id: alg-haken-jaco-tollefson-unknot-recognition

sources:
  references:
    - title: Joel Hass, Jeffrey C. Lagarias, and Nicholas Pippenger, The Computational
        Complexity of Knot and Link Problems, Journal of the ACM 46 (1999)
      url: https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hass/Research/Papers/Complexity/hlp.pdf
      locator: §§4–8 and §10, complete passages on normal-surface algorithms, finite
        bounds, triangulations and certificate analysis.
    - title: Jeff Erickson, Normal Surfaces and Knots, Computational Topology lecture
        notes (2009)
      url: https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/comptop/2009/notes/normal-surfaces.pdf
      locator: §§14.1–14.4, complete six-page note on normal disks, matching and
        unknot recognition.
---

## Definition

**Input:** A finite tagged Gauss code, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code, or oriented planar-diagram code in the code conventions of the planar-code definition, and a mode, either **Haken** or **JT**.

**Output:** The first validation error with its witness; **not-a-knot** for a valid code with more than one component; **disk-certificate** with a normal-coordinate vector and its finite witness data; or **no-candidate** after the selected search is exhausted.

**Procedure:**

1. Run the planar-code validation procedure. Return its first invalid result if validation fails. If the validated code represents more than one component, return **not-a-knot**.
2. Let $n$ be its crossing count. Construct the good triangulated exterior $E$ with $t\le C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and the marked original meridian path.
3. In Haken mode, enumerate all vectors $v\in\mathbb Z^{7t}$ with $0\le v_i\le t2^{7t+2}$ in lexicographic order. Retain a vector only if it satisfies all matching equations and quadrilateral restrictions and is fundamental. Fundamentalness supplies connectedness. Compute nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic, and mod-two meridian-intersection data from the compressed coordinates, without expanding the surface. Return **disk-certificate** at the first vector passing these tests; return **no-candidate** after the finite box is exhausted.
4. In JT mode, let $A$ be the integer matching matrix and put $m=7t$. Enumerate all subsets $Z\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ in lexicographic order. For each $Z$, append the equations $v_i=0$ for $i\in Z$ to $Av=0$. If the combined matrix has rank $m-1$ and its one-dimensional kernel contains a nonzero nonnegative vector, compute the unique relatively prime nonnegative integer generator $v$ of that ray. Require that its positive-coordinate support be exactly the complement of $Z$; this visits each ray once, at its exact zero-coordinate support. Discard vectors that violate the quadrilateral restriction. A primitive generator on an extreme ray is fundamental, so its surface is connected. Compute nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic, and mod-two meridian-intersection data from the compressed coordinates, without expanding the surface. Return **disk-certificate** at the first passing vector; return **no-candidate** after all subsets have been processed.

The candidate tests use the boundary arcs and Euler-characteristic data computed from the compressed normal coordinates. No correctness or complexity assertion is part of this algorithm definition.

## Definition references

[[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]] — accepted finite knot-code formats and peripheral crossing conventions.

[[alg-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-reconstruction]] — exact finite input validation and oriented component extraction.

[[thm-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-reconstruction-procedure-properties]] — termination and reconstruction output of that validator.

[[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]] — normal coordinates, admissibility, fundamentalness and extreme rays.

[[lem-normal-coordinate-matching-equations-and-finite-bounds]] — Haken and primitive-ray coordinate bounds.

[[lem-normal-disk-candidate-check-characterization]] — the disk tests applied to each retained vector.

[[lem-fundamental-normal-surfaces-are-connected]] — connectedness supplied by fundamentalness.

[[lem-good-linear-size-exterior-triangulation-from-diagram]] — finite marked exterior construction of linear size.

[Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger, §§5–8](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hass/Research/Papers/Complexity/hlp.pdf) — Haken and JT search architecture, bounds and triangulation interface.

  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
axiom_use: Countable Choice is inherited from the sequence model. AC is used only through the published Lindeberg–Feller theorem in the weighted chi-square limit; the finite likelihood-ratio expansion and asymptotic testing inequalities are choice-free.
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Yuri I. Ingster, Theofanis Sapatinas and Irina A. Suslina, Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems, Theorem 4.1 and the discussion after equation (4.3), PDF pp. 6–7"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.1853
    - title: "Evarist Giné and Richard Nickl, Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models, §6.2.3, PDF pp. 506–508"
      url: https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf
    - title: "Clément Marteau and Theofanis Sapatinas, A unified treatment for non-asymptotic and asymptotic approaches to minimax signal detection, §§3.1–3.2"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.5387
---

## Statement

Assume the $q=2$ ellipsoid detection-boundary theorem, Countable Choice, and the Axiom of Choice. Along a sequence for which $u_\varepsilon$ is bounded above and bounded away from zero and $w_{\varepsilon,0}\to0$, the minimax level-$\alpha$ type-II error and minimax total error satisfy
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)=\Phi(H_\alpha-u_\varepsilon)+o(1),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon))=2\Phi(-u_\varepsilon/2)+o(1),$$
where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function and $H_\alpha$ is defined by $\Phi(H_\alpha)=1-\alpha$. Let $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}=\inf\{t:\mathbb P_{\varepsilon,0}(T_\varepsilon\le t)\ge1-\alpha\}$; then $\mathbb P_{\varepsilon,0}(T_\varepsilon>c_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\le\alpha$ and $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\to H_\alpha$. The weighted tests with thresholds $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}$ and $u_\varepsilon/2$ attain these asymptotics, while the uncalibrated threshold $H_\alpha$ has asymptotic size $\alpha$. The vanishing-largest-weight condition is required for this Gaussian sharp branch.

## Statement references

[Ingster, Sapatinas and Suslina, *Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems*, Theorem 4.1 and equations (4.1)–(4.3), PDF pp. 6–7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.1853)

[Giné and Nickl, *Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models*, §6.2.3, PDF pp. 506–508](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

[Marteau and Sapatinas, *A unified treatment for non-asymptotic and asymptotic approaches to minimax signal detection*, §§3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.5387)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The q=2 detection-boundary statistic $T_\varepsilon$, finite-support extremal mean $\widetilde\eta_\varepsilon$, $u_\varepsilon$, and weights $w_{\varepsilon,j}$; AC and Countable Choice; $u_\varepsilon$ bounded above and away from zero; $w_{\varepsilon,0}\to0$.

[F1] [[thm-ip-ellipsoid-detection-boundary]]: $2\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}^2=1$, every alternative has statistic mean $m_\eta=\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}(\eta_j/\varepsilon)^2\ge u_\varepsilon$, and $\operatorname{Var}_\eta(T_\varepsilon)\le1+4w_{\varepsilon,0}m_\eta$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-weighted-chi-square-triangular-array-limit]]: under the null, $T_\varepsilon\Rightarrow N(0,1)$ when $w_{\varepsilon,0}\to0$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-gaussian-product-mixture-testing-bound]]: for the symmetric sign mixture on $\widetilde\eta_\varepsilon$, $L_\varepsilon=dP_{\pi}/dP_0=\prod_j e^{-\delta_j/2}\cosh(\sqrt{\delta_j}G_j)$, where $\delta_j=\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2/\varepsilon^2$ and $G_j=Y_j/\varepsilon$ under the null.

[F4] [[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment]] and [[lem-standard-normal-fourth-moment]]: under the null the $G_j$ are independent standard normals with even density and moments $\mathbb E G_j^2=1$ and $\mathbb E G_j^4=3$. The sixth and eighth moments are derived in step 1.2.

[F5] [[thm-slutsky-for-real-random-variables]]: adding a term converging to zero in probability preserves convergence in distribution.

[F6] [[thm-portmanteau-theorem]]: convergence in distribution gives convergence of bounded uniformly continuous test expectations and convergence of probabilities on Borel sets whose boundaries have limiting probability zero.

[F7] [[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]]: Chebyshev's inequality bounds a tail probability by the variance divided by the squared deviation.

[F8] [[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]] and [[thm-continuity-from-below-for-measures]]: probabilities of monotone event sequences converge to the probability of their intersection or union, respectively; the finite-measure hypothesis for continuity from above holds for probability laws.

[F9] [[thm-integration-by-parts]]: on a finite interval, differentiable functions with integrable derivatives satisfy integration by parts. The Gaussian density and the polynomial factors used in step 1.2 are continuously differentiable there, with continuous, integrable derivatives.

[F10] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: every fixed polynomial times the Gaussian exponential tends to zero at both ends of the real line.

[F11] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: nonnegative truncations of a measurable function on increasing intervals have integrals increasing to its full integral.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is used through the weighted Lindeberg–Feller theorem in [F2].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is inherited from the Gaussian sequence experiment.

## Proof

1.1 Under an alternative $\eta$, write $\mu_j=\eta_j/\varepsilon$ and let $G_j=\xi_j$ denote the independent standard-normal noise coordinates, so $Y_j/\varepsilon=\mu_j+G_j$. Then $$T_\varepsilon-m_\eta=\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}(G_j^2-1)+2\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}\mu_jG_j.$$ The first sum converges to $N(0,1)$ by [F2]. The second has mean zero and variance $4\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}^2\mu_j^2\le4w_{\varepsilon,0}m_\eta$. Thus for any sequence of alternatives with bounded $m_\eta$, the second sum tends to zero in probability by [F7], and [F5] gives $T_\varepsilon-m_\eta\Rightarrow N(0,1)$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F5, F7, given]

1.2 Put $\delta_j=\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2/\varepsilon^2=2u_\varepsilon w_{\varepsilon,j}$. Since $u_\varepsilon$ is bounded and $w_{\varepsilon,0}\to0$, $\max_j\delta_j\to0$ and $\sum_j\delta_j^2=2u_\varepsilon^2=O(1)$. For $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, direct differentiation gives $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$. For each $R>0$ and $k=3,4$, [F9] applied on $[-R,R]$ to $u(x)=x^{2k-1}$ and $v(x)=\phi(x)$ gives $$\int_{-R}^R x^{2k}\phi(x)\,dx=[-x^{2k-1}\phi(x)]_{-R}^R+(2k-1)\int_{-R}^R x^{2k-2}\phi(x)\,dx.$$ The boundary term tends to zero by [F10], and [F11] passes the nonnegative truncated integrals to the full real line. Starting from $\mathbb EG^4=3$ in [F4], the recurrence gives $\mathbb EG^6=5\cdot3=15$ and $\mathbb EG^8=7\cdot15=105$. Taylor's theorem applied to $f(x)=\log\cosh x$ gives $|f(x)-x^2/2+x^4/12|\le C|x|^6$ for all real $x$: on $[-1,1]$ use the bounded sixth derivative, and outside that interval use $|\log\cosh x|\le|x|$. Therefore the summed Taylor remainder in $\log L_\varepsilon$ has expected absolute value at most $C\sum_j\delta_j^3\mathbb E|G|^6\le C(\max_j\delta_j)\sum_j\delta_j^2\to0$. [A1, F3, F4, F9, F10, F11, given, algebra]

2.1 Put $F_\varepsilon(t)=\mathbb P_0(T_\varepsilon\le t)$ and $p=1-\alpha$. Since $T_\varepsilon$ is real-valued, the events $\{T_\varepsilon\le n\}$ increase to the whole space and $\{T_\varepsilon\le-n\}$ decrease to the empty set; [F8] shows that $F_\varepsilon(n)\to1$ and $F_\varepsilon(-n)\to0$. Thus $S=\{t:F_\varepsilon(t)\ge p\}$ is nonempty and bounded below, so $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}=\inf S$ is finite. For every $x>c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}$, the definition of the infimum gives some $s\in S$ with $s<x$, and monotonicity gives $F_\varepsilon(x)\ge F_\varepsilon(s)\ge p$. Hence $F_\varepsilon(c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}+1/n)\ge p$ for every positive integer $n$. The events $\{T_\varepsilon\le c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}+1/n\}$ decrease to $\{T_\varepsilon\le c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\}$, so [F8] gives $F_\varepsilon(c_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\ge p$ and therefore $\mathbb P_0(T_\varepsilon>c_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\le\alpha$. By [F2] and [F6], $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\to H_\alpha$, since the limiting normal distribution is continuous and strictly increasing. To bound maximal type-II error, consider any sequence $\eta_\varepsilon\in\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)$. If its means $m_{\eta_\varepsilon}$ are unbounded, pass to a subsequence on which they tend to infinity; the variance bound in [F1] and [F7] show $\mathbb P_{\eta_\varepsilon}(T_\varepsilon\le c_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\to0$. If they are bounded, pass to a subsequence on which $m_{\eta_\varepsilon}\to m\ge u_*$ and $u_\varepsilon\to u_*$, where $u_*>0$. Step 1.1 gives type-II limit $\Phi(H_\alpha-m)\le\Phi(H_\alpha-u_*)$. A subsequence contradiction therefore proves the uniform upper bound $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon),\psi_{\varepsilon,c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}})\le\Phi(H_\alpha-u_\varepsilon)+o(1)$. [F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, given]

2.2 The quartic term $\sum_j\delta_j^2G_j^4$ has mean $3\sum_j\delta_j^2=6u_\varepsilon^2$ and variance $96\sum_j\delta_j^4\le96(\max_j\delta_j)^2\sum_j\delta_j^2\to0$. Substituting the expansion from step 1.2 into [F3] gives $$\log L_\varepsilon=u_\varepsilon T_\varepsilon-u_\varepsilon^2/2+o_{P_0}(1).$$ Together with [F2], this implies that under $P_0$ the likelihood ratio converges along any subsequence with $u_\varepsilon\to u_*>0$ to $\exp(-u_*^2/2+u_*G)$ for $G\sim N(0,1)$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For any level-$\alpha$ test $\psi$, set $a_\varepsilon=\exp(u_\varepsilon c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}-u_\varepsilon^2/2)$. Pointwise, $L_\varepsilon(1-\psi)\ge\min(L_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)-a_\varepsilon\psi$. Hence the mixture-average type-II error is at least $\mathbb E_0\min(L_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)-a_\varepsilon\alpha$. Along a subsequence with $u_\varepsilon\to u_*>0$, step 2.1 gives $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\to H_\alpha$, and step 2.2 and [F6] yield the limit $\Phi(H_\alpha-u_*)$. Since maximal type-II error dominates the mixture average, this proves the matching lower bound for $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)$. [F1, F3, F6, step 2.1, step 2.2, given, algebra]

4.1 For every test $\psi$, $\psi+L_\varepsilon(1-\psi)\ge\min(1,L_\varepsilon)$ pointwise. Thus its total error against the null and mixture is at least $\mathbb E_0\min(1,L_\varepsilon)$. By step 2.2 and [F6] this expectation tends along $u_\varepsilon\to u_*$ to $2\Phi(-u_*/2)$, giving the matching minimax lower bound for $\gamma_\varepsilon$. The weighted test at threshold $u_\varepsilon/2$ has type-I limit $\Phi(-u_*/2)$ and maximal type-II upper limit $\Phi(-u_*/2)$ by the same bounded-mean/unbounded-mean split as step 2.1. Continuity in $u_*$ and compactness of the allowed range of $u_\varepsilon$ turn the subsequential bounds into the stated $o(1)$ formulas. [F1, F2, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 2.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal C$ be a ribbon category with chosen left duals and tensor unit $\mathbf 1$. A **finite oriented framed link colored in $\mathcal C$** is a finite disjoint union $L$ of oriented smoothly embedded circles in $S^3$, a homotopy class of nowhere-zero normal vector field on each component, and an assignment of an object of $\mathcal C$ to each component. A framed colored isotopy carries orientations, framings, and component colors. If $F_{\mathcal C}$ is the ribbon-tangle evaluation functor, define
$$\operatorname{RT}_{\mathcal C}(L):=F_{\mathcal C}(L)\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1).$$
This value depends only on the framed colored isotopy class. It is not automatically a field scalar; if $\mathcal C$ is $k$-linear and $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1)=k$, it is a scalar in $k$. The empty link is assigned $1_{\mathbf 1}$.

## Definition references

[[lem-multicolored-ribbon-coupon-evaluation|Multicolored framed-tangle evaluation lemma]]

[[def-rigid-object-and-rigid-monoidal-category|Rigid category and duality data]]

[[def-braiding|Braiding definition]]

[[def-twist-and-ribbon-structure|Ribbon twist definition]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable-choice axiom]]

[Turaev, *Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter I, Theorem 2.5 and §§3–4](https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/turaev5.pdf)

[Etingof, Gelaki, Nikshych, and Ostrik, *Tensor Categories*, §§8.9–8.10](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The ribbon category, its chosen left duals, a finite oriented framed link, and an object color on every component.

[F1] For arbitrary component colors, the ribbon evaluation assigns a morphism to each colored framed tangle, is invariant under framed graph isotopy, and preserves the empty graph ([[lem-multicolored-ribbon-coupon-evaluation]]).

[A1] Countable choice means every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data in the Definition and [A1].

1.1 Under [A1], the evaluator in [F1] exists. The colored framed link is a ribbon graph with no boundary endpoints, so it assigns a morphism from the tensor unit to itself. This is an element of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1)$, with no field-valued conclusion unless that endomorphism ring has been identified with a field. [F1, A1, given]

2.1 If two representatives are framed colored isotopic, [F1] gives equal evaluator morphisms; the empty graph has value $1_{\mathbf 1}$ by the same fact. Therefore the displayed assignment is well-defined on framed colored isotopy classes and has the stated empty-link value. [F1, A1, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Definition

Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary, let $x_0\in X$, and put $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$. A **finite relative disk-embedding datum** consists of proper generic immersions $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$, $1\le i\le n$, whose boundary circles are embedded and pairwise disjoint, together with framed generic immersions $g_i:S^2\looparrowright\operatorname{int}X$ that are algebraically dual to the disks. A topological generic immersion has the local models of a smooth generic immersion: at a point with one inverse image its image sheet is locally flat, with a proper half-space chart at boundary points in which the disk is a half-plane and its boundary lies on the ambient boundary, and each of its finitely many self-double points has exactly two preimages and the coordinate-plane model $\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb R^2$ in a chart of $X$. All mutual intersections among the disk and sphere maps are also required to be finite and transverse, so the equivariant intersection sums below are finite. Proper means that the inverse image of $\partial X$ is exactly the domain boundary. Each disk $f_i$ is supplied with a specified normal framing along $S^1$, equivalently the framing of its boundary attaching solid torus; this boundary framing is part of the datum and need not extend over $D^2$. Each sphere $g_i$ is supplied with a trivialization of its normal microbundle over $S^2$. Choose paths from $x_0$ to the immersed surfaces and orient the surfaces. Each transverse intersection $p$ of two surfaces contributes $\epsilon(p)g_p$ to $\lambda$, where $\epsilon(p)\in\{1,-1\}$ compares their induced local orientation with the chosen orientation of $X$, and $g_p\in G$ is the loop that travels along the chosen path to the first surface, then to $p$, and returns along the second surface and its chosen path. Thus $\lambda$ is a signed equivariant intersection sum in $\mathbb Z[G]$. Wall's self-intersection sum $\mu$ is the signed sum over self-double points in $\mathbb Z[G]/\langle g-g^{-1}:g\in G\rangle$, because interchanging the two sheets replaces a label by its inverse. The relative normal Euler (boundary-framing) obstruction of $f_i$ is zero precisely when its specified boundary framing extends over $D^2$; the datum does not assume that it vanishes. The spheres are **algebraically dual** when $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$ for every $i,j$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$ for every $i$. The disk data are **algebraically unobstructed** when also $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for every $i$.

## Definition

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with exterior $E_K$, positive meridian $\mu$, and preferred longitude $\lambda$. Define $\mathcal E_K\subset(\mathbb C^*)^2$ to consist of all pairs $(M,L)$ for which some representation $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ has a common invariant line on which $\rho(\mu)$ acts by $M$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ acts by $L$. The Zariski closure is the smallest Zariski-closed algebraic subset containing $\mathcal E_K$; let $V_K$ be the union of its one-dimensional irreducible components, where an irreducible component is a maximal irreducible closed subset. Zero-dimensional image components are omitted. The **ordinary A-polynomial** $A_K(M,L)$ is the Laurent polynomial generating the vanishing ideal of $V_K$, chosen square-free (no repeated irreducible factors) and with primitive integer coefficients (their greatest common divisor is one). It is determined up to multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$ for $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. Its reduced curve includes the abelian component $L=1$; equivalently, its representative in $\mathbb Z[M,L]$ is divisible by $L-1$.

## Definition

Let $X$ be a path-connected CW space. The oriented bordism set $\Omega_n^{SO}(X)$ consists of classes of pairs $(M,f)$, where $M$ is a closed smooth oriented $n$-manifold and $f:M\to X$. Two pairs are bordant when there is a compact oriented $(n+1)$-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M_0\sqcup(-M_1)$ and a map $F:W\to X$ restricting to $f_0$ and $f_1$ on the boundary. Disjoint union defines the operation. For a group $G$, $K(G,1)$ denotes a connected CW space with fundamental group $G$ and contractible universal cover.

## Definition

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude $\lambda_K$. Its smooth zero-trace $X_0(K)$ is the
compact smooth $4$-manifold obtained from $B^4$ by attaching a single $2$-handle
$D^2\times D^2$ to $\partial B^4=S^3$ along $K$, using the framing whose
parallel curve represents $\lambda_K$; corners are rounded.

## Definition references

[Piccirillo, Definition 1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §2.1, Definition 2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, a chosen tubular neighborhood,
and its preferred longitude.

[F1] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: the preferred longitude is
the degree-one peripheral curve whose class is zero in the first homology of
the knot exterior.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The attaching framing determines a parallel curve on the boundary torus of
the chosen tubular neighborhood. By [F1], the zero framing is the one whose
parallel represents the preferred longitude, which is the stated attaching
convention. [F1, given, def. preferred-longitude framing]

1.2 The construction uses the supplied preferred-longitude representative as
attaching data; it makes no uniqueness claim about such representatives and
does not change the chosen attachment. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice, take $Q>0$ and Sobolev-type weights $a_j\asymp j$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse model. If the singular values satisfy $s_j\asymp j^{-1}$, the minimax RMS error is of order $\epsilon^{2/5}$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$; if instead $s_j\asymp e^{-j}$, it is of order $[\log(1/\epsilon)]^{-1}$. ## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, where $\doteq$ denotes equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. For every Seifert surface $F$ of $K$ and every integral Seifert matrix $V$ of $F$ in the positive-push convention, the form represented by $V$ is S-equivalent over $\mathbb Z$ to the empty Seifert form.

## Statement references

[[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial|The determinant formula for the Alexander polynomial in this Seifert convention]]

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push matrix convention]]

[[def-seifert-form-s-equivalence|Integral basis changes and tube enlargements defining S-equivalence]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Full AC used by the current Seifert-form and determinant suppliers]]

Stavros Garoufalidis and Peter Teichner, “On Knots with Trivial Alexander Polynomial,” Lemma 4.2, https://people.math.gatech.edu/~stavros/publications/teichner1.pdf

H. F. Trotter, “On S-equivalence of Seifert Matrices,” *Inventiones Mathematicae* 20 (1973), 173–207, https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/download/pdf/PPN356556735_0020/LOG_0020.pdf

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a knot $K$ with $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, and one of its integral Seifert matrices $V$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is the choice-function axiom assumed by the Seifert-form and determinant suppliers.

[F1] [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]]: In the stated convention, $\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t)$ for each supplied Seifert matrix.

[F2] [[def-seifert-form-s-equivalence]]: S-equivalence is generated by integral basis changes and finite algebraic tube additions or their inverses.

[F3] [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]: $V-V^T=J_F$ is the integral unimodular alternating intersection form, with determinant $1$.

## Proof

1.1 By the actual determinant supplier, the supplied Seifert matrix has Laurent-unit determinant. Its skew part is the integral unimodular surface intersection form. The following finite matrix reduction applies to this very matrix and preserves the positive-push convention. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Let V be an integral 2g-by-2g matrix and J=V−V^T unimodular alternating. Suppose P(t)=det(V−tV^T) is a Laurent unit. Since P is a polynomial and P(t)=t^(2g)P(t^−1), it is t^g: a unit polynomial is ±t^m, reciprocity gives m=g, and P(1)=det J=1 fixes the sign. (The determinant of an integral unimodular alternating matrix is +1: choose any primitive vector, use the primitive row of J and Bezout to split off a symplectic pair, and repeat on its integral orthogonal direct summand. This determinant argument does not require a kernel vector of V, so it precedes the following deduction det V=0 without circularity.) For g>0 its constant coefficient det V is zero. Choose a nonzero rational kernel vector of V, clear denominators and divide by its coordinate gcd. This gives a primitive integral x with Vx=0. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 The row x^T V equals x^T J, since x^T V^T=(Vx)^T=0. It is primitive because multiplication by the unimodular J preserves primitive vectors. Bezout therefore gives an integral y with x^T V y=1. Then omega(x,y)=x^T J y=1. Put L={z:omega(x,z)=omega(y,z)=0}. Every z decomposes uniquely as [F1, F2, F3, algebra]
z = omega(z,y)x + omega(x,z)y + z_0,  z_0 in L. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.4 Thus Z^(2g)=Zx direct-sum Zy direct-sum L, and omega restricted to L is unimodular alternating. L is a free integral direct summand; its basis is obtained by applying the displayed integral projection to the coordinate generators and elementary Euclidean column operations. Repeating the primitive-vector/Bezout splitting in L gives an integral symplectic basis there. In that basis, followed by x,y, the Seifert matrix is [F1, F2, F3, algebra]
[[B,0,u],[0,0,1],[u^T,0,w]]. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.5 Indeed Vx=0 gives its zero x-column, and x^T V=x^T J gives the x-row. Orthogonality to y gives equality of the two old-to-y coupling vectors. Replace y by y−wx. This is a symplectic integral basis change and makes w zero, without changing B,u. We have exhibited exactly the algebraic tube enlargement in the ACTUAL S-equivalence Definition, not a rational enlargement. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.6 Expanding det(tV−V^T) along the x-row and then x-column gives [F1, F2, F3, algebra]
det(tV−V^T)=t det(tB−B^T). [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For even matrix size det(tV−V^T)=P(t) by transposition and multiplication by −1. Hence the reduced matrix B again has unit polynomial t^(g−1) and unimodular alternating skew part. Induct on g. This supplies a finite sequence of integral congruences and exact inverse tube additions down to the empty matrix. No stabilization theorem is assumed. It proves the full matrix assertion needed by the original S-equivalence carrier once its actual Seifert determinant/skew-pairing interfaces are applied. ∎ [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

## Statement

Assume AC. For a fixed prime-power cover degree and prime-power order character, the rationalized difference between the twisted and untwisted Casson–Gordon intersection-form Witt classes, divided by the bounding multiplicity $r$, is independent of the chosen multiple and bounding pair. It defines a class in $W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q$.

## Statement references

[[lem-casson-gordon-bordism-admissibility|Existence of a multiple bounding pair]]

[[lem-casson-gordon-twisted-intersection-form-is-nonsingular|Nonsingularity of the capped twisted form]]

[[def-oriented-bordism-group-of-a-space|Oriented bordism classes of maps]]

[[lem-oriented-bordism-classes-over-a-space-form-an-abelian-group|The bordism group operation]]

[Charles Livingston and Swatee Naik, *Introduction to Knot Concordance*, §§8.1, 8.4–8.5, pp. 164–172](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Concordance_Book.pdf)

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the fixed marked boundary character pair, and two smooth multiple bounding data.

[F1] Such data exist, and their twisted middle form is nonsingular on the actual cover-tensor module. [[lem-casson-gordon-bordism-admissibility]], [[lem-casson-gordon-twisted-intersection-form-is-nonsingular]]

[F2] For $B=K(C_d\times\mathbb Z,1)$, every closed four-manifold satisfies $d([Z,f]-[Z,\mathrm{constant}])=0$ in geometric smooth bordism. The proof constructs the requisite low-degree comparison, not merely rational signature equality. [[lem-low-degree-geometric-bordism-over-finite-cyclic-times-circle]]

[F3] The nonsingular image form over a unitary involutive field is zero on a closed four-boundary with extending coefficients and satisfies the whole-boundary Witt gluing identity. Its formation commutes with field extension. [[lem-unitary-field-witt-forms-respect-bordism-and-whole-boundary-gluing]]

[F4] Disjoint union and orientation reversal are the geometric bordism operations. [[def-oriented-bordism-group-of-a-space]], [[lem-oriented-bordism-classes-over-a-space-form-an-abelian-group]] Full AC is retained. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 Put $F=\mathbb C(t)$. For any smooth four-manifold $V$ over $B$ let $D(V)$ be its twisted nonsingular image Witt form minus the scalar extension to $F$ of its ordinary complex nonsingular image form. The representation $(a,n)\mapsto\zeta_d^at^n$ is unitary for the stipulated involution. By [F3], the two terms vanish on a closed five-bordism boundary with their respective extending systems. Hence on closed four-manifolds their difference is a homomorphism from $\Omega_4^{SO}(B)$ to $W(F)$. For a constant map the two coefficient systems are the same constant $F$ system, so $D(Z,\mathrm{constant})=0$. [F2, F3, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Applying that homomorphism to [F2] gives $dD(Z,f)=0$ for every closed $Z$ over $B$. In particular every closed ambiguity has torsion Witt difference and becomes zero after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$. This conclusion concerns the entire Witt class, not just its signature. No arbitrary-group analytic index theorem is required. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If the bounding multiplicities are $r_0,r_1$, take $r_1$ disjoint copies of $W_0$ and $r_0$ copies of $W_1$. Their whole marked boundaries are the same $r_0r_1$ copies. Glue them, reversing the second orientation, with the same boundary character maps. Whole-boundary Witt gluing [F3] gives $$D(Z)=r_1D(W_0)-r_0D(W_1).$$ This uses the ordinary nonsingular quotient even when the ordinary absolute form has a radical. The twisted boundary is acyclic by [F1], so that term uses precisely the absolute module of the Statement. By step 2.1 the left side is zero rationally. Dividing by $r_0r_1$ proves $D(W_0)/r_0=D(W_1)/r_1$. Disjoint union, repeated multiples and all marked gluing choices are therefore compatible. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 We also record the target enlargement needed for a disk extension. Embed $C_d$ in $C_D$ for $d\mid D$ by $a\mapsto(D/d)a$, and keep the infinite coordinate unchanged. With positive roots of unity, $\zeta_D^{(D/d)a}=\zeta_d^a$, so the two rank-one $F$ coefficient systems and their forms are literally the same. Regard any original bounding datum as a datum over the larger target. Even if its boundary map is not onto that target, the proof of steps 1.1–3.1 still applies: [F2] and [F3] allow arbitrary continuous maps to $B$, and acyclicity concerns the actual coefficient system. One may use the induced principal cover, which can be disconnected; its local coefficient module is unchanged. Thus a smooth filling over the larger finite cyclic target computes the same rational class. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Finally the specified one-sided signature is a well-defined homomorphism on this rational Witt group. The entries of a Hermitian rational matrix, its nonzero determinant, and a rational change-of-basis matrix have only finitely many zeros and poles on the unit circle unless the relevant function is identically zero. For a nonsingular representative choose a short interval $0<\theta<\epsilon$ avoiding those finite exceptional sets. Its evaluations are nonsingular Hermitian matrices, and their eigenvalue signs cannot change without a zero determinant, so the signature is constant there. Congruent representatives have congruent evaluations on a common such interval. A hyperbolic form evaluates to a hyperbolic form and has zero signature. Direct sums add signatures, and rationalization extends this homomorphism by rational linearity. This verifies exactly the one-sided limit specified in the invariant Definition; it does not substitute another averaging convention. Together with step 3.1 this completes the claimed rationalized Witt construction. [F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $P\subset S^2$ be the finite connected 4-valent graph underlying a regular link projection. Its complementary regions have exactly two colorings with two colors such that regions sharing an edge have different colors.

## Statement references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite connected 4-valent graph $P$ embedded in $S^2$.

[F1] Every crossing of a regular link projection is a transverse double point and has four local incident half-edges; there are finitely many crossings ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

[F2] A smooth embedded circle in the plane has exactly two complementary regions and bounds a closed disk on its bounded side, without a choice assumption. The corresponding separation fact on the projection sphere follows by choosing a point off the circle and using a stereographic chart ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-jordan-disk-parameters-and-prescribed-collars]]).

## Proof
1.1 Fix a point $x_0$ in a complementary region $R_0$. First decompose the edges of $P$ into finitely many edge-disjoint simple cycles. In a nonempty remaining even-degree graph, follow unused edges until a vertex first repeats; the segment between its two occurrences is a simple cycle, including a loop edge as a one-edge cycle. Removing that cycle subtracts two incident half-edges at each of its vertices and leaves every degree even. Repeat until no edge remains. This terminates because each removal deletes an edge; a vertex-free circle is already one cycle. Now choose two piecewise-smooth paths $\alpha,\beta$ from $x_0$ to the same point in a region $R$, avoiding the finitely many vertices and meeting open edges transversely in finitely many points. Their concatenation $\gamma=\alpha*\beta^{-1}$ is a closed test path; it need not be embedded or be an edge-path of $P$. Its intersections are counted with traversal multiplicity, so $I(\gamma,P)=I(\alpha,P)+I(\beta,P)$ modulo two. For each simple graph cycle, choose small vertex disks disjoint from the compact image of $\gamma$ and round that cycle inside them. The rounded cycle remains embedded and has exactly the same test-path intersections as its original edges. By [F2] it separates $S^2$ into two sides. Each transverse encounter switches the side occupied by $\gamma$, and a complete traversal returns to its initial side, even when the test path self-intersects or retraces an arc. Thus $\gamma$ meets each rounded cycle evenly. The graph cycles partition all open edges and $\gamma$ misses their vertices, so summing their intersection counts proves $I(\gamma,P)=0$ modulo two. Therefore $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have the same crossing parity. Coloring $R$ by this parity gives a well-defined function, independent also of the chosen endpoint inside $R$, since two such endpoints are joined within $R$ without crossing $P$. All decompositions, rounding choices and perturbations are finite; no choice axiom is used. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Crossing one edge changes the parity by one, so adjacent regions receive different colors. The dual adjacency graph of regions is connected because a generic path between any two regions crosses finitely many edges; hence fixing the color of $R_0$ forces every other color. The two choices for the color of $R_0$ give exactly two colorings. [step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $E$ be the compact exterior of a smooth knot with supplied product boundary torus $T=S^1\times S^1$, fibre meridian $\mu$, and unique degree-one zero-homology longitude class $[\lambda]$ from the product data. Let $D\subset E$ be a properly embedded piecewise-linear disk, meaning an embedded copy of the closed disk with $D\cap T=\partial D$. If $\partial D$ is not null-homotopic in $T$, then $[\partial D]=[\lambda]$ or $-[\lambda]$ in $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$, and its mod-two intersection number with $\mu$ is $1$.

## Statement references

[[lem-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude-via-mayer-vietoris]] — the kernel of boundary-to-exterior homology is generated by the degree-one longitude, and meridian/longitude form a basis.

[[lem-essential-simple-curve-on-torus-is-primitive]] — a non-null-homotopic simple curve on the torus represents a primitive class.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $E,T,\mu,\lambda$ and the properly embedded disk $D$ in the statement.

[F1] [[lem-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude-via-mayer-vietoris]]: $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ has basis $([\mu],[\lambda])$, the class $[\lambda]$ generates the kernel of $i_*:H_1(T)\to H_1(E)$, and product projection sends $[\mu]$ to $0$ and $[\lambda]$ to $1$.

[F2] [[lem-essential-simple-curve-on-torus-is-primitive]]: every non-null-homotopic embedded PL simple closed curve on a product torus has a nonzero primitive homology class.

## Proof

1.1 The boundary $\partial D$ is an embedded PL simple closed curve in $T$. Since it bounds the disk $D$ in $E$, its image under inclusion $i:T\hookrightarrow E$ is zero. By [F1], the kernel is $\mathbb Z[\lambda]$, so $[\partial D]=k[\lambda]$ for an integer $k$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 The hypothesis and [F2] say $[\partial D]$ is nonzero and primitive. Since $[\lambda]$ is a basis vector by [F1], the multiple $k[\lambda]$ is primitive only if $k=1$ or $k=-1$. Hence $[\partial D]=\pm[\lambda]$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put the boundary curve in PL transverse position to the fibre $\mu=p^{-1}(s_0)$, where $p:T\to S^1$ is product projection. Its intersection points are exactly the preimages of $s_0$ under $p|_{\partial D}$. A lift of this PL circle map to $\mathbb R$ changes by its degree, which is the product-projection coefficient of $[\partial D]$, namely $+1$ or $-1$ by step 2.1. For a regular value, the signed crossing count of the lift through the integer translates of that value equals this degree; reducing modulo $2$ removes the signs, so the number of preimages is odd. Thus $\partial D$ has mod-two intersection $1$ with $\mu$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 Steps 2.1 and 3.1 give the longitude class and the asserted parity. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Whenever the Haken branch of the Haken–Jaco–Tollefson search returns a disk-certificate, the associated normal surface is a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary in the triangulated knot exterior.

## Statement references

[[alg-haken-jaco-tollefson-unknot-recognition]] — Haken candidate acceptance tests.

[[lem-normal-disk-candidate-check-characterization]] — exact disk and essential-boundary characterization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid one-component knot code and a vector returned by the Haken branch as a disk-certificate.

[F1] [[alg-haken-jaco-tollefson-unknot-recognition]]: the Haken branch returns a vector only after checking matching, quadrilateral admissibility, fundamentalness, nonempty boundary, Euler characteristic $1$, and odd mod-two meridian intersection; fundamentalness gives connectedness by [F2].

[F2] [[lem-fundamental-normal-surfaces-are-connected]]: a fundamental normal surface is connected.

[F3] [[lem-normal-disk-candidate-check-characterization]]: an admissible normal vector passes the boundary, Euler-characteristic and meridian tests exactly when its normal surface is a properly embedded disk with essential boundary.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the returned vector satisfies the candidate tests in [F2], including normal matching and quadrilateral admissibility. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 By [F2], the returned fundamental normal surface is connected. The remaining tests in [F1], together with [F3], identify it as a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. In the Gaussian sequence detection experiment, let $v\in\Theta_q(r)$ have finite support $J$ and put
$$u(v)^2=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^4}\sum_{j\in J}v_j^4.$$
Let $\pi_v$ be the uniform probability law on the finite family of mean sequences whose $j$th coordinate is independently $+v_j$ or $-v_j$ for $j\in J$ and is zero off $J$, and let $P_{\pi_v}$ be the corresponding mixture sampling law. Then its likelihood ratio with respect to the null law is
$$L_v=\frac{dP_{\pi_v}}{dP_{\varepsilon,0}}=\prod_{j\in J}\exp\!\left(-\frac{v_j^2}{2\varepsilon^2}\right)\cosh\!\left(\frac{v_jY_j}{\varepsilon^2}\right),$$
it satisfies
$$\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}L_v^2=\prod_{j\in J}\cosh\!\left(\frac{v_j^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right),\qquad \mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}(L_v-1)^2\le \exp(u(v)^2)-1,$$
and the minimax risks obey
$$\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))\ge1-\frac12\sqrt{\exp(u(v)^2)-1},\qquad \beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)\ge1-\alpha-\frac12\sqrt{\exp(u(v)^2)-1}$$
for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$.

## Statement references

[Ingster, Sapatinas and Suslina, *Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems*, §4.1, equations (4.1)–(4.3), PDF pp. 6–7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.1853)

[Giné and Nickl, *Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models*, §6.2.3, Theorem 6.2.11 proof, PDF pp. 506–508](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $\varepsilon>0$, $v\in\Theta_q(r)$ of finite support, and the null and alternative laws in the Gaussian sequence detection experiment.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is inherited from the Gaussian sequence inverse model.

[F1] [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]] and [[thm-ip-white-noise-spectral-sequence-representation]]: after scaling the normalized observation by $s_j=\sigma_j^{-1}$, $Y_j=\eta_j+\varepsilon\xi_j$ with independent standard normal coordinates $\xi_j$.

[F2] [[def-ip-minimax-detection-risk-and-separation]]: $\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}\psi$, $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\sup_{\eta\in\Theta_q(r)}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,\eta}(1-\psi)$, and $\gamma_\varepsilon$ is the infimum of their sum.

[F3] [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]]: the standard normal density is $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and integrates to one.

[F4] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]: a finite tuple of independent coordinates has the product of its marginal laws.

[F5] [[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]]: probability measures agreeing on a generating pi-system agree on its generated sigma-algebra.

[F6] [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]: $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ over measurable events.

[F7] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]: translation of the standard normal density preserves its integral, so $\mathbb E e^{tG}=e^{t^2/2}$ for $G\sim N(0,1)$ by completing the square.

## Proof

1.1 For each sign vector $\tau\in\{-1,+1\}^J$, let $v^\tau_j=\tau_jv_j$ on $J$ and zero elsewhere. Absolute values and squares are unchanged, so every $v^\tau$ belongs to $\Theta_q(r)$. [A1, F1, given, construct]

1.2 Under the null, $X_j=Y_j/\varepsilon$ has density $\varphi$. For a fixed sign and coordinate, the density ratio for mean $\tau_jv_j$ versus zero is $\exp(\tau_jv_jY_j/\varepsilon^2-v_j^2/(2\varepsilon^2))$; completing the square using [F7] shows its null expectation is one. [F1, F3, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 Independence [F4] multiplies the one-coordinate ratios from step 1.2, giving the density ratio for the finite coordinate vector on each cylinder event. Its null expectation is the product of unit expectations, so it defines a probability measure on the full product space. [step 1.2, F4, algebra]

3.1 Cylinder events form a generating pi-system. The fixed-sign sampling law and the probability measure from step 2.1 agree on every cylinder, so [F5] gives equality on the product sigma-algebra and validates the full likelihood-ratio identity. [step 2.1, F5, algebra]

4.1 Averaging the fixed-sign likelihood ratios in step 3.1 over the finite sign set factors coordinatewise and gives $L_v=\prod_{j\in J}e^{-\delta_j/2}\cosh(\sqrt{\delta_j}X_j)$, where $\delta_j=v_j^2/\varepsilon^2$. This density is positive and has null expectation one. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For a standard normal $G$, [F7] and $\cosh^2t=(1+\cosh(2t))/2$ give $e^{-\delta}\mathbb E\cosh^2(\sqrt\delta G)=e^{-\delta}(1+e^{2\delta})/2=\cosh\delta$. Independence [F4] and step 4.1 therefore give $\mathbb E_0L_v^2=\prod_{j\in J}\cosh\delta_j$. [F4, F7, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The function $g(t)=t^2/2-\log\cosh t$ is even, has $g(0)=0$, and for $t\ge0$ has derivative $g'(t)=t-\tanh t\ge0$, since $(\tanh t)'\le1$ and $\tanh0=0$. Thus $\cosh t\le e^{t^2/2}$ for all real $t$. Since $\sum_j\delta_j^2=2u(v)^2$, step 5.1 yields $\mathbb E_0(L_v-1)^2=\prod_j\cosh\delta_j-1\le e^{\frac12\sum_j\delta_j^2}-1=e^{u(v)^2}-1$. [step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Since $\mathbb E_0(L_v-1)=0$, the positive and negative parts of $L_v-1$ have equal integrals; hence every event $E$ satisfies $|P_{\pi_v}(E)-P_0(E)|\le\frac12\mathbb E_0|L_v-1|\le\frac12\sqrt{\mathbb E_0(L_v-1)^2}$. Approximate a randomized test $\psi$ by $N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N\mathbf1_{\{\psi\ge k/N\}}$; the event bound [F6] and uniform approximation error $N^{-1}$ give $|\mathbb E_{\pi_v}\psi-\mathbb E_0\psi|\le\|P_{\pi_v}-P_0\|_{\rm TV}$. [F6, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 The maximal type-II error is at least its mixture average because every sign alternative lies in $\Theta_q(r)$. Therefore every test has total error at least $1-\|P_{\pi_v}-P_0\|_{\rm TV}$, and any level-$\alpha$ test has maximal type-II error at least $1-\alpha-\|P_{\pi_v}-P_0\|_{\rm TV}$. Taking the respective infima, then applying steps 6.1 and 7.1, proves both stated risk bounds. [F2, step 6.1, step 7.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The connected-sum construction and its fixed gluing convention]]

[[thm-isotopy-extension|Ambient extension of compact isotopies of ball-arc pairs]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and two smooth oriented knots with connected-sum data as in the Definition.

[F1] A knot is a smooth embedding of one oriented circle in the standard oriented three-sphere, and equivalence of oriented knots is by an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy. ([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]])

[F2] The connected-sum datum uses an orientation-preserving embedding of a standard ball-arc pair into each knot and a fixed standard boundary gluing. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]])

[F3] Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, an isotopy of embeddings of a compact manifold with boundary into a boundaryless manifold extends to an ambient isotopy supported near its track. ([[thm-isotopy-extension]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the sequence-choice principle stated in the item. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the two oriented knot embeddings, and two sets of connected-sum data.

1.1 A change of knot representative already comes with an oriented ambient isotopy by [F1]. Applying that isotopy to its ball-arc data carries the cut complement and its boundary collars to the new data, so the standard gluing produces an ambient-isotopic sum. A change of radius in one local straightening chart is the isotopy that rescales the standard ball radially while preserving its oriented diameter. This is an isotopy of compact ball-arc embeddings, so [A1] and [F3] extend it to an ambient isotopy of the knot sphere. [given, F1, F2, F3, A1, construct]

1.2 For two local oriented ball-arc charts centered at the same point, express them in one smooth coordinate chart. Their transition germ fixes the center, carries the positive tangent line of the knot to itself, and has positive determinant. Shrink to a common ball and use the smooth rescaling homotopy $G_s(x)=s^{-1}(G(sx)-G(0))$ for $s>0$, with $G_0(x)=DG_0(x)$. Taylor's formula gives the smooth extension at $s=0$. On a sufficiently small common ball the differentials stay uniformly close to the injective linear map $DG_0$, so every $G_s$ is an embedding and preserves the oriented diameter. The subgroup of invertible linear maps preserving that oriented line and the ambient orientation is path-connected: in line-normal coordinates its diagonal blocks lie in $(0,\infty)$ and $GL^+(2,\mathbb R)$, and the shear block contracts linearly to zero. Thus the chart germ is isotopic through oriented ball-arc embeddings to the fixed standard chart. [F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 If the marked points differ, move the parameter point along the knot circle by a smooth isotopy of that circle. The resulting family of knot embeddings carries the short oriented subarc along a finite chain of local straightening charts; compactness of the parameter interval gives a common sufficiently small ball radius. Apply [F3] to this isotopy and to the chart isotopies of steps 1.1 and 1.2. The resulting ambient isotopies identify the cut complements with their boundary collars and preserve the fixed endpoint pairing in the standard gluing. Hence they induce an oriented ambient isotopy between the two connected-sum outputs. [F1, F2, F3, A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the standing full AC convention. Give compact oriented smooth manifolds finite cellular models, and give their cellular complexes the local regular coefficients of any discrete group $G$. Put $A=\mathcal N G$. For each degree, let $p_Z$ and $p_B$ be the Hilbert projections onto cycles and the closure of boundaries after completion in $\ell^2(G)$. The algebraic reduced part is the finite projective $A$-module $P=(p_Z-p_B)A^n$, whereas completed reduced homology is the Hilbert module $H=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^n$. Algebraic homology with $A$ coefficients surjects onto $P$ with zero-dimensional kernel; its natural map into $H$ has dense image $P$ under $x\mapsto x\delta_e$, and need not be surjective onto $H$. The Hilbert completion of $P$ in this embedding is $H$. Pair and Mayer–Vietoris sequences become weakly exact on completed reduced homology: the closure of each image is the next kernel. Poincaré–Lefschetz cap duality induces bounded invertible maps on completed reduced homology and cohomology. In particular, the middle intersection operator of a closed oriented even-dimensional manifold is invertible. The cap boundary identity and the intersection/cup identities persist on these completed modules, with their ordinary orientation signs.

## Statement references

[[lem-finite-von-neumann-module-dimension-and-dense-quotients]]

[[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality-with-local-coefficients]]

[[thm-cellular-chains-compute-homology-with-local-coefficients]]

[[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[[thm-morse-functions-and-handle-decompositions-correspond]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite cellular complexes of the stated manifolds and pairs, with the stated regular local coefficients.

[F1] Closed invariant subspaces of finite Hilbert modules are projection ranges; spectral rank-nullity, the formula for the dimension of a quotient of a finite projective module by any submodule, and closure of zero-dimensional modules under submodules, quotients and extensions hold. [[lem-finite-von-neumann-module-dimension-and-dense-quotients]]

[F2] Cellular models compute local-coefficient homology; pair and Mayer–Vietoris sequences are exact and natural. Finite handle decompositions give the finite cellular models for compact smooth manifolds. [[thm-cellular-chains-compute-homology-with-local-coefficients]] [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]] [[thm-morse-functions-and-handle-decompositions-correspond]]

[F3] Cap with the relative fundamental class is Poincaré–Lefschetz duality, naturally with respect to restriction and boundary, for every complex vector local system. Apply it to the regular group-ring fiber, retaining the commuting right group-ring action. [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement; write $R=\mathbb CG$ and $A=\mathcal NG$.

1.1 For a finite matrix differential $d_i$, its algebraic kernel over $A$ is exactly $p_Z A^{n_i}$, where $p_Z$ projects onto its Hilbert kernel: the matrix equality $d_i p_Z=0$ gives one inclusion, and applying $p_Z$ to each column gives the other. Let $p_B$ project onto the closure of the image of $d_{i+1}$. Then $p_B\le p_Z$. Orthogonal projection onto the algebraic module $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^{n_i}$ induces a surjection from algebraic homology $H_i^{\mathrm{alg}}$, with kernel $T_i=p_B A^{n_i}/\operatorname{im}d_{i+1}$. This kernel has dimension zero by [F1]. The target $P_i$ is projective, so the surjection splits algebraically; in fact inclusion of the harmonic projection module into cycles gives a splitting. Thus $H_i^{\mathrm{alg}}\cong P_i\oplus T_i$. Separately, $P_i$ embeds in the Hilbert module $\mathscr H_i=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^{n_i}$ by applying its columns to $\delta_e$. This embedding is injective, since a group von Neumann operator annihilating $\delta_e$ annihilates all its right translates. Its image is dense because it contains $(p_Z-p_B)(\mathbb CG)^{n_i}\delta_e$. Consequently the natural map from $H_i^{\mathrm{alg}}$ to $\mathscr H_i$ has image this dense $P_i$, not necessarily all of $\mathscr H_i$. The same dictionary applies to the dual finite matrix complex. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 The cellular cap map in [F3] is represented by a map between finite free $R$ complexes, using the dual cellular decomposition or a finite common subdivision. Its homology maps are isomorphisms: apply [F3] to the regular $R$ fiber as a complex local system; all the constructions commute with right multiplication by $R$. Cellular cochains here are the finite dual matrix complex: on each relative cell the local-coefficient cochain is its freely specified fiber value, and induction over the finite cellular filtration gives the cochain comparison, just as for the cellular chain comparison in [F2]. The cap map's cone is therefore a bounded acyclic complex of finite free $R$ modules. Such a complex is contractible: start at its lowest nonzero degree, split the surjection onto that projective term, remove the resulting two-term identity complex, and continue over the finitely many degrees. All splittings are maps between finite projective summands of finite free modules and hence are finite matrices of elements of $R$. Every such matrix acts boundedly on $\ell^2(G)$. The cap map and its chain homotopy inverse consequently extend to bounded chain homotopy equivalences after completion. [F2, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 Consider three consecutive terms of an algebraically exact homology sequence in [F2], and decompose each as $P\oplus T$ by step 1.1. Every map from $T$ to a finite algebraic projection module vanishes: its image has dimension zero, whereas every nonzero element in a finite projection module generates a positive-dimensional submodule by the spectral quotient formula and faithfulness in [F1]. Hence the sequence induces maps $f_P,g_P$ on the algebraic projective reduced parts. These are restrictions of bounded maps on their Hilbert completions: restriction and inclusion come from finite cellular matrices, and connecting maps can be computed using the degreewise free splittings of the relative or cellular union chain sequence, again by finite matrices followed by harmonic projections. Let $K_A=\ker g_P$, a finite algebraic projection module whose Hilbert closure is the kernel $K_H$ of the completed map, by the same matrix-kernel argument as in step 1.1. View $K_A$ inside the middle algebraic homology using its harmonic-cycle splitting. Its image under the actual second homology map lies in the target $T$, so $K_A/\ker(g|_{K_A})$ has dimension zero. The quotient formula in [F1] makes $\ker(g|_{K_A})$ Hilbert-dense in $K_H$. Exactness identifies each of its elements with an actual preceding image; projecting that preimage off its $T$ summand does not change its projected image. Thus $\ker(g|_{K_A})\subseteq\operatorname{im}f_P\subseteq K_A$. The completed preceding image consequently has closure $K_H$. This proves weak exactness on completed reduced homology without identifying $P$ with its Hilbert completion. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Bounded chain homotopies descend to completed reduced homology, because differentials and all maps are bounded and therefore preserve closures of boundaries. Thus the maps in step 1.2 induce bounded mutually inverse maps on the Hilbert completions $\mathscr H_i$ of step 1.1. Orthogonal projection identifies completed reduced cohomology of the finite dual matrix complex with the Hilbert dual of completed reduced homology: both are the orthogonal complement of boundaries within cycles, and the involution on $R$ identifies the adjoint matrices. On a closed manifold the intersection map is exactly cap duality followed by this Riesz identification; it is therefore bounded and invertible. Its usual symmetry sign follows from the cellular cup/cap identity. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The cellular identity $\partial(c\cap z)=\pm((\delta c)\cap z)\pm c\cap\partial z$ proves compatibility with boundary and restriction before completion. The cup/cap and intersection identities likewise hold on cellular cycles, by their defining evaluation on the dual cells. Any chain homotopies involved are finite matrices, hence remain bounded after completion by step 1.2. They vanish on reduced homology, and every relevant map is continuous. The identities therefore persist on reduced homology with the same orientation signs. Together with steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2 this proves all assertions. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a fibered knot with exterior $E_K$ and fiber surface $F$. If $S\subset E_K$ is a connected, orientable, nonseparating, incompressible properly embedded surface whose boundary is a nonempty union of longitudes, then $S$ is isotopic to $F$. After their boundary curves are identified by an isotopy in the boundary torus and this alignment is extended across a collar, the concluding isotopy may be taken relative to the aligned boundary.

## Statement references

[Baldwin and Sivek, Proposition 4.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

[Waldhausen, Corollary 5.5](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970594)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The surface and fibered exterior in the Statement, with full AC as authorized for their homology and geometric suppliers. This is not a claimed choice-free proof.

[A1] Full AC implies the countable-choice assumptions used in the smooth surface and isotopy suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The exterior-homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and identifies the kernel of $H_1(\partial E_K)\to H_1(E_K)$ as $\mathbb Z[\lambda]$; it does not itself state the required relative group. Let $\pi:E_K\to S^1$ be the bundle projection with connected fiber $F$. Since $F$ is a fiber surface of a knot, its boundary is the single binding-parallel circle, of degree one on the knot. The boundary restriction is a circle bundle with fiber $\partial F$, which maps to zero in $H_1(E_K)$, so $[\partial F]=\pm[\lambda]$. The induced map $H_1(\partial E_K)\to H_1(S^1)$ is onto with kernel $\mathbb Z[\lambda]$, hence sends $[\mu]$ to $\pm1$. It factors through the inclusion into $H_1(E_K)$, so $\pi_*:H_1(E_K)\to H_1(S^1)$ is an isomorphism. The universal coefficient theorem, with $H_0(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ free on path components and $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$, identifies $H^1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(E_K),\mathbb Z)$; thus $\pi^*[S^1]$ generates it. Poincaré–Lefschetz duality identifies this generator with the relative class of a regular fiber, up to orientation sign: in a local product chart transverse to $F$, the degree-one base class caps with the oriented exterior class to give $[F]$. Therefore $H_2(E_K,\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[F]$, and its intersection-dual meridian class generates $H^1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]] [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]] [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality]]

[F2] Geometric incompressibility of a neat two-sided smooth surface is equivalent to fundamental-group injectivity. Broad smooth boundary-preimage surfaces first admit a boundary-fixed embedding neatification, and their actual smooth disk obstructions pass to that representative. [[thm-smooth-loop-theorem-and-incompressibility-criterion-in-orientable-three-manifolds]], [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]], [[lem-angular-boundary-neatification-preserves-smooth-disk-obstructions]]

[F3] A finite disjoint family of essential longitude curves on a smooth torus admits a simultaneous smooth normalization to the corresponding parallel affine circles. Its isotopy extends into the boundary collar by applying its time parameter times a collar cutoff. [[lem-choice-free-smooth-torus-curves-and-annulus-strips]]

[F4] An injective map of compact finite PL oriented surfaces with nontrivial source group is homotopic to a finite covering or to an annular boundary collapse. A boundary local homeomorphism can be fixed throughout. The actual thirteen-row proof gives subgroup cores, the boundary orientation-chain calculation, cutting-arc normalization and disk extension. Smooth compact surfaces have compatible finite cellulations; relative finite simplicial approximation gives the PL map in this interface, preserving an already matched boundary triangulation. [[thm-pi-one-injective-finite-pl-surface-maps-are-covers-or-annular-collapses]], [[lem-compact-c2-surfaces-admit-finite-cellulations-relative-to-a-finite-embedded-graph]], [[thm-finite-simplicial-approximation-for-maps-of-pairs]]

[F5] Connected subgroup covers and their map-lifting criterion exist. Finite surface graph thickenings give the disk conclusion for a simply connected compact surface with nonempty boundary; cellular relative homology computes the orientation-chain degree. [[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]], [[thm-covering-space-lifting-criterion]], [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]], [[thm-relative-cellular-homology-computes-relative-singular-homology]]

[F6] The actual boundary-relative homotopic-surface theorem supplies a downstairs embedded family-innermost product patch and the intersection-reducing isotopy. Its proof includes the relative half-product normalization and verifies the boundary-complement injections in the cut fiber product; it does not project an arbitrary cover isotopy. [[thm-boundary-relative-homotopic-incompressible-surfaces-in-fibered-exteriors-are-isotopic]]

[F7] Compact smooth manifolds with corners admit finite compatible triangulations relative to admissible triangulated boundary faces and protected collar neighborhoods. Cutting the smooth pair at its transverse surface faces gives exactly these compatible corner data; paired face subdivisions are matched before regluing. [[thm-compact-smooth-manifolds-with-corners-admit-relative-finite-triangulations]]

## Proof

1.1 Use [F2] to take a neat representative, preserving boundary and incompressibility. Nonseparation is preserved by its ambient topological extension. A short oriented transverse segment through $S$ closes through its connected complement to a loop intersecting $S$ once. Thus the intersection-dual cohomology class of $S$ is primitive. By [F1], $[S]=\pm[F]$ in $H_2(E_K,\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Every loop in $S$ may be represented in its interior and pushed slightly into its two-sided normal product, so its intersection with $S$ is zero. Its value under the fiber's meridian homomorphism is consequently zero. Therefore the inclusion lifts to the infinite cyclic fiber cover $\widetilde E_K=F\times\mathbb R$. The lift is an embedding, since equality of two lifted image points would imply equality of their projected points on the embedded $S$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Align the finitely many longitude boundary curves by [F3] with distinct fiber-boundary levels in the torus, extending across its collar. In the infinite cyclic cover their lifts are horizontal circles in $\partial F\times\mathbb R$. Straighten the neat surface's smaller boundary collars to the product collars using their simultaneous half-space coordinates, fixed on the boundary curves. The projection of the lifted inclusion is now a proper map $p:(S,\partial S)\to(F,\partial F)$ equal to a product near boundary; every boundary restriction is a diffeomorphism. Its fundamental-group map is injective: the lifted inclusion is injective on fundamental groups by [F2] and covering injection, and $F\times\mathbb R\to F$ is a homotopy equivalence. The relative fundamental class of $F\times\{t\}$ generates $H_2(F\times\mathbb R,\partial F\times\mathbb R)$ and pushes to $[F]$ downstairs. Consequently $[S]=\pm[F]$ from step 1.1 makes the relative degree of $p$ equal to $\pm1$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Give the compact smooth surfaces the finite triangulations of [F4], choosing matched boundary subdivisions through the actual boundary diffeomorphisms. On their product collars retain the boundary map and its linear collar coordinate; relatively approximate the remaining compact map by a finite PL map. Interior compact separation and sufficiently fine approximation keep it in the target interior, so this is a homotopy of pairs fixed on the original boundary. If $\pi_1S\ne1$, apply the full actual classifier [F4]. Its annular-collapse alternative induces zero on relative $H_2$, contrary to the degree $\pm1$ in step 2.1. Its finite covering alternative has absolute relative degree equal to its number of sheets, by summing the lifted oriented triangles. Thus it has one sheet and is a homeomorphism $h:S\to F$, homotopic to $p$ relative to the aligned boundary. If $\pi_1S=1$, [F5] makes $S$ a disk. Lift $p$ to the cover of $F$ for its trivial image subgroup. An infinite-sheeted cover has relative top homology zero: all coefficients of a finite two-cycle on adjacent oriented triangles agree, and connectedness forces a single coefficient on infinitely many triangles, which must vanish by finite support. A finite-sheeted cover pushes its fundamental class to its sheet number times $[F,\partial F]$. Nonzero degree $\pm1$ therefore forces this cover to have one sheet. Hence $F$ is simply connected and also a disk; its boundary map extends to a disk homeomorphism, homotopic to $p$ relative boundary by convex interpolation in disk coordinates. In either case $S$ has one boundary component. The height coordinate of its lifted inclusion can now separately be homotoped linearly to its one constant boundary height, fixed there. Combine these homotopies in $F\times\mathbb R$ and project to get an actual homotopy of the parametrized inclusion of $S$ to the corresponding fiber, relative to the aligned boundary. This asserts a homotopy of maps, not a projection of an arbitrary embedding isotopy. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The homeomorphism and actual boundary-relative homotopy in step 3.1 meet [F6]. Use [F7] on the pair cut along its transverse smooth surface faces and protected product collars, matching paired face subdivisions before regluing; this gives compatible finite structures retaining the already matched boundary triangulations. That theorem constructs an empty embedded product patch in the actual cut fiber product, verifies that the patch meets only one fiber face so embeds downstairs, and reduces the finite intersection system until the patch is the whole surface. Hence its ambient boundary-relative isotopy carries $S$ to the original marked fiber $F$. Restore the preliminary boundary-torus alignment and neatification if necessary. This proves both the isotopy assertion and its relative aligned-boundary refinement under the authorized AC assumptions. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎
