## Statement

Assume AC. Let $Q\subset\mathbb{CP}^2$ be the nonsingular complex conic parametrized by $[s:t]\mapsto[s^2:st:t^2]$, let $N(Q)$ be a closed tubular disk bundle, and let $B_2=\overline{\mathbb{CP}^2\setminus\operatorname{int}N(Q)}$. Then $B_2$ is a smooth compact four-manifold with $H_*(B_2;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$. Its boundary is the circle bundle of Euler number $4$ over $S^2$, hence is the lens space $L(4,1)$ up to orientation; orient $B_2$ so that the boundary agrees with the stated lens-space convention.

## Statement references

[[def-complex-projective-space-and-holomorphic-charts|The complex projective plane and its complex orientation]]

[[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention|The oriented lens-space surgery convention]]

[[thm-self-intersection-is-the-euler-number-of-the-normal-bundle|The normal Euler number equals self-intersection]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the complex-oriented projective plane, its conic $Q$, and a closed tubular disk bundle $N(Q)$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the UCT, tubular-neighbourhood, Thom, Poincare-duality, geometric-intersection, and self-intersection suppliers; AC implies the ACω hypotheses of the lens-space convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The standard filtration $\mathbb{CP}^0\subset\mathbb{CP}^1\subset\mathbb{CP}^2$ and affine charts give one cell in dimensions $0,2,4$; cellular and universal-coefficient comparison compute its integral homology and cohomology ([[def-complex-projective-space-and-holomorphic-charts]], [[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]], [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]).

[F2] Excision identifies $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^2,B_2;\mathbb Z)$ with $H^*(N(Q),\partial N(Q);\mathbb Z)$, and the normalized oriented rank-two Thom class identifies the latter with $H^{*-2}(Q;\mathbb Z)$ and evaluates $+1$ on each positive normal disk. Its relative-to-absolute image in degree two is the Poincare dual of $Q$, with sign $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$ ([[thm-excision-for-singular-cohomology]], [[thm-thom-isomorphism-for-oriented-vector-bundles]], [[def-thom-class-by-fiberwise-normalization]], [[lem-normal-thom-class-realizes-the-poincare-dual-of-a-submanifold]]).

[F3] The complex orientation supplies the fundamental class; Poincare duality identifies $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)$; the geometric intersection pairing equals the Poincare-dual cup pairing and depends only on homology classes; homotopic maps induce the same homology map; and the local sign of a transverse intersection is determined by the ordered tangent orientations ([[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]], [[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]], [[thm-geometric-intersection-equals-the-poincare-dual-cup-pairing]], [[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]], [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]], [[def-geometric-intersection-pairing-on-a-closed-oriented-manifold]], [[def-oriented-intersection-number]]).

[F4] The self-intersection of a compact oriented surface in an oriented four-manifold equals the Euler number of its oriented normal bundle ([[def-self-intersection-number-of-an-oriented-submanifold]], [[thm-self-intersection-is-the-euler-number-of-the-normal-bundle]]).

[F5] The lens-space convention defines $L(p,1)$ by $+p$ filling of the standard unknot exterior; the nonsingular surgery matrix gives $H_1\cong\mathbb Z/p$ ([[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention]], [[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix]]). The lens-space convention assumes countable choice, which follows from AC ([[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F6] The cohomology long exact sequence of the pair $(\mathbb{CP}^2,B_2)$ computes the cohomology of the complement from the relative and absolute groups ([[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-cohomology]]).

## Proof

1.1 Choose the filtration $\mathbb{CP}^0\subset P\subset\mathbb{CP}^2$ with $P=\{y=0\}\cong\mathbb{CP}^1$ and $\mathbb{CP}^0=[1:0:0]$. Its successive complements are $\mathbb C$ and $\mathbb C^2$, so the cellular boundary maps vanish for degree reasons and $H_2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[P]$, $H_4(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mathbb{CP}^2]$; UCT gives free cohomology, and put $h=\mathrm{PD}[P]$. The projective maps $T_t([x:y:z])=[x:y+tx:z]$ ($0\le t\le1$) give a homotopy from the inclusion of $P$ to that of $P'=\{y=x\}$. The two lines meet transversely at $[0:0:1]$ with positive sign, since a complex-linear isomorphism between their tangent complex lines and the ambient complex plane has positive real determinant. By [F3], $[P]^2=1$. On the charts $s\ne0$ and $t\ne0$, the conic map $[s:t]\mapsto[s^2:st:t^2]$ has target coordinates $(u,u^2)$ with $u=t/s$ and $(v^2,v)$ with $v=s/t$, respectively; these recover the source coordinate and have injective derivatives. Its image is exactly $xz-y^2=0$: if $x\ne0$ the point is $[1:y/x:(y/x)^2]$, and if $x=0$ then $y=0$ and the point is $[0:0:1]$. The same chart descriptions show the zero set is a smooth complex-oriented sphere and the map is an embedding. The line $P$ meets it at the two simple roots $st=0$, both transversely and positively in the complex orientations. Thus [F3] gives $[Q]\cdot[P]=2$; because $[P]$ generates $H_2$, this implies $[Q]=2[P]$, hence $[Q]\cdot[Q]=4$. [A1, F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The normal Euler number of $Q$ is therefore $4$ by [F4]. Its unit normal circle bundle is the boundary of its tubular disk bundle. Compute its genus-one gluing directly from the conic charts, without assuming an Euler-to-surgery identification. In the chart $x=1$ write the surface as $(y,z)=(u,u^2)$ and use normal coordinate $n=z-y^2$. In the chart $z=1$ use normal coordinate $n'=x-y^2$. Their change is $n'=(z-y^2)/z^2$; differentiating in the normal direction on the conic gives $n'=u^{-4}n$ in the normal line bundle. On the equator $u=e^{i\varphi}$ its unit normal circle transition is therefore $\theta_N=\theta_S-4\varphi$. Each closed hemisphere has its actual displayed complex normal frame, so its unit circle bundle is $D^2\times S^1$, a solid torus. On their common torus let $m$ be the equator loop at fixed $\theta_S$, and $l$ the fiber loop. The southern solid-torus meridian is $m$, and the northern meridian is $m+4l$, since holding $\theta_N$ fixed gives that exact slope. Identify the southern solid torus with the standard unknot exterior by $l=\mu_U$, $m=\lambda_U$: its fiber is the core circle, while its base disk is the exterior meridian disk. The second filling slope is therefore $4\mu_U+\lambda_U$, with the global boundary orientation determined by the product identifications. If those identifications reverse the desired global orientation, reverse the orientation of the total space; the statement permits exactly that choice. Thus [F5] identifies the total circle bundle with $L(4,1)$ up to orientation, by an actual meridian calculation. The complement has the opposite boundary orientation to its tubular neighborhood in the complex-oriented projective plane; choose the orientation of $B_2$ as allowed in the Statement so its boundary agrees with the declared lens-space convention. [A1, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 By [F2], the relative cohomology groups of $(\mathbb{CP}^2,B_2)$ are $\mathbb Z$ in degrees $2$ and $4$ and zero otherwise, since $Q\cong S^2$. The relative-to-absolute map in degree two sends the Thom generator to $\mathrm{PD}[Q]$: the normal-Thom sign is $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$ by [F2]. By step 1.1, $[Q]=2[P]$, so this map is multiplication by $2$ under $h=\mathrm{PD}[P]$. For degree four, let $a$ be the positive generator of $H^2(Q;\mathbb Z)$, with $\langle a,[Q]\rangle=1$. The Thom image of $a$ evaluates on $[\mathbb{CP}^2]$ as $\langle a,[Q]\rangle$: excision reduces the evaluation to the normal disk fibers, and the normalized Thom class evaluates $+1$ on each such fiber by [F2]. Thus the degree-four relative-to-absolute map sends a generator to a generator and is an isomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F6], the cohomology long exact sequence of the pair gives $H^1(B_2;\mathbb Z)=0$, $H^2(B_2;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/2$, and $H^j(B_2;\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $j\ge3$: in degree one the map $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ is injective multiplication by $2$, in degree two its cokernel is $\mathbb Z/2$ and the next relative group is zero, and in degree four the relative-to-absolute map is an isomorphism. In degree zero, the relative group vanishes, so $H^0(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)\to H^0(B_2;\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism; hence $B_2$ is connected. Repeat the relative calculation over $\mathbb Q$: the degree-two map is multiplication by $2$ and the degree-four map is the identity, both isomorphisms, so the pair sequence gives $H^j(B_2;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $j>0$ and $H^0(B_2;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$. The UCT over $\mathbb Q$ then gives the rational homology of a point. Together with step 2.1 this proves that $B_2$ is a rational homology ball bounded by $L(4,1)$. [A1, F1, F6, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎


## Remark

The picture is the one-component surgery diagram for the boundary circle bundle. The planar circle has no crossings and represents the unknot; its integer framing is specified by the label $+4$, meaning the chosen parallel has linking number $+4$ with the core. The proof identifies this handle attachment from the normal disk bundle and does not depend on the drawing.

\begin{tikzpicture}
  \draw[thick] (0,0) circle (0.7);
  \node at (0,1.05) {$+4$};
  \node at (0,-1.05) {$U$};
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot such that its double branched cover $M=\Sigma_2(K)$ is a rational homology sphere. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper embedded disk with boundary $K$, and let $B_D$ be the connected double cover of $B^4$ branched over $D$. Let $W$ be a compact connected smooth simply connected oriented four-manifold with boundary identified orientation-compatibly with $M$, and assume its boundary intersection form is positive definite. Assume also that the image of $\pi_1(M)\to\pi_1(B_D)$ normally generates $\pi_1(B_D)$, meaning its normal closure is the whole group. Then the oriented gluing $X=W\cup_M(-B_D)$ is a closed smooth simply connected positive-definite four-manifold, and inclusion induces an isometric full-rank embedding $Q_W\hookrightarrow Q_X$ of integral intersection lattices with $b_2(X)=b_2(W)$.

## Statement references

[[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot|The oriented double branched cover of a knot]]

[[lem-double-cover-branched-over-a-slice-disk-is-a-rational-homology-ball|A smooth slice disk has a rational-homology-ball double branched cover]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC; the knot, slice disk, rational-homology-sphere boundary, positive-definite simply connected filling, boundary identification, and normal-generation hypothesis in the statement.

[F1] For a smooth proper disk, the double cover branched over the disk is a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with rational homology of a point, and its boundary is the double branched cover of the boundary knot. The result does not assert a fundamental-group conclusion. [[lem-double-cover-branched-over-a-slice-disk-is-a-rational-homology-ball]]

[F2] The double branched cover is defined by the connected cover of the knot exterior classified by the positive-meridian map to $\mathbb Z/2$, filled along the closed lift of the squared meridian. [[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot]]

[F3] Smooth four-ball genus is the minimum genus of a smooth proper oriented surface in $B^4$; a smooth slice disk is the genus-zero case. [[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]]

[F4] The boundary form is the signed intersection pairing on the torsion-free quotient, and is rationally nondegenerate when the boundary is a rational homology sphere. [[def-intersection-lattice-of-a-four-manifold-with-boundary]] [[lem-boundary-intersection-pairing-well-defined-and-nondegenerate]]

[F5] Seifert–van Kampen computes the fundamental group of a union along a path-connected collar as the pushout of the two inclusion homomorphisms. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

[F6] Mayer–Vietoris gives the singular-homology exact sequence for the collar-thickened decomposition along $M$. [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

[F7] Smooth collars on the two boundaries allow the orientation-compatible gluing and its collar-thickened open cover. [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]

[F8] For any abelian group $A$, $A\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ is its positive-integer localization, and $a\otimes1=0$ exactly when some positive integer kills $a$. The natural coefficient map identifies $H_j(Y;\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb Q$ with $H_j(Y;\mathbb Q)$. [[lem-rationalization-is-exact-and-commutes-with-singular-homology]]

[A1] For this particular branched cover $B_D$, the boundary inclusion normally generates $\pi_1(B_D)$. This is an explicit additional hypothesis; it is not a consequence of the rational-homology-ball supplier [F1].

[A2] Full AC is assumed by the branched-cover and homology suppliers in [F1]–[F3].

## Proof

**Given:** The data and assumptions above.

1.1 By [F3], $D$ is a smooth proper slice disk; [F1] and [F2] then give a compact rational homology four-ball $B_D$ with boundary $M=\Sigma_2(K)$. The boundary identification in the statement permits the smooth oriented gluing $X=W\cup_M(-B_D)$; collars [F7] give a smooth closed oriented four-manifold. [given, F1, F2, F3, F7, A2, construct]

1.2 Applying [F5] to the collar-thickened union gives $\pi_1(X)=\pi_1(W)*_{\pi_1(M)}\pi_1(B_D)$. Since $\pi_1(W)=1$, this pushout is the quotient of $\pi_1(B_D)$ by the normal closure of the image of $\pi_1(M)$. That normal closure is all of $\pi_1(B_D)$ by [A1], so $\pi_1(X)=1$. [given, F5, A1, algebra]

2.1 In the rational Mayer–Vietoris sequence of [F6], $H_2(M;\mathbb Q)=H_1(M;\mathbb Q)=0$ and $H_i(B_D;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $i>0$ by [F1]. Thus inclusion induces an isomorphism $H_2(W;\mathbb Q)\cong H_2(X;\mathbb Q)$, so $b_2(X)=b_2(W)$. By [F8], $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb Q\cong H_2(W;\mathbb Q)$, and the kernel of the integral-to-rational map is exactly the torsion subgroup. If an integral class maps to torsion in $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$, its rational image vanishes; the isomorphism forces its rational class in $W$ to vanish, so it was torsion. Therefore the induced map on torsion-free quotients is injective and has full rank. [given, F1, F6, F8, A2, algebra]

2.2 Represent classes of $W$ by two-cycles in its interior and make two representatives transverse. Their signed intersection points are unchanged in the glued manifold, so the map of step 2.1 preserves the intersection form. Its rational extension is an isomorphism and transports the positive-definite form of $W$ to $X$; hence $Q_X$ is positive definite. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Unresolved proof obligations

The displayed gluing lemma is proved only with [A1]. A proof that every smooth slice-disk branched cover in this setting has boundary-normal-generated fundamental group has not been found in the inspected local suppliers. The rational homology conclusion [F1] does not supply [A1]. Consequently this lemma does not yet cover every smooth slice disk and cannot by itself certify unrestricted nonsliceness.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F$ be a fixed minimum-genus oriented Seifert surface, and let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H_1$ be admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagrams for the same pair $(K,F)$ whose hat complexes have total homology $\mathbb F_2$ and the same absolute Alexander normalization. Their diagramwise thresholds agree. Moreover, every grid presentation of $(K,F)$ gives this same value after the full filtered grid complex is converted to the normalized singly pointed model, with all basepoint-variable and stabilization factors accounted for. The common value is $\tau(K)$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau|The diagramwise threshold and absolute Alexander normalization]]

[[lem-tau-preserved-by-filtered-chain-homotopy-equivalence|Filtered chain homotopy equivalences preserve the threshold]]

[[thm-pointed-heegaard-floer-invariance-under-moves-and-stabilization|The claimed Heegaard-move comparison]]

[[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer|The claimed normalized grid-to-analytic comparison]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Knot Floer homology and the four-ball genus*, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0301149v4)

[Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, §§2.2–3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383v3)

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, Chapters 5, 6, and 13](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, a knot $K$, a fixed minimum-genus Seifert surface $F$, and two admissible doubly pointed diagrams with the stated one-dimensional total homology and common absolute normalization.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] states the axiom that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function; it is inherited by the current diagram/move suppliers that require selected finite data.

[F1] [[lem-tau-preserved-by-filtered-chain-homotopy-equivalence]] proves that a filtration-preserving chain homotopy equivalence between finite models with one-dimensional total homology preserves their tau thresholds.

[L1] [[thm-pointed-heegaard-floer-invariance-under-moves-and-stabilization]] supplies the actual finite filtered chain homotopy equivalences for admissible analytic diagrams, with the specified single-variable restriction and the Seifert-normalized doubly pointed origin. Specializing the actual finite identities at U=0 gives the filtered hat comparisons; this does not supply the separate grid-to-analytic identification.

[L2] [[thm-grid-commutation-stabilization-invariance-proof]] gives the local filtered equivalences for commutations and stabilizations, using the stated polygon maps and the stabilization cone comparison. Its simultaneous-collapse statement retains the extra $V$ factor; this local move comparison is separate from the analytic grid comparison in [L3].

[L3] [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] constructs the normalized comparison from the grid full filtered minus complex to the singly pointed analytic model. It distinguishes restriction to one variable action from simultaneous collapse, and accounts for the latter by $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$; its argument also identifies the grid Alexander origin with the Seifert-normalized one.

[L4] [[thm-grid-moves-generate-oriented-knot-isotopy]] gives a finite grid-move sequence for grids of the same oriented knot, by refining to bridge-like grids, applying an oriented Reidemeister sequence, and translating each local change using the stated arbitrary-exterior move supplier.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [L1] to the two analytic doubly pointed diagrams in the Statement. Its maps and inverse homotopies are finite polynomial identities preserving their Seifert-normalized Alexander filtration. Specialize those identities at U=0; no flatness assertion about homology is required. The resulting actual finite hat models are filtered chain homotopy equivalent and carry the nonzero total generators to each other. Therefore [F1] gives equality of their thresholds. This proves the analytic-diagram comparison in the first sentence. [F1, L1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Fix a grid $G$ with $n$ marking pairs and choose one marking variable $U_i$. Use the actual normalized grid-to-analytic comparison in [L3], together with the pointed-move comparison in [L1], to convert its full filtered minus complex to the finite singly pointed model for $(K,F)$. In this comparison first restrict scalars along $U\mapsto U_i$ and retain the other $U_j$ as independent module variables. The supplied chain maps and inverse homotopies preserve the Alexander filtration and the Seifert-normalized origin. Specializing these actual identities at the chosen $U=0$ gives the corresponding filtered equivalence to the singly pointed hat endpoint. The restricted grid module can still have infinite rank over $\mathbb F_2$ after this specialization, so it is not itself an input to the finite-complex definition of $\tau$; the grid value in the Statement is the threshold on the finite normalized singly pointed endpoint obtained by this conversion. [L1, L3, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 The separate simultaneous ordinary collapse sets all marking variables equal before taking the one-variable quotient. By [L3] and [L1] its filtered type is the singly pointed minus model tensored with $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$, with each $V$ carrying bidegrees $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. After quotienting the remaining variable by zero, this collapsed model has the extra $V$ homology factors and is not the finite complex with one-dimensional total homology required in the definition of $\tau$. Those factors are accounted for by the actual basepoint-pair cone and retraction comparison in [L1, L3]: use the retained-variable equivalence to the singly pointed model when defining the grid's value, and do not apply $\tau$ to the unreduced simultaneous-collapse complex. Thus no extra filtration shift from the $V$ factors is included in the claimed value. [L1, L3, given, algebra]

2.3 For any two grid presentations, [L3] supplies this conversion for each grid to a normalized singly pointed model. Compare those finite endpoints by the actual pointed-move equivalence [L1], specialize its maps and filtered inverse homotopies at $U=0$, and apply [F1]. This gives the same threshold as in step 1.1. The grid-move and grid-isotopy suppliers [L2, L4] describe additional combinatorial comparisons; they do not replace the filtered grid-to-analytic conversion or alter the variable-collapse distinction above. [A1, F1, L1, L2, L3, L4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. If a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ has Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, where $\doteq$ denotes equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, then there is a locally flat proper embedding $D^2\hookrightarrow B^4$ whose boundary is $K$. Here **topologically slice** means bounding such a locally flat proper disk; the conclusion asserts no smooth slice disk.

## Statement references

[[lem-alexander-one-knot-produces-a-good-group-disk-obstruction|The marked smooth Alexander-one complement and disk data]]

[[lem-freedman-casson-handle-skyscraper-and-surgery-modules|The smooth-input good-group construction with relative standard handle charts]]

[[thm-infinite-cyclic-group-is-good-for-disk-embedding|Goodness of the infinite cyclic group]]

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Local flatness and the prescribed boundary collar]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the stated smooth oriented Alexander-one knot.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]: Full AC supplies Countable Choice.

[F1] [[lem-alexander-one-knot-produces-a-good-group-disk-obstruction]]: In the literal radius-$3/2$ ball, the supplied smooth surface $\Sigma$ has a marked smooth complement $N$ with infinite cyclic fundamental group, smooth framed immersed compression disks and smooth algebraic dual spheres satisfying all the Wall vanishings. Their attaching annuli and framings match the short curves on $\Sigma$.

[F2] [[thm-infinite-cyclic-group-is-good-for-disk-embedding]]: This complement group is good.

[F3] [[lem-freedman-casson-handle-skyscraper-and-surgery-modules]]: Smooth framed data in the supplied smooth neighborhood $V=N$ give disjoint locally flat disks with disjoint standard product handle charts, preserving their attaching framings.

[F4] [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]]: The local pair charts and the unchanged outer knot collar give the asserted locally flat proper embedding.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to obtain the actual surface $\Sigma$, complement $N$, short curves $s_1,\ldots,s_g$, marked annuli and smooth disk/dual datum. By [A1] and [F2], [F3] applies with $V=N$. Its hypothesis concerns smooth maps and smooth collars; those are explicitly supplied here. Thus the compression disks have disjoint embedded standard product handle charts with the prescribed attaching framings. If $g=0$, the original $\Sigma$ is already the required disk and the following finite surgeries are empty. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Join each produced disk to its short curve on $\Sigma$ along the marked negative-normal annulus. These annuli are disjoint, and their interiors lie on the $\Sigma$ side of $\partial N$; the disks lie on its $N$ side. The supplied collars identify their product charts at the seam. The resulting joined disks therefore have product normal neighborhoods whose first boundary normal direction is the normal direction of $s_i$ within $\Sigma$. Choose mutually disjoint sufficiently small product neighborhoods. Replace the annulus $s_i\times(-\eta,\eta)$ in $\Sigma$ by the two disk parallels at $\pm\eta$ in that first normal direction, with opposite orientations. The attaching collars give two coordinate half-planes meeting on their common boundary line. Rounding their quadrant in those product coordinates yields a locally flat surface. This uses the product charts actually supplied by [F3], rather than a normal-neighborhood theorem for an arbitrary TOP surface. All changes fix the outer knot collar. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Cutting along the geometric short curves leaves a connected surface. Indeed, if its complementary-component graph had more than one vertex, choose a proper nonempty vertex subset with an edge to its complement. The oriented boundary of the corresponding union gives a nonzero signed relation among the independent classes $[s_i]$: every crossing edge occurs once, while edges internal to the union cancel. This is impossible. Hence capping these cut curves leaves the result connected. Removing the annuli changes no Euler characteristic, while the $2g$ disk caps raise it from $1-2g$ to $1$. The connected oriented one-boundary surface is a disk: the geometric cut-system polygon is a sphere with $2g+1$ boundary circles, and the caps fill its $2g$ inner circles. Its only outer boundary is still $K$, and its original boundary product collar is unchanged. Finally radial rescaling of the literal radius-$3/2$ ball to $B^4$ carries this locally flat proper disk to the desired one. ∎ [F1, F4, step 2.1, construct]

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot. Form the Newton polygon of the ordinary A-polynomial using the exponent convention that the lattice point $(a,b)$ represents the monomial $M^bL^a$, so edge slopes are measured in the preferred meridian-longitude convention. Every finite rational slope or infinite slope of an edge of this Newton polygon is a boundary slope of an incompressible, boundary-incompressible, orientable surface in the knot exterior. This statement does not assert that the realizing surface is non-fibered or that the slope is strict.

## Statement references

[Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long, and Shalen, Theorem 3.4](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~culler/papers/PlaneCurves/curves.pdf)

[Tillmann, §7](https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the nontrivial smooth knot with its chosen compact exterior and peripheral marking, and the stated Newton edge.

[A1] Full AC is retained. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The exterior is compact orientable and irreducible, with no proper compressing disk. Full AC supplies the countable choice needed by its smooth Schoenflies branch. Its tube is a smooth $S^1\times D^2$ product by the normal-circle frame supplier, so the boundary is the marked smooth torus. It is connected: join two distinct exterior points by an embedded spherical arc, perturb it relative to its endpoints to be transverse to the knot, and use $1+1<3$ to conclude it misses the knot. Radial projection of nonzero tube fibers to their boundary fixes the exterior and retracts that arc to an exterior path; equal endpoints need the constant path. [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]] [[lem-nontrivial-knot-exterior-boundary-incompressible]] [[lem-knot-normal-circle-bundle-trivialization]] [[lem-choice-free-relative-transversality-for-a-compact-smooth-embedding]]

[F2] Every selected Newton edge has an ACTUAL finite representation field and extending local curve valuation with peripheral eigenvalue pair a positive multiple of its primitive minimum normal. For an enhanced edge the representation is absolutely irreducible, including when its factor is also $L-1$. [[lem-newton-edges-have-valued-finite-peripheral-representation-models]]

[F3] For that valued representation, the actual lattice-tree/equivariant-map construction gives a connected orientable smooth essential surface with nonempty boundary whose primitive class annihilates the valuation pair. It proves both incompressibility and boundary-incompressibility by map-preserving compression complexity. With an absolutely irreducible representation it also proves that the chosen component cannot be a fiber. [[thm-nonelliptic-lattice-tree-actions-produce-essential-boundary-surfaces]]

[F4] In the stated marking $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$ has slope $b/a$, including $a=0$ as infinity. [[def-boundary-slope-of-an-incompressible-surface]]

## Proof

1.1 Let $e$ be any edge of the ordinary Newton polygon. Apply [F2] to the ordinary polynomial: it selects an irreducible peripheral curve factor with parallel minimum face, constructs the boundary-branch DVR by the unimodular toric chart, selects an actual finite-field generic representation by a closed point of the nonzero incidence fiber, and extends the valuation to that field. If $(u,v)$ is the primitive minimum normal in exponent coordinates $(a,b)$, its eigenvalues satisfy $(w(L),w(M))=d(u,v)$ for an integer $d>0$. Nothing in this step assumes that this ordinary representation is irreducible; it includes the abelian $L-1$ factor. [A1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 The manifold hypotheses of [F3] are exactly [F1]. Its valued-field hypotheses are supplied by step 1.1, and the valuation pair is nonzero. Thus [F3] gives a connected orientable neatly properly embedded smooth surface with nonempty boundary, no compression or boundary compression, and primitive boundary class $(a,b)$ satisfying $au+bv=0$. This is an actual associated midpoint surface after the finite compression and deletion homotopies, not an assumed Culler–Shalen witness. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Every direction $(\Delta a,\Delta b)$ of the original edge also satisfies $u\Delta a+v\Delta b=0$. Consequently its extended rational slope $\Delta b/\Delta a$ is exactly $b/a$ by [F4], including the vertical case where both denominators vanish and the value is infinity. This is a boundary slope realized by the surface of step 2.1, as required. The proof uses only the ordinary branch of [F2]–[F3] and makes no nonfiber or strictness assertion for that branch. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. There is an explicit functor $A$ from groups to groups and a natural transformation $\iota:\mathrm{id}\to A$ such that each $\iota_G:G\to A(G)$ is injective and
$$H_j(A(G);\mathbb Z)=0\quad(j>0),\qquad H_0(A(G);\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z.$$
One may take $A(G)$ to be the increasing union of the iterated mitoses $G_0=G$, $G_{r+1}=m(G_r)$, where
$$m(K)=\langle K,u,t\mid [h,ugu^{-1}]=1,\ t g t^{-1}=gugu^{-1}\ (g,h\in K)\rangle.$$
For every $n\ge0$ there is a specified partial chain homotopy, in degrees at most $n$, between the trivial homomorphism and $G\hookrightarrow G_n$ on integral unnormalized bar chains. It is zero in degree zero, has finite values on every basis simplex, and is natural in $G$. In particular every integral positive-degree bar cycle from any stage bounds after finitely many further mitoses. If $G$ is countable, $A(G)$ is countable.

## Statement references

[[def-unnormalized-homogeneous-bar-resolution]]

[Cha, Theorem 2.1 and section 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.1805)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, arbitrary groups, and homomorphisms. Products, free products and relative group presentations have their usual algebraic meanings. A chain homotopy from $a$ to $b$ has boundary $b-a$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] supplies the coset transversals in the HNN embedding supplier and implies the DC used by the supplied-resolution interpretation of group homology. The finite chain constructions below require no further choices.

[F1] [[def-hnn-extension-and-stable-letter]], [[cor-the-base-group-embeds-in-its-hnn-extension]] and [[prop-universal-property-of-an-hnn-extension]] give the relative presentation, base-group injection and extending homomorphisms for each HNN extension with injective associated maps.

[F2] The homogeneous bar complex has alternating vertex-deletion boundary. Passing to diagonal coinvariants and using consecutive increments identifies it with the free abelian complex $C_n(K)$ on all tuples $[g_1,\ldots,g_n]$, including identity entries, whose faces drop the first or last entry or replace consecutive entries by their product. Its homology is $H_*(K;\mathbb Z)$, naturally in $K$. [[def-unnormalized-homogeneous-bar-resolution]], [[lem-diagonal-bar-coinvariants-compute-group-homology]]

## Proof

1.1 Put $B=K\times K$. First adjoin $u$ with $u(g,1)u^{-1}=(1,g)$, an HNN extension between the two injective copies of $K$ in $B$. Next adjoin $t$ with $t(g,1)t^{-1}=(g,g)$; these associated maps remain injective after the first extension. By [F1], $B$ embeds after both adjunctions. Eliminating $(1,g)$ using the first relation leaves precisely the displayed presentation of $m(K)$: commutation between the two factors gives $[h,ugu^{-1}]=1$, and the diagonal relation becomes $tgt^{-1}=gugu^{-1}$. Conversely those relations define the commuting homomorphisms $(g,h)\mapsto g uhu^{-1}$ and satisfy both HNN relations, so the two presentation maps are inverse on generators. Thus $k_K:K\to m(K)$ is injective. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 We give the chain constructions needed for integral acyclicity, rather than using a field Kunneth splitting. The tuples of [F2] form a simplicial set $BK$: inserting $1$ gives degeneracies and the stated faces satisfy $d_i d_j=d_{j-1}d_i$ for $i<j$, by associativity, including the two end faces. Hence the alternating boundary squares to zero by pairing these faces. A tuple specifies a simplicial map from the standard simplicial simplex $\Delta^n$: a face edge from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$ is labelled by the product $g_{i+1}\cdots g_j$, with the empty product $1$. This uniquely describes all faces and degeneracies. Products obey $B(K\times L)=BK\times BL$ exactly. We use these unnormalized simplicial chains also for the finite standard simplex models below. [F2, algebra, construct]

2.1 A homomorphism $f:K\to L$ extends to $m(f)$ by applying $f$ to the old generators and sending $u,t$ to the respectively named generators. Every defining relation is preserved. Uniqueness on generators gives $m(1)=1$, $m(fg)=m(f)m(g)$ and $m(f)k_K=k_Lf$. Iterating gives a functorial sequence of injections $G_r\to G_{r+1}$. Its colimit may be represented as the disjoint union of the pairs $(r,g)$ modulo equality after transport to a common later stage; multiplication at a common stage is well-defined, and the stage maps are injective. This defines $A$ and the natural injective $\iota$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

2.2 For simplices $x,y$ of common dimension $n$, define the Alexander-Whitney map by $$D(x,y)=\sum_{i=0}^n x[0,\ldots,i]\otimes y[i,\ldots,n].$$ Define the shuffle $E(x\otimes y)$, for dimensions $p,q$, as the sum over the monotone lattice paths from $(0,0)$ to $(p,q)$ of their product simplices, with sign $(-1)^v$, where $v$ counts pairs consisting of a vertical step before a horizontal step. The coordinate simplex maps interpret a path vertex $(a,b)$ by the corresponding vertices of $x,y$, allowing repeated vertices. These formulas are natural. For $D$, the tensor boundary terms inside each front or back face reproduce the corresponding faces of $(x,y)$; the extra terms cutting at $i$ and $i+1$ cancel with opposite signs. Thus $dD=Dd$. For $E$, a face deleting the junction of steps of different types occurs in exactly the two paths interchanging those steps, with opposite signs. The remaining faces delete a vertex between two horizontal steps or between two vertical steps, or a first or last path vertex. These are exactly the shuffles of $dx\otimes y+(-1)^p x\otimes dy$, with the displayed signs, including paths with a zero-length coordinate. Consequently $dE=Ed$. Both maps agree with inverse identification of vertices in degree zero. [step 1.2, algebra, construct]

2.3 For $v\in L$, write $\mu_v(h)=vhv^{-1}$. The homomorphism $\mu_v$ is chain homotopic to the identity on $C(L)$ by the finite formula $$S_v[h_1,\ldots,h_j]=\sum_{i=0}^j(-1)^i[h_1,\ldots,h_i,v^{-1},\mu_v(h_{i+1}),\ldots,\mu_v(h_j)].$$ Indeed faces wholly before the inserted entry cancel with $S_vd$, as do those wholly after it with the shifted sign. The two faces crossing the inserted entry in adjacent summands cancel because $h_i v^{-1}=v^{-1}\mu_v(h_i)$. The only unpaired end faces are $\mu_v[h_1,\ldots,h_j]$ and $-[h_1,\ldots,h_j]$. Hence $dS_v+S_vd=\mu_v-1$, also in degree zero where both sides vanish. These formulas commute with any homomorphism taking $v$ to its specified image. [step 1.2, algebra, construct]

3.1 There is a specified natural homotopy $P$ with $dP+Pd=1-ED$ and $P_0=0$. Here are its model fillings. A simplex of $\Delta^n\times\Delta^n$ is a weakly increasing sequence of pairs in $\{0,\ldots,n\}^2$. Prepending $(0,0)$ defines a cone $c$; direct deletion gives $dc+cd=1-v\epsilon$, with $v\epsilon$ the augmentation projection onto that vertex, zero in positive degrees. Having defined $P$ below degree $n$, take the universal diagonal simplex $a_n$ in this product, set $z=(1-ED)a_n-P da_n$, and define $P a_n=cz$. For $n>0$, $dz=0$ by the lower identity and step 2.2; for $n=0$ set $P a_0=0$ since $z=0$. Thus $dP a_n=z$. For arbitrary $(x,y)$ push this fixed model chain forward by their uniquely specified simplex maps and extend linearly. The same rule defines its values on faces, so the identity holds on every generator. Composition of the simplex maps proves naturality. This construction does not require simplices to be nondegenerate, and every output is finite. [step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra, construct]

3.2 Suppose $\phi:\Pi\to K$ has a specified partial chain homotopy $Q$ with $dQ+Qd=\phi-e$ through degree $n-1$, where $n\ge1$, $e$ is the trivial homomorphism and $Q_0=0$. On $C(B\Pi\times B\Pi)$ put $L_1(x,y)=x\otimes[\ ]$, $L_2(x,y)=[\ ]\otimes y$ and $L=D-L_1-L_2$. Each is a chain map: the endpoint maps drop the other coordinate and tensor with the zero-cycle $[\ ]$. For positive degree $j$, $L$ has only tensor bidegrees $(i,j-i)$ with $1\le i\le j-1$. In degree zero $L=-[\ ]\otimes[\ ]$, which is killed by $Q\otimes\phi$ because $Q_0=0$. Therefore on degrees at most $n$ the signed tensor differential gives $$d((Q\otimes\phi)L)+(Q\otimes\phi)Ld=((\phi-e)\otimes\phi)L.$$ The terms involving the differential of the second factor cancel; the first factor only uses the stipulated identity below $n$. [step 2.2, given, algebra]

4.1 In step 3.2 let $U=\phi\times\phi$ and $V=e\times\phi$, as maps from $\Pi\times\Pi$ to $K\times K$. Set $$T=P(U-V)+E(Q\otimes\phi)L.$$ By naturality of $D$ and step 3.1, the boundary of the first summand is $(1-ED)(U-V)$. By step 3.2 the second boundary is $E((\phi-e)\otimes\phi)L$. Subtracting the $L$ contributions leaves the two endpoint terms: $E((\phi-e)\otimes\phi)L_1=\phi\times e-e\times e$ and $E((\phi-e)\otimes\phi)L_2=0$, since $\phi$ and $e$ agree on the vertex. Thus $$dT+Td=\phi\times\phi-\phi\times e-e\times\phi+e\times e$$ through degree $n$. Also $T_0=0$, using $P_0=Q_0=0$. All identities concern actual unnormalized chains; a trivial homomorphism is not replaced by the zero chain map. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra, construct]

5.1 Let $k=k_K$, and let $F:K\times K\to m(K)$ be $F(g,h)=k(g)u k(h)u^{-1}$, a homomorphism since its two factor images commute. On $\Pi$ let $i(g)=(g,1)$, $j(g)=(1,g)$, and $\delta(g)=(g,g)$. Put $a=F(\phi\times\phi)i=k\phi$, $b=F(\phi\times\phi)j=\mu_u a$, and $c=F(\phi\times\phi)\delta=\mu_t a$. The last two equalities are precisely the mitosis relations. Composing step 4.1 with $F$ and $\delta$ gives $d(FT\delta)+(FT\delta)d=c-a-b+e$. Step 2.3 gives boundaries $c-a$ for $S_ta$ and $b-a$ for $S_ua$. Consequently the explicit formula $$R=-FT\delta+S_ta-S_ua$$ satisfies $dR+Rd=a-e=k\phi-e$ through degree $n$. In degree zero, the two conjugation terms are $[t^{-1}]-[u^{-1}]$, independent of the single input vertex, while $FT\delta$ is zero there. To arrange zero degree-zero homotopy, replace $S_ta-S_ua$ in this formula by its difference from $(S_t-S_u)e$. Its boundary is unchanged, since $\mu_t e=\mu_u e=e$. Thus the required normalized formula is $$R=-FT\delta+(S_t-S_u)(a-e),\qquad R_0=0.$$ This supplies a full explicit one-degree improvement, with its sign checked by the three displayed boundary identities. [step 1.1, step 2.3, step 4.1, algebra, construct]

6.1 For $n=0$ the identity and trivial homomorphisms $G\to G$ agree on $C_0(G)=\mathbb Z$, so $Q^0=0$ is a partial homotopy through degree zero. Given $Q^{n-1}$ between the trivial map and $G\to G_{n-1}$, apply step 5.1 with $\Pi=G$, $K=G_{n-1}$, and $\phi$ that inclusion, obtaining $Q^n$. Each $Q^n_0=0$, so the induction applies at every stage. All constructions use finite sums, fixed simplex cones, named stable letters, and composition of natural maps. The formulas for $P,S,T,R$ therefore commute with a homomorphism on the original group; no choices of null-homology primitives are made in this induction. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.3, step 5.1, induction]

7.1 If $z\in C_j(G_r)$ is a cycle with $j>0$, apply step 6.1 to $G_r$ with $n=j$. Its image in $C_j(G_{r+j})$ differs from $e(z)$ by $dQ^jz$. The latter trivial-image cycle lies in the image of $C_*(1)$. This unnormalized point complex has one generator $e_l$ in each degree, with $de_l=e_{l-1}$ for positive even $l$ and zero for odd $l$. Its positive-degree contraction is $b e_l=e_{l+1}$ for odd $l$ and zero for positive even $l$, with $b e_0=0$; it satisfies $db+bd=1$ in positive degrees. Thus $e(z)$ bounds and so does the transported $z$. This handles identity entries without discarding degenerate simplices. [F2, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Every bar chain in $A(G)$ is a finite sum of tuples involving finitely many group elements. All those elements belong to a common stage, and injectivity of the stage maps means that an equation $dz=0$ in the union is already the identical equation in that stage's free bar complex. Step 7.1 then fills it at a later stage. Hence the positive integral bar homology of $A(G)$ vanishes; the unique vertex makes $H_0=\mathbb Z$. The identification [F2] yields the stated group homology. Countability follows because a group generated by a countable set has countably many finite words, each mitosis adds just two generators, and a countable union of countable explicitly generated groups is countable under [A1]. The trivial group, finite groups, arbitrary cardinalities and degree zero are all covered by the same constructions. [A1, F2, step 2.1, step 7.1] ∎

## Remarks

This group-theoretic result supplies no manifold bordism realization, topological bordism homology axiom, signature index theorem or rho independence. Those are separate prerequisites for applications to signature defects. The normalized homotopy in the proof fixes both its boundary sign and its degree-zero value explicitly.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every short exact sequence of discrete groups
$$1\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow 1,$$
the homological Serre spectral sequence of the induced map of classifying spaces
has
$$E^2_{p,q}\cong H_p\!\left(Q;H_q(N;\mathbb Z)\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H_{p+q}(G;\mathbb Z).$$
Here $H_p(Q;M)$ denotes homology of $BQ$ with the local coefficient system
determined by the left $Q$-module $M$, and group homology uses the bar
classifying spaces. The coefficient group $H_q(N;\mathbb Z)$ has the $Q$-action
induced by conjugation by lifts in $G$, and convergence is strong with the
finite Serre filtration in each total degree.

## Statement references

[McCleary, Theorem 8bis.14 and §8bis.2](https://pages.vassar.edu/mccleary/files/2011/04/MC08bis.fin_.pdf)

[Hatcher, §4.3, p. 408](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf)

[Milnor, Theorem 3 and proof, pp. 276–280](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorcw.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a short exact sequence $1\to N\to G\to Q\to1$ of discrete groups.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[L2] Full AC implies DC: apply AC to the family of nonempty successor sets of a serial relation, choose one initial element, and recursively follow the resulting choice function. [[def-dependent-choice]]

[L1] Under AC, Milnor's classifying space $BG$ is a connected CW model with $\pi_1(BG)\cong G$ and $\pi_k(BG)=0$ for $k>1$. [[cor-classifying-space-of-a-discrete-group-is-a-k-g-one]]

[F1] The homotopy long exact sequence of a Serre fibration computes the homotopy groups of its fiber. [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-homotopy-groups-of-a-fibration]]

[F2] For a Serre fibration over a path-connected CW complex, the homological Serre spectral sequence has $E^2_{p,q}=H_p(B;\mathcal H_q(F;\mathbb Z))$ and strongly converges to the homology of the total space. [[thm-homological-serre-spectral-sequence]]

[F3] The homology of a classifying space with the local system determined by a module is the usual bar-model group homology; the derived-functor identification in the library assumes DC. [[lem-diagonal-bar-coinvariants-compute-group-homology]], [[def-dependent-choice]]

[F4] Connected CW models with the same identified fundamental group and vanishing higher homotopy groups are homotopy equivalent under AC. [[thm-existence-and-homotopy-uniqueness-of-eilenberg-maclane-spaces]]

[F5] **External input:** For a map between CW complexes, its mapping-path homotopy fiber has CW homotopy type. This is the homotopy-fiber consequence of Milnor's compact-domain mapping n-ad theorem, stated explicitly in Hatcher's §4.3; the hypotheses here are satisfied by the classifying CW models in step 1.1. [[Hatcher §4.3, p. 408](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf)], [[Milnor, Theorem 3, pp. 276–280](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorcw.pdf)]

[F6] Classifying maps commute up to based homotopy with a based map and its induced fundamental-group homomorphism. [[lem-classifying-maps-are-natural-under-group-homomorphisms]]

## Proof

**Given:** The group extension and [A1].

1.1 Choose connected CW models from [L1]. Build a based map $BG\to BQ$ inducing $G\to Q$ by mapping the one-skeleton to loops representing the quotient images, filling each two-cell because its attaching word maps to the identity in $Q$, and extending over each higher cell because $\pi_k(BQ)=0$ for $k>1$. The finite cell extensions are simultaneous over a set of cells; [A1] supplies those choices. Replace this map by its mapping-path fibration $p:E\to BQ$; the total space $E$ is homotopy equivalent to $BG$, and the fiber $F$ is its homotopy fiber. [A1, L1, given, construct]

1.2 The map on fundamental groups is the quotient $G\to Q$. Exactness of [F1] gives $\pi_0(F)=\{*\}$, $\pi_1(F)\cong\ker(G\to Q)=N$, and $\pi_k(F)=0$ for every $k>1$, because both $BG$ and $BQ$ have zero higher homotopy groups by [L1]. By the external input [F5], $F$ has CW homotopy type. Choose a connected CW model $F'\simeq F$ and identify $\pi_1(F')$ with $N$. The uniqueness theorem [F4] gives $F'\simeq BN$, so $H_q(F;\mathbb Z)\cong H_q(N;\mathbb Z)$ for every $q$. [L1, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1]

1.3 A lift $g\in G$ of a loop class $q\in Q=\pi_1(BQ)$ transports the fiber fundamental group by $n\mapsto gng^{-1}$. Choose a based homotopy equivalence $h:F'\to F$ as in step 1.2 and a based homotopy inverse $\bar h:F\to F'$, using the basepoint path supplied by the transport. The map $T'_g=\bar h\circ T_g\circ h$ is a based self-map of $F'$ inducing $c_g(n)=gng^{-1}$ on $\pi_1(F')\cong N$. By [F6], the classifying map $c:F'\to BN$ satisfies $c\circ T'_g\simeq B(c_g)\circ c$, so the monodromy on $H_q(F')$ agrees under $h$ with the bar-classifying-space map induced by $c_g$. If a different lift is chosen, it differs by an element of $N$ and changes this map by an inner automorphism of $N$. Inner conjugation is homotopic to the identity on the bar classifying space: the conjugation functor on the one-object category of $N$ is naturally isomorphic to the identity by the conjugating element. Hence the induced action on $H_q(F;\mathbb Z)\cong H_q(N;\mathbb Z)$ depends only on $q$, and is exactly the stated $Q$-module action. [L1, F1, F4, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to $p:E\to BQ$. By step 1.2 the fiber homology is $H_q(N;\mathbb Z)$, and step 1.3 identifies its monodromy local system with the conjugation action. Therefore the $E^2$ page is $H_p(Q;H_q(N;\mathbb Z))$ and the spectral sequence strongly converges to $H_{p+q}(E;\mathbb Z)$. [F2, step 1.2, step 1.3]

2.2 The total-space equivalence from step 1.1 identifies $H_{p+q}(E;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_{p+q}(BG;\mathbb Z)$. By [F4], this classifying CW model is homotopy equivalent to the bar model used in [F3], so its homology is $H_{p+q}(G;\mathbb Z)$. The base and fiber are connected CW models, so the Serre filtration is first quadrant and finite on each total-degree diagonal. AC supplies the DC hypothesis of [F3] by [L2]. The fiber action and Serre filtration introduce no further choice. [A1, L2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On oriented ambient-isotopy classes of smooth knots in $S^3$, the connected-sum operation is associative and commutative, and the standard unknot is a two-sided identity. Here “commutative monoid” means a set with an associative binary operation, a two-sided identity, and equality after interchanging the two inputs.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|Connected-sum construction and standard unknot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and the oriented connected-sum construction.

[F1] The connected sum is formed by gluing the complements of trivial ball-arc pairs with a fixed standard orientation-reversing map, chosen symmetrically in the two-ball model. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]])

[F2] Changing the local representatives, charts, and sufficiently small ball-arc choices does not change the resulting oriented knot class. ([[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]])

[A1] AC$_\omega$ is the countable-choice hypothesis used by the local-choice lemma. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and oriented knot classes $[K],[J],[L]$.

1.1 For commutativity, choose the symmetric standard two-ball model in [F1]. The orientation-preserving half-turn exchanging its two lobes carries each oriented knot tangle to the corresponding tangle in the swapped model and carries the fixed joining map to itself. It therefore gives an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy between the model outputs for $K\#J$ and $J\#K$; [F2] transfers this equality to arbitrary connected-sum data. [given, F1, F2, A1, construct]

1.2 For associativity, place representatives of $K,J,L$ in three disjoint standard ball-arc pieces in a row and join consecutive pieces by the same fixed gluing. The constructions $(K\#J)\#L$ and $K\#(J\#L)$ then use the same three pieces and the same two joining maps; only the order in which the two gluings are performed differs. Since the gluings have disjoint boundary spheres, their order does not change the resulting oriented manifold or knot. By [F2], this common model represents both bracketings for arbitrary data. [given, F1, F2, A1, construct]

2.1 For the identity, choose the standard unknot summand with a small ball meeting it in a trivial arc. Its spanning disk shows that the complementary arc is boundary-parallel and hence trivial. The connected-sum gluing replaces a short trivial arc of $K$ by another standard trivial arc. The ball-arc isotopy of [F2] identifies the output with $K$. Reversing the order gives the same argument for the left identity. [given, F1, F2, A1, construct] ∎

## Sources

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

[[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]

[[def-countable-choice]]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If a connected compact oriented disk-and-band surface $F$ is built from $s$ disjoint disks by attaching $c$ rectangular bands along boundary intervals and has one boundary component, then $\chi(F)=s-c$ and $g(F)=(1-s+c)/2$. In particular, if the Seifert algorithm on an oriented knot diagram $D$ has $s$ Seifert circles and $c$ crossings, its output surface has genus $(1-s+c)/2$ and the knot genus satisfies $g(K)\le (1-s+c)/2$. This is an upper bound from one spanning surface, not a minimality assertion.

## Statement references

[[def-euler-characteristic-of-a-finite-cw-complex|Euler characteristic as an alternating finite cell count]]

[[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups|The compact oriented surface Euler formula under countable choice]]

[[lem-seifert-bands-embedded-orientable-boundary-correct|The algorithm output is an admissible surface for a knot]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|Knot genus is the minimum over all Seifert surfaces]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a connected disk-and-band surface made from $s$ disks and $c$ bands with one boundary component; for the final clause, $F$ is the output for an oriented knot diagram $D$ representing $K$.

[F1] The finite-cell Euler characteristic is the alternating sum of the numbers of cells. ([[def-euler-characteristic-of-a-finite-cw-complex]])

[F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a connected compact oriented surface with $b>0$ boundary circles has $\chi=2-2g-b$. ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

[F3] A connected compact oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$ is admissible in the set defining $g(K)$. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]])

[F4] For a one-component regular diagram with $s$ smoothed circles and $c$ crossings, the algorithm uses $s$ disk records and one band record per crossing. ([[alg-seifert-surface-from-diagram]])

[F5] For such a knot diagram, the realized disk-and-band surface is connected, oriented, embedded, and has boundary the represented knot. ([[lem-seifert-bands-embedded-orientable-boundary-correct]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the sequence principle stated in the item. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

1.1 Subdivide the disk boundaries so all band-attachment intervals are subcomplexes. Start with $s$ disjoint disks, each with Euler characteristic $1$. Relative to the two attaching intervals, a rectangular band has two free long sides and one square $2$-cell; collapsing the square across one free long side leaves one relative $1$-cell joining the intervals. Thus the band changes the alternating cell count by $-1$. By [F1], after $c$ bands $\chi(F)=s-c$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 The single boundary component gives $b=1$. By [F2] and [A1], $s-c=\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-1=1-2g(F)$, so $g(F)=(1-s+c)/2$. [step 1.1, F2, A1, algebra]

3.1 For the algorithm output on $D$, [F4] identifies the counts with its $s$ circles and $c$ crossings, and [F5] makes the output an admissible Seifert surface. By [F3], the minimum defining knot genus is at most this surface's genus, yielding $g(K)\le (1-s+c)/2$. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, the function $\Upsilon_K:[0,2]\to\mathbb R$ defined by the finite cycle minimax is continuous and piecewise linear with finitely many breakpoints, satisfies $\Upsilon_K(0)=0$ and $\Upsilon_K(t)=\Upsilon_K(2-t)$, and has right derivative $\Upsilon'_K(0+)=-\tau(K)$. For smooth oriented knots $K,J$ and $t\in[0,2]$,
$$ \Upsilon_{K\#J}(t)=\Upsilon_K(t)+\Upsilon_J(t),\qquad \Upsilon_{-K}(t)=-\Upsilon_K(t), $$
where $-K$ is the reverse mirror, the inverse under connected sum in the smooth concordance group. If $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ is the minimum genus of a smooth properly embedded compact connected oriented surface in the four-ball with boundary $K$, then
$$ |\Upsilon_K(t)|\le t\,g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)\qquad(0\le t\le1). $$

## Statement references

[[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex|Finite cycle-minimax definition and filtration convention]]

[[lem-tau-connected-sum-filtered-tensor-product|The supplied normalized bifiltered connected-sum tensor comparison]]

[[lem-upsilon-nu-minus-four-ball-bound|The auxiliary nu-minus genus estimate required for the Upsilon bound]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology*, §§2–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795)

[Livingston, *Notes on the knot concordance invariant Upsilon*, §§4–9](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Upsilon-revised.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot Floer complex with its finite bifiltered basis, normalized Maslov-zero total-homology generator, and the $F_t$ cycle-minimax convention.

[F1] [[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex]]: $\nu_t$ is the minimum of $F_t(z)$ over Maslov-zero cycles representing the normalized generator, and $\Upsilon_K(t)=-2\nu_t$; its finite candidate set makes the function piecewise linear.

[F5] The full geometric connected-sum comparison supplies the actual Maslov-graded bifiltered Laurent tensor equivalence, inverse and homotopies. [[lem-tau-connected-sum-filtered-tensor-product]]

[F9] The auxiliary threshold exists and is nonnegative by its local $V_s,H_s$ exponent proof. Its smooth genus upper bound uses the explicitly external OSS/Hom–Wu theorem in the exact same delta-threshold convention, with fixed finite/countable choice scope. [[lem-upsilon-nu-minus-four-ball-bound]]

[A3] [[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]]: the intended bound is the smooth four-ball genus branch; no locally flat/topological surface branch is used.

[F6] The supplied normalized doubly pointed polynomial complex $B=C\{i\le0\}$ has quotient $B/UB$ equal to the ordinary normalized hat model, whose total homology is $\mathbb F_2$ in degree zero. The differential retains every positive $z$ multiplicity as filtration. These are the accepted marked-variable/analytic knot interfaces, not arbitrary-link or cobordism assertions. [[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau]], [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]], [[lem-heegaard-floer-holomorphic-disk-regularity-compactness-gluing]]

[F2] [[lem-knot-floer-duality-and-filtration-swap]]: mirror duality negates both filtration coordinates, and conjugation exchanges the algebraic and Alexander filtrations. Its actual generator/class maps and absolute Seifert/Maslov origins are supplied without grid comparison.

[F3] [[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot]]: the reverse mirror is the reflected knot with its knot orientation reversed, using the fixed orientation-reversing reflection from the connected-sum convention.

[F7] The actual normalized model comparison supplies knot-level invariance of the two filtrations and hat threshold. The small-$t$ calculation below uses that threshold directly and does not use the still-held four-ball genus theorem. [[lem-tau-is-independent-of-heegaard-grid]]

[F8] The full normalized grid/analytic filtered equivalence is supplied, with the actual ordinary marked factors and absolute grading origins. [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]]

[F4] [[lem-upsilon-filtered-tower-splitting]] proves a filtered projection onto a minimizing rank-one tower and the exact real-series regrading comparison with maximal non-torsion degree $-2\nu_t$, for a supplied normalized complex.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], each fixed Maslov-zero cycle has filtration equal to the maximum of finitely many affine functions of $t$, and there are finitely many such cycles. Thus $\Upsilon_K$ is piecewise linear with finitely many breakpoints. The supplied model comparison [F8] makes this calculation a knot invariant. At $t=0$, $F_0$ is the algebraic filtration; the normalization in [F1] says the tower generator first appears at level zero, so $\nu_0=0$ and $\Upsilon_K(0)=0$. Exchanging the two bifiltration coordinates sends $F_t$ to $F_{2-t}$; [F2] therefore gives $\Upsilon_K(t)=\Upsilon_K(2-t)$. [given, F1, F8, F2, algebra]

1.2 Under the supplied geometric tensor comparison [F5], the connected-sum complex is the convolution-filtered Laurent tensor product. For a fixed $t$, apply the proved filtered splitting [F4] separately to the two factors. Their rank-one summands tensor to a zero-differential tower whose normalized generator has filtration $\nu_t(K)+\nu_t(J)$. Every other tensor summand contains an acyclic Laurent factor and is acyclic. To justify that last assertion without a filtered contraction assumption, normalize the factor's basis to Maslov degrees zero and one: its differential is given by finite binary matrices from degree one to zero and from degree zero to $U$ times degree one. Acyclicity makes the resulting finite parity complex acyclic, so finite vector-space complements give a contracting homotopy; the Laurent degree shifts insert only powers of $U$ or $U^{-1}$ to make it a chain homotopy. Tensoring this contraction with any other complex is a contraction, since the two cross terms cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Thus only the displayed tower carries total homology. The splitting is filtered, so no representative of its nonzero class can have a smaller filtration than that tower generator. This proves $\nu_t(K\#J)=\nu_t(K)+\nu_t(J)$ and Upsilon additivity. [given, F1, F5, F4, algebra]

1.3 First derive the actual minus normalization from [F6]. Since $B$ is finite free over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ with homogeneous generators, its chain groups vanish above a fixed Maslov degree. The exact sequence $0\to UB\to B\to B/UB\to0$ and $H(B/UB)=\mathbb F_2$ in degree zero imply that multiplication by $U$ is an isomorphism between adjacent even-degree homology groups below zero and between adjacent odd-degree groups; boundedness above gives $H_{>0}(B)=0$, $H_0(B)=\mathbb F_2$, and all odd groups zero. Thus $H(B)=\mathbb F_2[U]$ generated in degree zero. Every normalized minus cycle projects to the hat generator. Conversely, lift a Maslov-zero hat generator cycle to $c\in B$. Write $\partial c=Ud$; then $\partial d=0$ and $M(d)=1$. Since $H_1(B)=0$, write $d=\partial e$. The polynomial cycle $c+Ue$ lifts the SAME hat cycle and has the same leading $i=0$ terms. Therefore the least Alexander level among the $i=0$ parts of normalized minus cycles is exactly $\tau(K)$. Every normalized minus representative has a nonzero $i=0$ part, since a representative wholly in $UB$ would make the top homology generator $U$-divisible. The finite Maslov-zero Laurent cycle set admits a common positive $t$ interval in which any term with $i\ge1$ excludes a cycle from minimizing, and the maximum on a cycle with $i\le0$ comes only from its $i=0$ terms. Hence $\nu_t(K)=t\tau(K)/2$ on that interval and $\Upsilon'_K(0+)=-\tau(K)$. No genus estimate is used. [given, F1, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 By the actual normalized geometric duality [F2], the reverse-mirror complex is the filtered dual. Dualize the fixed-$t$ filtered splitting in [F4]. A filtration-preserving change of basis with filtration-preserving inverse has the same property after dualizing and negating the basis filtrations. The dual of the minimizing tower has normalized generator at filtration $-\nu_t(K)$. The dual complementary factor is acyclic, because the unfiltered finite Laurent contraction in step 1.2 dualizes to a contraction. Therefore the dual minimax equals $-\nu_t(K)$, and $\Upsilon_{-K}(t)=-\Upsilon_K(t)$. This uses no unproved identification of the homology of a dual torsion module. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Let $s=\nu^-(K)$ as defined in [F9], and put $g=g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$. Since $\delta(\mathcal A(K,s))=0$, there is a non-torsion homology class of Maslov grading zero represented by a cycle $z$ in $\mathcal A(K,s)$. For every finite basis generator $x_r$, all sufficiently large powers $U^n x_r$ satisfy $A(x_r)-n\le s$; hence localizing the inclusion $\mathcal A(K,s)\hookrightarrow C^-(K)$ gives the full $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ complex and induces an isomorphism on localized homology. The non-torsion class $[z]$ therefore maps to a nonzero degree-zero element of $H_*(C^-(K))\otimes_{\mathbb F_2[U]}\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$, whose only nonzero degree-zero element is the normalized generator. Thus $z$ represents that generator in $C^-(K)$ and in $C(K)$. Each term of $z$ has $i\le0$ and $j\le s$, so $F_t(z)=(1-t/2)i+(t/2)j\le ts/2$ for $0\le t\le1$. Therefore $\nu_t(K)\le ts/2\le tg/2$ by [F9], and $\Upsilon_K(t)\ge-tg$. A linear reflection extending the fixed reflection of $S^3$ to $B^4$ sends any smooth genus-$g$ surface bounded by $K$ to a genus-$g$ surface bounded by its mirror; reversing the surface orientation changes that boundary to the reverse mirror. Applying this diffeomorphism in both directions gives $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(-K)=g$. Apply the same threshold argument to $-K$ and use step 2.1 to obtain $\Upsilon_K(t)\le tg$. Combining both inequalities proves the bound, using the externally supplied genus upper estimate in [F9]. [given, F9, A3, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## External-input boundary

Every original clause follows from the displayed local minimax, derivative, tensor and dual arguments and the accepted normalized interfaces. The genus clause uses the explicitly external OSS/Hom–Wu smooth bound in [F9]; it is not inferred from a tau estimate or presented as a completed local surface-map construction. Its fixed finite/countable choice specialization is stated in that supplier.

## Example

Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty proper open set of line normals, invariant under $\theta\mapsto-\theta$, and suppose $S^1\setminus\overline{\Theta}$ contains an open arc. Restrict the Euclidean Radon incidence relation to
$$
Z_\Theta=\{(\theta,s,x)\in(\Theta\times\mathbb R)\times\mathbb R^2:s=x\cdot\theta\}.
$$
Give $Z_\Theta$ the standard nowhere vanishing analytic total density $|d\theta\,ds\,dt|$, with $x=s\theta+t\theta^\perp$, and constant weight $1$. This is a properly supported analytic double fibration.
For any $x_0\in\mathbb R^2$ and any nonzero covector $\xi_0\in T^*_{x_0}\mathbb R^2$ with $\xi_0/|\xi_0|\notin\Theta$, there are no $(\theta,s)\in\Theta\times\mathbb R$ and no data covector $\eta$ such that $(\theta,s,\eta;x_0,\xi_0)\in C_{Z_\Theta}$. In particular, this object covector has no data-side canonical pair for the restricted-angle transform.

## Example references

[[def-ip-2d-radon-transform|Euclidean Radon line and normal convention]]

[[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data|Measured angular set and visibility]]

[[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation|Incidence cotangent relation]]

[[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform|Analytic double-fibration transform]]

[[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel|Local incidence conormal formula]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open antipodally symmetric set $\Theta$, the incidence submanifold $Z_\Theta$, and the invisible covector $(x_0,\xi_0)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-2d-radon-transform]]: the line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is given by $s=x\cdot\theta$.

[F2] [[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data]]: a nonzero plane covector is visible exactly when its unit direction lies in $\Theta$; $\Theta$ is antipodally symmetric.

[F3] [[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation]]: $(\theta,s,\eta;x,\xi)$ belongs to the incidence relation exactly when $(\theta,s,x;\eta,-\xi)$ is a nonzero conormal to $Z_\Theta$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel]]: if $F(\theta,s,x)=0$ defines the incidence hypersurface, its conormal covectors are scalar multiples of $dF$.

[F5] [[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform]]: both incidence projections must be analytic submersions and the support condition is properness over compact object supports.

[F6] [[thm-real-analytic-inverse-and-implicit-function-theorems]]: a regular zero of a real-analytic scalar function is locally an analytic hypersurface.

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the example.

1.1 The defining function $F(\theta,s,x)=s-x\cdot\theta$ is real analytic and has $\partial_sF=1$. Thus $dF$ is surjective at every point of $Z_\Theta$, and [F6] makes $Z_\Theta$ an analytic hypersurface of dimension $3$. [F1, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 Use a local angular coordinate $\alpha$ on $S^1$, so $\partial_\alpha\theta=\theta^\perp$. The defining function $F(\theta,s,x)=s-x\cdot\theta$ has differential $ dF=ds-(x\cdot\theta^\perp)d\alpha-\theta\cdot dx. $ By [F4], a conormal covector is $\tau dF$ for a nonzero scalar $\tau$. Matching its data components and object component with the sign convention [F3] gives $ \eta_s=\tau,\qquad \eta_\alpha=-\tau x\cdot\theta^\perp,\qquad \xi=\tau\theta. $ Thus any object covector in the relation is parallel to the measured normal $\theta$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 A tangent vector satisfies $\dot s-\dot x\cdot\theta-x\cdot\dot\theta=0$. Given any data tangent pair $(\dot\theta,\dot s)$, choose $\dot x=(\dot s-x\cdot\dot\theta)\theta$; then $\pi_G$ has a tangent lift and is a submersion. Given any object tangent vector $\dot x$, choose $\dot\theta=0$, $\dot s=\dot x\cdot\theta$; hence $\pi_X$ is a submersion. Both maps are analytic restrictions of product projections and $4>3>2\ge2$. The displayed analytic total density is nowhere zero in these incidence coordinates. For compact $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ and compact $L\subset\Theta\times\mathbb R$, the preimage of $L$ under $\pi_G|_{\pi_X^{-1}(K)}$ is closed in $\operatorname{pr}_1(L)\times K$, which is compact because $\operatorname{pr}_1(L)\Subset\Theta$. Thus the restricted projection is proper and [F5] applies. [F5, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

3.1 If $(\theta,s,\eta;x_0,\xi_0)\in C_{Z_\Theta}$, step 1.2 implies $\xi_0/|\xi_0|=\theta$ or $-\theta$. Since $\Theta=-\Theta$, this would place $\xi_0/|\xi_0|$ in $\Theta$, contradicting the hypothesis. No such data covector exists. [F2, step 1.2, given] ∎

## Geometric diagram

The diagram chooses $\Theta$ to be two small antipodal arcs around the horizontal normals. The vertical covector $\xi_0$ lies in the open missing arc, so it cannot be parallel to a measured normal. The proof uses the conormal equation above, not the drawing.

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, the connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth disk in $B^4$ with only radial minima and saddles, is therefore also bounded by a locally flat topological disk, and satisfies $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K\#K^\dagger)=g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K\#K^\dagger)=0$. Its reverse-mirror summand represents the inverse of $[K]$ in each concordance group.

## Example references

[[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot|The reverse-mirror knot]]

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|The two slice-genus minima]]

[[thm-knot-concordance-is-an-abelian-group|The concordance group operations and inverse convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[F1] The reverse mirror is formed by applying the fixed orientation-reversing reflection and then reversing the knot orientation. ([[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot]])

[F2] A smooth proper disk is locally flat as a topological proper surface, and its genus is $0$ because $\chi(D^2)=1$. ([[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]], [[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]])

[F3] The smooth and topological slice genera are the least genera in the respective nonempty surface classes. ([[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]], [[lem-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus-minima-exist]])

[F4] The general reverse-mirror disk construction applies to every smooth oriented knot. ([[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]])

[F5] In the smooth concordance group, the reverse-mirror class is the additive inverse; the current theorem's smooth branch proves this using the disk in [F4]. ([[thm-knot-concordance-is-an-abelian-group]])

[F6] The full TOP group interface likewise gives the reverse-mirror class as the inverse for locally flat concordance, with the same countable-choice hypothesis. Its TOP connected-sum input includes the compact real-code/$L[r]$ specialization in the compatibility supplier at exactly this standard-product annulus scope; the unqualified literature assertion alone is not treated as an AC_omega theorem. No new local normal-neighborhood proof is asserted here. ([[thm-knot-concordance-is-an-abelian-group]])

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], the notation $K^\dagger$ refers to the fixed reverse-mirror operation. Apply [F4] to obtain a smooth disk $D$ bounded by $K\#K^\dagger$ with radial critical indices $0$ or $1$. Since the disk is smooth, [F2] makes it an admissible locally flat surface as well. Its Euler characteristic gives $g(D)=0$. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Every admissible surface genus is in $\mathbb N_0$, while $D$ contributes genus $0$ to both genus sets. Thus their least elements are $0$ by [F3]. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F5], the class of $K^\dagger$ is the inverse of $[K]$ in the smooth group; [F6] gives the same conclusion in the locally flat topological group. The common disk from step1.1 is admissible in both categories, and all input choice hypotheses are $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. This proves the entire example, including its group-class assertion. [F5, F6, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. If two finite signed Radon measures on $\Omega$ have the same integrals against every function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then the measures are equal.

## Statement references

[[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space|Finite Radon measures are regular on the open set Omega.]]

[[def-regular-complex-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space|The total variation of a finite signed Radon measure is a finite regular measure.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and finite signed Radon measures $\mu,\nu$ whose integrals agree on every compactly supported smooth test function.

[F1] Under the repository convention, each finite signed Radon measure has finite total variation on $\Omega$, and that total-variation measure is regular on all Borel sets. For $\lambda=\mu-\nu$, the partition definition gives $|\lambda|\le|\mu|+|\nu|$, so $|\lambda|$ is finite and regular as well: compact inner and open outer approximations for the finite regular sum $|\mu|+|\nu|$ also approximate $|\lambda|$. ([[def-regular-complex-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]], [[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]])

[F2] Rational balls give a countable base, and compact sets have finite subcovers. ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]], [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[thm-product-of-countable]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]])

[F3] A smooth bump can equal one on an inner ball and vanish outside a larger ball. ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]])

[F4] Dominated convergence applies to bounded pointwise-convergent cutoffs against the finite measure $|\lambda|$. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]])

## Proof

**Given:** The open set $\Omega$ and finite signed Radon measures $\mu,\nu$ with equal integrals on smooth compactly supported tests.

1.1 Set $\lambda:=\mu-\nu$. If $K\subset\Omega$ is compact and nonempty, then for every sufficiently large $m$, rational inner balls with doubled closures in $\Omega\cap\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,K)<1/m\}$ cover $K$; [F2] gives a finite subcover, and ordering finite rational lists by natural-number codes gives a least such cover. Put the fixed bump [F3] on each selected ball and combine them as $\eta_m=1-\prod_j(1-\psi_{m,j})$. Then $0\le\eta_m\le1$, it equals one on $K$, is supported in the $1/m$-neighborhood of $K$, and $\eta_m(x)\to\mathbf1_K(x)$. Since each $\eta_m$ is a smooth compactly supported test function, $\int\eta_m\,d\lambda=0$; dominated convergence [F4] with respect to the finite regular total-variation measure [F1] gives $\lambda(K)=0$. The empty compact set has measure zero directly. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, choose, construct]

2.1 For any Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ and $\varepsilon>0$, inner regularity of $|\lambda|$ [F1] gives a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $|\lambda|(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$. Since step 1.1 gives $\lambda(K)=0$, we have $|\lambda(A)|\le |\lambda|(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$. Thus $\lambda(A)=0$ for every Borel $A$, so $\mu=\nu$. [F1, step 1.1, given] ∎
