      locator: §§2–3, local meridian-conjugacy construction; knot case only
---

## Statement

Let $D$ be a finite oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled closed link or string link, with a chosen smooth realization and pairwise-disjoint product tubes. Choose a crossing whose two projected branches meet transversely and for which no other branch meets a sufficiently small neighborhood, and let $o$ be the over-strand. Orient the projection plane by the rule that $(v_1,v_2)$ is positive exactly when $(n,v_1,v_2)$ is positive in the ambient three-space, where $n$ is the viewing normal. Let $n_o$ be the positive in-plane normal characterized by $(v_o,n_o)$ being positive. The source side $s$ is the side from which $n_o$ points, and the target side $t$ is the side toward which it points.

Choose an orientation-preserving local crossing chart, whose existence follows from the transversality of the projected branches, in which the over-branch is $(x,0,0)$ oriented by $+\partial_x$, the under-branch is $(0,y,-h)$ for some $h>0$, the viewing normal is $+\partial_z$, and $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$ is the positive projection orientation. Use or radially shrink the chosen product tube near the under-branch to a radius $r$ with $0<r<h$. Choose $d,H>0$ small enough that the chart contains the points below. The source and target points on the upper boundary of the under-tube are $(0,-d,-h+r)$ and $(0,d,-h+r)$; join them by $\beta(y)=(0,y,-h+r)$ for $-d\le y\le d$. Choose a common basepoint in the chosen exterior above the chart and a path $\delta$ in the chosen exterior from it to $(0,0,H)$. The two sides of the triangle in $x=0$ from $(0,0,H)$ to the endpoints of $\beta$, together with $\delta$, give the compatible common-upper-collar access paths to the source and target meridian circles; denote them by $a_s,a_t$. Let $a_o$ be $\delta$ followed by an access arc in the punctured triangle to a small positive meridian circle around the over-strand. The oriented outer boundary of the punctured triangle represents this same based meridian. Base the positive over-meridian by the oriented boundary of this triangle after deleting a small disk about its intersection with the over-strand. Write the resulting based positive meridians as $m_o,m_s,m_t$. The chart, tube, and compatible paths are part of the data. All displayed based loops are in the link or string-link complement group, identified with the group of the chosen compact exterior by radial retraction in the product tubes.

For these compatible accesses,
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o.$$
Equivalently, the crossing relator is $m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}=1$. Reversing the direction of the under-strand does not change this side-based equation.

For arbitrary access paths $a'_e$ to the same chosen meridian circles, let $a_e$ be the compatible access, $c_e=a'_ea_e^{-1}$, and $m'_e=c_em_ec_e^{-1}$, for $e=o,s,t$. The exact relation for the independently based meridians is
$$m'_t=c_tc_o^{-1}(m'_o)^{-1}c_oc_s^{-1}m'_sc_sc_o^{-1}m'_oc_oc_t^{-1}.$$
A common change of base path conjugates all displayed meridians simultaneously.

## Statement references

[Friedl, §5.3, Claim 1a](https://friedl.app.uni-regensburg.de/papers/2024_knot-theory-final.pdf)

[Charbonneau, §§2–3](https://site.uvm.edu/cmcharbo/files/2021/12/knot-group-1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite regular oriented diagram and a smooth realization; the chosen pairwise-disjoint product tubes; an oriented crossing; its positive normal-disk meridians; and the common basepoint and compatible triangle accesses from the Statement.

[F1] At a regular crossing, the two projected branches are smooth and transverse; their oriented tangents determine local planar coordinates, and the chosen product tubes provide normal-disk meridians. [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[def-based-string-link-and-labeled-link-peripheral-system]]

[F2] The positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk whose orientation is fixed by the link tangent followed by the disk orientation agreeing with the ambient orientation. [[def-based-string-link-and-labeled-link-peripheral-system]]

[F3] The ambient orientation and viewing normal determine the positive orientation of the crossing chart and hence the orientation of the normal $(y,z)$ plane to the over-strand. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]

[F4] A $C^1$ map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$ whose derivative is invertible at a point restricts near that point to a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]

## Proof

1.1 Let the two projected branches be parametrized near the crossing by $\gamma_o(u)$ and $\gamma_s(v)$, with linearly independent derivatives at their common image $p$. The map $(u,v)\mapsto\gamma_o(u)+\gamma_s(v)-p$ has invertible derivative there, so the inverse function theorem gives local planar coordinates $x=u$, $y=v$. Choose the sign of $y$ so $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$ agrees with the oriented projection plane, and translate the crossing to $(0,0)$. Write the two height functions as $z=h_o(x)$ and $z=h_s(y)$, with $h_o(0)=0$ and $h_s(0)=-h<0$. The coordinate change
$$z'=z-h_o(x)-h_s(y)+h_s(0)$$
has Jacobian determinant $1$; it carries the over-branch to $(x,0,0)$ and the under-branch to $(0,y,-h)$, while preserving the ambient orientation. Shrink the chart so it excludes every other branch, as permitted by the isolated-crossing hypothesis in the Statement. The normal-disk product chart for the under-branch supplies the chosen small radius $r<h$. Since $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$ is positively oriented, $n_o=+\partial_y$, so $y<0$ is the source and $y>0$ is the target. [F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

1.2 The triangle boundary is the loop from its apex to the source endpoint, along $\beta$ to the target endpoint, and back to the apex. Its interior lies above the under-tube boundary and meets the over-branch exactly at $(0,0,0)$. With the boundary orientation induced by $(\partial_y,\partial_z)$, its transverse intersection sign is positive because $(\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z)$ is a positive ambient basis. Removing a small disk about that intersection leaves an annulus in the crossing complement from the triangle boundary to a positive normal meridian of the over-strand. Conjugating by the common path $\delta$ therefore identifies $a_s\beta a_t^{-1}$ with the stated $m_o$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, construct]

2.1 The product tube around the under-branch carries its positive meridian circles along the branch by an annulus. The top arc $\beta$ is the path on that tube boundary joining the chosen source and target circle basepoints. If $\mu_s,\mu_t$ denote the meridian loops based at those points, the annulus gives $\mu_s=\beta\mu_t\beta^{-1}$. With the access paths $a_s,a_t$ of the Statement, it follows that
$$m_s=(a_s\beta a_t^{-1})m_t(a_s\beta a_t^{-1})^{-1}.$$
The punctured-triangle argument in step 1.2 identifies $a_s\beta a_t^{-1}$ with $m_o$. Solving gives the asserted conjugation relation. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Multiplying the conjugation equality by $m_t^{-1}$ gives the displayed crossing relator. Reversing the under-strand orientation reverses both under-meridian loops, so inverting the equality leaves the same side-based equation. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For arbitrary access paths, $a'_e=c_ea_e$ gives $m'_e=c_em_ec_e^{-1}$. Substitute $m_o=c_o^{-1}m'_oc_o$ and $m_s=c_s^{-1}m'_sc_s$ into $m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o$, then conjugate by $c_t$. This gives exactly the correction formula in the Statement; simultaneous base-path change conjugates all meridians by the same loop. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

5.1 On a chosen product tube with normal coordinate $v\ne0$, the homotopy
$$v\longmapsto((1-s)|v|+s)\frac{v}{|v|},\qquad 0\le s\le1,$$
pushes the punctured tube radially to its boundary and fixes that boundary. Applying it on each disjoint tube and fixing the exterior identifies the based fundamental group of the open complement with that of the compact exterior. Thus the relation proved in the open complement is the same relation in the chosen exterior group. [given, F2, construct] ∎


## Remarks

The source/target labels determine which conjugation formula is used. Incoming/outgoing labels depend on the direction of the under-strand and should be derived from this equation, not substituted for it.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the minimax detection-risk definition with $q=2$. For each $\varepsilon$, suppose $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)$ is nonempty and has a finite-support fourth-power minimizer $\widetilde\eta_\varepsilon$ with profile $\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2=z_0^2\sigma_j^2(1-Aa_j^2)_+$ as in the extremal-profile lemma. Put
$$u_\varepsilon^2=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^4}\sum_j\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^4,\qquad w_{\varepsilon,j}=\frac{\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2}{\sqrt{2\sum_j\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^4}},\qquad w_{\varepsilon,0}=\max_jw_{\varepsilon,j},$$
and define
$$T_\varepsilon=\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}\bigl((Y_j/\varepsilon)^2-1\bigr),\qquad \psi_{\varepsilon,H}=\mathbf1_{\{T_\varepsilon>H\}}.$$
If $u_\varepsilon\to0$, then $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon))\to1$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$. If $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$, then for every fixed $c\in(0,1)$ the tests $\psi_{\varepsilon,cu_\varepsilon}$ have total error tending to zero.

For the extremal profile, define the finite sums
$$J_1=\sum_j\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+,\quad J_2=A\sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+,\quad J_0=\sum_j\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+^2.$$
The active constraints imply
$$r_\varepsilon^2=A\frac{J_1}{J_2},\qquad u_\varepsilon^2=\left(\frac{r_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^4\frac{J_0}{2J_1^2}.$$

## Statement references

[Ingster, Sapatinas and Suslina, *Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems*, Theorem 4.1 and equations (4.1)–(4.8)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.1853)

[Giné and Nickl, *Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models*, §6.2.3, Theorem 6.2.11 proof, PDF pp. 506–508](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

[Marteau and Sapatinas, *A unified treatment for non-asymptotic and asymptotic approaches to minimax signal detection*, §§3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.5387)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $q=2$; a nonempty class $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)$; a finite-support minimizing profile satisfying both active constraints; and the Gaussian sequence detection experiment.

[F1] [[def-ip-minimax-detection-risk-and-separation]]: $\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)=\mathbb E_0\psi$, $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r),\psi)=\sup_{\eta\in\Theta_2(r)}\mathbb E_\eta(1-\psi)$, and $\gamma_\varepsilon$ is the infimum total error.

[F2] [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-is-minimizer]]: $\widetilde\eta_j^2=z_0^2\sigma_j^2(1-Aa_j^2)_+$ minimizes $\sum_j\eta_j^4$ over $\Theta_2(r)$ and satisfies $\sum_j\sigma_j^2\widetilde\eta_j^2=r^2$, $\sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^2\widetilde\eta_j^2=1$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-gaussian-product-mixture-testing-bound]]: for a finite-support feasible $v$, its symmetric sign mixture has total-variation distance at most $\tfrac12\sqrt{\exp(u(v)^2)-1}$ from the null; consequently it gives the displayed minimax lower bounds.

[F4] [[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment]] and [[lem-standard-normal-fourth-moment]]: the noise coordinates are independent standard normals with even density, first and third moments zero, and second and fourth moments $1$ and $3$.

[F5] [[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]]: Chebyshev's inequality bounds a tail probability by the variance divided by the squared deviation.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is the assumption of the upstream Gaussian sequence model.

## Proof

1.1 The profile has finite support by the assumption on $S$. Its weights satisfy $2\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}^2=1$, so $\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}^2=1/2$. Under a parameter $\eta$, write $\mu_j=\eta_j/\varepsilon$; then $Y_j/\varepsilon=\xi_j+\mu_j$. Independence and [F4] give $$m_\eta:=\mathbb E_\eta T_\varepsilon=\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}\mu_j^2,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_\eta(T_\varepsilon)=1+4\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}^2\mu_j^2\le1+4w_{\varepsilon,0}m_\eta.$$ In particular, under the null the statistic has mean zero and variance one. [A1, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $u_\varepsilon\to0$. Apply [F3] to $v=\widetilde\eta_\varepsilon$. The resulting total-variation bound tends to zero, so every test has total error at least $1-o(1)$ and every level-$\alpha$ test has maximal type-II error at least $1-\alpha-o(1)$. The constant test $\psi\equiv0$ gives total error $1$, and the constant randomized test $\psi\equiv\alpha$ gives level $\alpha$ and maximal type-II error $1-\alpha$. These upper bounds prove both limits. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 For any $\eta\in\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)$, put $x_j=\eta_j^2$ and $\widetilde x_j=\widetilde\eta_j^2$. Since $1-Aa_j^2\le0$ off the profile support, $$\sum_j\widetilde x_jx_j=z_0^2\sum_{j\in S}\sigma_j^2(1-Aa_j^2)x_j\ge z_0^2(r_\varepsilon^2-A)=\sum_j\widetilde x_j^2,$$ where the inequality follows from $\sum_j\sigma_j^2x_j\ge r_\varepsilon^2$ and $\sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^2x_j\le1$. Thus $$m_\eta\ge\frac{\sum_j\widetilde\eta_j^4}{\varepsilon^2\sqrt{2\sum_j\widetilde\eta_j^4}}=u_\varepsilon.$$ [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$ and fix $c\in(0,1)$. Applying [F5] under the null gives $\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi_{\varepsilon,cu_\varepsilon})\le(cu_\varepsilon)^{-2}\to0$. For any alternative, step 2.1 and step 1.1 give $$\mathbb P_\eta(T_\varepsilon\le cu_\varepsilon)\le\frac{1+4w_{\varepsilon,0}m_\eta}{(m_\eta-cu_\varepsilon)^2}\le\frac{1}{(1-c)^2u_\varepsilon^2}+\frac{4w_{\varepsilon,0}}{(1-c)^2u_\varepsilon}.$$ The final bound uses that $m/(m-cu)^2$ decreases for $m\ge u$ and $w_{\varepsilon,0}\le1/\sqrt2$, which follows from $\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}^2=1/2$. It tends to zero uniformly over $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)$, proving consistency. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Substituting the profile into the active constraints gives $r_\varepsilon^2=z_0^2J_1$ and $1=z_0^2J_2/A$. Hence $r_\varepsilon^2=A J_1/J_2$. Also $\sum_j\widetilde\eta_j^4=z_0^4J_0$, and eliminating $z_0^2=r_\varepsilon^2/J_1$ gives $u_\varepsilon^2=(r_\varepsilon/\varepsilon)^4J_0/(2J_1^2)$. [F2, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$, $m\ge0$, and let $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ be a finite family in $\mathbb R^d$. For $S\subseteq[m]$, write
$$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_S):=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{a_i:i\in S\},$$
with $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_{\varnothing})=\{0\}$. The family $\Phi$ has the **complement property** if for every $S\subseteq[m]$,
$$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_S)=\mathbb R^d \quad\text{or}\quad \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_{[m]\setminus S})=\mathbb R^d.$$
The definition applies to labeled families, including repeated or zero vectors.

## Definition

Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

## Statement

Assume full AC. For a knot Seifert surface $F$ with Seifert matrix $V$, the function $q_F(x)=x^TVx\pmod2$ is well-defined on $H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)$ and satisfies
$$q_F(x+y)=q_F(x)+q_F(y)+x\cdot_F y.$$
Its polarization is nondegenerate. For any symplectic basis $(a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_g,b_g)$, the sum $\sum_iq_F(a_i)q_F(b_i)$ is independent of that basis. It is unchanged by either elementary Seifert enlargement, so it depends only on the knot.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-arf-invariant-from-seifert-form|The quadratic function and Arf convention]]

[[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection|The integral skew part and unimodular intersection form]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, an oriented knot, a connected genus-$g$ spanning surface, and its Seifert matrix $V$.

[A1] Full AC supplies the chosen integral homology basis and Seifert pairing. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]

[F1] $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank $2g$, and reduction modulo two identifies $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb F_2$ with $H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)$. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F2] $V-V^T=J_F$, where $J_F$ is the unimodular integral intersection matrix. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F3] An elementary enlargement adds a symplectic pair whose mod-two Seifert self-values are $(z,0)$ for some integer $z$. [[def-seifert-matrix-s-equivalence]]

## Proof

1.1 If two integral coordinate vectors $x,x'$ represent the same class modulo two, then $x'=x+2y$ for an integral vector $y$, and
$$(x+2y)^TV(x+2y)-x^TVx=2x^TVy+2y^TVx+4y^TVy$$
is even. Thus $x^TVx\pmod2$ is well-defined. Expanding the quadratic expression gives
$$q_F(x+y)-q_F(x)-q_F(y)=x^T(V+V^T)y\pmod2=x^T(V-V^T)y=x\cdot_Fy,$$
where plus and minus agree in $\mathbb F_2$. By [F2], this alternating form is nondegenerate. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 In a symplectic basis, every vector is uniquely $x=\sum_i(a_i a_i+b_i b_i)$ with $a_i,b_i\in\mathbb F_2$. The refinement identity gives
$$q_F(x)=\sum_i\bigl(a_iq_F(a_i)+b_iq_F(b_i)+a_ib_i\bigr).$$
Therefore the finite Gauss sum factors as
$$\sum_{x\in H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)}(-1)^{q_F(x)}=\prod_i\sum_{a,b\in\mathbb F_2}(-1)^{a q_F(a_i)+b q_F(b_i)+ab}=2^g(-1)^{\sum_iq_F(a_i)q_F(b_i)}.$$
The left side depends only on $q_F$, not on a basis, so the exponent defining the Arf value is basis-independent. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Under either enlargement in [F3], the new basis vectors $u,v$ have $u\cdot v=1$, $q(u)=z\pmod2$, and $q(v)=0$; moreover $v$ is orthogonal to all old basis vectors because its encircling disk misses them. If $u$ pairs nontrivially with old basis vectors, add a linear combination of the old symplectic basis to $u$ to obtain $u'$ orthogonal to all of them; the nondegenerate old intersection matrix gives the required coefficients, and $u'\cdot v=1$ remains unchanged. The old basis together with $u',v$ is symplectic; its new Arf contribution is $q(u')q(v)=0$, while the old $q$-values are unchanged. More precisely, put $u''=u'+q(u')v$. The refinement identity and $q(v)=0$, $u'\cdot v=1$ give $q(u'')=q(u')+q(u')=0$, while $u''\cdot v=1$ and both $u'',v$ remain orthogonal to the old subspace. Thus the enlarged quadratic space is isometric to the old one orthogonally summed with the hyperbolic plane $q_H(s,t)=st$: on $su''+tv$ the value is $st$. An integral congruence reduces to an invertible mod-two coordinate change and hence an isometry of quadratic spaces. Consequently, the stable isometry class is invariant under congruences, enlargements and their reverses. Here stable isometry means isometry after adjoining finitely many copies of $q_H$ on either side. Thus the Gauss-sum Arf value is unchanged by enlargement or reduction. By the knot-matrix S-equivalence lemma, all spanning surfaces give the same value. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$ with boundary an oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected oriented Seifert surface for $K$. After matching product collars and pushing the interior of $F$ slightly into $B^4$, the closed locally flat surface $\Sigma=F\cup_KD$ bounds a compact connected oriented locally flat three-manifold $R\subset B^4$. The conclusion includes an oriented ambient product neighborhood of $R$ on both sides, with the positive normal push-off along the $F$ portion of $\partial R=\Sigma$ lying on the complementary side of $R$.

## Statement references

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Properness, local-flatness charts, and product collars]]

[[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere|Alexander duality for compact locally contractible subsets]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the locally flat disk and surface of the Statement and their matching boundary collars. The first part additionally assumes that the disk is smooth; the final part proves the TOP branch using the explicitly cited external normal-bundle and transversality inputs.

[A1] Full AC implies the countable-choice hypotheses of the smooth approximation, ODE and transversality suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A locally flat surface has the pair charts and prescribed boundary collars in the Definition. For a smooth surface these are smooth charts. The Definition alone does not assert a global TOP normal disk bundle. [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]]

[F2] Local smooth ODEs, the inverse-function theorem and Euclidean smooth approximation apply with compact parameters. Parametric transversality applies to finite smooth perturbation families. [[thm-time-dependent-vector-fields-have-local-smooth-evolution-operators]], [[thm-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-on-manifolds]], [[thm-whitney-approximation-for-euclidean-valued-maps]], [[thm-parametric-transversality]]

[F3] Boundary linking equals the intersection of collared bounding chains in the four-ball. Smooth compact manifolds have finite CW homotopy models under countable choice. [[lem-linking-number-equals-four-dimensional-intersection-number]], [[lem-compact-smooth-manifolds-have-finite-cw-models-under-countable-choice]]

[F4] Mayer–Vietoris computes the actual collared decomposition homology; the oriented meridian is dual to a Seifert surface. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]], [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F5] Alexander duality gives the meridional complement class for the capped locally flat surface, but it supplies no regular fiber or collar at that surface. [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]

[F6] **External input — actual relative normal-bundle criterion.** Freedman–Quinn, original §9.3, Theorem 9.3A, printed p.137 (scan PDF143), states: if $N$ is a closed subspace of an ANR homology four-manifold $Y$, $Y\setminus N$ is a manifold, $N\times\mathbb R$ is a manifold, the specified local complement fundamental-group conditions hold (infinite cyclic when $\dim N=2$), and an actual normal vector bundle is given near a closed set $C\subset N$ containing $\partial N$, then there is a normal vector bundle which agrees with that given bundle on a neighborhood of $C$. The relative agreement is part of the existence conclusion, not an inference from uniqueness. In the 2013 reformatted edition this is §9.5, Theorem 9.7, printed pp.144–145/PDF158–159, https://archive.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/4789/2/FreedmanQuinn-TopologyOf4Manifolds-Reformatted2013.pdf. Its p.145 footnote warns that local $\pi_2$ vanishing may also be necessary; step 8.1 satisfies that stronger condition as well. Apply the criterion to the CLOSED doubled sphere in boundaryless $S^4$, with the actual seam-annulus bundle germ constructed there, not directly to $B^4$. This supplies only a normal vector bundle, not a circle-map fiber or a Seifert hypersurface. Full AC is retained.

[F7] **External input — strongly relative TOP transversality.** Quinn1988, Theorem printed145: for proper submanifolds $M,X\subset Y$, a specified normal microbundle $\xi$ of $X$, and closed $C\subset D\subset Y$, if $M$ is transverse to $\xi$ near $C$, an isotopy of $M$, supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $(D\setminus C)\cap M\cap X$, makes it transverse near $D$. Boundary properness is part of the theorem. Transversality means that the intersection is a manifold whose normal microbundle in $M$ is the restriction of the specified $\xi$. The theorem includes the dimensions used below, namely $4$-submanifolds of a $5$-manifold with intersection dimension $3$. This theorem is imported, not reconstructed locally.

[F8] **External input — circle representatives on TOP manifolds.** Metrizable TOP manifolds have CW homotopy type by the ANR/CW-type criterion of Milnor1959. On that homotopy type, Hatcher Proposition1B.9 for $S^1=K(\mathbb Z,1)$ represents every integral first-cohomology class by a continuous map to $S^1$; two such maps with the same induced integer homomorphism are homotopic. These classification inputs are used only to construct a continuous meridian map. They are not transversality assertions.


[F9] An actual compact TOP manifold with boundary has a TOP product collar of its entire boundary. Apply this only after the exterior has been constructed as such a manifold. [[thm-topological-collaring-for-manifold-boundaries]]

## Proof

**Given:** First take a smooth proper disk $D$, retaining the full AC of the Statement.

1.1 Use the given boundary product collar to extend $D$ a little beyond $S^3$. Its normal quotient planes are represented by smooth orthogonal projection matrices $Q$ in the ambient Euclidean space. Parametrize the original disk radially from one interior point. Along each radial segment solve $\dot U=[\dot Q,Q]U$ from one fixed oriented orthonormal frame. The skew-symmetric coefficient preserves norms, and compactness gives a bounded coefficient on the finite parameter disk and time interval, so the local solutions of [F2] extend over the entire interval and depend smoothly on the endpoint. This gives a smooth frame of the disk's normal quotient bundle. Choose an ambient metric product-shaped on the end collar, by a one-variable cutoff interpolation with its product metric. Its orthogonal normal bundle is isomorphic to the quotient and inherits the frame. Its geodesic map is the local flow of the smooth coordinate equation $\ddot x^k=-\tfrac12g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_jg_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij})\dot x^i\dot x^j$, whose transformation rule follows by the chain rule. At the zero section its derivative adds tangent and normal vectors, hence is invertible. Extend across the end collar and apply [F2] there. Compactness of the original disk gives a uniform injective tube radius: otherwise equal images of distinct normal vectors tending to zero have convergent basepoints, their limits are equal, and the local inverse at that zero vector is contradicted. Shrink also inside all local flow domains. This constructs an actual smooth disk tube $D^2\times D^2$, product-shaped at its boundary. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 A small nonzero constant frame vector gives a disjoint proper parallel disk $D'$. By [F3], the linking of its boundary with $K$ equals $D\mathbin\cdot D'=0$. Hence the tube's induced boundary framing is precisely the preferred zero framing. Remove its interior and round the product corners to obtain the actual compact smooth disk exterior $X$. In the decomposition $B^4=X\cup(D^2\times D^2)$ the overlap retracts to $D^2\times S^1$. Since the ball and tube are contractible, integral Mayer–Vietoris gives $H_1(X)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and $H_i(X)=0$ for $i>1$. Its marked boundary is the zero surgery $M(K)=E_K\cup_{T^2}(D^2\times S^1)$, with the disk meridian the zero longitude and the circle the positive meridian. The boundary meridian therefore induces an $H_1$ isomorphism to $X$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 We construct a boundary circle map with the actual prescribed fiber, rather than presuming that $K$ is fibered. Truncate $F$ at the knot tube to a proper surface in $E_K$, and cap its boundary with $D^2\times\{1\}$ in the inner solid torus. Call the resulting closed connected surface $\Sigma_0\subset M(K)$. Give a small normal product of $F$ the signed coordinate $u$ whose positive direction is the positive Seifert push, and put $f_0=\exp(2\pi i u)$ there. On the inner $D^2\times S^1$ put $f_0(x,z)=z$, matching these choices in the peripheral collar. Cut the rest of the knot exterior along that product of $F$. Its two faces have real phase values $\epsilon$ and $1-\epsilon$, and its remaining torus annulus has the ordinary lifted angular coordinate between them. These prescriptions agree in their product corner collars. Extend the real phase to the remaining compact cut manifold by finite smooth collar cutoffs and a partition of unity, with all values in $(0,1)$ and constant $1/2$ away from its prescribed boundary collars. Convexity keeps the extended values away from $0$ modulo $1$. Exponentiating gives a smooth map $f_0:M(K)\to S^1$ with $1$ as a regular value, fiber exactly $\Sigma_0$, and positive coorientation on the $F$ part. Its induced homomorphism on $H_1$ is the positive meridian map: crossing $F$ once positively increases the lifted phase by one, exactly the intersection convention in [F4]. [F2, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The same meridian class on $X$ is represented by a continuous map $g:X\to S^1$. To construct it, use the finite CW model of [F3]: send a maximal tree to the basepoint, the remaining one-cells to loops of the stipulated integer degrees, fill each two-cell because its relator has degree zero, and fill higher cells because the universal cover $\mathbb R$ of the circle is contractible. Transport the map by the actual homotopy model. The boundary homomorphism of $g$ equals that of $f_0$ by step 2.1. Smooth $g$ by viewing it in $\mathbb R^2$, extending constantly across boundary collars to the smooth double, applying [F2] within error $1/4$ and projecting the result radially to $S^1$. Normalized straight-line interpolation preserves its homotopy class. The smooth boundary ratio $f_0/g$ has zero degree on every loop, so it has a global smooth real argument: lift its argument along paths from a fixed point; zero loop increments make it path-independent, and local arguments prove smoothness. First make $g$ constant in a smaller boundary collar by a smooth reparametrization of the collar depth. Multiplication there by the exponential of the lifted boundary argument times a cutoff changes $g$ to a smooth $f:X\to S^1$ equal to $f_0$ on that smaller entire collar. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Make $1$ a regular value in the remaining compact interior while keeping that collar fixed. Cover the compact critical set on the fiber by finitely many interior charts with bumps positive on smaller cores. For small parameters $a_j$, the family $f_a=f\exp(2\pi i\sum_j a_j\phi_j)$ has derivative spanning the circle tangent in some parameter direction at each such core. Off these cores the original fiber map is already transverse, and sufficiently small parameters preserve that property by compactness and the inverse-function local rank criterion. Thus the total family is transverse to $1$. Parametric transversality [F2] supplies an arbitrarily small parameter with transverse slice. It is unchanged on the retained boundary collar. Its inverse image $R_0$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with product boundary $\partial R_0=\Sigma_0$; orient it with the normal-last product convention so that its boundary has the stated orientation of $\Sigma_0$. Since $\Sigma_0$ is connected, exactly one component of $R_0$ meets it; discard all closed components. [F2, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 On the inner tube boundary the fiber is exactly $D^2\times\{1\}$ and is product-shaped in its normal collar, so attach the radial product $D^2\times[0,r]$ down that fixed angle to the zero section $D$. At the common peripheral circle it joins the original $F$ collar; their quadrant coordinates agree with the zero-longitude marking in step 2.1. Round these product sectors. The result is a compact connected smooth embedded $R$ with boundary the rounded capped surface $F\cup_K(-D)$, with $F$ carrying its original orientation. Here, as in the Statement's collar adjustment, use a small collar embedding of the ball into its interior and the corresponding rounding to regard the capped closed surface and its spanning $R$ as interior representatives. This retains their identification with $F\cup_KD$ and all old $F$ homology curves; it does not leave an interior point of a closed capped surface on the outer boundary. The normal coorientation of $R_0$ on $F$ was the positive Seifert direction in step 3.1, so after the same collar transport the positive push-off lies on that complementary side of $R$. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 Finally the orientations of $R$ and of the four-ball supply a continuous unit smooth normal field on $R$. Extend it in finitely many coordinate neighborhoods by smooth cutoffs to an ambient smooth vector field. Along its small-time flow, the derivative in the normal/time direction together with the tangent directions is invertible at time zero. Local inverse charts, extended a little across the boundary collar of $R$, and compactness give one injective product $R\times[-\delta,\delta]$ in the ambient ball; the same convergent-basepoint contradiction as in step 1.1 proves injectivity after a uniform shrinking. Choose its positive direction to be the coorientation fixed on $F$. This gives the required oriented two-sided ambient product and positive-push compatibility. Thus the entire Seifert-hypersurface conclusion is proved when the supplied disk is smooth. [F2, step 1.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

8.1 Now let $D$ be the arbitrary locally flat disk of the Statement. First construct the actual boundary germ. The smooth knot $K\subset S^3$ has an oriented normal two-plane tube $\tau:K\times D^2_\delta\to S^3$: take the positive normal of the given smooth Seifert surface along $K$, complete it by the orientations of $K,S^3$, and use a uniformly small smooth tube over the compact circle, by the smooth inverse-chart/ODE construction [F2]. The matched disk and ambient product collars in the Given identify $D$ there with $K\times[0,\epsilon)\subset S^3\times[0,\epsilon)$. Thus $(q,t,v)\mapsto(\tau(q,v),t)$ is an ACTUAL rank-two normal-bundle germ over the entire boundary collar. No global TOP bundle is inferred from the Definition alone.  Double the standard ball and the collared disk to $(Y,N)=(S^4,D_+\cup_KD_-)$, where $N\cong S^2$. The tube doubles to the explicit product germ $K\times(-2a,2a)\times D^2_\delta$ for small $a>0$. Choose the CLOSED seam annulus $C=K\times[-a,a]\subset N$. This is the prescribed bundle on a neighborhood of $C$; restrict its fiber radius inside a slightly larger tube for the extendable-neighborhood convention. The doubled pair is locally flat: away from the seam use the given charts; at the seam its actual product chart is $(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\{0\})$.  Every hypothesis of [F6] is now literal. The ambient $S^4$ is a boundaryless smooth manifold and hence an ANR homology four-manifold; $Y\setminus N$ is an open four-manifold. The surface $N$ is closed, $N\times\mathbb R\cong S^2\times\mathbb R$ is a manifold and $\partial N=\varnothing$. Nested flat charts have complement homotopy type $S^1$; the local meridian maps give the infinite cyclic local fundamental group, and local $\pi_2=0$. Thus even the stronger condition in the reformatted erratum holds. The actual prescribed bundle near $C$ is the displayed product. Apply [F6] to obtain a normal vector bundle on $N$ whose embedding AGREES with that product on a smaller neighborhood of $C$.  Restrict to $D_+$. Near its boundary, agreement with the germ keeps the collar coordinate $t$ unchanged, so sufficiently short fibers stay in the original hemisphere. Away from a smaller seam collar, the zero section is a compact subset of the interior of that hemisphere; continuity and compactness give a uniform fiber radius whose image stays there. Choose a bundle norm equal to the product norm near the seam and shrink to the smaller of those radii. This gives an actual disk tube wholly in the original $B^4$, agreeing with the prescribed product on a smaller entire boundary collar. Relative agreement, not existence of some unspecified doubled tube, justifies restriction. Its oriented rank-two vector bundle over the disk is trivial. A global nonzero frame section gives a disjoint proper parallel disk, so its boundary has linking zero with $K$ by [F3]. Thus the induced boundary framing is the preferred zero framing. Any difference from the supplied zero-framed boundary trivialization has degree zero in $SO(2)$ and extends across the disk; adjust the global frame by that extension, and restrict the actual bundle neighborhood. This gives an actual framed TOP disk tube, with the prescribed product and angular marking on a smaller boundary collar. Its compact exterior $X$ is a TOP four-manifold. The same collared decomposition and integral Mayer–Vietoris calculation as in step2.1 give $H_1(X)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$, $H_i(X)=0$ for $i>1$, with boundary the actual zero surgery $M(K)$ and its marked inner $D^2\times S^1$. No smoothing of the disk or exterior is asserted. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

8.2 Construct on the actual boundary $M(K)$ the circle map $f_0$ of step3.1. Its knot-exterior part uses the given smooth $F$ and its positive Seifert collar; the solid-torus part is the actual framed tube's angular coordinate $f_0(x,z)=z$. Their zero-longitude boundary products agree by step8.1. The real-phase extension on the cut knot exterior stays in $(0,1)$, so the fiber over1 is exactly the capped surface $\Sigma_0$, with its prescribed whole product neighborhood and positive coorientation. On a collar of $\partial X$, extend $f_0$ constantly in collar depth. This is an actual TOP product-transverse boundary map even though it need not be smooth for the inherited structure of the original disk complement. [F1, F4, step 3.1, step 8.1, construct]

8.3 The meridian class in $H^1(X;\mathbb Z)$ has a continuous circle representative by [F8]. Its boundary class equals that of $f_0$ by step8.1. The boundary ratio therefore has a continuous real argument: lift along paths, with zero increments around every loop. First make the representative constant in a smaller boundary collar by reparametrizing collar depth, then multiply there by the exponential of that argument times a collar cutoff. This constructs a continuous $f:X\to S^1$ equal to $f_0$ on a whole smaller boundary collar. The argument uses [F8] only for a continuous map; no regular value is inferred from it or from Alexander duality. [F4, F8, F9, step 8.1, step 8.2, construct]

8.4 Apply [F7] in $Y=X\times S^1$ to the proper graph $M=\{(x,f(x)):x\in X\}$ and the proper submanifold $Z=X\times\{1\}$ with its specified trivial circle-normal line microbundle. Choose nested closed product collars $C_0\subset\operatorname{Int}C$ of $\partial X$ in the boundary collar where step8.3 fixes $f=f_0$, use $C$ as Quinn's protected set, and take the theorem's $D=Y$. The graph is already microbundle transverse near $C$ by step8.2. The closure of $(Y\setminus C)\cap M\cap Z$ is disjoint from $C_0$, so choose the theorem's support neighborhood disjoint from $C_0$. The isotopy may meet the outer frontier of $C$ but leaves the smaller collar $C_0$ fixed, preserving the whole boundary product and coorientation needed below. Parametrize its resulting graph image by $j_1:X\to M'$. It need not remain a graph over $X$: define instead $f'=\operatorname{pr}_{S^1}j_1$. Microbundle transversality says $R_0=(f')^{-1}(1)$ is a compact neat TOP three-manifold, with $\partial R_0=\Sigma_0$ and exactly the unchanged boundary product/coorientation. Its normal microbundle is the pullback of the specified trivial line, hence has an actual oriented product neighborhood after uniform shrinking over the compact fiber. The trivialization is the already prescribed one near the boundary. Orient $R_0$ by this normal direction and discard closed components; since $\Sigma_0$ is connected, exactly one component meets it. This is the required separate marked angular regular-fiber operation, using [F7], rather than a consequence claimed from [F6]. [F7, step 8.2, step 8.3, construct]

8.5 Attach the actual radial sector $D^2\times[0,r]$ at the fixed angular value down to the disk zero section, as in step6.1. The TOP tube products, zero-longitude peripheral marking and unchanged whole fiber collar make the attaching maps identical on their common products. In the disk's normal plane this sector is the positive coordinate ray; its transverse Cartesian coordinate supplies its two-sided normal product even at the zero-section boundary. It agrees with the angular coorientation for positive radius and with the positive Seifert normal along $F$. Round the product corners in these explicit two-dimensional sector coordinates. They paste with the product of $R_0$ from step8.4, giving the actual compact connected oriented locally flat $R$ with the stated two-sided product and positive-push alignment. Before the collar push this is the model meeting the outer sphere along $F$; the same collar embedding of the ball used in step6.1 gives the closed interior representative of $F\cup_KD$, retaining all marked $F$ homology curves and its normal direction. Together with the preserved smooth proof this proves the entire Statement under its full AC hypothesis. The normal-bundle and transversality theorems remain explicitly external inputs. [F1, F6, F7, step 6.1, step 8.1, step 8.2, step 8.4, construct] ∎

      locator: "Chapter 8, Theorem 8.2, printed pp. 79–81; full text used for the enlargement convention"
    - title: "Charles Livingston, A Survey of Classical Knot Concordance"
      url: "https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/living.pdf"
      locator: "§2.2, Definition 2.5 and Theorem 2.8, printed pp. 323–324"
---

## Statement

Assume full AC for any knot-derived Seifert matrix. Let $V$ be an integral Seifert matrix and let $E_0(V;x,y,z)$ or $E_1(V;x,y,z)$ be either elementary enlargement in the definition of S-equivalence, where $x,y\in\mathbb Z^{2g}$ and $z\in\mathbb Z$. Then $E_0(V;x,y,z)$ and $E_1(V;x,y,z)$ are integral Seifert lattices, and each represents the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$ as $V$.

## Statement references

[[def-seifert-matrix-s-equivalence|The two elementary enlargement matrices]]

[[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance|The integral algebraic concordance group and metabolic lattices]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integral Seifert matrix $V$ of size $2g$, integers $x,y,z$ of the stated sizes, and full AC only when $V$ is instantiated as a knot pairing.

[A1] Full AC is required by the knot Seifert-pairing interface; the matrix argument below is choice-free. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The elementary enlargement matrices are
$$E_0=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&0\\0^T&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_1=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&1\\0^T&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
[[def-seifert-matrix-s-equivalence]]

[F2] An integral Seifert lattice has even rank and unimodular skew part; it represents zero in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ when it has a rank-half direct summand on which its bilinear form vanishes, and direct sum is the group operation. [[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance]]

[F3] The negative lattice $-V$ represents the additive inverse of $V$ in $G_{\mathbb Z}$. [[lem-negative-seifert-form-represents-algebraic-inverse]]

## Proof

1.1 For each displayed enlargement, its skew part has block form
$$E_i-E_i^T=\begin{pmatrix}J&u&0\\-u^T&0&s_i\\0^T&-s_i&0\end{pmatrix},$$
where $J=V-V^T$, $u=x-y$, $s_0=-1$, and $s_1=1$. If $V$ is knot-derived, [A1] is the choice hypothesis for its Seifert-pairing convention; the following lattice calculation itself is choice-free. Since $J$ is unimodular, choose the integral vector $c=-J^{-1}u$ and replace the penultimate basis vector by itself plus the old-basis combination $c$. This integral basis change removes the $u$ block and leaves $J\oplus\begin{pmatrix}0&s_i\\-s_i&0\end{pmatrix}$. Both blocks are unimodular, so each enlargement is an integral Seifert lattice. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra, construct]

1.2 In $E_i\oplus(-V)$, take the subgroup generated by $(e_j; e_j)$ for the old basis vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_{2g}$ and by $(b;0)$, where $b$ is the last basis vector of the enlarged lattice. Its rank is $2g+1$, half the total rank. The two displayed enlargement matrices have zero old-to-$b$, $b$-to-old, and $b$-to-$b$ entries. The $V$ and $-V$ blocks cancel on the diagonal generators, while all pairings involving $(b;0)$ vanish. Therefore the form vanishes on this subgroup. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The subgroup in step 1.2 is a direct summand: its generators, together with $(a;0)$ and $(0;e_j)$ for every old basis vector, form an integral basis because subtracting $(0;e_j)$ from $(e_j;e_j)$ gives $(e_j;0)$. It is therefore a metabolizer. By [F2], $[E_i]+[-V]=0$, and [F3] gives $[E_i]=[V]$ in $G_{\mathbb Z}$. [F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1"

## Statement refuted

For every finite regular oriented diagram $D$, form the integral Khovanov state cube but omit the cohomological shift $-n_-$ and quantum shift $n_+-2n_-$. The false claim is that the resulting raw cohomology groups are invariant under oriented Reidemeister moves and that their graded rank Euler characteristic equals the Jones polynomial with the usual unreduced unknot factor $q+q^{-1}$, under $q=-A^{-2}$ and $t=q^2=A^{-4}$.

## Statement references

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|Normalized shifts and local algebra maps]]

[[lem-khovanov-reidemeister-chain-homotopies|Type-I chain-complex cancellations]]

[[lem-khovanov-graded-euler-characteristic-jones-normalization|Normalized Euler characteristic]]

[[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram|Raw state cube before normalization]]

[[thm-khovanov-euler-characteristic-is-jones|Jones Euler characteristic theorem]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial* (1999), §§2.2–2.4 and 5.1–5.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Bar-Natan, *On Khovanov's categorification of the Jones polynomial* (2002), §§3.1 and 3.5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0201043)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology* (2022), §§3–4](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

[Zhang, *Notes on Khovanov homology* (2025), §§3.5–3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The crossingless unknot, its positive and negative one-crossing curls, and the raw cube with both normalization shifts omitted.

[F1] The algebra $\mathcal A$ has basis $1,X$ in quantum degrees $1,-1$, and the edge operations are $m$ and $\Delta$ with the displayed values ([[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]).

[F2] In the declared smoothing chart, the positive one-crossing curl has a two-circle $0$-resolution and one-circle $1$-resolution joined by $m$; the negative curl has one-circle $0$-resolution and a two-circle $1$-resolution joined by $\Delta$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]], [[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]], [[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]]).

[F3] A crossingless one-circle diagram has a unique state with no differential ([[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]]).

[F4] Each oriented type-I curl is realized by an ambient isotopy, so the curled diagram and the crossingless diagram represent the same oriented unknot ([[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]], [[lem-each-oriented-reidemeister-move-is-realized-by-ambient-isotopy]]).

[F5] The signed cube differential squares to zero, and the raw cube is a bounded complex of finite-rank free abelian groups ([[lem-khovanov-cube-differential-squares-to-zero]], [[thm-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram-procedure-properties]]).


## Counterexample

1.1 The raw zero-crossing complex of $U$ is $\mathcal A$ in cohomological degree $0$ with zero differential by [F3]. Its generators $1,X$ have quantum degrees $1,-1$ by [F1], so its chain Euler polynomial is $q+q^{-1}$. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 In the positive curl, the $0$-state contributes $(q+q^{-1})^2$ and the $1$-state contributes $-q(q+q^{-1})$, because the state coordinate raises quantum degree by one and homological degree by one. Hence $\chi_q^{\mathrm{raw}}(U_+)=(q+q^{-1})^2-q(q+q^{-1})=1+q^{-2}=q^{-1}(q+q^{-1})$. In the negative curl, the $0$-state contributes $q+q^{-1}$ and the $1$-state contributes $-q(q+q^{-1})^2$. Hence $\chi_q^{\mathrm{raw}}(U_-)=(q+q^{-1})-q(q+q^{-1})^2=-q^3-q=-q^2(q+q^{-1})$. These computations use only the state modules and gradings before the writhe normalization. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For each quantum degree, tensor the bounded finite-rank free complex with $\mathbb Q$. Clearing denominators shows that kernels and images localize to the kernels and images of the rationalized maps; applying the same argument to a kernel modulo the preceding image identifies rationalized cohomology with integral cohomology tensored with $\mathbb Q$. Its dimension is therefore the integral rank of cohomology. In the bounded rational complex, rank-nullity gives $\dim C^i=\dim H^i+\dim\operatorname{im}d^i+\dim\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}$; alternating over $i$ cancels the image terms. Thus the raw cohomology Euler polynomials equal the chain Euler polynomials in steps 1.1–1.2. The distinct Laurent polynomials $q+q^{-1}$, $q^{-1}(q+q^{-1})$, and $-q^2(q+q^{-1})$ come from diagrams of the same unknot by [F4]. The raw groups are consequently not invariant, and the raw unknot factor is not the claimed $q+q^{-1}$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $D^2$ be the oriented closed disk and let $K\subset S^3=\partial B^4$ be a smooth oriented knot, meaning the image of an orientation-preserving smooth embedding of a circle. A **ribbon immersion** for $K$ is a smooth immersion $f:D^2\to S^3$ whose boundary restriction is an embedding onto $K$ and whose only multiple points form finitely many pairwise disjoint transverse double arcs $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m$. For each $i$, the full preimage of $\gamma_i$ consists of two disjoint embedded arcs $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_i$ in $D^2$: $\alpha_i$ is properly embedded, with its two endpoints on $\partial D^2$ and its interior in $\operatorname{Int}D^2$, while $\beta_i$ is compact and lies in $\operatorname{Int}D^2$. There are no triple points or other self-intersections. A **ribbon disk** for $K$ is such a ribbon immersion, and $K$ is a **ribbon knot** if it admits a ribbon disk.

A **band** on a link in $S^3$ is the image of a smoothly embedded rectangle whose two opposite attaching edges lie on the link and whose remaining points are disjoint from it. A **band move** removes the attaching edges, inserts the other two edges, and rounds the corners; the embedded band, including its half-twist data, is part of the move. A **no-maximum disk movie** is the family of regular level links of a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ is Morse in the disk interior and has only index-$0$ minima and index-$1$ saddles. A minimum creates a split unknot and a saddle performs an oriented band move; there are no maxima. The no-maximum disk movie is a second presentation convention used by the design for explicit ribbon examples. This movie model and the ribbon-immersion definition above describe the same class of knots: a finite birth-and-band induction converts the movie to an immersion, and cutting the proper double-arc preimages converts an immersion to a disk-and-band movie. The local resolution lemma proves only that a ribbon immersion pushes rel boundary to a smooth proper disk in $B^4$. The slice-ribbon conjecture asks whether every smooth slice knot admits a ribbon immersion as defined above.

## Example

Assume full AC. The unknot has the empty Seifert matrix, Alexander polynomial $1$, and a smooth slice disk. The right-handed trefoil has positive-push matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and Alexander polynomial $t^2-t+1$, so the Alexander-one theorem gives no conclusion for it and does not prove it nonslice. Let $Wh^+(T)$ denote the satellite of the right-handed trefoil $T$ by the positive-clasped, untwisted Whitehead pattern, embedded using the preferred longitude. This knot has Alexander polynomial $1$; by topologically slice we mean that it bounds a locally flat embedded disk in $B^4$. The established theorem gives that topological conclusion, not a smooth slice disk.

## Example references

[[thm-alexander-polynomial-one-implies-topologically-slice|The Alexander-one topological sliceness theorem]]

[[lem-positive-hopf-plumbing-has-trefoil-seifert-matrix|The right-handed trefoil matrix]]

[[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial|The determinant convention used in the calculations]]

[[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number|The satellite-pattern and winding-number conventions]]

Matthew Hedden and Juanita Pinzón-Caicedo, “Satellites of Infinite Rank in the Smooth Concordance Group,” §5.2.2 and Figure 2, printed pp.18–19, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.04186

Arunima Ray, *Slice Knots and Knot Concordance*, Definition 1.10, Theorem 1.13, and Figure 8, printed pp.5–6, https://aru-ray.github.io/documents/slicenotes.pdf

Stavros Garoufalidis and Peter Teichner, “On Knots with Trivial Alexander Polynomial,” Appendix A, https://people.math.gatech.edu/~stavros/publications/teichner1.pdf

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the unknot, the right-handed trefoil, and its positive untwisted Whitehead double.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: Full AC is the axiom used by the determinant supplier.

[F1] [[lem-positive-hopf-plumbing-has-trefoil-seifert-matrix]]: The right-handed trefoil has $V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ in the positive-push convention.

[F2] [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]]: $\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t)$.

[F3] [[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number]]: A satellite is obtained by inserting a pattern into a preferred-longitude tubular embedding of its companion; its winding number is the pattern's algebraic intersection with a meridional disk.

[F4] [[thm-alexander-polynomial-one-implies-topologically-slice]]: Under full AC, a smooth oriented Alexander-one knot bounds a locally flat proper disk in the standard four-ball.

[F5] [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]: In a positive handle basis $(a,b)$, the entries satisfy $V_{12}-V_{21}=a\cdot_F b=1$.

[F6] [[lem-seifert-pairing-well-defined]]: Linking is symmetric and the positive-push pairing is independent of the sufficiently small positive push and cycle representatives.

## Proof

1.1 For the unknot, the Seifert surface is a disk, so $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)=0$ and the empty determinant is $1$; the standard flat disk in $B^4$ proves sliceness. For the trefoil, [F1] and [F2] give $\det(V-tV^T)=t^2-t+1$, which is not a Laurent unit. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Construct the actual surface inside the preferred-longitude tube of $T$ from [F3]. Take a narrow annulus $A$ about its core with the zero product framing. In a small ball meeting $A$ in one square $Q$, plumb $A$ to a positive Hopf annulus $H$: identify their squares so the two annular core arcs are the two crossing coordinate axes in $Q$, and place the parts outside the square on opposite sides. Smooth the four square corners. Outside that ball the boundary is the two oppositely oriented zero-framed parallels of $T$; inside the ball the positive Hopf band joins them by its positive clasp. This is precisely the positive-clasped untwisted Whitehead pattern in the specified tube. The untwisted condition is the zero framing of $A$, and the construction uses the preferred longitude rather than an arbitrary longitude. It is also the $k=0$ surface of the cited Figure 2; that figure identifies the convention but is not a substitute for the following matrix calculation. [given, F3, construct]

2.1 Let $a$ be the annulus core and $b$ the Hopf core, with orientations chosen so their sole square intersection has $a\cdot_F b=1$. The plumbed surface is connected and oriented. Its Euler characteristic is $0+0-1=-1$, and tracing the alternating four attaching edges gives one boundary component. The two annuli retract to their two core loops with the square intersection identified, so $(a,b)$ is an integral handle basis and the surface has genus one. Choose the plumbing side in which the positive push of the $a$-arc is above the square. The unknotted Hopf core $b$ has a spanning disk in the local ball lying below the square except for its boundary arc; use the lower side for the remainder of $H$. Thus this disk misses $a^+$, including the part of $a^+$ outside the ball. This is a local disk for $b$, and does not assert that the companion $a=T$ bounds a disk. [F3, F6, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 The positive push of $a$ is a small parallel with the product annulus framing; its linking with $a$ is zero because that product longitude is the preferred longitude. Equivalently move the push to the annular side direction through nonzero normal directions, keeping it disjoint from $a$. The local square does not add a twist to this annular framing. Hence $V_{11}=0$. The two boundary components of the positive Hopf annulus, with induced orientations, link $+1$. Equally oriented core parallels therefore link $-1$, since one induced boundary orientation is reversed. Moving one core parallel to the positive normal push preserves this linking, so $V_{22}=-1$. The local spanning disk from step 2.1 and symmetry of linking give $V_{12}=\operatorname{lk}(a^+,b)=0$. Finally [F5] gives $V_{21}=-1$. Thus the ACTUAL Whitehead double of $T$, not just the pattern applied to the unknot, has matrix $V_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. [F2, F3, F5, F6, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Direct calculation gives $\det(V_0-tV_0^T)=t$. This is a Laurent unit, with inverse $t^{-1}$, so [F2] gives $\Delta_{Wh^+(T)}\doteq1$. Applying [F4] proves the stated locally flat proper slice disk in the standard $B^4$. The argument establishes the announced topological conclusion; it contains no smooth slice-disk construction and no inference that the trefoil is nonslice from its nonunit Alexander polynomial. Every claim in the example follows without a general satellite determinant theorem. ∎ [A1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

id: lem-kneser-haken-finiteness-for-incompressible-tori
kind: lemma
title: "Kneser–Haken finiteness for incompressible tori"
status: draft
origin: pipeline

  - lem-rectangular-normal-cut-components-are-interval-bundles
  - lem-connected-complement-surfaces-have-independent-mod-two-homology-classes
  - lem-haken-torus-bound-for-a-supplied-compatible-smooth-triangulation
  - thm-simplicial-and-singular-homology-agree-for-simplicial-complexes
justified_by: []
aliases: []
proof_strategy: direct
axiom_use: "The finite-position and isotopy steps use countable choice through relative transversality; the finite combinatorial bound itself is choice-free."
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Allen Hatcher, Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology"
      url: "https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf"
      locator: "Proposition 1.7 and Corollary 1.8, printed pp.11–13"
    - title: "Ryan Budney, JSJ-decompositions of knot and link complements in the 3-sphere"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0506523"
      locator: "§1, finiteness and minimality of the torus system, PDF pp.2–3"
---

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact connected irreducible orientable smooth $3$-manifold with nonempty boundary, and fix a finite triangulation of $M$ with $t$ triangular faces. If $\mathcal T$ is any finite family of pairwise disjoint, two-sided, incompressible tori in $M$ such that no component obtained by cutting $M$ along $\mathcal T$ is homeomorphic to $T^2\times[0,1]$, then
$$
|\mathcal T|\le 4t+\dim_{\mathbb Z_2}H_2(M;\mathbb Z_2)-1.
$$
Consequently, any iterative process that cuts along tori and for which every finite stage satisfies this no-product condition terminates after finitely many cuts.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Proposition 1.7 and Corollary 1.8](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Ryan Budney, *JSJ-decompositions of knot and link complements in the 3-sphere*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0506523)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a compact connected irreducible orientable smooth three-manifold $M$ with nonempty boundary, the fixed finite compatible triangulation with $t$ triangular faces, and the finite torus family in the Statement. Here compatible triangulation is used in the original smooth-manifold sense required by the smooth-strata transversality argument: its simplex maps and whole-star manifold charts are compatible with the given smooth structure. No new assertion for an arbitrary TOP marking unrelated to that structure is inferred.

[A1] Countable choice is [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] Incompressibility, irreducibility and a product cut component have the given conventions. [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]]

[F2] For this supplied compatible smooth triangulation, a finite incompressible smooth torus family has simultaneous smooth normal position. The actual cut tetrahedra and normal face disks retain their marked ball and rectangle parameters. [[lem-smooth-incompressible-tori-admit-normal-position-in-a-compatible-triangulation]]

[F3] A rectangular-only cut component with those actual parameters is an interval bundle. If it is not $T^2\times I$, it has a compact one-sided locally flat core whose removal leaves the component connected. [[lem-rectangular-normal-cut-components-are-interval-bundles]]

[F4] In a connected boundaryless three-manifold, disjoint compact locally flat closed surfaces with connected complement have independent mod-two homology classes, including one-sided surfaces. [[lem-connected-complement-surfaces-have-independent-mod-two-homology-classes]]

[F5] The accepted Haken bound proof constructs the finite normal face-cell and rectangle parameters and the finite inward collar push, and identifies finite simplicial and singular homology. These finite constructions and their declared countable-choice hypothesis apply to the exact same supplied triangulation here. [[lem-haken-torus-bound-for-a-supplied-compatible-smooth-triangulation]], Proof1.1 and4.1; [[thm-simplicial-and-singular-homology-agree-for-simplicial-complexes]]

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F2] to the given finite torus family for the very triangulation in the Statement. Its smooth ambient isotopy retains incompressibility, all cut-component homeomorphism types and the no-product condition. It puts the family into actual normal disks in each parametrized tetrahedron and disjoint arcs in each triangular face, joining distinct edges. This invokes the accepted marked normal-position construction rather than treating a surgery that changes a torus as an isotopy. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 In each triangular face group the arcs by the pair of distinct edges they join. Within each of the three types they occur in a parallel stack. Between consecutive arcs of a stack is a rectangle, and collapsing those strips leaves at most one arc of each type, hence at most four complementary regions. Every nonrectangular region survives distinctly in this collapsed picture, so there are at most $4t$ such regions over all faces. The successive finite face-disk cuts and the marked rectangle product maps are supplied by [F2] and [F5]; no unparametrized polygon or missing side matching is being assumed. [F2, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $m$ be the number of cut components meeting all faces only in rectangles. By [F3] each is an interval bundle. The torus-product possibility is excluded by hypothesis. Thus they have disjoint one-sided compact locally flat cores $Q_1,\ldots,Q_m$, and removing each core leaves its component connected. No ambient triangulation or smoothness of these cores is required. [F1, F3, step 1.2, construct]

2.2 Form the connected finite dual graph of all torus cuts, allowing loops, and choose a spanning tree. Let $k$ be the number of edges outside that tree. The corresponding $k$ tori, together with all the $Q_j$, have connected complement: remove the cores in the fully cut pieces, which remain connected by step2.1, and glue back the tree faces. A tree joins all the pieces and cannot create a new disconnection. Pass to $\operatorname{Int}M$ by the finite inward collar push in [F5], chosen disjoint from these compact surfaces; its homotopy fixes them and proves that the interior inclusion induces a homology isomorphism, while their complement remains connected. Now [F4] gives $k+m$ independent mod-two classes, so $k+m\le\beta$, where $\beta=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}H_2(M;\mathbb F_2)$. This number is finite because the supplied triangulation is finite and its simplicial homology computes singular homology. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

2.3 Write $n=|\mathcal T|$ and let $v$ be the number of cut components. The dual graph has $n$ edges, $v$ vertices and $k=n-v+1$ non-tree edges; thus $v=n-k+1$. Each component other than the $m$ rectangular-only ones contains a nonrectangular face region. A physical region belongs to just one cut component: its two tetrahedral sides are glued through its interior, or it is a boundary face with only one incident side. Distinct components therefore use distinct such regions, and step1.2 gives $v\le m+4t$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Combining these inequalities yields $n+1\le k+m+4t\le\beta+4t$, which is exactly the stated bound. It also holds for the empty family. If an accumulating cutting process continued past $4t+\beta-1$ cuts while each finite accumulated family retained the stated hypotheses, that stage would contradict the same bound for the fixed original triangulation. Thus no such process continues indefinitely. The proof retains the original countable-choice and smooth-compatible triangulation scope; it does not postulate an arbitrary unrelated TOP marking. [step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

id: lem-two-commuting-complex-2x2-matrices-are-simultaneously-triangularizable
kind: lemma
title: Two commuting complex 2x2 matrices are simultaneously triangularizable
status: draft
origin: pipeline

  2x2 matrix has a root.
provenance:

sources:
  references:
    - title: Léo Bénard, François Florens, and Adrien Rodau, A slope invariant and the
        A-polynomial of knots, §2.2
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151
    - title: Stephan Tillmann, Varieties associated to 3-manifolds, §§4.2–4.4
      url: https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf
---

## Statement

Let $A,B\in M_2(\mathbb C)$ commute. There is a one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$ invariant under both $A$ and $B$. Equivalently, in a basis beginning with a nonzero vector in that subspace, both matrices are upper triangular.

## Statement references

[Bénard, Florens, and Rodau, §2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151)

[Tillmann, §§4.2–4.4](https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two commuting complex $2\times2$ matrices $A,B$.

[F1] Every complex $2\times2$ matrix has an eigenvalue and a nonzero eigenspace because its characteristic polynomial has a complex root.

## Proof

1.1 If $A$ is scalar, choose an eigenvector of $B$ using [F1]; its span is preserved by $A$ and $B$. [F1, cases]

1.2 If $A$ is not scalar, choose an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$. Its eigenspace $E_\lambda$ is nonzero and has dimension one, since a two-dimensional eigenspace would force $A=\lambda I$. For $v\in E_\lambda$, commutation gives $A(Bv)=B(Av)=\lambda Bv$, so $Bv\in E_\lambda$; hence this line is invariant under both matrices. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 A basis beginning with a nonzero vector in the common invariant line makes both matrices upper triangular. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://site.uvm.edu/cmcharbo/files/2021/12/knot-group-1.pdf"
    - title: "Danny Calegari, Introduction to Knot Theory, §4.2, printed pp. 34–36"
      url: "https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf"
verification: {precheck: pass}

## Definition

Define a procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ on a finite planar code $D$ for one oriented knot and a designated under-arc $a_0$ as follows. First check all incidence, valence, branch-pairing, crossing over/under, edge-orientation, and one-component conditions in the code. For each pair of rational line segments in the drawing certificate, compute the determinant of their direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate linear intersection equations and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Accept an intersection only when it is a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence, and at a crossing verify that the two branch direction vectors have nonzero determinant. Reject self-intersections and all unrecorded intersections. If any check fails, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise traverse the oriented knot once starting at $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. For each crossing $v$, read its oriented over-tangent and positive in-plane normal. Let $a_s$ be the under-side from which that normal points and $a_t$ the side toward which it points, and read the over-arc $a_o$. Append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. Equivalently, if the incoming under-tangent follows that normal, append $x_o^{-1}x_{\rm in}x_ox_{\rm out}^{-1}$; otherwise append $x_ox_{\rm in}x_o^{-1}x_{\rm out}^{-1}$. The orientation of a positive meridian is fixed locally by requiring the knot tangent followed by the normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and this one relator per crossing.

      locator: "Printed pp.1450–1458 and 1470–1471; cobordisms, local relations, and the Frobenius TQFT"
    - title: "Louis H. Kauffman, An Introduction to Khovanov Homology, §5"
      url: "https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf"
      locator: "PDF pp.18–22; surface-cobordism state category and the four-tube, sphere, and torus relations"
---

## Definition

Let an object be a finite disjoint union of smooth embedded circles in the oriented plane $\mathbb R^2$, including the empty union. A cobordism from $C_0$ to $C_1$ is a compact smooth orientable surface properly embedded in $\mathbb R^2\times[0,1]$, with boundary $C_0\times\{0\}\sqcup C_1\times\{1\}$, product collars at those boundaries, and no other boundary. Surfaces are identified up to ambient isotopy fixed on the boundary collars. Compose cobordisms by gluing along their common boundary circles; the identity of $C$ is $C\times[0,1]$, and disjoint union gives the monoidal product. Let $\mathsf{Cob}_3$ be this additive monoidal category before imposing local relations.

Take the free abelian group on these isotopy classes of cobordisms and quotient by the following local relations, which are required to hold inside every surrounding cobordism. A sphere component is zero (the S relation). Adding a disjoint torus component multiplies a cobordism by $2$ (the T relation). For four disjoint disk patches numbered $1,2,3,4$, write $S_{ij}$ for the surface obtained by deleting the interiors of patches $i,j$ and joining their boundary circles by an orientable tube; the four-tube relation is $S_{12}+S_{34}=S_{13}+S_{24}$. The resulting additive monoidal category is denoted $\mathsf{Cob}_{BN}$.

## Definition references

[Bar-Natan, *Khovanov's homology for tangles and cobordisms*, §§3–4 and 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410495v2)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology*, §5](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

kind: lemma

status: draft

      url: "https://msp.org/agt/2009/9-1/agt-v9-n1-p06-p.pdf"
      locator: "§2, printed pp. 169–170"
    - title: "Charles Livingston, A Survey of Classical Knot Concordance"
      url: "https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/living.pdf"
      locator: "§3.4, printed pp. 326–328"
---

## Statement

Assume full AC for the knot Seifert-pairing convention. Let $V\in M_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be an invertible Seifert matrix and put $B=V+V^T$ and $T=V^{-1}V^T$ on $\mathbb Q^{2g}$. Then $B$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T$ is an invertible $B$-isometry, and $I-T$ is invertible; hence $(\mathbb Q^{2g},B,T)$ is a rational Seifert isometric structure.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push integral Seifert matrix]]

[[def-integral-witt-and-seifert-isometric-structures|The definition of a rational Seifert isometric structure]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and an invertible integral Seifert matrix $V$.

[A1] Full AC is the stated hypothesis of the Seifert-pairing interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For a knot Seifert matrix, $V-V^T$ is the unimodular surface intersection matrix. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F2] A rational Seifert isometric structure has a nonsingular symmetric form $B$, an invertible $B$-isometry $T$, and invertible $I-T$. [[def-integral-witt-and-seifert-isometric-structures]]

## Proof

1.1 The matrix $B=V+V^T$ is symmetric. Modulo $2$, $V+V^T\equiv V-V^T$; by [F1] the determinant of $V-V^T$ is odd, so $\det B$ is odd and in particular nonzero. Thus $B$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb Q$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Since $V$ and $V^T$ are invertible over $\mathbb Q$, $T=V^{-1}V^T$ is invertible. Direct multiplication gives
$$
T^TBT=V(V^T)^{-1}(V+V^T)V^{-1}V^T=V+V^T=B,
$$
because the two summands in the middle expression simplify respectively to $V$ and $V^T$. Therefore $T$ is a $B$-isometry. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Finally $I-T=V^{-1}(V-V^T)$, which is invertible by invertibility of $V$ and [F1]. The three defining conditions in [F2] hold, proving the claim. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Identify the oriented standard $S^3$ with the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$ and fix $h(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=x_4$. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, there is an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carrying $K$ to a smooth knot $K'$ for which $h|_{K'}$ has only nondegenerate critical points.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number|The fixed coordinate height and Morse representative convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ and the fixed height $h(x)=x_4$ under the standard identification $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$.

[F1] For a compact embedded smooth manifold $M\subset\mathbb R^N$, a generic direction $u\in S^{N-1}$ makes $x\mapsto u\cdot x$ a Morse function on $M$. [[thm-generic-height-functions-on-an-embedded-compact-manifold-are-morse]]

## Proof

**Given:** The smooth oriented knot $K$ and the fixed height in the statement.


1.1 Regard $K$ as a compact embedded smooth 1-manifold in $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. By [F1], the exceptional set $E$ of non-Morse directions is null in every smooth atlas of $S^3$. It cannot contain all of $S^3$, since a nonempty coordinate ball has positive Euclidean measure; choose $u\in S^3\setminus E$. Then $x\mapsto u\cdot x$ is Morse on $K$. [given, F1, choose]

2.1 Choose $R\in SO(4)$ with $R^Te_4=u$. Such a rotation is obtained in the plane spanned by $u$ and $e_4$; if $u=-e_4$, use a half-turn in a plane containing $e_4$. A rotation path $R_t$ from the identity to $R$ is an ambient isotopy of the oriented sphere. On $R(K)$, the fixed height equals $e_4\cdot R x=u\cdot x$, which is Morse by step 1.1. Thus $K'=R(K)$ is the required representative. [given, step 1.1, construct] ∎

[[thm-generic-height-functions-on-an-embedded-compact-manifold-are-morse]]
