## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$, with compact transversal $(M_0,g_0)$, and let $q_1,q_2\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ,\mathbb R)$. Assume zero is not a Dirichlet eigenvalue of either $-\Delta_g+q_j$, assume the unweighted scalar geodesic ray transform on $M_0$ is injective on compactly supported smooth functions, and suppose the full Schrödinger Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree:
$$\Lambda_{q_1}=\Lambda_{q_2}:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M).$$
Then $q_1=q_2$ on $M$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product domain and distinguished coordinate]]

[[def-ip-injective-geodesic-ray-transform|Unweighted transversal ray transform]]

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full Schrödinger DN map]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the DN identity and CGO solver suppliers [F1]--[F2].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the DN identity and CGO solver suppliers [F1]--[F2].

**Given:** the compact CTA product, real smooth interior-supported potentials, nonresonance of both operators, injectivity of the real scalar ray transform, and equality of full DN maps.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: under nonresonance, each Schrödinger DN map is a full boundary map on $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with normal derivative convention.

[F2] [[lem-ip-alessandrini-identity]] and [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: the Alessandrini Statement gives the Schrödinger identity for smooth boundary values, while the DN definition gives weak boundary forms on $H^{1/2}$. The exact $H^1$ solutions used below have only $H^{1/2}$ traces, so step 1.1 derives the needed extension directly from those forms.

[F3] [[def-ip-injective-geodesic-ray-transform]]: if a real compactly supported smooth function has zero unweighted integrals over all nontangential transversal geodesics, then it is zero; the same implication for complex functions follows by applying the real statement to real and imaginary parts.

[F4] [[cor-uniqueness-of-the-l-one-fourier-transform]]: two $L^1(\mathbb R)$ functions with equal Fourier transforms are equal almost everywhere.

[F5] [[thm-ip-cgo-solvability-and-remainder-bound]] now imports the $H^1$ real-weight right solver with $O(|\tau|^{-1})$ $L^2$ norm from Dos Santos Ferreira--Kurylev--Lassas--Salo, Proposition 2.1, PDF p. 10, with finite orientation-cover descent. The external result accepts arbitrary $L^2$ forcing and both signs of the real weight, rather than only the particular transport amplitude in that supplier's Statement.

[F6] [[lem-ip-cta-gaussian-beam-ray-limit]] supplies the normalized beam, arbitrarily small residual, and self-intersection ray limit, including nonorientable transversals by orientation-cover descent. The external source is Proposition 3.1, PDF p. 14, with the cross-term estimate on pp. 21--22. Proposition 2.2, PDF p. 11, gives the associated exact-solution correction. These external statements and the cross-term pages were inspected for the bounded repair; no complete new Carleman or beam proof is claimed.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 For exact $H^1$ solutions $u_j$ let $f_j=\operatorname{tr}u_j\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ and define $a_j(v,w)=\int_M(g(\nabla_gv,\nabla_g\overline w)+q_jv\overline w)\,dV_g$. By the weak DN definition, $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_1(u_1,u_2)$. Let $\widetilde u_1\in H^1(M)$ be the $q_2$ solution with trace $f_1$, which exists by nonresonant weak solvability. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_2(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, $a_2(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$, where the conjugation uses real-valuedness of $q_2$. Subtracting the weak pairings and using equality of the DN maps on all $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ gives $\int_M Q(x_1,x')u_1(x_1,x')\overline{u_2(x_1,x')}\,dV_g=0$, where $Q=q_1-q_2$. This derives the needed weak-trace extension of [F2]. Because $q_j\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ and $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$, extension of $Q$ by zero gives a smooth compactly supported function on $\mathbb R\times M_0$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, put $s=\tau+i\lambda$, and choose the beam $v_s$ of [F6] with residual $O(\tau^{-K})$. Use the signed real-weight solver [F5] to obtain exact solutions
$$u_1=e^{-s x_1}(v_s+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{s x_1}(v_s+r_2)$$
for the respective potentials, with $r_j\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_j\|_2=O(\tau^{-1})$. Indeed the conjugated residual is $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)v_s+q_jv_s$, of bounded $L^2$ norm on a fixed product cylinder; multiplication by $e^{\pm i\lambda x_1}$ is bounded there. Correcting with the real-weight solver gives precisely this bound. Their product in step 1.1 is $e^{-2i\lambda x_1}(v_s+r_1)(\overline{v_s}+\overline{r_2})$. Every error integral tends to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, the boundedness of $Q$, $\|v_s\|_2=O(1)$, and $\|r_j\|_2=o(1)$. Integrating first in $x_1$ gives the smooth compactly supported transversal test function $\widehat Q_\lambda$ below. Applying [F6] proves the attenuated ray identity for every $\lambda$ and every nontangential $\gamma$. This argument works on the base manifold; it does not assume injectivity of a ray transform on its orientation cover. [A1, A2, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Step 2.1 supplies
$$\int_{\gamma}\widehat Q_\lambda(\gamma(t))e^{-2\lambda t}\,dt=0 \quad\text{for every real }\lambda\text{ and every nontangential geodesic }\gamma,$$
where $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2i\lambda x_1}Q(x_1,x')\,dx_1$. At $\lambda=0$, [F3] gives $\widehat Q_0=0$. Assume inductively that $\partial_\lambda^j\widehat Q_0=0$ for every $j<k$. Differentiate the ray identity $k$ times at $\lambda=0$. Differentiation under the finite geodesic integral is valid because $Q$ is smooth with compact $x_1$ support. Leibniz' rule leaves the unweighted ray integral of $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0$; all other terms contain lower derivatives and vanish by the induction hypothesis. Thus [F3], applied to real and imaginary parts, gives $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0=0$. Induction proves that every Taylor coefficient of $\lambda\mapsto\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ vanishes for each fixed $x'$. [F3, given, step 2.1, induction, algebra]

3.2 For each fixed $x'$, compact $x_1$ support makes $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ entire in $\lambda$, so its zero Taylor series implies it vanishes for all real $\lambda$. This is the Fourier transform of the $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function $Q(\cdot,x')$ at every frequency $2\lambda$; [F4] gives $Q(\cdot,x')=0$ almost everywhere. Smoothness of $Q$ then yields $Q=0$ on $M$. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $A$ be an indeterminate, put $q=A^4$, $q_K=A^2$, and $q_L=A^{-2}=q_K^{-1}$, and work over $F=\mathbb Q(A)$. An oriented knot in $S^3$ means a smooth embedded circle with an orientation, considered up to orientation-preserving ambient isotopy. For an integer $r$, put
$$[r]=\frac{q_K^r-q_K^{-r}}{q_K-q_K^{-1}},\qquad [m]!=\prod_{r=1}^{m}[r]\quad(m\ge1),\qquad [0]!=1.$$
For each $N\ge1$, put $q_N=\exp(2\pi i/N)$.
For each integer $N\ge1$, let $V_N$ have basis $v_0,\ldots,v_{N-1}$ and define the $U_{q_L}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ action in the library coproduct convention by
$$K_Lv_j=q_L^{N-1-2j}v_j,\qquad Ev_j=[N-j]v_{j-1},\qquad Fv_j=[j+1]v_{j+1},$$
where $v_{-1}=v_N=0$. In the universal $R$-matrix formula use $q_K$ and $H v_j=(N-1-2j)v_j$; on $V_N\otimes V_N$ its action is the finite sum
$$\mathcal R_N=q_K^{H\otimes H/2}\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}q_K^{r(r-1)/2}\frac{(q_K-q_K^{-1})^r}{[r]!}\,E^r\otimes F^r,$$
and the positive crossing is $c_N=P\mathcal R_N$, where $P(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$. This is an irreducible module of dimension $N$. Equip these matrices with the Kauffman-bracket half-ribbon data: the twist matrix is the scalar $\theta_N=\lambda_N I$ with $\lambda_N=(-1)^{N-1}A^{N^2-1}$, and the matrix $G_N=(-1)^{N-1}\operatorname{diag}(A^{2(N-1-2j)})_{j=0}^{N-1}$ is the pivotal comparison used in the closure trace. The resulting generic quantum dimension is
$$d_N=\operatorname{Tr}(G_N)=(-1)^{N-1}\frac{A^{2N}-A^{-2N}}{A^2-A^{-2}}.$$
Use the contragredient left-dual action $(x\cdot f)(v)=f(S(x)v)$ on $V_N^*$, with evaluation $\operatorname{ev}(f\otimes v)=f(v)$ and coevaluation $1\mapsto\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}v_j\otimes v_j^*$. The ambient category is the $F$-linear category generated by the modules $V_N$ for all $N\ge1$ under finite tensor products, contragredient duals, finite direct sums and images of module-idempotents, whose morphisms are module homomorphisms, and whose tensor-product action is induced by the stated Hopf coproduct; its tensor unit is $F$ with the trivial action, so its tensor-unit endomorphism ring is $F$. These matrix data satisfy the ribbon-category axioms: braiding and inverse braiding, both duality snakes, monoidal pivotal comparison, balancing and dual compatibility of twist. Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice for the framed-tangle and Markov constructions. An oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ presented as the closure of an $n$-strand braid $\beta$ has generic normalized value
$$J_N^{\mathrm{gen}}(K;q)=\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(G_N^{\otimes n}\rho_N(\beta))}{d_N}\in F,$$
where, for a word $\beta=\sigma_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_m}^{\varepsilon_m}$ with $\varepsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}$, $w(\beta):=\sum_{j=1}^m\varepsilon_j$, and $\rho_N(\beta)$ is obtained by replacing each positive braid generator by $c_N$ on the corresponding adjacent tensor factors and each inverse generator by $c_N^{-1}$, then composing in word order. This quotient is an integral Laurent polynomial in $A^4$. Define the **normalized colored Jones sequence** by the unique $J_N(K;q)\in\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ satisfying $J_N(K;A^4)=J_N^{\mathrm{gen}}(K;A^4)$. Its root value $J_N(K;q_N)$ is obtained by substituting into this Laurent polynomial. The variable transport to the ordinary Jones convention is $t=q^{-1}=A^{-4}$.

## Definition references

[[lem-colored-jones-generic-ribbon-data|All-color ribbon identities]]

[[lem-colored-jones-generic-quotient-is-laurent|Integral Laurent representative and safe root evaluation]]

[[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra|Drinfeld–Jimbo generators and relations]]

[[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra|Library coproduct and antipode convention]]

[[def-quantum-sl2-fundamental-ribbon-module|Kauffman-bracket half-ribbon convention in dimension two]]

[[def-colored-framed-knot-evaluation-from-ribbon-category|Colored framed-link evaluation]]

[[thm-twist-correction-removes-framing|Scalar twist correction under Markov moves]]

[Etingof, Gelaki, Nikshych, and Ostrik, *Tensor Categories*, §§5.6 and 8.3](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf)

[Snyder and Tingley, *The half-twist for $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ representations*, §§3–5](https://msp.org/ant/2009/3-7/ant-v3-n7-p04-p.pdf)

[Murakami, *An Introduction to the Volume Conjecture*, §2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1002.0126)

[Habiro, *On the quantum $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ invariants of knots and integral homology spheres*, §§2.3 and 3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0211044)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $N\ge1$, the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, the generic module and matrices from the Definition, an oriented knot $K$, and a braid word $\beta$ whose closure represents $K$.

[F1] The library presentation has $K_L E K_L^{-1}=q_L^2E$, $K_L F K_L^{-1}=q_L^{-2}F$, and $EF-FE=(K_L-K_L^{-1})/(q_L-q_L^{-1})$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).

[F2] The library coproduct is $\Delta(E)=E\otimes K_L^{-1}+1\otimes E$ and $\Delta(F)=F\otimes1+K_L\otimes F$ ([[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]).

[F3] A ribbon category has a braiding, chosen duals, and a twist satisfying the balancing and dual-compatibility identities ([[def-braiding]], [[def-left-dual-and-right-dual-object]], [[def-twist-and-ribbon-structure]]).

[F4] For an absolutely simple color with scalar twist $\lambda I$, the generic framed trace corrected by $\lambda^{-w(\beta)}$ is invariant under oriented unframed Markov equivalence, under the stated Axiom of Choice ([[thm-twist-correction-removes-framing]]).

[F5] The framed colored-link value is the ribbon-tangle evaluation in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf1)$, and a closed braid is evaluated by the pivotal trace of its braid action ([[def-colored-framed-knot-evaluation-from-ribbon-category]]).

[F6] Absolute simplicity means $\operatorname{End}(V_N)=F I$ ([[def-absolutely-simple-object]]).

[F7] The finite matrices satisfy all ribbon identities for every $N\ge1$ and their pivotal trace of the identity is $d_N$ ([[lem-colored-jones-generic-ribbon-data]]).

[F8] The normalized generic quotient for every knot and color belongs to $\mathbb Z[A^4,A^{-4}]$ ([[lem-colored-jones-generic-quotient-is-laurent]]).

[A2] The Axiom of Choice supplies a choice function for every family of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A3] Countable choice supplies a choice function for every sequence of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Definition.

1.1 The diagonal weights give $K_L E K_L^{-1}v_j=q_L^2Ev_j$ and $K_L F K_L^{-1}v_j=q_L^{-2}Fv_j$. For the commutator, $EFv_j-FEv_j=([j+1][N-j-1]-[N-j][j])v_j=[N-1-2j]v_j$; the last equality follows by expanding the two quantum-number products over $q_K-q_K^{-1}$. Since $[r]_{q_K}=[r]_{q_L}$, this is $(K_L-K_L^{-1})(q_L-q_L^{-1})^{-1}v_j$. The generators therefore satisfy the defining $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ relations. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 The eigenvalues $q_L^{N-1-2j}$ of $K_L$ are pairwise distinct in $F$. Any module endomorphism is therefore diagonal in the given basis; commuting with $E$, whose successive coefficients $[N-j]$ are nonzero in $F$, forces all diagonal entries to be equal. Thus $\operatorname{End}_{U_{q_L}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)}(V_N)=F I$ and the color is absolutely simple by [F6]. [F6, given, algebra]

1.3 If $N=1$, $V_N$ is one-dimensional and irreducible. For $N>1$, let $W$ be a nonzero submodule and choose $x=\sum_j c_jv_j\in W$ nonzero. The eigenvalues of $K_L$ are distinct, so the polynomial spectral projection for any $j$ with $c_j\ne0$ maps $x$ to $c_jv_j$; hence $v_j\in W$. Repeated application of $E$ gives $v_0\in W$, since every coefficient $[N-k]$ encountered is nonzero. Repeated application of $F$ to $v_0$ gives each $v_k$ because the coefficients $[k]$ are nonzero. Thus $W=V_N$, proving irreducibility. [given, algebra]

1.4 The displayed sum for $d_N$ is a geometric sum, so $d_N=(-1)^{N-1}[N]$. Its numerator $A^{2N}-A^{-2N}$ is a nonzero Laurent polynomial and its denominator $A^2-A^{-2}$ is nonzero in $F$; hence the generic normalization is defined. The Hopf coproduct [F2] supplies the tensor-power action used in $\rho_N(\beta)$. By the braiding, dual, and ribbon axioms [F3] and the all-color ribbon identities [F7], these matrices define the framed evaluation, whose value is the pivotal trace by [F5]. [F2, F3, F5, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], [F7], and [A2], $\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}t_N(\beta)$ is unchanged by every conjugation and Markov stabilization, since $V_N$ is absolutely simple and its specified twist scalar is nonzero. Countable choice [A3] supplies the evaluator's hypothesis. Dividing by the fixed nonzero $d_N$ preserves that equality, so the displayed generic value is independent of the braid representative. [A2, A3, F4, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 1.4, given]

2.2 The unknot is represented by the one-strand identity braid, whose exponent sum is zero and whose pivotal trace is $\operatorname{Tr}(G_N)=d_N$. Hence $J_N^{\mathrm{gen}}(\bigcirc;q)=1$. For $N\ge2$, at $q_N=e^{2\pi i/N}$ choose $A_N=e^{\pi i/(2N)}$; then $A_N^4=q_N$ and $A_N^2-A_N^{-2}\ne0$, while $A_N^{2N}-A_N^{-2N}=e^{\pi i}-e^{-\pi i}=0$. Thus $d_N(q_N)=0$: the generic quotient cannot be evaluated there by dividing by $d_N$. [F5, step 1.4, given, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F8] to the given knot-closing braid and color under [A2] and [A3]. The generic quotient therefore has a unique integral Laurent representative in $q=A^4$. Substitution into that finite Laurent sum is defined for every nonzero complex $q$, including $q_N$; it does not divide by the specialized quantum dimension. Together with steps 2.1 and 2.2, this proves the stated representative independence, unknot normalization and root-evaluation convention. [A2, A3, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The all-color ribbon identities are proved by the finite-series interpolation argument in the first well-definedness supplier. The second proves integral Laurentness by cutting the knot into an integral scalar endomorphism and then proving invariance under $A\mapsto iA$. Thus root evaluation uses the resulting Laurent polynomial, even though the generic quantum dimension vanishes at the specified root for every $N\ge2$.

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356

## Example

Assume Countable Choice.

For a relative satellite radius $R>1$, identify the mean-zero real Fourier coefficients of a function on the unit circle with $X=\ell^2(\mathbb N;\mathbb R^2)$, where the two coordinates at frequency $n$ are its normalized cosine and sine coefficients, and give this space the canonical inner product $\langle(a_n,b_n),(c_n,d_n)\rangle=\sum_{n\ge1}(a_nc_n+b_nd_n)$. Interleaving the coordinates identifies it isometrically with real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so $X$ is a real Hilbert space. In these coordinates define the 2D satellite-gradiometry operator by
$$
(T_R(a_n,b_n))_{n\ge1}=(t_n a_n,t_n b_n)_{n\ge1},\qquad t_n=n(n+1)R^{-n-2}.
$$
This is the Fourier-coordinate map for recovering the mean-zero gravitational potential from the radial second derivative measured at relative satellite radius $R$. Take the truth to be the Fourier coefficient sequence of $f^\dagger(x)=\pi/2-|x|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$. Its constant coefficient is zero, so the omitted zero-frequency component is not part of this mean-zero model. The per-frequency eigenvalue of $T_R^*T_R$ is $\mu_n=n^2(n+1)^2R^{-2n-4}$, each with multiplicity two. For the inverse sequence model, order the cosine–sine modes by nonincreasing multiplier $t_n$, breaking ties by frequency and then placing cosine before sine; write the resulting ordered singular values as $(s_j)$ and their squares as $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Such an ordering exists because $t_n\to0$ and only finitely many modes exceed any positive threshold. Use the Tikhonov filter $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ and its continuous geometric-variance candidate grid in the SOLIT rule with known $\sigma>0$.

## Example references

[[alg-ip-solit-parameter-choice|The SOLIT selector used in this example]]

[[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index|Ordered filters and geometric-variance candidate grids]]

[Li and Werner, *Adaptive minimax optimality in statistical inverse problems via SOLIT*, §5.3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356)

[Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, complete lecture notes, Chapter 5](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real cosine–sine Fourier coefficient model on the circle, $R>1$, the multiplier sequence $t_n$, and the truth $f^\dagger(x)=\pi/2-|x|$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed for the upstream Fourier and compact singular-system coordinates.

[F1] [[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]]: The complex characters form a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2$ on the circle; their real and imaginary parts give the real cosine–sine coefficient basis.

[F2] [[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index]]: A candidate grid has geometric variance growth when its consecutive variance ratios lie in a fixed interval $[\theta_1,\theta_2]$ with $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$.

[F3] [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]: The positive-noise sequence experiment has observations $Y_j=\theta_j+\sigma s_j^{-1}\xi_j$ in singular coordinates.

[F4] [[alg-ip-solit-parameter-choice]]: SOLIT accepts a candidate only after its estimator differences from all finer candidates pass the two-index variance and Gaussian-quantile threshold.

[F5] [[lem-ip-solit-filter-risk-decomposition-and-monotone-bias]]: For each candidate, the regularized estimator is a measurable square-integrable Hilbert-valued random element.

[F6] [[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index]]: An ordered filter is nonnegative, satisfies $0\le\alpha q_\alpha(t)\le C_q'$ and $0\le tq_\alpha(t)\le1$, and increases pointwise as $\alpha$ decreases.

[F7] [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]]: Real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with its canonical inner product is complete.

## Verification

1.1 Interleaving $(a_n,b_n)_{n\ge1}$ as $(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots)$ is a linear isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so [F7] gives the stated real Hilbert structure. The integral of $f^\dagger$ over $[-\pi,\pi]$ is $\pi^2-\pi^2=0$, so its constant Fourier coefficient vanishes and its real Fourier coefficient sequence lies in the stated mean-zero coefficient space. The real cosine and sine modes are orthonormal because they are the real and imaginary parts of the orthonormal character basis in [F1]. [given, A1, F1, F7, algebra]

1.2 For every $n\ge1$, $t_n>0$ and $t_n\to0$ exponentially since $R>1$. The ratio of consecutive squared multipliers is $((n+1)/n)^2((n+2)/(n+1))^2R^{-2}$, which tends to $R^{-2}<1$; choose $\rho$ strictly between $R^{-2}$ and $1$, then the ratio is at most $\rho$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Thus $\sum_{n\ge1}2t_n^2<\infty$. The operator is injective because all its diagonal multipliers are positive. Its truncation to frequencies $n\le N$ is finite rank and the operator-norm error is $\sup_{n>N}t_n\to0$, so $T_R$ is compact and Hilbert–Schmidt. [given, algebra]

1.3 The frequency multipliers satisfy $t_{n+1}/t_n=(n+2)/(nR)$, which can exceed $1$ for small $n$; thus the frequency order is not always the singular-value order. The multiset of modes has a nonincreasing enumeration: at every stage a remaining maximum exists because $t_n\to0$ and only finitely many modes lie above any fixed positive threshold, and the fixed tie rule selects one uniquely. Every mode is eventually listed because only finitely many modes have multiplier at least its positive multiplier. The operator is diagonal on the orthonormal cosine–sine basis, so the frequency eigenvalue is $\mu_n=t_n^2=n^2(n+1)^2R^{-2n-4}$ twice at each frequency, and the enumerated singular system has these values in nonincreasing order. Since $(n+1)^2\asymp n^2$, $\mu_n\asymp n^4e^{-2n\log R}$, an exponential spectrum with exponent $\vartheta=1$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.4 For every $\lambda\ge0$, $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ is nonnegative, $\alpha q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$, and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$. If $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, then $\lambda+\widetilde\alpha<\lambda+\alpha$, so $q_\alpha(\lambda)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(\lambda)$. Thus it is an ordered filter with $C_q'=1$ by [F6]. Its trace variance is
$$
V(\alpha):=2\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\lambda_n}{(\lambda_n+\alpha)^2},\qquad \alpha>0.
$$
On every compact interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, each summand is continuous and is bounded above by $2\lambda_n/a^2$. Since $\sum_n2\lambda_n<\infty$ by step 1.2, the series converges uniformly there, so $V$ is continuous. Each summand strictly decreases as $\alpha$ increases, hence so does $V$. Also $V(\alpha)\le2\alpha^{-2}\sum_n\lambda_n\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. For every fixed $n$, $V(\alpha)\ge2\lambda_n/(\lambda_n+\alpha)^2\to2/\lambda_n$ as $\alpha\downarrow0$; because $\lambda_n\to0$, these lower bounds imply $V(\alpha)\to\infty$. Fix any $c>0$ and $\theta>1$. Continuity, strict decrease, and these endpoint limits give a unique $\alpha_m>0$ with $V(\alpha_m)=c\theta^m$ for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Thus $\alpha_m$ decreases to zero and the variances $v_m=\sigma^2V(\alpha_m)$ have the constant consecutive ratio $\theta$. The resulting infinite grid meets [F2], and the SOLIT rule truncates it at its finite $m_{\max}$. [given, F2, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 The truth lies in $L^2$ because it is bounded, and its Fourier coefficients are coordinates in the model by [F1]. The positive diagonal multipliers give the injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator verified in step 1.2; the Tikhonov filter satisfies [F6] and its candidates satisfy [F2], and the positive-noise experiment and finite selector are [F3]–[F4]. The well-definedness and moment properties of its estimators follow from [F5]. This example asserts no rate for the resulting estimator. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.2, step 1.4] ∎

## Finite checks

At frequencies $n=1,2$, $t_1=2R^{-3}$, $t_2=6R^{-4}$, $\lambda_1=4R^{-6}$, and $\lambda_2=36R^{-8}$. The first two Tikhonov variance terms are $2\lambda_1(\lambda_1+\alpha)^{-2}$ and $2\lambda_2(\lambda_2+\alpha)^{-2}$; both are finite, positive, and continuous for $\alpha>0$.

  without choice
status: draft

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, $o\in M$, and $R$ a unital ring. One can construct paths $\gamma_x$ from $o$ to every $x\in M$, with $\gamma_o$ constant, by fixed rules from one finite atlas and finitely many connecting paths. Let $\mathcal R$ be a right-$R$ local system with a supplied identification $\mathcal R_o=R$ and transport given by left multiplication by units, with monodromy image $H\le R^\times$. Its twisted singular complex has an explicit chain decomposition $C_*(M;\mathcal R)=C'_*\oplus Q_*$ after a change of free bases, where $C'_0=R$, $C'_* $ is free, and $Q_*$ is contractible with its only nonzero differential an identity from degree one to degree zero. Moreover
$$\operatorname{im}(d'_1)=\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R.$$
The decomposition and its dual cochain homotopy equivalences require no choice principle. In particular this image is principal if $H$ is cyclic, if it equals $R$, or if every right ideal of $R$ is principal.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact connected manifold, point, coefficient system, and base fiber identification.

[F1] A right-$R$ local system here means a functor from the fundamental groupoid to unital right-$R$ modules with right-linear transport isomorphisms. Forgetting the right action gives an abelian-group local system; the intrinsic first-vertex construction of [[def-singular-and-cellular-chain-complexes-with-local-coefficients]] applies with commutative base ring $\mathbb Z$. The additional arbitrary-ring linearity and square-zero calculation are supplied directly in step 1.1 below.

## Proof

1.1 For a singular simplex $\sigma:[v_0,\ldots,v_n]\to M$, put its coefficient in $\mathcal R_{\sigma(v_0)}$ and take the direct sum of those right modules over all singular simplices. For $n\ge1$ define $d(c\sigma)=T_{01}(c)\,\sigma[1,\ldots,n]+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^i c\,\sigma[0,\ldots,\widehat i,\ldots,n]$, and let the degree-zero differential be zero. Every face map is right-linear because transport is, so this defines right-$R$ linear differentials without assuming that $R$ is commutative. To check $d^2=0$, pair the two terms deleting vertices $i<j$. Their signs are $(-1)^{i+j-1}$ and $(-1)^{i+j}$. If $i>0$, both coefficients are $c$. If $i=0<1<j$, both coefficients are $T_{01}(c)$. If $(i,j)=(0,1)$, the coefficients are $T_{12}T_{01}(c)$ and $T_{02}(c)$, which agree because the two-edge path is endpoint-fixed homotopic to the direct edge in the simplex and transport is a groupoid functor. Thus every pair cancels. This includes degenerate simplices and degree one, where the next differential is zero. These are the underlying abelian local chains of [F1], now equipped with their verified right-$R$ structure. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose a finite cover by coordinate balls $U_1,\ldots,U_m$ with charts onto convex Euclidean balls, including a ball centered at $o$. This uses compactness and only a finite selection. Their intersection graph is connected: otherwise the unions belonging to different graph components would be disjoint nonempty open sets partitioning connected $M$. For each edge choose one point in the intersection, a finite selection; join it to each chart center by its straight coordinate segment. Choose a spanning tree by the finite index order and concatenate these segments to get paths from $o$ to every chart center. For $x\in M$, take the least-index chart containing it and follow its center path by the straight segment to $x$; at $o$ use the constant path. Denote this explicitly prescribed path by $\gamma_x$. This defines paths for all points from one finite list of charts and edge points, rather than selecting an infinite family of paths. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Transport the supplied basis $1\in\mathcal R_o$ along $\gamma_x$ to obtain a basis at each $x$. Thus [F1] makes every $C_j$ the free right $R$-module on its actual singular $j$-simplices. Write $e_x$ for the degree-zero basis and $e_\sigma$ for the degree-one basis of a path $\sigma:x\to y$. The degree-one boundary is $d_1e_\sigma=e_y g_\sigma-e_x$, where $g_\sigma\in H$ is the transition unit obtained by transporting first along $\gamma_x$, then along $\sigma$, and back along $\gamma_y$. For $x\ne o$, the path $\gamma_x$ is itself one singular one-simplex; denote its basis element by $p_x$. These basis elements are distinct because their terminal points are distinct, and $d_1p_x=e_x-e_o$. Put $p_o=0$. [F1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Change the degree-zero basis to $e_o$ and $b_x=e_x-e_o$ for $x\ne o$. This is invertible even with infinitely many vertices: the inverse is $e_x=b_x+e_o$, and every vector has finite support. Retain the degree-one basis elements $p_x$. For every other one-simplex $\sigma:x\to y$, replace its basis element by $q_\sigma=e_\sigma-p_y g_\sigma+p_x$. This is another invertible basis change, with inverse $e_\sigma=q_\sigma+p_y g_\sigma-p_x$. Direct substitution gives $d_1q_\sigma=e_o(g_\sigma-1)$, whereas $d_1p_x=b_x$. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Let $Q_1$ be free on the $p_x$, $Q_0$ free on the $b_x$, and $Q_j=0$ in other degrees, with differential $p_x\mapsto b_x$. Let $C'_1$ be free on the remaining $q_\sigma$, $C'_0=Re_o$, and $C'_j=C_j$ for $j\ge2$. The differential of a degree-two chain has zero $p_x$ coefficient for every $x$: applying $d_1$ would otherwise give a nonzero corresponding $b_x$ coefficient, contrary to $d_1d_2=0$ proved in step 1.1. Thus $d_2$ lands in $C'_1$, and higher differentials already stay in $C'$. This proves the claimed direct sum of complexes. Its contractible summand has the explicit homotopy $b_x\mapsto p_x$, zero on all other degrees. Dualizing this actual homotopy gives the cochain equivalences for any coefficient module; no exactness assertion about an infinite product or choice of primitives is needed. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The image of $d'_1$ is the right ideal generated by the elements $g_\sigma-1$. All transition units belong to $H$, so this ideal is contained in $\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R$. Conversely every $h\in H$ is realized by transport along a based loop at $o$. That loop is one singular one-simplex and is not one of the removed $p_x$, whose endpoints differ. Its reduced boundary is $e_o(h-1)$. Thus every generator of the displayed ideal occurs, and equality follows. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 If $H=\langle t\rangle$ is cyclic, $t^k-1$ is a right multiple of $t-1$ for every integer $k$: use the finite geometric sum for $k>0$, zero for $k=0$, and $t^{-k}-1=-t^{-k}(t^k-1)$ for negative powers. Since powers of $t$ commute with $t-1$, this last expression is also a right multiple. The ideal is therefore $(t-1)R$, including $H=\{1\}$ with zero ideal. The other two sufficient conditions for principality are literal. All basis changes and homotopies were explicit finite-support formulas, and the only initial choices were finite. This proves the stated choice scope. [step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid of grid number $n$ representing one oriented knot, and let $M_{\mathbb O}$, $M_{\mathbb X}$, and $A_G$ be the functions defined from its finite point sets and the pair-counting function $J$. Then $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integer-valued, and every rectangle $r$ from a grid state $\mathbf x$ to a grid state $\mathbf y$ satisfies $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$ and $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb X}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Consequently $A_G$ is integer-valued and $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot|The toroidal grid, its states, and the Maslov/Alexander formulas using $J$]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A knot grid $G$ with grid number $n$ and the functions in the preceding definition.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] defines grid states as one point on each horizontal and vertical circle, defines $J(P,Q)=(I(P,Q)+I(Q,P))/2$ by a finite pair count, and sets $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)=J(\mathbf x-\mathbb O,\mathbf x-\mathbb O)+1$ and $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)=J(\mathbf x-\mathbb X,\mathbf x-\mathbb X)+1$.

[F2] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] requires one $O$ and one $X$ in each row and column, and a one-component grid has a single $n$-cycle in the induced $O\to X\to O$ marking permutation.

## Proof

1.1 Each $I(P,Q)$ is an integer count. For $P=Q$, $J(P,P)=I(P,P)$, so the two self-pair terms in the formulas for $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integers; the cross terms occur doubled. Hence both Maslov functions are integer-valued. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Suppose a rectangle $r$ is contained in the chosen fundamental square. Write its southwest and northeast corners as $x_1,x_2\in\mathbf x$ and its northwest and southeast corners as $y_1,y_2\in\mathbf y$; all other state points are common. In $J(\mathbf x,\mathbf x)-J(\mathbf y,\mathbf y)$ the common-point terms cancel, the ordered corner pair contributes $1$, and each point of $\mathbf x$ strictly inside $r$ contributes twice, once against each changed corner. Thus this difference is $1+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. In $2J(\mathbf x,\mathbb O)-2J(\mathbf y,\mathbb O)$ the same cancellation leaves twice the number of $O$-markings in $r$. Substituting these two counts into [F1] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Replacing every $O$ by $X$ gives the stated formula for $M_{\mathbb X}$. [F1, construct, algebra]

1.3 For a marking set $P\in\{\mathbb O,\mathbb X\}$, write $M_P(\mathbf x)=J(\mathbf x-P,\mathbf x-P)+1$ and let $\mathrm{NW}(P_i)$ denote the northwest grid vertex of the cell containing the $i$th mark, read on the bottom edge when that cell is in the top row. Let $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}P}$ be the state consisting of these vertices. Expanding the $J$ formula in [F1] gives $M_P(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}P})=\#\{(i,j):\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<\mathrm{NW}(P_j)\}-\#\{(i,j):\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<P_j\}-\#\{(i,j):P_i<\mathrm{NW}(P_j)\}+\#\{(i,j):P_i<P_j\}+1.$ For distinct $i,j$ with neither mark in the top row, all four inequalities are equivalent and their signed contributions cancel. If $P_j$ is in the top row, the second and fourth inequalities are equivalent and the first and third are false; if $P_i$ is in the top row, the first and second inequalities are equivalent and the third and fourth are false. These contributions also cancel. For $i=j$, the only inequality that can hold is $\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<P_i$, and it holds exactly for the unique mark in the top row. The displayed count is therefore $-1+1=0$, proving $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})=M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X})=0$. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 For two complementary rectangles $r$ and $r'$ with the same vertical edges, let $v$ be their common width, counted in column strips. The one-$O$- and one-$X$-per-column conditions in [F2] give $n_{\mathbb O}(r)+n_{\mathbb O}(r')=v$ and $n_{\mathbb X}(r)+n_{\mathbb X}(r')=v$. The state has one point on each of the $v-1$ vertical circles strictly between those two edges, so $\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)+\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r')=v-1$. If the formula of step 1.2 holds for $r$ from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$, these three equalities give the formula for $r'$ from $\mathbf y$ to $\mathbf x$ by subtraction. The same argument applies to complementary rectangles sharing horizontal edges, counting rows instead of columns. Of the four torus rectangles for the two states, one lies in the fundamental square; successive horizontal or vertical complementations reach each of the other three, so the formulas hold for every torus rectangle. [F2, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Subtract the $M_{\mathbb X}$ change from the $M_{\mathbb O}$ change and divide by two. The constant terms and state-interior terms cancel, giving $\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)}2-\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)}2=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. The common normalization $-(n-1)/2$ in $A_G$ cancels, proving the rectangle-change formula and that all differences of $A_G$ are integers. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 The row and column connections from $O$ to $X$ and back form one $n$-cycle by [F2]. Equivalently, the relative permutation between $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X}$ and $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O}$ is an $n$-cycle. Factor that cycle into $n-1$ transpositions and apply them successively to obtain grid states between the two states. Two states that differ by one transposition have four intersection corners: the two row circles and two column circles cut the torus into four rectangles, and one of those rectangles has the first state at its southwest and northeast corners and the second state at its northwest and southeast corners. Thus each transition is realized by a torus rectangle, whether empty or not. Each rectangle changes $M_{\mathbb X}$ by an odd integer by steps 1.2 and 2.1, so $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})\equiv n-1\pmod 2$, using the zero normalization at $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X}$ from step 1.3. Since $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})=0$, the numerator $M_{\mathbb O}-M_{\mathbb X}-(n-1)$ defining twice $A_G(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})$ is even. Hence this value is integral. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 1.3, choose, algebra]

4.1 Any two grid states correspond to permutations, and a finite product of transpositions carries one to the other. Each transposition gives a rectangle transition. Step 3.1 shows that $A_G$ changes by an integer at every transition; since one state has integral Alexander value by step 3.2, all grid states do. [step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathsf{Cob}_3$ be the additive monoidal category of oriented cobordisms before the S, T, and four-tube relations are imposed, and let $\mathsf{Cob}_{BN}$ be its quotient by those relations. Suppose $F:\mathsf{Cob}_3\to\mathsf{GrAb}$ is a symmetric monoidal functor to graded abelian groups and homogeneous maps, with a circle sent to $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, a cup to $\eta(1)=1$, a cap to $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, a merge pair of pants to $m$, and a split pair of pants to $\Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\ \Delta(X)=X\otimes X$. Then every sphere component is sent to zero, every disjoint torus component acts by multiplication by $2$, and the two sides of the four-tube relation induce the same map. Therefore $F$ factors through an additive monoidal functor on $\mathsf{Cob}_{BN}$.

## Statement references

[[def-barnatan-tangle-cobordism-category|The surface category and its S, T, and four-tube relations]]

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|The integral Khovanov Frobenius algebra]]

[Bar-Natan, *Khovanov's homology for tangles and cobordisms*, Proposition 7.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410495v2)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology*, §5](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The additive monoidal category $\mathsf{Cob}_{BN}$ and the algebra $\mathcal A$ with the stated structure maps.

[F1] [[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]] gives the free basis $\{1,X\}$, the unit, counit, multiplication, and comultiplication formulas in the statement, and verifies the Frobenius identities on that basis.

[F2] [[def-barnatan-tangle-cobordism-category]] defines $\mathsf{Cob}_3$ by gluing and disjoint union, and defines $\mathsf{Cob}_{BN}$ by imposing the sphere, torus, and four-tube relations in every surrounding cobordism.

## Proof

1.1 By the assumed functoriality of $F$, gluing cobordisms is sent to composition of maps and disjoint union is sent to tensor product. Thus the only additional relations to check before factoring through the quotient are the three local relations in [F2]. [F2, given]

1.2 A sphere is evaluated by $\epsilon\eta$, and $\epsilon(\eta(1))=\epsilon(1)=0$. A torus is evaluated by $\epsilon m\Delta\eta$; on the generator $1$, $\Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1$, then $m\Delta(1)=2X$, and $\epsilon(2X)=2$. These are exactly the S and T relations, including when glued into any surrounding cobordism because the TQFT respects composition and tensor product. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 In the four-tube relation, each side consists locally of two ways to attach one tube. Applying the TQFT to the local four-disk input $1$, either side gives
$$
X\otimes1\otimes1\otimes1+ 1\otimes X\otimes1\otimes1+ 1\otimes1\otimes X\otimes1+ 1\otimes1\otimes1\otimes X.
$$
This follows by applying $\Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1$ at each tube attachment and $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$ at the two cut disks. The equality on the local input implies equality as maps: tensoring with identity maps and composing with the maps for the unchanged part of the surface preserves equality. Thus the four-tube relation is respected. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Every generating local relation of $\mathsf{Cob}_{BN}$ is respected by steps 1.2 and 1.3, while the Frobenius identities respect the isotopy and gluing presentation by step 1.1. Therefore the TQFT factors through the quotient defining $\mathsf{Cob}_{BN}$, as asserted. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Gamma$ be PTFA and let $k$ be either $\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field. The group ring $A=k[\Gamma]$ has no zero divisors, satisfies both Ore conditions, and has a fraction division ring $K$ in which every element is both a right and a left fraction of elements of $A$. The involution $\overline{\sum c_g g}=\sum c_g g^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive anti-automorphism of $K$.

Every intermediate unital ring $A\subseteq R\subseteq K$ has no zero divisors, satisfies both Ore conditions, and has this same $K$ as its fraction division ring. If $R$ is stable under the extended involution, that involution restricts to $R$ and descends to its additive quotient $K/R$. None of these assertions requires a choice principle.

## Statement references

[[lem-torsion-free-abelian-extensions-preserve-group-ring-domains]]

[[lem-ptfa-groups-have-finite-folner-sets]]

[[lem-folner-group-ring-domains-have-ore-fractions]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The coefficient ring, PTFA series and indicated intermediate ring when used.

[F1] Nonsplit extensions by torsion-free abelian quotients preserve absence of group-ring zero divisors over every commutative field. [[lem-torsion-free-abelian-extensions-preserve-group-ring-domains]]

[F2] PTFA groups have finite left Folner sets, and a group ring without zero divisors over a commutative field with these sets satisfies both Ore conditions and has a constructed right-fraction division ring. [[lem-ptfa-groups-have-finite-folner-sets]], [[lem-folner-group-ring-domains-have-ore-fractions]]

## Proof

1.1 If $k$ is a commutative field, apply [F1] finitely many times along the supplied subnormal PTFA series, starting with $k[\{1\}]=k$. Only normality of one subgroup in the next is needed. This gives absence of zero divisors in $A$. By [F2], $A$ satisfies both Ore conditions and embeds in a division ring $K$ whose elements are right fractions. Each right fraction $as^{-1}$ is also a left fraction: for $a\ne0$, the left Ore condition gives $ta=bs\ne0$, hence $as^{-1}=t^{-1}b$; zero uses denominator one. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For $k=\mathbb Z$, embed $A$ coefficientwise into $\mathbb Q[\Gamma]$ and use its division ring from step 1.1. The embedding is injective by the unique group basis, so $A$ has no zero divisors. A nonzero common right multiple of integral group-ring elements obtained over $\mathbb Q[\Gamma]$ has rational multiplier coefficients in two finite supports. Multiply both multipliers by a common positive integer clearing those finitely many denominators; this integer is central and nonzero, so the equality becomes a nonzero common right multiple over $A$. The same operation clears the left multipliers, proving both Ore conditions for $A$. A fraction $as^{-1}$ over $\mathbb Q[\Gamma]$ becomes $(Na)(Ns)^{-1}$ over $A$ for one common central positive integer $N$. Left fractions are cleared identically. Thus this same $K$ is the stated fraction division ring of $\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 On $A$ the displayed coefficient formula is additive, reverses products and has square the identity, directly from the group law and commutativity of $k$. Define on a right fraction $\jmath(as^{-1})=\bar s^{-1}\bar a$. To check independence, if $as^{-1}=bt^{-1}$ choose $su=tv=w\ne0$ in $A$; multiplication on the right by $w$ gives $au=bv$. Applying the original involution gives $\bar u\bar a=\bar v\bar b$, while $\bar w=\bar u\bar s=\bar v\bar t$. Multiplying on the left by $\bar w^{-1}$ proves $\bar s^{-1}\bar a=\bar t^{-1}\bar b$. Thus the formula is well-defined. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 With the same common denominator, the sum is $(au+bv)w^{-1}$, and $\bar w^{-1}(\bar u\bar a+\bar v\bar b)=\bar s^{-1}\bar a+\bar t^{-1}\bar b$, proving additivity. For a product $(as^{-1})(bt^{-1})$ with $b\ne0$, choose $bu=sv\ne0$. It is $av(tu)^{-1}$. Its image is $\bar t^{-1}\bar u^{-1}\bar v\bar a$, which equals $\bar t^{-1}\bar b\bar s^{-1}\bar a$ because $\bar u\bar b=\bar v\bar s$. This is the reverse product of the two images. Zero factors are immediate. The map preserves one and sends nonzero elements to nonzero elements, so it preserves inverses in reverse multiplication. Its square fixes $A$ and therefore every fraction, proving it is an involutive anti-automorphism. Every anti-automorphism extending the one on $A$ must have this fraction formula, proving uniqueness. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Let $A\subseteq R\subseteq K$. It has no zero divisors since $K$ is a division ring. For nonzero $a,b\in R$, express $a^{-1}b=cd^{-1}$ over $A$; then $bd=ac\ne0$ is a common right multiple with multipliers in $R$. Express $ba^{-1}=u^{-1}v$ over $A$; then $ub=va\ne0$ is a common left multiple. All elements of $K$ are already fractions over $A$, so are fractions over $R$. If $R$ is involution-stable, step 4.1 and the equality $\jmath^2=1$ give $\jmath(R)=R$; hence $q+R\mapsto\jmath(q)+R$ is well-defined on the additive quotient and has square one. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Each field-extension step uses the finite supplied series, each multiplier or denominator clearing uses two finite supports, and each fraction calculation chooses a single finite common multiple. No order, section or system of representatives on an infinite set was chosen. This proves the stated choice scope for the group ring, its involution and every intermediate ring. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $P\cup\eta$ be a smooth oriented two-component link in $S^3$ with unknotted axis $\eta$, and let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot. Supply disjoint closed product tubes and positive meridian/preferred zero-linking-longitude peripheral data for the knots and axis. Write $P(K)$ for infection along $\eta$ with the untwisted companion $K$. For a knot $L$, write $M(L)$ for its actual chosen zero-longitude filling, with the orientation extending its exterior. Let $w=\operatorname{lk}(P,\eta)$.

There is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $E$ with
$$\partial E=M(P)\sqcup M(K)\sqcup(-M(P(K))).$$
For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$, it has $H_1(E;R)=R$ and $H_2(E;R)=R^2$. The two first boundary components induce the displayed basis in degree two. If $s_L=\alpha_L\cap[M(L)]$ where $\alpha_L\in H^1(M(L);R)$ evaluates as $1$ on the positive meridian, then, in those coordinates,
$$i_*s_{P(K)}=i_*s_P+w\,i_*s_K.$$
In degree one the meridians of $P$, $K$ and $P(K)$ map to $1,w,1$, respectively.

Likewise, for any finite nonempty list of knots $K_1,\ldots,K_q$ with the same supplied peripheral data, there is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $C$ from $\bigsqcup_j M(K_j)$ to $M(K_1\#\cdots\#K_q)$, with $H_1(C;R)=R$ and $H_2(C;R)=R^q$. The incoming degree-two classes are its coordinate basis and the outgoing class maps to their sum. In particular, for $X=E$ or $C$, the outgoing inclusions are injective on $H_1,H_2$ and the union of incoming components surjects onto $H_2(X;R)$.

The peripheral and framing data are supplied, rather than selected by an existence theorem. Their subsequent construction and the homology assertions use no additional choice principle. This is an ordinary-coefficient assertion; arbitrary twisted-coefficient boundary generation is not asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite smooth knot data, product tubes and zero-linking peripheral systems in the Statement; all subsequent homology has constant coefficients $R$.

[F1] The small-chain Mayer–Vietoris exact sequences hold for these product-collared gluings, with no choice axiom. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[F2] Oriented cap duality and its boundary formula hold for compact collared manifolds and their closed boundaries, retaining constant $R$ actions by forgetting to abelian groups. [[thm-compact-collared-manifold-local-coefficient-lefschetz-duality-in-zf]], [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]], [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]]

## Proof

1.1 The elementary peripheral homology calculation is as follows. In $S^3=X_L\cup N(L)$, the degree-three orientation connector to $H_2(\partial N(L);R)$ is an isomorphism, represented by cutting a fundamental cycle along the torus. Mayer–Vietoris therefore gives $H_2(X_L;R)=0$ and an isomorphism $H_1(\partial N(L);R)\to H_1(X_L;R)\oplus H_1(N(L);R)$. The preferred longitude is zero in the exterior by its supplied peripheral property, while the positive meridian generates its $R$ summand. Thus $H_1(X_L;R)=R[\mu_L]$. The cohomology sequence gives the dual statement in degree one, with its generator evaluating as $1$ on $\mu_L$. Filling the preferred longitude gives, by the same two sequences, $H_1(M(L);R)=R[\mu_L]$ and $H^1(M(L);R)=R[\alpha_L]$. Closed cap duality [F2] identifies $H_2(M(L);R)$ with $R[s_L]$. The same exterior calculation with two removed tubes says that their meridians freely generate degree one. Filling one removed tube by its original solid torus drops that meridian coordinate and preserves the other one. Since $\lambda_P$ is zero in the one-knot exterior $X_P$, its $\mu_P$ coordinate on the two-component exterior is zero: $[\lambda_P]=v[\mu_\eta]$ for some integer $v$. Similarly $\lambda_\eta$ has zero $\mu_\eta$ coordinate; after filling the tube of $\eta$, its remaining coordinate is the class of the parallel axis in $X_P$, which by the definition of $w$ is $w[\mu_P]$. Thus $[\lambda_\eta]=w[\mu_P]$. Equality of $v$ and $w$ is not needed anywhere in this proof. These computations use finite torus/sphere product chains and the exact sequences, not a choice of Seifert surfaces. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $V_K$ be the filling solid torus in $M(K)$. Glue $M(P)\times[0,1]$ and $M(K)\times[0,1]$ along $N(\eta)\times\{0\}$ and $V_K\times\{0\}$ so that $\lambda_\eta$ maps to $\mu_K$ and $\mu_\eta$ to $\lambda_K$. The map extends over the solid tori: their core coordinates agree and their meridian disks agree up to the orientation fixed by the exterior filling. With the orientation on $V_K$ induced by the oriented filling, this is an orientation-reversing map of the boundary solid tori, as required for gluing the oriented four-dimensional products. The remaining bottom boundary is $(M(P)\setminus\operatorname{int}N(\eta))\cup X_K$. Its unfilled knot exterior is the infection exterior: it glues $X_K$ in place of $N(\eta)$ with the stated peripheral exchange. By step 1.1, the exchanged relation kills $\mu_\eta$, while $\mu_K=w\mu_P$; therefore the old longitude $\lambda_P=v\mu_\eta$ is still zero. Since the axis is unknotted, its exterior is a solid torus whose meridian is $\lambda_\eta$; after the peripheral exchange this fills the meridian $\mu_K$ of $K$, recovering $S^3$. The image of $P$ is the defined infection knot $P(K)$. The unchanged filling at $P$ is exactly its preferred zero-longitude filling, so the remaining boundary is $-M(P(K))$. Near the gluing-torus edge the local four-dimensional model is a product of that torus and two half-planes glued along one boundary ray. Rescaling the sector angle identifies it with a half-plane; this supplies the usual rounded smooth boundary chart and a collar, and is a product construction over the supplied torus. Away from this edge the existing product charts persist. Thus the finite gluing gives the stated smooth oriented collared cobordism, not merely a formal sum of boundary manifolds. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The product homotopies descend to a deformation retraction of $E$ onto $M(P)\cup_{N(\eta)=V_K}M(K)$, taking each interval coordinate to zero. In its Mayer–Vietoris sequence the solid torus has $H_2=0$ and $H_1=R$. Its degree-one map into $R[\mu_P]\oplus R[\mu_K]$ sends $1$ to $(w,-1)$, which is injective over every $R$. The degree-zero difference map is injective too. Exactness consequently gives $H_2(E;R)=H_2(M(P);R)\oplus H_2(M(K);R)=R^2$ and $H_1(E;R)=(R^2)/R(w,-1)=R$. The first meridian maps to its generator and the second to $w$ times it. The outgoing meridian of $P(K)$ is the original meridian of $P$ away from the infection torus, so its image is that same generator. Hence its degree-one inclusion is an isomorphism. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The cohomology Mayer–Vietoris sequence identifies $H^1(E;R)$ with the pairs $(a\alpha_P,b\alpha_K)$ satisfying $wa-b=0$: the preceding degree-zero difference map is surjective, and the following restriction to the common solid torus is $(a,b)\mapsto wa-b$. Let $\alpha$ be the resulting unique class restricting to $(\alpha_P,w\alpha_K)$. On the outgoing component it evaluates as $1$ on its meridian by step 3.1, so restricts there to $\alpha_{P(K)}$. Relative duality and the cap boundary identity give
$$\partial(\alpha\cap[E,\partial E])=-\alpha|_{\partial E}\cap[\partial E]=-s_P-w\,s_K+s_{P(K)}.$$
The cohomology-first cap boundary formula contributes the initial minus sign because $\alpha$ has degree one; the boundary orientations in step 2.1 give the displayed signs of the component classes. This is the boundary of a relative three-class, so its image in $H_2(E;R)$ is zero. It follows that $i_*s_{P(K)}=i_*s_P+w\,i_*s_K$. Its first coordinate is $1$, which proves the outgoing degree-two map injective even for a coefficient ring with zero divisors. The incoming degree-two surjectivity was already an isomorphism in step 3.1. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Realize connected sum as infection along a positive meridian of the first knot, whose winding number is $1$: the meridional disk meets one oriented arc, and replacing its straight product arc by the untwisted companion arc is precisely the connected-sum construction. Thus step 2.1 with this axis gives the two-knot connected-sum cobordism. For $q=1$ use a product. Inductively glue the next such infection piece to the current outgoing boundary. Equivalently attach the next surgery product along the meridional filling solid torus of the current outgoing manifold. Mayer–Vietoris has again a common solid torus whose degree-one map has the new component coordinate $-1$, and degree-two group zero. Hence each attachment adds one independent incoming $H_2$ generator and keeps $H_1=R$, with every meridian mapping to $1$. Step 4.1 with $w=1$ says that the new outgoing degree-two generator is the previous outgoing generator plus the new incoming generator. Induction therefore gives exactly the claimed coordinate basis and sum for arbitrary finite $q$. Orientation-reversed pieces are covered as well: reflection of the ambient sphere, reversing the knot orientation when taking the concordance inverse, preserves the zero slope and identifies its surgery with the oppositely oriented surgery manifold. The reflected product and filling give the same construction for a signed finite list. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 The only choices made after the supplied tubes and peripheral data were finite gluing parameters and individual representatives of exact-sequence classes. All homology and cohomology identities were proved with constant coefficients; no twisted surjectivity was inferred from them. The product-torus corner charts and outgoing collars are explicit and are independent of any proper locally flat annulus neighborhood theorem. Thus these computations prove precisely the ordinary inclusion properties needed for the boundary-cokernel gluing inequality, in the full finite infection and connected-sum scope stated above. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact oriented boundaryless Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold and let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with its integral orientation class induces isomorphisms
$$H^p(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;\mathcal L)$$
for every integer $p$, without a choice principle. The maps respect any coefficient-ring action commuting with transport, and in particular apply to local systems of modules over a noncommutative ring by forgetting to abelian groups and retaining that action. No smoothness, triangulation or prescribed finite CW structure is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact oriented manifold and the local system.

[F1] The actual support cap maps are well-defined and use compatible canonical integral support orientation classes, with no choice assumption. [[def-compactly-supported-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]], [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]], [[lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets]]

[F2] Cap duality holds on coordinate balls without choice. [[lem-choice-free-local-coefficient-duality-on-a-coordinate-ball]]

[F3] The compact-support local-coefficient Mayer–Vietoris ladder commutes with homology Mayer–Vietoris after its prescribed connector signs. [[lem-compact-support-local-coefficient-mayer-vietoris-and-cap-ladder]]

[F4] The five lemma compares the middle terms of exact five-term windows; local excision permits passage between a compact support in an open subspace and its ambient space. [[thm-five-lemma-for-a-morphism-of-long-exact-sequences]], [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 For every open $W\subset M$, define $D_W:H_c^p(W;\mathcal L)\to H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L)$ by the supportwise cap of [F1], using the restricted orientation. If $W=U\cup V$ and all three maps for $U,V,U\cap V$ are isomorphisms in every degree, the exact ladder [F3] and five lemma [F4] make $D_W$ an isomorphism in every degree. The five-term window centered on degree $p$ has the surrounding compact-support terms in degrees $p$ and $p+1$ on the intersection and on the two pieces; their homology comparisons are the assumed isomorphisms. Multiplying a connecting map by the specified sign preserves exactness. Thus this finite gluing implication is valid without a chosen splitting. [F1, F3, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $O$ be any open subset of one coordinate ball. In coordinates enumerate all bounded open boxes with rational endpoints whose closures lie in $O$, using the fixed elementary enumeration of finite rational tuples. They cover $O$: each point has a sufficiently small coordinate box with closure in $O$, and density supplies rational endpoints on either side of its coordinates. A box, and a nonempty intersection of finitely many boxes, is a coordinate ball; its local coefficient system is trivialized by the straight contraction inside the ambient coordinate chart, so [F2] applies. Prove duality for every finite union of these boxes by induction on their number. For the last box $B$ and preceding union $A$, the intersection $A\cap B$ is a union of fewer boxes, namely the nonempty intersections with $B$. The induction hypothesis applies to that union as well as to $A$, and step 1.1 proves duality on $A\cup B$. Empty intersections and the empty union have zero groups. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Let $O_j$ be the union of the admissible boxes among the first $j$ tuples in the fixed rational enumeration; inadmissible tuples contribute nothing. Every compact subset of $O$ is contained in some $O_j$, since finitely many of the boxes cover it and their indices have a finite maximum. Excision [F4] identifies a relative class supported on such a compact set with its class in that $O_j$; any equality of compact-support classes is witnessed on one larger compact support by [F1], hence in some common later stage. These two representative tests identify $H_c^p(O;\mathcal L)$ with the colimit of the $H_c^p(O_j;\mathcal L)$ under extension. A local homology cycle uses finitely many compact simplex images, as does any chain bounding it, so the identical finite-cover test identifies $H_{n-p}(O;\mathcal L)$ with the homology colimit of the stages. Cap commutes with these extension and inclusion maps by its support formula in [F1]. The stage maps are isomorphisms by step 2.1; surjectivity and injectivity at a common stage therefore make $D_O$ an isomorphism. This argument uses an explicitly enumerated family inside one supplied chart, rather than selecting a countable chart family on the manifold. [F1, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Compactness supplies a finite cover $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ of $M$ by coordinate balls, each with a specified chart; selecting that finite list requires only finite choice. Induct on the number of balls. The one-ball case is [F2]. If duality holds on $A=B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_{j-1}$, the intersection $A\cap B_j$ is an open subset of the single chart $B_j$, so step 3.1 proves duality there. Step 1.1 now proves duality on $A\cup B_j$. After finitely many steps this gives duality on all of $M$. Since $M$ is compact, its support $M$ is terminal and $H_c^p(M;\mathcal L)=H^p(M;\mathcal L)$; its support orientation class is the integral orientation class by [F1]. This is exactly the displayed map. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Compact disconnected manifolds have finitely many components, since their open components cover them; the same finite construction already applies without choosing data on an infinite component family. Empty manifolds give zero groups; dimension zero and all integer degrees are covered by [F2] and the same exact windows. All cap, transport, extension and inclusion maps commute with a commuting coefficient-ring action, so their inverses do too. Only the finite chart cover is selected, and the sole infinite family used was the fixed rational enumeration inside one chosen chart; all representative lifts are made one at a time. Thus no AC, countable choice, smooth or PL structure, or triangulation theorem has been used. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $D$ and $D'$ are finite regular diagrams of the same nonempty oriented link, then their rational Lee cochain complexes are related by a cochain homotopy equivalence whose maps and homotopies preserve the decreasing quantum filtrations after normalization. Consequently their Lee homology groups with induced filtrations are isomorphic, and the spectral sequences from the rational Khovanov page onward are isomorphic. These filtered groups and pages therefore depend only on the oriented link.

## Statement references

[[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex|Rational Lee complex and decreasing quantum filtration]]

[[lem-khovanov-signed-local-cancellation-models|Explicit signed local cancellation coordinates]]

[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem|Finite oriented Reidemeister sequence]]

[Rasmussen, *Khovanov homology and the slice genus* (2004), §§2.3 and 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131v1)

[McMullen, *4-Manifolds*, §§5.5–5.6](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/4Mnotes.pdf)

[Lee, *On Khovanov invariant for alternating links* (2002), §3.2 and §4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0210213v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, two finite oriented diagrams of the same link, and their Lee complexes with normalized gradings.

[F1] The rational Lee saddle maps differ from the degree-preserving Khovanov maps only by terms that raise quantum degree by $4$ ([[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex]]).

[F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, diagrams of the same oriented link are related by finitely many planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister I, II, and III moves ([[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]]).

[F3] The signed local cancellation coordinates, inverse blocks, and homotopies for the two-crossing and three-crossing cubes are explicit in [[lem-khovanov-signed-local-cancellation-models]].

[F4] In the signed Reidemeister II model, the four state modules retract by explicit identity pivots to the identity matching in local cohomological degree one and quantum shift upward by one; the two Reidemeister III cubes cancel to a common three-term complex ([[lem-khovanov-signed-local-cancellation-models]]).

[F5] Cochain homotopy equivalence induces cohomology isomorphisms ([[def-chain-homotopy-equivalence]]).

[F6] The associated-graded Lee differential is the integral Khovanov differential, and its filtered spectral sequence has rational Khovanov cohomology as its homology page ([[lem-lee-filtered-spectral-sequence-and-two-orientation-classes]]).

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the axiom that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement.

1.1 In $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$, multiplication by $X$ is a dot operator with $X^2=1$, and $\Delta_L(z)=1\otimes Xz+X\otimes z,\qquad \Delta_Lm_L(a\otimes b)=Xa\otimes b+a\otimes Xb.$ The first identity follows by substituting $z=1,X$; the second follows by substituting the four basis pairs $1\otimes1,1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$. Thus the split and merge circle coordinates in [F3] remain valid for the Lee algebra, and the neck-cutting relation required in the Reidemeister II retraction holds with $X^2=1$. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 For a positive curl, the local differential is $(u,v)\mapsto u+Xv$ from the small-circle coordinates $1\otimes u+X\otimes v$ to the continuing arc. Change coordinates to $(u',v')=(u+Xv,v)$. The retraction has inclusion $i(w)=(0,w)$, projection $p(u',v')=v'$, and contraction $h(w)=(w,0)$ on the target; hence $pi=1$ and $1-ip=dh+hd$. For a negative curl, the local differential is $v\mapsto(Xv,v)$ into the small-circle coordinates. Change target coordinates to $(w'_1,w_X)=(w_1-Xw_X,w_X)$; then the map is $v\mapsto(0,v)$, and the retraction onto $w'_1$ has inclusion $i(w)=(w,0)$, projection $p(w'_1,w_X)=w'_1$, and contraction $h(0,w) = w$ from the $w_X$ target summand to the source. These formulas give $pi=1$ and $1-ip=dh+hd$. Before the writhe shifts, the positive survivor has quantum shift $-1$ and the negative survivor has quantum shift $+2$; the new $+1$ and $-2$ writhe shifts cancel them, respectively. In both cases the normalized homological degree agrees with the original. For Reidemeister II use the local maps $i(v)=(v,tv,0)$ and $p(v,w_1,w_X)=v-sw_X$ from [F3]; the identity $ts=x+y$ used in $dh+hd=1-ip$ is exactly the second identity in step 1.1. Its local homological and quantum shifts are canceled by the one positive and one negative crossing normalization changes. For Reidemeister III, the two cancellations in [F4] use only identity pivots and the same split coordinates, while writhe normalization is unchanged. All coordinate changes have pivots $\pm1$ and entries given by the Lee saddle and dot maps, so they preserve the decreasing filtration after normalization. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The Lee deformation terms raise $q$ by $4$ by [F1]. Each local coordinate change in step 2.1 is triangular with diagonal entries $\pm1$; its off-diagonal entries are saddle maps, whose degree-preserving parts are the corresponding Khovanov maps and whose other terms raise $q$ by $4$. Therefore the maps, inverses, and contraction homotopies preserve the decreasing filtration after applying the normalization shifts. On the associated graded, the R1 retractions are the degree-preserving parts of the displayed curl maps, and the RII/RIII retractions are the local Khovanov equivalences of [F4]. Their filtered maps induce isomorphisms on filtered homology; their associated-graded maps induce isomorphisms on the Khovanov page and, by page iteration, on every later spectral-sequence page. [F1, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [A1] and [F2], choose a finite sequence of oriented Reidemeister moves and planar isotopies from $D$ to $D'$; if $D=D'$, the empty sequence gives the identity. Planar isotopies rel crossing data simply relabel state circles and preserve all degrees. Compose the filtered equivalences from step 3.1 along this finite sequence. The composite has a filtered inverse up to filtered homotopy, so [F5] gives an isomorphism of filtered Lee homology and step 3.1 gives isomorphisms of all pages from rational Khovanov onward. This proves diagram independence. The only choice used is the finite move sequence supplied by $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the local algebraic maps themselves are explicit and choice-free. [A1, F2, F5, step 3.1, given, construct] ∎

## Definition

Inputs are integers $m,n\ge1$, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ in the standard finite coordinate bases, a vector $y\in\mathbb R^m$, a radius $\epsilon\ge0$, positive real step sizes $\alpha,\beta$, an initial primal-dual state $x^0\in\mathbb R^n$, $p^0\in\mathbb R^m$, a nonnegative integer sweep cap $N$, positive integer proximal-call caps $C_f,C_{g^*}$, and deterministic finite solver programs with Boolean certificate checkers for the two proximal calls. Each solver/checker record must be complete and well-formed. Admissible solver/checker pairs satisfy the soundness condition that an accepted output is an exact minimizer of its stated proximal subproblem; this is an input assumption, not a finite proof search performed by the procedure.

Set $f(x)=\|x\|_1$ and $g(u)=0$ when $\|u-y\|_2\le\epsilon$, with $g(u)=+\infty$ otherwise. Define the Fenchel conjugate by $g^*(p)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R^m}(\langle p,u\rangle-g(u))$. For a proper closed convex function $q$ and $t>0$, $\operatorname{prox}_{tq}(v)$ denotes the unique minimizer of $q(w)+\|w-v\|_2^2/(2t)$. Let $A^*$ be the Euclidean adjoint and let $\|A\|_2=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\|Av\|_2$. The target is
$$\min_{z\in\mathbb R^n}\|z\|_1\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|Az-y\|_2\le\epsilon.$$

Return **invalid-input** if dimensions or vectors do not match, if $\epsilon<0$, if $N$ is not a nonnegative integer, if either proximal cap is not a positive integer, if either step size is nonpositive, if either solver/checker record is missing or malformed, or if the exact strict check $\alpha\beta\|A\|_2^2<1$ fails. For admissible inputs initialize $\bar x^0=x^0$ and perform the exact primal-dual hybrid-gradient recurrence for at most $N$ sweeps:
$$p^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\beta g^*}(p^k+\beta A\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha f}(x^k-\alpha A^*p^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
Use the supplied solver/checker pairs and caps for the corresponding proximal calls. Propagate any **invalid-input**, **prox-call-failed**, or **prox-cap-exhausted** status and the state returned by the primal-dual procedure. If all $N$ sweeps complete, let $(x,p)$ be the final primal-dual state and perform these exact tests in order:

- If $p\ne0$, $A^*p=0$, and $|\langle p,y\rangle|>\epsilon\|p\|_2$, return **infeasible**.
- Otherwise, if $\|Ax-y\|_2\le\epsilon$, $\|A^*p\|_\infty\le1$, and $\|x\|_1=-\langle p,y\rangle-\epsilon\|p\|_2$, return **success** with $x$.
- If neither certificate passes, return **budget-exhausted** with the final state.

For $N=0$, test the initial state. The certificate tests use exact real comparisons. The procedure makes no guarantee that a finite run finds a certificate and makes no convergence or finite-termination claim.

id: alg-ip-solit-parameter-choice
kind: algorithm
title: SOLIT parameter choice on a geometric-variance grid
status: draft

dependency_level: 5
deps:
  - def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index

  - def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model
  - def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment
  - thm-ip-white-noise-spectral-sequence-representation
  - def-countable-choice
justified_by: []
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: not-applicable
axiom_use: "Countable Choice is inherited through the fixed SVD coordinates in the sequence model; the finite selector search and minimum-index choice are otherwise choice-free."
verification:
  precheck: n/a
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Housen Li and Frank Werner, Adaptive minimax optimality in statistical inverse problems via SOLIT, §§3.2.1–3.2.2"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356
    - title: "Vladimir Spokoiny and Niklas Willrich, Bootstrap tuning in ordered model selection, §§2.1–2.4"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.05034
---

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces, let $S=T^*T$, and let $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ be a fixed positive singular system with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Let $Z$ be a real isonormal Gaussian process on $Y$, meaning that $g\mapsto Z(g)$ is linear into $L^2$, is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. In the weak observation experiment $Y_x(g)=\langle Tx,g\rangle_Y+\sigma Z(g)$ with known noise standard deviation $\sigma>0$, use the ordered filter $q_\alpha$, the geometric-variance candidates $\alpha_0>\cdots>\alpha_{m_{\max}}$, and variances $v_m=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2$ from the preceding definition. For each candidate index $m$, the regularized estimator $\widehat x_m$ is the $L^2$ limit of its finite singular-coordinate sums; its $j$th coordinate is $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$, where $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ and $\xi_j=Z(u_j)$.

Take as input the observed coordinates $y_j:=Y_x(u_j)$. For each candidate $m$ and truncation index $N$, compute
$$
\widehat x_{m,N}^{\mathrm{obs}}:=\sum_{j=1}^N s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)y_jv_j.
$$
Since $y_j=s_j\theta_j+\sigma\xi_j$, these partial sums have the displayed latent-coordinate coefficients and converge in $L^2(\Omega;X)$ to $\widehat x_m$ by the preceding risk-decomposition result. The quantities $v_{m_1,m_2}$ and $z_{m_1,m_2}(x)$ are determined by the known operator, filter, noise level and Gaussian coordinate law.

For $0\le m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, set
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2
$$
and let $N_{m_1,m_2}$ be the norm of the centered estimator difference divided by $\sigma$. For $x>0$, define its upper quantile by
$$
z_{m_1,m_2}(x):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N_{m_1,m_2}>z)\le e^{-x}\}.
$$
Given fixed $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$, put $x_m:=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)$ and $\eta_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma z_{m_1,m_2}(x_{m_1})+\beta\sqrt{v_{m_1,m_2}}$. Accept an index $m_1$ exactly when $\|\widehat x_{m_1}-\widehat x_{m_2}\|_X\le\eta_{m_1,m_2}$ for every $m_2$ with $m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, and output the smallest accepted index $\widehat m$ and parameter $\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\widehat m}$. The condition for $m_1=m_{\max}$ is vacuous, so the finite search always returns an index. This rule uses only the observed sequence, the known operator and filter, the noise level, the fixed candidate grid, and $\beta,\gamma$; it does not use $x$ or its source index $\varphi$.

## Definition references

[[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index|Ordered filters, source conditions, and candidate-grid variance]]

[[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model|The positive-noise SVD sequence experiment]]

[[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment|The weak isonormal observation process]]

[[thm-ip-white-noise-spectral-sequence-representation|Independent Gaussian coordinates of white noise]]

[[lem-ip-solit-filter-risk-decomposition-and-monotone-bias|Well-definedness and bias–variance properties of the regularized estimators]]

[Li and Werner, *Adaptive minimax optimality in statistical inverse problems via SOLIT*, §§3.2.1–3.2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356)

[Spokoiny and Willrich, *Bootstrap tuning in ordered model selection*, §§2.1–2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.05034)

## Rule diagram

The arrows show the order of the finite procedure: form the regularized estimates, compare each candidate with every finer one using the two-index threshold, then return the smallest candidate that passes all of its comparisons. The diagram illustrates the algorithm only; the proofs of its properties use the coordinate definitions and inequalities.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node[draw,rounded corners,align=center] (data) at (0,0) {observations $y_j=Y_x(u_j)$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,align=center] (est) at (3,0) {observed-data partial sums $\widehat x_{m,N}$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,align=center] (tests) at (6,0) {all finer-index two-index tests};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,align=center] (choose) at (9,0) {smallest accepted index $\widehat m$};
  \draw[->] (data) -- (est);
  \draw[->] (est) -- (tests);
  \draw[->] (tests) -- (choose);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Remarks

The constant $\gamma$ controls the strength of the noise quantiles, while $\beta$ controls the bias tolerance. The quantile definition remains meaningful when a pairwise Gaussian difference is degenerate; then its upper quantile is zero.
