## Definition

Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ and $(Q,\mathcal Q)$ be measurable data and target spaces, with $\mathcal Q$ the Borel sigma-algebra of the target metric space. Let $P$ be a probability measure on the product space $(\mathsf Y\times Q,\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal Q)$, and let $\ell:Q\times Q\to[0,+\infty]$ be product-measurable, where $\ell(t,a)$ is the loss for target $t$ and action $a$. For a point reconstruction rule $g:(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)\to(Q,\mathcal Q)$ measurable with respect to the stated sigma-algebras, its risk under $P$ is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(g):=\int_{\mathsf Y\times Q}\ell(t,g(y))\,P(dy,dt).$$
For a randomized reconstruction rule given by a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathsf Y$ to $Q$, define
$$R_P(K):=\int_{\mathsf Y\times Q}\!\left(\int_Q\ell(t,a)\,K(y,da)\right)P(dy,dt).$$
The inner integral is measurable in $(y,t)$ by kernel integration; a deterministic rule is the special case $K_y=\delta_{g(y)}$. When $P_{\rm train}$ and $P_{\rm test}$ are specified joint laws on the same input-target space, the corresponding training-law risk and test-law risk are $R_{P_{\rm train}}(K)$ and $R_{P_{\rm test}}(K)$. Either value may be $+\infty$. This definition imposes no inequality between the two risks: any such comparison requires an additional assumption relating the joint laws or the rule's behavior under them.

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N_2(0,C)$ with $C=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, so its support is the first coordinate axis. With unit-variance Gaussian noise, compare the one-coordinate measurements $A_\perp=(0,1)$ and $A_\parallel=(1,0)$. Their expected information gains are $0$ and $\frac12\log 2$, respectively. The log-determinant formula remains defined although $C$ is singular.

## Example references

[Clason, Chapter 13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00617)

[Dashti and Stuart, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.6989)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $C=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, unit observation noise, and the two row operators in the Example.

[A1] AC is inherited from the finite Gaussian and EIG/KL interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The support of $N_n(m,C)$ is $m+\operatorname{Ran}(C)$, including singular $C$. [[lem-ip-singular-gaussian-support-and-pseudoinverse]]

[F2] The linear-Gaussian EIG formula applies to every positive-semidefinite $C$ and positive-definite noise covariance. [[thm-ip-linear-gaussian-information-gain-logdet]]

[F3] The natural logarithm is strictly increasing and $\log1=0$. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Example.

1.1 The range of $C$ is $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)^T\}$, so [F1] gives the stated support. Also $A_\perp C A_\perp^T=0$ and $A_\parallel C A_\parallel^T=1$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Applying [F2] with noise covariance $1$ gives $\operatorname{EIG}(A_\perp)=\frac12\log(1+0)=0$ and $\operatorname{EIG}(A_\parallel)=\frac12\log(1+1)=\frac12\log2$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

1.3 Since $2>1$, [F3] gives $\log2>\log1=0$. The second coordinate therefore contributes no information under the prior, while the first-coordinate measurement has strictly positive EIG. No inverse or determinant of $C$ is taken. [F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\sigma$ be the surface measure on $S^1$ used in the polar-coordinate formula, let $\Sigma=S^1\times(0,2)$ with product measure $\sigma\times dt$, and for real Schwartz functions $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ define
$$(A_0u)(z,t)=t\int_{S^1}u(z+t\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega),\qquad z\in S^1,\quad 0<t<2.$$
The map $A_0$ has a unique bounded extension $A:L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\Sigma;\mathbb R)$. For full-space $TV_2$, exact datum $f=0$, zero truth $u^\dagger=0$, and certificate $p^\dagger=0$, the truth is a minimum-TV exact solution satisfying the source condition. For every sequence $\alpha_n>0$ tending to zero, $w_n=0$, and $u_n=0$, each $u_n$ is a global minimizer of the quadratic TV functional and all nonzero canonical level sets and boundaries of $u_n$ and $u^\dagger$ are empty; their measure and extended Hausdorff distances are zero.

[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space|The real $L^2$ norm and pairing are defined by the integral.]]

[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere|The circle carries the surface measure used in polar integration.]]

[Iglesias, Mercier, and Scherzer, *A note on convergence of solutions of total variation regularized linear inverse problems*, §5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06495)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The circle $S^1$, product data measure on $\Sigma$, the circular mean formula in the Statement, and the full-space functional $TV_2$.

[A1] Countable Choice is required by the polar-coordinate, completed-product integration, Schwartz-density, and $L^2$-completeness suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation]]: $TV_2$ is the supremum of $\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over compactly supported smooth vector fields with $\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1$, hence $TV_2\ge0$ and $TV_2(0)=0$.

[F2] [[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate]]: a source certificate for an exact minimum-TV truth is $p\in L^2(\Sigma)$ with $A^*p\in\partial TV_2(u^\dagger)$.

[F3] [[def-ip-tv-level-set-representatives-and-boundaries]]: the positive levels are density-one representatives of $\{u>t\}$, negative levels of $\{u<t\}$, and equal empty canonical boundaries have extended Hausdorff distance zero.

[F4] [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $\sigma$ is finite and $|\int_{S^1}g\,d\sigma|^2\le\sigma(S^1)\int_{S^1}|g|^2\,d\sigma$.

[F5] [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]: for nonnegative measurable $h$, $\int_{\mathbb R^2}h(x)\,dx=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^1}h(r\omega)r\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$.

[F6] [[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]: nonnegative measurable functions can be integrated in either order over the circle and Euclidean data variables.

[F7] [[lem-schwartz-space-is-dense-in-l-two]]: under Countable Choice, complex Schwartz classes are dense in complex $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$.

[F8] [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]: under Countable Choice, real $L^2$ on every measure space is complete with its real integral inner product.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct operator bound followed by completion and zero-objective verification.

1.1 Put $S=\sigma(S^1)<\infty$. For each fixed $z\in S^1$, polar coordinates [F5] give
$$\int_0^2\int_{S^1}|u(z+t\omega)|^2t\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dt=\int_{B(z,2)}|u(x)|^2\,dx<\infty,$$
so for almost every $t>0$ the circle section is square-integrable. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] then gives
$$|(A_0u)(z,t)|^2\le S t^2\int_{S^1}|u(z+t\omega)|^2\,d\sigma(\omega).$$
Integrating in $z,t$, using polar coordinates [F5] around each center and Tonelli [F6], yields
$$\|A_0u\|_{L^2(\Sigma)}^2\le S\int_{S^1}\int_{|x-z|<2}|x-z||u(x)|^2\,dx\,d\sigma(z)\le2S^2\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2,$$
where $|x-z|<2$ and $\sigma(S^1)=S$. Thus $A_0$ is real-linear and bounded on real Schwartz functions with norm at most $\sqrt2S$. [A1, F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F7], real Schwartz functions are dense in real $L^2$: approximate a real function by complex Schwartz classes and take real parts, which cannot increase the $L^2$ error. By [F8], the target real $L^2(\Sigma)$ is complete. For any real $u\in L^2$, choose real Schwartz $u_k\to u$; step 1.1 makes $(A_0u_k)$ Cauchy, and its limit is independent of the approximating sequence by the same bound. This defines a bounded real-linear extension $A$ with $\|A\|\le\sqrt2S$. If another bounded extension agrees with $A_0$ on the dense Schwartz subspace, continuity forces equality on all of $L^2$. [A1, F7, F8, step 1.1, choose, construct]


3.1 The zero vector $u^\dagger=0$ satisfies $Au^\dagger=f=0$ and $TV_2(u^\dagger)=0$. Since $TV_2\ge0$, it minimizes TV over the exact solution set, regardless of the kernel of $A$. Its adjoint certificate $p^\dagger=0$ satisfies $A^*p^\dagger=0\in\partial TV_2(0)$ because $TV_2(v)\ge0=TV_2(0)+\langle0,v\rangle$ for every $v\in L^2$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

4.1 For $w_n=0$, the regularized objective is $J_n(u)=\tfrac12\|Au\|_2^2+\alpha_nTV_2(u)\ge0$, and $J_n(0)=0$. Hence $u_n=0$ is a global minimizer for every $n$. If $t>0$, $\{u_n>t\}=\varnothing$; if $t<0$, $\{u_n<t\}=\varnothing$. The same holds for $u^\dagger$, so all canonical density-one sets and ambient boundaries agree as empty sets; symmetric-difference measures and the extended Hausdorff distances are zero. The noise ratio is $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n=0<2\sqrt\pi$, so the full-space threshold is met. [F1, F3, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and use the standard oriented four-crossing figure-eight code of the explicit oriented Wirtinger-code lemma, with its positive based under-arc meridians $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ and compatible diagram access paths. Put $u=x_1$, $v=x_2$, and $w=uv^{-1}u^{-1}v$. Then $$\pi_1(E_{4_1})=\langle u,v\mid vw=wu\rangle,$$ with $u$ a positive meridian. In this presentation $$X_3=uvu^{-1},\qquad X_4=v^{-1}uvu^{-1}v=w^{-1}v$$ are the old $x_3,x_4$. The preferred longitude based compatibly with $u$ is represented by $$\lambda=X_4u^{-1}vX_3^{-1}.$$ In particular its trace in any representation is the trace of this explicit word. The formula does not identify a zero-homology centralizing word as a longitude without the diagram-parallel calculation.

## Statement references

[[lem-explicit-unknot-and-figure-eight-oriented-wirtinger-codes|Actual oriented four-crossing code]]

[[lem-link-peripheral-longitude-word-from-diagram|Actual based blackboard-parallel and self-writhe correction]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated oriented figure-eight code, compatible positive based diagram meridians, and the selected initial strand $x_1$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is retained for the named knot-exterior branch; all new operations are finite.

[F1] [[lem-explicit-unknot-and-figure-eight-oriented-wirtinger-codes]] gives $R_1:x_1x_2=x_3x_1$, $R_2:x_1x_4=x_4x_2$, $R_3:x_3x_2=x_2x_4$, and $R_4:x_3x_4=x_1x_3$. Its full proof shows $R_4$ follows from the first three. Its actual oriented under-arc cycle is $x_1\to x_2$ at $R_2$, $x_2\to x_3$ at $R_1$, $x_3\to x_4$ at $R_3$, $x_4\to x_1$ at $R_4$; the local coordinate charts specify the source and target sides and positive crossing signs.

[F2] [[lem-link-peripheral-longitude-word-from-diagram]] proves that a positive component traversal contributes the over-meridian with exponent $+1$ for source-to-target underpasses and exponent $-1$ for target-to-source. Their ordered product is the based blackboard parallel; multiplying by the initial meridian to minus the self-writhe gives its preferred zero-self-linking longitude.

## Proof

1.1 In [F1] eliminate $x_3$ using $R_1$ to get $X_3=uvu^{-1}$, then eliminate $x_4$ using $R_3$ to get $X_4=v^{-1}X_3v=v^{-1}uvu^{-1}v$. These are eliminations of explicitly defined generators, reversible by substitution, so impose exactly the remaining relation $R_2$; $R_4$ adds none by [F1]. With $w=uv^{-1}u^{-1}v$ the expression is $X_4=w^{-1}v$. Hence $R_2$ reads $uw^{-1}v=w^{-1}v^2$, which after right cancellation of $v$ is $uw^{-1}=w^{-1}v$, equivalently $vw=wu$. This proves the asserted presentation with the original positive meridian $u=x_1$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Start the oriented traversal at $x_1$. The four successive underpasses in [F1] give the table $$(R_2,x_4,+1),\quad(R_1,x_1,-1),\quad(R_3,x_2,+1),\quad(R_4,x_3,-1),$$ listing crossing, over-meridian and source/target exponent. Indeed $R_2,R_3$ go from the lower source side to the upper target side in those actual coordinate charts, while $R_1,R_4$ go from the upper target side to the lower source side. The determinants of their ordered over/under tangents have these same signs: each over-tangent points right and the under-tangent points respectively upwards or downwards. Thus the self-writhe is $1-1+1-1=0$. This checks both the traversal order and the sign instead of deriving a longitude solely from homological exponent zero. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the based blackboard parallel for that actual code is $x_4x_1^{-1}x_2x_3^{-1}$. The self-writhe correction in step 1.2 is zero, so this very word is the preferred longitude. Substitution from step 1.1 gives $X_4u^{-1}vX_3^{-1}$. The positive component traversal has degree one in its peripheral tube by [F2], and the zero-writhe correction gives zero self-linking; this is the actual preferred peripheral representative with the chosen initial access path. Evaluating it in any representation proves the trace assertion. No other longitude convention or external two-bridge peripheral formula is assumed. [A1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra] ∎

title: Parameter-uniform Borel jet realization and ray-tube patching
status: draft

        Borel summation along a compact bicharacteristic segment."

        author lecture notes
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.08123v1
      locator: "§3.4.3–3.4.5, PDF pp. 35–38: phase and amplitude jets solved along a
        curve and Borel realized."

## Statement

Let $X$ be a smooth manifold with an auxiliary smooth Riemannian metric, let $J=[a,b]$ be a compact interval, and let $\beta:J\to X$ be a smooth embedding with nonzero derivative. The normal fiber at $s$ is $N_s\beta=\{v\in T_{\beta(s)}X:g(v,\dot\beta(s))=0\}$. A **formal scalar jet along $\beta$** means a family of symmetric coordinate Taylor coefficients $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$ on a finite coordinate cover of a tubular neighborhood, smooth in $s\in J$, whose formal Taylor series transform on overlaps by the ordinary chain rule for a scalar function. Then there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $\beta(J)$ and, for either scalar field $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an $F\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb K)$ whose transverse derivatives along $\beta$ realize every prescribed transverse coefficient $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$. The construction is uniform for a compact parameter family of such jets when all coefficient seminorms are uniformly bounded. The same assertion holds on a finite union $A$ of embedded compact segments provided the induced full ambient jets satisfy full Whitney compatibility on that compact union: in each coordinate chart, for every $k$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, the degree-$k$ Taylor polynomials $P_x^k$ satisfy $D^\alpha P_x^k(y)-D^\alpha P_y^k(y)=o(|x-y|^{k-|\alpha|})$ uniformly for $x,y\in A$ as $|x-y|\to0$. Tangential components of a full jet are obtained by differentiating the transverse coefficients along each segment and applying the coordinate chain rule. For parameter families on the same finite union, require these Whitney remainder moduli as well as all coefficient bounds to be uniform. The single-segment construction requires no choice axiom.

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-smooth-whitney-extension-on-compact-sets]]

[[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]

[[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-riemannian-geometry]]

[[thm-local-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-for-manifold-integral-curves]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth manifold $X$ with an auxiliary Riemannian metric; a compact interval $J$; an embedded smooth curve $\beta$ with $\dot\beta\ne0$; and compatible smooth formal scalar jets $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$ on a finite coordinate cover of a tube around $\beta(J)$.

[F1] [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]: the auxiliary metric is smooth and positive definite; [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-riemannian-geometry]] supplies its Levi–Civita connection.

[F3] [[lem-ip-smooth-whitney-extension-on-compact-sets]]: continuous all-order ambient jets on a compact Euclidean set with full Whitney remainder compatibility have a choice-free smooth realization, uniformly when the bounds and moduli are common.

[F2] [[thm-local-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-for-manifold-integral-curves]]: the geodesic ODE has local solutions with smooth dependence on initial data, so the normal exponential map is smooth and has the identity differential on each zero-section fiber.


## Proof

1.1 First handle the endpoints, rather than taking an inverse chart on a closed parameter interval. At each endpoint choose one of the given tube charts containing it and a short adjacent segment, and express the whole formal jet there. In that chart extend the coordinate curve through the endpoint as follows. For $t<0$ at $a$ use the Borel series $\sum_{j\ge0}v_jt^j\chi(t/r_j)/j!$, where $v_j=\partial_s^j\beta(a)$ and a fixed smooth $\chi$ equals one near zero and has compact support. Choose $r_j$ to be the largest dyadic number at most $2^{-j}$ for which every derivative of order $m<j$ of the $j$th summand is bounded by $2^{-j}$; such a radius exists since these bounds are constants times $r_j^{j-m}$. The tails converge with all fixed derivatives, and their derivatives at zero are the prescribed $v_j$. Join this negative-side series to the original curve for $t\ge0$; matching all one-sided derivatives makes the join smooth. Repeat with the reversed parameter at $b$. The nonzero endpoint derivatives persist after shrinking the two extensions. They remain embedded: within each endpoint chart a coordinate with nonzero tangent derivative is strictly monotone; the endpoint image is separated from the compact remainder of the original curve, and the two distinct endpoint neighborhoods can be made disjoint. Thus $\beta$ extends to an embedded open interval containing $J$.
For each transverse jet coefficient $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$ in the chosen endpoint chart, extend that scalar coefficient by the same endpoint Borel construction, using its derivatives $\partial_s^jT_{i,\alpha}$ and a dyadic radius $r_{j,i,\alpha}$. For fixed $j,i,\alpha$, the finitely many derivative bounds of order $m<j$ guarantee a radius because the relevant terms scale as $r^{j-m}$; choose the largest admissible dyadic radius. For a parameter family, choose each such radius using the uniform bounds for that fixed coefficient and the finitely many derivative orders, so it is common across the family. Keep the given jet on $J$. On the newly added endpoint segments, define its components in every other chart by the ordinary coordinate chain rule from the single extended endpoint-chart jet. On overlaps with $J$ these transformed components agree with the given ones by the original formal compatibility. This preserves compatibility across the extended curve without requiring independently chosen extensions to satisfy new overlap identities. The construction is deterministic for the countable coefficient family and uses no choice axiom. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For the extended curve the normal exponential map $E(s,y)=\exp_{\beta(s)}y$ maps its normal bundle into $X$. Its derivative at $(s,0)$ sends the parameter direction to $\dot\beta(s)$ and is the identity on the normal directions, hence is an isomorphism by [F1] and [F2]. The inverse function theorem gives open local tube charts, including at the original endpoints. A uniform tube over a slightly larger compact interval exists: if injectivity failed at every shrinking radius, compactness would give two collisions converging to zero-section points, which embeddedness identifies; one local inverse chart then excludes them. Thus the tube image contains an open neighborhood of all of $\beta(J)$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 In one tube chart write the extended prescribed transverse Taylor series as $\sum_{k\ge0}P_k(s,y)$, with $P_k$ homogeneous of degree $k$ in $y$. Fix a smooth transverse cutoff equal to one near zero. For each $m<k$, let $C_{k,m}$ bound the derivatives of total order at most $m$ of $P_k(s,y)\chi(|y|/\epsilon)$ after removing the factor $\epsilon^{k-m}$, on the slightly extended compact parameter interval. Define explicitly $$\epsilon_k=\min\left\{2^{-k},\min_{0\le m<k}\left(\frac{2^{-k}}{1+C_{k,m}}\right)^{1/(k-m)}\right\}.$$ Every derivative of order $m<k$ of the $k$th cutoff summand is then bounded by $2^{-k}$. Therefore $F_i=\sum_k P_k\chi(|y|/\epsilon_k)$ is smooth on the open tube and has exactly the prescribed transverse jet: a cutoff is constant near zero, so the homogeneous polynomial contributes its own degree and no other. Step 1.1 and uniform coefficient bounds make these choices common for the stated parameter families. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Choose a finite smooth partition supported in the tube charts and summing to one near $\beta(J)$. The local realizations have the same full jets along the curve, since transverse data and their tangential derivatives determine them and the given coordinate chain rule identifies them. The Leibniz formula therefore makes the partition-weighted sum realize the same jets. In particular, derivatives of the partition sum of positive order vanish, and its zeroth derivative is one. This proves the original single-segment claim on an open neighborhood, including its endpoints, with no choice axiom. [step 2.1, step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

5.1 For the finite union, first take the induced full ambient jets specified in the Statement. Cover its compact image by finitely many smaller coordinate patches with closures inside larger patches. The intersection of the union with each smaller closed patch is compact; by the full Whitney hypothesis its coordinate jets meet [F3] in every order. Apply [F3] componentwise (two real components for complex values) and restrict the resulting smooth realization to the smaller patch. A finite smooth partition of unity on a neighborhood of the union now combines these realizations: at each point of the union all active realizations have its same full jet, so the same Leibniz cancellation as in step 4.1 applies. Uniform coefficient bounds and uniform Whitney moduli give common extension scales in [F3], hence uniform seminorms after this fixed finite partition. Pointwise compatibility only at intersections would not suffice for this step; the stated Whitney remainder condition controls pairs of nearby points on different segments as well. This proves the entire finite-union assertion and its parameter-uniform form. [F3, step 4.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be compact between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, let $\psi$ be a bounded nonnegative spectral index with $\psi(0)=0$, and let $x=\psi(|K|)w$ for some $w\in X$. Then $x\in N(K)^\perp$; consequently, among all $z\in X$ satisfying $Kz=Kx$, $x$ is the unique vector of minimum norm.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model|Compact Hilbert-space inverse model]]

[Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Chapter 3](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

[Hofmann and Mathé, *A Note on the Modulus of Continuity*, Section 1](https://www.tu-chemnitz.de/mathematik/ip/fulltext/hofmann_b76.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, compact $K:X\to Y$ between real or complex Hilbert spaces, an admissible index function $\psi$ with $\psi(0)=0$, and $x=\psi(|K|)w$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed by the compact singular-value decomposition supplier.

[F1] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]: A compact operator has orthonormal right singular vectors spanning $N(K)^\perp$, with $|K|v_j=s_jv_j$ for each positive singular value $s_j$, and $X=N(K)^\perp\oplus N(K)$.

[F2] [[def-ip-index-source-ball]] and [[def-compact-spectral-filter-and-qualification]]: A bounded spectral index acts by $\psi(s_j)$ on each right singular vector and by $\psi(0)=0$ on the kernel.

[F3] [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], and [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]: The Hilbert norm is induced by the inner product; if $x\perp n$, then $\|x+n\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|n\|^2$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], write $w=w_0+\sum_j w_jv_j$ in norm, with $w_0\in N(K)$ and the $v_j$ an orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$. The compact spectral multiplier in [F2] gives $x=\psi(|K|)w=\psi(0)w_0+\sum_j\psi(s_j)w_jv_j=\sum_j\psi(s_j)w_jv_j$. If the positive singular set is empty, this sum is zero and $x=0$. In every case, each term is orthogonal to $N(K)$, so continuity of the inner product gives $x\perp N(K)$. [given, A1, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 If $Kz=Kx$, then $n:=z-x\in N(K)$. By step 1.1, $x\perp n$, so [F3] gives $\|z\|^2=\|x+n\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|n\|^2\ge\|x\|^2$, with equality only when $n=0$, that is, $z=x$. Thus $x$ is the unique minimum-norm solution. [given, step 1.1, F3, algebra] ∎

id: lem-ip-smooth-whitney-extension-on-compact-sets
kind: lemma
title: Smooth Whitney extension on compact sets
status: draft

pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19

## Statement

Let $d,N\ge1$ and let $A\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact. For every multi-index $\alpha$ prescribe a continuous function $f_\alpha:A\to\mathbb R^N$. Define $P_a^k(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}f_\alpha(a)(x-a)^\alpha/\alpha!$. Assume the full Whitney compatibility conditions: for every $k\ge0$ and $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha P_a^k(b)-f_\alpha(b)=o(|a-b|^{k-|\alpha|})\quad(a,b\in A,\ |a-b|\to0),$$
uniformly in $a,b$. Then a smooth $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^N$ exists with $D^\alpha F|_A=f_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$. The construction uses no choice axiom. For a compact parameter family of jets on the same $A$, all choices of scales can be made common, and the resulting extensions have uniformly bounded seminorms on compact sets, provided all coefficient bounds and all the Whitney remainder moduli are uniform in that family.

## Statement references

[[thm-whitney-extension-for-finite-order-euclidean-jets]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact set and all-order Whitney field in the statement, or a family on that fixed set with uniform coefficient bounds and remainder moduli.

[F1] [[thm-whitney-extension-for-finite-order-euclidean-jets]] gives a choice-free $C^k$ extension of each finite compatible jet by its explicit dyadic Whitney-cube partition and lexicographically selected nearest points.


## Proof

1.1 The empty-set case has the zero extension. Otherwise use the fixed Whitney cubes and partition $\psi_Q$ constructed in [F1]: outside $A$, their side lengths satisfy $\ell(Q)\asymp\operatorname{dist}(Q,A)$, enlarged cubes have bounded overlap and comparable sizes when they meet, and $|D^\alpha\psi_Q|\le C_\alpha\ell(Q)^{-|\alpha|}$. These facts follow from the fixed maximal dyadic retention test and rescaled bump quotient in that proof, independently of the jet order. Put $\sigma(z)=\sum_Q\ell(Q)\psi_Q(z)$. This is smooth and positive off $A$, and for $t=\operatorname{dist}(z,A)$ it satisfies $c t\le\sigma(z)\le C t$ and $|D^\alpha\sigma(z)|\le C_\alpha t^{1-|\alpha|}$. Each derivative estimate follows by bounded overlap and the side-length comparison. Fix $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\chi=1$ on $(-\infty,1]$ and $\chi=0$ on $[2,\infty)$. Then $\eta_\delta(z)=\chi(\sigma(z)/\delta)$ equals one for $t\le\delta/C$, vanishes for $t\ge2\delta/c$, and obeys $|D^\alpha\eta_\delta|\le B_\alpha t^{-|\alpha|}$ on its transition, with constants independent of $\delta$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For each integer $k\ge1$, take the actual extension $H_k$ produced by [F1]'s fixed cube formula for $P_a^k$. It is $C^k$ everywhere and smooth off $A$, since there it is a locally finite sum of smooth partition functions times polynomials. All these extensions are thereby specified without selecting elements of unspecified nonempty sets. Put $\Delta_k=H_{k+1}-H_k$. It is $C^k$ and all its derivatives through order $k$ vanish on $A$. Taylor's formula at a nearest point of $A$, on a fixed compact neighborhood of $A$, gives for every $|\beta|\le k$ $$|D^\beta\Delta_k(z)|=o(t^{k-|\beta|})\qquad(t=\operatorname{dist}(z,A)\downarrow0),$$ uniformly near $A$. Indeed the top derivative is uniformly continuous and zero on $A$, and the lower estimates follow by Taylor's integral remainder along the segment from the nearest point. In the parameter-family case these remainders are uniform: the finite-order cube proof bounds $D^\alpha H_k-D^\alpha P_{a_z}^k$ by a constant times the specified Whitney remainder modulus; away from $A$ on a compact set its locally finite formula bounds every derivative by the coefficient bounds. Hence the $C^k$ moduli at $A$ used here are common to the family. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The product rule and step 1.1 show that, for $|\alpha|\le k$, $D^\alpha(\eta_\delta\Delta_k)$ is bounded by a constant $B_k$ times $\max_{|\beta|\le k}t^{|\beta|-|\alpha|}|D^\beta\Delta_k|$, wherever $\eta_\delta$ is nonzero. Choose $\delta_k$ as the largest dyadic number $2^{-j}$ satisfying $\delta_k\le2^{-k}$, $\delta_k\le\delta_{k-1}/2$ when $k>1$, and the finitely many uniform inequalities $$B_k|D^\beta\Delta_k(z)|\le2^{-k}t^{k-|\beta|}\quad(0<t\le2\delta_k/c,\ |\beta|\le k).$$ The set of admissible integers $j$ is nonempty by step 2.1 and has a least element, so these scales are deterministic. Enlarge $B_k$ to include the finitely many binomial constants. Then $$|D^\alpha(\eta_{\delta_k}\Delta_k)(z)|\le2^{-k}t^{k-|\alpha|}\qquad(|\alpha|\le k).$$ Uniform moduli in step 2.1 give the same scales for the parameter family. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Define off $A$ $$F=H_1+\sum_{k\ge1}\eta_{\delta_k}(H_{k+1}-H_k),$$ and set $F(a)=f_0(a)$ on $A$. At each point off $A$ the sum is locally finite because $\delta_k\to0$, so $F$ is smooth there. Fix $K\ge1$. Sufficiently near $A$, all factors $\eta_{\delta_k}$ with $k<K$ equal one, and telescoping gives $F-H_K=\sum_{k\ge K}\eta_{\delta_k}\Delta_k$. For $|\alpha|\le K$, the single $k=K$ term is $o(t^{K-|\alpha|})$ by step 2.1 and the product rule, while the sum over $k>K$ is $O(t^{K+1-|\alpha|})$ by step 3.1 and a geometric series, taking $t<1/2$. Thus every derivative through order $K$ of this difference off $A$ is $o(t^{K-|\alpha|})$. Extend the difference by zero on $A$. These estimates make its order-$K$ derivatives continuous and zero there; for lower orders the first-order difference quotient at any $a\in A$ tends to zero since $t\le|z-a|$, so induction verifies that the continuous derivative extensions are actual derivatives. Therefore $F-H_K$ is $C^K$ with zero $K$-jet on $A$. Since $H_K$ has the prescribed $K$-jet and $K$ is arbitrary, $F$ is smooth and realizes the entire field. The same estimates are uniform for the parameter family near $A$, and local finiteness gives uniform bounds on every compact set away from $A$. This proves the uniform assertion and completes the choice-free construction. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K_0,K_1$ be strict Morse presentations of smooth oriented knots. Define a horizontal deformation to be a smooth family $K_s(x)=(z_s(x),t(x))$ that fixes neighborhoods of all height critical points. Define a critical-point move to be a smooth family fixed outside one local arc containing a single nondegenerate critical point in a horizontal slab, such that horizontal deformations can narrow the moving arc to every sufficiently small width $\varepsilon$, each horizontal disk meets that arc in at most two points, and its Morse charts remain uniformly bounded. Let a standard hump birth or death mean insertion or deletion of the fixed local maximum-minimum pair used in the normalization.

The normalized unframed series $I(K)=Z(K)Z(H)^{-r(K)}$ is unchanged by orientation-preserving reparametrizations, horizontal deformations, critical-point moves, and standard hump births or deaths, and hence by any finite sequence of these moves. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If $K_0$ and $K_1$ are related by a smooth ambient isotopy, then $I(K_0)=I(K_1)$. For a fixed parenthesization, the KZ holonomy of a geometric braid is invariant under homotopies of its configuration path with endpoints fixed. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, finite Markov moves preserve the normalized series of strict Morse knot presentations of their one-component braid closures, and oriented Reidemeister moves preserve the normalized series of strict Morse presentations of the knots they represent.

The diagram shows a horizontal deformation: the local arcs move in the complex coordinate while the height coordinate and critical neighborhoods remain fixed. It illustrates the move convention and is not used as proof.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.85,thick]
  \draw[->] (-1.5,0) -- (1.7,0) node[right] {$\operatorname{Re}z$};
  \draw[->] (-1.5,0) -- (-1.5,3) node[above] {$t$};
  \draw (-0.4,0.2) .. controls (-0.2,0.9) and (-0.8,1.4) .. (-0.25,2.1);
  \draw[dashed] (0.1,0.2) .. controls (0.7,0.9) and (0.55,1.4) .. (0.9,2.1);
  \draw[dotted] (-0.4,0.2) -- (0.1,0.2);
  \draw[dotted] (-0.25,2.1) -- (0.9,2.1);
  \node at (-0.8,2.45) {same critical data};
  \node at (1.25,1.25) {$s\mapsto z_s$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references

[[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids|Configuration integral and normalized series]]

[[lem-kontsevich-configuration-space-compactification-faces|Finite-degree integration faces]]

[[lem-kontsevich-configuration-integral-convergence-needle-estimates|Absolute convergence and critical-needle estimate]]

[[lem-kontsevich-critical-point-normalization-and-associator|Hump birth/death normalization]]

[[lem-kontsevich-morse-tangle-composition|Tangle factorization used in the horizontal-deformation proof]]

[[lem-kontsevich-morse-isotopy-decomposition|Finite generic Morse movie under countable choice]]

[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem|Reidemeister presentation under countable choice]]

[[lem-markov-moves-preserve-oriented-closure-isotopy|Markov moves preserve oriented closures under countable choice]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §§8.4–8.8 and 10.1.1–10.1.4, printed pp. 228–243 and 269–273](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §2.5, PDF pp. 12–15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

[Le and Murakami, §§3–4, PDF pp. 4–7](https://letu.math.gatech.edu/Papers/UN_PAPER.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Strict Morse oriented knots, the degreewise unframed configuration series, the KZ connection, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ only for the ambient-isotopy, Markov, and diagrammatic corollaries.

[F1] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: the degree-$m$ coefficient is the sum of the logarithmic configuration integrals in the unframed 4T+1T quotient, and $I(K)=Z(K)Z(H)^{-r(K)}$.

[F2] [[lem-kontsevich-configuration-space-compactification-faces]]: each degree-$m$ chamber has a compact manifold-with-corners resolution whose codimension-one faces are level collisions, outer endpoints, critical levels, and compatible endpoint-collision faces.

[F3] [[lem-kontsevich-configuration-integral-convergence-needle-estimates]]: degreewise coefficients converge absolutely, and the total contribution of pairings meeting a critical needle of width $\varepsilon$ is $O(\varepsilon)$.

[F4] [[lem-kz-connection-flatness-and-braid-relations]]: the KZ form is flat, and its degreewise holonomy is invariant under fixed-endpoint homotopy of a path in the configuration space.

[F5] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]] and [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: the tangle 4T relation is the same local alternating relation on its skeleton, and the closed unframed quotient kills an isolated chord.

[F6] [[lem-kontsevich-critical-point-normalization-and-associator]]: insertion or deletion of the fixed standard hump multiplies $Z$ by $Z(H)$ and leaves $I$ unchanged.

[F7] [[lem-kontsevich-morse-isotopy-decomposition]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every smooth isotopy with strict Morse endpoint heights has a fixed-endpoint perturbation with finitely many isolated critical-pair births/deaths and critical-value crossings.

[F8] [[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]: the allowed oriented diagram moves are planar isotopies and the stated R1, R2, R3 moves with their orientation variants.

[F9] [[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, ambient isotopic oriented links admit regular diagrams connected by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves.

[F10] [[lem-each-oriented-reidemeister-move-is-realized-by-ambient-isotopy]]: every oriented Reidemeister move is realized by an ambient isotopy of its smooth link realization.

[F11] [[def-markov-conjugation-and-stabilization-moves]]: Markov equivalence is generated by conjugation and positive or negative stabilization/destabilization.

[F12] [[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]: each geometric braid has a smooth oriented link closure in $S^3$.

[F13] [[lem-markov-moves-preserve-oriented-closure-isotopy]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, each Markov move preserves the oriented closure up to ambient isotopy.

[F14] [[lem-kontsevich-morse-tangle-composition]]: unframed tangle integrals converge absolutely degreewise and factor under vertical composition.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Fix a degree $m$ for all configuration-integral arguments; all diagram spaces at degree $m$ are finite-dimensional.

1.1 An orientation-preserving reparametrization of $K$ preserves the cyclic order of every chord endpoint, the set of points at each height, the down-endpoint sign, and the pulled-back differential form. Hence every degree coefficient of $Z(K)$ is unchanged, and the reparametrization preserves $r(K)$. A positive affine change $t\mapsto at+b$ of the height also preserves each coefficient: substitute $u_j=at_j+b$ in the ordered level integrals; the branch pairings and logarithmic forms correspond term by term. Thus $I(K)$ is unchanged under both operations. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Cut the knot at regular levels inside the fixed critical neighborhoods. Choose the tangle pieces containing critical points within the neighborhoods fixed by the horizontal deformation; each intervening tangle has no critical points and has fixed boundary points. By [F14], their degreewise integrals compose, and gluing the cut endpoints restores exactly the original circle pairing: the cuts add no integration levels. Thus it suffices to compare one no-critical tangle $T$. Fix a degree-$m$ branch chamber for $T$. Since $T$ is embedded and has no critical points, distinct branches at one height have a uniform positive horizontal separation on the compact closed chamber, so every logarithmic factor is smooth there. For a nonzero branch difference $\Delta=z_i-z_j$, $d\log\Delta=d\Delta/\Delta$ is closed because $d(d\Delta/\Delta)=-(d\Delta\wedge d\Delta)/\Delta^2=0$. Extend each factor to the full differential in $(t_1,\dots,t_m,s)$; the product sum $\omega_m$ is then closed, with equal-level coefficients interpreted in the 4T quotient. Apply Stokes to the compactified chamber cylinder from [F2]. [F1, F2, F5, F14, construct, algebra]

1.3 On an outer endpoint face of $T$, the boundary points are fixed by the cut inside a fixed critical neighborhood, so the restriction of $\omega_m$ has no $ds$ component and is zero. At an equal-level face, if the two chords use the same two branches, their logarithmic 1-forms coincide and their wedge is zero. If they use four distinct branches, swapping the two chord choices gives the same diagram with the opposite wedge sign, so the terms cancel. If they use exactly three branches, the 4T relation [F5] groups the six choices into the common diagram coefficient times
$\alpha_{12}\wedge\alpha_{23}+\alpha_{23}\wedge\alpha_{31}+\alpha_{31}\wedge\alpha_{12}$,
where $\alpha_{ij}=d\log(z_i-z_j)$. Set $f=z_1-z_2$, $g=z_2-z_3$, and $h=z_3-z_1=-(f+g)$. Direct expansion gives
$\alpha_{12}\wedge\alpha_{23}+\alpha_{23}\wedge\alpha_{31}+\alpha_{31}\wedge\alpha_{12}
=\bigl(\frac1{fg}-\frac1{g(f+g)}-\frac1{f(f+g)}\bigr)\,df\wedge dg=0$.
These cases exhaust equal-level pairings. Every remaining collision face is a corner of codimension at least two by [F2], so it does not occur in the codimension-one Stokes boundary. Therefore the only nonzero boundary integrals are the two ends $s=0,1$, which are equal. Summing the finitely many chambers proves equality of each intervening tangle series. The fixed critical pieces and the closure then give $Z(K_0)=Z(K_1)$ coefficientwise by [F14]; $r(K_s)$ is constant, so $I(K_0)=I(K_1)$. [F2, F5, F14, step 1.2, algebra]

1.4 By [F6], a standard hump birth multiplies the preliminary series by $Z(H)$ and increases $r(K)$ by one. Thus $I(K^+)=Z(H)Z(K)Z(H)^{-r(K)-1}=I(K)$; deleting the hump is the reverse equality. [F1, F6, algebra]

2.1 By definition of the move, horizontal deformations narrow the affected arcs in both presentations to needles of width $\varepsilon$ for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon$; steps 1.2–1.3 leave $I$ unchanged under these preliminary deformations. The pairings with no endpoint on the needle have identical integrals before and after the local move. The difference of the remaining degree-$m$ sums has norm at most the sum of the two needle contributions, at most $2C_m\varepsilon$ by [F3]. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives equality of each degree coefficient; the number of maxima is unchanged during this move, so the normalized series is equal. [F1, F3, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]


3.1 On an interval of the generic movie [F7] with no fold, each nondegenerate critical point follows a smooth branch by the implicit function theorem. Subdivide the interval finitely so that each moving critical point fits in one small local arc and the critical-value order is fixed on each open subinterval. Move the critical neighborhoods one at a time by small critical-point moves as in step 2.1 until their heights match a fixed reference slice; compactness of the parameter interval makes this a finite sequence. On each complementary monotone arc the endpoint heights then agree with those of the reference slice. Reparametrize that arc by the unique increasing map matching its height coordinate to the reference height. The inverse function theorem gives smooth dependence away from the fixed critical collars, and the local Morse coordinates extend the reparametrization smoothly to their endpoints. The remaining variation changes only the complex branch functions at fixed heights, hence is a horizontal deformation as in steps 1.2–1.3. At a transverse critical-value crossing, the two critical points are distinct in the embedded knot and their horizontal positions have positive separation. Subdivide the crossing into finitely many small moves of one critical point at a time; each stays in a needle arc and is covered by step 2.1. Thus $I$ is constant between and across all critical-value crossings. [F1, F3, F5, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1]

4.1 At a fold, [F7] gives one local maximum-minimum birth or death. The affected arc is isolated in a small ball and has nonzero complex tangent at the degenerate point. Rotate the complex coordinate so $u=\operatorname{Re}z$ is a local parameter, then shrink the ball so $u$ is strictly monotone along the entire arc. Interpolating $\operatorname{Im}z$ to zero at fixed $(u,t)$ remains an embedding because distinct arc points have distinct $u$. On the resulting planar arc, move the two nondegenerate critical points one at a time to the maximum and minimum of the fixed hump, using critical-point moves; choose the hump scaled so its endpoint and critical heights agree. Each monotone subarc now has the same endpoint heights as the standard hump, so the unique height-matching reparametrization is orientation-preserving and smooth up to the critical collars in their Morse coordinates. The birth is therefore, up to the reparametrizations, horizontal deformations, and critical-point moves already handled, the fixed standard hump insertion. Step 1.4 gives equality across the fold. Since [F7] supplies finitely many folds and crossings, steps 3.1–4.1 imply equality along the entire generic movie. [F3, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 1.4, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 If $K_0,K_1$ are smoothly ambient isotopic, restrict the isotopy to the oriented circles and apply [F7] to obtain a generic movie with the same endpoint embeddings. Steps 3.1–4.1 show that $I(K_0)=I(K_1)$. The only axiom used in this ambient-isotopy conclusion is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ from [F7] and the explicitly stated genericity supplier. [F7, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Each Markov move preserves the oriented braid closure under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ by [F13]; a finite Markov sequence therefore gives ambient isotopic closures, and step 5.1 gives equal normalized series. Each oriented Reidemeister move is likewise realized by ambient isotopy by [F10]; a finite sequence preserves $I$. Under [F9], any two regular diagrams of the same oriented link have such a finite move sequence. [F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 For a fixed parenthesization, a braid path is a path in the configuration space of distinct strand points. Its KZ holonomy is unchanged under fixed-endpoint path homotopy by [F4]. This use is choice-free; changes of parenthesization and the associator coherence equations are handled by a separate result. [F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $F\subset B^4\subset\mathbb R^4$ be a compact connected oriented smoothly properly embedded surface of genus $g$, with its supplied smooth boundary collar and oriented boundary the knot $K\subset S^3$. There is an orientation-preserving ambient diffeomorphism $\Psi:B^4\to B^4$ equal to the identity on a neighborhood of the outer boundary, and $0<\varepsilon<1$, such that $\Psi(F)\cap B^4_\varepsilon$ is exactly a flat two-disk in a plane through $0$. The surface $\Psi(F)\setminus\operatorname{int}B^4_\varepsilon$, in the explicitly round shell $B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}B^4_\varepsilon\cong S^3\times[0,1]$, is a connected smooth oriented knot cobordism between $K$ and a standard unknot, with genus $g$ and Euler characteristic $-2g$. Both boundary components have product collars in a shell identification fixing $K$ and the inner sphere. The ambient diffeomorphism $\Psi$ fixes a sufficiently small restriction of the supplied outer collar; the shell coordinates may be adjusted there to make that surface collar a product. No assertion about the complement of an arbitrary embedded four-ball is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice and the compact smoothly embedded surface in the unit Euclidean ball.

[F1] Compact embedding isotopies extend to ambient isotopies supported in any prescribed neighborhood of their tracks, under countable choice. The source may have boundary, and no endpoint stationarity is required by clause4 ([[thm-isotopy-extension]]).

[F2] Smooth proper surface charts, the supplied smooth boundary collar and its restrictions have the meaning specified in [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]].

[F3] The smooth Euclidean inverse function theorem holds without choice ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]]). Apply it to projection from a smooth surface chart for the local graph, and to the map sending a collar chart to its boundary parameter and radial coordinate for the collar reparametrization. At a boundary point use the smooth chart extension and restrict its inverse to the half-space.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is the precise axiom inherited from [F1].

## Proof

1.1 **Move a genuine ambient ball by translations.** Choose an interior point $p$ of $F$ and a radius $r>0$ with $|p|+r<1$. The embeddings of the closed radius-$r$ ball $D$ centered at $p$ given by $x\mapsto x-tp$, $0\le t\le1$, stay in the interior of $B^4$: the norm of a point in their image is at most $(1-t)|p|+r<1$. Their compact track has a neighborhood with closure in the interior of $B^4$. By [F1] this isotopy extends ambiently in $\mathbb R^4$ with support in that neighborhood. Its time-one map fixes an ambient neighborhood of the outer boundary, preserves orientation and takes $p$ to $0$, while agreeing with translation on the whole ball $D$. Replace $F$ by its image. No conclusion about any nonround ball complement has been drawn. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 **Flatten the surface on an actual neighborhood of zero.** Let $P$ be the tangent plane of the new surface at $0$. Orthogonal projection to $P$ has invertible derivative on that tangent plane, so [F3] writes the surface as $(u,h(u))$ in $P\oplus P^\perp$, with $h(0)=0$ and $Dh(0)=0$. Choose one sufficiently small closed disk in the $u$ coordinates. Its graph is a compact embedded disk in the interior of $B^4$. The maps $u\mapsto(u,(1-t)h(u))$ are an isotopy of that compact disk, since projection to $u$ remains injective with injective differential. Choose the disk small enough that its entire compact track lies in the interior of $B^4$. Apply [F1] again there, obtaining an ambient orientation-preserving diffeomorphism that fixes an ambient neighborhood of the outer boundary and maps the full graph disk to the flat disk. The surface is now exactly $P$ near $0$: the disk interior is an open neighborhood of $0$ within the embedded surface. Its complement outside a smaller such graph disk is compact and misses $0$, so it has positive distance from $0$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than that distance and the flat disk radius, and less than $1$. Then the surface meets the actual round ball $B^4_\varepsilon$ precisely in $P\cap B^4_\varepsilon$. Compose the two ambient diffeomorphisms to obtain $\Psi$. They fix a common ambient neighborhood $N$ of the outer boundary. For the supplied collar $c:K\times[0,\eta)\to F$, the open set $c^{-1}(N)$ contains $K\times\{0\}$. A finite cover of the compact circle by product neighborhoods gives one $0<\delta<\eta$ with $c(K\times[0,\delta])\subset N$. Thus $\Psi$ fixes this sufficiently small restriction of the supplied collar; no fixedness of its entire image is asserted. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 **Use only the concentric round shell.** The explicit map $(z,t)\mapsto(\varepsilon+(1-\varepsilon)t)z$ is a diffeomorphism $S^3\times[0,1]\to B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}B^4_\varepsilon$. The inner boundary curve is the great circle $P\cap S^3_\varepsilon$, hence a standard unknot after radial rescaling; an orthonormal basis of $P$ extends by finite linear algebra to an oriented orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^4$, giving an orientation-preserving linear rotation identifying it with the usual equator. Near the inner sphere the surface is a radial product in $P$, so this radial shell coordinate already supplies its product collar. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Respect a restriction of the given outer surface collar.** For completeness the original outer surface collar need not be radial. In its smooth proper half-space chart the radial coordinate has nonzero inward derivative along a transverse collar direction. In a supplied parametrization of that collar, [F3] and compactness of its boundary circle therefore reparametrize it, for $r$ near $1$, as $(r f_r(\theta))$ with $f_r:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ a smooth embedding family and $f_1$ the original parametrized $K$. By [F1] on $S^3$, choose a smooth ambient family $G_r$ with $G_1=\mathrm{id}$ and $G_r f_1=f_r$. Choose a smooth function $h(r)$ equal to $r$ near $1$ and to $1$ near the inner edge of this thin outer collar, with values in the parameter interval where $G$ is defined. The fiberwise diffeomorphism $(z,r)\mapsto(G_{h(r)}^{-1}z,r)$ is the identity at $r=1$ and near that inner edge, so extends as the identity over the rest of the shell; near the outer end it takes the surface to the literal product $K\times[1-\delta,1]$. Thus adjust the shell identification by this map. It leaves the inner sphere and the boundary knot fixed, and changes neither genus nor the fixedness of a sufficiently small restriction of the supplied outer collar by $\Psi$ from steps 1.1–2.1. Removing one interior disk from a connected surface leaves it connected, retains genus and adds one boundary circle; its Euler characteristic decreases from $1-2g$ to $-2g$. Orient the resulting shell surface as a cobordism from the inner unknot to $K$. Reversing the interval and the surface orientation gives the reverse direction if desired; a half-turn reverses the orientation of the standard unknot. This proves the full genus, orientation and collared-end assertions under countable choice, using only an explicitly concentric shell. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $a>b\ge2$ be coprime integers, choose integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $a\alpha+b\beta=1$, and put $G=\langle x,y\mid x^a=y^b\rangle$, $h=x^a=y^b$, $\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta$ and $\lambda=h\mu^{-ab}$. Consider all irreducible representations $\rho:G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$, where irreducible means having no common invariant complex line. The common peripheral eigenvalue pairs $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$ have reduced Zariski closure with vanishing ideal $$(1+M^{2a}L)\quad\hbox{if }b=2,\qquad (M^{2ab}L^2-1)\quad\hbox{if }b>2.$$ More precisely, $\rho(h)=\epsilon I$ with $\epsilon=-1$ when $b=2$ and $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ when $b>2$; each permitted sign occurs in a family realizing every point of the graph $L=\epsilon M^{-ab}$ except possibly finitely many meridian values. The displayed ideal is the ideal of the entire irreducible eigenvalue locus, not just of the exhibited families. No choice axiom is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite presentation and words in the Statement, with ordinary complex matrix algebra. Every nonconstant one-variable complex polynomial has a complex root; this is the fixed algebraic closure of $\mathbb C$, not a simultaneous selection of roots.

[F1] A two-by-two matrix satisfies $A^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)A+\det(A)I=0$, as entrywise multiplication verifies. A determinant-one matrix with two distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable by its two eigenvectors.

## Proof

1.1 **Only the specified scalar signs can occur.** The element $h$ commutes with $x$ and $y$, since it is a power of each. A nonscalar two-by-two complex matrix either has two distinct eigenvalues or has a repeated eigenvalue and a unique one-dimensional eigenspace. In the first case every commuting matrix preserves each eigenspace; in the second it preserves the kernel of the nonzero nilpotent part, which is that unique line. Thus a nonscalar $\rho(h)$ would provide a line invariant under both generator matrices, contradicting irreducibility. Consequently $\rho(h)=\epsilon I$, and determinant one forces $\epsilon=\pm1$. If $b=2$ and $\epsilon=1$, the equation $Y^2=I$ for $Y=\rho(y)$ makes $Y$ diagonalizable because $(z-1)(z+1)$ has distinct roots. Its determinant one forces its two eigenvalues to be equal, so $Y=I$ or $-I$. An eigenline of $\rho(x)$ would then be invariant under both generators. Hence only $\epsilon=-1$ is possible for $b=2$. In every case $\rho(\lambda)=\epsilon\rho(\mu)^{-ab}$, so every common peripheral eigenvalue pair satisfies $L=\epsilon M^{-ab}$, including nonsemisimple meridian matrices. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 **Choose noncentral roots with noncentral meridian powers.** Fix a permitted sign. For a positive integer $n\ge2$ choose $\zeta_n=\exp(2\pi i/n)$ when $\epsilon=1$ and $\zeta_n=\exp(\pi i/n)$ when $\epsilon=-1$. The first case is used only for $n\ge3$, since $\epsilon=1$ is permitted only when $a,b>2$. Set $\xi=\zeta_a$ and $\eta=\zeta_b$. They satisfy $\xi^a=\eta^b=\epsilon$ and neither is $\pm1$. Also $\xi^{\beta}\ne\xi^{-\beta}$ and $\eta^{\alpha}\ne\eta^{-\alpha}$. Indeed the Bezout identity gives $\gcd(\beta,a)=\gcd(\alpha,b)=1$. In the positive-sign case equality of the two powers would imply $a\mid2\beta$ or $b\mid2\alpha$, impossible for the relevant integer greater than two. In the negative-sign case the roots have orders $2a,2b$; equality would imply $a\mid\beta$ or $b\mid\alpha$, also impossible. These explicit roots require no choice family. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **An actual irreducible matrix family.** Put $s=\eta+\eta^{-1}$ and, for $v\in\mathbb C$, define $$X=\begin{pmatrix}\xi&0\\0&\xi^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y_v=\begin{pmatrix}v&1\\v(s-v)-1&s-v\end{pmatrix}.$$ The second matrix has determinant one and trace $s$, hence distinct eigenvalues $\eta,\eta^{-1}$. Therefore $X^a=Y_v^b=\epsilon I$, and these are actual representations of the displayed presentation for every $v$. Since $X$ has distinct eigenvalues, a common invariant line must be one of its coordinate lines. The upper-right entry of $Y_v$ is $1$, so the second coordinate line is never invariant. The first is invariant exactly when $v(s-v)-1=0$, whose two roots are $\eta,\eta^{-1}$. Thus the representation is irreducible for every $v$ other than these two values. [F1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 **The meridian trace varies with a nonzero linear coefficient.** Polynomial division modulo $(z-\eta)(z-\eta^{-1})$ gives $Y_v^\alpha=cY_v+dI$ for constants $c,d$ independent of $v$, including negative $\alpha$ because both eigenvalues are nonzero. Explicitly $c=(\eta^\alpha-\eta^{-\alpha})/(\eta-\eta^{-1})\ne0$ and $d=\eta^\alpha-c\eta$. With $r=\xi^\beta$, one obtains $$\operatorname{tr}(Y_v^\alpha X^\beta)=c(r-r^{-1})v+cr^{-1}s+d(r+r^{-1}).$$ The coefficient is nonzero by step 1.2. For each $M\ne0$ there is consequently exactly one $v$ giving meridian trace $M+M^{-1}$. The two forbidden $v$ values of step 2.1 exclude at most four meridian values, since each equation $M+M^{-1}=q$ is a quadratic after multiplication by $M$. Discard also $M=\pm1$. For every remaining $M$ the meridian has distinct eigenvalues $M,M^{-1}$, so an eigenline with eigenvalue $M$ exists and the longitude, being $\epsilon\mu^{-ab}$, acts there by $L=\epsilon M^{-ab}$. This gives the claimed cofinite graph family for each permitted sign. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Exact ideals, including all exceptional representations.** Evaluation $L\mapsto\epsilon M^{-ab}$ defines a surjection $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]\to\mathbb C[M^{\pm1}]$. Its kernel is $(LM^{ab}-\epsilon)$: multiplying by a monomial reduces any expression to a polynomial in $L$, and division by the monic $L-\epsilon M^{-ab}$ over $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1}]$ leaves exactly its evaluated constant remainder. A Laurent polynomial vanishing on the cofinite graph family of step 3.1 therefore has zero evaluated remainder, since a nonzero one-variable Laurent polynomial has only finitely many nonzero roots. Its ideal is precisely this graph ideal. Step 1.1 puts every irreducible eigenvalue pair, including all exceptional meridian values, in the permitted graphs, and step 3.1 supplies a dense family in each. The ideal of the entire locus and of its closure is consequently the intersection of these graph ideals. For $b=2$ the single sign gives $(LM^{2a}+1)$. For $b>2$ put $q=LM^{ab}$; the two ideals $(q-1)$ and $(q+1)$ are comaximal since their difference is $2$, an invertible scalar. Their intersection equals their product: writing $1=A+B$ with $A$ in one and $B$ in the other expresses an element of the intersection as a sum of two product elements. Thus their intersection is $(q^2-1)=(M^{2ab}L^2-1)$. Each graph ideal is prime because its quotient is the Laurent domain just displayed; their intersection is radical. This proves the exact reduced closure assertions by finite algebra with no assumption about completeness of an unspecified image. [step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC for the library KL/EIG convention.

Assume the finite-candidate algorithm's hypotheses. A candidate is admissible when it is dimension-valid and its symmetric noise covariance is positive definite; let $\mathcal V$ be the ordered list of admissible candidates and let $\mathcal F=(d\in\mathcal V:c_d\le B)$ in the inherited order. For each $d\in\mathcal F$, let $U_d=\operatorname{EIG}(d)-c_d$ be its exact utility. In exact-real mode, if $\mathcal F$ is nonempty, the algorithm returns the first index in $\mathcal F$ attaining $\max_{d\in\mathcal F}U_d$; if $\mathcal V$ is empty it returns `all-inadmissible`, and if $\mathcal V$ is nonempty but $\mathcal F$ is empty it returns `budget-exhausted`.

For the floating-point mode, suppose each $d\in\mathcal F$ has a computed score $\widehat U_d$, a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $\widehat Z_d$, a successful factor $\widehat R_d$, and certified radii $\delta_d\ge0$, $0\le\rho_d<1$, and $\lambda_d\ge0$ such that
$$\|\widehat Z_d-Z_d\|_2\le\delta_d,\qquad \|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I_{m_d}+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\rho_d,$$
where $Z_d$ is the exact Cholesky-whitened matrix in the algorithm's Definition, and
$$\left|\widehat U_d-\left(\frac12\log\det(\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T)-c_d\right)\right|\le\lambda_d.$$
For example, the matrix-radius component can use the information-matrix perturbation result in its single-design, unit-weight $W=I$ specialization: if $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$, $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$, $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$, and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$, then $\delta_d\ge2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$ is sufficient, with any separate formation residual added. A rounded triangular-solve backward-error bound must be converted to the needed forward matrix error using a verified conditioning bound. The rounded-Cholesky residual must follow from a successful factorization under its stated floating-point assumptions; in particular, the cited bound assumes $m u<1/5$, where $m=20m_d+20$ and $u$ is unit roundoff. The value $\lambda_d$ must bound the rounded logarithms, their summation, and cost evaluation. Set $\varepsilon_d=\frac{m_d}{2}\left(\delta_d+\frac{\rho_d}{1-\rho_d}\right)+\lambda_d$. If the algorithm returns a candidate $\widehat d$ with $\widehat U_{\widehat d}\ge\max_{d\in\mathcal F}\widehat U_d-\tau$, then
$$\max_{d\in\mathcal F}U_d-U_{\widehat d}\le\tau+\varepsilon_{d^*}+\varepsilon_{\widehat d}\le\tau+2\max_{d\in\mathcal F}\varepsilon_d,$$
where $d^*$ is any exact maximizer. If the certified score intervals show that the selected candidate's lower endpoint exceeds every earlier candidate's upper endpoint and is at least every later candidate's upper endpoint, it is the first exact maximizer. The matrix and factor radii must be certified under the published solve, information-matrix, rounded-Cholesky, and log-determinant error hypotheses; $\lambda_d$ must additionally cover rounded logarithm, summation, and cost evaluation.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-finite-candidate-information-design|The exact scan, feasible set, tie rule, and floating-point certificate interface.]]

[[lem-information-matrix-perturbation-bound|Uniform sensitivity errors control the weighted information-matrix error.]]

[[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability|A one-point design with the linear sensitivity maps and unit weight instantiates the finite-design perturbation setting.]]

[[lem-logdet-information-perturbation-bound|A common positive eigenvalue floor controls log-determinant error.]]

[[thm-rounded-cholesky-componentwise-and-normwise-backward-error|A successful rounded Cholesky factorization supplies a residual bound under its operationwise hypotheses.]]

[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws|The natural logarithm turns positive products into sums.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The algorithm and candidate data in the Statement, and, for each floating-point candidate, the certified matrices and error radii stated there.

[A1] AC is inherited through the algorithm's EIG/KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The exact candidate utility is the linear-Gaussian EIG minus its declared cost; exact-mode updates replace the stored candidate only on a strictly greater score, and floating mode selects the first score at least $\max_d\widehat U_d-\tau$. [[alg-ip-finite-candidate-information-design]]

[F2] For $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma_d\succ0$, $\operatorname{EIG}(d)=\frac12\log\det(I+\Gamma_d^{-1/2}A_dCA_d^T\Gamma_d^{-1/2})$. [[thm-ip-linear-gaussian-information-gain-logdet]]

[F3] A symmetric positive-definite matrix has a unique Cholesky factor; its triangular solves are the unique exact solutions and its triangular determinant is the product of its diagonal entries. [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] [[thm-cholesky-solves-hermitian-positive-definite-systems-and-has-half-the-lu-factorisation-cost]] [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]

[F4] Determinants are multiplicative on same-sized finite square matrices. [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]

[F5] A positive-semidefinite matrix has a unique positive-semidefinite square root. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]

[F6] For a one-point approximate design with $\xi=1$, linear sensitivity maps on $\mathbb R^{m_d}$, and symmetric positive-definite weight $W=I$, if $Z=J^TJ$, $\widehat Z=\widehat J^T\widehat J$, $\|J\|_2\le K$, and $\|\widehat J-J\|_2\le\eta$, the information-matrix perturbation is at most $2K\eta+\eta^2$. [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]] [[lem-information-matrix-perturbation-bound]]

[F7] For symmetric matrices on a segment with eigenvalue floor $\alpha>0$, $|\log\det B-\log\det A|\le p\|B-A\|_2/\alpha$ in dimension $p$. [[lem-logdet-information-perturbation-bound]]

[F8] A successful rounded Cholesky factorization has its stated spectral residual bound when the operationwise arithmetic and unit-roundoff hypotheses hold. [[thm-rounded-cholesky-componentwise-and-normwise-backward-error]]

[F9] A successful rounded triangular solve has a componentwise backward-error bound under its stated normal-range and unit-roundoff hypotheses. [[lem-rounded-triangular-substitution-componentwise-backward-error]]

[F10] The natural logarithm is multiplicative on positive products: $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$, and $\log(x^2)=2\log x$ for $x>0$. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 For a valid candidate, $\Gamma_d=L_dL_d^T$ and $V_d=L_d^{-1}A_d$, so $Z_d=V_dCV_d^T$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Hence $H_d=I_{m_d}+Z_d$ is positive definite and has the Cholesky factor used by the exact algorithm. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Put $Q_d=A_dCA_d^T$ and $W_d=\Gamma_d^{-1/2}$. The square-root identity [F5] gives $\Gamma_d+Q_d=\Gamma_d^{1/2}(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)\Gamma_d^{1/2}$. By [F4], $\det(\Gamma_d+Q_d)=\det(\Gamma_d^{1/2})^2\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)=\det(\Gamma_d)\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)$. Also step 1.1 gives $\Gamma_d+Q_d=L_dH_dL_d^T$, so [F3]–[F4] give $\det(\Gamma_d+Q_d)=\det(\Gamma_d)\det(H_d)$ with $\det(\Gamma_d)=(\det L_d)^2>0$. Dividing proves $\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)=\det(H_d)$. By [F2], the exact EIG is $\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)$. By [F3], $\det(H_d)=\det(R_dR_d^T)=(\prod_j(R_d)_{jj})^2$; all Cholesky diagonal entries are positive, so [F10] gives $\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)=\sum_j\log(R_d)_{jj}$. Thus the algorithm's exact score equals $U_d$. [A1, given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 For the exact scan, after the first feasible candidate the stored candidate is the first maximum of that one-element prefix. When the next candidate is processed, [F1] says a strictly larger score replaces it; an equal or smaller score leaves it in place, preserving the earliest maximizing index. Repeating this finite comparison through the ordered feasible list proves the final stored candidate is the first global maximizer. The validity and budget tests likewise make `all-inadmissible` and `budget-exhausted` exactly the two stated empty-feasible-set cases. [given, F1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 In floating-point mode, when $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$ and $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$, [F6] supplies $\delta_d\ge2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$ from certified bounds $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$ and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$; any rounded matrix-formation residual is included in the supplied $\delta_d$. Both $I+Z_d$ and $I+\widehat Z_d$ have eigenvalues at least $1$, and every matrix on their segment does too. Applying [F7] gives $|\log\det(I+\widehat Z_d)-\log\det(I+Z_d)|\le m_d\delta_d$. [given, F6, F7, algebra]

3.2 Put $E_d=\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I+\widehat Z_d)$. Every matrix $I+\widehat Z_d+tE_d$ has quadratic form at least $(1-t\rho_d)\|v\|_2^2\ge(1-\rho_d)\|v\|_2^2$, since $I+\widehat Z_d\succeq I$ and $\|E_d\|_2\le\rho_d<1$. Applying [F7] on this segment yields $|\log\det(\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T)-\log\det(I+\widehat Z_d)|\le m_d\rho_d/(1-\rho_d)$. Under the successful rounded-factorization hypotheses, [F8] provides such a residual radius. [F9] supplies only a backward-error constraint for triangular solves; any forward matrix error used in $\delta_d$ must additionally account for conditioning. [given, F7, F8, F9, algebra]

3.3 The certificate's $\lambda_d$ bounds the remaining rounded log, summation, and cost evaluation. Combining it with steps 3.1–3.2, the log-determinant perturbation [F7], and the factor $1/2$ in the EIG formula gives $|\widehat U_d-U_d|\le\varepsilon_d$. [given, F7, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

4.1 Let $d^*$ maximize exact utility and let $\widehat d$ be the selected computed $\tau$-maximizer. By [F1] and the hypothesis, $\widehat U_{\widehat d}\ge\max_d\widehat U_d-\tau$. Then $U_{d^*}\le\widehat U_{d^*}+\varepsilon_{d^*}\le\max_d\widehat U_d+\varepsilon_{d^*}$, while $U_{\widehat d}\ge\widehat U_{\widehat d}-\varepsilon_{\widehat d}\ge\max_d\widehat U_d-\tau-\varepsilon_{\widehat d}$. Subtracting gives the stated gap bound. [given, F1, step 3.3, algebra]

4.2 If the selected interval's lower endpoint exceeds each earlier upper endpoint and is at least each later upper endpoint, then every earlier exact utility is strictly smaller and every later exact utility is no larger. Thus the selected candidate is the first exact maximizer. [given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be an $n$-singular oriented knot with $n\ge0$ transverse double points and chord diagram $D\in\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$. Choose disjoint crossing balls and a common height presentation so that the two branches at every singular point are monotone in height inside their ball, all $2^n$ resolutions are strict Morse, and their height functions and number $r$ of local maxima agree outside the crossing balls. Define
$$
\Delta^n I(K):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\}^n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i\right)I(K_\epsilon).
$$
Then $\Delta^n I(K)$ has zero homogeneous components in degrees $m<n$, its degree-$n$ component is exactly $D$, and all remaining terms have degree greater than $n$. For $n=0$, the degree-zero component is the empty diagram with coefficient $1$. The conclusion is in the unframed 4T+1T chord-diagram completion and makes no rational-coefficient claim.

The drawing shows a singular crossing and the two oriented resolutions. The plus resolution is the one with positive determinant crossing sign; the drawing fixes no analytic estimate and is not used in the proof.

## Statement references

[[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative|Alternating resolution sum and singular-knot convention]]

[[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations|4T and unframed 1T quotient]]

[[lem-kontsevich-braid-and-knot-isotopy-invariance|Normalized knot-isotopy invariance under countable choice]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §8.8.1, printed pp. 239–240](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §2.6, PDF pp. 16–17](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, an $n$-singular oriented knot, its disjoint transverse crossing balls, and the common strict Morse height of all resolutions.

[F1] [[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative]]: an $n$-singular knot has $n$ disjoint transverse double points; its $n$th finite difference is the alternating sum of the $2^n$ positive and negative resolutions.

[F2] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: $Z(K)$ is the degreewise configuration integral in the unframed 4T+1T completion, and $I(K)=Z(K)Z(H)^{-r(K)}$.

[F3] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: an isolated chord is zero in the unframed target, and the 4T relation identifies the local endpoint slides.

[F4] [[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]: the positive crossing sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ in the positively oriented projection plane, with the positive Artin half twist assigned sign $+1$.

[F5] [[lem-kontsevich-configuration-integral-convergence-needle-estimates]]: each fixed-degree sum converges absolutely; contributions with an endpoint in a width-$\varepsilon$ critical needle are uniformly $O(\varepsilon)$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the countable-choice axiom used by the ambient-isotopy supplier.

[F6] [[lem-kontsevich-braid-and-knot-isotopy-invariance]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the normalized series is invariant under ambient isotopy, and changing a strict Morse presentation of a resolution does not change its value.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Fix a degree cutoff $N$ and work in the finite-dimensional quotient through degree $N$.

1.1 Choose pairwise disjoint balls around the $n$ singular points so each resolved pair of branches is monotone in height inside its ball. The same height function is used on every resolution, so $r(K_\epsilon)=r$ for all $\epsilon$. If necessary, move the singular knot by an isotopy supported in the balls to separate the singular heights and make the crossings monotone; each corresponding resolution is carried by the same ambient isotopy, so [F6] leaves $\Delta^n I(K)$ unchanged. [given, F1, F4, A1, F6, construct]

1.2 Expand the degree-$m$ part of $\Delta^n I(K)$ as a finite sum of pairing integrals over the resolution choices. If a pairing has no chord endpoint in the $i$th crossing ball, its integrand and diagram are independent of the sign $\epsilon_i$, because the two resolved knots agree outside that ball. Summing over $\epsilon_i=+1,-1$ therefore cancels that term. Hence every nonzero contribution to the $n$-fold difference must meet each of the $n$ balls. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 A chord joining endpoints in two different crossing balls, or one crossing ball and the complement, has denominator bounded away from zero: the balls are disjoint, and the singular immersion has no other intersections. Its endpoint-level interval in the shrinking local ball is $O(\varepsilon)$, so the mean-value bound for $d\log(z-z')$ makes its integral $O(\varepsilon)$. The other factors remain absolutely integrable by [F5], and there are finitely many degree-$m$ pairing types. Since the alternating resolution sum is unchanged when each crossing ball is shrunk by [F6], every term containing such a chord has zero limiting contribution and therefore vanishes in the finite difference. If $m<n$, a surviving pairing must touch all $n$ balls with only $m$ chords, so at least one chord joins distinct regions; its contribution vanishes by this estimate. Thus every homogeneous component of degree $m<n$ is zero. [A1, F1, F5, F6, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 For one singular point, let $w_\pm(t)=z_{1,\pm}(t)-z_{2,\pm}(t)$ be the relative complex coordinate of its two monotone branches in the positive and negative resolutions. The loop obtained by following $w_+$ and then the reverse of $w_-$ winds once positively around $0$: the two resolutions are the opposite half-turns of the relative vector. Hence $\frac1{2\pi i}\left(\int d\log w_+-\int d\log w_-\right)=1$. For two upward branches this is the difference of angular changes $+\pi-(-\pi)=2\pi$. Reversing both branch orientations leaves the determinant sign unchanged and changes the down count by two; reversing exactly one branch reverses both the crossing sign and the factor $(-1)^{\downarrow}$. Thus under [F4] the coefficient is $+1$ for every oriented positive resolution. Pairings with an endpoint outside the crossing ball vanish in the shrinking limit by step 2.1. The surviving degree-one local term is therefore exactly the one-chord diagram joining the two preimages. [F2, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 In degree $n$, the only terms that survive shrinking all crossing balls have one internal one-chord term in each ball; any cross-chord vanishes by step 2.1, and every ball must be met by step 1.2. The $n$ local level variables range independently over their crossing slabs. The global ordered simplex partitions into the finitely many possible orders of these variables; on each part the coordinate-permutation sign is canceled by the same wedge-permutation sign, so summing the regions is the product integral by Fubini. Each local factor is $1$ by step 3.1. The resulting circle chord diagram is exactly $D$, since its chord endpoints are the preimages of the corresponding double points and the chords are unordered. By [F3], it is interpreted in the unframed 4T+1T quotient, so the resulting class is $[D]$. Therefore the degree-$n$ component of $\Delta^n Z(K)$ is $[D]$. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra, construct]

5.1 The common factor $Z(H)^{-r}$ can be pulled outside the alternating sum because all resolutions have the same $r$. Its degree-zero coefficient is $1$, so multiplication by it preserves the first nonzero homogeneous component: the degree-$n$ component remains $D$, and all lower degrees remain zero. For $n=0$, the alternating sum is $I(K)$ and its degree-zero coefficient is $1$ by [F2]. Thus $\Delta^n I(K)=D+\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{>n}$ in every case. [F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎
