## Definition

Fix a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ and a bounded measurable functional
$f:E\to\mathbb R$, with $\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in E}|f(x)|<\infty$. All
target laws below are probability measures on this same space. If a model or
discretization originally uses another state space, specify its measurable
embedding into $E$ and compare its pushforward law; no identification of
different state spaces is implicit. A **posterior law** here is the probability
law for the unknown at the specified computation stage, conditional on the same
fixed observed data. For a probability law $\mu$, write
$\mu(f):=\int_E f\,d\mu$.

Name the successive posterior laws as follows: $\mu_\star$ is the intended
target; $\mu_{\rm model}$ is the posterior under the selected statistical or
physical model; $\mu_{\rm solver}$ is the posterior after replacing the exact
forward or PDE solution by the declared numerical solver output; and
$\mu_{\rm disc}$ is the posterior after the declared finite-dimensional
discretization. These labels refer to the exact adjacent laws recorded for the
computation, even when two stages happen to agree.

Let $K$ be the implemented probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$. An
**invariant law** $\pi_K$ for $K$ is a probability measure satisfying
$$\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi_K(dx)=\pi_K(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal E).$$
Choose and report which invariant law is used if $K$ has more than one. If no
invariant law has been established, the invariant-kernel and burn-in terms
below are unavailable; they are not set to zero. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a
time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative to its
natural filtration, with initial probability law $\lambda$. For burn-in length
$b\ge0$ and retained sample size $N\ge1$, set
$$\bar f_{b,N}:=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N f(X_{b+j}),$$
and let $\mathbb E_\lambda$ denote expectation under this initial law and the
chain's transition randomness.

When all stages are present, define the component errors
$$\begin{aligned}\delta_{\rm model}&:=|\mu_\star(f)-\mu_{\rm model}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm solver}&:=|\mu_{\rm model}(f)-\mu_{\rm solver}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm disc}&:=|\mu_{\rm solver}(f)-\mu_{\rm disc}(f)|,\\ \delta_K&:=|\mu_{\rm disc}(f)-\pi_K(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm burn}&:=|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|,\\ \delta_{\rm MC}&:=|\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}-\bar f_{b,N}|.\end{aligned}$$
The last component is random and the earlier components are fixed for the
declared data and computation. The **posterior computation error budget** is
$$\mathcal B_f:=\delta_{\rm model}+\delta_{\rm solver}+\delta_{\rm disc}+\delta_K+\delta_{\rm burn}+\delta_{\rm MC}.$$
If a computation stops before one of these stages, report the shorter reference
chain and its component terms. The term $\delta_K$ measures the invariant-law
discrepancy induced by the implemented transition rule; it is not a one-step
distance between kernels. A one-step kernel error cannot replace it without a
separate perturbation theorem with its own hypotheses.

The successive scalar references are arranged as this directed error chain;
each arrow is labelled by the absolute difference of its endpoints.

```tikzcd
\mu_\star(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm model}"] &
\mu_{\rm model}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm solver}"] &
\mu_{\rm solver}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm disc}"] &
\mu_{\rm disc}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_K"] &
\pi_K(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm burn}"] &
\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N} \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm MC}"] &
\bar f_{b,N}
```

The budget is a bookkeeping bound only when its components are supplied with
estimators or verified bounds; an unavailable component is reported as
unquantified rather than silently set to zero. In particular, invariance alone
does not provide a burn-in estimate, a mixing rate, or a Monte Carlo error
estimate.

[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable|A bounded functional has a finite expectation under a probability law.]]

[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel|A probability kernel has probability-measure rows and measurable event evaluations.]]

[[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel|An invariant law satisfies $\pi K=\pi$ on every measurable event.]]

[[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel|A Markov chain has the stated kernel as its conditional one-step law relative to its filtration.]]

[[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger|A scalar error ledger names successive reference targets and signed adjacent-stage errors.]]

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X=H=\mathbb R^2$, $K=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$, $C_0=I$, $m_0=0$, and $\epsilon=1$. Let $U$ be a Borel Gaussian prior with mean $0$ and covariance $I$, independent of a jointly Gaussian centered family $Z$ on $H$ that is linear into $L^2$ with covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(k)]=\langle g,k\rangle_H$, and set $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+Z(g)$. For $h=(1,1)$, the MAP feature operator is $B=K^*K=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)$, so $h$ is not an eigenvector. The test probe is $\Phi_h=(1/2,2/5)$ and the threshold is zero. For every $t>0$, the parameter $x_t=t(-1,1)$ is null for the feature $\langle x,h\rangle$, and the MAP test rejection probability is $G(3t/\sqrt{41})$, which tends to one as $t\to\infty$. Thus this unrestricted null class has supremum rejection probability one, although no finite $t$ attains it.

## Example references

[[alg-ip-gaussian-map-feature-test|Gaussian MAP feature test]]

[[thm-ip-map-test-level-and-power|Level, power, and weighted regularization of Gaussian MAP feature tests]]

[[thm-ip-unrestricted-map-test-can-have-level-one|A non-eigenfeature can give an unrestricted Gaussian MAP test level one]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-dimensional Gaussian inverse model and feature in the Example.

[F1] The MAP probe and threshold are $\Phi_h=K C_0^{1/2}(C_0^{1/2}K^*KC_0^{1/2}+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}C_0^{1/2}h$ and $c_h=\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle-\langle m_0,h\rangle$. [[alg-ip-gaussian-map-feature-test]]

[F2] The exact rejection probability for a nonzero probe is the Gaussian tail determined by its mean and noise variance. [[thm-ip-map-test-level-and-power]]

[F3] If the commuting MAP operator has a non-eigenfeature, the unrestricted null rejection supremum is one. [[thm-ip-unrestricted-map-test-can-have-level-one]]

## Proof

1.1 Since $C_0^{1/2}=I$ and $K^*K=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)$, one has $R=(B+I)^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/5)$ and $\Phi_h=KRh=(1/2,2/5)$. Also $c_h=0$. The vector $(1,1)$ is not an eigenvector because $B(1,1)=(1,4)$ is not a scalar multiple of it. Thus the compact finite-dimensional example satisfies the commutation and non-eigenfeature hypotheses of [F3]. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 For $x_t=t(-1,1)$, $\langle x_t,h\rangle=0$. The test mean is $\langle Kx_t,\Phi_h\rangle=-t/2+4t/5=3t/10$, while $\|\Phi_h\|^2=1/4+4/25=41/100$. Hence [F2] gives rejection probability $G((3t/10)/(\sqrt{41}/10))=G(3t/\sqrt{41})$, which tends to one. By [F3] the supremum over the unrestricted null is one; the finite $t$ tail is strictly below one. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ with its canonical real inner product, and for each $j\in\mathbb N$ let $e_j$ be the sequence whose $j$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are $0$. Then $(e_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H$. For every $x=(x_j)\in H$, the truncations $\sum_{j<N} x_je_j$ converge in $H$ to $x$ as $N\to\infty$ (the $N=0$ sum is empty and equals $0$), and $\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb N}|x_j|^2$.

## Statement references

[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set|the canonical square-sum norm and finite-tail property on real sequence space]]

[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis|an orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family with dense linear span]]

[[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space|real ell-two is complete for its canonical norm]]

[Teschl, §2.1, full notes](https://www.uomustansiriyah.edu.iq/media/lectures/9/9_2018_12_07!10_23_44_AM.pdf)

[Bühler and Salamon, Definition 2.62 and Exercise 2.64](https://uomustansiriyah.edu.iq/media/lectures/9/9_2021_09_21!12_02_01_AM.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real sequence Hilbert space $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ and the coordinate vectors $(e_j)$.

[F1] Square summability means $\sum_j|x_j|^2<\infty$, the norm squared is that sum, and finite tails of the sum can be made arbitrarily small. [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]

[F2] The canonical inner product makes real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ a complete real Hilbert space. [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]]

[F3] An orthonormal family is a Hilbert basis when its closed linear span is the whole Hilbert space. [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]

## Proof

**Given:** $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ and $e_j$ with coordinate $1$ at $j$ and $0$ elsewhere.

1.1 For all $i,j$, the canonical inner product gives $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$, so the coordinate family is orthonormal. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $x=(x_j)\in H$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By [F1], a finite set of coordinates has complement square-sum less than $\varepsilon^2$. Every finite subset of $\mathbb N$ is contained in $\{j:j<N\}$ for some $N\in\mathbb N$, so choose $N$ such that $\sum_{j\ge N}|x_j|^2<\varepsilon^2$. The coordinate formula gives $\|x-\sum_{j<N} x_je_j\|_2^2=\sum_{j\ge N}|x_j|^2<\varepsilon^2$. Thus finite linear combinations of the $e_j$ are dense in $H$; by [F3], the orthonormal family is a complete orthonormal basis. The same tail estimate proves the stated truncation convergence, and the norm identity is [F1]. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $W$ be a connected Hausdorff space with a supplied basis of contractible open neighborhoods, $o\in W$, $\pi=\pi_1(W,o)$, and $N\triangleleft\pi$. Put $G=\pi/N$ and let $k$ be any commutative unital ring. Use first-loop-first concatenation in $\pi$. There is a canonical based normal path-class cover $p:W_N\to W$ with $\pi_1(W_N)=N$, whose right deck action is
$$[\gamma]\cdot g=[a^{-1}*\gamma]\quad\text{when }a\in\pi\text{ represents }g.$$
Let $\mathcal R_x$ be the free $k$-module on $p^{-1}(x)$, with its induced right $k[G]$ action and transport along lifted paths. Each fiber is free of rank one as a right $k[G]$-module. Its base fiber is identified with $k[G]$ by the constant-path lift. Thus transport around a based loop $a$ is left multiplication by its quotient image $g^{-1}$.

For this specified right local system, the actual singular chain complex is naturally isomorphic to $C_*(W_N;k)$ as a complex of right $k[G]$-modules, and there is a natural isomorphism
$$H_1(W;\mathcal R)\cong (N/[N,N])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k.$$
The right action on the last group is $[u]\otimes c\mapsto[a^{-1}ua]\otimes c$ for $g=[a]\in G$. A based loop $u\in N$ with coefficient $1$ corresponds to $[u]\otimes1$. In particular it represents zero in $H_1(W;\mathcal R)$ exactly when it lies in the kernel of $N\to(N/[N,N])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k$. Taking $N=P^s\pi$ gives exactly the next mixed-series kernel $P^{s+1}\pi$ with coefficient ring $k$. For a based continuous map carrying $N$ into a normal subgroup $N\prime$ of the target fundamental group, these identifications commute with its induced homology maps and quotient-group coefficient maps. This includes every connected Hausdorff manifold, with boundary allowed, and every connected finite polyhedron. No finite CW structure, compactness, finite generation of $\pi$, or choice principle is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The based Hausdorff space, its basis of contractible open neighborhoods, the normal subgroup and coefficient ring. A singular chain is a finite linear combination of singular simplices. Its first-vertex local boundary transports the coefficient along the first edge on the face omitting the first vertex; the other faces retain that coefficient. Tensor products over $\mathbb Z$ are generated by pairs subject to the additive and balancing relations.

## Proof

1.1 The supplied contractible basis consists of path-connected open sets, so connectedness implies path-connectedness: path components are open and their complements are open. Form the set of paths $\gamma:o\to x$, identifying two with the same endpoint when the loop $\gamma*(\gamma')^{-1}$ belongs to $N$. The subgroup laws make this an equivalence relation. For a member $U$ of the supplied contractible basis and a path $\gamma$ ending in $U$, let $U_{[\gamma]}$ consist of $[\gamma*\eta]$ for paths $\eta$ lying in $U$ and starting at that endpoint. The projection to $U$ is bijective because any two such paths with the same endpoint are homotopic rel endpoints in $U$. If two such sets over $U$ meet they coincide; for two different basis neighborhoods, a smaller basis neighborhood of a common endpoint shows their intersections contain a basic set of this same form. They therefore define a topology for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets each homeomorphic to $U$. Surjectivity uses a path to each individual endpoint, rather than selecting all such paths. Thus this is an actual covering space constructed without a representative section. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For completeness the degree-one constant-coefficient calculation needs no universal-coefficient theorem. For any path-connected based space $Y$, concatenate paths by the first-loop-first rule. A constant edge is the boundary of a constant triangle; a path homotopy gives the boundary of its two-triangle prism up to constant endpoint edges; and $uv$ is homologous to $u+v$ by mapping a triangle to the concatenated path with vertex parameters $0,1/2,1$. A reversed path is homologous to the negative path, since its concatenation with the original contracts by retracing. These finite relations show that $[u]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c\mapsto c[u]\in H_1(Y;k)$ is a well-defined additive balanced map $S:\pi_1(Y)_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k\to H_1(Y;k)$. For a fixed finite cycle $z=\sum_e c_e e$, choose paths $\gamma_v$ from the basepoint to the finitely many endpoint images and put $$T_\gamma(z)=\sum_e [\gamma_{e(0)}*e*\gamma_{e(1)}^{-1}]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c_e.$$ Finite choice follows by finite induction in ZF, so these paths exist without an axiom of choice. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 A path $\gamma$ lifts from the constant-path point by $t\mapsto[\gamma|_{[0,t]}]$, with the restricted path reparametrized and held stationary after its endpoint. This is continuous on the basic sets of step 1.1, and reaches $[\gamma]$, so $W_N$ is path-connected. For any fixed starting lift, path lifting exists uniquely by finite subdivision into evenly covered basis neighborhoods. A homotopy lifts uniquely by the same finite-grid construction on its compact square: choose a finite fine grid subordinate to the inverse-image cover and extend sheet by sheet, with uniqueness on overlaps. The square is compact metric, so this finite construction uses no choice principle. Hence $p_*$ is injective on fundamental groups, and its image consists exactly of based loops whose lifted endpoint is the constant-path point, that is, exactly $N$. This identifies $\pi_1(W_N)$ with $N$ by the actual projection. The same lifting statement for a singular simplex follows directly by sending a point to the lift obtained along the straight segment from its first vertex; segments joined by a triangle are homotopic inside the simplex, so this gives the unique continuous lift with prescribed first vertex. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 Another finite path family changes each loop term by $d_{e(0)}-d_{e(1)}$ in the abelianization. After tensoring, its total coefficient at a vertex is that of the cycle boundary, hence zero. Thus $T_\gamma(z)$ has one uniquely defined value $T(z)$, independent of paths or enlargement of the finite endpoint list. On a singular triangle the loops for edges $01,12,02$ satisfy $L_{01}L_{12}=L_{02}$ because the triangle fills their concatenation, so $T$ kills its signed boundary. For any finite two-chain use the finite union of its vertex images to get the same conclusion termwise, with its $k$ coefficients. Thus $T$ descends to homology. The relations in step 1.2 say $\gamma_{e(0)}*e*\gamma_{e(1)}^{-1}$ is homologous to $\gamma_{e(0)}+e-\gamma_{e(1)}$; in the weighted sum the extra path terms cancel by the cycle condition. Hence $ST=\mathrm{id}$. On a based loop use the constant connector at its endpoint, giving $TS=\mathrm{id}$ on every generator $[u]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c$. This proves the natural isomorphism $H_1(Y;k)\cong\pi_1(Y)_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes k$. Naturality follows by mapping a finite connector family forward; independence then removes that family from the map. No paths to all points of $Y$ and no basis of an infinite vector space were chosen. [step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 For $g\in G$ and any representative loop $a$, define the right action by $[\gamma]\cdot g=[a^{-1}*\gamma]$. Replacing $a$ by another representative gives the same path class, since $N$ is normal; replacing $\gamma$ by an equivalent path also does. The action law follows from $b^{-1}*a^{-1}=(a*b)^{-1}$, and its maps carry the basic sets in step 1.1 to basic sets. On each fiber it is free and transitive: for paths $\gamma,\delta$ to the same endpoint take the quotient class of $\gamma*\delta^{-1}$, which sends $[\gamma]$ to $[\delta]$. The formula specifies the action uniquely without choosing representatives for all quotient elements. Free $k$-linearization of each fiber gives $\mathcal R_x$; path transport commutes with this right action because it appends a path at the end, while deck action prepends $a^{-1}$. Thus it is a right-$k[G]$ local system, each fiber individually having a torsor point as a free basis. At the basepoint the constant-path point is a specified basis, and transport along $a$ sends it to $[a]=[1]\cdot g^{-1}$, giving exactly the stated inverse convention and a right-linear map. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 A basis generator in the local chain group consists of a base singular simplex $\sigma$ together with one point of the covering fiber over its first vertex and a scalar in $k$. Send it to the unique lift of $\sigma$ with that first vertex, given in step 2.1, with the same scalar. Pairs of this kind are in bijection with covering singular simplices: projection gives the inverse map. Both directions are uniquely specified on generators, hence define inverse maps on all finite chains without selecting a lift for each base simplex. For the face omitting the first vertex, the first point of the lifted face is the transport of the old first point along that edge, exactly the local coefficient boundary rule. The other faces keep the first point. Thus the bijection commutes with all signed boundary terms. It commutes with the right deck action on generators too, so gives the claimed actual chain isomorphism of right $k[G]$-module complexes. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Apply steps 1.2 and 2.2 to $Y=W_N$ and combine with steps 2.1 and 4.1. A based loop $u\in N$ lifts to the based loop whose projection is $u$, so its coefficient-one class maps precisely to $[u]\otimes1$. For the right action, move the constant-path base lift by $g=[a]$. The lift of $a^{-1}$ joins the old base lift to that new one. Rebase the translated lift of $u$ by this path and its inverse; its projection is $a^{-1}ua$. Connector contributions cancel in first homology by step 1.2, so this gives the stated conjugation action on $N_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes k$. Different representatives of $g$ change it by an inner automorphism of $N$, trivial on $N_{\mathrm{ab}}$. The zero criterion is now exactly the displayed isomorphism and its coefficient-one formula; for $N=P^s\pi$ this is the defining next mixed-series kernel. For a based continuous map $f$ carrying $N$ into $N\prime$, the covering map is explicitly $[\gamma]\mapsto[f\circ\gamma]$; the equivalence relation makes it well-defined. It commutes with endpoint projection, the induced quotient-group action and simplex lifting, so step 4.1 is natural for its coefficient maps. Steps 1.2 and 2.2 already prove naturality of the constant-coefficient identification, yielding the stated commutative homology comparison. All covering, chain and homology maps were explicit quotient maps or uniquely defined finite-lift maps, so the full coefficient and choice scope in the Statement is proved. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the fixed orientation-reversing reflection used for the mirror convention sends the oriented curve $T(p,q)$ to the image-oriented curve $T(p,-q)$, and reversing the orientation of $T(p,q)$ gives $T(-p,-q)$.

## Statement references

[[def-coprime-torus-knot|The torus-knot parameterization and mirror convention]]

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, Proposition 5.1.4 and Lemma 5.1.5](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, and the parameterization in the torus-knot definition.

[A1] Countable Choice is the choice-function principle for sequences of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] [[def-coprime-torus-knot]] parameterizes $T(p,q)$ by $(r e^{2\pi i p s},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{2\pi i q s})$ and fixes reflection in the second coordinate as the mirror convention.

## Proof

1.1 Applying $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,\overline{z_2})$ to the parameterization changes its second angular coordinate from $q s$ to $-q s$ and leaves the first coordinate and parameter direction unchanged. Its image is therefore exactly the oriented curve $T(p,-q)$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Replacing the parameter $s$ by $-s$ traverses the same geometric curve in the opposite direction and changes the angular winding pair $(p,q)$ to $(-p,-q)$. Hence the reversed orientation is the orientation specified for $T(-p,-q)$. [A1, F1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, $m\ge0$, $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ with $[0]=\varnothing$, and let $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ be a finite family in $\mathbb R^d$. Use the standard dot product $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{k<d}u_kv_k$, identify $x,z\in\mathbb R^d$ when $z=x$ or $z=-x$, and write $[x]$ for the resulting class. Define $\mathcal I_\Phi([x])=(\langle a_i,x\rangle^2)_{i\in[m]}$, a formula independent of the representative because replacing $x$ by $-x$ leaves every square unchanged. For $S\subseteq[m]$, let $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_S)$ be the set of finite real linear combinations of its vectors, with the empty span equal to $\{0\}$. Then $\mathcal I_\Phi$ is injective on the global-sign classes if and only if for every $S\subseteq[m]$ at least one of $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_S)$ and $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_{[m]\setminus S})$ equals $\mathbb R^d$.

## Statement references

[Radu Balan, Pete Casazza, and Dan Edidin, complement-property equivalence, Theorem 2.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0412411)

[Philipp Grohs, Sarah Koppensteiner, and Martin Rathmair, complement-property equivalence and proof, Theorem 2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.07911v2)

[Radu Balan, complement-property criterion, Theorem 3.2](https://www.norbertwiener.umd.edu/Education/IMA2015/t4/lecture.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite real family $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ in $\mathbb R^d$, where $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$.

[F1] [[def-ip-real-frame-phase-retrieval]]: phase retrieval means injectivity of the intensity map on classes modulo one global sign; the real measurement at label $i$ is $\langle a_i,x\rangle$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-real-phase-retrieval-quotient-metric]]: the induced intensity map is well defined on those classes, and $[x]=[z]$ exactly when $x=z$ or $x=-z$.

[F3] [[def-ip-frame-complement-property]]: the complement property requires that for each $S\subseteq[m]$, the span indexed by $S$ or the span indexed by its complement is all of $\mathbb R^d$.

[F4] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]], [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]: the real coordinate pairing is bilinear, symmetric, and positive definite, so it is a real inner product; $v\in U^\perp$ means its pairing with every vector of $U$ is zero.

[F5] [[def-linear-combination-and-span]], [[def-linear-subspace]], [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]: the library span is the smallest real linear subspace containing its generators and equals the set of their finite real linear combinations. Bilinearity therefore extends orthogonality from the generators to their span.

[F6] [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], [[def-dimension]], [[def-linear-basis]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]: every subspace of $\mathbb R^n$ is finite-dimensional with dimension at most $n$, equality holds only for the whole space, and $\dim\mathbb R^n=n$, including $n=0$; finite dimension supplies a finite basis.

[F7] [[def-linear-map]], [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]], [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]], [[def-rank-and-nullity]], [[thm-rank-nullity]]: for a linear map with finite-dimensional domain, its kernel and image are subspaces, its rank is the image dimension, and domain dimension is nullity plus rank.

[F8] [[thm-reals-field]], [[thm-reals-ordered-field]]: $2=1+1>0$ in $\mathbb R$, so $2\ne0$ and cannot annihilate a nonzero real vector.

[A1] No form of the axiom of Choice is assumed; the dimension results are finite-dimensional and the selections in the proof are finite.

## Proof


1.1 Assume $\mathcal I_\Phi([x])=\mathcal I_\Phi([z])$. At every label $i$, equality of the intensity coordinates gives $\langle a_i,x\rangle^2=\langle a_i,z\rangle^2$. [given, F1]

2.1 Factoring the difference of squares over $\mathbb R$ yields $(\langle a_i,x-z\rangle)(\langle a_i,x+z\rangle)=0$ for every $i\in[m]$. This factorization also holds when $x=0$, $z=0$, or $a_i=0$; no nonzero-signal or nonzero-measurement hypothesis is used. [step 1.1, F4, F8, algebra]

3.1 Put $S=\{i\in[m]:\langle a_i,x-z\rangle=0\}$. For $i\in S$, $a_i\perp(x-z)$; for $i\notin S$, the first factor in step 2.1 is nonzero, so $a_i\perp(x+z)$. By [F5], each vector in either span is a finite linear combination of its generators, and bilinearity extends each orthogonality statement to the whole span. [step 2.1, F4, F5, construct]

4.1 By the complement property [F3], either $\operatorname{span}(\Phi_S)=\mathbb R^d$ or $\operatorname{span}(\Phi_{[m]\setminus S})=\mathbb R^d$. In the first case step 3.1 makes $x-z$ orthogonal to every vector of $\mathbb R^d$, hence to itself; positive definiteness [F4] gives $x-z=0$. In the second case it gives $x+z=0$. Thus $[x]=[z]$ by [F2], proving injectivity. [step 3.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

5.1 The forward implication is proved in step 4.1. For the converse, suppose the complement property fails; then some $S\subseteq[m]$ has the proper subspaces $U=\operatorname{span}(\Phi_S)$ and $V=\operatorname{span}(\Phi_{[m]\setminus S})$. We prove that every proper subspace $W\le\mathbb R^d$ has a nonzero orthogonal vector. Let $r=\dim W<d$ by [F6], choose a basis $w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1}$ of $W$, and define $L_W:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^r$ by $L_W(x)=(\langle x,w_j\rangle)_{j<r}$. Bilinearity makes $L_W$ linear. Its kernel is $W^\perp$: vanishing against the basis implies vanishing against every vector of $W$ because the basis spans $W$ and [F5] expresses each span vector as a finite linear combination; the converse is immediate. By [F7], the image is a subspace of $\mathbb R^r$, so [F6] gives $\operatorname{rank}L_W=\dim(\operatorname{im}L_W)\le r$. Rank-nullity [F7] and $\dim\mathbb R^d=d$ then give $\dim W^\perp=\dim\ker L_W=d-\operatorname{rank}L_W\ge d-r>0$. By [F6] a zero subspace has dimension zero, so $W^\perp$ contains a nonzero vector. Apply this argument to $U$ and $V$ and choose nonzero $u\in U^\perp$ and $v\in V^\perp$. [given, F5, F6, F7, A1, construct, choose]

6.1 Set $x=u+v$ and $z=u-v$. Since $v\ne0$, $x=z$ would imply $2v=0$, impossible by [F8]; since $u\ne0$, $x=-z$ would imply $2u=0$, also impossible. Hence $[x]\ne[z]$ by [F2]. [step 5.1, F2, F8, algebra]

6.2 If $i\in S$, then $a_i\in U$ and $u\perp a_i$, so $\langle a_i,x\rangle=\langle a_i,v\rangle$ and $\langle a_i,z\rangle=-\langle a_i,v\rangle$. If $i\notin S$, then $a_i\in V$ and $v\perp a_i$, so both measurements equal $\langle a_i,u\rangle$. If $a_i=0$, it lies in $U$ and both measurements are zero. Squaring shows equality of the intensity coordinates at every label, including when either component of the partition is empty. [step 5.1, F4, F5, algebra]

6.3 When $m=0$, the only partition has both sides empty, and both spans equal $\{0\}\ne\mathbb R^d$ by [F5] and $d\ge1$. The complement property fails, while steps 5.1–6.2 give distinct global-sign classes with the same unique empty data. Thus the zero-measurement case is included. [F2, F5, F6, F7, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 6.2]

7.1 Steps 6.1 and 6.2 give distinct quotient classes with the same intensity data, so $\mathcal I_\Phi$ is not injective. Together with step 4.1 and the definition of phase retrieval [F1], this proves the stated equivalence. [step 4.1, step 6.1, step 6.2, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. Then

$$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Here the positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and the preferred longitude has degree one around $K$ and maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Their homology classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so both classes are primitive.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-exterior|The chosen compact knot exterior]]

[[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude|The normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude]]

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, §§5.1.6–5.2.4](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

[Hatcher, §1.2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Calegari, §4.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the chosen knot exterior and based paths, and the specified Heegaard torus.

[A1] Full AC is the axiom that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[L1] Full AC implies the Axiom of Countable Choice, which is the hypothesis of the exterior and peripheral-system definitions ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] [[def-coprime-torus-knot]] identifies $K$ with the oriented primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$ on the standard unknotted Heegaard torus.

[F2] [[def-knot-exterior]] sets $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ with its boundary torus, and [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]] defines the positive meridian by the normal-disk boundary and the preferred longitude by degree one and zero exterior homology.

[F3] Under full AC, [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]] proves $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ generated by the positive meridian, proves existence and uniqueness of the preferred-longitude class, and proves that their boundary classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$.

[F4] [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]] identifies the fundamental group of a union from a path-connected open cover with the pushout of the two inclusion-induced maps from the intersection.

## Proof


**Given:** The knot, exterior, Heegaard splitting and AC hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$ is essential on the Heegaard torus. Removing a small annular neighborhood of $K$ from that torus leaves a closed annulus $A$. On either side, removing the corresponding half of the tube from a solid torus only removes a boundary collar, so the two pieces retract to solid tori $W_x,W_y$ and their overlap retracts to $A$. Thicken the pieces by half-collars to obtain path-connected open sets covering $E_K$ whose intersection retracts to $A$. The core of $A$ winds $p$ times around the core generator $x$ on one side and $q$ times around $y$ on the other. Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F2] by [L1]. [given, A1, F1, F2, L1, construct]

1.2 The action $\rho_t$ is isometric for the round metric. Its generic orbits have slope $(p,q)$ and trivial stabilizer because $\gcd(p,q)=1$; hence the metric tube chosen in the Statement is invariant. The coordinate circles $z_1=0$ and $z_2=0$ have stabilizer orders $|q|$ and $|p|$ respectively. The orbit space is a sphere: on each torus $|z_1|=r$ with $0<r<1$, quotienting by the primitive circle orbit leaves a circle, and the two end circles collapse to the two coordinate-orbit points. Removing the invariant tube removes a disk from the orbit sphere, so the exterior is fibered over a disk with the stated multiplicities. Multiplicity one is the regular local model; multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 The three fundamental groups in this cover are $\pi_1(W_x)=\langle x\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, $\pi_1(W_y)=\langle y\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, and $\pi_1(A)=\langle a\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, with inclusion maps $a\mapsto x^p$ and $a\mapsto y^q$. By [F4], $\pi_1(E_K)$ is their pushout. A group receiving maps from the two cyclic factors is determined by images of $x,y$; the maps agree on the intersection exactly when $x^p=y^q$. Hence the pushout has presentation $\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle$. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A regular orbit parallel to $K$ represents the annulus core $x^p=y^q=h$. This element commutes with $x$ because it is $x^p$, and commutes with $y$ because it is $y^q$; as $x,y$ generate the group from step 2.1, $h$ is central. [step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.2 Choose integers $c,d$ with $pd-qc=1$ and let $L=c\alpha+d\beta$ be the corresponding simple curve on the Heegaard torus; its algebraic intersection with $K$ is one. At the intersection, the boundary $m$ of a small normal disk splits into arcs $\gamma_x,\gamma_y$ on the two solid-torus sides, while $L$ splits into its crossing arc and complementary arc $L_1$. Inserting $L_1L_1^{-1}$ into $m=\gamma_x\gamma_y$ gives $m=(\gamma_xL_1)(L_1^{-1}\gamma_y)$. The first factor winds $c$ times around the $x$ core and the second winds $-d$ times around the $y$ core, hence $m=x^c y^{-d}$. Its abelianization under $x\mapsto q$, $y\mapsto p$ is $cq-dp=-1$, so it is opposite the positive normal-disk meridian, whose class is the positive generator by [F3]. Thus $\mu=m^{-1}=y^d x^{-c}$. Setting $\alpha=d$ and $\beta=-c$ gives $p\alpha+q\beta=1$ and the stated word; another Bezout solution changes the exponents by $(qk,-pk)$, so the word is unchanged because $y^{qk}=h^k=x^{pk}$ and $h$ is central. [A1, L1, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 Abelianizing the presentation in step 2.1 gives the relation $p[x]=q[y]$. The map $x\mapsto q$, $y\mapsto p$ is surjective because $\gcd(p,q)=1$, and its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(p,-q)$, exactly the relation vector; hence it identifies this quotient with $\mathbb Z$. Step 3.2 sends the positive meridian to $1$, so by [F3] it is the positive generator of $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Thus $[h]=p[x]=pq[\mu]$. The regular orbit $h$ is a degree-one parallel of $K$ on $\partial E_K$, and $\mu$ has degree zero there, so $\lambda=h\mu^{-pq}$ has degree one and zero image in $H_1(E_K)$. Uniqueness in [F3] identifies it with the preferred longitude; [F3] also proves that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so each is primitive. [L1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The square records the annulus-to-solid-torus inclusions used in steps 1.1–1.2. Its two composites agree on the annulus core precisely when $x^p=y^q$; the proof applies Seifert–van Kampen to establish that the lower-right group is the pushout and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node (a) at (0,1.1) {$\pi_1(A)=\langle a\rangle$};
  \node (x) at (3.3,1.1) {$\pi_1(W_x)=\langle x\rangle$};
  \node (y) at (0,-1.1) {$\pi_1(W_y)=\langle y\rangle$};
  \node (e) at (3.3,-1.1) {$\pi_1(E_K)$};
  \draw[->] (a)--node[above] {$a\mapsto x^p$}(x);
  \draw[->] (a)--node[left] {$a\mapsto y^q$}(y);
  \draw[->] (x)--node[right] {inclusion}(e);
  \draw[->] (y)--node[below] {inclusion}(e);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Definition

An **effective field** is a field whose elements have finite encodings and whose exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, equality test, and inversion of nonzero elements are terminating procedures. Input a finite-dimensional strict matrix realization of a $k$-linear ribbon category with $\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)=k$, finite-dimensional color objects with fixed bases, exact matrices for every braiding and inverse braiding used, the evaluation and coevaluation maps for the closure, the twist matrices, and the matrix $J_W$ of the ribbon-induced pivotal comparison $j_W=u_W\circ\theta_W:W\to W^{\vee\vee}$ for $W=V_{a_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{a_n}$, where $u_W$ is the Drinfeld morphism. Also input a finite braid word $\beta$ on $n\ge1$ strands and the top color tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$. The matrices are assumed to satisfy the stated ribbon-category axioms; an implementation does not infer those axioms from arbitrary matrices.

Use the strand-position permutation homomorphism $\pi:B_n\to\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$ given by $\pi(\sigma_i)=(i\ i+1)$. Read the braid letters in composition order, updating the current color tuple at each crossing by swapping its adjacent colors. For a positive letter $\sigma_i$, use the matrix of
$$1\otimes\cdots\otimes c_{V_{a_i},V_{a_{i+1}}}\otimes\cdots\otimes1,$$
and for a negative letter use its inverse. Let the blackboard-framed closure join the bottom and top endpoint at each position by the identity pairing. Reject the input if the final color tuple differs from the initial tuple: the tuple records the colors at the paired endpoints, so equality is exactly the condition that the closure carries a consistent color on every component. Starting with the identity matrix, multiply the typed crossing matrices in word order to obtain $M_\beta:W\to W$, then return the finite matrix contraction
$$\operatorname{ev}_{W^\vee}\bigl((J_WM_\beta)\otimes1_{W^\vee}\bigr)\operatorname{coev}_W\in k.$$
In ordinary dual-basis coordinates this contraction is the matrix trace $\operatorname{Tr}(J_WM_\beta)$.
This is the exact ribbon evaluation of the blackboard-framed colored braid closure in the given matrix realization. No algorithm is asserted for arbitrary abstract ribbon categories without effective finite matrix data.

## Definition references

[[def-colored-framed-knot-evaluation-from-ribbon-category|Colored framed-link value]]

[[lem-multicolored-ribbon-coupon-evaluation|Mixed-color ribbon-tangle evaluation]]

[[def-the-categorical-trace-of-a-morphism-into-the-double-dual|Categorical trace contraction]]

[[thm-a-braided-rigid-category-has-a-drinfeld-morphism|Drinfeld morphism and ribbon pivotal comparison]]

[[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation|Artin braid words]]

[[def-symmetric-group|Permutations of the strand labels]]

[Turaev, *Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter I, Theorem 2.5 and §§3–4](https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/turaev5.pdf)

[Etingof, Gelaki, Nikshych, and Ostrik, *Tensor Categories*, §§8.9–8.10](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The effective field, valid finite-dimensional matrix ribbon data, the braid word, and its top color tuple.

[F1] For $f:W\to W^{\vee\vee}$, the left categorical trace is the composite $\operatorname{ev}_{W^\vee}(f\otimes1_{W^\vee})\operatorname{coev}_W$ ([[def-the-categorical-trace-of-a-morphism-into-the-double-dual]]).

[F2] In a braided rigid category the Drinfeld morphism $u_W:W\to W^{\vee\vee}$ is natural, and a ribbon twist induces the pivotal comparison $j_W=u_W\circ\theta_W$ ([[thm-a-braided-rigid-category-has-a-drinfeld-morphism]]).

[F3] Each supplied crossing matrix is the morphism $c_{V_{a_i},V_{a_{i+1}}}$ or its inverse between the stated adjacent tensor factors, and the matrices satisfy the ribbon-category axioms by the input condition.

[F4] For $n\ge2$, $B_n$ is generated by $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{n-1}$ with the Artin braid and distant-commutativity relations, and $B_1$ is trivial ([[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]]).

[F5] $\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$ is the group of bijections of the strand-label set under composition, and $(i\ i+1)$ is the transposition interchanging $i$ and $i+1$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The valid input data in the Algorithm.

1.1 If $n=1$, there are no generators and $B_1$ is trivial, so $\pi$ is its unique homomorphism. If $n\ge2$, put $s_i=(i\ i+1)\in\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$. For $|i-j|>1$, $s_i$ and $s_j$ have disjoint supports and commute. For adjacent indices, both $s_i s_{i+1}s_i$ and $s_{i+1}s_i s_{i+1}$ equal $(i\ i+2)$, so the assignment $\sigma_i\mapsto s_i$ sends every Artin relator to the identity and [F4] gives the homomorphism $\pi$. At each position $i$, the positive matrix has source tensor factors $V_{a_i}\otimes V_{a_{i+1}}$ and target factors $V_{a_{i+1}}\otimes V_{a_i}$ by [F3]; the negative matrix is its typed inverse. Updating the color tuple by this same swap tracks the colors at the endpoints of each successive letter. The closure arcs pair equal strand positions, so the final tuple equals the initial tuple exactly when every paired endpoint has the same color; in that case the composite has source and target $W$ and the closure contraction is defined. [F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Induct on the number of letters already read. Before the first letter the running matrix is the identity action of the empty word. Each update composes with precisely the corresponding local braiding or inverse, so the induction hypothesis gives the action of the longer prefix. After the finite word is exhausted the result is $M_\beta$, the morphism represented by the input colored braid. [F3, F4, step 1.1, induction]

3.1 For a color-preserving tuple, the word composite is an endomorphism $M_\beta:W\to W$. Cut the finite blackboard-framed closure at a common level outside the braid rectangle. Its nested lower identity pairings are $\operatorname{coev}_W$, and its upper pairings are $\operatorname{ev}_{W^\vee}$ following the supplied pivotal comparison $J_W=j_W:W\to W^{\vee\vee}$. Inserting the braid word between these maps gives the finite closure composite $\operatorname{ev}_{W^\vee}((J_WM_\beta)\otimes1_{W^\vee})\operatorname{coev}_W$. By [F1] this is $\operatorname{Tr}_L(J_WM_\beta)$, whose finite matrix contraction is exactly the returned scalar. With standard dual bases, inserting $\operatorname{coev}_W=\sum_i e_i\otimes e_i^*$ and the canonical dual evaluation gives $\sum_i(J_WM_\beta)_{ii}$, the ordinary matrix trace. This argument evaluates only the given finite braid and its cup/cap word; it does not require constructing an evaluator on arbitrary framed graphs. Each of the finitely many letter updates and the final contraction uses finitely many exact field operations, so effectiveness proves termination. [F1, F2, step 2.1, given, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. If $D$ is a connected reduced alternating diagram of a knot $K$, then the library Jones polynomial has $t$-span exactly $c(K)=c(D)$, in the convention $t=A^{-4}$. The span of a nonzero Laurent polynomial is its largest exponent minus its smallest exponent.

## Statement references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a connected reduced alternating knot diagram $D$, and the crossing number of its underlying knot type.

[F1] Full AC implies countable choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F2] The crossing number is the least crossing count among regular diagrams of the same underlying unoriented link type ([[def-crossing-number-of-link]]).

[F3] Under full AC, a reduced alternating knot diagram with $c(D)$ crossings has Jones span $c(D)$, while every competing $c'$-crossing knot diagram has Jones span at most $c'$ ([[lem-alternating-state-adequacy-and-jones-span]]).

[F4] A reduced alternating diagram is connected and alternating by definition ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]]).

[A1] Full AC, the choice-function principle for arbitrary families of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Proof
1.1 By [A1] and [F1], the crossing-number definition [F2] applies. Since $D$ is a connected reduced alternating diagram by [F4], [F3] gives $\operatorname{span}_tV_K(t)=c(D)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 For every regular diagram $E$ of the same underlying knot type, choose its single-component orientation to match $K$. By [F3], $c(D)\le c(E)$ because the common Jones span is $c(D)$ and is at most $c(E)$. The diagram $D$ itself is one of the competitors in [F2], so $c(K)\le c(D)$; the preceding inequality for every $E$ gives $c(D)\le c(K)$. Thus $c(K)=c(D)$, and step 1.1 gives the asserted Jones span. [F2, F3, step 1.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, choose its compact exterior $E_K$ with boundary torus $T_K$, and let $\mu$ and $\lambda$ be its positive meridian and preferred longitude. The exterior homology theorem gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ be the composite of abelianization with the homomorphism $[\mu]\mapsto1$. For an integer $q\ge2$, let $\phi_q$ be the composite $\pi_1(E_K)\xrightarrow{\phi}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, and let $p_q:E_q\to E_K$ be the connected cover classified by $\ker\phi_q$. On $T_K$, the homomorphism sends $[\mu]\mapsto1$ and $[\lambda]\mapsto0$, so the preimage of $T_K$ is a connected torus cover whose fundamental group corresponds to $\langle\mu^q,\lambda\rangle$. Let $\widetilde\mu$ be the closed lift of $\mu^q$. Attach a solid torus to $E_q$ with its meridian identified with $\widetilde\mu$; the resulting oriented closed $3$-manifold is the $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$. In tubular coordinates near $K$, the extended map to $S^3$ has local form $(s,w)\mapsto(s,w^q)$, and the deck group $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ acts by $w\mapsto e^{2\pi i/q}w$.

## Definition

Let $\Gamma$ be a group. Say that $\Gamma$ is **good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem** when it has the $\pi_1$-null disk property: for every disk-like capped grope $G^c$ of height $1.5$ with a chosen basepoint and every homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(G^c)\to\Gamma$, there is a proper framed generic immersion $d:D^2\looparrowright G^c$ of a disk into the grope's actual four-dimensional framed block. Its boundary is the core attaching circle, with the normal framing specified by the attaching solid-torus neighborhood, and each double-point loop of $d$, regarded after basing as an element of $\pi_1(G^c)$, is sent to the identity by $\phi$. This definition of a good group is a hypothesis on $\Gamma$; it does not assert that any particular group is good.

## Definition

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

## Definition

A compact orientable three-manifold $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** if it admits no embedded disk whose interior misses the surface and whose boundary is an essential simple closed curve in it. A boundary subsurface is **$\pi_1$-injective** if the inclusion of each component induces an injection on fundamental groups. A **pared pair** is a pair $(M,P)$ in which $M$ is compact, orientable and irreducible, and $P$ is a possibly empty compact subsurface of $\partial M$ whose pairwise disjoint components are $\pi_1$-injective annuli or tori, every noncyclic abelian subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$ is conjugate into $\pi_1$ of a component of $P$ up to base-path conjugacy, and every map of pairs
$$
(S^1\times I,S^1\times\partial I)\longrightarrow(M,P)
$$
that induces injections on fundamental groups is homotopic through maps of pairs into $P$, so its boundary remains in $P$ during the homotopy. Write $\partial_0M=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}P$. A **horoball** is a region bounded by a horosphere, a Euclidean plane or sphere tangent to the ideal boundary at one point. The **peripheral subgroup** for a component of $P$ is the image of its fundamental group in $\pi_1(M)$, recorded up to conjugacy. A **hyperbolic structure** on $(M,P)$ is a curvature $-1$ metric on $\operatorname{int}M$ described by an atlas of charts into $\mathbb H^3$ whose transition maps are in $\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$. Its developing map $\operatorname{dev}$ from the universal cover and holonomy homomorphism $\rho:\pi_1(M)\to\operatorname{Isom}^+(\mathbb H^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{dev}(gx)=\rho(g)\operatorname{dev}(x)$. The metric is **complete** when it is geodesically complete. A **cusp** corresponding to a component of $P$ is a quotient of a horoball by the associated peripheral subgroup. The hyperbolic volume is the integral of the Riemannian volume density over $\operatorname{int}M$; the structure has **finite volume** when this integral is finite.

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

## Definition

For a link projection on $S^2$, a **checkerboard coloring** assigns one of two colors to each complementary region so that regions sharing an edge have different colors. Given such a coloring, the **black Tait graph** has one vertex for each black region and one edge for each crossing joining the two opposite black sectors at that crossing. The **white Tait graph** is defined by interchanging black and white. Loops and parallel edges are allowed.

## Definition references

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular link projection on $S^2$ and a checkerboard coloring of its complementary regions.

[F1] A regular link projection has finitely many transverse double points and no triple points ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

## Proof
1.1 At each crossing the four sectors alternate in color, so there is one unordered pair of opposite black sectors and one unordered pair of opposite white sectors. The crossing therefore determines one edge for each graph, with endpoints the region vertices named in the definition; if both sectors belong to one region, the edge is a loop. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 The crossings form a finite set by [F1], so each construction adds finitely many edges to the finite set of region vertices. The definition allows repeated endpoint pairs and equal endpoints, so it also covers parallel edges and loops without extra choices. [given, F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Example

Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot, let $E_{K_8}$ be the exterior obtained by deleting the binding neighborhood from its open-book presentation, and use the positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. The exterior admits a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric obtained by gluing two regular ideal tetrahedra, of total volume $2v_3=6\Lambda(\pi/3)\approx2.02988$, where $v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3)$ is the volume of one regular ideal tetrahedron and $\Lambda$ is the Lobachevsky function. The ordinary zero filling along $\lambda$ is a torus bundle over $S^1$ with monodromy matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ on the capped fiber homology, and the filled manifold admits no complete hyperbolic metric.

## Example references

[Danny Calegari, *Foliations and the Geometry of 3-Manifolds*, Construction 5.37, Theorem 5.38 and Example 5.39](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/books/foliations/oupbook.pdf)

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §§4.1–4.4](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

## Diagram

After capping, the punctured-torus fiber becomes $T^2$, and the displayed matrix is the monodromy action on its first homology. The separate circle marks the $S^1$ base. This schematic does not encode the knot projection or prove the bundle claim.

```tikz
  \draw[->,red,thick] (0,-0.32) arc (-90:270:0.30 and 0.30);

  \node[red] at (0.45,-0.75) {$b$};
  \node at (0,1.32) {$T^2$ fiber};
  \draw[->,thick] (0.72,0.78) .. controls (1.15,2.3) and (-1.15,2.3) .. (-0.72,0.78);
  \node[above] at (0,2.35) {$\varphi_* = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$};
  \draw[thick] (3.7,0) circle (0.30);
  \node[below] at (3.7,-0.48) {$S^1$ base};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard figure-eight knot with chosen compact exterior and peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$, with $\lambda$ the preferred longitude.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC selects from every family of nonempty sets.

[F1] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ selects from every countable family of nonempty sets.

[F2] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]: in ZF, $\mathrm{AC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[F3] [[lem-figure-eight-ideal-gluing-and-cusp-completeness]]: the standard two-tetrahedron gluing gives the figure-eight exterior a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric, with total volume $2v_3$.

[F4] [[lem-zero-filling-of-fibered-knot-is-a-torus-bundle]]: filling the figure-eight exterior along $\lambda$ caps its once-punctured torus fiber and gives the torus bundle whose homology matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

[F5] [[lem-closed-hyperbolic-three-manifold-has-no-z2-subgroup]]: a closed connected three-manifold with a complete curvature $-1$ metric has fundamental group with no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$.

[F6] [[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]]: ordinary filling along $\lambda$ attaches a solid torus with meridian disk boundary in that slope.

[F7] [[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]: the explicit pullback of a bundle along $\mathbb R\to S^1$ is a covering map.

[F8] [[thm-covering-maps-inject-fundamental-groups]]: every covering map induces an injective homomorphism on fundamental groups.

[F9] [[lem-figure-eight-complement-punctured-torus-bundle]]: the standard figure-eight knot is presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of one positive and one negative Hopf band, and deleting its binding neighbourhood gives the stated once-punctured-torus open-book exterior.

## Proof

1.1 First identify the two figure-eight models used here. In [F3], $K_8$ is the closure of $(\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2$, the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram. In [F9], the same standard figure-eight knot is presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of a positive and a negative Hopf band; Calegari's Example 5.39 identifies the boundary of the opposite-handed Hopf-band Murasugi sum as the figure-eight knot. Thus both are the same oriented $4_1$ knot class, and an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy identifies the braid closure with the plumbing boundary. Choose the binding and tubular neighborhoods compatibly under this isotopy. It identifies the compact exteriors and carries the positive meridian and preferred longitude to the corresponding peripheral classes (up to simultaneous reversal, which does not change the unoriented zero slope). The hyperbolic exterior from [F3] and the fibered exterior from [F9] are therefore the same marked exterior for this example. By [A1] and [F2], the countable-choice premise [F1] holds. The face gluing and regular-shape assignment in [F3] give the complete finite-volume metric and its two-tetrahedron volume. By [F4] and [F6], the zero filling along the preferred longitude is the stated torus bundle. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F9, construct]

2.1 Write the bundle as the mapping torus of its torus monodromy. Pull it back along the explicit universal cover $t\mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ of $S^1$; its total space is $T^2\times\mathbb R$, and the pullback projection is a covering because it is trivial over each lifted bundle chart. Its fundamental group is $\pi_1(T^2)\cong\mathbb Z^2$. By [F8], this subgroup injects into the fundamental group of the filled manifold. [F7, F8, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 If the filled manifold admitted a complete hyperbolic metric, it would be a closed connected three-manifold with curvature $-1$. By [F5] its fundamental group could contain no $\mathbb Z^2$ subgroup, contradicting step 2.1. Hence the zero filling is nonhyperbolic. The original complete structure has volume $2v_3=6\Lambda(\pi/3)$ by step 1.1. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, contradiction] ∎

## Sources

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §§4.1–4.4](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $D$ be a connected reduced alternating diagram with $c$ crossings. At every crossing, changing one smoothing from the all-$A$ state or from the all-$B$ state merges two distinct state circles; these are A- and B-adequacy. The Kauffman bracket has $A$-span $4c$. If $D$ represents a knot $K$, then the library Jones polynomial has $t$-span $c$, and every $c'$-crossing diagram of $K$ has $t$-span at most $c'$ under the convention $t=A^{-4}$. The span of a nonzero Laurent polynomial is its largest exponent minus its smallest exponent.

## Statement references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial*, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a connected reduced alternating diagram $D$ with $c$ crossings.

[F1] In a reduced alternating diagram, successive crossing visits along each component switch over-under, and no complementary region has a crossing more than once on its boundary ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]]).

[F2] For a connected reduced alternating diagram, each one-crossing change from either extreme state merges distinct circles, both extreme coefficients are nonzero, and the bracket span is $4c$; for any connected diagram its bracket span is at most $4c$ ([[lem-connected-diagram-bracket-span-bound-and-alternating-equality]]).

[F3] Under full AC, the library Jones polynomial satisfies $V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4})$, where $f_D(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle$ and $t=A^{-4}$ ([[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Choice supplies a choice function for every family of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Proof
1.1 By [F1], the input is a connected reduced alternating diagram, so the finite state-merging conclusion in [F2] applies. It establishes both A-adequacy and B-adequacy without invoking the separate Jones axiom branch, and gives $\operatorname{span}_A\langle D\rangle=4c$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Suppose $D$ represents a knot $K$. Let $E$ be any $c'$-crossing diagram of the same knot, with its component oriented to represent the chosen orientation of $K$. The projection of a one-component diagram is connected because it is the continuous image of a circle; thus [F2] gives $\operatorname{span}_A\langle E\rangle\le4c'$. Multiplication by the writhe-normalizing monomial $(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(E)}$ shifts all exponents equally and does not change span. By [A1] and [F3], substituting $t=A^{-4}$ divides the exponent span by $4$, so $\operatorname{span}_t V_K(t)\le c'$. Applying this to $D$ and using step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{span}_tV_K(t)=c$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth slice knot, let $q$ be a prime power, let $D$ be a smooth slice disk, and let $P_D$ be the induced metabolizer in $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$. For every prime-power-order character $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ that vanishes on $P_D$, the Casson–Gordon signature defect $\sigma(K,\chi)$ is zero.

## Statement references

[[def-casson-gordon-signature-defect|The specific Casson–Gordon signature defect]]

[[lem-casson-gordon-characters-and-linking-metabolizers|Character extension over the disk cover]]

[[lem-slice-disk-induces-branched-cover-metabolizer|The disk-induced linking metabolizer]]

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|The smooth-sliceness convention]]

[Charles Livingston and Swatee Naik, *Introduction to Knot Concordance*, Theorem 8.2.1, pp. 167–168](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Concordance_Book.pdf)

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the actual smooth slice disk, its prime-power branched cover and a prime-power-order character vanishing on the disk kernel.

[F1] The disk cover is a rational homology ball, its boundary kernel is a linking metabolizer, and the given character extends to its finite first homology with prime-power order, which may be larger than the original order. [[lem-prime-power-branched-cover-of-slice-disk-is-rational-homology-ball]], [[lem-slice-disk-induces-branched-cover-metabolizer]], [[lem-casson-gordon-characters-and-linking-metabolizers]]

[F2] Its unbranched exterior cover $X_{D,q}$ is filled by the branch-disk tube $D^2\times D^2$ along $D^2\times S^1$. The free coordinate is $\ell/q$, one on the lifted meridian. [[def-q-fold-branched-cover-of-a-slice-disk]], [[def-infinite-cyclic-cover-of-a-slice-disk-exterior]] Local Mayer–Vietoris applies to these actual collars. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[F3] For any prime-power finite character on that exterior cover, paired with this free coordinate, all $\mathbb C(t)$ homology vanishes. [[lem-prime-power-character-twists-of-knot-and-disk-covers-are-acyclic]]

[F4] The original rationalized Witt class is independent of its smooth bounding pair. Proof 4.1 also proves compatibility with embedding a smaller finite cyclic character image in a larger finite cyclic target without changing the root-of-unity coefficient system. [[lem-casson-gordon-bordism-independence-and-nonsingularity]] The signature is the stated one-sided homomorphism. [[def-casson-gordon-signature-defect]]

[A1] Full AC is retained. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] The smooth disk convention is [[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]].

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], choose an extending character $\widetilde\chi$ on the branched disk cover, and write its exact order as $D=p^a$. If the original nontrivial character has order $d=p^b$, then $d\mid D$. Restrict $\widetilde\chi$ to $H_1(X_{D,q})$ and pair it with $\ell/q$. Its finite coordinate vanishes on the lifted meridian because that circle bounds the branch-tube disk in the filled cover. Its infinite coordinate takes that circle to one. On the exterior of the boundary knot the finite coordinate is the original $\chi$; on the zero-filling solid torus it is zero. Thus its boundary is precisely the original $\eta$ followed by the inclusion $C_d\times\mathbb Z\to C_D\times\mathbb Z$, with the root representation unchanged. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct]

2.1 The actual oriented boundary of $X_{D,q}$ is $M_{0,q}$. Indeed the product disk tube at the base disk gives a longitude filling of the knot exterior: its framing is zero, since a parallel disk is disjoint and its boundary has linking zero with $K$. Passing to the meridional $q$-cover lifts the same longitude slope, while its normal circle is the closed lift of $\mu^q$. These are the zero-surgery cover coordinates in [F2], with the positive boundary orientation retained. Mayer–Vietoris in the rational homology ball $W_{D,q}=X_{D,q}\cup(D^2\times D^2)$, whose overlap is $D^2\times S^1$, gives $H_2(X_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ and $H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$ on that overlap circle. The higher groups vanish as well. In particular its ordinary middle nonsingular image form is zero. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The character in step 1.1 is of prime-power order on the actual exterior cover. Hence [F3] gives $H_2(X_{D,q};\mathbb C(t))=0$, so its twisted form is also zero. The difference of the two Witt forms of this actual single-boundary smooth filling is therefore zero. By [F4]'s larger-target comparison it computes the original rationalized class even when $D>d$: compare any original multiple bounding datum, viewed over $C_D\times\mathbb Z$, with the same number of copies of this filling and use the closed fourth-bordism ambiguity calculation. Thus $\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi)=0$ in $W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q$. Applying the specified one-sided signature homomorphism gives $\sigma(K,\chi)=0$, as claimed. This proves the full prime-power extension case rather than assuming extension with unchanged finite order. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Delta_C^\#(t)$ be the unique unit associate
of the knot Alexander generator that is symmetric under $t\mapsto t^{-1}$
and has $\Delta_C^\#(1)=1$. Then
$$\Delta_C^\#(t)=1.$$

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Introduction](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Freedman–Quinn, Theorem 11.11](https://archive.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/id/eprint/4789/2/FreedmanQuinn-TopologyOf4Manifolds-Reformatted2013.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the fixed Conway diagram and Alexander-polynomial
normalization.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. It supplies
countable choice through [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]].

[F1] [[lem-conway-seifert-surface-and-matrix]] constructs the actual embedded disk-and-band surface and an integral homology basis for the selected Conway diagram with the displayed matrix $V$, by a direct diagram transcription, local push-off counts and an explicit unimodular basis change.

[F2] [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]] identifies
the normalized Alexander polynomial with the determinant of a Seifert matrix
up to a unit $\pm t^m$ in $\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$.

[F3] [[cor-knot-alexander-normalization-symmetry-and-genus-bound]]: every knot
Alexander generator has a unique symmetric unit associate taking value $1$ at
$t=1$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $V$ be the matrix in [F1] and form $A(t)=V-tV^T$. Fraction-free Bareiss elimination uses, at stage $k$, the update $$ a_{ij}^{(k+1)}= \frac{a_{kk}^{(k)}a_{ij}^{(k)}-a_{ik}^{(k)}a_{kj}^{(k)}} {a_{k-1,k-1}^{(k-1)}}\qquad (i,j>k), $$ with initial divisor $1$. The successive pivots are $$ t-1,\quad 1-t+t^2,\quad -t+t^2,\quad t^2,\quad t-t^2+t^3-t^4,\quad t-2t^2+3t^3-2t^4+t^5. $$ At the seventh pivot exchange rows $7$ and $8$ once; the pivot is $t^2-t^3+t^4$ and the final Bareiss entry is $-t^4$. The one row exchange reverses the determinant sign, so $\det A(t)=t^4$. The recurrence has exact polynomial divisions at every stage; the finite pivot and exact-division certificate is recorded in the batch contract. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The monomial $t^4$ is a unit in $\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$. By [F2], the Alexander generator is associated to $1$. The polynomial $1$ is symmetric and takes value $1$ at $t=1$, so uniqueness in [F3] gives $\Delta_C^\#(t)=1$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

        surfaces and knots.
---

## Statement

Let $T=S^1\times S^1$ be the standard oriented product torus. If $C\subset T$ is an embedded piecewise-linear simple closed curve that is not null-homotopic, then its class $[C]\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ is nonzero and primitive, meaning that it is not $k x$ for any $x\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ and integer $|k|>1$.

## Statement references

[Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger, §4](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hass/Research/Papers/Complexity/hlp.pdf) — meridian and longitude use the two generators of the peripheral torus.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The product torus $T$ and the embedded PL circle $C$ in the statement.



## Proof

1.1 Give $T$ the one-vertex square cellulation with product generators $a=S^1\times\{1\}$ and $b=\{1\}\times S^1$. The cellular boundary of the square is the commutator $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$, whose signed incidence on each 1-cell is zero; the 1-cell boundary is also zero. Thus $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[a]\oplus\mathbb Z[b]$, and the two product projections read the two coordinates. For a PL loop $c:S^1\to S^1$, lift its finitely many arcs successively to the covering line $\mathbb R\to S^1$; the endpoint displacement is an integer, its degree. A degree-zero lift closes and contracts linearly, so $c$ is null-homotopic; conversely a null-homotopy lifts over a finite subdivision and keeps the integer displacement zero. Applying this to both coordinate projections shows that if $C$ is not null-homotopic, at least one homology coordinate of $[C]$ is nonzero. If $C$ separated $T$, the closure of either complementary component would be an oriented PL surface with boundary $C$; its finite oriented triangulation gives a $2$-chain with boundary $C$, so $[C]=0$. Hence $C$ is nonseparating, and cutting along it leaves a connected compact surface with two boundary copies. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose a vertex $p$ of a triangulation of $C$, and let $p_+$ and $p_-$ be its two copies on the boundary of the cut surface. A shortest edge path joining these corresponding copies has no repeated vertices; push its interior off any intermediate boundary edges to obtain a properly embedded PL arc. After gluing the boundary copies back, its endpoints become the same point $p$ and the arc crosses $C$ transversely exactly once. Orient the resulting simple closed PL curve $D$ arbitrarily; its signed intersection with $C$ is $+1$ or $-1$. [given, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For oriented transverse PL loops on an oriented torus, the signed crossing count is invariant under replacing either loop by a homologous cycle: across the boundary of each oriented triangle, the intersections with a closed transverse loop enter and leave with opposite signs. It is additive in each cycle. The product basis loops $a=S^1\times\{1\}$ and $b=\{1\}\times S^1$ meet once, while parallel copies of each are disjoint, so for classes $(p,q)$ and $(r,s)$ the pairing is $ps-qr$ up to the global orientation convention. Since $C\cdot D=\pm1$, this determinant is $\pm1$. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 If an integer $k$ with $|k|>1$ divided both $p$ and $q$, it would divide $ps-qr$, contradicting its value $\pm1$. Thus $\gcd(|p|,|q|)=1$, which says exactly that $[C]$ is primitive. Its nonzero status was established in step 1.1. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the ACω hat Floer disk-count theory for closed three-manifolds. For either orientation of $L(3,1)$, the standard genus-one pointed Heegaard diagram has three intersection generators and its $\widehat{CF}$ differential over $\mathbb F_2$ is zero. Consequently $\widehat{HF}(L(3,1);\mathbb F_2)$ has total rank three.

## Statement references

[[def-hat-heegaard-floer-complex-of-a-closed-three-manifold|Hat Floer generator and differential conventions]]

[[lem-os-disk-and-polygon-analytic-foundations|Analytic disk-count hypotheses]]

[[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention|Lens-space orientation convention]]

[Ozsváth and Szabó, *On the Heegaard Floer homology of branched double-covers*, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309170v1)

[Lipshitz, *Heegaard Floer Homologies*, §§2–5](https://floer.wiki/more/courses/floer-homology/2024/lipshitz_heegaard_floer_homology.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard genus-one splitting and the stated filling-orientation convention, and Countable Choice.

[F1] In the actual flat torus coordinates the meridians $\alpha=(1,0)$ and $\beta=(1,3\varepsilon)$, $\varepsilon=\pm1$, have exactly three intersections, no nonzero normalized periodic domain, no relative disk between different generators, and only the constant relative class at an equal generator. Its proof is the explicit compact-disk lift and affine contraction in the plane, independently of a holomorphic equation. ([[lem-straight-three-intersection-torus-diagram-has-no-nonconstant-disks]])

[F2] The actual allowed hat data have nonnegative region degrees and energy bounded by a fixed positive linear combination of those degrees. Relative homotopies preserve these degrees, since their boundary stays on the attaching circles, away from each region test point. ([[lem-nearly-symmetric-polygons-have-positive-domains-and-degree-energy-bounds]], [[lem-os-disk-and-polygon-analytic-foundations]])

[F3] The full hat complex and the proved actual move maps identify its homology with the full closed-manifold invariant. The filling convention identifies the unknot-exterior meridian with its preferred longitude $\lambda_U$, and the attached meridian for $L(3,1)$ with $\lambda_U+3\mu_U$. ([[def-hat-heegaard-floer-complex-of-a-closed-three-manifold]], [[thm-hat-heegaard-floer-is-a-closed-three-manifold-invariant]], [[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention]])

## Proof

1.1 Parametrize the splitting torus by $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ with $\lambda_U=(1,0)$ and $\mu_U=(0,1)$. Thus the two compression meridians are $(1,0)$ and $(1,3)$ by [F3]. They give exactly the positive-sign diagram in [F1]. Reversing the oriented splitting gives the negative sign diagram; equivalently conjugate the surface coordinate, retaining the same attaching sets. Both signs have three intersections and zero normalized periodic lattice. They therefore satisfy the corrected full-all-sector admissibility condition, including every empty sector; admissibility is not being inferred from a finite set of realized generators. [F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Take actual allowed generic hat data for either of these literal diagrams. This need not be the flat equation: its prescribed generator charts may be retained. A nonconstant strip would compactify to a relative disk. Distinct endpoints are impossible by [F1]. For equal endpoints the explicit plane contraction of [F1] is a boundary-preserving relative homotopy to the constant map. For each region point q its degree is invariant under this homotopy: the boundary never meets q, so the boundary winding of its small disk, or equivalently the pullback divisor degree, is constant. Every region degree is consequently zero. The ACTUAL positivity and energy inequality in [F2] force zero energy, hence a constant strip. Thus there is no index-one strip for any of these allowed data. At a constant generator its operator is the exact transverse operator of real index zero, as in [F1]; it does not enter the index-one count. This argument does not assume that merely seeing quadrilateral regions excludes arbitrary multiply covered disk domains. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The generator module is therefore $\mathbb F_2^3$ with zero differential. Its homology has total rank three. The actual closed-manifold invariance in [F3] identifies this diagram computation with $\widehat{HF}(L(3,1);\mathbb F_2)$; the negative-sign calculation proves the same for its reversed orientation. No individual Spin-c grading, absolute normalization or correction term has been inferred from this total rank calculation. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
