## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, there is a finite constant $C_\Omega>0$ such that every $u\in BV(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega),\qquad u_\Omega:=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions|Neumann TV is the interior distributional variation.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-compactness-lower-semicontinuity|Bounded-domain BV sequences are compact in L¹.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-extension-and-translation|Zero extension from a bounded Lipschitz domain has controlled BV norm.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality|In two dimensions, full-space BV embeds into L² with the stated TV bound.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, and the Neumann total-variation convention.

[A1] Countable Choice is used to choose a sequence contradicting the proposed $L^1$ Poincaré bound. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[lem-ip-bv-compactness-lower-semicontinuity]]: a BV sequence bounded in $L^1$ and TV has an $L^1$-convergent subsequence, and TV is lower semicontinuous.

[F2] [[lem-ip-bv-zero-gradient-constant-on-connected-domain]]: a locally integrable function with zero distributional gradient on a connected open set is a.e. constant.

[F3] [[lem-ip-bv-extension-and-translation]]: zero extension satisfies $\|\widetilde v\|_1+TV(\widetilde v;\mathbb R^2)\le C_{\rm ext}(\|v\|_1+TV(v;\Omega))$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality]]: $\|g\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le TV(g;\mathbb R^2)$ for $g\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$.

[F5] [[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions]]: adding a constant leaves Neumann TV unchanged.


## Proof

1.1 First there is $C_1<\infty$ such that every zero-mean $v\in BV(\Omega)$ satisfies $\|v\|_1\le C_1TV(v;\Omega)$. If no such constant existed, [A1] would select $v_k$ with $\int_\Omega v_k=0$, $\|v_k\|_1=1$, and $TV(v_k;\Omega)<1/k$. Their BV norms are bounded, so [F1] gives a subsequence converging in $L^1$ to $v$. The limit has mean zero and $\|v\|_1=1$, while lower semicontinuity gives $TV(v;\Omega)=0$. Hence every distributional derivative of $v$ is zero; [F2] makes $v$ constant a.e., and its mean forces $v=0$, contradicting $\|v\|_1=1$. [A1, F1, F2, given, choose, contradiction]

2.1 For any $u\in BV(\Omega)$ set $v=u-u_\Omega$. Then $v$ has mean zero, $TV(v;\Omega)=TV(u;\Omega)$ by [F5], and step 1.1 gives $\|v\|_1\le C_1TV(u;\Omega)$. By [F3], $\widetilde v\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and
$$TV(\widetilde v;\mathbb R^2)\le C_{\rm ext}(\|v\|_1+TV(v;\Omega))\le C_{\rm ext}(C_1+1)TV(u;\Omega).$$
Applying [F4] and using $\|\widetilde v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}=\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ proves the Statement with $C_\Omega=C_{\rm ext}(C_1+1)$. The same argument also shows every BV function on this bounded domain belongs to $L^2(\Omega)$. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $S\subset S^3$ be a smoothly embedded sphere transverse to $K$ in exactly two points. Cutting along $S$ gives two properly embedded arcs; cap each arc by an orientation-compatible simple arc on $S$, pushed slightly into the corresponding boundary collar to obtain oriented knots $K_1$ and $K_2$. Then the oriented isotopy class of $K$ is the connected sum $K_1\#K_2$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The connected-sum construction and orientation convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$, a smooth oriented knot $K$, and a smooth sphere $S$ transverse to $K$ in two points.

[F1] Smooth Schoenflies supplies an ambient isotopy taking $S$ to the equator; its endpoint identifies both ball sides simultaneously, with the same equatorial boundary parametrization. ([[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]])

[F2] The fixed standard ball-arc connected-sum construction is independent of its local choices under AC$_\omega$. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** The stated knot, sphere, and AC$_\omega$.

1.1 Apply [F1] and carry the knot through the same ambient isotopy. We now have the two standard hemispherical balls, each containing one proper arc of the knot. Cap each arc by a simple boundary arc, pushed slightly into a boundary collar; orient the cap to close the oriented original arc. Boundary caps give the same capped knot class: two simple arcs in a two-sphere joining the same two points are isotopic keeping the endpoints, with no other marked points to avoid. One explicit reduction puts the arcs transverse, removes an outermost bigon successively, and then slides the resulting disjoint arcs across the disk they cobound; all moves take place in surface disks and extend to their ball collars. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 A small collar neighbourhood of each cap arc is a ball meeting the capped knot in one trivial arc. Delete these two ball-arc neighbourhoods. The remaining arcs are precisely the original two knot pieces, with endpoint collars on the common equator. Gluing by the fixed orientation-matching two-ball convention recovers $K$; the simultaneous boundary parametrization in [F1] makes the two sides agree. Straighten the cap collar and its positive local frame before gluing, which is a change of the local data allowed by [F2]. Hence this is the connected sum $K_1\#K_2$ in the stated convention. Transporting back through the original ambient isotopy proves the assertion. No extension of an arbitrary prescribed sphere diffeomorphism is used. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let M be a closed oriented 3-manifold, Γ a discrete group, and φ:π₁(M)→Γ. If (W₀,ψ₀) and (W₁,ψ₁) are compact oriented 4-manifolds with boundary M over which φ extends, then sign_Γ^(2)(W₀,ψ₀)−sign(W₀)=sign_Γ^(2)(W₁,ψ₁)−sign(W₁). Hence the signature defect depends only on (M,φ).

## Statement references

[Lück–Schick, Theorem 1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209161)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC as in the coefficient Definition, the common boundary representation, and the extending compact oriented collared TOP bounds. Smooth bounds are a special case.

[A1] The coefficient Definition retains full AC. [[def-integral-half-solutions-strebel-and-l2-signatures]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The signature defect is the difference of the regular-coefficient von Neumann and ordinary signatures. [[def-integral-half-solutions-strebel-and-l2-signatures]]

[F2] Whole-boundary gluing preserves both ordinary and regular-coefficient signature additivity on actual compact collared manifolds. [[thm-topological-finite-projective-l2-duality-and-boundary-gluing]]

[F3] For closed smooth four-manifolds the regular-coefficient signature equals the ordinary signature. The smooth group-signature theorem also permits based paths, nononto maps and arbitrary targets. [[thm-l2-signature-theorem-for-closed-four-manifolds]], [[thm-smooth-group-signature-defects-are-independent-and-uniformly-bounded]]

[F4] **External TOP input, under the run-specific boundary in CLAUDE.md §12:** for a normal covering of a closed connected oriented topological manifold of dimension $4k$, its homological $L^2$ signature equals its ordinary signature. This includes dimension four; no smoothing of that manifold is required. Apply the normal-cover theorem to the coefficient image and use regular-module subgroup induction for a nononto target. This is imported, not reconstructed here. The actual v3 introduction and §1 opening were read to match its dimension-four TOP and normal-cover hypotheses; no complete reconstruction of its analytic proof is claimed. [Lück–Schick, *Various $L^2$-signatures and a topological $L^2$-signature theorem*, Theorem0.2 and §3, arXiv v3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209161v3).

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $W_0,W_1$ are smooth. Glue $W_0$ to $-W_1$ along their boundary collars to obtain a closed smooth four-manifold $X$. The extending homomorphisms agree on the based boundary representation; van Kampen therefore gives the coefficient map on $X$. If paths were used to identify boundary basepoints, send the connecting generators to their stipulated path elements, as in [F3]. By [F2], $$\operatorname{sign}(X)=\operatorname{sign}(W_0)-\operatorname{sign}(W_1),\qquad\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_\Gamma(X)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_\Gamma(W_0,\psi_0)-\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_\Gamma(W_1,\psi_1).$$ Apply the closed smooth equality in [F3] and rearrange these two identities. The two defects are equal, proving the entire smooth-bound conclusion for the same target of the Statement. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For the full TOP Statement glue the actual collared bounds to obtain the closed oriented TOP four-manifold $X=W_0\cup_M(-W_1)$, with the extending coefficient map supplied by van Kampen exactly as in step1.1. The local theorem [F2] supplies both signature-additivity identities on this actual nonsmooth manifold. The external TOP equality [F4] gives $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_\Gamma(X)=\operatorname{sign}(X)$. Subtract the ordinary identity from the group-signature identity to obtain equality of the two defects. Thus all supplied bounds in the Statement give the same value. Only the closed TOP equality is external; gluing and the resulting algebra are local, and no smooth-only equality is applied to a nonsmooth bound. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume ACω. Let a finite pointed Heegaard multidiagram have actual complete handlebody disk systems for closed oriented three-manifolds, with a basepoint in every one-system cut component. Ordered polygons use distinct labeled, pairwise transverse attaching systems; when an operation repeats a geometric system, use its separately labeled small transverse auxiliary copies. For the full hat operations impose global weak multidiagram admissibility: every nonzero full-curve multiperiodic domain vanishing at all basepoints has both signs. For operations in a specified total Spin-c family, ordinary weak admissibility is also allowed: every nonzero formal periodic domain difference in the capped Spin-c kernel, normalized at every mark and with Chern evaluation zero, has both signs. The same formal sector condition is imposed on each relevant boundary pair, including intended sectors with no generators. In this ordinary weak branch all basepoint multiplicities are fixed to zero, the required arities and compact auxiliary parameter families are finite, and counts use the corresponding fixed actual index bands. Strict all-mark normalized strong admissibility is a further allowed branch; it is not substituted for ordinary weakness. For a single diagram the full-module admissibility convention tests all intended Spin-c sectors, including empty sectors, and implies the required global weak domain condition.

In positive symmetric rank choose, among the auxiliary data, an arbitrarily small pointed Hamiltonian representative with no triple product-torus intersection, following its pair generators and transporting its domains, actual Spin-c labels and admissibility. Fix that representative. Compatible generic source-dependent perturbations, coherent over the required conformal faces and auxiliary parameter families, then make the disk and polygon spaces entering the hat differential, continuation, handleslide, stabilization and surgery operations regular with their actual expected dimensions. The common protected tensor and arbitrary constant product-angle end charts can be prescribed, and coherent perturbations can be arbitrarily small about a supplied compatible reference model. Auxiliary polygon and anchored-continuation parameter families here keep the autonomous end paths fixed and regular on the required energy budget; regular compatible parameter-boundary data may be retained. No slice-regularity assertion is made for arbitrary parameter-varying autonomous end paths. This does not assert regularity by almost-complex variations alone on an arbitrary fixed triple, or invariance under the preliminary curve choice.

Dimensions include every allowed conformal and auxiliary family parameter. Quotient only actual source automorphisms: longitudinal translation acts freely on autonomous nonconstant two-ended strips; an anchored source-dependent continuation strip and a three-marked triangle have no translation quotient. Every total zero-dimensional space used in a mod-two count is finite, across all its literal realized classes and with its specified labels. The one-dimensional spaces entering the chain-map, composition and homotopy identities compactify to actual compact one-manifolds. At fixed data their boundaries are precisely the matching rigid polygon–polygon conformal splittings and strip–polygon breakings. In an auxiliary family the broken configurations are the rigid joint fiber configurations at one common parameter, together with the prescribed parameter-boundary strata; they need not be products of individually rigid parameterized polygon spaces. Every such broken end has an exhaustive gluing collar. For the zero-basepoint operations no nonconstant sphere or one-torus boundary disk survives; thus the specified boundary-degeneration terms vanish, and there is no further escape or uncontrolled periodic-domain end. Boundary parity gives the differential square-zero identity and the polygon chain-map, composition and homotopy identities.

At symmetric rank zero retain the original empty systems and use the point target directly: the differential is zero, the matching constant triangle is counted once, higher rigid operations vanish, and the conformal and parameter boundary identities are the actual source-space identities. No triple-torus exclusion or free translation quotient is imposed on that point map.

This is the analytic count theorem. It does not construct a subordinate surgery diagram, prove that a named top generator is a cycle, identify the homology of a surgery total complex with a filling, or prove Heegaard-move invariance. Those remain duties of the respective operation constructions.

## Statement

Let $B$ be a smooth compact four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and oriented boundary the rational homology sphere $Y$, where $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. Let $\mathfrak t$ be a boundary Spin$^c$ structure extending over $B$. Removing an open four-ball from the interior gives a Spin$^c$ cobordism $W$ with boundary $-S^3\sqcup Y$, and each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism on rational homology. In both orientations, the induced Heegaard Floer infinity map is an isomorphism of degree zero and the corresponding plus-map inequality gives $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge0$ and $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\le0$.

## Statement references

[[def-heegaard-floer-plus-infinity-absolute-grading|The cobordism degree convention]]

[[lem-heegaard-floer-correction-term-heegaard-invariance|The generic Heegaard Floer package needed for correction terms]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Absolutely Graded Floer Homologies and Intersection Forms for Four-Manifolds with Boundary*, Theorem 9.6 and Proposition 9.9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0110170v1)

[Baranowski, Borodzik, and Serrano de Rodrigo, *Heegaard Floer Homologies and Rational Cuspidal Curves*, Section 4](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/wbln.12.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-punctured-rational-homology-balls-are-rational-cobordisms]] gives the two rational homology inclusion isomorphisms, the boundary orientations, $\chi(W)=0$ and the zero rational intersection module.

[F2] [[lem-rational-heegaard-floer-absolute-grading-and-cobordism-maps]] and [[lem-rational-heegaard-floer-infinity-standardness-and-rational-cobordism-isomorphism]] construct, for each fixed extending Spin$^c$ structure, the compatible infinity and plus maps and prove the degree-zero infinity isomorphism.

[F3] [[lem-heegaard-floer-correction-term-heegaard-invariance]] supplies the grading-preserving tower and its bottom degree, with $d(S^3)=0$; [[lem-commuting-laurent-and-plus-maps-give-bottom-degree-inequalities]] supplies the bottom-degree comparison for the commuting square.

## Proof

**Given:** The stated rational homology ball, its oriented boundary, and an extending Spin$^c$ structure; let $W$ be obtained by removing an interior open ball.

1.1 The two boundary inclusions are rational homology isomorphisms and $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)=0$. In particular the square of the Chern class is zero, and $\chi(W)=\sigma(W)=0$. The same assertions hold for the reverse cobordism from $Y$ to $S^3$. For each of the fixed induced Spin$^c$ structures, the constructed infinity map is an isomorphism with degree $(0-2\cdot0-3\cdot0)/4=0$, and the corresponding plus map commutes with the infinity-to-plus projection. This uses the individual fixed-structure conclusion, including torsion extensions. [F1, F2]

1.2 Apply the supplied commuting-square comparison first to $W:S^3\to Y$ and then to its reverse $Y\to S^3$. The degree-zero isomorphisms give respectively $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge d(S^3)=0$ and $d(S^3)=0\ge d(Y,\mathfrak t)$. These are exactly the two stated inequalities in both orientations. [F3, step 1.1] ∎

      url: "https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch2.pdf"

## Statement

Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth properly embedded disk with boundary knot
$K\subset S^3=\partial B^4$. Choose a product tubular neighborhood
$\nu(D)\cong D^2\times D^2$ whose intersection with $S^3$ is the chosen tube
$N(K)$, and let $X=\overline{B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu(D)}$. Then the
inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
carrying the positive meridian of $K$ to the positive normal-circle generator.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Lemma 1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hatcher, §2.2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch2.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth proper disk $D$ in the standard $B^4$, its product tubular neighborhood, and the induced knot exterior on the boundary.

[F1] [[lem-knot-exterior-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]: $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K]$.

[F2] [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] and [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]]: relative homology excision and the natural pair sequence apply to the compact manifold pairs below.

[F3] [[cor-homology-of-spheres]]: $B^4$ is contractible, so its positive-degree homology vanishes.

[F4] [[def-knot-exterior]] and [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]] fix the boundary exterior and positive-meridian orientation.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The portion of $\partial X$ added by deleting $\nu(D)$ is the normal-circle bundle $D^2\times S^1$, and it meets $E_K$ in $S^1\times S^1$. By excision [F2], the relative pair $(B^4,X)$ has the homology of $(D^2\times D^2,D^2\times S^1)$. The latter solid-torus subspace has $H_1\cong\mathbb Z$ generated by a normal circle and $H_2=0$, while $D^2\times D^2$ is contractible by [F3]. Its pair sequence [F2] therefore identifies $H_2(B^4,X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z$, generated by a normal disk whose boundary is that normal circle. [F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 In the pair sequence of $(B^4,X)$, the segment
$$H_2(B^4)\longrightarrow H_2(B^4,X)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_1(X)\longrightarrow H_1(B^4)$$
has zero end groups by [F3]. Hence $\partial$ is an isomorphism. The generator
from step 1.1 maps to the normal circle on $D^2\times S^1$. A path in the base
disk $D^2$ from an interior point to a boundary point gives a homotopy of
these normal circles to the boundary meridian of $K$, with orientation fixed
by [F4]. Thus $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_X]$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1,
algebra, construct]

3.1 The inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow X$ carries the boundary meridian $\mu_K$ to the same normal circle $\mu_X$. It is therefore an isomorphism between the infinite cyclic groups in [F1] and step 2.1. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the standard oriented unknot $U$ and its standard genus-zero one-pointed Heegaard diagram, the normalized Alexander-filtered hat complex has total homology $\mathbb F_2$ generated at filtration level $0$. Consequently the diagramwise threshold is $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(U)=0$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau|The normalized Alexander filtration and its first nonzero homology level]]

[[lem-standard-unknot-hat-diagram-rank-one|The one-generator genus-zero unknot diagram]]

[Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, §§2.1 and 3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383v3)

[Manolescu, *An Introduction to Knot Floer Homology*, §3.5](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/hfk.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard oriented unknot and its standard genus-zero one-pointed diagram.

[F1] [[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau]] fixes the absolute Alexander normalization with the one-generator standard unknot diagram at filtration zero.

[F2] [[lem-standard-unknot-hat-diagram-rank-one]] proves that this genus-zero one-pointed diagram has one generator and zero differential, so its total homology is $\mathbb F_2$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], the total complex has one generator and zero differential, so its only nonzero homology class is represented by that generator. [F2, given, construct]

2.1 By [F1] the generator has Alexander level $0$. For every $s<0$ its filtered subcomplex is zero, while at $s=0$ the inclusion is the identity on the one-dimensional homology. Thus the first level with nonzero image is $0$, which is the asserted value. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let K be a knot and W an integral (n+1/2)-solution for M(K). Let R be Q or F_p, let G be an amenable group in Strebel's class D(R) with G^(n+1)={e}, and let φ:π₁(M(K))→G extend over W. Assume φ sends a meridian of K to an infinite-order element of G. Then the rho invariant ρ(M(K),φ) vanishes.

## Statement references

[Cha, Theorem 3.2 and complete proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.1058)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data of the Statement, interpreted with the full AC and smooth solution convention of its coefficient Definition. In particular $W$ is an actual compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with boundary $M(K)$, and $n\ge0$.

[A1] Full AC, the integral solution convention and its equivariant intersection forms are fixed in the Definition. [[def-integral-half-solutions-strebel-and-l2-signatures]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] An integral $(n+1/2)$-solution has $H_1(M(K);\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(W;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$, $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$, height-$n$ isotropic classes with unit duals, and isotropic height-$(n+1)$ lifts of the former. [[def-integral-half-solutions-strebel-and-l2-signatures]]

[F2] Actual compact collared four-manifolds with these supplied lifted half-pairs have ordinary and $L^2$ signatures zero for amenable $G\in D(R)$, $R=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$, $G^{(n+1)}=1$, and infinite-order meridian image. Its proof includes finite-projective transfer, the boundary dimension calculation, the lifted-cycle span estimate, and arbitrary-group induction; it requires no rho independence premise. [[thm-topological-lifted-half-pairs-force-amenable-signature-defect-zero]]

[F3] For smooth bounds the signature defect is independent of the bound, extending map and injective target enlargement; it therefore defines the rho invariant in the coefficient Definition. [[thm-smooth-group-signature-defects-are-independent-and-uniformly-bounded]], [[def-integral-half-solutions-strebel-and-l2-signatures]]

## Proof

1.1 The supplied extending coefficient map $\psi:\pi_1W\to G$ satisfies $\psi((\pi_1W)^{(n+1)})\subset G^{(n+1)}=1$, by induction on commutators. Hence it factors through the height-$(n+1)$ quotient carrying the isotropic lifted classes in [F1]. The actual smooth $W$ has its smooth boundary collar and is in particular an admissible collared topological manifold for [F2]. Its integral homology, finite pair lists and unit dual pairings are exactly [F1]; its meridian has infinite image by the Statement. Thus every hypothesis of [F2], including $n=0$ and $R=\mathbb F_2$ when applicable, is satisfied by this same $W$ and extending map. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Applying [F2] gives $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W,\psi)=0=\operatorname{sign}(W)$. This invokes its actual weak-exactness and finite-projective calculation: no closed range, finite CW type of a TOP manifold, or lift of the height-$n$ dual classes to the height-$(n+1)$ coefficient system is inferred. The latter calculation uses only the lifted isotropic classes and their ordinary unit duals, precisely the supplied data checked in step 1.1. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since this very bound is smooth, [F3] identifies its actual defect with $\rho(M(K),\phi)$ under the Definition's smooth bounding convention. Therefore $\rho(M(K),\phi)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W,\psi)-\operatorname{sign}(W)=0$. The proof covers arbitrary target groups by [F2]'s same-image induction and [F3]'s target-enlargement independence. No comparison with a nonsmooth TOP bound or an analytic eta definition is required for this original smooth-solution Statement. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC_ω. Under connected sum, each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n} is an abelian group. The identity is the class of the unknot, and the inverse of [K] is the class of the reverse mirror of K. Each category retains the ambient and coefficient conditions in its definition.

## Statement references

[Livingston, §2.1 and Theorem 2.2](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/living.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The four concordance sets with their specified concordance relations.

[F1] The ambient and coefficient conditions defining the four concordance relations ([[def-cdr-satellite-concordance-categories]]).

[F2] The mirror-reverse connected sum K#−K bounds a ribbon disk in the standard 4-ball ([[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]]).

[F3] Connected sum is associative and commutative on oriented knot types, with the unknot identity ([[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]]).

[F4] Connected sum of knot concordances is the operation on concordance classes ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]).

[A1] AC_ω supplies the countable choice used by the cited ribbon and concordance constructions ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F5] **External TOP/exotic input.** In the category conventions of [F1], connected sum descends to an abelian group on $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{ex}}$, with unknot identity and reverse-mirror inverse. This is the group assertion in Cochran–Davis–Ray Section1, printed1–2. Its underlying TOP ambient gluing and relative-collar conclusion are imported under the run-specific external-source boundary; no new local proof of those unresolved ambient identifications is claimed. The cited CDR definitions and group assertion on printed1–2 were read directly.

[F6] **Compact finite-input convention.** The classical external results are initially used in ordinary ZFC, not assumed choice-free from their citations. For this one application take finitely many charts covering the given compact manifolds and finitely many pair charts covering each given compact disk or annulus, shrinking to closed inner charts inside open outer charts. Such finite subcovers exist by compactness; selecting this finite list uses no axiom of choice. Include the actual boundary/product collars and all supplied homeomorphisms in the list. Encode chart domains and overlaps by their rational balls, continuous maps and their inverses by dense rational data with moduli on the closed inner charts, and smooth maps by all finite-order derivative and Taylor-remainder data. The modulus at each integer scale is the least integer satisfying its uniform-continuity bound; restrictions to rational compact boxes use the least box index. These are uniquely defined choices from subsets of $\mathbb N$, not a countable family of freely selected charts. Include positive open-image and overlap margins, inverse identities, finite cover/Lebesgue bounds, and the pair-section identities with positive separation from the compact outside-patch remainder. On the standard disk/annulus parameters the latter certify the actual plane section, not merely a continuous embedding. One real $r$ codes these finitely many maps and their canonical countable data. The external relative-constructibility input is that $L[r]$ is an inner model of ZFC containing $r$ (Karagila, §8.3, p.42); no ambient choice hypothesis is required. All compact maps are decoded using these same moduli, so the inverse identities, covers, pair sections and collar equalities are checked on dense rational sets with their displayed buffers and remain valid in the ambient universe $V$. An internally produced compact witness is exported with the same certificates, and hence is an actual ambient compact witness. This uses the peer-checked compact annulus coding pattern of the standard connected-sum compatibility supplier only at its geometric scope; it does not assert that arbitrary homology or fundamental-group hypotheses are absolute.

## Proof

0.1 Specialize the TOP/exotic external assertion [F5] at each finite list of knot representatives and witnessing annuli actually used. For TOP these lie in the standard product; for exotic concordance the supplied boundary-marked homeomorphism to that product is part of the input code. The finite chart and pair-chart extraction in [F6] uses compactness, not a choice of an atlas for a countable family. Inside $L[r]$ use the ordinary CDR group operation, retain the actual output annulus and marked product homeomorphism, and export their compact forward/inverse and collar certificates. This proves the required finite compatibility and transitivity instances in $V$. Since each instance starts with its own given finite data, no simultaneous choice of representatives or witnesses for all classes is made. The quotient group operations and laws follow by universal quantification over these instances; the original $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis is therefore respected, rather than inferred from the unqualified source assertion. The localized category is handled directly by the subsequent homology calculations, with no TOP normal theorem needed. [F1, F5, F6, given, construct]


1.1 The supplied connected-sum theorem gives associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity at the level of oriented knot types. The retained standard smooth boundary-sum construction on witnessing annuli gives concordance compatibility in the standard smooth product; the TOP/exotic compatibility is the external input [F5], and the localized ambient verification is given by the subsequent homology calculations. The knot-type isotopies themselves are admissible annuli in every category. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 0.1, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $D\subset B^4$ be the smooth ribbon disk for $K\#K^\dagger$ supplied by [F2]. By local smooth coordinates and straightening of the embedded disk, choose an ambiently standard interior 4-ball $B$ such that $B\cap D$ is a standard 2-disk. An ambient isotopy supported in the interior carries $B$ to a concentric standard ball, so its complement in $B^4$ is diffeomorphic to $S^3\times I$. Removing $\operatorname{int}B$ from $B^4$ and the interior of $B\cap D$ from $D$ gives a smooth annulus. The outer and inner boundary collars give product collars for it. Order the ends with $K\#K^\dagger$ at the lower end and the inner standard unknot at the upper end, and orient the annulus so its boundary is $-(K\#K^\dagger)$ at the lower end and $U$ at the upper end. It is therefore an admissible inverse concordance in the smooth category, and the same product annulus satisfies the TOP, exotic and localized ambient conditions. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 The external input [F5] supplies the TOP and exotic ambient gluing/compatibility assertions at exactly the definitions in [F1]. For the localized smooth category, transitivity is stacking along the marked $S^3$: Mayer–Vietoris and the two boundary homology isomorphisms give another $R_n$-homology $S^3\times I$. Reflection gives symmetry and a product gives reflexivity, all with their smooth annulus collars. [F1, F5, step 0.1, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 For localized connected sum choose a smooth product neighborhood $D^3\times I$ of a proper spanning arc inside each witnessing annulus, with the annulus strip in its standard local position, and remove its interior. If $Q$ is the remaining ambient piece, excision gives $H_j(W,Q;R_n)=R_n$ only for $j=3$. The map $H_3(W;R_n)\to H_3(W,Q;R_n)$ is an isomorphism: the boundary fundamental class meets the spanning arc once. The pair sequence therefore makes $Q$ an $R_n$-homology ball. Glue the two such complements on $S^2\times I$, joining the annulus strips. Mayer–Vietoris gives $R_n$ in degrees0 and3 and zero in other positive degrees; the endpoint connected-sum spheres give the degree3 generator, so each end inclusion is a homology isomorphism. The resulting smooth annulus witnesses connected-sum compatibility in the original localized category. These calculations use no homeomorphism-to-product assertion. [F1, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Thus connected sum is well defined in every category: the retained standard smooth construction handles $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}$, [F5] handles TOP/exotic, and step2.2 handles the localized case. The oriented knot connected-sum monoid [F3] descends to each quotient, giving associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity. The ribbon inverse in [F2], admissible in all four ambients, supplies the stated reverse-mirror inverse. All ambient and coefficient conditions are those of [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ be a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$, and suppose $Y\setminus K$ fibers over $S^1$ with connected fiber a Seifert surface $F$ of genus $g$. Then the integral top Alexander group is one copy of the integers:

$$\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(Y,K,[F],g;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z.$$

## Statement references

[[def-top-alexander-grading-of-knot-floer-homology|The integral Alexander grading and Seifert class]]

[[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region|The product sutured manifold obtained by cutting along a fiber]]

[Ni, *Knot Floer homology detects fibred knots*, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0607156v4)

[Juhasz, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, Theorem 1.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609779v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-marked-fiber-admits-a-sutured-surface-diagram]] constructs the actual meridionally marked exterior diagram and identifies its fiber cut with the marked product.

[F2] [[lem-permissible-surface-niceification-preserves-admissibility]] gives a finite admissible adapted nice diagram.

[F3] [[lem-relative-sutured-diagrams-have-signed-move-equivalences]] gives the signed comparison for the specified transported orientation class and computes the product by the empty diagram.

[F4] [[lem-fiber-outer-grading-and-integral-cut-euler-matrix]] fixes the absolute Chern anchor: the outer summand has Alexander degree g.

[F5] [[lem-signed-outer-summand-cut-comparison-with-zero-periodic-cut]] identifies the entire outer differential with the cut differential over the integers when the cut periodic group vanishes.

## Proof

**Given:** A null-homologous knot K in the stated general closed oriented Y and its connected fiber F of genus g, with the meridional boundary trivialization in the definition of the integral Alexander grading.

1.1 Use the actual binding bridge and drilling construction to represent the exterior with two meridional sutures, carrying the actual page longitude and the class of F. The adapted surface cut is literally the result of cutting this mapping torus along its fiber, hence is F times an interval with its product sutures. Apply the finite permissible niceification. Signed relative diagram moves compare the resulting complex to the chosen defining complex, with its specified coherent orientation class transported. No restriction on Y or change of coefficient ring is made. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 In this marked adapted diagram the local Euler obstruction is minus 2g plus twice the number of interior polygon coordinates when evaluated on minus F. Therefore the Alexander degree is g minus that number: degree g is precisely the outer generator set, and no higher degree occurs. The product cut has zero periodic-domain group, either directly from its empty product diagram and the relative handle description, or from its vanishing relative integral homology. The signed cut comparison consequently identifies the whole degree-g differential with the cut differential, after harmless changes of generator signs. [F4, F5, step 1.1]

1.3 The empty diagram of the actual product has one empty-tuple generator and no nonconstant disk, so its integral chain complex is Z with zero differential. The signed relative move equivalences identify its homology with that of the actual cut diagram. Combining with the full top-summand chain identification gives the asserted integral group isomorphism. The exterior orientation character restricts trivially to the zero-periodic cut, so this conclusion holds for the specified defining class without asserting equivalence of arbitrary orientation systems on the uncut exterior. [F3, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The infinite cyclic group $\mathbb Z$ is good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem, in the sense of the $\pi_1$-null disk property defined for a good fundamental group.

## Statement references

[[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding|The $\pi_1$-null disk property defining a good group]]

[[def-countable-choice|Axiom of Countable Choice]]

Michael H. Freedman and Frank Quinn, *Topology of 4-Manifolds*, §2.9, https://archive.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/4789/1/FreedmanQuinn-TopologyOf4Manifolds-PMS39.pdf

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice and the definition of a good group.

[F1] [[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding]]: Goodness means the $\pi_1$-null disk property for all disk-like height-$1.5$ capped gropes and all homomorphisms to the group.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Every countable family of nonempty sets admits a choice function.

## Proof

1.1 **Section1: Precise input.** A finite framed four-dimensional capped-grope neighborhood is supplied, with its usual product collars and self-plumbing charts. Its body is embedded; only cap interiors have generic double points. An integer labeling means a homomorphism from the fundamental group of this actual neighborhood to Z. Paths to individual cap sheets are fixed once. Conjugating a based loop does not change its integer label. No arbitrary locally flat surface is given a tubular neighborhood by this hypothesis: the actual grope's framed block neighborhood is input. [F1, A1, construct]

1.2 **Operation.** Contract one top surface stage. Designate a finite subset of cap double points to be pushed off at that contraction, and choose a first and second sheet at each designated point. Then the resulting shorter capped grope has the same lower body, attaching circle and framing. Every old intersection not designated has parallel descendants with its old label. No designated old intersection remains. Every new cap intersection is a descendant of two designated intersections removed across dual caps at this same contraction, and its label is a difference of their labels, up to overall sign. Consequently, if all designated labels lie in an interval [a,b], every new label has absolute value at most b−a. [F1, A1, construct]

1.3 **Proof of the contraction operation.** Cut the top surface at each pair of symplectic attaching curves. Replace the cut part by two small parallel copies of each of its two caps and the small central square at their unique attaching-curve intersection. Cutting a genus-g one-boundary surface along its complete symplectic system leaves the disk region with paired edges; the four parallel cap sectors and this square fill each pair of edges. Thus this replaces the surface with its contracted disk. All replacements take place in the supplied framed block. Parallel copies are made in its chosen normal coordinate; the central square uses the untwisted product collar, so the external attaching framing is unchanged. The result may be immersed, which is allowed. [F1, A1, construct]

1.4 For a designated point, take an embedded path on its second cap from that point to its attaching boundary, with interior avoiding all other double-point preimages. Finitely many paths on one cap can be chosen with disjoint interiors by an embedded finite tree and small parallel offsets. The two parallel copies of that path, closed across the central square, bound a ribbon Whitney disk pairing the two intersections of the first sheet with the contracted cap. In a product rectangle around the path, this is just the rectangle between the two parallel copies, closed by the boundary square. Its interior is disjoint from the old body and all unmodified sheets. A generic sufficiently small choice of the finitely many product widths is possible because their unwanted incidences are finitely many closed disjoint compact sets. No appeal to a normal bundle over an arbitrary TOP surface occurs. [F1, A1, construct]

1.5 Push the first sheet across this ribbon. This removes precisely the two paired intersections. The only ribbons that can meet are ones running across dual cap sectors: their boundary paths cross in the central square. Resolving those crossings by the prescribed order of the pushes creates intersections between the pushed first sheets. Ribbons on the same cap have been chosen parallel and disjoint, and ribbons belonging to different handles have disjoint block neighborhoods. Therefore every new intersection has exactly the stated two designated ancestors. Repeating for all parallel descendants removes the designated old point altogether. This is a finite sequence of ordinary finger/Whitney operations in explicit smooth block charts; a small relative perturbation makes the resulting intersections transverse. [F1, A1, construct]

1.6 Here is the label calculation, including the path issue. Let the two designated points have based first-to-second loops g,h. A path to the new intersection follows the first pushed sheet along the ribbon to its second-sheet cap, crosses the common central square, and returns along the other ribbon in reverse. Cancel the common paths in the old body. The resulting word is g h^{-1}; changing starting path conjugates it and exchanging the two resulting sheets inverts it. This is a calculation in the original supplied neighborhood, since every ribbon and push lies there. Its Z label is consequently ±(phi(g)−phi(h)). An old point copied to parallel sheets has its old loop with a small contractible product strip added, so its label is unchanged. The construction, classification of new intersections and claimed bound follow. [F1, A1, construct]

1.7 **Section2: Halving and the finite stopping bound.** Suppose there are h top surface stages available for contraction and the absolute labels of all the actual cap-point generators are at most an integer N. Contract the top stage, designating all points whose labels are in [N/2,N]. Their new labels have absolute value at most N/2 by Section1. The unmodified old positive labels are less than N/2; old negative labels may still range to −N. Contract the next top stage and designate the labels in [−N,−N/2]. Again new labels have absolute value at most N/2. Old labels outside this interval already have absolute value at most N/2. Thus two contractions reduce the bound to N/2. The same construction works when N is odd, since inequalities refer to real bounds and labels remain integers. [F1, A1, construct]

1.8 After q pairs of contractions the bound is N/2^q. Choose the least integer q with 2^q>N; if N=0 take q=0. This is a finite integer algorithm. At that point every cap-point generator has label zero. The neighborhood group is generated by these loops: the abstract disk-like capped grope is simply connected (its symplectic basis loops are killed by its attached higher stages/caps), and each self-plumbing identifies two small simply connected sheet neighborhoods, adding its one double-point loop. Cutting the finite plumbing neighborhoods restores the abstract source. Van Kampen, adding them back one at a time, gives precisely these generators, with no assertion that an arbitrary ambient group is free. Hence the entire neighborhood image has zero Z label. [F1, A1, construct]

1.9 Contract the remaining body stages to a disk. Every operation stays in this neighborhood, so all double-point loops of the final framed immersed disk have zero image under the original homomorphism. Its boundary and framing are unchanged. This proves null-disk production **when sufficiently many actual stages have been constructed**; it does not yet manufacture those stages from height1.5. [F1, A1, construct]

1.10 In the symmetric height-raising construction, the precise quantitative target can be stated without the harmless factor-of-two compression in FQ2.9. If 2k raising steps give height at least 2^k and each resulting cap-point loop has word length at most 5^{2k} in the original finite cap-point generators, their absolute labels are at most 5^{2k}B. It suffices that
2^(−floor((2^k−1)/2)) · 5^(2k) · B < 1. [F1, A1, construct]

1.11 Reserve one bottom surface stage; the other stages supply the indicated number of contraction pairs. The displayed quantity tends to zero because its base-two logarithm is at most −2^(k−1)+O(k)+log2 B. Thus a least successful k is obtained by a terminating integer search. No infinite choice or convergence theorem is hidden in this numerical step. Sections3–4 prove the required height and word-length estimates starting from the asymmetric height1.5 input. [F1, A1, construct]

1.12 **Section3: The asymmetric bootstrap.** Start with one symplectic pair above the bottom surface: on the positive side a framed capped surface R of positive genus, on the negative side a framed immersed cap W. The same construction is repeated for the finitely many pairs; their body blocks are disjoint, and interactions between cap systems are allowed. All operations fix a neighborhood of the original bottom surface and its attaching region. [F1, A1, construct]

1.13 Take two small framed parallel copies of R, at negative and positive normal coordinate, and join their boundary circles by the normal annulus crossing the attaching curve of W once. The result is an embedded closed surface of genus twice that of R. Its caps are the corresponding parallel copies of the caps of R. This is a sphere-like capped surface F: compressing its symplectic system gives a sphere. Its body meets W in one point and is disjoint from R; its cap intersections with all the old caps are unrestricted. The annulus and the single crossing are read in the supplied symplectic handle block, not in a hypothetical neighborhood of an arbitrary locally flat surface. [F1, A1, construct]

1.14 Construct a small parallel copy of F and contract its top stage to an immersed framed sphere T. During contraction, push every other cap sheet off T by the ribbons of Section1, excluding the one prescribed body intersection T with W. This includes the original caps of F, the caps of R and the remaining parts of W. All intersections newly produced by those pushes are between those cap sheets. The sphere T is therefore disjoint from both R and the body/caps of F, and from the caps of R, and meets W at its one prescribed point only. Self-intersections of T are allowed. The ribbons have support near cap arcs and their central squares, away from the lower body, so they do not alter any of the displayed body intersections. [F1, A1, construct]

1.15 Use T as a Norman sphere to remove every intersection of W with a cap of R or F: for each such point, choose a path in W from that point to the unique point W meets T. Remove a small disk from the intersecting cap and connect it by an untwisted tube, along a parallel copy of that path, to T with a small disk removed. The second endpoint consumes the one intersection of that parallel T with W. The two disks removed and the tube are the boundary of a product neighborhood of the path, so the resulting cap misses W at the chosen point and has the same boundary and framing. Choose the finitely many paths as branches of a tree in the abstract disk W, with separate parallel approach paths at their common endpoint; their interiors avoid all other double-point preimages. Normal widths are chosen successively small. The added copies of T are framed immersed spheres; their self- and mutual intersections belong entirely to the modified CAPS. Thus they may create cap intersections but no body intersections. Their original intersections with R or the body of F are empty, and sufficiently small parallel copies retain that property. After this finite operation W is disjoint from every other part except its own self-intersections and the single point on the body of F. In particular F remains a proper capped surface transverse to W. [F1, A1, construct]

1.16 For each self-intersection of W, tube one of its sheets to a separate small parallel copy of the BODY of F, along the other sheet and then along a chosen arc in W to the transverse point. This is the same local Norman cancellation, now using a capped surface instead of the contracted sphere. The new body consists of W with that sheet disk deleted, the punctured closed body of F, and their connecting annulus. It is a one-boundary surface with additional genus, with the old W boundary/framing. The caps of the added F provide the symplectic caps for its new handles. Its body is embedded: before the tubing, distinct body copies were disjoint and met W only at their distinct transverse endpoints; the tube arcs avoid every other double-point preimage. Choose disjoint parallel branches of a finite tree in W and nested normal widths. The tube neighborhoods consequently miss all other body sheets. Every old self-intersection of W is removed once, and none is introduced into the new body. Its new caps may intersect each other or the old caps, but they miss every body: the prior operation made the old caps disjoint from W, and properness of F makes its caps disjoint from all the parallel body sheets. At the attaching collars this assertion is the defining product chart. Consequently W has become an actual proper framed capped surface, not merely a surface with unaccounted body intersections. [F1, A1, construct]

1.17 This changes the side heights (1,0) to (1,1), preserving the original bottom stage. All choices and moves were finite. The scorecard is: R/body(F) embedded and mutually disjoint throughout; T immersed auxiliary, intersecting W once; old caps arbitrary among themselves; after the Norman cancellations all old caps miss W; after the final tubing every new intersection lies among caps. The auxiliary T is discarded after its copies have been inserted into caps. No disjointness of its parallel copies is needed, because their intersections are allowed cap intersections. [F1, A1, construct]

1.18 **Section4: Height raising and word length.** Here the two side heights count stages ABOVE the fixed bottom surface. Section3 gives (1,0) to (1,1). The following side extension, used only finitely often in this bootstrap, supplies (1,1) to (2,1) to (2,3). Let P be the side to be raised and Q its other side, of heights p,q at least one. Construct F transverse to the bottom surface of P by taking two normal parallels of Q and closing their rims with the normal annulus. It is sphere-like of height q. Its body is embedded, meets P only at the specified first-stage point, and misses all other body stages; intersections of its caps with the old caps are allowed. [F1, A1, construct]

1.19 First make a contracted parallel sphere T transverse to the bottom of P, using Section1 and pushing off all original cap sheets and the caps of F. Its only body intersection is that prescribed transverse point. To make the caps of F disjoint from the old P caps, push an F-cap sheet at each intersection down the old P cap to its attaching stage and then down successive P stages to its bottom. A finger across one attaching collar replaces one intersection with two on the immediately lower stage; this is two parallel paths around the two ends of that collar. After p stages there are finitely many points on the bottom of P. Tube them off over parallel copies of T. These changes affect only caps of F. They cannot reintroduce intersections with old P caps because T misses those caps and the finger paths on the old caps avoid the other finitely many double-point preimages. The new intersections are among caps of F and possibly the old Q caps, which are still caps. All old body stages are fixed. [F1, A1, construct]

1.20 Now for an intersection of an old P cap with a Q cap, push the Q-cap sheet down the P stages and tube it off over T. The Q cap is still an immersed disk; its boundary and framing are fixed. It may acquire self/intersections with other caps, which are allowed. It remains disjoint from the old P caps and all body stages: the punctured T used in the tubing has had its unique bottom-P intersection removed. Crucially T is also disjoint from the body of F, so the Q caps miss every body piece to be added in the next step. [F1, A1, construct]

1.21 Finally treat every self/mutual intersection among the old P caps by pushing one of its P sheets down the P stages and tubing it off over copies of the full F, rather than T. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope: its first added stage is the old disk with punctured bodies of F attached, followed by the higher stages of those copies of F. Orient each added copy so its transverse intersection cancels the chosen point, and use the untwisted framed tubes. All old P-cap intersections have been removed; the added bodies are embedded and disjoint from each other because distinct body parallels of F are disjoint, and the tube paths avoid all other old preimages. The new caps are copies of F's caps. Those were made disjoint from ALL old P caps before this step, and properness makes them disjoint from F's parallel bodies. Consequently every new intersection is among caps, not on a new body. A cap with no intersections may be regarded as a genus-zero stage with no attached higher surface, as in the disk-like model. We have obtained side heights at least (p+q,q), with the previous body and its attaching framing preserved. The first and second steps are needed: merely asserting that tubing adds height would leave the old cap intersections on the new body. [F1, A1, construct]

1.22 All choices involve finite paths, parallels and normal widths in supplied framed blocks. Use the move first with p=q=1, then exchange the two sides and use p=1,q=2. Both sides then have height at least two, so the entire grope has height at least three. The induced integer labels on its finite plumbing generators are obtained by following their actual paths back to the original neighborhood; let B be the maximum of their absolute values. B exists without any growth estimate for this finite bootstrap. [F1, A1, construct]

1.23 Once both sides have height at least two, there is an efficient variant which contracts only the TOP stage of a transverse grope. For the side P to be extended, form the transverse grope from the opposite side Q. Its height is that of Q. Contract its top stage and push the old caps off that contraction by Section1. The transverse grope now has height one less and its caps are disjoint from all old caps. Push each intersection on a P cap down the P stages, and at the bottom tube off over this transverse grope. The same body/cap scorecard as Section4 applies: new bodies consist of separate parallel copies of the old embedded opposite-side bodies, and all cap intersections have been removed from the new body before it is declared a body. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope with the height of the contracted transverse grope. In terms of full path heights a,b INCLUDING the shared bottom, the updated path height is a+b−2. Alternate the sides. Starting with a_{−1}=a_0=3, the successive updated path heights obey a_n=a_{n−1}+a_{n−2}−2. The uniform height is the smaller of the two current path heights. Writing a_n−2 as a Fibonacci recursion gives, after 2k steps, uniform height at least 2^k: consecutive pairs increase the smaller Fibonacci term by at least a factor two. Additional initial height only improves the bound. [F1, A1, construct]

1.24 For clarity, the required estimate concerns WORDS, not numbers of double points. Base every old cap-point loop by a path in the old grope. Body-stage paths contribute no new plumbing generator. Contraction copies an old point without changing its generator. A push off a contraction creates the difference loop of Section1, a word of length at most two in the OLD cap-point generators. A new intersection among caps of the parallel transverse grope has length one, since its sheets are old parallel sheets. The only remaining type is a loop using a newly pushed-down finger: follow its first sheet across at most two old cap-point loops to the parallel transverse copy, cross its new cap intersection (one old generator), and return across at most two old loops on the other finger. The two bottom-stage paths cancel, as do the parallel collar paths. This is a concatenation of at most 2+1+2 old generators or inverses. These exhaust the new intersections: they occur on unchanged parallels, on a contraction push, or between two inserted fingers. Thus each step sends every NEW generator to a word of length at most five in the PRECEDING generators. Induction gives length at most 5^(2k) after 2k steps, and absolute Z label at most 5^(2k)B. No count of the possibly much larger number of points is substituted for this word bound. [F1, A1, construct]

2.1 Choose the least k satisfying Section2's displayed stopping inequality (if B=0 no raising is needed). Height supplies the required number of contraction pairs, and the label estimate supplies their initial bound. Section2 then gives zero image on every cap-point loop, and final contraction produces a framed immersed disk with the original framed attaching circle. Everything occurs in the original supplied grope neighborhood. For an arbitrary homomorphism to Z this is the pi1-null disk property of the existing goodness Definition. The construction is finite for each input: no countable-stage choice, limiting disk, tower standardization or arbitrary TOP normal-bundle theorem has been used in this cyclic part. ∎ [F1, A1, construct]

## Statement

Assume AC and ACω. For every nonempty oriented link $L\subset S^3$, there is a spectral sequence over $\mathbb F_2$ whose $E_2$ page is the reduced Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{*,*}(\overline L;\mathbb F_2)$ of the mirror link and whose abutment is $\widehat{HF}(\Sigma(L);\mathbb F_2)$ with its image filtration. The page identification is an isomorphism of bigraded vector spaces; this statement does not claim a diagram-independent filtered quasi-isomorphism type for the chain-level spectral sequence.

## Statement references

[[thm-os-spectral-sequence-for-a-fixed-link-diagram|Fixed-diagram spectral sequence]]

[[thm-reduced-khovanov-over-f2-link-invariance|Reduced Khovanov link invariance]]

[[lem-double-branched-cover-of-an-oriented-link-well-defined|Branched-cover invariance]]

[Ozsváth and Szabó, *On the Heegaard Floer homology of branched double-covers*, Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2, and §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309170v1)

[Lipshitz, *Heegaard Floer Homologies*, §5.3](https://floer.wiki/more/courses/floer-homology/2024/lipshitz_heegaard_floer_homology.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, ACω, a nonempty oriented link $L$, a diagram of $L$, and a basepoint on its mirror diagram.

[F1] The branched cover is well-defined up to oriented diffeomorphism ([[lem-double-branched-cover-of-an-oriented-link-well-defined]]).

[F2] For a fixed diagram, the surgery construction has $E_2$ equal to based reduced Khovanov cohomology and converges to the branched-cover Floer group ([[thm-os-spectral-sequence-for-a-fixed-link-diagram]]).

[F3] Over ACω, the reduced Khovanov group is independent of the chosen diagram and marked component up to bigraded isomorphism ([[thm-reduced-khovanov-over-f2-link-invariance]]).

[A1] AC is used by the link-complement and covering-space construction; ACω is separately used by the Reidemeister-move and generic Floer analytic branches ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Choose a finite regular diagram of $L$ and a point on its mirror away from crossings. By [F2], this fixed diagram gives a spectral sequence with the stated target and with $E_2$ equal to the based reduced Khovanov group of the mirror diagram. [F1, F2, A1, given, choose]

2.1 Apply [F3] to identify that page, up to bigraded isomorphism, with $\widetilde{Kh}(\overline L;\mathbb F_2)$ independently of the selected diagram and component. The convergence in [F2] and target invariance in [F1] give the stated invariant endpoints, with no diagram-independent filtered chain claim. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 The two deductions above are exactly the stated endpoint construction relative to [F2] and [F3]. They preserve the fixed-diagram scope of the filtered construction and use only the invariant isomorphism classes of its endpoints. Thus the formal assembly is complete relative to these two exact supplier interfaces. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## External-input boundary

The fixed-diagram supplier uses the explicitly labelled external Ozsváth–Szabó surgery and unlink-map inputs, with exact locators and reading limits recorded in those suppliers and the run source receipt. The reduced link-invariance supplier supplies the independent based-link passage. This proof assembles those results; it does not reconstruct their imported parts or claim a diagram-independent filtered chain type. AC for the branched cover and ACω for the analytic/Reidemeister branches remain the separate assumptions of the Statement.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every finite regular oriented diagram with exactly one component, the Seifert diagram procedure terminates after one finite smoothing scan and one finite band-record scan. It returns exactly one disk record for each Seifert circle and exactly one band record for each original crossing. Termination alone asserts no embeddedness, boundary equality, or genus minimality.

## Statement references

[[alg-seifert-surface-from-diagram|The exact finite procedure and its output]]

[[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram|Finiteness of the crossing set]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a regular oriented knot diagram $D$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the sequence principle stated in the item. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] The procedure performs one oriented smoothing at each crossing, records the Seifert circles, and then records one band for each crossing. ([[alg-seifert-surface-from-diagram]])

[F2] A regular oriented diagram has finitely many double points, all transverse, and no triple points. ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]])

[F3] Smoothing every crossing produces a finite disjoint union of oriented simple closed curves. ([[def-seifert-smoothing-and-seifert-circles-of-an-oriented-link-diagram]])

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], $D$ has a finite crossing set of cardinality $c$. The first loop in [F1] visits each crossing once and performs one smoothing, so it ends after $c$ iterations. No smoothing introduces a new crossing to be processed. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], the completed smoothing has a finite set of Seifert circles of cardinality $s$. The second loop in [F1] records one disk per circle and one band per original crossing, so it also has finitely many iterations and returns exactly $(s,c)$ with the prescribed records. No topological correctness claim follows from this finite termination argument. [given, A1, step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Input a valid finite planar code for one regular oriented knot diagram and a basepoint in the interior of an edge, away from every crossing and bend. Traverse the oriented code once starting at the basepoint. At each crossing, consider the first branch reached by this traversal. If that branch is under, record the crossing and exchange its over/under label; otherwise leave the crossing unchanged. Return the finite list of recorded crossing changes and the updated planar code. For a code with no crossings, return the empty list and the unchanged code. The input is the valid finite code defined for an oriented knot diagram; this procedure has no invalid-input branch.

## Definition

For the fixed root parameter, let $\mathcal C_p$ denote the semisimplified Temperley–Lieb category with labels $0,\ldots,r-2$, pivotal dimensions $d_j=[j+1]$, and Hopf-link data inherited from the Kauffman bracket. Put $\mathcal D_p^2=\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}d_j^2$ and choose $\mathcal D_p\in\mathbb C$ with that square. Choose $\kappa\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\kappa^6=A^{-6-(p+1)p/2}$. The root-specific extended data are the weighted Lagrangian ribbon bordisms whose objects are closed oriented labeled surfaces with a Lagrangian subspace of real first homology and whose morphisms are collared oriented labeled ribbon bordisms with integer weights. If $M_1:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ and $M_2:\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$ have relations $\Lambda_{M_1},\Lambda_{M_2}$ and boundary Lagrangians $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, define

$$K_1=\Lambda_{M_1}(\lambda_0),\qquad K_0=\lambda_1,\qquad K_2=\Lambda_{M_2}^{\,t}(\lambda_2), \qquad n(M_2\circ M_1)=n_2+n_1+\mu(K_1,K_0,K_2),$$

using the Wall-signature Maslov convention. The category composition, units, and anomaly weight are those specified by this formula and the weighted Lagrangian bordism definition; no ordinary oriented anomaly-free functor is part of this Definition.

## Remarks

The BHMV source uses $p_1$-structures, while the registered prerequisite map specifies Lagrangian-weighted data. This Definition supplies the latter using the existing local category carrier; the equality between its Maslov correction and the BHMV $p_1$/signature anomaly remains a theorem obligation and is not asserted here.

## Example

In the InverseBench black-hole-imaging case, very-long-baseline interferometry correlates telescope electric-field signals to produce complex visibilities of a nonnegative source-brightness image $z(\rho,\delta)$ on angular coordinates $(\rho,\delta)$. For a telescope pair $(a,b)$ at time $t$, the ideal visibility is the corresponding Fourier sample

$$I^t_{a,b}(z)=\iint z(\rho,\delta)e^{-2\pi i(u^t_{a,b}\rho+v^t_{a,b}\delta)}\,d\rho\,d\delta,$$

where $(u^t_{a,b},v^t_{a,b})$ is the projected baseline. The observed visibility is

$$V^t_{a,b}=g^t_ag^t_be^{-i(\phi^t_a-\phi^t_b)}I^t_{a,b}(z)+\eta^t_{a,b},$$

where $g^t_a,g^t_b$ are telescope amplitude gains, $\phi^t_a,\phi^t_b$ are phase errors, and $\eta^t_{a,b}$ is additive Gaussian thermal noise. For an oriented telescope triangle $(a,b,c)$, the closure phase is $\arg(V^t_{a,b}V^t_{b,c}V^t_{c,a})$; when a stored visibility has the opposite baseline orientation, the implementation uses its complex conjugate. For the ordered quadrangle $(a,b,c,d)$ returned by the implementation's closure-amplitude routine, the log closure amplitude is $\log\!\bigl(|V^t_{a,b}||V^t_{c,d}|/(|V^t_{a,d}||V^t_{b,c}|)\bigr)$. The closure phase is defined only when its triangle product is nonzero, and a log closure amplitude is defined only when all four relevant visibility amplitudes are nonzero. No value is assigned by these formulas at an undefined zero visibility; this domain restriction does not assert an implementation masking or rejection rule. The benchmark also uses total flux $\iint z(\rho,\delta)\,d\rho\,d\delta$. These derived data are nonlinear functions of the visibilities, so their noise is not additive. The training images are $50{,}000$ simulated general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic images resized to $64\times64$. Because those images are not public, the paper generates $5$ validation and $100$ test images from a pretrained diffusion model. The sparse, nonconvex closure-data model has multiple solutions compatible with the observations; the reported tests do not make a general uniqueness or posterior-calibration claim.

**Given:** A nonnegative image, telescope pairs and projected baselines, the complex visibility and gain/noise model, closure-data transformations on their stated nonzero-visibility domains, and the data-generation split stated in the Example.

## Example

Assume AC. For the square knot $K=T\#T^\dagger$, where $T$ is the positive trefoil and $T^\dagger$ is its reverse mirror, the double branched cover has $H_1\cong\mathbb Z/3\oplus\mathbb Z/3$ with linking form $\operatorname{diag}(1/3,-1/3)$. Its diagonal subgroup is a metabolizer, and the order-three character $\chi(a,b)=(a-b)/3\bmod\mathbb Z$ vanishes on it. The knot is smoothly slice.

## Example references

[[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon|A knot plus its reverse mirror is ribbon]]

[[lem-branched-cover-surgery-presentation-from-seifert-surface|The branched-cover surgery presentation]]

[[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix|The surgery-matrix linking-form formula]]

[Charles Livingston and Swatee Naik, *Introduction to Knot Concordance*, §3.1, pp. 44–51](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Concordance_Book.pdf)

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

[Rolfsen, *Knots and Links*, Chapter 8.D, pp. 212–215](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/rolfsen.pdf)

[[def-bounding-chain-torsion-linking-pairing|The oriented bounding-chain linking convention]]

[[def-finite-order-character-of-a-branched-cover|Finite-order characters]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The oriented connected-sum convention]]

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|The smooth sliceness convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive trefoil $T$, its reverse mirror $T^\dagger$, their boundary-connected-sum Seifert surface, the positive-push convention, and the double branched cover.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A positive trefoil Seifert matrix is $V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. [[lem-positive-hopf-plumbing-has-trefoil-seifert-matrix]]

[F2] The reverse-mirror surface is $-r(F)$; its positive normal is the reflected positive normal because the two orientation reversals cancel. Reflection negates linking, so the transported basis has positive-push matrix $-V$. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]] [[lem-seifert-pairing-well-defined]] [[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot]]

[F3] For $q=2$, a Seifert matrix $U$ gives a surgery presentation of the double branched cover with symmetric matrix $U+U^T$. [[lem-branched-cover-surgery-presentation-from-seifert-surface]]

[F4] For a nonsingular integral surgery matrix $A$, the first homology is $\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$ and the oriented linking form is $-A^{-1}\bmod\mathbb Z$. [[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix]]

[F5] Every knot plus its reverse mirror bounds a smooth ribbon disk. [[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]]

[F6] In a finite nonsingular linking form, an isotropic subgroup of square-root order is a metabolizer. [[def-finite-linking-form-and-metabolizer]]

[F7] The oriented torsion linking pairing is computed by the signed bounding-chain expression $(C\cdot y)/n\bmod\mathbb Z$. [[def-bounding-chain-torsion-linking-pairing]]

[F8] A finite-order character is a homomorphism to $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, with order measured in the character group. [[def-finite-order-character-of-a-branched-cover]]

[F9] The oriented connected sum joins the oriented knot arcs in the fixed two-ball model; the boundary-connected-sum surface in the Given therefore represents $T\#T^\dagger$. [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

[F10] A knot bounding a smooth proper disk in $B^4$ is smoothly slice. [[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]]

## Verification

1.1 The boundary-connected-sum surface for $K$ has block-diagonal Seifert matrix $U=V\oplus(-V)$: curves in the two summands are disjoint, so mixed linking entries vanish. Hence $U+U^T=A\oplus(-A)$, where
$$A=V+V^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}.$$
[F1, F2, F9, given, construct, A1]

2.1 The double-cover surgery presentation [F3] gives the linking group as $\operatorname{coker}(A)\oplus\operatorname{coker}(-A)$. Unimodular row and column operations reduce $A$ to $\operatorname{diag}(1,3)$, so each cokernel is $\mathbb Z/3$. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 Since $A^{-1}=-\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$, [F4] gives self-linking $2/3\equiv-1/3$ on a generator of the original-trefoil block. The reverse-mirror block has matrix $-A$, and therefore generator self-linking $-2/3\equiv1/3$. Choose the coordinates $(a,b)$ with the reverse-mirror block first and the original-trefoil block second. The mixed terms vanish, so in these explicitly ordered coordinates the linking form is $\operatorname{diag}(1/3,-1/3)$, as asserted. [F4, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The diagonal subgroup $P=\{(a,a):a\in\mathbb Z/3\}$ has order $3$ and $\lambda((a,a),(b,b))=ab/3-ab/3=0$. The ambient group has order $9$, so $|P|^2=9$ and [F6] makes $P$ a metabolizer. By [F8], the map $\chi(a,b)=(a-b)/3\bmod\mathbb Z$ is a character of order $3$ and vanishes on $P$. [F6, F8, given, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 By [F5], $T\#T^\dagger$ bounds a smooth ribbon disk and is smoothly slice by [F10]. This establishes sliceness independently of the homology and character calculation. [F5, F10, given] ∎

## Diagram

The following is the positive trefoil as the closure of the two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$. Here $\sigma_1$ means the strand entering from the left passes under the strand entering from the right; the closure arcs connect endpoints in equal horizontal positions. Three crossings exchange the two endpoints, so the closure has one component. The proof uses the Seifert-matrix calculations above and does not rely on the drawing.

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.9cm,y=0.9cm,baseline=(current bounding box.center)]
  \draw[thick] (-1,3)--(1,2)--(-1,1)--(1,0);
  \draw[thick] (1,3)--(-1,2)--(1,1)--(-1,0);
  \fill[white] (0,2.5) circle (2.5pt);
  \draw[thick] (-0.28,2.36)--(0.28,2.64);
  \fill[white] (0,1.5) circle (2.5pt);
  \draw[thick] (-0.28,1.36)--(0.28,1.64);
  \fill[white] (0,0.5) circle (2.5pt);
  \draw[thick] (-0.28,0.36)--(0.28,0.64);
  \draw[thick] (-1,0)..controls(-1.7,0)and(-1.7,3)..(-1,3);
  \draw[thick] (1,0)..controls(1.7,0)and(1.7,3)..(1,3);
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

The reverse mirror factor is obtained by reflecting the diagram and reversing its orientation; the square knot is their connected sum. The diagram only records the braid convention used to name $T$.

kind: lemma

      url: "https://www.ime.usp.br/~glaucio/mat6704/textos/GMTLecureNotes.pdf"

dependency_level: 0

## Statement

Let $n\ge2$. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $g_i:\mathbb R^{n-1}\to[0,\infty)$ be Lebesgue-measurable and integrable, with its arguments identified with all coordinates except $x_i$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_n)^{1/(n-1)}\,dx\le\prod_{i=1}^n\left(\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}g_i\right)^{1/(n-1)}.$$

## Statement references

[[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals|Hölder's inequality for integrals.]]

[[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces|Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative product integrals.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $n\ge2$ and nonnegative integrable functions $g_i$ on the coordinate hyperplanes.

[F1] Products of nonnegative measurable functions can be integrated iteratively by Tonelli's theorem. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[F2] For nonnegative integrable functions, Hölder's inequality bounds the integral of a product by the product of the corresponding norms. ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]])

[A1] For the induction step in dimension $n\ge3$, assume the inequality in dimension $n-1$.

## Proof

**Given:** The integer $n$ and nonnegative integrable coordinate functions $g_i$.

1.1 For $n=2$, Tonelli [F1] factors the left side as $(\int_{\mathbb R}g_1)(\int_{\mathbb R}g_2)$, which is the right side. [F1, given, base]

1.2 For $n\ge3$, assume [A1]. For $i<n$ define $h_i(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_{n-1}):=\int_\mathbb R g_i(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_{n-1},x_n)\,dx_n$. Tonelli [F1] makes each $h_i$ integrable. Applying Hölder [F2] in $x_n$ to the first $n-1$ factors and then Tonelli gives an upper bound for the left side of $\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}g_n(x')^{1/(n-1)}\prod_{i<n}h_i(\widehat{x_i}')^{1/(n-1)}\,dx'$. Set $H(x'):=\prod_{i<n}h_i(\widehat{x_i}')^{1/(n-2)}$. Hölder in $x'$ with exponents $(n-1)/(n-2)$ and $n-1$ bounds this by $(\int H)^{(n-2)/(n-1)}(\int g_n)^{1/(n-1)}$. The induction hypothesis [A1] bounds $\int H\le\prod_{i<n}(\int h_i)^{1/(n-2)}$, while Tonelli gives $\int h_i=\int g_i$. Substitution yields the claimed product bound in dimension $n$. [A1, F1, F2, given, IH]

2.1 Induction from the base case [step 1.1] through step 1.2 proves the inequality for every integer $n\ge2$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, discharge-induction: step 1.2] ∎

id: lem-lobachevsky-fourier-expansion-and-pi-third-bound
kind: lemma
title: "Lobachevsky Fourier expansion and a certified π/3 value"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 1
deps:
  - def-lobachevsky-function
justified_by: []

sources:
