## Statement

Let $X$ be a Hausdorff manifold, $X=U\cup V$ an open cover, and $\mathcal L$ a local system of abelian groups. There is a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_c^p(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_c^p(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_c^p(V;\mathcal L)\to H_c^p(X;\mathcal L)\to H_c^{p+1}(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots.$$
The maps into the union are extension maps obtained by excision. If $X$ is oriented of dimension $n$, cap with its compatible integral compact-support orientation classes compares this sequence with homology Mayer–Vietoris in degrees $n-p$. The ladder commutes when the homology connecting map leaving degree $n-p$ is multiplied by $(-1)^{p+1}$. No choice principle is assumed. All maps respect a coefficient-ring action commuting with the local transports.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The cover and ambient local system; in the cap assertion, the supplied orientation.

[F1] Compact-support classes have compact representatives and equality is witnessed at a common larger compact support. [[def-compactly-supported-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]]

[F2] Local chains admit the explicit least-subdivision small-chain deformation, excision and Mayer–Vietoris. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[F3] Compatible canonical support orientation classes exist without choice; the supplied orientation trivializes the orientation local system. [[lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets]]

[F4] The cohomology-first cap satisfies $\partial(\alpha\cap c)=(-1)^p(\alpha\cap\partial c-\delta\alpha\cap c)$ and is natural for coefficient transports. [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]]

## Proof

1.1 For compact $K,L\subset X$, write $C=C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathbb Z)$ and $A_K=C_*(X\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$, with analogous notation for $L$. Local cochains vanishing on $A_K$ are the relative local complex denoted $D_K$. Simplex by simplex, addition gives an onto map $D_K\oplus D_L\to D_{K\cup L}$: a simplex not entirely outside $K\cup L$ is not entirely outside at least one of $K,L$, so place its assigned coefficient in the first allowed summand. This is a degreewise lift, not asserted to commute with coboundaries. Its kernel consists of pairs $(a,-a)$ with $a$ vanishing on $A_K+A_L$. Thus there is a short exact cochain sequence with that kernel. The latter cochain complex computes the relative local cohomology supported in $K\cap L$. Indeed $X\setminus K$ and $X\setminus L$ are open and cover $X\setminus(K\cap L)$; [F2] replaces their small-chain sum by the full complement. To see the relative comparison on cochains explicitly, extend its small-chain homotopy $D$ to all ambient simplex generators by zero on simplices not contained in this complement. Then $1-\partial D-D\partial$ maps complement chains to their small-chain sum and fixes the sum, while $D$ vanishes on the sum. The resulting quotient maps are inverse up to the displayed chain homotopy; transporting coefficients along the same affine paths gives the identical local-cochain comparison. Taking cohomology gives the supported exact sequence. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Restrict to pairs $K\subset U$, $L\subset V$ compact. These unions are cofinal among compact supports in $X$. For any compact $Q\subset X$, choose finitely many relatively compact coordinate neighborhoods whose closures lie in one of $U,V$ and whose interiors cover $Q$. The union of the closures assigned to $U$, intersected with $Q$, is a compact $K\subset U$; the analogous construction gives $L\subset V$, with $Q=K\cup L$. Only one finite cover is selected. The intersections $K\cap L$ are cofinal for compact subsets of $U\cap V$, since one may take $K=L$ equal to any such compact set. Excision in [F2] identifies the groups supported in $K$, $L$ and $K\cap L$ with their groups in $U$, $V$ and $U\cap V$. Take the filtered colimit of the exact sequences of step 1.1. It is exact directly: a representative in a colimit kernel vanishes at one common larger pair of supports, where exactness supplies its lift; a zero representative of a lift also becomes zero at a common larger pair. With [F1] this gives exactly the displayed compact-support sequence and its extension maps. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For the cap assertion, use the support class of [F3] on $K\cup L$, whose restrictions are the two smaller support classes. Subdivide a finite representative orientation chain so that every simplex lies either in $U$ or outside $K$, and either in $V$ or outside $L$; the two open covers and the finite chain allow one common finite subdivision by [F2]. If $\alpha=\alpha_U+\alpha_V$ is a degree-$p$ supported cocycle lifted by the short exact sequence of step 1.1, then $\alpha_U\cap z$ is a chain in $U$ and $\alpha_V\cap z$ is a chain in $V$: the other simplices lie outside the corresponding support and their front evaluations vanish. Their sum is $\alpha\cap z$. The supported cohomology connector is represented by $\delta\alpha_U=-\delta\alpha_V$ in the intersection complex. The homology connector is represented by $\partial(\alpha_U\cap z)$. Since $\partial z$ lies outside $K\cup L$, [F4] gives $\partial(\alpha_U\cap z)=(-1)^{p+1}(\delta\alpha_U)\cap z$. To check the kernel-to-support comparison as well, put $\gamma=\delta\alpha_U$ and use $\rho=1-\partial D-D\partial$ from step 1.1. The actual cochain supported in $K\cap L$ is $\gamma\rho$. Since $\gamma$ is a cocycle, $\gamma\rho-\gamma=\delta\beta$ with $\beta=-\gamma D$. The homotopy $D$ vanishes on every simplex contained either outside $K$ or outside $L$, so $\beta$ vanishes there too. After the same cover subdivision, $\beta\cap z$ is a chain in $U\cap V$ and $\beta\cap\partial z=0$. The identity [F4] shows that $(\gamma\rho)\cap z-\gamma\cap z$ is the boundary $(-1)^{p+1}\partial(\beta\cap z)$ in that intersection. Thus the computed connector represents the cap of the actual supported cohomology class, not just of its small-complex model. This is the claimed connecting-square sign. The other squares commute by addition, the same support restrictions, and the cap formula. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Coefficient morphisms and restrictions commute with all simplex transports and the displayed maps, proving naturality; a commuting scalar action is respected for the same reason. Empty supports and intersections give zero groups, and the same formulas apply in degree zero and negative degrees. All subdivision choices are least integers, each compact support uses one finite cover, and colimit exactness chooses one representative and one lift at a time. No family of primitives, chart choices or inverse maps indexed by an infinite set is chosen. This proves the assertions without a choice principle. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be a closed oriented three-manifold, with a specified coefficient homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(M_j)\to\Gamma$ on each component $M_j$, where $\Gamma$ is PTFA. Let $k=\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field, put $A=k[\Gamma]$, and let $K$ be its fraction division ring with the involution fixing $k$ and inverting group elements. Let $A\subseteq R\subseteq K$ be an involution-stable unital intermediate ring, and assume $H_1(M;K)=0$.

Then $H_1(M;R)$ is an $R$-torsion module and the coefficient Bockstein, oriented duality and evaluation define its Blanchfield pairing with target $K/R$. This pairing is nonsingular provided that on each component at least one of the following holds: every right ideal of $R$ is principal; $H_0(M_j;R)=0$; or the image of $\phi|_{\pi_1(M_j)}$ is cyclic. The last condition includes the usual integral infinite-cyclic coefficient case $R=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, without asserting that this ring is a principal ideal domain. No choice principle is assumed.

## Statement references

[[def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant]]

[COT, Theorem 2.13 and proof, printed page 451](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908117)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The closed manifold, coefficient systems, coefficient rings and vanishing in the Statement; the additional alternative is imposed only for the nonsingularity conclusion.

[F1] The Blanchfield convention is the inverse coefficient Bockstein after oriented duality, followed by evaluation; its first argument is conjugate-linear and its second argument right-linear. [[def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant]]

[F2] Integral and field PTFA group rings and their intermediate rings have the asserted Ore fractions and compatible involutions. [[lem-ptfa-integral-and-field-group-rings-have-compatible-ore-involutions]]

[F3] Ore localization is exact, commutes with arbitrary chain homology, and annihilates exactly the elements with a nonzero right annihilator. [[lem-ore-localization-is-flat-and-detects-module-torsion]]

[F4] Twisted singular chains admit a choice-free one-vertex reduction with degree-zero boundary ideal $\sum_{h\in\operatorname{im}\phi}(h-1)R$. For a principal such ideal, degree-one evaluation with $K/R$ is an isomorphism. [[lem-compact-manifold-twisted-singular-chains-admit-one-vertex-reduction]], [[lem-principal-boundary-chain-evaluation-over-division-fractions]]

[F5] Involutive twisted-chain duals have the actual intrinsic local cochain models, and oriented duality identifies $H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))$ with $\overline{H_{3-p}(C_*)}$. [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]]

[F6] The low-degree coefficient Bockstein is exact at $H^1(K/R)$ and $H^2(R)$ without an infinite product lifting assumption. [[lem-choice-free-low-degree-coefficient-bockstein-on-compact-manifolds]]

## Proof

1.1 Work first on one nonempty connected component. Put $C_*=C_*(M;R)$ in the right-module convention. By [F2], $R$ has no zero divisors, satisfies both Ore conditions, and has fraction division ring $K$. The supplied homomorphism has unitary transport units for the given involution. By [F4], replace $C_*$ by its explicitly homotopy equivalent free complex $C'_*$ with $C'_0=R$. This replacement preserves homology, dual cohomology and the natural evaluation maps; the discarded summand has an explicitly contracted identity differential. [F2, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F3] and $H_1(M;K)=0$, one has $H_1(C_*)\otimes_RK=0$. The elementwise zero criterion of [F3] says that every element of $H_1(C_*)$ has a nonzero right annihilator. Thus the whole module equals its torsion submodule. This uses arbitrary-complex localization, so no finite CW or triangulation assumption is introduced. [F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.2 The degree-zero term of $C'_*\otimes_RK$ is $K$, and the image of its degree-one differential is either zero or $K$. In the first case $d_1=0$, and $H_1(M;K)=0$ implies that every degree-one chain is a boundary, so every degree-one dual cocycle vanishes. In the second case choose $z$ with $d_1z=1$; then $C'_1\otimes_RK=\ker d_1\oplus zK$. The same homology vanishing says $\ker d_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$, so every dual cocycle factors through $d_1$ and is the coboundary of its value on $z$. Hence $H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K))=0$, using the tensor adjunction in [F5]. Also [F5] directly identifies $H^2(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K))$ with $\overline{H_1(M;K)}=0$. The exact segment [F6], applied to the compatible dual local systems of [F5], therefore gives a Bockstein isomorphism $\beta:H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R))\to H^2(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))$. [F5, F6, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

2.3 Restriction of a cocycle to cycles always defines the left-$R$ linear evaluation map $\kappa:H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R))\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_1(C_*),K/R)$. Under the additional alternatives it is an isomorphism by [F4]. Indeed the reduced boundary image $B_0\subseteq C'_0=R$ is a right ideal, so it is principal if $R$ is right principal. If $H_0(M;R)=0$, it is all of $R$. If the coefficient image is cyclic generated by $t$, it is $(t-1)R$, including zero for trivial image. These verify precisely the hypothesis of the principal-boundary evaluation lemma, whose proof allows arbitrary $C'_1$. Thus no finite generation or principal-ideal assumption is silently imposed in the other two branches. [F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By [F5], the inverse oriented duality map is an isomorphism $\overline{H_1(C_*)}\to H^2(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))$. Compose it with $\beta^{-1}$ from step 2.2 and the evaluation map $\kappa$ from step 2.3. Evaluating the resulting functional on $y$ defines $B(x,y)\in K/R$. The composition is left-$R$ linear on the conjugate module and its values are right-$R$ linear functions of $y$, so $B(xr,y)=\bar rB(x,y)$ and $B(x,ys)=B(x,y)s$. This is exactly [F1]'s Bockstein–duality pairing, defined before any claim that $\kappa$ is invertible. Under the alternatives of step 2.3, all three maps in its adjoint are isomorphisms. Therefore $\overline{H_1(C_*)}\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_1(C_*),K/R)$ is an isomorphism, which is nonsingularity in the stated right-module convention. [F1, F5, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, construct, algebra]

4.1 A compact manifold has finitely many components, since its connected components are open and cover it. Apply the argument to each, using only finitely many basepoint and finite-atlas choices. Chains split over those components, and cochains are a finite product, so their cycle/boundary and Bockstein decompositions need no infinite primitive selection. The oriented fundamental class is the sum of the component classes, and the pairing is their orthogonal direct sum. Under the stated componentwise alternatives, each adjoint is an isomorphism, hence so is their finite direct sum. Empty $M$ gives the unique pairing on the zero module. In particular a cyclic integral coefficient image satisfies the third alternative even when $R=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ is not right principal. This proves the full stated scope without a choice axiom. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The unrestricted implication over an unlocalized multivariable group ring is false. The explicit $T^3$ example with coefficient image $\mathbb Z^2$ has nonzero torsion first homology and zero dual; it is recorded separately in the PTFA counterexample. This example is contextual evidence for the necessary coefficient hypothesis, not a supplier in the proof.

## Remarks references

[[cex-ptfa-ore-localization-alone-does-not-give-blanchfield-nonsingularity]]

## Statement

The integral signed Khovanov cubes have the local graded cancellation models described below. They are chain homotopy equivalences over every fixed exterior resolution, commute with exterior saddle differentials, and commute with multiplication by $X$ at every marked point outside the local disk. Consequently they also give chain homotopy equivalences after taking the reduced quotient. For the crossing with A-smoothing the identity matching and B-smoothing the cap-cup matching, the two three-crossing braid cubes with words $121$ and $212$ retract to the same three-term complex. The two-crossing inverse-pair cube retracts to the identity matching in local cohomological degree one and quantum shift upward by one. All retractions are integral; their homotopies and the two cancellations in the three-crossing cube are specified in the proof.

## Statement references

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]

[[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot]]

[[lem-khovanov-cube-differential-squares-to-zero]]

[[def-chain-homotopy-equivalence]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The algebra $A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, its Frobenius maps, and cube signs $(-1)^{\sum_{a<j}v_a}$, with local crossings ordered before exterior crossings.

[F1] The Frobenius maps and their basis values are those of [[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]. The corresponding signed cubes square to zero by [[lem-khovanov-cube-differential-squares-to-zero]].

[F2] In the reduced quotient the distinguished component has module $M=\mathbb Z$, with $X=0$, $m_M(1\otimes u)=u$, $m_M(X\otimes u)=0$ and $\Delta_M(u)=X\otimes u$ ([[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot]]).

## Proof

1.1 **Meaning of every local map.** Use rectangles with top boundary points $1,\ldots,n$ and bottom boundary points $1',\ldots,n'$, both listed left to right. Let $I$ join $a$ to $a'$. Let $E_i$ join top $i$ to $i+1$, bottom $i'$ to $(i+1)'$, and all other $a$ to $a'$. In a product $UV$, $U$ is above $V$ and equal middle labels are joined. Thus $E_iE_i$ is $E_i$ with one disjoint middle circle, and $E_1E_2E_1$ is boundary-fixing planar isotopic to $E_1$; likewise with $1,2$ interchanged. For the latter assertion, trace top $1,2$ to one cap, bottom $1',2'$ to one cup, and top $3$ to bottom $3'$ along the remaining arc; there is no closed component. Contracting the intervening bends gives the stated isotopy. Close any of these matchings by a fixed exterior resolution. Order the resulting circle factors by the least arc label on each circle, using a fixed total order on all local and exterior arcs; factor permutations have no Koszul signs. A dot on an arc means multiplication by $X$ on the circle containing that arc. A saddle replacing an occurrence of $I$ by $E_i$, or conversely, means precisely $m$ on the two ordered circle factors if they merge, and $\Delta$ if they split, followed by the indicated factor permutation. All unmentioned factors have the identity map. This defines the maps below on every tensor basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes k}$, even when several local arcs belong to the same global circle. In the based case use $M$ for the distinguished factor and [F2] for a saddle meeting it. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 **Circle coordinates and neck cutting.** For a disjoint middle circle put its factor first and write $w=1\otimes w_1+X\otimes w_X$. If a saddle splits that circle from an arc carrying dot operator $x$, its map in these coordinates is $u\mapsto(xu,u)$; if it merges the circle into an arc carrying dot operator $y$, its map is $(w_1,w_X)\mapsto w_1+yw_X$. These follow from $\Delta(a)=1\otimes Xa+X\otimes a$ and $m(a\otimes b)=ab$. Two successive opposite saddles between the same two local arcs equal the sum of a dot on each arc. If the arcs are on distinct circles, this is the identity $\Delta m(a\otimes b)=Xa\otimes b+a\otimes Xb$: on $1\otimes1,1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$, both sides are $X\otimes1+1\otimes X,X\otimes X,X\otimes X,0$. If they are on one circle it is $m\Delta(a)=2Xa$. The same formulas with the distinguished factor reduced modulo $X$ prove the assertion in that case too. These are the exact tensor interpretations of the local neck-cutting identities, including when two dot positions are on the same circle. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **An explicit cancellation rule.** Suppose a differential between consecutive degrees has block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\phi&\beta\\ \gamma&\delta\end{pmatrix}:A_0\oplus R\to B_0\oplus S$, with $\phi$ an isomorphism. Set $L(a,r)=(a+\phi^{-1}\beta r,r)$ and $T(b,s)=(b,s-\gamma\phi^{-1}b)$. These invertible integral changes of coordinates give $T d L^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(\phi,\delta-\gamma\phi^{-1}\beta)$. Conjugate the adjacent differentials too. The equation $d^2=0$ and invertibility of $\phi$ imply that the incoming differential has zero $A_0$ coordinate and the outgoing differential vanishes on $B_0$. Thus there is a direct summand $A_0\xrightarrow{\phi}B_0$, contracted by $h|_{B_0}=\phi^{-1}$, $h=0$ elsewhere. Inclusion and projection of the remaining coordinates, conjugated by $L,T$, are chain maps $i,p$ with $pi=1$ and $1-ip=dh+hd$. This supplies actual chain maps and a homotopy for every cancellation used below, rather than merely an acyclicity assertion. If the blocks are homogeneous, these maps have quantum degree zero and $h$ has cohomological degree $-1$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 **RII: all four modules and signs.** Take two strands and order the crossing with states $(I,E)$ first, the opposite crossing with states $(E,I)$ second. The four states $00,01,10,11$ are $U=E$, $V=I$, $W=E$ with a middle circle, and $Z=E$, respectively. The local differential is $d^0(u)=(su,xu,u),\qquad d^1(v,w_1,w_X)=tv-w_1-yw_X,$ where $s:E\to I$ and $t:I\to E$ are the two saddles, $x$ is the dot on the arc from which the middle circle splits, and $y$ is the dot on the arc into which it merges. Here $C^1=V\oplus W_1\oplus W_X$; the minus signs on the $10\to11$ edge are exactly the cube sign for the second crossing. Step 2.1 gives $ts=x+y$, so these displayed differentials square to zero. Define $i(v)=(v,tv,0),\qquad p(v,w_1,w_X)=v-sw_X,$ with $i,p$ zero in other local degrees, and define $h^1(v,w_1,w_X)=w_X,\qquad h^2(z)=(0,-z,0).$ Then $d i=0$, $p d=0$, and $pi=1$. In degree zero $hd=1$, in degree two $dh=1$, and in degree one $dh+hd$ sends $(v,w_1,w_X)$ to $(sw_X,w_1-tv+(x+y)w_X,w_X)$, which is exactly $1-ip$. The surviving $V$ has local degree one and quantum grading increased by one; in the shift conventions of the question this is $[-1]\{-1\}$. Thus both acyclic pairs and the signed quotient are explicitly identified. The other crossing order follows by swapping the two cube coordinates with state sign $(-1)^{v_1v_2}$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra, construct]

3.2 **RIII: ordered states and the first cancellation.** Let each crossing have states $(I,E_i)$, and form the word $121$ from top to bottom, with crossings ordered in that order. Write $P=E_1E_2$ and $Q=E_2E_1$. In degrees $0,1,2,3$ the ordered states are $I;\quad (E_1^{100},E_2^{010},E_1^{001});\quad(P^{110},(E_1\sqcup\bigcirc)^{101},Q^{011});\quad E_1^{111}.$ In the last term use the boundary-fixing isotopy $E_1E_2E_1\cong E_1$ of step 1.1. Denote a degree-one element by $(a,b,c)$ and the circle coordinates in state $101$ by $(w_1,w_X)$. Introduce four precisely located saddles: $u:E_1\to P$ inserts $E_2$ below $E_1$, $v:E_2\to P$ inserts $E_1$ above $E_2$, $w:E_1\to Q$ inserts $E_2$ above $E_1$, and $z:E_2\to Q$ inserts $E_1$ below $E_2$. Let $x$ and $y$ be the dot operators on the bottom cup and top cap of $E_1$, respectively. The degree-one differential is $d^1(a,b,c)=(-ua+vb,\ -xa+yc,\ -a+c,\ wc-zb),$ with output coordinates $(P,W_1,W_X,Q)$. Indeed the six cube edges are $100\to110$ with sign $-$, $010\to110$ with sign $+$, $100\to101$ with sign $-$, $001\to101$ with sign $+$, $010\to011$ with sign $-$, and $001\to011$ with sign $+$. The two edges to $101$ split the middle circle from the bottom cup or top cap, giving exactly the two displayed circle-coordinate pairs by step 2.1. The $101\to111$ edge has sign $-$ and merges that middle circle into the remaining through arc of $E_1E_2E_1$. Its $W_1\to E_1^{111}$ component is therefore $-1$, with its $W_X$ component minus the dot on that through arc. Cancel this $-1$ component by step 2.2. There are no remaining degree-three terms; the differential into $(P,W_X,Q)$ is the corresponding projection of the displayed $d^1$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra, construct]

4.1 **The second cancellation and the common residual matrix.** In the resulting complex, the $c\to W_X$ component is $+1$. Cancel it by step 2.2: its row is $-a+c$, so the residual coordinate substitution is $c=a$. The retained degree-one coordinates are $(a,b)$, the retained degree-two coordinates are $(P,Q)$, and the differentials become $I\xrightarrow{\binom{s_1}{s_2}}E_1\oplus E_2\xrightarrow{\begin{pmatrix}-u&v\\ w&-z\end{pmatrix}}P\oplus Q,$ where $s_i:I\to E_i$ is the saddle inserting $E_i$. The first map is obtained from the original $d^0=(s_1,s_2,s_1)$ by deleting the canceled coordinate; it is compatible with $c=a$. Repeat both cancellations for $212$ with $1$ and $2$ interchanged. Its retained coordinates before reordering are $(E_2,E_1)$ and $(Q,P)$, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-z&w\\ v&-u\end{pmatrix}$. Swapping both pairs, without a sign, gives exactly the preceding matrix and the preceding $d^0$. The four entries refer to the same saddles on the same labelled boundary matchings: for instance $E_2\to P$ inserts $E_1$ above, and $E_1\to P$ inserts $E_2$ below, on both sides. Hence these are actual equal tensor maps by step 1.1, not identifications of unlabelled spaces. Their kernels, composites and signs need no further $\tau$ identities. Composing the two explicit cancellation maps and their inverses gives the RIII equivalence; the homotopy for a composite of retractions $(i_1,p_1,h_1)$ and $(i_2,p_2,h_2)$ is $h_1+i_1h_2p_1$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra, construct]

5.1 **Quantum degrees.** A state of local height $r$ has quantum degree increased by $r$. In RII, $W_1$ has the underlying grading of $E$ increased by two, $W_X$ has the grading of $E$, and $Z$ has the grading of $E$ increased by two. Thus both canceled isomorphisms and the maps of step 3.1 preserve quantum degree. In RIII, $W_1^{101}$ and $E_1^{111}$ both have the grading of $E_1$ increased by three; $W_X^{101}$ and $E_1^{001}$ both have the grading of $E_1$ increased by one. The common residual complex has quantum increases $0,1,2$ in its three degrees. Every change of coordinates in step 2.2 is therefore homogeneous. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 **Exterior differentials and the marked quotient.** Dots commute with every exterior saddle: $m(Xa,b)=Xm(a,b)=m(a,Xb)$ and $\Delta(Xa)=(X\otimes1)\Delta(a)=(1\otimes X)\Delta(a)$. Two saddles in disjoint local disks commute before cube signs, including when their participating arcs lie on a common global circle, by associativity, coassociativity and the Frobenius identity in [F1]. A middle circle being delooped is contained in the local disk, so no exterior saddle meets it. Boundary-fixing isotopies of the matchings preserve the labelled exterior arcs. All matrix changes, inverses of $\pm1$ blocks, projections, inclusions and contractions above therefore commute with unsigned exterior saddles and with $X$ at a fixed exterior marked point. The total differential, with local crossings first, is $d_{\rm loc}+(-1)^r d_{\rm ext}$ on local degree $r$. A local homotopy lowers $r$ by one, so its two exterior terms in $dh+hd$ cancel; local degree-zero maps commute with the signed total differential. These identities prove the same retractions for the total cube. The identities descend modulo $\operatorname{im}X_p$ because every map and every homotopy commutes with $X_p$; this argument does not assume that every local saddle acts trivially on the distinguished interval. It proves all assertions, integrally and choice-free. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N$ be a compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold, with boundary allowed, and let $k$ be a commutative field with $\dim_k H_1(N;k)=1$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(N)\to G$ be nontrivial with $G$ PTFA, and let $K$ be the Ore fraction division ring of $k[G]$. Then $H_0(N;K)=H_1(N;K)=0$. No choice principle or finite CW model for $N$ is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact connected manifold, coefficient field, nontrivial homomorphism and PTFA fraction division ring.

[F1] Actual singular right-coefficient chains of a compact manifold have explicit finite-free domination, and Wall's finite algebraic construction gives a nonnegative bounded finite-projective chain model. [[thm-finite-geometric-complex-chains-dominate-compact-manifold-chains-in-zf]], [[lem-choice-free-wall-chain-finiteness-from-explicit-domination]]

[F2] For such a projective model the PTFA basechange inequality is $b_1^K\le b_1^k-1$ if $b_0^k=1$ and $b_0^K=0$. [[lem-ptfa-finite-projective-basechange-preserves-euler-characteristic]]

## Proof

1.1 Degree-zero local homology identifies all point fibers with the base fiber by paths. A based loop with image $g\ne1$ imposes $(g-1)K=K$, since $g-1$ is a nonzero element of the embedded group ring and is invertible in $K$. Hence $H_0(N;K)=0$, while ordinary connectedness gives $H_0(N;k)=k$. Only a finite set of paths is needed for any given zero-cycle. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F1] to the actual $k[G]$ coefficient complex. Tensoring its specified chain equivalence and homotopies with $k$ or $K$ preserves their identities; augmentation gives the ordinary complex because every group transport augments to $1$. Thus its two models have the actual $k$ and $K$ homology of $N$. By [F2] and step 1.1, $\dim_K H_1(N;K)\le1-1=0$, so it is zero. The models and every subsequent elimination are bounded finite projective; no arbitrary infinite vector-space splitting or triangulation theorem is used. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $k$ be a commutative unital ring and $H\le G$ a subgroup. Set $A=k[H]\subseteq B=k[G]$. Extension $-\otimes_A B$ on right modules is exact and faithful, and for each right $A$-module $M$ the map $m\mapsto m\otimes1$ is split injective as an $A$-module map. For every right-$A$ chain complex $C_*$, without a boundedness or finiteness assumption, there is the natural isomorphism
$$H_i(C_*)\otimes_A B\cong H_i(C_*\otimes_A B).$$
The corresponding left-module assertions hold with the tensor factors reversed.

Suppose additionally that $A$ and $B$ have $1\ne0$, no zero divisors and both Ore conditions, and are embedded in their right-fraction division rings $F$ and $K$, respectively. Then the inclusion $A\to B$ extends uniquely to an injective ring map $F\to K$. Under this identification,
$$F\cap B=A,\qquad F/A\longrightarrow K/B\text{ is injective as an }A\text{-bimodule map}.$$
All assertions require no choice principle, including when $G/H$ is infinite. No splitting of a group extension is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The group rings and, for the second clause only, the supplied Ore division rings. Group-ring elements are finite formal $k$-linear combinations of group elements.

[F1] A tensor product is the group on pairs modulo additivity and balancing relations; every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors. [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]

[F2] The homology of a chain complex is its cycles modulo its boundaries. [[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]

## Proof

1.1 For a finite set $S$ of left cosets $Hg$, let $B_S$ be the subgroup of $B$ consisting of sums supported on those cosets. It is a left $A$-submodule, and dropping all coefficients outside those cosets defines a left-$A$ linear projection $B\to B_S$ splitting inclusion. A finite choice of representatives $g_1,\ldots,g_r$ gives the explicit left-$A$ isomorphism $A^r\to B_S$, $(a_j)\mapsto\sum_j a_jg_j$: the supports of distinct summands are disjoint, and translating a supported sum by $g_j^{-1}$ proves surjectivity and uniqueness. Only representatives of this finite set of cosets are used; no global representative system is chosen. Every finite set of elements of $B$ lies in some such $B_S$, by taking the finitely many cosets that meet their supports. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For the fraction clause, send $as^{-1}\in F$, with $a,s\in A$ and $s\ne0$, to the same expression in $K$. If also $as^{-1}=bt^{-1}$ in $F$, choose a nonzero common right multiple $su=tv=w$ in $A$. Multiplying on the right by $w$ gives $au=bv$ in $A$, and the same identity in $K$ proves equality there. Thus the map is well-defined. At a common denominator the addition formula is $(au+bv)w^{-1}$ in both division rings. For a product $as^{-1}bt^{-1}$ with $b\ne0$, choose $bv=su$ nonzero in $A$. Then $s^{-1}b=uv^{-1}$ and the product is $au(tv)^{-1}$ in both rings; the case $b=0$ is immediate. Hence the map preserves multiplication, addition and unit. Its kernel is zero, since $as^{-1}=0$ implies $a=0$ in $K$ and hence in $A$. Uniqueness follows because a ring map extending $A$ must send the inverse of each nonzero $s\in A$ to its inverse in $K$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $f:M'\to M$ be injective. A tensor $z\in M'\otimes_A B$ lies in the image of $M'\otimes_A B_S$ for a finite $S$, by [F1] and step 1.1. If $(f\otimes1)z=0$, apply $1\otimes(B\to B_S)$ to see that its representative $z_S$ maps to zero in $M\otimes_A B_S$. The explicit finite-free coordinates of step 1.1 identify this map with a finite direct sum of copies of $f$, so $z_S=0$ and $z=0$. For arbitrary maps $L\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}N$ exact at $M$, the same finite projection sends a tensor in $\ker(g\otimes1)$ into a finite direct sum of copies of $\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$. Lifting its finitely many coordinates gives a tensor in the image of $f\otimes1$. Conversely that image lies in the kernel since $gf=0$. A surjective map also remains surjective, by lifting the finitely many first coordinates of a tensor expression. Thus extension is exact for arbitrary right modules. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Dropping all coefficients outside $H$ defines an $A$-bimodule map $p:B\to A$ with $p(1)=1$: multiplication by a group element of $H$ on either side preserves both $H$ and its complement. Balancing therefore defines $\rho_M:M\otimes_A B\to M$, $\rho_M(m\otimes b)=mp(b)$. It is right-$A$ linear and satisfies $\rho_M(m\otimes1)=m$. This proves the split unit assertion. If $f\otimes1=0$ for a module homomorphism $f$, then $f(m)=\rho_N((f\otimes1)(m\otimes1))=0$ for each $m$; the functor is faithful. Apply step 2.1 to the exact sequences defining cycles, boundaries and their quotient. It identifies tensor cycles with the kernel of the tensor differential, tensor boundaries with its image, and the tensor quotient with their quotient. The resulting map is $[z]\otimes b\mapsto[z\otimes b]$, proving the natural homology assertion degree by degree. Replacing left cosets by right cosets gives the same finite-coordinate proof for left modules, and the same coefficient projection splits their unit map. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Suppose $q\in F\cap B$. Write $q=as^{-1}$ with $a,s\in A$, $s\ne0$, so $qs=a$. Partition the finite support of $q$ into right cosets $gH$ and choose finitely many representatives, using $1$ for the coset $H$ if it occurs. Thus $q=\sum_j g_jq_j$ with $q_j\in A$. Right multiplication by $s$ preserves each of these coset supports. Since $a$ is supported on $H$, every summand outside that coset satisfies $g_jq_js=0$ as a group-ring element. The absence of zero divisors in $B$ and $s\ne0$ imply $q_j=0$ for each such summand. Therefore $q$ is supported on $H$, which means $q\in A$. The reverse inclusion is given, so $F\cap B=A$. The map of additive quotients $F/A\to K/B$ is well-defined, has kernel $(F\cap B)/A=0$, and respects both $A$ actions because all inclusions are ring maps. Every representative, denominator, lift and coordinate set in this proof belongs to a single finite argument; no simultaneous infinite family is selected. This proves all assertions without a choice principle. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every finite rational polygonal code that records one oriented circle, finitely many transverse double points, and one overpassing branch at each double point, and every basepoint in the interior of an edge, if the first encounter at each crossing is the overpassing branch, then the represented knot is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-planar-code|Finite planar code and represented knot diagram]]

[[alg-descending-diagram-unknotting-sequence|The based traversal that produces a descending diagram]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$, an admissible finite code $D$, its oriented diagram, and a basepoint in the interior of an edge.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written AC$_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] A valid code represents a smooth regular diagram after its finitely many bend vertices are smoothed; one base edge has a crossing-free subarc around the basepoint. [[def-knot-planar-code]]

[F2] Under AC$_\omega$, every smooth isotopy of embeddings of the compact source circle into the boundaryless $S^3$ extends to an ambient isotopy. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[F3] A proper arc with one height maximum or minimum in a height ball bounds a disk with any prescribed simple boundary arc on its level sphere. [[lem-one-extremum-arc-is-boundary-parallel]]

[F4] A smooth oriented knot bounds a genus-zero spanning surface if and only if it is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot. [[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]]

## Proof

**Given:** The code and hypotheses in the statement.


1.1 Cut the based circle at a small crossing-free subarc around the basepoint. Orient the cut subarc from the endpoint where the remaining long arc ends to the endpoint where it begins. Identify the plane with the equatorial sphere $S_0\subset S^3$ minus one point, and write the projected long arc as $\gamma(t)\in S_0$, $0\le t\le1$, and the cut subarc as $\delta(s)\in S_0$, $0\le s\le1$. Thus $\gamma(1)=\delta(0)$ and $\delta(1)=\gamma(0)$. Choose $a=1/2$ and lift these paths by
$$\widehat\gamma(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{1-a^2\cos^2(\pi t)}\,\gamma(t),\ a\cos(\pi t)\bigr),\qquad \widehat\delta(s)=\bigl(\sqrt{1-a^2\cos^2(\pi s)}\,\delta(s),\ -a\cos(\pi s)\bigr).$$
The first height strictly decreases from $a$ to $-a$ and the second strictly increases from $-a$ to $a$; their first derivatives vanish at the joins and their second derivatives match. Reparametrize the projected paths near their endpoints to match the smooth based-diagram jets. The resulting closed knot is smooth and has exactly one maximum and one minimum. The projected cut subarc is disjoint from the rest of the diagram except at its endpoints. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 At every double point of $\gamma$, the first encounter occurs at smaller $t$ and therefore has strictly larger fourth coordinate; hence the lifted knot has exactly the prescribed overpassing branch at every crossing. The long lifted arc is embedded because its fourth coordinate is strictly monotone, and the base subarc is disjoint from its projection away from the endpoints, so their union is an embedding. To identify this lift with the knot represented by the diagram, let $z_0$ be the smooth height function of any realizing lift over the same smoothed projected circle, and let $z_1$ be the height function specified in step 1.1. For $0\le u\le1$, set $z_u=(1-u)z_0+uz_1$. This is a jointly smooth family with values in $(-1,1)$, since the compact image of $z_0$ lies in $(-1,1)$ and $|z_1|\le1/2$. At every crossing the first-encounter inequality holds for both $z_0$ and $z_1$, so it holds strictly for every $z_u$; distinct projected points remain distinct, and the projected derivative is nonzero. Thus the corresponding lifts form a smooth isotopy of embeddings of the compact circle. By [F2] it extends to an ambient isotopy, proving that the constructed lift represents the same knot as the descending diagram. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Choose the regular level $S_0$ between the unique minimum and maximum. It cuts the lifted knot into an upper proper arc with one maximum and a lower proper arc with one minimum. Choose one simple joining arc on $S_0$. By [F3], each proper arc bounds an embedded disk with that same joining arc; push their interiors into the opposite open balls, so the disks intersect only in the joining arc. Their union, after smoothing its corner, is an embedded genus-zero spanning surface for the knot. [F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Apply [F4] to the spanning disk of step 3.1. The lifted knot, and therefore the represented descending diagram by step 2.1, is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nonempty oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere. Its rational Lee homology is a two-dimensional vector space. For every finite regular diagram of $K$, the two homology classes obtained from the two orientations by the oriented-resolution parity-of-nesting rule form a basis, and the induced quantum filtration is independent of the diagram.

## Statement references

[[lem-lee-filtered-spectral-sequence-and-two-orientation-classes|Canonical Lee orientation classes and their basis theorem]]

[[thm-lee-filtered-homology-is-an-oriented-link-invariant|Diagram-independent filtered Lee homology]]

[Rasmussen, *Khovanov homology and the slice genus* (2004), §§2.4 and 3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131v1)

[McMullen, *4-Manifolds*, §§5.5–5.6](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/4Mnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A knot diagram and its two possible orientations.

[F1] For a diagram with $c$ components, the $2^c$ canonical orientation cycles form a basis of Lee homology ([[lem-lee-filtered-spectral-sequence-and-two-orientation-classes]]).

[F2] Filtered Lee homology is independent of the diagram of the oriented link ([[thm-lee-filtered-homology-is-an-oriented-link-invariant]]).

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the countable-choice principle used by the finite diagram-move supplier ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a finite regular diagram $D$ of $K$.

1.1 A knot has exactly one component, so it has exactly $2^1=2$ orientations. Applying [F1] with $c=1$ shows that the associated canonical classes are linearly independent and span $H(C_L(D;\mathbb Q))$. Thus its dimension is two. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 If $D'$ is another diagram of the same oriented knot, [A1] supplies the axiom branch used in [F2], and [F2] gives an isomorphism of Lee homology preserving the induced filtration. Therefore the dimension and filtered vector-space type computed from $D$ agree with those computed from $D'$. The two canonical classes on each diagram form a basis by step 1.1; no identification of individual basis vectors across diagrams is needed for the claimed rank or filtration invariance. [A1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

      locator: "Chapter 2, Algorithm 2.1 and equation (2.30): Cholesky solves and log determinant from a positive-diagonal triangular factor."
    - title: "Kathryn Chaloner and Isabella Verdinelli, Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review, Statistical Science 10(3) (1995), 273–304"
      url: "https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps"

## Definition

Assume AC for the library KL/EIG convention. Input a prior covariance $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ symmetric positive semidefinite, a finite ordered list of raw candidate records $(A_d,\Gamma_d,c_d)_{d=1}^N$, and a real budget $B$. Each stored $A_d$ and $\Gamma_d$ is a finite real matrix, with its dimensions part of the input, and each declared cost $c_d$ is finite and real. A candidate is dimension-valid when $A_d$ has at least one row and exactly $n$ columns and $\Gamma_d$ is a symmetric square matrix whose dimension equals the row count of $A_d$; for a dimension-valid candidate write that common positive dimension as $m_d$. The prior mean is immaterial to the score.

Interpret each admissible candidate $d$ (dimension-valid with $\Gamma_d$ positive definite) as a separate singleton-design dominated inverse experiment with prior $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ for any $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, observation space $\mathbb R^{m_d}$ with Lebesgue measure, and observation $Y_d=A_d\theta+\eta_d$, where $\eta_d\sim N_{m_d}(0,\Gamma_d)$ is independent of $\theta$. Here $\operatorname{EIG}(d)$ is the expected information gain from the preceding definition for that singleton experiment. Different candidates may have different $m_d$ because each is evaluated on its own observation space. The score is independent of $m_0$.

In exact-real arithmetic, process the list in order. Mark a candidate inadmissible if it is not dimension-valid or if its noise covariance $\Gamma_d$ is not positive definite. For each remaining candidate with $c_d\le B$, compute the Cholesky factor $\Gamma_d=L_dL_d^T$ with positive diagonal, solve $L_dV_d=A_d$ by forward substitution, and form the symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $Z_d=V_dCV_d^T$. Set $H_d=I_{m_d}+Z_d$ and compute its Cholesky factor $H_d=R_dR_d^T$. Assign the utility
$$U_d=\sum_{j=1}^{m_d}\log (R_d)_{jj}-c_d=\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)-c_d.$$
Initialize the stored best candidate as unset. For each admissible candidate meeting the budget, set it if unset; otherwise replace it exactly when the new utility is strictly greater than the stored utility. After the scan, return the stored candidate. This update rule preserves the first index in any tie. If every candidate is inadmissible, return `all-inadmissible`; if at least one candidate is admissible but none meets the budget, return `budget-exhausted`.

In floating-point mode, treat each finite stored floating-point matrix entry, cost, budget, and tolerance as the exact real number represented by that value; no uncertainty in these input data is included. Use failure-aware Cholesky and triangular-solve procedures, and take a certificate provider as part of the floating-point input. Each provider result is a finite, independently checkable certificate; if the provider cannot certify a required fact, it returns `unresolved`.

Process the candidates in list order. Test dimensions and symmetry exactly, marking a dimension-invalid candidate inadmissible. For each dimension-valid noise matrix $\Gamma_d$, call `CertifyPositiveDefiniteness(\Gamma_d)`. It returns `positive-definite` only with a checkable positive-definiteness certificate, `not-positive-definite` only with a checkable certificate, or `unresolved`. For example, an exact factorization $\Gamma_d=L L^T$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal certifies positive definiteness, while a nonzero vector $v$ with $v^T\Gamma_dv\le0$ certifies that it is not positive definite. A failed rounded Cholesky factorization is not a certificate of non-positive-definiteness. If any required status is unresolved, return `numerically-unresolved`. After all statuses are certified, return `all-inadmissible` if none is admissible. Compare each admissible stored cost to the stored budget exactly; if none meets it, return `budget-exhausted`.

For each feasible candidate $d$ in inherited order, call `CertifyScore(d)`. It first runs failure-aware rounded Cholesky on $\Gamma_d$ and, on success, failure-aware forward substitution on each column of $A_d$ in order; any operation failure or unmet range hypothesis returns `unresolved`. After forming a certified positive-semidefinite $\widehat Z_d$, it forms a stored matrix $\widehat H_d$ and certifies both that $\widehat H_d$ is symmetric positive definite and that $\|\widehat H_d-(I_{m_d}+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\sigma_d$ for a rational bound $\sigma_d\ge0$. It then runs failure-aware rounded Cholesky on $\widehat H_d$; a failed definiteness check, factorization, or formation bound returns `unresolved`. The call then returns either `certified` with finite stored values $\widehat U_d$, $\widehat Z_d$, and $\widehat R_d$, nonnegative rational upper bounds $\delta_d,\rho_d,\lambda_d$, and certificates for all of the following, or `unresolved`:

- $\widehat Z_d$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $\|\widehat Z_d-Z_d\|_2\le\delta_d$, where $Z_d$ uses the exact Cholesky factor of the represented $\Gamma_d$. This bound includes rounding in forming the Cholesky factor and triangular solve for $\Gamma_d$, the covariance square root, and the matrix products.
- $\widehat R_d$ is a successful lower-triangular Cholesky factor with positive diagonal. If $\widetilde\rho_d$ is a certified upper bound for $\|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-\widehat H_d\|_2$, choose a rational $\rho_d\ge\widetilde\rho_d+\sigma_d$ with $\rho_d<1$; then $\|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I_{m_d}+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\rho_d$.
- $\left|\widehat U_d-\left(\frac12\log\det(\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T)-c_d\right)\right|\le\lambda_d$. Evaluate the exact expression as $\sum_j\log((\widehat R_d)_{jj})-c_d$ using the triangular determinant identity; $\lambda_d$ covers rounded logarithms, their summation, and cost evaluation.

The matrix radius may be certified by the published information-matrix perturbation bound in its single-design, unit-weight $W=I_n$ case. Factor $C$ as $C^{1/2}C^{1/2}$ and set $J_d=C^{1/2}V_d^T$; for a computed solve $\widehat V_d$, set $\widehat J_d=C^{1/2}\widehat V_d^T$. Then $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$ and $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$. The lemma's finite-design hypotheses hold for the one-point sensitivity maps $z\mapsto J_dz$ and $z\mapsto\widehat J_dz$ from $\mathbb R^{m_d}$ to $\mathbb R^n$, with weight $W=I_n$ and design weight $1$. If $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$ and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$, then $\delta_d$ may be any verified bound at least $2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$, enlarged by any separate matrix-formation residual. A rounded triangular-substitution bound may be used only after checking its $(m_d+3)u<1$ and normal-range, finite-operation hypotheses for every right-hand side. Convert its backward-error bound to the required forward matrix bound using verified conditioning; a solve backward-error bound alone does not certify $\eta_d$. For the published rounded-Cholesky normwise bound, verify success and its operationwise model, put $q=20m_d+20$ and $g=qu/(1-qu)$, and check $qu<1/5$ before using $100g\|\widehat R_d\|_F^2$ as a residual bound; if using its relative bound, also check $100\sqrt{m_d}g\le1/2$. The log-determinant perturbation bound is applied on the two symmetric matrix segments with eigenvalue floors $1$ and $1-\rho_d$. A missing or failed certificate returns `numerically-unresolved` and no optimum claim.

Set $\varepsilon_d=\frac{m_d}{2}\left(\delta_d+\frac{\rho_d}{1-\rho_d}\right)+\lambda_d$ and form the exact rational interval $[\widehat U_d-\varepsilon_d,\widehat U_d+\varepsilon_d]$. Given a finite nonnegative stored tolerance $\tau$, compute $M=\max_{d\text{ feasible}}\widehat U_d$ and return the first feasible candidate with $\widehat U_d\ge M-\tau$. Certify the comparisons exactly on the represented floating-point values and rational bounds; if any comparison needed for this branch or for its interval certificate is undecided, return `numerically-unresolved`. The returned candidate's true utility gap is at most $\tau+2\max_d\varepsilon_d$. If its lower interval endpoint exceeds every earlier candidate's upper endpoint and is at least every later candidate's upper endpoint, certify it as the first exact maximizer. The algorithm makes no bit-complexity claim for exact-real comparisons.

[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique|Every symmetric positive-definite matrix has a unique positive-diagonal Cholesky factor.]]

[[thm-cholesky-solves-hermitian-positive-definite-systems-and-has-half-the-lu-factorisation-cost|Cholesky triangular solves evaluate positive-definite systems without forming an inverse.]]

[[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix|The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.]]

[[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix|The log-determinant score uses the usual determinant of a finite square matrix.]]

[[def-natural-logarithm|The logarithm in the score is the natural logarithm.]]

## Remarks

This procedure is for the specified finite linear-Gaussian candidates. A Monte Carlo estimate of nonlinear EIG is a different procedure and inherits no exact finite optimum guarantee from this algorithm.

Any solve-error certificate must convert triangular-solve backward error to the required matrix error using a verified conditioning bound. Backward error alone is not a forward-error bound.

## Definition

Input a normalized sequence observation $z=(z_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ from the Gaussian sequence inverse model and a cutoff $D\in\mathbb N_0$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. Output the finite-support estimate $\widehat\theta_D(z)\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ defined by

## Definition

Let $n\ge1$, $\sigma,\gamma>0$, let $g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, let $\widetilde D_\sigma:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be a deterministic denoiser map, and choose $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Define
$$z_t=x_{t-1}-\gamma\nabla g(x_{t-1}),\qquad x_t=\widetilde D_\sigma(z_t)\quad(t=1,2,\ldots).$$
The output is the sequence $(x_t)_{t\ge0}$. This definition imposes no convexity, proximal representation, exact-MMSE identity, or convergence property on $\widetilde D_\sigma$.

id: ex-ip-exact-invariant-kernel-short-run
kind: example
title: An exact invariant kernel can be biased over a short run
status: draft
origin: pipeline

deps:

  AC is assumed only by the library time-homogeneous Markov-chain interface.
  Invariance and the finite-state expectation calculation use no choice.
provenance:

generation:
  role: example
sources:
  references:
    - title: "David A. Levin, Yuval Peres, and Elizabeth L. Wilmer, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition"
      url: https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/markovmixing.pdf
      locator: "§4.1, Example 4.1 and the total-variation discussion of the two-state chain."
---

## Example

Let $E=\{-1,+1\}$, and let the target posterior $\pi$ assign mass $1/2$ to
each state. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, define a transition kernel by
$$K_\varepsilon(x,\{x\})=1-\varepsilon,\qquad K_\varepsilon(x,\{-x\})=\varepsilon.$$
Take $\varepsilon=1/1000$, let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be the time-homogeneous Markov
chain with kernel $K_\varepsilon$ relative to its natural filtration and with
$X_0=+1$, and retain the next $N=100$ draws for the bounded functional
$f(x)=x$. The target law $\pi$ is
invariant for this exact kernel, but the expected reported average is
$$\mathbb E\left[\frac1{100}\sum_{j=1}^{100}X_j\right]=\frac{499}{100}\left(1-\left(\frac{499}{500}\right)^{100}\right)>0=\pi(f).$$
For the error ledger take each deterministic posterior stage to be $\pi$;
then the invariant-kernel error is zero while the finite-run burn-in error is
positive.

## Example references

[[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget|The invariant-kernel, burn-in, and Monte Carlo error components.]]

[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel|A probability kernel has probability rows and measurable event evaluations.]]

[[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel|Invariance means $\pi K=\pi$ on every event.]]

[[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel|The transition kernel gives the conditional one-step law.]]

[[prop-ip-bounded-posterior-functional-error|The pathwise error budget is bounded by its adjacent-stage terms.]]

[Levin, Peres, and Wilmer, §4.1, two-state chain](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/markovmixing.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-state target law, transition rule, deterministic initial state, and 100 retained draws in the Example.

[F1] A probability kernel has probability-measure rows and measurable event evaluations. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

[F2] A probability law $\pi$ is invariant for $K$ when $\int K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)$ for every event $A$. [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the library time-homogeneous Markov-chain interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F3] For a time-homogeneous Markov chain, $\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)$ almost surely. [[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel]]

[F4] The burn-in component is $|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|$; when the invariant target is $\pi$, this is the expected finite-run bias in the Example. [[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget]]

[F5] The mean and conditional expectation of a bounded real random variable are finite. [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]

## Verification

1.1 Each row of $K_\varepsilon$ sums to one. For either singleton $\{x\}$,
$$\pi K_\varepsilon(\{x\})=\tfrac12(1-\varepsilon)+\tfrac12\varepsilon=\tfrac12=\pi(\{x\}),$$
so additivity on the two-state space gives $\pi K_\varepsilon=\pi$ by [F2]. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Put $\lambda_0:=1-2\varepsilon=499/500$. Summing the two conditional probabilities in [F3] against the values $+1$ and $-1$, conditional on $X_n=x$,
$$\mathbb E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=(1-\varepsilon)x+\varepsilon(-x)=\lambda_0x.$$
Taking expectations and using $X_0=1$ gives $\mathbb E X_j=\lambda_0^j$ for every $j\ge1$ by induction. [A1, F3, F5, given, algebra]

2.2 Linearity gives $\mathbb E[100^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{100}X_j]=100^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{100}\lambda_0^j=\frac{499}{100}(1-(499/500)^{100})>0$. Since $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi$ is invariant by step 1.1, the kernel discrepancy vanishes, while [F4] identifies this positive difference as the burn-in component. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

        curves associated to character varieties of 3-manifolds, §2
      url: https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~culler/papers/PlaneCurves/curves.pdf
---

## Example

Let $K=J(2,-2)$ be the figure-eight knot with its positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. The enhanced A-polynomial is
$$\widetilde A_K(M,L)=M^4L^2+(-M^8+M^6+2M^4+M^2-1)L+M^4,$$
and the ordinary A-polynomial is $(L-1)\widetilde A_K(M,L)$, up to a Laurent unit.

## Example references

[[def-knot-a-polynomial|Ordinary A-polynomial and abelian component]]

[[def-enhanced-a-polynomial|Enhanced A-polynomial]]

[[lem-figure-eight-character-and-longitude-traces|Figure-eight character curve and longitude trace]]

[Petersen, §§3–4 and §7.2](https://nyjm.albany.edu/j/2015/21-39v.pdf)

[Bénard, Florens, and Rodau, Example 3.20 and §4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151)

[Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long, and Shalen, §2](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~culler/papers/PlaneCurves/curves.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard figure-eight knot, its positive meridian and preferred longitude, and the eigenvalue convention in which the peripheral matrices have diagonal entries $(M,M^{-1})$ and $(L,L^{-1})$ on a common invariant line.

[F1] On the one-dimensional irreducible character component, $x=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\mu))$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\lambda))=x^4-5x^2+2$ ([[lem-figure-eight-character-and-longitude-traces]]).

[F2] On a common invariant line of the commuting peripheral pair, $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\mu))=M+M^{-1}$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\lambda))=L+L^{-1}$ ([[def-sl-two-character-variety-and-peripheral-eigenvalues]]; [[lem-two-commuting-complex-2x2-matrices-are-simultaneously-triangularizable]]).

[F3] The Laurent polynomial ring over $\mathbb C$ is a localization of the finite-variable polynomial UFD ([[lem-finite-variable-polynomial-rings-over-fields-are-ufds]]); Gauss's lemma passes irreducibility from its fraction field to a primitive polynomial over this UFD ([[lem-gauss-lemma-over-a-ufd]]).

[F4] The concrete two-meridian presentation and preferred longitude are proved in [[lem-figure-eight-two-meridian-presentation-and-preferred-longitude-word]]. A reducible representation is upper triangular with equal diagonal characters on $u,v$, and this explicit longitude has exponent sum zero. Hence its longitude eigenvalue is one. Conversely $u=v=\operatorname{diag}(M,M^{-1})$ realizes $(M,1)$ for every $M\ne0$.

[F5] The full proof of [[lem-figure-eight-character-and-longitude-traces]] gives every irreducible representation its matrices $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}M&1\\0&M^{-1}\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}M&0\\t&M^{-1}\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and exact relation $F=t^2+(M^2+M^{-2}-3)t-(M^2+M^{-2}-3)=0$. Conversely $F=0,t\ne0$ gives an actual irreducible representation, including $M=\pm1$.

## Verification

1.1 Put $x=M+M^{-1}$. By [F1] and [F2], $L+L^{-1}=x^4-5x^2+2$. Since $x^2=M^2+2+M^{-2}$ and $x^4=M^4+4M^2+6+4M^{-2}+M^{-4}$, the right side is $M^4-M^2-2-M^{-2}+M^{-4}$. Multiplying by the unit $M^4L$ gives $$Q(M,L)=M^4L^2+(-M^8+M^6+2M^4+M^2-1)L+M^4=0.$$ Thus every eigenvalue pair from an irreducible representation lies on this explicit Laurent curve. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Irreducibility is checked by an exact factorization.** Put $X=M^2$ and $B(X)=-X^4+X^3+2X^2+X-1$. As a quadratic in $L$, $Q=X^2L^2+B(X)L+X^2$ has discriminant $$B(X)^2-4X^4=(X-1)^2(X+1)^2(X^2+X+1)(X^2-3X+1).$$ This follows by factoring $B-2X^2=-(X-1)^2(X^2+X+1)$ and $B+2X^2=-(X+1)^2(X^2-3X+1)$. A root $r$ of $X^2-3X+1$ is nonzero, is simple, and is neither $1,-1$ nor a root of $X^2+X+1$: subtracting the two quadratics at a common root would give $4r=0$. Each square root $M$ of $r$ is consequently a simple zero of the discriminant after substitution $X=M^2$, since $2M\ne0$. Thus the discriminant is not a square in $\mathbb C(M)$. The quadratic $Q$ is irreducible over $\mathbb C(M)$, and [F3] gives its irreducibility in the Laurent polynomial ring; its nonzero constant term excludes an inverted $L$ factor. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 **There are actual representations with infinitely many meridian values.** For every $M\ne0$ except the finitely many solutions of $M^2+M^{-2}-3=0$, the monic quadratic $F$ of [F5] has a complex root $t$ and neither root is zero. Hence [F5] gives an actual irreducible representation with meridian eigenvalue $M$. The preferred longitude commutes with the meridian, so the meridian eigenline $\mathbb C(1,0)$ in that matrix model is also a longitude eigenline whenever $M\ne\pm1$; discard these additional two values. Thus for infinitely many distinct $M$ there is an actual eigenvalue pair $(M,L)$ in the irreducible locus. These pairs satisfy $Q=0$ by step 1.1. No global eigenvalue-image completeness theorem is assumed here. [F2, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **The exact curve vanishing ideal follows by polynomial Euclid.** Suppose a Laurent polynomial $P(M,L)$ vanishes on all those irreducible eigenvalue pairs. If $Q$ does not divide $P$ in $\mathbb C(M)[L^{\pm1}]$, step 2.1 makes their gcd one. The finite Euclidean algorithm gives a Bezout identity there. Clearing its finitely many nonzero denominators in $M$, while retaining the already allowed Laurent powers of $L$, gives Laurent coefficients $U,V$ and a nonzero Laurent polynomial $h(M)$ with $UP+VQ=h(M)$. Step 2.2 would make $h(M)$ vanish at infinitely many nonzero meridian values, impossible for a nonzero one-variable Laurent polynomial. Therefore $Q$ divides $P$. Its primitive irreducible Laurent equation from step 2.1 and [F3] then divides $P$ in $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$ itself. The converse is step 1.1. Hence the vanishing ideal of the full irreducible peripheral eigenvalue locus is exactly $(Q)$, and its reduced closure is the whole $Q$ curve. This includes any exceptional central or parabolic pairs, since they too satisfy step 1.1, while the dense family already forces this ideal. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 Reducible representations contribute precisely $L=1$ by [F4]. Since $Q(M,1)=-M^8+M^6+4M^4+M^2-1$ is not identically zero, $Q$ and $L-1$ are distinct irreducible Laurent factors. The defining reduced union has ideal $(Q)\cap(L-1)=((L-1)Q)$ by [F3]. By the ordinary and enhanced definitions, the enhanced equation is $Q$ and the ordinary one is $(L-1)Q$, up to a Laurent unit. The displayed integer polynomials are primitive and square-free. This proves both formulas using the actual representation family and preferred longitude, rather than an assumed image-completeness premise. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The braid box records the word $\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}$ whose closure is $J(2,-2)$. In each positive crossing the left incoming strand passes over the right incoming strand; in each negative crossing the right incoming strand passes over the left. The boxes are read from top to bottom. The closure arcs outside the box are omitted, and the algebraic verification does not rely on the diagram.

  \node[left] at (0,3.5) {$\sigma_1$};
  \node[left] at (0,2.5) {$\sigma_2^{-1}$};
  \node[left] at (0,1.5) {$\sigma_1$};
  \node[left] at (0,0.5) {$\sigma_2^{-1}$};
  % First crossing: positive sigma_1, with the left strand over.
  \draw (1,4)--(0.58,3.58) (0.42,3.42)--(0,3);
  \draw (2,4)--(2,3);
  \draw (0,4)--(1,3);
  % Second crossing: negative sigma_2, with the right strand over.
  \draw (0,3)--(0,2);
  \draw (1,3)--(1.58,2.58) (1.42,2.42)--(2,2);
  \draw (2,3)--(1,2);
  % Third crossing: positive sigma_1.
  \draw (1,2)--(0.58,1.58) (0.42,1.42)--(0,1);
  \draw (2,2)--(2,1);
  \draw (0,2)--(1,1);

## Statement

Assume full AC. Put $T=(\mathbb C^*)^n$ and $R=\mathbb C[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}]$, with $n\ge0$. For a finite index set $B$, let $J_b$ be an ideal of $R[u_1,\ldots,u_{m_b}]$, where $m_b\ge0$, and let $X_b$ be its zero set in $T\times\mathbb C^{m_b}$. Let $S$ be the union of the coordinate projections of the $X_b$ to $T$. Then its Zariski closure $Z$ has radical vanishing ideal $$I(Z)=\bigcap_{b\in B}\bigl(\sqrt{J_b}\cap R\bigr).$$ Write the finite irreducible-component decomposition as $Z=\bigcup_i Z_i$, and let $C$ be the union of those $Z_i$ whose dimension is one. Then $$I(C)=\bigcap_{\dim Z_i=1}I(Z_i).$$ Thus one must select the one-dimensional components after radical elimination; the first intersection alone also retains any isolated or higher-dimensional components. Empty intersections are the unit ideal and an empty selected union is empty. If $S$ is preserved by every coordinatewise field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ (in particular, if all $J_b$ are generated by rational-coefficient Laurent polynomials), both $I(Z)$ and $I(C)$ are scalar extensions of radical ideals over $\mathbb Q$. No closedness of the projections or bound on their dimension is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the indicated finite incidence charts and coordinate projections.

[F1] The affine and relative Nullstellensatz identifies the vanishing ideal of a zero set with the radical of its defining ideal ([[thm-classical-affine-nullstellensatz-correspondence]]).

[F2] Every affine algebraic set has a unique finite irredundant decomposition into maximal nonempty irreducible closed subsets, including the empty decomposition ([[lem-classical-affine-algebraic-set-finite-irreducible-components]]).

[F3] Geometric dimension equals the dimension of the coordinate ring; the proof identifies both dimensions with lengths of strict chains of irreducible closed sets or prime ideals ([[thm-affine-variety-dimension-coordinate-ring]]).

[F4] A Laurent vanishing ideal stable under every field automorphism fixing $\mathbb Q$ is the scalar extension of its rational contraction, which is radical ([[lem-automorphism-stable-laurent-ideals-descend-to-rational-coefficients]]).

## Proof

1.1 **Exact radical contraction.** Realize $T\times\mathbb C^{m_b}$ as the closed affine set with coordinates $z_i,v_i,u_j$ and equations $z_iv_i=1$. Its coordinate ring is $R[u_1,\ldots,u_{m_b}]$: replace each $z_i^{-1}$ by $v_i$, and reduce any mixed positive powers using $z_iv_i=1$. Thus the relative assertion of [F1] gives $I(X_b)=\sqrt{J_b}$ in exactly this coordinate ring. A Laurent polynomial $f\in R$ vanishes on the projection of $X_b$ exactly when its pullback, the same expression independent of $u$, vanishes on $X_b$. Its ideal is consequently $\sqrt{J_b}\cap R$. Vanishing on a finite union means vanishing on every member, so $I(S)$ is the stated intersection. Moreover $I(S)=I(\overline S)$: each polynomial zero set containing $S$ contains its closure, and $S\subseteq\overline S$ gives the reverse inclusion. This proves the first formula without asserting that a projection is closed. For no charts, $S$ is empty and every polynomial vanishes on it. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Select actual curve components.** The set $Z$ is a closed subset of the displayed affine model for $T$, so [F2] gives its finite component list $Z_i$. Select precisely the members of dimension one, with dimension as in [F3]. This is a finite union of closed sets, hence closed. A polynomial vanishes on that union exactly when it vanishes on each selected member, giving the second formula directly. Each component ideal is radical, since $f^k$ vanishing at all its points forces $f$ to vanish; their intersection is radical as well. If no component is selected its vanishing ideal is the whole ring. The need for selection is literal: in $(\mathbb C^*)^2$, the closed set $V(L-1)\cup\{(2,2)\}$ has ideal $(L-1)\cap(M-2,L-2)$, whereas its selected curve ideal is $(L-1)$. These differ since $L-1$ has value $1$ at $(2,2)$. The line ideal formula follows by substitution $L=1$ in a Laurent polynomial (multiply by a monomial and divide by $L-1$); the point ideal follows by subtracting its value successively in $M$ and $L$. Thus even radical elimination does not itself discard isolated points. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Rational descent commutes with selection.** A field automorphism $\sigma$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ induces a bijection of $T$ taking $V(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ to $V(\sigma f_1,\ldots,\sigma f_r)$; the same assertion for arbitrary collections of equations makes it a Zariski homeomorphism. If $S$ is stable, its closure $Z$ is stable as well. This homeomorphism permutes the maximal irreducible closed subsets by maximality and preserves their dimensions by bijecting all strict chains of irreducible closed subsets, the convention in [F3]. Therefore it preserves $C$. Apply [F4] separately to the stable point sets $Z$ and $C$ to obtain both asserted radical rational contractions. Finally, rational generators for each $J_b$ make $X_b$ stable by applying $\sigma$ to the defining equations and their inverse implications; projection commutes with $\sigma$, so their union $S$ is stable. All arguments include $n=0$, empty charts, empty zero sets and the whole torus. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and put $M=\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega$ and $n=2d-2$. Give $M$ its product surface measure and choose a cube $D=(1/4,3/4)^n$ whose closure lies in $(0,1)^n$. Define $H^1(M)$ as the completion of smooth functions in the norm $\|h\|_{H^1(M)}^2=\int_M(|h|^2+|\nabla_Mh|^2)\,dS$; use the corresponding periodic $H^1$ norm on $\mathbb T^n$. There are a finite family of smooth bi-Lipschitz charts $(U_j,\phi_j)$ for $\partial\Omega$, with $\phi_j(U_j)\Subset(1/4,3/4)^{d-1}$, and smooth functions $\psi_j$ supported compactly in $U_j$ with $\sum_j\psi_j^2=1$. They induce bounded linear maps
$$G:L^2(M)\to\bigoplus_{j,k=1}^J L^2(\mathbb T^n),\qquad L:\bigoplus_{j,k=1}^J L^2(\mathbb T^n)\to L^2(M)$$
such that $LG=I_{L^2(M)}$. If $P_N$ is the orthogonal Fourier projection onto modes $\ell\in\mathbb Z^n$ with $\|\ell\|_\infty\le N$, applied componentwise, then for every compact $C\subset L^2(M)$,
$$\sup_{h\in C}\|P_NGh-Gh\|_{\oplus L^2(\mathbb T^n)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(N\to\infty).$$
The same maps are bounded between $H^1(M)$ and the direct-sum $H^1$ space, and there is $C_1<\infty$ such that
$$\|(I-P_N)Gh\|_{\oplus L^2(\mathbb T^n)}\le C_1(1+N)^{-1}\|h\|_{H^1(M)}\qquad(h\in H^1(M),\ N\ge0).$$

The maps and their left-inverse relation have the commutative diagram

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,node distance=2.4cm]
  \node[draw,rounded corners,align=center] (m) {$L^2(M)$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,align=center,right of=m] (local) {$\bigoplus_{j,k}L^2(\mathbb T^n)$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,align=center,below of=local] (out) {$L^2(M)$};
  \draw[->] (m) -- node[above] {$G$} (local);
  \draw[->] (local) -- node[right] {$L$} (out);
  \draw[->] (m) -- node[left] {$I$} (out);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Here $G$ localizes and pulls back by every chart pair, while $L$ multiplies by the same square-partition weights and sums the zero-extended chart components. The diagram records $LG=I$; the proof below establishes the identity by direct calculation.

## Statement references

[de Hoop et al., §4.3, local boundary charts and Lemma 4.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the smooth compact boundary product $M$, its product surface measure, and $D=(1/4,3/4)^n$.

[F1] Under Countable Choice, a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to any open cover. ([[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds]])

[F2] On a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, finite-chart integration is independent of the charts and subordinate partitions; in graph coordinates its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. ([[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]])

[F3] A $C^1$ diffeomorphism satisfies the nonnegative Lebesgue change-of-variables formula. ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]])

[F4] The torus characters form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, so their orthogonal Fourier projections are contractions converging strongly to the identity. ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]])

[F5] Fubini's theorem identifies the product chart integrals with iterated integrals on the two boundary factors. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed at the smooth partition and surface-measure interfaces. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and the smooth compact embedded hypersurface $\partial\Omega$.

1.1 The local graph charts of the smooth boundary form an open cover. Shrinking them gives graph-chart neighborhoods whose coordinate images have compact closure inside Euclidean balls; compactness selects a finite subcover. Rescale each coordinate ball affinely into $(1/4,3/4)^{d-1}$. On each compact chart closure, the map and inverse have bounded derivatives, so the restricted coordinate maps are bi-Lipschitz. Apply [F1] to the finite cover and combine partition functions sharing one chart to obtain nonnegative smooth $\theta_j$ compactly supported in $U_j$, with $\sum_j\theta_j=1$. Since $\sum_j\theta_j^2\ge J^{-1}$, $\psi_j=\theta_j/(\sum_i\theta_i^2)^{1/2}$ is smooth, has the same support, and satisfies $\sum_j\psi_j^2=1$. [A1, F1, given, construct]

2.1 For each pair set $\Phi_{jk}(x,y)=(\phi_j(x),\phi_k(y))$ and $\chi_{jk}(x,y)=\psi_j(x)\psi_k(y)$. Define $(Gh)_{jk}(z)=(\chi_{jk}h)(\Phi_{jk}^{-1}z)$ on $\Phi_{jk}(U_j\times U_k)$ and zero elsewhere, and define $(Lv)(x,y)=\sum_{j,k}\chi_{jk}(x,y)v_{jk}(\Phi_{jk}(x,y))$ on the chart pairs, zero outside. These are finite sums. The chart Jacobians and surface-density factors are bounded above and below on compact supports by bi-Lipschitz regularity and [F2]–[F3], with Fubini [F5] for the product chart factors. Thus the pullbacks, zero extensions and smooth multiplications are bounded on $L^2$, so $G$ and $L$ are bounded linear maps. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Substitution in the finite sum gives $(LGh)(x,y)=\sum_{j,k}\chi_{jk}(x,y)^2h(x,y)=(\sum_j\psi_j(x)^2)(\sum_k\psi_k(y)^2)h(x,y)=h(x,y)$ almost everywhere. Thus $LG=I$ as maps on $L^2(M)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For smooth $h$, the product and chain rules show that first derivatives of $(Gh)_{jk}$ are bounded chart coefficients times $h$ and its first tangential derivatives. The Jacobian bounds in step 2.1 give $\|Gh\|_{\oplus H^1}\le C\|h\|_{H^1(M)}$ and $\|Lv\|_{H^1(M)}\le C\|v\|_{\oplus H^1}$. Since the weights vanish near patch edges, zero extension remains smooth. Density in the completion definition extends these maps boundedly to $H^1$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 By [F4], $P_N$ is a contraction on the finite direct sum and converges strongly to the identity. The image $G(C)$ is compact by step 2.1. For $\varepsilon>0$, take a finite $\varepsilon/3$-net $v_1,\ldots,v_s$ for $G(C)$ and then take $N$ large enough that $\|P_Nv_i-v_i\|<\varepsilon/3$ for all $i$. For any $v\in G(C)$ choose $v_i$ with $\|v-v_i\|<\varepsilon/3$; contraction gives $\|P_Nv-v\|\le\|P_N(v-v_i)\|+\|P_Nv_i-v_i\|+\|v_i-v\|<\varepsilon$. This proves compact-uniform convergence. [F4, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

4.1 For $w\in H^1(\mathbb T^n)$, weak integration by parts against a character gives $\widehat{\partial_\ell w}(k)=2\pi i k_\ell\widehat w(k)$. Parseval [F4] yields $\|(I-P_N)w\|_2^2=\sum_{\|k\|_\infty>N}|\widehat w(k)|^2\le(2\pi N)^{-2}\sum_k|2\pi k|^2|\widehat w(k)|^2\le(2\pi N)^{-2}\|\nabla w\|_2^2$ for $N\ge1$. Apply this to each component of $Gh$ and use step 3.2. For $N=0$, $\|Gh\|_2\le\|Gh\|_{H^1}\le C\|h\|_{H^1}$; enlarging $C_1$ proves the stated tail estimate. [F4, step 3.2, algebra] ∎
