## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix a smooth bounded connected domain $\Omega$, an open $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and $0<m\le1\le M<\infty$. Let $\gamma,\gamma_0$ range over all measurable conductivities between $m$ and $M$ equal to one outside $\Omega'$. Let $(e_j,\lambda_j)$ be the mean-zero boundary spectral basis and put $w_j=1+\lambda_j$. There is $p\in(2,4)$ such that for every $L>0$,
$$\|\nabla u_{\gamma,e_j}\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C_Lw_j^{-L}.$$
Put $q=p/(p-2)>2$. For any fixed smoothing exponent $r\ge0$, the difference $(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0})(1-\Delta_{\partial\Omega})^{-r/2}$, extended to kill constants, is Hilbert–Schmidt and satisfies
$$\| (\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0})(1-\Delta_{\partial\Omega})^{-r/2}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le C_r\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^q(\Omega)}.$$
It also satisfies the same bound with the coefficient $L^\infty$ norm in place of $L^q$. Constants depend only on the displayed fixed geometry, ellipticity and exponents.

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-ntd-boundary-smoothing-for-fixed-background-collar|The fixed-collar boundary estimates.]]

[[lem-ip-meyers-higher-integrability-for-interior-conductivity-solutions|Uniform interior higher integrability.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the fixed domain, collar, conductivity bounds and basis in the Statement.

[F1] A harmonic function with zero normal derivative in a fixed smooth collar has every integer boundary Sobolev norm bounded by its collar $H^1$ norm, by the explicit boundary difference-quotient induction in step 1.2 of the collar lemma. The spectral and chart half-order norms are equivalent. ([[lem-ip-ntd-boundary-smoothing-for-fixed-background-collar]])

[F2] The interior higher-integrability estimate is uniform for measurable conductivities: on nested fixed domains, $\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(U)}\le C\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(V)}$ for some $p>2$; the proof permits $p<4$. ([[lem-ip-meyers-higher-integrability-for-interior-conductivity-solutions]])

[F3] Weak Neumann solutions obey the uniform energy estimate, and bounded coercive energy forms solve every bounded volume-gradient functional by Lax–Milgram. ([[lem-ip-mean-zero-neumann-problem-wellposedness]], [[thm-lax-milgram]])

[F4] For every $a>(d-1)/2$, $\sum_jw_j^{-a}<\infty$. ([[lem-ip-boundary-spectral-counting-and-sobolev-scale]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are assumed at those weak-solution, spectral, Sobolev and harmonic-analysis interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the fixed data in the Statement.

1.1 Cover $\overline{\Omega'}$ by finitely many balls $B_\ell$ whose concentric doubled balls $2B_\ell$ have closure in $\Omega$, and put $V=\bigcup_\ell2B_\ell$. Let $v\in L^2(V;\mathbb R^d)$. On the volume-mean-zero $H^1$ space, [F3] solves $\int_\Omega\nabla z\cdot\nabla\varphi=\int_Vv\cdot\nabla\varphi$, with $\|z\|_{H^1}\le C\|v\|_2$. This solution is harmonic with zero Neumann data in the fixed boundary collar. By [F1], its boundary trace has spectral $H^k_\Delta$ norm at most $C_k\|v\|_2$ for every integer $k$. Testing this equation with the background Neumann solution $u_{1,e_j}$, and that solution's equation with $z$, yields $|\int_Vv\cdot\nabla u_{1,e_j}|=|\langle e_j,z|_{\partial\Omega}\rangle|\le C_kw_j^{-k/2}\|v\|_2$. Taking the $L^2$ dual supremum proves $\|\nabla u_{1,e_j}\|_{L^2(V)}\le C_kw_j^{-k/2}$. No boundary regularity for a negative-order prescribed flux has been assumed in this argument. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct]

2.1 The correction $w=u_{\gamma,e_j}-u_{1,e_j}$ satisfies $\int\gamma\nabla w\cdot\nabla\varphi=\int_{\Omega'}(1-\gamma)\nabla u_{1,e_j}\cdot\nabla\varphi$. Coercivity and step 1.1 give $\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\|\nabla u_{1,e_j}\|_{L^2(\Omega')}\le C_kw_j^{-k/2}$. Adding the background gradient on $V$ gives $\|\nabla u_{\gamma,e_j}\|_{L^2(V)}\le C_kw_j^{-k/2}$. Apply [F2] on each smooth ball $2B_\ell$, restricted to $B_\ell$, and sum the finitely many bounds to obtain the stated rapid $L^p(\Omega')$ decay, choosing $k\ge2L$. All domains and constants were fixed before choosing $\gamma$ or $j$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The two weak Neumann equations, tested with the opposite solutions and subtracted, give $b_{ij}=\langle(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0})e_j,e_i\rangle=\int_{\Omega'}(\gamma_0-\gamma)\nabla u_{\gamma,e_j}\cdot\overline{\nabla u_{\gamma_0,e_i}}$. Hölder with $1/q+2/p=1$ and step 2.1 imply $|b_{ij}|\le C_L\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_q(w_iw_j)^{-L}$. Alternatively, the two rapid $L^2(V)$ bounds from that step and the coefficient supremum norm imply the identical bound with $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_\infty$. The conjugates and sign are consistent with the self-adjoint weak energy form; only the absolute value is used. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 In the boundary basis the smoothed matrix is $b_{ij}w_j^{-r/2}$. Choose $L$ with $2L>(d-1)/2$. By [F4], $\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2w_j^{-r}\le C_L^2\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_q^2(\sum_iw_i^{-2L})(\sum_jw_j^{-2L-r})<\infty$, with the asserted bound after taking the square root. A matrix with this sum finite defines its Hilbert–Schmidt operator: finite column sums converge in squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm and coincide with the given bounded operator on every finite spectral sum, hence on the dense span. The same proof uses the supremum-norm version of step 3.1. Extending by zero on constants preserves these norms. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-ip-solit-filter-risk-decomposition-and-monotone-bias
kind: lemma
title: Risk decomposition and monotone bias for ordered spectral filters
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 4
deps:

  - thm-ip-white-noise-spectral-sequence-representation
  - def-countable-choice
  - thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral
  - thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral
justified_by: []
proof_strategy: direct
axiom_use: "Countable Choice supplies the fixed compact singular system through the Gaussian sequence model; all series and risk calculations below are conditional on that fixed countable basis and use no further choice."
provenance:

  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Housen Li and Frank Werner, Adaptive minimax optimality in statistical inverse problems via SOLIT, Lemma 3.6 and §§3.1.1–3.2.1"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356
    - title: "Christian Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, complete lecture notes, Chapter 5 §5.1"
      url: https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf
---

## Statement
Assume Countable Choice and the positive-noise Gaussian sequence model with $\sigma>0$, a fixed complete positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ for an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator $T:X\to Y$, and a truth with coordinates $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ in $\ell^2$. Write $\lambda_j=s_j^2$ and let $\xi_j$ be the independent standard-normal noise coordinates. Let $q_\alpha$ be nonnegative and satisfy $0\le\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$, $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$, and $q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\le q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$ whenever $m_1<m_2$. For each candidate $m$, form the finite sums
$$
X_{m,N}:=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j\bigr)v_j.
$$
The conclusion below includes the existence of their limit $\widehat x_m$ in $L^2(\Omega;X)$. Put $f_m:=\mathbb E\widehat x_m$, $B_m:=\|f_m-x\|_X$, and $v_m:=\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-f_m\|_X^2$. Then $\widehat x_m$ is a measurable $X$-valued random element with finite second moment and
$$
\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=B_m^2+v_m,\qquad v_m=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
If $m_1<m_2$, then $B_{m_2}\le B_{m_1}$, $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$, and
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\mathbb E\| (\widehat x_{m_2}-f_{m_2})-(\widehat x_{m_1}-f_{m_1})\|_X^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2\le v_{m_2}.
$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index|The ordered-filter bounds and candidate-grid ordering]]

[[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model|The Gaussian sequence coordinate law]]

[[thm-ip-white-noise-spectral-sequence-representation|Independent standard-normal singular coordinates]]

[Li and Werner, *Adaptive minimax optimality in statistical inverse problems via SOLIT*, Lemma 3.6 and §§3.1.1–3.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356)

[Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, complete lecture notes, Chapter 5 §5.1](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the experiment and hypotheses in the Statement, a fixed complete positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and a fixed candidate $m$ or pair $m_1<m_2$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed by the SVD coordinate model; after its fixed countable basis is supplied, the proof below makes no further selections.

[F1] [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]: In the positive-noise sequence experiment, $Z_j=\theta_j+\sigma s_j^{-1}\xi_j$ with independent $\xi_j\sim N(0,1)$, and $\theta=(\theta_j)\in\ell^2$.

[F2] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]: The fixed positive singular vectors form complete orthonormal bases on the minimum-norm parameter space and the closure of the range, with $Tv_j=s_ju_j$ and $T^*Tv_j=\lambda_jv_j$.

[F3] [[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index]]: For each candidate $0\le\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$; if $m_1<m_2$, then $q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\le q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$; and $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$.


[F4] [[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment]]: The Gaussian coordinates are centered with variance one and independent on every finite orthonormal tuple.

[F5] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] permits passing increasing limits of nonnegative coordinate-square sums through the expectation.

[F6] [[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]] bounds the probability that a nonnegative random variable is at least a positive level by its expectation divided by that level.

## Proof
1.1 Put $c_j:=\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j$ and $d_j:=\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)$. By [F3], $|c_j|\le|\theta_j|$, so $(c_j)_j\in\ell^2$. Also $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ by [F2], so $\sum_jd_j^2=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2<\infty$. The partial sums of $Q:=\sum_jd_j^2\xi_j^2$ increase, and [F5] gives $\mathbb EQ=\sum_jd_j^2<\infty$. For each integer $r\ge1$, [F6] gives $\mathbb P(Q\ge r)\le\mathbb EQ/r$; since $\{Q=+\infty\}\subseteq\{Q\ge r\}$ for every $r$, $Q<\infty$ almost surely. Thus on a measurable event of probability one the coordinate series $\sum_j(c_j+d_j\xi_j)v_j$ converges in $X$; define its pointwise limit there and set it to zero on the null complement. The finite partial sums are measurable, and their pointwise limit on this event, extended by zero, is measurable because $X$ is separable. By Parseval and [F5], for each $N$, $\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-X_{m,N}\|_X^2=\sum_{j>N}\mathbb E(c_j+d_j\xi_j)^2=\sum_{j>N}c_j^2+\sum_{j>N}d_j^2$, where [F4] gives $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$. Both deterministic and noise tails tend to zero, so this constructed measurable pointwise limit is the $L^2(\Omega;X)$ limit. In particular it has finite second moment. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 For $m_1<m_2$, [F3] gives $0\le1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)\le1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)$. Squaring these nonnegative terms and summing against $\theta_j^2$ gives $B_{m_2}^2\le B_{m_1}^2$. Moreover, $f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}$ has coordinate $\lambda_j(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}-q_{\alpha_{m_1}})\theta_j$, whose multiplier equals $(1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_1}})-(1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_2}})$ and lies between zero and $1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_1}}$; coordinatewise comparison therefore yields $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Subtracting $x$ in each singular coordinate gives deterministic bias coefficient $-(1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j))\theta_j$ and centered noise coefficient $\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$. Since $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$ by [F1] and [F4], summing the coordinate second moments and using monotone convergence gives $\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=\sum_j(1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j))^2\theta_j^2+\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2=B_m^2+v_m$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The centered pairwise noise difference has coordinate variance $\sigma^2\lambda_j(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j))^2$. By [F3], each difference lies between zero and $q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$; summing its squared value against $\sigma^2\lambda_j$ proves $v_{m_1,m_2}\le v_{m_2}$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The $L^2$-limit definition is needed because white noise is not an $Y$-valued observation in infinite dimension. The estimator itself is $X$-valued because its filtered noise covariance has finite trace.

kind: lemma
title: Convergence and needle estimates for Kontsevich integrals
status: draft
origin: pipeline
proof_strategy: direct

deps:

  references:

      url: https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf
    - title: The Fundamental Theorem of Vassiliev Invariants, §2.5.1 and §2.5.3
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1

## Statement

Fix either a strict Morse knot presentation $K:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ or a compact strict Morse tangle $T\subset\mathbb C\times[a,b]$ with distinct regular boundary points, and a degree $m\ge0$. Each degree-$m$ coefficient of the unframed Kontsevich series is an absolutely convergent improper integral after summing its finitely many pairing terms in the 4T+1T quotient. A critical needle of width $\varepsilon$ in a horizontal slab is a local arc $N_\varepsilon$ whose intersection with each horizontal disk in the slab has at most two points and whose horizontal diameter is at most $\varepsilon$, with the knot or tangle fixed outside the slab and with the nondegenerate critical-point charts uniformly bounded in a compact smooth family. For every fixed $m$, the sum of degree-$m$ pairing integrals that have at least one endpoint on $N_\varepsilon$ has norm at most $C_m\varepsilon$, where $C_m$ is independent of $\varepsilon$. Thus these contributions tend to zero as the needle narrows.

The following figure illustrates a local maximum. The two branches meet at the critical point; the short chord is isolated if no higher endpoint interrupts the small oriented component arc, while a long chord joins a needle branch to a point outside the needle.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9,thick]
  \draw[->] (-1.2,0) -- (1.2,0) node[right] {$z$};
  \draw[->] (-1.2,0) -- (-1.2,2.5) node[above] {$t$};
  \draw (-0.7,0.25) .. controls (-0.42,1.35) and (-0.18,1.95) .. (0,2.2);
  \draw (0.7,0.25) .. controls (0.42,1.35) and (0.18,1.95) .. (0,2.2);
  \draw[dashed] (-0.4,1.2) -- (0.4,1.2);
  \draw[dashed] (-0.52,0.75) -- (0.52,0.75);
  \draw[dashed] (-0.95,0.75) -- (-0.52,0.75);
  \fill (0,2.2) circle (1.2pt);
  \node at (0.25,2.28) {$t_c$};
  \node at (0,1.42) {short};
  \node at (-0.72,0.9) {long};
  \node at (0.83,1.2) {$\varepsilon$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references

[[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids|Improper configuration-integral formula and 1T quotient]]

[[lem-kontsevich-configuration-space-compactification-faces|Morse branches and critical-level boundary coordinates]]

[[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations|Isolated-chord 1T relation]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §8.5, printed pp. 230–232](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §2.5.1 and §2.5.3, PDF pp. 13–15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A strict Morse knot or compact strict Morse tangle with regular boundary points, its degree-$m$ configuration cells, and the unframed 4T+1T chord quotient on its skeleton.

[F1] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: on each branch chamber the integrand is a finite sum of products of logarithmic forms $d\log(z_j-z'_j)$; tangle diagrams use the ordered tangle skeleton and the unframed quotient kills a chord whose endpoints are consecutive on one component.

[F2] [[lem-kontsevich-configuration-space-compactification-faces]]: each critical level has a local coordinate $s\ge0$ with $t_c-t=s^2$ at a maximum, branch evaluations extend smoothly, and all level/collision faces of knots and tangles have finite-dimensional corner coordinates.

[F3] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: 1T kills an isolated chord; on a circle its endpoints alternate with another chord exactly when the two chords intersect, and on a tangle arc the same local rule applies to consecutive endpoints.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Fix $m$; all constants below may depend on $K$, $m$, and the compact family, but not on $\varepsilon$.

1.1 Near a nondegenerate maximum, use the Morse coordinate $s=\sqrt{t_c-t}$ from [F2]. The two local branch functions satisfy $z_+(s)=z_c+a s+O(s^2)$ and $z_-(s)=z_c-a s+O(s^2)$ for some $a\ne0$; this follows because the tangle or knot immersion has nonzero tangent and $dt/ds=0$ at the critical point, so its tangent there is horizontal. Hence $|z_+(s)-z_-(s)|\asymp s$ and the short logarithmic form has absolute size at most $C\,ds/s$. A minimum has the same estimate after reversing $t$. [given, F2, construct, algebra]

1.2 For a long chord with one endpoint on a needle and one outside it, compactness of the family gives a uniform positive lower bound on its denominator. The two choices that put this endpoint on opposite needle branches have opposite factors $(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}$. Their endpoint positions differ by at most $\varepsilon$, so the mean-value estimate for $\log(z-z')$ away from $z=z'$ bounds the difference of their integrands by $C\varepsilon$ times bounded remaining factors. Integration over the fixed simplex preserves the $O(\varepsilon)$ bound. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Order the chord endpoints on the small oriented component arc between the two branches near the maximum. The endpoints of the level closest to $t_c$ are adjacent on this arc. If their chord joins the two branches, it is isolated under the tangle or circle 1T rule, so its diagram vanishes by [F1, F3]. Thus every nonzero pairing approaching this critical face either has no short chord or has short chords nested below an interrupting long chord. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For a surviving nested chain of $k$ short chords, write their branch separations as $0<\delta_k<\cdots<\delta_1<\varepsilon$. Each short factor is bounded by $C\,d\delta_j/\delta_j$ by step 1.1. The long chord interrupting the short chord nearest the critical point has denominator bounded away from zero; integrating its level variable produces a factor $O(\delta_k)$ because its logarithmic primitive is Lipschitz there and its endpoint limits differ by $O(\delta_k)$. The whole nested contribution is therefore bounded by a constant times $\int_0^\varepsilon \frac{d\delta_1}{\delta_1}\cdots\int_0^{\delta_{k-1}}\frac{d\delta_k}{\delta_k}\,\delta_k=\varepsilon$, by repeated use of $\int_0^a(d\delta/\delta)\delta=a$. This also covers $k=1$. At any noncritical level-collision face, each chord still joins two distinct points of the embedded knot or tangle, so every within-chord denominator remains nonzero and has a positive lower bound locally. If a within-chord denominator tends to zero, the endpoints lie on the two branches meeting at a critical point and are covered by steps 1.1–2.1. There are finitely many faces and pairing types at fixed $m$, so the degree-$m$ chamber integrals converge absolutely. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 A short chord joining the two needle branches is killed by 1T when it is the highest such chord; otherwise its nonzero diagram contains an interrupting long chord and the nested estimate of step 3.1 applies. Pairing the long-chord endpoint choices as in step 1.2 supplies an additional $O(\varepsilon)$ factor. There are finitely many pairing types in fixed degree $m$, so their sum is bounded by $C_m\varepsilon$ and tends to zero. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $p\ge4$ be even, $A\in\mathbb C$ a primitive $2p$-th root, and $r=p/2$. In the BHMV Temperley–Lieb quotient with loop value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ and planar pivotal trace, the complete simple-label set is $\{0,1,\ldots,r-2\}$, represented by the surviving Jones–Wenzl projectors $p_a$ obtained from the standard recursion using unit denominators $[2],\ldots,[a]$. Every simple is self-dual. Its fusion multiplicities are

$$N_{ab}^{c}=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |a-b|\le c\le\min(a+b,\,2r-4-a-b) \ \text{and }a+b+c\text{ is even},$$

and are zero otherwise. With the BHMV overcrossing map $c_i=A1_i+A^{-1}U_i$, where $U_i$ is the cup-cap generator, the full-framing ribbon structure has planar quantum dimensions $d_a=[a+1]$ and simple-object twists $\theta_a=(-1)^aA^{a(a+2)}$. Here the quantum integers use the fixed BHMV recurrence. The unnormalized Hopf-link matrix, whose $(a,b)$ entry is the pivotal trace of the double braiding on $p_a\otimes p_b$, is nondegenerate. Here modular means that this finite semisimple ribbon category has an invertible unnormalized Hopf-link matrix.

## Statement references

[[def-semisimplified-temperley-lieb-fusion-category|The quotient and planar pivotal convention]]

[[lem-root-jones-wenzl-recursion-and-negligible-ideal|Exact root negligible ideal and simple labels]]

[[thm-temperley-lieb-rank-one-pivotal-ribbon-conversion|Root parameter, ribbon comparison, and parity correction]]

[[thm-temperley-lieb-rank-one-tilting-quotient-fusion-category|Positive-pivotal root fusion rule and self-duality]]

[[thm-su2-root-unity-ribbon-category-is-modular|Positive-pivotal rank-one root category and sine matrix]]

[[def-modular-ribbon-category-and-hopf-link-data|Definition of modularity by the Hopf-link matrix]]

[Blanchet, Habegger, Masbaum, and Vogel, *Topological Quantum Field Theories Derived from the Kauffman Bracket*, §§3–4](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/bhmv.pdf)

[Gelca, *Topological Quantum Field Theory with Corners Based on the Kauffman Bracket*, §§3–4](https://www.math.ttu.edu/~rgelca/bra3.pdf)

[Sawin, *Quantum Groups at Roots of Unity and Modularity*, §§1–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0308281)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The fixed BHMV parameter, its negligible quotient, and the standard planar pivotal convention.

[F1] [[def-sl-two-root-of-unity-skein-parameter]]: $r=p/2$, $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, and $[j]$ is defined by $[0]=0$, $[1]=1$, $[j+1]=\delta[j]-[j-1]$.

[F2] [[lem-root-jones-wenzl-recursion-and-negligible-ideal]]: the quotient's negligible ideal is generated by $p_{r-1}$, and its complete simple labels are $0,\ldots,r-2$.

[F3] [[thm-temperley-lieb-rank-one-pivotal-ribbon-conversion]]: for $r\ge3$ and $q_0=e^{\pi i/r}$, the negative-loop diagram quotient at loop $-(q_0+q_0^{-1})$ with its diagram crossing and parity-corrected pivotal structure is ribbon-equivalent to the positive-pivotal rank-one tilting quotient. The diagram algebra is identified with the positive-loop algebra by $U_i\mapsto-e_i$.

[F4] [[thm-temperley-lieb-rank-one-tilting-quotient-fusion-category]]: the positive-pivotal quotient is semisimple, its simple objects are self-dual, and its tensor products have the truncated multiplicities.

[F5] [[thm-su2-root-unity-ribbon-category-is-modular]]: the positive-pivotal quotient at $q_0=e^{\pi i/r}$ has dimensions $d_a^+=\sin((a+1)\pi/r)/\sin(\pi/r)$, twists $\theta_a^+=e^{\pi i a(a+2)/(2r)}$, and invertible sine Hopf-link matrix.

[F6] [[def-modular-ribbon-category-and-hopf-link-data]]: modularity means that the unnormalized Hopf-link matrix of the finite semisimple ribbon category is invertible.

[F7] [[def-semisimplified-temperley-lieb-fusion-category]]: each fixed pair of object labels starts from a finite set of matching diagrams, and the quotient morphism space is a quotient of that finite-dimensional span.

## Proof

**Given:** The root parameter and quotient in the Statement.

1.1 If $r=2$, then $p=4$, $\delta=0$, and the sole proposed retained label is $0$. The boundary projector is $p_1=1_1$ and has zero trace. The tensor ideal it generates contains $1_n=1_1\otimes1_{n-1}$ for every $n\ge1$. Therefore every morphism with a positive source or target is zero in the quotient, because it factors through the corresponding identity. The endomorphism space of object $0$ is $\mathbb C$, and its trace is the identity, so it is non-negligible. The quotient's additive idempotent completion is thus finite-dimensional vector spaces with one self-dual simple $0$. Its fusion is $0\otimes0=0$, its unit twist is $1$, and its Hopf-link matrix is the $1\times1$ matrix $(1)$, which is invertible. [F1, F2, given, cases, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $r\ge3$ and first take the canonical root $A_0=e^{\pi i/(2r)}$, so $q_0=A_0^2=e^{\pi i/r}$ and the BHMV loop is $-(q_0+q_0^{-1})$. By [F3], the diagram quotient with its parity-corrected pivotal structure is ribbon-equivalent to the positive-pivotal quotient of [F4]–[F5]. Thus the quotient has exactly the labels $0,\ldots,r-2$, the displayed truncated fusion multiplicities, self-dual simples, and a nondegenerate Hopf-link matrix for that corrected pivotal structure. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given]

2.1 On the semisimple quotient define $\varepsilon_{p_a}=(-1)^a\,1_{p_a}$. This is a monoidal natural automorphism: each retained summand $p_c$ of $p_a\otimes p_b$ has $c\equiv a+b\pmod2$ by [F4], so $\varepsilon_{p_c}=\varepsilon_{p_a}\varepsilon_{p_b}$; it is dual-compatible because every $p_a$ is self-dual. The planar pivotal structure is $\varepsilon$ times the parity-corrected one of [F3]. Multiplying a pivotal structure $j$ by a dual-compatible monoidal automorphism $\varepsilon$ changes the twist $u^{-1}j$ to $\varepsilon\theta$, preserves balancing by monoidality, and preserves dual compatibility; hence the planar convention is also ribbon. Its dimensions are $d_a=(-1)^a d_a^+$, which equal the BHMV recurrence value $[a+1]$: the sequence $v_j=(-1)^{j-1}[j]_{q_0}$ has $v_0=0$, $v_1=1$ and satisfies $v_{j+1}=-(q_0+q_0^{-1})v_j-v_{j-1}$, so uniqueness of the recurrence gives $v_j=[j]$ for the BHMV loop. Its simple twists are $\theta_a=(-1)^a\theta_a^+=(-1)^aA_0^{a(a+2)}$. Its unnormalized Hopf-link entries are $s_{ab}=\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_b s_{ab}^+$, since the pivotal trace on $p_a\otimes p_b$ is multiplied by $\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_b$. Therefore its Hopf-link matrix is obtained from the invertible matrix in [F5] by multiplying row $a$ and column $b$ by $(-1)^a$ and $(-1)^b$, so it remains invertible. The criterion in [F6] proves modularity. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For any primitive $A$, write $A=A_0^k$ with $\gcd(k,4r)=1$. The automorphism of the cyclotomic field $\mathbb Q(A_0)$ sending $A_0$ to $A$ transports the finite diagram coefficients, the recursively defined projectors, the braiding and twist matrices, and the Hopf-link matrix. By [F7], every fixed Hom space is finite-dimensional, so this transport preserves all ranks and nonzero determinants. The fusion multiplicities are dimensions of these finite Hom spaces and so are unchanged under the field automorphism and extension to $\mathbb C$. Thus the canonical-root result applies to every primitive $2p$-th root with the exact stated BHMV convention; in particular $\theta_a=(-1)^aA^{a(a+2)}$. [F1, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $T$ be the trefoil represented by the standard oriented three-crossing diagram below. Choose a basepoint $x_0\in S^3\setminus T$ in the diagram's upper collar and use the common upper-collar paths from $x_0$ to base the positive-meridian generators. Its under-arcs are labelled $a,b,c$ so that the ordered triples $(o,L,R)$ of over-arc, upper target under-arc and lower source under-arc are $(b,c,a)$, $(c,a,b)$, and $(a,b,c)$ at the three crossings; read each triple in the orientation-preserving local chart that straightens the over-arc to point rightward. The knot group $G_T=\pi_1(S^3\setminus T,x_0)$, where $\pi_1$ is based loops modulo endpoint-fixed homotopy with multiplication by concatenation, has presentation $\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle$. This presentation denotes the free group on $a,b$ modulo the normal closure of the displayed relation. Its abelianization, the quotient by its commutator subgroup, is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$, but $G_T$ is nonabelian.

The drawing shows two oriented strands crossing three times; the two bottom endpoints join to the corresponding top endpoints by the outside arcs. The white gaps mark underpasses, and each redrawn strand is over. The crossing triples in the statement fix the generator labels and local chart convention.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
\foreach \j in {0,1,2} {
\draw[->] (-1,3-\j)--(-0.14,2.57-\j);
\draw[->] (0.14,2.43-\j)--(1,2-\j);
\draw[->,line width=1.2pt] (1,3-\j)--(-1,2-\j);
}
\draw[->] (-1,0)..controls(-1.7,0)and(-1.7,3)..(-1,3);
\draw[->] (1,0)..controls(1.7,0)and(1.7,3)..(1,3);
\node[above] at (-1,3) {$a$};
\node[above] at (1,3) {$b$};
\node[right] at (1,2) {$c$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references

[[thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctness|Wirtinger presentation theorem]]

[[lem-wirtinger-local-meridian-conjugacy|Local crossing conjugacy convention]]

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, *Knot Theory and Applications: Lecture Notes*, §4.2](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

[Charbonneau, *Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram*, §§3–4.1](https://site.uvm.edu/cmcharbo/files/2021/12/knot-group-1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard oriented trefoil diagram, crossing labels, chosen complement basepoint, and common upper-collar paths specified in the Statement.

[F1] For a valid finite knot diagram with chosen complement basepoint $x_0$, the Wirtinger presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing presents $\pi_1(S^3\setminus T,x_0)$ using the common upper-collar paths. [[thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctness]]

[F2] With a rightward over-strand and the common upper-collar basing paths, the upper target meridian $m_L$ and lower source meridian $m_R$ satisfy $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. [[lem-wirtinger-local-meridian-conjugacy]]

[F3] A group presentation $\langle a,b\mid r\rangle$ denotes the free group on $a,b$ modulo the normal closure of $r$.

## Proof

1.1 Applying [F2] to the three crossing triples gives $a=bcb^{-1}$, $b=cac^{-1}$, and $c=aba^{-1}$. Substitute the third equation into the first to obtain $a=baba^{-1}b^{-1}$; right multiplication by $ba$ gives $aba=bab$. Under this relation, $cac^{-1}=aba^{-1}aab^{-1}a^{-1}=abab^{-1}a^{-1}=bab b^{-1}a^{-1}=b$, so the second crossing equation follows. Therefore eliminating $c$ from the presentation in [F1] yields exactly $\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle$. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 In the abelianization, the relation becomes $2[a]+[b]=[a]+2[b]$, hence $[a]=[b]$. The abelianization is the free abelian group on $[a],[b]$ modulo this single relation, so it is $\mathbb Z$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Map $a\mapsto(12)$ and $b\mapsto(23)$ in $S_3$. Both $aba$ and $bab$ map to $(13)$, so the relation is satisfied. These two transpositions generate $S_3$, making the homomorphism surjective. Since $S_3$ is nonabelian, its surjective preimage $G_T$ is nonabelian. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://jmlr.org/papers/volume22/21-0806/21-0806.pdf"

---

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M=\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega$ for a nonempty bounded smooth domain $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$, $d\ge2$, and let $a,b\in\mathbb N$ be positive finite channel dimensions. If $T:L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)$ is continuous, then for every compact set $C\subset L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a generalized Fourier neural operator $\Psi:L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)$ using a fixed smooth globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation and the boundary charts of the statement such that
$$\sup_{h\in C}\|T(h)-\Psi(h)\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-generalized-fourier-neural-operator|The generalized FNO architecture, chart lifting and dimension-reduction layer.]]

[de Hoop et al., §4.4, Theorem 4.8 and proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

[Kovachki et al., Theorem 5 and Appendix D: compact-uniform FNO approximation](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume22/21-0806/21-0806.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\Omega$, $M$, $T$, compact $C$, and $\varepsilon$ as in the statement.

[F1] There are bounded chart maps $G_a:L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)\to\bigoplus_{j,k}L^2(\mathbb T^{2d-2};\mathbb R^a)$ and $L_a$ in the reverse direction, obtained by applying the scalar chart maps componentwise, with $L_aG_a=I$. ([[lem-ip-boundary-chart-lifting-and-fourier-projection]])

[F2] On a torus, a Fourier neural operator with the specified activation uniformly approximates every continuous map on every compact input set in the $L^2$ norm. ([[lem-ip-fno-torus-compact-universality]])

[F3] Zero extension from $L^2(\Omega)$ to $L^2(\mathbb T^d)$ is isometric because $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$; the product extension constant in the last $d-2$ coordinates is also isometric under normalized Haar measure.

[F4] The generalized-FNO architecture contains the zero operator by setting its finite-layer coefficients to zero. ([[def-ip-generalized-fourier-neural-operator]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed at the finite boundary-chart partition interface. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and the data in the statement.

1.1 If $C=\varnothing$, choose the zero generalized FNO from [F4]; the uniform error condition is vacuous. Otherwise let $n=2d-2$ and let $J_0:L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)\to L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^b)$ be zero extension. Let $I_{d,n}:L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^b)\to L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)$ send $g(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ to the function constant in the last $n-d=d-2$ coordinates. The chart-pair components identify $\bigoplus_{j,k}L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^a)$ with $L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^{J^2a})$. Define $S:=I_{d,n}J_0TL_a$ on this direct-sum space. This is continuous by [F1] and [F3], and $G_a(C)$ is compact because $G_a$ is continuous and $C$ is compact. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the continuous map $S:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^{J^2a})\to L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)$ on compact $G_a(C)$ with tolerance $\varepsilon$. There is a torus FNO $\Phi$ such that $\sup_{u\in G_a(C)}\|S(u)-\Phi(u)\|_{L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon$. [F2, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Set $\mathbb T^0=\{()\}$ with unit mass, so the following integral is the identity when $d=2$. For any finite channel dimension $c$, define $A_c:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^c)\to L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^c)$ by $(A_cv)(x)=\int_{\mathbb T^{d-2}}v(x,z)\,dz$, componentwise. Cauchy–Schwarz on the unit-measure torus and Fubini give $\|A_c\|\le1$. Let $R$ be restriction from $\mathbb T^d$ to $\Omega$, also of norm at most one. Since $A_bI_{d,n}=I$, $RJ_0=I$, and $L_aG_a=I$, the generalized FNO $\Psi:=R\circ A_b\circ\Phi\circ G_a$ satisfies
$$\|T(h)-\Psi(h)\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)}=\|RA_b(S(G_ah)-\Phi(G_ah))\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)}\le\|S(G_ah)-\Phi(G_ah)\|_{L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon$$
for every $h\in C$. Write the torus FNO as $\Phi=Q_\Phi\circ\Phi_0$, where $\Phi_0$ ends before its final constant affine channel map $Q_\Phi(v)=Wv+c$ and has $r$ output channels. Its initial affine channel lift is composed into the first affine part of $\Phi_0$ after $G_a$. Normalized averaging commutes with the final map, $A_bQ_\Phi=Q_\Phi A_r$, and restriction commutes with the same pointwise map. Hence $R A_b\Phi G_a=Q_\Phi R A_r\Phi_0G_a$. This has the generalized architecture: identity pointwise lift, chart lift $G_a$, torus layers $\Phi_0$, the constant-kernel dimension reduction $A_r$, restriction $R$, and final pointwise affine map $Q_\Phi$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot, and let $p,q$ be coprime integers with $q\ne0$. For the Dehn filling $Y_{p/q}=E_K(p/q)$ whose attached solid-torus meridian is identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the fundamental group $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ is nontrivial.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-exterior|Chosen knot exterior]]

[[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude|Meridian and preferred longitude]]

[[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling|Filling slope convention]]

[[lem-knot-surgery-first-homology-mayer-vietoris|First homology of knot fillings]]

[[lem-property-p-instanton-surgery-triangle-and-rank-input|Noncyclic SU(2) representations for numerator-one slopes]]

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Dehn surgery, the fundamental group and SU(2)*, Theorem 1](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/hrpthree.pdf)

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Knots, sutures and excision*, §7.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0807.4891)

[Motegi, *Dehn surgery on knots: survey*, pp. 19–21 and 26](https://www.math.tsukuba.ac.jp/~tange/diftop22/Dehn_surgery_survey.pdf)

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, published Theorem 1, p. 741](https://doi.org/10.4310/mrl.2004.v11.n6.a3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nontrivial smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, and a nonmeridional slope $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ with $\gcd(p,q)=1$ and $q\ne0$.

[F1] The filling has $H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$ for $p\ne0$, and $H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ for $p=0$. [[lem-knot-surgery-first-homology-mayer-vietoris]]

[F2] For a path-connected space, $H_1$ is naturally the abelianization of its fundamental group. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

[F3] If $|p|=1$ and $q\ne0$, the filling group admits a noncyclic homomorphism to $SU(2)$. The supplier derives this exact interface from the explicitly imported published Kronheimer–Mrowka Theorem 1, p. 741; its gauge-theoretic theorem is not claimed as locally reconstructed. [[lem-property-p-instanton-surgery-triangle-and-rank-input]]

[F4] The filling is obtained by attaching a solid torus to $E_K$ along its entire boundary torus, with meridian identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. [[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling]]

[F5] The chosen exterior is the complement of the interior of the closed tubular disk bundle over the connected knot $K$, with boundary $T_K=\partial N(K)$. [[def-knot-exterior]]

[A1] Full AC is the assertion that every set-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[L1] Applying [A1] to the set of members of any countable family gives the countable choice function required by [F1]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 By [F5], the chosen tubular neighbourhood is a disk bundle over the connected knot $K$, so its boundary $T_K$ is a circle bundle over $K$ with connected fibres and is connected. Indeed, a separation of $T_K$ would, since every fibre is connected, split it into two saturated open sets; their projections are open by the local bundle charts, disjoint, and cover the connected base $K$. Since $T_K$ is a connected smooth manifold, it is path-connected. The exterior $E_K$ is a compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary $T_K$. Because $T_K$ is connected, it lies in one component of $E_K$. Any other component is boundaryless, hence lies in $\operatorname{int}E_K$ and is open in $S^3$; it is also closed in $S^3$, since it is closed in $E_K$ and $E_K$ is closed in $S^3$ by [F5]. This contradicts connectedness of $S^3$. Thus $E_K$ is connected and, being a smooth manifold, path-connected. By [F4], $Y_{p/q}$ is the union of this path-connected exterior and an attached path-connected solid torus along $T_K$, so $Y_{p/q}$ is path-connected. [given, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 By [A1] and [L1], the countable-choice hypothesis of [F1] follows from the Statement, and step 1.1 verifies its connected-exterior hypothesis. If $p=0$, [F1] gives $H_1(Y_{p/q};\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. If $|p|\ge2$, it gives the nonzero finite group $\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$. Choose any basepoint $y_0$ of the path-connected filling. By [F2], $H_1(Y_{p/q};\mathbb Z)\cong\pi_1(Y_{p/q},y_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}$, so in either case the fundamental group is nontrivial. [given, A1, L1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $|p|=1$, the nonmeridional condition gives $q\ne0$, and [F3] supplies a homomorphism with noncyclic image. The trivial group has only the trivial, hence cyclic, image, so $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ is nontrivial. [given, F3, algebra]

4.1 Coprimality leaves exactly the cases $p=0$, $|p|=1$, or $|p|\ge2$, all covered by steps 2.1 and 3.1. Thus every nonmeridional filling has nontrivial fundamental group. [given, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## External dependency

The numerator-one case uses the external Kronheimer–Mrowka theorem through [F3], with its exact hypotheses and reading limits recorded in that supplier. The homology cases and the deduction of nontriviality from a noncyclic image are the local argument above.

## Definition

A finite rooted directed tree $T=(V,E)$ has root $o$, with all edges directed away from $o$, and a nonempty receiver set $R$ consisting of every leaf other than $o$. Every nonroot internal vertex has at least two children. For a vertex $v$, its children are the vertices joined to $v$ by an outgoing edge; $P(o,v)$ is the unique edge set on the path from $o$ to $v$. The root may have any finite number of children.

A finite probe design is a nonempty finite family $\mathcal C=((C_d,N_d))_{d=1}^D$, where each receiver set $C_d$ is a nonempty subset of $R$ and each probe count $N_d$ is a positive integer. A singleton receiver set is a unicast scheme; a receiver set of size at least two is a multicast scheme. Its used edge set is $E_d=\bigcup_{r\in C_d}P(o,r)$.

For a link-success parameter vector $p=(p_e)_{e\in E}\in(0,1)^E$, each design $d$ and probe $j\in\{1,\ldots,N_d\}$ has mutually independent link-success variables $X_{e,d,j}\in\{0,1\}$ for $e\in E_d$, with $\Pr_p(X_{e,d,j}=1)=p_e$. The same $p_e$ applies in every design and probe (temporal homogeneity). The observed receiver indicator is
$$
Y_{r,d,j}=\prod_{e\in P(o,r)}X_{e,d,j}\qquad(r\in C_d).
$$

For $y\in\{0,1\}^{C_d}$ let
$$
\Omega_{d,y}=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E_d}: y_r=\prod_{e\in P(o,r)}x_e\text{ for every }r\in C_d\right\},\qquad w_{p,d}(x)=\prod_{e\in E_d}p_e^{x_e}(1-p_e)^{1-x_e}.
$$
The one-probe outcome law is
$$
P_{p,d}(y)=\sum_{x\in\Omega_{d,y}}w_{p,d}(x).
$$
These probabilities sum to one because the sets $\Omega_{d,y}$ partition the finite link-state space and $\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{E_d}}w_{p,d}(x)=\prod_{e\in E_d}(p_e+(1-p_e))=1$. The complete experiment observes $N_d$ independent outcomes with law $P_{p,d}$ for each design, independently across designs. If the data are summarized by counts, $n_{d,y}\in\mathbb N_0$ is the number of probes in design $d$ with outcome $y$, and $\sum_y n_{d,y}=N_d$.

This is a finite statistical experiment: its parameter space is $(0,1)^E$ and its sampling law is the finite product of the stated receiver-outcome laws.

[[def-statistical-experiment|Statistical experiments]]

[Cáceres, Duffield, Horowitz, and Towsley, §§2.1–2.3](https://www.kiskeya.net/ramon/work/pubs/toit99.pdf)

[Lawrence, Michailidis, and Nair, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1079)

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\geq3$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded smooth domain contained in a ball $B(0,R)$, and let $q\in L^\infty(\Omega,\mathbb C)$. There are constants $C>0$ and $\tau_0\geq1$, depending only on $n$, $R$, and $\|q\|_{L^\infty}$, such that for every $\zeta\in\mathbb C^n$ satisfying $\zeta\cdot\zeta=0$ and $|\zeta|\geq\tau_0$, there is $r_\zeta\in H^1(\Omega,\mathbb C)$ for which
$$u_\zeta(x)=e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta(x))$$
solves $(-\Delta+q)u_\zeta=0$ distributionally in $\Omega$, and
$$\|r_\zeta\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C|\zeta|^{-1}\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad \|\nabla r_\zeta\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
The dot product in the null-phase condition is complex bilinear, and $|\zeta|=(\sum_{j=1}^n|\zeta_j|^2)^{1/2}$.

## Statement references

[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm|Euclidean Sobolev spaces and weak derivatives]]

[[def-riemannian-gradient|Gradient convention]]

[[def-laplace-beltrami-operator-as-trace-of-the-hessian|Euclidean Laplacian convention]]

[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus|Fourier basis and Parseval on the torus]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a bounded smooth domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$; $q\in L^\infty(\Omega,\mathbb C)$; and a null vector $\zeta$ above the stated size threshold.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed by the Fourier-basis supplier [F1].

[F1] [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]: on a normalized $n$-torus, the coordinate characters form a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2$ and satisfy Parseval's identity. Rescaling the fundamental cube and multiplying by a unit-modulus exponential preserve completeness and orthonormality.

[F2] [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-riemannian-gradient]], and [[def-laplace-beltrami-operator-as-trace-of-the-hessian]]: $H^1$ consists of $L^2$ functions with $L^2$ weak first derivatives, $D=-i\nabla$ has the same norm as $\nabla$, and $D^2=-\Delta$.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the Statement.

1.1 Write $\zeta=a+ib$. The null condition gives $|a|=|b|=:s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$ and $a\cdot b=0$. Choose an orthogonal map $U$ with $Ua=se_1$ and $Ub=se_2$. Work temporarily with $U\Omega$, $q\circ U^{-1}$, and the phase $U\zeta$, relabeling them $\Omega$, $q$, and $\zeta$ for the construction; the Euclidean Laplacian, Lebesgue norms, and null phase are invariant under this change, and the constructed remainder is pulled back by $U$ at the end. As $\Omega\subset B(0,R)$, choose $L>\max\{1,(R+1)/\pi\}$; then $\Omega\subset Q_L=(-\pi L,\pi L)^n$. Put $\eta_k=(k+\tfrac12e_2)/L$ and $w_k(x)=(2\pi L)^{-n/2}e^{i\eta_k\cdot x}$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$. By [F1], these form an orthonormal basis on $Q_L$: they are the rescaled standard Fourier characters multiplied by the unitary factor $e^{ix_2/(2L)}$. For $A_\zeta=D^2+2\zeta\cdot D$, one has $A_\zeta w_k=p_kw_k$, where $p_k=|\eta_k|^2+2\zeta\cdot\eta_k$ and $|\operatorname{Im}p_k|=2s|k_2+\tfrac12|/L\geq s/L$. If $|\eta_k|\leq4s$, then $|p_k|\geq s/L$ and $|\eta_k/p_k|\leq4L$. If $|\eta_k|>4s$, then $|\operatorname{Re}p_k|\geq|\eta_k|^2-2s|\eta_k|\geq|\eta_k|^2/2$, so $|p_k|^{-1}<1/(8s^2)\leq L/s$ and $|\eta_k/p_k|<1/(2s)$. Thus $\sup_k|p_k|^{-1}\leq L/s$ and $\sup_k|\eta_k/p_k|\leq C_L$. Define $G_\zeta f=\sum_k p_k^{-1}(f,w_k)w_k$. Parseval [F1] gives $\|G_\zeta f\|_2\leq (L/s)\|f\|_2$ and $\|\nabla G_\zeta f\|_2\leq C_L\|f\|_2$. For finite Fourier sums $f_N$, the corresponding partial sums $G_\zeta f_N$ satisfy $A_\zeta G_\zeta f_N=f_N$ termwise. Parseval and the multiplier bounds give $f_N\to f$ in $L^2(Q_L)$ and $G_\zeta f_N\to G_\zeta f$ in $H^1(Q_L)$. Since $A_\zeta:H^1(Q_L)\to H^{-1}_{\rm loc}(Q_L)$ continuously, passage to distributions yields $A_\zeta G_\zeta f=f$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra, construct]

2.1 Extend $q$ and $F:=-q$ by zero from $\Omega$ to $Q_L$. Multiplication by $q$ is bounded on $L^2(Q_L)$, and
$$\|qG_\zeta\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq \|q\|_\infty L/s.$$
Choose $\tau_0$ large enough that $s\geq2L\|q\|_\infty$ and $s\geq1$ whenever $|\zeta|\geq\tau_0$. Then the series $\widetilde F=\sum_{m=0}^\infty(-qG_\zeta)^mF$ converges in $L^2(Q_L)$, satisfies $(I+qG_\zeta)\widetilde F=F$, and has norm at most $2\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$. Set $r_\zeta=G_\zeta\widetilde F$ and restrict it to $\Omega$. Step 1.1 gives $A_\zeta r_\zeta+q r_\zeta=F=-q$ on $\Omega$, as well as $\|r_\zeta\|_2\leq (2L/s)\|q\|_2$ and $\|\nabla r_\zeta\|_2\leq2C_L\|q\|_2$. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 Since $D=-i\nabla$, conjugation gives
$$e^{-i\zeta\cdot x}(-\Delta+q)e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta) =(D^2+2\zeta\cdot D+\zeta\cdot\zeta+q)(1+r_\zeta).$$
The null condition removes $\zeta\cdot\zeta$, the constant amplitude has zero derivatives, and step 2.1 makes the remaining expression $q+A_\zeta r_\zeta+q r_\zeta=0$. Multiplication by the smooth exponential preserves $H^1(\Omega)$ for this fixed $\zeta$, so $u_\zeta\in H^1(\Omega)$ and solves the equation distributionally. The estimates in step 2.1 have $s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$, giving the asserted bounds after changing the constant. [F2, given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold $M$, and let $F$ be a normal surface. Its normal disks form polygonal cells with three or four sides. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite disjoint family of PL simple closed curves and properly embedded PL arcs on $F$. Suppose $\Lambda$ misses the normal-cell vertices, is transverse to the cell edges, and meets each normal disk in disjoint properly embedded arcs whose endpoints are on distinct sides of that disk.

Cut $F$ along $\Lambda$, retaining separate boundary copies of each cut. Let $P$ be the compact completion of one resulting component, and suppose $P\cap\partial F$ has $b$ components, all proper arcs. Define its edge weight by $w(P)=|P\cap T^{(1)}|$. If $w(P)=0$, its polygonal pieces have $k_j\ge2$ trace sides and satisfy

$$\chi(P)=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right)\le\frac b2.$$

Consequently, if $P$ is a disk and $b\le1$, then $w(P)>0$. This applies in particular to disk patches of a proper normal sum: an interior disk patch has one closed trace frontier and $b=0$, and a boundary disk patch has one trace-arc frontier and $b=1$.

The trace hypothesis is satisfied by the usual exchange rectangles: in each tetrahedron a rectangle has two opposite sides on distinct normal disks and the other two sides in distinct tetrahedral faces. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is imposed.

## Statement references

[[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]] — normal disks and their polygonal cell structure.

[[def-euler-characteristic-of-a-finite-cw-complex]] — finite cell count defining $\chi$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The triangulation, normal surface, trace family and cut component of the Statement.

[F1] A finite properly embedded polygonal arc in a polygonal disk cuts it into two disks. For a disjoint finite arc family, repeated cutting leaves disk regions. One verifies the one-arc assertion by joining the arc to each complementary boundary interval and applying polygonal separation and triangulation. ([[thm-polygonal-jordan-curve]], [[thm-simple-polygon-admits-a-triangulation]])

[F2] The normal disks and their sides give a finite cell structure on $F$; its vertices are exactly the normal surface's intersections with the triangulation edges. Each interior side is glued to one other side, and each side on $\partial M$ remains a boundary side. ([[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]])

[F3] The Euler characteristic of a finite cell structure is its number of vertices minus edges plus faces. For a PL disk this value is $1$: carry its one-skeleton to a plane disk by a PL disk parametrization. The connected plane graph has precisely its cell interiors as bounded faces and one exterior face, so the plane-graph formula gives $v-e+f=1$. Subdividing bent edges or subdividing to remove loops and multiple edges adds one vertex and one edge at a time and preserves this count. ([[def-euler-characteristic-of-a-finite-cw-complex]], [[thm-euler-formula-for-connected-plane-graphs]])

## Proof

1.1 Assume $w(P)=0$. Cut each normal disk along its trace arcs. The arcs are finite, disjoint and proper, so [F1] makes each remaining region a polygonal disk. Keep precisely the regions belonging to $P$, with distinct copies on opposite sides of any cut. Their finitely many sides and endpoints give a finite cell structure on the abstract cut completion $P$. The original normal-cell vertices do not occur in these regions, by the assumed zero weight and [F2]. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 A retained region cannot have two consecutive old side intervals: their meeting point would be an original normal-cell vertex. Nor can two trace sides meet: trace arcs are disjoint and transverse to the old edges, with distinct endpoints there. Thus the boundary of each retained region alternates trace sides and old side intervals. It contains a trace side, since a region with no trace side would be the entire original normal disk and would contain its vertices. If it had only one trace side, the complementary old interval would connect the two endpoints along one old side, so that trace arc would have both endpoints on that side, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore its number $k_j$ of trace sides is at least two, and it has exactly $k_j$ old side intervals. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Put $N=\sum_j k_j$, let $f$ be the number of retained regions, and let $e_i$ and $e_m$ count respectively the glued interior old intervals and the old intervals lying in $\partial F$. Every trace side is a boundary edge of the cut completion, so their number is $N$. An interior old interval has two incident retained region sides; a boundary old interval has one. Consequently $$N=2e_i+e_m.$$ This count concerns abstract sides of $P$, so it remains valid when the same component occurs on both sides of a trace or on both sides of an old cell edge. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Each component of $P\cap\partial F$ contains no original normal-cell vertex, again because $w(P)=0$. Such a component is, by hypothesis, a proper arc, with its two endpoints on the trace family. It therefore lies within one original boundary side. No trace endpoint lies in its interior, since cutting at any such endpoint terminates the corresponding boundary interval in the cut completion. Hence each of the $b$ components is exactly one boundary old edge, and $e_m=b$. [given, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Every vertex of the new cell structure is an intersection of a trace with an old side. It is consequently on the boundary of the cut completion. There are no other vertices, since the original vertices were excluded in step 1.1. The boundary is a finite disjoint union of polygonal circles, so its vertex count equals its edge count. Its edges are the $N$ trace sides and $b$ boundary old intervals, giving $v=N+b$. The full edge count is $e_i+N+b$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Apply [F3] and substitute the preceding counts: $$\chi(P)=(N+b)-(e_i+N+b)+f=f-e_i=f-\frac{N-b}{2}=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right).$$ Every summand is nonpositive by step 2.1, proving the asserted inequality. If $P$ is a disk and $b\le1$, then $\chi(P)=1$ whereas the inequality gives $\chi(P)\le1/2$, a contradiction. Thus every such disk patch has positive edge weight. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 For the exchange-rectangle application, each side of a rectangle lying on a normal disk joins its two face sides. Those face sides lie in distinct tetrahedral faces, so the endpoints lie on distinct sides of that normal disk. Disjoint exchange surfaces give disjoint traces, which can be chosen transverse to the old sides and away from their vertices by finite PL displacement. Thus their cut patches satisfy precisely the trace hypothesis already used. The stated interior and boundary disk patches have respectively zero and one proper original-boundary arcs, so step 6.1 applies without any additional ambient-manifold hypothesis. [given, F2, step 6.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $p,q$ are coprime nonzero integers and $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, then the oriented torus knot $T(p,q)$ is ambient isotopic in $S^3$ to the standard unknot with its standard orientation.

## Statement references

[[def-coprime-torus-knot|The torus-knot parameterization on the standard Heegaard torus]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The standard unknot and oriented ambient-isotopy convention]]

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, Remark 5.1.1 and Corollary 5.2.3](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, and $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$.

[F1] [[def-coprime-torus-knot]] realizes $T(p,q)$ as the primitive slope curve on the standard Heegaard torus, with the two coordinate circles bounding disks on opposite sides.

[F2] [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]] fixes the standard unknot as the standard oriented unit circle and uses orientation-preserving ambient isotopy for knot equivalence.

[F3] [[thm-isotopy-extension]] extends a smooth isotopy of a compact embedded circle to an ambient isotopy of the surrounding smooth manifold.

[A1] Countable Choice is the hypothesis of the torus-knot, unknot, and isotopy-extension interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $p=\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. Write the original oriented curve as $K(s)=(r e^{2\pi i\varepsilon s},\sin\theta_0 e^{2\pi i q s})$, where $r=\cos\theta_0\in(0,1)$. Put $\theta_t=(1-t)\theta_0$ and define $H_t(s)=(\cos\theta_t e^{2\pi i\varepsilon s},\sin\theta_t e^{2\pi i q s})$. Each $H_t$ lies in $S^3$; its first coordinate is an injective circle parameterization because $|\varepsilon|=1$ and $\cos\theta_t>0$, and the family is smooth including $t=1$. It begins with the given orientation and ends at the core circle with orientation sign $\varepsilon$. [A1, F1, construct]

1.2 If $q=\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$, the path $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(\cos t\,z_1+\sin t\,z_2,-\sin t\,z_1+\cos t\,z_2)$, $0\le t\le\pi/2$, lies in $SO(4)$ and isotopes the identity to $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_2,-z_1)$. The image of the curve is $(\sin\theta_0 e^{2\pi i\varepsilon s},-r e^{2\pi i p s})$. Let $\eta_0\in(0,\pi/2)$ satisfy $\cos\eta_0=\sin\theta_0$ and $\sin\eta_0=r$, put $\eta_t=(1-t)\eta_0$, and use $H_t(s)=(\cos\eta_t e^{2\pi i\varepsilon s},-\sin\eta_t e^{2\pi i p s})$. Its first coordinate has winding $\varepsilon=\pm1$, so the family is a smooth isotopy through embeddings to the core with orientation sign $\varepsilon$. The initial coordinate rotation also preserves the knot orientation because it is an ambient isotopy. [A1, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], each smooth isotopy of the compact embedded circle constructed above extends to an ambient isotopy of $S^3$. Its terminal core is the standard unknot, with orientation sign $\varepsilon$. If $\varepsilon=-1$, write $z_j=x_j+i y_j$ and define $R_\tau(x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2)=(x_1,y_1\cos\tau+y_2\sin\tau,x_2,-y_1\sin\tau+y_2\cos\tau)$. This is a rotation in the $(y_1,y_2)$-plane, so $R_\tau$ is an orientation-preserving isometry of $S^3$ from the identity to $R_\pi(z_1,z_2)=(\overline z_1,\overline z_2)$. On the core, $R_\pi(e^{2\pi i s},0)=(e^{-2\pi i s},0)$, so this ambient isotopy reverses its orientation. In either sign case the original oriented curve is ambient isotopic to the standard oriented unknot. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct] ∎

    - title: "Frederic Weidling, Variational Source Conditions and Conditional Stability Estimates for Inverse Problems in PDEs, Theorem 2.20"
      url: "https://univerlag.uni-goettingen.de/bitstream/handle/3/isbn-978-3-86395-411-6/weidling.pdf?sequence=1"
    - title: "Barbara Kaltenbacher, Convergence rates under a range invariance condition with application to electrical impedance tomography, Lemma 2 and Theorem 3"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18704"
---

## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $D(F)\subseteq X$, and $F:D(F)\to Y$. Let $R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, let $x^\dagger\in D(F)\cap\operatorname{dom}R$, set $y=F(x^\dagger)$, and choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$. Fix $1\le p<\infty$, $0\le\beta<1$, and a level $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$. Let $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(t)>0$ for $t>0$, and assume the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad\left(x\in L_{R_0}:=\{x\in D(F):R(x)\le R_0\}\right),$$

where $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}$. Extend $-\psi$ by $+\infty$ on negative arguments and write $H(q):=(-\psi)^*(-q)=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$; assume $H(q)$ is finite for sufficiently large $q$ and $H(q)\to0$ as $q\to\infty$. For sufficiently small noise levels $\delta>0$ and data $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, define $J_\alpha^\delta(x):=p^{-1}\|F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha R(x)$. Suppose $\alpha=\alpha(\delta)>0$ tends to zero, $0\le\varepsilon_\delta\le C_\varepsilon\delta^p$, and $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in D(F)$ is an $\varepsilon_\delta$-minimizer, meaning $J_\alpha^\delta(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})\le\inf_{z\in D(F)}J_\alpha^\delta(z)+\varepsilon_\delta$. Set $c_p:=2^{1-p}/p$ and $\rho_\delta:=H(c_p/\alpha(\delta))$. Assume that for constants $c_-,c_+,C_H>0$ independent of $\delta$,

$$c_-\delta^p\le\alpha(\delta)\rho_\delta\le c_+\delta^p,\qquad H(c_p/(2\alpha(\delta)))\le C_H\rho_\delta$$

for all sufficiently small $\delta$. Then for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}\in L_{R_0}$ and

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon},x^\dagger)=O(\rho_\delta),\qquad \|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta).$$

If, in addition, $\psi(C_0\delta^p)=O(\rho_\delta)$ for a fixed $C_0$ such that $T_\delta:=\|F(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\le C_0\delta^p$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$, then $|R(x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon})-R(x^\dagger)|=O(\rho_\delta)$. If also $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)\ge c_R\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^s$ on $L_{R_0}$ for constants $c_R,s>0$, then $\|x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}-x^\dagger\|_X^s=O(\rho_\delta)$.

In the Hilbert special case, set $p=2$ and suppose $X,Y$ are real Hilbert spaces, $F:U\to Y$ has the real open-domain interface of a nonlinear forward map, $x^\dagger$ is an $x_0$-minimum-norm exact solution, $R(x)=\frac12\|x-x_0\|_X^2$, and the source inequality on a regularizer sublevel contained in $U$ is

$$\langle x^\dagger-x_0,x^\dagger-x\rangle_X\le\beta_1\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2+\beta_2\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y$$

with $0\le\beta_1<1$ and $\beta_2\ge0$. For exact global minimizers of the nonlinear Tikhonov functional with $\alpha(\delta)\asymp\delta$, the theorem gives $\|x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X=O(\sqrt\delta)$ and $\|F(x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta)$. The assertion is conditional on such a global minimizer being supplied; it does not assert existence or cover local numerical minima.

## Statement references

[Christian Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, equation (10.17) and Theorem 10.7](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

[Frederic Weidling, *Variational Source Conditions and Conditional Stability Estimates for Inverse Problems in PDEs*, Theorem 2.20](https://univerlag.uni-goettingen.de/bitstream/handle/3/isbn-978-3-86395-411-6/weidling.pdf?sequence=1)

[Barbara Kaltenbacher, *Convergence rates under a range invariance condition with application to electrical impedance tomography*, Lemma 2 and Theorem 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18704)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** All hypotheses in the Statement hold. Write $x_\delta:=x_\alpha^{\delta,\varepsilon}$, $T_\delta:=\|F(x_\delta)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p$, and $r_\delta:=\|F(x_\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y$.

[A1] $\delta>0$, $x_\delta$ is an $\varepsilon_\delta$-minimizer of $J_\alpha^\delta$, and $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, with $0\le\varepsilon_\delta\le C_\varepsilon\delta^p$.

[A2] The VSC holds on $L_{R_0}$ with the chosen $\xi^\dagger$, $\beta$, and $\psi$.

[A3] $\alpha\rho_\delta\asymp\delta^p$, $H(c_p/(2\alpha))\le C_H\rho_\delta$, $\alpha\to0$, and $\rho_\delta\to0$.

[A4] For the optional penalty conclusion, $\psi(C_0\delta^p)=O(\rho_\delta)$ for a fixed $C_0$ that bounds $T_\delta/\delta^p$ for small $\delta$.

[A5] For the optional norm conclusion, $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)\ge c_R\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^s$ on $L_{R_0}$ for constants $c_R,s>0$.

[A6] For the Hilbert conclusion, $R(x)=\frac12\|x-x_0\|_X^2$, $\xi^\dagger(h)=\langle x^\dagger-x_0,h\rangle_X$, the displayed $x_0$-minimum-norm VSC holds with $0\le\beta_1<1$ and $\beta_2\ge0$, and $\alpha\asymp\delta$.

[F1] [[def-ip-banach-convex-subgradient-and-dual-pairing]]: for $x\in\operatorname{dom}R$, $\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}$.

[F2] [[def-ip-bregman-distance]]: $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}$ and is nonnegative.

[F3] [[def-ip-variational-source-condition]]: $-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p)$ on $L_{R_0}$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-index-function-young-conjugate-bound]]: from $c_1r+c_2\alpha e\le d+\alpha\psi(C_3r)$, the stated conjugate bounds hold for $e$ and $r$.

[F5] [[def-ip-nonlinear-forward-map]]: in the Hilbert specialization $F:U\to Y$ is a real-Hilbert forward map on an open domain.

[F6] [[def-ip-x0-minimum-norm-solution]]: the Hilbert specialization assumes the exact solution globally minimizes distance to $x_0$ over its exact solution set.

[F7] [[def-ip-nonlinear-tikhonov-functional]]: for a datum $y\in Y$, $J_{\alpha,y,x_0}(x)=\frac12\|F(x)-y\|_Y^2+\frac\alpha2\|x-x_0\|_X^2$.

[F8] [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]: each Banach norm satisfies the triangle inequality.

[F9] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: a real Hilbert norm satisfies $\|v\|_X^2=\langle v,v\rangle_X$.

[F10] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle_X|\le\|u\|_X\|v\|_X$.

## Proof


1.1 Comparing the approximate-minimum inequality with the exact solution gives $J_\alpha^\delta(x_\delta)\le\delta^p/p+\alpha R(x^\dagger)+\varepsilon_\delta$. Since the data term is nonnegative, $R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger)\le\delta^p/(p\alpha)+\varepsilon_\delta/\alpha=O(\rho_\delta)$ by [A1] and [A3]. As $\rho_\delta\to0$ and $R_0>R(x^\dagger)$, $x_\delta\in L_{R_0}$ for sufficiently small $\delta$. [given, A1, A3, algebra]

1.2 By [F5]–[F7] the special case uses the open-domain Hilbert map, the stipulated global $x_0$-minimum-norm exact solution, and the existing quadratic nonlinear Tikhonov functional. Under [A6], define $\xi^\dagger(h):=\langle x^\dagger-x_0,h\rangle_X$. By [F10] this is a bounded real-linear functional; expansion using [F9] gives $R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}=\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2\ge0$, so [F1] gives $\xi^\dagger\in\partial R(x^\dagger)$ and [F2] gives $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)=\frac12\|x-x^\dagger\|_X^2$. Taking $\psi(s)=(\beta_2+1)\sqrt{s}$, the stated Hilbert source inequality implies the VSC with $p=2$. [A6, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F9, F10, algebra]

2.1 By [F8], $T_\delta^{1/p}\le r_\delta+\delta$. For $p=1$, $(u+v)^p=u^p+v^p$; for $p>1$, $t\mapsto t^p$ is continuous at zero and has nonnegative second derivative $p(p-1)t^{p-2}$ on $(0,\infty)$, hence is convex on $[0,\infty)$, and its defining convexity inequality at the midpoint gives $(u+v)^p\le2^{p-1}(u^p+v^p)$. Taking $u=r_\delta$, $v=\delta$ yields $T_\delta\le2^{p-1}(r_\delta^p+\delta^p)$ and thus $r_\delta^p/p\ge c_pT_\delta-\delta^p/p$. Substituting into the comparison inequality from 1.1 gives $c_pT_\delta+\alpha(R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger))\le2\delta^p/p+\varepsilon_\delta$. [A1, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For $B:=\beta_2+1>0$, the conjugate is $H(q)=\sup_{u\ge0}(Bu-qu^2)=B^2/(4q)$, by completing the square. With $p=2$, $c_p=1/4$, so $\alpha H(c_p/\alpha)=B^2\alpha^2\asymp\delta^2$ and $\rho_\delta=H(c_p/\alpha)=B^2\alpha\asymp\delta$ when $\alpha\asymp\delta$. The scale comparability in [A3] also holds because $H(c_p/(2\alpha))=2H(c_p/\alpha)$. [A3, A6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By [F2] and [F3], $R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger)=D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)+\langle\xi^\dagger,x_\delta-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\ge(1-\beta)D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)-\psi(T_\delta)$. Combining this with the objective comparison in step 2.1 gives $c_pT_\delta+\alpha(1-\beta)D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)\le d_\delta+\alpha\psi(T_\delta)$, where $d_\delta:=2\delta^p/p+\varepsilon_\delta$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F4] with $c_1=c_p$, $c_2=1-\beta$, $C_3=1$, $r=T_\delta$, $e=D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)$, and $d=d_\delta$. It follows that $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)\le\frac1{1-\beta}\left(\frac{d_\delta}{\alpha}+\rho_\delta\right)$ and $T_\delta\le\frac2{c_p}\left(d_\delta+\alpha H(c_p/(2\alpha))\right)$. [F4, step 3.1]

5.1 From [A1] and [A3], $d_\delta=O(\delta^p)$, $d_\delta/\alpha=O(\rho_\delta)$, and $d_\delta+\alpha H(c_p/(2\alpha))=O(\delta^p)$. Thus $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x_\delta,x^\dagger)=O(\rho_\delta)$ and $T_\delta=O(\delta^p)$. The triangle inequality gives $r_\delta\le T_\delta^{1/p}+\delta$, so the noisy-data residual is $O(\delta)$. [A1, A3, F8, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For the penalty rate, [F2]–[F3] give $R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger)\ge-\psi(T_\delta)$, while step 1.1 supplies its upper bound. If [A4] holds for a fixed $C_0$ bounding $T_\delta/\delta^p$, then $|R(x_\delta)-R(x^\dagger)|=O(\rho_\delta)$. If [A5] also holds, the Bregman bound in step 5.1 gives $\|x_\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^s=O(\rho_\delta)$. [A4, A5, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 5.1]

7.1 Applying the Bregman bound from step 5.1 and the exact Bregman identity from step 1.2 gives $\|x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2=O(\delta)$ and $\|F(x_{\alpha(\delta)}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=O(\delta)$, hence the asserted $O(\sqrt\delta)$ solution error and $O(\delta)$ residual. [A6, step 5.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume AC. The input is either (a) a based $r$-component string-link diagram
with its endpoint collars and product-tube parallels equal to the diagram's
blackboard push-offs, or (b) a based finite regular
diagram of a closed $r$-component labeled oriented link with chosen product
tubes, one initial strand on each component, and a common basepoint and access
paths. The finite input records its compatible common-upper-collar reference accesses. In the compatible branch the actual accesses are these, up to a common base-path change, and the parallels are the blackboard parallels already specified. In the arbitrary-choice branch it additionally records finite words in the compatible strand meridians for each access difference $g_e$, the parallel endpoint differences $h_{0,j},h_{1,j}$, and its relative meridian winding $k_j$. These are word certificates for the chosen paths, part of the supplied based-word data; no evaluation of an unencoded smooth path is claimed. In closed-link mode the preferred longitude uses its own recorded access $h_j$, which may differ from the initial-meridian access $g_j$. Arbitrary parallels are allowed in this branch, with the recorded $k_j$. The input also includes a maximum index length $N\geq2$. The output is
the integer coefficients $\mu_\tau(I)$ in string-link mode, or the based
coefficients $\mu_L^b(I)$, their lower indeterminacy data $\Delta_I^b$, and
residues $\bar\mu_L^b(I)$ in closed-link mode, for every index sequence $I$
with $2\leq |I|\leq N$.

Set $d=N-1$ and work in the truncated noncommutative ring
$$R_d=\mathbb Z\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle/\mathfrak m^{d+1},$$
where $\mathfrak m$ is the ideal generated by the letters. Carry out the
following finite procedure.

1. Verify the finite crossing, orientation, over/under, and component data. If
   a closed-link component has no underpassing point, choose a crossing-free
   disk meeting only a short arc of that component and avoiding its chosen
   initial meridian point. Insert a small type-I curl there by the supported
   disk isotopy and record the resulting based diagram. Transport the
   basepoint, meridian circles, access paths, product tubes, parallels, and all
   supplied access, endpoint, and longitude word certificates through this
   isotopy. Before the curl, the component is one cyclic strand; the new
   underpass cuts it into one interval strand containing the chosen initial
   point. Identify that interval's reference meridian symbol with the
   transported old symbol. Every other strand is carried bijectively by the
   isotopy, with its reference symbol identified in the same way. In the finite
   certificates, apply this symbol substitution to every word; no unencoded
   path evaluation or additional certificate is required. Give every
   resulting strand $a$ the component label $j(a)$.

2. First compute in the compatible reference root symbols $x_j$, irrespective of the actual access choices. For every strand $a$, initialize its meridian series by
   $Y_a^{(1)}=1+X_{j(a)}$. For each degree $\ell=2,\ldots,d$, copy every
   $Y_a^{(\ell-1)}$ into the constant and lower-degree part of
   $Y_a^{(\ell)}$, with new degree-$\ell$ terms initially zero, and reset each
   chosen root strand to $1+X_j$. Then do one pass over each component in its
   oriented order. In closed-link mode start at the chosen initial strand and
   omit the final undercrossing back to that strand; in string-link mode start
   at the bottom endpoint and use every undercrossing through to the top
   endpoint. At an undercrossing with over-strand $o$ and source and target
   under-arcs $s,t$, use the already available $Y_o^{(\ell-1)}$ and the
   current $Y_s^{(\ell)}$ to set
   $$Y_t^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{trunc}_{\ell}\bigl((Y_o^{(\ell-1)})^{-1} Y_s^{(\ell)}Y_o^{(\ell-1)}\bigr)$$
   when the traversal is source-to-target, and set
   $$Y_s^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{trunc}_{\ell}\bigl(Y_o^{(\ell-1)} Y_t^{(\ell)}(Y_o^{(\ell-1)})^{-1}\bigr)$$
   when it is target-to-source. Here $\operatorname{trunc}_{\ell}$ discards
   monomials of degree greater than $\ell$, and every inverse is the finite
   geometric series in the nilpotent ideal of $R_d$.

3. For each component $j$, traverse its undercrossings in order and form
   $W_j=\prod_c (Y_{o(c)}^{(d)})^{\epsilon_c}$, where the factors are in
   traversal order and $\epsilon_c=+1$ for source-to-target and $-1$ for
   target-to-source. In string-link mode set $\Lambda_j=W_j$. In closed-link
   mode set
   $$\Lambda_j=(1+X_j)^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j,$$
   where $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is the sum of the determinant signs at
   self-crossings of component $j$.

4. In the arbitrary-choice branch first use the strand-symbol identification of step 1, then evaluate each supplied transport word by the strand series from step 2. Write $G_e$ for the resulting unit series, and $H_{0,j},H_{1,j}$ for the endpoint transport series. In string-link mode replace the compatible $\Lambda_j=W_j$ by
   $$H_{0,j}(1+X_j)^{k_j}W_jH_{1,j}^{-1}.$$
   In closed-link mode replace the compatible preferred series by
   $$H_j(1+X_j)^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_jH_j^{-1},$$
   where $H_j=H_{0,j}=H_{1,j}$ is the actual longitude access difference, independently of the initial-meridian difference $G_j$. The arbitrary parallel winding cancels in the preferred correction. All powers and inverses are finite truncated operations. To express this result in the actual component-meridian symbols, form
   $$G_j(1+X_j)G_j^{-1}=1+X_j+R_j(X),\qquad \deg R_j\ge2.$$
   With new letters $V_j$, initialize $Z_j^{(1)}=V_j$ and iterate
   $$Z_j^{(s+1)}=\operatorname{trunc}_d\bigl(V_j-R_j(Z^{(s)})\bigr),\qquad 1\le s<d.$$
   Substitute $X_j=Z_j^{(d)}(V)$ in the corrected longitude series. This is its expansion in the chosen actual meridians. For the compatible branch this step is the identity. Rename the final letters $V_j$ as $X_j$.

5. For every $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $1\leq k\leq d$, read the coefficient
   of $X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $\Lambda_j$. In string-link mode return this
   integer. In closed-link mode, also compute the gcd of the coefficients for
   all proper subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$ of lengths at least
   two, with empty gcd equal to zero, and return the corresponding residue
   class.

All scans, including the supplied transport words and the $d-1$ inverse-substitution iterations, are over finite crossing, strand, degree, and index sets. The
procedure makes no polynomial-time claim. If a finite-input validation fails,
return `invalid-input`.

## Definition references

[[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram|Finite regular diagrams and crossing data]]

[[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links|Truncated noncommutative ring and Magnus expansion]]

[[lem-link-wirtinger-local-meridian-conjugacy|Source-to-target meridian substitutions]]

[[lem-link-peripheral-longitude-word-from-diagram|Peripheral longitude word and self-writhe correction]]

[[def-milnor-integer-and-residue-invariants|Integer coefficients and based residues]]

## Remarks

The per-degree passes use over-strand series only through degree $\ell-1$:
their degree-$\ell$ terms cancel against the constant term of the conjugated
meridian. The output records the based residue data; its independence of
closed-link basing is the separate theorem on Milnor invariants.
