## Statement

Assume AC. Let $L$ be a nonempty labeled oriented link in $S^3$, let
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ have length at least two, and let $b,b'$ be any two
based meridian-longitude word systems used in the preceding definition. Then
the based residue candidates $\bar\mu_L^b(I)$ and $\bar\mu_L^{b'}(I)$ agree
under the canonical identification of their residue groups. If $L$ and $L'$ are
related by a finite sequence of self-crossing changes, the same residue is
preserved whenever the entries of $I$ are pairwise distinct. No invariance for
repeated-index sequences under self-crossing changes is asserted.

## Statement references

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§3–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

[Stees, §2.5](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/54c7d68f-d982-4e1f-9550-e54140ada5ea/content)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the closed-link peripheral system, and finite based word-lift data through the length of $I$.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] Integer coefficients, based residue candidates, and the gcd of proper subsequences and their cyclic permutations are defined by the preceding definition. [[def-milnor-integer-and-residue-invariants]]

[F2] Conjugating one longitude changes a degree-$m$ coefficient by an integer combination of coefficients on proper contiguous subwords. [[lem-magnus-conjugation-coefficients-use-shorter-subwords]]

[F3] The side-based meridian relation at a crossing is fixed by the local crossing chart. [[lem-link-wirtinger-local-meridian-conjugacy]]

[F4] Closed-link meridians lift to every finite nilpotent quotient, and the link group is computed by the crossing relations. [[lem-link-nilpotent-quotient-generated-by-component-meridians]], [[thm-link-wirtinger-presentation-correctness]]

[F5] The finite nilpotent peripheral presentation has kernel normally generated by $\Gamma_qF$ and $[x_a,l_{a,q}]$, for coherent diagram longitude words. Adding commutators of conjugate component meridians gives exactly the corresponding reduced-group quotient. [[lem-link-nilpotent-peripheral-presentation-from-diagram]]

[F6] The Magnus expansion of $\Gamma_qF$ is $1$ modulo degree $q$. [[lem-magnus-commutator-degree-and-truncation]]

[F7] Lower-central commutators add weights and induce biadditive pairings on graded layers. [[lem-hall-malcev-lower-central-commutators-add-weights]]

## Proof

**Given:** The link, finite peripheral word systems, and $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$; write $w=i_1\cdots i_k$.

1.1 Choose a finite regular diagram of the link. If a component has no underpass, insert a small type-I curl on a short arc in a ball meeting no other component, as in the local disk-push construction of the link-presentation theorem in [F4]. There are finitely many components, so the balls may be chosen disjoint and away from the common basepoint; the supported ambient isotopies carry the original chosen tubes, positive meridians, preferred longitudes and all access paths to their images. On each peripheral torus this transport preserves degree one and zero self-meridian coordinate. The induced based group isomorphism carries every original meridian to its transported meridian, so each original finite free word remains literally the same word and is still a lift of the corresponding transported longitude in every finite nilpotent quotient. This reduction imposes no upper-basing or coherence condition on the original word systems. The augmented diagram now has an underpass on every component, including originally crossingless components; its canonical upper basing will be compared with arbitrary transported basings and lifts by the subsequent variable-substitution and coefficient-ideal argument. First use the geometric root meridians and coherent longitude words $l_a$ from [F5], through degree $k$. For any index sequence $J$, write $c(J)$ for the corresponding coefficient of these words. Let $D_I$ be the ideal of $\mathbb Z$ generated by $c(J)$ for all proper subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$ of length at least two. Its nonnegative generator is the gcd in [F1]. Work in the ring $R_I$ with finitely many surviving monomials, obtained from $(\mathbb Z/D_I)\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle$ by setting to zero every monomial whose index word is not a subsequence of $w$. The discarded words span a two-sided ideal: adjoining letters cannot turn a word that is not a subsequence into one that is. Thus multiplication and inversion of series with constant term $1$ are well-defined finite operations. Occurrences, including repeated indices, are retained in their original order; no assumption of distinct indices is used here. [A1, F1, F4, F5, given, construct]

1.2 For a self-crossing change on component $a$, quotient the diagram group by the normal closure of all commutators of two conjugates of its meridian, doing this for every component. These quotients on the two sides of the crossing change have identical based presentations. To see this locally, cut both branches into incoming and outgoing arc symbols. The branch that is over has equal incoming and outgoing symbols. On the under-branch the Wirtinger equation conjugates its incoming meridian by the over-meridian; both are conjugates of the same component meridian and commute in this quotient, so its outgoing symbol also equals its incoming symbol. Switching the crossing interchanges which branch uses which argument and leaves precisely the same two equalities. All other crossing relations, and root paths chosen outside this small ball, are unchanged. Thus the identification preserves the component meridians, with no assertion of an isomorphism of the original unreduced groups. [F3, F4, F5, given, construct]

2.1 The coefficient of any surviving word in $E([x_a,l_a])-1$ is zero in $R_I$. Indeed put $E(l_a)=1+L_a$. The exact identity is $$E([x_a,l_a])-1=(X_aL_a-L_aX_a)(1+X_a)^{-1}(1+L_a)^{-1}.$$ Every summand contributing to a surviving word therefore contains one distinguished occurrence of $a$ and a nonempty block from $L_a$, as well as possibly other blocks. If that block has index word $B$, its coefficient is $c(Ba)$. The selected block and the distinguished $a$ occupy disjoint positions in a subsequence of $w$; starting just after that occurrence of $a$ and reading cyclically shows that $Ba$ is a subsequence of a cyclic permutation of $I$. It is proper, since its length is at most $k<|I|$. Hence $c(Ba)\in D_I$, and the whole summand vanishes. The same argument applies if $(1+L_a)^{-1}$ is expanded elsewhere in the expression; the distinguished block can always be taken from the displayed first factor. This proves the assertion for each relator, its inverse, conjugates and finite products. Also $E(\Gamma_{k+1}F)=1$ through degree $k$ by [F6]. Therefore [F5] makes the coefficient of $X_w$ independent modulo $D_I$ of every lift of a fixed longitude in $G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. [F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Under that reduced-group identification, the longitude of a component different from $a$ is unchanged: its traversal has no undercrossing factor in the altered ball, and its other arc meridians have the common images in step 1.2. For component $a$, the local factor lost or gained is a conjugate of its own meridian. It disappears on further quotienting by the normal subgroup generated by that meridian. The self-writhe normalization also differs by a power of this same meridian, so the preferred longitudes agree in this further quotient. These statements follow from the actual ordered undercrossing product, not solely from the meridian crossing relation. [F3, F5, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Consider a different basing. Each new meridian is a conjugate of the old one, and each new longitude is also a conjugate of the old degree-one zero-self-meridian curve. The conjugating loops may be different if the two accesses were chosen independently; retain both recorded loops. Lift the finitely many conjugating loops to $F/\Gamma_{k+1}F$ by [F4]. The resulting change of root variables is $\phi(x_a)=u_a^{-1}x_au_a$. This is an automorphism of the finite nilpotent free quotient. It is the identity on degree one, hence on every lower-central graded layer, whose commutators are generated by the degree-one generators by [F7]. To construct a preimage, correct a word successively in $\Gamma_s/\Gamma_{s+1}$ for $s=1,\ldots,k$; each correction has the prescribed image because the graded map is the identity. For injectivity, an element in the kernel is successively in $\Gamma_2,\ldots,\Gamma_{k+1}=1$. Its inverse is again a substitution by conjugates of the same respective generators. Thus the new longitude words are obtained by inverse variable substitution, their own independently recorded longitude conjugations, and elements of the transformed canonical kernel described in [F5]. No assertion that an independently based new meridian and longitude commute is needed; [F5] describes the reference presentation before these separate output conjugations. [F4, F5, F7, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 Now suppose the entries of $I$ are distinct. In the ring $R_I$ of step 1.1 every monomial containing an index twice is zero. For any word $u$, every term of $E(u^{-1}x_bu)-1$ contains $b$. Products of two such positive-degree expressions are therefore zero when both refer to $b$, and their units commute. The additional reduced-group relators $[u^{-1}x_bu,v^{-1}x_bv]$ are consequently annihilated. By [F5], the kernel of the map to the reduced nilpotent group consists exactly of these additional relators, the peripheral commutators already annihilated in step 2.1, and $\Gamma_{k+1}F$. If the changed component is $j$, the further normal-meridian subgroup in step 2.2 is annihilated too, since $j$ does not occur in $w$. Thus the two longitude coefficients agree modulo $D_I$. If the changed component is not $j$, their equality in the reduced group from step 2.2 already gives this conclusion. [F5, F6, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 In a variable substitution of this kind, $X_a$ is replaced by $X_a$ plus terms of degree at least two, every one of which contains an occurrence of $a$: this follows by expanding $E(u_a)^{-1}(1+X_a)E(u_a)-1$. A coefficient of $X_w$ in the substituted longitude therefore differs from its old coefficient only by integer multiples of $c(Bj)$ for proper subsequences $B$ of $w$. These are generators of $D_I$. A longitude conjugation has the same property by direct multiplication, or by [F2]: its constant term cancels and every correction uses a shorter longitude coefficient. The transformed kernel is also annihilated. In the argument of step 2.1, substituting conjugates preserves the distinguished occurrence of each original variable, so the selected $B$ and the distinguished $a$ still form a proper cyclic subsequence of $I$. Hence every permitted basing and lift change preserves the target coefficient modulo the ideal of the old proper coefficients. [F2, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 These assertions also identify the modulus exactly, including when it is zero. Induct on index length. At length two there are no lower coefficients; commutator kernels and all conjugation corrections start in degree two, so the degree-one coefficients agree as integers. For a longer $I$, apply the induction hypothesis to every proper cyclic subsequence $J$ of $I$. It says that its coefficient changes by an integer combination of coefficients on proper cyclic subsequences of $J$, all of which are proper cyclic subsequences of $I$. Order these finitely many sequences by length. The new coefficients thus lie in the ideal of the old proper coefficients. Conversely solve the same triangular relations in increasing length to express each old coefficient in the ideal of the new proper coefficients. The two ideals, their nonnegative gcd generators, and hence their residue groups are equal. Step 3.1 then proves equality of the target residues. Independent choices of word lifts at the separate finite degrees in [F1] are covered by step 2.1 and this same triangular argument; no unmentioned coherence hypothesis is imposed on those inputs. [F1, step 2.1, step 4.1, induction, algebra]

6.1 Induct again on the distinct index length. Length-two coefficients are preserved by step 3.2 with zero lower ideal. For larger $I$, apply the lower-length conclusions to its proper cyclic subsequences. The triangular ideal argument of step 5.1 shows that the old and new proper-coefficient ideals are equal; step 3.2 therefore gives equality in the canonically identical residue group. Step 4.1 permits arbitrary basings and finite word lifts at either endpoint. Composing along the stipulated finite sequence proves the self-crossing assertion. For repeated indices the square-zero argument in step 3.2 is unavailable, and no such assertion has been made. This proves both claims with the inherited AC and no extra choice principle. [A1, F1, step 5.1, step 3.2, induction, algebra] ∎

id: lem-von-neumann-inertia-and-coisotropic-reduction
kind: lemma
title: Von Neumann inertia, dense congruences, and coisotropic reduction
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19

  Neumann module and spectral suppliers.
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: Wolfgang Lück and Thomas Schick, Various L2-signatures and a topological
        L2-signature theorem
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209161
      locator: Section 3, finite Hilbert-module signatures; dense-form and isotropic
        calculations are supplied explicitly below.
---

## Statement

Work under the standing AC convention for finite von Neumann modules. Let $A=\mathcal N G$ with its finite trace, and let all Hilbert modules below be ranges of projections on finite sums of $\ell^2(G)$. For a bounded self-adjoint module operator $J$ define its positive and negative inertia by the traces of $\mathbf1_{(0,\infty)}(J)$ and $\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0)}(J)$, and its signature by their difference. Each inertia is the supremum of dimensions of closed module subspaces on which the form $\langle Jx,x\rangle$ is strictly positive or strictly negative, respectively. If $T:H_0\to H_1$ is bounded, injective and has dense image, then $T^*JT$ and $J$ have the same inertia. If $J$ is invertible, $V\subseteq H$ is closed, and $V^{\perp_J}\subseteq V$, then the form on $H$ and its restriction to $V$ have equal signatures. Kernels contribute zero. These statements include ordinary real signatures by complexification and the trivial-group trace.

## Statement references

[[lem-finite-von-neumann-module-dimension-and-dense-quotients]]

[Lück–Schick, Section 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209161)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite projection modules, their bounded module maps and self-adjoint forms in the Statement.

[F1] Matrix spectral projections, polar rank-nullity, trace faithfulness and normality, and Hilbert-closed submodule projections have the properties proved in the finite-module lemma. [[lem-finite-von-neumann-module-dimension-and-dense-quotients]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement.

1.1 The positive spectral subspace of $J$ is strictly positive for its quadratic form: integrating the positive spectral variable gives a positive number for every nonzero vector there. If a closed module subspace $U$ is strictly positive, its projection into that positive spectral subspace is injective, because a vector with no positive spectral part has nonpositive quadratic form. Polar rank-nullity in [F1] therefore bounds $\dim_A U$ by the trace of the positive spectral projection. This proves the positive characterization, and applying it to $-J$ proves the negative one. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For two projections $p,q$ on a common finite module, rank-nullity for $(I-q):pH\to(I-q)H$ gives $\tau(p\wedge q)\ge\tau(p)-\tau(I-q)$; its kernel is exactly their closed range intersection. If $T$ is injective with dense image, let $q_\varepsilon=\mathbf1_{[\varepsilon,\infty)}(TT^*)$. The traces $\tau(q_\varepsilon)$ tend to $\dim_A H_1$ by [F1], and $q_\varepsilon H_1$ lies in the image of $T$ with a bounded module inverse on it. Intersect this range with a positive spectral subspace $p_\delta H_1=\mathbf1_{[\delta,\infty)}(J)H_1$. Its trace tends to $\tau(p_\delta)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ by the intersection inequality. Pulling it back by the bounded inverse of $T$ gives a closed positive subspace for $T^*JT$ of the same dimension. Step 1.1 and then $\delta\downarrow0$ show that the positive inertia of $T^*JT$ is at least that of $J$. Conversely, on every closed positive subspace for $T^*JT$, project $T$ into the positive spectral subspace of $J$; this map is injective, giving the reverse inequality by [F1]. Repeat with $-J$. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Assume $J$ is invertible and put $L=V^{\perp_J}\subseteq V$, $K=V\cap L^\perp$ and $Q=V^\perp$, where unmarked orthogonals use the underlying Hilbert product. These are closed module subspaces and $H=L\oplus K\oplus Q$. The identity $L=J^{-1}Q$ says that $J|_L:L\to Q$ is a bounded isomorphism. In this decomposition the matrix of $J$ is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0&B\\0&C&E\\B^*&E^*&F\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, where $B^*:L\to Q$ is invertible. Replace $k\in K$ by $k-(B^*)^{-1}E^*k$. This bounded invertible triangular change makes $K$ orthogonal, for the form, to both $L$ and $Q$, leaving its form $C$ unchanged. In the remaining $L\oplus Q$ block, replace $l$ by $l-\tfrac12(B^*)^{-1}Fq$ to obtain $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&B\\B^*&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Conjugation by $\operatorname{diag}(I_L,-I_Q)$ negates this last form; its positive and negative spectral projections consequently have the same trace, so its signature is zero. Step 2.1 applies to the bounded invertible changes just used, proving that the original signature is the signature of $C$. [F1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The restriction of the form to $V=L\oplus K$ is $0\oplus C$, so it too has signature equal to that of $C$. This proves coisotropic reduction. For a map with a kernel, its pullback form vanishes on that kernel and has no cross terms with it; discard the kernel and use step 2.1 on its orthogonal complement whenever the remaining image is dense. For the trivial group, projection traces are ordinary complex dimensions; complexifying a real symmetric form preserves its real positive and negative dimensions by diagonalizing the finite real form. Thus the ordinary case is included. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf"
      locator: "Theorem 1.9 and its uniqueness proof, printed pp.14, 21–23"
---

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $M=E_{P(K)}$ be a satellite knot exterior with companion torus $T_c$. Suppose the pattern hypotheses of the essential-companion-torus lemma hold, both components of $M$ cut along $T_c$ are atoroidal or Seifert-fibered, and $M$ itself is neither atoroidal nor Seifert-fibered. Then the inclusion-minimal JSJ system of $M$ consists of a torus ambient isotopic to $T_c$. Cutting along that torus identifies the companion exterior $E_K$ as the component on the outside of the embedded companion solid torus. No conclusion is made for an essential companion torus that is absorbed into a Seifert-fibered union.

## Statement references

[Ryan Budney, *JSJ-decompositions of knot and link complements in the 3-sphere*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0506523)

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Theorem 1.9](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a satellite knot exterior $M$, its companion torus $T_c$, the stated pattern hypotheses, and the two pieces obtained by cutting along $T_c$.

[A1] Full AC is the assertion that every set-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], Definition).

[F1] The pattern and companion torus are defined in [[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number]].

[F2] Under the nontrivial companion and nonproduct pattern hypotheses, $T_c$ is essential ([[lem-satellite-torus-is-essential]], Statement).

[F3] A finite family of incompressible tori is a JSJ system when cutting along it gives only atoroidal or Seifert-fibered pieces; inclusion-minimality excludes every proper subfamily ([[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]], Definition).

[F4] For a compact knot exterior, an inclusion-minimal JSJ system is unique up to ambient isotopy ([[thm-jsj-decomposition-of-knot-exteriors]], Statement).

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], $T_c$ is incompressible. The hypothesis on the two cut components and [F3] show that the singleton family $\{T_c\}$ is a JSJ system. The empty family is not a JSJ system because its sole cut component is $M$, which by hypothesis is neither atoroidal nor Seifert-fibered. Thus $\{T_c\}$ is inclusion-minimal. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Apply [F4] to the minimal system $\{T_c\}$. It follows that the unique minimal system consists of one torus ambient isotopic to $T_c$. The decomposition of the satellite exterior in [F1] shows that the side inside the companion solid torus is the pattern exterior and the outside side is exactly $E_K$. The ambient isotopy supplied by [F4] is jointly smooth and starts at the identity. Apply its final diffeomorphism to the cut decomposition: it carries the original outside component $E_K$ to the corresponding outside component for the isotopic torus. The boundary of $M$ remains on the pattern side, so the component labels are unambiguous. [F1, F4, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Example

Let $X=G=S^2$ be the unit round sphere with its standard real-analytic structure, and give $Z$ the density induced by the product round metric. Let
$$
Z=\{(n,x)\in S^2\times S^2:n\cdot x=0\},
$$
so $n\in G$ labels the oriented great circle $C_n=\{x\in X:n\cdot x=0\}$. The transform uses the analytic density induced on $Z$ and the constant analytic weight $1$. Then $G\leftarrow Z\to X$ is an analytic double fibration, and the geodesic from $x$ to its antipode $-x$ along $C_n$ has conjugate endpoints. Moreover, for every $(n,x)\in Z$, the nonzero data covector $x^\flat\in T_n^*G$ is paired by the canonical relation with both $(x,-n^\flat)$ and $(-x,n^\flat)$. Thus the left projection of the canonical relation is not injective, so the Bolker condition fails globally.

## Example references

[[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform|Analytic double fibration and its proper-support condition]]

[[def-ip-bolker-condition|Global Bolker injectivity]]

[[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel|Incidence conormal formula]]

[[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold|Round metric]]

[[def-geodesic-variation|Geodesic variations]]

[[def-jacobi-field|Jacobi equation]]

[[def-conjugate-points-along-a-geodesic-and-their-multiplicity|Conjugate endpoints]]

[[ex-great-circles-as-round-sphere-geodesics|Great-circle geodesics]]

[[thm-variation-field-of-a-geodesic-variation-is-a-jacobi-field|Variation fields are Jacobi]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The unit round sphere, the incidence hypersurface $Z$, and the round arclength density on its great-circle fibers.

[F1] [[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform]]: both incidence projections must be analytic submersions, and the required support condition is properness over compact object sets.

[F2] [[def-ip-bolker-condition]]: Bolker requires the left cotangent projection to be globally injective.

[F3] [[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel]]: for a defining function $F$, the conormal bundle is generated by $dF$ and the relation uses $(\eta,-\xi)$.

[F4] [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]: the unit round metric identifies tangent vectors and cotangent vectors by $v\mapsto v^\flat$.

[F5] [[ex-sphere-as-a-regular-level-set]]: $T_xS^2=x^\perp$ for every $x\in S^2$.

[F6] [[thm-real-analytic-inverse-and-implicit-function-theorems]]: a regular zero of a real-analytic scalar function is locally an analytic graph.

[F7] [[def-geodesic-variation]]: a smooth family whose parameter curves are affinely parametrized geodesics is a geodesic variation.

[F8] [[def-jacobi-field]]: a Jacobi field satisfies $D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$.

[F9] [[def-conjugate-points-along-a-geodesic-and-their-multiplicity]]: endpoints are conjugate when a nonzero Jacobi field vanishes at both ends.

[F10] [[ex-great-circles-as-round-sphere-geodesics]]: constant-speed great-circle parametrizations are geodesics of the round sphere.

[F11] [[thm-variation-field-of-a-geodesic-variation-is-a-jacobi-field]]: the variation field of a smooth geodesic variation is Jacobi; this implication uses no choice axiom.

## Proof

**Given:** The incidence $Z$ and its round geometry.

1.1 Put $F(n,x)=n\cdot x$ on $S^2\times S^2$. At a point with $F=0$, the vector $x$ lies in $T_nS^2$ by [F5], and the tangent variation $(\dot n,\dot x)=(x,0)$ satisfies $dF(\dot n,\dot x)=x\cdot x=1$. Thus $dF\ne0$; [F6] makes $Z=F^{-1}(0)$ an analytic hypersurface of dimension $3$ in the $4$-dimensional product. [F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 A tangent vector to $Z$ satisfies $x\cdot\dot n+n\cdot\dot x=0$. Given any $\dot n\in T_nS^2$, set $\dot x=-(x\cdot\dot n)n$; then $\dot x\in T_xS^2$ by [F5], and the tangent equation holds. Hence $\pi_G$ is a submersion. Given any $\dot x\in T_xS^2$, set $\dot n=-(n\cdot\dot x)x$; the same calculation proves $\pi_X$ is a submersion. Both maps are analytic restrictions of product projections. Since $Z$ is compact, $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. The density induced by the positive-definite analytic product round metric has strictly positive analytic coefficient in every local incidence chart. The dimensions satisfy $4>3>2\ge2$, so [F1] applies. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

2.2 The defining differential on tangent vectors to the product is $dF=(x^\flat,n^\flat)$ by the metric identification [F4]. Therefore by [F3] the relation at $(n,x)$ consists of $ (n,\eta;x,\xi)=(n,\tau x^\flat;x,-\tau n^\flat),\qquad \tau\ne0. $ At the antipodal point $-x$, choose multiplier $-\tau$. Its data covector is $(-\tau)(-x)^\flat=\tau x^\flat$, the same as at $x$, while the object point changes from $x$ to $-x$. Both are nonzero relation points. Hence the left projection is not injective, and [F2] implies failure of global Bolker. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $v=n\times x$, a unit tangent vector at $x$. For $s$ near zero put $n_s=\cos(s)n+\sin(s)v$, $v_s=n_s\times x$, and $ \gamma_s(t)=\cos(t)x+\sin(t)v_s,\qquad 0\le t\le\pi. $ Each $n_s$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $x$, and $v_s$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $x$; hence $\gamma_s$ parametrizes a great circle at unit speed and is a geodesic by [F10]. Thus [F7] makes this a geodesic variation. Its endpoints are fixed: $\gamma_s(0)=x$ and $\gamma_s(\pi)=-x$. Differentiating in $s$ at zero gives $ J(t)=\left.\partial_s\gamma_s(t)\right|_{s=0} =\sin(t)(v\times x)=-\sin(t)n, $ because $(n\times x)\times x=-n$ when $n\cdot x=0$ and $|x|=1$. By [F11] this field is Jacobi and hence satisfies the Jacobi equation in [F8]. It is nonzero for $0<t<\pi$ and vanishes at both endpoints, so [F9] makes the endpoints conjugate. The proof uses no choice axiom; the sphere has no boundary, so this example lies outside the simple-surface hypotheses. [F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, given, algebra] ∎

## Geometric diagram

The great circle is drawn as a circle in its plane, with $n$ normal to the plane and $x,-x$ antipodal. At $n$, the data covector is represented by the same tangent vector $x$ for both relation points; the object covectors at the antipodes are opposite. The calculation in step 2.1, rather than the schematic, establishes noninjectivity.

  \fill (-1.35,0) circle (0.05) node[left] {$-x$};
  \draw[->,thick] (0,0) -- (0,1.45) node[above] {$n$};
  \draw[->,blue,thick] (0,1.45) -- (0.8,1.45) node[right] {$\eta=x^\flat$};
  \draw[->,red,thick] (1.35,0) -- (1.35,-0.75) node[below] {$\xi=-n^\flat$};
  \draw[->,red,thick] (-1.35,0) -- (-1.35,0.75) node[above] {$\xi'=n^\flat$};
  \node at (0,-1.65) {$C_n$};

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The subfield of $\mathbb C$ fixed by every field automorphism $\sigma:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ with $\sigma(q)=q$ for all $q\in\mathbb Q$ is exactly $\mathbb Q$.

## Statement references

[Milne, *Fields and Galois Theory*, §§3 and 9](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf)

[The Stacks Project, Section 9.26, Lemma 9.26.3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/030F)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the field inclusion $\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb C$, and an element $z\in\mathbb C$.

[F1] Under full AC, every algebraically independent subset extends to a maximal algebraically independent set, and a maximal set is a transcendence basis ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[lem-maximal-algebraically-independent-subset-is-a-transcendence-basis]]).

[F2] The algebraic numbers $\overline{\mathbb Q}=\{z\in\mathbb C:z\text{ is algebraic over }\mathbb Q\}$ form an algebraically closed algebraic extension of $\mathbb Q$: roots exist in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-the-complex-numbers-are-algebraically-closed]]) and remain algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ by transitivity ([[thm-transitivity-of-algebraicity]]).

[F3] Full AC is equivalent over ZF to Zorn's lemma ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[cor-ac-iff-zorn]]).

## Proof

1.1 Let $F\subset\Omega$ be a field extension with $\Omega$ algebraic over $F$, let $F_0$ be an intermediate field, and let $\phi_0:F_0\to\Omega'$ be an embedding into an algebraically closed field $\Omega'$. Order all extensions $\phi:E\to\Omega'$ with $F_0\subseteq E\subseteq\Omega$ by extension. A chain has the union embedding, so Zorn's lemma from [F3] gives a maximal one. If $E\ne\Omega$, choose $\alpha\in\Omega\setminus E$; it is algebraic over $E$. Apply $\phi$ to its minimal polynomial and choose a root $\beta\in\Omega'$. The transported minimal polynomial is irreducible over $\phi(E)$ because $\phi$ is an isomorphism onto its image, so sending $\alpha$ to $\beta$ extends $\phi$ to an embedding of $E(\alpha)$, contradicting maximality. Hence $\phi$ extends to $\Omega$. If $\phi_0$ maps $F$ onto $F$ and both source and target are algebraic closures of $F$, this extension is onto: its image is algebraically closed and contains $F$, so it contains every root of every polynomial over $F$, hence all of $\Omega$. [F3, given, algebra, choose]

1.2 Use [F2] to view $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ as a subfield of $\mathbb C$. By [F1], choose a transcendence basis $B$ of $\mathbb C$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$. Then $\mathbb C$ is algebraic over $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$ and, being algebraically closed, is an algebraic closure of that field. [F1, F2, given, choose]

1.3 If $z$ is algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ but $z\notin\mathbb Q$, its irreducible minimal polynomial has degree at least two and has distinct roots because its derivative is nonzero and relatively prime to it. Choose another root $z'\in\overline{\mathbb Q}$. By step 1.1, the embedding $\mathbb Q(z)\to\overline{\mathbb Q}$ sending $z$ to $z'$ extends to an automorphism of $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ over $\mathbb Q$. Extend it coefficientwise to $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$ while fixing $B$, then apply step 1.1 to extend it to an automorphism of $\mathbb C$. This automorphism moves $z$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra, choose]

1.4 If $z$ is transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, it is transcendental over the algebraic extension $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ by transitivity in [F2]. Extend $\{z\}$ to a transcendence basis $B$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ using [F1]. The assignment fixing $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ and every element of $B\setminus\{z\}$ while sending $z$ to $z+1$ defines an automorphism of $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$; its inverse sends $z$ to $z-1$. By step 1.1 it extends to an automorphism of $\mathbb C$, and it moves $z$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, choose]

2.1 Every complex number outside $\mathbb Q$ is either algebraic nonrational or transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, and steps 1.3–1.4 exhibit an automorphism fixing $\mathbb Q$ that moves it. Every element of $\mathbb Q$ is fixed by definition. Thus the common fixed field is exactly $\mathbb Q$. [step 1.3, step 1.4, given] ∎

title: An arc surgery enlarges a link Seifert matrix by two rows and columns

      url: https://ebooks.karbust.me/Mathematics/W.%20B.%20Raymond%20Lickorish%20-%20An%20Introduction%20to%20Knot%20Theory%20%281997%29%20%5B978-1-4612-0691-0%5D.pdf
      locator: "Chapter 8, Theorem 8.4, printed pp. 81–82: Seifert matrices under embedded arc surgery; the link-matrix calculation is proved here."
---
## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $L$ be a nonempty smooth oriented link with $r$ components, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented spanning surface of genus $g$, and let $F'$ be obtained by choosing an embedded solid cylinder $[0,1]\times D^2$ that meets $F$ exactly in its two end disks and lies on the same local side at both disks, then replacing those disks by the cylinder's lateral annulus with the compatible orientation. This surgery preserves $L$. Put $m=2g+r-1$, choose an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ represented away from the two end disks, and let $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ be its positive-push Seifert matrix. The surviving classes of that basis extend by two classes to an integral basis of $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)$, and for some column vectors $x,y\in\mathbb Z^m$ and integer $z$, the new Seifert matrix is one of
$$\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&0\\0^T&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&1\\0^T&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-link-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix for a link surface]]

[[def-seifert-surface-arc-surgery|The embedded product-cylinder arc surgery]]

[[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology|The homology calculation for the handle replacement]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty oriented link $L$, a connected compact oriented spanning surface $F$, an ordered basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, and one embedded arc surgery producing $F'$.

[A1] Full AC implies dependent choice and countable choice, supplying the Alexander-duality convention and compact-surface normal form. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The positive-push Seifert pairing is well-defined and bilinear on the homology of every connected link surface. [[lem-link-seifert-pairing-well-defined]]

[F2] An arc surgery replaces two disks by the lateral annulus of an embedded product cylinder, leaving the oriented boundary unchanged. [[def-seifert-surface-arc-surgery]]

[F3] Mayer–Vietoris computes the homology of two surfaces glued along a common boundary circle. [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

[F4] Linking is the signed intersection with a supplied spanning surface; linking of disjoint circles is symmetric. [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]], [[lem-link-seifert-pairing-well-defined]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data of the Statement.

1.1 The two surgery disks and a narrow strip in $F$ joining them have a disk neighbourhood $D$. Replacing the disks by the lateral annulus of the cylinder changes this neighbourhood into a once-punctured torus $P$ with the same boundary $\partial D$. Write $F_0=\overline{F\setminus D}$. Any old homology class can be represented in $F_0$: replace each of its finitely many arcs through $D$ by an arc along $\partial D$, which changes the cycle by a boundary in the disk. Take open collar neighbourhoods in $F$ and $F'$ so that $F_0$ and respectively $D$ or $P$ form open covers whose intersection retracts onto $\partial D$. In the Mayer–Vietoris sequence [F3], the map from $H_0(\partial D;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ to the direct sum of the two $H_0$ groups is $n\mapsto(n,-n)$ and is injective. For $F=F_0\cup D$, the $H_1$ map from the intersection circle has image generated by $([\partial D],0)$, since $H_1(D;\mathbb Z)=0$. For $F'=F_0\cup P$, the same image is generated by $([\partial D],0)$ because the oriented boundary of $P$ is zero in $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)$, while $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ on its longitudinal and meridional curves. Thus $H_1(F')\cong H_1(F)\oplus\mathbb Z^2$, with the old classes as a direct summand. Choose the added basis classes $b,c$ from those two curves; together with the old basis they are an integral basis. [A1, F2, F3, given, construct]

1.2 The surgery retains the old oriented surface outside the two attaching disks, so its positive normal there is unchanged and the old matrix block remains $V$. Use product coordinates $(t,w)$ on the cylinder, with $w\in D^2$, and take $c=\{t_0\}\times\partial D^2$. Let $b$ follow one longitudinal side of the tube and return through $F_0$; it crosses each cross-section disk once. The disks $\{t_0\}\times D^2$ and their sufficiently close parallel disks miss every old basis curve and its push-off, so [F4] gives zero for the two Seifert pairings between $c$ and every old basis curve. Along the lateral annulus, the positive normal points either out of or into the solid cylinder. If it points out, the radius-one cross-section disk misses $b^+$, giving $V(b,c)=0$, while the disk of slightly larger radius bounds $c^+$ and meets $b$ once; it gives $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=+1$ after orienting $c$, hence $V(c,b)=+1$ by the symmetry in [F4]. If it points in, the radius-one disk meets $b^+$ once, giving $V(b,c)=+1$ after orienting $c$, while the disk of slightly smaller radius bounds $c^+$ and misses $b$, giving $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=0$ and therefore $V(c,b)=0$. These intersection statements follow from the explicit single transverse point in the product coordinates and [F4]. In either case the concentric parallel meridians have $V(c,c)=0$. The remaining entries involving $b$ are integers $x$, $y$, and $z=\operatorname{lk}(b^+,b)$. Thus in the ordered basis $(a_1,\ldots,a_m,b,c)$ the matrix has exactly one of the two displayed forms. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

      locator: "Definition 1 and the bridge-position discussion, printed pp. 1–2"

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $D$ be an admissible finite planar code for a regular diagram of a representative of $K$, based at an interior point of an edge. The descending-diagram procedure changes at most $c(D)$ crossings, where $c(D)$ is the number of crossing records in the code, and its output diagram represents the standard unknot. Consequently the set of unknotting-sequence lengths for $K$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$, so the unknotting number $u(K)$ is finite and satisfies $u(K)\le c(D)$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number|The unknotting number and crossing-change convention]]

[[alg-descending-diagram-unknotting-sequence|The finite based traversal and crossing-change procedure]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a smooth oriented knot $K$, a finite regular diagram code $D$, and a basepoint in the interior of an edge.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The algorithm scans the finite crossing set once and returns the list of crossings whose first encounter is under, together with the updated code. [[alg-descending-diagram-unknotting-sequence]]

[F2] A code whose first encounter at every crossing is an overpass represents the standard unknot. [[thm-descending-diagram-is-unknot]]

[F3] The unknotting number is the minimum length of a crossing-change sequence from some regular diagram of a representative to the standard unknot diagram. [[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number]]

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a knot $K$, and an admissible finite code $D$ for a regular diagram of a representative of $K$, with a basepoint in an edge interior.


1.1 Apply [F1] to $D$. Since $D$ has $c(D)$ crossing records, the algorithm terminates after that finite scan and returns at most $c(D)$ crossing changes. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 After those changes every crossing is first encountered as an overpass, so [F2] says the updated code represents the standard unknot. It follows from [F3] that the returned list witnesses $u(K)\le c(D)$. In particular the set defining $u(K)$ is nonempty and its minimum is finite. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Let $U,V\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ commute and have a common invariant line on which their eigenvalues are $M,L$, respectively. For every primitive pair $(p,q)\in\mathbb Z^2$, if $M^pL^q=1$, then $U^pV^q=I_2$.

## Statement references

[[thm-a-polynomial-boundary-restriction-and-surgery-detector|Exact matrix relation for a filling representation]]

[[def-sl-two-character-variety-and-peripheral-eigenvalues|Common peripheral eigenline and eigenvalue convention]]

[[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling|Primitive filling-pair convention]]

[Baldwin and Sivek, §2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

[Bénard, Florens, and Rodau, §2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $U=I_2+N$, $V=I_2$, and the primitive pair $(p,q)=(1,0)$.

[F1] $N^2=0$, so $U$ is upper-triangular unipotent with determinant one and is not the identity.

[F2] The identity matrix commutes with every matrix, and the eigenvalues of an upper-triangular matrix are its diagonal entries.

## Counterexample

1.1 Since $N^2=0$, $U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $U\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$, has only eigenvalue $1$, and is not $I_2$. Also $V=I_2\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$. By [F2], the pair commutes and has common eigenline $\mathbb C(1,0)$ with eigenvalues $M=L=1$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 For $(p,q)=(1,0)$, the eigenvalue equation gives $M^pL^q=1^1 1^0=1$, while $U^pV^q=U\ne I_2$. This refutes the statement. The example is only a matrix pair and does not claim to extend to any knot-group representation. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix an even integer $p\ge4$ and a primitive $2p$-th root of unity $A\in\mathbb C$. Put

$$\zeta=A^2,\qquad q=-\zeta,\qquad r=p/2,\qquad \delta=-A^2-A^{-2}=q+q^{-1}.$$

The coefficient field after specialization is $\mathbb C$, and the Kauffman bracket loop coefficient is $\delta$ in the framed-link relation $[L\sqcup O]=\delta[L]$. Define the quantum integers by $[0]=0$, $[1]=1$, and $[j+1]=\delta[j]-[j-1]$ for $j\ge1$. Since $q^2=A^4$ has order $r\ge2$, these quantum integers also satisfy

$$[j]=\frac{q^j-q^{-j}}{q-q^{-1}}=(-1)^{j-1}\frac{A^{2j}-A^{-2j}}{A^2-A^{-2}}.$$

The BHMV simple-label convention is the finite set

$$\mathcal J_p=\{0,1,\ldots,r-2\}.$$

The pivotal loop and coefficient conventions throughout this page are the displayed $\delta$ and $\mathbb C$; no zero quantum integer is inverted.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $K\subset U$ be compact. There are constants $A,C>0$ and functions $\chi_N\in C_c^\infty(U)$ for each integer $N\ge1$ such that $0\le\chi_N\le1$, $\chi_N=1$ on a fixed neighborhood of $K$, and
$$
|\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)|\le C(AN)^{|\alpha|} \qquad (x\in\mathbb R^n,\ |\alpha|\le N).
$$
These are smooth compact cutoffs; no compactly supported analytic function is asserted.

## Statement references

[[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls|Smooth compact cutoff]]

[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables|Multi-index derivatives]]

[[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn|Compact support and integral]]

[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles|Compact-rectangle Fubini]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact set $K$ contained in an open set $U\subset\mathbb R^n$.

[F1] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: nested balls admit a smooth function between zero and one, equal to one on the smaller ball and supported in the larger ball.

[F2] [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]: $\partial^\alpha$ denotes the specified iterated coordinate derivatives, with $|\alpha|$ their order.

[F3] [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]: continuous compactly supported functions have finite integrals on containing rectangles.

[F4] [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]: for continuous functions on compact product rectangles, iterated integrals equal the product integral.

## Proof

**Given:** The compact set $K$ and open neighborhood $U$.

1.1 If $K=\varnothing$, set $\chi_N=0$ for all $N$; the empty set is a neighborhood of $K$, so every assertion is vacuous. Assume henceforth $K\ne\varnothing$. For each $x\in K$, choose concentric balls $B_{r_x}(x)\Subset B_{R_x}(x)\Subset U$. By [F1], take $b_x\in C_c^\infty(B_{R_x}(x))$ with $0\le b_x\le1$ and $b_x=1$ on $B_{r_x}(x)$. Compactness gives a finite subcover $B_{r_1}(x_1),\ldots,B_{r_m}(x_m)$ of $K$. The smooth function $ g=1-\prod_{j=1}^m(1-b_{x_j}) $ satisfies $0\le g\le1$, equals one on the open set $O=\bigcup_{j=1}^m B_{r_j}(x_j)$ containing $K$, and has compact support $S\Subset U$. This construction uses only finite subcover compactness. [given, F1, choose, algebra]

2.1 Choose a nonnegative smooth bump $\rho_0$ supported in the unit ball and equal to one on the ball of radius $1/2$, using [F1]. Its compactly supported integral is finite by [F3] and positive because it equals one on a ball. Normalize $\rho=\rho_0/\int\rho_0$, so $\int\rho=1$, $\rho\ge0$, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subset\overline B_1(0)$. Since $K\Subset O$ and $S\Subset U$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than one third of each distance $\operatorname{dist}(K,O^c)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(S,U^c)$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 For each $N\ge1$, put $\delta=\varepsilon/N$, $\rho_\delta(x)=\delta^{-n}\rho(x/\delta)$, and recursively $\eta_1=\rho_\delta$, $\eta_{j+1}=\eta_j*\rho_\delta$ for $1\le j<N$. Compact-rectangle Fubini [F4] and change of variables give $\int\eta_N=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_N\subset\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$; [F4] also permits reassociation of these compact convolution integrals. Define $\chi_N=g*\eta_N$. The integral defining $\chi_N$ is over a fixed compact rectangle. Differentiating the smooth kernel under this compact integral is justified by uniform convergence of its difference quotients on that rectangle, so $\chi_N$ is smooth. Positivity and unit mass give $0\le\chi_N\le1$. If $\operatorname{dist}(x,K)<\varepsilon$, then every $y\in\operatorname{supp}\eta_N$ satisfies $\operatorname{dist}(x-y,K)<2\varepsilon<\operatorname{dist}(K,O^c)$, hence $g(x-y)=1$ and $\chi_N(x)=1$. Also $\operatorname{supp}\chi_N\subset S+\overline B_\varepsilon(0)\Subset U$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

4.1 For smooth compactly supported $f,h$, write $\|h\|_1=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|h|$. Fubini on a rectangle containing their supports and the triangle inequality give $ \|f*h\|_{1}\le\int\!\!\int |f(x-y)||h(y)|\,dy\,dx =\|f\|_{1}\|h\|_{1}. $ Also $\partial_j(f*h)=(\partial_j f)*h=f*(\partial_jh)$ by differentiating under the compact integral and integration by parts; there is no boundary term because the factors have compact support. For $k=|\alpha|\le N$, distribute the $k$ coordinate derivatives to $k$ distinct convolution factors in $\eta_N$. Scaling gives $ \|\partial_j\rho_\delta\|_{1}=\delta^{-1}\|\partial_j\rho\|_{1}, $ so repeated use of the preceding inequality yields $ \|\partial^\alpha\eta_N\|_{1}\le (AN)^k,\qquad A=\varepsilon^{-1}\max\bigl(1,\max_j\|\partial_j\rho\|_{1}\bigr). $ For $k=0$ this is $\|\eta_N\|_{1}=1$. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Since $\|g\|_\infty\le1$, $ |\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)| =|g*(\partial^\alpha\eta_N)(x)| \le \|g\|_\infty\|\partial^\alpha\eta_N\|_{1} \le (AN)^{|\alpha|}. $ Thus the lemma holds with $C=1$ (or any larger fixed constant), uniformly for every $|\alpha|\le N$. The cutoffs are smooth and no analytic bump is used. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, its Seifert genus is zero if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The standard unknot convention]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|Seifert genus]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and a smooth oriented knot $K$.

[F1] Genus is the minimum genus of a connected compact oriented spanning surface; a genus-zero surface with one boundary circle is topologically a disk. For smooth input, the disk-and-band construction in steps 7.1–12.1 of [[lem-finite-c2-surface-carriers-have-smooth-normal-forms-and-relative-cap-approximations]] gives a smooth disk parametrization, including its boundary collar: its interval and circle extensions are smooth for smooth data, and all subsequent disk/band moves are smooth. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]], [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

[F2] An isotopy of an embedded compact circle extends to an ambient isotopy under AC$_\omega$. ([[thm-isotopy-extension]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and $K$.

1.1 If $K$ is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, carry its planar spanning disk through the isotopy. This is a genus-zero spanning surface, and nonnegativity gives $g(K)=0$. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Conversely, use [F1] to let a smooth embedding $e:D^2\to S^3$ parametrize a genus-zero spanning surface with oriented boundary $K$. For $0<r\le1$ the circles $x\mapsto e(rx)$, $x\in S^1$, are embedded and form a smooth isotopy from $K$ to a sufficiently small circle about $e(0)$. This contracts circles inside the embedded disk; it does not contract the final circle to a point. Choose a point outside this spanning disk and the fixed standard disk; their union has empty interior, since finitely many surface slice charts cover each compact disk. Its stereographic complement is one common positive chart $\mathbb R^3$ containing both disks. Write $p$ for the chart image of $e(0)$ and $E$ for the expression of $e$ translated by $-p$, so $E(0)=0$. For small fixed $r>0$, the maps $x\mapsto E(trx)/t$ for $0<t\le1$, continued at $t=0$ by $r\,dE_0(x)$, are an isotopy of embedded circles in that chart. Indeed Taylor's formula gives the smooth extension and, on a small disk, the derivatives are uniformly close to the injective linear map $r\,dE_0$; projection onto its image plane gives a uniform injectivity estimate by integration along line segments. Their images lie in the chart after decreasing $r$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 The final linear ellipse is isotopic to an oriented round circle in its plane: use the positive square root of its two-dimensional Gram matrix to deform its ordered independent spanning vectors to an orthonormal pair. Complete that pair by its positive normal to a positive ambient frame. Apply the same shrinking and linearization to the fixed standard disk in the common stereographic chart, obtaining an oriented round circle about its interior point $q$. Join the two round circles explicitly in this $\mathbb R^3$: move the center along the segment from $p$ to $q$, interpolate their positive radii, and rotate the first positive frame to the second through rotations in $SO(3)$ (successive rotations about coordinate axes suffice). Each intermediate circle is embedded, and the whole finite track is compact in the chart. A half-turn about a diameter reverses a circle orientation if required while preserving the ambient orientation. Reverse the standard disk shrinking to finish at the fixed standard unknot. Extend the concatenated circle isotopies by [F2]; each ambient diffeomorphism preserves orientation since it starts at the identity. Thus $K$ is the standard oriented unknot. [F2, step 1.2, construct] ∎

## Sources

[[thm-isotopy-extension]]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every nontrivial smooth oriented knot in $S^3$ is ambient isotopic to a finite connected sum of prime knots, and the prime factors are unique up to permutation and orientation-preserving ambient isotopy of the oriented factors.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|Connected sum, nontriviality, and primeness]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and a nontrivial smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[F1] Nontrivial knots have positive integer genus, genus is additive under connected sum, and the unknot has genus zero. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]], [[thm-knot-genus-additive-under-connected-sum]], [[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]])

[F2] A twice-transverse sphere realizes the oriented connected-sum factors; two prime sphere systems determine the same unordered list by the marked cut-and-paste lemma. ([[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum]], [[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-systems-cut-and-paste]])

[F3] Connected sum is associative and commutative with unknot identity, and a prime knot is a nontrivial knot that cannot split into two nontrivial factors. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]], [[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]])

[A1] The stated countable choice hypothesis supplies exactly the hypothesis of these surface, isotopy, and sphere suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and a nontrivial knot $K$.

1.1 Prove existence by induction on the positive integer $g(K)$. If $K$ is prime there is nothing to split. Otherwise the definition provides $K=J\#L$ with both factors nontrivial. By [F1], $g(J),g(L)\ge1$ and $g(J)+g(L)=g(K)$, so both genera are strictly smaller. The induction hypothesis gives each factor a finite prime decomposition; concatenate these lists using [F3]. For genus one the nonsimple case is impossible by the same inequalities. This establishes finite existence for every positive genus. [given, F1, F3, A1, induction]

2.1 Realize any finite connected-sum presentation by its standard separating spheres: take the gluing sphere in each two-ball construction, and place later summand constructions away from earlier small gluing collars. The resulting finite disjoint sphere system cuts the knot into arcs whose capped knots are exactly the original factors by [F2]. Conversely successive leaf regions of such a system give its connected-sum presentation, again by [F2] and associativity. Thus every prime presentation gives a prime sphere system with the same oriented factors. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For two prime presentations of $K$, use step 2.1 to obtain their two prime sphere systems in the same oriented knot sphere, transporting the standard constructions through the given ambient isotopies. Apply [F2]'s marked cut-and-paste comparison. Its replacements preserve oriented capped factors and reduce intersections until a common disjoint refinement compares the two lists. Therefore the lists have the same length and the same oriented prime knot classes, up to permutation. This is the full existence and uniqueness assertion. [F2, F3, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Remarks

No statement about prime decomposition of a three-manifold or knot exterior is used to infer this knot theorem. The sphere systems retain the two knot intersection points and their orientations throughout.

## Sources

[[thm-knot-genus-additive-under-connected-sum]]

[[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]]

[[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-systems-cut-and-paste]]

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N(0,1)$ and take two repeated observations with $A=(1,1)^T$ and noise covariance $\Gamma_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}$, where $-1<\rho<1$. The matrix $\Gamma_\rho$ is positive definite. The expected information gain is $\frac12\log\left(1+\frac{2}{1+\rho}\right)$. In particular, correlation $\rho=\frac12$ gives $\frac12\log(7/3)$, less than the independent-noise value $\frac12\log 3$ at $\rho=0$.

## Example references

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

[MacKay, §3.1](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, scalar prior covariance $C=1$, repeated-observation matrix $A=(1,1)^T$, and $-1<\rho<1$.

[A1] AC is inherited from the EIG/KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$, linear-Gaussian EIG is the log determinant in the Statement of the cited theorem. [[thm-ip-linear-gaussian-information-gain-logdet]]

[F2] The natural logarithm is strictly increasing. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Example.

1.1 The vectors $(1,1)^T$ and $(1,-1)^T$ are eigenvectors of $\Gamma_\rho$ with eigenvalues $1+\rho$ and $1-\rho$. Both are positive for $-1<\rho<1$, so $\Gamma_\rho\succ0$. The predictive covariance is
$S_\rho=ACA^T+\Gamma_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}2&1+\rho\\1+\rho&2\end{pmatrix}$
Thus $\det S_\rho=4-(1+\rho)^2$ and $\det\Gamma_\rho=1-\rho^2$. [given, algebra]

1.2 By [F1], $\operatorname{EIG}(\rho)=\frac12\log(\det S_\rho/\det\Gamma_\rho)=\frac12\log\left(\frac{4-(1+\rho)^2}{1-\rho^2}\right)$. Factoring numerator and denominator gives $\frac{4-(1+\rho)^2}{1-\rho^2}=\frac{(3+\rho)(1-\rho)}{(1-\rho)(1+\rho)}=1+\frac{2}{1+\rho}$, proving the formula. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 At $\rho=\frac12$, the ratio is $7/3$; at $\rho=0$, it is $3$. Since $7/3<3$, [F2] gives the strict EIG comparison in the Example. [F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

For every finite braid word $\beta$ whose closure is a knot in the declared generic matrix convention, the $N=1$ generic value is $1$; the one-strand identity braid has generic value $1$ for every $N\ge1$. Let $T$ be the closure of the positive two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$ in the declared crossing convention. With $t=q^{-1}=A^{-4}$, its $N=2$ generic value is $J_2^{\mathrm{gen}}(T;q)=t+t^3-t^4$. In addition, assuming the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, for every oriented knot $K\subset\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ the fundamental-color generic value satisfies $J_2^{\mathrm{gen}}(K;q)=V_K(q^{-1})$, where $V_K$ is the library Jones polynomial normalized by $V_{\bigcirc}=1$.

The braid diagram uses braid height increasing downward. At each positive generator, the strand entering on the right passes over the strand entering on the left; the closure joins each bottom endpoint to the top endpoint in the same position. The resulting closed braid has one component. For the diagram convention, closure arcs are routed outside the rectangular braid box without adding crossings. The diagram is explanatory; the verification uses the displayed matrices.

  \draw[->] (.56,2.44) -- (1,2);

  \node at (0,3.25) {$1$};

## Example references

[Murakami, *An Introduction to the Volume Conjecture*, §2.4 and Example 2.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1002.0126)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial*, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[[lem-quantum-sl2-ribbon-trace-matches-hecke-and-bracket|Fundamental ribbon trace and bracket formula]]

[[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization|Normalized bracket and library Jones polynomial]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The admissible generic color matrices, their normalization from the preceding definition, and the positive two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$; for the general fundamental-color identity, assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

[F1] The generic matrix value is $J_N^{\mathrm{gen}}(\beta;q)=\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}\operatorname{Tr}(G_N^{\otimes n}\rho_N(\beta))/d_N$, with $d_N\ne0$ in $\mathbb Q(A)$ ([[def-normalized-colored-jones-sequence]]).

[F2] For the fundamental ribbon color and any blackboard-framed braid closure, the ribbon trace satisfies $t_n(\beta)=\delta\langle\widehat\beta\rangle$, with $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ and twist scalar $-A^3$; this statement assumes Countable Choice ([[lem-quantum-sl2-ribbon-trace-matches-hecke-and-bracket]]).

[F3] Under the Axiom of Choice, the library Jones polynomial satisfies $V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4})$, where $f_K$ is the writhe-normalized Kauffman bracket and $t=A^{-4}$ ([[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization]]).

[F4] Every braid group element is represented by a finite word in the Artin generators and their inverses, and under AC the Artin presentation identifies these words with geometric braid classes ([[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]], [[thm-the-artin-presentation-is-complete-for-geometric-braids]]).

[F5] A geometric braid closure joins each strand endpoint to the endpoint prescribed by its permutation ([[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]).

[F6] The positive Artin half twist has determinant crossing sign $+1$ in the declared oriented projection ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F7] The opposite geometric half twist is the group inverse of the positive half twist ([[def-elementary-geometric-half-twist]]).

[F8] The exponent sum of a word is the sum of its signed generator exponents ([[def-exponent-sum-of-a-braid]]).

[F9] Under AC, every nonempty oriented link in $\mathbb R^3$ is equivalent to a closed geometric braid with at least one strand ([[thm-alexanders-closed-braid-theorem]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A2] Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct matrix evaluation.

**Given:** [F1] and the matrix data in the preceding definition.

1.1 For $N=1$, the basis has one vector, $E=F=0$, $K_L=1$, $c_1=G_1=1$, $d_1=\lambda_1=1$. Every braid generator therefore acts as $1$, and the normalized value of every such knot closure is $1$. For the unknot at any $N$, the one-strand identity braid has $w=0$ and trace $\operatorname{Tr}(G_N)=d_N$, so its normalized value is also $1$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 The strand permutation of $\sigma_1^3$ is $(12)^3=(12)$, so its two endpoints are interchanged; pairing each bottom endpoint with the top endpoint in the same position therefore produces one component. At $N=2$, the only nonzero terms of $\mathcal R_2$ are $r=0,1$. On the ordered basis $(v_+v_+,v_+v_-,v_-v_+,v_-v_-)$ they give $c_2=\begin{pmatrix}A&0&0&0\\0&0&A^{-1}&0\\0&A^{-1}&A-A^{-3}&0\\0&0&0&A\end{pmatrix}$ and $G_2\otimes G_2=\operatorname{diag}(A^4,1,1,A^{-4})$. The middle block $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&A^{-1}\\A^{-1}&A-A^{-3}\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(B^3)=A^3-A^{-9}$ by direct multiplication; the other two diagonal entries of $c_2^3$ are $A^3$, hence $\operatorname{Tr}((G_2\otimes G_2)c_2^3)=A^7+A^3+A^{-1}-A^{-9}$. Here $w(\sigma_1^3)=3$, $\lambda_2=-A^3$, and $d_2=-A^2-A^{-2}$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.3 Write a braid word as $\beta=\prod_{j=1}^m\sigma_{i_j}^{\varepsilon_j}$ with $\varepsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}$, using [F4] under [A1]. Each letter gives one crossing in the braid box. The closure pairs endpoints as prescribed by [F5]; in the diagram convention fixed in the Example, the joining arcs are routed outside the rectangular braid box without added crossings. A positive letter contributes $+1$ to writhe by [F6]. For a negative letter the opposite half twist [F7] exchanges the over- and under-strands; the determinant in the crossing-sign definition changes sign when its two vectors are exchanged, so that crossing contributes $-1$. Thus $\operatorname{wr}(\widehat\beta)=\sum_j\varepsilon_j=w(\beta)$ by [F8]. [A1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 Substitution into [F1] using step 1.2 yields $J_2^{\mathrm{gen}}(T;q)=\frac{A^{-9}(A^7+A^3+A^{-1}-A^{-9})}{A^2+A^{-2}}=A^{-4}+A^{-12}-A^{-16}=t+t^3-t^4$, where $t=A^{-4}=q^{-1}$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Given an oriented knot $K\subset\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$, choose a braid closure $\widehat\beta$ representing it by [F9]. By [F2], the fundamental-color ribbon trace is $\delta$ times the raw bracket and the twist is $-A^3$. Since $d_2=\delta$, formula [F1] gives $J_2^{\mathrm{gen}}(K;q)=(-A^3)^{-w(\beta)}\langle\widehat\beta\rangle$. By step 1.3 this is the writhe-normalized bracket $f_K(A)$. The use of [F9] requires [A1], and the framed trace in [F2] requires [A2]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F9, step 1.3, given, algebra]

3.1 The bracket/Jones theorem [F3] now gives $f_K(A)=V_K(t)$ at $t=A^{-4}=q^{-1}$. Its hypothesis uses AC [A1], while the ribbon-trace identification in [F2] uses ACω [A2], already supplied in step 2.2; the proof keeps those axiom branches separate. Therefore $J_2^{\mathrm{gen}}(K;q)=V_K(q^{-1})$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, step 2.2, given] ∎

## Remarks

The all-color ribbon and Laurent-polynomial prerequisites are now supplied locally. The general fundamental-color identification uses the actual matrix-to-bracket and bracket-to-Jones suppliers linked above, with their fixed A/B smoothing chart, positive Artin crossing convention, and separate AC and countable-choice hypotheses. The displayed finite matrix calculation fixes the variable transport $t=q^{-1}=A^{-4}$.

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.06490v3

## Statement

If a regular link diagram on $S^2$ is connected and alternating, then the represented link is nonsplit.

## Statement references

[Greene, *Alternating links and definite surfaces*, Corollary 3.2 and Theorem 5.1](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/lackenby/Fox.pdf)

[Kindred, *A geometric proof of the flyping theorem*, Fact 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.06490v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A connected alternating regular diagram $D$ and its represented link $L$.

[F1] Connectedness and alternation are properties of the projection and its crossing visits; a connected crossingless diagram consists of one circle. ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]])

[F2] The checkerboard construction gives a connected embedded surface $F$ with boundary $L$, a finite disk-and-band presentation, and a definite quadratic form on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ satisfying $q([c])=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)$ for all oriented rational multicurves. This also includes the zero-dimensional form of a crossingless spanning disk. ([[lem-alternating-checkerboard-normal-pairing-is-definite]])

[F3] A connected spanning surface with that definite normal-pairing property has nonsplit boundary. ([[lem-definite-normal-pairing-forces-nonsplit-boundary]])

[F4] A link is split if a sphere disjoint from it has link points on both complementary sides. ([[def-split-link]])

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F2] to the supplied connected alternating diagram. The resulting surface $F$ is connected, has the represented link as its entire boundary, and carries the stated definite normal pairing. If the diagram has no crossings, [F1] identifies it as a single circle and [F2] uses a spanning disk, so the same supplied-surface conclusions hold. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 The surface from step 1.1 satisfies every hypothesis of [F3], which therefore says that no sphere of the kind in [F4] splits its boundary $L$. Thus $L$ is nonsplit, with no reduction or choice assumption required. [F3, F4, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $g\geq0$ and let $V\in M_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ satisfy $\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$, where the empty skew matrix has determinant $1$. There is a connected compact smooth oriented surface $F\subset S^3$ with one boundary component and an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ whose positive-push Seifert matrix is exactly $V$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix of a chosen oriented surface and basis]]

[[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection|The skew part of a Seifert matrix is its surface intersection form]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and an integer $2g\times2g$ matrix $V$ with unimodular alternating part $J=V-V^T$.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom assumed by the knot Seifert-pairing convention and the supplied transversality interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For a knot Seifert matrix, $V-V^T$ is the unimodular oriented intersection matrix of the chosen surface. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F2] For disjoint oriented curves in a regular diagram, linking is one half the signed mixed-crossing sum. [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F3] The positive-push entry is $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]

## Proof

1.1 If $g=0$, $V$ is the empty matrix and a disk with its empty homology basis realizes it. Assume $g>0$. Put $J=V-V^T$ and $H=\mathbb Z^{2g}$. Choose a primitive vector $e\in H$. Since $J:H\to\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism, the functional $J(e,-)$ is primitive, so Bezout's identity gives $f\in H$ with $J(e,f)=1$. For every $x\in H$, the vector $x'=x-J(x,f)e+J(x,e)f$ satisfies $J(x',e)=J(x',f)=0$. Thus $H=\langle e,f\rangle\oplus\langle e,f\rangle^\perp$, and the restricted alternating form on the second summand is unimodular. Induction gives a basis with matrix $J_0=\bigoplus_{k=1}^g\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Let $P\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be the corresponding change of basis and put $W=P^TVP$; then $W-W^T=J_0$. [given, construct, induction]

2.1 Start with a disk and attach $2g$ oriented bands in the standard one-boundary handle pattern. Their core curves form an integral basis with intersection matrix $J_0$. The result is a connected compact smooth oriented surface with one boundary component. Write $W_0$ for its positive-push matrix; by [F1], $W_0-W_0^T=J_0$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 For each band core, inserting an integer number of full twists in a small subarc changes only its self-linking entry by the chosen integer. The twist box is disjoint from the other core arcs, and the surface intersection matrix is unchanged. Perform these finitely many modifications to make every diagonal entry of $W_0$ equal the corresponding diagonal entry of $W$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, construct]

3.1 For each pair $i<j$, choose subarcs of bands $i$ and $j$ in a ball disjoint from every other core and every earlier modification. Insert the oriented local clasp whose two new mixed crossings between $a_i^+$ and $a_j$ have the same sign $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. By [F2], their signed sum changes by $2\varepsilon$, so $W_{ij}$ changes by $\varepsilon$. The clasp preserves the abstract surface intersection form; by [F1], $W_{ij}-W_{ji}$ is unchanged, and therefore $W_{ji}$ also changes by $\varepsilon$. The move is supported away from every other core, so all other pair entries and all diagonal entries stay fixed. The target equation $W-W_0=(W-W_0)^T$ off the diagonal holds because both skew parts are $J_0$. A finite number of positive or negative clasps thus sets both entries to their target values for each pair, without changing previously treated pairs. The resulting surface has positive-push matrix exactly $W$. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.2, construct]

4.1 The basis change $P^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ on this surface changes its matrix from $W$ to $(P^{-1})^TW P^{-1}=V$. The constructed surface has one boundary component, so its boundary is an oriented knot and the matrix is a Seifert matrix for that knot. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The diagram records the positive oriented clasp between the positive push-off of one band core and the other core. At the left crossing the blue strand is over; at the right crossing the red strand is over. With both arrows oriented as shown, the two mixed crossing signs are positive, so their half-sum changes the linking number by $+1$; reversing both local crossing conventions gives $-1$. The proof uses the crossing formula and finite local modifications, not the drawing.

  \draw[thick,blue,->] (0.92,0) -- (2,0);

  \node[red] at (-1.45,-0.78) {$a_j$};
  \node at (-0.7,0.48) {$+$};
  \node at (0.7,0.48) {$+$};

## Statement

Let $r\ge0$, let $G$ be a group, and let $N\triangleleft G$ satisfy $N\subseteq G^{(r)}$, where $G^{(0)}=G$ and $G^{(i+1)}=[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}]$. Put $H=G/N$ and let $q:G\to H$ be the quotient. Supply a finite list of commutative unital rings $R_0,\ldots,R_{r-1}$. For a group $L$ define, through index $r$,
$$P^0L=L,\qquad P^{i+1}L=\ker\!\left(P^iL\longrightarrow (P^iL/[P^iL,P^iL])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R_i\right).$$
The tensor map sends an abelianized class $a$ to $a\otimes1$. Then for $0\le i\le r$, $N\subseteq P^iG$ and the restriction of $q$ induces
$$P^iG/N\cong P^iH,\qquad G/P^iG\cong H/P^iH.$$
For $0\le i<r$ it also induces
$$P^iG/P^{i+1}G\cong P^iH/P^{i+1}H.$$
These are the actual natural quotient maps. Every $P^iL$ is characteristic in $L$ and contains $L^{(i)}$. The same $q$ induces $G/G^{(r)}\cong H/H^{(r)}$. If all $R_i=\mathbb Q$, then $G/P^rG$ is PTFA. A final choice $R_i=\mathbb F_p$ is allowed in the quotient conclusions, but no PTFA assertion is made for such a series. No choice axiom is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The group, normal subgroup, integer and finite ring list in the Statement. A commutator subgroup means the subgroup of finite products of commutators and their inverses; all uses below are on such finite words. Tensor products are the abelian groups generated by pairs modulo the additive and balancing relations.

## Proof

1.1 Each $P^{i+1}L$ is a subgroup of $P^iL$. An automorphism of $L$ preserves $P^iL$ inductively, and induces an automorphism of its abelianization and of the displayed tensor group; their maps commute with $a\mapsto a\otimes1$. Its kernel is therefore preserved, proving that all $P^iL$ are characteristic and in particular normal. Also $L^{(i)}\subseteq P^iL$ by induction: the assertion is equality at zero, and commutators of elements of $L^{(i)}$ lie in $[P^iL,P^iL]$, which maps to zero under abelianization and hence lies in $P^{i+1}L$. Derived subgroups are descending by their finite commutator definition. Consequently $N\subseteq G^{(r)}\subseteq G^{(i)}\subseteq P^iG$ for every $i\le r$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 We prove $P^iH=q(P^iG)$ through index $r$. It holds at zero. Suppose it holds at $i<r$ and put $A=P^iG$. The restriction $q:A\to P^iH$ is onto with kernel $N$. Moreover $$N\subseteq G^{(r)}\subseteq G^{(i+1)}=[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}]\subseteq[A,A].$$ The abelianization of $A/N$ is $A/[A,A]$: expanding commutators shows $[A/N,A/N]=[A,A]/N$, since every finite commutator word in the quotient lifts by finitely many individual lifts. Thus the induced abelianization map is an isomorphism. Tensoring this isomorphism with $R_i$ is an isomorphism too, because tensoring its inverse gives an inverse on every generator $a\otimes u$; exactness of tensor is not being assumed. The two maps to these isomorphic tensor groups commute with $q$. Their kernels consequently satisfy $P^{i+1}H=q(P^{i+1}G)$: a fixed element of the former has a lift in $A$, and its tensor value is zero by the isomorphism, hence that lift is in $P^{i+1}G$. This proves the finite induction. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The kernel of each restricted $q:P^iG\to P^iH$ is $N$, already contained in $P^iG$ by step 1.1, proving the first displayed isomorphism. The preimage of $P^iH=q(P^iG)$ is $P^iG$, since it already contains $N$; this proves the second. Similarly the preimage in $P^iG$ of $P^{i+1}H$ is $P^{i+1}G$, giving the successive-quotient isomorphisms. For ordinary derived subgroups, expanding commutators and lifting each finite commutator word proves inductively $q(G^{(i)})=H^{(i)}$. Since $N\subseteq G^{(r)}$, the same preimage argument gives $G/G^{(r)}\cong H/H^{(r)}$. None of these conclusions follows merely from characteristicness: their actual kernels and preimages have been identified. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 When all $R_i=\mathbb Q$, each quotient $P^iG/P^{i+1}G$ embeds, by the kernel definition, in the additive group $(P^iG/[P^iG,P^iG])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$. That group is a rational vector space by scalar multiplication on the second tensor coordinate, so its additive group is torsion-free abelian: multiplication by a nonzero integer has inverse multiplication by its reciprocal. The finite normal series $$G/P^rG\ \trianglerighteq\ P^1G/P^rG\ \trianglerighteq\cdots\trianglerighteq\ P^rG/P^rG=1$$ therefore has torsion-free abelian factors and is precisely a PTFA series, with trivial factors permitted. For $r=0$ the quotient is trivial and the series is empty. For other ring lists steps 1.1–3.1 are unchanged, but a positive-characteristic tensor group can have additive torsion, so this last PTFA argument is intentionally not asserted. Every lift above concerned one finite word or one individual quotient element; no infinite set of representatives or vector-space basis was selected. This proves the full natural quotient assertions without a choice principle. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎
