## Statement

Let $k$ be a commutative field, let $G$ be PTFA and let $H\le G$. Put $A=k[H]$, $B=k[G]$ and let $F\subseteq K$ be their Ore fraction division rings, with the compatible standard involutions fixing $k$. Let $M$ be a closed oriented three-manifold, with a supplied homomorphism $\pi_1(M_j)\to H$ on each component. Use the canonical based coefficient systems, with base vector $1$ and the standard transported Hermitian structure. Suppose $H_1(M;F)=0$.

Then $H_1(M;K)=0$, and there is the natural isomorphism
$$H_1(M;B)\cong H_1(M;A)\otimes_A B.$$
The maps $x\mapsto x\otimes1$ are injective. The coefficient Bockstein, oriented duality and evaluation define linking pairings $B_A$ with target $F/A$ and $B_B$ with target $K/B$, and their values satisfy
$$B_B(x\otimes1,y\otimes1)=j(B_A(x,y)),\qquad j:F/A\hookrightarrow K/B.$$
In particular a nonzero self-pairing remains nonzero after subgroup extension. Neither pairing is asserted nonsingular without its additional coefficient hypotheses. No choice principle is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, groups, closed oriented manifold, based coefficient homomorphisms and vanishing in the Statement.

[F1] Subgroup group-ring extension is exact and faithful, commutes with arbitrary chain homology, and has a split unit on modules. Its division-fraction inclusion has $F\cap B=A$, so $j:F/A\to K/B$ is an injective $A$-bimodule map. [[lem-subgroup-group-ring-extension-is-faithfully-flat-and-preserves-fraction-quotients]]

[F2] PTFA group rings over $k$ have their two-sided Ore fractions and compatible standard involutions. Ore localization is exact on arbitrary chain complexes and annihilates precisely the elements having a nonzero right annihilator. [[lem-ptfa-integral-and-field-group-rings-have-compatible-ore-involutions]], [[lem-ore-localization-is-flat-and-detects-module-torsion]]

[F3] Intrinsic dual cochains have the unitary conjugate-chain model. Closed cap duality identifies their degree-two cohomology with conjugate degree-one homology. The one-vertex model and exact natural low-degree Bockstein require no infinite quotient-fiber lifting. [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]], [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]], [[lem-compact-manifold-twisted-singular-chains-admit-one-vertex-reduction]], [[lem-choice-free-low-degree-coefficient-bockstein-on-compact-manifolds]]

[F4] A finite subnormal series is the defining PTFA data. [[def-poly-torsion-free-abelian-group]]

## Proof

1.1 Intersect a PTFA series of $G$ with $H$. Each successive intersection is normal in the next, and its quotient embeds in the corresponding torsion-free abelian quotient of $G$. Subgroups of a torsion-free abelian group are torsion-free and abelian, directly from the definitions. Thus $H$ is PTFA, without choosing a global transversal. By [F2] both group rings have the asserted fractions and involutions. Apply [F1] to identify $F$ with its subring in $K$ and obtain the injective map $j$. The inclusions preserve involution because they agree on every group element and on $k$, and the inverse of a fraction denominator is forced in both rings. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 On a connected component use the finite-atlas based paths in [F3] for compatible fiber frames of all four coefficient systems. Their singular complexes are literally related by tensor base change on those generators. Hence [F1] gives $H_1(M;B)=H_1(M;A)\otimes_A B$, with the split injective unit asserted there. By [F2], vanishing over $F$ means that every $x\in H_1(M;A)$ has $xa=0$ for some nonzero $a\in A$. The composite functor $-\otimes_A B\otimes_B K$ is exact by [F1, F2], and therefore commutes with chain homology. Every such $x$ dies after tensoring with $K$, since $x\otimes z=(xa)\otimes a^{-1}z=0$. Thus $H_1(M;K)=0$. The same localization criterion says both first homology modules in the Statement are entirely torsion over their respective coefficient rings. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For either pair $(A,F)$ or $(B,K)$, the coefficient Bockstein $\beta:H^1(\operatorname{Hom}(C,F/A))\to H^2(\operatorname{Hom}(C,A))$ is an isomorphism, with the analogous notation for $(B,K)$. Indeed degree-two cohomology with values in the division ring is zero by closed duality and the proved first-homology vanishing. Its degree-one cohomology is zero by the one-vertex model: over the division ring $d_1$ has image zero or the whole degree-zero term. In the first case every degree-one cycle is a boundary; in the second split $d_1$ using one preimage of $1$, and a dual cocycle is a coboundary because it vanishes on $\ker d_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$. The exact coefficient segment in [F3] then proves $\beta$ is an isomorphism. Define $B_A$ by inverse duality, then $\beta_A^{-1}$, then evaluation, and define $B_B$ by the same procedure. This requires no inverse evaluation map, and hence asserts no unjustified general nonsingularity. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Coefficient inclusion gives actual morphisms between the two cochain coefficient sequences $A\to F\to F/A$ and $B\to K\to K/B$. On dual cochains the extension is explicit: if $f:C_A\to F/A$, set $f_B(c\otimes b)=j(f(c))b$, and use the identical formula for $A\to B$ and $F\to K$. Right-linearity of $f$ and the $A$-bimodule identity for $j$ make it balanced; the formula commutes with all differentials. The local cochain version is the same map on supplied simplex frames. The Bockstein is natural by [F3], so these maps commute with $\beta_A,\beta_B$. Cap duality also commutes with coefficient inclusion, by its finite simplex-and-transport formula using the same orientation class. Its unitary dual identifications commute because the base vector and standard form are the specified extensions of each other. No independent arbitrary gauge change is made. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 If $\nu_A$ is the inverse-Bockstein class associated by duality to $\bar x$, step 4.1 sends it to the inverse-Bockstein class associated to $\overline{x\otimes1}$, because $\beta_B$ is an isomorphism. Evaluating that cochain class on $y\otimes1$ gives exactly $j(\nu_A(y))$ by the displayed extension formula. This proves the stated value identity. Setting $y=x$ and using the injectivity of $j$ shows that a nonzero self-pairing cannot become zero. No nonsingularity theorem has entered this argument. [F1, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 A compact manifold has finitely many connected components, so apply the construction to each with only finitely many base-fiber data. Chains, Bockstein maps and cap classes split over that finite list, and the linking pairings are their orthogonal sum. Empty $M$ gives zero modules and the unique zero pairing. All potentially infinite cochain constructions above are actual formula maps on supplied whole cochains; the only Bockstein lifting is the already proved finite-generator construction of [F3]. The Ore annihilator and denominator arguments use one finite expression at a time. Thus all stated subgroup, field and topological scopes are proved without a choice axiom. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with a supplied boundary collar. Supply a unital involution-stable inclusion $R\subseteq K$ into an involutive division ring and a based rank-one right-$R$ coefficient system on $W$, with unitary monodromy and the transported standard Hermitian form. Suppose
$$H_2(W;K)=\operatorname{im}\{H_2(\partial W;K)\longrightarrow H_2(W;K)\}.$$
Let $N$ be a finite union of connected boundary components, each satisfying $H_1(N_j;K)=0$, with its induced boundary orientation and coefficient system. On each component define the linking form by inverse coefficient Bockstein, inverse oriented cap duality and evaluation; let $B_N$ be their orthogonal sum. Then
$$B_N(x,y)=0\quad\text{whenever }x,y\in\ker\{H_1(N;R)\longrightarrow H_1(W;R)\}.$$
No choice axiom or finite CW structure is assumed. No vanishing condition is imposed on the unselected boundary components.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The manifolds, collar, rings, parallel Hermitian structure and localized boundary-generation hypothesis in the Statement.

[F1] Absolute and relative cap duality hold for compact collared manifolds and closed manifolds, with arbitrary abelian-group local systems and commuting scalar actions. [[thm-compact-collared-manifold-local-coefficient-lefschetz-duality-in-zf]], [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]]

[F2] The supplied Hermitian structure identifies intrinsic dual coefficients with conjugate right coefficients, compatibly with scalar extension and restriction. [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]]

[F3] A compact connected closed manifold has a choice-free one-vertex right-chain model. Its low-degree coefficient Bockstein is natural and exact without requiring arbitrary products of quotient-fiber maps to be onto. [[lem-compact-manifold-twisted-singular-chains-admit-one-vertex-reduction]], [[lem-choice-free-low-degree-coefficient-bockstein-on-compact-manifolds]]

[F4] The pair exact sequences and the signed cap boundary identity identify homology and cohomology connectors. [[thm-pair-long-exact-sequences-with-local-coefficients]], [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]]

## Proof

1.1 Write $M=\partial W$. Under relative cap duality, the map $j:H^2(W,M;K^\vee)\to H^2(W;K^\vee)$ corresponds to the intersection map on $H_2(W;K)$. This map is zero under the given boundary-generation hypothesis. Indeed, if $z=i_*b$ for $b\in H_2(M;K)$, closed duality represents $\bar b$ by a degree-one cohomology class on $M$. Its pair connector is the relative dual class of $\bar z$, by the cap boundary identity, and its image under $j$ is zero by exactness. Every $z$ has this form by hypothesis. Thus $j=0$, with intrinsic dual systems identified using the supplied Hermitian form. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Extend $x$ by zero from $N$ to $H_1(M;R)$. Since it dies in $W$, the pair sequence supplies $a\in H_2(W,M;R)$ with $\partial a=x$. Absolute cap duality sends its conjugate to $u\in H^2(W;R^\vee)$, whose boundary restriction is the dual of $\bar x$, by the signed cap boundary formula in degree two. The image of $x$ in $H_1(M;K)$ is zero: on selected components this is the assumed vanishing and on other components $x$ was zero. Hence $u_K|_M=0$. Pair exactness puts $u_K$ in the image of $j$, which is zero by step 1.1. Choose one $R^\vee$-valued two-cocycle representing $u$. Since its image represents zero over $K$, one whole $K^\vee$-valued one-cochain $b$ satisfies $\delta b=u$. Its quotient $\nu=b\bmod R$ is a $(K/R)^\vee$-valued cocycle on $W$, and on each selected component its coefficient Bockstein is the dual of $\bar x$. This constructs a whole cochain, rather than choosing lifts of infinitely many quotient coefficients. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 On a selected connected component $N_j$, closed duality gives $H^2(N_j;K^\vee)=0$ from $H_1(N_j;K)=0$. Also $H^1(N_j;K^\vee)=0$. To see this without a universal-coefficient theorem, use the one-vertex model over $K$ from [F3], so $C_0=K$. Its $d_1$ image is either zero or $K$. In the first case $H_1=0$ says $C_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$, so every one-cocycle vanishes. In the second case one vector $v$ with $d_1v=1$ splits $C_1=\ker d_1\oplus vK$; a one-cocycle vanishes on $\ker d_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$, so equals a zero-cochain composed with $d_1$. The dual identification in [F2] preserves these assertions. Exactness [F3] therefore makes the degree-one coefficient Bockstein an isomorphism. Consequently the restriction of $[\nu]$ in step 2.1 is exactly the inverse-Bockstein class defining the linking form of $x|_{N_j}$. This applies to the finite component list separately. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Let $y$ also belong to the displayed kernel. Its image cycle in $W$ is the boundary of a single $R$-valued two-chain $c$. The sum of the component linking evaluations is therefore $\nu(y)=\nu(\partial c)=\delta\nu(c)=0$. Different components do not have cross terms because the chain and cochain groups on the finite disjoint union split componentwise; their cap fundamental classes carry their induced orientations. This is precisely $B_N(x,y)$. The proof used only finite component operations, exactness and one individual cochain witness, and made no assertion about the other boundary components. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf"
      locator: "§2.3, printed pp. 23–25, finite diagram traversal"
    - title: "Cole Charbonneau, Computing the Wirtinger Presentation of a Knot Group from a Knot Diagram"
      url: "https://site.uvm.edu/cmcharbo/files/2021/12/knot-group-1.pdf"
      locator: "§§1.2–3.2, finite diagram encodings and scans"
---

## Statement

For every admissible finite planar code of a regular oriented knot diagram and every basepoint in the interior of an edge, the descending-diagram procedure terminates, visits each crossing record once, and returns a finite updated code and a crossing-change list with at most one entry per crossing. The updated code is admissible and its first-encounter branch at each crossing is the overpassing branch. No claim about efficient minimization of $u(K)$ is made.

## Statement references

[[alg-descending-diagram-unknotting-sequence|The algorithm and its admissible input format]]

[[def-knot-planar-code|Finite edge, vertex, orientation, and crossing records]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An admissible finite planar code $D$ with $c$ crossing records and a basepoint in an edge interior.

[F1] The code contains finite vertex, edge, and half-edge sets, a coherent cyclic traversal of one oriented circle, and one over/under label at each crossing. [[def-knot-planar-code]]

[F2] The algorithm performs one oriented traversal, records a crossing only at its first encounter, and changes that crossing exactly when the first branch is under. [[alg-descending-diagram-unknotting-sequence]]

## Proof

**Given:** The admissible code and basepoint in the statement.


1.1 The code has finitely many edges and crossing records by [F1]. Following its coherent half-edge pairings from the basepoint returns to the starting edge after finitely many incidences, so the traversal terminates. It visits each crossing record once at first encounter, giving exactly $c$ processing operations. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Each operation either leaves the over/under label unchanged or exchanges the two labels once. It does not change vertices, edges, cyclic orders, branch pairings, orientations, or the rational drawing certificate; hence all validity conditions in [F1] remain satisfied. The resulting list has at most $c$ entries, and every recorded first underpass has become an overpass while first overpasses remain over. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[[def-knot-planar-code]]

[[alg-descending-diagram-unknotting-sequence]]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $A$ be an indeterminate and let $D$
be a nonempty regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere. Fix a
unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is
positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At each
crossing define $\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},
v_{\rm under})$ from the oriented projected tangents and set
$\operatorname{wr}(D)=\sum_c\operatorname{sgn}(c)$. At each crossing use the
local source chart in which the over-strand runs southwest to northeast; the
A-smoothing joins the left endpoints and the right endpoints with weight $A$,
and the B-smoothing joins the top endpoints and the bottom endpoints with
weight $A^{-1}$. Labels are transported by orientation-preserving changes of
local coordinates. Let $C(D)$ be the finite crossing set. A state is a map
$S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$; let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count its A- and B-smoothings, and
let $|S|$ be the number of circles after all crossings are smoothed. Set
$$\langle D\rangle= \sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1}.$$
Define
$$f_D(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle,$$
where $\operatorname{wr}(D)$ is the sum of the determinant signs of its
oriented crossings. If two such diagrams represent ambient-isotopic
oriented links, their $f_D(A)$ values are equal. Thus $f_D$ defines an
invariant of nonempty oriented links.

## Statement references

[[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value|Kauffman bracket state sum]]

[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing|Crossing sign and writhe]]

[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem|Oriented Reidemeister theorem]]

[Kauffman, *An Invariant of Regular Isotopy* (1990), §§III and VI](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kauffman/IRH.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §§4.1–4.4](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Funar, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter 3, §§1.1–2.3](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and two nonempty regular oriented
diagrams of ambient-isotopic oriented links.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the assumption $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The normalized bracket is unchanged by planar isotopy and every oriented
R1, R2, or R3 move ([[lem-kauffman-bracket-curl-and-writhe-correction]]).

[F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, two ambient-isotopic regular oriented link
diagrams are connected by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves ([[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]]).

[F3] Every oriented link may be moved off the point at infinity into $\mathbb R^3$,
and the directions giving regular projections are dense in $S^2$
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]],
[[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]).

## Proof
1.1 By [F1], each planar isotopy and each oriented Reidemeister move in a finite sequence preserves the normalized bracket value. Repeated equality along a finite sequence therefore preserves $f_D(A)$. [F1, induction]

2.1 By [A1] and [F2], the two given diagrams are joined by such a finite sequence. Applying step 1.1 to that sequence gives equal normalized bracket values. By [F3], every nonempty oriented link has a regular diagram. Hence $f_D$ defines a value on every nonempty oriented link type. [A1, F2, F3, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Input a real measurement matrix $A$ with $m$ rows indexed by $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $d$ columns indexed by $k<d$, where $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$. Use row $i-1$ of the ordinary zero-based $m\times d$ matrix for measurement label $i$. Input nonnegative intensities $b:[m]\to[0,\infty)$, a mode in $\{\mathrm{exact},\mathrm{noisy}\}$, a feasibility tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$, a maximum sign-pattern count $P\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and a linear-solve budget $L\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. Put $r_i=\sqrt{b_i}$.

For $m=0$, let $\mathcal S_m$ contain only the empty sign vector. For $m\ge1$, let
$$\mathcal S_m=\{s:[m]\to\{-1,+1\}:s_1=+1\},$$
ordered lexicographically with $+1$ before $-1$ and labels in increasing order. This gives one representative from each pair $\{s,-s\}$. A signed right-hand side is $y_s=(s_i r_i)_{i\in[m]}$, interpreted in the same zero-based row order as $A$.

If $P=0$ or $L=0$, return no candidates with status budget-exhausted. Otherwise compute one SVD of $A$, form its unique Moore–Penrose inverse $A^+$ and kernel $\ker A$, then process at most the first $P$ patterns in $\mathcal S_m$ and perform at most $L$ signed least-squares solves. Stop when either budget is exhausted. For each processed pattern $s$, compute the minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares solution $x_s=A^+y_s$ and signed residual $e_s=\|Ax_s-y_s\|_2$. The budget $L$ counts right-hand-side solves after the one SVD factorization.

* In exact mode, record the affine family $x_s+\ker A$ when $e_s\le\varepsilon$, together with $e_s$. Mark it exact-feasible if $e_s=0$ and tolerance-feasible if $0<e_s\le\varepsilon$. If $\varepsilon=0$ and all patterns are processed, return the union of the exact-feasible families modulo $x\sim -x$, or report infeasible if this union is empty. For $\varepsilon>0$, report only the tolerance-qualified least-squares families; this is a tolerance screen, not a list of every vector whose residual is at most $\varepsilon$.
* In noisy mode, initialize the incumbent as unset. For the first processed pattern, store $x_s$ and $J(x_s)$. For each later processed pattern, replace the incumbent by $x_s$ exactly when $J(x_s)$ is strictly smaller than the incumbent value; on a tie, keep the earlier pattern. Thus the incumbent has smallest $J$ among all processed candidates.
  Compute each visited candidate's squared amplitude residual
  $$J(x_s)=\sum_{i\in[m]}(|(Ax_s)_i|-r_i)^2$$
  before applying that update. The feasibility tolerance is not used in this mode.
* Return the candidates and a status. Exact mode returns exact-feasible/infeasible only when $\varepsilon=0$ and all patterns are processed; positive tolerance returns tolerance-feasible/no-tolerance-fit when all patterns are processed. Noisy mode returns a completed best candidate when all patterns are processed. If either budget stops enumeration before all patterns are processed, return budget-exhausted with any candidates found. A budget-exhausted result makes no claim about unvisited patterns.
* There are $1$ canonical pattern for $m=0$ and $2^{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$. Full enumeration is exponential in $m$. No statistical optimality or intensity-noise guarantee is part of this algorithm.

    - title: "Kathryn Chaloner and Isabella Verdinelli, Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review, Statistical Science 10(3) (1995), 273–304"
      url: "https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps"

## Statement refuted

The following implication is false: in every finite dominated inverse experiment, if expected information gain for a parameter is positive under a fixed nominal forward operator, then an unknown truth-operator pair is identifiable from the observation law, where identifiable means that distinct pairs induce distinct conditional observation laws.

## Statement references

[MacKay, §6.1 and Conclusion, model-correctness caveat](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §§1.2 and 2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

## Example

Take one scalar observation $Y=a\theta+\epsilon$ on $\mathsf Y=\{1,2,3\}$ with counting measure and independent noise $\epsilon$ uniform on $\{0,1\}$. In the actual model the unknown pair $H=(\theta,a)$ is uniform on $\{(1,1),(2,\frac12)\}$. In the nominal model the operator is fixed at $a=1$ and $\theta$ is uniform on $\{1,2\}$. Under the actual model both pairs give the same law, uniform on $\{1,2\}$; under the nominal model the expected information gain for $\theta$ is $\frac12\log 2>0$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-design-indexed-inverse-experiment|A finite parameter space, counting observation measure, proper prior, and dominated likelihood define an indexed experiment.]]

[[def-ip-expected-information-gain|EIG averages posterior-to-prior KL over the prior-predictive law.]]

[MacKay, §6.1, misspecified-model example](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the finite actual and nominal experiments in the Counterexample; the parameter priors and the counting measure on $\mathsf Y$.

[A1] AC is inherited from the library KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Expected information gain equals $D(P_{\theta,Y}\|P_\theta\otimes P_Y)$ for the specified dominated experiment. [[thm-ip-eig-is-joint-relative-entropy]]

[F2] The expected information gain is the prior-predictive integral of posterior-to-prior KL divergence. [[def-ip-expected-information-gain]]

[F3] KL divergence is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when the two probability measures agree. [[thm-kullback-leibler-is-nonnegative]]

[F4] The natural logarithm is strictly increasing and $\log1=0$. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

[F5] On a finite probability space, $D(P\|Q)=\sum_xP(\{x\})\log(P(\{x\})/Q(\{x\}))$, with zero-mass terms equal to zero. [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]

## Verification

**Given:** The finite models in the Counterexample.

1.1 In the actual model, $a\theta=1$ for both possible pairs. Hence $P(Y\in\{1,2\}\mid H=(1,1))=P(Y\in\{1,2\}\mid H=(2,\frac12))=1$, and both conditional laws assign probability $\frac12$ to each of $1$ and $2$. Thus $H$ and $Y$ are independent, so [F1] and [F3] give actual-pair EIG $D(P_{H,Y}\|P_H\otimes P_Y)=0$. The two distinct pairs have identical observation laws and are not identifiable. [A1, F1, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 In the nominal model, $\theta=1$ gives $Y\in\{1,2\}$ equiprobably and $\theta=2$ gives $Y\in\{2,3\}$ equiprobably. Therefore the predictive probabilities are $P(Y=1)=\frac14$, $P(Y=2)=\frac12$, and $P(Y=3)=\frac14$. [given, algebra]

2.1 The joint probabilities are $P(\theta=1,Y=1)=\frac14$, $P(\theta=1,Y=2)=\frac14$, $P(\theta=2,Y=2)=\frac14$, and $P(\theta=2,Y=3)=\frac14$. Dividing by the marginals in step 1.2 gives posterior $\delta_1$ at $Y=1$, the original uniform prior at $Y=2$, and $\delta_2$ at $Y=3$. By [F5], the corresponding KL values are $\log2$, $0$, and $\log2$. Thus [F2] gives nominal EIG $\frac14\log2+\frac12\cdot0+\frac14\log2=\frac12\log2>0$ by [F4]. [A1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By [F1] and [F3] as applied in step 1.1, the actual-pair EIG is zero although the pairs are distinct and observationally identical; by step 2.1 the nominal fixed-operator EIG is positive. Thus the claimed implication fails. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

id: def-ip-relaxed-range-invariance-objective
kind: definition
title: Joint and frozen-Newton objectives for range-invariant relaxations

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18704"

## Definition

Let $X,Y,Z$ be real Banach spaces, let $X_0$ be a closed linear subspace of $X$, and let $D\subseteq X$ contain $X_0$ and a nonempty set $U$. Fix $x_0\in X_0\cap U$, a map $F:D\to Y$, a bounded linear map $K:Z\to Y$, and a map $r:D\to Z$ such that $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ for every $x\in D$. Assume that $r|_U$ is a bijection from $U$ onto a set $\widetilde U\subseteq Z$, and that $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)\in X_0\cap D$ for every $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$ admitted below. Here $I$ is the identity on $X$ and $P:X\to X$ is a bounded linear projection with $P^2=P$, $P|_{X_0}=0$, and $(I-P)(X)\subseteq X_0$. Let $\check R:X_0\to[0,+\infty]$ be a proper convex regularizer, let $R_P:P(X)\to[0,+\infty]$ be a nonnegative penalty, and let $Q:Z\times Z\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfy $Q(a,b)=Q(b,a)$ and $Q(a,b)=0$ exactly when $a=b$. For $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$, set

$$\mathcal R(\widehat r):=\check R\big((I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)\big)+R_P\big(Pr^{-1}(\widehat r)\big).$$

For $p\in[1,\infty)$, data $y^\delta\in Y$, and parameters $\alpha,\beta>0$, the **joint relaxed objective** is

$$\mathcal J_{\alpha,\beta}^\delta(\widehat r,x):=\|K\widehat r+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha\mathcal R(\widehat r)+\beta Q(r(x),\widehat r)^p+\|Px\|_X^p,\qquad (\widehat r,x)\in\widetilde U\times U.$$

The joint source-condition objective takes $R_P=0$. The term $\beta Q(r(x),\widehat r)^p$ ties the relaxed range variable to the physical variable, while $\|Px\|_X^p$ penalizes the component outside $X_0$.

If $r$ is Gâteaux differentiable at a current iterate $x_n\in U$, the **frozen-Newton objective** with parameters $\alpha_n,\beta_n>0$ is

$$\mathcal J_n^\delta(\widehat r,x):=\|K\widehat r+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha_n\mathcal R(\widehat r)+\beta_n Q\big(r(x_n)+r'(x_n)(x-x_n),\widehat r\big)^p+\|Px\|_X^p.$$

Here $r'(x_n)$ is the bounded linear Gâteaux derivative used to form the affine range proxy; no minimizer existence or uniqueness is part of either definition.

## Example

For this example put $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$. On real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, let $e_j$ be the coordinate vectors and define $K_\gamma x=(\exp(-\gamma_j)x_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $\gamma_1=0$, $\gamma_j$ is strictly increasing, and $\gamma_j\to\infty$. For $\nu,q,\rho>0$, the power source ball $X_{\nu,\rho}(K_\gamma):=\{|K_\gamma|^\nu w:\|w\|_2\le\rho\}$ has coordinates $x_j=\exp(-\nu\gamma_j)w_j$, and the logarithmic source ball $X_{\log,q,\rho}(K_\gamma):=\{\psi_q(|K_\gamma|)w:\|w\|_2\le\rho\}$, where $\psi_q(0)=0$ and $\psi_q(t)=(1+\log(1/t))^{-q}$ for $0<t\le1$, has coordinates $x_j=(1+\gamma_j)^{-q}w_j$. The operator is compact and injective with $\|K_\gamma\|=1$. The choice $\gamma_j=j-1$ gives ordinary exponential decay; $\gamma_j=j(j-1)/2$ gives gaps with $s_{j+1}/s_j=\exp(-j)$. For this latter choice, write $s_j=\exp(-\gamma_j)$ and $\delta_j^\star=\rho(s_js_{j+1})^{(\nu+1)/2}$. Then $\varepsilon_{K_\gamma}(X_{\nu,\rho}(K_\gamma),\delta_j^\star)/((\delta_j^\star)^{\nu/(\nu+1)}\rho^{1/(\nu+1)})\to0$, so no matching constant lower bound holds at every sufficiently small $\delta$.

## Example

Assume a Conway skein function $\nabla$ on oriented links exists with $\nabla_U=1$ and $\nabla_{L_+}-\nabla_{L_-}=z\nabla_{L_0}$. For a knot $K$, put $a_2(K)=[z^2]\nabla_K(z)$. The unframed degree-one chord-diagram module is zero. The degree-two symbol of $a_2$ is the weight system $w_2$ that assigns $1$ to the intersecting two-chord diagram and $0$ to the diagram with two nonintersecting chords. In particular, $a_2(U)=0$ for the unknot and $a_2(T)=1$ for the positive trefoil $T$ that is the closure of the two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$. Under countable choice, the degree-two truncation of the normalized Kontsevich series recovers this example up to its unique degree-zero normalization: for every knot type $K$,
$$
a_2(K)=w_2(I_2(K))-w_2(I_2(U)).
$$
Here $I_2(K)$ is the degree-two coefficient of $I(K)$, and $I_0(K)=1$ is its degree-zero coefficient. This calculation is conditional on the existence supplier for $\nabla$ and asserts no rationality for the coefficients of $I(K)$.

The two degree-two chord patterns are shown below. Endpoints alternate in the first diagram and not in the second; the diagram only labels the two cases used in the algebraic check.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Conway skein function $\nabla$, the unframed chord-diagram module, the positive Artin crossing convention, and countable choice for knot-isotopy invariance of $I$.

[F1] [[def-conway-polynomial]]: $\nabla_U=1$ and $\nabla_{L_+}-\nabla_{L_-}=z\nabla_{L_0}$ for every oriented skein triple.

[F2] [[thm-conway-second-coefficient-is-type-two]]: $a_2$ has type at most two, its degree-two symbol is $w_2(D_{\times})=1$, $w_2(D_{\parallel})=0$, and $a_2(U)=0$, $a_2(T)=1$ for the specified positive trefoil.

[F3] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: degree-one diagrams are killed by 1T; at degree two the only circle diagrams are the intersecting and nonintersecting patterns shown.

[F4] [[thm-kontsevich-integral-is-universal]]: under countable choice, every type-at-most-two invariant has a complex-linear functional on the sum of unframed chord modules through degree two that recovers it; the degree-two part of this functional is its degree-two symbol.

[F5] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: $I_0(K)=1$ for every knot, since both $Z(K)$ and $Z(H)$ have degree-zero coefficient $1$.



[F6] **Discharged existence input.** [[def-conway-polynomial]] now supplies the actual unique $\mathbb Z[z]$-valued oriented ambient-link invariant by its explicitly external Garaev coefficient theorem and CDM ambient-link/skein interpretation, followed by the finite polynomial/uniqueness argument. Thus the Conway function in the Given is an actual available object, not an unresolved well-definedness premise. The finite coefficient/chord/trefoil arguments below are retained unchanged; no general rationality assertion for the Kontsevich coefficients is used.

## Verification

**Given:** As above.

1.1 The unique degree-one circle diagram has an isolated chord, so [F3] sets it to zero. In degree two, the two chord pairings are exactly $D_{\times}$ and $D_{\parallel}$: their four endpoints either alternate or do not. By [F2], $w_2$ evaluates them as $1$ and $0$, so it is a nonzero functional on the unframed quotient. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 The unknot normalization gives $a_2(U)=0$. For the positive Hopf link $H_2=\widehat{\sigma_1^2}$, switching one crossing cancels an adjacent positive and negative half twist and gives the two-component unlink; smoothing gives $\widehat{\sigma_1}=U$. A local type-I curl on one component of the two-component unlink has both crossing signs isotopic to that unlink and smoothing equal to the three-component unlink. The skein relation therefore gives $z\nabla_{U_3}=0$. Multiplication by the indeterminate $z$ is injective in $\mathbb Z[z]$, because a polynomial $f=\sum a_jz^j$ with $zf=0$ has every coefficient $a_j=0$; hence $\nabla_{U_3}=0$. Applying the same curl argument to the unknot gives $\nabla_{U_2}=0$. Thus $\nabla_{H_2}=z$. For $T=\widehat{\sigma_1^3}$, switching one crossing cancels an adjacent inverse pair and gives $U$, while smoothing gives $H_2$. Hence $\nabla_T-1=z\nabla_{H_2}=z^2$, so $a_2(T)=1$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $W$ be the functional supplied by [F4] for $a_2$. Its degree-two restriction is $w_2$ by [F2]; the only lower-degree summand is degree zero because [F3] makes degree one zero. Since $a_2(U)=0$ and $I_0(U)=1$ by [F5], the value of $W$ on the degree-zero unit is $-w_2(I_2(U))$. Therefore $W(I_{\le2}(K))=w_2(I_2(K))-w_2(I_2(U))$, which equals $a_2(K)$ by [F4]. This verifies the displayed universal-series recovery for every knot type. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the standing AC and canonical-trace convention of the $L^2$ signature definition. Let $W$ be a compact oriented four-manifold with a supplied finite CW pair model for its boundary and a surjection $\psi:\pi_1(W)\to G=\mathbb Z/d$, $d\ge1$. Let $\widetilde W_\psi$ be its actual degree-$d$ cover, and write $\zeta=\exp(2\pi i/d)$. For $0\le r<d$, let $\lambda_r$ be the character intersection form for the character sending the specified positive generator of $G$ to $\zeta^r$. Then, allowing arbitrary radicals,
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W,\psi)=\frac{\operatorname{sign}(\widetilde W_\psi)}d=\frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{sign}(\lambda_r).$$
Here the ordinary cover signature, like each character signature, means positive inertia minus negative inertia with the kernel discarded. Changing consistently from linear-first to conjugate-first pairings transposes the character matrices and does not change the formula. No independence of a bounding manifold, no infinite-cyclic integration and no arbitrary-group index assertion is part of this statement.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite pair, the oriented manifold, the surjection and the positive cyclic generator.

[F1] The canonical trace on $\mathcal N G$ is the coefficient at the identity, equivalently $\langle A\delta_e,\delta_e\rangle$. The $L^2$ signature is the trace of the positive spectral projection of the induced middle form minus that of its negative spectral projection, ignoring the radical. [[def-integral-half-solutions-strebel-and-l2-signatures]]

[F2] A finite-dimensional complex normal operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis. In particular a Hermitian matrix has real eigenvalues and its positive and negative projections have ranks the corresponding inertia counts. [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]

[F3] For the supplied finite CW pair, the cellular local complex computes its singular local homology, with the deck-incidence matrix of the supplied lifts acting through monodromy. [[thm-cellular-chains-compute-homology-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 Denote by $t$ the cyclic shift on the standard orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C[G]$. Its powers $1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1}$ are linearly independent, since their values on $\delta_e$ are the distinct basis vectors, and they span a finite-dimensional unital star algebra, hence a strongly closed algebra. Thus $\mathcal N G=\mathbb C[G]$. Put $$e_r=\frac1d\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\zeta^{-rk}t^k.$$ The geometric sum is $d$ if its exponent is divisible by $d$, and zero otherwise, by multiplying it by $1-\zeta^j$. Consequently $e_re_s=\delta_{rs}e_r$, $\sum_re_r=1$, $e_r^*=e_r$ and $te_r=\zeta^re_r$. Each $e_r$ has one-dimensional range on the regular representation and trace $1/d$, its identity coefficient. This includes $d=1$. Hence $\mathcal N G\cong\bigoplus_r\mathbb C e_r$ as a traced star algebra, with trace $d^{-1}\sum_r$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Lift the finitely many cells of the supplied pair to the cover. Their translates identify its complex cellular chains with the finite free $\mathbb C[G]$ chains of $W$. Multiplying by the finitely many $e_r$ gives a direct sum of complexes; on the $r$th summand every monodromy matrix is evaluated at $t=\zeta^r$. This is precisely the character cellular complex. Projection and inclusion commute with the differential, so kernels and images split in these summands. All the spaces have finite complex dimension, so every image is closed; reduced Hilbert homology and ordinary homology agree, including in relative degrees. Thus the actual middle homology splits as the sum of the character homologies, without a flatness or tensor-exactness assumption. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The intersection pairing respects this splitting. Its sesquilinearity gives, in the linear-first convention, $$\lambda(e_rx,e_sy)=e_r\lambda(x,y)e_s,$$ since $e_s^*=e_s$; this is zero for $r\ne s$. Within one summand its value is its scalar character form times $e_r$. This can also be seen directly on cells: lift one relative orientation chain from $W$ and add all its translates to get the orientation chain of the cover. Cup, cap, boundary and evaluation are finite linear formulas commuting with the central projections. The coefficient-at-identity pairing on a basis of lifted chains counts exactly their ordinary intersections in the cover. For Fourier-projected lift cycles $P_rx=d^{-1}\sum_k\zeta^{-rk}T^kx$, the ordinary cover pairing is the scalar character pairing divided by $d$; expand the two sums and put $j=b-a$ to get $$ I(P_rx,P_ry)=\frac1d\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}(x\mathbin{\cdot}T^jy)\zeta^{rj}.$$ Here $I$ is the ordinary real cover intersection form extended complex linearly in its first argument and conjugate linearly in its second. Thus all normalizations differ only by the positive scalar $d^{-1}$ on a character component. If the alternate inverse-deck convention is used it interchanges $r$ and $d-r$, which leaves the finite sum unchanged. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 In any character block choose a basis of middle homology. Its form matrix is Hermitian; its radical is exactly its kernel. By [F2] the positive and negative spectral spaces have dimensions $n_+(\lambda_r),n_-(\lambda_r)$, and the zero eigenspace is its radical. These dimensions do not depend on the chosen basis: a maximal positive subspace has dimension $n_+$, since projection to the positive spectral space is injective on any positive subspace, and that spectral space itself is positive. An invertible basis change bijects positive subspaces; repeat with the negative form for $n_-$. The same argument applies to a positive scalar multiple and to a transpose by complex conjugation. In the direct sum of step2 the full radical is the direct sum of these kernels, because all cross blocks vanish. No component is removed by assuming that a determinant is nonzero. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 On a finite $\mathcal N G$ module, a projection whose character ranks are $q_r$ has trace $\sum_rq_r/d$: represent it on a finite free module using step1, apply the ordinary matrix trace in each component, and sum the diagonal identity coefficients. Applied to the positive and negative homology projections of step4 this yields $$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W,\psi)=\frac1d\sum_r(n_+(\lambda_r)-n_-(\lambda_r)).$$ The ordinary cover form is the orthogonal sum of the same finite character blocks, with the positive normalization of step3, so its signature is the sum of their signatures. This proves both equalities, with every radical and the trivial character retained. The argument was for this actual finite cover and finite complex, and used neither a closed-signature index theorem nor a bordism-independence assertion. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ act by matrix multiplication in the standard finite coordinate bases, with row and column labels $1$ through their dimensions corresponding to library coordinates $0$ through one less, let $y\in\mathbb R^m$, and let $\epsilon\ge0$. Define $g:\mathbb R^m\to\{0,+\infty\}$ by $g(u)=0$ when $\|u-y\|_2\le\epsilon$ and $g(u)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $p\in\mathbb R^m$, define $g^*(p):=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R^m}\{\langle p,u\rangle-g(u)\}$. Then
$$g^*(p)=\langle p,y\rangle+\epsilon\|p\|_2\qquad(p\in\mathbb R^m).$$
Let $A^*:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be the Euclidean adjoint, characterized by $\langle A^*p,z\rangle=\langle p,Az\rangle$ for all $p,z$. If $x\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfies $\|Ax-y\|_2\le\epsilon$ and a vector $p\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfies $\|A^*p\|_\infty\le1$ and
$$\|x\|_1=-\langle p,y\rangle-\epsilon\|p\|_2,$$
then $x$ minimizes $\|z\|_1$ over that residual ball. If instead $p\ne0$, $A^*p=0$, and $|\langle p,y\rangle|>\epsilon\|p\|_2$, then the residual ball is disjoint from the range of $A$.

## Statement references

[[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space|Fenchel conjugate]]

[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces|Euclidean adjoint]]

[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension|Existence of the finite-dimensional adjoint]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one-, two-, and maximum norms]]

[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm|Cauchy–Schwarz for Euclidean norms]]

[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics|Positive definiteness of the Euclidean norm]]

[Chambolle and Pock, *A First-Order Primal-Dual Algorithm for Convex Problems with Applications to Imaging*, §2](https://optimization-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/06/2646.pdf)

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §4.3](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $m,n\ge1$, a real linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, its Euclidean adjoint $A^*$, a vector $y\in\mathbb R^m$, a radius $\epsilon\ge0$, and the residual ball $\{u:\|u-y\|_2\le\epsilon\}$.

[F1] [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]]: $g^*(p)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R^m}\{\langle p,u\rangle-g(u)\}$.

[F2] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: $\langle p,u\rangle$ is the finite Euclidean coordinate pairing and $\|p\|_2^2=\langle p,p\rangle$.

[F3] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|z\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^n|z_j|$, $\|u\|_2=(\sum_i|u_i|^2)^{1/2}$, and $\|v\|_\infty=\max_j|v_j|$ in positive dimensions.

[F4] [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]: $\langle A^*p,z\rangle=\langle p,Az\rangle$ for every $p,z$.

[F5] [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]: the Euclidean adjoint $A^*$ exists and is unique.

[F6] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle p,v\rangle|\le\|p\|_2\|v\|_2$.

[F7] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums of nonnegative terms are nonnegative.

[F8] [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]: the Euclidean $2$-norm is positive definite, so $\|p\|_2>0$ whenever $p\ne0$.

## Proof

1.1 In the supremum defining $g^*(p)$, only $u$ in the residual ball contributes. Write $u=y+v$ with $\|v\|_2\le\epsilon$. For $p\in\mathbb R^m$, define $g^*(p):=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R^m}\{\langle p,u\rangle-g(u)\}$. Then $g^*(p)=\langle p,y\rangle+\sup_{\|v\|_2\le\epsilon}\langle p,v\rangle.$ By [F6], the last supremum is at most $\epsilon\|p\|_2$. If $p=0$ or $\epsilon=0$, $v=0$ attains this value. Otherwise $v=\epsilon p/\|p\|_2$ is feasible and gives $\langle p,v\rangle=\epsilon\|p\|_2$. This proves the conjugate formula, including the zero cases. [given, F1, F2, F3, F6, F8, choose, algebra]

1.2 Let $z$ be any feasible vector and put $q=A^*p$. The condition $\|q\|_\infty\le1$ means $|q_j|\le1$ for every coordinate. Hence each term $|z_j|+q_jz_j$ is nonnegative, and [F7] gives $\|z\|_1+\langle q,z\rangle=\sum_j(|z_j|+q_jz_j)\ge0.$ By [F4], $\|z\|_1\ge-\langle p,Az\rangle$. Feasibility and [F6] give $|\langle p,Az-y\rangle|\le\epsilon\|p\|_2$, so $\|z\|_1\ge-\langle p,Az\rangle\ge-\langle p,y\rangle-\epsilon\|p\|_2.$ If $x$ is feasible and attains equality with the last quantity, it has objective no larger than any feasible $z$, proving the optimality certificate. [given, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 If $p\ne0$, $A^*p=0$, and $|\langle p,y\rangle|>\epsilon\|p\|_2$, then for every $z\in\mathbb R^n$, [F4] gives $|\langle p,Az-y\rangle|=|\langle A^*p,z\rangle-\langle p,y\rangle|=|\langle p,y\rangle|>\epsilon\|p\|_2.$ By [F6], this forces $\|Az-y\|_2>\epsilon$. Thus no $z$ is feasible, proving the infeasibility certificate. [given, F4, F6, F8, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$ use the one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$. Order the coordinates by decreasing $|x_j|$, breaking ties by increasing $j$, and let $S$ be the first $s$ indices. For every $U\subseteq[n]$, let $x_U$ agree with $x$ on $U$ and vanish on $U^c$. Then for every $T\subseteq[n]$ with $|T|\le s$,
$$\|x_T\|_1\le\|x_S\|_1\quad\text{and}\quad\|x_{S^c}\|_1\le\|x_{T^c}\|_1.$$
Consequently $\sigma_s(x)_1=\|x_{S^c}\|_1$, so the best $s$-term tail error is attained by retaining the first $s$ coordinates in the specified order.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-best-s-term-l1-error|Finite-minimum definition of the best s-term tail error]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one-norm]]

[[lem-finite-sum-laws|Monotonicity and additivity of finite sums]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §2.1 Definition 2.2, printed p. 42](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

[Mendelson, Rauhut, and Ward, *Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions*, §2.1](https://www.mathc.rwth-aachen.de/~rauhut/files/circulant-independent.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $n\ge1$, $1\le s\le n$, a vector $x\in\mathbb R^n$, its deterministic decreasing-magnitude order $j_1,\ldots,j_n$, the set $S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_s\}$, and an arbitrary $T\subseteq[n]$ with $|T|\le s$.

[F1] [[def-ip-best-s-term-l1-error]]: $\sigma_s(x)_1=\min\{\|x_{U^c}\|_1:U\subseteq[n],\ |U|\le s\}$.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|x_U\|_1=\sum_{j\in U}|x_j|$, and $\|x\|_1=\|x_U\|_1+\|x_{U^c}\|_1$ for every $U\subseteq[n]$.

[F3] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums preserve termwise inequalities and addition splits a finite sum over disjoint parts.

## Proof
1.1 If $T=\varnothing$, its retained mass is zero and is no larger than the nonnegative sum on $S$. Otherwise write the ranks of the elements of $T$ in increasing order as $r_1<\cdots<r_k$, where $k=|T|\le s$. Then $r_\ell\ge\ell$, so the specified ordering gives $|x_{j_{r_\ell}}|\le|x_{j_\ell}|$ for each $\ell$. Summing these inequalities and adding the remaining nonnegative terms among the first $s$ coordinates yields $\|x_T\|_1\le\|x_S\|_1$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Since $T$ and $S$ each partition the full coordinate set into retained and omitted coordinates, [F2] gives $\|x_{T^c}\|_1=\|x\|_1-\|x_T\|_1$ and $\|x_{S^c}\|_1=\|x\|_1-\|x_S\|_1$. Step 1.1 therefore implies $\|x_{S^c}\|_1\le\|x_{T^c}\|_1$. Applying this inequality to every admissible $T$, while $S$ itself is admissible, shows that the finite minimum in [F1] equals $\|x_{S^c}\|_1$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be compact between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, let $\nu>0$ and $w\in X$, and put $x=|K|^\nu w$. Then $\|x\|_X\le\|Kx\|_Y^{\nu/(\nu+1)}\|w\|_X^{1/(\nu+1)}$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model|Compact Hilbert-space inverse model]]

[Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Lemma 3.14](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

[Hofmann and Mathé, *A Note on the Modulus of Continuity*, Section 1](https://www.tu-chemnitz.de/mathematik/ip/fulltext/hofmann_b76.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, compact $K:X\to Y$ between real or complex Hilbert spaces, $\nu>0$, $w\in X$, and $x=|K|^\nu w$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed by the compact singular-value decomposition supplier.

[F1] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]: The positive singular system has orthonormal right and left singular vectors $v_j,u_j$ with $|K|v_j=s_jv_j$ and $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, and the closed span of the $v_j$ is $N(K)^\perp$.

[F2] [[def-ip-power-source-set]]: The power source multiplier is $|K|^\nu=(K^*K)^{\nu/2}$.

[F3] [[def-compact-spectral-filter-and-qualification]]: The compact spectral multiplier acts on an eigenvector by its scalar function, and the power multiplier has value zero at the zero eigenvalue.

[F4] [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], [[def-real-power]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-laws]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]], and [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]: For $a>0$ and $t>0$, $t^a>0$, $1^a=1$, and $(t^a)'=at^{a-1}>0$; hence the mean value theorem makes $t\mapsto t^a$ strictly increasing. For $0<\theta<1$, exponent laws give $t^{\theta-1}=1/t^{1-\theta}$, and reciprocation reverses positive inequalities.

## Proof

1.1 Let $J$ index the positive singular values in [F1]. Write $w=w_0+\sum_{j\in J}w_jv_j$ in norm, with $w_0\in N(K)$. By [F2]–[F3], $x=\sum_{j\in J}s_j^\nu w_jv_j$ and $Kx=\sum_{j\in J}s_j^{\nu+1}w_ju_j$, with norm-convergent expansions. For each finite $F\subseteq J$, orthonormality gives the squared norms of the partial sums as the sums of squared coefficients; taking limits by continuity of the norm gives $\|x\|_X^2=\sum_{j\in J}c_j$ and $\|Kx\|_Y^2=\sum_{j\in J}a_j$. The same finite-sum identity and $w_0\perp v_j$ give $\|w\|_X^2=\|w_0\|_X^2+\sum_{j\in J}b_j\ge\sum_{j\in J}b_j$, where $c_j=s_j^{2\nu}|w_j|^2$, $a_j=s_j^{2\nu+2}|w_j|^2$, and $b_j=|w_j|^2$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, construct]

1.2 Put $\theta=\nu/(\nu+1)\in(0,1)$. For a finite $F\subseteq J$, set $A_F=\sum_{j\in F}a_j$, $B_F=\sum_{j\in F}b_j$, and $C_F=\sum_{j\in F}c_j$. If $A_F=0$ or $B_F=0$, then every $w_j$ with $j\in F$ is zero because $s_j>0$, so $C_F=0$. Otherwise, for $j\in F$ put $p_j=a_j/A_F$ and $q_j=b_j/B_F$. The scalar inequality $t^\theta\le\theta t+1-\theta$ holds for $t\ge0$: for $t>0$ set $g(t)=\theta t+1-\theta-t^\theta$. By [F4], $g'(t)=\theta(1-t^{\theta-1})$. If $0<t<1$, strict increase of $u\mapsto u^{1-\theta}$ gives $t^{1-\theta}<1^{1-\theta}=1$; by [F4] and inverse order this implies $t^{\theta-1}>1$ and $g'(t)<0$. If $t>1$, the inequalities reverse and $g'(t)>0$. The mean value theorem then gives $g(t)\ge g(1)=0$ for every $t>0$, while $g(0)=1-\theta>0$. If $q_j>0$, apply the scalar inequality to $t=p_j/q_j$ to obtain $p_j^\theta q_j^{1-\theta}\le\theta p_j+(1-\theta)q_j$; if $q_j=0$, the same inequality is immediate. Since $c_j=a_j^\theta b_j^{1-\theta}$, summing and using $\sum p_j=\sum q_j=1$ gives $C_F\le A_F^\theta B_F^{1-\theta}$. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 Exhaust $J$ by its first $n$ indices when $J$ is infinite, and take $F=J$ when it is finite; if $J$ is empty, all three sums in step 1.1 are zero. Passing to the limit in step 1.2 gives $\|x\|_X^2\le\|Kx\|_Y^{2\theta}\|w\|_X^{2(1-\theta)}$. Taking nonnegative square roots and substituting $\theta=\nu/(\nu+1)$ proves the claimed inequality. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix either a strict Morse presentation $K:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ or a compact strict Morse tangle $T\subset\mathbb C\times[a,b]$, and an integer $m\ge1$. For each chamber of the ordered level simplex and each choice of the local branches paired at its levels, let $C_m$ be the resulting open configuration cell. The finite union of these cells has a compactification $\overline C_m$ that is a compact manifold with corners. Its boundary strata record exactly: adjacent level collisions $t_i=t_{i+1}$; the endpoint faces at $t_{\min},t_{\max}$ for a knot or at $a,b$ for a tangle; levels reaching a critical value of the height function; and compatible intersections of these events. Whenever endpoint positions coalesce, real oriented blow-up records their relative scale and limiting direction, including nested collision clusters. The branch-evaluation maps extend smoothly to the resolved faces. Orient each open cell by $dt_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dt_m$ and orient every new collision face by the outward-normal-first convention using its nonnegative radial coordinate; a critical-level face uses the local Morse coordinate $s\ge0$ with $t-c=\pm s^2$ and the same boundary-orientation convention.

## Statement references

[[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids|Ordered level cells, branch pairings, and the Kontsevich integral]]

[[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative|Smooth oriented knot convention]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §8.2, printed pp. 223–225](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §2.5, PDF pp. 12–13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Either a strict Morse knot presentation or a compact strict Morse tangle with regular boundary levels, its height function $t$, and a finite degree $m\ge1$.

[F1] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: the degree-$m$ integration domain is the ordered simplex between the boundary or extreme levels with critical levels removed; at each level a pairing chooses two distinct points on the knot or tangle and determines their chord endpoints.

[F2] [[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative]]: the knot skeleton is a compact smooth circle. For tangles, the compact one-dimensional skeleton and regular boundary levels are as in [F1]; nondegenerate critical points are isolated.

[F3] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: a degree-$m$ chord diagram has finitely many endpoints, each endpoint lying on the oriented parameter circle.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. All compactifications below are finite-degree and choice-free.

1.1 The critical points are isolated in the compact one-dimensional skeleton and absent from the tangle boundary, so there are finitely many critical points and critical values. On every open interval between consecutive critical values or boundary levels, the inverse image is a finite union of arcs on which $t$ is a local diffeomorphism. Thus the number of branches, and the finite set of allowed pairs at a level, are constant on each such interval. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 At a regular level, each branch is a smooth graph $z=z_\lambda(t)$, so its evaluation extends smoothly to any regular face. Near a critical point, choose a local parameter $x$ with $t(0)=c$, $t'(0)=0$, and $t''(0)\ne0$. The function $h(x)=(t(x)-c)/x^2$ extends smoothly with $h(0)=t''(0)/2\ne0$; after shrinking the coordinate interval, $s=x\sqrt{|h(x)|}$ is a smooth coordinate with nonzero derivative and $t=c+\operatorname{sgn}(h(0))s^2$. Since $z=z(x(s))$ is smooth, the two local branches and their limiting common point extend to the critical face in this coordinate. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Fix a chamber and let $k_r$ be the number of its ordered levels in the $r$th interval between critical or boundary levels. The chamber is a product of open simplices, one for each interval, with $k_r$ ordered coordinates. Its closure is the product of the corresponding closed simplices, hence compact. The facets of a closed simplex are exactly adjacent-coordinate equalities or a coordinate reaching one endpoint of its interval; across the finite family of chambers those endpoints are the knot extrema, tangle boundary levels, or critical values. Thus before resolving endpoint collisions the only faces are level collisions, outer endpoints, and critical-level events. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 In a regular-level collision, endpoints on distinct branches remain distinct because $K$ is embedded; endpoints on one branch coalesce along a smooth arc. In the latter case, use local parameters $s_1,\dots,s_k$ for the colliding endpoints, their center $p=k^{-1}\sum s_j$, the radius $r=(\sum_j|s_j-p|^2)^{1/2}$, and the normalized shape $(s_j-p)/r$. Replacing the diagonal $r=0$ by this shape data is the real oriented blow-up of that collision diagonal; its local coordinates are $r\ge0$ and smooth shape coordinates. At a critical point, step 1.2 supplies the same form with the Morse coordinate $s$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 For a cluster of several endpoints, first blow up the full collision diagonal and then each proper collision diagonal in its limiting shape space, from larger clusters to smaller ones. Collision subsets in any limiting configuration are either nested or disjoint, so these blow-ups introduce finitely many nonnegative radii $r_C$ and smooth shape coordinates. Each resulting chart is a product of half-lines $r_C\ge0$ and an open smooth coordinate set; transition maps are smooth because they are changes of center, scale, and unit direction. Hence the resolved cell is a manifold with corners. Each added boundary hypersurface is a collision cluster, and its boundary orientation is determined by the outward vector $-\partial_{r_C}$. The original simplex orientation and the local coordinates $s\ge0$ at critical levels give the stated orientations on all remaining faces. [F1, F3, step 2.2, construct]

4.1 Each chamber closure is compact by step 2.1, and real oriented blow-up replaces a closed collision diagonal by a compact sphere of limiting directions without losing compactness. Only finitely many chambers, branch pairings, and endpoint subsets occur at fixed $m$, so their resolved union is compact. The boundary labels from steps 2.1 and 3.1 exhaust its boundary faces; no additional face can occur because every boundary coordinate is either a level-gap, a distance to a critical/global endpoint, or one of the finitely many collision radii. The branch evaluations extend by steps 1.2 and 2.2. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive normal and Seifert-matrix convention]]

[[lem-seifert-pairing-well-defined|Linking, push-off, and cycle-representative independence]]

[[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups|The standard handle normal form for compact surfaces with boundary]]

[[def-oriented-intersection-number|Algebraic intersection number]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, an oriented knot $K$, a connected compact oriented spanning surface $F$, its oriented normal bicollar, and an integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom and supplies the stated countable-choice interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] A compact genus-$g$ surface with one boundary component has first homology free of rank $2g$; after capping its boundary, the supplied oriented normal form is the polygon word $\prod_{h=1}^g[a_h,b_h]$. Step 1.1 constructs the actual smooth handle curves and their intersection matrix. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F2] The Seifert pairing is bilinear on homology classes; linking is symmetric and positive push-offs may move through the positive normal collar. [[lem-seifert-pairing-well-defined]]

[F3] The positive normal is oriented so that $(n,u,v)$ is a positive ambient basis whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]

[F4] The algebraic intersection sign is the local orientation sign of the ordered tangent bases, with the curve factor and surface factor ordered as specified. [[def-oriented-intersection-number]], [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]

[F5] A basis curve $a_j$ is an oriented knot and therefore has a supplied compact oriented spanning surface; with a regular link diagram, linking with that curve is the signed intersection with the surface. [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]], [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]], [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]

[F6] Under countable choice, transversality and relative transversality apply to closed embedded targets, with the relative hypotheses as stated. The boundary-preimage theorem identifies the endpoints after restriction to the original surface halves, and the signed boundary count of a compact oriented one-manifold is zero. Step 2.1 uses boundaryless punctured interiors with protected collars and endpoint neighbourhoods; its unfixed part is compact. [[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], [[prop-relative-transversality-preserves-a-map-on-a-closed-good-region]], [[thm-transverse-preimage-for-manifolds-with-boundary]], [[lem-oriented-boundary-of-a-compact-oriented-one-manifold-has-zero-signed-count]]

[F7] Parametric transversality under countable choice gives a null exceptional set of slice parameters for a smooth family transverse to its target; the complement is dense in a positive-dimensional parameter ball. A smooth bump equal to one near a compact subset and supported in a chosen relatively compact open neighbourhood is supplied by the compact-set manifold bump theorem. Step 2.1 constructs the actual normalized-translation families, verifying their compact support, smallness, and transversality rather than attributing these extra conclusions to a transversality Statement. [[thm-parametric-transversality]], [[prop-a-null-set-has-dense-complement-in-a-positive-dimensional-manifold]], [[lem-manifold-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]]

## Proof

1.1 **Construct the smooth handle basis and its intersection matrix.** Cap the single boundary component by a disk and apply [F1] to obtain the oriented polygon normal form $\prod_{h=1}^g[a_h,b_h]$; remove the capping disk to recover the one-boundary surface. In this model the $h$th handle has two standard core curves, one meridional and one longitudinal, which meet once. Choose their orientations so the ordered tangent pair is positive at that crossing; curves from distinct handles are disjoint. The finite chart and disk-band construction in [F1] realizes this model on the given smooth surface: draw the curves as finite piecewise-smooth arcs in its bands and smooth their finitely many corners in disjoint coordinate disks, leaving their crossings fixed. In the model the surface retracts to the graph of these $2g$ core generators, so their homology classes form an integral basis; the same is true on $F$. Their intersection matrix is therefore the block sum $J_0=\bigoplus_{h=1}^g\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, with zero entries between distinct handles. [F1, construct]

2.1 **Compare positive and negative pushes in the constructed handle basis.** Use the curves $b_i,b_j$ constructed in step 1.1 and let $C_i=b_i\times[-\epsilon,\epsilon]$ be the product strip, oriented by $(n,u)$ so that $\partial C_i=b_i^+-b_i^-$. Write $V^0$ for the Seifert matrix in this basis. By [F5] choose a compact oriented spanning surface $\Sigma_j$ for $b_j$, and choose regular diagrams for the resulting link pairs. For $i=j$ the desired skew-entry identity is $0=0$, and the diagonal surface-intersection entry is zero by the handle model in step 1.1; hence take $i\ne j$ in the intersection construction. The boundary curves $b_i^+,b_i^-,b_j$ are pairwise disjoint. First let $X=\operatorname{Int}\Sigma_j$ with inclusion $f:X\to S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$ and closed target $\partial C_i$. Choose an open collar $G$ of $b_j$ disjoint from this target and protect a smaller collar. Its complement $K=X\setminus G$ is compact. By [F7] choose a smooth $\chi:X\to[0,1]$, equal to one near $K$, compactly supported in a relatively compact open neighbourhood of $K$ avoiding the smaller collar. Then $\chi=0$ only where $f$ is already transverse. For $\|v\|<1/2$ define $\mathcal F(p,v)=(f(p)+\chi(p)v)/\|f(p)+\chi(p)v\|$. Where $\chi>0$ its parameter derivative is $\chi/\|f+\chi v\|$ times the tangent projection onto $TS^3$, hence surjective; where $\chi=0$, $d\chi=0$ and old transversality applies. Thus the family is transverse. By [F7] every small parameter ball has a transverse slice. Compact support and direct differentiation give uniform $C^1$ convergence to the inclusion. A sufficiently small slice therefore extends by the unchanged boundary to an embedded spanning surface: finite compact coordinate subcharts keep a differential lower bound near the diagonal, and the remaining compact pairs keep positive image separation. Denote this surface again by $\Sigma_j$; it is transverse to $\partial C_i$. Let $P=C_i\cap b_j$. These points are finite, and the tangent of $b_j$ is not in $TC_i$ there because the handle curves cross transversely in $F$. Consequently $C_i$ is already transverse to $\Sigma_j$ near $P$. It is also transverse near $\partial C_i\cap\Sigma_j$, since $\Sigma_j$ was made transverse to $\partial C_i$. Put $U=S^3\setminus b_j$ and $X=\operatorname{Int}C_i\setminus P$. The target $Z=\Sigma_j\setminus b_j$ is a closed embedded boundaryless submanifold of $U$: $\Sigma_j$ is compact and all its boundary was removed. The inclusion $X\to U$ is a map between boundaryless manifolds. Protect a closed inner collar of $\partial C_i$ and, at every point of $P$, a sufficiently small punctured closed disk neighbourhood. These are closed subsets of $X$, and the inclusion is already transverse to $Z$ on their neighbourhoods. Choose these neighbourhoods small enough to retain all the original endpoint data. For the inclusion $f:X\to U\subset S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$, choose an open protected region $G$ containing all boundary ends and punctured disks at $P$, on which $f$ is transverse to $Z$; protect smaller such regions. Then $K=X\setminus G$ is compact. Choose a relatively compact open $W\subset X$ containing $K$ and missing the smaller protected regions, and use [F7] to choose $\chi\in[0,1]$ equal to one near $K$, with compact support in $W$. Where $\chi=0$ old transversality holds. Use the explicit family $\mathcal F(p,v)=(f(p)+\chi(p)v)/\|f(p)+\chi(p)v\|$. As above, where $\chi>0$ the parameter derivative surjects onto $TS^3$ and where $\chi=0$ the old derivative is unchanged, so the total family is transverse to $Z$. The compact set $f(\operatorname{supp}\chi)$ has positive distance from $b_j$; choosing $v$ small enough that the uniform displacement is less than half that distance keeps the entire family in $U$. Parametric transversality and the dense-complement statement [F7] now give an arbitrarily small transverse parameter. Direct differentiation on the compact support gives uniform $C^1$ convergence. Finite compact coordinate subcharts and off-diagonal separation, as in the preceding phase, ensure embeddedness. The family is identically the original inclusion on smaller punctured endpoint disks and boundary collars, so extends by the identity at $P$ and across $\partial C_i$, fixes all endpoint intersection germs, and creates no new intersection with $b_j$. Thus the original compact strip and spanning surface have been made transverse, preserving exactly the required endpoint sets. No added double half or disjointness assertion about one is used. Using the boundary-preimage theorem gives a compact oriented one-manifold $C_i\cap\Sigma_j$ with boundary exactly $(\partial C_i\cap\Sigma_j)\cup(C_i\cap b_j)$. Orient its tangent line by requiring $(n_{C_i},n_{\Sigma_j},\ell)$ to be positive in $S^3$, where the first two vectors are the positive normals of the oriented surfaces. The local determinant check at an endpoint on $\partial C_i$ gives boundary sign minus the ordered boundary-curve/surface sign; at an endpoint on $\partial\Sigma_j$ it gives boundary sign plus the ordered surface/boundary-curve sign. Explicitly, the first local model is $C_i=\{z=0,x\ge0\}$ with basis $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$ and boundary tangent $-\partial_y$, and $\Sigma_j=\{y=0\}$ with basis $(\partial_x,\partial_z)$; the intersection tangent is inward $+\partial_x$. The second model is $\Sigma_j=\{z=0,x\ge0\}$ with basis $(-\partial_x,\partial_y)$ and boundary tangent $+\partial_y$, and $C_i=\{y=0\}$ with basis $(\partial_x,\partial_z)$; the intersection tangent is again inward $+\partial_x$. Reversing either surface orientation reverses both signs in its endpoint identity. Thus the zero signed boundary sum is $$0=-(\partial C_i\cdot\Sigma_j)+(C_i\cdot b_j),$$ and therefore $$b_i^+\cdot\Sigma_j-b_i^-\cdot\Sigma_j=C_i\cdot b_j.$$ If $u,v$ are the positive tangents to $b_i,b_j$ at one of their crossings and $n$ is the positive normal to $F$, then the strip tangent basis is $(n,u)$ and adjoining $v$ gives $(n,u,v)$. By [F3] this has the ambient sign of $(u,v)$ in $F$, and [F4] fixes the ordered intersection convention; hence $C_i\cdot b_j=b_i\cdot_F b_j$. Applying [F5] to the transverse link pairs yields $$V^0_{ij}-\operatorname{lk}(b_i^-,b_j)=b_i\cdot_F b_j.$$ [A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, given, construct]

2.2 The pair $(b_i^-,b_j)$ can be translated through the normal collar by $+\epsilon$ while keeping the two curves disjoint; it becomes $(b_i,b_j^+)$. Hence $\operatorname{lk}(b_i^-,b_j)=\operatorname{lk}(b_i,b_j^+)$ by [F2]. Symmetry of linking in [F2] changes the latter to $\operatorname{lk}(b_j^+,b_i)=V^0_{ji}$. Therefore step 2.1 gives $V^0_{ij}-V^0_{ji}=b_i\cdot_F b_j$. [F2, step 2.1, given]

3.1 **Identify the intersection matrix in every basis.** Step 2.2 proves $V^0-(V^0)^T=J_0$. For any other integral basis $a_j=\sum_i b_iP_{ij}$, the change matrix $P$ lies in $\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$. Bilinearity of the Seifert pairing [F2] and of surface intersection gives $V=P^TV^0P$ and $J_F=P^TJ_0P$. Hence $V-V^T=J_F$, $J_F^T=-J_F$, and $\det J_F=(\det P)^2\det J_0=1$. If $g=0$, the matrices are empty and the determinant is the empty product $1$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The orientation sign can be checked in a local oriented chart: when the positive normal is the first vector, the strip orientation $(n,u)$ and the surface intersection orientation $(u,v)$ give the same sign. The proof uses that orientation check in step 2.1; the schematic below is not a proof premise.

  \draw[thick,->] (0,-0.6) -- (0.45,0.65) node[above] {$v$};

  \node at (0,-1.55) {$F\text{ tangent plane}$};

    \draw[->,red,thick] (1.4,-0.9) -- (1.4,0.95) node[above] {$n$};
    \draw[blue,thick] (0.55,0.58) -- (2.25,0.58) node[right] {$a_i^+$};
    \draw[blue,thick] (0.55,-0.58) -- (2.25,-0.58) node[right] {$a_i^-$};

## Statement

Let $A,B\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ and put $a=\operatorname{tr}A$, $b=\operatorname{tr}B$, $c=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$. Every word matrix in $A^{\pm1},B^{\pm1}$ is a linear combination of $I,A,B,AB$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Z[a,b,c]$, computed by finite word induction. Consequently its trace is a polynomial in those three traces. If $a=b=x$ and $c=y$, the coefficients specialize to $\mathbb Z[x,y]$. The assertion includes scalar, unipotent, reducible and irreducible pairs and uses no choice axiom.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two determinant-one complex $2\times2$ matrices, their indicated traces and any finite word in the matrices and their inverses.

[F1] For a $2\times2$ matrix $T$, the entrywise identity $T^2-(\operatorname{tr}T)T+(\det T)I=0$ follows by multiplying its four entries.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to $A$ and $B$. Since both determinants are one, $$A^{-1}=aI-A,\qquad B^{-1}=bI-B,\qquad A^2=aA-I,\qquad B^2=bB-I.$$ Thus it suffices to reduce positive words. Apply [F1] also to $A+B$ and subtract the identities for $A,B$. The entrywise determinant polarization is $\det(A+B)-\det A-\det B=ab-c$. Hence $$AB+BA=aB+bA+(c-ab)I,$$ an identity valid without any genericity or independence of the four matrices. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The span of $I,A,B,AB$ over $\mathbb Z[a,b,c]$ is stable under right multiplication by $A$ and $B$. Besides the products already displayed in step 1.1, the needed two are $$ABA=cA+B-bI,\qquad ABB=bAB-A.$$ For the first multiply the polarized identity by $A$ on the left and use $A^2=aA-I$; the second is $AB^2=A(bB-I)$. The other products are $IA=A$, $IB=B$, $AA=aA-I$, $AB=AB$, $BA=-AB+aB+bA+(c-ab)I$, $BB=bB-I$. This is the complete multiplication table needed for one-letter extension of a word. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Start the empty word at $I$ and apply the table of step 2.1 once per positive letter. Replace each inverse letter by its two-term expression from step 1.1, or use linearity to extend that same table to inverse letters. Induction gives a finite coefficient expression for every word. Taking traces uses only $\operatorname{tr}I=2$, $\operatorname{tr}A=a$, $\operatorname{tr}B=b$, $\operatorname{tr}AB=c$, proving the trace assertion. Substituting $a=b=x,c=y$ gives the stated equal-trace specialization. No matrix-basis independence, diagonalization or infinite choice of word expressions is required. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, induction, algebra] ∎
