## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $A\subseteq H_1$, and let $g:A\to H_2$. If a continuous, nondecreasing, concave function $\omega_\star:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ satisfies $\omega_\star(0)=0$ and
$$\|g(x)-g(y)\|_{H_2}\le\omega_\star(\|x-y\|_{H_1})\qquad(x,y\in A),$$
then the Hilbert-valued same-modulus extension theorem asserts that there is $\widetilde g:H_1\to H_2$ extending $g$ and satisfying the same inequality for every $x,y\in H_1$.

For the EIT inverse map, take the kernel input space to be $L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)$ viewed as a real Hilbert space with its usual complex $L^2$ norm. If IP-45 gives $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_2\le C_0[\log(1/\min\{\delta,t_0\})]^{-\rho}$ for $\delta=\|\dot\Lambda_\gamma-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}\|$, and the NTD kernel estimate transfers $\delta\le C_1\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_2^{1/2}$, then after decreasing $t_0$ and, if necessary, enlarging $C_0$ the concave modulus
$$\omega_\star(0)=0,\qquad \omega_\star(s)=C_0\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{C_1\sqrt{s},t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(s>0)$$
is an admissible modulus for that inverse map and can be extended by the Hilbert same-modulus theorem to the whole underlying real Hilbert space of complex-valued kernels.

## Statement references

[[thm-ip-calderon-logarithmic-l2-stability|The inverse stability estimate on the exact conductivity class.]]

[[lem-ip-ntd-smoothing-and-hilbert-schmidt-kernel-bound|The required NTD-kernel to DN-operator comparison.]]

[Benyamini–Lindenstrauss, Chapter 1, Theorem 1.12 and Proposition 1.13](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/048)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the real Hilbert spaces, subset, map and modulus in the Statement, and the EIT class data when applying the second paragraph.

[F1] IP-45 states $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_2\le C_0\omega(\|\dot\Lambda_\gamma-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}\|)$ with a saturated logarithmic modulus and $\omega(0)=0$. ([[thm-ip-calderon-logarithmic-l2-stability]])

[F2] For any concave nondecreasing modulus $\omega$ vanishing continuously at zero, source points $x_i$ and target points $y_i$ satisfying $\|y_i-y_j\|\le\omega(\|x_i-x_j\|)$ have $\bigcap_i\overline B(y_i,\omega(\|x_i-x\|))\ne\varnothing$ for every additional source point $x$. This includes arbitrary index sets and zero-radius balls. ([[lem-ip-concave-modulus-hilbert-ball-intersection]])

[F3] The actual kernel comparison is $\delta\le C_1s^{1/2}$, where $s$ is the $L^2$ kernel distance. ([[lem-ip-ntd-smoothing-and-hilbert-schmidt-kernel-bound]])

[F4] Under the Axiom of Choice, a nonempty poset whose every chain has an upper bound has a maximal element. ([[thm-zorn]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice supplies Zorn's lemma and implies the Countable Choice used by the Hilbert-ball and EIT interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the Statement.

1.1 Consider the set of pairs $(B,h)$ where $A\subseteq B\subseteq H_1$ and $h:B\to H_2$ extends $g$ and satisfies $\|h(u)-h(v)\|\le\omega_\star(\|u-v\|)$ for all $u,v\in B$. Order it by graph inclusion. It is nonempty, since $(A,g)$ is in it. Every nonempty chain has as upper bound the union of its graphs: every two of its domain points occur together in one member of the chain, so the same modulus inequality holds for their union. The empty chain has $(A,g)$ as an upper bound. By [F4] and [A1] there is a maximal pair $(B,h)$. [A1, F4, given, construct, choose]

1.2 For the EIT application first arrange $t_0\le e^{-(\rho+1)}$. If the original IP-45 constants have a larger cutoff, decrease it and enlarge $C_0$ if needed: the uniform class diameter is at most $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$, so taking $C_0\ge2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$ covers all DN distances above the new cutoff, while increasing $C_0$ preserves the old small-distance estimate. For $0<s<(t_0/C_1)^2$, put $L(s)=\log(1/(C_1\sqrt{s}))$ and $\varphi(s)=C_0L(s)^{-\rho}$. Then $\varphi'(s)=C_0\rho/(2sL(s)^{\rho+1})>0$ and $\varphi''(s)=C_0\rho[\rho+1-2L(s)]/(4s^2L(s)^{\rho+2})\le0$. At the cutoff it joins continuously to a constant and its derivative drops to zero; at zero it tends to zero. Thus the displayed $\omega_\star$ is continuous, nondecreasing and concave on the entire nonnegative half-line. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 If $B\ne H_1$, fix $x\in H_1\setminus B$. Apply [F2] to the source family $(u)_{u\in B}$ and target family $(h(u))_{u\in B}$. It gives a point $y\in H_2$ satisfying $\|y-h(u)\|\le\omega_\star(\|x-u\|)$ for every $u\in B$. Adding $h(x)=y$ gives a strictly larger admissible graph, contradicting maximality. This also covers $B=\varnothing$, since [F2]'s empty intersection is $H_2$, which contains zero. Thus $B=H_1$ and $\widetilde g=h$ proves the full same-modulus extension theorem for arbitrary real Hilbert spaces and arbitrary subsets. [F2, step 1.1, given, choose, algebra]

3.1 For an exact conductivity pair put $s=\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_{L^2(M\times M;\mathbb C)}$. By [F1], [F3] and monotonicity, $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_2\le C_0[\log(1/\min\{C_1\sqrt{s},t_0\})]^{-\rho}=\omega_\star(s)$ when $s>0$; if $s=0$, [F3] gives zero DN distance and [F1] gives equal conductivities. The operators $\mathscr R_\gamma$ and $C_M^{r_d/2}$ in the smoothed observation commute with complex conjugation: the weak Neumann problem has real coefficients and unique mean-zero representatives, while the real boundary Laplacian has conjugation-invariant eigenspaces and the spectral multiplier is real and constant on each eigenspace. Thus $\widetilde A_\gamma$ commutes with conjugation. Let $\kappa_\gamma$ be its unique complex $L^2$ kernel from the Hilbert–Schmidt kernel theorem. The kernel $\overline{\kappa_\gamma}$ also represents $\widetilde A_\gamma$, since its integral operator sends $f$ to $\overline{\widetilde A_\gamma\overline f}=\widetilde A_\gamma f$. Uniqueness of the kernel gives $\overline{\kappa_\gamma}=\kappa_\gamma$ almost everywhere. In particular, the exact kernel image lies in the real-valued subspace, while it is still regarded as a subset of the underlying real Hilbert space of complex-valued kernels. Therefore the exact-data inverse is well-defined and has this modulus on that real Hilbert space. Step 2.1 applies there and in the real conductivity $L^2$ Hilbert space, with concavity verified in step 1.2, to give its whole-space extension with exactly the same modulus. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For any two smooth oriented knots $K$ and $J$ in $S^3$, the bridge number of their oriented connected sum satisfies
$$b(K\#J)=b(K)+b(J)-1.$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number|Bridge number from local maxima of the fixed height]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The oriented connected-sum convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and smooth oriented knots $K,J\subset S^3$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written AC$_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The bridge-number minima are over nonempty subsets of $\mathbb N$ and are attained, and changing the connected-sum datum preserves the oriented knot class. [[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]

[F2] The connected sum is represented by removing a small trivial ball-arc neighborhood from each summand and gluing the two boundary spheres with the fixed arc-matching convention. [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

[F3] The essential-annulus normalization for the fixed bridge pair is [[lem-bridge-sphere-normalization]]. Its two final disk-intersection arcs end on $P\cap S$, away from the knot.

[F4] A knot exterior has $H_1(E;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. [[lem-knot-exterior-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]

[F5] Knot exteriors are irreducible under countable choice, and an incompressible boundary-compressible annulus in an irreducible smooth torus-boundary manifold is boundary-parallel. [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]], [[lem-boundary-compressible-annulus-is-boundary-parallel]]

[F6] Smooth Schoenflies gives an ambient isotopy of a smooth sphere to the equator with compatible ball-side parameters. Disk-window attachment and removal preserve the displayed ball type. [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]]

[F7] Compact smooth embedding isotopies extend ambiently. [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[F8] A two-puncture sphere determines the stated oriented connected-sum factors by boundary caps; the unknot is the connected-sum identity and has bridge number one. [[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum]], [[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]], [[thm-bridge-one-is-unknot]]

## Proof

1.1 We first justify using bridge spheres for the height-based minimum in [F1]. In the product of regular height levels $S^2\times(-1,1)$, a maximum can be raised without changing the number or kinds of critical points: take a small cap containing only that maximum, perturb its horizontal location so that its central vertical ray misses the rest of the knot, narrow the cap inside its original small chart to fit a tube about that ray, and lift it along the ray, lengthening its two descending ends monotonically. The horizontal location is available arbitrarily close to the initial cap: the projection of the remaining finite collection of compact smooth arcs has empty interior, as follows by covering each arc by finitely many intervals of derivative bound $C$, whose projected images lie in disks of radius $C\delta$ and have total area tending to zero as $\delta\to0$. Compact disjointness then gives a narrow tube about the ray avoiding the rest of the knot; its two thin parallel sides are the lengthened ends. A horizontal cap perturbation and the subsequent vertical move have embedding tracks with no new extrema; the moving cap has the translated local quadratic maximum and the ends have strictly positive or negative height derivative. Extend with [F7]. Do this finitely many times, choosing distinct rays avoiding earlier cap tracks, until all maxima lie above a regular level above all minima. The upper and lower pieces are trivial tangles with simultaneous disjoint spanning disks: sweep their endpoints between successive critical heights, extending the finite point motions on each level sphere by disjoint small coordinate vector fields. Transport disjoint joining arcs by these level isotopies. At a cap choose its joining arc in its small cap chart, away from the finitely many earlier arcs (move those arcs off that chart by a level isotopy before the birth). Their swept traces, capped at the extrema, give pairwise disjoint disks. Conversely, for any smooth bridge sphere and displayed disks, [F6] first carries the sphere to a regular level. Push each bridge through its own disk to a thin collar of its foot; in disk parameters use a positive rounded arch whose height is $\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ above, and $-\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ below, with compatible endpoint collars. The disjoint same-side disks allow these isotopies simultaneously; [F7] extends them, and rounding at endpoints gives exactly one maximum per upper arc and one minimum per lower arc. Thus the minimum number of upper arcs over bridge spheres is exactly the height-defined $b$. In particular a minimum-height representative supplies a bridge sphere with $b$ upper arcs, and any factor bridge sphere with $n$ upper arcs gives $b(\text{factor})\le n$. [A1, F1, F6, F7, construct]

1.2 Choose bridge representatives realizing $b(K)$ and $b(J)$, which is possible by [F1] and step 1.1. Each comes with its bridge sphere and disjoint upper and lower bridge-spanning disks. [A1, F1, step 1.1, choose]

2.1 Choose one point of each knot on its bridge sphere where an upper bridge arc and a lower bridge arc meet. Take product-coordinate balls around the two points so each ball meets the sphere in a disk, the knot in one short arc crossing that disk once, and each of the two incident bridge-spanning disks in a half-disk. Remove the ball interiors and glue the punctured spheres by the connected-sum map from [F2]. The two selected upper bridge arcs join into one proper upper arc, and the two selected lower bridge arcs join into one proper lower arc. The new upper spanning disk is the union of the two punctured upper disks and the gluing rectangle; two disks joined along one boundary interval form a disk. The same construction gives the lower spanning disk. Every unselected bridge arc and disk remains unchanged and disjoint from these disks. Thus the connected-sum position has $b(K)+b(J)-1$ upper arcs, so $b(K\#J)\le b(K)+b(J)-1$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 If either factor is the unknot, [F8] gives equality immediately. Suppose therefore both are nontrivial. Choose a bridge sphere $S$ of $L=K\#J$ with $b=b(L)$ upper arcs, by step 1.1. Transport the connected-sum construction's two-puncture sphere through the representative isotopy; this gives a smooth sphere $P$ cutting $L$ into the specified factors. Choose a sufficiently small product tube adapted to its two transverse punctures and form $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$. The annulus core is a positive or negative meridian in the tube: both its boundary components bound the normal disks $P\cap N(L)$ and its core is homotopic within $A$ to either boundary. By [F4], composing $\pi_1(A)=\mathbb Z\to\pi_1(E_L)$ with abelianization sends its generator to $\pm1\in\mathbb Z$. The inclusion is therefore injective. [F1, F2, F4, F8, step 1.1, construct]

3.2 There is no boundary compression of $A$. If there were, [F5] would give a parallelism to one of the two annuli $A_0$ on the boundary torus between its meridional boundaries. This implies that one factor is the unknot, as can be checked with the markings: write the tube over the corresponding subinterval of the core knot as $D^2\times I$, with side $A_0=\partial D^2\times I$ and end disks the two disks $P\cap N(L)$. Attach the annulus parallelism to this side, retaining its rim collars. It merely enlarges the radial disk coordinate in each $I$-fiber, so the result is a ball with boundary the original $P$ after rounding. Its knot arc is the core $\{0\}\times I$, and it cobounds with an arc on that ball's boundary a disk given by a fixed radial interval times $I$, rounded at its ends. Capping this arc on $P$ produces an unknot. The same construction works for either complementary annulus of the torus; it uses its actual product parameter, not just a homological slope. By [F8] the resulting unknot is one of the given factors, contradicting nontriviality. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold for this particular $P$, and we may apply its isotopy and disk changes without changing $(L,S)$ or the specified factors. [F3, F5, F6, F8, step 3.1, construct]

4.1 In the resulting normal form $P\cap S=C$ is one circle disjoint from $L$. The two disks $P_\pm=P\cap B_\pm$ each contain one puncture. Indeed the two disk-intersection arcs of [F3] have their puncture endpoints one on each side, as in that lemma's final normalization. Each $P_\pm$ is a proper disk cutting its bridge ball into two balls: cap it by either of the two disks on $\partial B_\pm$ bounded by its rim, round, and apply [F6]; the side not containing the exterior of $B_\pm$ is the required ball. Their collars give compatible markings. Let $S_1,S_2$ be the disks on $S$ bounded by $C$, labelled by the two sides of $P$, and put $r_i=|L\cap S_i|$. Then $r_1+r_2=2b$. In each original bridge ball exactly one bridge arc crosses $P_\pm$: it is the arc carrying its unique puncture. Its two endpoints on $S$ lie on opposite sides of $C$, because the bridge crosses that separating disk once. Every other bridge arc is wholly on one side. Consequently $r_i$ is odd. [F3, F6, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

4.2 Cap each of the two cut ball-arcs of $L$ by a boundary arc on $P$ running from the upper puncture to the lower puncture and crossing $C$ once, chosen as the two type-I traces joined by an arc of $C$ between their distinct foot endpoints, then rounded slightly in the collar of $C$ so that it crosses $C$ transversely just once. Push the two caps into their respective boundary collars. On each side this cap is a trivial ball-arc meeting the capped bridge sphere $S_i\cup$(cap disk) once. Its upper and lower portions extend the severed bridge arcs. Every uncut bridge disk remains in its original region. Each of the two cut bridge disks is cut along its one trace into two disks; on each side join its disk piece to the narrow cap strip. This is a disk attached along one boundary interval, so gives a spanning disk for the extended upper or lower arc. Choose the cap strips in disjoint small quadrant collars of the traces; other disks miss them, and on a given side all disk pieces were originally disjoint. Thus these are simultaneous disjoint spanning-disk systems. The upper and lower ambient pieces are balls: attach the cap half-balls along the displayed windows on $P_\pm$ and use [F6]. We have therefore constructed actual bridge spheres for the two specified oriented factors, not merely diagrams with a proposed number of bridges. Each has $r_i+1$ knot endpoints on its sphere, the extra endpoint being the single crossing of the cap. It follows that their upper arc counts are $n_i=(r_i+1)/2$, and $n_1+n_2=b+1$. Cap orientation is chosen to close the original oriented arc, so [F8] identifies the factors with $K,J$, up to their harmless interchange. [F3, F6, F8, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Step 1.1 applied to the two factor bridge spheres gives $b(K)\le n_1$ and $b(J)\le n_2$. Hence $b(K)+b(J)-1\le n_1+n_2-1=b=b(K\#J)$. Together with step 2.1 and the unknot case in step 3.1, this proves the formula for every pair of smooth oriented knots in the Statement. The constructions use finitely many extrema, disks, cuts and collars; their smooth extension and Schoenflies uses are precisely the stated countable-choice suppliers. [F1, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.2, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The schematic shows the local gluing at one bridge-sphere endpoint. The two selected upper disks join along a boundary strip to one upper disk, and the lower pair joins in the same way. The drawing records only the local count reduction by one; the lower-bound proof does not rely on it.

## Definition

Let $A$ be an indeterminate and let $\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$ be the Laurent
polynomial ring in $A$. A **nonempty unoriented regular link diagram** is the
finite planar projection and over/under data of a regular oriented link diagram
after its strand arrows are forgotten. Its finite crossing set is denoted
$C(D)$, and at least one closed component is required. The empty link diagram is
outside this definition.

At a crossing use the following local chart: the over-strand runs from the
southwest endpoint to the northeast endpoint and is drawn continuously over the
under-strand, which runs from northwest to southeast with a gap at the
intersection. Horizontal-right followed by vertical-up is the positive
orientation of this displayed chart. In this chart the **A-smoothing** joins the
two left endpoints and joins the two right endpoints; the **B-smoothing** joins
the two top endpoints and joins the two bottom endpoints. These labels are
attached to this displayed chart and are transported by orientation-preserving
changes of local coordinates. Thus turning right from an entering underpassing
half-strand gives the A-smoothing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.72, line cap=round, line join=round]
  \begin{scope}
    \draw[thick] (-1,1)--(-0.14,0.14);
    \draw[thick] (0.14,-0.14)--(1,-1);
    \draw[very thick] (-1,-1)--(1,1);
    \node at (0,-1.45) {crossing};
  \end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[xshift=3.4cm]
    \draw[thick] (-1,1) .. controls (-0.45,0.35) and (-0.45,-0.35) .. (-1,-1);
    \draw[thick] (1,1) .. controls (0.45,0.35) and (0.45,-0.35) .. (1,-1);
    \node at (0,-1.45) {$A$-smoothing, weight $A$};
  \end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[xshift=6.8cm]
    \draw[thick] (-1,1) .. controls (-0.35,0.45) and (0.35,0.45) .. (1,1);
    \draw[thick] (-1,-1) .. controls (-0.35,-0.45) and (0.35,-0.45) .. (1,-1);
    \node at (0,-1.45) {$B$-smoothing, weight $A^{-1}$};
  \end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

For a state $S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$, let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ be the numbers of
A- and B-smoothings, and let $|S|$ be the number of closed circles in the
crossingless diagram obtained by performing all smoothings. Set
$$\delta:=-A^2-A^{-2}$$
and define the **Kauffman bracket** of $D$ by
$$\langle D\rangle:=\sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}} A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}\in\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}].$$
Because $D$ is nonempty, every complete smoothing has $|S|\ge1$, so the loop
exponent is nonnegative. A crossingless $k$-component unlink with $k\ge1$ has
bracket $\delta^{k-1}$.

## Definition references

[[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram|Regular oriented link diagrams]]

[[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams|Planar isotopy of link diagrams]]

[Kauffman, *An Invariant of Regular Isotopy* (1990), §III, printed pp. 430–432](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kauffman/IRH.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §§4.1 and 4.3](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Funar, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter 3, §1.1](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty unoriented regular link diagram $D$ with finite crossing set $C(D)$.

[F1] A regular oriented link diagram has finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and an over/under datum at every crossing; forgetting the strand arrows leaves the input used here ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

[F2] A planar isotopy is an orientation-preserving smooth family of planar diffeomorphisms that transports the diagram and its over/under data and creates or deletes no crossings ([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]).

## Proof

1.1 Since $C(D)$ is finite by [F1], the set of all functions $S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$ is finite with exactly $2^{|C(D)|}$ elements. Each state replaces every crossing in a finite collection of disjoint crossing disks by one of the two specified pairings. The resulting finite 1-manifold has at least one circle because the input diagram has at least one component. Hence each term $A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}$ is a defined Laurent polynomial. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 The displayed sum is indexed by the set of states itself, so reordering a list of crossings merely gives a bijective reindexing of the same finite sum. By [F2], a planar isotopy carries crossings, local charts, states, and resulting circles bijectively to those of the isotoped diagram, preserving $a(S)$, $b(S)$, and $|S|$. Therefore the formula is well-defined on planar-isotopy classes and is choice-free. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $D_T$ be the standard three-crossing trefoil diagram with maximal underarcs
$a,b,c$. In cyclic order its crossing data are: overarc $c$ with underarcs
$a,b$; overarc $b$ with underarcs $c,a$; and overarc $a$ with underarcs
$b,c$. Thus its Fox equations are
$2a=b+c$, $2b=c+a$, and $2c=a+b$. Let $D_U$ be the standard one-arc,
zero-crossing unknot diagram. Then $D_T$ has exactly $9$ Fox $3$-colorings,
of which three are constant and six are nonconstant, while $D_U$ has exactly
$3$ colorings. Under the oriented Reidemeister theorem and the quandle-coloring
invariance result, these counts are knot invariants under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

The following diagram is the closure of the three-crossing two-strand braid;
the crossing data in the first paragraph, rather than the drawing, specifies

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The diagrams and crossing data in the Example, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[F1] [[alg-dihedral-fox-colorings]]: each crossing imposes $2x_o-x_i-x_j=0$ over $\mathbb F_p$.

[F2] [[thm-dihedral-fox-colorings-terminate-and-are-correct]]: the algorithm returns exactly the assignments satisfying the crossing equations.

[F3] [[thm-quandle-colorings-are-reidemeister-invariant]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, quandle coloring sets of diagrams of the same oriented link are bijective.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ supplies a choice function for every sequence of nonempty sets.

## Verification

1.1 For $D_T$, [F1] gives the three equations $2a-b-c=0$, $2b-c-a=0$, and $2c-a-b=0$. Modulo $3$, each left-hand side equals $2(a+b+c)$, so the system is equivalent to $a+b+c=0$. Choose $a,b$ freely and set $c=-a-b$; there are $3^2=9$ solutions. Exactly the three choices $a=b=c$ are constant, leaving six nonconstant colorings. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], these nine solutions are exactly the outputs of the Fox algorithm. The one-arc diagram $D_U$ has no crossing equations, so its single arc receives any of the three colors and it has three colorings. [F2, given, step 1.1]

3.1 The Reidemeister coloring theorem [F3] applies under [A1], so the counts just computed depend only on the represented knot types. ## Statement

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

## Statement references

[[def-hilbert-space|a Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space]]

[[def-separable-space|separable means having an at most countable dense subset]]

[[def-ip-prior-on-a-forward-domain|a prior on a forward domain requires full measure on that domain]]

[[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space|Borel Gaussian random elements are Borel measurable and have centered normal continuous-linear projections]]

[[lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summable-gaussian-series|square-summable independent Gaussian series have the corresponding scalar normal law under countable choice]]

[[def-countable-choice|the Axiom of Countable Choice]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice|the Axiom of Choice]]

[[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space|under countable choice, every bounded Hilbert-space functional is represented by an inner product vector]]

[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs|the covariance operator and covariance-induced RKHS of a Banach Gaussian]]

[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined|well-definedness of the covariance and RKHS construction]]

[[thm-fernique-integrability-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law|Fernique exponential-square integrability]]

[[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration|bounded linear functionals commute with Bochner integration]]

[Dashti and Stuart, §2.4, Theorem 2.4 and proof, full text](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.6989)

[Giné and Nickl, §§4.2–4.4.1, full book](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~nickl/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Separable real Hilbert spaces $H_0,H_1$ with the stated continuous inclusion and common orthogonal basis; positive weights $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2$; a probability space carrying independent real variables $\xi_j$ with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$; nonnegative $\lambda_j$ with $\sum_j\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. For the Gaussian conclusions, also assume each $\xi_j\sim N(0,1)$. AC and countable choice are assumed only for the stated Gaussian-law, covariance, and exponential-integrability branches.

[A1] AC is required by the library's Borel Gaussian, covariance/RKHS, and Fernique interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] Countable choice is used only by [F3] for scalar Gaussian-law identification and by [F8] for Hilbert-space Riesz representation. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] A prior on a declared Borel forward-map domain $D$ is a Borel probability $\mu$ on the parameter space with $\mu(D)=1$. [[def-ip-prior-on-a-forward-domain]]

[F2] A centered Borel Gaussian random element is Borel measurable and every continuous linear functional of it has a centered normal law. [[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space]]

[F3] Under countable choice, if independent standard normal variables have real coefficients with square-summable squares and their finite sums converge in probability to a supplied real random variable, that limit has the centered normal law with variance equal to the sum of coefficient squares. [[lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summable-gaussian-series]]

[F4] For nonnegative measurable $Y_N\uparrow Y$, monotone convergence gives $\mathbb E Y_N\uparrow\mathbb E Y$. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F5] Under AC, a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable Banach space has an exponential-square norm moment for some positive exponent. [[thm-fernique-integrability-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law]]

[F6] Under AC, the covariance operator of a centered Borel Gaussian is $C\ell=\mathbb E[\ell(S)S]$ and its covariance RKHS is the completion of the quotient by the covariance nullspace. [[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]]

[F7] Under AC, the Bochner covariance and the continuous injective embedding of the completed covariance RKHS into the Banach space are well-defined. [[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]]

[F8] Under countable choice, every bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space is the inner product with a unique vector, preserving the dual norm. [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

[F9] A bounded linear map commutes with the Bochner integral of an integrable vector-valued function. [[thm-bounded-linear-maps-commute-with-bochner-integration]]

## Proof

**Given:** $H_0,H_1,(e_j),(w_j),(\xi_j),(\lambda_j)$ as in the Statement, and AC and countable choice for the Gaussian-law, covariance, and Fernique conclusions.

1.1 Put $Y_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_jw_j\xi_j^2$ and $Y=\lim_NY_N$. The supplied second moments give $\mathbb EY_N=\sum_{j\le N}\lambda_jw_j$, so [F4] gives $\mathbb EY=\sum_j\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Therefore $Y<\infty$ almost surely: if $\mathbb P(Y=\infty)>0$, then $\mathbb EY\ge M\mathbb P(Y=\infty)$ for every $M>0$, contradicting finiteness. On the full-measure event $\Omega_0=\{Y<\infty\}$, orthogonality gives $\|S_m-S_n\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{n<j\le m}\lambda_jw_j\xi_j^2\to0$ as $m,n\to\infty$. Completeness of $H_1$ gives an almost-sure limit. This convergence argument uses no choice axiom. [F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Define $S$ to be this limit on $\Omega_0$ and $0$ on its measurable null complement. Each $S_N$ is Borel measurable. For any proper open $O\subset H_1$, let $C=H_1\setminus O$. The scalar functions $d(S_N,C)$ are measurable and on $\Omega_0$ converge to $d(S,C)$; because $S\in O$ exactly when $d(S,C)>0$, the set $S^{-1}(O)$ is $\Omega_0\cap\{\liminf_Nd(S_N,C)>0\}$, with $\Omega_0^c$ added exactly when $0\in O$. The liminf condition is a countable combination of measurable scalar inequalities, so $S^{-1}(O)$ is measurable. The cases $O=\varnothing$ and $O=H_1$ are immediate. Thus $S$ is Borel measurable. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 On $\Omega_0$, $\|S-S_N\|_{H_1}^2=Y-Y_N$. Since $\mathbb P(\Omega_0^c)=0$, [F4] and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E\|S-S_N\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j>N}\lambda_jw_j\to0$ and $\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_j\lambda_jw_j$. Hence $S_N\to S$ in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For any $\ell\in H_1^*$, let $z\in H_1$ be its Riesz vector and write $\ell_z(x)=\langle x,z\rangle$, so $\ell=\ell_z$. Set $c_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\ell_z(e_j)=\sqrt{\lambda_jw_j}\,\langle f_j,z\rangle$. Since $|\langle f_j,z\rangle|\le\|z\|$, $\sum_jc_j^2\le\|z\|^2\sum_j\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. By step 3.1, $\ell_z(S_N)\to\ell_z(S)$ in $L^2$, hence in probability; [F3] makes $\ell_z(S)$ centered normal with variance $\sum_jc_j^2$. Together with step 2.1 and [F2], this proves that $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element. For Riesz vectors $z,y\in H_1$, independence, centering, and unit variances give $\mathbb E[\ell_z(S_N)\ell_y(S_N)]=\sum_{j\le N}\lambda_jw_j\langle f_j,z\rangle\langle f_j,y\rangle$. The L² convergence from step 3.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz let these expectations pass to the limit, so the covariance form is $Q(\ell_z,\ell_y)=\sum_j\lambda_jw_j\langle f_j,z\rangle\langle f_j,y\rangle$. The series $v_z:=\sum_j\lambda_jw_j\langle f_j,z\rangle f_j$ converges in $H_1$, since $(\lambda_jw_j)$ is bounded and $(\langle f_j,z\rangle)$ is square-summable. Thus $Q(\ell_z,\ell_y)=\langle v_z,y\rangle$. By [F6]–[F7] the covariance Bochner integral exists, and [F9] shows that applying any Riesz coordinate functional commutes with that integral. Hence $v_z$ is the Riesz vector of $C\ell_z$, so the covariance operator transported to $H_1$ by Riesz is diagonal in $(f_j)$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, whose sum is finite. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F6, F7, F8, F9, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 If $D\subset H_1$ is a Borel forward-map domain with $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law $\mu$ of $S$ satisfies $\mu(D)=\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$. The definition [F1] therefore makes $\mu$ a prior on $D$. [F1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The space $H_1$ is a real separable Banach space, and step 4.1 supplies a centered Borel Gaussian random element in it. Under AC, [F5] applies and gives $a>0$ with $\mathbb E\exp(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2)<\infty$. [A1, F5, step 4.1] ∎

      url: https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/weibel/03-tor_and_ext.pdf

## Statement

Let $R$ be a unital ring with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors. Suppose both Ore conditions hold: any two nonzero elements have a nonzero common right multiple and a nonzero common left multiple. Let $R\subseteq K$ be a unital embedding into a division ring such that every element of $K$ is a right fraction $as^{-1}$ with $a\in R$ and $0\ne s\in R$.

For every right $R$-module $M$, the right $K$-module $M\otimes_RK$ is represented by fractions $[m,s]$ with $m\in M$ and $0\ne s\in R$, corresponding to $m\otimes s^{-1}$. The equality criterion is
$$[m,s]=[n,t]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exist }0\ne u,v\in R\text{ with }su=tv\text{ and }mu=nv.$$
In particular, $[m,s]=0$ if and only if $ma=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$. Thus the kernel of $M\to M\otimes_RK$, $m\mapsto m\otimes1$, is exactly the set of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, and $M\otimes_RK=0$ if and only if every element of $M$ has a nonzero right annihilator.

The functor $-\otimes_RK$ is exact on arbitrary right $R$-modules, so $K$ is flat as a left $R$-module. For every chain complex $C_\bullet$ of right $R$-modules, the canonical map gives a natural isomorphism
$$H_i(C_\bullet)\otimes_RK\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H_i(C_\bullet\otimes_RK)$$
for every integer $i$. No finite-generation, finite-presentation or boundedness assumption on the modules or complexes is required.

The corresponding left-module assertions also hold: $K$ is flat as a right $R$-module, $1\otimes m$ is zero in $K\otimes_RM$ precisely when $am=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$, and $K\otimes_R-$ commutes with the homology of arbitrary left-module chain complexes. All assertions require no choice axiom.

## Statement references

[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]

[[def-left-and-right-flat-modules-over-an-arbitrary-ring]]

[[def-chain-complex-with-coefficients-by-tensoring]]

[[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]

[[def-opposite-ring]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Exactly the ring embedding, two Ore conditions and right-fraction property in the Statement.

[F1] Right modules are unital additive groups with the right distributivity and associativity axioms; division rings are unital rings in which every nonzero element is invertible ([[def-ring]], [[def-division-ring]], [[def-left-and-right-modules]]).

[F2] A balanced biadditive map from a right module and a left module satisfies $b(mr,k)=b(m,rk)$. The tensor product is the free abelian group on pairs modulo these additivity and balancing relations, and its elements are finite sums of elementary tensors ([[def-balanced-and-bilinear-maps]], [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

[F3] Exactness means image equals kernel; a left module is flat when tensoring it with right modules is exact, and the right-flat definition has the sides reversed ([[def-exact-and-short-exact-sequences-of-modules]], [[def-left-and-right-flat-modules-over-an-arbitrary-ring]]).

[F4] Tensoring a chain complex means tensoring its terms and differentials, and homology is cycles modulo boundaries ([[def-chain-complex-with-coefficients-by-tensoring]], [[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]).

[F5] Opposite multiplication reverses factors while leaving addition and identity unchanged ([[def-opposite-ring]]).

## Proof

**Given:** An arbitrary right $R$-module $M$. Put $S=R\setminus\{0\}$.

1.1 On pairs $(m,s)\in M\times S$, impose the relation $(m,s)\sim(n,t)$ if $su=tv$ and $mu=nv$ for some $u,v\in S$. The right Ore condition supplies the common denominators. Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. For transitivity, suppose $su=tv$, $mu=nv$, and $tp=wq$, $np=lq$. Choose $e,f\in S$ with $ve=pf$. Then $sue=tve=tpf=wqf$ and $mue=nve=npf=lqf$, proving $(m,s)\sim(l,w)$. The needed products remain nonzero because $R$ has no zero divisors. Thus this defines a quotient set $L(M)$. Write its elements as $[m,s]$. Every pair has the same class as its refinement $(ma,sa)$ for $a\in S$. Moreover two equivalent pairs have a refinement with the same denominator and the same numerator, directly from the relation. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Define $[m,s]+[n,t]=[mu+nv,su]$ whenever $su=tv$ with $u,v\in S$. This is independent of the common denominator: if $su'=tv'=w'$, refine $w=su$ and $w'$ to $wc=w'c'$; cancellation by the nonzero $s$ and $t$ gives $uc=u'c'$ and $vc=v'c'$, so the two numerator sums agree after refinement. Replacing an input pair by a refinement also leaves the sum unchanged: refine the chosen common denominator and the refined input denominator once more and use the same cancellation argument. Since every equivalence is witnessed by equal refinements, addition is independent of input representatives. Any finite set of denominators has a common right multiple by finite induction. Computing three sums at one such denominator proves associativity and commutativity. The zero is $[0,1]$ and the negative of $[m,s]$ is $[-m,s]$. Consequently $L(M)$ is an abelian group. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Define $\alpha:L(M)\to M\otimes_RK$ by $[m,s]\mapsto m\otimes s^{-1}$. If $su=tv=w$, then $s^{-1}=uw^{-1}$ and $t^{-1}=vw^{-1}$ in $K$. Balancing therefore gives $m\otimes s^{-1}=mu\otimes w^{-1}$, and similarly for $n$. The equivalence relation makes $\alpha$ well-defined, and the common-denominator addition formula makes it additive. Conversely, for $k=as^{-1}\in K$ put $\beta(m,k)=[ma,s]$. If also $k=bt^{-1}$, choose $su=tv=w$ and multiply the equality in $K$ on the right by $w$ to obtain $au=bv$. This is equality in the embedded $R$, so $[ma,s]=[mb,t]$. Thus $\beta$ is independent of the right-fraction presentation. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 The map $\beta$ is biadditive: addition in $m$ uses one denominator, and addition of $as^{-1}$ and $bt^{-1}$ uses the common-denominator formula $(au+bv)w^{-1}$ with $su=tv=w$. It is balanced, since $\beta(mr,as^{-1})=[mra,s]=\beta(m,ras^{-1})$. Hence [F2]'s quotient presentation gives a homomorphism $\bar\beta:M\otimes_RK\to L(M)$. The two maps are inverse: $\bar\beta\alpha[m,s]=[m,s]$, while $\alpha\bar\beta(m\otimes as^{-1})=ma\otimes s^{-1}=m\otimes as^{-1}$, and elementary tensors generate. This proves the asserted fraction model and equality criterion. Right multiplication in $K$ defines $(m\otimes k)\ell=m\otimes k\ell$ and respects every tensor relation, so it equips this group with its stated right $K$-module structure. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By the relation in step 1.1, $[m,s]=[0,1]$ implies $mu=0$ for some $u\in S$. Conversely, if $ma=0$ with $a\in S$, then the common denominator $sa=1(sa)$ proves $(m,s)\sim(0,1)$. Thus the zero criterion holds for every denominator. At $s=1$ it gives the kernel assertion. If each $m$ has a nonzero right annihilator then each fraction is zero, hence the localized module is zero; the converse follows by applying the zero criterion to each $[m,1]$. This uses only individual existential annihilators, not a simultaneous choice of them. [step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 A right-module homomorphism $f:M\to N$ induces $L(f)[m,s]=[f(m),s]$, which agrees under step 4.1 with $f\otimes1$. If $f$ is injective and $[f(m),s]=0$, step 5.1 gives $f(m)a=f(ma)=0$ for some $a\in S$; hence $ma=0$ and $[m,s]=0$. Thus localization preserves injections. If $f$ is surjective, lift the one numerator of any $[n,s]$ to obtain a preimage fraction, proving surjectivity. For maps $P\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}N$ exact at $M$, a fraction $[m,s]$ in $\ker L(g)$ satisfies $g(m)a=0$ for some $a\in S$. Then $ma\in\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$, so take $p\in P$ with $f(p)=ma$. The refinement equality $[m,s]=[ma,sa]=L(f)[p,sa]$ proves $\ker L(g)\subseteq\operatorname{im}L(f)$; the reverse inclusion follows from $gf=0$. This proves exactness on all right modules and left flatness of $K$, without finiteness conditions. [F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 For an arbitrary right-module chain complex, put $Z_i=\ker d_i$ and $B_i=\operatorname{im}d_{i+1}$. Apply step 6.1 to $0\to Z_i\to C_i\to B_{i-1}\to0$ and to the inclusion $B_{i-1}\to C_{i-1}$. Their tensor images identify the kernel of $d_i\otimes1$ with $Z_i\otimes_RK$. Applying the same reasoning to $C_{i+1}\to B_i\to C_i$ identifies its image with the embedded $B_i\otimes_RK$. Finally exactness applied to $0\to B_i\to Z_i\to H_i(C)\to0$ identifies the quotient of these localized cycles by localized boundaries with $H_i(C)\otimes_RK$. The resulting isomorphism is the canonical map $[z]\otimes k\mapsto[z\otimes k]$. Each construction uses the original inclusions and quotient maps, so it commutes with every chain map and is natural. The proof works degree by degree and neither chooses bases nor imposes a bound on the complex. [F4, step 6.1, algebra, construct]

8.1 To obtain the left statements, every $k=as^{-1}\in K$ is also a left fraction: if $a\ne0$, use the left Ore condition to choose $t,b\in S$ with $ta=bs$, giving $k=t^{-1}b$; for $k=0$ use $1^{-1}0$. Thus $K^{\mathrm{op}}$ is a right-fraction division ring of $R^{\mathrm{op}}$, whose right Ore condition is the original left one. A left $R$-module is a right $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module by $m\cdot r=rm$. Apply steps 1.1–7.1 to these opposite rings. The tensor relation identifies $M\otimes_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}K^{\mathrm{op}}$ with $K\otimes_RM$ by $m\otimes k\mapsto k\otimes m$. The zero condition becomes $am=0$, flatness becomes right flatness, and the chain-homology result has the stated left-handed order. All denominators, refinements, lifts and annihilators in the argument were chosen only for a fixed finite collection in an individual assertion. There is no appeal to a choice axiom, even for arbitrary modules or unbounded complexes. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The choice-free PTFA Ore theorem supplies examples of the fraction-ring hypotheses: the PTFA fraction-ring theorem. The present lemma is ring-theoretic and also applies to other Ore subrings of a division ring whenever that same division ring is their ring of fractions. It asserts no nonsingularity, geometric duality or Blanchfield-pairing theorem.

## Statement

Let $F$ be a normal surface in a finite simplicial triangulation $T$. Cut $F$ along a finite disjoint trace family satisfying the distinct-normal-side hypothesis of the positive patch-weight lemma, and let $R$ be a connected compact cut patch missing $T^{(1)}$.

If $R$ is a disk with two trace-arc boundary sides and two original-boundary arc sides, then its normal-cell regions form a finite chain of quadrilaterals. The opposite trace arcs are parallel by a PL product parametrization of $R$: every intermediate arc meets each region of this chain in one arc joining its two old sides, and its endpoints stay within the two original boundary sides. These old sides lie in distinct tetrahedral faces.

If $R$ is an annulus whose two boundary components are trace circles and which misses $\partial F$, its normal-cell regions form a finite cycle of quadrilaterals. There is a PL product parametrization by $S^1\times[0,1]$ taking its two trace circles to the two end levels and keeping each intervening arc within its original normal-cell region. A Mobius patch instead has the twisted interval-bundle model and does not have two trace boundary components.

The parallelisms take place on the cut patch, cell by cell in the original triangulation. No ambient three-dimensional product region or cancellation of a separate exchange surface is asserted.

## Statement references

[[lem-normal-exchange-disk-patches-have-positive-edge-weight]]

[[lem-normal-exchange-disk-patches-have-positive-edge-weight]] — the exact zero-edge Euler cell count and distinct-side trace hypothesis.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The normal surface, trace family and zero-edge patch in either case of the Statement. An old side interval is a portion of an original normal-cell side; a trace side is a portion of a cut trace.

[F1] A zero-edge cut patch has normal-cell regions that are polygonal disks. A region with $k_j$ trace sides has $k_j$ old side intervals, alternating with those trace sides, and $k_j\ge2$. If the patch has $b$ original-boundary arcs, each is one old side interval, and $$\chi(R)=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right).$$ ([[lem-normal-exchange-disk-patches-have-positive-edge-weight]])

[F2] Each interior old interval is glued to precisely one other region side, while an original-boundary interval remains unglued. The trace sides are unglued boundary sides. Finite polygonal disk boundary identifications extend to PL disk parametrizations by triangulation and coning. ([[thm-polygonal-jordan-curve]], [[thm-simple-polygon-admits-a-triangulation]])

## Proof

1.1 In the disk case $\chi(R)=1$ and $b=2$; in the annulus or Mobius case $\chi(R)=0$ and $b=0$. In both cases the Euler formula [F1] says that a sum of nonpositive terms is zero. Thus every $k_j=2$. Each normal-cell region is a quadrilateral with two opposite trace sides and two opposite old sides. The old sides of one quadrilateral lie on distinct sides of its original normal disk: either trace side joins these two old sides, and the distinct-side trace hypothesis excludes their lying on the same normal-disk side. A normal disk has at most one side in any tetrahedral face, so these two faces are distinct. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Make a finite graph with one vertex for each quadrilateral and an edge for each glued pair of old intervals, retaining loops and repeated edges if present. It is connected. Indeed, the quadrilaterals reconstruct the connected surface patch by precisely these old-side gluings. They cannot connect only at a vertex: every vertex is a trace endpoint on an old interval, and its half-disk surface chart joins its incident regions across that interval. Each graph vertex has degree two minus its number of unglued old sides, counting a loop twice. In the disk case there are exactly two unglued old sides by [F1], so the connected graph is a path, possibly one vertex with both ends unglued. To check this without a graph classification, start at one unglued side and follow the unique continuation through each quadrilateral and glued old side. Encountering an earlier vertex before the other unglued side would produce a cycle with no possible exit, contradicting connectedness and the remaining unglued side. Thus all vertices are met once and the traversal ends at the other unglued side. In the closed-boundary-strip case all degrees are two, and the same traversal closes into one cycle containing all vertices. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Parametrize every quadrilateral by a rectangle, with its old sides at the two ends in the chain direction and its trace sides at transverse levels zero and one. These parametrizations may be made compatible along successive old-side gluings: choose a PL parameter on the first old side, transport it across each gluing, and choose any increasing PL parameter on the next old side. The resulting four boundary interval maps extend to a PL rectangle map by [F2]. A concrete extension triangulates the boundary breakpoints, adds an interior vertex, and cones the boundary intervals; it is a homeomorphism because its triangular interiors partition the polygonal disk. Each intermediate transverse level then maps to an embedded arc joining the two old sides within that quadrilateral. Gluing the chain gives a PL product rectangle for the entire disk patch. Its two transverse end levels are exactly the two trace arcs, and its other sides are the two original-boundary intervals. The maps therefore give the claimed cellwise trace parallelism without changing an original cell. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 In the cycle case cut along one old interval and perform the rectangle construction of step 3.1. Closing that cut identifies its two transverse parameter intervals by a PL interval homeomorphism. If the identification reverses their endpoint order, the two trace sides are joined into one boundary circle, giving the twisted rectangle model of a Mobius band. If it preserves endpoint order, reparametrize one of the end intervals by the inverse identification. The prescribed maps on the two old sides of the adjacent quadrilateral still extend by [F2], so this makes the closing identification the identity without changing the cell containing any point of an intermediate arc. The quotient is then a PL product $S^1\times[0,1]$. For the annulus in the Statement, its two distinct trace boundary circles rule out endpoint reversal. This proves both the product and the stated distinction from a Mobius patch, using only the finite original quadrilateral strip. [given, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $A$ be an indeterminate and let $D$ be a typed nonempty unoriented regular
link diagram with finite crossing set $C(D)$. At each crossing use the chart
with the over-strand southwest-to-northeast: A joins the left endpoints and the
right endpoints with weight $A$, while B joins the top endpoints and bottom
endpoints with weight $A^{-1}$. The Kauffman bracket state-sum algorithm
terminates after exactly $2^{|C(D)|}$ state visits and returns
$$\sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1},$$
where $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count the two smoothing types and $|S|$ counts the
circles in the smoothed diagram. The algorithm takes a mathematical diagram
as input and makes no claim about parsing strings or rejecting malformed
encodings.

## Statement references

[[alg-kauffman-bracket-state-sum|Kauffman bracket state-sum algorithm]]

[Kauffman, *An Invariant of Regular Isotopy* (1990), §III](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kauffman/IRH.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §4.3](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Funar, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter 3, §1.1](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A typed nonempty unoriented regular link diagram $D$ with finite
crossing set $C(D)$.

[F1] The algorithm initializes $p=0$, visits once each function
$S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$, adds $A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}$, and returns the final
accumulator, with $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$
([[alg-kauffman-bracket-state-sum]]).

[F2] The input diagram has at least one closed component, so every complete
smoothing has at least one circle and every term is a Laurent polynomial
([[alg-kauffman-bracket-state-sum]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $c=|C(D)|$, every state is a function from a $c$-element set to a two-element set, so the state set has exactly $2^c$ elements. This is finite, including the case $c=0$, where there is exactly one empty assignment. The algorithm processes every such function once and has no other loop. [F1, construct]

2.1 For each visited state, the prescribed smoothing produces a finite crossingless union of circles. By [F2], $|S|-1$ is a nonnegative integer, so $A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}$ is defined in $\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$. After any initial segment of the visits, the accumulator is the sum of exactly the terms already visited, by induction on the number of updates. After all $2^c$ visits it is the displayed state sum, which is returned. Therefore execution terminates with exactly the asserted output. [F1, F2, step 1.1, induction, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For an oriented Seifert surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary $K$ and ordered basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, let $V$ be the Seifert matrix with entries $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Here $\operatorname{lk}$ is the integer linking number of disjoint oriented cycles in $S^3$, and $a_i^+$ is a small push-off in the positive normal direction, chosen so that the positive normal followed by the oriented basis of $F$ gives the orientation of $S^3$. Use the standard knot-invariant conventions $\Delta_K(t)=\det(V-tV^T)$ up to units $\pm t^k$ and $\sigma_{-1}(K)=\operatorname{sign}(2(V+V^T))$, where the matrix sign is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues; independence of the chosen surface and basis is part of the Seifert-form invariance theorems. Let $T$ be the standard right-handed trefoil, let $T^*$ be its image under a fixed orientation-reversing reflection of $S^3$, and let $-T^*$ be that image with reversed knot orientation. Define $G=T\#T$ and $Q=T\#(-T^*)$. Then $\Delta_G(t)\doteq\Delta_Q(t)\doteq(t^2-t+1)^2$, and $|\sigma_{-1}(G)|=4$ while $\sigma_{-1}(Q)=0$. The oriented prime-factor multisets of $G$ and $Q$ are different. Thus equality of Alexander polynomials does not determine the prime knot summands.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|Connected sums and prime knots]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The full AC, knots $T,T^*,-T^*,G,Q$, positive-push and invariant conventions of the original Statement.

[A1] Full AC implies countable choice, as required by the prime and smooth knot suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] The actual right-handed trefoil bounds the standard positive two-Hopf-band plumbing, whose positive-push matrix in its ordered core basis is $V=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The handedness and negative diagonal signs are the established geometric convention, not the differently labeled positive matrix in the source-specific KT06 example. [[lem-positive-hopf-plumbing-has-trefoil-seifert-matrix]], [[lem-canonical-positive-three-crossing-braid-has-negative-trefoil-form]]

[F2] For every knot Seifert surface with the same positive normal and positive-meridian convention, $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)$. The actual boundary connected-sum surface has block matrix $V_K\oplus V_J$: the old bases lie in separated balls and both cross-linking blocks vanish. [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]], [[cor-alexander-polynomial-multiplies-under-connected-sum]], Proof2.1–4.1.

[F3] At every nonroot point $\omega$, the signature of $(1-\omega)V+(1-\bar\omega)V^T$ is an oriented knot invariant independent of surface and basis. The full knot-surface S-equivalence and stabilization proofs now establish this actual interface. [[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature]], [[lem-seifert-matrices-of-a-knot-are-s-equivalent]], [[lem-seifert-stabilization-preserves-levine-tristram-signature]]

[F4] The right trefoil is prime, reflection preserves nontriviality and primality, and the oriented prime decomposition is unique up to ordering and insertion/deletion of unknot factors. [[lem-right-trefoil-is-prime]], [[lem-mirroring-preserves-primality-of-a-knot]], [[thm-schubert-prime-decomposition-for-knots]], [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

## Refutation

**Given:** The actual right-trefoil matrix $V$ in [F1], with all the Statement's knot and orientation conventions.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], $$\Delta_T(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)=\det\begin{pmatrix}t-1&t\\-1&t-1\end{pmatrix}=(t-1)^2+t=t^2-t+1.$$ For $-T^*$ use the reflected spanning surface with its surface orientation reversed, so its boundary is the reversed reflected knot. Its positive normal is the reflected original positive normal: ambient reflection and surface reversal each negate the orientation, so their effects cancel in the normal-first convention. Reflection negates linking. The transported homology basis on this actual surface consequently has matrix $-V$. Its determinant is $\det(-V+tV^T)=\det(V-tV^T)$, since the matrix size is two. The two determinants evaluate to $3$ at $t=-1$, so this parameter is nonroot and [F3] applies directly, with no root-average ambiguity. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the actual boundary connected-sum surfaces of $G=T\#T$ and $Q=T\#(-T^*)$ have matrices $V\oplus V$ and $V\oplus(-V)$. Their block determinants both equal $(t^2-t+1)^2$, proving the two Alexander-polynomial identities up to units. Also $$H_{-1}(V)=2(V+V^T)=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-2\\-2&-4\end{pmatrix}.$$ Its eigenvalues on the vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ are $-6$ and $-2$, respectively. Thus $\sigma_{-1}(T)=-2$ and $\sigma_{-1}(-T^*)=2$. The corresponding block forms give $\sigma_{-1}(G)=-4$ and $\sigma_{-1}(Q)=-2+2=0$. These are actual knot-invariant values by [F3], since the sum polynomials at $-1$ equal $9\ne0$. In particular $|\sigma_{-1}(G)|=4$ as stated. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By [F4], $T$ and $T^*$ are nontrivial prime oriented knots. Reversal of knot orientation also preserves these properties: reverse both factors and the two local oriented arcs in any purported nontrivial connected-sum presentation of $-T^*$ to obtain a nontrivial presentation of $T^*$; reversing again is the inverse operation, and the unknot remains the unknot. Thus $-T^*$ is prime. The signatures in step2.1 show that $T$ and $-T^*$ are distinct oriented knot types, since an oriented ambient isotopy would preserve [F3]'s signature. Therefore the displayed two-prime decompositions have respective multisets $\{T,T\}$ and $\{T,-T^*\}$, which are different. By [F4]'s actual oriented Schubert uniqueness they are the prime-factor multisets of $G$ and $Q$, independent of a chosen decomposition. Together with their equal Alexander polynomials, this proves the entire original refutation. No planned matrix interface or conditional prime/invariant premise remains. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Definition

An oriented circle is a smooth one-dimensional manifold diffeomorphic to the standard oriented circle. An abstract oriented cobordism from an oriented circle $C_0$ to an oriented circle $C_1$ is a compact oriented smooth surface $F$ together with orientation-preserving identifications of its incoming and outgoing boundary components such that $\partial F=-C_0\sqcup C_1$. Here $-C_0$ denotes the same circle with its orientation reversed. The cobordism is abstract: no embedding of $F$, $C_0$, or $C_1$ into a common three- or four-manifold is included in the data.

## Definition

Let $Y_0,Y_1$ be closed smooth oriented three-manifolds, let $W$ be a compact smooth oriented four-manifold with boundary $-Y_0\sqcup Y_1$, where $-Y_0$ has the reversed orientation, and let $K_i\subset Y_i$ be images of smooth oriented embeddings of the circle. Every component of $Y_i$ is required to meet $K_i$; the boundary parametrizations and compatible product collars are part of the data. A **decorated knot cobordism** from $(Y_0,K_0)$ to $(Y_1,K_1)$ is a properly embedded smooth oriented surface $\Sigma\subset W$ with boundary $(-K_0)\sqcup K_1$, together with one $w$-basepoint and one $z$-basepoint on each end knot and a compact properly embedded one-manifold $\mathcal A\subset\Sigma$, which may have arc and closed-circle components. Every component of $W$ meets $\Sigma$, and every component of $\Sigma$ meets $\mathcal A$. The full dividing set $\mathcal A$ decomposes $\Sigma$ into subsurfaces $\Sigma_w,\Sigma_z$, with each $w$-basepoint in the closure of $\Sigma_w$, each $z$-basepoint in the closure of $\Sigma_z$, and $\mathcal A$ meeting the boundary transversely away from the marked points. Every component of $K_i\setminus\mathcal A$ contains exactly one of the two marked points; in particular each boundary knot meets the dividing set in two points, separating its $w$- and $z$-intervals. The basepoint labels, dividing set, two regions and their two-color assignment are part of the data.

For an end pair $(Y,K)$, a doubly pointed Heegaard diagram consists of a closed genus-$g$ oriented surface $S$, two $g$-tuples $\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta$ of pairwise disjoint simple closed curves giving a Heegaard splitting of $Y$, and points $w,z$ in the complement of those curves such that arcs in the two handlebodies from $w$ to $z$ form $K$. Each intersection point $\mathbf x\in\mathbb T_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\cap\mathbb T_{\boldsymbol\beta}$ determines a Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s_w(\mathbf x)$ on $Y$ from the homology class of the nonvanishing gradient vector field specified by $\mathbf x$ and $w$. For $\mathfrak t\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(Y)$, let $CFL^-_{UV}(Y,K,\mathfrak t)$ be generated over $R=\mathbb F_2[U,V]$ by those intersection points with $\mathfrak s_w(\mathbf x)=\mathfrak t$. A periodic domain is an integral two-chain in the regions of $S\setminus(\boldsymbol\alpha\cup\boldsymbol\beta)$ whose boundary is an integral sum of the attaching curves; its capped homology class in $Y$ is denoted $[P]$, and $n_w(P)$ is its multiplicity at $w$. Restrict to diagrams strongly admissible for $\mathfrak t$: there is a generator $\mathbf x$ with $\mathfrak s_w(\mathbf x)=\mathfrak t$, and for every nonzero periodic domain $P$ with $n_w(P)=0$ and $\langle c_1(\mathfrak t),[P]\rangle=2N\ge0$, some region of $P$ has multiplicity strictly greater than $N$. Here $c_1(\mathfrak t)$ is the first Chern class of its determinant line bundle. The symmetric product $\operatorname{Sym}^g(S)$ is the quotient of $S^g$ by permutations of the factors. The associated product tori $\mathbb T_{\boldsymbol\alpha},\mathbb T_{\boldsymbol\beta}\subset\operatorname{Sym}^g(S)$ determine the differential on each Spin-c summand by
$$
\partial \mathbf x=\sum_{\mathbf y}\ \sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\\ \mu(\phi)=1}} \#_2\bigl(\mathcal M(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)\,U^{n_w(\phi)}V^{n_z(\phi)}\mathbf y.
$$
Here $\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is the set of homotopy classes of Whitney disks, $\mu$ is the Maslov index, $\mathcal M(\phi)/\mathbb R$ is the moduli space of index-one disks modulo translation for chosen generic almost-complex data, $n_w,n_z$ are their local multiplicities at the marked points, and $\#_2$ is the finite count modulo two. This is the two-variable specialization of the colored link Floer complex. Its curvature vanishes: for a knot with one $w$- and one $z$-basepoint the curvature formula is $UV+VU=0$ in $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$, so $\partial^2=0$. The complex has the two-coordinate filtration induced by the $w$- and $z$-multiplicities.

For a chosen $\mathfrak s\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)$, the Floer map indexed by $\mathfrak s$ has the complexes for $(Y_0,K_0,\mathfrak s|_{Y_0})$ and $(Y_1,K_1,\mathfrak s|_{Y_1})$ as source and target; $\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)$ denotes the set of Spin-c structures on $W$. Zemke's Lemma 3.4 states the corresponding formula for $CFL^-$, and Remark 2.14 states that coloring with only two variables, one for all $w$-basepoints and one for all $z$-basepoints, makes the curvature zero. ## Definition

Let $Y$ be a closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold. A pointed genus-$g$ Heegaard diagram for $Y$ consists of an embedded splitting $Y=U_\alpha\cup_\Sigma U_\beta$, where $\Sigma=\partial U_\alpha$ is a closed oriented genus-$g$ surface and each $U$ is a handlebody, meaning a regular neighborhood of a finite connected graph; ordered systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_g)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_g)$ of pairwise disjoint smooth simple closed curves bounding specified disjoint proper compression disks in the respective handlebodies, each disk system cutting its handlebody into one ball; and one point $z$ off the curves. Opposite-system curves meet transversely in finitely many points. This is closed-manifold data; it includes neither a knot nor a second marked point.

Write $q:\Sigma^g\to\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)=\Sigma^g/S_g$ for the permutation quotient. The product tori are the images
$$T_\alpha=q(\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_g),\qquad T_\beta=q(\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_g).$$
The group $S_g$ acts on the ambient product, rather than on a fixed ordered product of distinct attaching circles. A generator is an intersection $x\in T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$; equivalently it selects one intersection point on each curve of each system. There are finitely many generators. For $g=0$ the symmetric product and both empty products are one point, with the empty generator.

A Whitney class $\phi\in\pi_2(x,y)$ is a relative homotopy class of maps of a closed disk with two marked boundary points into the symmetric product, taking its two boundary arcs into $T_\alpha,T_\beta$ and its marked points to $x,y$. Its domain is the integral two-chain of complementary regions; its coefficient at an interior point $p$ is the intersection multiplicity $n_p(\phi)$ with $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{g-1}(\Sigma)$. In particular $n_z(\phi)$ is the basepoint coefficient. A periodic domain is an integral region two-chain whose boundary is an integral sum of full attaching circles. The domain of a class $\psi\in\pi_2(x,x)$ is periodic. Such a class is normalized when $n_z(\psi)=0$. Write $\mu(\phi)$ for the real Fredholm index of the disk linearization, before quotienting longitudinal translation; well-definedness and its topological index formula are properties to be proved in the analytic and index theory.

For a periodic domain P, cap its full attaching-circle boundary with the specified compression disks, using the boundary multiplicities and orientations, to obtain the integral class $H(P)\in H_2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. A Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s$ is a lift of the oriented tangent frame bundle through $\operatorname{Spin}^c(3)\to SO(3)$; $c_1(\mathfrak s)$ is the first Chern class of its determinant line, with determinant character $[s,u]\mapsto u^2$. **Weak admissibility in the specified Spin-c sector $\mathfrak s$** means that EVERY nonzero integral periodic domain P with $n_z(P)=0$ and $\langle c_1(\mathfrak s),H(P)\rangle=0$ has both positive and negative region coefficients. This condition is imposed even when the sector has no diagram generators. It is a condition on domains and the intended sector, not only on periodic classes based at existing generators.

The ordinary sector module $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H,\mathfrak s)$ uses generators with Morse Spin-c label $\mathfrak s_z(x)=\mathfrak s$. The label is defined by compatible handle Morse data: replace the gradient in disjoint tubes around the generator's index-one/index-two trajectories and the basepoint's index-zero/index-three trajectory by nonsingular fields, and take the Spin-c lift of their oriented perpendicular planes. Its actual construction, independence properties and periodic-index formula are obligations of the Spin-c and index theory. In particular the equality between the index of a REALIZED normalized periodic class based at x and the Chern evaluation in $\mathfrak s_z(x)$ is not assumed as its own proof. A realized-generator test alone is not substituted for the stated domain condition.

An **admissible diagram for the full single-diagram hat module** satisfies this sector condition for EVERY Spin-c structure on Y, including the sectors with no generators. The full module below uses all generators and hence all intended sectors; an empty sector contributes a zero summand but is not omitted from the admissibility test. Equivalently this full-diagram condition is global weak admissibility: every nonzero periodic domain with $n_z=0$ has both signs. The equivalence uses the actual zero-Chern Spin-c sector constructed from complete Heegaard data in Complete Heegaard data have a zero-Chern Spin-c sector; it is not inferred from a generator existing in that sector. For a SINGLE specified sector, ordinary weak admissibility remains the stated Chern-kernel condition and need not imply global weakness. No assertion of the full group from a diagram tested only at its represented sectors is made.

For $g>0$ choose a complex structure $j$ and positive area form on $\Sigma$. Analytic data include a smooth path $J_t$ on the symmetric product, constant on actual neighborhoods of $t=0,1$. On a fixed neighborhood of the diagonal and the point-divisors for a chosen interior point of every complementary region, including $z$, it agrees with the integrable structure $\operatorname{Sym}^g(j)$; away from that neighborhood it is tame for the form descended from the product surface area form. The path is chosen in a sufficiently small nearly symmetric class. Product-integrable normal forms near the finitely many transverse generators may be included among its specified auxiliary choices. Existence of such choices and of the regular perturbations needed below remains a mathematical obligation. A holomorphic strip is an actual smooth finite-Dirichlet-energy map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)$ satisfying
$$u_s+J_t(u)u_t=0,\qquad u(s,0)\in T_\alpha,\quad u(s,1)\in T_\beta,$$
with uniform generator limits at both longitudinal ends. The space in class $\phi$ is $\mathcal M_J(\phi)$, and translation in $s$ acts on it. Regular means that its actual linearized operator is surjective at the solutions being counted. Local multiplicity positivity, Fredholmness, the class index and compactness are results to be proved, not choices of which maps to count.

The hat diagram-level module $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H;\mathbb F_2)$ is free over $\mathbb F_2$ on the generators. For regular data for which the displayed quotient sets are finite and, for each $x$, only finitely many nonempty pairs $(y,\phi)$ occur, its candidate count operator is
$$\widehat\partial x=\sum_y\ \sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(x,y)\\\mu(\phi)=1,\ n_z(\phi)=0}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M_J(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)y.$$
Here $\#_2$ is parity of an actual finite zero-dimensional quotient. For $g=0$ the operator is zero on the empty generator. That the required regular finite counts exist, that $\widehat\partial^2=0$, and that its homology is invariant under changing pointed admissible diagrams and auxiliary choices are separate analytic and move theorems. Once these hold, the common homology is denoted $\widehat{HF}(Y;\mathbb F_2)$. No filtered chain-homotopy invariant, integral orientations or absolute grading is asserted by this definition.

Comparisons of embedded diagrams permit orientation-preserving isomorphisms carrying $Y$, its two handlebodies, their oriented surface, the attaching systems and $z$ to the specified counterparts, equivalently compatible collared extensions of the surface map. Curve-factor reordering gives the corresponding product identification. Analytic data are transported by the induced symmetric-product map, including $j$, the area form, protected neighborhoods and $J_t$. The intended count identification is the actual pushforward of generators and disk classes with these transported data; its compatibility with the operator requires proof. An ambient isotopy is not assumed to act as the identity. Comparison of independently chosen perturbations likewise requires the continuation theorem.

## Definition

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere. Let $F$ be a compact connected oriented Seifert surface with boundary $K$, and let $\mathcal H=(\Sigma,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,w,z)$ be an admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagram representing $(K,F)$. The associated one-pointed hat chain complex $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is the finite-dimensional chain complex over $\mathbb F_2$ obtained from the minus complex by setting its basepoint variable to zero; its differential counts index-one disks with zero multiplicity at $w$. Assume for this specified data that the differential is nonincreasing in the Alexander filtration, that the absolute Alexander formula below takes integer values, and that $H(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))\cong\mathbb F_2$. Give a generator $\mathbf x$ its absolute Alexander filtration
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field assigned to $\mathbf x$ by the pointed Morse construction, with its prescribed boundary data near the two basepoints; $c_1$ is the first Chern class of the oriented plane field perpendicular to that vector field. To form the zero-framed surgery, remove a tubular neighborhood of $K$ and glue in a solid torus whose meridian is the longitude induced by $F$. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by deleting a boundary collar of $F$ and capping its longitude by the meridian disk of that solid torus. This is the standard integer normalization, with the one-generator diagram of the standard unknot at filtration zero. The subcomplex $F_s\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is spanned by generators of Alexander filtration at most $s$.

More generally, a finite integer-filtered chain complex is a finite-dimensional chain complex $C$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with subcomplexes $F_sC$ such that $F_sC=0$ for all sufficiently small integers $s$ and $F_sC=C$ for all sufficiently large integers $s$. If $H(C)\cong\mathbb F_2$, define
$$\tau(C):=\min\{s\in\mathbb Z:\operatorname{im}(H(F_sC)\longrightarrow H(C))\ne0\}.$$
For the fixed diagram and surface above, write $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)=\tau(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H),F_*\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))$. Once diagram and surface independence is proved, their common value is the knot invariant $\tau(K)$. Until that comparison is proved, $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)$ denotes only the value for the specified data.

**Given:** A finite integer-filtered chain complex $C$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with $H(C)\cong\mathbb F_2$.

## Verification

1.1 Since $F_sC=0$ for all sufficiently small $s$, the inclusion-induced map $H(F_sC)\to H(C)$ is zero at those levels. Since $F_sC=C$ for all sufficiently large $s$, this map is the identity on $H(C)$ at those levels and is nonzero by [A2]. [A1, A2, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $S=\{s\in\mathbb Z:H(F_sC)\to H(C)\text{ has nonzero image}\}$. Step 1.1 shows $S$ is nonempty, and [A1] gives an integer lower bound $m$ for $S$. Then $S-m$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N_0$; by [F1] it has a least element $k$. For every $s\in S$, $s-m\ge k$, so $m+k$ is the least element of $S$. This proves that $\tau(C)$ exists and is unique. [A1, A3, F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/rsplx.pdf"
      locator: "§§1.4, 1.7, PL maps and embeddings; §2.11–2.14, triangulations and common subdivisions, web text lines 177–229 and 482–514."

## Definition

Let $P$ and $Q$ be compact piecewise-linear polyhedra. A **piecewise-linear map** $f:P\to Q$ is a map that is simplicial after suitable finite subdivisions of triangulations of $P$ and $Q$. A **subpolyhedron** $A$ of $Q$ is a subset represented by the realization of a subcomplex in some finite linear triangulation of $Q$. A map $f:P\to Q$ is a **piecewise-linear embedding** if it is piecewise-linear, its image $f(P)$ is a subpolyhedron of $Q$, and $f:P\to f(P)$ is a piecewise-linear homeomorphism. A finite simplicial triangulation of a closed piecewise-linear $n$-manifold is **combinatorial** if the link of every $k$-simplex is a piecewise-linear sphere of dimension $n-k-1$. Thus in a closed combinatorial $3$-manifold every triangular face has link $S^0$ and is incident to exactly two tetrahedra.

[Rourke–Sanderson, §§1.4, 1.7, 2.14](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/rsplx.pdf) — piecewise-linear maps, embeddings and their simplicial subdivisions.

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, $q\ge2$, and $M=\Sigma_q(K)$ oriented as the boundary of the positive-meridian branched cover. When $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ is finite, its torsion linking form is the oriented pairing $\lambda_M:H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ given by $\lambda_M(x,y)=(C\cdot y)/n\bmod\mathbb Z$ for any integer $n>0$ and integral $2$-chain $C$ in $M$ with $\partial C=nx$; reversing the orientation negates $\lambda_M$. For a prime-power-order character $\chi$ of order $d$, the standard splitting $H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\langle\widetilde\mu\rangle$ of the $q$-fold cyclic cover $M_{0,q}$ of zero surgery extends $\chi$ to $\eta:H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z$ by identifying its cyclic image with $\mathbb Z/d$ and using the free-summand projection in the second factor. A Casson–Gordon bordism datum is a positive integer $r$ and a compact oriented $4$-manifold $W$ with a map to $K(\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z,1)$ whose boundary represents $r$ copies of $(M_{0,q},\eta)$.
