## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented smooth $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary and good fundamental group $G=\pi_1(X)$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_n:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$ be proper generic immersed disks with pairwise disjoint embedded boundary circles. Suppose they admit framed immersed algebraically dual spheres $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ with $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$, and suppose $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for all $i$, in the equivariant intersection conventions of the disk-embedding data definition. Then the disks are homotopic rel boundary, preserving the boundary framings, to pairwise disjoint locally flat properly embedded disks in $X$.

## Statement references

[[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data|The relative disk data and equivariant intersection hypotheses]]

[[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding|The good-group condition]]

[[thm-freedman-disk-embedding-theorem-proof-modules|The standardized-tower core construction]]

[[def-countable-choice|Axiom of Countable Choice used by the tower construction]]

Michael H. Freedman and Frank Quinn, *Topology of 4-Manifolds*, §5.1, Theorems 5.1A–5.1B, https://archive.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/4789/1/FreedmanQuinn-TopologyOf4Manifolds-PMS39.pdf

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, good $G$, and the stated finite algebraically unobstructed disk datum. The disk data specify actual boundary normal-microbundle framings, not merely stable classes; the relative extension obstruction is separate, and each dual sphere has a full normal-microbundle trivialization.

[F1] [[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data]] gives locally flat TOP sheet charts, prescribed disk-boundary normal framings, framed spheres and the signed group-labelled intersection conventions. A disk's relative framing-extension obstruction is tracked separately and is not assumed to vanish from the algebraic Wall conditions.

[F2] [[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding]] is the good-group property, invariant under a based group isomorphism.

[F3] [[lem-freedman-casson-handle-skyscraper-and-surgery-modules]] supplies the proved smooth-input good-group construction: in a supplied smooth neighborhood it gives disjoint locally flat disks in the original relative homotopy classes, with the supplied extending frames and retained geometric duals. Its Sections13–14 give relative approximation, finite affine-jet genericity and the relative Euler/intersection comparison; these operations are used below, rather than assuming TOP transversality. Its standard handle charts supply [[thm-freedman-disk-embedding-theorem-proof-modules]].

[F4] [[lem-finite-framed-locally-flat-links-in-smooth-three-manifolds-have-smooth-image-models]] gives, under CC, a supported boundary ambient TOP isotopy smoothing a finite locally flat link, positive source-circle reparametrizations, and smooth representatives of its full transported rank-two normal-microbundle framing classes.

[F5] [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]] and [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]] supply actual smooth collars and smooth tubes under CC.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is available. All subsequent choices beyond [F3]–[F5] are finite.

## Proof

1.1 The normal microbundle in [F1] is a neighborhood germ with its zero section and retraction, not merely an abstract stable vector bundle. On the embedded boundary of a proper locally flat sheet, its relative half-space chart is $(\mathbb R^2_+\times\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R^2_+\times0)$. Restricting the given normal trivialization to its boundary gives a TOP tube germ of that boundary circle in $\partial X$; its normal fiber is the second $\mathbb R^2$. Compactness permits a sufficiently small representative around each of the finitely many circles, and disjointness permits these representatives to be disjoint. This uses the GIVEN normal germ, not a theorem constructing normal neighborhoods for arbitrary TOP surfaces. Apply [F4] to this boundary link in the given compact smooth three-manifold $\partial X$. Denote its isotopy by $h_s$ and its smooth framing representatives by $\eta_i$. [given, F1, F4, A1]

2.1 Extend the actual isotopy over a smooth collar $c:\partial X\times[0,a)\to X$ from [F5]. Choose a cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near zero and zero before $a$. Set $H_s(c(x,r))=c(h_{s\beta(r)}(x),r)$, and use the identity outside the collar. The inverse uses $h_{s\beta(r)}^{-1}$, so $H_s$ is an orientation-preserving ambient TOP isotopy with joint inverse. Transport all maps, whiskers and normal classes by $H_1$. Every old signed intersection and group label is transported by the same based group isomorphism; goodness is unchanged. For the positive circle homeomorphism $\theta_i$ of [F4], let $\Theta_i:D^2\to D^2$ be its radial cone, and replace the disk temporarily by $H_1f_i\Theta_i$. Its boundary MAP is now a smooth regular parametrization. At the end we undo both $H_1$ and $\Theta_i$, so no change of the original boundary parameter is concealed. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 Construct a NEW smooth source collar. In the product of a smooth boundary-circle tube and the ambient collar, write the transported map on a small source collar as $(b_i(\theta,t),v_i(\theta,t),r_i(\theta,t))$, with boundary values $(\theta,0,0)$ and $r_i>0$ for $t>0$. Uniform continuity gives a unique small real lift of $b_i-\theta$ after restricting the collar. For $\kappa(t)$ equal to one on a smaller collar and zero outside the chosen one, interpolate these coordinates to $(\theta,0,\rho t)$ by $((1-s\kappa)b_i+s\kappa\theta,(1-s\kappa)v_i,(1-s\kappa)r_i+s\kappa\rho t)$. Choose the finite positive $\rho$ and collar small enough to stay in the coordinate tube. The last coordinate is positive for every interior point throughout this homotopy, and the boundary is fixed. At its end the smaller collar is smooth. The homotopy may pass through nongeneric maps: the conclusion requires a homotopy, not a regular homotopy of the old TOP ribbons. It can be arbitrarily small, and its support misses all old double points. [F1, F5, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Use [F3]'s relative smooth approximation and finite affine-jet perturbations simultaneously on the disks and spheres, fixed on these smaller smooth collars. In a target with boundary perform approximation in its smooth double, with error less than half the positive target-boundary distance on the remaining compact source interiors; the output therefore stays in $X$. The same retraction interpolation gives a homotopy fixed on the collars. Independent value and first-jet bumps avoid the rank-deficient jet strata, make the two-point evaluation transverse to the diagonal and avoid triple points; compactness then gives only finitely many double points. This is exactly the finite genericity operation already proved in [F3]. Denote the resulting smooth generic maps by $f'_i,g'_j$. [F3, A1, step 3.1]

5.1 Here is the full group-ring comparison. At each old transverse crossing choose its supplied oriented TOP sheet chart and two small parameter disks. On their four-dimensional product the chart difference of the old sheet maps has one zero, of local degree the old sign, and no zero on the product boundary. For a sufficiently close approximation its chart difference is joined to the old one by a straight homotopy nonzero on that compact boundary. The signed sum of its transverse zeros is therefore the same local degree. All their group labels are the old label, since their connectors lie in that contractible chart. This uses a degree of continuous maps in a TOP chart, not differentiation of that chart. Outside these finitely many products and a neighborhood of each source diagonal, the compact source-pair set has positive image separation. Thus there are no other intersections between DIFFERENT source surfaces. Near a source diagonal both preimages lie in one of finitely many embedded-sheet charts, so a new self-double loop is null in $X$. It follows that every off-diagonal $\lambda$, including every disk–sphere pairing, retains its full original value, and $\mu(f'_i)=n_i1$, $\mu(g'_j)=m_j1$ for integers $n_i,m_j$. These equalities are in the actual sheet-involution quotient, not just after augmentation. [F1, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 The self-pairing $\lambda(g'_j,g'_j)$ is still zero. To compute it without assuming TOP parametric transversality, take a small parallel using the original framed normal germ, with the same whisker. Apply the preceding degree comparison to that pair; it computes the original self-pairing. Approximate the two homotopic representatives smoothly and interpolate their maps in the smooth double, relative any protected collar. The ordinary finite smooth two-value transversality argument computes homotopy invariance of the pairing: the one-dimensional intersection tracks have cancelling signed interior endpoints, with unchanged group labels along each track. Thus the new self-pairing is the old zero. The same argument for a disk and its boundary parallel computes the relative intersection integer determined by a specified boundary framing. [F1, F3, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Track the actual relative Euler obstruction rather than declaring it zero. For a smooth oriented disk $u$ and a boundary frame $\eta$, a generic normal section extending its first boundary vector has isolated zeros; their signed sum is $e(u,\eta)$. A parallel sheet meets $u$ at those zeros, and at both ordered branches of every self-point. Hence its relative intersection integer is $e(u,\eta)+2\sum_p\epsilon(p)$. The analogous equivariant sphere identity is $\lambda(u,u)=e(u)1+\mu(u)+\overline{\mu(u)}$. These follow by the stated local zero count; the two self-point labels are inverses. Twisting a boundary frame changes its relative Euler integer by the corresponding signed winding, so every desired integer value is realized by a smooth frame, and the difference from $\eta$ is recorded. Vanishing relative Euler is precisely the obstruction to extending that frame over a disk: extend on a finite cell subdivision and move the integer zero indices into one interior two-cell, where index zero extends across the cell. [F1, F3, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 A signed interior cusp changes $(\mu,e)$ by $(\pm1,\mp2)$ and changes no relative map homotopy class or off-diagonal pairing. For concreteness the birth chart is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y^2,y^3-ty,xy)$: for $t<0$ it is immersed without a double point, and for $t>0$ its sole double pair is $(0,\sqrt t),(0,-\sqrt t)$, with independent tangent planes. Reflecting a normal coordinate changes its sign. Restrict to a small inner chart and join the unchanged outer sheet through the surrounding annulus; the modification is a homotopy in that coordinate ball fixed on its boundary. The change of $e$ is opposite twice the double-point sign by the parallel-sheet count of step 7.1, since the boundary parallel intersection is unchanged. The balls and joining sheets can miss every other source surface. Thus any finite prescribed sum of signed identity-labelled cusps is available without changing a nonidentity Wall coefficient. [F1, F3, step 7.1, construct]

9.1 Let $e_i=e(f'_i,\eta_i)$. Choose an auxiliary smooth boundary frame $\eta_i^a$ with $e(f'_i,\eta_i^a)=-2n_i$, and record its integer difference from the prescribed $\eta_i$. Insert cusps with signed sum $-n_i$. The resulting smooth disks have $\mu=0$ and extending auxiliary frames. For spheres, steps 5.1–7.1 give $0=\lambda(g'_j,g'_j)=(e(g'_j)+2m_j)1$, so the cusps of sum $-m_j$ give both $\mu=0$ and $e=0$. Their oriented smooth normal bundles are therefore trivialized: after choosing frames on the one-skeleton, the only two-cell obstruction is this Euler integer. All disk–sphere and off-diagonal pairings remain exactly those of the hypothesis. [F1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, construct]

10.1 If the prescribed original disk framing extended, its original boundary-parallel intersection integer was zero, since its Euler obstruction and original $\mu$ were zero. Steps 6.1–7.1 show that $e_i+2n_i=0$, so in that case $\eta_i^a$ is the prescribed class $\eta_i$ itself. If only an external boundary framing was specified, keep its recorded integer difference from $\eta_i^a$ on every later boundary tube. This preserves the specified external framing class and does not assert that a nonextending external class has become extending. Both readings of the literal datum are thus respected; no assertion that merely prescribing a frame forces $e_i=0$ was used. [F1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 9.1]

10.2 More explicitly, let $\tau_i$ be an auxiliary extending frame on an output product normal tube. Along its boundary write the recorded external frame as $\eta_i=\tau_i A_i$, with $A_i:S^1\to GL^+(2,\mathbb R)$; the smooth boundary representatives of [F4] allow this description. On a sufficiently thin boundary annulus use $(z,t,v)\mapsto(z,t,A_i(z)v)$, shrinking the fiber radii if necessary. Its inverse uses $A_i(z)^{-1}$, so this is a genuine change of collar coordinates carrying the entire prescribed boundary frame. It changes neither the zero-section disk nor its homotopy. An arbitrary winding of $A_i$ is allowed because these coordinates are required only on the annulus, not over the disk. Thus a nonzero relative Euler obstruction forbids an extending frame with that boundary value, but does not forbid retaining that value on the boundary of the embedded disk. The framing in the Statement is explicitly this boundary framing. [F1, F3, F4, step 10.1, construct]

11.1 Apply [F3] in the supplied smooth neighborhood $V=X$ to these corrected smooth framed maps. Their group is the original good group under the transport of step 2.1, and all hypotheses hold over its actual group ring. It gives pairwise disjoint proper locally flat disks and fixed-boundary homotopies, with extending auxiliary frames. Their actual product normal tubes carry the original external classes by the recorded boundary winding of step 10.1; when the input frame extended, it is already the extending output frame. No TOP-generic smoothing theorem or controlled five-dimensional normal-bundle theorem is being imported in this application. [F2, F3, A1, step 2.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, step 10.2]

12.1 Concatenate the finite collar, approximation, cusp and [F3] homotopies, then apply $H_1^{-1}$ and precompose each disk homotopy with $\Theta_i^{-1}$. At every time the boundary is $H_1^{-1}(H_1f_i\Theta_i\Theta_i^{-1})|_{S^1}=f_i|_{S^1}$ pointwise. Properness and local flatness survive the ambient and source homeomorphisms. The full normal-class comparisons of [F4] and step 10.1 pull back to the prescribed original boundary framings. This proves the stated TOP-input conclusion in the given smooth ambient manifold. Only the finite boundary operation and the accepted CC smooth construction were used; the seven accepted construction/Alexander/open-problem carriers require no alteration. ∎ [F1, F3, F4, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 8.1, step 11.1]

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $V_L(t)$ be the library Jones polynomial of a nonempty oriented link $L$, normalized by $V_{\bigcirc}(t)=1$. For every diagram $D$ of $L$, put $q=-A^{-2}$ and $t=q^2=A^{-4}$. Then the integral rank Euler characteristics satisfy
$$\sum_{i,j}(-1)^i\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}Kh^{i,j}(L)q^j=(q+q^{-1})V_L(t).$$
If $L=K$ is a knot with any basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, then
$$\sum_{i,\widetilde j}(-1)^i\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(K,p)q^{\widetilde j}=V_K(t).$$
The unreduced factor $q+q^{-1}$ and reduced factor $1$ are the respective unknot normalizations.

## Statement references

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Full Axiom of Choice]]

[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice|Full choice implies countable choice]]

[[lem-khovanov-graded-euler-characteristic-jones-normalization|Statewise Euler characteristic and bracket normalization]]

[[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization|Bracket-to-library Jones comparison]]

[[thm-khovanov-homology-is-an-oriented-link-invariant|Unreduced link invariance]]

[[thm-reduced-khovanov-basepoint-and-reidemeister-invariance|Reduced basepoint and diagram invariance]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial* (1999), §§2.4 and 7.1–7.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Bar-Natan, *On Khovanov's categorification of the Jones polynomial* (2002), §§3.1 and 3.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0201043)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology* (2022), §§3–4](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

[Zhang, *Notes on Khovanov homology* (2025), §§3.5–3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1)

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty oriented link $L$, its finite-diagram complexes, and the library Jones polynomial.

[A1] Full AC means every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] Full AC implies AC$_\omega$ ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F2] For a fixed finite diagram $D$, the integral rank Euler sums of its Khovanov cohomology are $(q+q^{-1})f_D(A)$ unreduced and $f_D(A)$ reduced, where $q=-A^{-2}$ and $f_D$ is the writhe-normalized state sum ([[lem-khovanov-graded-euler-characteristic-jones-normalization]]).

[F3] Under full AC, the normalized bracket state sum equals the library Jones polynomial at $t=A^{-4}$ ([[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization]]).

[F4] Under AC$_\omega$, the unreduced groups are independent of the diagram, and the reduced groups of a knot are independent of the diagram and basepoint ([[thm-khovanov-homology-is-an-oriented-link-invariant]], [[thm-reduced-khovanov-basepoint-and-reidemeister-invariance]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [A1] and [F1], full AC supplies AC$_\omega$. Hence [F4] identifies the bigraded groups computed from any finite diagram $D$ with $Kh^{i,j}(L)$, and in the knot case identifies the reduced groups with $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(K,p)$ for every allowed basepoint. The fixed-diagram complexes have finite rank and bounded support, so their rank Euler sums are finite. [A1, F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], those Euler sums are $(q+q^{-1})f_D(A)$ and $f_D(A)$, respectively. By [F3], $f_D(A)=V_L(A^{-4})$ under the stated full-AC hypothesis. Substituting $q=-A^{-2}$ and $t=q^2=A^{-4}$ gives exactly the two formulas in the Statement. For a crossingless unknot the unreduced complex has its two generators in quantum degrees $1,-1$, whereas the reduced interval module has one generator in reduced degree zero, so the respective factors are $q+q^{-1}$ and $1$. Since [F4] makes the groups diagram- and basepoint-independent, these are the claimed link and knot Euler characteristics. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For the Conway knot $C$ and Piccirillo partner $K_P$
fixed above, the zero-traces are diffeomorphic and
$$X_0(C)\cong X_0(K_P),\qquad s(K_P)=2.$$
This statement concerns the zero-trace $4$-manifolds; it asserts no smooth
concordance between $C$ and $K_P$.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Proposition 1.4 and Theorem 1.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the specified knots $C$ and $K_P$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, written AC, is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] AC implies dependent choice and hence countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; this supplies every retained local countable-choice hypothesis. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] [[lem-piccirillo-diagram-produces-dualizable-handle-link]] constructs
under full AC one actual framed handlebody with zero-trace descriptions
$X_0(C)$ and $X_0(K_P)$. The fixed twelve-collar $M$–$N$ transport is retained
locally; its terminal identification with the literal Figure 2 knot is the
explicit published framed input in that supplier, not a newly replayed local
arc map.

[F2] [[lem-piccirillo-knot-lee-computations]] supplies the established exact
rational Lee calculation on the two specified diagrams, giving $s(C)=0$
and $s(K_P)=2$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], the two zero-traces are diffeomorphic to the same framed
handlebody. Compose the first diffeomorphism with the inverse of the
second to obtain $X_0(C)\cong X_0(K_P)$. The terminal identification is
with the named Figure 2 knot, by the retained local construction and
the explicit published terminal input in [F1]. [A1, F1, construct]

1.2 Apply [F2] to that specified diagram to obtain $s(K_P)=2$. Together
with step 1.1 this gives both conclusions of the Statement. [A1, A2, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $K,J\subset S^3$ be smooth oriented knots that cobound a smooth properly embedded annulus in $S^3\times[0,1]$. Then there are finite-rank free $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ bifiltered chain complexes $A$ and $B$ with zero total homology such that
$$ \mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\oplus A\simeq\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(J)\oplus B, $$
where $\simeq$ denotes a Maslov-graded chain homotopy equivalence whose maps and chain homotopies do not increase either filtration. The complexes $A$ and $B$ are acyclic after the filtrations are forgotten; they need not be acyclic in either associated-graded complex.

## Statement references

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth annulus concordance and its direction conventions]]

[[lem-slice-knot-floer-complex-stably-equivalent-to-unknot|The slice-complex splitting with its explicit external Hom input]]

[[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer|The supplied normalized grid/analytic identification]]

[Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, Theorem 1 and §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383)

[Hom, *The knot Floer complex and the smooth concordance group*, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.6635)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth annulus concordance from $K$ to $J$, the filtered connected-sum tensor convention, and the normalized knot Floer complex of each boundary knot.

[F1] [[thm-knot-concordance-is-an-abelian-group]]: the smooth concordance classes form an abelian group with inverse represented by reverse mirror; the smooth proof branch is present and complete. The topological branch is not used.

[F5] The slice-complex stable-splitting lemma supplies exactly the finite-rank free totally acyclic stabilizations and filtered graded equivalence needed below. Its geometric slice input is explicitly external Hom, with the fixed finite/countable specialization stated there; no local movie theorem is inferred. [[lem-slice-knot-floer-complex-stably-equivalent-to-unknot]]

[F2] The supplied full connected-sum comparison is a Maslov-graded bifiltered Laurent chain homotopy equivalence, with inverse and filtered homotopies, and yields the actual tensor complex. [[lem-tau-connected-sum-filtered-tensor-product]]

[F3] The full normalized grid/analytic filtered comparison is supplied. [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]]

[F4] The actual chosen-data full-filtered disk analysis is supplied on its stated knot scope. [[lem-heegaard-floer-holomorphic-disk-regularity-compactness-gluing]]

## Proof

1.1 In the smooth concordance group, the annulus gives $[K]=[J]$, so $K\#(-J)$ is smoothly slice. Also $J\#(-J)$ is slice by the group inverse law. [given, F1]

2.1 Apply the exact stable form of [F5] to the slice knots $K\#(-J)$ and $J\#(-J)$. Write $C_L=CFK^\infty(L)$. It gives acyclic complexes $A_0,B_0,A_1,B_1$ with $C_{K\#(-J)}\oplus A_0\simeq\Lambda\oplus B_0$ and $C_{J\#(-J)}\oplus A_1\simeq\Lambda\oplus B_1$. It does not supply an unstabilized direct-sum splitting of either slice complex, and none is assumed. These equivalences are supplied by the exact slice stable-splitting input [F5]. The supplied model and disk comparisons [F3]–[F4] do not replace the geometric slice input. [given, F5, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Tensor the first equivalence with $C_J$ and the second with $C_K$. ## Statement refuted

Every Seifert surface for a fixed knot has minimum genus; equivalently, every admissible spanning surface $F$ for $K$ satisfies $g(F)=g(K)$.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface|The admissible spanning surfaces]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|The minimum defining knot genus]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a standard round unknot $U$ bounding a disk $D$, and the annular tube construction described above.

[F1] A Seifert surface is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is the given knot. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface]])

[F2] Knot genus is the least genus of any Seifert surface for the knot. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]])

[F3] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, compact subsurfaces have finite cellulations, and a connected compact oriented surface with $b>0$ boundary circles has $\chi=2-2g-b$. ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

[F4] The Euler characteristic of a finite CW complex is the alternating sum of its cell counts. ([[def-euler-characteristic-of-a-finite-cw-complex]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the sequence principle stated in the item. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Counterexample

1.1 Let $U$ be the standard round unknot and $D$ a smooth embedded spanning disk. Remove the interiors of two disjoint small disks from $\operatorname{Int}D$ to obtain a pair of pants $P$. Join the two new boundary circles by a simple arc in a small ball on one side of $D$ and disjoint from $U$; the lateral boundary of a sufficiently thin tubular neighborhood of that arc is an embedded annulus $A$ meeting $P$ only in its two attaching circles. Glue with matching orientations. Then $F=P\cup A$ is connected, compact, smooth, embedded, oriented, and has only boundary $U$. Choose finite cell structures with both attaching circles subcomplexes. Cell-count inclusion-exclusion gives $\chi(P)=\chi(D)-2\chi(D^2)+2\chi(S^1)=1-2+0=-1$; then $\chi(F)=\chi(P)+\chi(A)-2\chi(S^1)=-1+0-0=-1$. [given, F1, F3, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 The surface $F$ has $b=1$. By [F3] and [A1], $-1=\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-1$, hence $g(F)=1$. The original disk $D$ has $b=1$ and $\chi(D)=1$, so [F3] gives $g(D)=0$. [step 1.1, F3, A1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], both $D$ and $F$ are admissible spanning surfaces for $U$. Therefore [F2] and nonnegativity of surface genus give $g(U)=0$, while step 2.1 gives $g(F)=1$. Thus $F$ is not minimum genus and the refuted statement is false. [F1, F2, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the oriented $S^3$ with the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$ by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism and fix the standard height $h(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=x_4$. Its only critical points are the two poles, and each regular level is a 2-sphere. A **Morse representative** of a smooth oriented knot $K$ is a knot ambient isotopic to $K$ on which $h$ has only nondegenerate critical points. Define the **bridge number** $b(K)$ as the minimum number of local maxima of $h$ on a Morse representative of $K$. The standard unknot is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate 2-plane of $S^3$.

A **regular oriented diagram** is a projection of a smooth oriented knot with finitely many transverse double points, no other multiple points, and an over/under choice at each double point. A **crossing change** switches which branch is over at one chosen double point and leaves the projection and strand orientations unchanged. Define the **unknotting number** $u(K)$ as the minimum number of crossing changes needed to turn some regular diagram of a representative of $K$ into a diagram of the standard unknot. Both minima are taken in subsets of $\mathbb N$. The Morse-representative set is nonempty by the first well-definedness result below; under countable choice the regular-diagram existence result and the descending-diagram theorem below make the unknotting set nonempty. The bridge-number definition and the least-element argument in $\mathbb N$ require no choice; countable choice is used only to invoke the stated regular-projection supplier for $u(K)$.

## Example

Assume full AC. The positive trefoil is represented by the closure of the three-crossing two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$; its library Jones polynomial is $t+t^3-t^4$, of span $4-1=3$, and the corresponding connected reduced alternating diagram has crossing number $3$. The figure-eight knot is represented by the closure of the four-crossing three-strand braid whose levels from bottom to top are $\sigma_2^{-1},\sigma_1,\sigma_2^{-1},\sigma_1$; its library Jones polynomial is $t^{-2}-t^{-1}+1-t+t^2$, of span $2-(-2)=4$, and the corresponding connected reduced alternating diagram has crossing number $4$. The convention is $t=A^{-4}$.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9, line cap=round, line join=round]
  \begin{scope}
    \node at (0,1.7) {trefoil Tait graph};
    \fill (-0.7,0.5) circle (2pt) node[left] {$b_1$};
    \fill (0.7,0.5) circle (2pt) node[right] {$b_2$};
    \draw (-0.7,0.5) to[bend left=35] (0.7,0.5);
    \draw (-0.7,0.5) to (0.7,0.5);
    \draw (-0.7,0.5) to[bend right=35] (0.7,0.5);
  \end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[xshift=4cm]
    \node at (0,1.7) {figure-eight Tait graph};
    \fill (-0.9,0.5) circle (2pt) node[left] {$u$};
    \fill (0.9,0.5) circle (2pt) node[right] {$v$};
    \fill (0,-0.7) circle (2pt) node[below] {$w$};
    \draw (-0.9,0.5) to[bend left=28] (0.9,0.5);
    \draw (-0.9,0.5) to[bend right=28] (0.9,0.5);
    \draw (-0.9,0.5)--(0,-0.7)--(0.9,0.5);
  \end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

These are black Tait graphs; the white graphs are their plane duals. Each graph edge represents one crossing of the corresponding projected diagram.

## Example references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial*, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the two braid closures specified in the example, and the source-chart bracket convention.

[F1] A positive braid crossing expands as $A I+A^{-1}e_i$ and a negative one as $A^{-1}I+Ae_i$, where $I$ is through and $e_i$ is cup-cap ([[lem-kauffman-smoothing-operators-for-braid-crossings]]).

[F2] For each state $S$, the bracket contribution is $A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}$, with $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F3] The positive Artin generator has writhe sign $+1$, and the negative generator has sign $-1$ ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]], [[def-elementary-geometric-half-twist]]).

[F4] Components of a geometric braid closure correspond to cycles of its endpoint permutation ([[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]).

[F5] A connected reduced alternating knot diagram with $c$ crossings has Jones span $c$ and realizes crossing number $c$ ([[cor-jones-span-detects-crossing-number-for-reduced-alternating-knots]]).

[F6] A diagram is reduced when no region repeats a crossing on its boundary; connected alternating diagrams admit checkerboard colorings and have connected Tait graphs ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]], [[def-tait-graph-of-a-link-diagram]], [[lem-connected-projection-has-connected-tait-graphs]]).

[F7] Under full AC, $V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4})$ with $t=A^{-4}$ and $f_D(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle$ ([[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization]]).

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function principle for arbitrary families of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 For the closure of $\sigma_1^3$, the endpoint permutation is the transposition of the two strands, hence one cycle by [F4]. The three positive crossings form a connected projection. Starting on the left bottom strand, the successive crossing visits are under, over, under; after closure the right bottom strand visits over, under, over. Thus the diagram is alternating. Its black Tait graph has two vertices and three parallel edges, while the white dual graph is a triangle. Both graphs have no loops, so no crossing repeats a region on its boundary; the diagram is reduced by [F6]. [F3, F4, F6, construct]

1.2 For the four-level braid with levels $\sigma_2^{-1},\sigma_1,\sigma_2^{-1},\sigma_1$, the successive endpoint orders are $[1,3,2]$, $[3,1,2]$, $[3,2,1]$, and $[2,3,1]$. The resulting endpoint permutation is the cycle $1\mapsto3\mapsto2\mapsto1$, so the closure is one knot component by [F4]. Traversing it from the first bottom strand gives crossing visits under, over; from the third bottom strand gives under, over, under; and from the second gives over, under, over. The full cyclic sequence alternates. The black Tait graph is the theta graph with two parallel edges between $u,v$ and a two-edge path $u-w-v$; it has no loops or bridges. Its dual has no loops because the primal has no bridges. Thus both color pairs at every crossing are distinct and the diagram is reduced by [F6]. [F3, F4, F6, construct]

2.1 If exactly $k$ of the three positive crossings use the $B$-smoothing, the states and circle counts are: $k=0$: $1$ state with $2$ circles; $k=1$: $3$ states with $1$ circle; $k=2$: $3$ states with $2$ circles; $k=3$: $1$ state with $3$ circles. Stacking through pairings and cup-cap pairings and closing the two top endpoints to the corresponding bottom endpoints gives these counts. By [F1]–[F2], the grouped contributions are $A^3\delta+3A+3A^{-1}\delta+A^{-3}\delta^2=A^{-7}-A^{-3}-A^5$. The writhe is $3$ by [F3], so [F7] gives $V_{3_1}(t)=(-A^3)^{-3}(A^{-7}-A^{-3}-A^5)\big|_{t=A^{-4}}=t+t^3-t^4$. Its span is $3$, and [F5] gives crossing number $3$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Encode a state by four bits from bottom to top, with $0$ meaning through pairing and $1$ meaning cup-cap pairing. Let $p$ be the number of cup-cap choices at positive crossings and $q$ the number at negative crossings; [F1] gives weight exponent $2(q-p)$. Closing the pairings gives the exhaustive state data $\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{state}&\text{circles}&\text{exponent}\\0000&3&0\\0001&2&-2\\0010&2&2\\0011&1&0\\0100&2&-2\\0101&3&-4\\0110&1&0\\0111&2&-2\\1000&2&2\\1001&1&0\\1010&3&4\\1011&2&2\\1100&1&0\\1101&2&-2\\1110&2&2\\1111&1&0\end{array}$. Thus the five one-circle states contribute $5$, the eight two-circle states contribute $4(A^2+A^{-2})\delta$, and the three three-circle states contribute $(1+A^4+A^{-4})\delta^2$. Expanding $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ gives $\langle D_F\rangle=5+4(A^2+A^{-2})\delta+(1+A^4+A^{-4})\delta^2=A^8-A^4+1-A^{-4}+A^{-8}$. There are two positive and two negative crossings, so writhe is $0$ by [F3]. By [F7], $V_{4_1}(t)=t^{-2}-t^{-1}+1-t+t^2$, whose span is $4$. Applying [F5] gives crossing number $4$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F7, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $C_0(\Omega)$ in the uniform norm.

## Statement references

[[def-compact-support-c-c-and-c-zero-on-an-lch-space|C-zero functions vanish at infinity, and C-c functions have compact support.]]

[[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls|Smooth cutoffs exist between nested concentric balls.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a continuous function on $\Omega$ that vanishes at infinity.

[F1] Closed bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ are compact. ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]])

[F2] A smooth bump can be chosen equal to one on an inner ball and supported in a larger ball. ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]])

[F3] Dominated convergence holds on Lebesgue measure spaces without a choice assumption. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]])

## Proof

**Given:** The open set $\Omega$ and $f\in C_0(\Omega)$.

1.1 Let $f\in C_0(\Omega)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. The set $K:=\{x\in\Omega:|f(x)|\ge\varepsilon/3\}$ is compact by the definition of vanishing at infinity. If $K=\varnothing$, the zero function approximates $f$ within $\varepsilon/3$. Otherwise cover $K$ by finitely many inner balls whose doubled closed balls lie in $\Omega$, using compactness [F1]. Choose the corresponding bumps from [F2] and combine them as $\chi:=1-\prod_j(1-\chi_j)$. Then $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $\chi=1$ on $K$, so $\|f-\chi f\|_\infty\le\varepsilon/3$. [F1, F2, given, choose, construct]

2.1 Extend $g:=\chi f$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$. It is continuous and compactly supported, hence uniformly continuous. Fix a nonnegative smooth bump from [F2], normalize its integral to one, and rescale it as $\rho_\delta(x)=\delta^{-n}\rho(x/\delta)$. Then $$\|g*\rho_\delta-g\|_\infty\le\sup_{|h|\le\delta,\ x\in\mathbb R^n}|g(x-h)-g(x)|\to0.$$ To verify smoothness directly, for every multi-index $\alpha$ set $$G_\alpha(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}g(y)\,\partial^\alpha\rho_\delta(x-y)\,dy.$$ On each compact neighborhood of $x$, these integrands and their coordinate difference quotients are dominated by $C|g|\mathbf1_K$ for a common compact set $K$ and finite constant $C$, since the kernel derivatives have compact support and are bounded. Dominated convergence [F3] gives continuity of each $G_\alpha$ and $\partial_jG_\alpha=G_{\alpha+e_j}$ for every coordinate $j$. Induction on $|\alpha|$ therefore gives $g*\rho_\delta=G_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$. For sufficiently small $\delta$, its support remains in $\Omega$ because $\operatorname{supp}g$ is compactly contained there. Taking the uniform error below $2\varepsilon/3$ and restricting to $\Omega$ gives an element of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ within $\varepsilon$ of $f$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, construct] ∎

## Statement

For every path-connected CW space $X$, disjoint union makes $\Omega_n^{SO}(X)$ an abelian group with identity the empty manifold with its unique map to $X$ and inverse of $(M,f)$ represented by $(-M,f)$.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-bordism-group-of-a-space|Oriented bordism classes of maps to a space]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A path-connected CW space $X$ and the bordism classes of closed oriented $n$-manifolds equipped with maps to $X$.

[F1] A bordism class is represented by a pair $(M,f)$, and its equivalence is witnessed by a compact oriented bordism with an extending map to $X$. [[def-oriented-bordism-group-of-a-space]]

## Proof

1.1 The sum is well-defined: if $F_i:W_i\to X$ are bordisms witnessing equivalences of pairs for $i=0,1$, then $W_0\sqcup W_1$ with map $F_0\sqcup F_1$ is a bordism witnessing the equivalence of the disjoint unions. Boundary orientations are inherited componentwise. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Disjoint union is associative and commutative up to the orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that rebracket or permute its components; composing the maps with these diffeomorphisms preserves the bordism classes. The empty manifold with its unique map is a two-sided identity. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ with map $f\circ\operatorname{pr}_M$ has boundary $(M,f)\sqcup(-M,f)$ under the product orientation convention. Thus $(-M,f)$ is a two-sided inverse of $(M,f)$, so the operation is an abelian group operation. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.


## Statement references

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§1–2](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

[Stees, §2.5](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/54c7d68f-d982-4e1f-9550-e54140ada5ea/content)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the based string-link data in the statement.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The local Stallings supplier uses this axiom for its group-homology branch.

[F1] Each endpoint group is free of rank $r$, with the compatible positive meridian basis; independently based meridians are the recorded conjugates and give the same homology basis. The exterior inclusion maps are isomorphisms on $H_1$ and epimorphisms on $H_2$. [[lem-string-link-exterior-homology-and-meridian-maps]]

[F2] The natural degree-one Hurewicz maps identify group $H_1$ with abelianization. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

[F3] For a path-connected CW complex, the classifying map to the classifying space of its fundamental group is onto on $H_2$. [[lem-h2-classifying-map-is-surjective]]

[F4] Classifying maps commute up to based homotopy with maps of path-connected CW complexes and their induced fundamental-group homomorphisms. [[lem-classifying-maps-are-natural-under-group-homomorphisms]]

[F5] A group homomorphism inducing an isomorphism on $H_1(-;\mathbb Z)$ and an epimorphism on $H_2(-;\mathbb Z)$ induces isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient, under the stated AC branch. [[thm-stallings-integral-lower-central-isomorphism]]

[F6] Compact smooth manifolds with corners admit finite CW triangulations under AC. [[thm-compact-smooth-manifolds-with-corners-admit-relative-finite-triangulations]]

## Proof

**Given:** The endpoint inclusions $f_\pm:P_\pm\hookrightarrow X_\tau$.

1.1 By [F1], each $f_\pm$ induces an isomorphism on topological $H_1$ and an epimorphism on topological $H_2$. Naturality of [F2] identifies the $H_1$ map with the map between the abelianizations of $\pi_1(P_\pm)$ and $\pi_1(X_\tau)$. Thus each group homomorphism $(f_\pm)_*$ is an isomorphism on group $H_1$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 By [F6], $P_\pm$ and $X_\tau$ have CW structures, so choose classifying maps $c_\pm:P_\pm\to B\pi_1(P_\pm)$ and $c_X:X_\tau\to B\pi_1(X_\tau)$. For either sign and any $y\in H_2(\pi_1(X_\tau);\mathbb Z)$, choose $z\in H_2(X_\tau;\mathbb Z)$ with $(c_X)_*(z)=y$ using [F3]. By [F1] choose $w\in H_2(P_\pm;\mathbb Z)$ with $(f_\pm)_*(w)=z$. Write $\phi_\pm=(f_\pm)_*$. Naturality [F4] gives $$(B\phi_\pm)_*((c_\pm)_*(w))=(c_X)_*((f_\pm)_*(w))=y.$$ Thus every class $y$ in $H_2(\pi_1(X_\tau);\mathbb Z)$ is in the image of the induced group-homology map $H_2(\pi_1(P_\pm);\mathbb Z)\to H_2(\pi_1(X_\tau);\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 By [F5], each $(f_\pm)_*$ now satisfies both Stallings hypotheses. Applying it separately to $f_-$ and $f_+$ proves that each induced map on $F_r/\Gamma_q$ is an isomorphism for every finite $q\geq1$. [A1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Since both end maps are isomorphisms at every such $q$, their inverse/composite is defined and is an isomorphism. The meridian labels and basing path are carried through the same maps, so this is exactly the stated peripheral comparison. The proof uses full AC only through the classifying-space and Stallings suppliers; no additional choice is used in the elementwise quotient argument. [A1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Choose arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians. Their map $a:F_r\to\pi_1(P_\pm)$ is the identity on the ordered $H_1$ basis by [F1] and [F2]. Also $H_2(\pi_1(P_\pm);\mathbb Z)=0$: [F1] gives $H_2(P_\pm)=0$, and [F3] maps that group onto the group-homology group. Thus $a$ is onto on $H_2$, independently of its source's $H_2$. Apply [F5] to $a$. It induces an isomorphism at every finite lower-central quotient, even though $a$ need not be an isomorphism on the full groups. Compose it with the already proved end isomorphism of step 3.1. This proves the arbitrary-basing branch and its stated inverse/composite, using exactly the selected meridian conjugations rather than an incorrect free-basis assertion. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Example

Consider the complete original Fourier architecture and diagonal inverse question reproduced below. For every odd integer $m\ge3$, every $N\ge1$, and every admissible bounded parameter class with a measurable empirical minimizer, its risk satisfies
$$\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{ERM}}_{N,m}(S,B)\ge\frac{R^2(3^p-2^p)^2}{4\,3^{2(p+s)}}>0.$$
The same bound holds for every measurable learner whose realized predictor belongs to the stated coordinate-free Fourier class, whether or not it minimizes empirical risk. On the other hand, the unrestricted risk tends to zero as $m\to\infty$ for fixed $p,s,R,\sigma>0$, independently of $N$. Thus no growth of $N,S,B$ can make this original architecture attain the vanishing unrestricted risk along an odd-mesh subsequence. This is a partial resolution: no complete joint bounded-class rate, or corresponding fixed positive even-mesh floor, is asserted. The original question is retained verbatim under Original question.

## Example references

[Reinhardt, Wang, and Zech, full 2026 JMLR paper](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume27/25-0543/25-0543.pdf)

[de Hoop et al., full EIT inverse-map paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

[Bal, full inverse-problems lecture notes](https://www.stat.uchicago.edu/~guillaumebal/COURSES/E6901/LectureNotesIP.pdf)

[Kovachki et al., full 2023 JMLR paper](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume24/21-1524/21-1524.pdf)

## Original question

Let $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure and fix the real orthonormal Fourier basis
$$\phi_1(x)=1,\qquad \phi_{2k}(x)=\sqrt2\cos(kx),\qquad \phi_{2k+1}(x)=\sqrt2\sin(kx)\quad(k\ge1).$$
Use this basis to identify the real Hilbert space $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R)$. Fix integers $N,m\ge1$ and parameters $s,p,R,\sigma>0$, and define
$$\Theta_s(R)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2:\sum_{j\ge1}j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2\right\},\qquad (A_p\theta)_j=j^{-p}\theta_j,\qquad \mathcal X_p(R)=A_p\Theta_s(R).$$
The inverse map $G^\dagger:\mathcal X_p(R)\to\ell^2$ is $G^\dagger(A_p\theta)=\theta$. For $m\ge1$, let $P_m$ retain the first $m$ Fourier coefficients and let $I_m:\mathbb R^m\to\ell^2$ append zero coordinates.

Fix a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial function $\sigma_0:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, called the activation. For $x\in\mathbb R^m$, form the scalar input field $\bar u_0(x;z)=\sum_{j=1}^m x_j\phi_j(z)$. A pointwise affine lift $u_0(x;z)=V_{\mathrm{in}}\bar u_0(x;z)+b_{\mathrm{in}}$, with $V_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb R^{c_0}$ and $b_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb R^{c_0}$, creates $c_0$ channels. For fields $u_\ell(z)\in\mathbb R^{c_\ell}$ with positive integer channel counts $c_\ell$, apply an integer number $D\ge1$ of layers indexed by $\ell=0,\ldots,D-1$:
$$u_{\ell+1}(z)=\sigma_0\!\left(W_\ell u_\ell(z)+b_\ell+(\mathcal K_\ell u_\ell)(z)\right).$$
Here $\sigma_0$ acts coordinatewise, $W_\ell\in\mathbb R^{c_{\ell+1}\times c_\ell}$ and $b_\ell\in\mathbb R^{c_{\ell+1}}$ are pointwise channel weights, and $\mathcal K_\ell$ is a Fourier multiplier meaning $\widehat{(\mathcal K_\ell u)}(k)=R_{\ell,k}\widehat u(k)$, where $\widehat u(k)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}u(z)e^{-ikz}\,dz$ is computed componentwise, with matrices $R_{\ell,k}\in\mathbb C^{c_{\ell+1}\times c_\ell}$ satisfying $R_{\ell,-k}=\overline{R_{\ell,k}}$ and $R_{\ell,k}=0$ for $|k|>q$ for some integer cutoff $q\ge0$. A pointwise affine output map $v(x;z)=a_{\mathrm{out}}^\top u_D(z)+b_{\mathrm{out}}$ gives a real scalar field, and the network output is $\Psi_m(x)=(\langle v(x;\cdot),\phi_j\rangle_{L^2})_{j=1}^m$. Let $\mathcal F_{S,B}^{(m)}$ be the union of these maps over architectures whose depth, channel counts, Fourier cutoff, and number of real scalar parameters are each at most the integer $S\ge1$, with every trainable parameter bounded in absolute value by $B>0$. A parameter array used at mesh size $m$ is the same array at every other mesh size. For fixed $S$, there are finitely many allowed architecture indices; equip their disjoint union of bounded real parameter boxes with its Borel structure.

Write $\mathcal P(K)$ for the Borel probability laws on a Borel set $K$. For a Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\Theta_s(R)$, draw independent training truths $\theta_i\sim\mu$ and observations
$$X_{i,m}=P_mA_p\theta_i+\eta_{i,m},\qquad Y_{i,m}=P_m\theta_i,\qquad \eta_{i,m}\sim N(0,\sigma^2m^{-1}I_m),\quad i=1,\ldots,N,$$
with all noises independent, and write $D_{N,m}=((X_{i,m},Y_{i,m}))_{i=1}^N$. A selector is Borel into the finite disjoint union of architecture indices and their bounded parameter boxes, and its realized map minimizes the empirical loss. For each $N,m,S,B$, assume there is at least one such selector $\tau$ that, from $D_{N,m}$, returns a minimizer of
$$\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|\Psi(X_{i,m})-Y_{i,m}\|_2^2$$
over $\Psi\in\mathcal F_{S,B}^{(m)}$; let $\mathcal T_{N,m}(S,B)$ be the set of all such selectors. At test time, draw an independent $\theta\sim\mu$ and $\eta_m\sim N(0,\sigma^2m^{-1}I_m)$, and define
$$\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{ERM}}_{N,m}(S,B)=\inf_{\tau\in\mathcal T_{N,m}(S,B)}\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal P(\Theta_s(R))}E\left\|I_m\tau(D_{N,m})(P_mA_p\theta+\eta_m)-\theta\right\|_{\ell^2}^2.$$
Also define $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{all}}_{N,m}$ by the same infimum over all Borel predictors from $(D_{N,m},X_m)$ to $\mathbb R^m$, with $X_m=P_mA_p\theta+\eta_m$. Determine matching minimax upper and lower rates for $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{ERM}}_{N,m}(S,B)$ jointly in $N,m,S,B,p,s,R,\sigma$. In particular, characterize the joint growth regimes of $m=m_N$ and $S=S_N$ that separate statistical estimation, neural-operator approximation, and continuum truncation error, and determine when the bounded shared-parameter Fourier architecture attains the unrestricted rate $\mathfrak R^{\mathrm{all}}_{N,m}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The original real Fourier basis $\phi_1=1$, $\phi_2=\sqrt2\cos z$, $\phi_3=\sqrt2\sin z$ and all higher complete cosine/sine pairs; the architecture has only constant pointwise channel weights and biases, Fourier multipliers and a scalar pointwise Lipschitz activation. Its parameters may depend on all training data but are fixed during test evaluation.

[A1] Translation $T_\alpha u(z)=u(z-\alpha)$ is an isometry of $L^2(\mathbb T)$, sends $\phi_2$ to $\phi_3$ for $\alpha=\pi/2$, and preserves each full two-dimensional cosine/sine frequency pair. The first-m-coordinate subspace is translation-invariant when $m$ is odd.

[A2] A vector with distribution $N(0,\tau^2I_m)$ is invariant under every orthogonal matrix: its density is a constant times $e^{-\|x\|^2/(2\tau^2)}$, and orthogonal changes of variables preserve norm and volume.

[A3] $\|x-a\|^2+\|x-b\|^2\ge\|a-b\|^2/2$ by completing the square.

## Verification

**Given:** The original architecture, training and test model, and [A1]–[A3].

1.1 Each Fourier multiplier commutes with translation because the kth translated Fourier coefficient is multiplied by the scalar $e^{-ik\alpha}$, which commutes with its channel matrix. Every constant channel matrix, constant bias and coordinatewise scalar activation also commutes with translation. By induction through the lift, all layers and output map, the realized scalar output field is translation-equivariant. The layer fields are in $L^2$: a globally Lipschitz activation has linear growth, the pointwise weights are finite and the finite Fourier multipliers are bounded. For odd $m$, projection onto the first m coefficients commutes with translation by [A1]. Hence the zero-extended output map $F=I_m\Psi_m$ satisfies $F(U_\alpha x)=T_\alpha F(x)$, where $U_\alpha$ is the orthogonal translation matrix on the retained coefficients. This holds for every individual parameter array, also after data-dependent selection. [A1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Put $a=R3^{-(p+s)}$, choose $\theta_c=a2^pe_2$ and $\theta_s=a3^pe_3$, and let $\mu=(\delta_{\theta_c}+\delta_{\theta_s})/2$. These truths lie in the ellipsoid because their weighted squared norms are at most $a^23^{2(p+s)}=R^2$. Their forward coefficient vectors are respectively $ae_2$ and $ae_3$, related by $U=U_{\pi/2}$. Conditional on any training sample, the test truth is still an independent equal-probability draw from these two values. Couple the corresponding test noises as $\eta$ and $U\eta$; by [A2] both have the required $N(0,\sigma^2m^{-1}I_m)$ law. [A1, A2, given, construct, algebra]

1.3 To see unrestricted vanishing without training, put $k_m=\min\{m,\max\{1,\lfloor m^{1/(2(2p+1))}\rfloor\}\}$. Output $j^pX_{m,j}$ for $j\le k_m$ and zero otherwise. Its risk for every truth is at most $\sigma^2m^{-1}\sum_{j\le k_m}j^{2p}+R^2(k_m+1)^{-2s}\le\sigma^2m^{-1}k_m^{2p+1}+R^2(k_m+1)^{-2s}\to0$. It is a Borel predictor and is allowed in the unrestricted class. This proves the contrast with the positive odd-mesh architecture floor. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For fixed training data, let $F$ be its selected predictor. By step 1.1, $F(ae_3+U\eta)=T_{\pi/2}F(ae_2+\eta)$. Translating the first output and truth preserves their norm. Consequently the conditional average of the two squared risks is $\tfrac12E[\|T_{\pi/2}F(ae_2+\eta)-T_{\pi/2}\theta_c\|^2+\|T_{\pi/2}F(ae_2+\eta)-\theta_s\|^2]$, which is at least $\|T_{\pi/2}\theta_c-\theta_s\|^2/4=a^2(3^p-2^p)^2/4$ by [A3]. This lower bound is independent of the training sample. Integrating over it, taking the worst law and then the infimum over selectors proves the stated floor. [A1, A3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The mismatch arises because the diagonal inverse rescales the first cosine and sine by different factors $2^p$ and $3^p$, while the coordinate-free architecture must respect translation between them. It is independent of finite training or parameter-size limitations. The proof deliberately uses odd $m$ so both the input noise law and retained output subspace are translation-invariant; it supplies no identical assertion for even $m$, whose last frequency pair is incomplete. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Scope of the resolution

The odd-mesh consistency subquestion is answered negatively, and the unrestricted vanishing comparison is proved. The full requested joint N,m,S,B minimax rate is not resolved here; in particular even meshes break the complete-pair symmetry used by the lower bound, and different activations/parameter budgets may have distinct approximation behavior. This is not the EIT question: the generalized EIT architecture has coordinate/chart lifting, so this coordinate-free translation obstruction is not transferred to it.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $J=J_1\cup\cdots\cup J_n$ be an oriented link of $n\ge1$ smooth components in $S^3$. Choose pairwise disjoint closed tubular neighborhoods $N(J_i)$, let $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(\bigcup_iN(J_i))$, and let $\mu_i$ be the positive meridian of $J_i$. Let $\lambda_i$ be the longitude parallel to $J_i$ with zero self-linking. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^n$ on the meridian basis $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$; for $i\ne j$, define $\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ to be the $j$-th coordinate of $[\lambda_i]$, the usual oriented linking number. Use the boundary-torus intersection convention $\mu_i\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda_i=+1$. Give $J_i$ an integer framing $f_i$ and fill along $\delta_i=\lambda_i+f_i\mu_i$. Let $A$ be the symmetric integer matrix with $A_{ii}=f_i$ and $A_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$ for $i\ne j$. Assume $\det A\ne0$, and let $Y$ be the resulting oriented surgery manifold, oriented as the boundary of the 4-dimensional surgery handlebody with outward normal first. Then $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$. For torsion classes $[C],[D]\in H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ represented by oriented 1-cycles, choose $m>0$ and an integral 2-chain $F$ with $\partial F=mC$ and define $\lambda_Y([C],[D])=(F\mathbin{\cdot}D)/m\pmod{\mathbb Z}$, where the intersection is signed by the orientation of $Y$. If $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ are meridian-coordinate representatives of $[C],[D]$, then
$$
\lambda_Y([x],[y])=-x^TA^{-1}y\pmod{\mathbb Z}.
$$
## Statement references

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|Finite disjoint unions of smooth oriented circles in $S^3$]]

[[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold|The link exterior and its connected complement]]

[[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere|Alexander-duality meridian coordinates]]

[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link|Positive meridian normalization]]

[[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology|Homology exactness for the surgery filling]]

[Przytycki–Yasuhara, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0111203v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the framed link, its surgery slopes, the symmetric linking matrix $A$, and $\det A\ne0$.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom required by Alexander duality. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A finite oriented link in $S^3$ is compact and locally contractible; Alexander duality identifies the first homology of its complement with $\mathbb Z^n$, with the positive meridians as coordinate generators. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]

[F2] The open complement of a nonempty smooth link is connected and deformation retracts onto its compact exterior. [[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold]]

[F3] The positive meridians use the total-linking normalization: each positive component meridian maps to $1$ under the sum of the Alexander-duality component coordinates. [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F4] Mayer–Vietoris is exact for the collar-thickened cover by the exterior and the attached solid tori. [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data and boundary-torus intersection convention in the Statement. Write $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(J)$ for the compact exterior and use $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$ as its meridian-coordinate basis.

1.1 Radial motion in each punctured normal disk gives a deformation retraction from $S^3\setminus J$ to $X$. By [F1], Alexander duality identifies $H_1(S^3\setminus J;\mathbb Z)$ with $\widetilde H^1(J;\mathbb Z)=\bigoplus_iH^1(J_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n$. The inclusion of the compact exterior induces the same homology isomorphism by the retraction in [F2]. Thus $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 The boundary of a small positive normal disk to $J_i$ maps to the $i$-th Alexander-duality coordinate generator: it meets $J_i$ once positively and misses every other component. Hence $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_n]$ are the coordinate basis, with the positive orientation normalized as in [F3]. The $i$-th coordinate of $[\lambda_i]$ is zero by its zero self-linking convention, and for $j\ne i$ its $j$-th coordinate is the defined linking number $\operatorname{lk}_{S^3}(J_i,J_j)$. Therefore $[\delta_i]=[\lambda_i+f_i\mu_i]=\sum_jA_{ij}[\mu_j]$. [F3, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 In Mayer–Vietoris for the filling, the map $H_1(\partial V_i)\to H_1(V_i)$ is onto and its kernel is generated by the meridian-disk boundary $\delta_i$. The map $H_0(\bigsqcup_i\partial V_i)\to H_0(X)\oplus H_0(\bigsqcup_iV_i)$ is injective: in coordinates it sends $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ to $(\sum_i a_i,-a_1,\ldots,-a_n)$. Exactness therefore gives $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Since $A$ is invertible over $\mathbb Q$, for every $x\in\mathbb Z^n$ some positive integer $m$ clears the denominators of $A^{-1}x$, so $mx\in A\mathbb Z^n$ and each class is torsion. If $F,F'$ bound $mC,m'C$, pass to a common multiple $M$; the difference $(M/m)F-(M/m')F'$ is a 2-cycle $Z$. If $r[D]=0$, write $rD=\partial G$; the chain boundary identity gives $r(Z\mathbin{\cdot}D)=Z\mathbin{\cdot}\partial G=\partial Z\mathbin{\cdot}G=0$, hence $Z\mathbin{\cdot}D=0$. Thus the quotient is independent of the chosen bounding chain and multiple modulo integers. Replacing either cycle representative by a homologous one adds an integer by the same boundary identity. [step 3.1, given, algebra]

4.2 Let $B$ be the slope-coordinate matrix $[\delta]=B[\mu]$ in $H_1(X;\mathbb Q)$; step 2.1 gives $B=A$. In the reverse filling, the slope-coordinate matrix is $B^{-1}$. Let $\widetilde J_i$ denote the core of the attached solid torus, oriented so the boundary longitude $\ell_i$ mapping to it satisfies $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\ell_i=1$. Since $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\mu_i=-1$, the image of $\mu_i$ in that solid torus is $-[\widetilde J_i]$. Define $H_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_Y(\widetilde J_i,\widetilde J_j)$ for $i\ne j$, and let $H_{ii}$ be the reverse-surgery framing determined by the slope $\mu_i$. For $i\ne j$, clear denominators in $[\mu_i]=\sum_k(B^{-1})_{ik}[\delta_k]$ and cap each $\delta_k$ by its meridian disk. The chain in $X$ realizing this homology relation misses every core; with $\delta_k\mathbin{\cdot}\ell_k=+1$, the capped disk in $V_k$ meets the oriented core $\widetilde J_j$ once positively if $k=j$ and not at all otherwise. Hence $(B^{-1})_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_Y(\mu_i,\widetilde J_j)=-H_{ij}$. The reverse diagonal framing is the reverse slope coefficient divided by $\delta_i\mathbin{\cdot}\mu_i=-1$, so $H_{ii}=-(B^{-1})_{ii}$. Therefore $H=-B^{-1}=-A^{-1}$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

5.1 Each old meridian $\mu_i$ represents $-\widetilde J_i$ in its attached solid torus. Hence for distinct indices their linking equals the core-linking entry $H_{ij}$; for a self-pairing, a parallel meridian maps to the parallel core specified by the reverse framing, also giving $H_{ii}$. Thus $\lambda_Y([\mu_i],[\mu_j])=-(A^{-1})_{ij}$. The chain formula is additive in both cycles, by taking common multiples and summing bounding chains, so its matrix on the meridian basis gives $\lambda_Y([x],[y])=-x^TA^{-1}y\pmod{\mathbb Z}$. If $x$ is replaced by $x+Az$, the value changes by $-z^Ty$; if $y$ is replaced by $y+Az$, it changes by $-x^Tz$, both integers because $A$ is symmetric and integral. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The reverse filling restores $S^3$ by surgery on the core link. The diagram records the two surgery descriptions; the slope-basis calculation in steps 4.2–5.1 supplies the inverse-matrix sign.


## Statement

Assume full AC when the form is obtained from a knot. For every integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, the class represented by $(H,-V)$ is the additive inverse of the class represented by $(H,V)$ in $G_{\mathbb Z}$.

## Statement references

[[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance|The group presentation of algebraic concordance and the definition of a metabolic lattice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$ and the defining relations of $G_{\mathbb Z}$.

[A1] Full AC is inherited only when the abstract lattice is instantiated as a knot's Seifert pairing; the diagonal calculation below is choice-free. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] In $G_{\mathbb Z}$, direct sum is addition and every metabolic lattice represents zero. [[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance]]

## Proof

1.1 In $(H,V)\oplus(H,-V)$, the diagonal subgroup $\Delta H=\{(x,x):x\in H\}$ is a direct summand: it is the kernel of the surjection $(x,y)\mapsto x-y$ and that surjection has section $z\mapsto(z,0)$. Its rank is $\operatorname{rank}H$, half the rank of $H\oplus H$. For $x,y\in H$, $(V\oplus(-V))((x,x),(y,y))=V(x,y)-V(x,y)=0$, so $\Delta H$ is a metabolizer. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F1], the metabolic direct sum in step 1.1 represents zero, while the direct-sum relation identifies its class with $[V]+[-V]$. Hence $[-V]=-[V]$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $(B,G,R)$ be a dualizable framed handle link and
let $X(B,G,R)$ be its associated handlebody. There are finite sequences of
handle slides and cancellations, first sliding $G$ over $B$ and cancelling
the $1$-handle $R$ with the $2$-handle $B$, and then using the reversed roles,
that leave single $0$-framed attaching knots $K_G$ and $K_B$, respectively.
There are diffeomorphisms
$$
X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_G)\cong X_0(K_B).
$$

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Theorem 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice and a dualizable framed handle link $(B,G,R)$.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is [[def-countable-choice]].
It is used only through the handle-slide and cancellation suppliers below.

[F1] [[def-dualizable-handle-link]]: $R$ is a dotted $1$-handle, $B,G$ are
$0$-framed $2$-handles, each of $B\cup R$ and $G\cup R$ is a meridional
two-component link, and $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$.

[F2] [[def-handle-slide-of-one-k-handle-over-another]] and
[[lem-handle-slides-preserve-the-relative-diffeomorphism-type]]: a slide of
one $2$-handle over another replaces its attaching circle by a band sum with
a signed framed parallel copy and preserves the relative diffeomorphism type.

[F3] [[thm-handle-cancellation]]: a $1$-handle and $2$-handle whose attaching
and belt spheres meet transversely once cancel, preserving the diffeomorphism
type relative to the incoming boundary and transporting all remaining
attaching data.

[F4] [[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]]: the
half-sum of mixed crossing signs is invariant under regular diagram changes
and is symmetric in the two components.

[F5] [[lem-dualizable-slide-clears-meridian-disk]]: after finitely many slides
and isotopies, the remaining attaching circle can be made disjoint from a
spanning disk of the dotted circle. It constructs one framed slide and a product-bigon isotopy for each current intersection, reducing their finite count by one at every stage.

[F6] [[thm-oriented-linking-number-scan-terminates-and-is-correct]] and
[[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]]: on a finite
regular diagram of two oriented components, the scan returns the integer
half-sum of mixed crossing signs, and that half-sum is invariant under
orientation-preserving isotopy of the link. These suppliers do not identify
the integer with a homology coordinate.

[F7] [[lem-knot-exterior-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]: for a knot $K$ with
the chosen tube and positive meridian, $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K]$.

[F8] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: a preferred longitude has
zero class in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, and a degree-one parallel with zero class
is a preferred longitude.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix disjoint oriented knots $K,J\subset S^3$ with a regular oriented diagram $D$, and write $[J]=m[\mu_K]$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ using [F7]. The inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow S^3\setminus K$ is a homotopy equivalence: in the punctured tube $N(K)\setminus K$, radial motion in each normal disk retracts onto its boundary torus. Thus the same coefficient $m$ is obtained in the open complement. Let $\ell(D)$ be the half-sum of mixed crossing signs. At a mixed crossing where $K$ passes over $J$ with sign $\epsilon$, switching the crossing changes $\ell$ by $-\epsilon$. In an oriented crossing ball straighten $K$ to the positive $x$-axis. When $\epsilon=+1$, the old underpassing arc of $J$ runs in the positive $y$ direction, and the new arc above $K$ minus the old arc represents the negative positive-meridian class; when $\epsilon=-1$, reversing that tangent reverses the class. Hence the same switch changes $[J]$ by $-\epsilon[\mu_K]$, so it changes $m$ by $-\epsilon$. After switching all mixed crossings, $J$ passes over $K$ at every projected intersection. Raise $J$ in the viewing-normal direction and move its projection into a disk disjoint from the projection of $K$; this is an isotopy in $S^3\setminus K$. The final $J$ lies in a $3$-ball disjoint from $K$, so its homology class is zero, and a regular diagram with separated projections has half-sum zero. By [F6] the half-sum is unchanged by this isotopy. Since every crossing switch changed the half-sum and meridian coefficient by the same integer, their initial values agree: $\ell(D)=m$. In particular, for any framed parallel $L_f$ of a knot $L$, its framing integer measured by this half-sum is its meridian coefficient in $H_1(E_L)$; it is zero exactly when $[L_f]=0$. A degree-one parallel with zero class is a preferred longitude by [F8]. [F1, F6, F7, F8, given, construct]

2.1 Choose a spanning disk $D_R$ for the unknotted dotted circle $R$ so that $B$ meets it once, as allowed by [F1]. Apply [F5] to obtain a finite sequence of slides of $G$ over $B$ and isotopies after which the remaining attaching circle is disjoint from $D_R$. The supplier clears actual intersections one at a time; it does not infer geometric disjointness from a zero signed count. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given, construct]

3.1 At each slide of $G$ over $B$, the oriented band sum represents $[G]\pm[B_f]$ in $H_1(E_B)$, where $B_f$ is the signed framed parallel of $B$. By step 1.1, the meridian coordinate of $[B_f]$ is its framing integer $f(B)$. Thus the new linking number is $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)\pm f(B)$. The initial framing pushoff of $B$ is its preferred longitude by [F1], so [F8] makes its class zero and step 1.1 gives $f(B)=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ remains zero after every slide. [F1, F2, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, induction, construct]

4.1 For the same band sum, expanding the linking of the new attaching circle with its transported pushoff gives $$ f(G\#(\pm B))=f(G)+f(B)\pm2\operatorname{lk}(B,G). $$ The two self-pairings are the old framings and the two cross-pairings are equal by the symmetry in [F4]. The expansion is valid because the band and its pushoff are carried in disjoint product strips, so the four old pairings are unchanged outside the strips. Each framing integer is the meridian coordinate of its pushoff by step 1.1. All framing terms are zero initially by [F1], [F8] and step 1.1, and the mutual linking remains zero by step 3.1. Induction over the finite sequence in [F5] shows the final attaching framing is zero; isotopies preserve it. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, induction, algebra]

5.1 The circle $B$ still goes geometrically once over the $1$-handle $R$, while the remaining attaching circle is disjoint from the cancellation disk. Therefore the attaching sphere of the $2$-handle $B$ meets the belt sphere of the $1$-handle once, and [F3] cancels this pair. Since the remaining attaching circle and its framing lie outside the cancellation neighborhood, the transported remaining handle is a single $0$-framed $2$-handle on a $4$-ball. By [F1] this is $X_0(K_G)$. Slides preserve the handlebody by [F2], so $X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_G)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Interchange $B$ and $G$. The other meridional condition supplies the starting intersection for [F5], and the linking number remains zero by [F4]. The reversed slide sequence preserves both the zero mutual linking and zero framing by the calculations in steps 3.1 and 4.1. Cancel $(R,G)$ by the same one-intersection argument as in step 5.1. This gives $X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_B)$; combining with step 5.1 yields both trace descriptions. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=2.4cm,>=stealth]
  \node (x) {$B^4\cup_R h^1\cup_B h^2_0\cup_G h^2_0$};
  \node (kg) [below left of=x] {$B^4\cup_{K_G}h^2_0$};
  \node (kb) [below right of=x] {$B^4\cup_{K_B}h^2_0$};
  \draw[->] (x) -- node[left,align=center] {slide $G$ over $B$;\\cancel $(R,B)$} (kg);
  \draw[->] (x) -- node[right,align=center] {slide $B$ over $G$;\\cancel $(R,G)$} (kb);
  \draw[<->] (kg) -- node[below] {$X_0(K_G)\cong X_0(K_B)$} (kb);
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

The diagram records the two handle reductions. The dotted label $R$ means a
$1$-handle, and each subscript $0$ means a zero-framed $2$-handle. The proof
establishes both reductions by framed slides and geometric cancellation; no
handlebody conclusion is inferred from the diagram alone.

## Definition

A **2-tangle diagram** is a regular diagram in a disk of two properly embedded tangle arcs and possibly finitely many closed tangle components, with four specified endpoints on the disk boundary; the arcs and circles are disjoint in the represented 3-ball, while their projections may have crossings. A **flyping circle** is a simple closed curve in the projection sphere whose intersection with the diagram consists of exactly three points, exactly one of which is a crossing; the circle is transverse to both branches at that crossing and to the diagram at the other two points. A small annular neighborhood of this circle has two complementary tangle disks. A **flype** fixes the tangle in one disk, interchanges which pair of strands crosses in the annular neighborhood, and turns over the tangle in the other disk: its projected tangle is reflected and all its over-under crossing data are reversed. This turnover is a half-turn in three-dimensional space about an axis in the projection sphere. Component orientations are transported by this motion, and the exterior diagram is fixed. The move with the opposite choice of fixed disk is also allowed; a disk containing no crossings is allowed. A flype whose fixed tangle has no crossings is called an **entire flype**. Diagrams are drawn on the oriented projection sphere; a **sphere planar isotopy** is an orientation-preserving smooth isotopy of that sphere carrying the decorated diagram. A plane diagram is obtained by choosing a point of the sphere outside the projection and deleting it. At each crossing of a link diagram, a **crossing ball** is a small 3-ball in which the overpass lies on the upper hemisphere and the underpass lies on the lower hemisphere, with the rest of the link outside that ball. Replacing all crossing disks by upper hemispheres or by lower hemispheres gives the shifted projection spheres $S_+$ and $S_-$. A **saddle disk** in a crossing ball is a properly embedded disk whose boundary meets each of the two hemispheres in two arcs and whose interior passes across the equatorial crossing disk. For a closed embedded surface transverse to the link and to $S_+$ and $S_-$, each component $C$ of its intersection with either shifted sphere has a **bubble word**: read once around $C$, recording $P$ each time it crosses the link and $S$ each time it passes through a crossing ball along a saddle disk. The surface is in **bubble standard position** if every such word is nonempty and no word records the same crossing ball more than once. A **Conway sphere** is an embedded sphere meeting the link transversely in four points; it is in crossing-ball standard position when its intersection with the crossing balls consists of saddle disks and its shifted-sphere intersection curves satisfy the bubble-standard conditions.

The turnover convention is the one in Kindred's Definition 2.9 and Figure 1. In particular, an entire flype permits viewing the whole diagram from the opposite side of the sphere, as in his Definition 2.11. Closed components inside a tangle disk are carried along with its arcs.

## Definition references

[Kindred, *A geometric proof of the flyping theorem*, §2.2 (Definitions 2.9–2.11) and §§3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.06490v3)

[Menasco and Thistlethwaite, *The classification of alternating links* (1993)](https://doi.org/10.2307/2946636)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular link diagram with finite crossing set and its embedding in the projection sphere; a flype is specified by a supplied flyping circle and a choice of the fixed tangle disk.

[F1] A regular link diagram has finitely many crossings with transverse branches, over-under data, and component orientations ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

## Proof
1.1 A sufficiently thin annular neighborhood of the supplied flyping circle contains its distinguished crossing and no other crossing: the crossing set is finite by [F1], and the circle has just the prescribed three intersection points. Transversality lets us narrow this neighborhood so its diagram consists only of the local strands at those points. The specified flyping circle, the chosen fixed disk and the annular crossing determine the local flype replacement: reflect the other disk and reverse each of its crossings, then reconnect its four ends through the modified annular crossing. This also transports any closed tangle components and the component orientations. The move is reversible by the same turnover construction. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Each crossing ball is chosen inside a disjoint crossing neighborhood; its upper and lower hemispheres encode exactly the overpass and underpass of [F1]. The sphere intersections in the standard-position condition are finite transverse surfaces and saddle disks by definition, so the stated crossing-ball convention is well-defined for a supplied diagram and Conway sphere. [given, F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎
