## Example

For the two-mode posterior $\pi_w=w\delta_{-b}+(1-w)\delta_b$ with $b>0$ and $0<w<1/2$, $M\ge1$ independent exact draws miss the rare mode $-b$ with probability $(1-w)^M$. For any fixed $M$, this probability tends to one as $w\downarrow0$. If instead $w\in[w_{\min},1-w_{\min}]$ with $0<w_{\min}\le1/2$, then the probability of missing either mode is at most $2(1-w_{\min})^M$, so $M\ge\log(2/\alpha)/[-\log(1-w_{\min})]$ suffices to make it at most $\alpha\in(0,1)$.

## Example references

[[ex-ip-ideal-score-error-allows-unbounded-euler-wasserstein|A positive lower bound on posterior mode mass is one condition needed for uniform finite-budget guarantees.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $b>0$, a mixture weight $0<w<1/2$, $M\ge1$ independent draws from $\pi_w=w\delta_{-b}+(1-w)\delta_b$, and, for the final bound, $w\in[w_{\min},1-w_{\min}]$ with $0<w_{\min}\le1/2$.

[A1] Each draw independently equals the rare atom $-b$ with probability $w$ and the other atom with probability $1-w$.

## Verification

1.1 The event that no draw equals $-b$ is the intersection of $M$ independent events, each of probability $1-w$, hence has probability $(1-w)^M$. Its limit as $w\downarrow0$ is one for every fixed finite $M$. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 The event that at least one of the two atoms is absent is contained in the union of the event “no $-b$ draw” and the event “no $b$ draw.” Their probabilities are $(1-w)^M$ and $w^M$, each at most $(1-w_{\min})^M$ under the displayed weight interval. The union bound gives at most $2(1-w_{\min})^M$. If $M\ge\log(2/\alpha)/[-\log(1-w_{\min})]$, then $(1-w_{\min})^M\le\alpha/2$, proving the sufficient budget. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary, let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive, put $\rho=\sqrt{\gamma}$, and define $q=(\Delta_g\rho)/\rho$. If $v$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv)=0$ and $u=\rho v$, then $u$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q)u=0$. The potential $q$ has trivial Dirichlet kernel. For boundary data $f=v|_{\partial M}$, with $\rho_b=\rho|_{\partial M}$ and the physical flux convention $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v|_{\partial M}$, the exact boundary relation is
$$\Lambda_\gamma f=\rho_b\Lambda_q(\rho_b f)-\rho_b(\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}\rho)|_{\partial M}f.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Physical conductivity and Schrödinger DN maps]]

[[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity|Nonresonant elliptic solvability]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the weak conductivity and nonresonant Dirichlet solvability suppliers [F2]--[F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the weak conductivity and nonresonant Dirichlet solvability suppliers [F2]--[F3].

**Given:** the data in the statement, and the weak formulations of the conductivity and Schrödinger equations.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: the conductivity DN map is the physical flux $\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v$; the Schrödinger DN map is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u$; both are defined by their weak boundary forms, and the $H^1$ trace is continuous into $L^2(\partial M)$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness]]: for every boundary datum in $H^{1/2}$ and every smooth positive conductivity, the conductivity equation has a unique weak $H^1$ solution.

[F3] [[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity]]: if the Schrödinger Dirichlet kernel is zero, the weak Dirichlet problem is uniquely solvable, and smooth coefficients and data give solutions in every chartwise Sobolev space.

[F4] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]], [[def-riemannian-gradient]], and [[def-laplace-beltrami-operator-as-trace-of-the-hessian]]: $H^1$ is the completion of smooth functions in the fixed-atlas norm; the Laplacian is $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$ with the metric gradient. The scalar product rule used below follows in local charts from the weak Leibniz rule and this divergence convention; its distributional use is shown in step 1.1.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Let $v\in H^1(M)$ be a weak conductivity solution and put $u=\rho v$. Since $\rho$ is smooth, the distributional Leibniz rule in charts gives
$$\operatorname{div}_g(\rho^2\nabla_gv)=\rho^2\Delta_gv+2\rho\,g(\nabla_g\rho,\nabla_gv),\qquad \Delta_g(\rho v)=\rho\Delta_gv+2g(\nabla_g\rho,\nabla_gv)+v\Delta_g\rho.$$
The first expression is zero distributionally by the weak equation. Dividing by the smooth positive $\rho$ in that identity and substituting into the second gives $\Delta_g(\rho v)=v\Delta_g\rho=q(\rho v)$, hence $u\in H^1(M)$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q)u=0$ weakly. Equivalently, the same identity reads $\operatorname{div}_g(\rho^2\nabla_g(u/\rho))=\rho(\Delta_gu-qu)$, so the transformation also sends every weak Schrödinger solution in $H^1$ back to a weak conductivity solution. These distributional identities use only the divergence convention in [F4], and are independent of orientability. [F4, given, algebra]

1.2 If $w\in H_0^1(M)$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$, then $v=w/\rho$ lies in $H_0^1(M)$ because multiplication by the smooth functions $\rho$ and $\rho^{-1}$ preserves this space. The distributional identities of step 1.1 in reverse give $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv)=0$; by density this is the weak equation on all $H_0^1$ tests. Testing with $v$ yields $\int_M\gamma|\nabla_gv|_g^2\,dV_g=0$. Positivity of $\gamma$ implies $\nabla_gv=0$ almost everywhere; the zero trace then gives $v=0$, hence $w=0$. Therefore $q$ is nonresonant and $\Lambda_q$ is defined. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Let $f,h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, let $v_f$ be the conductivity solution, and put $u=\rho v_f$. Let $U_h$ be the Schrödinger solution with trace $\rho_bh$; it exists by step 1.2 and the nonresonant solvability supplier. Then $U_h/\rho$ is the conductivity solution with trace $h$ by step 1.1. Use these solutions as extensions in the weak DN pairings from [F1]. The weak product calculation, valid almost everywhere for $H^1$ functions and smooth $\rho$, is
$$\rho^2g\!\left(\nabla_g(u/\rho),\nabla_g(\overline{U_h}/\rho)\right)=g(\nabla_gu,\nabla_g\overline{U_h})+q\,u\overline{U_h}-\operatorname{div}_g\!\left(u\overline{U_h}\nabla_g\log\rho\right).$$
Here $q=\Delta_g\log\rho+|\nabla_g\log\rho|_g^2$. The product $u\overline{U_h}$ lies in $W^{1,1}(M)$. Approximate $u,U_h$ in $H^1$ by smooth functions using the completion defining $H^1$; their products converge in $W^{1,1}$, and their boundary products converge in $L^1$ by the trace bound in [F1]. Thus the smooth Gauss--Green formula passes to this product, whose trace is $(\rho_bf)\overline{(\rho_bh)}$. Integrating therefore gives $\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\langle\Lambda_q(\rho_bf),\rho_bh\rangle-\int_{\partial M}\rho_b(\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}\rho)f\overline h\,dS_g$. By duality, multiplication of an $H^{-1/2}$ distribution by $\rho_b$ is characterized by pairing against $\rho_bh$, so this is exactly the asserted operator identity for arbitrary $H^{1/2}$ data. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $L$ be a nonempty smooth oriented link in the oriented $3$-sphere, and let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with oriented boundary $L$. For disjoint oriented embedded circles $C,D\subset S^3$, define $\operatorname{lk}(C,D)$ as the coefficient of the positive meridian of $D$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus D;\mathbb Z)$, and extend it bilinearly to finite integral sums of oriented circles. This linking number is symmetric on disjoint circle cycles. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. The positive push-off $x^+$ of such a representative is a sufficiently small copy in the positive normal direction determined by the ambient and surface orientations. For representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between $x^+$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off level, and is bilinear. Hence it defines the positive-push Seifert pairing on $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$.

## Statement references

[[def-link-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The link Seifert pairing and positive-push matrix convention]]

[[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection|Meridian linking, signed intersection, and the mixed-crossing formula]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty oriented link $L$, and a connected compact oriented spanning surface $F$ with boundary $L$.

[A1] Full AC implies dependent choice and countable choice, supplying the compact-surface normal form and Alexander-duality conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F1] The compact surface has a finite cellulation, and its first homology is finitely generated and represented by integral cellular cycles. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F2] Linking of disjoint oriented circles is the meridian coefficient; when a regular diagram and spanning surface are supplied it agrees with the signed intersection and mixed-crossing half-sum. [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]], [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F3] After moving a finite oriented link off infinity, it has a regular projection, a finite decorated immersion with finitely many mixed crossings. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]

[F4] Every smooth oriented circle has a supplied connected compact oriented spanning surface, so the link-intersection theorem applies to it. [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]]

[F5] A smooth loop can be homotoped in the complement of a disjoint circle to meet a supplied spanning surface transversely. [[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], [[prop-relative-transversality-preserves-a-map-on-a-closed-good-region]]

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, $L$, and $F$ as in the Statement.

1.1 Fix a finite cellulation of $F$ from [F1]. An integral cellular $1$-cycle represents each class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Replace each edge with coefficient $n$ by $|n|$ parallel oriented copies, reversing orientation when $n<0$. At each vertex the cycle condition says that incoming and outgoing copies occur in equal number. Around the boundary of a small vertex disk there is therefore an adjacent incoming/outgoing pair; join that pair by a small arc and delete its endpoints, repeating finitely until all endpoints are paired. The resulting arcs can be chosen disjoint in the disk and oriented consistently with the copies. Each smoothing changes the chain only by the boundary of a $2$-chain in that disk. The result is a finite disjoint union of oriented embedded circles representing the original homology class. [A1, F1, given, construct]

1.2 For representatives $X,X'$ of the same class in $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, there is an integral singular $2$-chain $A$ in $F$ with $\partial A=X-X'$. Push the chain through a small positive normal level of $F$; its boundary is $X^+-X'^+$ and it is disjoint from any representative $Y\subset F$. Thus $X^+$ and $X'^+$ represent the same class in $H_1(S^3\setminus Y;\mathbb Z)$, so their meridian-coordinate linking sums with $Y$ agree. Varying the small positive level traces an annulus in the positive bicollar, also disjoint from $Y$, and gives the same class. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 If $Y,Y'$ represent the same class, choose an integral $2$-chain $B$ in $F$ with $\partial B=Y-Y'$. For each circle component of $X^+$ and each circle component of $Y-Y'$, [F4] supplies a spanning surface and [F5] permits a homotopy of the other circle in its complement to make it transverse to that surface. By [F3] choose a regular diagram of the pair. By [F2], linking is the half-sum of mixed crossing signs; exchanging the two components leaves the same mixed crossings with the same signs, so linking is symmetric. Bilinearity then gives $\operatorname{lk}(X^+,Y-Y')=\operatorname{lk}(Y-Y',X^+)$. The cycle $Y-Y'$ bounds $B$ in $S^3\setminus X^+$, so its total meridian coefficient there is zero. Hence the two linking sums agree in the second variable as well. Additivity of meridian coefficients gives bilinearity in both variables. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.2 The value in the Statement is therefore independent of the chosen cycle representatives and push-off level and is bilinear on homology. In any ordered integral basis its matrix entries are $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, as required. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot in $S^3$ admits a finite rational polygonal code recording a one-component diagram with only finitely many transverse double points and an overpassing choice at each, together with a finite sequence of changes that switch overpassing choices and whose final diagram represents the standard unknot.

## Statement references

[[lem-regular-projection-admits-finite-planar-code|Every smooth knot admits a finite planar diagram code]]

[[thm-descending-diagram-is-unknot|A descending diagram represents the unknot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written AC$_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Under AC$_\omega$, every smooth oriented knot has an admissible finite rational planar code for a regular diagram. [[lem-regular-projection-admits-finite-planar-code]]

[F2] The finite traversal algorithm outputs a list of crossing changes and changes at most one crossing per finite crossing record. [[alg-descending-diagram-unknotting-sequence]]

[F3] If every first encounter at a crossing is an overpass, the represented diagram is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot. [[thm-descending-diagram-is-unknot]]

## Proof

**Given:** The knot $K$ and AC$_\omega$.


1.1 Apply [F1] to choose an admissible finite code for a regular diagram of a representative of $K$, and choose a basepoint in the interior of one edge. There is such an edge because a one-component code has at least one edge, including in the crossing-free case. [A1, F1, given, choose]

2.1 Apply [F2] to that finite code. The algorithm terminates after the finite crossing records are scanned and produces a finite crossing-change list; after those changes, each crossing is first encountered as an overpass. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], the code after the listed changes represents the standard unknot. Thus the chosen code and its finite crossing-change list witness the asserted existence for $K$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement refuted

For every even $p\ge4$ and every primitive $2p$-th root $A$, the standard Jones–Wenzl recursion for the BHMV Kauffman bracket can be continued to every strand number by cancelling any zero quantum-integer denominator against a zero numerator.

## Statement references

[[def-sl-two-root-of-unity-skein-parameter|BHMV root and quantum-integer conventions]]

[[lem-jones-wenzl-idempotents-exist-below-root-order|The exact boundary of the standard recursion]]

[Kauffman and Lins, *Temperley-Lieb Recoupling Theory and Invariants of 3-Manifolds*, Chapters 2–3](https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781400882533_A27764847/preview-9781400882533_A27764847.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The BHMV conventions at $p=6$, a primitive twelfth root $A$, and the standard recursive formula for Jones–Wenzl projectors.

[F1] [[def-sl-two-root-of-unity-skein-parameter]]: $r=p/2$, $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, and $[1]=1$, $[2]=\delta$, $[3]=\delta[2]-[1]$.

[F2] [[def-temperley-lieb-jones-wenzl-recursion-over-unit-denominators]]: the next projector in the standard recursion uses the inverse of the next quantum integer.

## Counterexample

**Given:** Take $p=6$ and any primitive twelfth root $A$.

1.1 Here $r=3$, $q=-A^2$ has $q^2$ of order three, and $q+q^{-1}=-1$. Thus $\delta=-1$, $[2]=\delta=-1$, and $[3]=\delta[2]-[1]=(-1)(-1)-1=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The recursion for $p_3$ requires division by $[3]$. Since $[3]=0$ in $\mathbb C$, no multiplicative inverse exists, so this recursive expression is undefined. In particular, cancellation cannot assign it a value. The calculation refutes the asserted universal continuation; it makes no claim that a projector at rank three cannot be constructed by a different method. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty proper open antipodally symmetric set whose complement contains a nonempty open arc. Write $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$ and define the line Radon integral by $Rg(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}g(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$ using the compact-support Riemann integral in $t$. Choose a smooth function $\psi$ supported in $B_1(0)$ and equal to one on $\overline B_{1/2}(0)$. For every $h\in C_c^\infty(B_1(0);\mathbb C)$, equality of the restricted line data $Rh(\theta,s)=R\psi(\theta,s)$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$ and $s\in\mathbb R$ forces $h=\psi$. The Fourier-Laplace transforms of these compactly supported functions are entire in each complex frequency coordinate, so their agreement on the measured open wedge determines their values at every real frequency. In particular, $R\psi$ is not identically zero.

## Example references

[[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data|Measured Fourier wedge and blind directions]]

[[lem-ip-compact-support-fourier-laplace-is-entire|Compact-support entire Fourier-Laplace transform]]

[[cor-ip-limited-angle-compact-support-uniqueness|Choice-free compact-support uniqueness from an open set of angles]]

[Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

[Venkataswaran P. Krishnan and Eric Todd Quinto, Microlocal Analysis in Tomography, §1.3.2](https://math.tifrbng.res.in/~vkrishnan/Papers/Microlocal_Analysis_Tomography.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The set $\Theta$, a smooth bump $\psi$ supported in $B_1(0)$ and equal to one on $\overline B_{1/2}(0)$, and a compactly supported smooth function $h$ with the same restricted line data as $\psi$.

[F1] [[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data]]: the Fourier wedge of measured line normals is $W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\ne0\}$, a nonempty open sector when $\Theta$ is nonempty and open.

[F2] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: a smooth compactly supported function equal to one on a smaller concentric ball and supported in a larger ball exists.

[F3] [[lem-ip-compact-support-fourier-laplace-is-entire]]: the compact-support Riemann Fourier-Laplace transform is entire in each coordinate and restricts to the usual compact-support Fourier transform on real frequencies.

[F4] [[thm-ip-fourier-slice-identity]]: with the compact-support Riemann line-integral convention, the Fourier transform of Radon data equals the object Fourier transform on the ray $\sigma\theta$.

[F5] [[cor-ip-limited-angle-compact-support-uniqueness]]: zero limited-angle data for a compactly supported smooth function force that function to vanish everywhere, by the choice-free analytic-continuation argument.

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The ball $B_1(0)$ contains a smaller concentric ball, so [F2] supplies a bump with the stated support and plateau. It is nonzero because it equals one on the nonempty inner ball. [F2, given, construct]

1.2 If $h$ has the same restricted data as $\psi$, linearity of the line integral gives $R(h-\psi)(\theta,s)=0$ for every measured pair. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, let $\gamma,\widetilde\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive, let $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, and let $\xi_0\in T_{x_0}^*\partial\Omega$ have unit norm in the induced boundary metric. Choose a sufficiently small boundary patch and $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported there with $\chi=1$ near $x_0$. For every integer $N\geq1$ there are a smooth complex phase $\Phi$ in a collar of the patch and amplitudes $b_{\lambda,\gamma}$, $b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$, defined for $\lambda\geq1$, such that
$$v_{\lambda,\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\gamma},\qquad v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma},$$
have boundary values $\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\phi}\chi$, where $\phi$ is real with $|d\phi|=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, have $H^1(\Omega)$ norms bounded above and below by positive constants, and satisfy
$$\|\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} +\|\operatorname{div}(\widetilde\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
Here $\phi=\Phi|_{\partial\Omega}$ is real, $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$, and $\operatorname{Im}\Phi$ is comparable to the inward distance to the boundary on the collar. Let $u_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ be the exact conductivity solutions with the same respective boundary values. Their corrections satisfy
$$\|u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} +\|u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
For every fixed integer $k\geq0$ and continuous $F$ on $\overline\Omega$, choosing $N>k$ gives
$$\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda^k \int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k F(x) \nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}}\,dx =c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,\qquad c_k=2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt=\frac{k!}{2^k}>0.$$
The same limit holds with $v_{\lambda,\gamma},v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ replaced by their exact corrections.

## Statement references

[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts|Smooth Euclidean boundary charts]]

[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal|Outward normal and boundary distance]]

[[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness|Positive conductivity weak solvability]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is a hypothesis of the positive-conductivity solvability supplier [F3]; it is used only for the exact correction.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is a hypothesis of the positive-conductivity solvability supplier [F3]; it is used only for the exact correction.

**Given:** the smooth bounded domain, positive smooth conductivities, a boundary point and unit tangential covector, and a cutoff equal to one near that point.

[F1] [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] and [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]: a smooth boundary has local smooth charts flattening it, and a neighborhood of the compact boundary is smoothly parametrized by inward normal distance.

[F2] [[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds-with-boundary]]: a finite smooth partition of unity can localize and patch the chartwise constructions.

[F3] [[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness]]: a positive smooth conductivity has a unique weak Dirichlet solution for each $H^{1/2}$ boundary value, and its zero-trace Poincare inequality holds.

[F4] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: the exact corrections are measured in the chartwise $H^1$ norm and the zero-trace space is the closure of compactly supported smooth functions.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Choose boundary normal coordinates $(y,x_n)$ near $x_0$, with $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ and inward unit normal $\partial_{x_n}$. The induced metric on the boundary is smooth. Choose a smooth hypersurface $S$ in $\partial\Omega$ through $x_0$, orthogonal there to $\xi_0$ (if $n=2$, take $S=\{x_0\}$). The boundary geodesics starting normally from $S$ give, by smooth dependence of the geodesic ODE and the inverse function theorem, coordinates $(s,z)$ near $x_0$; define $\phi(s,z)=s$. Gauss' lemma gives $|d\phi|_{g_{\partial\Omega}}=1$ and $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$. Shrink the patch so these coordinates and $\chi$ are supported inside it. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 In boundary normal coordinates, $g^{nn}=1$ and $g^{n\alpha}=0$ at the boundary. Set $\Phi|_{x_n=0}=\phi$ and $\partial_n\Phi|_{x_n=0}=i$. Then $g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi=0$ at $x_n=0$ because $|d\phi|=1$. Differentiate this eikonal equation successively in $x_n$. At each order the newest unknown normal jet $\partial_n^{j+1}\Phi|_{x_n=0}$ occurs linearly with coefficient $2i g^{nn}=2i\ne0$; all other terms use already assigned jets and derivatives of $g$. Solve recursively for every normal jet. Realize the resulting jet sequence by the following local Borel construction: if $c_j(y)$ is the prescribed $j$th normal derivative, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\theta$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$, and set
$$\Phi(y,x_n)=\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{c_j(y)}{j!}x_n^j\theta(x_n/\varepsilon_j).$$
For all sufficiently large $j$, choose $\varepsilon_j<2^{-j}$ so that every derivative of order at most $j/2$ of the $j$th summand has sup norm at most $2^{-j}$; this is possible because those derivatives are bounded by constants times $\varepsilon_j^{j-m}$ with $m\leq j/2$. Choose any positive $\varepsilon_j$ for the finitely many smaller $j$. For each fixed derivative order, the tail then converges uniformly, so $\Phi$ is smooth and has the prescribed jets. In particular, the eikonal expression vanishes to infinite order at the boundary. Since $\partial_n\operatorname{Im}\Phi=1$ there, shrinking the collar gives $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.1 For $P_\gamma=\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$, direct differentiation gives
$$P_\gamma(e^{i\lambda\Phi}b)=e^{i\lambda\Phi}\big[-\lambda^2p_\gamma b+i\lambda L_\gamma b+P_\gamma b\big],$$
where $p_\gamma=\gamma g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi$ and
$L_\gamma b=2\gamma g^{ij}(\partial_i\Phi)(\partial_jb)+\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla\Phi)b$.
The phase is common to both conductivities and $p_\gamma=\gamma p_1$ vanishes to infinite order on the boundary by step 1.2. Prescribe $b_{0,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=\chi$ and $b_{-j,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ for $j\geq1$. In boundary normal coordinates the coefficient of the new normal derivative in $L_\gamma b$ is $2i\gamma$, which is nonzero. Therefore the normal derivatives of $b_{0,\gamma}$ can be chosen successively so that $L_\gamma b_{0,\gamma}=0$ to infinite order at the boundary; after choosing $b_{0,\gamma},\ldots,b_{-(j-1),\gamma}$, the same recursion chooses all jets of $b_{-j,\gamma}$ so that $iL_\gamma b_{-j,\gamma}+P_\gamma b_{-(j-1),\gamma}=0$ to infinite order. Realize each sequence by the Borel series in step 1.2 and multiply by a fixed collar cutoff equal to one near the boundary support. Repeat for $\widetilde\gamma$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, construct]

2.2 Let $b_{\lambda,\gamma}=\sum_{j=0}^K\lambda^{-j}b_{-j,\gamma}$, with the same construction for $\widetilde\gamma$. The order-$\lambda^2$ eikonal term and the order-$\lambda,\ldots,\lambda^{1-K}$ transport terms in step 2.1 vanish to infinite order at $x_n=0$. Thus each remaining coefficient is $O(x_n^R)$ for every prescribed integer $R$. On the collar, $|e^{i\lambda\Phi}|\leq e^{-\lambda x_n/2}$. For every fixed $a,R$, direct integration gives
$$\|\lambda^a x_n^R e^{-\lambda x_n/2}\|_{L^2(0,\delta)}=O(\lambda^{a-R-1/2}).$$
Choose $R$ and then $K$ large enough to make every residual term $O(\lambda^{-N})$. Derivatives of the collar cutoff are supported where $x_n\geq c>0$ and hence contribute $O(e^{-c\lambda})$. The same Gaussian integration shows $\|v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{L^2}=O(\lambda^{-1})$ and bounds its gradient norm above. Thus the $H^1$ norms are bounded above and the residual bounds hold for the arbitrary prescribed $N$. [F1, F2, given, step 2.1, algebra]

2.3 Let $r_\lambda=u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Its weak equation is $P_\gamma r_\lambda=-P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}$. Test with $r_\lambda$, use $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, and use the Poincare inequality in [F3]:
$$\gamma_*\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2^2\leq\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|r_\lambda\|_2 \leq C_P\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2.$$
If the last gradient norm is zero then $r_\lambda=0$ by [F3]; otherwise divide by it. This proves $\|r_\lambda\|_{H^1}=O(\lambda^{-N})$. The same argument applies to $\widetilde\gamma$. [A1, A2, F3, F4, step 2.2, algebra]

3.1 In the collar, write $J(y,x_n)dS(y)dx_n$ for Euclidean volume in boundary normal coordinates, with $J(y,0)=1$. Since $\Phi=\phi+ix_n+O(x_n^2)$, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi=x_n+O(x_n^2)$ and $g(d\Phi,\overline{d\Phi})=2+O(x_n)$. The boundary values of both leading amplitudes are $\chi$, and lower amplitudes vanish there. Differentiating $v_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ therefore gives
$$\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}} =2\lambda e^{-2\lambda x_n}|\chi(y)|^2+e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(1)+ e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(\lambda x_n),$$
uniformly for $0\leq x_n\leq\lambda^{-1/2}$. On this shrinking collar $\lambda x_n^2\leq1$, so after $t=\lambda x_n$ the phase remainder factor is uniformly bounded; boundedness of $F,J,\chi$ gives an integrable majorant $C t^ke^{-t}$ for the rescaled leading term. For each fixed $t$, the rescaled leading term tends to $2t^ke^{-2t}F(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2$. Each displayed remainder has an additional factor $\lambda^{-1}$ after scaling and is dominated by $C\lambda^{-1}(t^k+t^{k+1}+t^{k+2})e^{-t}$, including the phase error $e^{O(t^2/\lambda)}-1=O(t^2/\lambda)$; its integral tends to zero. On the rest of the fixed collar, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$ gives exponential decay $e^{-\lambda x_n}\leq e^{-\sqrt{\lambda}}$; every polynomial prefactor is therefore negligible. The cutoff region away from the collar is also exponentially small. Thus the limit for approximate beams is
$$2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,$$
whose constant is strictly positive. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 Taking equal conductivities, $F=1$, and $k=0$ in step 3.1 gives $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\int_\Omega|\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}|^2dx=c_0\int_{\partial\Omega}|\chi|^2dS>0$. Together with the upper bound in step 2.2 this proves the asserted two-sided $H^1$ norm bound. [F1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

3.3 The exact corrections satisfy $H^1$ errors $O(\lambda^{-N})$ by step 2.3, while both approximate beams have uniformly bounded $H^1$ norms by step 2.2. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the change in the weighted product integral, after multiplication by $\lambda^k$, by $C\lambda^k\lambda^{-N}$ because $0\leq\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k\leq C$ on the bounded domain. Choose $N>k$. The error tends to zero, so the same limit holds for the exact solutions. [F3, F4, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be disjoint finite rational $1$-cycles in the boundary $S^3$ of the standard oriented $4$-ball $B^4$, each represented as a finite rational linear combination of oriented knots. Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

## Statement references

[[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection|Linking is signed intersection with a spanning surface in the three-sphere]]

[[def-oriented-intersection-number|The signed intersection number of transverse chains]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, disjoint oriented boundary cycles in $S^3$, collared rational bounding chains in $B^4$, and general position for their interiors.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed in the supplied topological linking-number convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For disjoint oriented knots, linking is the signed intersection of the first knot with an oriented Seifert surface spanning the second. [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F5] Every oriented knot in $S^3$ bounds a compact oriented smooth Seifert surface. [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]]

[F2] A compact oriented $1$-manifold has signed boundary count zero. [[lem-oriented-boundary-of-a-compact-oriented-one-manifold-has-zero-signed-count]]

[F3] The standard $4$-ball is contractible, so its interior has zero second rational homology. [[cor-contractible-nonempty-spaces-have-the-homology-of-a-point]]

[F4] The local sign of a transverse intersection is determined by the ordered tangent bases and ambient orientation; boundary orientations use the outward-normal-first convention and product orientations preserve the stated factor order. [[def-oriented-intersection-number]], [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]], [[def-induced-boundary-orientation]], [[def-product-orientation]]

## Proof

1.1 First consider disjoint oriented knots $\alpha,\beta$ and two admissible choices $P,P'$ bounding $\alpha$ with the same product collar, while $Q$ is fixed. Their difference $C=P-P'$ is a closed rational $2$-cycle supported in the interior of $B^4$, because the common boundary collars cancel. By [F3], $C=\partial Z$ for a finite rational $3$-chain $Z$ supported in the interior. Put $Z$ and $Q$ in general position relative to their boundary collars. The transverse intersection $Z\cap Q$ is a compact oriented $1$-chain. The product-orientation convention in [F4] makes its boundary count equal to the intersection count $(P-P')\cdot Q$ plus the term from $Z\cap\partial Q$; the latter is empty because $Z$ lies in the interior and $\partial Q=\beta\subset S^3$. By [F2], its signed boundary count is zero, so $P\cdot Q=P'\cdot Q$. The same argument with $Q-Q'$ shows independence of the second bounding chain. Bilinearity gives this independence for finite rational combinations of knots. [A1, F2, F3, F4, given, construct]

1.2 By [F5], choose an oriented Seifert surface $S_\beta\subset S^3$ for each knot component of $\beta$, and similarly choose a cap for each component of $\alpha$. It suffices by bilinearity to consider one knot component of each. Choose a collar depth $0<\epsilon$ in $B^4$. Make $Q$ a graph of $S_\beta$ in the boundary collar with depth zero on $\beta$ and strictly between $0$ and $\epsilon/2$ on its interior. Make $P$ consist of the product collar $\alpha\times[0,\epsilon]$ followed by a cap at depth $\epsilon$. Then $P$ and $Q$ intersect exactly above $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. At each such point, the oriented tangent basis of the collar of $P$ is $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a)$, where $a$ is the positive tangent to $\alpha$ and $n_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outward normal of $B^4$; the tangent basis of $Q$ is a positive basis $(s_1,s_2)$ of $S_\beta$, up to radial components which do not change the determinant. By [F4], $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive exactly when $(a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive in the boundary orientation. Thus the $4$-dimensional intersection sign is exactly the $3$-dimensional sign of $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. Hence $P\cdot Q=\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ by [F1]. [F1, F4, F5, given, construct]

2.1 Step 1.1 shows the intersection number is independent of admissible collared bounding chains, and step 1.2 computes it for one convenient choice. Hence the equality holds for all such $P,Q$ when the boundaries are knots. Expanding finite rational cycles into their oriented knot components and using bilinearity of both signed intersection and linking proves the stated equality. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For the identification of the output with the normalized colored Jones knot invariant and its integral Laurent representative, assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. The finite fixed-braid rational operations below use only the supplied matrix data.

Input an integer $N\ge1$, an integer $n\ge1$, a finite word $\beta=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_m}^{\epsilon_m}$ with $\epsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}$ and $1\le i_j<n$, whose closure joins each bottom endpoint to the top endpoint in the same position outside the braid cylinder and has one component, and the generic matrix ribbon data for the color $V_N$ defined above in this pair. The coefficient field is $F=\mathbb Q(A)$, whose elements are encoded as exact rational functions and whose field operations, equality test, and inversion of a nonzero element terminate. The output is the generic rational value $J_N^{\mathrm{gen}}(\widehat\beta;A^4)\in F$. The procedure is:

1. Form the positive crossing matrix $c_N=P\mathcal R_N$ from the finite universal-$R$ sum in the color definition. The sum terminates at $r=N-1$ because $E^N=F^N=0$; its inverse is available because $c_N$ is the braiding in the proved ribbon data.

2. Invoke the finite colored-braid matrix evaluator with strand count $n$, the word $\beta$ in composition order, the constant color tuple $(V_N,\ldots,V_N)$, the positive matrix $c_N$, its inverse, and the pivotal matrix $G_N$. Record its exact output $t=\operatorname{Tr}(G_N^{\otimes n}\rho_N(\beta))$.

3. Compute the exponent sum $w(\beta)=\sum \varepsilon$ and the generic quantum dimension $d_N$.

4. Return $\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}t/d_N$ in $F$. Reject a malformed braid word, matrix data differing from the prescribed color data, or an input with $d_N=0$ in the coefficient field. This algorithm does not substitute a root of unity into the generic quotient; root evaluation is a separate operation on a proved Laurent-polynomial representative.

The generic output has a unique integral Laurent representative in $q=A^4$. To obtain it explicitly, perform exact Laurent-polynomial division of the rational output and collect powers of $A^4$; Laurentness guarantees zero remainder. Any subsequent root evaluation substitutes into that representative.

The positive generator convention is the braid-height convention used by the matrix $c_N$: strand $i+1$ passes over strand $i$.

```tikz

  \draw[->] (0,1) -- (.46,.08);

  \node at (-.2,-1) {$i+1$};

\end{tikzpicture}
```

The continuous strand is the overpassing strand. The diagram records the chosen positive generator only; the algorithm and any proof use the explicit matrix and ribbon identities, not the drawing.

## Definition

Assume countable choice. Let $K_0,K_1\subset S^3$ be smooth oriented knots. A smooth oriented knot cobordism from $K_0$ to $K_1$ is a compact smooth properly embedded oriented surface $\Sigma\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ whose boundary is $(-K_0\times\{0\})\sqcup(K_1\times\{1\})$, with product collars at both ends. A **generic movie** for $\Sigma$ is obtained by choosing a generic projection of the slices $S^3\times\{t\}$ to the plane and a Morse height function on $\Sigma$, then recording the oriented link diagram at each regular level. Intermediate regular levels may be links with any finite number of components. After choosing the projection and height generically, the finitely many exceptional levels are isolated and distinct: between them the diagrams change by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move, and at them the surface height has one nondegenerate minimum (a birth), one nondegenerate maximum (a death), or one index-one critical point (a saddle band move). A movie includes its ordered list of frames and these elementary changes; no claim that two movies of the same cobordism are equivalent is part of this definition.

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Properly embedded surfaces and product collars]]

[[lem-smooth-link-cobordisms-admit-finite-generic-movies|Finite generic movie existence for the actual collared surface]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable choice]]

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|Smooth oriented knots and links in the standard three-sphere]]

[Bar-Natan, *Khovanov's homology for tangles and cobordisms*, §§2 and 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410495v2)

[Jacobsson, *An invariant of link cobordisms from Khovanov homology*, §§3.2 and 4.2–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0206303)


## Diagram

For example, a saddle movie may merge two circles or split one circle, according to how its band is attached. The following schematic records the merge case only; the circles shown are level-set components, not a projection of the full embedded surface.

## Example

Let $\mathcal H=L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega)$ and $\mathcal Y=L^2(\Omega)$ for a bounded smooth EIT domain. Given any nonempty finite sample set $S=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\mathcal H$, any $x_*\in\mathcal H\setminus S$, and any $y_*\in\mathcal Y\setminus\{0\}$, there are continuous maps $F_0,F_1:\mathcal H\to\mathcal Y$ that agree at every sample input and differ by $y_*$ at $x_*$. Therefore exact fit on finitely many inputs alone cannot identify an arbitrary continuous inverse map. A continuum FNO approximation theorem concerns the full $L^2$ kernel input and $L^2$ conductivity output on a compact set; a finite-element experiment reports a finite discretization and finite train/test sample. Neither finite-data fit nor a discretized operator matrix supplies the continuum theorem's uniform bound or a statistical generalization guarantee.

## Example references

[[thm-ip-eit-fno-noise-robust-existence|The continuum compact-set existence statement and its precise scope.]]

[de Hoop et al., Theorem 4.8 and §5 numerical experiments](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** a nonempty finite $S\subset\mathcal H$, a point $x_*\notin S$, and $y_*\ne0$ in $\mathcal Y$.

[F1] The planned continuum theorem takes inputs in $L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega)$, outputs in $L^2(\Omega)$ and states a uniform existence bound on a compact continuum input set; it does not assert a training or finite-sample risk guarantee. ([[thm-ip-eit-fno-noise-robust-existence]])

## Proof

**Given:** the finite sample set $S$, the unsampled point $x_*$ and $y_*\ne0$.

1.1 The finite set $S$ is closed in the Hilbert metric and $d(x_*,S)>0$. Define $\varphi(x)=d(x,S)/d(x_*,S)$, $F_0(x)=0$ and $F_1(x)=\varphi(x)y_*$. Distance to a closed set is 1-Lipschitz, so both maps are continuous. For every $x_i\in S$, $\varphi(x_i)=0$, hence $F_0(x_i)=F_1(x_i)=0$; at $x_*$, $F_1(x_*)-F_0(x_*)=y_*$. [given, construct]

2.1 The construction shows that finite exact sample values do not determine an arbitrary continuous map on the ambient Hilbert input space. The distinction in the Example follows from the domains of the two claims: the continuum theorem quantifies over a compact subset of the full kernel $L^2$ space, whereas a finite-element experiment only evaluates finitely many discretized inputs and outputs. The finite-map construction is not asserted to belong to the generalized-FNO class or to contradict the continuum theorem. [F1, step 1.1, given] ∎

kind: lemma
title: Closed square-integrable adjoint one-forms on a cusped hyperbolic
  three-manifold are exact
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
deps:

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be an oriented hyperbolic three-manifold with compact complement to finitely many standard torus cusp ends, each isometric to $(T^2\times[0,\infty),dt^2+e^{-2t}g_T)$ for a flat metric $g_T$. The compact case is allowed. Let $E=\mathbb H^3\times_\Gamma\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ be the adjoint flat bundle. Give its fiber at a basepoint the Hilbert–Schmidt Hermitian product and transport this product by the homogeneous $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)/\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ construction. Write $d_E$ for its flat differential and $\delta_E$ for the metric formal adjoint.

There is $c>0$, depending only on the model normalization, such that every compactly supported smooth $E$-valued one-form satisfies
$$\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2.$$
Every smooth $E$-valued one-form $\alpha$ with $d_E\alpha=0$ and $\|\alpha\|_2<\infty$ has a smooth square-integrable primitive $b$, with $d_Eb=\alpha$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$.

## Statement references

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]

[Menal-Ferrer and Porti, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.2242)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the hyperbolic quotient with the stated finite cusp decomposition, the adjoint bundle, its homogeneous metric and the flat differential.

[A1] AC supplies Countable Choice and Dependent Choice for Hilbert projections, Riesz representation, countable localizations and the convergent approximation sequences below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] A Hilbert space is the orthogonal sum of a closed subspace and its orthogonal complement; bounded linear functionals have unique Riesz representing vectors. [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]], [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

## Proof

1.1 Put $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$, $K=\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ and $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$. Choose $X_1=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $X_2=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $X_3=\tfrac12\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ in $\mathfrak k$, and put $Y_j=iX_j$. These $Y_j$ are an orthonormal tangent basis for curvature $-1$ hyperbolic space; for example $\exp(tY_1)$ moves the basepoint distance $|t|$, and the $K$ action rotates this basis. The matrix commutators give $[X_i,X_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}X_k$ and $[Y_i,Y_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}Y_k$. On $V$ let $R_j=\operatorname{ad}Y_j$. Each $Y_j$ is Hermitian, so $R_j$ is self-adjoint for $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)$, by cyclicity of trace. The $K$ action is unitary for this product. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Represent $E$-valued forms by horizontal $K$-equivariant $V$-valued forms on $Q=\Gamma\backslash G$, expressing their coefficients in the left Maurer–Cartan frame. Indeed a frame $g$ identifies the fiber over $gK$ with $V$ by $\operatorname{Ad}g$, and replacing $g$ by $gk$ changes these coefficients by $\operatorname{Ad}k^{-1}$ and rotates the tangent indices. In these coefficients write $\varepsilon_j$ for exterior multiplication by the dual of $Y_j$ and $\iota_j$ for contraction by $Y_j$. The ordinary covariant differential of the $K$ connection is $D=\sum_j\varepsilon_jY_j$, because the horizontal part of $[Y_i,Y_j]$ is zero. Differentiating the fiber change $\operatorname{Ad}g$ gives $d_E=D+T$, where $T=\sum_j\varepsilon_jR_j$. These are actual coefficient formulas on all degrees, not definitions of a different connection. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The invariant volume on $Q$ is the product of hyperbolic volume and normalized compact-fiber volume. Integration in a local bundle chart and then a partition of unity shows that integration of a $K$-invariant coefficient norm on $Q$ equals its integration on $M$. The left invariant fields $Y_j$ have zero divergence for this volume: $G$ is unimodular, since $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}Z)=0$ for the displayed Lie algebra basis, hence for all $Z$, and $\det\operatorname{Ad}(\exp Z)=1$. Right translation therefore preserves its Haar volume. Integration by parts on compact supports now gives $D^*=-\sum_j\iota_jY_j$ and $T^*=\sum_j\iota_jR_j$. The relations $\varepsilon_i\iota_j+\iota_j\varepsilon_i=\delta_{ij}$ show that $DT^*+T^*D+TD^*+D^*T=0$: the two anticommutator sums are respectively $\sum_jR_jY_j$ and its negative, since coefficient differentiation commutes with the constant matrices $R_j$. Thus $d_E\delta_E+\delta_Ed_E=DD^*+D^*D+H$, where $H=TT^*+T^*T$. All statements are $K$-equivariant and descend from $Q$ to $M$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On one-form coefficients $a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\in V^3$, the exterior-contraction relations give $(Ha)_i=\sum_jR_j^2a_i+\sum_j[R_i,R_j]a_j$. This finite-dimensional self-adjoint operator is positive definite. If $Ha=0$, positivity of $TT^*+T^*T$ gives $Ta=0$, namely $R_ia_j=R_ja_i$ for all $i,j$. Since $[R_i,R_j]=i\epsilon_{ijk}R_k$, the commutator sum in the displayed formula is a multiple of $R_ka_j-R_ja_k$ and vanishes. Consequently $0=\langle Ha,a\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\|R_ja_i\|^2$. Each $a_i$ commutes with all $Y_j$, which span $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ over $\mathbb C$. A matrix commuting with all traceless matrices is scalar, and a traceless scalar is zero. Thus $a=0$. Compactness of the unit sphere in $V^3$ supplies $c>0$ with $H\ge cI$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For a compactly supported smooth one-form, integration by parts in step 3.1 and step 4.1 give $\|d_E\alpha\|_2^2+\|\delta_E\alpha\|_2^2=\|D\alpha\|_2^2+\|D^*\alpha\|_2^2+(H\alpha,\alpha)\ge c\|\alpha\|_2^2$. We next extend this inequality to the joint weak graph domain. On each cusp choose a smooth cutoff equal to one for $t\le R$, zero for $t\ge2R$, with derivative bounded by $C/R$, and set it equal to one on the compact core. These cutoffs $\chi_R$ have compact support and $|d\chi_R|\le C/R$. For a weak graph-domain form $v$, the product formulas $d_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_Rd_Ev+d\chi_R\wedge v$ and $\delta_E(\chi_Rv)=\chi_R\delta_Ev-\iota_{\nabla\chi_R}v$ show convergence to $v$ in the joint graph norm. The same conclusion holds separately for each differential and codifferential and for forms of every degree. In the compact case take the cutoff identically one. [A1, step 3.1, step 4.1, given, algebra]

6.1 Here are the local smoothing details needed to finish that graph-density argument. In a finite collection of trivializing charts around the support of $\chi_Rv$, every differential or codifferential is a first-order matrix operator $P=\sum_jA_j(x)\partial_j+B(x)$ with smooth coefficients. Multiplication by a subordinate smooth partition reduces to forms supported inside individual charts. For convolution with a smooth unit-mass kernel $\rho_\epsilon$, the difference $P(v*\rho_\epsilon)-(Pv)*\rho_\epsilon$ is a sum of integral operators with kernels $(A_j(x)-A_j(y))\partial_j\rho_\epsilon(x-y)+(\partial_jA_j)(y)\rho_\epsilon(x-y)$ and a zero-order coefficient commutator. The $L^1$ kernel bounds are uniform on the compact chart, by the mean-value bound for $A_j$ and scaling of $\rho_\epsilon$; thus these commutators are uniformly bounded on $L^2$. They tend to zero on smooth functions by differentiation of convolutions, hence on all $L^2$ functions by smooth approximation and the uniform bound. Therefore local mollification converges in each asserted graph norm, also for the direct sum operator $(d_E,\delta_E)$. The partition contributes only fixed zero-order commutators, so a finite sum completes the approximation by compactly supported smooth forms. Together with step 5.1 this proves the coercive inequality on the maximal joint graph domain. It also proves that maximal differentials are the adjoints of maximal formal codifferentials, since their compact-support integration-by-parts identities extend by this graph density. [A1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 Let $\mathcal H_p=L^2(\Lambda^pT^*M\otimes E)$ and let $d_p$ be the maximal weak differential. It is closed: convergence of a form and its differential in $L^2$ preserves the weak test-function identity. Flatness gives $d_1d_0=0$ distributionally. Put $Z=\ker d_1$, a closed subspace of $\mathcal H_1$, and $\delta=d_0^*$. Every $w\in Z^\perp$ belongs to $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ with $\delta w=0$, because it is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}d_0\subseteq Z$. Hence the orthogonal projection $P_Z$ maps $\operatorname{Dom}\delta$ into itself and $\delta P_Zv=\delta v$. On $Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, steps 5.1 and 6.1 give $\|v\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\delta v\|_2$. In particular $A=\delta|_{Z\cap\operatorname{Dom}\delta}$ is injective with closed range: a Cauchy sequence of its images is, by this estimate, the image under the closed operator $\delta$ of a convergent sequence in $Z$. [F1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Fix a weakly closed $\alpha\in\mathcal H_1$, so $\alpha\in Z$. On the closed range of $A$ define $\ell(Av)=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$. It is well defined and bounded, with norm at most $c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$, by step 7.1. Extend it to $\mathcal H_0$ by zero on the orthogonal complement of that range and use [F1] to obtain $b\in\mathcal H_0$ with $\langle Av,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ and $\|b\|_2\le c^{-1/2}\|\alpha\|_2$. For arbitrary $v\in\operatorname{Dom}\delta$, replace $v$ by $P_Zv$; its $\delta$ image is unchanged and its pairing with $\alpha$ is unchanged. Thus $\langle\delta v,b\rangle=\langle v,\alpha\rangle$ on the full domain of $\delta$. By the adjoint definition and the graph-density conclusion of step 6.1, $b\in\operatorname{Dom}d_0$ and $d_0b=\alpha$. This proves the primitive assertion in the weak sense without an external closed-range or harmonic-representative theorem. [A1, F1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 If $\alpha$ is smooth, the primitive $b$ is smooth. In a flat parallel frame on a coordinate ball, $d_Eb=\alpha$ is the ordinary componentwise distributional equation $db=\alpha$. A smooth closed one-form on a smaller star-shaped coordinate ball has a smooth primitive $b_0$, given by integrating along straight radial segments; differentiating the integral and using closedness verifies $db_0=\alpha$. Then $d(b-b_0)=0$ distributionally. Mollification on still smaller balls makes this difference a sequence of constants, so its distributional limit is constant as well. Thus $b=b_0+\text{constant}$ is smooth locally and hence globally. Its $L^2$ norm and the bound from step 8.1 remain unchanged. [step 8.1, algebra] ∎

## Source reading and scope

The complete 29-page Menal-Ferrer–Porti paper, including its principal-bundle appendix, was read. Its algebraic positivity proof is specialized above to the adjoint three-dimensional representation. Its externally stated Andreotti–Vesentini implication is replaced by the explicit graph-density and Hilbert-space argument in steps 5.1–9.1. Standard torus cusp models are hypotheses here; this lemma does not derive the geometric cusp decomposition. No triangulation or positivity of tetrahedron shapes is assumed.

## Statement

Let $F\subset S^3$ be a compact connected smoothly embedded surface with nonempty boundary $L$, supplied with a finite disk-and-band presentation. The surface may be nonorientable. A normal transfer $\tau c$ of an oriented rational multicurve $c$ in the interior of $F$ is its total inverse image in the boundary of a sufficiently small normal interval neighborhood of $F$, oriented by projection onto $c$. Suppose a quadratic form $q$ on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ is positive definite or negative definite and satisfies $q([c])=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)$ for every such rational multicurve. Then $L$ is nonsplit. Definiteness on the zero vector space is allowed.

## Statement references

[Greene, *Alternating links and definite surfaces*, Corollary 3.2 and Lemma 3.3](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/lackenby/Fox.pdf)

[Kindred, *A geometric proof of the flyping theorem*, Fact 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.06490v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The surface $F$, its boundary $L$, its finite presentation, and the definite form $q$ with the stated normal-transfer property.

[F1] A splitting sphere is a smooth sphere disjoint from $L$ with points of $L$ on both complementary sides. ([[def-split-link]])

[F2] Mayer–Vietoris gives the exact homology sequence of a two-open-set cover, with rational coefficients allowed. ([[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]])

[F3] $H_1(S^3;\mathbb Q)=H_2(S^3;\mathbb Q)=0$ and $H_0(S^3;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$. ([[cor-homology-of-spheres]])

[F4] Finite simplicial homology agrees with singular homology, without a choice assumption. ([[thm-simplicial-and-singular-homology-agree-for-simplicial-complexes]])

## Proof

1.1 Linking can be computed here using finite rational chains: a rational $1$-cycle $a$ in $S^3$ bounds a rational $2$-chain $C$ by [F3], and $\operatorname{lk}(a,b)=C\mathbin{\cdot}b$ for a disjoint rational cycle $b$. Independence of $C$ follows because the difference of two choices bounds a $3$-chain by [F3], whose intersection with the closed cycle $b$ has total boundary zero. In particular linking is zero if $a$ bounds a chain disjoint from $b$, and is unchanged under a homology of $b$ in the complement of $a$. All chains involved are finite. Curves and surfaces used below can be put in finite general position: subdivide their compact parameter domains finely in finitely many coordinate neighborhoods, approximate by polygonal patches within a tubular neighborhood, perturb the finitely many vertices to avoid the finitely many nontransverse affine incidences, and smooth the patches in smaller neighborhoods. Approximation sufficiently close to the original embedded patches preserves embedding and disjointness from the compact boundary $L$. These operations use finitely many choices, and no simultaneous choices indexed by an infinite family. [given, F3, construct]

1.2 We record elementary finite-surface facts needed below. Cutting the supplied presentation along a finite family of curves gives finite triangulations of its pieces. A connected triangulated surface with boundary has a graph spine: in the dual graph include a vertex for the boundary, choose a finite spanning tree rooted there, and remove triangles successively across their edge facing the already removed parent. The remaining $1$-complex is a deformation retract, and reversing these elementary collapses shows that the surface is a regular neighborhood of that graph. Consequently its rational first homology vanishes exactly when that graph is a tree, in which case its regular neighborhood is a disk, by successively removing leaf edges. Also, a two-sided simple closed curve $\gamma$ in the interior of $F$ with $[\gamma]=0$ bounds an orientable subsurface $F_0$ having $\gamma$ as its only boundary. To see this, triangulate with $\gamma$ as an edge cycle and take a rational $2$-chain bounding it using [F4]. Across edges outside $\gamma$ its coefficients agree with orientation signs. They vanish on the component touching $\partial F$ and jump by one across $\gamma$, so the nonzero component supplies precisely such an oriented $F_0$. The same coefficient argument shows that $H_1(F_0;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ is injective: any bounding chain for a cycle in $F_0$ has zero coefficients on the connected complementary surface, which touches $\partial F$. [given, F4, construct]

2.1 Suppose $D$ is a compressing disk for $F$: its interior misses $F$ and its boundary $\gamma$ does not bound a disk in $F$. Its boundary is two-sided in $F$, since a collar of the disk at $\gamma$ gives a side of the normal interval bundle there. The normal transfer of a sufficiently close parallel copy of $\gamma$ misses $D$; in a collar of $\gamma$, move the parallel copy slightly in the direction tangent to $F$ and transverse to $\gamma$, and take its normal lifts still closer to that copy. Thus $\operatorname{lk}(\gamma,\tau\gamma)=0$ by step 1.1. Definiteness forces $[\gamma]=0$. Step 1.2 supplies the subsurface $F_0$ bounded by $\gamma$. It is not a disk, and hence $V=H_1(F_0;\mathbb Q)$ is nonzero and injects into $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$. Cap $F_0$ with $D$ and smooth the corner, giving a closed connected orientable embedded surface $\Sigma$. Capping the unique boundary circle does not change $H_1$, so $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)=V$. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, contradiction, construct]

3.1 The surface $\Sigma$ has a two-sided collar. Apply [F2] to that collar and $S^3\setminus\Sigma$. Their overlap has two components, each retracting onto $\Sigma$. By [F3], the map from the overlap's $H_0=\mathbb Q^2$ into $\mathbb Q\oplus H_0(S^3\setminus\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ is injective and has cokernel $\mathbb Q$. Hence the complement has exactly two components, and the two collar sides belong to different ones. Let $A$ and $B$ be their closures. Thickening them to open sets, [F2] and [F3] give an isomorphism $V\to H_1(A;\mathbb Q)\oplus H_1(B;\mathbb Q)$. At least one projection has nonzero kernel: if both were injective, each target would have dimension at least $\dim V>0$, contradicting that their dimensions sum to $\dim V$. Thus a nonzero $a\in V$ bounds a rational $2$-chain on one side, say in $A$. Represent $a$ by an oriented rational multicurve in $\operatorname{int}F_0$. Both of its normal pushoffs have the same linking with it: the two normal directions are joined by a half-rotation in the normal plane of each oriented curve, giving a homology of the pushoffs in its complement. The pushoff into $\operatorname{int}B$ misses the bounding chain in $A$, so that linking is zero by step 1.1. The normal transfer therefore has linking zero as well. Step 1.2 makes $a$ nonzero in $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, contradicting definiteness of $q$. Thus $F$ has no compressing disk. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, contradiction]

4.1 By step 3.1, $F$ is incompressible. Suppose now that a splitting sphere $S$ exists. Make it transverse to $F$ by the finite perturbation of step 1.1, keeping it disjoint from $L$. Their intersection is a finite union of circles. At least one is essential in $F$: otherwise each bounds a disk in $F$, and removing the interiors of the outermost such disks leaves a connected surface containing every component of $\partial F=L$, disjoint from $S$. Its boundary would lie entirely on one side of $S$, contrary to [F1]. Choose a circle $\gamma$ innermost on $S$ among the circles essential in $F$, and let $D$ be the disk it bounds on $S$ with no other essential circle in its interior. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, choose, contradiction, construct]

5.1 Every circle of $\operatorname{int}D\cap F$ bounds a disk in $F$. If there are any, choose one $\beta$ whose disk $E\subset F$ is innermost among them. Its interior misses $D$: any intersection circle in that interior would itself be inessential in $F$ and would contradict the choice. The essential curve $\gamma$ cannot lie inside $E$. Replace the disk on $D$ bounded by $\beta$ by a small parallel copy of $E$, choosing the side that joins the remainder of $D$ and smoothing its boundary. Since $\operatorname{int}E$ misses $D$, this is again an embedded disk with boundary $\gamma$. It stays disjoint from $L$ and has strictly fewer intersection circles with $F$; the replacement disk is pushed off $F$ and all circles inside the discarded disk have disappeared. Repeating this finite reduction gives an embedded disk with boundary $\gamma$ and interior disjoint from $F$. This is a compressing disk, contrary to step 3.1. The splitting sphere cannot exist, so $L$ is nonsplit. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, contradiction] ∎

## Statement

Let $(M,o)$ be a compact connected based Hausdorff manifold, let $R$ be an involutive unital ring, and supply a rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$ with an identification $\mathcal R_o=R$. Assume every based-loop monodromy is left multiplication by a unit $u$ satisfying $\bar u=u^{-1}$. Equip the base fiber with the standard Hermitian form $h_o(a,b)=\bar a b$. Transport extends this to a path-independent parallel Hermitian form $h$ on $\mathcal R$. Put $C_*=C_*(M;\mathcal R)$. For a right $R$-module $P$, write $\overline P$ for its conjugate left module, with $r\cdot\bar p=\overline{p\bar r}$.

The left-$R$ cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R)$ is the intrinsic cochain complex of the left-$R$ local system with fiber $R$ and transport $a\mapsto au^{-1}$. Relative to the supplied parallel Hermitian form, that local system is naturally isomorphic to $\overline{\mathcal R}$ by $\bar v\mapsto[w\mapsto h(v,w)]$. The identifications are independent of unitary fiber frames; an arbitrary change of Hermitian structure is not asserted to preserve them. If $M$ is oriented, boundaryless and of dimension $n$, cap duality therefore gives
$$H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))\cong\overline{H_{n-p}(C_*)}.$$
If $R\subseteq K$ is an embedding into an involutive division ring extending the involution, the same conclusion is valid for $K$, with $C_*\otimes_R K$ in the homology target. If $R$ is involution-stable in $K$, the complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R)$ is the corresponding intrinsic left-$R$ cochain complex with fiber $K/R$ and transport by right multiplication by $u^{-1}$. These identifications require no choice principle and commute with the coefficient maps $R\to K\to K/R$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The supplied based coefficient system, standard Hermitian form on its identified base fiber, involutions and manifold data.

[F1] A left or right module local system here is a groupoid functor with linear transport; forgetting the action gives an abelian-group local system, to which the intrinsic definition applies at commutative base ring $\mathbb Z$. Finite atlas rules supply basepoint paths and specified rank-one bases in every fiber; the one-vertex supplier proves the arbitrary right-$R$ first-edge boundary and its square-zero identity directly. [[lem-compact-manifold-twisted-singular-chains-admit-one-vertex-reduction]], [[def-singular-and-cellular-chain-complexes-with-local-coefficients]]

[F2] Compact oriented manifold duality holds without choice for every abelian-group local system and respects commuting scalar actions. [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]]

## Proof

1.1 Use the finite-atlas paths of [F1] to transport the supplied base vector $1$ to a frame $e_x$ in every fiber. Two paths to $x$ give frames $e_x$ and $e'_x=e_xv$ where $v$ is unitary, because their difference is a based loop. Define $h_x(e_xa,e_xb)=\bar a b$. In the second frame the coordinates are $v^{-1}a,v^{-1}b$, and
$$\overline{v^{-1}a}\,v^{-1}b=\bar a(\bar v)^{-1}v^{-1}b=\bar a b.$$
Thus this definition is path-independent and every transport preserves $h$. The finite-atlas rule supplies all the paths by a formula, so no infinite family of choices is required. The resulting frames are unitary and their transition units are unitary. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Use the paths from [F1] to put a specified basis on every fiber, and let $u_{01}$ be the transition unit along the first edge of a singular simplex. In this gauge its right-chain boundary has first term $e_{\partial_0\sigma}u_{01}$ and its remaining terms $(-1)^i e_{\partial_i\sigma}$ for $i>0$. A right-linear cochain $f$ consequently has coboundary first term $f(e_{\partial_0\sigma})u_{01}$, with the same remaining signed terms. Intrinsic local cochains use inverse first-edge transport. Thus these are exactly the cochain formulas for the coefficient system whose transport is right multiplication by $u_{01}^{-1}$; that transport commutes with left multiplication by $R$. Sending $f$ to its values on these supplied simplex basis elements is a bijection, in every degree, with the intrinsic cochains, and the displayed formulas show that it commutes with coboundaries. No values in an infinite product are lifted or chosen. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Intrinsically send $\bar v$ to the right-linear functional $w\mapsto h(v,w)$. In a unitary frame this is $J:\overline R\to R$, $J(\bar a)=\bar a$, where the bar on the right is the ring involution. It is left-linear: $J(r\cdot\bar a)=\overline{a\bar r}=r\bar a$. It commutes with transport, since $\overline{ua}=\bar a\bar u=\bar a u^{-1}$. Hence it identifies the conjugate chain-coefficient local system with the dual system of step 1.2. Conjugation changes neither underlying abelian-group cycles nor boundaries and is involutive, so the homology of that dual system identifies with $\overline{H_*(C_*)}$. When $M$ is oriented and closed, apply [F2] to the actual dual local system from step 1.2, viewed as a local system of abelian groups with a commuting left-$R$ action. Its cap isomorphism gives precisely the displayed cohomology-to-conjugate-homology identification. [F2, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 For $K$ coefficients, every right-linear $f:C_j\to K$ extends uniquely to the right-$K$ linear map $C_j\otimes_RK\to K$, $c\otimes k\mapsto f(c)k$. Balancing proves that formula well-defined; its inverse is restriction to $c\otimes1$. These maps commute with the differentials and left $K$ actions. The chain coefficient system is now the scalar extension with fiber $K$, and its transport units have the same unitary involution property. Steps 1.2 and 2.1 applied to it give the asserted $K$ conclusion, including its left-$K$ linearity. This uses explicit tensor adjunction and no basis selection over $K$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The quotient $K/R$ is an $R$-bimodule because $R$ is a subring, and the involution descends because $\bar R=R$. Replace the value module in step 1.2 by this bimodule. Right multiplication by $u^{-1}$ is still well-defined and commutes with left $R$, so exactly the same simplex formula identifies its dual cochains. Inclusion and quotient of the three value modules commute with those multiplications, and therefore with the chain/cochain identifications. The dual-to-conjugate identification is intrinsic relative to $h$. Explicitly, under a unitary frame change $e'=ev$, vector coordinates change to $a'=v^{-1}a$ and right-linear functional coordinates to $q'=qv$. Then $\overline{a'}=\bar a(\bar v)^{-1}=\bar a v$, which is exactly the functional transformation. Equivalently its inverse sends $f$ to $\overline{e\,\overline{f(e)}}$; replacing $e$ by $ev$ leaves this unchanged since $v\bar v=1$. The same standard Hermitian structure extends to $K$, and these unitary frame identities hold there as well. All constructions used only the finite atlas data of [F1] and formula-defined maps on supplied generators. This proves every claimed compatibility without a choice principle. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC$_\omega$. Let $T$ be the standard right-handed trefoil, let $T^*$ be its image under the fixed orientation-reversing reflection of the connected-sum convention, and let $-T^*$ denote reversal of the image knot's orientation. Then $T\#(-T^*)$ bounds a smooth ribbon disk in $B^4$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The oriented connected-sum convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and the standard oriented trefoil $T$ with the fixed mirror convention.

[F1] Here a smooth ribbon disk means a smooth proper disk in the standard four-ball for which the radial function is Morse in the interior, with critical points only of indices $0$ and $1$; it has no interior local maxima. This is the radial convention for ribbon disks. ([Livingston, Definition 2.3, p.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0307077v4))

[F2] The standard ball-arc connected-sum convention is independent of local choices under AC$_\omega$. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]])

[F3] Under AC$_\omega$, good slices of a finite smooth transverse family are dense; compact-source isotopies extend ambiently. ([[thm-parametric-transversality]], [[thm-isotopy-extension]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and $T$.

1.1 Delete a small straight subarc of $T$ in a coordinate ball. Identify its complementary ball with $B^3$ and parametrize the remaining oriented arc by a smooth embedding $a:[0,1]\to B^3$ with endpoints on $S^2$, interior in the open ball, and transverse radial endpoint collars. These are the standard ball-arc data of [F2]. Move the arc slightly if necessary so that it misses the origin; this is possible by a small translation on its interior, fixed on endpoint collars, since a smooth compact arc in three-space has empty interior and its endpoint collars can be kept outside a small ball about the origin. Put $f(s)=|a(s)|^2>0$, with $f(0)=f(1)=1$ and $f<1$ in the interior; transversality gives $f'(0)<0<f'(1)$. [given, F2, construct]

2.1 Arrange that $f$ is Morse away from its endpoint collars, without changing the arc type. Here are finite perturbation details. The zeros of $f'$ lie in a compact subinterval. Cover that zero set by finitely many smaller open intervals on each of which a compactly supported smooth function $\phi_i$ has derivative $1$. For the family $f_u=f+\sum_i u_i\phi_i$, the map $(s,u)\mapsto f'_u(s)$ is a submersion near this zero set because one parameter derivative is $1$; on its compact complement $f'$ is bounded away from zero, so small parameters create no further zeros. Apply [F3] to this finite family and zero in $\mathbb R$. Choose arbitrarily small good $u$, so every zero of $f'_u$ is simple. Endpoint collars stay fixed and $0<f_u<1$ inside. Replace $a(s)$ by $\sqrt{f_u(s)/f(s)}a(s)$. For sufficiently small parameters this is an isotopy of embeddings, since on a finite chart cover immersion and local injectivity persist in $C^1$, while compact pairs outside the chart diagonals have a positive separation margin. Its squared radius is $f_u$. Rename this arc $a$ and this function $f$; the finitely many simple critical points lie in a compact subinterval, so there are only finitely many. [F3, step 1.1, construct, choose]

3.1 In $B^4=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R:|x|^2+t^2\le1\}$ take the surface $D=\{(a(s),t):0\le s\le1,\ t^2\le1-f(s)\}$. The strip map $(s,t)\mapsto(a(s),t)$ is an embedding. Its parameter domain is explicitly a smooth disk: the ellipse $v^2\le s(1-s)$ maps onto it by $(s,v)\mapsto(s,v\sqrt{q(s)})$, where $q(s)=(1-f(s))/(s(1-s))$ extends smoothly and positively to both endpoints because $f$ has simple transverse endpoint zeros of $1-f$. This map and its inverse are smooth, and every interior vertical fibre is an interval of positive length. Smoothness at those endpoints follows from the implicit function theorem applied to $f(s)+t^2=1$, because $f'$ is nonzero there; the domain boundary is locally $s=s(t)$ rather than a corner. Equivalently $D$ is the regular sublevel of $f(s)+t^2$ in a slightly extended embedded strip. Consequently it is a smooth compact properly embedded disk, its boundary lies in $S^3$, its interior lies in the open four-ball, and its intersection with $S^3$ is transverse. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The two boundary arcs of $D$ are $(a(s),\sqrt{1-f(s)})$ and $(a(s),-\sqrt{1-f(s)})$. The equatorial sphere $t=0$ meets their union only at $s=0,1$. The hemispheres are standard three-balls; projection to $x$ identifies their interiors with the interior of $B^3$, and their lifted arcs represent the original ball-arc pair by [F2]. To see this without a boundary-singular projection, first use transverse endpoint collars to straighten the arcs in smooth hemisphere collars, and then use projection on the compact remaining subarcs; the collar interpolation is an isotopy of the arcs fixing endpoints. Reflection $(x,t)\mapsto(x,-t)$ exchanges the hemispheres and reverses the boundary orientation of $S^3$. The orientation induced on $\partial D$ runs along one lifted arc with increasing $s$ and along the other with decreasing $s$. Thus the capped oriented boundary arcs are $T$ and $-T^*$, with the fixed mirror reflection transported by positive coordinate frames as in [F2]. Gluing these standard hemispherical arc data gives $\partial D=T\#(-T^*)$ as an oriented knot. [F2, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 On $D$ the squared radial function is $\rho(s,t)=f(s)+t^2$. Its interior critical points are exactly $(s,0)$ with $f'(s)=0$, and their Hessians are $\operatorname{diag}(f''(s),2)$. They are nondegenerate, with index $0$ or $1$, never $2$. Since $\rho>0$, taking its square root preserves these critical indices. Hence the standard radial function makes $D$ a ribbon disk by [F1], proving the full conclusion. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The construction works for any smooth knot arc; no alternating-diagram algorithm is required. The prohibition is on interior radial maxima. A compact proper disk necessarily has an interior radial minimum.

## Statement

Let $A$ and $B$ be Hermitian forms on the same finite-dimensional complex vector space, and suppose that the linear map representing $A-B$ has rank at most one. Then $|\operatorname{sign}(A)-\operatorname{sign}(B)|\le 2$, where the signature is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues, with multiplicity and with zero eigenvalues omitted.

## Statement references

[Signature and codimension-one restriction](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Hermitian forms $A$ and $B$ on the same finite-dimensional complex vector space, with $\operatorname{rank}(A-B)\le 1$.

[F1] For a Hermitian form $Q$, its positive index $n_+(Q)$ is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $Q(v,v)>0$ for every nonzero $v$; its negative index $n_-(Q)$ is defined using $Q(v,v)<0$. Its signature is $n_+(Q)-n_-(Q)$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $W=\ker(A-B)$. Rank-nullity and the rank hypothesis give $\operatorname{codim}W\le1$. If $P$ is a positive subspace for $A$ of dimension $n_+(A)$, then $\dim(P\cap W)\ge n_+(A)-1$. On $P\cap W$ the forms agree, so this intersection is positive for $B$. Thus $n_+(B)\ge n_+(A)-1$. Interchanging $A$ and $B$ proves $|n_+(A)-n_+(B)|\le1$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Apply the same argument to $-A$ and $-B$ to obtain $|n_-(A)-n_-(B)|\le1$. Therefore $|\operatorname{sign}(A)-\operatorname{sign}(B)|\le |n_+(A)-n_+(B)|+|n_-(A)-n_-(B)|\le2$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
