## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty proper open antipodally symmetric set whose complement contains a nonempty open arc, and let $W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\}$. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ and every measured normal $\theta\in\Theta$, the one-dimensional Fourier transform in the offset variable obeys $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta)$ for all $\sigma\in\mathbb R$. In particular, zero restricted data imply that $\widehat f$ vanishes on $W_\Theta$. If in addition $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, zero restricted data imply $f=0$ everywhere. For compactly supported inputs, the stated Countable Choice assumption identifies the Lebesgue line integrals here with the compact-support Riemann convention; the compact-support Fourier-slice and uniqueness results in that convention are proved without Countable Choice.

## Statement references

[Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

[Venkataswaran P. Krishnan and Eric Todd Quinto, Microlocal Analysis in Tomography, §1.3.2](https://math.tifrbng.res.in/~vkrishnan/Papers/Microlocal_Analysis_Tomography.pdf)

[Marco Mazzucchelli, Mikko Salo, and Leo Tzou, A general support theorem for analytic double fibration transforms, §§1.2–1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.05906)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The set $\Theta$, $W_\Theta$, and a function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$; in the compact-support conclusion also $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ and $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=0$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $s\in\mathbb R$.

[F1] [[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data]]: the measured Fourier wedge is $W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\ne0\}$.

[F2] [[def-ip-schwartz-radon-transform]]: $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=\int_\mathbb R f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$ with Lebesgue measure; under Countable Choice, this agrees on compactly supported smooth inputs with the compact-support Riemann line integral.

[F3] [[lem-ip-fourier-slice-identity-on-schwartz]]: for $f\in\mathcal S$, $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta)$.

[F4] [[thm-ip-fourier-slice-identity]]: for $f\in C_c^\infty$ and the IP-36 normalization, the same compact-support Fourier-slice identity holds.

[F5] [[cor-ip-limited-angle-compact-support-uniqueness]]: compactly supported smooth functions with zero data on a nonempty open set of line normals vanish everywhere; the proof uses the Riemann Fourier-Laplace transform and no Countable Choice.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is used by [F2] to identify the compact-support line-integral conventions and by [F3] for the general Schwartz Fourier-slice formula. The compact-support Fourier-slice and uniqueness results [F4]–[F5] themselves are choice-free in the Riemann convention.

## Proof

1.1 For each $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, [F3] gives the Fourier-slice identity. If the restricted data vanish, their one-dimensional Fourier transforms vanish, so $\widehat f(\sigma\theta)=0$. Every point of $W_\Theta$ has this form, hence $\widehat f$ vanishes on $W_\Theta$. [given, F1, F2, F3, A1]

2.1 Now assume $f\in C_c^\infty$ and its restricted data are zero. By [F2] and the stated Countable Choice assumption, those data use the compact-support Riemann line-integral convention. The compact-support Fourier-slice identity [F4] gives $\widehat f(\sigma\theta)=0$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, so the transform vanishes on the measured wedge. The compact-support uniqueness result [F5] then yields $f=0$ everywhere through its separate choice-free analytic-continuation proof. [F2, F4, F5, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $N$ be an oriented boundaryless Hausdorff $n$-manifold supplied with a finite coordinate atlas, and let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. The supportwise orientation-cap map is an isomorphism in every integer degree:
$$D_N:H_c^p(N;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(N;\mathcal L).$$
The manifold need not be compact. The maps respect every scalar action commuting with transport, including actions of noncommutative rings, and no choice principle is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The oriented manifold, finite atlas and abelian-group local system.

[F1] Supportwise cap is defined using compatible canonical integral orientation classes on compact subsets; its maps commute with support extension and restriction to open subspaces. [[lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets]], [[def-compactly-supported-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]], [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]]

[F2] Duality holds on coordinate balls for arbitrary abelian-group local systems without choice. [[lem-choice-free-local-coefficient-duality-on-a-coordinate-ball]]

[F3] The compact-support cap Mayer–Vietoris ladder has the prescribed connector signs and exact rows; five-term windows give the finite gluing implication for duality. [[lem-compact-support-local-coefficient-mayer-vietoris-and-cap-ladder]], [[thm-five-lemma-for-a-morphism-of-long-exact-sequences]]

[F4] Local excision compares compactly supported relative classes in an open subspace with those in the ambient space, by explicit small-chain operators. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 If $U,V$ are open and duality holds on $U,V,U\cap V$ in every degree, the signed exact ladder [F3] and the five lemma make it hold on $U\cup V$. On an open subset $O$ of a supplied chart, enumerate all rational open boxes whose closures lie in its coordinate image. They cover that image by density of the rationals and openness. A box and each nonempty finite intersection of boxes is a coordinate ball, so [F2] applies. Induction proves duality on every finite union of these boxes: for the last box $B$ and preceding union $A$, $A\cap B$ is a union of fewer boxes, namely their intersections with $B$; the induction hypothesis and the finite gluing implication apply. Empty intersections and unions have zero groups. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $O_j$ be the union of admissible boxes among the first $j$ tuples in the fixed enumeration of finite rational tuples. Every compact subset of $O$ lies in some $O_j$, since a finite subcover by boxes has a maximum index. For a support class, [F4] moves its representative to that stage; equality of support classes is witnessed at one larger compact support and hence at a common later stage. Thus $H_c^p(O;\mathcal L)$ is the colimit of the compact-support groups of these finite unions. A homology cycle uses finitely many compact simplex images, as does a chain bounding it; the same finite-cover argument identifies $H_{n-p}(O;\mathcal L)$ with the colimit of the stage homology groups. Cap commutes with these maps by [F1]. Surjectivity and injectivity at a common stage, using step 1.1, show that $D_O$ is an isomorphism. ## Statement

Let $k$ be a commutative field and $G$ a PTFA group. For every homomorphism $f:P\to Q$ between projective right-$k[G]$ modules, if
$$f\otimes1:P\otimes_{k[G]}k\longrightarrow Q\otimes_{k[G]}k$$
is injective under the augmentation $k[G]\to k$, then $f$ is injective. Projective means the lifting property for surjections, applied to right modules; it does not mean a supplied free basis. Thus this is the right-module defining property of Strebel's class $D(k)$. The left-module version holds too.

Moreover, if $k[G]\subseteq K$ is a supplied division ring of Ore fractions, every finite matrix $T$ over $k[G]$ satisfies
$$\operatorname{rank}_K(T\otimes K)\ge\operatorname{rank}_k(\varepsilon T).$$
Both assertions require no choice axiom. The group need not be finitely generated, its series need not be normal in all of $G$, and its successive extensions need not split.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, PTFA group, augmentation and, for the matrix consequence, the supplied Ore fraction division ring.

[F1] PTFA means a finite subnormal series with torsion-free abelian successive quotients. A torsion-free abelian group has a commutative group ring with no zero divisors over $k$: apply the nonsplit-extension domain theorem with trivial kernel. [[def-poly-torsion-free-abelian-group]], [[lem-torsion-free-abelian-extensions-preserve-group-ring-domains]]

[F2] Projectivity is the lifting property against each individual surjection; for right modules use the opposite-ring version of that definition. Tensor relations preserve compositions and split identities. [[def-projective-module]], [[def-opposite-ring]], [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]

[F3] Ore fraction extension is exact on arbitrary right modules, hence preserves each injection of finite free modules. [[lem-ore-localization-is-flat-and-detects-module-torsion]]

## Proof

1.1 Call the finite-free property for a group $L$ the implication that a right-$k[L]$ matrix map between finite free modules is injective if its augmentation is injective. If $L$ is torsion-free abelian, [F1] makes $k[L]$ a commutative ring without zero divisors. For an $n$ by $m$ matrix whose augmentation is injective, finite elimination over $k$ gives an $m$ by $m$ minor with nonzero augmented determinant. The determinant of that minor is therefore nonzero in $k[L]$. Multiplying a vector in its kernel by the adjugate shows that this nonzero determinant kills every coordinate. Absence of zero divisors forces all coordinates zero, so the original matrix is injective. This also covers the trivial group and empty matrices. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $N\trianglelefteq L$, and both $N$ and $L/N$ have the finite-free property. Let $T:k[L]^m\to k[L]^n$ have injective augmentation. Applying the quotient-ring map $k[L]\to k[L/N]$ gives $T_{L/N}$ with the same augmented matrix, hence injective. If $v\in\ker T$, its finitely many coordinates have finite group supports. Choose representatives for the finitely many right-$N$ cosets meeting those supports. In the input, the vectors $e_i g$ for these representatives form a basis of a finite free right-$k[N]$ submodule containing $v$. The finitely many images $T(e_i g)$ are contained in another finite free right-$k[N]$ submodule of the target, obtained by choosing representatives for their finitely many support cosets. Normality ensures that the quotient-ring map sends these coset bases to distinct quotient group elements. Thus the restricted finite $k[N]$ matrix has augmentation equal to the $k$-linear restriction of $T_{L/N}$ to the corresponding finite span of quotient basis elements. That restriction is injective, so the finite-free property of $N$ makes the restricted matrix injective. Consequently $v=0$. Only finite sets of coset representatives were selected; no global transversal or splitting was used. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Induct up a finite PTFA subnormal series. The trivial subgroup has the property by step 1.1; at each step the preceding subgroup is normal in the next and the quotient is torsion-free abelian. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 therefore prove the finite-free property for that next subgroup. This uses only the successive normalities given in [F1], not normality of the whole series in $G$. After finitely many steps, $G$ has the finite-free property. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The same detection property holds for a map between free $k[G]$ modules of arbitrary ranks. Indeed a proposed nonzero kernel vector uses finitely many input basis elements; their images use finitely many target basis elements. Restricting to those finite free submodules preserves injectivity of the augmented map, because their inclusions into the larger free modules are split coordinate inclusions and remain so after augmentation. The finite-free property of step 2.1 makes the restriction injective, contradicting the proposed vector. No arbitrary free module is being asserted projective in the absence of choice. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Put $A=k[G]$ and let $f:P\to Q$ be as in the Statement. The canonical free module $F_P=A^{(P)}$ on the underlying set of $P$ has a surjection $\pi_P:F_P\to P$ sending $e_p$ to $p$. Projectivity gives one section $s_P$, and similarly gives $\pi_Q:F_Q\to Q$ and a section $s_Q$. Set $e=s_P\pi_P$, so $e^2=e$. Define a map between actual free modules $$g:F_P\longrightarrow F_Q\oplus F_P,\qquad g(x)=(s_Qf\pi_Px,(1-e)x).$$ If an augmented vector $\xi$ lies in $\ker(g\otimes k)$, its second coordinate says $\xi=(s_P\otimes k)(\pi_P\otimes k)\xi$. Since $s_Q\otimes k$ has left inverse $\pi_Q\otimes k$, its first coordinate implies $(f\otimes k)(\pi_P\otimes k)\xi=0$. The assumed injectivity yields $(\pi_P\otimes k)\xi=0$, and hence $\xi=0$. Thus $g\otimes k$ is injective, so $g$ is injective by step 3.1. For $p\in\ker f$, $g(s_Pp)=0$; therefore $s_Pp=0$ and $p=0$. The two sections are supplied by the two individual projectivity assertions, not by a simultaneous lift selection. This proves the full right-projective assertion. [F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Inversion $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ and the identity on $k$ give an anti-isomorphism of $k[G]$ with itself that preserves augmentation. It converts left modules into right modules, preserves the individual lifting property, and converts the augmented injectivity question to the one proved in step 4.1. Hence the left-projective assertion holds too. This is an explicit opposite-ring change and chooses neither bases nor representatives. [F2, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Let $r$ be the rank of the finite augmented matrix $\varepsilon T$. Choose $r$ input columns and $r$ output rows giving an invertible augmented square minor; this is finite elimination over $k$. Its unaugmented square matrix is injective over $k[G]$ by step 2.1, and remains injective over $K$ by [F3]. Finite-dimensional division-ring elimination therefore gives it rank $r$ over $K$. It is a row projection of the corresponding $r$ columns of $T\otimes K$, so those columns are independent and the full matrix has rank at least $r$. The case $r=0$ is automatic. All eliminations, supports, sections and coset choices in the proof are finite or individually supplied; no basis of a projective module or infinite family of coset representatives was selected. Thus both detection and the stated rank comparison hold without a choice axiom. [F3, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Every centered Borel Gaussian probability on an infinite-dimensional separable Banach space has a density with respect to some nonzero translation-invariant Borel measure that is finite on every bounded Borel set.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator|small-ball MAP comparisons use posterior ball probabilities and do not require pointwise density values]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, countable choice, the real Hilbert space $\ell^2$ with standard basis $(e_j)$, independent standard normal variables $(\xi_j)$, and the displayed series.

[A1] AC and countable choice are assumed by the Gaussian branch of the weighted Hilbert Gaussian-series result. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] If $\sum_j\lambda_jw_j<\infty$, then $\sum_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}\xi_je_j$ converges almost surely in the selected Hilbert norm; with standard normal coefficients and AC, its limit is a centered Borel Gaussian random element. [[lem-ip-gaussian-series-prior-regularity]]

[F2] A measure is countably additive on pairwise-disjoint measurable sequences, and the measure of a countable union is at most the sum of the measures. [[def-measure]], [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]

[F3] The rationals are countable and dense in the reals; finite products and countable unions of countable sets are countable. [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]], [[thm-product-of-countable]], [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]]

[F4] A measure is monotone under inclusion of measurable sets. [[prop-measure-monotonicity]]

## Counterexample

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $B=\ell^2$ with its standard basis $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$, let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent standard normal variables, and define
$$ W=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{\xi_j}{\sqrt{j(j+1)}}e_j. $$
The weighted Hilbert Gaussian-series convergence result makes $W$ a centered Borel Gaussian probability on $\ell^2$. There is no nonzero translation-invariant Borel measure on $\ell^2$ that is finite on every bounded Borel set; here translation invariance means $\lambda(A+x)=\lambda(A)$ for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and $x\in\ell^2$. Thus this law has no density with respect to a locally finite translation-invariant analogue of Lebesgue measure.

1.1 In [F1], take $H_0=H_1=\ell^2$, $w_j=1$, and $\lambda_j=1/(j(j+1))$. The finite sums telescope as $\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j=\sum_{j=1}^N(1/j-1/(j+1))=1-1/(N+1)\le1$, so the required infinite sum is finite. Thus [F1] applies to the stated independent standard normals and proves that $W$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Suppose that $\lambda$ is a translation-invariant Borel measure finite on every bounded Borel set. Put $U_j=\{x:\|x-e_j\|_2<1/3\}$. For $j\ne k$, $\|e_j-e_k\|_2=\sqrt2>2/3$, so the $U_j$ are pairwise disjoint. Each lies in the bounded ball $\{x:\|x\|_2<2\}$ by the triangle inequality. Translation invariance gives $\lambda(U_j)=m$ independent of $j$. If $m>0$, the first $N$ disjoint balls have total measure $Nm$ for every $N$, contradicting finiteness of the radius-two ball. Hence $m=0$. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Translation invariance and step 1.2 make every radius-$1/3$ ball have measure zero. Let $D$ be the set of finitely supported rational sequences. [F3] makes $D$ countable: it is the countable union, over support lengths $N$, of the countable set $\mathbb Q^N$ padded with zeros. It is dense in $\ell^2$: for any $x\in\ell^2$ and $\epsilon>0$, choose $N$ so that the squared tail sum is less than $\epsilon^2/4$, then approximate the first $N$ coordinates by rationals with squared total error less than $\epsilon^2/4$; the resulting padded vector is within $\epsilon$ of $x$. The radius-$1/3$ balls centered at $D$ therefore form a countable cover of $\ell^2$. By [F2], $\lambda(\ell^2)=0$, and [F4] makes every Borel subset null. This contradicts that $\lambda$ is nonzero. Hence no such reference measure exists, refuting the statement; in particular, the displayed Gaussian has no density relative to one. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.2, given, algebra, choose] ∎

## Definition

Let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $0<\rho<1$ and $\tau>0$. In real scalar expressions, a natural number denotes its canonical real image. Use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, identifying coordinate label $j$ with library coordinate $j-1$. For $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and $S\subseteq[n]$, let $h_S$ agree with $h$ on $S$ and vanish on $S^c=[n]\setminus S$. The matrix $A$ satisfies the **$\ell^2$ robust nullspace property of order $s$ with constants $(\rho,\tau)$** if
$$\|h_S\|_2\le \frac{\rho}{\sqrt{s}}\|h_{S^c}\|_1+\tau\|Ah\|_2$$
for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$. This condition applies to all vectors, including vectors with $Ah\ne0$.

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Take the parameter space and prior domain to be $B=D=\mathbb R^d$ with the Euclidean norm. Let $d,m\ge1$, let $C$ and $\Gamma$ be symmetric positive-definite real matrices of sizes $d\times d$ and $m\times m$, let $A$ be an $m\times d$ real matrix, and observe the fixed datum $y=Au+\eta$ with prior $u\sim N(0,C)$ and independent noise $\eta\sim N(0,\Gamma)$. Define $\Phi_y(u)=\tfrac12(y-Au)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Au)$ and $I_y(u)=\Phi_y(u)+\tfrac12u^TC^{-1}u$. The posterior has a positive continuous Lebesgue density proportional to $e^{-I_y(u)}$; its density mode is the unique minimizer of $I_y$ and is a strong small-ball MAP.

## Example references

[[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator|the strong small-ball MAP is defined by ratios to the largest ball probability]]

[[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law|the fixed-data posterior normalizes likelihood-weighted prior mass]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, positive-definite covariance matrices $C,\Gamma$, a matrix $A$, the Gaussian prior $N(0,C)$, independent Gaussian observation noise $N(0,\Gamma)$, and datum $y$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the repository's normal-law and density interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A positive-definite multivariate normal has density proportional to $\exp(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m))$, and the fixed-data posterior normalizes the likelihood-weighted prior. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]], [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]], [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F2] A centered finite-dimensional Gaussian minimizes every bounded symmetric quasi-convex loss at its mean; applying the indicator of the complement of a closed Euclidean ball shows that a Gaussian ball probability is maximized at its mean. [[lem-gaussian-centering-for-bounded-symmetric-quasiconvex-loss]]

[F3] A strong small-ball MAP maximizes small-ball probabilities asymptotically relative to their supremum over all centers. [[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator]]

[F4] Translation preserves Lebesgue measure, so Euclidean balls of the same radius have equal volume. [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]

[F5] Write $B(z,r)=\{x:\|x-z\|_2<r\}$ and $\overline B(z,r)=\{x:\|x-z\|_2\le r\}$. AC implies countable choice. Every open Euclidean ball has positive finite Lebesgue measure; each closed Euclidean ball is Borel and hence measurable, and $B(z,r)\subseteq\overline B(z,r)\subseteq B(z,2r)$. Monotonicity therefore gives $0<\lambda(\overline B(z,r))<\infty$. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]], [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], [[prop-measure-monotonicity]]

[F6] The nonnegative Lebesgue integral is monotone and homogeneous for positive scalars. [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]

## Verification

1.1 By [F1], the prior and noise have positive continuous Gaussian densities proportional to $\exp(-\tfrac12u^TC^{-1}u)$ and $\exp(-\tfrac12(y-Au)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Au))$, respectively. For any $w$, $w^T\Gamma^{-1}w\ge0$: write $w=\Gamma v$, so $w^T\Gamma^{-1}w=v^T\Gamma v\ge0$. Thus $\Phi_y\ge0$ and $e^{-\Phi_y}\le1$, so the evidence is finite by [F6] and the fact that the prior is a probability. Write $f_0$ for the prior density. The function $f_0$ is positive and continuous at $0$, and $e^{-\Phi_y}$ is also positive and continuous there. On a sufficiently small open ball $O$ about $0$, there are constants $c_0,c_1>0$ with $f_0\ge c_0$ and $e^{-\Phi_y}\ge c_1$. By [F5], $\lambda(O)>0$; [F6] then gives $N(0,C)(O)=\int_O f_0\,d\lambda\ge c_0\lambda(O)>0$ and $Z\ge c_1N(0,C)(O)>0$. The posterior update [F1] is therefore defined. Its Lebesgue density is proportional to the product of the prior density and likelihood, hence to $e^{-I_y(u)}$. Put $Q=C^{-1}+A^T\Gamma^{-1}A$. For $v\ne0$, $v^TQv=v^TC^{-1}v+(Av)^T\Gamma^{-1}(Av)>0$: if $z=C^{-1}v$, then $v^TC^{-1}v=z^TCz>0$, and the second term is nonnegative by the preceding argument. Thus $Q$ is positive definite. Completing the square gives the unique minimizer $m=Q^{-1}A^T\Gamma^{-1}y$, and the posterior is the nondegenerate Gaussian $N(m,Q^{-1})$. [A1, F1, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 For every $r>0$, apply [F2] to this posterior and the loss $L_r(x)=\mathbf1_{\{\|x\|_2>r\}}$. Its sublevel sets are the closed radius-$r$ ball and the whole space, so it is bounded, symmetric and quasi-convex. Thus every ball of radius $r$ has posterior mass at most the ball centered at $m$, and the supremum in [F3] is attained at $m$. Consequently $m$ is a strong small-ball MAP. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Let $q$ be the positive continuous posterior density. By [F5], every closed Euclidean ball has positive finite Lebesgue measure; the inclusions $B(z,r)\subseteq\overline B(z,r)\subseteq B(z,2r)$ and the open-ball result in [F5] give the volume bounds, while [F4] makes the volumes of same-radius balls equal. For any fixed $z\in\mathbb R^d$, the absolute difference between $\lambda(\overline B(z,r))^{-1}\Pi(\overline B(z,r))$ and $q(z)$ is at most $\sup_{\|x-z\|_2\le r}|q(x)-q(z)|$, by [F6]; this tends to zero by continuity. The same holds at any $v$, and the common ball volume cancels; hence $\Pi(\overline B(z,r))/\Pi(\overline B(v,r))\to q(z)/q(v)$. Since $q$ is proportional to $e^{-I_y}$, the finite-dimensional small-ball ratio agrees with the density and Onsager–Machlup comparison. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

      locator: "§7.1, local cobordism maps for births, deaths, and saddles"
    - title: "Dror Bar-Natan, Khovanov's homology for tangles and cobordisms, §§7–8"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410495v2"
      locator: "Printed pp.1470–1480; Frobenius TQFT and movie-level maps"
    - title: "Louis H. Kauffman, An Introduction to Khovanov Homology, §5"
      url: "https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf"
      locator: "PDF pp.18–22; the surface-cobordism interpretation of Frobenius maps"
---

## Example

Let $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ be the Frobenius algebra with unit $\eta(1)=1$ and multiplication $m$. In the algebraic TQFT, consider the movie that first creates a disjoint circle and then attaches a saddle band merging that circle with one existing circle. The induced local map is
$$
\mathcal A\xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}\otimes\eta} \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\xrightarrow{m}\mathcal A,
$$
and this composite is the identity on $\mathcal A$.

The diagram records the two successive surface events; it is only a description of the movie, while the verification below is algebraic.

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}
\mathcal A
\arrow[r, "{\operatorname{id}\otimes\eta}"]
& \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
\arrow[r, "m"]
& \mathcal A
\end{tikzcd}
```

## Example references

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|The integral Frobenius algebra and local cobordism maps]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial*, §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Bar-Natan, *Khovanov's homology for tangles and cobordisms*, §§7–8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410495v2)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology*, §5](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The rank-two algebra $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, its unit $\eta(1)=1$, and its merge map $m$.

[F1] [[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]] gives the basis $\{1,X\}$, the unit $1\mapsto1$, and multiplication $m(a\otimes1)=a$ for $a\in\mathcal A$.

## Proof

1.1 On the basis element $1$, $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\eta)(1)=1\otimes1$, so $m(\operatorname{id}\otimes\eta)(1)=m(1\otimes1)=1$. On the basis element $X$, $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\eta)(X)=X\otimes1$, so $m(\operatorname{id}\otimes\eta)(X)=m(X\otimes1)=X$. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 The two basis elements generate $\mathcal A$ as an abelian group, and both are fixed by the composite in step 1.1. By linearity the composite fixes every element of $\mathcal A$, hence equals $\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-finite-homology-kernel-lines-have-rational-rank-charts
kind: lemma
title: Finite homology kernel lines have rational rank charts
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
deps:

provenance:

sources:
  references:
    - title: Bénard, Florens and Rodau, A slope invariant and the A-polynomial of
        knots
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151
      locator: Section3.3, Lemma3.10 proof, PDF/printed p9 asserts the algebraic
        homology kernel section. The explicit finite-matrix rank charts and
        base-change proof needed here are supplied below.
dependency_level: 0
---

## Statement

Let $A$ be a commutative integral domain with fraction field $F$. Let $B:A^s\to A^n$, $C:A^n\to A^t$ and $U=(u,v):A^2\to A^n$ be finite matrices with $CB=CU=0$. Put $\beta=\operatorname{rank}_F B$, $\gamma=\operatorname{rank}_F C$, and assume $$\operatorname{rank}_F(B\mid U)=\beta+1.$$ Then $h=n-\gamma-\beta\ge1$. There exists $0\ne f\in A$ such that, over $A_f$, the kernel, image and homology $H_f=\ker C_f/\operatorname{im}B_f$ have explicit free bases, with ranks $n-\gamma$, $\beta$ and $h$. The kernel $$L_f=\ker\{A_f^2\xrightarrow{U_f}H_f\}$$ is a free rank-one direct summand of $A_f^2$. In explicit homology coordinates the images of $u,v$ can be written $a e_1,b e_1$, with at least one of $a,b$ a unit of $A_f$. Hence $$L_f=A_f(-b,a).$$ All these assertions, including the displayed kernel, commute with any homomorphism $A_f\to E$ to a field. In particular they describe the actual homology kernel of the specialized matrices, not just a kernel before specialization.

If $A=\mathbb C[X]$ for a nonempty irreducible affine algebraic set $X$, this gives a regular projective kernel line $[-b:a]$ on a nonempty dense principal open subset and hence a rational map $X\dashrightarrow\mathbb P^1$. Its slope convention $-\text{second coordinate}/\text{first coordinate}$ is the projective value $[a:b]$, including zero and infinity. The rank-chart expressions agree wherever both are defined. The kernel line is unchanged by invertible changes of the three chain bases, by adding boundary columns to $U$, and by multiplying both columns of $U$ by the same invertible scalar. For rational changes it is unchanged after restricting to a common open set where their denominators and inverses are defined. No assertion that the matrix rank hypotheses hold for an arbitrary topological or representation-theoretic family is part of this lemma.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The domain, finite matrices, square-zero and cycle identities and the two generic rank numbers in the Statement.

[F1] A square matrix over a commutative ring satisfies $D\operatorname{adj}(D)=\operatorname{adj}(D)D=\det(D)I$ ([[thm-adjugate-identity-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Thus a nonzero determinant over a field gives its explicit inverse; after its determinant is made a unit the same formula works over the localized ring. Empty invertible blocks mean the unique identity on the zero module.

## Proof

1.1 **Finite field normal forms with all transformations retained.** Over $F$, Gaussian elimination is an actual finite algorithm: choose the first nonzero entry of the remaining rectangle in the fixed row/column order, swap its row and column into the next pivot position, divide the pivot row by that nonzero entry and subtract its multiples to clear its column and row. Each operation has an explicit inverse and removes one row and column from the remaining problem. It ends after at most the smaller matrix size, with a block identity and a zero rectangle. This proves that its number of pivots is the rank, since invertible operations preserve the column-span dimension and $\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)$ has rank $r$; the same normal form also gives row-span dimension $r$; no real-only rank-minor theorem is invoked. Apply this to $C$, recording its changes of bases in $F^n$ and $F^t$. Its kernel has basis the last $n-\gamma$ domain coordinates. The identity $CB=0$ places every column of the transformed $B$ in those coordinates. Apply the same algorithm to this $(n-\gamma)$-row matrix, using only row operations within $\ker C$ and column operations on $F^s$. Its first $\beta$ coordinates are now the image of $B$, and its remaining $h=n-\gamma-\beta$ coordinates represent the quotient homology. Thus the entire chain pair has a split block form over $F$, not just separately computed nullities. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Recover the kernel without changing its two prescribed coordinates.** Express $U$ in the chain basis from step 1.1. The identity $CU=0$ makes its first $\gamma$ coordinates zero. Ignore its next $\beta$ boundary coordinates and call the remaining $h\times2$ matrix $V$. The hypothesis on $(B\mid U)$ says exactly that $V$ has rank one: the image of $B$ already fills its own $\beta$ coordinates, while appending $U$ adds the dimension of its quotient image. In particular $h\ge1$. Choose the first nonzero row of $V$, call it $(a,b)$. If $a\ne0$, use $a$ as the pivot; if $a=0$, then $b\ne0$, and use $b$ as the pivot. Each other row is a multiple of $(a,b)$, since otherwise two rows would be independent and the matrix would have rank at least two. Compute each multiple using its first coordinate divided by $a$ when $a\ne0$, or its second coordinate divided by $b$ when $a=0$, and subtract that multiple of the pivot row. This makes every other row zero using only the chosen nonzero pivot. These are changes only of the homology basis; the two input coordinates of $U$ have not been altered. Consequently the quotient images are $a e_1,b e_1$ and the kernel consists precisely of $a x+b y=0$. If $a\ne0$, its vectors are $(-b,a)c$ with $c=y/a$; if $a=0$, then $b\ne0$, the kernel is $F(1,0)=F(-b,0)$. In either branch the generator has one nonzero coordinate, namely the selected pivot up to sign. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 **One finite localization makes every block calculation valid before specialization.** The algorithm used finitely many field entries: include every entry of its basis-change matrices, their inverse matrices, the transformed $B,C,U$, and the scalar divisions in step 2.1. If $a\ne0$, select the pivot $p=a$; otherwise select $p=b\ne0$. Write this pivot as a fraction of nonzero elements of $A$, and include its numerator and denominator among the finitely many elements to invert or clear, together with nonzero denominators for all other entries. Let $f$ be their product, omitting only zero entries and taking denominator $1$ where appropriate. It is nonzero because $A$ is a domain. Over $A_f$, all recorded transformations and their inverses are defined, and the specified pivot is a unit. All block identities valid over $F$ remain valid over $A_f$, since this ring injects into $F$. The identity blocks show directly that $\ker C_f$, $\operatorname{im}B_f$ and their quotient have the bases and ranks in the Statement. They also show that $L_f=A_f(-b,a)$: the field computation of step 2.1 uses only the specified unit in its branch, so the same solution formula holds in $A_f$. This generator has a unit coordinate and is therefore a direct summand, with a complement obtained by the other standard coordinate vector. Under any map $A_f\to E$ to a field the transformations retain their explicit inverses, the chosen unit stays nonzero, and the same identity and zero blocks persist. Hence the cycle, boundary, homology and kernel bases specialize to the actual bases of the specialized matrix complex. No flat-base-change theorem or choice of bases in an infinite module has been assumed. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Agreement of charts and invariance under representative changes.** Two choices of elimination data yield the same submodule of $A_{ff'}^2$: in either description a vector belongs to it exactly when its original $U$ image belongs to the original boundary image. Each gives a basis vector with a unit coordinate after the stated localizations. If these generators are $k,k'$, then $k'=c k$ and $k=d k'$ for some scalars in the common ring. Since $k$ has a unit coordinate, the equality $k=dc k$ gives $dc=1$; hence $c$ is a unit, and the two projective lines agree. An invertible change of any of the three chain bases carries cycles, boundaries and the two cycle columns together and induces an isomorphism of the quotient; its preimage kernel in the fixed two input coordinates is therefore unchanged. Replacing $U$ by $U+BT$ has the same quotient map. Replacing it by $cU$ for a common unit $c$ has the same kernel. For rational changes, invert their finitely many denominators and the numerator needed for each inverse, reducing to the same assertion. In particular a common rescaling of two peripheral cycle representatives does not require an independently normalized invariant vector. [step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

5.1 **The actual rational projective map.** For $A=\mathbb C[X]$, the nonzero element $f$ is a nonzero regular function, so $D_X(f)$ is nonempty; it is dense because $X$ is irreducible and a nonempty open subset of an irreducible space is dense. The coordinates $-b,a$ are regular there and have no simultaneous zero, since one is a unit. Thus they define a regular map to $\mathbb P^1$ there, with a regular affine ratio in whichever standard chart has nonzero denominator. Step4.1 proves agreement on intersections, so this is a well-defined rational kernel line independent of the chosen rank charts. Its coefficient pair in the prescribed order is $[-b:a]$, and applying $[x:y]\mapsto[-y:x]$ gives its slope $[a:b]$. If $a=0$ its value is zero and if $b=0$ its value is infinity; neither boundary case is discarded. Zero-sized chain blocks in steps 1.1–3.1 are interpreted by empty bases, while the rank-one hypothesis itself excludes $h=0$ or a zero quotient image. All choices were witnesses for one finite matrix calculation and one finite list of denominators. This proves the exact rationality, specialization and compatibility assertions without a choice principle and without asserting the rank hypotheses for a geometric family. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ act in the standard finite coordinate bases, with labels $j=1,\ldots,n$ corresponding to library coordinates $j-1$, $y\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\epsilon\ge0$. If
$$F:=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\|Az-y\|_2\le\epsilon\}$$
is nonempty, then $z\mapsto\|z\|_1$ attains a minimum on $F$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-nullspace-property|Finite matrix action and coordinate conventions]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one- and two-norms]]

[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics|Norm properties of the finite-dimensional norms]]

[[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric|Continuity and norm comparison on finite-dimensional spaces]]

[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm|Cauchy–Schwarz for finite coordinate lists]]

[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values|Compactness and attainment of extrema in finite-dimensional real spaces]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §4.3, the quadratically constrained basis-pursuit problem](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $m,n\ge1$, a real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, a vector $y\in\mathbb R^m$, a radius $\epsilon\ge0$, and a nonempty set $F=\{z:\|Az-y\|_2\le\epsilon\}$.

[F1] [[def-ip-nullspace-property]]: $(Au)_i=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}u_j$ under the one-based labels identified with library coordinate $j-1$.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|u\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^n|u_j|$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^n|u_j|^2)^{1/2}$.

[F3] [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]] and [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]: for $n\ge1$, $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a positive-definite norm, and every norm $N$ satisfies $|N(u)-N(v)|\le N(u-v)$, $\|u\|_1\le\sqrt{n}\|u\|_2$, and $\|u\|_2\le\|u\|_1$.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: for finite real coordinate lists, $|\sum_j a_jb_j|\le(\sum_j a_j^2)^{1/2}(\sum_j b_j^2)^{1/2}$.

[F5] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums preserve termwise inequalities and sums of nonnegative terms are nonnegative.

[F6] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]: for nonnegative reals $a,b$, $a^2\le b^2$ implies $a\le b$.

[F7] [[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]: in $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge1$, closed bounded sets are compact, and every continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum and maximum; this is a ZF theorem.

[F8] [[def-canonical-natural]]: $n$ is the canonical real image of the natural $n$ in scalar expressions.

[F9] [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]: because $n\ge1$, $n>0$.

## Proof
1.1 Put $M_A=(\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. For $u,v\in\mathbb R^n$, rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] and finite-sum monotonicity [F5] give $\|A(u-v)\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}(u_j-v_j)\right)^2\le M_A^2\|u-v\|_2^2.$ By [F6], $\|A(u-v)\|_2\le M_A\|u-v\|_2$. The reverse triangle inequality [F3] now gives $\big|\|Au-y\|_2-\|Av-y\|_2\big|\le\|A(u-v)\|_2\le M_A\|u-v\|_2.$ If $M_A=0$, the displayed bound gives $\|A(u-v)\|_2=0$ for every $u,v$; positive definiteness in [F3] gives $A(u-v)=0$, so the residual function is constant and nonemptiness gives $F=\mathbb R^n$. If $M_A>0$ and $z\notin F$, the positive gap $d=\|Az-y\|_2-\epsilon$ shows that every $u$ with $\|u-z\|_2<d/(2M_A)$ also lies outside $F$. Thus $F$ is closed. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, construct, algebra]

2.1 Fix one $z_0\in F$ and set $K=F\cap\{z:\|z\|_1\le\|z_0\|_1\}$. This set is nonempty because it contains $z_0$. If $\|z\|_1>\|z_0\|_1$, the positive gap $d=\|z\|_1-\|z_0\|_1$ and [F3] show that every $u$ with $\|u-z\|_2<d/(2\sqrt{n})$ still has $\|u\|_1>\|z_0\|_1$; the denominator is positive by [F9]. Thus the second factor is closed, and $K$ is closed by step 1.1. It is bounded since [F3] gives $\|z\|_2\le\|z\|_1\le\|z_0\|_1$ for every $z\in K$. By [F7], $K$ is compact. [given, F2, F3, F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 The function $z\mapsto\|z\|_1$ is continuous by [F3], so [F7] gives a minimizer on the nonempty compact set $K$. Every feasible point outside $K$ has $\|z\|_1>\|z_0\|_1$, while the minimum on $K$ is at most $\|z_0\|_1$. Hence this minimum is global on $F$. The proof selects only one witness $z_0$ and uses the stated ZF compactness theorem; no choice axiom is used. [given, F3, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be
bounded linear with Hilbert adjoint $T^*$, and let $e\in X$ and
$r\in Y\setminus\{0\}$. Suppose $0<\sigma<1$, $\gamma>1$, $\alpha>0$,
and $h$ is the unique minimizer of
$$h\longmapsto\frac12\|Th-r\|_Y^2+\frac\alpha2\|h\|_X^2.$$
Assume its residual forcing and the range-approximation condition are
$$\|Th-r\|_Y=\sigma\|r\|_Y,$$
$$\|Te+r\|_Y\le\frac\sigma\gamma\|r\|_Y.$$
Then
$$\|e\|_X^2-\|e+h\|_X^2\ge\|h\|_X^2+\frac{2(\gamma-1)\sigma^2}{\gamma\alpha}\|r\|_Y^2.$$
If also $\|T\|\le M$ for some $M>0$, then
$$\alpha\le\frac{\sigma M^2}{1-\sigma}.$$

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt|Regularized LM step and forcing rule]]

[[lem-ip-lm-product-condition-implies-range-approximation|Range-approximation condition]]

[[lem-ip-lm-step-existence-and-residual-forcing|Unique linearized minimizer and forcing parameter]]

[[def-countable-choice|Axiom of Countable Choice]]

[[def-hilbert-space-adjoint|Hilbert adjoint]]

[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space|Real Hilbert inner-product convention]]

[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties|Adjoint norm and product identities]]

[[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm|Triangle inequality for the Hilbert norm]]

[Christian Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Lemma 11.9 and proof of Theorem 11.11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00617v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; real Hilbert spaces $X,Y$; bounded linear $T:X\to Y$ with adjoint $T^*$; $e\in X$; $r\ne0$; $0<\sigma<1$, $\gamma>1$, $\alpha>0$; a unique minimizer $h$ with $\|Th-r\|=\sigma\|r\|$; and $\|Te+r\|\le(\sigma/\gamma)\|r\|$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the assumed principle used by the adjoint and shifted-normal-operator interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] In the substitution $T=F'(x)$ and $r=y^\delta-F(x)$, the regularized LM algorithm takes its exact increment to be a global minimizer of this same quadratic ([[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt]]).

[F2] The residual after the selected increment has norm $\sigma\|r\|$, and the range-approximation residual satisfies $\|Te+r\|\le(\sigma/\gamma)\|r\|$ ([[lem-ip-lm-step-existence-and-residual-forcing]], [[lem-ip-lm-product-condition-implies-range-approximation]]).

[F3] The adjoint identity gives $\langle T^*q,e\rangle_X=\langle q,Te\rangle_Y$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

[F4] For a real scalar $a$, $a\le|a|$; Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle q,w\rangle_Y|\le\|q\|_Y\|w\|_Y$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]).

[F5] The adjoint satisfies $\|T^*\|=\|T\|$ ([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]).

[F7] The operator norm of a bounded map is the supremum of $\|Sz\|$ over the unit ball ([[def-operator-norm]]).

[F8] The real Hilbert norm satisfies the triangle inequality ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]).

[F6] In a real Hilbert space, $\|e+h\|^2=\|e\|^2+2\langle e,h\rangle+\|h\|^2$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof



1.1 For any $z\in X$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, expansion using [F6] gives
$$\Phi_\alpha(h+tz)-\Phi_\alpha(h)=t\bigl(\langle Th-r,Tz\rangle_Y+\alpha\langle h,z\rangle_X\bigr)+\frac{t^2}{2}\bigl(\|Tz\|_Y^2+\alpha\|z\|_X^2\bigr).$$
Since $h$ is a global minimizer, this is nonnegative for every $t$. Its linear coefficient must therefore vanish: if it were nonzero, a sufficiently small $t$ of the opposite sign would make the displayed difference negative. By [F3], $\langle T^*(Th-r)+\alpha h,z\rangle_X=0$ for every $z$; taking $z=T^*(Th-r)+\alpha h$ and using positive definiteness gives $T^*(Th-r)+\alpha h=0$. Set $q:=r-Th$, so $\alpha h=T^*q$. Therefore [F3] gives $\alpha\langle h,e\rangle_X=\langle q,Te\rangle_Y$, and taking the inner product of $\alpha h=T^*q$ with $h$ gives $\alpha\|h\|_X^2=\langle q,Th\rangle_Y=\langle q,r\rangle_Y-\|q\|_Y^2$. [F3, F6, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $w:=Te+r$. By [F6] and step 1.1, $\|e+h\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2=\frac2\alpha\langle q,w\rangle_Y-\|h\|_X^2-\frac2\alpha\|q\|_Y^2.$ Indeed, $Te=w-r$; substitute this into $2\langle e,h\rangle+\|h\|^2$ and use $\langle q,r\rangle=\alpha\|h\|^2+\|q\|^2$. [F3, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F2], $\|q\|_Y=\sigma\|r\|_Y$ and $\|w\|_Y\le(\sigma/\gamma)\|r\|_Y$. Thus [F4] gives $2\langle q,w\rangle_Y\le2|\langle q,w\rangle_Y|\le2\|q\|_Y\|w\|_Y\le2\sigma^2\|r\|_Y^2/\gamma$. Substituting this and $\|q\|_Y^2=\sigma^2\|r\|_Y^2$ into step 2.1 yields $\|e\|_X^2-\|e+h\|_X^2\ge\|h\|_X^2+\frac{2(\gamma-1)\sigma^2}{\gamma\alpha}\|r\|_Y^2,$ which is the first claim. [F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Applying $T$ to $\alpha h=T^*q$ and using $q=r-Th$ gives $(TT^*+\alpha I_Y)q=\alpha r$. By [F8], $\alpha\|r\|_Y=\|(TT^*+\alpha I_Y)q\|_Y\le\|TT^*q\|_Y+\alpha\|q\|_Y$. The unit-ball definition [F7] gives $\|T^*q\|_X\le\|T^*\|\|q\|_Y$ and $\|T(T^*q)\|_Y\le\|T\|\|T^*q\|_X$: if an input vector is nonzero, divide it by its norm to place it in the unit ball; if it is zero, the bound is immediate. Then [F5] gives $\|TT^*q\|_Y\le\|T\|\|T^*\|\|q\|_Y=\|T\|^2\|q\|_Y$. Thus, using $\|T\|\le M$ and the forcing equality, $\alpha\|r\|_Y\le(M^2+\alpha)\sigma\|r\|_Y.$ Since $r\ne0$, divide by $\|r\|_Y$ and rearrange using $1-\sigma>0$ to obtain $\alpha\le\sigma M^2/(1-\sigma)$. [A1, F2, F5, F7, F8, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

Apply the lemma in the iteration with $T=F'(x)$, $e=x-x^\dagger$, and $r=y^\delta-F(x)$. By [F1], the algorithm's exact increment is the required minimizer. Then $Te+r$ is the negative of the linearized residual at $x^\dagger$, so their norms agree. The proof uses Countable Choice through the Hilbert-adjoint and normal-operator interfaces; it does not use full AC, DC, or HB. The first estimate is conditional on the exact residual-forcing step and the stated range-approximation inequality. It is not a claim about arbitrary inexact solutions of the normal equation.

kind: lemma
title: Stable extension of the EIT inverse map
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 10

  - def-axiom-of-choice
  - def-countable-choice

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361"
      locator: "Propositions 3.8 and 3.9, exact-data inverse map and stable Hilbert extension, printed pp. 16–18."

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, and let $X_d(R)$, $\kappa_\gamma$ and the concave modulus $\omega_\star$ be as in the mean-zero NTD observation and Hilbert extension statements. Regard $L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)$ as a real Hilbert space with its complex $L^2$ norm. The exact-data inverse map
$$\Psi^\star:\{\kappa_\gamma:\gamma\in X_d(R)\}\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma)=\gamma,$$
is well-defined and satisfies
$$\|\Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma)-\Psi^\star(\kappa_{\gamma_0})\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)}\le\omega_\star(\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)}).$$
Consequently the Hilbert-valued extension from the preceding theorem agrees with $\Psi^\star$ on the exact kernel image and retains this stability bound on the whole underlying real Hilbert space of complex-valued kernels. Each exact NtD kernel is real-valued, but the extension domain includes all complex-valued kernels.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-mean-zero-ntd-and-smoothed-kernel-observation|The exact NTD kernel data.]]

[[thm-ip-hilbert-map-extension-with-concave-modulus|The Hilbert extension with the same concave modulus.]]

[[thm-ip-calderon-logarithmic-l2-stability|IP-45 logarithmic stability.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the conductivity classes, the exact kernels, and the candidate modulus in the Statement.

[F1] The IP-45 stability theorem controls the conductivity difference by a saturated logarithmic function of the weak DN operator difference. ([[thm-ip-calderon-logarithmic-l2-stability]])

[F2] The NTD observation assigns a unique zero-mean-in-each-variable kernel by the smoothing and Hilbert–Schmidt theorem. ([[def-ip-mean-zero-ntd-and-smoothed-kernel-observation]], [[lem-ip-ntd-smoothing-and-hilbert-schmidt-kernel-bound]])

[F3] The concave same-modulus Hilbert extension agrees with the exact-data inverse map on its defining subset. ([[thm-ip-hilbert-map-extension-with-concave-modulus]])

[F4] The kernel distance $s$ controls the weak DN distance by $C_1s^{1/2}$, including at $s=0$. ([[lem-ip-ntd-smoothing-and-hilbert-schmidt-kernel-bound]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are inherited at the weak-solution, spectral and Hilbert-extension interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the Statement.

1.1 By [F2] every conductivity has its unique zero-mean kernel. If $\kappa_\gamma=\kappa_{\gamma_0}$, [F4] gives $\dot\Lambda_\gamma=\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}$ and [F1], with its value zero at zero, gives $\gamma=\gamma_0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. Thus assigning $\kappa_\gamma\mapsto\gamma$ defines a function on the exact image, independently of the conductivity representative. This remains valid if that image is empty. [A1, F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 For any exact pair, [F4] and [F1] give $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_2\le\omega_\star(\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_2)$ with $\omega_\star(s)=C_0[\log(1/\min\{C_1\sqrt{s},t_0\})]^{-\rho}$ for $s>0$ and value zero at zero. Its concavity and continuity are proved in [F3]. Applying that theorem to the function established in step 1.1 gives an extension to the entire underlying real Hilbert space of complex-valued kernels, with the same inequality for every pair of inputs and agreement on the exact image. If the class is empty, the zero map also supplies an extension. This proves both clauses. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

---
id: lem-kontsevich-critical-point-normalization-and-associator
kind: lemma
title: Tangential KZ regularization and the hump normalization
status: draft
origin: pipeline
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
deps:
  - def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids
  - lem-kontsevich-configuration-space-compactification-faces
  - lem-kontsevich-long-knot-closure-and-connected-sum
justified_by: []
dependency_level: 8
sources:
  references:
    - title: Introduction to Vassiliev Knot Invariants, §§8.4, 8.6–8.7, and 10.1.5–10.1.7
      url: https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf
    - title: The Universal Vassiliev–Kontsevich Invariant for Framed Oriented Links, §4
      url: https://letu.math.gatech.edu/Papers/UN_PAPER.pdf
    - title: The Fundamental Theorem of Vassiliev Invariants, §2.5.4
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1
---

## Statement

For each finite degree cutoff $N$, every parenthesized endpoint cluster of the KZ connection has a unique coefficientwise tangentially regularized transport, obtained by removing its local residue factor. For three strands, fix the normalized positions $(0,z,1)$ and put $a=t_{12}/(2\pi i)$ and $b=t_{23}/(2\pi i)$. The equation $G'(z)=\left(\frac{a}{z}+\frac{b}{z-1}\right)G(z)$ has unique solutions $G_0,G_1$ with $G_0(z)=f(z)z^a$, $G_1(z)=g(1-z)(1-z)^b$, where $f$ and $g$ are analytic near $0$ and $f(0)=g(0)=1$. Their ratio $\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}:=G_1(z)^{-1}G_0(z)$ is independent of $z$ and equals the regularized limit $\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\varepsilon^{-b}G_\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)\varepsilon^a,\qquad G_\varepsilon(\varepsilon)=1$.
If $K^+$ is obtained from a strict Morse knot presentation $K$ by inserting one copy of the fixed standard hump $H$, model the local birth by cutting the knot to a one-in one-out tangle $T_K$, composing with the standard one-in one-out hump tangle whose closure is $H$, and closing the composite. Then $Z(K^+)=Z(H)Z(K)$, $r(K^+)=r(K)+1$, and hence $I(K^+)=I(K)$. The inverse in $I(K)$ exists degreewise because the degree-zero coefficient of $Z(H)$ is $1$. The associator identities and independence under arbitrary changes of parenthesization are separate claims.

## Statement references

[[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids|KZ connection, tangential endpoint convention, and fixed hump normalization]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §§8.4, 8.6–8.7, and 10.1.5–10.1.7, printed pp. 228–240 and 273–277](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Le and Murakami, §4, PDF pp. 6–7](https://letu.math.gatech.edu/Papers/UN_PAPER.pdf)

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §2.5.4, PDF pp. 15–16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The completed strand algebra, the KZ form, the compactified level cells, the fixed standard hump $H$, and a finite degree cutoff $N$.

[F1] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: the KZ form is $\Omega_q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\sum_{i<j}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j)$; parenthesizations specify nested tangential collision directions; $Z(K)$ is the degreewise improper configuration integral in the unframed 4T+1T quotient; $I(K)=Z(K)Z(H)^{-r(K)}$.

[F2] [[lem-kontsevich-configuration-space-compactification-faces]]: each nested collision has a nonnegative radial coordinate and a smooth limiting direction; branch evaluations extend smoothly to its resolved face.

[F3] [[lem-kontsevich-long-knot-closure-and-connected-sum]]: closing the standard one-in one-out hump tangle gives $H$, and closure of a vertical composite multiplies the closed series by connected sum.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Work first in the finite-dimensional quotient through degree $N$; all limits and products below are coefficientwise. No choice axiom is used.

1.1 For a three-strand configuration, translation and positive scaling put the three points at $0,z,1$. The $t_{13}$ term of $\Omega_3$ is constant in these coordinates, while $d\log(z_1-z_2)=d\log z$ and $d\log(z_2-z_3)=d\log(z-1)$. Thus the reduced equation is exactly the displayed equation with residues $a$ at $0$ and $b$ at $1$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Near $z=0$, substitute $G_0(z)=f(z)z^a$ with $f(z)=1+\sum_{n\ge1}f_nz^n$. Comparing coefficients in the differential equation gives $(n-\operatorname{ad}_a)f_n=-b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}f_j$, where $\operatorname{ad}_a(x)=[a,x]$. On the degree-$N$ quotient, $\operatorname{ad}_a$ raises degree and is nilpotent, so $(n-\operatorname{ad}_a)^{-1}=\sum_{s=0}^{N}(\operatorname{ad}_a)^s/n^{s+1}$ is defined. This determines every $f_n$ uniquely. If $S_n=\sum_{j=0}^n\|f_j\|$ in any norm on the finite-dimensional quotient, the recurrence gives $S_n\le(1+C_N/n)S_{n-1}$ for a constant $C_N$; hence $S_n$ grows at most polynomially, and $f$ converges for $|z|<1$. It solves the equation by termwise differentiation. [given, F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Replacing $z$ by $1-z$ and interchanging $a,b$ gives the same recurrence at $z=1$ and uniquely constructs $G_1(z)=g(1-z)(1-z)^b$ with $g(0)=1$. Any other solution with the same tangential leading factor differs by a constant right multiplier; the prescribed leading coefficient $1$ makes that multiplier the identity. For a general parenthesized endpoint, each collision chart from [F2] has the form $\Omega_N=A_S\,d\rho/\rho+\eta(\rho)$ in its radial variable $\rho$, where $A_S=(2\pi i)^{-1}\sum_{i<j\in S}t_{ij}$ and $\eta$ is analytic in $\rho$ with the other corner coordinates as parameters. The same coefficient recursion, inductively in the specified nested collision tree, gives a unique regularized transport after removing $\rho^{A_S}$. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1, construct, induction]

4.1 Both $G_0$ and $G_1$ solve the same left differential equation. Differentiating $G_1^{-1}G_0$ therefore gives zero, so their ratio is constant. For $G_\varepsilon(z)=G_0(z)G_0(\varepsilon)^{-1}$, the endpoint expansions and $G_0(\varepsilon)^{-1}=\varepsilon^{-a}f(\varepsilon)^{-1}$ give
$$\begin{aligned} \varepsilon^{-b}G_\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)\varepsilon^a &=\varepsilon^{-b}f(1-\varepsilon)(1-\varepsilon)^a\varepsilon^{-a}f(\varepsilon)^{-1}\varepsilon^a\\ &=\varepsilon^{-b}g(\varepsilon)\varepsilon^b\,\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}\,\varepsilon^{-a}f(\varepsilon)^{-1}\varepsilon^a, \end{aligned}$$
where the second equality follows from $G_1(1-\varepsilon)\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}=G_0(1-\varepsilon)$. In each degree, $f(\varepsilon)^{-1}-1$ and $g(\varepsilon)-1$ are $O(\varepsilon)$. Since $a$ and $b$ have positive degree, conjugation by $\varepsilon^{\pm a}$ or $\varepsilon^{\pm b}$ is a finite polynomial in $\log\varepsilon$ in the degree-$N$ quotient. Thus both outside factors in the last expression differ from $1$ by $O(\varepsilon(1+|\log\varepsilon|)^N)$ in each degree, which tends to zero; the limit is $\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Let $T_K$ be the one-in one-out tangle obtained by cutting the chosen monotone arc of $K$, and let $Q$ be the fixed one-in one-out tangle that inserts one maximum-minimum pair. By construction, $K=\operatorname{cl}(T_K)$, $H=\operatorname{cl}(Q)$, and $K^+=\operatorname{cl}(Q\circ T_K)$. Applying [F3] gives $Z(K^+)=Z(H)\#Z(K)=Z(H)Z(K)$ in the completed closed diagram algebra. The degree-zero term of $Z(H)$ is $1$, so its inverse exists degreewise. Since $r(K^+)=r(K)+1$ and connected-sum multiplication is commutative, $I(K^+)=Z(H)Z(K)Z(H)^{-r(K)-1}=Z(K)Z(H)^{-r(K)}=I(K)$. Deleting a standard hump is the inverse equality. [given, F1, F3, algebra] ∎

---
id: lem-simultaneous-peripheral-full-turn-equations-have-small-solutions
kind: lemma
title: Simultaneous peripheral full-turn equations have unique small solutions
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
deps:
  - def-axiom-of-choice
  - thm-banach-fixed-point
proof_strategy: direct
axiom_use: Full AC is retained for the geometric consumers; the
  finite-dimensional contraction argument itself uses the stated constructive
  Banach theorem.
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: William P. Thurston, The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds
      url: https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/5.pdf
      locator: Section 5.8, the local generalized surgery map; its simultaneous
        existence and continuity step is proved directly here
dependency_level: 0
---

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $k\ge1$ and let $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_k$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^k$, with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(0)\ne0$. Put $v_i(u)=u_i\tau_i(u)$. At a coordinate with $u_i\ne0$, define real coefficients $(p_i,q_i)$ by
$$p_i u_i+q_i v_i(u)=2\pi i;$$
at $u_i=0$ define its parameter to be $\infty$ in the one-point compactification $S_i=\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$.

There are neighborhoods $U$ of $0$ and $V$ of $(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$ in $\prod_iS_i$ for which this parameter map is a homeomorphism $U\to V$. One may take $V=\prod_i(\{(p,q):p^2+q^2>R^2\}\cup\{\infty\})$ for a sufficiently large $R$. Every such tuple has a unique small simultaneous solution, with $u_i=0$ exactly at the unfilled coordinates. Uniformly as the tuple tends to the complete point, writing $w_i=2\pi i/(p_i+q_i\tau_i(0))$ for finite coordinates and $w_i=0$ at $\infty$, one has
$$u_i=w_i+O(|w_i|\|w\|_\infty),\qquad \|u\|_\infty\le\tfrac43\|w\|_\infty.$$
This analytic assertion allows real coefficients of either orientation. Primitive integral coefficients are included, but no geometric completion is asserted by the equations alone.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the positive integer $k$, the holomorphic functions and their nonreal complete values.

[A1] Full choice is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A contraction with constant strictly less than one on a nonempty complete metric space has a unique fixed point, given by its convergent iterates. [[thm-banach-fixed-point]]

## Proof

1.1 Shrink to a closed convex polydisc $B_\epsilon=\{\|u\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ inside the holomorphy domain. Its compactness and continuity of the derivatives give a common Lipschitz constant $L$ for all $\tau_i$ there, by integrating their derivatives along line segments. Put $A=\max_i|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(0)|^{-1}$ and shrink $\epsilon$ so that $AL\epsilon\le1/4$ and every $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)$ stays nonzero on $B_\epsilon$. For any nonzero real pair $(p,q)$, $p+q\tau_i(0)\ne0$ and $|q/(p+q\tau_i(0))|\le A$. Moreover $|p+q\tau_i(0)|\ge c\sqrt{p^2+q^2}$ for one common $c>0$: the real-linear maps $(p,q)\mapsto p+q\tau_i(0)$ are invertible, and their moduli have a positive minimum on the unit circle. [A1, given, algebra]

2.1 For a parameter tuple with finite pairs outside a sufficiently large radius $R$, define $a_i=q_i/(p_i+q_i\tau_i(0))$ and the $w_i$ in the Statement. At an infinite coordinate put $a_i=w_i=0$. On $B_\epsilon$ define $T_i(u)=w_i/[1+a_i(\tau_i(u)-\tau_i(0))]$. Step 1.1 makes every denominator have modulus at least $3/4$, hence $\|T(u)\|_\infty\le(4/3)\|w\|_\infty$. Also $\|T(u)-T(u')\|_\infty\le(16/9)AL\|w\|_\infty\|u-u'\|_\infty$. Since step 1.1 makes $\|w\|_\infty\le2\pi/(cR)$, choose $R$ so large that $\|w\|_\infty\le\epsilon/2$ and $(16/9)AL\|w\|_\infty\le1/2$. The closed polydisc is nonempty and complete, and $T$ maps it into itself, so [F1] supplies its unique fixed point. Its defining equations are exactly the simultaneous full-turn equations at finite coordinates, and $u_i=0$ at infinite ones. At a finite coordinate $w_i\ne0$, so its solution $u_i$ cannot vanish. Every solution in $B_\epsilon$ is such a fixed point and is therefore this one. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The fixed-point bound in step 2.1 gives $\|u\|_\infty\le(4/3)\|w\|_\infty$. Its coordinate equation also gives $|u_i-w_i|\le(4/3)A|w_i|\,|\tau_i(u)-\tau_i(0)|\le(16/9)AL|w_i|\|w\|_\infty$. This proves the stated uniform expansion, including every $w_i=0$ coordinate exactly. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Define the coefficient map $\Phi$ on the open polydisc by the equations in the Statement. If $u_i\ne0$, the real-linear equation $p_i+q_i\tau_i(u)=2\pi i/u_i$ has a unique real pair, continuously depending on $u$. If $u_i\to0$, the norms of these pairs tend to infinity uniformly with the other coordinates in $B_\epsilon$: boundedness of $\tau_i$ gives $2\pi/|u_i|=|p_i+q_i\tau_i(u)|\le C\sqrt{p_i^2+q_i^2}$. Thus $\Phi$ is continuous also at its infinite coordinates, with $\Phi(0)=(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$. Let $V$ be the product neighborhood specified using $R$ in step 2.1, and put $U=\Phi^{-1}(V)$ inside the open polydisc. This is an open neighborhood of $0$. Every parameter in $V$ has its unique solution in the interior by step 2.1, so $\Phi:U\to V$ is bijective. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Its inverse is continuous on the whole product neighborhood, including partially unfilled tuples. If parameter tuples converge, their fixed-point maps $T$ from step 2.1 converge uniformly on $B_\epsilon$. For a finite limiting coordinate, $a_i,w_i$ converge in the displayed rational formulas. For an infinite limiting coordinate, $w_i\to0$ while $|a_i|\le A$, so the corresponding $T_i$ tends uniformly to zero by the $3/4$ denominator bound, regardless of the directions of the real pairs. If $u,u'$ are the two fixed points and $T,T'$ their maps, then $\|u-u'\|_\infty\le\tfrac12\|u-u'\|_\infty+\sup_{B_\epsilon}\|T-T'\|_\infty$, proving continuity. This establishes the homeomorphism. No primitivity was used in this analytic proof; primitivity enters only when a later geometric construction identifies a smooth solid-torus meridian. [step 2.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $C(K)=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ have a finite homogeneous basis $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ with Maslov grading $M(x_r)$ and Alexander filtration $A(x_r)$. Let $C^-(K)$ be the subcomplex spanned over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by $U^n x_r$ for $n\ge0$, with $M(U^n x_r)=M(x_r)-2n$ and $A(U^n x_r)=A(x_r)-n$, and assume $H_*(C^-(K))\cong\mathbb F_2[U]$ with generator in Maslov degree zero. For each integer $s$, let $\mathcal A(K,s)$ be the subcomplex spanned over $\mathbb F_2$ by those terms $U^n x_r$ with $n\ge0$ and $A(x_r)-n\le s$. For any Maslov-graded $\mathbb F_2[U]$ complex $D$, let $\delta(D)$ be the maximal Maslov grading of a homogeneous non-torsion class in $H_*(D)$, with $\delta(D)=-\infty$ if no such class exists. Define $\nu^-(K)$ to be the least integer $s$ for which $\delta(\mathcal A(K,s))=0$. Then
$$ 0\le \nu^-(K)\le g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K), $$
where $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ is the minimum genus of a smooth compact connected oriented properly embedded surface in the four-ball bounded by $K$.

## Statement references

[[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex|The finite bifiltered complex and filtration-coordinate convention]]

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|The smooth four-ball genus branch]]

[[lem-knot-floer-large-surgery-and-filtered-cobordism-input|The separate tau cobordism inequality, which does not replace the nu-minus estimate]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology*, §2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795)

[Hom and Wu, *Four-ball genus bounds and a refinement of the Ozsvath-Szabo tau-invariant*, Proposition 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.1565)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot, its normalized minus complex, and the smooth four-ball genus.

[F1] [[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex]]: the finite bifiltered complex has a finite homogeneous basis, multiplication by $U$ lowers both filtration coordinates by one and Maslov grading by two, and its total localized homology has a normalized Maslov-zero generator.

[F2] The accepted normalized grid-to-analytic comparison identifies the knot complexes, with all marked-variable and stabilization factors accounted for. It is reused at that exact knot scope. [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]]

[A6] [[lem-heegaard-floer-holomorphic-disk-regularity-compactness-gluing]] supplies actual full-filtered chosen disk counts and compactification for knots in $S^3$, without the grid/Heegaard identification or the absolute large-surgery normalization.

[A7] [[def-countable-choice]]: the declared analytic cobordism branch uses countable choice; no full choice is inferred.

[F3] The accepted normalized analytic coordinate-swap equivalence is Maslov-zero and Laurent-linear, exchanges both filtrations, and preserves the normalized total generator, with its filtered inverse and homotopies. [[lem-knot-floer-duality-and-filtration-swap]]

[F4] **External genus input under CLAUDE.md §12:** for the normalized $\mathbb F_2[U]$ knot complex, the least $s$ with $\delta(\mathcal A(K,s))=0$ is at most the smooth four-ball genus. Its module, Maslov and Alexander conventions are exactly Definitions2.11–2.12 and Theorem2.14 of [Ozsváth–Stipsicz–Szabó, printed10–11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795v3). Proposition2.13 identifies this threshold with Hom–Wu's $\nu^+$; [Hom–Wu, Proposition2.4, printed5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.1565v1) supplies the smooth genus inequality. This imports the established large-surgery/cobordism bound, not just a formal triangle identity or a localized nonzero map. The exact OSS §2.3 statement and plus/minus proof on printed10–11 and Hom–Wu definition/propositions on printed3–5 were read; Rasmussen’s upstream proof is not represented as read or locally reconstructed.

[F5] **Choice scope of the external input:** use it for the fixed knot diagram and finite smooth concordance/surface under consideration, not for a simultaneous choice of data for every knot. Integer domains and Spin-c labels form countable sets; all coefficient matrices and final graded basis changes are finite. Compact source charts give separable Sobolev and almost-complex parameter spaces with countable bases. Their fixed Fredholm problems admit a countable family of finite-cokernel perturbation charts, selected using ACω; the usual finite-dimensional Sard reduction and least-basis nested-ball Baire construction select one datum regular for the countable list. Compactness/gluing is used pointwise for these data, with finite covers of the compact low-index moduli and least-integer shrinking thresholds, not an arbitrary family of choices. Thus the imported fixed-data construction has a finite/countable specialization; full AC is not substituted for the declared ACω branch. The cited papers are not claimed to contain an explicit foundational choice audit.

## Proof

1.1 Write $M_r=M(x_r)$ and $A_r=A(x_r)$. The terms of $\mathcal A(K,s)$ on the $r$th $U$-tower are $U^n x_r$ with $n\ge\max(0,A_r-s)$, so their Maslov gradings are at most $M_r-2\max(0,A_r-s)$. By [F1], this bound tends to $-\infty$ as $s$ tends to $-\infty$; since the basis is finite, choose $s_0$ so that it is strictly negative for every $r$ when $s\le s_0$. Then $H_*(\mathcal A(K,s))$ has no class of degree zero and $\delta(\mathcal A(K,s))\ne0$. For all $s\ge\max_r A_r$, $\mathcal A(K,s)=C^-(K)$ and its normalized tower gives $\delta=0$. Thus the set defining $\nu^-$ is nonempty and bounded below, and its least element exists. This argument does not prove that the least element is nonnegative. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Put $R=\mathbb F_2[U]$, $B=C^-(K)$ and $A_s=\mathcal A(K,s)$. The latter has finite free basis $U^{\max(0,A_r-s)}x_r$. Its actual inclusion $v_s:A_s\to B$ becomes the identity of $C(K)$ after localization. Therefore the kernel of its homology map is $U$-torsion and its image is a nonzero homogeneous ideal $U^{V_s}R$, with $V_s\ge0$. A homogeneous polynomial-torsion class is $U$-torsion: the different powers of $U$ have distinct Maslov degrees, so a polynomial annihilator implies a monomial annihilator for that class. Consequently homogeneous non-torsion classes are exactly the homogeneous classes having nonzero image in the localized tower. Their maximal grading is the top grading of the image ideal, and hence $\delta(A_s)=-2V_s$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.2 Reuse the supplied Maslov-zero Laurent-linear analytic coordinate-swap equivalence $\Phi:C(K)\to C(K)$, preserving the normalized total generator and swapping the two filtrations, with its swap-filtered inverse and homotopies. For $s\in\mathbb Z$, $h_s=\Phi U^s:A_s\to B$ is an actual polynomial-target map: a point with $i\le0,j\le s$ goes to $(j-s,i-s)$, whose first coordinate is at most zero. Its Maslov degree is $-2s$. It localizes to an isomorphism, so its homology image is $U^{H_s}R$, $H_s\ge0$. The same non-torsion-domain calculation gives $-2H_s=\delta(A_s)-2s$, and thus $H_s=V_s+s$. This argument permits negative $s$ in the Laurent intermediate complex and proves that the final target lies in the polynomial subcomplex; it does not treat $U^s$ alone as an endomorphism of $B$ for negative $s$. [F3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

2.3 If $s<0$, $V_s=H_s-s\ge -s>0$. Therefore $\delta(A_s)\ne0$ for every negative $s$. Together with step1.1 this proves existence of the threshold and $\nu^-(K)\ge0$. A direct local alternative for the upper inequality would require an actual surface input. Sufficient would be an $R$-linear Maslov-zero map from the unknot tower to $B$, with image in $A_g$, sending the homology generator to the normalized generator1. Its image cycle would force $V_g=0$ and $\nu^-(K)\le g$. A map with value a positive $U$-power, a localized nonzero map, or a tau inequality does not suffice. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

2.4 The finite free basis of $A_s$ in step2.1 is exactly the basis in the external Definition2.12, since its exponent condition is $n\ge\max(0,A_r-s)$, and the normalized top minus grading is zero in both conventions. Thus [F4] applies to the SAME threshold, not to a shifted plus invariant. It gives $\nu^-(K)\le g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ at the fixed data with [F5]. Combine this with step2.3 to obtain both original inequalities. The upper bound is explicitly external; the local exponent/nonnegativity argument is retained. [given, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite. Suppose $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ are independent, and observe $Y=A\theta+\eta$. With $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$, the expected information gain of this experiment is
$$\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I_m+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2}\right).$$
Here $\Gamma^{-1/2}$ is the inverse of the unique symmetric positive-definite square root of $\Gamma$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The matrix inside the log determinant is positive definite. This formula permits singular $C$ and never uses differential entropy of $\theta$; the mean $m_0$ cancels. Noise depending on $\theta$ is outside the hypotheses and need not satisfy the formula.

## Statement references

[[thm-ip-eig-is-joint-relative-entropy|Expected information gain is the joint KL divergence of parameter and observation from the product of their marginals.]]

[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior|For singular prior covariance and positive-definite observation noise, the finite linear Gaussian posterior exists and only the observation covariance is inverted.]]

[[def-multivariate-normal-law|A finite multivariate Gaussian law may have singular covariance.]]

[[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density|Positive-definite Gaussian covariance gives the stated Lebesgue density.]]

[[def-natural-logarithm|Logarithms use the natural logarithm.]]

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

[MacKay, §3.1](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

[Rasmussen and Williams, Chapter 2](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement, with the expected information gain defined for the dominated conditional Gaussian likelihood and its proper Gaussian prior.

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis of the finite Gaussian posterior interface and the library KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The joint-KL identity gives $\operatorname{EIG}=D(P_{\theta,Y}\|P_\theta\otimes P_Y)$ under the dominated model. [[thm-ip-eig-is-joint-relative-entropy]]

[F2] For $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and independent $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ with $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$, $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$ is positive definite and the posterior formula uses only $S^{-1}$; singular $C$ is permitted. [[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior]]

[F3] A finite independent stack of possibly singular Gaussian vectors is jointly Gaussian, and linear projections of a multivariate normal have the corresponding projected mean and covariance. [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] A positive-definite multivariate normal with covariance $V$ has density $(2\pi)^{-m/2}\det(V)^{-1/2}\exp(-\tfrac12(y-a)^TV^{-1}(y-a))$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F5] A positive-definite symmetric matrix has a unique positive-definite square root; determinants are multiplicative. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^m$, $v^TSv=(A^Tv)^TC(A^Tv)+v^T\Gamma v>0$ because $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$. Thus $S\succ0$ and both observation covariances have positive determinants. The same conclusion is recorded in [F2]. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 By [F3], $(\theta,\eta)$ is jointly Gaussian, so its linear image $Y=A\theta+\eta$ is Gaussian with mean $Am_0$ and covariance $S$. Conditional on $\theta$, $Y$ is a translate of $\eta$ and has covariance $\Gamma$. Since both $S$ and $\Gamma$ are positive definite, [F4] gives the positive conditional and predictive densities needed in [F1]. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Write $z=Y-Am_0$ and $e=Y-A\theta=\eta$. By [F4], the log likelihood ratio in [F1] is $\log\frac{p(Y\mid\theta)}{p_Y(Y)}=\frac12\log\frac{\det S}{\det\Gamma}-\frac12e^T\Gamma^{-1}e+\frac12z^TS^{-1}z$. The two quadratic terms have finite expectations: expanding each finite sum and using $\mathbb E[ee^T]=\Gamma$ and $\mathbb E[zz^T]=S$ gives $\mathbb E[e^T\Gamma^{-1}e]=\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma^{-1}\Gamma)=m$ and $\mathbb E[z^TS^{-1}z]=\operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}S)=m$. Their expectations cancel, so [F1] yields $\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log(\det S/\det\Gamma)$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Let $W=\Gamma^{-1/2}$. Since $\Gamma^{1/2}W=I_m$, matrix multiplication gives $S=\Gamma^{1/2}(I_m+WACA^TW)\Gamma^{1/2}$. The middle matrix is positive definite because $ACA^T\succeq0$. By [F5], $\det S=\det(\Gamma^{1/2})^2\det(I_m+WACA^TW)=\det\Gamma\,\det(I_m+WACA^TW)$. Substitution in step 2.1 proves the formula. No inverse or determinant of $C$ was used, so singular $C$ is included; centering by $m_0$ in $z$ proves the mean cancellation. [F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
