## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and let $R=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$ and
$\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. The Kauffman bracket skein module
$\mathcal K_A(S^3)$ is freely generated as an $R$-module by the empty link.
In particular, a zero-framed trivial circle represents
$\delta[\varnothing]$.

## Statement references

[[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold|Kauffman bracket skein module]]

[[lem-kauffman-bracket-evaluation-is-invariant-for-framed-links-in-s-three|Framed bracket evaluation]]

[Józef H. Przytycki, *Fundamentals of Kauffman Bracket Skein Modules* (1998), §2, Theorem 2.3(a)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9809113)

[Sean Pohorence, *3-manifold Invariants and TQFTs* (2016), §3.1](https://categorified.net/RTinvariants/Jan29-Feb3.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and the Kauffman bracket skein module of the oriented three-sphere.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the assumption $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The module is generated by framed-link isotopy classes modulo the crossing relation $[L_\times]=A[L_A]+A^{-1}[L_B]$ and the zero-framed trivial-circle relation $[L\sqcup O]=\delta[L]$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold]]).

[F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every framed link in $S^3$ has a regular planar diagram, and framed isotopies are represented by finite diagram moves ([[lem-framed-link-diagram-calculus]]).

[F3] Adding one positive or negative full twist to one component multiplies its skein class by $-A^3$ or $-A^{-3}$, respectively ([[lem-kauffman-bracket-module-framing-twist-factor]]).

[F4] Framed bracket evaluation is well-defined on $\mathcal K_A(S^3)$, is $R$-linear, and sends $[\varnothing]$ to $1$ ([[lem-kauffman-bracket-evaluation-is-invariant-for-framed-links-in-s-three]]).

## Proof


1.1 We prove by induction on the number of crossings of a regular diagram for a blackboard-framed link that its class is a scalar multiple of $[\varnothing]$. If the diagram has a crossing, the crossing relation in [F1] expresses its class as the sum of the two smoothing classes with coefficients $A$ and $A^{-1}$. The skein convention gives each smoothing its blackboard framing, and each has one fewer crossing, so the induction applies. A crossingless diagram is a finite disjoint union of planar circles. Choose an innermost circle; its planar disk has no other component in its interior and is disjoint from the remaining link. Its blackboard framing is the zero framing, so [F1] removes it with factor $\delta$. Remove this component and repeat; the crossingless link reduces to a scalar multiple of the empty link. For a general framed link, [F2] supplies a diagram and [F3], applied finitely many times to its framing-correction integer, reduces its class to a scalar multiple of the corresponding blackboard-framed diagram. Hence every class lies in $R[\varnothing]$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, induction, algebra]

2.1 Define $\phi:R\to\mathcal K_A(S^3)$ by $\phi(r)=r[\varnothing]$. Step 1.1 makes $\phi$ surjective. If $\phi(r)=0$, $R$-linearity and $E([\varnothing])=1$ give $r=E(\phi(r))=E(0)=0$. Thus $\phi$ is injective as well as surjective, so the empty class is a free $R$-module generator. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The trivial-circle relation in [F1], with $L=\varnothing$, gives $[O]=\delta[\varnothing]$, as claimed. [F1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. An oriented lens space is an oriented closed $3$-manifold obtained by gluing two solid tori by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism. For coprime integers $p>0$ and $q$, let $L(p,q)$ denote the oriented union of the exterior of the unknot in the oriented $3$-sphere and a solid torus whose meridian is identified with the slope $p[\mu_U]+q[\lambda_U]$ on the unknot exterior. Thus this library uses the convention $L(p,q)=E_U(p/q)$; no symbol $L(0,q)$ is assigned.

## Definition references

[[def-countable-choice|Countable-choice hypothesis for the chosen peripheral data]]

[[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling|The filling operation and slope convention used here]]

[Saveliev, Lecture 1 §1.5, genus-one gluings and lens spaces](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/3mani.pdf)

[Ozsváth–Stipsicz–Szabó, Exercise 1.2.14(b), with its opposite $-L(p,q)$ surgery-orientation convention](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/konyv9.pdf)

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The empty integral surgery diagram gives the standard oriented $S^3$. Surgery on the standard unknot with framing $0$ gives $S^1\times S^2$. For every integer $p>0$, surgery on the standard unknot with framing $p$ gives the oriented lens space $L(p,1)$ in the convention $L(p,q)=E_U(p/q)$.

## Example references

[[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram|Framed-link surgery convention]]

[[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling|Integer filling slope]]

[[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention|Orientation convention for lens spaces]]

[[def-knot-exterior|Chosen unknot exterior]]

[[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude|Meridian and preferred longitude]]

[[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude|Uniqueness of the preferred longitude]]

[Saveliev, Lecture 1 §1.5 and Lecture 2 §§2.2–2.3](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/3mani.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the empty link, and the standard oriented unknot $U(t)=(e^{2\pi i t},0)$ in $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; full AC also supplies the countable-choice hypotheses in the chosen tubular data.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ says that every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F1] [[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram]]: each component with integer $n$ is filled along $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$, and the empty link has surgery result $S^3$.

[F2] [[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling]]: the integer $n$ filling attaches a solid torus whose meridian maps to $n[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$.

[F3] [[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention]]: for $p>0$, $L(p,q)$ is the oriented filling of the unknot exterior with meridian slope $p[\mu_U]+q[\lambda_U]$.

[F4] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: a preferred longitude is a degree-one parallel curve whose homology class maps to zero in the chosen exterior.

[F5] [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]]: under full AC the positive meridian and unique preferred longitude form the peripheral basis of the unknot exterior.

## Verification

1.1 Applying [A1] to the range of any sequence $(X_n)$ in [A2] and composing the resulting choice function with $n\mapsto X_n$ gives the countable-choice function required by [A2]. Thus the chosen tubular and slope interfaces used below are available. [given, A1, A2, choose]

1.2 For the empty link there are no tubular neighbourhoods to remove and no solid tori to attach. The definition [F1] therefore leaves the standard oriented $S^3$ unchanged. [given, F1, construct]

1.3 Use $N(U)=\{|z_2|\le 1/\sqrt2\}$; its exterior is the solid torus $E_U=\{|z_2|\ge1/\sqrt2\}\cong D^2\times S^1$, with disk coordinate $z_1$ and core coordinate $\arg z_2$. The loop in the $z_1$ direction has degree one and bounds a disk in $E_U$, so [F4]–[F5] identify it with $\lambda_U$; the positive meridian $\mu_U$ runs once around the exterior core. For $0$-surgery, [F2] sends the attached meridian to $\lambda_U$, the meridian of $E_U$. The gluing-map convention in the slope definition permits the product gluing: the two disk factors glue to $S^2$ and the core circles glue to $S^1$, giving $S^1\times S^2$ with the induced surgery orientation. [given, F2, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 For $p>0$, [F2] identifies the $p$-framed unknot filling with the filling of $E_U$ along $p[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$. This is exactly $L(p,1)$ by [F3]. The case $p=1$ is included. [given, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The panels illustrate the examples only; the coordinate and gluing arguments in the verification establish the identifications.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact operator of infinite rank between real Hilbert spaces, with positive singular values $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots\downarrow0$. For every $\nu,\rho>0$, the coefficient sequences of the minimum-norm power source ball
$$X_{\nu,\rho}(K)=\{|K|^\nu w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$$
are exactly
$$\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^{-2\nu}\theta_j^2\le\rho^2\right\}.$$
Thus its ellipsoid weights are $a_j=s_j^{-\nu}$, a positive nondecreasing sequence.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model|Real SVD coordinate model and coefficient-space isometry]]

[[def-ip-statistical-ellipsoid-class|Weighted statistical ellipsoid class]]

[[def-ip-power-source-set|Power source ball]]

[[lem-ip-index-source-elements-are-minimum-norm|Power source elements lie in the minimum-norm subspace]]

[[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators|Compact singular system]]

[Litao Ding and Peter Mathé, *Minimax rates for statistical inverse problems under general source conditions*, Definition 2, equations (5)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.01706v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed by the compact singular-system and spectral-power definitions.

[F1] [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]: The right singular vectors form a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and their coefficient map identifies that subspace isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$.

[F2] [[def-ip-power-source-set]]: $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)=\{|K|^\nu w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$.

[F3] [[def-ip-statistical-ellipsoid-class]]: A weighted statistical ellipsoid is $\{\theta\in\ell^2:\sum_j a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\}$ for positive nondecreasing weights.

[F4] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]: $|K|v_j=s_jv_j$, and $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$.

[F5] [[def-compact-spectral-filter-and-qualification]]: A compact spectral multiplier acts on each singular eigenspace by its scalar multiplier and vanishes on the kernel for a positive spectral power.

[F6] [[lem-ip-index-source-elements-are-minimum-norm]]: Every element of the power source ball lies in $N(K)^\perp$.

[F7] [[def-real-power]] and [[thm-real-power-laws]]: Positive-base real powers obey $(s_j^2)^{\nu/2}=s_j^\nu$ and $s_j^{-\nu}=1/s_j^\nu$; [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] gives $(x^{-\nu})'=-\nu x^{-\nu-1}$ on $(0,\infty)$.

[F8] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: A function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on its interior has increment equal to its derivative at an intermediate point times the interval length.

**Given:** Countable Choice, the compact real infinite-rank operator $K$, its fixed positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$, and $\nu,\rho>0$.

## Proof


1.1 Write $w_j=\langle w,v_j\rangle_X$. By [F4] and the compact spectral multiplier [F5], the coefficient of $|K|^\nu w$ at $v_j$ is $s_j^\nu w_j$; the kernel component of $w$ contributes zero. [given, A1, F2, F4, F5, F7, algebra]

1.2 Conversely, take any $\theta\in\ell^2$ with $\sum_j s_j^{-2\nu}\theta_j^2\le\rho^2$ and put $w_j=s_j^{-\nu}\theta_j$. This sequence is square-summable with norm at most $\rho$; the coefficient isometry in [F1] gives a unique $w\in N(K)^\perp$ with these coefficients. [given, A1, F1, F7, construct]

2.1 For every $x=|K|^\nu w$ with $\|w\|_X\le\rho$, step 1.1 and Bessel's inequality for the orthonormal family $(v_j)$ give $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^{-2\nu}\langle x,v_j\rangle_X^2=\sum_{j\ge1}w_j^2\le\|w\|_X^2\le\rho^2$. Thus every source element has coefficient sequence in the stated ellipsoid. [given, F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Set $x=|K|^\nu w$ for the vector constructed in step 1.2. By [F5] its $j$th coefficient is $s_j^\nu w_j=\theta_j$; [F1] makes equality of the coefficient sequences equality of vectors in $N(K)^\perp$. Since $\|w\|_X\le\rho$, [F2] gives $x\in X_{\nu,\rho}(K)$. This proves the reverse inclusion. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Since $s_{j+1}\le s_j$ and $x\mapsto x^{-\nu}$ has negative derivative on $(0,\infty)$ by [F7], [F8] gives $s_{j+1}^{-\nu}\ge s_j^{-\nu}$ for every $j$. Hence $a_j=s_j^{-\nu}$ is positive and nondecreasing; by [F3] the right-hand set is a weighted statistical ellipsoid. Steps 2.1 and 2.2 prove the two set inclusions, completing the identification. [given, F3, F4, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $p,q\ge2$ be coprime integers. There is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F_{p,q}\subset S^3$ whose oriented boundary is $T(p,q)$ and whose genus is $(p-1)(q-1)/2$. It can be constructed from a disk by plumbing $(p-1)(q-1)$ positive Hopf bands: a positive Hopf band is the oriented annulus spanning the positively linked Hopf link, and plumbing along a square glues square neighborhoods of properly embedded arcs in two surfaces on opposite sides of a 3-ball, with the four boundary edges alternating between the surfaces and with orientations agreeing on the square. For a connected compact oriented surface with one boundary component, genus is defined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$.

## Statement references

[[def-coprime-torus-knot|The parameterized primitive torus-knot slope]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface|The connected compact oriented spanning-surface convention]]

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, §5.3.2](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

[Calegari, §3.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Akbulut and Ozbagci, §2](https://msp.org/gt/2001/5-1/gt-v5-n1-p10-p.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and coprime integers $p,q\ge2$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the choice-function principle for sequences of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] [[def-coprime-torus-knot]] parameterizes $T(p,q)$ on the standard Heegaard torus by the primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$.

[F2] [[def-oriented-seifert-surface]] defines a Seifert surface as a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with the knot as its oriented boundary, and gives $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$ for a one-boundary-component surface.

## Proof

1.1 Use the solid-torus side with core the first-coordinate circle, so the second coordinate is the meridional disk coordinate. At longitudinal angle $u\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ in the first coordinate, the knot meets this disk at the $p$ points with second-coordinate angles $2\pi q(u+k)/p$, $k=0,\ldots,p-1$. Place these points at the vertices of a regular $p$-gon. A counterclockwise rotation by $2\pi/p$, tapered to fix the disk boundary, carries each point to the next and crosses consecutive points once in the order $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{p-1}$; each $\sigma_i$ is the positive half twist of adjacent points. Thus one such increment is the braid block $\delta=\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_{p-1}$, and the rotation through $2\pi q/p$ gives $\delta^q$. The lifted curve has winding vector $(p,q)$ in the fixed Heegaard-torus coordinates, exactly the parameterization in [F1]. The braid block permutes the points by a $p$-cycle, so its $q$th power has one cycle because $\gcd(p,q)=1$. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 At each positive crossing replace the crossing by the orientation-compatible smoothing and then attach one half-twisted rectangle in the original crossing ball; this is the oriented braid Seifert-surface construction. It gives $p$ disks joined by $q(p-1)$ positively half-twisted bands, one for each crossing. The first block has one band between each adjacent pair of disks, so its incidence graph is a path; attaching bands along a tree joins the disks to a disk. Each of the remaining $q-1$ blocks has $p-1$ bands. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Add the remaining blocks in order, and within each block add the bands in the order $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{p-1}$. For each added band, a small ball containing it and the corresponding band from the preceding block can be chosen disjoint from the other crossing balls after sliding their strand rectangles along the Seifert disks. The two bands are positive half twists on the same adjacent pair; their union with the two intervening disk strips is an annulus whose boundary components have linking number $+1$, hence a positive Hopf band. The old band meets the already-built surface in a square, the new annulus lies on the opposite side of that square, and the orientations agree because both bands come from positive crossings. Thus each added band is exactly a plumbing along a square as defined in the Statement. Repeating this for all $(q-1)(p-1)$ later bands gives the stated grid of positive Hopf plumbings. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 A plumbing replaces the old square and the Hopf annulus by their union, so inclusion-exclusion for Euler characteristic gives $\chi(F_{p,q})=\chi(F_{p,q}^{\mathrm{old}})+0-1=\chi(F_{p,q}^{\mathrm{old}})-1$. Starting from the disk in step 2.1, after $(p-1)(q-1)$ plumbings the surface is connected and has $\chi(F_{p,q})=1-(p-1)(q-1)$. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The boundary of the constructed surface is the closure of the braid in step 1.1. Its permutation has one cycle, so the boundary has one component; the construction is connected and oriented at every band attachment. It is therefore a Seifert surface for $T(p,q)$ in the sense of [F2]. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Since $(p-1)(q-1)$ is even, the one-boundary-component identity $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$ and step 4.1 give $g(F_{p,q})=(p-1)(q-1)/2$. [F2, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

For $T(3,4)$ the grid has $(3-1)(4-1)=6$ positive Hopf-band plumbings. The three columns are the three later braid blocks and the two rows are their adjacent crossing bands; process columns left to right and each column in the crossing order from step 3.1. Each rectangle represents one annulus. The proof checks the boundary, orientation, connectedness, and Euler characteristic from the braid bands; it does not infer them from the drawing.

```tikz
      \node at (\x+0.41,\y+0.31) {$H^+$};

  \draw[->,thick] (1.5,1.9)--(2.55,1.9);
  \node[above] at (1.4,2.0) {plumb along the rectangular grid};
  \node[below] at (1.25,-0.25) {six positive Hopf bands};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ be a finite integral framed link in the standard oriented $S^3$. In its complement choose an oriented knot $K$ with any integer framing and a small meridian $U$ of $K$, lying in a ball about one short arc of $K$ and disjoint from $L$. Give $U$ its disk framing zero. Then $L\cup K\cup U$ and $L$ are related by a finite sequence of orientation-preserving ambient isotopies, fully framed handle slides, and insertions or deletions of split $+1$ or $-1$ framed unknots. The conclusion applies also to the inverse insertion move. No condition on the knot type of $K$ or on its linking with $L$ is imposed.

## Statement references

[[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram|Integral framings]]

[[def-kirby-moves-on-integral-framed-links|Allowed moves]]

[Roberts, p. 1 and the O3 move](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9812086)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The framed link $L\cup K\cup U$, the small meridional disk for $U$, and full AC.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is the hypothesis of the framed-link interface. All choices and move lists below are finite.

[F1] [[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram]]: the framing integer is measured from the preferred longitude in $S^3$.

[F2] [[def-kirby-moves-on-integral-framed-links]]: a slide is a band sum with the specified framed parallel; its full normal framing is carried across the band. Only a split signed-unit-framed unknot may be deleted directly.

## Proof

1.1 **Framing bookkeeping from bands.** For oriented components $A,B$ with integers $a,b$ and linking number $l$, a slide of $A$ over $sB$, $s=\pm1$, has framing $a+b+2sl$. Indeed choose small framed parallels and the parallel band. The linking of the new curve with its parallel is the sum of the old self-linkings $a,b$ and the two cross-linkings $sl,sl$; the two bands have disjoint interiors and contribute no further crossing. Its linking with a third component $C$ is $\operatorname{lk}(A,C)+s\operatorname{lk}(B,C)$. These are consequences of the actual parallel-and-band construction, not permissions to replace a geometric link by a matrix. We use bands with no added full twist; an existing twist of any component is carried with its strip. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 **The zero-meridian crossing operation.** A slide over $U$ can switch a crossing of a selected strand with the strand of $K$ encircled by $U$. Here is the local construction. Take the disk of $U$ transverse to the latter strand, and take a thin band from the selected strand to a disk-parallel copy of $U$. Put the interior of the band off the disk and all the link. In a cross-section perpendicular to the encircled strand, the band sum replaces a short detour on one side of the origin by that detour followed by one signed circuit about the origin. Round its two band corners. The result is the detour on the other side: the region between the circuit with its return segment and this detour is a disk in the punctured cross-section, so pushing across its product with the short strand interval is an ambient isotopy relative to the ends. Thus precisely the chosen crossing changes. Use the opposite band side for the opposite crossing. The disk-parallel framing of $U$ has no twist, so the strip is the transported framing of this operation, including any change of self-linking prescribed by step 1.1. The operation is valid when the selected strand is another part of $K$: use distinct disjoint short arcs as the two band ends. The encircled arc is unchanged, so $U$ remains its small zero-framed meridian. To use a different arc, move this meridian along a thin tubular neighbourhood of $K$; a meridional disk slides along the product tube, so this is an isotopy of $U$ in the complement of $K\cup L$, with its disk framing. The bands and their corners have smooth rounded product neighbourhoods; the disk pushes extend by a cutoff in those neighbourhoods to smooth orientation-preserving ambient isotopies. [given, F2, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 **Signed-unit blowdown as allowed moves.** Suppose an unknotted component $J$ has framing $\varepsilon=\pm1$ and a spanning disk $D$ transverse to the other strands. At a piercing of sign $d$, slide that strand over $-\varepsilon d$ times the oriented framed parallel of $J$. Route its band beside $D$. The parallel makes exactly $\varepsilon$ full turns around the disk-normal direction, so this banded detour removes that piercing and gives one signed twist of the remaining disk-piercing strands. This is a geometric disk operation: cut the strands at their small piercing intervals, carry their cut ends along disjoint narrow radial strips of $D$ to its boundary, and use the framed parallel there to join the ends on the same side of $D$. Nested radial strips are used one at a time; corners are rounded in the disk-normal product. After all piercings have been removed, $J$ bounds a disk missing the remaining link, so a small neighbourhood of that disk is a ball separating $J$. Delete it by [F2]. The remaining strands have acquired $-\varepsilon$ full twist about $D$; reversing this construction gives the corresponding blowup. The framing/linking updates are $a_i'=a_i-\varepsilon l_i^2$ and $l_{ij}'=l_{ij}-\varepsilon l_il_j$, where $l_i=\operatorname{lk}(A_i,J)$: apply step 1.1 successively to the signed slides, or count the crossings of the parallel strips in the displayed full twist. In the applications below each remaining component crosses $D$ only once. A full twist of one such strand is a curl of an unknotted arc; of two such strands it is their two-strand full twist. Thus this operation has an explicit geometric meaning, as well as the displayed integer update. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 **Splitting the pair from the old link.** Choose a regular finite projection of the compact smooth link, keeping a small meridional arc marked. Such a projection can be obtained by replacing finitely many short arcs inside disjoint tubular charts by polygonal arcs and rounding, followed by a small generic change of direction; the replacements are isotopies in their product tubes, and finitely many nonadjacent projected line segments have only finitely many transverse intersections after that change. At every mixed crossing of $K$ with $L$, use step 2.1 on the strand of $L$ to put $K$ above that strand. Its framing does not change: that component has linking zero with the small meridian $U$, and $U$ has framing zero, so step 1.1 gives the same integer. The local replacement changes no crossing between two strands of $L$. Consequently the old framed link, considered by itself, is still its original framed isotopy class. Once $K$ is above $L$ at every mixed crossing, lift $K$ and its very small meridian in the projection direction above a slab containing $L$, and move them into a ball disjoint from $L$. This lift has no obstruction at a mixed crossing because their height order was chosen precisely this way. From now on all operations are in that ball. [given, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 **Unknotting the companion.** Fix a base point away from the meridional arc. Switch self-crossings of $K$ by step 2.1 until its based diagram is descending: on traversing from the base point, the first encounter with each crossing is the overpass. A descending diagram is an unknot by the following explicit disk construction. Cut at the base point, and straighten the arc in traversal order, lifting each initial segment above all later segments; each lift is possible because the initial segment is the overpass at every first encounter. Join the endpoints by the short base-point arc outside the projection. This gives a simple planar circle after a final height isotopy, hence an embedded spanning disk. There are finitely many crossings, so these are finitely many moves and disk pushes. Keep $U$ tiny at an unchanged arc during each crossing operation and carry it by the subsequent isotopies. The result is the standard Hopf pair $K_n,U_0$ in the disjoint ball, for some integer $n$. Changes of $n$ have been carried by the strips; we do not assert that crossing changes preserve $n$. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 **Reducing the Hopf framing.** Orient the Hopf components to have linking $+1$. Sliding $K$ over either signed disk-parallel of $U$ changes $n$ by $+2$ or $-2$ by step 1.1. Choose the band in the standard Hopf solid torus $S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(U)=D^2\times S^1$, where $K$ is a core. A disk-framed parallel of $U$ is a meridian of this exterior solid torus. The band running radially from the core to that meridian makes the new curve, after pushing slightly inside, $(r w^{\pm1},w)$, $w\in S^1$, for small fixed $r>0$: the added meridian is the single turn of its disk coordinate. The curves $((1-t)r w^{\pm1},w)$, $0\le t\le1$, are embedded for every $t$, since the second coordinate is $w$. They give an isotopy to the core, supported away from the exterior boundary and hence away from $U$. Extend its velocity in a small tube by a cutoff to obtain an ambient isotopy; the full normal strip is transported. Thus the pair is again a Hopf pair, rather than merely having the same linking matrix. Repeating gives $K_0,U_0$ if $n$ is even and $K_1,U_0$ if $n$ is odd. Negative $n$ is covered by choosing the increasing sign. [F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 **The odd Hopf pair.** In $K_1,U_0$, the disk of $K$ has just one piercing, by $U$. Apply step 2.2 with $J=K$ and $\varepsilon=1$. The remaining component is the unknot $U$ with framing $-1$: the single strand receives one curl, which is removed by an ambient isotopy while retaining its changed normal framing. It is split from $L$, so delete it. This removes the odd pair by allowed moves alone. [F2, step 5.1, step 2.2, construct]

6.2 **The even Hopf pair.** In $K_0,U_0$, introduce a split $+1$ unknot $V$ in the same otherwise empty ball. Slide $U$ over $V$ along the untwisted band between their spanning disks, orienting the band so the new linking of $U$ and $V$ is $+1$. The band sum of these two unknots is still an unknot: its spanning disk is the band sum of their disjoint disks. Its framing is $1$. The three components are now the standard chain $K_0,U_1,V_1$, with adjacent linkings $+1$ and with $K,V$ unlinked. The disk of the middle component meets each end component once in separate straight product arcs. Blow down $U_1$ by step 2.2. Its two-strand twist makes the ends a standard Hopf pair of linking $-1$, with framings $K_{-1},V_0$. Each end remains unknotted, since its own arc has only received a curl; their mixed two crossings are the Hopf clasp. Blow down $K_{-1}$. The remaining $V$ is the unknot with framing $0-(-1)(-1)^2=1$, again with only a single-arc curl. Delete this split $+1$ unknot. Thus the even pair also disappears. The disk, band and full-twist descriptions identify every intermediate knot and not just its algebraic linking data. [F2, step 1.1, step 5.1, step 2.2, construct]

7.1 Steps 3.1 and 4.1 reduce the original configuration to the original framed $L$ and an isolated Hopf pair. Steps 5.1 and 6.1 and 6.2 remove that pair. All bands, disk pushes and lists are finite, and every deletion was a split signed-unit unknot deletion or its explicitly proved slide expansion. Orientations of components and their normal strips are transported at each move. Reversing the finite list proves the insertion assertion. [given, A1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 6.2] ∎

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9812086"
      locator: "pp. 1–4; the complete smooth oriented relative existence and marked calculus arguments are supplied by the proved local dependencies."
    - title: "Robion Kirby, A Calculus for Framed Links in S3"
      url: "https://math.berkeley.edu/~kirby/papers/Kirby%20-%20A%20calculus%20for%20framed%20links%20in%20S%5E3%20-%20MR0467753.pdf"
      locator: "Theorem 1 and complete proof, §§2–3, printed pp. 36–45"
    - title: "Nikolai Saveliev, Lectures on the Topology of 3-Manifolds"
      url: "https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/3mani.pdf"
      locator: "Theorem 3.1 and K1/K2 definitions, Lecture 3 §3.2, printed pp. 45–46"

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D_0$ and $D_1$ be finite integral framed-link surgery diagrams in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, with surgery results $M_0$ and $M_1$. Then $M_0$ and $M_1$ are orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic if and only if $D_0$ and $D_1$ are related by a finite sequence of ambient isotopies, framed handle slides, and additions or deletions of split $\pm1$-framed unknots.

## Statement references

[[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram|Integral framed-link diagrams and surgery results]]

[[def-kirby-moves-on-integral-framed-links|Ambient isotopy, framed handle slides, and stabilization]]

[[lem-relative-three-bordism-surgery-presentation|Proved marked relative surgery calculus]]

[[lem-zero-meridian-pairs-are-generated-by-kirby-moves-in-s-three|Elimination of zero-meridian pairs in the three-sphere]]

[Kirby, A Calculus for Framed Links in S3, Theorem 1 and proof](https://math.berkeley.edu/~kirby/papers/Kirby%20-%20A%20calculus%20for%20framed%20links%20in%20S%5E3%20-%20MR0467753.pdf)

[Saveliev, Lecture 3 §3.2, Theorem 3.1](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/3mani.pdf)


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, finite integral framed diagrams $D_0,D_1$ in the standard oriented $S^3$, and their oriented surgery results $M_0,M_1$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited by the suppliers below.

[F1] [[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram]] and [[def-kirby-moves-on-integral-framed-links]] specify the integer-framing, ambient-isotopy, fully framed band-slide and split signed-unit-unknot conventions.

[F2] [[lem-kirby-moves-preserve-surgery-manifold]] proves that each allowed move, and hence each finite sequence, preserves the orientation-preserving diffeomorphism type of the surgery output.

[F3] [[lem-relative-three-bordism-surgery-presentation]] proves marked relative surgery completeness. In the empty-decoration, closed-boundary case with fixed base $N=S^3$, any prescribed orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of two surgery outputs is realized by a finite sequence of exterior framed isotopies, split signed-unit-unknot moves O1, framed slides O2, and moves O3 inserting or deleting a framed knot together with its small disk-zero-framed meridian. The proof supplies the signature-adjusted marked five-bordism, common middle trace, based descending handle movie and its full framed conversion; none of those constructions is inferred from a generic function path alone.

[F4] [[lem-zero-meridian-pairs-are-generated-by-kirby-moves-in-s-three]] proves that every such O3 move in $S^3$ is a finite sequence of the moves in [F1], with the full component framings retained.

## Proof

1.1 If $D_0,D_1$ are related by the stated finite sequence, apply [F2] to each move and compose its orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms. The result is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $M_0\to M_1$. [given, A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Conversely, let $f:M_0\to M_1$ be an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism. Use the two given diagrams as undecorated presentations based in the same standard oriented $S^3$. Take empty external boundary, empty ribbon graph and arbitrary equal auxiliary weights; the global supplier's undecorated comparison is independent of its later decoration and evaluation clauses. Every component framing is its actual normal two-disk framing, as in [F1]. Thus [F3] applies to this specified $f$ and yields a finite O1/O2/O3 and framed-isotopy sequence from $D_0$ to $D_1$. In particular it compares the given endpoint diagrams; it does not merely produce some new presentations of their output manifolds. [given, A1, F1, F3, construct]

2.1 The O1 and O2 operations in this sequence are precisely the split signed-unit-unknot moves and fully framed slides of [F1]. Replace each O3 insertion or deletion by the finite sequence supplied by [F4]. That lemma has no restriction on the companion knot's linking with the rest of the diagram, so it applies at every intermediate stage. Its integer normal framings agree with [F1]. This replacement need not preserve the particular marked map $f$, which the present claim does not require, but it preserves the exact endpoint framed diagrams. A finite list with finitely many finite replacements is finite. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 The resulting sequence uses only ambient isotopy, fully framed handle slides and split $\pm1$ unknot stabilization or destabilization. It joins $D_0$ to $D_1$, proving the converse. Together with step 1.1 this establishes the equivalence with all stated orientation, smoothness and finiteness conventions. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement refuted

Every cyclic branched cover of a smooth oriented knot has finite first homology.

## Statement references

[[thm-knot-cyclic-cover-order-from-alexander-polynomial|The Alexander-polynomial criterion for cyclic-cover finiteness]]

[[thm-knot-determinant-is-order-of-double-cover-homology|Every double branched cover has finite first homology]]

[Livingston, “Seifert Forms and Concordance,” Theorem 3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0101035v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the right-handed trefoil matrix $V_T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and the primitive sixth root $\zeta_6=e^{i\pi/3}$.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom required by the cyclic-cover and Alexander-polynomial theorems. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The Seifert determinant $\det(V-tV^T)$ represents the Alexander polynomial up to a unit $\pm t^k$. [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]], [[def-alexander-polynomial-from-the-first-elementary-ideal]]

[F2] The cyclic-cover order theorem states that a zero at any nontrivial $q$-th root makes the first homology infinite. [[thm-knot-cyclic-cover-order-from-alexander-polynomial]]

[F3] The Alexander normalization gives $\Delta_K(1)=\pm1$, and the double-cover theorem gives finiteness when $|\Delta_K(-1)|$ is this nonzero odd integer. [[lem-square-seifert-presentation-and-alexander-normalization]], [[thm-knot-determinant-is-order-of-double-cover-homology]]

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Direct calculation gives $\det(V_T-tV_T^T)=\det\begin{pmatrix}t-1&-t\\1&t-1\end{pmatrix}=t^2-t+1$. By [F1], this represents the trefoil Alexander polynomial up to $\pm t^k$. Since $\zeta_6^2-\zeta_6+1=0$, the Alexander polynomial vanishes at this nontrivial sixth root. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Applying [F2] with $q=6$ shows that $H_1(\Sigma_6(T);\mathbb Z)$ is infinite, contradicting the refuted universal claim. For the boundary comparison, [F3] gives $\Delta_T(-1)$ odd and nonzero, so $H_1(\Sigma_2(T);\mathbb Z)$ is finite. Thus the failure occurs at a higher cyclic cover even though the double-cover case is always finite. The two supplier theorems use the Axiom of Choice in [A1]. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Definition

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, $E_K$ its exterior, and $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ a representation. The **adjoint local system** $\operatorname{Ad}\rho$ has fibre $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ and left group-module action $\gamma\cdot v=\rho(\gamma)v\rho(\gamma)^{-1}$. In the first-loop-first intrinsic convention, this means forward path transport $T_\gamma(v)=\rho(\gamma)^{-1}v\rho(\gamma)$; equivalently the corresponding right action is $v\cdot\gamma=\rho(\gamma)^{-1}v\rho(\gamma)$. Its twisted homology $H_*(E_K;\operatorname{Ad}\rho)$ is the intrinsic local-system homology with these transports, equivalently the homology of the cellular local-coefficient complex for a supplied CW structure; the same convention defines boundary-torus twisted homology and the inclusion map $i_*:H_1(\partial E_K;\operatorname{Ad}\rho)\to H_1(E_K;\operatorname{Ad}\rho)$. An **admissible adjoint representation** is one for which there is a nonzero vector $v_\rho\in\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ fixed by the peripheral adjoint action such that $\{[v_\rho\otimes\lambda],[v_\rho\otimes\mu]\}$ is a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\operatorname{Ad}\rho)$ and $\ker i_*$ is one-dimensional. For an irreducible affine character curve $X$, its function field $\mathbb C(X)$ is the fraction field of its coordinate domain. A **tautological representation** over $\mathbb C(X)$ is a homomorphism $\rho_X:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C(X))$ whose character is the generic character of $X$. A **smooth projective completion** consists of a smooth complete curve $\overline X$ with a dense open subset $U$ identified with the normalization $X^\nu$ of $X$, with its finite birational normalization map $\nu:U\to X$ recorded. When $X$ is smooth, $\nu$ identifies $U$ with $X$, recovering the usual completion. An **ideal point** is a point $x\in\overline X\setminus U$; points of $U$ over singular affine points of $X$ are affine branches and are retained inside $U$. Such an ideal point defines the discrete valuation $v_x(f)=\operatorname{ord}_x(f)$ on $\mathbb C(X)$. The valuation ring is $\mathcal O_x=\{f:v_x(f)\ge0\}$, and a **uniformizer** is an element $\pi\in\mathcal O_x$ with $v_x(\pi)=1$. Its residue field is $k_x=\mathcal O_x/(\pi)$. An $\mathcal O_x$-lattice in $\mathbb C(X)^2$ is a free rank-two $\mathcal O_x$-submodule spanning $\mathbb C(X)^2$; two lattices are homothetic if one is a nonzero scalar multiple of the other. The **Bruhat–Tits tree** has homothety classes of these lattices as vertices, with two vertices adjacent if representatives satisfy $\pi\Lambda\subsetneq\Lambda'\subsetneq\Lambda$ and $\Lambda/\Lambda'$ is one-dimensional over $k_x$. Whenever the tautological representation exists, it acts on this tree. The ideal point, valuation, action, and any essential surface produced from the action are its Culler–Shalen data; that surface is called the associated Culler–Shalen surface.

## Definition

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

## Definition references

[Piccirillo, §2, definition preceding Theorem 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A three-component link in $S^3$ with the component labels and framing
data in the Definition and countable choice.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is
[[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]: each component is
a smooth oriented embedded circle in the standard oriented $S^3$, and
ambient isotopy means an orientation-preserving isotopy of the ambient sphere.

[F2] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: a meridian is the boundary
of a normal disk to the component, oriented by the knot and ambient
orientations, and the preferred longitude is the degree-one peripheral curve
with zero exterior-homology class.

[F3] [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]] and
[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]: a regular
oriented diagram has finitely many transverse double crossings with over/under
data, each assigned the determinant crossing sign.

[F4] [[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]]: the half-sum
of mixed crossing signs is an integer independent of the regular oriented
diagram, and it is symmetric in the two components.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The definition specifies $R$ as dotted and $B,G$ as zero-framed attaching
circles. Thus $R$ contributes one $1$-handle, while $B$ and $G$ contribute
the two $2$-handles in the stated handlebody. [given, construct]

1.2 The two meridional-sublink conditions are invariant under ambient isotopy,
and each says that the indicated $2$-handle goes geometrically once over the
$1$-handle. The separately stated mixed-crossing condition is a link
invariant by [F4], while [F3] fixes the crossing-sign convention; it is not
inferred from either meridional-sublink condition. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $Y$ be a closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere, let $\mathfrak t$ be a Spin$^c$ structure, and suppose the Heegaard Floer groups, absolute rational grading, and natural map $\iota_*:HF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t)\to HF^+(Y,\mathfrak t)$ are defined and independent of the construction choices. View $HF^+$ as an $\mathbb F_2[U]$-module. An element is $U$-torsion if some positive power of $U$ annihilates it. The correction term $d(Y,\mathfrak t)$ is the minimum absolute grading of a nonzero homogeneous element in $\operatorname{im}\iota_*$. In the standard plus tower every element is $U$-torsion, although every element is divisible by every positive power of $U$; these two properties are compatible. The definition uses the nonzero homogeneous image elements, rather than imposing $U$-nontorsion. The standard normalization is $d(S^3,\mathfrak t_0)=0$ for the unique Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t_0$ on $S^3$. Existence of the minimum and independence of choices are separate proof obligations.

---

## Definition

Let $D$ be a finite regular diagram of a nonempty oriented link $L\subset S^3$ with ordered crossing set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. The resolution cube has vertices $I\in\{0,1\}^n$, and $D(I)$ is obtained by applying the indicated local smoothing at every crossing. The link-surgery filtered module associated to $D$ is the direct sum
$$
C_D=\bigoplus_{I\in\{0,1\}^n}\widehat{CF}(\Sigma(D(I));\mathbb F_2),
$$
with the summand for $I$ in increasing filtration degree $n-|I|$. Choose the subordinate Heegaard multi-diagram, compatible perturbation data and top-generator cycles for successive attaching-curve systems. The diagonal component of the candidate differential is the ordinary hat disk differential. For $I<J$ coordinatewise, sum over every ordered path $I=I_0<I_1<\cdots<I_r=J$ changing one coordinate at each step. Its summand counts the zero-dimensional holomorphic $(r+2)$-gon spaces with input at the $I$ vertex, the selected top-generator cycles between each pair of successive attaching systems, and output at the $J$ vertex. The count includes the allowed source conformal parameters and imposes zero basepoint multiplicity. These are the surgery polygon maps; the component is zero if $I\nleq J$. Thus changing several crossings is a sum over paths and polygon counts, not an arbitrary direct edge map. The increasing filtration is $F_pC_D=\bigoplus_{|I|\ge n-p}\widehat{CF}(\Sigma(D(I));\mathbb F_2)$, extended by zero below $0$ and by $C_D$ at and above $n$. Thus a component increasing $|I|$ lowers its filtration degree and preserves every $F_p$. The cube direction and the reduced Khovanov cochain degree remain separate indices. The polygon-count finiteness, square-zero, and total-homology identifications are justified by the surgery lemma, which labels its actual Ozsváth–Szabó construction and top-input/filling calculations as external inputs, separately from the retained local analytic theorem and finite filtration algebra.

The local smoothing labels are those of Ozsváth–Szabó Figure1: in the chart with northwest–southeast over-strand, 0 joins the two left and two right endpoints, and 1 joins the two top and two bottom endpoints. These become A and B on the mirror chart, respectively. This fixes the convention for the consumers without a diagram-invariance assertion. The general surgery lemma also applies to links in arbitrary closed connected oriented smooth three-manifolds; this definition is only its branched-cover instance.

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot bounding a smooth proper disk $D\subset B^4$, and let $q\ge2$. Write $X_D$ for the compact disk exterior and let the positive meridian induce $\pi_1(X_D)\to H_1(X_D;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/q$. Let $X_{D,q}$ be the connected cover classified by the kernel of this map. Attach $D^2\times D^2$ to $X_{D,q}$ along the connected cover of $D^2\times S^1$ using the normal-disk map $z\mapsto z^q$. The resulting compact oriented $4$-manifold $W_{D,q}$ is the $q$-fold cyclic cover of $B^4$ branched along $D$; its boundary is $\Sigma_q(K)$, and the local branched model is $(x,z)\mapsto(x,z^q)$.

## Definition

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and $C=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ a finitely generated free $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ complex. Choose a finite homogeneous basis $\{x_r\}$, with $M(x_r)$ and Alexander filtration $A(x_r)$. The translate $U^k x_r$ has Maslov grading $M(x_r)-2k$ and filtration coordinates $(i,j)=(-k,A(x_r)-k)$. The total homology is $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$; use the standard normalization in which its Maslov-zero tower generator first appears at algebraic filtration level $i=0$, and denote it by $\xi_K$.

For $t\in[0,2]$ and a nonzero finite chain $z$, define
$$ F_t(U^k x_r)=(1-t/2)(-k)+(t/2)(A(x_r)-k),\qquad F_t(z)=\max\{F_t(U^k x_r):U^k x_r\text{ has nonzero coefficient in }z\}. $$
Let $\mathcal Z_0(C)$ be the set of Maslov-zero cycles representing $\xi_K$. Set
$$ \nu_t(C)=\min_{z\in\mathcal Z_0(C)}F_t(z),\qquad \Upsilon_K(t)=-2\nu_t(C). $$
The minimum is over cycles representing the normalized homology generator, not over individual basis terms. For comparison, let $C^-(K)$ be the $\mathbb F_2[U]$-span of the chosen basis and form its $t$-modified complex over the ring $\mathcal R$ of formal sums $\sum_{\alpha\in S}c_\alpha v^\alpha$ whose support $S\subset[0,\infty)$ is well-ordered (every nonempty subset of $S$ has a least element). The coefficient extension uses $U=v^2$. In the extended Laurent complex, $v$ lowers both filtration coordinates by $1/2$ and Maslov grading by one, so a diagonal $U$-translation lowers the extended $t$-grading by two. On arbitrary homogeneous Laurent terms this grading is $M-t(j-i)$; the formula $M-tA$ below is specified on the chosen generators at $i=0$. A homogeneous generator $x$ has $t$-grading $M(x)-tA(x)$, extended by $\operatorname{gr}_t(v^\alpha x)=\operatorname{gr}_t(x)-\alpha$. If a term $U^k y$ occurs in $\partial x$, its $t$-modified differential coefficient is $v^{\operatorname{gr}_t(y)-\operatorname{gr}_t(x)+1}$; thus for $\partial x=\sum_y c_{xy}U^{(M(y)-M(x)+1)/2}y$, define $\partial_t x=\sum_y c_{xy}v^{\operatorname{gr}_t(y)-\operatorname{gr}_t(x)+1}y$. This differential lowers $t$-grading by one. The comparison between its non-torsion tower grading and the finite cycle minimum is the separate filtered tower-splitting claim.

## Definition references

[[lem-upsilon-real-series-valuation-domain|The real-exponent coefficient ring and its field of fractions]]

[[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau|The diagram-specific knot Floer filtration and tau convention]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology*, §§3–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795)

[Livingston, *Notes on the knot concordance invariant Upsilon*, §§2–7](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Upsilon-revised.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finitely generated free bifiltered knot Floer complex $C$ whose total homology has a normalized Maslov-zero generator, as stated in the definition.

[A1] [[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau]]: that item defines a diagram-specific hat threshold and does not itself prove diagram/surface independence or supply the Laurent filtration comparison. The current [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] separately supplies a normalized grid-to-analytic filtered comparison; localization gives the Laurent comparison under its stated prerequisites. This Definition remains algebraic on a supplied normalized complex.

## Proof

1.1 For each of the finitely many basis generators $x_r$, at most one Laurent translate has Maslov grading zero, since $M(x_r)-2k=0$ determines $k$ uniquely when it has an integer solution. Thus the Maslov-zero chain group is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb F_2$. A finite chain represents $\xi_K$, so $\mathcal Z_0(C)$ is nonempty; being a subset of a finite vector space, it is finite. The minimum defining $\nu_t$ therefore exists for every $t\in[0,2]$. The algebraic argument here does not establish knot-model independence; the current grid comparison theorem supplies the normalized comparison for its stated grid and analytic models. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 If $f:C\to C'$ is a bifiltered chain homotopy equivalence, then it sends every Maslov-zero cycle representing $\xi_K$ to one representing the normalized generator of $C'$. Each term of $f(z)$ has both filtration coordinates no larger than the corresponding input term, so $F_t(f(z))\le F_t(z)$ for $0\le t\le2$. Hence $\nu_t(C')\le\nu_t(C)$. Applying the same argument to a filtered inverse gives the reverse inequality, so $\nu_t(C')=\nu_t(C)$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For a fixed cycle support, $F_t(z)$ is the maximum of finitely many affine functions of $t$. Since $\mathcal Z_0(C)$ is finite, $\nu_t$ is the minimum of finitely many such finite maxima. A finite minimum or maximum of affine functions is continuous and piecewise linear with finitely many breakpoints. Therefore $\Upsilon_K(t)=-2\nu_t(C)$ is continuous and piecewise linear on $[0,2]$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For a differential term $U^k y$ in $\partial x$, the $i$-filtration gives $k\ge0$ and the $j$-filtration gives $A(y)-A(x)\le k$. The Maslov grading gives $M(y)-M(x)+1=2k$, so its exponent in $\partial_t x$ is $\operatorname{gr}_t(y)-\operatorname{gr}_t(x)+1=2k-t(A(y)-A(x))\ge(2-t)k\ge0$. For a two-step path $x\to y\to z$, the two exponents sum to $\operatorname{gr}_t(z)-\operatorname{gr}_t(x)+2$, independent of $y$. Thus the coefficient of each $z$ in $\partial_t^2x$ is the coefficient of $z$ in $\partial^2x$ multiplied by the same power of $v$; since $\partial^2=0$, $\partial_t^2=0$. [given, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Unresolved proof obligations

The diagramwise tau definition alone does not supply a normalized $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}$ model. The current [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] has an authored proof of the normalized grid-to-analytic comparison; localization gives the Laurent comparison under that supplier's stated prerequisites. The filtered tower-splitting item supplies the separate $t$-modified grading identification. This definition makes no assertion that $s=2\tau$ and does not itself prove model invariance.

## Example

Let $k$ be a field and let $V$ be a $d$-dimensional finite-dimensional vector space with the ribbon structure of finite-dimensional vector spaces, ordinary flip braiding, standard duality, and trivial twist. For each $n\ge1$ and $\beta\in B_n$, put $W=V^{\otimes n}$, let $\rho(\beta)$ be the braid action, and let $j_W:W\to W^{\vee\vee}$ be the ribbon-induced pivotal comparison. Define the finite blackboard-framed braid-closure value by the categorical trace $t_n^V(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(j_W\rho(\beta))$. Then
$$t_n^V(\beta)=d^{c(\pi(\beta))},$$
where $\pi:B_n\to\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$ is the homomorphism $\pi(\sigma_i)=(i\ i+1)$ and $c(\pi(\beta))$ is the number of cycles in its disjoint-cycle decomposition, including fixed points as one-cycles. Thus the one-component unknot has value $d$, the two-component unlink has value $d^2$, and the closure of the positive generator $\sigma_1\in B_2$ has value $d$.

The two-strand positive generator used in the last calculation is shown schematically below; its endpoint permutation is the transposition $(1\ 2)$.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current bounding box.center),scale=.8]
  \draw[->] (1,1) -- (.56,.08);
  \draw[->] (.44,-.08) -- (0,-1);
  \draw[->] (0,1) .. controls (.28,.5) and (.72,-.5) .. (1,-1);
  \node at (-.2,1) {$1$};
  \node at (1.2,1) {$2$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The vector space $V$, the flip ribbon structure, $n\ge1$, and a braid $\beta\in B_n$.

[F1] The left categorical trace of a morphism into the double dual is the coevaluation–morphism–evaluation composite ([[def-the-categorical-trace-of-a-morphism-into-the-double-dual]]).

[F2] The Drinfeld morphism in a braided rigid category is given by the evaluation–braiding–coevaluation composite ([[thm-a-braided-rigid-category-has-a-drinfeld-morphism]]).

[F3] Every permutation of a finite set has a disjoint-cycle decomposition, unique up to reordering and cyclic rotation, and fixed points are counted as one-cycles ([[thm-disjoint-cycle-decomposition]], [[def-permutation-support-disjoint-cycles-and-cycle-type]]).

[F4] In the specified vector-space ribbon structure, each positive and negative braid generator acts by the ordinary flip of the adjacent factors, and the twist is identity.

[F5] A generator assignment on $B_n$ that sends every Artin relator to the identity extends to a homomorphism ([[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]], [[thm-von-dyck]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data in the Example and [F1]–[F5].

1.1 If $n=1$, the braid group is trivial and $\pi$ is its unique homomorphism. If $n\ge2$, put $s_i=(i\ i+1)$. For $|i-j|>1$, $s_i$ and $s_j$ commute because they have disjoint supports; for adjacent indices, both $s_i s_{i+1}s_i$ and $s_{i+1}s_i s_{i+1}$ equal $(i\ i+2)$. These are the Artin relators, so [F5] gives the homomorphism $\pi$. By [F4], each positive or negative braid generator swaps its two adjacent tensor factors, so the action on $W=V^{\otimes n}$ is the factor permutation given by $\pi(\beta)$. The twist is identity. Let $w_1,\ldots,w_{d^n}$ be the tensor basis of $W$ and $w_1^*,\ldots,w_{d^n}^*$ its ordinary dual basis. Substitution in [F2]'s formula gives $u_W(w_r)(w_s^*)=1$ when $r=s$ and $0$ otherwise, so the pivotal comparison is the canonical double-dual identification. The categorical trace formula [F1] is therefore the ordinary matrix trace of that permutation operator. [F1, F2, F4, F5, given, construct]

2.1 Fix a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $V$. A basis tensor $e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$ is fixed by the factor permutation exactly when its indices are constant on each orbit of $\pi(\beta)$; by [F3], these orbits are exactly the cycles counted by $c(\pi(\beta))$, including fixed points. There are $d$ independent choices for each cycle, hence exactly $d^{c(\pi(\beta))}$ fixed basis tensors. A permutation matrix has trace equal to its number of fixed basis vectors, proving the formula. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The identity in $B_1$ has one permutation cycle, the identity in $B_2$ has two, and $\sigma_1$ has the transposition permutation with one cycle. Substitution into the formula gives $d$, $d^2$, and $d$, respectively; the latter closure is a single component because its endpoint permutation has one cycle. These calculations include $d=0$ because every listed cycle count is positive. [step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible atoroidal $3$-manifold whose boundary components are tori. If $M$ contains an incompressible, boundary-incompressible annulus $A$ whose boundary lies in $\partial M$, then $M$ is Seifert-fibered.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Lemma 1.16](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Walter Neumann and Gadde Swarup, *Canonical decompositions of 3-manifolds*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9712227)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact connected orientable irreducible atoroidal smooth three-manifold $M$ with torus boundary and the incompressible boundary-incompressible proper annulus $A$.

[F1] The geometric disk obstructions and atoroidality are [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]], Definition. In particular irreducibility supplies a parametrized smooth ball for each interior sphere.

[F2] The two circle-bundle bases used initially have injected boundary torus groups; their base groups are free of rank two and the bundle projection surjects onto them ([[lem-boundary-tori-circle-bundle-pants-punctured-mobius-pi1-injective]], Statement and Proof 1.1–1.2). Finite free-product reduced words are nontrivial, and a connected gluing gives the group pushout ([[thm-normal-form-for-free-products]], [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]], Statements).

[F3] Torus curves and their annulus strips have finite smooth parameters ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-torus-curves-and-annulus-strips]]). A nullhomotopic torus circle has a planar lift whose bounded disk has the smooth parameter of [[lem-choice-free-smooth-jordan-disk-parameters-and-prescribed-collars]]; different deck translates cannot nest bounded equal-area disks, so this disk projects injectively. Compact smooth embeddings admit relative transversality without choice ([[lem-choice-free-relative-transversality-for-a-compact-smooth-embedding]], Statement).

[F4] Marked smooth balls and disk windows have explicit standard parameters and collar-supported attachment/removal maps, without choice ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]], Statement).

[F5] Equal primitive Seifert fiber slopes admit actual smooth fiber matching and product-collar gluing, without choice ([[lem-equal-seifert-boundary-slopes-admit-smooth-fiber-matching-and-gluing]], Statement).

[F6] In a supplied smoothly parametrized $T^2\times I$, an incompressible smooth torus system has injective cut-piece groups, without choice ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-torus-incompressibility-in-a-supplied-flat-product]], Statement and full proof).

[F7] Finite compact-source isotopies extend smoothly ([[lem-choice-free-isotopy-extension-for-a-compact-smooth-source]]). Finite bundle transport uses the Euclidean flow and smooth parameter dependence in [[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] and [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]].

[F9] Every compact smooth boundary-preimage surface has a boundary-fixed smooth embedding neatification with an explicit topological ambient extension. The actual smooth disk obstructions and boundary-compressing witnesses transport as stated in the endpoint-witness supplier. Products here are the products in the original Definition; on a broad nonneat input their pullbacks are topological products, not newly asserted smooth collars. [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]] [[lem-angular-boundary-neatification-preserves-smooth-disk-obstructions]]

## Proof

1.1 First apply [F9] to the given surface, fixed pointwise on its boundary. The resulting surface is neat. Incompressibility passes to it, and a boundary-compressing witness passes in either direction; absence of boundary compressions therefore passes as well. Work with this neat representative for the following smooth collar constructions. The boundary-fixing topological ambient extension pulls any resulting boundary-parallel product back to the actual original surface. Thus this preparation does not add a neatness hypothesis to the Statement. Take a small product neighborhood of $A$ and collars of its incident boundary tori. They exist by a finite coordinate construction: choose the normal side using orientations of $M$ and $A$, combine finitely many adapted chart fields by normalized finite bumps, and use their short flow and the local inverse and compact separation arguments in [F7]. Normalize the two boundary curves on each incident torus by [F3]. Their parallel strip parameters and the product parameter of $A$ supply circle coordinates on the neighborhood, agreeing at the attaching rims. Circle parameter discrepancies have degree $\pm1$ and are adjusted by interpolation of their increasing, or decreasing, angular lifts; this is finite. Round the quadrant corners in the base coordinate, keeping the circle coordinate. The resulting neighborhood $N_0$ is an ordinary circle bundle with $A$ vertical. If the annulus meets two different original tori, its base is a pair of pants with two original boundary circles and one internal boundary. If it meets one original torus, its band attaches to the same base boundary circle: the two possible band identifications give a pair of pants with two internal boundaries, or a once-punctured Möbius band with one. The total space is orientable, since it is a submanifold of $M$; in the Möbius case the fiber orientation reverses with the base orientation. These are actual finite band-and-collar quotient parameters. The internal frontier consists of at most two tori. [F1, F3, F7, given, construct]

2.1 We first fill compressible frontier tori, before addressing boundary-parallel ones. For $N_0$, frontier groups inject into its group by [F2]. Use this injection for the initial iteration. After the only possible intermediate filling, its explicit group calculation below will verify the invariant before another iteration. If a frontier torus is compressible in $M$, choose a compressing disk and put it transverse to the other frontiers by [F3]. Its intersection consists of finitely many circles. Remove any inessential circle on a frontier by an innermost disk replacement: choose its frontier disk with interior disjoint from the compressing disk, replace the latter's subdisk by it and push slightly to the side of the retained disk. The disk parameters in [F3] and quadrant rounding give an embedded smooth disk with the same essential original boundary and fewer intersections. If a remaining intersection is essential on its frontier, an innermost circle on the disk cuts off a compressing disk whose interior misses the entire frontier. If no intersection remains, the original disk already has this property. Thus some frontier $T$ has a clean compressing disk $D$. It cannot lie in $N$, since its boundary class is nonzero on $T$ and $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(N)$ is injective. The connected disk interior consequently lies on the exterior side of $N$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Compress $T$ along $D$ and push the resulting sphere slightly off the frontier. Irreducibility supplies a ball $B$ bounded by it. The connected $N$ lies outside that ball: it misses the compressed sphere and contains an original boundary torus of $M$, whereas $B$ is an interior ball. The disk neighborhood restored by reversing compression is also on this non-ball side, because its rim strip is joined to $N$ through the gap removed from $T$. Hence reversal attaches a marked $1$-handle to $B$; it does not remove a possibly knotted handle from its interior. Its two disk windows have the parallel-copy parameters of $D$, and [F4] standardizes them. The result is a solid torus $U$ outside $N$, with boundary exactly $T$. It contains no other frontier, since $B$ and the small disk neighborhood miss $N$ except at $T$. The exterior component adjacent to $T$ is exactly $U$: its interior is both open and closed in that component and it has no other boundary. Adjoin it to $N$. [F1, F4, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The meridian of $U$ cannot be its attaching fiber slope. If it were, [F3] and its supported boundary collar formula give a smooth meridian disk bounded by that actual fiber. In $N$, choose a base arc from this frontier to the interior of the base arc underlying $A$, avoiding any previous cone point and meeting that arc only at its endpoint. Its inverse image is a vertical annulus meeting $A$ in its one boundary core. Join it to the meridian disk and round the common collar. This is a compression of $A$, a contradiction. In product coordinates $U=D^2\times S^1$, therefore, the primitive regular-fiber class is $a\mu+b\lambda$ with $b\ne0$. After reversing the fiber orientation take $b>0$. The action $$t\cdot(z,w)=(e^{iat}z,e^{ibt}w)$$ gives a Seifert model with that boundary slope and one possible multiplicity-$b$ core. Indeed the map $(\zeta,v)\mapsto(v^a\zeta,v^b)$ identifies $U$ with the quotient by $(\zeta,v)\mapsto(e^{-2\pi ia/b}\zeta,e^{2\pi i/b}v)$; since $\gcd(a,b)=1$, choose an inverse generator to obtain exactly the standard fibered-solid-torus cyclic model. Its boundary fibration has the same fiber class as the old one. Use [F5] to match it smoothly and glue the product collars. Thus this filling extends the actual Seifert structure, leaves $A$ vertical and caps that base boundary by a disk with cone order $b$ (regular if $b=1$). [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 There are initially at most two frontiers. The only filling that can leave another frontier is the pair-of-pants case with just one original boundary torus; its new base is an annulus with at most one cone. Its remaining boundary groups still inject, by this explicit finite calculation. Before filling the orientable circle bundle over a pair of pants has group $F(a,c)\times\langle h\rangle$: lift the two free base generators, and the oriented fiber $h$ is central and injective by [F2]. Filling adds the primitive relation $c^q h^p=1$, with $q\ge1$, by [F2]'s gluing pushout. The quotient by central $h$ is $\mathbb Z*C_q$. The two boundary base loops have images $a$ and $(ac)^{-1}$, both of infinite order by reduced words (for $q=1$, both are $a^{\pm1}$). Also $h$ has infinite order: the presentation maps to the additive reals by $h\mapsto1$, $c\mapsto-p/q$, $a\mapsto0$. Thus a boundary element projecting trivially must first have zero base exponent, then zero fiber exponent. This proves boundary-torus injection after the intermediate filling. Step 2.1 is therefore applicable again. After finitely many such steps, either no frontier remains or every remaining frontier is incompressible in $M$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 By atoroidality, each remaining frontier $T$ is parallel to an original boundary torus, with a supplied smooth product $P=T^2\times I$. If $P$ is on the exterior side of $N$, it is exactly the adjacent exterior component, so absorb it into $N$, extending the fibration as a product by [F5]. Suppose instead that $N$ lies on the $P$ side. It is then contained in $P$, since the latter occupies that whole component between $T$ and the original boundary. The product contains only one original boundary torus of $M$. Thus this is impossible if $N$ already contains two original boundary tori. If $N$ still has two frontiers, it is the original pair-of-pants bundle with one original boundary; the other frontier $T'$ is an incompressible smooth torus in $P$. By [F6], every cut piece of $P$ along $T'$ injects into $\pi_1(P)$. The connected $N$ is one such piece, since its only interior boundary in $P$ is $T'$. But $\pi_1(N)$ surjects onto the nonabelian free rank-two base group [F2], while $\pi_1(P)=\mathbb Z^2$ is abelian. This is a contradiction. This argument treats $N$ as a possible proper submanifold of the collar; it does not incorrectly infer that nonabelian $N$ cannot sit inside a product without an injection proof. [F1, F2, F5, F6, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 It remains to exclude the $N$-side collar when there is one frontier and one original boundary. In that case $N=P$, since it has exactly the two boundary tori of $P$ and no interior frontier in it. If its base is the once-punctured Möbius band, [F2]'s free rank-two quotient contradicts the abelian product group. Otherwise this is the intermediate annulus-with-one-possible-cone case. Its central-fiber quotient from step 5.1 is $\mathbb Z*C_q$, which is nonabelian for $q\ge2$. Hence $q=1$: the inherited structure is an ordinary circle bundle over an annulus. The vertical $A$ has both ends on the same original base boundary, so its base arc cuts off a disk. That disk has a smooth parameter by [F3] in an annulus cover. Trivialize the bundle over it by radial horizontal transport: combine finitely many local lifts by finite base bumps and solve the radial ODE from its center using [F7]. A fixed point of the initial fiber gives a section disk. Its boundary consists of an essential spanning arc of $A$ and an arc in the original boundary torus. This is a forbidden boundary compression of $A$. Thus the collar can never be on the $N$ side. Every remaining frontier is therefore an exterior product collar and can be absorbed. [F1, F2, F3, F7, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Each solid-torus filling or collar absorption removes a frontier, and initially there were at most two. At the end $N$ has no internal frontier; it is nonempty, closed and relatively open in connected $M$, hence equals $M$. Its fibration is the smooth Seifert structure constructed in steps 4.1 and 6.1. The neat representative of the annulus was retained throughout. The conclusion is a smooth Seifert structure on the unchanged ambient manifold, so it proves the original choice-free Statement without asserting that an original tangential annulus is smoothly ambient isotopic to a vertical one. The only product-group comparison used the explicit flat-product compression and cut-injection bridge [F6]; no arbitrary smooth/PL compatibility or general topological triangulation assertion entered. All choices and modifications were finite. [F1, F5, F6, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 7.1, construct] ∎
