## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot in $S^3$, let $F$ be a compact connected oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H_1$ be admissible multipointed Heegaard diagrams for $K$. For $i=0,1$, the diagram $\mathcal H_i$ has a closed genus-$h_i$ Heegaard surface and $m_i=h_i+k_i-1$ curves in each attaching system, with $k_i$ ordered $w$-points and $k_i$ ordered $z$-points; each component of either attaching-system complement contains one point of each type, and the connecting arcs represent $K$. A curve isotopy is an isotopy of one attaching curve through embedded curves in its attaching system, disjoint from the other attaching curves and all marked points. A handleslide replaces one attaching curve by its band sum with another curve in the same attaching system, along an embedded arc disjoint from the other attaching curves and the marked points. A Heegaard stabilization forms connected sum with the genus-one splitting of $S^3$ in a disk disjoint from all curves, marked points, and knot arcs; it raises the genus by one and leaves $k$ fixed. A basepoint-pair (index-zero/three) stabilization keeps the genus fixed and adds one curve to each system and one $w,z$ pair along the represented knot. Its inverse removes the following elementary configuration, after relabeling the cyclic pairs: curves $\alpha_0,\beta_0$ bound disks $A_0,B_0$ on the surface, are disjoint from every opposite-system curve except each other, and intersect transversely in two points; $A_0\cap B_0$ is a bigon containing just $w_0$, while $A_0\setminus B_0$ contains just $z_0$ and $B_0\setminus A_0$ contains the next $z$-point along the cyclic pairing. Remove $\alpha_0,\beta_0,w_0,z_0$ and concatenate the adjacent trivial knot arcs. The surviving marked points stay fixed. Thus the move inserts a pair along an existing knot arc rather than adjoining an isolated marked component in an empty disk. Both descriptions include the simultaneous boundary-parallel arc systems and require the stated one-$w$, one-$z$ condition in each attaching complement. Destabilizations are the respective inverse moves. Comparisons may apply the orientation-preserving diagram isomorphisms of the pointed-data definition, carrying the ordered marked points, attaching systems and simultaneous boundary-parallel arcs, before or after the listed geometric moves. Their complex identifications are induced by pushforward of generators, disk classes and almost complex data, rather than by assuming an isotopy acts as the identity. Comparisons also allow the fixed-splitting arc normalizations in that definition before or after the listed moves, retaining the simultaneous bridge witnesses and all ordered marks. They leave the surface attaching and analytic data fixed, so their identification of the actual count operators is the identity; they do not assert a diffeomorphism of a tangential and transverse surface-knot pair. With these identifications, any two such diagrams are related by a finite sequence of the listed moves through admissible multipointed diagrams, preserving the represented oriented knot.

For a diagram with $j$ basepoint pairs, regard its full filtered minus complex as a complex over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by restriction of scalars along $U\mapsto U_i$ for any one chosen basepoint variable. The resulting complexes of $\mathcal H_0$ and $\mathcal H_1$ are filtered chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb F_2[U]$, preserving relative Maslov grading and Alexander filtration, even when the diagrams have different numbers of basepoint pairs. The choice of the single variable action does not affect this type. Restriction retains the independent variables in the chain module; it is different from quotienting by $U_1=\cdots=U_j$. The latter ordinary quotient is the fully collapsed complex and has filtered chain homotopy type $CFK^-(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(j-1)}$, where $V$ has zero differential and bidegrees $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. Equivalently, a basepoint stabilization before quotienting is modeled by the cone of $U_{j+1}+U_i$ on the polynomial extension of the old complex; after the simultaneous quotient this is a zero-map cone and contributes the displayed extra factor.

For an admissible doubly-pointed diagram $\mathcal H_1$ for $(K,F)$, define $\widehat{HFK}(K)$ to be the homology of the Alexander-associated-graded complex obtained from its full filtered minus complex by quotienting by its sole variable $U$. For a generator $\mathbf x$ use the Alexander grading
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the relative $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ structure assigned by the pointed Heegaard construction from the gradient trajectories through $\mathbf x$ and the chosen basepoint pair, and $\widehat F$ is obtained by removing a tubular neighborhood of $K$ from $F$ and capping the resulting longitude with the meridian disk of the solid torus attached so that this longitude bounds it (zero-framed surgery). The vector-field representative is extended across small balls around the critical points, and its first Chern class is the Chern class of the orthogonal oriented plane field. Use the absolute Maslov normalization in which the unique generator of $\widehat{HF}(S^3)$ has degree zero.

For a diagram $\mathcal H$ with $j$ basepoint pairs, let $\widetilde C(\mathcal H)$ be the Alexander-associated-graded complex over $\mathbb F_2$ obtained from its full filtered minus complex by setting every $U_i=0$; its differential therefore counts only classes with all $n_{w_i}=n_{z_i}=0$. Its homology is $\widehat{HFK}(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(j-1)}$, where $V=\mathbb F_2\langle v_0,v_1\rangle$ has bidegrees $(M,A)(v_0)=(0,0)$ and $(M,A)(v_1)=(-1,-1)$.

## Statement

Assume AC. For every closed oriented smooth four-manifold $Z$ and every based homomorphism $\theta:\pi_1Z\to G$ to an arbitrary discrete group,
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(Z,\theta)=\operatorname{sign}(Z).$$
Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth three-manifold and $\phi:\pi_1M\to G$ any homomorphism. There exist an injective homomorphism $j:G\hookrightarrow\Gamma$ and a compact oriented smooth four-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M$ and a homomorphism $\pi_1W\to\Gamma$ restricting to $j\phi$. For any such data put
$$\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_\Gamma(W)-\operatorname{sign}(W).$$
This number is independent of the smooth bound, its extending map and the injective target enlargement. The same value is obtained from $r$ copies of $M$ bounding a smooth $W$ by dividing its defect by $r>0$. Embedding the target group preserves the number. There is a finite constant $C_M$, depending only on the given smooth manifold $M$, such that
$$|\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi)|\le C_M$$
for all $G$ and $\phi$, including nononto homomorphisms and uncountable targets. For a disconnected compact $M$, use its finitely many components and the sum of these values, equivalently the free-product convention for its based fundamental groups. This is a signature-defect invariant among smooth bounds. No comparison with a nonsmooth TOP bound or an analytic eta definition is asserted.

## Proof

1.1 We first identify the actual classifying-space homology used below. For a group $H$, use a CW $K(H,1)$ model from [F1], with universal cover $E$. The singular complex $C_*(E;\mathbb Z)$ is a free $\mathbb ZH$ complex: deck action is free on singular simplices, since a deck transformation fixing one simplex fixes its first vertex. Choose orbit representatives under [A1]. Its augmented complex is exact by contractibility. Taking deck coinvariants identifies it with singular chains of $BH$: every simplex lifts, and two lifts differ by a unique deck transformation, consistently on faces. Comparing this free resolution of $\mathbb Z$ with the bar resolution gives the same coinvariant homology. Explicitly lift the identity in degree zero and recursively lift each boundary of a free basis vector through the next differential of the exact resolution. This gives augmentation-preserving chain maps in both directions. The same recursion on their difference from the identity supplies chain homotopies. Tensoring with the trivial module retains these actual identities. Therefore $H_*(BH;\mathbb Z)=H_*(H;\mathbb Z)$; in particular $K=BA(H)$ is connected and integrally acyclic. All free-basis lifts are permitted by [A1]. [A1, F1, algebra, construct]

1.2 We need the labelled version of smooth collapse, and give its extension explicitly. For a CW space $K$ set $K_+=K\sqcup\{*\}$. A closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold with a map $f:M\to K$ gives a based map $S^{n+q}\to T_q\wedge K_+$: embed $M$, take the normal tube and its oriented classifying map as in [F2], and on a normal vector over $x$ retain the additional label $f(x)$. Collapse the tube exterior to the basepoint. Here $T_q$ is the Thom space of the universal oriented $q$-plane bundle and sufficiently large $q\ge\max(2,n+1)$ is allowed. Independence of the embedding, tube, normal metric and classifying homotopy follows from the same explicit tube comparisons and stabilization in [F2], with the label retained on each tracked base point of $M$. A smooth bordism carrying a map to $K$ embeds neatly with product boundary collars by [F2]; collapsing its tube and retaining its label gives a based homotopy after a common stabilization. The normal-first convention of [F2] gives negative incoming and positive outgoing boundary orientations. [F2, given, construct]

1.3 Now take connected integrally acyclic $K$. At a finite oriented Grassmannian stage let $T$ be its Thom space, with rank $q\ge2$. It is a finite based CW space with one basepoint zero-cell and all other cells in dimensions at least $q$: trivialize the oriented bundle over each base characteristic disk and collapse its sphere boundary, which shifts that disk's cell dimension by $q$. The ordinary product of a finite CW space with a CW space has the product CW structure. For this topology assertion, product with each compact disk preserves the quotient test for the characteristic-map presentation of $K$ by the ordinary compact-domain exponential law, iterated from the interval. The finite characteristic-disk quotient onto the Hausdorff finite complex $T$ is a closed map with compact fibers; its product with $K$ is still closed by the compact-fiber tube argument, hence quotient. Together these two tests are exactly the product-cell weak topology. The quotient $(T\times K)/(\{*\}\times K)=T\wedge K_+$ is therefore CW with all nonbasepoint cells of dimension at least $q$. Both it and $T$ are simply connected, by cellularly moving each loop into its single-vertex one-skeleton. [F2, F4, construct]

2.1 Maps to these $K(H,1)$ spaces realize group homomorphisms and classify them up to based homotopy on the smooth domains used here. Indeed replace a compact smooth domain by its finite CW model [F5]. Send a maximal tree to the basepoint and the remaining one-cells to loops representing the stipulated generator images. The relator condition extends this map across its two-cells; vanishing $\pi_jK(H,1)$ for $j>1$ extends it across every higher cell. A homotopy between maps with the same based fundamental-group homomorphism is built by the same relative cell induction on the cylinder; its obstruction on each cell lies in the corresponding zero higher homotopy group, with the one-cell case fixed by equality in $\pi_1$. Transport along the actual CW homotopy equivalence gives the map on the smooth domain. The same construction gives maps $Bf$ for group homomorphisms and their compositional compatibility up to specified based homotopies. On a boundary collar these homotopies can be inserted to make the restrictions exactly the specified maps. [A1, F1, F5, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 Conversely let $g:S^{n+q}\to T_q\wedge K_+$ be based. The Thom projection $p_T$, induced by $K_+\to S^0$, is continuous. Its zero preimage is compact and lies in the open set where $g$ has uniquely defined Thom and $K$ coordinates. Its Thom coordinate has compact image in a finite Grassmannian Thom space. On a compact buffer about the zero preimage apply [F2]'s controlled Euclidean smoothing/retraction and arbitrarily small transverse perturbation to that coordinate, keeping the $K$ coordinate unchanged. Cutoffs have support in this product-coordinate open set; on the compact outer buffer the Thom coordinate stays away from zero, so sufficiently small perturbations create no extra zeros. Off the buffer retain $g$. The result is based and has a compact smooth transverse zero preimage $P$ and its continuous retained map to $K$. The identical construction on a homotopy, constant on endpoint collars and protecting the basepoint track, gives a smooth normal bordism of the endpoint preimages with its retained $K$ map. Thus stable homotopies give actual labelled bordisms. [F2, step 1.2, construct]

2.3 Projection $T\times K\to T$ induces an integral homology isomorphism by [F3]: the Kunneth terms from $K$ are only its $H_0=\mathbb Z$, with no Tor contribution. The restriction $\{*\}\times K\to\{*\}$ is also an integral homology isomorphism. Their pair sequences imply an isomorphism on relative homology. The quotient comparison in [F3] thus shows that the actual projection $p:T\wedge K_+\to T$ is an integral reduced homology isomorphism, also an ordinary degree-zero isomorphism since both spaces are connected. To see it is a homotopy equivalence, replace it by its cellular CW mapping cylinder. The simply connected pair has zero relative integral homology by its pair sequence. Its relative degree one is zero by the homotopy pair sequence; if it is $(r-1)$-connected for $r\ge2$, the first relative Hurewicz isomorphism [F4] makes its degree-$r$ homotopy zero. Induction makes all relative homotopy groups zero. The homotopy sequence and Whitehead [F4] give a homotopy equivalence. It is based: its source basepoint is a CW subcomplex, so the inverse and its homotopies can be adjusted along their basepoint tracks, whose loops are null in the simply connected spaces. [F3, F4, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 These assignments are inverse, including surjectivity with the label. Near $P$, write the smooth Thom coordinate as $(b(x,v),a(x,v))$ on a small normal tube. Its normal derivative $A_x$ is invertible. As in [F2], transport the bundle along $b(x,tv)$ by its finite Grassmannian orthogonal projections and linearize $a$ to $A_xv$; a uniform $o(\|v\|)$ bound makes this homotopy zero-free off $P$. Simultaneously replace the continuous label $k(x,v)$ by $k(x,(1-s\chi(v))v)$, where the tube cutoff is one on a smaller tube and zero near its boundary. This homotopy is defined entirely in the product-coordinate region. On that smaller tube its final label is $k(x,0)$. A radial Thom map, homotopic to the identity, expands every radius at least this bound to the collapsed boundary; the resulting map is exactly the normally classified collapse of $P$ with label $k|_P$, up to the metric/tube comparisons in [F2]. Its normal orientation gives the original orientation on a collapsed $M$. Stabilization adds the same positive first normal coordinate as in [F2] and leaves the labels unchanged. Since $p_*$ is injective and $p s=1$, the labelled collapse and the constant-labelled version of its unlabelled collapse represent the same homotopy class already at this finite stage. The homotopy may have labels escaping finite subcomplexes near a basepoint preimage, which is harmless: its Thom projection remains in this same finite $T$, and step 2.2 perturbs only that projection on a compact zero buffer. Thus the equality passes to the same stable collapse group without any global compact-label claim. By step 2.2 this equality is witnessed by an actual compact smooth $(n+1)$-bordism over $K$, between $(M,f)$ and the same oriented $M$ with constant map. With constant coefficients the completed finite matrices are those of ordinary complex chains tensored with the regular Hilbert module, so each positive or negative scalar eigenspace contributes its ordinary multiplicity times the trace of $1$, equal to one. The constant-map $L^2$ signature is therefore the ordinary signature of $Z$. Group-subgroup induction [F6] identifies the original $G$ signature with its $A(G)$ signature, proving the first assertion for arbitrary $G$, without an analytic index theorem. [F1, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 Fix a connected smooth $M^3$, put $\Pi=\pi_1M$, and choose its map $M\to BA(\Pi)$ induced by $\iota_\Pi$. Step 4.1 gives a smooth four-bordism over $BA(\Pi)$ from $M$ to $M$ with constant map. Glue this actual filling with the bordism, respecting its collars and orientation, to obtain one fixed smooth $W_M$ with $\partial W_M=M$ and a map $\psi_M:\pi_1W_M\to A(\Pi)$ restricting to $\iota_\Pi$. Thus the same smooth $W_M$ is a valid bounding extension into $A(G)$ for every $G,\phi$, establishing existence with injective $G\to A(G)$. [F1, F5, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Compare any two smooth bounds $W_1,W_2$ for the same $(M,\phi)$, over target enlargements $j_i:G\hookrightarrow\Gamma_i$. Form $L=\Gamma_1*_G\Gamma_2$; [F7] embeds both targets into $L$. Their maps agree on the based boundary, and the collar gluing and van Kampen property supply the map on the smooth closed four-manifold $Z=W_1\cup_M(-W_2)$. If a boundary restriction was given only up to based homotopy, insert its actual cylinder homotopy first; its two maps then agree literally. Induction in [F6] preserves each signature under its target inclusion. Additivity and orientation reversal give the difference of their defects as $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_L(Z)-\operatorname{sign}(Z)$, zero by step 5.1. ## Statement refuted

Assume full AC. The false statement is: “For every $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$, the Levine–Tristram Hermitian matrix of every knot is nonsingular.” The positive trefoil matrix at a primitive sixth root is singular. At that root the nondegenerate signature calculation does not apply; the defined knot invariant is the one-sided-average value.

## Statement references

[[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature|The form and root-average convention]]

[[ex-knot-kt-07-worked-cases|The positive trefoil matrix and Alexander polynomial]]

[[lem-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-singular-set|Alexander roots are precisely singular parameters]]

[[lem-levine-tristram-one-sided-averages-exist|Existence of the one-sided limits at the root]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the positive trefoil matrix $V_T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and a primitive sixth root $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$.

[A1] Full AC supplies the positive-push Seifert matrix and signature conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature]]

[F1] $V_T$ is the positive-push trefoil matrix and its Alexander polynomial is $1-t+t^2$. [[ex-knot-kt-07-worked-cases]]

[F2] A root of the Alexander polynomial is exactly a singular parameter for $H_\omega$, and the invariant at such a root is the average of one-sided signatures. [[lem-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-singular-set]], [[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature]]

[F3] Each one-sided limit at this root exists as an integer, so the arithmetic mean prescribed by the definition is defined. [[lem-levine-tristram-one-sided-averages-exist]]

## Proof

1.1 Let $c=1-\omega$. Since $\omega+\bar\omega=1$, $|c|^2=(1-\omega)(1-\bar\omega)=2-(\omega+\bar\omega)=1$. Direct substitution gives $H_\omega(V_T)=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-\bar c\\-c&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det H_\omega=1-|c|^2=0$. The matrix is nonzero (its diagonal entries are $-1$), so it is singular. Also $1-\omega+\omega^2=0$, confirming this is an Alexander root. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The zero determinant refutes the universal nonsingularity statement. By [F2], this root is precisely where the definition uses the arithmetic mean of the two one-sided signature limits; [F3] guarantees that this average is defined. No signature formula requiring an invertible $H_\omega$ may be used at the root itself. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the maximal-abelian-cover convention. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link, with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L$ formed by deleting the interiors of pairwise-disjoint chosen closed normal-disk tubes, and basepoint $b\in E_L$. For a knot, $r=1$ and $E_L=E_K$. The full meridian abelianization group is $H_L=H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$, with the positive normal-disk meridians as its ordered basis. Choose a finite-rank free abelian group $H$ of positive rank and an epimorphism $\chi:H_L\to H$; write $\psi=\chi\circ\mathrm{ab}:G\to H$ for the induced map from $G=\pi_1(E_L,b)$. The identity choice $H=H_L$ is the full multivariable deck map; a coloring may identify its variables only through the explicitly stated map $\chi$. Let $\mathbb F$ be a field, let $d\ge1$, and let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$, the commutative Laurent-polynomial ring with monomial basis $H$, and $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$. On row vectors define the right $\mathbb F[G]$ action by $v\cdot g=v\rho(g)\psi(g)$, where $\psi(g)$ is central multiplication by its monomial in $\Lambda$. For a chosen finite based CW structure $X$ on $E_L$, orient and order its cells and choose one lift of each cell to the universal cover $\widetilde X$. The twisted cellular complex is

$$C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)=\Lambda^d\otimes_{\mathbb F[G]}C_*(\widetilde X;\mathbb F),$$

and its fraction-field complex is $C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;Q^d)=Q\otimes_{\Lambda}C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d)$. The lifted cell bases and the standard coordinate basis of $\mathbb F^d$ give the based $Q$-vector-space bases. If this fraction-field complex is not acyclic, define its twisted torsion to be $0$. If it is acyclic, choose in each degree a basis $\mathbf b_i$ of $B_i=\operatorname{im}\partial_{i+1}$ and lifts $\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}$ of $\mathbf b_{i-1}$ under $\partial_i$; with $\mathbf c_i$ the based cellular basis, set

$$\tau(C_*,\mathbf c)=\prod_i[\mathbf b_i,\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}/\mathbf c_i]^{(-1)^{i+1}}\in Q^\times,$$

where brackets denote the determinant of the change-of-basis matrix. The twisted Reidemeister torsion is this value modulo the subgroup $\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}=\{\pm\det(\rho(g))\psi(g)^d:g\in G\}\subset Q^\times$. This exact determinant image is contained in the commonly used coarser unit subgroup $\{\pm a h:a\in\det(\rho(G)),\ h\in H\}$. The choice-free statement uses the full abelianization chain model first and specializes it only by the declared coefficient map $\chi$.

    - title: "Jozef H. Przytycki and Akira Yasuhara, Linking Numbers in Rational Homology 3-Spheres, Cyclic Branched Covers and Infinite Cyclic Covers"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0111203v1"

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ bound a connected compact oriented Seifert surface $F$ of genus $g$. Choose a disk-band decomposition of $F$ with one disk and $2g$ bands, and use its band-core basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ to form the positive-push Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. For $q\ge2$, define the symmetric block matrix $M_q(V)$ of size $2g(q-1)$ by specifying its $2g\times2g$ blocks, indexed by $1\le k,\ell\le q-1$:
$$(M_q(V))_{k\ell}=\begin{cases}V+V^T,&k=\ell,\\-V^T,&\ell=k+1,\\-V,&k=\ell+1,\\0,&|k-\ell|\ge2.\end{cases}$$
Push the interior of $F$ into $B^4$ while keeping $K$ on $S^3=\partial B^4$, cut $B^4$ along a thickened copy of the pushed-in surface, and take $q$ copies. For $i=1,\ldots,q-1$, glue the positive face of copy $i$ to the negative face of copy $i+1$ by reflecting the normal coordinate; do not glue the last positive face to the first negative face. Call the resulting $q$-fold cyclic branched cover $W_q(F)$. It has one $0$-handle and $2g(q-1)$ $2$-handles, and its framed attaching link has linking matrix $M_q(V)$. The boundary branched cover, with the boundary marking induced by the covering map, is $\Sigma_q(K)$.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface|Connected compact oriented spanning surfaces and the genus convention]]

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix convention]]

[[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups|The disk-band handle form for a compact surface with one boundary component]]

[[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot|The exterior cover and meridional filling defining $\Sigma_q(K)$]]

[Akbulut–Kirby, “Branched Covers of Surfaces in 4-Manifolds,” §2](https://math.berkeley.edu/~kirby/papers/Akbulut%20and%20Kirby%20-%20Branched%20covers%20of%20surfaces%20in%204-manifolds%20-%20MR0593626.pdf)

[Przytycki–Yasuhara, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0111203v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the oriented knot $K$, a connected compact oriented Seifert surface $F$, its disk-band decomposition, the ordered band-core basis, and $q\ge2$.

[A1] Full AC implies the countable-choice hypothesis of the finite surface normal-form supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] A Seifert surface is connected, compact, smooth, oriented, and embedded with oriented boundary $K$; its genus is the integer $g$ with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. [[def-oriented-seifert-surface]]

[F2] Under countable choice, a connected compact surface with one boundary component has a disk-band handle form with $2g$ bands and a standard integral homology basis given by the band cores. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F3] The positive-push Seifert matrix has entries $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, with the positive normal determined by the surface and ambient orientations. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]

[F4] The $q$-fold branched cover of $S^3$ is formed from the meridian-mod-$q$ cover of the compact exterior by filling the lift of $\mu^q$. [[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot]]

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, the oriented knot $K$, the connected compact oriented Seifert surface $F$, its disk-band decomposition and band-core basis, the positive-push matrix $V$, and $q\ge2$.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], cut $B^4$ along the thickening of the pushed-in disk-band surface, producing cut copies $B_1^4,\ldots,B_q^4$. First glue these copies only along the disk $0$-handle of the branch surface. A disk thickening is a $3$-ball in the boundary of each cut $4$-ball; joining the two face balls for consecutive copies is the standard boundary-connected-sum operation, so the resulting $4$-manifold is again a $4$-ball with one $0$-handle. For each surface band, the positive face of copy $k$ glued to the negative face of copy $k+1$ joins the two band-core arcs; its regular neighborhood is a $2$-handle $D^2\times D^2$ attached along $S^1\times D^2$. There are $q-1$ such seams and $2g$ bands, so the construction gives $2g(q-1)$ $2$-handles and no other handles. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 For band $a_i$ and seam $k$, the attaching circle $C_{i,k}$ is obtained by joining its oriented core arc in the positive face of copy $k$ to the core arc in the negative face of copy $k+1$, with endpoints joined through the common disk $0$-handle. In the collar of $F$, closing either face arc through that disk gives the corresponding positive or negative push-off of the closed core cycle $a_i$. Simultaneously moving $a_i^-$ and $a_j$ through the product collar to $a_i$ and $a_j^+$ preserves linking, so symmetry of linking and [F3] give $\operatorname{lk}(a_i^-,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_j^+,a_i)=V_{ji}$. For two handles at the same seam, the positive-face and negative-face contributions are therefore $V_{ij}$ and $V_{ji}$, giving $V_{ij}+V_{ji}$; for the self-entry this is framing $2V_{ii}$. For handles at consecutive seams, only their common sheet contributes, and the reflection reverses one normal direction, giving $-\operatorname{lk}(a_j^+,a_i)=-V_{ji}$ in the upper block; symmetry gives $-V_{ij}$ in the lower block. If the seams are separated by at least one unused seam, the attaching circles lie in disjoint sheet neighborhoods, so their linking is zero. These cases exhaust all pairs and give exactly $M_q(V)$. [F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 In a normal disk to the branch surface, the $q$ cut sheets form the standard cyclic degree-$q$ branched disk; its map is $w\mapsto w^q$. Away from the branch locus, a positive meridian moves through the $q$ sheets cyclically, so the boundary exterior cover is the connected cover classified by the homomorphism $\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z/q$ sending $\mu$ to $1$. Its meridian boundary is the closed lift of $\mu^q$, which bounds the filling disk. By [F4] and uniqueness of the classified connected cover, the boundary with its branch marking is $\Sigma_q(K)$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

4.1 For $q=2$ there is one seam, so the block matrix has only its diagonal block $V+V^T$, as stated. [step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The boxes represent the $q$ copies of the cut $4$-ball; each arrow represents the $2g$ handles attached at one seam. The upper and lower matrix blocks record the opposite normal directions across that seam. The display sketches $q\ge4$; when $q=2$ there is one arrow. The proof computes the framed-link entries directly and does not rely on the schematic.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$. For $t>0$ set $E_t^+=\{x:u(x)>t\}$, and for $t<0$ set $E_t^-=\{x:u(x)<t\}$. Each set has finite area, almost every applicable level set has finite perimeter, and
$$TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The L² distributional-TV functional is the compactly supported test-field supremum.]]

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|Finite perimeter is the TV of the level-set indicator.]]

[Iglesias, Mercier, and Scherzer, *A note on convergence of solutions of total variation regularized linear inverse problems*, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06495)

[Terra, *Introduction to Geometric Measure Theory*, §5.3](https://www.ime.usp.br/~glaucio/mat6704/textos/GMTLecureNotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed for the BV coarea and test-field representation suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-cutoff-approximation]]: there are compactly supported $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1$ with $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ and $\limsup_RTV(v_R)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-bv-coarea-formula]]: for a globally integrable BV function, the positive superlevel and negative sublevel perimeters integrate to its total variation.

[F3] [[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]]: for an $L^1$ function, the extended test-field variation is lower semicontinuous in $L^1$; if finite, it equals the perimeter/TV defined by the distributional derivative.

[F4] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and [[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]: nonnegative level integrals may be interchanged, and absolutely integrable level/spatial functions satisfy Fubini.

[F5] [[thm-fatou-lemma]] and [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: Fatou bounds the limiting perimeter integrals, and increasing truncations of nonnegative level integrals converge to the full integral.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], choose compactly supported $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1$ with $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ and $\limsup_RTV(v_R)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$. For each fixed $t\ne0$, $\chi_{E_{R,t}}\to\chi_{E_t}$ in $L^1$: the symmetric difference is outside $B(0,R)$ for the cutoffs constructed in [F1] and contained in $\{|u|>|t|\}$, whose tail measure is at most $|t|^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus B(0,R)}|u|^2$. Here $E_{R,t}$ and $E_t$ are the corresponding signed superlevel or sublevel sets. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 For $t>0$, $|E_t^+|\le t^{-2}\|u\|_2^2$, and for $t<0$, $|E_t^-|\le |t|^{-2}\|u\|_2^2$. The indicator-valued maps are Borel on each half-line: on positive levels they are right-continuous in $L^1$ when $t_j\downarrow t>0$, by continuity from below of measure; on negative levels they are left-continuous when $t_j\uparrow t<0$. Composing with the lower semicontinuous extended variation in [F3] makes their perimeter functions measurable. Lower semicontinuity in [F3] and step 1.1 give $P(E_t^\pm;\mathbb R^2)\le\liminf_{R\to\infty}P(E_{R,t}^\pm;\mathbb R^2)$ for every applicable nonzero $t$. Fatou's lemma [F5], the BV coarea identity [F2], and the variation bound in step 1.1 imply, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\int_\varepsilon^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^{-\varepsilon}P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using monotone convergence [F5] proves that the full perimeter sum is at most $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$; its finiteness and [F3] give finite perimeter for almost every applicable level. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)$ with $\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1$. The signed layer-cake identity is $u(x)=\int_0^\infty\chi_{E_t^+}(x)\,dt-\int_{-\infty}^0\chi_{E_t^-}(x)\,dt$. On the compact support of $\operatorname{div}\varphi$, $\int |u|\,|\operatorname{div}\varphi|<\infty$, so Tonelli and Fubini [F4] permit integration of this identity against $\operatorname{div}\varphi$. At almost every level the absolute value of the resulting indicator test integral is at most its perimeter by [F3]. Therefore $\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is at most the perimeter sum in step 2.1. Taking the supremum over admissible $\varphi$ gives $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$ at most that sum, which together with step 2.1 proves equality. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $A$ be an indeterminate, $q_K=A^2$, $q_L=A^{-2}$, and $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. Use the fundamental module, positive crossing, duality maps, and twist fixed in the preceding definition. For every $n\ge1$ and $\beta\in B_n$, let $t_n(\beta)$ be the categorical ribbon trace of its blackboard-framed closure and let $w(\beta)$ be its exponent sum. With $t=A^{-4}$ and $z_0=-1/(t+1)$, the exact identities are
$$t_n(\beta)=\delta\langle\widehat\beta\rangle=\delta^n(-A)^{w(\beta)}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\big|_{v=t,\ z=z_0},$$
$$(-A^3)^{-w(\beta)}t_n(\beta)=\delta(-A^3)^{-w(\beta)}\langle\widehat\beta\rangle.$$
Here $\operatorname{tr}_n$ is the normalized type-A Hecke Markov trace with braid generator sent to $T_i$, and $\langle\widehat\beta\rangle$ is the Kauffman bracket in the fixed crossing chart. The second identity is a value-by-value normalization formula; it does not by itself assert a Jones-polynomial specialization.

## Statement references

[[def-quantum-sl2-fundamental-ribbon-module|Fundamental module matrices, duality, and twist]]

[[def-ribbon-evaluation-of-an-x-colored-closed-braid|Categorical braid-closure trace]]

[[thm-a-ribbon-object-defines-a-unique-framed-tangle-evaluation-functor|Framed tangle evaluator and generator assignments]]

[[lem-ribbon-trace-equals-the-framed-closure-evaluation|Ribbon trace as framed-closure evaluation]]

[[def-countable-choice|Axiom of Countable Choice]]

[[lem-hecke-bracket-trace-dictionary-and-local-descent|Hecke–bracket trace dictionary]]

[[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value|Kauffman bracket chart and state sum]]

[[def-exponent-sum-of-a-braid|Braid exponent sum]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $A$ is indeterminate, $n\ge1$, $\beta\in B_n$, and the fundamental ribbon module with its stated basis, braiding, and duality maps.

[F1] The fundamental module has the displayed positive braiding matrix $c_{V,V}$ and scalar twist $-A^3\operatorname{id}_V$ ([[def-quantum-sl2-fundamental-ribbon-module]]).

[F2] Its self-dual evaluation and coevaluation are the maps $B,U$ whose closed-loop value is $\delta$ ([[def-quantum-sl2-fundamental-ribbon-module]]).

[F3] The ribbon evaluation of the $V$-colored closed braid is the left categorical trace $t_n(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(j_{V^{\otimes n}}\rho_n(\beta))$ ([[def-ribbon-evaluation-of-an-x-colored-closed-braid]]).

[F4] The Kauffman bracket chart has the over-strand from southwest to northeast, its A-smoothing joins left endpoints, its B-smoothing joins top endpoints, and the loop value is $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F5] The positive Artin half twist has label $i$ pass below the midpoint and label $i+1$ pass above, and its over/under projected tangents are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$ in the stated projection coordinates ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F6] The Hecke–bracket trace dictionary states $\langle\widehat\beta\rangle=\delta^{n-1}(-A)^{e(\beta)}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))|_{v=t,z=z_0}$ for $q=A^{-2}$, $t=A^{-4}$, and $z_0=-1/(t+1)$ ([[lem-hecke-bracket-trace-dictionary-and-local-descent]]).

[F7] The braid exponent sum is a homomorphism with $w(\sigma_i^{\pm1})=\pm1$ ([[def-exponent-sum-of-a-braid]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, selects an element from every countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F8] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the framed tangle evaluator is monoidal, sends crossings to braidings and cups and caps to the chosen duality maps, and assigns equal values to framed-isotopic tangles ([[thm-a-ribbon-object-defines-a-unique-framed-tangle-evaluation-functor]]).

[F9] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the categorical ribbon trace $t_n(\beta)$ equals the framed tangle evaluation of the blackboard-framed closure ([[lem-ribbon-trace-equals-the-framed-closure-evaluation]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data in the Statement and [A1], [F1]–[F9].

1.1 In the ordered basis of [F1], direct subtraction gives $e:=A(c_{V,V}-AI)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\0&-A^2&1&0\\0&1&-A^{-2}&0\\0&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Writing $U(1)=-A^2v_+\otimes v_-+v_-\otimes v_+$ and $B(v_+\otimes v_-)=1$, $B(v_-\otimes v_+)=-A^{-2}$ shows entrywise that $e=UB$. Hence $B(U(1))=-A^2-A^{-2}=\delta$ and $e^2=\delta e$. The explicit snake equalities in [F2] give the adjacent tensor relations: $e_{12}e_{23}e_{12}=UB\otimes1$ because the middle composites $(1\otimes B)(U\otimes1)$ and then $(B\otimes1)(1\otimes U)$ are identities; the reversed calculation gives $e_{23}e_{12}e_{23}=e_{23}$. Distant placements commute because they act on disjoint tensor factors. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Use source coordinates $(u,v)$ with their standard positive orientation and positive projection coordinates $(t,x)$ on the braid box. For $h>0$, the map $(t,x)=(v,-2hu)$ has determinant $2h>0$. It sends the source over direction $(1,1)$ to $(1,-2h)$ and the source under direction $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is $4h>0$. The source left/right pairs have constant $u$, hence constant braid position $x$ and give the through pairing $I$; the source top/bottom pairs have constant $v$, hence constant braid time $t$ and give the cup-cap $e_i$. The displayed page coordinates $(x,t)$ reverse the positive projection orientation; their visual quarter-turn is not the orientation comparison. Thus the A/B crossing expansion is $C_i=AI+A^{-1}e_i$. Its inverse is $C_i^{-1}=A^{-1}I+Ae_i$, since their product is $I+(A^2+A^{-2}+\delta)e_i=I$. By [A1] and [F8]–[F9], the categorical ribbon trace is the framed tangle evaluation of this braid closure, and that evaluator is monoidal with the stated crossing and duality maps. Expanding a braid word into the two smoothing choices therefore gives the bracket weights in [F4]. Because the closure has $n\ge1$ strands, each complete smoothing is a nonempty closed 1-manifold, hence a union of at least one circle. Its categorical value is $\delta^{|S|}$ by monoidality in [F8] and the loop value [F2], whereas the bracket state sum uses $\delta^{|S|-1}$; the extra single factor is independent of the state. Thus $t_n(\beta)=\delta\langle\widehat\beta\rangle$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F8, F9, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The matrix trace $t_n$ in [F3] closes the tensor-word braid with the duality maps $B,U$ of [F2]. Substituting each crossing into the trace expansion from step 2.1 therefore gives the first identity in the Statement. The Hecke formula [F6] then yields $t_n(\beta)=\delta^n(-A)^{e(\beta)}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\big|_{v=t,z=z_0}$. By [F7], $e(\beta)=w(\beta)$. The twist in [F1] is $\lambda=-A^3$, so multiplying $t_n=\delta\langle\widehat\beta\rangle$ by $\lambda^{-w(\beta)}$ gives the second displayed identity. The only choice assumption is [A1], used in step 2.1 to invoke the published trace-to-closure identification; no stronger choice principle or division by $\delta$ is used. Since $A$ is indeterminate, the specialization is taken in the rational-function field where $t+1\ne0$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let $X$ be a certified based deficiency-one exterior spine with one $0$-cell, $n\ge2$ $1$-cells and $n-1$ $2$-cells, let $\psi:\pi_1(X)\twoheadrightarrow H\cong\mathbb Z^m$ have $m\ge1$, let $\rho:\pi_1(X)\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$, and let $H_1(C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\mathbb F[H]^d))$ be torsion over $\mathbb F[H]$. Form the Fox block matrix $J$ and a chosen Wada column quotient $W_j=\det(J_{\widehat j})/D_j$ with $D_j=\det(\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d)\ne0$. Then the fraction-field complex is acyclic, $\det(J_{\widehat j})\ne0$, and $W_j$ equals its based twisted Reidemeister torsion in $Q^\times/\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}$. Every admissible deleted column gives the same class. This conclusion applies only to the specified cellular spine; an abstract presentation of the same group is insufficient.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-wada-quotient-for-deficiency-one-presentation|Wada quotient and denominator]]

[[lem-twisted-fox-jacobian-is-cellular-boundary|Fox Jacobian as the cellular differential]]

[[lem-twisted-acyclicity-from-torsion-module|Localized acyclicity]]

[[lem-twisted-torsion-cell-basis-change-ambiguity|Torsion unit ambiguity]]

[Kirk and Livingston, Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.2](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Livingston_papers/1999_Twisted%20Alexander%20invariants%2C%20Reidemeister%20torsion%2C%20and%20Casson-Gordon%20invariants.pdf)

[Conway, §§2.3–2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.06678)

[Ranicki, Theorem 15](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/torsion.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the certified based deficiency-one exterior spine; a positive-rank free abelian deck epimorphism; a field-valued representation; torsion degree-one homology over the Laurent ring; and an index $j$ with $D_j\ne0$.

[A1] AC is inherited from the maximal-abelian-cover convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $J$ has blocks $\Phi(\partial r_i/\partial x_k)$, $D_j=\det(\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d)$, and $W_j=\det(J_{\widehat j})/D_j$ only for $D_j\ne0$. [[def-knot-wada-quotient-for-deficiency-one-presentation]]

[F2] With row coefficient vectors, $\partial_1$ sends $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ to $\sum_k y_kA_k$ for $A_k=\rho(x_k)\psi(x_k)-I_d$, and $\partial_2$ acts on the right by the Fox block matrix $J$. [[lem-twisted-fox-jacobian-is-cellular-boundary]]

[F3] Under the positive-rank deck and cell-count hypotheses, torsion $H_1$ implies the fraction-field complex is acyclic. [[lem-twisted-acyclicity-from-torsion-module]]

[F4] Changing cell lifts, orientations or certified simple-spine structure changes the torsion only by $\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}$. [[lem-twisted-torsion-cell-basis-change-ambiguity]]

[F5] For an acyclic based complex, torsion is the alternating product of determinants of boundary bases and their lifts in the chosen cellular bases. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

## Proof



1.1 By [A1] and [F3], the fraction-field complex $0\to Q^{(n-1)d}\xrightarrow{\partial_2}Q^{nd}\xrightarrow{\partial_1}Q^d\to0$ is acyclic. Therefore $\partial_2$ is injective and its image is $\ker\partial_1$, both of dimension $(n-1)d$. [A1, given, F3]

2.1 In the ordered $1$-cell basis, [F2] gives the stacked $d_1$ blocks $A_1,\ldots,A_n$; a row vector $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ lies in its kernel exactly when $\sum_k y_kA_k=0$. Since $A_j$ is invertible, projection $p_{\widehat j}:\ker d_1\to Q^{(n-1)d}$ onto all non-$j$ blocks is an isomorphism: for arbitrary non-$j$ row coordinates $y_k$, the unique missing coordinate is $y_j=-\left(\sum_{k\ne j}y_kA_k\right)A_j^{-1}$. Thus $p_{\widehat j}\partial_2$ is an isomorphism, and its row-coefficient matrix is $J_{\widehat j}$ by [F2]. In particular $\det(J_{\widehat j})\ne0$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\mathbf c_0,\mathbf c_1,\mathbf c_2$ be the standard cellular bases. In degree zero choose $\mathbf b_0=\mathbf c_0$. In degree one choose $\mathbf b_1=\partial_2\mathbf c_2$, and lift $\mathbf b_0$ to degree one using the $j$-block $A_j^{-1}$ and zero in the other blocks. After moving the $j$-block to the final position, the matrix of $[\mathbf b_1,\widetilde{\mathbf b}_0]$ in $\mathbf c_1$ is block triangular with diagonal blocks $J_{\widehat j}$ and $A_j^{-1}$; its determinant is $\pm\det(J_{\widehat j})/D_j$. The degree-zero and degree-two torsion brackets equal $1$, so [F5] gives $\tau=\pm W_j$. The sign lies in $\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}$ by [F4], proving the equality of classes. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The same construction applies to every index $k$ with $D_k\ne0$. Each quotient class equals the single torsion class of the same based complex by step 3.1; hence all admissible columns give the same class in $Q^\times/\mathcal U_{\rho,\psi}$. [F1, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

For the separated-mixture question reproduced below, there are admissible fixed one-dimensional parameters with $L=2$, fixed positive score-error allowance $\varepsilon_s$, and every fixed integer $J\ge2$, for which the supremum of the displayed expected fidelity loss over the original finite-valued Borel score class is $+\infty$, for every finite $M\ge1$. Each individual field in the construction has a finite-first-moment Euler chain and obeys the required score bound at every time. Thus the original ideal-marginal $L^2$ hypothesis supplies no finite uniform bound for the requested loss, however large the fixed budget $JM$ is. The original question is retained verbatim under Original question.

## Example references

[Burns and Fridovich-Keil, full 2026 paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.30330v1)

[Daras et al., full diffusion inverse-problems survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.00083v1)

[Blechschmidt et al., full 2026 flow-matching paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.02377v1)

[Prince, Chapter 18 full diffusion notes](https://csci4052u.science.ontariotechu.ca/generative_models/chapter_18_diffusion_models/notes.html)

## Original question

Fix dimension $d\ge1$, component count $L\ge2$, noise scale $\sigma>0$, diffusion horizon $T>0$, and a continuous schedule $\beta:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$. Assume the parameter choices below admit at least one component configuration and mixture weight vector. Consider a posterior density on $\mathbb R^d$ of the form
$$\pi(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L w_\ell\,\mathcal N(x;\mu_\ell,\Sigma_\ell),\qquad \sum_{\ell=1}^Lw_\ell=1,\quad w_\ell\ge w_{\min}>0,$$
Here $\mathcal N(\cdot;\mu_\ell,\Sigma_\ell)$ denotes the normal density with mean $\mu_\ell$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma_\ell$. The component means satisfy $\|\mu_\ell\|_2\le M_0$ and $\|\mu_\ell-\mu_r\|_2\ge\Delta>0$ for $\ell\ne r$, and every eigenvalue of each positive-definite $\Sigma_\ell$ lies in $[v_{\min},v_{\max}]$ for fixed $0<v_{\min}\le v_{\max}<\infty$. Assume $0<w_{\min}\le1/L$ and $\Delta\ge8\sqrt{d v_{\max}}$. For $t\in[0,T]$, let $p_t$ be the density of $X_t$ under
$$dX_t=-\tfrac12\beta(t)X_t\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t,\qquad X_0\sim\pi,$$
where $W_t$ is a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion, and let $s_t=\nabla\log p_t$ be its exact score. Let $\widehat s_t$ be a supplied jointly Borel, finite-valued score field satisfying the integrated error bound
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\|\widehat s_t(x)-s_t(x)\|_2^2p_t(x)\,dx\le\varepsilon_s^2.$$
Consider fields whose Euler chain has finite first moment. For $h=T/J$, use the reverse-time Euler convention $Z_0\sim p_T$ and
$$Z_{k+1}=Z_k+h\left[\tfrac12\beta(T-kh)Z_k+\beta(T-kh)\widehat s_{T-kh}(Z_k)\right]+\sqrt{h\beta(T-kh)}\,\zeta_k,\qquad k=0,\ldots,J-1,$$
with $\zeta_k\sim N(0,I_d)$ independent of $Z_0$ and of one another. Generate $M\ge1$ independent terminal values $X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(M)}$ and let $\widehat\pi_{J,M}=M^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^M\delta_{X^{(i)}}$; one score evaluation per reverse step gives online budget $B=JM$. Define disjoint mode regions $R_\ell=\{x:\|x-\mu_\ell\|_2<\Delta/4\}$, target masses $q_\ell=\pi(R_\ell)$, and empirical masses $\widehat q_\ell=\widehat\pi_{J,M}(R_\ell)$. For probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$, let $W_1$ be the infimum of $E\|X-Y\|_2$ over all couplings with the specified marginals. Determine whether the integrated score-error assumption alone yields finite minimax-sharp nonasymptotic upper and lower bounds, uniformly over the stated score-field class, for
$$E\,W_1(\widehat\pi_{J,M},\pi)+\Delta\sum_{\ell=1}^L E|\widehat q_\ell-q_\ell|+\Delta\,P\{\min_{1\le\ell\le L}\widehat q_\ell=0\}$$
as a function of $d,L,w_{\min},\Delta,v_{\min},v_{\max},M_0,T,\beta,\varepsilon_s,J,M$. In particular, characterize the compute regimes $B=JM$ that guarantee simultaneous control of distributional error and missed-mode probability uniformly over this family. This asks about score-based reverse diffusion with finite computation; it does not assume that the posterior is unimodal or that a good posterior mean certifies its mode weights.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Choose $d=1$, $\pi=(N(-a,v)+N(a,v))/2$ with $a,v>0$ and $2a\ge8\sqrt v$. Choose $L=2$, $w_{\min}=1/2$, $M_0=a$, $\Delta=2a$, $v_{\min}=v_{\max}=v$, $T>0$, $\beta=1$, $\varepsilon_s>0$, $J\ge2$ and $h=T/J$. The extraneous positive parameter called $\sigma$ in the original formulation may be arbitrary; it is not used by its displayed sampler.

[A1] The integrating factor $e^{t/2}$ in the scalar forward equation gives $X_t=e^{-t/2}X_0+e^{-t/2}\int_0^t e^{u/2}\,dW_u$. The stochastic integral is the mean-square limit of deterministic dyadic sums of independent Gaussian increments; these sums are centered Gaussian, with variances tending to $\int_0^te^u\,du=e^t-1$, and are independent of $X_0$. The limit is therefore Gaussian with that variance and independent of $X_0$, as follows by taking limits of its Gaussian characteristic functions. At time $t$, the noised target is the symmetric Gaussian mixture with means $\pm e^{-t/2}a$ and common variance $v_t=e^{-t}v+1-e^{-t}>0$. Its exact score is a posterior-weighted average of $-(x-e^{-t/2}a)/v_t$ and $-(x+e^{-t/2}a)/v_t$, so $|s_t(x)|\le(|x|+a)/\min\{v,1\}$ and is continuous. These formulas follow directly by differentiating the sum of the two Gaussian densities.

[A2] A convolution with a nondegenerate Gaussian has a strictly positive continuous density: continuity follows from the bounded Gaussian derivative, and positivity from its positive kernel. Gaussian densities have finite first moments and exponentially decaying tails.

## Verification

**Given:** The fixed parameters and Gaussian identities in [A1]–[A2].

1.1 Use the exact score at all grid times before the last two updates. All those states have finite first moment because each exact-score drift has linear growth by [A1]. Let $U$ be the state before the penultimate update, corresponding to ideal time $2h$. Its law has a strictly positive continuous density $\rho$: for $J=2$ it is exactly $p_T$, and otherwise the last preceding nondegenerate Euler noise gives [A2]. Since $p_{2h}$ is also positive and continuous, the density ratio $\rho/p_{2h}$ has positive minimum $c$ and finite maximum $C$ on $[-1,1]$. [A1, A2, construct]

2.1 For every sufficiently small $q>0$, choose the centered interval $A_q\subseteq[-1,1]$ with $\int_{A_q}p_{2h}(x)\,dx=q$. Such an interval exists by continuity and positivity of that density. Then $cq\le P\{U\in A_q\}\le Cq$. Put $b_q=\varepsilon_s/(2\sqrt q)$ and add $b_q\mathbf1_{A_q}$ to the score at time $2h$. Its squared ideal-marginal error is exactly $\varepsilon_s^2/4$. Set $f(x)=(1+h/2)x+hs_{2h}(x)$ and $H=\sup_{|x|\le1}|f(x)|<\infty$. After this update the state is $V=f(U)+hb_q\mathbf1_{A_q}(U)+\sqrt h\,G$. [A1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Let $I_q=[hb_q-H-\sqrt h,hb_q+H+\sqrt h]$, and let $r_q=\int_{I_q}p_h(x)\,dx>0$. On $\{U\in A_q,|G|\le1\}$ the state $V$ lies in $I_q$, so $P\{V\in I_q\}\ge cqP\{|G|\le1\}$. The ideal density $p_h$ is a fixed Gaussian mixture. Since the interval width is constant and its center $hb_q$ tends to infinity, its Gaussian density formula gives constants $C_1,c_1>0$, independent of small $q$, such that $r_q\le C_1e^{-c_1b_q^2}$. For example, once $hb_q\ge2(H+\sqrt h+a)$, every point of the interval is at distance at least $hb_q/2$ from either component mean; use the largest fixed variance in its Gaussian exponent and the constant interval length. [A1, A2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At the final evaluation time $h$ add $d_q\mathbf1_{I_q}$ to the exact score, where $d_q=\varepsilon_s/(2\sqrt{r_q})$. This second squared ideal-marginal error is also $\varepsilon_s^2/4$. At all other times use the exact score. These modifications at two distinct times define a jointly Borel finite-valued field with the original supremum-in-time score bound. Every individual field has finite first moments at all Euler steps: it is an affine-growth exact score plus two bounded, finite-amplitude additions. [A1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The first moment of $V$ is bounded uniformly as $q\downarrow0$: the added term has expectation at most $hb_qCq= hC\varepsilon_s\sqrt q/2$, while $E|f(U)|$ and $E|\sqrt hG|$ are fixed and finite. The terminal state is $X=(1+h/2)V+hs_h(V)+hd_q\mathbf1_{I_q}(V)+\sqrt hG'$. By [A1] the absolute expectation of the first two terms is uniformly bounded; $EG'=0$. Therefore $EX\ge h\varepsilon_scqP\{|G|\le1\}/(2\sqrt{r_q})-C_2\to+\infty$, because $b_q^2=\varepsilon_s^2/(4q)$ and the exponential bound in step 3.1 dominates every power of $q$. [A1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Every coupling of two finite-first-moment probabilities satisfies $|EX-EY|\le E|X-Y|$ by the integral triangle inequality. Thus $W_1(\widehat\pi_{J,M},\pi)\ge|M^{-1}\sum_iX^{(i)}|$ because the target mean is zero. Taking expectations gives $EW_1\ge|EX|$, which tends to infinity by step 5.1 for every finite $M$. The other two terms in the requested fidelity loss are nonnegative. Its supremum is consequently infinite despite fixed positive score-error allowance and fixed admissible target parameters. [given, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Scope of the resolution

The negative answer concerns every positive error allowance and every finite J>=2. It does not assert the same obstruction at J=1 or at exactly zero error. The mechanism is mismatch between ideal marginal mass and actual chain mass, not merely missing a mode by iid sampling. No numerical observation or source-specific failure experiment is used as the proof.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be a solid torus. Every connected, two-sided, properly embedded incompressible and boundary-incompressible surface $F\subset V$ with nonempty boundary is a disk, either a meridian disk or a boundary-parallel disk. In particular, if $F$ is not boundary-parallel, it is a meridian disk. Any two smooth meridian disks with the same boundary admit a smooth isotopy of embeddings relative to that boundary, with a boundary-fixing topological ambient extension. If both disks are neat, this can be a smooth ambient isotopy relative to the boundary. In addition, every two-sided embedded torus $T\subset\operatorname{int}V$ has a compressing disk in $V$.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Example preceding Lemma 1.10](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Walter Neumann and Gadde Swarup, *Canonical decompositions of 3-manifolds*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9712227)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the standard smooth solid torus $V$, the connected two-sided proper surface $F$ with nonempty boundary and the two disk-obstruction hypotheses; and, for the last assertion, an embedded two-sided torus $T$ in its interior.

[A1] Full AC is [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and implies countable choice ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], Statement; [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The disk obstructions and product definition of boundary-parallelity are [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]], Definition.

[F2] Every smooth sphere in $S^3$ bounds smooth balls on both sides ([[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]], Statement).

[F3] A smooth sphere boundary map extends over parametrized balls, as a product in their smaller boundary collars ([[lem-smooth-sphere-diffeomorphisms-extend-over-balls]], Statement). Smooth disk boundary maps extend retaining prescribed collars ([[lem-smooth-jordan-disk-boundary-maps-extend-to-diffeomorphisms]], Statement).

[F4] Essential torus circles in the same primitive class admit smooth finite bigon reductions and parallel-strip parameters ([[lem-relative-smooth-mapping-classes-of-annulus-and-torus]], Proof 1.1–2.1). Disk pushes across a ball have a smooth cap sweep with fixed boundary circle, explicitly parametrized in [[lem-gluing-irreducible-smooth-three-manifolds-across-injective-annuli]], Proof 3.1.

[F5] Finite relative general position and smooth ambient extension are [[lem-relative-transversality-for-embedded-surfaces]] and [[thm-isotopy-extension]], Statements.

[F6] For a compact two-sided neat surface in a compact orientable smooth three-manifold, geometric incompressibility is equivalent to injectivity on fundamental groups ([[thm-smooth-loop-theorem-and-incompressibility-criterion-in-orientable-three-manifolds]], Statement).

[F9] Boundary-fixed smooth embedding neatification, its explicit topological ambient extension and the smooth disk-obstruction transport retain both classification hypotheses. A neat input admits a smooth ambient extension; a broad input has only the stated topological ambient extension at its original tangencies. [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]] [[lem-angular-boundary-neatification-preserves-smooth-disk-obstructions]]

[F10] Full AC gives a finite PL triangulation of every compact TOP cut piece, with its entire boundary triangulated. The finite PL Loop theorem applies to a connected boundary component with nontrivial inclusion kernel; transporting its proper disk through that triangulation gives a TOP disk in the original piece. [[thm-compact-topological-three-manifolds-admit-finite-pl-triangulations]] [[thm-loop-theorem-for-finitely-triangulated-orientable-pl-three-manifolds]]

[F11] Connected-overlap van Kampen and amalgam normal form embed an injected common torus group. For a connected cut piece with two faces, the same collar van Kampen calculation gives the HNN presentation; its normal form embeds the vertex group and its associated subgroups, with transversals supplied by full AC. The torus group is $\mathbb Z^2$ and the standard solid-torus group is $\mathbb Z$. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]] [[thm-normal-form-for-free-products-with-amalgamation]] [[thm-hnn-normal-form-theorem]] [[thm-fundamental-group-of-the-circle]] [[thm-fundamental-group-of-a-product]]

## Proof

1.1 The solid torus is irreducible. Embed it as a standard unknotted solid torus in $S^3$. A sphere in its interior has two ball sides by [F2]. Its exterior solid torus is connected and misses the sphere, so lies entirely on one side; the other ball is contained in $V$. We will use the following disk-push consequence with its smooth interpretation. If two smooth disks meet just along their common boundary and bound such a ball, their faces admit a common-boundary disk sweep through the ball. To retain the actual faces, take a thin rim collar first. At a transverse rim its normal section is a quadrant; at a previously shared collar first separate the two faces by a small normal graph. Parametrize the two faces by smooth disks with their prescribed rim collars, using [F3]. Round and truncate the rim; the remaining boundary is a smooth sphere with these marked disk and collar portions. The two disk maps and the intervening product annulus give a smooth boundary diffeomorphism to the corresponding standard rounded lens; [F3] extends it over the ball. Restore the quadrant rim using those same product collars. This gives a lens parameter retaining both faces and their rim coordinates. In this parameter use [F4]'s spherical-cap sweep; in the rim section its inward tangent runs between the two face tangents and stays nonzero. The sweep is jointly smooth, including at the disk center, by [F4]'s displayed formulas. It can be continued just past either face in its normal collar and extended ambiently by [F5]. If another surface misses the ball except in one face, the push removes that face's intersections and creates none. The support can be restricted to the ball and arbitrarily thin face and rim collars. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given, construct]

2.1 For the classification first replace $F$ by its neat representative using [F9]; both disk-obstruction hypotheses pass to it. Its boundary and abstract surface are unchanged. The topological ambient extension pulls a boundary-parallel product back to the original surface, and no smooth product at an original tangency is asserted. In the rest of the classification denote this neat representative again by $F$. The surface $F$ is compact, since its inclusion is proper and $V$ is compact, and it is orientable, since it is two-sided in oriented $V$. If some component $c$ of $\partial F$ is nullhomotopic on $\partial V$, choose one with an innermost boundary disk $Q$ whose interior misses all of $\partial F$. A short inward push gives a disk with boundary $c$ on $F$ and interior disjoint from $F$. If $F$ is not a disk, $c$ is essential on $F$: a boundary circle of a connected surface can bound a disk in that surface only when that disk is the entire surface, by the local half-disk charts and connectedness. The pushed disk would therefore compress $F$. Thus in this case $F$ is a disk. For the rest of the classification suppose $F$ is not a disk; then every boundary circle is essential on $\partial V$. Disjoint essential circles on a torus have the same primitive unoriented slope, as the strip reductions of [F4] show. Use those reductions for the finite family and extend into a boundary collar by [F5] to make them parallel affine circles in coordinates $(\mu,\phi)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$, where $\phi$ is the longitude coordinate of $V$. If the slope is meridional, choose a standard meridian disk $D_0$ with boundary disjoint from them. Otherwise the affine circles have nonzero $\phi$ derivative and meet $\partial D_0=\{\phi=0\}$ transversely. [F9, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Put the interiors of $F$ and $D_0$ in finite transverse position. An innermost intersection circle on $D_0$ bounds a disk $D$ with interior missing $F$. Incompressibility makes its boundary bound a disk $D'$ on $F$. The sphere $D\cup D'$ bounds a ball in $V$ by step 1.1, with the corner interpreted there. The connected surface $F\setminus\operatorname{Int}D'$ reaches $\partial V$, misses the sphere off its rim, and hence lies on the exterior side of that ball. The disk push of step 1.1 replaces $D'$ by a disk just past $D$. It removes this circle and any additional circles in $D'$, and creates none. After finitely many pushes no circle remains. The isotopies have interior support and retain the normalized boundary curves. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Suppose an intersection arc remains. An outermost arc $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D$ in $D_0$, with other boundary arc $\beta\subset\partial D_0$ and interior missing $F$. Boundary-incompressibility implies that $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D'$ on $F$, with other boundary arc $\gamma$ contained in one component of $\partial F$. If the slope were meridional there would be no arc endpoints, by the chosen disjoint boundaries. Otherwise $\gamma$ is a nonconstant subarc of an affine boundary circle whose longitude coordinate is strictly monotone on its lift. Both its endpoints have $\phi=0$, so its lifted longitude displacement is a nonzero integer. But $\beta$ has constant longitude. The union $D\cup D'$, pushed a little along its common edge if necessary, gives a continuous disk cap for the loop $\beta\cup\gamma$ in $V$. Its longitude degree would therefore be zero, contradicting that nonzero integer. Thus there are no arcs. If the slope were nonmeridional, the affine boundary curves would necessarily meet $\partial D_0$, so this case is impossible. We have made $F$ disjoint from $D_0$. Cutting $V$ along $D_0$ leaves a ball. An innermost boundary circle of $F$ on its boundary sphere has a disk there with interior missing all boundary circles of $F$. Push it inward. Unless $F$ is a disk it is a compressing disk, by the boundary-circle argument of step 2.1. This contradicts our supposition that $F$ was not a disk. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

4.2 Let $D_1,D_2$ be meridian disks with the same boundary $C$. If either disk is not neat, first neatify each separately by [F9], fixing $C$. Apply the following neat-disk argument and then reverse the second embedding path. This gives a smooth embedding isotopy for the broad inputs; their two explicit topological ambient extensions and the middle smooth ambient path give a topological ambient extension. For neat inputs no preliminary change is necessary, and the entire argument below is smooth ambient. Now suppose both disks neat. In coordinates along $C$, use a small normal graph to separate their interior collars while fixing $C$ pointwise: with inward boundary coordinate $q\ge0$ and a transverse coordinate $y$ on $\partial V$, the two collars can be arranged as $y=\pm\varepsilon q$ on a common smaller strip. First each neat disk is straightened to such a graph by its full-rank collar coordinates; interpolation of the positive inward derivative gives an embedding path on a common compact strip, extended by [F5]. This keeps every boundary point fixed. General position relative to those collars then leaves only finitely many interior intersection circles. An innermost one on $D_1$ and its subdisk on $D_2$ bound a ball by irreducibility. The complement of that subdisk in $D_2$ reaches $C$ outside the ball, so the disk push from step 1.1 removes the circle and any circles inside that subdisk. Repeat until the interiors are disjoint. The resulting disks bound a ball with rim $C$, again by step 1.1 after the rim is rounded. Its common-boundary cap sweep carries one disk to the other, fixing $C$ throughout; at the rim every intermediate tangent is an inward direction between the two collar tangents, so the family remains neat in $V$. Undo the preliminary isotopies of $D_2$ and concatenate with stationary time changes. This gives a jointly smooth isotopy relative to $C$; The velocity vanishes on $C$ throughout this neat path. In a neat boundary chart it is $q$ times a smooth coefficient, as in [F9] and its neatification supplier Proof 5.2. Extend that coefficient and retain the factor $q$; the finite compact flow gives a smooth ambient isotopy fixing all of $\partial V$, not only $C$. [F9, A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 We have proved that $F$ is a disk. If $\partial F$ is essential on $\partial V$, it is a primitive class in the kernel of $\pi_1(\partial V)=\mathbb Z\mu\oplus\mathbb Z\phi\to\pi_1(V)=\mathbb Z\phi$, since $F$ caps it. It is therefore $\pm\mu$, so $F$ is a meridian disk. If $\partial F$ is inessential, let $Q$ be its disk on $\partial V$. The sphere $F\cup Q$, pushed slightly into the interior and rounded, bounds a ball there. Restore the boundary collar as in step 1.1 to get a ball with these two disk faces. Its marked lens parameter gives the boundary-parallel product: extend $Q$ a short distance beyond its rim in $\partial V$ and retain a smaller collar on $F$; in the normal section the two disk faces are separated by a rectangle, with its outer edge on $\partial V$. The lens parameter away from that rim and this rectangle near it identify the region with $D^2\times[0,1]$, with $D^2\times\{0\}=F$ and the other disk and lateral annulus in $\partial V$. Thus $F$ is boundary-parallel in exactly [F1]'s product sense. Conversely a boundary-parallel disk has no essential circle or essential proper arc, so it does satisfy both disk-obstruction hypotheses; this is why it must be retained in the conclusion. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Finally, if a two-sided torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ had no compressing disk, [F6] would inject $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ into $\pi_1(V)\cong\mathbb Z$. No such injection exists: for images $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ of the two generators, $(b,-a)$ is in the kernel when $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, and otherwise the entire group is the kernel. This contradiction yields a smooth compressing disk. This use of [F6] is within its compact smooth scope and does not turn a PL disk into a smooth disk without the supplied bridge. All earlier isotopies are smooth by the explicit cap, graph and finite extension constructions; the full AC assumption covers [F6] and implies the countable choice used elsewhere. [A1, F1, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

6.2 Finally allow the torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ to be TOP two-sided with its given product neighborhood, without assuming it smooth. Cut along that TOP collar. The cut pieces are compact orientable TOP3-manifolds; there are either two connected pieces with one torus face each, or one connected piece with two torus faces. Indeed every piece meets a face, and each face is connected. If any face map has nontrivial fundamental-group kernel, [F10] gives a proper disk in that cut piece whose boundary has nontrivial class on the face. Its image in $V$ is an embedded TOP compression of $T$ contained in $\operatorname{Int}V$, since its interior misses every cut boundary face and its boundary lies on only the chosen copy of $T$. Suppose therefore all face maps inject. In the two-piece case, [F11] embeds $\pi_1(T)$ in their amalgam $\pi_1(V)$. In the one-piece case choose a path in the cut piece joining the two face basepoints. Adjoining a thin copy of this path to the collar makes its overlap connected; van Kampen gives the presentation $\langle\pi_1(W),t\mid t i_+(a)t^{-1}=i_-(a),\ a\in\pi_1(T)\rangle$. One torus-overlap group maps to the collar's torus group and the other to its conjugate by the new path letter, which is exactly the displayed HNN relation. The two injected face groups are its associated subgroups, so HNN normal form [F11] again embeds $\pi_1(T)$ in $\pi_1(V)$. Both alternatives would inject $\mathbb Z^2$ into $\mathbb Z$, impossible: if the two basis images are $a,b$, then $(b,-a)$ is a nonzero kernel vector when either image is nonzero, and otherwise the whole group is the kernel. Thus some face kernel is nontrivial and the TOP compression exists. This closes the original unqualified torus clause without converting its input or its resulting disk to the smooth category. The preceding smooth classification and meridian-isotopy arguments are unchanged; their original convention/disposition remains owned by the parent assembly. [A1, F1, F10, F11, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $T$ be a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with $t\ge1$ tetrahedra. A nonzero nonnegative integer vector in $\mathbb Z^{7t}$ is the normal-coordinate vector of a normal surface exactly when it satisfies every face-matching equation and at most one quadrilateral type is nonzero in each tetrahedron. Every primitive integer generator of an extreme ray of the Haken cone has each coordinate at most $2^{7t-1}$. Every fundamental normal-surface vector has each coordinate at most $t\,2^{7t+2}$.

## Statement references

[[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]] — seven disk types per tetrahedron, face matching, quadrilateral admissibility, fundamental vectors and the Haken cone.

[Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger, Theorem 5.1 and Lemma 6.1](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hass/Research/Papers/Complexity/hlp.pdf) — matching characterization and coordinate bounds.

[Erickson, “Normal Surfaces and Knots,” §§14.1–14.3](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/comptop/2009/notes/normal-surfaces.pdf) — independent normal-coordinate conventions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite tetrahedral triangulation $T$ with $t\ge1$ tetrahedra and the seven normal disk types per tetrahedron.

[F1] [[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]]: normal vectors have $m=7t$ nonnegative integer coordinates; matching equations equate the counts of each normal-arc type across an interior face; the quadrilateral condition allows at most one quad type per tetrahedron.

[F2] [[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]]: a vector is fundamental exactly when it is not a sum of two nonzero admissible integer vectors, and the Haken cone is the nonnegative real solution set of the matching equations.

## Proof

1.1 For an existing normal surface, the arcs on the two sides of every interior face are the same finite set, so their type counts agree. Distinct quadrilateral types in one tetrahedron separate different opposite vertex pairs and intersect, so a disjoint normal surface can use at most one of them. Conversely, for a vector satisfying these conditions, place the prescribed parallel copies of each triangle type and the single permitted quadrilateral type in every tetrahedron. In each triangular face, arcs of a fixed type are nested parallel copies; put the endpoint blocks in the same order on its three edges on both incident tetrahedra. The matching equations give equal counts for every type, so pair the $j$th arc on one side to the $j$th arc on the other for each $j$. These gluings identify disk sides in pairs and do not identify interior points, producing a properly embedded normal surface with precisely the given counts. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Put $m=7t$. A one-dimensional face of the pointed cone $C(T)$ is cut out by the matching equalities together with active coordinate equations $x_i=0$ whose combined row rank is $m-1$. Choose $m-1$ independent active rows and form the integer matrix $R$ with those rows. Each matching row has four entries in $\{+1,-1\}$ and Euclidean norm $2$; each coordinate row has norm $1$. The cofactor vector $w\in\mathbb Z^m$, whose $j$th coordinate is the signed determinant of the matrix obtained by deleting column $j$, is nonzero and satisfies $Rw=0$ by Laplace expansion. Hadamard's inequality bounds each such determinant by the product of the row norms, hence $|w_j|\le2^{m-1}$. Dividing by the gcd of the coordinates gives the primitive integer generator on that ray and cannot increase any coordinate. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

1.3 The cone $C(T)$ is pointed because it lies in the nonnegative orthant. Intersect it with $\sum_i x_i=1$; this is a bounded rational polytope. Triangulate that finite polytope by coning a triangulation of each face from its first vertex in a fixed finite vertex order. Coning the simplices back to the origin decomposes $C(T)$ into finitely many simplicial cones, each generated by at most $m$ extreme rays of $C(T)$. [F1, construct]

2.1 Any nonzero vector satisfying the equations and quadrilateral condition is realized by step 1.1; counting its disk pieces returns the original vector. The zero vector has no disk pieces and represents the empty surface, which is admitted for coordinate addition. This proves the claimed characterization. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 Let $v$ be a fundamental admissible integer vector. If $v=x+y$ with nonzero integer vectors $x,y\in C(T)$, then $0\le x_i,y_i\le v_i$ for every coordinate. Since the support of the quadrilateral coordinates of $v$ uses at most one quad type per tetrahedron, the coordinatewise sub-vectors $x,y$ satisfy the same quadrilateral restriction. Step 2.1 realizes both as nonempty normal surfaces, contradicting fundamentalness. Thus $v$ is indecomposable in the integer semigroup $C(T)\cap\mathbb Z^m$. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1, contradiction]

4.1 Choose a simplicial cone from step 1.3 containing $v$, with primitive ray generators $r_1,\ldots,r_d$, where $d\le m$. Write $v=\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j r_j$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$. If some $\lambda_j>1$, then $v-r_j$ is a nonnegative integer vector in the same cone and is nonzero; hence $v=(v-r_j)+r_j$ contradicts indecomposability. Therefore every $\lambda_j\le1$, including the case $v=r_j$. For every coordinate $i$, step 1.2 gives $v_i\le\sum_j(r_j)_i\le d\,2^{m-1}\le7t\,2^{7t-1}\le t\,2^{7t+2}$. This proves the fundamental-vector bound. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
