## Statement

Let $R$ be an analytic double-fibration transform and let
$$
(z_0,\zeta_0;x_0,\xi_0)\in C_Z
$$
be a point of its incidence cotangent relation. Assume the Bolker condition holds at this point, meaning $\pi_L^{-1}(z_0,\zeta_0)=\{(z_0,\zeta_0;x_0,\xi_0)\}$ and $d\pi_L$ is injective at that relation point. For every compactly supported distribution $f\in\mathcal E'(X)$, if $(z_0,\zeta_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(Rf)$, then $(x_0,\xi_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(f)$. This is a qualitative microlocal implication; it asserts no noisy-data stability estimate.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform|Analytic transform]]

[[def-ip-bolker-condition|Bolker condition]]

[[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation|Incidence relation]]

[[def-ip-analytic-wavefront-fbi-transform|Gaussian FBI criterion]]

[[lem-ip-analytic-cutoff-sequence-and-fbi-invariance|Cutoff and FBI invariance]]

[[lem-ip-bolker-geometric-criteria|Bolker rank criteria]]

[[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel|Local conormal kernel]]

[[lem-ip-holomorphic-morse-normalization-and-gaussian-contour|Holomorphic Morse normalization]]

[[thm-ip-analytic-stationary-phase-with-exponential-remainder|Optimal analytic stationary phase]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The analytic transform $R$, the relation point with singleton full left fiber and injective left differential, and compactly supported $f$ with the stated data analytic regularity.

[F1] [[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform]]: the transform is properly supported on compact object supports and has a nowhere vanishing analytic incidence density and weight.

[F2] [[def-ip-bolker-condition]]: the pointwise condition gives the entire singleton left fiber and injective differential at this point.

[F3] [[lem-ip-analytic-nonstationary-incidence-localization]]: input support with no incidence cotangent relation over the supplied data covector has an exponentially small data Gaussian transform, with finite-order distributional estimates.

[F4] [[lem-ip-local-bolker-positive-packet-estimate]]: for distributions supported sufficiently near the supplied object point, data Gaussian regularity implies object Gaussian regularity, by the exact packet resolution, reduced positive phase, estimated stationary phase and elliptic packet criterion.

[F5] [[lem-ip-analytic-cutoff-sequence-and-fbi-invariance]]: the Gaussian criterion is independent of local cutoff and analytic chart and applies to distributional densities as well as scalar distributions.

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the statement.

1.1 Choose a smooth compact object cutoff $\rho$ equal to one near $x_0$ and supported in the small object neighborhood supplied by [F4]. Write $f=\rho f+(1-\rho)f$. The second summand is compactly supported away from $x_0$. By [F2] its support has no relation point over $(z_0,\zeta_0)$, because that full fiber consists of the supplied point over $x_0$. Hence [F3] gives $(z_0,\zeta_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(R((1-\rho)f))$. This includes all incidence points outside the local coordinate patch; it is not inferred merely from local injectivity. [F1, F2, F3, given, choose]

2.1 By hypothesis the Gaussian data transform of $Rf$ is exponentially small on some data parameter neighborhood. Subtract the exponential estimate from step 1.1, using the same data chart and a common smaller cutoff neighborhood by [F5]. Linearity gives the same estimate for $R(\rho f)$ at the supplied data covector. The differential clause of [F2] supplies the local Bolker hypothesis in [F4]. Since $\rho f$ is supported in its chosen small object neighborhood, [F4] yields $(x_0,\xi_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(\rho f)$. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The localized distributions $\rho f$ and $f$ agree on a neighborhood of $x_0$. Their Gaussian transforms with any common cutoff supported there agree exactly; all other cutoff choices differ only by the exponential Gaussian tails in [F5]. Thus step 2.1 gives $(x_0,\xi_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(f)$, as asserted. The two suppliers account separately for global fiber uniqueness and local differential injectivity, and all errors are controlled in the finite number of derivatives needed by the compact distribution. No stability or choice assumption has been added. [F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

## Definition references

[[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation|Incidence kernel, distribution operations, and relation]]

[[def-smooth-manifold|Smooth manifolds]]

[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds|Smooth maps and submersions]]

[[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density|Smooth density]]

[[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables|Real-analytic structure]]

[[def-multivariable-power-series|Power-series convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real-analytic double fibration, its density and nonvanishing analytic weight, and a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$.

[F1] [[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation]]: submersion pullback is defined by transposed fiber integration; density multiplication turns it into a distributional density; pushforward is defined when proper on support; the canonical relation uses $(\eta,-\xi)$.

[F2] [[def-smooth-manifold]]: local charts define the smooth manifold structures.

[F3] [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]: smooth submersions have smooth local coordinate representatives.

[F4] [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]: densities transform by absolute Jacobians and can be integrated without orientations.

[F5] [[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: the analytic maps and coefficients have holomorphic local complexifications.

[F6] [[def-multivariable-power-series]]: those complexifications are represented by convergent power series on smaller polydiscs.

## Proof

**Given:** The manifolds $G,Z,X$, maps $\pi_G,\pi_X$, density $\omega_Z$, weight $\kappa$, and input $u$.

1.1 The chart representatives are smooth submersions by [F2]–[F3], and their analytic representatives have local holomorphic extensions by [F5]–[F6]. Hence the fiber and incidence data in the statement are well-defined in the stated smooth and analytic categories. [given, F2, F3, F5, F6]

1.2 The pullback $\pi_X^*u$ exists by [F1]. Multiplying it by the nowhere vanishing analytic density $\omega_Z$ gives a distributional density; multiplication by the smooth function $\kappa$ preserves that type. If $\operatorname{supp}u\subset K$ with $K$ compact, the support of this product lies in $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$, on which $\pi_G$ is proper by hypothesis. [F1, given]

2.1 The proper pushforward in [F1] therefore defines $Ru$ as a distributional density on $G$. In coordinates, transposing fiber integration in the two submersions shows that it pairs a data test function with the integral over the corresponding incidence fiber, weighted by $\kappa\omega_Z$; the density Jacobians cancel by [F4]. The cotangent relation of the kernel is precisely $C_Z$ by the sign convention in [F1]. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

Let $b>0$, $0<w<1$, and let the two-mode posterior be $\pi_w=w\delta_{-b}+(1-w)\delta_b$ on $\mathbb R$. From $M\ge1$ independent exact posterior draws $X_1,\ldots,X_M$, define $\widehat w=M^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf 1\{X_i=-b\}$ and $\widehat\pi_M=\widehat w\delta_{-b}+(1-\widehat w)\delta_b$. The one-Wasserstein error and the probability that at least one posterior mode is absent from the sample are
$$W_1(\widehat\pi_M,\pi_w)=2b|\widehat w-w|,\qquad P\{\widehat w\in\{0,1\}\}=(1-w)^M+w^M,$$
and $E W_1(\widehat\pi_M,\pi_w)\le2b\sqrt{w(1-w)/M}$.

## Example references

[[ex-ip-ideal-score-error-allows-unbounded-euler-wasserstein|The finite-compute posterior-fidelity question, with score and time-discretization errors set to zero.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $b>0$, $0<w<1$, $M\ge1$, posterior $\pi_w=w\delta_{-b}+(1-w)\delta_b$, and independent draws $X_i\sim\pi_w$.

[A1] $W_1$ is the infimum of $E|X-X'|$ over couplings of the two probability measures.

## Verification

1.1 Put $\widehat w=M^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf 1\{X_i=-b\}$. In any coupling of $\widehat\pi_M$ and $\pi_w$, mass $\min\{\widehat w,w\}$ at $-b$ and $\min\{1-\widehat w,1-w\}$ at $b$ can be matched at zero cost; the remaining mass is $|\widehat w-w|$ and must move between the atoms, a distance $2b$. This coupling is feasible and no coupling can move less unmatched mass, so it is optimal and gives $W_1=2b|\widehat w-w|$. [given, A1, construct]

2.1 The count $M\widehat w$ is binomial $(M,w)$, so $E\widehat w=w$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat w)=w(1-w)/M$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $E|\widehat w-w|\le\sqrt{w(1-w)/M}$; step 1.1 yields the expected Wasserstein bound. The event of missing $-b$ has probability $(1-w)^M$, and the event of missing $b$ has probability $w^M$; for $M\ge1$ these events are disjoint, giving the displayed miss probability. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ and let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$. Fix an integer $s>n/2+2$ and a finite family $h_1,\ldots,h_m\in C^\infty(\partial M,\mathbb C)$. For $\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_m)\in\mathbb R^m$ sufficiently near zero, the equation
$$-\Delta_g u+q u^3=0\quad\text{in }M^\circ,\qquad u|_{\partial M}=\sum_{j=1}^m\epsilon_jh_j$$
has a unique solution in a fixed small $H^s(M)$ ball. The parameter map $\epsilon\mapsto u_\epsilon$ is $C^3$ into $H^s(M)$, and the corresponding nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann data $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_\epsilon|_{\partial M}$ is $C^3$ into $C^0(\partial M)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product geometry and Laplacian convention]]

[[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain|Chartwise Sobolev spaces]]

[[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity|Dirichlet inverse and higher regularity]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is assumed by the Sobolev algebra, embedding, and Banach implicit-function suppliers [F4]--[F6].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed by the Sobolev and elliptic regularity interfaces [F1], [F3].

**Given:** the product domain, real smooth $q$, integer $s>n/2+2$, and the fixed finite smooth boundary directions.

[F1] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: the chartwise integer Sobolev spaces are Banach spaces, and $H_0^1(M)$ is the closed zero-trace subspace.

[F2] [[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness]]: on a compact connected domain, $\|w\|_{L^2}\leq C_P\|\nabla w\|_{L^2}$ for zero-trace $w$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity]]: the zero Dirichlet operator $-\Delta_g$ is invertible; for integer $k\geq0$, zero-trace $F\in H^k$ gives $u\in H^{k+2}$ with $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k\|F\|_{H^k}$.

[F4] [[cor-sobolev-algebra-above-the-critical-index]]: for integer $s$ with $2s>n$ on a bounded smooth domain, multiplication is continuous in $W^{s,2}$, so the Sobolev space is a Banach algebra.

[F5] [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]]: for $s>n/2+2$ on a bounded smooth domain, $H^s$ embeds continuously in $C^2(\overline M)$.

[F6] [[thm-implicit-function-theorem-for-banach-spaces]]: if a $C^3$ map between Banach spaces vanishes at a point and its derivative in the unknown variable is a bounded isomorphism, its nearby zero set is the graph of a unique $C^3$ map.

[F7] [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]: boundary data on a compact smooth boundary extend smoothly into a collar by constant normal extension followed by a smooth cutoff and finite patching.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 For $q=0$, the Dirichlet kernel of $-\Delta_g$ is trivial: if $w\in H_0^1(M)$ is weakly harmonic, testing with $w$ gives $\int_M|\nabla w|^2dV_g=0$, and the zero-trace Poincare inequality in [F2] gives $w=0$. Thus [F3] supplies the zero-boundary inverse $G=(-\Delta_g)^{-1}:H^{s-2}(M)\to X_s$, where $X_s=\{w\in H^s(M):w\in H_0^1(M)\}$. The high-order estimate in [F3], together with its bounded $H^1$ inverse, makes $G$ bounded. [A2, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Since $s>n/2+2$, [F4] makes $H^s(M)$ an algebra by localizing to finitely many smooth charts, extending each localized representative to a bounded Euclidean chart domain, applying the Euclidean algebra estimate, and summing the finite norms. Thus the map $(\epsilon,w)\mapsto q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3$ is a continuous polynomial from $\mathbb R^m\times X_s$ into $H^{s-2}(M)$, where $f_\epsilon=\sum_j\epsilon_jh_j$ and $Ef_\epsilon$ is the smooth collar extension from [F7]. Define
$$\mathcal F(\epsilon,w)=w-G\big[\Delta_g(Ef_\epsilon)-q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3\big]\in X_s.$$
It is $C^3$ (indeed polynomial plus bounded linear maps) and $\mathcal F(0,0)=0$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, given, construct]

2.1 At $(0,0)$, the derivative $D_w\mathcal F(0,0)$ is the identity on $X_s$, because the derivative of $u\mapsto q u^3$ at $u=0$ vanishes. By [F6], there is a neighborhood of $\epsilon=0$ and a unique $C^3$ map $w(\epsilon)\in X_s$ near zero such that $\mathcal F(\epsilon,w(\epsilon))=0$. The fixed-point equation is exactly $-\Delta_g(Ef_\epsilon+w)+q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3=0$ with boundary trace $f_\epsilon$, so $u_\epsilon=Ef_\epsilon+w(\epsilon)$ gives the unique small solution. [A1, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 By [F5], $u_\epsilon\in C^2(\overline M)$ and the outward normal derivative has a continuous boundary trace. The trace map from $C^1(\overline M)$ to $C^0(\partial M)$ is bounded in the chartwise norms, so composing the $C^3$ map $\epsilon\mapsto u_\epsilon$ with this bounded linear trace of $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}$ proves $C^3$ dependence of the nonlinear DN data. [A1, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. The inclusion identifies $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ and preserves the positive-meridian classes. In particular, inclusion induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism

$$
H_1(p^{-1}(E_L);\mathbb Z)\cong A_L.
$$

## Statement references

[[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the link, its chosen pairwise-disjoint closed normal disk tubes $N(K_i)=\Phi_i(D_{\epsilon_i}\nu(K_i))$, the compact exterior $E_L$, the open complement $X_L$, a basepoint $b\in E_L$, and the maximal abelian cover $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$.

[A1] AC is assumed in the maximal-abelian-cover definition and its link-complement supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The cover $p$ is the connected regular cover classified by the kernel of abelianization, and its deck group is $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$ ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] A homotopy of maps into a base of a covering, together with an initial lift, has a unique homotopy lift ([[thm-homotopy-lifting-for-covering-maps]]).

[F3] Paths lift uniquely from a prescribed point of a covering fibre ([[thm-path-lifting-for-covering-maps]]).

[F4] Connected covers of a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected space are classified by their induced fundamental-group subgroups ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]).

[F5] A map defined continuously on the members of a finite closed cover, with agreeing restrictions on overlaps, is continuous ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]]).

[F6] The link complement is a connected smooth three-manifold under AC ([[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold]]).

[F7] In a connected regular covering, the deck group acts transitively on each fibre ([[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]]).

[F8] A deformation retract is fixed pointwise by a homotopy from the identity to the retraction-inclusion composite ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]).

[F9] Inclusion of a deformation retract induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups at every basepoint in the retract ([[prop-retracts-inject-fundamental-groups]]).

[F10] Homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on singular homology ([[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $x=\Phi_i(v)\in N(K_i)\setminus K_i$, write $\rho=\lVert v\rVert>0$ and define
$$
F_s(x)=\Phi_i\!\left(\left((1-s)\rho+s\epsilon_i\right)\frac{v}{\rho}\right),\qquad 0\le s\le1.
$$
On $E_L$ set $F_s(x)=x$. The formula is continuous on each punctured tube and agrees with the identity on its boundary $\rho=\epsilon_i$. The products with $I$ of the finitely many punctured closed tubes and $E_L$ form a finite closed cover of $X_L\times I$; [F5] therefore makes $F:X_L\times I\to X_L$ continuous. It starts at the identity, fixes $E_L$ pointwise, and at $s=1$ maps every punctured tube to its boundary, so it is a strong deformation retraction onto $E_L$. [given, F5, construct]

1.2 The link complement is path-connected by [F6], so its deformation retract $E_L$ is path-connected. The tube construction makes $E_L$ a smooth manifold with boundary, hence locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected. By [F8] and [F9], inclusion induces an isomorphism $i_*:\pi_1(E_L,b)\to\pi_1(X_L,b)$. By [F8] and [F10], it also induces an isomorphism $i_*:H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$. The positive meridians lie in $E_L$ and map to the same classes, so the meridian basis is preserved. An $E_L$-loop closes in the restricted cover exactly when its image under $i_*$ lies in $\ker\phi$, so the component containing $\widetilde b$ induces the subgroup
$$
i_*^{-1}(\ker\phi)=\ker(\phi\circ i_*).
$$
This subgroup is exactly the kernel of the abelianization of $\pi_1(E_L,b)$ because $i_*$ is an isomorphism. To check connectedness, take $y\in E_L$, a path $\delta$ in $E_L$ from $b$ to $y$, and a lift $\widetilde\delta$ from a chosen point $\widetilde b$ over $b$. Any other point over $y$ is $h\widetilde\delta(1)$ for some deck transformation $h$, by [F7]. Surjectivity of $i_*$ gives a loop $\alpha$ in $E_L$ whose lift from $\widetilde b$ ends at $h\widetilde b$. The reverse of $\widetilde\delta$, this lifted loop, and $h\widetilde\delta$ concatenate to a path in $p^{-1}(E_L)$ from $\widetilde\delta(1)$ to $h\widetilde\delta(1)$. Thus the restriction is connected. By [F4] it is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, with the same deck group $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to $F$ with initial lift the identity of $X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}$. For a point over $E_L$, its constant path is a lift of its path under $F$; uniqueness makes the lifted homotopy fix every point of $p^{-1}(E_L)$. At time $1$ the image lies in $p^{-1}(E_L)$, so the lifted homotopy is a strong deformation retraction of $X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}$ onto that restricted cover. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

2.2 For every deck transformation $h$, the maps $(x,s)\mapsto h\widetilde F_s(x)$ and $(x,s)\mapsto\widetilde F_s(hx)$ lift the same homotopy $F(p(x),s)$ and agree at $s=0$. Uniqueness in [F2] makes them equal. The retraction is therefore deck-equivariant, and its induced isomorphism on first homology is $\Lambda_r$-linear. By [F1] the target homology of the full cover is $A_L$, proving the asserted module isomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\psi\in C^\infty$ be real on a neighborhood of the transversal projection of $M$, with $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$. Suppose $a\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$2\partial_{x_1}a+2i\,g_0(\nabla_{g_0}\psi,\nabla_{g_0}a)+i(\Delta_{g_0}\psi)a=0.$$
Then, for all sufficiently large $\tau$, there is an exact solution
$$u_\tau=e^{-\tau(x_1+i\psi)}a+e^{-\tau x_1}r_\tau,\qquad (-\Delta_g+q)u_\tau=0\ \text{in }M^\circ,$$
with $r_\tau\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_\tau\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_{L^2(M)}$. No boundary value is prescribed for $r_\tau$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product metric and dimension]]

[[lem-ip-limiting-carleman-estimate-on-product|Product Carleman estimate and L2 right solvability]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is used for the Hahn--Banach extension in the product Carleman right solver [F2].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is used for its Hilbert-space Riesz representation [F2].

**Given:** the product domain, smooth real $q$, real eikonal function $\psi$ with unit transversal gradient, and smooth transport amplitude $a$.

[F1] [[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain]]: $g=dx_1^2\oplus g_0$ and $\Delta_g=\partial_{x_1}^2+\Delta_{g_0}$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-limiting-carleman-estimate-on-product]]: for $\varphi=x_1$, the conjugated operator $P_{\varphi,h,q}=e^{\varphi/h}h^2(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\varphi/h}$ has a distributional right inverse on $L^2$ with norm at most $C h^{-1}$.

[F3] [[def-riemannian-gradient]] and [[def-laplace-beltrami-operator-as-trace-of-the-hessian]]: the product metric extends the gradient bilinearly to complex phases, and $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$.

[F4] **External input:** Dos Santos Ferreira--Kurylev--Lassas--Salo, Proposition 2.1 (PDF p. 10), for a compact oriented CTA manifold, bounded potential, either sign of sufficiently large real $\tau$, and arbitrary $f\in L^2$, gives $r\in H^1$ solving $e^{\tau x_1}(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\tau x_1}r=f$, with $\|r\|_{H^\alpha}\le C|\tau|^{\alpha-1}\|f\|_2$ for $0\le\alpha\le1$, with no prescribed boundary value. We import this statement, not a reconstructed shifted Carleman proof. Its statement and the application in Propositions 2.1--2.2, PDF pp. 10--11, were inspected; the older Proposition 4.4 citation issue is not treated as a local proof.

[F5] The orientation restriction in [F4] is removed for scalar equations by the orientation double cover of $M_0$. Lift $M,q,f$ to its product cover, solve there, and average the solution with its deck transform. The invariant solution descends to $H^1(M)$ and solves the original equation. The degree-two factors in the squared $L^2$ norms cancel in the estimate; the same applies to the local Sobolev norms. A disconnected cover is handled componentwise, using only finitely many choices.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Put $\Phi=x_1+i\psi$. By [F1] and $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$,
$$g(d\Phi,d\Phi)=1+i^2|d\psi|_{g_0}^2=0.$$
Direct conjugation gives
$$(-\Delta_g+q)(e^{-\tau\Phi}a) =e^{-\tau\Phi}\left[\tau^2g(d\Phi,d\Phi)a+ \tau\left(2g(\nabla_g\Phi,\nabla_ga)+(\Delta_g\Phi)a\right) +(-\Delta_g+q)a\right].$$
The $\tau^2$ term vanishes by the eikonal equality, and the coefficient of $\tau$ is exactly the transport equation in the statement. Hence the residual is $e^{-\tau\Phi}(-\Delta_g+q)a$. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Set $h=\tau^{-1}$ and conjugate by the real weight $e^{-\tau x_1}$. The equation for the correction is
$$P_{x_1,h,q}r_\tau=-h^2e^{-i\tau\psi}(-\Delta_g+q)a.$$
The right side is in $L^2$ and has norm $h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2$. By [F4]--[F5], with the equation divided by $h^2$, there is an $H^1$ correction (and hence a distributional) $r_\tau\in L^2(M)$ with
$$\|r_\tau\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2 =C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2.$$
Thus the asserted remainder estimate and the equation hold distributionally. [A1, A2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

1.3 Choose the $H^1$ correction from step 1.2. Multiplication by the smooth exponentials preserves $H^1(M)$ for each fixed $\tau$, and the correction equation cancels the residual computed in step 1.1. Thus $u_\tau$ is exact, has the stated remainder bound, and has no imposed correction boundary value. The additional boundary regularity is the external input [F4], rather than a consequence asserted for the $L^2$ solver [F2]. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $a\ge b\ge1$ be coprime positive integers, and let $T_{a,b}\subset S^3$ be the corresponding torus knot. If a knot $K\subset S^3$ has the same enhanced A-polynomial as $T_{a,b}$ up to a Laurent unit and the same Alexander-polynomial breadth (highest exponent minus lowest exponent of its symmetrized Alexander polynomial), then $K$ has the same underlying unoriented knot type as $T_{a,b}$. When $b\ge2$, the absolute torus parameters of $K$ agree with $\{a,b\}$.

## Statement references

[[thm-enhanced-a-polynomial-newton-polygon-detects-torus-knots|Thin enhanced-A classification]]

[[thm-torus-knot-alexander-and-genus-formulas|Alexander breadth formula for torus knots]]

[Baldwin and Sivek, Corollary 1.4 and §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a knot $K$, a positive torus knot $T_{a,b}$, equality of enhanced A-polynomials up to a Laurent unit, and equality of Alexander breadths.

[F1] A knot whose enhanced A-polynomial has Newton polygon contained in a line is a torus knot. For a positive nontrivial torus knot $T_{a,b}$ with $a>b\ge2$, its enhanced A-polynomial has a line-segment Newton polygon of slope $ab$ in the stated convention; the unknot has enhanced A-polynomial $1$ ([[thm-enhanced-a-polynomial-newton-polygon-detects-torus-knots]]; [[lem-torus-knot-enhanced-a-polynomial]]). The same segment-slope formula holds for signed parameters: the mirror changes peripheral coordinates by $(M,L)\mapsto(M^{-1},L)$, reversing the knot orientation changes them by $(M,L)\mapsto(M^{-1},L^{-1})$, and these transformations are proved for the enhanced locus in [[thm-enhanced-a-polynomial-newton-polygon-detects-torus-knots]], Proof1.2. They send the positive segment slope $|pq|$ to the signed product $pq$.

[F2] For signed coprime parameters, the Alexander breadth of $T_{p,q}$ is $(|p|-1)(|q|-1)$; changing both signs reverses knot orientation and changing one sign takes the mirror ([[thm-torus-knot-alexander-and-genus-formulas]]; [[def-coprime-torus-knot]]).

[F3] A torus knot with one parameter of absolute value $1$ is the standard unknot ([[lem-torus-knot-unit-slope-is-unknot]]).

[A1] Full AC implies countable choice, the hypothesis used by [F3] ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F4] The classification used in [F1] is now complete with the explicit external input Baldwin–Sivek, arXiv:2405.19197v2, Theorem 1.2. Their Corollary 1.4 (p.2) independently states detection by the enhanced polynomial together with Alexander degree; the finite parameter-recovery proof below is retained locally. The source statement was consulted directly, not its gauge-theoretic proof reconstructed. The breadth used here is twice the degree of the symmetric polynomial for torus knots, so equality of breadths gives exactly the equality used in step2.1.

## Proof

1.1 Equality of enhanced A-polynomials up to a Laurent unit gives the same Newton polygon shape. By [F1], this polygon lies in a line, so write $K=T_{p,q}$ for signed coprime nonzero parameters. If $b\ge2$, both polygons are line segments and [F1] gives equality of slopes, hence $pq=ab$. If $b=1$, the target polygon is a point and no slope equation is asserted. [F1, given, cases, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $b\ge2$ and put $u=|p|$, $v=|q|$. From $pq=ab>0$, $p$ and $q$ have the same sign and $uv=ab$. Equality of Alexander breadths and [F2] give $(u-1)(v-1)=(a-1)(b-1)$. Expanding and substituting $uv=ab$ yields $u+v=a+b$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Suppose $b=1$. Then [F3] says $T_{a,1}$ is the unknot, whose Alexander breadth is zero. By [F2] and the assumed breadth equality, $(|p|-1)(|q|-1)=0$. Thus $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, and [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3], so $K=T_{p,q}$ is the unknot as well. Hence its underlying unoriented knot type equals $T_{a,1}$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The monic quadratics $x^2-(u+v)x+uv$ and $x^2-(a+b)x+ab$ are equal, so their root multisets agree and $\{u,v\}=\{a,b\}$. The same-sign conclusion in step 2.1 means that $K$ is $T_{a,b}$ up to orientation, so the underlying unoriented knot types agree. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 3.1 and 2.2 cover respectively the nontrivial and unknot target cases, proving the stated identification; in the nontrivial case step 3.1 also identifies the absolute parameters up to interchange. [step 3.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Example

Fix $R,a_0,\sigma>0$ and $0\le\rho_A<a_0/2$. The working inverse is $g(y)=y/a_0$. Under a test operator $a=a_0+\delta$ with $|\delta|\le\rho_A$, the observation is $Y=a\theta+\varepsilon$ for $\theta\in[-R,R]$ and independent $\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. For any two truth laws $\mu_0,\mu$ on $[-R,R]$, define $W_1(\mu,\mu_0)$ as the infimum of $E|\Theta-\Theta_0|$ over their couplings. The risk is
$$R_{\mu,\delta}(g)=E_{\theta\sim\mu,\varepsilon}|g((a_0+\delta)\theta+\varepsilon)-\theta|^2=\frac{\delta^2}{a_0^2}E_\mu\theta^2+\frac{\sigma^2}{a_0^2},$$
and it satisfies $R_{\mu,\delta}(g)\le(\rho_A^2R^2+\sigma^2)/a_0^2$ and
$$|R_{\mu,\delta}(g)-R_{\mu_0,\delta}(g)|\le\frac{2\delta^2R}{a_0^2}W_1(\mu,\mu_0).$$

## Example references

[[ex-ip-robust-ellipsoid-minimax-shift-rate|The bounded operator and test-law shift frontier illustrated by a conditioned scalar inverse.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $R,a_0,\sigma>0$, $0\le\rho_A<a_0/2$, $|\delta|\le\rho_A$, $\theta\in[-R,R]$, $\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ independent of $\theta$, and the working inverse $g(y)=y/a_0$.

[A1] The test law $\mu$ and source law $\mu_0$ are Borel probability measures on $[-R,R]$; $W_1$ is the infimum of expected absolute distance over their couplings.

## Verification

1.1 Substitution gives $g(Y)-\theta=((a_0+\delta)\theta+\varepsilon)/a_0-\theta=\delta\theta/a_0+\varepsilon/a_0$. Independence and $E\varepsilon=0$ make the cross term vanish, so the expected squared error is $\delta^2E_\mu\theta^2/a_0^2+\sigma^2/a_0^2$. Since $|\theta|\le R$ and $|\delta|\le\rho_A$, this is at most $(\rho_A^2R^2+\sigma^2)/a_0^2$. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 For any coupling $(\Theta,\Theta_0)$ of $\mu,\mu_0$, $|\Theta^2-\Theta_0^2|=|\Theta-\Theta_0||\Theta+\Theta_0|\le2R|\Theta-\Theta_0|$. Taking expectations, then the infimum over couplings, gives $|E_\mu\theta^2-E_{\mu_0}\theta^2|\le2R W_1(\mu,\mu_0)$. Multiplication by $\delta^2/a_0^2$ and step 1.1 yields the claimed risk-transfer bound. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ and, for $z=(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$, define $F(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x_1z_1+x_2z_2)}\,dx$ using the compact-support Riemann integral on any rectangle containing $\operatorname{supp}f$. This value is independent of the containing rectangle. Each coordinate slice of $F$ is entire, with $\frac{\partial F}{\partial z_j}(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(-2\pi ix_j)f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}\,dx$ for $j=1,2$, and the restriction of $F$ to $\mathbb R^2$ is the compact-support Fourier transform in the stated line-normal convention. The proof uses no Countable Choice.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-2d-radon-transform|Compact-support Fourier transform convention]]

[Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

[Venkataswaran P. Krishnan and Eric Todd Quinto, Microlocal Analysis in Tomography, §1.3.2](https://math.tifrbng.res.in/~vkrishnan/Papers/Microlocal_Analysis_Tomography.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compactly supported smooth complex function $f$ on $\mathbb R^2$, a rectangle containing its support, and a complex frequency $z\in\mathbb C^2$.

[F1] [[def-ip-2d-radon-transform]]: the compact-support Fourier transform uses $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$ and is defined by a compact-support Riemann integral.

[F2] [[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]: each continuous real function on a nondegenerate closed rectangle is Riemann integrable; apply this to real and imaginary parts.

[F3] [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]: the complex exponential is entire with derivative itself, so $(e^w-1)/w\to1$ as $w\to0$.

[F4] [[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]]: the Riemann integral is linear and its absolute-value estimate bounds an integral by the rectangle volume times a uniform bound; for complex functions apply the real estimate to both components.

[F5] [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]: a function complex differentiable at every point of $\mathbb C$ is entire.

## Proof

1.1 Choose a nondegenerate closed rectangle $B$ containing $\operatorname{supp}f$. For every $z\in\mathbb C^2$, the integrand $x\mapsto f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}$ is continuous on $B$, so [F2] makes its real and imaginary parts Riemann integrable. It vanishes outside $\operatorname{supp}f$; hence enlarging $B$ changes the integral only by adding regions on which the integrand is zero. This proves existence and independence of the containing rectangle. [F1, F2, given, choose]

1.2 Fix $j\in\{1,2\}$, fix the other complex coordinate, and let $h\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. By [F4], the coordinate difference quotient is the integral over $B$ of $f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}(e^{-2\pi i x_jh}-1)/h$. The coordinate $x_j$ is bounded on $B$; [F3] therefore makes $(e^{-2\pi i x_jh}-1)/h$ converge uniformly on $B$ to $-2\pi i x_j$ as $h\to0$. Multiplication by the fixed bounded continuous factor $f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}$ preserves uniform convergence, and [F4] passes the real and imaginary integrals to their limits. Thus the coordinate derivative exists and is the displayed integral. Since the other coordinate and the point were arbitrary, every coordinate slice is complex differentiable everywhere. [F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 By [F5], each coordinate slice is entire. At real $z=\xi$, the defining integral is exactly the compact-support Fourier integral of [F1], so $F(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi)$. This proves all claims without using a Lebesgue/Riemann identification theorem or Countable Choice. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ be a nonempty oriented smooth $r$-component link with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L$, and maximal abelian cover $E_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to E_L$ with deck group $H\cong\mathbb Z^r$ and group ring $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[H]$. For any finite CW structure on $E_L$, the inverse-image cells and one chosen lift of each open cell form a finite-rank free $\Lambda_r$ cellular chain complex. Its first homology is the absolute multivariable Alexander module $A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$, with the deck action specified by the positive meridians.

## Statement references

[[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]

[[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a nonempty oriented smooth $r$-component link with $r\ge1$; its chosen compact exterior $E_L$; its regular maximal abelian cover $E_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to E_L$ with deck group $H\cong\mathbb Z^r$; and a finite CW structure on $E_L$.

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis under which the maximal-abelian-cover definition is being used; selecting the finitely many cell lifts below itself needs no choice principle ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The absolute multivariable Alexander module is $A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$, with Laurent variables acting by the positive-meridian deck transformations ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] The compact exterior cover is the restriction of the open-complement cover; lifted deformation retraction gives a deck-equivariant isomorphism $H_1(E_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)\cong A_L$ ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]).

[F3] Cellular homology is naturally isomorphic to singular homology for every CW complex, and the isomorphism commutes with cellular maps ([[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]]).

## Proof

1.1 A finite CW structure has finitely many open cells. Each open cell is contractible, so its inverse image under a covering is a disjoint union of copies of that cell. The regular deck group $H$ acts freely and transitively on those copies. Choose one lifted copy for each cell; finitely many choices suffice. Every other lift is uniquely a deck translate of the chosen lift, so the lifted cellular chain group in degree $n$ is a free $\mathbb Z[H]=\Lambda_r$-module with one basis element per $n$-cell of $E_L$. [F1, given, choose]

1.2 Translating a lifted characteristic map by $h\in H$ translates all of its oriented boundary cells by the same $h$. Thus every cellular boundary map is $\Lambda_r$-linear. The cellular identity $\partial^2=0$ then makes these finite-rank free modules a chain complex over $\Lambda_r$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.1 Each deck transformation is cellular on the lifted CW structure. By the naturality in [F3], the cellular-to-singular homology isomorphism commutes with every deck transformation and hence is $\Lambda_r$-linear. In degree one it identifies the homology of the lifted cellular complex with $H_1(E_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F3, step 1.2]

2.2 Under the Axiom-of-Choice convention [A1], [F2] says inclusion of the restricted maximal abelian cover into $X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}$ induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism on first homology. Therefore the lifted cellular complex has first homology $A_L$ with the stated deck action. [A1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

**Inputs and admissible conditions.** Fix the domain $D$, wavenumber $k>0$, and library Fourier convention from the fixed-frequency data definition. Give nonempty finite lists of incident directions $d_1,\ldots,d_s\in S^2$ and observation directions $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\in S^2$. Give a finite measurable partition $D=\bigsqcup_{n=1}^N E_n$ with $|E_n|>0$, complex Born-data samples $y=(y_{ba})\in\mathbb C^{rs}$, a discrepancy threshold $\delta\ge0$, and an iteration budget $B\in\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. The sample frequency for pair $(\theta_b,d_a)$ is $\xi_{ba}:=k(\theta_b-d_a)/(2\pi)$. The declared finite discrete Born Fourier matrix $F\in\mathbb C^{rs\times N}$ has entries
$$F_{(b,a),n}:=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{E_n}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi_{ba}}\,dx.$$
For a piecewise-constant contrast $q_c:=\sum_{n=1}^N c_n1_{E_n}$, its sampled first Born data vector is exactly $Fc$.
The input also declares a reduced singular-value decomposition
$$Fc=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\sigma_j\langle c,v_j\rangle u_j\qquad(c\in\mathbb C^N),$$
where $p=\operatorname{rank}F$, the positive singular values $\sigma_j$ have orthonormal right vectors $v_j$ and orthonormal left vectors $u_j$, and the empty sum is used when $F=0$. Give a scalar filter $g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$ whose values at the $\sigma_j$ are finite and with $g(0)=0$. The threshold filter $g_\tau(\sigma)=1/\sigma$ for $\sigma>\tau$ and $g_\tau(\sigma)=0$ for $0\le\sigma\le\tau$ is the truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau\ge0$.

**Instructions and outputs.**

1. If $B=0$, return no estimate, no residual, and status **budget-exhausted**, with zero filter applications.
2. If $B\ge1$, form the coefficient estimate
   $$\widehat c:=\sum_{j:\sigma_j>0}g(\sigma_j)\langle y,u_j\rangle v_j,$$
   where $\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_\ell z_\ell\overline{w_\ell}$ is linear in its first argument. Return the piecewise-constant reconstruction $\widehat q:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\widehat c_n1_{E_n}$ after exactly one filter application.
3. Compute the finite data residual $R:=\|F\widehat c-y\|_2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\sum_\ell|z_\ell|^2)^{1/2}$. Return status **discrepancy** when $R\le\delta$, and **residual-above-threshold** when $R>\delta$; in either case also return $\widehat q$, $R$, and the application count $1$.

This procedure only defines one filtered finite-dimensional Born reconstruction and a residual status. The residual is not an exact-range test for an infinite-dimensional compact forward operator and does not establish a nonlinear solution, identifiability, stability, convergence, or correctness of the reconstructed contrast.

## Definition

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, meaning one oriented component of a finite smooth oriented link in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$. The grid orientation below fixes the sign convention for its Alexander grading.

For an integer $n\ge2$, put $T_n=\mathbb R^2/(n\mathbb Z)^2$, with horizontal circles $\alpha_i=\{y=i\}$ and vertical circles $\beta_j=\{x=j\}$ for $i,j\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$. A **toroidal grid diagram of grid number $n$** is a pair of disjoint sets $\mathbb O,\mathbb X$ of points in the open cells of this grid such that every row and every column contains exactly one point of each set. At each crossing of the projected link, the vertical segment is over and the horizontal segment is under. Orient each horizontal segment from its $O$-marking to its $X$-marking and each vertical segment from its $X$-marking to its $O$-marking. The markings and these segments determine an oriented link. Following each component from an $O$ along its row to an $X$ and then along that column to the next $O$ defines a permutation of the $n$ $O$-markings; its cycles are the link components. The grid represents a knot precisely when this permutation is one $n$-cycle.

A **grid state** is a subset $\mathbf x\subset\bigcup_{i,j}(\alpha_i\cap\beta_j)$ containing exactly one intersection on each horizontal and each vertical circle. After numbering the circles, grid states correspond bijectively to permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, so there are $n!$ states. For states $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$, a **rectangle from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$** is an embedded torus rectangle whose sides lie in grid circles, whose northeast and southwest corners lie in $\mathbf x$, whose northwest and southeast corners lie in $\mathbf y$, and whose remaining state points agree. Rectangles are subsets of the torus, so their lifts may cross a chosen fundamental-domain edge. Such a rectangle is **empty** when its interior contains no point of $\mathbf x$; write $\operatorname{Rect}^{\circ}(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ for the empty rectangles from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$.

To define the gradings, fix the fundamental square $[0,n)\times[0,n)$. For finite signed point sets $P,Q$ in this square, set $I(P,Q)=\#\{(p,q):p_1<q_1,\ p_2<q_2\}$ and $J(P,Q)=(I(P,Q)+I(Q,P))/2$, extended bilinearly to signed point sets. Regard $\mathbf x$, $\mathbb O$, and $\mathbb X$ as signed point sets and define

$$M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)=J(\mathbf x-\mathbb O,\mathbf x-\mathbb O)+1,\qquad M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)=J(\mathbf x-\mathbb X,\mathbf x-\mathbb X)+1.$$

For a knot grid, define the rational Alexander value

$$A_G(\mathbf x)=\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)}{2}-\frac{n-1}{2}.$$

The lemma establishing integrality and the rectangle-change formula is a well-definedness supplier for this grading. For any rectangle $r$, let $O_i(r)$ and $X_i(r)$ be $1$ if the interior of $r$ contains the corresponding marking and $0$ otherwise; let $n_{\mathbb O}(r)=\sum_iO_i(r)$ and $n_{\mathbb X}(r)=\sum_iX_i(r)$.

For illustration, this $3\times3$ marking pattern has one marking of each type in every row and column; its wraparound arrows are interpreted on the torus.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8]
  \draw[step=1,gray] (0,0) grid (3,3);
  \node at (0.5,0.5) {$O$}; \node at (1.5,0.5) {$X$};
  \node at (1.5,1.5) {$O$}; \node at (2.5,1.5) {$X$};
  \node at (2.5,2.5) {$O$}; \node at (0.5,2.5) {$X$};
  \node[left] at (0,0.5) {$1$}; \node[left] at (0,1.5) {$2$}; \node[left] at (0,2.5) {$3$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Example

Let $\Omega=B((1/2,1/2),1/4)\subset(0,1)^2$, let $\Omega'=B((1/2,1/2),1/8)$, and fix $m=1/2$, $M=3/2$, and contrast $a=1/4$. For every integer $N\ge1$, put $q=\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$, choose $N$ distinct cell centers from the $q\times q$ grid in $[7/16,9/16]^2$, set $r_N=1/(32q)$, and define $\gamma_N=1+a\mathbf1_{E_N}$, where $E_N$ is the union of the radius-$r_N$ disks about those centers. Then every $\gamma_N$ is a real, uniformly elliptic, individually finite-BV conductivity equal to $1$ outside $\Omega'$, but $TV(\gamma_N;\Omega)\ge(\pi a/32)\sqrt N$. Hence the family has no common finite BV bound $R$ and is not contained in any one class $X_2(R)$ as $N$ varies. This is a non-applicability example for a fixed uniform BV theorem, not a counterexample to its conclusion for members of that class.

## Example references

[[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class|The exact ellipticity, collar and BV-ball conventions.]]

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|The distributional total-variation norm.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc|The test-field formula for total variation of BV functions.]]

[de Hoop et al., §5, random finite conductivity samples and BV-class qualification](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

[Terra, §7.1, Definition 7.12 and Theorem 7.18: perimeter measure and Gauss–Green for Lipschitz domains](https://www.ime.usp.br/~glaucio/mat6704/textos/GMTLecureNotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the disk domain and parameters in the Example.

[F1] A conductivity in $X_2(R)$ must be uniformly elliptic, equal to the fixed background outside $\Omega'$, and satisfy the displayed BV norm bound. ([[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class]])

[F2] For $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\}$; symmetry under $\varphi\mapsto-\varphi$ makes this the supremum of absolute pairings. ([[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]])

[F3] A function is in $BV(\Omega)$ when its distributional derivative is a finite vector Radon measure, and its total variation is the mass of that measure; the distributional derivative is linear and annihilates constants. ([[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv]])

## Proof

**Given:** $N\ge1$ and the grid in the Example.

1.1 The square $[7/16,9/16]^2$ has side $1/8$ and lies in $\Omega'$ because its corner radius from $(1/2,1/2)$ is $\sqrt2/16<1/8$. The grid spacing is $s_N=1/(8q)$ and $r_N=s_N/4$. Distinct cell centers are separated by at least $s_N>2r_N$, and each disk lies inside its cell; hence the disks are disjoint and contained in $\Omega'$. Thus $1\le\gamma_N\le1+a=5/4<3/2$ and $\gamma_N=1$ on $\Omega\setminus\Omega'$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For a disk $B(c,r)$ and a smooth compactly supported vector field $\varphi$, polar coordinates give $\int_{B(c,r)}\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx=r\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(c+r(\cos\theta,\sin\theta))\cdot(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\,d\theta$. Indeed, in polar variables $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\rho^{-1}\partial_\rho(\rho\varphi_r)+\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta\varphi_\theta$; integrating against $\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta$ makes the angular derivative integrate to zero and the inner radial term vanish. The distributional definition therefore gives $D\mathbf1_{B(c,r)}=-\nu\,\mathcal H^1|_{\partial B(c,r)}$, whose variation has mass $2\pi r$. Summing these measures over the disjoint disks shows $D\mathbf1_{E_N}$ is finite with variation mass $2\pi r_NN$, so [F3] gives $\mathbf1_{E_N}\in BV(\Omega)$ and [F2] gives the stated upper bound. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The annuli of radii $(r_N/2,3r_N/2)$ about the chosen centers are pairwise disjoint: their outer radii sum to $3r_N=3s_N/4<s_N$, while distinct centers are at least $s_N$ apart. They lie in $\Omega$, since each center is within $\sqrt2/16$ of $(1/2,1/2)$ and $\sqrt2/16+3r_N/2\le\sqrt2/16+3/64<1/4$. On each annulus choose a smooth radial cutoff equal to one at radius $r_N$, vanishing outside the annulus and between zero and one. The sum of the corresponding radial unit-vector fields is smooth, compactly supported in $\Omega$, has norm at most one, and equals the outward normal on every circle. Its flux is $2\pi r_NN$, so [F2] gives the matching lower bound. Since $D\gamma_N=aD\mathbf1_{E_N}$ by [F3] and $a>0$, step 1.2 gives $TV(\mathbf1_{E_N};\Omega)=2\pi r_NN$ and $TV(\gamma_N;\Omega)=2\pi a r_NN=\pi aN/(16q)$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Since $q=\lceil\sqrt N\rceil\le2\sqrt N$, step 2.1 gives $TV(\gamma_N;\Omega)\ge(\pi a/32)\sqrt N$. The value and collar bounds were checked in step 1.1, and every finite union of disks has the finite perimeter computed in step 2.1. Thus each conductivity is individually finite-BV while the total variations diverge, so no fixed $R$ contains the whole family in $X_2(R)$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram on an oriented projection sphere. Choose either checkerboard color. Put a disk in each region of that color and join the opposite colored sectors at every crossing by a half-twisted band, with the twist chosen so that the boundary follows the over-under diagram. After rounding corners these disks and bands form a compact connected embedded spanning surface $F$ for the represented link. If $D$ has crossings, let $G$ be the corresponding Tait graph and orient its edges arbitrarily. Under the retraction of $F$ onto $G$, write a rational homology class as the unique graph cycle $a=\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e e$. There is a single sign $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ such that
$$q(a)=\epsilon\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e^2=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)$$
for every oriented rational multicurve $c$ representing $a$, where $\tau c$ is its normal transfer. Thus $q$ is positive definite or negative definite on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$. For a crossingless connected diagram, use either spanning disk and the zero-dimensional definite form.

## Statement references

[Greene, *Alternating links and definite surfaces*, Theorem 5.1](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/lackenby/Fox.pdf)

[Kindred, *A geometric proof of the flyping theorem*, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.06490v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The connected alternating diagram $D$, a checkerboard color, and an arbitrary orientation of the finite Tait graph's edges when crossings exist.

[F1] Connectedness and alternation refer to the projection graph and to the cyclic over-under crossing visits along each link component. Reducedness is not required here. ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]])

[F2] A connected projection admits a checkerboard coloring, and its Tait graph has one vertex per region of the chosen color and one edge per crossing. With at least one crossing this graph is connected. ([[lem-connected-regular-link-diagram-has-checkerboard-coloring]], [[def-tait-graph-of-a-link-diagram]], [[lem-connected-projection-has-connected-tait-graphs]])

[F3] The homology of a finite graph is its group of graph cycles, since it has no $2$-simplices, and finite simplicial homology agrees with singular homology. ([[thm-simplicial-and-singular-homology-agree-for-simplicial-complexes]])

[F4] A smooth Jordan curve on the projection sphere bounds a closed disk on either side, with no choice assumption; apply the choice-free smooth Jordan-disk result in a stereographic chart ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-jordan-disk-parameters-and-prescribed-collars]]).

## Proof

1.1 Suppose first that there is at least one crossing. Build a small regular neighborhood of the projection graph from disjoint crossing disks and narrow edge strips. To see that its complementary faces are disks, choose a finite spanning tree of the graph; its neighborhood is a disk, by adding each tree strip between two distinct disk components. Add the remaining edge strips one at a time. Each edge core is a properly embedded arc in one complementary disk; its strip cuts that disk along the arc. After rounding corners the two new boundary curves are smooth Jordan curves, and [F4] makes both closed sides disks. At each step the added edge lies in one old face and splits it into the two new faces, so these complementary disks correspond one-to-one to the regions of the projection. Their closures are disjoint from the graph and serve as disk cores. Put a disk in each core of the chosen color. At every crossing join the two appropriate disk cores by a narrow band with one half-twist; choose its direction so that its boundary strands have the diagram's prescribed overpass and underpass. The neighborhoods are disjoint, so the resulting surface is embedded. Its boundary is the usual height realization of $D$. Collapsing each disk to a vertex and each band to its core retracts $F$ onto the Tait graph $G$. This graph is connected by [F2], so $F$ is connected and has a supplied finite disk-and-band presentation. [given, F1, F2, F4, construct]

2.1 Measure the signed half-twist of a band relative to the planar framing of its two disk ends; call this incidence sign $\epsilon_e$. This is the unoriented crossing incidence, not the oriented link crossing sign. At two crossings joined by a projection edge, alternation changes which branch is over, while the chosen-color sector changes sides along that edge. The two changes cancel in the half-twist chart, giving the same incidence sign at the two crossings. Since the projection graph is connected, every band has one common sign $\epsilon$. Reversing the chosen orientation of a graph edge reverses its cycle coefficient, without changing this incidence sign. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 We compute the normal pairing in the disk-and-band presentation. After clearing rational denominators, represent a cycle by finitely many oriented parallel strands through each band, joined by arcs in the vertex disks; any extraneous arc pairs can be canceled inside those disks. The signed number of strands through band $e$ is its graph coefficient $a_e$. Normal transfer gives two local pushoffs of each strand, exchanged at a one-sided passage. In an untwisted planar disk the contributions of the two normal sides to the mixed-crossing count cancel. In a band with a signed half-turn, each ordered pair of an original strand and a transferred strand contributes $\epsilon_e$ to the total pairing: one normal side passes from one side of the original strand to the other during the half-turn, and the other normal side makes the complementary passage; the two mixed crossings have the same incidence sign, and the linking count is half their signed sum. Reversing either strand orientation reverses the corresponding contribution. Consequently the contribution of that band is $\epsilon_e(\sum_i s_i)(\sum_j s_j)=\epsilon_e a_e^2$, where $s_i=\pm1$ are the strand orientations. This is also a direct computation with the half-twisted strip $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v\cos(\pi u),v\sin(\pi u))$, reversing the half-turn for the other sign. The strips' end collars are included in this count; crossings of joining arcs in the planar disks cancel between the two normal sides. Linking here can be computed by the signed mixed-crossing count because a finite oriented smoothing of the first curve gives spanning disks and crossing bands, whose intersections with the second curve give that count. This finite construction uses the supplied drawing and does not use a link-diagram invariance theorem. Summing over all bands and restoring rational coefficients gives $\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)=\sum_e\epsilon_e a_e^2$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 By [F3] and the retraction in step 1.1, a homology class has a unique graph cycle vector. Thus $q(a)=\epsilon\sum_e a_e^2$ is a well-defined quadratic form on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, and step 3.1 proves the required normal-transfer formula for every representative. If $a\ne0$, some edge coefficient is nonzero, so $\sum_ea_e^2>0$. Therefore $q$ is positive definite if $\epsilon=1$ and negative definite if $\epsilon=-1$. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If the connected diagram has no crossings, it is a single circle. Either complementary disk is an embedded connected spanning disk with $H_1=0$. Every cycle in that disk bounds there and has zero linking with its normal transfer, so the zero-dimensional form has the asserted formula and definiteness. This also covers the zero-dimensional cycle space of a Tait tree in the preceding case. [given, F1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold with $k\ge1$ torus cusps and a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric. Choose a peripheral basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ on each cusp. On the augmented holonomy space obtained by selecting one common invariant line on each peripheral subgroup, near the complete structure write $u_i$ and $v_i$ for the logarithms of the eigenvalue ratios of the peripheral holonomies of $\mu_i$ and $\lambda_i$, with branches chosen so $u_i=v_i=0$ at the complete structure. There is a neighborhood of the complete point in the $k$ generalized parameter spheres such that primitive integral filling data $(p_i,q_i)$ in that neighborhood satisfying $p_i u_i+q_i v_i=2\pi i$ at every filled cusp produce a complete finite-volume hyperbolic structure on the ordinary filled manifold. The peripheral full-turn equations are solved simultaneously across the $k$ cusps; unfilled cusps retain their complete parabolic holonomy. No universal numeric length threshold is asserted.

## Statement references

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 5, §5.8](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/5.pdf)

[Petronio and Porti, *Negatively Oriented Ideal Triangulations and a Proof of Thurston’s Hyperbolic Dehn Filling Theorem*, Theorem 0.1 and §§1–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the full finite-volume $k$-cusped metric, the ordered peripheral bases and the primitive filling data.

[A1] AC supplies DC and countable choice. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] The given metric has a Kleinian quotient description and a compact smooth core with standard torus cusps. [[lem-complete-curvature-minus-one-manifolds-are-kleinian-quotients]], [[lem-finite-volume-hyperbolic-three-manifolds-have-finite-standard-cusp-decompositions]]

[F2] The augmented deformation germ is smooth of complex dimension $k$, with independent logarithms $u_i$ and $v_i=u_i\tau_i(u)$, where the complete $\tau_i$ are nonreal; for positive bases their imaginary parts are positive. [[thm-augmented-finite-volume-hyperbolic-holonomy-coordinates]]

[F3] These factors admit a product neighborhood of the complete generalized parameters with unique simultaneous small full-turn solutions, continuous also at partially unfilled tuples. [[lem-simultaneous-peripheral-full-turn-equations-have-small-solutions]]

[F4] Given such primitive solutions, the explicit developed ends extend to smooth solid-torus cores; the resulting metric is complete and has finite volume. Coordinates $u_i=0$ remain complete cusps. [[thm-small-augmented-holonomy-deformations-have-smooth-geometric-fillings]]

[F5] Ordinary fillings use primitive slopes modulo sign, and cusp lengths use chosen-section Euclidean norms. [[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]], [[def-cusp-slope-length]], [[def-pared-hyperbolic-structures-and-volume]]

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the input metric satisfies the standard cusp and quotient hypotheses of [F2]. Temporarily orient every peripheral basis positively by replacing its second element by its negative exactly where necessary. The augmented theorem [F2] supplies one common neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^k$ with holomorphic $\tau_i$ and $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(0)>0$. Changing back the second basis element negates $v_i$ and $\tau_i$, so their complete values remain nonreal for every original basis. The logarithms are taken on this augmented space; their branched relationship with ordinary trace-squared coordinates is part of [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 Shrink the small neighborhood enough for [F4]. Apply [F3] there to all $k$ factors simultaneously, rather than solving independent one-cusp deformations. It gives a radius $R$ and a product neighborhood $V=\prod_i(\{(p,q):p^2+q^2>R^2\}\cup\{\infty\})$ in which every tuple has its unique small solution. Its $i$th coordinate is zero exactly for the parameters $\infty$. At every finite coordinate it satisfies $p_i u_i+q_i v_i=2\pi i$. This is the asserted neighborhood and the full simultaneous solution. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 At a primitive integral coordinate, [F4] realizes the holonomy family by a metric and identifies the developed end as a punctured ordinary tube whose meridional angular period is precisely one full turn. It fills that end by a smooth geodesic core. Its complete proof treats the finite collection of ends together, proves metric completeness and finite volume, and leaves each $u_i=0$ end a complete translation cusp. If a supplied basis was negative, change $q_i$ to $-q_i$ along with $v_i$ to $-v_i$ before applying that supplier; the equation and unoriented primitive slope are unchanged. Return afterward to the supplied bases. Thus the construction applies to every allowed tuple and its ordinary filling data. By [F5], no nonprimitive coefficient is being called an ordinary slope. The constants depend on the original metric and the cusp coordinates, as permitted; no universal length bound is asserted. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-ip-bolker-geometric-criteria
kind: lemma
title: "Global fiber and local differential criteria for Bolker"
status: draft

      url: "https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/MazzucchelliSaloTzou2023.pdf"
      locator: "§3, Lemmas 3.2–3.3 and their proofs, printed pp. 19–24."
    - title: "Johannes Sjöstrand, Singularités analytiques microlocales"
      url: "https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1982__95__R3_0.pdf"
      locator: "§6, Proposition 6.2, printed pp. 37–38, for cotangent-coordinate invariance."
proof_strategy: direct
---

## Statement

Let $Z\subset G\times X$ be an analytic double fibration, and fix a local parameterization of its fibers over $G$,
$$
(g,s)\longmapsto (g,x(g,s)),
$$
where $s\in\mathbb R^d$ and $D_sx$ has rank $d$. Define
$$
E_g=\{(s,\xi):\xi\in T^*_{x(g,s)}X\setminus0,\ (D_sx(g,s))^T\xi=0\}, \qquad L_g(s,\xi)=(D_gx(g,s))^T\xi.
$$
On the cotangent relation over this incidence chart, the left projection is
$$
(g,s,\xi)\longmapsto(g,L_g(s,\xi)).
$$
Consequently it is injective on this chart portion exactly when each map $(s,\xi)\mapsto L_g(s,\xi)$ is injective on $E_g$. Its differential is injective exactly when the only $(\dot s,\dot\xi)$ satisfying
$$
(D_sx)^T\dot\xi+(D_s^2x[\dot s,\cdot])^T\xi=0,\qquad (D_sD_gx[\dot s,\cdot])^T\xi+(D_gx)^T\dot\xi=0
$$
is $(0,0)$. At a specified point of the full relation, the Bolker condition also requires that no point outside this chart portion has the same data covector; this is the global fiber-singleton clause. The displayed system is the local differential rank test.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform|Analytic double fibration]]

[[def-ip-bolker-condition|Bolker condition]]

[[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel|Incidence conormal coordinates]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The local fiber parameterization and its analytic double-fibration hypotheses.

[F1] [[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform]]: $\pi_G$ and $\pi_X$ are submersions and the incidence relation is defined by the conormal bundle.

[F2] [[def-ip-bolker-condition]]: the global condition is an injective immersion of the left projection; the pointwise condition is a singleton full fiber together with an injective differential at that point.

[F3] [[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel]]: local defining functions give the conormal relation with sign convention $(\eta,-\xi)$.

## Proof

**Given:** The parameterization $(g,s)\mapsto(g,x(g,s))$.

1.1 A tangent vector to $Z$ at $(g,x(g,s))$ has the form $ (\dot g,D_gx\,\dot g+D_sx\,\dot s). $ A pair $(\eta,-\xi)$ annihilates every such tangent vector exactly when $(D_sx)^T\xi=0$ and $\eta=(D_gx)^T\xi$. This follows by setting $\dot g=0$ and then varying $\dot g$ arbitrarily. Thus all conormal pairs, except the zero pair, are parameterized by $(g,s,\xi)\in E_g$. The rank condition on $D_sx$ makes this conormal parameterization smooth. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Under this parameterization, the left projection sends $(g,s,\xi)$ to $(g,(D_gx)^T\xi)$, as stated. Because the first component is retained, two points in this chart portion have the same left image exactly when their $g$ coordinates agree and their values under $L_g$ agree. This proves the chart-portion injectivity criterion; it says nothing about a second preimage outside this chart. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 A tangent vector in the kernel of the differential of the left projection has $\dot g=0$. Differentiating the defining equation $(D_sx)^T\xi=0$ along $(\dot s,\dot\xi)$ gives $ (D_sx)^T\dot\xi+(D_s^2x[\dot s, \cdot])^T\xi=0. $ Differentiating its output $(D_gx)^T\xi$ gives the second displayed equation in the statement. Therefore the differential is injective exactly when the simultaneous system has only the zero solution. This is the asserted rank test, and by [F2] it is precisely the local immersion clause of Bolker. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-kz-connection-flatness-and-braid-relations
kind: lemma
title: Flatness of the KZ connection and braid relations
status: draft
origin: pipeline

deps:

justified_by: []

      url: https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf
    - title: The Fundamental Theorem of Vassiliev Invariants, §§2.3–2.4
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1
---

## Statement

For every integer $q\ge2$, let $\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$ be the space of ordered $q$-tuples of pairwise distinct complex points, and let $\widehat{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb C}(q)$ and $t_{ij}$ be as defined for parenthesized braids. Write $\sigma_i$ for the positive geometric half twist interchanging adjacent strands $i$ and $i+1$ in a disk containing no other strand. The Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov form
$$\Omega_q=\frac1{2\pi i}\sum_{1\le i<j\le q}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j)$$
satisfies $d\Omega_q=0$ and $\Omega_q\wedge\Omega_q=0$. Consequently the degreewise iterated-integral holonomy depends only on the homotopy class of a path with fixed endpoints. On geometric braids this holonomy respects the distant commutation relations $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i$ for $|i-j|\ge2$ and the adjacent braid relations $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$.

## Statement references

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §§10.1.1–10.1.4, printed pp. 269–273](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §§2.3–2.4, PDF pp. 10–12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $q\ge2$, the configuration space $\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$, the completed strand algebra $\widehat{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb C}(q)$ with its infinitesimal braid relations, and the KZ form $\Omega_q$.

[F1] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: the strand algebra is degreewise completed, is generated by $t_{ij}=t_{ji}$, and satisfies $[t_{ij},t_{kl}]=0$ for distinct indices and $[t_{ij},t_{ik}+t_{jk}]=0$ for distinct $i,j,k$; the KZ form is the displayed logarithmic connection.

[F2] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: a 4T relation is the alternating four-diagram relation obtained by moving one endpoint past either endpoint of a fixed chord; the framed diagram quotient imposes 4T and does not impose 1T.

[F3] [[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative]]: the positive and negative resolutions of a transverse crossing are labelled by the determinant crossing sign, and the positive Artin half twist is positive.

## Proof

**Given:** As above; no choice axiom is assumed.

**Proof technique:** All power-series operations are performed after truncation at a fixed degree $N$. In that finite-dimensional quotient, only finitely many iterated integrals occur; the compatible truncations define the completed holonomy.

1.1 Put $\alpha_{ij}=d\log(z_i-z_j)$. Since $z_i-z_j$ is nonzero on $\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$, in local coordinates $\alpha_{ij}=d(z_i-z_j)/(z_i-z_j)$ and $d\alpha_{ij}=0$ by equality of mixed partial derivatives. Thus $d\Omega_q=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Write $a=t_{ij}$, $b=t_{kl}$ for two distinct chord generators. In the expansion of $\Omega_q\wedge\Omega_q$, the two ordered terms for these generators combine as $[a,b]\alpha_{ij}\wedge\alpha_{kl}$. If the pairs have four distinct indices, $[a,b]=0$ by [F1]; if they are the same pair, $\alpha_{ij}\wedge\alpha_{ij}=0$. Hence only pairs of generators supported on a common triple of strands can contribute. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $i<j<k$ and put $a=t_{ij}$, $b=t_{ik}$, $c=t_{jk}$, $x=\alpha_{ij}$, $y=\alpha_{ik}$, and $z=\alpha_{jk}$. The tangled 4T relation on these three strands is exactly the pair of infinitesimal braid relations $[a,b+c]=0$ and $[b,a+c]=0$. The contribution of this triple is $[a,b]x\wedge y+[a,c]x\wedge z+[b,c]y\wedge z$. The infinitesimal braid relations in [F1] give $[a,c]=-[a,b]$ and $[b,c]=[a,b]$, so this is $[a,b](x\wedge y-x\wedge z+y\wedge z)$. With $u=z_i-z_j$ and $v=z_j-z_k$, we have $x=du/u$, $z=dv/v$, and $y=d(u+v)/(u+v)$. Direct expansion gives $x\wedge z+z\wedge y+y\wedge x=(1/(uv)-1/(v(u+v))-1/(u(u+v)))du\wedge dv=0$, which is equivalent to $x\wedge y-x\wedge z+y\wedge z=0$. Thus every triple contribution vanishes. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The repeated-pair, disjoint-pair, and three-index cases exhaust the expansion of $\Omega_q\wedge\Omega_q$; steps 2.1–3.1 show that each contribution is zero. Together with step 1.1 this gives $d\Omega_q=0$ and $\Omega_q\wedge\Omega_q=0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Fix a smooth path $\gamma$ and let $U(t)$ solve $\dot U=A_tU$, $U(0)=1$, where $A_t=\Omega_q(\dot\gamma(t))$. In each degree this is a finite linear ODE system, solved recursively by the iterated-integral formula. For a homotopy $\gamma(s,t)$ with fixed endpoints, set $A_s=\Omega_q(\partial_s\gamma)$ and $W=U^{-1}(\partial_sU-A_sU)$. Differentiating and using $\partial_tU=A_tU$ gives $\partial_tW=U^{-1}(\partial_sA_t-\partial_tA_s+[A_t,A_s])U$. The coefficient in parentheses is the evaluation of the flatness expression from step 4.1, so it is zero. Since the initial endpoint is fixed, $W(s,0)=0$ and hence $W(s,t)=0$; at the fixed terminal endpoint $A_s=0$, so $\partial_sU(s,1)=0$. The holonomy is therefore constant throughout the homotopy. [given, F1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 The KZ form is unchanged by relabeling the strands, since its sum runs over every unordered pair; endpoint strand permutations therefore act on holonomy by the same permutation of the $t_{ij}$. For $|i-j|\ge2$, the paths for $\sigma_i$ and $\sigma_j$ lie in disjoint two-point disks, so exchanging their time intervals is a fixed-endpoint homotopy and step 5.1 gives $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i$. For three adjacent points, start at $(-1,0,1)$ and follow the configuration path $(-e^{\pi it},0,e^{\pi it})$, $0\le t\le1$. Its endpoints agree as unordered configurations with the three points reversed, and its pairwise distances stay bounded below by $1$. At $t=1/2$ the three real projections coincide. Small perturbations of the trajectories therefore remain collision-free and can separate the three projected crossing times in either of the two orders; both perturbed paths are homotopic to this rigid half-turn and give respectively $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i$ and $\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$. By step 5.1 their transports agree. [F1, F3, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $K^\dagger$ be the reverse mirror of an oriented knot $K$. Then
$$
s(K^\dagger)=-s(K).
$$

## Statement references

[[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot|Reverse-mirror convention]]

[[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex|Lee complex and quantum filtration]]

[[def-rasmussen-s-invariant|Filtration-level definition of s]]

[Rasmussen, *Khovanov homology and the slice genus* (2004), §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131v1)

[McMullen, *4-Manifolds*, §5.6](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/4Mnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite regular diagram $D$ of $K$.

[F1] The normalized Lee cube has state quantum degree $|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg_q(a)$ and the deformation differential preserves or raises this grading ([[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex]]).

[F2] For a knot, the two extremal Lee filtration levels differ by $2$, with $s=s_{\max}-1=s_{\min}+1$ ([[thm-lee-homology-of-a-knot-has-two-generators]], [[def-rasmussen-s-invariant]]).

[F3] The reverse mirror is obtained by the fixed orientation-reversing reflection followed by reversal of the knot orientation ([[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot]]).

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the axiom branch inherited from diagram independence of Lee filtration levels ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-rasmussen-s-invariant]]).

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the two-dimensional Lee homology of $K$, and its reverse mirror.

1.1 On $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$ use $\langle u,v\rangle=\epsilon_L(uv)$, whose matrix in the basis $1,X$ is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Thus $1,X$ are dual labels of opposite quantum degrees. The displayed Frobenius maps give $\langle m(a,b),c\rangle=\langle a\otimes b,\Delta(c)\rangle$ on the eight basis triples, and the analogous split identity follows by transposition. Number the crossings identically on $D$ and its mirror. For a mirror vertex $w$, its corresponding original vertex is $v=1-w$. The local smoothing chart interchanges A and B under reflection, so their resolved circles agree. On the dual complex put $(C^\vee)^i=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(C^{-i},\mathbb Q)$ and $d^\vee=(d)^*$; this convention squares to zero directly. For the mirror edge changing coordinate $j$, the original reversed edge has sign $(-1)^{\sum_{k<j}v_k}$, while its mirror sign is $(-1)^{\sum_{k<j}w_k}=(-1)^{j-1}(-1)^{\sum_{k<j}v_k}$. Multiply the tensor-pairing identification on mirror vertex $w$ by $\sigma(w)=(-1)^{\sum_j(j-1)w_j}$. Since $\sigma(w+e_j)/\sigma(w)=(-1)^{j-1}$, this makes every edge commute with the transposed original edge. It is therefore an actual cochain isomorphism, including cube signs. With $n=n_++n_-$, complementation gives $i'=-i$ and state shift $|w|+n'_{+}-2n'_{-}=-|v|-n_++2n_-$, the negative original shift. Dual tensor labels have opposite label degrees as well, giving $q'=-q$. Reversing the knot orientation leaves crossing signs and resolutions unchanged, so the same isomorphism applies to $K^\dagger$. [F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For a finite filtered cochain complex $C$, the just-described dual quantum filtration is $F^pC^\vee=\operatorname{Ann}(F^{1-p}C)$ in complementary cohomological degrees. Evaluation induces a perfect pairing $H(C^\vee)\times H(C)\to\mathbb Q$: cocycles are exactly the functionals vanishing on boundaries, and coboundaries are exactly those vanishing on cycles, by finite elimination. Its induced homology filtration is exactly the annihilator filtration. Indeed one direction follows by evaluating representatives. Conversely a homology functional vanishing on classes represented by cycles in $F^{1-p}C$ defines a functional on the sum of the cycle space and $F^{1-p}C$, using its given values on cycles and zero on the latter subspace. The intersection condition makes this well-defined. Extend it across a finite vector-space complement; it is a cocycle because it vanishes on boundaries and represents the required dual class in $F^p$. Thus the finite homology graded quotients occur in opposite degrees under duality. Applied to the two Lee lines, $s_{\max}(K^\dagger)=-s_{\min}(K)$ and $s_{\min}(K^\dagger)=-s_{\max}(K)$. By [A1] and [F2], $s_{\max}(K)=s(K)+1$ and $s_{\min}(K)=s(K)-1$, so $s(K^\dagger)=s_{\max}(K^\dagger)-1=-s(K)$. This finite basis argument adds no choice assumption. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Remark

The cited version of Dunfield, Lipshitz and Schütz's paper (v3, November 2025) reports that, as of April 2023, 17,991 prime knots with at most 19 crossings still had smooth sliceness status unknown in the cited census. Their reported refined LEO computations obstruct smooth sliceness for 890 of these knots; at least 832 of those 890 have Alexander polynomial one and are topologically slice by the criterion cited in that paper. These are dated source-reported computation results, not an independently recomputed or current census.

## Remark references

[[def-odd-khovanov-barnatan-and-leo-triple|LEO invariant data]]

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|Smooth and topological slice genus]]

[Dunfield–Lipshitz–Schütz, *Local equivalence and refinements of Rasmussen's s-invariant* (v3, 2025), §7.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.09114v3)

**Given:** The stated dated report from the cited version of the paper.

[F1] The paper's §7.1 reports the 17,991-knot cohort, 890 obstructions, and the lower bound of 832 topologically slice knots as of April 2023 (Dunfield–Lipshitz–Schütz, §7.1).

## Proof

**Given:** The numerical counts in [F1].

1.1 The paper's stated cohort is historical and date-qualified. Dividing the reported count by the cohort size gives $890/17{,}991\approx0.04947$, or approximately $4.95\%$, which rounds to the paper's “5%” description. Since $832\le890$, the reported lower bound for topologically slice knots is consistent with the reported obstructed subset. [F1, algebra]

2.1 No knot-by-knot calculation or present-day census is asserted in the Remark. Its claims are exactly the dated source report in [F1], with the percentage check from step 1.1; the topological sliceness count is attributed to the criterion cited by the source rather than re-proved here. [F1, step 1.1] ∎
