## Statement

Assume AC and let $G=\mathbb Z/d$ for any positive integer $d$. For every compact closed oriented smooth four-manifold $X$ and homomorphism $\psi:\pi_1(X)\to G$ (componentwise if needed),
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X,\psi)=\operatorname{sign}(X).$$
Surjectivity is not required.

Let $M$ be a closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold and $\phi:\pi_1(M)\to G$. Suppose $(W_i,\psi_i)$, $i=0,1$, are compact connected oriented smooth four-manifolds with their entire boundary identified with $M$, supplied smooth collars, and coefficient homomorphisms extending the same based $\phi$. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0,\psi_0)-\operatorname{sign}(W_0)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1,\psi_1)-\operatorname{sign}(W_1).$$
Whenever such a smooth extension exists, denote this common value by $\rho^{\mathrm{sm}}_d(M,\phi)$. In particular, for the actual zero surgery of every finite smooth oriented disk-band knot with its supplied first-variable positive-push matrix $V$ and positive meridional map $\phi_d$,
$$\rho^{\mathrm{sm}}_d(M_K,\phi_d)=\frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{sign}\bigl((1-\zeta_d^r)V+(1-\zeta_d^{-r})V^T\bigr),\qquad\zeta_d=e^{2\pi i/d}.$$
All singular character forms, the zero trivial-character term, $d=1$ and even $d$ are included.

These assertions establish independence among the indicated **smooth** bounding extensions. They assert neither existence of such an extension for every pair $(M,\phi)$, identification with an analytic eta invariant, independence from nonsmooth TOP bounding manifolds, an infinite-cyclic average nor a closed-index assertion for arbitrary groups.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite cyclic group and actual smooth geometric and coefficient data above.

[F1] Compact twisted signature operators define an integer-valued additive smooth bundle index. Every actual finite-character line has finite tensor order, so its index is the untwisted signature; the Hodge/chirality calculation identifies that index with its actual character intersection signature. [[thm-compact-twisted-signature-operators-give-additive-bundle-indices]]

[F2] The finite cyclic regular algebra splits by its explicit Fourier idempotents, each of trace $1/d$; for surjective coefficient maps the actual finite-cover signature is the sum of character signatures and its von Neumann signature is their normalized mean, including radicals. The finite algebra calculation, extended explicitly to possibly disconnected covers below, is what is used for nonsurjective maps. [[lem-finite-cyclic-von-neumann-signatures-are-character-averages]]

[F3] For compact oriented smooth four-manifolds glued along their common entire boundary and matching coefficient homomorphisms, ordinary and $L^2$ signatures subtract under $W_0\cup_M(-W_1)$, with the stated convention. [[lem-signature-additivity-under-gluing]]

[F4] The actual finite disk-band construction bounds the oriented zero surgery with the extending positive meridian map, and its canonical defect equals the displayed first-push signature average for every $d$. [[thm-canonical-finite-cyclic-knot-defects-equal-seifert-signature-averages]]

[F5] Smooth manifolds have universal covers by the path-class construction, since their coordinate balls are simply connected. Compact smooth manifolds have finite boundary-compatible triangulations. Matching homomorphisms glue by Van Kampen. [[thm-universal-cover-existence]] The universal deck group is the fundamental group with its stated traversal convention. [[thm-deck-group-of-a-universal-cover-is-the-fundamental-group]] [[thm-compact-smooth-manifolds-with-corners-admit-relative-finite-triangulations]] [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

## Proof

1.1 First take $X$ connected. The homomorphism $\psi$ gives an actual finite principal $G$-cover, even if its image is proper: form $(\widetilde X\times G)/\pi_1(X)$ using the action $\gamma\cdot(x,g)=(\gamma x,\psi(\gamma)^{-1}g)$, which is an action since $G$ is abelian, and retain right translation on the $G$ factor as the specified free fiber-transitive deck action. Over any simply connected coordinate ball choose one universal sheet; the quotient is that ball times the finite set $G$. These local identifications have locally constant sheet permutations, so define the smooth covering structure and orientation. At a chosen basepoint the lift of a loop $\gamma$ ends at $[\gamma\widetilde x,g]=[\widetilde x,\psi(\gamma)g]$, so this is the actual prescribed monodromy rather than its inverse. Its degree is exactly $d$, and its total space may be disconnected. It is compact by finitely many compact lift closures of smaller evenly covered charts. Pull back a Riemannian metric. By [F5] the base pair, and therefore its finite cover, have actual finite cellular complexes. Thus every Hilbert-module complex in [F2] is simply finite-dimensional in this application. A compact disconnected $X$ has finitely many components (its connected coordinate charts have a finite covering subfamily), so the subsequent construction applies on each and signatures add. [F5, given, construct]

2.1 Apply the projections $e_r=d^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\zeta_d^{-rk}t^k$ to the finite regular complex of step1.1. Their orthogonality, sum one and traces $1/d$ are the finite geometric-sum identities in [F2]; none uses surjectivity. Kernels, images and middle homology split literally by these projections, and every image is closed. Sesquilinearity makes different components orthogonal, so the positive and negative projections have trace $d^{-1}$ times the sum of their component ranks; the same statement holds after removing each component's radical. This proves the character-mean formula also for the actual possibly disconnected principal cover, without silently applying [F2]'s surjectivity hypothesis in a larger scope. Each character block is the one computed by [F1] on this actual finite cover, with a positive covering normalization. It has signature $\operatorname{sign}(X)$. If the cohomology pullback convention in [F1] reverses a character, all characters are still included and complex conjugation preserves each inertia count. The normalized sum of these $d$ identical integers is $\operatorname{sign}(X)$, proving the closed-index equality for every $\psi$. This step used only finite cyclic character lines; no approximation or general-group closed-index theorem is involved. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the bounding data, use their supplied collars to form the closed smooth oriented manifold $X=W_0\cup_M(-W_1)$. The coefficient homomorphisms agree on the common based boundary group, so [F5] gives the actual glued homomorphism $\psi:\pi_1(X)\to G$. The intersection is the connected full boundary collar; no injectivity of its group maps is required. Apply [F3] in precisely its smooth entire-boundary scope. It says $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X,\psi)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0,\psi_0)-\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1,\psi_1)$ and $\operatorname{sign}(X)=\operatorname{sign}(W_0)-\operatorname{sign}(W_1)$. Step2.1 identifies the two left sides. Rearranging gives the asserted equality of defects, without any surjectivity restriction on the boundary map or extensions. Hence the value is well-defined among all the supplied smooth extensions whenever at least one exists. [F3, F5, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 For the knot data, [F4] supplies an actual smooth bounding extension with the exact oriented zero-surgery boundary and positive meridional coefficient homomorphism. Thus the smooth common value of step3.1 exists, and evaluation on this particular extension is [F4]'s displayed average. Its proof treats nontrivial roots directly even when the Alexander form is singular, and treats the trivial character by a separate ordinary metabolic calculation; no invalid specialization at $t=1$ is introduced here. The convention is $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}-\operatorname{sign}$ throughout. The construction and equality now justify the indicated smooth finite-cyclic rho notation, but they do not compare it with a defect from a nonsmooth TOP bounding manifold or with an eta definition. All broader analytic and topological independence obligations remain separate. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented Hausdorff topological four-manifold and put $M=\partial W$, allowing $M$ empty. Let $k$ be a commutative field, $G$ a PTFA group, and $\phi:\pi_1(W)\to G$ a supplied coefficient homomorphism. Write $K$ for the fraction division ring of $k[G]$, with its standard involution, and use the induced rank-one right-coefficient systems. Suppose $\dim_kH_1(M_j;k)=1$ for each connected component $M_j$ of $M$. Then
$$\dim_K\operatorname{coker}\{H_2(M;K)\to H_2(W;K)\}\le\dim_k\operatorname{coker}\{H_2(M;k)\to H_2(W;k)\}.$$
All dimensions in the formula are finite. No choice axiom, smoothness, triangulation, or supplied finite CW model of $W$ is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact oriented manifold, field, group, coefficient homomorphism and boundary first-Betti hypothesis.

[F1] Singular right-coefficient chains of a compact manifold, with boundary allowed, have an actual basis and explicit domination by a bounded finite-free complex. The choice-free Wall construction converts that domination into a nonnegative bounded finitely generated projective chain model, with maps and homotopies. [[thm-finite-geometric-complex-chains-dominate-compact-manifold-chains-in-zf]], [[lem-choice-free-wall-chain-finiteness-from-explicit-domination]]

[F2] Finite projective PTFA base change preserves Euler characteristic and gives $b_1^K\le b_1^k-1$ when $b_0^k=1$ and $b_0^K=0$. The group-ring fractions and standard involution exist for the stated fields. [[lem-ptfa-finite-projective-basechange-preserves-euler-characteristic]], [[lem-ptfa-integral-and-field-group-rings-have-compatible-ore-involutions]]

[F3] Compact boundaries have collars, without choice. Relative and closed cap duality apply to arbitrary underlying abelian-group local systems with commuting actions. The standard unitary structure identifies dual cochains with conjugate chains; its simplexwise formula respects boundary subcomplexes. [[thm-topological-collaring-for-manifold-boundaries]], [[thm-compact-collared-manifold-local-coefficient-lefschetz-duality-in-zf]], [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]], [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]]

[F4] The homology pair sequence is exact with its actual inclusion and boundary maps. [[thm-pair-long-exact-sequences-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the actual $k[G]$ singular complex of $W$ and to each of the finitely many boundary components. Tensoring the specified chain equivalences and homotopies with $k$ or $K$ preserves their equations. On singular generators augmentation sends every group transport to $1$, so these are exactly the ordinary $k$ and twisted $K$ chains. The bounded projective models show that all homology dimensions are finite. By [F2] their alternating homology dimensions are equal; denote the common number by $\chi$. Apply [F1] over $k$ as well when needed. If a coefficient homomorphism is trivial, its actual singular $K$ complex is the constant singular $k$ complex tensored with $K$. Its bounded projective $k$ model is a bounded finite-dimensional vector-space complex; finite elimination splits it into its homology and contractible pairs. Tensoring those finite splittings with $K$ proves equality of all ordinary and $K$ Betti numbers in the trivial case, without a choice of a basis in an infinite vector space. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For a connected space with nontrivial $\phi$, $H_0(-;K)=0$: paths identify all point fibers with the base fiber in degree zero, and a based loop with image $g\ne1$ imposes $(g-1)K=K$, because the nonzero element $g-1$ is invertible in $K$. This argument uses one path for each individual zero-cycle, not a simultaneous path selection. If the homomorphism is trivial, $H_0(-;K)=K$. For $W$ write $\beta_i=\dim_k H_i(W;k)$ and $b_i=\dim_KH_i(W;K)$. If its homomorphism is nontrivial, $\beta_0=1,b_0=0$, so [F2] gives $b_1\le\beta_1-1$. This uses the nonnegative bounded projective model from step 1.1, not an unproved finite CW structure. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 Here is the exact rank formula for either coefficient system. Write $c_i$ for its dimensions on $W$ and $a_i$ for those on $M$. Finite projective models over the division field identify dual cohomology dimensions with homology dimensions by finite elimination, and [F3] therefore gives $H_i(W,M)$ dimension $c_{4-i}$ and boundary dimensions $a_i=a_{3-i}$. If $M$ is nonempty, $H_4(W)=0$: under relative duality it is degree-zero relative cohomology, whose parallel sections vanishing on the nonempty boundary vanish on connected $W$. The top of the pair sequence is then $$0\to H_4(W,M)\to H_3(M)\to H_3(W)\to H_3(W,M)\to H_2(M)\to H_2(W).$$ Successive image dimensions are $c_0$, $a_0-c_0$, $c_3-a_0+c_0$, and $c_1-c_3+a_0-c_0$. Hence the image of $H_2(M)\to H_2(W)$ has dimension $a_1-c_1+c_3-a_0+c_0$, and its cokernel has dimension $$r_*=c_2-a_1+c_1-c_3+a_0-c_0=\chi+2c_1-2c_0-a_1+a_0.$$ In the last equality $H_4(W)=0$ and higher homology vanishes by duality. If $M$ is empty, closed duality gives $c_4=c_0,c_3=c_1$ and $r_*=c_2$, yielding the same formula with $a_0=a_1=0$. Thus the formula is valid in both boundary cases. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For a boundary component write $\beta_i^j,b_i^j$ similarly. If its restricted homomorphism is trivial, step 1.1 gives $b_i^j=\beta_i^j$. Otherwise step 2.1 and [F2], applied to that component's projective model, give $b_0^j=0$ and $b_1^j\le\beta_1^j-1=0$. Thus $b_1^j=0$, while $\beta_0^j=\beta_1^j=1$. In both cases $$\beta_1^j-b_1^j=\beta_0^j-b_0^j.$$ Summing over the finitely many components gives the identical equality for the total boundary Betti numbers $\beta_i(M),b_i(M)$. It also holds for empty boundary, with all four numbers zero. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 If $\phi$ on $W$ is trivial, equality of all Betti numbers and natural ordinary coefficient base change in step 1.1 give equality of the two cokernel dimensions, or equivalently the identical formulas of step 2.2 do. Suppose it is nontrivial. Subtract the $K$ formula from the $k$ formula, using the common Euler number and $\beta_0=1,b_0=0$: $$r_k-r_K=2(\beta_1-1-b_1)-(\beta_1(M)-b_1(M))+(\beta_0(M)-b_0(M)).$$ The last two terms cancel by step 3.1, and the first is nonnegative by step 2.1. This proves the claimed inequality for empty or nonempty boundary. Every chain-model construction used actual domination maps and a finite projective strictification; every subsequent elimination and exact-sequence dimension computation was finite. Therefore no choice principle or smooth/PL/CW assumption on the manifold has been introduced. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U=\mathbb R$, write $B_s(a):=\{t\in\mathbb R:|t-a|<s\}$, and let $F(t)=t$, exact solution $x^\dagger=1$ with exact datum $y=1$, initial value $x_0=15/16$, noise bound $\delta=0$ and datum $y^\delta=1$, forcing fraction $\sigma=1/2$, and discrepancy factor $\tau=3$. For $n\ge0$, define $h_n$ as the minimizer of
$$h\longmapsto\frac12|h+x_n-1|^2+\frac{\alpha_n}{2}|h|^2$$
for some $\alpha_n>0$ satisfying $|h_n+x_n-1|=\sigma|x_n-1|$, and set $x_{n+1}=x_n+h_n$. The claim that this iteration reaches the zero discrepancy threshold $\tau\delta=0$ after finitely many updates is false. Indeed, $B_2(x_0)\subset U$, $x^\dagger\in B_1(x_0)$, $|F'(t)|\le1$, and for all $u,v\in B_2(x_0)$,
$$|F(u)-F(v)-F'(u)(u-v)|\le|u-v|\,|F(u)-F(v)|.$$
Also $e_0:=|x_0-x^\dagger|=1/16<\min\{1,1/8,1/4\}$, and $\tau=3>1/\sigma=2$.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt|Residual-forcing regularized LM iteration]]

[[thm-ip-lm-local-discrepancy-stopping|The positive-noise local stopping theorem]]

[[def-ip-product-tangential-cone-condition|Product-type tangential cone condition]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $F(t)=t$ on $\mathbb R$; $x^\dagger=y=y^\delta=1$; $x_0=15/16$; $\delta=0$; $\sigma=1/2$; $\tau=3$; and the residual-forcing update in the Counterexample section.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the general Hilbert-space LM definition through its adjoint interface ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The LM step minimizes the damped linearized residual and selects $\alpha_n$ so the linearized residual is multiplied by $\sigma$ ([[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt]]).

[F2] The stopping theorem requires $\delta>0$ and does not assert finite stopping at $\delta=0$ ([[thm-ip-lm-local-discrepancy-stopping]]).

[F3] The product condition compares the two-point remainder to the product of the distance and data residual ([[def-ip-product-tangential-cone-condition]]).

## Counterexample



1.1 The derivative of $F(t)=t$ is $F'(t)=1$, so $F(u)-F(\tilde u)-F'(u)(u-\tilde u)=0$ for every $u,\tilde u\in\mathbb R$. Thus the product condition holds on $B_2(x_0)\subset\mathbb R$ with $c=1$, and $|F'(t)|=1=M$. The exact solution lies in $B_1(x_0)$ and $B_2(x_0)\subset U$. Also $e_0=|x_0-x^\dagger|=1/16<1$, while $\frac{\sigma\tau-1}{c(1+\tau)}=\frac18,\qquad\frac{1-\sigma}{2c}=\frac14,$ so the theorem's local smallness clauses hold. Its positive-noise clause does not hold because $\delta=0$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Let $r_n:=1-x_n$. If $r_n>0$, the objective is $\frac12(h-r_n)^2+\frac{\alpha_n}{2}h^2$. Completing the square gives the unique minimizer $h_n=r_n/(1+\alpha_n)$ and $r_n-h_n=\alpha_n r_n/(1+\alpha_n)$. The forcing equation with $\sigma=1/2$ therefore requires $\alpha_n=1$ and gives $h_n=r_n/2$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $x_0=1-1/16$, $r_0=1/16>0$. Whenever $r_n>0$, step 1.2 gives $r_{n+1}=1-x_{n+1}=r_n-h_n=r_n/2$. By induction, $r_n=2^{-n}/16>0$ for every finite $n$. Therefore $|F(x_n)-y^\delta|=r_n>0=\tau\delta$ at every finite index, so no discrepancy crossing occurs. This refutes the stated finite-stopping extension to zero noise. [F2, step 1.2, given, induction, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The positive-noise theorem remains unchanged. This example isolates the boundary case it excludes: exact data with a zero threshold may require infinitely many contractive steps to attain residual zero.

## Definition

Let $Q\in[0,\infty)$ and let $a=(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a nondecreasing sequence of positive real numbers, so $0<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots$. The statistical ellipsoid of radius $Q$ and weights $a$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse model is
$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
No assumption that $a_j\to\infty$ is included. In particular, this definition does not assert that the ellipsoid is compact in $\ell^2$.

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D=[0,1]^3$, $k>0$, and let $r,s\ge1$. Take nonempty finite lists $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{obs}}$ and $d_1,\ldots,d_s\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{inc}}$, where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{obs}},\Gamma_{\mathrm{inc}}\subsetneq S^2$ are proper direction sets. 1.2 First compute the auxiliary positive two-strand closure, whose $A$-smoothing is the identity tangle and whose $B$-smoothing is the cap-cup tangle. With zero, one, two, or three cap-cup smoothings, the closure has respectively two, one, two, or three circles: composing cap-cups creates one additional internal circle each time after the first. Thus its four raw cochain degrees $0,1,2,3$ have modules $M\otimes\mathcal A$, $M^3$, $(M\otimes\mathcal A)^3$, and $M\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$, of ranks $2,3,6,4$. 1.3 Order crossings from top to bottom. The first differential sends $1\otimes1$ to $(1,1,1)$ and $1\otimes X$ to zero, so its image is the diagonal copy of $\mathbb Z$ and its kernel is $\mathbb Z\{1\otimes X\}$. After suppressing the common based factor $M$, the next differential is the signed incidence matrix
$$
\begin{pmatrix}-1&1&0\\-1&0&1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}
$$
with each integer entry multiplying the label $X$, because each edge splits the based circle and the reduced split sends $1$ to $1\otimes X$. Its image has rank two and its kernel is the diagonal copy of $\mathbb Z$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

1.4 Label the three two-circle states in crossing order and identify the two unbased factors in the all-$B$ state from left to right. The last differential is
$$
(a,b,c)\longmapsto a\otimes X-\Delta(b)+X\otimes c.
$$

Its image is exactly the subgroup generated by $1\otimes X$, $X\otimes1$, and $X\otimes X$, and its kernel consists of triples with equal coefficients of $1$ and with coefficients of $X$ satisfying $a_X-b_X+c_X=0$. ## Statement

Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold and $L\to X$ a smooth complex line bundle with a specified isomorphism $L^{\otimes d}\cong\mathbf1$ for a positive integer $d$. Let $K^0_{\mathrm{sm}}(X)$ denote the Grothendieck ring of finite-rank smooth complex vector bundles, with direct sum as addition, tensor product as multiplication and the trivial complex line as unit. Then $[L]-1$ is torsion in its additive group. Explicitly, a finite construction gives an integer $m\ge1$ for which
$$(1-[L])^m=0,\qquad d^{m-1}([L]-1)=0.$$
Consequently every additive homomorphism $I:K^0_{\mathrm{sm}}(X)\to\mathbb Z$ satisfies $I([L])=I(1)$. No stable triviality of $L$, rational characteristic-class formula or index theorem is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact smooth base, smooth line bundle and specified finite tensor-order isomorphism. The standing full AC convention may be retained. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Here the Grothendieck group is defined explicitly using pairs $(E,F)$ of finite-rank smooth complex bundles: $(E,F)$ and $(E',F')$ are equivalent when $E\oplus F'\oplus H\cong E'\oplus F\oplus H$ for some finite-rank smooth bundle $H$. Addition uses direct sums and multiplication uses $(E,F)(E',F')=(E\otimes E'\oplus F\otimes F',E\otimes F'\oplus F\otimes E')$. Bundle distributivity and the tensor flip make this a commutative ring; transitivity follows by adding the two witnessing isomorphisms and including their repeated middle summand in $H$. These formulas are part of the construction, not a claim of cancellation of actual bundles.

## Proof

1.1 Choose finitely many line-bundle trivializing charts with smaller precompact subcharts covering $X$. In each larger chart choose a smooth nonnegative Euclidean bump $\rho_i$, supported inside it and positive on the smaller closure. Their sum is positive, so divide by the sum to make $\sum_i\rho_i=1$. A local nonzero frame $v_i$ defines a global smooth section $s_i=\rho_i v_i$ by zero extension; the support is strictly inside its frame chart. At every point some $s_i$ is nonzero. Thus $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)$ is a nowherezero section of $L^{\oplus m}$. A Hermitian metric on $L$ is constructed by the same finite positive weighted sum of local squared frame norms, which is positive on every nonzero fiber vector. Normalize $s$ in the induced direct-sum metric. Its span is a trivial smooth line subbundle, and the smooth orthogonal projection $u\mapsto\langle u,s\rangle s$ exhibits a smooth complementary bundle $Q$ (in a local frame, extend the nonzero vector to a frame using a nonzero coordinate minor). Hence $L^{\oplus m}\cong\mathbf1\oplus Q$. For empty $X$ take $m=1$ and the zero bundle ring. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 For actual bundles define $\lambda_{-1}(E)=\sum_{k=0}^{\operatorname{rank}E}(-1)^k[\bigwedge^kE]$, componentwise if necessary. The fiberwise map which wedges an $i$-fold wedge from $E$ before a $j$-fold wedge from $F$ gives the smooth isomorphism $\bigwedge^k(E\oplus F)\cong\bigoplus_{i+j=k}\bigwedge^iE\otimes\bigwedge^jF$. Local basis wedges prove bijectivity and respect transitions, so finite distributivity gives $\lambda_{-1}(E\oplus F)=\lambda_{-1}(E)\lambda_{-1}(F)$. For a line $\lambda_{-1}(L)=1-[L]$ and $\lambda_{-1}(\mathbf1)=0$. Apply this actual-bundle identity to step1.1 to obtain $(1-[L])^m=\lambda_{-1}(L^{\oplus m})=\lambda_{-1}(\mathbf1\oplus Q)=0$. No exterior-power operation on virtual differences or splitting principle is used. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $x=[L]-1$ in the commutative ring of [F1]. The given tensor-power isomorphism implies $(1+x)^d=1$. Expanding the finite binomial gives $dx=-x^2q(x)$, where $q(x)=\sum_{j=2}^d\binom djx^{j-2}$ (zero if $d=1$). Induction then gives $d^k x=(-1)^k x^{k+1}q(x)^k$ for every nonnegative integer $k$: multiply the preceding identity by $d$ and substitute $dx=-x^2q(x)$, using commutativity. Step2.1 says $x^m=0$, so taking $k=m-1$ gives $d^{m-1}x=0$, including $m=1$. This is an actual integer annihilator, not just a rational equality. [F1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Applying an additive $I$ to step3.1 gives $d^{m-1}(I([L])-I(1))=0$ in $\mathbb Z$. The coefficient is a positive integer, so the difference is zero. All charts, sections, bundle splittings, powers and sums used above were finite; no triangulation, classification of line bundles, Chern character or infinite-dimensional operator argument entered the assertion. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$, let $y\in\mathbb R^m$, and let $\epsilon\ge0$. Define $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ by $f(x)=\|x\|_1$, and define $g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ by $g(u)=0$ when $\|u-y\|_2\le\epsilon$ and $g(u)=+\infty$ otherwise. Then $f$ and $g$ are proper (finite somewhere), closed (their epigraphs are closed), and convex (they satisfy the extended-real convex-combination inequality) on their respective finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive integers $m,n$, a center $y\in\mathbb R^m$, a radius $\epsilon\ge0$, the functions $f(x)=\|x\|_1$ and $g=\iota_C$ for $C=\{u:\|u-y\|_2\le\epsilon\}$.

[F1] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], and [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]: the one- and two-norms are finite-valued norms, satisfy homogeneity and both triangle inequalities, and $\|x\|_1\le\sqrt{n}\|x\|_2$ for $n\ge1$.

[F2] [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]: a function is proper when its finite domain is nonempty, convex under real convex combinations, and closed when its epigraph is closed.

[F3] [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]: for $0\le\theta\le1$, convexity is the inequality $q((1-\theta)a+\theta b)\le(1-\theta)q(a)+\theta q(b)$, with $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ at endpoints.

[F4] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: a set is convex when every segment between two of its points remains in it.

[F5] [[def-indicator-function-of-closed-convex-set]]: $\iota_C$ equals $0$ on $C$ and $+\infty$ outside it.

[F6] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the Euclidean norm on a product coordinate space is the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences.

[F7] [[def-canonical-natural]]: $n$ denotes the canonical real image of $n$.

[F8] [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]: $n>0$ for $n\ge1$.

[F9] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] and [[lem-of-square-monotone]]: finite sums preserve inequalities, and $a^2\le b^2$ for nonnegative reals implies $a\le b$.

## Proof

1.1 The function $f$ is finite everywhere because it is a finite sum of absolute values, and $f(0)=0$, so its effective domain is nonempty. For $0\le\theta\le1$, the triangle inequality and homogeneity in [F1] give $f((1-\theta)x+\theta z)\le f((1-\theta)x)+f(\theta z)=(1-\theta)f(x)+\theta f(z).$ Thus $f$ is proper and convex by [F2,F3]. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 For $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$ outside $\operatorname{epi}f$, the gap $d=f(x)-t$ is positive. Put $L=\sqrt{n}+1>0$. If $(x',t')$ has product Euclidean distance $D<d/(2L)$ from $(x,t)$, then coordinate-square domination gives $\|x'-x\|_2\le D$ and $|t'-t|\le D$. By [F1], $f(x')-t'\ge f(x)-t-|f(x')-f(x)|-|t'-t|\ge d-(\sqrt{n}+1)D>d/2>0.$ So the complement of $\operatorname{epi}f$ is open and its epigraph is closed. The scalar $L$ is positive by [F8]; the coordinate-square domination follows by comparing a partial sum with the full nonnegative sum and using [F9]. [given, F1, F6, F7, F8, F9, construct, algebra]

1.3 The residual ball $C$ contains $y$ because $\epsilon\ge0$. If $u,v\in C$ and $0\le\theta\le1$, homogeneity and the triangle inequality in [F1] give $\|(1-\theta)u+\theta v-y\|_2\le(1-\theta)\|u-y\|_2+\theta\|v-y\|_2\le\epsilon,$ so $C$ is convex. If $u\notin C$, the gap $d=\|u-y\|_2-\epsilon>0$ and the reverse triangle inequality show that every $v$ with $\|v-u\|_2<d/2$ also lies outside $C$. Thus $C$ is closed. [given, F1, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F5], $\operatorname{epi}g=C\times[0,\infty)$. If $(u,t)$ is outside this epigraph, either $u\notin C$ or $t<0$. In the first case step 1.3 supplies an open ball about $u$ disjoint from $C$, hence a product neighborhood disjoint from the epigraph; in the second case an interval about $t$ contained in $(-\infty,0)$ supplies such a product neighborhood. Therefore $\operatorname{epi}g$ is closed. Since $C$ is nonempty by step 1.3, $g$ is proper. If both endpoints lie in $C$, their convex combination lies in $C$ by step 1.3 and $g$ is zero there; if either endpoint has value $+\infty$ with positive coefficient, the convexity inequality has right side $+\infty$. Endpoint coefficients reduce to equality at the endpoint with coefficient one. Thus $g$ is convex, and [F2] proves that both functions have the asserted proper, closed, convex properties. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.3, construct, algebra] ∎

id: lem-ip-lm-product-condition-implies-range-approximation
kind: lemma
title: Product condition gives the LM range-approximation bound

## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let
$F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at every point of $U$ with
$x\mapsto F'(x)$ continuous in operator norm. Let $V\subseteq U$ and let
$c>0$ be such that, for every $u,\tilde u\in V$,
$$\|F(u)-F(\tilde u)-F'(u)(u-\tilde u)\|_Y\le c\|u-\tilde u\|_X\|F(u)-F(\tilde u)\|_Y.$$
Suppose
$x^\dagger,x\in V$, $F(x^\dagger)=y$, $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$ with
$\delta\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|x-x^\dagger\|_X\le e$. If
$R:=\|F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y>\tau\delta$, then

$$\|F'(x)(x^\dagger-x)+F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y\le\frac{1+ce(1+\tau)}{\tau}R.$$

In particular, if $\sigma\in(0,1)$, $e\le e_0$, and
$$\gamma:=\frac{\sigma\tau}{1+ce_0(1+\tau)}>1,$$
then
$$\|F'(x)(x^\dagger-x)+F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y\le\frac{\sigma}{\gamma}R.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-product-tangential-cone-condition|Product-type tangential cone condition]]

[[def-ip-nonlinear-forward-map|Nonlinear forward map and exact-data convention]]

[[def-hilbert-space|Real Hilbert spaces and their induced norms]]

[[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces|Fréchet differentiability and operator-norm derivative]]

[Christian Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Assumption 11.10 and proof of Theorem 11.11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00617v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The spaces, map, set, constant, exact solution, datum, noise bound, $\tau$, and points in the Statement.

[F1] For $x,\tilde x\in V$, the product condition gives
$$\|F(x)-F(\tilde x)-F'(x)(x-\tilde x)\|_Y\le c\|x-\tilde x\|_X\|F(x)-F(\tilde x)\|_Y$$
([[def-ip-product-tangential-cone-condition]]).

[F2] The exact-data convention is $F(x^\dagger)=y$ ([[def-ip-nonlinear-forward-map]]); the noise bound $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$ is an additional hypothesis in the Statement.

[F3] The induced real Hilbert norm satisfies the triangle inequality ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]).

## Proof



1.1 Set $E:=F(x)-F(x^\dagger)-F'(x)(x-x^\dagger)$. By [F1] with $\tilde x=x^\dagger$ and the point-distance bound, $\|E\|_Y\le ce\|F(x)-y\|_Y$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 The target residual equals $E+(y-y^\delta)$. Also [F3] gives $\|F(x)-y\|_Y\le R+\delta$. Therefore [F3] and [F2] yield $\|F'(x)(x^\dagger-x)+F(x)-y^\delta\|_Y\le ce(R+\delta)+\delta.$ [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $R>\tau\delta$ and $\tau>0$, $\delta<R/\tau$. Substituting into step 2.1 and collecting the coefficient of $R$ gives $ce(R+\delta)+\delta\le\left(ce\left(1+\frac1\tau\right)+\frac1\tau\right)R=\frac{1+ce(1+\tau)}{\tau}R,$ which is the first conclusion. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $e\le e_0$, then $1+ce(1+\tau)\le1+ce_0(1+\tau)=\sigma\tau/\gamma$. Applying this inequality to step 3.1 proves the stated $\sigma/\gamma$ range-approximation bound. [given, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

No choice principle is used: the proof applies the product condition to the two fixed points in the hypotheses and then uses norm inequalities.

## Statement

For the supplied $C^1$ objective and ambient gradient oracle, the displayed projected vector is the Frobenius metric-dual gradient of the restricted objective, and every polar trial is defined. For every input satisfying the finite-budget Stiefel gradient procedure, it returns after at most $K$ trial evaluations with an output frame $X_{\rm out}\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$. Every accepted update has nonincreasing objective value, and the returned status is `target-met` exactly when $r(X_{\rm out})\le\tau$; every other returned status has $r(X_{\rm out})>\tau$.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-stiefel-constrained-regularized-gradient|Finite-budget Stiefel gradient procedure]]

[[thm-stiefel-grassmann-tangent-projections|Stiefel tangent-space formula]]

[[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions|Polar retraction formula]]

[[thm-stiefel-retractions-are-first-order|Stiefel-valued polar retraction]]

[Absil, Mahony, and Sepulchre, *Optimization Algorithms on Matrix Manifolds*, Chapter 4, Example 4.1.3](https://assets.press.princeton.edu/chapters/absil/Absil_Chap4.pdf)

[Nicolas Boumal, *An Introduction to Optimization on Smooth Manifolds*, §7.3](https://www.nicolasboumal.net/book/IntroOptimManifolds_Boumal_2023.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and inputs of [[alg-ip-stiefel-constrained-regularized-gradient]], including $X_0\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, a finite integer $K\ge0$, and positive step sizes $\alpha_k$ for $0\le k<K$.

[F1] [[alg-ip-stiefel-constrained-regularized-gradient]] supplies a $C^1$ objective on the ambient open set and an oracle with $D\Phi(X)[Z]=\langle G(X),Z\rangle_F$. At each current frame $X$, the procedure forms $g=G-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G)$ and trials $\eta=-\alpha_k g$.

[F2] [[thm-stiefel-grassmann-tangent-projections]]: $T_X\operatorname{St}(n,p)=\{Z:X^{\mathsf T}Z+Z^{\mathsf T}X=0\}$.

[F3] [[thm-stiefel-retractions-are-first-order]]: the polar map on a Stiefel tangent input is defined and takes values in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$.

[F4] [[alg-ip-stiefel-constrained-regularized-gradient]]: an accepted candidate becomes the current frame, a rejected candidate returns the previous frame, the finite schedule index increases after each accepted nonterminal trial, and the residual test controls the returned status.

## Proof

1.1 For a current $X\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, put $M=X^{\mathsf T}G$. From [F1] and $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p$, the projected gradient satisfies $X^{\mathsf T}g+g^{\mathsf T}X=M+M^{\mathsf T}-2\operatorname{sym}(M)=0$. Thus $g\in T_X\operatorname{St}(n,p)$ by [F2], and multiplication by $-\alpha_k$ keeps $\eta$ tangent. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Put $S=\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G)$, so $S^{\mathsf T}=S$. If $Z\in T_X\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, then $A=X^{\mathsf T}Z$ is skew-symmetric by [F2]. Hence $\langle XS,Z\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(SA)=0$: transposing and cyclically reordering gives $\operatorname{tr}(SA)=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T})=-\operatorname{tr}(AS)=-\operatorname{tr}(SA)$. The derivative of the restriction on a tangent $Z$ is therefore $D\Phi(X)[Z]=\langle G,Z\rangle_F=\langle g,Z\rangle_F$. Together with step1.1 this makes $g$ its tangent metric-dual vector. It is unique, since two such tangent vectors differ by a tangent vector whose pairing with itself is zero. This uses only the supplied first derivative, so $C^1$ suffices. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 The initial frame is in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$ by the input condition. Whenever a current frame is in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, step1.1 makes the trial tangent. Then $(X+\eta)^{\mathsf T}(X+\eta)=I_p+\eta^{\mathsf T}\eta$, so for $v\ne0$ its quadratic form is $\|v\|_2^2+\|\eta v\|_2^2>0$. Thus $X+\eta$ has full column rank, the polar call is in the declared domain of [F3], and [F3] puts its candidate in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)\subset U$. In particular every subsequent objective, residual and oracle evaluation has an input in its supplied domain. An accepted candidate is the next current frame; a rejected candidate returns the previous frame. Hence every current frame and every possible returned frame remains in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$ by finite induction. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The index begins at zero, increases by one after each accepted nonterminal trial, and the loop ends when $k=K$; every other branch returns immediately. Therefore at most $K$ trial evaluations occur. The procedure accepts only candidates with objective no greater than the current value, and its residual test labels an output target-met exactly when its residual is at most $\tau$; every other return branch follows a failed target test and has residual greater than $\tau$. [given, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice, and let $I_m(K)$ be the degree-$m$ homogeneous coefficient of the normalized unframed Kontsevich series $I(K)$ of a smooth oriented knot type $K$. For $n\ge0$, put $I_{\le n}(K)=\sum_{m=0}^{n}I_m(K)$. A function on knot types is of type at most $n$ when its alternating resolution sum on every $(n+1)$-singular knot is zero. Then $I_{\le n}$ is a type-at-most-$n$ invariant with values in the sum of the unframed degree-$m$ chord-diagram modules for $0\le m\le n$. For every $n$-singular knot with chord diagram $D$, its $n$-fold finite difference satisfies $D_n I_{\le n}(K)=D$. In particular, the degree-$n$ symbol is the identity on rational chord diagrams after extending scalars to $\mathbb C$; no rational-coefficient claim is made about $I_m(K)$.

## Statement references

[[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative|Finite differences and type at most n]]

[[thm-kontsevich-universal-associated-graded-proof|Leading symbol of the normalized integral]]

[[lem-kontsevich-braid-and-knot-isotopy-invariance|Ambient-isotopy invariance under countable choice]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §8.8.1, printed pp. 239–240](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §2.6, PDF pp. 16–17](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a degree cutoff $n$, and the unframed normalized series of a strict Morse presentation of each oriented knot type.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: countable choice is assumed only through the ambient-isotopy invariance supplier.

[F1] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: $I(K)$ is the degreewise series in the completed unframed 4T+1T chord-diagram module.

[F2] [[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative]]: $D_kF(K)$ is the alternating sum over the $2^k$ resolutions of a $k$-singular knot; type at most $n$ means $D_{n+1}F=0$ on every $(n+1)$-singular knot.

[F3] [[thm-kontsevich-universal-associated-graded-proof]]: on a $k$-singular knot with chord diagram $D$, $D_kI(K)$ has zero degrees below $k$ and degree-$k$ component exactly $D$.

[F4] [[lem-kontsevich-braid-and-knot-isotopy-invariance]]: under countable choice, $I(K)$ is independent of the strict Morse presentation and is invariant under ambient isotopy of oriented knots.

[F5] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: each degreewise unframed chord-diagram module is the rational 4T+1T quotient, and its complexification is the target of $I_m$.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Let $\pi_{\le n}$ denote projection to homogeneous degrees $0,1,\ldots,n$; it is linear and commutes with finite sums.

1.1 By [F4] the normalized series is invariant under ambient isotopy and independent of its strict Morse presentation. Applying the degree projection $\pi_{\le n}$ preserves equality, so $I_{\le n}=\pi_{\le n}I$ is a well-defined invariant on oriented knot types with the stated target. [A1, F1, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Let $K$ be an $(n+1)$-singular knot with chord diagram $D$. By [F3], every homogeneous component of $D_{n+1}I(K)$ in degree at most $n$ is zero. Since $\pi_{\le n}$ commutes with the alternating resolution sum, $D_{n+1}I_{\le n}(K)=\pi_{\le n}D_{n+1}I(K)=0$. This is exactly the type-at-most-$n$ condition from [F2]. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $K$ instead be $n$-singular with diagram $D$. By [F3], the projection of $D_nI(K)$ to degrees at most $n$ has no terms below degree $n$ and has degree-$n$ term $D$. Therefore $D_nI_{\le n}(K)=\pi_{\le n}D_nI(K)=D$. For $n=0$, the same statement is the degree-zero unit term of [F1]. Thus the degree-$n$ symbol of the truncation is the identity on rational chord diagrams, with coefficients regarded in their complexification. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. An orientation-preserving diffeomorphism
between smooth oriented $3$-manifolds transports the full framing of every
link and induces an isomorphism of their Kauffman bracket skein modules. If
the diffeomorphism carries a specified product collar of a compact oriented
boundary surface productwise to another specified collar, the induced
isomorphism intertwines the two closed-link collar actions. A positive or
negative full framing twist on one link component multiplies its class by
$-A^3$ or $-A^{-3}$, respectively. In $\mathcal K_A(S^3)$, a positive twist
of a zero-framed trivial circle changes its class from
$\delta[\varnothing]$ to $-A^3\delta[\varnothing]$, with
$\delta[\varnothing]\ne -A^3\delta[\varnothing]$. In the solid-torus
module, a positive twist of the blackboard-framed core changes $[z]$ to
$-A^3[z]$, with $[z]\ne -A^3[z]$.

## Statement references
[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice|Choice implies countable choice]]


[[lem-general-3manifold-skein-quotient-isotopy-and-gluing|Functoriality and boundary-collar action]]

[[lem-kauffman-bracket-module-framing-twist-factor|Full framing twists]]

[[thm-skein-module-of-s-three-is-rank-one|S³ skein-module basis]]

[[thm-skein-module-of-solid-torus-has-core-multicurve-basis|Solid-torus skein-module basis]]

[Józef H. Przytycki, *Fundamentals of Kauffman Bracket Skein Modules* (1998), §2, Proposition 2.2(i), and §3, Theorem 3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9809113)

[Sean Pohorence, *3-manifold Invariants and TQFTs* (2016), §3.1](https://categorified.net/RTinvariants/Jan29-Feb3.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, oriented smooth three-manifolds, an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism, and matching specified product collars when a boundary action is considered.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}$ ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A2] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, means every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[A3] In ZF, $\mathrm{AC}$ implies $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F1] A diffeomorphism induces a skein-module isomorphism by transporting framed links, and a matching product collar carries the closed-link action by gluing and disjoint union; this action is natural under collar-preserving diffeomorphisms ([[lem-general-3manifold-skein-quotient-isotopy-and-gluing]]).

[F2] A positive or negative full framing twist on one component multiplies its skein class by $-A^3$ or $-A^{-3}$ ([[lem-kauffman-bracket-module-framing-twist-factor]]).

[F3] The empty class is a free $R$-basis of $\mathcal K_A(S^3)$ and a zero-framed trivial circle has class $\delta[\varnothing]$ ([[thm-skein-module-of-s-three-is-rank-one]]).

[F4] The blackboard-framed core classes $[z^n]$, $n\geq0$, are an $R$-basis of the solid-torus module ([[thm-skein-module-of-solid-torus-has-core-multicurve-basis]]).

[F5] Here $R=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$ is the Laurent-polynomial ring over the integral domain $\mathbb Z$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

## Proof


1.1 The quotient isomorphism and collar-action naturality are exactly [F1]. Under a diffeomorphism, the framing annulus is carried by the derivative along with its core, so this map preserves the full link framing rather than only the unframed core. A single full twist is changed according to [F2]. [F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 Apply [F2] to the zero-framed trivial circle $O$ in $S^3$. By [F3], $[O]=\delta[\varnothing]$, so its positive twist represents $-A^3\delta[\varnothing]$. The difference from $[O]$ is $(-A^3-1)\delta[\varnothing]$. In $R$, $\delta=-(A^2+A^{-2})\ne0$ and $-A^3-1\ne0$; the product is nonzero because the product of two nonzero Laurent polynomials over the integral domain $\mathbb Z$ is nonzero (its highest-exponent coefficient is the product of their nonzero highest-exponent coefficients). Since $[\varnothing]$ is a basis element by [F3], the two classes are unequal. [A1, A2, A3, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 For the solid-torus core, [F2] gives the twisted class $-A^3[z]$. Its difference from $[z]$ is $(-A^3-1)[z]$, which is nonzero because $-A^3-1\ne0$ in $R$ and $[z]$ is one of the free basis elements in [F4]. This proves the second displayed framing change is nontrivial. [A1, F2, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remark

For $\gamma>0$, a global proximal selection of an extended-real penalty $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ is a map $P:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that, for every $z\in\mathbb R$, $P(z)$ is a global minimizer of $x\mapsto\frac12|x-z|^2+\gamma h(x)$. The potential $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ in the exact-MMSE stationarity result is constructed from the conditional-mean map $D_\sigma$. Replacing $D_\sigma$ in PnP-ISTA by an arbitrary map $\widetilde D_\sigma$ does not in general give a global proximal representation or inherit that stationarity conclusion: for every $\gamma>0$, the map $z\mapsto-z$ is not a global proximal selection of any such $h$ that is finite somewhere and nowhere $-\infty$. This does not assert that a particular other denoiser has no different objective.

## Remark references

[[lem-ip-tweedie-mmse-jacobian-and-prox-potential]]

[[def-ip-pnp-ista-with-denoiser]]

[[thm-ip-exact-mmse-pnp-ista-stationarity]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exact-MMSE potential construction, the general PnP-ISTA input-map convention, and the global-proximal-selection counterexample claimed in the Remark.

[F1] [[lem-ip-tweedie-mmse-jacobian-and-prox-potential]]: for the exact Gaussian posterior-mean map, the constructed extended-real potential has that map as its unique global proximal minimizer.

[F2] [[def-ip-pnp-ista-with-denoiser]]: PnP-ISTA permits a deterministic map $\widetilde D_\sigma$ in the denoising step.

[F3] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: on $\mathbb R$, the norm is the absolute value and the squared Euclidean distance is the square of the scalar difference.

## Verification

**Given:** A step parameter $\gamma>0$ and the global-proximal-selection definition in the Remark.

1.1 Suppose an extended-real penalty $h$ that is finite somewhere and nowhere $-\infty$ had $P(z)=-z$ as a global minimizer of $\frac12|x-z|^2+\gamma h(x)$ for every $z$. Its objective has a finite competitor for every input, so each claimed global minimizer has finite value. For distinct $s,t\in\mathbb R$, compare the minimizer at input $s$ with competitor $P(t)$ and the minimizer at input $t$ with competitor $P(s)$, then add the inequalities. The finite penalty values cancel and expansion gives $(P(s)-P(t))(s-t)\ge0$. [given, F3, algebra]

2.1 Substituting $P(s)-P(t)=-(s-t)$ into step 1.1 yields $-(s-t)^2\ge0$, which is false for $s\ne t$. Thus no such $h$ exists for this map, so the exact-MMSE construction and stationarity result cannot be transferred to an arbitrary denoiser without a separate proof. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$
be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable everywhere with
$x\mapsto F'(x)$ continuous in operator norm. For $s>0$, write
$$B_s(x_0):=\{x\in X:\|x-x_0\|_X<s\}.$$
Suppose $B_{2r}(x_0)\subseteq U$ for some $r>0$, $x^\dagger\in B_r(x_0)$,
and $F(x^\dagger)=y$. Assume there are constants $M,c>0$ such that, for every
$x,\tilde x\in B_{2r}(x_0)$,
$$\|F'(x)\|\le M,$$
$$\|F(x)-F(\tilde x)-F'(x)(x-\tilde x)\|_Y\le c\|x-\tilde x\|_X\|F(x)-F(\tilde x)\|_Y.$$
Fix $\sigma\in(0,1)$ and $\tau>1/\sigma$. Put
$$e_0:=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X$$
and assume
$$e_0<\min\left\{r,\frac{\sigma\tau-1}{c(1+\tau)},\frac{1-\sigma}{2c}\right\}.$$
Set
$$\gamma:=\frac{\sigma\tau}{1+ce_0(1+\tau)};$$
the hypotheses give $\gamma>1$. For each exact iteration, use this $\gamma$ in
the range-approximation margin of the regularized LM procedure and select any
positive parameter satisfying its residual-forcing equality.
For every $\delta>0$ and $y^\delta\in Y$ satisfying
$\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, start at $x_0^\delta=x_0$ and, at each state
before stopping, let $h_n$ minimize
$$h\longmapsto\frac12\|F'(x_n^\delta)h+F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y^2+\frac{\alpha_n}{2}\|h\|_X^2$$
for a selected $\alpha_n>0$ satisfying
$$\|F'(x_n^\delta)h_n+F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y=\sigma\|F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y,$$
and set $x_{n+1}^\delta=x_n^\delta+h_n$. Let $N_\delta$ be the first
$n\in\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ such that
$$\|F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y\le\tau\delta.$$
Then this exact iteration is well-defined up to a finite first discrepancy
index $N_\delta$. Set
$$q:=\frac{\sigma+ce_0}{1-ce_0},\qquad K:=1+\|F(x_0)-y\|_Y,\qquad \delta_0:=\min\left\{1,\frac K\tau\right\}.$$
Here $q\in(0,1)$ and $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm. For
$0<\delta\le\delta_0$,
$$N_\delta\le1+\frac{\log(K/(\tau\delta))}{-\log q}.$$
Consequently $N_\delta=O(1+|\log\delta|)$ as $\delta\downarrow0$, with
constants depending only on the fixed problem and displayed parameters. A
finite run with update budget at least $N_\delta$ and successful exact calls
returns this first crossing; a shorter budget may return
`budget-exhausted`. No convergence rate for $x_{N_\delta}^\delta$ is asserted.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt|Exact residual-forcing regularized LM iteration and finite statuses]]

[[def-ip-nonlinear-forward-map|Nonlinear forward map and exact-solution convention]]

[[def-hilbert-space|Real Hilbert spaces]]

[[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces|Fréchet derivative and derivative operator norm]]

[[def-operator-norm|Operator norm]]

[[def-ip-product-tangential-cone-condition|Product-type tangential cone condition]]

[[lem-ip-lm-product-condition-implies-range-approximation|Range approximation from the product condition]]

[[lem-ip-lm-fejer-decrease-and-parameter-bound|Fejér decrease and upper bound for the regularization parameter]]

[[def-countable-choice|Axiom of Countable Choice]]

[[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm|Triangle inequality for the real Hilbert norm]]

[[def-natural-logarithm|Natural logarithm]]

[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws|Order and quotient laws for the logarithm]]

[[lem-cauchy-reals-archimedean|Natural numbers are unbounded in the real field]]

[Christian Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Assumption 11.10 and Theorem 11.11 with complete proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00617v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; real Hilbert spaces $X,Y$; an open domain $U$; a continuously Fréchet differentiable map $F:U\to Y$; $B_{2r}(x_0)\subseteq U$; an exact solution $x^\dagger\in B_r(x_0)$ with $F(x^\dagger)=y$; constants $M,c>0$; $\sigma\in(0,1)$; $\tau>1/\sigma$; the stated smallness bound on $e_0$; and positive noise $\delta$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|\le\delta$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the sole choice axiom assumed for Hilbert adjoints and the shifted normal equations ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] On the local ball, the product remainder is bounded by $c\|x-\tilde x\|\|F(x)-F(\tilde x)\|$ ([[def-ip-product-tangential-cone-condition]]).

[F2] If $\|x-x^\dagger\|\le e_0$ and $\|F(x)-y^\delta\|>\tau\delta$, then the linearized residual at $x^\dagger$ is at most $[1+ce_0(1+\tau)]/\tau$ times the current residual; when $\gamma=\sigma\tau/[1+ce_0(1+\tau)]>1$, this is at most $\sigma/\gamma$ times the current residual ([[lem-ip-lm-product-condition-implies-range-approximation]]).

[F3] The algorithm checks discrepancy before updates, uses the exact regularized linearized minimizer and the residual-forcing equality, and returns the first crossing when exact calls and its finite cap permit ([[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt]]).

[F4] Under the range-approximation condition, the exact step obeys
$$\|e_n\|^2-\|e_n+h_n\|^2\ge\|h_n\|^2+\frac{2(\gamma-1)\sigma^2}{\gamma\alpha_n}\|F(x_n)-y^\delta\|^2,$$
and if $\|F'(x_n)\|\le M$, then $\alpha_n\le\sigma M^2/(1-\sigma)$ ([[lem-ip-lm-fejer-decrease-and-parameter-bound]]).

[F5] The natural logarithm is strictly increasing, satisfies the quotient law, and is negative on $(0,1)$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).

[F6] For every real bound $b$, some natural number exceeds $b$ ([[lem-cauchy-reals-archimedean]]).

[F7] The real Hilbert norm satisfies the triangle inequality ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]).

[F8] A Fréchet derivative is a bounded linear map, and its norm is the operator norm defined on bounded linear maps ([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]], [[def-operator-norm]]).

[F9] For a nonzero residual and a vector meeting the range-approximation margin, the regularized linearized least-squares problem has a unique minimizer and some positive parameter attains the residual-forcing equality ([[lem-ip-lm-step-existence-and-residual-forcing]]).

## Proof


1.1 Define $\gamma:=\sigma\tau/[1+ce_0(1+\tau)]$. The bound $e_0<(\sigma\tau-1)/(c(1+\tau))$ gives $1+ce_0(1+\tau)<\sigma\tau$, so $\gamma>1$. Since $e_0=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X\ge0$ and $c>0$, the other smallness bound gives $0\le ce_0<(1-\sigma)/2$. Hence $1-ce_0>0$; also $\sigma+ce_0>0$ because $\sigma>0$, and $2ce_0<1-\sigma$ gives $\sigma+ce_0<1-ce_0$. Thus $q=(\sigma+ce_0)/(1-ce_0)$ lies in $(0,1)$. [given, algebra]

1.2 For each pre-stop index, the given derivative bound and [F8] give $\|F'(x_n^\delta)\|\le M$. Thus [F4] and $\alpha_n\le\sigma M^2/(1-\sigma)$ give $e_n^2-e_{n+1}^2\ge D\,R_n^2,\qquad D:=\frac{2(\gamma-1)\sigma(1-\sigma)}{\gamma M^2}>0,$ where $R_n:=\|F(x_n^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y$. [F4, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 We construct the exact path up to its first crossing by finite induction. Initially $x_0^\delta=x_0\in B_{2r}(x_0)$ and $e_0=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|$. Suppose $x_n^\delta\in B_{2r}(x_0)$ and $e_n:=\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|\le e_0$. If its residual is at most $\tau\delta$, the path stops. Otherwise [F2] with $e=e_0$ gives the range-approximation hypothesis with the $\gamma$ of step 1.1. Since $R_n>\tau\delta>0$, [F9] supplies the positive forcing parameter and unique minimizer. Applying [F4] shows $e_{n+1}\le e_n$ and $\|h_n\|\le e_n$. Hence $e_{n+1}\le e_0$ and $\|x_{n+1}^\delta-x_0\|_X\le\|x_{n+1}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X+e_0\le2e_0<2r,$ so the next state remains in the local ball and the induction continues. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F7, F9, given, induction]

3.1 If no crossing has occurred in the first $m$ updates, then $R_n>\tau\delta$ for $0\le n<m$. Summing step 1.2 telescopes and yields $m\tau^2\delta^2< D\sum_{n=0}^{m-1}R_n^2\le e_0^2.$ By [F6], choose a natural $m>e_0^2/(D\tau^2\delta^2)$. The displayed inequality is impossible for that $m$, so a crossing occurs at a finite index $N_\delta$. Summing step 1.2 through $N_\delta-1$ also gives $N_\delta\le e_0^2/(D\tau^2\delta^2)$. [F6, step 2.1, step 1.2, given, choose, algebra]

3.2 Fix $n<N_\delta$ and set $T_n:=F'(x_n^\delta)$, $h_n:=x_{n+1}^\delta-x_n^\delta$, $q_n:=y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)-T_nh_n$, and $\Delta_n:=F(x_{n+1}^\delta)-F(x_n^\delta)-T_nh_n.$ Both iterates lie in $B_{2r}(x_0)$ by step 2.1. Applying [F1] to the ordered pair $(x_n^\delta,x_{n+1}^\delta)$ gives $\|\Delta_n\|_Y\le c\|h_n\|_X\|F(x_{n+1}^\delta)-F(x_n^\delta)\|_Y$. The forcing rule gives $\|q_n\|_Y=\sigma R_n$, while $F(x_{n+1}^\delta)-y^\delta=-q_n+\Delta_n.$ Therefore, with $R_{n+1}:=\|F(x_{n+1}^\delta)-y^\delta\|_Y$, $R_{n+1}\le\sigma R_n+c\|h_n\|_X(R_{n+1}+R_n).$ Using $\|h_n\|\le e_n\le e_0$ from [F4] and $1-ce_0>0$ from step 1.1 yields $R_{n+1}\le\frac{\sigma+ce_0}{1-ce_0}R_n=qR_n.$ [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $K:=1+\|F(x_0)-y\|_Y$ and $\delta_0:=\min\{1,K/\tau\}$. By [F7] and the data-noise bound, $R_0\le K$ for $0<\delta\le\delta_0$. If $N_\delta\ge2$, the first-crossing definition gives $\tau\delta<R_{N_\delta-1}$, while repeated application of step 3.2 gives $R_{N_\delta-1}\le q^{N_\delta-1}R_0\le q^{N_\delta-1}K$. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing, $\log(\tau\delta/K)<(N_\delta-1)\log q$; by [F5], $\log q<0$, so division reverses the inequality and gives $N_\delta\le1+\frac{\log(K/(\tau\delta))}{-\log q}.$ The same bound holds for $N_\delta=0$ or $1$, since $\delta\le K/\tau$ makes its right side at least $1$. Finally, for $\delta\le\delta_0\le1$, [F5] gives $\log\frac{K}{\tau\delta}\le\left|\log\frac K\tau\right|+|\log\delta|,$ so, with $C:=1+[1+|\log(K/\tau)|]/(-\log q)$, the displayed bound is at most $C(1+|\log\delta|)$, with $C$ independent of $y^\delta$ and $\delta$. By [F3], a finite run with cap at least $N_\delta$ and successful exact calls returns this crossing. The proof asserts no convergence rate for the stopped iterate. [F3, F5, F7, step 3.2, given, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The source's logarithmic count uses the product-type remainder condition and a sufficiently small start. Positive noise is essential for finite discrepancy stopping; the B-page zero-noise counterexample verifies this boundary. This theorem proves an index bound only, not convergence of the stopped solution or an error rate.
