## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold with a compact smooth core and $k\ge1$ disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Choose positively oriented peripheral bases $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$. Let $\rho_u$, for $u$ near $0$ in $\mathbb C^k$, be the augmented holonomy family supplied by the augmented holonomy-coordinate theorem, based at the complete holonomy $\rho_0$. Thus the logarithms satisfy $v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$.

After shrinking this neighborhood, there are smooth hyperbolic metrics $g_u$ on $M$, possibly incomplete, with holonomy $\rho_u$. They depend smoothly on the real and imaginary parts of $u$ on every compact subset, and $g_0$ is the given complete metric. Each end with $u_i=0$ is a complete finite-volume translation cusp. Each end with $u_i\ne0$ has an explicit developing map onto the punctured tube about its peripheral axis, with the angular and axial periods specified by $u_i,v_i$.

Suppose $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and, for every $i\in J$, a primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ satisfies
$$p_i u_i+q_i v_i(u)=2\pi i,$$
while $u_i=0$ for $i\notin J$. Then $g_u$ extends across all ends in $J$ to a smooth complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on the ordinary Dehn filling whose meridians are $p_i\mu_i+q_i\lambda_i$. For arbitrary supplied orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphisms realizing these same slopes, the resulting topological filling is orientation-preservingly and core-preservingly homeomorphic to this realization, by a homeomorphism equal to the identity on the truncated original manifold. Transporting the realization's smooth structure and metric through this homeomorphism gives the asserted smooth hyperbolic metric on that supplied filling. No assertion is made about a separately prescribed smooth structure for an arbitrary topological gluing. The added cores are ordinary smooth geodesics, with no cone or orbifold singularity. Their lengths are
$$\ell_i=\frac{|u_i|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)}{2\pi}>0.$$
Along such filling parameters tending to zero, the metrics converge smoothly to $g_0$ on every compact subset of $M$, the core lengths tend to zero, and the filled volumes tend to $\operatorname{Vol}(M,g_0)$. No ideal triangulation is assumed. This theorem realizes given small holonomy solutions; it does not assert their existence for specified slopes.

## Statement references

[[thm-augmented-finite-volume-hyperbolic-holonomy-coordinates]]

[[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]]

[Petronio and Porti, Proposition 2.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the complete quotient, the compact core and standard cusp models, the peripheral bases, and the augmented representation family in the Statement.

[A1] AC supplies Countable Choice for smooth partitions of unity and for the holonomy supplier. The supplier also uses AC in its Hilbert-space and recursive formal-extension arguments. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] There are holomorphic representatives $\rho_u$ and holomorphically varying peripheral eigenlines. On each end a holomorphic change of frame sends that line to $\infty$, and the peripheral maps become $Z\mapsto e^{u_i}Z+a_i(u)$ and $Z\mapsto e^{v_i}Z+b_i(u)$, with $a_i(0)\ne0$, $v_i=\tau_i u_i$ and $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i>0$. On $u_i=0$, $v_i=0$ and $b_i/a_i=\tau_i$. [[thm-augmented-finite-volume-hyperbolic-holonomy-coordinates]]

[F2] A smooth open manifold has smooth partitions subordinate to an open cover under Countable Choice. A smooth map with invertible differential is a local diffeomorphism. [[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds]], [[thm-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-on-manifolds]]

[F3] The curvature-$-1$ model is the upper half-space $(Z,Y)\in\mathbb C\times(0,\infty)$, with its orientation-preserving projective matrix isometries. Its metric and volume formula are computed directly in step 1.1. [[lem-complete-curvature-minus-one-manifolds-are-kleinian-quotients]]

[F4] Ordinary filling attaches a solid torus by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism sending its meridian to the specified slope. Here equality of slopes means equality of unoriented ambient-isotopy classes of embedded curves on the torus, the standard ordinary-slope convention. A boundary homeomorphism between product solid tori extends core-preservingly, with the same orientation sign, if an ambient isotopy of the target boundary moves the image meridian to its target meridian. [[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]], [[lem-meridian-preserving-torus-homeomorphism-extends-over-solid-torus]]

## Proof

1.1 We first give an isometry-equivariant way of blending maps into $\mathbb H^3$. Use the Lorentz form $\langle X,X\rangle=X_1^2+X_2^2+X_3^2-X_4^2$ and embed upper half-space by $\Phi(Z,Y)=(\operatorname{Re}Z/Y,\operatorname{Im}Z/Y,(|Z|^2+Y^2-1)/(2Y),(|Z|^2+Y^2+1)/(2Y))$. Direct substitution gives $\langle\Phi,\Phi\rangle=-1$, positive last coordinate, and differentiation gives the upper half-space metric $(|dZ|^2+dY^2)/Y^2$. Its coordinate matrix in $(\operatorname{Re}Z,\operatorname{Im}Z,Y)$ is $Y^{-2}I_3$, so its volume coefficient is the positive square root of $Y^{-6}$, namely $Y^{-3}$. The action of $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ is linear on these Lorentz coordinates. Indeed the equivalent Hermitian-matrix coordinate is $Y^{-1}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}|Z|^2+Y^2&Z\\\overline Z&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; it is positive definite with determinant one, and $X\mapsto AXA^*$, for $A\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$, is linear on the four real Hermitian coordinates, preserves determinant and positivity, and is unchanged by replacing $A$ by $-A$. For positive weights summing to one, a weighted sum $S$ of future unit timelike vectors is future timelike: writing each vector as $(x,t)$ gives $t>|x|$, and the triangle inequality gives this strict inequality for the sum. Thus $B(S)=S/\sqrt{-\langle S,S\rangle}$ is well defined and smooth. It commutes with every $G$ action. If every input equals $X$, its value is $X$. This is a normalized Lorentz sum, rather than an undefined linear average inside a manifold. [F3, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Fix an end and omit its index temporarily. Choose the frames in [F1] so that at zero its original developing map is $(x,y,t)\mapsto(a(0)(x+\tau(0)y),e^t)$ on $\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)$. The deck generators add one to $x$ and $y$. Such a normalization is obtained by a fixed translation and dilation of a lift of the original horoball; it only fixes the origin and the level called $t=0$. Write $\zeta=x+\tau(u)y$, $L=u\zeta$, $w=(1-e^u)/a(u)$ and $B=\sqrt{(1+|w|^2)/(1+e^{2t}|w|^2)}$, choosing the positive square root. Put $E(z)=(e^z-1)/z$ with $E(0)=1$. Define an end map $\Psi_u=(Z_u,Y_u)$ by $Y_u=e^t|e^L|B$ and $Z_u=a(u)\zeta E(L)/E(u)+e^L(e^{2t}-1)\overline w/((1+e^{2t}|w|^2)(1+B))$. All these formulas are smooth in $(x,y,t,\operatorname{Re}u,\operatorname{Im}u)$, and in the other deformation coordinates: $a,\tau$ are holomorphic, $a$ and $E(u)$ are nonzero after shrinking, and every real denominator is positive. At $u=0$ they give precisely $(a(u)(x+\tau(u)y),e^t)$, including when other deformation coordinates are nonzero. At the complete parameter they give the original developing map. Consequently their convergence, with every derivative, is uniform on each fixed compact coordinate collar. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose product coordinates $T_i^2\times[0,\infty)$ on the ends, and include their collars through $t=2$ in a compact set $K$. The given complete developing map identifies the universal cover of $M$ with $\mathbb H^3$, with deck action $\rho_0$. Cover $K$ by finitely many simply connected evenly covered coordinate sets $U_j$ and choose one lift $\widetilde U_j$ for each. On an open neighborhood $V$ of $K$ covered by these sets, use [F2] to choose a subordinate smooth partition $\phi_j$. Pull each function to each component $\rho_0(\gamma)\widetilde U_j$ and extend it by zero; denote this lifted function by $\phi_{\gamma j}$. Its support stays inside that component. These functions are locally finite and sum to one on the inverse image of $V$. Put $D_{\gamma j}(x,u)=\rho_u(\gamma)\rho_0(\gamma)^{-1}x$ and let $D^{\mathrm{core}}_u(x)$ be the Lorentz blend of the points $D_{\gamma j}(x,u)$ with weights $\phi_{\gamma j}(x)$. The sums are locally finite and smooth. The deck identities for the weights and $D_{\delta\gamma,j}(\rho_0(\delta)x,u)=\rho_u(\delta)D_{\gamma j}(x,u)$ show exact $\rho_u$ equivariance. At zero every input is $x$, so $D^{\mathrm{core}}_0(x)=x$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 When $u\ne0$, put $c=1/w=a/(1-e^u)$ and $C=|c|$. The identity $(1-B)/w=(e^{2t}-1)\overline w/((1+e^{2t}|w|^2)(1+B))$ rewrites the preceding formula as $Z_u=c(1-Be^L)$, $Y_u=e^t|e^L|B$. On adding one to $x$, these become $Z\mapsto e^uZ+a$, $Y\mapsto e^{\operatorname{Re}u}Y$. Commutativity gives $a(e^v-1)=b(e^u-1)$, so $c(1-e^v)=b$; adding one to $y$ gives the other peripheral isometry. When $u=0$, the translation formula in step 1.2 gives the same equivariance because $v=0$ and $b=a\tau$. Compose $\Psi_u$ with the inverse of the frame from [F1]; this gives a map $D^{\mathrm{end}}_u$ on a chosen lifted end, equivariant under its peripheral subgroup. Extend to all its deck translates by $D^{\mathrm{end}}_u(\rho_0(\gamma)x)=\rho_u(\gamma)D^{\mathrm{end}}_u(x)$. This is well defined because two descriptions differ by a peripheral deck transformation. [F1, step 1.2, algebra, construct]

3.1 On the compact quotient $K$, the last construction converges to the identity in every derivative as $u\to0$, in fixed local lift charts. To see uniformity without an assertion about infinitely many deck transformations, cover $K$ by finitely many smaller relatively compact chart pieces and lift each piece once. Only finitely many of the locally finite functions $\phi_{\gamma j}$ meet those compact lifts. Only these finitely many matrices $\rho_u(\gamma)\rho_0(\gamma)^{-1}$ enter the derivative estimates there, and each converges smoothly to the identity. Invertibility of a matrix is open; compactness and [F2] therefore give one neighborhood of zero on which $D^{\mathrm{core}}_u$ is a local diffeomorphism at all points over $K$. Its pullback metric descends by equivariance, is hyperbolic, and converges smoothly to the original metric on $K$. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 The end map is a local diffeomorphism on its entire domain. For $u=0$ this follows directly from the translation formula and $\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$. For $u\ne0$ introduce Fermi coordinates about the vertical geodesic with endpoints $c,\infty$: $Z=c+e^s\tanh r\,e^{i\theta}$, $Y=e^s/\cosh r$. Direct differentiation using [F3] gives $dr^2+\sinh^2r\,d\theta^2+\cosh^2r\,ds^2$. The map in step 2.2 is precisely $r(t)=\operatorname{arsinh}(Ce^{-t})$, $s=\log\sqrt{C^2+1}+\operatorname{Re}L$, $\theta=\arg(-c)+\operatorname{Im}L$. The choice of the constant argument is immaterial modulo $2\pi$. The real linear map $(x,y)\mapsto(\operatorname{Re}L,\operatorname{Im}L)$ has determinant $\operatorname{Im}(\overline u v)=|u|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$, and $r'(t)\ne0$. Thus the differential is invertible everywhere for finite $t$. For $t\ge T$ its image is the whole punctured tube $0<r\le R(T)$, where $R(T)=\operatorname{arsinh}(Ce^{-T})$, and $(s,\theta)$ before angular reduction range over all $\mathbb R^2$. No discreteness of the full peripheral image is required for this local assertion. [F2, F3, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 We now join the core and the end maps. Take a fixed smooth function $\beta(t)$ equal to zero near $t=0$ and one for $t\ge1$. On the end collar $0\le t\le1$, Lorentz blend $D^{\mathrm{core}}_u$ and $D^{\mathrm{end}}_u$ with weights $1-\beta$ and $\beta$; use the core map below this collar and the end map above it. Both maps have the same $\rho_u$ equivariance, so the blend does too. The lifted end components are disjoint; their deck translates give the construction on all of the universal cover. At the complete parameter both inputs are the identity, and steps 3.1 and 1.2 show smooth convergence on the compact transition collars. Therefore, after one common shrinking for the finitely many ends, the blended differential is invertible throughout these collars. Above them step 3.2 applies; below them step 3.1 applies. We have constructed a global smooth equivariant local diffeomorphism $D_u:\widetilde M\to\mathbb H^3$. Its pullback of the hyperbolic metric is invariant under the original deck group and hence defines $g_u$ on $M$, with holonomy $\rho_u$. Local inverses from [F2] give its hyperbolic charts. The construction is smooth in parameters on compact subsets and gives $g_0$ exactly. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 If $u_i=0$, the metric above the collar is the translation-cusp metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}|a_i(u)|^2|dx+\tau_i(u)dy|^2$. It has volume $|a_i(u)|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)e^{-2T}/2$ for $t\ge T\ge1$, by integration on $[0,1]^2\times[T,\infty)$. Its end is complete: the length of any path dominates the total change in $t$, so reaching arbitrarily large $t$ requires unbounded length. This proves all assertions about unfilled ends, independently of what happens at the other cusps. [F3, step 1.2, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 Fix a filled cusp, so $u\ne0$ by its full-turn equation. Let $m=(p,q)$ be its primitive filling vector and choose integers $p',q'$ with $pq'-qp'=1$, using the integer Euclidean algorithm. Put $d=(p',q')$ and $W=p'u+q'v=A+iB_0$. Under the Fermi linear map in step 3.2, $m$ maps to $(0,2\pi)$ and $d$ to $(A,B_0)$. The determinant identity gives $-2\pi A=|u|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$. In particular $A\ne0$ and $|A|=|u|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau/(2\pi)$. The vectors $m,d$ are an integral basis, so the image of the deck lattice is exactly the lattice generated by $(0,2\pi)$ and $(A,B_0)$. It follows that the end $t\ge T\ge1$ with its actual metric is isometric to the punctured radius-$R(T)$ hyperbolic tube modulo the screw motion $(r,\theta,s)\mapsto(r,\theta+B_0,s+A)$. This is a bijective local isometry: the real linear map is invertible, $t\mapsto r$ is one-to-one onto $(0,R(T)]$, and its only identifications after reducing $\theta$ modulo $2\pi$ and then by the screw are precisely the original integral deck lattice. This checks the global quotient, beyond the local developing map. [step 3.2, step 4.1, given, construct, algebra]

6.1 Add the axis $r=0$ to this tube before taking its screw quotient. Its smooth structure and metric are ordinary hyperbolic ones. Explicitly, with $X=r\cos\theta$, $Y'=r\sin\theta$, the upper-half-space formula becomes $Z=c+e^s(\tanh r/r)(X+iY')$ and $Y=e^s/\cosh r$. The even smooth functions $\tanh r/r$ and $1/\cosh r$ extend at $r=0$ with value one. The map has invertible differential there and gives standard hyperbolic coordinates across the axis. The screw extends smoothly, freely and properly: it translates $s$ by the nonzero number $A$, so no nonidentity power fixes a point and only finitely many powers move one compact set to meet another. Its closed radius-$R(T)$ quotient is compact, as a closed disk times an $s$ interval of length $|A|$ with its ends identified by a rotation. More explicitly $(r,\theta,s)\mapsto(r e^{i(\theta-B_0s/A)},e^{2\pi i s/A})$ identifies the quotient smoothly with a product solid torus, including at $r=0$. The angular vector $m$, which changes $\theta$ by exactly $2\pi$ while fixing $s$, is its meridian. Thus the boundary identification furnished in step 5.2 attaches an ordinary solid torus with meridian $p\mu+q\lambda$, exactly as in [F4]. Its metric agrees on a whole punctured collar with $g_u$, so the attachment is smooth. The core is a geodesic of length $|A|=\ell_i$; no nonidentity screw power fixes a point on that core because the same screw has nonzero axial translation. [F2, F3, F4, step 5.2, construct, algebra]

7.1 These constructions are simultaneous and give the required topology. Choose the same level $T\ge1$ in the finitely many disjoint end products. Retain the compact truncated core, and attach the solid tori of step 6.1 on the filled boundary components, using the explicit boundary diffeomorphisms of step 5.2. Retain the translation ends on the unfilled components. This produces the ordinary partial filling with the indicated meridians, with its orientation extended from the core. The boundary maps reverse the induced boundary orientations because they identify the two sides of the same product collar; the constructed metric agrees there and fixes the oriented structure. Equivalently the removed open punctured solid torus in each completed tube has exactly the original $T^2\times[T,\infty)$ marking. Thus no separate identification of slopes, covering degree or core topology is being inferred merely from trivial peripheral holonomy. For precision concerning arbitrary supplied attaching maps, write $f_i:\partial V_i\to T_i$ for our explicit attachment and $h_i:\partial W_i\to T_i$ for a supplied orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism with the same meridian slope. By the ambient-isotopy convention in [F4], choose an ambient isotopy $J_{i,t}$ of $T_i$, starting at the identity, carrying $h_i(\partial D^2\times\{1\})$ onto $f_i(\partial D^2\times\{1\})$. For $e_i=f_i^{-1}h_i$, the conjugate isotopy $f_i^{-1}J_{i,t}f_i$ therefore satisfies exactly the meridian hypothesis of [F4]. Extend $e_i$ to a core-preserving homeomorphism $\overline e_i:W_i\to V_i$. It is orientation preserving because both $f_i,h_i$ reverse boundary orientation. The identity on the truncated manifold and these extensions glue to an orientation-preserving, core-preserving homeomorphism $P$ from the supplied filling to our constructed filling: on the attaching boundary, $f_i\overline e_i=h_i$. On the supplied topological filling declare charts to be $(P^{-1}U,\varphi\circ P)$ for every chart $(U,\varphi)$ of the constructed smooth filling. These charts have the same smooth transition functions as the constructed atlas; in this transported smooth structure $P$ is a diffeomorphism, and the metric defined by those same chart coefficients is $P^*g_u$. It makes $P$ an isometry. Because $P$ is the identity on the truncated original manifold, its original smooth structure and metric there are retained. Completeness, orientation, volume and core lengths are preserved by this isometry. This is transport of a smooth structure, not a claim that a given arbitrary boundary homeomorphism is smooth for some independently specified atlas. Smooth convergence on compact subsets of the marked original $M$ follows from step 4.1, since the explicit realized metrics agree with $g_u$ there. [F3, F4, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

8.1 The extended metric is complete and has finite volume. The union of the truncated core and the finitely many closed filled tubes is compact. The other ends are the explicit complete translation cusps of step 5.1. For metric completeness, define $f=0$ on that compact part and $f=t-T$ on each retained cusp. It is continuous and $1$-Lipschitz for the path metric: on cusp segments $|df|=1$, on the compact part it is zero, and splitting paths at the common boundary gives the global inequality. A Cauchy sequence has bounded $f$ and therefore stays in a compact union of that part and finitely many truncated cusps. A smooth Riemannian metric induces the manifold topology locally, since on a small relatively compact coordinate ball its positive-definite coefficients bound Euclidean lengths above and below; hence that compact union is metric compact. The sequence has a convergent subsequence, and being Cauchy converges. This proves completeness directly. The compact part has finite volume, each retained cusp has the finite volume in step 5.1, and each filled tube has finite volume: its Fermi density is $\sinh r\cosh r\,dr\,d\theta\,ds$, so its volume is $\pi|A|\sinh^2R(T)$. Curvature is $-1$ everywhere because the extension charts of step 6.1 are actual hyperbolic charts. [F3, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 Finally the same formulas give convergence of volume, including for varying simultaneous slope tuples. On a filled end $\sinh^2R(T)=|c|^2e^{-2T}$ and $|A|=|u|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau/(2\pi)$, so its completed tail volume is exactly $|a(u)|^2\operatorname{Im}\tau(u)e^{-2T}/(2|E(u)|^2)$, since $|1-e^u|^2=|u|^2|E(u)|^2$. On an unfilled end this formula has the same value by step 5.1 and $E(0)=1$. Thus, for any fixed $T\ge1$, each tail volume tends to its original complete-cusp volume as the full parameter tends to zero. On the compact part $t\le T$, step 4.1 gives smooth metric convergence, hence convergence of volume densities and their integrals; finitely many coordinate charts and a partition of unity reduce this to uniform convergence of smooth positive determinants on compact sets. Adding the finitely many tail volumes proves convergence of total volume. The displayed core-length formula in step 5.2 tends to zero as well, because $\tau$ stays bounded. All assertions of the Statement follow. [F2, F3, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 8.1, algebra] ∎

## Source reading and scope

The full 23-page Petronio–Porti paper was read, and its complete Proposition 2.7 proof, printed pp. 14–16, was reread for this construction. Thurston's complete Section 5.8, printed pp. 102–105, was read. The normalized Lorentz blending and the parameter-smooth explicit cusp formula are proved here; no deformation-of-structures theorem is imported from the references. The proof uses neither a positive triangulation nor a signed or flat triangulation realization theorem.

The compact core, original standard cusp decomposition, and the analytic augmented holonomy theorem are explicit prerequisites. The existence of small solutions to the simultaneous peripheral equations is a separate analytic supplier. This theorem supplies the full geometric realization and completion for every such solution, including partially filled manifolds.

## Definition

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

## Definition references

[[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram|Normalized unreduced Khovanov complex]]

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|Integral Frobenius algebra and edge maps]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial* (1999), §§8.1–8.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Zhang, *Notes on Khovanov homology* (2025), §6.3.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology* (2022), §§4–5](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A based knot diagram $(D,p)$ and the normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex defined in [[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]].

[F1] On a resolution circle, $X^2=0$, $\Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1$, and $\Delta(X)=X\otimes X$; multiplication is the product in $\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ ([[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]).

[F2] The differential is the signed sum of edge maps, each equal to multiplication or comultiplication on the factors meeting that edge and the identity on all other factors ([[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]]).

[F3] The signed cube differential squares to zero, so these state modules form a cochain complex ([[lem-khovanov-cube-differential-squares-to-zero]]).

## Proof

1.1 If an edge does not meet the basepoint circle, its map is the identity on the basepoint factor and hence commutes with $X_p$. If the edge merges the basepoint circle with another circle, associativity gives $m(Xa\otimes b)=X\,m(a\otimes b)$. If it splits the basepoint circle, the Frobenius identity gives $\Delta(Xa)=(X\otimes1)\Delta(a)=(1\otimes X)\Delta(a)$; on $a=1,X$ these are respectively $X\otimes X$ and $0$ on all three sides. Thus every edge map commutes with $X_p$, so $\operatorname{im}(X_p)$ is a subcomplex. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], the unreduced differential already squares to zero, and by step 1.1 it preserves $\operatorname{im}(X_p)$; thus the induced quotient differential also squares to zero. In each state the based factor is $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z\{1,X\}$, and $X_p$ has image $\mathbb Z\{X\}$. Therefore the quotient factor is $\mathbb Z\{1\}$, with raw quantum degree $+1$; subtracting one gives reduced degree $0$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 After cutting the based circle, every state has one distinguished interval factor $M$. The quotient identification sends the surviving based label $1$ to $1\in M$. For a merge into that interval, $m(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m(X\otimes1)=0$ in the quotient, exactly the displayed $m_M$; for a split, $\Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1$ and the term with $X$ on the distinguished interval is zero in $M$, leaving $X\otimes1$, exactly $\Delta_M(1)$. Edges away from the interval retain $m$ and $\Delta$. Hence this statewise identification commutes with every edge and gives the stated based tangle cube isomorphism. [F1, F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For $T(2,3)$, the exterior group is $\langle x,y\mid x^2=y^3\rangle$, a central fiber is $h=x^2=y^3$, a positive meridian is $\mu=y^2x^{-1}$, and a preferred longitude is $\lambda=h\mu^{-6}$. Its Alexander polynomial is $\Delta(t)\doteq t^2-t+1$ and its genus is $1$. For $T(1,5)$, the group presentation reduces to $\mathbb Z$, the knot is the unknot, the Alexander polynomial is $1$, and the genus is $0$.

## Example references

[[thm-torus-knot-group-presentation|The group, central fiber, and peripheral-word formulas]]

[[thm-torus-knot-alexander-and-genus-formulas|The Alexander polynomial and genus formulas]]

[[lem-torus-knot-unit-slope-is-unknot|The unit-slope unknot result]]

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, §§5.1.1 and 5.1.6–5.2.4](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

[Calegari, Example 1.2 and §4.3](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the coprime torus knots $T(2,3)$ and $T(1,5)$, and the formulas of the A page.

[A1] Full AC supplies the countable-choice hypotheses used by the knot and genus statements ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[L1] Full AC implies Countable Choice ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] [[thm-torus-knot-group-presentation]] gives $\pi_1(E_{T(p,q)})=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle$, $h=x^p=y^q$, and $\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta$, $\lambda=h\mu^{-pq}$ when $p\alpha+q\beta=1$.

[F2] [[thm-torus-knot-alexander-and-genus-formulas]] gives $\Delta_{T(p,q)}\doteq (t^{|pq|}-1)(t-1)/((t^{|p|}-1)(t^{|q|}-1))$ and $g(T(p,q))=(|p|-1)(|q|-1)/2$.

[F3] [[lem-torus-knot-unit-slope-is-unknot]] says $T(p,q)$ is the unknot when $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$.

## Verification

1.1 For $(p,q)=(2,3)$ the group relation is $x^2=y^3$, and this common element $h$ is central. The equation $2\alpha+3\beta=1$ has solution $(\alpha,\beta)=(2,-1)$, so [F1] gives $\mu=y^2x^{-1}$ and $\lambda=h\mu^{-6}$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Substituting $(2,3)$ into [F2] gives
$$\Delta(t)\doteq\frac{(t^6-1)(t-1)}{(t^2-1)(t^3-1)}=\frac{t^3+1}{t+1}=t^2-t+1,$$
and $g=(2-1)(3-1)/2=1$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

1.3 For $(p,q)=(1,5)$, the relation $x=y^5$ eliminates $x$ and leaves the infinite cyclic group generated by $y$. The meridian equation has solution $(\alpha,\beta)=(1,0)$, so [F1] gives $\mu=y$ and $\lambda=h\mu^{-5}=1$ in the group. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3] by [L1], so [F3] identifies $T(1,5)$ with the unknot. In [F2] the quotient cancels to $1$ and the genus expression is $0$, giving the stated Alexander polynomial and genus. [A1, L1, F2, F3, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, $m\ge0$, and $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ be a family in $\mathbb R^d$. Define $x\sim z$ by $z=x$ or $z=-x$, let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/\sim$, and put
$$d_{\pm}([x],[z])=\min\{\|x-z\|_2,\|x+z\|_2\}.$$
Let $Y_m=\{b:[m]\to[0,\infty)\}$ carry the metric induced from zero-based Euclidean $\mathbb R^m$ by the fixed relabeling $i\mapsto i-1$ when $m\ge1$, and the zero metric on the singleton $Y_0$ when $m=0$. Define
$$\mathcal M_\Phi([x])=(|\langle a_i,x\rangle|)_{i\in[m]},\qquad \mathcal I_\Phi([x])=(\langle a_i,x\rangle^2)_{i\in[m]}.$$
Then $\sim$ is an equivalence relation, $d_{\pm}$ is a metric on $Q_d$, $Y_m$ is a metric space, and both displayed measurement maps are well defined. Moreover, $\mathcal I_\Phi$ is coordinatewise the square of $\mathcal M_\Phi$, so the two maps are injective simultaneously.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-real-frame-phase-retrieval|Real phase-retrieval model and map conventions]]

[[def-metric-space|Metric-space axioms]]

[[lem-metrics-on-rn|The Euclidean metric on real coordinate spaces]]

[Philipp Grohs, Sarah Koppensteiner, and Martin Rathmair, quotient metric for phase retrieval, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.07911v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The definitions and hypotheses in the statement.

[F1] The sign relation is $x\sim z$ exactly when $z=x$ or $z=-x$, the quotient map sends $x$ to $[x]$, and the amplitude and intensity formulas use the real Euclidean pairing ([[def-ip-real-frame-phase-retrieval]]).

[F2] For each integer $n\ge1$, $d_2(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2$ is a metric on $\mathbb R^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F3] A metric satisfies separation, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; these axioms can be restricted to a subset ([[def-metric-space]]).

[F4] For real $t$, $|t|\ge0$, $|-t|=|t|$, and $|t|=0$ exactly when $t=0$ ([[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]).

[F5] A nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F6] Every real square is nonnegative ([[lem-of-square-positive]]).

[F7] The real order is total, so every two-element set of real numbers has a least element, which is its minimum ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-max-min]]).

## Proof



**Given:** A finite real family $\Phi$, $d\ge1$, and $m\ge0$.

1.1 The relation $\sim$ is reflexive because $x=x$, symmetric because $z=x$ implies $x=z$ and $z=-x$ implies $x=-z$, and transitive because multiplying the two signs in $z=\epsilon x$ and $w=\delta z$ gives $w=(\delta\epsilon)x$ with $\delta\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. Thus $Q_d$ is the quotient set and $q(x)=[x]$ is onto by the definition of equivalence classes. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 If $m\ge1$, the relabeling $J:Y_m\to[0,\infty)^m$ given by $J(b)_k=b_{k+1}$ is a bijection and $\rho_m(b,c)=d_2(Jb,Jc)$, so the metric axioms of [F2] restrict to $Y_m$. If $m=0$, $Y_0$ has one element and the zero function separates its only pair and is symmetric and triangular. Hence $Y_m$ is a metric space in both cases. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 Replacing representatives by $x'=\epsilon x$ and $z'=\delta z$, with $\epsilon,\delta\in\{1,-1\}$, changes the pair $(\|x-z\|_2,\|x+z\|_2)$ only by possibly interchanging its two entries, since $\|x'-z'\|_2=\|x-(\epsilon\delta)z\|_2$ and $\|x'+z'\|_2=\|x+(\epsilon\delta)z\|_2$. By [F7] the minimum is attained, so its value is independent of representatives. [given, F1, F7, algebra]

2.1 Replacing $x$ by $-x$ changes each amplitude coordinate from $|\langle a_i,x\rangle|$ to $|-\langle a_i,x\rangle|=|\langle a_i,x\rangle|$, and changes each intensity coordinate from $\langle a_i,x\rangle^2$ to $(-\langle a_i,x\rangle)^2=\langle a_i,x\rangle^2$. Every intensity coordinate is nonnegative by [F6], so both maps have the stated codomain and are well defined on $Q_d$, including zero rows and the zero signal. For $m=0$ both are the unique map to the empty tuple. [step 1.1, F1, F4, F6, algebra]

2.2 Choose signs $\epsilon,\delta\in\{1,-1\}$ attaining the two minima for $d_{\pm}([x],[y])$ and $d_{\pm}([y],[z])$; [F7] ensures these minima exist, and the choices are from finite two-element sets. The Euclidean triangle inequality and sign-invariance of the norm give $d_{\pm}([x],[z])\le\|x-\epsilon\delta z\|_2\le\|x-\epsilon y\|_2+\|y-\delta z\|_2=d_{\pm}([x],[y])+d_{\pm}([y],[z])$. Thus the triangle inequality holds. [step 1.3, F2, F7, choose, algebra]

3.1 Both candidate norms are nonnegative by the nonnegative-root convention [F5], and their minimum is symmetric under interchanging $x$ and $z$. The minimum is zero exactly when $x=z$ or $x=-z$, which is exactly $[x]=[z]$ by [F1] and separation of the Euclidean metric in [F2]. Together with the triangle inequality in step 2.2, this proves that $d_{\pm}$ is a metric. [step 1.3, step 2.2, F1, F2, F5]

4.1 Each amplitude coordinate is nonnegative and its square is the corresponding intensity coordinate. If two nonnegative amplitudes have the same square, uniqueness of nonnegative square roots [F5] makes the amplitudes equal; conversely equal amplitudes have equal squares. Coordinatewise, the amplitude and intensity maps therefore have the same fibers and are injective simultaneously. [step 2.1, F5, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Every group admitting a finite subnormal series with torsion-free abelian factors satisfies the left Folner condition: for each finite subset $S$ and each $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a finite nonempty subset $F$ with $|sF\triangle F|<\varepsilon|F|$ for every $s\in S$. This assertion requires no countability or finite-generation hypothesis and no choice axiom. More generally the finite Folner condition is preserved by arbitrary group extensions whose kernel and quotient satisfy it.

## Statement references

[[def-poly-torsion-free-abelian-group]]

[[def-folner-set-and-folner-condition]]

[[lem-finitely-generated-torsion-free-abelian-freeness-without-choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite Folner condition and a finite PTFA subnormal series.

[F1] The finite Folner condition is precisely the finite-set and symmetric-difference condition in the Statement ([[def-folner-set-and-folner-condition]]).

[F2] Finitely generated torsion-free abelian groups are finite-rank free abelian groups ([[lem-finitely-generated-torsion-free-abelian-freeness-without-choice]]).

[F3] A PTFA series has each successive subgroup normal in the next, with torsion-free abelian quotient; normality in the final group is not required ([[def-poly-torsion-free-abelian-group]]).

## Proof

**Given:** A finite test set and a positive error tolerance whenever the Folner condition is tested.

1.1 A torsion-free abelian group satisfies [F1]. Indeed the subgroup generated by a finite test set is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r$ by [F2]. For $r=0$ use the singleton identity set. For $r>0$ bound every test vector's coordinates in absolute value by $M\ge0$ and take the integer cube $E_n=[-n,n]^r\cap\mathbb Z^r$, with $n\ge M$. A translate by any test vector has intersection with $E_n$ of cardinality at least $(2n+1-M)^r$, whereas both sets have cardinality $(2n+1)^r$. Thus its relative symmetric difference is at most $2[1-(1-M/(2n+1))^r]$, which tends to zero. The transported cube witnesses the required condition in the original group. All choices concern a single finitely generated subgroup and a finite test set. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $1\to H\to G\xrightarrow{\pi}Q\to1$ is any group extension and both $H,Q$ satisfy [F1]. Fix finite $S\subseteq G$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a finite nonempty $(\pi(S),\varepsilon/2)$-Folner set $E\subseteq Q$. For the finite set $E\cup\pi(S)E$, choose lifts $t_q\in G$. For each $s\in S$ and $q\in E$ with $\pi(s)q\in E$, put $h_{s,q}=t_{\pi(s)q}^{-1}st_q\in H$. This is a finite collection of elements of $H$. Choose a finite nonempty set $B\subseteq H$ with $|h_{s,q}B\triangle B|<(\varepsilon/2)|B|$ for all of them, and let $F=\bigcup_{q\in E}t_qB$. Its cosets are disjoint, so $|F|=|E||B|$. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 For $s\in S$, the cosets present in exactly one of $sF,F$ contribute $|\pi(s)E\triangle E||B|$ elements to the symmetric difference. On a common coset indexed by $\pi(s)q$, the two subsets are $t_{\pi(s)q}h_{s,q}B$ and $t_{\pi(s)q}B$, whose difference has cardinality $|h_{s,q}B\triangle B|$. There are at most $|E|$ common cosets. Therefore $|sF\triangle F|\le|\pi(s)E\triangle E||B|+\sum_{q\in E,\,\pi(s)q\in E}|h_{s,q}B\triangle B|<\varepsilon|E||B|=\varepsilon|F|$. This proves the extension assertion for an arbitrary extension; the lifts were not required to form a homomorphism or a global transversal. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The trivial group satisfies [F1] using its singleton set. Induct up the given finite subnormal series. At each stage the kernel is the previous subgroup and the quotient is torsion-free abelian, so step 1.1 supplies the quotient condition and step 2.1 supplies the extension condition. This proves [F1] for every PTFA group in the full subnormal convention of [F3]. The construction uses only finitely many witnesses at each of finitely many stages. It constructs finite sets directly, without invariant means, ultrafilters or simultaneous choices over a family of tests, and hence adds no choice hypothesis. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $\mu,\nu$ be probability
measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with
$|f|\le M$ for some $0\le M<\infty$. Use the library convention
$$\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|.$$
Then
$$|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}.$$

For the complete posterior computation error budget defined above, the
pathwise total error satisfies
$$|\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}|\le\mathcal B_f.$$
This is a telescoping bound; it does not estimate any component.

Separately, let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with transition kernel $K$, invariant law $\pi_K$, and initial law
$X_0\sim\pi_K$, and use the same bounded functional $f$. Put
$$\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))\qquad(k\ge0).$$
If $\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|<\infty$, then for every burn-in $b\ge0$ and
sample size $N\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\left[|\bar f_{b,N}-\pi_K(f)|^2\right]=\frac{1}{N^2}\left[N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k\right]\le\frac{\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|}{N}.$$
The sample bound assumes stationarity; for a nonstationary start, the budget
keeps $|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|$ as a separate burn-in term.
This finite-$N$ variance bound is not a central limit theorem or a confidence
interval.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget|The six adjacent posterior, solver, discretization, kernel, burn-in, and Monte Carlo error terms.]]

[[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws|Total variation is the event supremum and has no factor $1/2$ in that convention.]]

[[thm-total-variation-bounds-for-expectations|With this convention, a measurable function bounded by $M$ has expectation difference at most $2M$ times total variation.]]

[[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel|An invariant law satisfies $\pi K=\pi$.]]

[[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel|The one-step conditional law is given by the transition kernel.]]

[[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift|Strict stationarity means all finite-dimensional laws are unchanged by time shifts.]]

[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance|Variance and covariance are expectations of centered products.]]

[[thm-pathwise-error-ledger-decomposition|A finite scalar reference chain telescopes into its adjacent signed errors.]]

[Gibbs and Su, §2, total-variation dual form](https://math.hmc.edu/su/wp-content/uploads/sites/10/2019/06/ON-CHOOSING-AND-BOUNDING-PROBABILITY.pdf)

[Levin, Peres, and Wilmer, §4.1, Proposition 4.5](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/markovmixing.pdf)

[Geyer, §1.1, stationary sample-mean variance](https://www.stat.umn.edu/geyer/f05/8931/n1998.pdf)

## Remarks

An ESS is functional-specific and is not a substitute for a Monte Carlo standard
error. The variance bound in this Proposition is a population statement under
its chain assumptions; it does not validate a finite-chain empirical ESS
estimate.

## Remarks references

[Vehtari et al., §3.2, functional-specific ESS and MCSE](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.08008v5)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement, the complete error budget when its pathwise bound is used, and a stationary Markov chain in the separate sample-error branch.

[F1] Total variation is the event supremum $\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$; it has no half-factor. [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]

[F2] If $\mu,\nu$ are probability measures and $|f|\le M$, then $|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}$. [[thm-total-variation-bounds-for-expectations]]

[F3] The error budget consists of the six absolute adjacent differences from $\mu_\star(f)$ through $\bar f_{b,N}$, and its Monte Carlo component is pathwise. [[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget]]

[F4] A stationary chain has marginal law $\pi_K$ at every time, and the covariance of $f(X_i),f(X_j)$ depends only on the lag $|j-i|$. [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]] [[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]

[F5] For square-integrable real random variables, variance is the expected squared centered value and covariance is the expected product of centered values. [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]

[F6] For a finite scalar reference chain, the total signed error telescopes and its absolute value is bounded by the sum of absolute adjacent errors. [[thm-pathwise-error-ledger-decomposition]]

[A1] AC is assumed only for the library time-homogeneous Markov-chain interface; this proposition assumes stationarity and makes no chain-existence claim. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 Since $|f|\le M$, [F2] applies to $\mu$ and $\nu$; [F1] fixes the event-supremum convention, so it yields the stated total-variation expectation bound. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 The successive scalar references in [F3] have signed adjacent differences whose sum is $\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}$. Apply [F6] to this finite reference chain to obtain $|\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}|\le\mathcal B_f$. [given, F3, F6, algebra]

2.1 For the stationary branch, set $Y_j=f(X_{b+j})-\pi_K(f)$. By [F4], each $Y_j$ has mean zero and $\mathbb E[Y_iY_j]=\gamma_{|i-j|}$. Expanding the finite square gives $\mathbb E[(N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N Y_j)^2]=N^{-2}(N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k)$: there are $N$ diagonal terms, and for each lag $k$ there are $N-k$ off-diagonal pairs, each counted twice. [A1, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.2 Since $0\le N-k\le N$ and $\gamma_0=\operatorname{Var}(f(X_0))\ge0$, the expression in step 2.1 is at most $N^{-1}(\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}|\gamma_k|)$, which is bounded by the claimed infinite-series expression. Absolute summability makes the bound finite. [step 2.1, F5, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $\nu_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $\nu_K\cong S^1\times\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K\to S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

## Statement references

[Hatcher, Theorem 3.44 and Corollary 3.45](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch3.pdf)

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, §§4.1 and 4.4](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

[Calegari, §3.3](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a smooth oriented knot $K:S^1\to S^3$, an oriented normal trivialization, a product tubular map on a disk neighbourhood of radius greater than $2\epsilon$, and the resulting closed product tube, exterior, and boundary torus.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]] defines $K$ as a smooth embedding of an oriented circle in the standard oriented $S^3$.

[F2] [[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]] defines the quotient normal bundle $\nu_K$.

[F3] [[def-knot-exterior]] defines the closed tube using a chosen smooth fibre norm, and fixes $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and the ambient orientation.

[F4] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]] defines the positive meridian as the oriented boundary of a normal disk and a preferred longitude as a degree-one parallel curve with zero image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$.

[F5] [[lem-knot-tubular-exterior-and-boundary]] supplies a product tubular map on a slightly larger disk bundle, the exterior retraction, and the product torus coordinates.

[F6] [[cor-homology-of-spheres]] gives $H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ and $H_1(S^3;\mathbb Z)=H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)=0$.

[F7] [[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]] gives homotopy invariance of singular homology.

[F8] [[lem-knot-exterior-has-peripheral-torus]] gives $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ with product meridian and section basis.

[F9] [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]] gives the exact homology sequence for an open cover.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under countable choice [A1], [F5] supplies a product tubular map and a closed product disk tube with the stated norm and radius data for every smooth oriented knot. [A1, F5, given, choose]

2.1 Write $D_r^2=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:|z|\le r\}$ in the product coordinates and set $U=\Phi(S^1\times\{|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$ and $V=S^3\setminus\Phi(S^1\times D^2_{\epsilon/2})$. The set $U$ is open because its source is open in the tubular domain and $\Phi$ maps that domain diffeomorphically onto an open set. The removed disk image is compact, hence closed in Hausdorff $S^3$, so $V$ is open. They cover $S^3$, and $U\cap V=\Phi(S^1\times\{\epsilon/2<|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$. [F1, F5, construct]

3.1 Radial homotopies retract $U$ onto $N(K)$ by replacing each fibre radius $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\min(r,\epsilon)$, fixing the zero vector; retract $V$ onto $E_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\max(r,\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon/2<r<2\epsilon$ and fixing points outside the product tube; and retract $U\cap V$ onto $T_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\epsilon$. Each formula remains within its domain, agrees with the identity at the relevant boundary, and fixes its target. Thus these are deformation retractions. [F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 On the overlap, composing its inclusion into $U$ with the first retraction gives radius $\min(r,\epsilon)$, while retracting first to $T_K$ and including into $N(K)$ gives radius $\epsilon$; linear interpolation stays in $N(K)$. For the inclusion into $V$, the corresponding radii are $\max(r,\epsilon)$ and $\epsilon$, and their interpolation stays in $E_K$. Hence, after the deformation-retraction identifications, the two maps in Mayer–Vietoris are the maps induced by $T_K\hookrightarrow N(K)$ and $T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$. By [F7], homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on homology. [F7, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 By [F9], the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the open cover of step 2.1 has the segment $$H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(U\cap V;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(U;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(S^3;\mathbb Z).$$ The outer groups vanish by [F6], so the middle map is an isomorphism. Under the identifications of step 4.1, it is induced by the two boundary inclusions. [F6, F7, F9, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 By [F8], $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ with basis $([\mu],[\sigma])$. The product tube $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$ retracts to its core $S^1$ by contraction in each disk fibre, so homotopy invariance [F7] and [F6] give $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Put $H=H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Steps 3.1–5.1 give $\mathbb Z^2\cong\mathbb Z\oplus H$. The isomorphism embeds $H$ as a subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$. Every subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$ is free of rank at most two: projection to one coordinate has cyclic image; if nonzero, choose a preimage of its positive generator to split it off, and the kernel is a subgroup of $\mathbb Z$; if zero, the subgroup already lies in $\mathbb Z$. Since the complementary $\mathbb Z$ has rank one and the total rank is two, $H$ has rank one. Therefore $H\cong\mathbb Z$. [F5, F6, F7, F8, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Choose $c$ to be the first component of the Mayer–Vietoris image of $[\sigma]$; it is a generator of $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)$ because the product section projects with degree one to the core of the product tube [F5, F8]. Choose a generator $h$ of $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, which exists by step 6.1. The meridian maps to zero in the $N(K)$ component because it bounds its fibre disk. In the bases $([\mu],[\sigma])$ and $(c,h)$, the Mayer–Vietoris isomorphism of step 5.1 has first column $(0,a)$ for some integer $a$ and second column whose first coordinate is $1$. Its determinant is therefore $\pm a$; since the map is an isomorphism over $\mathbb Z$, $a=\pm1$. Thus $[\mu]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. [F4, F5, F8, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer with $i_*[\sigma]=k[\mu]$, and put $[\lambda]=[\sigma]-k[\mu]$. Then $i_*[\lambda]=0$, $p_*[\lambda]=1$, and the change from the basis $([\mu],[\sigma])$ to $([\mu],[\lambda])$ has determinant $1$. In the new basis, $i_*(a[\mu]+b[\lambda])=a[\mu]$, so the kernel is exactly $\mathbb Z[\lambda]$, a primitive rank-one direct summand. Every degree-one class is $[\sigma]+a[\mu]$ and maps to zero exactly when $a=-k$, proving uniqueness. The curve $t\mapsto(e^{2\pi it},e^{-2\pi ikt})$ is embedded in $S^1\times S^1$ because its first coordinate is injective on $S^1$; it represents $[\lambda]$ and is a preferred longitude. [F4, F8, step 7.1, algebra, construct] ∎

      locator: §§I.2 and II.1, printed pp. 282–287; sign convention $F_A^-=0$ and $c_2(P)[X]=-1$
---

## Definition

Let $X$ be a closed oriented Riemannian four-manifold and let $P\to X$ be a smooth principal $SU(2)$-bundle with $c_2(P)[X]=-1$. The Hodge star on two-forms is $*$, and $F_A^-=(F_A-*F_A)/2$ denotes the anti-self-dual projection of the curvature of a connection $A$. The equation used in this item is $F_A^-=0$, so the curvature is self-dual; this convention and the negative second Chern number are fixed together for the positive-definite orientation. The self-dual moduli set is the set of smooth connections satisfying $F_A^-=0$, modulo the action of smooth gauge transformations of $P$. At a solution, the deformation complex is $0\to\Omega^0(X;\operatorname{ad}P)\xrightarrow{d_A}\Omega^1(X;\operatorname{ad}P)\xrightarrow{d_A^-}\Omega^-(X;\operatorname{ad}P)\to0$, and its gauge-fixed operator is $D_A=d_A^*\oplus d_A^-$. For index calculations, $D_A$ is completed from the first Sobolev space of one-forms to the direct sum of the zeroth Sobolev spaces of zero-forms and anti-self-dual two-forms.

    - title: "Jennifer Hom, Lecture notes on Heegaard Floer homology"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.01836v1"
      locator: "Sections 2.1–2.2; rational homology sphere Heegaard Floer groups and grading normalization"
---

## Definition

A rational homology sphere is a closed connected oriented three-manifold $Y$ with $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. Let $\mathfrak t$ be a Spin$^c$ structure on $Y$, meaning a principal $\mathrm{Spin}^c(3)$ lift of the oriented frame bundle. A pointed Heegaard diagram for $(Y,\mathfrak t)$ consists of a closed oriented surface $\Sigma$ of genus $g$, two systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_g)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_g)$ of pairwise disjoint simple closed curves which bound complete disk systems in the two genus-$g$ handlebodies of a Heegaard splitting of $Y$, and a basepoint $z\in\Sigma\setminus(\boldsymbol\alpha\cup\boldsymbol\beta)$; the diagram is restricted to the generators assigned to $\mathfrak t$. A periodic domain is an integral two-chain in the complementary regions whose boundary is an integral sum of attaching curves. The diagram is strongly admissible for $\mathfrak t$ when every nonzero periodic domain $P$ with $n_z(P)=0$ and $\langle c_1(\mathfrak t),[P]\rangle\ge0$ has at least one positive and one negative region coefficient.

For such a diagram, put $\mathbb T_\alpha=\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_g$ and $\mathbb T_\beta=\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_g$ in $\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)=\Sigma^g/S_g$. A generator is an intersection point $\mathbf x\in\mathbb T_\alpha\cap\mathbb T_\beta$. A Whitney disk class $\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a relative homotopy class of disks in $\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)$ with boundary arcs on the two product tori and endpoints $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$; its Maslov index is $\mu(\phi)$ and its local multiplicity at $z$ is $n_z(\phi)$. For a regular almost-complex datum for which every relevant count is finite and the disk-count operator squares to zero, define $CF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t)$ over $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ on generators $[\mathbf x,i]$, $i\in\mathbb Z$, with differential
$$
\partial^\infty[\mathbf x,i]=\sum_{\mathbf y}\sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\\\mu(\phi)=1,\ n_z(\phi)\ge0}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)[\mathbf y,i-n_z(\phi)].
$$
Here $\mathbb F_2$ is the field with two elements, $U[\mathbf x,i]=[\mathbf x,i-1]$, and $\#_2$ is the finite count modulo two. The submodule generated by $[\mathbf x,i]$ with $i<0$ is $CF^-(Y,\mathfrak t)$, $CF^+(Y,\mathfrak t)=CF^\infty/CF^-$, and $HF^\infty$ and $HF^+$ denote their homology when the differential is established. Relative Maslov gradings are fixed by the Fredholm index and the shift under $U$ is $-2$.

When the standard absolute rational Maslov grading is available, normalize it so that the generator of $HF^\infty(S^3)$ has degree zero. For a smooth Spin$^c$ cobordism $(W,\mathfrak s)$ between rational homology spheres, the induced map is assigned degree shift
$$
\frac{\langle c_1(\mathfrak s)^2\rangle-2\chi(W)-3\sigma(W)}{4},
$$
where $c_1(\mathfrak s)$ is the first Chern class, $\chi(W)$ is Euler characteristic, $\sigma(W)$ is the signature, and its square is evaluated using the rational intersection form of $W$. This is a convention for a Floer package when constructed; it asserts neither existence of generic regular data nor that the disk-count differential squares to zero. Heegaard invariance, the absolute grading on general $(Y,\mathfrak t)$, and cobordism-map properties are separate claims.

## Definition

A regular link diagram is **connected** when its underlying projection graph is connected. It is **alternating** when successive crossing visits along each component switch between overpasses and underpasses. It is **reduced** when no complementary region of the projection sphere has a crossing more than once on its boundary. A connected alternating diagram that is reduced is a **reduced alternating link diagram**.

## Definition references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, Definition 5.17](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Kindred, *A geometric proof of the flyping theorem*, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.06490v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular link diagram $D$ with its finite projection graph and over-under data.

[F1] A regular oriented link diagram has finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and an over-under datum at each crossing ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

## Proof
1.1 The projection graph, its complementary regions, and the cyclic order of crossing visits along each component are finite data by [F1]. Thus connectedness, alternation, and the stated repeated-region condition are properties determined by the given diagram. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Forgetting all strand orientations preserves the projection graph and the over-under data, so each condition is unchanged by reversing component orientations. The definition therefore applies consistently to the underlying unoriented diagram. [given, F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎

The dashed branch is the under-strand and each arrow points from bottom to top.
The labels at the top and bottom agree because the braid is pure. The diagram
records the word only; the proofs below use the explicit crossing sequence and
group words.

## Example references

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§4–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

[Stees, §2.5](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/54c7d68f-d982-4e1f-9550-e54140ada5ea/content)

[Wolfram MathWorld, Borromean Rings](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/BorromeanRings.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The based string link, the stated braid diagram, and its product-tube basing.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, supplies the classifying-space and nilpotent-quotient branch. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The positive Artin generator is the positive geometric half twist in the fixed crossing convention, and its inverse reverses the over/under choice. [[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]

[F2] The based string-link longitude is the ordered product of the over-meridians encountered at its undercrossings, with exponent determined by source-to-target direction. [[lem-link-peripheral-longitude-word-from-diagram]]

[F3] The finite lower-central quotient identifies the bottom and top peripheral systems, and the Magnus coefficient defines $\mu_{\tau_B}(1,2,3)$. [[thm-string-link-nilpotent-peripheral-identifications]], [[def-milnor-integer-and-residue-invariants]]

[F4] The diagram linking-number scan returns one half the signed mixed-crossing sum. [[alg-oriented-linking-number-from-diagram]], [[thm-oriented-linking-number-scan-terminates-and-is-correct]]

[F5] **External input:** The standard closure of the braid word $(\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2)^3$ is the Borromean rings. Wolfram MathWorld lists this exact word as a Borromean braid; this input identifies the closure, while the pairwise-linking and Milnor-coefficient calculations are proved below. [Wolfram MathWorld, Braid Word](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/BraidWord.html)

## Verification

**Given:** The braid word and the input conventions in the Example.

1.1 The rightmost factor is stacked lowest, so the factors from bottom to top are $\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1},\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1},\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1}$. Starting from the bottom positions, the component-position sequence after successive crossings is $(1,2,3)$, $(1,3,2)$, $(3,1,2)$, $(3,2,1)$, $(2,3,1)$, $(2,1,3)$, $(1,2,3)$. The six crossing-label pairs and signs in that order are respectively $(2,3,+1)$, $(1,3,-1)$, $(1,2,+1)$, $(2,3,-1)$, $(1,3,+1)$, and $(1,2,-1)$, as determined by the signed generators in the braid word and [F1]. Thus the closure returns each label to its own endpoint, and each component pair crosses twice with opposite signs. By [F4] each pairwise linking number is half the signed mixed-crossing sum, hence is zero. [F1, F4, given, construct]

2.1 At crossing 1, component 2 passes under component 3, so its meridian becomes $B=x_3^{-1}x_2x_3$. At crossing 2, component 3 passes under component 1 and contributes the longitude factor $x_1^{-1}$. At crossing 3, component 1 passes under component 2, so its meridian becomes $C=B^{-1}x_1B$. At crossing 5, component 3 passes under component 1 and contributes the factor $C$. The other crossings do not put component 3 under. Hence $\lambda_3=x_1^{-1}C=x_1^{-1}B^{-1}x_1B$. [F2, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 In $R_2$, $E(B)\equiv1+X_2\pmod{\mathfrak m^2}$, so
$$E(C)=E(B)^{-1}(1+X_1)E(B)=1+X_1+X_1X_2-X_2X_1\pmod{\mathfrak m^3}.$$
Since $E(x_1^{-1})=1-X_1+X_1^2$, multiplication gives
$$E(\lambda_3)=E(x_1^{-1})E(C)=1+X_1X_2-X_2X_1\pmod{\mathfrak m^3}.$$
Under [A1], the $X_1X_2$ coefficient is $+1$, so [F3] gives $\mu_{\tau_B}(1,2,3)=1$. [A1, F3, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 The computed longitude has zero degree-one term, as required by the chosen untwisted based peripheral system. Closing the endpoints along crossing-free arcs adds no undercrossing factor, and component 3 has self-writhe zero, so the same word is its based closed-link preferred longitude by [F2]. Every proper length-two subsequence in $\Delta_{123}^b$ is a pairwise linking number, so step 1.1 makes $\Delta_{123}^b=0$. Thus the same coefficient gives the closed-link residue candidate $1$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a knot. The input package required by the Baldwin–Sivek thin-knot and infinitely-many-abelian-surgeries arguments consists of the following conclusions with their stated hypotheses: (i) a nontrivial $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-averse knot has a unique rational accumulation slope and either it or its mirror is an instanton L-space knot; (ii) a nontrivial instanton L-space knot is fibered and its symmetrized Alexander polynomial has coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$ with nonzero coefficients alternating in sign; (iii) the L-space satellite restrictions and the pattern/companion surgery-transfer statements exclude the satellite cases used in §§3–5; and (iv) the hyperbolic Dehn-filling theorem and the knot-exterior JSJ classification reduce the remaining cases to torus knots. This carrier records the exact imported result interfaces and does not assert that these conclusions have been proved locally.

## Statement references

[Baldwin and Sivek, §§2–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

[Sivek and Zentner, Theorems 1.1 and 4.1, Proposition 10.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.01957v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the full original input-package scope. The finite representation/pillowcase argument below is retained. Its gauge-theoretic premises are explicit external inputs, not locally reconstructed instanton proofs.

[F1] Filling with primitive slope $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ imposes the actual group relation $\mu^p\lambda^q=1$. Abelianization of a knot group is generated by its meridian. A unitary reducible two-dimensional representation is simultaneously diagonal: the orthogonal complement of its invariant line is invariant as well. Consequently its image is abelian, and a representation with abelian image factors through the cyclic abelianization of the filled group. Thus SU2-abelian and SU2-cyclic are equivalent here, including the zero-slope case. [[def-sl-two-abelian-surgery]] [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]]

[F2] The actual finite representation and common-eigenline incidence varieties have finitely many irreducible components. For each component, dimension of its affine image is the transcendence degree of its coordinate function field. The generic adjoint trace pairing, cap identity, pair exact sequence and word derivations apply over the actual finitely generated characteristic-zero field. [[lem-sl2-representation-variety-is-affine]] [[lem-classical-affine-algebraic-set-finite-irreducible-components]] [[thm-affine-domain-dimension-transcendence-degree]] [[lem-generic-adjoint-peripheral-kernel-is-the-logarithmic-conormal-line]]

[F3] The ordinary A-polynomial is a nonzero square-free Laurent equation for the one-dimensional peripheral eigenvalue-image components, including the abelian component. It omits isolated image components but not points on a curve component. [[def-knot-a-polynomial]]

[F4] The actual marked pattern/companion filling transfers, including reducible nonabelian SL2 cases, and the closed hyperbolic holonomy lift are already supplied. They do not establish the instanton alternative [L1], L-space surgery, or Alexander coefficient restrictions. [[lem-satellite-sl2-abelian-fillings-transfer-to-pattern-and-companion]] [[lem-closed-oriented-hyperbolic-holonomy-has-a-faithful-sl2-lift]]

[L1] **External input:** Sivek–Zentner, *SU(2)-cyclic surgeries and the pillowcase*, arXiv:1710.01957v2, Theorem 4.1 (statement on pp.3–4 and in §4), proves for EVERY nontrivial knot the following alternative: either the entire vertical circle $\alpha=\pi/2$ is realized by irreducible SU2 representations, or there is an arc of irreducible representations with meridian $\operatorname{diag}(e^{is},e^{-is})$, $s\in[\pi/2,\pi/2+\epsilon)$, $\epsilon>0$. This is imported in its actual varying-meridian scope; neither isolated representation existence nor the local analytic complex is substituted for it.

[L2] **External inputs:** Baldwin–Sivek, arXiv:2405.19197v2, Theorem 2.7 and Corollary 2.8 (p.6) give boundedness of the FULL SU2-abelian slope set, its unique rational limit $r(K)$ with $|r(K)|>2$, the stated one-sided instanton L-space surgery range, and the knot-or-mirror instanton L-space conclusion. Theorems 2.1–2.2 and Corollary 2.3 (pp.4–5) give fiberedness, alternating nonzero unit Alexander coefficients, and the additional adjacent highest terms $\pm(t^g-t^{g-1}+O(t^{g-2}))$. Lemma 2.4, Proposition 2.16 and Proposition 3.1 give precisely the satellite restrictions with their displayed winding, pattern and companion hypotheses; Lemmas 5.3–5.4 give the filling transfers. The classical knot trichotomy used in their Proposition 2.15 and proofs in §§4–5 is imported at that knot-exterior scope: a nontrivial nontorus nonsatellite knot is hyperbolic. No arbitrary atoroidal manifold assertion is inferred from a definition. These are established external results, not new local proofs of their gauge or hyperbolization foundations.

[F5] **Reading boundary:** the cited primary theorem statements, hypotheses and Corollary 2.3 proof were consulted directly. The gauge-theoretic proofs underlying [L1]–[L2] have not been reconstructed here. Their use is authorized by the run-specific external-source rule; the accepted local filling and slope arguments remain in place.

## Proof

1.1 **The exact full slope set.** Write $\mathcal S(K)=\{p/q\in\mathbb Q:\gcd(p,q)=1,\ q>0,\ E_K(p/q)\text{ is SU2-abelian}\}$. Its elements are DISTINCT slopes, not a selected sequence. The meridional slope $\infty$ is isolated and is not a finite-surgery parameter in this set. A simultaneous peripheral diagonalization of an SU2 representation gives $\rho(\mu)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha})$ and $\rho(\lambda)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\beta},e^{-i\beta})$. The simultaneous inversion $(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto(-\alpha,-\beta)$ is the pillowcase quotient. For any continuous lifted path through peripheral images of irreducible representations, a slope in $\mathcal S(K)$ satisfies $p\alpha(t)+q\beta(t)\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$: equality would give an actual irreducible representation of the filled group, contradicting [F1]. Continuity puts this entire real function in one component of $\mathbb R\setminus2\pi\mathbb Z$. Thus for ANY two points of that path, $|p(\alpha_1-\alpha_0)+q(\beta_1-\beta_0)|<2\pi.$ This is a full-set exclusion, valid for positive, negative and zero numerators. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **The exact instanton interface selects a nonvertical path.** Under [L1], its first alternative makes $\mathcal S(K)$ empty: for any finite $p/q$ choose $\beta=-p\pi/(2q)$ modulo $2\pi$ on that full vertical circle, giving an actual irreducible filling representation. Hence an SU2-averse knot, for which $\mathcal S(K)$ is infinite, must satisfy the second alternative. On a smaller closed subinterval its meridian is noncentral and already diagonal. Its commuting longitude is diagonal too; its eigenvalue is a continuous circle-valued function, so subdivision into finitely many open semicircle charts gives a continuous real lift $\beta$. The meridian coordinate $\alpha=s$ has distinct endpoint values. This is the ONLY use of [L1] in the subsequent path argument; no bare nontrivial-knot representation-existence assertion is silently substituted for its varying-meridian conclusion. [F1, L1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Boundedness of ALL slopes.** Fix such a nonvertical path and endpoints, put $d=\alpha_1-\alpha_0\ne0$, $r_0=-(\beta_1-\beta_0)/d$ and $C=2\pi/|d|$. Step1.1 gives $|p/q-r_0|<C/q\le C$ for EVERY $p/q\in\mathcal S(K)$. Thus the full set is contained in the fixed bounded interval $[r_0-C,r_0+C]$; an unbounded exceptional subsequence is excluded. In a bounded interval there are only finitely many reduced fractions with denominator at most any fixed $Q$: for each $1\le q\le Q$ only finitely many integers $p$ satisfy the interval bound. Consequently, along EVERY sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $\mathcal S(K)$, $q\to\infty$ and the displayed inequality forces $p/q\to r_0$. The infinite set therefore has exactly one accumulation point in $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$, namely the finite $r_0$. This proves both quantifiers needed when passing to arbitrary infinite subsets. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **All lifted paths are straight and parallel.** Apply step1.1 to any two points of any continuous lifted irreducible peripheral path and to a sequence of distinct elements of the FULL set. Divide by $q$ and use step3.1 to obtain $r_0(\alpha_1-\alpha_0)+(\beta_1-\beta_0)=0.$ Thus $\beta+r_0\alpha$ is constant on each path, and any nonconstant one lies on a line of slope $-r_0$. In particular the varying-meridian path of step2.1 contains every point of a nontrivial interval of that line: its $\alpha$ coordinate covers the whole endpoint interval by continuity. No finite-component or semialgebraic path-selection assertion is required for this implication. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **A nonzero Laurent equation actually vanishes on this arc.** For completeness the needed image-dimension operation is the accepted field-linear adjoint calculation [F2], not an assumption that the A-polynomial Definition excludes larger images. If a generic irreducible eigenline-incidence component had algebraically independent $M,L$, its function field would admit two derivations independently differentiating $M,L$; extend these through its finite separable algebraic part by the minimal-polynomial derivative formula. The actual boundary homology has dimension two. Self-duality and the pair exact sequence make both boundary inclusion and cohomological restriction rank one. The actual word/eigenbasis pairing therefore puts ALL logarithmic derivative pairs $(DL/L,DM/M)$ in the same line, contradicting those two independent derivations. Reducible components have $L=1$ by knot abelianization. All peripheral images thus have dimension at most one. The finitely many zero-dimensional image components give only finitely many points. The nonconstant interval of step4.1, after discarding these points, lies in the union of the one-dimensional image curves; hence the nonzero Laurent polynomial $A_K$ in [F3] vanishes on it. By continuity it vanishes on the entire interval. This argument allows arbitrary dimensions of the underlying character components and does not confuse a one-parameter family with a maximal image component. [F1, F2, F3, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 **Rationality by a finite exponential calculation.** Write $A_K(M,L)=\sum_{(a,b)\in T}c_{ab}M^aL^b$, with finite distinct integral pairs and nonzero coefficients. On the interval $M=e^{i\alpha}$, $L=e^{i(c-r_0\alpha)}$, step5.1 gives $\sum_{(a,b)\in T} c_{ab}e^{ibc}e^{i(a-r_0b)\alpha}=0.$ If $r_0$ were irrational, all real numbers $a-r_0b$ would be distinct: equality for different pairs would either force identical pairs or express $r_0$ as a ratio of integers. Differentiate this finite identity $0,1,\ldots,|T|-1$ times at an interior point. Its coefficient matrix is a Vandermonde matrix in the distinct numbers $i(a-r_0b)$, multiplied by nonzero diagonal exponentials. Its determinant is nonzero, forcing every $c_{ab}e^{ibc}=0$, contrary to their choice. Thus $r_0\in\mathbb Q$. This proves rationality without importing a transcendence-number theorem or claiming arithmetic algebraicity of isolated pillowcase points. [F3, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 **Full package with explicit external inputs.** Steps1.1–6.1 prove the elementary full-set boundedness, uniqueness and rationality operation from [L1]. The actual alternative is now supplied externally by [L1], while [L2] supplies the additional nonzero bound, L-space surgery, fiberedness, Alexander and satellite interfaces. The accepted filling and closed-lift operations [F4], together with the external knot-exterior trichotomy in [L2], give the geometric reductions required in §§3–5. These establish all four parts of the original package under its stated hypotheses. This completion uses external gauge and classification results; it does not assert local reconstructions of those results. [F1, F2, F3, F4, L1, L2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎

## Statement

Let P be an oriented pattern of winding n≠0 and K an oriented knot. If P(U) bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B whose oriented boundary is identified with the standard oriented S³ and H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i, then for every K the zero surgeries M(P(K)) and M(K) are smoothly R_n-homology cobordant. For the positive meridians determined by the supplied orientations, their images in the cobordism satisfy [mu_K]=n[mu_{P(K)}]; in particular they differ by a unit of R_n. This is a winding-unit meridian comparison, not a claim of literal equality for arbitrary winding. If P has strong winding number ±1 and P(U) is pseudo-slice (respectively locally flat topologically slice), then M(P(K)) and M(K) are smoothly (respectively topologically) homology cobordant through a 4-manifold whose fundamental group is normally generated by the image of the fundamental group of either boundary component. The category and closure hypotheses are separate and cannot be inferred from winding alone.

## Statement references

[[def-cdr-satellite-concordance-categories|Pseudo-slice and localized concordance conventions]]

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|Smooth slice disks and locally flat topological slice disks]]

[[def-satellite-induced-concordance-operator|Pattern, winding and strong-winding conventions]]

[CFHH, Theorem 2.1 and complete proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5730)

[CDR, Theorems 4.1 and 4.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.5058v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A pattern of winding n≠0, a knot K, and the stated Z[1/|n|]-slice disk for P(U) in its compact smooth oriented homology ball, with its boundary orientation matched to the standard S³. The pseudo-slice convention likewise includes this orientation. No orientability is inferred solely from localized homology.

## Statement

If the underlying projection of a regular link diagram on $S^2$ is disconnected, then the represented link is split.

## Statement references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2 and Exercise 5.14](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Menasco, *Closed incompressible surfaces in alternating knot and link complements* (1984), Theorem 1(a)](https://www.scribd.com/document/471863717/1-s2-0-0040938384900235-main-2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular link diagram whose projection graph is a finite disconnected subset $P\subset S^2$.

[F1] A regular diagram is the projection of a finite disjoint union of embedded circles, and its projection has finitely many transverse double points ([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

[F2] A link is split if a sphere disjoint from it has link points on both sides ([[def-split-link]]).

[F3] A disconnected finite projection graph admits a Jordan curve in its complement with diagram points on both sides ([[lem-disconnected-projection-components-separated-by-jordan-curve]]).

[F4] The proof of [F3] constructs its separating curve as a smooth boundary component of a finite regular neighborhood. The choice-free smooth Jordan-disk result gives a closed disk on either side of that curve on $S^2$ ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-jordan-disk-parameters-and-prescribed-collars]]).

## Proof
1.1 By [F1], the projection graph has finitely many components and the link has compact image. Choose a point of $S^2\setminus P$ as infinity and work in the resulting finite projection plane. Apply the regular-neighborhood construction in the proof of [F3] in this chart; its smooth separating curve $\gamma$ misses the projection and has diagram points on both sides. Choose the bounded closed side as the disk $\Delta$, using [F4]. [given, F1, F3, F4, choose]

2.1 Regard $S^2$ as the projection sphere in $S^3$. The product $\Delta\times[-M,M]$ is a smoothly embedded 3-ball after rounding its corners, where $M$ exceeds the absolute height of every point of the compact link. Its rounded boundary consists of the side annulus over $\gamma$ and the two caps at heights $\pm M$; it is a sphere. Since $\gamma$ misses the projection and the caps lie above and below the link, this sphere misses the link. The two sides meet the link because $\Delta$ and its complementary disk each contain projection points, so [F2] says that the link is split. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct] ∎
