## Statement

Assume AC. Let $G$ be a discrete group, let $A=\mathcal N G\subseteq\mathcal B(\ell^2(G))$ have its canonical faithful normal trace $\tau$, and give matrices the unnormalized trace $\tau_r((a_{ij}))=\sum_{i=1}^r\tau(a_{ii})$. For a projection $p\in M_r(A)$ put $\dim_A(pA^r)=\tau_r(p)$; for any right $A$-module take the supremum of dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules. These dimensions are independent of the projective representation. If $L\subseteq pA^r$ is any submodule and $q$ is the projection onto its Hilbert closure in $p\ell^2(G)^r$, then $q\in M_r(A)$, $q\le p$, and
$$\dim_A L=\tau_r(q),\qquad \dim_A(pA^r/L)=\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q).$$
In particular a Hilbert-dense submodule has dimension-zero quotient. Modules of dimension zero are closed under submodules, quotients, extensions and filtered colimits. For any matrix $B\in M_{r,s}(A)$, its kernel and Hilbert-closed image are projection modules, its algebraic image is isomorphic to its support projection module, and
$$\tau_s(P_{\ker B})+\tau_r(P_{\overline{\operatorname{im}B}})=s.$$

## Statement references

[[def-tracial-state-and-faithful-normal-trace-on-a-von-neumann-algebra]]

[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-bounded-normal-operators-pvm-form]]

[[thm-polar-decomposition-for-bounded-operators]]

[Cha–Orr, Section 6.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0910.3700)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the group algebra von Neumann closure $A$, its canonical trace and the dimension convention in the Statement. Vectors in $A^r$ are columns and matrices act on the left, so their maps are right $A$-linear.

[F1] The canonical group trace is faithful, normal and tracial. Matrix traces inherit these properties by finite summation. [[def-tracial-state-and-faithful-normal-trace-on-a-von-neumann-algebra]]

[F2] A generated concrete von Neumann algebra is strongly closed and equals its double commutant. [[thm-double-commutant-theorem-for-concrete-von-neumann-algebras]]

[F3] Bounded self-adjoint operators have spectral projections and bounded Borel functional calculus. [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-bounded-normal-operators-pvm-form]]

[F4] A bounded operator has polar decomposition, with initial and final spaces the closures of its adjoint range and range. [[thm-polar-decomposition-for-bounded-operators]]

[A1] AC is the standing hypothesis of [F2]–[F4]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement.

1.1 A spectral projection of a self-adjoint matrix over $A$ belongs to the same matrix von Neumann algebra: it commutes with every element of that algebra's commutant by [F3], so belongs to its double commutant by [F2]. In the rectangular case apply this observation to $B^*B$ and $BB^*$; the polar partial isometry is the strong limit of $B(B^*B+\varepsilon I)^{-1/2}$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and belongs to the rectangular matrix algebra by [F2]–[F4]. Thus kernel, initial and final projections are matrices over $A$. The equality $\tau_s(v^*v)=\tau_r(vv^*)$, obtained by summing the trace identity for the matrix entries of $v$, gives the displayed rank-nullity formula. The algebraic kernel is exactly $P_{\ker B}A^s$, and $B$ maps $(I-P_{\ker B})A^s$ bijectively onto its algebraic image. [F1, F2, F3, F4, A1, algebra]

2.1 Every finite projective module has the form $eA^r$ for an idempotent $e$. Its Hilbert range is closed because $e^2=e$. Let $p$ be its orthogonal range projection, which lies in $M_r(A)$ by step 1.1. Since $ep=p$ and $pe=e$, one has $eA^r=pA^r$. Every module map between two such projection modules is given by a rectangular matrix: extend it to the ambient finite free module by composing with the source projection. If the algebraic map is injective, its Hilbert kernel projection is zero, since a nonzero kernel projection has a nonzero column in the algebraic kernel. Polar decomposition then implies that the source projection trace is at most the target projection trace. Applying this to an isomorphism and its inverse proves invariance of projective dimension. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For finitely many vectors of $L$, let $B$ have those vectors as columns. The corresponding range projection $q_B$ lies in $M_r(A)$ by step 1.1. As the finite subsets increase, the ranges increase, and their union has Hilbert closure equal to the closure of $L$: a vector $x\in A^r$ gives its Hilbert representative by applying its entries to $\delta_e$, while right translates of those representatives are also representatives of vectors of $L$. Their closed span contains the range of each column operator, because the coordinate vectors span $\ell^2(G)$ densely. The increasing projections converge strongly to their supremum $q\in M_r(A)$ by [F2]. Their ranges lie in the range of $p$, so $q\le p$. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For each such $B$, let $q_{B,\varepsilon}=\mathbf1_{[\varepsilon,\infty)}(BB^*)$ for $\varepsilon>0$. Then $q_{B,\varepsilon}\le q_B$ and $q_{B,\varepsilon}\uparrow q_B$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The bounded Borel function $f_\varepsilon(t)=t^{-1}\mathbf1_{[\varepsilon,\infty)}(t)$ gives $q_{B,\varepsilon}=BB^*f_\varepsilon(BB^*)$. Hence every column of $q_{B,\varepsilon}$ is a right $A$-linear combination of columns of $B$, and $q_{B,\varepsilon}A^r\subseteq L$. Normality of the trace first lets these traces approach $\tau_r(q_B)$ and then, over finite subsets, $\tau_r(q)$. Conversely any finite projective submodule of $L$ embeds in $qA^r$, so step 2.1 bounds its dimension by $\tau_r(q)$. Taking suprema proves $\dim_A L=\tau_r(q)$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The module $(p-q)A^r$ embeds in $pA^r/L$, giving lower dimension bound $\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q)$. For the reverse bound let a finite projective $P$ embed in that quotient. Projectivity lifts this map to a map $f:P\to pA^r$. For each projection $q_{B,\varepsilon}$ from step 3.1, the map $(p-q_{B,\varepsilon})f$ is injective: its kernel maps under $f$ into $q_{B,\varepsilon}A^r\subseteq L$, and therefore has zero image under the given embedding of $P$ into the quotient. Step 2.1 yields $\dim_A P\le\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q_{B,\varepsilon})$. Taking the projection traces arbitrarily close to $\tau_r(q)$ proves the quotient formula. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Submodules of a zero-dimensional module are zero-dimensional by the defining supremum. If a finite projective embeds in a quotient of a zero-dimensional module, projectivity lifts it to an injective map into the original module; hence its dimension is zero, proving quotient closure. For an exact sequence $0\to U\to V\to W\to0$ with $U,W$ zero-dimensional, take any finite projective $P\subseteq V$. Its kernel $K=P\cap U$ and its image $P/K\subseteq W$ are zero-dimensional. Apply steps 3.1 and 4.1 inside a projection representation of $P$: those formulas give $\dim_A P=\dim_A K+\dim_A(P/K)=0$. Thus $V$ is zero-dimensional. Finally, each image of a zero-dimensional module in a filtered colimit is zero-dimensional by quotient closure; these images form a directed family. Every finite set of generators of a finite projective submodule of the colimit lies in one member, so that projective has dimension zero. This proves filtered-colimit closure. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ be a rank-two lattice acting on $\mathbb H^3$ by horizontal translations, and let
$$
C=\{(x+iy,t):t\ge1\}/\Gamma
$$
be the quotient of the horoball $t\ge1$. If $A$ is the Euclidean area of a fundamental parallelogram for $\Gamma$, then the end is at infinite hyperbolic distance and $\operatorname{Vol}(C)=A/2$.

## Statement references

[Jessica S. Purcell, *Hyperbolic Knot Theory*, §4.3](https://users.monash.edu/~jpurcell/book/HypKnotTheory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The upper half-space metric and a rank-two translation lattice $\Gamma$.

[F1] [[def-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-and-cusp-holonomy]] gives $ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2)$ and its volume density $dx\,dy\,dt/t^3$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $Q$ be a fundamental parallelogram of area $A$. Integrating the density from [F1] over $Q\times[1,\infty)$ gives $\operatorname{Vol}(C)=\int_Q\int_1^\infty t^{-3}\,dt\,dx\,dy=A[1/(2t^2)]_1^\infty=A/2$. The improper integral converges because $t^{-3}$ is integrable on $[1,\infty)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Along any piecewise smooth path with height coordinate $t$, its hyperbolic length is at least $\int |dt|/t$, since the metric contains the term $dt^2/t^2$. A path escaping the end has $t\to\infty$, so this lower bound diverges as $\log t$. Thus the end is at infinite distance and is complete toward its ideal end. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

      url: "https://www.ime.usp.br/~glaucio/mat6704/textos/GMTLecureNotes.pdf"
      locator: "§7.4, distributional product rule and variation estimate"

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. If $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ and $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$, there exist smooth cutoffs $\chi_k$ with $0\le\chi_k\le1$, $\chi_k=1$ on $B(0,k)$, support in $B(0,2k)$, and $\sup_{k\ge1}k\|\nabla\chi_k\|_\infty<\infty$. For every family satisfying these four conditions, $v_k:=\chi_ku$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1(\mathbb R^2)$, has support in $B(0,2k)$, converges to $u$ in $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$, and
$$\limsup_{k\to\infty}TV(v_k;\mathbb R^2)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|Finite L² TV is the global mass of the distributional derivative.]]

[[lem-ip-tv-l2-finite-variation-has-radon-derivative|Finite L² distributional variation is represented by a finite vector Radon measure.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with finite $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the axiom used to obtain the finite Radon derivative from the test-field bound. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation]] and [[lem-ip-tv-l2-finite-variation-has-radon-derivative]]: $Du$ is a finite vector Radon measure and $|Du|(\mathbb R^2)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F2] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: a smooth cutoff exists that equals one on the unit ball and is supported in the ball of radius two; rescaling by $R$ bounds its gradient by a fixed constant times $R^{-1}$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $B(0,1)$, $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset B(0,2)$, and let $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ for integers $R\ge1$. This proves existence of a family with $\sup_R R\|\nabla\chi_R\|_\infty<\infty$. Now fix any family satisfying all four conditions in the statement, write $C=\sup_R R\|\nabla\chi_R\|_\infty$, and put $v_R=\chi_Ru$. Then $v_R\in L^2$ has compact support, hence is in $L^1$, and $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ because $\chi_R=1$ on $B(0,R)$ and $u\in L^2$. [A1, F2, given, choose, construct]

2.1 For every scalar $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, local integrability of $u$ and the definition of distributional derivative give $$-\int \chi_Ru\,\partial_i\psi=-\int u\,\partial_i(\chi_R\psi)+\int u\psi\,\partial_i\chi_R=\int\chi_R\psi\,dD_i u+\int u\psi\,\partial_i\chi_R.$$ Thus $D v_R=\chi_RDu+u\nabla\chi_R\,dx$. The variation of the first term is at most $|Du|(\mathbb R^2)$, and the second has variation at most $$\frac CR\int_{B(0,2R)\setminus B(0,R)}|u|\,dx\le C'\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus B(0,R))},$$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the annulus area bound $|B(0,2R)\setminus B(0,R)|^{1/2}\le C''R$. This error tends to zero. Since $v_R\in L^1$ and its derivative is a finite vector Radon measure, $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$, and [F1] yields $\limsup_R TV(v_R;\mathbb R^2)\le |Du|(\mathbb R^2)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$. The estimate applies to the arbitrary controlled family fixed in step 1.1 and proves the statement. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(W,\Sigma,\mathcal A)$ be a decorated knot cobordism between doubly pointed knots in $S^3$, and let $\mathfrak s\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)$. The representative maps from any two parametrized Kirby decompositions and admissible regular Heegaard choices are filtered $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$-equivariantly chain homotopic. If the decorated cobordism is a composite of $(W_1,\Sigma_1,\mathcal A_1)$ followed by $(W_2,\Sigma_2,\mathcal A_2)$, then for fixed Spin-c structures $\mathfrak s_i$ on $W_i$,
$$
\widetilde F_{W_2,\Sigma_2,\mathcal A_2,\mathfrak s_2}\circ \widetilde F_{W_1,\Sigma_1,\mathcal A_1,\mathfrak s_1} \simeq \sum_{\substack{\mathfrak s\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)\\ \mathfrak s|_{W_i}=\mathfrak s_i,\ i=1,2}} \widetilde F_{W,\Sigma,\mathcal A,\mathfrak s}.
$$
The sum is over Spin-c structures on the glued cobordism restricting to the specified structures on the two pieces. For $W=S^3\times[0,1]$, $\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)$ has one element, so the sum has one term and the composition law is ordinary composition up to filtered equivariant chain homotopy.

## Statement references

[[def-decorated-link-cobordism-and-floer-target|The decorated surface and filtered two-color target]]

[[def-knot-floer-cobordism-map|Maps for fixed decomposition data and one Spin-c structure]]

[[lem-knot-floer-holomorphic-triangle-transversality-compactness-gluing|Triangle analysis required by the map construction]]

[Zemke, *Link cobordisms and functoriality in link Floer homology*, Theorems A and B, §§10–13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.05207v3)

[Juhasz, *Cobordisms of sutured manifolds and the functoriality of link Floer homology*, §§8 and 11.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0910.4382v5)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] **External full naturality theorem.** Zemke, arXiv:1610.05207v3, Theorem A (p.3), gives a fixed-Spin-c $\mathbb Z^P$-filtered $\mathbb F_2[X_p:p\in P]$-equivariant chain map, invariant under diffeomorphism up to filtered equivariant chain homotopy. Diagram changes are compared by the transitive system of Definition 2.15 and Proposition 3.5 (§§2.2 and 3.3, pp.11–14). Theorem 11.5 and its proof (pp.74 and 84–85), followed by Theorem A' and its fourteen-move proof (§12.4, pp.91–95), supply changes of parametrized Kirby decomposition. Definition 12.8, Lemma 12.9 and the final proof of Theorem A (§12.5, pp.95–97) supply empty-end puncturing and its independence. These are imported results; their move checks are not claimed as locally reconstructed. ([Source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.05207v3))

[F2] **External Spin-c composition theorem.** Zemke, Theorem B (pp.3 and 97–98), gives the exact extension-sum formula in the Statement. Its proof stacks decompositions, reorders the elementary maps, applies the two-handle composition law (Proposition 5.10, p.43), and handles empty ends by puncturing. The sum and its chain-homotopy interpretation are part of this imported theorem; no unique global extension is assumed in a general gluing. ([Source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.05207v3))

[F3] The map Definition binds these imports to the specified full dividing-set category and to the two-color specialization, with actual representatives of the required auxiliary homology classes and natural endpoint transition maps. Its explicit finite/countable choice specialization supplies the stated CC scope; the publication is not assumed to have made that foundations analysis itself. The existing local analytic triangle theorem is preserved at its stated scope and is not used as a substitute for [F1] or [F2]. ([[def-knot-floer-cobordism-map]])

## Proof

1.1 Send the w-regions and z-regions of the given surface to the two colors $U,V$. The source ring is now exactly $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$ and its variable-power filtration is exactly the specified two-coordinate filtration. The curvature vanishes by the two-color identity. Hence [F1] applies to the actual maps of [F3] as genuine filtered equivariant chain maps, not merely as hat homology maps or uncolored counts. [F1, F3, given]

1.2 For different endpoint diagrams first use [F1]'s canonical transition chain-homotopy equivalences to compare maps on the same chosen endpoint representatives. Theorem A then gives a filtered equivariant chain homotopy for any two admitted decompositions and regular auxiliary choices. The source's fourteen Cerf moves include the band, basepoint and quasi-stabilization relations; §12.5 additionally handles components missing one or both ends. Boundary-fixed ambient isotopy preserves the given decorations and induces precisely the required diffeomorphism of decorated cobordisms, so it is covered by the same theorem. [F1, step 1.1]

1.3 Apply [F2] to the actual gluing and the two specified structures $\mathfrak s_1,\mathfrak s_2$. Restriction of each summand to the two pieces is exactly the condition displayed in the Statement; no unmarked or total-Spin-c map has replaced these maps. The two-color specialization respects the composition and homotopies, giving the displayed formula over $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

1.4 Finally $H^2(S^3\times[0,1];\mathbb Z)=0$ and the product is spin. Its nonempty Spin-c torsor therefore consists of one element. In the stated product case the extension set has precisely that element and the law reduces to ordinary composition up to filtered equivariant chain homotopy. The argument imports the established naturality/composition theorems, not an unproved assertion that the local triangle identity checks all movies. [given, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. If $Y$ is a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold with finite $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, then the bounding-chain torsion linking pairing $\lambda_Y$ is symmetric and nonsingular: its adjoint $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism.

## Statement references

[[def-bounding-chain-torsion-linking-pairing|The signed bounding-chain formula]]

[Charles Livingston and Swatee Naik, *Introduction to Knot Concordance*, §7.6, pp. 140–141](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Concordance_Book.pdf)

[Patrick Gilmer, *Slice Knots in S3*, §1, pp. 306–307](https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/gilmer3.pdf)

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$ with finite $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Poincaré duality for closed oriented manifolds gives $H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and $H^2(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(Y;\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]]

[F2] The cohomology universal coefficient sequence over $\mathbb Z$ identifies $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q)$ and $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$, since $H_0(Y;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ is free. [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]

[F3] The coefficient sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to0$ gives the long exact cohomology sequence and its natural Bockstein map $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. [[thm-long-exact-sequence-in-cohomology]]

[F4] **External triangulation input.** A compact topological $3$-manifold admits a finite manifold triangulation (Moise's theorem, as stated in Aschenbrenner–Friedl–Wilton, Theorem 3.1, p. 211, under their compact-manifold convention, p. 203). We use its barycentric dual cells as a chain model, not as an additional smoothness hypothesis on $Y$. Orient a dual cell so that its oriented transverse intersection with the corresponding primal cell is positive. The dual-cell description of Poincaré duality is recalled in Hatcher, §3.3, pp. 232–233; the specific bounding-chain/Bockstein identity is proved below, rather than assumed.

[F5] Cellular homology computes singular homology for every CW complex and every abelian coefficient group. Under [A1], cellular cochains compute singular cohomology for CW pairs with local coefficients, naturally for coefficient morphisms. Apply these comparisons to the finite triangulation and its dual CW complex, the pair $(Y,\varnothing)$, and the trivial coefficient systems $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$. Thus cellular cycles and bounding chains represent precisely the singular homology classes, and the cellular coefficient-sequence Bockstein and evaluation agree with their singular counterparts. [[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]] [[thm-cellular-cochains-compute-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 Since $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is finite, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$ by [F2], and $H^2(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$ by [F1]. Exactness of [F3] therefore makes $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ an isomorphism. Write $\operatorname{PD}:H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ for inverse cap duality. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra, A1]

2.1 We first fix the intersection sign and verify independence directly. For transverse oriented $2$-chains $C,T$ in an oriented $3$-manifold, orient their intersection so that
$$\partial(C\cap T)=(\partial C)\cap T-C\cap(\partial T).$$
This sign follows by the outward-normal-first boundary convention in an oriented coordinate ball: taking a boundary in the second sheet passes its outward normal past the one normal direction of the first sheet. Consequently, the total signed endpoint count gives
$$C\cdot\partial T=(\partial C)\cdot T.$$
These identities extend linearly to chains; the terms on paired interior faces cancel. For a closed $2$-chain $E$ and torsion cycle $y$, choose $m>0$ and $\partial T=my$. Then $m(E\cdot y)=E\cdot\partial T=0$, so $E\cdot y=0$. Thus if $\partial C=nx$ and $\partial C'=n'x$, the closed chain $n'C-nC'$ has zero intersection with $y$, giving $(C\cdot y)/n=(C'\cdot y)/n'$. Replacing $x$ by $x+\partial S$ permits replacing $C$ by $C+nS$ and changes the quotient by the integer $S\cdot y$. Replacing $y$ by $y+\partial T$ changes it by $(C\cdot\partial T)/n=x\cdot T$, also an integer. A change of transverse position is a chain homotopy: its prism has the moved-chain difference as boundary, so these same boundary identities apply. Hence the expression defines a pairing on the stated homology classes, independent of all these choices modulo $\mathbb Z$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.2 To identify that pairing with the Bockstein, use [F4] and [F5] and represent $x$ by a primal cellular $1$-cycle $a$, and $y$ by a dual cellular $1$-cycle $b$. Since $n[a]=0$, there is an integral primal cellular $2$-chain $C$ with $\partial C=na$. The dual-cell pairing gives the rational cellular $1$-cochain
$$u(e)=\frac{C\cdot e}{n}$$
on every oriented dual edge $e$. Let $z_a$ be the integral cellular $2$-cochain on the dual complex defined by $z_a(\sigma)=a\cdot\sigma$. The sign convention in step 2.1 gives, for every dual $2$-cell $\sigma$,
$$(\delta u)(\sigma)=\frac{C\cdot\partial\sigma}{n} =\frac{(\partial C)\cdot\sigma}{n} =a\cdot\sigma=z_a(\sigma).$$
There is no extra minus sign: in an oriented chart with $a$ tangent to the first coordinate and its dual $2$-cell tangent to the second and third coordinates, $a\cdot\sigma=+1$. A primal $2$-cell followed by its positive transverse dual edge likewise has intersection $+1$. These are precisely the oriented dual-cell representatives of inverse cap duality, so $[z_a]=\operatorname{PD}(x)$. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, construct]

2.3 Reducing $u$ modulo $\mathbb Z$ gives a cocycle $\bar u$, because $\delta u=z_a$ is integral. Under the natural comparison [F5], the connecting map in [F3] is constructed by lifting this cocycle to a rational cochain and taking its coboundary; therefore
$$\beta[\bar u]=[\delta u]=\operatorname{PD}(x),\qquad \langle[\bar u],y\rangle=u(b)\bmod\mathbb Z =\frac{C\cdot b}{n}\bmod\mathbb Z.$$
By step 2.1 this is also the bounding-chain expression for any representatives and any bounding multiple in the definition. Cellular representatives cause no restriction by [F5]: cellular and singular chain models represent the same classes, and changes of representatives and transverse positions have already been accounted for. Thus the precise identity is
$$\lambda_Y(x,y)=\bigl\langle\beta^{-1}\operatorname{PD}(x),y\bigr\rangle.$$
The evaluation is on the homology class $y$, not on a cohomology class called its Poincaré dual; equivalently it is the corresponding degree-$3$ cup-product evaluation on $[Y]$. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct]

3.1 Under [F2], evaluation identifies $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with the entire character group $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$. The displayed identity in step 2.3 identifies the adjoint of the bounding-chain pairing with the composite of this isomorphism, $\beta^{-1}$, and $\operatorname{PD}$. All three are isomorphisms, so the pairing is nonsingular. In particular its bilinearity also follows from these homomorphisms and evaluation. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 For torsion classes $x,y$, choose transverse representatives and chains $C,D$ with $\partial C=nx$ and $\partial D=my$. The boundary identity of step 2.1 applied to $C\cap D$ gives $n(x\cdot D)=m(C\cdot y)$. Interchanging a $1$-cycle and a $2$-chain in an oriented $3$-manifold changes the intersection sign by $(-1)^{(3-1)(3-2)}=+1$, so $x\cdot D=D\cdot x$. Divide by $nm$ and reduce modulo $\mathbb Z$ to obtain $\lambda_Y(x,y)=\lambda_Y(y,x)$. This proves symmetry with the signed bounding-chain convention of the definition. [step 2.1, step 2.3, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. There exists a dualizable framed handle link $(B,G,R)$ whose associated
handlebody is diffeomorphic to both zero-traces $X_0(C)$ and $X_0(K_P)$, with
the component orientations and zero-framings compatible with the diagrams
defining $C$ and $K_P$.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Proposition 1.4 and Figure 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The literal Conway and Figure 2 partner diagrams, with the handle
and zero-framing conventions of the Statement, and full AC.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, written AC, is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] AC implies dependent choice and hence countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; this supplies every retained local countable-choice hypothesis. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] [[def-piccirillo-conway-pair]] specifies the two diagram isotopy classes
$C$ and $K_P$; neither is identified by its invariants.

[F2] [[def-dualizable-handle-link]] requires the two meridional sublinks and
zero green–blue linking.

[F3] [[thm-dualizable-handle-link-has-two-knot-trace-descriptions]] supplies
the geometric finite-slide and cancellation construction for such links.
We use its actual framed handle calculus, rather than deducing a meridional
sublink from a linking number.

[F4] Finite encodings accompanying this proof are the previously established
`alternate-trace-certificate.json.gz` for the common source construction
through $K$, the `lm-local-worker` band/cancellation and $L$–$M$ records,
and the `conway-named` records `head-three-returns-prefix.json` and
`coupon-suffix-01.json`, `coupon-suffix-02.json`, `coupon-suffix-03.json`.
The last record includes the complete prescribed-exterior ribbon isomorphism
to literal $N$. The locally retained records end at literal $N$; the historical
$N$–$O$ and $O$–Figure 2 machine-readable records are unavailable.
The terminal framed identification is instead the explicitly imported
published input [F8]. No recovered arc map or fresh replay is claimed.
The local records and their exact research locations remain given under
Proof evidence.

[F5] [[lem-knot-exterior-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]: for every component
$L$ with its chosen tube and positive meridian,
$H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_L]$.

[F6] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: a degree-one parallel
whose exterior homology class is zero is a preferred longitude.

[F7] [[thm-oriented-linking-number-scan-terminates-and-is-correct]] and
[[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]]: the scan returns
the integer half-sum of mixed crossing signs, and the half-sum is invariant
under oriented link isotopy.

[F8] **External terminal framed identification:** Piccirillo, *The Conway knot is not slice*, Annals of Mathematics 191 (2020), Proposition 1.4 (p.583) and its proof in §2 (p.586), with Figure 2 (p.584) and Figure 4 (pp.587–588), supplies the terminal identification of the Figure 4 construction with the named knot $K'$ of Figure 2. The Figure 4 caption states that arrows denote handle slides, the $L$–$M$ transition includes cancellation, and the other changes are isotopies; in particular the terminal $N$–$O$ passage is an isotopy in this framed handle presentation. The terminal single attaching circle is marked $0$, and panel $O$ is the Figure 2 knot. This is used as an external framed-geometric input at the source's displayed zero-framing convention, not as a locally reconstructed complete arc map. The published source is classical differential topology and does not state a ZF or weakened-choice theorem; no such foundational improvement is inferred from its omission of an axiom discussion.

## Proof

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F$ be a compact smooth surface with boundary, let $M$ be a smooth three-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$ be a closed embedded smooth surface. If $i:F\to M$ is a smooth embedding whose boundary restriction $i|_{\partial F}$ is transverse to $S$, then there is a smooth isotopy $i_t:F\to M$ through embeddings, fixed on a neighbourhood of $\partial F$, such that $i_1(F)$ is transverse to $S$.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice|The choice hypothesis]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$, a compact smooth surface with boundary $F$, a smooth three-manifold $M$, a closed embedded surface $S\subset M$, and an embedding $i:F\to M$ with $i|_{\partial F}\pitchfork S$.

[F1] For a smooth map from a boundaryless manifold to a boundaryless target, there is a finite-dimensional smooth perturbation family through that map whose parameter map is a submersion at every source point. ([[lem-a-tubular-target-produces-a-submersive-finite-dimensional-perturbation-family]])

[F2] If a smooth family $G:X\times B\to M$ is transverse to $S$, then the parameters for which the slice $G_a:X\to M$ is not transverse to $S$ form a null subset of $B$. ([[thm-parametric-transversality]])

[F3] Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar. ([[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]])

[F4] Under AC$_\omega$, every smooth isotopy of embeddings of a compact source with boundary into a boundaryless target extends to an ambient isotopy. ([[thm-isotopy-extension]])

[F5] A smooth map transverse to an embedded submanifold has the tangent-space spanning property in the transversality definition; invertible differentials give local diffeomorphisms in charts. ([[def-a-smooth-map-transverse-to-an-embedded-submanifold]], [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]])

[F6] Under AC$_\omega$, every smooth manifold, including one with boundary, admits a Riemannian metric compatible with its manifold topology. ([[thm-every-smooth-manifold-admits-a-riemannian-metric]])

[A1] AC$_\omega$ is the sequence-choice principle used by [F1], [F2], and [F4]. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** The stated objects and hypotheses.

1.1 At every $x\in\partial F$, the inclusion $T_x\partial F\subset T_xF$ and the boundary transversality hypothesis imply $di_x(T_xF)+T_{i(x)}S=T_{i(x)}M$. Thus $i$ is transverse to $S$ along $\partial F$. Transversality is open in the point of the source, and $\partial F$ is compact, so there is a collar neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial F$ on which $i$ is transverse to $S$. [given, F3, F5, construct]

2.1 Choose a smooth collar coordinate $s$ on $U$ and a smooth function $\gamma:F\to[0,1]$ that vanishes on a smaller boundary collar and equals $1$ outside $U$. Such a function is obtained by composing the collar coordinate with a smooth one-variable cutoff and extending by $1$. Put $\tau=\gamma^2$. Then $d\tau=0$ wherever $\tau=0$, and the zero set of $\tau$ lies inside $U$. [F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Apply [F1] to the boundaryless interior $F^\circ$ and the map $i|_{F^\circ}$, obtaining a smooth family $\mathcal F:F^\circ\times B\to M$ with $\mathcal F(p,0)=i(p)$ and each parameter map a submersion. On $F^\circ$ define $G(p,a)=\mathcal F(p,\tau(p)a)$, restricting $B$ if necessary so $\tau(p)a\in B$. Where $\tau>0$, the parameter derivative of $G$ is surjective. Where $\tau=0$, $d\tau=0$, so $G(p,a)=i(p)$ and its source derivative is $di_p$; [F5] and step 1.1 make it transverse to $S$. Since $\tau=0$ on a boundary collar, setting $G=i$ on $\partial F$ extends $G$ smoothly to $F\times B$, fixed near the boundary. Thus the total family is transverse to $S$. [A1, F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Apply [F2] to $G|_{F^\circ\times B}$. Its good parameters are dense, because the bad set is null and every open parameter ball has positive measure. For each good parameter $a$, $G_a$ is transverse on $F^\circ$; near $\partial F$ it equals $i$, which is transverse by step 1.1. Hence $G_a$ is transverse on all of $F$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, choose]

5.1 Choose compatible Riemannian metrics on $F$ and $M$ using [F6]. At each $x\in F$, choose coordinate charts and a linear projection $P_x$ to a two-dimensional tangent plane so that $D(P_x\circ i)$ at $x$ is invertible. By [F5], shrink to a convex coordinate neighbourhood $U_x$ on which this derivative stays within one quarter of the least singular value of its value at $x$. Every sufficiently $C^1$-close map $j$ then has $P_x\circ j$ injective on $U_x$: integrate its derivative along the coordinate segment between two points to obtain a lower bound of one half that least singular value times their coordinate distance. Compactness gives a finite cover by such $U_x$ and a Lebesgue number $\delta>0$. For pairs at source distance at least $\delta$, compactness and injectivity of $i$ give a positive minimum target distance, which persists under sufficiently small $C^0$ perturbations. The differential of $i$ has a positive minimum norm on the compact unit tangent bundle, so immersion also persists under sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbations. Thus all sufficiently $C^1$-close maps are injective immersions; compactness of $F$ and the Hausdorff property of $M$ make them embeddings. Smoothness of $G$ and compactness of $F$ imply $G_b\to i$ in $C^1$ as $b\to0$, so there is a parameter ball about $0$ for which every $G_b$ is an embedding. By the density in step 4.1 choose a good $a$ in that ball; then $t\mapsto G_{ta}$ is an isotopy through embeddings fixed near $\partial F$. Apply [F4] to extend it to an ambient isotopy. Its endpoint carries $i(F)$ to a surface transverse to $S$, as required. [A1, F4, F5, F6, step 4.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

On oriented ambient-isotopy classes of smooth knots in the standard three-sphere, smooth concordance is an equivalence relation, and locally flat topological concordance is an equivalence relation.

## Statement references

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|The smooth concordance annulus and its product collars]]

[[def-locally-flat-topological-knot-concordance|The locally flat topological concordance annulus]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Smooth oriented knots $K_0,K_1,K_2\subset S^3$ and either category of concordance.

[F1] A smooth concordance is a proper smooth annulus with product collars and oriented boundary $-K_0\sqcup K_1$. ([[def-smooth-knot-concordance]])

[F2] A locally flat topological concordance is a proper locally flat annulus with product collars and the same oriented boundary convention. ([[def-locally-flat-topological-knot-concordance]])

[F3] Ambient isotopy of oriented knots is given by a smooth family of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$. ([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]])

[F4] Product collars and the local plane-pair charts are the boundary and interior conventions for proper surfaces. ([[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]])

## Proof

**Given:** Oriented knot types $[K_0],[K_1],[K_2]$ and one of the two concordance categories.

1.1 Reflexivity is witnessed by the product annulus $K_0\times I\subset S^3\times I$, oriented so its boundary is $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_0\times\{1\}$. If a representative is changed by an ambient isotopy $H_t$, reparameterize time so $H_t$ is constant near $t=0$ and $t=1$. Its trace $(x,t)\mapsto(H_t(x),t)$ then has product endpoint collars and is a concordance annulus; it is smooth in the smooth case and locally flat in the topological case because it is itself smooth. For an existing concordance, glue the trace to the matching product collar: use the reversed trace at the lower end and the forward trace at the upper end. The glued surface is an annulus in the same category, so replacing either endpoint by an ambient-isotopic representative preserves concordance. Thus the relation is well-defined on ambient-isotopy classes. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, construct]

1.2 If an annulus $A$ gives a concordance from $K_0$ to $K_1$, apply $(x,t)\mapsto(x,1-t)$ to its image. Reorient the resulting annulus so the boundary at the new lower end is $-K_1$ and the boundary at the new upper end is $K_0$. The map and reorientation preserve smoothness in the smooth category and local flatness and product collars in the topological category. This gives symmetry. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct]

1.3 Let $A$ be a concordance from $K_0$ to $K_1$ and $B$ one from $K_1$ to $K_2$ in the same category. Glue the upper product collar of $A$ to the lower product collar of $B$ along their common oriented knot $K_1$. The two collar coordinates combine to a single collar across the gluing hypersurface, so the annuli join without a corner in the smooth category and their local-flat pair charts join in the topological category. Gluing two annuli along one boundary circle gives an annulus; the intermediate boundary orientations $K_1$ and $-K_1$ cancel, leaving boundary $-K_0\sqcup K_2$. This gives transitivity. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Steps 1.1–1.3 prove reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and representative independence for both relations. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $B$ be a compact piecewise linear $3$-ball with a finite compatible triangulation, and let $T\subset\operatorname{int}B$ be a two-sided embedded torus, where two-sided means that $T$ has a product neighborhood with its given central inclusion. Then there is an embedded compressing disk $D\subset\operatorname{int}B$ with $D\cap T=\partial D$ and $\partial D$ essential on $T$. The disk is properly embedded in the closure of one component of $B\setminus T$: its boundary lies on that component's copy of $T$ and its interior lies in the interior of the component.
## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, §1.1 and §3.1](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Ryan Budney, *JSJ-decompositions of knot and link complements in the 3-sphere*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0506523)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the finite PL ball and the original unqualified two-sided embedded torus with product neighborhood. No PL or smooth compatibility of that torus is assumed.

[A1] Full AC is [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. It permits coset transversals for the possibly untriangulated cut-piece groups below.

[F1] Two-sidedness and a compressing disk have the geometric product-neighborhood and essential-boundary conventions of [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]]. A torus with a topological product neighborhood is locally flat, by its intrinsic surface charts crossed with the interval.

[F2] Under full AC every compact TOP3-manifold, boundary allowed, has a finite compatible PL triangulation with its boundary a subcomplex. The finite PL Loop theorem applies to any connected boundary component with nontrivial inclusion kernel. [[thm-compact-topological-three-manifolds-admit-finite-pl-triangulations]] [[thm-loop-theorem-for-finitely-triangulated-orientable-pl-three-manifolds]]

[F3] Van Kampen gives the pushout for spaces glued along the connected torus product collar. When both side maps are injective, amalgam normal form with coset transversals supplied by [A1] embeds the torus group. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]] [[thm-normal-form-for-free-products-with-amalgamation]]

[F4] A compact locally flat closed surface with connected complement in a boundaryless three-manifold has nonzero mod-two class, without choice or an ambient triangulation. [[lem-connected-complement-surfaces-have-independent-mod-two-homology-classes]] A contractible space has the homology of a point. [[cor-contractible-nonempty-spaces-have-the-homology-of-a-point]] For mod-two chains on a point, $\partial_2$ is multiplication by $3=1$, so its second homology is zero.

[F5] The torus group is $\mathbb Z^2$ by the circle and product computations. [[thm-fundamental-group-of-the-circle]] [[thm-fundamental-group-of-a-product]]

## Proof

1.1 The interior of the parametrized PL ball is a contractible boundaryless topological three-manifold. Its second mod-two homology is zero by [F4]. Hence [F1] and [F4] show that its complement of $T$ cannot be connected. The same is true in $B$: push its outer boundary collar slightly inward, fixing the compact interior torus; if $B\setminus T$ were connected, its connected pushed image and the collar homotopy would make the interior complement connected. There are exactly two components. Indeed the two open product-collar sides of connected $T$ are connected, and every complementary component must meet one: otherwise its closure misses $T$ and it is open and closed in connected $B$. More explicitly, at any point of $T$ in the closure of a component, a local flat chart puts some collar-side patch in that component; the connected full side collar then belongs to it. Thus there are at most two components. Their closures $W_1,W_2$ are compact orientable topological three-manifolds, with the corresponding copies of $T$ in their boundaries. [F1, F4, given, construct]

2.1 If both maps $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(W_i)$ were injective, choose their coset transversals by [A1]. The given topological product collar gives the connected-overlap van Kampen cover, and [F3] expresses $\pi_1(B)$ as their amalgam with $\pi_1(T)$ embedded. By [F5] this would embed $\mathbb Z^2$ into the trivial group of the ball, a contradiction. Thus one side boundary map has nontrivial kernel. This conclusion is topological and has required no triangulation of the cut pieces. [A1, F3, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F2]'s ACTUAL TOP triangulation theorem to that compact orientable side $W_i$, using [A1]. Let $q:|L|\to W_i$ be its resulting finite manifold triangulation. The preimage $q^{-1}(T)$ of the whole boundary component is a connected PL boundary surface subcomplex; no pre-existing compatibility of the original embedded torus with the original ball triangulation was needed. Conjugating by $q$ identifies its inclusion kernel with the nontrivial kernel from step 2.1. Apply finite PL Loop with that entire boundary component and normal subgroup $1$. It supplies a proper embedded PL disk in $|L|$ with boundary representing a nonidentity element of its torus group. Transport it by $q$ and then by the cut-side inclusion into $B$. These maps are homeomorphisms on the disk: the disk meets only this single boundary face and its interior misses all boundary faces. Hence its image $D$ is a TOP embedded disk in $\operatorname{int}B$, with $D\cap T=\partial D$ and essential boundary on $T$. It is proper in the cut side, as the Statement requires. This completes the unqualified TOP two-sided torus case with the original full AC hypothesis. [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 2.1, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The triangulation used in the proof is on the TOP cut side. Neither the original torus nor its transported disk has been asserted PL or smooth for the originally supplied ball triangulation. The distinct explicitly PL torus lemma remains the precise supplier for its finite PL consumers.

## Statement

Assume full AC. If $K\subset S^3$ is a nontrivial fibered knot that is not a torus knot, then either its exterior contains a connected, separating, incompressible surface whose boundary curves have slope zero, or $K$ has at least three distinct boundary slopes.

## Statement references

[[def-boundary-slope-of-an-incompressible-surface|Boundary slopes and the strict boundary-slope convention]]

[Baldwin and Sivek, Theorem 1.7 and §4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

[Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long, and Shalen, Theorem 3.4](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~culler/papers/PlaneCurves/curves.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a nontrivial fibered knot in $S^3$ that is not a torus knot.

[F1] In the present nontrivial-knot setting, zero is a boundary slope. The ordinary A-polynomial contains $L-1$; for the vertical weight its initial form is the product of the other factor’s initial form with this horizontal segment, so its minimum face is a horizontal edge. The ordinary edge theorem therefore supplies an actual incompressible boundary-incompressible orientable realizing surface. [[thm-ccgls-newton-edge-slope-is-boundary-slope]]

[F2] Every enhanced A-polynomial Newton-edge slope has a connected orientable incompressible boundary-incompressible nonfiber realizing surface, by the actual finite valued-model and equivariant compression construction. [[thm-enhanced-a-polynomial-newton-edge-is-strict-boundary-slope]]

[F3] A non-torus knot is not thin by the enhanced-A classification; its enhanced Newton polygon is therefore not contained in a line ([[thm-enhanced-a-polynomial-newton-polygon-detects-torus-knots]]).

[F4] A connected nonseparating incompressible longitudinal surface in this fibered exterior is isotopic to its actual fiber, including the boundary-relative refinement after alignment. The actual proof supplies the proper degree-one surface-map step and the downstairs family-innermost product extraction. [[lem-nonseparating-longitudinal-surface-in-fibered-exterior-is-fiber]]

[A2] The Newton-edge-to-essential-surface and strictness operations are supplied by [F1]–[F2]. The full enhanced-A classification [F3] now uses its explicit external Baldwin–Sivek Theorem 1.2 input; it does not claim a local reconstruction of gauge theory. Baldwin–Sivek Theorem 1.7 (p.3; §4.1) also states this exact two-boundary-slope alternative, with the same nontrivial fibered nontorus hypotheses.

## Proof

1.1 By [F3] the enhanced Newton polygon is not contained in a line. A nondegenerate planar polygon has at least two distinct unoriented edge directions, since otherwise all its vertices lie on one line. By [F2] these give two distinct strict boundary slopes. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 If there are at least three boundary slopes, the second alternative holds. Otherwise [F1] supplies slope zero, so the two distinct strict slopes from step1.1 exhaust the slope set and one is zero. Choose the connected orientable incompressible nonfiber zero-slope realizing surface supplied by [F2]. [F1, F2, step 1.1, cases]

3.1 If that surface were nonseparating, [F4] would make it isotopic to the fiber, contradicting its nonfiber property. It is separating and supplies the first alternative. These alternatives prove the full Statement, using the explicitly external classification input only at [F3]. [F4, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $B$ be a smooth compact four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and oriented boundary the rational homology sphere $Y$, where $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. If a boundary Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$ extends over $B$, then its Heegaard Floer correction term vanishes: $d(Y,\mathfrak t)=0$. The extension hypothesis is essential; no vanishing is asserted for Spin$^c$ structures that do not extend.

## Statement references

[[lem-rational-ball-spin-c-cobordism-map-inequality|The rational-ball cobordism-map inequalities]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Absolutely graded Floer homologies and intersection forms for four-manifolds with boundary*, Proposition 9.9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0110170v1)

[Baranowski, Borodzik, and Serrano de Rodrigo, *Heegaard Floer Homologies and Rational Cuspidal Curves*, Corollary 4.8](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/wbln.12.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth rational homology four-ball $B$, its oriented rational homology sphere boundary $Y$, and an extending boundary Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$.

[F1] For this extending structure, puncturing the ball yields both inequalities $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge0$ and $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\le0$ ([[lem-rational-ball-spin-c-cobordism-map-inequality]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** combine the two orientation-sensitive inequalities.

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 The forward punctured-cobordism map gives $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge0$ by [F1]. [F1, given]

2.1 The reversed punctured cobordism gives $d(Y,\mathfrak t)\le0$ by [F1]. A rational number satisfying both inequalities is zero, so $d(Y,\mathfrak t)=0$. The argument applies only to the Spin$^c$ structure that extends. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. There exists a closed connected simply connected oriented topological four-manifold $Y_{E_8}$ whose integral intersection form is isometric to the positive-definite even unimodular lattice $L_{E_8}$. This is a topological realization statement and does not assert a smooth structure on $Y_{E_8}$.

## Statement references

[Freedman, *The topology of four-dimensional manifolds*, Theorems 1.5 and 1.7](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/1982_The%20topology%20of%20four-dimensional%20manifolds.pdf)

[F2] **External TOP input — Freedman's realization theorem.** For every integral unimodular symmetric form $\omega$, there exists an oriented closed simply connected almost-smooth topological four-manifold whose integral intersection form is $\omega$. Here almost-smooth means smooth off a single point. This is the existence clause of Freedman, *The topology of four-dimensional manifolds*, Theorem 1.5, printed p. 368; Theorem 1.7, printed p. 371, separately records the E8 case. This input is imported from that source under the run-specific TOP exception; its plumbing, contractible cap and four-dimensional realization proof are not reconstructed here.

## Proof

**Given:** The local lattice calculation [F1] and the explicit external TOP realization input [F2].

1.1 Apply [F2] to the integral unimodular form $\omega=L_{E_8}$, which satisfies its exact algebraic hypothesis by [F1]. It gives an oriented closed simply connected topological four-manifold $Y_{E_8}$ with intersection form $L_{E_8}$. Simply connected includes path connectedness, so $Y_{E_8}$ has every property required in the statement. [F1, F2]

1.2 The source also gives smoothness away from a point, but no smooth structure on the whole closed manifold is asserted or used. This establishes precisely the stated topological realization. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The set of smooth oriented knot concordance classes in the standard three-sphere is an abelian group under connected sum, with identity the standard unknot and inverse of $[K]$ represented by the reverse mirror $K^\dagger$. Separately, the set of locally flat topological oriented knot concordance classes is an abelian group under connected sum, with the same identity and inverse convention.

## Statement references

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth oriented knot concordance]]

[[def-locally-flat-topological-knot-concordance|Locally flat topological oriented knot concordance]]

[[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot|The reverse-mirror inverse convention]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The oriented connected-sum operation and standard unknot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the smooth and topological concordance relations, and their oriented connected-sum operation.

[F1] Smooth and locally flat topological concordance are equivalence relations on oriented ambient-isotopy classes. ([[lem-smooth-and-topological-knot-concordance-is-an-equivalence-relation]])

[F2] Concordance respects connected sum in both categories under the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The smooth implication is the retained local annulus construction. The TOP implication uses the explicitly imported classical operation and the compact real-code/$L[r]$ specialization in the compatibility supplier; it is not inferred from bare-core straightening. ([[lem-knot-concordance-compatible-with-connected-sum]])

[F3] On oriented ambient-isotopy classes, connected sum is associative and commutative and has the standard unknot as two-sided identity under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. ([[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]])

[F4] For every smooth oriented knot $K$, $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$; the disk is locally flat as a topological proper surface. ([[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]], [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]])

[F5] A knot bounds a smooth proper disk in $B^4$ if and only if it is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot. ([[lem-smooth-slice-iff-concordant-to-unknot]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is used by the actual connected-sum and isotopy-extension supplier branches cited in this theorem; the TOP external input is specialized to the required compact data under that same hypothesis in [F2], rather than assuming ambient full Choice. ([[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]])

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and the two concordance relations.

1.1 In the smooth category, [F1] makes the smooth concordance classes a quotient set. [F2] ensures that replacing either connected-sum input by a concordant knot leaves the resulting class unchanged, so connected sum defines a binary operation on that quotient. [F3] supplies associativity, commutativity, and the two-sided identity on oriented knot types; these equalities pass to the quotient because the operation is well-defined. [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, construct]

2.1 For every $K$, [F4] gives a smooth disk bounded by $K\#K^\dagger$. By [F5], this connected sum is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot, so $[K]+[K^\dagger]=[U]$ in the smooth quotient. Together with the commutative monoid structure from step 1.1, every element has an inverse; thus the smooth quotient is an abelian group with the stated inverse. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, given]

3.1 In the locally flat topological category, [F1] again gives a quotient set, and the TOP implication of [F2] makes connected sum independent of both concordance representatives. Associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity descend from [F3] exactly as in step 1.1. For each smooth knot representative $K$, the smooth disk from [F4] and its smooth concordance to $U$ from [F5] are also locally flat by the surface/collar convention. Therefore $[K]+[K^\dagger]=[U]$ in the TOP quotient. Every element has the stated inverse, so this quotient too is an abelian group. The Countable Choice strength here is that of the bounded compatibility specialization [F2], not an unstated full-AC hypothesis. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable topological three-manifold, possibly with boundary. All embedded three-balls and two-spheres used in the connected-sum operation and in the definitions of prime and irreducible are required to be tame (locally flat). For manifolds, connected sum means deleting the interiors of embedded three-balls and gluing their boundary spheres by an orientation-reversing identification. A prime factor is a connected orientable three-manifold that is not a connected sum of two factors other than $S^3$. Then $M$ is a connected sum of finitely many prime factors, and the factors are unique up to order and insertion or deletion of $S^3$ factors. The factor $S^1\times S^2$ is prime but is not irreducible; irreducibility means every tame (locally flat) embedded $2$-sphere bounds a $3$-ball.


## Statement references

[Hatcher, Proposition1.4 and Theorem1.5, printed pp.4–8](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact connected orientable three-manifold of the Statement. Work with the ordinary tame (locally flat) embedded spheres and balls of three-manifold connected-sum theory. Full AC is used in the proof as specified below; a wild sphere is not a connected-sum cutting sphere.

[A1] Full AC. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A compact TOP three-manifold has a finite combinatorial PL triangulation. Prescribed finite boundary PL structures and TOP collars are retained on smaller collars. The proof constructs the actual finite atlas by compact-overlap handle straightening. [[thm-compact-topological-three-manifolds-admit-finite-pl-triangulations]]

[F2] For every index, a TOP coordinate embedding of a PL three-dimensional handle, PL near its attaching boundary, admits an ambient source TOP isotopy fixed there and outside twice its compact core, making the endpoint PL near the prescribed FIXED core. The finite PL vertex/edge/face/tetrahedron handle construction is given in [F1], Proof1.1, and its attaching-band protection in Proof2.1. [[thm-three-dimensional-topological-handles-admit-relative-pl-straightenings]]

[F3] A supplied finite orientable PL three-manifold has a finite prime connected-sum presentation with original boundary marks, actual cap parameters and gluing maps. Its nonirreducible prime factors are standard $S^1\times S^2$, which is PL prime; the other factors are PL irreducible. Its Proof1.1 gives finite cap-ball avoidance, and Proof3.1 gives the actual marked nonseparating-sphere handle model. No uniqueness is assumed. [[thm-finite-orientable-pl-three-manifolds-have-prime-connected-sum-decompositions]]

[F4] Finite PL Schoenflies in the standard three-sphere, finite marked ball-window gluing, and compatible finite convex-cell triangulations hold. A PL sphere boundary map extends over a parametrized ball by coning; the same formula extends any TOP sphere boundary map over a TOP parametrized ball. [[thm-finite-pl-schoenflies-in-dimension-three]] [[lem-parametrized-pl-balls-absorb-standard-boundary-windows]] [[lem-finite-convex-cell-complexes-admit-compatible-triangulations]]

[F5] A compact TOP three-manifold with its finite triangulated boundary has a TOP product collar. [[lem-compact-topological-three-manifolds-with-triangulated-boundary-have-collars]]

[F6] Finite simplicial chains compute singular homology, and the open-cover Mayer–Vietoris sequence is exact. [[thm-simplicial-and-singular-homology-agree-for-simplicial-complexes]] [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

## Proof

1.1 Fix the finite PL structure on $M$ supplied by [F1]. We give the compatibility operation needed below, rather than assume that an arbitrary TOP sphere was PL in this structure. For a finite disjoint locally flat sphere system, cut along its spheres using their local flat charts. The orientation of each sphere and of $M$ labels the two local sides consistently; the cut space is therefore a compact TOP manifold with two boundary copies of each sphere, and its old boundary unchanged. Assign the standard finite sphere PL parameter to one copy and the identical parameter under the cutting identification to the other. These finitely many new boundary components have collars by [F5]; keep also the old PL boundary collar of $M$, choosing all collars disjoint. Apply the relative assertion of [F1] to each cut component. On the smaller new boundary collars the cutting identification is the identity in the assigned sphere parameters, so gluing the collars gives an actual PL product across each seam. Finite product-cell subdivisions give a finite PL structure $\Sigma'$ on the original $M$ in which every sphere of the system is PL. It agrees with the original structure $\Sigma$ near $\partial M$. This operation also applies to any finite TOP connected-sum presentation: each gluing sphere receives matching parameters, and its cap balls have the cone parameters of [F4]. [A1, F1, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 Two such finite PL structures $\Sigma,\Sigma'$ on $M$ agreeing near its boundary are related by a homeomorphism $u:(M,\Sigma)\to(M,\Sigma')$ TOP isotopic to the identity, fixed on a smaller boundary collar. Here is the needed relative comparison construction. Cover the compact remainder of that collar by $\Sigma'$ coordinate domains. Subdivide the finite $\Sigma$ triangulation so finely that the closed thirty-two-fold star of each simplex meeting the remainder is in one of these domains; finite cover shrinking and the geometric mesh decrease give this subdivision. Form the vertex, edge, face and tetrahedron handles of [F1], Proof1.1, with all transverse extensions inside these stars. At each index straighten the current identity map in the chosen $\Sigma'$ coordinate chart using [F2]. Its source parameter is a $\Sigma$ PL handle; for positive index its attaching band lies in the already straightened region. Protect smaller earlier core neighborhoods and trim the attaching bands exactly as in [F1], Proof2.1. Here the coordinate control is finite and explicit. Choose the transverse extensions inside the closed two-fold star of their core simplex; at a fixed index their nonidentity supports are disjoint, after trimming the protected attaching bands. A correction can therefore carry a point only between simplices at most four adjacency steps apart, and at most one correction of that index moves it. Before the last index there have been at most three such stages. Consequently the current image of a handle and its transverse extension stays in the closed thirty-two-fold star of its core simplex, inside its chosen target coordinate domain. A sufficiently fine subdivision has this property because each fixed finite iterate of the star has mesh tending to zero. Thus every coordinate embedding to which [F2] is applied really has its whole domain in the chosen chart; no PL compatibility of the original TOP transition maps is assumed. Each correction is the identity on its attaching boundary and outside its own compact twice-core, so extends to all of $M$. Subsequent widths are chosen inside the remaining PL neighborhoods. The index-zero through index-three cores and their protected bands cover the remainder, just as in [F1], Proof2.1. At the endpoint the map is locally PL everywhere, including the unchanged boundary collar. Its inverse is locally PL on the same finite image subdivisions, hence it is a PL homeomorphism. Concatenating the finitely many supported isotopies gives $u$ and its TOP ambient isotopy. In particular, pulling the system of step1.1 back by $u$ makes it a PL sphere system in the ORIGINAL structure by an actual TOP ambient isotopy; this statement does not assert a smooth isotopy. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Consequently PL primeness and PL irreducibility for a finite PL manifold agree with their TOP tame versions. One recognition detail is needed in the reverse direction: if a closed finite PL manifold is TOP homeomorphic to $S^3$, pull its PL structure to standard $S^3$ and apply step2.1 (there is no boundary collar condition) to obtain a PL homeomorphism to standard PL $S^3$. If a finite PL manifold with sphere boundary is a TOP ball, its PL double is TOP $S^3$; the preceding recognition and [F4] make each half a PL ball. Thus neither a TOP sphere factor nor a TOP ball side is silently being recognized as PL without the comparison construction. Indeed a TOP splitting sphere can be moved to a PL sphere by steps1.1 and2.1, and the ambient homeomorphism identifies its two cut components. If its PL side is a parametrized ball, its TOP side is a parametrized TOP ball; conversely every PL splitting is an admitted TOP splitting. The same argument compares every finite TOP connected-sum presentation with a finite PL presentation. Capping choices do not affect the homeomorphism types: conjugate any boundary identification to a sphere map and extend by the cone formula $[x,t]\mapsto[f(x),t]$, which is a homeomorphism even when $f$ is only TOP. No assertion that a TOP ball parameter was PL in the old structure is used. Now apply [F3] to the fixed finite triangulation of $M$. It gives a finite connected sum of factors prime in the full tame TOP sense, with boundary allowed and every original boundary mark retained. This proves existence. It also proves the asserted prime-but-not-irreducible exception: [F3] proves $S^1\times S^2$ PL prime, hence TOP prime by this step, and $\{*\}\times S^2$ is nonseparating and cannot bound a ball. Every other prime is irreducible by [F3] and this same compatibility operation. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 We prove uniqueness first for finite PL presentations in one fixed PL manifold. A system $S$ will be said to reduce $M$ to a list $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ if cutting along $S$ and capping its cut faces gives precisely these manifolds together with some standard three-spheres having no original boundary marks. All original boundary components remain assigned to their cut component. Each $P_i$ is irreducible and is not $S^3$; balls and other factors with original boundary are retained. Given a prime presentation, take its separating connected-sum spheres and add one standard nonseparating sphere in each $S^1\times S^2$ summand. Their finite collars and the marked model in [F3], Proof3.1, show that they reduce $M$ to its irreducible nonspherical prime factors: cutting and capping the added sphere turns that summand into $S^3$. The cap-ball avoidance construction [F3], Proof1.1, realizes all these spheres disjointly in the original manifold. Conversely, if $S$ reduces to this list, adding any finite PL spheres disjoint from $S$ leaves the list unchanged. In a capped irreducible component each new sphere bounds a ball. Its cut-and-cap operation leaves that component and an unmarked $S^3$; in a capped $S^3$ this follows from [F4]. Move cap balls off the sphere as in [F3], Proof1.1, to carry out the cutting, or equivalently keep track of the cap balls as punctures on their respective sides. They introduce only extra punctures and do not erase an original boundary component. Induction over the finite added spheres proves the assertion. [F3, F4, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Let $S$ and $T$ be systems reducing $M$ to the irreducible lists from two prime presentations. Make their intersection transverse by a finite PL perturbation of one system. To see the finiteness and the local condition, take finite common subdivisions of their surface charts and ambient stars, and move their vertices by sufficiently small generic displacements in the finite linear charts. Avoid the finitely many affine incidences giving coincident vertices, tangencies or edge/face degeneracies; choose them one at a time outside these proper affine subsets. Finite compact disjoint simplices retain their positive separation, and the transverse link disks retain their embedding under such small moves. Use the boundary-fixed face-cone extensions in the ambient little stars to realize the moves, or just keep the parametrized perturbed surfaces; no factor changes. The intersection is now a compact one-manifold with a finite triangulation, hence finitely many disjoint polygonal circles. If there are no circles, keep the two systems. Otherwise choose a circle innermost on a component of $T$, bounding a PL disk $D$ whose interior misses $S$. The disk exists because a polygonal circle on a PL sphere bounds two parametrized disks by [F4]'s sphere boundary-disk construction. [F4, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Suppose $\partial D\subset S_j$. Surger $S_j$ along $D$: its two complementary disks capped by two close parallel copies of $D$ give spheres $S'_j,S''_j$. Small product pushes make both disjoint from $S_j$ and from all the other spheres of $S$. These are actual finite PL surfaces: in the finite disk and circle collar charts take two levels, triangulate the product strips, and flatten their quadrant corners by finite face-cone maps. The three spheres $S_j,S'_j,S''_j$ bound a parametrized three-punctured sphere $P$. For its parameter, take the collar of $S_j$ on the $D$ side and the narrow disk prism thickening $D$; it is the standard collar with a disk two-handle on one end. Cut the sphere parameter along the common circle into its two parametrized disks. The two disk prisms and their circle strip give, by the marked window gluing of [F4], a ball with two disjoint parametrized interior balls removed. This verifies the three-punctured-sphere description with its three specified boundary components, not just its homology. Add both new spheres to $S$. By step4.1 this enlarged system reduces to the same list. Then delete $S_j$. This attaches $P$ to the component on the other side of $S_j$ along exactly that one boundary sphere; the other two boundary spheres stay cut. After capping these two faces, the operation just fills the old $S_j$ face by a parametrized ball. Thus the capped component is unchanged, and all other capped components are unchanged. This remains true if the two sides belonged to the same component before adding the new spheres, since $P$ is an isolated component AFTER the two new cuts. The new system therefore reduces to the same list. [F3, F4, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 The surgery reduces the number of intersections with $T$. Choose its disk levels on opposite sides of $D\subset T$ and the circle collar so that the two cap disks miss $T$. Every remaining old intersection circle lies in one of the two complementary disks of $S_j$ and is merely carried to the corresponding new sphere. The chosen circle disappears, and no new one is created; all other members of $S$ are unchanged. Repeat step6.1 until the finite nonnegative intersection count is zero. The resulting $S^*$ is disjoint from $T$ and reduces to precisely the original $P_i$ list. Their union is now an enlargement both of $S^*$ and of $T$. Step4.1 says its capped components consist of the $P_i$ together with unmarked $S^3$'s and also of the $Q_i$ together with unmarked $S^3$'s. Hence the nonspherical irreducible factors occur with identical multiplicity and homeomorphism types, up to permutation. Original boundary marks may be retained throughout, though the Statement does not require that stronger marking. [F4, step 4.1, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 The remaining number of $S^1\times S^2$ factors is also determined. Work over $\mathbb Q$. The finite triangulation and [F6] make $b_1(M)=\dim H_1(M;\mathbb Q)$ finite. For a separating connected-sum sphere, use its collar to form an open two-set cover; the intersection retracts to $S^2$. This sphere has $H_1=0$ and connected $H_0=\mathbb Q$, and its map to the two connected sides' $H_0$ groups is $a\mapsto(a,-a)$, injective. Exactness in [F6] gives $H_1(M;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(P;\mathbb Q)\oplus H_1(Q;\mathbb Q)$; filling the boundary spheres has no effect on $H_1$ by the same cover sequence with a ball. For $S^1\times S^2$ use two proper overlapping open circle arcs whose intersection has two interval components, and multiply by $S^2$. Each of the two open sets retracts to $S^2$ and the overlap retracts to two copies of $S^2$. The sphere has zero $H_1$ by its finite boundary-of-a-tetrahedron chain complex in [F6]. The degree-zero map $\mathbb Q^2\to\mathbb Q^2$ sends both component generators to $(1,-1)$, so its kernel is one-dimensional. The same exact sequence gives $b_1(S^1\times S^2)=1$. Thus a presentation with irreducible list $P_i$ and $\ell$ such factors satisfies $b_1(M)=\sum_i b_1(P_i)+\ell$. Step7.1 identifies the sum for the two presentations, so their numbers $\ell$ are equal. [F6, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 Finally take any two admitted finite tame TOP prime presentations of the original $M$. By steps1.1 and2.1 move each of their finite cutting systems to a PL system in the fixed structure. Their capped factors are homeomorphic to the original factors by step3.1. TOP prime factors become PL prime, so [F3]'s prime-versus-irreducible assertion applies; the explicit nonseparating handle model identifies the possible $S^1\times S^2$ factors. Steps4.1–8.1 therefore compare these two presentations and give precisely the required equality of prime factors up to order and insertion or deletion of $S^3$. A single-factor presentation and $M=S^3$ are included: the reducing system may be empty and its only capped component may be an unmarked $S^3$; the same refinement argument forces every nonspherical irreducible list to be empty, and step8.1 forces zero handle factors. Existence and the exceptional prime factor were proved in step3.1. All boundary cuts and cap maps used actual parameters, the only TOP-to-PL compatibility used the explicit relative operation of steps1.1 and2.1, and full AC entered through [A1], [F1] and [F2] exactly as declared. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, step 3.1, step 7.1, step 8.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a finite regular projection diagram $D$ having $n$ crossings and a supplied product tube. There is a polygonal knot $P$ inside that tube with the same crossing code as $D$ and a smooth rounding $K^\sharp$ of $P$ such that $K^\sharp$ is smoothly ambient isotopic to $K$. The compact exterior of this same $P$ has a good triangulation with at most $C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and a marked path for the original meridian with at most $C(n+1)$ boundary edges, for one universal constant $C$. The peripheral-preserving exterior homeomorphism transfers this model to $K^\sharp$.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]] — smooth knot and ambient-isotopy convention.

[[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]] — finite regular diagram and crossing-code conventions.

[[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]] — finite regular diagram and crossing-code conventions.

[[lem-smooth-to-pl-knot-exterior-ambient-isotopy]] — code-preserving polygonal approximation, smooth rounding and peripheral-preserving exterior homeomorphism.

[[lem-good-linear-size-exterior-triangulation-from-diagram]] — linear-size triangulation of the supplied polygonal realization and marked meridian.

[Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger, §7](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hass/Research/Papers/Complexity/hlp.pdf) — diagram-to-exterior triangulation and linear-size bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a smooth knot $K$, its finite regular diagram $D$, and a supplied product tube.

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only through the smooth isotopy extension in [[lem-smooth-to-pl-knot-exterior-ambient-isotopy]].

[F1] [[lem-smooth-to-pl-knot-exterior-ambient-isotopy]]: $D$ admits a polygonal knot $P$ with the same code; a smooth rounding $K^\sharp$ is smoothly ambient isotopic to $K$; and a homeomorphism carries $P$'s exterior and marked meridian to those of $K^\sharp$.

[F2] [[lem-good-linear-size-exterior-triangulation-from-diagram]]: for a specified polygonal realization $P$ of the code, the construction triangulates that same exterior with at most $C_0(n+1)$ tetrahedra and a meridian path of at most $C_0(n+1)$ edges.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the supplied knot and diagram. It gives the polygonal realization $P$ with the same code, the smooth rounding $K^\sharp$ ambient isotopic to $K$, and the peripheral-preserving exterior homeomorphism. [given, A1, F1, construct]

2.1 Apply [F2] to this same specified polygonal knot $P$. It gives its good exterior triangulation and marked meridian path with the stated $C_0(n+1)$ bounds. Transport both through the peripheral-preserving homeomorphism in [F1]; homeomorphism does not change the number of tetrahedra or boundary edges in the combinatorial model. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Taking $C=C_0$ (or a larger fixed constant covering the zero-crossing template) proves the two bounds for the exterior of $K^\sharp$. Its smooth ambient isotopy to $K$ is supplied by [F1]. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

For every nontrivial companion knot and every pattern in its solid torus, the companion torus in the satellite exterior is essential.

## Statement references

[[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number]]

## Construction

Let $K$ be any nontrivial knot. Take the core pattern $P=S^1\times\{0\}\subset V=S^1\times D^2$, choose its tubular neighbourhood to be a smaller concentric solid torus inside a companion neighbourhood $V=e(S^1\times D^2)$ of $K$, and use the induced companion embedding. Then $P(K)=K$. The companion torus is the boundary of the larger chosen neighbourhood, while the satellite exterior has boundary the boundary of the smaller tube around $K$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The pattern, the companion embedding, and the two nested tubular neighbourhoods specified in the Counterexample.

[F1] [[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number]] defines the core pattern, satellite knot, pattern exterior, and companion torus.

[F2] [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]] defines boundary-parallel torus and essential torus.

## Proof

1.1 The companion embedding sends the core $S^1\times\{0\}$ to $K$, so the satellite knot $P(K)$ is exactly $K$ with the specified smaller tubular neighbourhood. The companion torus is the boundary of the larger neighbourhood. [F1, given]

1.2 The shell between the two concentric tubular neighbourhoods is explicitly $T^2\times[0,1]$, by radial interpolation in the $D^2$ coordinate. It lies in the satellite exterior and has the companion torus and the satellite exterior boundary as its end tori. Thus the companion torus is boundary-parallel and, by [F2], is not essential. This refutes the unrestricted statement. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Remarks

This example shows why a nonproduct condition on the pattern exterior is needed in the essential-companion-torus lemma.

[[lem-satellite-torus-is-essential]]
