## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let $L$ be a nonempty oriented link, let $E_L$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $X$ be a finite based two-dimensional CW complex with one $0$-cell, $n\ge2$ oriented $1$-cells $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, and $n-1$ oriented $2$-cells attached by based words $r_1,\ldots,r_{n-1}$. The supplied data include a based cellular spine certificate: a finite sequence of elementary cellular expansions and collapses identifying the simple-homotopy type of $X$ with the selected finite CW structure on $E_L$. Thus an abstract group isomorphism $\pi_1(X)\cong\pi_1(E_L)$ alone is not a spine certificate. Let $G=\pi_1(E_L)$, let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ and $\psi:G\twoheadrightarrow H$ be the representation and declared free-abelian deck map, and put $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb F[H])$. The associated deficiency-one presentation is $\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_{n-1}\rangle$ through the certified spine map. For $w\in F_n$, define Fox derivatives recursively by $\partial x_k/\partial x_j=\delta_{kj}$, $\partial(uv)/\partial x_j=\partial u/\partial x_j+u\,\partial v/\partial x_j$, and $\partial x_k^{-1}/\partial x_j=-x_k^{-1}\delta_{kj}$. Extend them linearly to the group ring and let $\Phi:\mathbb F[F_n]\to M_d(Q)$ be the ring homomorphism induced by $x_k\mapsto\rho(x_k)\psi(x_k)$. Form the block Fox matrix $J=(\Phi(\partial r_i/\partial x_k))_{i,k}$, of size $(n-1)d$ by $nd$. For a chosen column index $j$, let $J_{\widehat j}$ be obtained by deleting its entire $d$-column block and let $D_j=\det(\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I_d)$. The Wada quotient for this column is defined only when $D_j\ne0$, and then is $W_j=\det(J_{\widehat j})/D_j\in Q$; a zero denominator makes that column inadmissible even when another column is valid. No abstract deficiency-one presentation is assigned exterior torsion unless its presentation complex is the stated based spine.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $M$ is a closed connected orientable three-manifold with a complete Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$, then its fundamental group contains no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$.

## Statement references

[Gongopadhyay and Kulkarni, *z-Classes of Isometries of the Hyperbolic Space*, §1 and Appendix A.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.0487)

[Ved Datar, *Lectures on Riemannian Geometry*, §24.1 and §24.3](https://math.iisc.ac.in/~vvdatar/Lecture_Notes/RG_Lectures_typesett_published.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A closed connected three-manifold $M$ with a complete metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$ and the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ selects from every countable family of nonempty sets.

[F1] [[def-pared-hyperbolic-structures-and-volume]]: a hyperbolic structure is a curvature $-1$ metric described by charts into $\mathbb H^3$.

[F2] [[thm-cartan-hadamard]]: the complete simply connected universal cover of a connected complete manifold with $K\le0$ is identified with its tangent space by the exponential map.

[F3] [[ex-jacobi-fields-in-constant-sectional-curvature]]: along a unit-speed geodesic in curvature $-1$, a normal Jacobi field with $J(0)=0$ and $D_tJ(0)=w$ is $J(t)=\sinh(t)P_t w$, where $P_t$ is parallel transport.

[F4] [[def-universal-covering-space]] and [[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]: the universal cover is a covering and its deck group acts freely; [[thm-deck-group-of-a-universal-cover-is-the-fundamental-group]] identifies that group with $\pi_1(M)$. The lifted metric makes the covering a local isometry by [[def-riemannian-isometry-and-local-isometry]], local isometries send geodesics to geodesics by [[lem-local-isometries-send-geodesics-to-geodesics]], and covering paths lift by [[thm-path-lifting-for-covering-maps]].

[F5] Gongopadhyay and Kulkarni, *z-Classes of Isometries of the Hyperbolic Space*, §1 and Appendix A.1: orientation-preserving isometries of $\mathbb H^3$ are Möbius transformations of the boundary sphere, with hyperbolic/parabolic/elliptic types identified by their fixed-point behavior.

## Proof

1.1 The lift of the complete metric to $\widetilde M$ is complete: every geodesic upstairs projects by [F4] to a geodesic downstairs, which extends for all time; path lifting extends the original geodesic upstairs, and a local isometry preserves its geodesic equation. [given, F4, construct]

2.1 By [F2], the complete simply connected universal cover $\widetilde M$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^3$. Along each radial unit-speed geodesic from a fixed point, [F3] says the differential of the exponential map multiplies angular vectors by $\sinh r$, while its radial differential preserves length. Thus in polar coordinates the pulled-back metric is $dr^2+\sinh^2(r)g_{S^2}$, the standard hyperbolic metric; the exponential map identifies $\widetilde M$ isometrically with $\mathbb H^3$. By [F4], $\Gamma=\pi_1(M)$ acts freely and properly discontinuously by deck isometries; compactness of $M$ makes the action cocompact. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Every nonidentity element of $\Gamma$ is loxodromic. A Möbius map $z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)$ has fixed-point equation $cz^2+(d-a)z-b=0$ on the boundary sphere. If there are two distinct fixed points, conjugate them to $0,\infty$; the map then has form $z\mapsto \lambda z$. If $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda\ne1$, its extension fixes the axis joining $0$ to $\infty$, contrary to the free deck action [F4]. If $|\lambda|\ne1$, it preserves that axis and translates it nontrivially. If the fixed-point equation has a double root, conjugate it to $\infty$; the map has form $z\mapsto az+b$, and its only fixed point is $\infty$ precisely when $a=1$ and $b\ne0$. This is parabolic: the upper-half-space distance formula gives $\cosh d((0,t),(b,t))=1+|b|^2/(2t^2)$, so its displacement tends to zero as $t\to\infty$. To exclude such a parabolic in a cocompact deck group, choose compact $K$ with $\Gamma K=\mathbb H^3$ and points $y_n$ whose displacement tends to zero. Choose $h_n\in\Gamma$ so $x_n=h_ny_n\in K$ and put $\gamma_n=h_n\gamma h_n^{-1}$. The points $x_n$ and $\gamma_nx_n$ lie in a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, so proper discontinuity permits only finitely many $\gamma_n$. Along a subsequence this element is constant and $x_n$ converges in $K$; the displacement limit makes it fix the limit point, contradicting freeness. Hence every nonidentity element has two fixed endpoints and preserves a unique axis with nonzero translation. [F4, F5, step 2.1, given, algebra, contradiction]

4.1 Fix $\gamma\ne1$ and let $C_\Gamma(\gamma)=\{\delta\in\Gamma:\delta\gamma=\gamma\delta\}$. Commutation preserves the attracting and repelling endpoints of $\gamma$ individually, hence preserves its axis and acts there by a signed translation. The signed translation map $\tau:C_\Gamma(\gamma)\to\mathbb R$ is a homomorphism. It is injective: an element in its kernel fixes every point on the axis, and [F4] makes it the identity. Its image is discrete: if infinitely many elements had bounded signed translations, their images of a fixed point on the axis would lie in a compact segment, contradicting proper discontinuity in [F4]. Every discrete subgroup of $(\mathbb R,+)$ is cyclic, so $C_\Gamma(\gamma)$ is cyclic. [F4, F5, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 If $H\le\Gamma$ were isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$, choose $\gamma\in H\setminus\{1\}$. Since $H$ is abelian, $H\subseteq C_\Gamma(\gamma)$, contradicting step 4.1 because a cyclic group has no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Therefore no such $H$ exists. [given, step 4.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[Gongopadhyay and Kulkarni, *z-Classes of Isometries of the Hyperbolic Space*, §1 and Appendix A.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.0487)

[Ved Datar, *Lectures on Riemannian Geometry*, §24.1 and §24.3](https://math.iisc.ac.in/~vvdatar/Lecture_Notes/RG_Lectures_typesett_published.pdf)

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $TV_2(\cdot;\Omega)$ be the extended distributional total variation on $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. It is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous in the $L^2$ norm, and positively one-homogeneous for nonnegative scalars. For every $u\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)$, it agrees with spatial TV: $TV_2(u;\Omega)=TV(u;\Omega)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The extended L² distributional-TV functional is a supremum over smooth compactly supported vector fields.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc|For globally integrable BV functions, that test-field supremum equals the measure total variation.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, the functional $TV_2$ on $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and the spatial BV total variation.

[F1] [[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation]]: $TV_2(u;\Omega)$ is the supremum of $\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields with Euclidean norm at most one.

[F2] [[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]]: for $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $TV(u;\Omega)$ equals the same test-field supremum.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: each test functional $u\mapsto\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is continuous on $L^2$, with absolute value at most $\|u\|_2\|\operatorname{div}\varphi\|_2$.

## Proof

1.1 The zero function has $TV_2(0;\Omega)=0$, so the functional is proper; its defining test class is symmetric under $\varphi\mapsto-\varphi$, hence its supremum is nonnegative. For $\lambda>0$, linearity of every test integral gives $TV_2(\lambda u;\Omega)=\lambda TV_2(u;\Omega)$, and the equality also holds for $\lambda=0$. For $\theta\in[0,1]$, every admissible field gives $\int(\theta u+(1-\theta)v)\operatorname{div}\varphi\le\theta TV_2(u;\Omega)+(1-\theta)TV_2(v;\Omega)$; taking the supremum proves convexity, with the extended-real cases automatic. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], every fixed test integral is a continuous linear functional on $L^2$. For each real $a$, the sublevel set $\{u:TV_2(u;\Omega)\le a\}$ is the intersection, over all admissible $\varphi$, of the closed half-spaces $\{u:\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi\le a\}$; hence it is closed and $TV_2$ is lower semicontinuous. If $u\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)$, [F1] and [F2] give $TV_2(u;\Omega)=TV(u;\Omega)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $B$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$ and connected rational homology sphere boundary $Y$. Assume $Y$ has a nonsingular framed-link surgery presentation with the boundary orientation and linking convention of the surgery linking-form result. The coefficient sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to0$ gives an isomorphism $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. Define the cohomological linking pairing by
$$\lambda_Y(x,y)=\langle\beta^{-1}(x)\smile y,[Y]\rangle\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z.$$
Let $M$ be the image of restriction $H^2(B;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and $M^\perp=\{x:\lambda_Y(m,x)=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$. Then the boundary Spin$^c$ structures extending over $B$ form one affine coset of $M$, the pairing is nonsingular, $M=M^\perp$, and $|M|^2=|H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)|$.

## Statement references

[[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix|The chain torsion linking form and its nonsingular surgery-matrix convention]]

[[lem-spin-c-structures-form-an-h2-torsor|The affine H2 action on Spin-c structures]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the compact connected oriented smooth rational homology four-ball $B$, connected boundary $Y$, and the nonsingular surgery presentation specified in the statement.

[A1] AC is assumed by the finite-triangulation, Poincare-Lefschetz, UCT, and Bockstein suppliers used below ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] Compact smooth manifolds admit finite triangulations, so the integral homology groups of $B$ are finitely generated ([[thm-compact-smooth-manifolds-with-corners-admit-relative-finite-triangulations]]).

[F2] For a compact oriented four-manifold with boundary, cap product gives $H^j(B,Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_{4-j}(B;\mathbb Z)$ and $H^j(B;\mathbb Z)\cong H_{4-j}(B,Y;\mathbb Z)$ under AC ([[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality]]).

[F3] The pair $(B,Y)$ has the cohomology and homology long exact sequences, and cohomology of a free integral chain complex satisfies the UCT exact sequence ([[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-cohomology]], [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]], [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]).

[F4] The connecting map for a short exact coefficient sequence is defined by lifting cocycles and taking the coboundary; it is independent of the chosen lift and representative ([[def-bockstein-connecting-operation]], [[lem-the-bockstein-is-independent-of-lift-and-cocycle-representative]]).

[F5] Cup product is natural under inclusion; for a rational homology sphere, Poincare duality identifies $H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, and the surgery supplier fixes the chain-linking convention as $-A^{-1}$ for a nonsingular matrix $A$ ([[prop-cup-product-is-natural-unital-and-associative]], [[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]], [[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix]]).

[F6] Once a Spin$^c$ lift is given, the isomorphism classes of lifts form an affine $H^2(-;\mathbb Z)$-space ([[lem-spin-c-structures-form-an-h2-torsor]]). Boundary restriction is the actual normal-first rank-four-to-rank-three principal reduction and is equivariant for the restriction of line bundles and $H^2$ ([[lem-boundary-spin-c-restriction-and-line-twists-are-equivariant]]).

[F7] Every compact connected oriented smooth rational homology four-ball admits at least one Spin$^c$ structure ([[lem-rational-homology-four-ball-admits-spinc]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** compute the restriction subgroup from the cohomology sequence, prove it isotropic by the coefficient Bockstein formula, and compare orders.

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 Since $B$ has finite CW type by [F1] and has zero positive rational homology, each $H_i(B;\mathbb Z)$ for $i>0$ is finite. Put $a=|H_1(B;\mathbb Z)|$ and $b=|H_2(B;\mathbb Z)|$. The UCT [F3] gives $|H^2(B;\mathbb Z)|=a$ and $|H^3(B;\mathbb Z)|=b$, because the Hom terms from finite groups vanish and $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb Z/m,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/m$. Poincare-Lefschetz duality [F2] gives $|H^2(B,Y;\mathbb Z)|=b$ and $|H^3(B,Y;\mathbb Z)|=a$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 In the pair sequence, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$ because $Y$ is a rational homology sphere and its first integral cohomology is $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y),\mathbb Z)$. Thus $H^2(B,Y)\to H^2(B)$ is injective. Also $H^3(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, so the map from the finite group $H^3(B;\mathbb Z)$ to $H^3(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; exactness makes $H^3(B,Y)\to H^3(B)$ surjective. It follows that the restriction image $M$ has order $a/b$, and that $H^2(Y)/M$ has order $a/b$. Hence $|H^2(Y)|=(a/b)^2$ and $|M|^2=|H^2(Y)|=|H_1(Y)|$, the last equality following from UCT and Poincare duality for the rational homology sphere. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For any $m\in M$, choose $u\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$ restricting to $m$, and let $c$ be an integral cocycle representing $u$. Since $H^2(B;\mathbb Q)=0$, the rational cocycle $c$ is $\delta q$ for a rational $1$-cochain $q$; reducing $q$ modulo $\mathbb Z$ gives a cocycle $v\in H^1(B;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with $\beta(v)=u$. It is unique because $H^1(B;\mathbb Q)=0$. Restriction of this cochain lift gives $\beta(v|_Y)=m$. For $Y$, both $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q)$ and $H^2(Y;\mathbb Q)$ vanish, so the same coefficient sequence proves that $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism. By UCT, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$; by Poincare duality, $H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. Cup evaluation is therefore the perfect character-evaluation pairing under these identifications. If $X,D$ are torsion $1$-cycles with $mX=\partial F$, the cochain represented by the rational bounding chain $F/m$, reduced modulo integral cochains, is $\beta^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}^{-1}[X])$; its evaluation against $\mathrm{PD}^{-1}[D]$ is $F\cdot D/m$ modulo $\mathbb Z$. Thus this cohomological formula agrees with the chain linking form up to the global orientation sign, which does not change annihilators. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 If $x\in M$ is the restriction of $w\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$, naturality of cup product [F5] gives $\lambda_Y(m,x)=\langle v|_Y\smile w|_Y,[Y]\rangle=\langle v\smile w,i_*[Y]\rangle=0$, since $i_*[Y]=0$ in $H_3(B;\mathbb Z)$ by the homology pair sequence: $[Y]$ is the boundary of the relative fundamental class $[B,Y]$. Therefore $M\subseteq M^\perp$. For a nonsingular finite pairing on a group $G$, restriction of characters $G\to\operatorname{Hom}(G,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is onto. To see this, extend a character from a subgroup $H$ one generator $g$ at a time: if the least $n>0$ with $ng\in H$ is fixed, choose $z\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ with $nz=f(ng)$ (possible because multiplication by $n$ is onto), and set $f'(h+kg)=f(h)+kz$; the relation $ng\in H$ makes $f'$ well defined. Since $G$ is finite this process terminates. Hence $|M^\perp|=|G|/|M|$. Apply this with $G=H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and use step 2.1 to obtain $|M^\perp|=|M|$. Thus $M=M^\perp$. [F5, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 By [F7], choose a Spin$^c$ structure on $B$. Then [F6] makes the Spin$^c$ structures on $B$ an affine $H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$-space. Restriction is equivariant, so the image of this nonempty affine space is one affine coset of the image subgroup $M$. This proves the extension-set assertion. If $M=0$, the same sequence gives $|H^2(Y)|=1$, so the trivial subgroup is its own annihilator; the empty-boundary case is excluded by the connected-boundary hypothesis. [F6, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with exactly one component, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Perform the following construction in its projection sphere $S^2$.

1. Choose a point $q\in S^2$ outside the finite diagram. In pairwise disjoint small disks about the crossings, replace each crossing by the unique noncrossing smoothing compatible with the strand orientations. Let the resulting oriented circles be the Seifert circles and let $s$ be their number.
2. For each Seifert circle $C$, take the closure of the component of $S^2\setminus C$ that does not contain $q$. Under the stated choice axiom, each such region is an embedded compact disk. The finite family of disk regions is nested or disjoint. Orient each disk to induce the given orientation of its boundary circle, then place nested disks at distinct nearby heights ordered by inclusion; the resulting disk interiors are pairwise disjoint in $S^3$.
3. For every original crossing, attach one rectangular band along short boundary intervals on the two smoothing arcs. A half-twist means a single $180$-degree turn of the band across the crossing neighborhood. Choose its direction, endpoint orientations, and over/under order to match the original crossing.
4. Return the finite disk-and-band construction data together with $(s,c)$.

The returned data are a finite attached two-dimensional complex. This algorithm's definition alone does not assert that the resulting image is embedded, is a surface, is connected, or has the original knot as boundary; the separate correctness lemma establishes those properties.

## Definition

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. A nontangential maximal geodesic segment is a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$, with $L>0$, whose initial velocity points strictly inward at $\partial M_0$, whose terminal velocity points strictly outward at $\partial M_0$, and whose points for $0<t<L$ lie in $M_0^\circ$. For $f\in C_c^\infty(M_0^\circ,\mathbb R)$ define its geodesic ray transform by $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=\int_0^L f(\gamma(t))\,dt$. The unweighted scalar ray transform is called injective on compactly supported smooth functions if $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=0$ for every such segment implies $f=0$. For complex-valued $f$, injectivity means injectivity of its real and imaginary parts separately.

## Example

In the finite-dimensional Gaussian credible-ball question reproduced below, choose $d=n=1$, $R=1$, $\sigma=1$, $T=1$, $\beta(t)=1$, and $\gamma=1/4$, with arbitrary positive $p,s,a$. Take the numerical operator equal to the true operator, so $\delta_A=0$. For every integer $K\ge1$ there is a jointly Borel finite score field with integrated score error exactly zero, whose Euler terminal law is $N(1,K^{-1})$ for every observation. With $M=K$ independent terminal draws, the resulting empirical ball has frequentist coverage tending to zero at truth $\theta=0$, although the stated uniform boundary-margin condition holds with exponent $\kappa=1$. The exact credible-ball baseline satisfies $\delta^0_{1,1/4}<3/4$. Consequently no bound in that question can have $\Phi\to0$ uniformly over its original score class as $(\delta_A,\varepsilon_s,K^{-1},M^{-1/2})\to(0,0,0,0)$. The original formulation is retained verbatim under Original question.

## Example references

[Knapik, van der Vaart, and van Zanten, full paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1103.2692)

[Szabó, van der Vaart, and van Zanten, full paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.4489v5)

[Giné and Nickl, full textbook](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

[Narnhofer et al., full paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.12499v2)

## Original question

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$, parameters $p,s,a,R,\sigma>0$, a credibility error $\gamma\in(0,1)$, and a continuous schedule $\beta:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ with $T>0$. Let
$$\Theta_s(R)=\left\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:\sum_{j=1}^d j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2\right\},\qquad A_p=\operatorname{diag}(1^{-p},2^{-p},\ldots,d^{-p}).$$
Observe $Y_i=A_p\theta+\varepsilon_i$, $1\le i\le n$, with independent $\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_d)$. Use the proper Gaussian prior $\Pi_0=N(0,\operatorname{diag}(j^{-1-2a})_{j=1}^d)$, and let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid Y)$ be its exact posterior under the stated forward operator and noise law. Let $m_n(Y)$ be the posterior mean and let $r_{n,\gamma}(Y)$ be the unique radius for which the Euclidean ball
$$C_{n,\gamma}(Y)=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u-m_n(Y)\|_2\le r_{n,\gamma}(Y)\}$$
has posterior probability $1-\gamma$. Define the exact frequentist coverage $c_{n,\gamma}(\theta)=P_{n,\theta}\{\theta\in C_{n,\gamma}(Y)\}$ and its baseline error $\delta^0_{n,\gamma}=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s(R)}|c_{n,\gamma}(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|$.

For a deterministic numerical matrix $\widehat A_n\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with $\delta_A\ge0$ and $\|\widehat A_n-A_p\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\delta_A$, let $\widehat\Pi_n(\cdot\mid Y)$ be the Gaussian posterior formed with $\widehat A_n$ and the same prior and noise variance. Write $\widehat p_{n,t}^Y$ for the density obtained by applying the forward variance-preserving diffusion $dX_t=-\tfrac12\beta(t)X_t\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t$ to $X_0\sim\widehat\Pi_n(\cdot\mid Y)$, and set $\widehat s_{n,t}^Y=\nabla\log\widehat p_{n,t}^Y$. A jointly Borel learned score field $s_{n,t}^Y$ is required to satisfy
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s(R)}E_{Y\sim P_{n,\theta}}\left[\frac1T\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R^d}\|s_{n,t}^Y(x)-\widehat s_{n,t}^Y(x)\|_2^2\widehat p_{n,t}^Y(x)\,dx\,dt\right]\le\varepsilon_s^2.$$
For $h=T/K$, define the reverse-time Euler chain by $Z_0\sim\widehat p_{n,T}^Y$ and, for $k=0,\ldots,K-1$,
$$Z_{k+1}=Z_k+h\left[\tfrac12\beta(T-kh)Z_k+\beta(T-kh)s_{n,T-kh}^Y(Z_k)\right]+\sqrt{h\beta(T-kh)}\,\zeta_k,$$
where the $\zeta_k$ are independent $N(0,I_d)$ vectors independent of $Z_0$ and the observations. Draw $M$ independent copies of this chain conditionally on $Y$ and denote their terminal values by $X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(M)}$. Let $\bar X=M^{-1}\sum_iX^{(i)}$, let $\widehat r$ be the empirical $1-\gamma$ quantile of $\{\|X^{(i)}-\bar X\|_2\}_{i=1}^M$ (the smallest order statistic whose empirical cumulative mass is at least $1-\gamma$), and put $\widehat C_{n,K,M}(Y)=\{u:\|u-\bar X\|_2\le\widehat r\}$. Suppose the exact credible-ball boundary satisfies the uniform margin condition
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s(R)}P_{n,\theta}\left(\left|\|\theta-m_n(Y)\|_2-r_{n,\gamma}(Y)\right|\le u\right)\le C_{\mathrm{ac}}u^\kappa\quad(0<u\le u_0)$$
for fixed $C_{\mathrm{ac}},u_0>0$ and $\kappa>0$. Determine whether a minimax-sharp nonasymptotic function $\Phi$ exists uniformly over all such score fields and, if it does, find it as a function of $d,n,p,s,a,R,\sigma,T,\gamma,C_{\mathrm{ac}},u_0,\kappa,\delta_A,\varepsilon_s,K^{-1}$, and $M^{-1/2}$ such that
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s(R)}\left|P_{n,\theta,\mathrm{sampler}}\{\theta\in\widehat C_{n,K,M}(Y)\}-(1-\gamma)\right|\le\delta^0_{n,\gamma}+\Phi,$$
with matching lower bounds that identify when $\Phi\to0$. The probability includes observation noise and sampler randomness. The target concerns the additional coverage error introduced by the approximate forward operator, learned score, finite reverse discretization, and finite posterior sample; it does not assume that the exact Bayesian credible ball is already calibrated on every truth class.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The scalar parameter choices in the Example and the original score-error, Euler and empirical-ball definitions reproduced below it.

[A1] Write $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and $\Phi(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x\phi(z)\,dz$. A standard Gaussian has density $\phi$, mean zero, variance one and tail probability tending to zero at infinity.

[A2] Let $q=3/4$ and let $r>0$ solve $P\{|G|\le\sqrt2r\}=q$ for a standard Gaussian $G$. Continuity and strict positivity of $\phi$ give existence and uniqueness of $r$.

## Verification

**Given:** The scalar model and [A1]–[A2].

1.1 Completing the square in $e^{-u^2/2}e^{-(Y-u)^2/2}$ gives posterior $N(Y/2,1/2)$, so its exact credible interval is $[Y/2-r,Y/2+r]$. Under truth $\theta\in[-1,1]$, $Y=\theta+G$ and the exact coverage is $c(\theta)=P\{|\theta/2-G/2|\le r\}$. This is a continuous strictly positive function of $\theta$, and is at most one. By compactness of $[-1,1]$ it has a positive minimum $c_*>0$. Therefore $\delta^0_{1,1/4}\le\max\{q-c_*,1-q\}<q$. [A1, A2, algebra]

2.1 Put $h=1/K$ and let $\mathcal G_K=\{1-kh:0\le k<K\}$. Away from this finite set of times, use the exact noised-posterior score. At each $t\in\mathcal G_K$ set $s_t^Y(x)=(1-x)/h-x/2$. This finite-valued jointly Borel field has zero integrated score error: its discrepancy from the exact score is supported on the finite, Lebesgue-null set $\mathcal G_K$ in time. The noised posterior has mean $e^{-t/2}Y/2$ and variance $1-e^{-t}/2$: the integrating-factor solution of the linear forward equation is $e^{-t/2}X_0+e^{-t/2}\int_0^te^{u/2}\,dW_u$, whose independent Gaussian integral has variance $1-e^{-t}$ (use dyadic Brownian-increment sums and pass their Gaussian characteristic functions to the mean-square limit). Its exact score is therefore affine in $x$, so the inner Gaussian error integral is finite at every time. The zero-error conclusion holds for every observation and hence uniformly over all truths. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 The variable $\theta/2-G/2$ has a density bounded by $2/\sqrt{2\pi}$ uniformly in $\theta$. The event $\bigl||\theta/2-G/2|-r\bigr|\le u$ is contained in two intervals of total length at most $4u$. Thus its probability is at most $8u/\sqrt{2\pi}$. The required margin holds, for example with $\kappa=1$, $u_0=1$ and $C_{\mathrm{ac}}=8/\sqrt{2\pi}$. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At every Euler step the deterministic update becomes $x+h(x/2+s_t^Y(x))=1$. Thus each new state is $1+\sqrt h\,\zeta_k$, independently of its input and of $Y$, and the terminal law is $N(1,h)$. For $M=K$, write the independent terminal draws as $1+K^{-1/2}G_i$. If $V_K=\max_{i\le K}|G_i|$, then the empirical center differs from one by at most $K^{-1/2}V_K$ and every empirical distance to that center is at most $2K^{-1/2}V_K$. Hence the empirical radius has that same upper bound. [A1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The Gaussian density gives $P\{|G|>v\}\le2e^{-v^2/2}$ for $v\ge1$: integrate $x\phi(x)/v$ on $[v,\infty)$ and use $1/(v\sqrt{2\pi})\le1$. The union bound then gives $P\{V_K>K^{1/4}\}\le2K e^{-\sqrt K/2}\to0$. On the complementary event the center is at least $1-K^{-1/4}$ and the radius at most $2K^{-1/4}$, so for all sufficiently large $K$ the empirical interval excludes truth zero. Its coverage therefore tends to zero, and its deviation from $q$ tends to $q>\delta^0_{1,1/4}$. Since both error norms are zero and $K^{-1},M^{-1/2}\to0$, a uniformly vanishing $\Phi$ would contradict this strict gap. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Scope of the resolution

This resolves the requested uniformly vanishing-error guarantee negatively under the original score hypothesis. Time-integrated error does not control pointwise values at a deterministic solver grid. A constant worst-case coverage bound remains possible; no impossibility of all numerical functions is asserted. No Bayesian calibration claim is imported from a conformal theorem.

## Statement

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary and let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$ be a unit-speed nontangential geodesic segment. For every real $\lambda$ and every $K>0$, there is a family $v_{\tau+i\lambda}\in C^\infty(M_0)$, $\tau\geq1$, such that
$$\|(-\Delta_{g_0}-(\tau+i\lambda)^2)v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(\tau^{-K}),\qquad \|v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(1),$$
and for every $\psi\in C(M_0)$,
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_{M_0}|v_{\tau+i\lambda}|^2\psi\,dV_{g_0} =\int_0^L e^{-2\lambda t}\psi(\gamma(t))\,dt.$$
The statement permits transversal manifolds without an orientability assumption and makes no boundary condition assertion for the quasimodes.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Transversal manifold]]

[[def-ip-injective-geodesic-ray-transform|Nontangential geodesic segment]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the compact Riemannian transversal, a nontangential segment, a real attenuation $\lambda$, and $K>0$.

[F1] [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]: geodesic normal coordinates, the metric volume density, and the Laplace-Beltrami operator are defined locally without choosing an orientation.

[F2] [[thm-local-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-for-manifold-integral-curves]]: the geodesic ODE has local solutions and smooth dependence on initial data, so parallel frames and exponential-coordinate maps vary smoothly along an embedded geodesic subsegment.

[F3] **External input:** Dos Santos Ferreira--Kurylev--Lassas--Salo, Proposition 3.1, PDF p. 14, supplies exactly the residual, norm, and attenuated ray limit in the statement on an oriented compact transversal of dimension at least two. Its finite Taylor-jet construction and distinct-branch cross-term estimate (equation (3.6), PDF pp. 21--22) are imported, including overlap matching at self-intersections. For this repair the proposition and the cross-term argument on pp. 21--22 were inspected; the entire proof on pp. 14--22 is not claimed as newly reconstructed. Historical source coverage is distinct from this reading extent.

[F4] The construction for each fixed $K$ uses finitely many charts, finite Taylor orders, and linear transport and matrix ODEs with fixed initial data. Increasing the finite order suffices for that $K$; no simultaneous choice of quasimodes for unrelated $K$ or $\lambda$ is required. The parameter $\tau$ then enters the resulting explicit formula. Thus the use here adds no choice axiom to the statement.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Embed the segment in a collar extension across $\partial M_0$ and cover it by finitely many coordinate neighborhoods. On an embedded subsegment, parallel transport an orthonormal normal frame and set $F(t,y)=\exp_{\gamma(t)}(\sum_\alpha y_\alpha E_\alpha(t))$. The inverse function theorem gives local Fermi coordinates with $g_{jk}(t,0)=\delta_{jk}$ and $\partial_i g_{jk}(t,0)=0$. This construction is along an interval and uses no orientation of $M_0$. [F1, F2, given]

1.2 In one such chart, seek $v_s=e^{is\Theta}a$, $s=\tau+i\lambda$, with $\Theta(t,0)=t$ and $\operatorname{Im}\Theta(t,y)\geq c|y|^2$. Expand $\Theta$ into homogeneous transverse Taylor polynomials. The quadratic polynomial is $\frac12H(t)y\cdot y$; substituting into $g(d\Theta,d\Theta)=1$ gives the matrix Riccati equation $H'+H^2=F(t)$, where $F$ is determined by the second transverse Taylor coefficient of the inverse metric. An initial complex symmetric $H(t_0)$ with positive-definite imaginary part yields a smooth solution with positive imaginary part on a short subsegment. Each higher homogeneous phase term then solves a linear first-order ODE along $t$, because its newest coefficient occurs linearly in the eikonal equation. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Substituting $a=\tau^{(m-1)/4}\sum_{j=0}^N s^{-j}a_{-j}$ into $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)e^{is\Theta}a$ cancels successive powers of $s$ by linear transport ODEs for the transverse Taylor coefficients of each $a_{-j}$. The leading coefficient solves $a_0(t,0)=c_0\exp(-\frac12\int_{t_0}^t\operatorname{tr}H(r)\,dr)$. A finite Taylor realization to the order required for the fixed $K$ and a transverse cutoff produce a smooth local beam; Gaussian integration gives bounded $L^2$ norm and a residual that tends to zero faster than any prescribed power after increasing the Taylor order. [F1, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 On an oriented transversal of dimension at least two, apply [F3] to complete the finite overlap matching and eliminate all distinct-branch cross terms. This gives the stated global family and limit; steps 1.1--2.1 describe its local ingredients, without claiming a new proof of the imported global estimates. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 For a nonorientable transversal let $\pi:\widetilde M_0\to M_0$ be its orientation double cover, with deck involution $\sigma$, and lift $\gamma$ to $\widetilde\gamma$. Let $w_s$ be the oriented beam from [F3] along that lift. Define the descended function by $\pi^*v_s=w_s+\sigma^*w_s$. The residual and norm bounds follow by a finite sum and the covering integral formula. The two lifted segments have no common tangent branch: equality of position and velocity at different times would make the geodesic periodic, contrary to its nontangential boundary exit; opposite velocities at a repeated point would force a zero midpoint velocity by geodesic uniqueness. There are only finitely many crossing branches, by compactness and local uniqueness. The distinct-branch estimate in [F3], applied to these two lifts, therefore gives a zero mixed-term limit. For every continuous $\psi$ the covering formula is
$$\int_{M_0}|v_s|^2\psi\,dV=\int_{\widetilde M_0}|w_s|^2(\psi\circ\pi)\,dV+\operatorname{Re}\int_{\widetilde M_0}w_s\overline{\sigma^*w_s}(\psi\circ\pi)\,dV.$$
The first term has precisely the required ray limit and the second tends to zero. In particular there is no extra factor two in the normalization. The same argument works if the cover is disconnected. [F1, F3, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

3.3 If the transversal has dimension one, the component containing the segment is an interval with arclength coordinate $t$ beginning at its incoming endpoint. Set $v_s=e^{ist}$ on this component and zero on all other components. The residual is zero and the asserted integral formula is exact. In dimension zero the given unit-speed segment cannot exist. This covers the dimensions not needed in the CTA application as well. [F1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $E$ be a triangulated compact exterior of a smooth knot with peripheral torus $T$ and a marked simple fibre meridian $\mu$ in the boundary triangulation. For an admissible normal-coordinate vector $v$ and its associated normal surface $S$, the following tests hold exactly when $S$ is a connected properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary in $T$: (i) $S$ is connected; (ii) $\partial S\ne\varnothing$; (iii) $\chi(S)=1$; and (iv) $\partial S$ has odd mod-two intersection with $\mu$. If $v$ is fundamental, connectedness follows from fundamentalness.

## Statement references

[[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]] — normal-coordinate and admissibility conventions.

[[lem-normal-coordinate-matching-equations-and-finite-bounds]] — admissible vectors represent normal surfaces.

[[lem-fundamental-normal-surfaces-are-connected]] — fundamental normal surfaces are connected.

[[lem-connected-normal-surface-chi-one-is-disk]] — a connected surface with boundary and Euler characteristic one is a disk.

[[lem-essential-disk-boundary-is-longitude]] — essential disk boundaries in this exterior meet the original meridian oddly.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The triangulated knot exterior $E$, its peripheral torus $T$, marked fibre meridian $\mu$, and admissible vector $v$.

[F1] [[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]]: an admissible vector is a nonnegative integer vector satisfying all normal matching equations and the quadrilateral condition.

[F2] [[lem-normal-coordinate-matching-equations-and-finite-bounds]]: every admissible integer vector is realized by a properly embedded normal surface with that vector.

[F3] [[lem-connected-normal-surface-chi-one-is-disk]]: a connected compact triangulated surface with nonempty boundary and Euler characteristic $1$ is a disk.

[F4] [[lem-essential-disk-boundary-is-longitude]]: every properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary in $T$ has boundary $\pm[\lambda]$ and odd mod-two intersection with $\mu$.

[F5] [[lem-fundamental-normal-surfaces-are-connected]]: every nonempty fundamental normal surface is connected.

## Proof

1.1 The hypothesis that $v$ is admissible has the meaning fixed in [F1]. By [F2], it determines a properly embedded normal surface $S$, so its boundary lies in $T$. If tests (i)–(iv) pass, then $S$ is connected, has nonempty boundary, and has Euler characteristic one. By [F3], it is a disk. [given, F1, F2, F3, construct]

1.2 Conversely, suppose $S$ is a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. A disk is connected, has nonempty boundary, and has Euler characteristic one. By [F4], its boundary has odd mod-two intersection with $\mu$, so all four tests pass. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 If $\partial S$ were null-homotopic in $T$, its product projection would have degree zero. After a PL transverse perturbation, the mod-two intersection with the fibre meridian equals the parity of the preimages of a regular point under this projection; a lift to $\mathbb R$ with zero net change crosses that regular level an even number of times. This contradicts test (iv). Thus the disk has non-null-homotopic boundary. [given, step 1.1, construct, contradiction]

3.1 If $v$ is fundamental, [F5] already supplies test (i); the other tests remain exactly those stated. Steps 1.1–1.2 prove the equivalence. [given, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented three-sphere, and let $F$ be a connected compact oriented smooth embedded surface with oriented boundary $K$. Fix the standard round metric on $S^3$. A normal field along $K$ assigns to every point $p\in K$ a nonzero vector in the plane orthogonal to $T_pK$; two such fields represent the same framing class when they are homotopic through nonzero normal fields. The inward unit vector tangent to $F$ along $K$, together with the positive quarter-turn in each oriented normal plane, gives a reference frame. In this frame the relative normal field is a map $K\cong S^1\to S^1$, and its degree gives a bijection from framing classes to $\mathbb Z$. Adding $n$ positive full twists changes this integer by $n$.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|The smooth oriented knot model in the three-sphere]]

[[thm-fundamental-group-of-the-circle|Based circle loops are classified by integer degree]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot $K$, a spanning surface $F$ as in the statement, and the standard orientation and metric on $S^3$.

[F1] An oriented link in $S^3$ is a smooth embedding of a finite disjoint union of oriented circles, with the fixed standard orientation of $S^3$. ([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]])

[F2] The degree map from $\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])$ to $(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism, and two based circle loops are homotopic exactly when they have equal degree. ([[thm-fundamental-group-of-the-circle]])

## Proof

1.1 At each point of $K$, the inward unit vector in $T F$ perpendicular to $T K$ is a smooth nonzero normal vector. The orientation of $S^3$, the orientation of $K$, and the metric orient the normal plane; its positive quarter-turn supplies a smooth second unit vector. These vectors give an oriented orthonormal frame of the normal plane along all of $K$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Normalize any nonzero normal field to unit length and express it in this reference frame as $(\cos 2\pi\theta(p),\sin 2\pi\theta(p))$. This defines a map $r:K\to S^1$. The frame identifies homotopies through nonzero normal fields exactly with free homotopies of these circle maps, since normalization is continuous and the frame is defined at every point. [step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 Fix a point of $K$. Any free loop $r$ can be made based by a constant rotation of the target sending its value at that point to $1$; the rotation is homotopic to the identity because $S^1$ is path-connected. By [F2], based homotopy classes are classified by degree and every integer occurs. Undoing the constant rotations shows that free homotopy classes are also classified by degree. Therefore the winding parameter is a bijection to $\mathbb Z$, and multiplication by the degree-$n$ loop adds $n$, giving a free transitive twist action. [F2, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume AC and Countable Choice. Fix $\alpha,\beta,p,L>0$. For each $0<\epsilon<1/e^{\alpha+p}$, use the centered Gaussian Borel prior on $\ell^2$ with independent coordinates $\theta_j\sim N(0,e^{-2\alpha j})$, independent of the observation noise. Under the fixed-truth law, observe $Y_j=e^{-pj}\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$ with independent $N(0,1)$ noise and a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger$ in the exponential ellipsoid $\{\theta\in\ell^2:\sum_{j\ge1}e^{2\beta j}(\theta_j)^2\le L^2\}$. Then the posterior contracts in the $\ell^2$ norm at rate $r_\epsilon=\epsilon^{\min(\alpha,\beta)/(\alpha+p)}$, meaning that for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$ the expected posterior mass outside radius $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ tends to zero as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model|The sequence inverse experiment uses positive singular values and product-Borel observations.]]

[[def-ip-posterior-contraction-rate|The rate means expected posterior tail convergence for every diverging multiplier under the fixed-truth data law.]]

[[thm-ip-conjugate-gaussian-sequence-contraction|The exact posterior moment formula supplies the bias, sampling variance, and posterior variance terms.]]

[Ding and Mathé, *Minimax rates for statistical inverse problems under general source conditions*, §3 and Table 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.01706)

[Johnstone, *Gaussian estimation: Sequence and wavelet models*, §2.3](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jbradic/math281a/Johnstone.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; $\alpha,\beta,p,L>0$; $0<\epsilon<1/e^{\alpha+p}$; the exponential ellipsoid and independent Gaussian prior in the Example; and the exact posterior moment formula for the coordinate model.

[A1] AC is the declared assumption for the Gaussian product posterior construction. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] Countable Choice is inherited from the compact-SVD sequence model. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The posterior coordinate mean and variance are $\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and $v_j$, and the expected posterior squared error is the displayed nonnegative sum; posterior tail mass is bounded by that sum divided by the squared radius. [[thm-ip-conjugate-gaussian-sequence-contraction]]

[F2] A rate is established when expected posterior mass outside every diverging multiple tends to zero under the fixed-truth law. [[def-ip-posterior-contraction-rate]]

[F3] The Gaussian sequence inverse model has $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$, positive singular values, product-Borel observations, and independent standard-normal noise coordinates. [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]

[F4] For positive bases, real powers obey $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$ and the exponent laws; the natural logarithm is the inverse of the exponential and $\log 1=0$, so $\log e=1$ and $\exp(0)=1$. [[def-real-power]], [[thm-real-power-laws]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

[F5] The exponential is positive, strictly increasing, tends to infinity at infinity, and obeys $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$. [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]], [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[F6] If $0<r<1$, the geometric series $\sum_{k\ge0}r^k$ converges to $(1-r)^{-1}$. [[thm-geometric-series]]

[F7] The canonical real square-summable sequence space $H=\ell^2$ is complete, hence a real Hilbert space. Positive-index coordinates are identified with the $\mathbb N_0$-indexed sequence space by the isometry $(x_j)_{j\ge1}\mapsto(x_{n+1})_{n\ge0}$. [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]] The set of finite-support sequences with rational coordinates is countable and dense: truncate any square-summable sequence so the tail norm is arbitrarily small, then approximate the finitely many retained coordinates by rationals. Hence $H$ is separable. For the diagonal covariance, positivity and self-adjointness follow from $\langle\Gamma x,x\rangle=\sum_j\tau_j^2x_j^2\ge0$ and $\langle\Gamma x,y\rangle=\langle x,\Gamma y\rangle$. Finite-rank truncations converge in operator norm, so $\Gamma$ is compact; its diagonal rank-one expansion has nuclear sum $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$, so it is trace class. [[thm-hilbert-space-with-a-given-orthonormal-basis-is-ell-two-of-the-index-set]], [[def-separable-space]], [[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]], [[thm-norm-limit-of-compact-operators-is-compact]], [[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]]

[F8] A positive self-adjoint trace-class covariance on a separable real Hilbert space defines a Borel centered Hilbert-valued Gaussian random element with that covariance. [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]]

[F9] A finite vector is multivariate normal when all its linear projections are normal. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F10] Finite jointly Gaussian blocks with zero cross-covariance are independent, including for singular covariance matrices. [[lem-uncorrelated-jointly-gaussian-blocks-are-independent]]

[F11] The notation $N(m,\sigma^2)$ denotes the law of a normal variable with mean $m$ and variance $\sigma^2$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

[F12] For positive bases, $a>1$ makes $x\mapsto a^x$ increasing, $0<a<1$ makes it decreasing, and for $t>0$ the map $a\mapsto a^t$ is increasing while $a\mapsto a^{-t}$ is decreasing, since $a^{-t}=1/a^t$. For $0<\epsilon<1$, $\log\epsilon<0$, so $u\ge v$ implies $\epsilon^u\le\epsilon^v$. Finally, for $\eta>0$ and any $M>0$, if $0<\epsilon<\exp(-M/\eta)$ then $\eta\log\epsilon<-M$, so $\epsilon^\eta<\exp(-M)$; the latter tends to zero as $M\to\infty$. These follow from [F4] and [F5]: $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, $\log$ and $\exp$ are strictly increasing, $\log1=0$, and $\exp(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$. [[def-real-power]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Example and facts [A1], [F1]–[F12].

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Example and facts [A1], [A2], [F1]–[F12].

1.1 Let $H=\ell^2$ with standard basis $(e_j)$ and set $\tau_j^2=e^{-2\alpha j}$. Since $e=\exp(1)$, real-power definition and logarithm inversion give $e^{-2\alpha}=\exp(-2\alpha)$; strict increase, positivity and $\exp(0)=1$ imply $0<e^{-2\alpha}<1$. By the exponent laws, $\tau_j^2=(e^{-2\alpha})^j$, so [F6] gives $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$. Define $\Gamma e_j=\tau_j^2e_j$. It is positive and self-adjoint; its truncations $\Gamma_N$ have finite rank, and $\|\Gamma-\Gamma_N\|\le\sup_{j>N}\tau_j^2\le\sum_{j>N}\tau_j^2\to0$, so [F7] makes $\Gamma$ compact. The expansion $\Gamma x=\sum_j\langle x,\tau_j^2e_j\rangle e_j$ has nuclear sum $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$, so [F7] also makes it trace class. By [F8] there is a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G$ in $H$ with covariance $\Gamma$. For each finite coordinate vector, every linear projection is centered normal by [F8], hence it is jointly Gaussian by [F9]; its covariance matrix is diagonal with entries $\tau_j^2$. Repeatedly applying [F10] to the first coordinate and the remaining block proves that the coordinates are independent, and [F11] identifies their laws as $N(0,\tau_j^2)$. Thus the law of $G$ is the stated prior on $\ell^2$. [A1, A2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Put $q=\alpha+p$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, let $J$ be the largest positive integer with $e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon$. Since $q>0$, the exponential is increasing and unbounded, so $J$ exists and $J\to\infty$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Maximality gives $e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon<e^q e^{qJ}$, hence $e^{-q}/\epsilon<e^{qJ}\le1/\epsilon$. The posterior variance satisfies $v_j\le\min\{e^{-2\alpha j},\epsilon^2e^{2pj}\}$. Reversing the finite geometric sum for $j\le J$ and summing the tail gives $\sum_{j\ge1}v_j\le C_{\alpha,p}(\epsilon^2e^{2pJ}+e^{-2\alpha J})\le C'_{\alpha,p}\epsilon^{2\alpha/q}$. For the first term, $e^{2pJ}=(e^{qJ})^{2p/q}\le\epsilon^{-2p/q}$ by positive-power order; for the second, $e^{qJ}>e^{-q}/\epsilon$ gives $e^{-2\alpha J}<e^{2\alpha}\epsilon^{2\alpha/q}$ by exponent order. [F4, F5, F6, F12, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Write $b_j=1-\lambda_j=\epsilon^2/(\epsilon^2+e^{-2qj})\le\min\{1,\epsilon^2e^{2qj}\}$. The truth ellipsoid implies $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le L^2\sup_j b_j^2e^{-2\beta j}$. For $j\le J$, this is bounded coordinatewise by $\epsilon^4e^{(4q-2\beta)j}$; its maximum is at $J$ if $\beta\le2q$, and then is at most $\epsilon^4(e^{qJ})^{4-2\beta/q}\le\epsilon^{2\beta/q}$. If $\beta>2q$, the exponent is negative and the maximum is at $j=1$, bounded by a constant times $\epsilon^4$. For $j>J$, the source weight gives $b_j^2e^{-2\beta j}\le e^{-2\beta J}=(e^{qJ})^{-2\beta/q}\le e^{2\beta}\epsilon^{2\beta/q}$. Thus the squared-bias term is at most $C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{\min\{2\beta/q,4\}}$. The exponent-order comparisons use $e>1$, [F12], and $0<\epsilon<1$. [F3, F4, F5, F12, given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Since $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j\le1$, one has $v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2=v_j\lambda_j\le v_j$. Combining [F1] with steps 1.2–2.1 gives $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{2\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/q}$. To see the exponent comparison, put $\delta=\min\{2\beta/q,4\}$. If $\beta\le\alpha$, then $\delta=2\beta/q\le2\alpha/q$. If $\beta>\alpha$, then $\delta>2\alpha/q$, because $2\beta/q>2\alpha/q$ and $4>2\alpha/q$ (as $\alpha<q$). Since $0<\epsilon<e^{-q}<1$, [F12] shows that the sum of the bias bound $O(\epsilon^\delta)$ and variance bound $O(\epsilon^{2\alpha/q})$ is $O(\epsilon^{2\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/q})$. Set $\eta=\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/q>0$. Then [F12] gives $r_\epsilon=\epsilon^\eta\to0$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. [F1] bounds the expected posterior tail outside $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ by $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$. By [F2], this is the claimed posterior contraction rate. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F4, F12, given, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\Lambda_q^{\rm NL}$ be the small-data nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann map for $-\Delta_g u+qu^3=0$. For smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$, let $v_j$ be the harmonic solution with boundary value $h_j$. If
$$w_{123}=\left.\partial_{\epsilon_1}\partial_{\epsilon_2}\partial_{\epsilon_3}u_\epsilon\right|_{\epsilon=0},$$
where $u_\epsilon$ has boundary value $\epsilon_1h_1+\epsilon_2h_2+\epsilon_3h_3$, then
$$-\Delta_gw_{123}+6qv_1v_2v_3=0,\qquad w_{123}|_{\partial M}=0,$$
and
$$\left\langle (D^3\Lambda_q^{\rm NL})_0[h_1,h_2,h_3],h_4\right\rangle =6\int_Mq\,v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g.$$

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-cubic-dn-small-data-differentiability|Small-data cubic solution and DN map differentiability]]

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Boundary normal derivative and pairing]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the small-data differentiability supplier [F1] and nonresonant regularity supplier [F2].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the small-data differentiability supplier [F1] and nonresonant regularity supplier [F2].

**Given:** the data in the statement and the finite-parameter solution family from the small-data lemma.

[F1] [[lem-ip-cubic-dn-small-data-differentiability]]: for every finite list of smooth boundary directions, the small solution and nonlinear DN data depend $C^3$ on the real parameters $\epsilon_j$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity]]: the zero-Dirichlet Laplacian has a unique weak inverse and smooth data yield smooth solutions.

[F3] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: the smooth Schrödinger DN convention is the outward normal derivative, and the boundary pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.

[F4] [[def-riemannian-volume-density]] and [[def-laplace-beltrami-operator-as-trace-of-the-hessian]]: integration by parts for $\Delta_g$ is performed with the positive density $dV_g$ and outward boundary density $dS_g$.

[F5] [[thm-sobolev-gauss-green-formula-on-c-one-domains]]: on a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain, integration by parts for smooth functions has the outward-normal boundary term; the Riemannian identity follows chartwise from the coordinate divergence formula and positive volume density.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Differentiate $-\Delta_g u_\epsilon+q u_\epsilon^3=0$ once in $\epsilon_j$ at $\epsilon=0$. Since $u_0=0$, the derivative $v_j=\partial_{\epsilon_j}u_\epsilon|_0$ solves $-\Delta_gv_j=0$ with trace $h_j$. Differentiating twice in distinct parameters gives $-\Delta_g(\partial_{\epsilon_i}\partial_{\epsilon_j}u_\epsilon|_0)=0$ with zero trace, so this second derivative vanishes by [F2]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 The third mixed derivative of $u_\epsilon^3$ at zero has exactly the six permutations of $v_1v_2v_3$, hence equals $6v_1v_2v_3$; all other chain-rule terms contain $u_0$ or one of the vanishing second derivatives from step 1.1. Differentiating the equation gives $-\Delta_gw_{123}+6qv_1v_2v_3=0$, with zero boundary trace. By [F1], the third derivative of the nonlinear DN data is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}w_{123}|_{\partial M}$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Since $v_4$ is harmonic and $w_{123}$ has zero trace, chartwise Green's formula and a finite partition of unity give
$$\int_{\partial M}(\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}w_{123})\overline{h_4}\,dS_g =\int_M(\Delta_gw_{123})\overline{v_4}\,dV_g.$$
Indeed, the second Green identity has boundary term $w_{123}\partial_{\nu}\overline{v_4}$ equal to zero, and interior term $w_{123}\Delta_g\overline{v_4}=0$. In each boundary chart, write $\Delta_g w=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i(|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}\partial_jw)$ and apply [F5] to the coordinate components; summing with the finite partition leaves the displayed Riemannian boundary integral by [F4]. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 The equation in step 1.2 gives $\Delta_gw_{123}=6qv_1v_2v_3$. Substituting this into step 2.1 and using the definition of the third DN derivative proves the displayed identity. [F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On the unit sphere $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$ with height $h(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=x_4$, let $c$ be a regular value and let $a$ be a smooth properly embedded arc in the upper ball $B_+=\{x_4\ge c\}$, with endpoints on $S_c=\{x_4=c\}$, such that $h|_a$ has exactly one nondegenerate interior maximum and no other critical point. For every simple smooth arc $\beta\subset S_c$ joining those endpoints, there is an embedded disk in $B_+$ with boundary $a\cup\beta$. The corresponding statement for one nondegenerate minimum in the lower ball $B_-=\{x_4\le c\}$ also holds.

## Statement references

[[thm-isotopy-extension|Extension of an isotopy of a compact embedded source]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the standard coordinate height on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$, a regular level sphere $S_c$, the upper ball $B_+=\{x_4\ge c\}$, a smooth proper arc $a\subset B_+$ with one nondegenerate maximum and endpoints on $S_c$, and a simple arc $\beta\subset S_c$ with the same endpoints.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The regular level spheres of $h$ are explicitly identified by $\Phi_r:S^2\to S_r$, $\Phi_r(v)=(\sqrt{1-r^2}\,v,r)$ for $-1<r<1$.

[F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a smooth isotopy of embeddings of a compact source into a boundaryless manifold extends to an ambient isotopy. [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

## Proof

**Given:** The upper-ball arc and the hypotheses in the statement.


1.1 Let $m$ be the unique maximum. The two components of $a\setminus\{m\}$ are strictly monotone in height, so each intermediate regular level meets $a$ in exactly two points. In a Morse chart on $a$ near $m$, the height is $h(m)-t^2$; a short level arc joining the two nearby points and the subarc through $m$ bound a small embedded cap disk. Under [F1], the two points on all lower regular levels form a smooth path of distinct ordered pairs in $S^2$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the two-point isotopy of step 1.1, starting at the cap level. The extended sphere isotopy transports the short cap arc through simple arcs on the intervening levels. Their union is an embedded strip because distinct levels are disjoint; adjoining the cap disk gives an embedded disk with boundary $a\cup\beta_0$ for a simple arc $\beta_0\subset S_c$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Let $\gamma_0$ be the initial cap arc on the reference $S^2$, and let $f_r$ be the ambient isotopy from [F2] carrying its endpoint pair to the two intersection points on level $S_r$. The arc $f_c^{-1}(\beta)$ is a simple arc with the same endpoints as $\gamma_0$. Bigon elimination gives an isotopy $g_t$ of $S^2$, fixed at those endpoints, with $g_1(\gamma_0)=f_c^{-1}(\beta)$. Precompose the transported cap arc by $g_{\lambda(r)}$ before applying $f_r$, where $\lambda$ is zero near the cap level and increases smoothly to $1$ at $r=c$. Every $g_t$ fixes the reference endpoints, so the joining arcs still have the required endpoint tracks; at $r=c$ the joining arc is exactly $\beta$. The union of this family with the cap disk is therefore an embedded disk bounded by $a\cup\beta$. Reversing height proves the lower-ball statement. [A1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $0<\epsilon$, let $(s_j)_{j\ge1}$ be the positive singular values in the Gaussian sequence inverse model, and let a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger=(\theta^\dagger_j)_{j\ge1}$ belong to $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$. In particular, if $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$ for a constant $C$ and a positive $r_\epsilon\to0$, then $r_\epsilon$ is a posterior contraction rate in the sense of the preceding definition.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model|The compact-SVD coordinates have a square-summable parameter space, product-Borel data, and normalized observations.]]

[[def-ip-posterior-contraction-rate|A contraction rate is defined by expected posterior mass outside every diverging multiple of the rate tending to zero under the fixed-truth data laws.]]

[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior|Finite Gaussian conditioning gives the scalar posterior mean and variance used coordinatewise.]]

[[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel|Under AC, a consistent countable family of finite Gaussian laws has a probability law on the coordinate cylinder sigma-algebra.]]

[Knapik, van der Vaart, and van Zanten, *Bayesian inverse problems with Gaussian priors*, §§3–4 and §7.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1103.2692)

[Johnstone, *Gaussian estimation: Sequence and wavelet models*, §§1.2 and 2.3](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jbradic/math281a/Johnstone.pdf)

[Ding and Mathé, *Minimax rates for statistical inverse problems under general source conditions*, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.01706)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; the positive-noise Gaussian sequence inverse experiment; a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$; an independent-coordinate Gaussian prior with $\tau_j>0$ and $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$; and prior/noise independence.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] Countable Choice supplies a choice function for every countable family of nonempty sets; this is the branch assumed by the compact-SVD coordinate model. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The Gaussian sequence inverse model has parameter $\theta\in\ell^2$, product-Borel data $Z\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, and coordinates $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j$ with independent standard normal $\xi_j$. Multiplying by $s_j>0$ gives $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$. [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]

[F2] In a finite linear Gaussian model with Gaussian prior $N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and positive-definite observation-noise covariance $\Gamma$, the posterior law is multivariate normal with mean $m_0+C_0A^T(AC_0A^T+\Gamma)^{-1}(y-Am_0)$ and covariance $C_0-C_0A^T(AC_0A^T+\Gamma)^{-1}AC_0$. [[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior]]

[F3] Under AC, a consistent family of finite Gaussian laws on countably many real coordinates has a unique probability law on the product cylinder sigma-algebra. [[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]]

[F4] Independence of random elements is independence of their generated sigma-algebras; the assumed independent prior and noise coordinates give independent coordinate pairs. [[def-independent-random-elements]]

[F5] Finite measures that agree on a generating $\pi$-system and on the whole space agree on its generated sigma-algebra. [[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]]

[F6] A $\pi$-system contained in a Dynkin system has its generated sigma-algebra contained in that Dynkin system. [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]

[F7] Increasing nonnegative measurable functions satisfy convergence of their integrals to the integral of their pointwise limit. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F8] For a nonnegative measurable function $f$ and $t>0$, $\mu\{f\ge t\}\le t^{-1}\int f\,d\mu$. [[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]]

[F9] A posterior contraction rate is defined by the expected fixed-truth posterior tail condition in the Statement. [[def-ip-posterior-contraction-rate]]

[F10] In a jointly multivariate-normal vector, blocks with zero cross-covariance are independent, including when the covariance is singular. [[lem-uncorrelated-jointly-gaussian-blocks-are-independent]]

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement.

1.1 For each fixed coordinate $j$, apply [F2] with one-dimensional prior variance $C_0=\tau_j^2$, observation map $A=s_j$, and noise variance $\Gamma=\epsilon^2$. Then $AC_0A^T+\Gamma=s_j^2\tau_j^2+\epsilon^2>0$, and [F2] gives posterior mean $\tau_j^2s_jY_j/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and variance $\tau_j^2-\tau_j^4s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=v_j$. [A1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For every finite coordinate set $J$, the prior/noise pairs indexed by $J$ are independent of the pairs outside $J$: independence of the prior element from the noise element and independence within each coordinate family factor the probabilities of finite coordinate rectangles into the product of the pair marginals, and [F5] extends this factorization from the generating rectangles to the corresponding product-Borel events. Each $Y_j$ is a measurable function of its pair $(\theta_j,\xi_j)$, so $(\theta_J,Y_J)$ is independent of $Y_{J^c}$. For the finite block, put $D_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_j^2)_{j\in J}$ and $D_s=\operatorname{diag}(s_j)_{j\in J}$. [F2] gives posterior covariance
$$D_\tau-D_\tau D_s^T(D_sD_\tau D_s^T+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}D_sD_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(v_j)_{j\in J},$$
and posterior mean with coordinates $\lambda_jY_j/s_j$. Since each $v_j>0$, the Gaussian coordinates have zero cross-covariance, and repeated application of [F10] shows they are independent. Thus the finite-block conditional law is the product of the scalar laws from step 1.1. Independence of the complement makes this also the conditional law given the full data: the conditional identity first holds on data rectangles by finite-block conditioning and independence, and [F5] extends it to all product-Borel data events. The product Gaussian law $Q_y=\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jy_j/s_j,v_j)$ exists on $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ by [F3]. On finite-coordinate cylinders its evaluations are Borel functions of $y$; the class of Borel sets $B$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(B)$ is measurable is a Dynkin system containing the generating cylinder $\pi$-system, so [F6] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. The same finite-block conditional identity holds on data cylinders, and [F5] applied successively in the data and parameter coordinates extends it to all product-Borel events. Thus $Q_y$ is the prior-predictive conditional law on the product coordinate space. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F10, given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Put $m_j(y)=\lambda_jy_j/s_j$ and $Y_0=\{y:\sum_jm_j(y)^2<\infty\}$. This is Borel because each $m_j$ is coordinate-measurable and $\ell^2=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:\sum_{j=1}^Nx_j^2\le k\}$. Since $v_j\le\tau_j^2$, [F7] gives $\int\sum_jx_j^2\,Q_y(dx)=\sum_j(m_j(y)^2+v_j)<\infty$ on $Y_0$, so $Q_y(\ell^2)=1$ there. Under the prior-predictive law, $\mathbb E m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2\tau_j^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=\lambda_j\tau_j^2\le\tau_j^2$; under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)=\lambda_j\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$ and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2\le(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\tau_j^2$. Applying [F7] to the partial sums shows $Y_0$ has full measure under both laws. Restrict $Q_y$ to $\ell^2$ on $Y_0$ and set it equal to $\delta_0$ outside $Y_0$; this is a posterior version on $\ell^2$ and is defined for fixed-truth-almost every observation. [A1, A2, F3, F6, F7, given, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 For $y\in Y_0$, the product posterior has coordinate mean $m_j(y)$ and variance $v_j$, so its expected squared coordinate error is $(m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j$. The partial sums of these nonnegative errors increase to $\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$; [F7] therefore gives $\int\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid y)=\sum_j((m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j)$, with the value $+\infty$ allowed. [F7, given, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger=-(1-\lambda_j)\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$. The noise has mean zero and variance one, so its cross term has expectation zero and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}(m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2=(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2$. The identity $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j$ gives $\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2$. Taking expectations in step 4.1 and applying [F7] to the nonnegative partial sums proves the displayed exact series identity. [F1, F7, given, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For each fixed data sequence, apply [F8] to the posterior probability measure with $f(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$ and threshold $R^2>0$. This gives posterior tail mass at most $R^{-2}$ times the posterior second moment. Taking fixed-truth expectation and using step 5.1 yields the stated bound. If $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$, substitute $R=M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ to obtain expected tail mass at most $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$; [F9] identifies $r_\epsilon$ as a posterior contraction rate. [F8, F9, step 5.1, given, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

At $s_j=\tau_j=\epsilon=1$, the coordinate posterior is $N(Y_j/2,1/2)$ and the prior-predictive law of $Y_j$ is $N(0,2)$. The finite check of this one-coordinate case does not test the infinite product or the $\ell^2$ support argument.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain whose Euclidean metric is isometric to the product metric $dx_1^2\oplus g_0$ on a compact subdomain of $\mathbb R\times D^\circ$, where $(D,g_0)$ is a compact connected simple Riemannian surface with smooth boundary. Let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive. If their full physical scalar conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree on every boundary datum, then $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ in $\overline\Omega$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full physical scalar conductivity DN map]]

[[lem-ip-conductivity-liouville-transform-and-dn-conjugacy|Liouville potential and boundary conjugacy]]

[[thm-ip-boundary-determination-of-scalar-conductivity|Equality of all boundary conductivity jets]]

[[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform|Simple transversal surface convention]]

[[thm-ip-euclidean-schrodinger-calderon-uniqueness|Euclidean Schrödinger full-data uniqueness]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the boundary determination and Euclidean potential uniqueness suppliers [F1]--[F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the boundary determination and Euclidean potential uniqueness suppliers [F1]--[F3].

**Given:** the Euclidean CTA product domain, a compact simple transversal surface, two positive smooth conductivities, and equality of their full physical DN maps.

[F1] [[thm-ip-boundary-determination-of-scalar-conductivity]]: equal full conductivity DN maps imply equality of every inward boundary-normal derivative of the two conductivities.

[F2] [[lem-ip-conductivity-liouville-transform-and-dn-conjugacy]]: for $\rho_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$, $q_j=\Delta_g\rho_j/\rho_j$, the conductivity equation is conjugated by $u=\rho_jv$ to $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u=0$, and $\Lambda_{\gamma_j}f=\rho_{j,b}\Lambda_{q_j}(\rho_{j,b}f)-\rho_{j,b}(\partial_\nu\rho_j)f$.

[F3] [[thm-ip-euclidean-schrodinger-calderon-uniqueness]]: on a bounded smooth Euclidean domain in dimension at least three, equality of the full Schrödinger DN maps for real smooth nonresonant potentials implies equality of the potentials.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 By [F1], all boundary-normal jets of $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ agree, so the boundary values and first normal derivatives of $\rho_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$ agree. Put $q_j=\Delta_g\rho_j/\rho_j$. Their Liouville boundary relations in [F2], together with $\Lambda_{\gamma_1}=\Lambda_{\gamma_2}$, now give $\Lambda_{q_1}g=\Lambda_{q_2}g$ for every $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$: substitute $f=g/\rho_b$ into the physical-flux relation, using the common positive boundary value $\rho_b$ and common $\partial_\nu\rho_j$. Multiplication and division by smooth positive $\rho_b$ preserve $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Each $q_j$ is nonresonant. If $w\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)w=0$, then $v=w/\rho_j\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solves $-\operatorname{div}(\gamma_j\nabla v)=0$ by [F2]. Testing weakly with $\overline v$ gives $\int_\Omega\gamma_j|\nabla v|^2dx=0$. Positivity of $\gamma_j$ implies $v=0$, hence $w=0$. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The domain is bounded and smooth in $\mathbb R^3$, the potentials are real and smooth, both operators are nonresonant by step 1.2, and their full Schrödinger DN maps agree by step 1.1. Thus [F3] applies and yields $q_1=q_2=:q$ in $\Omega$. [A1, A2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 Each $\rho_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q)\rho_j=0$ and the two functions have the same boundary value by step 1.1. Their difference is a zero-trace solution of the nonresonant operator from step 1.2, hence vanishes. Therefore $\rho_1=\rho_2$ and $\gamma_1=\rho_1^2=\rho_2^2=\gamma_2$ in $\Omega$; continuity extends this equality to $\overline\Omega$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_2(0,\operatorname{diag}(4,1))$,
$\eta\sim N_2(0,\operatorname{diag}(1,4))$ independently, $A=I_2$, and
observe $y=(2,4)^T$ in $Y=AX+\eta$. Put
$L=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$ and
$W=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/2)$. The coordinate change $x=Lz$ makes the
prior on $z$ standard Gaussian, and $W$ whitens the observation noise in
that $W\Gamma W^T=I_2$. The
preconditioned Tikhonov objective is
$$ \|WALz-Wy\|_2^2+\|z\|_2^2 =\|\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2)z-(2,2)^T\|_2^2+\|z\|_2^2. $$
The posterior mean, MAP point, and minimizer in the original parameter
coordinates are $(8/5,4/5)^T$, and the posterior covariance is
$(4/5)I_2$.

## Example references

[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior|The posterior formula handles general positive-definite observation covariance.]]

[[cor-ip-gaussian-map-equals-tikhonov-minimizer|Prior whitening gives the support-coordinate Tikhonov objective whose unique minimizer is the MAP and posterior mean.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the model and datum in the Example.

[A1] AC is inherited from the Gaussian-law and finite Gaussian-conditioning
interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The finite linear Gaussian posterior formula is valid for singular or
positive-definite prior covariance and positive-definite noise covariance.
[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior]]

[F2] The finite Gaussian MAP and posterior mean equal the support-restricted
Tikhonov minimizer. [[cor-ip-gaussian-map-equals-tikhonov-minimizer]]

[F3] For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov objective is
$\|Dz-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|z\|_2^2$, with unique minimizer
$(D^TD+\lambda I)^{-1}D^Tb$. [[def-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares]],
[[thm-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares-has-a-unique-minimiser]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses and facts in the Example and Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Here $S=C_0+\Gamma=5I_2$, so [F1] gives $m(y)=C_0S^{-1}y=(8/5,4/5)^T$ and $C(y)=C_0-C_0S^{-1}C_0=(4/5)I_2$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The whitening matrices satisfy $W\Gamma W^T=I_2$ and $D=WAL=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2)$, while $b=Wy=(2,2)^T$. Applying [F3] with $\lambda=1$ gives $\widehat z=(D^TD+I_2)^{-1}D^Tb=(4/5,4/5)^T$.
