## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\gamma>0$. There is a constant $C_P>0$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|\nabla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv,\nabla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain|Fixed-atlas Sobolev and trace spaces]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; this is assumed by the Rellich, trace-right-inverse, higher-order regularity, and Sobolev embedding suppliers.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; this is assumed by the Lax--Milgram, partition, and collar suppliers.

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; the compact connected smooth Riemannian domain and positive smooth conductivity in the statement; and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: $H^1(M)$ is defined by finitely many chartwise $W^{1,2}$ norms, and $H_0^1(M)$ is the $H^1$ closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$.

[F2] [[thm-rellich-compactness-from-w-one-p-zero-to-lp]]: on a bounded Euclidean open set, $W_0^{1,2}$ is compactly embedded in $L^2$.

[F3] [[thm-lax-milgram]]: a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on a Hilbert space has a unique weak solution.

[F4] [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]: on a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain, the trace is a bounded operator from $H^1$ to $L^2$ and agrees with restriction for smooth functions; therefore every class in the closure $H_0^1$ has zero trace.

[F5] [[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace]]: on a bounded smooth Euclidean domain, every $H^{1/2}$ boundary datum has an $H^1$ extension; after localization this supplies boundary-chart extensions on $M$.

[F6] [[thm-higher-order-boundary-regularity-for-dirichlet-problems]]: a zero-trace weak solution of a smooth uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation on a bounded smooth Euclidean domain gains two Sobolev derivatives when its right-hand side has the corresponding Sobolev regularity.

[F7] [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]]: membership in every chartwise integer Sobolev space gives a smooth representative up to the boundary.

[F8] [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]: smooth boundary data extend smoothly into a collar by constant normal extension and a cutoff.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement, including $h\in L^2(M)$.

1.1 There is a constant $C_P$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(M)}$ for $w\in H_0^1(M)$. Otherwise choose $w_j\in H_0^1(M)$ with $\|w_j\|_{L^2}=1$ and $\|\nabla w_j\|_{L^2}\to0$. The sequence is bounded in $H^1$. A finite chart partition and [F2] give an $L^2$-convergent subsequence; a further subsequence converges weakly in the Hilbert space $H^1$, so its limit $w$ belongs to the weakly closed subspace $H_0^1(M)$, has weak gradient zero, and has $L^2$ norm one. In each connected coordinate ball, convolution of a function with zero weak gradient is constant on smaller balls; overlapping balls force the constants to agree, so connectedness makes $w$ constant on $M^\circ$. Its trace is zero by [F4], whereas the trace of a nonzero constant is that same nonzero constant on the nonempty boundary. This contradiction proves the inequality. [A1, F1, F2, F4, given, contradiction]

2.1 Compactness of $M$ and positivity of $\gamma$ give $\gamma_*:=\min_M\gamma>0$. Thus $a_\gamma(w,z)=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)\,dV_g$ is bounded on $H_0^1(M)$ and $a_\gamma(w,w)\geq c\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2$ by step 1.1 and $\gamma_*$. By [F3], for any bounded conjugate-linear functional $G$ on $H_0^1(M)$ there is a unique $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with $a_\gamma(w,z)=G(z)$ for all $z$. [A2, F1, F3, step 1.1, given]

2.2 Flatten each boundary chart, apply the local half-space trace lift, and patch the finitely many chart lifts with a smooth partition. The resulting $Ef\in H^1(M)$ has trace $f$ and norm bounded by $C\|f\|_{H^{1/2}(\partial M)}$ by [F5]. For $h\in L^2(M)$ take $G(z)=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g-a_\gamma(Ef,z)$ in step 2.1 and set $v=Ef+w$. Then $v$ has trace $f$ and satisfies the weak equation. If $v_1,v_2$ are two such solutions, their difference $w$ lies in $H_0^1$ and $a_\gamma(w,w)=0$; since $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, $\nabla w=0$, and step 1.1 gives $w=0$. [A1, A2, F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $h$ and $f$ are smooth. By [F8], extend $f$ smoothly from the boundary into a collar and multiply by a cutoff to obtain a smooth extension $Ef$ on $M$. Then $w=v-Ef$ has zero trace and solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gw)=h-\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gEf)$, whose right-hand side is smooth. In each boundary chart, flatten the boundary and write the principal matrix as $|g|^{1/2}\gamma g^{ij}$; it is smooth and uniformly elliptic because $g$ is positive definite and $\gamma$ has a positive minimum. For the base case, localize $w$ by a cutoff; its equation has an $L^2$ right-hand side since $w\in H^1$, so [F6] gives local $H^2$ regularity. If $w\in H^{m+1}$, each cutoff commutator contains derivatives of $w$ of order at most $m+1$ with smooth bounded coefficients, hence lies in $H^m$; the localized right-hand side is therefore in $H^m$, and [F6] gives $H^{m+2}$ regularity. Induction over $m$ and a finite chart cover give $w\in H^m(M)$ for every integer $m$. By [F7], $w$ and hence $v=Ef+w$ are smooth up to the boundary. [A1, A2, F1, F6, F7, F8, step 2.2, induction, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $L$ be a nonempty oriented $r$-component link with $r\ge1$ and maximal-abelian-cover module $A_L$ over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. Then $A_L$ is finitely presented, every elementary/Fitting ideal $E_j(A_L)$ is independent of the chosen finite triangulation and of the chosen lifts of its cells, and the order $\operatorname{ord}(A_L)$—the greatest common divisor of the generators of $E_q(A_L)$, where $q=\dim_{\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)}(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r))$—is defined up to a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. The diagonal ring map $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, $t_i\mapsto t$, specializes the lifted chain complex by coefficient extension to the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex. This statement concerns the chain complex only; it does not identify $A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ with the first homology of the specialized complex. For $r\ge2$, the diagonal map is nonflat and such an identification need not hold because homology need not commute with nonflat base change.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a nonempty oriented $r$-component link $L$ with $r\ge1$; its maximal-abelian-cover module $A_L$; $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$; a basepoint $b\in E_L$, and the first Hurewicz map $\phi_E:\pi_1(E_L,b)\to H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$.

[A1] AC, as assumed by the link-complement and one-variable-cover suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The maximal-abelian-cover module is $A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$ with its $\Lambda_r$ deck action ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] The ring $\Lambda_r$ is Noetherian and a UFD, with units exactly signed Laurent monomials ([[lem-multivariable-laurent-ring-noetherian-ufd]]).

[F3] For a finitely presented module, the $j$th elementary ideal is the ideal generated by all minors of the prescribed size in a finite presentation matrix ([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]).

[F4] For every commutative ring and finitely presented module, each elementary ideal is independent of the finite presentation and invariant under module isomorphism ([[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]]).

[F5] A finite CW structure on $E_L$ lifts to a finite-rank free $\Lambda_r$ cellular chain complex whose first homology is $A_L$ ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-cellular-chain-model]]).

[F6] The one-variable Alexander module is first homology of the cover classified by total linking, whose defining map sums the Alexander-dual meridian coordinates ([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]).

[F7] Connected covers are classified by their induced fundamental-group subgroups ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]).

[F8] The maximal abelian cover deformation retracts equivariantly onto the restricted compact-exterior cover ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]).

[F9] A connected regular cover has deck group the quotient of its fundamental group by the induced subgroup ([[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write the lifted finite free complex from [F5] as $C_2\xrightarrow{d_2}C_1\xrightarrow{d_1}C_0$. Since $\Lambda_r$ is Noetherian by [F2], every submodule of a finite free module is finitely generated: induct on the rank $n$ of $\Lambda_r^n$; project a submodule $N$ to the first coordinate, choose lifts of finitely many generators of its image ideal, and apply the induction hypothesis to the kernel in $\Lambda_r^{n-1}$. Thus $Z_1=\ker d_1$ is finitely generated, and $B_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$ is generated by the finitely many columns of $d_2$. The quotient $A_L=Z_1/B_1$ is finitely generated. Choose a surjection $\Lambda_r^m\to A_L$ with finite $m$; its kernel is a submodule of $\Lambda_r^m$ and hence finitely generated by the same argument. This is a finite presentation of $A_L$. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given, construct]

1.2 Use the resulting finite presentation to define each $E_j(A_L)$ as in [F3]. Any other triangulation of the same marked exterior lifts to another CW structure on the same topological cover; [F5] identifies the homology of either lifted cellular complex with the same singular module $A_L$, and the deck action in both identifications is the same. A different lift of a cell multiplies its basis element by a deck monomial, also leaving the resulting singular module unchanged. Hence the modules computed from the two choices are isomorphic. By [F4] all their elementary ideals agree. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

2.1 Put $K=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)$ and $q=\dim_K(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}K)$. For a finite presentation matrix with $n$ target generators, tensoring with $K$ shows its rank is $n-q$. Therefore at least one $(n-q)\times(n-q)$ minor is nonzero (with the empty minor equal to $1$ when $n=q$), so $E_q(A_L)\ne0$. This ideal has finitely many generators by its finite presentation, and in the UFD [F2] their gcd exists and is unique up to a unit. Since [F4] makes the ideal presentation-independent, the gcd is well-defined up to a unit of $\Lambda_r$, which by [F2] is $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\bar\eta:H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ be the total-linking map. By [F1] the positive meridians are the coordinate basis, so the coordinate-sum definition [F6] sends each one to $1$. Define $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1$ to be its induced ring map $t_i\mapsto t$. By [F7], quotienting the maximal abelian cover of $E_L$ by $\ker\bar\eta$ gives the connected cover classified by $\ker(\bar\eta\circ\phi_E)$; this quotient cover is regular with deck group $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)/\ker\bar\eta\cong\mathbb Z$ by [F9]. The equivariant deformation retraction [F8] descends to a deformation retraction of this quotient cover onto the corresponding quotient of the open-complement cover; by [F6] the latter is the one-variable total-linking cover. For every lifted cell orbit, tensoring its free rank-one $\Lambda_r$ summand with $\Lambda_1$ along $\eta$ identifies the quotient-orbit generator with a free rank-one $\Lambda_1$ generator, and sends each boundary coefficient to its image under $\eta$. Therefore $C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(E_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ is the cellular chain complex of the total-linking cover of $E_L$. [F1, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, construct]

3.2 Homology does not in general commute with this coefficient extension. For $r=1$, $\eta$ is the identity; for $r\ge2$, consider the finite free chain complex $C_1=\Lambda_r\xrightarrow{\,t_1-t_2\,}C_0=\Lambda_r$ with all other chain groups zero. The ring $\Lambda_r$ is a domain and $t_1-t_2\ne0$, so $H_1(C_*)=0$. After diagonal base change $\eta$, the differential is multiplication by $t-t=0$, hence $H_1(C_*\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1)=\Lambda_1$, while $H_1(C_*)\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$. The multiplication map $\Lambda_r\xrightarrow{t_1-t_2}\Lambda_r$ is injective before tensoring and becomes the zero map afterward, so $\Lambda_1$ is nonflat over $\Lambda_r$ for $r\ge2$. Thus for $r\ge2$ the chain specialization does not in general identify the specialized chain-complex homology with the tensor product of $A_L$, and no equality of specialized homology orders follows without additional hypotheses. [F2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

For every probability density $p$ on $\mathbb R$ with finite first absolute
moment and at least one global maximizer, every maximum a posteriori (MAP)
point, meaning every global maximizer of $p$, equals its mean
$\int_{\mathbb R}t\,p(t)\,dt$.

## Statement references

[[cor-ip-gaussian-map-equals-tikhonov-minimizer|The Gaussian result has explicit prior, likelihood, support, and quadratic-posterior hypotheses.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a prior uniform on $[0,1]$; independent standard-normal
observation noise; and the observation model in the Counterexample.

[A1] AC is assumed by the standard-normal law. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The standard-normal noise has a strictly positive Gaussian density.
[[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]],
[[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F2] A normalized potential update is the prior reweighted by its likelihood
and divided by its evidence when the evidence is positive and finite.
[[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F3] The equality of MAP, posterior mean, and support-restricted Tikhonov
minimizer proved for the finite Gaussian model uses Gaussian prior and
likelihood assumptions. [[cor-ip-gaussian-map-equals-tikhonov-minimizer]]

## Counterexample

**Given:** Let $\theta$ have the uniform probability density
$\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$ on $\mathbb R$. Independently let
$\epsilon\sim N(0,1)$, observe $Y=\theta+\epsilon$, and condition on $y=0$.
The likelihood potential is $\Phi_0(\theta)=\theta^2/2$ on $[0,1]$ and the
posterior density relative to Lebesgue measure is
$$ p(\theta\mid 0)= \frac{e^{-\theta^2/2}}{\int_0^1 e^{-t^2/2}\,dt}\, \mathbf 1_{[0,1]}(\theta). $$

1.1 The evidence in [F2] is $Z=\int_0^1e^{-t^2/2}\,dt$. Since $e^{-1/2}\le e^{-t^2/2}\le1$ on $[0,1]$, one has $0<e^{-1/2}\le Z\le1$. Thus the displayed normalized posterior density is proper. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 On $(0,1]$, the derivative of $e^{-\theta^2/2}$ is $-\theta e^{-\theta^2/2}<0$. The posterior density vanishes outside $[0,1]$, so its unique global maximizer is $\theta=0$. Its support is the bounded interval $[0,1]$ and it is not a point mass. A nondegenerate one-dimensional Gaussian has a strictly positive density on all of $\mathbb R$ by [F1], whereas a zero-variance Gaussian is a point mass. Therefore this posterior is non-Gaussian. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The posterior mean is $$ \frac{\int_0^1 t e^{-t^2/2}\,dt}{Z} =\frac{1-e^{-1/2}}{Z}>0, $$ which differs from the MAP point $0$. This refutes the universal claim. It also shows why [F3] is restricted to the Gaussian model. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

## Definition references

[[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain|Fixed-atlas Sobolev and trace spaces]]

[[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness|Positive conductivity weak solvability]]

[[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity|Schrodinger weak solvability under nonresonance]]

[[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold|Riemannian volume density]]

[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal|Outward unit normal]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; the compact smooth Riemannian domain; positive smooth $\gamma$; a real smooth nonresonant $q$; and the weak solutions in the Definition.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is assumed by the Euclidean trace-kernel and Gauss-Green suppliers [F2, F5].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed by the local weak-solution, trace-lift, and collar suppliers [F3, F4, F6, F8].

[F1] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: $H_0^1(M)$ is the closure of interior compactly supported smooth functions in a fixed finite chartwise $H^1$ norm; the trace is defined chartwise and the fixed finite atlas admits a smooth partition of unity.

[F2] [[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero]]: on a bounded Euclidean $C^1$ domain, an $H^1$ function has zero trace if and only if it belongs to the $H^1$ closure of compactly supported interior smooth functions.

[F3] [[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness]]: for each $H^{1/2}$ boundary value, the positive-conductivity weak solution exists uniquely, its weak equation vanishes on every $H_0^1$ test, and smooth boundary data with smooth forcing give a solution smooth up to the boundary.

[F4] [[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity]]: under the stated trivial Dirichlet-kernel condition, the Schrödinger weak solution is unique and smooth for smooth boundary data.

[F5] [[thm-sobolev-gauss-green-formula-on-c-one-domains]]: for smooth functions on a bounded Euclidean $C^1$ domain, integration by parts produces the outward-normal boundary term.

[F6] [[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace]]: each $H^{1/2}$ boundary datum has an $H^1$ extension in a smooth Euclidean chart; finite chart localization supplies such extensions on $M$.

[F7] [[lem-trace-commutes-with-smooth-boundary-cutoffs-and-charts]]: multiplying by a smooth cutoff multiplies the trace by its boundary restriction, and flattening charts transport the trace to the Euclidean chart trace.

[F8] [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]: smooth boundary data extend smoothly into a collar by constant normal extension and a cutoff.

[F9] [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]: the trace is a bounded map on $H^1$ and agrees with restriction for smooth functions.

## Verification

**Given:** the data in the Definition and two $H^1$ extensions $V_h^{(1)},V_h^{(2)}$ of the same boundary datum $h$.

1.1 Their difference $W=V_h^{(1)}-V_h^{(2)}$ has zero trace. Localize $W$ by the fixed finite partition in [F1]. On each boundary chart, [F7] shows that the localized function has zero Euclidean trace after flattening; [F2] then approximates it in $H^1$ by compactly supported interior smooth functions. On interior charts, ordinary compactly supported mollification gives the same approximation. Pulling back and summing the finitely many approximations shows $W\in H_0^1(M)$. [A1, F1, F2, F7, given, construct]

2.1 For the conductivity pairing, [F3] gives $\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline W)\,dV_g=0$, since $W\in H_0^1(M)$. Therefore replacing $V_h^{(1)}$ by $V_h^{(2)}$ changes the displayed pairing by zero. For the Schrödinger pairing, the same argument with the weak equation in [F4] gives $\int_M(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline W)+qu_f\overline W)\,dV_g=0$. Thus both definitions are independent of the chosen extension and are well-defined. [A2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3] and [F4], smooth boundary data yield solutions smooth up to $\partial M$. For smooth test data $h$, choose a smooth collar extension $V_h$ by [F8]. In a boundary chart, write $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv)=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i(|g|^{1/2}\gamma g^{ij}\partial_jv)$ and $\Delta_gu=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i(|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}\partial_ju)$. Apply the Euclidean Gauss-Green identity [F5] to the coordinate fluxes; summing over the finite partition gives the Riemannian boundary flux, while artificial chart boundaries cancel and the density transforms to $dS_g$. For the conductivity equation it yields
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_{\partial M}\gamma\,\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f\,\overline h\,dS_g,$$
since $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$. For the Schrödinger equation it yields
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_{\partial M}\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f\,\overline h\,dS_g,$$
since $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$. The extensions required for the weak pairings exist by [F6], and smooth test extensions exist by [F8]. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Take $\Omega=B_2(0)$, $K=\overline B_1(0)$, $\Theta=\{\theta\in S^1:|\theta_1|<1/2\}$, and $v=(1,0)$. Write $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$ and define $R_\Theta u(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}u(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$ for $\theta\in\Theta$, $s\in\mathbb R$. Give the data space $D=L^2(\Theta\times\mathbb R,d\theta\,ds)$ the norm $\|g\|_D=(\int_\Theta\int_{\mathbb R}|g(\theta,s)|^2\,ds\,d\theta)^{1/2}$, with arc-length measure $d\theta$ and Lebesgue measure $ds$, and define $\|u\|_{H^1}=(\|u\|_2^2+\|\partial_1u\|_2^2+\|\partial_2u\|_2^2)^{1/2}$ using Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$. Then $\Theta$ is open and antipodally symmetric, its complement contains open horizontal arcs, and $\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}|v\cdot\theta^\perp|=\sqrt3/2$. For every $M>0$, the class of smooth functions supported in $K$ with $H^1$ norm at most $M$ has no uniform Hölder stability estimate from the restricted Radon data. More explicitly, choose a real bump $\psi\in C_c^\infty(B_1(0))$ with $\|\psi\|_2=1$, set $\lambda_M=M/[2(1+\|\nabla\psi\|_2+2\pi)]$, and let $u_N(x)=\lambda_MN^{-1}e^{2\pi iNx_1}\psi(x)$ for integers $N\ge1$. These functions have the same compact support, satisfy $\|u_N\|_{H^1}\le M$ and $\|u_N\|_2=\lambda_MN^{-1}$, while for every integer $m\ge1$ there is $C_m<\infty$ with $\|R_\Theta u_N\|_D\le C_mN^{-m-1}$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data|Line-normal and blind-direction conventions]]

[[prop-ip-limited-angle-data-no-holder-stability|High-frequency modulation and the no-Hölder estimate]]

[Venkataswaran P. Krishnan and Eric Todd Quinto, Microlocal Analysis in Tomography, §1.5.1](https://math.tifrbng.res.in/~vkrishnan/Papers/Microlocal_Analysis_Tomography.pdf)

[Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and the stated domain $\Omega$, fixed support $K$, measured normals $\Theta$, direction $v$, and bump $\psi$.

[F1] [[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data]]: $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$ is the unit line tangent, so for $v=(1,0)$ one has $|v\cdot\theta^\perp|=|\theta_2|$.

[F2] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: a smooth bump supported in $B_1(0)$ and equal to one on a smaller ball exists.

[F3] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]: a nondegenerate box has strictly positive Lebesgue measure, so a bump equal to one on a ball has positive $L^2$ norm and can be normalized.

[F4] [[prop-ip-limited-angle-data-no-holder-stability]]: if a fixed-support bump is normalized in $L^2$ and $|v\cdot\theta^\perp|$ is uniformly bounded below on $\Theta$, its modulations $u_N=\lambda N^{-1}e^{2\pi iNv\cdot x}\psi$ have $H^1$ norm bounded by $\lambda(1+\|\nabla\psi\|_2+2\pi)$ and restricted data bounded by $C_mN^{-m-1}$ for every $m$; this is the proposition's proved integration-by-parts estimate.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is used in the box-measure supplier [F3] and in [F4]'s Lebesgue change-of-variables and integration-by-parts estimates.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The set $\Theta$ is the inverse image of the open interval $(-1/2,1/2)$ under the continuous coordinate map $\theta\mapsto\theta_1$, so it is open; changing $\theta$ to $-\theta$ preserves $|\theta_1|$, so it is antipodally symmetric. Its complement contains arcs around $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, $|\theta_2|=\sqrt{1-\theta_1^2}>\sqrt3/2$, hence the infimum is at least $\sqrt3/2$; approaching either boundary $|\theta_1|=1/2$ shows the infimum is exactly $\sqrt3/2$. By [F1] this is $\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}|v\cdot\theta^\perp|$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 A translated or rescaled bump from [F2] has compact support in $B_1(0)$ and equals one on a smaller ball. That inner ball contains a nondegenerate box, which has positive measure by [F3]; compact support makes its $L^2$ norm finite, and the plateau makes the norm positive. Divide by this norm to obtain the required real $\psi$ with $\|\psi\|_2=1$. Since $K=\overline B_1(0)$ lies inside $\Omega=B_2(0)$, its support is contained in the fixed set $K$. [A1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 The formula in the Example is the modulation family in [F4]. The chosen $\lambda_M$ satisfies $\lambda_M(1+\|\nabla\psi\|_2+2\pi)=M/2\le M$, and the geometric verification in step 1.1 supplies the positive lower bound required there. Thus the family has the stated fixed support, $H^1$ and $L^2$ bounds, and rapid restricted-data decay. [F4, A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 If a uniform Hölder estimate with exponent $\alpha>0$ and constant $C\ge0$ held on the fixed-support class, choose an integer $m\ge1$ with $\alpha(m+1)>1$. Step 2.1 would imply $\lambda_MN^{-1}\le C(C_mN^{-m-1})^\alpha$, so $\lambda_M\le CC_m^\alpha N^{1-\alpha(m+1)}\to0$, contradicting $\lambda_M>0$. Therefore no such estimate holds. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. Let $W$ and $X$ be compact manifolds with supplied boundary collars and decompositions $\partial W=A\sqcup D$ and $\partial X=A\sqcup B$, where each summand is a union of boundary components. Glue the two copies of $A$ by a supplied homeomorphism, obtaining $Y=W\cup_A X$ with $\partial Y=D\sqcup B$. All homology below has constant coefficients $R$. Suppose
$$H_1(A;R)\longrightarrow H_1(X;R)\ \text{is injective},\qquad H_2(B;R)\longrightarrow H_2(X;R)\ \text{is surjective}.$$
Then inclusion of $W$ induces a well-defined surjection
$$\frac{H_2(W;R)}{\operatorname{im}H_2(\partial W;R)} \twoheadrightarrow \frac{H_2(Y;R)}{\operatorname{im}H_2(\partial Y;R)}.$$
In particular, if $R$ is a field and the first quotient is finite dimensional, the dimension of the second quotient is at most that of the first. No injectivity assumption on $H_2(A;R)\to H_2(X;R)$, orientability, or choice principle is needed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The manifolds, collars, gluing and coefficient ring in the Statement, and the two homology hypotheses.

[F1] Constant $R$ coefficients are a local system, and an excisive cover gives its homology Mayer–Vietoris sequence. The actual small-chain construction uses only least subdivision integers and finite chain operations. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 The supplied collars give an open cover of $Y$ by a neighborhood of $W$ and a neighborhood of $X$, retracting onto $W,X$, with intersection retracting onto $A$. In collar coordinates this is obtained by adding a short collar segment across the seam to each side; shrinking its height linearly gives the three retractions. Hence [F1] gives the exact window
$$H_2(A;R)\xrightarrow{(i_W,-i_X)} H_2(W;R)\oplus H_2(X;R)\xrightarrow{j_W+j_X} H_2(Y;R)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_1(A;R) \xrightarrow{(i_W,-i_X)}H_1(W;R)\oplus H_1(X;R).$$
The last arrow is injective, since its $X$ coordinate is injective by hypothesis. Exactness therefore says that $j_W+j_X$ is surjective. This statement is elementwise and does not choose a simultaneous family of preimages. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Write $Q_Y=H_2(Y;R)/\operatorname{im}H_2(D\sqcup B;R)$ and let $\pi$ be its quotient map. Every $x\in H_2(X;R)$ is the image of a class in $H_2(B;R)$, by hypothesis. Its image in $H_2(Y;R)$ therefore lies in the boundary image, so $\pi j_X=0$. For any $y\in H_2(Y;R)$ choose, for this one $y$, a preimage $(w,x)$ under the surjection of step 1.1. Then $\pi(y)=\pi j_W(w)$. Thus $\pi j_W:H_2(W;R)\to Q_Y$ is surjective. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 A class from $H_2(D;R)$ maps to zero under $\pi j_W$ because $D$ is a component union of $\partial Y$. A class $a\in H_2(A;R)$ has $j_Wi_W(a)=j_Xi_X(a)$ by the zero composite of the first two Mayer–Vietoris arrows. step 2.1 makes the latter class zero in $Q_Y$. Since $\partial W=A\sqcup D$, every boundary class of $W$ is a sum of these two kinds, so $\pi j_W$ vanishes on the full boundary image. It therefore factors uniquely through the displayed source quotient, and the factored map is surjective by step 2.1. This proves the claimed canonical map, without any assumption on $H_2(A;R)\to H_2(X;R)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If the source quotient is a vector space with a finite basis of size $r$, its $r$ images span the target. Finite elimination deletes linearly dependent images until a basis remains, so the target has dimension at most $r$. Only finitely many operations and selections occur. The proof also covers an empty seam or empty outer boundary, zero homology groups and the zero coefficient ring. No step selects representatives for infinitely many classes; surjectivity is used for a single class at a time. Thus the result and the finite-dimensional consequence require no choice principle. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $W,X$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds with supplied boundary collars and decompositions $\partial W=A\sqcup D$, $\partial X=A\sqcup B$. Glue their copies of $A$ by a supplied orientation-reversing identification, obtaining $Y=W\cup_A X$ with $\partial Y=D\sqcup B$. Supply one ambient rank-one right-$R$ local system on $Y$, where $R$ is an involutive unital ring. On each connected component supply a base-fiber identification with $R$ and unitary monodromy, and use its transported standard Hermitian form. Use its restrictions and the induced orientations on $W,X$.

For the intersection pairings defined by inverse relative cap duality, passage to absolute cohomology and evaluation,
$$\lambda_Y(i_*p,i_*q)=\lambda_W(p,q)\qquad(p,q\in H_2(W;R)).$$
In particular all isotropic and dual-pair identities for homology classes in $W$ persist under their inclusion in $Y$. The result applies to topological manifolds and requires no geometric surface transversality or choice principle.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The collared gluing, compatible orientations, single ambient coefficient system and parallel form.

[F1] Relative duality identifies $\overline{H_2(W;R)}$ with $H^2(W,\partial W;\mathcal R^\vee)$, and likewise for $Y$. The dual-system identification is relative to the supplied form and is compatible with restriction. [[thm-compact-collared-manifold-local-coefficient-lefschetz-duality-in-zf]], [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]]

[F2] Local excision holds with actual small-chain homotopy inverses. Support and relative cap commute with those maps by their face formulas, and orientation classes are characterized by their local images. These facts apply to the underlying abelian-group systems at base ring $\mathbb Z$, retaining the right or left actions commuting with transport. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]], [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]], [[lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets]]

## Proof

1.1 Put $T=X\cup D\subset Y$. This contains $\partial Y$. Restriction induces an isomorphism $$H^2(Y,T;\mathcal R^\vee)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^2(W,A\cup D;\mathcal R^\vee).$$ To see the actual excision condition, remove from $X$ a closed core outside a short open collar of its seam $A$. That core is closed in $Y$ and lies in $\operatorname{int}_Y T$, because it misses the seam. Excision [F2] then leaves $W$ together with that short seam collar, and the remaining relative subspace is $D$ together with the collar. Pushing the collar to $A$ is a homotopy equivalence of pairs with $(W,A\cup D)$. Coefficient transports along the collar give its local-system comparison. This proves the isomorphism; it is restriction and commutes with forgetting relative conditions. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $u_p\in H^2(W,\partial W;\mathcal R^\vee)$ be the dual of $\bar p$, and let $v_p$ be its inverse image under step 1.1. Map $v_p$ into $H^2(Y,\partial Y;\mathcal R^\vee)$ since $\partial Y\subset T$. Its cap with $[Y,\partial Y]$ is $\overline{i_*p}$. Indeed the image of the orientation class in the excised pair restricts to $[W,\partial W]$, since their pointwise orientation images on the interior of $W$ agree. The support/relative cap comparison of [F2] therefore identifies the cap with $u_p$ on $W$, followed by inclusion in $Y$. On representatives one may first apply the image-preserving small-chain operator: the portion in $X$ caps to zero because $v_p$ vanishes on $T$, and the portion on the remaining collar core gives precisely the cap on $W$. Changes of the orientation representatives are a boundary plus a chain in the relative subspace; the cap boundary identity makes their caps a boundary plus zero. Thus this is the actual cap map, not an unsupported geometric push of cycles. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Relative duality [F1] now says that the class in step 2.1 is the relative dual of $\overline{i_*p}$. Its absolute cohomology image restricts to the absolute image of $u_p$ on $W$, by the last sentence of step 1.1. Naturality of evaluation gives $$\lambda_Y(i_*p,i_*q)=\langle j_Yv_p,i_*q\rangle=\langle i^*j_Yv_p,q\rangle=\langle j_Wu_p,q\rangle=\lambda_W(p,q).$$ Here each cochain system uses the restriction of the same ambient parallel Hermitian form, so no unrestricted frame change or independent coefficient identification is being inserted. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The displayed equality immediately preserves any finite list of zero self-pairings and unit dual-pairings. Empty seam or empty outer boundary causes no change in the restriction and relative maps; a disconnected gluing is treated on its finitely many compact components with the supplied coefficient systems. Every collar core and representative comparison is chosen for one finite calculation, and the small-chain operators are fixed formulas. Thus the full stated topological and coefficient scope uses no choice axiom. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses and notation of the fixed-frequency far-field definition. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ put $\rho=\rho_k(q)$. Uniformly over all incident and observation directions,
$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M}{4\pi}\|q\|_\infty\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.$$
Whenever $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, this implies
$$\sup_{\theta,d\in S^2}\left|\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{M C_D}{4\pi}\frac{\|q\|_\infty^2}{1-C_D\|q\|_\infty}.$$
For each fixed $(\theta,d)$, the scalar map $q\mapsto\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)$ on the open domain $\mathcal U_{D,k}$, with $L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$ and $\mathbb C$ viewed as real Banach spaces, is Fréchet differentiable at $q=0$ and has derivative $h\mapsto\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)$. The remainder bound is uniform in $(\theta,d)$; it asserts no nonlinear uniqueness or stability result.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-fixed-frequency-far-field-data|The exact scattering family, small-norm domain, and first Born data formula.]]

[[lem-ip-small-contrast-scattering-map-well-defined|The small-norm solution, data integrals, and open contrast domain are well-defined.]]

[[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded|The operator-norm estimate $\rho_k(q)\le C_D\|q\|_\infty$.]]

[[thm-volume-integral-scattering-born-neumann-error|For $\rho<1$, the Lippmann–Schwinger solution satisfies the first partial-sum tail bound.]]

[[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces|Fréchet differentiability means a bounded real-linear first-order approximation with remainder $o(\|h\|)$.]]

[[thm-complex-lp-completeness-and-almost-everywhere-subsequences|Countable Choice makes complex $L^\infty$ complete.]]

[[def-countable-choice|The declared axiom for L-infinity completeness and volume-scattering suppliers.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the data in the fixed-frequency definition; a contrast $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$; and directions $\theta,d\in S^2$.

[F1] The definition fixes $K_{q,k}$, $\rho_k(q)$, $\mathcal S_k(q)$, and $\mathcal B_kq$ on the stated quotient spaces and gives $C_D=\sqrt{M\operatorname{diam}(D)/(4\pi)}$ ([[def-ip-fixed-frequency-far-field-data]]).

[F2] The volume operator is linear in $q$ and obeys $\|K_{q,k}\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le C_D\|q\|_\infty$ ([[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]]).

[F3] For $\rho<1$, the unique solution $u=f+K_{q,k}u$ satisfies $\|u-\sum_{j=0}^{N}K_{q,k}^jf\|_2\le \rho^{N+1}\|f\|_2/(1-\rho)$ ([[thm-volume-integral-scattering-born-neumann-error]]).

[F4] The complex L2 pairing is representative-independent and satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz ([[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]]).

[F5] The Fourier transform convention is $\widehat g(\xi)=\int g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$ for $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]).

[F6] Under Countable Choice, $L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$ is complete; realification leaves its norm and metric unchanged. The same completeness fact applies to $\mathbb C$ as a finite-dimensional complex L-infinity space ([[thm-complex-lp-completeness-and-almost-everywhere-subsequences]], [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]).

[F7] Between real Banach spaces, a Fréchet derivative is a bounded real-linear map whose remainder divided by the input norm tends to zero ([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]], [[def-banach-space]]).

[F8] For real $t$, $|e^{it}|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[F9] A measurable representative of the complex contrast satisfies $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere ([[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound]]).

[F10] The domain $\mathcal U_{D,k}$ is open and contains zero ([[lem-ip-small-contrast-scattering-map-well-defined]]).

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed through [F3] and [F6] ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 For any $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, [F8] gives $|e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}e^{ikd\cdot y}|=1$ and [F9] gives $\int_D|h|\le M\|h\|_\infty$. The integral definition therefore yields $|\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)|\le M\|h\|_\infty/(4\pi)$. By [F5] and the Fourier formula in [F1], this integral is the stated Born functional. It is complex-linear in $h$, hence bounded and real-linear for every fixed pair of directions. [F1, F5, F8, F9, given]

1.2 Let $f=f_{k,d}$. By the definition and [F8], $|f|=1$ on $D$, so $\|f\|_2=\sqrt M$. The case $N=0$ of [F3] gives $\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2\le\rho\sqrt M/(1-\rho)$. [F1, F3, F8, given]

2.1 Subtracting the integral formulas in [F1] yields $\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)-\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)\bigl(u_{q,k,d}(y)-f(y)\bigr)\,dy.$ By [F9], $q(u_{q,k,d}-f)$ has $L^2$ norm at most $\|q\|_\infty\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2$. The same unit-modulus calculation as step 1.2, with $d$ replaced by $\theta$, gives $\|e^{ik\theta\cdot(\cdot)}\|_2=\sqrt M$. By [F4], the integral's absolute value is at most $\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|u_{q,k,d}-f\|_2/(4\pi)$; then [F3] and step 1.2 give the first bound, uniformly in the directions. [F1, F3, F4, F9, step 1.2]

3.1 By [F2], $\rho\le C_D\|q\|_\infty$. When $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, monotonicity of $t\mapsto t/(1-t)$ on $[0,1)$ gives $\rho/(1-\rho)\le C_D\|q\|_\infty/(1-C_D\|q\|_\infty)$. Substitution into step 2.1 proves the second bound. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For nonzero $q$ with $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, divide the second bound by $\|q\|_\infty$; the quotient is at most $\frac{M C_D}{4\pi}\frac{\|q\|_\infty}{1-C_D\|q\|_\infty}$, which tends to zero as $\|q\|_\infty\to0$. Since [F10] makes zero an interior point, the bounded real-linear map from step 1.1 satisfies the Fréchet remainder criterion [F7], with the Banach-space hypotheses in [F6]. Also $\mathcal S_k(0)=0$ by its definition. Thus $D\mathcal S_k(0)(\theta,d)h=\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)$ for each fixed pair, with the same remainder estimate uniformly over the full direction family. [A1, F1, F6, F7, F10, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

At zero contrast the first Born data are
$$\mathcal B_kh(\theta,d)=\frac1{4\pi}\widehat{h_0}\!\left(\frac{k}{2\pi}(\theta-d)\right).$$
Thus each fixed-frequency direction pair samples one Fourier frequency on the corresponding Ewald surface. The result is local at $q=0$ and does not extend a derivative or inverse-uniqueness assertion to arbitrary contrasts.

## Fourier-transfer geometry

For fixed $k>0$ and unit directions $d,\theta$, the wavevectors $kd$ and $k\theta$ lie on the radius-$k$ sphere in their span. The arrow from $kd$ to $k\theta$ is exactly $k(\theta-d)$; the Fourier variable in the library's $2\pi$ convention is that chord divided by $2\pi$. The diagram is only a geometric description of the frequency label; the Fréchet estimate above is proved by the integral and norm bounds, not by the drawing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,scale=1.2]
  \coordinate (O) at (0,0);
  \coordinate (D) at (2,0);
  \coordinate (T) at (1.2,1.6);
  \draw[gray,dashed] (O) circle (2);
  \draw[->,thick] (O) -- (D) node[midway,below] {$kd$};
  \draw[->,thick] (O) -- (T) node[midway,left] {$k\theta$};
  \draw[->,very thick,blue] (D) -- (T) node[midway,right] {$k(\theta-d)$};
  \node[below left] at (O) {$0$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

      url: https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/AG.pdf

      url: https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00CM
---

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $C$ be a finite union of distinct irreducible one-dimensional closed algebraic subsets of $(\mathbb C^*)^2$. Suppose its radical vanishing ideal in $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$ is the scalar extension of a radical ideal in $\mathbb Q[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$; this is what it means here for the reduced union to be defined over $\mathbb Q$. Then its complex vanishing ideal is generated by a square-free Laurent polynomial $F$ with primitive integer coefficients. Any two such primitive integer-coefficient generators differ by multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb Z$.

## Statement references

[Milne, *Algebraic Geometry*, v6.10, §§1–3](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/AG.pdf)

[The Stacks Project, Section 10.9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00CM)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the two-dimensional algebraic torus $(\mathbb C^*)^2$, and the reduced finite union $C$ of distinct irreducible one-dimensional closed subvarieties, with a rational structure on the union.

[F1] Every prime ideal of height one in a finite-variable polynomial ring over a field is principal and generated by an irreducible element ([[lem-finite-variable-polynomial-rings-over-fields-are-ufds]]).

[F2] For an affine domain of finite type over a field, its Krull dimension is the transcendence degree of its fraction field ([[thm-affine-domain-dimension-transcendence-degree]]).

[F3] Geometric dimension of an affine algebraic set over an algebraically closed field equals Krull dimension of its coordinate ring, under full AC ([[thm-affine-variety-dimension-coordinate-ring]]; [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The torus is affine: $(M,L)\mapsto(M,L,M^{-1},L^{-1})$ identifies it with $\{(M,L,U,V):MU=LV=1\}\subset\mathbb C^4$.

[F4] For a finite-type domain $A$ and prime $P$, full AC gives $\operatorname{ht}(P)+\dim(A/P)=\dim A$ ([[cor-height-plus-quotient-dimension-affine-domain]]; [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F5] Prime ideals disjoint from a localization set correspond by extension and contraction, preserving inclusions ([[thm-prime-spectrum-of-a-localisation-bijection]]).

[F6] The Laurent polynomial ring is the localization of $\mathbb C[M,L]$ obtained by inverting $M$ and $L$; its units are nonzero scalars times monomials, as follows from polynomial factorization in [F1].

[F7] The fixed field of all automorphisms of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb Q$ ([[lem-fixed-field-of-automorphisms-of-c-over-q-is-q]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $R=\mathbb C[M,L]$ and $S=\{M^aL^b:a,b\ge0\}$. The coordinate ring of $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ is $A=S^{-1}R$, a finite-type domain with fraction field $\mathbb C(M,L)$ of transcendence degree two. Each irreducible curve $Y$ in $C$ has prime ideal $P_Y\subset A$, and its quotient coordinate ring has dimension one by [F3]. Thus [F2] gives $\dim A=2$ and $\dim(A/P_Y)=1$; [F4] yields $\operatorname{ht}(P_Y)=1$. [F2, F3, F4, given]

1.2 Contract $P_Y$ to $p_Y=P_Y\cap R$. It avoids $S$ because every element of $S$ is a unit in $A$. By [F5], contraction and extension identify all primes below $P_Y$ with primes below $p_Y$, so $p_Y$ has height one. By [F1], $p_Y=(f_Y)$ for an irreducible polynomial $f_Y\in R$. Since $p_Y$ avoids $M$ and $L$, neither variable divides $f_Y$. In the localization of the UFD $R$, an irreducible remains prime unless it divides an inverted element; therefore $f_Y/1$ is a nonunit prime and $P_Y=(f_Y/1)$. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Distinct components have distinct prime ideals, hence their irreducible generators $f_Y$ are pairwise nonassociate in the Laurent ring. A Laurent polynomial belongs to every $(f_Y)$ exactly when each pairwise nonassociate prime factor divides it; unique factorization then makes it divisible by their product. If $C$ is empty, the vanishing ideal is the unit ideal and the empty product is $F_0=1$; otherwise the same product over the components generates the vanishing ideal. In either case the generator is square-free, and any other generator differs by a Laurent unit. [F1, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 By the stated rational structure, every automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ preserves the vanishing ideal. Shift the finite support of $F_0$ so its lexicographically least exponent pair is $(0,0)$, then scale its coefficient there to $1$. This gives a unique normalized generator: by [F6] any two generators differ by a Laurent unit, and the support shift and specified coefficient remove that unit. Every such field automorphism preserves the normalization, hence fixes each coefficient. By [F7] the coefficients are rational. Clearing denominators and dividing by their integer gcd gives a primitive integer Laurent polynomial. Any two primitive integer-coefficient generators differ by a Laurent unit with rational scalar part; primitivity forces that scalar to be $\pm1$. [F6, F7, given, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 Steps 1.1–2.2 prove existence of the square-free primitive integer equation and show that its only ambiguity is $\pm M^aL^b$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot in $S^3$ has an admissible finite planar code whose rational polygonal drawing certificate represents a regular oriented diagram of that knot.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-planar-code|The finite rational polygonal code requirements]]

[[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram|Regular projections, transverse double points, and over/under data]]

[[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection|Existence of a regular projection under countable choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the knot can be moved off infinity and projected regularly; the projection has finitely many transverse double points and no triple points. [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]

[F2] A finite planar code records a rational polygonal path for every edge, exact incidence and over/under data, transverse crossing vertices, and one oriented component. [[def-knot-planar-code]]

[F3] Regularity is the condition that the projected knot is an immersion with only finitely many transverse double points and no higher multiple points. [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]

[F4] An isotopy of embeddings of a compact circle extends to an ambient isotopy under AC$_\omega$. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

## Proof

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.


1.1 Apply [F1] and list the finitely many crossings of the resulting projection. Around each crossing choose a closed disk meeting the image in exactly two transverse arcs, with all such disks pairwise disjoint. Subdivide the remaining compact arcs into finitely many subarcs contained in planar coordinate disks where each arc is a graph over a line interval and where nonincident pieces are separated. Compactness and finiteness give a positive minimum for the separations between the disjoint pieces. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct]

2.1 In each crossing disk, choose a nearby rational point $q$ and move the crossing there by a small planar isotopy supported in that disk. Choose four rational points on the four branch germs in the same cyclic order, and join each to $q$ by a rational straight segment; choose them close enough that the two lines through $q$ have nonzero determinant and stay in the same four sectors. Outside these disks, approximate each graph arc from step 1.1 by a sufficiently fine polygonal graph and perturb its finitely many vertices to rational coordinates. Choose all perturbations smaller than one third of the positive separation bound, so distinct nonincident pieces remain disjoint and every adjacent segment stays in its graph chart. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Orient the polygonal edges by the original circle parameter, pair the four crossing half-edges as on the original branches, and retain each crossing's over/under label. In each graph chart interpolate linearly between the original graph and the rational polygonal graph; the graphs remain embedded, their boundary endpoints agree, and their disjoint neighborhoods prevent new intersections. In each crossing disk the two interpolated branches keep the same four sectors and nonzero crossing determinant at the fixed rational point. Smooth each bend inside a smaller disk disjoint from all crossings. This gives an isotopy through diagrams with exactly the original crossing data. Lift the over/under heights continuously; strict height inequalities at each crossing persist, so this is an isotopy of embedded circles, which extends to an ambient isotopy by [F4]. The resulting rational polygonal data satisfy all clauses of [F2]. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

      url: "https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf"
---

## Statement


Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ and $t$ be formal variables and $K$ a
nonempty oriented link. At each crossing of a regular diagram $D$ use the
source chart with over-strand southwest-to-northeast: A joins left and right
endpoints with coefficient $A$, and B joins top and bottom endpoints with
coefficient $A^{-1}$. A state $S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}$ assigns one smoothing at every
crossing; let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count these choices and $|S|$ count the
resulting circles. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection
plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the
ambient oriented $3$-sphere. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under}), \qquad \operatorname{wr}(D)=\sum_c\operatorname{sgn}(c),$$
$$f_K(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)} \sum_{S:C(D)\to\{A,B\}}A^{a(S)-b(S)}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|S|-1}.$$
For an $n$-strand braid $\beta$ whose oriented closure is $K$, let
$e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism $e(\sigma_i)=1$, where $\sigma_i$
is the positive geometric Artin half twist. Let $H(n)$ be the type-A Hecke
algebra with generators $T_i$, quadratic relation $T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v$, braid
relations, and distant commutation, and let $\pi_n(\sigma_i)=T_i$. Its
normalized Markov trace $\operatorname{tr}_n$ satisfies
$\operatorname{tr}_n(1)=1$, cyclicity, tower restriction, and
$\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$. Define the library
Jones value by
$$V_K(t)=s^{e(\beta)}\left(-\frac{s^2+1}{s}\right)^{n-1} \operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\Big|_{v=s^2,\,z=-1/(s^2+1),\,t=s^2},$$
where $s=t^{1/2}$. With $A=t^{-1/4}$, these values satisfy
$$V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4}).$$
## Statement references

[[def-temperley-lieb-quotient-and-jones-specialization|Hecke-trace Jones specialization]]

[[thm-normalized-bracket-is-an-oriented-link-invariant|Normalized bracket invariance]]

[[lem-hecke-bracket-trace-dictionary-and-local-descent|Braid closure trace dictionary]]

[Kauffman, *An Invariant of Regular Isotopy* (1990), §§III and VI](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kauffman/IRH.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §§4.1–4.4](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Funar, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter 3, §§1.1–2.3](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty oriented link $K$, a braid closure of $K$, and
the two polynomial constructions in the statement.

[A1] Full AC means that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] Full AC implies countable choice
([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F2] The positive Artin half twist has determinant crossing sign $+1$; the
opposite reflected half twist exchanges over and under and has sign $-1$
([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]],
[[def-elementary-geometric-half-twist]]).

[F3] The braid exponent sum is additive, with $e(\sigma_i)=1$ and
$e(\sigma_i^{-1})=-1$
([[def-exponent-sum-of-a-braid]]).

[F4] For every braid closure, the normalized bracket satisfies
$$f_{\widehat\beta}(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(\widehat\beta)} \langle\widehat\beta\rangle,$$
and its value is independent of the regular diagram under AC$ _\omega$
([[thm-normalized-bracket-is-an-oriented-link-invariant]]).

[F5] For every $n$-braid, the raw bracket has the trace expression
$$\langle\widehat\beta\rangle =\delta^{n-1}(-A)^{e(\beta)}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta)) \big|_{v=A^{-4},\,z=-1/(A^{-4}+1)},\qquad \delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$$
([[lem-hecke-bracket-trace-dictionary-and-local-descent]]).

[F6] The library Jones value is invariant under braid equivalence and Markov
moves under full AC, and is given by the trace formula in the Statement
([[thm-the-hecke-trace-construction-is-an-oriented-link-invariant]],
[[def-temperley-lieb-quotient-and-jones-specialization]]).

[F7] Every nonempty oriented link has a braid closure under full AC
([[thm-alexanders-closed-braid-theorem]],
[[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]).

[F8] Every element of $B_n$ is represented by a finite word in the Artin
generators and their inverses; each letter is one geometric half twist or its
opposite, and the closure joins the braid endpoints
([[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]],
[[def-elementary-geometric-half-twist]],
[[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]).

## Proof

1.1 A closed braid diagram has one crossing for each letter in a finite Artin word and no crossings at its closure arcs. Each positive generator contributes $+1$ to writhe by [F2]. In the reflected inverse half twist, the over- and under-strands exchange while their oriented projected tangent vectors retain their respective directions; exchanging the two vectors negates their determinant, so each inverse generator contributes $-1$. Summing over the word and using the homomorphism in [F3] and the finite word representation in [F8] gives $$\operatorname{wr}(\widehat\beta)=e(\beta).$$ [F2, F3, F8, algebra]

2.1 Put $q=A^{-2}$ and $t=q^2$. Then $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}=-(q+q^{-1})=-(t+1)/q$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $$\begin{aligned} f_{\widehat\beta}(A) &=(-A^3)^{-e(\beta)}\delta^{n-1}(-A)^{e(\beta)} \operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\\ &=q^{e(\beta)}\delta^{n-1}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\\ &=q^{e(\beta)}\left(-\frac{q^2+1}{q}\right)^{n-1} \operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta)). \end{aligned}$$ This is exactly the library trace normalization with $s=q$ and $t=s^2$ from [F6]. Thus the two constructions agree on every braid closure. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The target coefficient ring in [F6] is $T=\mathbb Z[s^{\pm1},(s^2+1)^{-1}]$. The substitution $s\mapsto A^{-2}$, $t=s^2\mapsto A^{-4}$ defines a ring map $T\to R_A$. It is injective because distinct Laurent powers $s^k$ map to distinct Laurent monomials $A^{-2k}$, and the localization denominator maps to the unit $A^{-4}+1$. Hence the equality from step 2.1 is an equality in $T$, with $t=s^2$, rather than only after embedding the two values in a larger ring. [F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [A1] and [F1], full AC supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F4]. By [F7], choose a braid closure for the given nonempty link $K$. The calculation in step 2.1 and its ring identification in step 3.1 prove equality on that closure; the invariance in [F4] and [F6] makes both values independent of the chosen regular diagram and braid representative. Therefore $V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4})$ for every nonempty oriented link. [A1, F1, F4, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $L$ be a finite geometric simplicial complex with an ordered vertex set, and let $\mathcal R$ be a local system of rank-one free right modules over an arbitrary unital ring $R$. Its finite simplicial chain complex $F_*(L;\mathcal R)$ and intrinsic singular chain complex $C_*(L;\mathcal R)$ admit $R$-linear chain maps
$$P:C_*(L;\mathcal R)\to F_*(L;\mathcal R),\qquad J:F_*(L;\mathcal R)\to C_*(L;\mathcal R)$$
with $PJ=1$ and an explicitly constructed chain homotopy $JP\simeq1$. Choices of bases at its finitely many vertices make $F_*$ bounded finite-free.

Consequently, for every compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, and every such local system supplied with a base-fiber identification with $R$, its nonnegative singular chain complex is free with a formula-specified basis and is $R$-linearly chain-homotopy dominated by a bounded finite-free complex. No choice principle, triangulation of $M$, or assertion of finite CW type for $M$ is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The ordered finite geometric complex and coefficient functor; for the consequence, the compact manifold and based coefficient system.

[F1] The least-subdivision small-chain construction supplies a chain map $\rho$ into chains subordinate to an open cover and a homotopy $1-I\rho=dD+Dd$; it preserves the image of each simplex. Applied to underlying abelian-group systems it respects any commuting right-$R$ action, since all coefficient transports are right-linear. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[F2] A compact Hausdorff manifold with boundary is a retract of a finite Euclidean cubical complex, without choice. [[thm-compact-manifolds-are-retracts-of-finite-polyhedra-without-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 Here the right-module singular complex is defined intrinsically: $C_n=\bigoplus_\sigma\mathcal R_{\sigma(v_0)}$, and on a coefficient $a$ its first face has coefficient $T_{01}a$ over $v_1$, while face $i>0$ has coefficient $(-1)^ia$ over $v_0$. The signs include the first face sign $+1$. The identities $d_id_j=d_{j-1}d_i$ pair and cancel faces for $i<j$; the only two potentially different transport composites are along edges $01,12$ and edge $02$, equal because their paths are homotopic in the simplex. Thus $d^2=0$ for arbitrary noncommutative $R$. The same formula on affine simplices defines $F_*$, and affine inclusion defines a chain map $J$. All formulas are right-linear. Choosing one basis in each of the finitely many vertex fibers makes each $F_n$ finite-free, and $F_n=0$ above the dimension of $L$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Cover $L$ by its finitely many open vertex stars. A simplex is called small if its image lies in one of them. Apply [F1] to obtain the small chain complex $C_*^{\mathrm{sm}}$, inclusion $I$, map $\rho:C_*\to C_*^{\mathrm{sm}}$ and homotopy $D$. The proof of [F1] transports coefficients only along paths within the domain simplex; hence its face cancellations and least-integer subdivision formula apply to the right-module complex of step 1.1, or equivalently to its underlying abelian-group complex. In particular $\rho$ and $D$ are right-$R$ linear and preserve every subcomplex generated by simplices whose images lie in a specified subcomplex of $L$. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For a small singular simplex $\sigma$, let $A_\sigma$ be the finite subcomplex generated by the geometric simplices whose relative interiors meet its image. If $v$ is a vertex whose open star contains that image, every such geometric simplex contains $v$. Therefore $A_\sigma$ is a cone with apex $v$: joining $v$ to any of its faces remains in it. If $\tau$ is a face of $\sigma$, then $A_\tau\subseteq A_\sigma$. Choose as apex the least vertex whose open star contains the image. Both its simplicial chains and its singular chains have explicit augmented cone contractions: join to $v$, using straight segments in the geometric cone, and transport coefficients along those segments. For a simplex map $f$, the singular cone is $t_0v+(1-t_0)f(t_1/(1-t_0),\ldots)$, extended by $v$ at $t_0=1$; boundedness makes it continuous there. The boundary is the original chain minus the cone on its boundary, with the usual augmentation term in degree zero. The simplicial cone is the oriented join, zero when the vertex already occurs. These identities follow by the finite face cancellations. The coefficient system trivializes on the cone by its straight paths, so the identities apply to all its fibers without choosing trivializations independently at every point. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Define $S:C_*^{\mathrm{sm}}\to F_*$ by induction. For a point simplex, send its coefficient to the least apex vertex of its carrier along their straight segment. For degree $n>0$, the already defined $S(d\sigma)$ is a cycle in $A_\sigma$; in degree zero its transported augmentation is zero. Put $S\sigma$ equal to its simplicial cone at the chosen apex. The cone identity gives $dS\sigma=S(d\sigma)$. Images of all faces lie in their nested carriers, so each operation stays in $A_\sigma$. Extend linearly on each coefficient fiber. This constructs the entire chain map by a formula on generators, with finite sums and least vertices, rather than an infinite set of individually chosen fillings. [step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Construct $H:C_*^{\mathrm{sm}}\to C_{*+1}$ similarly. After lower degrees are defined, the chain $\sigma-JS\sigma-H(d\sigma)$ is a cycle in $A_\sigma$, with zero augmentation in degree zero. Cone it singularly at the chosen apex and call the result $H\sigma$. Its boundary is precisely that cycle, so $dH+Hd=I-JS$. Put $P=S\rho$. Then $$1-JP=(1-I\rho)+(I-JS)\rho=d(D+H\rho)+(D+H\rho)d.$$ Thus the displayed homotopy is actually right-linear and defined on all singular generators. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 For an affine simplex $\tau$ of $L$, image preservation in step 2.1 and the carriers of step 3.1 put $PJ\tau$ in the simplicial chains of $\tau$ itself. On a vertex $PJ$ is the identity. Inducting on dimension, $d(PJ\tau-\tau)=0$. For a positive-dimensional geometric $n$-simplex, its top simplicial chain group is one fiber and its top boundary is injective: each codimension-one face occurs with coefficient the transported original coefficient, so zero boundary forces that coefficient zero. Hence $PJ\tau=\tau$. This proves $PJ=1$, including degenerate singular simplices, which were never discarded from the source complex. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 For the manifold consequence, take the actual retraction $e:M\hookrightarrow L$ and $r:L\to M$ from [F2]. Triangulate each grid cube by its coordinate-order simplices: for each permutation of the axes take the successive vertices from its lower vertex by adding those coordinate edges in that order. These finitely many simplices cover the cube, and on shared faces the same ordering of the remaining coordinates gives the same triangulation. Pull the coefficient system to $L$ along $r$. With $F_*$ its finite simplicial complex, set $i_C=P\,C(e)$ and $r_C=C(r)J$. The homotopy of step 5.1 gives $r_Ci_C\simeq C(r)C(e)=1$, since $re=1$ literally. The coefficient maps have these same identities on fibers, so this is domination in right-$R$ chain complexes, not just ordinary homology. [F2, step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

8.1 Finally the singular modules on $M$ have actual formula-defined free bases. Take its finite convex ball/half-ball atlas. The finite intersection graph is connected; choose a finite spanning tree, one point for each tree-edge intersection, and coordinate-straight paths through these points joining the finitely many chart centers to the basepoint. For a point $x$, use the first chart containing it and append that chart's straight path from its center to $x$. This specifies a based path $\gamma_x$ for every point without pointwise selection. Transport the supplied base vector $1$ along $\gamma_x$ to obtain a basis of its fiber. Each singular generator then has its specified first-vertex basis. The differential and homotopies of the preceding steps respect those right-module structures. For disconnected finite complexes the first argument already works componentwise with finitely many vertex bases; empty complexes give zero maps. All manifold choices were finite atlas/tree data, and the only infinite constructions were recursive formulas on generators. This proves the full choice-free assertion. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard oriented three-sphere,
$$
|s(K)|\le 2g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K),
$$
where $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ is the minimum genus of a connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surface in the standard four-ball with oriented boundary $K$.

## Statement references

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|Smooth four-ball genus]]

[[lem-lee-cobordism-filtration-genus-bound|Filtered Lee maps for connected smooth cobordisms]]

[[def-rasmussen-s-invariant|Rasmussen's s convention]]

[Rasmussen, *Khovanov homology and the slice genus* (2004), §4.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131v1)

[McMullen, *4-Manifolds*, §5.7](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/4Mnotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a knot $K$, and its smooth slice genus.

[F1] The smooth slice genus is the minimum genus of a connected smooth orientable proper surface bounded by $K$ ([[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]]).

[F2] Rasmussen's convention is $s(K)=s_{\max}(K)-1$ ([[def-rasmussen-s-invariant]]).

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used by the smooth slice-genus minimum and finite movie branches ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F3] A connected genus-$g$ smooth cobordism between knots admits a filtered Lee homology isomorphism of degree $-2g$ ([[lem-lee-cobordism-filtration-genus-bound]]).

[F4] Every connected smooth properly embedded genus-$g$ surface in the standard four-ball can be punctured after supported interior ambient modifications so that the removed region is a concentric round ball meeting it in a flat disk. The remaining literal round shell has a collared genus-$g$ knot-to-unknot cobordism and Euler characteristic $-2g$ ([[lem-puncturing-smooth-four-ball-surfaces-gives-genus-preserving-knot-cobordisms]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement.

1.1 For the standard crossingless unknot diagram, the Lee complex is the one-term vector space $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$ with basis $1,X$ in quantum degrees $1,-1$ and zero differential. Its induced filtration levels are therefore $s_{\max}(U)=1$ and $s_{\min}(U)=-1$, so [F2] gives $s(U)=0$. [F2, algebra]

1.2 Let $F\subset B^4$ be any connected smooth orientable proper spanning surface of genus $g$ with boundary $K$. Apply [F4] under the countable-choice hypothesis [A1]. It moves and flattens a small interior surface disk by ambient diffeomorphisms fixed on a sufficiently small restriction of the supplied outer collar, then removes an actual concentric round ball. The remaining round shell is explicitly $S^3\times I$, with unchanged boundary knot $K$, an inner standard unknot and product collars. Its surface is connected of the same genus $g$ and has Euler characteristic $-2g$; reverse its direction if needed. This uses neither a slice-only Statement for a positive-genus surface nor a claim about arbitrary embedded four-ball complements. [A1, F1, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Apply the Lee cobordism construction to this surface and to its reverse. By [F3], each map is a filtered isomorphism of degree $-2g$. Choose a nonzero class of maximal level in $V_K$; its image is nonzero in $V_U$ and has level at least $s_{\max}(K)-2g$, which is at most $s_{\max}(U)=1$. Hence $s_{\max}(K)\le1+2g$ and $s(K)\le2g$. Apply the reverse map to a nonzero class of maximal level in $V_U$: its nonzero image in $V_K$ has level at least $1-2g$, so $s_{\max}(K)\ge1-2g$ and $s(K)\ge-2g$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Under [A1], [F1] supplies a nonempty set of smooth spanning-surface genera with a least element. Minimize $g$ over $F$ in step 1.2. Step 2.1 then gives the asserted inequality. This gives the inequality in the Statement. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\varepsilon$ have the standard normal law, let $Y=\theta+\varepsilon$, and let $g(x)=(x-Y)^2/2$. For any noise parameter $\sigma>0$, deterministic map $\widetilde D_\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, step $\gamma>0$, and initialization $x_0\in\mathbb R$, define $z_t=x_{t-1}-\gamma(x_{t-1}-Y)$ and $x_t=\widetilde D_\sigma(z_t)$. The false claim is that Gaussian measurement noise forces $z_t-\theta$ to have a Gaussian law at every iteration $t\ge1$, for every such denoiser, step, and initialization.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-pnp-ista-with-denoiser]]

[[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a standard normal random variable $\varepsilon$, $Y=\theta+\varepsilon$, the scalar least-squares function $g(x)=(x-Y)^2/2$, and the PnP-ISTA recurrence in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: the Axiom of Choice is assumed.

[F1] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: under AC, $N(0,1)$ is the probability law with density $\phi(u)=\exp(-u^2/2)/\sqrt{2\pi}$, which is strictly positive for every real $u$.

[F2] [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]: under AC, every positive-variance normal law has a strictly positive Lebesgue density on all of $\mathbb R$; a zero-variance normal law is a point mass.

[F3] [[def-ip-pnp-ista-with-denoiser]]: the gradient step is $z_t=x_{t-1}-\gamma\nabla g(x_{t-1})$ and the next iterate is $x_t=\widetilde D_\sigma(z_t)$.

## Counterexample

**Given:** The probability model and recurrence in the Statement. Choose $\theta=0$, $x_0=0$, $\sigma=1$, $\gamma=1/2$, and the deterministic plug-in map $\widetilde D_1(z)=z^2$.

1.1 Since $\nabla g(x)=x-\varepsilon$, [F3] gives $z_1=\varepsilon/2$, $x_1=\varepsilon^2/4$, and $z_2=x_1-\frac12(x_1-\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2/8+\varepsilon/2=(\varepsilon+2)^2/8-1/2$. Thus $z_2\ge-1/2$ almost surely. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The event $-1/2<\varepsilon<1/2$ has positive probability by [A1, F1] and gives $-7/32<z_2<9/32$. The event $-5/2<\varepsilon<-3/2$ also has positive probability and gives $-1/2\le z_2<-15/32$. These disjoint output intervals show that $z_2$ is not almost surely constant. [A1, F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 A nondegenerate Gaussian law has positive probability below $-1/2$ by [A1, F2], whereas $z_2$ has none by step 1.1; a degenerate Gaussian is a point mass, whereas step 2.1 shows $z_2$ is not. Therefore $z_2$ is not Gaussian and the universal iterative-AWGN claim is false. [A1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
