## Definition

Use coordinates $(z,t)\in\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ on oriented $\mathbb R^3$, with $t$ increasing upward. A knot is a smooth embedding $K:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$ with the orientation of $S^1$. A strict Morse presentation is one for which $t|_K$ has nondegenerate critical points, meaning its second derivative in a local coordinate is nonzero there, and pairwise distinct critical values. Write $t_{\min}:=\min_{x\in K}t(x)$, $t_{\max}:=\max_{x\in K}t(x)$, and $r(K)$ for the number of local maxima. A parenthesized $q$-braid is a smooth braid with $q$ strands, each strictly increasing in $t$, together with an ordered binary parenthesization of its lower endpoints and an ordered binary parenthesization of its upper endpoints.

For $n\ge0$, a degree-$n$ chord diagram is an oriented circle with $n$ disjoint unordered pairs of distinct points, called chords. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ be the rational vector space on these diagrams modulo 4T, and let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$ be its quotient by 1T as well. A 4T relation fixes one chord $pq$ and another chord endpoint $r$, moves the other endpoint of the second chord to just before or after $p$ and just before or after $q$, and takes the alternating sum of those four diagrams. A chord is isolated when it intersects no other chord, where intersection means that chord endpoints alternate around the circle; 1T sets every such diagram to zero. Put $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{fr/un}}_{\mathbb C}:=\prod_{n\ge0}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{fr/un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C)$, with multiplication induced by connected sum of diagrams and unit the empty diagram. For $q$ ordered upward strands, let $\widehat{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb C}(q)$ be the completion of the associative algebra generated by $t_{ij}=t_{ji}$ for $1\le i<j\le q$, with relations $[t_{ij},t_{kl}]=0$ when $i,j,k,l$ are distinct and $[t_{ij},t_{ik}+t_{jk}]=0$ when $i,j,k$ are distinct. The generator $t_{ij}$ is a horizontal chord joining strands $i$ and $j$; multiplication stacks diagrams from bottom to top.

More generally, a compact strict Morse tangle $T$ is a compact oriented smooth one-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb C\times[a,b]$, with distinct boundary points on the planes $t=a$ and $t=b$, transverse to those planes, and with nondegenerate interior critical points of height having distinct critical values. A tangle chord diagram is a finite set of unordered pairs of distinct interior points on the oriented tangle skeleton. Its 4T relation is the same local alternating relation as above on the skeleton. The unframed tangle quotient also sets to zero any chord whose endpoints are consecutive in the order along the same skeleton component; for a circle the order is cyclic and for an arc it is linear. The completed degreewise tangle diagram space is denoted $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}(T)$.

The unframed configuration series of a strict Morse presentation $K$ is the formal degreewise series
$$
Z(K):=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac1{(2\pi i)^m}\int_{t_{\min}<t_m<\cdots<t_1<t_{\max}}\ \sum_{P}(-1)^{\downarrow(P)}[D_P]_{\mathrm{un}}\bigwedge_{j=1}^m\frac{dz_j-dz'_j}{z_j-z'_j}\ \in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}.
$$
The ordered simplex is divided into chambers by the critical values of $t|_K$. In each chamber, $P$ ranges over choices, at each level $t_j$, of an unordered pair of distinct points $(z_j,t_j),(z'_j,t_j)$ of $K$. The diagram $D_P$ joins the corresponding preimages on the oriented parameter circle. The integer $\downarrow(P)$ counts endpoints at which $t$ decreases along the orientation of $K$. The differential form is pulled back to the chamber by the selected local branches. The degree-zero term is the empty diagram with coefficient $1$; the displayed integrals are interpreted as improper integrals on each chamber.

For a compact strict Morse tangle $T$, $Z(T)$ is given by the same formula with $T$ in place of $K$, the interval $(a,b)$ in place of $(t_{\min},t_{\max})$, the chord diagrams on the tangle skeleton in place of circle diagrams, and the corresponding unframed tangle quotient in place of $\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C}$. A parenthesized braid is a special case with no interior critical points.

For a parenthesized braid path $\gamma$ in the configuration space of $q$ distinct complex points, define its Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov (KZ) series by the degreewise iterated-integral holonomy of
$$\Omega_q=\frac1{2\pi i}\sum_{1\le i<j\le q}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j).$$
Explicitly, if $\gamma:[0,1]\to\operatorname{Conf}_q(\mathbb C)$ is an ordinary path with noncolliding endpoints, its holonomy is
$$1+\sum_{m\ge1}\int_{0<t_m<\cdots<t_1<1}\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_1)\cdots\gamma^*\Omega_q(t_m).$$
A tangential endpoint is a limiting collision configuration together with a specified nonzero first-order direction of approach for each colliding cluster. When endpoints have such clusters prescribed by the parenthesizations, the holonomy is the constant term after removing the local logarithmic factors $\exp(t_{ij}\log\varepsilon/(2\pi i))$ at each tangential endpoint. A change between the two parenthesizations of three consecutive strands is encoded by the regularized transport $\Phi_{\mathrm{KZ}}$.

For parenthesized braids the KZ holonomy takes values in the framed strand algebra, where only tangled 4T is imposed; passing from a closed framed strand diagram to an unframed knot applies the quotient by isolated-chord 1T. Fix a standard hump $H$ by starting with the two-critical-point unknot and inserting one local birth of a maximum-minimum pair; thus $H$ has two local maxima. The normalized unframed Kontsevich series of $K$ is
$$
I(K):=Z(K)\,Z(H)^{-r(K)}\in\widehat{\mathcal A}^{\mathrm{un}}_{\mathbb C},
$$
The normalization uses one copy of $Z(H)$ for each local maximum; its degree-zero term is $1$, so its inverse is interpreted in the product completion. This definition makes no assertion that the unnormalized KZ coefficients are rational or that equal Kontsevich series separate knot types.

The following figure illustrates the positive Artin generator $\sigma_1$ and parenthesization conventions. Height increases upward, the right-bottom strand is the overstrand under the determinant crossing convention, and the labels at the ends record the ordered parenthesizations; no proof below relies on the drawing.

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\varepsilon,\alpha,\delta>0$, let
$\sigma\in(0,1)$, and consider the scalar forward map $F_\varepsilon:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $F_\varepsilon(t)=
\varepsilon t$ at a current point $x$ with exact datum $y=F_\varepsilon(x)$
and noisy datum $y^\delta$ satisfying $0<r:=y^\delta-F_\varepsilon(x)\le\delta$.
The regularized linearized step with fixed damping $\alpha$ is the unique
minimizer of
$$h\longmapsto\frac12|\varepsilon h-r|^2+\frac\alpha2|h|^2,$$
namely $h_\alpha=\varepsilon r/(\varepsilon^2+\alpha)$; hence
$|h_\alpha|\le\delta/(2\sqrt\alpha)$, uniformly in $\varepsilon$. The
unregularized Gauss–Newton increment, defined by $\varepsilon h_0=r$, is
$h_0=r/\varepsilon$ and satisfies only $|h_0|\le\delta/\varepsilon$. If
instead $\alpha$ is selected by the residual-forcing equality
$|\varepsilon h_\alpha-r|=\sigma r$, then
$\alpha=\sigma\varepsilon^2/(1-\sigma)$ and
$h_\alpha=(1-\sigma)r/\varepsilon$, so the forcing-selected increment is not
uniformly bounded over $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ at a fixed noise bound. For the finite-dimensional
safeguarded LM trial on this same scalar linear residual, with exact arithmetic,
$D=1$, current damping $\lambda=\alpha$, damping floor
$0<\lambda_{\min}\le\alpha$, factors $\gamma=2$, $\eta_1=1/4$,
$\eta_2=3/4$, trust radius $\Delta>|h_\alpha|$, one-attempt budget, and a
supplied exact reduced QR factorization of the augmented matrix, the trial is
accepted with ratio $1$ and unchanged damping.

## Example references

[[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt|Residual-forcing regularized LM step]]

[[alg-safeguarded-levenberg-marquardt|Finite-budget safeguarded LM trial]]

[Christian Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, §11.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00617v2)

[Barbara Kaltenbacher, *Inverse Problems – Applications and Solution Strategies*, slide 80](https://me.aau.at/~bkaltenb/AD12_kaltenbacher.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $\varepsilon,\alpha,\delta>0$; $0<\sigma<1$; $F_\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon t$; exact datum $y=F_\varepsilon(x)$; and $0<r=y^\delta-F_\varepsilon(x)\le\delta$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the axiom required by the general Hilbert-space regularized LM definition ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The regularized LM method selects $\alpha_n$ by the displayed residual-forcing equality ([[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt]]).

[F2] In exact mode the safeguarded LM trial minimizes the damped least-squares objective with the supplied scaling matrix ([[alg-safeguarded-levenberg-marquardt]]).

[F3] An exact safeguarded trial is accepted only when the actual-to-predicted ratio is at least $\eta_1$; damping is reduced only when the ratio is at least $\eta_2$ and the scaled step reaches the trust boundary ([[alg-safeguarded-levenberg-marquardt]]).

[F4] Each positive real has a positive square root, and $2\varepsilon\sqrt\alpha\le\varepsilon^2+\alpha$ follows from $(\varepsilon-\sqrt\alpha)^2\ge0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

## Verification



1.1 Completing the square gives $\frac12|\varepsilon h-r|^2+\frac\alpha2|h|^2=\frac{\varepsilon^2+\alpha}{2}\left(h-\frac{\varepsilon r}{\varepsilon^2+\alpha}\right)^2+\frac{r^2}{2}-\frac{\varepsilon^2r^2}{2(\varepsilon^2+\alpha)}.$ Since $\varepsilon^2+\alpha>0$, the unique minimizer is $h_\alpha=\varepsilon r/(\varepsilon^2+\alpha)$. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $2\varepsilon\sqrt\alpha\le\varepsilon^2+\alpha$, so $|h_\alpha|=\varepsilon r/(\varepsilon^2+\alpha)\le r/(2\sqrt\alpha)\le\delta/(2\sqrt\alpha)$, with a bound independent of $\varepsilon$. The unregularized linearized equation $\varepsilon h_0=r$ instead gives $|h_0|=r/\varepsilon\le\delta/\varepsilon$, which is unbounded as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ for fixed $r>0$. [F4, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The linearized residual after the regularized step is $\varepsilon h_\alpha-r=-\alpha r/(\varepsilon^2+\alpha)$. Since $r>0$, the residual-forcing equality is equivalent to $\alpha/(\varepsilon^2+\alpha)=\sigma$, hence $\alpha=\sigma\varepsilon^2/(1-\sigma)$ and $h_\alpha=(1-\sigma)r/\varepsilon$. This forcing-selected step grows like $1/\varepsilon$ when $r$ is held fixed; the fixed-$\alpha$ bound above does not give a uniform bound for this varying-parameter family. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 For the finite safeguarded procedure, the augmented matrix is the column $A=(\varepsilon,\sqrt\alpha)^T$. Put $s:=\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+\alpha}$, $Q:=A/s$, and $R:=(s)$. Then $s>0$, $Q^TQ=1$, and $QR=A$, so $A=QR$ is an exact reduced QR factorization. Its augmented residual vector is $b=(-r,0)^T$, and the exact damped least-squares minimizer is the same $p=h_\alpha$ from step 1.1. [F2, F4, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Take residual map $g(t)=\varepsilon t-y^\delta$, Jacobian $J=\varepsilon$, $D=1$, current damping $\lambda=\alpha$, a floor $0<\lambda_{\min}\le\alpha$, factors $\gamma=2$, $\eta_1=1/4$, $\eta_2=3/4$, trust radius $\Delta>|h_\alpha|$, and one allowed attempt. The exact gradient is nonzero since $J^Tg(x)=-\varepsilon r\ne0$. The model residual equals the actual residual because $g$ is affine. The predicted reduction is positive because $|\varepsilon h_\alpha-r|=\alpha r/(\varepsilon^2+\alpha)<r$, so the actual-to-predicted ratio is $1$. The trial lies inside the trust radius, hence it is accepted and does not meet the boundary condition for lowering damping; it returns the same damping $\lambda=\alpha$. [A1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, given, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The fixed-damping bound and the residual-forcing parameter rule are different comparisons. The finite safeguarded procedure is used here for its exact finite-dimensional damped-step mechanics; its trust-ratio update does not replace the residual-forcing rule in the regularizing Hilbert-space iteration.

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $\rho:\Gamma\to SL_2(F)$ be a representation of a finitely generated group which is absolutely irreducible, meaning that no line is invariant under all its matrices after extension to any field containing $F$. Let $K\subseteq F$ be the subfield generated by the prime field and all traces $\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$, $g\in\Gamma$. There are words $A=\rho(a)$ and $B=\rho(b)$ and an element $\xi$ satisfying $\xi^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)\xi+1=0$, with $\xi\ne\xi^{-1}$, such that over $F(\xi)$ the representation is conjugate by a matrix in $GL_2(F(\xi))$ to one whose generator matrices all lie in $SL_2(K(\xi))$. Thus the required model field has degree at most two over $K$. The entries are obtained by explicit finite formulas from $\xi$ and the traces of $A,B,AB,C,AC,BC,ABC$ for each generator matrix $C$. If $K(\xi)\ne K$, its nonidentity automorphism is realized on this model by simultaneous conjugation with one explicit matrix in $GL_2(K(\xi))$. In particular, suppose a projective point $z\in\mathbb P^r(K(\xi))$ is obtained from the model by a construction commuting with field automorphisms and invariant under simultaneous $GL_2$ conjugation. Then $z$ is defined over $K$. This last clause requires the stated compatibility and invariance; it asserts no analytic, homology-rank or quotient-existence theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, finitely generated group, absolutely irreducible representation and trace subfield in the Statement.

[F1] For a two-by-two matrix $T$, direct multiplication gives $T^2-\operatorname{tr}(T)T+\det(T)I=0$. A matrix with two distinct eigenvalues has the corresponding eigenvectors as a basis. A quadratic polynomial with distinct roots gives either the trivial extension or a separable quadratic extension, whose nonidentity automorphism exchanges the roots.

## Proof

1.1 **Find a noncentral semisimple word and a word meeting both eigenspaces.** Some group matrix has trace different from $2,-2$. Otherwise, if all matrices were scalar the representation would be reducible; choose a nonscalar $D=\epsilon I+N$ with $\epsilon=\pm1$, $N\ne0$ and $N^2=0$ by [F1]. For every group matrix $C$ and integer $m\ge0$, $$\operatorname{tr}(D^mC)=\epsilon^m\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C+m\epsilon^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(NC)\bigr).$$ All these traces belong to $\{2,-2\}$ by the supposition. In characteristic zero a nonconstant affine function on the nonnegative integers takes infinitely many values, so $\operatorname{tr}(NC)=0$ for every $C$. In a basis over $F$ with $N=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ this forces the lower-left entry of every $C$ to be zero. Its first coordinate line would be invariant, a contradiction. Thus choose a word $A$ with trace different from $\pm2$, and adjoin one root $\xi$ of its characteristic polynomial. Its two distinct eigenvalues are $\xi,\xi^{-1}$, so it is diagonalizable already over $F(\xi)$. In that eigenbasis some group word $B$ has both off-diagonal entries nonzero. Indeed the elements preserving the first and second eigenlines form two proper subgroups of $\Gamma$ by absolute irreducibility. A group cannot be the union of two proper subgroups: for elements in their respective differences, their product belongs to neither. Choose $B$ outside that union. These are finitely many existential selections, not an infinite choice principle. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Normalize and recover every generator by trace equations.** In the chosen $A$ eigenbasis write $B_{12}=u\ne0$ and conjugate by $\operatorname{diag}(u^{-1},1)$ to make this entry one. The lower-left entry becomes the nonzero product $q=B_{12}B_{21}$. Put $a=\operatorname{tr}A$, $b=\operatorname{tr}B$, $c=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$. In the normalized basis $$A=\begin{pmatrix}\xi&0\\0&\xi^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}d_1&1\\q&d_2\end{pmatrix},\quad d_1=\frac{c-\xi^{-1}b}{\xi-\xi^{-1}},\quad d_2=b-d_1,\quad q=d_1d_2-1\ne0.$$ All these entries lie in $K'=K(\xi)$. For each generator $C$ put $e=\operatorname{tr}C$, $f=\operatorname{tr}(AC)$, $g=\operatorname{tr}(BC)$ and $h=\operatorname{tr}(ABC)$, which belong to $K$ by its definition. Its diagonal entries are $$c_{11}=\frac{f-\xi^{-1}e}{\xi-\xi^{-1}},\qquad c_{22}=e-c_{11}.$$ Its off-diagonal entries are uniquely solved from $$c_{21}+q c_{12}=g-d_1c_{11}-d_2c_{22},\qquad \xi c_{21}+\xi^{-1}q c_{12}=h-\xi d_1c_{11}-\xi^{-1}d_2c_{22}.$$ The determinant of this two-by-two linear system is $q(\xi^{-1}-\xi)\ne0$. Thus every normalized generator matrix has entries in $K'$. These are the actual conjugated original matrices in $F(\xi)$, not merely formal matrices with the correct traces: the normalization was performed first and the displayed linear equations uniquely recover their entries. Therefore their determinant-one equations and every group relation hold in $K'$, by its injection into $F(\xi)$. The conjugated representation is an actual model over $K'$, with no new relator-existence assumption. [F1, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 **The quadratic swap is explicit conjugation.** If $K'=K$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise its automorphism $\tau$ exchanges $\xi$ and $\xi^{-1}$ and fixes every word trace. The formulas of step 2.1 give $\tau(d_1)=d_2$, $\tau(q)=q$. Put $$P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\q&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&q^{-1}\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ Direct multiplication gives $PAP^{-1}=\tau A$ and $PBP^{-1}=\tau B$. For each generator $C$, both $PCP^{-1}$ and $\tau C$ have traces $e,f,g,h$ when paired respectively with $I,\tau A,\tau B,(\tau A)(\tau B)$: conjugation preserves trace, and $\tau$ fixes the four word traces. The diagonal/off-diagonal recovery in step 2.1 applies to this swapped pair as well; its determinant is still nonzero. Uniqueness therefore gives $PCP^{-1}=\tau C$ for every generator, hence for all group words. This proves simultaneous conjugacy over $K'$ itself, without an appeal to pointwise complex-character classification. [F1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Projective descent for compatible invariant constructions.** Under the hypotheses on $z$, applying $\tau$ to its construction yields the point constructed from $\tau\rho$, while conjugation invariance and step 3.1 identify that point with $z$. Hence $\tau z=z$. Choose one nonzero homogeneous coordinate $z_j$ and normalize it to $1$. Equality of projective points implies that each ratio $z_i/z_j$ is fixed by $\tau$. Every element of the quadratic field has the unique form $u+v\xi$ with $u,v\in K$; being fixed gives $v(\xi-\xi^{-1})=0$, so $v=0$. Thus every normalized coordinate lies in $K$, proving that $z$ is a $K$-point. In the trivial-extension case this is immediate. The argument uses only finite matrix and field operations; it neither asserts that an arbitrary merely pointwise invariant assignment is rational nor supplies any analytic or chain-complex prerequisite for constructing $z$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Every finitely generated torsion-free abelian group $A$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r$ for some finite integer $r\ge0$. Here torsion-free means $na=0$ with $n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ implies $a=0$. More precisely, a fixed finite generating list yields an embedding of $A$ into a finite-rank integer lattice, and every subgroup of $\mathbb Z^r$ has a basis of at most $r$ elements. These conclusions require no form of the Axiom of Choice and no general PID factorization or structure theorem.

## Statement references

[[def-group]]

[[def-vector-space]]

[[thm-rat-field]]

[[lem-subgroups-of-z-are-cyclic]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An abelian group $A$ generated by a finite list $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, with no nonzero integer torsion.

[F1] The rationals with their fraction operations form a field ([[thm-rat-field]]); the vector-space axioms are those of [[def-vector-space]].

[F2] Every subgroup of the additive integers is $d\mathbb Z$ for a unique $d\ge0$, with $d$ the least positive element when the subgroup is nonzero ([[lem-subgroups-of-z-are-cyclic]]). Its proof uses the integer division algorithm and the well-ordering of the natural numbers, without a choice hypothesis.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data in the Statement and the fixed generating list.

1.1 On pairs $(a,n)$ with $a\in A$ and positive integer $n$, put $(a,n)\sim(b,m)$ when $ma=nb$. This is an equivalence relation. Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. If $ma=nb$ and $pb=mc$, then $m(pa-nc)=0$, so torsion-freeness gives $pa=nc$, proving transitivity. Denote the class of $(a,n)$ by $[a,n]$ and its quotient set by $V$. Define $[a,n]+[b,m]=[ma+nb,nm]$, $-[a,n]=[-a,n]$, $0=[0,1]$, and $(r/s)[a,n]=[ra,sn]$ for integer $r$ and positive integer $s$. These are independent of representatives: if $n'a=na'$ and $m'b=mb'$, multiplying the first relation by $mm'$ and the second by $nn'$ gives the cross-multiplied equality for the two proposed sums. If also $r/s=r'/s'$, then $rs'=r's$ and $s'n'ra=snr'a'$, which gives the scalar equality. Negation and zero respect the relation as well. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For completeness, every subgroup $H\le\mathbb Z^d$ is free on at most $d$ elements, by induction on the finite integer $d$. The case $d=0$ has the empty basis. For $d>0$, project to the first coordinate. Its image is $c\mathbb Z$ by [F2]. The kernel is identified by the remaining coordinates with a subgroup of $\mathbb Z^{d-1}$, so the induction hypothesis gives it a basis of at most $d-1$ elements. If $c=0$, this kernel is all of $H$. If $c>0$, take one element $h\in H$ with first coordinate $c$. Every $x\in H$ has first coordinate $nc$ for a unique integer $n$, and $x-nh$ is in the kernel. Hence the kernel basis together with $h$ generates $H$. It is independent, because the first coordinate of a relation first forces the coefficient of $h$ to be zero, and then independence of the kernel basis forces all remaining coefficients to be zero. This proves the induction step for every subgroup, without assuming it is finitely generated in advance. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The operations make $V$ a rational vector space. Addition is commutative because $ma+nb=nb+ma$, and both associations of a three-term sum have representative $[mpa+npb+nmc,nmp]$ for inputs $[a,n],[b,m],[c,p]$. Zero is an identity and the negative sums to $[0,n^2]=[0,1]$. The identities $(r/s)([a,n]+[b,m])=(r/s)[a,n]+(r/s)[b,m]$ and $(r/s+t/u)[a,n]=(r/s)[a,n]+(t/u)[a,n]$ follow by cross multiplication, reducing respectively to $r(ma+nb)=mra+nrb$ and $(ru+ts)a=rua+tsa$. Scalar associativity follows from $[rta,sun]$ for $(r/s)(t/u)[a,n]$, and scalar $1$ acts as the identity. These are all axioms in [F1]. The map $\eta:A\to V$, $\eta(a)=[a,1]$, is additive and injective, since $[a,1]=[0,1]$ forces $a=0$. Every $[a,n]$ equals $(1/n)\eta(a)$, so $V$ is spanned over $\mathbb Q$ by the fixed finite list $\eta(a_1),\ldots,\eta(a_m)$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Process that finite spanning list in its given order, retaining a vector exactly when it does not belong to the span of those previously retained. The resulting list $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ spans $V$, because each discarded vector was already in the span of an earlier retained sublist. It is independent: in a nonzero finite relation, the last vector with nonzero coefficient would belong to the span of the earlier ones, contrary to its retention rule. Thus it is a basis, constructed by a finite recursion rather than by an arbitrary basis-selection theorem. Each $\eta(a_j)$ has unique rational coordinates in this basis. Take $D>0$ to be the product of the positive denominators of the finitely many coordinates, using $D=1$ for the empty product. For $a\in A$, define $\Phi(a)$ as $D$ times the coordinate vector of $\eta(a)$. Every $a$ is an integer linear combination of the $a_j$, so $\Phi(a)\in\mathbb Z^r$. The map $\Phi:A\to\mathbb Z^r$ is additive and injective, since $D\ne0$, coordinates are unique and $\eta$ is injective. [F1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Apply step 1.2 to $H=\Phi(A)\le\mathbb Z^r$. Its finite basis and the injective map in step 3.1 identify $A$ with $\mathbb Z^t$ for some $t\le r$, giving the asserted finite freeness (rename $t$ to $r$ in the first assertion). The only selections were a single finite generating list, finitely many unique coordinate tuples, and at most one lift at each of finitely many integer-coordinate induction stages. Existence of such finitely many witnesses does not require any choice axiom. The explicit rationalization and integer-subgroup proof used no general PID structure or factorization theorem. [step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-ip-compact-manifold-dirichlet-spectrum-and-regularity

title: Compact-manifold Dirichlet spectrum and boundary regularity
status: draft

pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19

dependency_level: 1
deps:

      url: https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf
      locator: §4.10 compact self-adjoint resolvent construction; §4.12, Theorems
        4.30–4.31, printed pp. 114–116 (PDF pp. 120–122); the higher boundary
        induction and finite-atlas transfer are supplied below.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact smooth Riemannian manifold of positive dimension with smooth boundary and $q$ a smooth real function. Set $H=L^2(M,dV_g)$, $V=H^1_0(M)$ and $c=1+\|q\|_\infty$. Then
$$b(u,v)=\int_M(\langle\nabla u,\nabla\bar v\rangle+(q+c)u\bar v)\,dV_g$$
is an equivalent Hilbert inner product on $V$. There are an $H$-orthonormal sequence $(e_j)$ complete in $H$ and positive numbers $\mu_j\to\infty$ such that $b(e_j,v)=\mu_j(e_j,v)_H$ for every $v\in V$, and
$$b(u,u)=\sum_j\mu_j|(u,e_j)_H|^2\qquad(u\in V).$$
For $A=-\Delta_g+q$, weak solutions $v\in V$ of $Av=f\in H^k(M)$ satisfy
$$\|v\|_{H^{k+2}(M)}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k(M)}+\|v\|_{L^2(M)}),\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.$$
Here integer Sobolev norms use any finite smooth atlas. For every integer $a$, the inclusion $H^k(M)\to C^a(M)$ is bounded for all sufficiently large integers $k$.

## Statement references

[[thm-lax-milgram]]

[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]]

[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]]

[[lem-ip-riemannian-green-boundary-traces-and-wave-lifting]]

[[def-countable-choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and the compact smooth metric and real smooth potential in the statement; complex spaces use conjugation in the second slot.

[F1] [[thm-lax-milgram]] gives a unique inverse for bounded coercive forms on a Hilbert space under Countable Choice.

[F2] [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]] supplies the complete nonzero-eigenvalue decomposition of a compact self-adjoint operator on the orthogonal complement of its kernel.

[F3] [[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]] gives the $H^2$ estimate for smooth uniformly elliptic divergence-form operators on bounded smooth domains, including flattened boundary localizations.

[F4] [[lem-ip-riemannian-green-boundary-traces-and-wave-lifting]] gives the coordinate divergence formula and smooth boundary collar.


## Proof

1.1 On each of finitely many relatively compact coordinate charts, metric eigenvalues and the volume density have positive lower and finite upper bounds. Thus the intrinsic $H^1$ norm is equivalent to the sum of coordinate $H^1$ norms of a fixed smooth partition of unity. A Cauchy sequence has $L^2$ limits for the localized functions and their first derivatives; testing against a smooth function and passing to the limit identifies the derivative limits as the weak derivatives of the function limit. This proves completeness; $V$, being a closure, is closed. Moreover $1\le q+c\le1+2\|q\|_\infty$, so $b$ and the $H^1$ inner product have equivalent norms. Local mollification of compactly supported functions and a finite partition prove density of $V$ in $H$. [F4, given, algebra]

2.1 The inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is compact without an arbitrary-index choice argument. Indeed, a localized $v\in V$ extends by zero across a flattened boundary: approximate in $H^1$ by localized interior smooth functions, extend those, and pass to the weak-derivative identities. All extensions have bounded support in a fixed coordinate box. On a cube $C$ of side $\delta$, successively average in its $n$ coordinate variables. The one-variable identity $f(s)-f(t)=\int_t^s f'(r)dr$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|f-\operatorname{avg}_C f\|_{L^2(C)}\le n\delta\|Df\|_{L^2(C)}$ by telescoping those averages; density extends this to $H^1$. Replacement by the mean on each cube of a fixed finite grid is therefore a finite-rank approximation to each coordinate inclusion, with error $O(\delta)$ uniformly on the $H^1$ unit ball. Sum the finitely many coordinate reconstructions to approximate $V\hookrightarrow H$ in operator norm by finite-rank maps. A bounded finite-dimensional set has finite nets; choosing $\delta=2^{-k}$ makes the inclusion's image totally bounded, and completeness of $H$ makes its closure compact. Only countably many finite nets are involved. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 In a coordinate chart $Av=f$ is $$-\partial_i(\rho g^{ij}\partial_jv)+\rho qv=\rho f,\qquad \rho=\sqrt{\det g}.$$ The principal matrix is smooth uniformly positive on each compact chart. Localize by a smooth cutoff; its commutator with $A$ has order one. In a boundary chart flatten to $x_n\ge0$ and localize away from the chart sides. The localization can be regarded as a zero-Dirichlet function on a bounded smooth domain agreeing with the half-space near its support and rounded elsewhere. Applying [F3] and the same interior estimate, then summing the finite cover, gives $\|v\|_{H^2}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_{H^1})$. Testing the equation with $v$ gives $\|v\|_{H^1}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_2)$ by absorbing the gradient term, so this is the stated $k=0$ estimate. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $f\in H$, use [F1] to solve $b(Kf,v)=(f,v)_H$. The map $K:H\to V$ is bounded, and step 2.1 makes $K:H\to H$ compact. Symmetry gives $(Kf,h)_H=b(Kf,Kh)=(f,Kh)_H$, positivity gives $(Kf,f)_H=b(Kf,Kf)>0$ for $f\ne0$, and density of $V$ makes $K$ injective. Its range is dense since a vector orthogonal to the range lies in the kernel by self-adjointness. Apply [F2] to obtain positive eigenvalues $\kappa_j\to0$ and a complete $H$-orthonormal family; put $\mu_j=\kappa_j^{-1}$. Repeated finite multiplicities are included. The vectors $e_j/\sqrt{\mu_j}$ are $b$-orthonormal and complete in $V$: if $b(v,e_j)=0$ for every $j$, then $(v,e_j)_H=0$ for every $j$, hence $v=0$. Orthogonal projection and completeness therefore give the asserted $b$-Parseval identity and convergence of the spectral projections in $V$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Here is the boundary induction for higher orders. Suppose $f\in H^k$ and $v\in H^{k+1}$ is already known. In a flattened boundary chart apply a tangential derivative $D_{x'}^\alpha$, $|\alpha|=k$, to the localized equation. Its commutator with the second-order operator contains derivatives of $v$ of order at most $k+1$ with bounded smooth coefficients. The localized $D_{x'}^\alpha v$ has zero trace and lies in $H^1$; this follows first for tangential difference quotients, which preserve zero trace, and then by their $H^1$ limit. The $k=0$ local estimate of step 2.2 gives its $H^2$ bound in terms of $\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}}$. If a derivative has total order $k+2$ and at least three normal factors, differentiate the equation $k$ times, isolating the term $\rho g^{nn}D_n^2v$. Divide by the positive coefficient $\rho g^{nn}$. Each other highest-order derivative has fewer normal factors because its two principal derivatives include a tangential derivative; all commutators have order at most $k+1$. Induction on the number of normal factors therefore bounds every derivative of order $k+2$. Interior patches allow derivatives in all directions. Difference quotients justify each differentiation before regularity is established; the bounds are uniform in their increments, and testing their weak limits identifies the claimed derivatives. Nested cutoffs and the finite cover give $\|v\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}})$, and the previous induction level absorbs the last term into $C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_2)$. This proves all asserted elliptic estimates. [step 2.2, given, algebra]

4.1 For completeness the needed high-order embedding also has a finite-chart proof with this axiom base. In a half-chart extend across $x_n=0$ by $\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}a_jv(x',-jx_n)$ for $x_n<0$, where the finite Vandermonde system $\sum_j a_j(-j)^\ell=1$ for $0\le\ell\le k$ matches the derivatives at the interface. After a cutoff this is a bounded $H^k$ extension; the assertion follows first on smooth functions and then by the weak derivative identities and approximation. On a bounded support box, iterated one-dimensional integration gives $\|D^\alpha w\|_\infty\le C\|D_1\cdots D_nD^\alpha w\|_2$ for smooth compactly supported $w$. Apply this also to first derivatives of $D^\alpha w$ and to differences of mollifications. For $k\ge n+a+1$ these mollifications and all derivatives through order $a$ are uniformly Cauchy and their limits are continuous, with the asserted norm bound; passing to the coordinate segment integral identifies them as classical derivatives. Sum the finite chart extensions. This proves the embedding and completes the lemma. [step 1.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be
a bounded linear operator, let $r\in Y$ be nonzero, and let
$\sigma\in(0,1)$ and $\gamma>1$. Suppose that a fixed $v\in X$ satisfies
$$\|Tv-r\|_Y\le\frac{\sigma}{\gamma}\|r\|_Y.$$
For each $\alpha>0$, the functional
$$\Phi_\alpha(h):=\frac12\|Th-r\|_Y^2+\frac\alpha2\|h\|_X^2\qquad(h\in X)$$
has the unique global minimizer
$$h_\alpha=(T^*T+\alpha I_X)^{-1}T^*r,$$
where $T^*$ is the Hilbert adjoint and $I_X$ is the identity on $X$. Moreover,
there exists at least one $\alpha>0$ for which
$$\|Th_\alpha-r\|_Y=\sigma\|r\|_Y.$$

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-regularized-levenberg-marquardt|The regularized linearized LM subproblem and forcing rule]]

[[lem-ip-lm-product-condition-implies-range-approximation|Local range-approximation bound]]

[[def-hilbert-space|Real Hilbert spaces]]

[[def-bounded-linear-operator|Bounded linear operators]]

[[def-operator-norm|Operator norm]]

[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space|Real inner-product identities]]

[[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm|Triangle inequality for the Hilbert norm]]

[[def-hilbert-space-adjoint|Hilbert adjoint under Countable Choice]]

[[def-hilbert-space|Real Hilbert spaces]]

[[def-countable-choice|Axiom of Countable Choice]]

[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible|Shifted normal operator is invertible]]

[[thm-intermediate-value|Intermediate value theorem]]

[Christian Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Theorem 11.8 and its proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00617v2)

[Barbara Kaltenbacher, *Inverse Problems – Applications and Solution Strategies*, slide 80](https://me.aau.at/~bkaltenb/AD12_kaltenbacher.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; real Hilbert spaces $X,Y$; a bounded linear map $T:X\to Y$ with Hilbert adjoint $T^*$; $r\ne0$; $0<\sigma<1$; $\gamma>1$; and $v\in X$ with $\|Tv-r\|\le(\sigma/\gamma)\|r\|$.

[A1] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, permits a choice from each countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]). It is the only choice axiom assumed here.

[F1] The Hilbert adjoint satisfies $\langle Tx,z\rangle_Y=\langle x,T^*z\rangle_X$ for every $x\in X,z\in Y$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

[F2] For every $\alpha>0$, $T^*T+\alpha I_X$ is bijective with inverse norm at most $1/\alpha$ ([[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]).

[F3] Since $T$ is bounded linear, there is an operator norm with $\|Tw\|_Y\le\|T\|\,\|w\|_X$ for every $w\in X$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]).

[F4] In a real Hilbert space, $\|w\|^2=\langle w,w\rangle$ and the inner product is symmetric and bilinear ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

[F5] A continuous real function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values ([[thm-intermediate-value]]).

[F6] The norm satisfies the triangle inequality, hence $|\|u\|-\|v\||\le\|u-v\|$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]).

## Proof



1.1 Fix $\alpha>0$ and write $B_\alpha:=T^*T+\alpha I_X$. By [F2], $B_\alpha$ is bijective, so $h_\alpha:=B_\alpha^{-1}T^*r$ is defined and satisfies $T^*(Th_\alpha-r)+\alpha h_\alpha=0$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 For any $h\in X$, set $d:=h-h_\alpha$. Expanding with [F4] gives $\Phi_\alpha(h)-\Phi_\alpha(h_\alpha)=\langle Th_\alpha-r,Td\rangle_Y+\alpha\langle h_\alpha,d\rangle_X+\frac12\|Td\|_Y^2+\frac\alpha2\|d\|_X^2.$ The first two terms sum to $\langle T^*(Th_\alpha-r)+\alpha h_\alpha,d\rangle_X=0$ by [F1] and step 1.1. The remaining terms are nonnegative, and because $\alpha>0$ their sum vanishes only when $d=0$. Thus $h_\alpha$ is the unique global minimizer and $\Phi_\alpha(h_\alpha)\le\Phi_\alpha(0)$, so $\|h_\alpha\|_X\le\|r\|_Y/\sqrt\alpha$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Define $f(\alpha):=\|Th_\alpha-r\|_Y$. For $\alpha,\beta>0$, the inverse identity $B_\alpha^{-1}-B_\beta^{-1}=(\beta-\alpha)B_\alpha^{-1}B_\beta^{-1}$ and [F2] give $h_\alpha-h_\beta=(\beta-\alpha)B_\alpha^{-1}h_\beta$. Therefore, when $\alpha,\beta$ lie near a fixed $\alpha_0>0$, $\|h_\alpha-h_\beta\|_X\le|\beta-\alpha|\frac{\|r\|_Y}{\alpha\sqrt\beta},$ which tends to zero with $|\beta-\alpha|$. Thus $h_\alpha$ and $f(\alpha)$ are continuous on $(0,\infty)$, using [F6] for continuity of the norm. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 By step 2.1 and [F3], $\|Th_\alpha\|_Y\le\|T\|\|r\|_Y/\sqrt\alpha\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. The reverse triangle inequality from [F6] gives $|f(\alpha)-\|r\|_Y|\le\|Th_\alpha\|_Y$, so $f(\alpha)\to\|r\|_Y>\sigma\|r\|_Y$. [F3, F6, step 2.1, given, algebra]

3.3 Comparing the minimizer with the fixed vector $v$ gives $f(\alpha)^2+\alpha\|h_\alpha\|_X^2\le\|Tv-r\|_Y^2+\alpha\|v\|_X^2.$ Because $\|Tv-r\|_Y\le(\sigma/\gamma)\|r\|_Y<\sigma\|r\|_Y$, there is a strict squared-norm gap below $\sigma^2\|r\|_Y^2$. Also $v\ne0$, since $v=0$ would contradict the range bound and $r\ne0$. Choose $a>0$ small enough that $\|Tv-r\|_Y^2+a\|v\|_X^2<\sigma^2\|r\|_Y^2$. The minimizer comparison in this step gives $f(a)^2\le\|Tv-r\|_Y^2+a\|v\|_X^2<\sigma^2\|r\|_Y^2$, so $f(a)<\sigma\|r\|_Y$. [given, step 2.1, construct, choose, algebra]

4.1 By step 3.2, choose $b>a$ with $f(b)>\sigma\|r\|_Y$. Continuity from step 3.1 and [F5] give $\alpha\in[a,b]$ such that $f(\alpha)=\sigma\|r\|_Y$. Since $a>0$, this is an admissible positive parameter and proves the forcing claim. [F5, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, construct] ∎
## Remarks

The proof uses Countable Choice through the stated Hilbert-adjoint and normal-operator interfaces; it does not use full AC, DC, or HB. The scalar bisection or root-finding cost of a numerical parameter selector is not covered by this existence lemma.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$ that is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane, and let $\sigma,\gamma>0$. Put
$$\rho_\sigma(w)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|w\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad p_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du),$$
and define the normalized posterior measure and its mean by
$$\nu_{\sigma,z}(E)=\frac{\int_E\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)}{p_\sigma(z)}\quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)),\qquad D_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
The omitted normalizing constant of the $N(0,\sigma^2I)$ likelihood is independent of $u$ and cancels in $\nu_{\sigma,z}$. Writing $U(u)=u$ for the identity random vector under $\nu_{\sigma,z}$, its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u-D_\sigma(z))(u-D_\sigma(z))^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and smooth, each $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ has finite second moment, and $D_\sigma(z)$ uniquely minimizes the posterior squared-error risk $a\mapsto\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)$. Moreover, $D_\sigma$ is smooth and
$$J D_\sigma(z)=\sigma^{-2}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)$$
is symmetric positive definite. Hence $D_\sigma$ is injective with open image $X_\sigma=D_\sigma(\mathbb R^n)$ and smooth inverse on $X_\sigma$. Put $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ and, for $x\in X_\sigma$, define
$$h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=-\frac{\|x-D_\sigma^{-1}(x)\|_2^2}{2\gamma}+\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma}q_\sigma(D_\sigma^{-1}(x));$$
set $h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=+\infty$ outside $X_\sigma$. The restriction of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ to $X_\sigma$ is smooth. For any extended-real $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, define
$$\operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h}(z)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h(x)\right\},$$
where the argmin is the set of global minimizers and $h$ need not be convex. Then
$$D_\sigma(z)=z+\sigma^2\nabla\log p_\sigma(z)=z-\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(z),\qquad \operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}}(z)=\{D_\sigma(z)\}\quad(z\in\mathbb R^n).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-learned-reconstruction-estimator]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The integer $n\ge1$, a Borel probability $\mu$ not concentrated on an affine hyperplane, and $\sigma,\gamma>0$, with $\rho_\sigma,p_\sigma,\nu_{\sigma,z},D_\sigma,q_\sigma$ and $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ as in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: on $\mathbb R^n$, $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$ and $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$.

[F2] [[def-probability-measure]]: $\mu$ is a measure on its Borel sigma-algebra with total mass $\mu(\mathbb R^n)=1$.

[F3] [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]: if an integrand is integrable for each parameter, its parameter derivative is measurable, and that derivative has one integrable majorant on an open interval, then the integral is differentiable and its derivative is the integral of the derivative.

[F4] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of the limit through the integral.

[F5] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: the real exponential is smooth and $\exp'=\exp$.

[F6] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: for $r>0$, $\log$ is differentiable with $\log'(r)=1/r$.

[F7] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable Euclidean maps, the total derivative of a composite is the composite of the total derivatives.

[F8] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums, products, scalar multiples, and quotients obey their derivative formulas wherever their denominators are nonzero.

[F9] [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]: finite componentwise sums, products, scalar multiples, and composites of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$.

[F10] [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: a Euclidean map is smooth when it is $C^k$ for every finite $k$.

[F11] [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]]: in positive-dimensional Euclidean space, a smooth map with invertible derivative at a point restricts to a smooth diffeomorphism between open neighborhoods; this theorem uses no choice axiom.

[F12] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a continuous scalar function on a closed interval, differentiable in its interior, has an interior derivative equal to its endpoint difference divided by interval length.

[F13] [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]: a multi-index is an element $\alpha\in\mathbb N^n$, and $\partial^\alpha$ is the corresponding iterated coordinate derivative.

[F14] [[def-measure-with-density]]: for nonnegative Borel $w$, $E\mapsto\int_Ew\,d\mu$ is a measure.

[F15] [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]: the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative simple function is its simple integral.

[F16] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous under positive finite scalars.

[F17] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions.

[F18] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: increasing pointwise limits of nonnegative measurable functions commute with the integral.

## Proof

1.1 Since $0<\rho_\sigma(z-u)\le1$, $p_\sigma(z)\le1$. For fixed $z$, the measurable sets $E_k=\{u:\rho_\sigma(z-u)\ge1/k\}$, $k\ge1$, cover $\mathbb R^n$. By [F2] and countable subadditivity, some $E_k$ has positive $\mu$-measure; hence $p_\sigma(z)\ge\mu(E_k)/k>0$. For $j=1,2$, the function $u\mapsto\|u\|_2^j\rho_\sigma(z-u)$ is bounded because a polynomial factor is dominated at infinity by the Gaussian exponential, so its $\mu$-integral is finite. Put $w_{\sigma,z}(u)=\rho_\sigma(z-u)/p_\sigma(z)$. This is a nonnegative Borel function. By [F14], $E\mapsto\int_Ew_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu$ is a measure; [F16] identifies it with $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ and gives total mass $\int w_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu=p_\sigma(z)^{-1}p_\sigma(z)=1$. Hence $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ is a probability measure. [given, F1, F2, F14, F16, algebra]

1.2 For a nonnegative simple Borel function $\varphi=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ on disjoint Borel sets, $\varphi w_{\sigma,z}\in L^1(\mu)$ because $\varphi$ is bounded and $w_{\sigma,z}\in L^1(\mu)$ by step 1.1. By [F15] and [F17], $$\int\varphi\,d\nu_{\sigma,z}=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\nu_{\sigma,z}(A_j)=\int\varphi w_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu.$$ For arbitrary nonnegative Borel $\varphi$, set $\varphi_k(u)=2^{-k}\lfloor2^k\min\{\varphi(u),k\}\rfloor$. These are finite-valued Borel simple functions, increase pointwise, and converge to $\varphi$. Applying [F18] under $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ and $\mu$ yields $$\int\varphi\,d\nu_{\sigma,z}=\lim_k\int\varphi_k\,d\nu_{\sigma,z}=\lim_k\int\varphi_kw_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu=\int\varphi w_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu=p_\sigma(z)^{-1}\int\varphi\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,d\mu.$$ For real Borel $\varphi$ with $\int|\varphi|\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,d\mu<\infty$, apply this identity to $\varphi^+$ and $\varphi^-$ and use [F17] to obtain the same formula for $\varphi$. Taking $\varphi(u)=\|u\|_2^2$ and using its weighted bound in step 1.1 proves the finite-second-moment claim; the finite first moment follows from $\|u\|_2\le1+\|u\|_2^2$. Thus $D_\sigma(z)$ is well-defined. [F2, F15, F16, F17, F18, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Let $\alpha\in\mathbb N^n$ be a multi-index as in [F13]. At order zero, $\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma=\rho_\sigma$. If $\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(w)=P(w)\rho_\sigma(w)$ for a polynomial $P$, then $\partial_j(P(w)\rho_\sigma(w))=(\partial_jP(w)-w_jP(w)/\sigma^2)\rho_\sigma(w)$, again a polynomial times $\rho_\sigma$. Induction on $|\alpha|$ proves the stated form for every finite derivative. On each compact set of $z$ values, both $|\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(z-u)|$ and $|u_i\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(z-u)|$ are bounded uniformly in $u$, since every polynomial times the Gaussian tends to zero at infinity. Apply [F3] coordinate by coordinate to $p_\sigma$ and to each numerator $N_i(z)=\int u_i\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)$; the uniform bounds supply an integrable majorant and [F4] justifies passage of each derivative limit through the integral. The same bounds for derivatives of order $|\alpha|+1$ give a uniform bound $M$ for the first derivatives of each resulting derivative on any compact ball $K$. For $z,w\in K$, apply [F12] to that derivative along $z+t(w-z)$, $0\le t\le1$, to obtain a difference bound $\sqrt n M\|z-w\|_2$; thus each resulting derivative is continuous. Iterating over $\alpha$ makes $p_\sigma$ and every $N_i$ smooth. Since $p_\sigma>0$, the reciprocal $r(s)=1/s$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$: its first derivative is $-r(s)^2$ by the difference quotient, and repeated use of [F8] shows every higher derivative is a polynomial in $r$. Thus [F9] makes $D_\sigma=(N_i/p_\sigma)_{i<n}$ smooth; [F6], [F8], and positivity of $p_\sigma$ also make $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ smooth. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, F10, F12, F13, step 1.2]

3.1 For $a\in\mathbb R^n$, expand $u-a=(u-D_\sigma(z))+(D_\sigma(z)-a)$ and integrate. The cross term vanishes because $\int(u-D_\sigma(z))\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)=0$, giving $$\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)=\int\|u-D_\sigma(z)\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)+\|a-D_\sigma(z)\|_2^2.$$ Thus $D_\sigma(z)$ is the unique posterior squared-error minimizer. Differentiating $N_i/p_\sigma$ using [F3], [F5], [F7], [F8], and [F9] gives $$\partial_jD_{\sigma,i}(z)=\frac1{\sigma^2}\left(\int u_i u_j\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)-D_{\sigma,i}(z)D_{\sigma,j}(z)\right),$$ because the terms containing $z_j$ cancel. This is exactly the stated symmetric covariance formula. [F1, F3, F5, F7, F8, F9, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For each coordinate $j$, $\partial_j\rho_\sigma(z-u)=(u_j-z_j)\rho_\sigma(z-u)/\sigma^2$. Differentiating under the integral by [F3] and using step 1.2 gives $\nabla p_\sigma(z)=p_\sigma(z)(D_\sigma(z)-z)/\sigma^2$. Since $p_\sigma(z)>0$, [F6] gives $\nabla\log p_\sigma=\nabla p_\sigma/p_\sigma$, proving both Tweedie identities in the Statement. [F3, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 For nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $$v^{\mathsf T}J D_\sigma(z)v=\sigma^{-2}\int\langle v,u-D_\sigma(z)\rangle^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$ If this were zero, then for each $k\ge1$ the set where $|\langle v,u-D_\sigma(z)\rangle|\ge1/k$ would have $\nu_{\sigma,z}$-measure zero; their union is the complement of the affine hyperplane $\{u:\langle v,u\rangle=\langle v,D_\sigma(z)\rangle\}$. Hence that hyperplane has full $\nu_{\sigma,z}$-measure. The density $\rho_\sigma(z-u)/p_\sigma(z)$ is strictly positive, so $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ and $\mu$ have the same null sets: if $\nu_{\sigma,z}(E)=0$, then each set $E\cap\{\rho_\sigma(z-u)/p_\sigma(z)\ge1/k\}$ has zero $\mu$-measure, and these sets cover $E$. Thus the hyperplane has full $\mu$-measure, contradicting the hypothesis. Therefore $J D_\sigma(z)$ is positive definite. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 3.1]

4.2 Fix $z$ and write $$\Psi_z(u)=\frac12\|D_\sigma(u)-z\|_2^2-\frac12\|D_\sigma(u)-u\|_2^2+\sigma^2q_\sigma(u).$$ By the definition of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$, this equals $\frac12\|D_\sigma(u)-z\|_2^2+\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}(D_\sigma(u))$. Differentiate using [F7] and the symmetry of $J D_\sigma$ from step 3.1: $$\nabla\Psi_z(u)=J D_\sigma(u)(D_\sigma(u)-z)-(J D_\sigma(u)-I)(D_\sigma(u)-u)+\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(u)=J D_\sigma(u)(u-z),$$ where the last equality uses $D_\sigma(u)-u=-\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(u)$ from step 3.2. [F1, F7, step 3.1, step 3.2]

5.1 If $z\ne w$, put $v=w-z$ and $\psi(t)=\langle D_\sigma(z+tv),v\rangle$ on $[0,1]$. By [F7] and step 4.1, $\psi'(t)=v^{\mathsf T}J D_\sigma(z+tv)v>0$. The mean-value theorem [F12] yields $\langle D_\sigma(w)-D_\sigma(z),w-z\rangle>0$, so $D_\sigma(w)\ne D_\sigma(z)$ and $D_\sigma$ is injective. [F1, F7, F12, step 4.1]

6.1 At every $z$, the derivative $J D_\sigma(z)$ is invertible by step 4.1. Apply [F11] at each $z$: every point has an open neighborhood mapped diffeomorphically onto an open neighborhood. Their images cover $X_\sigma$, so $X_\sigma$ is open. Injectivity from step 5.1 makes the local inverse maps agree on overlaps, giving the global inverse $D_\sigma^{-1}:X_\sigma\to\mathbb R^n$, which is smooth. Since $q_\sigma$ is smooth by step 2.1, the formula in the Statement makes $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ smooth on $X_\sigma$. [F9, F10, F11, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1]

7.1 For any $v\ne0$, let $\chi(t)=\Psi_z(z+tv)$ on $[0,1]$. Step 4.2 gives $\chi'(t)=t\,v^{\mathsf T}J D_\sigma(z+tv)v>0$ for every $t\in(0,1]$ by step 4.1. By [F12], $\Psi_z(z+v)>\Psi_z(z)$. Thus $u=z$ is the unique global minimizer of $\Psi_z$. Every $x\in X_\sigma$ has a unique form $D_\sigma(u)$ by step 6.1, while $h_{\sigma,\gamma}=+\infty$ outside $X_\sigma$; consequently $D_\sigma(z)$ is the unique global minimizer of $\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)$ over all $x\in\mathbb R^n$. [F12, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 4.2] ∎

---
id: lem-kontsevich-morse-isotopy-decomposition
kind: lemma
title: Generic isotopies have finite Morse movies
status: draft
origin: pipeline
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
deps:
  - def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids
  - def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy
  - def-countable-choice
  - thm-parametric-transversality
  - thm-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-on-manifolds
  - lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-compact-embedded-submanifolds-extends-to-an-ambient-isotopy
justified_by: []
dependency_level: 4
sources:
  references:
    - title: Introduction to Vassiliev Knot Invariants, §§8.6–8.7
      url: https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf
    - title: "Gualtieri, Topology I: Smooth Manifolds, §3.4, Theorem 3.26"
      url: https://www.math.toronto.edu/mgualt/courses/17-1300/docs/17-1300-notes-10.pdf

---

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K_s:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\times\mathbb R$, $0\le s\le1$, be a smooth isotopy of oriented embeddings that is constant near $s=0,1$, and suppose its endpoint height functions are strict Morse functions with distinct critical values. For every $\delta>0$, there is a smooth family of embeddings $\widetilde K_s$ fixed near $s=0,1$ and within $\delta$ of $K_s$ in the $C^1$ topology such that:

1. except at finitely many parameter values, $t|_{\widetilde K_s}$ is strict Morse with distinct critical values;
2. at each exceptional value, either one nondegenerate maximum-minimum pair is born or dies, or two distinct nondegenerate critical points have a transverse crossing of their critical values;
3. no two exceptional events occur at the same parameter, no three critical values coincide, and a birth or death does not coincide in height with another critical point.

The perturbation can be made in the height coordinate alone, so every $\widetilde K_s$ remains in the same oriented knot class as $K_s$. The diagram is a schematic of the allowed event types; the proof uses the jet conditions, not the drawing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9,thick]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (3,0) node[right] {$s$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1.4) -- (0,1.5) node[above] {critical value};
  \draw (0.1,0) .. controls (0.65,0) and (0.85,0.65) .. (1.35,0.72);
  \draw (0.1,0) .. controls (0.65,0) and (0.85,-0.65) .. (1.35,-0.72);
  \fill (0.1,0) circle (1.4pt);
  \node at (1.2,1.05) {birth/death};
  \draw (1.65,-1.1) -- (2.85,1.1);
  \draw (1.65,1.1) -- (2.85,-1.1);
  \fill (2.25,0) circle (1.4pt);
  \node at (2.65,1.35) {value crossing};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references

[[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids|Strict Morse height convention]]

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|Smooth isotopy of oriented knots]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §§8.6–8.7, printed pp. 233–240](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Gualtieri, Topology I: Smooth Manifolds, §3.4, Theorem 3.26, PDF pp. 34–35](https://www.math.toronto.edu/mgualt/courses/17-1300/docs/17-1300-notes-10.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth compact one-parameter family of oriented embeddings with fixed strict Morse endpoint heights, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[F1] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: a strict Morse presentation is an embedding of the compact oriented circle whose height has only nondegenerate critical points with distinct critical values.

[F2] [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]: oriented knot equivalence is ambient isotopy of the embedded oriented circle.

[F3] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the axiom of countable choice.

[F4] [[thm-parametric-transversality]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if a smooth finite-dimensional parameter family is transverse to a submanifold, then almost every parameter gives a transverse slice.

[F5] [[thm-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-on-manifolds]]: a smooth map with invertible derivative has a smooth local inverse.

[F6] [[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-compact-embedded-submanifolds-extends-to-an-ambient-isotopy]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a smooth isotopy through embeddings of the compact circle extends to an ambient isotopy.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Write $K_s(x)=(z(s,x),h(s,x))$ with $x\in S^1$. All perturbations below vanish on fixed collars of $s=0,1$.

1.1 The set of embeddings of the compact circle into $\mathbb R^3$ is open in the $C^1$ topology. To verify this for the given compact family, cover $S^1$ by finitely many parameter intervals on which the derivative of each $K_s$ has a uniform positive lower bound; a sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation remains an immersion there. On the compact complement of a neighborhood of the diagonal in $S^1\times S^1$, injectivity has a uniform positive separation because $(s,x,y)\mapsto\|K_s(x)-K_s(y)\|$ is continuous and positive. A sufficiently small $C^0$ perturbation preserves that separation. Thus a small perturbation of $h$ alone keeps every slice embedded and fixed at the two endpoint collars. The straight interpolation between $h$ and its perturbation is also $C^1$-small, hence stays embedded; [F6] extends this path to ambient isotopy. [given, F1, F2, F6, construct, algebra]

1.2 For a smooth height family $h$ on $S^1\times[0,1]$, use finitely many coordinate intervals and smooth bump functions supported away from the endpoint collars to form a finite-dimensional perturbation family $h_a=h+\sum_j a_j\phi_j$. Cutoff multiples of $x$, $x^2/2$, $x^3/6$, and $(s-s_0)x$ prescribe, independently, $h_x,h_{xx},h_{xxx},h_{xs}$ at a point; finitely many smaller intervals cover the compact cylinder. The universal maps for $h_x$, $(h_x,h_{xx})$, $(h_x,h_{xx},h_{xxx})$, and $(h_x,h_{xx},h_{xs})$ are transverse to zero because the parameter derivatives span the corresponding target coordinates. By [F4], choose one arbitrarily small parameter for which all four slices are transverse. The zero set of $h_x$ is then a one-manifold; the zero set of $(h_x,h_{xx})$ is zero-dimensional; and the two three-coordinate maps have no zeros because their two-dimensional source has smaller dimension than their target. Thus every degeneracy has $h_x=h_{xx}=0$, $h_{xxx}\ne0$, and $h_{xs}\ne0$. The fold condition is open, so later perturbations can be chosen small enough to preserve it. [given, F3, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 The fold set from step 1.2 is a compact zero-dimensional transverse preimage in the two-dimensional cylinder, hence finite. Near a fold $(s_0,x_0)$, the equation $h_x(s,x)=0$ has $h_x=h_{xx}=0$, $h_{xxx}\ne0$, and $h_{xs}\ne0$. By [F5], solve it locally as $s=\psi(x)$; differentiating gives $\psi'(x_0)=0$ and $\psi''(x_0)=-h_{xxx}/h_{xs}\ne0$. Thus on one side of $s_0$ there are exactly two nondegenerate critical points and on the other side none. Between these finitely many fold values, $h_x=0$ is a finite union of smooth branches by the implicit function theorem. At the birth, the two new critical values are distinct away from the fold: $h_x$ has constant nonzero sign between its two roots, so $h(s,x_+)-h(s,x_-)=\int_{x_-}^{x_+}h_x(s,x)\,dx\ne0$. [F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Remove small disjoint fold neighborhoods and endpoint collars from the parameter cylinder. On the remaining compact set, distinct critical points have a positive separation in the circle coordinate. Cover it by finitely many charts and add bump functions with disjoint small supports so that, at any two distinct critical points, the parameter derivatives independently span the two derivative values and the difference of the function values. For a pair $(x,y)$, the event map $(s,x,y)\mapsto(h_x(s,x),h_x(s,y),h(s,x)-h(s,y))$ is therefore transverse to zero for generic coefficients by [F4]. Its source and target both have dimension three, so its zeros are isolated. At a zero the derivative matrix has determinant $h_{xx}(s,x)h_{xx}(s,y)(h_s(s,x)-h_s(s,y))$. The first two factors are nonzero because the fold neighborhoods were removed; transversality makes the third nonzero. Thus the two critical values cross transversely. These zeros stay away from the removed diagonal neighborhoods by the fold model of step 2.1, so they form a compact zero-dimensional set and are finite. [F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Use further bump functions supported near mutually distinct critical points, so their value and derivative jets can be changed independently. For three distinct critical points, the event map with their three $x$-derivatives and two value differences has five scalar components on a four-dimensional parameter-and-point domain; [F4] makes its zero set empty. For two disjoint value crossings, four critical-point equations and two value differences give six components on a five-dimensional domain, so simultaneous crossings are absent. A birth/death coinciding in height with another critical point imposes $h_x=h_{xx}=0$ at the fold, $h_x=0$ at the other point, and equality of their values: four independent conditions on a three-dimensional domain, so this event is absent. A fold simultaneous with a value crossing at two other critical points imposes five independent conditions on a four-dimensional domain and is absent. Two folds at the same parameter impose four equations on a three-dimensional domain and are absent as well. The same finite-dimensional bump family can impose all these conditions simultaneously: the bad parameter set for each map is null by [F4], their finite union is null, and every coefficient ball contains a point outside that union. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Outside the finite fold and crossing parameters, every critical point is nondegenerate and the critical values are pairwise distinct, so each height slice is strict Morse. Steps 2.1–4.1 show that the only exceptional events are isolated max-min births or deaths and transverse crossings of two distinct critical values; the imposed three-point, four-point, and fold-pair conditions exclude simultaneous events and triple values. The total perturbation can be chosen arbitrarily small, so step 1.1 keeps every slice embedded and in the same oriented knot class. The perturbation vanishes near $s=0,1$, hence leaves the specified endpoint presentations fixed. [given, F1, F2, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ have a finite presentation. There is a finite list of words $w_1,\ldots,w_N\in G$ whose trace functions generate the coordinate ring of $X(E_K)$, so the map $[\rho]\mapsto(\operatorname{tr}\rho(w_1),\ldots,\operatorname{tr}\rho(w_N))$ is a closed embedding into $\mathbb C^N$, with defining ideal the kernel of the induced map $\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_N]\to\mathbb C[\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2)]^{SL_2}$. On the irreducible-character locus, equal trace coordinates determine conjugate representations; on the reducible locus, the quotient records the semisimplified diagonal character, not the possibly non-diagonalizable representative.

## Statement references

[Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long, and Shalen, §2](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~culler/papers/PlaneCurves/curves.pdf)

[Tillmann, §§4.2–4.8](https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the finite Wirtinger presentation of the knot group.

[F1] The character quotient coordinate ring is generated by traces of words ([[lem-sl2-character-trace-coordinate-algebra]]).

[F2] The character quotient is affine with finitely generated reduced coordinate algebra, the quotient map is onto, and generators give its actual closed coordinate model ([[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]]).

[F3] [[lem-equal-irreducible-sl2-traces-determine-conjugacy]] proves by the actual rank-two matrix-algebra and trace-pairing argument that equal irreducible trace characters are conjugate in $SL_2(\mathbb C)$, and a reducible representation has the trace character of its diagonal semisimplification. This is a pointwise proof, not an assertion of a representation over a function field.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], choose a finite algebra generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_s$ for the character coordinate algebra. Each $f_j$ is a polynomial in finitely many word traces by [F1]. The union of these finitely many word lists is finite; denote it by $w_1,\ldots,w_N$. Their traces generate an algebra containing all $f_j$, hence the entire coordinate algebra. This establishes one fixed finite list for the quotient, rather than just a separate list for each function. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Send $z_i$ to $t_{w_i}$. Step 1.1 makes this polynomial-ring map onto the reduced invariant coordinate algebra. Its kernel is therefore radical. The actual affine coordinate-ring construction in [F2] identifies the quotient with the closed zero locus of that kernel in $\mathbb C^N$ and its point map with the displayed trace-coordinate map. Thus this is the asserted closed embedding with exactly the stated defining ideal. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Equal listed coordinates give equal values of every element of the coordinate algebra by step 1.1. In particular they give equal traces on every group word. The irreducible claim follows from [F3], including preservation of irreducibility. A reducible representation is triangular in an invariant-line basis, and [F3] gives its diagonal semisimplification with identical traces. Since the listed traces are the quotient coordinates, both have exactly the same quotient point. This records the semisimplified character and does not assert conjugacy of a nonsemisimple triangular representation to that diagonal one. All full-AC hypotheses are retained from [F1] and [F2]; the pointwise conjugacy argument adds no choice axiom. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every finite ordered triangulation of a compact link exterior with certified positive-meridian edge loops and a label vector on each oriented edge, execution terminates. It returns exactly the finite free graded modules and boundary matrices prescribed by the procedure if and only if edge reversal, every oriented 2-simplex cocycle sum, and every marked-meridian image check pass; otherwise it returns invalid-labeling. The procedure does not recognize whether the supplied triangulation is a link exterior or whether the certified peripheral loops are genuine meridians; those are geometric input hypotheses.

## Statement references

[[alg-abelian-cover-chain-model-from-triangulated-exterior]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite ordered triangulation of a compact link exterior with certified positive meridian edge loops, and an encoded integer vector label on every oriented edge. Prove the procedure terminates and has exactly the stated validation behavior.

[F1] The procedure checks edge reversal, each oriented 2-simplex sum, and each meridian-loop evaluation, returns `invalid-labeling` upon a failed check, and otherwise constructs one boundary matrix entry for each oriented face incidence of each simplex ([[alg-abelian-cover-chain-model-from-triangulated-exterior]]).

[A1] The finite complex is a valid triangulation of the compact exterior, its 1-skeleton is connected, and the listed boundary loops are already certified as positive meridians. These geometric facts are input hypotheses; the procedure does not test them ([[alg-abelian-cover-chain-model-from-triangulated-exterior]]).

## Proof

1.1 There are finitely many edges, 2-simplices, meridian-loop edges, vertices, simplices, and face incidences in the finite input. Each validation pass performs finitely many additions and comparisons of integer vectors, so it terminates. It returns `invalid-labeling` at the first failed edge-reversal, face-sum, or meridian-image check; if none fails, it proceeds to construction. By [F1] there are no other label-rejection branches, so rejection occurs exactly for the stated failed checks. [given, F1, A1, construct]

2.1 By [A1] the 1-skeleton is finite and connected. The procedure scans its finite ordered edge list, adds an edge exactly when its endpoints lie in different current components, and merges those components. Each addition reduces the number of components by one; connectedness therefore yields a spanning tree after finitely many additions, with exactly $|V|-1$ edges. The paths in this tree have finite length, and the sum of their integer edge labels is a finite computation for each vertex. Each simplex has finitely many edges and faces, so the prescribed exponent and signed Laurent coefficient are computed by finitely many additions, comparisons, and table insertions. There are finitely many simplices, hence all boundary matrices are produced and the algorithm terminates with exactly the free modules and face-incidence entries in [F1]. [A1, F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$. Use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$, and interpret natural numbers in real scalar expressions as their canonical real images. Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and suppose that for some $0<\rho<1$ and $\tau>0$,
$$\|h_S\|_2\le\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{s}}\|h_{S^c}\|_1+\tau\|Ah\|_2$$
for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$, where for any vector $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $v_S$ agrees with $v$ on $S$ and vanishes on $S^c=[n]\setminus S$. Let $x^\dagger\in\mathbb R^n$, $\epsilon\ge0$, and $e\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfy $y=Ax^\dagger+e$ and $\|e\|_2\le\epsilon$. Define
$$\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1:=\min\{\|x^\dagger_{T^c}\|_1:T\subseteq[n],\ |T|\le s\}.$$
The indexing family is finite and nonempty, so this minimum is attained; it also equals the minimum of $\|x^\dagger-z\|_1$ over vectors $z$ with at most $s$ nonzero coordinates. Then the basis-pursuit denoising problem
$$\min_{z\in\mathbb R^n}\|z\|_1\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|Az-y\|_2\le\epsilon$$
has a minimizer. Every minimizer $\widehat x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_2\le C_1\frac{\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1}{\sqrt{s}}+C_2\epsilon,\qquad \|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_1\le C_3\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1+C_4\sqrt{s}\,\epsilon,$$
where
$$C_1=\frac{2(1+2\rho)}{1-\rho},\quad C_2=\frac{6\tau}{1-\rho},\quad C_3=\frac{2(1+\rho)}{1-\rho},\quad C_4=\frac{4\tau}{1-\rho}.$$
If the certified finite basis-pursuit denoising procedure returns **success**, its returned vector is a minimizer and satisfies these same bounds. Only reconstruction error is bounded; the theorem asserts neither uniqueness nor support recovery.
## Statement references

[[lem-ip-bpdn-dual-certificates|Exact success certificate implies optimality]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §4.3, Theorem 4.22, printed pp. 87–88](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

[Mendelson, Rauhut, and Ward, *Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions*, §2.1, Theorem 2.2, printed p. 5](https://www.mathc.rwth-aachen.de/~rauhut/files/circulant-independent.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $m,n\ge1$, $1\le s\le n$, a real matrix $A$ satisfying the robust nullspace inequality, a truth $x^\dagger$, a radius $\epsilon\ge0$, a perturbation $e$ with $y=Ax^\dagger+e$ and $\|e\|_2\le\epsilon$, and any minimizer $\widehat x$ of the residual-constrained $\ell^1$ problem.

[F1] [[def-ip-robust-nullspace-property]]: for every $h$ and every $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|\le s$, $\|h_S\|_2\le\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{s}}\|h_{S^c}\|_1+\tau\|Ah\|_2$.

[F2] [[def-ip-best-s-term-l1-error]] and [[lem-ip-best-s-term-l1-sparse-vector-formulation]]: $\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1$ is the finite coordinate-tail minimum and equals the minimum $\ell^1$ error over vectors with at most $s$ nonzero coordinates.

[F3] [[lem-ip-largest-s-coordinates-attain-best-s-term-l1-error]]: the first $s$ largest coordinates attain this minimum and maximize the retained $\ell^1$ mass over all sets of size at most $s$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-robust-nsp-block-tail-estimate]]: if $S$ is the first $s$ coordinates of $h$ ordered by decreasing absolute value with increasing-index tie breaks, then $\|h_{S^c}\|_2\le\|h_S\|_2+\|h_{S^c}\|_1/\sqrt{s}$.

[F5] [[lem-ip-bpdn-minimizer-exists]]: nonempty finite-dimensional residual balls admit a global $\ell^1$ minimizer.

[F6] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]: the finite-dimensional one- and two-norms obey their triangle and homogeneity laws.

[F7] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $\|v\|_1\le\sqrt{k}\|v\|_2$ on a coordinate set of size $k$.

[F8] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums preserve coordinatewise inequalities and split over disjoint sets.

[F9] [[def-canonical-natural]]: $\sqrt{s}$ means $\sqrt{s}$ in real scalar expressions.

[F10] [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]: $s>0$, so all divisions by $\sqrt{s}$ are defined.

[F11] [[alg-ip-basis-pursuit-denoising]]: a returned **success** vector is accompanied by the exact feasibility and primal-dual certificate checks stated in the Algorithm.

[F12] [[lem-ip-bpdn-dual-certificates]]: those exact checks imply that the returned feasible vector is a global minimizer.

## Proof

1.1 The truth $x^\dagger$ is feasible because $\|Ax^\dagger-y\|_2=\|e\|_2\le\epsilon$. Thus the feasible set is nonempty, and [F5] supplies at least one minimizer. Fix any minimizer $\widehat x$ and put $h=\widehat x-x^\dagger$. [given, F5, F6, construct]

1.2 Order the coordinates of $x^\dagger$ by decreasing magnitude, breaking ties by increasing index, and let $T$ be the first $s$ indices. By [F2,F3], $\|x^\dagger_{T^c}\|_1=\sigma_s(x^\dagger)_1=:\sigma$. Minimality of $\widehat x$ and the triangle inequality give $\|x^\dagger_T+h_T\|_1+\|x^\dagger_{T^c}+h_{T^c}\|_1\le\|x^\dagger_T\|_1+\|x^\dagger_{T^c}\|_1.$ Applying $\|a+b\|_1\ge\|b\|_1-\|a\|_1$ to the two disjoint restrictions yields $\|x^\dagger_T\|_1-\|h_T\|_1+\|h_{T^c}\|_1-\|x^\dagger_{T^c}\|_1\le\|x^\dagger_T\|_1+\|x^\dagger_{T^c}\|_1.$ After cancellation this is $\|h_{T^c}\|_1-\|h_T\|_1\le2\sigma$, hence the cone estimate $\|h_{T^c}\|_1\le\|h_T\|_1+2\sigma$. [given, F2, F3, F6, F8, construct, algebra]

2.1 Independently order $h$ by decreasing magnitude with the same deterministic tie break and let $S$ be its first $s$ indices. Since $T$ has size $s$, [F3] gives $\|h_T\|_1\le\|h_S\|_1$ and $\|h_{S^c}\|_1\le\|h_{T^c}\|_1$. Step 1.2 therefore yields $\|h_{S^c}\|_1\le\|h_S\|_1+2\sigma.$ The data relation and feasibility give $Ah=(A\widehat x-y)+e$, so the triangle inequality gives $\|Ah\|_2\le2\epsilon$. [given, F3, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Set $u=\|h_S\|_2\ge0$. Applying [F1] to this $S$, then using step 2.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz on its $s$ coordinates, gives $u\le\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{s}}\|h_{S^c}\|_1+\tau\|Ah\|_2 \le\rho u+\frac{2\rho\sigma}{\sqrt{s}}+2\tau\epsilon.$ Since $1-\rho>0$, rearranging proves $u\le\frac{2\rho}{1-\rho}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{s}}+\frac{2\tau}{1-\rho}\epsilon.$ [F1, F7, F9, F10, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F4] to $h$ and its chosen largest-coordinate set $S$. Step 2.1 and [F7] show $\|h_{S^c}\|_2\le u+\frac{\|h_{S^c}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}} \le u+\frac{\sqrt{s}\,u+2\sigma}{\sqrt{s}} =2u+\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt{s}}.$ By the triangle inequality on $h=h_S+h_{S^c}$, $\|h\|_2\le3u+2\sigma/\sqrt{s}$. Substitute step 3.1 and simplify: $\|h\|_2\le\left(\frac{6\rho}{1-\rho}+2\right)\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{s}}+\frac{6\tau}{1-\rho}\epsilon =\frac{2(1+2\rho)}{1-\rho}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{s}}+\frac{6\tau}{1-\rho}\epsilon.$ [F4, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 Disjoint coordinates and step 2.1 give $\|h\|_1\le\|h_S\|_1+\|h_{S^c}\|_1\le2\sqrt{s}\,u+2\sigma$ by [F7]. Substituting step 3.1 yields $\|h\|_1\le\left(\frac{4\rho}{1-\rho}+2\right)\sigma+\frac{4\tau}{1-\rho}\sqrt{s}\,\epsilon =\frac{2(1+\rho)}{1-\rho}\sigma+\frac{4\tau}{1-\rho}\sqrt{s}\,\epsilon.$ This proves both bounds for the arbitrary minimizer fixed at step 1.1. [F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If the finite procedure returns success, [F11] gives the same exact feasibility and certificate conditions, and [F12] makes its vector a minimizer. Steps 1.2, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1, and 4.2 therefore apply to that vector as well. No step uses uniqueness or identifies a support. [F11, F12, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎
