## Statement

Assume countable choice. For each Carter–Saito movie move, the two movie segments have the same incoming and outgoing oriented link diagrams and represent isotopic portions of an oriented surface cobordism relative to their boundary collars. The induced maps on the integral even Khovanov homology groups of those diagrams differ by multiplication by a single overall sign. The same conclusion holds when two disjoint critical points of the height function are interchanged.

## Statement references

[[def-khovanov-cobordism-map-up-to-sign|The map associated to a fixed generic movie]]

[[lem-khovanov-frobenius-tqft-respects-barnatan-relations|The Frobenius TQFT and the S, T, and four-tube relations]]

[[lem-barnatan-formal-kink-retractions|Explicit formal kink retractions]]

[[lem-barnatan-formal-inverse-boundary-crossings|Both inverse-crossing retractions]]

[[lem-barnatan-formal-third-reidemeister-equivalence|Both third-move constructions]]

[[lem-barnatan-open-pairings-have-scalar-degree-zero-endomorphisms|Scalar endomorphisms of pairings]]

[[lem-barnatan-planar-homotopies-and-conditional-boundary-crossing-simplicity|Planar homotopies and crossing simplicity]]

[[lem-barnatan-morse-movie-matrices|The five explicit Morse movie checks]]

[[lem-integral-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-defines-a-cobordism-functor|The integral Frobenius functor]]

[[def-carter-saito-euclidean-local-movie-moves|The fifteen local geometric models]]

[Bar-Natan, *Khovanov's homology for tangles and cobordisms*, §8.3 and Theorem 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410495v2)

[Jacobsson, *An invariant of link cobordisms from Khovanov homology*, Lemmas 5.1–5.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0206303)

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial*, §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice and either one of the fifteen Euclidean local movie relations in a fixed planar outside, or an interchange of two disjoint surface-height critical events. Work first in the additive formal surface category and apply the closed-surface functor only after inserting the outside.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited by the geometric disk-system and link-homology suppliers. The finite cubes and matrix compositions require no further choice.

[F1] [[def-khovanov-cobordism-map-up-to-sign]] fixes the actual Bar-Natan local systems, their inverses, crossing permutations and normalization; it does not permit arbitrary automorphisms as replacement maps.

[F2] [[lem-barnatan-formal-kink-retractions]], [[lem-barnatan-formal-inverse-boundary-crossings]] and [[lem-barnatan-formal-third-reidemeister-equivalence]] provide actual internal degree zero equivalences for the three Reidemeister moves, with their displayed inverses and homotopies.

[F3] [[lem-barnatan-open-pairings-have-scalar-degree-zero-endomorphisms]] says that the degree-zero endomorphisms of a crossingless pairing form $\mathbb Z$ generated by its identity. Its degree-zero homotopy automorphisms are therefore exactly $\pm1$.

[F4] [[lem-barnatan-planar-homotopies-and-conditional-boundary-crossing-simplicity]] gives invariance of this simplicity under degree-zero equivalence and under adjoining a boundary crossing when both crossing inverse equivalences exist. The latter premises are supplied by the two physical orders in [F2]. It also gives signed planar insertion of homotopies.

[F5] [[lem-barnatan-morse-movie-matrices]] proves the five Morse relations MM11–MM15 for exactly the selected systems, including both directions and the cube signs.

[F6] [[lem-integral-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-defines-a-cobordism-functor]] constructs the actual integral functor on closed surfaces, not only a conditional factorization. [[lem-khovanov-frobenius-tqft-respects-barnatan-relations]] makes it descend through S, T and four-tube. Finite matrices and chain homotopies therefore pass to the stated integral cube complexes.

[F7] [[def-carter-saito-euclidean-local-movie-moves]] specifies the fifteen coordinate models. [[def-barnatan-open-tangle-cobordism-complexes]] specifies their formal cubes and signed planar totalization.

## Proof

1.1 **Inverse clips.** For MM1–MM5, a Reidemeister move is followed by its selected inverse, possibly with a planar change of frame between them. The equations in [F2] make the composite homotopic to the identity. All reflections and compatible strand orientations use the corresponding specified local coordinate identification in [F1]; the cochain and internal shifts agree at both ends. Thus the five inverse clips satisfy their formal movie relation before any closed evaluation. [given, A1, F1, F2, F7, construct]

1.2 **Simple base frames for the five circular clips.** Each of MM6–MM10 consists solely of Reidemeister moves, so it gives a degree-zero homotopy automorphism of its starting tangle complex by [F2]. The following explicit starting frames of the models in [F7] are simple. For MM7 choose the frame before the small cusp loop: it is a single bent arc, hence a pairing. For MM8 choose the frame before the cusp crosses the third strand: its two arcs have one transverse crossing and no small loop; peeling this sole boundary crossing leaves a pairing. For MM9 choose the frame before the cubic double-curve turn: it likewise has two arcs with one crossing, which peels off at the boundary. The MM6 starting frame is two parallel arcs crossed by a third transverse arc. Its two crossings peel in order from an end of the transverse arc, leaving three disjoint arcs. More explicitly, the outermost crossing has two adjacent free legs in the disk boundary; cut a small collar rectangle containing that crossing and those legs, leaving one boundary-crossing addition to the smaller tangle. After removing it the other crossing has the same property. For MM10 the initial frame is the four small affine strand segments resolving the projected quadruple point, with six pairwise crossings. Choose a linear height not perpendicular to any segment and place upper and lower cuts beyond all six crossings. Each segment is a graph over that height. Order the six crossing heights after a small planar perturbation; the highest crossing is between adjacent outgoing strands, so its two free legs give a boundary-crossing collar rectangle. Remove it and repeat down the ordered list. This peels all six crossings and leaves a pairing, for every retained over/under order. These cuts merely parametrize the local disk and straighten its outside arcs; no crossing change is used. Thus the boundary-crossing equivalences in [F4] and [F2], beginning with [F3], prove simplicity of all five base frames. Starting the same circular clip at a different frame conjugates its endomorphism by a product of equivalences, so [F4] also gives simplicity there. [F2, F3, F4, F7, construct]

1.3 **The five Morse clips.** For MM11 use the explicit disk cancellation. For MM12 and MM13 use the two columns $D_a-T,D_b-T$ and the integral identity $D_a+D_b=2T$; the upward clips have their separately checked cap/saddle maps. For MM14 use its two circle-birth columns, with the reverse-order RII cube sign retained in both. For MM15 use the residual saddle column $(\alpha,\beta)^T$, or its actual target-retract row in the upward version, with the middle cube permutation and last-vertex sign. These are exactly the five proved calculations of [F5]. Hence the two formal maps agree up to a single sign for every nonreversible clip as well. [F1, F2, F5, construct]

2.1 **Circular clips.** The degree-zero homotopy automorphism of each MM6–MM10 base frame is therefore homotopic to $\varepsilon1$, where $\varepsilon=1$ or $-1$. This is one scalar in the formal endomorphism group of the whole local complex, not a separate sign on its states. Changing a base frame conjugates that equation by equivalences and preserves the same assertion. A relation presented as two alternative paths is equivalent to its circular clip: compose one path with the selected inverse of the other; its homotopy inverse exists by [F2]. Multiplying the circular equation by the other path therefore makes the two path maps equal up to this one sign. This proves all five circular relations without assuming that arbitrary maps between two homology groups agree up to sign. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 **Outside complexes and distant events.** Insert each formal equation or homotopy into the fixed planar outside by [F4]. For two distant elementary events, decompose their disjoint support disks and the outside as one planar operation. Their maps have cochain degree zero; a Morse map can have nonzero quantum degree, but the totalization signs use cochain degree alone. Acting in the first disk and then the second therefore gives the same matrix as acting in the opposite order. The crossing-order changes in [F1] are exactly the signed tensor interchanges of [F7], so the assertion also holds when a Reidemeister event changes the number or order of crossings. In particular it holds for the two distant surface-height critical events in the statement. Now all objects are closed resolutions. Apply [F6] entry by entry; its additivity, gluing and relation factorization preserve each formal chain-map equality and homotopy. The images are precisely the integral maps fixed in [F1], including empty resolutions and the identity on unaffected circles. [F1, F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

4.1 Pass to homology in step 3.1. A chain homotopy becomes equality, and the one scalar $\varepsilon$ becomes multiplication by that same overall sign on the full integral homology group. The construction covered MM1–MM5, MM6–MM10 and MM11–MM15, all their stated variants, and the distant interchanges. Thus every relation asserted in the statement preserves the selected map up to one sign. No assertion about spherical sweep-around follows from these Euclidean local computations. [A1, F1, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.3, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and a smooth winding-zero pattern $P$ whose axis has nonzero integral classical Blanchfield self-value. Use oriented zero surgery $M(K)$ and the first-positive-push Levine–Tristram signature function $\sigma_J$. Let $L>0$ exceed the uniform Cheeger–Gromov bound for every rho value of $M(P(U))$ under every group representation. For every $n,m\ge1$, there are distinct odd primes $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ outside the finite exceptional set for reduction of this self-value and finite disk-band companion knots $J_i$ such that, writing $\zeta_p=\exp(2\pi i/p)$,
$$D_i=\frac1{p_i}\sum_{r=0}^{p_i-1}\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i}^{r})>mnL,$$
with $\sigma_{J_i}(1)=0$, $\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i})=\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i}^{-1})>p_i mnL/2$, all other nonidentity $p_i$-th-root signatures zero, and every $p_j$-th-root signature zero for $j\ne i$. Thus $D_i$ is the canonical $\mathbb Z/p_i$ cyclic defect of $M(J_i)$. In any candidate smooth bounding bordism for a nonzero integer vector $(a_i)$ used in the actual finite-prime infection obstruction assembly, choose $i_*$ with $|a_{i_*}|=\max_i|a_i|$. Its supplied quotient using $p_{i_*}$ gives signed bottom boundary contribution $a_{i_*}D_{i_*}$; the remaining $n\sum_i|a_i|$ pattern terms have total absolute value less than $nL\sum_i|a_i|\le nmL|a_{i_*}|<|a_{i_*}|D_{i_*}$. Thus the total signed boundary rho value has the sign of $a_{i_*}$ and is nonzero.

For every $n\ge1$, the three-branch obstruction assembly also admits a finite disk-band companion knot with a canonical cyclic defect $D>3nL$. For any supplied candidate smooth homology-circle bound in that assembly, its quotient kills the distinguished negative bottom branch and gives either $0$ or $D$ on each positive bottom branch, with at least one value $D$. Its $3n$ remaining pattern terms have total absolute value less than $3nL$, so the total boundary rho value is positive. For a locally flat TOP pair-family application, the initial bordism must supply the actual height-$n$ pairs and height-$(n+1)$ isotropic lifts; for a TOP three-branch application it must supply the actual homology-circle bound. In either case the finite-projective coefficient quotient must satisfy the stated survival and vanishing hypotheses, and the boundary rho values must agree with the smooth bounding defects by the closed TOP bordism equality. Pairwise relatively prime Alexander polynomials belong only to the separate Theorem C comparison of distinct patterns; they are not hypotheses of Theorems A or B.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F2] For any finite distinct odd primes and positive heights, explicit finite disk-band knots have nonnegative signature functions whose own selected primitive pair has value $2N_i$ exceeding its height, whose other selected roots have value zero, and whose other selected-prime means vanish. Thus the same smooth uniform bound applies to that boundary invariant; no smoothing of the given four-manifold is used. [[thm-topological-finite-projective-l2-duality-and-boundary-gluing]], [[thm-topological-lifted-half-pairs-force-amenable-signature-defect-zero]], [[thm-cheeger-gromov-uniform-rho-bound]]

[[lem-cha-kim-integral-solvability-and-blanchfield-bordism]], [[thm-unimodular-infection-tower-data-force-mixed-derived-meridian-survival]], [[thm-three-branch-infection-data-admit-nonhomomorphism-coefficient-quotients]]

**Given:** The actual finite-stage data and AC. First take the smooth bounding-defect application.

1.1 Fix the stage $n\ge1$ and desired family size $m$. Choose $L>0$ greater than [F1]'s bound for the one fixed pattern surgery $M(P(U))$. The integral axis reduction has one finite exceptional-prime set, already checked on the actual coefficient maps in [F3]. Choose distinct odd $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ outside that set, and apply [F2] at heights $p_i mnL/2$. Its actual first-push surfaces give $2N_i>p_i mnL/2$, hence $D_i=4N_i/p_i>mnL$, with zero selected cross-prime means. This proves the normalized inequality for the actual companion term; a large point-signature value alone, without its factor of $p_i$, would not prove it. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For any nonzero signed coefficient vector $(a_i)$, choose $i_*$ with maximal $|a_i|$. The simultaneous finite-forest map of [F3] gives order exactly $p_{i_*}$ on every actual bottom meridian. Its restriction there is cyclic, and its extension over the canonical companion bound has that same positive meridian image. Actual same-complex subgroup induction and smooth independence in [F3] therefore make the signed bottom sum exactly $a_{i_*}D_{i_*}$; changing a cyclic generator only permutes the normalized roots. There are exactly $n\sum_i|a_i|$ remaining signed pattern terms, each of absolute value below $L$. Their sum has absolute value below $nL\sum_i|a_i|\le nmL|a_{i_*}|<|a_{i_*}|D_{i_*}$. The selected bottom sum thus has the fixed sign of $a_{i_*}$ and cannot be cancelled. This is the precise domination used in Theorem A. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Each of its two positive bottom branches has value zero or $D$, and at least one is $D$. All asserted choices are finite and no coprime Alexander assumption has entered either construction. The separate source statement in section6 compares two different patterns under relative primeness of their closure Alexander polynomials; that hypothesis was neither used nor silently transferred here. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 For a supplied TOP initial bound, [F5] supplies the actual quotient maps and bottom orders, and [F4] gives its actual half-pair zero defect and identifies every remaining boundary term with the invariant bounded in [F1]. ## Statement

Let $P\subset S^2$ be the finite projection graph of a regular link diagram. If $P$ is disconnected, there is a simple closed curve $\gamma\subset S^2\setminus P$ such that $P$ has points on both sides of $\gamma$.

## Statement references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2 and Exercise 5.14](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Menasco, *Closed incompressible surfaces in alternating knot and link complements* (1984), §2](https://www.scribd.com/document/471863717/1-s2-0-0040938384900235-main-2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite disconnected projection graph $P\subset S^2$.

[F1] A regular projection is a finite graph with finitely many transverse double points and no triple points; crossingless link components are embedded circles ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

[F2] A smooth Jordan curve on $S^2$ separates the sphere into two sides. To obtain the spherical form of the choice-free smooth Jordan-disk result, choose a point off the curve, apply a stereographic chart, and use the two disk sides supplied by [[lem-choice-free-smooth-jordan-disk-parameters-and-prescribed-collars]].

## Proof
1.1 Choose one connected component $P_0$ of $P$. Around each of its finitely many vertices take a small closed disk, and around each edge take a narrow closed strip joining the incident vertex disks; for a crossingless circle take an annular neighborhood. Round the finitely many corners. Because the graph is finite and its distinct components are disjoint compact sets, the disks and strips can be chosen so that their union $N$ is a compact connected subsurface of $S^2$ with smooth finite boundary, contains $P_0$ in its interior, and misses every other component of $P$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Choose points $p_0\in P_0$ and $p_1$ in another component of $P$. Choose a piecewise-smooth path from $p_0$ to $p_1$ transverse to the finite smooth boundary $\partial N$. Its endpoints lie respectively in the interior of $N$ and outside $N$, so it crosses $\partial N$ an odd number of times. The boundary has finitely many disjoint simple closed components; at least one, call it $\gamma$, is met an odd number of times. The curve $\gamma$ lies in $S^2\setminus P$, since $N$ contains $P_0$ in its interior and misses every other component. By [F2], every transverse crossing of $\gamma$ switches sides, so $p_0$ and $p_1$ lie on opposite sides of $\gamma$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The construction uses finitely many neighborhoods and applies also when $P_0$ is a crossingless circle; therefore it proves the asserted separation for every disconnected regular projection. Its chosen separating curve is a smooth boundary component of $N$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, cases] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be an oriented topological $4$-manifold with boundary, and let $V\subset X$ be a connected relatively open neighborhood endowed with a specified smooth structure compatible with its smooth boundary collar and the given framed disk data, whose specified boundary collars and normal framings are smooth in this structure. Assume $\pi_1(V)$ is good for disk embedding. Let $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(V,V\cap\partial X)$ be a finite proper smooth generic disk datum with pairwise disjoint embedded framed boundaries, and framed smooth immersed spheres $g_i$ satisfying $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$, $\mu(g_i)=0$, $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$, and $\mu(f_i)=0$, computed in $\mathbb Z[\pi_1(V)]$.

There is a finite family of proper framed one-story capped-grope towers in $V$, of first-story height at least four, whose attaching regions are the Whitney circles for a regular homotopy of the $f_i$. Their bodies extend to embedded convergent skyscraper pinched neighborhoods, each with a relative standard-two-handle parameterization preserving its attaching solid torus and framing. The corresponding embedded framed Whitney disks give pairwise disjoint proper locally flat disks $\bar f_i$ homotopic to $f_i$ rel boundary and framing. They carry product normal neighborhoods supplied by this construction and framed immersed geometric duals $\bar g_i$ homotopic in $V$ to $g_i$.

In particular one may take $V=X$ when $X$ and the given maps, boundary collars and framings are smooth. No existence of a smoothing of a general topological neighborhood is asserted. The towers are capped-grope skyscrapers; an unrestricted Casson-handle construction is not assumed.

## Statement references

[[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data|Framed disk data and equivariant Wall obstructions]]

[[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding|The exact good-group null-disk property]]

[[def-disk-like-capped-grope-height-one-and-one-half|Framed grope neighborhoods and height conventions]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated smooth neighborhood, good group, framed disk datum and Countable Choice.

[F1] [[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data]]: The Wall coefficients use the specified whiskers, sheet involution, local signs and disk-boundary normal framings. The relative extension obstruction is separate; the immersed spheres carry their own extending normal framings.

[F2] [[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding]]: Every based homomorphism from a supplied height-$1.5$ grope has a framed immersed null-double-loop disk in that grope neighborhood.

[F3] [[def-disk-like-capped-grope-height-one-and-one-half]]: The grope is its supplied framed four-dimensional block neighborhood, with body embedded and only allowed cap plumbings.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable families of nonempty choices admit a choice function; the shrinking constructions below also specify their successive finite choices.

[F4] [[thm-whitney-approximation-for-manifold-valued-maps]]: Its actual full proof supplies a proper Euclidean embedding, a smooth neighborhood retraction, and arbitrary positive pointwise approximation bounds under Countable Choice.

[F5] [[thm-parametric-transversality]]: A transverse evaluation family has a null bad-parameter set; the finite affine-jet families below verify that evaluation hypothesis explicitly.

[F6] Boundary framing and extending framing are different data. The output $\bar f_i$ retains the specified framing on its boundary normal bundle; this does not say that an arbitrary such boundary frame extends over $\bar f_i$. In the preceding Statement, “embedded framed Whitney disks” refers to the Whitney disks and their extending Whitney framings. A product normal neighborhood of a final disk supplies an auxiliary extending frame, independently of its prescribed boundary marking. On a boundary annulus with coordinates $(z,t)$, write the prescribed oriented boundary frame relative to that auxiliary frame as $A(z)\in GL^+(2,\mathbb R)$. The same $A(z)$ on $(z,t)$ carries that marking through the annulus. Only this annulus is used: no extension of $A$ over $D^2$ is asserted. These finite collar choices require no choice principle beyond the stated Countable Choice.

## Proof

1.1 **Section1: Finite contraction and cyclic-label cancellation.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data. [given, construct]

1.2 A finite framed four-dimensional capped-grope neighborhood is supplied, with its usual product collars and self-plumbing charts. Its body is embedded; only cap interiors have generic double points. An integer labeling means a homomorphism from the fundamental group of this actual neighborhood to Z. Paths to individual cap sheets are fixed once. Conjugating a based loop does not change its integer label. No arbitrary locally flat surface is given a tubular neighborhood by this hypothesis: the actual grope's framed block neighborhood is input. [construct]

1.3 Contract one top surface stage. Designate a finite subset of cap double points to be pushed off at that contraction, and choose a first and second sheet at each designated point. Then the resulting shorter capped grope has the same lower body, attaching circle and framing. Every old intersection not designated has parallel descendants with its old label. No designated old intersection remains. Every new cap intersection is a descendant of two designated intersections removed across dual caps at this same contraction, and its label is a difference of their labels, up to overall sign. Consequently, if all designated labels lie in an interval [a,b], every new label has absolute value at most b−a. [construct]

1.4 Cut the top surface at each pair of symplectic attaching curves. Replace the cut part by two small parallel copies of each of its two caps and the small central square at their unique attaching-curve intersection. Cutting a genus-g one-boundary surface along its complete symplectic system leaves the disk region with paired edges; the four parallel cap sectors and this square fill each pair of edges. Thus this replaces the surface with its contracted disk. All replacements take place in the supplied framed block. Parallel copies are made in its chosen normal coordinate; the central square uses the untwisted product collar, so the external attaching framing is unchanged. The result may be immersed, which is allowed. [construct]

1.5 For a designated point, take an embedded path on its second cap from that point to its attaching boundary, with interior avoiding all other double-point preimages. Finitely many paths on one cap can be chosen with disjoint interiors by an embedded finite tree and small parallel offsets. The two parallel copies of that path, closed across the central square, bound a ribbon Whitney disk pairing the two intersections of the first sheet with the contracted cap. In a product rectangle around the path, this is just the rectangle between the two parallel copies, closed by the boundary square. Its interior is disjoint from the old body and all unmodified sheets. A generic sufficiently small choice of the finitely many product widths is possible because their unwanted incidences are finitely many closed disjoint compact sets. No appeal to a normal bundle over an arbitrary TOP surface occurs. [construct]

1.6 Push the first sheet across this ribbon. This removes precisely the two paired intersections. The only ribbons that can meet are ones running across dual cap sectors: their boundary paths cross in the central square. Resolving those crossings by the prescribed order of the pushes creates intersections between the pushed first sheets. Ribbons on the same cap have been chosen parallel and disjoint, and ribbons belonging to different handles have disjoint block neighborhoods. Therefore every new intersection has exactly the stated two designated ancestors. Repeating for all parallel descendants removes the designated old point altogether. This is a finite sequence of ordinary finger/Whitney operations in explicit smooth block charts; a small relative perturbation makes the resulting intersections transverse. [construct]

1.7 Here is the label calculation, including the path issue. Let the two designated points have based first-to-second loops g,h. A path to the new intersection follows the first pushed sheet along the ribbon to its second-sheet cap, crosses the common central square, and returns along the other ribbon in reverse. Cancel the common paths in the old body. The resulting word is g h^{-1}; changing starting path conjugates it and exchanging the two resulting sheets inverts it. This is a calculation in the original supplied neighborhood, since every ribbon and push lies there. Its Z label is consequently ±(phi(g)−phi(h)). An old point copied to parallel sheets has its old loop with a small contractible product strip added, so its label is unchanged. The construction, classification of new intersections and claimed bound follow. [construct]

1.8 **Section2: The finite asymmetric bootstrap.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data. [given, construct]

1.9 Start with one symplectic pair above the bottom surface: on the positive side a framed capped surface R of positive genus, on the negative side a framed immersed cap W. The same construction is repeated for the finitely many pairs; their body blocks are disjoint, and interactions between cap systems are allowed. All operations fix a neighborhood of the original bottom surface and its attaching region. [construct]

1.10 Take two small framed parallel copies of R, at negative and positive normal coordinate, and join their boundary circles by the normal annulus crossing the attaching curve of W once. The result is an embedded closed surface of genus twice that of R. Its caps are the corresponding parallel copies of the caps of R. This is a sphere-like capped surface F: compressing its symplectic system gives a sphere. Its body meets W in one point and is disjoint from R; its cap intersections with all the old caps are unrestricted. The annulus and the single crossing are read in the supplied symplectic handle block, not in a hypothetical neighborhood of an arbitrary locally flat surface. [construct]

1.11 Construct a small parallel copy of F and contract its top stage to an immersed framed sphere T. During contraction, push every other cap sheet off T by the ribbons of Section1, excluding the one prescribed body intersection T with W. This includes the original caps of F, the caps of R and the remaining parts of W. All intersections newly produced by those pushes are between those cap sheets. The sphere T is therefore disjoint from both R and the body/caps of F, and from the caps of R, and meets W at its one prescribed point only. Self-intersections of T are allowed. The ribbons have support near cap arcs and their central squares, away from the lower body, so they do not alter any of the displayed body intersections. [construct]

1.12 Use T as a Norman sphere to remove every intersection of W with a cap of R or F: for each such point, choose a path in W from that point to the unique point W meets T. Remove a small disk from the intersecting cap and connect it by an untwisted tube, along a parallel copy of that path, to T with a small disk removed. The second endpoint consumes the one intersection of that parallel T with W. The two disks removed and the tube are the boundary of a product neighborhood of the path, so the resulting cap misses W at the chosen point and has the same boundary and framing. Choose the finitely many paths as branches of a tree in the abstract disk W, with separate parallel approach paths at their common endpoint; their interiors avoid all other double-point preimages. Normal widths are chosen successively small. The added copies of T are framed immersed spheres; their self- and mutual intersections belong entirely to the modified CAPS. Thus they may create cap intersections but no body intersections. Their original intersections with R or the body of F are empty, and sufficiently small parallel copies retain that property. After this finite operation W is disjoint from every other part except its own self-intersections and the single point on the body of F. In particular F remains a proper capped surface transverse to W. [construct]

1.13 For each self-intersection of W, tube one of its sheets to a separate small parallel copy of the BODY of F, along the other sheet and then along a chosen arc in W to the transverse point. This is the same local Norman cancellation, now using a capped surface instead of the contracted sphere. The new body consists of W with that sheet disk deleted, the punctured closed body of F, and their connecting annulus. It is a one-boundary surface with additional genus, with the old W boundary/framing. The caps of the added F provide the symplectic caps for its new handles. Its body is embedded: before the tubing, distinct body copies were disjoint and met W only at their distinct transverse endpoints; the tube arcs avoid every other double-point preimage. Choose disjoint parallel branches of a finite tree in W and nested normal widths. The tube neighborhoods consequently miss all other body sheets. Every old self-intersection of W is removed once, and none is introduced into the new body. Its new caps may intersect each other or the old caps, but they miss every body: the prior operation made the old caps disjoint from W, and properness of F makes its caps disjoint from all the parallel body sheets. At the attaching collars this assertion is the defining product chart. Consequently W has become an actual proper framed capped surface, not merely a surface with unaccounted body intersections. [construct]

1.14 This changes the side heights (1,0) to (1,1), preserving the original bottom stage. All choices and moves were finite. The scorecard is: R/body(F) embedded and mutually disjoint throughout; T immersed auxiliary, intersecting W once; old caps arbitrary among themselves; after the Norman cancellations all old caps miss W; after the final tubing every new intersection lies among caps. The auxiliary T is discarded after its copies have been inserted into caps. No disjointness of its parallel copies is needed, because their intersections are allowed cap intersections. [construct]

1.15 **Section3: Finite bootstrap to height three.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data. [given, construct]

1.16 Here the two side heights count stages ABOVE the fixed bottom surface. Section2 gives (1,0) to (1,1). The following side extension, used only finitely often in this bootstrap, supplies (1,1) to (2,1) to (2,3). Let P be the side to be raised and Q its other side, of heights p,q at least one. Construct F transverse to the bottom surface of P by taking two normal parallels of Q and closing their rims with the normal annulus. It is sphere-like of height q. Its body is embedded, meets P only at the specified first-stage point, and misses all other body stages; intersections of its caps with the old caps are allowed. [construct]

1.17 First make a contracted parallel sphere T transverse to the bottom of P, using Section1 and pushing off all original cap sheets and the caps of F. Its only body intersection is that prescribed transverse point. To make the caps of F disjoint from the old P caps, push an F-cap sheet at each intersection down the old P cap to its attaching stage and then down successive P stages to its bottom. A finger across one attaching collar replaces one intersection with two on the immediately lower stage; this is two parallel paths around the two ends of that collar. After p stages there are finitely many points on the bottom of P. Tube them off over parallel copies of T. These changes affect only caps of F. They cannot reintroduce intersections with old P caps because T misses those caps and the finger paths on the old caps avoid the other finitely many double-point preimages. The new intersections are among caps of F and possibly the old Q caps, which are still caps. All old body stages are fixed. [construct]

1.18 Now for an intersection of an old P cap with a Q cap, push the Q-cap sheet down the P stages and tube it off over T. The Q cap is still an immersed disk; its boundary and framing are fixed. It may acquire self/intersections with other caps, which are allowed. It remains disjoint from the old P caps and all body stages: the punctured T used in the tubing has had its unique bottom-P intersection removed. Crucially T is also disjoint from the body of F, so the Q caps miss every body piece to be added in the next step. [construct]

1.19 Finally treat every self/mutual intersection among the old P caps by pushing one of its P sheets down the P stages and tubing it off over copies of the full F, rather than T. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope: its first added stage is the old disk with punctured bodies of F attached, followed by the higher stages of those copies of F. Orient each added copy so its transverse intersection cancels the chosen point, and use the untwisted framed tubes. All old P-cap intersections have been removed; the added bodies are embedded and disjoint from each other because distinct body parallels of F are disjoint, and the tube paths avoid all other old preimages. The new caps are copies of F's caps. Those were made disjoint from ALL old P caps before this step, and properness makes them disjoint from F's parallel bodies. Consequently every new intersection is among caps, not on a new body. A cap with no intersections may be regarded as a genus-zero stage with no attached higher surface, as in the disk-like model. We have obtained side heights at least (p+q,q), with the previous body and its attaching framing preserved. The first and second steps are needed: merely asserting that tubing adds height would leave the old cap intersections on the new body. [construct]

1.20 All choices involve finite paths, parallels and normal widths in supplied framed blocks. Use the move first with p=q=1, then exchange the two sides and use p=1,q=2. Both sides then have height at least two, so the entire grope has height at least three. The induced integer labels on its finite plumbing generators are obtained by following their actual paths back to the original neighborhood; let B be the maximum of their absolute values. B exists without any growth estimate for this finite bootstrap. [construct]

1.21 **Section4: Efficient symmetric raising and the word bound.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data. [given, construct]

1.22 Once both sides have height at least two, there is an efficient variant which contracts only the TOP stage of a transverse grope. For the side P to be extended, form the transverse grope from the opposite side Q. Its height is that of Q. Contract its top stage and push the old caps off that contraction by Section1. The transverse grope now has height one less and its caps are disjoint from all old caps. Push each intersection on a P cap down the P stages, and at the bottom tube off over this transverse grope. The same body/cap scorecard as Section3 applies: new bodies consist of separate parallel copies of the old embedded opposite-side bodies, and all cap intersections have been removed from the new body before it is declared a body. This replaces each old P cap by a capped grope with the height of the contracted transverse grope. In terms of full path heights a,b INCLUDING the shared bottom, the updated path height is a+b−2. Alternate the sides. Starting with a_{−1}=a_0=3, the successive updated path heights obey a_n=a_{n−1}+a_{n−2}−2. The uniform height is the smaller of the two current path heights. Writing a_n−2 as a Fibonacci recursion gives, after 2k steps, uniform height at least 2^k: consecutive pairs increase the smaller Fibonacci term by at least a factor two. Additional initial height only improves the bound. [construct]

1.23 For clarity, the required estimate concerns WORDS, not numbers of double points. Base every old cap-point loop by a path in the old grope. Body-stage paths contribute no new plumbing generator. Contraction copies an old point without changing its generator. A push off a contraction creates the difference loop of Section1, a word of length at most two in the OLD cap-point generators. A new intersection among caps of the parallel transverse grope has length one, since its sheets are old parallel sheets. The only remaining type is a loop using a newly pushed-down finger: follow its first sheet across at most two old cap-point loops to the parallel transverse copy, cross its new cap intersection (one old generator), and return across at most two old loops on the other finger. The two bottom-stage paths cancel, as do the parallel collar paths. This is a concatenation of at most 2+1+2 old generators or inverses. These exhaust the new intersections: they occur on unchanged parallels, on a contraction push, or between two inserted fingers. Thus each step sends every NEW generator to a word of length at most five in the PRECEDING generators. Induction gives length at most 5^(2k) after 2k steps, and absolute Z label at most 5^(2k)B. No count of the possibly much larger number of points is substituted for this word bound. [construct]

1.24 **Section5: The special relative disk-to-disk operation in standardness.** The following finite construction and its limiting steps use the supplied framed data. [given, construct]

1.25 This is the operation of FQ4.6, with the actual relative data made explicit. Let f:B^4→B^4 be continuous and onto, with a homeomorphic boundary restriction. Its point-inverse collection is null (only finitely many fibres have diameter at least any positive epsilon), its singular IMAGE is nowhere dense, and E is a closed subset of the target containing the whole boundary. Suppose f:f^−1(E)→E is a homeomorphism. Then there is a homeomorphism h:B^4→B^4 equal to f on f^−1(E). Here E CONTAINS the boundary; it is not merely a subset of that boundary. The latter misreading would make the relative assertion too weak for the collared-tower application. [construct]

1.26 Use the following intermediate configuration. W is compact metrizable; e,f:B^4→W and g:W→B^4 are onto. The composites ge,gf are identity on the boundary. The fibres of g,ge,gf are null; their relevant singular images Sigma_g, g(Sigma_e),g(Sigma_f) are nowhere dense and pairwise well separated: neither set meets the closure of another. A protected closed set E_0 containing the boundary is disjoint from all three, and the relation e^−1 f is fixed there. Nullity makes each singular image countable (group the nontrivial fibres by diameter at least1/m). We will decrease both e- and f-fibre diameters while controlling the relations e^−1 f and f^−1 e between the TWO fixed domain balls. [construct]

1.27 Here is the local replacement. Choose a closed round ball B in the TARGET of g, disjoint from E_0,Sigma_g,g(Sigma_f), and a smaller concentric ball B_0 whose boundary misses g(Sigma_e). The restrictions over B for g and over the sphere boundary of B_0 for ge are homeomorphisms: they are continuous bijections of compact spaces to Hausdorff spaces. We require no open neighborhood of that sphere free of e singular values, which may accumulate on it. Replace g^−1(int B_0) in W by (ge)^−1(B_0), gluing their boundaries by e. The result is W'. On the inserted piece define e' to be the identity and g' to be ge; outside use the old e,g. These maps match at the gluing and satisfy g'e'=ge. The map e' is a homeomorphism over the inserted piece, so every e-fibre with g-image in B_0 has been eliminated. This is a finite compact adjunction, not a claim that W' is already a manifold. [construct]

Take a fresh family of capped-torus parallels with bodies in4/6<t<5/6 and contract it, pushing nothing off, to obtain spheres S_j geometrically dual to D'_j. [construct]

1.115 Pair the C–C' points by framed immersed Whitney disks. Their boundaries lie above t=4/6, and their nullhomotopies can be chosen there: deleting t<4/6 from a boundary collar is a homotopy equivalence with an explicit collar-push inverse. Tube these disks over S_j to make their interiors disjoint from all D'_j. The tube paths and spheres stay above the fresh lower collar slabs. Apply the geometric Casson move to C and C'. Its supports miss D'_j and all unused torus BODIES below4/6. Thus the new caps miss each other as the two collections, while arbitrary self/intersections within each cap collection are still allowed and remain algebraically cancelling. [construct]

1.116 Push the C' self/mutual points down D'_j and tube full capped-torus parallels with bodies in3/6<t<4/6. This adds the second surface stages, producing height-two capped gropes D''_j. Their body is embedded by the same scorecard as Section3. Separate their new caps C'' from C exactly as before, now using contracted parallels in2/6<t<3/6 and Whitney nullhomotopies outside t<2/6. All remaining torus bodies may now be taken in0<t<2/6. They and their caps are geometrically dual to the entire height-two gropes, including their caps. Raise the latter to any required finite height, keeping their first two stages, and successively contract one extra top stage to make their caps pairwise disjoint, with their self-points in canonical cancelling pairs. These neighborhood operations miss the dual capped surfaces because those were made disjoint from the whole starting grope except at the bottom transverse point. [construct]

1.117 Now the actual good-group Definition applies in its exact place. Choose grope height n+2.5. Each disjoint top height-1.5 component is a supplied disk-like framed grope. Apply goodness to its homomorphism into pi1(M') to obtain the framed null disk in that canonical model. Section14 smooths it within a neighborhood with trivial group image while retaining its attaching frame; thus it supplies the smooth immersed disk required here, with double-point loops null in M'. Distinct replacement disks lie in disjoint component neighborhoods. The retained grope has height n+1. Contract one top stage symmetrically: the new cap double loops are parallel copies or differences of the null loops, hence null; the cap self-points come in algebraically cancelling finger pairs. The first n stages have been kept EXACTLY. Taking n≥4 is sufficient for Sections7–12. [F2, construct]

1.118 Fill those double-point loops by framed immersed accessory disks. Their boundaries miss t<2/6, so their fillings may be pushed off that collar. Hence they miss the torus BODIES reserved there, although they may intersect its caps and the grope arbitrarily. Contract fresh dual capped surfaces with bodies in1/6<t<2/6 to get spheres S''_j. Correct the accessory framings, push their body intersections down, and tube over S''_j to clear the whole grope body. The resulting accessories are the proper tower top caps. Finally take the LAST capped-torus parallels with bodies in0<t<1/6 and contract them, pushing every tower-cap sheet off the contraction. Their bodies already miss the accessories by the collar choice. The resulting spheres R_j therefore miss the ENTIRE tower except for their prescribed bottom transverse point. This final contraction/push-off is the step which the uncontrolled use of the original spheres in Section6 could not provide. [construct]

1.119 The R_j are nullhomotopic in the ORIGINAL M. Indeed symmetric contraction of a fixed capped surface is independent up to homotopy of its caps: it is regularly homotopic to surgery on only the first cap of each pair; switch the unused second caps; it is also homotopic to surgery on only the second caps; then switch the first caps. Thus in M replace the caps built from g_i by the original small meridional caps. The contracted Clifford torus is now contained in the original double-point four-ball, and is null there. This proves [R_j]=0 in pi2(M), despite its being a useful nonzero class in pi2(M'). [construct]

1.120 Remove intersections of the original g_i with the towers by pushing them down the tower to the bottom and tubing over R_j. They still meet the f_i only at their one original dual point, since all these changes lie in M'. They now miss the entire tower. The changes of g_i are homotopies and additions of whiskered R_j, which are null in M, so preserve their original homotopy classes. Perform Sections7–12 inside neighborhoods of the towers disjoint from these g_i, with their one dual intersection moved into the protected attaching collar. The resulting embedded framed Whitney disks are disjoint from every g_i. Their Whitney moves on the f_i give disjoint properly locally flat embedded disks, regularly homotopic rel boundary/framing to the original f_i, and with the g_i still geometrically dual. They also provide the product normal charts required in the final surface-compression application: on the untouched pieces keep the old smooth disk frames; on each Whitney replacement use the pulled-back standard two-handle frame, glued by the Whitney framing along its two boundary arcs. This is a finite construction of a normal disk bundle over the resulting disk, trivialized by those compatible frames. Compactness permits sufficiently small widths so different patches overlap only by their prescribed bundle transitions and the resulting total-space map is injective. Thus the constructed disks have their OWN product tubes, without using the later general TOP normal-bundle theorem. Thus the original disk theorem's homotopy conclusion is supplied by WHITNEY MOVES, rather than assumed from an arbitrary standard-core choice. [construct]

1.121 **Section14: Smoothing a framed null disk inside a canonical grope neighborhood.** The following construction makes the relevant framing and foundation inputs explicit. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.122 This operation addresses the category of the disk obtained from GOODNESS, whose boundary is the canonical smooth attaching region of the framed model grope. It does not smooth an arbitrary original boundary knot or a TOP-generic disk in an unrelated ambient manifold. Its input is a generic immersed disk with the supplied extending framing/product germs which make its boundary the model attaching region. If 'framed boundary' were read as an arbitrary external integer without an extending framed immersion, the following parity argument would not apply; that is not the framed-disk convention used here. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.123 Let Q be the smooth framed model neighborhood, phi:pi1(Q)→Gamma, and d:D^2→Q the supplied generic framed disk with phi-null double-point loops. Its compact image A is homeomorphic to a finite polyhedron P: subdivide the parameter disk with the finitely many paired double-point preimages as vertices and with their stars disjoint, identify those vertex pairs, and subdivide once more. The resulting finite quotient complex maps continuously bijectively onto A and hence homeomorphically, by compactness and the Hausdorff target. Its fundamental group is generated by the finitely many double-point loops, since the disk before identifying the pairs is simply connected. Thus phi kills the entire image of pi1(A). [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.124 Here is an explicit neighborhood-retraction argument, avoiding a general normal-bundle theorem. Realize P as a finite subcomplex of a standard simplex, subdivide barycentrically, and note that its subdivision is FULL: a simplex whose chain of face-vertices all belong to P belongs to P. On the open star of P in that subdivided simplex, delete the barycentric coordinates at vertices outside P and normalize the remaining positive sum. Fullness makes this a continuous retraction onto P. A small neighborhood in Euclidean space first retracts to the simplex, by taking nonnegative coordinates and normalizing their sum. Composing gives a Euclidean neighborhood retraction onto P. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.125 Extend the finitely many coordinates of the inverse homeomorphism A→P continuously to Q as follows. For a residual continuous scalar function r_n on compact A with sup norm at most c_n, choose the least positive integer L_n such that
|r_n(a)−r_n(b)| ≤ c_n/2 + L_n dist(a,b)   for all a,b in A. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.126 Uniform continuity and boundedness give such an integer. Put h_n(x)=inf_(a in A)(r_n(a)+L_n dist(x,a)), clamped to[−c_n,c_n]. It is bounded and L_n-Lipschitz; on A its error from r_n lies between0 and c_n/2. Define r_(n+1)=r_n−h_n|A and c_(n+1)=c_n/2. The uniformly convergent sum of the h_n extends the original coordinate function exactly. All constants are suprema/infima or least integers, so this is a definable recursion. For a zero starting function use the zero extension. The finite coordinate extensions give a map Psi:Q→R^N. On the inverse image of the preceding Euclidean retraction neighborhood, compose with its retraction and P→A. This gives a continuous retraction r:U→A from an actual open neighborhood U of A. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.127 Form the smooth double $Q^{\mathrm{dbl}}$ from the two copies of the supplied smooth grope neighborhood, using its given product boundary collar, as in Section13. Use the proper Euclidean embedding j of this BOUNDARYLESS double and its smooth neighborhood retraction R supplied by the actual Whitney-approximation proof. There is a continuous fold c:Q^{dbl}→Q: it is the identity on the first copy, identifies the second copy with the first by the doubling identification, and in the shared collar is (x,t)→(x,|t|). For x in a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood U' of compact A in U⊂Q, the segment between j(x) and j(r(x)) stays in the domain of R. Indeed r fixes A, and compact j(A) has positive distance from the closed complement of that domain. The formula c(R((1−t)j(x)+t j(r(x)))) is a continuous homotopy IN Q from the inclusion U'→Q to r|U', fixed on A. Hence every loop in U' has phi-trivial image in Q. No smooth retraction onto the boundary of Q is used, and no smoothness of the fold is claimed. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.128 Carry out the smooth relative approximation and finite jet perturbation of d in the DOUBLE, fixing its supplied smooth attaching collar pointwise. Choose a smaller closed source boundary collar inside the collar where d is already smooth; keep a neighborhood of that smaller collar fixed by the cutoff. The complement of that neighborhood in the compact parameter disk is a compact set mapped into IntQ, since d is proper. Its image therefore has positive distance from the boundary of Q in the doubled metric. It also has a positive tolerance for remaining in U', by relative openness and compactness. Choose the approximation and subsequent finite perturbations below both tolerances. On the fixed collar the map remains d; everywhere else it stays in IntQ∩U'. Thus the resulting map is a smooth proper generic disk IN Q, with the original attaching collar and framing, and all its double-point loops lie in U'. The continuous fold used in1.127 is NOT applied to this smooth approximation. For the framing, take the supplied framed parallel of the original d with its disjoint boundary parallel. Its ordinary relative intersection with d is twice the signed self-point count, and is therefore even; the normal-zero term is absent because that frame extends. The relative intersection number is unchanged under homotopy fixing these boundary parallels. For the smooth approximation it equals2mu+e, by the local parallel-sheet count and the zeros of a generic normal section. Thus its relative Euler number e is even. Interior cusps change e by2, so finitely many restore e=0 and the required frame. Their new loops are trivial in the same small coordinate balls, so phi-nullness survives. The resulting SMOOTH framed generic null disk has the original attaching region. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.129 This operation shows why the goodness step can be consumed in the canonical smooth grope model with the framed-disk convention, without using arbitrary TOP neighborhood smoothing, stable5 integration, or the full boundary/collar smoothing needed for an unrelated original TOP-generic input. That boundary/collar bootstrap is not claimed here. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.130 **Section15: Countable Choice versus the successive tower choices.** The following construction makes the relevant framing and foundation inputs explicit. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.131 Countable Choice is not being identified with Dependent Choice. Saying 'choose a next tower at each stage' would not justify this foundation claim. The geometric selections in this particular smooth-model construction can instead be made by a single-valued least-code rule, after fixing the Euclidean embedding/retraction of the smooth neighborhood once. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.132 For a new disk with a specified smooth boundary collar, list pairs consisting of a dyadic collar width and a finite tuple of rational polynomials on the standard parameter disk. Use its supplied boundary-collar map b and a fixed smooth radial cutoff alpha, equal to1 on a smaller collar and0 off that collar. Form the Euclidean candidate alpha j(b)+(1−alpha)P and apply the fixed neighborhood retraction R. The term alpha j(b) is extended by zero only where alpha already vanishes; it is smooth there. Candidates are retained only when the Euclidean values lie in the retraction domain and the resulting map has the required proper boundary collar, genericity, support and finite intersection conditions. Framed candidates are listed simultaneously: project rational polynomial vector fields to the smooth normal plane of the candidate disk, blend them with the prescribed boundary frame on the same collar, and retain those with oriented linearly independent normal vectors everywhere. Orthogonal projection is computed from the ambient embedding metric and the derivative matrix, so is part of the fixed formula. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.133 Whenever an admissible smooth framed filling exists, some listed candidate exists. Choose the dyadic collar inside a collar on which that filling agrees with b. Rational polynomials approximate its Euclidean coordinates and its normal frame uniformly with the required first derivatives. Here is the needed C1 density calculation. Extend each smooth coordinate function slightly past the compact disk, using its finitely many local extensions and a finite smooth partition, and restrict to a containing square rescaled to[0,1]^2. Its Bernstein polynomial is the finite sum of f(k/n,l/n) times the two binomial basis polynomials. Uniform convergence follows from uniform continuity: the binomial weights are probabilities, and the weight outside a fixed distance eta of(x,y) is at most1/(2n eta^2) by the sum of their variances. Its x derivative is the analogous degree(n−1,n) sum of n(f((k+1)/n,l/n)−f(k/n,l/n)), each an average of the x derivative on an interval of length1/n; uniform continuity of that derivative and the same variance bound give uniform derivative convergence. The y derivative is identical. Approximate the finitely many coefficients by rationals with error smaller than the desired C1 tolerance divided by4n: the basis sums to1 and the derivative difference has bound2n times that error. Restrict back to the disk. This proves the claimed rational-polynomial C1 density rather than assuming an analytic power series for an arbitrary smooth function. The values stay in the open retraction domain; properness away from the fixed collar, the normal-frame determinant and the finite transversality angles have positive compact lower bounds. Thus sufficiently close candidates preserve them. Near a generic immersion the double points and their labels persist in disjoint coordinate balls and no new double points occur outside them, by compactness off the local-injectivity diagonal. For a group-null filling use Section14's open neighborhood with null group image: sufficiently close candidates lie there, so retain all null-loop conditions. Candidates which are required to lie in a prescribed relative homotopy class do so for sufficiently close approximations, by the straight retraction homotopy fixed on the boundary collar. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.134 The least natural-number code satisfying these actual predicates therefore specifies the disk and its frame uniquely. Decidability of the predicates is not asserted or needed for set-theoretic definability. This is not a choice function on arbitrary subsets of a mapping space: it is minimization in a specified COUNTABLE list which has just been proved nonempty for each geometric step. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

1.135 The other choices have the same form. Paths and finger arcs are finite polygonal/rational smooth approximations in the already specified charts, with endpoint templates and finite disjointness conditions. Parallel widths and modification balls use the first dyadic radius meeting the strict compact separation conditions. Finite orderings of double points can be obtained lexicographically from their distinct parameter preimage coordinate tuples, and every finite tree or interval subdivision is chosen in that ordering. The local shrinking Baire step of Section5 has its own explicit countable rational bump rule, preserving every earlier finite avoidance margin. The successive approximations of Sections9–12 use least cofinal story levels and least integer tolerances. No choice is made over an uncountable family of possible future branches. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

2.1 Thus each next finite stage is a uniquely defined function of the previous finite stage, the original input and the fixed embedding/retraction. Ordinary recursion on the natural numbers constructs the entire sequence. The single fixed smooth embedding/retraction and the actual transversality/approximation suppliers use their stated Countable Choice hypothesis; once those are fixed, no additional Dependent Choice principle is introduced by the tower or shrinking recursion. This is the precise foundation claim of the current smooth-input candidate. It does not turn the open unrestricted problem into a theorem and does not supply a TOP smoothing theorem. ∎ [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, construct]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth knot in $S^3$ that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, and assume its compact exterior $E_K$ is atoroidal and not Seifert-fibered. Then every smoothly embedded $2$-sphere in $\operatorname{int}E_K$ bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $E_K$, and there is no smoothly embedded disk in $E_K$ whose interior misses $\partial E_K$ and whose boundary is essential in $\partial E_K$.

## Statement references

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nontrivial smooth knot exterior $E_K$, and the assumptions that it is atoroidal and not Seifert-fibered.

[A1] Full AC is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]] defines irreducible to mean every interior $2$-sphere bounds a $3$-ball, incompressible boundary to mean no compressing disk with essential boundary, atoroidal to mean every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel, and Seifert-fibered to mean decomposed into circles with the specified fibered-solid-torus local models.

[L1] Full AC implies the countable-choice assumption of [F1] by applying a choice function to the countable family of nonempty smooth-manifold data. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F2] [[lem-knot-exterior-irreducible-and-boundary-incompressible-kt18-local]] proves that every knot exterior with non-unknot core is irreducible and has incompressible boundary under AC.

## Proof

1.1 Full AC supplies the countable-choice premise in [F1] by [L1]. The supplied atoroidality and non-Seifert assumptions have the exact meanings in [F1]; they impose additional hypotheses on the exterior and do not remove either conclusion of [F2]. [given, A1, L1, F1, F2]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the stated nontrivial knot and its chosen compact exterior. It gives irreducibility and absence of a compressing disk on the boundary; by [F1], these are exactly the two conclusions asserted here. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Sources

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open, $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $TV_2(u;\Omega)<\infty$, then each distributional derivative of $u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure. Their vector measure $Du$ has finite Radon variation and $|Du|(\Omega)=TV_2(u;\Omega)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The extended distributional-TV functional on L² is defined by its smooth test-field supremum.]]

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|The distributional derivative uses the negative-transpose test convention.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, and $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $M:=TV_2(u;\Omega)<\infty$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the axiom required by the Euclidean real Radon-representation supplier. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation]]: $M$ is the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields with $\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1$.

[F2] [[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv]]: $D_i u$ acts on a smooth compactly supported scalar test $\psi$ by $-\int u\,\partial_i\psi$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-smooth-compact-support-dense-in-c0]]: smooth compactly supported functions are uniformly dense in $C_0(\Omega)$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-euclidean-radon-representation-under-countable-choice]]: every bounded real linear functional on $C_0(\Omega)$ is integration against a unique finite signed Radon measure.

[F5] [[lem-ip-vector-radon-variation-is-radon]]: for a finite vector of signed Radon measures, partition variation is Radon and its mass equals the supremum over continuous compactly supported vector fields of norm at most one.

## Proof

1.1 Every $L^2$ function is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz, so its distributional derivatives are defined. For $i=1,2$, set $L_i(\psi):=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\psi\,dx$ on $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. If $\psi\ne0$, the vector field $\varphi=\psi e_i/\|\psi\|_\infty$ and its negative are admissible in [F1]; hence $|L_i(\psi)|\le M\|\psi\|_\infty$. The same bound is immediate for $\psi=0$. By [F3], $L_i$ extends uniquely to a bounded real linear functional on $C_0(\Omega)$. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Countable Choice and [F4] represent each extension by a finite signed Radon measure $\mu_i$. Formula [F2] identifies $\mu_i$ with $D_i u$, so $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ has finite vector Radon variation by [F5]. For every continuous compactly supported $g$ with $\|g\|_\infty\le1$, approximate uniformly by a smooth compactly supported $h$ with $\|h-g\|_\infty<\varepsilon$, and replace $h$ by $h/\max\{1,\|h\|_\infty\}$. The replacement has norm at most one and differs from $g$ by at most $2\varepsilon$. Since $\sum_i|\mu_i|(\Omega)<\infty$, its integral against $\mu$ approaches that of $g$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Thus the supremum over smooth unit fields equals the continuous-field supremum in [F5]. By [F2], $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi=-\int\varphi\cdot d\mu$; symmetry of the unit test class removes this minus sign. Consequently $|Du|(\Omega)=M=TV_2(u;\Omega)$, proving the assertion. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $C(K)=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ be its normalized bifiltered complex over $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$. The complex of the reverse mirror $-K$ is filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to the dual complex $C(K)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]}(C(K),\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}])$, with dual differential $d\phi(x)=\phi(\partial x)$ and dual basis elements at negated bifiltration coordinates. There is also a Maslov-graded filtered-chain-homotopy equivalence from $C(K)$ to the complex obtained by exchanging the algebraic and Alexander filtrations. These are distinct symmetries: duality negates both filtration coordinates, while conjugation exchanges them.

## Statement references

[[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot|Reverse-mirror convention for the smooth concordance inverse]]

[F1] Actual admissible doubly pointed S3 diagrams have the full filtered minus count complex, retaining positive multiplicities at BOTH marks. ## Proof

1.1 **The actual bifiltered model.** Choose one supplied doubly pointed diagram $\mathcal H=(\Sigma,\alpha,\beta,w,z)$ and good count data in [F1]. Write $R=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$. Its finite free localized module has generator $x$ in coordinates $(0,A(x))$, and $U^k x$ in $(-k,A(x)-k)$ of Maslov degree $M(x)-2k$. Equivalently write $[x,i,j]$ with $j-i=A(x)$ and degree $M(x)+2i$. Its differential is the actual sum of $[y,i-n_w(\phi),j-n_z(\phi)]$ over index-one classes $\phi:x\to y$. This dictionary follows directly from [F2], and records both positive marked degrees. All ensuing comparisons concern this finite free module and actual classes, not an abstractly postulated symmetry. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Geometric diagrams and their knot labels.** Swapping the two attaching systems while keeping the oriented surface gives $\mathcal H^\vee=(\Sigma,\beta,\alpha,w,z)$. Physically the two handlebodies exchange their roles and both of their ambient orientations reverse, so this is $(-S^3,-K)$: the old beta bridge is now traversed from w to z and the old alpha bridge from z to w. After the fixed orientation-reversing ambient reflection, it is the reverse mirror [F5]. The compatible Morse function changes from $f$ to $-f$. The diagram $\mathcal H^c=(-\Sigma,\beta,\alpha,z,w)$ instead has the ORIGINAL ambient orientation (surface reversal cancels the handlebody exchange), and the ORIGINAL knot orientation (mark exchange cancels the bridge reversal). Explicitly, the new alpha arc is the OLD beta arc directed from old z to old w, and the new beta arc is the OLD alpha arc directed from old w to old z. Both are their ORIGINAL directions; only the starting point of the closed traversal changed. The surface reversal restores the original orientations on both physical handlebodies after their role exchange, so their identity gluing identifies the ambient oriented manifold with the original one. Thus this is the same oriented $(S^3,K)$ with its carried bridge disks, not an assumed oriented isotopy from K to its reverse. All complete compression data remain present. Their normalized periodic domains have zero coefficient at one mark precisely as before, and reversing labels or region orientations transports the admissibility sign tests. Use the transported count data rather than require the same arbitrary almost-complex path on every diagram. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 **Actual dual classes and counted operators.** For $\phi:x\to y$ represented by $u(s,t)$ put $u^\vee(s,t)=u(-s,1-t)$ and $J_t^\vee=J_{1-t}$. Its ends are y,x and its boundary lies on beta at t=0 and alpha at t=1. The equation becomes $u_s^\vee+J_t^\vee u_t^\vee=-(u_s+J_{1-t}u_t)=0$. The source map reverses both real coordinates and is orientation preserving; every individual divisor degree $n_w,n_z$ is unchanged. Precomposition is an invertible map of the actual weighted domains and targets of the linearized real operators, so kernels, cokernels and Fredholm indices agree. It reverses the translation parameter but induces a bijection of its orbits, hence of the actual zero-dimensional counted moduli spaces. It also gives the inverse on literal continuous classes and identifies broken ends. Thus if $\partial x$ contains $U^a y$ with coefficient $e\in\mathbb F_2$, the actual dual diagram differential contains $U^a x^\vee$ in $\partial y^\vee$ with the SAME coefficient. This is exactly the R-linear transpose $d\phi(x)=\phi(\partial x)$, without discarding any positive marked terms. [F1, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Dual absolute origins.** On the physical exterior, $f\mapsto-f$ negates the selected negative Morse field while the ambient orientation also reverses. Its perpendicular plane therefore retains its physical orientation: its orientation is determined by the ambient orientation and the field direction, and both changed sign. Its determinant and Euler obstruction on the physical surface are unchanged. The reverse-mirror Seifert surface has the opposite surface orientation, so the capped pairing changes sign. The zero-Euler cap stays zero under this transport (a constant reversal of its boundary frame has winding zero). Hence $A^\vee(x^\vee)=-A(x)$ with NO affine shift. The relative index equation and [F2]'s Whitney connectivity give $M^\vee(x^\vee)=-M(x)+d$ for one integer d. After setting U=0, step3.1 is the finite vector-space dual of the actual TOTAL hat complex, including its positive-z differential. The homology of this dual is the dual of the original homology: a functional is a cycle exactly when it vanishes on boundaries, and quotient by functionals vanishing on cycles gives the dual of cycles modulo boundaries. Its sole homology class has degree zero when the basis degrees are $-M(x)$. Uniqueness of [F2]'s hat normalization therefore gives d=0. Sending $x^\vee$ to the R-dual basis functional $x^*$ is now an actual graded chain isomorphism with dual basis coordinates $(0,-A(x))$. An arbitrary shifted dual basis has coordinates $(-i,-j)$, exactly as stated. [F2, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.2 **Actual conjugate classes.** For $\mathcal H^c$ use $u^c(s,t)=C(u(s,1-t))$ and $J_t^c=-C_*J_{1-t}$. Direct substitution gives $u_s^c+J_t^c u_t^c=C_*(u_s+J_{1-t}u_t)=0$. This time the ends x,y are unchanged. Source t reflection and target complex conjugation each reverse the relevant orientation, so their two signs cancel in every divisor degree. Since the mark labels were exchanged, $n_{w^c}(\phi^c)=n_z(\phi)$ and $n_{z^c}(\phi^c)=n_w(\phi)$. The same invertible real-operator conjugacy as step3.1 gives the actual index and count equality; C is defined by conjugating the coefficients of each unordered-root polynomial, not by the generally nonsmooth symmetric power of an arbitrary surface map. The protected integrable divisor neighborhoods, product generator charts and taming forms are transported to the conjugate surface, so the chosen data remain in the allowed class. On the physical exterior f changes to -f with the SAME ambient orientation, so the negative selected field reverses and its perpendicular plane is conjugated. The knot and Seifert surface orientations are unchanged by step2.1. The cap again has relative Euler zero. Thus its actual capped Chern pairing gives $A^c(x^c)=-A(x)$. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 **The raw swapped map and its one possible Maslov shift.** Define $S[x,i,j]=[x^c,j,i]$. Step4.2 and $A^c=-A$ make this an R-linear chain isomorphism: each term of the target differential lowers its first coordinate by $n_z$ and second by $n_w$. It and its inverse interchange the two filtrations EXACTLY. The actual relative index equations give $M^c(x^c)-M^c(y^c)=M(x)-M(y)-2(A(x)-A(y))$. Therefore $\Phi^2$ and its inverse preserve the ORIGINAL bifiltration, and their inverse homotopies do also: compose the given homotopies with the swap maps on both sides, so two swaps cancel. In particular they restrict to the algebraic sublevel $i\le0$, the actual full minus module of step1.1; quotienting by U gives inverse chain homotopy equivalences of the actual total hat complex. The square is homogeneous of degree 2c. Its induced homology map is an isomorphism of a one-dimensional vector space supported only in degree zero by [F2]. Consequently 2c=0 as an INTEGER, and c=0. This uses neither a grid identification nor an unproved equality of the two independently normalized w/z Maslov origins. No grid/analytic equality, four-dimensional degree formula, concordance-map nonvanishing or numerical knot computation is a premise. ## Statement

Let $F_r$ be the free group and $E$ the Magnus expansion from the preceding
definition, with augmentation ideal $\mathfrak m$. If
$u\in\Gamma_pF_r$ and $v\in\Gamma_qF_r$ for $p,q\ge1$, then
$$
E([u,v])\in 1+\mathfrak m^{p+q}.
$$
Consequently $E(\Gamma_qF_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m^q$ for every $q\ge1$.
In particular, reduction of $E$ modulo $\mathfrak m^{d+1}$ factors through
$F_r/\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$ and its coefficients through degree $d$ are independent
of the representative word.

## Statement references

[[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links|Lower-central series and Magnus expansion]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The free group, lower-central series, Magnus map, and augmentation
ideal from the preceding definition.

[F1] The series map $E$ is a group homomorphism, $E(F_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m$,
and $\mathfrak m^a\mathfrak m^b\subseteq\mathfrak m^{a+b}$.
[[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links]]

## Proof

1.1 In any filtered associative ring, write $U=1+a$ and $V=1+b$ with
$a\in\mathfrak m^p$ and $b\in\mathfrak m^q$. Since $U,V$ are units,
$$
[U,V]-1=(UV-VU)U^{-1}V^{-1}=(ab-ba)U^{-1}V^{-1}.
$$
By [F1], $ab-ba\in\mathfrak m^{p+q}$, and multiplication by units preserves
this two-sided ideal. Therefore $[U,V]\in1+\mathfrak m^{p+q}$. Applying this
to $U=E(u)$ and $V=E(v)$ proves the first claim. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Every free generator and its inverse map to a series with constant term
$1$, so [F1] gives $E(\Gamma_1F_r)=E(F_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m$. Assume
$E(\Gamma_qF_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m^q$. Each generator
$[u,v]$ of $\Gamma_{q+1}F_r=[F_r,\Gamma_qF_r]$ has $u\in F_r$ and
$v\in\Gamma_qF_r$, so step 1.1 puts its image in $1+\mathfrak m^{q+1}$.
Products and inverses of elements in $1+\mathfrak m^{q+1}$ remain in that
subgroup; hence the inclusion holds for all of $\Gamma_{q+1}F_r$. Induction
proves it for every $q$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra, induction]

2.1 If two words represent the same element of $F_r/\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$, their
quotient lies in $\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$. By step 1.2 its expansion is
$1$ modulo $\mathfrak m^{d+1}$. Multiplicativity of $E$ then makes the two
truncated expansions equal, proving representative-independence of every
coefficient of degree at most $d$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Over $\mathbb Q$, the Rasmussen invariants of the
oriented Conway knot $C$ and its Piccirillo partner $K_P$ are
$$s(C)=0,\qquad s(K_P)=2.$$
The calculation is the finite Lee-filtered Khovanov calculation on the two
specified diagrams, including the rational Khovanov ranks and the surviving
Lee filtration levels needed to determine these values.
