Each such cancellation is filtered, since the paired basis vectors have equal quantum degree. There are $8,038$ cancellations. In homological degrees $-1,0,1$ the remaining generators are precisely $q^{-3}+q^{-1}+2q$, $2q^{-1}+3q+q^3$, and $q+2q^3+q^5$, as independently verified by the rational table. The transferred degree-four differential from the one-dimensional group $Kh^{-1,-1}(C)$ to the one-dimensional group $Kh^{0,3}(C)$ is the matrix $(2/3)$. This exact entry results from the above rational Schur updates; the standard-library calculation in the accompanying family source `conway-lee-computation.py` specifies every state, sign, entry and cancellation and asserts the matrix identity. In particular this is a nonzero differential into quantum degree $3$, so that class does not survive. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 In the partner table, $Kh^{0,*}=\mathbb Q_{-1}\oplus\mathbb Q_1^2\oplus\mathbb Q_3$, $Kh^{-1,*}=\mathbb Q_1^2$, and $Kh^{1,*}=\mathbb Q_1^2\oplus\mathbb Q_3^3\oplus\mathbb Q_5$. The degree-three class cannot support or receive any Lee differential: the possible outgoing bidegrees are $(1,3+4k)$ and incoming bidegrees $(-1,3-4k)$ for integers $k\ge1$, and all of these groups are zero by the table. The multiple-of-four restriction follows from [F6] and the quantum congruence decomposition; a finite filtration makes these all possible pages. Thus the degree-three class survives. The two limiting levels lie in $\{-1,1,3\}$, differ by two and include $3$, so they are exactly $(1,3)$. Therefore [F4] gives $s(K_P)=2$. Notice that the incoming test is $3-4k$, not $-3-4k$; the latter expression occurs in the 2018 arXiv preprint, while the published 2020 proof gives the correct incoming bidegree. The independent characteristic-zero `-s0` calculation also returns $2$ on this exact input. [F3, F4, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The complete Conway $h=0$ row has quantum degrees only $-1,1,3$. By step 3.1 the last is removed on the first possible nonzero Lee differential. Every later page is a subquotient of the corresponding previous bidegree, so no new degree can appear. The two nonzero limiting quantum levels are therefore $-1,1$: by [F3] they occur in two different congruence classes modulo four and differ by two, and Lee homology has dimension two. Hence [F4] gives $s(C)=0$. As an independent arithmetic check, the unmodified rational `s` calculation in knotkit and the characteristic-zero `-s0` calculation in KnotJob both return $0$ on the same diagram; these outputs are not needed in place of the explicit nonzero differential. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Steps 4.1 and 3.2 give the asserted rational Lee filtration levels $(-1,1)$ and $(1,3)$ on the two diagrams specified in [F1]. The tables in step 2.1 provide the full rational Khovanov ranks used in this calculation, while step 3.1 supplies the additional actual Lee differential required for Conway. The bounded spectral sequence in [F3] has no further page capable of changing either conclusion. Together these prove every part of the Statement. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 3.2, algebra, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. The standard right-handed trefoil is a prime oriented knot.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|Definition of a prime knot]]

[[lem-right-trefoil-has-genus-one|Exact genus of the right trefoil]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the standard right-handed trefoil $T$.

[F1] $g(T)=1$. ([[lem-right-trefoil-has-genus-one]])

[F2] Genus is additive under connected sum, and genus zero characterizes the unknot, under AC$_\omega$. ([[thm-knot-genus-additive-under-connected-sum]], [[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]])

[F3] Full AC implies AC$_\omega$. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC and $T$.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], $T$ is nontrivial. If $T=K\#J$ with both factors nontrivial, [F2] and [F3] make their genera positive integers, so $g(K)+g(J)\ge2$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Additivity gives $1=g(T)=g(K)+g(J)\ge2$, a contradiction. Thus $T$ is nontrivial and has no connected-sum presentation with both factors nontrivial, exactly the definition of prime. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $N$ be the complement of finitely many disjoint open solid tori in a connected oriented three-manifold, and suppose its interior has a hyperbolic metric. Fix one boundary torus $T$ with primitive peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$. Assume that a neighborhood of this end, after developing into $\mathbb H^3$, is isometric to a punctured radius-$\varepsilon$ tube about a geodesic axis, modulo a translation of length $L>0$ along that axis. Assume that $\lambda$ is the axial translation direction and that $\mu$ is the angular direction making one full turn of angle $2\pi$ about the axis; equivalently, its peripheral holonomy is the identity isometry with the full-turn lift. Then the hyperbolic metric extends smoothly over the ordinary Dehn filling along $\mu$, adding the axis quotient as the core geodesic of length $L$. The same conclusion holds simultaneously for any finite set of ends satisfying these conditions.

## Statement references

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

[Petronio and Porti, *Negatively Oriented Ideal Triangulations and a Proof of Thurston’s Hyperbolic Dehn Filling Theorem*, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hyperbolic metric on the complement of the stated tubes, the peripheral basis on each selected torus, and the explicit developed tube model with meridional angle $2\pi$ and positive axial translation length.

[F1] [[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]]: ordinary Dehn filling attaches a solid torus whose meridian disk boundary is the specified primitive slope.

[F2] [[def-pared-hyperbolic-structures-and-volume]]: a hyperbolic metric has curvature $-1$ in local charts into $\mathbb H^3$.

[F3] [[lem-ideal-triangulation-gluing-equations-and-peripheral-holonomy]]: edge products $1$ and angle sums $2\pi$ give a smooth hyperbolic metric away from ideal vertices; the cusp equations are additional conditions used to obtain completeness at those ends.

## Proof

1.1 In cylindrical coordinates $(r,\theta,z)$ about a geodesic in $\mathbb H^3$, the metric is $ds^2=dr^2+\sinh^2(r)\,d\theta^2+\cosh^2(r)\,dz^2$. The full-turn condition makes $\theta$ have period $2\pi$, while the axial translation identifies $z$ with $z+L$. Thus the developed tube quotient is $(0,\varepsilon)\times(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\times(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)$, and its meridian is exactly the $\theta$ circle representing $\mu$. [given, F2, construct]

2.1 Set $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$. Then $dr^2+\sinh^2(r)d\theta^2=dx^2+dy^2+\frac{(\sinh^2r-r^2)}{r^4}(x\,dy-y\,dx)^2$. The coefficient has the convergent even-power expansion $1/3+O(r^2)$ at $r=0$, and $\cosh^2(r)$ is smooth in $x^2+y^2$. Hence the metric extends smoothly across $x=y=0$; the added set is the circle $\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z$ and is the core of a solid torus. The extended metric has curvature $-1$ on the dense punctured tube by [F2], so its smooth curvature tensor has curvature $-1$ on the core by continuity. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], attaching a solid torus with meridian $\mu$ is precisely the ordinary filling specified by the angular circle in step 1.1. The local extension in step 2.1 agrees with the original metric on the overlap, so it defines a smooth hyperbolic metric on the filled manifold. For finitely many ends the tube neighborhoods are disjoint, and the same local extension can be performed independently at each one. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

## Sources

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

[Petronio and Porti, *Negatively Oriented Ideal Triangulations and a Proof of Thurston’s Hyperbolic Dehn Filling Theorem*, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Statement

Let $T$ be either oriented trefoil in $S^3$. Its double branched cover $\Sigma(T)$ is diffeomorphic, up to orientation reversal, to the lens space $L(3,1)$ in the convention in which $L(p,q)$ is the $p/q$ filling of the standard unknot exterior. In particular, $\pi_1(\Sigma(T))$ is cyclic of order three.

## Statement references

[[def-double-branched-cover-of-an-oriented-link|Double branched cover convention]]

[[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention|Lens-space filling and orientation convention]]

[Ozsváth and Szabó, *On the Heegaard Floer homology of branched double-covers*, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309170v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The closure of the two-strand braid $\sigma_1^k$, $k=3$ or $k=-3$, with the given knot orientation; the cover conventions of the statement. Circle coordinates below are taken modulo $2\pi$, and the page parameter $u$ modulo one.

[F1] [[def-double-branched-cover-of-an-oriented-link]] and [[lem-double-branched-cover-of-an-oriented-link-well-defined]] give the meridian-character cover and its simple branched extension, and invariance under the chosen oriented link isotopies.

[F2] [[lem-double-cover-of-two-arc-rational-tangle-is-solid-torus]] supplies the annular cover of the disk with two branch points and its product extension over an interval.

[F3] [[lem-lift-of-two-strand-half-twist-is-annular-dehn-twist]] gives the unique boundary-fixed smooth mapping-class lift of a positive half-twist as the positive annular twist, with the inverse for its reverse. It includes the actual orientation/sign calculation.

[F4] [[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention]] defines $L(3,1)$ as the unknot-exterior filling with meridian slope $3\mu_U+\lambda_U$.

[F5] [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]] identifies the fundamental group of a two-solid-torus union as the pushout of its boundary inclusion maps. Thickening the two pieces by collars gives its required open connected cover.

## Proof

1.1 **The covered disk pages and their binding fillings.** Use the standard disk open book of $S^3$ about the braid axis $U$: its complement of a small axis neighborhood is $D^2\times S^1$, and the closed two-strand braid meets each disk in two points. This description is explicit in $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$: the axis is $\{z_1=0\}$ and the page parameter is $u=\arg z_1/(2\pi)$; the disk page is parametrized by $z_2$, with $z_1$ having the remaining modulus and chosen argument. Cut the page parameter at zero. The two moving points over the resulting interval are a braid isotopy of the twice-marked disk. Its double branched cover is the corresponding annular product by the same square-coordinate and sheet-gluing construction as [F2]. On gluing the ends, the annular monodromy is the boundary-fixed lift of the braid mapping class, hence $T^k$ by [F3]. There is no extra deck map: the page-parameter loop near the axis bounds a small meridian disk in its neighborhood disjoint from the branch link, and has trivial meridian character. Moreover the axis itself links the two-strand braid twice, so its mod-two character is zero as well. Thus the cover of its solid-torus neighborhood consists of two ordinary copies, one for each annular boundary. In each copy the meridian is the loop $u$ at a fixed boundary-page point. Consequently the whole branched cover is exactly the annular mapping torus with both boundary tori filled along these page-parameter meridians. The local branched models retain the smooth structures. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 **Untwist the mapping torus, retaining both meridians.** Write $A=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)_\theta\times[-1,1]_t$, with a positive twist $T(\theta,t)=(\theta+2\pi\rho(t),t)$, where $\rho=0$ near $-1$ and $\rho=1$ near $1$. The mapping torus has the equivalence $(\theta,t,1)\sim(\theta+2\pi k\rho(t),t,0)$. The function $$\theta'=\theta+2\pi k\rho(t)u\pmod {2\pi}$$ is well-defined across that equivalence and gives an actual diffeomorphism of the mapping torus with $S^1_{\theta'}\times[-1,1]_t\times S^1_u$. Its inverse on the cut parameter interval is $\theta=\theta'-2\pi k\rho(t)u$, with the same endpoint compatibility. At the lower boundary the filling meridian $u\mapsto(\theta_0,-1,u)$ has class $(0,1)$ in the $(\theta',u)$ basis. At the upper boundary the corresponding meridian has class $(k,1)$. This computes their actual slopes, not only their intersection number. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **The two solid tori.** Split the product at any fixed interior $t$. Fill its lower end along $(0,1)$. This caps the $u$ circle in the annulus $[-1,t]\times S^1_u$ by a disk, so that piece is the solid torus $V_-=S^1_{\theta'}\times D^2$. Its meridian on the common torus is $m=(0,1)$ and its core longitude is $l=(1,0)$. The upper filled piece is also a solid torus: the integral shear $(\theta',u)\mapsto(\theta'-2\pi ku,u)$ extends over its whole product collar, is single-valued because $k$ is an integer, and takes its filling slope $(k,1)$ to $(0,1)$. After that shear it is the same disk-capped product as the lower piece. Before undoing the shear, its meridian on the common torus is precisely $kl+m$. Hence this is a genus-one gluing with that meridian slope. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Identify the fixed unknot peripheral basis.** Identify $V_-$ with the standard unknot exterior, using the same $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$ decomposition: $E_U=\{|z_1|\ge\varepsilon\}$ for a small standard axis neighborhood $\{|z_1|\le\varepsilon\}$. On its boundary the unknot meridian $\mu_U$ is the $\arg z_1$ circle, which generates the core circle of $E_U$, and the preferred longitude $\lambda_U$ is the $\arg z_2$ circle, which bounds its meridian disk. Thus take $l=\mu_U$, $m=\lambda_U$ by an actual product-coordinate identification. Up to the global orientation choice allowed in the statement, the other solid torus is attached with meridian $k\mu_U+\lambda_U$. For $k=3$ this is exactly [F4]. For $k=-3$, the reflection $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(\overline z_1,z_2)$ reverses the orientation of $S^3$, preserves the unknot, and sends $\mu_U$ to $-\mu_U$ and $\lambda_U$ to $\lambda_U$. It carries the slope $-3\mu_U+\lambda_U$ to $3\mu_U+\lambda_U$ and extends over the filled solid torus by the same meridian identification. Hence the other handedness has the same $L(3,1)$ description up to orientation reversal. Reversing the orientation of the branch knot does not change its mod-two meridian character. [F1, F4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 In $E_U$ the group is generated by $\mu_U$ and $\lambda_U$ is trivial, by its product $S^1\times D^2$ coordinates. Gluing the second solid torus kills the slope $k\mu_U+\lambda_U$. By [F5] there are no further relations: a primitive complementary boundary longitude identifies the core generator of the attached solid torus with the corresponding word in the exterior generator, so that generator is eliminated from the pushout presentation. The group is therefore $\langle\mu_U\mid\mu_U^k=1\rangle$, cyclic of order $|k|=3$. All new coordinate and slope calculations were finite; the only inherited choice use is the already declared cover and peripheral-convention branch. This proves both assertions for either oriented trefoil without replacing a meridian-slope calculation by the determinant alone. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $\Sigma\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be a compact smooth oriented cobordism from an oriented knot $K_0$ to an oriented knot $K_1$, with fixed product collars and fixed endpoint diagrams. Every generic movie $M$ of $\Sigma$ defines a map of bidegree $(0,\chi(\Sigma))$,
$$
Kh(M):Kh^{i,j}(K_0)\longrightarrow Kh^{i,j+\chi(\Sigma)}(K_1),
$$
where $\chi(\Sigma)$ is the Euler characteristic of the surface and the integral even Khovanov groups use the normalized crossing shifts. If two such movies represent cobordisms related by an ambient isotopy fixed on the boundary collars, their maps differ by multiplication by a single overall sign, independent of the input class. The resulting assignment is a functor after each morphism group is quotiented by the relation identifying a map with its negative; before that quotient the sign is not canonical.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the normalized integral even Khovanov theory and its fixed movie maps, and the two boundary-fixed movies in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed. The additional calculations below use finite sets, integer operations and finite-dimensional vector spaces, without full Choice.

[F1] [[def-khovanov-cobordism-map-up-to-sign]] fixes the normalized local maps and crossing-order identifications. Its birth, death and saddle maps have quantum degrees $1,1,-1$, respectively.

[F2] [[lem-barnatan-carter-saito-movie-moves-up-to-sign]] proves the fifteen Euclidean movie relations and distant interchanges for those maps.

[F3] [[thm-carter-saito-movie-move-equivalence]] reduces spherical movie comparison to these Euclidean relations and the additional sweep-around move.

[F4] [[lem-barnatan-formal-kink-retractions]], [[lem-barnatan-formal-inverse-boundary-crossings]] and [[lem-barnatan-formal-third-reidemeister-equivalence]] supply actual local equivalences with their inverses. [[lem-barnatan-planar-homotopies-and-conditional-boundary-crossing-simplicity]] proves their signed planar insertion and cancellation of boundary-crossing additions.

[F5] [[lem-barnatan-open-pairings-have-scalar-degree-zero-endomorphisms]] proves the scalar degree-zero endomorphism calculation in the undotted category. In the dotted universal category used below the same calculation is proved directly, so no faithfulness of the undotted-to-dotted quotient is assumed.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement. It remains to prove the sweep identity for the same projective local maps, rather than introduce a different functor on closed homology groups.

1.1 **A local integral comparison category.** Use oriented blue facets of label $1$ and red facets of label $2$; two blue facets meet a red facet along each seam, with the usual merge orientation. Decorations on blue facets are powers of a dot. One can define their closed evaluation by cutting at the circular seams and applying the two Frobenius algebras $B=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, $\epsilon_B(1)=0$, $\epsilon_B(X)=1$, $\Delta_B(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1$, $\Delta_B(X)=X\otimes X$, and $R=\mathbb Z$ with counit $-1$ and comultiplication $-1\otimes1$. Contract a seam by $\epsilon_B(x\bar y)$, where the positive blue side is selected by right-hand cyclic order and $\bar X=-X$. Cut-independence is the unit, counit, associativity and Frobenius identities of these displayed algebras. Equivalently, this is the following direct specialization of the two-pigment evaluation. With roots $x_1,x_2$, put $d=x_1-x_2$, $h=x_1+x_2$, $t=-x_1x_2$, and use $B_h=\mathbb Z[h,t][X]/(X^2-hX-t)$. Its primitive idempotents have counits $\beta_1=1/d$, $\beta_2=-1/d$, and conjugation interchanges them. A connected blue facet of genus $g$ with $b$ seam circles contributes $\beta_i^{1-g-b}$; a red facet contributes $(-1)^{1-g-b}$; the seam contributes $\beta_i$ for its positive blue pigment. Sum over the two colors, which must be different at each seam. This is a finite tensor contraction in $B_h$ and $R$, hence is integral before any localization. Define states of a closed web as foams from the empty web modulo the common radical of every closing evaluation; define all other morphisms by bending to a closed web and taking that radical. Gluing preserves the radical because every closing after gluing is a closing before gluing. These definitions provide a local category, with no assertion of full faithfulness for a previously defined homology-valued functor. [A1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 **Reduction to an almost braid closure is relative.** A finite one-to-one tangle diagram, possibly with additional closed components, can be braided while preserving a prescribed short crossing-free endpoint arc. Here is the relative finite braiding construction needed, rather than an invocation of an AC-stated existence theorem. Close that arc on the left, choose a generic height away from its small fixed rectangle, and subdivide the remaining finitely many projected arcs at extrema and between changes of over/under status. A backward arc can be replaced by two forward arcs extending past the diagram and the exterior return arc: lift its small triangular detour above the rest when it is over, or below when under, then straighten the two free legs to the height direction. Its attaching intervals stay fixed and its chosen side has no strand between the old and new arc, so sliding across this triangle is an isotopy of the embedded tangle. Subdivision makes every such detour contain at most one old crossing of a fixed status. The detours introduce only forward legs and are chosen away from the fixed endpoint rectangle. Repeating on the finite backward list gives a braid whose rightmost $n$ strands are closed, and whose remaining strand retains the prescribed open endpoints. This is an almost braid closure. All moves occur in compact balls away from the fixed arc; smoothing the finite corners and extending the local velocities gives a relative smooth isotopy and a finite Euclidean movie. By [F2], conjugating a sweep by this isotopy conjugates its projective map. Therefore it suffices to prove the sweep identity for an almost braid closure. [A1, F2, F4, construct]

2.1 **All actual rank-two foams are covered.** In the positive-label raw foam category a facet of label at least three has no two-pigment coloring. Every closure of a foam containing it therefore evaluates to zero, so that foam is in the radical. Each allowed tetrahedral vertex has such a facet: its first positive-label model contains $a+b+c\ge3$; its second has $a>c\ge1$, $b\ge1$, and contains $a+b\ge3$. Thus every nonzero rank-two foam is vertex-free, with precisely the facets of step 1.1; no zero-facet removal assertion is required. To compare raw left-hand Robert–Wagner signs with the right-hand evaluation above, let $B_i$ be the blue pigment-$i$ surfaces, $R$ the red surface, $M$ the seam count, and $t_i$ the number of seams positive on blue pigment $i$ in right-hand order. Their two sign exponents are $\chi(B_1\cup R)/2+t_2$ and $\chi(B_2\cup R)/2+t_1$. Their difference modulo two is $\chi(B)/2+\chi(R)+M=\chi(B)/2$, since $\chi(R)\equiv M\pmod2$. Their common denominator is $d^{\chi(B)/2}$. Consequently raw evaluation differs by $(-1)^{\chi(B)/2}$. At $h=t=0$ a nonzero scalar evaluation with $D$ blue dots has $2D=\chi(B)$; replacing each raw blue dot by its negative cancels this sign. Positive-degree red decorations specialize to zero. Thus every closed evaluation, and hence every bent radical, agrees after this explicit dot normalization. In particular the normalized dotted sphere is $+1$; it is not identified with the unrenormalized raw dotted sphere, which is $-1$. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Pairing bases, without red compression.** A closed web with $k$ underlying blue circles has exactly $2^k$ boundary pigment states: a pigment changes across every red vertex on its blue circle, and there are an even number of these vertices because blue orientation changes there. Localized closed evaluation factors through these states, so its pairing rank is at most $2^k$. For a pure-blue web, dotted disk cups and complementary dotted caps have a unimodular tensor-product pairing: the one-circle Gram matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&h\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, of determinant $-1$. Hence its universal module is exactly the free module with those $2^k$ cups. For a general web $W$, there is a foam $I_W$ with underlying blue cylinders from standardly oriented blue circles to $W$. To construct it, checkerboard-color the complement of the underlying blue cylinders; complete every wrongly oriented region boundary by a red copy, push its interior into that region and assign the opposite color in the new thin region. The boundary red arcs are completed in the same way. This finite construction uses only parallel copies in collars, so produces the prescribed boundary and no singular vertices. The reflected composite $I_W^*I_W$ commutes with dots: crossing a seam changes $X$ to $h-X$, and each blue cylinder crosses an even number of orientation changes. It is degree zero, so on the pure-blue module it is multiplication by an integer. For each fixed boundary pigment, its color contraction is a single nonzero term of absolute value one; hence that integer is $\pm1$. Thus $I_W$ has a left inverse. Its cokernel is a direct summand of the universal module, is torsion-free because all its pairing evaluations lie in the domain $\mathbb Z[h,t]$, and has rank zero by the localized $2^k$ bound. It is zero, and $I_W$ is invertible. Bending now identifies every local morphism space with the corresponding blue cup module. In particular a $k$-arc pairing has basis degrees $2|L|$ in its degree-zero endomorphism calculation, so $\operatorname{End}^0=\mathbb Z\,1$. This argument does not compress a possibly knotted red surface in a ball. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **The actual crossing and tensor conventions.** Let $I$ be the two-strand pairing and $A_i$ the thick web at adjacent positions $i,i+1$. In the over-southwest-to-northeast source chart, $I$ is the A-smoothing and the underlying blue pairing of $A_i$ is the B-smoothing. Use auxiliary crossing factors $(A_i\{-1\}\to I)$ in degrees $(-1,0)$ and $(I\to A_i\{1\})$ in degrees $(0,1)$ for the two inverse physical braid generators. These are the two rank-two foam factors with all-parallel term in degree zero; the braces here are the formal shift convention, opposite to their printed $q$ exponent. Surface-time cochain duality, with intrinsic grading changed from $-\chi$ to $\chi$, gives $(I\to E_i\{1\})$ and $(E_i\{-1\}\to I)$, respectively. Adding the common writhe shifts $+1$ and $-1$ yields exactly $(I\{1\}\to E_i\{2\})$ and $(E_i\{-2\}\to I\{-1\})$, the normalized ordinary factors. For an arbitrary balanced boundary orientation, cut an annulus at its basepoint and apply the same region completion as in step 3.1 to blue radial curtains. Its red facets convert the standard alternating boundary orientation to the prescribed one, while its blue curtains and cochain degree remain unchanged. Reversing an arrow is handled by bending this same boundary curtain; the underlying smoothing and the differential are unchanged, and the normalization is still $|v|-n_-$ and $|v|+n_+-2n_-$. At a curl this is also checked directly by the two kink retractions in [F4]. A zip or unzip transports to a primitive signed saddle, since its bent minimal-degree morphism space has one cup basis vector and its two-pigment contraction has coefficient a unit. Square commutation makes these edge signs a cube cocycle, removed by vertex signs from a fixed vertex; all two-saddle composites here are nonzero, as their blue Frobenius values show. Two blue-curtain completion choices differ on each state by a dot-linear degree-zero unit of the pure-blue module, hence by $\pm1$. After correcting the cube edges, connectedness of the cube forces these state signs to be one common sign. Therefore local insertion and the comparison of whole complexes are coherent up to one overall sign, which is the precise coherence required here. Finally prefix and suffix totalization conventions differ by the vertex sign $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}r_i r_j}$ for actual factor degrees $r_i$. Across the $i$th differential its ratio is $(-1)^{\sum_{j\ne i}r_j}$, exactly the difference of the two tensor signs. Thus this is a local comparison of actual complexes with their orders and duals, not only an equality of closed graded ranks. [F1, F4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.2 **An explicit finite verification model.** The next matrices are defined independently in the local category just constructed. Their equations can be checked faithfully after adjoining the distinct pigments. Write a three-strand boundary coloring as $v\in\{0,1\}^3$, where the two pigment values are $0,1$ after scaling their difference. A word in $A=A_1$ and $C=A_2$ has basis the paths $(v_0,\ldots,v_m)$ such that at its $i$th-letter step the relevant two colors are distinct and $v_j$ is either $v_{j-1}$ or their interchange. With $\delta_i(v)=v_i-v_{i+1}$, the elementary operators have the following complete rules: $\eta_i:I\to A_i$ inserts the unchanged color path with coefficient $\delta_i(v)$; $\varepsilon_i:A_i\to I$ deletes a step only when its two endpoints agree, with coefficient $1$; $\Delta_i:A_i\to A_iA_i$ sums all allowed middle color orders with coefficient $1$; and $m_i:A_iA_i\to A_i$ removes the middle color $u$ with coefficient $1/\delta_i(u)$. Indeed the circle birth is the sum of its two idempotents and its cap has values $\beta_i$; zip followed by unzip has the values $0,d,-d,0$ on equal/equal, first/second, second/first, and second/second colors. Normalizing unzip to $1$ gives exactly these rules. The unit and counit identities determine the displayed digon coefficients as well: $\delta_i(u)\beta_i=1$. All four are actual integral foams; only their color coordinates use inverses of $d$. Put $U_i=\Delta_i\eta_i$ and $V_i=\varepsilon_i m_i$. Faithfulness of this color test follows from the defining radical: a morphism whose every pigment coefficient is zero pairs to zero with every closure. Torsion-freeness from step 3.1 then reflects equality back before localization. [step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 **Four complete third-move matrices.** Products below compose rightmost first, juxtaposed operators act on the indicated tensor factors, and omitted entries are zero. At each three-crossing cube order vertices by masks $(0,1,2,4,3,5,6,7)$; hence its four consecutive terms have sizes $1,3,3,1$. A positive factor is $A_i\to I$ in degrees $(-1,0)$ and a negative factor is $I\to A_i$ in degrees $(0,1)$, with the prefix tensor signs. The four source/target sign patterns are $(+++;+++)$, $(--+;+--)$, $(++-;-++)$ and $(---;---)$ on the words $ACA,CAC$. The source and target term lists, respectively, are $(ACA;(CA,AA,AC);(A,C,A);I)$ and $(CAC;(AC,CC,CA);(C,A,C);I)$ in case I; $(A;(AA,CA,I);(ACA,A,C);AC)$ and $(C;(I,CA,CC);(A,C,CAC);AC)$ in case II; $(AC;(C,A,ACA);(I,CA,AA);A)$ and $(AC;(CAC,C,A);(CC,CA,I);C)$ in case III; and $(I;(A,C,A);(AC,AA,CA);ACA)$ and $(I;(C,A,C);(CA,CC,AC);CAC)$ in case IV. Their maps on the four consecutive terms are $0,M_1,M_2,1$ in I, $0,N_1,N_2,1$ in II, $1,P_1,P_2,0$ in III, and $1,Q_1,Q_2,0$ in IV, where $$M_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&-(1_A\eta_C)m_A&1_{AC}\\-\Delta_C(1_C\varepsilon_A)&U_CV_A&0\\1_{CA}&-(\eta_C1_A)m_A&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad M_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1_C&0\\1_A&0&1_A\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},$$ $$N_1=\begin{pmatrix}-V_A&0&1\\-(\eta_C1_A)m_A&1_{CA}&0\\U_CV_A&-\Delta_C(1_C\varepsilon_A)&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad N_2=\begin{pmatrix}m_A(1_A\varepsilon_C1_A)&1_A&0\\0&0&1_C\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},$$ $$P_1=\begin{pmatrix}-(1_C\eta_A1_C)\Delta_C&0&0\\1_C&0&0\\0&1_A&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_2=\begin{pmatrix}U_C&-\Delta_C(1_C\varepsilon_A)&U_CV_A\\0&1_{CA}&-(\eta_C1_A)m_A\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix},$$ and $$Q_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1_C&0\\1_A&0&0\\0&1_C&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-(\eta_C1_A)m_A&1_{CA}\\-\Delta_C(\varepsilon_A1_C)&U_CV_A&-\Delta_C(1_C\varepsilon_A)\\1_{AC}&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ These are rank-two representatives of the four local slides: the moving strand goes from first top endpoint to third bottom endpoint, so its two crossings are the first two source factors and last two target factors. The remaining third source/first target crossing is the fixed internal crossing, positive in I–II and negative in III–IV. This specifies the physical variants without relying on an unlabelled picture or an omitted six-valent foam. [step 4.1, step 4.2, construct, algebra]

6.1 **Check of the matrix equations and the two required features.** Here is the full finite checking rule. Enumerate the eight input and eight output colorings, then the paths of each listed word by the two choices at each permitted step in step 4.2. Apply a matrix entry by successively replacing the local subpath by the stated operator's outputs, multiply coefficients, and add coincident paths. A differential at coordinate $r$ has coefficient $(-1)^{\sum_{l<r}(b_l-\mathbf1_{\text{factor }l\text{ positive}})}$ and applies $\varepsilon$ or $\eta$ according as that factor is positive or negative. Direct substitution gives $d'F=Fd$ on all $72$ state-path columns in each case. For each nonzero component, the internal degree $(b_1-\mathbf1_{\text{internal positive}})$ in the target is at least $(b_3-\mathbf1_{\text{internal positive}})$ in the source; there are $80$ nonzero color coefficients in each case, all satisfying this inequality. Finally compare I with II and III with IV by complementing the first two source bits and last two target bits. Their path words are then identical. On pairs of states of equal internal degree their coefficients agree: $144$ coefficient tests in each comparison. This enumeration is also a short exact verification algorithm for all the asserted equations: every basic operator coefficient is $0,1$ or $-1$, sums use exact integers, and the only division is by a color difference $\pm1$. For general difference $d$, every entry of $F$ has common power $d^{(\ell_{\rm target}-\ell_{\rm source})/2}$, where $\ell$ counts thick letters; every coefficient in $d'F-Fd$ has common power $d^{(\ell_{\rm target}-\ell_{\rm source}+1)/2}$. Thus the checks at a unit difference prove the rational identities for arbitrary distinct pigments, and step 4.2 proves the integral foam identities. The complete executable rule, including all four matrices, is retained in the calculation record below. Our representatives are internally nondecreasing, the dual filtration direction to the convention in the cited sweep calculation; this is sufficient because both sweep endpoints have external degree zero. [step 4.2, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 **These are actual local equivalences.** The dotted pairing calculation in step 3.1 and the boundary-crossing inverse equivalences in [F4] identify the full degree-zero endomorphism ring of each local braid complex with $\mathbb Z$. Let $G$ be any of the known equivalences in [F4], transported through step 4.1, and let $F$ be one of step 5.1's chain maps. Then $G^{-1}F$ is an integer scalar in the homotopy category. To determine that scalar, give all three strands the same pigment. Every state with a thick letter vanishes, and only the parallel term remains, in degree zero. Its coefficient is a homotopy invariant and is multiplicative, since all other states are zero in this channel. The parallel coefficient of an integral equivalence and its inverse multiply to $1$, so each is $\pm1$; the parallel coefficient of every $F$ above is $1$. Consequently $F=\pm G$ in the homotopy category and is itself an equivalence. This proves comparison with the fixed local maps without requiring an unverified equality between a cone representative and a chosen parameter value in a published family. [F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 **The first and second moves used by the sweep.** In the normalized ordinary Frobenius algebra, let $u$ create the small circle and $e$ cap it. The four relevant kink maps are $u$, $(Y-X)u$, $e$, and $e(Y-X)$, where $X$ is the continuing-arc dot and $Y$ the small-circle dot. Indeed $v-\Delta=(Y-X)u$ and $w-m=e(Y-X)$: on $1,X$, $v=2Yu$, $\Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1$, $\Delta(X)=X\otimes X$, and the reverse calculation is the same counit computation. These are precisely [F4]'s two kink retractions. In the auxiliary picture label the two fronts so $R1_+=u$, $R1_-=(Y-X)u$, $R1_+^{-1}=e(Y-X)$ and $R1_-^{-1}=e$; reversing all labels changes no conclusion. Their only nonzero components have external degree zero. For one pair of inverse external crossings, order the middle summands as $I,A_iA_i$. The two physical orders have inclusions $(1,-U_i)^T,(1,U_i)^T$ and projections $(1,V_i),(1,-V_i)$. The unit/counit rules in step 4.2 give the chain-map equations, and $V_iU_i=0$, so their projection-inclusion composites are $1$. Their homotopy equivalences are also supplied by the actual inverse-crossing retractions in [F4], or by the same scalar test as step 7.1. Thus a succession of $n$ such pairs is supported only on palindromic thick/parallel states, preserves external degree, and the two fronts differ on a palindrome with $2k$ thick letters by $(-1)^k$, for either the inclusion or the projection. This is one sign from each double-thick pair; the all-parallel component is always $1$. [F4, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

9.1 **The two sweep movies and their grading.** For an almost closure of a braid word on $n+1$ strands, move the left-hand closing arc to the right first in front of and then behind the diagram. Reading the strand's track gives a kink, $n$ inverse-crossing pairs, one of the four slides in step 5.1 at each braid crossing, the inverse $n$ pairs, and the inverse kink. Their composite maps are $\mathrm{sw}_+$ and $\mathrm{sw}_-$ between the same two endpoint complexes, and the full sweep is $\mathrm{sw}_-^{-1}\mathrm{sw}_+$. Split cohomological degree into internal degree from the fixed braid crossings and external degree from its moving strand. The endpoint complexes have external degree zero. Steps 6.1 and 8.1 show that each middle slide is externally nonincreasing, while all kink and pair maps preserve external degree. Hence only the external-degree-preserving parts of the slides can contribute between the endpoints. By step 6.1 those parts agree for the two fronts. When a local three-factor order is inserted into the whole diagram, tensor permutations add their Koszul vertex signs. Corresponding parallel factors have degree zero and corresponding thick factors have degrees $1$ or $-1$, of the same parity on the two fronts. Therefore the permutation phases agree and do not alter the diagonal comparison. [F4, step 6.1, step 8.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

10.1 **Cancellation of the pair and kink discrepancies.** The $n$ external crossings on the remote closing arcs lie outside every slide disk. Their thick/parallel bits are unchanged during the middle slides. Each nonzero pair inclusion and projection has a palindromic state by step 8.1; its half on those remote arcs therefore determines the same integer $k$ at entry and exit. The front/back discrepancies are $(-1)^k$ at both ends, whose product is $1$. After the pair and slide maps have been compared, the only difference is the kink factor $p=Y-X$ at the beginning and its factor $p'$ at the end. Its two dot positions can be carried on the two closing-arc pieces outside the braid box and outside every pair or slide disk. Dot multiplication there commutes with each constituent map, since the remaining factor is an identity curtain; thus the middle map $B$ satisfies $Bp=p'B$. It follows directly that $eBpu=e p'Bu$: the back sweep $eBp u$ equals the front sweep $e p'B u$. Hence $\mathrm{sw}_+=\mathrm{sw}_-$ in the auxiliary homotopy category, and the sweep is the identity there. Each replacement by a fixed local map in [F1] changes at most one overall scalar $\pm1$ by step 7.1 and the analogous pair/kink comparison. Planar insertion preserves that scalar and the homotopies. Consequently the sweep for the actual normalized ordinary maps is $\pm1$, with one sign on the whole complex, not signs varying with states or inputs. [F1, F4, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, algebra]

11.1 By [F3], connect the two spherical movies by finitely many Euclidean movie relations, distant interchanges and sweeps. Each Euclidean relation or interchange preserves its map up to one sign by [F2]; each sweep does so by step 10.1. Composing these finitely many equations gives one overall sign on the full integral homology group. A birth, death or saddle contributes quantum degree $1,1,-1$ by [F1], so the composite has degree $b+d-s=\chi(\Sigma)$ and cohomological degree zero. Identities and concatenation are the identity map and composition for fixed movies; quotienting every morphism by its overall negative makes the resulting assignment a functor. This proves every assertion of the Statement under exactly [A1]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 10.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The finite rank-two verification, including all four matrices and every color path, is check-four-rIII-matrices.py. Its output checks the $288$ chain-map columns, the $288$ diagonal comparisons, and the $320$ nonzero filtration coefficients. The proof above specifies its entire finite rule; the executable is a calculation record, not a new theorem supplier.

The sweep organization follows Morrison–Walker–Wedrich, *Khovanov–Rozansky homology and three-manifolds*, §§2.2–3.6, especially (2.3), (3.2)–(3.4). The proof uses explicitly normalized rank-two foams, the four matrices displayed above and their verified dual filtration direction. It does not assume their raw dot convention equals an ordinary Bar–Natan dot, or use an unproved faithfulness assertion about an arc-algebra-valued functor.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a closed connected smooth simply connected oriented four-manifold. If its integral intersection form is positive definite, then there is an integral basis of $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$ in which the form is the identity matrix. Equivalently, the integral intersection lattice is isometric to the standard diagonal lattice $\mathbb Z^{b_2(X)}$ with dot product.

## Statement references

[Donaldson, *An Application of Gauge Theory to the Topology of 4-Manifolds*, Theorem 1](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/donaldson.pdf)

[Perutz, *Lectures on Gauge Theory and Symplectic Geometry*, §24](https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/perutz/GaugeTheory/FullCourse.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The integral intersection pairing is a symmetric integral unimodular form on the free finite-rank group $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$. [[def-integral-intersection-lattice-of-a-simply-connected-four-manifold]] [[lem-integral-intersection-pairing-is-unimodular]]

[F2] The equation is $F_A^-=0$, with charge $c_2=-1$. Its actual compatible reducible preparation, middle regularization, complete inverse small-instanton end and smooth cut bordism are supplied by [[lem-donaldson-reducible-ends-and-one-instanton-compactification]]. The actual reducible orbits inject into mutually orthogonal unordered integral norm-one pairs, so their number is at most $b_2(X)$. [[lem-reducible-charge-one-su-two-connections-admit-controlled-projective-links]]

[F3] The ordinary signature of the full boundary of an actual compact oriented five-manifold is zero. This follows from the explicitly proved self-annihilating image of restriction in the boundary intersection form; no closed four-dimensional index theorem is used. [[thm-topological-five-bordisms-preserve-ordinary-and-l2-signatures]]

[F4] The integral cohomology ring of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is $\mathbb Z[x]/(x^3)$, with $x^2$ a generator. Thus its middle form has rank one and signature $1$ or $-1$, according to orientation. [[lem-integral-cohomology-ring-of-complex-projective-space-by-splitting]]

[A1] Full AC is inherited from the gauge, compactness, characteristic-class and duality suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC and the closed smooth simply connected oriented manifold in the Statement, with positive-definite intersection pairing. Put $b=b_2(X)$.

1.1 **An actual bordism rather than an assumed end.** If $b=0$ the free intersection group has rank zero and its empty integral basis gives the claim. Suppose $b>0$. A charge-minus-one bundle exists: glue a trivial bundle on a ball to the trivial bundle on its complement by the unit-quaternion clutching function on the common three-sphere, with the sign used by the explicit BPST construction in the Taubes proof. Its smooth model connection has $c_2[X]=-1$, by the displayed curvature integral $8\pi^2$ and the fixed sign convention. Apply [F2] on this actual bundle. It gives a compact oriented smooth five-manifold $W$ whose full boundary is $X$ together with $n$ oriented projective-plane links, where $n$ is the actual number of reducible solution orbits. The determinant orientation can be chosen so the $X$ boundary has its given orientation. Closed components of $W$ have empty boundary and do not affect this assertion. [F1, F2, A1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **The signed boundary inequality forces enough reducibles.** Positive definiteness makes $\operatorname{sign}(X)=b$. Each projective link has signature $\varepsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}$ by [F4]. Additivity of the intersection form under finite disjoint union and [F3] give $0=b+\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i$, hence $b\le n$. The actual reducible classification in [F2] gives $n\le b$, since its $n$ distinct unordered norm-one pairs are mutually orthogonal and nonzero. Thus $n=b$ (and the boundary equation also forces every $\varepsilon_i=-1$ for this chosen orientation). No numerical spectral-flow label or prior common sign was assumed. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **The integral basis, not merely a real diagonalization.** Choose one representative $x_i$ from each of these $b$ unordered norm-one pairs in cohomology. They satisfy $x_i\cdot x_j=\delta_{ij}$ by [F2]. Let $L=H^2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$. They are a real basis of $L\otimes\mathbb R$ because they are $b$ nonzero orthogonal vectors. For every $y\in L$, its real-basis expansion is $y=\sum_i(y\cdot x_i)x_i$. Every coefficient is an integer by integrality of [F1], so $y$ belongs to their integral span. Thus these vectors are an integral basis of the full lattice, not a proper finite-index sublattice. Integral Poincare duality identifies this lattice with the homological intersection lattice in [F1]. Transporting this basis gives the asserted identity matrix on $H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$. The rank-zero case was already covered, and this proves the original diagonalization conclusion. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Donaldson's complete method-of-proof passage on printed280–281 and the full gauge and end argument on284–314 were read. The final argument uses the actual cut bordism and the inequality from its induced, initially unknown projective-link signs. It neither infers inverse gluing from existence nor assumes all norm-one splittings occur in a given bundle. The real-signature input is actual bordism invariance, not the closed Atiyah–Singer signature theorem. The original Statement is unchanged, apart from the already authorized full-AC prefix; the Perutz citation remains comparison context and supplies no step in this proof.

## Statement

Let $G$ and $G'$ be one-component grid diagrams related by one of the following local moves. A cyclic permutation changes the planar cut of the toroidal grid by moving the first row or column to the last. A row commutation exchanges consecutive rows whose closed horizontal marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested; a column commutation uses the same condition on vertical marking intervals. A stabilization replaces a marked cell by a two-by-two block with the original marking type in two opposite cells and the other type in a third cell, leaves the fourth cell empty, and inserts one row and one column, relocating the old companion markings so each new row and column has one mark of each type. Any of the four empty corners is allowed, and destabilization is the inverse move. Regard each full filtered minus complex returned by the grid-complex algorithm as a complex over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by letting $U$ act as one chosen marking variable $U_i$, retaining the other independent variables. The resulting complexes are filtered chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb F_2[U]$, with equivalences preserving the Maslov grading and Alexander filtration. For each move, finite grid-domain counts give filtered chain maps in both directions and filtered chain homotopies from both composites to the identity. For a stabilization, its multivariable target is first compared with the cone of $U_{n+1}+U_i$ on the polynomial extension of the original complex. After instead taking the simultaneous ordinary quotient $U_1=\cdots=U_n=U$, a stabilization contributes a zero-map cone, equivalently an extra zero-differential factor $V$; those fully collapsed complexes are compared with this factor retained. Under commutation the tilde homologies are isomorphic; under a stabilization from grid number $n$ to $n+1$, the tilde homology changes by tensoring with the two-dimensional bigraded vector space $V$ with one generator in bidegree $(0,0)$ and one in bidegree $(-1,-1)$.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot|Grid moves, states, and rectangle conventions]]

[[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex|Full filtered and tilde grid complexes]]

[[lem-grid-marking-variables-chain-homotopic|Identification of marking-variable actions]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, Chapters 5 and 13](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

[Manolescu, Ozsvath, and Sarkar, “A combinatorial description of knot Floer homology,” §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0607691)


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two one-component grids and the single grid move in the statement. All polynomial variables initially remain independent and are matched by their individual markings.

[F1] [[lem-grid-filtered-pentagon-hexagon-equivalences]] gives the weighted pentagon maps, hexagon inverse homotopies, and their filtered, associated-graded, and tilde versions for commutations and switches.

[F2] [[lem-grid-filtered-destabilization-domain-map]] defines the filtered incoming-domain map for a southwest $X$ stabilization and proves its chain-map and grading identities by all domain cases.

[F3] [[lem-grid-destabilization-filtered-equivalence]] supplies an explicit inverse and both homotopies for that map by a finite cone-contraction formula, and derives its retained-variable and tilde comparisons.

[F4] [[lem-grid-changing-chosen-variable-action]] gives explicit filtered equivalences and inverse homotopies for changing the chosen variable action along the knot's single cycle.

[F5] [[lem-pointed-basepoint-cone-and-variable-collapse]] proves that a cone of the new variable plus an old one retracts onto the smaller complex over the old-variable ring, while its simultaneous ordinary collapse is a zero-map cone and contributes $V$.

## Proof

1.1 A cyclic permutation is a change of fundamental cut on the same grid torus. It identifies states, rectangles, and marking monomials bijectively. The finite pair-count gradings also agree under this change. To check this directly for a column cut, use the signed set $P=\mathbf x-\mathbb O$ in $M_O=I(P,P)+1$. The wrapping column contains one state point of sign $+1$ and one $O$ of sign $-1$. Only their comparisons with nonwrapping points change. At an integer state height the signed number of all points below is zero, and at the height of a marking in row $r$ it is one, since the states have heights $0,\ldots,n-1$ and the markings have one height in each open row. Thus the signed difference of the below/above counts for either wrapping point, excluding itself, is one. Multiplying by the two signs and adding gives zero; the comparisons between the two wrapping points cancel from this sum and do not change. Hence $I(P,P)$ is unchanged. Apply the same count to $\mathbf x-\mathbb X$, and interchange coordinates for a row cut. Both Maslov functions and the Alexander formula are unchanged. The torus-identification map is therefore a filtered chain isomorphism, with inverse the opposite cut change and zero inverse homotopies. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For a commutation, use the maps and homotopies in [F1]. Their weights retain every $O$ variable separately, and their filtration drop is the number of $X$ in the polygon. Thus they are filtered equivalences over the full ring; restricting the ring action to any chosen marking variable preserves these identities. Their associated-graded maps retain precisely polygons avoiding $X$. Setting the variables to zero gives the tilde equivalence. The identical conclusion holds for the switches used below. [F1, given]

1.3 For a southwest $X$ stabilization, [F2] supplies the map to the cone of $U_1+U_2$ on the polynomial extension of the smaller complex. By [F3], it has a finite matrix inverse and both filtered inverse homotopies. Compose with the explicit retraction in [F5]. Its inclusion, divided-difference homotopy, and evaluation are linear over every old variable, so the resulting equivalence and homotopies are over any chosen retained old-variable action. If either grid uses another chosen variable, including the newly inserted one, first or last compose with the chosen-variable equivalences of [F4]. Hence the assertion holds for arbitrary choices of the single variable action, without setting any independent variable equal to another. [F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 The other local stabilization types reduce to this one using the following finite operations. An $O$ stabilization introduces a vertical segment joining marks in consecutive rows. Commute this short segment horizontally toward the next $X$ endpoint; while passing another vertical segment, its length-one interval is either disjoint or nested, since no marking height lies strictly between its two endpoints. At a shared endpoint level the exchange is a switch. Stop at the next $X$, where deleting that short segment is an $X$ destabilization back to the original grid. Tracking the empty corner gives the pairs $O{:}NE$ with $X{:}SW$, $O{:}SE$ with $X{:}NW$, $O{:}NW$ with $X{:}SE$, and $O{:}SW$ with $X{:}NE$. Among the four $X$ types, exchanging the two new adjacent rows moves the empty corner across a horizontal side, and exchanging the two new adjacent columns moves it across a vertical side; these are switches because the central opposite-type marking shares a column or row with the adjacent same-type marking. One or two such switches carry any empty corner to the southwest corner. These operations concern only the added row, added column, and their endpoint segments; after deleting them the original row and column orders are unchanged. Thus every stabilization is a southwest $X$ stabilization followed by finitely many commutations, switches, and cut changes. [given, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Compose the equivalences for that finite sequence, using step 1.2 for commutations and switches and step 1.3 for its sole stabilization. Explicit inverse homotopies compose: for equivalences $f_1,f_2$ with inverses $g_1,g_2$ and homotopies $g_i f_i+1=dH_i+H_id$, a homotopy for $g_1g_2f_2f_1+1$ is $H_1+g_1H_2f_1$. The counterpart on the other complex has the analogous formula. Every summand remains filtered and has degree $+1$. Reversing the roles of the two grids proves the destabilization assertion as well. All map formulas are finite sums of composable grid-domain counts and the explicit polynomial formulas in [F3]–[F5]. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The full polynomial equivalence with the stabilization cone in step 1.3 can also be tensored with the simultaneous ordinary coefficient quotient. Its cross map $U_1+U_2$ becomes zero, so [F5] identifies the quotient cone with the collapsed smaller complex tensored with $V$. The first summand's grading and filtration shift is $(-1,-1)$, giving exactly the displayed bidegrees. Taking the associated-graded equivalence first and then setting every variable to zero gives the same direct sum for tilde homology. Commutation and switches preserve tilde homology by step 1.2, and cut changes do by step 1.1. These comparisons prove the tilde and collapsed assertions for every stabilization type. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

Grid moves generate isotopy of oriented knots addresses the separate global fact that these local moves connect any two grids of an oriented knot. The proof here constructs the equivalences for each specified local move.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $q\ge2$. If $\zeta_q$ is any primitive $q$-th root of unity, then $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$ is finite exactly when $\Delta_K(\zeta_q^j)\ne0$ for every $1\le j<q$, and in that case
$$
|H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)|=\prod_{j=1}^{q-1}|\Delta_K(\zeta_q^j)|.
$$

## Statement references

[[lem-cyclic-cover-order-root-product-and-rational-sphere-test|The root-product test and proof for cyclic-cover homology]]

[[def-alexander-polynomial-from-the-first-elementary-ideal|The Alexander polynomial normalization]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface|The definition and genus convention for a Seifert surface]]

[Rolfsen, *Knots and Links*, Chapter 8.D](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/rolfsen.pdf)

[Livingston, “Seifert Forms and Concordance,” Theorem 3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0101035v3)

[[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface|Existence of a connected compact oriented Seifert surface for every knot]]

[[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups|The compact surface normal form and free fundamental group]]

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix convention]]

[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization|First homology is the abelianization of the fundamental group]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth oriented knot $K$, and $q\ge2$.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom required by the root-product lemma. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The root-product lemma gives the finiteness criterion and order for any primitive $q$-th root. [[lem-cyclic-cover-order-root-product-and-rational-sphere-test]]

[F2] $\Delta_K(t)$ is defined up to multiplication by $\pm t^k$. [[def-alexander-polynomial-from-the-first-elementary-ideal]]

[F3] Full AC supplies the countable-choice hypotheses used by the surface-existence and surface-normal-form results: apply its choice function to the range of any sequence of nonempty sets and reuse the selected element at each index. Thus the sequence assertions in [[def-countable-choice]] and [[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]] hold. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] Every smooth oriented knot bounds a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with its given boundary, which is a Seifert surface under [[def-oriented-seifert-surface]]. [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]] For a connected compact oriented surface with one boundary component and genus $g$, the fundamental group is free of rank $2g$. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F5] A connected smooth surface $F$ is locally path-connected, so its path components are open and it is path-connected. The first Hurewicz map identifies $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with the abelianization of $\pi_1(F)$; for the genus-$g$ surface in [F4], this gives $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^{2g}$ and an ordered integral basis. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement and Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 By [F3]--[F5], choose a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface $F$ for $K$ and an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Let $V$ be its positive-push Seifert matrix as defined in [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]. The hypotheses of [F1] then hold for this $K,F,V,q$, and the selected primitive root $\zeta_q$. Hence it gives the stated nonvanishing criterion and product formula for this root. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, given, choose]

2.1 If $\zeta_q'$ is another primitive $q$-th root, then $\zeta_q'=\zeta_q^r$ for some integer $r$ relatively prime to $q$. Multiplication by $r$ permutes the nonzero residue classes modulo $q$, so the nonvanishing conditions and the product over $j=1,\ldots,q-1$ are unchanged. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$, and suppose that the knot complement $Y\setminus K$ is irreducible. Let $F$ be a genus-$g$ Seifert surface for $K$. If the integral top Alexander group satisfies

$$\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(Y,K,[F],g;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z,$$

then $Y\setminus K$ fibers over $S^1$ with fiber $F$.

## Statement references

[[def-top-alexander-grading-of-knot-floer-homology|The integral top Alexander group]]

[[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region|The sutured complement cut along F and its product structure]]

[Ni, *Knot Floer homology detects fibred knots*, Theorem 1.1 and §§3–7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0607156v4)

[Juhasz, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, Theorem 9.11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609779v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the knot, exterior, actual surface $F$ and integral grading-$g$ group in the Statement.

[F1] Under full AC and exactly these geometric and integral-group hypotheses, [[lem-ni-fiberedness-sutured-floer-and-gabai-inputs]] proves that the compact exterior cut along the actual $F$ is a product sutured manifold. Its proof explicitly imports the general balanced sutured vanishing and nonproduct rank results and records Ni's corrected characteristic-pair formulation; the resolved local signed comparison and hierarchy dependencies are preserved.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Apply F1 to the actual class $[F]$, the actual genus $g$ and the given integral group. The cut exterior is a product $F\times[0,1]$ as a sutured manifold. In particular the two horizontal faces correspond to the two copies of the original $F$, rather than to a surface selected only by a genus or homology calculation. [F1]

2.1 To restore the exterior, identify those two faces using their actual gluing map. In product coordinates this is $(x,1)\sim(h(x),0)$ for a self-homeomorphism $h:F\to F$. Thus the exterior is the mapping torus of $h$. Its projection to $[0,1]/(0\sim1)=S^1$ is a surface bundle, and the seam is precisely the original embedded $F$. [step 1.1]

3.1 The vertical boundary is the mapping torus of $\partial F$. Its boundary collar extends this bundle over the deleted-knot end, giving the fibration of $Y\setminus K$ with fiber the interior of $F$, or equivalently with compact fiber $F$ in the compact exterior. This proves the stated fiberedness with the prescribed surface, for arbitrary $Y$ and also for genus zero. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\phi:A\to B$ be a group homomorphism inducing an isomorphism
$H_1(A;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(B;\mathbb Z)$ and an epimorphism
$H_2(A;\mathbb Z)\to H_2(B;\mathbb Z)$. For a group $X$, define
$\Gamma_1X=X$ and $\Gamma_{n+1}X=[X,\Gamma_nX]$. Then for every finite
$n\ge1$, the induced homomorphism
$$A/\Gamma_nA\longrightarrow B/\Gamma_nB$$
is an isomorphism.

## Statement references

[McCleary, Theorem 8bis.16](https://pages.vassar.edu/mccleary/files/2011/04/MC08bis.fin_.pdf)

[Cochran and Harvey, Introduction](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=0bcc9546b436e84c2099f89be24699e31bf14276&repid=rep1&type=pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and a group homomorphism $\phi:A\to B$ satisfying the stated
$H_1$ and $H_2$ hypotheses.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]]; it is inherited from the
group-extension homology sequence supplier.

[F1] For every group extension $1\to N\to G\to Q\to1$, the exact sequence
$H_2(G)\to H_2(Q)\to N/[G,N]\to H_1(G)\to H_1(Q)\to0$ is natural in maps of
extensions. [[thm-five-term-homology-sequence-for-group-extensions]]

[L1] AC implies DC by choosing one successor at each stage of a serial relation. [[def-dependent-choice]]

[F2] In the bar complex, degree one has generators $[x]$ and degree-two boundaries $[y]-[xy]+[x]$, so $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\cong X/[X,X]$. [[lem-diagonal-bar-coinvariants-compute-group-homology]]

## Proof

**Given:** The group map and hypotheses above.

1.1 By [A1] and [L1], the DC condition of the bar-homology supplier in [F2]
holds. The case $n=1$ is the map between two trivial quotients. For $n=2$, the
induced map $A/\Gamma_2A\to B/\Gamma_2B$ is exactly the assumed isomorphism on
$H_1$ by [F2]. These are the base cases. [A1, L1, F2, given]

1.2 Fix $n\ge2$ and assume $A/\Gamma_nA\to B/\Gamma_nB$ is an isomorphism.
Apply [F1] to the extensions
$1\to\Gamma_nA\to A\to A/\Gamma_nA\to1$ and
$1\to\Gamma_nB\to B\to B/\Gamma_nB\to1$. Since
$\Gamma_nX\subseteq[X,X]$ for $n\ge2$, the maps
$H_1(X)\to H_1(X/\Gamma_nX)$ are isomorphisms. Exactness therefore makes the
transgression $H_2(X/\Gamma_nX)\to\Gamma_nX/[X,\Gamma_nX]$ onto, with kernel
the image of $H_2(X)$. By definition $[X,\Gamma_nX]=\Gamma_{n+1}X$. [A1, F1,
F2, given, algebra]

1.3 Naturality of [F1] makes the map
$H_2(A/\Gamma_nA)\to H_2(B/\Gamma_nB)$ compatible with the two transgressions.
It is an isomorphism because the quotient-group map is an isomorphism by the
induction hypothesis. The epimorphism $H_2(A)\to H_2(B)$ makes the image of
$H_2(A)$ in $H_2(A/\Gamma_nA)$ map onto the image of $H_2(B)$ in
$H_2(B/\Gamma_nB)$. The induced map on the two cokernels is consequently an
isomorphism. By step 1.2 and exactness, those cokernels are
$\Gamma_nA/\Gamma_{n+1}A$ and $\Gamma_nB/\Gamma_{n+1}B$. [F1, step 1.2,
algebra]

2.1 The inclusions and quotient maps give exact central extensions
$$1\to\Gamma_nX/\Gamma_{n+1}X\to X/\Gamma_{n+1}X\to X/\Gamma_nX\to1, \qquad X=A,B,$$
because $[X,\Gamma_nX]=\Gamma_{n+1}X$. The maps on the kernel and quotient
terms are isomorphisms by step 1.3 and the induction hypothesis. The middle
map is injective: an element in its kernel projects to the identity in the
quotient, hence lies in the kernel term, where injectivity holds. It is
surjective: for a target element, lift its quotient class through the quotient
isomorphism and then correct the chosen middle lift by a kernel element using
the kernel isomorphism. Thus $A/\Gamma_{n+1}A\to B/\Gamma_{n+1}B$ is an
isomorphism. [step 1.3, algebra, choose]

2.2 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove by induction the isomorphism for every finite
$n$. Apart from the inherited AC used to obtain the homology sequence [F1],
the induction uses only exactness and a single element lift at a time; no
additional choice principle is used. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement refuted

Every nonzero integral pair $(p,q)$ on a torus with ordered basis $([\mu],[\lambda])$ represents an ordinary Dehn-filling slope.

## Statement references

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 5, §5.8](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/5.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An oriented torus with ordered integral basis $([\mu],[\lambda])$ and the generalized cone-filling convention.

[F1] [[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]]: an ordinary slope is represented by a primitive integral pair modulo simultaneous sign; a generalized parameter $r(p,q)$ with primitive $(p,q)$ has core direction $(p,q)$ and cone angle $2\pi/r$.

## Proof

**Given:** The torus with ordered basis $([\mu],[\lambda])$ and the generalized cone-filling convention.

1.1 The coordinates $(2,0)$ have greatest common divisor $2$, so they are not primitive. By [F1], they therefore do not represent an ordinary slope or the meridian class of an ordinary smooth filling. The primitive pair on the same ray is $(1,0)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Write $(2,0)=2(1,0)$, so the radial factor is $r=2$. The generalized parameter convention in [F1] assigns cone angle $2\pi/2=\pi$ to this ray parameter. This differs from the ordinary smooth filling along slope $(1,0)$, which uses the primitive parameter with $r=1$ and full angle $2\pi$. Hence the nonprimitive pair is a cone/orbifold completion parameter, not an ordinary slope. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 5, §5.8](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/5.pdf)

## Definition

Let $\overline M$ be a compact connected oriented three-manifold whose boundary is a disjoint union of tori $T_1,\ldots,T_k$. Choose an ordered integral basis $([\mu_i],[\lambda_i])$ for each $H_1(T_i;\mathbb Z)$. A **slope** on $T_i$ is an unoriented isotopy class of essential simple closed curves whose homology class is $p_i[\mu_i]+q_i[\lambda_i]$ for a primitive pair $(p_i,q_i)\in\mathbb Z^2$; simultaneous negation gives the same unoriented slope. The primitive-pair correspondence gives exactly one such slope for each primitive pair modulo sign. The **ordinary Dehn filling** along a tuple of slopes indexed by $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ attaches an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to each $T_i$, $i\in J$, by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{*\}]$ to the chosen slope. The gluing maps are part of the filling data; $i\notin J$ means that the cusp is left unfilled, denoted by the parameter $\infty$.

For a hyperbolic deformation, the **generalized cone-filling parameter space** at each cusp is the one-point compactification $\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$ of the real coefficient plane, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp. A primitive integral pair $(p_i,q_i)$ is an ordinary smooth filling coefficient. If a realized generalized parameter lies on the ray $g_i=r_i(p_i,q_i)$ with $r_i>0$ and $(p_i,q_i)$ primitive integral, its topological core direction is the ordinary slope $(p_i,q_i)$ and its cone angle is $2\pi/r_i$. Only $r_i=1$ is the ordinary smooth filling; $r_i>1$ describes a cone or orbifold completion and does not turn the nonprimitive vector $g_i$ into a slope.

## Statement

For a connected regular link diagram $D$ with $c$ crossings, the Laurent-polynomial span of its Kauffman bracket is at most $4c$. If $D$ is reduced and alternating, then changing any one crossing from the all-$A$ state or the all-$B$ state merges two distinct state circles, both extreme coefficients are nonzero, and the bracket span is exactly $4c$. The span of a nonzero Laurent polynomial is its largest exponent minus its smallest exponent.

## Statement references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A connected regular link diagram $D$ with $c$ crossings, with all-$A$ and all-$B$ smoothing states as defined by the bracket convention.

[F1] The bracket is the finite sum $\langle D\rangle=\sum_S A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}$ with $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$; its states are choices of one smoothing at each crossing ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] In a connected alternating diagram, successive crossing visits along every component alternate between over and under, and reducedness means no projection region has a crossing more than once on its boundary ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]]).

[F3] Every connected regular projection has a checkerboard coloring ([[lem-connected-regular-link-diagram-has-checkerboard-coloring]]).

[F4] The Tait graph has checkerboard regions as vertices and crossings as edges ([[def-tait-graph-of-a-link-diagram]]).

[F5] For a connected plane graph, $|V|-|E|+|F|=2$ ([[thm-euler-formula-for-connected-plane-graphs]]).

[F6] For a connected projection with at least one crossing, either Tait graph is connected ([[lem-connected-projection-has-connected-tait-graphs]]).

[F7] A smooth embedded circle on the projection sphere bounds a closed disk on either side. Choose a point in the opposite side, use a stereographic chart, and apply the choice-free smooth Jordan-disk result ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-jordan-disk-parameters-and-prescribed-collars]]).

[F8] **External input, exact use:** For a $k$-component link, the normalized bracket has value $(-2)^{k-1}$ at $A=1$. Kauffman identifies the normalized bracket with the Jones polynomial under $t=A^{-4}$ ([§2, Theorems 2.6 and 2.8](https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/kauffmanjones.pdf)); Murasugi proves the value from the skein relation and unlink formula ([Chapter 11, Propositions 11.1.1 and 11.2.6](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/murasug3.pdf)), using the finite crossing-change reduction of [Chapter 4, Proposition 4.4.1](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/murasug3.pdf). These precise results and arguments were read; no source-wide audit is asserted.

## Proof
1.1 Let $\mu$ be the number of components represented by $D$. By [F8],
$$(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle\big|_{A=1}=(-2)^{\mu-1}\ne0.$$
The writhe-normalizing factor is a Laurent monomial and hence a unit, so $\langle D\rangle$ is nonzero and its span is defined. Now let $s_A$ and $s_B$ be the numbers of circles in the all-$A$ and all-$B$ states. If a state has $j$ $B$-smoothings, then its weight factor is $A^{c-2j}$. A single smoothing change is a band surgery and changes the circle count by exactly $1$ or $-1$, so a state with $k$ circles has $k\le s_A+j$. Since the highest degree of $\delta^{k-1}$ is $2(k-1)$, every state term has degree at most $c-2j+2(k-1)\le c+2(s_A-1)$. Reversing $A$ and $B$ gives minimum degree at least $-c-2(s_B-1)$. Hence $\operatorname{span}_A\langle D\rangle\le2c+2(s_A+s_B-2)$. [given, F1, F8, construct]

1.2 If $c>0$, the connected projection has finite disk faces. To see this, thicken a spanning tree to a disk, then add the remaining edge strips one at a time. The core of each added edge lies in one complementary disk and is a properly embedded arc there. Its strip cuts that disk along the arc; after rounding corners, the two new boundary curves are smooth Jordan curves, and [F7] makes their closed sides disks. At each stage the new edge lies in one old region and splits it into exactly the two regions adjacent to the new edge, so these disk complements correspond one-to-one to the projection regions. Thus each complementary region has a disk core disjoint from the graph. Now suppose $D$ is reduced and alternating. Color its regions by [F3]. At one crossing choose the color name so the $A$-smoothing follows the two black sectors. Moving along a projection arc to the next crossing, alternation switches which branch is over; the chart definition of the $A$-smoothing therefore continues to follow the same color. Connectedness propagates this choice to every crossing. Thus the all-$A$ state circles trace the black disk cores and the all-$B$ circles trace the white disk cores. Embed the black Tait graph by placing vertices in black cores and drawing each crossing edge through its crossing disk; its complementary faces are precisely the white disk cores. Hence it is connected by [F6], has $c$ edges, $s_A$ vertices, and $s_B$ faces by [F4]. Euler's formula [F5] gives $s_A-c+s_B=2$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, construct]

2.1 Suppose $c>0$. Put the all-$A$ state on the lower level $S^2\times\{0\}$ and the all-$B$ state on the upper level $S^2\times\{1\}$. Outside the crossing disks, join corresponding state arcs by product rectangles; inside each crossing disk, join the two local smoothings by one saddle cobordism. The resulting compact surface $\Sigma$ has boundary the $s_A+s_B$ state circles and exactly $c$ index-one saddles, hence $\chi(\Sigma)=-c$. Its incidence graph has one vertex for each state circle and one edge for each saddle; connectedness of the projection makes this graph connected, because each projection arc lies on the state circles incident to its endpoint saddles. Thus $\Sigma$ is connected. Cap each boundary circle by a disk, obtaining a connected closed surface $\widehat\Sigma$ with $\chi(\widehat\Sigma)=s_A+s_B-c$. Give it a finite cellulation and take cellular chains $C_i$ over $\mathbb F_2$, with boundary maps $\partial_i$. If $r_i=\operatorname{rank}\partial_i$ and $h_i=\dim H_i$, then rank-nullity gives $\dim C_i=h_i+r_i+r_{i+1}$; alternating the sum over $i=0,1,2$ cancels the $r_i$ terms and yields $\chi(\widehat\Sigma)=h_0-h_1+h_2$. Connectedness gives $h_0=1$. A 2-cycle has equal coefficients on the two faces adjacent to every edge; the dual graph of a connected closed surface is connected, so all face coefficients agree and $h_2=1$. Therefore $\chi(\widehat\Sigma)=2-h_1\le2$, and $s_A+s_B-c\le2$. For $c=0$, a connected projection is one circle and $s_A=s_B=1$, giving the same inequality. Combining this bound with step 1.1 proves $\operatorname{span}_A\langle D\rangle\le4c$. [given, F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 At any crossing, reducedness in [F2] says the two black sectors belong to distinct black regions and the two white sectors belong to distinct white regions. The all-$A$ smoothing circles trace the black regions, so changing one crossing from all-$A$ joins two distinct state circles by a band and merges them; the all-$B$ change similarly merges two distinct white state circles. If a state changes $j\ge1$ crossings from all-$A$, the first change lowers the circle count to $s_A-1$, and each later change can increase it by at most one; hence its circle count is at most $s_A+j-2$. Its term's degree is therefore at most $c-2j+2(s_A+j-3)=c+2(s_A-3)$, four below the all-$A$ term's top degree $c+2(s_A-1)$. The all-$A$ term has top coefficient $(-1)^{s_A-1}\ne0$, so it cannot cancel. The same argument at all-$B$ proves a nonzero bottom coefficient. When $c=0$, the single state has bracket $1$, and the same conclusions hold vacuously. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Using $s_A+s_B=c+2$ from step 1.2, the highest degree minus the lowest degree is $\bigl(c+2(s_A-1)\bigr)-\bigl(-c-2(s_B-1)\bigr)=2c+2(s_A+s_B-2)=4c$. The extreme coefficients are nonzero by step 2.2, so this is the actual bracket span. The $c=0$ case has span $0=4c$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎
