## Statement

Let $X$ be a locally compact second-countable metric space, let $\lambda$ be a finite positive Radon measure on $X$, and let $\nu:X\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous with $|\nu(x)|=1$ for every $x$. Define the vector measure $\mu(A):=\int_A\nu\,d\lambda$ on Borel sets. Its partition variation satisfies $|\mu|=\lambda$.

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-vector-radon-variation-is-radon|Partition variation for finite vectors of Radon measures.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A locally compact second-countable metric space $X$, a finite positive Radon measure $\lambda$, and a continuous unit-vector field $\nu$.

[F1] The partition variation is defined by taking the supremum of sums of vector norms over Borel partitions. ([[lem-ip-vector-radon-variation-is-radon]])

[F2] A finite Radon measure has compact inner approximation on the open set $X$. ([[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]])

[F3] Each coordinate formula $\mu_i(A):=\int_A\nu_i\,d\lambda$ defines a finite signed Borel measure. Countable additivity follows by dominated convergence for disjoint Borel unions, since $|\nu_i|\le1$ and $\lambda(X)<\infty$. Its partition variation satisfies $|\mu_i|(A)\le\lambda(A)$ by the triangle inequality, and $|\mu_i|$ is a measure by [[thm-total-variation-is-a-measure]]. Although the Radon convention for $\lambda$ states compact inner approximation only on open sets, finiteness upgrades it to all Borel sets: for Borel $A$ and $\epsilon>0$, choose compact $C\subset X$ with $\lambda(X\setminus C)<\epsilon/2$ and open $G\supset X\setminus A$ with $\lambda(G\cap A)<\epsilon/2$; then $C\setminus G$ is compact in $A$ and $\lambda(A\setminus(C\setminus G))<\epsilon$. Thus $\lambda$ is regular on all Borel sets, and domination transfers compact inner and open outer approximations to $|\mu_i|$. By the repository convention that a finite signed measure is Radon when its total variation is regular, each coordinate measure is finite signed Radon and the vector-variation result [F1] applies. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[thm-total-variation-is-a-measure]], [[def-radon-measure-on-an-lch-space]], [[def-regular-complex-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]])

## Proof

**Given:** The space $X$, the finite Radon measure $\lambda$, and the continuous unit field $\nu$.

1.1 By [F3], the coordinate measures of $\mu$ are finite signed Radon measures, as required before applying [F1]. For any countable Borel partition $(A_j)$ of a Borel set $A$, the triangle inequality for vector integrals gives $\sum_j|\mu(A_j)|\le\sum_j\int_{A_j}|\nu|\,d\lambda=\lambda(A)$. Thus $|\mu|(A)\le\lambda(A)$. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\lambda(X)=0$, step 1.1 already gives $|\mu|(X)=0$. Otherwise fix $0<\varepsilon<1$ and also choose it small enough that $\varepsilon<\lambda(X)$. By [F2] choose compact $K\subset X$ with $\lambda(X\setminus K)<\varepsilon$; then $K$ is nonempty. Uniform continuity of $\nu$ on $K$ gives a finite Borel partition $K=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^N A_j$ such that $|\nu(x)-\nu(y)|<\varepsilon$ for all $x,y\in A_j$. Choose $x_j\in A_j$ for each nonempty part. Then $$|\mu(A_j)|\ge\nu(x_j)\cdot\mu(A_j)=\int_{A_j}\nu(x_j)\cdot\nu(x)\,d\lambda(x)\ge(1-\varepsilon^2/2)\lambda(A_j),$$ since $\nu(x_j)\cdot\nu(x)=1-\tfrac12|\nu(x_j)-\nu(x)|^2$. The partition of $X$ consisting of these $A_j$ and $X\setminus K$ therefore gives $|\mu|(X)\ge(1-\varepsilon^2/2)\lambda(K)\ge(1-\varepsilon^2/2)(\lambda(X)-\varepsilon)$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using step 1.1 proves $|\mu|(X)=\lambda(X)$. Applying the same argument to each Borel subset with the restricted measure proves equality on every Borel set. [F1, F2, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 The preceding equality on all Borel subsets is precisely equality of the two positive measures $|\mu|$ and $\lambda$. [step 2.1] ∎

    - title: "Arunima Ray, Slice Knots and Knot Concordance, Winter Braids Lecture Notes 8"
      url: "https://numdam.org/item/10.5802/wbln.39.pdf"
      locator: "§1.2.3, Definition 1.17 and Remark 1.69, printed pp.31–33"

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard oriented three-sphere, let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera $g(F)\in\mathbb N_0$ of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$, and let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the corresponding set for locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces. For each surface, $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Both sets are nonempty and have least elements.

## Statement references

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Properness, local flatness, and boundary charts]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|The genus convention for connected orientable spanning surfaces]]

[[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface|Existence of a smooth oriented Seifert surface under countable choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[F1] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $K$ bounds a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $\Sigma\subset S^3$ with oriented boundary $K$. ([[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]])

[F2] For a connected compact orientable surface with one boundary component, $g(\Sigma)\in\mathbb N_0$ is determined by $\chi(\Sigma)=1-2g(\Sigma)$. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]])

[F3] A smooth boundary has a smooth collar; in the standard unit ball the boundary collar is $(x,u)\mapsto(1-u)x$ for $x\in S^3$ and sufficiently small $u\ge0$. ([[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]], [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]])

[F4] A proper surface is locally flat when it has the stated plane-pair charts at interior and boundary points; a smooth proper surface has such topological charts. ([[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the sequence-choice principle stated in the supplier. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $K$.

1.1 By [F1], choose a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface $\Sigma\subset S^3$ with $\partial\Sigma=K$. By [F3], choose $0<\varepsilon<1$ and identify a collar of $S^3=\partial B^4$ with $S^3\times[0,\varepsilon)$, where $(x,u)$ maps to $(1-u)x$. Apply the collar theorem in [F3] also to $\Sigma$ and write $r\ge0$ for its inward boundary-collar coordinate. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi(r)$ equal to $1$ near $r=0$ and $0$ before the collar ends, and a constant $c\in(0,\varepsilon)$; set $h=\chi(r)r+(1-\chi(r))c$ in the collar and $h=c$ beyond it. Since $0\le r,c<\varepsilon<1$, $h$ takes values in $[0,1)$; it is smooth, vanishes exactly on $\partial\Sigma$, and is positive on the interior. [F1, F3, A1, construct]

2.1 The graph $F=\{((1-h(x))x):x\in\Sigma\}\subset B^4$ is embedded because the radial collar projection to $S^3$ recovers $x$. It is compact and connected, its boundary is exactly $K$, and all its nonboundary points lie in the interior of $B^4$. Its smooth charts give the local-flat pair charts in [F4]. The graph is homeomorphic to $\Sigma$, so it has genus $g(\Sigma)$ from [F2]. Thus this one surface contributes an element to each of $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ and $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Each set is therefore a nonempty subset $A\subseteq\mathbb N_0$. Choose one $n\in A$. The finite set $A\cap\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$ is nonempty, so it has a least element $m$ by the ordinary finite ordering. If $a\in A$ and $a<m$, then $a\le n$ and hence $a\in A\cap\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$, contradicting the choice of $m$. Thus $m$ is least in $A$. Applying this argument to each of the two sets gives both minima; no well-ordering principle or additional choice axiom is used. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]]

## Statement refuted

Assume Countable Choice. The assertion that every sequence $(u_N)_{N\ge1}$ in $BV((0,1))$ with bounded $L^1(0,1)$ norms has uniformly bounded total variations is false. For $k\ge1$ let $I_k=(2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k})$ and define $u_N:=\sum_{k=1}^N(-1)^k\chi_{I_k}$. Then $\|u_N\|_{L^1(0,1)}=\sum_{k=1}^N|I_k|<1/2$, while the adjacent jumps have total magnitude $2N$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|The definitions of spatial BV and total variation.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc|Finite-test-field characterization of total variation detects the growing jump variation.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the interval $\Omega=(0,1)$, and the sequence of step functions $u_N$ defined above.

[A1] Countable Choice is used to identify interval Lebesgue integrals with their Riemann values and to use countably additive Lebesgue measure. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] Distributional derivatives use the negative-transpose test convention, and BV total variation is the mass of the derivative measure. ([[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv]])

[F2] For BV functions, total variation is the supremum over compactly supported smooth unit-bounded scalar test fields in one dimension; this clause is choice-free. ([[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]])

[F3] Smooth cutoffs supported in small intervals can be chosen equal to one at a prescribed interior point. ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]])

[F4] Under Countable Choice, Lebesgue measure of a bounded interval is its length. ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-radon-measure-on-rn]])

[F5] A bounded Riemann-integrable function on a compact interval has the same Lebesgue and Riemann integrals. ([[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]])

[F6] The integral of a continuous derivative over an interval is the endpoint difference. ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]])

## Counterexample

**Given:** The step functions $u_N$ and their pointwise limit $u$ on $(0,1)$.

1.1 The intervals are disjoint and have Lebesgue measure $2^{-(k+1)}$ by [F4], so $\|u_N\|_1=\sum_{k=1}^N2^{-(k+1)}<1/2$. Integration by parts on each interval, justified by [F5] and [F6], shows that $Du_N$ is an atomic signed measure: its jump at $1/2$ has magnitude $1$, its $N-1$ interior jumps at $2^{-2},\ldots,2^{-N}$ have magnitude $2$, and its jump at $2^{-(N+1)}$ has magnitude $1$. These are all jumps in $(0,1)$, so $u_N\in BV((0,1))$ and $TV(u_N;(0,1))=1+2(N-1)+1=2N$. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 The sequence converges in $L^1$ to $u=(-1)^k$ on each $I_k$ and $u=0$ on $(1/2,1)$, since $|u_N-u|\le1$ and its support lies in $(0,2^{-(N+1)})$, whose measure tends to zero by [F4]. For each $M$, choose disjoint small intervals around $x_j=2^{-j}$, $1\le j\le M$, avoiding every other dyadic jump, and smooth bumps equal to one at these points, with signs chosen opposite to the jumps of $u$. Their sum is a compactly supported smooth test function $\phi_M$ with $|\phi_M|\le1$. Its support is bounded away from zero, so only finitely many intervals $I_k$ meet it; integration by parts on those intervals, using [F5] and [F6], gives $$\int_0^1u\,\phi_M'\,dx=1+2(M-1)=2M-1.$$ Thus the test-field supremum for $u$ is infinite. If $u$ were in $BV((0,1))$, [F2] would make that supremum equal its finite total variation, a contradiction. This proves the refuted assertion fails despite the uniform $L^1$ bound. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given, construct] ∎

## Example

Let $\Omega=B(0,1)\subset\mathbb R^3$ and let $\Gamma=\{x\in\partial\Omega:x_3>1/2\}$, a proper nonempty open boundary cap. A measurement protocol that knows only $\Lambda_\gamma f|_\Gamma$ for inputs $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$ is a partial-data protocol. It is outside the full-data conductivity uniqueness theorem, whose hypothesis is equality of the DN operators on every boundary input; this example asserts no nonuniqueness for the partial-data protocol.

## Example references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full-data conductivity DN map]]

[[cor-ip-euclidean-cta-conductivity-uniqueness|Full-data conditional conductivity uniqueness]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the unit ball, the open cap $\Gamma$, and the partial input/output restriction in the statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: full-data equality is equality of the operators on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$.

[F2] [[cor-ip-euclidean-cta-conductivity-uniqueness]]: the full-data theorem's hypothesis is equality of the scalar DN maps on every boundary datum.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 The set $\Gamma$ is nonempty because it contains the north pole and is open in the sphere because it is the inverse image of $(1/2,\infty)$ under the continuous coordinate $x\mapsto x_3$. It is proper because the south pole is not in it. A nonzero smooth bump supported in a small lower cap defines boundary data outside $C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$, so the allowed inputs form a proper subset of the full boundary-data space. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 By [F1] and [F2], the full-data theorem requires the map on every $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ input and the corresponding full boundary output. The stated protocol restricts both input and output to $\Gamma$, so it does not satisfy that hypothesis. This classifies the configuration as outside the theorem's scope and asserts no uniqueness or nonuniqueness conclusion. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $X$ be a real-analytic manifold, let $x_0\in X$, and let $\Sigma$ be a $C^2$ hypersurface through $x_0$, meaning that in a smooth local chart it is the graph of a $C^2$ function with nonzero conormal $\nu_0\in T^*_{x_0}X$. Let $f\in\mathcal D'(X)$ vanish on one side of $\Sigma$ in a neighborhood of $x_0$, meaning that in such a chart its restriction is zero on either the strict epigraph or strict subgraph of that defining function. If either $(x_0,\nu_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(f)$ or $(x_0,-\nu_0)\notin\operatorname{WF}_A(f)$, then $f=0$ in a neighborhood of $x_0$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-analytic-wavefront-fbi-transform|Gaussian FBI definition of analytic wavefront]]

[[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation|Distribution support and local pairing]]

[[lem-ip-analytic-cutoff-sequence-and-fbi-invariance|Cutoff and chart/packet invariance]]

[[def-support-of-a-distribution|Distribution support]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real-analytic manifold $X$, a $C^2$ hypersurface $\Sigma$ through $x_0$, a distribution $f$, one-sided vanishing, and the stated analytic-wavefront hypothesis.

[F1] [[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation]]: distributions are continuous functionals on compactly supported smooth densities, so localization to a chart is defined.

[F2] [[def-support-of-a-distribution]]: the support is the complement of the largest open set on which the distribution vanishes.

[F3] [[lem-ip-flat-one-sided-analytic-support]]: a distribution supported in a closed half-space at a support point has both oriented normal covectors in its Gaussian analytic wavefront set.

[F5] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]] supplies the local inverse used to put the $C^2$ hypersurface in graph form; differentiating the inverse identity preserves its $C^2$ regularity.

[F4] [[lem-ip-analytic-cutoff-sequence-and-fbi-invariance]]: analytic coordinate changes preserve the Gaussian criterion with its cotangent transformation.

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the statement.

1.1 Work in an analytic ambient chart centered at $x_0$. The hypersurface remains $C^2$ in that chart, since changing from its given smooth chart is a smooth diffeomorphism. A real linear coordinate change makes its tangent plane nonvertical. The $C^2$ implicit graph theorem then writes it as $x_n=\psi(x')$, with $\psi$ of class $C^2$: the inverse of a $C^2$ map with invertible derivative is $C^2$, by differentiating the identity for its inverse twice. Translate to have $\psi(0)=0$. Shrink to a convex $x'$ ball on which $\|D^2\psi\|\le 2C$. Taylor's integral formula gives $ q_-(x'):=D\psi(0)x'-C|x'|^2\le\psi(x')\le D\psi(0)x'+C|x'|^2=:q_+(x'). $ Both supporting quadratics are real analytic and have the same differential as $\psi$ at $0$. [F1, F5, given, algebra, construct]

2.1 Suppose first that $f$ vanishes on the strict subgraph of $\psi$. Its local support lies in $x_n\ge\psi(x')$, hence in $x_n\ge q_-(x')$. The analytic shear $(x',x_n)\mapsto(x',x_n-q_-(x'))$ has analytic inverse $(y',y_n)\mapsto(y',y_n+q_-(y'))$, determinant $1$, and sends this latter closed side into $y_n\ge0$. If instead $f$ vanishes on the strict epigraph, its support lies in $x_n\le\psi(x')\le q_+(x')$ and use the corresponding analytic shear with $q_+$. In either case the pulled-back normal $dy_n$ at $0$ is $dx_n-D\psi(0)dx'$, a nonzero scalar multiple of the supplied conormal $\nu_0$. This flattens an analytic supporting quadratic; it does not flatten the original $C^2$ graph analytically. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 If $f$ already vanishes near $x_0$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $x_0\in\operatorname{supp}f$ by [F2]. Localize inside the chart. Under the appropriate shear, [F3] then puts both $dy_n$ and $-dy_n$ in the analytic wavefront set at the origin. By [F4] these are exactly both conormal orientations at $x_0$, up to positive frequency scaling. Either absence hypothesis in the statement contradicts this conclusion. Thus $f=0$ near $x_0$. Every construction used finite-dimensional coordinates and explicit quadratics; it introduces no choice assumption. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose two boundary components, with their induced orientations, have linking number $+1$. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push convention on ordered core curves]]

[[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection|The skew part of a Seifert matrix is the oriented surface intersection matrix]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated positive Hopf plumbing, its oriented core curves $a,b$, the positive-push convention, and full AC for the knot Seifert-pairing interface.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom assumed by the knot Seifert-pairing convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The Seifert matrix entry is $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, with the stated positive normal. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]

[F2] The stated plumbing convention gives $a\cdot_F b=1$ and the specified bounding disk for $a^+$ is disjoint from $b$; each Hopf annulus has boundary linking $+1$ by the definition in the Statement.

[F4] The canonical three-positive-crossing closure has a genus-one disk-and-band surface, whose three pair-of-band Hopf annuli all have core self-pairing $-1$. [[lem-canonical-positive-three-crossing-braid-has-negative-trefoil-form]]

[F3] The skew matrix of the positive-push form is the oriented intersection matrix in the same ordered basis. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

## Proof

1.1 The standard plumbing has the three crossing bands of the positive two-strand three-crossing closure: its two annular strips use successive pairs of the three bands, and their common disk is the plumbing square with its four alternating attaching edges. In oriented braid coordinates $(x,y,t)$ use $(X,Y,Z)=(x,-t,y)$, of determinant $+1$, to draw the closure on the $(X,Y)$ page with viewer $+Z$. The overpass runs down-left and the underpass down-right at each of the three crossings, while the two outside closure arcs are crossing-free. This is precisely the right-hand trefoil diagram of Rolfsen printed146, identified as right-hand on printed201; the comparison fixes the handedness using actual crossing data. The two core classes have intersection number $a\cdot_F b=1$ by [F2]. Since $F$ has genus one and one boundary component, its first homology has rank two; the intersection matrix in the core classes has determinant $1$. Therefore $a,b$ form an integral basis. [A1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], each diagonal is the self-linking of a Hopf core. Equally oriented parallel cores transport to the two boundary components with one orientation reversed, so their linking is minus the boundary linking, namely $-1$. A small positive normal push returns to the first core through curves disjoint from the second. Thus $V_{11}=V_{22}=-1$. The disk specified in [F2] bounds $a^+$ in the complement of $b$, hence $\operatorname{lk}(a^+,b)=0$ and $V_{12}=0$. By [F3], $V_{12}-V_{21}=a\cdot_F b=1$, so $V_{21}=-1$. These four entries give the displayed matrix. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

This schematic shows the plumbing square and the oriented core classes. Red and blue identify the two Hopf bands; the horizontal core is $a$ and the vertical core is $b$. The orientation of the core tangents and the oriented surface gives $a\cdot_F b=+1$. The diagram records the local basis convention only; the matrix proof uses the linking and intersection calculations above.

## Statement

Assume full AC. The stable isometry class of the Seifert quadratic enhancement and its Arf value are independent of the spanning surface and integral symplectic basis of an oriented knot $K$. Stable isometry means isometry after orthogonally adjoining finitely many hyperbolic planes $q_H(s,t)=st$ on either side. Under the convention $\Delta_K(t)=\nabla_K(t^{1/2}-t^{-1/2})$ with $\Delta_K(1)=1$, the coefficient $a_2(\nabla_K)$ of $z^2$ satisfies
$$\operatorname{Arf}(K)\equiv a_2(\nabla_K)\pmod2.$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-arf-invariant-from-seifert-form|The Seifert quadratic enhancement and Arf definition]]

[[def-seifert-s-equivalence-and-conway-normalization|The Conway and symmetric Alexander conventions]]

[[lem-conway-polynomial-from-seifert-determinant|The determinant realization and skein relation]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[A1] Full AC supplies the Alexander and Seifert-pairing conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Any two spanning-surface Seifert matrices are S-equivalent. [[lem-seifert-matrices-of-a-knot-are-s-equivalent]]

[F2] The quadratic enhancement is well-defined, has basis-independent Arf value, and each enlargement orthogonally adds a hyperbolic plane up to isometry; hence its stable isometry class and Arf value are unchanged. [[lem-arf-quadratic-enhancement-from-seifert-form]]

[F3] The normalized Conway determinant is independent of surface and basis and has the declared skein normalization. [[lem-conway-polynomial-from-seifert-determinant]]

[F4] In the symmetric normalized variable, $\Delta_K^\#(t)=\nabla_K(t^{1/2}-t^{-1/2})$. [[def-seifert-s-equivalence-and-conway-normalization]]

[F5] The Seifert determinant near $t=-1$ is $1+\operatorname{Arf}(K)(1+t)^2/t$ modulo $(2,(1+t)^4)$. [[lem-arf-seifert-determinant-congruence-near-minus-one]]

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], matrices from any two spanning surfaces are connected by congruences and elementary enlargements. Congruence transports the quadratic form by an isometry, while the explicit hyperbolic-pair splitting in [F2] preserves its stable isometry class and Arf value through each enlargement or reduction. Composing these finitely many operations proves independence of the stable class and the Arf value from surface and basis. The unstabilized quadratic spaces themselves can have different dimensions: a disk for the unknot has dimension zero, whereas attaching an ordinary tube gives a genus-one spanning surface with a two-dimensional hyperbolic enhancement. Thus stable isometry is the required surface-independent assertion. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 Write $\nabla_K(z)=1+a_2z^2+a_4z^4+\cdots$. For a knot the matrix size is $2g$, so $D_K(u^{-1})=\det(u^{-1}V-uV^T)=\det(uV^T-u^{-1}V)=D_K(u)$, using even size in the first equality and transposition in the second. Since replacing $u$ by $u^{-1}$ sends $z=u-u^{-1}$ to $-z$, and substitution into the Laurent polynomial ring is injective (the highest Laurent power of a nonzero polynomial in $z$ cannot cancel), this identity gives $\nabla_K(z)=\nabla_K(-z)$ and hence all odd coefficients vanish. Set $u^2=t$. Then $z^2=(u-u^{-1})^2=t+t^{-1}-2\equiv(1+t)^2/t\pmod{(2,(1+t)^4)}$, and $z^4$ is divisible by $(1+t)^4$ in that quotient. Hence [F4] gives
$$\Delta_K^\#(t)\equiv1+a_2(\nabla_K)(1+t)^2/t\pmod{(2,(1+t)^4)}.$$
Comparing with [F5], and using that $(1+t)^2/t$ is nonzero modulo $(1+t)^4$, yields $a_2(\nabla_K)\equiv\operatorname{Arf}(K)\pmod2$. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty proper open antipodally symmetric set such that $S^1\setminus\overline\Theta$ contains a nonempty open arc. Choose an open arc $J$ with $\overline J\subset S^1\setminus\overline\Theta$, put $V=\{r\omega:1<r<2,\ \omega\in J\}$, choose a nonzero smooth function $q\in C_c^\infty(V;\mathbb C)$, and define $f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}q(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ write $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$ and, for a Schwartz function $g$, define $R_{\mathcal S}g(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}g(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$ using Lebesgue measure $dt$. Let $Y=L^2(\Theta\times\mathbb R,d\theta\,ds)$, where $d\theta$ is arc-length measure and $ds$ is Lebesgue measure. Then $f$ is a nonzero Schwartz function in $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ with Lebesgue measure, its Fourier transform is $q$, and $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=0$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, so both $0$ and $f$ give datum $0$ in $Y$ without either truth being required to have compact support. For the two-truth class $\{0,f\}$ with target loss $\|g-h\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}$, every deterministic estimator $\Phi:Y\to L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfies $\max\{\|\Phi(0)\|_2,\|\Phi(0)-f\|_2\}\ge \|f\|_2/2>0$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data|Measured Fourier wedge and blind directions]]

[[lem-ip-fourier-slice-identity-on-schwartz|Fourier-slice identity for Schwartz inputs]]

[[thm-ip-kernel-directions-preclude-unrestricted-recovery|Two-truth lower bound for deterministic estimators]]

[Venkataswaran P. Krishnan and Eric Todd Quinto, Microlocal Analysis in Tomography, §1.3.2](https://math.tifrbng.res.in/~vkrishnan/Papers/Microlocal_Analysis_Tomography.pdf)

[Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, the normal set $\Theta$, the blind arc $J$, the annular sector $V$, and the nonzero smooth function $q$ supported in $V$ from the Example.

[F1] [[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data]]: $W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\ne0\}$, while the directions in $S^1\setminus\overline\Theta$ are unmeasured.

[F2] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: every nonempty open ball contains a nonzero smooth compactly supported function, by translating and rescaling a concentric bump.

[F3] [[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]]: under Countable Choice the negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform maps Schwartz functions to Schwartz functions.

[F4] [[thm-fourier-inversion-on-schwartz-space]]: under Countable Choice, $g(x)=\int\widehat g(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$ for every Schwartz function $g$.

[F5] [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]: $\widehat g(\eta)=\int g(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\eta}\,dx$ for integrable $g$.

[F6] [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]: under Countable Choice, the reflection $x\mapsto-x$ preserves Lebesgue integrals because its absolute determinant is one.

[F7] [[lem-schwartz-functions-and-all-derivatives-are-integrable]]: under Countable Choice every Schwartz function belongs to $L^p$ for each $1\le p\le\infty$.

[F8] [[lem-ip-fourier-slice-identity-on-schwartz]]: under Countable Choice, $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}g}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat g(\sigma\theta)$ for Schwartz $g$.

[F9] [[lem-ip-schwartz-radon-well-defined]]: for fixed $\theta$, $R_{\mathcal S}g(\theta,\cdot)$ is a Schwartz function.

[F10] [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]: the $L^2$ quotient norm is a norm and gives the triangle inequality and separation.

[F11] [[thm-ip-kernel-directions-preclude-unrestricted-recovery]]: if two truths share one exact datum, every deterministic data-only estimator has maximum target loss at least half their target distance.

[F12] [[def-metric-space]]: a metric satisfies separation (M1), symmetry (M2), and the triangle inequality (M3); the metric induced by an $L^2$ norm here is $d(g,h)=\|g-h\|_2$.


[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed by the Fourier transform, inversion, Lp integrability, Fourier-slice, and Lebesgue substitution suppliers [F3], [F4], [F6]–[F9].

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The sector $V$ is a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^2$ because $(r,\omega)\mapsto r\omega$ maps the open parameter set $(1,2)\times J$ to an open polar-coordinate sector. It therefore contains a ball; [F2] supplies a nonzero $q\in C_c^\infty(V)$. This establishes the required bump choice. [F2, given, construct]

1.2 By the Fourier definition [F5], the function in the Example is $f(x)=\widehat q(-x)$. Since $q$ is smooth with compact support, every Schwartz seminorm of $q$ is bounded, so $q\in\mathcal S$. By [F3] its transform is Schwartz, and reflection preserves each Schwartz seminorm up to sign, hence $f$ is Schwartz; [F7] gives $f\in L^2\cap L^1$. The reflection substitution [F6] and inversion [F4] give $\widehat f(\eta)=\int\widehat q(-x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\eta}\,dx=\int\widehat q(y)e^{2\pi i y\cdot\eta}\,dy=q(\eta)$. Since $q\ne0$, this identity implies $f$ is nonzero as an $L^1$ and $L^2$ class. [F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, A1, given, algebra]

1.3 For $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\sigma\ne0$, the point $\sigma\theta$ is outside the support of $q$ because every frequency in $V$ has direction in $J$ and $\overline J$ is disjoint from $\overline\Theta$; also $q(0)=0$ since $V$ avoids the origin. Thus [F8] gives $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)=q(\sigma\theta)=0$ for all real $\sigma$. By [F9], the offset function is Schwartz, so Fourier inversion [F4] in one dimension gives $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=0$ for every $s$. [A1, F1, F4, F8, F9, given]

2.1 Let the parameter and target metric spaces both be $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ with distance $d(g,h)=\|g-h\|_2$, let the admissible truth class be $U=\{0,f\}$, and let the target map $q:U\to L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ be inclusion. Give the data space $Y=L^2(\Theta\times\mathbb R)$ its norm metric and define $F:U\to Y$ by the restricted line integrals. The normed-space result [F10] and the metric axioms [F12] give the parameter, target, and data metrics used here. Theorem [F11] applies directly to this truth class and target map. Step 1.3 gives $F(0)=F(f)=0$, while step 1.2 gives $d(q(0),q(f))=\|f\|_2>0$. Apply [F11] with shared datum $0$ and radius $0$ to any deterministic estimator $\Phi:Y\to L^2(\mathbb R^2)$; its maximum target loss is at least $\|f\|_2/2$. This proves the asserted lower bound on the stated two-truth class. [F10, F11, F12, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, $\theta\in S^1$, and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the one-dimensional Fourier transform in the offset variable, using the phase $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$, satisfies $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta)$, where the two-dimensional transform uses the phase $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. On compactly supported smooth inputs the formula has the same line parameterization and normalization as the Euclidean Radon transform.

## Statement references

[Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

[Venkataswaran P. Krishnan and Eric Todd Quinto, Microlocal Analysis in Tomography, §1.3.2](https://math.tifrbng.res.in/~vkrishnan/Papers/Microlocal_Analysis_Tomography.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, $\theta\in S^1$, and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$.

[F1] [[def-ip-schwartz-radon-transform]]: $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=\int_\mathbb R f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-schwartz-radon-well-defined]]: for fixed $\theta$, the offset function is Schwartz and its line integral is absolutely convergent.

[F3] [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]: $\widehat g(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}g(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx$ for integrable $g$.

[F4] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: for $0<r<R$, there is a smooth cutoff equal to one on the radius-$r$ closed ball and supported in the radius-$R$ open ball.

[F5] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: pointwise convergence under a single integrable majorant permits passage to the limit under an integral.

[F6] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: an absolutely integrable function on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces has integrable sections almost everywhere and its iterated integrals equal its product integral.

[F7] [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]: assuming Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism changes an $L^1$ Lebesgue integral by the absolute Jacobian determinant.

[F8] [[lem-schwartz-functions-and-all-derivatives-are-integrable]]: under Countable Choice every Schwartz function and each of its derivatives is in $L^1$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed for the compact-support Lebesgue/Riemann compatibility in [F1], the Lebesgue change-of-variables supplier [F7], and Schwartz integrability [F8].

## Proof

1.1 The Schwartz seminorms and the estimate proved in [[lem-ip-schwartz-radon-well-defined]] give $|f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|\le C_N(1+|s|+|t|)^{-N}$ for every $N$, after changing the constant. For $N>2$ this is integrable on $\mathbb R^2$ in $(s,t)$. The offset integral is absolutely convergent, and [F6] applied to the absolutely integrable function $f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)e^{-2\pi i\sigma s}$ yields $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)e^{-2\pi i\sigma s}\,ds\,dt$. The Lebesgue Fourier-transform definitions in [F3] are applicable by [F8]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F6, F8, given]

1.2 Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\chi_R$ equal to one on the radius-$R$ ball and supported in the radius-$2R$ ball, using [F4], and put $f_R=\chi_Rf$. Then $f_R\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$. The matrix with columns $\theta,\theta^\perp$ is a positively oriented orthogonal matrix, so its determinant is one. Apply the Lebesgue change-of-variables formula [F7] to the integrable compactly supported function $x\mapsto f_R(x)e^{-2\pi i\sigma x\cdot\theta}$ and the map $(s,t)\mapsto s\theta+t\theta^\perp$; its pullback integral is $\int_{\mathbb R^2}f_R(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)e^{-2\pi i\sigma s}\,ds\,dt=\widehat{f_R}(\sigma\theta)$. [F4, F7, A1, given]

2.1 As $R\to\infty$, $f_R(x)\to f(x)$ and $|f_R(x)|\le |f(x)|$. The function $f$ is integrable by [F8], and the same Schwartz estimate in $(s,t)$ gives an integrable majorant for $f_R(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)$. Dominated convergence [F5] passes both integrals in step 1.2 to their limits; step 1.1 identifies the data-side limit with $\widehat{R_{\mathcal S}f}(\theta,\sigma)$, while the spatial-side limit is $\widehat f(\sigma\theta)$. This proves the formula. [A1, F5, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

      url: "https://msp.org/agt/2009/9-1/agt-v9-n1-p06-p.pdf"
      locator: "§2, the definition of Witt-trivial integral Seifert matrices, printed p. 170"

## Statement

Let $H$ be a free abelian group of rank $2g$ and let $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ be a bilinear form. Write $H_{\mathbb Q}=H\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and extend $V$ $\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to $H_{\mathbb Q}$. If $L\subset H_{\mathbb Q}$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace of dimension $g$ and $V(x,y)=0$ for all $x,y\in L$, then $M=H\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand of $H$ and $V|_{M\times M}=0$.

## Statement references

[[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance|A metabolizer is a primitive rank-half direct summand on which the integral Seifert pairing vanishes]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-rank free abelian group $H$, an integral bilinear form $V$, and a $g$-dimensional rational isotropic subspace $L\subset H_{\mathbb Q}$, where $\operatorname{rank}H=2g$.

[A1] The displayed hypotheses are the complete input; no choice axiom is used.

## Proof

1.1 Choose a $\mathbb Q$-basis $v_1,\ldots,v_g$ of $L$. Clearing the finitely many denominators in the coordinates of each $v_i$ gives nonzero integer multiples $x_i\in H\cap L$. The $x_i$ remain $\mathbb Q$-linearly independent, so $M=H\cap L$ has rank at least $g$; it has rank at most $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=g$. Hence $\operatorname{rank}M=g$. [given, A1, choose, algebra]

1.2 If $n\ne0$, $x\in H$, and $nx\in M$, then $nx\in L$ and therefore $x=n^{-1}(nx)\in L$ because $L$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace. Thus $x\in M$, so $M$ is saturated in $H$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 We prove by induction on $r$ that every saturated subgroup $P\subset\mathbb Z^r$ is a direct summand. The cases $P=0$ and $P=\mathbb Z^r$ are immediate. Otherwise choose a nonzero $p\in P$, divide its coordinates by their greatest common divisor, and use saturation to see that the resulting primitive vector $e_1$ still lies in $P$. The Euclidean algorithm gives a unimodular change of basis carrying $e_1$ to the first standard basis vector, so write $\mathbb Z^r=\mathbb Ze_1\oplus H'$. Every $p'\in P$ has a unique form $ae_1+h'$ with $h'\in H'$, and $h'=p'-ae_1\in P\cap H'$. Therefore $P=\mathbb Ze_1\oplus(P\cap H')$. The subgroup $P\cap H'$ is saturated in $H'$; its rank is $\operatorname{rank}P-1$, since the projection of $P$ to $\mathbb Ze_1$ is onto. Induction makes $P\cap H'$ a direct summand of $H'$, hence $P$ a direct summand of $\mathbb Z^r$. [given, A1, step 1.2, induction, construct]

2.2 Apply step 2.1 to the saturated rank-$g$ subgroup $M\subset H\cong\mathbb Z^{2g}$ from step 1.2. It is a direct summand of $H$. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1]

3.1 Since $M\subset L$ and $V$ vanishes on $L\times L$, its restriction to $M\times M$ vanishes. Together with rank $g$ and the direct-summand conclusion of step 2.2, this proves the claim. [given, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a three-dimensional transversally anisotropic product domain with compact connected simple surface transversal $(M_0,g_0)$. Let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$. Suppose that for every finite family of smooth boundary directions, the corresponding small-data nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps for
$$-\Delta_g u+q_j u^3=0$$
agree for all sufficiently small real parameter values. Then $q_1=q_2$ on $\overline M$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product geometry]]

[[lem-ip-cubic-dn-small-data-differentiability|Small-data nonlinear DN maps]]

[[lem-ip-cubic-dn-third-linearization-identity|Third derivative identity]]

[[lem-ip-intersecting-gaussian-beam-four-factor-limit|Four-factor concentration]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the small-data, third-linearization, and four-factor suppliers [F1]--[F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the small-data, third-linearization, and four-factor suppliers [F1]--[F3].

**Given:** the CTA product with simple surface transversal, real smooth cubic coefficients, and equality of the finite-parameter nonlinear DN maps for every finite list of smooth boundary directions.

[F1] [[lem-ip-cubic-dn-small-data-differentiability]]: each finite-parameter solution and its nonlinear DN data are $C^3$ in the real parameters near zero.

[F2] [[lem-ip-cubic-dn-third-linearization-identity]]: the third DN derivative determines $6\int_Mq\,v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g$ for any four harmonic boundary solutions.

[F3] [[lem-ip-intersecting-gaussian-beam-four-factor-limit]]: the claimed four-factor limit at any transversal intersection is a nonzero constant times the longitudinal Fourier transform of the coefficient difference.

[F4] [[cor-uniqueness-of-the-l-one-fourier-transform]]: an $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function with identically zero Fourier transform vanishes almost everywhere.

[F5] The four-factor supplier imports the smooth harmonic-product density theorem of Lassas--Liimatainen--Lin--Salo, Proposition 5.1, PDF p. 14; its hypotheses are a compact oriented CTA manifold of dimension at least three, a $C^1$ coefficient, and four or more smooth harmonic factors. The orientation hypothesis follows here because the local simple-surface definition [F1] agrees with Paternain--Salo--Uhlmann, Definition 3.8.1: their Theorem 3.8.2 and Propositions 3.8.4--3.8.5 yield unique geodesics and show $M_0$ is diffeomorphic to a closed disk, hence orientable; $M$ inherits the product orientation. See *Geometric inverse problems, with emphasis on two dimensions*, Section 3.8 ([author-hosted full text](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/GIP2D_driver.pdf)). The complete proof of LL--LS Proposition 5.1 in Section 5, PDF pp. 14--23, including Lemma 5.2, was inspected for this repair; only its density conclusion is imported, not locally reconstructed. The four-factor witnesses are smooth on $\overline M$, depend on the coefficient being tested, and are constant in $\tau$, so the smooth-boundary identity [F2] applies directly; no extension of that identity to arbitrary $H^1$ boundary traces is required. Theorem 1.3, pp. 5--6, is the corresponding nonlinear uniqueness theorem, not a replacement local proof here.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Fix four smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$. Equality of the finite-parameter DN maps for $q_1$ and $q_2$ implies equality of their mixed third derivatives at the origin. Applying [F2] to each coefficient and subtracting gives
$$\int_M(q_1-q_2)v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g=0$$
for every four harmonic functions $v_j$ arising from smooth boundary data. [A1, A2, F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 The identity in step 1.1 holds also for complex smooth harmonic functions: write their boundary values as real and imaginary parts and expand the separately linear or conjugate-linear expression. Since the Laplacian has real coefficients, conjugation preserves harmonicity; replacing the fourth function by its conjugate therefore gives $\int_M Qw_1w_2w_3w_4\,dV=0$ for every four smooth complex harmonic functions, where $Q=q_1-q_2$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Fix $p\in M_0^\circ$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R$. Choose the transverse boundary-to-boundary geodesic segments through $p$ supplied by [F3] (their existence is established in that supplier's proof). Apply [F3] with $Q=q_1-q_2$. Its witnesses are smooth by [F5], so their product integral is zero for every $\tau$ by step 1.2. Taking their stated limit gives
$$c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}(q_1-q_2)(x_1,p)\,dx_1=0,$$
where $c>0$ is the crossing normalization. The coefficient transform therefore vanishes for every $\xi$ and every $p$. [A1, A2, F3, F5, step 1.2]

2.2 For each $p$, extend $x_1\mapsto(q_1-q_2)(x_1,p)$ by zero outside $I_p$. It is a compactly supported $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function. By step 2.1, [F4] makes this section zero almost everywhere; its smoothness in the interior of $M$ then makes $q_1-q_2=0$ on $M^\circ$, and continuity gives equality on $\overline M$. Thus the theorem follows. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$,
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for all
$v\in\mathbb R^n$,
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ symmetric with $u^T\Gamma u>0$ for all
nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Let
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ be independent, and
observe $Y=AX+\eta$. Put
$S_0=m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$ and
$r=\dim\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$. The $r$-dimensional Euclidean Lebesgue
measure on $S_0$ is the pushforward of Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^r$
under any affine isometry onto $S_0$; this measure is independent of the
chosen orthonormal coordinates. A MAP point means a maximizer of the
posterior density with respect to this measure; for $r=0$, the unique point
of $S_0$ is the MAP point. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse $C_0^\dagger$
satisfies
$$ C_0C_0^\dagger C_0=C_0,\qquad C_0^\dagger C_0C_0^\dagger=C_0^\dagger, $$
and $C_0C_0^\dagger$ and $C_0^\dagger C_0$ are symmetric. The optimization
below is restricted to $S_0$. Then for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$, the unique
MAP point equals the posterior mean and the unique minimizer over $x\in S_0$ of
$$ J_y(x)=(Ax-y)^T\Gamma^{-1}(Ax-y) +(x-m_0)^TC_0^\dagger(x-m_0). $$
All objects are finite-dimensional; no minimization over points outside the
prior support is asserted when $C_0$ is singular.

## Statement references

[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior|The finite Gaussian posterior mean and covariance are given by the displayed conditioning formulas.]]

[[lem-ip-singular-gaussian-support-and-pseudoinverse|A singular Gaussian prior is supported on the mean plus the covariance range, and its pseudoinverse has range coordinates.]]

[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse|The pseudoinverse is characterized by the four Penrose equations.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the finite linear Gaussian inverse model with
$C_0\succeq0$, $\Gamma\succ0$, and the support and MAP conventions in the
Statement.

[A1] AC is inherited from the finite Gaussian posterior and multivariate-normal
interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The posterior update is the finite Gaussian law with the stated mean and
covariance, defined for every datum. [[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior]]

[F2] There are orthonormal range coordinates
$C_0=U\Lambda U^T$, $C_0^\dagger=U\Lambda^{-1}U^T$, and the prior support
is $m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(U)$. [[lem-ip-singular-gaussian-support-and-pseudoinverse]]

[F3] The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse is characterized by the four Penrose
equations. [[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]

[F4] A finite-dimensional non-negative matrix has a unique non-negative
square root, and a non-negative self-adjoint matrix has an orthonormal
eigenbasis. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]], [[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]

[F5] The Tikhonov objective is
$\|Dz-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|z\|_2^2$ for $\lambda>0$. [[def-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares]]

[F6] For this objective the unique minimizer is
$(D^TD+\lambda I)^{-1}D^Tb$. [[thm-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares-has-a-unique-minimiser]]

[F7] A positive-definite Gaussian law has a density proportional to its
positive quadratic exponential. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

## Proof
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 If $r=0$, [F2] gives $C_0=0$ and $S_0=\{m_0\}$. The posterior is the point mass at $m_0$ by [F1], so its mean and unique MAP point are $m_0$. The objective $J_y$ has only this admissible point, hence it has the same unique minimizer on $S_0$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $r>0$. By [F2], choose $U,\Lambda$ with $C_0=U\Lambda U^T$, $C_0^\dagger=U\Lambda^{-1}U^T$, and write $L=U\Lambda^{1/2}$. The map $z\mapsto m_0+Lz$ is a bijection from $\mathbb R^r$ onto $S_0$. For $x=m_0+Lz$, $(x-m_0)^TC_0^\dagger(x-m_0)=z^Tz$. [F2, F3, given, algebra, construct]

2.1 Let $W$ be the non-negative square root of $\Gamma^{-1}$. Since $\Gamma\succ0$, $W$ is symmetric positive definite and $W^TW=\Gamma^{-1}$ by [F4]. Set $D=WAL$ and $b=W(y-Am_0)$. Substituting $x=m_0+Lz$ into the objective in the Statement gives $J_y(m_0+Lz)=\|Dz-b\|_2^2+\|z\|_2^2$. This is the Tikhonov objective in [F5] with $\lambda=1$, so [F6] gives the unique minimizer $\widehat z=(D^TD+I_r)^{-1}D^Tb$. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By the Gaussian representation in [F2], the prior coordinate $z$ has standard Gaussian density. The likelihood is proportional to $\exp(-\tfrac12\|Dz-b\|_2^2)$ by [F7]. Thus the posterior density in $z$ is proportional to $\exp[-\tfrac12(\|Dz-b\|_2^2+\|z\|_2^2)]$. Its precision matrix $H=I_r+D^TD$ is positive definite, and completing the square gives a Gaussian density with mean $H^{-1}D^Tb=\widehat z$ and covariance $H^{-1}$. This density has its unique maximum at its mean. The affine bijection in step 1.2 has constant positive Jacobian in orthonormal coordinates on $S_0$, so its image has the unique MAP point $\widehat x=m_0+L\widehat z$. Its posterior mean is also $m_0+L\widehat z$, and step 2.1 makes this point the unique minimizer of $J_y$ on $S_0$. [A1, F1, F2, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

For the robust minimax value $\mathfrak R_N(\rho_X,\rho_A)$ in the original question reproduced below, fix $p,s>0$, $R,\sigma>0$, $N\ge1$, $\rho_X\ge0$ and $0\le\rho_A<1/2$. Put
$$Q_{p,s}(R,\sigma)=R^2\min\left\{1,(\sigma/R)^{4s/(2s+2p+1)}\right\}.$$
There is $c_{p,s}>0$, depending only on $p,s$, such that
$$c_{p,s}\bigl(Q_{p,s}(R,\sigma)+R^2\rho_A^2\bigr)\le\mathfrak R_N(\rho_X,\rho_A)\le\min\left\{R^2,2Q_{p,s}(R,\sigma)+R^2\rho_A^2\right\}.$$
These bounds hold for every training size and truth-law shift radius. For fixed positive $p,s,R$, along any sequence of the remaining parameters the risk tends to zero if and only if both $\sigma\to0$ and $\rho_A\to0$. In particular, increasing $N$ with fixed positive noise does not force the worst-law risk to zero. The original question, including both distinct shift classes, is retained verbatim under Original question.

## Example references

[van Maarschalkerwaart et al., full 2026 paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.30230v1)

[Zheng et al., ICLR 2025 InverseBench paper](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/e297068f5ec7f483a017948715b591fb-Paper-Conference.pdf)

[Bal, full inverse-problems lecture notes](https://www.stat.uchicago.edu/~guillaumebal/COURSES/E6901/LectureNotesIP.pdf)

## Original question

Fix an integer $N\ge1$, parameters $p,s,R,\sigma>0$, a shift radius $\rho_X\ge0$, and an operator radius $0\le\rho_A<1/2$. Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, with norm $\|\theta\|_2^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\theta_j^2$, and define the compact truth class
$$\Theta_s(R)=\left\{\theta\in\mathcal H:\sum_{j\ge1}j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2\right\},\qquad (A_p\theta)_j=j^{-p}\theta_j.$$
Let $\mathcal Y=\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ have its product Borel sigma-algebra. A sequence observation with forward operator $A$ is $Y_j=(A\theta)_j+\sigma\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables; this defines a probability law on $\mathcal Y$ even though the white-noise sequence need not lie in $\ell^2$. Write $\mathcal P(K)$ for the Borel probability laws on a Borel set $K$. For a Borel probability law $\mu_0$ on $\Theta_s(R)$, the training data are $D_N=((\theta_i,Y_i))_{i=1}^N$ with independent $\theta_i\sim\mu_0$ and $Y_i=A_p\theta_i+\sigma\xi_i$. At test time, $\theta\sim\mu$ for another Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\Theta_s(R)$ and the unknown forward operator is $A_{p,E}=A_p(I+E)$, where $E:\ell^2\to\ell^2$ is bounded linear and $\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\rho_A$. Write $\mathcal L(\ell^2)$ for the bounded linear operators from $\ell^2$ to itself. The learner receives $D_N$ and the test observation $Y$, but not $E$.

For probability laws $\mu,\mu_0$ on $\Theta_s(R)$, define their Wasserstein distance by
$$W_1(\mu,\mu_0)=\inf_{\Gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\mu_0)}\int_{\Theta_s(R)\times\Theta_s(R)}\|\theta-\theta_0\|_2\,\Gamma(d\theta,d\theta_0),$$
where $\Pi(\mu,\mu_0)$ is the set of couplings with those marginals. A learner is a Borel map $G_N:(\Theta_s(R)\times\mathcal Y)^N\times\mathcal Y\to\ell^2$. For fixed training data its test risk is
$$R_{\mu,E}(G_N\mid D_N)=E_{\theta\sim\mu,\,\xi}\left\|G_N(D_N,A_p(I+E)\theta+\sigma\xi)-\theta\right\|_2^2,$$
where $\xi$ is an independent standard Gaussian sequence. Define the robust minimax value
$$\mathfrak R_N(\rho_X,\rho_A)=\inf_{G_N}\sup_{\substack{\mu_0,\mu\in\mathcal P(\Theta_s(R)),\ W_1(\mu,\mu_0)\le\rho_X\\ E\in\mathcal L(\ell^2),\ \|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\rho_A}}E_{D_N\sim(\mu_0,A_p)}R_{\mu,E}(G_N\mid D_N).$$
Determine matching upper and lower bounds for $\mathfrak R_N(\rho_X,\rho_A)$ as a function of $N,\rho_X,\rho_A,p,s,R,\sigma$, and identify necessary and sufficient joint regimes in which it tends to zero. In particular, the bound must distinguish source-to-test truth-law shift from perturbation of the conditional measurement law induced by $E$; no access to $E$ is available at deployment.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** All data spaces, training laws, test laws, learners and shift classes in the original question. Let $e_j$ denote the jth coordinate vector. Let $\Phi$ be the standard normal distribution function and put $b=\Phi(-1)>0$.

[A1] A scalar observation $V=\delta U+\sigma G$ with $U$ uniform on $\{-1,1\}$ and independent standard Gaussian $G$ has minimum sign-testing error $\Phi(-\delta/\sigma)$ for $\delta>0$: the two Gaussian densities cross at zero, and choosing the larger density pointwise minimizes the error integral. Their ratio is $\exp(2\delta V/\sigma^2)$.

[A2] For vectors $x,a,b$ in a real Hilbert space, $\|x-a\|^2+\|x-b\|^2=2\|x-(a+b)/2\|^2+\|a-b\|^2/2$. This identity follows by expansion of the squares.

## Verification

**Given:** The original robust minimax model and [A1]–[A2].

1.1 The zero estimator gives risk at most $R^2$ for every allowed law and operator. If $\sigma<R$, put $t=(R/\sigma)^{2/(2s+2p+1)}>1$ and $k=\lfloor t\rfloor\ge1$. Use the Borel finite-coordinate estimator $\widehat\theta_j=j^pY_j$ for $j\le k$ and zero otherwise; it ignores the training data. Under any test truth its retained error is $P_kE\theta+(\sigma j^p\xi_j)_{j\le k}$ and its omitted error is $-(I-P_k)\theta$. These components are orthogonal, and the centered noise is independent of the truth. Hence its expected squared error is at most $R^2\rho_A^2+R^2(k+1)^{-2s}+\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^k j^{2p}$. Because $k+1>t$ and $\sum_{j\le k}j^{2p}\le k^{2p+1}\le t^{2p+1}$, the last two terms are at most $2R^2t^{-2s}=2Q_{p,s}$. If $\sigma\ge R$, $Q_{p,s}=R^2$ and the zero estimator already gives the asserted upper bound. Taking the better of the zero and cutoff rules proves the displayed upper bound uniformly over both shift classes. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For the noise lower bound first suppose $\sigma\ge R$. Set $E=0$ and $\mu=\mu_0=(\delta_{Re_1}+\delta_{-Re_1})/2$. These laws have Wasserstein distance zero and are admissible at every $\rho_X$. The training sample is independent of the fresh test sign, and all other test coordinates are independent pure noise. Given those ancillary variables, testing the fresh sign reduces to [A1] with $\delta=R$. Thus any prediction of its first coordinate has squared error at least $R^2$ whenever its induced sign test is wrong, and its integrated risk is at least $R^2\Phi(-R/\sigma)\ge bR^2=bQ_{p,s}$. At a zero predicted coordinate, choose either sign; the squared error is still $R^2$. [A1, given, construct, algebra]

1.3 Put $r=\rho_A$. If $r>0$, define $a=R/(1+r)$, $b_0=R$ and take the same source and test law $\mu_0=\mu=(\delta_{ae_1}+\delta_{b_0e_1})/2$. Compare the two allowed operators $E_1=0$ and $E_2=-r(1+r)^{-1}P_1$, whose norms are at most $r$. In the first world, the test truth $ae_1$ has observation mean $ae_1$; in the second, truth $b_0e_1$ has the same mean because $(I+E_2)b_0e_1=ae_1$. The joint law of the full training sample and this conditional test observation is identical in the two cases, including every noisy coordinate. Calling that common law $H$, the corresponding two full test risks satisfy $R_1\ge\tfrac12E_H\|G-ae_1\|^2$ and $R_2\ge\tfrac12E_H\|G-b_0e_1\|^2$. Therefore [A2] gives $\max(R_1,R_2)\ge(b_0-a)^2/8=R^2r^2/[8(1+r)^2]\ge R^2r^2/18$. This holds for every Borel learner and all training sizes. If $r=0$, the asserted zero operator lower bound is immediate. [A2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $\sigma<R$, use $t$ from step 1.1 and $k=\lceil t\rceil\le2t$. On the coordinate block $k\le j<2k$, put $a=2^{-s-1}Rk^{-s-1/2}$ and let $\mu_0=\mu$ be the uniform law on the $2^k$ vectors having independent coordinates $\theta_j=\pm a$ on this block and zero elsewhere. Each such vector lies in the ellipsoid because $\sum_jj^{2s}\theta_j^2\le k(2k)^{2s}a^2=R^2/4$. Again choose $E=0$. For every block coordinate, its test sign is independent of the whole training sample and of all other test coordinates. Its signal amplitude is $j^{-p}a\le k^{-p}a\le\sigma$, by the definition of $t$ and $k\ge t$. Applying the density-crossing argument in [A1], conditional on all ancillary data, gives sign error at least $b$. Summing the coordinate squared errors gives risk at least $bka^2=b2^{-2s-2}R^2k^{-2s}\ge b2^{-4s-2}Q_{p,s}$. Finite averaging over the sign prior and integration over the independent ancillary observations suffice; no choice of an unknown prior by the learner is being assumed. [A1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Steps 1.2 and 2.1 give $\mathfrak R_N\ge c_0Q_{p,s}$ with $c_0=b\min\{1,2^{-4s-2}\}>0$, and step 1.3 gives $\mathfrak R_N\ge R^2\rho_A^2/18$. The maximum of these bounds is at least $\tfrac12\min\{c_0,1/18\}(Q_{p,s}+R^2\rho_A^2)$, proving the lower bound with that explicit positive $c_{p,s}$. For fixed $p,s,R>0$, the upper bound tends to zero when $\sigma,\rho_A\to0$, and the lower bound forces both limits whenever the risk tends to zero. Both lower constructions have $\mu=\mu_0$, so they remain admissible even at zero truth-law shift; the upper construction ignores the training law entirely. This explains why $N$ and $\rho_X$ do not enter the matching-order rate for this worst-law formulation. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Scope of the resolution

This gives matching-order upper and lower bounds for the exact original worst-law problem, including simultaneous unknown relative-operator shift and truth-law Wasserstein shift. It neither identifies the exact minimax constant nor says that finite-sample distribution learning is unimportant for a fixed restricted prior family. The source paper's conditional-law DRO bound is adjacent context; the two shift mechanisms and finite sign-prior proofs above are local and do not substitute its finite-dimensional hypotheses.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$ be a three-dimensional transversally anisotropic product domain with compact connected simple surface transversal $(M_0,g_0)$. For every $p\in M_0^\circ$ choose two nontangential unit-speed geodesic segments $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ meeting transversely at $p$ and nowhere else. For every $\xi\in\mathbb R$ and every $Q\in C^\infty(\overline M)$, there are four exact harmonic solutions $u_{\tau,1}^+,u_{\tau,1}^-,u_{\tau,2}^+,u_{\tau,2}^-\in H^1(M)$, with no prescribed boundary values, such that
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_MQ(x_1,x')u_{\tau,1}^+u_{\tau,1}^-u_{\tau,2}^+u_{\tau,2}^-\,dV_g =c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}Q(x_1,p)\,dx_1,$$
where $I_p=\{x_1\in\mathbb R:(x_1,p)\in M^\circ\}$ and $c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)>0$ is the nonzero Gaussian normalization divided by $|\sin\angle(\dot\gamma_1(p),\dot\gamma_2(p))|$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product domain]]

[[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform|Simple transversal and nontangential geodesics]]

[[thm-ip-cgo-solvability-and-remainder-bound|Exact CGO solutions and remainder]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the CGO solver supplier [F2].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the CGO solver supplier [F2].

**Given:** the simple surface product, an interior transversal point, two crossing nontangential geodesics, a longitudinal frequency $\xi$, and $Q\in C^\infty(\overline M)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform]]: strict convexity and unique geodesic segments define the simple surface convention.

[F2] [[thm-ip-cgo-solvability-and-remainder-bound]]: the intended supplier constructs exact harmonic solutions from transport amplitudes and controls the correction in $L^2$.

[F3] **External input:** Lassas--Liimatainen--Lin--Salo, Proposition 5.1, arXiv:1903.12562v1, PDF p. 14: on a compact oriented transversally anisotropic manifold of dimension at least three, if $f\in C^1(M)$ satisfies $\int_M f v_1\cdots v_m\,dV=0$ for all smooth harmonic $v_j$, with $m\ge4$, then $f=0$. We import this density statement. The complete proof in Section 5, PDF pp. 14--23, including the supporting Lemma 5.2, was inspected for this repair; it is not claimed to be reconstructed locally.

[F4] The literal quantifiers in the statement permit the four witnesses to depend on $Q$. They impose no uniformity in $Q$, no nonzero-solution requirement, and no quantitative remainder or beam-profile estimate. The proof below uses density to obtain smooth witnesses constant in $\tau$; it does not assert a uniform Gaussian-beam family. The Gaussian calculation fixes the allowed positive geometric normalization.

[F5] **External geometric input:** Paternain--Salo--Uhlmann, *Geometric inverse problems, with emphasis on two dimensions*, Section 3.8, Theorem 3.8.2 and Propositions 3.8.4--3.8.5 ([author-hosted full text](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/GIP2D_driver.pdf)). The local simple-surface conditions in [F1] agree with their Definition 3.8.1. Under these hypotheses Theorem 3.8.2 gives the equivalent simple-manifold formulations, Proposition 3.8.4 gives a unique minimizing geodesic between any two points, and Proposition 3.8.5 gives a diffeomorphism with a closed ball. Thus $M_0$ is diffeomorphic to a disk and is orientable; the isometric embedding of $M$ in $\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$ gives $M$ the product orientation. These consequences verify the orientation hypothesis of [F3] and the uniqueness use in step 1.1.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Since $M_0$ is a surface, choose two unit directions $v_1,v_2\in S_pM_0$ with $v_2\ne\pm v_1$. Nontrapping extends each geodesic through $p$ in both directions to a boundary-to-boundary segment, and strict convexity makes its boundary intersections nontangential. Their distinct tangent lines make the segments transverse at $p$. If they met again at a distinct point $z$, the two different subsegments from $p$ to $z$ would violate the unique-geodesic conclusion of [F5]. Thus the only intersection is $p$. [F1, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix unit tangent vectors $e_1,e_2$ at the crossing and their normal linear forms $\ell_1,\ell_2$ on the tangent plane. Their determinant has absolute value $|\sin\angle(e_1,e_2)|$. The normalized Gaussian
$$\frac{\tau}{\pi}e^{-\tau(\ell_1(y)^2+\ell_2(y)^2)}$$
has integral $c=|\sin\angle(e_1,e_2)|^{-1}>0$, by the linear substitution $z_j=\sqrt\tau\,\ell_j(y)$. Choose this unit Gaussian normalization for the constant in the statement. This calculation fixes $c$ and does not claim estimates for any exact-solution beam remainders. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Put $T=c\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}Q(x_1,p)\,dx_1$, which is finite because $M$ is compact and $Q$ is bounded. If $Q=0$, four constant harmonic functions give the assertion. Otherwise, since [F5] verifies the orientation hypothesis of [F3], contraposition of [F3] gives smooth harmonic functions $w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4$ with $S=\int_M Qw_1w_2w_3w_4\,dV\ne0$. For every $\tau$ set
$$u_{\tau,1}^+=(T/S)w_1,\quad u_{\tau,1}^-=w_2,\quad u_{\tau,2}^+=w_3,\quad u_{\tau,2}^-=w_4.$$
They are exact harmonic smooth functions, hence belong to $H^1(M)$, with no prescribed boundary values. Their product integral equals $T$ for every $\tau$, so the required limit holds. This includes $T=0$. These are explicitly $Q$-dependent, constant-parameter witnesses; no estimate stronger than the unchanged statement is inferred from the $L^2$ CGO bound. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every integer $r\ge1$, the commutative ring
$$
\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]
$$
is Noetherian and a unique factorisation domain. Its units are exactly the elements $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $r\ge1$ and commuting indeterminates $t_1,\ldots,t_r$.

[F1] The one-variable Laurent ring $\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1}]$ is Noetherian and a UFD, and its units are $\pm t_1^k$ ([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]]).

[F2] A polynomial ring in finitely many variables over a Noetherian commutative ring is Noetherian ([[cor-finite-variable-polynomial-ring-noetherian]]).

[F3] Every localization of a Noetherian commutative ring is Noetherian ([[thm-noetherian-ring-quotients-and-localisations]]).

[F4] Products of primitive polynomials over a UFD are primitive, and a primitive positive-degree polynomial is irreducible over the UFD exactly when it is irreducible over its fraction field ([[lem-gauss-lemma-over-a-ufd]]).

[F5] For every field $K$, $K[x]$ is a UFD ([[thm-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-ufd]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $r=1$ the statement is [F1]. Suppose $r>1$, put $P_r=\Lambda_1[t_2,\ldots,t_r]$, and let $S_r$ be the multiplicative set generated by $t_2,\ldots,t_r$. Clearing negative powers identifies $\Lambda_r$ with $S_r^{-1}P_r$. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 By [F2], $P_r$ is Noetherian because $\Lambda_1$ is Noetherian by [F1]. Its localization $S_r^{-1}P_r=\Lambda_r$ is Noetherian by [F3]. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

2.1 We prove by induction on the number of added variables that $\Lambda_1[t_2,\ldots,t_r]$ is a UFD. The base is [F1]. For the induction step let $R$ be the preceding UFD and $K$ its fraction field. Every nonzero $f\in R[x]$ is its content $c\in R$ times a primitive polynomial $f_0$: since $f$ has finitely many coefficients, take the product over irreducibles of their minimum exponents in those coefficients. Factor $c$ in $R$ and factor $f_0$ in $K[x]$ using [F5]. Clear denominators in each positive-degree irreducible factor and divide by its content to obtain primitive polynomials $q_1,\ldots,q_m\in R[x]$. By [F4], their product $q$ is primitive and is associated to $f_0$ in $K[x]$. Write this scalar as $a/b$ with coprime $a,b\in R$, so $bf_0=aq$. Any irreducible divisor of $a$ then divides every coefficient of $f_0$, and any irreducible divisor of $b$ divides every coefficient of $q$; primitiveness forces $a$ and $b$ to be units. Thus $f_0$ is associated in $R[x]$ to the product of the $q_i$. Each $q_i$ is irreducible in $R[x]$ by [F4], and the content factors in $R$, so every nonzero nonunit of $R[x]$ factors into irreducibles. [given, F1, F4, F5, induction, construct]

2.2 For uniqueness in the same induction step, contents have unique factorization in $R$. Two factorizations of the primitive part become factorizations in the UFD $K[x]$, so their primitive positive-degree factors pair up up to scalar associates. If primitive $f,g\in R[x]$ satisfy $f=(a/b)g$ for coprime $a,b\in R$, then $bf=ag$; any irreducible factor of $a$ must divide every coefficient of $f$, and any irreducible factor of $b$ must divide every coefficient of $g$. Primitiveness forces $a,b$ to be units, so the scalar is a unit of $R$. This proves uniqueness in $R[x]$ and completes the induction. [given, F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, induction, algebra]

3.1 Localizing the UFD $P_r$ at $S_r$ preserves unique factorization: factor a numerator in $P_r$ and discard the irreducible factors that divide an element of $S_r$, since precisely those factors become units. Every remaining irreducible stays prime: if it divides a product of localized fractions, clearing denominators gives divisibility of the product of their numerators in $P_r$, so primality in $P_r$ makes it divide one numerator; it cannot divide a cleared denominator because it was not inverted. Uniqueness follows by clearing denominators and using uniqueness in $P_r$. Thus $\Lambda_r$ is a UFD. [given, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 If $u=f/s\in S_r^{-1}P_r$ is a unit, then $fg=sq$ for some $q\in S_r$. Every irreducible factor of $f$ therefore divides a product of powers of $t_2,\ldots,t_r$, so it is associated in $P_r$ to one of these variables. The only units already in $P_r$ are the units of $\Lambda_1$, namely $\pm t_1^k$, by degree in $t_2,\ldots,t_r$ and [F1]. Consequently the units of $\Lambda_r$ are exactly $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. [given, F1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 1.2, 3.1 and 3.2 prove Noetherianity, unique factorization, and the stated unit description for every $r\ge1$. [given, step 1.2, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume Countable Choice. The claim that every minimum-TV exact truth in a two-dimensional Neumann model has an $L^2$ source certificate is false. Let $\Omega=(-1,1)^2$, let $X=Y=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, let $A:X\to Y$ be the identity, let $f=u^\dagger$ with $u^\dagger(x_1,x_2)=|x_1|$, and let the regularizer be the Neumann total variation $R(u)=|Du|(\Omega)$ on $BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)$ and $R(u)=+\infty$ otherwise. The exact equation $Au=f$ has the unique solution $u^\dagger$, so it is a minimum-TV exact truth. Nevertheless, there is no $p\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ such that $A^*p=p\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $p\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$ means $R(v)\ge R(u^\dagger)+\int_\Omega p(v-u^\dagger)\,dx$ for every $v\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|A dual source certificate is an L² vector whose adjoint image is a TV subgradient.]]

[[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions|Neumann TV counts the distributional derivative inside the open domain.]]

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|BV, distributional derivatives, and total variation.]]

[Chambolle, Duval, Peyré, and Poon, *Geometric properties of solutions to the total variation denoising problem*, §§1.3 and 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.00087)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\Omega=(-1,1)^2$, $X=Y=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, $A=I$, $u^\dagger(x_1,x_2)=|x_1|$, $f=u^\dagger$, and $R=TV_N$ as specified in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv]]: $Du$ is the vector of distributional derivatives and $TV(u;\Omega)$ is the partition variation $|Du|(\Omega)$.

[F2] [[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions]]: in the Neumann convention, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ for $u\in BV(\Omega)$.

[F3] [[def-ip-banach-convex-subgradient-and-dual-pairing]]: $p\in\partial R(u)$ exactly when $R(v)\ge R(u)+\langle p,v-u\rangle_{L^2}$ for every $v\in L^2(\Omega)$.

[F4] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the real $L^2$ inner product is $\langle p,v\rangle=\int_\Omega pv\,dx$; Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its absolute value by $\|p\|_2\|v\|_2$. ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]])

[F5] [[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]: integrable functions on this rectangle may be integrated by iterated one-dimensional integration.

[F6] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-radon-measure-on-rn]]: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$ is Radon; an integrable density gives a finite Radon measure on the bounded domain.

[F7] [[lem-ip-vector-radon-variation-is-radon]]: the partition variation of a finite vector Radon measure is a finite positive Radon measure.

[F8] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: pointwise convergence almost everywhere under an integrable majorant permits convergence of integrals; it applies to the difference quotients bounded by $|\nabla\varphi|$.

[F9] [[thm-integrable-simple-functions-are-dense-in-l-one]]: every real integrable function admits integrable finite-valued simple approximants in $L^1$; apply it separately to the two coordinates of a vector-valued density.

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct directional-derivative contradiction.

For any integrable real vector density $g=(g_1,g_2)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, apply [F9] to each coordinate with $L^1$ error less than $\varepsilon/2$ and refine the two finite partitions in common. The resulting finite-valued vector simple function $s$ satisfies $\|g-s\|_{L^1}<\varepsilon$, since the Euclidean pointwise norm is at most the sum of the absolute coordinate errors. Thus the vector approximation used in step 1.2 follows from the scalar supplier coordinatewise. The dominated-convergence supplier [F8] also applies there: the difference quotients are bounded by the integrable function $|\nabla\varphi|$.

1.1 The function $u^\dagger=|x_1|$ is bounded on the bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega$, hence belongs to $L^2(\Omega)$. Fubini and one-dimensional integration by parts show that its distributional gradient is $Du^\dagger=\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)e_1\,dx$: for every compactly supported smooth vector field $\varphi$, the $x_1$ derivative pairing is $-\int |x_1|\partial_1\varphi=\int\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)\varphi_1$, and the $x_2$ derivative pairing vanishes. This bounded density defines a finite vector Radon measure by [F6], so $u^\dagger\in BV(\Omega)$. Since $A=I$, its Hilbert adjoint is also $I$. The equation $Au=f$ forces $u=f=u^\dagger$, so $u^\dagger$ is the unique exact solution and therefore minimizes $R$ among exact solutions. [F1, F2, F5, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, the distributional gradient of $u^\dagger+t\varphi$ has density $g_t=\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)e_1+t\nabla\varphi$. For any integrable vector density $g$, its partition variation mass is $\int|g|$: every partition gives $\sum_j|\int_{B_j}g|\le\int|g|$; conversely, for $\varepsilon>0$ choose a finite-valued measurable simple function $s=\sum_{k=1}^N c_k\mathbf1_{B_k}$ with $\|g-s\|_1<\varepsilon$, where the disjoint $B_k$ partition the set and $s=0$ off their union. Then this partition gives $\sum_k|\int_{B_k}g|\ge\sum_k|c_k||B_k|-\|g-s\|_1=\|s\|_1-\|g-s\|_1\ge\|g\|_1-2\varepsilon$. Taking arbitrary $\varepsilon$ proves the formula. Consequently $$R(u^\dagger+t\varphi)=\int_\Omega|\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)e_1+t\nabla\varphi|\,dx.$$ For almost every $x$, the vector $q=\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)e_1$ has norm one and $\lim_{t\downarrow0}(|q+t h|-|q|)/t=q\cdot h$. The quotient is bounded in absolute value by $|h|$, by the reverse triangle inequality. Dominated convergence with $h=\nabla\varphi$ therefore yields the one-sided derivative $$L(\varphi):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{R(u^\dagger+t\varphi)-R(u^\dagger)}{t}=\int_\Omega\operatorname{sgn}(x_1)\partial_1\varphi\,dx=-2\int_{-1}^1\varphi(0,x_2)\,dx_2,$$ where the last equality is integration by parts on $(-1,0)$ and $(0,1)$; compact support removes the endpoint terms. Replacing $\varphi$ by $-\varphi$ gives directional derivative $-L(\varphi)$. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, given, algebra]

2.1 Suppose a certificate $p\in L^2(\Omega)$ existed. The subgradient inequality [F3] applied to $u^\dagger+t\varphi$ for $t>0$, divided by $t$ and passed to the limit in step 1.2, gives $\int_\Omega p\varphi\le L(\varphi)$. Applying the same inequality to $u^\dagger-t\varphi$ gives $-\int_\Omega p\varphi\le-L(\varphi)$. Thus $\int_\Omega p\varphi=L(\varphi)$ for every compactly supported smooth $\varphi$. [F3, step 1.2, given]

3.1 Choose $\eta,\psi\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$ with $\eta(0)=1$ and $\int_{-1}^1\psi\ne0$, and for $0<\varepsilon<1$ set $\varphi_\varepsilon(x_1,x_2)=\eta(x_1/\varepsilon)\psi(x_2)$. Then $\varphi_\varepsilon\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $\|\varphi_\varepsilon\|_2=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\|\eta\|_2\|\psi\|_2\to0$. But step 2.1 and the formula in step 1.2 give $\int_\Omega p\varphi_\varepsilon=-2\int_{-1}^1\psi(x_2)\,dx_2$, a fixed nonzero number, whereas Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] forces these integrals to tend to zero. This contradiction proves that no $L^2$ source certificate exists. [F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set with $0<M:=|D|<\infty$, and let $k>0$. Write $S^2:=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:|v|=1\}$ and $C_D:=\sqrt{M\,\operatorname{diam}(D)/(4\pi)}$. For $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, extended by zero off $D$, set $G_k(z):=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ and $G_k(0):=0$, and let
$$K_{q,k}v(x):=\int_D G_k(x-y)q(y)v(y)\,dy,\qquad \rho_k(q):=\|K_{q,k}\|_{L^2(D)\to L^2(D)}.$$
The **small-norm contrast class** is
$$\mathcal U_{D,k}:=\{q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C):\rho_k(q)<1\}.$$
For $d\in S^2$, put $f_{k,d}(x):=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ on $D$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, let $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ denote the unique solution of $u=f_{k,d}+K_{q,k}u$. For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, define the exact far-field data family by
$$\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)u_{q,k,d}(y)\,dy,\qquad (\theta,d)\in S^2\times S^2.$$

For $h\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$, define its first Born data by
$$\mathcal B_k h(\theta,d):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_D e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}h(y)e^{ikd\cdot y}\,dy=\frac1{4\pi}\widehat{h_0}\!\left(\frac{k}{2\pi}(\theta-d)\right),$$
where $h_0$ is the zero extension of $h$ to $\mathbb R^3$ and $\widehat g(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$ for $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. No uniqueness or stability outside $\mathcal U_{D,k}$ is asserted.

## Definition references


[[def-metric-bounded-diameter|The diameter is $\operatorname{diam}(D)=\sup\{|x-y|:x,y\in D\}$.]]

[[def-euclidean-inner-product|The norm and dot product on $\mathbb R^3$ are the Euclidean ones.]]

[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions|The spaces $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ consist of measurable functions modulo equality almost everywhere.]]

[[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure|The $L^\infty$ norm is the essential supremum with respect to Lebesgue measure.]]

[[def-operator-norm|The operator norm is the least bound on a bounded linear map between normed spaces.]]

[[def-volume-integral-scattering-model|The outgoing volume model fixes $G_k(z)=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ and the far-field convention $e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}q(y)v(y)/(4\pi)$.]]

[[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded|The displayed volume kernel defines a bounded operator on complex $L^2(D)$.]]

[[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded|The far-field map is continuous and is the uniform outgoing limit of the exterior volume potential.]]

[[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn|The library Fourier transform uses $\widehat g(\xi)=\int g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$, giving the frequency $k(\theta-d)/(2\pi)$.]]

[[thm-volume-integral-scattering-born-neumann-error|For the strict operator norm bound, the volume equation has a unique L2 solution, which supplies the field used here.]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice is the declared axiom branch for the L2 volume model and its Neumann result.]]
