## Example

Let $N\ge1$ and let $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in[0,1]$ be arbitrary training inputs. For every deterministic learning rule that returns a prediction function $g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ from the observed pairs $(x_i,f(x_i))$, there are two $1$-Lipschitz functions $f_0,f_1:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ agreeing with each other and taking the common value $0$ at every training input but satisfying
$$\|f_1-f_0\|_{\infty}\ge\frac{1}{2(N+1)}.$$
Consequently, at the midpoint of a largest sample-free interval, the returned prediction function $g$ has absolute prediction error at least $1/(4(N+1))$ for at least one of these two indistinguishable target functions.

## Example references

[[op-ip-neural-operator-sample-complexity-for-inverse-maps|A finite-sample limit that motivates explicit inverse-map and architecture classes.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge1$, arbitrary sample sites $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in[0,1]$, exact labels $f(x_i)$, and a deterministic learning rule depending only on these observed pairs.

[A1] A function is $1$-Lipschitz when $|f(x)-f(y)|\le|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in[0,1]$.

## Verification

1.1 Sort the distinct sample sites together with endpoints $0$ and $1$. The at most $N+1$ consecutive gaps have total length one, so one open gap $(a,b)$ has length $\ell=b-a\ge1/(N+1)$. Let $x_*=(a+b)/2$, $r=\ell/2$, $f_0(x)=0$, and $f_1(x)=\max\{0,r-|x-x_*|\}$. The tent has slopes of magnitude at most one, vanishes at every sample site, and has height $r\ge1/(2(N+1))$ at $x_*$. Thus $f_0,f_1$ are both $1$-Lipschitz and yield identical training pairs. [given, A1, construct]

2.1 Because the training pairs are identical, the deterministic rule returns the same value $g(x_*)$ for both target functions. Since $|g(x_*)-f_0(x_*)|+|g(x_*)-f_1(x_*)|\ge|f_1(x_*)-f_0(x_*)|=r$, one of the two errors is at least $r/2\ge1/(4(N+1))$. Their uniform distance is $r\ge1/(2(N+1))$, proving both claims. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let a smoothly embedded surface in a horizontal slab of $\mathbb R^3$ have regular boundary on the two boundary planes and have at most one critical point of the height function, a nondegenerate one. Cut off its regular end collars and cap every resulting boundary circle by its planar disk, at slightly separated heights when disks are nested, rounding the seams. Every connected component of the resulting closed surface that is a sphere bounds a smoothly embedded standard $3$-ball. This includes the caps obtained by successively doing innermost horizontal-disk surgeries on a smooth sphere at finitely many regular levels separating all its critical values.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[lem-smooth-ball-windows-and-boundary-disk-absorption]]

[[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a component of the surface piece, its height function $z$, and the disjoint horizontal caps specified above.

[F1] A regular embedded nullhomotopic circle in an oriented surface bounds an embedded compact disk region under countable choice ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]], clause 4). In the plane its nullhomotopy is the linear contraction. For smooth input the disk is smooth: the disk-and-band construction in steps 7.1–12.1 of [[lem-finite-c2-surface-carriers-have-smooth-normal-forms-and-relative-cap-approximations]] uses smooth collars, smooth interval maps and smooth circle-map extensions throughout. Thus its smooth-input construction gives a smooth disk parametrization, including a prescribed smooth boundary collar.

[F2] The local form at a nondegenerate surface critical point is $z=z(p)\pm u^2\pm v^2$ ([[thm-morse-lemma]]). A compact smooth embedding isotopy extends to a compactly supported ambient isotopy under countable choice ([[thm-isotopy-extension]]).

[F3] Two smooth balls glued along a disk window form a ball; removing a boundary-attached ball from a ball leaves a ball, after corner rounding ([[lem-smooth-ball-windows-and-boundary-disk-absorption]]).

[A1] The hypothesis is [[def-countable-choice]]. It is used through [F1]–[F2]; every selection and modification particular to the finite collection of caps is finite.

## Proof

**Given:** The surface piece, the caps and the assumptions above.

1.1 On a compact height band without critical points, the restriction of height to the surface has a smooth field $X$ with $dz(X)=1$: in any surface chart divide a coordinate field by its nonzero height derivative, and combine finitely many such fields by a smooth partition near the compact band. Its flow carries the level circles through the band. Existence for the entire height interval follows by covering the compact band by finitely many flow charts, choosing a common positive short time, and restarting; the trajectory remains in the band until its height reaches an endpoint. Projecting each moving circle to its horizontal plane gives a smooth isotopy of disjoint plane curves. Its velocity has a smooth planar extension near the circles by their normal collar charts; finitely many cutoffs give a compactly supported extension. Its planar flow therefore straightens these curves simultaneously, level by level. In ambient coordinates use $(x,z)\mapsto(g_z(x),z)$ for these plane diffeomorphisms, cutting it off beyond the end levels. Consequently every regular end of the piece can be made vertical. The construction can be made fixed near its attachment to a critical neighborhood. [F2, construct]

2.1 Move the horizontal caps toward the critical level, stopping in a sufficiently thin slab about that level; in a regular collar this is exactly shortening a vertical cylinder and translating its cap. With nested caps perform the move on the innermost disk first and keep the stopping heights distinct in the order imposed by disjointness. This prevents intersections: outside the moving collar the only possible obstruction is another cap over a nested planar disk, and that cap has already been moved to a nearer stopping height or is kept beyond the moving one. Use positive, strictly monotone changes of the height coordinate along each cylinder, constant near its fixed end, to implement these moves; on the cap use the corresponding translation. Smooth corner rounding is done in disjoint collar neighborhoods. These are isotopies of the capped surface, and [F2] extends them ambiently. The same shortening applies in a component with no critical point, using any intermediate level. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 At a saddle use the chart $z=z(p)+u^2-v^2$. Outside a small rectangle about the saddle the regular sheets can be made vertical by step 1.1. Viewed in the horizontal plane, the two circles on the two-component side are joined by the projected saddle rectangle; its interior misses those circles. There are exactly two possibilities: their bounded disks are disjoint, or one disk lies inside the other. To justify completeness, each circle bounds the unique disk in the plane by [F1]. The connected second circle avoids the first and hence lies entirely in its disk interior or its exterior; applying the same argument with the two interchanged gives precisely disjoint or nested disks. The rectangle lies in the region adjacent to both of its attaching arcs: outside both disks in the disjoint case and in the annulus between them in the nested case. A different region would force it to cross one of the two circles. The saddle's other level circle is the boundary obtained by the band reconnection. Reverse height if necessary so this is the one-component side. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 With no critical point the connected uncapped piece is a cylinder: the flow in step 1.1 identifies it with one level circle times an interval. After shortening and straightening it is the vertical wall over a plane circle, with one disk cap at each end. Its bounded region is $D^2\times I$ in the disk coordinates from [F1]. This is a ball after rounding: replace the product corners in the disk-radius/height half-plane by circular arcs; the rounded solid is a smooth convex cylinder with rounded ends, radially parametrizable from its center. If there is a maximum or a minimum, the critical chart in [F2] is a paraboloid disk. The regular part is a cylinder attached to its boundary, by step 1.1. Shorten that cylinder into the chart. The paraboloid and its opposite planar cap bound a region $\{(u,v,t):0\le t\le c-u^2-v^2\}$, or its reflection. It is a ball, since rounding its edge gives a convex solid with a smooth radial parametrization; a radial rescaling is constant linear near the center and adjusted near the boundary. Thus these three cases give standard balls. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 In the disjoint-disk case, straighten the two attaching arcs in the boundary collars of their planar disks. The projected union of the two disks and the connecting rectangle is a disk: shrink the disks in their parametrizations to end caps, straighten the rectangle in its product coordinates, and round to a stadium. All remaining interval parametrizations extend over their collars by increasing interpolation, so this is an actual disk parametrization. The capped saddle bounds the solid made from the two short disk cylinders by a single thickened rectangle joining one disk window of each. Indeed, away from the rectangle its boundary is exactly the two vertical walls and their horizontal caps; across the rectangle its boundary has the reconnection prescribed by $u^2-v^2$. Rounding the rectangle's two lower or upper edges produces that saddle chart, and rounding the other edges gives precisely the cap collars. The two cylinders are balls by step 3.1. The thickened rectangle is a ball meeting the first cylinder in one disk, and its union with that cylinder meets the second cylinder in one disk. Two applications of [F3] therefore make this solid a ball. [F2, F3, step 3.1, step 2.2, construct]

4.2 In the nested-disk case let $D_i\subset\operatorname{Int}D_o$ be the inner and outer disks. Their intervening closed annulus is a smooth annulus by the two marked-disk/annulus construction of numbered clauses 12.1–13.1 of [F1]'s smooth-input normal-form proof. The joining rectangle is a crosscut of this annulus. Cutting along its central joining arc leaves a connected surface: a path can be rerouted from one side of the cut to the other around either of the two boundary circles before their marked attaching intervals are removed. Its boundary is one circle and its Euler characteristic is $0+1=1$, since cutting the rectangle replaces one band by two boundary intervals. The finite surface normal form in [F1] therefore gives a topological disk, and its smooth-input construction gives a smooth disk. Equivalently the curve on the one-component side bounds the annulus slit along the joining rectangle. The bounded solid of the capped saddle is an outer short disk cylinder with an inner short disk cylinder indented into one end; the indent's boundary window is opened to the outer wall by the thickened joining rectangle. The indented cylinder together with that rectangle is a ball meeting the outer cylinder's boundary in one disk: this window is the union of its inner disk window and the strip running to the outer boundary, rounded along their shared interval. This description is checked fiberwise away from the rectangle: a point of $D_o\setminus D_i$ has the full outer vertical interval and a point of $D_i$ has that interval shortened by the inner cap. Along the rectangle these intervals join at their endpoints in the single local reconnection $u^2-v^2$; rounding gives the prescribed saddle. The indented cylinder and joining rectangle are balls glued along one window, hence their union is a ball by [F3]. Removing this boundary-attached ball from the outer cylinder leaves a ball by [F3]. This proves the nested case. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, step 2.2, construct]

5.1 A connected regular piece has one circle at each end; an extremum piece has one; and a saddle piece has the three boundary circles just analyzed. There are no additional ends in the connected component: the regular flow supplies cylinders and the single critical chart supplies respectively the disk or the single band. Thus steps 4.1–4.2 exhaust the capped components that are spheres. Every straightening used an embedding isotopy, so it carries the constructed ball back to a smooth embedded standard ball bounded by the original capped sphere. For surgeries performed successively at finitely many regular levels, the innermost choice ensures that each cap interior misses the remaining surface, and sufficiently small distinct collar widths keep all new caps disjoint. Their components have exactly the form used in steps 1.1–2.1, so the final assertion follows as well. [F2, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

## Statement

Supply a finite polygonal disk-band oriented Seifert surface, its local ambient smooth roundings, and the resulting smooth oriented knot $K=\partial F\subset S^3$. Supply a compatible closed product tube $N(K)$, a positive meridian $\mu$, a preferred zero longitude $\lambda$ obtained by trimming and paralleling $F$, and peripheral base paths. Put $X_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and let $M(K)$ be its zero-longitude filling. Then
$$H_1(X_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu],\qquad \lambda\in\pi_1(X_K)^{(2)}.$$
Both $\pi_1(X_K)$ and $\pi_1(M(K))$ are normally generated by their marked meridian images. These conclusions use no choice principle. The finite model and tubes are part of the input; no existence theorem for a neighborhood of an arbitrary locally flat surface is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The supplied finite disk-band model, local roundings, compatible product tube, peripheral loops and base paths. A derived subgroup is the subgroup of finite products of commutators.

[F1] Product-collared decompositions have Mayer–Vietoris with actual inclusion maps, and $H_1(S^3;\mathbb Z)=H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)=0$. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]], [[cor-homology-of-spheres]]

[F2] The first Hurewicz map is the natural quotient onto the abelianization, without choice or a CW hypothesis. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

[F3] Van Kampen gives the actual fundamental-group pushout for a path-connected collared decomposition, without overlap injectivity. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

## Proof

1.1 On the peripheral torus $T$, the supplied meridian and longitude give $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]\oplus\mathbb Z[\lambda]$, as its finite square cell model shows. The tube retracts onto its core and has $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$. The longitude bounds the trimmed parallel Seifert surface in $X_K$, so its class there is zero, while it maps to the core generator in $N(K)$; the meridian maps to zero in that tube. Apply [F1] to $S^3=X_K\cup N(K)$ with slightly thickened collars. The segment $0=H_2(S^3)\to H_1(T)\to H_1(X_K)\oplus H_1(N(K))\to H_1(S^3)=0$ makes its middle map an isomorphism. Its values on the two displayed generators therefore give $H_1(X_K)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ exactly, including the marked generator. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For normal generation apply [F3] to $S^3=X_K\cup N(K)$. In the tube group the meridian becomes $1$ and the longitude becomes its core $c$, so the pushout is $(\pi_1(X_K)*\langle c\rangle)/\langle\!\langle\mu,\lambda c^{-1}\rangle\!\rangle$, naturally $\pi_1(X_K)/\langle\!\langle\mu\rangle\!\rangle$. This group is trivial: cover $S^3$ by the complements of its north and south poles; each is $\mathbb R^3$ and contracts, and their overlap is path-connected, so [F3] gives $\pi_1(S^3)=1$. This proves normal generation of the exterior group. In the zero filling the meridian becomes the filling core and the longitude becomes $1$; the identical pushout calculation gives $\pi_1(M(K))=\pi_1(X_K)/\langle\!\langle\lambda\rangle\!\rangle$. It too is normally generated by the image of $\mu$. No incompressibility or injection assertion about a torus group is used. [F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Signed intersection with the properly trimmed Seifert surface defines a homomorphism $H_1(X_K;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ taking $\mu$ to one. In this finite model its chain-level justification is explicit. Undo the supplied finite local roundings, work with its finite polygonal faces, and move each fixed finite loop or chain into general position with these faces by finite subdivision and small piecewise-linear perturbations. Each perturbation excludes only finitely many improper affine incidences, so finite rational choices suffice. These operations preserve the homology class by the straight simplex prisms in sufficiently small convex coordinate boxes. For a two-chain in the interior of $X_K$, its transverse intersection with the oriented surface is a finite oriented one-chain. Its boundary is the intersection with the two-chain boundary: no boundary term comes from the surface boundary, which lies on $T$ outside that interior. The signed sum of this one-chain's endpoints is zero, so intersection counts agree on homologous one-cycles. Boundary collars move any fixed finite chain into the interior before this calculation. The meridian meets the surface once with positive sign by the supplied peripheral orientation. Thus step 1.1 makes this intersection homomorphism an isomorphism. All loops in a small positive parallel copy $F^+$ of the trimmed surface miss the original surface, so their images in $H_1(X_K)$ are zero. The parallel copy and its boundary longitude are supplied by the finite oriented ribbon charts and tube. [F1, given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By [F2], step 2.1 implies that the entire image of $\pi_1(F^+)$ in $\pi_1(X_K)$ lies in its commutator subgroup. The oriented boundary loop of $F^+$ represents zero in $H_1(F^+;\mathbb Z)$: a finite triangulation of the supplied disk-band surface gives an oriented two-chain whose boundary is exactly that boundary loop, with all internal edges cancelling. Apply [F2] to $F^+$ to conclude that its boundary element belongs to $[\pi_1(F^+),\pi_1(F^+)]$. Its image in $\pi_1(X_K)$ therefore belongs to $[\pi_1(X_K)^{(1)},\pi_1(X_K)^{(1)}]=\pi_1(X_K)^{(2)}$. The compatible tube identifies this boundary with the preferred longitude up to conjugation. Derived subgroups are normal, as conjugation sends each finite commutator product to another, so the marked $\lambda$ has the same conclusion. [F2, given, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The proof used the actual supplied finite surface model only to define and justify intersection counts and its finite fundamental two-chain. The marked tube, trimming and parallel copy were input or finite product constructions. All perturbations concerned one finite chain at a time; all homology comparisons and pushout maps were natural or uniquely defined. Consequently no simultaneous choice of representatives, triangulation of an arbitrary topological manifold, or locally flat four-dimensional normal-bundle assertion has been imported. This proves all stated peripheral and group conclusions in their full supplied-data scope. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

kind: lemma

status: draft

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361"
      locator: "§2.3, boundary spectral smoothing exponent and eigenvalue summability, printed pp. 9–11."
---

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, put $M=\partial\Omega$, and set $n=d-1$. Define $H^1(M)$ as the completion of smooth functions in the norm $\|u\|_{H^1(M)}^2=\int_M(|u|^2+|\nabla_Mu|^2)\,dS$. Define $-\Delta_M$ by its weak form: $-\Delta_Mu=f$ when $u\in H^1(M)$, $f\in L^2(M)$, and $\int_M\nabla_Mu\cdot\overline{\nabla_Mv}\,dS=\langle f,v\rangle_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1(M)$. Then the nonnegative Laplace–Beltrami operator $-\Delta_M$ on $L^2(M)$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis $(e_j)_{j\ge0}$ with eigenvalues $0\le\lambda_0\le\lambda_1\le\cdots$ repeated with multiplicity and tending to infinity. Its counting function satisfies
$$N_M(\Lambda):=\#\{j:\lambda_j\le\Lambda\}\le C_M(1+\Lambda)^{n/2}\qquad(\Lambda\ge0).$$
For $s\ge0$, define the spectral Sobolev space and norm by
$$H^s_{\Delta}(M)=\left\{f=\sum_j c_je_j:\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)^s|c_j|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad \|f\|_{H^s_\Delta}^2=\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)^s|c_j|^2.$$
At $s=1$, this norm equals the quadratic-form norm $\int_M(|f|^2+|\nabla_Mf|^2)\,dS$. In particular, for every $\tau>0$,
$$\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)^{-n/2-\tau}<\infty.$$

The compact-resolvent construction factors through the compact embedding:

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,node distance=2.5cm]
  \node[draw,rounded corners] (l2a) {$L^2(M)$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,right of=l2a] (h1) {$H^1(M)$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,right of=h1] (l2b) {$L^2(M)$};
  \draw[->] (l2a) -- node[above] {$\widetilde K$} (h1);
  \draw[->] (h1) -- node[above] {$J$ (compact)} (l2b);
  \draw[->,bend right=30] (l2a) to node[below] {$K=J\widetilde K$} (l2b);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Here $\widetilde K$ is the weak resolvent map and $J$ is the compact inclusion; the lower arrow is their composition.

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-boundary-chart-lifting-and-fourier-projection|Finite boundary charts and compact Fourier-tail estimates.]]

[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface|The surface measure and boundary gradient convention.]]

[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators|The compact self-adjoint spectral theorem.]]

[de Hoop et al., §2.3: boundary spectral smoothing exponent](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice, $\Omega$, $M$ and $n=d-1$ as in the statement.

[F1] The boundary chart lemma supplies a finite family of boundary charts with compactly supported smooth weights satisfying $\sum_j\psi_j^2=1$; its displayed chart maps are for the product boundary. The single-boundary maps and their bounds used here are constructed in step 1.1. ([[lem-ip-boundary-chart-lifting-and-fourier-projection]])

[F2] A bounded coercive sesquilinear form on a Hilbert space has a unique weak solution with the standard norm estimate. ([[thm-lax-milgram]])

[F3] A compact positive self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has finite-multiplicity positive eigenvalues tending only to zero, and its nonzero eigenspaces span the closure of its range. ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]])

[F4] Fourier characters form an orthonormal basis on $\mathbb T^n$ and Parseval holds. ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is used at the compact self-adjoint spectral theorem interface. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[A2] Countable Choice is used at the chart partition, weak-solution and Hilbert interfaces. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice, the Axiom of Choice, and the smooth compact boundary $M$.

1.1 Let $(U_j,\phi_j)_{j=1}^J$ and $(\psi_j)_{j=1}^J$ be the boundary charts and square partition supplied by [F1], with $\phi_j(U_j)\Subset(1/4,3/4)^n$. Define
$$\mathcal Gf=\bigl((\psi_j f)\circ\phi_j^{-1}\bigr)_{j=1}^J,\qquad \mathcal L(v_1,\ldots,v_J)=\sum_{j=1}^J\psi_j(v_j\circ\phi_j),$$
where each chart component is extended by zero outside its chart image and each summand by zero off $U_j$. Since every $\psi_j$ is compactly supported in $U_j$, the zero extensions preserve smoothness for smooth inputs. Change of variables, the bounded chart Jacobians, and the product and chain rules show that $\mathcal G$ and $\mathcal L$ are bounded on $L^2$ and $H^1$. Direct substitution gives $\mathcal L\mathcal Gf=\sum_j\psi_j^2f=f$ almost everywhere. For $N\ge1$, Fourier Parseval [F4] gives componentwise
$$\|(I-P_N)\mathcal Gf\|_{\oplus L^2(\mathbb T^n)}^2\le (2\pi N)^{-2}\|\nabla\mathcal Gf\|_{\oplus L^2(\mathbb T^n)}^2\le C N^{-2}\|f\|_{H^1(M)}^2.$$
For $N=0$, boundedness of $\mathcal G$ on $H^1$ gives the same estimate after increasing $C$. Therefore
$$\|f-\mathcal L P_N\mathcal Gf\|_2\le C(1+N)^{-1}\|f\|_{H^1(M)}.$$
The finite Fourier sums $\mathcal L P_N\mathcal Gf$ are smooth functions on $M$ and converge to $f$ in $L^2$, so smooth functions are dense in $L^2(M)$. [F1, F4, given, construct]

2.1 The estimate in step 1.1 proves $H^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is compact: the finite-rank maps $\mathcal L P_N\mathcal G$ approximate the identity uniformly on the $H^1$ unit ball, and their images are bounded subsets of finite-dimensional spaces, hence have finite nets of every positive radius. Thus the unit ball is totally bounded in the complete space $L^2(M)$. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Put $q(u,v)=\int_M(u\overline v+\nabla_Mu\cdot\overline{\nabla_Mv})\,dS$ on $H^1(M)$. For $f\in L^2(M)$, [F2] gives a unique $u=\widetilde Kf\in H^1(M)$ with $q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for every $v\in H^1(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^1}\le\|f\|_2$. Let $J:H^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ and $K=J\widetilde K$. By step 2.1, $K$ is compact. Hermitian symmetry of $q$ gives $\langle Kf,g\rangle=\langle f,Kg\rangle$ and $\langle Kf,f\rangle=q(\widetilde Kf,\widetilde Kf)\ge0$. If $Kf=0$, the weak equation and smooth density from step 1.1 imply $\langle f,v\rangle=0$ for every $v\in L^2(M)$, so $f=0$. Thus $K$ is compact, positive, self-adjoint and injective. [A2, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F3], $K$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_j$ with positive eigenvalues $\mu_j\to0$; order these so that $\mu_j$ is nonincreasing. Put $\lambda_j=\mu_j^{-1}-1$. From $Ke_j=\mu_je_j$ and the weak equation, $\int_M\nabla_Me_j\cdot\overline{\nabla_Mv}\,dS=\lambda_j\langle e_j,v\rangle$ for every $v\in H^1(M)$. Taking $v=e_j$ gives $\lambda_j=\int_M|\nabla_Me_j|^2\,dS\ge0$, and these are the eigenvectors of the stated weak Laplace–Beltrami operator. In the form inner product $q$, the vectors $(1+\lambda_j)^{-1/2}e_j$ are orthonormal and complete: a vector $v$ orthogonal to every $e_j$ in $q$ satisfies $(1+\lambda_j)\langle v,e_j\rangle=0$ for every $j$, hence vanishes in $L^2$. Form Parseval gives $q(v,v)=\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)|\langle v,e_j\rangle|^2$, proving the $s=1$ norm identity. [A1, F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Let $E_\Lambda=\operatorname{span}\{e_j:\lambda_j\le\Lambda\}$. For $u\in E_\Lambda$, step 4.1 gives $\|u\|_{H^1}^2\le(1+\Lambda)\|u\|_2^2$. If $\dim E_\Lambda$ exceeded the rank of $P_N\mathcal G|_{E_\Lambda}$, rank-nullity would give nonzero $u\in E_\Lambda$ with $P_N\mathcal Gu=0$. Since $\mathcal L\mathcal G=I$ and $\mathcal L$ is bounded, step 1.1 then gives $\|u\|_2\le C(1+N)^{-1}\|u\|_{H^1}\le C\sqrt{1+\Lambda}(1+N)^{-1}\|u\|_2$. Choose $N\ge2C\sqrt{1+\Lambda}$ to contradict $u\ne0$. Thus $N_M(\Lambda)=\dim E_\Lambda\le\operatorname{rank}(P_N\mathcal G)\le J(2N+1)^n\le C'(1+\Lambda)^{n/2}$. [F1, step 1.1, step 4.1, choose, algebra]

6.1 For $p=n/2+\tau$, group eigenvalues into $[2^k,2^{k+1})$. The bound from step 5.1 gives $\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)^{-p}\le C\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-kp}N_M(2^{k+1})\le C'\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k(p-n/2)}<\infty$; the finitely many eigenvalues below $1$ contribute finitely. This proves the stated summability for every $\tau>0$. Defining $H^s_\Delta(M)$ by the weighted coefficient norm in the Statement completes the spectral-scale claim. [step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a link with $c$ components, and form its rational Lee cochain complex using the normalized crossing cube and decreasing quantum filtration. The associated bounded spectral sequence has the rational Khovanov cohomology of $D$ on its homology page and converges to the associated graded of Lee homology with its induced filtration. For the empty link, both rational complexes use the one-term empty tensor complex $\mathbb Q$ in bidegree $(0,0)$ with zero differential, so the spectral sequence is constant. For each of the $2^c$ orientations $o$ of the link, let $D_o$ be the oriented resolution and set $a=1+X$ and $b=X-1$ in $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$. For each Seifert circle $C$ in $D_o$, let $\delta(C)\in\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ be the parity of the number of other Seifert circles separating $C$ from infinity, and let $\kappa(C)=1$ if $C$ is counterclockwise in the oriented projection plane and $\kappa(C)=0$ if it is clockwise in that plane. Label $C$ by $a$ exactly when $\delta(C)+\kappa(C)$ is even, and by $b$ otherwise. These labels define a canonical Lee cycle $s_o$, and the cycles form a basis of Lee homology. For the empty link, its unique orientation class is the empty-tensor unit and spans its one-dimensional Lee homology. For a knot, the two canonical classes $s_o,s_{\bar o}$ have equal least filtration level, while $s_o+s_{\bar o}$ and $s_o-s_{\bar o}$ are nonzero classes in the two distinct quantum-degree congruence summands modulo $4$.


### Local crossing convention

For the proof’s local convention, the four segment ends are numbered clockwise, and sectors $(1,2)$ and $(3,4)$ are black. The textual endpoint and arrow rules in step 2.1 determine all labels; the drawing is illustrative and is not used in the proof.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.1]
  \fill[black!18] (0,0) -- (0.72,0) arc (0:90:0.72) -- cycle;
  \fill[black!18] (0,0) -- (-0.72,0) arc (180:270:0.72) -- cycle;
  \node at (0.48,0.48) {$B$};
  \node at (-0.48,-0.48) {$B$};
  \draw[line width=5pt] (-0.8,0) -- (0.8,0);
  \draw[white,line width=5pt] (-0.2,0) -- (0.2,0);
  \draw[line width=1pt] (-0.8,0) -- (-0.2,0);
  \draw[line width=1pt] (0.2,0) -- (0.8,0);
  \draw[line width=1pt] (0,0.8) -- (0,-0.8);
  \node[above] at (0,0.82) {$1$};
  \node[right] at (0.82,0) {$2$};
  \node[below] at (0,-0.82) {$3$};
  \node[left] at (-0.82,0) {$4$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references

[[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex|Rational Lee cochain complex and decreasing quantum filtration]]

[[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram|Normalized even Khovanov state cube]]

[[thm-bounded-filtered-complex-spectral-sequence-abuts-to-filtered-homology|Bounded filtered-complex abutment]]

[Rasmussen, *Khovanov homology and the slice genus* (2004), §§2.3–2.4 and 3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131v1)

[McMullen, *4-Manifolds*, §§5.5–5.6](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/4Mnotes.pdf)

[Lee, *On Khovanov invariant for alternating links* (2002), §§2–4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0210213v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite regular oriented link diagram, its oriented resolution cube, and the rational Lee operations.

[F1] The Lee complex has the finite signed state cube, quantum degree, and decreasing filtration specified in [[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex]].

[F2] The even Khovanov procedure assigns the integral Frobenius algebra to each state and the signed saddle maps to its edges ([[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]]).

[F3] The integral cube differential squares to zero, and it is the degree-preserving part of the Lee differential ([[lem-khovanov-cube-differential-squares-to-zero]]).

[F4] A finite filtration on each chain object yields a spectral sequence whose limiting page is the associated graded of homology ([[thm-bounded-filtered-complex-spectral-sequence-abuts-to-filtered-homology]]).

[F5] The cochain-to-chain reindexing $C^\sharp_n=C^{-n}$ and the translation $G_p=F^{-p}$ convert a decreasing filtered cochain complex to an increasing filtered chain complex without changing its differential or finite filtration ([[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], [[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

## Proof

**Given:** $D$, the finite cube and its crossing signs and order.

**Empty-link case:** If $D$ is empty, both cubes are the one-term empty tensor complex $\mathbb Q$ in bidegree $(0,0)$ with zero differential. The spectral sequence is constant, and the unique orientation class is its empty-tensor unit. This proves the empty-link assertions. Assume henceforth that $D$ is nonempty.


1.1 Put $a=1+X$ and $b=X-1$ in $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$. The relation $X^2=1$ gives $m_L(a\otimes a)=2a,\quad m_L(b\otimes b)=-2b,\quad m_L(a\otimes b)=m_L(b\otimes a)=0, \qquad \Delta_L(a)=a\otimes a,\quad\Delta_L(b)=b\otimes b.$ The counit takes value $1$ on each of $a,b$. In the basis $1,X$, the degree-preserving part of each saddle is the integral Khovanov saddle, and the only remaining terms replace $X\otimes X$ by $1$ under multiplication or replace $X$ by $1\otimes1$ under comultiplication. Each replacement raises the quantum degree by $4$, including the state shift, so the associated-graded differential is precisely the even Khovanov differential. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 The projection of $D$ is a finite four-valent plane graph (with crossingless components as disjoint Jordan curves), so checkerboard-color its regions with the unbounded region white. Define the color of a region by the parity of intersections of a path from infinity to it with the projection; this is path-independent because every closed curve in the plane has even mod-$2$ intersection with the closed diagram. For each segment between crossing disks, assign label $a$ and direct it so that the black region is on its right, or assign label $b$ and direct it so that black is on its left. At a crossing, list the four incident segment ends clockwise as $1,2,3,4$, choosing the convention that sectors $(1,2)$ and $(3,4)$ are black, as in the local drawing. The arrows point outward/inward at ends $1,3$ according as their labels are $a/b$, and inward/outward at ends $2,4$ according as their labels are $a/b$. Thus the four patterns $aabb,abba,bbaa,baab$ are exactly those for which opposite ends have opposite arrows; in each case exactly one adjacent pairing connects equal labels and an incoming to an outgoing arrow. It is the oriented smoothing. All-equal patterns have two equal-label smoothings but do not orient the original crossing, while alternating and three-to-one patterns have no compatible smoothing. Thus, among segment labelings compatible with a smoothing at every crossing, having no all-equal crossing is equivalent to determining exactly one oriented state and an orientation of the link. For an oriented state, each circle has one label. Let $\delta(C)$ be the parity of the number of other Seifert circles separating it from infinity. The outside region of $C$ is black exactly when $\delta(C)=1$; its inside has the opposite color. As the interior is left of a counterclockwise circle and right of a clockwise circle, the black-right rule labels $C$ by $a$ exactly when $\delta(C)+\kappa(C)$ is even, where $\kappa(C)=1$ for counterclockwise and $0$ for clockwise. This is the parity rule in the Statement. [given, construct]

2.1 The cube has finitely many states and each state module is finite-dimensional, hence only finitely many quantum filtration levels occur. Reindex the cochain degrees and filtration by [F5], then apply [F4] to obtain a convergent spectral sequence with abutment $\operatorname{gr}H(C_L(D))$; reversing the filtration index changes only the page's filtration label. Index its first page as the associated-graded chain complex and its next as its cohomology. By step 1.1 and [F2], this cohomology is rational Khovanov cohomology. This is the convention in which the homology page is denoted $E_2$; changing page names does not change the limiting filtered homology. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Restrict an enhanced state to the diagram segments between crossing disks; its circle labels determine one segment labeling. From the operations in step 1.1, an edge map is nonzero exactly when the four labels at its crossing agree. Every nonzero edge preserves all segment labels, so the complex is a direct sum over segment labelings. For a fixed labeling, each all-equal crossing is a free coordinate with both smoothings and an invertible saddle; each other crossing has at most one compatible smoothing. If any crossing has no compatible smoothing the summand is zero; otherwise its compatible states form a Boolean cube on precisely the all-equal crossings. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 On any nonempty cube from step 2.2, every edge coefficient is nonzero in $\mathbb Q$. Let $u(e)$ be the coefficient of a directed edge and let $s(e)=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v_i}$ be the standard cube sign on the edge changing coordinate $j$. The equation $d^2=0$ gives $u(e_1)u(e_2)=-u(e_3)u(e_4)$ around each square, and the standard signs satisfy the same equation. Hence $u(e)/s(e)$ has product $1$ around every square. Rescale each vertex basis by the product of these ratios along a path from a fixed vertex; square faces generate all path changes in a Boolean cube, so the rescaling is path-independent and identifies its differential with the standard tensor differential. If there is a free coordinate, its factor is $\mathbb Q\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}\mathbb Q$; contracting that factor with the tensor-product Koszul sign contracts the whole cube. If there is no free coordinate, the cube is a single zero-differential line. When $D$ is empty, this is the unique empty-state line $\mathbb Q$, whose class is the empty-tensor unit. In all cases, step 1.2 identifies the singleton lines bijectively with the orientations of the link, so they form a basis of Lee homology. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra, construct]

4.1 For a knot, reversing orientation leaves the oriented resolution fixed and interchanges $a$ and $b$ on each of its $k\ge1$ Seifert circles. Write the two singleton representatives as $u=\bigotimes_{i=1}^k c_i$ and $\bar u=\bigotimes_{i=1}^k\bar c_i$, where $c_i\in\{a,b\}$ and $\bar c_i$ is the other basis vector. Their state shift is $r=|v|+n_+-2n_-$. A tensor term with exactly $j$ labels equal to $1$ has quantum degree $r-k+2j$. In the expansions of $u$ and $\bar u$, its coefficients differ by $(-1)^j$: each selected $1$ contributes opposite signs from $a=1+X$ and $b=X-1$, while every $X$ contributes coefficient $1$. Thus $u+\bar u$ contains exactly the even-$j$ terms and $u-\bar u$ exactly the odd-$j$ terms. Their least chain degrees are $r-k$ and $r-k+2$, which give lower bounds for their induced homology filtration levels; boundary changes may improve those levels. The differential changes quantum degree by $0$ or $4$, so the whole filtered complex splits into its quantum congruence summands modulo $4$. The two nonzero homology classes $[u+\bar u]$ and $[u-\bar u]$ lie in distinct such summands and span homology by step 3.1. Each summand therefore contributes one filtered homology line, with level in its own congruence class. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Choose a point $p$ away from the crossings. Let $X_p$ multiply the circle containing $p$ by $X$ in each state. It commutes with each edge: the identities $m(Xz,w)=Xm(z,w)=m(z,Xw)$ and $\Delta(Xz)=(X\otimes1)\Delta(z)=(1\otimes X)\Delta(z)$ hold for $z,w=1,X$, hence for all inputs. It is a chain map with $X_p^2=1$. Its terms have quantum degrees $-2$ (sending $1$ to $X$) and $+2$ (sending $X$ to $1$), so it has filtered degree $-2$. At the mark the labels of $u,\bar u$ are opposite, with $Xa=a$ and $Xb=-b$. Hence $X_p$ interchanges the two homology lines of step 4.1, up to an overall sign. If their filtration levels are $\ell_+,\ell_-$, its filtered degree in both directions gives $\ell_-\ge\ell_+-2$ and $\ell_+\ge\ell_--2$. They lie in congruence classes differing by two modulo four, so $|\ell_+-\ell_-|=2$. Every knot-state quantum grading is odd: at the oriented state its parity is $n+k$, and the connected Seifert disk-band surface has $k-n=1-2g$; a cube edge changes $|v|+k(v)$ by an even integer. Finally $[u]$ and $[\bar u]$ are half the sum and difference of these two lines, so both have the smaller level, by the filtered direct sum into congruence summands. Thus their common level is $s_{\min}$, the larger line has level $s_{\max}=s_{\min}+2$, and the asserted equal-level and congruence properties hold. This argument concerns induced homology filtrations and makes no assertion that a fixed canonical cycle is already a maximal-filtration representative. [F1, step 4.1, algebra, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with supplied boundary collar, and let $R$ be an involutive unital ring. Supply a based rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$, a base-fiber identification with $R$, unitary monodromy and its parallel standard Hermitian form. For $p\in H_2(W;\mathcal R)$ let $a_p\in H^2(W,\partial W;\mathcal R^\vee)$ be the inverse cap-duality image of $\bar p$, using the form to identify the intrinsic dual system with $\overline{\mathcal R}$. Define
$$\lambda(p,q)=\langle j(a_p),q\rangle,$$
where $j$ forgets the relative condition and the last pairing is intrinsic cochain evaluation. Then
$$\lambda(p,q)=\overline{\lambda(q,p)}$$
for all $p,q$. In particular $\lambda(\ell_i,d_j)=\delta_{ij}$ implies $\lambda(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$. No choice axiom, triangulation or geometric transversality of surfaces in dimension four is required.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact collared manifold, ring, unitary local system and its supplied standard Hermitian structure.

[F1] Relative cap duality holds for arbitrary abelian-group local systems and commuting scalar actions; unitary Hermitian structures identify intrinsic dual systems with conjugate systems. [[thm-compact-collared-manifold-local-coefficient-lefschetz-duality-in-zf]], [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]]

[F2] Cup and cap are given by front/back faces and coefficient transport, and their associativity identity is checked on these faces. The relative orientation class is represented by a finite integral chain with boundary in $\partial W$. [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]], [[lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets]]

## Proof

1.1 On the dual coefficient fibers and their conjugates, the natural evaluation pairing is the ring-valued pairing $(a,\bar b)\mapsto a\bar b$ in a unitary frame. This is transport-invariant: dual transport is $a\mapsto au^{-1}$, conjugate-dual transport on the second factor corresponds to $\bar b\mapsto u\bar b$, and their product is unchanged. Its transposed conjugate pairing has the same value, since $\overline{b\bar a}=a\bar b$. Thus the reversed-factor cup product followed by involution can be compared with the original product in the same constant abelian-group coefficient system $R$. This does not exchange factors inside a noncommutative product without applying the involution. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose relative dual two-cocycles $\alpha,\beta$ representing $a_p,a_q$. Conjugation turns $\beta$ into a right-coefficient cocycle whose relative cap is $q$. The front-evaluation cap in [F2] retains the back face: $\overline\beta$ is evaluated on the front face to give the coefficient of $q$, while $\alpha$ evaluates its retained back face. Consequently the exact formulas, with the transport evaluation of step 1.1, are $$\lambda(p,q)=\langle\tau(\overline\beta\smile\alpha),[W,\partial W]\rangle,\qquad\overline{\lambda(q,p)}=\langle\alpha\smile\overline\beta,[W,\partial W]\rangle.$$ Here $\tau$ means reverse the two coefficient factors and use the pairing of step 1.1, so the coefficient product in the second expression is still ordered as the value of $\alpha$ followed by the conjugate value of $\beta$. Both cocycles vanish on simplices contained in $\partial W$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The needed cup interchange is an explicit finite cochain identity. For a singular three-simplex with ordered vertices $0123$, put $$H(0123)=\alpha(013)\,\overline{\beta(123)}-\alpha(023)\,\overline{\beta(012)}.$$ Every factor is transported to the first vertex before pairing; for the first product this transports the second factor from vertex1 to vertex0. On each singular four-simplex the pulled-back local systems are trivialized by its straight vertex paths, so coefficient transports obey the face identities and the calculation reduces to the same displayed ring products. Expanding the five terms of $\delta H(01234)$ and using $\delta\alpha=\delta\beta=0$ gives $$\delta H(01234)=\alpha(012)\,\overline{\beta(234)}-\alpha(234)\,\overline{\beta(012)}.$$ For clarity the unreduced expansion is $\alpha(124)\overline{\beta(234)}-\alpha(134)\overline{\beta(123)}-\alpha(024)\overline{\beta(234)}+\alpha(034)\overline{\beta(023)}+\alpha(014)\overline{\beta(134)}-\alpha(034)\overline{\beta(013)}-\alpha(014)\overline{\beta(124)}+\alpha(024)\overline{\beta(012)}+\alpha(013)\overline{\beta(123)}-\alpha(023)\overline{\beta(012)}$; substituting the four-face cocycle identities groups it into the two displayed terms. Coefficient multiplication retains its order throughout. Hence $\delta H=\alpha\smile\overline\beta-\tau(\overline\beta\smile\alpha)$. This is the degree-two cup-one homotopy written out locally; no commutative-ring cup-interchange theorem is being applied in a broader scope. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Since $\alpha,\beta$ are relative, $H$ vanishes on every simplex in $\partial W$. If $z$ is the finite relative orientation cycle, then $\langle\delta H,z\rangle=\langle H,\partial z\rangle=0$. Evaluating the identity of step 3.1 and using step 2.1 proves the asserted Hermitian equality. For the cross terms, apply the equality and $\bar1=1,\bar0=0$. The cochains were chosen only for the two given classes, each simplex calculation involved finitely many faces, and the evaluation used a single finite orientation chain. All coefficient identifications were relative to the supplied standard form. Thus no choice principle or surface transversality assertion has entered. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. For every supplied finite smooth oriented disk-band Seifert surface $F$ with one-boundary knot $K$, ordered homology basis and first-variable positive-push matrix $V$, let $W_F$ and its meridional extension $\psi_d:\pi_1(W_F)\to\mathbb Z/d$ be the actual construction of the finite disk-band bounding-manifold construction. For every positive integer $d$, set $\zeta_d=\exp(2\pi i/d)$ and
$$D_d(F)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_{\mathbb Z/d}(W_F,\psi_d)-\operatorname{sign}(W_F).$$
Then
$$D_d(F)=\frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{sign}\bigl((1-\zeta_d^r)V+(1-\zeta_d^{-r})V^T\bigr).$$
The sign is exactly the positive $L^2$ signature minus ordinary signature convention. The formula allows singular character forms and all $d$, including $d=1$ and even $d$. The term $r=0$ is defined by the zero Hermitian matrix and contributes zero; its equality to the trivial-character signature follows from the ordinary metabolic calculation, not from specialization of a localized homology basis.

The boundary is the actual oriented zero surgery and its positive meridian map, not the knot exterior or a simply connected trace. The displayed formula proves this **canonical bounding defect**. Whenever a separately proved applicable bordism-independence assertion identifies the rho invariant with the defect of this bounding extension, it consequently gives the same value for that rho invariant. No such general independence assertion, global signature invariance, rho identification, uniform bound, infinite-cyclic formula or arbitrary-group index theorem is asserted here.

## Statement references

[[lem-finite-disk-band-surfaces-give-cyclic-zero-surgery-bounding-manifolds|Finite disk-band bounding-manifold construction]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite smooth surface, its actual first-push matrix, AC and the positive integer $d$.

[F1] The first supplier constructs $W_F$ with actual zero-surgery boundary and meridional fundamental group, proves its ordinary signature zero, and computes its actual nontrivial-character form as $(1-z)V+(1-z^{-1})V^T$; the ordinary form is handled separately. [[lem-finite-disk-band-surfaces-give-cyclic-zero-surgery-bounding-manifolds]]

[F2] For an actual finite cyclic cover of a finite pair, its $L^2$ signature is the arithmetic mean of all character signatures, with kernels discarded only within their own blocks. [[lem-finite-cyclic-von-neumann-signatures-are-character-averages]]

[F3] The compact smooth manifold and its smooth boundary have a compatible finite triangulation. This supplies an actual finite CW pair, with the boundary a subcomplex. [[thm-compact-smooth-manifolds-with-corners-admit-relative-finite-triangulations]]

[F4] The rho definition uses a supplied bounding extension and the convention $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}-\operatorname{sign}$; independence is a separate obligation. [[def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant]]

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the supplied finite geometry. It gives an oriented boundary identification $\partial W_F=M_K$ and an isomorphism $\pi_1(W_F)=\mathbb Z$ whose generator is the positive meridian of that boundary. Reducing this actual generator modulo $d$ gives a surjection and restricts to the positive meridian map on the actual zero surgery. In particular the prescribed coefficient map extends, which would not follow from merely taking the simply connected zero-framed two-handle trace. The smooth compact pair supplied by [F1] has the finite relative triangulation of [F3]. Thus all hypotheses of [F2] hold for this actual covering pair. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 For each nontrivial character $r$, [F1] identifies the actual middle character form, including its possible radical, with the displayed Hermitian matrix at $z=\zeta_d^r$, up to a positive basis normalization which changes no inertia. Its proof obtained that character homology directly from the cut complex and the invertibility of $1-z$, without assuming an Alexander determinant was nonzero. For $r=0$, the actual character form is the ordinary form of $W_F$, whose signature is zero by its explicit half-dimensional isotropic subspace and nonsingularity. The displayed matrix at $1$ is zero and also has signature zero, so this term has the same signature even though it is not a basis matrix for the ordinary form. Applying [F2] therefore gives precisely the arithmetic mean in the Statement for $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}(W_F,\psi_d)$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], $\operatorname{sign}(W_F)=0$. Subtracting it from step2.1 proves the claimed defect formula with the stated sign. For $d=1$ there is only the zero term and both ordinary and trivial-group signatures coincide; for even $d$ the $-1$ character is included like every other nontrivial character, with no nonsingularity exception. Finally, if an independently established applicable bordism-independence theorem identifies [F4]'s rho with this particular supplied defect, substitution of the proven equality gives its same value. Without that additional assertion the already proved conclusion is exactly $D_d(F)$. This logical implication invokes no unproved independence supplier and makes no claim that the canonical defects are already independent of the supplied surface. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be a closed connected oriented Hausdorff topological three-manifold, with a specified based loop $\mu$ freely generating $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Use the associated right infinite-cyclic coefficient system, with first-loop-first convention and transport around $a$ given by left multiplication by $t^{-\phi(a)}$, where $\phi(\mu)=1$. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[t,t^{-1}]$, and $\Lambda_p=\mathbb F_p[t,t^{-1}]$. All systems have their based standard parallel Hermitian structure with involution $t^*=t^{-1}$. Define $B_{\mathbb Z}$, $B_{\mathbb Q}$ and $B_p$ on the respective first local homology modules by inverse coefficient Bockstein, inverse oriented cap duality and evaluation, with targets $\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda$, $\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ and $\mathbb F_p(t)/\Lambda_p$.

These forms are defined on the whole respective first homology modules. There is a primitive annihilator $\Delta\in\mathbb Z[t]$, $\Delta(1)=1$, for $H_1(M;\Lambda)$. Put $\delta=\Delta^*$. For the actual coefficient images $x_{\mathbb Q},x_p,y_{\mathbb Q},y_p$ of any $x,y\in H_1(M;\Lambda)$,
$$B_{\mathbb Q}(x_{\mathbb Q},y_{\mathbb Q})=j\bigl(B_{\mathbb Z}(x,y)\bigr),\qquad B_p(x_p,y_p)=\rho_{p,\delta}\bigl(B_{\mathbb Z}(x,y)\bigr).$$
Here $j$ is the natural integral-to-rational quotient map, and $\rho_{p,\delta}$ is the well-defined fraction reduction on the $\delta$-annihilated subgroup, $[a/\delta]\mapsto[a_p/\delta_p]$. Its denominator is nonzero modulo every prime. Consequently, if $B_{\mathbb Z}(x,x)\ne0$, then $B_{\mathbb Q}(x_{\mathbb Q},x_{\mathbb Q})\ne0$ and $B_p(x_p,x_p)\ne0$ for all primes outside a finite explicit set. No choice principle, finite CW model, smoothness, Seifert presentation, or global rational-function reduction map is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The closed oriented manifold, marked integral homology generator and the explicit right coefficient convention.

[F1] A primitive polynomial $\Delta$ with $\Delta(1)=1$ annihilates the integral first local homology, and its coefficient image annihilates the corresponding first local homology over every commutative constant ring, with natural coefficient maps. [[thm-compact-betti-one-manifolds-have-primitive-alexander-annihilators-without-choice]]

[F2] For a primitive Laurent polynomial $\delta$, the integral-to-rational quotient map is injective on its annihilated subgroup, and the reductions $[a/\delta]\mapsto[a_p/\delta_p]$ are well-defined and preserve each nonzero class outside finitely many explicitly bounded primes. [[lem-primitive-laurent-annihilators-preserve-nonzero-values-under-rational-and-prime-reduction]]

[F3] Localization into the fraction field is exact and commutes with arbitrary chain homology. [[lem-ore-localization-is-flat-and-detects-module-torsion]]

[F4] Closed oriented cap duality holds without choice for arbitrary underlying abelian-group local systems and commuting scalar actions. The supplied Hermitian structure identifies intrinsic dual systems with conjugate right systems, naturally under the stated coefficient maps. [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]], [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]]

[F5] Compact-manifold right singular chains have a free basis prescribed from one finite atlas and finite path data, with an explicit one-vertex reduction. The low-degree coefficient Bockstein is natural and exact without an infinite-product lifting premise. [[lem-compact-manifold-twisted-singular-chains-admit-one-vertex-reduction]], [[lem-choice-free-low-degree-coefficient-bockstein-on-compact-manifolds]]

## Proof

1.1 Choose $\Delta$ from [F1] and put $\delta=\Delta^*=\Delta(t^{-1})$. Both are primitive and evaluate to one at $t=1$. In each field coefficient case their reductions are nonzero. By [F3], localization annihilates the first homology because its annihilator becomes invertible; thus $H_1(M;\mathbb Q(t))=0$ for the integral and rational systems and $H_1(M;\mathbb F_p(t))=0$ for every prime system. The unlocalized first homology is torsion in each case, since the same nonzero annihilator kills it. These are statements about the actual coefficient homology of $M$ by [F1] and arbitrary-chain localization; no finite CW structure is used. [F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For any of these coefficient inclusions $R\subset K$, the degree-two dual $K$ cohomology is zero by [F4] and $H_1(M;K)=0$. The degree-one dual $K$ cohomology is zero too: use [F5]'s one-vertex chain model with $C_0=K$. Its $d_1$ image is zero or all of $K$. In the first case $H_1=0$ makes every degree-one chain a boundary, so every dual one-cocycle is zero. In the second choose one $v$ with $d_1v=1$; split off $vK$, and use $\ker d_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$ to see that each dual one-cocycle is a coboundary. The natural exact coefficient segment in [F5] therefore makes $\beta:H^1(M;(K/R)^\vee)\to H^2(M;R^\vee)$ an isomorphism. Closed cap duality and evaluation consequently define all the displayed linking forms on the whole first homology. This step does not assert that the final evaluation map is an isomorphism. [F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Fix $x,y$ and take an integral dual two-cocycle $a$ representing the inverse-cap class of $\bar x$. Since $x\Delta=0$ by [F1] and duality is linear on the conjugate module, $\delta[a]=0$. Thus one whole integral dual one-cochain $c$ satisfies $\partial^*c=\delta a$. The $K$-cochain $b=c/\delta$ satisfies $\partial^*b=a$, so its quotient is a one-cocycle with Bockstein $[a]$. Uniqueness of the inverse in step 2.1 gives $$B_{\mathbb Z}(x,y)=[c(y)/\delta]\in\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda.$$ In particular this value lies in the $\delta$-annihilated subgroup. This construction uses one integral cochain witness from a zero cohomology class; it neither chooses quotient representatives on all simplices nor asks an infinite product of surjections to be onto. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Use the actual finite-atlas path frames of [F5] simultaneously for the coefficient systems. The integral singular chain group is free on its actual singular simplices and its reduction is the corresponding $\Lambda_p$ chain group, with the same transition monomials reduced coefficientwise. Hence every integral dual cochain has a canonical forward reduction: reduce its value on each basis simplex and extend $\Lambda_p$-linearly. This defines a function without selecting any preimages, and commutes with the cochain differential. Thus $\partial^*c_p=\delta_p a_p$; since $\delta_p\ne0$, $c_p/\delta_p$ is a field-valued primitive of $a_p$. Cap and evaluation are finite simplex formulas, so coefficient change sends $[a]$ to the inverse-cap class of $\overline{x_p}$ and gives $c_p(y_p)=(c(y))_p$. By step 2.1 the actual mod-$p$ pairing therefore equals $[c_p(y_p)/\delta_p]=\rho_{p,\delta}(B_{\mathbb Z}(x,y))$. The same argument over $\mathbb Q$ uses the honest inclusion $\Lambda\to\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ and the same fraction $c/\delta$, giving exactly the asserted rational quotient identity. In a chosen unitary frame $e$, the inverse intrinsic-dual identification sends a functional $f$ to $\overline{e\,\overline{f(e)}}$; reducing its coefficient and then taking this expression is the same as reducing that expression, because the involution and all ring operations commute with reduction. Thus the intrinsic-dual/conjugate identifications in [F4] respect these fixed frames as well, so no scalar side or unmarked gauge change occurs. [F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 If the integral self-value is nonzero, it belongs to $T_\delta$ by step 3.1. Apply [F2]. Its rational image is nonzero, and its specified prime reductions are nonzero away from the finite exceptional integer constructed there. The identities in step 4.1 identify these values with the actual rational and prime Blanchfield self-values. Every prime denominator is valid because $\delta_p(1)=1$. Compactness was used in the proved finite-presentation/annihilator and finite-atlas cochain suppliers; all remaining primitive, reduction, cap and evaluation operations were forward maps or individual cochain witnesses. Thus the full integral-to-rational and integral-to-prime nonzero conclusions hold without any added choice, smoothness, CW or global fraction-field reduction assumption. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[lem-smooth-ball-windows-and-boundary-disk-absorption]]

[[lem-capped-elementary-height-spheres-bound-smooth-balls]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice and the smooth embedded sphere $S\subset S^3$.

[F1] A generic linear height on a compact Euclidean embedded smooth manifold is Morse ([[thm-generic-height-functions-on-an-embedded-compact-manifold-are-morse]]). Its finitely many critical values can be separated by arbitrarily small local bump perturbations without changing its critical points or Hessians ([[lem-finitely-many-critical-values-can-be-separated-locally]]).

[F2] Under countable choice a regular nullhomotopic circle on an oriented surface bounds a compact disk; on a sphere both complementary closures are disk regions ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]], clause 4). In the plane use the explicit linear contraction. Smooth disk parametrizations, including collar-compatible boundary maps, are obtained by the smooth-input disk-and-band construction in steps 7.1–13.1 of [[lem-finite-c2-surface-carriers-have-smooth-normal-forms-and-relative-cap-approximations]]. In particular the two disks obtained by cutting a smooth sphere along a regular circle are smooth disks.

[F3] Each sphere obtained by capping a height piece with at most one critical point bounds a smooth standard ball ([[lem-capped-elementary-height-spheres-bound-smooth-balls]]).

[F4] A disk attachment or its reverse is absorbed without changing the smooth manifold type, and an embedded standard ball is ambient isotopic to a coordinate round ball ([[lem-smooth-ball-windows-and-boundary-disk-absorption]]).

[F5] Smooth isotopies of compact embedded submanifolds extend to ambient isotopies under countable choice ([[thm-isotopy-extension]]).

[A1] Countable choice is [[def-countable-choice]]. Its use is inherited from the local disk, smooth normal-form and isotopy-extension suppliers [F2]–[F5]; it is an assumption of this local proof, not a claim that the classical theorem requires that axiom intrinsically. The surgeries and their reversal form finite constructions.

## Proof

**Given:** The sphere and assumptions above.

1.1 Choose a point of $S^3$ outside $S$ and use its stereographic chart to regard $S$ as a compact smoothly embedded sphere in $\mathbb R^3$. By [F1] choose a direction whose restricted height is Morse, and rotate it to the $z$ direction. Separate its finitely many critical values by the finite small perturbation in [F1]. Realize that perturbation geometrically by retaining the $x,y$ coordinates and changing only $z$. A sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation and its straight interpolation are embeddings: finitely many graph charts retain a nonzero rank-two minor and local injectivity, while pairs of source points outside those chart neighborhoods have a positive image-separation minimum by compactness. Choose the perturbation below both bounds. By [F5] this is an ambient isotopy of $S^3$, supported away from the stereographic point. It therefore suffices to prove that the resulting sphere, with excellent Morse height, bounds a smooth standard ball in $\mathbb R^3$. [F1, F5, A1, construct]

1.2 Choose finitely many regular heights between consecutive critical values. A level meets the sphere in finitely many smooth disjoint circles: its preimage is a compact regular one-manifold, and finitely many connected local interval charts cover it. Each circle bounds a planar smooth disk by [F2]. Choose an innermost circle, so that this disk's interior misses every other level circle and hence misses the sphere. In a sufficiently thin regular band around the level remove the sphere's annular collar of that circle and replace it by the two horizontal disks at the band's ends. The level curves vary smoothly, so their disks at nearby heights remain disjoint from the rest of the surface after a sufficiently small band shrink. Round the two seams in that band. This is surgery on the sphere along a disk whose interior misses the surface. [F2, construct]

2.1 Every such surgery replaces one smooth sphere by two smooth spheres. Indeed its circle splits that sphere into two disk regions by [F2], and each region, with the added cap, is a smooth sphere: the boundary gluing is a smooth circle map and extends over a disk by the angular interpolation used in [F2]'s normal-form construction. Now repeat step 1.2 on each remaining circle of that regular level, always innermost among the remaining circles and with a new sufficiently small collar width. Earlier horizontal caps are kept at distinct nearby levels, and the new width is chosen smaller than their positive distances from the chosen level. There are finitely many circles. Then repeat at the finitely many other chosen regular levels, with disjoint level neighborhoods. The outcome is a finite disjoint collection of smooth spheres, each made from a connected piece of the original sphere between successive cutting levels, together with horizontal caps. Each such piece contains at most one height critical point. [F2, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 By [F3] each final sphere bounds a smooth embedded standard ball. We shall reverse the surgeries and prove inductively that each sphere then present bounds a smooth embedded standard ball. No assertion that all their chosen balls are disjoint is needed: balls bounded by disjoint spheres may be nested. [F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Consider the reverse of the last unreversed surgery, whose two output spheres bound balls $A$ and $B$ by the inductive assertion. In its product disk neighborhood the two added cap disks can be moved toward each other until both occupy the original surgery disk $D$; equivalently shrink the normal coordinate of the deleted annular collar to zero. Their remaining boundaries are disjoint. The move is an isotopy up to its endpoint on each individual ball, because the cap has a product collar and its boundary annulus is shortened monotonically; at the endpoint it merely meets the other ball's boundary in $D$. An arbitrarily small corner rounding reverses this motion and recovers the pre-surgery sphere. The balls now have either disjoint interiors and intersection exactly $D$, or one is contained in the other, with their boundaries meeting exactly in $D$. To check that these alternatives exhaust the possibilities, first take their disjoint cap positions. The complement of a known embedded ball in $\mathbb R^3$ is connected: [F4] carries that ball to a round one by a compactly supported ambient isotopy. Hence each connected sphere disjoint from the other's boundary lies wholly inside or wholly outside its ball. If neither ball contains the other's boundary, their interiors are disjoint; otherwise one ball is inside the other. The product cap motion preserves the corresponding alternative and makes their boundary contact exactly $D$. [F4, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 In the disjoint-interior case the pre-surgery sphere is the rounded boundary of $A\cup_D B$. This union is a ball by disk absorption [F4]. In the nested case, relabel so that $B\subset A$; the pre-surgery sphere is the rounded boundary of $A\setminus\operatorname{Int}B$, where $B$ meets $\partial A$ in the disk $D$. Disk removal [F4] says that this too is a ball. These boundary identifications can be checked in $D\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$: the pre-surgery annular wall is the side $\partial D\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$, whereas surgery inserts the faces $D\times\{-\varepsilon,\varepsilon\}$; all surfaces agree outside that neighborhood. Thus the induction gives a smooth standard ball bounded by the original excellent-height sphere. Undoing the initial small ambient isotopy gives a smooth embedded standard ball bounded by the given $S$. [F4, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Apply [F4] to that parametrized embedded ball, using the stereographic chart, to carry it by an ambient isotopy to a small Euclidean round ball. Translation and positive dilation in $\mathbb R^3$ extend smoothly across its compactifying point: they are the usual stereographic conformal transformations of $S^3$, and their parameter paths give smooth ambient isotopies. They carry the round boundary sphere to the unit sphere, the standard equator in this stereographic convention. Concatenate with the preceding isotopies, using smooth stationary reparametrizations. This gives the claimed $H_t$, starting at the identity. The two components and both ball diffeomorphisms are now the inverse images of the two standard open hemispheres and their closures under $H_1$. The two restrictions agree on $S$ because they restrict one ambient diffeomorphism, and pulling back the standard equator's two-sided collar gives a common collar with the same property. [F4, F5, A1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The boundary map is the one furnished simultaneously by the ambient isotopy. The proof does not assert extension of an arbitrary preassigned diffeomorphism of $S^2$. For decomposing-sphere applications one may transport the two marked intersection points and the chosen boundary cap arc by this common map and choose all ball coordinates and collars together.

## Statement refuted

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

The false claim is that if two integral framed-link surgery diagrams in $S^3$ have orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic surgery results, then the framed links are ambient isotopic.

## Statement references

[[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram|Integral surgery diagrams]]

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|Ambient isotopy of oriented links]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the empty surgery diagram $D_0$, and the diagram $D_1$ consisting of a single $+1$-framed standard unknot.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ says that every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. Full AC [A1] implies this by applying its choice function to the range of the sequence and composing with the index map.

[F1] [[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram]]: the empty diagram has surgery result $S^3$, and the integer $n$ filling uses meridian slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$.

[F2] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: $\mu$ is the positive meridian and $\lambda$ is the degree-one preferred longitude that maps to zero in the knot exterior.

[F3] [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]]: under full AC the preferred longitude is the unique degree-one class in the kernel of the exterior inclusion.

[F4] [[def-kirby-moves-on-integral-framed-links]]: adding a split $+1$-framed unknot is a Kirby stabilization.

[F5] [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]: ambient isotopy identifies links by a diffeomorphism of their component domains, so it preserves the number of components.

## Counterexample

1.1 By [F1], surgery on $D_0$ leaves the standard oriented $S^3$ unchanged. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Give $S^3$ its unit-sphere model in $\mathbb C^2$ and let $U(t)=(e^{2\pi i t},0)$. With $N(U)=\{|z_2|\le1/\sqrt2\}$, the exterior is $D^2\times S^1$ with disk coordinate $z_1$ and core coordinate $w=z_2/|z_2|$. The preferred longitude $\lambda_U$ is the disk-meridian class and $\mu_U$ is the core-longitude class by [F2]–[F3]. The diffeomorphism $g(z,w)=(w^{-1}z,w)$ preserves orientation and sends $[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$ to $[\mu_U]$. Let $f_0$ be the original $S^3$ gluing, which sends the meridian of the removed unknot neighbourhood to $[\mu_U]$, and choose the $+1$-filling map $f_1=g^{-1}\circ f_0$. It sends the attached meridian to $[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$, the required slope by [F1]. The map equal to $g$ on the exterior and the identity on the attached solid torus is well-defined because $g\circ f_1=f_0$; it is a smooth orientation-preserving diffeomorphism to the original $S^3$. Thus $D_1$ also presents $S^3$. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 The diagrams are not ambient isotopic: $D_0$ has zero components and $D_1$ has one, while [F5] implies ambient isotopy preserves component count. Yet they have the same oriented surgery result by steps 1.1–1.2. Moreover [F4] identifies their difference as a permitted stabilization. Hence the false claim fails. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The left panel is the empty diagram and the right panel is a split unknot labelled $+1$. The labels are integer framings; the circles are schematic projections of the standard unknot and contain no crossing information.

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node at (0,0) {$\varnothing$};
  \draw[->,thick] (0.7,0) -- (2.0,0);
  \node at (1.35,0.35) {stabilize};
  \draw[thick] (2.7,0) circle (0.48);
  \node at (3.55,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

## Definition

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.
