## Example

Let the target posterior $\pi$ be uniform on $E=\{-1,+1\}$ and define
$$K_\varepsilon(x,\{x\})=1-\varepsilon,\qquad K_\varepsilon(x,\{-x\})=\varepsilon,$$
with $\varepsilon=1/100$. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be the time-homogeneous Markov
chain with kernel $K_\varepsilon$ relative to its natural filtration, started
with $X_0\sim\pi$, and take $f(x)=x$. Define its lag-$k$ autocorrelation by
$$\rho_f(k):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))}{\operatorname{Var}(f(X_0))}.$$
For every $k\ge1$, $\rho_f(k)=(49/50)^k$. Its integrated autocorrelation
time $\tau_f:=1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\rho_f(k)$ is therefore $99$, so the
theoretical functional-specific effective sample size of $N=10{,}000$ draws is
$$\operatorname{ESS}_f(10{,}000)=\frac{10{,}000}{99}\approx101.01.$$
The invariant law is exactly the target posterior, while this functional has
only about one percent of the nominal independent-sample size. This is the
theoretical ESS from the stationary autocorrelation sequence, not an empirical
finite-run ESS estimate, and it asserts no central limit theorem.

## Example references

[[def-functional-specific-effective-sample-size|The theoretical ESS uses a stationary functional with positive finite variance, absolutely summable autocorrelations, and positive integrated autocorrelation time.]]

[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary|An invariant initial law makes the Markov chain strictly stationary under AC.]]

[[prop-ip-bounded-posterior-functional-error|The stationary sample-average variance bound requires its own covariance-summability assumption.]]

[Vehtari et al., §3.2, functional-specific ESS](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.08008v5)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-state probability kernel, its initial law $\pi$, and the bounded functional $f$ in the Example.

[F1] A probability kernel has probability-measure rows and measurable event evaluations. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]

[F2] Invariance means $\pi K(A)=\pi(A)$ for every measurable event $A$. [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]

[F3] A time-homogeneous Markov chain has one-step conditional law given by its transition kernel. [[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the library Markov-chain and invariant-initial-law interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] If the initial law is invariant, the chain is strictly stationary. [[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]]

[F5] The theoretical functional ESS is $N/(1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_f(k))$ when the process is strictly stationary, has positive finite variance, absolutely summable autocorrelations, and positive integrated autocorrelation time; this definition asserts no CLT. [[def-functional-specific-effective-sample-size]]

[F6] For a stationary chain with absolutely summable lag covariances, the finite-sample mean-square error is bounded by $N^{-1}(\gamma_0+2\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|)$. [[prop-ip-bounded-posterior-functional-error]]

[F7] Variance is the expected squared centered value, and covariance is the expected product of centered values. [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]

## Verification

1.1 For either singleton $\{x\}$, $\pi K_\varepsilon(\{x\})=\tfrac12(1-\varepsilon)+\tfrac12\varepsilon=\tfrac12=\pi(\{x\})$; additivity gives $\pi K_\varepsilon=\pi$ by [F2]. The rows are probability measures by [F1]. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Since $X_0\sim\pi$ and $\pi$ is invariant by step 1.1, [A1] permits the invariant-initial-law result [F4], which makes the chain strictly stationary. Its one-time law is symmetric, so $\mathbb E X_j=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_j)=1$. [A1, F2, F4, F7, step 1.1, given]

2.1 Put $\lambda=1-2\varepsilon=49/50$. By [F3], $\mathbb E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=\lambda X_n$. Hence $\mathbb E[X_0X_{k+1}]=\lambda\mathbb E[X_0X_k]$ and $\mathbb E[X_0X_0]=1$, so induction gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_k)=\lambda^k$ and $\rho_f(k)=\lambda^k$. [F3, F5, F7, given, algebra]

2.2 The autocorrelations are absolutely summable because $0<\lambda<1$, with $\sum_{k\ge1}\lambda^k=\lambda/(1-\lambda)=49$. Thus $\tau_f=1+2\cdot49=99>0$, and [F5] gives $\operatorname{ESS}_f(10{,}000)=10{,}000/99$. The covariance bound [F6] applies, but neither it nor the ESS definition supplies a CLT. [F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal A$ be a planar annulus
and identify the solid torus with $\mathcal A\times[-1,1]$. Let
$R=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$, $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, and let $z$ be a formal
polynomial variable. For a regular annular diagram $D$, a state $S$ smooths
every crossing. Let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ count its A- and B-smoothings, let
$u(S)$ count the resulting circles that bound disks in $\mathcal A$, and let
$e(S)$ count the resulting circles that do not bound disks in $\mathcal A$;
call a circle that does not bound a disk essential.
If $m$ is the total full-twist correction from the blackboard framing to the
specified framing, counting an A-type twist positively and its inverse
negatively as in the framed diagram calculus, set
$$
\Psi(D,m)=(-A^3)^m\sum_S A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{u(S)}z^{e(S)}.
$$
This value is independent of the regular annular diagram and twist correction
of the framed link and induces an $R$-linear map
$$
\Psi:\mathcal K_A(\mathcal A\times[-1,1])\longrightarrow R[z].
$$
For the empty link, the empty diagram has its unique empty state and the
formula gives $\Psi(\varnothing)=1$.

The diagram below shows one essential core curve and one contractible circle
in an annular state; every smoothed component is classified by these two
types.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.75,line cap=round]
  \draw[thick] (0,0) circle (1.6);
  \draw[thick] (0,0) circle (0.65);
  \draw[very thick] (0,0) circle (1.05);
  \draw[very thick] (1.30,0) circle (0.16);
  \node at (0,1.05) [above] {$z$};
  \node at (1.45,0.25) [right] {$\bigcirc$};
  \node at (0,-1.95) {essential core and contractible circle};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references
[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice|Choice implies countable choice]]


[[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold|Kauffman bracket skein module]]

[[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value|Kauffman bracket smoothing and loop value]]

[[lem-framed-link-diagram-calculus|Framed annular diagram calculus]]

[[lem-two-disjoint-circles-in-s-two-cobound-an-annulus|Two disjoint smooth circles cobound an annulus]]

[Józef H. Przytycki, *Fundamentals of Kauffman Bracket Skein Modules* (1998), §3, Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9809113)

[Thang T. Q. Le, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds* (2016), §6.2, Proposition 6.2 and Example 6.5](https://letu.math.gatech.edu/Papers/Lectures_Luminy_2014_new.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, a framed link in the solid torus $\mathcal A\times[-1,1]$, and a regular annular diagram with its full-twist correction.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}$ ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A2] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, means every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[A3] In ZF, $\mathrm{AC}$ implies $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F1] At a crossing, the Kauffman bracket state sum uses the A-smoothing with weight $A$, the B-smoothing with weight $A^{-1}$, and the loop value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The module is generated by framed-link classes modulo the crossing and trivial-circle relations ([[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold]]).

[F3] Every framed link in the solid-torus product admits a regular annular diagram with signed full-twist correction marks, and framed isotopies of links are represented by annular planar isotopies and finitely many R1, R2, and R3 moves; R1 changes the blackboard twist correction by the opposite unit ([[lem-framed-link-diagram-calculus]]).

[F4] In the fixed source-chart convention, the crossing operators cancel under R2 and satisfy the three-strand braid relation under R3; these are equalities of local Temperley–Lieb tangles ([[lem-kauffman-bracket-r2-r3-identities]]).

[F5] For two disjoint smoothly embedded circles in $S^2$, the complement consists of two open disks and a unique open annulus bounded by the circles ([[lem-two-disjoint-circles-in-s-two-cobound-an-annulus]]).

## Proof


1.1 Let $B_i$ and $B_o$ be the inner and outer boundary circles of the planar annulus. For any embedded state circle $C$, apply [F5] to $C$ and $B_i$. Their complement has a disk component on the $B_i$ side, a disk component on the $C$ side, and an annulus component. Since $B_o$ lies outside the disk bounded by $B_i$, it lies either in the annulus component or in the disk component on the $C$ side. In the first case the disk component on the $C$ side lies inside the disk bounded by $B_o$ and outside the disk bounded by $B_i$, so $C$ bounds a disk in $\mathcal A$. In the second case $C$ separates $B_i$ from $B_o$, and the annulus component between $C$ and $B_i$ lies inside the disk bounded by $B_o$ and outside the disk bounded by $B_i$. The two disk sides of $C$ then contain $B_i$ and $B_o$, respectively, so neither is contained in $\mathcal A$; hence $C$ is essential exactly in this second case. Thus an essential $C$ has $B_i$ and $B_o$ on opposite disk sides. For two disjoint essential state circles, apply [F5] to the pair. Each disk side containing $B_i$ contains the disk bounded by $B_i$, while $B_o$ lies on the opposite side of both; therefore the curves are nested and the complementary annulus between them lies outside the disk bounded by $B_i$ and inside the disk bounded by $B_o$, hence in $\mathcal A$. Ordering the finitely many essential circles by disk inclusion shows every consecutive pair bounds such an annular band, so they are parallel. Thus $u(S)$ and $e(S)$ are unambiguous finite counts, and each state contributes a Laurent-polynomial multiple of $z^{e(S)}$. [A1, F1, F5, given, cases, construct]

2.1 The state set is finite. At a chosen crossing, partition it into states using the A-smoothing and states using the B-smoothing. In a framed skein triple the exterior annular strips agree; place the same twist marks on those common arcs and none on the blackboard-framed local crossing or smoothings. Their total correction $m$ is common to all three, so the partition gives $\Psi(D_\times,m)=A\Psi(D_A,m)+A^{-1}\Psi(D_B,m)$. Adding a zero-framed trivial circle increases $u(S)$ by one in every state, so it multiplies $\Psi$ by $\delta$. Hence the state expansion annihilates both relation generators in [F2]. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Annular planar isotopy preserves which state circles bound disks. Under R2 and R3, the local tangle identities in [F4] remain equal after attaching the same exterior annular tangle; evaluating each resulting contractible loop by $\delta$ and each essential circle by $z$ is an $R$-linear operation, so the state expansions agree. For an A-type R1 kink the local state factor is $A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^3$; for the opposite B-type kink it is $A+A^{-1}\delta=-A^{-3}$. By [F3] the correction decreases by one for the A-type kink and increases by one for the B-type kink, so the factor $(-A^3)^m$ cancels the raw state-sum change. The value is therefore independent of diagram and framing correction. [A2, A3, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F3], every framed-link generator has a regular annular diagram and framing correction. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 show that the state expansion is independent of that choice and vanishes on both generators of the defining submodule [F2]. Its $R$-linear extension therefore factors through the quotient and gives the stated map $\Psi$. [A3, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth oriented $3$-manifolds, and let
$f:M\to N$ be an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism. Then
$[L]\mapsto[f(L)]$ induces an $R$-module isomorphism
$f_*:\mathcal K_A(M)\to\mathcal K_A(N)$. These maps respect identity
diffeomorphisms and composition.

Let $\Sigma$ be a compact oriented surface with a specified product collar
$\iota:\Sigma\times[0,1]\hookrightarrow M$ whose lower face lies in
$\partial M$. Give $\Sigma\times[0,1]$ the orientation pulled back from $M$
by $\iota$; the skein module and stacking product below use this orientation.
The stacking product on
$\mathcal K_A(\Sigma\times[0,1])$ and collar gluing define a unital left
action on $\mathcal K_A(M)$: a closed framed link in the surface product is
placed in a sufficiently thin outer subcollar and united with a framed link
in the interior of $M$. The action is independent of the thin-collar width,
associative, and natural under orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that
respect the specified collars. Only closed framed links are glued; no relative
boundary endpoints are part of this action.

## Statement references

[[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold|Kauffman bracket skein module]]

[Józef H. Przytycki, *Fundamentals of Kauffman Bracket Skein Modules* (1998), §2, Proposition 2.2(i)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9809113)

[Sean Pohorence, *3-manifold Invariants and TQFTs* (2016), §1.2 and §3.1](https://categorified.net/RTinvariants/Jan29-Feb3.pdf)

[Thang T. Q. Le, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds* (2016), §6.1](https://letu.math.gatech.edu/Papers/Lectures_Luminy_2014_new.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Smooth oriented $3$-manifolds $M,N$, an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:M\to N$, an oriented surface collar in $\partial M$, and the Kauffman bracket skein quotients defined above.

[F1] The free module is generated by framed unoriented link isotopy classes; its relation submodule is generated by the local crossing relation and the zero-framed trivial-circle relation with $R=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$ and $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold]], [[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The collar product is oriented by pullback under $\iota$, so its embedding carries each defining crossing and trivial-circle relation to the identical relation in $M$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold]]).

## Proof


1.1 Define $\widetilde f:\mathcal F_R(M)\to\mathcal F_R(N)$ on basis elements by $\widetilde f([L])=[f(L)]$ and extend $R$-linearly. A diffeomorphism sends ambient-isotopic framed annuli to ambient-isotopic framed annuli and sends the framing annuli by its derivative, so this is well-defined on the free modules. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 Fix framed-link representatives $P$ in $\Sigma\times(0,1)$ and $L$ in the interior of $M$. To check independence of isotopy representatives, take any isotopy track of either framed link. Its framing annuli have compact trace in the interior. Place the trace of the product-factor link in a sufficiently thin outer collar layer disjoint from the trace of the $M$-factor link. The disjoint-union family is a smooth isotopy of framed annuli in $M$. In finitely many submanifold charts of its compact trace, extend the annulus velocity to ambient charts with cutoffs and combine these extensions with a partition of unity; the resulting compactly supported time-dependent vector field has a flow that realizes this isotopy by ambient diffeomorphisms. Thus the union class is independent of both representatives. For the quotient relations, rescale $P$ into a boundary layer disjoint from $L$. A change of $P$ by either defining relation becomes the identical local relation after the collar embedding by [F2]; a change of $L$ by either relation remains the identical relation with the disjoint collar link outside its ball. The same local check in two successive collar layers shows that stacking descends to the skein quotients. Hence collar gluing gives a bilinear action. Decreasing the collar width uses an orientation-preserving product rescaling isotopy supported in a thin boundary layer and disjoint from $L$, so the resulting skein class is unchanged. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 The image of an oriented crossing ball is an oriented ball. Its transported chart preserves the over/under crossing and both endpoint pairings, so $\widetilde f([L_\times]-A[L_A]-A^{-1}[L_B])$ is the corresponding defining relation in $N$. A zero-framed trivial circle bounding a disk in the ball maps to another zero-framed trivial circle bounding the image disk. Thus $\widetilde f(\mathcal R_A(M))\subseteq\mathcal R_A(N)$ and $\widetilde f$ descends to $f_*$. Applying the same construction to $f^{-1}$ gives the inverse; applying it to a composite gives the composite map on every link generator. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Place two algebra links in successive subcollars and the $M$-link deeper inside. Both $(P*Q)\cdot L$ and $P\cdot(Q\cdot L)$ are represented by the same ordered union, up to an orientation-preserving product rescaling, and the empty link acts as the identity. Thus the action is associative and unital. If an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism carries one specified collar productwise to another, it sends each stacked or glued link union to the corresponding union, so its module maps intertwine the actions. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $I$ be any set, let $x\in H_1$, and let $(x_i)_{i\in I}\subset H_1$ and $(y_i)_{i\in I}\subset H_2$. Let $\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\omega(0)=0$. If
$$\|y_i-y_j\|\le\omega(\|x_i-x_j\|)\qquad(i,j\in I),$$
then
$$\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline B\bigl(y_i,\omega(\|x_i-x\|)\bigr)\ne\varnothing.$$
The intersection over an empty index set means all of $H_2$.

## Statement references

[[thm-projection-onto-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set|Existence of Hilbert projections under Countable Choice.]]

[[thm-hilbert-projection-variational-characterization|The projection variational inequality.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the Hilbert spaces, points, index set and modulus in the Statement.

[F1] Every nonempty closed convex Hilbert set has a unique nearest point under Countable Choice, and if $p$ is nearest to zero, then $\langle p,z-p\rangle\ge0$ for every point $z$ of the set. ([[thm-projection-onto-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]], [[thm-hilbert-projection-variational-characterization]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice implies Countable Choice and supplies the countable near-supremum selections used below. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the Statement.

1.1 For a nonnegative function $\delta$ with $\delta(0)=0$, consider the finite weighted inequality $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j[\delta(\|v_i\|)^2+\delta(\|v_j\|)^2-\delta(\|v_i-v_j\|)^2]\ge0$ for Hilbert vectors $v_i$ and nonnegative scalars $a_i$. The function $\delta(t)=t$ satisfies it, since the sum is $2\|\sum_i a_iv_i\|^2$. Each truncated function $\delta_A(t)=\min\{t,A\}$, $A>0$, also satisfies it. Indeed, for the subsum with BOTH $\|v_i\|,\|v_j\|<A$, replacing the negative truncated-distance square by the negative full-distance square can only decrease the sum, and this subsum is then $2\|\sum_{\|v_i\|<A}a_iv_i\|^2\ge0$. Every remaining summand is separately nonnegative, because at least one of its two positive squares is $A^2$ while its negative square is at most $A^2$. The property is closed under pointwise limits, and under taking $\delta=(\sum_{k=1}^N c_k\delta_k^2)^{1/2}$ with $c_k\ge0$, since the weighted expression is linear in $\delta^2$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The function $\eta(t)=\omega(\sqrt t)^2$ is nondecreasing, continuous, zero at zero and concave. Here is a proof that covers nonsmooth moduli. Interpolate $\omega$ on grids $0,1/n,2/n,\ldots,n$ and extend constantly after $n$; these concave nondecreasing polygonal functions converge pointwise to $\omega$. On each affine piece $\omega_n(r)=a+br$, its slope $b$ is nonnegative and its intercept $a$ is nonnegative because concavity and $\omega_n(0)=0$ imply $\omega_n(r)\ge r\omega_n'(r)$. Thus $\omega_n(\sqrt t)^2=a^2+2ab\sqrt t+b^2t$ is concave on that piece. At a junction its one-sided derivatives are $\omega_n(r)b/r$, so the slope drops when $b$ drops. Continuity at zero then proves global concavity for $\eta_n$, and passing to the pointwise limit proves it for $\eta$. Interpolate $\eta$ on the same type of grids and flatten the final slope to zero. Every such polygonal $\eta_n$ is a finite sum $\sum_k c_k\min\{t,t_k\}$ with $c_k\ge0$: take $c_k$ to be the decrease of slope at the breakpoint $t_k$. Hence $\sqrt{\eta_n(t^2)}=(\sum_k c_k\min\{t,\sqrt{t_k}\}^2)^{1/2}$ has step 1.1's property. Passing to the limit gives that property for $\omega(t)=\sqrt{\eta(t^2)}$. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 First suppose the index set is finite and nonempty. If $\omega$ is identically zero, the pairwise hypothesis makes all the $y_i$ equal and their common value works. Otherwise $\omega(t)>0$ for every $t>0$: if $\omega(t_*)=0$ with $t_*>0$, monotonicity makes it zero on $[0,t_*]$, and concavity bounds every subsequent slope by zero, forcing it to be identically zero. If some $x_i=x$, then $y=y_i$ works directly by the pairwise hypothesis. In the remaining case all $r_i=\|x_i-x\|$ and $b_i=\omega(r_i)$ are positive. In the finite-dimensional affine span of the $y_i$, minimize $h(y)=\max_i\|y-y_i\|^2/b_i^2$. A minimum exists because this continuous function tends to infinity with $\|y\|$ in that span; its perpendicular projection from $H_2$ never increases any distance. Let $y$ be a minimizer and let $J$ be its active set. The origin belongs to the convex hull of $(y-y_i)/b_i^2$, $i\in J$: otherwise that finite convex hull has a nonzero nearest point $z$, whose variational inequality gives $\langle z,(y-y_i)/b_i^2\rangle\ge\|z\|^2>0$ for every active $i$. Moving a sufficiently small distance in direction $-z$ strictly decreases all active functions and keeps the finitely many inactive ones below the old maximum, a contradiction. [A1, F1, step 2.1, given, choose, algebra]

4.1 Choose nonnegative coefficients $\beta_i$, summing to one over $J$, with $\sum_{i\in J}\beta_i(y-y_i)/b_i^2=0$, and normalize $a_i=(\beta_i/b_i^2)/(\sum_{j\in J}\beta_j/b_j^2)$. Then $\sum a_i=1$ and $y=\sum a_iy_i$. Write $h(y)=\lambda^2$; every active index has $\|y-y_i\|^2=\lambda^2b_i^2$. The Hilbert variance identity gives $\sum_{i,j\in J}a_ia_j\|y_i-y_j\|^2=2\sum_{i\in J}a_i\|y_i-y\|^2=2\lambda^2\sum_i a_ib_i^2$. Apply the pairwise hypothesis and step 2.1's weighted inequality to $v_i=x_i-x$. They bound that same sum above by $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j\omega(\|v_i-v_j\|)^2\le2\sum_i a_i\omega(\|v_i\|)^2=2\sum_i a_ib_i^2$. The latter scalar is positive, so $\lambda\le1$. The minimizer therefore belongs to EVERY target ball, proving finite intersection. [step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 Now let $I$ be arbitrary and nonempty, and fix $i_0\in I$. For every finite $J\subset I$ containing $i_0$, the set $C_J=\bigcap_{i\in J}\overline B(y_i,b_i)$ is nonempty by step 4.1, closed and convex. Let $p_J$ be its nearest point to zero by [F1]. Since $C_J$ lies in the fixed ball with center $y_{i_0}$ and radius $b_{i_0}$, the numbers $\|p_J\|^2$ have a finite supremum $D$. By [A1], choose finite $J_n$ with $\|p_{J_n}\|^2>D-1/n$ and replace them by their cumulative unions, preserving this inequality. They are increasing. For $m\ge n$, [F1] gives $\|p_{J_m}-p_{J_n}\|^2\le\|p_{J_m}\|^2-\|p_{J_n}\|^2\le D-\|p_{J_n}\|^2$, so they form a Cauchy sequence and converge to a point $p\in H_2$. [A1, F1, step 4.1, given, choose, algebra]

6.1 For any fixed $i\in I$, let $q_n=p_{J_n\cup\{i\}}$. Again [F1] gives $\|q_n-p_{J_n}\|^2\le\|q_n\|^2-\|p_{J_n}\|^2\le D-\|p_{J_n}\|^2\to0$. Hence $q_n\to p$; since every $q_n$ lies in the closed ball $\overline B(y_i,b_i)$, so does $p$. This works for each $i$ without enumerating $I$, and proves the required full intersection. If $I$ is empty, zero belongs to its intersection by convention. This proves all cases. [F1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded connected smooth domain, let $U\Subset\Omega$ be open, and fix $0<m\le M<\infty$. There are $p\in(2,4)$ and $C<\infty$, depending only on $d,m,M,\Omega,U$, such that every real measurable $\gamma$ with $m\le\gamma\le M$ and every weak solution $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ of $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u)=0$ satisfy
$$\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(U)}\le C\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
In particular, for a weak Neumann solution with quotient flux $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$, the right side is at most $C\|F\|_{\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}}$, uniformly in $\gamma$.

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-mean-zero-neumann-problem-wellposedness|The weak Neumann solution and quotient flux norm.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the domain, compactly contained set and uniform ellipticity bounds in the Statement.

[F1] The Riesz transforms have multipliers $-i\xi_j/|\xi|$, are bounded on every $L^r$, $1<r<\infty$, and their compositions agree on intersections of those spaces. ([[lem-hilbert-and-riesz-transforms-are-calderon-zygmund-operators]], [[thm-calderon-zygmund-singular-integrals-are-bounded-on-lp]])

[F2] Riesz–Thorin interpolation bounds the intermediate complex scalar $L^r$ operator norm by the geometric mean of its two endpoint bounds; Plancherel computes $L^2$ Fourier multiplier norms. ([[thm-riesz-thorin-interpolation]], [[thm-plancherel]])

[F3] On the fixed smooth domain, $H^1$ embeds into $L^{2d/(d-2)}$ if $d>2$, and into every finite $L^r$ if $d=2$. Subtracting the volume mean bounds the $H^1$ norm by the gradient norm. ([[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]], [[thm-critical-sobolev-embedding-into-every-finite-lq]], [[thm-poincare-wirtinger-on-bounded-connected-extension-domains]])

[F4] The uniformly elliptic weak Neumann solution satisfies $\|\nabla u\|_2\le C\|F\|_{\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}}$. ([[lem-ip-mean-zero-neumann-problem-wellposedness]])

[F5] Young’s convolution inequality holds on Lebesgue spaces under Countable Choice. ([[thm-young-convolution-inequality]])

[F6] The normalized locally integrable kernel $\Phi_-$ is $-|S^{d-1}|^{-1}\log|x|$ for $d=2$ and $|x|^{2-d}/((d-2)|S^{d-1}|)$ for $d\ge3$, and satisfies $-\Delta\Phi_-=\delta_0$ distributionally. ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], [[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]])

[A1] The two choice assumptions are inherited at the stated harmonic-analysis, Sobolev and weak-solution interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the Statement and a weak solution $u$.

1.1 On vector fields on $\mathbb R^d$ put $P=-\bigl(R_iR_j\bigr)_{i,j}$, with multiplier $\xi\xi^T/|\xi|^2$ away from zero. This is the orthogonal gradient projection, so $\|P\|_{L^2(\ell^2)\to L^2(\ell^2)}=1$ by [F2]. The finitely many compositions in [F1] give a finite $L^4(\ell^4)$ bound $C_4\ge1$. Apply scalar [F2] on the product of Lebesgue measure and counting measure on $\{1,\ldots,d\}$ to this matrix operator, whose $L^2$ norm there is exactly one. If $1/p=(1-\theta)/2+\theta/4$, then $\|P\|_{L^p(\ell^p)\to L^p(\ell^p)}\le C_4^\theta$. Since $\|z\|_{\ell^p}\le\|z\|_{\ell^2}\le d^{1/2-1/p}\|z\|_{\ell^p}$ for $p>2$, its Euclidean-vector $L^p$ norm is at most $D_p=d^{1/2-1/p}C_4^\theta$, which tends to one as $p\downarrow2$. These extensions agree with the $L^2$ projection on common inputs by density. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Put $a=(m+M)/2$ and $k=(M-m)/(M+m)<1$. Extend $\gamma$ outside $\Omega$ by $a$ and set $c=(a-\gamma)/a$, so $\|c\|_\infty\le k$. Choose $p\in(2,4)$ sufficiently close to two that $kD_p<1$ and, when $d>2$, $p<2d/(d-2)$. The operators $Pc$ then have norms less than one both on $L^2(\ell^2)$ and on $L^p(\ell^2)$. For every vector field $F$ in their intersection, the series $\sum_{j\ge0}(Pc)^j a^{-1}PF$ converges in BOTH spaces. The two limits agree as distributions, since convergence in either space implies convergence against compactly supported smooth tests. In particular, any $v\in H^1(\mathbb R^d)$ solving $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v)=\operatorname{div}F$ satisfies $\nabla v=a^{-1}PF+Pc\nabla v$ in $L^2$: subtracting the two sides gives a gradient field of zero divergence, whose Fourier transform vanishes away from zero and hence vanishes in $L^2$. Thus $\|\nabla v\|_p\le a^{-1}D_p(1-kD_p)^{-1}\|F\|_p$. [step 1.1, given, choose, algebra]

3.1 Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one on a neighborhood of $\overline U$, set $u_0=u-u_\Omega$ and extend $v=\chi u_0$ by zero. The product rule and the weak equation give $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v)=\operatorname{div}(\gamma u_0\nabla\chi)+g$, where $g=\gamma\nabla u\cdot\nabla\chi$ is compactly supported, $\|g\|_2\le C\|\nabla u\|_2$, and $\int g=0$ by testing the original weak equation with $\chi$. Put $\Phi=-\Phi_-$ using [F6], so $\Delta\Phi=\delta_0$, and set $W=\nabla\Phi*g$. The radial formula in [F6] gives $\partial_i\Phi=x_i/(|S^{d-1}||x|^d)$ and $\partial_{ij}\Phi=\delta_{ij}/(|S^{d-1}||x|^d)-d x_ix_j/(|S^{d-1}||x|^{d+2})$ away from zero, hence $|\nabla\Phi(x)|\le C|x|^{1-d}$ and $|D^2\Phi(x)|\le C|x|^{-d}$. This convolution defines a locally integrable distribution with $\operatorname{div}W=g$: integrate the fundamental-solution identity against compactly supported tests and use local integrability of $|x|^{1-d}$. Its low-frequency behavior is controlled by the zero integral of $g$, as quantified next. [F6, step 2.1, given, construct]

4.1 Enclose $\operatorname{supp}g$ in a fixed ball of radius $L$. On $|x|\le2L+1$, $W$ only uses the restriction of $\nabla\Phi$ to a fixed larger ball; that kernel is in $L^r$ for $1\le r<d/(d-1)$. The convolution inequality with $1+1/p=1/2+1/r$ gives $\|W\|_{L^p(|x|\le2L+1)}\le C\|g\|_2$, because the chosen $p<2d/(d-2)$ makes this $r$ admissible (there is no finite upper restriction for $d=2$). The same argument with $r=1$ gives the local $L^2$ bound. Outside that ball, subtract $\nabla\Phi(x)\int g=0$ in the integral and use $|D^2\Phi(x-y)|\le C|x|^{-d}$ to obtain $|W(x)|\le C|x|^{-d}\|g\|_1$. This is integrable to both the second and the $p$th power at infinity. Thus $\|W\|_2+\|W\|_p\le C\|\nabla u\|_2$. The convolution estimates are [F5]. [F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Set $F=\gamma u_0\nabla\chi+W$. By [F3], the first term belongs to $L^2\cap L^p$ with norm at most $C\|\nabla u\|_2$; step 4.1 gives the same bound for the second. Step 3.1 now reads $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v)=\operatorname{div}F$. Apply step 2.1 and use $\nabla v=\nabla u$ on $U$ to obtain $\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(U)}\le C\|\nabla u\|_2$, with all constants depending only on the fixed data. For Neumann solutions [F4] gives the final estimate. Every construction used a fixed finite cutoff and bounded operators, so the two choice assumptions enter only through [A1]. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2"
    - title: "Justin Roberts, Knots Knotes, §§4.1 and 4.3, printed pp. 21–22 and 24–25"
      url: "https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf"
    - title: "François Funar, A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds, Chapter 3, §1.1"
      url: "https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf"
---

## Statement

Let $A$ be an indeterminate and let $D$ be a nonempty regular oriented link
diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient its
projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive
in the ambient $3$-space. At each crossing define
$\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$
from the oriented projected tangents, and set
$\operatorname{wr}(D)=\sum_c\operatorname{sgn}(c)$. With
$\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, adding a positive type-I kink multiplies the
raw bracket by $-A^3$ and increases writhe by $1$; adding a negative type-I
kink multiplies it by $-A^{-3}$ and decreases writhe by $1$. Deleting either
kink multiplies by the reciprocal factor. Consequently
$$f_D(A):=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle$$
is unchanged by every oriented type-I, type-II, and type-III Reidemeister move
and by planar isotopy.

## Statement references

[Kauffman, *An Invariant of Regular Isotopy* (1990), §§III and VI](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kauffman/IRH.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §§4.1 and 4.3](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Funar, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter 3, §1.1](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty regular oriented link diagram $D$ and a type-I, type-II,
or type-III move applied to it.

[F1] In the positively oriented chart with over-strand southwest–northeast,
the A-smoothing pairs left endpoints and right endpoints, while the B-smoothing
pairs top endpoints and bottom endpoints. A crossing contributes $A$ for its
A-smoothing and $A^{-1}$ for its B-smoothing; a state with $k$ circles contributes the factor
$\delta^{k-1}$, and $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$
([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The total writhe is the sum of the signs
$\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$;
the positive Artin half twist has sign $+1$
([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F3] A type-I kink creates or deletes one crossing of either sign; type II
creates or deletes two crossings of opposite signs; type III preserves the
signs of its three crossings ([[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]).

[F4] The raw bracket is unchanged under every R2 and R3 local replacement
([[lem-kauffman-bracket-r2-r3-identities]]).

## Proof

1.1 Label the crossing ports northwest $1$, northeast $2$, southeast $3$, and southwest $4$, in the chart of [F1]. The over-strand joins $4$ to $2$ and the under-strand joins $1$ to $3$. For the left exterior cap $(1,4)$ the remaining ports are $2,3$. Orient its through strand from $2$ to $3$: it traverses the over-strand northeast to southwest, then the cap, then the under-strand northwest to southeast. The tangent vectors may be taken as $(-1,-1)$ and $(1,-1)$, whose determinant is $2>0$. This is a positive kink. The A-pairing $(1,4)(2,3)$ closes one additional circle against the cap; the B-pairing $(1,2)(3,4)$ gives just the through arc. Hence its bracket factor is $A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^3$. Reversing the component negates both tangent vectors and preserves the determinant. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 For the top exterior cap $(1,2)$ the remaining ports are $4,3$. Orient its through strand from $4$ to $3$: it traverses the over-strand southwest to northeast, then the cap, then the under-strand northwest to southeast. The tangent vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ have determinant $-2<0$, so this is a negative kink. Here the A-pairing gives only the through arc, while the B-pairing closes one additional circle. Its factor is $A+A^{-1}\delta=-A^{-3}$. The right and bottom cap cases are the respective $180$-degree rotations; orientation-preserving chart changes and reversal of the component preserve the calculation. These are all oriented type-I variants. The calculation is inside the move disk and permits every exterior connectivity and any additional components. Deletion uses the reciprocal Laurent-unit factor. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 The positive kink changes writhe from $w$ to $w+1$, and the negative kink changes it to $w-1$. Their respective normalized values are $$(-A^3)^{-(w+1)}(-A^3)\langle D\rangle=(-A^3)^{-w}\langle D\rangle,$$ and $$(-A^3)^{-(w-1)}(-A^{-3})\langle D\rangle=(-A^3)^{-w}\langle D\rangle.$$ Thus both type-I additions and their inverse deletions preserve $f_D$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 A type-II move creates or deletes two opposite signs, and a type-III move preserves all three signs, so writhe is unchanged. Their raw bracket is unchanged by [F4]. Planar isotopy transports the determinant crossing signs, smoothing states and state-circle counts bijectively. Therefore it preserves both factors of $f_D$, and the normalized value is invariant under every listed move. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-kontsevich-morse-tangle-composition
kind: lemma
title: Convergence and composition of Morse tangle integrals

      url: https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf

      url: https://letu.math.gatech.edu/Papers/UN_PAPER.pdf

## Statement

Let $T_1\subset\mathbb C\times[a,c]$ and $T_2\subset\mathbb C\times[c,b]$ be compact strict Morse tangles whose boundary points and orientations match at the regular level $c$, with the joined tangle $T=T_2\circ T_1$ smooth and embedded. Their unframed configuration integrals converge absolutely degreewise and satisfy
$$
Z(T_2\circ T_1)=Z(T_2)\,Z(T_1),
$$
where multiplication stacks tangle diagrams with $T_2$ above $T_1$. The equality holds in the completed unframed tangle diagram space and uses only the finite-degree integrals defined on the matched pieces.

## Statement references

[[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids|Morse tangle integral and vertical stacking convention]]

[[lem-kontsevich-configuration-integral-convergence-needle-estimates|Absolute convergence for strict Morse tangles]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §§8.4.1 and 8.5, printed pp. 229–232](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Le and Murakami, §3, PDF pp. 4–5](https://letu.math.gatech.edu/Papers/UN_PAPER.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Matched compact strict Morse tangles $T_1,T_2$, their regular joining level $c$, and the unframed degreewise tangle integrals.

[F1] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: $Z(T)$ integrates over the ordered levels on a compact tangle skeleton, sums pairings at each level, and places the upper tangle factor to the left in the vertical-stacking product.

[F2] [[lem-kontsevich-configuration-integral-convergence-needle-estimates]]: for each fixed degree, the tangle pairing sum is an absolutely convergent improper integral in the unframed 4T+1T quotient.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Fix a degree $m$ and work with its finitely many branch chambers and pairing types.

1.1 In the degree-$m$ ordered simplex, the set where some level $t_j=c$ has measure zero. Absolute convergence from [F2] allows removal of this set without changing the integral. The remaining domain is the disjoint union, for $k=0,\ldots,m$, of regions with exactly $k$ levels above $c$ and $m-k$ below it; each such region is the product of the corresponding ordered simplex for $T_2$ and that for $T_1$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 On the region indexed by $k$, every selected pair at a level above $c$ lies on $T_2$, and every pair below $c$ lies on $T_1$. Thus a pairing on the composite decomposes uniquely into a pairing on each piece. The product differential form separates into the upper and lower factors in height order, and the resulting chord diagram is their vertical stack. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Fubini's theorem applies to each product region because both factors are absolutely integrable by [F2]. Therefore its integral is the product of the degree-$k$ coefficient for $T_2$ and the degree-$(m-k)$ coefficient for $T_1$. Summing over the finite set $k=0,\ldots,m$ is exactly the degree-$m$ coefficient convolution of $Z(T_2)Z(T_1)$. Since $m$ was arbitrary, the displayed completed-series identity follows. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

      url: https://doi.org/10.1016/0001-8708(76)90027-X

      url: https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf
---

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $G$ be a finitely presented group. Every regular function on $\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2(\mathbb C))$ invariant under simultaneous conjugation is a polynomial in finitely many word-trace functions $t_w(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(w))$. Equivalently, the coordinate algebra of the affine character quotient is generated by trace functions of words in $G$.

## Statement references

[Procesi, *The invariant theory of $n\times n$ matrices*, Theorem 1.3](https://doi.org/10.1016/0001-8708(76)90027-X)

[Tillmann, §§4.2–4.8](https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a finite presentation of $G$, its affine representation variety, and the simultaneous conjugation action.

[F1] For any finite presentation, the determinant and adjugate relator equations give the actual closed invariant representation subset in the matrix tuple space, including its reduced coordinate algebra. This general finitely presented group statement is proved directly in [[lem-sl2-matrix-invariants-by-epsilon-contractions-and-traces]], not restricted to knot groups.

[F2] Every word trace is a regular conjugation-invariant function ([[lem-sl2-trace-functions-are-regular-and-invariant]]).

[F3] The invariant coordinate algebra is finitely generated and defines the affine categorical quotient ([[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]]).

[F4] [[lem-sl2-matrix-invariants-by-epsilon-contractions-and-traces]] proves trace generation for the full simultaneous matrix action by explicit epsilon tensor contractions and polarization, and proves the passage to every closed invariant reduced subset using the actual reductive quotient theorem.

## Proof

1.1 Use the finite presentation of $G$ to realize its representations as the determinant-one matrix tuples satisfying the relator equations from [F1]. This is a closed invariant reduced subset of the finite matrix space; no assumption that $G$ is a knot group is needed. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Apply [F4] to that actual subset. Every invariant regular function is a polynomial in finitely many restricted word traces. On determinant-one matrices an adjugate in that calculation is the inverse matrix, so the words are words in $G$, and their regular invariant functions agree with [F2]. Thus the invariant coordinate algebra is generated by the stated trace functions. The full-AC quotient branch is exactly the branch of [F3] and [F4], rather than an unproved assertion of exactness for the relator ideal. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice used by the bridge-number definition. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard $S^3$, $b(K)=1$ if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the fixed oriented coordinate circle used as the standard unknot.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number|Bridge number and the standard unknot]]

[[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot|A genus-zero spanning disk characterizes the standard unknot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard $S^3$.

[A1] The definition of $b(K)$ is the least number of local maxima over Morse representatives, and the standard unknot is the fixed coordinate circle. [[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number]]

[F1] The set of Morse representatives is nonempty for every smooth knot. [[lem-knot-admits-morse-height-representative]]

[F2] A proper arc with one height maximum (or minimum) in a height ball bounds a bridge disk with any prescribed simple boundary arc joining its endpoints on the level sphere. [[lem-one-extremum-arc-is-boundary-parallel]]

[F3] A smooth oriented knot bounds a genus-zero spanning surface exactly when it is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot. [[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]]

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and the knot $K$.


1.1 Suppose $b(K)=1$. By [A1] and [F1], the nonempty set of maximum counts has least value $1$, so choose a Morse representative $K'$ with exactly one local maximum. On the circle, nondegenerate critical points alternate between maxima and minima; compactness gives finitely many, and a function on a circle has at least one minimum. Hence $h|K'$ has exactly one minimum. Choose a regular value between these two critical values. Its level sphere meets $K'$ in exactly two points, and the upper and lower balls contain one proper arc each, with respectively one maximum and one minimum. [A1, F1, given, choose]

2.1 Fix a simple arc $\beta$ on the level sphere joining the two intersection points. Apply [F2] to the upper arc and the lower arc, using this same $\beta$. The resulting bridge disks lie in opposite balls and meet only along $\beta$; their union, with its corner smoothed, is an embedded disk whose boundary is $K'$. Thus $K'$ has genus zero, and [F3] makes it ambient isotopic to the standard unknot. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Conversely, choose an orientation-preserving rotation in $SO(4)$ carrying the fixed coordinate 2-plane of the standard unknot $U$ to the plane spanned by $e_1$ and $e_4$. A path of rotations from the identity gives an ambient isotopy, and on the rotated circle the fixed height is a sine or cosine with exactly one maximum. Hence $b(U)\le1$. Every Morse function on a compact circle has at least one maximum, so $b(U)\ge1$ and $b(U)=1$. Ambient-isotopic knots have the same set of representative maximum counts, so every unknot has bridge number one. [A1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number]]

[[lem-one-extremum-arc-is-boundary-parallel]]

[[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]]

## Diagram

The dashed line represents a regular level sphere in a two-dimensional cross-section; the two solid arcs are the upper and lower height arcs. The figure is only a cross-sectional schematic. The proof uses the bridge disks from [F2], not the drawing.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be compact between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field and $\nu,\rho>0$. For every $\delta\ge0$, $\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\delta)\le\delta^{\nu/(\nu+1)}\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}$. For every positive singular value $s_j$ with right singular vector $v_j$, equality holds at $\delta_j=\rho s_j^{\nu+1}$, witnessed by $x_j=\rho s_j^\nu v_j$. If $K$ has infinite rank, these $\delta_j$ form a null sequence; if $K$ has finite positive rank, equality is asserted only at its finitely many positive singular values; if $K=0$, the source ball and modulus are $\{0\}$ and $0$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model|Compact Hilbert-space inverse model]]

[Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Theorems 4.11–4.12](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

[Hofmann and Mathé, *A Note on the Modulus of Continuity*, Section 1](https://www.tu-chemnitz.de/mathematik/ip/fulltext/hofmann_b76.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, compact $K:X\to Y$ between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, $\nu,\rho>0$, the power source ball, its centered modulus, and $\delta\ge0$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed by the compact singular-value decomposition supplier.

[F1] [[def-ip-power-source-set]]: $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)=\{|K|^\nu w:\|w\|_X\le\rho\}$.

[F2] [[def-ip-centered-modulus-of-continuity]]: $\varepsilon_K(M,\delta)$ is the supremum of $\|x\|_X$ over $x\in M$ with $\|Kx\|_Y\le\delta$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-index-source-elements-are-minimum-norm]]: Every element of the power source ball lies in $N(K)^\perp$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-spectral-interpolation-for-power-source-balls]]: If $x=|K|^\nu w$, then $\|x\|_X\le\|Kx\|_Y^{\nu/(\nu+1)}\|w\|_X^{1/(\nu+1)}$.

[F5] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]] and [[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]: Each positive singular value $s_j$ has a unit right singular vector $v_j$ with $|K|v_j=s_jv_j$ and $\|Kv_j\|_Y=s_j$; an infinite positive singular sequence tends to zero.

## Proof

1.1 If $\delta=0$ and $x$ belongs to the centered-modulus set, then $Kx=0$. By [F3], $x\in N(K)^\perp$ as well, so $x=0$ and $\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),0)=0$. If $K=0$, [F3] likewise forces every member of the power source ball to be zero, so the asserted bound holds with no positive singular direction. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Suppose $\delta>0$ and let $x$ be any element of the centered-modulus set. By [F1], choose $w\in X$ with $x=|K|^\nu w$ and $\|w\|_X\le\rho$. Applying [F4] and using $\|Kx\|_Y\le\delta$ gives $\|x\|_X\le\delta^{\nu/(\nu+1)}\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}$; taking the supremum over the centered-modulus set proves the bound. [given, A1, F1, F2, F4, choose]

2.1 Fix a positive singular value $s_j$ and its unit right singular vector $v_j$ from [F5]. Set $w_j=\rho v_j$ and $x_j=|K|^\nu w_j=\rho s_j^\nu v_j$. Then $\|Kx_j\|_Y=\rho s_j^{\nu+1}=\delta_j$ and $\|x_j\|_X=\rho s_j^\nu=\delta_j^{\nu/(\nu+1)}\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}$. Thus $x_j$ is feasible in the centered-modulus supremum at $\delta_j$ and attains the upper bound from step 1.2. If there are infinitely many positive singular values, compactness gives $s_j\to0$ and hence $\delta_j\to0$; finite positive rank gives only the stated finite list, while $K=0$ was handled in step 1.1. [given, A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, F5, construct, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://www.stat.purdue.edu/~xbw/research/xi_tomo_jasa1206.pdf"
      locator: "§4.2, PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 1434–1435): latent link successes, conditional expectations, and expected-success/probe-count update"
    - title: "E. Lawrence, G. Michailidis, and V. N. Nair, Statistical Inverse Problems in Active Network Tomography, IMS Lecture Notes–Monograph Series 54 (2007), 24–44"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1079"
      locator: "§3.2, PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 29–30): flexicast multinomial outcomes and the EM E/M steps"
---

## Definition

**Inputs.** Use a finite-tree multicast loss experiment with observed counts $n_{d,y}$, where $n_{d,y}\in\mathbb N_0$, $\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{C_d}}n_{d,y}=N_d$, and $p_e$ is the success probability for edge $e$. Supply an initial vector $p^{(0)}\in(0,1)^E$, a likelihood tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and an iteration cap $M\in\mathbb N_{>0}$. The data are admissible only when every pattern with positive count has $\Omega_{d,y}\ne\varnothing$ and every link is traversed by at least one probe, that is,
$$
N_e:=\sum_{d:e\in E_d}N_d>0\qquad(e\in E).
$$

For algorithm calculations, extend the finite law to candidate vectors in the closed cube as follows. For $a\in[0,1]$ and $z\in\{0,1\}$, let $b(a,z)=a$ if $z=1$ and $b(a,z)=1-a$ if $z=0$. For $p\in[0,1]^E$, set
$$
w^{\mathrm{cl}}_{p,d}(x):=\prod_{e\in E_d}b(p_e,x_e),\qquad Z_{d,y}(p):=P^{\mathrm{cl}}_{p,d}(y):=\sum_{x\in\Omega_{d,y}}w^{\mathrm{cl}}_{p,d}(x).
$$
The sets $\Omega_{d,y}$ partition the link-state space and $\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{E_d}} w^{\mathrm{cl}}_{p,d}(x)=\prod_{e\in E_d}((1-p_e)+p_e)=1$, so $P^{\mathrm{cl}}_{p,d}$ is a probability law for every $p\in[0,1]^E$.
For $p\in(0,1)^E$, $P^{\mathrm{cl}}_{p,d}(y)=P_{p,d}(y)$ from the tree-experiment definition. This closed-cube extension is used only to evaluate candidate iterates; the experiment's parameter space remains $(0,1)^E$. When $Z_{d,y}(p)>0$ define
$$
m_{e,d,y}(p):=\frac{\sum_{x\in\Omega_{d,y}}x_e w^{\mathrm{cl}}_{p,d}(x)}{Z_{d,y}(p)}\qquad(e\in E_d).
$$
The algorithm's observed log likelihood on the closed cube is
$$
\ell(p):=\sum_{d=1}^D\sum_{y:n_{d,y}>0}n_{d,y}\log Z_{d,y}(p),
$$
with $\ell(p)=-\infty$ if any positive-count pattern has zero probability.

**Output.** Return the finite iterate list and one status: `invalid-input`, `zero-likelihood-current`, `zero-likelihood-candidate`, `likelihood-tolerance-met`, or `iteration-cap-reached`. For admissible input, the list begins with $p^{(0)}$ and every later iterate lies in $[0,1]^E$. If an input check fails, the list is the one-element list $(p^{(0)})$ containing the supplied initial vector.

**Procedure.**

1. Validate the count constraints, pattern feasibility, interior initial vector, nonnegative tolerance, positive iteration cap, and $N_e>0$ for each link. If any check fails, return the one-element iterate list $(p^{(0)})$ and status `invalid-input`.

2. Initialize the list with $p^{(0)}$. At each current iterate $p^{(t)}$, compute $Z_{d,y}(p^{(t)})$ for every positive-count pattern. If any is zero, return the current iterate list, ending in $p^{(t)}$, with status `zero-likelihood-current`.

3. For each link $e$, compute its expected number of latent successes
$$
\widehat S_e^{(t)}=\sum_{d:e\in E_d}\sum_{y:n_{d,y}>0}n_{d,y}m_{e,d,y}(p^{(t)}).
$$
Set
$$
p_e^{(t+1)}=\widehat S_e^{(t)}/N_e\qquad(e\in E).
$$
This finite sum is the E-step conditional expectation of the complete-data success count; the displayed ratio is the M-step update instruction and lies in $[0,1]$ for each edge. Coordinates equal to $0$ or $1$ are allowed after an update.

4. Compute $\ell(p^{(t+1)})$. If any positive-count pattern has zero probability, return the current iterate list, ending in the last valid iterate $p^{(t)}$, with status `zero-likelihood-candidate`. Otherwise append $p^{(t+1)}$. If $|\ell(p^{(t+1)})-\ell(p^{(t)})|\le\tau$, return the list with status `likelihood-tolerance-met`. If not, continue from $p^{(t+1)}$ until $M$ updates have been made, then return the list with status `iteration-cap-reached`.

All state sums are finite, and the finite link-state conditional probabilities are calculated directly; the generic measure-space/KL branch of the EM procedure is not invoked. The status records only the stopping rule that fired; it asserts neither parameter convergence nor a global optimum.

    - title: "Ciprian Manolescu, An Introduction to Knot Floer Homology, §§3.3–3.5 and 4.2–4.3"
      url: "https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/hfk.pdf"
      locator: "Printed pp.12–18; holomorphic knot Floer complex and its toroidal grid specialization"

## Definition

Work in the smooth category inherited from the oriented-link convention. In particular, an embedded bridge witness disk means the image of a smooth rank-two embedding of a planar disk, with ordinary smooth boundary or smooth transverse corners at its two marked endpoints; smoothness at a boundary or corner means local smooth extension in its charts. Witness parametrizations can be chosen for the finite disk families. This category convention does not require the knot arcs to meet the Heegaard surface transversely: tangential smooth crossings remain permitted.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $h$, let $k\ge1$, and put $m=h+k-1$. A **handlebody** is a compact three-manifold that is a regular neighborhood of a finite connected graph. A **$2k$-pointed Heegaard diagram for $S^3$** consists of a splitting $S^3=U_{\alpha}\cup_{\Sigma}U_{\beta}$ into handlebodies, two systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m)$ of pairwise disjoint simple closed curves on $\Sigma$ that bound pairwise disjoint properly embedded disks in $U_{\alpha}$ and $U_{\beta}$, respectively, cutting each handlebody into exactly $k$ three-balls, and two ordered sets of distinct points $\mathbf w=(w_1,\ldots,w_k)$ and $\mathbf z=(z_1,\ldots,z_k)$ disjoint from the curves. Curves from different systems intersect transversely in finitely many points. Each component of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$ contains exactly one $w$-point and exactly one $z$-point. The diagram also includes trivial arc systems in the two handlebodies: the $\alpha$-arcs join $w_i$ to $z_i$, and the $\beta$-arcs join $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$, with indices modulo $k$. Each system is disjoint from its compression disks and is simultaneously boundary parallel: its arcs cobound pairwise disjoint embedded disks with arcs in the corresponding components of the attaching-system complement on $\Sigma$. Thus each ball obtained by compression contains one unknotted arc. Together the arcs form an oriented knot, oriented from $w_i$ to $z_i$ in $U_{\alpha}$ and from $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$ in $U_{\beta}$. The diagram is **compatible with $K$** when this knot is orientation-preservingly ambient isotopic to $K$. For a grid diagram, compatibility uses the row and column orientation fixed in the grid definition, with $w$-points at $O$ and $z$-points at $X$. For a grid representing one knot, the basepoint pairs can be numbered cyclically in reverse order of travel along the oriented knot so that $w_i,z_i$ lie in the same component $A_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and $w_i,z_{i+1}$ lie in the same component $B_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$.

Comparisons of these embedded diagrams allow **orientation-preserving diagram isomorphisms**: an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^3$ carrying the two handlebodies, their oriented Heegaard surface, the two attaching systems, the ordered $w,z$ points, and the two simultaneously boundary-parallel arc systems to the corresponding data. Equivalently one may specify the surface isomorphism together with its compatible collared extensions over both handlebodies carrying those arcs. The attaching systems are carried as systems; reordering their curve factors induces the corresponding product identification. Comparisons also allow **arc normalizations in the fixed splitting**: a smooth isotopy of the represented oriented knot, supported near the ordered marks and fixing each mark, during which every open connecting arc stays in its original handlebody and the two simultaneous boundary-parallel witness systems are retained or replaced by embedded witnesses for those same arcs. The surface, attaching curves, marked points and compression disks stay fixed. Such a normalization may replace a tangential marked crossing by a transverse one; the original data are not required to have neat arcs. This is a change of knot representative relative to the fixed surface, not a diagram isomorphism carrying both objects. Analytic and assigned grading data depending on the fixed surface diagram can be kept identical; the corresponding generator and disk-count identification is then the identity. Existence of normalizations with the required witnesses is a separate geometric assertion, not part of this definition. Such a comparison transports the represented oriented knot and any specified Seifert surface as well. For analytic data, it transports $j$, the surface area form, all chosen divisor neighborhoods and $J_t$ by the induced symmetric-product diffeomorphism. The comparison maps on generators and disk classes are their pushforwards under this map; compatibility with the count differential is a mathematical property to be proved. No identity action is part of this convention, even when the ambient diffeomorphism is isotopic to the identity.

The $m$-fold symmetric product $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)=\Sigma^m/S_m$ is the space of unordered $m$-tuples of points of $\Sigma$, where $S_m$ permutes coordinates. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ be the quotient map. The product tori are the images $\mathbb T_{\alpha}=q(\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_m)$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}=q(\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_m)$. Their intersection points are the generators. A **Whitney disk class** $\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a relative homotopy class of maps from a disk to $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ whose two boundary arcs lie on $\mathbb T_{\alpha}$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}$ and whose endpoints are $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$. Its domain is the integral two-chain of complementary regions with coefficients equal to local multiplicities. Write $n_{w_i}(\phi)$ and $n_{z_i}(\phi)$ for its local multiplicities at the marked points. An almost complex structure $J$ on $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ is a smooth endomorphism of the tangent bundle with $J^2=-1$. Fix a complex structure $j$ and an area form on $\Sigma$. For $m>0$, choose a smooth path $\mathbb J=(J_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ of nearly symmetric almost complex structures, constant near $t=0,1$: each $J_t$ agrees with the induced integrable structure $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(j)$ on a fixed neighborhood of the diagonal and of every divisor $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ for a chosen interior point $p$ of every complementary region, including every marked point, and tames the form descended from the product area form off that neighborhood. The path is a sufficiently small perturbation in this class. For $m=0$ the symmetric product is a point. Local multiplicities are intersection numbers with these divisors; positivity is a mathematical property to be proved, not an additional choice of disk counts. A $\mathbb J$-holomorphic strip representative is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ satisfying $\partial_{\tau}u+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$, with $u(\tau,0)\in\mathbb T_{\alpha}$, $u(\tau,1)\in\mathbb T_{\beta}$, and limits $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$ as $\tau\to-\infty,+\infty$. Translation in $\tau$ defines an $\mathbb R$-action. The Maslov index $\mu(\phi)$ is the Fredholm index of the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator at a representative of $\phi$; the relative Maslov grading convention is $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf y)=\mu(\phi)-2\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_{w_i}(\phi)$, up to one overall additive constant.

A **periodic domain** is an integral two-chain in the complementary regions whose boundary is an integral sum of full $\alpha$- and $\beta$-curves; its local multiplicity at a marked point is the coefficient of the containing region. The pointed diagram is **admissible** when every nonzero periodic domain with $n_{w_i}=0$ for all $i$ has at least one positive and at least one negative region coefficient. A path $\mathbb J$ is **regular for a set of disk classes** when the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator at every holomorphic-strip representative in those classes is surjective. For a path regular on the classes used, let $\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)$ be the space of strip representatives. If, for each generator $\mathbf x$, only finitely many pairs $(\mathbf y,\phi)$ with $\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)\ne\varnothing$, $\mu(\phi)=1$, and $n_{w_i}(\phi)\ge0$ for every $i$ occur, and each quotient is finite, the multipointed full filtered minus module is the free module over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_k]$ generated by $\mathbb T_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb T_{\beta}$, with differential
$$\partial^-\mathbf x=\sum_{\mathbf y}\sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y),\;\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)\ne\varnothing\\\mu(\phi)=1,\; n_{w_i}(\phi)\ge0\ \forall i}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)\,U_1^{n_{w_1}(\phi)}\cdots U_k^{n_{w_k}(\phi)}\mathbf y.$$
Here $\#_2$ is the count modulo two of the zero-dimensional quotient when it is finite. Quotienting by all $U_i$ leaves the fully blocked multipointed chain complex (the hat chain complex when $k=1$), with terms only from classes satisfying $n_{w_i}=0$ for every $i$; its Alexander-filtered associated-graded complex further retains only classes with every $n_{z_i}=0$. The relative Alexander grading convention is $A(\mathbf x)-A(\mathbf y)=\sum_i n_{z_i}(\phi)-\sum_i n_{w_i}(\phi)$, with an overall additive constant. Each $U_i$ lowers Maslov grading by two and Alexander filtration by one. In a grid diagram, $\Sigma=T^2$, $h=1$, $k=n$, and $m=n$; the horizontal circles are the $\alpha$-curves, the vertical circles are the $\beta$-curves, and the $w$-points and $z$-points are the $O$- and $X$-markings respectively.

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $n\ge3$. On the unit ball $B^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:|x|<1\}$ take the constant matrix conductivity $\gamma(x)=I_n$, the $n\times n$ identity matrix. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, define $F_\varepsilon:\overline{B^n}\to\overline{B^n}$ by $F_\varepsilon(x)=(1+\varepsilon(1-|x|^2))x$ and define $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon=(F_\varepsilon)_*\gamma$ by the anisotropic conductivity pushforward formula. For $\eta=\gamma$ or $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon$, let $\Lambda_\eta$ be the weak energy map on $\mathcal B_{B^n}=H^1(B^n)/H_0^1(B^n)$ given by $\langle\Lambda_\eta f,h\rangle=\int_{B^n}\eta\nabla u_{\eta,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx$, where $u_{\eta,f}$ is the unique weak solution with boundary class $f$ and $V_h$ is any representative of $h$. Then $F_\varepsilon$ is a smooth diffeomorphism that fixes $\partial B^n$ pointwise, $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon$ is smooth and uniformly positive definite, and $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon\not\equiv I_n$; nevertheless $\Lambda_{\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon}=\Lambda_{I_n}$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-anisotropic-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Anisotropic conductivity and weak DN map]]

[[thm-ip-boundary-fixing-diffeomorphism-preserves-dn-map|Boundary-fixing diffeomorphism invariance]]

[Salo, §1, pp. 170–171](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book60/files/30salo.pdf)

[Daudé, Kamran, and Nicoleau, §1, equation (1.6)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.00910)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; an integer $n\ge3$; the unit ball $B^n$; the identity matrix conductivity $I_n$; and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, as assumed by the local anisotropic DN map and gauge theorem. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] If $F$ is a smooth boundary-fixing diffeomorphism and $\gamma$ is a smooth uniformly positive-definite symmetric conductivity, then $(F_*\gamma)(x)=DF(y)\gamma(y)DF(y)^T/|\det DF(y)|$ for $y=F^{-1}(x)$ is smooth uniformly positive definite and $\Lambda_{F_*\gamma}=\Lambda_\gamma$. ([[thm-ip-boundary-fixing-diffeomorphism-preserves-dn-map]], Statement)

[F2] The weak DN map is the energy form on $\mathcal B_\Omega=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$, defined using the unique weak solution and any $H^1$ representative of the second boundary datum. ([[def-ip-anisotropic-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]], Definition)

## Verification

1.1 Write $R_\varepsilon(r)=r(1+\varepsilon(1-r^2))$ for $0\le r\le1$. Then $R_\varepsilon(0)=0$, $R_\varepsilon(1)=1$, and $R_\varepsilon'(r)=1+\varepsilon-3\varepsilon r^2\ge1-2\varepsilon>0$. Thus $R_\varepsilon$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $[0,1]$ to itself; $F_\varepsilon$ preserves each radial ray, is bijective on the ball, and fixes the boundary pointwise. [given, algebra]

1.2 At the origin $DF_\varepsilon(0)=(1+\varepsilon)I_n$ and $J_{F_\varepsilon}(0)=(1+\varepsilon)^n>0$. At $r>0$ the radial derivative is $R_\varepsilon'(r)>0$ and each tangential eigenvalue is $R_\varepsilon(r)/r=1+\varepsilon(1-r^2)>0$. By continuity, $R_\varepsilon'$ stays positive on $[0,1+\delta]$ for some $\delta>0$. The same radial formula extends $F_\varepsilon$ to a smooth diffeomorphism from the ball of radius $1+\delta$ onto its image, which contains a neighborhood of $\overline{B^n}$; its inverse is smooth there. Thus the inverse is smooth through the boundary and the differential is nonsingular on the closed ball. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Since $F_\varepsilon(0)=0$, the pushforward formula in [F1] gives $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon(0)=DF_\varepsilon(0)DF_\varepsilon(0)^T/J_{F_\varepsilon}(0)=(1+\varepsilon)^{2-n}I_n$. Because $n\ge3$ and $\varepsilon>0$, this differs from $I_n$, so the pushed-forward conductivity is nontrivial. [F1, given, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 The hypotheses of [F1] hold for $\gamma=I_n$ and $F_\varepsilon$, so $\Lambda_{\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon}=\Lambda_{I_n}$. The example therefore exhibits a distinct smooth anisotropic conductivity with exactly the same boundary energy map, caused by the stated boundary-fixing change of variables. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold with a basepoint, and let $0\to\mathcal A\xrightarrow{i}\mathcal B\xrightarrow{q}\mathcal C\to0$ be a short exact sequence of local systems of abelian groups on $M$. There is a natural coefficient Bockstein making the sequence
$$H^1(M;\mathcal B)\xrightarrow{q_*}H^1(M;\mathcal C)\xrightarrow{\beta}H^2(M;\mathcal A)\xrightarrow{i_*}H^2(M;\mathcal B)$$
exact at its two middle terms. In particular $\beta$ is an isomorphism if $H^1(M;\mathcal B)=H^2(M;\mathcal B)=0$. No choice principle is assumed. If the local systems and maps have a commuting coefficient-ring action, the sequence and Bockstein respect it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The based manifold and the fiberwise exact coefficient sequence.

[F1] Based paths $\gamma_x$ to all points can be specified from finite atlas data, with $\gamma_o$ constant; the fundamental group has a finite generating list. [[lem-compact-manifold-twisted-singular-chains-admit-one-vertex-reduction]], [[lem-compact-connected-manifold-fundamental-group-has-finite-generators-in-zf]]

[F2] Intrinsic local cochains take values in the fiber over the first vertex, and their coboundary uses inverse transport along the first edge. [[def-homology-and-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 Fix the paths from [F1]. For a degree-one cocycle $\alpha$ in a local system $\mathcal E$, the two-simplex identity of [F2] gives $\alpha(uv)=\alpha(u)+T_u^{-1}\alpha(v)$ for concatenated paths, with the second term transported to the initial fiber. A triangle realizing the concatenation proves this formula, and a triangulated homotopy square proves invariance for endpoint-fixed path homotopies; common internal edges cancel with their inverse transports. A constant two-simplex shows that a cocycle evaluates to zero on a constant path, and the concatenation formula then handles reversed paths. Define a zero-cochain $v_x=T_{\gamma_x}\alpha(\gamma_x)$ and $v_o=0$. The normalized cocycle $\alpha^0=\alpha-\delta v$ vanishes on every $\gamma_x$. If $g_\sigma=[\gamma_x\sigma\overline\gamma_y]$ for a path $\sigma:x\to y$, the concatenation formula consequently gives $\alpha^0(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_x}d(g_\sigma)$, where $d(g)=\alpha^0(g)$ on based loops. Here $d(gh)=d(g)+\rho(g)d(h)$ with $\rho(g)=T_g^{-1}$ in the cohomological convention. This is a crossed homomorphism; conversely that formula assigns a normalized cocycle to every such $d$, since the three edges of a singular two-simplex satisfy the same loop relation. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to a $\mathcal C$-cocycle. Choose one lift $b_s\in\mathcal B_o$ of $d(s)$ for each of the finitely many generators $s$ of $\pi_1(M,o)$ from [F1]. For its inverse use $b_{s^{-1}}=-\rho(s^{-1})b_s$. Order the finite alphabet and use shortlex order on its finite words. Every group element $g$ has a least representing word $w(g)$; the identity has the empty word. On a word $t_1\cdots t_k$ form the finite sum $D(w)=\sum_j\rho(t_1\cdots t_{j-1})b_{t_j}$ in $\mathcal B_o$, and put $Q(g)=D(w(g))$. Its image in $\mathcal C_o$ is $d(g)$ by the crossed-homomorphism law. Thus $b(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_x}^{\mathcal B}Q(g_\sigma)$ gives an actual $\mathcal B$-valued one-cochain lifting $\alpha^0$ on every singular path, without selecting a fraction representative for each path. Its coboundary has zero $\mathcal C$-image, so unique inverse images under the injective fiber maps $i$ define a two-cochain $a$ in $\mathcal A$ with $i(a)=\delta b$. It is a cocycle since $i$ is injective and $\delta^2b=0$. Define $\beta[\alpha]=[a]$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Any other lift of the same normalized one-cochain differs from $b$ by the image of a unique $\mathcal A$-valued one-cochain, so its coboundary gives the same class $[a]$. This includes changes in the finite generators, their lifts and the shortlex order. If $\alpha$ is changed by $\delta c$ for a $\mathcal C$ zero-cochain, its normalization changes by $\delta\widehat c$, where $\widehat c_x=T_{\gamma_x}c_o$: indeed the change in the normalizing zero-cochain is $c_x-T_{\gamma_x}c_o$. A single lift of $c_o$ in $\mathcal B_o$, transported along all $\gamma_x$, lifts $\widehat c$. Its coboundary adjusts $b$ without changing $\delta b$. Thus $\beta$ depends only on the cohomology class. Sums of lifts are lifts of sums, and their coboundaries add, proving additivity. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The map also does not depend on the finite-atlas path assignment. Compare a second family $\eta_x$ with $\gamma_x$, and first use the $\gamma$-normalized cocycle. Its evaluation on $\eta_x$ is $d(k_x)$, where $k_x=[\eta_x\overline\gamma_x]$. Thus its $\eta$-normalizing zero-cochain is $T_{\eta_x}^{\mathcal C}d(k_x)$. The explicit $\mathcal B$ zero-cochain $T_{\eta_x}^{\mathcal B}Q(k_x)$ lifts it, so subtracting its coboundary from $b$ produces a lift of the $\eta$ normalization with the same two-coboundary. Step 3.1 removes the initial change of representative. Coefficient morphisms commute with transport and the formulas, and images of chosen finite lifts are valid lifts for the image cocycle; independence of lifts therefore proves naturality. A commuting scalar action is treated by taking scalar multiples of lifts and using step 3.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.2 If $[\alpha]$ comes from a $\mathcal B$ one-cocycle, normalize that cocycle using its own path evaluations. It lifts the normalized image cocycle and has zero coboundary, so its Bockstein is zero. Conversely if $\beta[\alpha]=0$, the lift $b$ from step 2.1 has $\delta b=i(\delta a_1)$ for some $\mathcal A$ one-cochain $a_1$. Then $b-i(a_1)$ is a $\mathcal B$ one-cocycle whose image is $\alpha^0$, so $[\alpha]$ is in the image of $q_*$. This proves exactness at $H^1(M;\mathcal C)$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Every Bockstein two-cocycle becomes a coboundary in $\mathcal B$ by construction. Conversely let an $\mathcal A$ two-cocycle $a$ become a coboundary $i(a)=\delta b$ for one $\mathcal B$ one-cochain $b$. Its image $\alpha=q(b)$ is a $\mathcal C$ one-cocycle. The $\mathcal B$ zero-cochain $v_x=T_{\gamma_x}^{\mathcal B}b(\gamma_x)$, with $v_o=0$, lifts the normalizing zero-cochain for $\alpha$. Hence $b-\delta v$ lifts $\alpha^0$ and still has coboundary $i(a)$. By step 3.1 it computes the same Bockstein, so $\beta[\alpha]=[a]$. This proves exactness at $H^2(M;\mathcal A)$ and the asserted isomorphism when the two surrounding groups vanish. All lifts used either finitely many generator values, one base-fiber value, or a previously supplied whole cochain. No surjectivity of an infinite product of coefficient quotients was assumed. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.2, construct, algebra] ∎
