## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a finite based diagram of a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$ with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$. The singular instanton resolution complex admits a finite filtration whose first page, with its first differential, is isomorphic to the reduced Khovanov cube of the reflected based diagram $\overline D$. Its spectral sequence converges to $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$. The cube sign at the edge changing $c_j$ is $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v_i}$, and the edge operation is multiplication for a merge or comultiplication for a split. Thus its $E_2$ page is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology of $\overline D$. The claim includes coherent instanton orientations and the unlink group and saddle-map identifications; it asserts no diagram-invariance of intermediate pages.

## Statement references

[[def-instanton-knot-homology-and-canonical-class|Singular instanton homology]]

[[def-singular-instanton-knot-and-sutured-closure-data|Admissible resolution data]]

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|Integral Frobenius operations and cube signs]]

[[lem-instanton-knot-complex-asd-analytic-foundations|Analytic instanton complex]]

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Khovanov homology is an unknot-detector* (2011), §§6–8.7](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/khovanov-unknot.pdf)

[Yang, *An Overview of Floer Homologies* (2025), §5.7](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/286.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The actual based-link complexes, finite integral critical orientation modules, all-class cylindrical counts and continuation are [[thm-based-link-earring-complexes-and-resolution-unlink-groups-are-well-defined]]. Only its based-link invariant is used here, not a sutured closure or nonvanishing assertion.

[F2] Actual compatible backgrounds are [[lem-earring-skein-cobordisms-admit-compatible-marked-orbifold-backgrounds]]. Finite all-class oriented parameter counts and exhaustive collars are [[thm-admissible-earring-cobordisms-have-finite-oriented-family-counts-and-gluing]].

[F3] The integral skein maps, null homotopies, degree-one pentagon contribution and mapping-cone quasi-isomorphism, relative to the disjoint parameter families, are [[thm-earring-skein-cobordisms-give-integral-exact-triangles]]. This includes the genuine reducible-cap calculation, rather than assuming an exact triangle from the existence of cylindrical Floer homology.

[F4] The primitive integral unlink bases, their finite planar compatibility and actual merge/split maps are [[thm-integral-earring-unlink-saddles-are-the-reduced-frobenius-operations]]. They use no unproved general split-link excision or arbitrary concordance formula.

[F5] The reduced Frobenius cube convention is [[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]] and [[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot]]. Its signed differential is checked in [[lem-khovanov-cube-differential-squares-to-zero]]. The finite-filtration spectral sequence is [[thm-bounded-filtered-complex-spectral-sequence-abuts-to-filtered-homology]].

## Proof

**Given:** The finite based ordered diagram, full AC and the actual marked analytic data. Every parameter construction below is finite; the analytic suppliers carry their declared AC uses.

1.1 **The multi-saddle parameter spaces and their entire boundary.** Use the resolution labels of the reflected diagram, with an edge increasing one coordinate. Write $C_v$ for the actual based-link complex of that planar resolution. For $v<w$, let $S$ be its set of changed crossings, $k=|S|$. Put one standard saddle at time $\tau_j$ in each of its disjoint crossing balls; collisions of times are allowed, since the spatial balls are disjoint. Divide simultaneous translation out of $\mathbb R^S$, giving a parameter space of dimension $k-1$. Its broken compactification is constructed as follows. A boundary chart is indexed by an ordered partition $S=B_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup B_l$: retain the centered finite times within each block, and give successive block centers gaps $T_r$, with boundary coordinate $q_r=e^{-T_r}\ge0$. At $q_r=0$ the corresponding cylinder is broken. Refining a block gives the corner charts. On chart overlaps centering changes a gap by a smooth bounded function of the retained block times, so $q_r$ changes by a smooth positive factor; two successive subdivisions give the same ordered gaps. These are manifold-with-corners charts. They cover a compact space: in any sequence normalize one time, pass to a fixed order of the finitely many labels, and select successive gaps which are bounded or diverge to positive infinity. The bounded clusters give finite centered limits after subdivision into their own bounded/divergent clusters, and there are at most $k$ labels. This proves sequential compactness in these finite partition charts; their countable coordinate basis and Hausdorff gap coordinates give compactness. Its facets are exactly the two nonempty ordered blocks. Such a facet is the product of the two smaller saddle parameter spaces, with the intermediate resolution as its cut; higher corners are their ordered iterates. Actual metrics are the fixed saddle metrics translated to these times, with product critical collars between separated blocks. Use their existing product metrics on every boundary chart and extend over the remaining compact interior by a finite partition in the convex cone of positive metrics. Here the background compatibility can be made literal. Put the planar resolution curves and the saddle surfaces in projection-plane times time; a local saddle has graph $t=x^2-y^2$ and normal coordinate $z=0$. The constant viewing-normal vector $\partial_z$ is a nonzero normal section on every such panel and every unchanged planar strand strip. Fix the product normal model on the separate earring annulus. Thus the normal splitting in [F2] uses the SAME section on every cube face, rather than separately chosen graph-spine sections. The sheet cover is cut along the SAME vertical marking arcs, outside all crossing balls. Construct the exterior determinant line by the degree-one angular Thom clutch around the fixed marking rectangle; it is the fixed product line outside the crossing balls and the fixed trivial line inside each ball, since the rectangle misses them. On the normal tube use the explicit common sheet gluing $\rho(v)w=v\bar w$ of [F2], with these normal coordinates. Restriction at an intermediate resolution, and commuting two disjoint saddles, now preserve these very transition functions and their determinant trivializations. Hence all backgrounds and all corner identifications agree as actual gluing data. Relative perturbations from [F2], by induction on $k$, therefore agree on all corners. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 **The total differential and the exact edge signs.** Orient $\mathbb R^S/\mathbb R$ by the ordered crossing coordinates together with the positive simultaneous-translation direction. Retain the parameter orientation line instead of making separate arbitrary signs on its faces. At vertex $v$ tensor $C_v$ with the top exterior line $E_v=\bigwedge^{|v|}\mathbb Z^{\{j:v_j=1\}}$, of parity $|v|$. For an edge increasing $j$, identify the line map with insertion of $e_j$ and reorder into increasing crossing order. Its sign is exactly $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v_i}$. For a larger $S$, use the analogous ordered exterior insertion and the parameter orientation line to define the signed zero-dimensional count $D_{wv}$. Include the vertex differential as $D_{vv}$. The relative grading shift makes each total map odd: its unshifted parity is $1-k$, from its $k-1$ parameters and the even local saddle degree, whereas exterior insertion changes parity by $k$. A one-dimensional parameter moduli space has only end-trajectory breaks and the two-block facets of step 1.1; it has no unlisted bubbles or extra class ends by [F2]. Ordered determinant excision identifies each boundary count with its corresponding composition $D_{wu}D_{uv}$. Its sign is precisely the exterior shuffle sign: move the ordered first block past the second in the exact sequence of their time-coordinate spaces, separating the positive gap and translation factors. For one element in each block this is the anticommutation $e_ie_j=-e_je_i$; for general blocks it is its repeated shuffle. Thus the algebraic boundary-zero identity is the coefficient of $D^2$ at every vertex pair. The finite direct sum $T=\bigoplus_v C_v\otimes E_v$ with $D=\sum_{v\le w}D_{wv}$ is an integral complex. Checkerboard boundary orientations of the planar regions orient all the surfaces consistently; their product determinant orientations are those of [F4]. If the skein labels are initially decreasing, reversing all labels contributes the fixed edge factor $(-1)^{j-1}$, removed by the vertex sign $(-1)^{\sum_j(j-1)v_j}$. The displayed increasing edge sign is therefore literal in [F5]'s convention. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Why this total complex is the original instanton complex.** Leave one crossing unresolved and keep the other resolution parameters. The total complex obtained by resolving that crossing decomposes into its two face totals and their off-diagonal saddle-family map; by step 2.1 this is its actual mapping cone, with the indicated shifts. Use [F3]'s cone comparison on that crossing relative to every already fixed disjoint saddle family. Its components with other crossings changed are the counts over the same disjoint time families, with the local two-saddle homotopy and three-saddle pentagon inserted. Their boundary strata are exactly those already specified in [F3] and step 1.1. The relative perturbations agree on their common faces, and their boundary formulas are exactly the assertion that these components give a filtered chain map from the partially unresolved total to this cone. Filter both by the other crossings. On its associated graded this map is the vertexwise cone quasi-isomorphism of [F3]. A finite filtered comparison with quasi-isomorphic associated graded is itself a quasi-isomorphism: induct on the filtration length, use the short exact sequence of a final filtration piece and its quotient, and chase the long exact sequences in cohomology. No convergence of an infinite filtration is used. Resolve the crossings one at a time. This gives a composite quasi-isomorphism between $T$ and the original complex $C(K)$, including the zero-crossing case, which is the identity. Hence $H(T,D)\cong I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$. This is an actual filtered-cone construction, not an inference that matching vertex ranks determines the abutment. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **The first two pages.** Filter $T$ by $F^pT=\bigoplus_{|v|\ge p}C_v\otimes E_v$. Every count increases the number of resolved coordinates, so this is a bounded filtration by subcomplexes. On the associated graded the differential is just the vertex differential, hence $E_1=\bigoplus_v I^\natural(D_v;\mathbb Z)\otimes E_v$. Its first differential is exactly the one-crossing saddle map, with the insertion sign computed in step 2.1; all larger saddle sets increase filtration by at least two. By [F4], the ordered planar unlink groups have the primitive reduced Frobenius bases and every one of these actual saddle maps is multiplication on a merge or comultiplication on a split, with the identity on the remaining factors. The marked circle uses the one-dimensional reduced factor. The local tetrahedral smoothing chart interchanges its two planar pairings when the over- and under-strands are reflected; these are precisely the A- and B-resolutions of the reflected diagram in [F5]. Thus the identified signed first-page complex is the reduced integral Khovanov cube of $\overline D$, not merely a vector space with the same rank. Its cohomology is the stated reduced integral $E_2$ page. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 **Convergence and exact scope.** The filtration has only $n+1$ nonzero levels and the even and odd total chain groups are finite free abelian. Forget any finer instanton grading. To apply the ordinary integer-graded finite-filtration theorem literally, unroll this parity complex by $\widehat T^{2q+r}=T^r$, $r=0,1$, with the repeated differential, and reverse cohomological indices if using [F5] in its chain convention. Every integer degree has the same finite filtration bounds. The cycles, boundaries and pages are two-periodic, so [F5] applies degreewise and the result folds back to the two parity degrees. The uniform finite filtration length makes every differential with filtration change greater than $n$ vanish. Thus it gives a finite spectral sequence with finite total pages and abutment the associated graded of the induced finite filtration on $H(T,D)$. Step 3.1 identifies this abutment with $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$ in the usual filtered-homology sense. All counts used their actual integral determinant orientations, exhaustive collars and all-class finiteness. Full AC is inherited from their analytic and bundle constructions; once these finite chain groups and maps exist, the filtration, exterior signs and finite exact-sequence arguments introduce no additional choice. The construction is for the fixed finite based diagram; neither an invariance theorem for its intermediate pages nor a sutured/KHI nonvanishing statement has been used or asserted. This proves every claim of the original Statement. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC, using Sobolev norms formed from the $L^p$ norms of Euclidean ordered derivative tensors. There exist constants $\varepsilon,C,C_3>0$ with the following property. Let $A$ be a smooth $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued one-form on the closed Euclidean ball $B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$, with Frobenius target norm and curvature $F_A=dA+A\wedge A$. If $\|F_A\|_{L^2(B_r)}\le\varepsilon$, then there exists $g:B_r\to SU(2)$ belonging to $W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p\ge2$ such that
$$a=A^g=g^{-1}dg+g^{-1}Ag,\qquad d^*a=0,$$
and $a$ belongs to the $W^{1,3}$ closure $Y_3$ of smooth one-forms with zero normal component on the sphere. In particular the normal condition is valid in the weak integration identity. The form $a$ belongs to every $W^{1,p}$ with finite $p\ge2$ and satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_2+\|\nabla a\|_2+\|a\|_4\le C\|F_A\|_2,\qquad r^{-1}\|a\|_3+\|\nabla a\|_3\le C_3\|F_A\|_3.$$
The constants are independent of $r$ and $A$; no uniform bound on the gauge's higher norms in terms of the critical curvature norm alone is asserted.

If a fixed finite $\Gamma\le O(4)$ acts on the ball and $\tau$ is an action of $\Gamma$ on $SU(2)$ by constant unitary conjugations, assume $\gamma^*A=d\tau_\gamma(A)$. Then $g$ may be chosen with $g(\gamma x)=\tau_\gamma(g(x))$. This includes prescribed conjugation actions coming from $PU(2)$ representations, without choosing a lift to an $SU(2)$ representation.

For a finite collection of balls with smooth local connection forms $A_i$ and given smooth $SU(2)$ transition maps $t_{ij}$ satisfying $A_j=A_i^{t_{ij}}$ and $t_{ij}t_{jk}=t_{ik}$, apply the construction on each ball where its curvature bound holds. The transformed maps $h_{ij}=g_i^{-1}t_{ij}g_j$ are continuous $W^{2,3}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ transition maps on the overlaps, satisfy the cocycle identities pointwise, and identify the transformed connection forms by $a_j=a_i^{h_{ij}}$.

## Statement references

[[lem-strong-lp-neumann-inverse-on-four-dimensional-balls|Constructed strong Neumann inverse]]

[[lem-normal-boundary-hodge-estimate-on-four-dimensional-balls|Constructed normal Hodge estimate]]

[[lem-neumann-coulomb-gauge-correction-by-contraction|Constructed nonlinear gauge correction]]

[Tao–Tian, Theorem 4.6 and §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209352)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] On $B_1$ the constructed normal-boundary Hodge estimate applies to the closure classes $Y_p$ and, for $p=2,3$, absorbs the curvature nonlinearity when $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$. It then bounds $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}$ by $C_p\|F_a\|_p$ for Coulomb forms ([[lem-normal-boundary-hodge-estimate-on-four-dimensional-balls]]).

[F2] For $a\in Y_3$ Coulomb with $\|a\|_4\le\rho_c$, and $\lambda\in Y_3$ with sufficiently small $W^{1,3}$ norm, the proved contraction constructs a Neumann gauge $h=e^u$ with $b=(a+\lambda)^h\in Y_3$ Coulomb, and $\|b-a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_c(1+\|a\|_{W^{1,3}})\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}$. It preserves given finite constant-conjugation equivariance. Its Neumann gauge class is the $W^{2,3}$ closure $\mathcal G_N$ of smooth $SU(2)$ maps with zero normal derivative ([[lem-neumann-coulomb-gauge-correction-by-contraction]]).

[F3] The constructed strong Neumann inverse supplies the unique mean-zero weak solution in $W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p\ge2$ and preserves normal polynomial approximation ([[lem-strong-lp-neumann-inverse-on-four-dimensional-balls]]).

[F4] On the ball, $W^{1,2}\hookrightarrow L^4$, $W^{1,3}\hookrightarrow L^{12}$, and $W^{2,3}\hookrightarrow L^\infty$. Also $W^{2,6}$ has bounded first derivatives. These follow from the proved first- and higher-order embeddings and the ball's extension property ([[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]], [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]], [[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]]).

[F5] Holder gives the product estimates below, and smooth approximation gives weak product rules. In particular the embeddings in [F4] prove continuity of multiplication $W^{2,3}\times W^{2,3}\to W^{2,3}$ and $W^{2,3}\times W^{1,3}\to W^{1,3}$: second-derivative cross terms use $L^6\cdot L^6\subset L^3$, and first derivatives of mixed products use $L^{12}\cdot L^4\subset L^3$ ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-meyers-serrin-density-on-an-arbitrary-open-set]]).

[F6] Full AC is inherited from these analytic suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC and the smooth connection of the statement. Work first on the unit ball.

1.1 **A constructed radial gauge.** Put $M(s,x)=\sum_i x_iA_i(sx)$ and define $P(s,x)$ by the convergent iterated-integral series $I+\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^k\int_{0<t_k<\cdots<t_1<s}M(t_1,x)\cdots M(t_k,x)\,dt_k\cdots dt_1$. On the compact parameter set every term has norm at most $L^k/k!$; any fixed number $N$ of spatial derivatives is bounded by $C_N k^N L_N^k/k!$. Uniform convergence of these derivative series, followed by the coordinate-segment fundamental theorem, identifies them as the derivatives of the sum. The series also gives the integral equation $P(s,x)=I-\int_0^sM(t,x)P(t,x)\,dt$, which also gives smoothness in $s$. It satisfies $\partial_sP=-MP$, $P(0,x)=I$. Since $M$ is skew-Hermitian and trace zero, differentiation gives $\partial_s(P^*P)=0$; thus $P$ is unitary, and the two-by-two determinant derivative gives $\partial_s\det P=-\operatorname{tr}(M)\det P=0$, so $P\in SU(2)$. Uniqueness of the integral equation follows by iterating its difference estimate $k$ times and taking $k\to\infty$ using $L^k/k!\to0$. Set $U(x)=P(1,x)$. Rescaling the integration parameters gives $U(sx)=P(s,x)$, so $x\cdot dU=-(x\cdot A)U$. Therefore $C=A^U$ is smooth and $x\cdot C=0$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Gauge algebra and the scaling path.** The matrix identity $d(g^{-1})=-g^{-1}(dg)g^{-1}$ gives $F_{A^g}=g^{-1}F_Ag$ and $(A^g)^h=A^{gh}$ by expansion and cancellation. It applies to smooth gauges first; [F4]–[F5] pass it to $W^{2,3}$ gauges and their $W^{1,3}$ connection forms. Unitarity preserves pointwise curvature norms. Define $A_t(x)=tC(tx)$ for $0\le t\le1$. It is a smooth path of smooth zero-normal forms, starts at zero, and ends at $C$. Its curvature is $F_{A_t}(x)=t^2F_C(tx)$, hence $\|F_{A_t}\|_2=\|F_C\|_{L^2(B_t)}\le\|F_A\|_2$ for $t>0$, and $\|F_{A_t}\|_3=t^{2/3}\|F_C\|_{L^3(B_t)}\le\|F_C\|_3$. The same inequalities at $t=0$ are immediate. There are finite constants $L,X$ for which $\|A_t-A_s\|_{W^{1,3}}\le L|t-s|$ and $1+\sup_t(\|A_t\|_{W^{1,3}}+\|F_{A_t}\|_3)\le X$: differentiate $tC(tx)$ and $t^2DC(tx)$ in $t$, using bounded derivatives of the fixed smooth $C$ through order two. [F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Uniform critical improvement in any admissible gauge.** Choose $\rho>0$ no larger than $\rho_c,\rho_2,\rho_3$ in [F1]–[F2]. Call $t$ admissible if some $g\in\mathcal G_N$ has $a=A_t^g\in Y_3$, $d^*a=0$ and $\|a\|_4\le\rho$. All such forms belong to $Y_2$ by finite-volume norm comparison of their smooth normal approximants. By [F1], curvature covariance and [F4], there is a fixed $K_0$ such that $\|a\|_{W^{1,2}}\le C_2\|F_A\|_2$ and $\|a\|_4\le K_0\|F_A\|_2$. Also $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_3\|F_{A_t}\|_3\le C_3X$. Choose the theorem's fixed $\varepsilon>0$ so that $K_0\varepsilon\le\rho/4$. Consequently every admissible gauge has the improved margin $\|a\|_4\le\rho/4$, and its higher connection norm is bounded by a constant depending only on $X$. These estimates require only the given curvature bound, once admissibility holds. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 2.1, choose, construct, algebra]

4.1 **A uniform bound on the transported perturbation.** In an admissible gauge, $dg=g a-A_tg$ holds as a weak matrix identity. Unitarity and [F4] give $\|dg\|_{12}\le C(\|a\|_{12}+\|A_t\|_{12})\le C_X$, with $C_X$ independent of $t$ and of the chosen admissible gauge. For another parameter $s$, set $\lambda=g^{-1}(A_s-A_t)g$. Product differentiation, $g^{-1}=g^*$, Holder and $W^{1,3}\hookrightarrow L^4$ give $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C(1+\|dg\|_{12})\|A_s-A_t\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_XL|s-t|$. Moreover $\lambda\in Y_3$: approximate $g$ by the defining smooth Neumann gauges of $\mathcal G_N$; conjugating the smooth zero-normal form $A_s-A_t$ by these gauges preserves zero normal component, and [F5] gives convergence in $W^{1,3}$. [F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 **A uniform admissibility step.** Let $K_4$ be the fixed embedding norm from $W^{1,3}$ to $L^4$. Using the uniform bound for $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}$ in step 3.1, choose $\delta_X>0$ below the perturbation threshold of [F2] and so small that $K_4C_c(1+C_3X)\delta_X\le\rho/4$. Choose $\kappa>0$ so that $C_XL\kappa<\delta_X$, replacing $L$ by $1+L$ in this choice if necessary. Whenever $t$ is admissible and $|s-t|<\kappa$, step 4.1 allows [F2] to correct $a+\lambda$ by $h\in\mathcal G_N$. The result is $b=(a+\lambda)^h=A_s^{gh}\in Y_3$, Coulomb, and $\|b-a\|_4\le\rho/4$. The group $\mathcal G_N$ is closed under multiplication by the Sobolev product and approximation argument in [F2], so $gh\in\mathcal G_N$. Step 3.1 gives $\|b\|_4\le\rho/2<\rho$. Thus $s$ is admissible, with the same step length $\kappa$ for every admissible $t$. [F2, F4, F5, step 3.1, step 4.1, choose, algebra]

6.1 **Finite construction reaches the original connection.** At $t=0$, take $g=I$ and $a=0$, so admissibility holds. Choose a positive integer $N$ with $1/N<\kappa$ and successively apply step 5.1 to $t_j=j/N$, $j=0,\ldots,N$. This finite induction constructs an admissible $G\in\mathcal G_N$ at $t=1$, with $a=C^G$ Coulomb and in $Y_3$. Take the total gauge $g=UG$. Step 2.1 gives $a=A^g$, and step 3.1 gives $\|a\|_{W^{1,2}}+\|a\|_4\le(C_2+K_0)\|F_A\|_2$ and $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_3\|F_A\|_3$. In particular the construction obtains a gauge from small curvature alone. It used no assumed small potential norm of the original connection: the admissible small potentials were constructed from the zero starting connection by finitely many proved correction steps. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, choose, construct, induction, algebra]

7.1 **Higher regularity from the constructed Neumann inverse.** The family gauge $G$ is in $W^{2,3}$ and obeys $\partial_iG=G a_i-(A_1)_iG$. Contracting its derivative and using $\sum_i\partial_i a_i=0$ gives $\Delta G=\sum_i((\partial_iG)a_i-(A_1)_i\partial_iG)-(\operatorname{div}A_1)G$. Initially $\nabla G,a\in L^{12}$ by [F4], while $A_1$ is smooth and $G$ is bounded; hence the right side belongs to $L^6$. The form $dG$ belongs to $Y_3$ with target the real eight-dimensional matrix space, by the defining smooth Neumann approximation of $G$. The integration identity of [F1] applied to $dG$ therefore gives the zero-normal weak identity for each component of $G$. In particular $-\Delta G$ has zero mean. Apply [F3] at $p=6$ to each component, after subtracting its mean, and use weak-solution uniqueness to conclude $G\in W^{2,6}$. By [F4] its first derivatives are now bounded; the displayed equation then has bounded right side, because $a=G^{-1}dG+G^{-1}A_1G$ is bounded as well. For every finite $p\ge2$, apply [F3] again to this same zero-mean source and uniqueness to obtain $G\in W^{2,p}$. The smooth factor $U$ preserves this regularity for the total gauge $g$, and the gauge formula gives $a\in W^{1,p}$ by ordinary weak product differentiation. This proves exactly the claimed Sobolev regularity, without asserting unproved smooth boundary bootstrapping. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 6.1, algebra]

7.2 **Given finite equivariance.** Suppose the stated $\Gamma,\tau$ data are present. The equality $M(s,\gamma x)=d\tau_\gamma(M(s,x))$ follows from the equivariance of $A$ evaluated on the radial vector. Constant conjugation commutes with all products and integrals in step 1.1, so $U(\gamma x)=\tau_\gamma(U(x))$. Hence $C$ and every $A_t$ have the same equivariance. The initial gauge $I$ is equivariant. If an admissible family gauge is equivariant, its transported perturbation in step 4.1 is equivariant, and [F2] supplies an equivariant correction. The finite induction of step 6.1 therefore produces equivariant $G$ and total $g=UG$. Only the conjugation action is used; scalar representatives of a projective unitary element act trivially, so a lift to an $SU(2)$ representation is unnecessary. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 **Scaling and overlap compatibility.** For $B_r$, pull back the connection as $A_r(y)=rA(ry)$. Its critical curvature norm equals $\|F_A\|_2$. Apply the unit-ball construction and define the physical gauge by $g(x)=g_r(x/r)$. The transformed one-form obeys $a_r(y)=r a(ry)$, so $\|a_r\|_2=r^{-1}\|a\|_2$, $\|\nabla a_r\|_2=\|\nabla a\|_2$, $\|a_r\|_4=\|a\|_4$, and the derivative/curvature $L^3$ norms have common factor $r^{2/3}$. This gives both stated estimates and preserves the approximation class, regularity and equivariance. Finally, on the given overlaps the continuous representatives of $g_i$ supplied by [F4] make $h_{ij}=g_i^{-1}t_{ij}g_j$ continuous and $W^{2,3}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by [F5]. Direct multiplication gives $h_{ij}h_{jk}=h_{ik}$ pointwise, and the gauge composition identity of step 2.1 gives $a_j=a_i^{h_{ij}}$; smooth approximation justifies the equality for the Sobolev forms. Full AC is used only through the actual analytic suppliers [F1]–[F6]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 7.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be a connected oriented complete finite-volume hyperbolic three-manifold, with a compact smooth core $N$ and $k\ge1$ standard rank-two torus cusp ends. Thus $M$ is the interior of $N$ and each end has metric $dt^2+e^{-2t}g_i$, where $g_i$ is a flat torus metric. Let $\rho_0:\pi_1(N)\to G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be its holonomy. Choose a positively oriented basis $(\mu_i,\lambda_i)$ for each oriented horotorus, so its translation lattice can be normalized to $\langle1,\tau_i^0\rangle$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0>0$.

The germ of representations modulo conjugacy at $[\rho_0]$ is a smooth complex manifold of dimension $k$. The functions $s_i(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu_i)$ are local holomorphic coordinates near their values $s_i=4$. Trace squared is well defined in $G$, independently of an $SL_2$ lift.

Augment a nearby representation by choosing one common invariant line for each peripheral subgroup, and quotient these data by simultaneous conjugacy. The germ of this augmented space at the complete representation and its unique peripheral fixed lines is a smooth complex $k$-manifold. It has holomorphic coordinates $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$, where $u_i$ is the eigenvalue-ratio logarithm for $\mu_i$ on the selected line, and the forgetful map is
$$s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2).$$
The corresponding logarithms $v_i$ for $\lambda_i$ are holomorphic and satisfy
$$v_i(u)=\tau_i(u)u_i,\qquad \tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\tau_i(u)>0$$
on a sufficiently small neighborhood. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and for $k=1$ one has $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. No positive or nondegenerate ideal triangulation is assumed. The statement concerns the augmented space, not a single-valued eigenvalue logarithm on the ordinary conjugacy quotient.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the finite-volume quotient, its supplied compact core and standard cusp models, the complete holonomy and the positively oriented peripheral bases.

[A1] AC supplies DC and Countable Choice for the listed suppliers, finite-dimensional choices and the sequence of formal extensions below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] Every closed smooth square-integrable one-form with values in the homogeneous-metric adjoint bundle has a smooth square-integrable primitive. [[lem-adjoint-hyperbolic-ltwo-one-forms-are-exact]]

[F2] The compact core has a finite CW model, and the local-coefficient pair sequence and Poincaré–Lefschetz duality apply. Over $\mathbb C$, the invariant nondegenerate pairing $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ identifies the adjoint local system with its dual. [[lem-compact-smooth-manifolds-have-finite-cw-models-under-countable-choice]], [[thm-pair-long-exact-sequences-with-local-coefficients]], [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality-with-local-coefficients]]

[F3] A holomorphic equation with invertible partial Jacobian has a unique local holomorphic solution. [[thm-holomorphic-implicit-function-theorem]]

[F4] Commuting affine holonomies $w\mapsto e^{u_i}w+a_i$ and $w\mapsto e^{v_i}w+b_i$, with nonzero complete translations and nonreal complete ratio, satisfy $v_i=\tau_i u_i$ for a holomorphic $\tau_i$ extending that ratio, on arbitrary reduced analytic parameter spaces. [[lem-commuting-affine-peripheral-holonomy-logarithm-factorization]]

## Proof

1.1 The complete holonomy is irreducible and its adjoint invariants vanish. Indeed one cusp subgroup is a rank-two translation lattice fixing $\infty$. If all of $\Gamma$ fixed $\infty$, its elements would be similarities $z\mapsto az+b$. An element with $|a|\ne1$ would conjugate a fixed nonzero lattice translation to translations tending to the identity, contradicting discreteness. An element with $|a|=1$ and $a\ne1$ is elliptic about a vertical line, impossible in a torsion-free discrete group. Hence all elements would be translations, and the quotient would have infinite volume as height tends to zero. This contradicts the finite-volume hypothesis. Thus some element does not fix $\infty$. A traceless matrix invariant under the cusp group is a multiple of $E=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, by direct commutation with a nontrivial unipotent. A nonzero such matrix invariant under all of $\Gamma$ would force preservation of its kernel line, hence of $\infty$, a contradiction. Thus $H^0(M;E_{\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0})=0$. The same argument excludes a common invariant line for the holonomy matrices. The group centralizer in $G$ is trivial as well: a Möbius map commuting with the cusp translations fixes $\infty$ and is itself a translation, by its affine formula; a nonidentity such translation has unique fixed point $\infty$, so commuting with the entire group would force the whole group to fix $\infty$. [given, algebra]

1.2 We specify the cohomology comparisons being used. The flat adjoint bundle has local parallel frames, obtained on simply connected balls by trivializing its defining covering construction. In such frames its differential is the componentwise ordinary exterior differential; integration of forms over simplices is compatible with the constant transition matrices and with Stokes. The usual local Poincaré contraction is explicit: integrate contraction by the radial vector along radial coordinate segments. A locally finite good cover by sufficiently small strongly convex metric balls therefore gives a Čech double complex whose form columns resolve the parallel local sections. Its positive Čech rows are contracted by $(hc)_{i_0\ldots i_{r-1}}=\sum_j\phi_jc_{ji_0\ldots i_{r-1}}$, for a subordinate partition of unity. The small-singular-cochain double complex has the same degree-zero columns, since every intersection is contractible; subdivision makes singular simplices subordinate to the cover, and the Čech rows contract by assigning a containing index to each small simplex. The two edge comparisons identify flat de Rham cohomology with singular cohomology with this local system, naturally for restrictions. These constructions also apply to compact support and to collars, so relative classes are represented by forms supported away from the ends. Finally $M$ is aspherical, with universal cover $\mathbb H^3$ contractible. Its lifted cellular or singular chains form a free resolution of $\mathbb C$ as a $\mathbb C\Gamma$-module; comparison of free resolutions by successive lifts gives the same cohomology as group cocycles. In degree one, this comparison is concretely integration of an equivariant closed form along a lifted group loop. These arguments establish the coefficient comparisons, rather than invoking an unproved twisted de Rham theorem. [A1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

1.3 The representation scheme of a torus is smooth near its noncentral complete peripheral pair. Use local $SL_2$ lifts $A,B$ of the two generators, both near nontrivial commuting unipotents; their commutator is $I$ because its sign is locally constant and is positive at the basepoint. Choose a fixed vector $v$ with $v,Av$ independent at that point and hence nearby. For a commuting matrix $B$, write $Bv=av+bAv$; commutation then forces $B=aI+bA$ by applying both sides to the basis $v,Av$. This argument works over truncated power-series rings too, because the basis determinant is a unit. Put $C=A-(\operatorname{tr}A)I/2$ and write $B=\alpha I+\beta C$. Its determinant condition is $\alpha^2-\beta^2((\operatorname{tr}A)^2/4-1)=1$. At the complete pair $\alpha=1$, so [F3] solves uniquely for $\alpha$ in terms of $A$ and $\beta$. Thus the commuting-pair scheme is locally a smooth four-dimensional space, parametrized by the three coordinates of $A$ and one of $\beta$. In particular every representation over $\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1})$ near this pair extends one order further. [F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Write $E_0=E_{\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0}$. The restriction $r_1:H^1(N;E_0)\to H^1(\partial N;E_0)$ is injective. If a closed smooth form represents a class in its kernel, on each cusp tail it equals $d_{E_0}b_i$ for a smooth section, by step 1.2. Subtract $d_{E_0}(\chi_i b_i)$ using a cutoff equal to one sufficiently far along that end and zero near the core. The resulting cohomologous closed form is compactly supported, hence square integrable, and is exact by [F1]. Thus the original class is zero. Equivalently the map $H^1(N,\partial N;E_0)\to H^1(N;E_0)$ vanishes. By [F2], its transpose, up to the harmless cap-boundary sign, is the map $H^2(N,\partial N;E_0)\to H^2(N;E_0)$, so that map also vanishes. The pair sequence therefore gives $r_2:H^2(N;E_0)\to H^2(\partial N;E_0)$ injective. It is onto because its cokernel embeds in $H^3(N,\partial N;E_0)$, which is dual to $H^0(N;E_0)=0$ by step 1.1. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 We give the full obstruction construction. Suppose $\rho^{(n)}$ is a representation over $\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1})$ with constant term $\rho_0$. Choose arbitrary one-order lifts $\widetilde\rho(\gamma)$ of its values. The defect is uniquely $\widetilde\rho(\gamma)\widetilde\rho(\delta)\widetilde\rho(\gamma\delta)^{-1}=I+t^{n+1}c(\gamma,\delta)$ modulo $t^{n+2}$, with $c$ in the adjoint Lie algebra; this expression is read in the identity chart of $G$. Associativity gives $c(\gamma,\delta)+c(\gamma\delta,\epsilon)=\operatorname{Ad}_{\rho_0(\gamma)}c(\delta,\epsilon)+c(\gamma,\delta\epsilon)$, exactly the group two-cocycle relation. Replacing the lift at $\gamma$ by $(I+t^{n+1}b(\gamma))\widetilde\rho(\gamma)$ changes $c$ by $b(\gamma)+\operatorname{Ad}_{\rho_0(\gamma)}b(\delta)-b(\gamma\delta)$. Hence a one-order extension exists if and only if the class $[c]\in H^2(\Gamma;\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0)$ vanishes. The formulas commute with restriction to every subgroup. [A1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 At a cusp the adjoint invariants are $\mathbb CE$, of dimension one. Torus duality and the Euler characteristic of a finite cellular local system give $\dim H^0(T_i;E_0)=\dim H^2(T_i;E_0)=1$ and $\dim H^1(T_i;E_0)=2$. Indeed every cell contributes three coefficient dimensions, so the alternating chain dimension is $3\chi(T_i)=0$. The pair sequence and step 2.1 give a short exact sequence $0\to H^1(N;E_0)\to H^1(\partial N;E_0)\to H^2(N,\partial N;E_0)\to0$. The last group is dual to the first by [F2]. Consequently $\dim H^1(N;E_0)=k$, while $r_2$ identifies $H^2(N;E_0)$ with $\mathbb C^k$. All these spaces are finite dimensional by the finite CW model in [F2]. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 On each peripheral subgroup the obstruction in step 2.2 is zero by the smooth formal chart of step 1.3. The map on $H^2$ restricting to all peripheral subgroups is injective by step 2.1 and the comparisons in step 1.2, so the global obstruction vanishes. Starting with any first-order cocycle, repeat step 2.2 and choose corrections at each order. AC supplies this countable recursive sequence. Every first-order representation tangent vector therefore has a full formal representation curve with that tangent. No convergence assertion about this curve is needed. [A1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 1.3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 We compute the cusp classes and trace derivatives. Normalize the cusp lattice as $z=x+\tau_i^0 y$, with deck translations $x\mapsto x+1$ and $y\mapsto y+1$, and put $F=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and $n(z)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&z\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The forms $\eta_i=dx\otimes E$ and $\omega_i=dz\otimes\operatorname{Ad}_{n(z)}F$ are equivariant and closed: $E$ is translation invariant and the polynomial $\operatorname{Ad}_{n(z)}F=F+zH-z^2E$ depends only on $z$, so its derivative wedges to zero with $dz$. Their trace-paired cup product is $\operatorname{tr}(\eta_i\wedge\omega_i)=\tau_i^0dx\wedge dy$, while each self-pairing is zero. Thus these two classes are independent and form a basis by step 3.1. The form $\eta_i$ is square integrable on its cusp: at height $t$, $|dx|$ grows as $e^t$ and the homogeneous norm of $E$ decays as $e^{-t}$, whereas volume decays as $e^{-2t}$. [step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

5.1 Let $L$ be the span of the $k$ classes $\eta_i$ in $H^1(\partial N;E_0)$. The image of $r_1$ meets $L$ only in zero. If a global closed form restricts cohomologically to a combination of these $\eta_i$, subtract exact cutoff terms on the ends as in step 2.1 to arrange equality with that combination on each tail. The resulting global form is square integrable by step 4.1 and compactness of the remaining core, hence exact by [F1]. Since both $H^1(N;E_0)$ and the span of the $\omega_i$ have dimension $k$, there is a global cohomology basis whose boundary images are $\omega_i+\sum_jc_{ij}\eta_j$. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 A group one-cocycle $a$ represents the infinitesimal representation $(I+\epsilon a(\gamma))\rho_0(\gamma)$ modulo $\epsilon^2$, as direct multiplication verifies; infinitesimal conjugacies are precisely coboundaries. Thus representation tangent vectors modulo infinitesimal conjugacy are $H^1(N;E_0)$. For the positive local lift of the normalized cusp meridian, $\rho_0(\mu_i)=n(1)$, integration in step 1.2 gives $a_{\eta_i}(\mu_i)=E$ and $a_{\omega_i}(\mu_i)=\int_0^1(F+xH-x^2E)\,dx=F+H/2-E/3$. Therefore $d\operatorname{tr}_{\mu_i}(\eta_i)=\operatorname{tr}(En(1))=0$ and $d\operatorname{tr}_{\mu_i}(\omega_i)=1$. For trace squared the latter derivative is $4$, since the complete trace is $2$. Classes supported at other cusps contribute only their own restrictions. By the basis in step 5.1, $(ds_1,\ldots,ds_k)$ is an isomorphism from $H^1(N;E_0)$ to $\mathbb C^k$. This is a tangent calculation; smoothness is proved next. [step 1.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Here is why formal integrability implies analytic smoothness in this setting, without an approximation theorem for formal solutions. Take a finite presentation from [F2] and express its relators near $\rho_0$ as an analytic map $R:\mathbb C^{3g}\to\mathbb C^{3r}$ by using local coordinates on $G$ for the generators and the identity logarithm for each relator. Put $K_0=\ker dR_0$, choose a complement $W$ in the source and a projection $\pi$ onto $\operatorname{im}dR_0$ in the target. By [F3], the equation $\pi R(z,w)=0$ has the unique solution $w=\psi(z)$, with $z\in K_0$, $\psi(0)=0$ and $d\psi_0=0$. Thus the representation germ is the zero set of $\kappa(z)=(I-\pi)R(z,\psi(z))$. If $\kappa$ were nonzero, let $P_d$ be its first nonzero homogeneous Taylor term. A formal representation curve of arbitrary tangent $a\in K_0$, supplied by step 3.2, has $z(t)=ta+O(t^2)$ and $w(t)=\psi(z(t))$; the latter identity follows recursively from the invertible partial Jacobian defining $\psi$. Its relators then give $P_d(a)=0$. This holds for every $a\in K_0$, contradicting that $P_d$ is a nonzero polynomial. Hence $\kappa$ vanishes identically by convergence of its analytic Taylor series. The representation scheme is smooth with tangent $K_0=Z^1(\Gamma;\operatorname{Ad}\rho_0)$ and dimension $k+3$: $H^1$ has dimension $k$, and the coboundaries have dimension three because the invariants vanish in step 1.1. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 6.1, step 3.2, algebra]

8.1 To pass to ordinary conjugacy, choose three linear coordinate conditions transverse to the conjugation orbit at $\rho_0$. The orbit derivative is injective by step 1.1. The analytic inverse theorem, equivalently [F3] applied to the conjugation map, gives a local product of a three-dimensional identity neighborhood in $G$ and a slice $S$ of dimension $k$. This slice represents the actual conjugacy quotient germ. To exclude extra identifications by large conjugations, suppose instead that arbitrarily near $\rho_0$ there were conjugate pairs requiring conjugators away from the identity in $G$. Choose such a sequence, lift its conjugators to nonzero matrices and normalize their Euclidean matrix norms to one. After a subsequence the normalized matrices have a nonzero limit $P$. Choose local lifts of the finitely many generator matrices. Their intertwining equations have signs $\pm1$; after another subsequence each sign is fixed. If $P$ had rank one, these equations would make its kernel a common invariant line of the limiting holonomy matrices, contradicting step 1.1. Thus $P$ is invertible, and its projective class centralizes the complete holonomy. That projective centralizer is trivial by step 1.1, so the conjugators tend projectively to the identity, a contradiction. The local product uniqueness therefore excludes all extra slice identifications after shrinking. This proves smoothness of the ordinary quotient germ. By step 6.1 the trace-squared map on $S$ has invertible differential, and [F3] makes $(s_1,\ldots,s_k)$ its holomorphic coordinates. [F3, step 1.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

9.1 Let $u\in\mathbb C^k$ be small. Step 8.1 gives a unique slice representation $\rho(u)$ whose trace-squared coordinates are $s_i=4\cosh^2(u_i/2)$; it depends holomorphically on $u$. Choose local $SL_2$ lifts $A_i(u)$ of $\rho(u)(\mu_i)$ with trace near $2$. Their traces equal $2\cosh(u_i/2)$, because their squares agree and the near-$2$ branch is unique. Thus $e^{u_i/2}$ is an eigenvalue. The matrix $A_i(u)-e^{u_i/2}I$ has rank one throughout a small neighborhood, including $u_i=0$, since it has zero determinant and stays near a nonzero rank-one matrix. A fixed nonzero column of its adjugate gives a holomorphic kernel line $\ell_i(u)$ after shrinking. This line is invariant under the whole peripheral subgroup by commutation. Conversely, given a nearby slice representation with a chosen peripheral line, its meridian eigenvalue on that line is holomorphic and near $1$; its unique near-zero ratio logarithm defines $u_i$. The trace relation forces precisely the representation just constructed, and the rank-one kernel forces precisely its chosen line. Both constructions are holomorphic: the eigenvalue is read by applying the matrix to a local nonzero vector of the line. They are inverse maps on the augmented germ. Hence that germ is smooth of dimension $k$ with coordinates $u$. [F3, step 1.3, step 8.1, construct, algebra]

10.1 The local lift of $\rho(u)(\lambda_i)$ commutes with $A_i(u)$: the commutator sign is locally constant and positive at the complete point. It acts on $\ell_i(u)$ by a nonzero holomorphic eigenvalue near its complete value; choose its sign to make this value $1$, and define $v_i$ as twice its near-zero logarithm. Choose a holomorphic change of frame sending $\ell_i(u)$ to $\mathbb Ce_1$, by adjoining a fixed complementary vector and normalizing the determinant locally. The resulting peripheral Möbius maps fix $\infty$ and act on its finite complement as $z\mapsto e^{u_i}z+a_i(u)$ and $z\mapsto e^{v_i}z+b_i(u)$. At $u=0$, their translations satisfy $a_i(0)\ne0$ and $b_i(0)/a_i(0)=\tau_i^0$. Apply [F4] to get $v_i=\tau_i(u)u_i$ with $\tau_i$ holomorphic and $\tau_i(0)=\tau_i^0$. Positivity of the imaginary part persists on a sufficiently small common neighborhood. For one cusp the holomorphic Taylor expansion gives $v(u)=\tau^0u+O(u^2)$. All constructions used representation matrices and cusp models; none used an ideal triangulation, or a positivity assumption about tetrahedra. [F4, step 9.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Source reading and precise scope

The complete 29-page *Twisted cohomology* paper and the complete 13-page *Local coordinates* paper were read, together with Kapovich's full Sections 8.8 and 8.10 (printed pp. 179–190, obtained from PDF pages 200–211 by OCR). The present proof supplies the degree-one analytic vanishing through its local supplier, constructs the obstruction cocycles rather than citing their existence, and replaces the source's Artin-approximation invocation with the lowest-nonzero-Taylor-term argument in step 7.1.

This theorem gives the full analytic representation and augmented holonomy germ. Its geometric inputs are the compact core and standard cusp models. It does not assert a positive ideal triangulation exists, does not identify the unaugmented quotient with the eigenvalue-coordinate cover, and does not by itself construct the completed Dehn-filled metric. Those geometric realizations remain separate suppliers.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every nonempty closed connected oriented smooth $3$-manifold $M$, there is a finite oriented link $L=\bigcup_{i\in I}K_i\subset S^3$ and an integer $n_i$ for each component such that the oriented manifold obtained by simultaneous surgery with meridian slopes $n_i[\mu_i]+[\lambda_i]$ is orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic to $M$. The empty link is allowed and presents $S^3$.

## Statement references

[[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram|Integral framed-link surgery convention]]

[[lem-relative-three-manifolds-admit-parametrized-link-surgery-presentations|Proved smooth oriented link-surgery existence]]

[Saveliev, Lecture 2 §2.2, Theorem 2.1 and proof](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/3mani.pdf)

[E, Lei, and Li, A Proof of Lickorish and Wallace’s Theorem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.1376)


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a nonempty closed connected oriented smooth $3$-manifold $M$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is the hypothesis of both local suppliers.

[F1] [[lem-relative-three-manifolds-admit-parametrized-link-surgery-presentations]]: for connected nonempty compact oriented smooth $N,M$ with their prescribed common parametrized boundary, a finite framed link in $N$ has surgery orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic to $M$. The proof supplies actual normal disk framings and the prescribed smooth output identification, including the closed case $N=S^3$.

[F2] [[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram]]: a component's preferred longitude is the unique degree-one parallel with zero homology class in its individual knot exterior. Its positive meridian and preferred longitude form the peripheral basis, and integer surgery fills along $n\mu+\lambda$. The empty diagram gives $S^3$.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] with the standard oriented $N=S^3$, target $M$, and empty external boundary. The hypotheses hold: both manifolds are connected, nonempty, compact and oriented, and their boundaries have the unique empty identification. The supplier gives a finite framed link $L\subset S^3$ with disjoint actual attaching tubes and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism from its simultaneous framed surgery to $M$. Its normal disk framings are the actual attaching framings of its four-dimensional two-handle trace; no arbitrary rational filling has been introduced. [given, A1, F1, construct]

2.1 Orient each of the finitely many components. In a component's oriented framed tube $S^1\times D^2$, the framed parallel is $t\mapsto(t,v)$ for a fixed nonzero normal vector $v$. Its projection to the core has degree $+1$. In the positive-meridian/preferred-longitude basis from [F2], the meridian has degree zero and the preferred longitude has degree one, so this parallel has class $n_i[\mu_i]+[\lambda_i]$ for an integer $n_i$. This also follows by writing the normal vector in the preferred trivialization: its winding is the integer $n_i$. The surgery meridian of a framed two-handle is precisely this parallel, by the explicit exchanged disk-factor construction in [F1]. Thus every component has exactly the required integer slope, with the full original normal framing retained. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The disjoint attaching tubes in step 1.1 permit these fillings simultaneously; step 2.1 identifies each of them with the integral convention in [F2]. Their result is therefore the stated integral surgery manifold and has the orientation-preserving diffeomorphism to $M$ supplied in step 1.1. If the link is empty, [F2] identifies its result with $S^3$; conversely the empty diagram is an allowed presentation of $S^3$. This proves the full claim. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume countable choice. The raw tilde grid homology is not a knot invariant by itself. The two specified grid diagrams both represent the oriented unknot, but their tilde homology ranks are $2$ and $4$. For these grids the grid-to-knot-Floer comparison gives $\widetilde{GH}(G_n)\cong\widehat{HFK}(U)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)}$, where $n=2,3$, $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}V=2$, and $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}\widehat{HFK}(U)=1$ by the standard genus-zero diagram and pointed-diagram invariance. Removing the factor $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ would therefore falsely identify different raw ranks with the same rank-one knot invariant.

## Definition

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen compact exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$. A simple closed curve on a surface is **essential** if it is not null-homotopic there. A surface $S\subset E_K$ is properly embedded if $S\cap\partial E_K=\partial S$ and its interior lies in the interior of $E_K$. It is **incompressible** if it has no embedded disk with interior disjoint from $S$ and essential boundary in $S$; it is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no embedded disk whose boundary is the union of an arc in $S$ that does not cut off a disk and an arc in $\partial E_K$. A **boundary slope** of $K$ is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ that occurs as the boundary of a properly embedded, orientable, incompressible, boundary-incompressible surface. Using the positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$ as a homology basis, a primitive class $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$ has slope $b/a\in\mathbb Q\cup\{\infty\}$, with $a=0$ interpreted as $\infty$. A boundary slope is **strict** if it has a realizing orientable, incompressible, boundary-incompressible surface which is not a fiber of any locally trivial fibration $E_K\to S^1$; a fiber is the inverse image of a point under that bundle projection.

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.6635"
      locator: "§§2–3, PDF pp.4–7; the maps F_s and G_s, the three epsilon cases, and the reduced-complex convention"
    - title: "Jennifer Hom, A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance, §3.1"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383"

## Definition

Work over $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $C=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ be its finitely generated free $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ chain complex with Maslov grading $M$ and bifiltration coordinates $(i,j)$. Multiplication by $U$ lowers each filtration coordinate by one and lowers $M$ by two; the differential lowers $M$ by one and does not increase either filtration. The total homology is $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ with its generator normalized in Maslov grading zero.

For a filtration region $R$, write $C\{R\}$ for the corresponding subquotient of the bifiltered complex; in particular $C\{i=0\}$ is the vertical complex, $C\{j=s\}$ is the horizontal complex at Alexander level $s$, and $C\{i=0,j\le s\}$ is the subcomplex of the vertical complex at levels at most $s$. Define
$$ \tau(C)=\min\{s\in\mathbb Z: H_*(C\{i=0,j\le s\})\longrightarrow H_*(C\{i=0\})\text{ is nonzero} \}. $$
For each integer $s$, let $F_s$ be the homology map induced by the chain map from $C\{i=0\}$ to $C\{\min(i,j-s)=0\}$ obtained by quotienting by $C\{i=0,j<s\}$ and then including the quotient. Let $G_s$ be the homology map from $C\{\max(i,j-s)=0\}$ to $C\{i=0\}$ obtained by quotienting by $C\{i<0,j=s\}$ and then including. The epsilon invariant is
$$ \epsilon(C)=\begin{cases} 1,&F_{\tau(C)}=0,\\ -1,&G_{\tau(C)}=0,\\ 0,&F_{\tau(C)}\ne0\text{ and }G_{\tau(C)}\ne0. \end{cases} $$
Here zero and nonzero refer to the induced homology maps. This definition fixes the sign convention; invariance under stable equivalence is a separate claim.

## Definition references

[[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau|The diagram-specific knot Floer filtration and tau convention]]

[Hom, *The knot Floer complex and the smooth concordance group*, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.6635)

[Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finitely generated bifiltered knot Floer complex $C$ with the grading, filtration, and rank-one vertical homology conventions stated above.

[A1] [[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau]]: that item defines the threshold for specified normalized filtered hat data and does not itself prove diagram/surface independence or state the Laurent subquotient interface used here. The current [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] separately supplies a normalized grid-to-analytic filtered comparison; localization gives the Laurent comparison under its stated prerequisites. This Definition remains an algebraic definition on a supplied complex.

[F1] [[lem-bifiltered-two-hook-maps-cannot-both-vanish]] proves that a vertical class represented at $j\le s$ and killed by $F_s$ is in the image of $G_s$, by explicit northeast/southwest hook projections. It uses no simultaneous horizontal simplification theorem.

## Proof

1.1 The quotient and inclusion constructions defining $F_s,G_s$ are chain maps between the stated subquotient complexes, since the differential cannot increase either coordinate. The vertical complex is finite-dimensional: translate each of the finitely many homogeneous Laurent basis generators to algebraic level zero. Its remaining basis has finitely many integer Alexander levels. Since its homology is one-dimensional by the Given data, some finite cycle represents its nonzero class. Below the least basis level the filtered subcomplex is zero, and above the greatest level it is the whole vertical complex. Thus the minimum defining $\tau(C)$ exists. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $s=\tau(C)$ and let $\xi$ be the nonzero vertical homology class, with a cycle representative supported at $j\le s$. If $F_s=0$, [F1] produces a southwest-hook cycle whose image under $G_s$ is $\xi$, so $G_s\ne0$. Hence the two maps cannot both vanish. Their remaining zero/nonzero possibilities are exactly the three displayed cases, proving the algebraic trichotomy and the value set $\{-1,0,1\}$. This argument assumes no horizontal-representative equivalence, and supplies no model independence. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Unresolved proof obligations

The diagramwise tau definition alone does not supply an analytic $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}$ model. The current [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] has an authored proof of the normalized grid-to-analytic comparison; localization gives the Laurent comparison under that supplier's stated prerequisites. This Definition's two-hook proof establishes only the algebraic trichotomy for a supplied finite based bifiltered complex with rank-one vertical homology. It does not prove stable-equivalence or concordance invariance, nor the simultaneous horizontal-representative normal form supplied separately by [[lem-epsilon-stable-core-from-finite-filtered-splittings]].

## Definition

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

## Definition

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

## Definition

Let $V$ be an integral Seifert matrix in the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Two integral Seifert forms are **S-equivalent** when they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular basis changes and algebraic tube additions or their inverses. A basis change replaces $V$ by $P^T V P$ for $P\in\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb Z)$. A tube addition replaces $V$ by
$$\begin{pmatrix} V&0&\rho\\ 0&0&1\\ \rho^T&0&0 \end{pmatrix},\qquad \rho\in\mathbb Z^m,$$
where the two new basis elements are the short and long curves of the added tube. The **empty Seifert form** is the unique bilinear form on the zero module, represented by the $0\times0$ matrix.

## Definition references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push convention and integral Seifert matrices]]

Stavros Garoufalidis and Peter Teichner, “On Knots with Trivial Alexander Polynomial,” §3, Definition 3.2 and the tube-addition matrix, https://people.math.gatech.edu/~stavros/publications/teichner1.pdf

H. F. Trotter, “On S-equivalence of Seifert Matrices,” *Inventiones Mathematicae* 20 (1973), 173–207, https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/download/pdf/PPN356556735_0020/LOG_0020.pdf

## Example

Assume $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=e^{\alpha j}$, and $\sigma_j=j^\beta$ in the Gaussian sequence detection experiment. The minimax separation rate over $\Theta_2(r)$ has order
$$r_\varepsilon^*\asymp\varepsilon(\log\varepsilon^{-1})^{\beta+1/4}.$$

## Example references

[Ingster, Sapatinas and Suslina, *Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems*, Theorem 4.5 and equation (4.6), PDF p. 14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.1853)

[Giné and Nickl, *Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models*, §6.2.3](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=e^{\alpha j}$, $\sigma_j=j^\beta$, and a nonempty $\Theta_2(r)$ with a finite extremal profile for sufficiently small $r$. For this rate comparison, $X_\varepsilon\asymp Y_\varepsilon$ means the ratio is bounded above and away from zero by constants independent of $\varepsilon$.

[F1] [[thm-ip-ellipsoid-detection-boundary]]: $r^2=A J_1/J_2$, $u_\varepsilon^2=(r/\varepsilon)^4J_0/(2J_1^2)$, and the $u_\varepsilon$ boundary determines minimax distinguishability.

[F2] [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-exists-for-small-r]] and [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-is-minimizer]]: a finite active profile exists and its cutoff $m$ satisfies $A\asymp e^{-2\alpha m}$.
## Verification

1.1 Let $m$ be the largest active index. Then $A e^{2\alpha m}<1\le A e^{2\alpha(m+1)}$, so $t=Ae^{2\alpha m}\in[e^{-2\alpha},1)$. For $j=m-\ell$ with $0\le\ell<m$, the profile factor is $\rho_\ell=1-te^{-2\alpha\ell}$. For $\ell\ge1$, $1-e^{-2\alpha}\le\rho_\ell\le1$. Hence the terms with $1\le\ell\le m/2$ give a lower bound for $J_1$ and $J_0$, while the full sums are bounded above by $\sum_{j\le m}j^{4\beta}\le m^{4\beta+1}$. Thus $J_1\asymp J_0\asymp m^{4\beta+1}$. In $J_2$, the summand at $\ell$ is $t e^{-2\alpha\ell}(m-\ell)^{4\beta}\rho_\ell$. Its sum is at most $m^{4\beta}\sum_{\ell\ge0}e^{-2\alpha\ell}\le C_\alpha m^{4\beta}$, and the $\ell=1$ term is at least $c_{\alpha,\beta}m^{4\beta}$ for $m\ge2$. Therefore $J_2\asymp m^{4\beta}$. Formula [F1] gives $$r^2\asymp e^{-2\alpha m}m,\qquad u_\varepsilon^2\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^4m^{-(4\beta+1)}.$$ Taking logarithms of the first relation shows $m\asymp\log(1/r)$. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Set $L=\log\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $r_\varepsilon^*=\varepsilon L^{\beta+1/4}$. At this radius, $\log(1/r_\varepsilon^*)\sim L$, so [F1] and step 1.1 give $u_\varepsilon^2\asymp1$. If $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, then $\log(1/r_\varepsilon)\ge\log(1/r_\varepsilon^*)\sim L$ and $$u_\varepsilon^2\asymp(r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*)^4\left(\frac{\log(1/r_\varepsilon^*)}{\log(1/r_\varepsilon)}\right)^{4\beta+1}\to0.$$ If $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$ and $r_\varepsilon\to0$, the logarithm ratio is at least one, so $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$. If the radii do not tend to zero, use $\bar r_\varepsilon=\sqrt{r_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon^*}$. Nonempty alternatives satisfy $r_\varepsilon^2\le a_1^{-2}$ because $\sum_j\sigma_j^2\eta_j^2\le a_1^{-2}\sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^2\eta_j^2\le a_1^{-2}$. Hence $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$, $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$, and $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_2(\bar r_\varepsilon)$; consistent tests for the larger class work on the original class. The two risk implications in [F1] prove the claimed rate. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $T_{2,3}$ be the right-handed trefoil and $-T_{2,3}$ its reverse mirror. A filtered basis for $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(T_{2,3})$ is $x_0,x_1,x_2$ with $(M,A)(x_0)=(0,1)$, $(M,A)(x_1)=(-1,0)$, $(M,A)(x_2)=(-2,-1)$ and differential $\partial x_1=Ux_0+x_2$, $\partial x_0=\partial x_2=0$. Under the conventions of this page,
$$ \epsilon(T_{2,3})=1,\qquad \Upsilon_{T_{2,3}}(t)=\begin{cases}-t,&0\le t\le1,\\ t-2,&1\le t\le2.\end{cases} $$
The graph has its unique interior breakpoint at $t=1$. For the reverse mirror, $\epsilon(-T_{2,3})=-1$ and $\Upsilon_{-T_{2,3}}(t)=-\Upsilon_{T_{2,3}}(t)$.

## Example references

[[def-epsilon-from-filtered-knot-floer-complex|Epsilon sign convention]]

[[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex|Cycle-minimax Upsilon convention]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology*, §§2 and 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795)

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, §§4.1–4.6 and 13.2](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

## Diagram

The horizontal and vertical coordinates are the algebraic and Alexander filtrations $(i,j)$. Arrows point from $x_1$ to the two terms in its differential, $Ux_0$ and $x_2$. The dotted vertex is the translated cycle $U^{-1}x_2$ used in the Upsilon minimax. All diagonal $U$-translates are omitted; the differential and filtration calculations in the proof use the displayed algebraic data, not the drawing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1.1cm,y=1.1cm,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1.35,0) -- (1.65,0) node[right] {$i$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1.45) -- (0,1.55) node[above] {$j$};
  \node[circle,fill=black,inner sep=1.5pt,label=above left:$x_0$] at (0,1) {};
  \node[circle,fill=black,inner sep=1.5pt,label=above right:$x_1$] at (0,0) {};
  \node[circle,fill=black,inner sep=1.5pt,label=below left:$x_2$] at (0,-1) {};
  \node[circle,fill=black,inner sep=1.5pt,label=below:$Ux_0$] at (-1,0) {};
  \node[circle,draw=black,dashed,inner sep=1.7pt,label=below right:$U^{-1}x_2$] at (1,0) {};
  \draw[->] (0,0) -- (-0.82,0);
  \draw[->] (0,-0.08) -- (0,-0.82);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The displayed staircase complex, the epsilon map convention, and the Upsilon cycle-minimax definition.

[F1] [[def-epsilon-from-filtered-knot-floer-complex]]: epsilon is $1$ when the distinguished vertical class is a horizontal boundary, $-1$ when it is not a horizontal cycle, and $0$ when it is a horizontal cycle but not a boundary.

[F2] [[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex]]: $\Upsilon=-2\nu_t$, where $\nu_t$ is the minimum $F_t$-level of a Maslov-zero cycle representing the normalized generator.

[F4] [[lem-epsilon-stable-equivalence-and-not-a-homomorphism]] steps 4.3 and 6.1 give a finite signed-code admission of the positive trefoil grid and compute its normalized three-generator staircase. [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] supplies the stated normalized grid-to-analytic comparison; its current Proof includes the absolute Maslov and Alexander normalizations and has its [F1]–[F5] prerequisites recorded there.

[F3] [[lem-knot-floer-duality-and-filtration-swap]]: the reverse-mirror complex is filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to the dual, which negates the two filtration coordinates; the actual analytic diagram identification and its absolute grading are supplied without requiring admission of this particular staircase.

[F5] [[thm-grid-upsilon-equals-oss-upsilon]] now has a proof of the grid Upsilon comparison, using the normalized comparison in [F4] and the locally supplied t-modification and tower splitting. Its precise analytic prerequisites are those recorded by [F4].

## Proof

1.1 In the vertical complex, the differential is $x_1\mapsto x_2$, so its degree-zero homology generator is $x_0$ and first appears at Alexander level $1$. The normalized comparison in [F4], after quotient by the chosen $U$ action, identifies this filtered hat complex with the specified-data complex in [[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau]]; hence $\tau(T_{2,3})=1$. For the exact epsilon maps at $s=1$, the target of $F_1$ contains $U^{-1}x_1$ with boundary $x_0$: its other differential term $U^{-1}x_2$ has $j<1$ and is killed there. Thus $F_1=0$. The source of $G_1$ contains the degree-zero cycle $x_0$, while $U^{-1}x_1$ has $i>0$ and is excluded, so that class survives and maps to the nonzero vertical class. Thus $G_1\ne0$ and the exact three-case definition gives epsilon $1$ for this complex. [given, F1, F4]

1.2 A Maslov-zero cycle representing the normalized total generator is either $x_0$ or $U^{-1}x_2$: the Maslov-zero chain group in the displayed basis is spanned by these two cycles, and $\partial(U^{-1}x_1)=x_0+U^{-1}x_2$ makes their homology classes equal. Their coordinates are $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$, so their filtration levels are $t/2$ and $1-t/2$. Therefore $\nu_t=\min(t/2,1-t/2)$ and $\Upsilon_{T_{2,3}}(t)=-2\nu_t$, which gives the stated two linear pieces. They agree at $t=1$, where the slope changes. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 The algebraic Laurent dual of the displayed complex has generators $x_0^*,x_1^*,x_2^*$ at Maslov/Alexander values $(0,-1),(1,0),(2,1)$ and differential $\partial x_0^*=Ux_1^*$, $\partial x_2^*=x_1^*$, $\partial x_1^*=0$. In its vertical complex $x_2^*$ maps to $x_1^*$, leaving $x_0^*$ as generator at Alexander level $-1$. At $s=-1$, the $F_{-1}$ target kills $Ux_1^*$ because $i<0$, so $x_0^*$ becomes a cycle; its only degree-one basis vector is $x_1^*$ with zero differential, so the class is not a boundary and $F_{-1}\ne0$. The $G_{-1}$ source has only $x_0^*$ in degree zero, and its differential $Ux_1^*$ is retained; $Ux_2^*$ lies above $j=-1$ and is excluded. Hence $G_{-1}=0$ and the exact epsilon convention gives $-1$. The degree-zero chain space has basis $x_0^*,Ux_2^*$; their individual differentials are both $Ux_1^*$, so the only nonzero cycle is $x_0^*+Ux_2^*$, and it represents the normalized generator. Its two terms have coordinates $(0,-1)$ and $(-1,0)$, giving $\nu_t^*=\max(-t/2,-1+t/2)=-\min(t/2,1-t/2)$. Thus its Upsilon is the negative of the value in step 1.2 by an explicit cycle computation. Fact [F3] identifies the dual of an ADMITTED knot complex with its actual reverse-mirror complex. Both numerical knot-level values here still require admission of this specific staircase from an actual trefoil diagram. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Under [F5], the same calculation is obtained from the diagonal grid complex after accounting for its $W^{\otimes(n-1)}$ factors, whose nonzero t-grade shifts are nonpositive on $[0,1]$. The factor is retained and does not change the maximal non-torsion grading. [given, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

## Unresolved proof obligations

The positive staircase is identified with the actual right-handed trefoil by the signed-code proof and finite staircase computation in [F4]. Its normalized grid-to-analytic comparison and the grid-Upsilon equality are supplied by [F4] and [F5], under their stated prerequisites; the reverse-mirror identification is supplied by [F3]. The previous missing-grid-comparison and missing-diagram qualifications are resolved.

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible $3$-manifold whose boundary components are tori. Let $A\subset M$ be a connected properly embedded incompressible annulus with $\partial A\subset\partial M$. If $A$ is boundary-compressible, then $A$ is boundary-parallel.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Lemma 1.10](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Walter Neumann and Gadde Swarup, *Canonical decompositions of 3-manifolds*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9712227)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact connected orientable irreducible smooth three-manifold with torus boundary, the incompressible proper annulus $A$, and a boundary-compressing disk $D$.

[F1] The disk obstructions, irreducibility and boundary-parallel product have the conventions of [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]], Definition.

[F2] Smooth essential torus curves are primitive, finite disjoint families admit smooth affine normalization, and their complementary strips have smooth annulus parameters, without choice ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-torus-curves-and-annulus-strips]], Statement).

[F3] A parametrized ball with a parametrized boundary disk window is the standard marked pair; with supplied collars, disk attachment and removal preserve ball type, without choice ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]], Statement).

[F9] Every compact smooth boundary-preimage surface has a boundary-fixed smooth embedding neatification with an explicit topological ambient extension. The actual smooth disk obstructions and boundary-compressing witnesses transport as stated in the endpoint-witness supplier. Products here are the products in the original Definition; on a broad nonneat input their pullbacks are topological products, not newly asserted smooth collars. [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]] [[lem-angular-boundary-neatification-preserves-smooth-disk-obstructions]]

## Proof

1.1 First apply [F9] to the given surface, fixed pointwise on its boundary. The resulting surface is neat. Incompressibility passes to it, and a boundary-compressing witness passes in either direction; absence of boundary compressions therefore passes as well. Work with this neat representative for the following smooth collar constructions. The boundary-fixing topological ambient extension pulls any resulting boundary-parallel product back to the actual original surface. Thus this preparation does not add a neatness hypothesis to the Statement. Write $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha$ is the essential proper arc in $A$ and $\beta$ lies in a boundary torus $T$. In an annulus every essential proper arc joins its two boundary circles: cut along a radial spanning arc and use a lift to the strip; an arc returning to the same boundary cuts off a disk there. Consequently both boundary circles of $A$ lie on this same $T$. They are essential on $T$: otherwise choose an innermost disk bounded by one of them in $T$, push it inward off the annulus collar, and obtain a compression of $A$. By [F2] the two circles cut $T$ into two parametrized annuli. The interior of $\beta$ misses them and joins them, so it spans one of these annuli, denoted $A_0$. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Push the interior of $A_0$ a little into its inward collar, keeping its rim on $A$, and round the rim. The union $S=A\cup A_0$ is a torus with a displayed corner before rounding. The curve $\alpha\cup\beta$ on it meets a core of $A$ once algebraically, not merely modulo two: $\alpha$ is a spanning arc of the annulus. It is therefore a nonseparating essential circle. Compress $S$ along $D$, taking two parallel copies of $D$ in its disk neighborhood; the result is a sphere. Irreducibility supplies a parametrized ball bounded by it. The disk neighborhood lies outside this ball: its strip along $\beta$ is joined to $\partial M$ through the gap left when that strip was removed from $A_0$, without crossing the compressed sphere. A ball in the interior cannot contain that boundary collar. Restoring the disk neighborhood therefore attaches one marked $1$-handle to the ball, rather than removing a possibly knotted handle from it. Its two attaching disk windows have the actual parallel-copy parameters of $D$. They can be put in standard positions by [F3]: standardize one window, shrink the other in the connected complement of the first on the boundary sphere, and move it to the opposite standard disk by the finite supported construction in [F3]'s Proof 1.1–2.1, fixing the first. Thus the restored region $U$ is a smooth solid torus with meridian disk the cocore of this handle. Its boundary is the displayed $S$; all corner changes are restored by the original quadrant collars. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The marking is essential. In the product coordinates $U=D^2\times S^1$ supplied by that ball and handle, let $(\mu,\lambda)$ denote the meridian-longitude basis of its boundary. Each rim circle of $A$ meets the cocore boundary once algebraically, because it meets $\alpha\cup\beta$ once. Hence its slope is $p\mu+q\lambda$ with $q=\pm1$. By [F2] normalize the two rim circles to affine circles of that slope. The entire boundary isotopy extends into a radial annulus of $D^2\times S^1$: in the boundary radial coordinate use the same formula $(r,x)\mapsto(r,h_{\eta(r)t}(x))$ as [F3], identity near the inner solid torus. The product diffeomorphism $(z,e^{i\theta})\mapsto(e^{ip\theta}z,e^{iq\theta})$, with inverse $(z,e^{i\varphi})\mapsto(e^{-ipq\varphi}z,e^{iq\varphi})$, carries longitudinal circles to that slope, up to replacing $p$ by its negative according to the chosen inverse. Apply its inverse. The two complementary boundary annuli now correspond to the two arcs between two points on $\partial D^2$, times $S^1$. The disk with one of these marked arcs is a rectangle with its bottom edge marked, with the usual rounded-corner interpretation, by [F3] in dimension two. Taking its product with $S^1$ gives a product between the corresponding annuli: the first is $A\times\{0\}$, and $A\times\{1\}\cup\partial A\times[0,1]$ is the second annulus $A_0$. Restore the retained quadrant collars to get this product for the actual original $A$ and boundary annulus in $\partial M$. This proves boundary-parallelity in [F1]'s precise sense. The winding-one condition from $D$ is what justifies this product; complementary annuli in an arbitrary solid torus do not suffice. All selected charts, windows and curve moves were finite, and [F2]–[F3] require no choice. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎
