## Statement

Let $n\ge1$. Supply a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold $V$ with boundary a marked knot zero surgery, $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ and $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$, and exactly $r$ integral pairs $x_i,y_i\in H_2(V;\mathbb Z[\pi/\pi^{(n)}])$, $\pi=\pi_1(V)$, satisfying $\lambda(x_i,x_j)=0$ and $\lambda(x_i,y_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Form $W$ by any finite sequence of the actual marked standard connected-sum and winding-zero infection cobordism adjunctions along outgoing knot-surgery components, including orientation reversals, using supplied smooth peripheral products and collars. Let $\phi:\pi_1(W)\to\Gamma$ have PTFA target and restrict on $V$ through $\pi/\pi^{(n)}$. Take $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$ and put $A=k[\Gamma]$, with involutive Ore fraction division ring $K$ and the based standard parallel Hermitian structure.

The image pairs $\ell_i,d_i\in H_2(W;A)$ satisfy $\lambda(\ell_i,\ell_j)=0$ and $\lambda(\ell_i,d_j)=\lambda(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$. Their localized boundary-intersection cokernel has dimension at most $2r$. For each boundary component $M_0$ on which $\phi$ is nontrivial, $H_1(M_0;K)=0$, its coefficient Bockstein–duality linking form is defined, and its actual inclusion kernel is isotropic:
$$B_{M_0}(z,w)=0\quad\text{for all }z,w\in\ker\{H_1(M_0;A)\to H_1(W;A)\}.$$
Thus every boundary class with nonzero self-pairing survives in $H_1(W;A)$ and lies outside every isotropic submodule. If a component's coefficient image is cyclic, its form additionally has the nonsingularity furnished by the cyclic-image coefficient theorem; no unrestricted PTFA nonsingularity is asserted.

For a finite forest of iterated winding-zero infections with these initial data, suppose each top meridian generates $H_1(W_n;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ up to sign, and each pattern-axis integral classical self-pairing is nonzero. Use the actual intermediate $W_j$, rational mixed coefficients through index $n$, and one bottom field $\mathbb F_p$. For every odd prime outside the explicit finite exceptional set of the axis values, every branch meridian has a nonzero class in $P^{n-j}\pi_1(W_j)/P^{n-j+1}\pi_1(W_j)$, of infinite order when $j>0$ and order $p$ when $j=0$. All these conclusions hold for the supplied locally flat topological bordisms and smooth bordisms without a choice principle. Existence of the initial $V$ and its lifted pairs from a concordance relation is a separate hypothesis, as are analytic rho invariance and signature vanishing.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The actual initial integral homology and pair data, finite marked standard adjunctions, coefficient homomorphism and field, and the extra finite-forest hypotheses when that conclusion is invoked.

[F1] Integral pair data persist under the actual standard adjunctions, whose ordinary boundary homology maps give nonincreasing boundary cokernel dimension. For PTFA targets factoring through the initial derived quotient, the localized bound and every selected boundary-kernel isotropy follow in the full supplied topological scope. [F2] The full simultaneous finite-forest induction gives actual mixed-derived meridian survival and exact orders from one supplied initial integral-pair bordism, using the finite exceptional-prime set for nonzero integral axis self-values. [[thm-unimodular-infection-tower-data-force-mixed-derived-meridian-survival]]

[F3] Integral and field PTFA group rings have the compatible involution and fractions; a closed component's cyclic coefficient image gives nonsingularity when its fraction-field first homology vanishes. [[lem-ptfa-integral-and-field-group-rings-have-compatible-ore-involutions]], [[lem-higher-order-blanchfield-pairings-are-nonsingular]]

## Proof

1.1 The supplied height-$n$ integral pairs and the factorization of $\phi|_{\pi_1(V)}$ verify the exact input of [F1]. Its coefficient extension, cap naturality and Hermitian symmetry give the zero and both unit cross-pairings for their actual images in $W$. The ordinary homology computation bounds $\dim_k\operatorname{coker}(H_2(\partial W;k)\to H_2(W;k))$ by $2r$; its full topological rank comparison bounds the localized cokernel by this ordinary dimension. Thus the displayed pairs and localized rank bound are established for the actual supplied $W$, including all orientations and finite attachment orders. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Every remaining boundary component is a marked knot zero surgery and has ordinary first Betti number one over $k$. By [F1], a nontrivial restricted PTFA system makes its first $K$ homology zero, so its Bockstein–duality form is defined. The same theorem applies the finite pairs and the localized bound from step 1.1 to give exactly the asserted kernel isotropy, without a vanishing assumption on any other boundary component. This is the boundary-kernel conclusion used in the source's Blanchfield-bordism argument. It does not require invertibility of an arbitrary noncommutative universal-coefficient evaluation map. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 If $B_{M_0}(z,z)\ne0$, the class $z$ cannot belong to the inclusion kernel of step 2.1, since all self-values in that kernel are zero. Its image in $H_1(W;A)$ is therefore nonzero. The same reasoning excludes it from every isotropic submodule. If the coefficient image on a closed component is cyclic, step 2.1 verifies the fraction-field vanishing required by [F3], and that theorem supplies its additional nonsingularity. For a general PTFA image only the defined form and the proved isotropic kernel are used. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 In the finite-forest situation, each intermediate $W_{j+1}$ is obtained from the same $V$ by a finite list of standard adjunctions. Its coefficient target $\Gamma_j=\pi_1(W_{j+1})/P^{n-j}\pi_1(W_{j+1})$ has rational-prefix derived length at most $n-j\le n$, so the restriction to $V$ factors through $\pi/\pi^{(n)}$. Step 1.1 supplies the finite intersection data required in [F2] for all these actual intermediate manifolds and fields. The stipulated top-meridian homology condition supplies its base case, and its integral-axis reduction gives the common finite exceptional prime set. Apply [F2] to obtain precisely the simultaneous nonzero mixed factors and infinite/prime orders in the Statement, with the actual inclusion quotient maps. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The constructions use only the stated initial integral-pair data and the actual supplied finite adjunctions; [F1] and [F2] establish them without smoothing the initial topological manifold or choosing arbitrary infinite bases. The resulting multi-boundary bordisms have the finite Lagrangian-pair and kernel-isotropy properties proved above. These properties do not identify a nonzero-self axis with an isotropic kernel, and do not assert that such a multi-boundary manifold is itself an integral half-solution. No analytic rho conclusion or existence of initial pair data was used. This completes every stated supplied-data conclusion. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

The original carrier incorrectly described the iterated multi-boundary infection bordism as an integral half-solution and its infection axes as a metabolizer. An integral knot half-solution has a single prescribed surgery boundary; moreover an axis with nonzero self-value cannot lie in an isotropic metabolizer. The actual source uses an initial solution $V$ and proves finite Lagrangian-pair and Blanchfield-kernel properties for its standard adjunctions. ## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a closed simply connected oriented smooth Riemannian four-manifold with positive-definite intersection form, and let $P\to X$ be an $SU(2)$ bundle with $c_2(P)[X]=-1$. Use the unbased $H^3/H^4$ quotient and the determinant-line orientation. There is a compatible perturbation procedure as follows: prepare the finitely many reducible circle-slice obstruction maps by arbitrarily small equivariant finite-rank smoothing perturbations, and make a further generic bounded smoothing perturbation on finitely many bounded irreducible slice collars in a middle region. The procedure is fixed near the prepared reducibles and vanishes on the entire small-instanton end. The further choices may be made arbitrarily small; they form a relatively open dense transverse class on the prescribed smaller middle collars.

The resulting regular irreducible zero set is an oriented five-manifold. Its ideal completion is compact, has one small-instanton boundary stratum identified with $X$, and has exactly the finitely many prepared reducible cone points, with no other strata. A neighborhood of each cone point is a cone on $\mathbb{CP}^2$. Delete smaller open cone neighborhoods and add the small-instanton boundary. The result is a smooth compact oriented five-manifold with boundary $X$ and one projective-plane link for each actual reducible orbit, with their induced orientations. Each projective link has one of the two complex-orientation signs; no common sign or numerical spectral-flow computation is asserted. The orientation on the component with the small-instanton end can be chosen so that this boundary is $X$ with its given orientation. The number of projective links is at most $b_2(X)$.

## Statement references

[Donaldson, *An Application of Gauge Theory to the Topology of 4-Manifolds*, §§II.1–II.4 and III.3–III.4](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/donaldson.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The original equation, charge and unbased conventions are fixed by [[def-asd-moduli-fredholm-index-and-lattice-setup]].

[F2] The actual reducible classification, its bound by $b_2(X)$, and equivariant finite obstruction perturbations with local cone $\mathbb C^3/S^1$ are proved in [[lem-reducible-charge-one-su-two-connections-admit-controlled-projective-links]].

[F3] On finite bounded irreducible slice collars, bounded smoothing sections give open dense transversality and an oriented five-dimensional zero set. The proof applies around any fixed bounded smoothing section, using its actual compact zero-container and finite cokernel directions. [[lem-asd-regularity-perturbation-and-orientability]]

[F4] Unperturbed ideal compactness and the full inverse small-instanton collar, including exhaustion and uniqueness, are proved in [[lem-uhlenbeck-compactness-and-removable-singularities]] and [[thm-taubes-small-instanton-gluing-and-compactified-end]].

[F5] The high-order Coulomb Green estimate and compact $H^4\hookrightarrow H^3$ inclusion hold also at a reducible smooth center, after retaining its finite kernel term in the estimate. Full AC is inherited from the analytic and topological providers. [[lem-high-sobolev-coulomb-slices-for-irreducible-su-two-connections]] [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The manifold, bundle, sign and quotient in the Statement, with full AC.

1.1 **Prepare precisely the actual reducibles.** Apply [F2] to their finite set and choose disjoint bounded invariant slice neighborhoods. Its constructed smoothing section $\sigma_r$ is supported in their union and vanishes at the central reducible points. On smaller neighborhoods its zeros are equivariant smooth graphs over $\mathbb C^3$; the punctured quotients are smooth oriented five-manifolds, and cutting their graph-radius gives projective links. There are no additional reducible solutions inside these slice neighborhoods: the stabilizer of a nearby orbit is a subgroup of the center's circle by the local slice construction; a reducible orbit must therefore be fixed by that circle. On its fixed diagonal subspace the equivariant off-diagonal perturbation is zero. The diagonal equation is the abelian self-dual equation, whose only local slice solution is the center because its $H^1$ is zero. Outside these neighborhoods the equation remains unperturbed, so [F2] lists all remaining reducibles. The construction is bounded and smooth into $H^3$ in these finitely many slices. [F1, F2, F5, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Compactness for this prepared equation and a genuine middle region.** The supports in step 1.1 are in bounded $H^3$ slice balls. For a zero in such a ball the equation $d_{A_i}^-a=-F_{A_i}^--(a\wedge a)^--\sigma_r(a)$ has bounded $H^3$ right side, since $H^3$ is an algebra and the section is uniformly $H^3$ bounded. Together with $d_{A_i}^*a=0$, the Green estimate [F5] bounds $a$ in $H^4$. Thus zeros there have compact $H^3$ closure, including along the edges of the support. Any sequence of zeros outside these balls is unperturbed, so [F4] supplies its smooth or ideal subsequence. The bounded balls cannot approach an ideal point: their curvature has a uniform $L^4$ bound from the $H^3$ bound, so its energy on a ball of volume tending to zero tends uniformly to zero by Holder. Therefore a sufficiently small whole ideal collar from [F4] misses all the supports. The prepared equation is literally unperturbed there, retaining its entire regular end. Delete a smaller portion of that collar and smaller reducible cone neighborhoods. The remaining zero set is compact and irreducible, by the two sequence arguments just given. Cover this compact set by finitely many bounded irreducible Coulomb-slice collars, avoiding the protected smaller end and cone neighborhoods, and choose larger/smaller radii as in [F3]. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Relative middle transversality with all ends preserved.** Apply the finite-dimensional cokernel-direction and Sard proof of [F3] to $\Phi+\sigma_r$ on these middle collars, multiplying its new directions by bumps supported there. The fixed $\sigma_r$ is allowed in those charts: transition gauges on bounded chart sets have uniform $H^4$ bounds, and its original finite smooth target vectors and coordinate cutoffs consequently have uniformly bounded $H^3$ representatives. The derivative is a compact perturbation of the original Fredholm slice derivative, so its index remains five. The actual compact zero-container in [F3] and its positive-minimum argument exclude all new middle zeros outside the chosen smaller covering neighborhoods when the finite parameters are small. Around the protected cone and ideal collars the equation and its regularity remain exactly as in steps 1.1–2.1; on the compact transition overlaps, openness of surjectivity preserves their regularity. Thus a sufficiently small regular finite parameter makes every irreducible zero transverse. The same proof gives openness and density for all further allowed small middle sections. Both perturbations are zero outside the finite original and middle slice neighborhoods. For every resulting zero sequence in their union the same bounded-section $H^4$ estimate gives a converging $H^3$ subsequence; outside their union [F4] applies unchanged. This proves compactness of the full ideal completion and excludes any other ends, without applying an unperturbed compactness theorem to a nonzero perturbation. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **The actual smooth cut bordism.** The determinant line orients the transverse irreducible zero set by [F3], and its compact-derivative homotopy includes the fixed reducible preparation. At the ideal stratum, [F4]'s actual center-scale diffeomorphism and homeomorphic ideal extension provide a smooth collar $X\times[0,\lambda_0)$. At each reducible, [F2]'s graph-radius coordinate gives the smooth punctured cone collar $(0,\delta)\times\mathbb{CP}^2$. Delete its part of radius less than a smaller positive number. These finitely many collars are disjoint from each other and from the ideal collar. Step 3.1 makes the remaining interior compact up to the displayed collars, so the cut completion is a compact smooth five-manifold with exactly those boundary components. The induced boundary orientation on each projective link is its complex orientation or its negative. On the unique component meeting the connected ideal boundary choose the determinant orientation's global sign so this boundary orientation agrees with the given orientation of $X$; arbitrary other components cause no additional boundary strata. The number of links is exactly the number of actual reducibles, bounded by [F2]. This proves the compatible perturbation, compactified-strata and smooth cut-bordism assertions. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Donaldson's actual printed280–281, full reducible and perturbation argument on287–295, full end proof on300–311 and Appendix312–314 were read. Two necessary corrections to the original formalization are explicit: arbitrary regular perturbations need not preserve the prescribed end, and the raw compactification has reducible cone points rather than being a smooth manifold there. The controlled procedure and deleting cone neighborhoods give the actual source's smooth bordism. The source explicitly leaves its projective boundary signs undetermined at this stage; the induced determinant orientations suffice for the subsequent signature inequality, without fabricating a spectral-flow calculation.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $L$ be a free abelian group of rank $n$ with an integer-valued symmetric bilinear form whose Gram determinant is $1$ or $-1$, and let $f:L\to\mathbb Z^n$ be an isometric homomorphism, where $\mathbb Z^n$ has its standard dot product. Then $f(L)=\mathbb Z^n$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A rank-$n$ free abelian group $L$, a unimodular integral symmetric form on $L$, and an isometric homomorphism $f$ to the standard dot-product lattice $\mathbb Z^n$.

[A1] The stated Gram determinant has absolute value one; the argument is finite integral linear algebra and uses no choice axiom.

[F1] If $A\in M_n(\mathbb Z)$ has nonzero determinant, then the subgroup $A\mathbb Z^n$ has index $|\det A|$ in $\mathbb Z^n$. [[cor-index-of-a-full-rank-integer-sublattice-is-the-absolute-determinant]]

## Proof

1.1 Choose an integral basis of $L$ and let $B$ be the integer $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are the images of that basis under $f$. Since $f$ is isometric, the Gram matrix of $L$ is $B^{\mathsf T}B$. [given, A1, choose, construct]

1.2 Taking determinants gives $1=|\det(B^{\mathsf T}B)|=|\det B|^2$, hence $\det B=1$ or $-1$. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and step 1.2, the image subgroup $B\mathbb Z^n=f(L)$ has index $|\det B|=1$ in $\mathbb Z^n$. The quotient therefore has one element, which means $B\mathbb Z^n=\mathbb Z^n$ and $f(L)=\mathbb Z^n$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

## Statement references

[Jessica S. Purcell, *Hyperbolic Knot Theory*, Lemma 4.6](https://users.monash.edu/~jpurcell/book/HypKnotTheory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A positively oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized upper half-space position with shape $z$, $\operatorname{Im}z>0$.

[F1] [[def-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-and-cusp-holonomy]] defines its edge parameters as $z$, $1/(1-z)$ and $(z-1)/z$, one for each opposite-edge pair.

## Proof

1.1 Since $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, the imaginary parts of $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$ and $z''=1-1/z$ are all positive: the second is $\operatorname{Im}z/|1-z|^2$, and the third is $\operatorname{Im}z/|z|^2$. Thus their principal arguments lie in $(0,\pi)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Multiplication gives $zz'z''=z\cdot(1-z)^{-1}\cdot(z-1)z^{-1}=-1$. The sum of the three arguments is therefore an odd multiple of $\pi$; because it lies strictly between $0$ and $3\pi$, it must equal $\pi$. The arguments are the dihedral angles by the edge cross-ratio convention in [F1]. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, $1-\omega=\omega^{-1}$ and $\omega-1=\omega^2$. Hence $1/(1-\omega)=\omega$ and $(\omega-1)/\omega=\omega$; each parameter has argument $\pi/3$. Each of the three parameter arguments occurs on a pair of opposite edges, proving the regular-angle assertion. [given, F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[Jessica S. Purcell, *Hyperbolic Knot Theory*, Lemma 4.6](https://users.monash.edu/~jpurcell/book/HypKnotTheory.pdf)

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Every $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$ satisfies
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The full-space L² TV is the extended distributional test-field supremum.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality|For globally integrable BV functions in two dimensions, $\|v\|_2\le TV(v)$.]]

[[lem-ip-tv-l2-cutoff-approximation|Compactly supported BV cutoffs approximate every finite-variation L² function.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with finite $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[A1] Countable Choice supplies the finite-Radon representation used in the cutoff approximation. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-cutoff-approximation]]: there are $v_k\in BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ with $v_k\to u$ in $L^2$ and $\limsup_kTV(v_k;\mathbb R^2)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality]]: every globally integrable $v\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfies $\|v\|_2\le TV(v;\mathbb R^2)$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], choose $v_k\in BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ with $v_k\to u$ in $L^2$ and the stated variation upper bound. Apply [F2] to each $v_k$ to obtain $\|v_k\|_2\le TV(v_k;\mathbb R^2)$. [A1, F1, F2, given, choose]

2.1 Norm continuity gives $\|v_k\|_2\to\|u\|_2$, so
$$\|u\|_2=\lim_k\|v_k\|_2\le\limsup_kTV(v_k;\mathbb R^2)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$
This is the required inequality. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(S,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\gamma,w,z)$ be a strictly strongly admissible pointed Heegaard triple for a decorated knot cobordism, with the strong condition normalized at ALL $w$ marks. Fix one Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s$ and nonnegative $w,z$-multiplicities. In positive symmetric rank $m=h+k-1>0$, among the auxiliary Heegaard data first choose an arbitrarily small pointed Hamiltonian representative with no common intersection of three attaching families, following the pair generators and transporting the actual Spin-c label and strict admissibility. Such positive-rank representatives exist. Fix that representative; this is an explicit curve choice, not a claim that varying the almost-complex tensor alone regularizes constant triangles on the original arbitrary fixed triple.

At rank $m=0$, keep the original empty attaching systems: the target is one point and no triple-torus exclusion is imposed. Its unique constant triangle, when its assigned Spin-c label and zero marked-degree vectors match the specified ones, is regular of index zero and contributes one; all other specified-label or positive-degree sets are empty. The fixed index-one and universal index-minus-one spaces are empty, and a matching one-parameter family is the parameter interval.

In positive rank choose regular end data in the open dense set of allowed genuine constant-collar paths described in the proof. For generic fixed source-dependent almost-complex data compatible with those ends, the Maslov-index-zero triangle moduli spaces used in the triangle-count map are regular zero-manifolds and finite. For generic one-parameter families with those fixed regular ends, the universal triangle moduli spaces are regular with the parameter included in the expected dimension; slice counts are taken at regular parameter values. The compactified one-dimensional Maslov-index-one triangle spaces have precisely the broken triangle/strip strata, with actual gluing collars. In these dimensions no nonconstant one-torus boundary degeneration is allowed: its index contribution is at least two and the remaining triangle would have negative count dimension. In a one-parameter family the compactified universal index-zero spaces additionally have the two parameter-endpoint strata; the zero-dimensional universal index-minus-one spaces define the homotopy terms.

The mod-two boundary counts give the weighted bilinear triangle chain-map equation and its chain homotopy. Inserting an actual intermediate cycle gives the corresponding one-input chain-map equation. All nonnegative marked multiplicities and the fixed Spin-c extension are retained, including intermediate closed three-manifolds beyond $S^3$ and multiple mark pairs. No additional ends arise from sphere bubbling, escape through nonzero periodic domains or uncontrolled marked-point multiplicities. This analytic assertion does not itself establish that a named top generator is a cycle or prove invariance under changing the chosen attaching curves.

## Statement references

[[def-admissible-pointed-heegaard-floer-data|Pointed Heegaard data and admissibility]]

[[thm-strictly-admissible-triple-free-polygons-have-full-marked-low-dimensional-counts|Independent raw full-marked polygon counts and their fixed Spin-c labels]]

[[lem-heegaard-floer-holomorphic-disk-regularity-compactness-gluing|The disk-analysis supplier and its stated scope]]

[[lem-weighted-moduli-boundary-counts-give-floer-chain-identities|The finite weighted boundary-count assembly, conditional on the actual analytic boundary theorem]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Holomorphic disks and topological invariants for closed three-manifolds*, §§3.2–3.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0101206)

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, Chapter 16](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the actual strictly strongly admissible balanced triple, fixed Spin-c extension and marked multiplicities, and the auxiliary curve and end choices specified in the Statement.

[F1] In positive rank, small pointed Hamiltonian representatives avoiding triple torus intersections exist, with pair generators followed without births, an integral swept-annulus transport of domains and an actual smooth source-dependent transport of polygon map spaces. This uses no global symmetric power of a nonholomorphic surface map. ([[lem-pointed-transverse-multidiagrams-admit-small-triple-free-curve-representatives]])

[F2] The actual finite Morse Spin-c construction, capped-domain difference, attaching-curve collar transport and strict positive-domain bounds are proved. The collar transport carries the lift including torsion and preserves the Chern functional and all old admissibility witnesses. ([[lem-heegaard-polygon-spin-c-difference-is-the-capped-periodic-domain]], [[lem-strong-polygon-admissibility-bounds-indices-and-positive-domains]])

[F3] Actual full-marked low-dimensional polygon analysis proves the open dense good end choices, source-dependent universal transversality, finite counts, index budgets, compact one-manifold boundaries and exhaustive gluing, on general balanced intermediate three-manifolds. Its proof includes the finite lower-index band and excludes all nonconstant nonpositive-index strips before analyzing limiting levels. ([[thm-strictly-admissible-triple-free-polygons-have-full-marked-low-dimensional-counts]])

[F4] **Raw count convention, independent of any cobordism-map construction.** Put $R=\mathbb F_2[U,V]$ and let $C_{\alpha\beta},C_{\beta\gamma},C_{\alpha\gamma}$ be the free $R$-modules on the actual finite pair-intersection generators, with the differentials supplied by [F3]. For the fixed total Spin-c label define $F:C_{\alpha\beta}\otimes_R C_{\beta\gamma}\to C_{\alpha\gamma}$ on basis pairs by counting the actual rigid triangles of [F3], each with weight $U^{\sum n_w}V^{\sum n_z}$, and extend $R$-bilinearly. Define $H$ by the corresponding universal index-minus-one counts for a fixed-end one-parameter family. Finiteness and label/degree additivity are [F2]–[F3]; the finite weighted boundary assembly is [[lem-weighted-moduli-boundary-counts-give-floer-chain-identities]]. An auxiliary chain $\Theta$ is used only if actually supplied, with finite support and $d\Theta=0$; its substitution is an algebraic operation. No distinguished top class, elementary cobordism map, decomposition independence or movie theorem is a premise of these raw counts.

## Proof

1.1 Treat rank zero directly. The target and all empty product tori are one point. The fixed-map operator is the zero map from the zero section space to the zero forcing space; it is onto of index zero. The three-marked source has no conformal parameter or automorphism. Hence its unique map is a regular isolated triangle with all marked degrees zero, in its assigned constant-class Spin-c extension. With another prescribed label or a nonzero degree vector the relevant set is empty. A fixed index-one triangle or universal index-minus-one triangle cannot occur. A matching one-parameter family is exactly its compact parameter interval, with its two identical endpoint counts; there are no nonconstant strips, spheres or boundary disks. Thus its differential is zero and its triangle and parameter-boundary identities hold directly. No strip translation is divided out and no empty tuple is claimed to supply a constituent surface point. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Now suppose that $m>0$ and apply [F1] with the marked points and one witness in every original region protected. The resulting representative has no triple torus intersection and has the same followed pair generators. [F2]'s actual collar extension carries the compression disks and Morse data, identifies the actual Spin-c lift and capped classes, and preserves every old strict witness coefficient under the swept-annulus lattice isomorphism. Thus the new triple has the same required strict admissibility and Spin-c indexing. Its polygon spaces represent exactly the transported literal continuous classes, not classes modulo a sphere or fundamental-group action. A constant triangle would lie in all three tori, so none occurs. This explicitly permitted auxiliary curve choice is necessary: at a constant triangle the almost-complex parameter derivative vanishes because $du=0$, so no J-only universal argument can be substituted for it. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F3] to this actual triple and its restricted pair sectors. The geometric strict-domain theorem first supplies a finite lower strip index and finite nonnegative domains in every upper-index band. Its actual auxiliary all-index regular path and bubble budget then produce the open dense good genuine-collar end data with no nonconstant index at most zero and index-one regularity. Hence the ensuing polygon limits have the required regular strip levels; a claim of index-one regularity alone would not justify that conclusion. The source-local Hilbert perturbations give actual fixed-data and one-parameter universal transversality at every nonconstant triangle, preserving the protected divisors, tori and exact product-angle end charts. There are no constant triangles by step1.2. [F2, F3, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 A triangle has three marked ends and no conformal modulus or translation action. Its fixed count index is therefore $\mu$, and a one-parameter universal count has index $\mu+1$. The domain bounds in [F2] and actual domain-area inequality in [F3] give one energy bound for each required low-dimensional set, across all its literal classes and all nonnegative degree vectors. Every limiting nonconstant strip has positive index. Every nonconstant disk bubble contributes at least two, every sphere at least $2k$, and every regular triangle vertex has nonnegative count dimension. The unconditional determinant index budget of [F3] thus excludes all bubbles in count dimensions zero and one. The only broken one-dimensional ends have one rigid triangle and one rigid strip. The same calculation with the family parameter counted ONCE gives rigid universal index-minus-one triangles and the stated universal index-zero ends. This retains $k=1$ and general intermediate $Y$; it does not borrow a knot-in-$S^3$ disk theorem outside its scope. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The actual product-chart, correction and exhaustion proof in [F3] supplies exactly one collar for every such compatible broken pair. Its global tail estimate promotes compact-core convergence to the true Sobolev chart, so a rigid total set is compact discrete and finite under Countable Choice. Its explicit Hausdorff collar compactification of a one-dimensional space is a compact one-manifold with finite boundary. Degree vectors and the actual total Spin-c structure are carried by each neck smoothing; restricting either these labels or an actual class gives the corresponding open-and-closed part. Thus neither multiple classes with the same domain nor the Spin-c extension orbit creates a missing or an extra end. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Count the boundary of this actual compact one-manifold over $\mathbb F_2$. Writing $F$ for the bilinear triangle count, the strip breaks give $dF+F(d\otimes1)+F(1\otimes d)=0$. The marked vectors add at each actual gluing, so the component weights multiply, with every $w,z$ exponent retained. For a fixed-end one-parameter family its universal one-manifold also has the two parameter endpoints; the universal index-minus-one counts $H$ give $F_1+F_0=dH+H(d\otimes1)+H(1\otimes d)$. These are finite weighted equations, also after specializing every $w$ color to $U$ and every $z$ color to $V$. If the intermediate input $\Theta$ is an actual cycle, substituting it removes the $F(1\otimes d)$ term and gives the required one-input chain map and homotopy. Together with the direct point model in step1.1 and the raw convention [F4], this proves exactly the analytic identities. No existence or cycle property of a distinguished top input, elementary cobordism-map construction, or movie-invariance theorem has been assumed to obtain them. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Logical scope of the raw construction

The geometric and analytic inputs [F1]–[F3] precede this lemma and contain no hypothesis that a decorated cobordism map already exists. Fact [F4] is a finite bilinear count definition and an auxiliary-cycle substitution, not such a map theorem. Distinguished auxiliary cycles and the independently sourced cobordism construction are downstream uses. This ordering preserves the full closed-three-manifold, two-color, marked-degree and fixed-label Statement.

## Statement

Let $F_r$ be the free group with Magnus expansion $E$, let $u,\lambda\in F_r$,
and let $w$ be a nonempty word of length $m$. The coefficient of $X_w$ in
$E(u^{-1}\lambda u)-E(\lambda)$ is an integer linear combination of
coefficients of $E(\lambda)$ on proper contiguous subwords of $w$. Thus, when
$w$ is the prefix of a Milnor index $I=(w,j)$, conjugating the longitude can
change its degree-$m$ coefficient only by an integer combination of
coefficients indexed by proper subsequences of $I$.

## Statement references

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§3–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

[Stees, §2.5](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/54c7d68f-d982-4e1f-9550-e54140ada5ea/content)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The noncommutative formal-series ring, augmentation ideal $\mathfrak m$, and Magnus expansion in the preceding definition.

[F1] Every Magnus expansion has constant term $1$, its positive-degree part lies in $\mathfrak m$, and multiplication concatenates words. [[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links]]

## Proof

1.1 Write $E(u)=1+U$ and $E(\lambda)=1+V$ with $U,V\in\mathfrak m$. Then
$$E(u^{-1}\lambda u)-E(\lambda) =(1+U)^{-1}V(1+U)-V.$$
Expand $(1+U)^{-1}=\sum_{a\geq0}(-U)^a$. The term with no $U$ on either side is $V$ and cancels the subtracted $V$. Every remaining term is a product $(-U)^a VU^b$ with $a+b\geq1$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 A coefficient of degree $m$ in such a product uses a degree-$p$ monomial of $U^a$, a degree-$s$ monomial of $V$, and a degree-$q$ monomial of $U^b$ with $p+s+q=m$ and $p+q\geq1$. The $V$ monomial therefore has degree $s<m$ and occupies a contiguous middle block of the target word $w$, while the nonempty left or right block comes from $U$. Summing the finitely many decompositions of $w$ expresses its coefficient as an integer linear combination of coefficients of $E(\lambda)$ on proper contiguous subwords. Appending the longitude index $j$ makes each such index a proper subsequence of $(w,j)$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $Q$ be a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron with a fixed finite linear triangulation $T$. If $f:P\to Q$ is a piecewise-linear embedding of a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron, then some finite subdivision $T'$ of $T$ contains $f(P)$ as the realization of a subcomplex.

## Statement references

[[def-pl-embedding-and-subpolyhedron]] — the image of a piecewise-linear embedding is a subpolyhedron in some finite triangulation.

[[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]] — a subcomplex is closed under taking faces.

[[lem-two-finite-linear-subdivisions-have-a-common-simplicial-refinement]] — finite linear triangulations of the same polyhedron have a common refinement.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compact piecewise-linear polyhedron $Q$, a finite linear triangulation $T$ of $Q$, and a piecewise-linear embedding $f:P\to Q$.

[F1] [[def-pl-embedding-and-subpolyhedron]]: $f(P)$ is a subcomplex in some finite linear triangulation $T_0$ of $Q$.

[F2] [[lem-two-finite-linear-subdivisions-have-a-common-simplicial-refinement]]: two finite linear triangulations of the same polyhedron have a common finite linear refinement.

[F3] [[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]]: a subcomplex is closed under taking faces.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], choose a finite linear triangulation $T_0$ of $Q$ in which $f(P)$ is a subcomplex. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Apply [F2] to $T$ and $T_0$ to obtain a common finite linear refinement $T'$. It is a subdivision of $T$, and it refines every simplex of the subcomplex representing $f(P)$; therefore the simplices of $T'$ contained in $f(P)$ form a subcomplex by [F3], with realization exactly $f(P)$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let P be a pattern and let K be a knot. Choose a transverse meridional disk for P and a short product slab about it. Form a pattern P_K by replacing all strands of P across that slab by parallel untwisted copies of a long-knot representative of K, with the individual strand orientations inherited from P; this is simultaneous companion insertion, rather than tying K into just one arc. For every knot J, the satellite P(K#J) is isotopic as an oriented knot to P_K(J). The pattern P_K has the same winding number as P.

## Statement references

[CDR, Lemma 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.5058v3)

[Livingston, §9](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/living.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The pattern $P$, knots $K,J$, the transverse meridional disk and product slab specified in the Statement, and the preferred zero framings.

[F1] A satellite inserts the complete pattern into the companion's zero-framed tubular neighborhood, matching its meridian and preferred longitude. [[def-satellite-induced-concordance-operator]], [[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number]]

[F2] Connected sum joins two long-knot representatives end to end with their endpoint product coordinates matched. [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

[F3] Coordinate disks have smooth cutoffs, and an everywhere invertible derivative gives a smooth local inverse. [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]], [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]

## Proof

1.1 A transverse meridional disk exists for every smooth pattern, without a selection axiom. Parametrize $P$ by its supplied circle embedding and compose with the angular projection of the solid torus to obtain a smooth circle map $f$. Its angular derivative is a continuous real function on the parameter circle. For $0<\delta<1/2$, uniform continuity allows a partition into finitely many equal short intervals such that on any interval meeting the zero set of $f'$ one has $|f'|<\delta$. Make the intervals short enough to lift the map to real angular coordinates there. The images of these intervals have total arc length at most $\delta$, by integrating this derivative bound over intervals of total length at most one. Those finitely many image arcs cannot cover the target circle of length one: cutting at their finitely many endpoints and adding the lengths proves this finite covering inequality directly. Choose an angle outside them. Every preimage is regular, so its meridional disk is transverse; the case of empty preimage is allowed. Only one angle and finitely many intervals are selected. The specified transverse disk in the Statement may be any such disk. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Represent $K\#J$ by concatenating long representatives of $K$ and $J$, each constant in its endpoint product collars, and then closing by the fixed trivial outside arc. Use their zero-framed tubular products, glued by the identity on the two normal disk coordinates. This is the zero-framed product of the connected sum: a longitude and the core have linking zero on each of the two separated summand portions, their connecting parallel arcs are untwisted, and cross linking vanishes because those portions lie in disjoint balls. Their total linking is therefore zero. This checks the framing rather than introducing an unspecified meridional twist at the concatenation. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let the disk meet $P$ in the finite transverse set $p_1,\ldots,p_m$. Finiteness follows because this inverse image is a compact discrete subset of the compact knot. Shrink the slab so that its intersection with $P$ consists of exactly $m$ arcs crossing from one disk face to the other. Indeed transversality gives each intersection a local graph over the slab coordinate; finitely many disjoint such neighborhoods suffice, and the compact remaining part of $P$ is disjoint from the central disk and hence from a sufficiently short slab. Straighten the graph arcs in disjoint small disks about the $p_j$. Explicitly, if the $j$th graph has disk coordinate $p_j(t)$, use $(q,t)\mapsto(q+\chi_j(q)(p_j(0)-p_j(t)),t)$, with $\chi_j=1$ near that graph and zero outside its disk. Work first in a slightly larger slab and multiply the displacement by a smooth time-coordinate cutoff $\tau(t)$ equal to one on the inner slab and zero near the larger slab faces. Thus the isotopy is the identity at the outside faces and glues to the identity off the larger slab. After shortening the slab its derivative in $q$ differs from the identity by norm less than $1/2$; the straight-line interpolation has the same bound and is an isotopy. Each disk map is a diffeomorphism: solve its inverse by the uniformly contracting iteration $q_{k+1}=z-\tau(t)\chi_j(q_k)(p_j(0)-p_j(t))$, and use [F3] at its everywhere invertible derivative to obtain smooth local inverses, which agree with this unique inverse. Thus the pattern can be represented as one remaining tangle joined to $m$ straight parallel strands across the chosen slab, with some of their orientations possibly reversed. [F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Cut a small standard arc from $K$, leaving a long knot in a product ball whose two end neighborhoods are straight. Its zero-framed normal product yields $m$ disjoint parallel copies, one for each supplied point $p_j$ after a disk-coordinate rescaling. The product is constant at the ends and its framing has no full twist. Insert this whole string link in the straight-strand slab and retain the other tangle from step 2.1. All endpoint coordinates agree, so the result is a smooth embedded oriented knot in the original solid torus, denoted $P_K$. Negative-oriented strands follow the same geometric parallel copy with the opposite orientation; they are not omitted or replaced by a differently framed tangle. [F1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Insert the tangle description of $P$ from step 2.1 into the product of step 1.2. Across the long $K$ portion it has exactly the $m$ parallel strands constructed in step 3.1. Across the long $J$ portion it has the corresponding parallel strands of $J$, and the remainder is the unchanged tangle of $P$. One may now absorb the $K$ portion into that remainder, leaving $J$ as the sole companion portion. The resulting tangle is precisely $P_K$ inserted into the zero-framed neighborhood of $J$. The disk products agree on every common face, so these are the same glued oriented embedding after the chosen product reparametrizations; smoothing the matching straight collars gives an oriented isotopy. Hence $P(K\#J)$ is isotopic to $P_K(J)$. No step replaces all $m$ strands by a local knot in one strand. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 Both the original straight $m$-strand tangle and its replacement lie in a product ball inside a slightly smaller meridional-disk slab containing all $p_j$, and they agree on its boundary. Their oriented difference is a one-cycle in that ball, hence bounds there (contract the ball linearly). They therefore represent the same class in the homology of the solid torus. Their algebraic coefficient of its core, namely the winding number, is unchanged. This proves the second conclusion as well, including winding zero and mixed strand orientations. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a supplied product tubular embedding $\Phi:S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}\to S^3$. There is a polygonal knot $P$ inside this tube and a smooth rounding $K'$ of $P$ such that $K'$ is smoothly ambient isotopic to $K$ by an isotopy supported in the tube. If $K$ is supplied with a finite regular projection diagram $D$, the polygonal approximation and rounding can be chosen to have the same crossing code as $D$. A homeomorphism supported in the larger tube carries $P$ to $K'$, preserves the boundary torus of the radius-$\epsilon$ tube, and sends each marked fibre meridian to itself up to orientation. Conversely, every polygonal knot $P$ with a finite product regular neighborhood can be rounded in pairwise disjoint vertex balls to a smooth knot $P^\sharp$; a homeomorphism supported in those balls carries its compact exterior and marked meridian to those of $P^\sharp$. If a regular projection diagram is supplied, the rounding balls can be chosen away from crossing charts, so the crossing code is unchanged. These clauses compare smooth knot type through smooth knots and polygonal exterior models through homeomorphisms; they do not treat a nonsmooth polygonal curve as a smooth isotopy slice.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]] — smooth knots and smooth ambient isotopy.

[[def-knot-exterior]] — the supplied product tube and compact exterior convention.

[[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]] — fibre meridian and peripheral marking.

[[thm-isotopy-extension]] — extension of the constructed smooth knot isotopy with support in the supplied tube.

[[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]] — regular projection and finite crossing-code conventions preserved by the approximation.

[[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]] — regular projection and finite crossing-code conventions preserved by the approximation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a smooth oriented knot $K$, its supplied product tube, and optionally a finite regular projection diagram $D$.

[F1] [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]: $K$ is a smooth embedding of $S^1$; smooth ambient isotopy is a path of ambient diffeomorphisms carrying the embedding at every time.

[F2] [[def-knot-exterior]]: the chosen tube defines a compact exterior and boundary torus.

[F3] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: a fibre circle of the normal disk tube is the marked meridian; an ambient map of the product tube transports this peripheral class.

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used through the existing smooth isotopy extension theorem; all partitions, approximations and local disk maps below use only finite constructions.

[F4] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ supplies the cutoff data in the smooth isotopy extension theorem.

[F5] [[thm-isotopy-extension]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a smooth isotopy of a compact source embedding whose track lies in an open set extends to a smooth ambient isotopy supported in that open set.

[F6] [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]] and [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]]: a finite regular diagram has finitely many transverse crossings, disjoint small crossing disks, and compact arc portions separated away from those disks; its crossing code records the local incidence and over/under order.

## Proof

1.1 Choose a point outside the compact tube image and use its stereographic chart to place that entire tube in $\mathbb R^3$. Reparameterize $K$ by arclength on the circle. The tubular projection to $K$ is smooth and has derivative equal to the identity along $K$. Compactness of $K$ and continuity of this derivative give a uniform $\delta>0$ such that every chord joining $K(s)$ to $K(s+h)$, with $0<h<\delta$, lies in the tube and has strictly increasing tubular projection from $s$ to $s+h$. Indeed, the chord direction divided by $h$ converges uniformly to $K'(s)$ as $h\to0$, and the differential of the projection converges uniformly to its value on the tangent. Choose a uniform finite partition of the parameter circle with mesh less than $\delta$ and join successive samples by these chords. Strict increase of the projection on each chord makes their union an embedded polygonal circle $P$ and makes its projection to $K$ a homeomorphism. If $D$ is supplied, its finitely many disjoint crossing disks and separated compact arc portions from [F6] give positive margins away from the transverse crossing neighborhoods; choose the mesh still finer so each polygonal strand stays within those margins and remains transverse with the same over/under height order in each crossing disk. Thus no new crossing occurs off those disks and exactly the declared crossing occurs in each disk. [given, F1, F6, construct]

1.2 For a polygonal knot $P$, choose pairwise disjoint small balls around its finitely many vertices, disjoint from the marked meridian point and any crossing charts. In each ball the knot is a single embedded polygonal arc with two straight end segments. Choose a linear coordinate along which both segments project monotonically; then the arc is the graph of a piecewise-linear transverse section over an interval. Smooth that section inside a smaller interval, fixed near its endpoints, to obtain a rounded arc. The changed arcs fit the unchanged edges smoothly, so the resulting $P^\sharp$ is a smooth knot and its diagram code is unchanged when crossing charts are avoided. [given, F1, F3, F6, construct]

2.1 In tube coordinates $P$ is the graph of a continuous, piecewise-smooth normal section $u:S^1\to D^2_{\epsilon/4}$. Smooth each of its finitely many corners inside pairwise disjoint short parameter intervals, leaving the section unchanged outside those intervals, to obtain a smooth section $q$ uniformly close to $u$. The graph $K'(s)=\Phi(s,q(s))$ is a smooth embedding because its first coordinate is $s$. The family $K_t(s)=\Phi(s,tq(s))$ consists of embeddings for the same reason, starts at $K$, ends at $K'$, and stays inside the supplied tube. [step 1.1, F1, construct]

3.1 Apply [F5] to the smooth isotopy $K_t$ with an open support neighborhood whose closure lies inside the radius-$2\epsilon$ tube. It gives an ambient smooth isotopy supported there carrying $K$ to $K'$. Its time-one diffeomorphism transports the chosen tube and its fibre meridians. This is the only use of $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in the argument. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1]

3.2 The two sections $u$ and $q$ lie in the interior quarter-disk. In each fibre disk, rescale to the unit disk and use the orientation-preserving disk automorphisms $M_a(z)=(z-a)/(1-\overline a z)$: the map $M_{q(s)}^{-1}\circ M_{u(s)}$ sends $u(s)$ to $q(s)$. These maps depend continuously on $s$ and send each boundary circle to itself. On the outer radial collar between radii $\epsilon$ and $2\epsilon$, lift each boundary-circle map to an increasing angle function $h_s(\theta)$ close to $\theta$ and interpolate it linearly with $\theta$ as the radius increases; convex combinations of increasing lifts remain increasing. The resulting fibre maps agree at radius $\epsilon$, are the identity at radius $2\epsilon$, and are homeomorphisms on every fibre. Their union, extended by the identity outside the larger tube, is a homeomorphism of $S^3$ carrying $P$ to $K'$. It preserves the radius-$\epsilon$ boundary torus and each fibre circle as a set, so it transports the marked meridian and identifies the compact exteriors. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 In each such ball, the old and rounded arcs are graphs of two close sections in a product chart. A fibrewise disk homeomorphism taking one section to the other, extended across a collar to be the identity near the ball boundary, gives a homeomorphism supported in the ball. The finitely many disjoint homeomorphisms paste together; they carry the regular neighborhood, exterior, boundary torus and meridian class to those of $P^\sharp$. This proves the converse rounding clause. Combining it with steps 3.1–3.2 proves all stated comparison clauses. [F2, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 1.2, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The PL and smooth maps are kept separate because the library's link definition uses smooth embeddings and diffeomorphisms, while a polygonal curve has corners. Smooth ambient isotopy is asserted only between smooth embeddings; exterior comparison with a polygonal model uses a peripheral-preserving homeomorphism.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $X$ be a closed oriented Riemannian four-manifold, let $P$ be a fixed principal $SU(2)$-bundle with charge $k=-\langle c_2(P),[X]\rangle$, and let $(A_j)$ be smooth connections satisfying $F_{A_j}^-=0$ and $\sup_j\int_X|F_{A_j}|^2\,d\mathrm{vol}<\infty$. Then a subsequence, bundle isomorphisms, and a finite set $S\subset X$ exist such that the transported connections converge in local Sobolev gauge on compact subsets of $X\setminus S$ to a self-dual connection on a possibly lower-charge bundle of charge $k_\infty$. For each $p\in S$ there is a positive integer bubble charge $m_p$, and $k=k_\infty+\sum_{p\in S}m_p$. The limiting connection extends smoothly across every puncture after gauge transformation, and the compactified moduli space is obtained by adjoining the lower-charge limits together with the finite bubble points and their integer charge labels.

## Statement references

[Donaldson, *An Application of Gauge Theory to the Topology of 4-Manifolds*, §§III.1–III.2](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/donaldson.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the fixed closed oriented smooth Riemannian four-manifold, the smooth $SU(2)$ bundle and the self-dual sequence in the Statement. Use the real Frobenius form on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ for coefficient energy. Changing this norm by a fixed positive convention factor changes only the displayed energy unit, not the integer charges.

[F1] The actual smooth-ball small-curvature theorem constructs Euclidean Coulomb gauges with $\|a\|_4+\|a\|_{W^{1,2}}\le C\|F\|_2$ on a unit ball. It applies to arbitrary smooth connections, with exact unitary curvature covariance. ([[lem-small-critical-curvature-coulomb-gauges-on-four-balls]])

[F2] For a smooth metric sufficiently $C^0$ close to Euclidean, the new curved-metric weak Coulomb theorem proves smoothness, uniform interior coefficient bounds for small $L^4$ potential, and the actual estimate $r^2\|F\|_\infty\le C\|F\|_2$. Its constants are uniform on the rescalings of finitely many fixed compact coordinate charts. It covers either Hodge sign. ([[lem-weak-coulomb-asd-connections-for-smooth-four-metrics-are-interior-smooth]])

[F3] The annular transport proof gives a frame bounded by the uniform annular curvature, using two spherical path families and quaternionic normalization. The punctured critical-gauge proof aligns adjacent frames by constants and sums a dyadic annular $L^4$ bound. The point-removal proof retains the full quadratic cutoff curvature and constructs a limiting gauge after Coulomb extraction. Their Euclidean-ASD Statements are NOT invoked for a curved metric: the required extensions of these actual arguments are supplied below with [F2]. ([[lem-small-uniform-curvature-gauges-on-four-dimensional-annuli]], [[lem-finite-energy-punctured-euclidean-asd-connections-have-l-four-gauges]], [[lem-finite-energy-euclidean-asd-point-singularity-is-removable]])

[F4] Close $SU(2)$ cocycles are intertwined by the explicitly proved normalized quaternionic average. Its finite algebra works on any finite chart cover with compactly supported smooth scalar weights; below it is written again for the present smooth data. A countable smooth matrix cocycle glues a smooth vector bundle. For $SU(2)$ transitions its preserved metric, complex structure and determinant give the corresponding principal $SU(2)$ frame bundle. ([[lem-close-su-two-cocycles-admit-constructed-sobolev-isomorphisms]], [[thm-vector-bundle-construction-from-a-smooth-cocycle]])

[F5] The second Chern form is $c_2(A)=\operatorname{tr}(F_A\wedge F_A)/(8\pi^2)$ for the trace-zero rank-two connection and represents the integral topological class over the reals. Closed exact top forms integrate to zero. On a coordinate ball, the divergence theorem gives zero integral for the derivative of a smooth three-form with zero tangential boundary trace. Thus, for the sign $F_A^-=0$, $\int|F_A|^2=-8\pi^2\langle c_2(P),[X]\rangle$. These signs follow from the given Frobenius norm and the stated determinant normalization. ([[thm-chern-weil-forms-represent-the-at-characteristic-classes-over-the-reals]], [[def-chern-pontryagin-and-euler-characteristic-forms]], [[lem-finite-chart-localization-defines-choice-free-integration-and-compact-stokes]], [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]])

[F6] Arzela–Ascoli, smooth cutoffs, Holder and absolute continuity hold in the stated finite-dimensional smooth charts. Countable diagonal extractions and choices are permitted by full AC. ([[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]], [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]], [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-absolute-continuity-of-the-integral]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** The data above, and write $M=\sup_n\int_X|F_{A_n}|^2$.

1.1 Fix finitely many positive coordinate-ball charts with compactly contained working subcharts covering $X$. A positive linear change makes the metric Euclidean at each chart center; shrink the charts so its coefficient matrix is within [F2]'s fixed small $C^0$ neighborhood throughout. For each sequence member, a frame at a chart center extends over that ball by radial parallel transport. This exists intrinsically: the ordered matrix integral series constructs transport in each bundle chart; finite subdivision of each compact path and uniqueness patch those solutions, and smooth parameter dependence makes the endpoint frame smooth. It is smooth at the center by the same local radial equation there. Thus the coordinate-ball trivializations can be chosen even for a sequence of different bundles; no common topological trivialization is being assumed. Metric energy and Euclidean coefficient energy are uniformly comparable on this finite list. List the coordinate balls with rational centers and radii whose quadrupled closures are in a chart. By successive bounded real subsequence extraction and one diagonal, arrange that the energy integral on every quadrupled listed ball has a limit. Choose $\theta>0$ so energy less than $2\theta$ on such a ball implies the Euclidean curvature smallness in [F1] and the resulting potential smallness in [F2], after dilation. Let $S$ be the points not lying in any listed ball whose quadrupled-ball limiting energy is less than $\theta$. Its complement is open. If $N$ distinct points lie in $S$, choose $N$ listed balls containing them with pairwise disjoint quadrupled closures; this is possible by the coordinate basis and finitely many positive distances. Each limiting energy is at least $\theta$, so $N\theta\le M$. Thus $S$ is finite. For every compact set in its complement finitely many good balls suffice, and all their required smallness bounds hold eventually. [F1, F2, F3, F6, given, choose, construct, algebra]

2.1 On each good ball apply [F1] on its quadruple. The pulled-back form is Euclidean Coulomb, while its curvature satisfies the actual curved self-duality equation by gauge covariance. Apply [F2] on smaller subballs: the potentials have uniform bounds in every fixed derivative order on the working ball. The constructed gauges are smooth there: their weak equation $du=u a-A_nu$, with smooth $A_n,a$, first gives every local first Sobolev order and then every higher order by differentiation. On an overlap, its transformed transition $h_{ij}^n$ is unitary and satisfies $dh_{ij}^n=h_{ij}^n a_j^n-a_i^n h_{ij}^n$, with the fixed coordinate pullback on $a_j^n$ understood. This identity and the uniform local coefficient bounds give uniform derivative bounds on every smaller overlap, inductively; a bound on the transition itself is supplied by compact $SU(2)$. There is no assumption that two different coordinate charts define the same Euclidean Coulomb operator. Apply [F6] on countably many smaller compact balls, to all coefficient and transition derivatives, and diagonalize. This gives smooth limits $a_i,h_{ij}$, convergence in every local derivative norm, the transition equation and the exact cocycle identities. The latter pass pointwise by uniform convergence on triple-overlap compacts. By [F4] they define one smooth bundle $P_\infty$ and connection $A_\infty$ on $X\setminus S$. The equation passes to the smooth limits, so $F_{A_\infty}^-=0$. On each compact subset its energy is the limit of the original energy and is at most $M$. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Establish removal for the possibly nontrivial limiting bundle near a point of $S$. The needed small punctured curvature gauge has an intrinsic construction. On a dyadic coordinate annulus, choose a frame at one basepoint and transport it along the two spherical path families of [F3]'s annular proof. Transport is defined in finitely many bundle charts along each path, and its variation identity is intrinsic: the covariant derivative of the endpoint frame is the integral of transported curvature over the path variation. The two caps' transports differ by the holonomy of the same explicit spherical lune of area at most $2\pi$. Thus their quaternionic average supplies a global annular frame with potential at most $C r\|F\|_\infty$, without assuming that the punctured bundle already has a global trivialization. On a sufficiently small punctured ball, finite energy and [F2] give, for $r_j=2^{-j}$ and $E_j$ the energy on $\{r_j/4<|x|<4r_j\}$, the bounds $\|F\|_{L^\infty(\{r_j/2<|x|<2r_j\})}\le C r_j^{-2}\sqrt{E_j}$ and $\sum_jE_j\le5E$. These are applications on ordinary balls away from the puncture; all rescaled metric bounds are uniform. Make the total energy small enough for the annular threshold. Align neighboring frames by their relative value at one fixed point of each overlap, as in [F3]. The relative frame then differs from identity by at most $C(\sqrt{E_j}+\sqrt{E_{j+1}})$ on that overlap, by integrating its gauge equation along bounded-length angular/radial paths. Average these aligned frames with a dyadic partition having only adjacent overlaps and normalize their quaternionic norm. This gives ONE smooth frame on the whole punctured smaller ball. Its potential $B$ obeys $|B|\le C r_j^{-1}(\sqrt{E_j}+\sqrt{E_{j+1}})$ on the $j$th band, hence $\int|B|^4\le C\sum_j(E_j^2+E_{j+1}^2)\le CE^2$. This reconstructs the punctured $L^4$ argument for the curved metric; no Euclidean-ASD theorem is applied to $A_\infty$. [F2, F3, F6, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 In this actual punctured frame choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_j=0$ on $B_{r_j}$ and $1$ outside $B_{2r_j}$, with $|d\chi_j|\le C/r_j$. The potentials $B_j=\chi_jB$ extended by zero are smooth on the full fixed ball. If $\mathcal F$ is the punctured curvature extended as an $L^2$ class, their exact curvatures are $F_{B_j}=\chi_j\mathcal F+d\chi_j\wedge B+(\chi_j^2-\chi_j)B\wedge B$. Holder and absolute continuity show $F_{B_j}\to\mathcal F$ in $L^2$: the cutoff derivative term is bounded by $C\|B\|_{L^4(\{r_j<|x|<2r_j\})}$ and the quadratic term by its square. Choose the punctured ball initially small enough that all these curvatures are below [F1]'s threshold. Construct full-ball Coulomb gauges $u_j$ and potentials $b_j$ with bounded $W^{1,2}$ and small $L^4$ norms. Weak Hilbert extraction and Rellich give weak $W^{1,2}$ and strong $L^p$, $p<4$, limits; the actual argument in [F3]'s point-removal proof passes $b_j\wedge b_j$ first in $L^1$ and then the bounded curvature in weak $L^2$, giving $F_b$. The $g$-anti-self-dual projections of $F_{B_j}$ tend to zero in $L^2$ because $\pi_{-,g}$ is a fixed smooth bounded coefficient operator. Unitary covariance gives the same assertion for $b_j$, so $d_e^*b=0$ and $F_b^{-,g}=0$ weakly on the ENTIRE ball. By [F2], $b$ is smooth across the point. On punctured compact sets the gauge equations $du_j=u_jb_j-Bu_j$ give bounded $W^{1,4}$ norms; Rellich and a diagonal yield a unitary limit $u$ with $du=ub-Bu$. Passing the products uses strong $L^3$ convergence of $b_j$ and strong $L^{12}$ convergence of the bounded matrices. Smooth $b,B$ bootstrap this equation to a smooth $SU(2)$ map on the puncture. Thus $B^u=b$ there. Glue a new trivial ball using this actual gauge; it extends the limiting bundle and connection smoothly. Repeat at the finitely many points of $S$, obtaining a smooth self-dual $A_\infty$ on a bundle over ALL of $X$. This is the full curved point removal argument, including its actual limiting gauge. [F1, F2, F3, F6, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Construct comparison isomorphisms, not merely unrelated local gauges. On a compact core $K\Subset X\setminus S$, select finitely many working charts from step2.1 and smaller charts covering a neighborhood of $K$. Choose smooth weights $\phi_j$ with compact support in the larger charts, summing to one on that neighborhood. In chart $i$ put $T_i^n=\sum_j\phi_jh_{ij}^nh_{ji}$. Since the two transition cocycles converge smoothly on the finitely many compact supports, $T_i^n\to I$ in every derivative norm. For large $n$ its quaternionic norm is bounded below by one half. Set $\sigma_i^n=T_i^n/(\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}((T_i^n)^*T_i^n))^{1/2}$. The cocycle laws give $T_i^n=h_{ik}^nT_k^nh_{ki}$; their scalar norms agree, so $h_{ik}=(\sigma_i^n)^{-1}h_{ik}^n\sigma_k^n$. Therefore these are actual smooth bundle isomorphisms from the limiting bundle to the original one on the core neighborhood. The transferred connections $(a_i^n)^{\sigma_i^n}$ converge smoothly to $a_i$. This is [F4]'s finite averaging proof with smooth manifold weights, not its Euclidean-cover Statement outside scope. [F4, F6, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Choose increasing cores by deleting shrinking disjoint balls about $S$. Apply step5.1 and diagonal selection so that the $n$th chosen comparison is within $1/n$ in every derivative order at most $n$ on the $n$th core. Extend each comparison to the WHOLE punctured manifold. Indeed near a deleted sphere both bundles have the smooth ball trivializations, one original and one from step4.1. On the collar the comparison is an $SU(2)$ function $h(\vartheta,r)$. Choose a smooth radial function $f(r)$ equal to $r$ on its outer collar and equal to one interior collar radius for all sufficiently small positive $r$. Then $h(\vartheta,f(r))$ extends the comparison across the remaining punctured end and agrees with it near its original domain boundary. No extension across the center is requested. Perform this on each disjoint punctured ball. These are actual bundle isomorphisms on $X\setminus S$ for each sequence member, and the extensions change nothing on the exhausting cores. Consequently the transported connections converge in $C^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(X\setminus S)$, in particular in the asserted local Sobolev gauges. No assertion that $P_\infty$ and $P$ extend isomorphically across $S$ has been made. [F4, F6, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 Identify the lost energy before calling it an integer. Choose disjoint coordinate balls $B_r(p)$ about the finite points of $S$ and one decreasing radius sequence tending to zero at each point. Extract further so the integrals of $|F_{A_n}|^2$ on all these balls converge. Smooth convergence on every compact annulus shows $\lim_n\int_{B_r(p)}|F_{A_n}|^2-\int_{B_r(p)}|F_{A_\infty}|^2$ is independent of these sufficiently small radii: subtract two radii and use smooth annular convergence. Denote it $\lambda_p$. It is positive. In fact, because $p$ was bad in step1.1, every neighborhood contains a listed ball containing $p$ whose limiting energy on its quadruple is at least $\theta$; choose that quadruple inside $B_r(p)$. Hence the first limiting integral is at least $\theta$, while the smooth extended connection's ball energy tends to zero as $r\to0$. Thus $\lambda_p\ge\theta>0$. For a continuous test function $f$, split its integral over these balls and their complement. On the complement use smooth convergence; on each ball replacing $f$ by $f(p)$ costs at most its oscillation there times the bounded total energy. Let their radii tend to zero. This proves actual weak energy-measure convergence to $|F_{A_\infty}|^2d\mathrm{vol}+\sum_p\lambda_p\delta_p$ and the identity $\lim_n E(A_n)=E(A_\infty)+\sum_p\lambda_p$. No bubble-tree energy identity has been assumed. [F2, F6, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

8.1 Prove individual charge quantization by clutching. Fix one sufficiently small ball $B=B_r(p)$ as in step7.1 and use the comparison from step6.1 on its fixed boundary collar. In its limiting smooth frame the transported connection $a_n$ converges smoothly to $A_\infty$ there. Modify $a_n$ by a fixed collar cutoff to equal $A_\infty$ near $\partial B$, and transport this modification back to the original frame. It defines a smooth connection $A_n'$ on the original bundle over $B$, equal to $A_n$ away from the collar. Since the modification tends to zero with all derivatives in the comparison frame, $\int_Bc_2(A_n')-\int_Bc_2(A_n)\to0$, by the actual curvature polynomial and gauge invariance. Glue this ball bundle to the oppositely oriented limiting ball bundle using the comparison on the boundary. To make the connections match smoothly, flatten each near its boundary to the product pullback of its common tangential connection. This changes neither Chern integral: for a path of connections, direct differentiation and Bianchi give $\partial_t\operatorname{tr}(F_t\wedge F_t)=2d\operatorname{tr}(\dot A_t\wedge F_t)$; a deformation fixing the tangential boundary connection has zero tangential transgression trace. Explicitly write that three-form as $\sum_i(-1)^{i-1}V_i\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\widehat{dx_i}\cdots\wedge dx_4$; its derivative is $(\operatorname{div}V)dx$ and its zero tangential trace is $V\cdot\nu=0$. The actual ball divergence theorem in [F5] therefore makes its derivative integral zero. Product collars then glue a smooth connection on an actual $SU(2)$ bundle over the doubled ball $S^4$. Its Chern number is the integer $q_n=\int_Bc_2(A_n')-\int_Bc_2(A_\infty)$. By [F5] and step7.1, $q_n\to-\lambda_p/(8\pi^2)$. A convergent integer sequence is eventually constant, so $m_p=\lambda_p/(8\pi^2)$ is an integer; step7.1 makes it positive. This argument constructs the clutching bundle and uses integrality of its Chern class, not an unproved instanton profile or a classification of all bundles on $S^4$. [F4, F5, F6, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

9.1 Let $k_\infty=-\langle c_2(P_\infty),[X]\rangle$. The extended bundle is smooth, so [F5] makes this an integer and $E(A_\infty)=8\pi^2k_\infty\ge0$. The same calculation gives $E(A_n)=8\pi^2k$ for every sequence member. Substitute step8.1 into step7.1 to get $k=k_\infty+\sum_pm_p$. In particular there are at most $k$ bubble points counting multiplicity. If $S$ is empty the comparison in step5.1 is over all of $X$ and the bundles are isomorphic, as expected. A sequence with negative prescribed $k$ cannot exist by the energy formula. All claims about the smooth limit, gauges and integer loss are now established. [F5, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 Specify the compactification and verify that no extra ideal data are required. An ideal connection is a smooth self-dual gauge orbit on a bundle of charge $j\ge0$, together with a finite unordered collection of points of total positive integer weight $k-j$. Its topology is the actual convergence of connections modulo smooth local comparison gauges off those points, together with weak convergence of the energy measure $|F|^2d\mathrm{vol}+8\pi^2\sum m\delta_p$. Steps1.1–9.1 prove that every original sequence has an ideal subsequential limit in this topology. The same proof works for a sequence of background bundles, since no fixed-bundle hypothesis was used before the comparison construction. For a sequence of ideal connections, first pass to a fixed background charge in the finite range $0,\ldots,k$. The finite point configurations have a convergent subsequence by compactness of $X$: list their finitely many repeated points, extract in $X$ and forget that listing. Apply steps1.1–9.1 to the background connections and add their new bubble weights to the limiting old weights at coincident points. The exact charge equation persists. Thus the ideal space, and in particular the closure of the original moduli, is sequentially compact. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, construct, algebra]

11.1 For completeness this topology is second-countable and Hausdorff, so sequential compactness really gives compactness. Here is a countable local-data construction. Use the fixed countable coordinate-ball basis, finite deleted-ball lists and finite chart subcovers of their compact complements. Smooth potentials and smooth transition maps on each such finite arrangement have countable $C^r$ coefficient bases: use rational polynomial approximations on finitely many smaller boxes, smooth fixed cutoffs, rational tolerances and integer $r$. Their subspaces satisfying the unitary and transition identities inherit those bases. Arbitrary changes of local frames act by homeomorphisms, so the open saturations of these countable bases form a countable basis on the corresponding gauge quotients. Combine these tests with the countable uniform-dense family of continuous functions on compact $X$, constructed by the same rational-chart approximation, for the weak energy tests. Require also that all listed ideal points lie in the chosen deleted balls. That condition follows locally from finitely many open energy tests: outside those balls the limiting smooth energy measure has no atom, so cover the compact remainder by finitely many smaller balls with test-function integrals less than $4\pi^2$. For sufficiently close energy measures these integrals remain less than $8\pi^2$, excluding every positive integer ideal atom where a test function is one. Thus these saturated finite-chart and energy tests give a countable basis for exactly the convergence in step10.1. No classification of bundle isomorphism types or global Coulomb slice is used. For uniqueness of a limit, compare two proposed limits on the complement of their finite exceptional sets. Gauges between their smoothly convergent representatives satisfy $dh_n=h_nb_n-a_nh_n$. Unitarity and the smooth coefficient bounds control all gauge derivatives locally, so a diagonal gives a smooth limiting gauge intertwining the two background connections. Weak energy measures have unique limits against the continuous test functions, so their atomic weights and positions agree; the smooth background measure has no atoms. This gauge extends over every exceptional point: in their two smooth extension frames its derivative is bounded by the same equation, and the length distance on a punctured four-ball has the Euclidean completion, so it has a unique continuous limit at the puncture. The bounded derivative gives a weak Lipschitz extension, and the equation then bootstraps to smoothness. The ideal limits are therefore the same. With the countable neighborhood bases just constructed, failure of Hausdorff separation would select a point in every intersection of two shrinking neighborhood bases, giving a sequence with those two different limits. Thus the topology is Hausdorff. Finally second-countability gives a countable subcover of every open cover under AC. If no finite subcover existed, choose a point outside its first $n$ members; a convergent subsequence would contradict the member containing its limit. The sequential compactness in step10.1 therefore gives compactness of the ideal space and of the closed original-moduli closure. This is precisely the compactification by lower-charge smooth limits and integer point labels in the Statement. [F4, F6, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 7.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, construct, algebra] ∎

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151
    - title: Allen Hatcher, Boundary slopes of incompressible surfaces
      url: https://www.math.unl.edu/~mbrittenham2/classwk/990s08/public/hatcher.bdyslopes.pdf
