[[def-axiom-of-choice|Full AC, implying the countable-choice hypothesis of the ribbon-disk supplier]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the right-handed trefoil $T$, and the fixed reverse-mirror and connected-sum conventions.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies a choice function for each family of nonempty sets.

[A2] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]: Full AC implies the countable-choice axiom used by the ribbon-disk construction.

[F1] [[lem-positive-hopf-plumbing-has-trefoil-seifert-matrix]]: For the stated positive Hopf plumbing, $V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$.

[F2] [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]: In the positive-push convention, the Seifert matrix is $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ in the chosen integral basis.

[F3] [[lem-seifert-matrix-of-reverse-mirror-is-negative-original]]: The reverse-mirror matrix in the image basis is $-V$.

[F4] [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]]: $\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t)$ for the supplied Seifert matrix.

[F5] [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]: The connected sum is formed by deleting small balls around trivial arcs and gluing the complements by the fixed orientation-reversing boundary identification.

[F7] [[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]]: Under AC$_\omega$, $T\#T^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded ribbon disk in $B^4$.

[F8] [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]]: Smooth surface charts are also topological locally flat charts.

## Proof

1.1 The right-handed trefoil matrix is $V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ by [F1] in the convention [F2]. Choose the connected-sum balls around short boundary arcs where the Seifert surfaces are standard collars, disjoint from their basis curves and small positive push-offs. The fixed gluing [F5] joins those collars. A basis cycle in one summand and its push-off lie in a ball disjoint from the other summand's curves, so the first cycle bounds a $2$-chain there away from the second; hence all cross linking entries vanish. The combined matrix is therefore $W=\operatorname{diag}(V,-V)$ by [F3]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, construct]

2.1 Direct calculation gives $\det(V-tV^T)=\det\begin{pmatrix}t-1&t\\-1&t-1\end{pmatrix}=(1-t)^2+t=t^2-t+1$. For the reverse-mirror block, $-V-t(-V^T)=-(V-tV^T)$, whose determinant equals $\det(V-tV^T)$ because the rank is two. Since $W-tW^T$ is block diagonal, its determinant is $(t^2-t+1)^2$. By [F2] and [F4], this is a representative of $\Delta_S(t)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Expanding $(t^2-t+1)^2$ gives $t^4-2t^3+3t^2-2t+1$, which has nonzero coefficients in degrees $0$ and $1$ and is therefore not a monomial $\pm t^k$. Since these monomials are exactly the units of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, the Alexander polynomial is nonunit. On the other hand, [A2] supplies AC$_\omega$ from full AC, so [F7] gives a smooth ribbon disk; by [F8] this disk is locally flat. Thus $S$ is topologically slice despite its nonunit Alexander polynomial, refuting the asserted converse. For $T$, the same calculation gives $\Delta_T=t^2-t+1\not\doteq1$, which only means that the Alexander-one theorem does not apply. [A1, A2, F4, F7, F8, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

## Example

Fix $n\ge1$, $\sigma,\tau>0$, and $0<\gamma<1$. Observe independent $Y_i\sim N(\theta,\sigma^2)$ under truth $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and use prior $N(0,\tau^2)$. Let $v_n=(\tau^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1}$, $a_n=v_n n\sigma^{-2}$, and $z_\gamma=\Phi^{-1}(1-\gamma/2)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The exact posterior credible interval is $[a_n\bar Y-z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n},a_n\bar Y+z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n}]$. Since $0<a_n<1$, its repeated-sampling coverage at fixed $n$ tends to zero as $|\theta|\to\infty$, despite exact posterior computation and exact sampling.

## Example references

[[op-ip-calibration-under-score-and-solver-error|The calibrated-inversion question and its exact Bayesian baseline.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The scalar normal observation model and proper prior in the Example, with $n\ge1$, $\sigma,\tau>0$, and $0<\gamma<1$.

[A1] Completing the Gaussian likelihood and prior gives posterior mean $a_n\bar Y$, variance $v_n=(\tau^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1}$, and central credible radius $r_n=z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n}$.

[A2] The standard normal cumulative distribution has vanishing tails: $\Phi(t)\to0$ as $t\to-\infty$ and $\Phi(t)\to1$ as $t\to+\infty$.

## Verification

1.1 At every fixed $n$, $a_n=n\tau^2/(\sigma^2+n\tau^2)$ lies strictly between zero and one, and $r_n$ is finite and independent of the observation. Under truth $\theta$, $a_n\bar Y-\theta$ has mean $-(1-a_n)\theta$ and fixed positive standard deviation $a_n\sigma/\sqrt n$. [given, A1, algebra]

1.2 Standardizing the event in the Example gives $c_n(\theta)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{r_n+(1-a_n)\theta}{a_n\sigma/\sqrt n}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{-r_n+(1-a_n)\theta}{a_n\sigma/\sqrt n}\right)$. [A1, algebra]

2.1 As $\theta\to+\infty$, both arguments in step 1.2 tend to $+\infty$, so both cumulative probabilities tend to one by [A2] and their difference tends to zero. As $\theta\to-\infty$, both arguments tend to $-\infty$ and their difference again tends to zero. Thus the infimum coverage over $\theta\in\mathbb R$ is zero at each fixed $n$. [A1, A2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Every Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ with finite area and finite perimeter satisfies
$$4\pi |E|\le P(E;\mathbb R^2)^2.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|Area is Lebesgue measure and perimeter is the total variation of the distributional derivative of the indicator.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and a measurable $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ with $|E|<\infty$ and $P(E;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$.

[A1] Countable Choice is used by strict smooth approximation and the regular-level selections. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] Every finite-perimeter $L^1$ function on $\mathbb R^2$ has compactly supported smooth strict approximants $u_j$: $u_j\to u$ in $L^1$ and $\int|\nabla u_j|\to TV(u;\mathbb R^2)$. ([[lem-ip-bv-strict-approximation]])

[F2] For $u\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1$ with integrable gradient, the integral of its gradient norm equals the integral of the perimeters of its positive and negative superlevel sets; outside a null set of levels the levels are regular and have finite perimeter. ([[lem-ip-bv-smooth-coarea]], [[thm-morse-sard-for-euclidean-maps]])

[F3] The distributional total variation is the supremum over smooth compactly supported vector fields of norm at most one; on a compact smooth planar domain, Stokes gives the boundary flux formula needed to identify the distributional derivative of its indicator. ([[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]], [[cor-greens-theorem-from-general-stokes]])

[F4] The partition variation of a vector Radon measure is a Radon measure; for a unit normal field $\nu$ on a compact smooth curve, the variation of $\nu\,\mathcal H^1$ is $\mathcal H^1$. ([[lem-ip-vector-radon-variation-is-radon]])

[F5] A nonempty compact connected smooth one-dimensional manifold without boundary is diffeomorphic to a circle. ([[lem-a-compact-connected-one-dimensional-manifold-without-boundary-is-a-circle]])

[F6] Parseval's identity holds for Fourier series on the circle: the squared $L^2$ norm is the sum of squared Fourier coefficients. ([[thm-parseval-identity-for-fourier-series]])

## Proof

1.1 First suppose $G\subset\mathbb R^2$ is a bounded open set with compact smooth boundary $\Gamma$. The boundary is a compact smooth one-dimensional manifold without boundary. Connected coordinate arcs cover $\Gamma$; compactness gives a finite subcover, so $\Gamma$ has finitely many connected components. By [F5] each component is a smooth embedded circle. Parametrize component $i$ by an orientation-compatible unit-speed smooth periodic curve $\gamma_i:[0,L_i]\to\mathbb R^2$, where $L_i$ is its length. The divergence formula in [F3] gives $D\chi_G=-\nu\,\mathcal H^1|_\Gamma$ with $\nu$ the outward normal, and [F4] therefore gives $P(G;\mathbb R^2)=\mathcal H^1(\Gamma)=\sum_iL_i$. Applying Stokes in [F3] to $\omega=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/2$, whose exterior derivative is $dx\wedge dy$, gives
$$|G|=\frac12\sum_i\int_0^{L_i}(\gamma_{i,1}\gamma'_{i,2}-\gamma_{i,2}\gamma'_{i,1})\,ds.$$
For each $i$, translating $\gamma_i$ by its arclength mean $\bar\gamma_i=L_i^{-1}\int_0^{L_i}\gamma_i(s)\,ds$ does not change this integral, since each coordinate derivative integrates to zero over a period. Write $z_i=\gamma_i-\bar\gamma_i$. [F3, F4, F5, given, construct]

1.2 For a smooth $L$-periodic scalar function $z$ of mean zero, set $v(\theta)=z(L\theta/(2\pi))$. Its zeroth Fourier coefficient vanishes. Integration by parts gives $\widehat{v'}(k)=ik\widehat v(k)$ for every integer $k$. Parseval [F6] and $k^2\ge1$ for $k\ne0$ imply $\int_0^{2\pi}|v|^2\,d\theta\le\int_0^{2\pi}|v'|^2\,d\theta$. Changing variables yields
$$\int_0^L|z(s)|^2\,ds\le\left(\frac L{2\pi}\right)^2\int_0^L|z'(s)|^2\,ds.$$
Apply this to both coordinates of $z_i$ and add. Since $|z'_i|=|\gamma'_i|=1$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives
$$\left|\frac12\int_0^{L_i}(z_{i,1}z'_{i,2}-z_{i,2}z'_{i,1})\,ds\right|\le\frac12\|z_i\|_{L^2}\|z'_i\|_{L^2}\le\frac{L_i^2}{4\pi}.$$
Summing over the finitely many boundary components and using $\sum_iL_i^2\le(\sum_iL_i)^2$ proves $4\pi|G|\le P(G;\mathbb R^2)^2$. [F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Now let $E$ be as in the Statement and put $u=\chi_E$. By [F1], choose $u_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $e_j:=\|u_j-\chi_E\|_1\to0$ and $a_j:=\int|\nabla u_j|\to P(E;\mathbb R^2)$. If $|E|=0$, the result is immediate. If some $e_j=0$, continuity forces $u_j$ to take only the values $0$ and $1$ everywhere; connectedness of $\mathbb R^2$ and compact support then force $u_j=0$, contradicting $|E|>0$. Thus $e_j>0$. Let $\tau_j=\sqrt{e_j}$ and discard finitely many terms so $0<\tau_j<\min\{1/2,|E|/2\}$. For every $t\in I_j:=[\tau_j,1-\tau_j]$, a point where $\chi_E$ and $\chi_{\{u_j>t\}}$ differ contributes at least $\tau_j$ to $|u_j-\chi_E|$; hence $|\{u_j>t\}\mathbin\triangle E|\le e_j/\tau_j=\tau_j$. [A1, F1, given, choose]

2.2 By [F2], the measurable level-perimeter function has integral at most $a_j$ on $I_j$, whose length is $1-2\tau_j$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, the set of $t\in I_j$ with $P(\{u_j>t\};\mathbb R^2)\le a_j/(1-2\tau_j)+\varepsilon$ has positive measure; otherwise its integral over $I_j$ would exceed $a_j$. The critical values of $u_j$ form a null set by [F2], so choose such a regular value $t_j$ and take $\varepsilon=1/j$. Since $t_j>0$ and $u_j$ is compactly supported, $G_j:=\{u_j>t_j\}$ is bounded and its closure is a compact smooth domain with boundary $\{u_j=t_j\}$. Thus step 1.2 applies to $G_j$, and
$$|G_j\mathbin\triangle E|\le\tau_j,\qquad P(G_j;\mathbb R^2)\le\frac{a_j}{1-2\tau_j}+\frac1j.$$
The right side has limit $P(E;\mathbb R^2)$, while $|G_j|\to|E|$. [A1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, choose]

3.1 Step 1.2 gives $4\pi|G_j|\le P(G_j;\mathbb R^2)^2$ for every selected $j$. Taking upper limits, the convergence $|G_j|\to|E|$ and the perimeter upper bound from step 2.2 give $4\pi|E|\le P(E;\mathbb R^2)^2$. This proves the claimed inequality for every finite-measure finite-perimeter set. [step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For the standard right-handed trefoil in $S^3$, the minimum genus among its connected compact smooth oriented spanning surfaces is exactly $1$.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|Definition of knot genus]]

[[thm-seifert-algorithm-boundary-euler-and-genus|The disk-and-band genus formula]]

[[lem-the-trefoil-does-not-bound-a-smooth-proper-disk-in-the-four-ball|The full-AC nonsliceness result for the trefoil]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the standard right-handed trefoil $T$.

[F1] Oriented smoothing replaces a crossing by its orientation-compatible noncrossing pairing; the Seifert algorithm records one disk per resulting circle and one band per crossing. Under AC$_\omega$, the bands realize a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with the original knot as boundary, and its genus is $(1-s+c)/2$ for $s$ circles and $c$ crossings. ([[def-seifert-smoothing-and-seifert-circles-of-an-oriented-link-diagram]], [[alg-seifert-surface-from-diagram]], [[lem-seifert-bands-embedded-orientable-boundary-correct]], [[thm-seifert-algorithm-boundary-euler-and-genus]])

[F2] Under full AC, $T$ does not bound a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$. ([[lem-the-trefoil-does-not-bound-a-smooth-proper-disk-in-the-four-ball]])

[F3] A genus-zero connected compact orientable surface with one boundary component is topologically a disk. For smooth input the disk-and-band normal-form construction gives a smooth disk parametrization: steps 7.1–12.1 use smooth circle extensions and smooth disk/band collar moves. ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]], [[lem-finite-c2-surface-carriers-have-smooth-normal-forms-and-relative-cap-approximations]])

[F4] A smooth disk in the boundary $S^3$ can be pushed through a collar into $B^4$, fixing its boundary, to give a smooth proper disk. ([[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]])

[F5] Knot genus is the minimum nonnegative integer among the genera of spanning surfaces. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]])

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[A2] Full AC implies AC$_\omega$. ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC and the standard right-handed trefoil $T$.

1.1 Use the standard right-trefoil diagram, the closure of the positive two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$, with both braid strands directed downward and the closing arcs directed back to the top. It has exactly three crossings. At each crossing the oriented smoothing pairs each upper endpoint with the lower endpoint in the same vertical position, rather than the diagonal pairing. Smoothing all three crossings therefore leaves two vertical strands; each joins its own closing arc to form one circle. Thus $s=2$ and $c=3$. The unsmoothed braid has the transposition permutation (three interchanges), so its closure has one knot component. The algorithm attaches three half-twisted bands between the two disk records, with twist directions restoring these three positive crossings. By [F1] and [A2] the result is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded spanning surface for $T$, and its genus is $(1-2+3)/2=1$ (equivalently $\chi=2-3=-1$). Hence the nonnegative minimum in [F5] satisfies $g(T)\le1$. [given, F1, F5, A1, A2, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $g(T)=0$, a minimizing surface exists by [F5], and [F3] makes it a smooth disk $D\subset S^3$. Let $c:S^3\times[0,\epsilon)\to B^4$ be a collar from [F4]. A boundary collar of $D$ gives a smooth function $h:D\to[0,\epsilon)$ that equals the inward collar coordinate near $\partial D$, is positive on $\operatorname{Int}D$, and vanishes exactly on $\partial D$. The map $x\mapsto c(x,h(x))$ is injective because the collar projection is $x$, and its differential is injective because its first coordinate is the inclusion of $D$; at $\partial D$, the positive derivative of $h$ in the inward conormal makes the disk proper and transverse to $\partial B^4$. Thus it is a smooth proper disk in $B^4$ with boundary $T$, contradicting [F2]. Hence $g(T)\ne0$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, A2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 A nonnegative integer at most $1$ and not equal to $0$ is $1$. Hence $g(T)=1$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and let the based diagram, peripheral data, and maximum index length
$N\geq2$ satisfy the input conditions of the preceding algorithm. Put
$d=N-1$. The algorithm terminates after finitely many diagram, degree, and
monomial operations. In string-link mode, its output for each $I$ with
$2\leq|I|\leq N$ equals the integer coefficient of the based longitude in the
bottom-end quotient $F_r/\Gamma_{|I|}F_r$. In closed-link mode, its output
equals the based coefficient, gcd indeterminacy, and residue candidate defined
from the chosen peripheral word lifts. It makes no polynomial-time claim.

## Statement references

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§3–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

[Stees, §2.5](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/54c7d68f-d982-4e1f-9550-e54140ada5ea/content)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a valid based diagram input with finite maximum length $N$.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, supplies the choice branch in the string-link quotient theorem and implies the countable-choice hypothesis for crossing and framing data. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-string-link-nilpotent-peripheral-identifications]]

[F1] The procedure uses finitely many strand, crossing, degree, monomial, and subsequence scans. [[alg-truncated-milnor-invariants-from-based-diagram]]

[F2] Crossing meridians satisfy the stated source-to-target conjugation relation, and the link group is presented by these relations. [[lem-link-wirtinger-local-meridian-conjugacy]], [[thm-link-wirtinger-presentation-correctness]]

[F3] For compatible accesses the literal diagram word is the blackboard parallel, with its self-writhe correction giving the closed preferred longitude. For arbitrary accesses the exact formulas are $h_0x_j^kW_jh_1^{-1}$ for a string link and $h_jx_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j}W_jh_j^{-1}$ for the closed preferred longitude. The access-word inputs record those differences. [[lem-link-peripheral-longitude-word-from-diagram]]

[F4] Component meridians generate each finite closed-link nilpotent quotient, and both string-link end inclusions identify the corresponding finite nilpotent quotients. [[lem-link-nilpotent-quotient-generated-by-component-meridians]], [[thm-string-link-nilpotent-peripheral-identifications]]

[F5] The Magnus expansion through degree $d$ factors through the quotient by $\Gamma_{d+1}$ and its coefficients are representative-independent. [[lem-magnus-commutator-degree-and-truncation]]

[F6] The coefficient and based residue outputs are those specified in the preceding definition. [[def-milnor-integer-and-residue-invariants]]

## Proof

**Given:** The algorithm input and the facts above.

1.1 Under [A1], the validation stage scans a finite diagram. The degree loop runs from $2$ to $d$, each component traversal visits finitely many undercrossings, and each multiplication, inverse, and truncation in $R_d$ involves only finitely many monomials of degree at most $d$. The output stage scans finitely many index sequences and their finitely many proper subsequences and cyclic permutations. Thus every loop is finite and the procedure terminates. [A1, F1, given, construct]

1.2 At degree one, every arc meridian on component $j$ maps to $1+X_j$: conjugate meridians have the same abelianization, and the component meridians are the chosen basis in the free source. This is exactly the initialization $Y_a^{(1)}$. If step 1 inserts a curl, the original underpass-free component had one cyclic strand and the new curl cuts it into one interval strand. The supported isotopy transports its initial meridian, paths, and supplied words to that strand; all other strand symbols are transported bijectively. Thus every existing certificate used by the algorithm is interpreted in the post-curl reference system, including the case with no original underpass. [F2, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Assume the series $Y_a^{(\ell-1)}$ correctly represent every strand meridian through degree $\ell-1$, and that $Y_s^{(\ell)}$ represents the source meridian through degree $\ell$. At a source-to-target crossing the group relation is $m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o$; at a target-to-source crossing it is $m_s=m_om_tm_o^{-1}$ by [F2]. In a conjugation $Y_o^{-1}Y_sY_o$, replacing the over-series by another series with the same terms through degree $\ell-1$ changes the product only in degree at least $\ell+1$: the degree-$\ell$ discrepancy in $Y_o$ commutes with the constant term $1$ and first meets a positive-degree term of $Y_s$ in degree $\ell+1$. The two update formulas therefore give the correct target meridian through degree $\ell$. Induction over the finite spanning paths and then over $\ell=2,\ldots,d$ proves every assigned strand series is correct through degree $d$. [F2, step 1.2, algebra, induction]

3.1 By [F3], multiplying the ordered over-meridian factors gives the based string-link longitude or the closed-link blackboard parallel with its self-writhe correction. The arc-series just established make $\Lambda_j$ its Magnus expansion through degree $d$. [F3, step 2.1]

4.1 In the arbitrary-choice branch, evaluating the finite transport words gives their actual compatible-coordinate expansions by step 2.1 and [F5]; when step 1 inserted a curl, these words have already been transported through the explicit old-to-new strand-symbol identification of step 1.2. The formulas of [F3] therefore give the actual selected longitude expansion before changing root variables. The actual root meridian is $g_jx_jg_j^{-1}$, so its series is $1+X_j+R_j$ with $R_j$ of degree at least two. Substitution of two letter systems agreeing through degree $s$ into $R_j$ gives results agreeing through degree $s+1$, since each monomial has at least two letters. Hence the displayed iteration improves the inverse equation by one degree at each pass, starting correctly at degree one. At pass $d$ it solves $Z_j+R_j(Z)=V_j$ exactly in the truncated ring. The same degree argument proves uniqueness, and consequently also the other composition identity. Thus it is the inverse formal change from compatible to actual meridian coordinates. This also agrees with the group-theoretic change on the finite nilpotent quotient: substitution by the conjugates has identity degree-one map and induces an isomorphism on each finite free nilpotent quotient: apply the arbitrary-basing branch of [F4] to the trivial string link, whose compatible endpoint group is $F_r$, with these exact independently conjugated meridians. Its Magnus series satisfies the same unique inverse equations. The corrected-and-substituted series is therefore exactly the longitude expansion in the chosen actual symbols, including independently based endpoints and all supplied relative winding. No full-group free-basis assertion or unrecorded access cancellation is used. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, induction, algebra]

5.1 Under the stated axiom branch [A1], for $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\leq d$, [F5] says the coefficient of $X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ depends only on the longitude class in $F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}$ and is independent of the chosen representative. In string-link mode, [F4] identifies that class uniquely via the bottom-end isomorphism. In closed-link mode, [F4] supplies the required component-meridian lift; the procedure uses the based lift determined by its root arcs and traversal. Thus the coefficient read from $\Lambda_j$ is exactly the based coefficient in [F6]. [A1, F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 In closed-link mode, each lower coefficient used for $\Delta_I^b$ is computed by the same procedure at its own finite degree; the finite gcd and quotient operation are exactly those in [F6]. Hence the returned indeterminacy and residue candidate are correct for the selected based word-lift data. The theorem asserts no independence of those choices; that is the separate basing theorem. [F1, F6, step 5.1] ∎

## Example

Let $p,s,R>0$, $m\ge1$, $\theta\in\ell^2$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2$, and let $(A_p\theta)_j=j^{-p}\theta_j$. Given data $y=A_p\theta+\eta$ with $\|\eta\|_{\ell^2}\le\delta$, the mesh-$m$ truncated inverse is $g_m(y)=(j^py_j)_{j\le m}$ with zero output coordinates for $j>m$. It satisfies the continuum error bound
$$\|g_m(y)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}\le m^p\delta+R(m+1)^{-s}.$$
This separates measurement-noise amplification from the mesh truncation tail; it makes no statistical or neural-operator claim.

## Example references

[[op-ip-neural-operator-sample-complexity-for-inverse-maps|A mesh-transfer example on the compact diagonal inverse-map domain.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $p,s,R>0$, $m\ge1$, $\sum_{j\ge1}j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2$, data $y=A_p\theta+\eta$, and $\|\eta\|_{\ell^2}\le\delta$.

[A1] $g_m(y)$ retains the first $m$ coordinates $j^py_j$ and sets all later coordinates to zero.

## Verification

1.1 For $j\le m$, $j^py_j=\theta_j+j^p\eta_j$. The norm of the first-$m$ noise vector is at most $m^p\|\eta\|_{\ell^2}\le m^p\delta$. [given, A1, algebra]

1.2 The omitted truth tail satisfies $\sum_{j>m}\theta_j^2\le(m+1)^{-2s}\sum_{j>m}j^{2s}\theta_j^2\le R^2(m+1)^{-2s}$. Its norm is at most $R(m+1)^{-s}$. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 The error vector is the sum of the retained-coordinate noise error and the omitted truth tail. The triangle inequality with steps 1.1 and 1.2 gives $\|g_m(y)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}\le m^p\delta+R(m+1)^{-s}$. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\phi$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^n$, with $d\phi(0)=0$ and complex Hessian $H=\phi''(0)$ invertible. There is a local biholomorphic coordinate map $w=\Psi(z)$ with $\Psi(0)=0$ such that
$$
\phi(z)=\phi(0)+\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^n w_j^2.
$$
Its linear part satisfies $(\det D\Psi(0))^2=\det H$. For a continuous parameter family of invertible Hessians $H(p)$, near any fixed parameter $p_0$ the determinant remains in a disc avoiding $0$; choosing one square root at $p_0$ therefore fixes a continuous branch on that neighborhood. If $\operatorname{Re}H$ is positive definite, then
$$
\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\lambda x^THx/2}\,dx =(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2},\qquad \lambda>0,
$$
with the integral interpreted as an absolutely convergent improper integral and the branch analytically continued from real positive-definite matrices. Finally, deforming a holomorphic contour preserves the integral of a holomorphic top-degree form when the contours are homologous through a region of holomorphy and the swept boundary integrals tend to zero.

## Statement references

[[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables|Analytic complexification]]

[[def-multivariable-power-series|Convergent multi-index series]]

[[thm-power-series-define-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables|Holomorphic power-series sums]]

[[thm-holomorphic-inverse-function-theorem-several-variables|Local holomorphic inverse]]

[[thm-identity-theorem-in-several-complex-variables|Holomorphic identity theorem]]

[[thm-stokes-theorem-for-smooth-singular-chains|Stokes theorem]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A holomorphic germ $\phi$ with a critical point at $0$ and invertible Hessian.

[F1] [[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: real-analytic germs complexify to holomorphic germs.

[F2] [[def-multivariable-power-series]]: the defining series converges absolutely on smaller polydiscs.

[F3] [[thm-power-series-define-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables]]: holomorphic power series can be differentiated termwise.

[F4] [[thm-holomorphic-inverse-function-theorem-several-variables]]: an invertible complex derivative gives a local biholomorphism.

[F5] [[thm-identity-theorem-in-several-complex-variables]]: holomorphic functions agreeing on a nonempty open subset of a connected domain agree throughout it.

[F6] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: pointwise convergence under a common integrable majorant permits passage of limits through integrals.

[F7] [[thm-stokes-theorem-for-smooth-singular-chains]]: the integral of a closed differential form over the boundary of a smooth chain is zero.

[F8] [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]: a real symmetric positive-definite matrix has a Cholesky factor with positive diagonal.

[F9] [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]: the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

[F10] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]: $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$.

[F11] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-compact-jordan-sets]]: a $C^1$ diffeomorphism changes compact Jordan integrals by its absolute Jacobian.

[F12] [[thm-nonnegative-improper-multiple-integral-by-exhaustion]]: a compact Jordan exhaustion computes the nonnegative improper integral.

[F13] [[thm-gaussian-integral]]: $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-t^2}\,dt=\sqrt\pi$, by a proof that adds no choice axiom.

[F14] [[thm-substitution-for-improper-integrals]]: a monotone differentiable substitution preserves convergent improper integrals on corresponding truncations.

[F15] [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]: continuous functions on compact product rectangles have equal product and iterated Riemann integrals.

[F16] [[cor-determinant-is-a-polynomial-in-the-matrix-entries]]: determinant is a polynomial in the matrix entries, with linear term $\operatorname{tr}(M)$ in $\det(I+tM)$ at $t=0$.

## Proof

**Given:** The function $\phi$ and Hessian $H$ in the statement.

1.1 Because $H$ is complex symmetric and invertible, some vector $v$ has $v^THv\ne0$: otherwise polarization would give $u^THv=0$ for every $u,v$, contradicting invertibility. Extend $v$ to a basis and use this as a complex linear coordinate change, so $H_{11}\ne0$. From now on, compose each coordinate change with the preceding ones; $\Psi$ denotes the final map from the original coordinates. The holomorphic equation $\partial_{z_1}\phi(z_1,z')=0$ has a unique holomorphic solution $z_1=\psi(z')$ near $0$ by [F3] and [F4], since $\partial_{z_1}\phi(0)=0$ and $\partial_{z_1}^2\phi(0)=H_{11}\ne0$. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Set $t=z_1-\psi(z')$. Taylor's formula in $t$, with the linear term zero, gives $ \phi(\psi(z')+t,z')=\phi(\psi(z'),z')+t^2a(t,z'),\quad a(t,z')=\int_0^1(1-s)\partial_{z_1}^2\phi(\psi(z')+st,z')\,ds. $ The integral is holomorphic by locally uniform convergence of the power series [F2]; $a(0, 0)=H_{11}/2\ne0$. Shrink the polydisc so $a=a(0, 0)(1+b)$ with $|b|<1$. The binomial series for $(1+b)^{1/2}$ converges absolutely by [F2], so $w_1=t\sqrt{2a(t, z')}$ is holomorphic and has nonzero $t$-derivative at $0$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 By [F4], $(t, z')\mapsto(w_1, z')$ is biholomorphic near $0$, and the phase becomes $\phi(\psi(z'), z')+w_1^2/2$. The Hessian of the reduced phase in $z'$ is the Schur complement $H_{22}-H_{21}H_{11}^{-1}H_{12}$. It is invertible because the block determinant formula gives $\det H=H_{11}\det(H_{22}-H_{21}H_{11}^{-1}H_{12})$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For real symmetric positive-definite $H$, [F8] gives $H=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal. Since $H$ is real, $\overline L$ is another such factorization; uniqueness in [F8] gives $L=\overline L$, so $L$ is real and $H=LL^T$. On each ball $B_R$, the map $x\mapsto L^Tx$ sends a compact Jordan set to a compact Jordan set; [F11] changes variables by $|\det L|^{-1}$. Letting $R\to\infty$ and using [F12] gives the corresponding nonnegative improper-integral equality. Since $\det L>0$, [F9]–[F10] give $\det H=(\det L)^2$. Repeated compact-rectangle Fubini [F15] factors the standard Gaussian integral on $[-R, R]^n$ into one-dimensional integrals, and [F12] lets $R\to\infty$. By [F13] and the substitution $t=x/\sqrt2$ in [F14], each one-dimensional integral of $e^{-x^2/2}$ is $\sqrt{2\pi}$. Finally, $z=\sqrt\lambda w$ scales the integral by $\lambda^{-n/2}$, proving the formula for real positive-definite $H$ with the positive determinant root. [F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, F14, F15, algebra, step 2.1]

4.1 Repeating steps 1.1–2.1 on the reduced phase proves the normal form by induction on $n$, with the constant phase as the $n=0$ case. Because $\Psi$ is the composite from the original coordinates, differentiating $\phi(z)=\phi(0)+\frac12\Psi(z)^T\Psi(z)$ twice at $0$ gives the original Hessian identity $H=(D\Psi(0))^TD\Psi(0)$; taking determinants gives the asserted square relation. For a continuous parameter family, continuity of $\det H$ lets one restrict to a neighborhood whose determinant image lies in a disc avoiding zero, where a square-root branch can be fixed from its base value. [step 3.1, induction, algebra, given]

4.2 For complex symmetric $H$ with positive-definite real part, the Gaussian integral is holomorphic in its entries: on each compact subset of this matrix domain, the integrand and its entry derivatives are bounded by a polynomial times $e^{-c|x|^2}$ for some $c>0$, so [F6] permits differentiation under the integral. This domain is convex, hence connected, and $\det H\ne0$ there because $Hv=0$ would imply $\operatorname{Re}(v^*Hv)=v^*(\operatorname{Re}H)v>0$ for $v\ne0$. For $H_t=I+t(H-I)$, [F16] and determinant multiplicativity give $\frac{d}{dt}\det H_t=(\det H_t)\operatorname{tr}(H_t^{-1}(H-I))$. Thus $ L(H)=\int_0^1\operatorname{tr}(H_t^{-1}(H-I))\,dt $ depends holomorphically on $H$, satisfies $e^{L(H)}=\det H$, and is zero at $I$. When $H$ is real positive definite, its segment $H_t$ is real positive definite, so $L(H)$ is real and the branch $e^{L(H)/2}$ is positive. The real Gaussian formula from step 3.2 and the complex integral formula agree on a real open set of positive-definite matrices. In a polydisc centered at any point of that set, apply the one-variable identity theorem successively in the independent entries of a complex symmetric matrix; then [F5] extends the identity from that polydisc to the connected matrix domain. [F5, F6, F10, F16, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 The holomorphic $n$-form in the statement is closed: in complex coordinates its exterior derivative has repeated holomorphic differentials and no antiholomorphic coefficients. The difference of two homologous admissible contours is the boundary of the swept chain. By [F7], its integral is the boundary integral on the truncation of that chain; the stated decay makes this term tend to zero as the truncation expands. Therefore the contour integrals agree. [F7, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a nontrivial smooth knot with a specified companion solid torus $V=e(S^1\times D^2)$, let $P\subset\operatorname{int}(S^1\times D^2)$ be a pattern, and assume the outer torus of its pattern exterior $X_P$ has no compressing disk and is not product-parallel to the inner pattern torus. Let $T_c=\partial V=e(\partial(S^1\times D^2))\subset E_{P(K)}$ be the companion torus. Then $T_c$ is incompressible and is not boundary-parallel in $E_{P(K)}$; hence it is essential.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, §1.2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Ryan Budney, *JSJ-decompositions of knot and link complements in the 3-sphere*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0506523)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nontrivial smooth knot $K$, the supplied orientation-preserving companion product embedding $e:S^1\times D^2\to S^3$, and the specified pattern exterior with incompressible outer boundary and nonproduct ends.

[F1] The pattern exterior and satellite exterior are defined in [[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number]]. With $V=e(S^1\times D^2)$, the common torus is $\partial V=e(\partial(S^1\times D^2))$. Identifying the pattern exterior with its image, the satellite exterior is $X_P\cup_{\partial V}E_K$.

[A1] Full AC permits coset-transversal choices ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F2] A nontrivial knot with a supplied smooth product tube has injective exterior boundary. Its proof also verifies exterior connectedness. [[lem-nontrivial-knot-with-supplied-product-tube-has-injective-exterior-boundary]]

[F3] Strong smooth Loop applies to a connected boundary subsurface of a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold. Thus absence of essential-boundary proper smooth disks implies injection of that subsurface group. [[thm-smooth-loop-theorem-and-incompressibility-criterion-in-orientable-three-manifolds]]

[F4] Van Kampen identifies the union group with the pushout; when both side maps are injective, the normal form with fixed transversals embeds the common group. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]] [[thm-normal-form-for-free-products-with-amalgamation]]

[F5] Finite compact-source transversality avoids a curve by an embedded arc in a three-manifold; finite graph fields and compact flows give smooth collars. [[lem-choice-free-relative-transversality-for-a-compact-smooth-embedding]] [[lem-choice-free-isotopy-extension-for-a-compact-smooth-source]]

[F6] Incompressibility, boundary-parallelity and essentiality have the smooth conventions of [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]].

## Proof

1.1 Put $X=e(X_P)$ and $Y=E_K$. They are compact orientable smooth three-manifolds with common boundary torus $T_c$. The exterior $Y$ is connected by [F2]. For completeness $X$ is connected as well: in the standard connected solid torus join two points of $X_P$ by a path consisting of finitely many smooth chart arcs. Remove repeated arcs and perturb finitely many joins in small coordinate balls to obtain an embedded arc, fixed near its endpoints; in dimension three finitely many arcs can be made disjoint except at consecutive endpoints by small finite chart perturbations. By [F5] perturb it to avoid the pattern core $P$. On the punctured supplied tube of $P$, radial projection to its boundary, extended by the identity outside that tube, is continuous and sends this path into $X_P$. Consequently all exterior points are connected by paths. The outer torus has no compressing disk by hypothesis, so [F3], with the entire outer boundary component as subsurface and normal subgroup $1$, gives $\pi_1(T_c)\hookrightarrow\pi_1(X)$. The companion product tube is exactly the supplied input of [F2], so $\pi_1(T_c)\hookrightarrow\pi_1(Y)$ too. Both applications are smooth; an abstract finite PL disk has not been treated as a smooth disk. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given, construct]

2.1 Use finite smooth collars of the common torus to enlarge the two sides to a connected open cover whose intersection retracts to $T_c$. Van Kampen and the amalgam normal form [F4], with transversals supplied by [A1], then make $\pi_1(T_c)$ inject into $\pi_1(E_{P(K)})$. Any compressing disk would make its essential torus boundary nullhomotopic in the union, contradicting that injection. Thus $T_c$ is incompressible. [A1, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The only boundary of the satellite exterior is the inner pattern torus $T_{\mathrm{in}}=\partial e(N(P))$. The two components cut along $T_c$ are the connected pieces $X$ and $Y$ from step 1.1; only $X$ meets $T_{\mathrm{in}}$. Suppose there were a boundary-parallel product region $R$ with ends $T_c,T_{\mathrm{in}}$. Its interior must lie in $X$: it cannot cross either of its two boundary tori, and its collar at $T_{\mathrm{in}}$ is on the $X$ side. Moreover $R$ exhausts $X$. Indeed $\operatorname{Int}R$ is open in $\operatorname{Int}X$ by the smooth full-dimensional product charts, and closed relative to $\operatorname{Int}X$ because $R$ is compact and its boundary lies in $\partial X$. The interior of the connected manifold $X$ is connected, as is seen by pushing any boundary portions of a path into its finite collar. Hence $\operatorname{Int}R=\operatorname{Int}X$, and taking closures gives $R=X$. Transporting that product by $e^{-1}$ would identify $X_P$ with a product between its two marked ends, contrary to hypothesis. Therefore $T_c$ is not boundary-parallel. For this closed torus boundary-incompressibility is vacuous, so it is essential by [F6]. [F1, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen compact exterior $E_K$. There exists a finite inclusion-minimal collection $\mathcal T$ of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori in the interior of $E_K$ such that every component of $E_K$ cut along $\mathcal T$ is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. Any two such inclusion-minimal collections are ambient isotopic in $E_K$. Atoroidal pieces in this statement are not asserted to be hyperbolic.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Theorem 1.9](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Stefan Friedl, *An Introduction to 3-Manifolds*, Theorem 6.1](https://www.math.csi.cuny.edu/abhijit/gt3m/Friedl-3mfds.pdf)

[Walter Neumann and Gadde Swarup, *Canonical decompositions of 3-manifolds*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9712227)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the smooth oriented knot and its chosen compact exterior $E_K$.

[F1] Full AC implies countable choice. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F2] The chosen tube and exterior are those of [[def-knot-exterior]]. The oriented normal plane bundle has a smooth global frame by [[lem-knot-normal-circle-bundle-trivialization]], Statement and full finite-frame proof. Under countable choice the exterior is irreducible by [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]], Statement.

[F3] The compact smooth exterior admits a supplied finite compatible whole-star manifold triangulation, taking the empty interior surface family. [[lem-compact-smooth-three-manifold-pairs-admit-compatible-whole-star-triangulations]]

[F4] For that very compatible triangulation, with $t$ triangular faces and $\beta=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}H_2(E_K;\mathbb F_2)$, every finite incompressible torus family with no $T^2\times I$ cut component has at most $4t+\beta-1$ members. [[lem-haken-torus-bound-for-a-supplied-compatible-smooth-triangulation]]

[F5] Cutting along a finite incompressible smooth torus family preserves smooth irreducibility and injects every cut-piece group into the original group, including for nonseparating cuts. [[lem-smooth-incompressible-torus-cuts-inject-groups-and-preserve-irreducibility]]

[F6] Geometric smooth incompressibility is fundamental-group injectivity. Compact embedded paths admit finite supported transversality relative to their endpoint neighborhoods. [[thm-smooth-loop-theorem-and-incompressibility-criterion-in-orientable-three-manifolds]] [[lem-choice-free-relative-transversality-for-a-compact-smooth-embedding]]

[F7] In a compact connected orientable irreducible smooth manifold with nonempty torus boundary, any two finite inclusion-minimal good torus systems are carried to one another by a jointly smooth ambient isotopy fixed near the original boundary. Its full proof treats the exceptional product and twisted-Klein-bundle overlaps and the final disjoint-system comparison. [[lem-smooth-minimal-torus-splittings-have-unique-isotopy-class]]

[F8] Incompressibility, atoroidality, the Seifert models and inclusion-minimal good systems have the conventions of [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]].

## Proof

1.1 The exterior is a compact oriented smooth manifold with torus boundary. To verify the last assertion, orthonormalize the global normal frame of [F2] in the metric used for the tube's disk subbundle. Its chosen tube is then smoothly parametrized by $S^1\times D^2$, so its boundary is $T^2$. The exterior is connected as well: any two distinct points in it are joined by an embedded great-circle arc in $S^3$ (choose a half great circle in the antipodal case). Apply [F6]'s compact relative transversality to this arc and the knot, fixing its endpoint neighborhoods. A transverse one-dimensional arc cannot meet the one-dimensional knot in a three-manifold, so it avoids the knot. There is a continuous retraction $S^3\setminus K\to E_K$, equal to the identity outside the tube and sending a nonzero normal vector of length $r\le\epsilon$ radially to the vector of length $\epsilon$ in the same direction. It is continuous at the tube boundary and fixes both endpoints. The retracted arc is a path in the exterior. The coincident-endpoint case is constant. Thus $E_K$ is connected, and it is irreducible by [F1]–[F2]. [F1, F2, F6, given, construct]

2.1 Choose the finite compatible triangulation of [F3] once. If $E_K$ itself is atoroidal or Seifert, the empty family proves existence and is minimal. Otherwise start with the empty family, and whenever a current component $C$ is neither atoroidal nor Seifert, choose an incompressible torus not boundary-parallel in $C$, by [F8]'s definition of failure of atoroidality. It is two-sided: the torus and ambient orientations orient its normal line, and a finite normal-field flow gives a smooth product neighborhood. Every cut component has nonempty torus boundary. Indeed a boundaryless cut component would have no cutting face and no original boundary, hence would give a closed component of the original connected exterior, impossible by step 1.1. Irreducibility of the successive pieces will follow from [F5]. This construction is needed only for a bounded finite number of steps, as established below. [F3, F5, F8, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Suppose a finite accumulated family is incompressible in $E_K$. By [F5] its cut pieces inject into $E_K$ and are irreducible. A new torus chosen in $C$ injects into $C$ by [F6], and then into $E_K$ by composition. It is therefore incompressible in $E_K$ by [F6]. The empty family starts this induction. Thus every finite stage consists of incompressible tori in the original exterior and has irreducible cut pieces, and all applications of [F4]–[F5] are within their smooth categories. [F5, F6, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 No finite stage has a product cut component. Initially the exterior is not good, hence is not $T^2\times I$. If a product first appears after a new cut along $T\subset C$, it must be one of the new components and must contain a boundary copy of $T$. If its other end is an old boundary face of $C$, the displayed product makes $T$ boundary-parallel in $C$, contradicting its choice. If both ends are the two copies of $T$, regluing them makes the entire connected old component $C$ a closed torus bundle; this contradicts the nonempty boundary of $C$ verified in step 2.1. Components unaffected by this cut were already nonproducts. This finite induction proves the no-product condition required by [F4], without assuming that selected tori separate. [F4, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Put $B=4t+\beta-1$, a fixed finite integer from [F4]. If no stage had become good after at most $B$ cuts, the construction could be extended through $B+1$ cuts by finite induction: at each of these finitely many stages use step 2.1. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 would then give an incompressible torus family with no product cut component and $B+1$ members, contradicting [F4]. Thus a finite good family exists. This argument selects only a bounded finite list of cuts, rather than postulating an infinite sequence of independent choices. The zero-cut empty family in the nongood initial case also satisfies [F4], so $B\ge0$ there. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Among the subfamilies of that particular finite good family, take a good subfamily of least cardinality. There is at least one, and its finite power set suffices for the selection. No proper subfamily can be good, so it is inclusion-minimal in exactly [F8]'s sense. This proves existence with all the original hypotheses and no additional condition on the knot. [F8, step 5.1, construct, choose]

7.1 Finally let two finite inclusion-minimal systems as in the Statement be given. Step 1.1 verifies that their ambient exterior is compact, connected, orientable and irreducible with nonempty torus boundary. Their tori and good cut pieces have exactly [F7]'s smooth hypotheses. Apply that full uniqueness supplier to obtain a jointly smooth ambient isotopy of $E_K$, even fixed near its boundary, carrying one system to the other. The underlying convention is the ordinary smooth ambient isotopy of the knot definitions; no homeomorphism isotopy has replaced it. The conclusion asserts only atoroidal or Seifert pieces and introduces no hyperbolicity assertion. [F1, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 6.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty open set of unit line normals and let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$. If the line integral $Rf(\theta,s)$ is zero for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, then $f$ is zero everywhere. The assertion holds without Countable Choice.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data|Line-normal and Fourier-wedge convention]]

[Mikko Salo, On geometric inverse problems and microlocal analysis, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

[Venkataswaran P. Krishnan and Eric Todd Quinto, Microlocal Analysis in Tomography, §1.3.2](https://math.tifrbng.res.in/~vkrishnan/Papers/Microlocal_Analysis_Tomography.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty open set $\Theta\subset S^1$, a compactly supported smooth complex function $f$, and the hypothesis $Rf(\theta,s)=0$ for every measured normal and offset.

[F1] For this proof, put $W_\Theta=\{\sigma\theta:\theta\in\Theta,\ \sigma\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\}$. Since $\Theta$ is nonempty and open, it contains an open arc $J$, and the positive-radius sector $\{r\theta:r>0,\ \theta\in J\}$ is a nonempty open subset of $W_\Theta$.

[F2] [[thm-ip-fourier-slice-identity]]: for compactly supported smooth input and the line-normal convention, $\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta)$ for all real $\sigma$; the supplier proof uses no Countable Choice.

[F3] [[lem-ip-compact-support-fourier-laplace-is-entire]]: the compact-support Riemann Fourier-Laplace transform of a smooth compactly supported function is entire in each coordinate, with coordinate derivatives given by integrals with polynomial factors; the proof is choice-free.

[F4] [[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]]: the real Riemann integral is linear, monotone, and bounded by volume times a uniform absolute bound; apply it componentwise to complex functions.

[F5] [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]]: a holomorphic function on a connected domain that vanishes on a set with an accumulation point in the domain vanishes everywhere.

[F6] [[thm-real-stone-weierstrass-for-compact-metric-spaces]]: real polynomials on a compact subset of $\mathbb R^2$ are dense in its real continuous functions because they form a unital point-separating algebra.

## Proof

1.1 The hypothesis and the compact-support Fourier-slice identity [F2] give $\widehat f(\sigma\theta)=0$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$. By [F1], this includes the nonempty open positive-radius sector generated by $J$; choose a product of open real intervals $I_1\times I_2$ inside that sector. For each real $\xi_2\in I_2$, the entire function $z_1\mapsto\widehat f(z_1,\xi_2)$ vanishes on $I_1$, so [F5] makes it zero for every complex $z_1$. Then for every real $\xi_1$ the entire second-coordinate slice vanishes on $I_2$, and [F5] makes it zero everywhere. Thus $\widehat f$ vanishes on all of $\mathbb R^2$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given, choose]

2.1 Let $K=\operatorname{supp}f$. If $K=\varnothing$, then $f=0$. Otherwise, fix a rectangle $B$ whose interior contains $K$ and interpret all integrals below as compact-support Riemann integrals over $B$. Repeated use of the coordinate derivative formula in [F3] shows $\int_B x^\alpha f(x)\,dx=0$ for every multi-index $\alpha$, since all real-frequency derivatives of $\widehat f$ vanish at the origin. The real polynomials restricted to $K$ form a unital subalgebra separating points, because the coordinate functions distinguish distinct points. By [F6], approximate $\operatorname{Re}\overline f$ and $\operatorname{Im}\overline f$ uniformly on $K$ by real polynomials; combine these approximations into complex polynomials $p_j$. Every moment is zero, so $\int_Bfp_j=0$. Also $f=0$ outside $K$, so $\int_B|f|^2=\left|\int_Bf(\overline f-p_j)\right|\le\sqrt2\,\operatorname{vol}(B)\|f\|_{C(B)}\|p_j-\overline f\|_{C(K)}\to0$, using the real Riemann integral bound [F4] on both components. If $f$ were nonzero at a point, continuity would bound $|f|^2$ below by a positive number on a nondegenerate box inside $B$, forcing its nonnegative Riemann integral to be positive. Thus $f=0$ everywhere. This proof uses neither Fourier inversion nor Countable Choice. [F3, F4, F6, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Let
$X\sim N_2(0,\operatorname{diag}(1,0))$,
$\eta\sim N_2(0,I_2)$ independently, $A=I_2$, and observe
$y=(2,3)^T$ in the model $Y=AX+\eta$. The prior support is
$S_0=\{(t,0)^T:t\in\mathbb R\}$. The Gaussian posterior version has mean
$(1,0)^T$ and covariance $\operatorname{diag}(1/2,0)$. On $S_0$, the
support-restricted objective is
$$ J_y(x)=(x_1-2)^2+(x_2-3)^2+x_1^2, $$
and its unique minimizer is $(1,0)^T$.

## Example references

[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior|The posterior formula allows a singular state covariance when the observed covariance is positive definite.]]

[[cor-ip-gaussian-map-equals-tikhonov-minimizer|The MAP, posterior mean, and support-restricted minimizer agree for the finite Gaussian model.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the model and datum in the Example.

[A1] AC is inherited from the Gaussian-law and finite Gaussian-conditioning
interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The finite linear Gaussian posterior mean and covariance are given by the
displayed conditioning formulas, even for singular prior covariance.
[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior]]

[F2] The posterior MAP and mean equal the unique support-restricted
Tikhonov minimizer. [[cor-ip-gaussian-map-equals-tikhonov-minimizer]]

[F3] A rank-one Gaussian prior with covariance $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ has
support $\{(t,0)^T:t\in\mathbb R\}$ and pseudoinverse
$\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$. [[lem-ip-singular-gaussian-support-and-pseudoinverse]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses and facts in the Example and Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Here $C_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$. Thus $C_0S^{-1}y=(1,0)^T$ and $C_0-C_0S^{-1}C_0=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,0)$, which gives the posterior mean and covariance in the Example by [F1]. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 On $S_0$, $x_2=0$ and $C_0^\dagger=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ by [F3]. The objective becomes $(x_1-2)^2+9+x_1^2 =2(x_1-1)^2+11$, so it has the unique minimizer $(1,0)^T$. By [F2] this point is also the posterior MAP and mean, as asserted. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\varphi=\sigma x_1$ for $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$. For $0<h\leq h_0$ define
$$P_{\varphi,h,q}=e^{\varphi/h}h^2(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\varphi/h}.$$
There is a constant $C$ such that every $w\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|P_{\varphi,h,q}w\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
Moreover, for every $F\in L^2(M)$ there is an $R\in L^2(M)$ solving $P_{\varphi,h,q}R=F$ in distributions on $M^\circ$ and satisfying
$$\|R\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
No boundary trace is prescribed for $R$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product metric and distinguished coordinate]]

[[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain|Sobolev spaces and distributional interpretation]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice, a compact product subdomain $(M,g)\Subset(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$, a real smooth $q$, a sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$, and $0<h\leq h_0$.

[F1] [[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain]]: the metric is the product $dx_1^2\oplus g_0$, so its coefficients are independent of $x_1$ and $|\nabla_gx_1|=1$.

[F2] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: $L^2$ and $H^1$ are defined by the Riemannian density and fixed chartwise Sobolev norms; compactly supported interior smooth functions have no boundary terms in integration by parts.

[F3] [[def-laplace-beltrami-operator-as-trace-of-the-hessian]]: $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is assumed through [[thm-complex-hahn-banach-norm-preserving-extension]] to extend the bounded complex functional from the range of the adjoint to all of $L^2(M)$.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed through [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] to represent the extended bounded functional by an $L^2$ vector.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Put $s=\varphi$ and first set $q=0$. For a real smooth weight $\psi$, direct differentiation gives
$$P_{\psi,h,0}=e^{\psi/h}(-h^2\Delta_g)e^{-\psi/h} =-h^2\Delta_g-|\nabla_g\psi|^2+2h\nabla_g\psi\cdot\nabla_g+h\Delta_g\psi.$$
For $\psi=s$, $|\nabla s|=1$ and $\Delta s=0$, so $P_{s,h,0}=A+C$ with $A=-h^2\Delta_g-1$ self-adjoint and $C=2h\partial_s$ skew-adjoint on compactly supported functions. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Convexify by $\psi=f(s)=s+\frac{h}{2\varepsilon}s^2$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is fixed small and then $h/\varepsilon$ is small. Since $M$ is compact, choose $h$ so $f'=1+hs/\varepsilon>1/2$ on $M$. The conjugated operator is $P_{\psi,h,0}=A_\varepsilon+C_\varepsilon$ with
$$A_\varepsilon=-h^2\Delta_g-(f')^2,\qquad C_\varepsilon=2hf'\partial_s+hf'',\qquad f''=h/\varepsilon.$$
Here $A_\varepsilon$ is self-adjoint and $C_\varepsilon$ is skew-adjoint. Product independence of $s$ makes $-\Delta_g=-\partial_s^2-\Delta_{g_0}$, with $\Delta_{g_0}$ commuting with $C_\varepsilon$. Direct differentiation in the $s$ coordinate therefore gives the exact commutator
$$[A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon]=4h(f')^2f''-4h^3f''\partial_s^2.$$
For compactly supported $w$, integration by parts yields
$$\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2^2 =\|A_\varepsilon w\|_2^2+\|C_\varepsilon w\|_2^2+ 4h f''\|(f')w\|_2^2+4h^3f''\|\partial_sw\|_2^2 \geq c h^2\varepsilon^{-1}\|w\|_2^2.$$
The same identity implies $\|A_\varepsilon w\|_2\leq\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2$. Since
$\|h\nabla w\|_2^2=\langle A_\varepsilon w,w\rangle+\|f'w\|_2^2$,
the $L^2$ bound just obtained gives $\|w\|_2+\|h\nabla w\|_2\leq C_\varepsilon h^{-1}\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

1.3 The convexified and unconvexified weights are related by multiplication with $m=e^{s^2/(2\varepsilon)}$: $P_{\psi,h,0}(mw)=mP_{s,h,0}w$. On compact $M$, $m$ and $m^{-1}$ are bounded, so step 1.2 yields $\|w\|_2\leq C h^{-1}\|P_{s,h,0}w\|_2$. Adding the potential changes the conjugated operator by $h^2q$. Its norm on $w$ is at most $h^2\|q\|_\infty\|w\|_2$, which is absorbed in the preceding estimate for sufficiently small $h$. Replacing $s$ by either sign of $x_1$ proves the a priori estimate in the statement. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $P=P_{\varphi,h,q}$ and apply the a priori estimate also to $P^*=P_{-\varphi,h,q}$, which has the same real potential and the opposite allowed sign. On $E=P^*(C_c^\infty(M^\circ))\subset L^2(M)$ define the complex-linear functional $\ell(P^*w)=\int_M\bar Fw\,dV_g$. The estimate makes this well-defined: $P^*w=0$ implies $w=0$. It also gives $|\ell(P^*w)|\leq\|F\|_2\|w\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_2\|P^*w\|_2$. By [A1] extend $\ell$ to $L^2(M)$ with the same bound; by [A2] there is $R\in L^2(M)$ with $\ell(z)=\int_Mz\bar R\,dV_g$ and $\|R\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_2$. Taking complex conjugates gives $\int_MR\overline{P^*w}\,dV_g=\int_MF\bar w\,dV_g$ for every test $w$, which is precisely $PR=F$ distributionally on $M^\circ$. [F2, A1, A2, given, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

---
id: lem-smooth-ball-windows-and-boundary-disk-absorption
kind: lemma
title: "Smooth ball windows and absorption along a boundary disk"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 0
deps: [def-countable-choice, lem-isotopy-extension-for-a-compact-source-with-boundary]
justified_by: []
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Allen Hatcher, Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology"
      url: "https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf"
      locator: "Chapter 1, Lemma 1.3 and its proof, printed p.3"
---

## Statement

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[lem-isotopy-extension-for-a-compact-source-with-boundary]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice; a smooth ball embedding $e:D^n\to N$ for $n=2,3$; and, for the last assertions, a smooth disk window and a rounded disk attachment.

[F1] An isotopy of embeddings of a compact manifold with boundary into a boundaryless manifold of the same dimension, made stationary near its time endpoints, extends to a smooth ambient isotopy with support in any prescribed neighborhood of its track ([[lem-isotopy-extension-for-a-compact-source-with-boundary]]).

[A1] The choice assumption is [[def-countable-choice]] and is used through [F1]. All ball shrinkings, coordinate interpolations and collar choices below are finite constructions.

## Proof

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses above.

1.1 Shrink the parametrized ball without collapsing it: $e_t(x)=e(r(t)x)$, where $r$ decreases smoothly from $1$ to a fixed positive $\varepsilon$ and is constant near both ends. Every slice is an embedding. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, its last image lies in one coordinate chart centered at $e(0)$. Write the chart representative of $e$ near $0$ as $f$, with $f(0)=0$ and $L=Df(0)$ invertible. Let $m>0$ satisfy $|Lv|\ge m|v|$. Choose $\varepsilon$ so that $\|Df(y)-L\|<m/2$ for $|y|\le\varepsilon$. The interpolation $f_s(x)=\varepsilon Lx+(1-s)(f(\varepsilon x)-\varepsilon Lx)$ has invertible differential and is injective: its difference from $\varepsilon L$ is Lipschitz with constant less than $\varepsilon m/2$, so $|f_s(x)-f_s(y)|\ge\varepsilon m|x-y|/2$. All images lie in the chart after a further shrink. This is an isotopy from the small ball to a linear ellipsoid. [given, construct]

2.1 Write $L=QP$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $P$ positive definite. The positive definite path $(1-s)P+s\lambda I$, for small $\lambda>0$, gives an isotopy from that ellipsoid to a coordinate round ball. Reparametrize and concatenate the finite paths smoothly with stationary endpoints. By [F1] the resulting embedding isotopy extends to an ambient isotopy carrying $e(D^n)$ to that round ball. A coordinate ball can be moved along any prescribed finite chain of overlapping charts, shrinking it inside each overlap before the next move; a path between its center and any prescribed target center has such a finite chart subdivision. Within a chart, translation and positive dilation of a sufficiently small round ball are embedding isotopies. Hence any two sufficiently small coordinate balls in the same connected component are ambient isotopic. [F1, A1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Parametrize the given $3$-ball $B$ by $D^3$. Its boundary is thereby the standard $S^2$. Apply steps 1.1–2.1 in dimension two to a parametrization of its disk window $W\subset S^2$, then move and enlarge the resulting small round disk to a hemisphere by latitude disks. The endpoint parametrization in step 2.1 is linear orthogonal followed by a positive scalar; its orthogonal factor is the restriction of a fixed orthogonal symmetry of $S^2$. Consequently the standardization can retain the specified disk parametrization, up to that fixed symmetry, rather than only its image. Thus there is an isotopy $h_t$ of $S^2$, starting at the identity, that carries $W$ to a hemisphere, and, if needed, a fixed orthogonal symmetry makes its endpoint agree with the specified standard disk coordinates. This isotopy extends over $D^3$ explicitly: in a radial annulus use $(r,x)\mapsto(r,h_{\alpha(r)t}(x))$, where $\alpha=0$ near the inner edge and $\alpha=1$ near $r=1$, and use the identity on the smaller ball. Each slice is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $(r,y)\mapsto(r,h_{\alpha(r)t}^{-1}(y))$. It is smooth across the inner edge because it is the identity there; the fixed orthogonal symmetry also extends linearly over $D^3$. This proves standardization of the ball-window pair with its disk coordinates, without extending an arbitrary sphere diffeomorphism. [F1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Standardize the added ball's window using its actual attaching parametrization, as permitted by step 3.1. Its collar map is then the product $(x,t)\mapsto(x,t)$ in the receiving disk coordinates. The standard ball-window pair can be represented as a cap over a flat disk: its remaining boundary is a dome meeting the window at its edge. This representation follows by viewing a round ball as two hemispherical graphs and flattening one graph in its collar; the strictly positive normal-coordinate derivative makes the flattening a diffeomorphism. Making the cap thinner is a positive rescaling of its normal coordinate. Therefore in the collar of a disk $D$ in the receiving boundary the attached ball may be represented as a thin cap, with its attaching map retained. A coordinate neighborhood of the whole closed disk exists: extend its full-rank parametrization across the boundary circle using finitely many boundary charts; the extensions agree with it on the disk, and sufficiently small extensions remain injective by compactness and the inverse function theorem. [step 3.1, construct]

5.1 In these coordinates the receiving manifold is $t\ge0$. After rounding the edge, its union with the thin cap is $t\ge\gamma(x)$, where $\gamma\le0$ is smooth and compactly supported in the disk coordinate neighborhood. Take a smooth cutoff $\rho(t)$ equal to one near the cap and zero beyond the chosen receiving collar. Choose the cap thin enough that $\|\gamma\rho'\|_\infty<1$. Then $(x,t)\mapsto(x,t-\gamma(x)\rho(t))$ sends $t\ge\gamma(x)$ diffeomorphically to $t\ge0$: its normal derivative is $1-\gamma(x)\rho'(t)>0$, its boundary value is zero, and it is the identity at the far end of each collar fiber. It is the identity outside this neighborhood, so it pastes to the identity elsewhere. This proves disk absorption. Applying the inverse construction proves disk removal, with the same support assertion. [step 4.1, construct]

6.1 The first assertion is established by steps 1.1–2.1, the window assertion by step 3.1, and both attachment assertions by step 5.1. In particular two balls glued along one boundary disk form a ball; and a boundary-attached ball indented into a ball can be removed leaving a ball. Every use of isotopy extension is in dimensions two or three with compact source and stationary endpoints, as required by [F1]. [F1, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1] ∎

id: cex-knot-kt-36-boundary-case
kind: counterexample
title: One finite sequence value does not determine asymptotic growth
status: draft

dependency_level: 0

    - title: Hitoshi Murakami and Jun Murakami, The colored Jones polynomials and the
        simplicial volume of a knot, §5
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9905075
    - title: Hitoshi Murakami, An Introduction to the Volume Conjecture, §§1–4
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1002.0126
---

## Statement refuted

For every positive real sequence $(a_N)_{N\ge1}$, every real $V>0$, and every integer $N_0\ge1$, if $(2\pi/N_0)\log(a_{N_0})=V$, then $\lim_{N\to\infty}(2\pi/N)\log(a_N)=V$.

## Statement references

[Hitoshi Murakami and Jun Murakami, *The colored Jones polynomials and the simplicial volume of a knot*, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9905075)

[Hitoshi Murakami, *An Introduction to the Volume Conjecture*, §§1–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1002.0126)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A positive real sequence $(a_N)_{N\ge1}$, a target value $V>0$, and a finite index $N_0\ge1$.

[F1] For every positive real $x$, $\log x$ is defined, and $\log 1=0$.

## Counterexample

1.1 Define $a_{N_0}=\exp(VN_0/(2\pi))$ and $a_N=1$ for every $N\ge1$ with $N\ne N_0$. Each term is positive, and $(2\pi/N_0)\log(a_{N_0})=(2\pi/N_0)(VN_0/(2\pi))=V$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 For every $N>N_0$, $a_N=1$, so $(2\pi/N)\log(a_N)=0$. The sequence of normalized logarithms is therefore eventually zero and has limit $0\ne V$. This contradicts the asserted conclusion. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

This is a sequence-level witness about the information in one finite evaluation. It is not asserted to be a colored Jones sequence and does not refute the volume conjecture.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

## Definition references

[[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model|Compact linear inverse model between Hilbert spaces]]

[[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators|Compact-operator singular system and expansion]]

[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis|Complete orthonormal systems and Hilbert bases]]

[[thm-hilbert-space-with-a-given-orthonormal-basis-is-ell-two-of-the-index-set|A complete orthonormal basis identifies a Hilbert space isometrically with $\ell^2$]]

[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set|Square-summable families and $\ell^2$]]

[[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment|Functional isonormal white-noise experiment]]

[[thm-ip-white-noise-spectral-sequence-representation|Independent Gaussian coordinates in a white-noise experiment]]

[[def-countable-choice|The Axiom of Countable Choice]]

[Litao Ding and Peter Mathé, *Minimax rates for statistical inverse problems under general source conditions*, §1, equations (1)–(4), PDF pp. 1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.01706)

[Iain M. Johnstone, *Gaussian estimation: Sequence and wavelet models*, §3.8, equations (3.63)–(3.67), printed pp. 77–79](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jbradic/math281a/Johnstone.pdf)

## Coordinate diagram

The deterministic square commutes: $\Phi_X(x)=(\langle x,v_j\rangle)_j$ and $\Phi_{H_0}(y)=(\langle y,u_j\rangle)_j$ are the coefficient isometries, and $D_s(\theta)=(s_j\theta_j)_j$ is well defined because $s_j\le s_1$. The compact SVD expansion gives $\Phi_{H_0}(Kx)=D_s(\Phi_X(x))$. The noisy coordinates add $\epsilon\xi_j$ before division by $s_j$; the diagram is not a claim that white noise is an $H_0$-valued sample and is not used as a proof.

```tikzcd
N(K)^\perp \arrow[r, "\Phi_X"] \arrow[d, "K"'] & \ell^2(\mathbb{N},\mathbb{R}) \arrow[d, "D_s"] \\
H_0 \arrow[r, "\Phi_{H_0}"'] & \ell^2(\mathbb{N},\mathbb{R})
```

## Example

Fix a truth bound $R>0$. For every absolute operator-shift radius $\rho_A>0$, take the working scalar operator $A_0=\rho_A/2$, the true operator $A=0$, the noiseless datum $Y=A\theta$ at truth $\theta=R$, and the working inverse $g(y)=y/A_0$. Then $|A-A_0|=\rho_A/2\le\rho_A$ but $|g(Y)-\theta|^2=R^2$. Thus no recovery modulus tending to zero with the absolute operator error can hold uniformly when the baseline inverse conditioning is allowed to vanish.

## Example references

[[ex-ip-robust-ellipsoid-minimax-shift-rate|The robust-inversion frontier and its need for explicit conditioning hypotheses.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $R>0$, any $\rho_A>0$, working operator $A_0=\rho_A/2$, true operator $A=0$, truth $\theta=R$, noiseless data $Y=A\theta$, and working inverse $g(y)=y/A_0$.

[A1] In the scalar model the operator norm is absolute value, and the recovery loss is squared absolute error.

## Verification

1.1 The absolute operator discrepancy is $|A-A_0|=|0-\rho_A/2|=\rho_A/2\le\rho_A$. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 By step 1.1 this is an allowed perturbation. The true noiseless datum is $Y=A\theta=0$, so $g(Y)=0/A_0=0$. The squared reconstruction error is $|0-R|^2=R^2$, independent of $\rho_A$. Since $R>0$ is fixed while $\rho_A$ can be arbitrarily small, a uniform modulus depending only on absolute operator shift cannot tend to zero. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

kind: lemma
title: Local-coefficient cap duality on a coordinate ball without choice
status: draft
origin: pipeline
deps:
  - def-compactly-supported-cohomology-with-local-coefficients
  - def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings
  - lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets
  - thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients

sources:

        local coefficients
      url: https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 0
