## Statement

Let $B$ be an oriented coordinate ball of dimension $n\ge0$ and let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups on $B$. Cap with the integral support orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$H_c^k(B;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-k}(B;\mathcal L)$$
in every integer degree. Under a coordinate contraction trivialization with fiber $A$, both sides are $A$ for $k=n$ and zero otherwise, and the displayed nonzero map is the identity on $A$. No choice principle is assumed; any commuting coefficient-ring action is respected.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The coordinate ball, its orientation, and the local system. Use the given chart to identify the ball with $\mathbb R^n$.

[F1] Compact-support representatives and their equality criterion are defined by relative local cohomology. [[def-compactly-supported-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]]

[F2] Pair sequences and Mayer–Vietoris hold for local coefficients by explicit small-chain homotopies. [[thm-pair-long-exact-sequences-with-local-coefficients]], [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[F3] Integral support orientation classes exist without choice, and the actual cap product is front-face evaluation followed by retention of the back face. [[lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets]], [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]]

## Proof

1.1 Fix the coordinate center $0$. Transport along straight radii trivializes $\mathcal L$ with fiber $A=\mathcal L_0$; triangular straight homotopies show that these identifications intertwine every path transport, since the ball is contractible. A contraction induces the usual singular prism homotopy by triangulating each simplex times the interval into its finitely many standard prisms, carrying constant coefficients unchanged. Its boundary identity proves directly that a contractible space has cohomology $A$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees, with no universal-coefficient theorem or chosen primitive family. It also computes homology as $A$ in degree zero and zero elsewhere. For two points the cochain complex splits as two such complexes, so its reduced degree-zero cohomology is $A$ by the difference of the two values. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The same coefficient calculation gives $\widetilde H^k(S^m;A)=A$ for $k=m$ and zero otherwise, for each $m\ge0$. Start with the two-point sphere from step 1.1. For $m\ge1$, cover $S^m$ by the complements of the two poles; both are contractible and their intersection retracts onto $S^{m-1}$. The reduced cohomology Mayer–Vietoris sequence in [F2] identifies each group with the preceding degree on that intersection. This is a finite induction. These identifications are normalized by evaluation on the oriented sphere cycle: split a triangulated sphere into its two oriented hemispheres; the connecting cochain evaluates on their sum as the preceding cochain evaluates on their common boundary. This follows from $(\delta a)(c)=a(\partial c)$ with the difference signs of Mayer–Vietoris. Starting with the oriented difference of the two points, induction proves that evaluation on the oriented fundamental sphere cycle is the resulting isomorphism to $A$, including its sign. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For $n\ge1$, closed concentric balls are cofinal among compact supports in $\mathbb R^n$. The complement of a closed radius-$r$ ball retracts radially onto any larger concentric sphere. Since the ambient space is contractible, its pair sequence in [F2] and step 2.1 identify $H^k(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^n\setminus\overline B_r;A)$ with $A$ for $k=n$ and with zero otherwise. The isomorphism is evaluation on a positively oriented relative ball cycle: the pair connector and $(\delta a)(c)=a(\partial c)$ identify it with the sphere evaluation of step 2.1. Enlargement from $r$ to a larger radius preserves this normalization, since the two oriented sphere cycles bound the oriented intervening annulus and the relative ball cycles restrict to the same local orientation. Hence the direct limit in [F1] has exactly the asserted groups, without a choice of representatives at infinitely many radii. For $n=0$ the ball is a point and the same conclusion is step 1.1. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 A finite triangulated coordinate ball enclosing the support, with boundary disjoint from it, represents the canonical support class by [F3]. In degree $n$, the cap formula sends a relative cocycle $\alpha$ and this oriented cycle $z$ to a zero-chain whose sum of coefficients is $\alpha(z)$: each retained back face is a vertex and each coefficient is the front evaluation on that simplex. The coefficient sum identifies $H_0(B;A)$ with $A$ by the contraction in step 1.1. Step 3.1 shows that $\alpha\mapsto\alpha(z)$ is exactly the source identification with $A$. Thus cap is the identity in its only nonzero degree, and it is the unique zero-group isomorphism in all other degrees. Every transport, prism, finite hemisphere induction, and cofinal-support comparison commutes with any commuting scalar action. Only one center and finitely many geometric data at a time were used, so no choice axiom is needed. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

title: Disk-band Seifert surfaces give actual cyclic zero-surgery bounding manifolds
status: draft
origin: pipeline

  - thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality-with-local-coefficients

  proof: ai-generated
sources:

        group
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0206059
      locator: Appendix5, Lemmas5.4–5.6 and their proofs, PDF20–24. Their
        second-variable positive-push matrix S is the transpose of the
        first-variable positive-push matrix V used here.
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19

## Statement

Assume AC. Supply a finite smooth oriented disk-and-band presentation of a connected Seifert surface $F\subset S^3$ of genus $g$ with one boundary component $K$, including its boundary product collar. Supply an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and its **first-variable positive-push** matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The positive normal is determined by the surface and ambient orientations. Use the preferred longitude and positive meridian of this actual surface and tube in the zero-surgery manifold $M_K$.

A finite smooth construction gives a compact connected oriented four-manifold $W_F$ with its actual oriented boundary identified with $M_K$, and an isomorphism $\pi_1(W_F)\cong\mathbb Z$ taking the positive meridian to $1$. Thus the positive meridian map $\pi_1(M_K)\to\mathbb Z/d$ extends over $W_F$ for every positive integer $d$. The ordinary intersection form of $W_F$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb R$, has dimension $2g$, contains an isotropic subspace of dimension $g$, and has signature zero.

More precisely, put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$ and $R=\Lambda[(1-t)^{-1}]$. The positive deck generator is denoted $T$. With the equivariant pairing **linear in the first variable**
$$\lambda(x,y)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(x\mathbin{\cdot}T^ky)t^k,$$
the localized second homology has a basis of size $2g$ and matrix
$$H(t)=(1-t)V+(1-t^{-1})V^T.$$
For every unit complex number $z\ne1$, the corresponding character component has actual second homology of dimension $2g$ and intersection matrix $H(z)$, up to a positive scalar if Fourier-projected lift cycles are used as basis. This assertion includes singular matrices $H(z)$: no Alexander-polynomial nonvanishing is required. Equivalently, in the conjugate-first convention the matrix is the transpose, with the same signature. The trivial-character component is the ordinary metabolic form just described; the zero matrix $H(1)$ is not asserted to be its homology-basis matrix.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the actual finite smooth surface, collar, basis and push data of the Statement.

[F1] Preferred-longitude filling defines the oriented zero-surgery manifold; it does not supply a four-dimensional extension. [[def-zero-surgery-on-a-knot]]

[F2] Finite smooth surface presentations with equal Euler characteristic and boundary count admit orientation-preserving matches with prescribed boundary maps and collars, under Countable Choice, hence under AC. The proof explicitly realizes polygon cuts and handle extraction on smooth ribbon neighborhoods. [[lem-finite-smooth-surface-presentations-have-prescribed-collar-matches]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F3] Van Kampen gives the group pushout for connected collared gluings. Excision and Mayer–Vietoris apply to one ambient local system and its restrictions. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]] [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]] The cellular complex of a supplied finite CW pair computes its local singular homology. [[thm-cellular-chains-compute-homology-with-local-coefficients]]

[F4] Poincare–Lefschetz duality over the constant field identifies relative middle homology with the dual of absolute middle homology, and identifies the absolute-to-relative map with the intersection form. [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality-with-local-coefficients]]

[F5] Parametric transversality applies to a finite smooth perturbation family transverse to an embedded target; its Countable Choice hypothesis follows from AC. [[thm-parametric-transversality]]

## Proof

1.1 Work in an inward collar $S^3\times[0,\epsilon)$ of the standard ball. Push $F$ to the graph of a smooth positive interior depth function, zero on its boundary and with positive inward derivative there. Such a function is obtained from the supplied finite band and disk charts and positive finite bump sums, retaining the prescribed boundary collar. Round its finitely many seams in those charts. Denote this neat pushed surface by $F'$, and remove the interior of a small product normal disk neighborhood. The result $V_F$ is a compact smooth manifold after the displayed corner roundings. Its boundary is the knot exterior $E_K$ glued to $F\times S^1$ along their common torus: a normal disk to $F'$ has boundary the positive meridian, and the surface boundary direction is the preferred zero-linking longitude. This already fixes the peripheral marking, before any new handle is attached. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Here is a useful cut model, including why its chamber is a ball. The trace of the inward push gives a three-dimensional sheet from $F'$ back to its original position in $S^3$. Cut $V_F$ open along the portion of this sheet outside the removed normal neighborhood. The two banks are copies of a thickening of $F$, and the resulting chamber $Q$ is a ball with these marked banks. This last assertion has a collar construction. In each normal two-plane the removed disk and the cut trace are a rounded slit reaching the outside boundary. Cutting the slit opens it into an indentation attached to that boundary. Over a small three-dimensional neighborhood of $F$ in $S^3$, straighten that indentation to a depth graph $s=h(x)$; the graph has support in that neighborhood. The straightening in a normal section is the increasing reparametrization between two rounded intervals, and agrees with the identity at the outer section endpoints. The product coordinates along $F$ paste these reparametrizations; at its boundary use the supplied half-disk collar, so the slit endpoint is the same rounded half-section on both sides. All widths can be chosen common over the finitely many compact disk/band pieces. For a collar of depth $L>\max h$, the formula $(x,s)\mapsto(x,h(x)+(L-h(x))s/L)$ is a diffeomorphism from the original collar onto the graph indentation, agrees with the unchanged interior along a smaller interpolated collar, and has strictly positive normal derivative. It is identity outside the graph support. Undoing this indentation identifies $Q$ with the standard ball. The banks retain precisely the positive and negative normal push copies of $F$ in its boundary. This is a cut-and-collar parameterization, not a claim that an arbitrary smooth four-ball is standard. [step 1.1, construct]

2.2 We now change the boundary to actual zero surgery. Let $H$ be a smooth genus-$g$ handlebody whose oriented boundary is the union of a copy of $F$ and a disk along $\partial F$. Such a marked handlebody is supplied by the finite standard disk with $2g$ bands on the boundary of the standard genus-$g$ three-dimensional handlebody. The given disk-band surface has a finite smooth triangle presentation by subdividing its finitely many rectangles and disks in their coordinates. Both surfaces have Euler characteristic $1-2g$ and one boundary, so [F2] matches them with the exact given boundary map and collar. This transfers the handlebody parameter to the given $F$. Glue $H\times S^1$ to $V_F$ along $F\times S^1$, using the normal circle as the second factor and opposite boundary orientations. Round the product corners in those same collars, and call the result $W_F$. The remaining boundary is exactly $E_K\cup(D^2\times S^1)$, where the disk meridian is the actual preferred longitude and the circle core is the actual positive meridian. Its orientation restricts to the original oriented exterior. Therefore the boundary identification is the oriented [F1] zero surgery, rather than a homology-equivalent substitute. Equivalently, this gluing attaches the $g$ round handles which compress $F$ to the displayed disk. It is not the simply connected two-handle trace of zero surgery. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Form the infinite cyclic cut space by taking chambers $Q_k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, and identifying the positive bank of $Q_k$ with the negative bank of $Q_{k-1}$. Fix the indexing so the positive meridian crosses to the next chamber; its deck motion is $T$. Finite consecutive unions of chambers are simply connected by [F3]: each chamber is a ball and each joining thickened $F$ is connected, so the tree of trivial vertex groups has trivial pushout. A compact loop or homotopy meets only finitely many chambers, since the chamber pattern is locally finite. Hence the full cut space is simply connected and is the universal cover, with deck group generated by $T$. Thus $\pi_1(V_F)=\mathbb Z$, generated by the actual positive meridian. The cover's Mayer–Vietoris sequence, or its degreewise short exact small-chain sequence, has the form of the mapping cone of the difference of the two bank inclusions, from $C_*(F)\otimes\Lambda$ to $C_*(Q)\otimes\Lambda$. The same assertion holds directly with a specified character in place of $\Lambda$: coefficients are trivial within each bank and chamber, and the second bank map has the character factor. Since $Q$ is a ball and $F$ has one boundary component, it gives $$H_2(V_F;\Lambda)\cong H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda,\qquad H_3(V_F;\Lambda)=0.$$ On degree-zero homology the difference map is $1-t$ up to its invertible sign/deck factor. For every $z\ne1$ this factor is invertible, while the degree-one chamber homology is zero. Directly using the character small-chain sequence therefore gives $H_2(V_F;\mathbb C_z)\cong H_1(F;\mathbb C)$, without a possibly nonflat specialization argument. [F3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 We calculate the ordinary part separately over $\mathbb R$. Mayer–Vietoris for the original decomposition of the ball into $V_F$ and $F\times D^2$ identifies the rim-torus map $$H_1(F)\otimes H_1(S^1)=H_2(F\times S^1)\longrightarrow H_2(V_F)$$ as an isomorphism: its adjacent ball homology groups vanish and $H_2(F\times D^2)=0$. It also gives $H_1(V_F)=\mathbb R$, generated by the meridian, since the other degree-one summand is $H_1(F)$ and the overlap map to it is the identity. One has $H_3(V_F)=0$ since the adjacent degree-three product group and ball groups are zero. For $W_F=V_F\cup(H\times S^1)$ the degree-two overlap map is $(\mathrm{id},j_*)$ in this rim identification, where $j_*:H_1(F)\to H_1(H)$ is onto of ranks $2g\to g$. Its cokernel has dimension $g$. The degree-one overlap map is $$(x,n)\longmapsto(n,j_*x,n)\in H_1(V_F)\oplus H_1(H)\oplus H_1(S^1),$$ with an immaterial minus sign on one gluing summand. Its kernel has dimension $g$. Exactness therefore gives $\dim H_2(W_F)=2g$. The image of $H_2(H\times S^1)$ is injective: the graph image $(x,j_*x)$ meets $0\oplus H_2(H\times S^1)$ only in zero. It has dimension $g$. Choose the $g$ disjoint framed longitude curves of the explicit three-dimensional handlebody. Their products with $S^1$ are disjoint embedded tori with disjoint normal pushes. They represent this image, so it is isotropic. [F3, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 We calculate the form with its signs. Represent the finitely many basis cycles by oriented smooth one-cycles on $F$, with transverse intersections, and choose independent normal levels for any coinciding pieces. For $a_i$ take a cap of its positive push in $Q_1$ and a cap of its negative push with reversed orientation in $Q_0$. Their union across the banks is an oriented smooth two-cycle $\Sigma_i$ representing the connecting class in step3.1. Caps can be obtained by coning a smooth cycle in the supplied ball parameter and smoothing the cone as a map relative to its boundary; immersion is unnecessary. For intersection counts take two independent copies. Cover their compact interior overlap by finitely many coordinate charts, add coordinate-vector perturbations with supported bumps, and apply [F5] to the product evaluation map and the diagonal of the product ball. Its derivative in those independent target-translation parameters spans the normal to the diagonal. Thus a sufficiently small parameter makes the two maps transverse, while their already separated boundary collars remain fixed. The intersection points are finite, and self-intersections of either separate map do not affect the resulting intersection of cycles. The ordinary intersection number of two such caps in a ball is the linking number of their boundary cycles: choose a spanning two-chain for one boundary in the boundary three-sphere and push its interior inward, where its intersections with the other cap are exactly the signed crossings defining linking. Changing either cap adds a closed two-cycle in the ball and hence changes the count by zero. At each transverse intersection its chart orientation sign is exactly the local orientation evaluation in cap duality, so this geometric count is the homological intersection form of [F4]. Thus the same rule applies to these cycle representatives and to an independent copy for a self-pairing. [F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

4.2 Every loop of $F$ is trivial in $\pi_1(V_F)$: its pushed bank copy lies in the ball $Q$. The map $\pi_1(F)\to\pi_1(H)$ is onto, as is seen in the standard handlebody by its $g$ longitude curves on the punctured boundary. Its kernel kills only these boundary relations. Applying [F3] to $V_F\cup(H\times S^1)$ therefore kills all of the free handlebody group and identifies its circle factor with the positive meridian of $V_F$. No relation kills any power of that meridian: the maps to $\mathbb Z$ which are zero on $\pi_1(H)$ and one on the circle and meridian agree on the overlap. Hence $\pi_1(W_F)=\mathbb Z$ with exactly the specified generator. Reduction modulo $d$ gives the claimed extensions on the actual boundary. [F3, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

5.1 For completeness the four cap pairings give the following finite table, in our first-positive-push convention: $$\begin{array}{c|c}k&\Sigma_i\mathbin{\cdot}T^k\Sigma_j\\\hline 0&V_{ij}+V_{ji}\\ 1&-V_{ij}\\ -1&-V_{ji}\\ |k|>1&0. \end{array}$$ Indeed the two same-chamber upper-upper and lower-lower boundary pairings are respectively $\operatorname{lk}(a_i,a_j^+)=V_{ji}$ and $\operatorname{lk}(a_j,a_i^+)=V_{ij}$, by moving the two chosen normal levels simultaneously without crossing either curve. The lower cap has opposite boundary orientation; at a neighboring chamber exactly one of the two caps is lower, giving the minus sign. The positive neighboring translate pairs the positive push of $a_i$ with $a_j$, and the negative neighboring translate pairs the opposite order. Nonneighboring chamber interiors are disjoint. This also proves the diagonal entries by using an independent parallel cycle before taking the same class. Hence the table sums to $(1-t)V+(1-t^{-1})V^T$. It is Hermitian for $t^*=t^{-1}$. With this displayed pairing, $\lambda(Tx,y)=t\lambda(x,y)$ and $\lambda(x,Ty)=t^{-1}\lambda(x,y)$ by shifting the summation index, explicitly fixing the coefficient convention. [step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For coefficients with $1-t$ invertible, the complexes of both $F\times S^1$ and $H\times S^1$ are contractible. Explicitly the cellular circle complex is $0\to R\xrightarrow{t-1}R\to0$ (or its inverse-deck version, differing by a unit); its contraction sends degree zero to degree one by $(t-1)^{-1}$. In the product total complex the contraction is $(-1)^p$ times this map on a degree-$p$ base chain; direct substitution in the total differential gives $ds+sd=1$. The finite product cells on $F,H$ give the same result for local singular homology by subdivision and their ordinary cellular comparison. The same calculation works directly for each $z\ne1$, with $(z-1)^{-1}$, including every singular Alexander root. Mayer–Vietoris in [F3] now makes $H_2(V_F)\to H_2(W_F)$ an isomorphism for these coefficients. The cycles of the cap calculation can be pushed into the interior of $V_F$, so their intersections computed in $W_F$ have exactly the same orientation and signs. This proves the localized and every nontrivial-character form assertions. Nothing here divides by $\det H(z)$. [F3, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

7.1 The ordinary first homology of $M_K$ is one-dimensional, generated by the meridian. One can compute this with the same supplied exterior/tube: Mayer–Vietoris for $S^3=E_K\cup(S^1\times D^2)$ says that the torus first homology maps isomorphically to the direct sum of the two first homologies, because $H_2(S^3)=H_1(S^3)=0$. The tube kills the meridian, so the exterior homology is generated by it; its kernel slope is the preferred longitude since $F$ bounds it in the exterior. The zero filling kills precisely that longitude and retains the meridian. By step4.2 the map $H_1(M_K)\to H_1(W_F)$ is consequently an isomorphism. The pair exact sequence and [F4] then show that $H_2(W_F)\to H_2(W_F,M_K)$ is onto between vector spaces of equal dimension, hence an isomorphism. Its intersection form is therefore nonsingular. Its $g$-dimensional isotropic subspace from step3.2 has half its dimension. In a basis beginning with that subspace its matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&B\\B^*&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $B$ invertible; the linear-first basis change $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&0\\-\tfrac12DB^{-1}&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ gives $GHG^*=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&B\\B^*&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, removing $D$. The resulting off-diagonal form has equal positive and negative inertia (negating one summand negates the form). Thus its signature is zero. The same argument covers $g=0$ with empty matrices. This establishes the ordinary part without substituting $t=1$ into the localized basis, which would be invalid. All constructions used the supplied smooth disk-band geometry; no spin, Arf-zero, finite-cover nonsingularity or TOP smoothing premise was added. [F3, F4, step 4.2, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded incidence submanifold of codimension $k>0$, and let $(g_0,x_0)\in Z$. Choose coordinates near this point and a submersion $F:G\times X\to\mathbb R^k$ with $Z=\{F=0\}$. Write $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_k)$. For every $\tau\in\mathbb R^k\setminus\{0\}$, the conormal covector at $(g,x)\in Z$ is
$$
(g,x;D_gF(g,x)^T\tau,\ D_xF(g,x)^T\tau).
$$
Consequently the incidence kernel has local delta representation $b(g,x)\delta(F(g,x))|dg\,dx|$, with a smooth density coefficient $b$, and its cotangent relation consists exactly of
$$
(g,D_gF^T\tau;\ x,-D_xF^T\tau),\qquad (g,x)\in Z,\quad \tau\ne0.
$$
No general Fourier-integral-operator composition calculus is used.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation|Incidence kernel and relation convention]]

[[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform|Analytic incidence data]]

[[cor-local-normal-form-for-submersions|Submersion normal form]]

[[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density|Density transformation rule]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The incidence submanifold $Z$, its two submersions, and a local defining submersion $F$ of codimension $k$.

[F1] [[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation]]: the kernel is integration on $Z$ against a smooth density, and the relation pairs conormal $(\eta,-\xi)$.

[F2] [[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform]]: $Z$ is embedded and both projections are submersions.

[F3] [[cor-local-normal-form-for-submersions]]: a submersion is locally equivalent to coordinate projection.

[F4] [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]: density coefficients transform by absolute Jacobians.

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the statement.

1.1 Since $F$ is a submersion, its differential has rank $k$. The tangent space of its zero level is $T_{(g,x)}Z=\ker DF(g,x)$. In finite-dimensional linear algebra, the annihilator of the kernel of a rank-$k$ linear map is the image of its transpose: inclusion follows from $\tau^TDFv=0$ for $v\in\ker DF$, and both spaces have dimension $k$. Hence every conormal is uniquely $DF^T\tau=(D_gF^T\tau,D_xF^T\tau)$. [F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 By [F1], the incidence functional is integration of a test function against a smooth density on $Z$. Complete $F$ to submersion coordinates $(s,t)$ with $t=F(g,x)$, using [F3]. In these coordinates its action is $\int_{t=0}\Phi(s,0)c(s)|ds|$ for a smooth coefficient $c$. Rewriting the ambient density as $|dg\,dx|$ and applying the ordinary change-of-variables rule gives $b(g,x)\delta(F(g,x))|dg\,dx|$ for a smooth $b$; the Jacobian factor is nonzero because the coordinate map is a diffeomorphism. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 The cotangent relation uses the conormal $(\eta,-\xi)$ by [F1]. Substituting the formula from step 1.1 gives $\eta=D_gF^T\tau$ and $-\xi=D_xF^T\tau$, so $\xi=-D_xF^T\tau$. Since $DF^T$ is injective, $\tau\ne0$ gives a nonzero conormal. This proves the displayed relation, with every sign fixed by the kernel convention. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular diagrams of the same oriented smooth knot, with marks away from crossings. Remove a small open arc about each mark and regard each complementary diagram as a one-interval tangle diagram in a disk, using the complementary disk in the projection sphere. Identify their two boundary endpoints and short oriented product collars. The resulting proper arcs can be realized in one standard smooth three-ball so that they are smoothly isotopic with those endpoints and collars fixed. Their diagrams are connected by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves supported away from those collars. This holds when the two diagrams coincide and only the mark has moved along the knot.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]]

[[lem-a-generic-isotopy-of-links-has-only-reidemeister-singular-times]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and the two finite based diagrams of the same oriented knot.

[F1] A smooth isotopy of embeddings of a compact manifold, including a compact three-ball, extends under AC$_\omega$ to an ambient isotopy; end stationarity can be retained ([[thm-isotopy-extension]], clauses 1 and 4).

[F2] Parametric transversality and transverse preimages have the meanings and countable-choice hypotheses of [[thm-parametric-transversality]] and [[thm-transverse-preimage-theorem]]. The finite-jet proof, codimension counts, exclusion of accumulation on source diagonals, and construction of planar isotopies on regular intervals are given in [[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]], proof steps 1.1–5.1.

[F3] An ordinary cusp, quadratic double tangency and transverse triple event give respectively R1, R2 and R3, with all actual orientations and height orders retained ([[lem-a-generic-isotopy-of-links-has-only-reidemeister-singular-times]], proof steps 1.1–2.1; [[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]).

## Proof

1.1 **The endpoint realizations and the common cap.** Regard a planar diagram as a diagram on the projection sphere, and choose a small closed disk $U$ about its mark meeting the diagram in one crossing-free arc only. The complementary disk contains a proper interval diagram; its two endpoints can be put at any prescribed two boundary points by an orientation-preserving disk coordinate change, preserving the interval orientation. Realize its crossings at small distinct positive or negative heights in a thickening of that disk, and straighten short end collars. Round the thickening to a standard three-ball $B$. Closing the interval by a fixed unknotted arc in the complementary ball $B_*$ gives exactly the original diagram on the sphere: the two projected disks glue along their boundary and the cap is the single deleted arc. This operation changes no crossing, sign, or resolution; it replaces the marked circle in every resolution by one interval. Make these choices for both diagrams with the same $B,B_*$, endpoints and cap $J$. The cap and slightly longer knot collars may be chosen identical as parametrized embeddings at both ends. Indeed an orientation-preserving change of circle parametrization can prescribe its parametrization on an interval; it extends over the remaining interval by a strictly increasing smooth map. Such circle reparametrizations are isotopic to the identity, as seen by interpolating their increasing lifts $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x+1)=f(x)+1$, with the identity lift. Thus there is a smooth isotopy $F_t$ of the closed parametrized knots with these endpoint embeddings and this common source interval $J$. Reparametrize time to make it stationary near $0,1$. Here the existence of $F_t$ is exactly the hypothesis that the two closed diagrams represent the same oriented knot. [given, construct]

2.1 **Trivialize a moving ball, including its endpoint charts.** Along the track of the slightly enlarged source interval $J$, choose a smooth pair of normal vectors to the nonzero knot tangent, equal to the same standard pair near $t=0,1$. Such a pair exists on the rectangle $J\times I$: start with local transverse frames, extend them along the interval and then in time, and correct their terminal angle by a smooth rotation, equal to zero initially and to that angle terminally. The terminal angle has a smooth real lift on an interval. Regarding $S^3$ as the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$, use the explicit tube $(F_t(s)+u n_1(s,t)+v n_2(s,t))/\sqrt{1+u^2+v^2}$, with the two normals tangent to $S^3$. Its derivative is injective along the zero section. For uniformly small transverse coordinates it is an embedded tube; compactness gives a common width and excludes intersections with the rest of the knot outside the enlarged interval. Rounded end caps give a smooth family of embedded three-balls $b_t:B_*\to S^3$ about the cap, intersecting the knot in the chosen cap and its standard end collars. At the two stationary ends this family is the same specified ball chart: $b_0=b_1$. Apply [F1] to $b_t$ and, if necessary, a slightly larger ball chart, to get $H_t$ with $H_t b_0=b_t$. Then $G_t=H_t^{-1}F_t$ fixes the cap and its collar throughout. Its restriction to the complementary source interval is a proper-arc isotopy in the fixed $B=S^3\setminus\operatorname{Int}B_*$. At $t=0$ it is the first tangle; at $t=1$ it is $h$ applied to the second, where $h=H_1^{-1}|_B$ is a diffeomorphism equal to the identity on a boundary collar, because $b_1=b_0$ on the slightly larger ball. No identification of the terminal ball chart with an arbitrary initial chart has been assumed. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 **Correct the terminal diffeomorphism on the arc.** Identify $B$ with the unit ball and choose the coordinate origin off the second compact arc $T$. The chart can have this property by a small interior change fixing its boundary collar. Since $h$ is the identity near the boundary, for $0<r\le1$ the maps $h_r(x)=\begin{cases}r h(x/r),&|x|\le r,\\ x,&|x|\ge r\end{cases}$ are smooth diffeomorphisms, agreeing smoothly at $|x|=r$, and equal to the identity on a fixed boundary collar. Put $h_0=1$. For $r$ less than the positive distance from the origin to $T$, $h_r|_T$ is exactly the identity. Thus $(s,r)\mapsto h_r(T(s))$ is a smooth isotopy of proper arcs even at $r=0$, although the ambient Alexander formula need not be smooth at $(x,r)=(0,0)$. Each slice is embedded, its endpoints and collars are fixed, and its final slice is $h(T)$. Reverse this arc isotopy and concatenate it with step 2.1, using stationary time changes at the join. The resulting smooth arc isotopy runs from the first tangle to the second relative to the same boundary endpoints and collars. This argument uses no claim that the diffeomorphism group of a three-ball is smoothly contractible. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 **Projection and relative perturbations.** Choose the standard ball model as a rounded thickening of the projection disk, with the two fixed endpoint collars radial in that disk and with constant height. The rest of the compact arc track is in the interior of the ball. Shorten the protected collars if needed. Compactness then separates their projected endpoint neighbourhoods from every other branch: off a slightly larger source collar the radial coordinate in the disk is uniformly bounded away from its boundary. On the remaining transition collars the projection is still a fixed regular embedded arc. Reparametrize the isotopy in time to be stationary near its two regular end diagrams. In the finite-dimensional family of [F2], replace the time cutoff $\lambda(t)$ by $\lambda(t)\rho(s)$, where $\rho$ vanishes on the protected source collars and is positive on their complement. Embed the compact source rectangle in Euclidean space; multiplying coordinate polynomials of degree at most $43$ by this cutoff independently prescribes jets through order three at any at most six distinct free source points. Explicitly, at points $X_i$, the polynomials $\prod_{j\ne i}|X-X_j|^8$ times suitable cubic Taylor polynomials prescribe the required jets, since multiplication by the nonzero cutoff is invertible on jets. Keep the spatial height coordinate unchanged. Small parameters preserve slice embeddings by compact local immersion and distant-point separation, fix the time-end diagrams, and fix the protected endpoint collars. The collars meet no singular stratum, and the transition region is regular with no other projected branch, so absence of perturbations on the collars loses no needed transversality. [F2, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 **All singularities remain interior and finite.** Apply [F2] to that family on the free source configurations. The equations $g_s=0$ have codimension two in $(s,t)$; the extra degeneracy $\det(g_{ss},g_{sss})=0$ has total codimension three and is avoided. Distinct-point equality has codimension two in $(s_1,s_2,t)$; equality plus tangent dependence has codimension three, giving isolated quadratic double tangencies with nonzero relative normal velocity. Triple equality has codimension four in $(s_1,s_2,s_3,t)$; adding tangent dependence or a vanishing derivative increases codimension and is avoided. Quadruple equality has codimension six in dimension five and is absent. Simultaneous distinct events have combined codimension larger than the shared-time configuration dimension; independent jets at up to six points exclude them. Countably many coordinate charts and AC$_\omega$ allow a parameter outside the resulting countable null union. As in [F2], near a regular source point a projected coordinate is strictly monotone, excluding accumulation along deleted diagonals; near an ordinary cusp its Taylor form $(b s^2,e(t-t_0)s+c s^3)$, $bec\ne0$, has a single local double arc with no accumulation of other event types. Elsewhere the relevant configurations are compact, and isolated transverse events are finite. There are no endpoint accumulations because the protected endpoint neighbourhoods are fixed and isolated, and no end-time accumulations because those diagrams are stationary and regular. These arguments prove the required relative version directly; they do not apply a closed-source statement to an interval without modification. [F2, step 4.1, algebra, construct]

6.1 **The relative movie.** By [F3], each exceptional time of step 5.1 gives one oriented R1, R2 or R3 in an interior disk disjoint from the protected endpoint collars. Between events, continue crossings by the inverse function theorem and extend the motions of the intervening embedded edges by normal-coordinate cutoffs, as in [F2]. The cutoffs can vanish on the protected collars, since those arcs are stationary and isolated. Hence the intervening planar isotopies fix them too. A finite subdivision of time and composition produces the asserted finite relative movie. The construction starts with either pair of marks, including two different marks on one diagram, so it proves that case as well. AC$_\omega$ has been used only in [F1], [F2] and their countable chart unions. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard oriented three-sphere has its connected sum with its reverse mirror represented by the boundary of a smooth immersed disk in $S^3$ whose only multiple points are finitely many transverse double arcs, each having one proper preimage arc and one interior preimage arc. Consequently $K\#K^\dagger$ is ribbon in the ribbon-immersion sense.

## Statement references

[[def-ribbon-disk-and-ribbon-knot|Ribbon immersions and their double-arc condition]]

[[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot|The reverse mirror]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|Oriented connected sum]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** ACω and a smooth oriented knot $K$.

[A1] ACω is the countable choice assumption of the regular-projection and smooth isotopy-extension suppliers. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] Every smooth knot already contained in the standard $\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ has a regular projection under ACω. It is an immersion with finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and over/under data specified by strict height inequalities. [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]

[F2] Under ACω, every smooth isotopy of a compact smooth manifold embedded in $S^3$ extends to an ambient isotopy. In particular, this applies to a point and to an embedded circle; each extending ambient isotopy is orientation-preserving because it starts at the identity. [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[F3] Gluing a ball-arc tangle to its reflected copy, traversed in the opposite direction, gives the oriented connected sum of the tangle's knot closure with its reverse mirror. Its oriented knot type is unchanged when either factor is replaced by an oriented ambient-isotopic representative or when the small trivial closing arc is changed. [[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot]], [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]

[F4] The ribbon condition requires finitely many disjoint transverse double arcs with one proper preimage arc and one interior preimage arc, and no other multiple points. [[def-ribbon-disk-and-ribbon-knot]]

## Proof

**Given:** $K$ and ACω.

1.1 Choose $p\in S^3\setminus K$ and a smooth path $p_t$ from $p$ to $\infty$, constant near both endpoints of $I$. This is an isotopy of embeddings of the compact $0$-manifold consisting of one point. By [F2] it extends to an ambient isotopy $H_t$ of $S^3$. Set $K':=H_1(K)$, so $K'\subset S^3\setminus\{\infty\}=\mathbb R^3$, and take a regular diagram of $K'$ by [F1]. Delete a short open subarc of an edge incident to the unbounded complementary region. Its remaining projected arc can be placed in a closed planar disk with its two endpoints on the disk boundary, all its other points in the disk interior, and the deleted closing arc outside that disk: draw the boundary through the deleted edge along the adjacent unbounded region and round it away from the diagram. Parameterize the remaining immersed planar arc by $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^2$, straight near its endpoints. It has nonzero derivative, finitely many transverse crossing pairs $(u_i,v_i)\in(0,1)^2$, no triples, and no endpoint multiple points. The closing arc has no crossing. At each crossing mark which of $u_i,v_i$ is over according to the diagram of $K'$. Since $H_t$ is orientation-preserving, the conjugate isotopy $rH_t r^{-1}$ shows $K'^\dagger$ is oriented ambient-isotopic to $K^\dagger$. By [F3], the oriented connected-sum type $K'\#K'^\dagger$ is therefore $K\#K^\dagger$ under the fixed gluing convention. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Choose a smooth function $q:[0,1]\to(0,\infty)$ so that $h(s)=\sqrt{s(1-s)q(s)}$ has the prescribed strict over-minus-under sign at every crossing pair. This is a finite interpolation: assign positive heights $2$ and $1$ at the over and under parameters, respectively, and prescribe $q(s)=h(s)^2/(s(1-s))$ at these finitely many distinct parameters; interpolate the positive $q$ values by disjoint nonnegative smooth bumps against a positive constant. Distinct crossing parameters are disjoint because there are no triples. Make $q$ constant near the endpoints. Put $\Omega=\{(s,t):0\le s\le1,\ t^2\le s(1-s)q(s)\}$. The map $(s,v)\mapsto(s,v\sqrt{q(s)})$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from the round disk $v^2\le s(1-s)$ onto $\Omega$, including its two endpoint tips. Thus $\Omega$ is a smooth disk. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Define $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ by $f(s,t)=(\gamma(s),t)$. Since $\gamma'(s)\ne0$, its two derivative vectors $(\gamma'(s),0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ are independent, so $f$ is an immersion, including in the smooth disk charts at the tips. The only possible multiple points occur at the crossing pairs of $\gamma$. For a pair $(u,v)$, assume $h(u)<h(v)$. The image double arc is $\{(\gamma(u),t):|t|\le h(u)\}$, with preimages $\{u\}\times[-h(u),h(u)]$ and $\{v\}\times[-h(u),h(u)]$. The first is properly embedded in $\Omega$, whereas the second lies entirely in its interior because $h(u)<h(v)$. The image sheets are transverse: their planar tangent directions are independent, and both contain the vertical tangent. Double arcs from different crossings are disjoint because their planar crossing points are distinct. There are no triple points. No two boundary points have the same image, since boundary heights at a crossing are $\pm h(u)$ and $\pm h(v)$, all distinct. Thus $f$ satisfies exactly [F4]. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The plane $t=0$, completed by the point at infinity, is an equatorial sphere of $S^3$. It cuts the boundary of $f(\Omega)$ at exactly the two tips. The upper boundary arc is $(\gamma(s),h(s))$ and the lower is its reflection $(\gamma(s),-h(s))$ with opposite boundary orientation. Both are smooth proper ball-arc tangles: near a tip the equation $t^2=s(1-s)q(s)$ solves smoothly for $s$ as a function of $t^2$, so the arc is transverse to the equatorial plane. Close the upper arc by the deleted trivial arc in the equatorial sphere and round its two corners in crossing-free endpoint neighborhoods. This closure represents $K'$: it has exactly the projected crossings of the diagram in step 1.1 and their original height ordering. Explicitly, after choosing smooth endpoint roundings, interpolate its heights to those of the regular diagram realization of $K'$ while keeping the planar immersion fixed. At every crossing, each endpoint height difference is positive in its marked ordering, so their convex interpolation stays positive; the planar immersion ensures immersion of every slice. This gives a smooth isotopy of embedded circles, and [F2] makes it ambient. The endpoint rounding takes place in disjoint balls without other strands and changes no knot type. Consequently [F3] identifies the oriented boundary of $f(\Omega)$ with $K'\#K'^\dagger$, which represents $K\#K^\dagger$ by step 1.1. Together with step 3.1, this is the required ribbon immersion. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Remarks

This direct construction does not require conversion of an arbitrary disk with a radial Morse function without maxima to a ribbon immersion. That general equivalence is a separate theorem.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the prescribed generic matrix ribbon data for the $N$-dimensional color, where $N\ge1$. For every finite braid word $\beta$ on $n\ge1$ strands whose closure is a knot, the algorithm performs finitely many exact operations, including exactly one crossing-matrix update per letter and one finite pivotal-trace contraction, and returns the generic normalized value $J_N^{\mathrm{gen}}(\widehat\beta;q)$. If two such braid words close to the same oriented unframed knot, their returned generic values agree. The unique Laurent representative belongs to $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$, and its evaluation at any nonzero complex $q$ is defined, including at $q_N=e^{2\pi i/N}$.

## Statement references

[[alg-colored-jones-from-ribbon-evaluation|Finite colored Jones procedure]]

[[def-normalized-colored-jones-sequence|Generic normalization and color data]]

[[thm-ribbon-evaluation-from-colored-braid-word-procedure-properties|Colored-braid evaluator correctness and termination]]

[[thm-twist-correction-removes-framing|Scalar twist correction and Markov invariance]]

[Etingof, Gelaki, Nikshych, and Ostrik, *Tensor Categories*, §§8.9–8.10](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf)

[Murakami, *An Introduction to the Volume Conjecture*, §§2.4–2.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1002.0126)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, an integer $N\ge1$, the prescribed generic matrix ribbon data, a finite braid word $\beta$ of length $m$ on $n\ge1$ strands, and a knot closure.

[F1] The procedure forms the positive and inverse crossing matrices, calls the finite matrix ribbon evaluator, computes the exponent sum, and returns $\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}t_N(\beta)/d_N$ over the exact field $\mathbb Q(A)$ ([[alg-colored-jones-from-ribbon-evaluation]]).

[F2] For valid finite-dimensional matrix data over an effective field and a color-preserving braid word of length $m$, the ribbon evaluator makes exactly $m$ crossing-matrix updates and one finite pivotal-trace contraction and returns the framed colored-braid value ([[thm-ribbon-evaluation-from-colored-braid-word-procedure-properties]]).

[F3] In the generic definition, $d_N\ne0$ in $\mathbb Q(A)$, $\lambda_N\ne0$, and $J_N^{\mathrm{gen}}=\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}t_N(\beta)/d_N$ ([[def-normalized-colored-jones-sequence]]).

[F4] For an absolutely simple color with scalar twist $\lambda I$, the corrected framed trace $\lambda^{-w(\beta)}t_n(\beta)$ is invariant under conjugation and both Markov stabilizations when the Axiom of Choice is assumed ([[thm-twist-correction-removes-framing]]).

[F5] The framed ribbon-tangle evaluator is defined under Countable Choice ([[def-colored-framed-knot-evaluation-from-ribbon-category]]).

[F6] The Axiom of Choice implies Countable Choice ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[F7] The quotient has a unique integral Laurent representative in $q=A^4$, proved by [[lem-colored-jones-generic-quotient-is-laurent]].

[A1] The Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A2] Countable Choice has its usual sequence-of-nonempty-sets meaning ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and [A1].

1.1 The universal-$R$ sum used for $c_N$ has only the terms $0\le r<N$, since $E^N=F^N=0$ on the displayed $N$-dimensional module. The braid word has finitely many letters, and [F2] performs exactly one matrix update per letter followed by one finite trace contraction. All remaining arithmetic is addition, multiplication, equality testing, and inversion of the nonzero generic scalar $d_N$ in $\mathbb Q(A)$, so every operation terminates. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 By [F2], the evaluator returns $t_N(\beta)$, the pivotal trace of the framed colored closure. The last step in [F1] multiplies this value by $\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}$ and divides by $d_N$, exactly the formula in [F3]. Hence the returned value is $J_N^{\mathrm{gen}}(\widehat\beta;q)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given]

3.1 If $\beta$ and $\beta'$ close to the same oriented unframed knot, Markov's theorem under [A1] relates them by finitely many conjugations, stabilizations, and destabilizations. The scalar-twist theorem [F4] preserves $\lambda_N^{-w}t_N$ under each move; both braids use the same nonzero $d_N$, so division by $d_N$ preserves equality. The abstract framed evaluation used to identify the matrix trace is defined under Countable Choice [F5], which follows from [A1] by [F6] and has the meaning in [A2]. Thus the algorithm outputs agree without adding an axiom beyond AC. Finally [F7] proves that their unique common representative is an integral Laurent polynomial, whose substitution at a nonzero complex number has no vanishing denominator. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $V$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with boundary a chosen zero-longitude surgery $M(J)$. Suppose
$$H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z,\qquad H_2(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^{2r}.$$
Put $\pi=\pi_1(V)$ and $\Pi_s=\pi/\pi^{(s)}$, where $s\ge0$ and the superscript denotes the ordinary derived series. Supply classes $x_1,\ldots,x_r,y_1,\ldots,y_r\in H_2(V;\mathbb Z[\Pi_s])$ satisfying
$$\lambda(x_i,x_j)=0,\qquad\lambda(x_i,y_j)=\delta_{ij}.$$
These are actual integral intersection-pair data; existence of such data is not asserted.

Form $W$ by finitely many oriented attachments of standard connected-sum or infection cobordisms, allowing their orientation reversals, along each piece's marked outgoing surgery component. Use the supplied peripheral models in those constructions. Let $\phi:\pi_1(W)\to G$ be a supplied homomorphism to a PTFA group whose restriction to $\pi_1(V)$ factors through $\Pi_s$. In particular the factorization is automatic if $G^{(s)}=1$. Let $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$ for a prime $p$, put $A=k[G]$, and let $K$ be its fraction division ring with standard involution.

Then there are image classes $\ell_i,d_i\in H_2(W;A)$ with
$$\lambda_A(\ell_i,\ell_j)=0,\qquad\lambda_A(\ell_i,d_j)=\lambda_A(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij},$$
and both cokernel dimensions satisfy
$$\dim_K\operatorname{coker}\{H_2(\partial W;K)\to H_2(W;K)\}\le\dim_k\operatorname{coker}\{H_2(\partial W;k)\to H_2(W;k)\}\le2r.$$
For every boundary component $M_0$ with nontrivial restricted homomorphism, $H_1(M_0;K)=0$ and its Bockstein-duality pairing has
$$B_0(a,b)=0\quad\text{for all }a,b\in\ker\{H_1(M_0;A)\to H_1(W;A)\}.$$
Consequently every boundary class with nonzero self-pairing has nonzero image in $H_1(W;A)$. The theorem applies to locally flat topological bordisms as well as smooth ones and introduces no choice principle.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The actual integral homology and lifted pairing data, finite framed cobordism attachments, coefficient homomorphism and field in the Statement.

[F1] Standard infection and connected-sum pieces have outgoing injections on ordinary $H_1,H_2$ and incoming degree-two surjectivity. A collared gluing with outgoing $H_1$ injection and remaining-boundary $H_2$ surjection induces a surjection on boundary homology cokernels. [[lem-standard-infection-cobordisms-have-boundary-generated-second-homology]], [[lem-boundary-homology-cokernels-surject-under-excisive-bordism-gluing]]

[F2] Ambient unitary coefficients preserve intersection pairings under collared gluing, and the pairings are Hermitian. [[lem-equivariant-intersection-pairings-are-preserved-by-collared-bordism-gluing]], [[lem-relative-unitary-equivariant-intersection-pairing-is-hermitian]]

[F3] A compact oriented four-manifold with boundary components of ordinary first Betti number one has localized boundary-cokernel dimension at most the ordinary one. A nontrivial PTFA coefficient system on a compact Betti-one manifold kills localized first homology. [[thm-ptfa-localized-boundary-intersection-rank-is-no-larger-than-ordinary-rank]], [[lem-ptfa-localization-kills-first-homology-of-betti-one-manifolds]]

[F4] Integral pairs and the localized cokernel bound force each selected acyclic boundary kernel to be isotropic for the Bockstein-duality form. [[thm-unimodular-intersection-pairs-force-boundary-blanchfield-kernel-isotropy]]

[F5] Relative cap duality holds with arbitrary underlying abelian-group local systems. Constant rational localization is exact; compact manifold boundaries have collars without choice. [[thm-compact-collared-manifold-local-coefficient-lefschetz-duality-in-zf]], [[lem-ore-localization-is-flat-and-detects-module-torsion]], [[thm-topological-collaring-for-manifold-boundaries]]

## Proof

1.1 The factorization supplies an involution-preserving ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z[\Pi_s]\to A$, and hence maps of all actual coefficient chain systems on $V$. Cap, dual-system identification and evaluation commute with this change of coefficients. Explicitly a dual cochain $f$ changes to $c\otimes a\mapsto\rho(f(c))a$; balancing and the finite face formulas show compatibility with coboundaries and cap. Both relative cap maps are isomorphisms by [F5], so their inverse duality maps commute too. Thus the image classes on $V$ retain the displayed zero and unit pairings. The standard base vector $1$ gives compatible transported Hermitian structures before and after change of ring. Hermitian symmetry [F2] supplies the reverse cross-pairing $\lambda_A(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$. [F2, F5, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 The ordinary group $H_2(V;k)$ has dimension $2r$. For $k=\mathbb Q$ this is exact rational localization of the integral singular complex, using [F5]. For $k=\mathbb F_p$ one can check the coefficient sequence directly without an infinite lifting assertion. Lift the finitely many coefficients of an $\mathbb F_p$ two-cycle $z$ to an integral chain $\widetilde z$. Write $\partial\widetilde z=pw$; then $w$ is an integral one-cycle and $p[w]=0$. Since $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$, $w=\partial v$ for some two-chain $v$, so $\widetilde z-pv$ is an integral cycle lifting $z$. Conversely, if an integral two-cycle becomes a boundary mod $p$, lift that one finite bounding three-chain and subtract its boundary; the difference is $p$ times an integral two-cycle, since integral chain groups have no $p$-torsion. Thus $H_2(V;\mathbb F_p)\cong H_2(V;\mathbb Z)/p=\mathbb F_p^{2r}$. Its quotient by the boundary image therefore has dimension at most $2r$. [F5, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Give $V$ its collar from [F5] and use the actual product collars of the finite standard pieces. At each attachment the outgoing $H_1$ injection and incoming $H_2$ surjection of [F1] give a surjection from the preceding boundary cokernel to the new one. Its dimension cannot increase, so after finitely many attachments the ordinary cokernel is at most $2r$. The single coefficient system on final $W$ restricts to each intermediate manifold, and [F2] preserves every pair identity under inclusion. Thus the images $\ell_i,d_i$ in final $W$ satisfy all pair identities in the Statement. Orientation reversal of a piece does not change its ordinary injection and surjection properties; the orientation on the embedded preceding manifold is unchanged, which is the orientation used in [F2]. All the resulting manifolds are compact and oriented with the actual remaining boundary components. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Every remaining boundary component is a chosen zero-longitude surgery on a knot. Its ordinary first homology over $k$ is $k$: in the exterior/filling Mayer–Vietoris sequence the preferred longitude maps to zero, the filling core identifies with the meridian, and that meridian remains the single free generator, exactly as in the peripheral calculation of [F1]. Hence [F3] applies to final $W$ and gives the first cokernel inequality in the Statement. If the restriction to $M_0$ is nontrivial, the second assertion of [F3] gives $H_1(M_0;K)=0$. Thus the finite pairs of step 2.1 and the localized dimension bound verify every hypothesis of [F4], with $R=A$ and the standard involutive fraction ring $K$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F4] to obtain $B_0(a,b)=0$ for all classes in that inclusion kernel. If $B_0(a,a)\ne0$, the class $a$ therefore cannot lie in the kernel, and its image in $H_1(W;A)$ is nonzero. This is the survival implication used for infection axes in the source bordism argument. Every isotropic submodule has zero self-pairings, so such a surviving class lies outside every isotropic submodule. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For actual integral $s$-solution data, these hypotheses are precisely its homology and lifted-pairing part; passage to a quotient target of derived length at most $s$ factors because a homomorphism carries the ordinary derived series into the target derived series. Every coefficient lift in step 1.2 involved one finite chain; all other arguments used the supplied finite pair list and actual collared attachments. The proof therefore preserves smooth and topological scopes and introduces no choice axiom beyond none in these data. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

This theorem supplies the pairing and kernel-isotropy data once the actual initial bordism and attachments are given. Deriving that initial bordism from a topological concordance relation, the mixed-derived-series meridian maps, and the analytic signature constraints are separate requirements for the full Cha–Kim Theorems A and B.

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold with $k\ge1$ torus cusps and a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric. Choose an ordered peripheral basis on each cusp. For cusp $i$, let the generalized filling parameter sphere be $S_i=\mathbb R^2\cup\{\infty\}$, with $\infty$ denoting the complete cusp and primitive integral pairs modulo sign denoting ordinary slopes. There is a neighborhood $U$ of $(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$ in $\prod_{i=1}^k S_i$ such that every tuple in $U$ whose finite coordinates are primitive integral slopes determines a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on the corresponding ordinary Dehn filling; coordinates equal to $\infty$ remain unfilled complete cusps. Consequently, one may choose neighborhoods $U_i$ of $\infty$ with $\prod_i U_i\subseteq U$, and only finitely many primitive integral pairs at each cusp lie outside $U_i$. Thus every simultaneous filling whose slopes all lie in their respective $U_i$ is hyperbolic. Nonprimitive ray parameters may describe cone or orbifold completions but are not ordinary smooth fillings. No universal numeric length threshold or universal bound on the number of exceptional slopes is asserted.

## Statement references

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 5, §5.8, Theorem 5.8.2](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/5.pdf)

[Petronio and Porti, *Negatively Oriented Ideal Triangulations and a Proof of Thurston’s Hyperbolic Dehn Filling Theorem*, Theorem 0.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the complete finite-volume metric with $k\ge1$ torus cusps and the chosen ordered peripheral bases.

[A1] AC and its countable-choice consequence are retained. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] The full $k$-cusped local deformation-and-completeness theorem gives a product neighborhood of the complete generalized parameters and smooth complete finite-volume ordinary fillings for every primitive tuple therein, with the other cusps unfilled. [[lem-dehn-filling-deformation-and-completeness]]

[F2] Slopes and arbitrary supplied ordinary gluing maps have the stated primitive-pair convention. [[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]]

[F3] The input metric and volume convention are [[def-pared-hyperbolic-structures-and-volume]]. Each chosen-section cusp length is a norm on its rank-two peripheral lattice; changing section rescales it by a positive constant. [[def-cusp-slope-length]]

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the entire given $k$-cusped metric. It supplies a product neighborhood $U$ of $(\infty,\ldots,\infty)$ and the required complete finite-volume metric for every tuple with primitive finite coordinates. Coordinates $\infty$ retain their complete translation cusps, so the conclusion includes every partial filling and the unchanged complete manifold. These are the ordinary fillings of [F2], including their supplied gluing data, rather than just representations solving the peripheral equations. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Choose cuspwise open neighborhoods $U_i$ of $\infty$ with $\prod_iU_i\subseteq U$; one may use the product neighborhood in [F1] itself. The complement $S_i\setminus U_i$ is a closed subset of the compact sphere $S_i$ missing $\infty$, hence a compact subset of $\mathbb R^2$ and therefore bounded. A bounded set contains only finitely many integer lattice points: if its norm is at most $B$, each coordinate is one of the finitely many integers between $-\lceil B\rceil$ and $\lceil B\rceil$. Restricting to primitive pairs and quotienting by simultaneous sign cannot increase their number. This proves the finite-exception assertion at every cusp and hence the simultaneous conclusion. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], any sequence of primitive slopes whose chosen-section lengths tend to infinity leaves every bounded coefficient set, so it eventually lies in its $U_i$. Rescaling a horotorus multiplies all these lengths by one positive constant and does not alter this conclusion. A nonprimitive ray parameter does not specify an ordinary primitive meridian; by [F2] its cone-angle convention is separate from the smooth fillings proved here. All neighborhoods are allowed to depend on the given manifold and its metric, so the proof asserts neither a universal numeric threshold nor a universal number of exceptions. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume countable choice. The framed self-linking number of a framed oriented knot is the linking number of the knot with a sufficiently small push-off along its framing. Let $D_1$ be the degree-one chord diagram consisting of an oriented circle with one chord. The framed self-linking invariant has a degree-one weight system $w$ with $w(D_1)=2$. Since $D_1$ is isolated, the unframed 1T quotient sets it to zero. Therefore $w$ does not factor through the unframed 4T+1T quotient. This counterexample distinguishes the framed and unframed diagram targets and makes no claim about separating knot types.

The diagram shows the isolated one-chord generator; the circle orientation fixes its cyclic skeleton and no proof relies on the picture.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9,thick]
  \draw (0,0) circle (1);
  \draw[->] (0.05,0.99) .. controls (0.28,0.96) and (0.47,0.87) .. (0.60,0.80);
  \draw[very thick] ({cos(55)},{sin(55)}) -- ({cos(235)},{sin(235)});
  \fill ({cos(55)},{sin(55)}) circle (1.5pt);
  \fill ({cos(235)},{sin(235)}) circle (1.5pt);
  \node at (0,-1.35) {$D_1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references

[[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations|Framed 4T and unframed 4T+1T quotients]]

[[thm-vassiliev-invariant-induces-weight-system|Framed self-linking symbol on one chord]]

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §1.1, PDF pp. 3–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §§3.4 and 4.1–4.2, printed pp. 70–75 and 89–94](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, the degree-one framed chord module, and its unframed quotient.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: countable choice is the hypothesis used for the framed normal-bundle branch.

[F1] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: the framed module imposes 4T; the unframed module additionally sets every isolated chord to zero.

[F2] [[thm-vassiliev-invariant-induces-weight-system]]: under countable choice, framed self-linking has type at most one and its degree-one derivative is a framed weight system taking value $2$ on the one-chord diagram.

## Counterexample

**Given:** As above.

1.1 The diagram $D_1$ has one chord and no other chords, so that chord is isolated. In degree one there is no 4T generator, since 4T has two chords. Thus [F2] gives a valid framed weight system with $w(D_1)=2$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Every functional on the unframed quotient must vanish on $D_1$, because [F1] imposes $D_1=0$. If $w$ factored through that quotient, it would satisfy $w(D_1)=0$, contrary to $w(D_1)=2\ne0$ in $\mathbb Z$. Hence the framed weight system does not descend through 1T. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

In the first two cases take $A=I_2:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$, $s=1$, $\rho=\tfrac12$, and $\tau=1$. This matrix satisfies the robust nullspace property for every vector: for each $S\subseteq\{1,2\}$ with $|S|\le1$, $\|h_S\|_2\le\|h\|_2=\|Ah\|_2$, while the other term on the right side of the robust inequality is nonnegative.

1. **Bounded noise.** Let $x^\dagger=(1,0)$, $e=(0,\tfrac1{10})$, $y=(1,\tfrac1{10})$, and $\epsilon=\tfrac1{10}$. The truth is feasible, the noise bound is attained, and $\sigma_1(x^\dagger)_1=0$. Every minimizer therefore obeys the recovery bounds with $C_1=8$, $C_2=12$, $C_3=6$, and $C_4=8$.

2. **Compressible truth.** Let $x^\dagger=(1,\tfrac15)$, $e=(0,\tfrac1{100})$, $y=(1,\tfrac{21}{100})$, and $\epsilon=\tfrac1{100}$. The truth is feasible and $\sigma_1(x^\dagger)_1=\tfrac15$. Every minimizer obeys the same constants and hence
$$\|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_2\le\tfrac{43}{25},\qquad \|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_1\le\tfrac{32}{25}.$$

3. **A large nullspace component outside the theorem's hypothesis.** Let $A_0:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $A_0(z_1,z_2)=z_1$, take $s=1$, $x^\dagger=(0,M)$ for any $M>0$, $e=0$, $\epsilon=0$, and $y=0$. The only minimum-$\ell^1$ feasible vector is $\widehat x=(0,0)$, so $\|\widehat x-x^\dagger\|_2=M$ while $\sigma_1(x^\dagger)_1=0$. The robust nullspace property fails for $A_0$, witnessed by $h=(0,1)$ and $S=\{2\}$; this case is outside the theorem and shows why its matrix hypothesis cannot be omitted.

[Mendelson, Rauhut, and Ward, *Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions*, §2.1](https://www.mathc.rwth-aachen.de/~rauhut/files/circulant-independent.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The three finite-dimensional examples in the Example section and the constants and conclusions stated there.

[F1] [[def-ip-robust-nullspace-property]]: the inequality must hold for every vector and every coordinate set of size at most $s$.

[F2] [[def-ip-best-s-term-l1-error]] and [[lem-ip-largest-s-coordinates-attain-best-s-term-l1-error]]: $\sigma_s(x)_1$ is the least coordinate-tail $\ell^1$ error and is obtained by retaining the largest $s$ coordinates.

[F3] [[thm-ip-robust-nsp-noisy-recovery-bound]]: under the robust property, every BPDN minimizer obeys the two displayed error bounds with the stated constants.

Since $\rho\|h_{S^c}\|_1\ge0$, the robust inequality holds with $\rho=1/2,\tau=1$. The best-term lemma gives $\sigma_1(1,0)_1=0$ and $\sigma_1(1,1/5)_1=1/5$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

## Example

Let $\theta$ have the uniform prior on $[0,1]$, regarded as a Borel probability on $\mathbb R$, and let an observation $Y\in\{0,1\}$ satisfy $\mathbb P(Y=1\mid\theta)=\theta^2(1-\theta)$. After observing $Y=1$, the posterior has density $12\theta^2(1-\theta)$ on $[0,1]$ and zero outside. Its unique density mode, at $\theta=2/3$, is a strong small-ball MAP, while its posterior mean is $3/5$. Thus the posterior mean and a small-ball MAP differ.

## Example references

[[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator|the strong small-ball MAP is defined by small-ball probabilities relative to their global supremum]]

[[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law|the fixed-data posterior normalizes likelihood-weighted prior mass]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Borel probability prior that is uniform on $[0,1]$, the binary sampling rule with success probability $\theta^2(1-\theta)$, and observation $Y=1$.

[F1] The posterior at a fixed datum is the likelihood-weighted prior divided by its evidence when the evidence is positive and finite. [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F2] A point is a strong small-ball MAP when its posterior ball probability divided by the supremum over all centers tends to $1$. [[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator]]

[F3] Let $\pi$ be the stipulated uniform Borel probability on $[0,1]$. Its Lebesgue density is $\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$; thus $\pi([a,b])=b-a$ for $0\le a\le b\le1$, every singleton has mass zero, and $\pi(J\cap[0,1])\le\operatorname{length}(J)$ for every interval $J$. [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]

[F4] The nonnegative Lebesgue integral is monotone and agrees with the simple integral on nonnegative simple functions. [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]

[F5] The Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions. [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]

## Verification

1.1 For $k=1,2,3,4$, put $a_k=\int_{[0,1]}\theta^k\,d\pi$. These bounded continuous functions are integrable because $0\le\theta^k\le1$ on the support of the probability $\pi$. For each $N\ge1$, partition $[0,1]$ into $I_{j,N}=[j/N,(j+1)/N)$ for $j<N-1$ and $I_{N-1,N}=[(N-1)/N,1]$. The simple lower and upper step functions with values $(j/N)^k$ and $((j+1)/N)^k$ on $I_{j,N}$ bound $\theta^k$ pointwise; [F3] gives $\pi(I_{j,N})=1/N$, and [F4] therefore gives
$$L_{N,k}:=N^{-(k+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}j^k\le a_k\le N^{-(k+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{N}j^k=:U_{N,k}.$$
Their difference is $U_{N,k}-L_{N,k}=1/N$. Also the binomial identity telescopes to
$$N^{k+1}=(k+1)\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}j^k+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\binom{k+1}{i}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}j^i.$$
For each $i<k$, $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}j^i\le N^{i+1}$, so after division by $N^{k+1}$ all terms in the second sum tend to zero. Hence $L_{N,k}\to1/(k+1)$, and the squeeze gives $a_k=1/(k+1)$. Also $\int_{[0,1]}1\,d\pi=1$. [F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 On $[0,1]$, $p(\theta)=\theta^2(1-\theta)\ge0$. Its derivative is $p'(\theta)=\theta(2-3\theta)$, so its maximum is $p(2/3)=4/27<1$. Therefore $p$ and $1-p$ define valid conditional probabilities for $Y=1$ and $Y=0$. [given, algebra]

1.3 By [F1] and [F5], the evidence for $Y=1$ is
$$Z=\int_{[0,1]}p(\theta)\,d\pi=\int\theta^2\,d\pi-\int\theta^3\,d\pi=\frac13-\frac14=\frac1{12}>0,$$
using step 1.1. The posterior formula [F1] gives density $p/Z=12\theta^2(1-\theta)$ relative to $\pi$. Since $\pi$ has Lebesgue density $\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$, the posterior Lebesgue density is $q(\theta)=12\theta^2(1-\theta)$ on $[0,1]$, extended by zero on $\mathbb R\setminus[0,1]$. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.1 On $(0,1)$, $q'(\theta)=12\theta(2-3\theta)$, so $q$ increases up to $2/3$ and decreases after it; $q(0)=q(1)=0$. Thus $q_{\max}=q(2/3)>0$ is the unique density maximum. For any center $x\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$, the posterior density relative to $\pi$ and [F3] give $m_r(x)\le q_{\max}\pi([x-r,x+r]\cap[0,1])\le2r q_{\max}$. For $0<r<1/3$, $[2/3-r,2/3+r]\subseteq[0,1]$ and its $\pi$-mass is $2r$. Continuity of $q$ then gives
$$\left|\frac{m_r(2/3)}{2r}-q_{\max}\right|\le\sup_{|\theta-2/3|\le r}|q(\theta)-q_{\max}|\longrightarrow0.$$
Hence
$$1\ge\frac{m_r(2/3)}{\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}m_r(x)}\ge\frac{m_r(2/3)}{2r q_{\max}}\longrightarrow1.$$
By [F2], $2/3$ is a strong small-ball MAP. [F2, F3, step 1.3, given, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], [F5], and steps 1.1 and 1.3, the posterior mean is
$$\int_{[0,1]}\theta q(\theta)\,d\pi=12\left(\int\theta^3\,d\pi-\int\theta^4\,d\pi\right)=12\left(\frac14-\frac15\right)=\frac35.$$
Since $3/5\ne2/3$, the posterior mean differs from the strong small-ball MAP. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $n\ge0$, let $R_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}]$ and $R_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}]$, and let $I\subseteq R_{\mathbb C}$ be an ideal invariant under coefficientwise application of every field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$. Then $$I=(I\cap R_{\mathbb Q})R_{\mathbb C}.$$ If $I$ is radical, then $I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$ is radical as well. In particular, if $S\subseteq(\mathbb C^*)^n$ is preserved by all such coordinatewise automorphisms, the radical vanishing ideal of its Zariski closure is the scalar extension of a radical ideal over $\mathbb Q$. This includes the empty set, the whole torus and zero variables. No algebraicity or closedness of $S$ is assumed.

## Statement references

[[lem-fixed-field-of-automorphisms-of-c-over-q-is-q|The exact fixed field]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the indicated Laurent rings, ideal or point set, and coefficientwise field automorphisms.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited through the fixed-field supplier.

[F1] [[lem-fixed-field-of-automorphisms-of-c-over-q-is-q]] proves that a complex number fixed by every automorphism fixing $\mathbb Q$ belongs to $\mathbb Q$. Its proof includes the extension of embeddings to algebraic closures and the transcendence-basis argument under full AC.

## Proof

1.1 **Finite stable linear spaces have rational bases.** Let $W\subseteq\mathbb C^N$ be a complex linear subspace invariant under coordinatewise application of all the automorphisms in [F1]. Choose any finite basis and put its row matrix in reduced row-echelon form, deleting zero rows. Finite elimination terminates by choosing successive pivot columns in the fixed order. The resulting nonzero rows are independent of the initial basis: the pivot columns are characterized successively by the dimensions of the projections of $W$ to initial coordinate blocks; once these columns are fixed, each row is the unique vector of $W$ whose pivot coordinates are its specified standard basis vector. Indeed the pivot-coordinate projection is an isomorphism $W\to\mathbb C^{\dim W}$ by row reduction. Applying a field automorphism preserves row-echelon equations, zero entries, leading ones and the increasing pivot order. It takes the row space to $W$, so uniqueness fixes every entry of this matrix. By [F1] all entries are rational. Thus its rows belong to $W\cap\mathbb Q^N$ and their complex span is $W$. If $W=0$ the row list is empty and the same conclusion holds. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Apply finite descent to each support box.** For $d\ge0$ let $V_d$ be the finite-dimensional complex span of monomials $z^\alpha$ with $-d\le\alpha_i\le d$, in a fixed lexicographic order. For $n=0$ take the single monomial $1$. Coefficientwise automorphisms preserve $V_d$ and preserve $W_d=I\cap V_d$. Step 1.1 expresses each element of $W_d$ as a finite complex linear combination of elements of $I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$. Every Laurent polynomial has finite support and belongs to some $V_d$. Hence every element of $I$ belongs to $(I\cap R_{\mathbb Q})R_{\mathbb C}$. The reverse inclusion holds because $I$ is an ideal containing that rational intersection. This proves the asserted scalar-extension equality without choosing an infinite family of generators or invoking an elimination theorem. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 **Radical contraction and stable point sets.** If $f\in R_{\mathbb Q}$ and $f^k\in I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$ for an integer $k\ge1$, radicality of $I$ gives $f\in I\cap R_{\mathbb Q}$. Thus the contracted ideal is radical. For the point-set assertion let $I(S)$ be the Laurent polynomials vanishing on every point of $S$. It is radical, since a complex number whose positive power vanishes is zero. For an automorphism $\sigma$ and $s\in S$, one has $(\sigma f)(s)=\sigma(f(\sigma^{-1}s))=0$ whenever $f\in I(S)$, so $\sigma I(S)=I(S)$ using the inverse automorphism too. The Zariski closure has exactly the same vanishing ideal: each zero set of a polynomial vanishing on $S$ is closed and contains the closure, and the reverse inclusion follows from $S\subseteq\overline S$. Apply step 2.1 to $I(S)$, then the radical contraction just proved. Empty $S$ gives the unit ideal and the full torus gives zero; step 2.1 also handles $n=0$ directly. These are finite row computations plus the precise full-AC fixed-field theorem, with no extra choice assumption. [A1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

      locator: "Printed pp.77–83 and 252–254; index-two rectangle decompositions, annulus terms, and grading drops"
    - title: "Ciprian Manolescu, Peter Ozsvath, and Sucharit Sarkar, A combinatorial description of knot Floer homology, §1"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0607691"
