## Statement

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid representing a knot, and use the three differentials defined by the grid-complex algorithm. For any fixed source and target states, every non-annular composite of two counted rectangles has exactly two ordered rectangle decompositions; the two decompositions have equal $O$-monomial weights and are either both counted or both excluded in each mode. Returning composites consist of thin annuli, one horizontal annulus for each row and one vertical annulus for each column. Every such annulus contains one $X$ and one $O$, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode, each horizontal annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking, and each vertical annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking; every $O$-variable occurs once in each family and therefore twice in total. Thus all returning terms cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Every counted rectangle term has Maslov degree $-1$ and lowers Alexander filtration by exactly the number of $X$-markings in its interior; the modes excluding $X$ preserve Alexander grading.

## Statement references

[[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex|The three grid-complex modes and their coefficient weights]]

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot|Grid states, empty rectangles, markings, and gradings]]

[[lem-grid-alexander-grading-integral|The rectangle-change formula for the grid Alexander grading]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A knot grid $G$, its finite set of states, and one of the three differential modes in the grid-complex algorithm.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)=J(\mathbf x-\mathbb O,\mathbf x-\mathbb O)+1$, the analogous $M_{\mathbb X}$ formula, and the one-$O$/one-$X$-per-row-and-column conditions.

[F2] [[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex]] defines the tilde mode by excluding both markings, the associated-graded minus mode by excluding $X$ and weighting each $O_i$ by $U_i$, and the full filtered minus mode by allowing $X$ and weighting each $O_i$ by $U_i$; each $U_i$ lowers Maslov grading by two and Alexander filtration by one.

[F3] [[lem-grid-alexander-grading-integral]] proves the Maslov rectangle-change formulas and $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$ for every rectangle from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$.

## Proof

1.1 For two successive rectangles $r_1,r_2$, let $\psi=r_1+r_2$ be their cellwise sum as a two-chain, and let $\mathbf x,\mathbf z$ be the initial and terminal states. The state permutation changes by one transposition at each rectangle. If $\mathbf x\ne\mathbf z$, their relative permutation is either a product of two disjoint transpositions, so four points move, or a $3$-cycle, so three points move. These are the only nonidentity products of two transpositions. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For a counted rectangle $r$ the interior contains no state point, so [F3] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. The coefficient $\prod_iU_i^{O_i(r)}$ lowers Maslov degree by $2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$ by [F2]; hence the full term has degree $-1$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 In the four-point case, the two transpositions are disjoint and commute. Exchanging their order gives the alternate intermediate state; the first rectangle in one decomposition has the same support as the second rectangle in the other, and conversely. Thus both decompositions have the same two rectangle interiors and are empty together. No third decomposition is possible, because the four distinct changing corners must be paired into the same two disjoint transpositions fixed by the endpoint permutation and the domain boundary. [step 1.1, construct]

2.2 In the three-point case, following the boundary of $\psi$ gives a six-corner region with five right-angle corners and one reflex corner of angle $270^\circ$; every cell coefficient is zero or one. At the reflex corner the boundary can be cut in exactly two ways into two rectangles. Each cut gives the required intermediate grid state, and the resulting interiors contain no additional state point because any such point would already lie in the interior of one of the original empty rectangles. The six-corner boundary has no other concave corner at which to make a cut, so these are exactly the two decompositions. [step 1.1, construct]

2.3 If $\mathbf x=\mathbf z$, the two rectangles reverse the same state transposition and their union is a periodic annulus. If the annulus were not thin, its transverse width would include at least two grid strips; the interior would then contain a state point on an intervening grid circle, contradicting emptiness. Hence every returning domain is one of the $n$ horizontal thin annuli, each occupying one row strip, or one of the $n$ vertical thin annuli, each occupying one column strip. Conversely, the two state points on the boundary circles of any one-row strip split that strip into two empty rectangles, and the same holds for every one-column strip, so all $2n$ listed annuli occur as returning composites. Each contains exactly one $O$ and one $X$ by the row and column marking conditions, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode, the horizontal annulus through the row of $O_i$ contributes $U_i$, and the vertical annulus through its column also contributes $U_i$. Every $O_i$ therefore occurs twice among all returning domains, and the total is zero over $\mathbb F_2$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In either non-annular case the two decompositions have the same cellwise domain $\psi$. A forbidden $O$- or $X$-marking occurs in one rectangle of a decomposition exactly when its cell has positive coefficient in $\psi$; hence a mode excluding that marking accepts either both decompositions or neither. For each $O_i$, the exponent in the product coefficient is its multiplicity in $\psi$, so the two accepted terms have the same monomial. They cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. [F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The Alexander change in [F3] is $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. Multiplication by the coefficient lowers filtration by $n_{\mathbb O}(r)$, so the output filtration is $A_G(\mathbf x)-n_{\mathbb X}(r)$. Thus the full filtered term drops by exactly $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$, and the tilde and associated-graded modes, which count only rectangles with $n_{\mathbb X}(r)=0$, preserve Alexander grading. [F2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<1$. Let $X_d(R)$ be the BV conductivity class for $d=2$ and the bounded $C^{1,\alpha}$ class for $d\ge3$, with the same ellipticity and background collar in both cases. Then $X_2(R)$ is compact in $L^1(\Omega)$ and each $X_d(R)$ for $d\ge3$ is compact in $C^1(\overline\Omega)$. In dimension two there is an exponent $q>2$ and a constant $C$ such that
$$\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega)}\le C\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\qquad(\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_2(R));$$
for $d\ge3$ the same kernel map is continuous in the $C^1(\overline\Omega)$ topology. Consequently the exact kernel image $\{\kappa_\gamma:\gamma\in X_d(R)\}$ is compact in $L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class|The exact BV and C1,alpha conductivity classes.]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice|The Axiom of Choice used in the d≥3 compactness argument.]]

[[def-countable-choice|The Countable Choice axiom used in the dimension-two BV closure argument.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-translation-modulus-for-conductivity|The uniform BV translation modulus.]]

[[lem-ip-ntd-smoothing-and-hilbert-schmidt-kernel-bound|The continuum kernel observation and its Hilbert-space norm.]]

[de Hoop et al., Corollary 4.3, Lemma 4.5 and Corollary 4.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

[Rondi, Theorem 4.2 and Remark 4.5: forward NtD continuity and Meyers estimate](https://www.aimsciences.org/article/doi/10.3934/ipi.2008.2.397)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the domain, parameters, conductivity class and kernel convention in the statement.

[F1] In $d=2$, the background extensions $\gamma_e=1+\operatorname{zeroextend}(\gamma-1)$ have uniform $L^1$ translation-difference bounds and the stated finite-$L^p$ translation moduli. Therefore $h_\gamma=\operatorname{zeroextend}(\gamma-1)$, supported in $\overline{\Omega'}$, has those SAME translation differences and a uniform $L^1$ bound. ([[lem-ip-bv-translation-modulus-for-conductivity]])

[F2] A bounded-support family with bounded $L^p$ norms and uniform translation continuity is relatively compact in $L^p(\mathbb R^d)$. ([[thm-frechet-kolmogorov-compactness-criterion-in-lp]], [[lem-bounded-support-makes-frechet-kolmogorov-tail-control-automatic]])

[F3] A uniformly bounded and equicontinuous family on a compact metric domain has compact closure in the uniform topology; its limit preserves a common Hölder bound. ([[cor-real-and-euclidean-vector-valued-ascoli-arzela]])

[F4] The weak conductivity solutions and DN maps are well-defined on the trace quotient, and the mean-zero NtD observation is defined by the weak Neumann problem. ([[lem-ip-calderon-rough-dn-map-wellposedness]], [[def-ip-mean-zero-ntd-and-smoothed-kernel-observation]])

[F5] For $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^d),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\}$; symmetry under $\varphi\mapsto-\varphi$ gives the absolute-pairing form. ([[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]])

[F6] Assuming Countable Choice, for real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed test-field supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, and then it equals $TV(u;\Omega)$. ([[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]])

[F7] For some $p\in(2,4)$ and $q=p/(p-2)>2$, the fixed-collar NtD kernel difference is bounded by $C\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^q}$; in every dimension it is also bounded by $C\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_\infty$. This is proved by uniform interior Meyers estimates, rapid boundary-mode decay and the weak energy identity. ([[lem-ip-interior-neumann-modes-and-kernel-forward-continuity]])

[A3] Countable Choice is assumed in the statement and is used at the arbitrary-$L^1$ test-field characterization in [F6] and the upstream spectral and higher-integrability interfaces. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[A4] The Axiom of Choice is assumed in the statement and supplies the Ascoli–Arzelà compactness step in dimension $d\ge3$. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 In dimension two, set $h_\gamma=\operatorname{zeroextend}(\gamma-1)$. It is supported in $\overline{\Omega'}$, has $\|h_\gamma\|_1\le(M+1)|\Omega|$, and satisfies $\|\tau_yh_\gamma-h_\gamma\|_1=\|\tau_y\gamma_e-\gamma_e\|_1\le C|y|$ by [F1]. Apply the Fréchet–Kolmogorov criterion [F2] to the bounded-support family $\{h_\gamma\}$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^2)$; restriction to $\Omega$ followed by addition of one gives relative compactness of $X_2(R)$ in $L^1(\Omega)$. If $\gamma_j\to\gamma$ in $L^1$, pass to an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence; the ellipticity bounds and background-collar equality pass to the limit almost everywhere. For each admissible smooth test field $\varphi$, its divergence is bounded, so the pairing with $\gamma_j$ converges to the pairing with $\gamma$. By [F5], the absolute value of each approximating pairing is at most $TV(\gamma_j;\Omega)$; taking the supremum over $\varphi$ yields $V(\gamma)\le\liminf_jTV(\gamma_j;\Omega)$. Assumption [A3] lets [F6] infer $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ and $TV(\gamma;\Omega)=V(\gamma)\le R$. Thus the class is closed and compact in $L^1$. [A3, F1, F2, F5, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 For $d\ge3$, the uniform $C^{1,\alpha}$ bound gives uniform bounds and equicontinuity for both the functions and their first derivatives. Apply [F3] with [A4] to the finite vector $(\gamma_j,D\gamma_j)$ to extract a subsequence converging in $C^1(\overline\Omega)$. The limit derivatives retain the same $\alpha$-Hölder bound by passing to the limit in $|D\gamma_j(x)-D\gamma_j(y)|\le R|x-y|^\alpha$; the ellipticity and collar conditions are closed under uniform convergence. Hence $X_d(R)$ is compact in $C^1$. [A4, F3, given, choose, algebra]

1.3 Apply [F7], using the observation convention [F4], with the actual fixed smoothing exponent $r_d$. The Hilbert–Schmidt difference there has, by the kernel isometry in the smoothing lemma, exactly the norm $\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_2$. In dimension two this gives the stated $L^q$ Lipschitz estimate with $q>2$. In dimensions at least three its supremum-norm estimate gives continuity in $C^1(\overline\Omega)$, since convergence in that topology implies uniform convergence of the coefficients. Thus the asserted kernel continuity is established in both branches. [F4, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 To use step 1.1's $L^1$ compactness in dimension two, note that all conductivities have the same uniform $L^\infty$ bound. Hence $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_q^q\le(2M)^{q-1}\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_1$. The estimate in step 1.3 therefore makes the kernel map continuous also for the $L^1$ topology on this class. Its image is compact as the continuous image of the compact class from step 1.1. For $d\ge3$, use the $C^1$ compactness in step 1.2 and the continuity in step 1.3. This proves the final assertion without a finite-dimensional measurement restriction. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, let $0<m\le1\le M<\infty$, and let $m\le\gamma\le M$ be measurable with $\gamma=1$ outside $\Omega'$. Put $M_\partial=\partial\Omega$ and give the NtD maps their total-boundary-mean-zero representatives. The spectral space $H^{1/2}_\Delta(M_\partial)$ is equivalent to the chart trace space $H^{1/2}(M_\partial)$, including their quotients by constants and mean-zero duals. Uniformly in $\gamma$,
$$\|\mathscr R_\gamma f\|_{H^1_\Delta(M_\partial)}\le C\|f\|_{L^2(M_\partial)}\quad\left(\int_{M_\partial}f=0\right).$$
For every integer $q\ge0$ there is $C_q$ such that
$$\|(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_1)F\|_{H^q_\Delta(M_\partial)}\le C_q\|F\|_{H^{-1/2}_\Delta(M_\partial)}$$
for every mean-zero weak Neumann flux $F$. If $w_j=1+\lambda_j$ and $(e_j)$ is any orthonormal boundary Laplace–Beltrami basis on the total-mean-zero subspace, the matrix $b_{ij}=\langle(\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0})e_j,e_i\rangle$ of any two such conductivities satisfies, for every $L>0$,
$$|b_{ij}|\le C_L(w_iw_j)^{-L}.$$
The constants depend only on the displayed fixed data and $q$ or $L$. More generally, any $v\in H^1$ harmonic with zero weak normal derivative on a fixed smooth boundary collar has $\|v|_{M_\partial}\|_{H^q_\Delta}\le C_q\|v\|_{H^1(\text{collar})}$ for every integer $q\ge0$, using a fixed smaller collar for the boundary estimate.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-mean-zero-ntd-and-smoothed-kernel-observation|The actual NtD and boundary spectral convention.]]

[[lem-ip-calderon-boundary-trace-quotient-identification|Chart trace spaces and quotient norms.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the domain, fixed collar, ellipticity bounds and spectral conventions in the Statement.

[F1] Weak Neumann solutions exist modulo constants and obey the uniform $H^1/\mathbb R$ energy estimate in the quotient flux norm. ([[lem-ip-mean-zero-neumann-problem-wellposedness]])

[F2] The quotient trace norm agrees up to fixed constants with the chart $H^{1/2}$ norm modulo constants. ([[lem-ip-calderon-boundary-trace-quotient-identification]])

[F3] The spectral boundary basis is complete, its $H^1_\Delta$ norm is the gradient form norm, and its counting function is at most $C(1+\Lambda)^{(d-1)/2}$. Finite chart localization and reassembly are bounded on $L^2,H^1$ and are left inverses. ([[lem-ip-boundary-spectral-counting-and-sobolev-scale]], [[lem-ip-boundary-chart-lifting-and-fourier-projection]])

[F4] Bounded tangential difference quotients give the corresponding weak derivatives, with the integral integration-by-parts identity valid for compactly supported tests; smooth-coefficient interior equations gain arbitrarily many derivatives by nested local estimates. ([[thm-difference-quotient-characterisation-of-w-one-p-for-p-greater-than-one]], [[thm-interior-h-k-plus-two-elliptic-regularity]])

[F5] Euclidean Fourier Parseval and the spectral basis Parseval hold. ([[thm-plancherel]], [[lem-ip-boundary-spectral-counting-and-sobolev-scale]])

[A1] The two choice assumptions enter at the weak Neumann, trace, spectral and Sobolev interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the fixed geometry and conductivities in the Statement.

1.1 Here is the needed half-order identification, without assuming an unproved equivalence for the full spectral scale. For a Hilbert pair $(E_0,E_1)$ use $K(t,f)^2=\inf_{f=f_0+f_1}(\|f_0\|_{E_0}^2+t^2\|f_1\|_{E_1}^2)$. In the spectral $L^2,H^1$ pair, independent minimization of each coefficient gives $K(t,f)^2=\sum_j|f_j|^2t^2w_j/(1+t^2w_j)$. Integration against $t^{-2}\,dt$ yields a fixed positive multiple of $\sum_jw_j^{1/2}|f_j|^2$, by substituting $t\sqrt{w_j}$ and Tonelli. Use the single-boundary versions of the chart maps: $Gf=((\psi_jf)\circ\phi_j^{-1})_j$ and $L(v)=\sum_j\psi_j(v_j\circ\phi_j)$, with zero extension. The finite chart Jacobian bounds and product rule give their $L^2,H^1$ bounds, while $\sum_j\psi_j^2=1$ gives $LG=I$, exactly as in [F3] with one chart factor. These maps bound the respective $K$ functionals in both directions (apply either map to every decomposition, using its endpoint bounds and its left inverse). For a compactly supported chart function the identical Fourier calculation gives weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$. This is equivalent to its Slobodeckij norm: Parseval applied to $f(\cdot+h)-f$ and integration against $|h|^{-n-1}\,dh$ give the homogeneous weight $c_n|\xi|$, with $0<c_n<\infty$ by splitting $|h|\le1$ and $|h|>1$. Smooth compact chart cutoffs and bi-Lipschitz changes of coordinates preserve this norm by the difference definition, using $|\psi(x)-\psi(y)|\le C|x-y|$ for the product term. Thus [F2] identifies the trace quotient with $H^{1/2}_\Delta/\mathbb R$, and duality identifies its mean-zero dual with $H^{-1/2}_\Delta$. Subtracting the total surface mean is bounded in every norm here, even when the boundary is disconnected. [A1, F2, F3, F5, given, construct]

1.2 We record the local homogeneous-Neumann estimate used below. In boundary normal coordinates $(y,t)$ on a fixed collar, the Laplace equation is $\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_jv)=0$ with smooth positive coefficients, $a^{t\ell}=0$ for every tangential index $\ell$, and homogeneous conormal condition $\partial_tv=0$ on $t=0$. For a compactly supported collar cutoff $\eta$, tangential testing with $-\delta_{-h}(\eta^2\delta_hv)$ gives $c\|\eta\nabla\delta_hv\|_2^2\le C\|v\|_{H^1}^2+(c/2)\|\eta\nabla\delta_hv\|_2^2$: the coefficient difference is bounded by $C|h|$ before division by $h$, the cutoff terms by $C\|v\|_{H^1}$, and $2ab\le\epsilon a^2+\epsilon^{-1}b^2$ absorbs them. There is no boundary term because these are admissible weak Neumann tests. Applying [F4] gives all second derivatives with at least one tangential derivative. The equation then solves for $\partial_{tt}v$, since $a^{tt}\ge c>0$. Iterating with nested cutoffs proves $\|v\|_{H^k(V)}\le C_k\|v\|_{H^1(V_0)}$ for every integer $k$, with $V$ a smaller collar. In detail, tangentially differentiating $r$ times introduces only terms $\partial_i((D_y^\beta a^{ij})\partial_jD_y^{r-\beta}v)$ with $|\beta|\ge1$; their energy pairings are bounded by the already known derivatives of total order at most $r$, leaving $\nabla D_y^rv$ on the left. Derivatives with two or more normal indices are recovered successively by differentiating the equation and isolating $a^{tt}D^\alpha\partial_{tt}v$; every other derivative of the same total order has fewer normal indices, while differentiated coefficient terms have lower total order. This induction proves the asserted estimate, rather than importing a Neumann boundary theorem. For a smooth forcing the same induction includes its finitely many derivatives on the right; a smooth nonzero normal datum can first be subtracted using a smooth collar function $t f(y)$ with cutoff and the appropriate normal sign. [F4, given, construct]

2.1 It suffices first to treat real fluxes; real and imaginary parts give the complexified estimates with the same uniform dependence. Choose a smooth vector field $X$ supported in the fixed harmonic collar with $X=\nu$ on the boundary. For smooth mean-zero flux $f$, the weak solution is smooth in a smaller collar: subtract the smooth normal-data lifting in step 1.2 and apply that step's inhomogeneous induction. For its harmonic part, direct differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}(X|\nabla u|^2-2(X\cdot\nabla u)\nabla u)=(\operatorname{div}X)|\nabla u|^2-2\partial_iX_j\partial_iu\partial_ju$. Integrate on the collar, where $X$ vanishes near its inner edge. The outer flux is $|\nabla_Mu|^2-|f|^2$, so $\|\nabla_Mu\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2^2+C\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. With the trace normalized to surface mean zero, [F1], the bounded $L^2$-to-quotient-flux inclusion from [F2], and the trace $L^2$ estimate bound $\|u|_M\|_{H^1}\le C\|f\|_2$. Approximate an arbitrary mean-zero $L^2$ flux by smooth mean-zero fluxes. Apply the same estimate to their differences with the SAME conductivity and use [F1] for convergence of the weak solutions; their traces converge in $H^1$, proving the displayed uniform bound by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.2 For an arbitrary weak flux $F$, put $v=u_{\gamma,F}-u_{1,F}$. Its $H^1/\mathbb R$ norm is at most $C\|F\|$ by [F1], and it is harmonic with ZERO normal derivative throughout the fixed collar. Apply step 1.2 to a representative of bounded $H^1$ norm. Tangential boundary derivatives are controlled by collar derivatives: for each smooth $z(y,t)$, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem applied to $|z|^2$ between $0$ and a fixed interior slice, averaged over that slice, gives $\|z(\cdot,0)\|_2^2\le C(\|z\|_2^2+\|z\|_2\|\partial_tz\|_2)$; apply this to all tangential derivatives. Thus all integer chart norms of the trace are bounded by $C_q\|F\|$. Applying the tangential differential operator $(1-\Delta_M)^k$ to this smooth trace and using [F5] gives $\sum_jw_j^{2k}|v_j|^2\le C_k\|F\|^2$; integration by parts against the weak eigenfunctions is justified by their local smoothness from [F4] in boundary charts. Smaller spectral exponents follow from $w_j\ge1$. Finally subtract the boundary mean, a bounded operation, and use step 1.1 to obtain the second displayed estimate. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 The weak energy identity makes $\mathscr R_\gamma$ self-adjoint on mean-zero $L^2$: $\langle\mathscr R_\gamma f,g\rangle=\int\gamma\nabla u_f\cdot\overline{\nabla u_g}$. Hence $b_{ij}=\overline{b_{ji}}$. By step 1.1 the quotient flux norm of $e_j$ is at most $Cw_j^{-1/4}$; step 2.2 applied twice gives $|b_{ij}|\le C_q w_i^{-q/2}w_j^{-1/4}$. Symmetry gives also $|b_{ij}|\le C_q w_j^{-q/2}w_i^{-1/4}$. Their geometric mean is $C_q(w_iw_j)^{-q/4-1/8}$. Choose an integer $q$ with $q/4+1/8\ge L$ to obtain the asserted two-sided estimate, uniformly for every pair of conductivities. This also covers additional mean-zero zero eigenmodes caused by a disconnected boundary, since all $w_j\ge1$. [step 1.1, step 2.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and let $R=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$ and
$\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. For a nonempty framed unoriented link $L$ in $S^3$,
choose a regular planar diagram $D$ of its core. Let $m_j\in\mathbb Z$ be
the full-twist correction on the $j$th component from the blackboard framing
of $D$ to the specified framing of $L$, counting an A-type twist positively
and its inverse negatively as in the framed diagram calculus, and put
$m=\sum_jm_j$. For a state
$S$ of $D$, let $a(S)$ and $b(S)$ be its numbers of A- and B-smoothings and
$|S|$ its number of resulting circles. The assignment
$$E(\varnothing)=1,\qquad E(L)=\delta(-A^3)^m\sum_{S}A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}$$
is independent of the diagram and twist corrections and extends
$R$-linearly to a map $E:\mathcal K_A(S^3)\to R$ satisfying
$E([\varnothing])=1$.

## Statement references

[[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold|Kauffman bracket skein module]]

[[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value|Kauffman bracket smoothing and loop value]]

[[lem-framed-link-diagram-calculus|Framed diagram calculus]]

[Józef H. Przytycki, *Fundamentals of Kauffman Bracket Skein Modules* (1998), §2, Theorem 2.3(a)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9809113)

[Sean Pohorence, *3-manifold Invariants and TQFTs* (2016), §3.1](https://categorified.net/RTinvariants/Jan29-Feb3.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a framed unoriented link in $S^3$, and its regular diagram and framing corrections.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] For a nonempty regular diagram $D$, the Kauffman bracket is the finite sum $\langle D\rangle=\sum_S A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}$ with $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The raw bracket is unchanged by every local Reidemeister II and III replacement in the fixed source-chart convention ([[lem-kauffman-bracket-r2-r3-identities]]).

[F3] Framed isotopies in $S^3$ admit finite planar-isotopy/Reidemeister sequences; a type-I move changes the blackboard framing by one signed twist ([[lem-framed-link-diagram-calculus]]).

[F4] The skein module imposes $[L_\times]=A[L_A]+A^{-1}[L_B]$ and $[L\sqcup O]=\delta[L]$ for a zero-framed trivial circle ([[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold]]).

## Proof


1.1 The state sum in [F1] is invariant under planar isotopy because that isotopy bijects crossings, states, and state circles. By [F3], diagrams of the same framed link are connected by a finite move sequence. For RII and RIII, [F2] leaves the raw bracket unchanged and the framing correction is unchanged. For an A-type R1 kink, the local state contribution is $A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^3$; for the opposite B-type kink it is $A+A^{-1}\delta=-A^{-3}$. For the A-type kink [F3] decreases the correction by one and for the B-type kink it increases the correction by one, so the product $(-A^3)^m\langle D\rangle$ is unchanged. Hence $E(L)$ is independent of diagram and framing correction. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 At a crossing, partition the finite state set by whether that crossing is smoothed A or B. This gives $\langle D_\times\rangle=A\langle D_A\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_B\rangle$. In a framed skein triple the exterior framed strips agree; place the same twist marks on those common arcs and none on the blackboard-framed local tangles. Their total correction $m$ is the same for the crossing and both smoothings. Multiplying the state identity by $\delta(-A^3)^m$ proves that $E$ sends the crossing relation in [F4] to zero. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $L$ is nonempty, adjoining a disjoint zero-framed trivial circle adds one circle to every state and multiplies the bracket by $\delta$. Thus $E(L\sqcup O)=\delta E(L)$. For the empty link, its one-circle diagram has bracket $1$, so the defining assignment gives $E(O)=\delta E(\varnothing)$. The evaluation therefore annihilates every trivial-circle relation in [F4]. Its $R$-linear extension to the free module factors through the quotient $\mathcal K_A(S^3)$ and sends the empty class to $1$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. For any finite $r\ge0$, every polynomial in the entries of $r$ complex $2\times2$ matrices invariant under simultaneous conjugation by $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is a polynomial in traces of words in those matrices. For each given invariant only finitely many words are needed. If $Z\subseteq M_2(\mathbb C)^r$ is any closed reduced invariant algebraic subset, every invariant regular function on $Z$ is likewise a polynomial in the restricted word traces. In particular this applies to the representation variety of any finitely presented group in $SL_2(\mathbb C)$, with its determinant and relator equations. The assertion does not identify a nonsemisimple representation from its character or assert a generic representation over the character function field.

## Statement references

[[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient|Closed invariant subsets and their quotient coordinate maps]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard two-dimensional space $V=\mathbb C^2$, its determinant form $\varepsilon(v,w)=v_1w_2-v_2w_1$, the finite tuple of matrices and, when used, the closed invariant reduced subset $Z$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited only through the quotient theorem below.

[F1] In [[def-reductive-and-linearly-reductive-over-c]], a unipotent subgroup has a nonzero fixed vector in each nonzero finite-dimensional rational module; a complex affine algebraic group is reductive if it has no nontrivial closed normal unipotent subgroup.

[F2] [[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]] proves for a complex reductive group that a closed invariant inclusion induces a closed immersion of affine quotients. On coordinate rings this is the surjection from the ambient invariant algebra to the subset invariant algebra. The proof gives precisely this surjection via the Reynolds operator, including the reduced relator quotient.

## Proof

1.1 **The invariant tensor dimension.** In the tensor power $V^{\otimes d}$ use the standard orthonormal tensor basis with letters $+$ and $-$. Let $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, let $E(-)=+$, $E(+)=0$, and let $F(+ )=-$, $F(-)=0$; on tensor powers each acts by the sum of its actions in each slot. Then $E^*=F$ and $[E,F]=H$ by direct multiplication in each slot, with distinct-slot terms commuting. Invariance under the diagonal matrices forces weight zero, and invariance under the upper unipotents forces $Ew=0$. Conversely, for weight-zero $w$ with $Ew=0$, the identity $\|Fw\|^2-\|Ew\|^2=\langle Hw,w\rangle$ gives $Fw=0$. Both unipotent one-parameter groups then fix $w$ by their finite exponential series. They generate $SL_2(\mathbb C)$: Gaussian elimination handles a matrix with nonzero upper-left entry; a zero entry is first made nonzero by an elementary row operation, and diagonal matrices are also products of elementary upper and lower matrices. Thus these are exactly the invariant tensors. Odd $d$ gives zero invariants, since the central element $-I$ acts by $-1$. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 **The group hypothesis for the quotient passage is proved.** If $U$ is a closed normal unipotent subgroup of $SL_2$, its action on the nonzero rational module $V$ has a nonzero fixed vector by [F1]. The subspace $V^U$ is $SL_2$-stable: for $v\in V^U$, $g\in SL_2$ and $u\in U$, normality gives $u(gv)=g(g^{-1}ug)v=gv$. The standard representation is irreducible; a nonzero vector can be carried to any other by a determinant-one change of basis, obtained by completing each vector to a basis with determinant one. Hence $V^U=V$. The standard representation is faithful, so $U$ is trivial. By [F1] $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is reductive in precisely the convention used by [F2]. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **A finite rank computation.** Put $d=2n$. The weight-zero space has dimension $\binom{2n}{n}$ and weight-two space has dimension $\binom{2n}{n-1}$, with the latter zero when $n=0$. The adjoint of $E:W_0\to W_2$ is $F:W_2\to W_0$. This $F$ is injective: if $Fw=0$ for a weight-two vector, the commutator identity gives $-\|Ew\|^2=2\|w\|^2$, so $w=0$. Finite-dimensional orthogonal-complement linear algebra therefore makes $E:W_0\to W_2$ surjective. Step 1.1 gives invariant dimension $\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}$. This computation includes the one-dimensional empty tensor power. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Actual epsilon tensors form a basis.** For each noncrossing matching of the ordered $2n$ positions, insert the invariant tensor $+\otimes- - -\otimes+$ in each matched pair, smaller position first, and permute tensor slots to their specified positions. All these tensors are invariant because the determinant form and its inverse are preserved by $SL_2$. Order tensor words lexicographically with $+>-$. The leading word has $+$ at every left endpoint and $-$ at every right endpoint. It is a Dyck word: each initial segment has at least as many left endpoints as right endpoints. Noncrossing matchings correspond bijectively to these words by closing the most recent unclosed endpoint. Distinct matchings therefore have distinct leading words, so their tensors are independent: in any nonzero linear relation choose the largest leading word among its nonzero coefficients. The number of Dyck words is $\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}$, by reflecting the initial segment through the first negative partial sum in each bad balanced word. The dimension computation in step 2.1 shows these actual tensors form a basis of the entire invariant space. The same holds for invariant multilinear forms, using the equivariant identification $V\to V^*$ given by the nondegenerate determinant form. For $n=0$ the matching is empty and gives the scalar $1$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Polarize invariant polynomials.** Separate an invariant polynomial into its homogeneous degrees; the action is linear, so each part is invariant. For a homogeneous degree-$d$ polynomial on $W=M_2(\mathbb C)^r$, its polarization is the symmetric multilinear form $$T(w_1,\ldots,w_d)=\frac1{d!}\sum_{A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}(-1)^{d-|A|}f\Bigl(\sum_{j\in A}w_j\Bigr).$$ Expansion of each monomial shows that terms missing any argument cancel and the surviving terms use each argument once. Hence it is multilinear and $T(w,\ldots,w)=f(w)$. The formula also proves invariance. Expand each slot according to the finite direct sum of $r$ matrix spaces; each resulting form is an invariant multilinear form on $d$ copies of $\operatorname{End}(V)$. The determinant identification $\operatorname{End}(V)=V\otimes V^*\cong V\otimes V$ turns it into the invariant $2d$-tensor problem of step 3.1. Consequently it is a linear combination of pairwise epsilon contractions of the two legs of each matrix. Degree zero is simply a scalar and needs no polarization. [step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

5.1 **Every contraction is a product of word traces.** Write $J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The tensor of a matrix $A$ in $V\otimes V$ is $AJ$: indeed $(gAg^{-1})J=g(AJ)g^T$ because $gJg^T=J$. Contract tensor legs by $J^{-1}$. Regard a complete pairing as a graph with one two-legged vertex for each matrix and one edge for each contraction. It is a disjoint union of cycles, allowing loops and doubled edges. Traverse a cycle and sum its repeated indices. Passing a vertex in its given leg order contributes $(AJ)J^{-1}=A$; passing it in the reverse order contributes $(AJ)^TJ^{-1}=-JA^TJ^{-1}=-\operatorname{adj}(A)$. Reversing an edge pairing merely changes a sign because $(J^{-1})^T=-J^{-1}$. Closing the repeated indices is exactly a trace. Thus each cycle is, up to a sign, a trace of a word in the matrices and their adjugates, and different cycles multiply. Finally $$\operatorname{adj}(A)=(\operatorname{tr}A)I-A$$ is the explicit $2\times2$ entry identity. Expanding each adjugate in every word expresses the contraction as a polynomial in ordinary word traces, with $\operatorname{tr}I=2$ for an empty word. Together with polarization, this proves the ambient matrix-polynomial assertion. [step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 **Pass to the actual reduced representation equations.** For a closed invariant reduced $Z\subseteq M_2^r$, apply [F2] and step 1.2 to its inclusion. The invariant coordinate algebra of $Z$ is a quotient of $\mathbb C[M_2^r]^{SL_2}$. Every ambient invariant is a polynomial in word traces by step 5.1, so their restrictions generate the quotient. A finitely presented group representation variety is such a $Z$: determinants equal one and relators equal the identity are finite polynomial equations after inverse letters are replaced by adjugates. The vanishing ideal of their point set is radical and invariant, whether or not the displayed raw equation ideal is radical. Thus [F2] applies to this actual reduced variety and yields the asserted invariant trace generation. On determinant-one matrices the adjugates used along the way are precisely inverse matrices, so the traces are traces of group words. Every polynomial calculation and pairing list was finite; full AC enters only in [F2]. No classification of individual orbits or rational descent of generic representations has been substituted for this calculation. [A1, F2, step 5.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\nabla_L(z)$ be a Conway skein invariant of oriented links, and for a knot $K$ put $a_2(K):=[z^2]\nabla_K(z)$. Then $a_2$ has type at most two: its third finite difference vanishes on every three-singular knot. If $D$ is the degree-two chord diagram of a two-singular knot, then $D_2a_2(K)=1$ when the two chords intersect and $D_2a_2(K)=0$ when they do not. Thus its degree-two symbol is a nonzero weight system on the unframed 4T+1T quotient. Moreover, $a_2(U)=0$ for the unknot, and $a_2(T)=1$ for the positive trefoil $T$ represented by the closure of a two-strand braid with three successive positive Artin half twists; closure joins each upper endpoint to the corresponding lower endpoint outside the braid cylinder.

The two possible degree-two chord patterns are shown below. The first has alternating endpoints and the second has an isolated chord. The diagrams illustrate the symbol values; the proof is algebraic.

## Statement references

[[def-conway-polynomial|Conway normalization and skein relation]]

[[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative|Finite-difference and type conventions]]

[[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations|Degree-two diagrams, intersections, 4T, and 1T]]

[[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids|Positive Artin half-twist and braid conventions]]

[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing|Positive crossing sign convention]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §2.3, printed pp. 35–37, and §3.1.1](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Chmutov, Cap Khoury, and Rossi, §§3.4–4.2, PDF pp. 4–8](https://math.osu.edu/~chmutov.1/preprints/chmutov-khoury-rossi.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Conway skein invariant $\nabla$ on oriented links, the finite-difference convention for singular knots, and the degree-two chord-diagram convention.

[F1] [[def-conway-polynomial]]: $\nabla_U=1$ and $\nabla_{L_+}-\nabla_{L_-}=z\nabla_{L_0}$ for an oriented skein triple.

[F2] [[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative]]: the $r$-fold finite difference is the alternating sum over independent positive/negative resolutions, and type at most two means that every third finite difference is zero.

[F3] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: a two-chord diagram is either intersecting or has an isolated chord; 1T kills the latter, and 4T has the alternating four-term sign convention.

[F4] [[def-kontsevich-integral-on-parenthesized-braids]]: the positive Artin half twist is the positive two-strand braid generator, and stacking an inverse half twist beside it cancels to the identity braid.

[F5] [[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]: a positive crossing has sign $+1$ under the determinant convention, and the positive Artin half twist has that sign.

[F6] **Discharged existence input.** [[def-conway-polynomial]] now supplies the actual unique $\mathbb Z[z]$-valued oriented ambient-link invariant by its explicitly external Garaev coefficient theorem and CDM ambient-link/skein interpretation, followed by the finite polynomial/uniqueness argument. Thus the Conway function in the Given is an actual available object, not an unresolved well-definedness premise. The finite coefficient/chord/trefoil arguments below are retained unchanged; no general rationality assertion for the Kontsevich coefficients is used.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. All arguments use the unframed branch and no choice axiom.

1.1 For any skein triple, the constant coefficients of $\nabla_{L_+}$ and $\nabla_{L_-}$ agree because their difference is divisible by $z$. Hence $c_0(L):=[z^0]\nabla_L$ is unchanged by crossing switches. Choose a basepoint on each component of a link diagram and a finite order of the components; switch each crossing so its first encounter in that traversal is the overpass. The resulting diagram is descending: starting at each basepoint, every arc can be pulled successively over the portions it meets, in the chosen component order, until each component is a round circle in a separate ball. Thus every link can be changed by crossing switches to an unlink. For the $r$-component unlink $U_r$, the normalization gives $c_0(U_1)=1$. Add a local curl to one component of $U_r$; its positive and negative versions are both $U_r$, while its oriented smoothing is the split unlink $U_{r+1}$. The skein relation gives $z\nabla_{U_{r+1}}=0$. Multiplication by the indeterminate $z$ is injective in $\mathbb Z[z]$: if $f=\sum_{j=0}^{N}a_jz^j$ and $zf=0$, then each coefficient $a_j$ is zero. Hence $\nabla_{U_{r+1}}=0$. Therefore $c_0(L)=1$ for knots and $c_0(L)=0$ for links with at least two components. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Comparing the coefficient of $z^1$ in the skein relation gives $c_1(L_+)-c_1(L_-)=c_0(L_0)$. In a two-component link, smoothing a mixed crossing yields a knot and therefore difference $1$; smoothing a self-crossing yields a three-component link and therefore difference $0$, by step 1.1. The value of this first difference depends only on whether the crossing is mixed, not on any other crossing resolution. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At one singular crossing of a knot, the skein relation gives $D_1a_2(K)=c_1(L_0)$ for its oriented two-component smoothing $L_0$. On a three-singular knot, resolve one marked point first and apply the two remaining differences to this $c_1(L_0)$. By step 2.1, taking the difference at either remaining crossing gives $c_0$ of its oriented smoothing; that smoothing has either one or three components, so its $c_0$ is constant across the resolution of the last marked crossing by step 1.1. The final alternating difference is therefore zero. Since the marked point chosen first was arbitrary, every third finite difference of $a_2$ vanishes. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For a two-singular knot, smooth the first marked point. Its two preimages split the circle into two arcs, which become the two components of $L_0$. The other marked crossing is mixed exactly when its two preimages lie on different arcs, equivalently when the two chord endpoints alternate with those of the first chord. By step 2.1 the resulting second difference is $1$ in that case and $0$ otherwise. [F2, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Define $w(D)=1$ on the intersecting two-chord diagram and $w(D)=0$ on the nonintersecting one. The latter is zero by 1T [F3]. If the cyclic order of the three fixed points is $p,q,r$, the four diagrams $D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4$ in the 4T generator have intersection indicators $(0,1,1,0)$; if the order is $p,r,q$, they have indicators $(1,0,0,1)$. These exhaust the cyclic orders up to rotation. In either case $w(D_1)-w(D_2)+w(D_3)-w(D_4)=0$. Thus $w$ factors through the unframed quotient. Since $w(D_{\times})=1$, that class is nonzero and the degree-two symbol in step 3.2 is nonzero. [F3, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 The unknot normalization gives $\nabla_U=1$, hence $a_2(U)=0$. Let $H$ be the closure of a two-strand braid with two successive positive Artin half twists. Switching one crossing creates adjacent positive and negative half twists, which cancel by [F4] to the two-component unlink $U_2$; smoothing that crossing leaves a one-half-twist closure, an unknot with a removable type-I curl. Step 1.1 gives $\nabla_{U_2}=0$, so the skein relation yields $\nabla_H=z$. For the positive trefoil $T$, the closure of three successive positive half twists, switching one crossing leaves an adjacent positive-negative pair that cancels and hence an unknot; smoothing that crossing leaves $H$. Therefore $\nabla_T-1=z\nabla_H=z^2$, so $a_2(T)=1$. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

id: thm-ip-unrestricted-map-test-can-have-level-one
kind: theorem
title: A non-eigenfeature can give an unrestricted Gaussian MAP test level one
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 4
deps:

axiom_use: The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the Gaussian posterior construction; Countable Choice is used by the shifted-operator and Hilbert-space interfaces. The null-direction scaling argument uses no further choice.
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Remo Kretschmann and Frank Werner, Maximum a posteriori testing in statistical inverse problems, Theorem 2.6 and its proof"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00686
---

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,H$ be separable real Hilbert spaces, $K:X\to H$ bounded and linear, $\epsilon>0$, and let $U$ be a Borel Gaussian prior with mean $m_0$ and positive self-adjoint, injective, trace-class covariance $C_0$, independent of a jointly Gaussian centered family $Z$ indexed by $H$, linear into $L^2$ with covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(k)]=\langle g,k\rangle_H$. Put $S=C_0^{1/2}$, $B=SK^*KS$, $R=(B+\epsilon^2I_X)^{-1}$. For a feature vector $h\in X$, define $\Phi_h=KSRSh$, $c_h=\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle_H-\langle m_0,h\rangle_X$, and the raw test $\delta_h=\mathbf1\{Y_x(\Phi_h)>c_h\}$, where $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$. Suppose $C_0K^*K=K^*KC_0$, $h\ne0$, and $Bh$ is not a scalar multiple of $h$. Then the unrestricted null set $H_0=\{x\in X:\langle x,h\rangle_X\le0\}$ satisfies
$$\sup_{x\in H_0}\mathbb P_x\{\delta_h=1\}=1.$$
The supremum need not be attained at any finite parameter value.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-gaussian-map-feature-test|Gaussian MAP feature test]]

[[thm-ip-map-test-level-and-power|Level, power, and weighted regularization of Gaussian MAP feature tests]]

[Kretschmann and Werner, *Maximum a posteriori testing in statistical inverse problems*, Theorem 2.6 and its proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00686)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Gaussian inverse model, operators, feature, and test in the Statement, together with the commutation and non-eigenfeature hypotheses.

[F1] Under the commutation hypothesis, $K^*\Phi_h=B(B+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}h$, and the raw test has rejection probability $G((\langle x,K^*\Phi_h\rangle-c_h)/(\epsilon\|\Phi_h\|))$ when $\Phi_h\ne0$. [[thm-ip-map-test-level-and-power]]

[F2] The shifted normal operator $B+\epsilon^2I$ is invertible, and its inverse commutes with $B$. [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]

[F3] The adjoint identity is $\langle Kx,\Phi\rangle_H=\langle x,K^*\Phi\rangle_X$, and inner products satisfy Cauchy–Schwarz. [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the posterior and polar-decomposition branches; Countable Choice is used for Hilbert adjoints and shifted-operator inversion. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]



## Proof
1.1 Put $A=B(B+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}$. By [F1] and its inherited Axiom of Choice hypothesis [A1], $K^*\Phi_h=Ah$. If $Ah=\eta h$ for a real scalar $\eta$, multiply the identity by $B+\epsilon^2I$ and use [F2] to obtain $Bh=\eta(B+\epsilon^2I)h$, hence $(1-\eta)Bh=\eta\epsilon^2h$. The case $\eta=1$ forces $h=0$, contrary to the hypothesis; otherwise $Bh=\eta\epsilon^2(1-\eta)^{-1}h$. Thus any scalar dependence of $Ah$ and $h$ would make $Bh$ a scalar multiple of $h$. The assumed non-eigenfeature condition therefore implies $Ah\notin\operatorname{span}\{h\}$. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $w=Ah-\frac{\langle Ah,h\rangle_X}{\|h\|_X^2}h$. Then $w\ne0$, $\langle w,h\rangle_X=0$, and $\langle Ah,w\rangle_X=\|w\|_X^2>0$ by orthogonal projection. For $t>0$, $x_t=tw$ belongs to $H_0$. Moreover $Ah\ne0$, since otherwise $Bh=0$ by invertibility of $B+\epsilon^2I$ and $h$ would be an eigenvector with eigenvalue zero; so $K^*\Phi_h=Ah$ implies $\Phi_h\ne0$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By [F3] and the inherited Axiom of Choice hypothesis [A1], the test statistic at $x_t$ has mean $\langle x_t,K^*\Phi_h\rangle_X=t\langle w,Ah\rangle_X=t\|w\|_X^2$ and positive standard deviation $\epsilon\|\Phi_h\|_H$. The exact tail formula [F1] gives $\mathbb P_{x_t}\{\delta_h=1\}=G\!\left(\frac{t\|w\|_X^2-c_h}{\epsilon\|\Phi_h\|_H}\right)\longrightarrow1$ as $t\to\infty$. Every $x_t$ is null, so the supremum over $H_0$ is at least this limit and at most one; it is therefore one. Since a nondegenerate normal tail is strictly below one at every finite threshold, the limiting sequence does not assert attainment. [given, A1, F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the proposed universal statement is that for every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ and every regular oriented diagram $D$ of a representative of $K$ (a projection with finitely many transverse double points, no other multiple points, oriented strands, and an over/under choice at each double point), the number $c(D)$ of double points equals the unknotting number $u(K)$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number|The separate definitions of diagram crossing count and unknotting number]]

[[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves|Reidemeister-I kink creation and deletion]]

[[def-countable-choice|The countable-choice hypothesis used to define the unknotting number]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$, the standard crossing-free unknot diagram, and a positive integer $k$.

[A1] AC$_\omega$ is the countable-choice axiom under which $u(K)$ is defined. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The standard unknot has bridge number one and unknotting number zero by their definitions. [[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number]]

[F2] Each oriented Reidemeister-I creation adds exactly one transverse double point, and each oriented Reidemeister move preserves the represented knot type by an ambient isotopy. [[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]], [[lem-each-oriented-reidemeister-move-is-realized-by-ambient-isotopy]]

## Counterexample

Let $U$ be the standard unknot and start from its crossing-free regular diagram. Perform $k$ oriented Reidemeister-I kink creations in pairwise disjoint disks along the diagram, obtaining a regular diagram $D_k$ of the same unknot. Then $c(D_k)=k$, whereas $u(U)=0$ and $b(U)=1$. For every $k\ge1$, this gives $c(D_k)\ne u(U)$ and refutes the proposed universal equality.

1.1 By [F2], each of the $k$ moves preserves the represented knot type and adds exactly one crossing, while disjoint supports ensure that no move changes crossings created in another disk. Induction on the finite number of moves gives $c(D_k)=k$ and shows that $D_k$ still represents $U$. [F2, given, induction]

2.1 By [F1], $u(U)=0$ and $b(U)=1$. Since $k\ge1$, step 1.1 yields $c(D_k)=k\ne0=u(U)$, proving the counterexample. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

This local schematic shows the one-crossing kink created by an R1 move. The horizontal segment is the underpassing branch, the diagonal segment is the overpassing branch, and the outer curved portion returns the strand to itself. Repeating the move in disjoint disks produces the family $D_k$; the count proof uses only the R1 definition, not the drawing.

## Definition

A **sutured manifold** $(M,\gamma)$ consists of a compact oriented $3$-manifold $M$ with boundary and a union $\gamma$ of pairwise disjoint annuli and tori in $\partial M$. Each annulus contains a suture, its oriented core circle; write $A(\gamma)$ for the annuli and $s(\gamma)$ for the union of their cores. Orient each component of $R(\gamma)=\partial M\setminus\operatorname{int}(\gamma)$ so that its boundary orientation agrees in the annulus with the homology class of the suture. The regions whose normal points out of $M$ form $R_+(\gamma)$ and those whose normal points into $M$ form $R_-(\gamma)$. The sutured manifold is **balanced** when $M$ has no closed component, $\chi(R_+)=\chi(R_-)$, and every component of $\partial M$ meets an annular component of $\gamma$. It is **irreducible** when every embedded $2$-sphere in $M$ bounds a $3$-ball in $M$. A properly embedded surface is **incompressible** when it has no compressing disk, meaning an embedded disk whose boundary is a loop on the surface that does not bound a disk on that surface. For a compact surface $S$ put $x(S)=\sum_{S_j}\max(0,-\chi(S_j))$, where the sum is over its connected components. The Thurston norm of a relative homology class in $H_2(M,\gamma;\mathbb Z)$ is the minimum of $x(S)$ over properly embedded oriented representatives. A balanced sutured manifold is **taut** when it is irreducible and $R(\gamma)$ is norm-minimizing in $H_2(M,\gamma;\mathbb Z)$.

A **product sutured manifold** is $(R\times[0,1],\partial R\times[0,1])$ for a compact oriented surface $R$, with positive and negative regions $R\times\{1\}$ and $R\times\{0\}$. A properly embedded oriented surface $S\subset M$ is a **decomposing surface** when every component $\lambda$ of $S\cap\gamma$ is either a properly embedded nonseparating arc in an annular component meeting its suture once, a simple closed curve in an annular component homologous to that suture, or a homotopically nontrivial curve in a toroidal component, with all such curves in one torus component representing the same homology class. A **product disk** is a decomposing surface that is a disk and meets the sutures in exactly two points. A **product annulus** is a decomposing annulus with one boundary circle in $R_+$ and one in $R_-$. A **horizontal surface** $S$ in a balanced sutured manifold has no closed component, $|\partial S|=|s(\gamma)|$, $[S]=[R_+]$ in $H_2(M,\gamma;\mathbb Z)$, and $\chi(S)=\chi(R_+)$. The sutured manifold is **vertically prime** when every horizontal surface is parallel to $R_+$ or $R_-$, where parallel means that the surfaces cobound an embedded product between them.

When $(M,\gamma)$ is irreducible, $\gamma$ has no torus component, and $R_+$ and $R_-$ are incompressible and diffeomorphic, a **product region** is a submanifold $\Phi\times[0,1]\subset M$ for a compact possibly disconnected surface $\Phi$ such that $\Phi\times\{0\}$ and $\Phi\times\{1\}$ are incompressible subsurfaces of $R_-$ and $R_+$, respectively. A **characteristic product region** is a product region $E\times[0,1]$ such that every product region $\Phi\times[0,1]$ can be carried into it by an ambient isotopy of $M$.

[Juhasz, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, §§2 and 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609779v3)

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D=B(x_0,1/4)\subset(0,1)^2$ and $D'=B(x_0,1/8)$, where $x_0=(1/2,1/2)$. With $m=1/2$, $M=3/2$, $R=1$, define $\gamma(x)=1+\tfrac12\chi_{B(x_0,1/16)}(x)$ on $D$. Then $\gamma\in X_2(1)$ for the planar BV class on $(D,D')$, and its almost-everywhere class has no continuous representative on $D$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class|The planar class $X_2(R)$ and its BV norm.]]

[[ex-ip-bv-jump-across-smooth-curve|The indicator of a disk has total variation equal to its circumference.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $D=B(x_0,1/4)$, $D'=B(x_0,1/8)$, $m=1/2$, $M=3/2$, $R=1$, and $\gamma=1+\tfrac12\chi_{B(x_0,1/16)}$.

[F1] In dimension two, $X_2(R)$ consists of measurable coefficients equal to $1$ almost everywhere on $D\setminus D'$, satisfying $m\le\gamma\le M$, and with $\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(D)},TV(\gamma;D)\}\le R$. ([[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class]], [[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv]])

[F2] For every disk $B(x_0,r)$, its indicator has distributional derivative $-\nu\mathcal H^1|_{\partial B(x_0,r)}$ and total variation $2\pi r$. ([[lem-ip-calderon-disk-inclusion-perimeter-scaling]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed in the cited disk-perimeter scaling proof. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The disk $B(x_0,1/16)$ is contained in $D'$ because $1/16<1/8$, and $\gamma=1$ on $D\setminus D'$. Almost everywhere its only values are $1$ and $3/2$, so $1/2\le\gamma\le3/2$. Thus the support and ellipticity conditions in [F1] hold. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $|D|=\pi/16$ and $|B(x_0,1/16)|=\pi/256$, the integral satisfies $\|\gamma\|_{L^1(D)}=\pi/16+\pi/512=33\pi/512<1$. By [F2] and homogeneity of distributional variation, $TV(\gamma;D)\le\tfrac12(2\pi/16)=\pi/16<1$; restriction to $D$ cannot increase the full-space variation. Therefore the BV norm is at most $1$, so [F1] gives $\gamma\in X_2(1)$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At every point of the circle $\partial B(x_0,1/16)$ lying inside $D$, every neighborhood meets the interior disk and its exterior in sets of positive measure. The function equals $3/2$ almost everywhere on the former and $1$ almost everywhere on the latter. A continuous representative would be constant $3/2$ on the interior and constant $1$ on the exterior by continuity and almost-everywhere equality, contradicting continuity across the circle. Hence the conductivity class is discontinuous. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-commuting-affine-peripheral-holonomy-logarithm-factorization
kind: lemma
title: Commuting affine peripheral holonomies factor their logarithms on
  singular parameter spaces
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19

sources:

        and a Proof of Thurston's Hyperbolic Dehn Filling Theorem
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045
      locator: Lemma 2.6 and its commutativity identity, printed pp. 13–14; Theorem
        2.2(1,3); Proposition 3.6
dependency_level: 0
---

## Statement

Let $Z$ be a reduced complex analytic space with point $o$, and suppose $u_i,v_i,a_i,b_i$ are holomorphic germs on $Z$ for $1\le i\le k$, with $k<\infty$, $u_i(o)=v_i(o)=0$, $a_i(o)\ne0$ and $\tau_i^0=b_i(o)/a_i(o)\notin\mathbb R$. Suppose the affine maps
$$L_i(w)=e^{u_i}w+a_i,\qquad P_i(w)=e^{v_i}w+b_i$$
commute at every parameter point. Then, after shrinking around $o$, there are holomorphic germs $\tau_i$ such that $v_i=\tau_i u_i$, $\tau_i(o)=\tau_i^0$ and $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i\ne0$ throughout. In particular $u_i=0$ if and only if $v_i=0$, and $v_i/u_i\to\tau_i^0$ as the parameter tends to $o$ through $u_i\ne0$. No smoothness, dimension or rank hypothesis on $Z$ is required.

For $u_i\ne0$, there is a unique real pair $(p_i,q_i)$ solving $p_iu_i+q_iv_i=2\pi i$. With
$$\widetilde u_i=\frac{2\pi i}{p_i+\tau_i^0q_i},$$
one has
$$|\widetilde u_i-u_i|\le\frac{|\tau_i-\tau_i^0|}{|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0|}|u_i|.$$
Set $\widetilde u_i=0$ when $u_i=0$. The functions $\widetilde u_i$ are continuous at such points, and $\|\widetilde u-u\|=o(\|u\|)$ as the parameter tends to $o$ through $u\ne0$.

## Statement references

[Petronio and Porti, Lemma 2.6 and Proposition 3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite collection of holomorphic germs, their values at $o$ and the commuting affine maps in the Statement.

## Proof

1.1 If $k=0$, the collection of germs and every indexed assertion are empty. Both vectors are the unique vector of $\mathbb C^0$, with norm zero; there is no parameter with $u\ne0$, so the final limiting assertion is vacuous. This proves the Statement in that case. Henceforth suppose $k\ge1$. Composition of the two affine maps shows that commutativity is exactly $a_i(e^{v_i}-1)=b_i(e^{u_i}-1)$. Let $E(t)=(e^t-1)/t$ for $t\ne0$ and $E(0)=1$; its convergent series is $\sum_{n\ge0}t^n/(n+1)!$, so it is holomorphic and nonzero near zero. Since $a_i(o)\ne0$, the holomorphic function $\tau_i=(b_i/a_i)E(u_i)/E(v_i)$ is defined near $o$. The commutativity equation becomes exactly $v_i=\tau_i u_i$, and $\tau_i(o)=b_i(o)/a_i(o)$. The finitely many nonreal values permit one common neighborhood on which all $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i$ are nonzero. Thus all $\tau_i$ are nonzero, proving the equivalence of their zero logarithms and the asserted quotient limit. The argument is an identity of holomorphic functions on $Z$, so singular points cause no difficulty. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 When $u_i\ne0$, real linear independence of $u_i$ and $v_i=\tau_i u_i$ follows from $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i\ne0$. Hence the real linear map $(p,q)\mapsto pu_i+qv_i$ is invertible and gives the unique real pair. Its equation is $(p_i+q_i\tau_i)u_i=2\pi i$. Since $\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0\ne0$, the denominator $p_i+q_i\tau_i^0$ cannot vanish: if it did, its imaginary part would give $q_i=0$, then its real part $p_i=0$, contrary to the full-turn equation. Therefore $\widetilde u_i/u_i=(p_i+q_i\tau_i)/(p_i+q_i\tau_i^0)$ and $(\widetilde u_i-u_i)/u_i=q_i(\tau_i-\tau_i^0)/(p_i+q_i\tau_i^0)$. The elementary bound $|p_i+q_i\tau_i^0|\ge |q_i|\,|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0|$ proves the estimate, including $q_i=0$ where its left side is zero. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood all $\tau_i$ are bounded, so step 2.1 gives $|\widetilde u_i|\le C|u_i|$. Thus extending $\widetilde u_i$ by zero across $u_i=0$ is continuous there; elsewhere its formula is continuous because it comes from an invertible real linear system. Put $\eta(z)=\max_i |\tau_i(z)-\tau_i^0|/|\operatorname{Im}\tau_i^0|$. Finiteness of $k$ and continuity give $\eta(z)\to0$ as $z\to o$. Applying the scalar estimates coordinatewise, also where $u_i=0$, gives $\|\widetilde u-u\|\le\eta(z)\|u\|$. This proves the final assertion. No claim that $u$ is a coordinate system or has nonvanishing derivative has entered the argument. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Scope

The affine normalization retains a chosen peripheral fixed point or eigenline. This lemma supplies the logarithmic quotient and the filling-parameter comparison even when the shape space is singular. It supplies neither a holomorphic coordinate on an ordinary character quotient nor the analytic-space openness, isolated-complete-point, geometric realization or triangulation-existence prerequisites needed for general hyperbolic Dehn filling.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If two integral framed-link surgery diagrams are related by one ambient isotopy, handle slide, or split $\pm1$-unknot stabilization or destabilization as defined for this page, then their oriented surgery results are orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic. The same holds for any finite sequence of these moves.

## Statement references

[[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram|Integral surgery result]]

[[def-kirby-moves-on-integral-framed-links|The three allowed moves]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable-choice consequence of full AC used by the trace and slide suppliers]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, two integral framed-link diagrams, and one allowed Kirby move between them.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Applying it to the range of any sequence of nonempty sets gives the countable-choice axiom required by the framed handle-slide and surgery-trace interfaces.

[F1] [[def-integral-framed-link-surgery-diagram]]: component $K_i$ is filled with a solid torus whose meridian maps to $n_i[\mu_i]+[\lambda_i]$.

[F2] [[def-kirby-moves-on-integral-framed-links]]: a handle slide replaces a component by the band sum with a framed parallel of another component, and stabilization adds or removes a split unknot with coefficient $+1$ or $-1$.

[F3] [[def-handle-slide-of-one-k-handle-over-another]]: the slid attaching sphere is the band sum of the first attaching sphere with a signed framed parallel copy of the second, with the full framing carried across the band.

[F4] [[lem-handle-slides-preserve-the-relative-diffeomorphism-type]]: for $1\le k\le n-2$, a handle slide gives a diffeomorphism of the handle attachments relative to the incoming boundary.

[F5] [[def-surgery-trace-cobordism]]: a framed surgery trace is the cylinder with a handle attached along the framed sphere.

[F6] [[thm-upper-boundary-of-the-surgery-trace-is-the-surged-manifold]]: the outgoing face of a framed surgery trace is diffeomorphic, as a smooth manifold, to the corresponding surgered manifold; the identification is the identity on the complement of the surgery neighbourhood. The orientation agreement needed here is checked in step 1.2.

[F7] [[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling]]: the integer $r$ filling slope is $r[\mu]+[\lambda]$, and the orientation-reversing gluing gives a filled orientation agreeing with the oriented exterior.

[F8] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ says that every sequence of nonempty sets $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ has a choice function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$.

## Proof

1.1 For an ambient isotopy, carry each component neighbourhood, meridian, and preferred longitude along the isotopy. The endpoint diffeomorphism of $S^3$ therefore maps every filling meridian to the same framed slope on the corresponding endpoint torus. Extend it over each attached solid torus by the product identification used in the filling. The resulting map is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of the filled manifolds. [given, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Applying [A1] to the family of values of any sequence $(X_n)$ in [F8] gives a choice function on that range; composing it with $n\mapsto X_n$ supplies the choice function required by [F8]. Thus the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis of [F3]–[F6] holds. For a diagram $D$, form its $4$-dimensional surgery trace from $S^3\times[0,1]$ by attaching one $2$-handle for each framed link component. Orient the product by $dt$ followed by the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient each handle so its attaching identification reverses the induced boundary orientations of the handle and cylinder, as required by [F5]; this is possible because each attaching region $S^1\times D^2$ is connected. The trace is connected. On the outgoing face, the unaltered part $E_D=S^3\setminus\bigcup_i\operatorname{int}N(K_i)$ has the standard $S^3$ orientation from the upper product face, exactly the orientation that the filling conventions [F1, F7] extend over the attached solid tori. The link exterior is nonempty and connected (paths in $S^3$ can be perturbed off the one-dimensional link; for the empty diagram $E_D=S^3$). Thus the identity-on-$E_D$ identification in [F6] preserves the surgery orientation. The link slide of [F2] is exactly the $k=2$ handle slide of [F3], including its full transported normal framing. Since $1\le2\le4-2$, [F4] supplies a diffeomorphism between the two traces relative to the incoming $S^3$ face. Both traces have the product orientation there and the diffeomorphism fixes that face; its tangent derivative is the identity and its normal derivative preserves the interior side, so it preserves the trace orientation. Its restriction preserves the induced orientations on the outgoing faces. Composing with the identifications in [F6] gives the required orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of surgery results. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, construct]

1.3 Suppose a split unknot is added with coefficient $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ in a ball disjoint from the rest of the link. The separating sphere shows that the filled manifold is the connected sum of the old surgery result with the filling of the unknot exterior along $\varepsilon[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$. For the standard unknot, take $E_U=\{|z_2|\ge1/\sqrt2\}\subset S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, identified with $D^2\times S^1$ by $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_1,z_2/|z_2|)$. Its preferred longitude $\lambda_U$ is the meridian of this solid torus, and $\mu_U$ is its core longitude. The diffeomorphism $g_\varepsilon(z,w)=(w^{-\varepsilon}z,w)$ of $D^2\times S^1$ preserves orientation, fixes $[\lambda_U]$, and sends $[\mu_U]$ to $[\mu_U]-\varepsilon[\lambda_U]$; hence it sends the slope $\varepsilon[\mu_U]+[\lambda_U]$ to the unoriented meridional slope $[\mu_U]$. Choose the $S^3$ gluing with meridian $[\mu_U]$ and the $\varepsilon$-filling gluing as its pullback by $g_\varepsilon^{-1}$. The map $g_\varepsilon$ on the exterior and the identity on the attached solid torus then give an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism between the two fillings. Filling along $[\mu_U]$ restores the original unknot neighbourhood, so the $\varepsilon$-framed unknot filling is orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic to $S^3$. Hence the connected sum is the original manifold: deleting a ball and regluing the complementary ball of $S^3$ restores the same manifold. Removing a split $\varepsilon$-framed unknot is the inverse operation. [given, A1, F1, F2, F7, construct]

2.1 Each allowed move preserves the oriented surgery manifold by steps 1.1–1.3. Composing the finitely many orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms along a move sequence proves the assertion for Kirby-move-equivalent diagrams. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U$ be the standard oriented unknot and take its genus-zero one-pointed Heegaard diagram: $\Sigma=S^2$, each handlebody is a three-ball, there are no $\alpha$- or $\beta$-curves, and one $w$-point and one $z$-point are joined by trivial arcs in the two balls. The associated-graded hat chain complex has one generator, zero differential, and homology of rank one over $\mathbb F_2$. This is a computation for the stated diagram; it makes no invariance claim for other diagrams.

## Statement references

[[def-admissible-pointed-heegaard-floer-data|The pointed Heegaard diagram and associated-graded hat complex]]

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|The oriented unknot in the standard three-sphere]]

[Manolescu, Ozsvath, and Sarkar, “A combinatorial description of knot Floer homology,” §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0607691)

[Manolescu, *An Introduction to Knot Floer Homology*, §3.5](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/hfk.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The genus-zero, one-pointed diagram specified in the statement.

[F1] [[def-admissible-pointed-heegaard-floer-data]] defines $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$, the product tori, and their intersection points as generators; its hat specialization sets the basepoint variable to zero.

[F2] [[def-admissible-pointed-heegaard-floer-data]] defines the differential by counts of classes of Maslov index $1$.

## Proof

1.1 Here $h=0$ and $k=1$, so $m=h+k-1=0$. The empty products of $\alpha$- and $\beta$-curves both map to the unique point of $\operatorname{Sym}^{0}(S^2)$, which is a singleton. By [F1], this intersection is the entire generator set, so the chain group has dimension one. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Every map into a singleton is constant, so there is only the constant class in $\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf x)$. Its pullback tangent bundle is zero-dimensional; hence the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator has zero kernel and cokernel and Maslov index $0$. Thus there is no class of Maslov index $1$ to contribute under [F2]. The differential is zero, and the homology equals the one-dimensional chain group. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every odd prime $p$ and every finite regular oriented link diagram $D$,
the algorithm in the Definition terminates and returns exactly
$\operatorname{Col}_p(D)$. If its reduced system has $f$ free variables, it
returns $p^f$ colorings. It uses at most $a$ pivot steps and at most $ca$
row-entry elimination scans for a diagram with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings.

## Statement references

[[alg-dihedral-fox-colorings]].

[[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]].

[Przytycki, *3-coloring and other elementary invariants of knots*, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0608172).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An odd prime $p$ and a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings.

[F1] [[alg-dihedral-fox-colorings]]: the input equations are $2x_o-x_i-x_j=0$ over $\mathbb F_p$; each pivot is selected in the leftmost available column and row, normalized, and cleared in every other row.

[F2] [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]: a regular diagram has finitely many crossings and finitely many arcs between crossings.

[A1] $p$ is prime; thus every nonzero residue modulo $p$ is invertible by Bézout's identity.

## Proof

1.1 Each crossing contributes one linear equation in the $a$ arc variables, so the algorithm forms a $c\times a$ matrix over $\mathbb F_p$. Addition and multiplication of residue classes are well-defined because congruence modulo $p$ is preserved by sums and products. If a residue $r$ is nonzero, then $\gcd(r,p)=1$, so integers $u,v$ satisfy $ur+vp=1$ and $u$ is the inverse of $r$ modulo $p$. The field hypothesis in [A1] therefore supplies every division used by the pivot instructions in [F1]. [given, F1, F2, A1, construct]

2.1 Every row operation in [F1] preserves the solution set of the homogeneous system. A row swap is reversible by the same swap; multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar is reversible by multiplying by its inverse; and adding a multiple of one row to another is reversible by subtracting the same multiple. Each transformed system is therefore equivalent to the preceding one. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 The algorithm visits each of the $a$ columns once. Each pivot search inspects at most $c$ rows, for at most $ca$ entry tests in total. Every pivot clears its column in at most $c-1$ other rows, so at most $a(c-1)\le ca$ row-entry elimination scans occur. A pivot increases the unused-row index, and there are at most $a$ columns, so there are at most $a$ pivots. The loops are finite and the chosen first nonzero entry makes the procedure deterministic. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 At termination, each pivot column has a single $1$ in its pivot row and zeros in every other row; earlier pivot columns stay cleared because each later pivot row is zero in those columns. Each nonpivot column is free. The pivot equations uniquely determine the pivot variables from arbitrary free-variable values, and every such assignment satisfies the reduced system. By step 2.1 the reduced system has exactly the original solution set, so the returned assignments are exactly the Fox colorings. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 There are exactly $p^f$ choices of the $f$ free variables, and each determines one distinct solution. If $a=0$, then $f=0$ and the empty diagram has its unique empty assignment; if $c=0$, every arc variable is free and all $p^a$ assignments are returned. The stated pivot and scan bounds follow from step 2.2. [given, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[[alg-dihedral-fox-colorings]].

[[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]].
