## Statement

Assume countable choice.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link, after
inserting a small type-I curl on any component that has no underpassing point.
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be the positive meridians of the strands between
successive underpassing points, with the compatible common-upper-collar accesses of the local crossing rule. At a crossing $c$, write $o(c)$ for the
over-strand and $s(c),t(c)$ for the source and target under-sides defined using
the positive in-plane normal to the over-strand. Set
$$r_c=x_{o(c)}^{-1}x_{s(c)}x_{o(c)}x_{t(c)}^{-1}.$$
Then the assignment of each generator to its based positive meridian induces
an isomorphism
$$\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_c\ (c\text{ a crossing})\rangle \cong \pi_1(E_L).$$
Any one crossing relator may be omitted without changing the represented
group. The theorem makes no claim that all relators are independent.

Arbitrary independently based positive strand meridians remain recorded: if $g_e$ is the access difference for strand $e$, its actual class is $y_e=g_ex_eg_e^{-1}$ in this reference presentation. This gives their exact group elements without claiming that the independently conjugated $y_e$ themselves freely generate the upper region or give the displayed uncorrected presentation. A common access change conjugates every generator and preserves the displayed presentation map.

## Statement references

[Friedl, Proposition 5.5 and §5.3](https://friedl.app.uni-regensburg.de/papers/2024_knot-theory-final.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The link diagram, its labels, crossing conventions, a smooth realization $L$, and common based meridian paths. Here $E_L$ denotes the exterior of arbitrary specified pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$ about the components of $L$, with their product parametrizations; thus $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(\bigcup_iN(K_i))$. Choose the group basepoint in $E_L$. Compatible diagram meridians may first be represented in $X=S^3\setminus L$; their images under the product-tube radial retraction are the based positive meridians in the displayed exterior group. These are auxiliary choices for the exterior and its marking, not extra restrictions on the link.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] For the normalized realization, $X=S^3\setminus L$ has an open cover whose upper piece is generated freely by the strand meridians, whose lower piece is contractible, and whose overlap is a punctured sphere with crossing circles normally generating its fundamental group even after one is omitted. For the specified product tubes the cover supplier also gives the radial deformation retraction $R:X\to E_L$, fixed on $E_L$. [[lem-link-wirtinger-crossing-ball-cover]], [[lem-link-diagram-upper-region-free-meridians]]

[F2] The Seifert–van Kampen theorem identifies the fundamental group of a union with the pushout of the two inclusion maps from a path-connected overlap. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]], [[thm-group-pushout-as-an-amalgamated-quotient]]

[F3] Under the upper-region meridian basis, the image of a small puncture circle at crossing $c$ is conjugate to $r_c$ or $r_c^{-1}$; these have the same normal closure. [[lem-link-wirtinger-local-meridian-conjugacy]]

[F4] A group presentation is the quotient of the free group on the stated generators by the normal closure of the stated relators. [[def-group-presentation]], [[def-free-group]]

[F5] A regular link diagram whose components have underpasses has an ambient-isotopic height realization with every underpass at height $-1$ and all other points above $-1$. [[lem-regular-link-diagram-admits-normalized-height-realization]]

## Proof

1.1 If a component has no underpassing point, insert a small type-I curl in a disk meeting only that component. The local curl is the boundary of a disk pushed into a ball disjoint from the rest of the link, so removing it by the reverse isotopy identifies the resulting link with the original. After this finite operation each component has an underpass. Apply [F5] to obtain the normalized height model required by the cover supplier. If $h$ is the resulting ambient isotopy's endpoint, transport each specified tube parametrization by $h$, together with the basepoint and all based paths. Then $h(E_L)$ is exactly the exterior of these transported tubes, and $h$ identifies its based positive meridians with the original ones. Work in this normalized model and retain the names $L,E_L$. [F5, given, construct]

2.1 By [A1, F1], the upper-region group is free on $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the lower-region group is trivial, and the overlap group is normally generated by the crossing circles $c_1,\ldots,c_n$. Applying [F2] to the open cover of $X$, the pushout with a trivial lower group is the quotient of the upper group by the normal closure of the images of these circles. This quotient initially computes $\pi_1(X)$. Use common basepoint-change paths when passing between the overlap basepoint and the reference upper basepoint; this conjugates all generator images by the same path, consistently with the given common basing. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F3], the normal closure in the upper group of the images of the crossing circles is the normal closure of the relators $r_c$. By [F4], the pushout quotient is therefore the stated Wirtinger presentation of $\pi_1(X)$. Now apply the radial retraction from [F1]: in each punctured product tube, write a point as $(\theta,r\omega)$ with $0<r\leq1$ and $|\omega|=1$, and use $(\theta,r\omega)\mapsto(\theta,((1-t)r+t)\omega)$ for $0\leq t\leq1$, fixing the exterior. These formulas agree with the identity at $r=1$, so they give the based deformation retraction $R:X\to E_L$. It sends a positive small normal circle to the corresponding positive tube-boundary meridian, and fixes any already exterior-based loop. Thus composing the presentation isomorphism with $R_*$ gives exactly the stated isomorphism to $\pi_1(E_L)$ with its positive-meridian marking; retracting the common basepoint-change paths gives the same based identification. Transporting back by $h^{-1}$ restores the originally specified exterior. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The cover lemma also states that any $n-1$ of the crossing circles normally generate the overlap group. Replacing the full list by any list omitting one circle therefore gives the same normal closure in the upper group, hence the same group $\pi_1(X)$ and, under the fixed isomorphism $R_*$, the same marked exterior-group presentation from step 3.1. [F1, step 3.1]

5.1 For an arbitrary access $a_e'$ to the same positive meridian circle reached by the reference access $a_e$, set $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$. Cancellation of reversed paths gives $a_e'\mu_e(a_e')^{-1}=g_e(a_e\mu_ea_e^{-1})g_e^{-1}=g_ex_eg_e^{-1}$ in the actual exterior group and hence, by step 3.1, in its reference presentation. If one common based loop is prepended to all accesses, this is simultaneous conjugation and so an inner automorphism of the target. Independent $g_e$ need not define an automorphism or even a generating tuple, which is why no such assertion is made. All geometric based meridian data are retained by these explicit words. [given, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The universal implication that a knot with $\tau(K)=0$ is smoothly slice is false. In the twist convention of Hedden and Ording, the positive-clasped two-twisted Whitehead double $D_+(T_{2,3},2)$ has $\tau=0$ and $s=2$, so its smooth four-ball genus is at least one and it is not smoothly slice.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau|The tau invariant]]

[[def-rasmussen-s-invariant|Rasmussen's s invariant]]

[[thm-rasmussen-s-bounds-smooth-four-ball-genus|The smooth genus bound for s]]

[[lem-knot-kt41-whitehead-double-values|The proved values for this Whitehead double]]

[Hedden and Ording, *The Ozsvath-Szabo and Rasmussen concordance invariants are not equal*, Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0512348v1)

[Rasmussen, *Khovanov homology and the slice genus*, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, the universal implication, and the specified Whitehead double with the source's positive-clasp and two-twist conventions.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is the axiom branch inherited by the knot invariants and smooth genus.

[L1] [[lem-knot-kt41-whitehead-double-values]] proves $\tau=0$ and $s=2$ for the specified positive-clasped two-full-twist knot, using its actual finite Lee and normalized full grid computations.

[L2] [[thm-rasmussen-s-bounds-smooth-four-ball-genus]] states $|s(K)|\le2g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$, for an actual smooth spanning surface.

[L3] [[lem-lee-cobordism-filtration-genus-bound]] is the exact supplier required by [L2]; its hypothesis is a smoothly properly embedded surface in $S^3\times[0,1]$ with product collars, not an abstract oriented surface with knot labels.

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice, the proposed implication, and the actual Whitehead double in the Statement.

1.1 The joint value lemma [L1] gives $\tau(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=0$ and $s(D_+(T_{2,3},2))=2$ in precisely the stated convention. Apply the smooth embedded-surface bound [L2], with its geometric supplier [L3]. It gives $2\le2g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(D_+(T_{2,3},2))$, so this genus is at least one. [A1, L1, L2, L3, given, algebra]

2.1 A smoothly slice knot bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in the four-ball and therefore has smooth four-ball genus zero. This contradicts the lower bound in step 1.1 for the displayed knot. It is consequently not smoothly slice even though its tau value is zero, giving the required counterexample to the universal implication. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $Y$ be a closed oriented $3$-manifold and let $x,y\in\operatorname{Tor}H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. For choices of an integer $n>0$ and an integral $2$-chain $C$ with $\partial C=nx$, the bounding-chain expression is $(C\cdot y)/n\bmod\mathbb Z\in\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, where $C$ and $y$ are placed transversely and intersection signs use the orientation of $Y$. This expression is the torsion linking pairing when its independence of the choices is established.

## Definition

A finite nonsingular linking form is a pair $(A,\lambda)$, where $A$ is a finite abelian group and $\lambda:A\times A\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is symmetric and induces an isomorphism $A\to\operatorname{Hom}(A,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$. For $P\le A$, put $P^\perp=\{a\in A:\lambda(a,p)=0\text{ for every }p\in P\}$. A metabolizer is a subgroup $P$ with $P=P^\perp$; equivalently, $\lambda$ vanishes on $P\times P$ and $|P|^2=|A|$.

## Definition

Let $K_0,K_1$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$, and let $I=[0,1]$. They are locally flat topologically concordant if there is a topological proper embedding $f:S^1\times I\to S^3\times I$ whose image is a locally flat annulus, whose boundary circles are $K_0\times\{0\}$ and $K_1\times\{1\}$, and whose annulus orientation induces the boundary $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_1\times\{1\}$. The annulus must have product collars at both ends. No differentiability of the annulus is assumed.

## Definition

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $p,q\in\mathbb Z$ be coprime and not both zero, and let $E_K(p/q)$ be the Dehn filling whose attached solid-torus meridian is identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. A closed 3-manifold $Y$ is **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$-abelian** if every homomorphism $\pi_1(Y)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ has abelian image. The slope $p/q$ is an **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$-abelian surgery slope** for $K$ if $E_K(p/q)$ is $SL_2(\mathbb C)$-abelian. The knot admits infinitely many such surgeries if infinitely many distinct rational slopes have this property.

## Example

Assume $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=j^\alpha$, and $\sigma_j=j^\beta$ in the Gaussian sequence detection experiment. The minimax separation rate over $\Theta_2(r)$ has order
$$r_\varepsilon^*\asymp\varepsilon^{4\alpha/(4\alpha+4\beta+1)}.$$

## Example references

[Ingster, Sapatinas and Suslina, *Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems*, Theorem 4.2 and equation (4.3), PDF pp. 12–13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.1853)

[Giné and Nickl, *Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models*, §6.2.3](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=j^\alpha$, $\sigma_j=j^\beta$, and a nonempty $\Theta_2(r)$ with the finite extremal profile supplied for sufficiently small $r$. For this rate comparison, $X_\varepsilon\asymp Y_\varepsilon$ means the ratio is bounded above and away from zero by constants independent of $\varepsilon$.

[F1] [[thm-ip-ellipsoid-detection-boundary]]: $r^2=A J_1/J_2$, $u_\varepsilon^2=(r/\varepsilon)^4J_0/(2J_1^2)$, and $u_\varepsilon\to0$ or $\infty$ gives the corresponding indistinguishability or consistency branch.

[F2] [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-exists-for-small-r]] and [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-is-minimizer]]: for sufficiently small $r$, a finite-support extremal profile exists and has $\widetilde\eta_j^2=z_0^2j^{2\beta}(1-Aj^{2\alpha})_+$.
## Verification

1.1 Let $m$ be the largest active index, so $A m^{2\alpha}<1\le A(m+1)^{2\alpha}$ and $(m+1)^{-2\alpha}\le A<m^{-2\alpha}$. For $j\le m/2$, $1-Aj^{2\alpha}\ge1-2^{-2\alpha}>0$. For any fixed $p>0$, $\sum_{j\le m}j^p\le m^{p+1}$ and $\sum_{m/4\le j\le m/2}j^p\ge c_pm^{p+1}$ for all sufficiently large $m$, by counting at least $m/8$ terms each at least $(m/4)^p$. Applying these bounds with $p=4\beta$ and $p=4\beta+2\alpha$ gives $$J_1\asymp m^{4\beta+1},\qquad J_0\asymp m^{4\beta+1},\qquad J_2=A\sum_{j\le m}j^{4\beta+2\alpha}(1-Aj^{2\alpha})\asymp m^{4\beta+1}.$$ Thus [F1] yields $r^2\asymp A\asymp m^{-2\alpha}$ and $u_\varepsilon^2\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^4m^{-(4\beta+1)}$. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Since $m\asymp r^{-1/\alpha}$, the last expression becomes $u_\varepsilon^2\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^{4+(4\beta+1)/\alpha}=(r/\varepsilon^{4\alpha/(4\alpha+4\beta+1)})^{4+(4\beta+1)/\alpha}$. Hence radii with ratio tending to zero give $u_\varepsilon\to0$, and [F1] gives the indistinguishability limits. For a ratio tending to infinity, if $r_\varepsilon$ does not tend to zero, replace it by $\bar r_\varepsilon=\sqrt{r_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon^*}$: nonempty alternatives satisfy $r_\varepsilon\le a_1^{-1}$, so $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$, $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$, and $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_2(\bar r_\varepsilon)$. The consistent tests from [F1] at $\bar r_\varepsilon$ therefore also work at $r_\varepsilon$. This proves the stated separation rate. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

[[thm-fibered-knot-has-rank-one-top-knot-floer-homology|The converse rank-one implication used for the S3 examples]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, Chapter 4](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Heegaard Floer homology and alternating knots*, Theorem 1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209149v3)

[Manolescu, *An Introduction to Knot Floer Homology*, Theorems 2.3 and 2.5](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/hfk.pdf)


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the right-handed trefoil and standard alternating knot $5_2$ with the original integral normalization and classical choice branch declared in the dependencies.

[F1] **External input.** Ozsváth–Szabó, *Heegaard Floer homology and alternating knots*, Geometry & Topology 7 (2003), Theorem 1.3, printed p.230 (PDF p.6 of arXiv:math/0209149v3): if $K$ is alternating and its normalized symmetric Alexander polynomial is $a_0+\sum_{s>0}a_s(t^s+t^{-s})$, then
$$\widehat{HFK}(S^3,K,s;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^{|a_s|},$$
supported in Maslov degree $s+\sigma(K)/2$. This is the INTEGRAL theorem, including freeness; no integral conclusion is inferred from the retained mod-two grid comparison. Its signature convention has left trefoil signature $+2$.

[F2] **External finite table input.** Knot Atlas, pages `3_1` and `5_2`, section “Polynomial invariants / Alexander polynomial”, records respectively $t-1+t^{-1}$ and $2t-3+2t^{-1}$. These two finite entries and their standard knot diagrams identify the table knots. The same polynomials result from the standard genus-one disk/band Seifert matrices
$$V_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V_5=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$$
(up to simultaneous handedness/sign conventions): $\det(V_3-tV_3^T)=1-t+t^2$ and $\det(V_5-tV_5^T)=2-3t+2t^2$. Multiplying by $t^{-1}$ gives the stated symmetric polynomials. The TABLE/diagram identification is external input; the two determinant calculations are finite local checks, not an assertion that an abstract matrix by itself identifies a knot.

[F3] **External input at the exact $S^3$, integral scope.** Manolescu, *An Introduction to Knot Floer Homology*, printed/PDF p.5, Theorem 2.3, gives $g(K)=\max\{s:\widehat{HFK}(K,s;\mathbb Z)\ne0\}$ for every knot in $S^3$. Theorem 2.5 on that same page gives that a knot in $S^3$ is fibered if and only if its integral top genus group is $\mathbb Z$. These exact specializations of the established Ozsváth–Szabó/Ghiggini/Ni/Juhász results are imported. This does not assert completion of the held local general-$Y$ signed comparison or product-criterion proofs. The source explicitly states these as integral groups.

Actual reading limits: the complete Theorem 1.3 statement and its preceding conventions on printed pp.229–230 of the primary alternating paper; the two named Alexander-polynomial table entries (not all table invariants); the full Theorems 2.3 and 2.5 statements and surrounding geometric-applications text on Manolescu p.5. No reading or local reconstruction of the full alternating theorem proof, Ni proof, or entire survey is claimed. These are explicitly authorized external imports under the run-specific source boundary. The original full-choice branch is retained; no integral full-choice theorem is silently cast as a CC theorem.

## Proof

1.1 Both named diagrams are alternating. Apply [F1] with the two polynomials in [F2]. In the trefoil case the coefficients in Alexander degrees $1,0,-1$ have absolute values $1,1,1$, with zero coefficients elsewhere. Thus the maximum nonzero Alexander grading is $1$ and its integral group is $\mathbb Z$. In the $5_2$ case the corresponding absolute values are $2,3,2$, with zero coefficients elsewhere. Its maximum grading is again $1$, with integral top group $\mathbb Z^2$. The formula for the supporting Maslov degree is exactly that of [F1]; no signature sign is guessed from a drawing. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3] the genus is one for both knots. The trefoil's integral top group is $\mathbb Z$, so the fiberedness equivalence in [F3] proves that it is fibered. For $5_2$, $\mathbb Z^2$ is not isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$ (tensoring with $\mathbb Q$ already distinguishes their dimensions), so the same equivalence proves that it is not fibered. These arguments prove every Example clause at its full integral coefficient scope. They do not invoke an unearned generic-$Y$ local supplier or weaken a rank over integers to a mod-two rank. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with rational-homology-sphere boundary $M$. The signed intersection pairing on interior two-cycles descends to a symmetric integer-valued bilinear form on $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$, this group is free of finite rank, and the form is nondegenerate after extending scalars to $\mathbb Q$. The form need not be unimodular.

## Statement references

[[def-intersection-lattice-of-a-four-manifold-with-boundary|Boundary intersection lattice and rational-homology-sphere convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M$ and $H_*(M;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$.

[F1] The long exact sequence of the pair contains $H_2(M;\mathbb Q)\to H_2(W;\mathbb Q)\to H_2(W,M;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(M;\mathbb Q)$. Both end groups vanish by the boundary hypothesis. [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]]

[F2] Poincaré–Lefschetz duality identifies $H_2(W,M;\mathbb Q)$ with $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality]]

[F3] Over the field $\mathbb Q$, the universal-coefficient theorem identifies $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H_2(W;\mathbb Q),\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]

[F4] Double $W$ along a boundary collar; the resulting closed smooth manifold has finite CW homotopy type under full AC. Folding the second copy into the first makes $W$ a homotopy retract of the double, so $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$ is a direct summand of a finitely generated group. [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]] [[lem-a-closed-smooth-manifold-has-the-homotopy-type-of-a-finite-cw-complex]]

[F5] The boundary intersection form is the signed intersection pairing on interior representatives. [[def-intersection-lattice-of-a-four-manifold-with-boundary]]

[A1] Full AC is assumed for the finite-CW homotopy-type supplier [F4].

## Proof

**Given:** The data and suppliers [F1]–[F5].

1.1 The collar of $M$ lets every absolute two-cycle be moved into $\operatorname{int}W$. The signed transverse intersection number is integer-valued and bilinear. Since $H_2(M;\mathbb Q)=0$, [F1] shows that $H_2(W;\mathbb Q)\to H_2(W,M;\mathbb Q)$ is an isomorphism. [given, F1, F5, construct]

1.2 The pairing map over $\mathbb Q$ is the composite $H_2(W;\mathbb Q)\to H_2(W,M;\mathbb Q)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{PD}^{-1}}H^2(W;\mathbb Q)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H_2(W;\mathbb Q),\mathbb Q)$. Every map in this composite is an isomorphism by step 1.1, [F2], and [F3], so the form is rationally nondegenerate. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 By [F4] and [A1], $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$ is finitely generated, so its torsion-free quotient is a finite-rank free abelian group. If $x$ has finite order $m$, bilinearity gives $mQ_W(x,y)=Q_W(mx,y)=0$ in $\mathbb Z$, hence $Q_W(x,y)=0$; the same argument applies in the other variable. Thus the form descends to the torsion-free quotient. The four-dimensional cup-product sign is $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$, so the form is symmetric. [F4, F5, A1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a based map of path-connected CW
complexes, let $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$ and $H=\pi_1(Y,y_0)$, and put
$\phi=f_*:G\to H$. Let $c_X:X\to BG$ and $c_Y:Y\to BH$ be based classifying
maps inducing the identity on the identified fundamental groups. There is a
based map $B\phi:BG\to BH$ inducing $\phi$, and
$$
B\phi\circ c_X\simeq c_Y\circ f
$$
by a based homotopy. Consequently the induced maps on singular homology commute.

## Statement references

[Davis and Kirk, Theorem 7.20 and Corollary 7.24](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Davis_Kirk_Lecture%20notes%20in%20algebraic%20topology.pdf)

[Miller, Lectures 13–14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-906-algebraic-topology-ii-spring-2020/e8a061a73ca1a451df8809c7a7fbc846_MIT18_906S20_notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the based map $f$, the classifying maps $c_X,c_Y$, and the CW models in the statement.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A classifying CW model is connected, has its specified fundamental group, and has zero higher homotopy groups. [[cor-classifying-space-of-a-discrete-group-is-a-k-g-one]]

[F2] Under AC, connected CW models $K(G,1)$ exist for every group and the classifying-space construction is available for the stated groups. [[thm-existence-and-homotopy-uniqueness-of-eilenberg-maclane-spaces]]

[F3] Homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on singular homology. [[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data above and [A1].

1.1 Construct $B\phi$ on the one-skeleton of $BG$ by sending each based loop representing $g\in G$ to a based loop representing $\phi(g)\in H$. Every two-cell attaching loop represents the identity in $G$, so its image represents the identity in $H$ and extends over the two-cell. For a cell of dimension $k\geq3$, the attaching map is a sphere map into $BH$ and extends over the disk because $\pi_{k-1}(BH)=0$ by [F1]. AC chooses the extensions over the set of cells. This gives a based map inducing $\phi$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 The maps $B\phi\circ c_X$ and $c_Y\circ f$ induce the same homomorphism $\phi$ on fundamental groups. On the vertices choose based paths joining their values, and on each one-cell fill the resulting boundary loop; that loop is null because the two induced fundamental-group maps agree. Inductively, the obstruction to extending the homotopy across each $k$-cell is a map $S^k\to BH$, and it is null for $k\geq2$ by [F1]. AC supplies the cell extensions. Hence the maps are based homotopic. [A1, F1, step 1.1, given, construct]

2.1 By [F3], the homotopy of step 1.2 gives $(B\phi)_*\circ(c_X)_*=(c_Y)_*\circ f_*$. This is the asserted naturality, including degree two. [F3, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F$ be a connected compact oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $V$ be its positive-push Seifert matrix in any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Then
$$
H_1(\Sigma_2(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{coker}(V+V^T).
$$
For $g=0$, the matrix is empty and the cokernel is trivial.

## Statement references

[[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot|The definition of the double branched cover $\Sigma_2(K)$]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface|The connected compact oriented spanning surface and genus convention]]

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix convention]]

[[lem-cyclic-branched-cover-seifert-block-matrix|The cyclic-cover homology presentation by $M_q(V)$]]

[Rolfsen, *Knots and Links*, Chapter 8.D](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/rolfsen.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth oriented knot $K$, a connected compact oriented Seifert surface $F$, an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, and its positive-push matrix $V$.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom used by the cyclic-cover construction. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The double branched cover is $\Sigma_2(K)$ from the connected meridian-mod-$2$ exterior cover with its lifted meridian filled. [[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot]]

[F2] For every $q\ge2$, $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{coker}(M_q(V))$, with diagonal blocks $V+V^T$ and adjacent blocks $-V$ and $-V^T$. [[lem-cyclic-branched-cover-seifert-block-matrix]]

## Proof

1.1 The block indices in $M_q(V)$ run from $1$ to $q-1$. At $q=2$ there is only one index, so there are no adjacent blocks and $M_2(V)$ consists of the single diagonal block $V+V^T$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Substitute $q=2$ in [F2]. By [F1], the resulting manifold is the double branched cover $\Sigma_2(K)$; hence its first homology is the cokernel of $V+V^T$. If $g=0$, the block has size zero and the cokernel is the zero group by the empty-matrix convention. The required AC hypothesis is inherited through [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Every nonempty fundamental normal surface in a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold is connected.

## Statement references

[[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]] — a normal surface has a finite normal-coordinate vector and fundamentalness means no nonzero admissible decomposition.

[Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger, Lemma 5.3](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hass/Research/Papers/Complexity/hlp.pdf) — fundamental normal surfaces are connected.

[Erickson, “Normal Surfaces and Knots,” §14.3](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/comptop/2009/notes/normal-surfaces.pdf) — connectedness of fundamental normal surfaces.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty fundamental normal surface $S$ in a finite tetrahedral triangulation.

[F1] [[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]]: $v(S)$ is an admissible integer vector and fundamentalness excludes every decomposition into two nonzero admissible integer vectors.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $S$ is disconnected. Since $S$ is a finite normal surface, its connected components are finite in number; let $S_1$ be one component and let $S_2$ be the union of all remaining components. Both are nonempty properly embedded normal surfaces: each normal disk and each face-matched arc belongs to exactly one component. Disk counts add coordinatewise, so $v(S)=v(S_1)+v(S_2)$, and both summands are admissible nonzero integer vectors. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 The decomposition in step 1.1 contradicts the defining indecomposability of the fundamental vector $v(S)$. Therefore $S$ is connected. [F1, step 1.1, contradiction] ∎

## Statement

Let an orientable finite ideal triangulation have exactly one ideal vertex, whose link is a torus. Suppose its tetrahedra carry positive shapes whose edge products equal $1$ and whose dihedral angles sum to $2\pi$ around every edge. If the cusp multipliers $H(\alpha)$ and $H(\beta)$ are $1$ for a basis $\alpha,\beta$ of the torus fundamental group, then the glued hyperbolic metric is complete at that cusp.

## Statement references

[Jessica S. Purcell, *Hyperbolic Knot Theory*, Proposition 4.15](https://users.monash.edu/~jpurcell/book/HypKnotTheory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite face-glued ideal triangulation, its positive shapes, the edge equations, and a basis of loops on the torus vertex link.

[F1] [[def-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-and-cusp-holonomy]] defines the upper half-space metric, the shape at each corner of a truncated ideal vertex, and the product $H(\gamma)$ recording the linear scale and rotation accumulated around a cusp path.

[F2] [[lem-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-parameter-relations]] identifies the argument of each positive shape with its dihedral angle.

## Proof

1.1 The positive shapes determine nondegenerate ideal tetrahedra. The face maps are hyperbolic isometries. Around each finite edge, the edge product $1$ makes the accumulated complex similarity the identity, and the $2\pi$ angle sum removes a cone angle. Thus the tetrahedra glue to a smooth hyperbolic metric away from the ideal vertex. Horospherical truncations give Euclidean triangles on the torus link; their face identifications are Euclidean similarities, maps of the form $x\mapsto aRx+b$ with $a>0$, $R$ a rotation, and have no cone singularities. They define a Euclidean similarity structure: an atlas with these transition maps. Its linear holonomy, the product $aR$ accumulated around a loop, need not yet be trivial. [given, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 For a loop $\gamma$ on the link, the linear part of its similarity holonomy is $H(\gamma)$: transporting a tangent vector across each corner multiplies it by the corner parameter or its reciprocal according to the side used. The basis loops have multiplier $1$, so the linear holonomy is trivial on $\pi_1(T)$, since every loop is a word in that basis. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Trivial linear holonomy lets a Euclidean metric in one similarity chart be transported consistently to every chart: two transport paths differ by a loop, whose linear holonomy is the identity by step 1.2. The local Euclidean metrics therefore agree on overlaps and give a global flat metric on the compact torus link. A compact Riemannian manifold is complete. [given, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Lift the flat metric of step 2.1 to the simply connected universal cover and integrate its Euclidean charts along paths to obtain a local isometry into $\mathbb R^2$; simple connectivity makes this construction path-independent up to one rigid motion. Completeness lets the local isometry extend along every straight segment, so it is a covering onto $\mathbb R^2$ and hence an isometry. Its deck group acts by Euclidean isometries. Every deck transformation has identity linear part by step 1.2, so acts by translation; compactness of the quotient makes this group a rank-two lattice. The cusp is the corresponding horoball quotient. [given, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 In horospherical coordinates the quotient end has metric $ds^2=dr^2+e^{-2r}g_T$ for $r\ge0$, where $g_T$ is the complete flat torus metric from step 2.1. A path escaping toward the ideal vertex has $r\to\infty$ and length at least the change in $r$, hence infinite length. Thus the glued metric is complete at its only end, the torus cusp. [given, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Sources

[Jessica S. Purcell, *Hyperbolic Knot Theory*, Proposition 4.15](https://users.monash.edu/~jpurcell/book/HypKnotTheory.pdf)

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be second-countable oriented hyperbolic three-manifolds, and let $f:M\to N$ be an isometry. Then
$$
\int_M d\operatorname{vol}_M=\int_N d\operatorname{vol}_N.
$$
In particular, if either volume is finite, then both are finite and the values agree.

## Statement references

[John M. Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*, Proposition 16.6(d)](https://julianchaidez.net/materials/reu/lee_smooth_manifolds.pdf)

[John M. Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*, Propositions 15.29–15.33 and Corollary 15.34](https://dokumen.pub/introduction-to-smooth-manifolds-2nd-ed-9781441999818-9781441999825-1441999817-1441999825.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, second-countable oriented hyperbolic three-manifolds $M,N$, and an isometry $f:M\to N$.

[A1] Countable choice, written AC$_\omega$, is [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] [[def-riemannian-volume-density]] defines the density in coordinates as $\sqrt{\det G}\,|dx^1dx^2dx^3|$.

[F2] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]] states that for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ between open subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ and every nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $h$ on $V$, $\int_V h=\int_U(h\circ T)|\det DT|$ under AC$_\omega$.

[F3] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] identifies the integral over a countable increasing union with the limit of the integrals over its finite partial unions.

[F4] [[def-pared-hyperbolic-structures-and-volume]] defines volume as the nonnegative integral of the Riemannian volume density.

## Proof

1.1 Since $f$ is an isometry, $f^*g_N=g_M$. In any coordinate charts, if $J=Df$ is the coordinate derivative, then the metric matrices satisfy $G_M=J^{\mathsf T}(G_N\circ f)J$. Taking determinants gives $\sqrt{\det G_M}=|\det J|\sqrt{\det(G_N\circ f)}$. Thus $f$ pulls the Riemannian volume density of $N$ back to that of $M$, regardless of whether it preserves orientation. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Consider the set of ALL coordinate-neighborhood pairs $(U,V)$ with $f(U)\subset V$. It covers $M$. Fix a countable basis of $M$; for each basis member contained in some such $U$, use [A1] to select one containing pair. Their selected $U$ neighborhoods form a countable cover $(U_j)_{j\ge1}$, with corresponding $V_j$. Thus no point-indexed choice of charts is required. Make it disjoint by setting $A_1=U_1$ and $A_j=U_j\setminus\bigcup_{i<j}U_i$; these are Borel, disjoint and cover $M$. In coordinates on $U_j,V_j$, apply [F2] to the nonnegative measurable function equal to the target density times the indicator of $f(A_j)$. The Jacobian identity in step 1.1 yields $\operatorname{Vol}_M(A_j)=\operatorname{Vol}_N(f(A_j))$. The sets $f(A_j)$ are disjoint and cover $N$. [given, A1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The indicators of the finite unions $\bigcup_{j\le n}A_j$ increase to $1_M$. By [F3] and [F4], the volume of $M$ is the limit of the sums $\sum_{j\le n}\operatorname{Vol}_M(A_j)$, and the same holds for $N$ and the sets $f(A_j)$. These finite sums agree term by term by step 2.1; their limits therefore agree in $[0,\infty]$. If one volume is finite, their common value is finite. [F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[John M. Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*, Proposition 16.6(d)](https://julianchaidez.net/materials/reu/lee_smooth_manifolds.pdf)

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $S$ be a connected compact smooth oriented surface properly embedded in $S^3\times[0,1]$, with product collars and oriented boundary $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_1\times\{1\}$ for smooth oriented knots $K_0,K_1$. Let $g$ be the genus of $S$, and use the standard absolute Alexander normalization for the endpoint knot Floer complexes. Then
$$|\tau(K_1)-\tau(K_0)|\le g.$$
In particular, a smooth concordance annulus gives equal tau values, and a genus-$g$ surface from a knot to the unknot gives the four-ball genus estimate.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau|The normalized tau value from the filtered complex]]

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth cobordisms with oriented boundary and product collars]]

[[def-knot-floer-cobordism-map|The representative map for a decorated knot cobordism]]

[[lem-knot-floer-holomorphic-triangle-transversality-compactness-gluing|The required triangle moduli spaces]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Knot Floer homology and the four-ball genus*, Theorem 1.1 and §§3.3–3.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0301149v4)

[Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, §§3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383v3)

[Zemke, *Link cobordisms and absolute gradings on link Floer homology*, Theorem 10.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.03454v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, the collared smooth oriented cobordism $S$, its endpoint knots, and the fixed Alexander normalization.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] states that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function; the normalized analytic knot models use the declared countable-choice branch.

[F1] [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] supplies the normalized full filtered comparison between the local knot model and the standard knot Floer invariant used in the cited genus theorem.

[F2] **External input, authorized by the run-specific source boundary.** Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, §3.1, Theorem 3.1(2), printed p.8, states $|\tau(K)|\le g_4(K)$ for every smooth knot $K\subset S^3$. Hom states on printed p.2 that the paper works throughout with $\mathbb F_2$ coefficients. In §3.1 the threshold is the least Alexander level at which the filtered inclusion surjects onto $\widehat{HF}(S^3)\cong\mathbb F_2$; this agrees with the nonzero-image convention here because the target is one-dimensional. For any actual smooth genus-$h$ spanning surface, $g_4(K)\le h$, so the imported theorem gives $|\tau(K)|\le h$. This is a direct $\mathbb F_2$ genus input; it does not infer a mod-two nonvanishing map from an integral map.

[F3] [[lem-tau-connected-sum-filtered-tensor-product]] supplies connected-sum additivity, and [[lem-knot-floer-duality-and-filtration-swap]] identifies the normalized reverse-mirror complex with the bifiltered dual. Step 1.3 gives the finite filtered threshold calculation needed for $\tau(-K)=-\tau(K)$.

[F4] [[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau]] fixes the standard unknot generator at filtration zero, so its diagramwise threshold is $\tau(U)=0$.

[F5] [[lem-puncturing-smooth-four-ball-surfaces-gives-genus-preserving-knot-cobordisms]] supplies the product-collar puncturing of an actual spanning surface when the four-ball corollary is phrased as a knot cobordism.

**Coefficient boundary for retained source context.** Ozsváth–Szabó, *Knot Floer homology and the four-ball genus*, Proposition 3.1 and Lemma 3.5 are stated in that paper's integral setup (in particular, it identifies $\widehat{HF}(S^3)$ with $\mathbb Z$). Their nonvanishing and disk-bundle statements are not used here as $\mathbb F_2$ statements. Hom's direct genus theorem [F2] is the only external genus input used in the proof. The relevant passages checked were Hom's coefficient convention and Theorem 3.1(2), and the compatible threshold definition in §3.1; no whole-paper reading or reconstruction of Hom's cited proof is claimed.

## Proof

1.1 Let $C$ be the normalized finite filtered hat complex for a knot and put $t=\tau(C)$. Choose a cycle $x\in F_tC_n$ representing the generator of $H(C)\cong\mathbb F_2$ in degree $n$. By minimality of $t$, every cycle in $F_{t-1}C_n$ is a boundary. Hence $x\notin B_n+F_{t-1}C_n$, where $B_n=\operatorname{im}(\partial_{n+1})$; otherwise $x-b$ would be a cycle in $F_{t-1}C_n$ representing the same nonzero class. Extend a linear functional $\lambda:C_n\to\mathbb F_2$ that vanishes on $B_n+F_{t-1}C_n$ and satisfies $\lambda(x)=1$. It is a cocycle and represents the nonzero class in the dual homology, since it evaluates nontrivially on the cycle $x$. By [F3], the reflected knot's normalized Laurent complex is the R-dual with both coordinates negated. In the normalized $i=0$ hat slice, the $U^0$ terms are exactly the hat differential, while positive $U$ powers leave that slice in both original and dual complexes; transposing therefore gives the finite hat dual. Negating the Alexander coordinate gives its annihilator filtration $F_sC^\vee=\{\mu:\mu(F_{-s-1}C)=0\}$. Thus $\lambda\in F_{-t}C^\vee$, so $\tau(C^\vee)\le -t$. If $s<-t$, then $-s-1\ge t$ and every functional in $F_sC^\vee$ annihilates $F_tC$, hence pairs trivially with $[x]$. The evaluation pairing identifies $H(C^\vee)$ with $H(C)^\vee$ and is nondegenerate; therefore no such lower filtration level maps nontrivially to total dual homology. This gives $\tau(C^\vee)\ge -t$, and hence $\tau(-K)=-\tau(K)$ in the normalized knot setting. [F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose a smooth embedded arc on $S$ joining its two boundary components. Cut $S$ along a thin strip about that arc, and remove from $S^3\times I$ the interior of a compatible tubular neighborhood of the arc. A properly embedded arc joining the two boundary spheres in this simply connected four-dimensional product is isotopic to a product arc relative its ends: a generic homotopy of such arcs is a path of embeddings, since the coincidence condition for two distinct arc points at the same time has dimension $1+1+1-4<0$, and the derivative-zero condition is also avoidable. These are finitely many compact smooth general-position choices. Removing the product arc neighborhood turns the ambient shell into $B^4$, after rounding its product corners. The cut surface has one boundary component $K_1\#(-K_0)$ and Euler characteristic $\chi(S)+1=1-2g$, hence genus $g$. Its product collars supply the ordinary connected-sum boundary convention. Thus it is an actual smooth genus-$g$ spanning surface for $K_1\#(-K_0)$. [given, construct]

1.3 By [F2] and the surface from step 1.2,
$$|\tau(K_1\#(-K_0))|\le g_4(K_1\#(-K_0))\le g.$$
Using connected-sum additivity from [F3] and the threshold sign established in step 1.1 gives $\tau(K_1\#(-K_0))=\tau(K_1)-\tau(K_0)$. This proves the stated inequality. If $g=0$, it gives concordance invariance. If one boundary knot is the standard unknot, [F4] gives the four-ball genus estimate; equivalently, puncture an actual spanning surface and use [F5] to obtain that cobordism case. The only external genus assertion used is Hom's direct $\mathbb F_2$ theorem [F2]; no coefficient transfer from the integral surgery-trace maps is made. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If a smooth oriented knot $K$ is nontrivial and prime, then its mirror image under the fixed reflection from the connected-sum convention, with the image orientation, is also nontrivial and prime.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|Definitions of nontrivial and prime knots]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$, a nontrivial prime oriented knot $K$, and a fixed orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$.

[F1] A prime knot is nontrivial and has no connected-sum presentation with both summands nontrivial. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]])

[F2] The connected-sum operation is well-defined, and its fixed gluing map commutes with the reflection in the standard model. ([[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]], [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]])

[A1] AC$_\omega$ is the countable-choice hypothesis for the connected-sum choice-independence result. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** AC$_\omega$, $K$, and $r$.

1.1 If $r(K)$ were ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, conjugating that isotopy by $r$ would give an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy from $K$ to $r^{-1}(U)$. The reflection image $r^{-1}(U)$ is a round circle and hence a standard unknot; if its orientation is reversed, a half-turn in its plane is an orientation-preserving isotopy to the chosen orientation. Thus $K$ would be trivial, contrary to [F1], and $r(K)$ is nontrivial. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Suppose $r(K)=J\#L$ with both $J,L$ nontrivial. Reflect the connected-sum model. By [F2], its image is the connected sum of the reflected summands, $K=r^{-1}(J)\#r^{-1}(L)$ up to oriented ambient isotopy. Reflection preserves nontriviality by the argument in step 1.1, contradicting primeness of $K$. Hence $r(K)$ is prime. [given, F1, F2, A1, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Sources

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

[[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]

[[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]]

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $q=p^k$ for a prime $p$ and $k\ge1$. Then $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$ is finite, so $\Sigma_q(K)$ is a rational homology sphere and carries a nonsingular torsion linking form.

## Statement references

[[lem-cyclic-cover-order-root-product-and-rational-sphere-test|The cyclic-cover root-product criterion]]

[[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection|The Seifert skew part is the unimodular surface intersection form]]

[[thm-cyclotomic-polynomials-are-irreducible-over-the-rationals|Irreducibility of cyclotomic polynomials]]

[[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-homology-over-a-pid|The homology universal coefficient theorem]]

[[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds|Poincaré duality]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth oriented knot $K$, and $q=p^k$ with $p$ prime and $k\ge1$.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For any connected Seifert surface with positive-push matrix $V$, the group $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$ is finite exactly when $D(\zeta_q^j)\ne0$ for all $1\le j<q$, where $D(t)=\det(V-tV^T)$. [[lem-cyclic-cover-order-root-product-and-rational-sphere-test]]

[F2] $D(1)=\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$, since $V-V^T$ is the integral intersection matrix of the Seifert surface. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F3] For each $s\ge1$, the minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ of a primitive $p^s$-th root is the monic cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_{p^s}(t)$, which has integer coefficients and $\Phi_{p^s}(1)=p$. [[thm-cyclotomic-polynomials-are-irreducible-over-the-rationals]]

[F4] If $Y$ is closed, connected, oriented and has finite first homology, its bounding-chain torsion linking pairing is nonsingular. [[lem-linking-pairing-on-rational-homology-sphere-is-nonsingular]]

[F5] For a closed oriented $3$-manifold with finite first homology, the homology universal coefficient theorem and Poincaré duality give rational homology of $S^3$. [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-homology-over-a-pid]] [[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]]

## Proof

1.1 Suppose a nontrivial $q$-th root of unity $\omega$ were a zero of $D$. Its order is $p^s$ for some $1\le s\le k$. By [F3], the minimal polynomial $\Phi_{p^s}$ divides $D$ in $\mathbb Q[t]$. Since $\Phi_{p^s}$ is monic and both polynomials have integer coefficients, polynomial long division gives an integer-coefficient quotient with zero remainder. Thus $p=\Phi_{p^s}(1)$ divides $D(1)$. [F3, given, algebra, A1]

2.1 This contradicts $D(1)=\pm1$ from [F2]. Therefore $D$ has no zero at any nontrivial $q$-th root of unity. The criterion [F1] gives finiteness of $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F5], the finite first homology from step 2.1 makes $\Sigma_q(K)$ a rational homology sphere. Its torsion linking form is nonsingular by [F4], which proves the final assertion. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let P⊂S¹×D² be a smooth oriented pattern. If oriented knots K₀ and K₁ are concordant in one of the four categories C_sm, C_top, C_ex or C^{1/n}, then P(K₀) and P(K₁) are concordant in the same category. Thus P induces a well-defined set map on each of these concordance sets.

## Statement references

[CDR, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.5058v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A pattern P and a concordance annulus A from K₀ to K₁ in one of the stated ambient categories.

[F1] Satellite insertion uses a zero-framed tubular copy of S¹×D² around each endpoint knot ([[def-satellite-induced-concordance-operator]]).

[F2] Each category specifies the ambient 4-manifold and regularity of its concordance annulus ([[def-cdr-satellite-concordance-categories]]).

[F3] **External TOP input (not reconstructed here).** A locally flat proper surface in a topological four-manifold has an actual rank-two normal VECTOR-bundle neighborhood; where such a neighborhood is prescribed near a closed subset, including the boundary collars, it can be chosen to agree with that germ on a smaller neighborhood. This is Freedman–Quinn Theorem9.3A, printed137–141, used under the run-specific external-source boundary. It supplies the actual tube, not automatic agreement of arbitrary global framings. The cited statement and proof pages137–141 were read; no full-book reading or local reconstruction is claimed.

[F4] Every ambient concordance manifold here is oriented and is an $R$-homology $S^3\times I$, with $R=\mathbb Z$ in the standard, TOP and exotic cases and $R=R_n$ in the localized case. This follows from the defining ambient conditions. [[def-cdr-satellite-concordance-categories]]

[F5] **Compact finite-input convention.** The classical external results are initially used in ordinary ZFC, not assumed choice-free from their citations. For this one application take finitely many charts covering the given compact manifolds and finitely many pair charts covering each given compact disk or annulus, shrinking to closed inner charts inside open outer charts. Such finite subcovers exist by compactness; selecting this finite list uses no axiom of choice. Include the actual boundary/product collars and all supplied homeomorphisms in the list. Encode chart domains and overlaps by their rational balls, continuous maps and their inverses by dense rational data with moduli on the closed inner charts, and smooth maps by all finite-order derivative and Taylor-remainder data. The modulus at each integer scale is the least integer satisfying its uniform-continuity bound; restrictions to rational compact boxes use the least box index. These are uniquely defined choices from subsets of $\mathbb N$, not a countable family of freely selected charts. Include positive open-image and overlap margins, inverse identities, finite cover/Lebesgue bounds, and the pair-section identities with positive separation from the compact outside-patch remainder. On the standard disk/annulus parameters the latter certify the actual plane section, not merely a continuous embedding. One real $r$ codes these finitely many maps and their canonical countable data. The external relative-constructibility input is that $L[r]$ is an inner model of ZFC containing $r$ (Karagila, §8.3, p.42); no ambient choice hypothesis is required. All compact maps are decoded using these same moduli, so the inverse identities, covers, pair sections and collar equalities are checked on dense rational sets with their displayed buffers and remain valid in the ambient universe $V$. An internally produced compact witness is exported with the same certificates, and hence is an actual ambient compact witness. This uses the peer-checked compact annulus coding pattern of the standard connected-sum compatibility supplier only at its geometric scope; it does not assert that arbitrary homology or fundamental-group hypotheses are absolute.

## Proof

0.1 For the TOP annulus the ambient manifold is the standard compact product, and the given annulus and end collars have exactly the finite pair-code description in [F5]. Apply the external normal theorem [F3] inside $L[r]$ with those collars. Restrict the resulting tube to a compact disk bundle, still with a slightly wider domain, and export its forward/inverse, pair and collar certificates as in [F5]. This gives an actual relative tube in $V$ without ambient AC. For the smooth annuli in the other three categories, a finite chart partition of unity gives a metric and connection along the compact annulus; parallel transport and the compact inverse-function construction give the smooth tube. Only finitely many chart choices and least integer radii are needed. Thus the external TOP input used below is earned at this particular finite input; no global choice-free version of FQ is being asserted. [F2, F3, F5, given, construct]


1.1 In the smooth product category, choose a tubular neighborhood of the smooth annulus A. Its oriented normal 2-plane bundle over A has relative Euler obstruction in H²(A,∂A;Z)≅Z. The boundary trivializations are the zero framings of K₀ and K₁; the relative obstruction is the difference of their self-linking numbers, hence zero. A relative framing therefore identifies a neighborhood of A with A×D² and agrees with the two prescribed endpoint zero-framed neighborhoods. [F1, F2, given]

1.2 In that framed neighborhood insert $P$ in every disk fiber. Orient the inserted annulus by the interval direction followed by the pattern orientation. Its oriented boundary is then $-P(K_0)$ at the lower end and $P(K_1)$ at the upper end. The product collars of $A$ and the endpoint framings give product collars matching the ambient end collars, and the two endpoint patterns use the preferred zero framings. This proves concordance preservation for smooth annuli in a standard product. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 In the exotic and localized cases the annulus is smooth, so the same smooth tubular construction is available in its given smooth ambient manifold. In the TOP case use the external input [F3] relative to the two actual smooth endpoint collars. In every case this gives an oriented rank-two vector normal bundle over $A$. Its obstruction to a framing extending the two preferred zero framings is its relative Euler number in $H^2(A,\partial A;\mathbb Z)$. Cap $A$ by boundary Seifert chains with opposite boundary orientations and push the caps into the product collars. Their union is a closed two-cycle. Its intersection with a relative small parallel copy of $A$ is the relative Euler number, because the two cap terms are precisely the endpoint zero-linking numbers. The cycle is zero over $R$ by [F4], so that Euler number is zero in $R$. The inclusion $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow R$ is injective, hence it is zero integrally. Classification of oriented plane bundles with boundary framing now gives a framing of the actual normal bundle agreeing with both preferred endpoint framings. This proves the required relative framing, rather than inferring it from absolute triviality. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 0.1, given, algebra]

2.2 Insert the product annulus $P\times I$ into this framed neighborhood, as in step1.2. Its endpoint knots are the untwisted satellites because both endpoint framings are the preferred zero framings. In the TOP case the product model makes the new annulus locally flat; in the three smooth categories it is smooth. The ambient manifold is the original $W$, so its homeomorphism or $R$-homology conditions do not change. Thus the satellite assignment preserves concordance in all four categories and descends to the stated set maps. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $E\to X$ be an oriented real vector bundle over a path-connected paracompact Hausdorff compactly generated weak Hausdorff space of CW homotopy type, and suppose one numerable Spin$^c$ lift of its oriented frame bundle is given. Among numerable Spin$^c$ lifts of that same frame bundle, isomorphism classes form a torsor for $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$: tensoring a lift by a complex line bundle defines a free and transitive action, identified with $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ by the first Chern class. For a continuous map $f:X\to Z$ between bases with these hypotheses and an oriented bundle $E_Z\to Z$, the pullback action on lifts of $f^*E_Z\to X$ is equivariant for $f^*:H^2(Z;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$.

## Statement references

[[def-given-spin-and-spinc-structures-and-associated-spinor-bundles|Spin-c lifts of the oriented frame bundle]]

[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle|Principal bundles and associated bundles]]

[[prop-associated-bundle-is-locally-trivial-and-functorial-under-pullback|Local triviality and pullback naturality of associated bundles]]

[[thm-first-chern-class-classifies-complex-line-bundles|Classification of complex line bundles by the first Chern class]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A path-connected paracompact Hausdorff base $X$ of CW homotopy type, an oriented real vector bundle $E\to X$, and one fixed Spin$^c$ lift $P_0$ of its oriented frame bundle.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed by the first-Chern-class classification used to identify line-bundle classes with $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] A Spin$^c$ structure is a principal $\mathrm{Spin}^c(n)$-bundle lifting the oriented frame bundle through $\mathrm{Spin}^c(n)\to\mathrm{SO}(n)$; the kernel is the central $U(1)$ ([[def-given-spin-and-spinc-structures-and-associated-spinor-bundles]]).

[F2] A principal $U(1)$-bundle has the associated complex line bundle for the standard scalar representation; its unit circle subbundle is canonically the original principal bundle, and associated bundles are locally trivial and natural under pullback ([[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]], [[prop-associated-bundle-is-locally-trivial-and-functorial-under-pullback]]).

[F3] For a path-connected CW-type paracompact Hausdorff compactly generated weak Hausdorff base, the first Chern class gives a natural group isomorphism from isomorphism classes of complex line bundles under tensor product to $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$, under AC ([[thm-first-chern-class-classifies-complex-line-bundles]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** construct the difference line bundle between two lifts and use its first Chern class.

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 For any second lift $P_1$, define $L(P_0,P_1)_x$ to be the set of Spin$^c$-equivariant maps from $(P_0)_x$ to $(P_1)_x$ covering the identity map of the common oriented frame fiber. Since both are lifts of that same frame fiber, two such maps differ by a unique element of the central kernel $U(1)$ from [F1]. In local lift trivializations, the transition functions of $P_0$ and $P_1$ project to the same $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ functions, so their pointwise quotient lies in central $U(1)$; the cocycle identity for each lift makes these quotients a $U(1)$-valued cocycle. Thus the difference fibers form a principal $U(1)$-bundle $L(P_0,P_1)$ over $X$. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Associate to the principal difference bundle in step 1.1 the standard complex line. By [F2], its unit circle bundle is that principal bundle. The diagonal central action defines the twist $P_0\otimes L=(P_0\times_X L)/U(1)$; evaluation of each difference map gives a Spin$^c$-equivariant isomorphism $P_0\otimes L(P_0,P_1)\cong P_1$. If $P_0\otimes L\cong P_0$, its difference bundle is trivial, so the action is free; the construction for arbitrary $P_1$ proves transitivity. Tensor product of line bundles gives the group law and pullback commutes with the fiberwise construction. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 By [F3], the isomorphism class of the associated line $L$ is uniquely identified with $c_1(L)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$, compatibly with tensor product and pullback. Thus the free transitive line-bundle action is precisely a free transitive $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$ action and is natural under $f^*$. If $X$ is a point, $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)=0$ and the given lift is the only class in its torsor; no existence of an initial lift is asserted. AC is used only through [A1] and [F3]. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $C=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ be the finite-rank free $\Lambda=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ knot Floer complex of a smooth oriented knot, with its Maslov grading, algebraic filtration $i$, Alexander filtration $j$, and weighted filtration $F_t=(1-t/2)i+(t/2)j$ for a fixed $t\in[0,2]$. Assume its total homology is $\Lambda$ generated in Maslov grading zero. Then the filtered graded complex $(C,F_t)$ admits a filtered direct-sum decomposition $C=T\oplus A$, where $T=\Lambda\alpha$, $\partial\alpha=0$, $\alpha$ represents the normalized homology generator at filtration $\nu_t(C)$, and $A$ is acyclic as a graded complex. In the t-modified complex, the non-torsion tower from $T$ has maximal grading $-2\nu_t(C)$; hence this maximum equals the cycle-minimax definition of $\Upsilon_K(t)$.

## Statement references

[[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex|The finite cycle-minimax and t-grading conventions]]

[Livingston, *Notes on the knot concordance invariant Upsilon*, Appendix A and §15](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Upsilon-revised.pdf)

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology*, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite-rank free $\Lambda$ complex with a homogeneous bifiltered basis as in the Statement, differential of Maslov degree $-1$, and total homology $\Lambda$ generated in Maslov degree zero.

[F1] [[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex]] defines $\nu_t$ using the maximum weighted filtration of a finite cycle representing the normalized Maslov-zero class. Its Maslov-zero chain group, hence its candidate set over $\mathbb F_2$, is finite.

[F2] [[lem-upsilon-real-series-valuation-domain]] proves the coefficient domain $\mathcal R$ and its field of fractions $\mathcal K$, including the least-exponent criterion and that a common monomial clears the lower exponents of finitely many elements of $\mathcal K$.

[F3] [[lem-upsilon-finite-series-complex-homogeneous-splitting]] proves finite homogeneous homology decomposition over $\mathcal R$, so non-torsion homology generators and their maximal grading are justified without a Noetherian assumption.

## Proof

1.1 Put $\nu=\nu_t(C)$ and choose a Maslov-zero representing cycle $\alpha$ with $F_t(\alpha)=\nu$, using [F1]. Let $C_0,C_1$ be the finite-dimensional chain groups in Maslov degrees zero and one. Set $B_0=\partial C_1$ and $L=\{z\in C_0:F_t(z)<\nu\}$, including zero. The maximum-filtration rule makes $L$ a subspace. One has $\alpha\notin B_0+L$: otherwise $\alpha=b+\ell$ would make $\ell$ a cycle representing the same nonzero class at a smaller filtration. Finite-dimensional linear algebra therefore gives a functional $\lambda:C_0\to\mathbb F_2$ with $\lambda(\alpha)=1$ and $\lambda(B_0+L)=0$. Translate each homogeneous Laurent basis vector by the unique power of $U$ putting its Maslov degree in $\{0,1\}$. Define a $\Lambda$-linear map $P:C\to\Lambda\alpha$ by $P(x)=\lambda(x)\alpha$ on these degree-zero basis vectors and $P(y)=0$ on the degree-one ones. Boundaries from degree one are annihilated by $\lambda$, and the differential of a degree-zero vector lies in $UC_1$, on which $P$ is zero. Thus $P$ is a chain map and $P(\alpha)=\alpha$. If $P(x)\ne0$, then $F_t(x)\ge\nu$ because $\lambda(L)=0$; the $U$-translation rule gives the same inequality for every translate. Hence $P$ preserves filtration. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Write $\alpha$ in the degree-zero basis and choose a term of largest filtration, which has filtration $\nu$. Replacing that basis vector by $\alpha$ is invertible and preserves filtration in both directions, since all other terms in $\alpha$ have filtration at most $\nu$. For every remaining degree-zero basis vector $x$, replace it by $x+\lambda(x)\alpha$. When the extra term is present, $F_t(x)\ge\nu$, so this and its inverse preserve filtration. The degree-one basis is unchanged. The resulting basis consists of $\alpha$ and a basis of $\ker P$. Since $P$ is a chain map, this is a filtered graded direct-sum decomposition $C=T\oplus A$, with $T=\Lambda\alpha$ and $A=\ker P$. Its total homology on $T$ already maps isomorphically to $H(C)=\Lambda$, so $H(A)=0$. This proves the first assertion by an explicit filtered projection, without assuming that an arbitrary unfiltered acyclic complex is filtered contractible. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Return to the original basis $x_r$ at algebraic level zero, and put $m_r=M(x_r)$ and $a_r=A(x_r)$. Its differential has coefficients $c_{rs}U^{(m_s-m_r+1)/2}$ with $c_{rs}\in\mathbb F_2$. Extend scalars to $\mathcal K$ by $U=v^2$, and write $e_r=v^{m_r}x_r$. The differential is then $\partial e_r=v\sum_s c_{rs}e_s$. Let $W$ be the finite $\mathbb F_2$-space on these formal $e_r$, with differential $d_0e_r=\sum_sc_{rs}e_s$. It squares to zero, since the two-step coefficient in the original differential has the same $U$ exponent for every intermediate index. Separate $W$ by the parity of $m_r$. The even space identifies with $C_0$ by $e_r\mapsto U^{m_r/2}x_r$, and the odd space with $C_1$ by $e_r\mapsto U^{(m_r-1)/2}x_r$. The two matrices of $d_0$ are respectively those of $\partial:C_1\to C_0$ and $U^{-1}\partial:C_0\to C_1$. Consequently $H(W)_{\mathrm{even}}=\mathbb F_2$ and $H(W)_{\mathrm{odd}}=0$, by the given total graded homology. Finite vector-space splittings extend to $\mathcal K$; since $v$ is invertible, $\partial=v d_0$ has one-dimensional homology over $\mathcal K$, detected by the same even homology functional. [F2, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 Let $C_t$ be the exact $t$-modified polynomial-basis complex in the definition, and put $g_r=m_r-ta_r$. The $\mathcal K$-linear map $\Phi(x_r)=v^{ta_r}x_r$ from its scalar extension to the scalar extension of $C$ is a grading-preserving chain isomorphism. Indeed, a differential term on the source has coefficient $v^{m_s-m_r+1-t(a_s-a_r)}$, and multiplying its target by $v^{ta_s}$ gives exactly $v^{ta_r}v^{m_s-m_r+1}$, the differential of the image. The weighted filtration on the latter scalar extension is defined by $F_t(v^\beta x_r)=ta_r/2-\beta/2$, extended to a series by its least nonzero exponent and to a finite basis expansion by the maximum. Thus the image of $C_t$ is exactly the lattice $F_t\le0$: its $r$th coefficient has least exponent at least $ta_r$. This is the explicit coordinate change, and it uses $U=v^2$. [F1, F2, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 A cycle in $C_t$ is non-torsion in homology exactly when its class remains nonzero over $\mathcal K$. One direction follows by inverting a nonzero annihilating coefficient. Conversely, if the cycle becomes a boundary over $\mathcal K$, the bounding chain has finitely many coefficients; a single monomial $v^c$ with $c\ge0$ shifts all their least exponents into $[0,\infty)$ by [F2]. Multiplying the bounding equation by $v^c$ gives an annihilator of the original class over $\mathcal R$. Now a homogeneous cycle of degree $g$ in $C_t$ has the form $z=\sum_r\epsilon_rv^{g_r-g}x_r$, with $\epsilon_r\in\mathbb F_2$, all occurring exponents nonnegative. Its image is $v^{-g}\sum_r\epsilon_re_r$, so the vector $\zeta=\sum_r\epsilon_re_r$ is a $d_0$-cycle. If $z$ is non-torsion, step 3.1 shows that the even part of $\zeta$ represents the nonzero even homology class. Hence $z_0=\sum_{m_r\text{ even}}\epsilon_rU^{m_r/2}x_r$ is an original Maslov-zero cycle representing the normalized generator. For every term in $z_0$, the nonnegative-exponent condition gives $g\le m_r-ta_r$, and therefore $F_t(z_0)\le-g/2$. It follows that every homogeneous non-torsion degree satisfies $g\le-2\nu$. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 4.1, given, algebra]

6.1 Conversely write a minimizing original Maslov-zero cycle as $\alpha=\sum_{m_r\text{ even}}\epsilon_rU^{m_r/2}x_r$ and put $g=-2\nu$. Each exponent $m_r-ta_r-g$ in its support is nonnegative by the definition of $F_t(\alpha)=\nu$. Thus $z_t=\sum_r\epsilon_rv^{m_r-ta_r-g}x_r$ is a homogeneous cycle in $C_t$, since its image under step 4.1 is $v^{-g}\alpha$ and $\Phi$ is injective. Its scalar-extended homology class is nonzero by step 3.1, so it is non-torsion by step 5.1. Its degree is $g=-2\nu$, attaining the upper bound. Finally the filtered projection and direct sum in steps 1.1–2.1 extend over $\mathcal K$ and restrict to the lattice $F_t\le0$. On $T$ this lattice is $\mathcal R v^{2\nu}\alpha$, with zero differential and generator degree $-2\nu$; the complementary lattice has only torsion homology, since its scalar extension is acyclic. By step 4.1 this is precisely the non-torsion tower in the $t$-modified complex. This proves the complete tower/minimax identification, including irrational $t$ and both endpoints. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[Livingston, Appendix A and Section15](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Upsilon-revised.pdf)

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz and Szabo, Definition4.1 and Lemma4.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795)

## Remarks

This is an algebraic theorem for a supplied normalized graded bifiltered complex. It proves no existence or invariance of analytic knot Floer complexes, no connected-sum identification, and no smooth cobordism genus estimate.

## Statement

Assume full AC. For every smooth oriented knot $K$, $b(K)=1$ if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the fixed oriented coordinate circle, and the classical signature satisfies $|\sigma_{-1}(K)|\le 2u(K)$, where $u(K)$ is the minimum number of crossing changes needed to reach that circle.

## Statement references

[[thm-bridge-one-is-unknot|The bridge-number-one characterization]]

[[thm-unknotting-number-at-least-half-levine-tristram-signature|The signature lower bound for unknotting number]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a smooth oriented knot $K$.

[A1] Full AC implies the countable-choice hypothesis of the bridge-number-one theorem. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] Under countable choice, $b(K)=1$ if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the fixed oriented coordinate circle. [[thm-bridge-one-is-unknot]]

[F2] Under full AC, the classical signature is well-defined and satisfies $|\sigma_{-1}(K)|\le2u(K)$. [[thm-unknotting-number-at-least-half-levine-tristram-signature]]

## Proof

1.1 By [A1], the hypotheses of [F1] hold, so it supplies both implications of the asserted bridge-number characterization, with the specified oriented standard unknot. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the same knot. It gives the asserted signature inequality with the same unknotting-number convention. Combining it with step 1.1 proves the conjunction without changing either interface. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial knot. Every finite rational or infinite slope of an edge of the Newton polygon of the enhanced A-polynomial is a strict boundary slope of $K$: it is realized by an incompressible, boundary-incompressible, orientable surface in the exterior which is not a fiber of any exterior fibration over $S^1$.

## Statement references

[[def-enhanced-a-polynomial|Enhanced A-polynomial with the reducible component removed]]

[[def-boundary-slope-of-an-incompressible-surface|Boundary and strict boundary slopes]]

[Baldwin and Sivek, Theorem 4.4 and Remark 4.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

[Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long, and Shalen, §3](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~culler/papers/PlaneCurves/curves.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the nontrivial smooth knot with its chosen compact exterior and peripheral marking, and the stated Newton edge.

[A1] Full AC is retained. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The exterior is compact orientable and irreducible, with no proper compressing disk. Full AC supplies the countable choice needed by its smooth Schoenflies branch. Its tube is a smooth $S^1\times D^2$ product by the normal-circle frame supplier, so the boundary is the marked smooth torus. It is connected: join two distinct exterior points by an embedded spherical arc, perturb it relative to its endpoints to be transverse to the knot, and use $1+1<3$ to conclude it misses the knot. Radial projection of nonzero tube fibers to their boundary fixes the exterior and retracts that arc to an exterior path; equal endpoints need the constant path. [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]] [[lem-nontrivial-knot-exterior-boundary-incompressible]] [[lem-knot-normal-circle-bundle-trivialization]] [[lem-choice-free-relative-transversality-for-a-compact-smooth-embedding]]

[F2] Every selected Newton edge has an ACTUAL finite representation field and extending local curve valuation with peripheral eigenvalue pair a positive multiple of its primitive minimum normal. For an enhanced edge the representation is absolutely irreducible, including when its factor is also $L-1$. [[lem-newton-edges-have-valued-finite-peripheral-representation-models]]

[F3] For that valued representation, the actual lattice-tree/equivariant-map construction gives a connected orientable smooth essential surface with nonempty boundary whose primitive class annihilates the valuation pair. It proves both incompressibility and boundary-incompressibility by map-preserving compression complexity. With an absolutely irreducible representation it also proves that the chosen component cannot be a fiber. [[thm-nonelliptic-lattice-tree-actions-produce-essential-boundary-surfaces]]

[F4] In the stated marking $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$ has slope $b/a$, including $a=0$ as infinity. [[def-boundary-slope-of-an-incompressible-surface]]

## Proof

1.1 Let $e$ be any edge of the enhanced Newton polygon. By [F2], choose its minimum-normal valued model using the irreducible-character incidence charts in that supplier, not merely a factor of the ordinary polynomial. The finite word-matrix determinant certificate is inverted before the generic-fiber closed point is selected; hence it stays nonzero in the resulting finite field. Thus the constructed representation is absolutely irreducible, its peripheral eigenvalues are the actual coordinate functions, and their valuation pair is a positive multiple of the primitive normal to $e$. This also treats a factor $L-1$ contributed by irreducible characters. [A1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Apply [F3] in the exterior verified by [F1]. It yields a connected orientable essential surface with nonempty boundary and the primitive kernel slope of that nonzero valuation pair. That is the edge slope by the same orthogonality equation as in [F4]. Moreover the last clause of [F3] applies to the ACTUAL absolutely irreducible representation from step 1.1. If the selected component were a fiber, its normal subgroup would fix an edge; integrality of all stable-letter conjugates would force the representation to be reducible, the contradiction proved there. Thus this surface is not a fiber of any fibration having it as fiber. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The surface is precisely a realizing orientable incompressible boundary-incompressible nonfiber surface in [F4]'s definition of strict boundary slope. Hence every specified enhanced edge slope is strict, including zero or infinity when those occur. No claim that the ordinary abelian $L-1$ edge is strict has been used: enhanced strictness depends on the actual irreducible-character model, while the ordinary boundary-slope theorem retains its weaker valid conclusion. [F4, step 2.1] ∎
