## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $G_0,G_1$ be finite planar grid diagrams, with vertical segments over horizontal segments and orientation from $O$ to $X$ in rows and $X$ to $O$ in columns, representing the same oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere. A cyclic permutation moves the first row or column to the last position. A row commutation exchanges adjacent rows when the closed intervals between their respective $O$- and $X$-mark abscissae are disjoint or one lies in the interior of the other; a column commutation is defined by the same condition on the intervals between marking heights. A stabilization chooses a marked cell and temporarily removes its marking together with the other markings in its row and column. It splits that row and column into two, places the three removed markings, and adds one new $O$-mark and one new $X$-mark so that every row and column again has one of each. In the four-cell subdivision of the chosen cell, exactly three cells are marked: the chosen marking type appears twice, the other type once, and any one corner may be the empty cell; the two other markings removed from the original row and column are placed outside this block in the new row and column. A destabilization is the inverse operation. Then a finite sequence of cyclic permutations, commutations, stabilizations, and destabilizations carries $G_0$ to $G_1$.
## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot|Planar and toroidal grid conventions and oriented knot diagrams]]

[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem|Finite Reidemeister sequences for ambient-isotopic oriented knots]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable choice]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, Theorem B.4.1](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)



## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice and the two finite grids representing the same oriented knot, with the full marked move conventions in the Statement.

[F1] [[lem-grid-bridge-like-refinement]] refines any nonempty grid to a bridge-like grid by actual marked stabilizations and legal commutations, preserving the decorated planar-isotopy class after smoothing.

[F2] [[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]] connects regular diagrams of equivalent oriented links by finitely many planar isotopies and oriented R1/R2/R3 moves under countable choice.

[F3] [[lem-planar-isotopy-preserves-grid-move-class]] connects arbitrary bridge rectifications of planar-isotopic bridge diagrams by finitely many permitted grid moves.

[F4] [[lem-grid-reidemeister-moves-with-arbitrary-exterior]] supplies bridge representatives of the endpoints of any local Reidemeister move and connects arbitrary rectifications of any such bridge representatives, with arbitrary exterior and every oriented sign variant.

## Proof

1.1 A knot grid is nonempty. Apply [F1] to each $G_i$, obtaining a finite grid-move sequence to a bridge-like grid $B_i$. Smooth $B_i$ as in that supplier to a bridge diagram $D_i$. Its crossing decorations and strand orientation agree with the original grid diagram, and the supplier proves planar isotopy after smoothing. Thus $D_0,D_1$ represent the same oriented knot. The three-mark splits and strict interval commutations in [F1] are among those specified here: the retained exterior row and column partners provide the two markings outside the stabilization block in the Statement. No unlisted shared-endpoint switch has been used. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 By [F2] choose a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves from $D_0$ to $D_1$. Compose successive planar isotopies, and regard each remaining Reidemeister move as an edge between its two decorated planar-isotopy classes. The sequence now traverses finitely many such classes, with the first and last represented by $D_0,D_1$. If there is no Reidemeister edge, these two diagrams are planar isotopic. Otherwise each intermediate class is incident to a Reidemeister edge and has a bridge representative by [F4]. Choose one bridge representative for each occurrence of a class in this finite sequence, keeping $D_0,D_1$ at its ends, and choose a bridge rectification there. The choices are finite; no stronger choice principle is invoked. [F2, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Across a Reidemeister edge, the chosen bridge representatives need only be planar isotopic to that edge's original endpoint diagrams. This is exactly the relative-representative interface of [F4], so their chosen grid rectifications are joined by actual grid moves, with every exterior strand included. Across an interval with only planar isotopy, [F3] joins the chosen rectifications. This also treats the sequence with no Reidemeister edge. The endpoint rectifications may be taken to be precisely $B_0,B_1$, because both suppliers apply to arbitrary rectifications. Concatenating the finitely many constituent finite sequences gives a sequence of allowed commutations, stabilizations and destabilizations from $B_0$ to $B_1$. [F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, cases]

4.1 Prepend the refinement from $G_0$ to $B_0$ and append the reversed refinement from $B_1$ to $G_1$. Reversing a stabilization gives a destabilization and reversing a legal commutation gives a legal commutation, so all operations remain allowed. This produces the required finite sequence from $G_0$ to $G_1$. The proof needs no cyclic permutation, but allowing those additional moves in the Statement does not change the conclusion. The local suppliers cover all marking types and strand orientations, so the sequence preserves the prescribed oriented-knot convention throughout. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $g(K)$ be the least genus of a compact connected oriented embedded surface in $S^3$ with boundary $K$. With the integral Alexander normalization, the maximum Alexander grading in which the hat knot Floer homology of $K$ is nonzero is $g(K)$:

$$g(K)=\max\{i\in\mathbb Z:\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^3,K,i;\mathbb Z)\ne0\}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|The minimum genus among embedded Seifert surfaces]]

[[def-top-alexander-grading-of-knot-floer-homology|The integral absolute Alexander grading]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Holomorphic disks and genus bounds*, Theorem 1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0311496)

[Juhasz, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, Corollary 8.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609779v3)

[Manolescu, *An Introduction to Knot Floer Homology*, Theorem 2.3](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/hfk.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]] gives the two ball sides of a smooth embedded sphere in the actual three-sphere.

[F2] [[lem-integral-sutured-floer-taut-hierarchy-nonvanishing]] gives a split copy of Z in the integral homology of a taut balanced sutured manifold, with its specified coherent orientation class induced through the finite hierarchy.

[F3] [[lem-ni-holomorphic-disk-and-jsj-analytic-inputs]] constructs the actual marked adapted diagram and identifies the entire integral degree-g differential with the cut differential, with the specified orientation character retained.

[F4] [[lem-fiber-outer-grading-and-integral-cut-euler-matrix]] computes the absolute Alexander degree of every adapted generator as g minus its number of interior polygon coordinates.

[F5] [[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]] defines the minimum among compact connected oriented embedded Seifert surfaces. Such surfaces exist. Their nonnegative integer genera have a least realized value; this finite integer minimization uses no additional choice principle beyond the assumptions of the statement.

[F6] **Classical analytic input and exact axiom boundary.** Under the Axiom of Choice in the Statement, use the general integral sutured analytic framework explicitly imported in F5 of [[lem-integral-sutured-floer-compactness-and-orientations]], at the actual balanced/adapted diagrams, admissibility, boundary-region/divisor and coherent-orientation conditions of F2–F4. This supplies the pointwise Fredholm, regularity, compactification and strip/polygon gluing prerequisite; the preserved local area, grading, signed cut and hierarchy constructions then use it at their stated targets. The published framework is Juhász, *Holomorphic discs and sutured manifolds*, §§3,6–7, especially Definition7.1 and Theorems7.2/7.5, together with the referenced Ozsváth–Szabó analytic framework, and Juhász, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, Proposition7.6 and Theorems1.4–1.5. These are explicit external inputs in the classical setting, not a newly reconstructed weak-choice theorem. [[lem-countable-analytic-choice-for-fixed-sutured-floer-data]] retains its conditional Countable Choice conclusion: GIVEN the actual pointwise constructions, its fixed finite diagram/cut and at-most-two-parameter choices are finite or countable. It does not itself prove that those pointwise constructions follow under Countable Choice. The Countable-Choice-only genus strengthening is not certified here; neither its falsity nor an independent new geometric open problem is asserted. [Juhász2006](https://msp.org/agt/2006/6-3/agt-v6-n3-p16-s.pdf), [Juhász2008](https://msp.org/gt/2008/12-1/gt-v12-n1-p07-s.pdf)

## Proof

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot K in S³, the stated choice assumptions, and its integral meridional Alexander normalization.

1.1 Choose a Seifert surface F realizing the least genus g=g(K), and let E be the compact exterior. The exterior is irreducible: a sphere in its interior bounds two balls in S³ by F1; the connected knot neighborhood lies entirely on one side, so the other ball is disjoint from it and lies in E. A small oriented meridian loop meets F once, so F is nonseparating: a separating two-sided surface would have algebraic intersection zero with every closed loop. Cut E along the connected F to obtain connected M with the product annular suture and the two F faces. Their Euler characteristics agree and the boundary meets that suture, so M is balanced. A sphere in M is disjoint from F in E. Its E-ball is also disjoint from F: since F is connected, disjoint from the sphere, and has its boundary on ∂E outside that interior ball, it lies entirely on the other side. Thus that ball remains a ball in M. This proves irreducibility of the actual cut without a general-Y irreducibility assertion. [F1, F5, construct]

1.2 The two faces are incompressible. A compression of F along a nonseparating essential circle produces a connected Seifert surface of genus g−1. A separating compression produces a boundary-bearing Seifert component and a closed component. The latter has positive genus, since otherwise the original compression circle bounded a disk on F; discarding it again gives a Seifert surface of genus strictly less than g. Both contradict minimality. A face compression in M would be such a compression in E. For g=0 the disk has no essential compression circle. [F5, construct]

1.3 To prove the actual sutured norm-minimality, take any compact oriented properly embedded competitor T representing the positive face class in H₂(M,γ;Z). Its total oriented boundary in H₁(γ;Z) is one copy of the longitude. Put its boundary circles in the interior of the annular suture. Cap an innermost contractible boundary circle by its disk in the annulus, pushed into the boundary collar; this operation increases Euler characteristic and cannot increase the Thurston complexity. Continue until every boundary circle is essential. Whenever both orientations remain, choose an adjacent opposite pair. The annulus between them contains no other boundary circle. Glue it to T in a thin boundary collar and round the corners. This gives an embedded oriented surface and removes the pair. Euler characteristic is unchanged; if two components merge, the inequality max(0,−(χ₁+χ₂))≤max(0,−χ₁)+max(0,−χ₂) shows that total complexity cannot increase. For two circles on one component its Euler characteristic, hence complexity, is unchanged. The finite sequence ends with exactly one essential boundary circle, since its total winding is one. Delete all closed components, which also cannot increase complexity. The remaining connected surface embeds in E and extends across the knot collar to an actual Seifert surface for K of the same genus. Its genus is at least g by minimality. For g≥1 its complexity is therefore at least 2g−1=x(F); for g=0 it is at least zero=x(F). It follows that x(T)≥x(F). The same argument applies to the negative face. Thus M is the actual taut balanced sutured manifold, by irreducibility and norm-minimality. The boundary cancellations were used only to derive a lower bound and need not preserve the competitor's relative class after it is mapped to E. [F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

2.1 Work under the full-Choice analytic framework F6 on the actual fixed finite hierarchy and marked adapted diagram. Its admitted sutured operator problems retain the boundary/divisor barriers, periodic-domain and area conditions and the specified coherent orientation class. With the regular data and compactification/gluing construction supplied at that scope, apply F3 to the marked Seifert surface F. Its meridional frame, rather than an unspecified closure framing, gives an admissible adapted representative. By F4 every generator has Alexander degree g−n_P(x), with n_P(x) a nonnegative integer. Hence its whole integral chain complex has no generator, and thus no homology, in a grading greater than g. [F3, F4, F6, step 1.3]

2.2 The entire degree-g summand is the outer summand, and F3 identifies its signed differential with the actual cut complex of M. Since M is taut, F2 gives that this cut homology contains a split copy of Z for the orientation class induced by the given knot complex. Consequently the integral knot Floer group at degree g is nonzero. This also covers g=0: the taut cut argument and the same signed chain map apply to the minimum disk, without a genus-one connected-sum or field-coefficient substitution. [F2, F3, step 1.3, step 2.1]

2.3 Degree g is nonzero and every larger degree is zero, so the maximum of the stated nonvanishing degree set is exactly g(K). The proof uses only the literal S³ ball-side and minimum-Seifert-genus arguments above; it makes no claim of arbitrary general-Y Thurston norm detection. [step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot and let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular oriented diagrams of $K$ with basepoints away from all crossings. Then the reduced integral groups $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$ and $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D',p')$ are isomorphic for every $(i,\widetilde j)$. In particular, they are invariant under Reidemeister moves supported away from the basepoint and under transport of the basepoint along the knot.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice|Countable choice axiom]]

[[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot|Reduced quotient and based interval module]]

[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem|Oriented Reidemeister equivalence]]

[[thm-isotopy-extension|Ambient extension of a marked-knot isotopy]]

[[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position|General-position link isotopy]]

[[lem-a-generic-isotopy-of-links-has-only-reidemeister-singular-times|Finite Reidemeister event sequence]]

[[lem-khovanov-reidemeister-chain-homotopies|Local based chain homotopies]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial* (1999), §§8.1–8.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Bar-Natan, *On Khovanov's categorification of the Jones polynomial* (2002), §§3.5.1–3.5.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0201043)

[Zhang, *Notes on Khovanov homology* (2025), §6.3.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1)

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** AC$_\omega$, two finite regular based diagrams of the same oriented knot, and their reduced quotient complexes.

[F1] AC$_\omega$ is the axiom that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F2] An isotopy of smooth embeddings of a compact knot circle extends under AC$_\omega$ to an ambient isotopy ([[thm-isotopy-extension]]).

[F3] The cut one-interval tangles of any two based diagrams of the same oriented knot admit a smooth isotopy relative to the two endpoints and collars, and a finite relative Reidemeister movie. The moving-ball and terminal Alexander-scaling constructions, and the spatial-cutoff general-position proof, are supplied by [[lem-marked-knot-cut-tangles-have-relative-reidemeister-movies]], proof steps 1.1–6.1.

[F4] Every local move away from the mark induces a bigraded chain homotopy equivalence of the reduced quotient complexes; all local chain maps and homotopies commute with $X_p$ before quotienting ([[lem-khovanov-reidemeister-chain-homotopies]]).

[F5] A cochain homotopy equivalence induces mutually inverse maps on cohomology ([[def-chain-homotopy]], [[def-chain-homotopy-equivalence]]).

## Proof

1.1 Under AC$_\omega$ in [F1], apply [F3] to $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$. Its moving-ball construction uses the compact isotopy-extension clause of [F2]. It gives a finite Reidemeister movie of their cut one-interval diagrams whose endpoints and short product collars remain fixed throughout. Closing the boundary collars by the same crossing-free cap recovers the two based diagrams. In each resolution this closure replaces the distinguished interval by the based circle and adds no crossing, so it preserves $n_+,n_-$, cohomological degree and reduced quantum degree. The quotient/interval identification is the one proved in the defining reduced-complex item. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Every interior R1, R2 or R3 in the movie avoids the distinguished end collars. By [F4], its chain maps and contractions descend to the reduced quotient. A planar isotopy of the tangle identifies resolution factors and preserves every signed edge map; it fixes the distinguished interval and its degree-zero module. Thus each movie segment gives a bigraded chain homotopy equivalence of the reduced complexes. By [F5], the induced cohomology maps are mutually inverse, and finite composition gives the asserted isomorphisms in every $(i,\widetilde j)$. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Taking a movie with just one local move gives the based-move clause. Taking the same diagram with two marks gives the basepoint-transport clause by [F3]; orientation-preserving reparametrization of the single knot circle can carry either mark to the other. The relative supplier proves this case using an actual isotopy of cut arcs and fixed collars, so no relative-boundary statement for closed-link isotopies is being assumed. Together with step 2.1 this proves the full Statement. AC$_\omega$ is used only through that supplier's isotopy extension and transversality, and the local algebra is choice-free. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $M$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological manifold with supplied boundary collar, and supply a based homomorphism on each component to a discrete group $G$, with compatible paths when maps or gluings are considered. Use $R=\mathbb CG$, with involution conjugating complex scalars and sending $g$ to $g^{-1}$, and its based right regular local system with standard parallel Hermitian form. Let $A=\mathcal NG$ have the canonical group trace. Then its singular coefficient complex has an actual bounded finite-projective $R$ chain-homotopy model. Absolute, relative and finite whole-component gluing diagrams admit such models and finite matrix comparison maps.

After extending these finite projective matrices to $\ell^2(G)$, write $\mathscr H_i(M)$ for completed reduced homology, with boundaries replaced by their Hilbert closures. If $p_Z,p_B$ are the cycle and boundary-closure projections in a finite ambient projection module, the corresponding algebraic reduced module is $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^r$, and
$$H_i(M;A)\twoheadrightarrow P_i\hookrightarrow\mathscr H_i(M)=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^r.$$
The first map has dimension-zero kernel, and the second is injective with dense image and need not be onto. Pair and whole-component Mayer–Vietoris sequences are weakly exact on the completed modules. Oriented cap duality gives bounded mutually inverse maps on their completed reduced homology and cohomology, with the cap-boundary and restriction identities. These structures and the resulting spectral signature do not depend on the finite-projective model.

For a four-manifold the middle intersection form is the bounded Hermitian form defined by inverse relative cap duality, restriction and evaluation. Its Hilbert radical is the kernel of its self-adjoint operator. Its signature is the trace of the positive spectral projection minus the trace of the negative projection; no closed range or bounded inverse is required for a manifold with boundary. For a closed four-manifold its middle intersection operator is boundedly invertible.

Let $W_0,W_1$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds, let $N$ be a union of entire closed boundary components, and glue the two marked copies of $N$ by an orientation-reversing identification and the supplied collars. Put $W=W_0\cup_N W_1$ and supply one compatible regular coefficient system on $W$. Other boundary components may remain. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1),\qquad\operatorname{sign}(W)=\operatorname{sign}(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}(W_1).$$
Orientation reversal changes the corresponding sign. No finite CW type, triangulation, smoothing of a topological four-manifold, equality of ordinary and $L^2$ signatures on arbitrary closed manifolds, or analytic eta-to-defect comparison is asserted or assumed. For an arbitrary possibly uncountable $G$, the finite-matrix construction has the same dimensions and signatures as its countable coefficient image, so it agrees with the countable-group convention.

**Given:** Full AC, compact oriented topological manifolds, actual boundary collars, based regular coefficient systems and whole-component gluing data in the Statement. No seam with boundary or corners along a seam is included.

[[thm-finite-geometric-complex-chains-dominate-compact-manifold-chains-in-zf]], [[lem-choice-free-wall-chain-finiteness-from-explicit-domination]]

[F2] Oriented cap duality holds on compact collared topological manifolds and their closed boundaries for all underlying abelian-group local systems, with commuting scalar actions. Intrinsic dual cochains are identified with conjugates by the supplied parallel Hermitian form. [[thm-compact-collared-manifold-local-coefficient-lefschetz-duality-in-zf]], [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]], [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]]

[F3] Finite von Neumann matrix kernels and Hilbert-closed images are projection modules. Quotient dimension is the trace difference of closure projections; dimension-zero modules are closed under submodules, quotients and extensions. Dense injective pullback preserves inertia, and restricting an invertible Hermitian form to a closed coisotropic submodule preserves signature. [[lem-finite-von-neumann-module-dimension-and-dense-quotients]], [[lem-von-neumann-inertia-and-coisotropic-reduction]]

[F4] Topological equivariant intersections are Hermitian, retain their same-piece values under collared inclusion, and are compatible with the actual support/excision cap comparison. [[lem-relative-unitary-equivariant-intersection-pairing-is-hermitian]], [[lem-equivariant-intersection-pairings-are-preserved-by-collared-bordism-gluing]]

[F5] Small-chain excision, pair and Mayer–Vietoris sequences hold for the collared gluings. Fundamental classes have finite orientation representatives and compatible local images. The cohomology-first cap convention is $\partial(\alpha\cap z)=(-1)^p(\alpha\cap\partial z-\delta\alpha\cap z)$ for a degree-$p$ cochain. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]], [[thm-pair-long-exact-sequences-with-local-coefficients]], [[lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets]], [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]]

## Statement refuted

Assume AC. The assertion that every nonsingular linking form on a finite group of odd prime-power order has a metabolizer is false: the double branched cover of the positive trefoil has cyclic first homology of order three and no metabolizer.

## Statement references

[[def-finite-linking-form-and-metabolizer|The metabolizer definition]]

[[def-bounding-chain-torsion-linking-pairing|The oriented linking-pairing convention]]

[[lem-positive-hopf-plumbing-has-trefoil-seifert-matrix|The positive trefoil Seifert matrix]]

[[lem-branched-cover-surgery-presentation-from-seifert-surface|The branched-cover surgery presentation]]

[[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix|The surgery linking form formula]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

[Rolfsen, *Knots and Links*, Chapter 8.D, pp. 212–215](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/rolfsen.pdf)

[Przytycki and Yasuhara, *Linking Numbers in Rational Homology 3-Spheres, Cyclic Branched Covers and Infinite Cyclic Covers*, §§1 and 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0111203v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive trefoil, its Seifert matrix $V$, and the double branched-cover orientation convention.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. [[lem-positive-hopf-plumbing-has-trefoil-seifert-matrix]]

[F2] The double-cover surgery matrix is $A=V+V^T$. [[lem-branched-cover-surgery-presentation-from-seifert-surface]]

[F3] The oriented linking form on the surgery cokernel is $-A^{-1}\bmod\mathbb Z$. [[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix]]

[F4] A finite nonsingular linking form has a metabolizer only if some subgroup has square-root order. [[def-finite-linking-form-and-metabolizer]]

[F5] The surgery linking matrix computes the same oriented torsion linking pairing as the signed bounding-chain formula. [[def-bounding-chain-torsion-linking-pairing]] [[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix]]

[F6] A closed oriented $3$-manifold with finite first homology has nonsingular torsion linking form. [[lem-linking-pairing-on-rational-homology-sphere-is-nonsingular]]

## Counterexample

1.1 Computing gives $A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $3$, and unimodular row and column operations reduce it to $\operatorname{diag}(1,3)$. Therefore $H_1(\Sigma_2(T);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/3$. The matrix formula [F3] gives generator self-linking $2/3\equiv-1/3\bmod\mathbb Z$ under [F5], so the full group is not isotropic. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given, algebra, A1]

2.1 The only subgroups of $\mathbb Z/3$ have order $1$ or $3$, while a metabolizer would have order $\sqrt3$ by [F4]. The form is nonsingular by [F6] and step 1.1, so it satisfies the assertion's nonsingularity hypothesis. No subgroup has that order, so no metabolizer exists. This finite nonsingular form of odd prime-power order refutes the assertion. [F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F$ be a connected compact oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $V$ be its positive-push Seifert matrix in an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Write $\Delta_K(t)$ for the Alexander polynomial normalized up to multiplication by $\pm t^k$, and let $q\ge2$ with $\zeta_q$ a primitive $q$-th root of unity. Then $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$ is finite if and only if $\Delta_K(\zeta_q^j)\ne0$ for every $1\le j<q$, and, when it is finite,
$$
|H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)|=\prod_{j=1}^{q-1}|\Delta_K(\zeta_q^j)|.
$$
The same criterion and order hold when $\Delta_K(t)$ is replaced by $\det(V-tV^T)$.

## Statement references

[[lem-cyclic-branched-cover-homology-is-alexander-module-coinvariants|Cyclic branched-cover homology as Alexander-module coinvariants]]

[[thm-seifert-matrix-presents-knot-alexander-module|The Seifert-matrix presentation of the Alexander module]]

[[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial|The Seifert determinant represents the Alexander polynomial]]

[[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection|The Seifert matrix skew part is unimodular surface intersection]]

[[lem-square-integer-cokernel-finiteness-and-order|The determinant criterion for a square integer presentation]]

[Rolfsen, *Knots and Links*, Chapter 8.D](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/rolfsen.pdf)

[Livingston, “Seifert Forms and Concordance,” Theorem 3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0101035v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, $K,F,V,q$, and the primitive root $\zeta_q$ in the Statement.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom required by the cyclic-cover definition and coinvariant lemma. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\cong A_K/(t^q-1)A_K$, where $A_K$ is the infinite-cyclic-cover Alexander module with positive-meridian deck action $t$. [[lem-cyclic-branched-cover-homology-is-alexander-module-coinvariants]]

[F2] $A_K$ has presentation $\operatorname{coker}(V-tV^T)$ over $\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$. [[thm-seifert-matrix-presents-knot-alexander-module]]

[F3] $V-V^T$ is the matrix of the integral intersection form on $F$, hence has determinant $\pm1$. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F4] $\det(V-tV^T)$ represents $\Delta_K(t)$ up to multiplication by $\pm t^k$. [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]]

[F5] The cokernel of a square integer matrix is finite exactly when its determinant is nonzero, and then its order is the absolute determinant. [[lem-square-integer-cokernel-finiteness-and-order]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement and Facts & Assumptions. Put $D(t)=\det(V-tV^T)$ and $R_q=\mathbb Z[t]/(t^q-1)$.

1.1 Quotienting the module presentation in [F2] by $(t^q-1)A_K$ gives $A_K/(t^q-1)A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}(V-tV^T:R_q^{2g}\to R_q^{2g})$ as abelian groups. The group $R_q^{2g}$ is free abelian of rank $2gq$ on $t^ka_i$ for $0\le k<q$ and $1\le i\le2g$, so this map is represented by a square integer matrix $Q_q$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 After tensoring with $\mathbb C$, multiplication by $t$ on $R_q\otimes\mathbb C$ is diagonalizable: its eigenvalues are the $q$ distinct roots $\zeta_q^j$ for $0\le j<q$, each with one-dimensional eigenspace. On the corresponding $2g$-dimensional summand, $Q_q$ acts by $V-\zeta_q^jV^T$. Therefore $\det Q_q=\prod_{j=0}^{q-1}\det(V-\zeta_q^jV^T)$. The $j=0$ factor is $\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$ by [F3]. Thus $\det Q_q\ne0$ exactly when every factor with $1\le j<q$ is nonzero, and its absolute value is the product of the absolute values of those factors. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], the group in question is $\operatorname{coker}(Q_q)$. Applying [F5] shows it is finite exactly when $\det Q_q\ne0$, with order $|\det Q_q|$; if any nontrivial-root factor vanishes, the square integer cokernel has positive free rank and is infinite. [F1, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F4], $D(t)=\pm t^k\Delta_K(t)$ for some integer $k$. At every root of unity, $|\pm(\zeta_q^j)^k|=1$, so $|D(\zeta_q^j)|=|\Delta_K(\zeta_q^j)|$. Hence the determinant-root criterion and product from step 3.1 give exactly the Alexander-polynomial criterion and order in the Statement, including the empty-matrix case $g=0$. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\sigma_i$ be the positive geometric Artin braid crossing in a braid rectangle whose parameter increases from bottom to top, with strand $i$ passing below and strand $i+1$ passing above. Use the bracket chart in which the over-strand runs southwest to northeast, the $A$-smoothing joins left to left and right to right with weight $A$, and the $B$-smoothing joins top to top and bottom to bottom with weight $A^{-1}$. Let $I$ be the through pairing and let $e_i$ be the pairing with a top cap and a bottom cup at positions $i,i+1$. Then the positive crossing has bracket operator $A I+A^{-1}e_i$, and the negative crossing has bracket operator $A^{-1}I+A e_i$.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.82, line cap=round, line join=round]
  \begin{scope}
    \draw[thick] (-0.55,-1)--(-0.55,1);
    \draw[thick] (0.55,-1)--(0.55,1);
    \node at (0,1.35) {$I$};
  \end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[xshift=2.6cm]
    \draw[thick] (-0.55,1) .. controls (0.25,0.55) and (0.25,-0.55) .. (0.55,-1);
    \draw[thick] (0.55,1) .. controls (-0.25,0.55) and (-0.25,-0.55) .. (-0.55,-1);
    \node at (0,1.35) {$e_i$};
  \end{scope}
  \node at (1.25,0) {$\sigma_i=A I+A^{-1}e_i$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §II](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial*, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive geometric half twist, its inverse, the determinant crossing-sign convention, and the Kauffman bracket chart specified in the statement.

[F1] In the positive geometric generator, strand $i$ moves from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint and strand $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to $x=-h$ above it; the inverse reverses the crossing ([[def-elementary-geometric-half-twist]]).

[F2] The crossing sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, and this convention assigns sign $+1$ to the positive geometric Artin half twist ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F3] In the stated chart a crossing contributes $A$ times its $A$-smoothing plus $A^{-1}$ times its $B$-smoothing; the loop value is $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

## Proof
1.1 Use source coordinates $(u,v)$ with their standard positive orientation and positive projection coordinates $(t,x)$ on the braid box. For $h>0$, the map $(t,x)=(v,-2hu)$ has determinant $2h>0$. It sends the source over direction $(1,1)$ to $(1,-2h)$ and the source under direction $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is $4h>0$. The source left/right pairs have constant $u$, hence constant braid position $x$ and give the through pairing $I$; the source top/bottom pairs have constant $v$, hence constant braid time $t$ and give the cup-cap $e_i$. The displayed page coordinates $(x,t)$ reverse the positive projection orientation; their visual quarter-turn is not the orientation comparison. The two terms in [F3] are therefore $A I$ and $A^{-1}e_i$. [F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 The inverse half twist reverses which diagonal is over. Reflection of the local crossing interchanges the two pairings while retaining the bracket rule that assigns coefficient $A$ to the chart's $A$-smoothing and $A^{-1}$ to its $B$-smoothing. Consequently the through pairing now has coefficient $A^{-1}$ and the cap-cup pairing has coefficient $A$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let $X$ be a connected finite based two-dimensional CW complex with one $0$-cell, $n\ge2$ $1$-cells and $n-1$ $2$-cells, so $\chi(X)=0$. Let $G=\pi_1(X)$, let $\psi:G\twoheadrightarrow H\cong\mathbb Z^m$ be an epimorphism with $m\ge1$, let $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation over a field, set $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$ and $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$, and form the based twisted cellular complex from the preceding definition. If every element of $H_1(C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;\Lambda^d))$ is annihilated by some nonzero element of $\Lambda$, then $C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;Q^d)$ is acyclic. No assumption that its degree-two homology vanishes before localization is required.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion|Twisted coefficient complex and deck action]]

[Conway, Lemma 2.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.06678)

[Kirk and Livingston, §§3–4](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Livingston_papers/1999_Twisted%20Alexander%20invariants%2C%20Reidemeister%20torsion%2C%20and%20Casson-Gordon%20invariants.pdf)

[Ranicki, Example 17](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/torsion.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the finite based $2$-complex and its cell counts; a positive-rank free abelian quotient $\psi:G\twoheadrightarrow H$; a field $\mathbb F$; and the torsion hypothesis on $H_1$ over $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$.

[A1] AC is inherited from the maximal-abelian-cover convention used to define the coefficient complex. The finite-dimensional linear-algebra argument below itself uses no choice principle. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The twisted complex is formed from the chosen based universal-cover cellular chains using the right action $v\cdot g=v\rho(g)\psi(g)$; the boundary of a lifted oriented $1$-cell $x$ is multiplication by $\rho(x)\psi(x)-I_d$. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F2] The field of fractions of an integral domain is a field, and the canonical map embeds the domain. [[def-field-of-fractions]]; [[thm-field-of-fractions-is-a-field-and-the-domain-embeds]]

## Proof



1.1 By [A1], use the prescribed AC-based twisted coefficient convention. Choose an ordered basis $t_1,\ldots,t_m$ of $H$. Then $\Lambda$ is the Laurent-polynomial ring $\mathbb F[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_m^{\pm1}]$. Order exponent vectors lexicographically. For nonzero Laurent polynomials $f,g$, their finite supports have largest exponents $a,b$ with nonzero coefficients $f_a,g_b$; the largest exponent of $fg$ is $a+b$ and its coefficient is $f_ag_b\ne0$. Thus $\Lambda$ is an integral domain, and [F2] makes $Q$ a field containing $\Lambda$. [A1, given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $z/s\in C_1\otimes_\Lambda Q$ be a fraction-field cycle, with $z\in C_1$ and $0\ne s\in\Lambda$. Since $d_1(z)/s=0$ and each coordinate of $C_0$ lies in the domain $\Lambda$, $d_1(z)=0$. The torsion hypothesis gives $0\ne f\in\Lambda$ and $w\in C_2$ with $fz=d_2(w)$. Hence $z/s=d_2(w/(fs))$, so every fraction-field $1$-cycle is a boundary and $H_1(C_*\otimes Q)=0$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Because $\psi$ is onto a positive-rank free abelian group, some $1$-cell generator $x$ has $\psi(x)=h\ne1$. In the corresponding $d_1$ block, $A=\rho(x)h-I_d$. Its determinant is a polynomial in the distinct monomials $1,h,\ldots,h^d$ whose top coefficient is $\det\rho(x)\ne0$, so $\det A\ne0$ in $\Lambda$. Thus $A$ is invertible over $Q$, this block makes $d_1:C_1\otimes Q\to C_0\otimes Q$ surjective, and $H_0(C_*\otimes Q)=0$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The fraction-field chain dimensions are $d(n-1),dn,d$, whose alternating sum is $d((n-1)-n+1)=0$. Euler–Poincaré for this finite-dimensional complex gives $\dim_QH_0-\dim_QH_1+\dim_QH_2=0$. Steps 2.1 and 2.2 make the first two terms zero, hence $H_2=0$; there are no chain groups above degree $2$. The localized complex is acyclic. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

A pattern has strong winding number ±1 if and only if its closure P(U) is the unknot.

## Statement references

[[def-satellite-induced-concordance-operator|Strong-winding definition]]

[CDR, Definition 1.1 and §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.5058v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nontrivial knot J and the pattern P_J obtained by tying J into a small arc of the solid-torus core.

[F1] The closure of the local-knot pattern is J and its winding number is 1 ([[def-satellite-induced-concordance-operator]]).

[F2] Strong winding is the normal-generation property of the axis meridian in the closure complement ([[def-satellite-induced-concordance-operator]]).

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The pattern P_J has winding number 1 because tying a local knot does not change its homology class in the solid torus. Its closure is J, which is not the unknot by the choice of J. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 The axis meridian is a meridian of J in this local-knot construction. Meridional filling of the knot exterior yields S³, whose fundamental group is trivial; van Kampen implies that the normal closure of the meridian is the entire group. Hence P_J is strong winding +1 although P_J(U) is not the unknot. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 This disproves the forward implication from strong winding to an unknotted closure, while leaving the reverse implication untouched. The counterexample makes no claim that ordinary winding ±1 always implies strong winding ±1. [step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Definition

A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

## Example

Let $D=\{x'\in\mathbb R^2:|x'|\leq1\}$ with its Euclidean metric and let
$$M=\{(x_1,x')\in\mathbb R\times D:x_1^2+4|x'|^2\leq1\}$$
with the restricted Euclidean product metric. Then $M$ is a compact smooth three-dimensional product subdomain compactly contained in $\mathbb R\times D^\circ$, and the transversal $D$ is a simple surface whose unweighted scalar geodesic ray transform is injective on real-valued compactly supported smooth functions.

## Example references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product-domain convention]]

[[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform|Simple surface and scalar ray transform]]

[[thm-ip-2d-simple-surface-xray-injectivity|Injectivity on simple surfaces]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the disk $D$, the ellipsoid $M$, and the Euclidean product metric in the statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain]]: a compact smooth three-dimensional domain compactly contained in a product $\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$ with product metric is transversally anisotropic.

[F2] [[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform]]: a compact surface is simple when its boundary is strictly convex, there are no conjugate points, and geodesics exit in finite time.

[F3] [[thm-ip-2d-simple-surface-xray-injectivity]]: for a real $f\in C_c^\infty(D^\circ)$, zero integrals over all nontangential boundary-to-boundary geodesics on a simple surface imply $f=0$.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 The boundary of $M$ is the level set $x_1^2+4|x'|^2=1$. Its defining function has gradient $(2x_1,8x_2,8x_3)$, which cannot vanish on that level set, so $M$ is a compact smooth three-dimensional domain. Every point of $M$ has $|x'|\leq1/2<1$, hence $M\Subset\mathbb R\times D^\circ$; the ambient metric is exactly $dx_1^2\oplus g_D$. By [F1], this is a transversally anisotropic product domain. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The disk has strictly convex boundary: its outward unit normal is $x'$ on $|x'|=1$ and $g(\nabla_w\nu_{\rm out},w)=|w|^2>0$ for every nonzero tangent $w$. Its curvature is zero, so a normal Jacobi field has scalar coefficient $a+bt$; if it vanishes at two distinct times then $a=b=0$, proving no conjugate points. Every unit-speed straight line exits the bounded disk in finite forward and backward time, and the segment between two points in the disk is unique. Thus $D$ is simple by [F2]. [F2, given, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] to this simple surface. Its unweighted scalar geodesic ray transform is injective on the stated compactly supported smooth real functions. This verifies the injective-transversal condition for $M$. [F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and suppose $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-TV exact solution with a source certificate $p^\dagger$. For $\alpha_n>0$ tending to zero and noises $w_n\in L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$, assume $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n\le\eta$ and let $u_n$ be supplied global minimizers of $\frac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_2^2+\alpha_n TV(u)$. Define $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$ and $v_n=A^*p_n$. Use $TV_2$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ for full-space TV, zero-extension Dirichlet TV on a bounded Lipschitz domain, and relative Neumann TV on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain; for bounded-domain geometry use the ambient zero-extended level sets and their topological boundaries in $\mathbb R^2$.

For full-space or Dirichlet TV, assume $\eta<2\sqrt\pi$; in the bounded Dirichlet case also assume $\Omega$ has global obstacle curvature $\kappa_\Omega\in L^1(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $\kappa_\Omega\ge g$ almost everywhere outside $\Omega$ for some real-valued $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Omega;\mathbb R)$. For Neumann TV, let $C_\Omega$ be a constant from the BV Sobolev–Poincaré inequality $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ and assume $\eta<1/C_\Omega$.

For almost every nonzero $t$, the level set $E_n(t)$ has finite measure and perimeter, minimizes the branch-specific perimeter minus $\int_{E}\operatorname{sgn}(t)v_n$ under compactly supported perturbations, and satisfies $P(E_n(t))=\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_{E_n(t)}v_n$. There are constants $c>0$ and $r_0>0$, independent of $n$ and almost every such $t$, such that for every $x\in\partial E_n(t)$ and $0<r<r_0$,
$$|B(x,r)\cap E_n(t)|\ge c|B(x,r)|,\qquad |B(x,r)\setminus E_n(t)|\ge c|B(x,r)|.$$
In the full-space branch all these level sets are contained in one common ball; in the bounded branches they lie in $\overline\Omega$. The same density and support conclusions are asserted for any selected minimum-TV exact limit that carries the inherited source certificate, using zero noise. Whenever the corresponding level sets converge in measure, their canonical boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-level-set-representatives-and-boundaries|Canonical level sets use density-one representatives and ambient boundaries.]]

[[def-ip-tv-variational-curvature|Variational curvature uses the full-space, Dirichlet, or Neumann perimeter convention.]]

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|A source certificate places its adjoint image in the subdifferential at an exact minimum-TV truth.]]

[[lem-ip-neumann-bv-sobolev-poincare|The Neumann threshold uses the bounded-domain BV Sobolev–Poincaré constant.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the linear map and TV branch, a minimum-TV exact source-certified truth, the noise condition, and supplied global regularized minimizers as in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice is used by the coarea, BV representation, and compactness suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[lem-ip-tv-dual-attainment-and-certificate-limit]]: each supplied minimizer has $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$, $v_n=A^*p_n\in\partial TV(u_n)\cap\partial TV(0)$, the exact-data fields $v_{\alpha_n,0}$ converge strongly in $L^2$ to $v_0$, and $\|v_n-v_{\alpha_n,0}\|_2\le\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n\le\eta$.

[F2] [[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate]]: the initial exact truth is minimum-TV and the source certificate supplies a subgradient in the real Hilbert pairing.

[F3] [[def-ip-tv-level-set-representatives-and-boundaries]]: for $t>0$ use the density-one representative of $\{u>t\}$; for $t<0$ use that of $\{u<t\}$; bounded-domain sets are viewed by zero extension solely for their ambient geometry.

[F4] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-coarea-formula]] and [[lem-ip-bv-coarea-formula]]: full-space finite-variation $L^2$ functions and bounded-domain BV functions have the corresponding positive-superlevel/negative-sublevel coarea identities.

[F5] [[def-ip-tv-variational-curvature]]: variational curvature means minimization of the branch-specific perimeter minus the signed integral of its curvature over compactly supported symmetric-difference perturbations.

[F6] [[lem-ip-planar-isoperimetric-inequality-for-finite-perimeter-sets]]: $4\pi|E|\le P(E;\mathbb R^2)^2$ for finite-area finite-perimeter planar sets.

[F7] [[lem-ip-neumann-bv-sobolev-poincare]]: on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain, $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ for the stated Neumann constant.

[F8] [[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]]: the spatial test-field variation is lower semicontinuous under $L^1$ convergence and equals perimeter on finite-perimeter indicators.

[F9] [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]: every bounded scalar real sequence has a convergent subsequence. Applying it to the first coordinate and then to the second coordinate of that subsequence gives a convergent subsequence in $\mathbb R^2$, since the first-coordinate convergence is retained.

[F10] Actual ball-cut and obstacle comparisons, uniform two-sided density in all three branches, and a common full-space support bound follow from distributional ball products and radial-tail extinction. [[lem-ip-tv-finite-perimeter-ball-cut-calculus]], [[lem-ip-tv-uniform-density-and-radial-support-for-curvature-minimizers]]

[F12] The distributional L2 TV is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous and positively one-homogeneous, and agrees with BV TV on integrable functions. [[lem-ip-tv-l2-functional-properties]]

[F11] A bounded Lipschitz-domain BV indicator has a BV zero extension, so its ambient perimeter is finite even in the Neumann branch. Completed Fubini and Tonelli apply to the signed layer-cake integrals when their absolute integral is finite. [[lem-ip-bv-lipschitz-trace-and-zero-extension]], [[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]

[F13] The real Hilbert pairing satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]

## Proof

1.1 The TV functional is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous and positively one-homogeneous by [F12]. On a bounded domain $L^2\subset L^1$, so the relative functional agrees with that test-field functional by [F8]; the Dirichlet version is its composition with the linear isometric zero-extension map into full-space $L^2$. Thus the hypotheses of [F1] hold. Comparison of each objective with its finite value at zero also gives finite TV at a supplied minimizer. Put $z_n=v_{\alpha_n,0}=A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}$. By [F1], $z_n\to v_0=A^*p_0$ strongly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and $v_n=z_n+e_n$ with $\|e_n\|_2\le\eta$. Thus the exact-field sequence, its limit and the noisy fields have precisely the coefficient decomposition required by [F10]. In particular their uniform small-measure moduli and, in full space, exact-field tail moduli follow from strong convergence, as proved there, without an assumed uniform integrability of the noisy perturbations. [F1, F8, F10, F12, given, construct]

1.2 For each supplied minimizer, [F1] and positive one-homogeneity imply $R(u_n)=\langle v_n,u_n\rangle$ and $v_n\in\partial R(0)$. The selected TV is even, since its test-field class is symmetric and zero extension is linear. Applying its inequality to both $\chi_F$ and $-\chi_F$ gives $P_*(F)\ge\sigma\int_Fv_n$ for either sign $\sigma$, for every finite-area finite-selected-perimeter competitor; $P_*$ denotes the selected branch perimeter throughout this proof. Indeed these indicators belong to $L^2$ and their selected TV is exactly $P_*$ by [F8] and the boundary conventions. In full space every nonzero level has finite area by $|\{|u_n|>|t|\}|\le\|u_n\|_2^2/t^2$. Bounded-domain levels have finite area automatically. Coarea [F4] gives finite selected perimeter for almost every nonzero level. Relative-perimeter Neumann levels also have finite ambient perimeter by [F11]. Signed layer cake and Cauchy–Schwarz give an absolutely integrable level pairing: the integral over levels of $\int_{E_n(t)}|v_n|$ is $\int|u_n||v_n|\le\|u_n\|_2\|v_n\|_2$. Hence [F11] and coarea show that the integral of the nonnegative gaps $P_*(E_n(t))-\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_{E_n(t)}v_n$ equals $R(u_n)-\langle v_n,u_n\rangle=0$. Each gap therefore vanishes almost everywhere. Their value zero is the global minimum of $P_*(F)-\operatorname{sgn}(t)\int_Fv_n$, since every competitor has nonnegative value. This proves the stated equality and even global branch minimization, which in particular implies compact-perturbation variational curvature [F5]. Taking the countable union of exceptional level sets makes this true simultaneously for all $n$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, F8, F11, F13, algebra]

2.1 The threshold and actual obstacle assumptions are exactly those of [F10]. Apply it to every calibrated set from step 1.2, with either level sign. It supplies one $c,r_0>0$ for both ambient density inequalities at every point of each canonical boundary, independently of the index and the nonexceptional level. In the Dirichlet branch the actual obstacle extension uses perimeter submodularity from [F10]; in the Neumann branch its proof uses relative cuts and the specified $C_\Omega$, and at points on $\partial\Omega$ it uses the uniform Lipschitz exterior area for the ambient complement. Thus no false relative-complement estimate is imposed on the valid case $E=\Omega$. In full space [F10] compares $E$ with actual radial cuts and proves finite-radius extinction of $|E\setminus B(0,r)|$, giving one common ball containing the density-one sets and their topological boundaries. Bounded-domain representatives and boundaries lie in $\overline\Omega$. These are the full density and support conclusions, rather than assumptions for the transfer below. [F3, F6, F7, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, construct]

3.1 The limiting field calibrates every minimum-TV exact solution $u_0$ under consideration. More explicitly, the dual supplier [F1] defines $p_0\in\{p:A^*p\in\partial R(0),\ \langle f,p\rangle=R(u^\dagger)\}$. For any such exact minimum $Au_0=f$ and $R(u_0)=R(u^\dagger)$, one has $\langle v_0,u_0\rangle=\langle p_0,f\rangle=R(u_0)$, while $v_0\in\partial R(0)$. Its subgradient inequality is therefore also the inequality at $u_0$. Repeat step 1.2 with $u_0,v_0$; its almost-everywhere level sets are calibrated global minimizers. Adjoin the limiting exact field with perturbation zero in [F10]. The very same coefficient moduli and noise threshold used in step 2.1 then give the same uniform density and support conclusions for this limit. This includes any selected minimum-TV exact limit carrying the inherited certificate; it does not identify that solution with $u^\dagger$ without uniqueness. [F1, F2, F4, F10, F11, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Fix a nonzero nonexceptional level for which the corresponding sets converge in measure to such a canonical limit $E_0$. If $E_0=\varnothing$ and infinitely many $E_n$ are nonempty, their bounded common support makes each boundary nonempty: a boundaryless subset of connected $\mathbb R^2$ is clopen, and the only bounded clopen set is empty. Choose a boundary point and one fixed $0<r<r_0$; the density estimate gives $|E_n\triangle E_0|\ge c\pi r^2$, a contradiction. If $E_0$ is nonempty, it has positive measure by its density-one definition, so convergence rules out infinitely many empty $E_n$. The empty status therefore agrees eventually; two empty boundaries have Hausdorff distance zero. In the nonempty case, if $x_n\in\partial E_n$ stays at distance at least $\delta>0$ from $\partial E_0$, common compact support and [F9] give a subsequence $x_n\to x$. For $r<\min(r_0,\delta/4)$ the connected ball $B(x_n,r)$ misses $\partial E_0$ and is entirely in $E_0$ or entirely outside it. The two-sided density of $E_n$ forces symmetric difference at least $c\pi r^2$, again a contradiction. Conversely, if $y_n\in\partial E_0$ stays at distance at least $\delta$ from $\partial E_n$, take a convergent subsequence with limit $y\in\partial E_0$. A fixed smaller connected ball about $y$ misses every corresponding $\partial E_n$, so along a further subsequence its status is always full or always empty. Measure convergence makes $E_0$ full or empty almost everywhere on that ball. By the density-one definition it is then actually full or empty in a smaller ball, contradicting $y\in\partial E_0$. Both directed Hausdorff distances tend to zero, with all point and subsequence selections allowed by [A1]. [A1, F3, F9, step 2.1, step 3.1, choose, construct, contradiction] ∎

## Statement

For the fixed root parameter, the normalized double-handlebody pairing on the admissible spine states of a marked handlebody is nondegenerate after quotienting by its radical. The inverse pairing defines the sewing map for gluing along a closed marked surface, and these maps satisfy the stated weighted Lagrangian anomaly correction.

## Statement references

[[def-skein-tqft-state-space-and-handlebody-pairing|State-space pairing]]

[[lem-root-handlebody-spine-state-space-finite-generation|Finite spine spanning set]]

[[def-extended-skein-cobordism-anomaly-data|Weighted Lagrangian anomaly convention]]

[Blanchet, Habegger, Masbaum, and Vogel, *Topological Quantum Field Theories Derived from the Kauffman Bracket*, §§1 and 4–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/bhmv.pdf)

[Kauffman and Lins, *Temperley-Lieb Recoupling Theory and Invariants of 3-Manifolds*, Chapters 6–7](https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781400882533_A27764847/preview-9781400882533_A27764847.pdf)

[Pohorence, *3-manifold Invariants and TQFTs*, §3](https://categorified.net/RTinvariants/Jan29-Feb3.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite spanning set of admissible spine states and the normalized gluing pairing.

[F1] [[def-skein-tqft-state-space-and-handlebody-pairing]] defines the radical quotient and pairing.

[F2] [[lem-root-handlebody-spine-state-space-finite-generation]] supplies the finite admissible spine spanning set via its explicitly labelled external BHMV input.

[F3] [[def-extended-skein-cobordism-anomaly-data]] fixes the weight and Maslov convention.

[F4] **External input — perfect pairing and sewing.** BHMV, Theorem1.4 p.887, property(F) on p.886, Proposition1.9 p.891, and Theorem4.11 p.909: in this even-root theory the radical quotient is finite free with unimodular dual pairing, the admissible spine states form a basis with unit diagonal norms in the double pairing, and the universal gluing maps satisfy the TQFT axioms. Proposition1.9 permits the complementary handlebody giving $S^3$, rather than assuming the self-double and $S^3$ pairings have the same matrix. Their normalization is the $Z_p$ normalization explicitly fixed in [F1]. Only perfectness/basis/sewing at this actual convention is imported.

[F5] **External input — actual weighted variant.** Gilmer–Masbaum, arXiv:0912.4706v3, §2 equation(1) pp.4–6 and §11 pp.23–25, states the colored TQFT with Lagrangians and integer weights and one-weight multiplier $\nu=\kappa^3$ in BHMV notation. The finite sign comparison $\mu_{GM}=-\mu_{Wall}$ is as recorded in the Kirby lemma, so its composition is exactly that of [F3]. The source states rational Lagrangians. For the real Lagrangians of [F3], take the rational handlebody-kernel reference on each marked surface and transport by the weight-zero identity cylinder to its specified real Lagrangian; the reverse cylinder is its inverse because $\mu(L,L',L)=0$. Conjugating morphisms by these cylinders is a functor to the rational-reference category, with the integer weights computed by [F3], so the imported functor extends to these real objects. This is a finite categorical transport, not an assumption that every real Lagrangian is rational.

## Proof

**Given:** A marked handlebody spine, its admissible colorings, and the gluing pairing.

1.1 On a fixed finite spine, each admissible coloring gives a finite colored graph state. Gluing a pair of handlebodies evaluates the resulting closed colored graph using the specified root bracket and anomaly normalization. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 By [F4], the radical quotients for the two orientations are finite-dimensional dual spaces and their normalized pairing is perfect. This is stronger than left nondegeneracy by the definition of a radical alone. Choose bases $v_i,w_j$ and let $B_{ij}$ be their pairing matrix. Its inverse gives the coevaluation tensor $\sum_{i,j}(B^{-1})_{ji}v_i\otimes w_j$; contraction with $B$ on either side is the identity. This finite linear-algebra identity is exactly the sewing contraction in the imported gluing theorem and is independent of the chosen dual bases. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The imported weighted gluing in [F5] gives the prescribed anomaly factor, with weight law [F3]. Its parameter is the cube of the selected sixth root, not an independently chosen square root with an unchecked sign. The real-Lagrangian transport in [F5] respects composition because the intervening reference cylinders cancel. Thus the inverse-pairing sewing maps satisfy precisely the registered weighted law. No unweighted anomaly cancellation or positivity of every complex-root Hermitian form is asserted. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

**Inputs.** A nonempty oriented $r$-component link $L$; its compact exterior $E_L$; a finite oriented simplicial triangulation $K$ of $E_L$ with connected 1-skeleton, an ordering of its vertices and simplices, and least vertex $v_0$ as the based point used to classify the cover; one certified positive-meridian edge loop in the boundary triangulation for each component, each loop oriented as the boundary of a normal disk whose positive tangent followed by its positive normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$; and a label $\ell(e)\in\mathbb Z^r$ for every oriented edge $e$ of $K$.

**Admissible input conditions.** The input is admissible when edge reversal gives $\ell(\bar e)=-\ell(e)$, the sum of the labels around every oriented 2-simplex is zero, and the sum around the $i$th certified positive meridian loop is the standard basis vector $e_i\in\mathbb Z^r$. The last check verifies the marking: by the Alexander-dual meridian basis and the compact-exterior retraction, these loops give the standard basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$, so their evaluations determine the full abelianization. The edge labels define a covering model by assigning to each oriented edge $e:v\to w$ the transition $(v,g)\mapsto(w,g+\ell(e))$ on vertex exponents $g\in\mathbb Z^r$; the face check makes all simplex lifts compatible. The procedure takes the geometric status of the supplied triangulation and peripheral curves as input data; it does not recognize a 3-manifold or discover meridians.

**Output.** Either `invalid-labeling`, or the finite free graded $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$ modules with one basis element per simplex orbit and the prescribed Laurent-polynomial boundary matrices. The main theorem on this page proves that these matrices make the output a chain complex and that its first homology is $A_L$.

**Instructions.**

1. Check the edge-reversal rule, each oriented 2-simplex sum, and each meridian-loop evaluation. Return `invalid-labeling` if any check fails.
2. Order the 1-simplices by their supplied simplex order. Start with no tree edges and with each vertex in its own component. Scan the edges in that order, adding an edge exactly when its endpoints lie in different current components and then merging those components. Because the 1-skeleton is connected, this finite scan produces the lexicographically first spanning tree. Use the least-ordered based vertex $v_0$ as root, assign its lift to the identity deck element, and assign every other vertex lift by summing edge labels along its unique tree path from the root.
3. For each oriented simplex $\sigma$, choose its least-ordered vertex as anchor and use the label sums along edges of $\sigma$ to determine the lift incident to the already chosen anchor lift. For each oriented face $\tau$ of $\sigma$, compute the unique deck exponent $g(\sigma,\tau)\in\mathbb Z^r$ taking the chosen lift of $\tau$ to that face of the chosen lift of $\sigma$.
4. If $\tau$ occurs with incidence sign $\epsilon(\sigma,\tau)\in\{-1,1\}$ in $\partial\sigma$, place the coefficient $\epsilon(\sigma,\tau)t_1^{g_1(\sigma,\tau)}\cdots t_r^{g_r(\sigma,\tau)}$ in the corresponding matrix entry. Repeat for every simplex and dimension.
5. Return the chain groups and boundary matrices in the input simplex order. Coning a closed edge path in a simplex to its anchor expresses it as a sum of triangular face boundaries, so the face-sum check makes its edge-path sum independent of path; the meridian checks ensure the deck group is the prescribed full abelianization.

The following triangle records the local consistency check. Each arrow is oriented as drawn and its label lies in $\mathbb Z^r$. The face check in instruction 1 is exactly the equation $g_{01}+g_{12}+g_{20}=0$.

  \coordinate (v2) at (1.5,2);
  \draw[->] (v0) -- (v1) node[midway,below] {$g_{01}$};
  \draw[->] (v1) -- (v2) node[midway,right] {$g_{12}$};
  \draw[->] (v2) -- (v0) node[midway,left] {$g_{20}$};
  \fill (v0) circle (1.5pt) node[below left] {$v_0$};
  \fill (v1) circle (1.5pt) node[below right] {$v_1$};
  \fill (v2) circle (1.5pt) node[above] {$v_2$};

## Definition

Let $u$ be a distribution, not necessarily compactly supported, or a distributional density (a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions), on a real-analytic $n$-manifold $X$. Let $x_0$ lie in an analytic coordinate chart and let $\xi_0\in T^*_{x_0}X\setminus\{0\}$ have coordinate components in that chart. For $\chi\in C_c^\infty$ supported in the chart and equal to $1$ near $x_0$, define the Gaussian FBI packet
$$
\mathcal F_\chi u(x,\lambda\omega) =\left\langle u(y),\chi(y) \exp\!\left(i\lambda(x-y)\cdot\omega-\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|x-y|^2\right)\right\rangle, \quad \lambda\ge1,\quad |\omega|=1.
$$
When $u$ is a scalar distribution, the pairing is with the displayed function times coordinate density $|dy|$; when $u$ is a distributional density, the pairing is with the displayed scalar function. In both cases $\lambda\omega$ is the cotangent frequency. The covector $(x_0,\xi_0)$ is analytically regular for $u$ in this chart if there are such a cutoff $\chi$, a neighborhood $U$ of $x_0$, an open neighborhood $\Gamma$ of $\xi_0/|\xi_0|$ in the unit sphere, and constants $c,C>0$ such that
$$
|\mathcal F_\chi u(x,\lambda\omega)|\le C e^{-c\lambda} \quad(x\in U,\ \omega\in\Gamma,\ \lambda\ge1).
$$
The analytic wavefront set $\operatorname{WF}_A(u)$ is the set of nonzero cotangent vectors for which this exponential estimate fails. This is a chart-local definition. The separate local FBI-invariance claim needed for a geometric interpretation is stated by the companion lemma.

## Definition references

[[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation|Distribution and density pairing]]

[[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables|Analytic coordinate charts]]

[[def-multivariable-power-series|Power-series convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A distribution or distributional density $u$, an analytic chart, a point $x_0$, and a nonzero cotangent vector $\xi_0$.

[F1] [[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation]]: distributions act continuously on compactly supported smooth densities; multiplication by the compactly supported cutoff localizes any distribution to the chart.

[F2] [[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: analytic charts have holomorphic complexifications near each point.

[F3] [[def-multivariable-power-series]]: the chart complexifications and their derivatives are represented by convergent power series on smaller polydiscs.

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the definition.

1.1 For fixed $x,\lambda,\omega$, the function of $y$ in the displayed pairing is smooth and supported in $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, hence it is a test density. Therefore the packet is a well-defined complex number by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Replacing $\xi_0$ by a positive multiple leaves the unit direction $\xi_0/|\xi_0|$ unchanged; the definition quantifies over all $\lambda\ge1$ and an open cone of unit directions. Thus analytic regularity is conic in the cotangent variable, and its complement defines a conic subset of $T^*X\setminus0$. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2]–[F3], an analytic coordinate change near $x_0$ extends to a holomorphic map on a smaller complex neighborhood, so its cotangent action and Gaussian packet phase are locally defined there. The definition makes no claim that the numeric packet is unchanged under this change; the next lemma proves equivalence for the packet families actually used on this page. [F2, F3, given] ∎

## Example

Assume AC and Countable Choice. Fix $\alpha,\beta,p,L>0$. For each $0<\epsilon\le1$, use the centered Gaussian Borel prior on $\ell^2$ with independent coordinates $\theta_j\sim N(0,j^{-1-2\alpha})$, independent of the observation noise. Under the fixed-truth law, observe $Y_j=j^{-p}\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$ with independent $N(0,1)$ noise and a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger$ in the power ellipsoid $\{\theta\in\ell^2:\sum_{j\ge1}j^{2\beta}(\theta_j)^2\le L^2\}$. Then the posterior contracts in the $\ell^2$ norm at rate $r_\epsilon=\epsilon^{2\min(\alpha,\beta)/(1+2\alpha+2p)}$, meaning that for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$ the expected posterior mass outside radius $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ tends to zero as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model|The sequence inverse experiment fixes the data-coordinate convention used in this example.]]

[[def-ip-posterior-contraction-rate|The rate means expected posterior tail convergence for every diverging multiplier under the fixed-truth data law.]]

[[thm-ip-conjugate-gaussian-sequence-contraction|The exact moment sum has squared bias, posterior-mean sampling variance, and posterior variance terms.]]

[Knapik, van der Vaart, and van Zanten, *Bayesian inverse problems with Gaussian priors*, §§3–4 and §7.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1103.2692)

[Johnstone, *Gaussian estimation: Sequence and wavelet models*, §2.3](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jbradic/math281a/Johnstone.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; $\alpha,\beta,p,L>0$; $0<\epsilon\le1$; the power ellipsoid and Gaussian prior in the Example; and the exact posterior moment formula for the coordinate model.

[A1] AC is the declared assumption for the Gaussian product posterior construction. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] Countable Choice is inherited from the compact-SVD sequence model. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The posterior coordinate mean and variance are $\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and $v_j$, and the expected posterior squared error is the displayed nonnegative sum; posterior tail mass is bounded by that sum divided by the squared radius. [[thm-ip-conjugate-gaussian-sequence-contraction]]

[F2] A rate is established when expected posterior mass outside every diverging multiple tends to zero under the fixed-truth law. [[def-ip-posterior-contraction-rate]]

[F3] The Gaussian sequence inverse model has $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$, positive singular values, product-Borel observations, and independent standard-normal noise coordinates. [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]

[F4] For positive bases, real powers satisfy $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$ and the ordinary exponent laws. [[def-real-power]], [[thm-real-power-laws]]

[F5] For every $q>0$, the geometric series $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2qk}$ converges and equals $(1-2^{-2q})^{-1}$. [[thm-geometric-series]]

[F6] The canonical real square-summable sequence space $H=\ell^2$ is complete, hence a real Hilbert space. Positive-index coordinates are identified with the $\mathbb N_0$-indexed sequence space by the isometry $(x_j)_{j\ge1}\mapsto(x_{n+1})_{n\ge0}$. [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]] The set of finite-support sequences with rational coordinates is countable and dense: truncate any square-summable sequence so the tail norm is arbitrarily small, then approximate the finitely many retained coordinates by rationals. Hence $H$ is separable. For the diagonal covariance, positivity and self-adjointness follow from $\langle\Gamma x,x\rangle=\sum_j\tau_j^2x_j^2\ge0$ and $\langle\Gamma x,y\rangle=\langle x,\Gamma y\rangle$. Finite-rank truncations converge in operator norm, so $\Gamma$ is compact; its diagonal rank-one expansion has nuclear sum $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$, so it is trace class. [[thm-hilbert-space-with-a-given-orthonormal-basis-is-ell-two-of-the-index-set]], [[def-separable-space]], [[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]], [[thm-norm-limit-of-compact-operators-is-compact]], [[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]]

[F7] A positive self-adjoint trace-class covariance on a separable real Hilbert space defines a Borel centered Hilbert-valued Gaussian random element with that covariance. [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]]

[F8] A finite vector is multivariate normal when all its linear projections are normal. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F9] Finite jointly Gaussian blocks with zero cross-covariance are independent, including for singular covariance matrices. [[lem-uncorrelated-jointly-gaussian-blocks-are-independent]]

[F10] The notation $N(m,\sigma^2)$ denotes the law of a normal variable with mean $m$ and variance $\sigma^2$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

[F11] For positive bases, $a>1$ makes $x\mapsto a^x$ increasing, $0<a<1$ makes it decreasing, and for $t>0$ the map $a\mapsto a^t$ is increasing while $a\mapsto a^{-t}$ is decreasing, since $a^{-t}=1/a^t$. In particular, for $q>0$, $0<2^{-2q}<1$, because $\log2>\log1=0$ and $\exp$ is positive and increasing. For $0<\epsilon<1$, $\log\epsilon<0$, so $u\ge v$ implies $\epsilon^u\le\epsilon^v$. Finally, for $\eta>0$ and any $M>0$, if $0<\epsilon<\exp(-M/\eta)$ then $\eta\log\epsilon<-M$, so $\epsilon^\eta<\exp(-M)$; the latter tends to zero as $M\to\infty$. These facts use $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, strict increase of $\log$ and $\exp$, $\log1=0$, positivity of $\exp$, and its limit at $-\infty$. [[def-real-power]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Example and facts [A1], [F1]–[F11].

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Example and facts [A1], [A2], [F1]–[F11].

1.1 Let $H=\ell^2$ with standard basis $(e_j)$ and set $\tau_j^2=j^{-1-2\alpha}$. Each dyadic block $2^k\le j<2^{k+1}$ has at most $2^k$ terms, each at most $2^{-k(1+2\alpha)}$, so [F5] gives $\sum_j\tau_j^2\le\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}<\infty$; here the geometric ratio satisfies $0<2^{-2\alpha}<1$ by [F11]. Define $\Gamma e_j=\tau_j^2e_j$. It is positive and self-adjoint; its truncations $\Gamma_N$ have finite rank, and $\|\Gamma-\Gamma_N\|\le\sup_{j>N}\tau_j^2\le\sum_{j>N}\tau_j^2\to0$, so [F6] makes $\Gamma$ compact. The expansion $\Gamma x=\sum_j\langle x,\tau_j^2e_j\rangle e_j$ has nuclear sum $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$, so [F6] also makes it trace class. By [F7] there is a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G$ in $H$ with covariance $\Gamma$. For each finite coordinate vector, every linear projection is centered normal by [F7], hence it is jointly Gaussian by [F8]; its covariance matrix is diagonal with entries $\tau_j^2$. Repeatedly applying [F9] to the first coordinate and the remaining block proves that the coordinates are independent, and [F10] identifies their laws as $N(0,\tau_j^2)$. Thus the law of $G$ is the stated prior on $\ell^2$. [A1, A2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Put $d=1+2\alpha+2p$ and $J=\lceil\epsilon^{-2/d}\rceil$. Since $\epsilon^{-2/d}\ge1$, one has $\epsilon^{-2/d}\le J\le2\epsilon^{-2/d}$. The posterior variance satisfies $v_j\le\min\{j^{-1-2\alpha},\epsilon^2j^{2p}\}$. Therefore $\sum_{j\ge1}v_j\le\epsilon^2\sum_{j\le J}j^{2p}+\sum_{j>J}j^{-1-2\alpha}\le\epsilon^2J^{2p+1}+2J^{-2\alpha}\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-2\alpha k}\le C_{\alpha,p}\epsilon^{4\alpha/d}$. The finite sum has at most $J$ terms each at most $J^{2p}$; for the tail, the block $2^kJ<j\le2^{k+1}J$ has at most $2^{k+1}J$ terms, each at most $(2^kJ)^{-1-2\alpha}$. The conversions between powers of $J$ and $\epsilon$ use the positive-base power order in [F11]. [F3, F4, F5, F11, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Write $b_j=1-\lambda_j=\epsilon^2/(\epsilon^2+j^{-d})\le\min\{1,\epsilon^2j^d\}$. The ellipsoid condition gives $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le L^2\sup_j b_j^2j^{-2\beta}$. For $j\le J$, this supremum is bounded by $\epsilon^4J^{2d-2\beta}$ when $\beta\le d$, and by $\epsilon^4$ when $\beta>d$. For $j>J$, it is at most $J^{-2\beta}$. The bounds on $J$ in step 1.2 give $\sum_jb_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{\min\{4\beta/d,4\}}$. This treats the equality case $\beta=d$ in the first branch. The power-order comparisons use $0<\epsilon\le1$ and the positive-base facts in [F11]. [F3, F4, F11, given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Since $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j\le1$, one has $v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2=v_j\lambda_j\le v_j$. The exact sum [F1] and steps 1.2–2.1 therefore give $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C_{\alpha,\beta,p,L}\epsilon^{4\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/d}$; here $4\alpha/d<4$. Put $\eta=2\min\{\alpha,\beta\}/d>0$. By [F11], $r_\epsilon=\epsilon^\eta\to0$, as required in the rate definition. Since $0<\epsilon\le1$, [F11] also permits the posterior-moment bound to be written as $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$. The expected posterior tail outside $M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ is therefore at most $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$. By [F2], this is the stated contraction rate. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F4, F11, given, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
