## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty bounded open set, let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be measurable, and use arc-length measure $d\theta$ on $S^1$. For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$, the function $(\theta,s)\mapsto R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)$ belongs to $L^2(\Theta\times\mathbb R,d\theta\,ds)$ and satisfies $\|R_{\mathcal S}f\|_{L^2(\Theta\times\mathbb R)}^2\le \operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\,|\Theta|\,\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$, a measurable $\Theta\subset S^1$, and $f\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-schwartz-radon-transform]]: the data on the line with normal $\theta$ and offset $s$ is $\int_\mathbb R f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$.

[F2] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]: for square-integrable functions $u,v$, $\int|uv|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$.

[F3] [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]: under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism transforms an $L^1$ Lebesgue integral by the absolute Jacobian determinant.

[F4] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: absolutely integrable functions on product spaces satisfy the iterated-integral formula.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is used by [F3] for the Lebesgue change-of-variables formula; the remaining estimates are direct.

## Proof

1.1 Choose $R>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq\overline B_R(0)$. If $|t|>R$, then $|s\theta+t\theta^\perp|\ge|t|>R$ and the integrand in [F1] is zero. On any compact set of $(\theta,s)$, uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact image of $(s,\theta,t)$ for $|t|\le R$ shows that the line integrals vary continuously: the difference of two such integrals is at most $2R$ times the uniform difference of their integrands. Hence the data function is continuous and measurable. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 Put $D=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)$ and $T_{\theta,s}=\{t\in\mathbb R:s\theta+t\theta^\perp\in\Omega\}$. Any two points of $T_{\theta,s}$ differ by at most $D$, so this open set is contained in an interval of length at most $D$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F2] on $T_{\theta,s}$, where the constant function $1$ has squared integral at most $D$, gives $|R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)|^2\le D\int_{\mathbb R}|f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|^2\,dt$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 The function $(\theta,s,t)\mapsto|f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|^2$ is bounded and vanishes unless $|s|,|t|\le R$, so it is integrable on the finite-measure set $\Theta\times[-R,R]^2$. Apply [F4] to exchange the iterated integrals, and for each $\theta$ apply [F3] to the orthogonal diffeomorphism $(s,t)\mapsto s\theta+t\theta^\perp$, whose absolute Jacobian is one. This gives $\int_\Theta\int_{\mathbb R^2}|f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|^2\,ds\,dt\,d\theta=|\Theta|\,\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. Integrating step 1.2 yields the claimed bound and square-integrability. [F3, F4, A1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. For every $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$, changing an ordered basis by an integral unimodular congruence or changing a knot Seifert matrix by either elementary enlargement or reduction preserves the signature of $H_\omega$. Consequently, the nonroot Levine–Tristram signature and its one-sided-average value at every Alexander root are independent of the spanning surface and basis.

## Statement references

[[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature|The Hermitian matrix and signature convention]]

[[def-seifert-matrix-s-equivalence|The two elementary enlargement matrices]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, an oriented knot Seifert matrix $V$, its two enlargement matrices, and $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$.

[A1] Full AC supplies the Seifert pairing and surface hypotheses. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A basis change is $V\mapsto P^TVP$ for $P\in GL_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$; knot surfaces are related by isotopies and the two enlargements. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]], [[lem-seifert-matrices-of-a-knot-are-s-equivalent]], [[def-seifert-matrix-s-equivalence]]

[F2] Signature is the positive eigenvalue count minus negative eigenvalue count of a finite Hermitian matrix. [[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature]]

[F3] The one-sided signature limits at every Alexander root exist, so their arithmetic averages are defined. [[lem-levine-tristram-one-sided-averages-exist]]

## Proof

1.1 Since $P$ is real, $H_\omega(P^TVP)=P^TH_\omega(V)P$. An invertible congruence is a change of coordinates in the associated Hermitian form, so its positive and negative indices are unchanged: a maximal positive subspace maps bijectively by $P$, and likewise for negative subspaces. Hence the signature is invariant under basis change. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Put $c=1-\omega\ne0$. For either enlargement, the enlarged Hermitian matrix has block form
$$\widetilde H=\begin{pmatrix}H&b&0\\b^*&z(c+\bar c)&\lambda\\0&\bar\lambda&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad |\lambda|=|c|>0,$$
where $H=H_\omega(V)$, $b$ is the column determined by the enlargement vectors, and $z\in\mathbb Z$. The lower $2\times2$ block $D$ has determinant $-|c|^2<0$, hence one positive and one negative eigenvalue. Its inverse has $(D^{-1})_{11}=0$. The block congruence eliminating $b$ therefore has Schur complement $H-b(D^{-1})_{11}b^*=H$, so $\widetilde H$ is congruent to $H\oplus D$. The block $D$ contributes signature $0$, proving enlargement invariance for every $\omega\ne1$, including singular parameters. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], any two knot matrices are connected by the operations of steps 1.1 and 2.1, so their signatures agree at every nonroot parameter. The one-sided signatures are equal as functions on each punctured neighboring arc; by [F3] their arithmetic averages are defined and agree at a root as well. Reductions reverse the same equalities. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $n$ ordered crossings, the procedure that enumerates all $2^n$ smoothing states, assigns one copy of $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ per resolution circle, places a generator in degrees $i=|v|-n_-$ and $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$, and sums the signed merge or split edge maps terminates after finitely many operations. Its output is a finite direct sum of finite-rank free abelian groups with a differential of bidegree $(1,0)$ satisfying $d^2=0$; hence it is a bounded bigraded cochain complex.

## Statement references

[[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram|State enumeration and edge-map procedure]]

[[lem-khovanov-cube-differential-squares-to-zero|Square-zero property of the signed differential]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial* (1999), §§3.3–4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Bar-Natan, *On Khovanov's categorification of the Jones polynomial* (2002), §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0201043)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology* (2022), §4](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

[Zhang, *Notes on Khovanov homology* (2025), §§3.5–3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1)

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ with an ordered crossing set of cardinality $n$ and the finite state procedure in the Theorem.

[F1] The procedure traverses each function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$ once, uses a finite number of edge maps per state, and assigns $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$ with the stated gradings ([[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]]).

[F2] The signed edge sum has square zero for every such finite ordered diagram ([[lem-khovanov-cube-differential-squares-to-zero]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $n=|C(D)|$, there are exactly $2^n$ states; each complete smoothing of a finite closed diagram has finitely many circles. Since $\mathcal A$ is free of rank two with basis $1,X$, each state module is finite-rank free, and the finite sum of these modules is finite-rank free. The procedure visits each of finitely many states and at most $n$ outgoing edges per state, so it terminates. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Each edge changes $|v|$ and $i$ by $+1$ and changes the algebraic degree by $-1$ through $m$ or $\Delta$, so its total quantum-degree change is $+1-1=0$. By [F2] the returned differential squares to zero. The state set is finite, so only finitely many homological degrees occur; this is a bounded bigraded cochain complex. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\ell>0$ be the unique real satisfying $\ell^4=\pi/(2\sqrt3)$, take $D=[0,\ell]^3$, $k=1$, and the unit contrast $q=1_D$. Then $C_D=1/(2\sqrt2)<1$, so $\rho_1(q)<1$ and the exact far-field data lie on the small-norm Born branch. Uniformly over all incident and observation directions, the first Born amplitude error is at most $\ell^3/(4\pi(2\sqrt2-1))$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-fixed-frequency-far-field-data|The small-norm domain is $\rho_k(q)<1$.]]

[[lem-ip-born-linearization-of-the-scattering-map|The uniform error estimate in terms of $M$, $C_D$, and $\rho_k(q)$.]]

[[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded|The operator-norm bound $\rho_k(q)\le C_D\|q\|_\infty$.]]

[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind|The cube $\lbrack0,\ell\rbrack^3$ has Lebesgue measure $\ell^3$.]]

[[thm-nth-roots-exist|A positive real has a unique positive fourth root.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $D=[0,\ell]^3$ with $\ell>0$ and $\ell^4=\pi/(2\sqrt3)$, $k=1$, and $q=1_D$.

[F1] The small-norm domain is $\mathcal U_{D,1}=\{q:\rho_1(q)<1\}$ ([[def-ip-fixed-frequency-far-field-data]]).

[F2] The volume operator satisfies $\rho_1(q)\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{|D|\operatorname{diam}(D)/(4\pi)}$ ([[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]]).

[F3] For $q\in\mathcal U_{D,1}$, the uniform Born remainder is at most $\frac{M}{4\pi}\|q\|_\infty\frac{\rho_1(q)}{1-\rho_1(q)}$ and, when $C_D\|q\|_\infty<1$, at most $\frac{MC_D}{4\pi}\frac{\|q\|_\infty^2}{1-C_D\|q\|_\infty}$ ([[lem-ip-born-linearization-of-the-scattering-map]]).

[F4] The Lebesgue measure of the closed cube $[0,\ell]^3$ is $\ell^3$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F5] The Euclidean norm in $\mathbb R^3$ is $\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2}$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F6] The unique nonnegative real $\ell$ satisfying $\ell^4=\pi/(2\sqrt3)$ exists, and it is positive because the right-hand side is positive ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]).

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed in the L2 operator and Neumann-series suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Verification

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 By [F4], $M=|D|=\ell^3$. The coordinate formula [F5] shows that the largest distance in the cube is attained by opposite corners and is $\operatorname{diam}(D)=\sqrt3\,\ell$. Also $\|q\|_\infty=1$. [given, F4, F5]

2.1 Substituting the values from step 1.1 into [F2] gives $\rho_1(q)\le C_D=\sqrt{\frac{\ell^3\sqrt3\ell}{4\pi}}=\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt3\ell^4}{4\pi}}=\frac1{2\sqrt2}<1.$ The final strict inequality follows from $\sqrt2>1$. Hence $q\in\mathcal U_{D,1}$ by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TCv\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$X$ be a random vector with law $N_n(m,C)$, and define
$\mu_X(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. Write
$\operatorname{Ran}(C)=\{Cv:v\in\mathbb R^n\}$, and put
$r=\dim\operatorname{Ran}(C)$. For a Borel probability $\mu$ on
$\mathbb R^n$, define its topological support by
$$ \operatorname{supp}(\mu)=\{x:\mu(B(x,\varepsilon))>0\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0\}, $$
where $B(x,\varepsilon)$ is the open Euclidean ball. If $r>0$, there are
$U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}$ and a symmetric positive-definite
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ with $U^TU=I_r$ such that
$$ C=U\Lambda U^T,\qquad \operatorname{Ran}(C)=\operatorname{Ran}(U),\qquad C^\dagger=U\Lambda^{-1}U^T. $$
Moreover, $X$ has the same law as $m+U\Lambda^{1/2}Z$, where
$Z\sim N_r(0,I_r)$, and
$$ \operatorname{supp}(\mu_X)=m+\operatorname{Ran}(C). $$
Here $C^\dagger$ is the unique matrix satisfying
$CC^\dagger C=C$, $C^\dagger CC^\dagger=C^\dagger$, and such that
$CC^\dagger$ and $C^\dagger C$ are symmetric. If $r=0$, then
$C=0$, $X=m$ almost surely, $C^\dagger=0$, and the support is $\{m\}$.

## Statement references

[[def-multivariate-normal-law|A finite Gaussian law permits singular positive-semidefinite covariance and has the corresponding square-root representation.]]

[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse|The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse is defined by the four Penrose equations.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, a symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariance matrix $C$, a mean vector $m$, and a supplied
law $X\sim N_n(m,C)$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the multivariate-normal and standard-normal construction
interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A finite-dimensional non-negative operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis
with non-negative eigenvalues. [[thm-non-negative-operator-characterisations]]

[F2] A finite-dimensional non-negative operator has a unique non-negative
square root. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]

[F3] A multivariate-normal law permits singular covariance and is the law of
its mean plus the covariance square root applied to a vector of independent
standard-normal coordinates. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] A positive-definite multivariate-normal covariance gives a Lebesgue
density that is strictly positive everywhere. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F5] A matrix is a Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse when it satisfies the four
Penrose equations, and every finite real matrix has a unique such matrix.
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]], [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]]

## Proof
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $C$ and order it so the positive eigenvalues are $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. Let $U$ have the corresponding eigenvectors as columns and set $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)$. The zero eigenspace is the orthogonal complement of these columns, so $C=U\Lambda U^T$ and $\operatorname{Ran}(C)=\operatorname{Ran}(U)$. When $r=0$, the eigenbasis gives $C=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 If $r>0$, set $P=U\Lambda^{-1}U^T$. The decomposition in step 1.1 gives $CP=PC=UU^T$, hence $CPC=C$ and $PCP=P$; also $CP$ and $PC$ are symmetric. Thus $P$ satisfies all four equations in [F5], so uniqueness gives $P=C^\dagger$. If $r=0$, the zero matrix satisfies the four equations for $C=0$, and uniqueness gives $C^\dagger=0$. [F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Suppose $r>0$. By [F2], the square root is $C^{1/2}=U\Lambda^{1/2}U^T$. By [F3], $X$ has the law of $m+U\Lambda^{1/2}U^TZ_n$ for a standard-normal vector $Z_n$. For every $a\in\mathbb R^r$, the scalar $a^TU^TZ_n=(Ua)^TZ_n$ is centered normal with variance $\|Ua\|_2^2=\|a\|_2^2$, so $U^TZ_n$ has law $N_r(0,I_r)$. Therefore $X$ has the stated representation. When $r=0$, [F3] makes $X=m$ almost surely. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $r>0$, let $x=m+U\Lambda^{1/2}z$ be any point of $m+\operatorname{Ran}(C)$. The continuous map $t\mapsto m+U\Lambda^{1/2}t$ sends $z$ to $x$, so the preimage of every open ball about $x$ contains an open ball about $z$. By [F4], $N_r(0,I_r)$ assigns positive measure to every nonempty open ball. The representation in step 2.2 therefore gives positive $\mu_X$-mass to every neighborhood of $x$. Conversely, the law in step 2.2 is concentrated on the finite-dimensional closed affine subspace $m+\operatorname{Ran}(C)$; every point outside it has a neighborhood of zero mass. Hence the support is exactly that subspace. If $r=0$, the point-mass law from step 2.2 has support $\{m\}$. [F4, step 2.2, given, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded open set containing a closed ball $K=\overline B_R(x_0)$ of positive radius, and let $\Theta\subset S^1$ be a nonempty open antipodally symmetric set. Write $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$ and, for a Schwartz function $g$, define $R_{\mathcal S}g(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}g(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$; use the same integral for smooth functions supported in $K$. Suppose a unit vector $v\in S^1$ satisfies $c:=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}|v\cdot\theta^\perp|>0$. For each smooth complex function $u$ supported in $K$, define $\|u\|_{H^1}:=(\|u\|_2^2+\|\partial_1u\|_2^2+\|\partial_2u\|_2^2)^{1/2}$ using Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$, and set $\|R_\Theta u\|_D:=(\int_\Theta\int_{\mathbb R}|R_{\mathcal S}u(\theta,s)|^2\,ds\,d\theta)^{1/2}$, where $ds$ is Lebesgue measure and $d\theta$ is arc-length measure. For every $M>0$ there are $a_M>0$, functions $u_N\in C_c^\infty(\operatorname{int}K;\mathbb C)$ for all integers $N\ge1$, and constants $C_m>0$ for all integers $m\ge1$, such that all $u_N$ have one fixed compact support and $\|u_N\|_{H^1}\le M$, $\|u_N\|_2=a_MN^{-1}$, and $\|R_\Theta u_N\|_D\le C_mN^{-m-1}$. Consequently, for every fixed $M>0$, no $\alpha>0$ and $C\ge0$ satisfy $\|u\|_2\le C\|R_\Theta u\|_D^\alpha$ for every smooth $u$ supported in $K$ with $\|u\|_{H^1}\le M$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data|Line-normal and blind-direction convention]]

[Venkataswaran P. Krishnan and Eric Todd Quinto, Microlocal Analysis in Tomography, §§1.3.2 and 1.5.1](https://math.tifrbng.res.in/~vkrishnan/Papers/Microlocal_Analysis_Tomography.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, $\Omega$, $K$, $\Theta$, $v$, $c>0$, and the definitions and hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-visible-covector-for-limited-angle-data]]: $\theta$ is the unit line normal and $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$ is the line tangent direction.

[F2] [[def-ip-schwartz-radon-transform]]: $R_{\mathcal S}u(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}u(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$.

[F3] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: for $0<r<R$, a smooth function equal to one on the closed radius-$r$ ball and supported in the open radius-$R$ ball exists.

[F4] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]: the integral of a product is bounded by the product of the two $L^2$ norms.

[F5] [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]: under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism changes an $L^1$ Lebesgue integral by the absolute Jacobian determinant.

[F6] [[lem-complex-integration-by-parts-on-intervals-and-decaying-lines]]: under Countable Choice, complex $C^1$ functions on a finite interval satisfy $\int u'v=[uv]-\int uv'$.

[F7] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: the product of differentiable real functions satisfies the product rule; the complex-valued formula follows by applying it to real and imaginary parts.

[F8] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: composing a smooth function with an affine line map differentiates by applying its differential to the line direction.

[F9] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]: differentiating $\cos(at)+i\sin(at)$ gives $ia(\cos(at)+i\sin(at))$ by the real chain rule.

[F10] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]: every nondegenerate box has positive Lebesgue measure equal to the product of its side lengths.

[F11] [[lem-ip-limited-angle-radon-data-is-l2-on-compact-support]]: for every smooth input with fixed compact support, the restricted data have finite $L^2(\Theta\times\mathbb R)$ norm.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is used by the box-measure supplier [F10], L2 data bound [F11], Lebesgue change-of-variables [F5], and complex integration-by-parts [F6] suppliers.

## Proof

1.1 Choose $0<r<R$ and apply [F3] to obtain a bump supported in $B_R(x_0)$ and equal to one on a smaller ball; translation of the concentric bump places it inside $K$. Its $L^2$ norm is finite and positive because it is bounded with compact support and equals one on a ball containing a nondegenerate box, whose measure is positive by [F10]. Rescale it to a real-valued $\psi$ with $\|\psi\|_2=1$. Choose $\lambda>0$ so that $\lambda(1+\|\nabla\psi\|_2+2\pi)\le M$, and put $u_N(x)=\lambda N^{-1}e^{2\pi iNv\cdot x}\psi(x)$. Then all supports equal $\operatorname{supp}\psi\Subset\operatorname{int}K$ and $\|u_N\|_2=\lambda N^{-1}$. By [F7]–[F9], $\partial_j u_N=\lambda N^{-1}e^{2\pi iNv\cdot x}(\partial_j\psi+2\pi iNv_j\psi)$, so $\|\nabla u_N\|_2\le\lambda N^{-1}\|\nabla\psi\|_2+2\pi\lambda\|v\|\,\|\psi\|_2\le\lambda(\|\nabla\psi\|_2+2\pi)$. Therefore $\|u_N\|_{H^1}\le M$; set $a_M=\lambda$. [A1, F3, F7, F8, F9, F10, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Put $a=v\cdot\theta^\perp$, so $|a|\ge c>0$. The line formula gives $R_{\mathcal S}u_N(\theta,s)=\lambda N^{-1}e^{2\pi iNs(v\cdot\theta)}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{2\pi iNat}\psi(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$. For each integer $m\ge1$, integrate the last integral by parts $m$ times over an interval containing the support of its integrand. The boundary terms vanish because $\psi$ and all its derivatives vanish near the endpoints. Applying [F6] repeatedly gives $\left|\int_{\mathbb R}e^{2\pi iNat}\psi(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt\right|\le(2\pi N|a|)^{-m}\int_{\mathbb R}|(\theta^\perp\cdot\nabla)^m\psi(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|\,dt$. [F1, F2, F6, F8, F9, A1, given, construct]

2.1 Let $D=\operatorname{diam}(\operatorname{supp}\psi)$. The set of $t$ values on a fixed line meeting this support has measure at most $D$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] bounds the square of the last integral in step 1.2 by $D\int_{\mathbb R}|(\theta^\perp\cdot\nabla)^m\psi(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|^2\,dt$. Integrate in $s$ and apply [F5] to the orthogonal change of variables $(s,t)\mapsto s\theta+t\theta^\perp$, whose absolute Jacobian is one. Expanding $(\theta^\perp\cdot\nabla)^m$ gives an $L^2$ bound independent of $\theta$, since there are finitely many derivatives and all coefficients are bounded by one. Since $|a|\ge c$ and $|\Theta|\le2\pi$, step 1.2 yields a finite constant $C_m>0$, independent of $N$, with $\|R_\Theta u_N\|_D\le C_mN^{-m-1}$. [F4, F5, A1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Fix $\alpha>0$ and choose an integer $m\ge1$ with $\alpha(m+1)>1$. The square-integrability bound [F11] makes the data norm finite for every member of the fixed-support class. If a uniform Hölder estimate with constant $C\ge0$ held on the class in the Statement, steps 1.1 and 2.1 would give $\lambda N^{-1}\le C(C_mN^{-m-1})^\alpha$ for every $N\ge1$. Multiplication by $N$ makes the right side $CC_m^\alpha N^{1-\alpha(m+1)}$, which tends to zero as $N\to\infty$, contradicting $\lambda>0$. Therefore no such estimate exists. [A1, F11, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Let $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ with unit $\eta(1)=1$ and counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$. On a movie with one unaffected circle, birth a disjoint circle and then cap that same circle by a death. The composite operator is
$$
\mathcal A\xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}\otimes\eta} \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}\otimes\epsilon} \mathcal A,
$$
which is zero and therefore is not the identity, even after allowing multiplication by an overall sign.

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}
\mathcal A
\arrow[r, "{\operatorname{id}\otimes\eta}"]
& \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
\arrow[r, "{\operatorname{id}\otimes\epsilon}"]
& \mathcal A
\end{tikzcd}
```

The movie is a cylinder on the original circle disjoint union a born-and-capped sphere; the diagram specifies the local birth and death sequence and is not used as a proof.

## Statement references

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|The unit, counit, and integral Frobenius algebra]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial*, §7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Bar-Natan, *Khovanov's homology for tangles and cobordisms*, §§7–8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410495v2)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology*, §5](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The free abelian group $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\eta(1)=1$, $\epsilon(1)=0$, and $\epsilon(X)=1$.

[F1] [[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]] gives the unit and counit formulas and the nonzero basis element $1\in\mathcal A$.

## Proof

1.1 The birth map sends $1\in\mathbb Z$ to $1\in\mathcal A$, and the following death sends this element to $\epsilon(1)=0$. Thus $\epsilon\eta=0:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Tensoring the zero map $\epsilon\eta$ with $\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$ gives the zero endomorphism of $\mathcal A$, which is the composite in the statement. The identity of $\mathcal A$ is nonzero because it sends $1$ to $1\neq0$; its negative also sends $1$ to $-1\neq0$. Hence the composite is neither the identity nor its negative. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric parameter and data spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth class, let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map, and let $(Q,d_Q)$ be a metric target space. All metric spaces in this definition carry their Borel sigma-algebras. Give $U$ the subspace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(U):=\{U\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and assume that $q:U\to Q$ is measurable from $(U,\mathcal B(U))$ to $(Q,\mathcal B(Q))$. The target $q(x)$ is the recovery object assigned to truth $x$; $Q$ may be the parameter space itself or a quotient solution-class space. A **point reconstruction rule** is a Borel map $g:Y\to Q$, and its output at data $y$ is $g(y)$. A **learned point estimator** is such a map $\widehat q_\phi$ with a fitted parameter $\phi$ in a specified parameter set. A complete training description names the probability law $P_{\rm fit}$ of all variables used to fit $\phi$; those variables may be paired or unpaired. A complete test description names a probability law $P_{\rm test}$ for evaluation pairs $(Y,q(X))$. No equality between fitting and test laws is assumed.

A finite **unrolled learned update** consists of an integer $K\geq1$, a Borel initialization $u_0:Y\to Q$, and Borel maps $T_{\phi,k}:Q\times Y\to Q$ for $0\leq k<K$, with $u_{k+1}(y)=T_{\phi,k}(u_k(y),y)$. Its output $u_K(y)$ is a point reconstruction rule. An **amortized inverse map** is a learned point estimator applied to multiple data inputs after a single fit; this term adds a reuse convention, not an accuracy guarantee.

For a real Hilbert signal space $H$, a **denoiser** is a Borel map $D_\phi:H\to H$ trained under a specified signal-corruption law and used to transform a corrupted signal into a signal estimate or an update. A denoiser is the exact minimum mean-square error map only when it equals the conditional mean for the specified signal and corruption laws. A **learned prior** is a supplied Borel probability measure $\rho_\phi$ on $H$; one construction is the pushforward law $\rho_\phi(A)=\nu(G_\phi^{-1}(A))$ for $A\in\mathcal B(H)$, where $\nu$ is a specified probability measure on a measurable source space $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ and $G_\phi:(Z,\mathcal Z)\to(H,\mathcal B(H))$ is measurable. The law or generator alone is not a data-to-target estimator.

For a finite horizon $T>0$, a specified parameter set $\Phi$, and $\phi\in\Phi$, a **score field model** in a finite-dimensional signal space $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel map $s_\phi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ intended to approximate the target field $s^*(t,x)=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ for a specified family $(p_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ of positive continuously differentiable probability densities for which $s^*$ is jointly Borel. Its complete description names a probability law $P_{\rm fit}$ for all variables used to fit $\phi$ and a probability law $P_{\rm test}$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$ for evaluation inputs $(t,x)$; the target on those inputs is $s^*(t,x)$. These laws need not agree, and no approximation guarantee under either law is implied. A score field is not itself a posterior law, posterior sample, or point reconstruction rule. A **posterior sampler** is a probability kernel $S:Y\to Q$; relative to a supplied posterior target kernel $\Pi_y$, it is exact on a data domain $D$ when $S_y=\Pi_y$ as probability measures for every $y\in D$. A draw from $S_y$ is random; obtaining a point estimate from it requires an additional summary rule. The name “learned” by itself asserts no exact recovery, stability, convergence, calibration, or train-to-test guarantee.

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. At wavenumber $k=1$, let $D=[0,1/4]^3$ and let the contrast be the constant $q(y)=512\pi$ on $D$, extended by zero outside. In the outgoing volume model, the associated operator satisfies $\|K_{q,1}\|_{L^2(D)\to L^2(D)}>2$. Thus this contrast lies outside the small-norm domain used for the Born linearization. This example makes no claim that the exact scattering equation has no solution or is nonunique.

## Example references

[[def-ip-fixed-frequency-far-field-data|The small-norm domain is $\rho_k(q)=\|K_{q,k}\|<1$.]]

[[def-volume-integral-scattering-model|The outgoing operator uses $G_k(z)=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$.]]

[[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded|The L2 operator is well-defined and bounded for bounded contrasts on finite-volume sets.]]


[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound|A vector-valued function with derivative norm at most $L$ is $L$-Lipschitz.]]


[[def-operator-norm|The operator norm is the supremum over the unit ball.]]

[[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero|The constant $\pi$ is positive.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the cube $D=[0,1/4]^3$, $k=1$, $q=512\pi\,1_D$, and the volume operator $K_{q,1}$.

[F1] The volume model defines $K_{q,1}$ by the kernel $e^{i|x-y|}/(4\pi|x-y|)$ off the diagonal and uses the zero representative on the diagonal; the operator lemma identifies its L2 value with this a.e. kernel integral ([[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]], [[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]]).

[F2] The closed box $D$ is Lebesgue measurable and has volume $(1/4)^3=1/64$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F3] The Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^3$ is $\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2}$, so every $x,y\in D$ satisfy $|x-y|\le\sqrt3/4<1/2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F4] For real $t$, $|\exp(it)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[F5] For real $r\ge0$, the curve $s\mapsto \exp(irs)$ has derivative $ir\exp(irs)$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]); a differentiable curve with derivative norm bounded by $r$ is $r$-Lipschitz ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]).

[F6] The constant function $1_D$ is a nonzero vector of $L^2(D)$ with norm $\sqrt{|D|}$, and the complex $L^2$ pairing obeys Cauchy–Schwarz ([[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]]).

[F7] The operator norm is $\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\|Tx\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

[F8] The number $\pi$ is positive ([[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]).

[F9] The small-norm domain is $\mathcal U_{D,k}=\{q:\|K_{q,k}\|<1\}$ ([[def-ip-fixed-frequency-far-field-data]]).



[A1] Countable Choice is assumed in the volume model and bounded-operator supplier ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Verification

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 By [F2], $M=|D|=1/64$. By [F3], every distance in $D$ is at most $\sqrt3/4$, and opposite corners attain this value, so $d:=\operatorname{diam}(D)=\sqrt3/4<1/2$. The indicator $1_D$ is a nonzero $L^2$ class. [given, F2, F3]

2.1 For $0\le r\le d$, the curve $\gamma(s)=e^{irs}$ on $[0,1]$ has derivative $\gamma'(s)=ir e^{irs}$, whose modulus is $r$ by [F4]. Fact [F5] gives $|e^{ir}-1|\le r$, and hence $\operatorname{Re}(e^{ir})\ge1-r\ge1-d>1/2$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For almost every $x\in D$, the kernel integral in [F1] represents $K_{q,1}1_D(x)$. For such an $x$, almost every $y\in D$ has $r=|x-y|$ in $(0,d]$ by step 1.1, and [F1] gives $\operatorname{Re}G_1(x-y)=\frac{\operatorname{Re}(e^{ir})}{4\pi r}>\frac{1}{8\pi d}.$ Integrating this pointwise lower bound against the positive constant $q=512\pi$ yields $\operatorname{Re}(K_{q,1}1_D)(x)>qM/(8\pi d)=1/d=4/\sqrt3>2$ for almost every $x\in D$; the last inequality follows by squaring the positive sides of $\sqrt3<2$. [A1, F1, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By step 3.1, $g:=|K_{q,1}1_D|^2-4$ is positive almost everywhere on $D$; [F1] and [A1] put $K_{q,1}1_D$ in $L^2(D)$, so $g$ is integrable. Since $M>0$ by step 1.1, the sets $\{x\in D:g(x)>1/n\}$ cannot all be null, as their countable union contains the positive-measure set where $g>0$. Thus for some $n$, the set $\{x\in D:g(x)>1/n\}$ has positive measure, so $\int_D g\ge |\{g>1/n\}|/n>0$; hence $\|K_{q,1}1_D\|_2^2>4M=4\|1_D\|_2^2$. The unit-ball supremum in [F7] gives $\|K_{q,1}\|>2$. By [F9] the contrast lies outside $\mathcal U_{D,1}$, so the small-norm model branch does not apply; no nonexistence or nonuniqueness conclusion follows. [A1, F1, F6, F7, F9, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Work in ZF. Let $A$ be any associative unital ring and let $C$ be a chain complex of unital right $A$-modules with $C_n=0$ for $n<0$. Supply a chain complex $F$ with $F_n=0$ outside $0\le n\le m$, each $F_n$ supplied as a finite free right $A$-module, chain maps $f:C\to F$ and $g:F\to C$, and right $A$-linear maps $h_n:C_n\to C_{n+1}$ such that
$$1_C-gf=d_Ch+hd_C.$$
Then there is a chain complex $E$ of finitely generated projective right $A$-modules, zero outside $0\le n\le N$ for some finite $N$, together with explicitly constructed chain maps $a:C\to E$, $b:E\to C$ and chain homotopies
$$1_C-ba=dH+Hd,\qquad 1_E-ab=dL+Ld.$$
The modules of $E$ below its top degree can be taken finite free, and its top module is the image of an explicit idempotent on $\bigoplus_{j=0}^mF_j$.

Neither freeness nor projectivity nor finite generation of the modules of $C$ is required. Thus the result applies in particular to the nonnegative singular or cellular free chain complexes with specified bases. More generally it applies after reindexing whenever $C$ and $F$ have a common finite lower bound. It makes no assertion for inputs unbounded below and no assertion that $E$ is finite free or that any underlying space has finite CW type. No form of the Axiom of Choice is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The ring, nonnegative complexes and explicit domination data in the Statement. Maps are composed from right to left; $d=d_C$ and $\partial=d_F$. A composition containing a zero degree module is zero. A power $h^s$ denotes the specified successive degree-one maps, and $h^0=1$.

[F1] Chain maps commute with differentials. A degree-one homotopy has boundary $dH+Hd$; mutually inverse maps up to these boundaries are a chain homotopy equivalence. These conventions are [[def-chain-map]], [[def-chain-homotopy]] and [[def-chain-homotopy-equivalence]], applied to right module homomorphisms.

[F2] Projectivity means the lifting property for surjective module homomorphisms. The left-module convention of [[def-projective-module]] is applied to $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ for right modules. Only finite free modules and their explicit summands will be used; their lifting property is proved below.

[F3] A finite list of nonempty sets admits a simultaneous choice in ZF. [[lem-finite-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 Put $u=gf$ on $C$. Repeatedly substituting $dh=1-u-hd$ gives, for every integer $s\ge1$, $$dh^s=(-1)^sh^sd+\epsilon_s h^{s-1}-\sum_{\ell=0}^{s-1}(-1)^\ell h^\ell u h^{s-1-\ell},\qquad \epsilon_s=\begin{cases}1&s\text{ odd},\\0&s\text{ even}.\end{cases}$$ For $s=1$ this is the given equation. Multiplying the formula on the right by $h$ and substituting $dh$ in its first term proves the next case: the identity coefficient changes from $\epsilon_s$ to $\epsilon_s+(-1)^s=\epsilon_{s+1}$ and the last summand acquires index $s$. This is finite induction on a specified identity, with no choices. [given, algebra]

1.2 Define $D_n=\bigoplus_{j=0}^nF_j$ for $n\ge0$, and $D_n=0$ for $n<0$. Define maps $\delta_n:D_n\to D_{n-1}$ by their finite blocks, with column $j$, row $k$, where $0\le j\le n$ and $0\le k\le n-1$: $$ (\delta_n)_{kj}=\begin{cases} 0&j\ge k+2,\\ (-1)^{n+k+1}\partial_j&j=k+1,\\ 1_{F_j}-f_jg_j&j=k,\ n+k\text{ odd},\\ f_jg_j&j=k,\ n+k\text{ even},\\ (-1)^{n+k}f_kh^{k-j}g_j&j<k. \end{cases}$$ All blocks have the displayed source and target, regardless of noncommutativity of $A$. Also define $\alpha_n:C_n\to D_n$ to have only its final component $f_n$, define $\beta_n:D_n\to C_n$ by the row $(h^ng_0,h^{n-1}g_1,\ldots,g_n)$, and let $s_n:D_n\to D_{n+1}$ be inclusion into the first $n+1$ summands. These are specified finite formulas in every degree. We next verify that $D$ is a chain complex and that the named maps have all claimed properties; these are not assumed from a matrix citation. [given, construct]

2.1 The final column of $\delta_n$ has only its final block $+\partial_n$. Therefore $\delta_n\alpha_n=\alpha_{n-1}d_n$, using $\partial f=fd$. To check $\beta_{n-1}\delta_n=d_n\beta_n$, consider column $j$. If $j=n$, the assertion is $g_{n-1}\partial_n=d_ng_n$. Otherwise put $t=n-j\ge1$. The superdiagonal contribution is $(-1)^t h^tdg_j$ (zero if $j=0$); the diagonal contribution is $\epsilon_t h^{t-1}g_j-(-1)^{t-1}h^{t-1}ug_j$. Reindexing the lower contributions by $\ell=n-1-k$ gives $-\sum_{\ell=0}^{t-2}(-1)^\ell h^\ell u h^{t-1-\ell}g_j$. The total is exactly $dh^tg_j$ by step 1.1. Thus both intertwining identities hold, without yet assuming $\delta^2=0$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.2 Directly in the blocks, $$\delta_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}\delta_n=1_{D_n}-\alpha_n\beta_n.$$ Indeed for rows $k<n$ the off-diagonal blocks cancel when $n$ is replaced by $n+1$, and the two diagonal blocks sum to $1$. In row $n$ only the first term is present: its blocks are $-f_nh^{n-j}g_j$ for $j<n$ and $1-f_ng_n$ for $j=n$. They are exactly the final row of $1-\alpha\beta$. 3.1 We prove $\delta_{n-1}\delta_n=0$ by induction on $n$. It holds at $n=1$ since $D_{-1}=0$. On the remaining summand $F_n$, the two final-column observations give $\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$. Thus the composite vanishes on every summand. This proves $\delta^2=0$. Now step 2.1 says that $\alpha,\beta$ are chain maps, and step 2.2 together with $1-\beta\alpha=dh+hd$ gives a chain homotopy equivalence $C\simeq D$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F1, induction, algebra]

4.1 Set $T=\bigoplus_{j=0}^mF_j$. For all $n\ge m$, $D_n$ is canonically $T$, because all subsequent summands are zero. For $n\ge m+1$, the square matrix $\delta_n:T\to T$ depends only on the parity of $n$. Write $p$ for its value when $n$ is even. The formulas show that its value when $n$ is odd is $1-p$: the off-diagonal blocks change sign and the diagonal blocks are complementary. Taking two consecutive such degrees in $\delta^2=0$ gives $p(1-p)=0=(1-p)p$, hence $p^2=p$. No assertion that the homotopy idempotent $fg$ itself is strictly idempotent has been made. [step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Choose the explicit even integer $N=2(m+1)$, and let $q=p:T\to T$. Define $E_n=D_n$ for $0\le n<N$, $E_N=qT\subseteq T=D_N$, and $E_n=0$ otherwise. Restrict $\delta_N$ to $qT$ at the top, and keep $\delta_n$ below it. The square-zero identities remain valid by step 3.1. The maps $J:E\to D$ are the evident inclusions. Define $I:D\to E$ to be identity below $N$, $q$ in degree $N$ and zero above $N$. At degree $N$, $\delta_Nq=\delta_N$ because $1-q=\delta_{N+1}$ and $\delta_N\delta_{N+1}=0$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Define $t_n:D_n\to D_{n+1}$ to be zero for $n<N$ and the canonical identity $T\to T$ for $n\ge N$. Then $$1_D-JI=\delta t+t\delta.$$ Below $N$ both sides are zero. In degree $N$ the right side is $\delta_{N+1}=1-q$, which is the left side. Above $N$ it is the sum of the two complementary matrices $p$ and $1-p$, hence identity, as is the left side. Thus $I,J$ give a specified chain homotopy equivalence between $D$ and the bounded complex $E$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, construct, algebra]

6.2 The modules $E_n$ below $N$ are finite direct sums of the supplied finite free modules, so their concatenated bases are finite. The module $qT$ is generated by the finitely many vectors $q(e_i)$, where $(e_i)$ is that concatenated basis of $T$, and $T=qT\oplus(1-q)T$: write $x=qx+(1-q)x$, and apply $q$ to an element in the intersection to show it is zero. For completeness its projectivity is choice-free. Given a surjection $v:U\to V$ and a right-linear $w:qT\to V$, take, for each of the finitely many $e_i$, a lift in $U$ of $w(qe_i)$. Their simultaneous existence is [F3]. Extend this finite assignment right-linearly to a map $\widetilde w:T\to U$. Then $v\widetilde w=wq$, and restriction to $qT$ is the requested lift. The same proof with $q=1$ gives projectivity of the lower finite free modules. This verifies the actual lifting property, not the general claim that arbitrary free modules are projective in ZF. [step 5.1, F2, F3, algebra]

7.1 Set $a=I\alpha$, $b=\beta J$. These are chain maps and $$1_C-ba=d(h+\beta t\alpha)+(h+\beta t\alpha)d,$$ since $1_C-\beta JI\alpha=(1_C-\beta\alpha)+\beta(1_D-JI)\alpha$. Similarly, using $IJ=1_E$ and step 2.2, $$1_E-ab=\delta_E(IsJ)+(IsJ)\delta_E.$$ Indeed $I(1_D-\alpha\beta)J=1_E-I\alpha\beta J$. These are the explicit required homotopies $H=h+\beta t\alpha$ and $L=IsJ$. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, F1, algebra]

8.1 Every degree of $D$, every matrix product used to define its maps, and each component of the homotopies uses a finite sum and finitely many compositions of supplied maps. The single family indexed by all nonnegative degrees is defined by these formulas; it is not obtained by independently selecting a lift or basis in each degree. The only lifts selected in the entire projectivity verification are a finite list for one supplied lifting problem. If the two input complexes vanish below a common integer $b$, reindex $C'_n=C_{n+b}$, $F'_n=F_{n+b}$ with the same differentials and domination equations, apply the construction, and reindex the result back. No infinite recursion of choices and no unbounded-below input is involved. The proof therefore establishes exactly the stated ZF conclusion for the required bounded-below setting. [step 1.2, step 5.1, step 6.2, step 7.1, F3] ∎

The explicit algebraic strictification follows Ranicki's displayed matrices and Proposition 3.1, with all signs fixed and all needed identities verified locally above. In the scanned printed p.119, the piecewise expression and the displayed even/odd matrices have inconsistent signs/parities; the formulas here follow the displayed matrices and the verified final-column chain-map and homotopy identities. ## Statement

Let $R$ be an associative unital ring with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors, embedded as a unital subring in a division ring $K$, let $N=K/R$ as a right $R$-module, and let $C_*$ be a chain complex of right $R$-modules with $C_0,C_1$ finite free and $C_j=0$ for $j<0$. If either $H_0(C_*)=0$ or every right ideal of $R$ is principal, then restriction to cycles induces an isomorphism of abelian groups
$$\kappa:H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,N))\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_1(C_*),N).$$
If the coefficient Hom groups carry a compatible commuting left action, this is an isomorphism for that action as well. No choice principle is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The displayed ring embedding, finite supplied free bases in degrees zero and one, and one of the two alternatives in the Statement. Write $Z_1=\ker d_1$, $B_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$, and $B_0=\operatorname{im}d_1$.

## Proof

1.1 A cochain $f:C_1\to N$ is a cocycle precisely when $f(B_1)=0$. Restricting to $Z_1$ therefore induces a map $H_1=Z_1/B_1\to N$. A coboundary $g d_1$ vanishes on $Z_1$, so this induces the stated well-defined map $\kappa$. It is onto if every map $Z_1\to N$ vanishing on $B_1$ extends to $C_1$. It is injective if every map $B_0\to N$ extends to $C_0$: indeed a cocycle restricting to zero on $Z_1$ factors uniquely through $d_1:C_1\to B_0$, and such an extension expresses it as a coboundary. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For the principal-right-ideal alternative, $N$ is right divisible: given $n=q+R\in N$ and $0\ne a\in R$, the element $q a^{-1}+R$ multiplied on the right by $a$ equals $n$. We prove by induction on $m$ that any right-linear map $f:S\to N$ from any right submodule $S\subseteq R^m$ extends to $R^m$. For $m=0$ this is immediate. Let the projection of $S$ to the last coordinate be the right ideal $J$. If $J=0$, apply induction on the first $m-1$ coordinates and give the last basis vector value zero. Otherwise write $J=aR$ with $a\ne0$ and take $z=(z',a)\in S$. Then $S=S'\oplus zR$, where $S'=S\cap(R^{m-1}\times0)$: subtract $zr$ from an element with last coordinate $ar$, and uniqueness follows from the absence of zero divisors. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $H_0=0$, then $d_1:C_1\to C_0$ is onto. Lift the finitely many given basis vectors of $C_0$ and extend linearly to a section $s:C_0\to C_1$. This gives $C_1=Z_1\oplus s(C_0)$. Extend a map from $Z_1$ by zero on the second summand to prove surjectivity in step 1.1. Here $B_0=C_0$, so the extension required for injectivity is automatic. The section uses only finitely many selections. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 Extend $f|_{S'}$ to $g:R^{m-1}\to N$ by induction. Right divisibility supplies $v\in N$ with $va=f(z)-g(z')$. Define the extension on $R^m$ by $(u,r)\mapsto g(u)+vr$. It agrees with $f$ on $S'$ and on $z$, hence on all of $S$. This completes the finite induction, using one ideal generator, one lift, and one division at each of finitely many stages. It does not use a maximal extension argument or an infinite family of choices. [step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Apply the extension result of step 2.2 first to $Z_1\subseteq C_1$ and then to $B_0\subseteq C_0$, using the supplied finite bases. These are exactly the surjectivity and injectivity requirements of step 1.1. The first alternative was established in step 2.1, so $\kappa$ is an isomorphism in either case. Restriction and passage to cycles commute with every compatible left coefficient action; thus the inverse, being unique, also respects that action. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $1\le p<\infty$. Let $X,Y,Z$ be real Banach spaces, let $X_0$ be a closed linear subspace of $X$, and let $D,U\subseteq X$. Let $x_0,x^\dagger\in D\cap U\cap X_0$, let $F:D\to Y$, $K\in\mathcal L(Z,Y)$, and $r:D\to Z$ satisfy $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ for all $x\in D$. Assume $r|_U:U\to\widetilde U$ is a bijection, $r$ is Lipschitz on $D$ with constant $L_r$, and $r$ has bounded linear Gâteaux derivatives on $U$. Let $P:X\to X$ be a bounded linear projection with $P^2=P$, $P|_{X_0}=0$, and $(I-P)(X)\subseteq X_0$. Assume $P(x^\dagger)=0$ and $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)\in D\cap X_0$ for each admitted $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$.

Let $\check R:X_0\to[0,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial\check R(x^\dagger)$, and write

$$D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(z,x^\dagger):=\check R(z)-\check R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle_{X_0^*,X_0}.$$

Suppose that, on the stated sublevel $\check R(z)\le R_0$, the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle_{X_0^*,X_0}\le bD_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(z,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(z)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)$$

holds for some $R_0\ge\check R(x^\dagger)$ and $0\le b<1$. Assume that $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is continuous, nondecreasing and concave, with $\psi(0)=0$, and that for a constant $C_\psi>0$,

$$\psi(a+b)\le C_\psi\bigl(\psi(a)+\psi(b)\bigr)\qquad(a,b\ge0).$$

Let $H(q):=\sup_{s\ge0}(\psi(s)-qs)$, and assume the values of $H$ used below are finite. Let $\gamma>C_\psi$, $C_P\ge2^{p-1}\|K\|^pL_r^p$, and $\widetilde C_Q>0$. Let $R_P:P(X)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfy $R_P(0)=0$ and

$$R_P(z)\ge\gamma\psi(C_P\|z\|_X^p)\qquad(z\in P(X)).$$

For each admitted $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$, put $u(\widehat r):=r^{-1}(\widehat r)$ and $\check x(\widehat r):=(I-P)u(\widehat r)$. Assume the compatibility bound

$$\|\widehat r-r(x^\dagger)\|_Z^p\le\widetilde C_Q\left(D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x(\widehat r),x^\dagger)+\psi(C_P\|Pu(\widehat r)\|_X^p)\right).$$

Choose $c_{\beta\alpha}>0$ with $c_{\beta\alpha}\le\min\{1-b,\gamma-C_\psi\}/(4\widetilde C_Q)$, and set

$$m:=\min\{1-b,\gamma-C_\psi\},\quad a:=2^{1-p},\quad \lambda:=2^{1-p},\quad t:=2^{2-2p}-2^{p-1}c_{\rm tcr}^p,\quad v:=(1+2^{p-1})c_{\rm tcr}^p,\quad \overline C:=C_\psi 2^{2p-2}.$$

Assume $0<c_{\rm tcr}<1$ and $t>0$, and for all $x_1,x_2\in U$ assume

$$\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)-r'(x_2)(x_1-x_2)\|_Z\le c_{\rm tcr}\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)\|_Z.$$

Assume the candidate projected point satisfies $\check R(\check x(\widehat r_{n+1}))\le R_0$.

Let $Q(a,b):=\|a-b\|_Z$. Fix $\delta>0$, $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y\le\delta$, and $\alpha_n>0$, with $\beta_n:=c_{\beta\alpha}\alpha_n$. Suppose $(\widehat r_{n+1},x_{n+1})\in\widetilde U\times U$ satisfies, for some $\eta_n\ge0$,

$$\mathcal J_n^\delta(\widehat r_{n+1},x_{n+1})\le\mathcal J_n^\delta(\widehat r,x)+\eta_n\qquad((\widehat r,x)\in\widetilde U\times U),$$

where $\mathcal J_n^\delta$ is the frozen objective in the Joint and frozen-Newton objectives definition, with regularizer $\mathcal R(\widehat r)=\check R(\check x(\widehat r))+R_P(Pu(\widehat r))$ and distance $Q$.

Define

$$E_{n+1}:=\frac{c_{\beta\alpha}}{C_\psi}\left(\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r(x^\dagger)\|_Z^p+t\|r(x_{n+1})-r(x^\dagger)\|_Z^p\right),$$

$$S_{n+1}:=\frac{1}{C_\psi}\left(2^{1-p}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r(x^\dagger))\|_Y^p+\|Px_{n+1}\|_X^p\right),$$

and

$$d_n:=\frac{c_{\beta\alpha}}{C_\psi}\alpha_n v\|r(x_n)-r(x^\dagger)\|_Z^p+\frac{2\delta^p+\eta_n}{C_\psi}.$$

Then

$$S_{n+1}+\alpha_nE_{n+1}\le d_n+\alpha_n\psi(\overline C S_{n+1}).$$

Consequently,

$$E_{n+1}\le\frac{d_n}{\alpha_n}+H\!\left(\frac{1}{\overline C\alpha_n}\right),\qquad S_{n+1}\le2\left(d_n+\alpha_nH\!\left(\frac{1}{2\overline C\alpha_n}\right)\right).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-differential-range-invariance|Range-invariance factorization and domains]]

[[def-ip-relaxed-range-invariance-objective|Joint and frozen-Newton objective definitions]]

[Barbara Kaltenbacher, *Convergence rates under a range invariance condition with application to electrical impedance tomography*, equations (2.31)–(2.41)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18704)

[Frederic Weidling, *Variational Source Conditions and Conditional Stability Estimates for Inverse Problems in PDEs*, Theorem 2.20](https://univerlag.uni-goettingen.de/bitstream/handle/3/isbn-978-3-86395-411-6/weidling.pdf?sequence=1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** All spaces, maps, penalties, parameters, source inequalities, compatibility inequalities, and the approximate frozen step satisfy the hypotheses in the Statement.

[A1] The projected point $\check x(\widehat r_{n+1})$ belongs to the regularizer sublevel where the VSC holds.

[F1] [[def-ip-differential-range-invariance]]: $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ on the specified domain, and $r|_U$ is invertible onto $\widetilde U$.

[F2] [[def-ip-relaxed-range-invariance-objective]]: the frozen objective has data term $\|K\widehat r+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|^p$, regularizer $\alpha_n\mathcal R(\widehat r)$, coupling $\beta_n\|\ell_n(x)-\widehat r\|^p$, and penalty $\|Px\|^p$, where $\ell_n(x)=r(x_n)+r'(x_n)(x-x_n)$.

[F3] [[def-ip-banach-convex-subgradient-and-dual-pairing]]: $\xi^\dagger\in\partial\check R(x^\dagger)$ means $\check R(z)\ge\check R(x^\dagger)+\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle$ for every $z\in X_0$.

[F4] [[def-ip-bregman-distance]]: $D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(z,x^\dagger)=\check R(z)-\check R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle$.

[F5] [[def-ip-variational-source-condition]]: $-\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle\le bD_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(z,x^\dagger)+\psi(\|F(z)-F(x^\dagger)\|^p)$ on the stated sublevel.

[F6] [[lem-ip-index-function-young-conjugate-bound]]: if $r+\alpha e\le d+\alpha\psi(Cr)$, then $e\le d/\alpha+H(1/(C\alpha))$ and $r\le2(d+\alpha H(1/(2C\alpha)))$.

## Proof

1.1 Write $r^\dagger:=r(x^\dagger)$, $u:=r^{-1}(\widehat r_{n+1})$, $\check x:=(I-P)u$, and $\ell_n(x):=r(x_n)+r'(x_n)(x-x_n)$. Compare the approximate-minimum inequality with $(\widehat r,x)=(r^\dagger,x^\dagger)$. The competitor has data residual at most $\delta^p$, penalty $R_P(0)=0$, and $Px^\dagger=0$. If $g:=K\widehat r_{n+1}+F(x_0)-y^\delta$, then $K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)=g+(y^\delta-y)$; convexity of $s\mapsto s^p$ gives $\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p\le2^{p-1}(\|g\|^p+\delta^p)$. Thus the comparison gives $2^{1-p}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p+\alpha_n(\mathcal R(\widehat r_{n+1})-\check R(x^\dagger))+\beta_n\|\ell_n(x_{n+1})-\widehat r_{n+1}\|^p+\|Px_{n+1}\|^p\le2\delta^p+\eta_n+\beta_n\|\ell_n(x^\dagger)-r^\dagger\|^p$. The remainder hypothesis at $(x^\dagger,x_n)$ and $c_{\rm tcr}<1$ imply $\|\ell_n(x^\dagger)-r^\dagger\|^p\le c_{\rm tcr}^p\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $A:=\|r(x_{n+1})-\widehat r_{n+1}\|$, $B:=\|\ell_n(x_{n+1})-\widehat r_{n+1}\|$, and $D_n:=\|r(x_{n+1})-\ell_n(x_{n+1})\|$. The triangle inequality gives $A\le B+D_n$, hence $B^p\ge2^{1-p}A^p-D_n^p$. Applying the same power inequality to $\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|\le A+\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|$ gives $A^p\ge2^{1-p}\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p-\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p$. The Taylor hypothesis and another triangle-power estimate give $D_n^p\le2^{p-1}c_{\rm tcr}^p(\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p+\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p)$. Therefore $\|\ell_n(x_{n+1})-\widehat r_{n+1}\|^p\ge t\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p-\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p-2^{p-1}c_{\rm tcr}^p\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p$, with $t=2^{2-2p}-2^{p-1}c_{\rm tcr}^p$ and $\lambda=2^{1-p}$. [given, algebra]

1.3 Set $z:=Pu$. Since $\|r(\check x)-r(u)\|\le L_r\|z\|$, the factorization and power inequality give $\|F(\check x)-F(x^\dagger)\|^p\le2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p+2^{p-1}\|K\|^pL_r^p\|z\|^p$. By the VSC [F5], the Bregman identity [F4], the penalty lower bound, and $\psi(a+b)\le C_\psi(\psi(a)+\psi(b))$, we obtain $\mathcal R(\widehat r_{n+1})-\check R(x^\dagger)\ge m(D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger)+\psi(C_P\|z\|^p))-C_\psi\psi(2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p)$. Indeed, the VSC yields coefficient $1-b$ on the Bregman term, and the penalty leaves coefficient $\gamma-C_\psi$ on the penalty-index term; their minimum is $m$. [A1, F1, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Substituting steps 1.1–1.3 into the objective comparison and applying the compatibility inequality gives $C_\psi S_{n+1}+\alpha_nmT+\beta_nt\|r(x_{n+1})-r^\dagger\|^p\le\beta_nv\|r(x_n)-r^\dagger\|^p+\beta_n\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p+\alpha_nC_\psi\psi(2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger)\|^p)+2\delta^p+\eta_n$, where $T:=D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger)+\psi(C_P\|Pu\|^p)$. By [F3], $D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger)\ge0$, so $T\ge0$. Since $\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p\le\widetilde C_QT$ and $\beta_n\lambda\widetilde C_Q\le\alpha_nm/4$, the left regularizer term absorbs the displayed compatibility term and a second copy of it, leaving $\alpha_nmT/2$; in particular it bounds another $\beta_n\lambda\|\widehat r_{n+1}-r^\dagger\|^p$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

3.1 Divide step 2.1 by $C_\psi$ and use $\beta_n=c_{\beta\alpha}\alpha_n$. Applying [F6] with $c_1=c_2=1$, $C_3=\overline C$, $r=S_{n+1}$, and $e=E_{n+1}$ proves both conjugate bounds. [step 2.1, F6, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold with one torus cusp and a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric. In a neighborhood of its complete holonomy, the representation deformation space modulo conjugacy is a complex one-dimensional manifold, with local coordinate $s=\operatorname{tr}^2\rho(\mu)$ near $s=4$ for a chosen peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$.

Augment a representation by choosing a common invariant line of its peripheral holonomy. The augmented deformation space is a smooth complex curve, with holomorphic eigenvalue-ratio logarithm coordinate $u$ vanishing at the complete point. The forgetful map to the ordinary conjugacy quotient is $s=4\cosh^2(u/2)$. The corresponding logarithm $v(u)$ for $\lambda$ satisfies $v(0)=0$ and $v(u)=\tau u+O(u^2)$. Here $\operatorname{Im}\tau\ne0$; it is positive for a positively oriented basis of the oriented horotorus, and changes sign if the basis orientation is reversed. In particular the eigenvalue logarithm is a coordinate on the augmented space, rather than a single-valued holomorphic coordinate on the ordinary quotient.

The pair $(u,v)$ records the local generalized filling parameters. The primitive slope equation $p u+q v(u)=2\pi i$ has its full-turn holonomy meaning for ordinary smooth filling when $\gcd(p,q)=1$; sufficiently large primitive coefficients admit such small solutions and smooth complete hyperbolic fillings. Nonprimitive ray parameters are not ordinary slopes.

## Statement references

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 5, §5.8](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/5.pdf)

[Danny Calegari, *Kleinian Groups*, §§2.3.2–2.4.1](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/kleinian_groups_2015/kleinian_groups.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the complete one-cusped metric and the chosen ordered peripheral basis.

[A1] AC supplies DC and countable choice for the analytic and geometric suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] A complete oriented curvature-minus-one manifold is a Kleinian quotient, and finite volume supplies a compact smooth core with finitely many standard rank-two cusps. [[lem-complete-curvature-minus-one-manifolds-are-kleinian-quotients]], [[lem-finite-volume-hyperbolic-three-manifolds-have-finite-standard-cusp-decompositions]]

[F2] For any such finite-volume quotient, the ordinary conjugacy quotient has independent trace-squared coordinates; its augmented space has independent eigenvalue-ratio logarithms, the stated branched forgetful map and peripheral factorization. [[thm-augmented-finite-volume-hyperbolic-holonomy-coordinates]]

[F3] Holomorphic peripheral factors with nonreal complete values admit unique simultaneous small full-turn solutions for all sufficiently large real coefficient tuples, including the partially unfilled coordinates. [[lem-simultaneous-peripheral-full-turn-equations-have-small-solutions]]

[F4] Small augmented solutions with primitive full-turn meridians give smooth complete finite-volume ordinary fillings. [[thm-small-augmented-holonomy-deformations-have-smooth-geometric-fillings]]

[F5] Ordinary slopes are primitive pairs modulo sign, and the chosen-section length is a lattice norm up to a fixed invertible real-linear map. [[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]], [[def-cusp-slope-length]], [[def-pared-hyperbolic-structures-and-volume]]

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the given complete metric. Its one cusp has the standard quotient description needed by [F2]. First choose a positively oriented basis. Specializing [F2] to $k=1$ gives the smooth ordinary curve with coordinate $s$, the smooth augmented curve with coordinate $u$, $s=4\cosh^2(u/2)$, and the holomorphic factorization $v(u)=u\tau(u)$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau(0)>0$. Holomorphy gives $\tau(u)=\tau(0)+O(u)$, hence the asserted first-order expansion. This uses no ideal triangulation. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 For an arbitrary supplied basis, keep its first element $\mu$. If its orientation is negative, replace $\lambda$ by $-\lambda$ temporarily to apply step 1.1, then return to the supplied basis by $v\mapsto-v$ and $\tau\mapsto-\tau$. This preserves $u$, the ordinary trace coordinate, the branched forgetful map, and all deformations. It proves precisely the signed nonreal assertion for every ordered basis. A holomorphic logarithm coordinate on the ordinary curve cannot replace this augmentation: differentiating $s=4\cosh^2(u/2)$ at $u=0$ gives $ds=0$ if $u$ were a holomorphic function on that curve, contradicting that $s$ is its local coordinate. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The coefficient equation has unique real coefficients when $u\ne0$, because $1,\tau(u)$ are real-linearly independent; $u=0$ is the complete parameter. Apply [F3] for the small-solution assertion. For a negatively oriented supplied basis, the simultaneous equation is unchanged after replacing $q$ by $-q$ and $v$ by $-v$, so [F4] supplies the same geometric completion after returning to the positive basis. By [F5], primitivity is exactly the ordinary meridian convention and nonprimitive multiples do not become ordinary slopes. Thus the full analytic and ordinary-filling conclusions hold for the entire given one-cusped class. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $f:D^2\to S^3$ be a smooth immersion of an oriented disk whose boundary is an embedded oriented knot $K$. Suppose that its only self-intersections are finitely many pairwise disjoint transverse double arcs, and that the two preimage arcs of each double arc are one properly embedded arc in $D^2$ and one compact arc contained in $\operatorname{Int}D^2$. Then there is a smooth proper embedding $\widetilde f:(D^2,\partial D^2)\to(B^4,S^3)$ with $\widetilde f|_{\partial D^2}=f|_{\partial D^2}$.

## Statement references

[[def-ribbon-disk-and-ribbon-knot|The local preimage convention for ribbon double arcs]]

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Properness and smooth boundary collars]]

[Owens, *Knots and 4-Manifolds*, Lecture 1, PDF p.2](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~bowens/papers/WB.pdf)

[Ray, *Slice Knots and Knot Concordance*, §1.1](https://aru-ray.github.io/documents/slicenotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth immersion $f:D^2\to S^3$ satisfying the ribbon-double-arc hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] For each self-intersection arc, its two preimages are disjoint embedded arcs, one proper with endpoints on $\partial D^2$ and one compact in $\operatorname{Int}D^2$, and these are all the multiple points. ([[def-ribbon-disk-and-ribbon-knot]])

[F2] An embedding of a surface into a manifold with boundary is proper when the preimage of the ambient boundary is exactly the surface boundary; smooth proper surfaces have smooth boundary collars. ([[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]])

## Proof

1.1 Identify $B^4$ with the unit ball in $\mathbb R^4$ and use the explicit boundary collar $c:S^3\times[0,\varepsilon)\to B^4$, $c(y,s)=(1-s)y$, with $0<\varepsilon<1$. On the unit disk set $r(x)=1-\lVert x\rVert^2$, so $r=0$ on $\partial D^2$, $r>0$ in the interior, and $dr$ is nonzero in the inward normal direction at the boundary. By [F1], the finitely many preimage arcs form disjoint compact subsets of $D^2$. Choose pairwise disjoint neighborhoods of the interior arcs $\beta_i$, all disjoint from every proper arc $\alpha_j$ and from $\partial D^2$, and choose smooth bump functions $\phi_i$ supported in those neighborhoods with $\phi_i=1$ on $\beta_i$ and $0\le\phi_i\le1$. This is a finite choice of smooth functions on a disk. [given, F1, construct, choose]

2.1 Let $M=\max\{0,\max_{i,s}(r(\alpha_i(s))-r(\beta_i(s)))\}$ when there is at least one double arc, and let $M=0$ otherwise. Choose $\delta>0$ so that $\delta(2M+3)<\varepsilon$, set $a=2\delta(M+1)$, and define $h=\delta r+a\sum_i\phi_i$. The supports are disjoint, so $0<h<\varepsilon$ on $\operatorname{Int}D^2$ and $h=0$ exactly on $\partial D^2$. For every double arc and every parameter $s$, $h(\beta_i(s))-h(\alpha_i(s))=a+\delta(r(\beta_i(s))-r(\alpha_i(s)))\ge\delta(M+2)>0$. Near $\partial D^2$ all bumps vanish, so $h=\delta r$ there and has positive inward derivative. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Define $\widetilde f(x)=c(f(x),h(x))$. If $\widetilde f(x)=\widetilde f(y)$, injectivity of the collar coordinates gives $f(x)=f(y)$ and $h(x)=h(y)$. By [F1], either $x=y$ or $x,y$ are the two preimages of one of the double arcs; the strict height inequality in step 2.1 excludes the latter. Thus $\widetilde f$ is injective. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The map $f$ is an immersion, so its derivative is injective; adjoining the height coordinate preserves injectivity of the derivative, and the collar map $c$ is a local diffeomorphism. Hence $\widetilde f$ is an immersion. A continuous injection from compact $D^2$ to the Hausdorff space $B^4$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, so this injective immersion is a smooth embedding. Since $h^{-1}(0)=\partial D^2$, its preimage of $S^3=\partial B^4$ is exactly $\partial D^2$; the nonzero inward derivative established in step 2.1 gives the proper boundary collar condition in [F2]. The disk orientation transports through the embedding and its boundary remains the original oriented knot $K$. [given, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The height separation is choice-free: there are finitely many disjoint compact arcs, finitely many bump functions, and a single positive scale $\delta$ satisfying the displayed bound. The approved dependency map also names $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and the knot-concordance group theorem; neither is used by these four geometric steps, so that declared supplier interface remains an explicit reconciliation item.

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, with boundary allowed, with a specified based loop $\mu$ whose integral homology class freely generates $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(M)\to\mathbb Z$ be the abelianization taking $\mu$ to $1$, put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, and use its associated normal-cover right coefficient system, whose transport around a loop $a$ is left multiplication by $t^{-\phi(a)}$ in the based fiber.

There is a finite Laurent matrix $A(t)$ such that
$$H_1(M;\Lambda)\cong\operatorname{coker}A(t),$$
naturally on changing the constant coefficient ring from $\mathbb Z$ to any commutative unital ring $k$. More precisely the actual coefficient map gives
$$H_1(M;\Lambda)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k\cong H_1(M;k[t,t^{-1}]).$$
There is a polynomial $\Delta(t)\in\mathbb Z[t]$ with $\Delta(0)\ne0$ and $\Delta(1)=1$ annihilating $H_1(M;\Lambda)$; its coefficient image annihilates $H_1(M;k[t,t^{-1}])$ for every $k$. In particular $\Delta$ is primitive and its reduction modulo any prime is nonzero. No choice principle, finite CW type, triangulation, smoothness or Seifert presentation for $M$ is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact manifold, marked homology generator and coefficient convention.

[F1] There is a finite one-vertex presentation two-complex $K$ and a based map $K\to M$ inducing a fundamental-group isomorphism, with a marked one-cell mapping exactly by $\mu$. Its underlying space is a finite polyhedron. [[thm-compact-manifolds-have-finite-presentation-complexes-without-choice]]

[F2] Normal-cover local first homology is naturally the covering subgroup's abelianization tensored with the constant coefficient ring. This applies to both spaces of [F1] and their actual map. [[lem-normal-cover-local-homology-detects-mixed-derived-kernels-without-choice]]

[F3] For a finite CW complex with supplied cell lifts the cellular local chains, with their transported signed incidence matrices, compute singular local homology. Here the coefficient rings are commutative, so the left/right distinction is just the corresponding identical scalar action. [[thm-cellular-chains-compute-homology-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1], and pull the given coefficient system to $K$. The induced fundamental-group map is an isomorphism and matches $\mu$, so [F2] identifies the actual $H_1$ of $K$ with that of $M$ for $\Lambda$ and every $k[t,t^{-1}]$. Use [F3] on this actual finite two-complex. Its chain groups are finite free, with $C_0=\Lambda$, a basis of one-cells including $e_\mu$, and a finite basis of two-cells. Cell lifts and orientations require only finitely many choices. Their incidence coefficients reduce under every constant-ring map, so coefficient change on these finite cellular chains is literally coefficientwise change in their Laurent matrices. In particular augmentation $t=1$ gives exactly the ordinary integral cellular complex of $K$. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 If the other oriented one-cells have images $n_j\in\mathbb Z$, their degree-one boundaries are $t^{-n_j}-1$, while $d_1e_\mu=t^{-1}-1$. Set $z=-t e_\mu$, so $d_1z=t-1$. Write $q_j=(t^{-n_j}-1)/(t-1)\in\Lambda$, an explicit finite geometric sum also for negative exponents, and replace $e_j$ by $f_j=e_j-zq_j$. This is an invertible triangular basis change with $C_1=\Lambda z\oplus\Lambda^r\langle f_j\rangle$ and $d_1f_j=0$. Multiplication by $t-1$ is injective in $k[t,t^{-1}]$ for every commutative $k$: the top nonzero coefficient of a nonzero finite Laurent list remains a nonzero top coefficient after multiplication by this monic polynomial. Thus $\ker d_1$ is exactly the $f_j$ summand, both integrally and after every constant-ring change. Since $d_1d_2=0$, the $z$ row of $d_2$ is zero. Let $A(t)$ be its remaining $r\times s$ matrix, giving $H_1(K;\Lambda)=\operatorname{coker}A(t)$ and $H_1(K;k[t,t^{-1}])=\operatorname{coker}A_k(t)$. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 At $t=1$, $d_1=0$ and the integral first homology is therefore $\mathbb Z[z]\oplus\operatorname{coker}A(1)$. The marked class $z$ maps to $-[\mu]$, a free generator of $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ by hypothesis and [F1]–[F2]. Hence $\operatorname{coker}A(1)=0$ and $A(1):\mathbb Z^s\to\mathbb Z^r$ is onto. For each of the finitely many coordinate vectors choose one preimage, giving an integer $s\times r$ matrix $S$ with $A(1)S=I_r$. Put $D(t)=A(t)S$ and $\Delta_0(t)=\det D(t)$. Then $\Delta_0(1)=1$. The adjugate identity $D\,\operatorname{adj}D=\Delta_0 I_r$, proved by finite signed minor expansion, gives $\Delta_0\Lambda^r\subseteq\operatorname{im}D\subseteq\operatorname{im}A$. Thus $\Delta_0$ annihilates the presented first homology. The same identity is an identity of integer Laurent matrices, so holds after every coefficient change as well. For $r=0$, use the empty determinant one; the corresponding first homology is zero. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Normalize $\Delta_0$ by a power of $t$ so its smallest exponent is zero, obtaining the asserted polynomial $\Delta$ with nonzero constant term. This multiplies it by a Laurent unit and retains $\Delta(1)=1$ and every annihilation assertion. The coefficients sum to one, so their greatest common divisor is one; reduction modulo any prime still evaluates to one at $t=1$ and is therefore nonzero. Finally finite presentation cokernels commute with the change $\mathbb Z\to k$ here directly: tensoring the presentation generators imposes exactly the same finite-column relations with their coefficients in $k$, so $\operatorname{coker}A\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k=\operatorname{coker}A_k$ by the tensor generators-and-relations construction. Via the natural identifications in steps 1.1–2.1 this is the actual coefficient map on local $H_1$, not just an abstract isomorphism of modules. All selections in step 3.1 were finite preimages of a finite standard basis, and the remaining operations were finite integer or Laurent-matrix calculations. This proves the full scope without a choice axiom or a finite CW claim about $M$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $A:L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)\to L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and suppose $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-TV exact solution with a dual source certificate $p^\dagger$, meaning $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Use $R=TV_2$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ for full-space TV; for a bounded connected Lipschitz domain use either Dirichlet TV of the zero extension or Neumann TV relative to $\Omega$. Let $\alpha_n>0$ tend to zero, let $w_n\in L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n\le\eta$, and suppose a global minimizer $u_n$ is supplied for each functional
$$u\longmapsto\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_2^2+\alpha_nR(u).$$
For full-space or Dirichlet TV, assume $\eta<2\sqrt\pi$; for bounded Dirichlet TV also assume $\Omega$ has global obstacle curvature $\kappa_\Omega\in L^1(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $\kappa_\Omega\ge g$ almost everywhere outside $\Omega$ for some real-valued $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Omega;\mathbb R)$. For Neumann TV, let $C_\Omega$ be a constant satisfying $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ on $BV(\Omega)$ and assume $\eta<1/C_\Omega$. In the Neumann case with $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, choose the minimizers after subtracting their means.

There is a subsequence $(u_{n_k})$ and a selected minimum-TV exact solution $u_0$ such that $Au_0=f$ and, for almost every nonzero $t$, the canonical level sets of $u_{n_k}$ converge in measure to the canonical level set of $u_0$, while their canonical ambient boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance. The limit $u_0$ need not equal the initially named truth $u^\dagger$ unless the minimum-TV exact solution is unique.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|The source condition is $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$ at a minimum-TV exact solution.]]

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|Full-space TV on L² uses the extended distributional test-field functional.]]

[[def-ip-tv-level-set-representatives-and-boundaries|Canonical levels use density-one representatives and ambient boundaries.]]

[[def-ip-tv-variational-curvature|The obstacle and relative curvature conditions use the selected boundary convention.]]

[[lem-ip-neumann-bv-sobolev-poincare|The Neumann threshold uses a specified BV Sobolev–Poincaré constant.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the bounded linear forward map, a minimum-TV exact source-certified truth, the branch-specific parameter threshold, and supplied global regularized minimizers.

[A1] Countable Choice supplies the subsequence selections in primal compactness and the level-integral diagonal argument. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[lem-ip-tv-vanishing-noise-primal-compactness]]: after a subsequence, $u_n$ converges weakly in $L^2$ and strongly in $L^1$ on bounded domains or locally in $L^1$ in full space to a selected minimum-TV exact solution $u_0$; any certificate at $u^\dagger$ remains a subgradient at $u_0$.

[F2] [[def-ip-tv-level-set-representatives-and-boundaries]]: use $\{u>t\}$ for $t>0$ and $\{u<t\}$ for $t<0$, with their canonical density-one representatives and ambient topological boundaries.

[F3] [[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]: the layer-cake representation of $|u_n-u_0|$ may be integrated over space and levels.

[F4] [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]: every bounded scalar real sequence has a convergent subsequence. Applying it successively to the two coordinates gives the needed subsequence in $\mathbb R^2$, retaining the first coordinate convergence when selecting for the second.

[F5] The density supplier now proves uniform ambient two-sided density and common support for all regularized and source-certified selected exact-limit level sets, including full-space radial support and both bounded-domain boundary conventions. [[lem-ip-tv-level-set-uniform-density-and-hausdorff]]

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the supplied minimizers, retaining its subsequence, and call its limit $u_0$. Then $Au_0=f$, $R(u_0)$ is minimal among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$. In bounded domains the subsequence already converges strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$. In full space, [F5] supplies a common ball containing the regularized and limit level sets for almost every nonzero level. By [F2] and the positive and negative layer-cake identities, for each fixed $n$ the integral of $|u_n|$ outside that ball is the integral over levels of the measures of those level sets outside it; Tonelli [F3] makes this integral zero. The same argument applies to $u_0$, so local $L^1$ convergence from [F1] is global $L^1$ convergence. [F5, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], for each real-valued $u$ the positive and negative level sets use $\{u>t\}$ for $t>0$ and $\{u<t\}$ for $t<0$. They satisfy the pointwise layer-cake identity $$|u(x)-u_0(x)|=\int_0^\infty|\mathbf1_{\{u>t\}}-\mathbf1_{\{u_0>t\}}|\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0|\mathbf1_{\{u<t\}}-\mathbf1_{\{u_0<t\}}|\,dt.$$ Integrating and applying [F3] gives $$\|u_n-u_0\|_1=\int_0^\infty|E_n^+(t)\mathbin\triangle E_0^+(t)|\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0|E_n^-(t)\mathbin\triangle E_0^-(t)|\,dt.$$ The right side tends to zero by step 1.1. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $g_n(t)$ denote the symmetric-difference measure of the positive level sets for $t>0$ and of the negative level sets for $t<0$. Step 2.1 says $g_n\to0$ in $L^1(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})$. Choose a further subsequence with $\sum_k\|g_{n_k}\|_1<\infty$; Tonelli implies $\sum_k g_{n_k}(t)<\infty$ for almost every nonzero $t$, hence the level sets converge in measure there. [A1, F3, step 2.1, choose, construct]

4.1 Fix a nonzero level for which step 3.1 gives measure convergence. If the limit level set is empty and infinitely many regularized level sets are nonempty, [F5] gives compact common support, so each such set has a boundary point; choose one for each index using [A1]. Its two-sided density estimate at a fixed radius $r<r_0$ forces symmetric-difference measure at least $c\pi r^2$, contradicting convergence to the empty limit. If the limit set is nonempty, it has positive measure because it is a nonempty density-one representative; measure convergence therefore rules out infinitely many empty regularized sets. Hence empty status agrees eventually, and the empty boundaries have Hausdorff distance zero by [F2]. For the remaining nonempty sets, [F5] supplies the two-sided density and support bounds. If boundary points of $E_{n_k}(t)$ stayed a fixed distance from $\partial E_0(t)$, choose them using [A1]; bounded support and [F4] give a convergent subsequence. A ball around its limit lies on one side of $E_0(t)$, while the two-sided density bound forces a fixed positive symmetric-difference measure, contradicting step 3.1. Conversely, if a boundary point of $E_0(t)$ stayed a fixed distance from every $\partial E_{n_k}(t)$, choose these points using [A1]; compact support and [F4] give a subsequence converging to $y\in\partial E_0(t)$. A connected ball around $y$ misses those boundaries for all large $k$, so each $E_{n_k}(t)$ is either full or empty there. A subsequence with one fixed status and measure convergence would make $E_0(t)$ full or empty almost everywhere on a smaller ball, contradicting that $y$ lies on the boundary of its canonical density-one representative. Thus the canonical boundaries converge in Hausdorff distance. The limit is the selected solution from [F1]; if the exact minimum-TV solution is unique it equals $u^\dagger$, and otherwise no such identification is asserted. [A1, F5, F1, F2, F4, step 3.1, choose, construct, contradiction] ∎
