## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let $\beta\in B_n$ be a geometric braid with $n\ge2$ strands, let $X$ be the compact exterior of its oriented closure, and let $Y$ be the compact exterior of the closure together with the braid axis. Suppose finite based deficiency-one two-dimensional spine certificates are supplied for $X$ and $Y$, with compatible cell bases for the filling decomposition $X=Y\cup_T V$, where $T$ is the boundary torus and $V\cong D^2\times S^1$ is the filled solid torus. The certificate for $X$ has generators $g_1,\ldots,g_n$, where $g_i=x_1\cdots x_i$ are cumulative positive meridians, and relators $r_i=g_i^{-1}\beta_*(g_i)$ for $1\le i<n$; the certificate for $Y$ has generators $g_1,\ldots,g_n,x$, where $x$ is the axis meridian, and relators $s_i=\beta_*(g_i)(x^{-1}g_ix)^{-1}$ for $1\le i\le n$. The gluing certificate gives $T$ its one-vertex cell structure with $1$-cells $x,g_n$ and one commutator $2$-cell, and gives $V$ its one-vertex and one-core-edge structure, with compatible based cell bases. Assume these are actual compatible based spine and gluing certificates; an abstract group isomorphism or matching relator list alone is insufficient.

Let $H_L=H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ have its ordered positive-meridian basis, let $\chi:H_L\twoheadrightarrow H\cong\mathbb Z^m$ be the declared color map with $m\ge1$, and write $\psi$ for the induced deck map. Let $\mathbb F$ be a field, let $\rho:\pi_1(X)\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation, and use the coefficient systems on $Y,T,V$ pulled back or extended across the filling; thus $x$ acts as the identity and the core $g_n$ of $V$ acts by $M_n=\rho(g_n)\psi(g_n)$. Put $D=\det(M_n-I_d)$ and assume $D\ne0$. Compute the reduced colored Burau block $\overline B_\rho(\beta)$ in the cumulative-meridian basis as in the finite procedure, and put $N=\det(\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I_{(n-1)d})$. For the declared convention that torsion is zero on a nonacyclic fraction-field complex, if the twisted complex of $X$ is acyclic then its torsion is represented by $N/D$ modulo the exact determinant and deck-unit subgroup of the coefficient system. If the complex is nonacyclic then $N=0$ and $\tau(X)=N/D=0$ in $Q$. The acyclic identity follows from the braid-axis filling product.

The diagram records only the supplied gluing certificate; it is schematic and is not a substitute for the cell or spine data.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth, node distance=2.5cm]
  \node (T) {$T$};
  \node (Y) [right of=T] {$Y$};
  \node (V) [below of=T] {$V=D^2\times S^1$};
  \node (X) [right of=V] {$X=Y\cup_TV$};
  \draw[->] (T) -- node[above] {inclusion} (Y);
  \draw[->] (T) -- node[left] {inclusion} (V);
  \draw[->] (Y) -- node[right] {glue along $T$} (X);
  \draw[->] (V) -- node[below] {glue along $T$} (X);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

[Ranicki, Definitions 4 and 6 and Theorem 15](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/torsion.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the actual compatible based spine and filling certificates; the full positive-meridian abelianization followed by the explicit color map; a field-valued representation of $\pi_1(X)$; and $D\ne0$.

[A1] The maximal-abelian-cover and twisted-chain conventions explicitly assume AC. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F1] For a based acyclic twisted complex, torsion is the alternating determinant product in the cellular bases; nonacyclic torsion is defined to be zero. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F2] For a certified deficiency-one exterior spine with torsion degree-one homology over the Laurent ring and an admissible deleted column, the Fox minor divided by its boundary determinant equals the based torsion class. [[thm-wada-deleted-minor-equals-twisted-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F3] The finite braid procedure fixes the positive Artin convention, the cumulative meridians $g_i$, the closure relators, the reduced Fox block $\overline B_\rho(\beta)$, and the numerator and denominator $N,D$. [[alg-twisted-burau-determinant-for-colored-braid-closure]]

[F4] The closure and axis exteriors, their meridian generators, and the Artin action use the stated geometric braid and punctured-disk conventions; the assignment of generator automorphisms extends to a well-defined Artin representation and agrees with the geometric action on meridians; the standard positive puncture meridians form a free basis. [[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]; [[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]]; [[def-the-artin-representation-on-a-free-group]]; [[prop-the-geometric-action-on-meridians-is-the-artin-representation]]; [[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]]; [[thm-the-punctured-disk-fundamental-group-is-free-on-standard-meridians]]

[F5] The based Fox block matrix is the cellular boundary matrix of the based presentation complex under the row-coefficient convention. [[lem-twisted-fox-jacobian-is-cellular-boundary]]

[F6] The chain-model theorem proves that the full positive-meridian cellular model computes the maximal-abelian-cover module. The colored-braid algorithm separately requires forming the full positive-meridian basis before applying the declared map $\chi$. [[thm-abelian-cover-chain-model-computes-alexander-module]]; [[alg-twisted-burau-determinant-for-colored-braid-closure]]

[F7] Filling the axis torus kills its meridian in the fundamental group, and the gluing fundamental group is determined by the inclusions of the common boundary torus. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]; [[def-knot-exterior]]

[F8] The Laurent coefficient ring is an integral domain embedded in its fraction field, so clearing a nonzero denominator in a free module is valid. [[def-field-of-fractions]]; [[thm-field-of-fractions-is-a-field-and-the-domain-embeds]]

[F9] **External relative-cellular gluing input.** For the actual braid-axis filling $X=Y\cup_T(D^2\times S^1)$ with agreeing local coefficients, use finite CW representatives relative to the common boundary torus, with the based simple comparisons to the supplied exterior spines. The cellular inclusion and difference maps give the degreewise split exact gluing sequence. The based comparison is with those relative models, not with a core circle as a boundary-containing subcomplex. This is the geometric gluing/excision operation used in Conway, *Burau Maps and Twisted Alexander Polynomials*, arXiv:1510.06678v2, proof of Theorem 3.15, printed/PDF pp. 16–17; its based-chain multiplicativity is Proposition 2.4, printed/PDF p. 7. This finite relative-cellular comparison is an explicit external input, not a locally reconstructed relative-CW theorem. In the present proof the solid-torus comparison is additionally computed in step 2.3. The cellular operation applies after the declared color map as well: its degreewise splittings use individual lifted cells, so applying the coefficient representation preserves exactness; the only inverse needed in the solid-torus computation is the assumed invertible $M_n-I_d$. No acyclicity is assumed before that specialization. [Conway, Proposition 2.4 and proof of Theorem 3.15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.06678v2)

## Proof



1.1 Let $\alpha(g)=\rho(g)\psi(g)$ denote the coefficient matrix. Under [A1], the supplied filling certificate and [F7] identify $\pi_1(X)$ as the quotient of $\pi_1(Y)$ that kills the axis meridian $x$. Pulling the coefficient system back from $X$ therefore gives $\alpha(x)=I_d$ and $\psi(x)=1$; the core of $V$ is represented on $T$ by $g_n$, with matrix $M_n$. The algorithm forms the full positive-meridian basis on $X$ before applying $\chi$, while the compatible filling certificate specifies the resulting pulled-back or extended coefficient systems on $Y,T,V$ and makes them agree on overlaps. The chain-model theorem [F6] supplies the maximal-abelian-cover module computation on the full system; it does not prescribe the specialization order. The map $\pi_1(Y)\to\pi_1(X)$ is surjective, so the pulled-back deck map on $Y$ is still onto and the coefficient-unit images for the two exteriors agree. Since $D\ne0$, $M_n-I_d$ is invertible. [A1, given, F3, F4, F6, F7]

2.1 First compute the core-circle spine $V_{\mathrm{core}}$ with one $0$-cell and one $1$-cell for $g_n$. Its twisted boundary is $M_n-I_d$, so this core complex is acyclic and its torsion is $D^{-1}$. This core is not used as a CW pair containing $T$; a separate relative model and its torsion comparison are established before applying the gluing sequence. Give $T$ the standard one-vertex CW structure with $1$-cells $x,g_n$ and one commutator $2$-cell $xg_nx^{-1}g_n^{-1}$. The Fox boundary blocks are $d_1=(0,M_n-I_d)^\mathsf{T}$ and $d_2=(I_d-M_n,0)$: hence $d_1$ is onto, $d_2$ is injective onto $\ker d_1$, and $T$ is acyclic. In the torsion determinant product, the factors $\det(I_d-M_n)$ and $\det((M_n-I_d)^{-1})$ cancel up to $(-1)^d$, so $\tau(T)=(-1)^d$. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For $X$, Fox differentiation of $r_i=g_i^{-1}\beta_*(g_i)$ gives block row $M_i^{-1}(\widetilde B_{i,*}-e_i)$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th identity block row and $M_i=\rho(g_i)\psi(g_i)$. Thus, after deleting the $g_n$ column, the Fox block is $\operatorname{diag}(M_1^{-1},\ldots,M_{n-1}^{-1})(\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I)$, whose determinant is $\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\det(M_i^{-1})\right)N$. The prefactor is a nonzero coefficient unit. The $d_1$ block for $g_n$ is $M_n-I_d$, which is invertible, so $d_1$ is onto and projection from $\ker d_1$ to the first $n-1$ coordinate blocks is an isomorphism. By [F5], the projected $d_2$ is the displayed deleted Fox block. Therefore $N\ne0$ implies $d_2$ injective and, by dimensions and $d_1d_2=0$, the complex is acyclic; if the complex is acyclic, the same projection makes $d_2$ injective and forces $N\ne0$. Hence nonacyclicity is equivalent to $N=0$. [F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Give $D^2$ its boundary vertex, boundary edge $x$, and meridian disk cell $a$, and give $S^1$ its vertex and core edge $g_n$. Their product is a finite CW model $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ of the actual solid torus containing exactly the specified torus CW structure as its boundary subcomplex. Besides the cells of $T$, it has the $2$-cell $a\times\{*\}$, still denoted $a$, and the $3$-cell $b=a\times g_n$. Put $A=M_n-I_d$ and let $q$ denote the torus $2$-cell, with the orientation in step 2.1. For a coefficient row $v$, the product boundaries are $$\partial a(v)=x(v),\qquad \partial q(v)=x(-vA),\qquad \partial b(v)=q(v)+a(vA).$$ The first formula is the meridian disk boundary, the second is the torus Fox boundary from step 2.1, and the third is the oriented boundary of disk times core edge; its two terms have cancelling images under $\partial$. Replace the degree-two block $q(v)$ by $q'(v)=q(v)+a(vA)$. This block-triangular basis change has determinant one, $\partial q'=0$, and $\partial b(v)=q'(v)$. Split off the unit two-term pair $(b,q')$, then the unit pair $(a,x)$. The remaining based complex is exactly the core complex with $\partial g_n(v)=vA$. Each split pair has identity incidence and torsion one up to the sign unit, and the triangular change contributes determinant one. Hence $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ has the same homology and torsion class as $V_{\mathrm{core}}$, so it is acyclic and its torsion is $D^{-1}$ up to the declared units. This calculation supplies the missing based comparison while retaining $T$ in the actual gluing model. [F1, F5, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Use the relative-cellular gluing operation [F9] for the actual decomposition in the supplied certificate. For $V$ use $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ from step 3.1, not its core spine. For the exterior pieces the operation uses the compatible relative CW representatives and the supplied based simple-spine comparisons. Equivalently, a boundary map into a spine is represented by its finite cellular mapping cylinder: each added prism over a torus cell pairs with its source face, with lifted incidence a unit; these pairs are removed in decreasing cell dimension. Their torsion changes lie in the declared unit subgroup. Thus the based torsion classes used below are those of the supplied spines, without identifying the boundary torus with a subcomplex of a core circle or of an abstract presentation. In the common relative models each cell of $T$ occurs in both pieces, and each other cell occurs in exactly one. Inclusion into the first piece and its negative into the second, followed by the difference quotient to the union, therefore give the degreewise split short exact sequence $$0\longrightarrow C_*(T)\longrightarrow C_*(Y_{\mathrm{rel}})\oplus C_*(V_{\mathrm{rel}})\longrightarrow C_*(X_{\mathrm{rel}})\longrightarrow0.$$ Choose the shared lifts compatibly; any permitted adjustment changes only the declared determinant/deck units. Since $T$ and $V_{\mathrm{rel}}$ are acyclic by steps 2.1 and 3.1, the long exact homology sequence identifies $H_*(Y;Q^d)$ with $H_*(X;Q^d)$. Thus $Y$ is acyclic exactly when $X$ is. Subsequent references to the gluing sequence mean these relative models and their certified based comparisons. [F9, given, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 In the acyclic case, choose boundary bases in the short exact sequence compatibly: lift a basis of each quotient boundary space, append a basis of the subcomplex boundary space, and lift the resulting boundary bases to chain groups. The change-of-basis matrices are block triangular with diagonal blocks the matrices for the subcomplex and quotient, so their determinants multiply degree by degree; the alternating torsion product therefore gives $\tau(Y)\tau(V)=\pm\tau(T)\tau(X)$. As $\tau(T)=\pm1$ and both signs lie in the declared unit subgroup, step 2.1 yields $\tau(Y)\doteq\tau(X)D$. [F1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 Suppose $X$ and hence $Y$ are acyclic over $Q$. The finite based chain modules over $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$ are free. If $z\in C_1(Y;\Lambda^d)$ is a $1$-cycle, acyclicity over $Q$ gives $z/1=d_2(y)/s$ for some $y\in C_2(Y;\Lambda^d)$ and nonzero $s\in\Lambda$. By [F8], equality in the fraction field means that some nonzero $u\in\Lambda$ annihilates $sz-d_2(y)$; since $C_1(Y;\Lambda^d)$ is free over the domain $\Lambda$, multiplication by $u$ is injective, so $sz=d_2(y)$. Every degree-one homology class is therefore killed by a nonzero element of $\Lambda$. [given, F1, F8, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Apply [F2] to the certified spine of $Y$ and delete the $g_n$ column, whose denominator is $D\ne0$. For $s_i=\beta_*(g_i)(x^{-1}g_ix)^{-1}$, the $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ Fox blocks evaluate to $\widetilde B-I$, where $\widetilde B$ is the full cumulative-meridian Fox matrix, and the $x$-column blocks are $I_d-M_i$ with $M_i=\rho(g_i)\psi(g_i)$. Because $\beta_*(g_n)=g_n$, the last row of $\widetilde B-I$ is zero; after deleting its $g_n$ column, the remaining matrix has upper-left block $\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I$, arbitrary upper-right block, zero lower-left block, and lower-right block $I_d-M_n$. It is block upper triangular, so its determinant is $(-1)^dND$. Dividing by $D$ gives $(-1)^dN$, which represents $N$ modulo the sign unit. Consequently $\tau(Y)\doteq N$. [F2, F3, F5, step 5.2, algebra]

7.1 If the complex is acyclic, combine steps 5.1 and 6.1 to obtain $\tau(X)D\doteq N$, hence $\tau(X)\doteq N/D$. If it is nonacyclic, step 2.2 gives $N=0$, and the declared convention sets $\tau(X)=0=N/D$. This proves the statement in both branches. [F1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For an oriented link type $L$ in $S^3$, the Conway polynomial is the polynomial $\nabla_L(z)\in\mathbb Z[z]$ characterized by the normalization $\nabla_U(z)=1$ for the unknot $U$ and the skein relation
$$\nabla_{L_+}(z)-\nabla_{L_-}(z)=z\,\nabla_{L_0}(z).$$
Here $L_+$ and $L_-$ are identical oriented links outside a ball and have respectively a positive and negative crossing inside it, while $L_0$ is obtained in that ball by the orientation-preserving smoothing. For each integer $k\ge0$, the $k$th Conway coefficient is $c_k(L):=[z^k]\nabla_L(z)$. This carrier records the conventional skein interface; existence and uniqueness of the invariant are a separate well-definedness obligation. The skein characterization is on nonempty oriented links. If the link domain also includes the empty link, extend the invariant by the separate conventional value $\nabla_{\varnothing}(z)=0$; this empty-link value is not determined by the nonempty skein axioms.

## Definition references

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|Oriented links and ambient-isotopy classes]]

[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing|Positive crossing convention]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §2.3, printed pp. 35–37](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Chmutov, Cap Khoury, and Rossi, §§3.4–4.2, PDF pp. 4–8](https://math.osu.edu/~chmutov.1/preprints/chmutov-khoury-rossi.pdf)

[Garaev, “Elementary proof of existence of the Alexander-Conway polynomial,” §§1–4, PDF pp. 1–9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.03086v1)



## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite diagrams of nonempty oriented links, with no ordering of their components, the declared positive/negative crossing convention and oriented smoothing. The link isotopy and diagram conventions are those of the Definition.

[F1] **External input — existence of the Conway coefficient invariants.** T. Garaev, *Elementary proof of existence of the Alexander-Conway polynomial*, arXiv:2012.03086v1 (5 December 2020), Section1, Theorem1, PDF p.2, with the equivalence and skein charts on p.1, supplies a sequence $c_{-1}=0,c_0,c_1,\ldots$ of invariants of oriented link diagrams with unordered components. They are invariant under all oriented Reidemeister moves and planar isotopies, have $c_0(U)=1$ and $c_j(U)=0$ for $j>0$, and satisfy
$$c_j(L_+)-c_j(L_-)=c_{j-1}(L_0),\qquad j\ge0.$$
This is an imported established coefficient-existence result, not a claim to reconstruct its Reidemeister-III argument. The source's crossing sign agrees with the declared convention: it is positive when the ordered over/under tangent pair has positive planar determinant. Its Figure2 is the oriented smoothing in this Definition. Polynomial finiteness, integrality and uniqueness are earned below rather than falsely attributed to the coefficient-sequence statement alone.

[F2] **External input — ambient-link interpretation and conventional normalization.** Chmutov–Duzhin–Mostovoy, *Introduction to Vassiliev Knot Invariants*, §1.2.1, printed p.11/PDF19, gives the Reidemeister diagram criterion with its oriented extension; §2.3.1, printed pp.35–36/PDF43–44, states the Conway invariant of ORIENTED LINKS with values in $\mathbb Z[t]$, normalized to one on the unknot and satisfying its displayed positive-minus-negative skein relation. It uses links with unnumbered components. These are the ambient-link interpretation and the standard skein convention of [F1]; the letter $t$ is renamed $z$. The book's §2.3.2 expressly notes that existence is nontrivial. Here existence is EXTERNALLY supplied, not inferred from that observation or from a formal definition. The empty link, if included in the ambient link domain, is assigned the separate conventional zero value in the Definition; the imported skein characterization is only for nonempty links.

Actual reading limits: the complete Garaev v1 Section1/Theorem1 statement and crossing-sign definitions on PDF pp.1–2, including visual inspection of Figures1–3; the coefficient-extension setup on p.3; CDM's complete §1.2.1 text and its oriented extension on printed p.11, and the complete §2.3.1 definition and displayed skein normalization plus the opening §2.3.2 text on printed pp.35–36. No full Garaev proof, Reidemeister-III reconstruction or full book reading is claimed. These exact established external inputs are used under the run-specific external-source permission.

## Proof

1.1 Form the coefficientwise formal expression $C_D(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}c_j(D)z^j$ from [F1]. It is a diagram invariant, has value $1$ on an unknot, and satisfies $C_{D_+}-C_{D_-}=zC_{D_0}$ coefficientwise. A local positive and negative curl on any component of the $r$-component unlink are both that unlink; the oriented smoothing is the $(r+1)$-component unlink. Thus $c_j(U_r)-c_j(U_r)=c_{j-1}(U_{r+1})$ for every $j\ge1$. All coefficients of $U_{r+1}$ vanish. Therefore the unlink values of the formal expression are $1$ for one component and $0$ for more than one. This is also the forced unlink value for ANY polynomial-valued invariant satisfying the Definition. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Here is the finite argument that the expression is actually in $\mathbb Z[z]$. In a diagram choose finitely many component basepoints and an order. Call a crossing bad when its first encounter in this traversal is the underpass. If none is bad, the first component passes over every later component and has a descending self-diagram. Pull its successive arcs above everything they first encounter to isolate a round circle; repeat for the remaining components. Thus a descending diagram is an unlink. At a bad crossing the skein relation writes its value as the value of the switched diagram, plus or minus $z$ times its oriented smoothing. The switched diagram has one fewer bad crossing and the same number $N$ of crossings; the smoothing has $N-1$ crossings. Reset the finite component data on a smoothing if necessary. The nonnegative integer $N(N+1)/2+b$, with $b$ the number of bad crossings, decreases in each branch. Hence this is a FINITE resolution tree. Its leaves have values $0$ or $1$ by step1.1. Working back through the tree uses only integer addition/subtraction and multiplication by $z$, so $C_D\in\mathbb Z[z]$. In fact every branch has at most $N$ smoothing operations, giving degree at most $N$. This proves finiteness and integrality without assuming an integer-valued formal sequence theorem or making an infinite selection. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Apply the SAME finite tree to any two polynomial-valued invariants satisfying the stated normalization and skein relation. Their unlink leaves agree by step1.1, and each internal skein relation then forces agreement. Their values agree on every diagram. Existence follows from [F1], step1.2 and the ambient-link interpretation [F2], and this argument proves uniqueness. The separately fixed empty-link extension is unique as well, since its prescribed value is zero. Consequently the separate existence/uniqueness obligation mentioned in the Definition is now discharged: the resulting actual link invariant is exactly $\nabla$, and its coefficient $[z^k]\nabla_L$ is well-defined for every $k$. The finite local arguments use no choice axiom; the external constructive coefficient/diagram inputs are explicitly distinguished from them. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=H=\mathbb R^2$ with the Euclidean inner product, let $K(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,x_2/2)$, fix $\epsilon>0$, and let $Z$ be a jointly Gaussian centered family on $H$, linear into $L^2$ with covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(k)]=\langle g,k\rangle_H$. Define $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ and consider the feature $\phi(x_1,x_2)=x_1$. The map $K$ is compact, $K^*(1,0)=(1,0)$, and the observation $Y_x(1,0)$ is an unbiased exact estimator of $\phi(x)$ with variance $\epsilon^2$. Thus the feature vector lies in the adjoint range and is exactly estimable by one probe.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-dimensional inverse model and feature in the Example, with $\epsilon>0$.

[F1] A feature $x\mapsto\langle x,h\rangle$ is exactly estimable by one probe precisely when $h\in R(K^*)$. [[def-ip-feature-estimability-through-adjoint-range]]

[F2] In a compact inverse model, the parameter and data spaces are Hilbert spaces and the forward map is compact and linear. [[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model]]

[F3] Every bounded finite-rank operator is compact. [[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]

## Proof

1.1 The matrix of $K$ in the standard basis is $\operatorname{diag}(1,1/2)$, so its range is two-dimensional and it is bounded. It is compact by [F3], hence it satisfies the compact inverse-model hypothesis [F2]. The matrix is self-adjoint, so $K^*=K$ and $K^*(1,0)=(1,0)$, the Riesz vector of $\phi$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

## Example

For this example put $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$. On real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, let $e_j$ be the coordinate vectors and define $K_ax=(j^{-a}x_j)_{j\ge1}$ for $a>0$. For $\nu,q,\rho>0$, the power source ball $X_{\nu,\rho}(K_a):=\{|K_a|^\nu w:\|w\|_2\le\rho\}$ has coordinates $x_j=j^{-a\nu}w_j$, while the logarithmic source ball $X_{\log,q,\rho}(K_a):=\{\psi_q(|K_a|)w:\|w\|_2\le\rho\}$, where $\psi_q(0)=0$ and $\psi_q(t)=(1+\log(1/t))^{-q}$ for $0<t\le1$, has coordinates $x_j=(1+a\log j)^{-q}w_j$. The operator is compact and injective with $\|K_a\|=1$. For the power ball the centered modulus has the bound in the conditional-modulus theorem, with equality at $\delta_j=\rho j^{-a(\nu+1)}$; this does not assert equality for every $\delta$.

[F2] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]] and [[def-operator-norm]]: The inner product satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator norm is the supremum of $\|Tx\|$ over $\|x\|\le1$.

[F3] [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], and [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]: Every bounded operator on a Hilbert space has a unique adjoint satisfying $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$; self-adjointness is $T^*=T$, and positivity is $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every $x$.

[F4] [[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]] and [[thm-norm-limit-of-compact-operators-is-compact]]: Bounded finite-rank maps are compact, and a norm limit of compact maps into a Banach space is compact under Countable Choice.

[F5] [[lem-positive-square-root-of-a-compact-positive-operator]] and [[def-compact-spectral-filter-and-qualification]]: The positive square root of a compact positive operator is unique and acts on an eigenvector of eigenvalue $\lambda$ by $\sqrt{\lambda}$; compact spectral multipliers act eigenvalue by eigenvalue.

[F6] [[def-ip-index-source-ball]] and [[def-ip-power-source-set]]: The source ball is the image of the radius-$\rho$ vector ball under its spectral index multiplier; the power index is $t^\nu$, and the logarithmic candidate defines a source ball once it is bounded on the compact spectrum.

[F7] [[thm-ip-source-ball-modulus-of-continuity]]: The centered power-source modulus is at most $\delta^{\nu/(\nu+1)}\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}$ and attains this value at the radii $\rho s_j^{\nu+1}$.

## Statement

Let $G$ be any group and $\rho,\rho':G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ be representations with $$\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)=\operatorname{tr}\rho'(g)\qquad(g\in G).$$ If $\rho$ is irreducible, then $\rho'$ is irreducible and there is $P\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ such that $\rho'(g)=P\rho(g)P^{-1}$ for every $g$. If $\rho$ is reducible, it has the same trace character as its diagonal semisimplification $g\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(\chi(g),\chi(g)^{-1})$, where $\chi:G\to\mathbb C^*$ is the character on a common invariant line. The two diagonal characters $\chi,\chi^{-1}$ determine the same semisimple conjugacy class. This is a pointwise statement; it does not assert that an irreducible character component admits a tautological representation over its function field or prove rational quotient descent.

## Statement references

[Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long and Shalen, §2.1](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~culler/papers/PlaneCurves/curves.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The group and two representations with the stated equal traces. A representation is irreducible if it has no common invariant complex line in $\mathbb C^2$.

[F1] The complex span of the matrices in a group representation is a unital matrix algebra, since products of image matrices are image matrices. Every complex $2\times2$ characteristic polynomial splits, by its explicit quadratic formula and existence of complex square roots.

## Proof

1.1 **The actual rank-two matrix-algebra argument.** Let $A\subseteq M_2(\mathbb C)$ be a unital subalgebra acting irreducibly. It contains a nonscalar element, since scalar matrices preserve every line. If some $T\in A$ has distinct eigenvalues, conjugate to an eigenbasis. Its two rank-one spectral projections belong to $A$, being degree-one polynomials in $T$, so $E_{11},E_{22}\in A$. Irreducibility forces an element $B\in A$ with $b_{12}\ne0$, since otherwise every element preserves the second coordinate line; it also forces $C\in A$ with $c_{21}\ne0$, since otherwise every element preserves the first coordinate line. Thus $E_{11}BE_{22}=b_{12}E_{12}$ and $E_{22}CE_{11}=c_{21}E_{21}$ put all four matrix units in $A$. If no element initially has distinct eigenvalues, take a nonscalar $T$ and subtract its repeated eigenvalue. The resulting nonzero nilpotent is conjugate, after scaling one basis vector, to $N=E_{12}$. Irreducibility again supplies $B$ with $b_{21}\ne0$. Then $NB=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}b_{21}&b_{22}\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ has distinct eigenvalues $b_{21},0$ and reduces to the previous case. Hence every such algebra is $M_2(\mathbb C)$. In particular an irreducible group image spans the full matrix algebra by [F1]. [F1, given, cases, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Irreducibility is detected by the trace character.** Choose four group elements $g_i$ whose images under an irreducible $\rho$ are a basis of $M_2$; such a finite basis can be extracted from its spanning image in step 1.1. The trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is nondegenerate: pairing with $E_{ij}$ reads the $(j,i)$ matrix entry. Therefore its Gram matrix $\bigl(\operatorname{tr}\rho(g_ig_j)\bigr)_{i,j=1}^4$ is invertible. The equal character gives the identical Gram matrix for the four $\rho'(g_i)$. Those four matrices are independent, because a dependence would give a kernel vector of that Gram matrix. A reducible representation is triangular in an invariant-line basis and its image spans at most the three-dimensional upper-triangular algebra. Thus $\rho'$ cannot be reducible. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Trace equality defines an algebra isomorphism.** Both images now span $M_2$. Define on finite linear combinations $$\Phi\Bigl(\sum_i c_i\rho(g_i)\Bigr)=\sum_i c_i\rho'(g_i).$$ This is well defined. Indeed if the source combination is zero, its proposed image pairs to zero with every $\rho'(h)$, since $$\sum_i c_i\operatorname{tr}\rho'(g_ih)=\sum_i c_i\operatorname{tr}\rho(g_ih)=0.$$ The second image spans $M_2$ and its trace pairing is nondegenerate, so that proposed image is zero. The inverse construction with the representations exchanged proves bijectivity. Multiplication on the group image, then bilinearity, proves that $\Phi$ is a unital algebra isomorphism and $\Phi(\rho(g))=\rho'(g)$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **The algebra isomorphism is explicitly inner.** Put $Q_{ij}=\Phi(E_{ij})$. The nonzero proper idempotent $Q_{11}$ has rank one, because $Q_{11}^2=Q_{11}$ and $Q_{22}=I-Q_{11}$ is also nonzero. Choose $v_1\ne0$ in its image and put $v_2=Q_{21}v_1$. The identity $Q_{12}Q_{21}=Q_{11}$ implies $v_2\ne0$ and $Q_{12}v_2=v_1$. Also $Q_{11}v_1=v_1$ and $Q_{11}v_2=0$, so $v_1,v_2$ are independent. The matrix-unit identities now show $Q_{ij}v_k=\delta_{jk}v_i$. Hence, for the invertible matrix $P_0$ with these columns, $\Phi(A)=P_0AP_0^{-1}$ for every $A$. Multiplying $P_0$ by a scalar whose square is $(\det P_0)^{-1}$ makes its determinant one without changing conjugation; a nonzero complex number has such a square root. Thus the asserted $P\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ exists. These selections involve only finitely many nonempty sets. [F1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 **The reducible character is its diagonal one.** In a basis beginning with a common invariant-line vector, write $$\rho(g)=\begin{pmatrix}\chi(g)&c(g)\\0&\chi(g)^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$ The product law makes $\chi$ a multiplicative map to $\mathbb C^*$, and the trace of every group word is $\chi(g)+\chi(g)^{-1}$, exactly the trace of the diagonal representation. Conjugation by $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in SL_2$ exchanges its two diagonal characters. This proves the semisimplification assertions, not conjugacy of every triangular representative to its diagonal part. Steps 1.1–4.1 prove the irreducible conclusion. All spans, bases, roots and matrix operations used are finite, so no choice axiom is introduced. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every one-component toroidal grid and each of the tilde, associated-graded minus, and full filtered minus modes, the differential defined by the grid-complex algorithm satisfies $\partial^2=0$ over its stated coefficient ring.

## Statement references

[[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex|The three finite grid differential definitions]]

[[lem-grid-rectangle-boundary-square-zero-and-filtration|Rectangle-composition pairings and annulus weights]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A one-component toroidal grid $G$ and one of the three differential modes defined by the algorithm.

[F1] [[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex]] defines each differential as a finite sum over empty-state rectangles, with the stated mode-specific marking restriction and coefficient.

[F2] [[lem-grid-rectangle-boundary-square-zero-and-filtration]] proves that every non-annular two-rectangle composite has two equal contributions and that the only possible annular contributions either vanish by mode restriction or occur twice with the same monomial.

## Proof

1.1 Fix initial and terminal states $\mathbf x,\mathbf z$. The coefficient of $\mathbf z$ in $\partial^2\mathbf x$ is the sum over all ordered pairs of counted empty rectangles with an intermediate state. By [F2], every non-annular composite contributes in a pair of decompositions with equal coefficient, and so its total is zero in $\mathbb F_2$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 If $\mathbf z\ne\mathbf x$, all composites are non-annular and step 1.1 gives zero coefficient. If $\mathbf z=\mathbf x$, the only additional composites are thin annuli; [F2] shows these are excluded in the first two modes and cancel in the full filtered mode. Thus every matrix coefficient of $\partial^2$ is zero, for every mode. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~carlen/502S13/Topology502.pdf"

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ and let $\sigma\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ be globally Lipschitz and not a polynomial. For a compact set $K\subset\mathbb R^n$, let $\mathcal N_{\sigma,n}(K)$ be the restrictions to $K$ of functions
$$x\longmapsto c_0+\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_j\sigma(a_j\cdot x+b_j),$$
where $J\ge0$, $c_0,c_j,b_j\in\mathbb R$ and $a_j\in\mathbb R^n$. Then $\mathcal N_{\sigma,n}(K)$ is uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

## Statement references

[Leshno, Lin, Pinkus and Schocken, Theorem 1 proof: smooth finite differences generate polynomial ridge functions](https://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/14329/1/IS-92-13.pdf)

[Carlen, §1.6, Theorem 1.26 and Lemmas 1.27–1.28: real Stone–Weierstrass theorem and proof](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~carlen/502S13/Topology502.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subset\mathbb R^n$, and a globally Lipschitz, smooth nonpolynomial activation $\sigma$.

[L1] Every unital point-separating real function algebra on a compact Hausdorff space is uniformly dense in its continuous real-valued functions. ([[thm-real-stone-weierstrass-general]])

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the statement.

1.1 Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb R^n$. Since $\sigma$ is not a polynomial, $\sigma^{(m)}$ is not identically zero; choose $b_m$ with $\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)\ne0$. For $h\ne0$ define $R_{m,h}(x):=\frac{1}{\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)h^m}\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^{m-j}\binom mj\sigma(b_m+jh(a\cdot x))$. This is a finite linear combination of permitted units. The repeated-integral formula for the $m$th forward difference gives $R_{m,h}(x)=\frac{(a\cdot x)^m}{\sigma^{(m)}(b_m)}\int_{[0,1]^m}\sigma^{(m)}(b_m+h(a\cdot x)(t_1+\cdots+t_m))\,dt$. Because $a\cdot x$ is bounded on compact $K$ and $\sigma^{(m)}$ is uniformly continuous on a compact interval around $b_m$, $R_{m,h}\to(a\cdot x)^m$ uniformly on $K$ as $h\to0$. [given, choose, algebra]

2.1 For $m\ge1$ and arbitrary real $x_1,\ldots,x_m$, the polarization identity $x_1\cdots x_m=\frac{1}{2^m m!}\sum_{\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^m}(\prod_{j=1}^m\epsilon_j)(\sum_{j=1}^m\epsilon_jx_j)^m$ expresses each monomial of total degree $m$ in $n$ variables as a finite linear combination of powers of linear forms. Step 1.1 places every such power in the uniform closure of the network family, and that closure is a vector space because finite network sums are represented by concatenating their hidden units. Constants are present through $c_0$. Hence every real polynomial restricted to $K$ belongs to that closure. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The restrictions of real polynomials to $K$ form a unital real function algebra and separate distinct points, since a coordinate function distinguishes any two different points. Compact subsets of Euclidean space are compact Hausdorff, so [L1] makes these polynomial restrictions uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. The network closure contains them by step 2.1 and is therefore all of $C(K,\mathbb R)$. [L1, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$. Write $M=\partial\Omega$, $n=d-1$, and let $A_\gamma$ and $\widetilde A_\gamma$ be the mean-zero smoothed NtD observation and its extension from the preceding definition. Then $\widetilde A_\gamma$ is Hilbert–Schmidt on $L^2(M)$ and has a unique zero-mean-in-each-variable kernel $\kappa_\gamma\in L^2(M\times M)$, with
$$\|\kappa_\gamma\|_{L^2(M\times M)}=\|\widetilde A_\gamma\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.$$
The Hilbert–Schmidt norms are uniformly bounded over $X_d(R)$. Moreover, there is $C<\infty$, depending only on the fixed class and domain, such that
$$\|\dot\Lambda_\gamma-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\dot{\mathcal D},\dot{\mathcal D}^{*})}\le C\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_{L^2(M\times M)}^{1/2}\qquad(\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-mean-zero-ntd-and-smoothed-kernel-observation|The mean-zero NtD observation and its zero-mean kernel convention.]]

[[lem-ip-boundary-spectral-counting-and-sobolev-scale|The boundary eigenvalue counting bound and spectral Sobolev norms.]]

[[thm-ip-hilbert-schmidt-operator-admits-square-integrable-kernel|The Hilbert–Schmidt to square-integrable kernel correspondence.]]

[de Hoop et al., Lemmas 3.4–3.7 and Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the domain, conductivity class and smoothing exponent in the statement.

[F1] For $n=d-1$, the boundary eigenvalues satisfy $N_M(\Lambda)\le C(1+\Lambda)^{n/2}$, so $\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)^{-1-r_d}<\infty$. ([[lem-ip-boundary-spectral-counting-and-sobolev-scale]])

[F2] The smoothed observation is $A_\gamma=\mathscr R_\gamma C_M^{r_d/2}$ on mean-zero $L^2$, extended to kill constants and have mean-zero range. ([[def-ip-mean-zero-ntd-and-smoothed-kernel-observation]])

[F3] Every Hilbert–Schmidt operator on the compact boundary has a unique $L^2$ kernel with the same norm, and the zero-mean operator extension gives the zero-mean-in-each-variable kernel convention. ([[thm-ip-hilbert-schmidt-operator-admits-square-integrable-kernel]])

[F4] An $L^2$ kernel defines a Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator with norm equal to the kernel norm. ([[thm-l-two-kernels-give-hilbert-schmidt-operators]])

[F5] Uniformly in the conductivity, $\mathscr R_\gamma:L^2_0(M)\to H^1_\Delta(M)$ is bounded. For $B=\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0}$, every $L>0$ gives $|b_{ij}|\le C_L(w_iw_j)^{-L}$ in the boundary basis, with $w_j=1+\lambda_j$. The spectral half-order norms equal the quotient trace norms up to fixed constants. ([[lem-ip-ntd-boundary-smoothing-for-fixed-background-collar]])

[F6] The weak DN and NtD maps are bounded mutually inverse maps on the quotient trace and its dual; the DN bounds are uniform in the ellipticity class. This also follows directly from the two weak formulations and uniqueness. ([[lem-ip-calderon-rough-dn-map-wellposedness]], [[def-ip-mean-zero-ntd-and-smoothed-kernel-observation]])

[F7] A compact self-adjoint Hilbert operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis on the complement of its kernel. ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are inherited at the weak-solution, spectral and trace interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the Statement. If the conductivity class is empty, its uniform assertions are vacuous; otherwise its collar forces $m\le1\le M$.

1.1 Write $r=r_d\ge0$, $n=d-1$ and $w_j=1+\lambda_j$ on the total-mean-zero subspace. The counting estimate [F1] implies $w_j^{-1/2}\le C(1+j)^{-1/n}$, after enlarging the constant for finitely many low modes. By [F5], $R=\mathscr R_\gamma$ maps the $L^2$ unit ball into a uniformly bounded $H^1_\Delta$ ball. If $P_J$ is the first $J$-mode projection, then $R_J=P_JR$ has rank at most $J$ and $\|R-R_J\|\le C(1+J)^{-1/n}$. Likewise $S=C_M^{r/2}$ has the rank-$J$ approximation $S_J=P_JS$ with $\|S-S_J\|\le C(1+J)^{-r/n}$; for $r=0$ this means the bound one and does not assert that $S$ is compact. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given, construct]

2.1 The rank-at-most-$2J$ map $R_JS+(R-R_J)S_J$ approximates $RS$ with error $(R-R_J)(S-S_J)$, bounded by $C(1+J)^{-(1+r)/n}$. The compact operator $RS$ therefore has singular values $s_j\le C(1+j)^{-(1+r)/n}$. To justify this implication, apply [F7] to $(RS)^*(RS)$: truncating its orthogonal singular expansion gives a rank-$k$ approximation with error $s_{k+1}$, and any other rank-$k$ approximation has a kernel vector in the span of the first $k+1$ right singular vectors, so its error is at least $s_{k+1}$. Since $2(1+r)>n$ by the actual dimension-dependent choice of $r$, $\sum_js_j^2<\infty$ uniformly. Thus $A_\gamma=RS$ and its zero extension are Hilbert–Schmidt. Apply [F3] to obtain the unique $L^2$ kernel and norm equality. Input and output annihilation of the constant mode mean that its integral in either variable is zero, by testing the integral operator and its adjoint on the constant function. [F3, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $B=\mathscr R_\gamma-\mathscr R_{\gamma_0}$ and $s=\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_2$. By [F4], $s^2=\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2w_j^{-r}$. Choose $L$ so large that both $\sum_iw_i^{1-2L}$ and $\sum_jw_j^{r+1-2L}$ converge by [F1]. Then [F5] gives $T:=\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2w_iw_j^{r+1}\le C$, uniformly over every conductivity pair. Cauchy–Schwarz now yields $\sum_{i,j}w_i^{1/2}w_j^{1/2}|b_{ij}|^2\le (\sum|b_{ij}|^2w_j^{-r})^{1/2}(\sum|b_{ij}|^2w_iw_j^{r+1})^{1/2}\le C s$. The left side is the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm from $H^{-1/2}_\Delta$ to $H^{1/2}_\Delta$: the normalized input basis is $w_j^{1/4}e_j$. Taking square roots and [F5]'s quotient norm equivalence gives $\|B\|_{\mathcal L(\dot{\mathcal D}^*,\dot{\mathcal D})}\le C s^{1/2}$, also when $s=0$. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For clarity, the inverse assertion in [F6] uses no boundary pointwise differentiability: the Dirichlet weak solution with boundary class $g$ has Neumann functional $\dot\Lambda_\gamma g$, and uniqueness of the weak Neumann problem gives $\mathscr R_\gamma\dot\Lambda_\gamma g=g$; conversely the weak Neumann solution satisfies its own Dirichlet problem, giving $\dot\Lambda_\gamma\mathscr R_\gamma F=F$. Therefore $\dot\Lambda_\gamma-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}=\dot\Lambda_\gamma(\mathscr R_{\gamma_0}-\mathscr R_\gamma)\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}$. Uniform DN operator bounds in [F6] and step 3.1 prove the displayed square-root comparison. Together with step 2.1 this establishes all assertions. [F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be a smooth oriented $3$-manifold and let $L$ be a framed unoriented
link in its interior with a specified component. A positive full framing twist is the local blackboard
curl whose $A$-smoothing is the straight strip with one additional
zero-framed trivial circle; a negative full framing twist is the curl whose
$B$-smoothing is the straight strip with one additional zero-framed trivial
circle. Write $L^+$ and $L^-$ for the links obtained by inserting these twists
on one component. With $R=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1}]$ and
$\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, the module classes satisfy
$$
[L^+]=-A^3[L],\qquad [L^-]=-A^{-3}[L].
$$

## Statement references

[[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold|Kauffman bracket skein module]]

[[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value|Kauffman bracket smoothing and loop value]]

[Józef H. Przytycki, *Fundamentals of Kauffman Bracket Skein Modules* (1998), §2, framing relation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9809113)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented $3$-manifold $M$, a framed unoriented link $L$ in its interior, and the two local full-twist insertions from the Statement.

[F1] A crossing triple in $\mathcal K_A(M)$ satisfies $[L_\times]=A[L_A]+A^{-1}[L_B]$, and adjoining a zero-framed trivial circle multiplies a class by $\delta$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-skein-module-of-a-three-manifold]]).

[F2] The loop value is $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ and the coefficients of the two smoothings are $A$ and $A^{-1}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

## Proof


1.1 In the positive curl from the Statement, the $A$-smoothing is $L$ with one zero-framed trivial circle and the $B$-smoothing is $L$. By [F1] and [F2], $[L^+]=A\delta[L]+A^{-1}[L] =\bigl(A(-A^2-A^{-2})+A^{-1}\bigr)[L] =-A^3[L].$ [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 In the negative curl, the $A$-smoothing is $L$ and the $B$-smoothing is $L$ with one zero-framed trivial circle. Hence $[L^-]=A[L]+A^{-1}\delta[L] =\bigl(A+A^{-1}(-A^2-A^{-2})\bigr)[L] =-A^{-3}[L].$ These are equalities in the framed-link quotient and use no ambient-isotopy identification that forgets the framing. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $S\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be a connected compact oriented smoothly properly embedded surface of genus $g$, with product collars and oriented boundary $(-K_0\times\{0\})\sqcup(K_1\times\{1\})$ for oriented knots $K_0,K_1$ in the standard three-sphere. A **finite movie** for $S$ is a finite ordered sequence of regular-level link diagrams whose changes are planar isotopies, oriented Reidemeister moves, births, saddles or deaths. Such a movie defines a map on rational Lee homology that preserves the induced decreasing filtration with degree $\chi(S)=-2g$. The map is an isomorphism; consequently
$$
|s(K_1)-s(K_0)|\le 2g.
$$

## Statement references

[[def-generic-movie-of-an-oriented-knot-cobordism|Properly embedded smooth knot cobordism in the standard product, with product collars]]

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth embeddings and product collars]]

[[thm-adapted-excellent-morse-functions-exist-on-compact-cobordisms|Finite adapted Morse decomposition]]

[[def-generic-movie-of-an-oriented-knot-cobordism|Generic movies and their elementary changes]]

[[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex|Lee saddle operations and filtration]]

[Rasmussen, *Khovanov homology and the slice genus* (2004), §§4.1–4.3 and §6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131v1)

[McMullen, *4-Manifolds*, §5.7](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/4Mnotes.pdf)


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a connected smoothly properly embedded oriented knot cobordism in $S^3\times[0,1]$ with product collars, and finite regular diagrams at its boundary.

[F2] A birth uses $\eta_L(1)=1$, a death uses $\epsilon_L(1)=0,\epsilon_L(X)=1$, and a saddle uses $m_L$ or $\Delta_L$ ([[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex]]).

[F3] Each oriented Reidemeister move induces a filtered chain homotopy equivalence of degree zero on Lee homology ([[thm-lee-filtered-homology-is-an-oriented-link-invariant]]).

[F4] The two canonical orientation classes form a basis of knot Lee homology ([[thm-lee-homology-of-a-knot-has-two-generators]]).

[F5] For a $c$-component link the $2^c$ canonical orientation classes form a basis, with labels fixed by the checkerboard convention ([[lem-lee-filtered-spectral-sequence-and-two-orientation-classes]]).

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the axiom used by the adapted-Morse and finite diagram/movie inputs ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F6] Every compact smooth collared oriented link cobordism admits a finite generic movie representing its actual embedded trace, relative to smaller end collars, under countable choice ([[lem-smooth-link-cobordisms-admit-finite-generic-movies]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement.

1.1 Under [A1], [F6] supplies a finite movie of the actual collared surface, with fixed regular endpoint diagrams and only planar isotopies, Reidemeister events, births, saddles and deaths. It represents the same oriented embedded surface up to ambient isotopy relative to smaller collars, so it has the same connectedness, genus and Euler characteristic. No assertion that all movies give the same homology map is needed here; choose one supplied movie and its reverse. [A1, F6, given, construct]

1.2 For every Reidemeister disk choose a marked point on each link component outside that disk, carried through the move. On the Lee cube let $X_p$ multiply the circle containing the point by $X$. Each $X_p$ is a chain map: $m(Xu,v)=Xm(u,v)=m(u,Xv)$ and $\Delta(Xu)=(X\otimes1)\Delta(u)=(1\otimes X)\Delta(u)$, verified on $u,v=1,X$. The local Reidemeister maps commute with these operators. Indeed the retractions used in [F3] consist of saddles, dots, factor relabelings, and inverses of scalar identity pivots; the displayed identities show that each constituent commutes with every exterior $X_p$, so their composites and homotopies do too. In the canonical basis $a=1+X$, $b=X-1$, one has $Xa=a$, $Xb=-b$. The checkerboard convention for the canonical labels is unchanged outside the disk. At one fixed mark on each component its sign determines the orientation of that component; consequently the $2^c$ orientation classes are distinct simultaneous eigenlines of the exterior marked actions. A Reidemeister homology isomorphism intertwining those actions must carry each eigenline to the line with the same signs, and cannot kill it. Thus it carries each orientation class to a nonzero multiple of the class with the induced orientation. This argument covers every orientation and exterior connectivity of RIII without an omitted case census. [F2, F3, F5, algebra, construct]

2.1 In the basis $a,b$ the Morse maps are $\eta_L(1)=\tfrac12(a-b)$, $m_L(aa)=2a$, $m_L(bb)=-2b$, $m_L(ab)=m_L(ba)=0$, $\Delta_L(a)=aa$, $\Delta_L(b)=bb$, and $\epsilon_L(a)=\epsilon_L(b)=1$. The local label compatibility is explicit: in an empty band disk put its two attaching segments parallel. The middle strip has a single checkerboard color. The black-right rule of [F5] then assigns equal labels exactly when the segment arrows are opposite, and different labels exactly when they agree; inspect the two possible strip colors, which exchange both labels. An orientation extends across an oriented band exactly in the opposite-arrow case. The exterior checkerboard colors remain fixed, so the surviving equal label is the canonical label after the saddle. This includes segments on the same circle, nested circles or disjoint circles. Track orientations of each partial surface: components meeting the incoming knot have their forced orientation, while each other component has its two possible orientations. A birth creates precisely the two possibilities with nonzero coefficients. A split or a band within one surface component extends its orientation uniquely and multiplies its coefficient by a nonzero scalar. A band joining distinct components retains precisely the compatible choices and kills the others: each orientation of the joined component restricts to a unique compatible pair, so no two retained terms cancel. For a death the disappearing boundary circle belongs to a surface component with another boundary, unless that component becomes closed. A closed component of a partial surface cannot later join another component, and would be a closed component of $S$; connectedness and its incoming boundary exclude this. Thus distinct permitted orientations remain distinct on the surviving boundary after a death, and $\epsilon_L(a)=\epsilon_L(b)=1$ preserves their nonzero coefficients. Step 1.2 treats the Reidemeister events. At the final level every component meets the incoming boundary because $S$ is connected. Hence exactly one permitted orientation extends either incoming orientation, and its coefficient is nonzero. The two input classes map to nonzero multiples of the two output classes. [F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra, construct]

2.2 Assign to a planar isotopy the relabeling of state circles, to a Reidemeister move the filtered map of [F3], and to a Morse event the cube map induced by the corresponding Lee Frobenius operation in [F2]. These are actual cochain maps: the move disk misses the crossings, and its unsigned operation commutes with every cube saddle by associativity, coassociativity and the Frobenius/unit/counit identities proved for [F2]; the crossing set and its cube signs remain fixed. The map for a birth is $\eta_L(1)=1$, whose new circle label has quantum degree $+1$. The death map sends only the $X$ term to $1$, raising quantum degree by $+1$. Each degree-preserving term of a saddle has quantum degree $-1$, while each Lee deformation term raises that saddle degree by $4$; hence a saddle map has filtration degree $-1$. If the movie has $b$ births, $s$ saddles and $d$ deaths, composition has filtered degree $b-s+d=\chi(S)$. For a connected genus-$g$ surface with two boundary components, $\chi(S)=2-2g-2=-2g$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Step 2.1 and [F4] show that the movie map is an isomorphism between two-dimensional Lee homology groups. Its forward and reverse maps both have filtered degree $-2g$ by step 2.2. Applying the forward map to a nonzero class of level $s_{\max}(K_0)$ gives $s_{\max}(K_1)\ge s_{\max}(K_0)-2g$; applying the reverse map to a class of level $s_{\max}(K_1)$ gives $s_{\max}(K_0)\ge s_{\max}(K_1)-2g$. Since $s=s_{\max}-1$, these inequalities give $|s(K_1)-s(K_0)|\le2g$. The same argument applies to every supplied finite movie, and step 1.1 supplies one for every surface in the Statement. Thus all asserted conclusions follow. [A1, F3, F4, F6, step 2.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

        A-polynomial of knots, §2.1
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151
    - title: Stephan Tillmann, Varieties associated to 3-manifolds, §4.2
      url: https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf
---

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be a finite presentation of a knot-exterior group. The set of homomorphisms $G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is the affine algebraic subset of $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ cut out by the matrix-entry equations $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=I_2$ for $1\le j\le m$. After each inverse letter is replaced by the adjugate of its determinant-one matrix, these equations have integer coefficients in the matrix-entry coordinates.

## Statement references

[Bénard, Florens, and Rodau, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151)

[Tillmann, §4.2](https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the finite presentation $G=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$.

[F1] The knot group has a finite Wirtinger presentation ([[thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctness]]).

[F2] If $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$, then $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$, an integer-polynomial expression in its entries: multiplying by the displayed matrix gives $\det(A)I=I$ entrywise.

## Proof

1.1 Work with the fixed finite presentation in the Statement. Fact [F1] ensures the existence of finite presentations for the knot group, but no change from the specified presentation to different Wirtinger generators is presumed here. Write each generator matrix as four coordinate variables and impose the polynomial determinant equation $\det(A_i)=1$. These finitely many equations cut out $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ in affine $4n$-space. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Evaluate each relator word by matrix multiplication, replacing each inverse letter by the adjugate matrix from [F2]. Every entry of $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)-I_2$ is therefore a polynomial in the coordinates. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A tuple in $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ satisfies all these matrix equations exactly when its generator assignment extends to a homomorphism from the presented group $G$. Hence their common zero set is precisely $\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2(\mathbb C))$, a closed algebraic subset of affine space. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://www.tu-chemnitz.de/mathematik/ip/fulltext/hofmann_b76.pdf"

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be compact between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, $\nu,\rho>0$, and let $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)$ be its power source ball. For any deterministic reconstruction map $A:Y\to X$ and any $\delta\ge0$, define $E_\delta(A):=\sup\{\|A(Kx+\eta)-x\|_X:x\in X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\ \eta\in Y,\ \|\eta\|_Y\le\delta\}$. Then $E_\delta(A)\ge\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\delta)$, and therefore $\inf_{A:Y\to X}E_\delta(A)\ge\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\delta)$. For any $M\subseteq X$ with $0\in M$, define the two-truth modulus $\widetilde\varepsilon_K(M,\delta):=\sup\{\|x_1-x_2\|_X:x_1,x_2\in M,\ \|K(x_1-x_2)\|_Y\le2\delta\}$. Then $\widetilde\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\delta)=2\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\delta)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model|Compact Hilbert-space inverse model]]

[Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Theorem 4.10](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

[Hofmann and Mathé, *A Note on the Modulus of Continuity*, equations (6)–(7)](https://www.tu-chemnitz.de/mathematik/ip/fulltext/hofmann_b76.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, compact $K:X\to Y$ between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, $\nu,\rho>0$, the power source ball $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)$, a noise level $\delta\ge0$, and a deterministic map $A:Y\to X$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is required by the compact spectral multiplier used to define the power source ball; the indistinguishable-data argument below uses no further choice.

[F1] [[def-ip-power-source-set]]: $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)=\{|K|^\nu w:\|w\|_X\le\rho\}$.

[F2] [[def-ip-centered-modulus-of-continuity]]: $\varepsilon_K(M,\delta)=\sup\{\|x\|_X:x\in M,\|Kx\|_Y\le\delta\}$ when $0\in M\subseteq N(K)^\perp$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-index-source-elements-are-minimum-norm]]: Every element of $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)$ lies in $N(K)^\perp$.

[F4] [[def-hilbert-space]] and [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]: The Hilbert norm is induced by the inner product, and its triangle inequality holds.

## Proof

1.1 The class $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)$ contains $0$ by taking $w=0$ in [F1]. It is symmetric: if $x=|K|^\nu w$ with $\|w\|_X\le\rho$, then $-x=|K|^\nu(-w)$ with $\|-w\|_X\le\rho$. It is convex: for $x_i=|K|^\nu w_i$ with $\|w_i\|_X\le\rho$ and $0\le t\le1$, $tx_1+(1-t)x_2=|K|^\nu(tw_1+(1-t)w_2)$, while the triangle inequality gives $\|tw_1+(1-t)w_2\|_X\le t\rho+(1-t)\rho=\rho$. By [F3], this class is contained in $N(K)^\perp$, so [F2] applies. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, choose, algebra]

2.1 Let $x\in X_{\nu,\rho}(K)$ satisfy $\|Kx\|_Y\le\delta$. The two admissible truths $x$ and $-x$ with noises $-Kx$ and $Kx$ both produce the same observed datum $0$. Their reconstruction errors are $\|A(0)-x\|_X$ and $\|A(0)+x\|_X$, and the triangle inequality yields $2\|x\|_X=\|(A(0)+x)-(A(0)-x)\|_X\le\|A(0)+x\|_X+\|A(0)-x\|_X$. Hence the larger error is at least $\|x\|_X$, so taking the supremum over all such $x$ gives $E_\delta(A)\ge\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\delta)$. Taking the infimum over $A$ preserves this lower bound. [given, step 1.1, F2, F4, algebra]

3.1 If $x_1,x_2\in X_{\nu,\rho}(K)$ and $\|K(x_1-x_2)\|_Y\le2\delta$, then $z=(x_1-x_2)/2$ lies in the class by symmetry and convexity from step 1.1 and satisfies $\|Kz\|_Y\le\delta$; thus $\|x_1-x_2\|_X=2\|z\|_X\le2\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\delta)$. Conversely, for every $z$ in the centered-modulus set, the pair $(z,-z)$ lies in the source ball and has $\|K(z-(-z))\|_Y=2\|Kz\|_Y\le2\delta$, so the two-truth supremum is at least $2\varepsilon_K(X_{\nu,\rho}(K),\delta)$. Taking suprema proves the claimed factor of two. [given, step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with nonempty smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $q\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time. Let $dV_g$ be Riemannian volume and $L^2(M)=L^2(M,dV_g)$. A weak coordinate derivative $D_iw$ is defined by $\int w\,\partial_i\psi=-\int D_iw\,\psi$ for every smooth compactly supported coordinate test $\psi$. Let $H^1(M)$ be the space of $L^2$ functions whose weak coordinate first derivatives are locally $L^2$ in smooth charts and whose weak differential has finite metric $L^2$ norm; write $\nabla_gu$ for the metric dual of that weak differential. Give it norm
$$\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2=\int_M(|w|^2+|\nabla_gw|_g^2)\,dV_g,$$
and let $H_0^1(M)$ be the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in this norm. For $u_0\in H_0^1(M)$, $u_1\in L^2(M)$, and $F\in L^1((0,T);L^2(M))$, there is a unique energy solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem
$$u_{tt}-\Delta_gu+q(x)u=F,\qquad u|_{(0,T)\times\partial M}=0,\qquad (u(0),u_t(0))=(u_0,u_1),$$
where energy solution means
$$u\in C([0,T];H_0^1(M))\cap C^1([0,T];L^2(M)),$$
and, for every $\phi\in H_0^1(M)$ and every $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$, the weak equation is
$$\int_0^T(u(t),\phi)_{L^2}\zeta''(t)\,dt+\int_0^T\!\int_M\big(\langle\nabla_gu(t),\nabla_g\phi\rangle_g+q\,u(t)\phi\big)\zeta(t)\,dV_gdt=\int_0^T(F(t),\phi)_{L^2}\zeta(t)\,dt.$$
There is a constant $C=C(M,g,q,T)<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|u(t)\|_{H^1(M)}+\|u_t(t)\|_{L^2(M)}\big)\le C\big(\|u_0\|_{H^1(M)}+\|u_1\|_{L^2(M)}+\|F\|_{L^1((0,T);L^2(M))}\big).$$
In particular, the solution $w$ with zero initial data satisfies the correction estimate
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|w(t)\|_{H^1(M)}+\|w_t(t)\|_{L^2(M)}\big)\le C\|F\|_{L^1((0,T);L^2(M))}.$$
The corresponding assertion for prescribed terminal data follows by time reversal. For smooth Dirichlet data compactly supported away from the time endpoints, the boundary lifting in the Riemannian Green-and-lifting lemma reduces the problem to this homogeneous-boundary assertion.

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-riemannian-green-boundary-traces-and-wave-lifting]]

[[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]

[[def-riemannian-volume-density]]

[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]

[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]

[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]

[[def-countable-choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the manifold, metric, static potential, initial data, and Bochner-integrable forcing in the statement.

[F1] [[lem-ip-compact-manifold-dirichlet-spectrum-and-regularity]] supplies the shifted form $b$, its equivalent $H^1_0$ norm, the $L^2$ eigenbasis $(e_j)$ with eigenvalues $\mu_j>0$, and convergence of its projections both in $L^2$ and in the form norm.

[F2] [[lem-ip-riemannian-green-boundary-traces-and-wave-lifting]] supplies a smooth lift of smooth time-compact boundary data, zero near both temporal endpoints.


## Proof

1.1 Set $c=1+\|q\|_\infty$, $a(u,v)=b(u,v)-c(u,v)_{L^2}$, and let $P_J$ be projection on $e_1,\ldots,e_J$. Solve the scalar equations $d_j''+(\mu_j-c)d_j=(F,e_j)$ with the projected initial data, and put $u_J=\sum_{j\le J}d_je_j$. The scalar solutions exist for $L^1$ forcing by integration against the sine/hyperbolic-sine fundamental solution (at zero frequency use $t$); they have continuous first derivatives and absolutely continuous first derivatives on compact intervals. For $E_J=(\|u_J'\|_2^2+b(u_J,u_J))/2$, multiply each equation by $\bar d_j'$ and take real parts to obtain $$E_J'=\operatorname{Re}(P_JF+cu_J,u_J')\le C E_J+\sqrt{2E_J}\|F\|_2.$$ Apply this to $\sqrt{E_J+\eta}$ and let $\eta\downarrow0$ after integrating: multiplication by $e^{-Ct}$ gives $\sqrt{E_J(t)}\le C_T(\sqrt{E_J(0)}+\int_0^T\|F\|_2dt)$. This is exactly the asserted estimate, uniformly in $J$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For $J>K$, the same estimate for $u_J-u_K$ has data $(P_J-P_K)u_0,(P_J-P_K)u_1$ and forcing $(P_J-P_K)F$. These data tend to zero in $V\times H$ by [F1]. The forcing tends to zero in $L^1_tH$ because the projections converge pointwise in $H$ and are contractive, so dominated convergence applies. Hence $u_J$ is Cauchy in $C([0,T];V)$ and $u_J'$ in $C([0,T];H)$. Their limits $u,w$ satisfy $u(t)-u(s)=\int_s^t w(r)dr$, so $u\in C^1([0,T];H)$ with derivative $w$ and the exact strong initial traces. Pass to the limit in the integrated finite-dimensional equation first for a finite spectral test and then for every $\phi\in V$, using boundedness of $a$ and the form-density in [F1]. This gives precisely the displayed weak equation and energy bound. No weak-in-time limiting trace is substituted for a strong trace. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 If two energy solutions have the same data and forcing, test their difference against $e_j$. The scalar coefficient is a distributional solution of $d_j''+(\mu_j-c)d_j=0$ with zero strong data. Its integral equation, or the scalar fundamental solution, gives $d_j=0$. Completeness in [F1] makes the difference zero for every time. The estimate of step 1.1 passes to the strong limit, including its zero-data version. Replacing $t$ by $T-t$ proves terminal well-posedness with the same bound. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 We also establish the classical regularity needed by the last assertion and the DN interfaces. Let $h$ be smooth and zero near the temporal endpoints, take the smooth lift $H$ from [F2], and solve for $w=u-H$ with zero Dirichlet and initial data and forcing $G=-L_qH$. This $G$ is smooth and zero near $t=0$. For every integer $\ell\ge0$, solve the same zero-data energy problem with forcing $\partial_t^\ell G$. Integration in time and uniqueness in step 3.1 identify these solutions successively with $\partial_t^\ell w$: for example integrating the solution with forcing $G_t$ gives a solution with forcing $G-G(0)=G$ and zero data. Thus all time derivatives of $w$ are continuous in $V$. At every time, $Aw=G-w_{tt}$; the right side is continuous in $L^2$, so [F1]'s elliptic estimate gives continuity of $w$ in $H^2$, by applying the estimate to time differences. Apply this argument to every time derivative. Inductively if all time derivatives are continuous in $H^k$, the identity $A\partial_t^\ell w=\partial_t^\ell G-\partial_t^{\ell+2}w$ and [F1] give continuity in $H^{k+2}$. Thus all mixed derivatives have arbitrarily high spatial Sobolev regularity, and [F1]'s embedding gives a smooth representative on the closed cylinder, in particular $C^2$. Adding $H$ proves the stated smooth boundary reduction and actual classical forward solvability; time reversal gives the terminal version. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

In $\mathbb C^2$ use $a_1=(1,0)$, $a_2=(0,1)$, and $a_3=(1,1)$, and define $\langle a,x\rangle=\overline{a^{(1)}}x_1+\overline{a^{(2)}}x_2$ for $a=(a^{(1)},a^{(2)})$. Identify signals by global phase, $x\approx z$ when $z=\lambda x$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $|\lambda|=1$, and use intensity data $(|\langle a_j,x\rangle|^2)_{j=1}^3$. Here the complex complement property means that every subset of the three labels or its complement spans $\mathbb C^2$. Each pair spans $\mathbb C^2$, so the family has this property; nevertheless, $x=(1,i)$ and $z=(1,-i)$ have equal intensity data and are not related by a global phase. Thus the real complement-property criterion and its real full-spark count cannot be transferred to complex phase retrieval.

## Statement references

[[thm-ip-real-phase-retrieval-complement-property|The complement-property theorem is stated for real measurements and a global sign]]

[[cor-ip-full-spark-sharp-real-phase-measurement-count|The sharp full-spark count is a real-field result]]

[Philipp Grohs, Sarah Koppensteiner, and Martin Rathmair, real/complex distinction in phase retrieval, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.07911v2)

[Radu Balan, Pete Casazza, and Dan Edidin, discussion of the real-field hypothesis after Theorem 2.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0412411)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The three vectors in $\mathbb C^2$, the Hermitian pairing and global-phase relation defined in the counterexample, and the real-field scope of the cited theorem.

[F1] [[thm-ip-real-phase-retrieval-complement-property]]: the complement-property equivalence proved here has hypotheses over $\mathbb R^d$ and identifies only the pair $x,-x$.

[F2] [[cor-ip-full-spark-sharp-real-phase-measurement-count]]: the $2d-1$ full-spark sufficiency statement is for finite real measurement families.

[F3] [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]: $\mathbb C$ is a field with imaginary unit $i$ satisfying $i^2=-1$.

[F4] [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]: $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and $|z|^2=z\overline z$.

[F5] [[def-linear-combination-and-span]], [[def-linear-subspace]]: each span is a complex linear subspace containing its generators, so every displayed linear combination belongs to that span.

## Counterexample


1.1 For arbitrary $(u,v)\in\mathbb C^2$, the three identities $$ (u,v)=u a_1+v a_2=(u-v)a_1+v a_3=u a_3+(v-u)a_2 $$ show that each of the pairs $\{a_1,a_2\}$, $\{a_1,a_3\}$, and $\{a_2,a_3\}$ spans $\mathbb C^2$: the span is a subspace containing the pair, so it contains the corresponding displayed combination for every $(u,v)$. Any partition of three labels has at least two labels on one side, and a set containing a spanning pair also spans; hence the complex complement property holds. [given, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 The measurements of $x=(1,i)$ are $(1,i,1+i)$ and those of $z=(1,-i)$ are $(1,-i,1-i)$. By [F3] and [F4], their squared moduli are $(1,1,2)$ in both cases. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 If $z=\lambda x$ with $|\lambda|=1$, the first coordinate forces $\lambda=1$, while the second would then force $-i=i$, which is false in the field [F3]. Thus $x\not\approx z$, and step 1.2 proves noninjectivity despite step 1.1. By [F1] and [F2], this does not contradict either real-field result: the ambient field, phase relation, and measurements differ. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

    - title: "P. B. Kronheimer and T. S. Mrowka, Knots, sutures and excision, §§7.1–7.8"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/0807.4891"
    - title: "Kimihiko Motegi, Dehn surgery on knots: survey, pp. 7–10"
      url: "https://www.math.tsukuba.ac.jp/~tange/diftop22/Dehn_surgery_survey.pdf"
verification:

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and ordered meridian-longitude basis $(\mu,\lambda)$. A **surgery triad** is a cyclically ordered triple of primitive unoriented slopes $s_0,s_1,s_\infty$ on $\partial E_K$ whose pairwise geometric intersection numbers are one, together with the oriented fillings $Y_j=E_K(s_j)$ and the three 2-handle surgery cobordisms in the cyclic order $Y_0\to Y_1\to Y_\infty\to Y_0$. Choose primitive representatives $v_j=(p_j,q_j)$ in the ordered basis $(\mu,\lambda)$ so that $\det(v_0,v_1)=\det(v_1,v_\infty)=\det(v_\infty,v_0)=1$; the cyclic order is the one for which this orientation convention holds. The geometric intersection number of $s_j$ and $s_k$ is $|p_jq_k-p_kq_j|$.

For a closed oriented Riemannian 3-manifold $Y$, a principal $SO(3)$-bundle $P\to Y$ is a locally trivial bundle with fiber $SO(3)$ and right structure-group action. A connection $A$ is a smooth right-$SO(3)$-invariant horizontal distribution on $P$ complementary to its vertical tangent spaces. In a local trivialization its curvature is $F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A]$; it is **flat** when $F_A=0$. Let $\mathcal A(P)$ be the space of smooth connections and let $\mathcal G(P)$ be the group of bundle automorphisms covering the identity of $Y$. The configuration space is the quotient $\mathcal B(P)=\mathcal A(P)/\mathcal G(P)$. The associated oriented rank-three real vector bundle has second Stiefel–Whitney class $w_2(P)\in H^2(Y;\mathbb Z/2)$.

Fix an $SO(3)$-invariant inner product on $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and normalize the Chern–Simons functional on its covering of $\mathcal B(P)$ so that its differential at $A$ in a connection variation $a$ is $d\mathrm{CS}_A(a)=\int_Y\langle a\wedge F_A\rangle$. A **holonomy perturbation** is a finite sum of gauge-invariant terms formed by integrating smooth class functions of holonomy around a finite family of embedded loops against compactly supported smooth weights. A critical point of a perturbed Chern–Simons functional is called a perturbed flat connection. At a nondegenerate critical point, the gauge-fixed Hessian is self-adjoint; the **spectral flow** along a path of such Hessians is the signed count of eigenvalues crossing zero and supplies the relative grading convention. Give $\mathbb R\times Y$ the product metric and orientation $dt\wedge\mathrm{or}(Y)$. Fix a holonomy perturbation $f_\pi$ and write $V_\pi(B)=\nabla_{L^2}f_\pi(B)$ for its gradient. A **finite-energy perturbed anti-self-dual trajectory** is a gauge-equivalence class with a temporal-gauge representative $A=B(t)$ on the pullback bundle satisfying
$$\frac{dB}{dt}=-\bigl(*_YF_B+V_\pi(B)\bigr)=-\nabla_{L^2}(\mathrm{CS}+f_\pi)(B),$$
with specified limiting critical points $\beta_-,\beta_+$ of that same perturbed functional at the two ends, and with finite flow energy
$$E_\pi(B):=\int_{\mathbb R}\left\|\frac{dB}{dt}\right\|_{L^2(Y)}^2\,dt=\int_{\mathbb R}\|*_YF_B+V_\pi(B)\|_{L^2(Y)}^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Equivalently, in this gauge its four-dimensional equation is $F_A^++\widehat V_\pi(A)=0$, where $\widehat V_\pi(A)=\tfrac12(dt\wedge V_\pi(B)+*_YV_\pi(B))$. When $\pi=0$ this reduces to the ordinary anti-self-duality equation. On a chosen real lift of the Chern–Simons functional along the trajectory, the chain rule gives $d(\mathrm{CS}+f_\pi)(B(t))/dt=-\|dB/dt\|_{L^2}^2$; whenever the functional has the specified endpoint limits, the energy is their difference. For nonzero perturbations those endpoints need not be flat, so no finiteness of the unperturbed curvature integral $\int_{\mathbb R\times Y}|F_A|^2$ is imposed. If the analytic Fredholm construction is established, the expected dimension is the index of the gauge-fixed linearization of the perturbed equation with the stated asymptotic conditions; translation decreases dimension by one for a nonconstant trajectory.

The **candidate instanton surgery-triangle input data** consist of a principal $SO(3)$-bundle on each $Y_j$, compatible bundle identifications on the three cobordisms, the invariant inner product and Chern–Simons normalization, the allowed perturbation class, and the grading convention. After separate proofs of analytic existence, regularity, compactness and gluing, these data may be used to define critical-point complexes and cobordism maps. Chain complexes, exactness of the three-term Floer sequence, and independence of the choices are separate theorem obligations. This definition asserts none of those analytic or Floer-theoretic conclusions.

## Definition references

[[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling|Slope coordinates, meridian-longitude basis and oriented fillings]]

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Dehn surgery, the fundamental group and SU(2)*, §§2–4](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/hrpthree.pdf)

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Knots, sutures and excision*, §§7.1–7.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0807.4891)

[Motegi, *Dehn surgery on knots: survey*, pp. 7–10](https://www.math.tsukuba.ac.jp/~tange/diftop22/Dehn_surgery_survey.pdf)

## Remarks

The ordinary closed-manifold $SO(3)$ theory in this definition is distinct from the singular earring complex and sutured closure used for Khovanov detection. No Khovanov or singular-instanton rank detector is a logical input to Property P in the proof route considered here.

## Remarks references

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Dehn surgery, the fundamental group and SU(2)*, §2](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/hrpthree.pdf)
