## Example

Assume Countable Choice. On the real Hilbert space $X=H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with standard basis $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$, define $Kx=(x_j/j)_{j\ge1}$ and the feature vector $h=(1/j)_{j\ge1}$. Fix $\epsilon>0$, let $Z$ be a jointly Gaussian centered family indexed by $H$, linear into $L^2$ with covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(k)]=\langle g,k\rangle_H$, and define $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$. The map $K$ is compact and self-adjoint. Its adjoint range contains every finitely supported sequence, so $\overline{R(K^*)}=\ell^2$. The vector $h$ belongs to $\ell^2$ but not to $R(K^*)$, since any preimage would have all coordinates equal to $1$. Thus this feature lies in the closure of the adjoint range but is not exactly estimable by one probe.

## Example references

[[def-ip-feature-estimability-through-adjoint-range|Exact linear feature estimability through the adjoint range]]

[[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model|Compact linear inverse model between Hilbert spaces]]

[[thm-p-series-real-exponents|Convergence and divergence of real p-series]]

[Giné and Nickl, *Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models*, §1.2.2](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real square-summable sequence Hilbert space, its standard basis, the diagonal map and feature in the Example.

[F1] The real square-summable sequences form a Hilbert space with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_jx_jy_j$ and norm squared $\sum_jx_j^2$. [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]

[F2] For a square-summable sequence, its coordinate truncations converge in norm; the standard coordinate vectors form a complete orthonormal basis. [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]

[F3] The series $\sum_{j\ge1}j^{-2}$ converges. [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]]

[F4] Every bounded finite-rank operator is compact, and under Countable Choice an operator-norm limit of compact operators into a Banach space is compact. [[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]], [[thm-norm-limit-of-compact-operators-is-compact]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F5] The adjoint identity is $\langle Kx,y\rangle=\langle x,K^*y\rangle$. [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]

[F6] A feature vector is exactly estimable by one probe iff it belongs to $R(K^*)$. [[def-ip-feature-estimability-through-adjoint-range]]

[F7] The compact inverse model has Hilbert parameter and data spaces and a compact forward map. [[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model]]

[A1] Countable Choice is used only through the compactness of norm limits in [F4]. [[def-countable-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 The map is linear and $\|Kx\|_2^2=\sum_jx_j^2/j^2\le\|x\|_2^2$, so it is bounded. For $N\ge1$, let $K_Nx$ retain only the first $N$ output coordinates. Its range is spanned by $e_1,\ldots,e_N$, and $\|K_Nx\|_2\le\|x\|_2$ makes it bounded, so [F4] makes $K_N$ compact. Also $\|(K-K_N)x\|_2^2=\sum_{j>N}x_j^2/j^2\le(N+1)^{-2}\|x\|_2^2$, with equality in the operator norm on $e_{N+1}$. Thus $\|K-K_N\|=1/(N+1)\to0$, and [F4] makes $K$ compact. The diagonal real entries show $\langle Kx,y\rangle=\sum_jx_jy_j/j=\langle x,Ky\rangle$; by [F5], $K^*=K$. For every finitely supported $z$, the sequence $x_j=jz_j$ is finitely supported and $Kx=z$, so $c_{00}\subseteq R(K^*)$. Truncations are dense in $\ell^2$ by [F2], proving $\overline{R(K^*)}=\ell^2$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, F7, A1, algebra, construct]

2.1 By [F3], $h=(1/j)$ is square-summable. If $K^*x=h$, self-adjointness and the coordinate equations give $x_j/j=1/j$, hence $x_j=1$ for every $j$. But the first $N$ squared coordinates of such an $x$ sum to $N$ for every $N$, so no finite bound can contain all partial sums; this contradicts $x\in\ell^2$. Therefore $h\notin R(K^*)$. Since $h\in\overline{R(K^*)}$ by step 1.1, [F6] shows that the feature is not exactly estimable by a single probe despite lying in the closure of the adjoint range. [given, F1, F3, F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

dependency_level: 1

## Statement

For an odd prime $p$, let $\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ and define
$a*b=2b-a$. Then $(\mathbb F_p,*)$ is a quandle.

## Statement references

[[def-quandle-and-knot-coloring]].

[Manturov, *Knot Theory*, Chapter 5](https://varf.ru/rudn/manturov/book.pdf).

[Carter, *A Survey of Quandle Ideas*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1002.4429).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An odd prime $p$ and $a,b,c\in\mathbb F_p$, with $a*b=2b-a$.

[F1] [[def-quandle-and-knot-coloring]]: a quandle has bijective right translations, is idempotent, and is right self-distributive.

[A1] $p$ is prime, so a nonzero residue class modulo $p$ has an inverse.

## Proof

1.1 Addition and multiplication of residue classes are well-defined because congruence modulo $p$ is preserved by sums and products. If $\bar r\ne0$ in $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, choose an integer representative $r$ not divisible by $p$. Since $p$ is prime, $\gcd(r,p)=1$; Bézout's identity gives integers $u,v$ with $ur+vp=1$, so $\bar u\bar r=1$. Hence the residue classes form a field. For fixed $b$, the right translation is $R_b(a)=2b-a$ and satisfies $R_b(R_b(a))=2b-(2b-a)=a$. It is therefore a bijection. [given, A1, construct]

1.2 Idempotency holds because $a*a=2a-a=a$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For all $a,b,c$, $(a*b)*c=2c-(2b-a)=a-2b+2c$, while $(a*c)*(b*c)=2(2c-b)-(2c-a)=a-2b+2c$. Thus right self-distributivity holds; together with step 1.1 and step 1.2, [F1] gives the quandle axioms. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[[def-quandle-and-knot-coloring]].

      url: https://friedl.app.uni-regensburg.de/papers/2024_knot-theory-final.pdf

        pp. 72–73
---

## Statement

Assume countable choice.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link with
$n\geq1$ crossings. Fix a smooth height realization
$L_D=\{(\gamma(s),\eta(s))\}\subset\mathbb R^2\times[-1,0]$ such that
$\eta(s)=-1$ exactly at the $n$ underpassing points and $\eta(s)>-1$
elsewhere, and assume each component has at least one underpassing point. Put
$$M=(\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\setminus L_D.$$
Cut every component parameter circle at its underpassing points; the resulting
$n$ open intervals are the strands. For each strand interval $I_j$, its
vertical sheet is
$$D_j=\{(\gamma(s),z):s\in I_j,\ -1<z<\eta(s)\}\subset M.$$
Set $Z=M\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^nD_j$. Choose a common basepoint in $Z$, and
for each strand choose a positive meridian circle meeting only its own sheet
once, with its access path in $Z$. Then $\pi_1(M)$ is free on these based
positive meridians $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. The inclusion $M\hookrightarrow A_L$
also induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups.

## Statement references

[Friedl, §5.3, Claim 2](https://friedl.app.uni-regensburg.de/papers/2024_knot-theory-final.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The diagram, height realization, product-tube data, and based positive meridians specified in the statement.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The inclusion of the upper half-space with its point at infinity into $A_L$ is a homotopy equivalence by the variable-width level-sphere collar. [[lem-link-wirtinger-crossing-ball-cover]]

[F2] For an open cover by two path-connected sets with path-connected intersection, Seifert–van Kampen identifies the fundamental group of the union with the pushout. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

[F3] Under countable choice, every closed smooth embedded submanifold has an open tubular neighborhood in its normal bundle. [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F4] Cutting along a closed simply connected hypersurface with a two-sided simply connected tube and a one-tube corridor in the complement adds one free cyclic factor to the fundamental group. [[lem-simply-connected-hypersurface-complement-adds-free-generator]]

[F5] A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, with orientation fixed by the link tangent followed by disk orientation. [[def-based-string-link-and-labeled-link-peripheral-system]]

## Proof

**Given:** The diagram and height realization in the statement.

1.1 Let $A_L^\circ=((\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\})\setminus L_D$. By [F1], $\pi_1(A_L^\circ)\cong\pi_1(A_L)$. A small neighborhood $H$ of $\infty$ in $A_L^\circ$ is the open upper half-ball together with its cone vertex $\infty$, disjoint from $L_D$; other points of the level-sphere boundary have been deleted. The open cover $A_L^\circ=M\cup H$ has intersection $H\setminus\{\infty\}$, which is homeomorphic to $(0,1)\times\operatorname{int}(S^2_+)$ and is contractible because the open hemisphere $\operatorname{int}(S^2_+)$ is an open disk. Since $H$ is also contractible, [F2] gives $\pi_1(M)\cong\pi_1(A_L^\circ)$. [F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 Each $D_j$ is the image of the open region $(s,t)\mapsto(\gamma(s),-1+t(\eta(s)+1))$ with $s\in I_j$ and $0<t<1$; this is an embedded open disk. At a projected double point, the underpassing branch has height $-1$ and is absent from $M$, while the overpassing branch has height greater than $-1$. Thus sheets over distinct intervals are disjoint. Each sheet is closed in $M$: its only limit points outside itself lie on the excluded plane $z=-1$ or on the excluded link. Hence it is a proper smooth embedded simply connected surface. [given, construct]

2.1 At a fixed vertical line, every point of $Z$ lies above all link points on that line. Since every link height is at most $0$, the straight homotopy $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,(1-t)z+t)$ ($0\le t\le1$) stays above those link points and contracts $Z$ onto the plane $z=1$. This plane is contained in $Z$, so $Z$ is contractible. [step 1.2, given, construct]

3.1 For $j=1,\ldots,n$, put $M_j=M\setminus\bigcup_{k>j}D_k$. Then $M_0=Z$ and $M_j=M_{j-1}\cup D_j$. At each stage $M_{j-1}$ is path-connected: it contains path-connected $Z$, and every point of an earlier sheet joins to $Z$ along a short normal segment. Orient $D_j$ by its interval and height coordinates. The ambient orientation orients its normal line, so that line bundle is trivial; a bundle metric gives the unique positive unit vector in each fibre. By [A1, F3], choose a tubular neighborhood disjoint from the other sheets. Radial contraction shows the whole neighborhood and each of its two side components are simply connected. Choose a small positive meridian circle around an interior point of the $j$th strand in a ball disjoint from all other sheets. It meets $D_j$ transversely once. Remove a short open arc about that intersection; the remaining compact arc lies in $M_{j-1}$ and joins the two sides of $D_j$. Shrink the tubular neighborhood so that it meets this arc only in two end balls. This gives the corridor required by [F4], and its complement hypothesis holds because $M_j\setminus D_j=M_{j-1}$ is path-connected. [A1, F3, F4, given, step 1.2, step 2.1, induction, construct]

4.1 The cut lemma [F4] gives $\pi_1(M_j)\cong\pi_1(M_{j-1})*\mathbb Z$. Its cyclic generator is represented by the short meridian arc crossing $D_j$ followed by the complementary arc from step 3.1. Joining this loop to the basepoint by its access path in $Z$ gives exactly $x_j$, with positive orientation fixed by [F5]. Since $\pi_1(M_0)=\pi_1(Z)=1$, induction yields that $\pi_1(M)$ is free on $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. Step 1.1 identifies this with $\pi_1(A_L)$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, induction, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The cross-section shows one sheet below a strand between two underpassing points. The embedded sheet is a disk strip, and its two side collars are the two components used in the van Kampen step; the proof uses these products, not the drawing.

~~~tikz
  \draw[thick,->] (-1.5,2) .. controls (-0.5,2.3) and (0.5,2.3) .. (1.5,2);
  \draw[dashed] (-1.5,0) .. controls (-0.5,0.5) and (0.5,0.5) .. (1.5,0);
  \draw[dotted] (-1.5,0) -- (-1.5,2);
  \draw[dotted] (1.5,0) -- (1.5,2);
  \node at (-1.5,-0.25) {$p_-$};
~~~

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a fixed finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let $r>0$, and write $B_r=B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$. For each $f\in L^2(B_r;V)$ with $\int_{B_r}f=0$ there exists a unique $u\in W^{2,2}(B_r;V)$ with $\int_{B_r}u=0$ satisfying the Neumann problem in the weak form
$$\int_{B_r}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{B_r}\langle f,v\rangle\qquad\bigl(v\in W^{1,2}(B_r;V)\bigr).$$
Thus $-\Delta u=f$ distributionally, and the zero-normal boundary condition is included in the displayed all-test-function identity. The inverse $f\mapsto u$ is linear and obeys
$$\|D^2u\|_2\le\|f\|_2,\qquad r^{-2}\|u\|_2+r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2+\|D^2u\|_2\le C\|f\|_2,$$
with $C$ independent of $r$ and $f$. The Hessian norm is the Euclidean norm on all ordered second derivatives. If $f$ is the restriction of a polynomial and has mean zero, then $u$ is the restriction of a polynomial with classical $\partial_\nu u=0$ on $\partial B_r$.

If a fixed finite $\Gamma\le O(4)$ and an orthogonal representation $\sigma:\Gamma\to O(V)$ satisfy $f(\gamma x)=\sigma(\gamma)f(x)$ almost everywhere, the unique solution satisfies $u(\gamma x)=\sigma(\gamma)u(x)$ almost everywhere. This includes $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with its Frobenius norm and a prescribed action by orthogonal Lie-algebra automorphisms.

The compatibility $\int f=0$ is necessary. This is a linear $L^2$ boundary-solvability result; higher-$L^p$ Neumann estimates and nonlinear Coulomb-gauge existence are separate assertions.

## Statement references

[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains|Divergence theorem]]

[[lem-mean-zero-poincare-estimate-on-bounded-connected-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n|Mean-zero Poincare estimate]]

[Axler–Shin, *The Neumann problem on ellipsoids*, §2](https://www.axler.net/NeumannSpringer.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The divergence theorem holds for smooth vector fields on the closed ball and gives integration by parts with the outward unit normal ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]).

[F2] On $B_1$ there is $P>0$ with $\|v\|_2\le P\|\nabla v\|_2$ for scalar mean-zero $v\in W^{1,2}$. Summing the squared scalar inequalities in an orthonormal basis gives the same inequality for $V$-valued functions ([[lem-mean-zero-poincare-estimate-on-bounded-connected-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]]).

[F3] The polynomial algebra on the compact closed unit ball is uniformly dense in its real continuous functions, by the unital point-separating algebra criterion of [[thm-real-stone-weierstrass-for-compact-metric-spaces]]. Smooth compactly supported functions in $B_1$ are dense in $L^2(B_1)$ ([[lem-smooth-compactly-supported-functions-are-dense-in-ltwo-of-an-open-set]]).

[F4] $L^2$ is complete, and Holder controls its pairings and means ([[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[F5] The ball has a bounded Sobolev extension operator. Extend a $W^{1,2}$ class to $\mathbb R^4$ and approximate there by smooth functions to obtain restrictions of functions smooth on a neighbourhood of $\overline B_1$ converging in $W^{1,2}(B_1)$ ([[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]], [[thm-meyers-serrin-density-on-an-arbitrary-open-set]]).

[F6] Full AC supplies the Countable Choice used by the analytic suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, the space $V$, the radius and mean-zero datum of the statement. Work first on $B_1$.

1.1 **A finite harmonic decomposition.** If $p$ is homogeneous of degree $d$ on $\mathbb R^4$, put $N=\lfloor d/2\rfloor$, $c_0=1$, and $c_j=-c_{j-1}/(4j(d-j+1))$ for $1\le j\le N$. Define $H=\sum_{j=0}^Nc_j|x|^{2j}\Delta^jp$. For homogeneous $Q$ of degree $d-2j$, product differentiation and Euler's identity give $\Delta(|x|^{2j}Q)=4j(d-j+1)|x|^{2j-2}Q+|x|^{2j}\Delta Q$. Hence successive terms cancel in $\Delta H$, and $\Delta^{N+1}p=0$ gives $\Delta H=0$. All denominators are positive in their stated range. Moreover $p-H$ is divisible by $|x|^2$. Induction on $d$, starting with degrees zero and one, therefore writes $p$ as a finite sum $\sum_k|x|^{2k}H_{d-2k}$ with homogeneous harmonic $H_{d-2k}$. Decomposing each homogeneous piece of an arbitrary polynomial and then restricting to the unit sphere writes its restriction as $\sum_{l=0}^L G_l|_{\partial B_1}$ with each $G_l$ homogeneous harmonic of degree $l$. All constructions apply coefficientwise to $V$. [given, construct, induction, algebra]

1.2 **A polynomial antiderivative of the Laplacian.** On a monomial $x_1^a x_2^{b_2}x_3^{b_3}x_4^{b_4}$ define $I$ to multiply by $x_1^2/((a+1)(a+2))$; extend linearly to polynomials. Then $\partial_1^2I=\mathrm{id}$, and $I$ commutes with $\Delta'=\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2+\partial_4^2$. For a polynomial $f$, choose $M$ so that $(\Delta')^{M+1}f=0$ and set $p=-\sum_{k=0}^M(-1)^kI^{k+1}(\Delta')^kf$. Applying $\partial_1^2+\Delta'$ telescopes the finite sum and gives $\Delta p=-f$. [given, construct, algebra]

1.3 **Mean-zero polynomial density.** Given an $L^2$ function on $B_1$, first approximate it in $L^2$ by a compactly supported smooth function using [F3]. Extend this smooth function by zero near the boundary; it is continuous on the compact closed ball. Apply the polynomial density of [F3] uniformly, which also gives $L^2$ approximation by [F4]. Thus polynomials are dense in $L^2(B_1)$, coefficientwise for $V$. For mean-zero $f$, take polynomial approximants $p_j\to f$ and replace $p_j$ by $f_j=p_j-(p_j)_{B_1}$. Holder gives $\|(p_j)_{B_1}\|\,|B_1|^{1/2}\le\|p_j-f\|_2$, so these mean-zero polynomials still converge to $f$ in $L^2$. Full AC permits this sequential selection. [F3, F4, F6, construct, choose, algebra]

2.1 **The normal correction for polynomial data.** Suppose the polynomial $f$ has zero mean on $B_1$, choose $p$ from step 1.2, and let $g=-x\cdot\nabla p$ restricted to $\partial B_1$. By [F1], $\int_{\partial B_1}g=-\int_{B_1}\Delta p=\int_{B_1}f=0$. Decompose $g=\sum_lG_l|_{\partial B_1}$ by step 1.1. For $l\ge1$, Euler's identity and [F1] give $l\int_{\partial B_1}G_l=\int_{\partial B_1}\partial_\nu G_l=\int_{B_1}\Delta G_l=0$. Thus the constant $G_0$ is zero: its sphere integral vanishes and the sphere has positive area, since [F1] applied to $x$ gives $|\partial B_1|=4|B_1|>0$. The harmonic polynomial $h=\sum_{l\ge1}G_l/l$ satisfies $\partial_\nu h=g$ on the sphere. Hence $u=p+h$ satisfies $-\Delta u=f$ and $\partial_\nu u=0$. Subtracting its volume mean preserves these equations and gives a mean-zero polynomial solution. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 **The exact boundary Hessian estimate.** For a scalar smooth $u$ with $\partial_\nu u=0$ on $\partial B_1$, consider $Z=(\Delta u)\nabla u-D^2u\,\nabla u$. Direct differentiation cancels the third derivatives and gives $\operatorname{div}Z=(\Delta u)^2-|D^2u|^2$. On the sphere $\nabla u$ is tangential. Differentiating $\nabla u\cdot\nu=0$ in that tangential direction gives $D^2u(\nabla u,\nu)=-|\nabla u|^2$, because $\nabla_{\nabla u}\nu=\nabla u$ there. Thus $Z\cdot\nu=|\nabla u|^2$. By [F1], $\|\Delta u\|_2^2=\|D^2u\|_2^2+\int_{\partial B_1}|\nabla u|^2$. Sum the identity over an orthonormal basis of $V$. In particular every polynomial solution of step 2.1 satisfies $\|D^2u\|_2\le\|f\|_2$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **The remaining terms and the weak identity.** Integration by parts [F1] for a mean-zero polynomial solution gives $\|\nabla u\|_2^2=\int\langle f,u\rangle\le\|f\|_2\|u\|_2\le P\|f\|_2\|\nabla u\|_2$ by [F2] and [F4]. Dividing when the gradient norm is nonzero, and treating zero separately, gives $\|\nabla u\|_2\le P\|f\|_2$ and $\|u\|_2\le P^2\|f\|_2$. Together with step 3.1 this yields $\|u\|_2+\|\nabla u\|_2+\|D^2u\|_2\le(1+P+P^2)\|f\|_2$. The all-test-function weak identity first holds for tests smooth near the closed ball by [F1], since the normal term vanishes; it then holds for every $W^{1,2}$ test by [F4]–[F5]. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **Completion constructs the strong inverse.** For each $f_j$ choose the polynomial mean-zero solution $u_j$ of step 2.1. Their differences are polynomial mean-zero solutions for $f_j-f_k$, so steps 3.1–4.1 make $u_j$, all its first derivatives and all its second derivatives Cauchy in $L^2$. Completeness [F4] gives limits for each of these finitely many components. Passing in the weak derivative identities against a compactly supported smooth test identifies the first-derivative limits as the weak derivatives of the limit $u$, and then identifies the second-derivative limits as derivatives of those first derivatives. Hence $u\in W^{2,2}(B_1)$ and $u_j\to u$ strongly in that space. Its mean is zero by Holder. Passing to the limit in the weak identity of step 4.1 gives the displayed equation for every $W^{1,2}$ test. Norm continuity passes both estimates of steps 3.1–4.1 to $u$, including the constant-one Hessian bound. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

6.1 **Uniqueness, linearity and compatibility.** If two mean-zero $W^{1,2}$ solutions have the same datum, test their difference equation with the difference itself. Its gradient has zero $L^2$ norm; [F2] makes its $L^2$ norm zero, so the solutions agree. This proves uniqueness in the claimed $W^{2,2}$ class as well. Linear combinations satisfy the same linear weak identity and mean-zero normalization; uniqueness proves linearity of the inverse. Testing any weak solution with each constant vector in $V$ gives $\int f=0$, proving necessity. The polynomial solution of step 2.1 equals the completed solution by this uniqueness. [F2, F4, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 **Every radius.** For data $f$ on $B_r$, put $f_r(y)=r^2f(ry)$ on $B_1$ and solve there for $v$ by step 5.1. Set $u(x)=v(x/r)$. Changing variables in the weak identity proves the required identity and mean-zero normalization on $B_r$. In four dimensions, $\|f_r\|_{L^2(B_1)}=\|f\|_{L^2(B_r)}$, $\|D^2v\|_2=\|D^2u\|_2$, $\|\nabla v\|_2=r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2$, and $\|v\|_2=r^{-2}\|u\|_2$. Thus the bounds follow with $C=1+P+P^2$, independent of $r$. The construction preserves polynomiality for polynomial data. [step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

8.1 **Given finite equivariance and conclusion.** For $\gamma\in\Gamma$ let $T_\gamma u(x)=\sigma(\gamma)^{-1}u(\gamma x)$. Orthogonal changes of variables preserve the ball, volume, the gradient pairing and the zero mean; orthogonality of $\sigma(\gamma)$ preserves the target pairing. Therefore $T_\gamma u$ solves the same weak equation as $u$ when $T_\gamma f=f$. Uniqueness from step 6.1, rescaled as in step 7.1, gives $T_\gamma u=u$. This proves the equivariance for every element of the given finite group, including the stated Lie-algebra case. All existence, uniqueness and estimate claims are proved; full AC enters only through the analytic suppliers and the sequential approximation choices [F2]–[F6]. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Axler–Shin's full Proposition 2.1, Theorem 2.2, Lemma 2.3 and Theorem 2.4 proofs, printed pp.263–268 (PDF pp.3–8), were read in the author-hosted full paper. Their generalized polynomial Neumann construction uses a polynomial anti-Laplacian and a harmonic normal correction. The ball case above supplies its own finite homogeneous-harmonic decomposition, so no unproved Fischer decomposition or polynomial Dirichlet theorem is imported. The boundary Hessian identity and the completion to all mean-zero $L^2$ data are proved explicitly here.

This constructs the strong mean-zero $L^2$ Neumann inverse and preserves a prescribed finite equivariance by uniqueness. It does not supply the higher-$L^p$ or Hodge estimates, nonlinear exponential iteration, or small-critical-curvature gauge construction needed in the full instanton foundations.

## Statement

Let $D$ be a nonempty unoriented regular link diagram with $c$ crossings and $m\ge1$ components, and let $\langle D\rangle=\sum_j z_jA^j$ be its exact Kauffman bracket. Its Laurent exponents satisfy $|j|\le 3c+2m-2$, and its signed-magnitude coefficient-bit size, as defined in the encoded diagram size definition, is at most $m+2c+1$. Consequently, a knot diagram ($m=1$) has Laurent degree and coefficient-bit size bounded linearly in $c+1$.

The state-sum algorithm admits a naive exact implementation taking
$O(2^c(c+m+1)^4)$ elementary bit steps in the following model. Its typed
input gives $c$ and the number $u$ of crossingless components in
self-delimiting binary: each number is encoded by $b$ ones, a zero, and its
$b$ ordinary binary digits, with $b\ge1$ the number of those digits.
These fields are followed by the edge-pairing table on the $4c$
endpoints indexed by crossing and local port. Its entries are ordered by
endpoint index and each uses $\max(1,\lceil\log_2(4c+1)\rceil)$ bits.
At each crossing the ports are northwest, northeast,
southeast, southwest in the bracket's fixed local chart; the two smoothing
pairings are therefore fixed pairs of port indices. The table is assumed to
be the incidence data of the given diagram. Polynomial arithmetic uses dense
arrays of signed binary integer coefficients, and one tape-cell read, write,
or head move on a fixed finite number of binary work tapes costs one step.
For knots this bound is $O(2^c(c+1)^4)$. It is a bound for this explicit
indexed implementation, not for arbitrary black-box polynomial operations.
Constructing the indexed input from an arbitrary literal code of length $L$,
reading other labels or padding, and processing geometric coordinates are
outside this bound.

## Statement references

[[def-encoded-diagram-size-and-exact-output]]

[[alg-kauffman-bracket-state-sum]]

[[thm-kauffman-bracket-state-sum-procedure-properties]]

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §4.3](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory* (2025), §5.1](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty unoriented regular link diagram $D$ with $c$ crossings and $m\ge1$ components.

[F1] [[def-encoded-diagram-size-and-exact-output]]: $c$ is the crossing count, $m$ is the component count, and a Laurent coefficient $z$ has signed-magnitude bit length $1+\lceil\log_2(|z|+1)\rceil$ when $z\ne0$.

[F2] [[alg-kauffman-bracket-state-sum]]: the bracket term of a state $S$ is $A^{a(S)-b(S)}\delta^{|S|-1}$ with $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$; $a(S)+b(S)=c$, and $|S|$ is the number of circles after smoothing.

[F3] [[thm-kauffman-bracket-state-sum-procedure-properties]]: the state-sum procedure visits exactly the $2^c$ maps from the crossing set to $\{A,B\}$ and returns the displayed sum.

## Proof

1.1 The state set has exactly $2^c$ elements by [F3]. A complete smoothing starts with $m$ circles. At each crossing the four local endpoints lie on one or two current circles, and either smoothing reconnects them into one or two circles. Thus the circle count increases by at most one at each of the $c$ smoothings. Every state has $1\le |S|\le m+c$. [F2, F3, construct]

2.1 For a fixed state, put $r=|S|-1$, so $0\le r\le m+c-1$. The binomial theorem gives $\delta^r=(-1)^r\sum_{k=0}^r\binom{r}{k}A^{2r-4k}$. These exponents are distinct, so its coefficient l1 norm is $\sum_{k=0}^r\binom{r}{k}=2^r$; multiplication by the monomial $A^{a(S)-b(S)}$ only shifts the exponents. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Since $a(S)+b(S)=c$, one has $|a(S)-b(S)|\le c$. The exponents in $\delta^r$ lie between $-2r$ and $2r$. Using $r\le m+c-1$, every exponent in every state term, and thus in the sum, has absolute value at most $c+2(m+c-1)=3c+2m-2$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Put $q=c+m+1\ge2$. Represent a crossing endpoint by an integer from $1$ to $4c$, grouped into four successive ports at each crossing, and write $\alpha$ for the supplied edge-pairing involution. For a state, let $\beta$ pair the two left and two right ports for A, or the two top and two bottom ports for B. The multigraph on the $4c$ endpoints with one $\alpha$-edge and one $\beta$-edge at every vertex is two-regular, allowing parallel edges. Each connected component follows one smoothed circle, and the $u$ supplied crossingless components add $u$ further circles. Thus a traversal marking a vertex when first queued computes $|S|$ exactly. The same traversal, with the opposite ports paired instead of smoothing ports, computes the original component count $m$; perform it once initially and then compute $q$ for allocation. Use binary counters and linear scans for all table and mark lookups: there are $O(q)$ endpoint visits, each using a bounded number of scans of $O(q)$ records with $O(\log q)$ index bits. Even with a work-tape queue or stack scanned linearly, each visit costs $O(q^2)$ bit steps, so tracing costs $O(q^3)$. Computing $a(S)-b(S)$ and adding $u$ use counters of $O(\log q)$ bits and fit this bound. Enumerate the states with a $c$-bit binary counter, making exactly $2^c$ visits; the $c=0$ case is one empty mask with $|S|=u=m$. Reading the stated input takes $O(q\log q)$ steps and is included. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Summing over all $2^c$ states, the l1 norm of the final coefficient sequence is at most the sum of the state-term l1 norms, hence at most $2^c2^{m+c-1}=2^{m+2c-1}$. Every individual coefficient therefore has absolute value at most $2^{m+2c-1}$. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $M=m+2c\ge1$. By step 3.1, a nonzero coefficient $z_j$ satisfies $|z_j|\le2^{M-1}$, so $|z_j|+1\le2^M$ and $\ell_{\mathbb Z}(z_j)=1+\lceil\log_2(|z_j|+1)\rceil\le M+1=m+2c+1$. The support lies in at most $6c+4m-3$ integer exponents by step 2.2, so storing the exact polynomial as a dense coefficient array takes $O((c+m)^2)$ bits. For a knot, $m=1$, giving degree at most $3c$ and coefficient-bit size at most $2c+2$, both linear in $c+1$. [F1, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.2 Use coefficient slots for every exponent from $-3q$ to $3q$, padded with zeros, and use $2q+3$ bits per signed-magnitude slot, plus $O(\log q)$-bit position counters. These arrays have $O(q^2)$ tape cells. Every partial accumulator, not just the final sum, has coefficient l1 norm at most $2^c2^{m+c-1}$: apply the triangle inequality in step 3.1 to the subset of states already processed. Hence its coefficients fit the chosen width, since $m+2c-1<2q$. For one state compute $r=|S|-1$ and start with the array for $P_0=1$. For $k=0,\ldots,r-1$, form a new array by the exact recurrence $(P_{k+1})_j=-(P_k)_{j-2}-(P_k)_{j+2}$, reading absent coefficients as zero. This is multiplication by $\delta$, so $P_r=\delta^r$. All intermediate powers have degree at most $2r<2q$ and l1 norm at most $2^r\le2^{m+c-1}$, so they too fit the arrays and widths. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra, construct]

5.1 Here is a direct tape bound without unit-cost access or integer arithmetic. To retrieve or write a coefficient, scan an entire array of $O(q)$ slots of $O(q)$ bits, advancing a binary slot counter and comparing it with the desired index. The counter work is $O(q\log q)$ and the scanned data have $O(q^2)$ bits, so one lookup or write costs $O(q^2)$ bit steps. Addition or subtraction of two signed integers in these slots is performed by sign comparison, a linear magnitude comparison, and the usual binary carry or borrow scan, costing $O(q)$ steps; the extra carry bit fits the reserved width. For each of the $O(q)$ destination coefficients in the recurrence of step 4.2, make at most two source lookups, one such addition, and one destination write. A multiplication by $\delta$ therefore costs $O(q^3)$ steps. There are $r<q$ repetitions, giving $O(q^4)$ work. Shift this state polynomial by $a(S)-b(S)$ and add it to the accumulator coefficient by coefficient using the same linear scans; the state shift has magnitude at most $c$, its support stays inside the slots by step 2.2, and this accumulation costs $O(q^3)$. Clearing arrays, moving the state counter, and loop-index bookkeeping are bounded by the same charges. [step 2.2, step 2.3, step 4.2, construct, algebra]

6.1 Summing the per-state bounds in steps 2.3, 4.2, and 5.1 over exactly $2^c$ visits gives $O(2^cq^4)$ bit steps. The initial component-count traversal costs $O(q^3)$ by step 2.3; coefficient-array initialization and writing the dense exact output cost $O(q^2)$. These are absorbed because $2^c\ge1$ and $q\ge2$. The loop tracing and arithmetic realize exactly the state terms in [F2], so [F3] identifies the result with the bracket. When $c=0$, the single state computes $\delta^{m-1}$ with the same bound; when $m=1$, $q=c+2$ gives $O(2^c(c+1)^4)$. All choices and operations are finite. The bit-cost argument concerns only the specified indexed table and elementary binary operations, so it makes no claim about parsing arbitrary code strings of length $L$ or the cost of an unspecified arithmetic library. [F1, F2, F3, step 4.1, step 2.3, step 4.2, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $V$ be its positive-push Seifert matrix, with entries $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ in an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the Alexander polynomial normalized by $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)$, where $p\doteq q$ means $p=\pm t^kq$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$. If the integral Seifert lattice is metabolic, then there is an $f(t)\in\mathbb Z[t]$ such that $\Delta_K(t)\doteq f(t)f(t^{-1})$. The same factorization is necessary if $K$ bounds a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$. This is a necessary condition for either algebraic or locally flat sliceness, not a sufficient condition. The factorization concerns the Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K$, not the separate knot-normalized fraction $D_K(t)=\Delta_K(t)/(1-t)$.

[[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance|The integral metabolizer condition]]

[[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial|The determinant normalization of the Alexander polynomial]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, an oriented knot $K$, a connected oriented Seifert surface $F$, its positive-push matrix $V$, and either a metabolizer for $V$ or a locally flat proper slice disk for $K$.

[A1] Full AC is the family-of-nonempty-sets choice axiom used by the knot Seifert-pairing convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The positive-push matrix represents the integral Seifert pairing, with the stated linking convention. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]

[F2] The generator of the zeroth Alexander elementary ideal satisfies $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)$ in this convention. [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]]

[F3] A metabolic Seifert lattice has a rank-$g$ direct summand on which the pairing vanishes. [[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance]]

[F4] For any integral rank-$2g$ bilinear form with unimodular skew part and a rank-$g$ direct-summand metabolizer, its determinant is $t^gf(t)f(t^{-1})$ for some $f\in\mathbb Z[t]$. [[lem-metabolic-seifert-form-implies-fox-milnor-factorization]]

[F5] Under full AC the actual slice-metabolizer supplier proves that every locally flat proper slice disk induces the required integral rank-$g$ primitive metabolizer. Its TOP branch uses the explicitly sourced geometric inputs of the Seifert-hypersurface supplier and retains the local duality, isotropy and integral-saturation argument. [[lem-slice-disk-induces-seifert-metabolizer]]

## Proof

1.1 If the Seifert lattice is metabolic, [F3] supplies a rank-$g$ direct-summand metabolizer for the positive-push matrix [F1]. Its skew part is unimodular by the knot Seifert convention, so [F4] gives $\det(V-tV^T)=t^gf(t)f(t^{-1})$. By [F2], $\Delta_K(t)$ differs from this determinant by a Laurent unit, proving the algebraic factorization claim. This matrix calculation uses no choice beyond the stated full-AC convention for the Seifert data. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 If $K$ bounds the locally flat proper disk of the Statement, [F5] provides the actual integral metabolizer for the positive-push Seifert lattice on the given $F$. Apply step1.1 to obtain $\Delta_K(t)\doteq f(t)f(t^{-1})$. This includes a smooth slice disk as a special case. The conclusion is the stated necessary condition for $\Delta_K$, and does not assert sufficiency or a factorization of $D_K$. [A1, F5, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement refuted

Let $C=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(T_{2,3})$ be the right-handed trefoil staircase on generators $x_0,x_1,x_2$ with $(M,A)(x_0)=(0,1)$, $(M,A)(x_1)=(-1,0)$, $(M,A)(x_2)=(-2,-1)$ and differential $\partial x_1=Ux_0+x_2$, $\partial x_0=\partial x_2=0$. The claim that $\Upsilon_{T_{2,3}}(1)$ is obtained by minimizing $F_1(x)$ over the individual displayed basis terms $x_0,x_1,x_2$, instead of over Maslov-zero cycles representing the normalized generator, is false. Under the diagonal-grid convention, every grid diagram of the trefoil also has grid Upsilon value $-1$ at $t=1$.

## Statement references

[[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex|The cycle-minimax definition, including the normalized-generator condition]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Zoltan Szabo, *Concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology*, §§2 and 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795)

[Livingston, *Notes on the knot concordance invariant Upsilon*, §§4–6](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Upsilon-revised.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The explicitly displayed right-handed trefoil staircase and the definition of $F_1$ on a finite chain.

[F1] [[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex]]: $F_1(z)$ is the maximum weight among terms in the support of $z$, and $\nu_1$ minimizes this value over Maslov-zero cycles representing the normalized generator.

[F2] [[thm-grid-upsilon-equals-oss-upsilon]] now contains a proof of the grid-value comparison using the normalized grid/Heegaard supplier, whose own current Proof is present and whose [F1]–[F5] prerequisites remain explicit. MOS Proposition 2.3 supplies the chosen-variable filtered comparison and tilde-homology $V$-factor, and Theorem 3.3 identifies the grid filtered complex with the knot filtration; the current in-run comparison proof supplies the chain-level collapse factor and its absolute normalization argument.

## Counterexample

1.1 The only Maslov-zero basis terms in the displayed staircase are $x_0$ and $U^{-1}x_2$; $x_1$ has odd Maslov parity, so no integral $U$-translate of $x_1$ has Maslov grading zero. Both even-degree terms are cycles, and $\partial(U^{-1}x_1)=x_0+U^{-1}x_2$ shows they represent the same nonzero generator. Their coordinates are $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$, each of $F_1$-weight $1/2$. The sum is a boundary, so every Maslov-zero cycle representing the normalized generator has filtration $1/2$. Thus $\nu_1=1/2$ and $\Upsilon(1)=-2(1/2)=-1$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The displayed basis term $x_2$ has coordinates $(0,-1)$ and weight $F_1(x_2)=-1/2$, which is less than $1/2$. It has Maslov grading $-2$, so it is excluded from the Maslov-zero representative set; although it is a cycle, its homology class is not the normalized degree-zero generator. The false rule would return $-2(-1/2)=+1$, contradicting step 1.1. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F2], the diagonal grid complex has the same Upsilon value as the original invariant, so step 1.1 gives the stated grid value $-1$. The grid comparison uses the supplier prerequisites recorded in [F2]. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

The finite staircase refutation is complete. Its right-handed trefoil identification is supplied by the signed three-crossing grid proof in [[lem-epsilon-stable-equivalence-and-not-a-homomorphism]], step 4.3, together with that item's finite staircase computation. The universal grid-value clause is supplied by [F2] under the comparison prerequisites it records; the earlier missing-comparison escalation is no longer current.

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $q$ be a prime power, and let $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ have prime-power order $d$. Choose a Casson–Gordon bordism datum $(M_{0,q},\eta,r,W)$. Write $G=\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z$, let $Y\to W$ be the regular cover determined by $\eta$, and give $\mathbb C(t)$ the $G$-action $(a,n)z=\exp(2\pi ia/d)t^n z$ and involution $\overline{t}=t^{-1}$ with complex conjugation on constants. Define
$$H_2^t(W;\mathbb C)=H_2(Y;\mathbb C)\otimes_{\mathbb C[G]}\mathbb C(t).$$
The Casson–Gordon Witt class is
$$\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi)=\frac{1}{r}\bigl([H_2^t(W;\mathbb C)]-[Q_0(W)\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C(t)]\bigr)\in W(\mathbb C(t))\otimes\mathbb Q,$$
using the nonsingular twisted form and the ordinary nonsingular image form. Precisely, put $Q_0(W)=H_2(W;\mathbb C)/\operatorname{rad}(\lambda_W)$ with its induced form; the untwisted term in the display is understood as $Q_0(W)\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C(t)$. The twisted boundary complex is acyclic, so its algebraic Poincare cap preserves the absolute twisted module. This does not assert that an arbitrary ordinary absolute intersection form is nonsingular. Here $W(\mathbb C(t))$ is the Witt group of nonsingular Hermitian forms over the field with involution, modulo hyperbolic forms. Its signature defect is $\sigma(K,\chi)=\sigma_1(\tau(\Sigma_q(K),\chi))$, where $\sigma_1$ evaluates a Hermitian representative at $t=e^{i\theta}$ and takes the one-sided limit as $\theta\to0^+$. This is the specified Casson–Gordon invariant and signature homomorphism; it is not an arbitrary rho invariant or an unspecified difference of signatures.

## Definition

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $q\ge2$, and let $M=\Sigma_q(K)$ be its $q$-fold cyclic branched cover. A character is a homomorphism $\chi:H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$. Its order is its order in $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(M;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$; it is finite-order when this order is finite and has prime-power order when its order is $p^e$ for a prime $p$ and $e\ge1$. It vanishes on a subgroup $P$ when $\chi(x)=0$ for every $x\in P$.

## Definition

Let $X$ be a closed connected oriented smooth four-manifold. Its integral intersection lattice is the abelian group $L_X=H_2(X;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$ with the integer-valued symmetric bilinear pairing $Q_X(\bar x,\bar y)=\langle \operatorname{PD}^{-1}(x)\smile\operatorname{PD}^{-1}(y),[X]\rangle$. Here $\operatorname{Tor}$ is the subgroup of elements of finite order, $[X]\in H_4(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the orientation class, and $\operatorname{PD}:H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\to H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the Poincaré duality isomorphism. The rank is $b_2(X)=\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_2(X;\mathbb Q)$. The lattice is positive definite when $Q_X(x,x)>0$ for every nonzero $x\in L_X$; it is unimodular when a Gram matrix in an integral basis has determinant $1$ or $-1$.

## Definition

For any group $G$, define its lower-central series by $\Gamma_1G=G$ and
$\Gamma_{q+1}G=[G,\Gamma_qG]$, where $[G,H]$ is the subgroup generated by
$ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$ for $g\in G$ and $h\in H$. For $r\ge1$, let
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$ be the free group on the formal meridian
symbols $x_i$, with the free-group convention of its stated generators.

Let $\mathcal A_r=\mathbb Z\langle\!\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle\!\rangle$
be the ring of formal integer sums $\sum_w a_wX_w$ over all finite words $w$
in the letters $X_i$, with multiplication given by concatenation of words.
This is the degree-complete ring for the word-length filtration; a series with
invertible constant coefficient is a unit, with inverse determined recursively
degree by degree.
Filter it by total degree (word length), and let $\mathfrak m$ be the ideal of
series with zero constant term.
The Magnus expansion is the group homomorphism
$$E:F_r\longrightarrow \mathbb Z\langle\!\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle\!\rangle^\times, \qquad E(x_i)=1+X_i.$$
It sends $x_i^{-1}$ to $(1+X_i)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kX_i^k$. For an
integer $d\ge0$, calculations through degree $d$ use the truncated ring
$R_d=\mathbb Z\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle/\mathfrak m^{d+1}$. As a
$\mathbb Z$-module it has the finite monomial basis of words of length at most
$d$. In $R_d$, the inverse of $1+A$ for $A\in\mathfrak m$ is the finite sum
$1-A+A^2-\cdots+(-A)^d$.

For a based string link, $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ may be used as formal symbols
corresponding to the positive bottom-end meridians. No freeness or
lower-central quotient isomorphism is asserted here; those properties require
separate proofs.

## Remarks

The commutator convention is $[a,b]=aba^{-1}b^{-1}$. Truncation to degree $d$
retains the constant and homogeneous terms of degrees at most $d$.

## Definition

Assume full AC. Let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ be the group of a smooth oriented knot exterior, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. For a finite presentation $G=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$, the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ representation variety** is the algebraic set of tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ for which every relator matrix $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)$ equals the identity. The group $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ acts on this set by simultaneous conjugation. Its affine categorical quotient, whose coordinate ring is the invariant ring of regular functions, is the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ character variety** $X(E_K)$. For a representation $\rho$, its character is the function $\gamma\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\gamma))$. A representation is **reducible** if its matrices preserve a common one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$; otherwise it is irreducible. The peripheral torus group is $\pi_1(T_K)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, generated by the meridian and preferred longitude; its image in $G$ is generated by their commuting classes and need not be isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Their image under any representation is a commuting pair of matrices, so it has a common invariant line and is simultaneously triangularizable over $\mathbb C$. Choosing a common invariant line gives meridian and longitude eigenvalues $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$; the unordered boundary character identifies $(M,L)$ with $(M^{-1},L^{-1})$. Simultaneous diagonalizability is stronger than simultaneous triangularizability.

## Example

Assume Countable Choice and let $Q=\rho>0$, $\nu=1$, and $K$ be a compact real infinite-rank operator. Over its minimum-norm power source ball $X_{1,\rho}(K)$, if $s_j\asymp j^{-1}$ then the minimax RMS error in the Gaussian sequence inverse model is of order $\epsilon^{2/5}$; if $s_j\asymp e^{-j}$ then it is of order $\epsilon^{1/2}$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. The constants may depend on $\rho$ and the fixed singular-value comparison constants.

## Example references

[[lem-ip-power-source-class-as-statistical-ellipsoid|Power source balls are weighted statistical ellipsoids]]

[[cor-ip-mild-and-severe-estimation-rates|Polynomial and exponential minimax estimation rates]]

[Litao Ding and Peter Mathé, *Minimax rates for statistical inverse problems under general source conditions*, Definition 2 and §3, Table 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.01706v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-ip-power-source-class-as-statistical-ellipsoid]]: $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)$ has ellipsoid weights $a_j=s_j^{-\nu}$ and radius $Q=\rho$.

[F2] [[cor-ip-mild-and-severe-estimation-rates]]: For polynomial singular values with polynomial axes, the rate is $\epsilon^{\kappa/(\kappa+p+1/2)}$; for exponential singular values with exponential axes, the rate is $\epsilon^{\kappa/(p+\kappa)}$.

[F3] [[def-ip-power-source-set]] and [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]: The source class is $X_{\nu,\rho}(K)=\{|K|^\nu w:\|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ in the real Gaussian sequence inverse model.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is inherited through the compact singular system.

**Given:** Countable Choice, $\rho>0$, $\nu=1$, and either $s_j\asymp j^{-1}$ or $s_j\asymp e^{-j}$.

## Verification

1.1 If $s_j\asymp j^{-1}$, [F1] gives $a_j=s_j^{-1}\asymp j$, so the first formula of [F2] applies with $p=\kappa=1$ and gives $\epsilon^{2/5}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 If $s_j\asymp e^{-j}$, [F1] gives $a_j=s_j^{-1}\asymp e^j$, so the fourth formula of [F2] applies with $p=\kappa=1$ and gives $\epsilon^{1/2}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By [A1], the compact singular-system coordinate model is interpreted with its stated Countable Choice prerequisite. Both substitutions use the exact coefficient ellipsoid from [F1] and preserve the stated radius $\rho$, so they yield the two source-ball rates in the Example. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

For the crossingless oriented unknot code, triangulate its solid-torus exterior $D^2\times S^1$ by triangulating $D^2$ as one triangle with vertices $a_0,a_1,a_2$ and $S^1$ as the three-edge cycle $b_0b_1b_2b_0$. In the prism over $b_0b_1$, write $a_i^0=(a_i,b_0)$ and $a_i^1=(a_i,b_1)$ and use the tetrahedra
$$T_1=[a_0^0,a_1^0,a_2^0,a_2^1],\qquad T_2=[a_0^0,a_1^0,a_1^1,a_2^1],\qquad T_3=[a_0^0,a_0^1,a_1^1,a_2^1].$$
The properly embedded normal disk $D^2\times\{s_*\}$ at the midpoint $s_*$ of $b_0b_1$ meets $T_1$ in the triangle cutting off $a_2^1$, $T_2$ in the quadrilateral separating $\{a_0^0,a_1^0\}$ from $\{a_1^1,a_2^1\}$, and $T_3$ in the triangle cutting off $a_0^0$; every other normal coordinate is zero. It is connected, has nonempty boundary and Euler characteristic one, and its boundary meets the marked original meridian $\mu=\{a_0\}\times S^1$ once mod two.

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1]
\coordinate (A0) at (0,0); \coordinate (A1) at (2,0); \coordinate (A2) at (1,1.5);
\coordinate (B0) at (0.6,0.7); \coordinate (B1) at (2.6,0.7); \coordinate (B2) at (1.6,2.2);
\draw (A0)--(A1)--(A2)--cycle; \draw (B0)--(B1)--(B2)--cycle;
\draw (A0)--(B0) (A1)--(B1) (A2)--(B2);
\draw[dashed] (A0)--(B1) (A0)--(B2) (A1)--(B2);
\coordinate (M0) at (0.3,0.35); \coordinate (M1) at (2.3,0.35); \coordinate (M2) at (1.3,1.85);
\draw[red,very thick] (M0)--(M1)--(M2)--cycle;
\node[below left] at (A0) {$a_0^0$}; \node[below right] at (A1) {$a_1^0$}; \node[left] at (A2) {$a_2^0$};
\node[left] at (B0) {$a_0^1$}; \node[right] at (B1) {$a_1^1$}; \node[above] at (B2) {$a_2^1$};
\node[red] at (1.35,0.8) {$D^2\times\{s_*\}$};
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

The dashed edges indicate the staircase prism subdivision specified by $T_1,T_2,T_3$; the red section is the geometric disk whose intersections with those tetrahedra give the stated triangle–quadrilateral–triangle vector. The formula for the tetrahedra, not the schematic projection, fixes the exact triangulation.

## Example references

[[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]] — triangle and quadrilateral normal disk types.

[[lem-good-linear-size-exterior-triangulation-from-diagram]] — fixed crossingless solid-torus exterior model and marked meridian path.

[Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger, §4 and §5](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hass/Research/Papers/Complexity/hlp.pdf) — unknot exterior and normal disk coordinates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The product triangulation $D^2\times S^1$ of the exterior and its marked meridian path.

[F1] [[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]]: a triangle or quadrilateral normal disk meets tetrahedral faces in matching normal arcs; admissibility allows at most one quadrilateral type per tetrahedron.

[F2] [[lem-good-linear-size-exterior-triangulation-from-diagram]]: at zero crossings the exterior is a fixed triangulated solid torus with the original meridian represented by a three-edge fibre cycle.

## Verification

1.1 For the prism over $b_0b_1$, write $a_i^0=(a_i,b_0)$ and $a_i^1=(a_i,b_1)$. Use the staircase tetrahedra
$$T_1=[a_0^0,a_1^0,a_2^0,a_2^1],\qquad T_2=[a_0^0,a_1^0,a_1^1,a_2^1],\qquad T_3=[a_0^0,a_0^1,a_1^1,a_2^1].$$
Their common faces are triangulated by the same ordered diagonals, so the three tetrahedra form the triangular-prism block; repeating this order on the three-cycle of $S^1$ gives the product triangulation in [F2]. [given, F2, construct]

2.1 The level disk at the midpoint of the product edge separates the bottom vertices $a_i^0$ from the top vertices $a_i^1$. In $T_1$ it cuts off the single top vertex $a_2^1$, giving one triangle; in $T_2$ it separates the pair $\{a_0^0,a_1^0\}$ from $\{a_1^1,a_2^1\}$, giving one quadrilateral; in $T_3$ it cuts off the single bottom vertex $a_0^0$, giving one triangle. It misses all tetrahedra in the other two prism blocks. Its intersections on shared faces agree because they are the same level section of the product, so the matching equations hold. Only one quadrilateral coordinate is nonzero, so [F1] gives an admissible normal disk vector. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The geometric surface is exactly $D^2\times\{s_*\}$, hence is a connected disk. Its boundary is $\partial D^2\times\{s_*\}$, which is nonempty and has $\chi=1$. The marked meridian $\{a_0\}\times S^1$ passes through exactly one point of this boundary at $(a_0,s_*)$, in the interior of the chosen fiber edge; the intersection is transverse and has parity $1$. [given, F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Thus the explicit vector satisfies the matching, quadrilateral, connectedness, boundary, Euler-characteristic and mod-two meridian checks claimed in the statement. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

kind: lemma
title: "Boundary tori inject into the circle-bundle group"

      locator: "Lemma 1.16 proof, printed pp.20–21"
    - title: "Ryan Budney, JSJ-decompositions of knot and link complements in the 3-sphere"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0506523"
      locator: "§1, Seifert pieces in the torus decomposition, PDF pp.2–4"
---

## Statement

Let $B$ be either a pair of pants or a once-punctured Möbius band, and let $p:N\to B$ be a circle bundle whose total space is orientable. For each boundary torus $T$ of $N$, the inclusion $T\hookrightarrow N$ induces an injective homomorphism $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(N)$.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Lemma 1.16 proof](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Ryan Budney, *JSJ-decompositions of knot and link complements in the 3-sphere*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0506523)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A circle bundle $p:N\to B$ over a pair of pants or once-punctured Möbius band, with orientable total space, and a boundary torus $T$ of $N$.

[F1] A Seifert fibration is locally a circle bundle away from exceptional fibers ([[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]], Definition).

[F2] A fibration has the long exact sequence of homotopy groups, so when $\pi_2(B)=0$ the fiber group injects into the total-space group and its image is the kernel of projection ([[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-homotopy-groups-of-a-fibration]], Statement).

## Proof

1.1 Each of the two possible bases has nonempty boundary and deformation-retracts to a graph, so $\pi_2(B)=0$. The homotopy exact sequence [F2] therefore injects the fiber subgroup $\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb Z$ into $\pi_1(N)$, with image the kernel of $p_*:\pi_1(N)\to\pi_1(B)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 The fundamental group of a pair of pants is free on two generators $a,b$, and its three boundary loops represent $a$, $b$, and $(ab)^{-1}$, each of infinite order. The once-punctured Möbius band has free generators $x,c_1$ and boundary loops represented by $c_1$ and $c_1^{-1}x^{-2}$; both are nontrivial cyclically reduced words and have infinite order in the free group. Thus every boundary circle of $B$ injects on fundamental groups. [given, algebra]

2.1 The restriction $T\to\partial B$ is a circle bundle over a circle, hence induces a surjection $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(\partial B)$. If $g\in\pi_1(T)$ maps trivially to $\pi_1(N)$, its projection is a power of the corresponding boundary loop and is trivial in $\pi_1(B)$; step 1.2 forces that power to be zero. Therefore $g$ lies in the fiber subgroup, whose inclusion into $\pi_1(N)$ is injective by step 1.1, so $g=1$. This proves that $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(N)$ is injective. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let A be a proper annulus in a compact oriented 4-manifold W, with boundary knots K₀ and K₁ in the two boundary 3-spheres. Assume A has an oriented normal disk neighborhood A×D² whose endpoint framings are the preferred zero-linking longitudes. Let R be Z or R_n=Z[1/|n|], and assume each end S³→W is an R-homology isomorphism. Removing A×D² and attaching D²×S¹×I along the annular side, with ∂D² matched to the annulus longitude and the core matched to the normal meridian, produces a cobordism V from M(K₀) to M(K₁). The statement predicts that the boundary inclusions M(K_i)→V are R-homology isomorphisms. If W is simply connected, it also predicts that π₁(V) is normally generated by either endpoint knot-group image.

## Statement references

[[def-cdr-satellite-concordance-categories|Concordance ambient and coefficient conventions]]

[[def-zero-surgery-on-a-knot|Preferred-longitude zero surgery]]

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Proper annuli and local flatness]]

[CDR, Proposition 3.2 and §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.5058v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $W$, the proper annulus $A$, its supplied relative normal disk neighborhood $N=A\times D^2$, its endpoint zero framings, and the stated $R$-homology isomorphisms.

[F1] Zero surgery fills the preferred longitude. [[def-zero-surgery-on-a-knot]]

[F2] The supplied proper product collars permit the displayed cut-and-paste constructions at both ends. [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]]

[F3] Excisive covers have the natural small-chain Mayer–Vietoris sequence, including with constant $R$ coefficients; the chain construction descends to relative pairs. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[F4] The fundamental group of a union with connected overlap is the pushout of the two factor groups. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

## Proof

1.1 Put $E=\overline{W\setminus N}$, $C=A\times S^1$, and $E_i=E\cap S_i^3$, $N_i=N\cap S_i^3$, $C_i=C\cap S_i^3$. The supplied product identifies $N$ with $S^1\times I\times D^2$, $N_i$ with $S^1\times\{i\}\times D^2$, $C$ with $S^1\times I\times S^1$, and $C_i$ with its endpoint torus. Attach $F=D^2\times S^1\times I$ along $C$, identifying its disk-boundary circle with the annulus longitude and its other circle with the normal meridian. Each endpoint boundary is then $E_i$ filled by $F_i=D^2\times S^1\times\{i\}$ along the preferred longitude, precisely $M(K_i)$ by [F1]. The common annular-side collar gives a manifold after gluing, with the same smooth or topological category as the supplied data; in the smooth case round the product corners. This constructs $V=E\cup_C F$ with the prescribed oriented ends. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Here is the relative chain comparison in every degree. Thicken the pieces slightly along their supplied common collars to make excisive covers, using the same thickening at the ends; the thickenings retract onto the indicated pieces and intersections as pairs. For either decomposition $X=P\cup_C Q$ with corresponding endpoint $X_i=P_i\cup_{C_i}Q_i$, the small-chain sequence underlying [F3], quotiented by the endpoint sequence, is degreewise exact: $0\to C_*(C,C_i;R)\to C_*(P,P_i;R)\oplus C_*(Q,Q_i;R)\to C_*^{\mathrm{small}}(X,X_i;R)\to0$, with maps $c\mapsto(c,-c)$ and $(p,q)\mapsto p+q$. Exactness follows simplex by simplex, and subdivision and its prism preserve the endpoint chains, so the last complex computes $H_*(X,X_i;R)$. Its connecting map sends a relative cycle $p+q$ to the class of $\partial p=-\partial q$ in the intersection quotient. Thus it supplies the relative exact sequence in all degrees, including degrees zero and one, rather than only a comparison of absolute ranks. [F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The endpoint inclusions $N_i\to N$ and $C_i\to C$ are deformation retractions up to inverse inclusion, by linearly contracting the $I$ coordinate to $i$. Their relative homology groups therefore vanish in every degree. Apply step 2.1 to $(W,S_i^3)=(E,E_i)\cup(N,N_i)$: the exact sequence gives $H_k(E,E_i;R)\cong H_k(W,S_i^3;R)$ for every $k$. The latter groups vanish because $S_i^3\to W$ induces homology isomorphisms in every degree, as follows directly from the long exact sequence of this pair. Next $F_i\to F$ is also a product deformation retraction. Applying the same exact sequence to $(V,M(K_i))=(E,E_i)\cup(F,F_i)$ gives $H_k(V,M(K_i);R)\cong H_k(E,E_i;R)=0$ for every $k$. The pair sequence now proves that each $M(K_i)\to V$ is an $R$-homology isomorphism, including in degree zero and the top degrees. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 Suppose finally that $\pi_1(W)=1$. The exterior $E$ is connected: $W$ is connected, $N$ and its side $C$ are connected, and any other component of the manifold $E$ would be a component of $W$ disjoint from the gluing side. Choose basepoint paths in $C$ and write $\ell,m$ for its annulus and meridian circles. The map $\pi_1(C)\to\pi_1(N)$ is surjective with kernel normally generated by $m$. The pushout [F4] consequently identifies $\pi_1(W)$ with $\pi_1(E)/\langle\!\langle m\rangle\!\rangle$; this follows also directly by eliminating the generator $\ell$ of the second factor in its amalgamated presentation. Thus $m$ normally generates $\pi_1(E)$. For the second gluing, $\pi_1(C)\to\pi_1(F)$ is surjective with kernel generated by $\ell$, so the same elimination gives $\pi_1(V)=\pi_1(E)/\langle\!\langle\ell\rangle\!\rangle$. The image of $m$ still normally generates this quotient and lies in each endpoint knot-exterior group, hence in its zero-surgery group image. This proves the stated endpoint normal-generation conclusion. The proof uses the normal neighborhood already assumed in the Statement and makes no assertion that local flatness alone constructs it. [F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

id: lem-dualizable-slide-clears-meridian-disk
kind: lemma
title: "A dualizable link can slide off a meridian disk"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923"
      locator: "Theorem 2.1 proof, printed p. 585 (PDF p. 4), finite slides removing intersections with $D_R$"
    - title: "Jennifer Hom, Getting a handle on the Conway knot"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171"
      locator: "§3, dualizable-link cancellation argument"
---

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $(B,G,R)$ be a dualizable framed handle link, and
isotope $R$ to an unknot bounding a disk $D_R$ that meets $B$ transversely in
one point. Then there is a finite sequence of slides of the $2$-handle $G$ over
the $2$-handle $B$, together with link isotopies, after which the attaching
circle for $G$ is disjoint from $D_R$.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Theorem 2.1 proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a dualizable handle link, and the stated spanning
disk $D_R$.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is
[[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] [[def-dualizable-handle-link]]: both $B\cup R$ and $G\cup R$ are
meridional pairs, and the components carry the specified zero framings.

[F2] [[def-handle-slide-of-one-k-handle-over-another]]: a slide of $G$ over
$B$ replaces its attaching circle by a band sum with a signed framed parallel
copy of $B$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $q$ be the unique point of $B\cap\operatorname{int}D_R$, and put the current attaching circle $G$ transverse to $D_R$. Its intersection set is finite: it is a compact zero-dimensional transverse submanifold, disjoint from $\partial D_R=R$. If it is empty there is nothing to do. Otherwise choose $p\in G\cap\operatorname{int}D_R$. A sufficiently close framed parallel $B'$ of $B$ is disjoint from $B\cup G\cup R$ and meets $D_R$ once, at a point $q'$ close to $q$. Indeed near $q$ the transverse arc $B$ has product coordinates in which $D_R$ is $z=0$ and $B$ is a vertical interval; choose the parallel's displacement there tangent to the disk. Away from this coordinate ball the compact sets $B$ and $D_R$ are disjoint, so a sufficiently small parallel creates no other intersection. The displacement can be interpolated in the framed normal disk bundle without changing the prescribed parallel's framing. [A1, F1, F2, given, choose, construct]


2.1 Orient the signed parallel $B'$ so that its intersection sign with $D_R$ at $q'$ is opposite to the sign of the intersection of $G$ with $D_R$ at $p$. Reversing the orientation of the parallel changes this sign without changing its underlying framed curve, and [F2] permits either signed parallel. Join $p$ to $q'$ by a smooth embedded arc $a$ in $\operatorname{int}D_R$ whose interior misses $G\cap D_R$, $q$, and $q'$. Such an arc is obtained by a polygonal path in the disk minus the finitely many forbidden points, removing loops in its finite subdivision and smoothing its corners in small disjoint disks. A thin strip about $a$ misses the remaining intersections and $B$. Choose the strip's normal product neighborhood so that the short branches of $G$ at $p$ and the chosen oriented $B'$ at $q'$ are vertical, while its interior misses all three retained components. In its positive side, join short intervals of these vertical branches by an embedded band running just above $a$. Give the band its product framing and choose the band-end coordinates by the full seam convention in [F2], so its orientation extends the orientation of $G$ over the selected signed parallel. Band summing $G$ with this $B'$ is therefore an allowed slide over $B$. [F2, step 1.1, choose, construct]


3.1 One of the new band-sum arcs runs along one edge of the band between $p$ and $q'$. Together with a parallel of $a$ in $D_R$, it bounds an embedded product disk in the positive half-neighborhood. Of the two endpoints, one has positive intersection sign and the other negative sign. Orienting this arc from the positive-sign crossing to the negative-sign crossing, it enters the positive side of $D_R$ at the first endpoint and exits at the second; thus the entire arc lies on the positive side. Its interior misses the slid circle and the retained components: the other edge of the band is chosen on the opposite transverse side of this disk, and the rest of $B'$ and $G$ misses the neighborhood. Push this arc across the disk and slightly into the negative side of $D_R$, rounding its ends. In strip coordinates this replaces the arch above $z=0$ joining the two opposite-sign intersections by an arc below $z=0$; extend the motion to its thin tubular neighborhood. This is a link isotopy supported away from $B\cup R$. It removes precisely $p,q'$ and creates none, while all old intersections away from $p$ persist. Thus a slide followed by this isotopy changes $|G\cap D_R|$ from $N$ to $N+1-2=N-1$. Transport the attaching framing by this isotopy. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]


4.1 Repeat steps 1.1–3.1 for the current attaching circle whenever an intersection remains. Each new parallel and strip can be chosen sufficiently thin for that finite stage, and the fixed $B,R,D_R$ are retained. The nonnegative integer intersection count drops by one at every stage, so after exactly the original number of intersections the current attaching circle is disjoint from $D_R$. The resulting finite sequence consists solely of the permitted framed slides and link isotopies and proves the full statement. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, induction, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

## Statement references

[[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot|The reverse-mirror knot]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The fixed oriented connected-sum convention]]

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Proper surface embeddings]]

[[def-morse-function-and-excellent-morse-function|Morse functions]]

[[def-nondegenerate-critical-point-nullity-index-and-coindex|Nondegenerate critical points and Morse index]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[F1] A knot is a smooth embedding of an oriented circle in the standard oriented $S^3$; a small ball meeting it in a short trivial arc leaves a properly embedded smooth arc in the complementary ball. ([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]])

[F2] The connected sum uses the fixed reflection and orientation-reversing boundary gluing, and changing the local trivial arcs and ball charts does not change its oriented knot type under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]])

[F3] If a smooth family of maps is transverse as a total map to $\{0\}\subset\mathbb R$, then outside a null set of parameters its slice is transverse to $0$. ([[thm-parametric-transversality]])

[F4] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, an isotopy of embeddings of a compact source with boundary into the boundaryless manifold $S^3$ extends to an ambient isotopy supported in any prescribed neighborhood of its track. ([[thm-isotopy-extension]])

[F5] The reverse mirror is obtained by applying the fixed orientation-reversing reflection and reversing the knot orientation. ([[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot]])

[F6] A proper surface embedding has boundary preimage equal to its surface boundary; smooth surface charts give the required boundary behavior in the unit four-ball. ([[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]])

[F7] A Morse function has nondegenerate critical points, and the index is the maximal dimension of a subspace on which its Hessian is negative definite. ([[def-morse-function-and-excellent-morse-function]], [[def-nondegenerate-critical-point-nullity-index-and-coindex]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the sequence-choice principle stated in the extension and transversality suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $K$.

1.1 Cut a short trivial arc from $K$ inside a small ball. Identify its complementary ball with the unit ball $B^3\subset\mathbb R^3$ so that the remaining arc is a smooth embedding $a:[0,1]\to B^3$, its endpoints lie on $S^2$, and its interior lies in the open ball. Straighten its endpoint collars to be radial and transverse to $S^2$. A small perturbation supported away from the endpoints makes $a$ avoid the origin; compactness and the fact that a one-dimensional embedded arc has empty interior allow the perturbation to be chosen arbitrarily small in $C^1$, so it remains embedded and fixed on the endpoint collars. Put $f(s)=\lVert a(s)\rVert^2$. Then $f>0$ on $[0,1]$, $f(0)=f(1)=1$, $f<1$ on $(0,1)$, and transversality gives $f'(0)<0<f'(1)$. [F1, F2, A1, construct]

2.1 The zeros of $f'$ lie in a compact subinterval of $(0,1)$ because $f'$ is nonzero on the endpoint collars. Cover the zero set by finitely many intervals carrying smooth functions $\phi_i$ supported in $(0,1)$ whose derivatives equal $1$ on smaller intervals still covering the zero set. For $u=(u_i)$ define $f_u=f+\sum_i u_i\phi_i$. On a neighborhood of every zero of $f'$ the total family $\mathcal F(s,u)=f'_u(s)$ is a submersion in the parameter direction, since some $\partial\mathcal F/\partial u_i=\phi_i'(s)=1$. On the compact complement of that neighborhood, $|f'|$ has a positive lower bound, so for all sufficiently small $u$ no new zeros occur there. Thus the total map is transverse to $0$ for parameters in a sufficiently small ball. By [F3], choose a parameter in that ball for which $0$ is a regular value of $f'_u$. The critical points of $f_u$ are then nondegenerate and finite. Shrink the parameter ball so $0<f_u<1$ on the perturbation support. The radial arcs $a_\lambda(s)=\sqrt{f_{\lambda u}(s)/f(s)}\,a(s)$, $0\le\lambda\le1$, form a smooth isotopy of embeddings fixed near the endpoints: the formula is smooth since $f>0$, and sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbations preserve immersion and injectivity on the compact source. By [F4], extend this isotopy in an ambient isotopy supported away from the removed trivial arc, so replacing $a$ by $a_u$ preserves the knot type of its closure. Rename $a_u$ as $a$ and $f_u$ as $f$. [F3, F4, A1, step 1.1, construct, choose]

3.1 In the unit ball $B^4=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R:\lVert x\rVert^2+t^2\le1\}$ define $\Omega=\{(s,t):0\le s\le1,\ t^2\le1-f(s)\}$ and $D=\{(a(s),t):(s,t)\in\Omega\}$. The map $(s,t)\mapsto(a(s),t)$ is an injective immersion, hence an embedding because $\Omega$ is compact. The function $q(s)=(1-f(s))/(s(1-s))$ extends smoothly and positively to $s=0,1$, with $q(0)=-f'(0)>0$ and $q(1)=f'(1)>0$. Consequently $(s,v)\mapsto(s,v\sqrt{q(s)})$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from the round disk $v^2\le s(1-s)$ onto $\Omega$. The boundary of $\Omega$ is regular: at an interior boundary point $t\ne0$, and at its two endpoints $f'(s)\ne0$, so the differential of $f(s)+t^2$ is nonzero. Thus $D$ is a smooth disk, its boundary lies in $S^3$, and its interior lies in the open four-ball. By [F6], its boundary is exactly the boundary knot specified by properness. [F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The two boundary arcs of $D$ are the lifts $(a(s),\pm\sqrt{1-f(s)})$ and meet the equatorial $S^2=\{t=0\}\cap S^3$ only at their endpoints. Each hemisphere of $S^3$ is a standard three-ball. Away from a small collar of its equator, projection $(x,t)\mapsto x$ is a smooth diffeomorphism onto the corresponding truncated ball and identifies the lifted arc with $a$. At an endpoint, use the equator collar coordinate $t\ge0$ (or $-t\ge0$ in the lower hemisphere). Since $f'(0)\ne0$ and $f'(1)\ne0$, the implicit function theorem writes the lifted arc near each endpoint as $s=\sigma(t^2)$, with $\sigma$ smooth; in a chart $y$ on the equator its tangential coordinates are $y(t)=y_0+O(t^2)$, while $t$ is the inward collar coordinate. Choose a cutoff $\chi(y,t)$ supported in this chart and equal to $1$ near the arc, and use $(y,t)\mapsto(y-\chi(y,t)(y(t)-y_0),t)$. Its derivative is the identity plus $O(t)$, so after shrinking the collar it is a diffeomorphism and straightens the arc to $\{y_0\}\times[0,\epsilon)$. This is the same standard ball-arc collar as the radial endpoint collar of $a$. Thus the lifted upper arc is the original ball-arc tangle and the lower one is its image under $(x,t)\mapsto(x,-t)$, up to collar-supported isotopy. The boundary orientation traverses one lifted arc in the direction of $a$ and the other in the reverse direction. By [F2] and [F5], closing these two arcs with the fixed connected-sum gluing gives precisely the oriented type $K\#K^\dagger$. Therefore $\partial D$ has the required oriented knot type. [F2, F5, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 On $D$, the squared radial function is $\rho(s,t)=f(s)+t^2$. Its interior critical points are exactly $(s,0)$ where $f'(s)=0$. At each such point the Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(f''(s),2)$, which is nondegenerate and has index $0$ when $f''(s)>0$ and index $1$ when $f''(s)<0$ by [F7]. Thus there are no index-$2$ critical points, and step 4.1 identifies the boundary knot as $K\#K^\dagger$. This proves the statement. [F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The picture is a schematic of the parameter domain $\Omega$ in step 3.1. The horizontal coordinate is $s$, the vertical coordinate is $t$, and the two boundary arcs meet at $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$. The marked point represents one possible interior critical point $(s_j,0)$; its presence and index are determined by the proof's Morse perturbation and Hessian calculation. The diagram contains no knot-crossing information and is not used in the proof.

## Statement

Let an oriented finite ideal triangulation of the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold have $k\ge1$ ideal vertices, each with torus link. Assign a positive ideal-tetrahedron shape to every tetrahedron. Suppose that around every finite edge the product of its incident complex shape parameters is $1$ and the sum of its dihedral angles is $2\pi$. For each ideal vertex $v$, choose a basis $(\alpha_v,\beta_v)$ of the fundamental group of its torus link and suppose the cusp multipliers satisfy $H(\alpha_v)=H(\beta_v)=1$. Then the face gluings define a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on the manifold interior, with one rank-two cusp for each ideal vertex.

## Statement references

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §§4.1–4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

[Petronio and Porti, *Negatively Oriented Ideal Triangulations and a Proof of Thurston’s Hyperbolic Dehn Filling Theorem*, Theorem 0.1 and §§1–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Diagram

Opposite edges of a normalized ideal tetrahedron carry the same shape parameter. The wire drawing records that convention only; all edge classes, products and angle sums in the proof are computed from the given face pairings, not from the drawing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.0,line cap=round,line join=round]

  \draw[thick] (a)--(b)--(c)--cycle;
  \draw[thick,dashed] (d)--(a) (d)--(b) (d)--(c);

  \node[below right] at (b) {$1$};

  \node at (1,-0.35) {$z$ on $01,\infty z$};

  \node at (1.0,2.05) {$z''$ on $1\infty,0z$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```
