## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite face-paired ideal triangulation, its positive shapes, all edge equations and angle sums, and a homology basis on each torus vertex link.

[F1] [[def-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-and-cusp-holonomy]]: a positive shape determines a nondegenerate ideal tetrahedron in $\mathbb H^3$, its corner factors, and the cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ along a path in a torus vertex link.

[F2] [[lem-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-parameter-relations]]: the argument of each positive shape parameter is the corresponding dihedral angle.

[F3] [[lem-ideal-torus-cusp-holonomy-criterion]]: for one torus vertex, edge products $1$, angle sums $2\pi$, and cusp multipliers $1$ on a fundamental-group basis imply a complete hyperbolic cusp.

[F4] [[lem-horocusp-truncation-has-finite-volume]]: a rank-two translation-lattice horocusp with Euclidean cross-section area $A$ has volume $A/2$.

[F5] [[def-pared-hyperbolic-structures-and-volume]]: a hyperbolic structure is a curvature $-1$ metric on the manifold interior, and a torus cusp is a horoball quotient by its peripheral subgroup.

## Proof

1.1 For each tetrahedron, [F1] supplies a nondegenerate ideal simplex, and the assigned face maps are hyperbolic isometries because their three corresponding ideal vertices have the same cross-ratio shape. Around a finite edge, the product equation makes the accumulated complex similarity the identity, while the angle sum $2\pi$ makes the total rotation one full turn. Thus the simplices glue to a smooth curvature $-1$ metric away from the ideal vertices. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Fix an ideal vertex $v$ and let $T_v$ be its torus link. Truncate the corners at $v$ by small horospheres. The resulting finite collection of Euclidean corner triangles triangulates $T_v$, and the face identifications restrict to Euclidean similarities. At a vertex of this link triangulation, corresponding to an incident edge of the ideal triangulation, the edge-shape product equation makes the accumulated complex similarity equal to $1$, while the $2\pi$ angle sum makes the total cone angle exactly $2\pi$. Thus the link similarity structure has no cone singularities. For a loop $\gamma$ on $T_v$, the linear part of its similarity holonomy is the multiplier $H_v(\gamma)$: crossing a corner contributes its shape factor or reciprocal according to the side traversed. The two assumed basis multipliers are $1$, so this linear part is the identity for every loop in $\pi_1(T_v)$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 Fix a Euclidean metric in one link chart and transport it through the similarity charts. The metric is independent of the transport path, because every loop has identity linear holonomy and translations preserve the Euclidean metric. This gives a global flat metric $g_v$ on the compact torus $T_v$, hence a complete one. Its lift to the universal cover is complete as well: any geodesic projects to a geodesic on the complete torus, extends there, and the extension lifts through the covering. The lifted Euclidean charts develop to a local isometry into $\mathbb R^2$. Every finite straight segment starting at a point in the image lifts to its endpoint: a partial lift has finite length, is therefore Cauchy, and extends from its limit by the local isometry. Hence the development is onto. For a small Euclidean ball about any point, lifting its radial segments from each preimage gives disjoint isometric copies of that ball; lifting the reverse radial segments shows these copies exhaust its preimage. Thus the development is a covering, and since $\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected it is an isometry. Deck transformations have identity linear part by the trivial link holonomy, so act by translations. Compactness of $T_v$ makes their translation vectors a rank-two lattice $\Lambda_v$. The assembled end is therefore the quotient of a horoball by $\Lambda_v$, with metric $dr^2+e^{-2r}g_v$ in horospherical depth $r$. A path escaping toward the ideal vertex has length at least the change in $r$, so the end is complete. Repeating this argument at each of the finitely many vertices proves completeness at every end. This is the local cusp argument underlying [F3], carried out separately on every link; the one-vertex Statement of [F3] is not applied to the full triangulation. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, construct]

3.1 A horospherical truncation of each ideal tetrahedron is compact and has finite volume because its smooth hyperbolic volume density is bounded on that compact region. Each removed vertex tail is contained in a rank-two horocusp and has finite volume by [F4]. There are finitely many tetrahedra and vertices, so the glued manifold has finite total volume. [given, F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The part remaining after all cusp neighborhoods are removed is a compact union of truncated tetrahedra. Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence. If infinitely many terms lie in that compact part, a subsequence converges there and the Cauchy property forces the whole sequence to the same limit. Otherwise the sequence eventually lies in the union of the finitely many disjoint cusp ends; sufficiently deep points in distinct ends have positive separation through the compact core, so the Cauchy property forces it eventually into one end, where it converges by step 2.1. Thus the full metric is complete. Together with step 3.1 and the curvature $-1$ charts from step 1.1, this is a complete finite-volume hyperbolic structure as defined in [F5]. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Whenever the JT branch of the Haken–Jaco–Tollefson search returns a disk-certificate, its primitive vertex normal surface is a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary in the triangulated knot exterior.

## Statement references

[[alg-haken-jaco-tollefson-unknot-recognition]] — JT primitive-ray enumeration and candidate tests.

[[lem-normal-disk-candidate-check-characterization]] — exact disk and essential-boundary characterization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid one-component knot code and a primitive ray vector returned by the JT branch as a disk-certificate.

[F1] [[alg-haken-jaco-tollefson-unknot-recognition]]: a returned JT vector is primitive on an extreme ray, admissible, and passes the nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic-one and odd-meridian-intersection tests.

[F2] [[lem-fundamental-normal-surfaces-are-connected]]: a fundamental normal surface is connected.

[F3] [[lem-normal-disk-candidate-check-characterization]]: an admissible normal vector with those three tests represents a properly embedded disk with essential boundary.

[F2] [[lem-fundamental-normal-surfaces-are-connected]]: a fundamental normal surface is connected.

[F3] [[lem-normal-disk-candidate-check-characterization]]: the boundary, Euler-characteristic and meridian tests characterize a properly embedded disk with essential boundary.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the returned vector is admissible and is the primitive integer generator of an extreme ray. If it split into two nonzero admissible integer vectors, both summands would lie on that same extreme ray; primitivity forbids such a positive integral split. Hence the vector is fundamental, and [F2] makes its surface connected. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The remaining tests checked by [F1], together with [F3], identify the connected surface as a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a supplied regular admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagram and normalized finite filtered hat complex $C_K$ whose total homology is $\mathbb F_2$. Let $K^\dagger$ be its reverse mirror under the fixed orientation-reversing reflection convention, with the reflected Seifert surface and reflected regular diagram. For a finite filtered complex $C$, define its dual complex $C^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2}(C,\mathbb F_2)$ with transposed differential and filtration
$$F_sC^\vee=\{\lambda\in C^\vee:\lambda(F_{-s-1}C)=0\}.$$
Then the reflected diagram's normalized filtered hat complex is filtered chain isomorphic to $C_K^\vee$. In particular, its total homology is $\mathbb F_2$ and
$$\tau_{\mathcal H^\dagger,F^\dagger}(K^\dagger)=-\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K).$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau|The absolute Alexander filtration and tau threshold]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The fixed reflection convention for the mirror knot]]

[[def-admissible-pointed-heegaard-floer-data|The pointed diagram and holomorphic-strip differential]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Holomorphic disks and knot invariants*, §3.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209056v3)

[Hom, *The knot Floer complex and the smooth concordance group*, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.6635)

[Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite integer-filtered chain complex $C_K$ with $H(C_K)\cong\mathbb F_2$, a regular pointed Heegaard diagram for $K$, and the reflected regular diagram for $K^\dagger$.

[F1] [[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau]] defines tau as the least filtration level whose inclusion has nonzero image in the one-dimensional total homology.

[F2] [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]] fixes the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ used to form the mirror convention.

[F3] [[def-admissible-pointed-heegaard-floer-data]] defines the differential by mod-two counts of index-one holomorphic strips and the relative Alexander change by the difference of the marked-point multiplicities.

## Proof

1.1 Put $t=\tau(C_K)$ and let $[x]$ be its nonzero total homology class in degree $n$. There is a cycle $x\in F_tC_{K,n}$ representing $[x]$. Since $H(F_{t-1}C_K)\to H(C_K)$ has zero image, every cycle in $F_{t-1}C_{K,n}$ is a boundary. Thus $x\notin B_n+F_{t-1}C_{K,n}$, where $B_n$ is the subspace of boundaries. Extend a linear functional $\lambda$ that vanishes on $B_n+F_{t-1}C_{K,n}$ and satisfies $\lambda(x)=1$. It is a cocycle. For a finite-dimensional chain complex, $\ker(\partial^\vee)=B^\perp$ and $\operatorname{im}(\partial^\vee)=Z^\perp$, so evaluation identifies $H(C_K^\vee)=B^\perp/Z^\perp$ with $H(C_K)^\vee$; hence $\lambda$ represents the nonzero dual class. It belongs to $F_{-t}C_K^\vee$. If $s<-t$, every element of $F_sC_K^\vee$ vanishes on $F_tC_K$, so its induced class pairs trivially with $[x]$ and maps to zero in total dual homology. Therefore $\tau(C_K^\vee)=-t$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Write the pointed holomorphic-strip equation on the symmetric product of $\Sigma$ as $\partial_su+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$. On the reflected surface $-\Sigma$ use the reflected almost-complex structure $-J_t$ and define $u^\dagger(s,t)=u(-s,t)$. Then $\partial_su^\dagger+(-J_t)(u^\dagger)\partial_tu^\dagger=-(\partial_su+J_t(u)\partial_tu)(-s,t)=0$. The map reverses the two asymptotic ends, so an index-one strip from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$ corresponds bijectively to an index-one strip from $\mathbf y^\vee$ to $\mathbf x^\vee$; conjugation of the linearized operators preserves regularity and the mod-two counts agree. Consequently the reflected differential is the transpose. Under the orientation-reversing identification, the relative $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ structure is conjugated, which reverses the orientation of its orthogonal plane field and negates its first Chern class; the capped Seifert class is carried forward by the reflection. Hence the Alexander pairing changes sign and the dual generator has filtration $-A_F(\mathbf x)$. The reflected complex is therefore $C_K^\vee$, and step 1.1 gives the tau sign formula. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ be a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$, let $Y\setminus K$ be irreducible, and let $F$ be a genus-$g$ Seifert surface. If the integral top Alexander group $\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(Y,K,[F],g;\mathbb Z)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$, then the sutured manifold obtained by cutting the compact knot exterior along $F$ is a product sutured manifold. The argument uses Ni's homology-product reduction, the horizontal and separating product-annulus decompositions, the characteristic product region, and Gabai's taut-foliation input under their stated hypotheses.

## Statement references

[[def-top-alexander-grading-of-knot-floer-homology|The integral top Alexander group and normalization]]

[[def-balanced-taut-sutured-manifold-and-product-region|Product sutured manifold and characteristic product region]]

[[def-sutured-floer-chain-complex|Sutured Floer homology notation and coefficients]]

[Ni, *Knot Floer homology detects fibred knots*, §§3–7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0607156v4)

[Juhasz, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, §§8–9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609779v3)

[Gabai, *Foliations and the topology of 3-manifolds III*](https://doi.org/10.2307/1971333)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The knot, exterior, surface and integral group in the Statement. Full Choice is available through [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A Seifert surface is connected, compact, oriented and properly embedded in the compact exterior, with its one boundary component the preferred longitude.

[F1] The resolved signed top/outer comparison in [[lem-ni-holomorphic-disk-and-jsj-analytic-inputs]] identifies the actual grading-$g$ complex with the actual $F$-cut complex, with its induced coherent orientation class. Thus it identifies their integral homologies. This is also the exact external Theorem 1.5 of Juhász, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, published p.300, for a null-homologous knot in any closed connected oriented $Y$ and any Seifert surface $F$; no three-sphere or rational-homology-sphere hypothesis occurs.

[F2] **External vanishing input:** Juhász, *Holomorphic discs and sutured manifolds*, Proposition 9.18, published pp.1452–1453: if a balanced sutured manifold is irreducible and not taut, its integral sutured Floer homology is zero. This is used by contrapositive, independently of the resolved taut-to-nonzero hierarchy theorem.

[F3] **External nonproduct input:** Juhász, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, Theorem 9.7, published pp.343–348: every taut balanced sutured manifold which is not a product has integral sutured Floer homology containing a copy of $\mathbb Z^2$. Its geometric reduction, including the characteristic-pair step, is an external input here, not a locally reconstructed consequence of the $S^3$ JSJ theorem. The source's proof reduces by horizontal/product-annulus operations and produces two taut decompositions with disjoint outer $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ sets. Their nonzero summands and signed cut maps agree with the scopes of the preserved local hierarchy and analytic suppliers. In particular no integral homology tensor formula without Tor is assumed.

[F4] **Corrected external characteristic-pair input:** the original Ni characteristic-product-region citation is not imported uncorrected. Ni's Corrigendum, author-version pp.1–3, Theorem 4 and Definitions 5–6, uses a characteristic Seifert pair for a Haken manifold pair and a maximal gapless product pair containing its characteristic product pair. Theorem 6.2-prime assumes irreducible balanced, connected suture, vertically prime, and $\widehat{\mathrm{HFS}}\cong\mathbb Z$; it says that product-annulus homologies span $H_1(M)$. Corollary 7 says that the characteristic product pair then surjects onto $H_1(M)$. The corrected main proof on p.3 supplies the product reduction in the original arbitrary-$Y$ setting. These are source qualifications for the external product argument in F3 and Ni's Theorem 1.1, not assertions of the false universal ambient enclosure used in the uncorrected paper. None is deduced from the retained $S^3$ knot-exterior JSJ Statement.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct, with the explicitly identified external inputs F2–F4.

1.1 Let $E$ be the compact exterior and $(M,\gamma)$ its cut along $F$. Its two faces are copies of $F$, and its vertical boundary is the annulus $\partial F\times I$. It is balanced: both faces have Euler characteristic $1-2g$, no component is closed, and every boundary component meets the vertical annulus. A meridian intersects $F$ algebraically once, so $F$ is nonseparating and the cut is connected. [Given]

1.2 The irreducibility assumption applies to $E$: pushing away the deleted-knot end identifies every compact sphere question with that in $Y\setminus K$. A sphere in the interior of $M$ is therefore a sphere disjoint from $F$ in $E$ and bounds a ball in $E$. Since $F$ is connected and disjoint from this sphere, if it entered the ball it would lie wholly in its interior, contradicting $\partial F\subset\partial E$. The ball is consequently disjoint from $F$; shrink the cut collar if necessary to obtain the same ball in $M$. Thus $M$ is irreducible. [Given, step 1.1]

2.1 The signed cut comparison gives $\operatorname{SFH}(M,\gamma;\mathbb Z)\cong\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(Y,K,[F],g;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. The grading uses the supplied class $[F]$ and genus of this actual surface; no genus-detection theorem for a different ambient manifold is substituted. [F1]

3.1 If $(M,\gamma)$ were not taut, its integral sutured Floer homology would vanish by the external vanishing input, contradicting step 2.1. Therefore it is taut. This is the contrapositive of F2, not a reversal of taut hierarchy nonvanishing. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 If the taut balanced $(M,\gamma)$ were not a product, F3 would give $\mathbb Z^2\hookrightarrow\operatorname{SFH}(M,\gamma;\mathbb Z)$. Such an injection into $\mathbb Z$ is impossible: images $a,b$ of its two basis vectors satisfy the nontrivial integer relation $b a-a b=0$ when either is nonzero, and an image zero itself contradicts injectivity. The two disjoint outer summands in the source argument therefore contradict step 2.1. Hence the actual $F$-cut exterior is a product sutured manifold. This includes $g=0$ and uses the corrected characteristic-pair qualification F4. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk, let $p$ be prime, and let $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$. The $q$-fold cyclic cover $W_{D,q}$ of $B^4$ branched along $D$ is a compact connected oriented $4$-manifold with $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$ for every $i>0$ and boundary $\Sigma_q(\partial D)$.

## Statement references

[[def-q-fold-branched-cover-of-a-slice-disk|The cyclic branched cover of the disk]]

[[lem-prime-power-cyclic-cover-homology-of-slice-disk-exterior|Homology of the prime-power exterior cover over its defining field]]

[Charles Livingston and Swatee Naik, *Introduction to Knot Concordance*, Theorem 7.8.4, pp. 142–145](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Concordance_Book.pdf)

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth proper disk $D$, a prime $p$, and $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $W_{D,q}$ is obtained by gluing the $q$-fold exterior cover $X_{D,q}$ to $D^2\times D^2$ along $D^2\times S^1$; the overlap circle maps to the closed lift of the $q$th meridian. [[def-q-fold-branched-cover-of-a-slice-disk]]

[F2] $H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$ and $H_i(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)=0$ for $i\ge2$. [[lem-prime-power-cyclic-cover-homology-of-slice-disk-exterior]]

[F3] Compact smooth manifolds have finite CW models under countable choice, so the integral homology groups of $W_{D,q}$ are finitely generated. Full AC supplies countable choice. [[lem-compact-smooth-manifolds-have-finite-cw-models-under-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] Mayer–Vietoris is exact for the collar-thickened gluing in [F1]. [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

[F5] The homology universal coefficient sequence over $\mathbb Z$ applies with coefficients $\mathbb F_p$. [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-homology-over-a-pid]]

## Proof

1.1 The core circle of $D^2\times S^1$ is the lift of $\mu^q$. Lift that loop to the infinite cyclic cover $X_{D,\infty}$: it is a path from a point $\widetilde x$ to $t^q\widetilde x$. The connecting map of the chain sequence for the $q$-fold quotient sends its homology class to $[\widetilde x]\in H_0(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)$. By the proof of [F2], this connecting map is an isomorphism in degree one, so the overlap map $H_1(D^2\times S^1;\mathbb F_p)\to H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)$ is an isomorphism. [F1, F2, given, construct, A1]

2.1 The filling piece $D^2\times D^2$ is contractible and the overlap has homology only in degrees zero and one. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence [F4], using the isomorphism from step 1.1, gives $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)=0$ for every $i>0$. The two glued pieces and their overlap are connected, so $W_{D,q}$ is connected; orientation is inherited from the cyclic branched covering map away from the branch set and extends over the local model. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], each integral homology group $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)$ is finitely generated. The injection $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb F_p\hookrightarrow H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)$ from [F5] makes that tensor product zero for $i>0$. A finitely generated abelian group with zero tensor product with $\mathbb F_p$ has rank zero; hence $H_i(W_{D,q};\mathbb Q)=0$. Its boundary is $\Sigma_q(\partial D)$ by [F1], proving the statement. [F1, F3, F5, step 2.1, algebra, A1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a single knot, and let the Seifert algorithm supply its finite disk-and-band construction data. These disks and bands can be realized in $S^3$ as a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F$ with exactly one boundary component, whose oriented boundary is the knot represented by $D$. The bands can be chosen mutually disjoint and disjoint from disk interiors except at their attaching intervals.

## Statement references

[[def-seifert-smoothing-and-seifert-circles-of-an-oriented-link-diagram|Oriented smoothing and Seifert circles]]

[[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups|Embedded disk regions for nullhomotopic circles under countable choice]]

[[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected|Simple connectivity of the projection sphere]]

[[alg-seifert-surface-from-diagram|The finite disk-and-band construction data]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a regular oriented knot diagram $D$, and the finite output data of the Seifert algorithm.

[F1] At each crossing the unique noncrossing pairing compatible with the strand orientations is used; performing this at all crossings gives a finite disjoint union of oriented simple closed curves in $S^2$. ([[def-seifert-smoothing-and-seifert-circles-of-an-oriented-link-diagram]])

[F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle in an oriented surface without boundary bounds an embedded compact disk region; in a sphere component both complementary disk regions are available. ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

[F3] The sphere $S^2$ is simply connected. ([[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]])

[F4] For each crossing the algorithm records one band between the two oriented smoothing arcs, and it uses one disk record for each Seifert circle. ([[alg-seifert-surface-from-diagram]])

[F5] A Seifert surface is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface in $S^3$ whose oriented boundary is the given knot. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the sequence principle stated in the item. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the smoothing gives finitely many disjoint embedded circles in the projection sphere. Choose a point $q$ outside them. By [F3], each circle is nullhomotopic; [F2] and [A1] supply both complementary disk regions, so for each circle choose the region not containing $q$ and orient it to induce the Seifert-circle orientation. Disjoint Jordan circles have disk regions that are nested or disjoint, so their finite strict-inclusion order admits a linear extension. Place nested disks at distinct nearby heights in that order; their interiors are then pairwise disjoint as subsets of $S^3$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, choose, construct]

2.1 Choose pairwise disjoint crossing neighborhoods small enough to avoid all other Seifert-circle boundaries. Put the two projected tangent lines on the coordinate axes. Up to reversing both orientations and exchanging axes, the strand directions are east-and-north or east-and-south. In the first case the orientation-compatible noncrossing pairings are west-to-north and south-to-east; in the second they are north-to-east and west-to-south. Thus in each case the two smoothing arcs are locally parallel and equally directed. Any disk region for a third circle whose interior meets this crossing neighborhood contains the neighborhood and both affected circles, so it is an ancestor of each; its assigned height is lower than their disk heights. Raise narrow collars of both attaching intervals into a local slab above every disk sheet meeting the neighborhood. Attach a rectangle along those intervals with one half-twist. Of the two twist directions, choose the one whose long sides project to the original overpassing and underpassing branches. The equal arrow directions on the smoothing arcs permit opposite boundary parameterizations at the two attaching edges of the rectangle, so its orientation extends the orientations of both disks across the gluing. The crossing neighborhoods are disjoint; finiteness lets all collars and bands be thin enough to avoid every other disk sheet and one another. [F1, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Gluing the finitely many rectangles to disjoint boundary intervals of the disks and rounding the collar corners gives a smooth embedded compact two-manifold. The orientations agree along each attaching interval, so the surface is oriented. Outside a crossing neighborhood its boundary follows the original diagram arcs; inside each neighborhood the two long sides of the half-twisted band restore the specified crossing and its orientation. Hence the boundary is exactly the original oriented knot. [F1, F4, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Every disk has an unused boundary arc because only finitely many short attaching intervals were chosen; each band attachment replaces two boundary intervals by its two long sides, so no component of the resulting disk-and-band surface becomes closed. Each connected surface component therefore contributes at least one boundary component. Step 3.1 gives a total boundary consisting of the one knot component, so the surface has exactly one connected component and satisfies [F5]. [F4, F5, step 3.1, given, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let P be a pattern of strong winding number ±1. For every oriented knot K, regard P(K) as the pattern obtained by tying K into each strand of P in the companion solid torus. Then this new pattern P(K) also has strong winding number ±1. A pattern obtained from any strong-winding pattern by taking connected sum with a local knot also has strong winding number ±1.

## Statement references

[CDR, Proposition 2.5 and complete proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.5058v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A pattern P, its unknotted-solid-torus closure P(U), strong-winding meridian η, and a knot K inserted as companion.

[F1] Strong winding means the axis meridian normally generates the closure complement group ([[def-satellite-induced-concordance-operator]]).

[F2] The knot exterior has meridian μ_K and preferred longitude λ_K on its boundary torus ([[def-knot-exterior]], [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]).

[F3] The knot-group meridian normally generates π₁(S³\K): meridional filling gives S³, and van Kampen quotients by the normal closure of μ_K to π₁(S³)=1 ([[def-knot-exterior]], [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]).

[F4] Connected sum is formed by joining the two knot exteriors along a meridional annulus ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]).

## Proof

1.1 Let λ denote the longitude of the pattern solid torus. Filling the outer boundary of the pattern exterior along λ produces S³∖P(U), so the induced epimorphism π₁(ST∖P)→π₁(S³∖P(U)) has kernel normally generated by λ. By [F1], the target is normally generated by the image of η; hence π₁(ST∖P) is normally generated by η and λ. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For a local connected sum with any knot J, the closure-complement group is the amalgamated product of the two knot groups along their common meridian, by cutting at the connected-sum sphere and applying van Kampen. Each knot-group factor is normally generated by its meridian. [F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Decompose the complement of P(K) along the companion torus into ST∖P and S³∖K. Van Kampen gives a generating set normally contained in the images of these two groups. The first is normally generated by η and λ by step 1.1; the second is normally generated by μ_K by [F3]. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Under the torus gluing, λ is identified with λ_K and η with μ_K. Since μ_K normally generates the companion-knot group, λ becomes redundant, and η normally generates the entire satellite-complement group. The outer solid-torus meridian for the pattern P(K) is isotopic in the complement to η, so it too normally generates. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The solid-torus meridian normally generates the strong-winding factor by hypothesis; quotienting the amalgamated product by that meridian kills this factor and the common meridian. The other knot-group factor is then killed because its meridian normally generates it. Thus the whole closure-complement group is normally generated by the solid-torus meridian. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot with compact exterior obtained by deleting the binding neighborhood from its open-book presentation and peripheral basis $(\mu,\lambda)$, where $\mu$ is the positive meridian and $\lambda$ is the preferred zero-homology longitude. The exterior fibers over $S^1$ with fiber a once-punctured torus and monodromy fixing its boundary pointwise. Filling along the slope $\lambda$ produces a torus bundle over $S^1$. For the fiber and ordered core basis in the figure-eight plumbing convention, the induced action on the capped torus homology is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

## Statement references

[Danny Calegari, *Foliations and the Geometry of 3-Manifolds*, Construction 5.37 and Example 5.39](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/books/foliations/oupbook.pdf)

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The chosen exterior of the standard figure-eight knot, its positive meridian and preferred longitude, and the square-plumbed fiber and monodromy convention.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F1] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ selects from every countable family of nonempty sets.

[F2] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]: in ZF, $\mathrm{AC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[F3] [[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling]]: with the stated peripheral basis, the integer coefficient $0$ is the unoriented slope represented by $\lambda$; ordinary filling attaches a solid torus whose meridian is that slope.

[F4] [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]]: under AC the preferred longitude is the unique primitive boundary class that maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, and $(\mu,\lambda)$ is a basis.

[F5] [[lem-figure-eight-complement-punctured-torus-bundle]]: the exterior is the mapping torus of a once-punctured torus, with boundary-fixing monodromy whose capped homology matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

[F6] [[def-multicusped-dehn-filling]]: a filling along a selected boundary slope is obtained by attaching an oriented solid torus with the specified meridian slope.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2] and [A1], the needed countable-choice hypothesis [F1] holds. Let $F$ be the fiber from [F5]. Cutting the exterior along $F$ gives $F\times[0,1]$, with its interval ends reidentified by the monodromy $\varphi$; because $\varphi$ fixes $\partial F$ pointwise, the boundary torus is identified with $\partial F\times S^1$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F5, construct]

2.1 The curve $\partial F$ on the peripheral torus is an essential parallel of the knot and bounds the fiber in the exterior, so its homology class maps to zero in $H_1(E_{K_8};\mathbb Z)$. It is primitive because it is a simple essential curve. By uniqueness in [F4], it represents $\lambda$ up to orientation, hence it is exactly the unoriented filling slope $0$ by [F3]. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Write the filling solid torus as $D^2\times S^1$, using its second coordinate for the mapping-torus direction. Its meridian disk boundary is identified with $\partial F\times\{t\}$ by [F3] and step 2.1. The filling is therefore the mapping torus of $\overline F=F\cup_{\partial F}D^2$: extend $\varphi$ over the added disk by the identity. This extension is continuous and fixes the seam because $\varphi|_{\partial F}=\mathrm{id}$. If the chosen boundary gluing differs by a twist along the meridian slope, that twist extends over $D^2\times S^1$ by rotating the disk as the second coordinate varies, so it does not change the resulting bundle up to homeomorphism. [F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The surface $\overline F$ is obtained from a once-punctured torus by capping its sole boundary component with a disk, so it is a closed torus. The mapping torus of the extended homeomorphism $\overline\varphi$ is consequently a torus bundle over $S^1$. Inclusion $F\hookrightarrow\overline F$ induces an isomorphism on first homology, and the extension is the identity on the cap, so its matrix remains the matrix in [F5]. [F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[Danny Calegari, *Foliations and the Geometry of 3-Manifolds*, Construction 5.37 and Example 5.39](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/books/foliations/oupbook.pdf)

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be compact smooth properly embedded oriented surfaces from fixed oriented knots $K_0$ to $K_1$, with the same boundary parametrizations and product collars. Suppose their generic movies represent ambient isotopic cobordisms by an isotopy fixed on those collars. Then one movie can be changed to the other by a finite sequence of the fifteen Carter–Saito movie moves, sweep-around moves, and interchanges of two disjoint elementary movie events (including disjoint critical points of the surface-height function). A sweep-around moves a closing arc of a one-interval tangle over the tangle to its other side and back underneath, or reverses that movie; geometrically it is a local sheet passage through the missing vertical arc in a spatial chart $S^3\setminus\{\infty\}$. Every intermediate movie represents a generic surface cobordism with the same fixed boundary data.

## Statement references

[[def-generic-movie-of-an-oriented-knot-cobordism|Generic movies and boundary collars]]

[[lem-spherical-cobordism-isotopies-reduce-to-sweep-around-events|The additional spherical sweep-around events]]

[[def-carter-saito-euclidean-local-movie-moves|The fifteen local Euclidean models and distant interchanges]]

[[lem-euclidean-surface-isotopies-have-carter-saito-movie-decompositions|The complete unframed Euclidean movie decomposition]]

[Carter and Saito, *Reidemeister moves for surface isotopies and their interpretations as moves to movies*, pp.251–284](https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/pdf/10.1142/S0218216593000167)

[Jacobsson, *An invariant of link cobordisms from Khovanov homology*, §4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0206303)

[Hunt, *Movie presentations of isotopies*, §5.2](https://tqft.net/web/research/students/HilaryHunt/thesis.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, the two fixed-boundary generic movies and the stated ambient isotopy of their oriented traced cobordisms in $S^3\times I$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is used through the two geometric suppliers.

[F1] [[def-generic-movie-of-an-oriented-knot-cobordism]] supplies traced movies, their actual orientations, parametrized boundary and product collars.

[F2] [[lem-spherical-cobordism-isotopies-reduce-to-sweep-around-events]] proves that an actual spherical comparison of two Euclidean traced cobordisms factors into finitely many Euclidean ambient isotopies and local sheet passages through the missing vertical arc, the sweep-around events.

[F3] [[lem-euclidean-surface-isotopies-have-carter-saito-movie-decompositions]] proves the finite Euclidean decomposition into the fifteen types and distant interchanges, with its independent-jet, local normal-form and finiteness arguments. The local types and all orientation/height variants are [[def-carter-saito-euclidean-local-movie-moves]].

## Proof

1.1 Use the actual smooth traced realizations of the two planar movies, with their prescribed endpoint realizations and collars. These lie in the standard spatial chart $S^3\setminus\{\infty\}$; by [F1] and the hypothesis, their oriented traces have the specified spherical isotopy relative to those collars. Apply [F2]. The comparison is a finite sequence of Euclidean isotopies and isolated sweep-around events, with the same parametrized boundary. At the intermediate cuts choose generic movies fixed on the retained collars; the same finite-jet construction in [F3] applies with these cuts protected. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 On each Euclidean isotopy interval, [F3] replaces its comparison by finitely many of the fifteen local moves, distant interchanges and planar isotopies. All hidden-coordinate height orders and orientations are preserved. At each missing-arc passage retain the sweep-around supplied by [F2]; it is not silently replaced by a Euclidean move. The two boundary movies of each interval match those at the adjacent pieces, because the construction fixes the chosen cuts and collars. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Concatenate these finite lists. There are finitely many intervals and passages, so the total list is finite. Every retained frame is a regular frame of a generic traced surface, and every elementary replacement has its stated oriented local trace with the same outside and boundary data. Consequently all intermediate movies have the prescribed parametrized knots and collars. The total sequence starts and ends at the given movies and proves the claimed spherical comparison. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Source and scope note

The fifteen Euclidean types are derived locally from the unframed smooth-sheet calculations in Queffelec–Walker, not from a citation standing in for a proof. Their full framed-foam theorem and its seam moves are not premises here. The spherical step uses the separately proved missing-arc incidence reduction, in accordance with the explicit distinction on p.2 of Morrison–Walker–Wedrich. The original Carter–Saito publisher text was not retrieved; no reading of that unavailable article is claimed. A homology theory must still prove its own sweep-around map identity; this geometric theorem does not establish one.

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot. For a nonzero Laurent polynomial $f(M,L)$, its Newton polygon is the convex hull in $\mathbb R^2$ of exponent pairs $(a,b)$ for which the coefficient of $M^bL^a$ is nonzero. The enhanced A-polynomial is **thin** when this polygon is contained in an affine line; the constant polynomial $1$ has a one-point Newton polygon and is thin. Then the enhanced A-polynomial of $K$ is thin if and only if $K$ is a torus knot, including the unknot.

## Statement references

[[def-enhanced-a-polynomial|Enhanced A-polynomial and reducible component]]

[[def-coprime-torus-knot|Coprime torus-knot convention]]

[Baldwin and Sivek, Theorem 1.2 and §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

[Ni and Zhang, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1712.04012)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the smooth knot in the Statement. The accepted local torus, hyperbolic and conditional satellite arguments are retained. The remaining established classification is imported explicitly in [F11].

[F1] The positive coprime torus-knot formula, with its separate $b=2$ and $b>2$ cases, and the unknot formula are proved by the explicit irreducible peripheral matrix calculation. [[lem-torus-knot-enhanced-a-polynomial]], [[lem-torus-presentation-irreducible-peripheral-eigenvalue-curves]], [[def-coprime-torus-knot]], [[lem-torus-knot-unit-slope-is-unknot]]

[F2] Complete one-cusped holonomy has an actual smooth complex ordinary deformation curve and an augmented eigenvalue-ratio logarithm coordinate $u$, with longitude logarithm $v(u)=\tau u+O(u^2)$ and $\operatorname{Im}\tau\ne0$. The forgetful map is the stated branched trace-squared map, so this is not an unproved choice of a logarithm on the ordinary quotient. [[lem-one-cusped-deformation-parameters-and-holonomy]], [[thm-augmented-finite-volume-hyperbolic-holonomy-coordinates]] The cited augmented-coordinate supplier's proof locators are rows 8.1 (ordinary holomorphic slice) and 9.1 (augmented holomorphic family).

[F3] The exterior retracts from the complement of the smooth knot; Alexander duality computes its integral homology, and the universal coefficient theorem computes its mod-two cohomology. Its compact smooth core has a compatible finite triangulation. [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]], [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]], [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]], [[thm-compact-smooth-manifolds-with-corners-admit-relative-finite-triangulations]]

[[lem-sl2-representation-variety-is-affine]], [[def-sl-two-character-variety-and-peripheral-eigenvalues]], [[def-enhanced-a-polynomial]]

[F5] The actual proof of the generic adjoint peripheral kernel computes its boundary inclusion rank by Lefschetz duality and pair exactness, and pairs arbitrary field derivations with actual word cycles, including a moving peripheral eigenbasis. These particular field-linear arguments do not require its Statement's curve hypothesis; their extension to the generic field used below is explicitly supplied in step 2.5. Affine-domain dimension is transcendence degree, and Noetherian algebraic sets have finitely many irreducible components. [[lem-generic-adjoint-peripheral-kernel-is-the-logarithmic-conormal-line]], [[thm-affine-domain-dimension-transcendence-degree]], [[lem-noetherian-space-has-finitely-many-irreducible-components]]

[[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]], [[thm-seifert-matrix-presents-knot-alexander-module]], [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]], [[thm-torus-knot-alexander-and-genus-formulas]]

This makes all constants of the thin peripheral graphs finite order; it does not exclude a vertical segment. [[lem-knot-newton-edge-roots-are-roots-of-unity]]

[F8] For an actual fibered satellite with essential companion torus, winding is nonzero, the genus is $g(P(U))+|w|g(C)$, and the actual top-adjacent Alexander condition implies that $P(U)$ is nontrivial. The proof constructs the marked fiber cut products, preserves the base class under the changed target gluing, caps the pattern piece and proves minimal genera by actual Alexander-cover breadth. Its smooth disk/window rerun retains the smooth category. A nontrivial smooth knot has positive genus by the actual genus-zero unknot equivalence; full AC supplies its countable-choice hypothesis. Compactness, connectedness and the single torus boundary are verified in the JSJ proof1.1; exterior irreducibility and nontrivial-knot boundary incompressibility have their actual proved suppliers. No JSJ uniqueness input is missing. [[thm-seifert-fibered-smooth-knot-exteriors-have-torus-knot-models]], [[lem-smooth-tori-in-s-three-give-marked-unknotted-or-satellite-models]], [[thm-jsj-decomposition-of-knot-exteriors]], [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]], [[lem-nontrivial-knot-exterior-boundary-incompressible]]

For the full classification, including exclusion of the unit or meridian-constant possibilities, [F11] supplies the exact result directly.

[L2] The residual metric step in the retained conditional geometric derivation has exactly the Statement of [[thm-thurston-hyperbolization-for-atoroidal-knot-exteriors]] as its input. Its local proof is not claimed here. The direct external classification [F11] completes the original theorem without requiring this carrier to certify a new proof of that metric theorem. The accepted local satellite and Seifert cases remain valid independently.


[F11] **External classification:** Baldwin–Sivek, *Torus knots, the A-polynomial, and SL(2,C)*, arXiv:2405.19197v2, Theorem 1.2 (p.2; proof in §4), states that a knot in $S^3$ is thin if and only if it is a torus knot. Their §2.3 and (1.1) define the same enhanced polynomial by irreducible peripheral curves, with $A_K=\operatorname{lcm}(\widetilde A_K,L-1)$; their torus convention includes the unknot (§2 opening). Laurent units translate the Newton polygon and do not affect thinness; the named-variable exponent convention agrees with the Statement. The statement and conventions were consulted directly; no new local reconstruction of the gauge/classification proof is claimed.

## Proof

1.1 The unknot and all positive nontrivial torus knots are thin by [F1]: their enhanced curves have respectively the unit equation and the two explicitly calculated monomial terms. These are actual proved formulas, rather than assumptions on an uncomputed torus character variety. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 This proves the forward direction for every signed torus knot as well. Reflection carries its oriented meridian to the inverse positive meridian of the reflected knot: it preserves the carried knot orientation and reverses the ambient normal-plane orientation. It carries its preferred longitude to the preferred longitude, because the degree along the knot remains one and its exterior homology class remains zero; uniqueness in [F3] excludes any meridian shift. Composition of representations with this exterior diffeomorphism therefore identifies the peripheral loci by $(M,L)\mapsto(M^{-1},L)$, preserving irreducibility and all closure dimensions. Their reduced curve equations differ by that Laurent substitution and a unit. Reversing the knot orientation instead inverts both peripheral generators and gives $(M,L)\mapsto(M^{-1},L^{-1})$. These invertible integral changes of exponents preserve containment in an affine line. Finally swapping the two complex coordinates of the standard $S^3$ interchanges the two torus parameters and preserves ambient orientation; the radial torus parameter may be changed by a smooth radial isotopy. Thus, using the mirror and orientation conventions in [F1], every coprime torus knot reduces to the positive case, or to the unknot if one parameter has absolute value one. In the latter case the actual sine-cosine circle isotopy and ambient extension in the unit-slope supplier [F1] give the unknot, with its countable-choice hypothesis supplied by full AC. This is a proof of thinness for mirrors, not an assertion that the displayed positive formula applies unchanged to a negative knot. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Suppose now that the knot exterior has the complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric. We first construct the necessary SL2 lift on this EXTERIOR; no lift of the holonomy of a closed filling is assumed. Alexander duality in [F3], in degrees one and two, gives $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ and $H_2(E_K;\mathbb Z)=0$, since the knot is a connected circle. The universal coefficient exact sequence therefore gives $H^2(E_K;\mathbb Z/2)=0$. On a finite triangulation choose a spanning tree and the associated finitely many vertex base paths. A PSL2 representation labels each oriented edge by its based transport; the labels multiply to identity around every triangle. Lift each edge label to SL2, choosing the reverse lift as its inverse. A triangle product is a central sign. The four triangle signs around each tetrahedron sum to zero in $\mathbb Z/2$: after conjugating to one vertex the intermediate edge factors cancel and the remaining signs commute. They are therefore a simplicial two-cocycle. Its cohomology class is zero, so it is the coboundary of a one-cochain. Multiply each edge lift by its corresponding sign. Every triangle product is now identity, and edge-path homotopy gives an actual SL2 representation lifting the specified PSL2 one. This finite argument uses the space cohomology directly and inserts no spin or closed-three-manifold parallelizability theorem. [F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 The lift works for the local holonomy family, not merely its central point. Use the actual local slice representations constructed in [F2], not just the abstract quotient coordinate. The augmented-coordinate supplier cited in [F2] proves that three conditions transverse to the conjugation orbit give a holomorphic slice, with no large-conjugator identifications, and then gives its holomorphic family after the branched substitution $s=4\cosh^2(u/2)$. The complete cusp group is nonelementary. Indeed, if the full discrete group fixed its cusp point, put that point at infinity. It contains a rank-two translation lattice. An element with dilation of modulus different from one would conjugate a nonzero translation to translations tending to identity, contrary to discreteness. The translations in the group form a discrete rank-two lattice containing the cusp lattice; conjugation preserves it. The linear parts therefore belong to the finite orthogonal symmetry group of this lattice, and the Euclidean quotient of each horizontal horosphere has the same finite positive area. Its hyperbolic volume is the area times $\int_0^\infty z^{-3}\,dz=\infty$, contradicting finite volume. Thus the holonomy has no common invariant line and its SL2 lift is irreducible. The same is true in a neighborhood: otherwise invariant lines for a convergent sequence of reducible tuples have a convergent subsequence in compact $\mathbb{CP}^1$, giving an invariant line at the complete point. Now choose the local edge lifts holomorphically, with their values at the center equal to those of step 2.1. Each triangle product is a continuous central sign, hence stays identity. This yields the actual local family of irreducible SL2 representations. On the augmented curve its chosen common peripheral line has eigenvalues $M(u)=\epsilon_\mu e^{u/2}$ and $L(u)=\epsilon_\lambda e^{v(u)/2}$ for fixed signs, because their squares are the eigenvalue ratios in [F2]. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

2.3 This nonconstant peripheral arc lies in the enhanced curve of [F4]. To check the dimension condition rather than assume it, take the algebraic irreducible-character component through the complete irreducible point. The ordinary local quotient in [F2] is a smooth complex curve, so that component has dimension one; the local finite lift from PSL2 to SL2 does not change this dimension. Adjoining a peripheral eigenline away from $u=0$ is a finite choice of the two eigenlines, so its component is again one-dimensional. Its algebraic peripheral image closure has dimension at most one, and at least one because $M(u)$ is nonconstant. Hence this is an actual one-dimensional irreducible-character image component, not an isolated representation discarded by the enhanced Definition. The enhanced polynomial vanishes on the entire local arc. [F2, F4, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

2.4 A nonzero Laurent polynomial with collinear integral support has the form $M^aL^b P(M^rL^s)$, where $(r,s)$ is a primitive nonzero integral vector and $P$ is a one-variable Laurent polynomial; subtract one support point and divide all support differences by their common primitive direction. If the support is a single point, it has no zero in $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ and already cannot vanish on the arc in step 2.3. Otherwise $P$ has finitely many nonzero complex roots. A connected local arc on its zero set has $M^rL^s$ equal to one fixed root. Applying step 2.2 and differentiating at $u=0$ gives $r+s\tau=0$. Since $\operatorname{Im}\tau\ne0$, this forces $s=0$ and then $r=0$, a contradiction. Thus the enhanced polynomial of a finite-volume hyperbolic knot is not thin. This proves the complete hyperbolic exclusion without treating a PSL2 filling representation as an already lifted SL2 representation. [F2, F4, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra]

2.5 We also need global image control before the SU2 filling operation, since the enhanced Definition alone omits rather than excludes higher-dimensional images. Take any irreducible component of the finite algebraic representation variety together with one common peripheral eigenline, and its actual generic matrices over its finitely generated function field $F$. Cover the eigenline projective coordinate by its two affine charts. If its peripheral image were two-dimensional, $M,L$ would be algebraically independent by [F5]; in particular a peripheral matrix generically has distinct eigenvalues. Its adjoint system is self-dual by trace. The explicit nonparabolic torus computation in [F5] gives boundary homology dimension two. Here is the rank computation over this arbitrary $F$, without assuming that its transcendence degree is one. Dualizing chains over the field, Lefschetz cap identifies restriction on $H^1$ with the pair connector on $H_2$, up to its degree sign, while restriction is transpose to inclusion on $H_1$. Exactness therefore gives $2=\dim\ker i_*+\operatorname{rank}i_*=2\operatorname{rank}i_*$; both image and kernel have dimension one. The extension of functionals needed to dualize is permitted by the standing full AC, exactly as in [F5]. For any $\mathbb C$-derivation $D:F\to F$, differentiating actual word matrices gives the cocycle $Z(g)=D\rho(g)\rho(g)^{-1}$. The finite word pairing with $u=\rho(\delta)-\operatorname{tr}\rho(\delta)I/2$ annihilates every relator boundary and has peripheral values one common nonzero factor times $(DL/L,DM/M)$, as the explicit moving-eigenbasis calculation in [F5] shows. Hence ALL these pairs annihilate the SAME one-dimensional boundary kernel. But extend $M,L$ to a finite transcendence basis of $F/\mathbb C$ and use the two coordinate derivations on that rational function field. Each extends over its finite algebraic extension to $F$: for a minimal polynomial $p(\alpha)=0$, set $D\alpha=-(Dp)(\alpha)/p'(\alpha)$; characteristic zero ensures $p'(\alpha)\ne0$, and the product/quotient rules verify the extension. Their resulting logarithmic pairs are independent, contradicting that common annihilator line. Thus no image component is two-dimensional. Components with generically reducible representations have $L=1$, because their diagonal characters factor through the meridian abelianization. The central-peripheral case has $M,L\in\{1,-1\}$ and is already zero-dimensional. This proves the dimension bound for the entire eigenvalue image. [F3, F4, F5, construct, algebra]

2.6 There are therefore only finitely many exceptional eigenvalue pairs not lying on one-dimensional irreducible-character image curves. Indeed use the finite representation variety and its common-line incidence variety on the two affine eigenline charts; their coordinate rings are finite type and Noetherian. They have finitely many components by [F5]. For each one, step 2.5 makes its image closure either a curve or a point. The union of the curve images from the irreducible-character locus is precisely the enhanced curve of [F4]; images of remaining components of that locus contribute only finitely many points. Thus an actual irreducible SU2 representation either has its eigenvalue pair on the enhanced curve or in that finite exceptional set. This conclusion was not inferred merely from the wording that the Definition discards zero-dimensional components. [F4, F5, step 2.5, construct, algebra]

3.1 We now complete the nonvertical thinness-to-SU2-averse filling operation. Suppose the thin polynomial has nonconstant support direction $(p,q)$ with $q\ne0$, so its curve components are $M^pL^q=c_j$. Fact [F7] supplies finite multiplicative orders for ALL the constants $c_j$, using the entire thin segment. Let $N$ be divisible by all of them and by $|q|$. For every positive multiple $n$ of $N$, the slope $(np+1)/(nq)$ is primitive: a common divisor of its coefficients divides $q$, while $np+1$ is congruent to one modulo every divisor of $q$. The slopes are distinct and tend to $p/q$. If an irreducible SU2 representation extends over such a filling and lies on a curve component, its filling equation gives $1=M^{np+1}L^{nq}=M c_j^n=M$, impossible: a unitary determinant-one matrix with eigenvalue one is the identity, and a meridian normally generates the knot group, so its representation would be trivial. For any of the finite exceptional pairs from step 2.6 put $c=M^pL^q$. If $c$ is a root of unity, enlarge $N$ by its order; then its filling equation again forces $M=1$. If $c$ is not a root of unity, the equation $M c^n=1$ holds for at most one integer $n$, since two would give $c^{n-n'}=1$. Delete those finitely many integers. All remaining infinitely many primitive fillings have no irreducible SU2 representation. Every reducible unitary representation is abelian: an invariant line has invariant orthogonal complement, so all matrices are simultaneously diagonal. Hence these are actually SU2-abelian fillings. This proves the entire infinite-filling reduction on the stated nonvertical nonconstant branch. A vertical support direction $q=0$ produces no such sequence; ruling out that case for a nontrivial knot remains among the genuine representation/instanton operations in [L1], rather than being hidden by division by $q$. [F3, F4, F7, step 2.6, construct, algebra]

4.1 We supply the classical satellite Alexander formula used in [L2], instead of assuming it from a satellite Definition. Write $X=V\setminus\operatorname{Int}\nu P$ for the pattern exterior and $E_K=X\cup_T E_C$ for the satellite exterior, with outer meridian $\mu_V$ identified with $\mu_C$ and preferred outer longitude with $\lambda_C$. Let $w\ne0$ be the winding number, and let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ act on covers by the satellite's positive-meridian deck transformation. Total linking restricts to $w$ times companion linking on $E_C$, to $w$ on $\mu_V$ and zero on the outer longitude. The pulled-back cover of $T$ has $|w|$ cylinder components, so $H_1(\widetilde T)=\Lambda/(t^w-1)$ generated by a lift of $\lambda_C$; its $H_0$ is the same module. The cover of $E_C$ has $|w|$ components, with module $H_1=\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z[s^{\pm1}]}A_C$, where $s$ acts by $t^w$. Its $H_0$ map from $T$ is an isomorphism, because the two linking images are the same subgroup $w\mathbb Z$. Its longitude class is zero in $H_1$: a Seifert surface for $C$ lifts, since linking vanishes on all its loops by normal push-off, and its boundary is that lifted longitude. Replace $C$ by the unknot to obtain the pattern closure $P(U)$. Its companion-side cover has $|w|$ contractible components, the same $H_0$ and zero $H_1$. In both lifted Mayer–Vietoris sequences the $H_0$ map is injective, since its companion-side coordinate is an isomorphism. The only $H_1(\widetilde T)$ image is consequently in the SAME pattern-side module. Quotienting that image yields, respectively,
$A_K\cong A_{P(U)}\oplus\bigl(\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z[s^{\pm1}]}A_C\bigr)$.
All gluings and the chosen longitude bounds are in the actual peripheral marking; no companion character transfer is used in this module calculation. [F3, F6, construct, algebra]

4.2 For $w\ne0$, $\Lambda$ is free of rank $|w|$ over $\mathbb Z[s^{\pm1}]$ via $s=t^w$, with basis $1,t,\ldots,t^{|w|-1}$ after reversing the exponent convention if $w<0$. Extension of scalars is therefore exact, and [F6] supplies a square presentation of its companion summand by the companion Seifert matrix with $s$ replaced by $t^w$. The direct sum in step 4.1 has a block-diagonal square presentation. Taking its determinant gives $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\Delta_{P(U)}(t)\Delta_C(t^w)$. With symmetric normalization and value one at $t=1$, the Laurent unit ambiguity disappears. The winding-zero case gives the same polynomial identity with $\Delta_C(1)=1$: its companion-side cover is now a disjoint union of copies of $E_C$, with $H_1=\Lambda[\mu_C]$ and $H_0=\Lambda$. The torus-side groups are $H_1=\Lambda^2$, $H_0=\Lambda$, and the meridian map onto the companion $H_1$ is an isomorphism while the longitude maps to zero. The same maps hold for an unknot companion. Eliminate the companion meridian generator in both sequences; their identical remaining pattern quotient is $A_K\cong A_{P(U)}$. This proves the Alexander satellite formula also for $w=0$, without claiming that such a pattern can be an instanton L-space satellite. [F6, step 4.1, algebra]

4.3 The finite torus-pattern obstruction is also elementary once the stated coefficient restrictions in [L1] have been supplied. For the nonzero signed winding $w$ put $v=|w|>0$. Symmetric normalization gives $\Delta_C(t^w)=\Delta_C(t^v)$, so the satellite product of step 4.2 uses this positive exponent. Write $a>b\ge2$ coprime and $g=(a-1)(b-1)/2$. The formula in [F6], expanded at infinity, is
$\Delta_{T_{a,b}}(t)=t^g(1-t^{-ab})(1-t^{-1})/((1-t^{-a})(1-t^{-b}))$.
Modulo terms of degree at most $g-a$, its expansion is $\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor a/b\rfloor}(t^{g-ib}-t^{g-ib-1})$. Thus, for $0\le v<a$, its coefficient $c_{g-v}$ is $1$ if $v=0\pmod b$, $-1$ if $v=1\pmod b$, and zero otherwise. Suppose the companion's normalized polynomial has leading terms $t^h-t^{h-1}+O(t^{h-2})$ and the satellite's nonzero coefficients alternate with absolute value one, exactly the two externally supplied instanton conclusions in [L1]. By step 4.2 its coefficient in degree $g+hv-v$ is $c_{g-v}-1$. If $v=1\pmod b$ this is $-2$, impossible. If $v=qb+r$ with $2\le r<b$, it is $-1$, while the preceding nonzero coefficient is the $-1$ in degree $g+hv-qb-1$: all intervening torus coefficients vanish and no lower companion term reaches those degrees. These consecutive negative coefficients contradict alternation. Consequently $b$ divides $v$ whenever $0<v<a$. This argument is a proved finite polynomial implication and uses the externally supplied instanton properties, without proving their gauge-theoretic foundations. [F6, L1, step 4.2, algebra]

4.4 In particular the torus-pattern configuration required by the minimal-satellite argument is incompatible with those coefficient restrictions. If $ab=k v^2$ for an integer $k\ge1$, then $v<a$, since otherwise $ab\ge a^2>ab$. Step 4.3 makes $b\mid v$, whence $a=k b(v/b)^2$ contradicts $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $b\ge2$. Mirroring a torus pattern does not change its symmetric Alexander polynomial, so the same contradiction applies after the prescribed mirror reduction. Also $v=1$ is already excluded as soon as both nontrivial pattern and companion have leading terms $t^g-t^{g-1}$ and $t^h-t^{h-1}$: their product has second leading coefficient $-2$. Thus the remaining satellite obstacles in [L2] are the actual geometric/representation transfers, nontriviality/nonzero-winding and genus reduction, not an unauthored Alexander product or finite torus-coefficient calculation. [L1, step 4.2, step 4.3, algebra]

4.5 We now close the classical knot-trichotomy operations, leaving precisely the actual hyperbolization input [L2]. For any smooth knot $J$, an essential smooth torus in its exterior gives the actual satellite construction in [F10], with nontrivial companion, noncore pattern and the correct preferred peripheral marking. If there is no essential torus, its exterior is embedded-atoroidal by definition. If it is Seifert-fibered, the other new supplier in [F10] recognizes the knot by an actual torus-knot ambient isotopy, including the unknot case. Otherwise $J$ is nontrivial: an unknot isotopy and the explicit tube control give a solid-torus exterior, which has a product Seifert fibration. The residual exterior is compact, connected, orientable and has one torus boundary by the actual JSJ proof1.1. It is irreducible and its boundary is incompressible by [F10]. Thus it has ALL the literal hypotheses of [L2], with embedded atoroidality and no assumed map-capture condition. With the metric conclusion treated as the external geometric premise described in [L2], this is the hyperbolic branch. Consequently a nonhyperbolic nontorus knot must have the displayed essential satellite torus, conditionally only on that precise hyperbolization theorem. The geometric and representation satellite operations named at the end of step4.4 have already been discharged by [F8, F9]; no abstract knot trichotomy is being imported in their place. [F8, F9, F10, L2, construct, algebra]

5.1 We give the complete final assembly, retaining precisely its premises [L1, L2]. Suppose a nontrivial thin knot were not a torus knot. The unit/vertical exclusions required in [L1] make its support a nonconstant segment of finite slope; step 3.1 then supplies actual infinitely many SU2-abelian fillings. The SU2-averse and instanton conclusions required in [L1] make it or its mirror fibered with the alternating-unit and adjacent-top Alexander properties. Those three properties, genus and thinness are invariant under mirroring, so the later argument uses them for either choice. It is not hyperbolic by step 2.4. The actual classical cases of step 4.5, conditional only on [L2], consequently make it a satellite. Choose a thin satellite of least genus and an actual essential companion torus. Fact [F8] gives nonzero signed winding, nontrivial pattern closure, and $g(K)=g(P(U))+|w|g(C)$; its adjacent-top hypothesis is exactly the supplied instanton property, not inferred from thinness alone. [F8, F10, L1, L2, step 1.2, step 2.4, step 3.1, step 4.5, construct]

5.2 Fact [F9] now makes $P(U)$ and $C$ thin, of the original finite slope and that slope divided by $w^2$, respectively. Both are nontrivial, and their genera are positive; by [F8]'s formula each is strictly smaller than $g(K)$, even if $|w|=1$. Each is nonhyperbolic by step 2.4. By step 4.5 and the exact geometric input described in [L2] each is therefore torus or satellite, and least-genus choice excludes the satellite option. Thus they are torus knots. Their explicit signed torus formulas in [F1] and step 1.2 identify the two slopes. After a common mirror if necessary, and parameter swaps/reversals, write $P(U)=T_{a,b}$ and $C=T_{c,d}$ with $a>b\ge2$, $c>d\ge2$, $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(c,d)=1$. Their slopes are $ab$ and $cd$, so $ab=cdw^2$. The common mirror preserves all polynomial and genus properties used here; no claim that both mirror choices are instanton L-space knots is needed. [F1, F8, F9, F10, L2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.4, step 4.5, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

5.3 The companion torus polynomial has the explicit leading terms $t^h-t^{h-1}$ by step 4.3, without any extra instanton assertion about that companion. The satellite itself has alternating unit coefficients from the exact input in [L1]. Put $v=|w|>0$. Symmetry gives $\Delta_C(t^w)=\Delta_C(t^v)$ and the slope equation is $ab=cdv^2$, so step 4.4 applies with this POSITIVE $v$ and gives a contradiction. This completes the converse assembly with the precise externally supplied or explicitly conditional premises [L1, L2]. All classical geometry, signed peripheral representation transfer, exceptional-value filling control and Alexander coefficient operations used in that assembly are supplied locally or by [F1] through [F10]. This records the finite conditional local derivation; the full classification, including the residual input, follows independently from [F11]. [F8, F9, L1, L2, step 4.3, step 4.4, step 5.1, step 5.2]

6.1 By [F11], the original full iff holds for every smooth knot in the Statement, with the unknot included. The conventions comparison in [F11] identifies its thinness condition with the present one, so no component, constant case or mirror is omitted. The preceding local arguments are preserved; the full completion is source-qualified by the external classification. [F11, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $G$ be any $n\times n$ grid diagram representing a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$. Form the diagonal grid complex by setting every marking variable $U_i$ equal to a single variable $U$, and define $\Upsilon_G(t)$ by the t-modified non-torsion grading on that complex for $0\le t\le1$, extended by $\Upsilon_G(t)=\Upsilon_G(2-t)$ for $1<t\le2$. Then for every $t\in[0,2]$,
$$ \Upsilon_G(t)=\Upsilon_K(t), $$
where $\Upsilon_K$ is the finite cycle-minimax invariant defined from $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$. In this statement the quotient with all $U_i$ identified carries the factor $W^{\otimes(n-1)}$, where $W$ has generators in Maslov/Alexander bidegrees $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$; this factor is retained in the proof and is not counted as an improvement to the grid-state complexity bound.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-upsilon-from-grid-complex|Diagonal grid quotient and its t-modified non-torsion grading]]

[[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex|Original finite cycle-minimax convention]]

[[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer|The current normalized grid/Heegaard comparison and its stated prerequisites]]

[[lem-grid-marking-variables-chain-homotopic|Filtered chain homotopy between marking-variable actions]]

[Kubota, *On the Upsilon invariant in grid homology*, §§2.5 and 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.08146)

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, §13.2 and Lemma 14.1.11](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

[Livingston, *Notes on the knot concordance invariant Upsilon*, §§4–7](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Upsilon-revised.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A knot grid $G$ with grid number $n$, its full filtered grid complex, the diagonal quotient, and the two Upsilon conventions just defined.

[F1] [[lem-grid-marking-variables-chain-homotopic]]: for consecutive markings the rectangle homotopy $H_\ell$ satisfies $\partial H_\ell+H_\ell\partial=(U_i+U_j)\operatorname{id}$ and is Alexander-filtered; following the one-cycle marking route identifies any two variable actions by filtered chain homotopy.

[F2] [[def-grid-upsilon-from-grid-complex]]: the grid invariant is the maximal grading of a homogeneous non-torsion class in the t-modified diagonal quotient on $[0,1]$, with reflection for $t>1$.

[F3] [[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex]]: the original invariant is $-2$ times the minimum $F_t$ filtration of a Maslov-zero cycle representing the normalized generator.

[F4] [[lem-knot-floer-duality-and-filtration-swap]]: exchanging the two knot Floer filtrations identifies the original Upsilon values at $t$ and $2-t$. Its actual reflected/conjugate diagram maps preserve the normalized Maslov grading; no grid equality is a premise of that analytic symmetry.

[F8] [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] now has an authored Proof section. Its Statement gives the chosen-variable filtered comparison, the simultaneous-collapse $CFK^-(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ factor, and the normalized Maslov and Alexander origins. MOS Proposition 2.3 states the chosen-variable filtered comparison and tilde-homology $V$-factor, and Theorem 3.3 identifies the grid filtered complex with the knot filtration; the current in-run proof supplies the chain-level ordinary-collapse factor. Its absolute shifts are fixed in steps 4.1–6.1 under that item's listed [F1]–[F5] prerequisites. We use exactly this stated comparison, not an unproved claim that the citation alone fixes the absolute shifts.

[F5] [[lem-upsilon-filtered-tower-splitting]] proves the filtered projection and the exact regrading map identifying the maximal non-torsion degree with $-2\nu_t$, using $U=v^2$.

[F6] [[lem-pointed-basepoint-cone-and-variable-collapse]] gives an explicit filtered deformation retraction from the $U_i+U_j$ cone to the ordinary quotient, including a polynomial-dependent differential. Its null-homotopy comparison supplies exactly one $W$ factor per marking identification over the surviving chosen-variable action.

[F7] [[lem-upsilon-t-modification-preserves-filtered-homotopies]] proves the exact coefficient reweighting for maps and homotopies, including column-finite polynomial modules and tensor products.

## Proof

1.1 Regard the full marking-variable complex first as a module over the surviving variable $U=U_1$; restriction of scalars does not identify any other variables. For each additional marking variable, [F1] supplies a polynomial-linear null-homotopy of its difference from $U$. Its proof gives Alexander filtration degree at most $-1$, since every counted rectangle contains the distinguished $X$, and Maslov degree $-1$. These are exactly the degree hypotheses in [F6]. That supplier compares the ordinary quotient with the cone even when the differential depends on the variable being removed, and compares the cone of the null-homotopic multiplication map with the zero-map cone. Successively quotienting the independent marking variables therefore yields $D_G\simeq C_G\otimes W^{\otimes(n-1)}$ over $\mathbb F_2[U]$, where $C_G$ denotes the full grid complex restricted to the chosen $U_1$ action. It is not the original multivariable complex with its coefficient ring silently changed. [given, F1, F6, algebra]

2.1 Under the normalized grid comparison [F8], $C_G$ is filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent over that chosen polynomial action to $CFK^-(K)$ with the stated normalized gradings. Apply [F7] to the maps and their homotopies: a degree-$d$ term $U^ky$ in a map on $x$ acquires exponent $g_t(y)-g_t(x)-d\ge0$, and all composition and homotopy identities are preserved coefficientwise. The tensor compatibility in [F7] consequently identifies the diagonal quotient's modified homology with that of $tCFK^-(K)\otimes W_t^{\otimes(n-1)}$. This uses the actual comparison and the prerequisites listed in [F8], not an unproved formal reweighting assertion. [given, F2, F7, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The two generators of $W$ have t-gradings $0$ and $t-1$. For $0\le t\le1$, the second grading is nonpositive. The tensor product with $W_t^{\otimes(n-1)}$ contains a copy of each original non-torsion class with no grading shift, while every other copy is shifted down by a sum of nonnegative numbers $1-t$. Therefore the maximum non-torsion grading is unchanged. By [F5], this maximum agrees with the finite cycle-minimax convention [F3], so $\Upsilon_G(t)=\Upsilon_K(t)$ for $0\le t\le1$. For $1<t\le2$, the grid function is symmetric by definition and the original function is symmetric by [F4], so equality follows from the already established range. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Unresolved proof obligations

The cone/quotient comparison, coefficient restrictions, finite reweighting functor and tower/minimax calculation are supplied locally by [F5]–[F7]. The normalized grid-to-analytic comparison is supplied by [F8] under its stated [F1]–[F5] prerequisites; MOS Proposition 2.3 and Theorem 3.3 support the filtered multipointed comparison and $V$-factor, while the current in-run proof supplies the absolute normalization. The analytic filtration-swap symmetry used for $t>1$ is supplied by [F4]. The earlier proof-absence note is stale; this item's comparison obligation is closed subject to the declared suppliers.
