## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For any smooth oriented knots $K,J\subset S^3$, the Seifert genus of their oriented connected sum satisfies $g(K\#J)=g(K)+g(J)$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|Connected-sum convention]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|Knot genus]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and smooth oriented knots $K,J$.

[F1] The minimum genus surfaces for $K$ and $J$ exist by the definition of genus and the nonempty spanning-surface theorem. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]])

[F2] Under AC$_\omega$, a connected compact oriented surface with $b$ boundary circles satisfies $\chi=2-2g-b$. ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

[F3] A compact spanning surface can be isotoped rel its boundary to be transverse to the standard connected-sum sphere when its boundary is already transverse to that sphere. ([[lem-relative-transversality-for-embedded-surfaces]])

[F4] Every smooth embedded circle in the standard sphere is nullhomotopic and bounds an embedded disk there under AC$_\omega$. ([[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]], [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

[F5] The connected-sum model supplies a standard separating sphere meeting the sum knot in two points and separating the two summand pieces. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]])

[L1] Cutting at a decomposing sphere and capping on its boundary recovers the oriented connected-sum factors. ([[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum]])

[A1] AC$_\omega$ is the sequence-choice principle used by the genus and transversality suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** AC$_\omega$, $K,J$, and minimum genus spanning surfaces $F_K,F_J$.

1.1 Remove a small boundary half-disk from each minimum genus surface $F_K,F_J$ in the chosen connected-sum balls and glue their exposed boundary intervals. This is an embedded oriented boundary connected sum with boundary $K\#J$. Attaching the single connecting band changes Euler characteristic by $-1$, so $\chi(F)=\chi(F_K)+\chi(F_J)-1$. By [F2], $\chi(F_K)=1-2g(K)$ and $\chi(F_J)=1-2g(J)$; hence $\chi(F)=1-2(g(K)+g(J))$ and $g(K\#J)\le g(K)+g(J)$. [given, F1, F2, A1, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose a minimum genus surface $F$ for $K\#J$ and, among such surfaces transverse to the standard sum sphere $S$, one minimizing the finite number of circular components of $F\cap S$. Such a surface exists by [F1], [F3], and well-ordering of the nonnegative integers. The intersection is a compact one-manifold whose boundary is the two points $(K\#J)\cap S$, hence consists of one arc $\alpha$ and finitely many circles. [given, F1, F3, F5, A1, choose]

2.1 If circles occur, choose one innermost on $S$. Since the intersection circles are disjoint and the arc $\alpha$ is connected and misses them, finite nesting gives a disk side of some circle containing neither $\alpha$ nor another intersection component. By [F4] this is an embedded disk $D\subset S$, disjoint from $K$. [given, F4, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 If the selected circle $c$ is nonseparating on $F$, cut $F$ along $c$ and cap the two new boundary copies by parallel copies of $D$, rounded in a product neighbourhood of $c$. The caps are disjoint and the boundary remains the original knot. Cutting along a circle preserves Euler characteristic and the two caps add $2$, so by [F2] the new genus is $g(F)-1$, contradicting minimality. [given, F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 If $c$ separates $F$, cutting gives a component $F_K$ containing the knot boundary and a component $F_0$ with boundary $c$. Let their genera be $h_K,h_0$. Since $F_K$ has two boundary components and $F_0$ has one, Euler characteristic additivity along the cut and [F2] give $g(F)=h_K+h_0$. Cap $F_K$ by a parallel copy of $D$ and discard $F_0$. If $h_0>0$ this is a lower genus spanning surface, contradiction; if $h_0=0$, it is another minimum genus surface with fewer intersection circles, contradicting the choice in step 1.2. The cap is embedded after rounding in the local product neighbourhood from step 2.1. Thus no circle can occur. [given, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 With no circles, $F\cap S=\alpha$. Since $S$ separates the two knot pieces in the standard sum model, the proper arc $\alpha$ separates $F$ into two connected surfaces $F_1,F_2$, each with one boundary component. Cutting along an arc increases total Euler characteristic by $1$, so [F2] gives $g(F)=g(F_1)+g(F_2)$. The two surfaces are connected because any component of either side not incident to $\alpha$ would already be a separate component of $F$; the sole arc has just one collar on each side. Their boundary circles consist of the corresponding knot subarc and $\alpha\subset S$, and hence represent $K$ and $J$ by [L1] and the original connected-sum datum. Thus $g(K)+g(J)\le g(F_1)+g(F_2)=g(F)=g(K\#J)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the full equality. [given, F2, F5, L1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume ACω. For every nonempty oriented link $L\subset S^3$, the bigraded $\mathbb F_2$ vector spaces $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,j}(L;\mathbb F_2)$ obtained by reducing the normalized Khovanov complex at a point on any chosen component are independent, up to noncanonical bigraded isomorphism, of the diagram and the chosen component. No filtered structure from a Floer construction is part of this invariance statement.

## Statement references

[[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-based-link-over-f2|Based reduced Khovanov cohomology]]

[[lem-reduced-khovanov-over-f2-basepoint-independence|Component independence for a fixed diagram]]

[[lem-based-link-reduced-khovanov-reidemeister-equivalences|Local reduced equivalences for arbitrary based links]]

[Ozsváth and Szabó, *On the Heegaard Floer homology of branched double-covers*, §5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309170v1)

[Shumakovitch, *Torsion of the Khovanov homology*, §§2.2 and 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0405474v2)

[Turner, *A hitchhiker’s guide to Khovanov homology*, §1.2](https://www.i2m.univ-amu.fr/perso/luisa.paoluzzi/Turner1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** ACω, two finite regular diagrams of the same nonempty oriented link, and a basepoint on a component of each diagram.

[F1] Under ACω, two diagrams of the same oriented link are connected by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves ([[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]]).

[F2] For every oriented link Reidemeister move with an unchanged exterior mark, the actual normalized integral maps and inverse homotopies commute with the marked actions and descend to bigraded equivalences of the quotient complexes; reducing the same identities modulo two proves the corresponding based-link equivalences over $\mathbb F_2$ ([[lem-based-link-reduced-khovanov-reidemeister-equivalences]]).

[F3] For a fixed diagram, the reduced $\mathbb F_2$ cohomology is independent of which link component carries the basepoint ([[lem-reduced-khovanov-over-f2-basepoint-independence]]).

[F4] The based reduction is the quotient by the image of the basepoint action ([[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-based-link-over-f2]]).

## Proof


1.1 By [F1], choose a finite sequence $D=D_0,D_1,\ldots,D_r=D'$ of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister moves. For a Reidemeister step choose a marked point on an unchanged exterior arc and carry it to the corresponding arc on the other diagram. Such an arc exists: the move models contain a continuing strand meeting the boundary of their disk, and a closed regular link diagram continues that strand outside the disk. For a planar isotopy choose any mark and carry it by the isotopy. There are finitely many steps and every diagram is nonempty, so these are finite point choices, adding no choice hypothesis beyond [F1]. These auxiliary marks need not all lie on a single tracked component. [F1, given, choose, construct]

2.1 At the start of a step, [F3] identifies the current reduced group with the reduction at its chosen auxiliary mark, even if that mark lies on another component. For a Reidemeister move, [F2] then gives a bigraded cochain homotopy equivalence between the reductions at the two unchanged exterior marks. Its integral maps and contractions commute with the marked action before quotienting, and their explicit equations remain true over $\mathbb F_2$. For a planar isotopy the relabeling of circles preserves that marked factor and every normalized degree. Thus each step supplies a bigraded cohomology isomorphism, followed if necessary by another fixed-diagram change of mark using [F3]. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Compose these finitely many isomorphisms, using [F3] at the first and last diagram to reach the originally selected marks. This proves independence of the diagram and chosen component. For an empty move sequence only [F3] is needed. Each vector space has finite support in its bigrading, so finite choices of its isomorphisms assemble the asserted noncanonical bigraded isomorphism. The proof uses neither a canonical identification of different move sequences nor a relative movie theorem for multi-component cut tangles. ACω is used only in [F1]; the local tensor equations and fixed-diagram mark changes are finite and choice-free. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $Y$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological five-manifold with supplied boundary collar, and let $X=\partial Y$ have its boundary orientation. Supply a based homomorphism $\psi:\pi_1Y\to G$ on each component, where $G$ is an arbitrary discrete group, with the standard unitary regular coefficient systems. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X,\psi|_X)=0,\qquad \operatorname{sign}(X)=0.$$
In particular, when $X=X_1\sqcup(-X_0)$, the ordinary and $L^2$ signatures of these closed oriented four-manifolds agree across this actual coefficient-extending TOP bordism. The equality is unchanged under embedding the target group in a larger group. This theorem asserts bordism invariance and does not assert existence of a bordism between arbitrary closed coefficient manifolds.

## Statement references

[[thm-topological-finite-projective-l2-duality-and-boundary-gluing]]

[Cha, section2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.1805)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the actual collared oriented $Y$, its boundary $X$, and the compatible regular coefficient maps in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is the standing spectral and projective-comparison hypothesis of the finite-projective supplier.

[F1] For compact collared TOP manifolds in every dimension, bounded finite-projective coefficient chain models and their pair diagrams transfer actual cap duality to bounded isomorphisms on completed reduced homology and cohomology. Pair sequences are weakly exact; algebraic harmonic parts are dense. Cap-boundary and restriction identities hold after completion. For a closed oriented four-manifold its middle Hermitian operator is boundedly invertible. Model independence and coefficient-subgroup induction hold by finite matrices and identical coset operator blocks. [[thm-topological-finite-projective-l2-duality-and-boundary-gluing]]

[F2] Restriction of a boundedly invertible Hermitian form on a finite Hilbert von Neumann module to a closed coisotropic submodule preserves its signature; a zero form has zero signature. [[lem-von-neumann-inertia-and-coisotropic-reduction]]

## Proof

1.1 Use [F1] for $Y,X$ and $(Y,X)$ with $R=\mathbb CG$ and $A=\mathcal NG$. Write $V=\mathscr H^2(X)$ for completed reduced cohomology. Transport the middle intersection form of $X$ to $V$ by its bounded cap isomorphism, and denote it by $Q$. It is a bounded Hermitian form with boundedly invertible operator, since $X$ is closed. Let $r:\mathscr H^2(Y)\to V$ be restriction and $\delta:V\to\mathscr H^3(Y,X)$ the completed connecting map of the pair. These are bounded maps of finite Hilbert $A$ modules. Set $U=\overline{\operatorname{im}r}$, an actual closed submodule; no assertion that $\operatorname{im}r$ is closed is made. [A1, F1, given, construct]

2.1 Cap duality on $Y$ and Riesz duality give a bounded nondegenerate scalar sesquilinear pairing $\mathscr H^2(Y)\times\mathscr H^3(Y,X)\to\mathbb C$: take evaluation of the first class on the cap of the second with $[Y,X]$, followed by the canonical trace, initially on algebraic harmonic parts. Riesz and the bounded cap isomorphism extend this pairing to the Hilbert completions and identify either factor boundedly with the Hilbert dual of the other. No $A$-valued pairing is asserted on arbitrary $\ell^2$ vectors. The boundary identity identifies $Q(ra,b)$ with this pairing of $a$ and $\delta b$, up to the fixed conjugation convention, for all $a\in\mathscr H^2(Y)$ and $b\in V$. Concretely, for an actual degree-two boundary cocycle $\beta$ extend it to a cochain $\widetilde\beta$ on $Y$. The relative cocycle $d\widetilde\beta$ represents $\delta\beta$, and the cohomology-first cap formula gives $\partial(\widetilde\beta\cap[Y,X])=\beta\cap[X]-(d\widetilde\beta)\cap[Y,X]$. Thus $i_*\mathrm{PD}_X\beta=\mathrm{PD}_{Y,X}\delta\beta$ in absolute homology. Pairing with $a$ proves the asserted identity on algebraic harmonic parts. Such parts are dense, all displayed maps and pairings are bounded, and [F1] transfers this actual identity to the completed modules. This uses cochains and the finite orientation chain, with no geometric transverse intersections in dimension four or five. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1 and nondegeneracy of the perfect pairing, $Q(ra,b)=0$ for every $a$ if and only if $\delta b=0$. Continuity replaces $\operatorname{im}r$ by its closure without changing this annihilator, giving $U^{\perp_Q}=\ker\delta$. Weak exactness of the actual pair sequence in [F1] gives $\ker\delta=\overline{\operatorname{im}r}=U$. Therefore $U$ is a closed self-annihilating, hence coisotropic, submodule, and $Q|_U$ is identically zero. These are equalities of Hilbert-closed submodules; no algebraic exactness has been promoted to closed-range exactness. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F2] to the invertible closed-boundary form $Q$ and $U$. Its signature is the signature of the zero restriction, namely zero. The bounded cap change of coordinates preserves inertia, so this is precisely $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X)$. Apply the same argument to the trivial group: its complex Hermitian intersection form is the complexification of the real symmetric form, with equal positive and negative multiplicities, and hence gives the ordinary signature zero. All arguments allow finite disconnected boundaries and empty boundary; in the latter case the middle module is zero. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 A disjoint union is an orthogonal direct sum of the finite-projective complexes and forms; orientation reversal negates cap and the form. Thus $X=X_1\sqcup(-X_0)$ in step 4.1 yields the two asserted bordism-invariance equalities. For an embedded coefficient subgroup $G\hookrightarrow K$, construct the same finite models over $\mathbb CG$ and extend the matrices to $\mathbb CK$. Every left-$G$ matrix decomposes on $\ell^2(K)=\bigoplus_{G\gamma}\ell^2(G\gamma)$ into identical copies of its $\ell^2(G)$ operator. Kernel, harmonic and positive/negative projections have the same identity-coordinate diagonal trace. By [F1] this preserves the signatures on both ends and on $X$, for arbitrary cardinalities of $K$. No equality between ordinary and $L^2$ signatures on arbitrary closed four-manifolds and no TOP bordism realization theorem was assumed. [F1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

The false claim is: if a closed oriented three-manifold $Y$ with $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$ bounds a smooth compact four-manifold $B$ with $H_*(B;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$, then a nonzero correction term $d(Y,\mathfrak t)$ for any boundary Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$ obstructs the existence of $B$.

## Statement references

[[thm-correction-term-obstruction-from-rational-ball|The actual vanishing theorem, which requires extension over the ball]]

## Example

Let $B_2$ be the rational homology ball bounded by $L(4,1)$ constructed as the complement of a tubular neighborhood of a conic in $\mathbb{CP}^2$. The canonical Spin$^c$ label $i=0$ has $d(L(4,1),0)=3/4$. The extension set has exactly two elements and every extending structure has correction term zero. Therefore label $i=0$ is nonextendible, even though this rational-ball filling exists.

## Example references

[[lem-rational-ball-b2-bounds-lens-l4|The explicit rational ball bounded by the four-surgery lens space]]

[[lem-rational-ball-spin-c-extension-set-metabolizer|The extension-set size and metabolizer]]

[[lem-heegaard-floer-correction-terms-lens-space-lp1|The lens-space correction-term calculation]]

[[thm-correction-term-obstruction-from-rational-ball|Vanishing on extending structures]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the rational ball $B_2$ with boundary $L(4,1)$, and the lens-space label $i=0$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the construction and the extension-set supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The conic complement is a rational homology four-ball with boundary $L(4,1)$ in the selected orientation ([[lem-rational-ball-b2-bounds-lens-l4]]).

[F2] The surgery matrix for $L(4,1)$ is nonsingular and its first homology has order $4$ ([[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix]]).

[F3] Over a rational-ball boundary, the extending Spin$^c$ structures form a coset of order $\sqrt{|H_1(Y)|}$, and every extending structure has zero correction term ([[lem-rational-ball-spin-c-extension-set-metabolizer]], [[thm-correction-term-obstruction-from-rational-ball]]).

[F4] For the selected orientation, $d(L(4,1),i)=((2i-4)^2-4)/16$ ([[lem-heegaard-floer-correction-terms-lens-space-lp1]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** compute the extension-set size and the correction term at a label outside that set.

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], $B_2$ is a rational homology ball with $|H_1(L(4,1))|=4$. Therefore [F3] gives exactly $\sqrt4=2$ extending Spin$^c$ structures. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 At label $i=0$, [F4] gives $d(L(4,1),0)=(16-4)/16=3/4\ne0$. Every extending structure has $d=0$ by [F3], so label $0$ is not in the two-element extension set. Thus a nonextending structure has nonzero correction term while the rational-ball filling exists, refuting the stated claim. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. For each such surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Define the smooth slice genus and the locally flat topological slice genus by

$$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

## Example

Let $X=\mathbb R^2$, $G=S^1\times\mathbb R$, and
$$
Z=\{(\theta,s,x):s=x\cdot\theta\}.
$$
Write $x=s\theta+t\theta^\perp$ on $Z$, use the analytic total density $|d\theta\,ds\,dt|$ and constant weight $1$, so $R$ is the full Euclidean Radon transform. This is a properly supported analytic double fibration. Its canonical relation satisfies the global Bolker condition. Using the Euclidean metric to identify covectors with vectors and its associated norm, for every $x\in\mathbb R^2$ and every $\xi\in T_x^*\mathbb R^2\setminus0$, set
$$
\theta=\xi/|\xi|,\qquad \tau=|\xi|,\qquad s=x\cdot\theta,\qquad \eta_s=\tau,\quad \eta_\theta=-\tau\,x\cdot\theta^\perp.
$$
Then $(\theta,s;\eta_\theta,\eta_s;x,\xi)$ is a canonical pair. Thus every nonzero Euclidean covector is visible. In particular, for a compactly supported distribution $f$, the analytic wavefront recovery theorem implies that if $(x,\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_A(f)$, then this data covector belongs to $\operatorname{WF}_A(Rf)$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-2d-radon-transform|Radon lines and normal convention]]

[[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation|Incidence relation]]

[[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform|Analytic transform]]

[[def-ip-bolker-condition|Bolker condition]]

[[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel|Incidence conormal calculation]]

[[lem-ip-bolker-geometric-criteria|Bolker rank test]]

[[thm-ip-analytic-wavefront-recovery-under-bolker|Analytic wavefront recovery]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The full Euclidean Radon incidence, its constant analytic weight and line density, and a nonzero covector $(x,\xi)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-2d-radon-transform]]: lines are parameterized by $s=x\cdot\theta$, with $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-double-fibration-conormal-kernel]]: the defining function $F(\theta,s,x)=s-x\cdot\theta$ gives conormal components by differentiating $F$, with the relation sign $(\eta,-\xi)$.

[F3] [[def-ip-bolker-condition]]: the Bolker condition requires a singleton left fiber and injective differential at its point.

[F4] [[thm-ip-analytic-wavefront-recovery-under-bolker]]: data-side analytic regularity at a Bolker pair implies object-side analytic regularity.

[F5] [[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform]]: both incidence projections must be analytic submersions and the support condition is properness over compact object supports.

[F6] [[thm-real-analytic-inverse-and-implicit-function-theorems]]: a regular zero of a real-analytic scalar function is locally an analytic hypersurface.

## Proof

**Given:** The incidence and the covector $(x,\xi)$.

1.1 The defining function $F(\theta,s,x)=s-x\cdot\theta$ is analytic and has $\partial_sF=1$. Thus [F6] makes $Z=F^{-1}(0)$ an analytic hypersurface of dimension $3$. [F1, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 In a local angle coordinate $\alpha$ with $\partial_\alpha\theta=\theta^\perp$, the defining function has differential $ dF=ds-(x\cdot\theta^\perp)d\alpha-\theta\cdot dx. $ By [F2], the canonical relation consists of $ \xi=\tau\theta,\qquad \eta_s=\tau,\qquad \eta_\theta=-\tau x\cdot\theta^\perp,\qquad \tau\ne0. $ These signs follow by matching $(\eta,-\xi)=\tau dF$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 A tangent vector satisfies $\dot s-\dot x\cdot\theta-x\cdot\dot\theta=0$. Given any data tangent pair $(\dot\theta,\dot s)$, choose $\dot x=(\dot s-x\cdot\dot\theta)\theta$; this lifts it to $TZ$, so $\pi_G$ is a submersion. Given any object tangent vector $\dot x$, take $\dot\theta=0$ and $\dot s=\dot x\cdot\theta$, so $\pi_X$ is a submersion. Since $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ is parameterized by the compact set $S^1\times K$ for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^2$, the restriction to $G$ is proper. The specified analytic total density is nowhere zero. The dimensions satisfy $4>3>2\ge2$, so [F5] applies. [F5, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

2.2 For fixed $(\theta,s,\eta_s,\eta_\theta)$ in the image, $\tau=\eta_s\ne0$ and $ x=s\theta-\frac{\eta_\theta}{\tau}\theta^\perp,\qquad \xi=\tau\theta. $ Thus the left fiber is a singleton. To check the differential, let a tangent variation be in the kernel of the left projection. Then $\dot\theta=0$, $\dot s=0$, $\dot\tau=\dot\eta_s=0$, and $ 0=\dot s=\dot x\cdot\theta,\qquad 0=\dot\eta_\theta=-\tau\,\dot x\cdot\theta^\perp. $ Since $\tau\ne0$ and $(\theta,\theta^\perp)$ is a basis, $\dot x=0$ and $\dot\xi=0$. Hence the left projection is an injective immersion, so [F3] gives global Bolker. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 For the specified object covector, $\theta=\xi/|\xi|$ and $\tau=|\xi|$ satisfy $\xi=\tau\theta$. With $s$ and $\eta$ chosen in the statement, step 1.2 supplies the remaining relation equations. Therefore the data-side canonical pair exists for every nonzero $\xi$. [F2, step 1.2, given]

3.1 The contrapositive of [F4] shows that $(x,\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_A(f)$ forces $(\theta,s;\eta_\theta,\eta_s)\in\operatorname{WF}_A(Rf)$. Its hypotheses hold by the analytic nonvanishing density, properness and full Bolker calculations in steps 1.1–2.2. [F4, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, contrapositive] ∎

## Geometric diagram

The line has normal $\theta$, so its conormal covectors are scalar multiples of $\theta$. The point $x$ determines the offset $s=x\cdot\theta$; the tangential component of the data covector records $-x\cdot\theta^\perp$. The drawing fixes these conventions only; the proof computes the full data covector and verifies Bolker directly.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.0]

  \draw[->] (0,-0.4) -- (0,3.0) node[above] {$\theta$};
  \draw[thick,blue] (-0.3,1.2) -- (3.4,1.2) node[right] {$x\cdot\theta=s$};
  \fill (2.0,1.2) circle (0.06) node[below right] {$x$};
  \draw[->,red,thick] (2.0,1.2) -- (2.0,2.4) node[above] {$\xi=\tau\theta$};
  \draw[->,red,thick] (0,0) -- (0,1.2) node[left] {$\theta$};
  \node at (3.1,2.35) {$\xi$ visible};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement

For $0<\zeta<\pi/2$, let
$$\mathcal O_\zeta= \{(x+iy,t)\in\mathbb H^3: 0\le x\le\cos\zeta,\quad 0\le y\le x\tan\zeta,\quad t\ge\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}\}.$$
Its hyperbolic volume in the upper half-space metric is $\frac12\Lambda(\zeta)$.

## Statement references

[Jessica S. Purcell, *Hyperbolic Knot Theory*, Lemma 9.8](https://users.monash.edu/~jpurcell/book/HypKnotTheory.pdf)

## Diagram

The shaded triangle is the vertical projection of $\mathcal O_\zeta$. The dashed arc is the unit circle; the vertex $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$ lies on it. The region in $\mathbb H^3$ lies above the corresponding unit hemisphere and is unbounded toward the ideal point at infinity. This is a projection only; the proof uses the stated coordinate inequalities and integral.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=2.2]
  \def\a{38}
  \coordinate (O) at (0,0);
  \coordinate (A) at ({cos(\a)},0);
  \coordinate (B) at ({cos(\a)},{sin(\a)});
  \fill[blue!12] (O)--(A)--(B)--cycle;
  \draw[thick,blue!70!black] (O)--(A)--(B)--cycle;
  \draw[dashed] (0,0) arc[start angle=0,end angle=\a,radius=1];
  \draw[->] (-0.08,0)--(1.13,0) node[right] {$x$};
  \draw[->] (0,-0.08)--(0,0.92) node[above] {$y$};
  \draw (0.16,0) arc[start angle=0,end angle=\a,radius=0.16];
  \node[below left] at (O) {$O$};
  \node[below] at (A) {$A=(\cos\zeta,0)$};
  \node[above right] at (B) {$B=(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$};
  \node at (0.28,0.09) {$\zeta$};
  \node[below right] at (0.92,0.12) {$x^2+y^2=1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The region $\mathcal O_\zeta$ and $0<\zeta<\pi/2$.

[F1] [[def-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-and-cusp-holonomy]] gives the upper half-space metric with volume density $dx\,dy\,dt/t^3$.

[F2] [[def-lobachevsky-function]] defines $\Lambda(\theta)=-\int_0^\theta\log|2\sin u|\,du$.

[F3] [[lem-lobachevsky-fourier-expansion-and-pi-third-bound]] proves that $\Lambda$ is odd and $\pi$-periodic, $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$, and $\Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2)$.

## Proof

1.1 Integrating the volume density in $t$ gives $\operatorname{Vol}(\mathcal O_\zeta)=\int_0^{\cos\zeta}\int_0^{x\tan\zeta}\frac{dy\,dx}{2(1-x^2-y^2)}$. For fixed $x$, put $A=\sqrt{1-x^2}$; since $x\tan\zeta<A$ for $0\le x<\cos\zeta$, the inner integral is $\frac1{4A}\log\frac{A+x\tan\zeta}{A-x\tan\zeta}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Set $x=\cos\theta$, so $\zeta\le\theta\le\pi/2$. Sine addition identities change the logarithm ratio to $\sin(\theta+\zeta)/\sin(\theta-\zeta)$, and therefore $\operatorname{Vol}(\mathcal O_\zeta)=\frac14\int_\zeta^{\pi/2}\log\frac{\sin(\theta+\zeta)}{\sin(\theta-\zeta)}\,d\theta=\frac14(\Lambda(2\zeta)-\Lambda(\pi/2+\zeta)+\Lambda(\pi/2-\zeta))$. The logarithmic singularity at $\theta=\zeta$ is integrable, so the substitution and improper endpoint evaluation are valid. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By oddness and period $\pi$ from [F3], $\Lambda(\pi/2-\zeta)=-\Lambda(\pi/2+\zeta)$. Also [F3] gives $\Lambda(2\zeta)=2\Lambda(\zeta)+2\Lambda(\zeta+\pi/2)$. Substitution in step 2.1 cancels the two $\Lambda(\zeta+\pi/2)$ terms and leaves $\operatorname{Vol}(\mathcal O_\zeta)=\frac12\Lambda(\zeta)$. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Sources

[Jessica S. Purcell, *Hyperbolic Knot Theory*, Lemma 9.8](https://users.monash.edu/~jpurcell/book/HypKnotTheory.pdf)

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let $L$ be a nonempty oriented link and let $X$ be a certified finite based two-dimensional spine of its compact exterior with one $0$-cell, $n\ge2$ $1$-cells and $n-1$ $2$-cells. Let $\psi:\pi_1(X)\twoheadrightarrow H\cong\mathbb Z^m$ be an epimorphism with $m\ge1$, let $\rho:\pi_1(X)\to\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$ be a representation over a field, and form the twisted chain complex over $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$ and its localization over $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$. If its degree-one homology over $\Lambda$ is a torsion module, then its fraction-field complex is acyclic.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion|Twisted exterior chain complex]]

[[lem-twisted-acyclicity-from-torsion-module|General localized acyclicity lemma]]

[Conway, Lemma 2.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.06678)

[Kirk and Livingston, §3](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Livingston_papers/1999_Twisted%20Alexander%20invariants%2C%20Reidemeister%20torsion%2C%20and%20Casson-Gordon%20invariants.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a based two-dimensional simple spine of a nonempty link exterior with one $0$-cell, $n$ $1$-cells and $n-1$ $2$-cells; a positive-rank free abelian deck quotient; a field-valued representation; and the torsion hypothesis on degree-one homology.

[A1] AC is inherited from the full abelianization convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The based twisted complex is built from the exterior spine and its prescribed coefficient action; a certified spine has the same based simple-homotopy type as the selected exterior cell structure. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]; [[def-knot-wada-quotient-for-deficiency-one-presentation]]

[F2] For a finite based two-dimensional complex with one $0$-cell, $n$ $1$-cells and $n-1$ $2$-cells, positive-rank free-abelian deck map and torsion $H_1$ over the Laurent coefficient ring, localization yields an acyclic complex. [[lem-twisted-acyclicity-from-torsion-module]]

## Proof



1.1 The stated cell counts give $\chi(X)=1-n+(n-1)=0$, and the two-dimensional spine has no cellular chain groups above degree $2$. The declared deck group has positive rank, the coefficient field and representation are as in [F1], and the degree-one torsion hypothesis is exactly the remaining module assumption of [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to this $X$, $\rho$, and $\psi$. It gives $H_i(C_*^{\rho,\psi}(X;Q^d))=0$ in every degree; hence the fraction-field complex is acyclic. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let $X$ be a finite based CW model of a link exterior, let $G=\pi_1(X)$, let $\alpha(g)=\rho(g)\psi(g)\in\mathrm{GL}_d(Q)$ be its declared twisted coefficient representation, and suppose the based fraction-field complex is acyclic. Let $\mathcal U=\{\pm\det(\alpha(g)):g\in G\}$. Changing the lift or orientation of any cell multiplies the based Reidemeister torsion by an element of $\mathcal U$, so its class in $Q^\times/\mathcal U$ is unchanged. An elementary simple expansion or collapse, meaning addition or deletion of a pair of adjacent-dimensional cells whose lifted incidence block is $\pm g$ for some $g\in G$, has the same property.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion|Based chain and torsion convention]]

[Ranicki, basis changes and Theorem 15](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/torsion.pdf)

[Conway, §§2.3–2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.06678)

[Kirk and Livingston, §3](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Livingston_papers/1999_Twisted%20Alexander%20invariants%2C%20Reidemeister%20torsion%2C%20and%20Casson-Gordon%20invariants.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite based cellular model, its acyclic twisted complex, the fixed coefficient representation $\alpha$, and the torsion convention of the preceding definition.

[A1] AC is inherited from the maximal-abelian-cover convention; the finite basis-change argument uses only finite-dimensional linear algebra. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For an acyclic based complex with bases $\mathbf c_i$, torsion is the alternating product of determinants $[\mathbf b_i,\widetilde{\mathbf b}_{i-1}/\mathbf c_i]^{(-1)^{i+1}}$; the bases are the chosen cellular lifts tensored with the fixed coefficient basis. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F2] A lifted oriented cell is a basis vector in a free $Q[G]$-module; translating its lift by $g$ applies $\alpha(g)$ to its coefficient block, and reversing its orientation multiplies that block by $-I_d$. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F3] The determinant map $g\mapsto\det(\alpha(g))$ is a group homomorphism to $Q^\times$, and $\mathcal U$ is its image together with the sign unit. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

## Proof

1.1 If a chosen lift of one $q$-cell is translated by $g$, [F2] changes exactly its $d$-vector block in $\mathbf c_q$ by $\alpha(g)$. The only torsion bracket whose denominator basis changes is the degree-$q$ bracket in [F1], so the torsion is multiplied by $\det(\alpha(g))^{(-1)^q}$ (or its inverse under the opposite bracket-order convention). This factor belongs to $\mathcal U$ by [F3]. Reversing the cell orientation gives the factor $(-1)^{d(-1)^q}$, also in $\mathcal U$. Applying finitely many such changes multiplies by a product of elements of the subgroup $\mathcal U$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 In an elementary expansion, order the new cell bases last and clear the old-cell entries of the new boundary column by adding multiples of old basis columns; these are triangular basis changes with determinant $1$. Because the new $q$-cell is a free face, the lifted boundary matrices have the old blocks together with a single invertible diagonal block $\pm\alpha(g)$ between the new $(q+1)$- and $q$-cell blocks; clearing the other entries in that new column by the described triangular basis changes splits off the two-term complex $0\to Q^d\xrightarrow{\pm\alpha(g)}Q^d\to0$. The torsion formula [F1] for this two-term summand is $\det(\alpha(g))$ or its inverse according to the degree parity, hence lies in $\mathcal U$ by [F3]. The direct-sum torsion formula multiplies the old torsion by that factor, so the class is unchanged. A collapse is the inverse operation. Iterating proves invariance under every finite sequence of these elementary simple moves. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Assume full AC. The positive one-crossing type-I kink of the unknot is connected and alternating but not reduced; its diagram has one crossing while the represented unknot has crossing number zero, and its normalized library Jones polynomial has $t$-span zero.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9, line cap=round, line join=round]
  \draw[->,thick] (-0.22,-0.22)--(-0.045,-0.045);
  \draw[->,thick] (0.045,0.045)--(0.22,0.22);
  \draw[->,very thick] (-0.22,0.22)--(0.22,-0.22);
  \draw[->,thick] (0.22,0.22) .. controls (0.95,1.0) and (-0.95,1.0) .. (-0.22,0.22);
  \draw[->,thick] (0.22,-0.22) .. controls (0.95,-1.0) and (-0.95,-1.0) .. (-0.22,-0.22);
  \node at (0,1.25) {positive type-I kink};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

The arrows orient the single component; at the central crossing, the diagonal from northwest to southeast is over and the southwest-to-northeast diagonal has a gap.

## Statement references

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the positive type-I kink diagram $D_+$ of the unknot, and the bracket and Jones conventions in the statement.

[F1] A crossing contributes $A$ for its $A$-smoothing and $A^{-1}$ for its $B$-smoothing, a state with $k$ circles contributes $\delta^{k-1}$, and $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The positive geometric crossing has sign $+1$, and writhe is the sum of crossing signs ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F3] A connected diagram has connected projection graph, alternation switches over-under at successive visits, and reducedness excludes a crossing repeated on a region boundary ([[def-reduced-alternating-link-diagram]]).

[F4] A type-I Reidemeister move is realized by an ambient isotopy of the represented link ([[lem-each-oriented-reidemeister-move-is-realized-by-ambient-isotopy]]).

[F5] Under full AC, the normalized bracket state sum specializes to the library Jones polynomial by $V_K(t)=f_K(t^{-1/4})$ with $t=A^{-4}$ ([[thm-bracket-state-sum-matches-library-jones-specialization]]).

[F6] The crossing number is the least crossing count among regular diagrams of the same underlying unoriented link type ([[def-crossing-number-of-link]]).

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function principle for arbitrary families of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Counterexample
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The two states of a positive kink consist of an $A$-smoothing that leaves the original arc and creates one trivial circle, and a $B$-smoothing that leaves only the original arc. By [F1] their total bracket factor is $A\delta+A^{-1}=A(-A^2-A^{-2})+A^{-1}=-A^3$, so $\langle D_+\rangle=-A^3$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 The kink has one positive crossing, so [F2] gives $\operatorname{wr}(D_+)=1$. Its normalized bracket is $f_{D_+}(A)=(-A^3)^{-1}(-A^3)=1$. By [A1] and [F5], the library Jones polynomial is therefore $1$, whose $t$-span is $0$. The one-crossing projection is connected; its unique component visits the crossing once over and once under, so it is alternating; the kink region has the crossing twice on its boundary, so it is not reduced by [F3]. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F4], the type-I move carries $D_+$ to the crossing-free unknot diagram. Thus the represented link has a diagram with zero crossings. Since crossing counts are nonnegative by [F6], its crossing number is zero, strictly less than the one crossing in $D_+$. This verifies the claimed failure of crossing minimality at a non-reduced alternating diagram. [F4, F6, given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D_T$ be the standard closure of the two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$, let $D_8$ be the standard closure of the three-strand braid $\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}$, and let $D_U$ be the round unknot diagram with one Reidemeister-I kink. Here each $\sigma_i$ is the elementary geometric half twist of adjacent strands and closure joins the bottom endpoints to the corresponding top endpoint set. These are the standard trefoil, figure-eight, and kinked-unknot diagrams. Their Seifert-algorithm data and output-surface genera are

| Diagram | Seifert circles $s$ | Crossings $c$ | Output genus $g(F)$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Trefoil | 2 | 3 | 1 |
| Figure-eight | 3 | 4 | 1 |
| Kinked unknot | 2 | 1 | 0 |

Thus the corresponding knot genera are at most $1$, at most $1$, and exactly $0$, respectively. The first two rows compute particular spanning surfaces and do not assert that those surfaces have minimum genus.

The arrows orient the first diagram, and at each crossing the unbroken strand is the overpass.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.82, line cap=round, line join=round]
  % Close bottom endpoints to top endpoints on the same side.
  \draw[thick,->] (0.8,-1.5) .. controls (1.8,-1.5) and (1.8,1.5) .. (0.8,1.5);
  \draw[thick,->] (-0.8,-1.5) .. controls (-1.8,-1.5) and (-1.8,1.5) .. (-0.8,1.5);
  % The right-to-left strand is under at each of the three crossings.
  \draw[thick] (0.8,1.5)--(-0.8,0.5);
  \draw[thick,white,line width=4pt] (0.12,1.075)--(-0.12,0.925);
  \draw[thick] (-0.8,0.5)--(0.8,-0.5);
  \draw[thick,white,line width=4pt] (-0.12,0.075)--(0.12,-0.075);
  \draw[thick] (0.8,-0.5)--(-0.8,-1.5);
  \draw[thick,white,line width=4pt] (0.12,-0.925)--(-0.12,-1.075);
  % The left-to-right strand passes over at all three crossings.
  \draw[thick,->] (-0.8,1.5)--(0.8,0.5);
  \draw[thick,->] (0.8,0.5)--(-0.8,-0.5);
  \draw[thick,->] (-0.8,-0.5)--(0.8,-1.5);
  \node[below] at (0,-1.9) {three-crossing two-strand closure};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

The picture is a projection schematic: the white gaps mark the underpassing strand, and each closing arc joins a bottom endpoint to the top endpoint on the same side. The smoothing and surface claims below are proved from the finite strand and band data, not from the picture.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and the three finite oriented knot diagrams described above.

[F1] Each crossing is replaced by the unique orientation-compatible noncrossing smoothing, giving finitely many oriented Seifert circles. ([[def-seifert-smoothing-and-seifert-circles-of-an-oriented-link-diagram]])

[F2] The algorithm smooths every crossing once, records one disk per circle and one band per crossing. ([[alg-seifert-surface-from-diagram]])

[F3] For a one-component diagram, the realized surface is connected, oriented, embedded, and has one boundary component equal to the knot. ([[lem-seifert-bands-embedded-orientable-boundary-correct]])

[F4] A connected one-boundary disk-and-band surface with $s$ disks and $c$ bands has genus $(1-s+c)/2$, and its knot genus is at most that value. ([[thm-seifert-algorithm-boundary-euler-and-genus]])

[F5] Knot genus is the minimum genus of an admissible Seifert surface, so every such surface gives an upper bound. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]])

[F6] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a connected compact oriented surface with $b$ boundary circles satisfies $\chi=2-2g-b$. ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

[F7] The elementary half twist at adjacent positions has endpoint permutation the corresponding transposition, and its opposite is the inverse half twist. ([[def-elementary-geometric-half-twist]])

[F8] Endpoint permutations multiply under braid stacking, and the standard closure has one component for each cycle of that permutation. ([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]], [[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is the sequence principle stated in the item. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Verification

1.1 The word $\sigma_1^3$ has three crossings, and its endpoint permutation is $(12)^3=(12)$ by [F7] and [F8], so its closure is one knot component. Smoothing each braid crossing continues its oriented strand to the adjacent lower segment, leaving the identity two-strand closure with two cycles; hence $c=3$ and $s=2$. [given, F1, F2, F7, F8, algebra]

1.2 The word $\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}$ has four crossings. Since $\sigma_i$ and $\sigma_i^{-1}$ both induce the adjacent transposition, its endpoint permutation is $(12)(23)(12)(23)$, a $3$-cycle; [F8] therefore makes its closure one knot component. Smoothing each crossing straightens its adjacent oriented strands, leaving the identity three-strand closure with three cycles. Hence $(s,c)=(3,4)$. [given, F1, F2, F7, F8, algebra]

1.3 The kinked unknot diagram has one crossing; its oriented smoothing separates the small kink loop from the remaining circle, so $(s,c)=(2,1)$. In the zero-crossing boundary case, the round unknot has one smoothing circle and no bands, so $(s,c)=(1,0)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], all three outputs are connected oriented spanning surfaces. Applying [F4] gives $(1-2+3)/2=1$, $(1-3+4)/2=1$, and $(1-2+1)/2=0$. For the round unknot the disk surface has genus $0$, and all surface genera are nonnegative by [F6]; therefore its minimum is exactly $0$. For the trefoil and figure-eight, [F5] yields only the upper bound $g(K)\le1$, as claimed. [F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and assume $u^\dagger$ is an exact solution minimizing a proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, positively one-homogeneous TV functional $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with a source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Use full-space $R=TV_2(\cdot;\mathbb R^2)$ if $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$; for a bounded connected Lipschitz $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, use either Neumann $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ or Dirichlet $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ for the zero extension $\widetilde u$, assigning $+\infty$ outside the respective finite-variation domain. A bounded connected Lipschitz domain here is a bounded open set with a finite Lipschitz graph cover of its boundary, with the domain on one side of each graph, and it has no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets.

Let $\alpha_n>0$ tend to zero, let $w_n\in Y$, and suppose $\|A^*\|\,\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta$ for some finite $\eta$. For each $n$, suppose a supplied global minimizer $u_n\in X$ minimizes
$$J_n(u)=\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u).$$
In the Neumann case, if $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, take $u_n$ after subtracting its mean $|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$; this leaves $J_n$ unchanged. Then a subsequence converges weakly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and, in addition, strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$ when $\Omega$ is bounded or strongly in $L^1$ on every bounded ball when $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$. Its limit $u_0$ is an exact solution $Au_0=f$ minimizing $R$ among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|A TV source certificate is an adjoint image in the convex subdifferential at a minimum-TV exact solution.]]

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|Full-space TV on L² is the extended distributional test-field supremum.]]

[[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions|Dirichlet TV counts zero-extension boundary variation; Neumann TV counts only interior variation.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement, including supplied global minimizers of $J_n$.

[A1] Countable Choice supplies the countable diagonal selections in the compactness and weak-subsequence arguments. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate]]: $Au^\dagger=f$, $R(u^\dagger)$ is minimal over exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$; the Hilbert adjoint satisfies $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-tv-dual-attainment-and-certificate-limit]]: every supplied global minimizer has $p_{\alpha,w}=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$, the exact-data fields $p_{\alpha,0}$ remain bounded as $\alpha\to0$, and $\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\|w\|_Y/\alpha$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-bv-compactness-lower-semicontinuity]]: bounded-domain BV sequences with bounded $L^1$ norm and variation have an $L^1$-convergent subsequence, and TV is lower semicontinuous under $L^1$ convergence.

[F4] [[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality]]: in two dimensions, $\|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le TV(v;\mathbb R^2)$ for $v\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$.

[F5] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-sobolev-inequality]]: the same estimate holds for $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ with finite extended variation: $\|u\|_2\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F6] [[lem-ip-bv-zero-gradient-constant-on-connected-domain]]: a locally integrable function with zero distributional gradient on a connected open domain is a.e. constant.

[F7] [[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions]]: Neumann TV is unchanged by adding constants; Dirichlet TV is the full-space TV of the zero extension and dominates the interior variation.

[F8] [[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]]: spatial TV is lower semicontinuous in $L^1$ and finite whenever the extended test-field variation is finite under Countable Choice.

[F9] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-finite-variation-has-radon-derivative]]: finite $TV_2$ gives a finite vector Radon derivative measure, whose restriction to bounded balls has variation at most $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F10] [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]: bounded scalar real sequences have convergent subsequences.

[F11] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$.

[F12] [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]: bounded linear functionals on a real Hilbert space are inner products with vectors in that space.

[F13] [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]: two locally integrable functions that define the same distribution are equal almost everywhere.

[F14] [[lem-ip-neumann-bv-sobolev-poincare]]: on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain, $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ for a fixed finite $C_\Omega$.

## Proof

1.1 If $\|A^*\|=0$, the adjoint identity implies $A=0$ and $f=0$. Since $0$ is exact, minimality gives $R(u^\dagger)=0$. The data term of $J_n$ is then constant, so every global minimizer has $R(u_n)=0$. In the full-space case [F6] makes $u_n$ constant and $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ forces it to be zero; in the Dirichlet case apply [F6] to its zero extension, which vanishes outside bounded $\Omega$, and again obtain zero; in the Neumann case [F6] makes it constant and the prescribed zero-mean choice makes it zero. Thus $u_0=0$ is an exact minimum-TV solution. Since $R\ge0$ and $R(0)=0$, $0\in\partial R(0)=\partial R(u_0)$, so $A^*p^\dagger=0\in\partial R(u_0)$ and the assertion holds. For the remainder assume $\|A^*\|>0$. [F1, F6, F7, given, cases, algebra]

2.1 Put $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$. By [F2], $p_n=p_{\alpha_n,w_n}$ and $p_{\alpha_n,0}$ is bounded. The noise hypothesis gives $\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta/\|A^*\|$, hence [F2] makes $(p_n)$ bounded and $\|w_n\|_Y\to0$. The identity $Au_n=f+w_n-\alpha_np_n$ therefore gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly in $Y$. Comparing the objective at $u_n$ and $u^\dagger$ gives
$$\tfrac12\|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u_n)\le\tfrac12\|w_n\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u^\dagger),$$
so $R(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\|w_n\|_Y^2/(2\alpha_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\eta^2\alpha_n/(2\|A^*\|^2)$. In particular the variations are bounded and $\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

3.1 In the Neumann branch on bounded connected $\Omega$, write $m_n=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$ and $v_n=u_n-m_n$. The Poincaré inequality [F14] gives $\|v_n\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(v_n;\Omega)=C_\Omega R(u_n)$, which is uniformly bounded by step 2.1. [F7, F14, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 If $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, subtracting $m_n$ leaves both $Au_n$ and Neumann TV unchanged, so we use the zero-mean minimizer specified in the Statement, which is uniformly bounded in $L^2$ by step 3.1. If $A\mathbf1_\Omega\ne0$, then [F1] and step 2.1 give bounded $\|Au_n\|_Y$ and
$$|m_n|\,\|A\mathbf1_\Omega\|_Y=\|Au_n-Av_n\|_Y\le\|Au_n\|_Y+\|A\|\|v_n\|_2,$$
so the means, and therefore $\|u_n\|_2$, are bounded. In the full-space case [F5] gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. In the Dirichlet case [F4] applied to $\widetilde u_n$ gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. Thus in every branch the selected sequence is bounded in $L^2$. [F1, F4, F5, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.1 If $\Omega$ is bounded, the $L^2$ bound gives an $L^1$ bound by [F11]; the interior variation is bounded by $R(u_n)$ in both boundary conventions [F7]. [F3] therefore supplies a subsequence converging strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, restrict to each ball $B(0,m)$: the $L^1$ norms are bounded by $|B(0,m)|^{1/2}\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$, and [F9] bounds the variation there. Applying [F3] on each ball and taking a countable diagonal subsequence using [A1] gives convergence in $L^1$ on every bounded ball. [A1, F3, F7, F9, F11, step 3.2, construct]

4.2 The resulting sequence is still bounded in the Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega)$. Its closed linear span is separable, since rational finite linear combinations of its terms are dense. Gram–Schmidt gives a finite or countable orthonormal family with dense span. Each coordinate sequence is bounded by [F11]; repeated use of [F10] and [A1] yields a subsubsequence on which every coordinate converges. Pythagoras applied to each finite orthogonal projection bounds the sums of squared limiting coordinates by the common squared norm bound, so these coordinates define a vector $u_0$ in the closed span. Approximation by finite linear combinations proves convergence of inner products against every vector in the span. For any $z\in L^2(\Omega)$, [F12] represents $x\mapsto\langle x,z\rangle$ restricted to that span by a vector in the span, so the convergence is weak in all of $L^2$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions shows that this weak limit and the strong $L^1$ or local-$L^1$ limit from step 4.1 define the same distribution; injectivity [F13] makes them equal almost everywhere. [A1, F10, F11, F12, F13, step 4.1, construct]

5.1 Weak convergence and boundedness of $A$ imply $Au_n\rightharpoonup Au_0$, while step 2.1 gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly; hence $Au_0=f$. In the full-space case, for every admissible test field $\varphi$, local $L^1$ convergence gives $\int u_0\operatorname{div}\varphi=\lim_n\int u_n\operatorname{div}\varphi\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$; taking the supremum gives $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$. In the Neumann case the same lower semicontinuity follows from [F8] and strong $L^1(\Omega)$ convergence. In the Dirichlet case the zero extensions converge strongly in $L^1(\mathbb R^2)$, so [F8] gives the same inequality for their full-space TV. Thus $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)\le\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$. Exactness and the minimum property of $u^\dagger$ force equality, so $u_0$ is a minimum-TV exact solution. [F1, F8, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Let $\xi=A^*p^\dagger$. Since $Au_0=Au^\dagger=f$, the adjoint identity in [F1] gives $\langle\xi,u_0-u^\dagger\rangle_X=\langle p^\dagger,A(u_0-u^\dagger)\rangle_Y=0$. For every $v\in X$, the subgradient inequality at $u^\dagger$ therefore gives
$$R(v)\ge R(u^\dagger)+\langle\xi,v-u^\dagger\rangle_X=R(u_0)+\langle\xi,v-u_0\rangle_X.$$

## Statement

Let $H$ be a handlebody with a fixed finite trivalent spine $G$, and let every edge carry one of the labels $0,\ldots,r-2$. Call a labeling admissible when the three labels at each trivalent vertex satisfy the root fusion rule. In the radical-quotient state space of $H$, the states represented by admissible labeled spines span, and the set of such labelings is finite. This statement asserts spanning, not linear independence.

## Statement references

[[def-skein-tqft-state-space-and-handlebody-pairing|Handlebody state space]]

[[lem-root-fusion-rules-and-simple-object-completeness|Root fusion rule]]

[Blanchet, Habegger, Masbaum, and Vogel, *Topological Quantum Field Theories Derived from the Kauffman Bracket*, §§4–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/bhmv.pdf)

[Kauffman and Lins, *Temperley-Lieb Recoupling Theory and Invariants of 3-Manifolds*, Chapters 4–7](https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781400882533_A27764847/preview-9781400882533_A27764847.pdf)

[Chen, *The Temperley-Lieb Categories and Skein Modules*, Chapter 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.06845v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite handlebody spine and the root state-space construction.

[F1] [[def-skein-tqft-state-space-and-handlebody-pairing]] defines the state space as a radical quotient of a specialized handlebody skein module.

[F2] [[lem-root-fusion-rules-and-simple-object-completeness]] proves that the finite label set is $\{0,\ldots,r-2\}$ and gives the exact local fusion rule; it does not itself prove that arbitrary handlebody skeins are spanned by spine states.

[F3] **External input — actual handlebody quotient and spine basis.** BHMV, Proposition1.9 p.891 and Theorem4.11 p.909, identify the radical-quotient handlebody model with the universal state space and give an orthogonal basis represented by the $p$-admissibly colored fixed banded spine. For even $p=2r$, the source's $q=(p-2)/2=r-1$ and colors $<q$ are exactly $0,\ldots,r-2$; $p$-admissibility is the registered truncated fusion rule. Coefficients are specialized through the given complex primitive root, with no vanishing quantum denominator inverted. This imports the actual spanning theorem, rather than inferring it from abstract semisimplicity alone.

## Proof

**Given:** The fixed finite spine $G$ and the finite label set $\{0,\ldots,r-2\}$.

1.1 The edge set of $G$ is finite and each edge has only $r-1$ candidate labels by [F2]. Therefore the set of all labelings, and hence its subset of admissible labelings, is finite. [given, F2, construct]

2.1 Apply [F3] to the supplied handlebody marking and spine, using [F1] for the identical radical-quotient model and [F2] for its root labels. Every vector is a linear combination of the admissible spine states. Together with the finite count in step1.1 this proves the full Statement. Linear independence, although present in the imported theorem, is not needed for this spanning conclusion. No infinite skein reduction or additional choice campaign is performed. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

**Inputs.** An integer $n\ge2$; a finite Artin word $\beta\in B_n$ in the positive-half-twist convention where $\sigma_i$ sends the $i$th meridian $x_i$ to $x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1}$ and $x_{i+1}$ to $x_i$; a surjective color map $c$ from the cycles of the endpoint permutation to $\{1,\ldots,\mu\}$, written on strands as $c_1,\ldots,c_n$ and constant around each cycle; a field $\mathbb F$ with encoded exact arithmetic and equality; a positive integer $d$ and invertible matrices $\rho(x_i)\in\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbb F)$; and compatible finite certificates of based deficiency-one $2$-spines for the closure exterior $X$ and the closure-with-axis exterior $Y$. The $X$ spine has generators $g_i=x_1\cdots x_i$ and relators $r_i=g_i^{-1}\beta_*(g_i)$ for $1\le i<n$. The $Y$ spine has generators $g_1,\ldots,g_n,x$ and relators $s_i=\beta_*(g_i)(x^{-1}g_ix)^{-1}$ for $1\le i\le n$; $x$ is the meridian of the axis. The certificates include a based cell structure on $T$ with one vertex, $1$-cells $x,g_n$, and the commutator $2$-cell; the one-vertex, one-core-edge structure on $V=D^2\times S^1$; and compatible cell bases for $X=Y\cup_TV$. These spine and gluing certificates are geometric input and are not recognized by the procedure. Put $H=\langle t_1,\ldots,t_\mu\rangle\cong\mathbb Z^\mu$, $\psi(x_i)=t_{c_i}$, $g_n=x_1\cdots x_n$, $\Lambda=\mathbb F[H]$, and $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$.

**Instructions.**

1. Read the supplied $X$ and $Y$ spine/presentation correspondences and compatible gluing as certified geometric input; check their finite cell counts and relator lists, but do not attempt to recognize whether the data describe exterior spines. Return `not-applicable` if either certificate is absent. Compute the induced free-group automorphism $\beta_*$ by substituting the displayed Artin rules in the declared word order. Return `not-applicable` if the coloring is not preserved on endpoints, if the representation fails any closure relator, or if, after setting the axis meridian to the identity, it fails any mapping-torus relator $s_i=\beta_*(g_i)(x^{-1}g_ix)^{-1}$. Equivalently the braid invariance checks $\rho(\beta_*(x_i))=\rho(x_i)$ must hold for all meridians.

2. Set $\psi(x)=1$ on the axis meridian. Verify the deck map on the relators $r_i$ and the axis relators $s_i$, and verify the colors are surjective, so $\psi$ descends to both spine groups and is an epimorphism. Compute the positive-meridian full abelianization basis first, then use the explicit color map $H_L\to H$; no unannounced equal-variable or total-linking specialization is performed.

3. Rewrite $\beta_*(g_i)$ in the free basis $g_1,\ldots,g_n$, using $x_i=g_{i-1}^{-1}g_i$ and $g_0=1$. Compute the block Fox matrix $B_\beta$ with $(i,j)$ block $\Phi(\partial\beta_*(g_i)/\partial g_j)$, using the product and inverse recursions of the Wada definition and $\Phi(g)=\rho(g)\psi(g)$. The braid fixes the boundary word $g_n$, so its last block row is $(0,\ldots,0,I_d)$. Let $\overline B_\rho(\beta)$ be the upper-left $(n-1)d$-square block.

4. Compute $D=\det(\rho(g_n)\psi(g_n)-I_d)$. If $D=0$, return `not-applicable`: this designated deleted column is inadmissible, even if another column of the Fox matrix could be used.

5. Form the twisted cellular boundary matrices $d_1,d_2$ of the supplied spine from the Fox lemma. Use exact Gaussian elimination over $Q$ to check the chain identity $d_1\circ d_2=0$ (the row-matrix product $J A_{\rm stack}=0$). If this identity fails, return `not-applicable` because the encoded data do not define a chain complex. If it holds but the ranks are not $\operatorname{rank}(d_1)=d$ and $\operatorname{rank}(d_2)=(n-1)d$, return $0$ under the declared torsion convention. Otherwise compute $N=\det(\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I_{(n-1)d})$ and return the rational function $N/D$ as the twisted Burau determinant value, modulo the determinant/deck units of the based torsion convention.

The braid convention is shown for two adjacent downward-oriented strands. The left strand crosses over the right strand for $\sigma_i$; the gap records the underpass. The word, color map, and algebraic action above, rather than the diagram, determine the computation.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1.2cm,y=1.0cm,>=stealth,line width=1pt]

  \node at (1,2.2) {$x_{i+1}$};
  \draw (0,2) -- (1,0);

\end{tikzpicture}
```

The displayed generator interchanges endpoint positions, with the original left strand passing over; the colors must follow the same permutation along each link component.

## Definition

Assume full AC for the library Jones invariant. An oriented link is a finite
disjoint union of oriented smooth circles embedded in $S^3$, considered up to
ambient isotopy; an oriented classical knot is the one-component case. For an
oriented link $L\subset S^3$, let $V_L(x)\in\mathbb Z[x^{\pm1}]$ be the
library-normalized Jones polynomial, with $V_U(x)=1$ for the unknot $U$;
write $V_K$ for its value on a knot $K$. Here $x=t^{1/2}$ in the library
convention $t=A^{-4}$, so an oriented skein triple satisfies
$$x^{-2}V_{L_+}(x)-x^2V_{L_-}(x)=(x-x^{-1})V_{L_0}(x).$$
Set $p=x-x^{-1}$. By the unique Laurent decomposition, write
$$V_K(x)=\sum_{q\ge0}(a_q(K)+b_q(K)x)p^q,$$
where $a_q(K),b_q(K)\in\mathbb Z$ and only finitely many are nonzero. The
**Jones–Vassiliev coefficient vector of order $q$** is
$$f_q(K):=(a_q(K),b_q(K))^{\mathsf T},$$
and $c_q(K):=a_q(K)+b_q(K)$. This is the algebraic coefficient-vector
definition used by Carmi and Cohen. The claim that the coordinates of $f_q$
are finite-type invariants of order at most $q$ is a separate theorem and is
not part of this definition.

## Example

Let $n\ge1$, $\sigma,\tau>0$, and $0<\gamma<1$. Given a scalar truth $\theta\in\mathbb R$, observe independent $Y_i\sim N(\theta,\sigma^2)$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, and use the proper prior $\theta\sim N(0,\tau^2)$. Write $\bar Y=n^{-1}\sum_iY_i$, $v_n=(\tau^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1}$, $a_n=v_n n\sigma^{-2}$, and $z_\gamma=\Phi^{-1}(1-\gamma/2)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The exact posterior is $N(a_n\bar Y,v_n)$ and its central $(1-\gamma)$ credible interval is $C_n(\bar Y)=[a_n\bar Y-z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n},a_n\bar Y+z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n}]$. Its frequentist coverage at truth $\theta$ is
$$P_\theta\{\theta\in C_n(\bar Y)\}=\Phi\!\left(\frac{z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n}+(1-a_n)\theta}{a_n\sigma/\sqrt n}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{-z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n}+(1-a_n)\theta}{a_n\sigma/\sqrt n}\right).$$

## Example references

[[op-ip-calibration-under-score-and-solver-error|The calibration frontier whose exact-computation baseline is isolated here.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The normal observation model, the proper $N(0,\tau^2)$ prior, the posterior credible interval, $n\ge1$, $\sigma,\tau>0$, and $0<\gamma<1$ from the Example.

[A1] The likelihood is proportional to $\exp(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\theta)^2)$ and the prior density is proportional to $\exp(-\theta^2/(2\tau^2))$.

[A2] $\Phi(t)=P(Z\le t)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and $z_\gamma$ is its $(1-\gamma/2)$ quantile.

## Verification

1.1 Multiplying the likelihood by the prior and completing the square in $\theta$ gives posterior precision $\tau^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2}$ and posterior mean $(\tau^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1}n\sigma^{-2}\bar Y=a_n\bar Y$. Thus the posterior variance is $v_n$ and the stated interval has posterior mass $1-\gamma$. [given, A1, A2, algebra]

2.1 Under the fixed truth $\theta$, $a_n\bar Y-\theta$ is normal with mean $-(1-a_n)\theta$ and standard deviation $a_n\sigma/\sqrt n$. The event $\theta\in C_n(\bar Y)$ is exactly $-z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n}\le a_n\bar Y-\theta\le z_\gamma\sqrt{v_n}$; standardizing the two endpoints gives the displayed difference of normal cumulative probabilities. [given, A1, A2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ and every $\theta\in S^1$, the defining line integral for $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)$ converges absolutely for every $s\in\mathbb R$, and $s\mapsto R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)$ belongs to $\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$. For each pair of nonnegative integers $k,N$, its $k$th derivative is bounded by $C_{k,N}(1+|s|)^{-N}$ with a finite constant $C_{k,N}$ independent of $s$ and $\theta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ and $\theta\in S^1$.

[F1] [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]: every seminorm $p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$ is finite.

[F2] [[def-ip-schwartz-radon-transform]]: $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$.

[F3] [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]: if each parameter slice is integrable, the integrand is differentiable in the parameter almost everywhere, its derivative is measurable, and the derivatives have one integrable majorant uniform in the parameter interval, then the integral is differentiable with derivative equal to the integral of the derivative.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition of totally differentiable Euclidean maps is the composition of their derivatives.

[F5] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: for a real differentiable function on an interval, its increment equals an interior derivative times the interval length; apply to real and imaginary parts for complex functions.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a derivative multi-index $\beta$ and an integer $N\ge1$, and choose an integer $m\ge N$. Since $(1+|x|)^N\le(1+|x_1|)^m(1+|x_2|)^m$, expanding the right side and using the finite Schwartz seminorms in [F1] gives a finite $C_{\beta,N}(f)$ with $|\partial^\beta f(x)|\le C_{\beta,N}(f)(1+|x|)^{-N}$. For $x=s\theta+t\theta^\perp$, orthogonality gives $|x|=(s^2+t^2)^{1/2}\ge(|s|+|t|)/\sqrt2$, so the line integrand is bounded by a constant times $(1+|s|+|t|)^{-N}$. Taking $N>1$ makes this majorant integrable in $t$, proving absolute convergence. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $D_\theta=\theta\cdot\nabla$. The chain rule [F4] gives $\partial_s^k f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)=(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)$. Expanding $D_\theta^k$ gives finitely many partial derivatives with coefficients bounded uniformly for $\theta\in S^1$. For the target decay order $N$, apply step 1.1 with spatial decay order $N+2$ to each such derivative. Integrating $(1+|s|+|t|)^{-N-2}$ in $t$ gives $\left|\int_{\mathbb R}(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt\right|\le C'_{k,N}(1+|s|)^{-N-1}\le C'_{k,N}(1+|s|)^{-N}$, uniformly in $\theta$ and $s$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and a bounded open interval $I$ containing $s_0$. For each $k\ge0$, set $g_k(t,s)=(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)$. Every slice $g_k(\cdot,s)$ is integrable by step 1.1; it is differentiable in $s$ with derivative $g_{k+1}$ by [F4], and this derivative is measurable. Step 1.1 with spatial decay order $3$ bounds $|g_{k+1}(t,s)|\le C(1+|t|)^{-3}$ uniformly for $s\in I$, an integrable majorant. Thus [F3] proves $\frac{d}{ds}\int g_k(t,s)\,dt=\int g_{k+1}(t,s)\,dt$. To see each resulting derivative is continuous, if $s=s'$ the difference is zero; otherwise apply [F5] to real and imaginary parts on the segment joining $s$ and $s'$. The same majorant gives $|g_k(t,s)-g_k(t,s')|\le C|s-s'|(1+|t|)^{-3}$, and integration proves local continuity. Repeating for all $k$ and using the estimates in step 2.1 shows the offset function is Schwartz. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
