## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $D\subset B^4$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk with oriented boundary $K$. Then the positive-push Seifert lattice $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is metabolic: it has a rank-$g$ primitive direct summand on which $V$ vanishes identically.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert pairing on integral first homology]]

[[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance|The rank-half primitive direct-summand definition of a metabolizer]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a Seifert surface $F$ of genus $g$, and a locally flat slice disk $D$ with the same oriented boundary knot.

[A1] Full AC is the family-of-nonempty-sets choice axiom used by the Seifert-pairing convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, the matrix entries are $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, and $V$ is bilinear on homology. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]], [[lem-seifert-pairing-well-defined]]

[F2] Poincaré–Lefschetz duality for a compact oriented $3$-manifold $R$ with boundary $\Sigma$ identifies $H_i(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ with $H^{3-i}(R;\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality]]

[F3] The linking number of disjoint rational boundary cycles in $S^3=\partial B^4$ is the signed intersection number of collared rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ that bound them. [[lem-linking-number-equals-four-dimensional-intersection-number]]

[F4] A $g$-dimensional rational subspace on which $V$ vanishes saturates to a rank-$g$ direct summand of the integral lattice, still with vanishing restriction. [[lem-rational-isotropic-subspace-saturates-to-integral-metabolizer]]

[F5] For the given locally flat slice disk the hypersurface supplier constructs the compact oriented locally flat Seifert three-manifold with an actual two-sided product and positive-push alignment. Its pre-collar-push model meets the outer sphere in $F$, with the stated product corners at $K$. Its smooth branch remains the previously supplied smooth construction; its TOP branch explicitly imports separate relative normal-bundle and microbundle-transversality theorems. [[lem-locally-flat-slice-surface-bounds-seifert-hypersurface]]

[F6] Smooth chains compute continuous real homology, including for a smooth manifold with boundary. This is invoked below only in smooth ambient neighborhoods, not by treating a locally flat $R$ as an already smooth submanifold. [[thm-smooth-singular-chains-compute-singular-homology]]

[F7] Under full AC a compact TOP three-manifold has a finite compatible PL triangulation, with boundary a subcomplex. In particular its Betti numbers and Euler characteristic are finite. This is intrinsic to the three-manifold and does not smooth its embedding in the four-ball. [[thm-compact-topological-three-manifolds-admit-finite-pl-triangulations]]

[F8] The positive-push pairing on $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has skew part equal to the algebraic intersection form on $F$, which is unimodular. Hence $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is an integral Seifert lattice in the sense of the metabolic-form definition. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F9] A connected compact oriented surface of genus $g$ with one boundary component has $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ free of rank $2g$, and capping that boundary gives a closed genus-$g$ surface of Euler characteristic $2-2g$. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F10] The homology sequence of a pair is exact, including $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_0(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_0(R;\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]]

[F11] The compact TOP manifold $R$ has a collar of $\Sigma$; open thickenings of the two copies in its double retract to the copies of $R$, and their overlap retracts to $\Sigma$. Mayer–Vietoris with constant rational coefficients therefore gives $\chi(\widehat R)=2\chi(R)-\chi(\Sigma)$; the Betti ranks are finite by [F7]. [[thm-topological-collaring-for-manifold-boundaries]], [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[F13] For the finite CW models supplied by [F7], the alternating rank-nullity identity on the rational cellular chain complex gives $\chi(X)=\sum_i(-1)^i\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_i(X;\mathbb Q)$. This is the Euler–Poincaré calculation for a finite complex. [[thm-euler-poincare-formula-for-finite-cw-complexes]]

[F12] The closed oriented double $\widehat R$ is a compact TOP three-manifold with finite Betti ranks by [F7]. Poincaré duality over $\mathbb Q$ pairs its Betti numbers in complementary degrees, so [F13] gives $\chi(\widehat R)=0$. [[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]]

[F14] Over $\mathbb Q$, the universal coefficient theorem identifies $H^i(R;\mathbb Q)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H_i(R;\mathbb Q),\mathbb Q)$ because the $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Q}$ term vanishes. By [F7], these homology groups are finite-dimensional, so $\dim H^i(R;\mathbb Q)=b_i(R)$. [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]

## Proof

1.1 First assume the given disk is smooth. Construct $R$ by [F5], and write $\Sigma=\partial R=F\cup D$ after matching collars. The Axiom of Choice [A1] is the hypothesis under which the supplied Seifert-pairing and duality interfaces are invoked. Capping the sole boundary circle of $F$ by a disk does not change $H_1$ because that circle is already the boundary of the oriented fundamental $2$-chain of $F$; by [F9] and exactness [F10], $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $2g$. In the pair sequence [F10], $H_0(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_0(R;\mathbb Q)$ is an isomorphism because both are connected. Exactness therefore makes $H_1(R;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ surjective. By [F2] and [F14], the target has dimension $b_2(R)$, so the image of $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $b_1(R)-b_2(R)$. [A1, F2, F5, F9, F10, F14, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Let $\widehat R$ be the double of $R$ along $\Sigma$, with the second copy oppositely oriented so the orientations glue. Its two copies have open collar thickenings with intersection retracting to $\Sigma$, so [F11] gives $\chi(\widehat R)=2\chi(R)-\chi(\Sigma)$. By [F12] and [F13], $\chi(\widehat R)=0$, and by [F9], $\chi(\Sigma)=2-2g$; hence $\chi(R)=1-g$. Also [F2] gives $H_3(R;\mathbb Q)\cong H^0(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)=0$: a relative zero-cocycle is locally constant on the connected $R$ and vanishes on the nonempty connected $\Sigma$, so it is zero. With $b_0(R)=1$, the rational Euler-characteristic identity [F13] implies $b_1(R)-b_2(R)=g$. Thus the kernel $L=\ker(H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q))$, identified with a subspace of $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, has dimension $2g-g=g$. [F2, F9, F11, F12, F13, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Let $x,y\in L$, represented by finite rational smooth cycles on $F$ away from $K$. Their rational bounding chains in $R$ can be taken smooth. Indeed [F6] first supplies finite smooth real bounding chains; their boundary equations are one finite rational linear system on the real coefficients of finitely many smooth simplices, so rational Gaussian elimination supplies rational coefficients solving the same equations. Use the pre-collar-push model in [F5] to place the boundary cycles back on the actual $F\subset S^3$. A finite intrinsic collar push moves the interiors of their bounding chains off the boundary of $R$, fixing the prescribed boundary collars, so the chains miss the product corner $K$. The model is smooth on a neighborhood of these compact supports. Its positive normal field is tangent to $S^3$ along $F$ and points in the positive Seifert direction; extend it by finitely many bumps to an ambient field tangent to $S^3$ there. Its small-time flow pushes the first bounding chain $X$ off $R$, with boundary exactly $x^+$ in $S^3$, while the second chain $Y$ stays in $R$ with boundary $y$. Compactness and the product neighborhood keep the two supports disjoint. Their common standard end collars and empty intersection make them admissible for [F3], so $\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)=X^+\mathbin\cdot Y=0$. By [F1] this is $V_{\mathbb Q}(x,y)$. Hence $L$ is a rational Seifert-isotropic subspace. [F1, F3, F5, F6, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.2 By [F4], $M=H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand and $V|_{M\times M}=0$. By [F8], $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is an integral Seifert lattice; the metabolic-form definition therefore makes $M$ a metabolizer. This proves the entire metabolic conclusion whenever the supplied slice disk is smooth. [F4, F8, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 For the arbitrary locally flat disk use the TOP $R$ and its actual product from [F5]. The duality and pair-sequence computation of steps 1.1–1.2 applies to this compact oriented TOP three-manifold: [F7] supplies finite homology and [F13] gives its Euler-characteristic formula, [F2] applies in the TOP category, and [F11]–[F12] give the double's Euler characteristic. By [F9], $\chi(\Sigma)=2-2g$ and $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $2g$. Thus, without putting a smooth structure on the embedding, the rational kernel $L=\ker(H_1(F;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q))$ has dimension $g$. [A1, F2, F5, F7, F9, F11, F12, F13, F14, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.2 Represent $x,y\in L$ by finite rational smooth cycles in the given $F$, away from $K$, and choose finite rational CONTINUOUS bounding chains in $R$. Use its pre-collar-push model and the actual positive normal product of [F5]. Push the first chain into the positive complementary side, with boundary the actual positive Seifert push $x^+$; leave the second chain in $R$ with boundary $y$. An intrinsic boundary-collar push of their interiors and the common product near $F$ give the usual collared bounding chains in $B^4$, missing the corner $K$. Their supports are disjoint compact sets by the actual two-sided product. Choose disjoint relatively open smooth ambient neighborhoods $U,V\subset B^4$ of those supports, including their boundary cycles; these are smooth manifolds with boundary as open subsets of the standard smooth ball. In $U$, [F6] makes the smooth cycle $x^+$ bound a finite smooth real chain, since it bounds continuously there; likewise $y$ bounds in $V$. In each finite set of occurring simplices the equations for the boundary coefficients are rational, so rational Gaussian elimination replaces the real coefficients by rational ones without enlarging support. Near $S^3$, move the interiors inward and attach the standard product of the fixed boundary cycle with the collar interval. This puts both chains in common standard end collars, still in disjoint $U,V$. They therefore have empty interior intersection, and [F3] gives $V_{\mathbb Q}(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)=0$. The smoothing here concerns only chains in the disjoint SMOOTH ambient regions; it assumes no smooth structure on $R$ or its TOP normal chart. [F1, F3, F5, F6, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

3.3 Apply the unchanged integral-saturation result [F4] to this $g$-dimensional rational isotropic subspace: $M=H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\cap L$ is a primitive rank-$g$ direct summand with $V|_{M\times M}=0$. By [F8] the pairing is on an integral Seifert lattice, so the metabolic-form definition makes $M$ a metabolizer. This proves the full locally flat Statement, with the external geometric inputs explicitly located in [F5]'s hypersurface supplier and the resolved smooth/rank/saturation arguments retained. [F4, F8, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude. Call $K$ smoothly slice when it bounds a smooth
properly embedded disk in the standard $B^4$, with a product collar at its
boundary. Then $K$ is smoothly slice if and only if the compact smooth
$4$-manifold $X_0(K)$, formed using that preferred-longitude framing, admits a
smooth codimension-zero embedding into the standard $S^4$.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Lemma 1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with its fixed tubular
neighborhood and preferred longitude; the standard decomposition
$S^4=B_1\cup_{S^3}B_2$ into two $4$-balls; and the zero-trace convention.
The tube and peripheral curve are fixed data throughout; no choice principle
is used to select a family of them.

[F1] [[def-smooth-zero-trace]]: $X_0(K)$ is $B^4$ with a $2$-handle attached
using the framing whose pushoff represents the preferred zero-linking
longitude.

[F2] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: the preferred longitude is
the degree-one peripheral class whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero.

[F3] [[lem-slice-disk-complement-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]: for a proper
slice disk $D$, the boundary exterior $E_K$ includes into the disk exterior $X$
with $H_1(E_K)\to H_1(X)$ an isomorphism carrying meridian to meridian.

[F4] [[def-smooth-immersion-and-embedding-for-manifolds-with-boundary]]: a
smooth embedding is a smooth immersion and homeomorphism onto its image; here
both source and target have dimension four.

[F5] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]: a $C^1$ map between open
subsets of $\mathbb R^4$ with invertible derivative at a point is a local
diffeomorphism there.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $D\subset B_1$ is a smooth proper slice disk for $K$. Its oriented
normal $2$-plane bundle is trivial because $D$ is a disk. Choose a nowhere-zero
normal section and push $D$ slightly along it to a parallel disk $D'$ in the
exterior $X$ of a tubular neighborhood of $D$. The boundary $K'$ is a
degree-one parallel of $K$ in $E_K$, and it bounds $D'$ in $X$. By [F3], its
class in $H_1(E_K)$ is zero. By [F2], it is the preferred longitude. [F2, F3,
given, construct]

1.2 A tubular neighborhood of $D$ is $D^2\times D^2$ and meets the other
hemisphere $B_2$ in the attaching region $S^1\times D^2$. Consequently
$B_2\cup\nu(D)$ is obtained from a $4$-ball by attaching one $0$-framed
$2$-handle along $K$, hence is diffeomorphic to $X_0(K)$ by [F1]. This union
is a smooth codimension-zero submanifold of $S^4$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.1 Conversely, suppose $i:X_0(K)\hookrightarrow S^4$ is a smooth
codimension-zero embedding. In the $0$-handle of $X_0(K)$ take the cone on $K$
from an interior point $p$, and join that cone disk to the core disk
$D^2\times\{0\}$ of the $2$-handle along their common boundary $K$. After
smoothing the join, this is a piecewise-smooth embedded $2$-sphere, smooth
away from the cone point $p$. [F1, given, construct]

2.2 In oriented coordinates at $p$ and $i(p)$, the derivative of $i$ is
invertible by [F4], because its differential is injective and both dimensions
are four. By [F5], $i$ is a local diffeomorphism near $p$. If its local
orientation sign is negative, compose it with a fixed orientation-reversing
reflection of the standard $S^4$; this preserves the existence of the
embedding and makes the local sign positive. Thus its derivative $A$ lies in
$\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$. [F4, F5, given, construct]

2.3 Identify the cone near $p$ with the radial cone on $K\subset S^3$. Along
each direction $u\in K$, the derivative at the cone point of the target
distance is $\lVert Au\rVert>0$. Compactness of $K$ makes this derivative
uniformly positive, so [F5] gives a smooth radial intersection parameter for
all sufficiently small target spheres. Taylor expansion in $C^1$ along $K$,
followed by radial normalization, makes the resulting link
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ $C^1$-close to $\phi_A(K)$, where
$\phi_A(u)=Au/\lVert Au\rVert$. The polar decomposition $A=QP$ joins $A$ to
the identity through $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$: join the positive-definite
$P$ to $I$ linearly and join $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(4)$ to $I$ by a path in the
connected group $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Hence $\phi_A(K)$ is isotopic to $K$. The
chosen normal-disk tube of $K$, transported by $\phi_A$, is a tube of
$\phi_A(K)$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the tubular projection
restricts to a local diffeomorphism from $\Gamma_\epsilon$ to $\phi_A(K)$.
It is homotopic to the identity because the curves are $C^1$-close, so it has
degree one; a local diffeomorphism of circles with degree one is a
diffeomorphism. Thus $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is the graph of a small normal section. Scaling that
section to zero gives a smooth knot isotopy to $\phi_A(K)$, so
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ is isotopic to $K$. [F2, F5, step 2.2, algebra, construct]

2.4 Choose the coordinate ball bounded by that small sphere. Its complement
$W=S^4\setminus\operatorname{int}(B_\epsilon)$ is a standard $4$-ball. The
image sphere is smooth away from the cone point; transversality makes its
remainder after deleting the cone cap a smooth properly embedded disk in $W$
with product boundary collar and boundary $\Gamma_\epsilon$. Append the trace
annulus of the isotopy in step 2.3 inside a boundary collar of $W$, with the
isotopy stationary near its ends. The result is a smooth slice disk with
boundary exactly $K$. [step 2.1, step 2.3, construct]

3.1 Steps 1.1–1.2 construct an embedding from a slice disk, and steps
2.1–2.4 construct a slice disk from an embedding. These are the two
implications in the statement. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, given] ∎

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9]
  \draw[thick] (0,0) circle (1.15);
  \node at (0,1.42) {$K\subset\partial B^4$};
  \draw[thick] (-0.72,0.05) .. controls (-0.55,0.62) and (0.55,0.62) .. (0.72,0.05);
  \draw[thick] (-0.72,0.05) .. controls (-0.55,-0.52) and (0.55,-0.52) .. (0.72,0.05);
  \fill (0,0.04) circle (1.5pt);
  \node[below] at (0,-0.05) {$p$};
  \node at (2.15,0.38) {$\text{cone disk}$};
  \draw[->] (1.8,0.32) -- (0.66,0.22);
  \node at (2.15,-0.15) {$\text{2-handle core}$};
  \draw[->] (1.8,-0.15) -- (0.65,-0.18);
  \draw[dashed] (0,0.04) circle (0.34);

~~~

The sketch records the cone-on-$K$ disk and the $2$-handle core that form the
piecewise-smooth sphere. The dashed circle marks the cap removed near the cone
point. The proof uses the local coordinate-ball argument above, not the sketch.

## Example

Let $\Lambda_2=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},t_2^{\pm1}]$, $\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and let $\eta:\Lambda_2\to\Lambda_1$ send $t_1,t_2$ to $t$. Choose standard pairwise-disjoint radius-$\epsilon$ tubes with $0<\epsilon<1/\sqrt2$. Let $H$ be the standard Hopf link $\{z=0\}\cup\{w=0\}$ in $S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, orienting its components so the increasing phase meridians are positive, and let $U$ be the standard two-component unlink whose components lie in separate $3$-balls. Choose a common basepoint for the two based positive-meridian loops in the unlink exterior and use it for the unlink cover. For $H$, the complement is $T^2\times(0,1)$ and the compact exterior is $T^2\times I$; its maximal abelian cover is $\mathbb R^2\times I$, so its absolute multivariable Alexander module is $A_H=0$. Its total-linking cyclic cover is $S^1\times\mathbb R\times I$, with trivial $t$-action on first homology, so the one-variable Alexander module is $\Lambda_1/(t-1)$, whereas $A_H\otimes_{\Lambda_2,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$. For $U$, the compact exterior has free fundamental group on its two positive meridians. The meridian map from $S^1\vee S^1$ induces an isomorphism on first homology of the corresponding maximal abelian covers, whose graph-cover chain complex is $\Lambda_2^2\xrightarrow{(t_1-1,\ t_2-1)}\Lambda_2$; its first homology is free of rank one, so $A_U\cong\Lambda_2$. The total-linking cyclic graph-cover complex computing its first homology is $\Lambda_1^2\xrightarrow{(t-1,\ t-1)}\Lambda_1$, with first homology $\Lambda_1$. These computations distinguish chain specialization from tensoring the multivariable homology module.

The projection below is schematic: the upper crossing has the first component $K_1$ (blue) over, and the lower crossing has the second component $K_2$ (red) over. The calculations use the stated coordinate and meridian graph-cover homology models, not the drawing.

## Example references

[[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the standard Hopf link $H$ and two-component unlink $U$ specified in the Example; and the maximal-abelian and total-linking covers of their compact exteriors.

[A1] AC is the assumption of the maximal-abelian-cover definition ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The multivariable module is absolute first homology of the maximal abelian cover, with the positive-meridian deck action ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] The one-variable module is first homology of the cover classified by total linking, whose defining homomorphism sums the Alexander-dual meridian coordinates ([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]).

[F3] Connected covers are classified by the subgroups they induce ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]).

[F4] Cellular homology agrees naturally with singular homology for CW complexes ([[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]]).

[F5] $\Lambda_2$ is a domain and UFD, with signed monomials as its units ([[lem-multivariable-laurent-ring-noetherian-ufd]], [[prop-retracts-inject-fundamental-groups]]).

[F6] Diagonal coefficient extension of the maximal-abelian-cover chain complex is the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex ([[lem-multivariable-alexander-order-and-specialization]]).

[F7] The compact-exterior maximal abelian cover and the open-complement maximal abelian cover are deck-equivariantly homotopy equivalent and have the same module ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]).

[F8] Homotopies into a covering base lift uniquely after an initial lift is specified ([[thm-homotopy-lifting-for-covering-maps]]).

[F9] A deformation retract induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups at every basepoint in the retract ([[prop-retracts-inject-fundamental-groups]]).

[F10] Seifert--van Kampen applies to the collar-thickened split-sphere union; its overlap is simply connected. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]], [[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]]

[F11] The degree-one Hurewicz map naturally identifies first homology with the abelianization of fundamental group. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Verification

1.1 Every point of $S^3\setminus H$ has $z\ne0$ and $w\ne0$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto(z/|z|,w/|w|,|z|)$ has inverse $(u,v,s)\mapsto(su,\sqrt{1-s^2}v)$, so the open complement is $T^2\times(0,1)$ and a compact exterior is $T^2\times I$. The two phase loops are positive meridians of the two coordinate-circle components, hence form the basis of $\pi_1(E_H)=H_1(E_H;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^2$. By [F3], the maximal abelian cover is the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$, whose first homology vanishes. The compact-exterior/open-complement identification [F7] therefore gives $A_H=0$. [A1, F1, F3, F7, given, construct]

1.2 By [F1], the two positive meridians form the coordinate basis; the coordinate-sum definition [F2] therefore sends both to $1$, so its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(1,-1)$. Quotienting the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$ by this rank-one translation subgroup gives $S^1\times\mathbb R\times I$. Its first homology is $\mathbb Z$ generated by the circle. Every deck transformation is represented by a translation, and the path of translations from the identity to that translation is a homotopy, so $t$ acts as $1$. Thus the cyclic module is $\Lambda_1/(t-1)\ne0$, whereas $A_H\otimes_{\Lambda_2,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$ because $A_H=0$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 For the standard unknot $K=\{w=0\}$ in $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, the exterior of the tube $|w|\le\epsilon$ is homeomorphic to $D^2_{\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2}}\times S^1$ by $(z,v)\mapsto(z,\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\,v)$; hence it is a solid torus. For the split unlink use its given separating sphere, with one component and its tube in each ball. The exterior is a collared union along that sphere of two ball-minus-tube pieces. Each piece is a solid-torus unknot exterior with the interior of one disjoint standard ball removed. Reattaching the ball does not change fundamental group, by van Kampen with the simply connected sphere overlap. Thus each piece has group $\mathbb Z$ generated by its positive meridian. Van Kampen on their separating-sphere union gives $\pi_1(E_U)\cong\mathbb Z*\mathbb Z$ with these meridian generators. This does not identify $E_U$ with a handlebody or assert a graph deformation retraction. [A1, F3, F10, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 Let $G=S^1\vee S^1$ map its two based oriented loops to these meridians in $E_U$. It induces the computed fundamental-group isomorphism and intertwines abelianization to $\mathbb Z^2$. Lift it to the connected maximal abelian covers after fixing the base lift. The induced map on fundamental groups identifies the kernels of abelianization, hence is an isomorphism. Degree-one Hurewicz then makes its map on first homology an isomorphism. This is Laurent-linear: conjugation by each meridian implements its deck action on the kernel abelianization, and the map intertwines those conjugations. The same argument for total linking to $\mathbb Z$ compares the cyclic-cover $H_1$. Only first homology is compared; the separating sphere is not removed by a false homotopy equivalence. The lifted graph cellular boundary is $C_1=\Lambda_2^2\xrightarrow{(t_1-1,\ t_2-1)}C_0=\Lambda_2$, so this graph complex computes the desired first homology. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F7, F11, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

2.3 The quotient $\Lambda_2/(t_1-1)$ is $\mathbb Z[t_2^{\pm1}]$, a domain by [F5], so $t_1-1$ is prime. It does not divide $t_2-1$, whose image under $t_1\mapsto1$ is the nonzero element $t_2-1$. If $(a,b)$ lies in the kernel, $(t_1-1)a=-(t_2-1)b$, so primality forces $t_1-1$ to divide $b$. Write $b=(t_1-1)c$; cancellation in the domain gives $a=-(t_2-1)c$. Thus the kernel is generated by $(-(t_2-1),t_1-1)$; it is free because its second coordinate can vanish only when $c=0$. Hence $A_U\cong\Lambda_2$. [F4, F5, step 2.2, algebra]

3.1 Under total linking, both loop edges map to $t$, so [F6] gives the cyclic-cover boundary $(t-1,t-1):\Lambda_1^2\to\Lambda_1$. Since $\Lambda_1$ is a domain, its kernel consists of $(a,-a)$ and is free of rank one. This confirms the stated cyclic-cover module and completes the example. [F2, F5, F6, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. For every $F\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in H^1(M)$ of $(-\Delta_g+q)u=F$ with trace $f$. If $f=0$, $F\in H^m(M)$ and $m\geq0$ is an integer, then $u\in H^{m+2}(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^{m+2}}\leq C_m\|F\|_{H^m}$. If $F$ and $f$ are smooth, this solution belongs to $H^m(M)$ for every integer $m\geq0$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain|Fixed-atlas Sobolev and trace spaces]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; this is assumed by the Rellich compactness and abstract Fredholm suppliers used in steps 1.2 and 2.1.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; this is assumed by the Lax--Milgram, partition, and trace suppliers used in steps 1.1 and 2.2.

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; the compact smooth Riemannian domain; a real smooth potential with trivial Dirichlet kernel; $F\in L^2(M)$; and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: $H_0^1(M)$ is the closure of compactly supported interior smooth functions in $H^1(M)$; the boundary space $H^{1/2}$ is defined by finite chartwise Euclidean $W^{1/2,2}$ norms.

[F2] [[thm-lax-milgram]]: a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on a Hilbert space has a unique weak solution.

[F3] [[thm-rellich-compactness-from-w-one-p-zero-to-lp]]: on a bounded Euclidean open set, $W_0^{1,2}$ is compactly embedded in $L^2$.

[F4] [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-identity-minus-compact]]: for compact $K$ on a Banach space, $I-K$ is injective if and only if it is surjective, and then it is boundedly invertible.

[F5] [[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace]]: a smooth bounded Euclidean domain has a bounded right inverse from its $H^{1/2}$ boundary space to $H^1$.

[F6] [[thm-higher-order-boundary-regularity-for-dirichlet-problems]]: a zero-trace weak solution of a uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation on a bounded smooth Euclidean domain gains two derivatives, with the stated $H^{m+2}$ estimate.

## Proof

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice and the data in the statement.

1.1 Choose a real constant $Q>1+\|q\|_{L^\infty(M)}$ and let $A=-\Delta_g+Q$ on $H_0^1(M)$, with form $a(w,z)=\int_M(g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)+Qw\bar z)\,dV_g$. The form is bounded and coercive in the chartwise $H^1$ norm, so [F2] gives a bounded inverse $A_D^{-1}:(H_0^1(M))^*\to H_0^1(M)$. [A2, given, F1, F2]

1.2 Multiplication by $Q-q$ maps $H_0^1(M)$ boundedly to $L^2(M)$, and the inclusion $H_0^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is compact: localize with the finite atlas and partition, apply [F3] on each bounded chart piece (using zero extension at a boundary face), then extract a finite diagonal subsequence and sum the localized limits. Hence $K:=A_D^{-1}(Q-q)$ is compact on $H_0^1(M)$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 For $w\in H_0^1(M)$, $(I-K)w=0$ is equivalent, after applying $A$, to $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$. The latter has only the zero solution by hypothesis, so $I-K$ is injective. By [F4], $I-K$ is boundedly invertible. This gives a unique weak zero-trace solution for every bounded functional on $H_0^1(M)$, in particular for every $F\in L^2(M)$ after subtracting any fixed boundary lift. [A1, F4, given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 A finite collection of flattened boundary charts, the collar neighborhood, and [F5] give a bounded extension $E:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^1(M)$ with trace $f$. Set $u=Ef+w$ and solve for $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with weak right-hand-side functional $z\mapsto\int_MF\bar z\,dV_g-a_q(Ef,z)$ by step 2.1. This proves existence for the stated data. The difference of any two solutions has zero trace and lies in the assumed trivial kernel, proving uniqueness. [A2, F1, F5, step 2.1, construct]

3.1 First take zero boundary data and $F\in L^2$. In each interior chart the operator has smooth uniformly elliptic divergence-form coefficients $|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}$; in each boundary chart the collar flattens the boundary and the pulled-back coefficients remain smooth and uniformly elliptic. Applying the $m=0$ case of [F6] to localized zero-trace equations gives $u\in H^2$ and the estimate with the additional $L^2$ term. If $f$ is smooth, extend it smoothly in a boundary collar by keeping its chart representative constant in the normal variable near the boundary and multiplying by a cutoff; a finite partition patches these extensions to a smooth $Ef$. Then $w=u-Ef$ has zero trace and solves an equation with smooth datum, so the same local estimates apply to $w$. [F1, F6, step 2.2]

3.2 If $u\in H^{k+1}$ and $F\in H^k$, differentiating the localized zero-trace equation $k$ times leaves the same uniformly elliptic principal part; each commutator contains a bounded derivative of a smooth coefficient and a derivative of $u$ of order at most $k+1$, so it belongs to $L^2$. Tangential derivatives retain zero trace. Applying [F6] at order $k$ on each boundary patch and the corresponding interior estimate gives $u\in H^{k+2}$ and $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k(\|F\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{L^2})$. The bounded inverse in step 2.1 controls $\|u\|_{H^1}$ by $\|F\|_{L^2}$ for zero trace; hence the local estimate and this inverse bound give $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k\|F\|_{H^k}$. Induction gives the claimed zero-trace estimate; for smooth nonzero $f$ apply the same induction to $u-Ef$. [F1, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, induction] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ be a nonempty oriented smooth $r$-component link with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$ obtained from pairwise-disjoint closed normal disk tubes, a finite oriented simplicial triangulation $K$ of $E_L$ with ordered vertices and simplices, with least vertex $v_0$ as the basepoint used in the cover definition, and one certified positive-meridian edge loop $\mu_i$ per component. Orient each normal disk so the positive tangent to its component followed by the positive disk basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$, and assume the resulting classes form the standard basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$. If an integer-vector edge labeling is antisymmetric under edge reversal, sums to zero on every oriented 2-simplex, and evaluates to the $i$th standard basis vector on $\mu_i$, then the chain procedure returns a finite free chain complex over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. The first homology of this complex is the absolute maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module $A_L$. Its Fitting ideals are independent of the triangulation and cell lifts, and its order is defined up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$.

## Statement references

[[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]

[[alg-abelian-cover-chain-model-from-triangulated-exterior]]

[[lem-multivariable-alexander-order-and-specialization]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a nonempty oriented smooth $r$-component link; its chosen compact exterior and finite ordered oriented simplicial triangulation; certified positive-meridian edge loops forming the basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$; and an edge labeling accepted by the chain procedure.

[A1] AC is assumed in the maximal-abelian-cover definition and its link-complement supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The module $A_L$ is $H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$ with Laurent variables acting by positive-meridian deck transformations ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] Inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement lifts to a deck-equivariant homotopy equivalence of maximal abelian covers and preserves the positive-meridian basis ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]).

[F3] The procedure checks edge reversal, all oriented 2-simplex sums and the marked meridian images, returning invalid-labeling upon any failed check ([[alg-abelian-cover-chain-model-from-triangulated-exterior]]).

[F4] On each encoded admissible input the procedure terminates and rejects exactly inputs that fail one of its three label checks ([[thm-abelian-cover-chain-model-from-triangulated-exterior-procedure-properties]]).

[F5] A finite CW structure on $E_L$ lifts to a finite-rank free $\Lambda_r$ cellular chain complex whose first homology is $A_L$ ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-cellular-chain-model]]).

[F6] For every CW complex, cellular homology agrees naturally with singular homology and the comparison is natural for cellular maps ([[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]]).

[F7] The first Hurewicz homomorphism identifies $\pi_1(E_L,b)^{\mathrm{ab}}$ with $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ ([[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]).

[F8] The Fitting ideals of $A_L$ and its order are independent of finite triangulation and cell lifts; the order has the signed Laurent-monomial unit ambiguity ([[lem-multivariable-alexander-order-and-specialization]]).

[F9] Connected covers of a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected space are classified by their induced subgroups ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]).

[F10] For each lifted face incidence, the procedure inserts the signed incidence number times the deck monomial of its lift displacement ([[alg-abelian-cover-chain-model-from-triangulated-exterior]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [F4], an admissible input passes all three label checks and the finite procedure terminates. Thus its output is the finite free complex whose cells and boundary matrices are prescribed in [F3]. [A1, F3, F4, given]

1.2 Antisymmetry makes the edge labels a homomorphism from the cellular 1-chain group of $K$ to $\mathbb Z^r$. The zero sum on each oriented triangle says this homomorphism vanishes on every cellular 2-boundary. Its restriction to cellular 1-cycles therefore descends to a homomorphism $H_1^{\mathrm{cell}}(E_L;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z^r$. By [F6] and the meridian-basis assertion in [F2], this map sends the basis $[\mu_i]$ to $e_i$, so it is precisely the isomorphism that records the full meridian abelianization. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

1.3 By [F7], the corresponding homomorphism on $\pi_1(E_L,b)$ factors through its abelianization and has kernel equal to the commutator subgroup. Thus the cover represented by the labels is the maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, with deck exponents indexed by the stated meridian basis. [F2, F7, step 1.2]

2.1 Let $\lambda(v)$ be the sum of edge labels along the unique spanning-tree path from the least vertex $v_0$ to $v$. Construct a simplicial cover with vertices $(v,g)$, $g\in\mathbb Z^r$, and with each oriented edge $e:v\to w$ lifting from $(v,g)$ to $(w,g+\ell(e))$. In a simplex, assign a vertex exponent by summing labels along an edge path from its least vertex; if two such paths have the same endpoints, their difference is a 1-cycle, and coning that cycle to the least vertex expresses it as a sum of triangular face boundaries. The face checks make each such sum zero. Thus every simplex has a unique lift through each of its vertex lifts, and the lifted simplices agree on common faces. At each vertex $(v,g)$, each simplex incident to $v$ has a unique lift through $(v,g)$; therefore the open star maps homeomorphically to the open star of $v$, proving the covering condition. A loop lifts closed exactly when its label sum is zero; by steps 1.2–1.3 this subgroup is the kernel of abelianization. Whiskering the certified meridian loops to $v_0$ and back gives loops with label sums $e_i$, so the whole fiber over $v_0$ is connected. The spanning tree paths then connect every vertex in every other fiber to that fiber, hence the cover is connected. By [F9] the constructed cover is the maximal abelian cover. [F2, F3, F9, step 1.2, step 1.3, construct]

2.2 The tree assignments select the vertex lifts $(v,\lambda(v))$. The procedure then selects each simplex lift through its anchor lift. For a face $\tau$ of $\sigma$, the difference between the exponent of this face occurrence and the selected lift of $\tau$ is exactly $g(\sigma,\tau)$ computed in instruction 3. Therefore its lifted boundary coefficient is $\epsilon(\sigma,\tau)t_1^{g_1(\sigma,\tau)}\cdots t_r^{g_r(\sigma,\tau)}$, as in instruction 4. These are the cellular face-incidence boundaries in the constructed cover, so the procedure matrices satisfy $\partial^2=0$ and form its lifted cellular chain complex. [F10, step 2.1, construct]

3.1 By [F1] and [F5], the first homology of that complex is $A_L$ as a $\Lambda_r$-module. By [F8], its Fitting ideals and order are independent of the triangulation and lift choices, with the stated unit ambiguity. This proves every conclusion. [F1, F5, F8, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement refuted

For every closed oriented three-manifold $M$, PTFA coefficient homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(M)\to\Gamma$, group ring $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\Gamma$ and fraction skew field $K$, the condition $H_1(M;K)=0$ implies that the Blanchfield pairing on $TH_1(M;\Lambda)$ is nonsingular over $\Lambda$.

## Statement references

[COT, Theorem 2.13, printed page 451](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908117)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $M=T^3=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^3$ with its product orientation, $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^2=\langle x,y\rangle$, and $\phi(m,n,p)=(m,n)$. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[x^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]$, $K=\mathbb Q(x,y)$, $a=x-1$, $b=y-1$, and $I=(a,b)$.

[F1] Supplied lifted oriented cells compute local homology by their group-ring incidence boundaries. [[thm-cellular-chains-compute-homology-with-local-coefficients]]

## Counterexample

1.1 The group $\Gamma$ is torsion-free abelian, hence PTFA with its one-step series. The ring $\Lambda$ is a commutative domain: after multiplying nonzero Laurent polynomials by monomials, lexicographically leading nonzero terms of ordinary polynomials have nonzero product over $\mathbb Z$. Its fraction field is $K$. Give each circle its one-vertex, one-edge cell structure, use their eight product cells on $T^3$, and lift them to the oriented coordinate cells of $\mathbb R^3$. Opposite faces differ by $x,y,1$, respectively. Thus [F1] identifies the coefficient complex with the exterior algebra on $e_1,e_2,e_3$, with differential the graded derivation $d(e_1)=a$, $d(e_2)=b$, $d(e_3)=0$. In particular $d_1(u,v,w)=au+bv$ and $d_2(p,q,r)=(-bp,ap,aq+br)$ in the ordered bases $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(e_1\wedge e_2,e_1\wedge e_3,e_2\wedge e_3)$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Evaluation at $x=1$ identifies $\Lambda/(a)$ with the domain $\mathbb Z[y^{\pm1}]$; its kernel is exactly $(a)$ by multiplying by a power of $x$ and applying the ordinary identity $x^j-1=(x-1)(1+\cdots+x^{j-1})$. If $au+bv=0$, reduction modulo $a$ gives $b\bar v=0$, whence $v=at$ and $u=-bt$. Therefore every degree-one cycle has a unique expression $(-bt,at,w)$. The image of $d_2$ consists precisely of those expressions with arbitrary $t=p$ and $w\in I$. Consequently $H_1(M;\Lambda)\cong\Lambda/I\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the third circle. It is nonzero, and all of it is $\Lambda$-torsion because $a\ne0$ annihilates it. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Over $K$, multiplication by $a$ is invertible. The operator $h(\omega)=a^{-1}e_1\wedge\omega$ satisfies $dh+hd=1$ by the displayed graded-derivation differential. Hence the entire coefficient chain complex over $K$ is contractible and in particular $H_1(M;K)=0$. This verifies the vanishing assumption of the refuted statement without any finiteness or rank inference. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Any $\Lambda$-linear map $\Lambda/I\to K/\Lambda$ is determined by the image $q+\Lambda$ of $1+I$, where $aq,bq\in\Lambda$. Set $r=aq$ and $s=bq$. Then $br=as$. Reducing this identity modulo $a$ and using the domain $\Lambda/(a)$ from step 2.1 gives $r=at$ for some $t\in\Lambda$. Since $a\ne0$ in the field $K$, the identity $aq=at$ forces $q=t\in\Lambda$. Thus the image of $1+I$ is zero, and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(\Lambda/I,K/\Lambda)=0$. The conjugate dual is also zero; the involution $x\mapsto x^{-1},y\mapsto y^{-1}$ preserves $I$ because $x^{-1}-1=-x^{-1}a$ and $y^{-1}-1=-y^{-1}b$. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By steps 2.1 and 3.1, the adjoint of any sesquilinear pairing on $TH_1(M;\Lambda)$ with target $K/\Lambda$ has nonzero source and zero target, and therefore is not an isomorphism. This includes the coefficient Bockstein–duality pairing whenever expressed in those conventions. Together with step 2.2 this refutes the asserted implication. Every object and calculation is explicit and finite; no choice assumption is needed. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

COT Theorem 2.13 does not assert the refuted generality. Its printed statement assumes $\beta_1(M)=1$ and a nontrivial coefficient system, and obtains nonsingularity with the extra condition that the intermediate coefficient ring is a principal ideal domain or an augmentation-ideal element becomes invertible. Those conditions are absent from the refuted statement. The example above has $\beta_1(T^3)=3$ and no such coefficient localization.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$
\theta_1\le\frac{V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)}{V_{T,q}(\alpha_{m-1})}\le\theta_2\qquad(m\ge1).
$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.


## Definition references

[[def-ip-index-source-ball|The singular-value source ball convention and spectral multiplier for an index function]]

[[def-compact-spectral-filter-and-qualification|Compact spectral multipliers, source powers, and regularizing filters]]

[[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators|Positive singular systems and the compact SVD]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice for the upstream countable singular-system construction]]

[Li and Werner, *Adaptive minimax optimality in statistical inverse problems via SOLIT*, §§3.1.1–3.2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356)

[Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, complete lecture notes, Chapter 5 §§5.1–5.2](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

## Remarks

The source class agrees with the earlier singular-value convention because its multiplier at a singular value $s_j$ is $\psi(s_j)=\varphi(s_j^2)=\varphi(\lambda_j)$. The variance function is finite for every fixed $\alpha>0$: the filter bound gives $q_\alpha(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$.

## Example

Let $U=(-6,6)^2\subset\mathbb R^2$, let $\phi(s):=s+9\int_0^s e^{-u^2}\,du$, and define the partially observed map $F:U\to\mathbb R$ by $F(s,t):=\phi(s)$. With basepoint $x_0=(0,0)$, set $Z=\mathbb R^2$, $K(a,b):=10a$, and $r(s,t):=(\phi(s)/10,t)$. Then $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ for every $x\in U$, and $r$ is bi-Lipschitz on $U$. Nevertheless, the local tangential cone condition at $x_0$ fails on radius $5$ for every allowed constant $0\le\eta<1$. The second parameter $t$ is unobserved: all points $(0,t)$ give the datum $0$.

## Example references

[[def-ip-differential-range-invariance|The Banach-space range-invariance factorization]]

[[def-ip-tangential-cone-condition|The local tangential cone inequality tested here]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real Hilbert spaces $X=\mathbb R^2$ and $Y=\mathbb R$, the open set $U=(-6,6)^2$, the basepoint $x_0=(0,0)$, and the function and operators in the Example.

[F1] [[def-ip-differential-range-invariance]]: range invariance at $x_0$ means $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ for a fixed bounded linear $K$ and a map $r$.

[F2] [[def-ip-tangential-cone-condition]]: on a closed ball about $x_0$, the local tangential cone condition requires $\|F(x_0+h)-F(x_0)-F'(x_0)h\|\le\eta\|F(x_0+h)-F(x_0)\|$ for every admissible $h$, with $0\le\eta<1$.

## Verification

1.1 Differentiating gives $\phi'(s)=1+9e^{-s^2}$, so $1\le\phi'(s)\le10$. For $s>s'$, directly from the integral, $s-s'\le\phi(s)-\phi(s')\le10(s-s')$. Thus $\phi$ is strictly increasing and both $s\mapsto\phi(s)/10$ and its inverse are Lipschitz; with the unchanged second coordinate, $r$ is bi-Lipschitz on $U$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The linear map $K(a,b)=10a$ is bounded since $|K(a,b)|\le10\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. Also $F(x_0)=0$ and $Kr(s,t)=10(\phi(s)/10)=\phi(s)=F(s,t)$, so [F1] holds throughout $U$. Further, $F'(x_0)(h_1,h_2)=10h_1$, whose kernel contains the unobserved $t$-axis. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The closed radius-$5$ ball about $x_0$ lies in $U$. At $h=(5,0)$ the TCC remainder is $|\phi(5)-50|$. Since $\int_0^5e^{-u^2}\,du\le1+\int_1^\infty ue^{-u^2}\,du=1+e^{-1}/2<3/2$, we have $0<\phi(5)<5+27/2<25$. Consequently $|\phi(5)-50|=50-\phi(5)>\phi(5)=|F(x_0+h)-F(x_0)|$. This contradicts [F2] for every $\eta<1$. [F2, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For every $t\in(-6,6)$, $F(0,t)=\phi(0)=0$. Hence the observation does not distinguish the points $(0,t)$, even though the range-invariance factorization from step 2.1 holds. [given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every integer $N\ge1$ and every finite braid word $\beta$ on $b\ge1$ strands whose closure is a knot, the normalized generic quotient
$$\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(G_N^{\otimes b}\rho_N(\beta))}{d_N}$$
belongs to $\mathbb Z[A^4,A^{-4}]$. Consequently there is a unique $J_N(K;q)\in\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ whose substitution $q=A^4$ equals that quotient. It is independent of the braid representative, has $J_N(\bigcirc;q)=1$, and agrees with the normalized colored Jones convention of Murakami’s explicit matrix definition in the variable $q$. Its value at every nonzero complex $q$, in particular $q_N=e^{2\pi i/N}$, means evaluation of this Laurent polynomial; it never means division by the specialized quantum dimension.

## Statement references

[[def-normalized-colored-jones-sequence]]

[[lem-colored-jones-generic-ribbon-data]]

[[lem-quantum-pascal-recurrence-and-gaussian-integrality]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $N\ge1$, $b\ge1$, the knot-closing braid word $\beta$, and the two choice assumptions.

[F1] The generic matrices, nonzero $d_N$, scalar $\lambda_N$, absolute simplicity of $V_N$, representative independence under the choice hypotheses and unknot normalization are established in [[def-normalized-colored-jones-sequence]]. Their admissibility is proved, for every $N$, in [[lem-colored-jones-generic-ribbon-data]].

[F2] Symmetric Gaussian quotients $\begin{bmatrix}m\\r\end{bmatrix}_{q_K}$ are integral Laurent polynomials in $q_K$, and their Gauss product and alternating-sum identities hold ([[lem-quantum-pascal-recurrence-and-gaussian-integrality]]).

[F3] Under Countable Choice a colored framed tangle is evaluated by its ribbon matrices; compositions, tensor products and closures agree with their corresponding contractions ([[def-colored-framed-knot-evaluation-from-ribbon-category]], [[thm-a-ribbon-object-defines-a-unique-framed-tangle-evaluation-functor]], [[lem-ribbon-trace-equals-the-framed-closure-evaluation]]). Absolute simplicity says that every color endomorphism is a scalar ([[def-absolutely-simple-object]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement. Put $a=N-1$, $z=q_K-q_K^{-1}$ and $R_0=\mathbb Z[A,A^{-1}]$.

1.1 On the displayed color basis, $E^r/[r]!$ sends $v_i$ to $\begin{bmatrix}a-i+r\\r\end{bmatrix}_{q_K}v_{i-r}$, with zero outside the index range, while $F^rv_j=\prod_{s=1}^r[j+s]v_{j+r}$. By [F2] each coefficient in the finite $R$ series therefore belongs to $R_0$, including the weight factor $A^{hk}$. Its inverse is $\bigl(\sum_{r\ge0}(-1)^rq_K^{-r(r-1)/2}z^rE^r\otimes F^r/[r]!\bigr)D^{-1}$, again a finite integral matrix by the same argument. To check the inverse formula, the coefficient of $(E\otimes F)^m$ in the product of the two nilpotent series is, after multiplication by $[m]!/z^m$, $\sum_{r=0}^m(-1)^{m-r}q_K^{r(r-1)/2-(m-r)(m-r-1)/2}\begin{bmatrix}m\\r\end{bmatrix}_{q_K}$. Its exponent equals $(m-1)r-m(m-1)/2$, so for $m>0$ it vanishes by [F2]'s alternating Gauss sum; at $m=0$ it is $1$. Thus both $c$ and $c^{-1}$ are integral matrices. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Ordinary dual evaluation and coevaluation have entries $0,1$. The pivotal matrices $G_N$ and $G_N^{-1}$ are diagonal Laurent monomials with signs. Accordingly both orientations of cup and cap are integral: one uses ordinary evaluation/coevaluation, the other their composites with the pivotal comparison or its inverse. Crossings involving a dual strand are obtained by bending one or both strands of $c$ or $c^{-1}$ with those maps, as follows from braiding naturality at evaluation and the snakes; concretely this is a partial transpose followed by the just-listed integral contractions. It introduces no matrix inverse other than $c^{-1}$ and $G_N^{-1}$. Every elementary matrix of a tangle colored by $V_N$ and its dual is thus over $R_0$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 It remains to prove the stronger exponent assertion. Work temporarily over $\mathbb Q(i)(A)$, and let a prime denote substitution $A\mapsto iA$. On the basis $v_0,\ldots,v_a$ put $Qv_j=(-1)^{j(j-1)/2}v_j$ and $Dv_j=(-1)^jv_j$. The $r$th term of $R$ sends input $(u,v)$ to $(u-r,v+r)$, before the flip. Every nonzero Laurent monomial in its coefficient has degree, modulo $4$, $ (a-2u)(a-2v)+2r(a-u+v+r)\equiv a^2-2a(u+v)+2r(a-u+v+r)\pmod4.$ Indeed $[m]$ has all degrees congruent to $2(m-1)$, $z$ has degree $2$, $q_K^{r(r-1)/2}$ has degree $r(r-1)$, and the weight factor is evaluated at the output weights. The quotient of the output and input $Q\otimes Q$ signs is $(-1)^{r(v-u+r)}$. Comparing these two explicit expressions yields $c'=(Q\otimes Q)c(Q\otimes Q)^{-1}\quad(a\text{ even}),$ $c'=i(Q\otimes Q)(D\otimes1)c(D\otimes1)(Q\otimes Q)^{-1}\quad(a\text{ odd}).$ For the second formula, the remaining sign is $(-1)^{u+v+r}$, exactly the product of the left input and left output $D$ signs after the flip. No asymptotic or numerical specialization is used in these matrix equalities. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Cut a small oriented arc of the framed knot closure of $\beta$. The remaining framed $(1,1)$-tangle is a morphism $f:V_N\to V_N$ (choose its endpoint orientation accordingly). A generic planar projection decomposes it into finitely many elementary crossings, cups and caps, so step 2.1 makes every entry of $f$ an element of $R_0$. By [F1] and [F3], $f=sI$ for a scalar $s\in F$; its $v_0$ diagonal entry gives $s\in R_0$. Closing that cut arc is the pivotal trace of $f$, namely $d_Ns$, and is the same framed knot value as $\operatorname{Tr}(G_N^{\otimes b}\rho_N(\beta))$ by [F3]. Since $d_N\ne0$ generically, the quotient in the Statement is $\lambda_N^{-w(\beta)}s\in R_0$. This proves integral Laurentness in $A$ without dividing in an integral ring or after specialization. [A1, F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

3.2 If $a$ is even, let $T=Q^{\otimes b}$. Step 2.2 gives $\rho'=T\rho T^{-1}$ for every braid word, including inverses. Direct substitution gives $G_N'=G_N$, $d_N'=d_N$ and $\lambda_N'=\lambda_N$, because $a$ and $a(a+2)$ are even and divisible by $4$, respectively. Since $T$ commutes with $G_N^{\otimes b}$, cyclicity of the ordinary trace shows that the normalized quotient is unchanged by $A\mapsto iA$. [F1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.3 If $a$ is odd, put $H=D^0\otimes D^1\otimes\cdots\otimes D^{b-1}$ and $T=Q^{\otimes b}H$. The operator $c$ preserves the sum of basis indices, so it commutes with $D\otimes D$. Consequently conjugating an adjacent $c$ by $H$ has the effect $(D\otimes1)c(D\otimes1)$, regardless of which adjacent position has odd exponent. Step 2.2 thus gives $\rho'=i^{w(\beta)}T\rho T^{-1}$. Here $G_N'=-G_N$, $d_N'=-d_N$, and $\lambda_N'=-i\lambda_N$, since $a(a+2)\equiv3\pmod4$. Taking the trace and normalizing therefore multiplies the quotient by $(-1)^{b-1+w(\beta)}$. The strand permutation of a knot-closing braid is a single $b$-cycle, so its sign is $(-1)^{b-1}$. Each positive or negative generator is a transposition, so that same sign is $(-1)^{w(\beta)}$. The multiplier is $1$. This proves invariance under $A\mapsto iA$ also for odd $a$. [F1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Write the integral Laurent polynomial from step 3.1 as $\sum_k n_kA^k$, where $n_k\in\mathbb Z$ and only finitely many are nonzero. Steps 3.2 and 3.3 imply $\sum_kn_k(i^k-1)A^k=0$. Linear independence of Laurent monomials over $\mathbb Q(i)$ gives $n_k=0$ unless $4\mid k$. Replacing $A^{4m}$ by $q^m$ gives the required unique integral Laurent polynomial. Its representative independence and unknot value follow from [F1]. Evaluation of a finite Laurent sum at a nonzero complex number is defined without any denominator other than a power of that number, even when the generic quantum dimension specializes to zero. This proves every assertion, including the root-evaluation interpretation. [F1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, algebra]

5.1 To check the conventional variable explicitly, write $a=N-1$ and $\{m\}=q^{m/2}-q^{-m/2}$, $\{m\}!=\prod_{s=1}^m\{s\}$. Murakami's defining positive matrix on basis $e_0,\ldots,e_a$ has coefficient, for input $(k,l)$ and output $(I,J)=(l-r,k+r)$, $\frac{\{l\}!\{a-k\}!}{\{l-r\}!\{r\}!\{a-k-r\}!}q^{(I-a/2)(J-a/2)-r(I-J)/2-r(r+1)/4},$ with $0\le r\le\min(l,a-k)$, and pivotal diagonal $\mu e_j=q^{(2j-a)/2}e_j$; these are the explicit defining formulas in §2.4, not an invoked invariance theorem. At $q=A^4$, change basis by $v_j=A^{j^2}([j]![a-j]!)^{-1}e_{a-j}$. For input $(u,v)$, reversal makes the output $(v+r,u-r)$. The factorial coefficient changes to $z^r[a-u+r]![v+r]!/([a-u]![v]![r]!)$, exactly the one in step 1.1. Before scaling, the exponent of $A$ differs from the declared $R$ coefficient by $2r(v-u+r)$; the change-of-basis factor $A^{u^2+v^2-(u-r)^2-(v+r)^2}$ is its inverse. Thus the two positive crossing matrices are conjugate, as are their inverses, and $\mu$ becomes $K=q_K^H$. Murakami's twist-normalizing scalar is $A^{a(a+2)}$. Replacing this unsigned pivotal and twist by the signed ones of our definition multiplies the normalized closed-braid quotient by $(-1)^{a(b-1-w(\beta))}=1$, by the knot-permutation parity proved in step 3.3. Consequently the Laurent polynomial just established is exactly that source's normalized colored Jones polynomial with $q=A^4$. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Supply distinct odd primes $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ with $m\ge1$ and positive real numbers $C_1,\ldots,C_m$. Put $\omega_j=\exp(2\pi i/p_j)$. A finite construction gives smooth oriented knots $K_1,\ldots,K_m$, each with a supplied connected one-boundary oriented Seifert surface and ordered integral basis with exact positive-push matrix $V_i$. Define its chosen-surface signature function by
$$s_i(z)=\operatorname{sign}\bigl((1-z)V_i+(1-\bar z)V_i^T\bigr),\qquad z\in S^1.$$
There are positive integers $N_i$ such that
$$s_i(\omega_i)=s_i(\omega_i^{-1})=2N_i>C_i,$$
while $s_i(\omega_i^r)=0$ when $r\not\equiv\pm1\pmod{p_i}$, and $s_i(\omega_j^r)=0$ for all integers $r$ when $j\ne i$. Each $s_i$ is nonnegative on the entire unit circle. In particular,
$$\frac1{p_i}\sum_{r=0}^{p_i-1}s_i(\omega_i^r)=\frac{4N_i}{p_i}>\frac{2C_i}{p_i},\qquad \frac1{p_j}\sum_{r=0}^{p_j-1}s_i(\omega_j^r)=0\quad(j\ne i).$$
The surface for $K_i$ has genus $4N_i$. No choice principle, concordance classification, cabling formula, signature-to-rho formula or uniform analytic bound is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite prime list and real target heights.

[F1] For any angle in $(0,\pi)$ and containing open interval, an explicit integral $8\times8$ matrix has signature two at that angle, signature zero outside that interval in $[0,\pi]$, nonnegative signature everywhere and conjugate symmetry. Its two four-dimensional blocks have standard skew matrices with opposite signs. Its proof establishes finite inertia invariance under congruence and block-sum additivity. [[lem-explicit-integral-seifert-matrices-realize-arbitrarily-small-signature-bumps]]

[F2] Any integral matrix with fixed standard symplectic skew part has a finite smooth disk-band realization with its exact positive-push matrix, one boundary component and specified basis, without choice. [[lem-finite-standard-skew-seifert-matrices-have-choice-free-disk-band-realizations]]

## Proof

1.1 Let $\Theta$ be the finite set $\{0,\pi\}\cup\{2\pi r/p_j:1\le j\le m,\ 1\le r\le(p_j-1)/2\}$. All displayed interior angles are distinct except when both indices and residues agree: equality $r/p_j=s/p_\ell$ for distinct primes would force $p_j$ to divide $r$ or $p_\ell$, impossible in the stated residue ranges. The target $\theta_i=2\pi/p_i$ is one of these interior angles. Its distance from every other member of $\Theta$ is positive; let $\delta_i$ be one third of the finite minimum of these distances. Thus $I_i=(\theta_i-\delta_i,\theta_i+\delta_i)\subset(0,\pi)$ contains none of the other angles in $\Theta$. Choose the least positive integer $N_i$ with $2N_i>C_i$, which exists by the Archimedean property of the reals. All these are finite operations on the supplied list. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Use [F1] with $\theta_i,I_i$ to obtain the exact matrix $B_i$ there, and let $\widetilde V_i$ be the block sum of $N_i$ copies of $B_i$. Its signature is $N_i$ times that of $B_i$ by finite inertia additivity. In each positive four-dimensional skew block reorder $(e_1,e_2,f_1,f_2)$ as $(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2)$; in each negative skew block use $(e_1,-f_1,e_2,-f_2)$. Their block sum is an explicit signed permutation $P_i$ for which $V_i=P_i^T\widetilde V_iP_i$ has standard symplectic skew part. Congruence preserves every Hermitian signature by [F1]. Apply [F2] with $g=4N_i$ to realize exactly $V_i$ on an actual smooth one-boundary surface, whose oriented boundary is $K_i$. Thus the constructed knot and chosen matrix have the required nonnegative, conjugate-symmetric signature function, equal to $2N_i$ at $\omega_i$. No mirroring or change of knot orientation is needed to make its sign positive. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 At any nonidentity $p_j$-th root, complex conjugation puts its angle in $\Theta\setminus\{0,\pi\}$. If $j\ne i$, that angle is outside $I_i$, so its signature is zero by [F1]. If $j=i$, only the residues $r\equiv\pm1$ give the angle $\theta_i$; every other nonidentity residue gives another angle of $\Theta$ outside $I_i$ and has signature zero. At the identity all Hermitian matrices in the definition are zero, so their signature is zero as well. The two residues $\pm1$ are distinct because $p_i$ is odd. Their values are both $2N_i$, so summing the exact finite list gives the displayed averages, with no integration or analytic identification. These constructions and the matrix-realization choices are finite and explicit; the statement concerns the actual supplied Seifert surfaces. This proves the full finite separation and height assertions. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $1\le p<\infty$. Let $X,Y,Z$ be real Banach spaces, $X_0\subseteq X$ a closed linear subspace, $D\subseteq X$ a domain containing $X_0$ and $U$, and $x_0\in U\cap X_0$. Let $F:D\to Y$, $K\in\mathcal L(Z,Y)$, and $r:D\to Z$ satisfy $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ on $D$, with $r|_U:U\to\widetilde U$ bijective and $r$ Lipschitz with constant $L_r$ on $D$. Let $P:X\to X$ be a bounded linear projection such that $P|_{X_0}=0$, $(I-P)(X)\subseteq X_0$, and $P(x_0)=P(x^\dagger)=0$ for an exact solution $x^\dagger\in U\cap X_0$; put $y:=F(x^\dagger)$. Assume the projected points $(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)$ belong to $D\cap X_0$ for all admitted $\widehat r\in\widetilde U$.

Let $\check R:X_0\to[0,+\infty]$ be proper and convex, choose $\xi^\dagger\in\partial\check R(x^\dagger)\subseteq X_0^*$, and suppose that for some $R_0\ge\check R(x^\dagger)$, $b\in[0,1)$, and continuous nondecreasing concave $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\psi(0)=0$, the variational source inequality

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,\check x-x^\dagger\rangle\le bD_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger)+\psi\big(\|F(\check x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\big)$$

holds whenever $\check x\in D\cap X_0$ and $\check R(\check x)\le R_0$, where $D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x,x^\dagger):=\check R(\check x)-\check R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,\check x-x^\dagger\rangle$. Set $R_P=0$ in the joint objective. Let $Q:\widetilde U\times\widetilde U\to[0,\infty]$ satisfy $Q(a,b)=Q(b,a)$ and $Q(a,b)=0$ exactly when $a=b$, and assume there is a constant $C_Q\ge0$ such that

$$\|P(r^{-1}(a))-P(r^{-1}(b))\|_X\le C_Q Q(a,b)\qquad(a,b\in\widetilde U).$$

For $\delta>0$, let $y^\delta\in Y$ satisfy $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$. Let $\alpha,\beta>0$, $C_\eta\ge0$, and let $(\widehat r_\delta,x_\delta)\in\widetilde U\times U$ be an $\eta_\delta$-minimizer of the joint objective, meaning

$$\mathcal J_{\alpha,\beta}^\delta(\widehat r_\delta,x_\delta)\le\mathcal J_{\alpha,\beta}^\delta(\widehat r,x)+\eta_\delta\qquad((\widehat r,x)\in\widetilde U\times U),\qquad 0\le\eta_\delta\le C_\eta\delta^p.$$

Assume $\check x_\delta:=(I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r_\delta)$ lies in the stated VSC sublevel. Define

$$s_\delta:=2^{1-p}\|K(\widehat r_\delta-r(x^\dagger))\|_Y^p+\beta Q(r(x_\delta),\widehat r_\delta)^p+\|Px_\delta\|_X^p,\qquad e_\delta:=D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(\check x_\delta,x^\dagger),$$

and

$$C_*:=2^{2p-2}\max\left\{1,\|K\|^pL_r^p,\frac{\|K\|^pL_r^pC_Q^p}{\beta}\right\},\qquad d_\delta:=(2+C_\eta)\delta^p.$$

Then

$$s_\delta+(1-b)\alpha e_\delta\le d_\delta+\alpha\psi(C_*s_\delta).$$

## Statement references

[Barbara Kaltenbacher, *Convergence rates under a range invariance condition with application to electrical impedance tomography*, equations (2.10)–(2.14)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18704)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Banach spaces, range factorization, projection, regularizer, VSC, compatibility inequality, exact datum, noise bound, and approximate minimizer in the Statement.

[A1] The candidate projected point $\check x_\delta$ belongs to $D\cap X_0$ and satisfies $\check R(\check x_\delta)\le R_0$, so the VSC applies to it.

[A2] The noisy datum and approximate-minimizer tolerance satisfy the bounds in the Statement.

[A3] The projection-coupling bound holds for all range variables in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-differential-range-invariance]]: $F(x)-F(x_0)=Kr(x)$ for every $x$ in the range-factorization domain.

[F2] [[def-ip-relaxed-range-invariance-objective]]: with $R_P=0$, the joint objective is $\|K\widehat r+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha\check R((I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r))+\beta Q(r(x),\widehat r)^p+\|Px\|_X^p$.

[F3] [[def-ip-banach-convex-subgradient-and-dual-pairing]]: $\xi^\dagger\in\partial\check R(x^\dagger)$ means $\check R(z)\ge\check R(x^\dagger)+\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle$ for every $z\in X_0$.

[F4] [[def-ip-bregman-distance]]: $D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(z,x^\dagger)=\check R(z)-\check R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle$.

[F5] [[def-ip-variational-source-condition]]: on the named regularizer sublevel, $-\langle\xi^\dagger,z-x^\dagger\rangle\le bD_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(z,x^\dagger)+\psi(\|F(z)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p)$.

## Proof

1.1 Compare the approximate-minimum inequality with $(\widehat r,x)=(r(x^\dagger),x^\dagger)$. By [F1], $Kr(x^\dagger)+F(x_0)=F(x^\dagger)=y$, while $Q(r(x^\dagger),r(x^\dagger))=0$ and $Px^\dagger=0$. Since $r^{-1}(r(x^\dagger))=x^\dagger$ and $P(x^\dagger)=0$, the comparison regularizer is $\check R(x^\dagger)$, so its objective is at most $\delta^p+\alpha\check R(x^\dagger)$. Writing the estimated data residual as $K(\widehat r_\delta-r(x^\dagger))+(y-y^\delta)$, the triangle inequality gives $\|K(\widehat r_\delta-r(x^\dagger))\|\le\|K\widehat r_\delta+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|+\delta$. For $p=1$ the power inequality is equality; for $p>1$, $f(t)=t^p$ has $f\prime\prime(t)=p(p-1)t^{p-2}\ge0$ for $t>0$ and is continuous at zero, so it is convex on $[0,\infty)$; midpoint convexity gives $(a+b)^p\le2^{p-1}(a^p+b^p)$ for $a,b\ge0$. Rearranging yields $2^{1-p}\|K(\widehat r_\delta-r(x^\dagger))\|^p\le\|K\widehat r_\delta+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|^p+\delta^p$. Combining this with the comparison and $\eta_\delta\le C_\eta\delta^p$ gives $s_\delta+\alpha(\check R(\check x_\delta)-\check R(x^\dagger))\le d_\delta$. [A2, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], $\xi^\dagger$ is a subgradient at $x^\dagger$, and [F4] gives $\check R(\check x_\delta)-\check R(x^\dagger)=e_\delta+\langle\xi^\dagger,\check x_\delta-x^\dagger\rangle$. The VSC [F5] therefore implies $\check R(\check x_\delta)-\check R(x^\dagger)\ge(1-b)e_\delta-\psi(\|F(\check x_\delta)-F(x^\dagger)\|^p)$. Substituting this lower bound in step 1.1 yields $s_\delta+(1-b)\alpha e_\delta\le d_\delta+\alpha\psi(\|F(\check x_\delta)-F(x^\dagger)\|^p)$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Put $u_\delta=r^{-1}(\widehat r_\delta)$, so $\check x_\delta=(I-P)u_\delta$. Since $r^{-1}(r(x_\delta))=x_\delta$, assumption [A3] and the triangle inequality give $\|Pu_\delta\|\le\|Px_\delta\|+C_QQ(r(x_\delta),\widehat r_\delta)$. Lipschitz continuity of $r$ gives $\|r(\check x_\delta)-\widehat r_\delta\|=\|r((I-P)u_\delta)-r(u_\delta)\|\le L_r\|Pu_\delta\|$. Applying [F1] at $\check x_\delta$ and $x^\dagger$, then applying $(a+b)^p\le2^{p-1}(a^p+b^p)$ twice, yields $\|F(\check x_\delta)-F(x^\dagger)\|^p\le2^{p-1}\|K(\widehat r_\delta-r(x^\dagger))\|^p+2^{2p-2}\|K\|^pL_r^p(\|Px_\delta\|^p+C_Q^pQ(r(x_\delta),\widehat r_\delta)^p)\le C_*s_\delta$. Monotonicity of $\psi$ gives $\psi(\|F(\check x_\delta)-F(x^\dagger)\|^p)\le\psi(C_*s_\delta)$. [A3, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substitute the last bound from step 2.2 into the inequality from step 2.1. This gives $s_\delta+(1-b)\alpha e_\delta\le d_\delta+\alpha\psi(C_*s_\delta)$, as claimed. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$ and $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[t,t^{-1}]$. Let $\Delta\in\Lambda$ be nonzero and primitive, meaning that the greatest common divisor of its finitely many integer coefficients is one. Define
$$T_\Delta=\{x\in\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda:\Delta x=0\}.$$
The natural map $\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda\to\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ is injective on $T_\Delta$.

For a prime $p$ such that $\bar\Delta\ne0$ in $\Lambda_p=\mathbb F_p[t,t^{-1}]$, there is a well-defined additive reduction map
$$\rho_{p,\Delta}:T_\Delta\longrightarrow\mathbb F_p(t)/\Lambda_p,\qquad [a/\Delta]\longmapsto[\bar a/\bar\Delta],\quad a\in\Lambda.$$
It satisfies $\rho_{p,\Delta}(b x)=\bar b\,\rho_{p,\Delta}(x)$ for $b\in\Lambda$. For every nonzero $x\in T_\Delta$, one can compute a nonzero integer $D$ from $\Delta$ and a chosen representative $a/\Delta$ such that $\rho_{p,\Delta}(x)\ne0$ for every prime $p\nmid D$. No choice principle or factorization theorem for arbitrary rings is assumed. This is a map on the specified annihilated quotient module; no global reduction homomorphism from $\mathbb Q(t)$ to $\mathbb F_p(t)$ is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The primitive finite Laurent polynomial and, for the last assertion, one nonzero annihilated quotient class with a representative. Laurent polynomials are finite coefficient lists. Over a field the product of two nonzero Laurent polynomials is nonzero, since its lowest and highest nonzero terms have nonzero product coefficients.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $x\in T_\Delta$ maps to zero in the rational quotient. It has a representative $r\in\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$, and $\Delta r\in\Lambda$. Let $m\ge1$ be the least positive integer clearing the finitely many denominators of $r$ and put $f=mr\in\Lambda$. If $m>1$, take a prime divisor $p$ of $m$; the least divisor greater than one is prime, so this requires no choice principle. Not every coefficient of $f$ is divisible by $p$, since otherwise $m/p$ would also clear the denominators of $r$, contrary to minimality. Primitivity likewise says $\bar\Delta\ne0$ modulo $p$. Thus $\bar\Delta\bar f\ne0$ in the field Laurent polynomial ring. But $\Delta f=m(\Delta r)$ has all coefficients divisible by $p$, a contradiction. Hence $m=1$, so $r\in\Lambda$ and $x=0$. This proves the asserted injection. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Every $x\in T_\Delta$ has a representative $a/\Delta$ with $a\in\Lambda$: take any rational-function representative $r$ of $x$ and use $a=\Delta r$, which is in $\Lambda$ by the annihilation condition. For two such representatives $a/\Delta,a'/\Delta$, equality of their classes means $a'-a=\Delta b$ for some $b\in\Lambda$. If $\bar\Delta\ne0$, their reduced fractions differ by $\bar b$ and so define the same class in $\mathbb F_p(t)/\Lambda_p$. The additive and $\Lambda$-scalar identities follow by reducing their actual finite numerators. This constructs precisely the claimed map and uses no reduction of arbitrary rational-function coefficients or denominators. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Fix a nonzero $x$. Multiply $\Delta$ by a power of $t$ to obtain a polynomial $d(t)$ with nonzero constant and leading coefficient; this unit change does not change its annihilated module. Adjust its numerator accordingly, then multiply $x$ by a power $t^m$ so that $y=t^m x=c(t)/d(t)$ with $c\in\mathbb Z[t]$. The class $y$ is nonzero, and step 1.1 implies $c/d\notin\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$. Ordinary finite polynomial division over $\mathbb Q$ gives $c=dQ+R$, with $\deg R<\deg d$. Its remainder is nonzero, since a zero remainder would give $c/d\in\mathbb Q[t]$. Clear the finitely many coefficient denominators: $$q c=d A+B,\qquad q\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\quad A,B\in\mathbb Z[t],\quad B\ne0,\quad\deg B<\deg d.$$ In particular $\deg d>0$. Choose the first nonzero coefficient $C$ of $B$ in increasing exponent order and set $D=q\,d(0)\,\operatorname{lead}(d)\,C\ne0$. All choices here are finite coefficient operations and polynomial division. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 If $p\nmid D$, then $\bar d$ has its original positive degree and nonzero constant term, $\bar B\ne0$ and $\deg\bar B<\deg\bar d$, and $\bar q$ is invertible. The reduced identity gives $$[\bar c/\bar d]=\bar q^{-1}[\bar B/\bar d]\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p(t)/\Lambda_p.$$ The latter class cannot be zero. If $\bar B=\bar d\,L$ for $L\in\Lambda_p$, the nonzero constant term of $\bar d$ and the polynomial nature of $\bar B$ force the lowest exponent of $L$ to be nonnegative: lowest exponents add and their coefficients do not cancel. Hence $L$ is a polynomial, contradicting $\deg\bar B<\deg\bar d$. Thus $\rho_{p,\Delta}(y)\ne0$, with the unit changes in $\Delta$ cancelled between numerator and denominator. By step 1.2, $\rho_{p,\Delta}(y)=t^m\rho_{p,\Delta}(x)$; the unit $t^m$ preserves nonzero classes. This proves the nonzero reduction assertion for the explicit finite exceptional integer $D$. If $\Delta$ is a Laurent unit, $T_\Delta=0$ and the nonzero case is vacuous. The argument used only finitely many integer and polynomial operations, proving the full choice scope. [step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

For an actual Blanchfield self-pairing, applying this lemma requires a proved primitive annihilator of the value and an exact identification of its reduced value with the geometric mod-$p$ pairing. Neither a Seifert presentation nor that coefficient comparison is supplied by this purely algebraic statement.
