## Statement

Fix even $p\ge4$, a primitive $2p$-th root $A$, and $r=p/2$. In the Temperley–Lieb diagram category over $\mathbb C$ with loop value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, call $f:m\to n$ negligible when $\operatorname{Tr}_m(g\circ f)=0$ for every reverse morphism $g:n\to m$, where $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the unnormalized diagram-closure trace. A tensor ideal is a family of linear subspaces of the morphism spaces closed under composition on either side and tensor product on either side by arbitrary morphisms. The negligible morphisms form a tensor ideal. This ideal is generated, as a tensor ideal, by the Jones–Wenzl projector $p_{r-1}$, defined by the standard recursion through its first zero quantum integer; in particular the quotient has precisely the surviving projector labels $0,\ldots,r-2$.

## Statement references

[[def-sl-two-root-of-unity-skein-parameter|Root and loop conventions]]

[[lem-jones-wenzl-idempotents-exist-below-root-order|Existence and zero trace of the boundary projector]]

[[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category|Temperley–Lieb diagram category]]

[Chen, *The Temperley-Lieb Categories and Skein Modules*, §§5.1–5.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.06845v1)

[Kauffman and Lins, *Temperley-Lieb Recoupling Theory and Invariants of 3-Manifolds*, Chapters 3–7](https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781400882533_A27764847/preview-9781400882533_A27764847.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The specialized Temperley–Lieb category, its unnormalized closure trace, and the root-order projectors.

[F1] [[lem-jones-wenzl-idempotents-exist-below-root-order]]: $p_{r-1}$ is a nonzero idempotent with zero closure trace.

[F2] [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]: each morphism is a finite $\mathbb C$-linear combination of noncrossing matching diagrams; cups and caps bend strands, and composition is stacking with each closed component weighted by $\delta$.

[F3] [[def-temperley-lieb-negligible-morphisms]]: $f:m\to n$ is negligible exactly when $\operatorname{Tr}_m(g\circ f)=0$ for every $g:n\to m$.

[F4] [[lem-temperley-lieb-negligible-morphisms-form-tensor-ideal]]: the negligible subspaces form a two-sided tensor ideal in the planar Temperley–Lieb category for every complex loop value.

[F5] [[lem-temperley-lieb-closure-trace-component-identities]]: the unnormalized closure trace is cyclic and its identities do not divide by $\delta$.

[F6] [[lem-temperley-lieb-jones-wenzl-partial-trace-and-uniqueness]]: the corner of each defined $p_n$ is $\mathbb C p_n$.

[F7] [[thm-temperley-lieb-rank-one-pivotal-ribbon-conversion]]: at the canonical root with order parameter $r\ge3$, the negative-loop quotient has kernel equal to the embedded ideal generated by $p_{r-1}$ and its ribbon quotient is equivalent to the specified rank-one tilting quotient.

[F8] [[thm-temperley-lieb-root-negligible-quotient-is-semisimple]]: for the positive-loop root $q=e^{\pi i/r}$, the boundary projector ideal is the exact negligible ideal and the quotient has simple labels $0,\ldots,r-2$ with the truncated fusion rule.

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement.

1.1 By the boundary-projector result, $p_{r-1}$ is an idempotent with trace zero. The diagram category [F2] supplies the endomorphism algebra $\mathrm{TL}_{r-1}$ and its closure trace. For any $g\in\mathrm{TL}_{r-1}$, [F6] gives $p_{r-1}gp_{r-1}=\lambda p_{r-1}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C$. Cyclicity [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}_{r-1}(g\circ p_{r-1})=\operatorname{Tr}_{r-1}(p_{r-1}gp_{r-1})=\lambda\operatorname{Tr}_{r-1}(p_{r-1})=0$. Thus $p_{r-1}$ itself is negligible by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], the negligible morphisms form a tensor ideal. Since [F3] and step 1.1 place $p_{r-1}$ in that ideal, the tensor ideal it generates is contained in the negligible ideal. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Put $A_0=e^{\pi i/(2r)}$. For $r\ge3$, $A_0$ is a primitive $4r$-th root, $q_0=A_0^2=e^{\pi i/r}$, and $-A_0^2-A_0^{-2}=-(q_0+q_0^{-1})$. Thus the negative-loop category in [F7] is exactly the BHMV Temperley–Lieb category at $A_0$; its quotient kernel is the ideal generated by $p_{r-1}$, and [F8] gives the complete label list. [F1, F7, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 If $r=2$, the loop value is zero and $p_1=1_1$ has zero trace by step 1.1. The tensor ideal it generates contains every identity $1_n$ for $n\ge1$, while the object $0$ has endomorphism algebra $\mathbb C$ with trace $1$. Hence the quotient is equivalent to finite-dimensional vector spaces with the single simple label $0$; its negligible ideal is exactly the ideal generated by $p_1$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra, cases]

3.1 For arbitrary primitive $A$, write $A=A_0^k$ with $\gcd(k,4r)=1$. The cyclotomic automorphism $\sigma_k$ of $\mathbb Q(A_0)$ sends $A_0$ to $A$, sends $\delta(A_0)$ to $\delta(A)$, and sends every coefficient of each recursively defined projector and every closure-trace pairing matrix to its specialized coefficient at $A$. For each fixed pair of object labels, the matching set is finite by [F2], so the Hom spaces and trace-pairing matrices are finite-dimensional. The field automorphism preserves the ranks and kernels of all these matrices, the exact boundary ideal, and the quotient's simple labels. This completes the canonical-to-arbitrary-root transport and the proof. [F1, F2, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The canonical-root quotient and its boundary ideal use the full-rank path decomposition and the exact diagram-to-tilting comparison. Both supplier statements and their complete local proofs were inspected. The proof is transported to other primitive roots by the finite cyclotomic-field argument in step 3.1; no source-only acceptance is asserted.

## Statement

Let $W$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold with boundary $A$ and a supplied boundary collar $c:A\times[0,1)\to W$. Let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with the integral relative orientation class $z=[W,A]$ gives isomorphisms in every integer degree:
$$H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L),\qquad H^p(W;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W,A;\mathcal L).$$
The maps commute with every coefficient action commuting with transport, including noncommutative ring actions on the underlying abelian-group systems. No choice principle, smoothness, triangulation or finite CW structure is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The oriented compact manifold, supplied collar and abelian-group local system.

[F1] Canonical support classes and the relative orientation class exist without choice; the boundary of $z$ is the outward-normal-first orientation class $[A]$. The oriented assertion is the trivialized integral orientation-system case. [[lem-canonical-twisted-fundamental-classes-over-compact-subsets]]

[F2] Compact-support duality holds on a boundaryless finite-atlas manifold, and ordinary duality holds on a compact oriented boundaryless manifold. [[thm-finite-atlas-manifold-compact-support-duality-in-zf]], [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]]

[F3] Local pair sequences, excision, and homotopy invariance apply to abelian-group local systems by using the commutative base ring $\mathbb Z$. Pair cochain connectors use the explicit zero extension on simplex functions. [[thm-pair-long-exact-sequences-with-local-coefficients]], [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]], [[prop-local-coefficient-homology-and-cohomology-are-functorial-for-a-map-with-a-coefficient-morphism]]

[F4] Local cap satisfies the cochain-first boundary formula and commutes with restriction and passage to relative groups; compact-support groups are the support colimit. [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]], [[def-compactly-supported-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]]

[F5] The five lemma applies to commutative exact five-term windows. [[thm-five-lemma-for-a-morphism-of-long-exact-sequences]]

## Proof

1.1 If $A$ is empty, both maps are [F2]'s compact duality, so assume it is nonempty. Put $N=W\setminus A$, $C_d=c(A\times[0,d))$ and $K_d=W\setminus C_d$ for $0<d<1/2$. Every compact $L\subset N$ lies in some $K_d$: intersect it with the closed compact collar segment of height at most $1/2$; on the nonempty intersection the continuous height has a positive minimum since $L$ misses $A$. Choose $d$ below that minimum; if the intersection is empty any sufficiently small $d$ works. Compactness supplies a finite atlas of $W$ by ordinary and half-space charts. Restricting these charts to $N$ gives a finite atlas by open Euclidean subsets. Thus [F2]'s finite-atlas duality applies to $N$. Pushing the collar inward with the function $t\mapsto t+\varepsilon\chi(t)$, where $\chi=1$ near zero and vanishes before height $1/2$ and $\varepsilon>0$ is small enough, gives a homotopy inverse to $N\hookrightarrow W$. Linear interpolation of this push gives the homotopies, stays inside the collar, and restricts to positive heights on $N$. [F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The collar deformation retraction $C_d\to A$, its coefficient transports, and the exact pair sequences imply that $H^p(W,C_d;\mathcal L)\to H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)$ is an isomorphism. Excision identifies its domain with $H^p(N,N\setminus K_d;\mathcal L|_N)$. These maps commute with decreasing $d$. The cofinality of the $K_d$ from step 1.1 and the representative definition of the support colimit therefore give a canonical isomorphism $H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_c^p(N;\mathcal L|_N)$. To verify independence, move two representatives to a common smaller collar core; the natural relative maps and common-support equality identify them there. This selects representatives for a single class only. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], the image of $z$ in $H_n(W,C_d;\mathbb Z)$ is the excision image of the support orientation class of $N$ at $K_d$. A relative cocycle on $(W,C_d)$ vanishes on $C_d$. Cap with two chains representing this equality differs by a boundary and by a cap term supported in $C_d$; the latter is zero. The cap boundary formula [F4] turns the former difference into a target boundary. Thus under step 2.1 the relative cap map on $W$ is exactly compact-support cap on $N$ followed by inclusion $N\hookrightarrow W$. Both maps are isomorphisms by step 1.1 and [F2], proving $H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Compare the exact cohomology window $$H^{p-1}(A;\mathcal L)\to H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\to H^p(W;\mathcal L)\to H^p(A;\mathcal L)\to H^{p+1}(W,A;\mathcal L)$$ with the homology window $$H_{n-p}(A;\mathcal L)\to H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L)\to H_{n-p}(W,A;\mathcal L)\to H_{n-p-1}(A;\mathcal L)\to H_{n-p-1}(W;\mathcal L).$$ Use cap with $[A]$ in the first and fourth vertical positions, the isomorphism of step 3.1 in the second and fifth, and cap with $z$ in the middle. The boundary is compact and boundaryless, so its two cap maps are isomorphisms by [F2]. All rows are exact by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The two squares involving inclusions and relative quotients commute directly on the cap representatives. For the first connector square, extend a degree-$(p-1)$ cocycle $a$ on $A$ by zero to a cochain $\widetilde a$ on $W$. The cap identity gives $$\delta\widetilde a\cap z=\widetilde a\cap\partial z+(-1)^p\partial(\widetilde a\cap z).$$ Together with $\partial z=[A]$ this proves the required square on homology. For the last connector square, a degree-$p$ cocycle $b$ gives $\partial(b\cap z)=(-1)^p b|_A\cap[A]$. Multiplying that homology connector by $(-1)^p$ therefore makes the square commute. Multiplication by this unit preserves exactness. The signed ladder is now commutative, so [F5] and the four isomorphisms of step 4.1 prove the middle cap map is an isomorphism. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The argument applies to arbitrary abelian-group fibers; it never lifts a cochain through a quotient of infinite products. The only cochain extension was the explicit zero extension for a subspace. Compactness supplies finitely many charts; all other operations use a single compact support or finitely many chains at a time. Any commuting scalar action commutes with cap, transport, extension and restriction, so all the maps and their inverses retain it. Empty manifolds, empty boundary, dimension zero, disconnected manifolds and all integer degrees obey the same formulas, with negative complexes zero. Hence the stated full coefficient and topological scope is obtained without a choice axiom. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and let
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning
$u^T\Gamma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Suppose
$X$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with laws
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law|A positive finite evidence defines the normalized potential update, and the dominated version convention identifies it as a conditional law.]]

[[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws|Finite Gaussian conditioning permits singular prior and predictive covariance blocks when the observed covariance is positive definite.]]

[[lem-ip-singular-gaussian-support-and-pseudoinverse|For a singular finite Gaussian prior, the affine support is the mean plus the covariance range.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a finite-dimensional Gaussian prior $N_n(m_0,C_0)$ with
$C_0\succeq0$; independent Gaussian observation noise $N_m(0,\Gamma)$ with
$\Gamma\succ0$; and the linear observation map $A$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the repository's multivariate-normal, Gaussian-process,
and finite Gaussian conditioning interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A finite Gaussian law is characterized by its Gaussian scalar
projections, permits singular covariance, and has the covariance-square-root
representation. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F2] The prior is supported on $m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$ and admits
coordinates $C_0=U\Lambda U^T$ with a standard Gaussian vector on that range.
[[lem-ip-singular-gaussian-support-and-pseudoinverse]]

[F3] A real process is Gaussian when all its finite linear combinations are
normal. [[def-gaussian-process]]

[F4] Independence of random elements is independence of their generated
sigma-algebras. [[def-independent-random-elements]]

[F5] Measurable functions of independent random elements remain independent.
[[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]]

[F6] For a finite Gaussian process with independent Gaussian observation noise,
if the observed covariance is positive definite, the conditional law of the
test vector is the Gaussian with mean
$m_*+K_{*X}(K_{XX}+R)^{-1}(y-m_X)$ and covariance
$K_{**}-K_{*X}(K_{XX}+R)^{-1}K_{X*}$, defined for every $y$ even when the
prior or conditional covariance is singular.
[[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]]

[F7] A positive-definite Gaussian observation-noise covariance has the
Lebesgue density proportional to
$\exp(-\tfrac12 z^T\Gamma^{-1}z)$, which is strictly positive everywhere.
[[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F8] The inverse-problem potential update is the prior reweighted by
$e^{-\Phi_y}$ and normalized by its evidence when that evidence is positive
and finite. [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F9] A finite continuous potential with lower envelope $0$ under a proper
prior on a separable Banach space has positive finite evidence at every datum.
[[thm-ip-function-space-posterior-propriety]]

## Proof
**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For $v\in\mathbb R^m\setminus\{0\}$, $v^TSv=(A^Tv)^TC_0(A^Tv)+v^T\Gamma v>0$, since the first term is nonnegative and the second is positive. Thus $S\succ0$ and $S^{-1}$ exists. [given, algebra]

1.2 Let $T$ be the finite index set with state indices $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ and observation indices $o_1,\ldots,o_m$. Define $f_{s_i}=X_i$ and $f_{o_j}=(AX)_j$. Every finite linear combination of these coordinates is a linear projection of $X$, so it is normal by [F1] and $f$ is a Gaussian process by [F3]. Its covariance blocks are $K_{SS}=C_0$, $K_{SO}=C_0A^T$, and $K_{OO}=AC_0A^T$. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

1.3 For each fixed $y$, $\Phi_y$ is finite, continuous, and nonnegative on $\mathbb R^n$, and $(x,y)\mapsto\Phi_y(x)$ is jointly continuous. The prior $\mu_0$ is a probability on the separable Banach space $\mathbb R^n$, and the envelope $M_1(r)=0$ satisfies $\int e^{M_1(\|x\|_2)}\,\mu_0(dx)=1$. Therefore [F9] gives $0<Z(y)<\infty$ for every $y$, and [F8] defines $\Pi^y$. The likelihood density from [F7] is a positive constant independent of $x$ times $e^{-\Phi_y(x)}$; its constant cancels in the normalized update. [F7, F8, F9, given, algebra]

2.1 The vector $f$ is a measurable function of $X$, so [F4] and [F5] make $\eta$ independent of $f$. The observed covariance is $K_{OO}+\Gamma=S\succ0$ by step 1.1. Applying [F6] with test list $S$ and observation list $O$ gives the displayed Gaussian conditional-law version for every $y$. [A1, F4, F5, F6, given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Suppose $r=\operatorname{rank}(C_0)>0$. By [F2], write $C_0=U\Lambda U^T$ and represent $X$ as $m_0+L\xi$, where $L=U\Lambda^{1/2}$ and $\xi\sim N_r(0,I_r)$. Put $B=AL$ and $d=y-Am_0$. By the pushforward formula for $\mu_0$ and the likelihood in [F7], the density of the normalized update in these coordinates is proportional, for every $y$, to $$ \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\left[\xi^T\xi+(d-B\xi)^T\Gamma^{-1}(d-B\xi)\right]\right). $$ This is a pointwise fixed-data calculation; it does not replace the all-data version convention in step 1.3. [F2, F7, F8, step 1.3, given]

3.1 Set $Q=I_r+B^T\Gamma^{-1}B$ and $h=B^T\Gamma^{-1}d$. Then $Q\succ0$, and expansion gives $$ \xi^T\xi+(d-B\xi)^T\Gamma^{-1}(d-B\xi) =(\xi-Q^{-1}h)^TQ(\xi-Q^{-1}h)+d^T\Gamma^{-1}d-h^TQ^{-1}h. $$ Thus the update in step 2.2 is the Gaussian law of $\xi$ with mean $Q^{-1}h$ and covariance $Q^{-1}$, so the update of $X=m_0+L\xi$ has mean $m_0+LQ^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}d$ and covariance $LQ^{-1}L^T$. [F2, F7, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Since $S=\Gamma+BB^T$, multiplication gives $QB^T=B^T\Gamma^{-1}S$, hence $Q^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}=B^TS^{-1}$. Also $Q(I_r-B^TS^{-1}B)=Q-QB^TS^{-1}B=I_r$, so $Q^{-1}=I_r-B^TS^{-1}B$. Substituting these identities into step 3.1 yields $$ m_0+LQ^{-1}B^T\Gamma^{-1}d=m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}d $$ and $$ LQ^{-1}L^T=C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0. $$ These are exactly the mean and covariance in the Statement. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $r=0$, [F2] gives $C_0=0$ and $X=m_0$ almost surely. Reweighting a point mass by the positive likelihood leaves that point mass, while the displayed formulas reduce to mean $m_0$ and covariance $0$. This also matches the conditional version from step 2.1 and proves the rank-zero boundary. Thus the fixed-data update and the stated all-data conditional version have the displayed law in every rank case. [F2, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with a supplied boundary collar, and put $M=\partial W$. Let $R\subseteq K$ be a unital involution-stable subring of an involutive division ring. Supply a based rank-one right-$R$ coefficient system $\mathcal R$ on $W$, with its base fiber identified with $R$, unitary monodromy and the transported standard Hermitian form. Write $H_*(W;R)$ and $H_*(W;K)$ for its homology and scalar-extended homology.

Define the equivariant intersection pairing $\lambda_R$ by sending $\bar p\in\overline{H_2(W;R)}$ through inverse relative cap duality to $H^2(W,M;\mathcal R^\vee)$, then into $H^2(W;\mathcal R^\vee)$, then evaluating on $q\in H_2(W;R)$. Here $\mathcal R^\vee$ is the intrinsic dual coefficient system, identified with the conjugate system by the supplied Hermitian form. Thus $\lambda_R(p,q)$ is conjugate-linear in $p$ and right-linear in $q$. Define $\lambda_K$ by the same construction over $K$.

Suppose $m\ge0$ and classes $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m,d_1,\ldots,d_m\in H_2(W;R)$ satisfy
$$\lambda_R(\ell_i,\ell_j)=0,\qquad\lambda_R(\ell_i,d_j)=\lambda_R(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij},$$
and suppose
$$\dim_K\bigl(H_2(W;K)/\operatorname{im}H_2(M;K)\bigr)\le2m.$$
Let $M_0$ be one connected boundary component with $H_1(M_0;K)=0$. Its coefficient Bockstein, oriented cap duality and evaluation define the linking form $B_0$ with values in $K/R$. Then
$$B_0(x,y)=0\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\ker\{H_1(M_0;R)\longrightarrow H_1(W;R)\}.$$
No vanishing condition on the other boundary components is imposed. No choice axiom, finite CW structure, or general noncommutative universal-coefficient theorem is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The manifolds, collar, rings, unitary coefficient system, finite list of intersection pairs and dimension bound in the Statement.

[F1] Oriented relative cap duality holds for a compact collared manifold with arbitrary abelian-group local systems and commuting scalar actions; closed cap duality holds on its boundary. [[thm-compact-collared-manifold-local-coefficient-lefschetz-duality-in-zf]], [[thm-compact-oriented-manifold-local-coefficient-duality-in-zf]]

[F2] Supplied standard parallel Hermitian structures identify intrinsic dual coefficient systems with conjugate right systems. The cochain identification is simplexwise, so restriction to a subspace and the relative cochain subcomplex preserve it. [[lem-involutive-twisted-chain-duals-realize-local-coefficient-duality]]

[F3] A compact connected closed manifold has a choice-free one-vertex right-chain model with degree-zero term its coefficient ring. The low-degree coefficient Bockstein is natural and exact, without lifting an infinite product of quotient fibers. [[lem-compact-manifold-twisted-singular-chains-admit-one-vertex-reduction]], [[lem-choice-free-low-degree-coefficient-bockstein-on-compact-manifolds]]

[F4] The pair exact sequences use explicit zero extension for subspace cochains. The cap boundary formula identifies their connectors after the prescribed degree signs. [[thm-pair-long-exact-sequences-with-local-coefficients]], [[def-cup-and-cap-products-with-local-coefficient-pairings]]

## Proof

1.1 All coefficient maps and pair maps in the definitions of $\lambda_R,\lambda_K$ commute with cap, conjugation and evaluation: on simplex representatives these are transport, the ring inclusion and finite sums. Thus scalar extension carries each displayed $R$ intersection identity to its $K$ counterpart. In a unitary frame a right-linear functional is conjugate to a right vector by the standard form, as in [F2]; this calculation is valid equally on simplices of a manifold with boundary and on its relative subcomplex. All cap and exact-sequence arguments below can therefore be performed on the intrinsic underlying abelian-group systems, retaining the left coefficient actions. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The pairing $\lambda_K$ descends in both variables to $V=H_2(W;K)/\operatorname{im}H_2(M;K)$. For the first variable, take $b\in H_2(M;K)$. Closed duality represents $\bar b$ by a class of degree one on $M$ with dual coefficients. Its pair cohomology connector maps to the relative duality preimage of $\overline{i_*b}$: extending the cocycle to $W$, the identity $\delta a\cap[W,M]=a|_M\cap[M]+\partial(a\cap[W,M])$ in this degree proves the equality on homology. ## Definition

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Use one-based labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, identifying label $j$ with library coordinate $j-1$. For $T\subseteq[n]$, let $x_{T^c}$ retain the coordinates outside $T$ and vanish on $T$, where $T^c=[n]\setminus T$. Define the best $s$-term $\ell^1$ approximation error by
$$\sigma_s(x)_1:=\min\{\|x_{T^c}\|_1:T\subseteq[n],\ |T|\le s\}.$$
The indexing family is finite and nonempty, so the displayed minimum exists and is attained.

## Definition references

[[def-ip-nullspace-property|One-based coordinate labels and coordinate restrictions]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|The finite-dimensional one-norm]]

[[def-max-min|Minimum of a real set]]

[[lem-finite-set-has-max|Attainment of minima on finite nonempty real sets]]

[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set|Finiteness of the power set of a finite set]]

[[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set|Finiteness of a subfamily of a finite set]]

[[def-countable|Finite-set convention]]

[[def-finite-cardinality|Cardinalities of finite sets, including the empty set]]

[[def-equinumerous|Bijection convention for equinumerous sets]]

[[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor|Every nonzero natural number is a successor]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §2.1 Definition 2.2, printed p. 42, and §4.3](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

[Mendelson, Rauhut, and Ward, *Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions*, §2.1](https://www.mathc.rwth-aachen.de/~rauhut/files/circulant-independent.pdf)

## Remarks

The attainment clause follows from an explicit finite enumeration. The canonical relabeling $j\mapsto j-1$ identifies $[n]$ bijectively with the library index set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, so $[n]$ is finite and its power set is finite; the family $\mathcal T_s:=\{T\subseteq[n]:|T|\le s\}$ is a subset of that power set and is therefore finite. It is nonempty because $\varnothing\in\mathcal T_s$. Since $\mathcal T_s$ is finite, there are a natural number $k$ and a bijection $e:k\to\mathcal T_s$. Nonemptiness implies $k\ne0$, so write $k=\ell+1$. For each $0\le j\le\ell$, put $a_j:=\|x_{e(j)^c}\|_1$. Surjectivity of $e$ gives
$$\{\|x_{T^c}\|_1:T\in\mathcal T_s\}=\{a_0,\ldots,a_\ell\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set of real numbers. Applying the finite-list minimum result to $a_0,\ldots,a_\ell$ gives a minimum that is one of these values, hence belongs to the displayed value set. Therefore the displayed minimum in the Definition is attained.

## Example

Let $a,\sigma>0$ and use the scalar two-point prior assigning mass $1/2$ to each of $-a$ and $a$, whose exact Gaussian posterior-mean map is $D_\sigma(z)=a\tanh(az/\sigma^2)$, where $\tanh(s)=(\exp(s)-\exp(-s))/(\exp(s)+\exp(-s))$. For any tolerance $\eta>0$, choose $b$ with $0<|b|<\eta$ and define the one-pixel convolutional neural network (CNN) map
$$\widetilde D_\sigma(z)=a\tanh(az/\sigma^2)+b.$$
This map is implemented by a $1\times1$ convolution, a $\tanh$ activation, output scaling, and an output bias $b$. It satisfies $\sup_{z\in\mathbb R}|\widetilde D_\sigma(z)-D_\sigma(z)|=|b|<\eta$, while $\widetilde D_\sigma(0)\ne D_\sigma(0)$. It is approximate and does not meet the exact-denoiser hypothesis of the stationarity theorem; this example makes no claim that it lacks some other objective.

## Example references

## Network diagram

For this one-channel, one-pixel input, a $1\times1$ convolution with weight $w$ is scalar multiplication $z\mapsto wz$. The architecture applies weight $a/\sigma^2$, then $\tanh$, then output scaling by $a$ and bias addition by $b$. The arrows depict function composition, and the sequence computes exactly $\widetilde D_\sigma(z)=a\tanh(az/\sigma^2)+b$.

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1.45cm,y=0.8cm,>=stealth]
  \node (input) at (0,0) {$z$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,minimum width=2.3cm,minimum height=0.9cm] (conv) at (2,0) {$1\times1$ conv: $a/\sigma^2$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,minimum width=1.4cm,minimum height=0.9cm] (act) at (4.5,0) {$\tanh$};
  \node[draw,rounded corners,minimum width=2cm,minimum height=0.9cm] (out) at (7,0) {scale $a$, bias $b$};
  \node (result) at (9.2,0) {$\widetilde D_\sigma(z)$};
  \draw[->] (input) -- (conv);
  \draw[->] (conv) -- node[above] {$az/\sigma^2$} (act);
  \draw[->] (act) -- node[above] {$\tanh(az/\sigma^2)$} (out);
  \draw[->] (out) -- (result);
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $a,\sigma,\eta>0$, a nonzero bias $b$ with $|b|<\eta$, and the finite two-point prior and Gaussian likelihood in the Example.

[F1] [[def-dirac-measure]]: $\delta_{x_0}(E)=1$ when $x_0\in E$ and $0$ otherwise.

[F2] [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]: each Dirac set function is a probability measure.

[F3] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$ for all real $x,y$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-tweedie-mmse-jacobian-and-prox-potential]]: for a Borel probability measure not concentrated on an affine hyperplane, the Gaussian posterior-mean map is defined by the normalized likelihood integral and uniquely minimizes posterior squared-error risk.

[F5] [[thm-ip-exact-mmse-pnp-ista-stationarity]]: the stationarity conclusion assumes the plug-in map is exactly the analytic posterior-mean map $D_\sigma$.

## Verification

**Given:** The prior, noise parameter, tolerance, bias, and network map in the Example.

1.1 By [F1]–[F2], $\mu=\frac12\delta_{-a}+\frac12\delta_a$ is a Borel probability. Because $a>0$, the atoms are distinct, each has positive mass, and every affine hyperplane in $\mathbb R$ is a singleton, so $\mu$ is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane. Its posterior mean is $D_\sigma(z)=a\frac{\rho_\sigma(z-a)-\rho_\sigma(z+a)}{\rho_\sigma(z-a)+\rho_\sigma(z+a)}=a\tanh(az/\sigma^2)$, where the second equality follows by factoring the common Gaussian term and using [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 For every $z$, $|\widetilde D_\sigma(z)-D_\sigma(z)|=|b|<\eta$, so the uniform error is $|b|$. At $z=0$, $D_\sigma(0)=0$ while $\widetilde D_\sigma(0)=b\ne0$; hence the network is not the exact MMSE map and [F5] does not apply. No conclusion about a different objective follows. [F4, F5, given, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $a,\sigma,\gamma>0$ and let the scalar prior put mass $1/2$ at each of $-a$ and $a$. Under the Gaussian likelihood kernel $\rho_\sigma(z-u)=\exp(-(z-u)^2/(2\sigma^2))$, its exact posterior-mean map is

The normalizing constant of the Gaussian likelihood cancels in the posterior. For every $z$, $D_\sigma(z)$ uniquely minimizes the posterior squared-error risk and, with the potential $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ constructed from this prior, is the unique global minimizer of $x\mapsto (x-z)^2/2+\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)$.

## Statement

For every $0<\theta_0<\pi$ and open interval $I\subset(0,\pi)$ containing $\theta_0$, there is a smooth oriented knot $K$ with a supplied compact connected oriented genus-four Seifert surface, ordered integral homology basis and positive-push Seifert matrix $V$ such that
$$\operatorname{sign}\bigl((1-e^{i\theta_0})V+(1-e^{-i\theta_0})V^T\bigr)=2,$$
and the same signature is zero for all $\theta\in[0,\pi]\setminus I$. It is nonnegative on $[0,\pi]$, constant equal to two on a neighborhood of $\theta_0$, and symmetric under $\theta\mapsto-\theta$. The surface, basis and knot are given by finite disk-band data; no choice principle or algebraic concordance classification is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The parameter $\theta_0$ and the containing open interval $I$.

[F1] An explicit integral eight-dimensional matrix $V=V_-\oplus(-V_+)$ has exactly the claimed Hermitian signature bump, with $V_\pm=\begin{pmatrix}A&I_2\\0&B_\pm\end{pmatrix}$ and symmetric two-dimensional $A,B_\pm$. Each $V_\pm-V_\pm^T$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0&I_2\\-I_2&0\end{pmatrix}$. [[lem-explicit-integral-seifert-matrices-realize-arbitrarily-small-signature-bumps]]

[F2] Every integral matrix with fixed standard two-dimensional symplectic skew blocks has a finite smooth disk-band realization with its exact positive-push Seifert matrix and a specified homology basis, without choice. [[lem-finite-standard-skew-seifert-matrices-have-choice-free-disk-band-realizations]]

## Proof

1.1 Take the exact matrix $V$ of [F1]. In the first four-dimensional block, replace the coordinate order $(e_1,e_2,f_1,f_2)$ by $(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2)$. In the second block, whose skew part is the negative of the first, use $(e_1,-f_1,e_2,-f_2)$. These define an explicit signed permutation $P$ with $P^T(V-V^T)P=\bigoplus_{j=1}^4\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Thus $W=P^TVP$ meets [F2] exactly. Apply its finite construction with $g=4$ to obtain a smooth one-boundary surface and ordered basis with positive-push matrix $W$. Reorder and reverse the basis cores by the signed permutation $P^{-1}$; their linking numbers change by the corresponding row and column permutations and signs, giving matrix $(P^{-1})^TW P^{-1}=V$ on the same surface. Its oriented boundary is the required knot $K$. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 This actual surface matrix is exactly the integer matrix in [F1], not just an algebraic concordance class or a rational equivalence class. Its Hermitian matrices therefore coincide entry for entry with those in [F1]. The full signature conclusions, including the values at the two jump parameters and at zero, follow from that finite calculation. The surface has genus four and one boundary component by [F2], and every basis change in step 1.1 was an explicit signed permutation. Only finite constructions and the individual integer witnesses of [F1] were used. This proves the stated knot and supplied-surface realization without invoking an arbitrary Seifert-surface choice or any additional axiom. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The conclusion gives an actual knot together with an actual Seifert surface and its signature function. Surface independence, concordance invariance, signature-to-rho formulas, cable reparametrization and companion coefficient-system bookkeeping are separate assertions; none is inferred from this realization lemma.

## Statement

Let $A$ be an indeterminate, $R_A=\mathbb Z[A^{\pm1},(A^{-4}+1)^{-1}]$,
$q=A^{-2}$, $t=q^2=A^{-4}$, $\delta=-(q+q^{-1})=-A^2-A^{-2}$, and
$z_0=-1/(t+1)$. For a nonempty regular diagram $D$, define
$\langle D\rangle$ by summing its crossing smoothings with weights $A$ and
$A^{-1}$ and the factor $\delta^{k-1}$ for a state with $k$ circles. Let
$B_n$ be the $n$-strand Artin braid group with positive geometric generators
$\sigma_i$ (label $i$ passes below the midpoint and label $i+1$ passes above),
drawn with braid parameter increasing from bottom to top; let
$e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism $e(\sigma_i)=1$. Let $H(n)$ be
the type-A Hecke algebra with generators $T_i$, quadratic relation
$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v$, braid relations, and distant commutation; let $\pi_n$
send $\sigma_i$ to $T_i$. Its normalized Markov trace $\operatorname{tr}_n$
satisfies $\operatorname{tr}_n(1)=1$, cyclicity, tower restriction, and
$\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$. Let
$\mathrm{TL}_n$ be the noncrossing pairing algebra with loop value $\delta$,
and let $\operatorname{Tr}_n(D)=\delta^{c(D)}$ be the unnormalized trace,
where $c(D)$ is the number of circles after joining corresponding top and
bottom endpoints outside the rectangle; set
$\tau_n=\delta^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}_n$. For $\beta\in B_n$,
$n\ge1$, orient its closure in the braid direction. Under the specialization
$v\mapsto t$, $z\mapsto z_0$ of the Hecke tower, one has
$$\langle\widehat\beta\rangle =\delta^{n-1}(-A)^{e(\beta)}\operatorname{tr}_n(\pi_n(\beta))\big|_{v=t,\,z=z_0}.$$
The identity gives bracket value $1$ on the one-strand identity closure. Its
positive and negative Markov stabilizations multiply the raw bracket by
$-A^3$ and $-A^{-3}$, respectively.

## Statement references

[Kauffman, *An Invariant of Regular Isotopy* (1990), §III](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kauffman/IRH.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §§4.1–4.4](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Funar, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter 3, §§1.1–2.3](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, an $n$-strand braid $\beta$, the Laurent coefficient ring
$R_A$, and the definitions and relations named below.

[F1] A crossing in the source chart is the A-smoothing with coefficient $A$
plus the B-smoothing with coefficient $A^{-1}$, and the loop value is
$\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$
([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The positive geometric half twist has the explicit diamond path with label
$i$ passing below the midpoint and label $i+1$ above it; the reflected path is
its inverse ([[def-elementary-geometric-half-twist]]).

[F3] $B_n$ is generated by $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{n-1}$ with the Artin
braid and distant-commutation relations, and the closure joins corresponding
top and bottom endpoints with the strand orientations respected
([[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]],
[[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]).

[F4] The vertical identity diagram has $n$ through strands; $e_i$ has a top
cap and bottom cup at positions $i,i+1$; stacking removes each closed loop
with coefficient $\delta$
([[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]).

[F5] The generators satisfy $e_i^2=\delta e_i$,
$e_ie_{i+1}e_i=e_i$, $e_{i+1}e_ie_{i+1}=e_{i+1}$, and distant commutation
([[lem-temperley-lieb-generators-satisfy-local-relations]]).

[F6] The local crossing operators satisfy R2 cancellation and the R3 braid
identity in the declared source chart
([[lem-kauffman-bracket-r2-r3-identities]]).

[F7] The unnormalized diagram closure trace is cyclic,
$\operatorname{Tr}_{n+1}(x\otimes1)=\delta\operatorname{Tr}_n(x)$, and
$\operatorname{Tr}_{n+1}((x\otimes1)e_n)=\operatorname{Tr}_n(x)$;
when $\delta$ is a unit, $\tau_n=\delta^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}_n$
([[def-temperley-lieb-closure-trace-and-partial-trace]],
[[lem-temperley-lieb-closure-trace-component-identities]]).

[F8] The Hecke tower has quadratic relation
$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v$, and its Ocneanu trace satisfies the tower restriction,
cyclicity, and $\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$
([[def-markov-trace-on-the-type-a-hecke-tower]],
[[thm-the-ocneanu-markov-trace-exists-and-is-unique]]).

[F9] The assignment $\sigma_i\mapsto T_i$ is a group homomorphism to Hecke
units, and $T_i^{-1}=v^{-1}T_i+(v^{-1}-1)$
([[lem-the-hecke-generators-satisfy-the-artin-relations-and-are-units]]).

[F10] The Hecke tower has the decomposition
$H(n+1)=H(n)\oplus H(n)T_nH(n)$ as an $H(n)$-bimodule
([[lem-the-hecke-tower-is-free-over-the-previous-level]]).

[F11] The exponent sum is a homomorphism $e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ with
$e(\sigma_i)=1$ ([[def-exponent-sum-of-a-braid]]).

## Proof

1.1 Use source coordinates $(u,v)$ with their standard positive orientation and positive projection coordinates $(t,x)$ on the braid box. For $h>0$, the map $(t,x)=(v,-2hu)$ has determinant $2h>0$. It sends the source over direction $(1,1)$ to $(1,-2h)$ and the source under direction $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is $4h>0$. The source left/right pairs have constant $u$, hence constant braid position $x$ and give the through pairing $I$; the source top/bottom pairs have constant $v$, hence constant braid time $t$ and give the cup-cap $e_i$. The displayed page coordinates $(x,t)$ reverse the positive projection orientation; their visual quarter-turn is not the orientation comparison. Thus its two smoothings are $I$ with weight $A$ and $e_i$ with weight $A^{-1}$. For the opposite crossing the pairings exchange. Hence the local operators are $$C_i=AI+A^{-1}e_i,\qquad C_i^{-}=A^{-1}I+Ae_i.$$ The relations [F5] and [F6] show these operators satisfy the Artin relations and are mutual inverses; distant generators commute by [F5]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, construct]

2.1 Define $\rho_n(\sigma_i)=C_i$ and $S_i:=-A^{-1}C_i=-I-qe_i$. With $t=q^2$ and $\delta=-(q+q^{-1})$, direct multiplication gives $$S_i^2=I+(2q+q^2\delta)e_i=I+(q-q^3)e_i =(t-1)S_i+t.$$ The braid and distant-commutation relations for $S_i$ follow from [F5] and step 1.1; thus $T_i\mapsto S_i$ defines a homomorphism from the Hecke tower specialized at $v=t$ into the diagram algebra. For a braid word, this map sends $\pi_n(\beta)$ to the product of the corresponding $S_i^{\pm1}$. [F5, F8, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The element $A^{-4}+1$ is a unit in $R_A$ and $\delta=-A^2(A^{-4}+1)$ is therefore a unit. Set $\tau_n=\delta^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}_n$. By [F7], $\tau_n(1)=1$, $\tau_{n+1}(x\otimes1)=\tau_n(x)$, and $\tau_n$ is cyclic. Since $S_n=-I-qe_n$, the last closure rule of [F7] gives $$\tau_{n+1}((x\otimes1)S_n) =-\tau_n(x)-q\delta^{-1}\tau_n(x) =-\frac{1}{q^2+1}\tau_n(x)=z_0\tau_n(x).$$ Thus $\tau\circ\rho_H$ satisfies all specialized Markov-trace rules, where $\rho_H(T_i)=S_i$. [F7, F8, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Any specialized Markov trace is determined by its restriction to $H(n)$: on $H(n+1)=H(n)\oplus H(n)T_nH(n)$, restriction determines the first summand, while cyclicity and the Markov rule force $\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_ny)=z_0\operatorname{tr}_n(yx)$ on every product in the second summand. Starting at $H(1)$, induction proves uniqueness, without dividing by any specialized parameter. The scalar extension of the Ocneanu trace exists by [F8], so the trace in step 3.1 equals that specialized trace. [F8, F10, step 3.1, induction, algebra]

5.1 Expand each crossing of $\beta$ by $C_i$ or $C_i^{-}$ and close the resulting Temperley–Lieb diagrams. The unnormalized trace counts each closed state circle with a factor $\delta$, whereas the bracket state sum counts it with $\delta^{|S|-1}$; hence $$\langle\widehat\beta\rangle =\delta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}_n(\rho_n(\beta)) =\delta^{n-1}\tau_n(\rho_n(\beta)).$$ Since $C_i=-A S_i$ and $C_i^{-}=(-A)^{-1}S_i^{-1}$, multiplying along an Artin word gives $\rho_n(\beta)=(-A)^{e(\beta)}\rho_H(\pi_n(\beta))$. Step 4.1 now gives the displayed trace identity. [F1, F3, F7, F9, F11, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The closure of the identity in $B_1$ has one circle; the state sum gives $\delta^{1-1}=1$, and its trace expression gives $\delta^0(-A)^0\operatorname{tr}_1(1)=1$. For positive stabilization, the Markov trace factor is $z_0=-1/(q^2+1)$, so the bracket formula changes by $$(-A)\delta z_0=-A^3.$$ For negative stabilization, [F9] and [F8] give trace factor $$z_-:=t^{-1}(z_0+1-t)=-\frac{q^2}{q^2+1};$$ the bracket formula changes by $$\delta(-A)^{-1}z_-=-A^{-3}.$$ This proves the unknot value and both stabilization normalizations. [F7, F8, F9, F11, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\sigma\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ be globally Lipschitz and nonpolynomial. Let $T:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^a)\to L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)$ be continuous, let $C$ be a compact subset of the input space, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Then a finite Fourier neural operator on $\mathbb T^n$, with finitely many channels and layers, finite Fourier multipliers, continuous periodic bias functions, coordinatewise activation $\sigma$, and a final pointwise affine output map, satisfies
$$\sup_{f\in C}\|T(f)-\Phi(f)\|_{L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-generalized-fourier-neural-operator|The Fourier multiplier layer and generalized FNO architecture.]]

[[lem-ip-finite-dimensional-neural-universal-approximation|Finite-dimensional activation approximation on compact sets.]]

[Kovachki et al., Theorem 5 and Appendix D: complete compact-uniform FNO approximation proof](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume22/21-0806/21-0806.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and $n,a,b,\sigma,T,C,\varepsilon$ as in the statement.

[F1] Fourier characters form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$; finite Fourier projections are contractions converging strongly to the identity. ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]])

[F2] Finite sums of affine hidden units with activation $\sigma$ are uniformly dense in continuous maps on every compact subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. ([[lem-ip-finite-dimensional-neural-universal-approximation]])

[F3] A Fourier neural operator layer can apply any finite Fourier multiplier, inject any continuous periodic bias channel, and apply a pointwise affine map followed by $\sigma$; finite compositions with an affine output map have the architecture stated above. ([[def-ip-generalized-fourier-neural-operator]])

[A1] Countable Choice is used by the Fourier-basis supplier for completed Lebesgue $L^2$, including density of continuous periodic functions and Hilbert completeness. The finite coefficient extraction, finite-dimensional neural approximation and synthesis steps require only finite choices. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and the data in the statement.

1.1 If $C=\varnothing$, the zero operator from [F3] suffices. Otherwise let $P_N$ be the orthogonal projection onto real Fourier modes of frequency at most $N$. Strong convergence in [F1] is uniform on compact $C$: for $\eta>0$, choose a finite $\eta/3$-net $f_1,\ldots,f_s$ for $C$, then take $N$ so that $\|P_Nf_i-f_i\|_2<\eta/3$ for every $i$. For $f$ within $\eta/3$ of $f_i$, contraction of $I-P_N$ gives $\|(I-P_N)f\|_2<2\eta/3$. Hence $\sup_{f\in C}\|P_Nf-f\|_2\to0$. [A1, F1, F3, given, choose]

2.1 For each $f\in C$, let $m(f)$ be the least nonnegative integer such that $T$ has oscillation less than $\varepsilon/8$ on $B(f,2^{-m(f)})$, and set $r_f=2^{-m(f)}$. Continuity ensures that such an integer exists, so this defines all radii canonically without a simultaneous choice. Choose a finite subcover $B(f_i,r_i/2)$ of $C$ by the HALF-radius balls, and take a positive $\delta<\min_i r_i/4$. By step 1.1, increase $N$ until $\sup_{f\in C}\|P_Nf-f\|_2<\delta$. For every $f\in C$ choose $i$ with $\|f-f_i\|_2<r_i/2$; then $\|P_Nf-f_i\|_2<3r_i/4$, so both points lie in the full continuity ball $B(f_i,r_i)$ and $\|T(P_Nf)-T(f)\|_2<\varepsilon/8<\varepsilon/4$. The set $P_NC$ and its continuous image $T(P_NC)$ are compact. Fourier projections converge uniformly on the latter by the finite-net argument of step 1.1, so choose $M$ with $\sup_{z\in P_NC}\|P_MT(z)-T(z)\|_2<\varepsilon/4$. [F1, step 1.1, given, choose]

3.1 The range of $P_N$ is finite dimensional. In a real orthonormal trigonometric basis, define $g:P_NC\to\mathbb R^q$ by listing the coefficients of $P_MT(z)$. By [F2], approximate $g$ uniformly on compact $P_NC$ by a finite $\sigma$-network with Euclidean coefficient error less than $\varepsilon/8$; orthonormality makes the corresponding output-polynomial error less than $\varepsilon/8$ in $L^2$. [F2, step 2.1]

4.1 First apply the finite Fourier multiplier $P_N$ from step 2.1, retaining the WHOLE real Fourier polynomial, including both sine and cosine components of each nonzero frequency. Its coefficient vectors lie in a compact set, so all its pointwise values are uniformly bounded. Inject the finitely many retained real basis functions $\varphi_j(x)$ as periodic bias channels. The multiplication map $(z,t)\mapsto zt$ is continuous on the compact ranges of $(P_Nf)(x)$ and $\varphi_j(x)$; approximate it by the pointwise networks of [F2], then use a zero-frequency multiplier to average each product. Since $\int(P_Nf)(x)\varphi_j(x)\,dx$ is exactly the real coefficient of $\varphi_j$, these constant channels approximate ALL desired coefficients without using an impossible translation-invariant cosine-only projection. Mandatory activations can be passed with arbitrarily small error on these bounded channels: choose $c$ with $\sigma'(c)\ne0$, encode $z$ as $c+\tau z$, and decode affinely by $(\sigma(c+\tau z)-\sigma(c))/(\tau\sigma'(c))$, which converges uniformly to $z$ on every bounded interval as $\tau\to0$. Approximate the finite products and implement the coefficient network from step 3.1 using finitely many such layers. At each stage uniform continuity on the compact finite coefficient ranges propagates arbitrarily small errors through the finite composition; zero-mode averaging has norm one. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Inject the finitely many output basis functions $\varphi_k(x)$ as periodic bias channels. The output coefficient vector from step 4.1 ranges over a compact set; the continuous map from that vector and $(\varphi_k(x))_k$ to $\sum_kc_k\varphi_k(x)$ is uniformly approximated on their compact product by [F2]. The final affine output approximates this output Fourier polynomial with arbitrarily small uniform, hence $L^2$, error because normalized torus measure is one. [F2, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Choose the coefficient-extraction and Fourier-synthesis errors in steps 4.1–5.1 so their sum is less than $\varepsilon/4$. Combining this with the input truncation, output truncation and finite coefficient-map errors from steps 2.1 and 3.1 yields $\sup_{f\in C}\|T(f)-\Phi(f)\|_2<\varepsilon/4+\varepsilon/4+\varepsilon/8+\varepsilon/4<\varepsilon$. All cutoffs and channel counts are finite. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $h\in\mathbb R^n$ use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$. In real scalar expressions, a natural number denotes its canonical real image. Order the coordinates by decreasing $|h_j|$, breaking ties by increasing $j$. Let $S$ consist of the first $s$ indices, and partition $S^c$ in this same order into consecutive nonempty blocks $T_1,\ldots,T_q$ of size $s$, with only the last block possibly smaller; if $S^c=\varnothing$, take $q=0$. Then
$$\|h_{S^c}\|_2\le \|h_S\|_2+\frac{\|h_{S^c}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-nullspace-property|One-based finite coordinate restrictions]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one- and two-norms]]

[[def-canonical-natural|Canonical real image of the natural scalar $s$]]

[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics|Triangle inequality for the finite-dimensional two-norm]]

[[lem-of-naturals-positive|Positivity and strict increase of canonical natural scalars]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §4.3, proof of Theorem 4.25, printed pp. 89–90](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

[Mendelson, Rauhut, and Ward, *Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions*, §2.1, Theorem 2.2, printed p. 5](https://www.mathc.rwth-aachen.de/~rauhut/files/circulant-independent.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $n\ge1$, $1\le s\le n$, a vector $h\in\mathbb R^n$, the deterministic ordered coordinate list $j_1,\ldots,j_n$, its first-$s$ set $S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_s\}$, and the finite successive tail blocks $T_1,\ldots,T_q$.

[F1] [[def-ip-nullspace-property]]: $h_S$ agrees with $h$ on $S$ and is zero on $S^c$; the coordinate labels are one-based with label $j$ identified with library coordinate $j-1$.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|v\|_1=\sum_j|v_j|$ and $\|v\|_2=(\sum_j|v_j|^2)^{1/2}$ on finite-dimensional real coordinate spaces.

[F3] [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]: $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm and obeys the triangle inequality.

[F4] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums preserve termwise inequalities and a sum of nonnegative terms is nonnegative.

[F5] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]: for nonnegative $a,b$, $a^2\le b^2$ implies $a\le b$.

[F6] [[def-canonical-natural]]: a natural number used as a real scalar denotes its canonical real image.

[F7] [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]: the canonical real image of $s$ is positive for $s\ge1$; if $k_r\le s$ as natural numbers, then their canonical real images satisfy $k_r\le s$.

## Proof
1.1 If $q=0$, then $S^c=\varnothing$ and the conclusion is $0\le\|h_S\|_2$. If $q\ge1$, write $r=|T_1|\le s$. The order gives $T_1=\{j_{s+1},\ldots,j_{s+r}\}$ and $S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_s\}$, with $|h_{j_{s+k}}|\le|h_{j_k}|$ for every $1\le k\le r$. Termwise squaring and finite-sum monotonicity therefore give $\|h_{T_1}\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^r|h_{j_{s+k}}|^2\le\sum_{k=1}^r|h_{j_k}|^2\le\sum_{k=1}^s|h_{j_k}|^2=\|h_S\|_2^2.$ Both norms are nonnegative, so [F5] gives $\|h_{T_1}\|_2\le\|h_S\|_2$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 For each $2\le r\le q$, the preceding block $T_{r-1}$ has size $s$. Its last ordered coordinate has magnitude no greater than any earlier entry, hence no greater than the average magnitude on $T_{r-1}$. Every entry of $T_r$ is no greater than that last entry. Put $c=\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1/s$. Then each entry of $T_r$ has magnitude at most $c$. If $k_r=|T_r|$, termwise comparison gives
$$\|h_{T_r}\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in T_r}|h_j|^2\le k_r c^2\le s c^2=\frac{\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1^2}{s},$$
using $k_r\le s$ as natural numbers: padding the sum of $k_r$ copies of the nonnegative number $c^2$ by the remaining nonnegative copies gives the sum of $s$ copies, by [F4]; [F6,F7] interpret these counts as real scalars. Since both sides are nonnegative, [F5] gives $\|h_{T_r}\|_2\le\frac{\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$ The blocks are disjoint and finite. By [F6], [F7], the triangle inequality, step 1.1, and this block bound, $\|h_{S^c}\|_2=\Big\|\sum_{r=1}^q h_{T_r}\Big\|_2\le\sum_{r=1}^q\|h_{T_r}\|_2\le\|h_S\|_2+\frac1{\sqrt{s}}\sum_{r=1}^{q-1}\|h_{T_r}\|_1\le\|h_S\|_2+\frac{\|h_{S^c}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$ This proves the claimed estimate, including a final block smaller than $s$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The tie-breaking rule makes the block partition deterministic. The proof uses only finite coordinate comparisons and the Euclidean triangle inequality; no choice axiom is used.

## Statement

Let $A$ be an indeterminate and $n\ge2$. In a vertical $n$-strand braid box
whose longitudinal parameter increases from bottom to top, let $I$ be the
straight tangle and, for
$1\le i<n$, let $e_i$ be the cup-cap tangle with a cap at the top and a cup
at the bottom on strands $i,i+1$, and straight strands elsewhere. Each closed
loop has value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. For the positive crossing, use positive projection coordinates $(t,x)$, with $t$ longitudinal and $x$ transverse, and over and under tangent vectors $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$ for $h>0$. Transport the source chart by $(t,x)=(v,-2hu)$: its A-smoothing is the left/right pairing with coefficient $A$, giving $I$, and its B-smoothing is the top/bottom pairing with coefficient $A^{-1}$, giving $e_i$. Set
$$C_i:=AI+A^{-1}e_i.$$
For the opposite crossing, the smoothings exchange their through and cup-cap
pairings; set
$$C_i^{-}:=A^{-1}I+Ae_i.$$
Then $C_iC_i^{-}=C_i^{-}C_i=I$, and for adjacent strands
$$C_iC_{i+1}C_i=C_{i+1}C_iC_{i+1}.$$
Consequently the bracket is unchanged by every local Reidemeister II or III
replacement; arbitrary strand orientations do not change these unoriented
tangle identities.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8, line cap=round]
  \draw (-0.35,-0.25) rectangle (2.35,1.25);
  \foreach \x in {0,1,2} {
    \fill (\x,1) circle (1.4pt);
    \fill (\x,0) circle (1.4pt);
  }
  \draw (0,1) .. controls (0,0.68) and (1,0.68) .. (1,1);
  \draw (0,0) .. controls (0,0.32) and (1,0.32) .. (1,0);
  \draw (2,0) -- (2,1);
  \node[above] at (0,1.06) {$t_1$};
  \node[above] at (1,1.06) {$t_2$};
  \node[above] at (2,1.06) {$t_3$};
  \node[below] at (0,-0.06) {$b_1$};
  \node[below] at (1,-0.06) {$b_2$};
  \node[below] at (2,-0.06) {$b_3$};
  \node at (1,-0.55) {$e_1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

The picture names the cap, cup, and through strand that define $e_1$; the
algebraic equalities above are proved below without using the picture as an
inference.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves|Oriented Reidemeister moves]]

[Kauffman, *An Invariant of Regular Isotopy* (1990), §III, printed pp. 430–432](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kauffman/IRH.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §4.1](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Funar, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter 3, §1.2](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular link diagram with one of the local R2 or R3 replacements described in the statement.

[F1] In the source crossing chart, the A-smoothing has weight $A$, the B-smoothing has weight $A^{-1}$, and a closed trivial loop has value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The identity $I$ is the vertical through tangle; $e_i$ is the cap on top and cup on bottom, stacking removes loops with coefficient $\delta$, and the stacking product is associative and bilinear ([[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]], [[thm-temperley-lieb-diagram-category-laws]]).

[F3] The generators satisfy $e_i^2=\delta e_i$, $e_ie_{i+1}e_i=e_i$, $e_{i+1}e_ie_{i+1}=e_{i+1}$, and distant generators commute ([[lem-temperley-lieb-generators-satisfy-local-relations]]).

[F4] R2 creates or deletes two opposite crossings, and every allowed R3 has a strict height order with the cyclic over/under pattern excluded ([[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]).

## Proof
1.1 Use source coordinates $(u,v)$ with their standard positive orientation and positive projection coordinates $(t,x)$ on the braid box. For $h>0$, the map $(t,x)=(v,-2hu)$ has determinant $2h>0$. It sends the source over direction $(1,1)$ to $(1,-2h)$ and the source under direction $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is $4h>0$. The source left/right pairs have constant $u$, hence constant braid position $x$ and give the through pairing $I$; the source top/bottom pairs have constant $v$, hence constant braid time $t$ and give the cup-cap $e_i$. The displayed page coordinates $(x,t)$ reverse the positive projection orientation; their visual quarter-turn is not the orientation comparison. For the opposite crossing, rotating the source chart by a positive quarter-turn exchanges the two endpoint pairings, so its A/B smoothings are respectively $e_i$ and $I$. By [F1] these expansions are $C_i=AI+A^{-1}e_i$ and $C_i^{-}=A^{-1}I+Ae_i$. Using [F2] and [F3], $$C_iC_i^{-}=(AI+A^{-1}e_i)(A^{-1}I+Ae_i)=I+(A^2+A^{-2}+\delta)e_i=I.$$ The same multiplication in the other order gives $C_i^{-}C_i=I$, since both factors are polynomials in $e_i$. Thus the two opposite crossings in an R2 pair cancel in either order. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Put $x=e_i$ and $y=e_{i+1}$. Expanding and using [F3] gives $$C_iC_{i+1}C_i=A^3I+A(2x+y)+A^{-1}(xy+yx+\delta x)+A^{-3}x,$$ while interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives $$C_{i+1}C_iC_{i+1}=A^3I+A(2y+x)+A^{-1}(yx+xy+\delta y)+A^{-3}y.$$ Their difference is $A^{-1}(A^2+\delta+A^{-2})(x-y)=0$. Hence the two sides of the braid-like R3 move have equal bracket operators. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Near the three-strand event, choose a linear longitudinal coordinate nonzero on each of the three tangent lines, shrink the event disk, and orient the unoriented local tracks in its increasing direction. All three tracks are then monotone; these temporary arrows do not affect the bracket. Label the tracks $1,2,3$ at the incoming end. The two R3 sides meet their pairs in orders $(12,13,23)$ and $(23,13,12)$, and a strict height order permits exactly the exponent triples $+++, --- , ++-, -++, +--, --+$. The triples $+-+$ and $-+-$ would require a cyclic height order. Put $a=C_i$ and $b=C_{i+1}$. Besides $aba=bab$ from step 1.2 and its inverse from step 1.1, the four needed identities are $$ab a^{-1}=b^{-1}ab,\qquad a^{-1}ba=bab^{-1},\qquad ab^{-1}a^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}b,\qquad a^{-1}b^{-1}a=ba^{-1}b^{-1}.$$ The first follows by multiplying $aba=bab$ on the left by $b^{-1}$ and on the right by $a^{-1}$; the second follows by multiplying on the left by $a^{-1}$ and on the right by $b^{-1}$; the last two are their inverses. Thus each of the six height orders gives equality with exactly its actual over/under choices. For R2, choose a longitudinal coordinate along the common tangent at the bigon event, shrink the disk, and temporarily orient both tracks increasingly; the two local crossings have opposite types and cancel by step 1.1. Reversing any original strand arrow leaves all smoothing weights unchanged. Tensoring or stacking with the unchanged exterior preserves each equality by bilinearity and associativity, proving every R2/R3 variant. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic different from $2$, and let $L,M\in SL_2(F)$ commute. Write $t=\operatorname{tr}M$ and suppose $\Delta=t^2-4\ne0$. Give the torus $T^2$ an ordered pair of based oriented generating loops $(\lambda,\mu)$, and give its adjoint local system intrinsic monodromies $P=\operatorname{Ad}L$ and $Q=\operatorname{Ad}M$ on $V=\mathfrak{sl}_2(F)$. Here monodromy acts on column coefficient vectors on the left. Set
$$v=M-\frac t2 I,\qquad W=\{X\in V:\operatorname{tr}(vX)=0\}.$$
Then $V=Fv\oplus W$, both summands are preserved by $P,Q$, and $P,Q$ are the identity on $Fv$. There is an explicit split chain model
$$0\longrightarrow V\xrightarrow{d_2}V\oplus V\xrightarrow{d_1}V\longrightarrow0,$$
where $d_2z=((I-Q)z,(P-I)z)$ and $d_1(x,y)=(P-I)x+(Q-I)y$, in the ordered edge coordinates $(\lambda,\mu)$. Its $W$ subcomplex is contractible, so
$$H_0(T^2;V)=F[v],\qquad H_1(T^2;V)=F[v\otimes\lambda]\oplus F[v\otimes\mu],\qquad H_2(T^2;V)=F[v\otimes[T^2]].$$
In particular the two displayed peripheral classes are an actual basis, without imposing any norm-one normalization on $v$. The splitting, contraction and classes commute with field extensions and simultaneous conjugation of $L,M$. All their matrix entries are rational expressions in the entries of $L,M$, with denominators powers of $2$ and $\Delta$. This assertion concerns boundary-torus homology only: it makes no claim about the rank of its inclusion into the homology of a knot exterior.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, commuting matrices, nonzero discriminant, ordered torus generators and specified left intrinsic monodromies in the Statement.

[F1] Cellular chains with local coefficients compute intrinsic singular local homology; for supplied lifts their boundary is the signed attaching-incidence matrix acting by the specified monodromies ([[thm-cellular-chains-compute-homology-with-local-coefficients]]). We use its left coefficient convention and do not regard a left action as a right action without inversion.

## Proof

1.1 **The fixed line and a rational complementary plane.** The direct $2\times2$ determinant identity gives $M^2-tM+I=0$, and therefore $v^2=(\Delta/4)I$, $\operatorname{tr}v=0$, and $\operatorname{tr}(v^2)=\Delta/2\ne0$. In particular $v\ne0$. The map $\pi:V\to Fv$ defined by $\pi(X)=2\operatorname{tr}(vX)v/\Delta$ is a projection: $\pi(v)=v$, its image is $Fv$ and its kernel is $W$. Thus $V=Fv\oplus W$. Commutation of $L,M$ implies $P(v)=Q(v)=v$. For either $A=L$ or $A=M$, the direct identity $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(vAXA^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}vAX)=\operatorname{tr}(vX)$. Hence $P,Q$ preserve $W$ and commute with $\pi$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **An actual inverse on the complementary plane.** On $W$ the inverse of $Q-I$ is the explicit operator $R=(Q+(3-t^2)I)/\Delta$. To check this without a splitting-field assumption, the polynomial $z^2-tz+1$ either has a root in $F$ or is irreducible, in which case its quotient gives a quadratic extension. In that field its two distinct roots are $r,r^{-1}$, and a change of basis diagonalizes $M$, since the two kernels of $M-rI$ and $M-r^{-1}I$ are distinct one-dimensional subspaces. In these coordinates $v=\operatorname{diag}((r-r^{-1})/2,-(r-r^{-1})/2)$, $W$ is exactly the off-diagonal plane, and $Q$ has eigenvalues $r^2,r^{-2}$ on it. Consequently $Q^2-(t^2-2)Q+I=0$ on $W$, and multiplication gives $(Q-I)(Q+(3-t^2)I)=\Delta I$ there. This identity descends to $F$, because scalar extension of a finite matrix over a field is injective. The two factors commute, so $R$ is a two-sided inverse. It commutes with $P$ because $P$ commutes with $Q$. This finite calculation uses no chosen eigenvectors in the final formulas. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

2.2 **The actual torus chain complex.** Use one vertex, the two oriented edges and the square whose attaching path is $\lambda\mu\lambda^{-1}\mu^{-1}$. Lift its lower left corner and transport a coefficient from that corner along its four sides. The bottom and oppositely oriented top edges give coefficients $z$ and $-Qz$ in the $\lambda$ coordinate; the right and oppositely oriented left edges give $Pz$ and $-z$ in the $\mu$ coordinate. Thus the square boundary is $((I-Q)z,(P-I)z)$. An edge with monodromy $S$ has boundary $(S-I)$ on its coefficient, which gives $d_1$ as stated. The two composites cancel because $PQ=QP$. This is the supplied-lift cellular model in [F1], so it computes the actual intrinsic homology, rather than an independently assumed complex. The direct-sum decomposition of step1.1 splits this entire complex into its $Fv$ and $W$ parts. [F1, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 **A chain contraction, including both ends of the complex.** On the $W$ part define $h_0:W\to W\oplus W$ by $h_0(z)=(0,Rz)$ and $h_1:W\oplus W\to W$ by $h_1(x,y)=-Rx$, and put all other homotopy maps zero. Then $d_1h_0=I$. Also $h_1d_2=R(Q-I)=I$. Finally $d_2h_1(x,y)=(x,-(P-I)Rx)$ and $h_0d_1(x,y)=(0,R(P-I)x+y)$; their sum is $(x,y)$ because $R$ commutes with $P$. Thus $dh+hd=I$ in each of degrees $0,1,2$. The $W$ summand contributes no homology. On $Fv$ both differentials vanish, leaving one, two and one copies of $Fv$ in those degrees. Their cycles are precisely the vertex, the two supplied oriented edges, and the supplied oriented square with coefficient $v$. This proves the stated basis and not merely a dimension count. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Compatibility and exact scope.** For a field extension, the same formulas for $v,\pi,R,d,h$ remain defined because $2$ and $\Delta$ remain nonzero; the split contractible and zero-differential summands persist, so their classes identify the actual extended homology. For simultaneous conjugation by an invertible matrix $A$, the map $X\mapsto AXA^{-1}$ sends $v$ to the new $v$, intertwines $P,Q$, and preserves all traces in $\pi$; it therefore carries the splitting and contraction to the displayed new ones and takes each named peripheral cycle to its corresponding cycle. The formulas use only addition, multiplication and division by $2$ and $\Delta$ in the entries of the original matrices (the inverse of an $SL_2$ matrix is its polynomial adjugate). The eigenvalue extension in step2.1 verified an identity, and supplies no extra scalar choice to these formulas. The hypothesis $\Delta\ne0$ excludes the parabolic and scalar cases; neither their homology nor any exterior inclusion rank is asserted. All conclusions, including the fixed order of the two peripheral classes, follow. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. For every word $w$ in the generators of a finitely presented group $G$, the function $\rho\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(\rho(w))$ is a regular function on $\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2(\mathbb C))$ and is invariant under simultaneous conjugation.

## Statement references

[Bénard, Florens, and Rodau, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151)

[Tillmann, §§4.2–4.4](https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a finite presentation of $G$, its affine representation variety, and a word $w$ in the generators and their inverses.

[F1] For the given finite presentation, impose determinant-one equations and the matrix-entry relator equations in the finite generator matrix space. By the inverse formula [F2], these are polynomial equations for every finitely presented group, not just a knot group.

[F2] If $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$, then $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$, as verified by direct multiplication using $ad-bc=1$.

## Proof

1.1 The equations of [F1] cut out exactly the representation tuples, since a generator assignment satisfies them precisely when it respects every presented relator. Evaluate $w$ by multiplying its generator matrices and the adjugates for inverse letters from [F2]. Each entry of the resulting matrix is a polynomial in the representation coordinates, so its trace is regular. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 For any $P\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$, conjugation sends the word matrix $W$ to $PWP^{-1}$. The identity $\operatorname{tr}(PWP^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(WP^{-1}P)=\operatorname{tr}(W)$ proves invariance. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Thus each word trace defines an element of the conjugation-invariant coordinate ring of the representation variety. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a design $d$ in a design-indexed dominated inverse experiment, with prior $\mu_0$, likelihood density $p_d(y\mid\theta)$ relative to the common sigma-finite measure $\nu$, predictive density $p_d(y)$, and posterior $\mu_d^y$ on $G_d=\{y:0<p_d(y)<\infty\}$. Let $P_d$ be the joint law of $(\theta,Y)$, so on measurable rectangles
$$P_d(A\times B)=\int_B\int_Ap_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)\,\nu(dy),$$
let $P_{Y\mid d}(B)=\int_Bp_d(y)\,\nu(dy)$, and let $Q_d=\mu_0\otimes P_{Y\mid d}$. Then
$$\operatorname{EIG}(d)=D(P_d\|Q_d)\in[0,+\infty].$$
On $G_d$, the Radon–Nikodym density $dP_d/dQ_d$ is $p_d(y\mid\theta)/p_d(y)$ almost everywhere. The identity is valid as an extended integral: its negative part is finite, its positive part may be infinite, and no subtraction of two infinite entropies occurs.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-design-indexed-inverse-experiment|The common proper prior, dominated likelihood, predictive density, and posterior on positive finite evidence fibers.]]

[[def-ip-expected-information-gain|EIG is the prior-predictive expectation of posterior-to-prior KL divergence.]]

[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence|KL is the directional RN log-density integral with a finite negative part.]]

[[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels|The predictive density and posterior kernel identities hold on positive finite evidence fibers, and exceptional fibers have zero predictive mass.]]

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

[MacKay, §2](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement, including AC and the finite design-indexed dominated experiment.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice supplies the Radon–Nikodym convention used by the library KL definition. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A design-indexed experiment has a proper prior, a jointly measurable probability-kernel density, predictive density $p_d(y)=\int p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)$, and posterior $\mu_d^y(d\theta)=p_d(y\mid\theta)\mu_0(d\theta)/p_d(y)$ on positive finite evidence fibers. [[def-ip-design-indexed-inverse-experiment]]

[F2] For a dominated probability kernel, the observation marginal has density $p_d$ and the posterior formula is a conditional-law version on $0<p_d<\infty$; the zero and infinite normalizer fibers have zero marginal mass. [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]]

[F3] Tonelli's theorem makes section integrals measurable and equates a nonnegative product integral with either iterated integral on sigma-finite measure spaces. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F4] Measures on a sigma-finite product that agree on the generating measurable rectangles agree on the product sigma-algebra. [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]]

[F5] A nonnegative measurable function with integral zero vanishes almost everywhere. [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]

[F6] For $P\ll Q$ with RN derivative $r$, $D(P\|Q)=\int r\log r\,dQ$ with $0\log0=0$ and finite negative part; on a probability space, $\int (r\log r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$. [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]

[F7] KL divergence between probability measures is nonnegative. [[thm-kullback-leibler-is-nonnegative]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1] and [F3], Tonelli gives $\int_{\mathsf Y}p_d(y)\,\nu(dy)=\int_\Theta\int_{\mathsf Y}p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\nu(dy)\,\mu_0(d\theta)=1$. Thus $P_{Y\mid d}$ is a probability measure and $p_d(y)<\infty$ for $\nu$-almost every $y$. By [F2], its mass on $\{p_d=0\}\cup\{p_d=\infty\}$ is zero, and the posterior formula in [F1] is the conditional-law version on $G_d$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The joint law $P_d$ has density $p_d(y\mid\theta)$ relative to $\mu_0\otimes\nu$ by [F2]. For a measurable rectangle $A\times B$, $Q_d(A\times B)=\mu_0(A)\int_Bp_d(y)\,\nu(dy)=\int_{A\times B}p_d(y)\,d(\mu_0\otimes\nu)$, so [F4] makes $p_d(y)$ the density of $Q_d$ on the full product sigma-algebra. On $G_d$ define $r_d(\theta,y)=p_d(y\mid\theta)/p_d(y)$, and set it to zero elsewhere and on any product-null set where $p_d(y\mid\theta)=\infty$. The latter set is null because the joint density has total integral one. On $\{p_d=0\}$, [F1] gives $\int_\Theta p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)=0$, so [F5] makes the joint density zero for $\mu_0$-almost every $\theta$ on that fiber. The $\{p_d=\infty\}$ fibers are $\nu$-null by step 1.1. Consequently, for every product-measurable set $C$, $\int_C r_d\,dQ_d=\int_Cp_d(y\mid\theta)\,d(\mu_0\otimes\nu)=P_d(C)$, so $r_d=dP_d/dQ_d$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For each $y\in G_d$, [F1] makes $r_d(\cdot,y)$ a probability density relative to $\mu_0$, so [F6] gives $D(\mu_d^y\|\mu_0)=\int r_d(\theta,y)\log r_d(\theta,y)\,\mu_0(d\theta)$ and bounds the fiber's negative part by $1/e$. Weighting by $p_d(y)$ and using step 1.1 bounds the full negative part by $\frac1e\int_{G_d}p_d(y)\,\nu(dy)=1/e$. Tonelli [F3] on the positive and negative parts separately, together with the product density in step 2.1, therefore gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d)=\int r_d\log r_d\,dQ_d$ with finite negative part and possibly infinite positive part. [F1, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Substituting the fiber identity from step 3.1 into the definition of EIG and using the separate Tonelli exchanges from that step gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d)=\int r_d\log r_d\,dQ_d$. By [F6] and step 2.1, this is $D(P_d\|Q_d)$; [F7] gives nonnegativity. The finite negative part from step 3.1 rules out an $\infty-\infty$ subtraction, proving the stated extended identity. [A1, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.06020v2"

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty simple Riemannian background of dimension $n\ge2$, with smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $q_1,q_2\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ;\mathbb R)$ be static interior potentials. Suppose the full time-dependent forward Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps for $\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q_1$ and $\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q_2$ agree for every smooth Dirichlet input compactly supported in $(0,T)\times\partial M$. Let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M$ be any unit-speed geodesic segment with $\gamma(0),\gamma(L)\in\partial M$, $\gamma((0,L))\subset M^\circ$, directed inward at $0$ and outward at $L$, and with length $0<L<T$. Then
$$\int_0^L(q_1-q_2)(\gamma(s))\,ds=0.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-simple-riemannian-background]]

[[def-ip-hyperbolic-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]

[[lem-ip-wave-alessandrini-identity]]

[[lem-ip-simple-geometry-global-eikonal-geometric-optics]]

[[def-countable-choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two real static interior potentials on the stated simple manifold, equal full forward DN maps on all smooth time-compact inputs, and a maximal unit-speed ray of length $L<T$.

[F1] [[lem-ip-wave-alessandrini-identity]] gives the bilinear forward/terminal identity with outward classical traces.

[F2] [[lem-ip-simple-geometry-global-eikonal-geometric-optics]] gives exact smooth forward and terminal waves with time-compact smooth boundary traces, uniformly bounded approximate $L^2$ norms, vanishing $L^2$ correction errors, and the unweighted ray-product limit.

[F3] [[def-ip-hyperbolic-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]] specifies equality on the entire smooth time-compact boundary input space and the terminal map convention.

## Proof

1.1 First use [F1] with both potentials equal to a single real $q$. Its left side is zero, so for every $h,k$ in the boundary input space $$\int_\Sigma k\Lambda_q^+h\,dS_gdt=\int_\Sigma h\Lambda_q^-k\,dS_gdt.$$ This is a bilinear transposition identity and uses exactly the classical forward and terminal solutions, whose endpoint terms vanish. Therefore the right side of [F1] for $q_1,q_2$ equals $\int_\Sigma k(\Lambda_{q_1}^+-\Lambda_{q_2}^+)h\,dS_gdt$, which is zero under the assumed equality of forward maps. Hence $\int_Q(q_1-q_2)uv\,dV_gdt=0$ for every admitted forward $q_1$ wave and terminal $q_2$ wave. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Choose $t_0\in(0,T-L)$ and insert the exact waves of [F2] into step 1.1. Their boundary traces belong to the full input space for each $\lambda$, so the zero identity applies without a limit or density assumption on boundary data. The product convergence of [F2], with $A(t,x)=q_1(x)-q_2(x)$, gives $$0=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\int_Q(q_1-q_2)u_{1,\lambda}u_{2,\lambda}\,dV_gdt=\int_0^L(q_1-q_2)(\gamma(s))\,ds.$$ The test is legitimate either by [F2]'s closed-cylinder conclusion or by a temporal cutoff equal to one on all approximate packets; its omitted exact-product terms contain vanishing correction factors. Since the ray was arbitrary subject to $L<T$, every claimed ray integral is determined. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

For every separable real Banach space $X$, Borel set $D\subseteq X$, and Borel probability $\mu_0$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$ and positive mass on a bounded subset of $D$. Give $D$ the relative norm topology. Let $\Phi,\Phi_N:D\to\mathbb R$ be finite continuous potentials indexed by integers $N\ge1$, let $M_1,M_2:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Borel and nondecreasing, and let $\psi_N\ge0$ tend to zero. If $\Phi,\Phi_N\ge-M_1(\|u\|_X)$ and $|\Phi_N(u)-\Phi(u)|\le M_2(\|u\|_X)\psi_N$ for every $u,N$, and their evidence normalizers are positive and finite, then there are $C<\infty$ and $N_0$ such that the library root-L2 Hellinger distance satisfies $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\le C\psi_N$ for every $N\ge N_0$, even without assuming $\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}(1+M_2(\|u\|_X)^2)\,d\mu_0<\infty$.

## Statement references
