[[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws|The library Hellinger distance is the root-L2 norm of the difference of square-root densities.]]

[[def-banach-space|A Banach space is complete for its norm metric.]]

[[def-separable-space|A separable space has an at most countable dense subset.]]

[[def-norm-and-normed-space|A norm induces the metric used on the parameter space.]]

[[def-borel-sigma-algebra|The Borel sigma-algebra is generated by open sets.]]

[[def-probability-measure|A probability measure has total mass one.]]

[[def-metric-topology|The metric topology declares a set open when every point has an open ball inside it.]]

[[def-subspace-topology-top|The relative topology consists of intersections of ambient open sets with the subspace.]]

[[def-continuous-map-top|Continuity means inverse images of open sets are open.]]

[Dashti and Stuart, full lecture notes, §4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.6989)

[Cotter, Dashti, and Stuart, full paper, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0909.2126)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A counterexample is required to the no-integrability claim in Statement refuted.

[F1] For a fixed-data potential, $Z=\int e^{-\Phi}\,d\mu_0$ and the posterior density relative to $\mu_0$ is $e^{-\Phi}/Z$ on positive finite evidence fibers. [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F2] For supplied densities $p,q$ relative to the same measure, the library Hellinger distance satisfies $h^2=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu_0$. [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]]

[F3] The series $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$ converges, while $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-1}$ diverges. [[thm-p-series-rational]]

[F4] The valid potential-discretization result assumes $\int e^{M_1}(1+M_2^2)\,d\mu_0<\infty$ to conclude a linear Hellinger rate. [[thm-ip-posterior-potential-discretization-error]]

[F5] The real exponential is continuous and strictly increasing, with $e^{-x}=1/e^x$ and $e^1>1$. [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]

[F6] The real line with its absolute-value metric is a separable Banach space. For each $n\ge1$, the intervals $(x-|x-n|/2,x+|x-n|/2)$, indexed by $x\ne n$, cover $\mathbb R\setminus\{n\}$ and omit $n$, so $\{n\}$ is closed. Hence $D=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{n\}$ is Borel. Also $(n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)\cap D=\{n\}$ for each $n\ge1$, so every singleton is relatively open, $D$ is discrete, and every real-valued function on $D$ is continuous. [[def-banach-space]], [[def-separable-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]], [[def-continuous-map-top]]

[F7] The assigned values of $\mu_0$ are nonnegative, and the empty set has measure zero by the empty sum. For pairwise disjoint Borel sets $A_j\subseteq\mathbb R$, the nonnegative series in the definition of $\mu_0$ partitions across the disjoint sets $A_j\cap D$, so $\mu_0(\bigcup_j A_j)=\sum_j\mu_0(A_j)$. By [F3], $c>0$ is finite and $c\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}=1$, hence $\mu_0$ is a Borel probability measure with $\mu_0(D)=1$. [[def-probability-measure]]

## Counterexample

Let $X=\mathbb R$ with its usual norm, $D=\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ with the trace Borel sigma-algebra, and $c=(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-2})^{-1}$. For Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, define $\mu_0(A):=c\sum_{n\in A\cap D}n^{-2}$, so $\mu_0(\{n\})=c/n^2$. Let $\Phi(n)=0$, $\Phi_N(n)=n/N$ for integers $N\ge1$, and set $M_1(s)=0$, $M_2(s)=s$, and $\psi_N=1/N$. The potentials have common lower envelope zero and satisfy $|\Phi_N(n)-\Phi(n)|=M_2(|n|)\psi_N$, but the weighted error envelope is not prior-integrable.

1.1 By [F3], $0<\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}<\infty$, so $c$ is finite and positive and [F7] makes $\mu_0$ a probability with $\mu_0(D)=1$. By [F6], $D$ is Borel and has the discrete relative topology, so every real-valued function on $D$, including $\Phi,\Phi_N$, is continuous. The real line with its usual norm is a separable Banach space by [F6]. Thus all $\Phi,\Phi_N$ are finite continuous functions on $D$. They satisfy $\Phi,\Phi_N\ge0$ and $|\Phi_N(n)-\Phi(n)|=n/N=M_2(|n|)\psi_N$. But $\int_D e^{M_1(|u|)}(1+M_2(|u|)^2)\,\mu_0(du)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}(1+n^2)=+\infty,$ since the second summand contributes $c$ for each $n$. This is precisely the integrability hypothesis used by [F4], and it fails here. [F3, F4, F6, F7, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The base evidence is $Z=1$. For each $N$, the approximate evidence $Z_N=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}e^{-n/N}$ is positive and at most one, so both posterior updates exist. Moreover $Z_N\to1$: given $\epsilon>0$, choose $m$ with $\sum_{n>m}c/n^2<\epsilon/2$ by [F3]. The finite sum $\sum_{n=1}^m(c/n^2)(1-e^{-n/N})$ tends to zero by continuity of the exponential [F5], while the remaining tail of $1-Z_N$ is at most $\sum_{n>m}c/n^2<\epsilon/2$. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, given, choose, algebra]

3.1 Since $e^{-1}<1$, the number $\alpha:=(1+e^{-1})/2$ is less than one. From $Z_N\to1$, for all sufficiently large $N$ we have $Z_N\ge\alpha$. For $n\ge N$, $\frac{e^{-n/N}}{Z_N}\le\frac{e^{-1}}{\alpha}=\frac{2}{e+1}<1,$ so $1-\sqrt{e^{-n/N}/Z_N}\ge\kappa:=1-\sqrt{2/(e+1)}>0$. [F5, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 The posterior density of the base law relative to $\mu_0$ is $1$, and that of the approximation is $e^{-n/N}/Z_N$. By [F2] and step 3.1, $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)^2=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c}{n^2}\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{e^{-n/N}}{Z_N}}\right)^2\ge\kappa^2\sum_{n=N}^{2N-1}\frac{c}{n^2}\ge\frac{\kappa^2c}{4N},$ because the block has $N$ terms and each $n$ in it satisfies $n<2N$. Therefore $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\ge(\kappa\sqrt c/2)N^{-1/2}$, while $\psi_N=N^{-1}$. The ratio $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)/\psi_N$ is at least $(\kappa\sqrt c/2)\sqrt N$ and is unbounded, so the claimed $O(\psi_N)$ rate fails. [F2, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary. Write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. Let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite, so some $0<c\le C<\infty$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le \xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

The weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is the bilinear-form candidate $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given, whenever the weak solution exists, by

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

where $V_h\in H^1(\Omega)$ is any representative of $h$. The local anisotropic conductivity well-posedness lemma proves existence and uniqueness for every boundary class, independence of the representative $V_h$, and boundedness on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$; it therefore makes this candidate a bounded bilinear map. The map is the boundary energy form for the equation $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u)=0$. Under the trace-quotient isomorphism and the local boundedness result, this form gives the usual weak map into the dual $H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ with the scalar convention.

## Statement

Let $k$ be a commutative field and let $G$ satisfy the finite left Folner condition. If $k[G]$ has no zero divisors, then it satisfies both Ore conditions: for nonzero $a,b\in k[G]$ there exist nonzero $x,y$ with $ax=by$, and nonzero $u,v$ with $ua=vb$. Moreover it embeds as a unital subring in a division ring $D$ in which each element has the form $as^{-1}$ for $a\in k[G]$ and $0\ne s\in k[G]$. Thus this is a skew field of fractions, rather than only a ring in which some denominators are invertible. The construction uses no choice axiom.

## Statement references

[[def-group-ring]]

[[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]

[[def-folner-set-and-folner-condition]]

[[def-division-ring]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The commutative field $k$, group $G$, and ring $R=k[G]$ with no zero divisors.

[F1] The group ring has the group elements as a $k$-basis and its product is induced by the group law ([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

[F2] For every finite $S\subseteq G$ and $\delta>0$ there is finite nonempty $F\subseteq G$ with $|sF\triangle F|<\delta|F|$ for all $s\in S$ ([[def-folner-set-and-folner-condition]]).

[F4] A linear map with finite-dimensional source satisfies rank-nullity ([[thm-rank-nullity]]).

[F3] A division ring is a unital ring with $1\ne0$ in which every nonzero element has a two-sided inverse ([[def-ring]], [[def-division-ring]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data in the Statement. A right ideal below is an additive subgroup closed under right multiplication by $R$; its homomorphisms are additive maps commuting with that multiplication.

1.1 Fix nonzero $a,b\in R$ and let $S$ contain the identity and both finite supports. Choose $F$ by [F2] with $\delta=1/(2|S|)$. The union bound gives $|SF|\le |F|+\sum_{s\in S}|sF\setminus F|<(3/2)|F|<2|F|$. Let $kF$ and $k(SF)$ denote the subspaces with the indicated group bases. The linear map $kF\oplus kF\to k(SF)$ defined by $(x,y)\mapsto ax-by$ has source dimension $2|F|$ and strictly smaller target dimension, so rank-nullity [F4] gives a nonzero kernel vector. Neither component of that vector is zero, since $R$ has no zero divisors and $a,b\ne0$. Its common product is also nonzero. Thus $aR\cap bR$ contains a nonzero element, proving the right Ore condition. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra, construct]

2.1 The $k$-linear map $\jmath(\sum_gc_gg)=\sum_gc_gg^{-1}$ satisfies $\jmath(rs)=\jmath(s)\jmath(r)$ and $\jmath^2=1$, by [F1] and commutativity of the coefficient field. Apply step 1.1 to $\jmath(a),\jmath(b)$, and then apply $\jmath$ to the resulting nonzero common right multiple. This gives a nonzero common left multiple $\jmath(x)a=\jmath(y)b$. Hence the left Ore condition holds as well. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 We construct the fraction division ring for any unital ring $R$ with $1\ne0$, no zero divisors and the right Ore condition just proved. Any two nonzero right ideals $I,J$ intersect nontrivially: choose $0\ne s\in I$, $0\ne t\in J$, and a nonzero common right multiple in $sR\cap tR\subseteq I\cap J$. Finite intersections remain nonzero by induction. Every right-linear map $f:I\to R$ on a nonzero right ideal is either the zero map or injective. To see this, if $f(s)\ne0$ but $0\ne t\in\ker f$, choose $0\ne su=tv$ by the right Ore condition; here $u\ne0$. Right linearity gives $f(s)u=f(t)v=0$, contradicting absence of zero divisors. [step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 Form the set of pairs $(I,f)$ with $I$ a nonzero right ideal and $f:I\to R$ right-linear. Identify two pairs when their maps agree on some nonzero right ideal contained in both domains. Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate, and transitivity follows by intersecting the two nonzero agreement ideals using step 2.2. This defines a quotient set $D$. Denote the class of a map by $[f]$. The class is zero exactly when its map is identically zero: a nonzero map is injective by step 2.2 and cannot vanish on a nonzero ideal. Define addition by the sum on the intersection of domains, and define $[f][g]=[f\circ g]$ on $g^{-1}(I)$ if $I$ is the domain of $f$ and $J$ is the domain of $g$. That preimage is a right ideal. It is nonzero if $g=0$, when it is all $J$; otherwise choose $t\in J$ with $g(t)\ne0$ and a nonzero element $g(t)r\in g(t)R\cap I$. Then $tr\ne0$ belongs to the preimage. Thus multiplication is always represented on a nonzero right ideal. [step 2.2, algebra, construct]

4.1 These operations are independent of representatives. For addition, intersect the two agreement ideals and all relevant domains. For multiplication, if $f=f'$ on a nonzero ideal $U$ and $g=g'$ on a nonzero ideal $V$, restrict to $V\cap g^{-1}(U)$. This is nonzero by step 2.2 and the preimage argument of step 3.1, and both composites agree there. Zero maps cause no exception: they may be represented by the zero map on all $R$, and equivalent maps representing zero are actually zero on their domains. Thus addition and multiplication are well-defined. The additive zero is the zero map on $R$, additive inverse is $-f$, and the multiplicative identity is the identity map on $R$. [step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The ring identities hold on nonzero common restriction ideals, hence in $D$. For addition and its commutativity and associativity, use the intersection of all three domains and the ordinary additive identities of $R$. For multiplication of nonzero representatives $f,g,h$, the two associative composites agree on the nonzero ideal of those $x$ for which $h(x)$ lies in the domain of $g$ and $g(h(x))$ lies in the domain of $f$; successive preimages are nonzero because the maps are injective and the preimage argument of step 3.1 applies. If a representative is zero, both composites are zero. For $f(g+h)=fg+fh$, restrict first to the common domain of $g,h$, then to the intersection of the preimages of the domain of $f$ under each nonzero one of $g,h$. These are nonzero ideals and their intersection is nonzero; zero summands impose no restriction. Both $g(x),h(x)$ and their sum then lie in the domain of $f$, and additivity of $f$ proves equality there. For $(f+g)h=fh+gh$, restrict to the preimage under $h$ of the intersection of the domains of $f,g$; the same argument applies. Identity and zero laws hold by their defining maps. This verifies every unital ring axiom without a formal-fraction associativity assumption. [F3, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Map $r\in R$ to the class of left multiplication $L_r:R\to R$, $L_r(x)=rx$. This is a unital ring homomorphism, since $L_r+L_s=L_{r+s}$ and $L_r\circ L_s=L_{rs}$. It is injective: for $r\ne0$, its restriction to every nonzero ideal is nonzero by absence of zero divisors, so its class is not zero by step 3.1. In particular $1\ne0$ in $D$. For a nonzero class $[f]$, the representative $f:I\to R$ is injective by step 2.2 and its image $f(I)$ is a nonzero right ideal. The inverse function $f^{-1}:f(I)\to I\subseteq R$ is right-linear. Its two composites with $f$ are the identity maps on $I$ and $f(I)$ respectively, hence represent $1$ in $D$. Thus every nonzero class has a two-sided inverse, and [F3] makes $D$ a division ring. [F3, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra, construct]

7.1 Finally choose $0\ne s\in I$ for a representative $f:I\to R$ and put $a=f(s)$. The composite $f\circ L_s$ is defined on all $R$, because $sR\subseteq I$, and sends $x$ to $ax$. Thus $[f]L_s=L_a$, and in the embedded-ring notation $[f]=as^{-1}$. Every element of $D$ is therefore a right fraction and every nonzero original denominator is invertible. All maps, ideals and equivalence classes used above form sets over the fixed underlying set $R$. The only selections were finitely many elements in individual nonempty sets at each proof step; no choice function on an infinite family was used. Together with steps 1.1 and 2.1 this proves every assertion. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $F:S^1\times[0,1]\to S^3$ be a smooth isotopy of oriented knots, stationary in end collars, with a specified marked source point. Suppose its two endpoint diagrams are regular compatible long presentations with the same standard oriented exterior marked arc, parametrized identically on a neighborhood of that point. Use the corresponding spatial endpoint coordinates, in which this common marked arc is a standard small round arc through the stereographic point at infinity; its puncture is closed in the planar diagrams by the same standard exterior arc. Then these prescribed endpoint diagrams are related by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented R1, R2 and R3 moves, whose closed support disks miss the mark. The marked neighborhood remains fixed. There are no births, saddles or deaths. The movie represents the given marked isotopy up to a spatial coordinate family equal to the identity in both end collars and a small isotopy relative those collars.

Here compatible long endpoints include the displayed common oriented arc and its spatial coordinate identifications. This statement does not silently identify arbitrary physical endpoint coordinates. Spherical endpoint recharting may first be used to choose such common compatible presentations; no algebraic invariance of that recharting or of these movies is asserted here.

## Statement references

[[lem-marked-knot-concordances-admit-finite-movies-away-from-the-mark|Relative long-tangle construction]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The marked knot isotopy and the specified common parametrized marked arc and endpoint coordinates in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed for the smooth extension and generic projection suppliers.

[F1] [[thm-isotopy-extension]] proves extension for compact sources with boundary. Its proof extends the prescribed velocity in finitely many track charts, multiplies by cutoffs, and integrates a smooth compactly supported field. The same construction with an extra compact parameter is smooth in that parameter, since the chart extensions and cutoffs can be chosen on the compact total track; it is zero at parameter values where the prescribed velocity is identically zero.

[F2] [[lem-marked-knot-concordances-admit-finite-movies-away-from-the-mark]] constructs product strip coordinates and compact long-tangle projections in its steps 3.1–4.1, and its step 6.1 repeats the independent-jet genericity proof relative the protected exterior arc. Its earlier four-dimensional arc straightening and its Morse perturbation are unnecessary for an already levelwise knot isotopy.

[F3] [[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]] proves actual independent-jet evaluation, exclusion of higher events, and finiteness including deleted diagonals. [[lem-a-generic-isotopy-of-links-has-only-reidemeister-singular-times]] identifies the isolated generic events as oriented R1, R2 and R3.

## Proof

1.1 **Small marked arcs and their relative center–tangent data.** Parametrize a uniformly small marked interval by oriented arclength $v$ near zero, smoothly in the isotopy parameter $t$; the resulting reparametrization changes neither knot nor mark and is stationary in the end collars. Let $b(t)=F(0,t)$ and let $u(t)$ be its unit tangent. Identify $S^3$ with unit quaternions. The imaginary unit quaternion $c(t)=b(t)^{-1}u(t)$ lies in $S^2$, and $(b(t),c(t))$ is a smooth loop in $S^3\times S^2$, constant in the end collars. The two endpoint marked arcs are the same by hypothesis. In exponential coordinates at $b(t)$ the small actual arc has the form $vu(t)+O(v^2)$, with derivative $u(t)+O(v)$ uniformly in $t$. Interpolating its error to zero gives a smooth family of embedded intervals for a sufficiently small uniform width: projection onto $u(t)$ has strictly positive derivative. This interpolation is stationary in the end collars if their common model is taken to be the geodesic round arc, as stipulated. Its inverse will later restore the actual marked germ. [given, construct]

2.1 **An explicit contraction fixes both parameter ends.** A smooth loop in either $S^d$, $d=2,3$, misses a point. Indeed a derivative bound makes its $n$ equal parameter intervals map into $n$ balls of radius $C/n$; their total spherical $d$-volume is at most $C'n^{1-d}$, which tends to zero. They cannot cover the positive-volume sphere. Choose one omitted point for each of the two loops from step 1.1. Stereographic coordinates from those points send each loop into Euclidean space. The straight interpolation from its constant endpoint value to its value at $t$ contracts it through loops constant on the same end collars; inverse stereographic projection gives smooth loops $b_s(t),c_s(t)$, with $s=0$ constant and $s=1$ the given data. Thus $$A_{s,t}(v)=b_s(t)\bigl(\cos v+c_s(t)\sin v\bigr)$$ is a smooth family of geodesic marked interval embeddings, with $A_{0,t}$ the common standard arc and $A_{s,t}$ equal to it in both end collars. Concatenate with the inverse error interpolation in step 1.1, using stationary smooth parameter joins. This constructs a two-parameter family of embedded intervals from the constant common arc to the actual moving marked arcs; at $t$ in either end collar the entire family is the constant arc. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Relative ambient coordinates really are identity at both ends.** Extend the velocity in the contraction parameter $s$ of step 2.1 by the actual construction in [F1], with $t$ an additional parameter. To spell out the relative point: the track in $S^3\times[0,1]_s\times[0,1]_t$ is embedded because its last two coordinates retain $s,t$ and each interval slice is embedded. In finite track charts extend the three spatial velocity components constantly in normal coordinates, patch by a smooth partition, and apply a compact cutoff equal to one on the smaller interval track. The prescribed velocity is zero on both $t$ end collars; choose all extended components zero there, using charts of the constant product arc on those collars and a cutoff in $t$ on their complement. Integrate in $s$. Uniqueness of the ODE gives a smooth family $H_t$ of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms with $H_t(A_{0,t})$ the actual marked interval and $H_t=\mathrm{id}$ on both time end collars. Consequently $H_t^{-1}F_t$ is a knot isotopy retaining exactly the given endpoints and fixing one common marked interval for every $t$. This contraction argument is necessary: simply extending the moving interval in the parameter $t$ would not by itself force the terminal ambient map to be the identity. [A1, F1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 **Puncture without changing height or endpoints.** Apply the product-strip and puncture construction of [F2] to this fixed common interval, with spatial coordinates independent of $t$. In a smaller neighborhood the knots agree with that interval for all $t$; compactness gives uniform separation from the rest after shortening it once. Puncturing at its central point gives an isotopy of compact long tangles, fixed on their two spatial end collars, closed by one fixed exterior arc carrying the mark. The spatial coordinate changes in step 3.1 were level-preserving, so its trace is still exactly a cylinder of knot embeddings with time coordinate $t$. In particular the restriction of time to this cylinder has nonzero derivative everywhere. There is no need for a Morse perturbation, and none is made. There is an explicit planar endpoint comparison if the displayed closed diagrams initially use a pole in the adjacent face rather than the spatial puncture at the mark. Write their common round compact projection disk as $D=\{|z|\le R\}$ and their common marked point as $p$, where $|p|>R$. Choose a small marked germ and $\delta>0$ so that its closed neighborhood misses $W=\{|z|<R+\delta\}$. Set $$b_u=\frac{uR^2}{\overline p},\qquad f_u(z)=\frac{z-b_u}{1-\overline b_u z/R^2},\qquad 0\le u\le1.$$ These are disk automorphisms, starting at the identity: on $|z|=R$ one has $|z-b_u|^2=R^2|1-\overline b_u z/R^2|^2$, and their inverse fractional linear maps have the same disk property. Their complex derivative has nonzero numerator $1-|b_u|^2/R^2>0$. Their pole is $p/u$, with infinity at $u=0$, so it stays outside $D$ and ends at the marked point. Thus $f_u|_D$ is an actual smooth isotopy of compact disk embeddings onto $D$, including $u=1$. It is an orientation-preserving coordinate chart on the punctured projection sphere. Its endpoint pole is the spatial puncture point; postcomposition by a positive planar similarity identifies it with a rotation-induced stereographic chart with that pole if such a chart is used for the spatial coordinates. One may instead retain this very chart in the puncture construction. Apply [F1] to $f_u|_D$ in the plane, with extension support in $W$. Its disk velocity is tangent to the boundary; the extension theorem for a compact source with boundary applies and gives an ambient plane isotopy $\Phi_u$ equal to $f_u$ on $D$ and identity outside $W$. Consequently it fixes the specified marked germ pointwise throughout. Choose the long closing arc to be $\Phi_1$ of the original common exterior arc. It is outside $D$, since $\Phi_1$ preserves $D$, and retains exactly the same marked germ. This supplies protected planar isotopies from the displayed endpoints to the punctured-and-reclosed endpoints; prepend and append those isotopies. For two normalized endpoints use the same $D,p,b_u,\Phi_u$ and closing arc. No arbitrary ambient extension or equality of different planar charts is being assumed: both the prescribed endpoint diagrams and their fixed marked germ are retained by the recorded relative extension. [F1, F2, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 **Relative finite projection genericity.** Repeat the family of [F3] on this compact tangle isotopy with bumps zero on smaller parameter end collars and spatial tangle-end collars. At every movable source point these bumps are positive, so the same finite monomial Hermite interpolation prescribes the required independent jets; its evaluations at protected source points are not needed. The exterior closing arc and the two joining collars have fixed regular projection, separated from the compact moving portion. Thus no bad projection stratum involving the protected mark is present. On the moving portion the cusp, tangent-double and triple equations, exclusions of their coincidences and higher degeneracies, and deleted-diagonal estimates are precisely those proved in [F3]. Arbitrarily small parameter choices give finitely many separated generic events relative the stationary endpoint diagrams. The perturbations change spatial coordinates of the slice embeddings only, so their trace remains a height-submersive cylinder. Straight interpolation between the original and sufficiently close perturbed slice maps is an embedding isotopy by the uniform local immersion and distant-pair separation bounds used in [F3]. It is fixed on every protected collar. [A1, F2, F3, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 The event identification in [F3] gives only oriented R1, R2 and R3 moves; between them the projected decorated diagrams vary by planar isotopy. Each exceptional event has compact support inside the projection disk and therefore misses the fixed marked exterior arc. The finite time list yields the required sequence. No surface critical point has been introduced, so births, saddles and deaths do not occur. Undoing $H_t^{-1}$ identifies its trace with the given marked isotopy, up to the small relative perturbation in step 5.1. Since $H_t$ is identity on both end collars, the spatial endpoint identifications are retained exactly; the explicitly recorded planar endpoint isotopies in step 4.1 return the displayed prescribed diagrams. This proves the stated relative comparison and no algebraic map assertion. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Derivative tensors carry their Euclidean norms, and Sobolev norms are sums of the resulting $L^p$ norms. Fix a finite-dimensional real inner-product space $V$, $2\le p<\infty$, and $r>0$. Every $f\in L^p(B_r(0);V)$ with zero volume mean has a unique mean-zero $u\in W^{2,p}(B_r;V)$ satisfying
$$\int_{B_r}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{B_r}\langle f,v\rangle\qquad(v\in W^{1,2}(B_r;V)).$$
The inverse is linear and obeys
$$r^{-2}\|u\|_p+r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_p+\|D^2u\|_p\le C_{p,V}\|f\|_p,$$
with $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ and $f$. Its solution is the $W^{2,p}$ limit of mean-zero polynomial solutions with classical zero normal derivative. In particular it belongs to the $W^{2,p}$ closure of smooth zero-normal-derivative functions on the closed ball.

On $B_1$, let $X_p$ be the $W^{2,p}$ closure of the $V$-valued polynomials with zero normal derivative on the sphere, and let $X_p^0$ be its mean-zero subspace. Then $-\Delta:X_p^0\to L^p_0(B_1;V)$ is a bounded bijection with the above inverse. Here $L^p_0$ denotes the zero-mean subspace; $X_p^0$ is complete for the equivalent norm $\|u\|_{X_p^0}=\|\Delta u\|_p$. A prescribed finite orthogonal equivariance of $f$ is preserved by the inverse, as in the $L^2$ case. No endpoint $p=\infty$ or nonlinear gauge existence is asserted.

## Statement references

[[lem-strong-l-two-neumann-inverse-on-four-dimensional-balls|Constructed L2 Neumann inverse]]

[[thm-global-w-two-p-estimate-for-the-laplacian-on-rn|Whole-space Laplace estimate]]

[[lem-lp-interpolation-absorbs-lower-order-derivatives|Interpolation absorption]]

[Tao–Tian, Proposition 3.6 and §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209352)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The proved [[lem-strong-l-two-neumann-inverse-on-four-dimensional-balls]] constructs the unique mean-zero weak Neumann solution, with its $W^{2,2}$ bound on $B_1$, and gives polynomial solutions for polynomial data.

[F2] The whole-space Laplace estimate bounds $D^2z$ by $C_p\Delta z$ in $L^p$ for $z\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^4)$. The interpolation estimate gives $\|\nabla z\|_p\le\eta\|D^2z\|_p+C_{p,\eta}\|z\|_p$, after finite-dimensional norm comparisons ([[thm-global-w-two-p-estimate-for-the-laplacian-on-rn]], [[lem-lp-interpolation-absorbs-lower-order-derivatives]]).

[F3] The unit ball is a $W^{2,2}$ extension domain; the critical higher-order Sobolev embedding there gives $\|z\|_{L^p}\le C_p\|z\|_{W^{2,2}}$ for every finite $p$ ([[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]], [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]]).

[F4] Polynomials uniformly approximate real continuous functions on the closed ball. Smooth approximation on $\mathbb R^4$ is available also in order zero, $L^p$ is complete, and Holder compares norms on finite-volume sets ([[thm-real-stone-weierstrass-for-compact-metric-spaces]], [[thm-meyers-serrin-density-on-an-arbitrary-open-set]], [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[F5] A fixed smooth cutoff can equal one near $\overline B_1$ and vanish outside $B_2$ ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]). Full AC supplies the countable choices of the analytic suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, $V$, $2\le p<\infty$, and the stated datum. Work first on $B_1$.

1.1 **Reflection matching.** Let $u$ be smooth near $\overline B_1$ with $\partial_\nu u=0$. On $1<|x|<2$ put $\jmath(x)=x/|x|^2$ and $v(x)=u(\jmath(x))$, and put $v=u$ on $B_1$. At $|x|=1$, $D\jmath=I-2\nu\otimes\nu$; since $\nabla u$ is tangential, the outside gradient $D\jmath^T\nabla u$ equals the inside gradient. The values match as well. Thus $v$ is $C^1$ across the sphere, smooth on each side, and has locally bounded piecewise second derivatives. Integration by parts on the two sides cancels the interface terms for $v$ and its first derivatives, so these piecewise derivatives are its weak derivatives through order two. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **The reflected equation.** Writing $s=|x|$, one has $D\jmath=s^{-2}(I-2x\otimes x/s^2)$, $D\jmath D\jmath^T=s^{-4}I$, and $\Delta\jmath_j=-4s^{-4}x_j$ in four dimensions. The chain rule therefore gives $\Delta v=s^{-4}(\Delta u)(\jmath x)-4s^{-4}x\cdot(\nabla u)(\jmath x)$. Since $x\cdot\nabla v=-s^{-2}x\cdot(\nabla u)(\jmath x)$, this is $\Delta v=s^{-4}(\Delta u)(\jmath x)+4s^{-2}x\cdot\nabla v$. All coefficients are bounded on the annulus. The inversion Jacobian has absolute value $s^{-8}$ and maps that annulus into $B_1\setminus\overline B_{1/2}$, so change of variables bounds its reflected $u$, first-derivative and Laplacian norms by constant multiples of their norms on $B_1$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **A whole-space estimate for the extension.** Choose the cutoff $\chi$ of [F5] equal to one near $\overline B_1$, and define $Eu=\chi v$ on $B_2$, zero elsewhere. Step 1.1 gives $Eu\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^4)$ with compact support. Step 2.1 and $\Delta(\chi v)=\chi\Delta v+2\nabla\chi\cdot\nabla v+(\Delta\chi)v$ give $\|Eu\|_p\le C\|u\|_p$ and $\|\Delta Eu\|_p\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|\nabla u\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. Since $Eu=u$ on $B_1$, $\|\nabla u\|_p\le\|\nabla Eu\|_p$. Apply [F2] to obtain $\|D^2Eu\|_p\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|\nabla Eu\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. Interpolate the middle term by [F2] with $\eta>0$ chosen so $C_p\eta\le1/2$, and absorb it. Then interpolate once more for the first derivatives and restrict to $B_1$. The result is $\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(B_1)}\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. No estimate was applied before the reflected function's $W^{2,p}$ membership was proved. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

4.1 **Removing the zeroth-order term for Neumann solutions.** For mean-zero polynomial $f$, [F1] gives a polynomial mean-zero solution $u$ with classical zero normal derivative and $\|u\|_{W^{2,2}}\le C\|f\|_2$. By [F3], $\|u\|_p\le C_p\|f\|_2\le C_p|B_1|^{1/2-1/p}\|f\|_p$, where the final Holder bound uses $p\ge2$. Substitution in step 3.1, with $-\Delta u=f$, proves $\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(B_1)}\le C_{p,V}\|f\|_p$ for these polynomial solutions, uniformly in their degrees. [F1, F3, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **Construction for all mean-zero Lp data.** Extend $f$ by zero to $\mathbb R^4$, approximate in $L^p$ by smooth functions using [F4], and restrict to the closed ball. Each approximant is continuous there and hence uniformly approximable by polynomials by [F4]. A choice of uniform error tending to zero gives polynomial approximants in $L^p$; subtract their means to obtain mean-zero $f_j\to f$ in $L^p$, since $\|(f_j-f)_{B_1}\|\,|B_1|^{1/p}\le\|f_j-f\|_p$ before normalization. Let $u_j$ be the polynomial solutions from [F1]. Applying step 4.1 to their differences makes all derivative components through order two Cauchy in $L^p$. Completeness [F4] and passage in the weak-derivative test identities give a limit $u\in W^{2,p}$ with $u_j\to u$ strongly and the same bound. Finite volume and $p\ge2$ imply $u_j\to u$ in $W^{1,2}$ and $f_j\to f$ in $L^2$; their weak Neumann identities pass to the limit for every $W^{1,2}$ test. Thus the solution is the unique $L^2$ Neumann solution of [F1], now with the stronger regularity and norm estimate. [F1, F4, F5, step 4.1, construct, choose, algebra]

6.1 **The complete normalized domain.** By step 5.1 the inverse maps into $X_p^0$ and is bounded there. Conversely let $u\in X_p^0$ and choose polynomial zero-normal approximants $u_j\to u$ in $W^{2,p}$. Subtracting their means preserves the normal condition and convergence. The sources $f_j=-\Delta u_j$ have zero mean, by the polynomial weak identity of [F1], and converge to $f=-\Delta u\in L^p_0$. Each $u_j$ is the normalized solution for $f_j$, so the bounded inverse from step 5.1 sends $f$ to $u$. This proves bijectivity. Also $\|\Delta u\|_p\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,p}}$ and the inverse bound gives the reverse norm comparison. The zero-mean subspace of $L^p$ is closed, since its mean functional is bounded by Holder, hence complete by [F4]. Its isomorphism with $X_p^0$ gives completeness for $\|\Delta u\|_p$. [F1, F4, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 **Scaling, uniqueness and symmetry.** For $B_r$ put $f_r(y)=r^2f(ry)$, solve on $B_1$ and set $u(x)=u_r(x/r)$. Direct change of variables gives $\|f_r\|_p=r^{2-4/p}\|f\|_p$, $\|D^2u_r\|_p=r^{2-4/p}\|D^2u\|_p$, $\|\nabla u_r\|_p=r^{1-4/p}\|\nabla u\|_p$, and $\|u_r\|_p=r^{-4/p}\|u\|_p$. Divide the unit-ball bound of step 5.1 by $r^{2-4/p}$ to obtain the displayed estimate; polynomial approximations rescale as well. The weak identity passes by change of variables. Uniqueness, linearity and preservation of prescribed finite orthogonal equivariance follow from [F1], since all these solutions belong to its unique mean-zero $W^{1,2}$ solution class. Full AC is inherited through [F2]–[F5] and the sequential approximation choices. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

Tao–Tian's complete Proposition 3.6 proof and §9 nonlinear iteration were read in the full paper. The proof above constructs the ball's linear inverse directly: inversion reflection gives its strong estimate, and the previously constructed polynomial Neumann solutions give surjectivity by completion. It invokes no quoted strong Neumann solvability theorem, no boundary Schauder theorem and no merely formal weak-to-strong upgrade. This is the strong linear boundary supplier needed before a nonlinear gauge iteration can be justified.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y,Z$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over one scalar field. Let compact linear maps $F:X\to Y$ and $G:Y\to Z$ have a common singular system indexed by a finite or countable set $J$: $(x_j)_{j\in J}$, $(y_j)_{j\in J}$, and $(z_j)_{j\in J}$ are orthonormal bases of $\overline{R(F^*)}$, $\overline{R(F)}=\overline{R(G^*)}$, and $\overline{R(G)}$, and $Fx_j=\lambda_jy_j$, $F^*y_j=\lambda_jx_j$, $Gy_j=\mu_jz_j$, and $G^*z_j=\mu_jy_j$ with $0<\lambda_j,\mu_j\le1$. Put $A:=G\circ F$. Let $\nu_0>2$, $1<\nu\le\nu_0-1$, $\rho>0$, $x^\dagger=|A|^\nu w$ with $\|w\|_X\le\rho$, and $z:=Ax^\dagger\ne0$; set $y^\dagger:=Fx^\dagger$. The common system gives the compatible minimum-norm factorization on this exact datum: $A^\dagger z=F^\dagger G^\dagger z=x^\dagger$ and $G^\dagger z=Fx^\dagger=y^\dagger$. For $H=F,G$, let $R^H_\eta=f^H_\eta(H^*H)H^*$ and $p^H_\eta(t):=1-tf^H_\eta(t)$. Assume finite constants $C_H,S_H,K_H>0$ satisfy $\|HR^H_\eta\|\le C_H$, $\|I-HR^H_\eta\|\le S_H$, and $\|R^H_\eta\|\le K_H\eta^{-1/2}$ for every $\eta>0$; and, for each $0<s\le\nu_0$, $\sup_{j\in J}s_{H,j}^{s}|p^H_\eta(s_{H,j}^2)|\le D_H(s)\eta^{s/2}$ for finite $D_H(s)$, where $s_{F,j}=\lambda_j$ and $s_{G,j}=\mu_j$. Fix $\tau_G>S_G$ and $\tau_F>S_FC_G$. Let $\alpha_k,\gamma_\ell>0$ be decreasing sequences with successive ratios in $[\theta,1)$ for one fixed $0<\theta<1$. For noisy data $z^\delta$ with $\|z^\delta-z\|_Z\le\delta$, choose first indices $k,\ell$ (when they exist) such that $\|GR^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta-z^\delta\|_Z\le\tau_G\delta<\|GR^G_{\alpha_i}z^\delta-z^\delta\|_Z$ for every $i<k$, and $\|AR^F_{\gamma_\ell}R^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta-GR^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta\|_Z\le\tau_F\delta<\|AR^F_{\gamma_i}R^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta-GR^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta\|_Z$ for every $i<\ell$. For any sequence $\delta\downarrow0$ for which both selected indices exist for all sufficiently small $\delta$, there are constants $C_1,C_2$ independent of $\delta$ and $\rho$ such that, for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $\|x^\dagger-R^F_{\gamma_\ell}R^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta\|_X\le C_1\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}\delta^{\nu/(\nu+1)}+C_2\rho^{2/(\nu+1)}\delta^{(\nu-1)/(\nu+1)}.$ In particular, for fixed $\rho$ this two-stage reconstruction converges to $x^\dagger$. The statement is conditional on existence of both stopping indices and makes no claim that $(G\circ F)^\dagger=F^\dagger G^\dagger$ for arbitrary factorizations.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-composite-double-regularization|Composite estimator and order]]

[[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model|Compact Hilbert inverse model]]

[[def-ip-power-source-set|Power source ball and minimum-norm convention]]

[[lem-ip-spectral-interpolation-for-power-source-balls|Spectral interpolation inequality]]

[[def-ip-unbounded-hilbert-moore-penrose-inverse|Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose inverse]]

[[def-hilbert-space-adjoint|Hilbert adjoint convention]]

[[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators|Compact-operator singular system]]

[[def-compact-spectral-filter-and-qualification|Spectral filter and residual conventions]]

[Brandt and Horn, Theorem 6, proof, and conclusion on optimality](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.13483)

[Clason, Theorem 5.11 and complete proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.00617)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; compact real or complex Hilbert maps $F:X\to Y$ and $G:Y\to Z$ with the common positive singular system in the Statement; $A=G\circ F$; $x^\dagger=|A|^\nu w$, $\|w\|\le\rho$, $z=Ax^\dagger\ne0$; the compatible minimum-norm factorization; spectral filters with the stated residual, norm, and qualification bounds; the two geometric first-crossing rules; and noisy data $\|z^\delta-z\|\le\delta$ for a sequence $\delta\downarrow0$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function selecting one member from each set.

[F1] [[def-ip-composite-double-regularization]]: The forward map is $A=G\circ F$ and the reconstruction applies $R^G_\alpha$ first, then $R^F_\gamma$.

[F2] [[def-ip-compact-linear-inverse-model]]: A compact Hilbert inverse model has a compact linear forward map and exact data $z=Ax^\dagger$ for a truth $x^\dagger$.

[F3] [[def-ip-power-source-set]]: $X_{\nu,\rho}(A)=\{|A|^\nu w:\|w\|\le\rho\}$, where $|A|=(A^*A)^{1/2}$; source elements lie in $(\ker A)^\perp$ and are minimum-norm representatives.

[F4] [[def-ip-unbounded-hilbert-moore-penrose-inverse]]: The inverse domain is $R(A)\oplus R(A)^\perp$, and on exact range data it returns the unique minimum-norm solution.

[F5] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]: A compact Hilbert operator has a positive singular system with orthonormal right and left singular families and the corresponding operator expansion.

[F6] [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]: The adjoint is characterized by $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$.

[F7] [[def-compact-spectral-filter-and-qualification]]: For a filter family, the residual multiplier is $1-tf(t)$ and qualification bounds positive spectral powers times the absolute residual.

[F8] [[lem-ip-spectral-interpolation-for-power-source-balls]]: If $e=|H|^\nu v$, then $\|e\|\le\|He\|^{\nu/(\nu+1)}\|v\|^{1/(\nu+1)}$.

## Proof

1.1 Because $F$ and $G$ are compact, hence bounded, $A=G\circ F$ is compact: the image under $F$ of any bounded sequence is bounded, and compactness of $G$ gives a subsequence whose images under $G$ converge. Put $a_j=\lambda_j\mu_j$ and $w_j=\langle w,x_j\rangle$. The adjoint identity [F6] and the singular-vector equations show $N(F)=\{x_j:j\in J\}^{\perp}$ and $N(G)=\{y_j:j\in J\}^{\perp}$: each kernel vector is orthogonal to the indicated family, and conversely a vector orthogonal to the family is orthogonal to the full range of the adjoint, hence is killed by the operator. Since $G$ is injective on $\overline{R(F)}=\overline{R(G^*)}$ (its coefficients there are the positive $\mu_j$), $\ker A=\ker F$; hence $(x_j)$ is a basis of $N(A)^\perp$. By [F1], $Ax_j=a_jz_j$. The adjoint identity [F6] gives $A^*=F^*G^*$, so [F5] yields $A^*z_j=a_jx_j$, $A^*Ax_j=a_j^2x_j$, and $|A|x_j=a_jx_j$. The vectors $z_j$ span $\overline{R(A)}$, since the range of $A$ is generated by $Ax_j=a_jz_j$ and $a_j>0$. Compact spectral calculus and [F3] therefore give $x^\dagger=\sum_{j\in J}a_j^\nu w_jx_j$ and $z=Ax^\dagger=\sum_{j\in J}a_j^{\nu+1}w_jz_j$. The source element is perpendicular to $\ker A$, so [F4] gives $A^\dagger z=x^\dagger$. Thus $y^\dagger=Fx^\dagger$ lies in $N(G)^\perp$ and $x^\dagger$ lies in $N(F)^\perp$; since $Gy^\dagger=z$ and $Fx^\dagger=y^\dagger$, the minimum-norm property [F4] gives $G^\dagger z=y^\dagger$ and $F^\dagger y^\dagger=x^\dagger$. Finally, $v:=\sum_j\lambda_j^{\nu+1}w_jy_j$ satisfies $y^\dagger=|G|^\nu v$ and $\|v\|^2=\sum_j\lambda_j^{2\nu+2}|w_j|^2\le\|w\|^2\le\rho^2$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra, construct]

2.1 Let $e_G:=R^G_\alpha z-y^\dagger$. On each $y_j$, $I_Y-R^G_\alpha G$ has multiplier $p^G_\alpha(\mu_j^2)$, whose absolute value is at most $S_G$ because $I_Z-GR^G_\alpha$ has that same multiplier on $z_j$. Thus $e_G=-|G|^\nu p^G_\alpha(G^*G)v=|G|^\nu v'$ with $\|v'\|\le S_G\|v\|\le S_G\rho$. Also $Ge_G=GR^G_\alpha z-z$. The difference between the exact and noisy first residuals is $(GR^G_\alpha-I_Z)(z-z^\delta)$, of norm at most $S_G\delta$; the stopping inequality therefore gives $\|Ge_G\|\le(\tau_G+S_G)\delta$. Applying [F8] to $e_G=|G|^\nu v'$ proves $\|R^G_\alpha z-y^\dagger\|\le((\tau_G+S_G)\delta)^{\nu/(\nu+1)}(S_G\rho)^{1/(\nu+1)}$. [given, step 1.1, F3, F7, F8, algebra]

2.2 Put $e_A:=x^\dagger-R^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha z$. On the common singular system, $R^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha A$ has multiplier $(1-p^F_\gamma(\lambda_j^2))(1-p^G_\alpha(\mu_j^2))$. The bounds on $FR^F_\gamma$ and $GR^G_\alpha$ bound the two factors by $C_F,C_G$; on $N(A)$ the product with $A$ is zero. Therefore $e_A=|A|^\nu u$ with $u=(I-R^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha A)w$ and $\|u\|\le(1+C_FC_G)\rho$. The same coefficient formula, now on $Z$, gives $\|AR^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha\|\le C_FC_G$. The exact composite residual decomposes as $(z-z^\delta)+(z^\delta-GR^G_\alpha z^\delta)+(GR^G_\alpha z^\delta-AR^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha z^\delta)+AR^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha(z^\delta-z)$. These four terms have norms at most $\delta,\tau_G\delta,\tau_F\delta,C_FC_G\delta$, respectively, by the noise bound, the two stopping rules, and the composite operator bound. Since $Ae_A=z-AR^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha z$, it follows that $\|Ae_A\|\le(1+\tau_G+\tau_F+C_FC_G)\delta$. Applying [F8] to $e_A=|A|^\nu u$ proves $\|e_A\|\le C_1\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}\delta^{\nu/(\nu+1)}$. [given, step 1.1, F1, F3, F7, F8, algebra]

2.3 Replace $D_H(\nu+1)$ by $\max\{D_H(\nu+1),0\}+1$ for $H=F,G$; the qualification bounds remain valid and these constants are positive. Define $q_\gamma(h):=AR^F_\gamma R^G_\alpha h-GR^G_\alpha h$. Its common-system multiplier on $z_j$ is $-p^F_\gamma(\lambda_j^2)(1-p^G_\alpha(\mu_j^2))$. Since $a_j^{\nu+1}=\lambda_j^{\nu+1}\mu_j^{\nu+1}$, qualification at $s=\nu+1$, $\mu_j\le1$, and $|1-p^G_\alpha(\mu_j^2)|\le C_G$ give $\|q_\gamma(z)\|\le D_F(\nu+1)C_G\rho\,\gamma^{(\nu+1)/2}$. On arbitrary noise coordinates, $|p^F_\gamma(\lambda_j^2)|\le S_F$ and $|1-p^G_\alpha(\mu_j^2)|\le C_G$, so $\|q_\gamma(z^\delta-z)\|\le S_FC_G\delta$. If $\ell\ge2$, the preceding noisy discrepancy is greater than $\tau_F\delta$; subtracting the noise bound gives $\|q_{\gamma_{\ell-1}}(z)\|>(\tau_F-S_FC_G)\delta$. The exact-data bound just proved then yields $\gamma_{\ell-1}>[(\tau_F-S_FC_G)/(D_F(\nu+1)C_G)]^{2/(\nu+1)}(\delta/\rho)^{2/(\nu+1)}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge\theta\gamma_{\ell-1}$ gives the same lower bound with factor $\theta$. Hence $\|R^F_{\gamma_\ell}\|\le K_F/\sqrt{\gamma_\ell}\le C''\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}\delta^{-1/(\nu+1)}$. If $\ell=1$, then $\gamma_\ell=\gamma_1$ is fixed. The common system and $\lambda_j,\mu_j\le1$ give $\|A\|\le1$, so $0<\delta<\|z\|=\||A|^{\nu+1}w\|\le\rho$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$. Thus $(\rho/\delta)^{1/(\nu+1)}\ge1$, and $\|R^F_{\gamma_1}\|\le K_F/\sqrt{\gamma_1}\le C''(\rho/\delta)^{1/(\nu+1)}$ after enlarging $C''$. [given, step 1.1, F3, F7, algebra]

3.1 If $k\ge2$, the preceding noisy residual is greater than $\tau_G\delta$. Its difference from the exact-data residual is $(GR^G_{\alpha_{k-1}}-I_Z)(z-z^\delta)$, of norm at most $S_G\delta$, so $\|GR^G_{\alpha_{k-1}}z-z\|>(\tau_G-S_G)\delta$. Expanding $z=G|G|^\nu v$ in the common basis and applying the qualification bound at $s=\nu+1$ gives $\|GR^G_{\alpha_{k-1}}z-z\|\le D_G(\nu+1)\rho\,\alpha_{k-1}^{(\nu+1)/2}$. Thus $\alpha_{k-1}>[(\tau_G-S_G)/D_G(\nu+1)]^{2/(\nu+1)}(\delta/\rho)^{2/(\nu+1)}$, and $\alpha_k\ge\theta\alpha_{k-1}$ gives the same lower bound for $\alpha_k$ with the extra factor $\theta$. Consequently $\|R^G_{\alpha_k}(z^\delta-z)\|\le K_G\delta/\sqrt{\alpha_k}\le C\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}\delta^{\nu/(\nu+1)}$, where $C$ is independent of $\rho,\delta$. If $k=1$, then $\alpha_k=\alpha_1$ is fixed. Since $\rho>0$, we have $\delta\le\rho$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$, and hence $\|R^G_{\alpha_1}(z^\delta-z)\|\le K_G\delta/\sqrt{\alpha_1}\le K_G\alpha_1^{-1/2}\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}\delta^{\nu/(\nu+1)}$. Combining this noise bound with step 2.1 and the triangle inequality gives $\|R^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta-y^\dagger\|\le C'\rho^{1/(\nu+1)}\delta^{\nu/(\nu+1)}$. [given, step 2.1, F7, algebra]

4.1 The exact/noisy decomposition is $x^\dagger-R^F_{\gamma_\ell}R^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta=e_A+R^F_{\gamma_\ell}R^G_{\alpha_k}(z-z^\delta)$. By linearity, $\|R^G_{\alpha_k}(z-z^\delta)\|\le\|R^G_{\alpha_k}z-y^\dagger\|+\|R^G_{\alpha_k}z^\delta-y^\dagger\|$, and these terms are bounded by steps 2.1 and 3.1. Combining those estimates with the exact composite bias from step 2.2 and the outer norm bound from step 2.3 gives the two terms in the Statement, with constants independent of $\delta$ and $\rho$. Since $\nu>1$, both powers of $\delta$ are positive, so the error tends to zero for fixed $\rho$. [given, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let G be a PTFA group and let QG be its group ring over the rational field. Then QG has no zero divisors and satisfies both the left and right Ore conditions. Consequently QG embeds in a skew field of fractions in which every nonzero element of QG is invertible.

## Statement references

[[lem-torsion-free-abelian-extensions-preserve-group-ring-domains]]

[[lem-ptfa-groups-have-finite-folner-sets]]

[[lem-folner-group-ring-domains-have-ore-fractions]]

[COT, §2.1, Proposition 2.5 and its cited group-ring argument](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908117)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A PTFA group G with a finite subnormal series whose factors are torsion-free abelian.

[F1] PTFA means that G has such a finite subnormal series; each subgroup need only be normal in the next ([[def-poly-torsion-free-abelian-group]]).

[F2] The rational group ring has the group elements as a basis, bilinear group-law multiplication and a nonzero identity ([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

[F3] If $H\trianglelefteq L$ with $L/H$ torsion-free abelian and $\mathbb Q[H]$ has no zero divisors, then $\mathbb Q[L]$ has no zero divisors, including for nonsplit extensions ([[lem-torsion-free-abelian-extensions-preserve-group-ring-domains]]).

[F4] Every group with the finite subnormal series in [F1] satisfies the finite left Folner condition without a choice axiom ([[lem-ptfa-groups-have-finite-folner-sets]]).

[F5] A group-ring with no zero divisors and finite left Folner sets has both Ore common-multiple properties and an explicitly constructed division ring of fractions in which every element is a right fraction $as^{-1}$ ([[lem-folner-group-ring-domains-have-ore-fractions]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement.

1.1 Fix a finite series $1=G_0\trianglelefteq G_1\trianglelefteq\cdots\trianglelefteq G_m=G$ as in [F1]. Its base ring $\mathbb Q[G_0]=\mathbb Q$ has no zero divisors. For each $j<m$, apply [F3] to $G_j\trianglelefteq G_{j+1}$ and its torsion-free abelian quotient. Induction gives absence of zero divisors in $\mathbb Q[G]$. The domain supplier keeps the conjugation automorphisms and cocycle units of the extension in its leading-coefficient product, so this induction assumes neither a splitting nor normality of each $G_j$ in the final group. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F4], the same finite subnormal series gives finite left Folner sets in $G$. That supplier constructs finite sets directly across each group extension, with only finitely many coset lifts for each test, rather than assuming an invariant mean or adding a choice principle. [F1, F4, given]

2.1 Apply [F5] to the ring from step 1.1 and the finite sets from step 1.2. It gives nonzero common right multiples $ax=by$ of every nonzero $a,b$, and the group-inversion anti-automorphism gives nonzero common left multiples. It then constructs a division ring from equivalence classes of right-linear maps on nonzero right ideals, embeds $\mathbb Q[G]$ injectively, and shows every element of that division ring is $as^{-1}$ with $0\ne s\in\mathbb Q[G]$. These are exactly both Ore conditions and the required skew field of fractions. The length-zero case is already included by the base field. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

      locator: "§3, same trace but distinct concordance discussion"
---

## Statement refuted

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The proposed statement is that for every pair of
smooth oriented knots $K_0,K_1\subset S^3$, a smooth diffeomorphism
$X_0(K_0)\cong X_0(K_1)$ implies that $K_0$ and $K_1$ are smoothly concordant.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Introduction and §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the Conway knot $C$ and its Figure 2 trace partner $K_P$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, written AC, is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] AC implies dependent choice and hence countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; this supplies every retained local countable-choice hypothesis. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] [[def-smooth-knot-concordance]]: a smooth concordance is a properly embedded smooth annulus in $S^3\times[0,1]$ with product collars.

[F2] [[lem-piccirillo-knot-lee-computations]] gives $s(C)=0$ by its direct Conway Lee computation. Only its Conway conclusion is used here.

[F3] [[lem-lee-cobordism-filtration-genus-bound]] gives $|s(K_1)-s(K_0)|\le2g$ for an actual smoothly properly embedded oriented genus-$g$ cobordism with product collars.

[F4] [[thm-piccirillo-conway-trace-partner-has-s-two]] proves under full AC that $X_0(C)\cong X_0(K_P)$ and $s(K_P)=2$, using the retained local framed construction with its explicit published terminal input and the direct rational Lee calculation.

## Counterexample

1.1 The oriented knots $C,K_P$ of [F4] have diffeomorphic zero-traces. Suppose they were smoothly concordant. By [F1] the concordance is a properly embedded product-collared annulus, hence a genus-zero cobordism. [A1, A2, F1, F4, given, contradiction]

2.1 Apply [F3] with $g=0$. It gives $|s(C)-s(K_P)|\le0$, so the two invariants must agree. [A1, A2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 But [F2] and [F4] give $s(C)=0$, $s(K_P)=2$. Their difference has absolute value two, contradicting step 2.1. Thus these actual equal-zero-trace knots are not smoothly concordant, refuting the unchanged universal Statement. [A2, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, contradiction] ∎

## Definition

Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, and it has product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, with product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

## Definition

A **finite triangulation of a compact PL surface** is a finite two-dimensional simplicial complex $K$ in which each edge is incident to one or two triangles and the link of each vertex is homeomorphic to a circle or a closed interval. Its realization $|K|$ is the surface; its boundary is the subcomplex formed by edges incident to one triangle and their vertices. If $V,E,F$ are the numbers of vertices, edges and triangles, its simplicial Euler characteristic is $\chi(K)=V-E+F$.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold whose boundary $M$ is a rational homology three-sphere, meaning $H_*(M;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. The boundary intersection lattice has underlying group $L_W=H_2(W;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Poincaré–Lefschetz duality identifies each $x\in H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$ with a class $\alpha_x\in H^2(W,M;\mathbb Z)$. Define $Q_W(\bar x,\bar y)=\langle\alpha_x\smile\alpha_y,[W,M]\rangle$, where $\smile$ is the relative cup product and $[W,M]\in H_4(W,M;\mathbb Z)$ is the relative orientation class; equivalently, this is the signed intersection number of interior two-cycle representatives. Its rank is $b_2(W)=\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_2(W;\mathbb Q)$. A nondegenerate positive-definite $Q_W$ is called a positive-definite filling lattice. It is not required to be unimodular; the boundary linking form can make its determinant have absolute value greater than one.

## Definition

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

## Definition references

[[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links|Lower-central quotients and finite Magnus expansion]]

[[def-based-string-link-and-labeled-link-peripheral-system|Based string-link longitudes and closed-link peripheral data]]

[[lem-magnus-commutator-degree-and-truncation|Representative-independent truncated coefficients]]

[[thm-string-link-nilpotent-peripheral-identifications|End isomorphisms on finite lower-central quotients]]

[[lem-link-nilpotent-quotient-generated-by-component-meridians|Component meridians generate finite closed-link nilpotent quotients]]

[[lem-string-link-exterior-homology-and-meridian-maps|Existence of preferred zero-self-meridian longitudes]]

## Remarks

The length of $I$ is $k+1$; its final index names the longitude component, and the preceding indices name the Magnus word. The gcd convention records exactly the lower-order data used in the classical residue definition. The isotopy theorem later proves that the based residue candidate is independent of its choices.

## Definition

Let $K_0,K_1$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$, and let $I=[0,1]$. A smooth concordance from $K_0$ to $K_1$ is the image of a smooth proper embedding $f:S^1\times I\to S^3\times I$ whose lower and upper boundary circles are $K_0\times\{0\}$ and $K_1\times\{1\}$. The embedding has product collars at both ends: in a neighborhood of each boundary circle it is the corresponding knot embedding crossed with the interval coordinate. Orient the annulus so that its boundary, with the boundary-orientation convention, is $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_1\times\{1\}$. The knots are smoothly concordant when such an annulus exists.

## Example

Assume $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=e^{\alpha j}$, and $\sigma_j=e^{\beta j}$ in the Gaussian sequence detection experiment. A minimax separation rate over $\Theta_2(r)$ is
$$r_\varepsilon^*\asymp\varepsilon^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}.$$

## Example references

[Giné and Nickl, *Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models*, §6.2.3](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=e^{\alpha j}$, $\sigma_j=e^{\beta j}$, and the finite-support extremal profile for sufficiently small $r$. For this rate comparison, $X_\varepsilon\asymp Y_\varepsilon$ means the ratio is bounded above and away from zero by constants independent of $\varepsilon$.

[F1] [[thm-ip-ellipsoid-detection-boundary]]: $r^2=A J_1/J_2$, $u_\varepsilon^2=(r/\varepsilon)^4J_0/(2J_1^2)$, and the $u_\varepsilon$ boundary determines minimax distinguishability.

[F2] [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-exists-for-small-r]] and [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-is-minimizer]]: the active cutoff $m$ satisfies $A\asymp e^{-2\alpha m}$.

1.1 Let $m$ be the largest active index and put $t=Ae^{2\alpha m}\in[e^{-2\alpha},1)$. For $j=m-\ell$, the profile factor is $\rho_\ell=1-te^{-2\alpha\ell}$. For every $\ell\ge1$, $1-e^{-2\alpha}\le\rho_\ell\le1$, while $0\le\rho_0\le1$. The sums for $J_1$ and $J_0$ are geometric in $\ell$; their $\ell=1$ terms give positive lower bounds and the full geometric sums give upper bounds, so $J_1\asymp J_0\asymp e^{4\beta m}$. In $J_2$, the summands are $t e^{-(2\alpha+4\beta)\ell}\rho_\ell e^{4\beta m}$; the $\ell=1$ term is bounded below by a positive constant times $e^{4\beta m}$, and the geometric series gives the matching upper bound. Thus $J_2\asymp e^{4\beta m}$. By [F1], $$r^2\asymp A\asymp e^{-2\alpha m},\qquad u_\varepsilon^2\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^4e^{-4\beta m}\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^{4+4\beta/\alpha}.$$ [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The last expression is comparable to $(r/\varepsilon^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)})^{4+4\beta/\alpha}$. Thus radii below the displayed scale by a factor tending to zero have $u_\varepsilon\to0$, and radii above it by a factor tending to infinity have $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$ when $r_\varepsilon\to0$. If $r_\varepsilon$ does not tend to zero, reduce to $\bar r_\varepsilon=\sqrt{r_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon^*}$. Nonempty alternatives satisfy $r_\varepsilon^2\le a_1^{-2}$ by the two q=2 constraints, so $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$ and $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$. The inclusion $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_2(\bar r_\varepsilon)$ transfers consistent tests to the original class. The risk implications in [F1] establish the separation rate. ## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, where $\doteq$ denotes equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. Then $K$ has a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface $F$ and an ordered geometric basis, represented by embedded simple closed curves $s_1,\ldots,s_g,\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_g$ for $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, such that $s_i\cdot_Fs_j=0=\ell_i\cdot_F\ell_j$ and $s_i\cdot_F\ell_j=\delta_{ij}$, and the Seifert matrix in this basis has block form
$$V=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_g+U\\U^T&W\end{pmatrix},$$
where $U$ is strictly upper triangular and $W$ is symmetric with zero diagonal. Such a geometric symplectic basis and block matrix are called a trivial Alexander basis.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface|Connected compact oriented Seifert surfaces and their genus]]

[[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface|Existence of a Seifert surface under countable choice]]

[[lem-alexander-one-seifert-form-is-s-equivalent-to-empty|The Alexander-one S-equivalence claim needed for the basis construction]]

Stavros Garoufalidis and Peter Teichner, “On Knots with Trivial Alexander Polynomial,” Definition 4.1 and Lemma 4.2, https://people.math.gatech.edu/~stavros/publications/teichner1.pdf

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and an oriented knot $K$ with $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is the choice-function axiom used by the Seifert-form interfaces.

[F1] [[def-oriented-seifert-surface]]: A Seifert surface is connected, compact, smooth, oriented, and has boundary the given oriented knot.

[F2] [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]]: Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every smooth oriented knot bounds such a surface.

[F3] [[lem-alexander-one-seifert-form-is-s-equivalent-to-empty]]: The actual proof gives primitive kernel-vector splittings and exact integral inverse tube enlargements, rather than an unspecified stabilization.

[F4] [[def-seifert-form-s-equivalence]]: The displayed symmetric coupling enlargement is an allowed algebraic tube addition.

[F5] [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]: Its finite disk-and-band/polygon construction provides a geometric handle graph. On the supplied smooth surface, its finitely many piecewise smooth handle curves can be rounded in chart disks, preserving their finite transverse crossing pattern. Thus the finite twist construction below starts with actual smooth curves, not a claimed arbitrary TOP smoothing.

## Proof

1.1 Full AC implies Countable Choice, so choose the actual connected smooth Seifert surface supplied by [F2]. The proved reduction [F3] splits its given lattice by symplectic pairs and the exact inverse tube enlargements of [F4]. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, choose]

1.2 Reversing these reductions also produces the claimed trivial Alexander block. Keep all short vectors first and all long vectors second. A reverse tube addition introduces a new short x with zero column and only the entry 1 in its own long column, and a new long y with zero diagonal. Its couplings to earlier short vectors occupy precisely the new LAST column of U, so U stays strictly upper triangular. Its couplings to earlier long vectors give a symmetric new row/column of W, with zero new diagonal. Starting from the empty matrix therefore gives [[0,I+U],[U^T,W]] with exactly the advertised conditions. This is an integral symplectic basis of the original lattice; the finite construction below realizes it geometrically rather than assuming that arbitrary integral basis changes are surface homeomorphisms. [F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 Fix a standard geometric basis a_i,b_i on the actual compact oriented genus-g surface with one boundary circle. Its existence follows by cutting a finite disk-and-handle model of the surface, not from an arbitrary homology basis. Put omega(a_i,b_j)=delta_ij. An annular Dehn twist about an embedded curve v acts by the transvection T_v(z)=z+omega(z,v)v, choosing the twist sign accordingly. This formula is proved by cutting each transverse arc at the annulus: the twisted arc acquires one oriented copy of its core. Curves representing a_i+a_j, b_i+b_j and a_i+b_j for i≠j are embedded band sums on distinct handles. The joining arc lies in the complement of the other standard handles; the band gives the indicated homology class. Thus these transvections and their inverses are actual boundary-fixed surface homeomorphisms (smooth diffeomorphisms in the smooth model). [F5, construct]

1.4 For orthogonal u,v, direct expansion gives
T_(u+v) T_u^−1 T_v^−1(z)
=z+omega(z,u)v+omega(z,v)u. [F5, construct]

1.5 Taking u=a_i,v=b_j, i≠j, realizes the elementary block-GL operation a_j to a_j+a_i and b_i to b_i−b_j. Its powers realize arbitrary integral elementary additions. Handle permutations and simultaneous sign reversal of a_i,b_i are also realized; the latter is the square of the two-twist rotation on that handle. Euclidean elimination consequently realizes every block action (x,y) to (A x,A^−T y) for A in GL_g(Z). Likewise the a_i and a_i+a_j twists realize every symmetric upper shear, because the diagonal rank-one matrices and the identity (e_i+e_j)(e_i+e_j)^T−E_ii−E_jj=E_ij+E_ji generate all symmetric integral matrices; the b_i analogues realize every symmetric lower shear. [F5, construct]

1.6 Here is a complete generation argument, so this is not an appeal to mapping-class surjectivity. Given a primitive vector v=(x,y), first interchange the a and b directions on a handle if necessary to make x nonzero. A block-GL operation makes x=(d,0,...,0), d>0. If some y_j is not divisible by d, reduce d strictly: for j=1 use the ordinary Euclidean two-twist SL_2 algorithm on (d,y_1); for j≠1 an upper diagonal shear inserts y_j in x_j, then block-GL Euclidean reduction replaces d by gcd(d,y_j). Repeat. The positive integer d decreases until every y_j is divisible by d; primitivity then forces d=1. A lower symmetric shear with first column −y clears y while keeping x=e_1. Thus an actual finite product of the specified twists takes every primitive vector to a_1. [F5, construct]

2.1 Let A be an arbitrary symplectic integral matrix. Apply this procedure to its first column, so the resulting matrix fixes a_1. Its image of b_1 has the form b_1+c a_1+z, with z in the span W of the remaining handles. The displayed orthogonal-transvection combination for u=a_1 and each basis vector v of W fixes a_1. Its k-th power subtracts k v from that image of b_1 and only changes its a_1 coefficient in addition. Use these powers to clear all coordinates of z. Then a power of T_(a_1) clears c. The resulting matrix fixes both a_1,b_1, and hence restricts symplectically to W. Induct on g. We have reduced A to the identity by actual twists; reversing the finite list realizes A. In particular the symplectic lattice basis from the preceding primitive-vector/tube reduction is represented by an ACTUAL geometric basis, with disjoint short curves, disjoint long curves and exactly one transverse short–long intersection on each matching pair. ∎ [F5, construct]
