## Example

Let $C_3=\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, put $\omega=(-1-i\sqrt3)/2$, and for a real signal $f:C_3\to\mathbb R$ define its unnormalised discrete Fourier transform by $\widehat f(k)=\sum_{n=0}^{2}f(n)\omega^{kn}$ for the representatives $k=0,1,2$. Its Fourier magnitude data are $(|\widehat f(k)|)_{k=0}^{2}$. Define translation by $(\tau_1 f)(n)=f(n-1)$ and reflection by $(Rf)(n)=f(-n)$, with indices in $C_3$. For $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=2$, and $f(2)=0$, both $\tau_1f$ and $Rf$ have the same Fourier magnitude data as $f$, while neither equals $f$ or $-f$.

## Example references

[Philipp Grohs, Sarah Koppensteiner, and Martin Rathmair, finite Fourier translation and conjugate-reflection ambiguities, Proposition 3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.07911v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The cyclic group $C_3$, $\omega=(-1-i\sqrt3)/2$, the stated DFT convention, and the real signal $f$ in the example.

[F1] Complex arithmetic is a field operation system; conjugation and modulus are given by $\overline{a+bi}=a-bi$ and $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, and conjugation respects sums, products and modulus ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F2] The nonnegative square root of $3$ squares to $3$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

## Verification


1.1 Write $s=\sqrt3$. By [F1] and [F2], $\omega^2=(-1+is)/2$, $\omega^3=1$, and $|\omega|^2=1$, hence $|\omega|=1$. Reindexing the finite sum with $j=n-1$ gives $\widehat{\tau_1f}(k)=\sum_j f(j)\omega^{k(j+1)}=\omega^k\widehat f(k)$. Multiplicativity of the modulus [F1] gives $|\omega^k|=1$, so every Fourier magnitude is unchanged. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Since $|\omega|=1$, [F1] gives $\overline\omega=\omega^{-1}$. Reindexing with $j=-n$ gives $\widehat{Rf}(k)=\sum_j f(j)\omega^{-kj}$. Because every $f(j)$ is real, this equals $\overline{\sum_j f(j)\omega^{kj}}=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$ by the conjugation laws in [F1], so reflection preserves every Fourier magnitude. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 The support of $f$ is $\{0,1\}$, that of $\tau_1f$ is $\{1,2\}$, and that of $Rf$ is $\{0,2\}$. These differ from $\{0,1\}$, so neither transformed signal is $f$; each is nonzero, so neither is $-f$ either. Combined with the invariances in steps 1.1 and 2.1, both transformed signals are distinct from the original up to global sign but have identical Fourier magnitude data. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $G_2$ be the toroidal $2\times2$ grid whose bottom row has $O$ in its left cell and $X$ in its right cell, and whose top row has $X$ in its left cell and $O$ in its right cell. With the row and column orientation convention for grid diagrams, this is a one-component unknot grid. The tilde grid complex over $\mathbb F_2$, whose differential counts empty-state rectangles disjoint from both marking sets, has homology of rank two.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9]
  \draw[step=1,gray] (0,0) grid (2,2);
  \node at (0.5,0.5) {$O$}; \node at (1.5,0.5) {$X$};
  \node at (0.5,1.5) {$X$}; \node at (1.5,1.5) {$O$};
  \node[left] at (0,0.5) {bottom row};
  \node[left] at (0,1.5) {top row};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot|The grid orientation and toroidal rectangle convention]]

[[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex|The tilde differential]]

[[lem-grid-rectangle-differential-squares-to-zero|The tilde differential squares to zero]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, Exercise 4.4.3](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

[Manolescu, Ozsvath, and Sarkar, “A combinatorial description of knot Floer homology,” §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0607691)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The specified 2-by-2 marking array on a torus.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] traces each component by following the row from $O$ to $X$ and the column from $X$ to the next $O$; it identifies the components with cycles of this finite marking permutation and gives exactly two grid states for a 2-by-2 knot grid.

[F2] [[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex]] defines the tilde differential by counting empty-state rectangles whose interiors contain no $O$- or $X$-marking.

[F3] [[lem-grid-rectangle-differential-squares-to-zero]] establishes that the tilde differential is a chain-complex differential.

## Verification

1.1 Starting at the bottom-left $O$, the oriented route follows its row to the bottom-right $X$, then follows that column to the top-right $O$, then that row to the top-left $X$, then that column back to the starting $O$. Thus the link has one component. Its planar projection has no transverse self-intersection: the four segments meet only at these marked turning points, and smoothing the four corners gives a simple closed planar curve, which bounds a disk. Therefore it is an unknot. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 There are exactly two grid states, the two permutations of two columns. For either ordered pair of distinct states, the rectangles from the first state to the second are the bottom-left and top-right cells, each containing one $O$; the reverse rectangles are the bottom-right and top-left cells, each containing one $X$. No such rectangle is counted in tilde mode, and there are no rectangles from a state to itself. Hence the tilde differential is zero. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 The tilde chain group has its two grid states as a basis, and its differential is zero by step 1.2. The chain condition is supplied by [F3], so its homology equals this two-dimensional chain group and has rank two. [F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and work on the closed Euclidean unit ball in four dimensions. Use sums of $L^p$ norms of Euclidean ordered derivative tensors for Sobolev norms; these are equivalent to the cited scalar Sobolev norms and invariant under orthogonal coordinate changes. Let $X$ be the mean-zero $W^{2,3}$ closure of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued polynomials with zero normal derivative on the sphere. Let $Y$ be the $W^{1,3}$ closure of smooth $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued one-forms with zero normal component on the sphere. Let $\mathcal G_N$ be the $W^{2,3}$ closure of smooth maps to $SU(2)$ with zero normal derivative on the sphere.

There exist fixed positive constants $\rho,\eta,\delta,C$ such that, if $a\in Y$ satisfies $d^*a=0$, $\|a\|_4\le\rho$, and $\lambda\in Y$ satisfies $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le\delta$, there exists $u\in X$, unique among $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta$, such that $h=e^u\in\mathcal G_N$ and
$$b=h^{-1}dh+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h\in Y,\qquad d^*b=0.$$
Moreover
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}},\qquad \|b-a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C(1+\|a\|_{W^{1,3}})\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}.$$
All constants are independent of the higher norm of $a$.

Given a finite $\Gamma\le O(4)$ and an action $\tau$ of $\Gamma$ on $SU(2)$ by constant unitary conjugations, suppose $\gamma^*a=d\tau_\gamma(a)$ and $\gamma^*\lambda=d\tau_\gamma(\lambda)$. Then $u(\gamma x)=d\tau_\gamma(u(x))$ and $h(\gamma x)=\tau_\gamma(h(x))$. A representation into $PU(2)$ supplies such a conjugation action; no lift of that representation to $SU(2)$ is required.

## Statement references

[[lem-strong-lp-neumann-inverse-on-four-dimensional-balls|Constructed strong Neumann inverse]]

[[lem-normal-boundary-hodge-estimate-on-four-dimensional-balls|Normal-boundary Hodge class and identity]]

[Tao–Tian, Proposition 9.2, Step 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209352)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The constructed inverse $S$ for $-\Delta$ maps $L^3_0$ boundedly onto the complete normalized space $X$, with $\|Sf\|_{W^{2,3}}\le K_N\|f\|_3$. It preserves prescribed finite orthogonal equivariance ([[lem-strong-lp-neumann-inverse-on-four-dimensional-balls]]).

[F2] Every $R\in Y$ satisfies $\int d^*R=0$, by the normal-boundary integration identity tested with constants ([[lem-normal-boundary-hodge-estimate-on-four-dimensional-balls]]).

[F3] On the ball $W^{2,3}\hookrightarrow L^\infty$ and $\|Dv\|_{12}\le K\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}$; also $W^{1,3}\hookrightarrow L^{12}$. These follow from the proved higher-order and first-order embeddings and the ball's extension property ([[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]], [[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]], [[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]]).

[F4] Holder controls products and changes of exponent on the fixed ball. $L^3$ is complete, smooth approximation is available, and a contraction on a nonempty complete metric space has a unique fixed point ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], [[thm-meyers-serrin-density-on-an-arbitrary-open-set]], [[thm-banach-fixed-point]]).

[F5] Full AC is inherited through the analytic suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC and the classes $X,Y,\mathcal G_N$ and data of the statement. All norms in this proof are on the fixed unit ball.

1.1 **Sobolev matrix algebra and boundary approximation.** By [F3]–[F4] and the weak product rule obtained by smooth approximation, $\|vw\|_{W^{2,3}}\le K_A\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}\|w\|_{W^{2,3}}$: the second-derivative cross terms obey $\|DvDw\|_3\le\|Dv\|_6\|Dw\|_6$, and [F3] controls both $L^6$ norms. Similarly $\|cv\|_{W^{1,3}}+\|vc\|_{W^{1,3}}\le K_A\|c\|_{W^{1,3}}\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Passing the derivative test identities to $L^3$ limits proves completeness of the ambient Sobolev spaces from [F4]. The power series for $e^u$ therefore converges in $W^{2,3}$, locally uniformly in that norm, and defines a continuously differentiable composition there; termwise differentiation is justified by the convergent exponential majorants. For $u\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ pointwise, $u^2=-s^2I$ for a real $s$, so $e^u=\cos s\,I+(\sin s/s)u$ (with the continuous value at zero) is unitary with determinant one. Polynomial Neumann approximants to $u\in X$ exponentiate to smooth $SU(2)$ maps with zero normal derivative; continuity gives $e^u\in\mathcal G_N$. Products of maps in $\mathcal G_N$ remain in it, and inverse is matrix adjoint and hence continuous. Gauge transformation by such maps sends $Y$ to $Y$, by approximating both inputs with smooth zero-normal inputs and using the above product estimates. Also $du\in Y$ for $u\in X$. [F1, F3, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 **The exact nonlinear remainder.** Put $h=e^u$ and define $R(u)=h^{-1}dh-du+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h-a$. By step 1.1, $R(u)\in Y$ whenever $u\in X$. Let $E(u)=e^{-u}d(e^u)-du$. Differentiating the convergent matrix series, or integrating the series termwise, gives $e^{-u}d(e^u)=\int_0^1e^{-tu}(du)e^{tu}\,dt$, hence $E(u)=A(u)du$ where $A(0)=0$ and $A$ and its first two matrix derivatives are uniformly bounded for $|u|\le1$. More precisely $|A(u)|\le C|u|$ there. Thus $R(u)=E(u)+(e^{-u}ae^u-a)+e^{-u}\lambda e^u$, with $R(0)=\lambda$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **The quadratic differential term.** Suppose $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}},\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta$ with $\eta$ small enough that [F3] gives $|u|,|v|\le1$. The formula in step 2.1 gives $|d^*E(u)|\le C(|u||D^2u|+|Du|^2)$. Subtracting the two formulas, using bounded first and second derivatives of $A$, and applying [F3]–[F4] gives $\|d^*E(u)\|_3\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}^2$ and $\|d^*(E(u)-E(v))\|_3\le C\eta\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Indeed terms with two first derivatives use $L^6\cdot L^6\subset L^3$, while a second derivative is paired with an $L^\infty$ factor; differences of coefficients are bounded by $C|u-v|$, and the resulting terms use the same two estimates. These formulas hold for the Sobolev classes by the smooth approximation and product continuity of step 1.1. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **The critical Coulomb coefficient and the perturbation.** In $d^*(e^{-u}ae^u-a)$ the term $e^{-u}(d^*a)e^u-d^*a$ vanishes. Only derivatives falling on the exponentials remain, so their pointwise norm is at most $C|a||Du|$ for $|u|\le1$. Subtracting at $u,v$ gives at most $C|a|(|D(u-v)|+|u-v|(|Du|+|Dv|))$. By $L^4\cdot L^{12}\subset L^3$, this gives a difference bound $C\|a\|_4\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$ when $\eta\le1$. The contracted derivative of $e^{-u}\lambda e^u$ consists of $e^{-u}(d^*\lambda)e^u$ and terms bounded by $C|\lambda||Du|$. The same subtraction, [F3] and Holder give a difference bound $C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Thus, after choosing one universal $C_0$, the preceding estimates prove $\|d^*(R(u)-R(v))\|_3\le C_0(\eta+\|a\|_4+\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}})\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. The cancellation of $d^*a$ is why no higher norm of $a$ occurs in this bound. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **A well-defined contraction, including compatibility.** Define $T(u)=S(-d^*R(u))$ on the closed radius-$\eta$ ball in $X$. Step 2.1 and [F2] show $-d^*R(u)\in L^3_0$, so the Neumann solve is well defined for every iterate. Choose positive $\eta,\rho$ so that $\eta\le1$, the $L^\infty$ restriction of step 3.1 holds, and $K_NC_0(\eta+\rho)\le1/4$. Then choose $\delta>0$ so small that $K_NC_0\delta\le1/4$ and $K_N\|d^*\lambda\|_3\le\eta/4$ whenever $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le\delta$; the latter follows from the fixed finite coefficient bound for $d^*$. For $\|a\|_4\le\rho$ and such $\lambda$, step 4.1 gives contraction constant at most $1/2$, and $\|T(0)\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta/4$. Hence $\|T(u)\|_{W^{2,3}}\le3\eta/4$ on that ball. It is a complete metric space by [F1] and the equivalence of its domain norm with $W^{2,3}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, choose, construct, algebra]

6.1 **The correction and uniqueness.** By [F4], $u_{j+1}=T(u_j)$ starting at zero converges to the unique fixed point $u$ in that ball. The equation $-\Delta u=-d^*R(u)$ and $d^*du=-\Delta u$ give $d^*(du+R(u))=0$. Since $d^*a=0$, the form $b=a+du+R(u)=h^{-1}dh+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h$ is Coulomb and belongs to $Y$ by step 1.1. Conversely any $u\in X$ in the stated ball for which $b$ is Coulomb satisfies this same Neumann equation, so uniqueness of [F1] makes it a fixed point and thus this $u$. Also $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\|T(0)\|_{W^{2,3}}+\tfrac12\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le K_N\|d^*\lambda\|_3+\tfrac12\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, giving the first quantitative bound. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 **The correction size in the connection norm.** The matrix power series and product estimates of step 1.1 imply $\|e^{-u}d(e^u)\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, $\|e^{-u}ae^u-a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, and $\|e^{-u}\lambda e^u\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}$ on the fixed small ball. For the middle bound, write $e^{-u}ae^u-a=(e^{-u}-1)ae^u+a(e^u-1)$; the terms with derivatives on $a$ have a factor bounded by $C\|u\|_\infty$, and the other terms use $L^4\cdot L^{12}\subset L^3$. Adding the three bounds and using step 6.1 proves the claimed estimate for $b-a$, with $C$ independent of $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 **Prescribed finite equivariance.** Orthogonal pullback preserves the Laplacian, codifferential, means and all the domain norms. Constant unitary conjugation preserves matrix products, the Frobenius norm and the exponential. Therefore the transformation $u(x)\mapsto d\tau_\gamma^{-1}(u(\gamma x))$ preserves $X$ and commutes with $T$ when $a,\lambda$ have the stated equivariance; this uses the equivariant inverse of [F1]. The zero starting iterate is invariant, so every iterate and its limit are invariant. Exponentiation gives the assertion for $h$. A central unitary scalar acts trivially by conjugation, which explains why a $PU(2)$ action suffices. The existence, uniqueness, estimates and boundary compatibility are all supplied in steps 5.1–7.1; full AC is inherited as stated in [F5]. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The full exponential Neumann iteration in Tao–Tian, Proposition 9.2, Step 3 (PDF pp.38–39), was read. Here its linear solve is the constructed local strong Neumann inverse, and every iterate's mean-zero compatibility is proved through the normal approximation class. The nonlinear estimates exploit the critical $L^4$ norm of the Coulomb coefficient, with its contracted derivative cancelling exactly. This lemma corrects nearby given Coulomb data; a subsequent scaling-path construction is needed to obtain a gauge from small curvature alone.

## Statement

Let $k$ be a commutative field and let $H\trianglelefteq G$ be a normal subgroup with torsion-free abelian quotient $G/H$. If $k[H]$ has no zero divisors, then $k[G]$ has no zero divisors. The group extension need not split; neither finite generation of $G/H$ nor an order on all of $G$ is assumed.

## Statement references

[[def-group-ring]]

[[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]

[[lem-finitely-generated-torsion-free-abelian-freeness-without-choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $k$, normal subgroup $H\trianglelefteq G$, and torsion-free abelian quotient $A=G/H$.

[F1] Group-ring elements have unique finite expansions, multiplication is $k$-bilinear with $[g][h]=[gh]$, and each $[g]$ is a unit ([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

[F2] Every finitely generated torsion-free abelian group is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r$ for some finite $r$ ([[lem-finitely-generated-torsion-free-abelian-freeness-without-choice]]).

[A1] The ring $k[H]$ has no zero divisors.

## Proof

**Given:** Two nonzero elements $f,g\in k[G]$ and [A1].

1.1 Let $B$ be the subgroup of $A$ generated by the images of the finite supports of $f$ and $g$. It is finitely generated, torsion-free and abelian, so [F2] identifies it with $\mathbb Z^r$. Transport the lexicographic order from $\mathbb Z^r$ to $B$. This is a total order invariant under addition. No order on the whole quotient or on $G$ is needed. Let $X,Y\subseteq B$ be the finite quotient supports of $f,g$. Choose lifts $t_x\in G$ for the finitely many elements of $X\cup Y\cup(X+Y)$, using the same lift for any repeated element. By grouping terms in each coset, [F1] gives unique expressions $f=\sum_{x\in X}r_xt_x$ and $g=\sum_{y\in Y}s_yt_y$ with $0\ne r_x,s_y\in k[H]$. Distinct cosets have disjoint group bases, so these grouped coefficients are nonzero. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 For these lifts put $\alpha_x(s)=t_xst_x^{-1}$ on $k[H]$ and $h_{x,y}=t_xt_yt_{x+y}^{-1}\in H$. Normality makes $\alpha_x$ a ring automorphism, with inverse conjugation by $t_x^{-1}$. Direct multiplication gives $(r_xt_x)(s_yt_y)=r_x\alpha_x(s_y)h_{x,y}t_{x+y}$. This is the crossed-product multiplication on the finite supports. The factor $h_{x,y}$ is retained and is a unit; it is not assumed to be $1$. Its compatibility with iterated multiplication is inherited from associativity in $G$. Thus the calculation applies to a nonsplit extension. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $x_0=\max X$ and $y_0=\max Y$. Every other pair $(x,y)$ satisfies $x+y<x_0+y_0$: if $x<x_0$, then $x+y\le x+y_0<x_0+y_0$, and if $x=x_0$ but $y<y_0$, addition invariance gives the same strict inequality. Hence the coefficient of $t_{x_0+y_0}$ in $fg$ is the single term $r_{x_0}\alpha_{x_0}(s_{y_0})h_{x_0,y_0}$. It is nonzero by [A1], invertibility of $h_{x_0,y_0}$ and injectivity of $\alpha_{x_0}$. By disjointness of coset bases, $fg\ne0$. Since $f,g$ were arbitrary, $k[G]$ has no zero divisors. Only finitely many lifts were chosen, so the proof introduces no choice axiom. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at every point with $F':U\to\mathcal B(X,Y)$ continuous in operator norm. Fix $x_0\in U$ and $r>0$ such that $\overline B_{2r}(x_0)\subseteq U$, and suppose an exact solution $x^\dagger\in\overline B_r(x_0)$ satisfies $y=F(x^\dagger)$. Assume $\|F'(x)\|\le1$ for every $x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ and that, for some $0\le\eta<1/2$,

$$
\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)-F'(x)(x-\widetilde x)\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)\|_Y
$$

for every $x,\widetilde x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$. This is a uniform two-point hypothesis with the derivative based at the first point. Assume Countable Choice so that the bounded derivatives have Hilbert adjoints. For $\delta\ge0$ and $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, set $x_0^\delta=x_0$ and define the ideal Landweber sequence by

$$
x_{n+1}^\delta=x_n^\delta+F'(x_n^\delta)^*(y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)).
$$

Let $\tau>2(1+\eta)/(1-2\eta)$. For $\delta>0$, let $N(\delta,y^\delta)$ denote the first $n\in\mathbb N_0$ with $\|y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)\|_Y\le\tau\delta$, if it exists. Put $d_0=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X$ and $c_\tau=1-2\eta-2(1+\eta)/\tau>0$. Then the following hold.

1. For every update before the first discrepancy stop, writing $R_n^\delta=\|y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)\|_Y$, the squared-error estimate is

   $$
   \|x_{n+1}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le R_n^\delta\bigl(2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)R_n^\delta\bigr).
   $$

   In particular, the iterates are Fejér monotone relative to $x^\dagger$ up to the stop: their distance to $x^\dagger$ does not increase. Here Fejér monotonicity means exactly this nonincrease of distance to the stated solution.

2. If $\delta>0$, the first discrepancy index exists and

   $$
   N(\delta,y^\delta)<C\delta^{-2},\qquad C:=1+\frac{d_0^2}{c_\tau\tau^2}.
   $$

   A run of the finite-budget algorithm with budget $M\ge N(\delta,y^\delta)$ returns `stopped` at this first index; if $M<N(\delta,y^\delta)$, it returns `budget_exhausted` at $M$.

3. For exact data ($\delta=0$ and $y^\delta=y$), the ideal sequence is defined for every $n$, satisfies

   $$
   (1-2\eta)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2\le d_0^2,
   $$

   and converges strongly to some $\bar x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ with $F(\bar x)=y$. No finite stopping index is claimed in the exact-data case.

4. For noisy data ($\delta>0$), the ideal stopped iterates converge uniformly over the admissible noise ball to that same exact-data limit:

   $$
   \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\ \sup_{\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta}\|x_{N(\delta,y^\delta)}^\delta-\bar x\|_X=0.
   $$

   For finite-budget runs this conclusion concerns outputs only when their budgets reach the first discrepancy indices. The theorem asserts neither a convergence rate nor that $\bar x$ is an $x_0$-minimum-norm solution.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-nonlinear-landweber-discrepancy|Nonlinear Landweber update and discrepancy test]]

[[def-ip-nonlinear-forward-map|Real-Hilbert forward maps and exact solutions]]

[[def-ip-tangential-cone-condition|Pointwise local tangential-cone inequality; the theorem assumes its uniform two-point form on the outer ball]]

[[def-hilbert-space-adjoint|Hilbert adjoints under Countable Choice]]

[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties|Hilbert-adjoint identities and operator-norm equality]]

[[def-countable-choice|Axiom of Countable Choice]]

[Christian Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, Chapter 11, Assumption 11.2, Lemma 11.3, and Theorems 11.4–11.6](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

[S. Hubmer, E. Sherina, S. Kindermann, and K. Raik, *A numerical comparison of some heuristic stopping rules for nonlinear Landweber iteration*, §2.1](https://epub.oeaw.ac.at/0xc1aa5576_0x003dd6da.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** All hypotheses in the Statement. For any current iterate $u$ in the outer ball, write $A=F'(u)$ and $q=y^\delta-F(u)$. The update is $u^+=u+A^*q$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: the Axiom of Countable Choice, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is assumed. No stronger form of choice is assumed.

[A2] The data satisfy $y=F(x^\dagger)$ and $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$.

[A3] The closed outer ball lies in $U$, $x^\dagger$ is within distance $r$ of $x_0$, $F'$ is continuous in operator norm on $U$, and the derivative bound and uniform two-point tangential-cone inequality in the Statement hold on that ball.

[F1] [[alg-ip-nonlinear-landweber-discrepancy]]: the iteration is $x_{n+1}^\delta=x_n^\delta+F'(x_n^\delta)^*(y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta))$ and the discrepancy check is made before the finite-budget check.

[F2] [[def-ip-tangential-cone-condition]]: at a base point $x$, the local TCC bounds $\|F(x+h)-F(x)-F'(x)h\|_Y$ by $\eta\|F(x+h)-F(x)\|_Y$. The theorem assumes this exact orientation uniformly for pairs in the outer ball.

[F3] [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]] and [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]: $\langle Au,v\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*v\rangle_X$ and $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ for every bounded Hilbert-space operator $A$.

[F4] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the real inner product is symmetric and $\|u\|_X^2=\langle u,u\rangle_X$; the corresponding expansion is $\|u+v\|_X^2=\|u\|_X^2+2\langle u,v\rangle_X+\|v\|_X^2$.

[F5] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$.

[F6] [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]: $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$ in each real Hilbert space.

[F7] [[def-hilbert-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $X$ for the induced norm converges in $X$.

[F8] [[def-series]] and [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]]: a series with nonnegative real terms and bounded partial sums converges, and its tails tend to zero.

[F9] [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and [[thm-of-archimedean]]: the real field is complete and its natural numbers are unbounded above.

[F10] [[thm-well-ordering-principle]]: every nonempty set of natural indices has a least member.

[F11] [[def-operator-norm]]: for every bounded linear $T$, $\|Tu\|\le\|T\|\,\|u\|$.

[F12] [[def-ip-nonlinear-forward-map]]: a real-Hilbert forward map is $F:U\to Y$ on an open domain, and exact solutions satisfy $F(x^\dagger)=y$.

[F13] [[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]: each Fréchet derivative is a bounded real-linear operator, and differentiability on $U$ defines the derivative map $F':U\to\mathcal B(X,Y)$.

## Proof


1.1 Fix a current point $u$ and any exact solution $z$ in the outer ball, and set $e=u-z$, $R=F(u)-y^\delta$, and $w=F(u)-F(z)-F'(u)e$. The uniform TCC gives $\|w\|_Y\le\eta\|F(u)-F(z)\|_Y$. Since $y=F(z)$, $y^\delta-F(u)+F'(u)e=y^\delta-y-w$, so by the noise bound and the triangle inequality, $\|y^\delta-F(u)+F'(u)e\|_Y\le\delta+\eta\|F(u)-y\|_Y\le(1+\eta)\delta+\eta\|R\|_Y$. [given, A2, A3, F2, F6, algebra]

1.2 The update has $e^+=e+A^*(y^\delta-F(u))$. Expanding its squared norm and using the adjoint identity yields $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2=2\langle y^\delta-F(u),Ae\rangle_Y+\|A^*(y^\delta-F(u))\|_X^2$. Since [F13] makes $A$ a bounded operator, [F11] gives $\|A^*(y^\delta-F(u))\|_X\le\|A^*\|\,\|R\|_Y=\|A\|\,\|R\|_Y\le\|R\|_Y$. [A1, A3, F3, F4, F11, F13, algebra]

2.1 Write $Ae=-(y^\delta-F(u))+(y^\delta-F(u)+Ae)$. By [F5] and step 1.2, $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2\le-\|R\|_Y^2+2\|R\|_Y\,\|y^\delta-F(u)+Ae\|_Y$. Substituting step 1.1 gives the stated one-step estimate $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2\le\|R\|_Y\bigl(2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y\bigr)$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F5, algebra]

3.1 If $\delta>0$ and $\|R\|_Y>\tau\delta$, then $2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y<0$ by the strict lower bound on $\tau$, so the squared error decreases. For exact data $\delta=0$, the same bound is $-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y^2\le0$ for every residual, including zero. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Put $c_\tau:=1-2\eta-2(1+\eta)/\tau$, which is positive by the strict hypothesis on $\tau$. For each $n<N(\delta,y^\delta)$, the residual is greater than $\tau\delta$; step 2.1 then gives $\|x_{n+1}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le-c_\tau(R_n^\delta)^2$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 For exact data, step 2.1 gives $\|x_{n+1}-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le-(1-2\eta)\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2$ for every $n$. Summing the first $K$ inequalities telescopes and yields $(1-2\eta)\sum_{n<K}\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2\le d_0^2-\|x_K-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le d_0^2$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The initial point satisfies $\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X=d_0\le r$. At every update before the noisy stop, or at every exact-data update, step 3.1 keeps $\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X\le d_0$; consequently $\|x_n^\delta-x_0\|_X\le\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X+d_0\le2r$. Induction therefore keeps every iterate needed by the recurrence in the declared outer ball and proves Fejér decrease relative to $x^\dagger$. [given, A3, step 3.1, F1, F6, induction]

4.2 Suppose $\delta>0$ and the discrepancy test never succeeds. Summing step 3.2 over the first $K$ updates telescopes, while every residual exceeds $\tau\delta$, so $K\tau^2\delta^2<\sum_{n<K}(R_n^\delta)^2\le d_0^2/c_\tau$ for every natural $K$. The Archimedean property in [F9] supplies a natural $K>d_0^2/(c_\tau\tau^2\delta^2)$, contradicting this bound. Hence the first stopping index is finite. [given, step 3.2, F9, assume-contra, choose, algebra]

4.3 The partial sums of the nonnegative residual-square series are bounded by step 3.3. By [F8] the series converges, its tails tend to zero, and its terms tend to zero; thus $\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y\to0$ and the claimed infinite-series bound holds. [step 3.3, F8, algebra]

4.4 Let $e_j:=x_j-x^\dagger$, $a_j:=\|e_j\|_X^2$, and $\rho_j:=\|F(x_j)-y\|_Y$. The sequence $a_j$ is nonincreasing by step 3.1. Hence $\Delta_j:=a_j-a_{j+1}\ge0$, and the partial sums satisfy $\sum_{j<K}\Delta_j=a_0-a_K\le a_0$. Applying [F8] again shows that the tail sums $D_n:=\sum_{j\ge n}\Delta_j$ tend to zero. [step 3.1, step 3.3, F8, algebra]

5.1 If $d_0>0$, the same telescoping through the finite first index gives $N(\delta,y^\delta)\tau^2\delta^2<d_0^2/c_\tau$, hence $N(\delta,y^\delta)<C\delta^{-2}$. If $d_0=0$, then $x_0=x^\dagger$ and the initial residual is at most $\delta<\tau\delta$, so $N=0$ and the same bound holds for the stated positive $C$. By [F1], a budget reaching $N$ returns the first stop, while a shorter budget returns `budget_exhausted`. [given, A2, step 3.2, step 4.2, F1, algebra]

5.2 Fix $m\ge n$ and choose $k\in\{n,\ldots,m\}$ minimizing the finite set of residuals $\rho_j$; [F10] supplies a least index among minimizers. For $n\le j<m$, put $A_j=F'(x_j)$, $w_j=F(x_j)-y-A_je_j$, and $v_{j,k}=F(x_j)-F(x_k)-A_j(x_j-x_k)$. The uniform TCC gives $\|w_j\|_Y\le\eta\rho_j$ and $\|v_{j,k}\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x_j)-F(x_k)\|_Y\le\eta(\rho_j+\rho_k)\le2\eta\rho_j$. Since $A_je_k=\bigl(F(x_j)-y-w_j\bigr)+\bigl(F(x_k)-F(x_j)+v_{j,k}\bigr)=F(x_k)-y-w_j+v_{j,k}$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle y-F(x_j),A_je_k\rangle_Y|\le\rho_j(\rho_k+\|w_j\|_Y+\|v_{j,k}\|_Y)\le(1+3\eta)\rho_j^2$. [given, A3, step 4.1, F2, F5, F10, choose, algebra]

5.3 For any fixed finite number of executed updates, the noisy iterates converge to the exact iterates as $\delta\to0$ along data sequences whose discrepancy stop occurs no earlier. Indeed, the update map $(x,z)\mapsto x+F'(x)^*(z-F(x))$ is continuous: $F$ is continuous by Fréchet differentiability, $F'$ is continuous by hypothesis, and [F3] together with [F11] gives operator-norm continuity of the adjoint action. Induction from the common initial point proves the fixed-index assertion. [A3, F1, F3, F11, F13, step 4.1, induction, algebra]

6.1 The exact update gives $e_{j+1}-e_j=A_j^*(y-F(x_j))$. Summing this identity and using [F3] shows $\langle e_k-e_m,e_k\rangle_X\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j=k}^{m-1}\rho_j^2\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$, and likewise $\langle e_k-e_n,e_k\rangle_X\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j=n}^{k-1}\rho_j^2\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$. [step 5.2, F3, algebra]

7.1 Real inner-product expansion gives $\|e_m-e_k\|_X^2=2\langle e_k-e_m,e_k\rangle_X+a_m-a_k\le2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$, since $a_m\le a_k$. It also gives $\|e_k-e_n\|_X^2=2\langle e_k-e_n,e_k\rangle_X+a_n-a_k\le2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2+D_n$, because $a_n-a_k=\sum_{j=n}^{k-1}\Delta_j\le D_n$. [step 4.4, step 6.1, F4, algebra]

8.1 By the triangle inequality, $\|e_m-e_n\|_X\le\sqrt{2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2}+\sqrt{2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2+D_n}$, which tends to zero uniformly in $m\ge n$ by steps 4.3 and 4.4. Thus $(e_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness of $X$ gives $x_n\to\bar x$. By Fréchet differentiability at $\bar x$, $F(x_n)-F(\bar x)=F'(\bar x)(x_n-\bar x)+o(\|x_n-\bar x\|_X)$, so boundedness of $F'(\bar x)$ implies $F(x_n)\to F(\bar x)$; step 4.3 gives $F(\bar x)=y$. step 4.1 and the triangle inequality give $\|x_n-x_0\|_X\le2r$, so passage to the limit gives $\bar x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$. [step 4.1, step 4.3, step 4.4, step 7.1, F6, F7, F12, F13, A3, algebra]

9.1 Suppose the uniform noisy-data conclusion fails. Then some $\varepsilon>0$ and, for every $j$, a positive $\delta_j<1/j$ and admissible datum $y_j$ can be selected so that the stopped iterate is at least $\varepsilon/2$ from $\bar x$; [A1] supplies this countable selection from the nonempty bad-data sets. Let $N_j=N(\delta_j,y_j)$. Passing to a subsequence, either $N_j$ is a fixed integer or $N_j\to\infty$: a bounded sequence of natural indices has a value occurring infinitely often, and an unbounded one has an increasing subsequence chosen recursively by least indices. [A1, F10, step 8.1, choose, assume-contra]

9.2 In the fixed-index case, write $N_j=N$. Step 5.3 gives $x_N^{\delta_j}\to x_N$. Fréchet differentiability at $x_N$ and boundedness of $F'(x_N)$ imply $F(x_N^{\delta_j})\to F(x_N)$. The discrepancy test and noise bound give $\|F(x_N^{\delta_j})-y\|_Y\le\tau\delta_j+\delta_j$, so $F(x_N)=y$. The exact update at $x_N$ is then zero, so $x_n=x_N$ for every $n\ge N$ and therefore $x_N=\bar x$. Step 5.3 now gives $x_N^{\delta_j}\to\bar x$, contradicting the selected distance lower bound. [A2, step 8.1, step 5.3, F1, F12, F13, algebra]

9.3 In the case $N_j\to\infty$, choose $L$ with $\|x_L-\bar x\|_X<\varepsilon/4$ by step 8.1. For all sufficiently large $j$, $N_j\ge L$ and step 5.3 gives $\|x_L^{\delta_j}-x_L\|_X<\varepsilon/4$. Each noisy iterate before its stop stays in the outer ball by step 4.1, and $\bar x$ lies there by step 8.1; applying the one-step estimate of step 2.1 with the exact solution $\bar x$ makes the noisy iterates Fejér monotone relative to $\bar x$ up to $N_j$. Hence $\|x_{N_j}^{\delta_j}-\bar x\|_X\le\|x_L^{\delta_j}-\bar x\|_X<\varepsilon/2$, again contradicting the selected lower bound. [A3, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 8.1, step 5.3, F6, algebra]

10.1 Both subsequence cases contradict the failure assumption in step 9.1. Therefore the supremum over all data satisfying $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$ tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. [step 9.1, step 9.2, step 9.3, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Remarks

The lower bound on $\tau$ is sufficient, not necessary. The local TCC constant can be difficult to verify and is often not known numerically; when it is unknown, a chosen $\tau$ cannot be certified by this theorem merely because it is a common practical value. The nonlinear residual sequence need not be monotone, which is why the exact-data Cauchy proof selects a minimum residual on each finite block. The result is local to the declared ball and gives neither a rate nor a minimum-norm selection.

## Remarks references

[S. Hubmer, E. Sherina, S. Kindermann, and K. Raik, *A numerical comparison of some heuristic stopping rules for nonlinear Landweber iteration*, §2.1](https://epub.oeaw.ac.at/0xc1aa5576_0x003dd6da.pdf)

## Statement

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3) =\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).$$

## Statement references

[Jessica S. Purcell, *Hyperbolic Knot Theory*, Theorem 9.3 and Example 9.4](https://users.monash.edu/~jpurcell/book/HypKnotTheory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular positively oriented ideal tetrahedron in $\mathbb H^3$.

[F1] [[def-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-and-cusp-holonomy]] specifies the upper half-space model; a normalized tetrahedron with vertices $0,1,\infty,\omega$, $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, is regular.

[F2] [[lem-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-parameter-relations]] proves that this tetrahedron has all dihedral angles $\pi/3$.

[F3] [[lem-ideal-orthoscheme-volume]] gives $\operatorname{Vol}(\mathcal O_\zeta)=\frac12\Lambda(\zeta)$ for the explicit region $\mathcal O_\zeta$ in upper half-space.

[F4] [[lem-lobachevsky-fourier-expansion-and-pi-third-bound]] gives the absolutely convergent series for $\Lambda(\pi/3)$.

## Proof

1.1 Apply a Euclidean similarity of the boundary plane, extended by the same scaling of height, sending the circumcircle of the three finite ideal vertices to the unit circle centered at $0$; this upper half-space isometry fixes $\infty$. The three vertices become points $p,q,r$ on that circle and remain equilateral. Hence $(0,0)$ lies in the interior of their triangle, so the vertical ray from $(0,0,1)$ to $\infty$ lies inside the tetrahedron. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 On the unit-hemisphere face, draw the perpendicular arcs from $(0,0,1)$ to its three edges and the arcs from $(0,0,1)$ to $p,q,r$. Cone the six resulting sectors to $\infty$. Because the vertical ray lies in the tetrahedron, the six simplices have disjoint interiors and cover the tetrahedron; their common faces have three-dimensional volume zero. Each simplex has two finite vertices and two ideal vertices. Its three right dihedral angles come from the perpendicular cuts; among its other angles, two equal the corresponding original tetrahedron edge angle $\zeta$ and the third is $\pi/2-\zeta$. The tetrahedron is regular, so [F2] gives $\zeta=\pi/3$ for each of the six simplices. [F2, given, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Normalize one simplex by a hyperbolic isometry so its ideal vertices are $\infty$ and $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$ and one finite vertex is $(0,0,1)$. The three right angles place the projected right-angle vertex at $(\cos\zeta,0)$: the two legs are horizontal and vertical. The angle at the origin is $\zeta$, so the other ideal point has coordinates $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$. The projected triangle is the intersection of the half-planes $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$, $x\le\cos\zeta$ and $y\le x\tan\zeta$. The unit hemisphere through $(0,0,1)$ has equation $x^2+y^2+t^2=1$, and the tetrahedral side is above it. Thus the simplex is exactly $\mathcal O_\zeta$ from [F3] with $\zeta=\pi/3$. [F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 By [F3], each of the six simplices has volume $\frac12\Lambda(\pi/3)$. Their interiors are disjoint and their union is the tetrahedron up to faces of volume zero, so additivity gives $\operatorname{Vol}=6\cdot\frac12\Lambda(\pi/3)=3\Lambda(\pi/3)$. Substitution of the absolutely convergent series in [F4] gives the second displayed expression; absolute convergence follows by comparison with $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot admitting a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ (a smooth embedding of the closed disk with interior in $\operatorname{int}B^4$ and boundary $K\subset S^3$). Let $W_D$ be its connected double cover branched along $D$, so $H_*(W_D;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(\mathrm{point};\mathbb Q)$, and let $Y=\Sigma_2(K)$ be the oriented double branched cover of $S^3$ using the positive-meridian convention. Then $H_*(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. Define the torsion linking pairing $\lambda_Y$ on $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ by $\lambda_Y([C],[D])=(F\cdot D)/n\pmod{\mathbb Z}$ when $\partial F=nC$, with signed intersection in the oriented $Y$. Under Poincare duality, the restriction image of $\operatorname{Spin}^c(W_D)$ in $\operatorname{Spin}^c(Y)$ is an affine coset of a subgroup $M\subseteq H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ with $M=M^\perp$, where $M^\perp=\{x:\lambda_Y(m,x)=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$; such a subgroup is a metabolizer. It has $|M|^2=|H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)|$. Every extending structure $\mathfrak t$ in this coset satisfies $d(Y,\mathfrak t)=0$. No conclusion is asserted for a merely locally flat topological disk (a topological embedding with local flat disk charts but no smoothness hypothesis) or for nonextending boundary structures.

## Statement references

[[lem-slice-disk-double-cover-is-rational-homology-ball|The smooth slice-disk double cover is a rational homology ball]]

[[lem-rational-ball-spin-c-extension-set-metabolizer|The extension coset is a self-annihilating subgroup]]

[[thm-correction-term-obstruction-from-rational-ball|Correction-term vanishing for extending structures]]

[[lem-branched-cover-surgery-presentation-from-seifert-surface|The Seifert-surface surgery presentation]]

[[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix|The positive-meridian surgery linking convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and a smooth proper slice disk $D\subset B^4$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the smooth slice-cover and extension-set suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The connected cover branched over $D$ is a rational homology four-ball and its boundary is $Y=\Sigma_2(K)$ under the positive-meridian convention ([[lem-slice-disk-double-cover-is-rational-homology-ball]]).

[F2] For a rational ball with connected rational-homology-sphere boundary, the extending Spin$^c$ structures form one affine coset of a self-annihilating subgroup of the boundary torsion cohomology, and that subgroup has square-root order ([[lem-rational-ball-spin-c-extension-set-metabolizer]]).

[F3] A Spin$^c$ structure extending over a smooth rational homology four-ball has correction term zero ([[thm-correction-term-obstruction-from-rational-ball]]).

[F4] The double branched cover has the nonsingular Seifert-surface surgery presentation; its meridian linking form uses the matrix inverse convention fixed by the positive-meridian surgery supplier ([[lem-branched-cover-surgery-presentation-from-seifert-surface]], [[lem-cyclic-cover-linking-form-inverse-matrix]]).

## Proof
**Proof technique:** apply the slice-cover, extension-set, and vanishing results in sequence.

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 Apply [F1] to $D$. It gives a rational homology four-ball $W_D$ and identifies the oriented boundary with $Y$; in particular $Y$ is a rational homology sphere. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 Apply [F2] to $(W_D,Y)$. It identifies the restriction image as one affine coset of a self-annihilating subgroup $M$ for the torsion linking form and gives $|M|^2=|H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)|$. The boundary orientation and linking convention agree with the stated one by [F4]. [F2, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Every structure in that restriction image extends over $W_D$, so [F3] gives $d(Y,\mathfrak t)=0$ for each such structure. The proof used a smooth disk in [F1]; it does not apply to a merely locally flat topological disk. It makes no statement about structures outside the restriction image. [F1, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ have admissible adjoint local system, and let $v_\rho$ be a nonzero peripheral-adjoint-invariant vector for which $[v_\rho\otimes\lambda],[v_\rho\otimes\mu]$ form the specified ordered basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\operatorname{Ad}\rho)$. If a generator of the one-dimensional kernel of inclusion is $a[v_\rho\otimes\lambda]+b[v_\rho\otimes\mu]$, the **Bénard–Florens–Rodau slope** is $s_K(\rho)=-b/a\in\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$, with $a=0$ interpreted as $\infty$. Rescaling $v_\rho$ or the kernel generator does not change this projective ratio. A rational function on an irreducible character component means an element of its function field, the fraction field of its coordinate domain. A projective-valued rational function means a point of the projective line over that field; it may be identically $\infty$. The slope's rational extension has this projective meaning. Unless its generic value is $\infty$, it is an ordinary rational function, whose individual infinite values are poles. Its rational extension is not a value assigned to every singular or inadmissible character.

## Definition

For a smooth knot $K$ with chosen compact exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K$, a finite-volume hyperbolic knot exterior structure is a complete Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$ on $\operatorname{int}(E_K)$ with finite volume and exactly one cusp whose torus cross-section is isotopic in $\operatorname{int}(E_K)$ to a parallel copy of $T_K$. ---

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice and use the Gaussian sequence inverse model with singular values $s_j>0$, inverse-noise weights $\sigma_j=s_j^{-1}$, and parameter coordinates $\theta=(\theta_j)\in\ell^2$. Let $a=(a_j)$ be a positive nondecreasing sequence with $a_j\to\infty$, and let $\sigma=(\sigma_j)$ be a positive nondecreasing sequence with $\sigma_j\to\infty$. For $\varepsilon>0$, put $\eta_j=\theta_j/\sigma_j$ and observe $Y_j=Z_j/\sigma_j=\eta_j+\varepsilon\xi_j$, where $Z$ is the normalized observation in the Gaussian sequence inverse model and the $\xi_j$ are independent standard normal random variables. For $0<q\le2$ and $r>0$, define
$$\Theta_q(r)=\left\{\eta\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}:(\sigma_j\eta_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}|a_j\sigma_j\eta_j|^q\le1,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sigma_j^2\eta_j^2\ge r^2\right\}.$$
Test $H_0:\eta=0$ against $H_1:\eta\in\Theta_q(r)$ by a product-Borel measurable randomized test $\psi:\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\to[0,1]$, where $\psi(y)$ is the rejection probability. Its type-I error and maximal type-II error are
$$\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}\psi,\qquad \beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\sup_{\eta\in\Theta_q(r)}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,\eta}(1-\psi).$$
When $\Theta_q(r)=\varnothing$, define $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=0$, the convention that no type-II error occurs when no alternative is possible. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$ define
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\inf_{\psi:\,\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)\le\alpha}\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=\inf_\psi\{\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)+\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)\}.$$
A positive family $r_\varepsilon^*\to0$ is a minimax separation rate if $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))\to1$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, while $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))\to0$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to0$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$.

## Definition

Let $M$ be a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation $T$ consisting of $t$ tetrahedra. A **normal arc** in a triangular face is a properly embedded arc whose endpoints lie in the interiors of two distinct edges and which cuts off the third vertex. A **normal disk** in a tetrahedron is a properly embedded disk whose boundary is a union of normal arcs, one on each face it meets, and whose disk type is one of the following: one of four **triangle types**, each cutting off one tetrahedron vertex, or one of three **quadrilateral types**, each separating one pair of opposite vertices from the other pair. Disks of the same type are parallel copies. A **normal surface** is a properly embedded piecewise-linear surface that meets every tetrahedron in a finite disjoint union of these normal disks and whose arcs match across every interior face. The empty surface is admitted for coordinate addition and has the zero vector.

For each of the seven disk types in each tetrahedron, the **normal coordinate vector** $v(S)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{7t}$ records the number of disks of that type in a normal surface $S$. For an interior face shared by tetrahedra $\Delta$ and $\Delta'$, and for each of the three normal-arc types $\tau$ in that face, its **face-matching equation** is the equality between the sum of coordinates of disk types in $\Delta$ whose boundary contributes an arc of type $\tau$ and the corresponding sum for $\Delta'$. A disk type contributes either one such arc or none. A nonnegative integer vector is **admissible** when it satisfies all these equations and, in each tetrahedron, at most one of the three quadrilateral coordinates is nonzero. The **Haken cone** $C(T)\subseteq\mathbb R^{7t}$ is the set of nonnegative real vectors satisfying only the face-matching equations; it does not impose quadrilateral restrictions. A nonzero admissible integer vector is **fundamental** if it is not the sum of two nonzero admissible integer vectors. A **primitive vertex vector** is the unique nonnegative integer vector with relatively prime coordinates on a one-dimensional face (extreme ray) of $C(T)$.

A standard schematic records the two disk shapes in a tetrahedron. The vertices are $A,B,C,D$; each red polygon is the intersection of a normal disk with the tetrahedron boundary.

\draw (A)--(B)--(C)--cycle; \draw (A)--(D)--(B); \draw (C)--(D);
\node[below left] at (A) {$A$}; \node[below right] at (B) {$B$}; \node[above] at (C) {$C$}; \node[right] at (D) {$D$};
\draw[red,thick] (0.39,0.20)--(0.68,0.30)--(0.65,0.45)--(0.43,0.48)--cycle;

\begin{scope}[xshift=4.1cm]
\coordinate (A) at (0,0); \coordinate (B) at (2.7,0); \coordinate (C) at (1.35,2.2); \coordinate (D) at (1.45,0.95);
\draw (A)--(B)--(C)--cycle; \draw (A)--(D)--(B); \draw (C)--(D);

**Given:** $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=j^\alpha$, $\sigma_j=e^{\beta j}$, and the finite-support extremal profile for sufficiently small $r$. For this rate comparison, $X_\varepsilon\asymp Y_\varepsilon$ means the ratio is bounded above and away from zero by constants independent of $\varepsilon$.

[F1] [[thm-ip-ellipsoid-detection-boundary]]: $r^2=A J_1/J_2$, $u_\varepsilon^2=(r/\varepsilon)^4J_0/(2J_1^2)$, and $u_\varepsilon\to0$ or $\infty$ gives the two minimax risk regimes.

[F2] [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-exists-for-small-r]] and [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-is-minimizer]]: the active cutoff $m$ satisfies $A\asymp m^{-2\alpha}$.
## Verification

1.1 Let $m$ be the largest active index, so $(m+1)^{-2\alpha}\le A<m^{-2\alpha}$, and write $\ell=m-j$. For $1\le\ell\le m/2$, the mean-value theorem applied to $x^{2\alpha}$ on $[1/2,1]$ gives $$c_\alpha\frac{\ell+1}{m}\le1-A(m-\ell)^{2\alpha}\le C_\alpha\frac{\ell+1}{m}.$$ For $\ell>m/2$, the profile factor is at most one. Summing against $\sigma_j^4=e^{4\beta m}e^{-4\beta\ell}$, the near terms are bounded by the convergent sums $\sum_{\ell\ge0}(\ell+1)e^{-4\beta\ell}$ and $\sum_{\ell\ge0}(\ell+1)^2e^{-4\beta\ell}$, and the far tail is exponentially smaller than $m^{-2}$. The $\ell=1$ term supplies matching lower bounds. Thus $$J_1\asymp J_2\asymp e^{4\beta m}/m,\qquad J_0\asymp e^{4\beta m}/m^2.$$ For $J_2$, its extra factor $Aa_j^2$ is at most one and is bounded below by a positive constant at $j=m-1$. Consequently [F1] gives $r^2\asymp A\asymp m^{-2\alpha}$ and $u_\varepsilon^2\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^4e^{-4\beta m}$. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The cutoff relation implies $m\asymp r^{-1/\alpha}$. For $r_\varepsilon^*=(\log\varepsilon^{-1}/\beta)^{-\alpha}$, if $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, then $m/(\log\varepsilon^{-1}/\beta)\to\infty$, so the expression in step 1.1 tends to zero. If the ratio tends to infinity while $r_\varepsilon\to0$, then $m=o(\log\varepsilon^{-1})$ and $\log u_\varepsilon^2=4\log\varepsilon^{-1}-4\beta m+4\log r_\varepsilon+O(1)\to\infty$, because $\log(1/r_\varepsilon)=O(\log\log\varepsilon^{-1})$. If $r_\varepsilon$ does not tend to zero, reduce to $\bar r_\varepsilon=\sqrt{r_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon^*}$. Nonempty alternatives satisfy $r_\varepsilon^2\le a_1^{-2}$ by the two q=2 constraints, so $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$ and $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$. The inclusion $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_2(\bar r_\varepsilon)$ transfers consistent tests to the original class. By [F1], these limits prove the displayed rate. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$. There is a connected compact smooth Seifert surface $F$ with a geometric symplectic basis $s_1,\ldots,s_g,\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_g$ whose positive-push matrix is
$$V=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_g+U\\ U^T&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad U\text{ strictly upper triangular}.$$
Place $F$ on the unit sphere in the literal radius-$3/2$ ball and join its boundary to the outer copy of $K$ by the radial product collar, rounding the inner junction away from that outer collar. Write $\Sigma$ for this proper surface. Its actual smooth normal thickening can be chosen so that the rounded complement
$$N=B^4_{3/2}\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu\Sigma$$
is compact, connected and smooth, with $\pi_1(N)\cong\mathbb Z$ generated by the positive normal meridian of $\Sigma$.

The fixed negative normal pushoffs of the short curves give disjoint framed circles $\delta_i\subset\partial N$. They bound proper framed smooth generic disks $\Delta_i$ in $N$ admitting framed smooth immersed spheres $f_i$ such that
$$\lambda(\Delta_i,f_j)=\delta_{ij},\quad \lambda(\Delta_i,\Delta_j)=0\ (i\ne j),\quad \mu(\Delta_i)=0,\quad \lambda(f_i,f_j)=0,\quad\mu(f_i)=0$$
in $\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z]$ with the specified Wall conventions. Along the fixed annuli from $\delta_i$ to $s_i\subset\Sigma$, their boundary framings agree with the normal directions of $s_i$ within $\Sigma$. Thus the data retain the actual ambient ball, complement, attaching circles and compression framings. The group is good when the infinite-cyclic good-group theorem is supplied. For $g=0$ the disk and sphere families are empty and the geometric complement assertion remains valid.

## Statement references

[[lem-alexander-one-knot-has-trivial-alexander-basis|The required trivial Alexander basis on a Seifert surface]]

[[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data|Relative immersed disk data and Wall obstructions]]

[[thm-infinite-cyclic-group-is-good-for-disk-embedding|Goodness of the infinite cyclic group]]

Stavros Garoufalidis and Peter Teichner, “On Knots with Trivial Alexander Polynomial,” Appendix A, https://people.math.gatech.edu/~stavros/publications/teichner1.pdf

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the smooth oriented Alexander-one knot, and the disk-data conventions.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]: Full AC supplies the countable-choice interfaces.

[F1] [[lem-alexander-one-knot-has-trivial-alexander-basis]]: The proved construction supplies an actual smooth geometric basis with the stated triangular and symmetric blocks.

[F2] [[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data]]: The Wall coefficients use the fixed paths, local signs, sheet involution and specified disk-boundary normal framings. The proof separately constructs extending normal framings for these particular compression disks; it does not infer extension from the disk-data convention.

[F3] [[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding]] and [[thm-infinite-cyclic-group-is-good-for-disk-embedding]]: Goodness is the null-disk property, and the cyclic theorem supplies it for the computed complement group.

[F4] [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]] and [[lem-seifert-pairing-well-defined]]: $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i,a_j^-)$, with symmetric bilinear linking.

[F5] [[thm-whitney-approximation-for-manifold-valued-maps]] and [[thm-parametric-transversality]]: Smooth relative fillings and the explicitly submersive finite affine-jet perturbations in the proof give generic immersed disks under Countable Choice.

## Proof

1.1 Use [F1] to fix the actual geometric trivial Alexander basis. The following integral shear preserves its short–long intersection convention and makes its long–long block zero. [given, A1, F1, F4, construct]

1.2 The current general disk carrier demands vanishing mutual/self Wall numbers for its dual spheres, not merely the triangular disk–sphere matrix in the short GT application. The following integral operation removes a potential extra obstruction rather than assuming those two interfaces coincide. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.3 Suppose a supplied geometric trivial Alexander basis has matrix V=[[0,I+U],[U^T,W]], with U strictly upper triangular and W symmetric. Put N(C)=CU+U^T C on symmetric integral g-by-g matrices. Left multiplication by U^T and right multiplication by U commute and each has gth power zero. The binomial expansion therefore gives N^(2g−1)=0: in every summand one of the two exponents is at least g. Hence I+N has the integral inverse sum_{r=0}^{2g−2}(−N)^r (the g=0 case is empty). Set C=−(I+N)^(−1)W. This is an explicit symmetric INTEGRAL matrix, since N preserves symmetry. The block change S=[[I,C],[0,I]] is symplectic: its new long basis vectors are ell'_j=ell_j+sum_i s_i C_ij, and their intersections are −C_ij+C_ji=0; short–long intersections remain the identity. Direct multiplication gives
S^T V S = [[0,I+U],[U^T,W+C(I+U)+U^T C]]
= [[0,I+U],[U^T,0]]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.4 Thus the same triangular block admits an entirely zero long–long Seifert block. This does NOT assert minimal Seifert rank: U may be nonzero. The initial basis is supplied by [F1]. This particular shear has an explicit geometric realization, so no general surjectivity assertion about the mapping-class group is needed for THIS step. For any vector v among e_i and e_i+e_j, realize its short-class sum by an embedded circle: use s_i for e_i; for e_i+e_j use a band sum of parallel copies of s_i,s_j along a simple arc avoiding all short curves. Such an arc exists because cutting along all the short curves leaves a connected surface. If that cut were disconnected, the oriented boundary of one complementary component would give a nontrivial integral relation among the independent short classes, a contradiction. The band sum and its small annular neighborhood can be chosen disjoint from every original short curve. A Dehn twist in that annulus, written in annular coordinates as (theta,r) to (theta+2pi rho(r),r), is a homeomorphism fixed on the annulus boundary; choose rho constant zero/one near its two ends. Tracking an oriented transverse arc gives on homology the transvection x to x+(x intersection v)v, with sign reversed by the inverse twist. It fixes every short class and sends the long classes by the symmetric rank-one shear vv^T, with the sign chosen according to the intersection convention. Now
E_ij+E_ji = (e_i+e_j)(e_i+e_j)^T−E_ii−E_jj. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.5 Every symmetric integral C is a finite integer sum of these rank-one matrices. Compose the corresponding positive/negative twist powers. Each action fixes the short Lagrangian, so their shear matrices ADD even when their supporting annuli are not disjoint. The composition is an actual orientation-preserving boundary-fixed surface homeomorphism. Applying it to the entire original geometric basis preserves all its geometric intersection counts and realizes S. In the smooth category choose smooth annular cutoffs to obtain a diffeomorphism. Thus the zero-W basis is genuinely geometric and has exactly the same triangular U. The basis supplier [F1] supplies that initial input. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.6 Apply the preceding shear to [F1]. We obtain a smooth geometric basis s_i,ell_i with V=[[0,I+U],[U^T,0]], not only the existential lattice statement. The following construction retains the ambient ball and all attaching data. It is stated before invoking any disk-embedding conclusion. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.7 Use the literal ball of radius1.5 and its unit sphere. Place the original surface F in that unit sphere and add the exterior collar K times [1,1.5]. Round its junction with F, retaining the outer K product collar; call this proper smooth surface Sigma. Near F its normal coordinates are the radial coordinate x and the positive normal coordinate y of F in S3. Choose its open normal thickening there to be .9<x<1.1, |y|<epsilon, with the compatible product continuation near K. This is an ACTUAL smooth thickening, supplied by the radial product and the normal line of the oriented surface in S3. Put N=the complement of that open thickening, with corners rounded away from the marked circles. It is compact, connected, smooth, and the original ball/surface have not been replaced by an abstract four-manifold. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.8 A disk-and-band handle decomposition of F has one disk and2g bands. Make its height increase from that disk across the bands to the boundary, and realize that height as a small radial displacement in the displayed collar. The complement has one0handle, one1handle from the surface minimum and2g2handles from its bands, with no higher handles. This local complement recipe follows by taking the product normal2disk to a surface0handle or1handle: its complement adds respectively the normal meridian1handle or the2handle whose core crosses the band. The product collars identify the attaching pieces; no arbitrary embedded4ball is identified with the standard ball. The resulting complement deformation retracts onto a2complex with one vertex, one1cell and2g2cells. Name the positive normal meridian of its one1handle a. The local2handle at an oriented surface band identifies its endpoint meridians by transport through the band: its attaching relation is m_1 w m_2^−1 w^−1. To see the signs, take the boundary of a normal2disk and transport it along the band core; the two boundary ends of the resulting normal-annulus strip have opposite induced boundary orientations. Both endpoint meridians come from the same original disk and represent a in the one-generator1skeleton. Any winding of a knotted band only changes the transport word w, which is a power of a there. Thus the attaching word is a a^k a^−1 a^−k=1, for every band. Consequently pi1(N)=Z, and the same2complex is homotopy equivalent to a circle wedge2g spheres. This is the actual group/attaching-word computation, not an inference from H1 alone. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.9 Choose generic immersed disks Delta(s_i) in the inner unit ball with boundaries s_i-down. Run their boundary collars in the negative-y side of the marked normal strip, bending into the interior of N immediately off each boundary circle. Choose disks Delta(ell_i) bounding the long curves and trim their radial collars to x=.8; they then have boundaries ell_i at x=.8 and lie in the ball x<=.8. The short disks consist of disks in that inner ball and their mutually disjoint negative-y collars. Their union lies in a simply connected part of N: the inner ball together with those product collars retracts onto the inner ball. Thus all their equivariant intersection labels are1. Their ordinary intersections are the boundary linking numbers, which are V(s_i,s_j)=0. To justify this relative4-ball identity, compare one filling disk with a Seifert surface for the same boundary curve pushed into a thin boundary collar. Their difference is a two-cycle, null in the ball. Its intersection with the other proper disk is therefore zero, by the boundary-of-intersection identity for a bounding three-chain. The collar surface counts exactly the linking number on the boundary sphere, with the outward-normal-first orientation. This proves the identity for immersed fillings, rather than assuming disjoint embedded disk fillings. The boundary framings are the prescribed surface pushoffs. A generic filling disk with that zero longitude can be made framed: the parallel-intersection identity gives 0=2mu+e, so its relative normal Euler number e is even; an interior cusp changes e by2. Use finitely many cusps to make e0. The same identity then gives mu0. These changes are local in the inner ball and preserve the boundary circle/frame. Mutual intersection numbers are invariant under those rel-boundary homotopies. Accordingly lambda(Delta(s_i),Delta(s_j))=0 and mu(Delta(s_i))=0 in the precise integral group-ring convention, not merely after augmentation. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.10 For each long curve construct the torus T_i=ell_i times the boundary of the normal rectangle [.8,1.2] times [−2epsilon,2epsilon]. The long curves are geometrically disjoint, so these tori are disjoint. They lie in N. A short disk meets T_i at the point of ell_i intersection s_j on its negative-y radial collar, hence with geometric signed count delta_ij. Remove an annular neighborhood of the long curve at x=.8,y=0 in T_i, and cap its two boundary circles by opposite oriented framed parallel copies of the trimmed Delta(ell_i). This is a smooth immersed sphere g_i in N. The long–long Seifert block is ZERO, so these long disks have zero boundary linking and can be chosen with the zero extending normal framing as above. The torus product framing matches both caps explicitly: along x=.8 the first common normal is the direction in F transverse to ell_i; the second rotates from the radial direction on the torus to the y-direction on each disk across the chosen rectangle corner. The opposite upper/lower cap orientations give opposite half-rotations, not an extra full twist. The long disk's extending zero frame supplies the remainder. Hence the untwisted attaching annuli give a trivial normal2plane bundle on g_i. Thus these are framed spheres, not tori called spheres without a framing check. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.11 Fix orientations explicitly before the coefficient calculation. At a positive short–long intersection let u be the short tangent and v the long tangent, so (u,v) orients F. The ambient ball orientation is (x,y,u,v), with x outward radial and y the positive surface normal in S3. Orient the rectangle boundary counterclockwise in (x,y), and orient T_i by its rectangle tangent FIRST and its long tangent SECOND. At its x=.8 side the torus tangent basis is (−y,v), while the outward-radial collar of the short disk has basis(x,u); their ordered determinant relative to(x,y,u,v) is positive. Thus the old torus–short point contributes +delta_ij. Removing the annulus |y|<epsilon' at that side leaves its upper boundary oriented +ell_i and its lower boundary −ell_i. Consequently the surgery uses −Delta(ell_i) on the upper cap and +Delta(ell_i) on the lower cap. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.12 Take t to be the counterclockwise meridian in the oriented (x,y) normal plane and base through the inner ball on the lower side. Traveling in the retained torus from the lower cap to the upper one goes around the rectangle's outer three sides counterclockwise; returning through the inner ball closes the positive meridian. Thus the upper cap path differs from the lower by t, with no arbitrary relabeling of the prescribed positive meridian. Use common basing paths through the inner ball. The old torus–short-disk point contributes delta_ij. Every intersection of the long disk with a short disk gives two sphere–short intersections of opposite signs. Their paths differ by precisely the short meridian, so
lambda(g_i,Delta(s_j))=delta_ij+(1−t)lk(ell_i,s_j-down)
=delta_ij+(1−t)(U^T)_ij. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.13 For two DIFFERENT g spheres the tori and their annular surgery pieces contribute no points, because the long curves are geometrically disjoint. Each long-disk intersection contributes four points from the two cap parallels, with factors1,−t,−t^−1,1. Hence
lambda(g_i,g_j)=(1−t)lk(ell_i,ell_j-down)(1−t^−1)=0. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.14 For a self-double point the same parallel-sheet accounting gives two identity-label contributions and the negative t,t^−1 contributions, modulo the sheet-exchange relation. The long disk has framed relative Euler number0 and self-intersection sum0, so mu(g_i)=0. No extra intersections occur at the surgery seam: its two parallel attaching annuli are disjoint in the explicit product torus, with their normal framings already matched. This verifies the additional dual-sphere vanishings demanded by the ACTUAL local disk-data Definition, not just the weaker duality assertion quoted in AppendixA. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

1.15 The displayed disk–sphere matrix is lower unitriangular. Set f_i=g_i−sum_(k<i) T_ik f_k, inductively, using whiskered parallel sphere copies and framed connected sums. For j<i the sum cancels T_ij; for j=i the earlier rows vanish and the diagonal stays1; for j>i both terms vanish. A whisker around t^r left-multiplies the first-variable coefficient by t^r in [F2], so each Laurent coefficient is realized with its stated sign. Its result has lambda(f_i,Delta(s_j))=delta_ij, and the zero lambda/mu conditions among the spheres persist by direct sesquilinearity and the self-sum formula (all cross terms vanish). Taking conjugate transpose gives lambda(Delta(s_i),f_j)=delta_ij in the original disk-data order. The output is therefore the ACTUAL good-group disk problem in this particular N, with exactly the short-circle boundaries and product normal framings needed to compress Sigma. Goodness of Z is [F3]; disjoint embedded replacement disks still require the separate tower/standardness proof. This construction makes no such replacement by definition. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 The relative smooth filling step used above is justified without TOP smoothing. Approximate a filling map in the smooth ball, fix its supplied boundary collar by cutoff interpolation in the Euclidean embedding/retraction from [F5], and choose finite affine coordinate bumps which independently vary its first jets. Rank-one jets have codimension3>2, so parametric transversality gives an immersion. Independent bumps at distinct pairs make the double locus zero-dimensional; triple configurations have codimension8>6 and are absent. Compactness away from the uniform local-injectivity diagonal gives finitely many double points. Boundary collars are fixed throughout. The explicit cusp and sphere operations above are in those smooth charts. ∎ [A1, F5, construct]

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $q$ be a prime power, and let $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ have prime-power order $d$. Under the standard splitting $H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\langle\widetilde\mu\rangle$, the character extends to $\eta:H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z$ by identifying its cyclic image with $\mathbb Z/d$ and using the free-summand projection in the second factor. Some positive multiple of $(M_{0,q},\eta)$ bounds a compact oriented $4$-manifold with an extending map to $K(\mathbb Z/d\oplus\mathbb Z,1)$.

## Statement references

[[def-torsion-linking-form-and-casson-gordon-bordism|The Casson–Gordon character and bordism conventions]]

[[def-cyclic-zero-surgery-cover|The cyclic zero-surgery cover]]

[[def-finite-order-character-of-a-branched-cover|Finite-order characters]]

[[lem-zero-surgery-cyclic-cover-homology-splitting|The zero-surgery cover homology splitting]]

[[def-oriented-bordism-group-of-a-space|Oriented bordism groups of maps]]

[[lem-oriented-bordism-classes-over-a-space-form-an-abelian-group|The bordism group operation]]

[Charles Livingston and Swatee Naik, *Introduction to Knot Concordance*, §8.1, pp. 164–166](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Concordance_Book.pdf)

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the smooth oriented knot, its prime-power cover and character, and the marked splitting in the Statement.

[F1] The actual integral splitting is $H_1(M_{0,q})=H_1(\Sigma_q(K))\oplus\mathbb Z[\widetilde\mu]$, with free coordinate one on the closed lift of $\mu^q$. [[lem-zero-surgery-cyclic-cover-homology-splitting]]

[F2] The geometric smooth third bordism group of the specified $K(C_d\times\mathbb Z,1)$ is finite. Its proof supplies the full prime-power calculation. [[thm-casson-gordon-third-bordism-group-finite]]

[F3] A zero geometric bordism class means an actual compact smooth oriented filling with its extending map; disjoint union is the group operation. [[def-oriented-bordism-group-of-a-space]], [[lem-oriented-bordism-classes-over-a-space-form-an-abelian-group]] Finite smooth CW presentations exist under AC. [[thm-compact-smooth-manifolds-with-corners-admit-relative-finite-triangulations]]

[A1] Full AC is the convention of this item. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 On [F1]'s branched-cover summand send a class to its character value, identifying its cyclic image with $C_d$; send $\widetilde\mu$ to zero in that factor. In the other factor use the integral free projection. This is the stated homomorphism $\eta$ on actual integral homology and hence on the fundamental group. It is represented by a continuous map to the specified $K(G,1)$: on a finite CW presentation send each one-cell to a loop with the assigned group image, fill each two-cell because its relation has trivial image, and extend over higher cells because the target's higher homotopy groups vanish. The extensions agree on cell boundaries; their finite pasting is continuous. AC permits these finite choices, and changing them alters the map only within its homotopy class by the same cell-by-cell argument. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Its geometric class belongs to [F2]'s finite group. Some positive integer $r$ kills that element (indeed the explicit calculation permits $r=d$). By [F3], zero means that the disjoint union of those $r$ actual marked copies bounds a compact smooth oriented four-manifold with a map to $K(G,1)$ restricting to their maps. This is exactly the required bordism datum, with the positive orientations and both prescribed character coordinates unchanged. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For a connected regular link projection on $S^2$ with at least one crossing and either checkerboard coloring, both Tait graphs are connected.

## Statement references

[Kauffman, *New Invariants in the Theory of Knots*, §III](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1988__163-164__137_0.pdf)

[Calegari, *Introduction to Knot Theory*, §5.2](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A connected regular link projection and a checkerboard coloring of its complementary regions.

[F1] A connected projection is a connected finite 4-valent graph, with crossingless components represented by embedded circles ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

[F2] Its complementary regions admit a checkerboard coloring ([[lem-connected-regular-link-diagram-has-checkerboard-coloring]]).

[F3] Each Tait graph has one vertex per region of its color and one edge per crossing joining the opposite sectors ([[def-tait-graph-of-a-link-diagram]]).

## Proof
1.1 Associate to each crossing the edge of a chosen Tait graph. Along any projection edge joining crossings, the region of the chosen color on one side is the same at both ends, so the two corresponding Tait edges share that region vertex. Since the projection graph is connected, a path between any two crossings gives a sequence of Tait edges in which consecutive edges share a vertex. Every region vertex is incident to an edge because every face boundary of a connected projection with crossings contains a crossing. Therefore the Tait graph is connected. The same argument applies to the other color. [given, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 The only excluded connected projection is a crossingless circle, which is not covered by this statement; it will be treated directly in the bracket-span proof. This closes the claimed case. [given, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable Seifert-fibered $3$-manifold and let $A\subset M$ be an incompressible, boundary-incompressible neatly embedded annulus. After an ambient isotopy and, if necessary, replacement by another Seifert fibration of $M$, $A$ is vertical. A change of fibration is needed only when the underlying manifold is $T^2\times I$ or the orientable twisted $I$-bundle over the Klein bottle. The twisted $I$-bundle over $T^2$ and $K\times I$ are nonorientable and do not occur under these hypotheses.

For an arbitrary smooth boundary-preimage annulus with the same disk-obstruction hypotheses, the conclusion holds by a smooth isotopy of embeddings with a topological ambient extension. The smooth ambient conclusion above requires neatness.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Lemma 1.14](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Walter Neumann and Gadde Swarup, *Canonical decompositions of 3-manifolds*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9712227)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a compact connected orientable Seifert-fibered $3$-manifold $M$ and an incompressible, boundary-incompressible annulus $A$, neat for the smooth ambient conclusion and otherwise a boundary-preimage embedding for the broader variant.

[A1] Full AC is the axiom that every set-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], Definition).

[F1] Every essential annulus in a Seifert-fibered piece is isotopic to a vertical or horizontal annulus ([[lem-essential-surface-in-seifert-piece-is-vertical-or-horizontal]], Statement).

[F2] A proper two-sided horizontal annulus in an orientable Seifert piece admits a smooth refibering that makes that very annulus vertical; the underlying manifold is $T^2\times I$ or the orientable twisted Klein-bottle interval bundle ([[lem-horizontal-annuli-in-orientable-seifert-pieces-admit-vertical-refiberings]], Statement).

[F3] [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]] defines vertical and horizontal surfaces and exceptional fibers.

[F4] A compact connected orientable Seifert piece with nonempty boundary is irreducible ([[lem-orientable-seifert-pieces-with-boundary-are-irreducible]], Statement).

[F9] The explicit boundary-fixed neatification and disk-witness transport preserve the annulus disk obstructions. Its initial path is a smooth isotopy of embeddings with a topological ambient extension; it has a smooth ambient extension when the initial annulus is neat. [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]] [[lem-angular-boundary-neatification-preserves-smooth-disk-obstructions]]

## Proof

1.1 For a broad input first use [F9] to pass to a neat representative, retaining both disk-obstruction hypotheses. At the end prepend that smooth embedding path and its explicit topological ambient extension. For a neat input use the argument directly. Properness of the annulus makes the boundary of $M$ nonempty, so $M$ is irreducible by [F4]. A boundary-parallel annulus has a boundary compression: in its product with a boundary annulus, a spanning arc crossed with the product interval is a boundary-compressing rectangle. Therefore the given boundary-incompressible annulus is not boundary-parallel and is essential. All hypotheses of [F1], including irreducibility, are now discharged. Apply it to isotope $A$ to a vertical or horizontal annulus. [F9, A1, F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 If it is vertical, retain the original fibration. If it is horizontal, apply [F2] to refiber $M$ while leaving the annulus in place. The new fibration makes it vertical, and [F2] identifies the only possible underlying orientable manifolds where this change is needed. Compose with the initial isotopy to obtain the stated conclusion for the original annulus. There is no use of a hypothetical circle foliation on a horizontal annulus: the refibering supplier constructs an invariant circle foliation from its actual finite deck action. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct] ∎
