There is ONE winding number making every prescribed diagram and every isotopy interval in this finite word globally weak. At finitely many diagram vertices, test evaluations are rational linear functions of the opposite boundary coefficients, whose injectivity follows from the complete moving system. For each compact isotopy interval choose the test points to be regular values of its finite moving traces. Their finite preimage counts bound all partial traces uniformly. Across a slide there are only finitely many new endpoint relation matrices; take the maximum of these finitely many linear bounds. Thus the same $\pm N$ calculation in [F2], with N larger than that maximum, supplies strict opposite signs for EVERY nonzero periodic chain throughout the word. The initial winding path remains globally weak because its supports miss every initial region representative. On an isotopy interval apply the actual maps of [F2]. At a slide use its actual circular representative, which is globally weak by that theorem; it is isotopic as a whole family to the prescribed slid system. Both endpoints of this last isotopy are globally weak for the wound opposite family, so its actual isotopy equivalence aligns them. A joint own-family isotopy is factored into single-curve ones by a finite subdivision into graphs in disjoint annuli. This proves actual equivalences along the prepared word, without counting on an inadmissible slice. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Consequently any two globally weak diagrams on the SAME embedded splitting have equivalent chosen complexes. Apply step 2.1 to their alpha systems. Wind the first beta system to prepare that finite alpha word by step 3.1, and perform it, ending with the target alpha and the wound beta, globally weak. Now apply step 2.1 to that beta and the target beta. Wind the fixed target alpha to prepare this beta word, and perform it. Its result is $(\alpha',\beta_{\rm target})$, globally weak, where alpha-prime is isotopic to the target alpha. The target diagram itself is globally weak. The two-endpoint isotopy theorem [F2] therefore removes this last alpha winding while keeping the target beta fixed. The same construction covers mere changes of auxiliary disk witnesses: their boundary curves did not change, and all counts depend on those curves rather than the chosen interior preparation. Every map and its inverse homotopy in this comparison is the actual one in [F2] or [F4]. [F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The location restriction in [F3] causes no gap. For a geometric stabilization elsewhere, choose a path on the old surface carrying its small disk to a disk in the z-region, avoiding z. A compact supported surface flow and its two-sided collar extension carry the stabilizing ball and its torus bubble along that path. This is an actual ambient transport of the stabilized splitting fixing z and carrying both handlebodies. It need NOT preserve their attaching systems. After transport, those systems and the standard z-region stabilized systems are complete systems in the SAME two handlebodies. Step 2.1 gives their based same-genus slide/isotopy comparison, and step 4.1 supplies its actual equivalences whenever globally weak chosen representatives are used. Hence [F3] is applied only at a z-region disk; all other location changes use actual same-splitting moves. In particular no assertion that $n_q=0$ at a point in an arbitrary old region, and no unproved target-degeneration gluing, has been inserted into the product stabilization proof. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Take the finite geometric word of [F5]. For every supplied intermediate splitting choose a complete globally weak diagram on that splitting by the finite winding theorem in [F1]; at the two ends use the given admissible diagrams. This preparation changes the disk systems, not the splitting or Y. A genus-preserving step or ambient diagram transport now compares diagrams on the same splitting after the actual transport, so step 4.1 applies. For a genus increase first stabilize its chosen lower diagram at a z-region disk by [F3]. Step 5.1 identifies its higher splitting with the prescribed higher splitting; the actual transported data are identified by [F4]. Step 4.1 then compares this higher global diagram with the chosen global diagram there. For a genus decrease use exactly the reverse equivalence, including the literal inverse P of [F3]. Thus there is an actual chain homotopy equivalence for each step of the word. Intermediate geometric diagrams themselves were never assumed admissible and received no count matrix. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 Match the actual analytic choices, including independently supplied generator data and area forms. Fix one set of smooth separate-root generator charts for each of the finitely many geometric diagrams. Construct a canonical reference on its off-diagonal locus as follows. In each two-dimensional surface factor choose a smooth positive tensor with the required two real axes at its crossings. Relative to j take its Cayley matrix separately in each root factor, multiply by a symmetric configuration cutoff equal to one near the two tori and zero near the protected discriminant and point divisors, and retain the block diagonal matrix. It is permutation-equivariant, is the standard symmetric tensor near the protected set, and extends smoothly there because the cutoff vanishes on a neighborhood. Each two-dimensional block is positive; hence this reference is tame for the product form of EVERY positive surface area form. It need not be asserted to be a symmetric power of a nonholomorphic surface map. For the finite list of forms used by the actual small-triangle operations, choose generic perturbations sufficiently close to this reference to retain all their positive tameness margins and its prescribed generator and boundary tensors. Now canonical choices at a shared diagram are tame for one common selected form and have the common prescribed generator charts. The raw-identity trivialization near the tori keeps the prescribed tensor there. Thus the maps in step 6.1 compose on the actual endpoint complexes. This supplies the independent-chart and finite-area junctions explicitly, instead of extending a common-chart theorem by omission. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

8.1 Compose these finitely many actual equivalences. The resulting chain maps induce inverse isomorphisms on homology. This identifies the two hat groups for the given arbitrary closed oriented Y. ## Statement

Let $M=S^3\times[0,1]$. Let $\alpha:[0,1]\to M$ be a locally flat proper embedding with endpoints $(p,0)$ and $(p,1)$ and with product collars at those endpoints. Then there is a continuous family of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, $t\in[0,1]$, such that $H_0$ is the identity, every $H_t$ preserves the two boundary levels and is the identity near them, and $H_1(\alpha([0,1]))=\{p\}\times[0,1]$. If in addition $\alpha(s)=(p,s)$ on neighborhoods of $0$ and $1$, the family can be chosen so that $H_1(\alpha(s))=(p,s)$ for every $s$.

## Statement references

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|The locally flat pair charts and proper endpoint collars]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The locally flat proper arc and its endpoint product collars.

[F1] A locally flat proper parametrized arc in the standard product, smooth near its source endpoints, admits a relative ambient topological isotopy to a smooth parametrized arc, fixed near the two boundary levels. Its finite-chart proof uses explicitly presented controlled smooth embedding classes and inverse-controlled back-and-forth limits, without a choice axiom. [[lem-locally-flat-collared-arcs-admit-relative-ambient-smoothing]]

[F2] A smooth proper collared arc in this product is ambiently smoothly isotopic, fixed near the boundary levels, to the vertical arc. With the standard source parametrization near the endpoints, its terminal parametrization is the standard one. [[lem-smooth-collared-arcs-in-the-four-dimensional-product-are-unknotted]]

## Proof

**Given:** $\alpha$ and the specified collars.

1.1 In those collars the image of $\alpha$ is vertical, so write $\alpha(t)=(p,h_0(t))$ near zero and $\alpha(t)=(p,h_1(t))$ near one. Each $h_i$ is an increasing homeomorphism onto its height interval: it is continuous and injective, and the endpoint heights fix its orientation. Choose an increasing homeomorphism $\theta:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ agreeing with the two inverse height functions near the endpoints and interpolate monotonically between them on the remaining middle interval. Then $\beta(s)=\alpha(\theta(s))$ has the same image as $\alpha$ and satisfies $\beta(s)=(p,s)$ on neighborhoods of the source endpoints. In the additional parametrized case take $\theta=\operatorname{id}$. This changes only the parameter used to describe the input image. [given, construct]

2.1 Apply [F1] to $\beta$, obtaining an ambient topological isotopy $A_t$ whose final arc $\gamma(s)=A_1(\beta(s))$ is smoothly embedded. Since $A_t$ is fixed near the boundary levels, $\gamma(s)=(p,s)$ near its endpoints. Apply the parametrized clause of [F2] to $\gamma$, obtaining an ambient smooth isotopy $B_t$ fixed near the boundary levels and satisfying $B_1(\gamma(s))=(p,s)$ for every $s$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Concatenate $A_{2t}$ for $0\le t\le1/2$ with $B_{2t-1}A_1$ for $1/2\le t\le1$. They agree at the joining time. This is a continuous ambient family of homeomorphisms starting at the identity, fixed on a common neighborhood of the two boundary levels. Its terminal map sends the image of $\beta$, and hence the image of $\alpha$, to $\{p\}\times[0,1]$. In the additional parametrized case $\theta=\operatorname{id}$, so it sends $\alpha(s)$ to $(p,s)$ for every $s$. This proves both conclusions without an added choice hypothesis. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

## Parametrization convention

The general conclusion concerns the image of an arc. A boundary-fixed ambient isotopy cannot change a nonstandard source parametrization in its fixed endpoint neighborhood. For example, $\alpha(s)=(p,\varphi(s))$ for an increasing homeomorphism $\varphi$ not equal to the identity near an endpoint already has the required straight image, but cannot satisfy $H_1(\alpha(s))=(p,s)$ there if $H_1$ fixes that neighborhood. The extra endpoint parametrization hypothesis in the second clause is therefore necessary. The image-unknotting assertion is proved above, including the locally flat category.

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $\mathcal C$ be a ribbon category with chosen left duals. If two finite colored braids have color-preserving endpoint permutations and their blackboard-framed closures are isotopic as oriented framed links by an isotopy preserving each component color, then their evaluations agree in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf1)$. Thus the framed colored evaluation of a closed braid is independent of its colored-braid representative whenever the represented framed colored links are the same.

## Statement references

[[def-colored-framed-knot-evaluation-from-ribbon-category|Colored framed-link evaluation]]

[[lem-multicolored-ribbon-coupon-evaluation|Multicolored framed-tangle isotopy invariance]]

[Turaev, *Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter I, Theorem 2.5 and §§3–4](https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/turaev5.pdf)

[Etingof, Gelaki, Nikshych, and Ostrik, *Tensor Categories*, §8.10](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/egnobookfinal.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a ribbon category, two finite colored braids, and a framed colored isotopy between their closures.

[F1] The colored framed-link evaluation is the framed ribbon-tangle functor applied to the closed link and takes values in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf1)$ ([[def-colored-framed-knot-evaluation-from-ribbon-category]]).

[F2] The multicolored ribbon-tangle evaluator is invariant under every boundary-relative framed graph isotopy and handles arbitrary object colors with the chosen duality maps ([[lem-multicolored-ribbon-coupon-evaluation]]).

[A1] Countable choice is assumed for the cited construction of the multicolored tangle evaluator ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data in the Statement and [A1].

1.1 Under [A1], each braid closure is a framed colored link with empty boundary. By [F1], its value is the endomorphism of the tensor unit assigned by the multicolored framed-tangle evaluator, and its component labels are exactly the colors carried around the permutation cycles. [F1, F2, A1, given]

2.1 The isotopy hypothesis is a framed graph isotopy that preserves the labels. By [F2], the two closed tangles have equal evaluation morphisms. Applying [F1] identifies those morphisms with the two braid-closure values, proving equality in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf1)$. This statement concerns framed isotopy; an ordinary Markov stabilization that changes framing is not an additional move here. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. For every smooth oriented knot $K$, the classical signature $\sigma_{-1}(K)$ of the positive-push Seifert form is independent of the chosen connected spanning surface and integral basis, and it satisfies
$$|\sigma_{-1}(K)|\le 2u(K).$$
Zero eigenvalues are omitted when computing the signature of a Hermitian matrix.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a smooth oriented knot $K$.

[A1] Full AC implies the countable-choice hypothesis of the unknotting-number definition. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] The unknotting set is nonempty and $u(K)$ is its least element, measured by finite sequences of crossing changes in regular diagrams. [[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number]]

[F2] A single crossing change admits corresponding Seifert matrices with difference zero or $\pm vv^T$. [[lem-seifert-matrices-differ-rank-one-under-crossing-change]]

[F3] Two Hermitian matrices differing by rank at most one have signatures differing by at most two, with zero eigenvalues omitted. [[lem-rank-one-hermitian-signature-perturbation]]

[F4] The positive-push matrix gives $H_{-1}(V)=2(V+V^T)$; surface and basis changes preserve its signature. At a nonroot this is the declared invariant $\sigma_{-1}$. [[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature]], [[lem-seifert-stabilization-preserves-levine-tristram-signature]], [[lem-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-singular-set]]

[F5] The skew part $V-V^T$ is the unimodular intersection pairing of a knot Seifert surface. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

## Proof

1.1 At $\omega=-1$ the form is nonsingular for every knot. Indeed $V+V^T\equiv V-V^T\pmod2$, so its determinant is odd by [F5] and in particular is not zero. Thus $H_{-1}=2(V+V^T)$ is nonsingular. By [F4], $-1$ is not an Alexander root and the actual matrix signature is precisely $\sigma_{-1}(K)$; its surface and basis independence also follows from [F4]. This removes any need to use a root-average convention at $-1$. [A1, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 For two successive knots in a crossing-change sequence, use the two corresponding bases from [F2]. If their Seifert matrix difference is $\pm vv^T$, their $H_{-1}$ difference is $\pm4vv^T$, of rank at most one; if the difference is zero, the same bound holds. By [F3], the absolute signature change is at most two. Step 1.1 identifies the signatures of these particular matrices with the knot invariants, regardless of which diagram surfaces occur at other stages. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], take a sequence of length $u(K)$ ending at the standard unknot. Its disk Seifert surface has an empty matrix and signature zero. Apply the estimate of step 2.1 to each consecutive pair and add the finitely many inequalities. The triangle inequality yields $|\sigma_{-1}(K)|\le2u(K)$, including a length-zero sequence. Together with step 1.1 this proves both claims. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $M$ be the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold with a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric and torus cusps $C_1,\ldots,C_k$. For a chosen cusp $C_i$, choose a horospherical section $T_i$ and identify its Euclidean universal cover with $\mathbb R^2$ so its deck group is a rank-two translation lattice. A slope on $T_i$ is represented by a primitive lattice vector $v$ modulo sign. Its **Euclidean slope length on the chosen section** is $\ell_{T_i}(v)=\lVert v\rVert$ in the induced Euclidean metric. In upper half-space coordinates, if the section is the quotient of the horosphere of height $h>0$ by lattice $\Lambda$, then $\ell_{T_i}(p,q)=|p u+q w|/h$, where $u,w$ are the translation vectors representing the chosen basis. Replacing height $h$ by $h'>0$ multiplies every slope length by $h/h'$; therefore the length depends on the chosen section and is not an intrinsic number until that section is fixed.

## Definition

Assume countable choice as required by the chosen tubular-neighborhood and peripheral-system data. Let K be a smooth oriented knot with compact exterior E_K, positive meridian mu_K, and preferred longitude lambda_K on the boundary torus. The zero-framed surgery manifold M(K) is the closed oriented 3-manifold obtained by gluing D²×S¹ to E_K so that the meridian boundary circle of D²×{1} is identified with lambda_K and the core {0}×S¹ is identified with mu_K. The orientation extends the orientation of E_K across the filling. Thus the filling slope is the preferred zero-linking longitude; the definition asserts no 4-manifold bounded by M(K).

## Example

Assume full AC. Use the positive-push Seifert matrices
$$V_T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V_F=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$$
for the positive trefoil and the figure-eight knot, respectively. At $\omega=-1$, their Levine–Tristram signatures are $-2$ and $0$. In the displayed symplectic bases both quadratic forms have $q(a)=q(b)=1$, so both Arf invariants are $1$. Their normalized Conway polynomials are $1+z^2$ and $1-z^2$, respectively.

## Example references

[[ex-knot-kt-07-worked-cases|The trefoil and figure-eight matrices and determinants]]

[[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature|The $\omega=-1$ signature convention]]

[[lem-conway-polynomial-from-seifert-determinant|The determinant formula for the normalized Conway polynomial]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the two displayed oriented knot Seifert matrices in the positive-push convention.

[A1] Full AC is the ambient hypothesis for the Seifert pairing. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The trefoil matrix $V_T$ is the positive-push matrix for the positive trefoil. [[ex-knot-kt-07-worked-cases]]

[F2] The figure-eight matrix $V_F$ is a positive-push Seifert matrix; its skew part is the standard symplectic block. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]], [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F3] The Arf invariant is $q(a)q(b)$ for a genus-one symplectic basis and equals $a_2$ modulo two. [[def-knot-arf-invariant-from-seifert-form]], [[thm-arf-equals-second-conway-coefficient-mod-two]]

[F4] For a Seifert matrix $V$, the determinant substitution gives the normalized Conway polynomial $D_K(u)=\det(uV-u^{-1}V^T)=\nabla_K(u-u^{-1})$. [[lem-conway-polynomial-from-seifert-determinant]]

[F5] The Levine–Tristram signature of the knot is independent of the chosen surface and basis, including the one-sided-average value at an Alexander root. [[lem-seifert-stabilization-preserves-levine-tristram-signature]]

## Proof

1.1 Since $1-(-1)=2$, $H_{-1}(V)=2(V+V^T)$. For the trefoil, $V_T+V_T^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $-1,-3$, so the signature is $-2$. For the figure-eight, $V_F+V_F^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-5<0$, hence one positive and one negative eigenvalue, so the signature is $0$. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 The standard intersection block is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ for both matrices. The quadratic values on the basis vectors are their diagonal entries modulo two, namely $(1,1)$ for each matrix. Therefore $\operatorname{Arf}=1\cdot1=1$ for each knot. Their Alexander determinants are $\det(V_T-tV_T^T)=1-t+t^2$ and $\det(V_F-tV_F^T)=-1+3t-t^2$. Substituting $t^{1/2}-t^{-1/2}=z$ with the symmetric normalization gives $\nabla_T=1+z^2$ and $\nabla_F=1-z^2$; both $z^2$ coefficients are odd, agreeing with the Arf values. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge2$. Every $u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies $$\|u\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathbb R^n)}\le TV(u;\mathbb R^n).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|Spatial BV and total variation.]]

[[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space|The Lp spaces are defined using Lebesgue measure on Rn.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, an integer $n\ge2$, and $u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$.

[A1] Countable Choice is needed for the strict smooth approximation used below. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] Every full-space BV function has a compactly supported smooth strict approximation converging in $L^1$ and in gradient integral. ([[lem-ip-bv-strict-approximation]])

[F2] The Loomis–Whitney integral inequality bounds the coordinate-product integral by the product of its $(n-1)$-dimensional integrals. ([[lem-ip-lw-integral-inequality]])

[F3] For a smooth function with continuous derivative, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem gives its value from the integral of its derivative along each coordinate line. ([[lem-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-banach-valued-continuous-curves]])

[F4] Tonelli allows the coordinate-line integrals to be assembled into the full-space integrals below. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses listed above.

1.1 First let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$. For each $i$, put $$g_i(x_{\widehat i}):=\int_\mathbb R|\partial_i f(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},s,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n)|\,ds.$$ Tonelli [F4] shows $g_i$ is nonnegative measurable and integrable. By [F3], integrating from a point to the left of the compact support up to $x_i$ gives $|f(x)|\le g_i(x_{\widehat i})$ for every coordinate $i$. Multiplication and raising to the power $1/(n-1)$ yield $$|f(x)|^{n/(n-1)}\le\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(x_{\widehat i})^{1/(n-1)}.$$ [F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Integrating this inequality and applying [F2] gives $$\|f\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}}\le\prod_{i=1}^n\|\partial_i f\|_1^{1/n}\le\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\partial_i f\|_1\le\frac1{\sqrt n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}|\nabla f|\,dx.$$ The middle inequality is arithmetic-geometric mean; the last follows pointwise from $\sum_i|\partial_i f|\le\sqrt n|\nabla f|$. Thus the desired inequality holds for smooth compactly supported $f$, with the stronger constant $1/\sqrt n$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [A1] and [F1], choose $f_k\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $f_k\to u$ in $L^1$ and $\int|\nabla f_k|\to TV(u;\mathbb R^n)$. Select a subsequence with $\|f_{k_j}-u\|_1<2^{-2j}$; Tonelli [F4] gives $\int\sum_j|f_{k_j}-u|<\infty$, hence $f_{k_j}\to u$ almost everywhere. Fatou and step 2.1 imply $$\int|u|^{n/(n-1)}\,dx\le\liminf_j\int|f_{k_j}|^{n/(n-1)}\,dx\le TV(u;\mathbb R^n)^{n/(n-1)}.$$ Taking the $(n-1)/n$ power proves the stated inequality and at the same time shows $u\in L^{n/(n-1)}$. [A1, F1, F4, step 2.1, choose] ∎

title: A punctured-sphere cover from a labeled link diagram

    - title: Stefan Friedl, Knot Theory, §5.3, proof of the Wirtinger Presentation
        Proposition
      url: https://friedl.app.uni-regensburg.de/papers/2024_knot-theory-final.pdf
      locator: Chapter 5, §5.3, printed pp. 69–72, PDF pp. 70–73
    - title: John Milnor, Link Groups
      url: https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf
      locator: §§1–2, PDF pp. 1–6, for the link-complement and meridian conventions
---

## Statement

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link with labeled components $K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive, and with
$n\geq1$ crossings and at least one underpassing point on each component. Fix a
smooth height realization $L_D=\{(\gamma(s),\eta(s))\}\subset\mathbb R^2\times[-1,0]$
such that $\eta(s)=-1$ exactly at the $n$ underpassing points and
$\eta(s)>-1$ elsewhere; at each crossing the overpassing point has height
strictly greater than $-1$. Choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$ about the components of $L_D$, and let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior. Put
$$A=(\mathbb R^2\times[-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\},\quad B=(\mathbb R^2\times(-\infty,-1])\cup\{\infty\},\quad \Sigma=(\mathbb R^2\times\{-1\})\cup\{\infty\},$$
and write $X=S^3\setminus L_D$, $A_L=A\cap X$, $B_L=B\cap X$,
and $\Sigma_L=\Sigma\cap X$. Also put
$A_L^\circ=((\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\})\cap X$.
Then $\Sigma_L$ is a path-connected sphere
with $n$ punctures, $A_L\cup B_L=X$, and $A_L\cap B_L=\Sigma_L$. There are
path-connected open sets $U,V\subset X$ such that $X=U\cup V$, $U$ deformation
retracts onto $A_L$, $V$ deformation retracts onto $B_L$, and $U\cap V$
deformation retracts onto $\Sigma_L$. The set $B_L$ is contractible. The small
circles in $\Sigma_L$ around the $n$ punctures normally generate
$\pi_1(\Sigma_L)$, and they still normally generate after any one circle is
omitted. The inclusion $A_L^\circ\hookrightarrow A_L$ is a homotopy
equivalence. Radial retraction in each chosen product tube identifies
$\pi_1(X)$ with the fundamental group of the chosen exterior $E_L$.

## Statement references

[Friedl, §5.3, punctured-sphere cover and Claims 0–1](https://friedl.app.uni-regensburg.de/papers/2024_knot-theory-final.pdf)

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§1–2](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The regular diagram, height realization, labels, and product-tube data in the statement.

[F1] A regular diagram has finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and finite oriented over/under data. [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]

[F2] The link exterior is formed from pairwise disjoint product tubes; positive meridians are oriented boundaries of normal disks. [[def-based-string-link-and-labeled-link-peripheral-system]]

[F3] Attaching disks along loops in a path-connected space kills exactly their normal closure in the fundamental group. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

## Proof

1.1 The height condition says that the link meets the level sphere $\Sigma$ exactly at the $n$ underpassing points. Hence $A_L\cup B_L=X$ and $A_L\cap B_L=\Sigma_L$. The one-point compactification of the plane $\mathbb R^2\times\{-1\}$ is a sphere, so removing those $n$ points gives the stated punctured sphere. The punctured sphere is path connected: remove one puncture to obtain a plane, in which a polygonal path detours around the remaining finite points. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 Because the crossing set is finite, choose pairwise disjoint coordinate balls about its points, then shrink the product tubes so each crossing ball meets precisely the two prescribed local branches and contains no other tube. Shrinking a product tube radially is an isotopy of its boundary and leaves the exterior homeomorphic. Use the unit-sphere stereographic coordinates $(u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4)=(2x,2y,2z,x^2+y^2+z^2-1)/(1+x^2+y^2+z^2)$. Here $\Sigma$ is $h\cdot u=c$, with $h=(0,0,1,-1)/\sqrt2$, $c=-1/\sqrt2$. Write $q=c h+\sin(3\pi/4)w$, $w\perp h$, $|w|=1$. Its explicit unit-speed normal collar is $\cos(3\pi/4-t)h+\sin(3\pi/4-t)w$, for $|t|<\rho=\pi/8$; it is injective since its angle stays in $(0,\pi)$, and positive $t$ is the $A$ side. In particular no general tubular-neighborhood or choice theorem is required. For $q\in\Sigma_L$, set $\epsilon(q)=\min\{\rho/4,d(q,L)/4\}$. This is positive and continuous. The points $\exp_q(t\nu_q)$ with $|t|<\epsilon(q)$ avoid $L$, since their distance from $q$ is less than $d(q,L)$. The variable-width collar $C=\{\exp_q(t\nu_q):q\in\Sigma_L,\ |t|<\epsilon(q)\}$ is embedded and open in $X$. Set $U=A_L\cup C_{<0}$ and $V=B_L\cup C_{>0}$, where $C_{<0}$ and $C_{>0}$ are its negative and positive normal halves. Then $U,V$ are open, cover $X$, and $U\cap V=C$. Clamping the normal coordinate to $0$ retracts $U$ to $A_L$ and $V$ to $B_L$, while the collar itself retracts to $\Sigma_L$. For the final assertion, choose a continuous function $\chi:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ equal to $1$ on $[0,1/4]$ and $0$ on $[1/2,1]$. On the positive collar of $A_L$, the homotopy $t\mapsto t+s\epsilon(q)\chi(t/\epsilon(q))/4$ ($0\le s\le1$) pushes every boundary point into $A_L^\circ$, fixes points outside the collar, and stays below $\epsilon(q)$; it stays in $X$ by the distance bound. It maps $A_L^\circ$ to itself, so the inclusion $A_L^\circ\hookrightarrow A_L$ is a homotopy equivalence. [F1, F2, given, construct]

1.3 Every finite point of $B_L$ has height at most $-1$. For $0\leq t<1$, move $(x,y,z)$ vertically to $(x,y,z-t/(1-t))$, and send $\infty$ to itself; at $t=1$ send every point to $\infty$. This is continuous in the one-point compactification, avoids $L_D$ because the link lies in $z\geq-1$, and contracts $B_L$ to $\infty$. [given, construct]

1.4 Choose disjoint small coordinate disks about the punctures on $\Sigma$. Within each punctured disk, the radial homotopy $r\mapsto(1-t)r+t\max\{r,\varepsilon\}$ pushes its punctured cap onto its boundary collar, fixing points outside the cap. Thus $\Sigma_L$ retracts to the compact sphere with $n$ open disks removed. Base the $n$ boundary circles along any specified accesses. Filling all $n$ boundary circles by disks gives $S^2$, which is simply connected: two slightly enlarged hemispheres are contractible with path-connected annular overlap, so [F3] gives the trivial group. Filling all but the $j$th boundary circle gives a disk, also simply connected. The radial retraction extends by the identity on the newly attached disks. Consequently attaching disks to the original noncompact punctured sphere gives spaces homotopy equivalent to these filled compact models, rather than literally the compact models. The van Kampen quotient in [F3] proves that all the based puncture circles normally generate, and that the $n-1$ circles other than $c_j$ still normally generate. For $n=1$ the omitted list is empty and $\Sigma_L\cong\mathbb R^2$ is contractible, as required. Independent access changes conjugate each relator, leaving its normal closure unchanged. [F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The lower piece is contractible by step 1.3. For the upper piece, a finite point outside the link has a small relative ball disjoint from the link. Move within that ball to a point whose plane projection misses the whole projected diagram; such projections are dense because a finite regular immersed compact curve has locally finitely many one-dimensional graph branches and empty interior. The vertical path from that point to height $1$ now avoids the link. The height-$1$ plane is connected. The point at infinity first moves into this finite upper piece along the explicit positive collar in step 1.2. Thus the upper piece too is path connected. This uses explicit paths rather than a general-position theorem for arbitrary arcs. The retractions of step 1.2 now show that $U,V,U\cap V$ are path connected as well: any point is joined to its retraction image by that retraction path. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

3.1 In a product tube $S^1\times D^2$, the punctured tube $S^1\times(D^2\setminus\{0\})$ retracts radially onto $S^1\times\partial D^2$. Applying this on each of the finitely many disjoint tubes and fixing the exterior gives a deformation retraction of $X$ onto the chosen exterior. Thus the induced map on fundamental groups is an isomorphism. [F2, given, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The proof uses the height realization as explicit input. For any finite diagram with a component having no underpass, inserting a small type-I curl creates one underpass on that component and is realized by an isotopy supported in a disk; the link-presentation theorem applies to the resulting diagram.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The Conway knot $C$ bounds a locally flat proper
disk in the standard $B^4$, but it bounds no smooth proper disk there.

## Statement references

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[L1] AC supplies countable choice through
[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], which is used by
the handle and Lee branches.

[F1] [[lem-conway-knot-alexander-polynomial-one]] gives the actual normalized equality $\Delta_C(t)=1$.

[F2] [[thm-alexander-polynomial-one-implies-topologically-slice]]: under full AC, every smooth oriented Alexander-one knot bounds a locally flat proper disk in standard $B^4$. This is its smooth-input application; no broader TOP-generic disk-embedding assertion is used.

[F3] [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]] fixes the proper local-flatness and boundary-collar conclusion.

[F4] [[thm-knot-slice-iff-zero-trace-embeds-in-s-four]]: a smooth knot is smoothly slice if and only if its zero-trace smoothly embeds in standard $S^4$.

[F5] [[thm-piccirillo-conway-trace-partner-has-s-two]]: under full AC, the Figure 2 partner $K_P$ has $X_0(C)\cong X_0(K_P)$ and $s(K_P)=2$.

[F6] [[thm-rasmussen-s-bounds-smooth-four-ball-genus]]: under countable choice, $|s(K)|\le2g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$, with its collared properly embedded cobordism hypotheses satisfied by an actual smooth slice disk.

1.1 By [A1] and [F1], the smooth oriented Conway knot has Alexander polynomial one. Apply [F2] to this actual knot, and use [F3] for the boundary convention. This gives a locally flat proper disk in the standard $B^4$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, construct]

Compose this embedding with the actual trace diffeomorphism in [F5] to embed $X_0(K_P)$, and apply [F4] to obtain a smooth proper slice disk for $K_P$. ## Definition

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

## Definition references

[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set|Test functions and compact support]]

[[def-test-function-topology|Test-function topology]]

[[def-distribution|Continuous distributions]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth manifold $M$, a submersion $p:Y\to M$, an embedded incidence submanifold $Z\subseteq G\times X$ whose two projections are submersions, and a smooth density on $Z$.

[F1] [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]: test functions are compactly supported smooth functions.

[F2] [[def-test-function-topology]]: test functions carry the locally convex test-function topology.

[F3] [[def-distribution]]: a distribution is a continuous linear functional on test functions.

[F4] [[def-support-of-a-distribution]]: support is the complement of the largest vanishing open set; tests supported away from it pair to zero.

[F5] [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]: a density transforms by the absolute coordinate Jacobian and can be integrated without an orientation.

[F6] [[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]: cotangent vectors are dual tangent vectors and transform by the inverse transpose of the tangent coordinate change.

[F7] [[def-smooth-manifold]]: chart transitions are smooth.

[F8] [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]: smooth maps have smooth coordinate representatives.

[F9] [[thm-compactly-supported-distributions-are-tempered]]: a compactly supported Euclidean distribution has a unique tempered extension.

[F10] [[lem-compactly-supported-distributions-extend-to-smooth-functions]]: a compactly supported distribution has a unique continuous extension to smooth functions by a cutoff equal to one near its support.

[F11] [[cor-local-normal-form-for-submersions]]: near any point a submersion has coordinates $(x,v)\mapsto x$.

[F12] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: nested coordinate balls admit smooth cutoffs equal to one on the smaller ball and supported in the larger ball.

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the definition.

1.1 In submersion coordinates $(x,v)$, a compactly supported test density on $Y$ is $\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|$. Its fiber integral is $\widetilde\psi(x)=\int\psi(x,v)|dv|$. The integrand has compact support, so differentiation under the integral gives a smooth function; its support lies in the compact projection of $\operatorname{supp}\psi$. Thus $\widetilde\psi(x)|dx|$ is a test density and transposing this operation defines $p^*u$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, F11, algebra]

1.2 If $q$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$ and $K$ is compact in $M$, then $Q_K=q^{-1}(K)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose one smooth cutoff $\beta_K$ equal to one near $Q_K$. For every test function $\varphi$ supported in $K$, define $\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta_K(\varphi\circ q)\rangle$. If another cutoff is used, the difference of the two test functions vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}V$: it vanishes near $Q_K$ because both cutoffs equal one there, and away from $Q_K$ either $V$ vanishes or $\varphi\circ q=0$. Hence [F4] gives the same pairing. The chain and product rules bound every fixed-support seminorm of $\beta_K(\varphi\circ q)$ by finitely many fixed-support seminorms of $\varphi$, so continuity of $V$ proves continuity of $q_*V$. A finite cover by coordinate balls and [F12] supplies $\beta_K$. Multiplication by a smooth density is defined by the stated transpose formula, so the typed pushforward is well-defined. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F7, F8, F12, given, algebra]

1.3 In coordinates where $Z=\{t=0\}$, the incidence functional is integration of the restricted test function against $\omega_Z$. Under a change of coordinates on $Z$, the coefficient of $\omega_Z$ transforms by the absolute tangential Jacobian [F5]. Thus the functional is independent of the defining chart. [F5, F7, F8, given]

1.4 A covector annihilating $T_zZ$ transforms by the inverse transpose rule [F6], so $N^*Z$ and $C_Z$ are coordinate independent. If a conormal has the form $(\eta,0)$, it annihilates the image of $d\pi_G:T_{(g,x)}Z\to T_gG$, which is all of $T_gG$ because $\pi_G$ is a submersion; therefore $\eta=0$. Applying the same argument to $\pi_X$ shows that $(0,\xi)$ can only be zero. [F6, F11, given, algebra]

2.1 On overlapping submersion charts, the full absolute Jacobian factors into the base Jacobian and the fiber-density quotient. The fiber integral therefore transforms as a base density. This proves that the transposed functional in step 1.1 is chart independent. [F5, F7, F8, F11, algebra, step 1.1]

3.1 Cover $\operatorname{supp}u$ by finitely many smaller coordinate balls $B_i$ whose closures lie in coordinate balls $U_i$. Using [F12] in each chart, choose $\beta_i$ supported in $U_i$ and equal to one on $B_i$, and put $\sigma=\sum_i\beta_i$. Then $\sigma>0$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$. By compactness and another finite use of [F12], choose a compactly supported smooth $\theta$ in $\{\sigma>0\}$ equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}u$. Define $\chi_i=\theta\beta_i/\sigma$ on $\{\sigma>0\}$ and extend by zero outside; this is smooth and compactly supported in $U_i$, and $\sum_i\chi_i=\theta$. Thus $u=\sum_i\chi_i u$, since $1-\theta$ vanishes near $\operatorname{supp}u$ by [F4]. Each summand is a compactly supported Euclidean distribution in one chart; [F9] and [F10] give its unique tempered and smooth-function realizations. Uniqueness makes these local realizations agree on overlaps, so the packet pairings recover the chartwise definition without a global coordinate choice or choice axiom. [F4, F9, F10, F12, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

A group G is poly-torsion-free abelian (PTFA) if it admits a finite subnormal series
1=G_0 ◁ G_1 ◁ ⋯ ◁ G_m=G
in which every quotient G_{j+1}/G_j is torsion-free abelian. The trivial group is PTFA, using the length-zero series. The term “subnormal” means each G_j is normal in G_{j+1}; normality in all of G is not required.

## Example

Assume countable choice. Let $U$ be the standard unknot. Its zero-trace is
diffeomorphic to $S^2\times D^2$ and embeds in the standard $S^4$ as a tubular
neighborhood of an unknotted $S^2$. It also has the following dualizable-link
description: take a dotted unknot $R$ and two zero-framed meridian circles
$B,G$ at distinct points of $R$, with their normal spanning disks disjoint.
Then $B\cup R$ and $G\cup R$ are meridional pairs, $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$,
and cancelling either meridional $1$–$2$ pair leaves the zero-framed unknot
trace.

## Example references

[Piccirillo, Definition 1.2 and Theorem 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, the standard unknot $U$, and the framed link
described in the Example.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is
[[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] [[def-smooth-zero-trace]]: $X_0(U)$ is obtained by attaching a single
zero-framed $2$-handle to $B^4$ along $U$.

[F2] [[def-dualizable-handle-link]]: a dotted $R$ represents a $1$-handle,
and the meridional sublinks and zero mutual linking are the dualizability
conditions.

[F3] [[thm-handle-cancellation]]: a $1$-handle and $2$-handle with one
transverse attaching/belt-sphere intersection cancel, transporting remaining
attaching data.

[F4] [[thm-knot-slice-iff-zero-trace-embeds-in-s-four]]: a smooth slice disk
for $U$ gives a smooth embedding of $X_0(U)$ in $S^4$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The standard spanning disk for $U$ in $B^4$ is a smooth proper slice disk.
By [F4], its zero-trace embeds smoothly in $S^4$. [A1, F4, given, construct]

1.2 Glue the spanning disk for $U$ in the boundary $S^3$ to the core disk of
the attached $2$-handle. Their union is an embedded $S^2$, and its regular
neighborhood is the disk bundle over $S^2$ whose clutching map along the
equator has degree equal to the handle framing. The framing is zero by [F1],
so this clutching map has degree zero. Since $SO(2)\cong S^1$ and a degree-zero
map $S^1\to S^1$ is null-homotopic, the oriented disk bundle is trivial.
Therefore $X_0(U)\cong S^2\times D^2$. [F1, construct, algebra]

1.3 The standard unknotted $S^2$ in $S^4$ has trivial oriented normal bundle:
in the round model one normal vector is radial in $\mathbb R^3$ and the other
is the constant fourth-coordinate vector. Its tubular neighborhood is thus
$S^2\times D^2$, giving the stated embedding of $X_0(U)$. [step 1.2,
construct]

2.1 Each of $B$ and $G$ bounds its chosen normal disk meeting the core $R$
once, so both indicated sublinks are a knot and its meridian. The disks are
disjoint, so $B$ and $G$ have zero linking number. Their framings are zero by
the stated preferred-longitude pushoffs. Thus $(B,G,R)$ satisfies [F2].
[F1, F2, given, construct]

2.2 Cancel the $1$-handle represented by $R$ with the $2$-handle $B$ using
their single transverse meridional intersection. The other normal disk is
disjoint from this cancellation neighborhood; after cancellation it is a
spanning disk for the remaining attaching circle. The transported framing is
zero, so the remaining handle is $X_0(U)$. Reversing the roles gives the same
result after cancelling $R$ with $G$. This verifies both cancellations
described in the Example. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, construct] ∎

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=2.5cm,>=stealth]
  \node (x) {$B^4\cup_R h^1\cup_B h^2_0\cup_G h^2_0$};
  \node (g) [below left of=x] {$B^4\cup_U h^2_0$};
  \node (b) [below right of=x] {$B^4\cup_U h^2_0$};
  \draw[->] (x) -- node[left,align=center] {cancel $(R,B)$;\\retain $G$} (g);
  \draw[->] (x) -- node[right,align=center] {cancel $(R,G)$;\\retain $B$} (b);
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

The sketch shows handle incidence only: dotted $R$ denotes the $1$-handle and
subscript $0$ denotes zero framing. The proof uses the disjoint normal disks and
the single-intersection cancellation, not the sketch.

## Statement

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.


## Statement references

[Friedl, §7.1, Longitudes](https://friedl.app.uni-regensburg.de/papers/2024_knot-theory-final.pdf)

[Elhamdadi, Hajij, and Istvan, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.10257v6)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The diagram, based strand meridians, base arcs, and product tubes in the statement.

[F1] At each crossing, based positive meridians on the source and target under-sides satisfy the side-based conjugation relation. [[lem-link-wirtinger-local-meridian-conjugacy]]

[F2] In the meridian basis of [F3], the class of a word is its vector of meridian exponent sums. Positive arc meridians on the same component differ by tube transport and conjugation, hence have the same homology class. The choice-free first Hurewicz theorem identifies loop concatenation with addition in $H_1$ and kills conjugation. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] No crossing-count theorem with an additional choice hypothesis is needed.

[F3] The positive component meridians form a basis of exterior $H_1$, and the degree-one class with zero self-meridian coordinate is the preferred closed-link longitude class. [[lem-string-link-exterior-homology-and-meridian-maps]], [[def-based-string-link-and-labeled-link-peripheral-system]]

[F4] The crossing sign is the determinant sign of the ordered over- and under-tangents in the oriented projection plane. [[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]

## Proof

1.1 Set $v_0=1$. Suppose the current strand meridian on $K_j$ is represented by $v_{i-1}^{-1}x_jv_{i-1}$. At crossing $c_i$, if the component passes source-to-target, [F1] replaces it by $x_{o(c_i)}^{-1}v_{i-1}^{-1}x_jv_{i-1}x_{o(c_i)}$, which is $v_i^{-1}x_jv_i$ for $v_i=v_{i-1}x_{o(c_i)}$. If it passes target-to-source, solving the same relation for the source meridian gives the same formula with $v_i=v_{i-1}x_{o(c_i)}^{-1}$. Thus after one traversal the ordered product is exactly $W_j(D)$. [F1, given, induction, algebra]

2.1 In the local product chart at each undercrossing, the narrow band between the component and its parallel has boundary access paths whose difference is the over-meridian factor just computed in step 1.1. Away from crossings the parallel and the core run in a product annulus and contribute no group letter. Concatenating these finitely many local annuli from bottom to top gives the based string-link longitude; concatenating once around a closed component gives its based blackboard-parallel loop. In both cases the ordered word is $W_j(D)$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 In the closed-link case the parallel in step 2.1 has degree $+1$ on $K_j$. By [F2] and [F3], its self-meridian coordinate is the exponent sum of those factors in $W_j(D)$ whose over-strand belongs to $K_j$. Each self-crossing contributes exactly once, at its underpass. Source-to-target means the under-tangent has positive determinant with the over-tangent, so its exponent is the crossing sign $+1$; target-to-source gives both signs $-1$ by [F4]. Consequently the coordinate is exactly $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$. Every mixed-crossing factor lies in a different meridian coordinate and contributes zero to this coordinate. This proves the needed self-writhe correction directly from the actual group word and homology basis, without invoking a countable-choice framing or linking-number theorem. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For arbitrary strand accesses, path concatenation gives $y_e=g_ex_eg_e^{-1}$ and hence $x_e^{\epsilon}=g_e^{-1}y_e^{\epsilon}g_e$ for $\epsilon=\pm1$. Substitution in the finite ordered product proves $\widehat W_j=W_j$ exactly, without asserting that independent meridian conjugations cancel. A common base-path change conjugates every factor and the entire word by that one path, recovering the literal-word branch with its correspondingly based meridians. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 In the closed-link case, multiplication by $x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}$ changes the self-meridian coordinate by $-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ and leaves the degree on $K_j$ equal to $+1$. Its self-meridian coordinate is therefore zero. By [F3], this is the preferred zero-self-meridian longitude class. In the string-link case, step 2.1 already gives the based longitude specified by the tube and access paths. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The tube annulus of a string component is $[0,1]\times S^1$. Two paths between its fixed endpoint coordinates differ, relative endpoints, by the integer winding of their concatenation in $S^1$: lift that coordinate to $\mathbb R$ and linearly interpolate paths with the same lifted endpoints. Thus $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$. On a closed component the same calculation on $S^1\times S^1$ gives the unique class $(k,1)$ of a degree-one parallel relative to the blackboard section; its based loop is $\mu_0^k\beta$. Concatenating actual accesses now gives $$a_0'\beta'(a_1')^{-1}=h_0(a_0\mu_0^ka_0^{-1})(a_0\beta a_1^{-1})h_1^{-1}=h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$ For a closed component $h_0=h_1=h$ and conjugation changes no homology coordinate. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 give coordinate $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$. Multiplication by the actual initial meridian $(hx_jh^{-1})^{-(k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D))}$ cancels both the chosen extra winding and the self-writhe, leaving $h x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j h^{-1}$. It has degree one and zero self-coordinate, so [F3] identifies precisely the preferred class. These formulas cover no undercrossings, $k=0$, independently changed endpoints, and common conjugation, and preserve the arbitrary data of the peripheral definition. [F3, given, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a Seifert surface $F$ and ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$, using $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ for the positive-push Seifert matrix. Let $K^\dagger$ be the reverse mirror defined by the fixed orientation-reversing reflection followed by reversal of the knot orientation, and use the image basis on the reflected surface. The Seifert matrix of $K^\dagger$ in that basis is $-V$.

## Statement references

[[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot|The fixed reverse-mirror convention]]

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert-matrix convention]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice|The full Axiom of Choice assumed by the knot Seifert-pairing interface]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the oriented surface, and the ordered basis from the statement.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is the choice-function axiom used by the Seifert-pairing interface.

[F1] [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]: The matrix entry is $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, where the positive normal is determined by the ambient and surface orientations.

[F2] [[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot]]: The reverse mirror applies the fixed orientation-reversing reflection and reverses the knot orientation.

## Proof

1.1 Give the reflected surface $r(F)$ its transported orientation. Its boundary is $r(K)$ with the transported knot orientation. Therefore the Seifert surface for the specified reverse mirror is $F^\dagger=-r(F)$, with the opposite surface orientation. Let $(u,v)$ be a positive tangent frame of $F$ and let $n$ be its positive normal, so $(n,u,v)$ is ambient-positive by [F1]. A positive tangent frame for $F^\dagger$ is $(-dr(u),dr(v))$: reversing exactly one tangent reverses the surface orientation. Since $r$ reverses ambient orientation, the frame $(dr(n),-dr(u),dr(v))$ is ambient-positive. Consequently the positive normal of $F^\dagger$ is $dr(n)$, and the positive push of the image basis curve $r(a_i)$ is precisely $r(a_i^+)$. This computation includes both orientation reversals; reversing both tangent vectors instead would preserve the surface orientation. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Reflection negates linking. Indeed an oriented normal disk to an oriented curve $D$ is positive when its disk orientation follows the tangent of $D$ in the ambient orientation. The reflected disk has the opposite normal-disk orientation relative to $r(D)$, since $r$ reverses the ambient orientation. Thus $r$ takes the positive meridian class to minus the positive meridian class, and taking meridian coefficients in the complement gives $\operatorname{lk}(r(C),r(D))=-\operatorname{lk}(C,D)$. Using the actual positive pushes from step 1.1, the image-basis entries are therefore $\operatorname{lk}(r(a_i^+),r(a_j))=-\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)=-V_{ij}$. This proves the matrix is $-V$, including the empty matrix in genus zero. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

Reflection alone, without reversal of the knot and spanning-surface orientations, takes the positive normal to the reflected negative normal and gives the negative transpose. The reverse mirror in the fixed definition includes that additional orientation reversal and gives the negative original matrix in the transported basis. Arbitrary changes of basis remain ordinary unimodular congruences.

## Diagram

The panels label tangent frames; the normal is drawn out of the page as $\odot$. Take the orientation-reversing reflection $r(x,y,z)=(x,-y,z)$. The right frame $(-r(u),r(v))$ reverses exactly one transported tangent vector and has positive normal $r(n)$, as proved above.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,scale=1.05]
  \draw[thick] (-3.2,-0.7) rectangle (-0.8,0.7);
  \node at (-2,0.95) {$F$};
  \draw[->,thick] (-2,-0.15)--(-1.15,-0.15) node[right] {$u$};
  \draw[->,thick] (-2,-0.15)--(-2,0.52) node[above] {$v$};
  \node[blue] at (-1.25,0.45) {$\odot\ n$};
  \node at (0,0) {$r(x,y,z)=(x,-y,z)$};
  \draw[thick] (0.8,-0.7) rectangle (3.2,0.7);
  \node at (2,0.95) {$F^\dagger=-r(F)$};
  \node at (2,1.25) {surface orientation reversed};
  \draw[->,thick] (2, -0.15)--(1.15,-0.15) node[left] {$-r(u)$};
  \draw[->,thick] (2, -0.15)--(2,-0.52) node[below] {$r(v)$};
  \node[blue] at (2.8,-0.45) {$\odot\ r(n)$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Statement refuted

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. The standard right-handed trefoil is a ribbon knot.

## Statement references

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Full Axiom of Choice used by the nonsliceness supplier]]

[[def-ribbon-disk-and-ribbon-knot|Definition of a ribbon knot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the standard right-handed trefoil $T$.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function principle. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] Under full AC, the standard right-handed trefoil does not bound a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$. ([[lem-the-trefoil-does-not-bound-a-smooth-proper-disk-in-the-four-ball]])

[F2] Under ACω, every ribbon knot bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$. ([[thm-ribbon-knot-is-smoothly-slice]])

[F3] Full AC implies ACω. ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]])

## Counterexample

The standard right-handed trefoil $T$ has no smooth proper disk in $B^4$, so it cannot admit a ribbon disk whose resolution is such a disk.

1.1 The given full AC is the choice-function principle in [A1]. Applying [F1] under that hypothesis, no smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$ has boundary $T$. [given, A1, F1]

1.2 If $T$ were ribbon, [F3] would supply the ACω hypothesis of [F2], and [F2] would give a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$ with boundary $T$. [given, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Step 1.2 contradicts step 1.1. Therefore the trefoil is not ribbon, refuting the statement. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, contradiction] ∎

The box denotes the three-crossing positive two-strand braid whose closure is the standard right-handed trefoil. The closure arcs join equal endpoint positions outside the box. ## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link with $r\ge1$ components, and let $X_L=S^3\setminus L$ be its open complement. For each component choose a smooth fibrewise norm on its normal plane bundle $\nu(K_i)$ and a tubular map $\Phi_i$ from an open neighborhood of the zero section, fixing the zero section, together with a radius $\epsilon_i>0$ whose closed disk subbundle lies in that neighborhood. Require the resulting closed tubes $N(K_i)=\Phi_i(D_{\epsilon_i}\nu(K_i))$ to be pairwise disjoint, and put $N(L)=\bigcup_{i=1}^rN(K_i)$ and $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(L)$, the resulting compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary. The tube choices are part of the input. Choose a basepoint $b\in E_L\subset X_L$. Orient each normal disk so that the positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by its positive normal basis agrees with the fixed orientation of $S^3$. A **positive meridian** $\mu_i$ of $K_i$ is the oriented boundary of the radius-$\epsilon_i$ normal disk in one fibre of $\nu(K_i)$; the curve lies on $\partial E_L$ and is disjoint from every component of $L$; its spanning normal disk meets $K_i$ transversely once with positive sign and misses every other component. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ and identifies the classes of $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ with its standard basis. Write $G=\pi_1(X_L,b)$ and let $\phi:G\to H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ be the first Hurewicz homomorphism, equivalently abelianization. The subgroup $\ker\phi$ is normal. The connected covering $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ classified by $\ker\phi$ is the **maximal abelian cover**; it is regular and its deck group is identified with $G/\ker\phi\cong H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$. Put $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)]\cong\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$, where $t_i$ is the deck transformation corresponding to $[\mu_i]$. The isomorphism sends each variable to its group-ring basis element; monomials $t_1^{n_1}\cdots t_r^{n_r}$ correspond bijectively to the basis elements indexed by $n_1[\mu_1]+\cdots+n_r[\mu_r]$. Define the absolute multivariable Alexander module by

$$A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z),$$

as a left $\Lambda_r$-module under the deck action. “Absolute” means this is ordinary homology of the covering space, not relative homology with respect to a fibre over the basepoint.

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be the positively oriented trefoil, the closure of the positive two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$, and use the trivial one-dimensional representation and the single-color deck map sending each positive meridian to $t$. Use the standard genus-one Heegaard decomposition of $S^3$ with $K$ the $(2,3)$ curve on the splitting torus. Its two exterior pieces are solid tori meeting in an annulus whose core maps with degrees $2$ and $3$ to their oriented cores; the associated based simple-spine certificate has one vertex, core generators $a,b$, and one $2$-cell with attaching word $a^2b^{-3}$. The full abelianization sends $a$ to $t^3$ and $b$ to $t^2$. Deleting the $a$ column in this spine gives Wada quotient $-(t^4+t^2+1)/(t^3-1)=(t^2-t+1)/(1-t)$. In the cumulative-meridian basis, the reduced colored Burau block for $\sigma_1$ is $[-t]$, so for $\sigma_1^3$ it is $[-t^3]$; its numerator and boundary denominator are $-(t^3+1)$ and $t^2-1$. Their quotient is also $(t^2-t+1)/(1-t)$, the twisted torsion value for this based spine up to the declared units. Interpreting that ratio as the output of the full braid-axis procedure additionally requires the compatible axis-exterior and filling certificate in the procedure hypotheses.

The braid portion shown below uses the positive crossing convention from the colored procedure. The closure joins bottom endpoint $i$ to top endpoint $i$; because the endpoint permutation is a transposition, the closure is one component.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the standard genus-one splitting and $(2,3)$ torus-knot certificate; the trivial representation; the positive-meridian deck map; and the positive braid convention.

[A1] AC is inherited from the maximal-abelian-cover and twisted-chain conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F1] For an admissible deficiency-one exterior-spine column, the Wada quotient is the deleted Fox minor divided by $\det(\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I)$. [[def-knot-wada-quotient-for-deficiency-one-presentation]]

[F2] The based torsion uses the declared acyclic fraction-field determinant convention and is invariant under certified simple spine changes modulo determinant and deck units. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]; [[thm-knot-wada-quotient-equals-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F3] The braid procedure uses $\sigma_1(x_1)=x_1x_2x_1^{-1}$, $\sigma_1(x_2)=x_1$, the cumulative basis $g_1=x_1$, $g_2=x_1x_2$, and the reduced block obtained from the evaluated Fox Jacobian. [[alg-twisted-burau-determinant-for-colored-braid-closure]]

[F4] Seifert–van Kampen computes the group of a union from the two solid-torus pieces and their annular intersection. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

[F5] The colored Burau formula identifies the procedure value with exterior torsion only when the compatible based spine and axis-filling certificates are supplied. [[thm-twisted-burau-determinant-formula-under-extension-hypotheses]]

[F6] The positive meridian generates the first homology of a knot exterior. [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]]; [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]

[F7] In the standard torus-knot construction, the finite complex $X_{m,n}$ is the union of mapping cylinders of the degree-$m$ and degree-$n$ maps of a circle, and the compact exterior is the mapping cylinder of a map from the boundary torus to $X_{m,n}$. [Hatcher, §1.2, Example 1.24](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch1.pdf)

## Proof



1.1 Under [A1], let $A$ be the annulus left on the Heegaard torus after removing an open annular neighborhood of the $(2,3)$ curve. The torus-knot model identifies its core with the common source circle $c$ in the finite spine $X=M_2\cup_c M_3$, where $M_2$ and $M_3$ are mapping cylinders of the degree-two and degree-three maps of a circle and their target core circles are $a$ and $b$. By [F7], the compact exterior is the mapping cylinder of an explicit map from its boundary torus to $X$. Choose finite cell structures compatible with this map and the two degree maps, and take the unique vertex of $X$ as basepoint. In the resulting mapping-cylinder CW structure, each prism over a boundary-torus cell $\sigma$ pairs with its unglued face $\sigma\times\{0\}$; removing these pairs in decreasing cell dimension gives a finite sequence of elementary collapses onto $X$, fixing $X$ and its chosen basepoint. Thus this specific exterior-to-$X$ equivalence is simple. Give $X$ its natural finite CW structure with one vertex, core edges $a,b,c$, and $2$-cells $\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ attached by $r_2=a^2c^{-1}$ and $r_3=b^3c^{-1}$. Slide $\lambda_3$ over the oppositely oriented $\lambda_2$, replacing its attaching word by
$$r_3r_2^{-1}=(b^3c^{-1})(a^2c^{-1})^{-1}=b^3a^{-2}.$$
This elementary based $2$-cell slide removes $c$ from that attaching map. The edge $c$ now occurs exactly once in the boundary of $\lambda_2$ and nowhere else, so $(c,\lambda_2)$ is a free $1$- and $2$-cell pair and collapses. Reversing the orientation of the remaining $2$-cell gives the attaching word $a^2b^{-3}$. Thus the resulting one-vertex complex with core edges $a,b$ and one $2$-cell is based simple-homotopy equivalent to the chosen compact exterior and supplies the required certificate. [A1, given, F4, F7, construct, algebra]

2.1 The abelianization of this spine has generators $[a],[b]$ and relation $2[a]-3[b]=0$. By [F6], the positive meridian class $[m]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Write $[a]=p[m]$ and $[b]=q[m]$; the relation gives $2p=3q$, and $a,b$ generate the abelianization, so $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Hence $(p,q)=(3,2)$ or $(-3,-2)$; orient the two core generators consistently with the positive meridian to choose $(3,2)$. Thus the full positive-meridian deck map sends $a\mapsto t^3$ and $b\mapsto t^2$. [F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $r=a^2b^{-3}$, the Fox product and inverse rules give $\partial r/\partial a=1+a$ and $\partial r/\partial b=-a^2(b^{-1}+b^{-2}+b^{-3})$. Evaluating at $a=t^3$, $b=t^2$ gives $1+t^3$ and $-(t^4+t^2+1)$. The $a$ denominator is $t^3-1\ne0$, so the deleted-$a$ quotient is $-(t^4+t^2+1)/(t^3-1)$. Factoring $t^4+t^2+1=(t^2+t+1)(t^2-t+1)$ and $t^3-1=(t-1)(t^2+t+1)$ reduces it to $(t^2-t+1)/(1-t)$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 In the cumulative basis, $g_1=x_1$ and $g_2=x_1x_2$. The positive Artin rule gives $\sigma_1(g_1)=g_2g_1^{-1}$ and fixes $g_2$. The Fox row of $g_2g_1^{-1}$ is $(-g_2g_1^{-1},1)$, which evaluates to $(-t,1)$ under the trivial representation and equal strand colors; the fixed boundary word contributes the second row $(0,1)$. Therefore the reduced block for $\sigma_1$ is $[-t]$. For automorphisms $\beta,\gamma$ of the free group, the product and inverse recursions imply $\partial(\beta(u))/\partial g_j=\sum_k\beta(\partial u/\partial g_k)\,\partial(\beta(g_k))/\partial g_j$: it holds for generators and inverses, and the product rule extends it to every word by induction. After evaluation, the braid-preserved color map makes coefficient substitution by $\beta$ leave the coefficients unchanged, so the full Fox matrices compose by matrix multiplication; their block form has bottom row $(0,1)$, so the reduced scalar blocks multiply. The two strands close to one component, hence this coloring is preserved, and the reduced block for $\sigma_1^3$ is $[-t]^3=[-t^3]$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, induction]

4.1 The fraction-field $d_1$ has the invertible block $t^3-1$, so it is onto. The deleted Fox minor from step 3.1 is nonzero, so $d_2$ is injective; since the chain dimensions are $1,2,1$ and $d_1d_2=0$, its image is the one-dimensional kernel of $d_1$. The complex is acyclic. Moreover, any Laurent-ring $1$-cycle becomes a boundary over $\mathbb Q(t)$; clearing its denominator and using that the chain module is free over the domain $\mathbb Q[t^{\pm1}]$ shows that the cycle's homology class is annihilated by a nonzero Laurent polynomial. Thus the degree-one Laurent-ring homology is torsion, and the hypotheses of the exterior-spine Wada theorem hold. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Apply [F2] to the certified spine and admissible $a$ column. Its Wada quotient from step 3.1 represents the twisted torsion class. This identifies the displayed rational function with the torsion computed from the torus-spine certificate. [F2, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 The Burau numerator and boundary denominator are $N=\det([-t^3]-[1])=-(t^3+1)$ and $D=t^2-1$. Hence $N/D=-(t^3+1)/(t^2-1)=-((t+1)(t^2-t+1))/((t-1)(t+1))=(t^2-t+1)/(1-t)$. This is exactly the quotient in step 3.1, so the finite determinant calculation equals the based-spine torsion value. If the compatible axis-filling certificate is supplied as well, [F5] identifies the same ratio with the procedure output. [F1, F5, step 3.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram, order its crossings as $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and form the direct sum of state modules $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$ over all functions $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$. Here $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, each crossing is changed from its A-smoothing at $0$ to its B-smoothing at $1$, and the edge map is the multiplication $m$ for a merge or comultiplication $\Delta$ for a split, multiplied by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ on the edge at $c_j$. Then the sum $d$ of all edge maps satisfies $d^2=0$.

## Statement references

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|Frobenius algebra, smoothing and sign conventions]]

[[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram|Finite state cube and edge maps]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial* (1999), §§3.3–4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Bar-Natan, *On Khovanov's categorification of the Jones polynomial* (2002), §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0201043)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology* (2022), §4](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

[Zhang, *Notes on Khovanov homology* (2025), §§3.5–3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1)

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The finite ordered crossing set, the state modules and edge maps in the Lemma.

[F1] The multiplication and comultiplication on $\mathcal A$ obey associativity, coassociativity, commutativity, cocommutativity, and the Frobenius identities $(m\otimes\mathrm{id})(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)=\Delta m=(\mathrm{id}\otimes m)(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})$ ([[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]).

[F2] The differential is the sum of the signed edge maps, and the sign on the edge changing coordinate $j$ is $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ ([[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix a state $v$ and two distinct coordinates $i<j$ with $v(c_i)=v(c_j)=0$. The two length-two paths from $v$ to $v+e_i+e_j$ induce equal unsigned maps: saddles on disjoint circles commute as tensor maps; when the two saddles meet one component, the three possible merge/split patterns give respectively associativity, coassociativity, or one of the two equal Frobenius composites in [F1]. These are all possibilities because each edge changes one smoothing by one saddle. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The sign on the path that changes $i$ then $j$ has exponent $\sum_{r<i}v(c_r)+\sum_{r<j}v(c_r)+1$, while the path that changes $j$ then $i$ has exponent $\sum_{r<j}v(c_r)+\sum_{r<i}v(c_r)$. Their signs are opposite, so the two equal unsigned composites from step 1.1 cancel in the sum defining the component of $d^2$ from $v$ to $v+e_i+e_j$. If there are fewer than two crossings, no length-two paths occur and $d^2$ is the empty sum; otherwise every term of $d^2$ lies in exactly one such pair. Hence $d^2=0$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
