## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty smooth oriented link, let $F$ be a compact smooth oriented embedded surface with oriented boundary $L$, and put $X=S^3\setminus L$. For each component $K_i$, let $\mu_i$ be the positive meridian, oriented as the boundary of a small normal disk so that a positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by the disk's positive basis gives the ambient orientation. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with the free abelian group on $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_r]$. Define the total-linking homomorphism $\varphi:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ by $\varphi(\sum_i m_i[\mu_i])=\sum_i m_i$. If a smooth oriented loop $J\subset X$ is transverse to the interior of $F$, define its signed intersection number $J\cdot F$ by counting $+1$ when $J$ crosses from the negative to the positive side of the oriented normal of $F$ and $-1$ for the reverse crossing. Then $J\cdot F=\varphi([J])$.

## Statement references

[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link|Alexander-duality coordinates and the total-linking homomorphism]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty smooth oriented link $L$, a compact oriented spanning surface $F$ with boundary $L$, and a smooth loop $J$ in $X=S^3\setminus L$ transverse to the interior of $F$.

[A1] Full AC is the ambient choice hypothesis for the Alexander-duality convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The link complement $X$ is connected, and Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ on the positive meridian basis; total linking is the sum of the component coordinates. [[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold]], [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F2] Smooth loops and homotopies in $X$ can be perturbed to be transverse to the interior of $F$, while a prescribed closed region on which the map is already suitable is kept fixed. [[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], [[prop-relative-transversality-preserves-a-map-on-a-closed-good-region]]

[F3] The degree-one Hurewicz map sends $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ onto $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ and factors through abelianization. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, $L$, $F$, $X$, $J$, and the conventions of the Statement.

1.1 Choose a basepoint $x_0\in X\setminus F$, which exists on a local side of any interior point of $F$. Represent any class of $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ by a smooth loop transverse to $\operatorname{Int}F$, using [F2]. Define $I_F$ on that class to be its signed intersection count. If two such loops are homotopic in $X$, perturb the homotopy relative to its boundary by [F2]. The inverse image of $\operatorname{Int}F$ is then a compact oriented one-manifold in the homotopy annulus; it is compact because the annulus image is disjoint from $L=\partial F$. Orient it using the orientations of the annulus and the normal of $F$. Its oriented boundary signs at the two ends are the intersection signs of the endpoint loops with opposite signs on the two boundary circles. The total signed boundary count is zero, so the endpoint intersection counts agree. Concatenation adds counts, hence $I_F:\pi_1(X,x_0)\to\mathbb Z$ is a homomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 By [F3], this homomorphism factors through a homomorphism $\overline I_F:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$. The signed intersection convention in the Statement agrees with this induced map on the class represented by $J$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Near a point of $K_i$, choose oriented local coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in which $K_i$ is the $x$-axis and $F$ is the half-plane $y\ge0$, $z=0$. The boundary orientation and the stated positive-meridian convention make $(x,y,z)$ ambient-positive. The small positive meridian crosses this half-plane exactly once, at $(0,\rho,0)$ for some $\rho>0$, in the $+z$ direction. Thus $\overline I_F([\mu_i])=1$ for every $i$. [F1, given, construct]

2.2 By [F1], the classes $[\mu_i]$ form a basis of $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$. The homomorphisms $\overline I_F$ and $\varphi$ agree on every basis element by step 2.1 and [F1], so they are equal. Evaluating this equality on $[J]$ gives $J\cdot F=\varphi([J])$. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice convention of the twisted-chain definition. Let a finite colored geometric braid, a field with exact arithmetic, a representation of the closure exterior group, the full positive-meridian abelianization followed by a declared surjective color map, and compatible based spine and axis-filling certificates satisfy all input conditions of the colored twisted Burau procedure. Assume its designated denominator $D=\det(\rho(g_n)\psi(g_n)-I_d)$ is nonzero, so the procedure is applicable, and assume the representation and deck map extend over the filling with the axis meridian acting trivially. Then the procedure returns the class of the twisted Reidemeister torsion of the closure exterior. If the fraction-field complex is acyclic, the returned value is $N/D$, where $N=\det(\overline B_\rho(\beta)-I_{(n-1)d})$; if it is nonacyclic, the procedure returns $0$ and $N=0$, in agreement with the declared zero-torsion convention. The geometric certificates are essential hypotheses: matching a group presentation alone does not certify an exterior spine or the axis-filling decomposition.

[[thm-twisted-burau-axis-torsion-product|Braid-axis torsion product]]

[[thm-knot-wada-quotient-equals-reidemeister-torsion|Exterior-spine Wada quotient theorem]]

[[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion|Twisted coefficient and torsion convention]]

[Conway, Theorem 3.15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1510.06678)

[Kirk and Livingston, §§2–4](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Livingston_papers/1999_Twisted%20Alexander%20invariants%2C%20Reidemeister%20torsion%2C%20and%20Casson-Gordon%20invariants.pdf)

[Ranicki, Definitions 4 and 6 and Theorem 15](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/torsion.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; all finite encoded procedure inputs; a nonzero designated denominator; the actual based spine and compatible axis-filling certificates; and the stated coefficient extension across filling.

[A1] AC is inherited from the full abelianization and twisted-chain convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F1] The finite procedure checks its declared input conditions, evaluates $D$ before the acyclicity branch, returns zero for a nonacyclic complex, and otherwise returns $N/D$. [[alg-twisted-burau-determinant-for-colored-braid-closure]]

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0201043"

      url: "https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf"
    - title: "Melissa Zhang, Notes on Khovanov homology, arXiv:2501.03115v1, §§3.5–3.7"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1"

## Statement

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a link with $n_+$ positive crossings, $n_-$ negative crossings, writhe $w=n_+-n_-$, and $n=n_++n_-$. For each resolution state $v$, let $k(v)$ be its number of circles and let $D_v$ use the A-smoothing at coordinates $0$ and B-smoothing at coordinates $1$. Put $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ and define the normalized bracket
$$f_D(A):=(-A^3)^{-w}\sum_{v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}} A^{n-2|v|}\delta^{k(v)-1}.$$
For integral unreduced Khovanov cohomology, define $\chi_q(Kh(D))=\sum_{i,j}(-1)^i\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}Kh^{i,j}(D)q^j$. For reduced cohomology use its basepoint quantum grading $\widetilde j$ and define $\widetilde\chi_q=\sum_{i,\widetilde j}(-1)^i\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)q^{\widetilde j}$. Under $q=-A^{-2}$ and $t=q^2=A^{-4}$,
$$\chi_q(Kh(D))=(q+q^{-1})f_D(A),\qquad \widetilde\chi_q(D,p)=f_D(A).$$
Thus the unreduced unknot factor is $q+q^{-1}$ and the reduced unknot factor is $1$.

## Statement references

[[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value|Bracket smoothing weights and loop value]]

[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing|Crossing signs and writhe]]

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|Khovanov state-module and grading conventions]]

[[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram|State complex construction]]

[[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot|Reduced quotient and quantum shift]]

[Khovanov, *A categorification of the Jones polynomial* (1999), §§2.2–2.4 and 7.1–7.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9908171v2)

[Bar-Natan, *On Khovanov's categorification of the Jones polynomial* (2002), §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0201043)

[Kauffman, *An Introduction to Khovanov Homology* (2022), §§3–4](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/kaufmann.pdf)

[Zhang, *Notes on Khovanov homology* (2025), §§3.5–3.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.03115v1)

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A finite oriented link diagram, its ordered Khovanov state cube, and the integral unreduced and based reduced cochain complexes.

[F1] The Kauffman state sum is $\langle D\rangle=\sum_v A^{n-2|v|}(-A^2-A^{-2})^{k(v)-1}$, with each state using the prescribed A/B smoothing chart ([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The writhe is the sum of crossing signs, so $w=n_+-n_-$ ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F3] A state with circle labels $1,X$ has cohomological degree $i=|v|-n_-$ and quantum degree $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$; $\deg(1)=1$, $\deg(X)=-1$, and edge maps preserve $j$ ([[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]).

[F4] The reduced state module kills the based-circle $X$ label and subtracts one from the original quantum degree, so the surviving based label $1$ contributes degree zero ([[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot]]).

[F5] The Khovanov procedure returns a bounded bigraded cochain complex with finite-rank free state groups ([[thm-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram-procedure-properties]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix a quantum degree and tensor the finite free complex with $\mathbb Q$. For an integer matrix $d$, the kernel after tensoring is $(\ker d)\otimes\mathbb Q$: if $d(a/r)=0$ with $a$ integral and $r\ne0$, then $d(a)=0$ because the target is torsion-free. The image after tensoring is $\operatorname{im}(d)\otimes\mathbb Q$ by clearing denominators, so rationalized homology is $H^i(C)\otimes\mathbb Q$ and has dimension $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}H^i(C)$. Rank-nullity in this bounded rational complex gives $\dim C^i=\dim H^i+\dim\operatorname{im}d^i+\dim\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}$; alternating over $i$ cancels the image dimensions. The same argument applies to the reduced complex, whose terms are finite-rank free. [F5, given, algebra]

2.1 On a state $v$, summing $q^{\sum\deg(a)}$ over its $k(v)$ independent labels gives $(q+q^{-1})^{k(v)}$, so the unreduced chain Euler sum is $\sum_v(-1)^{|v|-n_-}q^{|v|+n_+-2n_-}(q+q^{-1})^{k(v)}$. With $q=-A^{-2}$, one has $q+q^{-1}=\delta$ and, term by term, $(-1)^{|v|-n_-}q^{|v|+n_+-2n_-}A^{-(n-2|v|)}=(-A^3)^{-w}$. The state contribution is consequently $(q+q^{-1})(-A^3)^{-w}A^{n-2|v|}\delta^{k(v)-1}$. For the reduced cube, the based label contributes degree zero by [F4], leaving $(q+q^{-1})^{k(v)-1}$ in place of $(q+q^{-1})^{k(v)}$, so its state contribution is $(-A^3)^{-w}A^{n-2|v|}\delta^{k(v)-1}$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Summing the state contributions in step 2.1 gives the two displayed formulas for the chain Euler sums. Step 1.1 identifies those sums with the Euler characteristics of integral cohomology. When $D$ is the crossingless unknot, $n_+=n_-=0$ and $k=1$, so the unreduced value is $q+q^{-1}$ and the reduced value is $1$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, and let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive. If their full physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree on all boundary data, then every inward boundary-normal derivative agrees:
$$\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_1|_{\partial\Omega} =\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_2|_{\partial\Omega} \qquad(k=0,1,2,\ldots),$$
where $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ in a boundary normal collar.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full physical conductivity DN map]]

[[lem-ip-alessandrini-identity|Conductivity Alessandrini identity]]

[[lem-ip-boundary-quasimode-jets-and-borel-correction|Boundary concentrating quasimodes and exact correction]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the DN identity and exact correction suppliers [F1]--[F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the DN identity and exact correction suppliers [F1]--[F3].

**Given:** the smooth bounded domain, two strictly positive smooth conductivities with equal full-data DN maps, and the fixed-atlas trace convention.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: $\Lambda_\gamma$ is the weak full-boundary map of $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$ with physical flux $\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-alessandrini-identity]]: for conductivity solutions $u_j$ with boundary values $f_j$, $\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle=\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_1\cdot\overline{\nabla u_2}\,dx$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-boundary-quasimode-jets-and-borel-correction]]: for every boundary point, unit tangential covector, cutoff $\chi=1$ near that point, integer $k\geq0$, and residual order $N>k$, the approximate solutions have residual and exact-correction $H^1$ errors $O(\lambda^{-N})$; their weighted gradient product satisfies $\lambda^k\int \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^kF\nabla v_1\cdot\overline{\nabla v_2}\,dx\to c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS$ with $c_k>0$.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Fix $x_0\in\partial\Omega$ and a sufficiently small patch. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported in the patch and equal to one near $x_0$, and use [F3] to construct approximate beams for $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ with the same boundary trace. Let $u_{\lambda,j}$ be their exact conductivity solutions. Equality of the DN maps and [F2] give
$$\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_{\lambda,1}\cdot\overline{\nabla u_{\lambda,2}}\,dx=0.$$
Replacing each exact solution by its approximate beam changes this integral by $O(\lambda^{-N})$: the coefficient is bounded, the beam $H^1$ norms are uniformly bounded, and each exact correction is $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$ by [F3]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Set $k=0$ in [F3] and let $\lambda\to\infty$ in step 1.1. Since $c_0>0$,
$$\int_{\partial\Omega}(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)|\chi|^2\,dS=0.$$
If $\gamma_1-\gamma_2$ were positive or negative at any boundary point, continuity would give a patch on which it has that strict sign; choosing $\chi$ supported in that patch and equal to one near the point would make this integral nonzero. Thus $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ on $\partial\Omega$. [F3, step 1.1, contradiction]

2.1 Fix an integer $k\geq1$ and suppose inductively that $\partial_{x_n}^j(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)=0$ on a boundary patch for every $j<k$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder in the inward normal coordinate gives
$$\gamma_1(y,x_n)-\gamma_2(y,x_n)=x_n^kF_k(y,x_n),\qquad F_k(y,0)=\frac{\partial_{x_n}^k(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)(y,0)}{k!},$$
for a smooth $F_k$. Apply [F2] to the exact beams from [F3], replace them by their approximate beams, and multiply the resulting integral identity by $\lambda^k$. The replacement error is $O(\lambda^{k-N})$, since the weight $x_n^k$ is bounded and the corrections are $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$. Choose $N>k$ and apply the weighted limit in [F3]; then
$$c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F_k(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2\,dS(y)=0.$$
Since $c_k>0$, the same localized sign argument as in step 1.2 gives $F_k(y,0)=0$ throughout the patch. Therefore the $k$th inward normal derivatives agree there. [A1, A2, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Step 1.2 is the base case for the induction. Step 2.1 proves each subsequent order on a patch that may be chosen around any prescribed boundary point. Thus every boundary point has a neighborhood on which the order-$k$ normal derivative difference is zero for every integer $k\geq0$, proving the full boundary-jet assertion. [step 1.2, step 2.1, induction] ∎

## Definition

Let $M$ be a closed oriented three-manifold with a specified coefficient homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(M_j)\to\Gamma$ on each component, where $\Gamma$ is PTFA. The integral coefficient ring is $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ with its fraction division ring $K\Gamma$. More generally let $k$ be $\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field, let $K$ be the fraction division ring of $k[\Gamma]$, and let $k[\Gamma]\subseteq R\subseteq K$ be an involution-stable unital intermediate ring. The involution fixes $k$ and sends $g$ to $g^{-1}$; on fractions it is the involutive anti-automorphism extending this formula. Taking $k=\mathbb Z$ and $R=\Lambda$ recovers the integral convention.

If $H_1(M;K)=0$, the coefficient Bockstein, oriented Poincaré duality and evaluation define the Blanchfield linking pairing
$$B_{M,\phi,R}:TH_1(M;R)\times TH_1(M;R)\longrightarrow K/R.$$
Here $T$ denotes the submodule of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, the first variable is conjugate-linear, and the second is right-linear. Nonsingularity means that the adjoint
$$\overline{TH_1(M;R)}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(TH_1(M;R),K/R)$$
is an isomorphism of left $R$-modules, where $r\cdot\bar x=\overline{x\bar r}$ on the conjugate module. This is equivalent to the conjugate-dual formulation in the right-module convention. For $\Gamma=\mathbb Z$ with generator $t$, $R=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ and $K=\mathbb Q(t)$ give the classical coefficient convention. Nonsingularity is a separate property of the defined pairing, with its coefficient hypotheses supplied by the nonsingularity theorem.

For a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G over a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, define the signature defect by ρ(M,φ;W,ψ)=sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is an invariant of (M,φ) only when a separate bordism-independence theorem applies.

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0210213v2
      locator: §§2–3, the rational deformation of the Frobenius maps
---

## Definition

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram in the standard oriented $3$-sphere. Use the oriented Khovanov resolution cube, crossing order, signs, and shifts fixed in the integral Khovanov construction. Over $\mathbb Q$, replace its circle algebra by $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$, with $\deg_q(1)=1$ and $\deg_q(X)=-1$, and structure maps
$$
\eta_L(1)=1,\quad \epsilon_L(1)=0,\quad \epsilon_L(X)=1,
$$
$$
m_L(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m_L(1\otimes X)=m_L(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m_L(X\otimes X)=1,
$$
$$
\Delta_L(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad \Delta_L(X)=1\otimes1+X\otimes X.
$$
For a resolution state $v$ with $k(v)$ circles, assign $A_L^{\otimes k(v)}$ and cohomological degree $i(v)=|v|-n_-$. On a tensor basis element whose circle labels are $a_1,\ldots,a_{k(v)}\in\{1,X\}$, set
$$
q(v;a_1,\ldots,a_{k(v)})=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{j=1}^{k(v)}\deg_q(a_j).
$$
The differential is the signed sum of the edge maps $m_L$ and $\Delta_L$. The resulting finite cochain complex is the **Lee-deformed Khovanov complex** $C_L(D;\mathbb Q)$. Its decreasing quantum filtration $F^pC_L(D;\mathbb Q)$ is spanned by basis elements of quantum degree at least $p$. Its homology with the induced filtration is the Lee homology of the diagram. The diagram-level definition does not by itself assert invariance under changing $D$.

For the empty link diagram, use its single empty resolution state and empty tensor term $\mathbb Q$ in cohomological and quantum degree $0$, with zero differential. Its induced decreasing filtration is $F^pC_L(\varnothing;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$ for $p\leq0$ and $F^pC_L(\varnothing;\mathbb Q)=0$ for $p>0$.

The two equal composites in the diagram below are the Frobenius compatibility maps used on merge-split faces. The drawing names maps only; the proof checks the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$.

```tikzcd
A_L\otimes A_L \arrow[r,"m_L"] \arrow[d,"\Delta_L\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & A_L \arrow[d,"\Delta_L"] \\
A_L\otimes A_L\otimes A_L \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m_L"'] & A_L\otimes A_L
```

## Definition references

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions|The crossing order, signed resolution cube, and quantum shift being deformed]]

[[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category|The cochain-complex convention]]

[[def-filtered-chain-complex|Filtered-complex convention]]

[[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object|Increasing and decreasing filtrations]]

[Rasmussen, *Khovanov homology and the slice genus* (2004), §§2.3–2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0402131v1)

[McMullen, *4-Manifolds*, §§5.5–5.6](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/4Mnotes.pdf)

[Lee, *On Khovanov invariant for alternating links* (2002), §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0210213v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite regular oriented diagram $D$, an ordering of its crossing set, and the coefficient field $\mathbb Q$.

[F1] The normalized Khovanov cube uses a finite state set, the state degree $|v|-n_-$, the quantum shift $|v|+n_+-2n_-$, and a cube sign that reverses on opposite routes around each square face. ([[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]])

[F2] A cochain complex has a degree-$+1$ differential whose square is zero. ([[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]])

## Proof

**Given:** The finite oriented resolution cube of $D$ and the operations in the Definition.

**Empty-link case:** For $D=\varnothing$, the state set is the singleton empty function, its empty tensor term is $\mathbb Q$ in degrees $(0,0)$, and there are no edges. The differential is zero and the degree-zero generator gives exactly the filtration stated in the Definition. Assume henceforth that $D$ is nonempty for the remaining checks.

1.1 The quotient $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$ has basis $1,X$, and its multiplication table is the displayed $m_L$. Hence multiplication is associative and commutative with unit $1$. The counit identities follow on $1,X$: $(\epsilon_L\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_L(1)=1$, $(\epsilon_L\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_L(X)=X$, and the other counit composite gives the same values. [given, algebra]

2.1 For input $1$, both composites $(\Delta_L\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta_L$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta_L)\Delta_L$ equal $1\otimes X\otimes X+X\otimes1\otimes X+1\otimes1\otimes1+X\otimes X\otimes1$. For input $X$, both equal $1\otimes1\otimes X+1\otimes X\otimes1+X\otimes1\otimes1+X\otimes X\otimes X$. Thus $\Delta_L$ is coassociative. Cocommutativity follows by swapping tensor factors in its two displayed values. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On the ordered basis $1\otimes1,1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$, each of $(m_L\otimes\mathrm{id})(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta_L)$, $\Delta_Lm_L$, and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes m_L)(\Delta_L\otimes\mathrm{id})$ has outputs $1\otimes X+X\otimes1$, $1\otimes1+X\otimes X$, $1\otimes1+X\otimes X$, and $1\otimes X+X\otimes1$. The Frobenius identities therefore hold. On a cube square, two changes on disjoint circles commute by tensor functoriality; two merges give the same composite by associativity of $m_L$; two splits give the same composite by coassociativity of $\Delta_L$; and a merge-split pair gives the same composite by the Frobenius identities just checked. In each case the cube signs on the two routes are opposite, so the square contribution to $d_L^2$ is zero. Every length-two path in the cube lies in one such square, so summing over squares proves $d_L^2=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The terms of $m_L$ and $\Delta_L$ inherited from $\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2)$ have total quantum degree $0$ after the state shift. The new multiplication term $m_L(X\otimes X)=1$ changes the label degree from $-2$ to $1$, and the edge state shift adds $1$, so it raises $q$ by $4$. The new term $1\otimes1$ in $\Delta_L(X)$ changes label degree from $-1$ to $2$, and its edge state shift again adds $1$, so it raises $q$ by $4$. Thus every differential term preserves or raises $q$, making each $F^pC_L$ a subcomplex. The state set and each state module are finite, so only finitely many $q$-degrees occur and the filtration is finite. All algebra and cube checks use finite bases and no choice axiom. [F1, F2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356
    - title: "Christian Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems, complete lecture notes, Chapter 5"
      url: https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf

## Example

Assume Countable Choice.

Let the real periodic Fourier coefficient space be $X=Y=\mathbb R\oplus\ell^2(\mathbb N;\mathbb R^2)$, with one constant coordinate and cosine–sine coordinate pairs for each positive frequency, and give it the canonical inner product $\langle(c_0,(a_n,b_n)),(d_0,(c_n,d_n))\rangle=c_0d_0+\sum_{n\ge1}(a_nc_n+b_nd_n)$. The interleaving map $(c_0,(a_n,b_n))\mapsto(c_0,a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots)$ is an isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so this is a real Hilbert space. For a heat time $\bar t>0$, define the periodic heat forward operator by
$$
T_{\bar t}(c_0,(a_n,b_n)_{n\ge1})=(c_0,(e^{-n^2\bar t}a_n,e^{-n^2\bar t}b_n)_{n\ge1}).
$$
Its eigenvalues for $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$ are $1$ on the constant mode and $e^{-2n^2\bar t}$ on both modes of frequency $n$. The singular system for the sequence model is ordered as the constant mode, then cosine and sine modes in increasing positive frequency; its singular values are nonincreasing. Use the truth whose function is $f^\dagger(x)=\pi/2-|x|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$, and observe its weak Gaussian white-noise data with known standard deviation $\sigma>0$. Li and Werner report an empirical SOLIT simulation at $\bar t=0.1$ using $10^4$ Monte Carlo runs: SOLIT appears close to the oracle, while the minimax behavior is unclear and the empirical adaptation behavior for spectral cut-off is irregular. These are reported simulation findings, not a theorem or a simulation performed for this library.

For the spectral-cutoff candidate sequence $\alpha_n=e^{-2n^2\bar t}$, indexed by $n\in\mathbb N_0$, the variance sums $V_n=1+2\sum_{k=1}^n e^{2k^2\bar t}$ do not have a uniformly bounded consecutive ratio: $V_n/V_{n-1}\to\infty$. Thus this infinite spectral-cutoff sequence does not meet the uniform geometric-variance-grid condition. A continuous Tikhonov filter $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ does admit such a grid because its variance function is continuous, decreases from $+\infty$ to $0$, and can be sampled at successive fixed variance ratios.

## Example references

[[alg-ip-solit-parameter-choice|The SOLIT selector used in this example]]

[[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index|Ordered filters and geometric-variance candidate grids]]

[Li and Werner, *Adaptive minimax optimality in statistical inverse problems via SOLIT*, §§5.3.3 and 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10356)

[Clason, *Regularization of Inverse Problems*, complete lecture notes, Chapter 5](https://imsc.uni-graz.at/clason/preprints/InverseNotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The periodic real Fourier coefficient space, the multiplier operator $T_{\bar t}$ with $\bar t>0$, and its constant and positive-frequency modes.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed for the upstream Fourier and compact singular-system coordinates.

[F1] [[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]]: The complex characters form a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2$ on the circle; their real and imaginary parts give the real Fourier modes.

[F2] [[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index]]: The grid condition requires consecutive candidate variances to have ratios in a fixed interval $[\theta_1,\theta_2]$ with $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$.

[F3] [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]: Positive-noise observations in a fixed singular basis have independent Gaussian coordinates with the stated singular-value scaling.

[F4] [[alg-ip-solit-parameter-choice]]: SOLIT compares the filtered estimator at each candidate with every finer candidate and returns the smallest index passing all comparisons.

[F5] [[lem-ip-solit-filter-risk-decomposition-and-monotone-bias]]: For each candidate, the filtered noise has finite trace variance, and the estimator is a measurable square-integrable Hilbert-valued random element.

[F6] [[def-ip-ordered-filter-grid-and-source-index]]: An ordered filter is nonnegative, satisfies $0\le\alpha q_\alpha(t)\le C_q'$ and $0\le tq_\alpha(t)\le1$, and increases pointwise as $\alpha$ decreases.

[F7] [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]]: Real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with its canonical inner product is complete.

## Verification

1.1 Interleaving the constant coordinate and cosine–sine pairs is a linear isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so [F7] gives the stated real Hilbert structure. The real Fourier modes are orthonormal by taking real and imaginary parts of the character basis in [F1]. On each positive frequency, $\partial_{xx}\cos(nx)=-n^2\cos(nx)$ and $\partial_{xx}\sin(nx)=-n^2\sin(nx)$, so solving $\partial_tu=\partial_{xx}u$ multiplies both coefficients by $e^{-n^2\bar t}$; the constant mode is unchanged. Therefore the operator in the Example is the periodic heat forward map in Fourier coordinates. [given, A1, F1, F7, algebra]

1.2 Every multiplier of $T_{\bar t}$ is positive, so $T_{\bar t}$ is injective. The positive-frequency multipliers tend to zero, so finite-frequency truncations converge in operator norm and $T_{\bar t}$ is compact. Moreover, $\sum_{n\ge1}2e^{-2n^2\bar t}<\infty$ by comparison with the geometric series $\sum_{n\ge1}2e^{-2n\bar t}$, so the operator is Hilbert–Schmidt. Squaring the multipliers gives the stated eigenvalues of $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$. [given, algebra]

1.3 For spectral cut-off, the inverse-eigenvalue contribution at frequency $n$ is $2e^{2n^2\bar t}$. Since $V_{n-1}\le(2n-1)e^{2(n-1)^2\bar t}$,
$$
\frac{V_n}{V_{n-1}}=1+\frac{2e^{2n^2\bar t}}{V_{n-1}}\ge1+\frac{2}{2n-1}e^{2(2n-1)\bar t}\longrightarrow\infty.
$$
Hence no finite $\theta_2$ bounds all consecutive ratios in this sequence, as claimed. [F2, algebra]

2.1 For every $\lambda\ge0$, $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ is nonnegative, $\alpha q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$, and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$. If $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, then $\lambda+\widetilde\alpha<\lambda+\alpha$, so $q_\alpha(\lambda)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(\lambda)$. Thus it is an ordered filter with $C_q'=1$ by [F6]. Its variance is $V(\alpha)=1/(1+\alpha)^2+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-2n^2\bar t}(e^{-2n^2\bar t}+\alpha)^{-2}$. On each compact interval $\alpha\ge a>0$, the summands are continuous and bounded by $2a^{-2}e^{-2n^2\bar t}$, a summable sequence, so $V$ is continuous there by uniform convergence. It is strictly decreasing. For $\alpha\ge1$, $V(\alpha)\le\alpha^{-2}(1+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-2n^2\bar t})\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. It tends to infinity as $\alpha\downarrow0$: for every $N$, its first $N$ positive-frequency terms tend to $2\sum_{n=1}^N e^{2n^2\bar t}$, and these partial sums are unbounded in $N$. The intermediate value theorem therefore selects recursively a decreasing sequence with any prescribed fixed ratio $\theta_1>1$ between consecutive variance values; its upper ratio is the same $\theta_1$. The estimator and each finite comparison are well-defined by [F3]–[F5]. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra] ∎

## Finite checks

At frequencies $0$ and $1$, the eigenvalues of $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$ are $1$ and $e^{-2\bar t}$ (with multiplicity two for frequency $1$). For $n=1$, $V_1=1+2e^{2\bar t}$; for $n=2$, $V_2=1+2e^{2\bar t}+2e^{8\bar t}$. The displayed consecutive-ratio lower bound is $V_2/V_1>1$.

kind: lemma
title: Compact manifold fundamental groups have finite generators without choice
status: draft

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold and $o\in M$. There is a finite based graph mapped continuously into $M$ such that its induced fundamental-group map is onto. Consequently $\pi_1(M,o)$ has a finite generating list, without a choice principle. No triangulation or smooth structure on $M$ is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact connected manifold and specified basepoint.

## Proof

1.1 First construct a compatible metric from finite data. Compactness supplies finitely many coordinate balls $V_i$ whose closures lie in larger coordinate balls with charts $\varphi_i$; take their coordinate images concentric balls of radii $r_i<R_i$. A continuous radial function $\chi_i$ equals one on $\overline V_i$, decreases linearly to zero before the larger chart boundary, and is zero elsewhere on $M$. The finitely many functions $\chi_i$ and $\chi_i\varphi_i$, extended by zero, are continuous because their coordinate supports are compactly contained in the charts. Their combined map $F$ into a finite Euclidean space is injective: for $x$, choose $i$ with $x\in V_i$, so $\chi_i(x)=1$; equality $F(x)=F(y)$ forces $\chi_i(y)=1$ and $\varphi_i(x)=\varphi_i(y)$, hence $x=y$. A continuous injection of a compact space into a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image: images of closed subsets are compact and hence closed. Therefore $d(x,y)=|F(x)-F(y)|$ is a compatible metric. All choices so far are finite. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose a finite cover of $M$ by contractible coordinate balls. It has a positive Lebesgue number $\lambda$: for a finite open cover the functions $x\mapsto d(x,M\setminus U)$, with the empty-complement case assigned a positive constant, are continuous; their finite maximum is everywhere positive and has a positive minimum on compact $M$. A sufficiently small number below that minimum makes every set of diameter less than $\lambda$ lie in some member, by taking a point in the set and using the corresponding distance bound. Choose $0<\epsilon<\lambda/10$. There is a finite cover by smaller coordinate balls $B_j$ of $d$-diameter less than $\epsilon$, because one can shrink a coordinate neighborhood inside a metric ball of radius less than $\epsilon/2$ and then take a finite subcover. Choose $0<\delta<\epsilon$ that is a Lebesgue number for this second finite cover. Any pair of points of distance less than $\delta$ can therefore be joined inside one $B_j$ by its straight coordinate path, of diameter less than $\epsilon$. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Compactness gives a finite $\delta/4$-net of anchors $a_0=o,a_1,\ldots,a_s$, with the basepoint added first. For each unordered distinct anchor pair of distance less than $\delta$, put an edge in a finite graph and map it to the straight coordinate path in the least-index $B_j$ containing that pair; the reverse orientation uses the reversed path. Map each vertex to its anchor. For any $x\in M$, let $a(x)$ be the least-index anchor at distance less than $\delta/4$. Join $x$ to $a(x)$ by the straight path in the least-index $B_j$ containing them. These connectors have diameter less than $\epsilon$ and are defined by finite lists and the chart formulas, without choosing a family of paths. At $o$ take the constant connector. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Let $\ell$ be any based loop in $M$. Uniform continuity on its compact interval gives a finite subdivision such that each segment has image diameter less than $\delta/4$. Write its successive endpoints as $x_i$ and anchors as $a_i=a(x_i)$. Then $d(a_i,a_{i+1})<3\delta/4$, so the selected graph has an edge between successive distinct anchors; repeated anchors give the constant path. The loop formed by this edge, the original loop segment and the two endpoint connectors is contained in a set of diameter less than $4\epsilon$: each connector and edge has diameter less than $\epsilon$, and its initial or terminal point lies within $\delta/4$ of an endpoint of the original short segment. This entire small loop therefore lies in one of the contractible coordinate balls of step 2.1. Contract it there. Gluing these finitely many homotopies, with adjacent connectors cancelling, shows that $\ell$ is based homotopic to the resulting graph edge loop at $a_0=o$. Thus the fundamental-group map of the component of this finite graph containing $a_0$ is onto. [step 2.1, step 3.1, given, construct, algebra]

5.1 Choose a spanning tree of that finite graph component by its finite vertex order. For every oriented edge outside the tree, follow the tree path from the base vertex to its initial vertex, traverse the edge, and return along the tree path from its terminal vertex. These finitely many loops generate all graph edge loops: insert the corresponding tree paths at successive vertices of an edge loop; the intervening inverse tree paths cancel, and a tree-edge loop contracts by deleting immediate reversals. Step 4.1 then makes their images generate $\pi_1(M,o)$. All graph data, covers, nets and tree paths were finite; a loop uses its own one finite subdivision and finite homotopy construction. No infinite family of generators, partitions or primitives was selected. This proves the statement without AC. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix $n\ge1$ and a finite marked smooth infection sequence $J_{j+1}=P_j(J_j)$, $0\le j<n$, with unknotted axes $\eta_j$ and winding number zero. Supply compatible product tubes, peripheral paths and finite disk-band Seifert-surface models with local ambient roundings for all knots $J_j$ and $P_j(U)$. Let $E_j$ be their actual standard infection cobordisms. Let $W_n$ be any compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with a supplied collared boundary component $M(J_n)$, and form
$$W_j=W_{j+1}\cup_{M(J_{j+1})}E_j\qquad(j=n-1,\ldots,0)$$
using the marked collars. Other boundary components of $W_n$ are allowed. Base paths are supplied coherently through the finite gluings. Write $\mu_j$ for the positive meridian of $J_j$ and $G_j=\pi_1(W_j)$.

For $0\le k<n$, inclusion induces an epimorphism $q_k:G_{k+1}\to G_k$ and a natural isomorphism
$$G_{k+1}/G_{k+1}^{(n-k+1)}\cong G_k/G_k^{(n-k+1)}.$$
Moreover $\mu_k\in G_k^{(n-k)}$. For any supplied finite commutative-ring list $R_0,\ldots,R_n$, define the mixed series by
$$P^0G=G,\qquad P^{i+1}G=\ker\!\left(P^iG\longrightarrow(P^iG/[P^iG,P^iG])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R_i\right).$$
The same $q_k$ identifies $G_{k+1}/P^iG_{k+1}$ with $G_k/P^iG_k$ for $i\le n-k+1$, and identifies $P^iG_{k+1}/P^{i+1}G_{k+1}$ with $P^iG_k/P^{i+1}G_k$ for $0\le i<n-k+1$. These are assertions for the actual inclusion maps. No nontriviality or order assertion about a meridian in a mixed quotient is included; such an assertion requires the separate Blanchfield argument. No choice principle or smoothing of $W_n$ is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite marked knot models, zero-winding axes, actual product cobordisms, collared $W_n$, paths and finite coefficient-ring list.

[F1] Adjoining the actual standard infection cobordism along its outgoing surgery induces precisely the quotient by the normal closure of the companion longitude, and its companion meridian is the marked pattern-axis core. [[lem-standard-infection-cobordism-adjunction-kills-the-companion-longitude]]

[F2] For the supplied finite knot models, exterior and zero-surgery groups are normally generated by their meridian, and the preferred exterior longitude lies in the exterior group's second derived subgroup. [[lem-finite-disk-band-knot-longitudes-lie-in-the-second-derived-subgroup]]

[F3] Killing a normal subgroup contained in $G^{(r)}$ preserves the ordinary derived quotient at index $r$ and all mixed-series quotients and factors through index $r$, for the actual quotient map. [[lem-killing-deep-derived-normal-subgroups-preserves-mixed-derived-quotients]]

[F4] The standard product-spine markings identify the outgoing satellite meridian with the pattern meridian. The peripheral calculation gives $H_1(M(P_j(U));\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_{P_j}]$ and the axis class $[\eta_j]=\operatorname{lk}(P_j(U),\eta_j)[\mu_{P_j}]=0$: this is the longitude calculation in the two-component exterior, before filling back the axis tube. [[lem-standard-infection-cobordisms-have-boundary-generated-second-homology]]

[F5] Zero first-homology class is equivalent to membership in the commutator subgroup, without choice. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Proof

1.1 Fix $k<n$ and work first in $G=G_{k+1}$. For $k+1\le j<n$, the piece $E_j$ is already present in $W_{k+1}$. Let $A_j$ be the image of the group of its pattern boundary $M(P_j(U))$ in $G$. Its meridian is the image of $\mu_{j+1}$ by [F4], so [F2] implies $A_j\subseteq\langle\!\langle\mu_{j+1}\rangle\!\rangle_G$. By [F4] and [F5], its axis lies in the commutator subgroup of that pattern-boundary group. Its image is $\mu_j$ by [F1]. Hence $$\mu_j\in[A_j,A_j]\subseteq[\langle\!\langle\mu_{j+1}\rangle\!\rangle_G,\langle\!\langle\mu_{j+1}\rangle\!\rangle_G].$$ Only this inclusion is needed; no equality between a single axis normal closure and an entire commutator subgroup is asserted. [F1, F2, F4, F5, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Starting with $\mu_n\in G^{(0)}$, descend through the finite range $j=n-1,\ldots,k+1$. If $\mu_{j+1}\in G^{(n-j-1)}$, its normal closure is contained in that derived subgroup because derived subgroups are normal: conjugation preserves every finite commutator word. Step 1.1 then gives $\mu_j\in G^{(n-j)}$. Consequently $\mu_{k+1}\in G^{(n-k-1)}$; when $k=n-1$ this just says $\mu_n\in G$. The companion exterior $X_{J_k}$ is an actual subspace of the outgoing boundary $M(J_{k+1})$. By normal generation of that surgery group in [F2], the entire image of its group, and hence the image of the companion-exterior group, lies in $\langle\!\langle\mu_{k+1}\rangle\!\rangle_G\subseteq G^{(n-k-1)}$. Its longitude lies in its second derived subgroup by [F2]. Expanding the finite commutator products under the inclusion homomorphism therefore puts the longitude image $\lambda_k$ in $G^{(n-k+1)}$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], the actual inclusion gives $G_k=G/\langle\!\langle\lambda_k\rangle\!\rangle_G$. Derived subgroups are normal, so step 2.1 puts the entire kernel in $G^{(n-k+1)}$. Apply [F3] with $r=n-k+1$ to obtain exactly the ordinary and mixed-quotient isomorphisms in the Statement, for the actual inclusion map and every supplied finite ring prefix. To check the remaining meridian depth, observe in the new piece $E_k$ that the image $A_k$ of its pattern-boundary group lies in the normal closure of $q_k(\mu_{k+1})$, and that $\mu_k\in[A_k,A_k]$, by the same argument as step 1.1. The image of $\mu_{k+1}$ has depth at least $n-k-1$ by step 2.1, because a homomorphism sends each finite commutator word to the corresponding word of its images. Thus $\mu_k\in G_k^{(n-k)}$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The topological adjunctions used only supplied three-dimensional boundary collars and the explicit smooth product pieces. Finite paths fix all based inclusions; changing any such path conjugates its relevant image and does not affect normal closures or derived-depth statements. The calculation never asserted that a derived meridian is nonzero, of infinite order, or of prime order: those require additional homological and Blanchfield inputs. Likewise positive-characteristic mixed factors are not called PTFA merely because the rational prefixes are. Every commutator, representative and path used above belongs to a fixed finite calculation, and [F3] proves the kernel comparisons without an infinite representative selection. Thus the full stated finite-tower naturality and depth assertions hold in the supplied TOP/smooth scope without a choice axiom. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

    - title: "Otmar Scherzer and Leonidas Mindrinos, Inverse Problems: Lecture Notes, University of Vienna, Sommersemester 2015"
      url: "https://www.csc.univie.ac.at/files/InverseProblems_SS15/InverseProblems_full.pdf"

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses and notation of the definition of fixed-frequency far-field data. For each $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ there is an $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\|q'-q\|_\infty<\varepsilon$ implies $q'\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$; in particular this metric neighborhood condition holds at zero. For every $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ and every $d,\theta\in S^2$, the solution $u_{q,k,d}$ exists uniquely in $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the integrals defining $\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)$ and $\mathcal B_kq(\theta,d)$ are absolutely convergent and independent of representatives, and $\mathcal S_k(q)(\cdot,d)$ is continuous. If $R_0>\sup_{y\in D}|y|$ and $r\ge2R_0$, then
$$\sup_{\theta\in S^2}\left|r e^{-ikr}V_k u_{q,k,d}(r\theta)-\mathcal S_k(q)(\theta,d)\right|\le\frac{2R_0+|k|R_0^2}{4\pi r}\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\,\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2.$$
Thus $\mathcal S_k(q)(\cdot,d)$ is the uniform outgoing far-field amplitude in the stated convention.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-fixed-frequency-far-field-data|The small-norm domain, volume operator, incident plane wave, scattering data, and first Born data family.]]

[[def-volume-integral-scattering-model|The volume model uses equivalence classes in complex L2 and the stated outgoing Green kernel.]]

[[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded|The far-field map is continuous and has the uniform outgoing-wave error bound.]]

[[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded|The volume operator is linear and satisfies the Hilbert–Schmidt norm bound used to show openness.]]

[[thm-volume-integral-scattering-born-neumann-error|For operator norm strictly below one, the Lippmann–Schwinger equation has a unique L2 solution.]]

[[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz|Complex L2 Cauchy–Schwarz and representative-independent pairings.]]

[[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound|An L-infinity representative is bounded almost everywhere by its essential norm.]]

[[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn|The L1 Fourier transform is defined at every frequency and is representative-independent.]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice is the declared axiom branch of the volume and L2 suppliers.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a bounded Lebesgue-measurable $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ with $0<M:=|D|<\infty$; $k>0$; a contrast $q\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$; and directions $d,\theta\in S^2$.

[F1] The volume model defines $K_{q,k}$ on complex $L^2(D)$ by the outgoing kernel, treats inputs as equivalence classes, sets the diagonal representative to zero, and uses $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere ([[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]]).

[F2] For $\operatorname{diam}(D)<\infty$, $\|K_{q,k}\|_{L^2\to L^2}\le C_D\|q\|_\infty$, where $C_D=\sqrt{M\operatorname{diam}(D)/(4\pi)}$ ([[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]]).

[F3] The plane wave has modulus one, so its restriction to $D$ is in $L^2(D)$ with norm $\sqrt M$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[F4] If $\rho_k(q)<1$ and $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, then $u=f+K_{q,k}u$ has a unique solution in $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ ([[thm-volume-integral-scattering-born-neumann-error]]).

[F5] For $a,b\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the pairing is representative-independent and $|\int_D a\overline b|\le\|a\|_2\|b\|_2$ ([[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]]).

[F6] For $g\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, $\widehat g(\xi)=\int g(y)e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\xi}\,dy$ is absolutely convergent at every $\xi$ and unchanged by null-set modifications ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]).

[F7] For a measurable representative with finite essential norm, $|q|\le\|q\|_\infty$ almost everywhere ([[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound]]).

[F8] For $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, the far-field map is continuous in observation direction and its values are the uniform outgoing-wave limits of the exterior volume potential, with the displayed explicit remainder ([[lem-volume-far-field-map-is-bounded]]).

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the volume model and the Neumann theorem used here ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement, with $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$.

1.1 The integral operator depends linearly on $q$, so $K_{q,k}-K_{q',k}=K_{q-q',k}$ for any $q,q'\in L^\infty(D;\mathbb C)$. By [F2], $\|K_{q,k}-K_{q',k}\|\le C_D\|q-q'\|_\infty$. The operator-norm triangle inequality then gives $|\rho_k(q)-\rho_k(q')|\le C_D\|q-q'\|_\infty$. Thus $q\mapsto\rho_k(q)$ is continuous, $\mathcal U_{D,k}=\{\rho_k<1\}$ is open, and $0\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$ because $K_{0,k}=0$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 By [F3], $f_{k,d}(x)=e^{ikd\cdot x}$ belongs to $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ and has norm $\sqrt M$. Since $q\in\mathcal U_{D,k}$, [F4] applies with $f=f_{k,d}$ and gives exactly one $u_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$. [A1, F3, F4, given]

1.3 By [F7], $qu_{q,k,d}\in L^2(D)$ with norm at most $\|q\|_\infty\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2$, while [F3] puts $e^{ik\theta\cdot y}$ in $L^2(D)$. Their pairing in [F5] is the stated integral, so it is absolutely convergent and independent of the representatives. Cauchy–Schwarz gives its absolute value at most $\|q\|_\infty\sqrt M\|u_{q,k,d}\|_2$. [F1, F3, F5, F7, given]

1.4 By [F7], $\|q\|_2\le\sqrt M\|q\|_\infty$; pairing $|q|$ with $1_D$ in [F5] then gives $\int_D|q(y)|\,dy\le M\|q\|_\infty$. Hence $q_0\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. By [F6], its transform is finite and representative-independent. Since $e^{-ik\theta\cdot y}e^{ikd\cdot y}=e^{-2\pi i y\cdot(k(\theta-d)/(2\pi))}$, the Fourier and integral formulas for $\mathcal B_kq$ agree and are well-defined. This proves the assertion for both data families. [F5, F6, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F8] to $v=u_{q,k,d}$, whose existence is established in step 1.2. It supplies continuity in observation direction and the stated uniform outgoing-wave limit estimate, so the defined data are the physical far-field amplitude for this volume branch. [F8, step 1.2] ∎
## Remarks

The proof establishes only the small-norm branch selected by $\rho_k(q)<1$. It does not import global scattering uniqueness from smoother coefficient models.

id: lem-ptfa-finite-projective-basechange-preserves-euler-characteristic
kind: lemma
title: PTFA finite projective base change and Euler characteristic
status: draft
origin: pipeline

## Statement

Let $k$ be a commutative field, let $G$ be PTFA, put $A=k[G]$, and supply its Ore fraction division ring $K$. Subscripts $k$ and $K$ mean tensor base change along augmentation $A\to k$ and inclusion $A\to K$, respectively.

For every finitely generated projective right-$A$ module $P$,
$$\dim_K P_K=\dim_k P_k<\infty.$$
For a homomorphism $f:P\to Q$ between such modules,
$$\dim_K\operatorname{im}f_K\ge\dim_k\operatorname{im}f_k.$$
Consequently, for any bounded complex $P_*$ of finitely generated projective right-$A$ modules,
$$\sum_i(-1)^i\dim_K H_i(P_K)=\sum_i(-1)^i\dim_k H_i(P_k).$$
If additionally the complex is nonnegative, $\dim_k H_0(P_k)=1$ and $H_0(P_K)=0$, then
$$\dim_K H_1(P_K)\le\dim_k H_1(P_k)-1.$$
No choice principle or free basis for a projective module is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, group, fraction division ring and the finite projective modules or bounded complex in the relevant assertion.

[F1] PTFA augmentation detects projective injectivity, and finite matrices over $A$ have $K$-rank at least their augmented $k$-rank, without a choice principle. [[thm-ptfa-augmentation-detects-projective-injectivity-without-choice]]

[F2] Projectivity is the individual lifting property for surjections, with right modules read over the opposite ring. Tensor base change preserves compositions, sums and split identities. [[def-projective-module]], [[def-opposite-ring]], [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]

## Proof

1.1 Choose a finite generating list for $P$, giving a surjection $\pi:A^n\to P$. Projectivity gives one section $s:P\to A^n$. The matrix $E=s\pi$ is idempotent, and after either base change $P$ identifies with the image of that idempotent. Put $r=\operatorname{rank}_k E_k$. By [F1], $\operatorname{rank}_K E_K\ge r$ and $\operatorname{rank}_K(1-E)_K\ge n-r$. Idempotency gives the actual complementary decomposition $K^n=\operatorname{im}E_K\oplus\operatorname{im}(1-E)_K$: every vector is the sum of its two displayed images, and their intersection is zero after applying $E_K$. Their dimensions therefore add to $n$, forcing equality in both inequalities. Hence $\dim_K P_K=r=\dim_k P_k$. Only one finite generating list and one projectivity section were used. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Take finite split surjections $\pi_P:A^m\to P$ and $\pi_Q:A^n\to Q$, with sections $s_P,s_Q$. The finite matrix $T=s_Qf\pi_P$ has, after either base change, the same image dimension as $f$: the map $\pi_P$ remains surjective and $s_Q$ remains injective by their split identities. Applying [F1] to $T$ yields $\dim_K\operatorname{im}f_K\ge\dim_k\operatorname{im}f_k$. This argument does not treat $P$ or $Q$ as free. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For a bounded complex after either base change all chain groups are finite-dimensional. If $d_i:P_i\to P_{i-1}$ is its differential, finite-dimensional rank-nullity and cycles modulo boundaries give $$\dim (P_i)_*=\operatorname{rank}(d_i)_*+\dim H_i(P_*)+\operatorname{rank}(d_{i+1})_*,$$ where $*$ is $k$ or $K$. Summing with signs over the finite range cancels every differential rank, so the alternating homology dimension equals the alternating chain dimension. The latter sums are equal under the two base changes by step 1.1. This proves the asserted Euler equality, with no boundedness or generation conclusion inferred for an unrelated singular complex. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 In the nonnegative case, $d_0=0$. Write $n_i=\dim_k(P_i)_k=\dim_K(P_i)_K$. The degree-zero hypotheses give $\operatorname{rank}(d_1)_k=n_0-1$ and $\operatorname{rank}(d_1)_K=n_0$. Step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{rank}(d_2)_K\ge\operatorname{rank}(d_2)_k$. Therefore $$\dim_K H_1(P_K)=n_1-n_0-\operatorname{rank}(d_2)_K\le n_1-n_0-\operatorname{rank}(d_2)_k=\dim_k H_1(P_k)-1.$$ Every section and generating set needed for the bounded complex belongs to one finite list; finite elimination over $k$ and $K$ requires no choice axiom. This proves all assertions in their stated projective scope. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $E$ be the actual standard infection cobordism from $M(P)\sqcup M(K)$ to $M(P(K))$, constructed from the two surgery products by identifying $N(\eta)$ with the filling solid torus $V_K$. Supply the oriented product tubes and peripheral paths, with $\mu_\eta=\lambda_K$ and $\lambda_\eta=\mu_K$ on the common torus, where $\lambda_K$ is the companion's preferred longitude. No winding-number condition is needed. The inclusion-induced homomorphism is onto and induces
$$\pi_1(M(P(K)))/\langle\!\langle\lambda_K\rangle\!\rangle\ \cong\ \pi_1(E).$$
The marked companion meridian and pattern-axis core have the same image in $\pi_1(E)$, with the supplied base paths.

More generally, if a connected manifold $W$ with supplied boundary collar is glued to $E$ along the marked outgoing component $M(P(K))$, the inclusion-induced map is onto and gives
$$\pi_1(W)/\langle\!\langle i_*(\lambda_K)\rangle\!\rangle\ \cong\ \pi_1(W\cup_{M(P(K))}E).$$
Changing a peripheral base path changes the relator by conjugation and leaves its normal closure unchanged. The statements hold for topological collared $W$ as well as smooth $W$ and use no choice axiom.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The actual finite product infection construction, marked peripheral data, and, in the second assertion, the connected collared gluing manifold $W$.

[F1] The standard infection construction glues the bottom solid tori of the two surgery products; its remaining bottom boundary is the marked surgery $M(P(K))$, with explicit torus corner charts and collars. [[lem-standard-infection-cobordisms-have-boundary-generated-second-homology]]

[F2] On a path-connected two-set open cover with path-connected overlap, the actual inclusion maps give the fundamental-group pushout; overlap injections are not required. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

## Proof

1.1 Put $A=M(P)\setminus\operatorname{int}N(\eta)$, $X_K=M(K)\setminus\operatorname{int}V_K$ and $S=N(\eta)=V_K$. Collapse the interval coordinates in the two defining products to their identified bottom ends. The homotopies agree on $S$, so descend to a deformation to $Z=M(P)\cup_S M(K)$. Rewriting $M(P)=A\cup S$ and $M(K)=X_K\cup S$ gives $$Z=(A\cup_{\partial S}X_K)\cup_{\partial S}S=M(P(K))\cup_{\partial S}S.$$ The deformation fixes $A$ and $X_K$ at their bottom ends; the explicit rounded torus collars identify this fixed union with the outgoing boundary. It therefore supplies the relative homotopy equivalence needed for the actual outgoing inclusion, rather than just an unmarked homotopy equivalence of spaces. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to product-collared open neighborhoods in this last spine. On its overlap torus the two generators, written using companion peripheral coordinates, are $\mu_K,\lambda_K$. The solid torus $S$ has infinite-cyclic group generated by its core $c$, and the gluing sends $\mu_K$ to $c$ and $\lambda_K$ to $1$. Thus the pushout group has presentation relative to $G=\pi_1(M(P(K)))$ as $$\bigl(G*\langle c\rangle\bigr)/\langle\!\langle\,\mu_Kc^{-1},\lambda_K\,\rangle\!\rangle.$$ Eliminate $c$: the map from $G/\langle\!\langle\lambda_K\rangle\!\rangle$ to this group is induced by $G$, while the reverse map is induced by the quotient on $G$ and $c\mapsto[\mu_K]$. They respect the displayed relations and are inverse on both generating factors. This proves the first asserted isomorphism and surjectivity for the actual inclusion. The core $c$ was precisely $\lambda_\eta$, the oriented axis core; hence it also proves the marked meridian-axis identity. Neither torus-to-manifold map was assumed injective. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For the manifold adjunction, the supplied boundary collars give open neighborhoods with the same homotopy types as $W$, $E$ and their common surgery component. Apply [F2] again. Put $B=\pi_1(W)$ and let $f:G\to B$ be its marked boundary inclusion map. By step 2.1, the other pushout factor is the quotient $G/\langle\!\langle\lambda_K\rangle\!\rangle$. Every compatible pair of homomorphisms from these two factors is uniquely determined by a homomorphism from $B$ that kills $f(\lambda_K)$: its values on the second factor are forced by its values on $G$, and they descend exactly when that relator is killed. The group $B/\langle\!\langle f(\lambda_K)\rangle\!\rangle$ has precisely this universal property, with the actual inclusion from $B$. Explicitly send its coset of $b$ to the inclusion image of $b$; in the reverse direction use the quotient on $B$ and the homomorphism from $G/\langle\!\langle\lambda_K\rangle\!\rangle$ induced by $f$. The composites are identities on the two pushout factors. This proves the second isomorphism and its stated map without an injectivity hypothesis on $f$. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Replacing a chosen path to a peripheral loop by another changes its based group element by conjugation. The normal closure of a conjugate is the same normal subgroup, so both quotient descriptions and their inclusion-induced maps are independent of that change in the asserted sense. All geometric operations above are the actual supplied product homotopies and collar neighborhoods; the group calculations use finite words and the unique maps of the pushout property. The van Kampen supplier constructs these maps from finite loop and homotopy subdivisions rather than a global family of representatives. Thus no choice principle, smooth structure on $W$, or locally flat annulus product theorem has entered the proof. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

id: thm-compact-manifolds-have-finite-presentation-complexes-without-choice
kind: theorem
title: Compact manifolds have finite fundamental-group presentation complexes
  without choice
status: draft
origin: pipeline
deps:

  - thm-seifert-van-kampen

      url: https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, with boundary allowed, and $o\in M$. Supply any finite list of based loops $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_\ell$. There is a finite connected two-dimensional CW complex $K$ with one vertex $v$, a based map $f:(K,v)\to(M,o)$ inducing an isomorphism on fundamental groups, and marked oriented one-cells which $f$ parametrizes by the specified loops. In particular $\pi_1(M,o)$ is finitely presented without a choice axiom.

For any normal subgroup $N\triangleleft\pi_1(M,o)$ and commutative unital ring $k$, use on $M$ the associated right $k[\pi_1(M)/N]$ normal-cover system and on $K$ its pullback. The actual induced map on $H_1$ with these coefficients is an isomorphism. No finite CW type, triangulation or smoothing of $M$ is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The based compact manifold and finite marked loop list.

[F1] A compact Hausdorff manifold is a strict retract $M\xrightarrow{i}L\xrightarrow{r}M$ of a finite geometric polyhedron, with $ri=\mathrm{id}$. [[thm-compact-manifolds-are-retracts-of-finite-polyhedra-without-choice]]

[F2] Fundamental groups of connected collared open gluings are their actual group pushouts, without an overlap-injectivity assumption or global choice of loop representatives. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

[F3] Normal-cover right local first homology is naturally the abelianized covering subgroup tensored with $k$, for actual based maps and induced coefficient maps, without choice. The supplied contractible-neighborhood-basis scope includes finite polyhedra. [[lem-normal-cover-local-homology-detects-mixed-derived-kernels-without-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 Use [F1] and retain the component of $L$ containing connected $i(M)$; it is still finite and still retracts onto $M$. Triangulate the finite polyhedron by its given finite geometric structure, choose a spanning tree of its finite one-skeleton, and take one generator for each oriented edge outside the tree. Each two-simplex gives its finite boundary-word relation. These give a finite presentation of $\pi_1(L,i(o))$. Here is the finite van Kampen verification: a tree contracts by successively deleting leaf edges, so the one-skeleton has the free group on the edges outside it. Attaching a two-cell adds the normal relation given by its boundary, by [F2] applied to the cell with a thin based connector strip; the overlap retracts to its boundary circle, and the cell side contracts. Attaching a cell of dimension at least three adds no relation or generator because the same overlap is its simply connected boundary sphere. A sphere of dimension at least two is simply connected by [F2] on its two punctured-coordinate charts: they are Euclidean spaces and contract, and their overlap is path-connected. This verifies the presentation through the finite list of cells. A path from $i(o)$ to a chosen tree vertex changes basepoint and only conjugates these finitely many loops. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $P=\pi_1(L,i(o))=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_a\mid r_1,\ldots,r_b\rangle$. The based endomorphism $e=i_*r_*$ is idempotent and has image $i_*\pi_1(M,o)$, with $i_*$ injective because $r_*i_*=\mathrm{id}$. Choose a finite word $w_j$ representing $e(x_j)$ for each of the finitely many generators. Consider $$Q=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_a\mid r_1,\ldots,r_b,\ x_1w_1^{-1},\ldots,x_aw_a^{-1}\rangle.$$ The map $e:P\to\operatorname{im}e$ kills these additional relations because $e^2=e$, so descends to $Q$. Conversely include $\operatorname{im}e$ in $P$ and pass to $Q$. This gives inverse maps: on $e(x_j)$ the first composite is $e^2(x_j)=e(x_j)$; on the generating $x_j$ of $Q$ the second is $w_j=x_j$ by its new relation. Hence $Q\cong\operatorname{im}e\cong\pi_1(M,o)$, proving finite presentability by an explicit finite quotient, rather than assuming retracts preserve finite presentation. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Realize the finite presentation $Q$ by a bouquet of its generator circles and one two-cell per relator; the same [F2] calculation gives fundamental group $Q$. Map each generator circle to its based loop in $M$ under the isomorphism in step 2.1. Each relator has trivial based class, so has a based nullhomotopy; choose one for each of the finitely many relators and extend over its two-cell. This gives a based map inducing exactly that isomorphism. For each specified $\gamma_h$, choose one finite word $v_h$ in these generators representing its based class, add a new generator $y_h$ and the relation $y_hv_h^{-1}$, and map $y_h$ exactly by $\gamma_h$. A nullhomotopy of its relation extends this map. The added generator can be eliminated from the presentation, so the induced fundamental-group map is still the same isomorphism. This particular presentation complex has a finite polyhedral model. Triangulate every generator circle by three edges and read each nonempty relator on a subdivided boundary circle, so each boundary edge maps homeomorphically to one graph edge. Insert its mapping cylinder before attaching the disk. Each cylinder rectangle has distinct bottom endpoints in the graph and distinct private top endpoints; triangulate it by a fresh center and its four boundary edges. The private center distinguishes different rectangles even when their bottom edges coincide, and neighboring vertical sides agree, so these are finitely many honest simplices. Cone each top circle to a fresh vertex to attach its disk. The cylinder plus disk is just a disk with an extra annular collar, so this changes no underlying presentation space or graph marking. Empty relators may be omitted without affecting the group; with no generators the point suffices until marked generators are added. Thus $K$ has a finite simplicial triangulation of its underlying space, and its contractible open-star basis, while retaining its original one-vertex CW description. These operations produce the asserted finite two-complex with its actual marked loops. [F2, given, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The normal subgroup pulled back along this isomorphism maps isomorphically onto $N$. Apply the explicit normal path-class construction and finite-cycle comparison of [F3] to the map in step 3.1; the finite triangulation in step 3.1 supplies its required contractible-neighborhood basis. Its chain-map naturality identifies the actual map on local $H_1$ with the isomorphism of the covering subgroups' abelianizations tensored with $k$, which is an isomorphism with its explicitly induced inverse. Only the finite polyhedron, its group presentation, individual words and finitely many nullhomotopies were selected. No homotopy equivalence between $M$ and $K$ or finite CW type of $M$ was inferred. This proves precisely the stated choice-free presentation and degree-one comparison. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

kind: theorem
title: Level, power, and weighted regularization of Gaussian MAP feature tests
status: draft

  - thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion
  - thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family
