  proof: ai-altered
axiom_use: The raw and calibrated Gaussian-tail arguments add no choice. The weighted-minimizer clause constructs the real polar partial isometry from the common eigenbasis and uses Countable Choice through the compact spectral and square-root suppliers. The posterior input inherits the Axiom of Choice from its separate RCD proof.
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Remo Kretschmann and Frank Werner, Maximum a posteriori testing in statistical inverse problems, Theorems 2.4–2.5"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00686
    - title: "Remo Kretschmann, Tanja Wachsmuth, and Frank Werner, Optimal regularized hypothesis testing in statistical inverse problems, §1.2 and Theorem 2.3"
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.12897
---

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,H$ be separable real Hilbert spaces, $K:X\to H$ bounded and linear, $\epsilon>0$, and let $U$ be a Borel Gaussian prior with mean $m_0$ and positive self-adjoint, injective, trace-class covariance $C_0$, independent of a jointly Gaussian centered family $Z$ indexed by $H$, linear into $L^2$ with covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(k)]=\langle g,k\rangle_H$. Fix $h\in X$, define $S=C_0^{1/2}$, $B=SK^*KS$, $R=(B+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}$, $\Phi_h=KSRSh$, and $c_h=\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle_H-\langle m_0,h\rangle_X$. Let $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ and let the raw MAP test reject exactly when $Y_x(\Phi_h)>c_h$. Define $G(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-s^2/2}\,ds$, the standard normal cumulative distribution function. For every $x\in X$ its rejection probability is
$$\mathbb P_x\{Y_x(\Phi_h)>c_h\}=\begin{cases}G\!\left(\dfrac{\langle x,K^*\Phi_h\rangle_X-c_h}{\epsilon\|\Phi_h\|_H}\right),&\Phi_h\ne0,\\[6pt]\mathbf1\{0>c_h\},&\Phi_h=0.\end{cases}$$

Let $P_Y$ be the prior-predictive law of the field $Y(g)=\langle KU,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ on $\mathbb R^H$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra, and let $\Pi_y$ and $M_y$ be the data-indexed posterior kernel and mean supplied by the Gaussian posterior-law theorem, using supplied finite or countable complete orthonormal bases of $X$ and $H$ as in that theorem. For every $y$, the scalar feature marginal under $\Pi_y$ is normal with mean $\langle M_y,h\rangle_X$ and variance $\langle C_{\rm post}h,h\rangle_X$; its mode is its mean, with the support point serving as the mode when the variance is zero. For each fixed $h$, the raw MAP test agrees for $P_Y$-almost every $y$ with rejection exactly when this posterior marginal mode is positive. The exceptional null set may depend on $h$. If $h=0$, then $\Phi_h=c_h=0$, and the raw test returns $0$ almost surely under every sampling law and under $P_Y$.

For a further real Hilbert space $V$ and a continuous linear injection $i:V\to X$, define the residual functional $r_\Phi\in V^*$, where $V^*$ is the continuous dual of $V$, by
$$r_\Phi(v)=\langle Ki(v),\Phi\rangle_H-\langle i(v),h\rangle_X,\qquad \|r_\Phi\|_{V^*}=\sup_{\|v\|_V\le1}|r_\Phi(v)|.$$
For $0<\alpha<1$ let $z_{1-\alpha}$ satisfy $G(z_{1-\alpha})=1-\alpha$. If $\Phi\ne0$, the calibrated probe test rejects exactly when
$$Y_x(\Phi)>\epsilon\|\Phi\|_H z_{1-\alpha}+\|r_\Phi\|_{V^*}.$$
Its rejection probability at every $x\in X$ is the same displayed Gaussian-tail formula with $\Phi$ in place of $\Phi_h$ and calibrated threshold in place of $c_h$. If $x=i(v)$ satisfies $\|v\|_V\le1$ and $\langle x,h\rangle_X\le0$, this test has rejection probability at most $\alpha$. For $\Phi=0$ it never rejects and has level zero.

As an additional weighted-regularization identity, assume Countable Choice and suppose that $C_0K^*K=K^*KC_0$. Let $J$ be the real partial isometry in the polar decomposition $K=J(K^*K)^{1/2}$. Let $\mathcal D=\{C_0^{1/2}x:x\in X\}$, and define $C_0^{-1/2}$ as the inverse of $C_0^{1/2}$ on $\mathcal D$. On $\Psi\in H$, set
$$J_h(\Psi)=\|K^*\Psi-h\|_X^2+\epsilon^2\|C_0^{-1/2}J^*\Psi\|_X^2$$
when $J^*\Psi\in\mathcal D$, and set $J_h(\Psi)=+\infty$ otherwise. Then $\Phi_h$ is a minimizer of $J_h$, and
$$K^*\Phi_h=B(B+\epsilon^2I_X)^{-1}h.$$

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-gaussian-map-feature-test|Gaussian MAP feature test]]

[[thm-ip-isonormal-gaussian-posterior-law|Gaussian posterior law in an isonormal inverse experiment]]

[Kretschmann and Werner, *Maximum a posteriori testing in statistical inverse problems*, Theorems 2.4–2.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00686)

[Kretschmann, Wachsmuth, and Werner, *Optimal regularized hypothesis testing in statistical inverse problems*, §1.2 and Theorem 2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.12897)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Gaussian model and hypotheses in the Statement, a feature vector $h$, a truth space $V$ when the calibrated test is used, and the commutation hypothesis for the final clause.

[F1] The MAP feature test has probe $\Phi_h=K C_0^{1/2}(C_0^{1/2}K^*KC_0^{1/2}+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}C_0^{1/2}h$ and threshold $c_h=\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle-\langle m_0,h\rangle$. [[alg-ip-gaussian-map-feature-test]]

[F2] At any fixed $x$ and probe $\Phi$, $Y_x(\Phi)$ is normal with mean $\langle Kx,\Phi\rangle_H$ and variance $\epsilon^2\|\Phi\|_H^2$; the zero probe is the constant zero. [[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment]]

[F3] The standard normal distribution is continuous, strictly increasing, symmetric, and its upper $1-\alpha$ quantile satisfies $1-G(z_{1-\alpha})=\alpha$. [[lem-standard-normal-cdf-quantiles-and-symmetry]]

[F4] A positive injective trace-class covariance is compact and has a positive square root; its compact positive operator admits a complete orthonormal eigenbasis under Countable Choice. [[def-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-positive-square-root-of-a-compact-positive-operator]], [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]]

[F5] The cited partial-isometry definition uses nonzero complex Hilbert spaces; it supplies only the terminology here. The real operator $J$ is constructed and its defining properties are verified directly in step 1.2. [[def-isometry-coisometry-and-partial-isometry]]

[F6] A self-adjoint operator on each finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis, and Hilbert-basis expansions converge in norm with Parseval's identity. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]], [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]

[F7] The Hilbert adjoint satisfies $\langle Kx,\Phi\rangle_H=\langle x,K^*\Phi\rangle_X$. [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]

[F8] For $\sigma>0$, the density of $N(a,\sigma^2)$ is uniquely maximized at $a$; when $\sigma=0$, $N(a,0)$ is the point mass at $a$, whose support point is its mode.

[F9] For every fixed $h$, the posterior-law theorem gives $\langle M_y,h\rangle_X=\langle m_0,h\rangle_X+y(\Phi_h)-\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle_H$ for $P_Y$-almost every $y$, and gives the scalar posterior marginal stated in the Statement. [[thm-ip-isonormal-gaussian-posterior-law]]

[A1] The posterior input inherits the Axiom of Choice from its separate conditional-law construction. Countable Choice is used for the compact spectral and square-root suppliers in the weighted clause; its real partial isometry is constructed in the proof. The Gaussian-tail and calibration calculations use no additional choice principle. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]



## Proof
1.1 For fixed $x$ and $\Phi\ne0$, [F2] gives $Y_x(\Phi)=\langle Kx,\Phi\rangle_H+\epsilon\|\Phi\|_H Z_0$ in law, where $Z_0$ is standard normal. By [F7], the mean is $\langle x,K^*\Phi\rangle_X$. Hence $\mathbb P_x\{Y_x(\Phi)>c\}=1-G((c-\langle x,K^*\Phi\rangle)/(\epsilon\|\Phi\|)$, which equals the stated formula by symmetry in [F3]. For $\Phi=0$, $Y_x(0)=0$ and the probability is exactly $\mathbf1\{0>c\}$. Substituting $\Phi_h,c_h$ proves the raw MAP formula. [given, F1, F2, F3, F7, algebra]

1.2 For the weighted clause, [F4] gives the compact positive injective spectral decomposition $C_0v_j=c_jv_j$ with $c_j>0$, finite-dimensional eigenspaces, and a complete orthonormal family spanning $X$. The commutation hypothesis makes each such eigenspace invariant under the self-adjoint positive operator $K^*K$. By [F6], diagonalize its finite-dimensional restriction in each eigenspace. This gives a common complete orthonormal basis with $C_0v_j=c_jv_j$ and $K^*Kv_j=\lambda_jv_j$, $\lambda_j\ge0$. For $\lambda_j>0$, put $w_j=Kv_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}$; then $\langle w_i,w_j\rangle_H=\delta_{ij}$ by [F7]. Define $Tv_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}v_j$ and define $Jv_j=w_j$ for $\lambda_j>0$ and $Jv_j=0$ for $\lambda_j=0$. For a finite sum $x=\sum_j a_jv_j$, orthonormality gives $\|Tx\|^2=\sum_j\lambda_j|a_j|^2\le\|K\|^2\|x\|^2$ and $\|Jx\|^2=\sum_{\lambda_j>0}|a_j|^2\le\|x\|^2$. Thus both rules extend by completeness to bounded real-linear operators on $X$, with $T$ self-adjoint and positive and $T^2=K^*K$. Any bounded self-adjoint positive square root $Q$ of $K^*K$ commutes with its square and therefore preserves each eigenspace; on an eigenspace with eigenvalue $\lambda\ge0$, it equals $\sqrt\lambda I$. Indeed, for $Q^2=\lambda I$, $a=\sqrt\lambda$, and a vector $x$ in that eigenspace, $V=(Q-aI)x$ satisfies $QV=-aV$, which positivity forces to vanish; when $\lambda=0$, $\|Qx\|^2=\langle Q^2x,x\rangle=0$. Hence $T=(K^*K)^{1/2}$. Also $\|Kx\|^2=\sum_j\lambda_j|\langle x,v_j\rangle|^2$, so $\ker K$ is the closed span of the zero-eigenvalue vectors and $(\ker K)^\perp$ is the closed span of the positive-eigenvalue vectors. The extended $J$ vanishes on $\ker K$, is isometric on $(\ker K)^\perp$, and has $\ker J=\ker K$ by its coordinate formula; these real-space properties verify that $J$ is a partial isometry as characterized in [F5], including when the basis is empty. The expansions of $Kx$ and $Jx$ show $K=JT$ and $\overline{R(K)}=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{w_j:\lambda_j>0\}$. Since $w_j$ are orthonormal, with $\xi_j=\langle\Psi,w_j\rangle_H$ the adjoint identities and Fourier expansion in $X$ give $J^*\Psi=\sum_{\lambda_j>0}\xi_jv_j$ and $K^*\Psi=\sum_{\lambda_j>0}\sqrt{\lambda_j}\xi_jv_j$. If $h_j=\langle h,v_j\rangle_X$, the Fourier expansions give $\|K^*\Psi-h\|_X^2=\sum_{\lambda_j>0}|\sqrt{\lambda_j}\xi_j-h_j|^2+\sum_{\lambda_j=0}|h_j|^2$ and $\|C_0^{-1/2}J^*\Psi\|_X^2=\sum_{\lambda_j>0}|\xi_j|^2/c_j$ whenever the second term is defined. Components of $\Psi$ in $\overline{R(K)}^\perp$ affect neither expression. [given, A1, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

1.3 For each fixed $h$, [F9] gives for $P_Y$-almost every $y$ that $\langle M_y,h\rangle_X=\langle m_0,h\rangle_X+y(\Phi_h)-\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle_H=y(\Phi_h)-c_h$. For every $y$, the posterior feature marginal has the normal law stated in the theorem. If its variance $\sigma^2$ is positive, its density is $(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}\exp(-(t-\langle M_y,h\rangle_X)^2/(2\sigma^2))$, uniquely maximized at $\langle M_y,h\rangle_X$; if its variance is zero, it is the point mass at that same value. Thus its mode is $\langle M_y,h\rangle_X$ in both cases. On the probability-one set where the displayed identity holds, the raw comparison $y(\Phi_h)>c_h$ is therefore equivalent to a positive posterior marginal mode; its exceptional null set may depend on $h$. If $h=0$, the definitions give $\Phi_h=c_h=0$, and [F2] gives $Y_x(0)=0$ almost surely under each $P_x$ and $Y(0)=0$ almost surely under $P_Y$, so the raw test returns $0$ under all those laws. [F2, F8, F9, algebra]

2.1 For $x=i(v)$ in the stated null ball, [F7] gives $\langle Kx,\Phi\rangle=\langle x,K^*\Phi\rangle_X=\langle x,h\rangle_X+r_\Phi(v)\le|r_\Phi(v)|\le\|r_\Phi\|_{V^*}$. Thus the calibrated threshold is at least $\langle Kx,\Phi\rangle+\epsilon\|\Phi\|z_{1-\alpha}$. Applying step 1.1 to that threshold and using [F3] bounds the rejection probability by $1-G(z_{1-\alpha})=\alpha$. The same substitution gives the exact stated power formula at every $x$. If $\Phi=0$, then $r_0(v)=-\langle i(v),h\rangle$ and its norm is nonnegative, so the strict comparison is $0>\|r_0\|_{V^*}$, which is false; the level and power are zero. [given, F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each $\lambda_j>0$, the scalar quadratic $|\sqrt{\lambda_j}\xi-h_j|^2+\epsilon^2|\xi|^2/c_j$ is minimized at $\xi_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}c_jh_j/(\lambda_jc_j+\epsilon^2)$. These coefficients define a vector in $H$ and lie in the inverse-square-root domain because $|\xi_j|^2/c_j=\lambda_jc_j|h_j|^2/(\lambda_jc_j+\epsilon^2)^2\le|h_j|^2/(4\epsilon^2)$, using $t/(t+\epsilon^2)^2\le1/(4\epsilon^2)$ for $t\ge0$; Parseval makes the bound summable. The corresponding vector is $KSRSh=\Phi_h$, since $SRS$ has coefficient $c_jh_j/(\lambda_jc_j+\epsilon^2)$ on $v_j$. Each coordinate minimizes its summand, while the $\lambda_j=0$ terms are fixed and the orthogonal observation component is irrelevant, so $\Phi_h$ minimizes $J_h$. Finally [F7] and the diagonal action of $B$ show that $K^*\Phi_h$ has coefficient $\lambda_jc_jh_j/(\lambda_jc_j+\epsilon^2)$, which is the coefficient of $B(B+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}h$. [step 1.2, F4, F6, F7, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The raw MAP formula uses a prior fixed independently of the observation whose rejection is tested. If prior covariance is tuned using the same sample, this theorem does not establish the displayed level or power formula for that empirical procedure.

## Remarks references

[Kretschmann and Werner, *Maximum a posteriori testing in statistical inverse problems*, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00686)
## Polar factorization diagram

The triangle records the real polar factorization $K=J(K^*K)^{1/2}$. On the common eigenbasis in step 3.1, the upper arrow sends $v_j$ to $\sqrt{\lambda_j}v_j$; the right arrow then sends it to $\sqrt{\lambda_j}w_j$ when $\lambda_j>0$, and to zero when $\lambda_j=0$. This agrees with the lower arrow $K$ on the basis and therefore on all of $X$ by boundedness and density. The diagram summarizes step 1.2 and is not used in any proof step.

```tikzcd
X \arrow[r, "(K^*K)^{1/2}"] \arrow[dr, "K"'] & X \arrow[d, "J"] \\
& H
```

## Definition

The **grid-complex algorithm** takes a finite encoded grid and a mode from $\{\mathrm{tilde},\mathrm{minus\text{-}associated\text{-}graded},\mathrm{minus\text{-}filtered}\}$. It requires an integer grid number $n\ge2$, disjoint $O$- and $X$-markings with exactly one of each in every row and column, and an induced component permutation that is one $n$-cycle. If $n<2$ or the marking conditions fail, return `invalid-grid`; if the component permutation has more than one cycle, return `link-input-not-supported`. No chain complex is returned on either branch.

For a valid knot grid, number the horizontal and vertical circles $1,\ldots,n$ and enumerate all permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ in lexicographic order. The state for a permutation $\sigma$ consists of the $n$ intersections $(i,\sigma(i))$. For each ordered pair of states $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$, if they agree in other than exactly $n-2$ points, add no rectangle terms. Otherwise enumerate the at most two torus rectangles with the four nonshared state points as corners, retain those whose interiors contain no point of $\mathbf x$, and apply the selected mode. In the full filtered mode, each term drops filtration by $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$; the associated-graded mode retains precisely the terms with zero drop, which are the rectangles with no $X$-marking:

1. **Tilde mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2$. Count a retained rectangle with coefficient $1$ exactly when its interior contains no $O$- or $X$-marking.
2. **Associated-graded minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count a retained rectangle exactly when its interior contains no $X$-marking, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$.
3. **Full filtered minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count every retained rectangle, regardless of its $X$-markings, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$. Use the grid Alexander value for each state and assign filtration drop $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$ to this term.

Return the ordered state list, the mode and coefficient ring, the exact differential matrix obtained by summing coefficients modulo two, the state Maslov and Alexander values, and the filtration data for the full filtered mode. The algorithm returns this finite presentation only; its identification with knot Floer homology and its independence of the chosen grid are separate theorems. The factor $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ is not multiplied into the output.

and define the raw threshold
$$c_h=\langle Km_0,\Phi_h\rangle_H-\langle m_0,h\rangle_X.$$
Input a white-noise observation field $y\in\mathbb R^H$. Compute $q=y(\Phi_h)-c_h$. Return $1$ when $q>0$ and return $0$ when $q\le0$. This strict raw comparison defines the **Gaussian MAP feature test** for every field input $y$.

## Definition references

[[thm-ip-isonormal-gaussian-posterior-law|Gaussian posterior law in an isonormal inverse experiment]]

[Kretschmann and Werner, *Maximum a posteriori testing in statistical inverse problems*, §1.2 and Theorems 2.3–2.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.00686)

[Stuart, *Inverse problems: A Bayesian perspective*, §6.3](https://web.stanford.edu/class/ee378a/REFS/stuart.pdf)

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the library's Kullback–Leibler divergence convention. For a design $d$ in a design-indexed dominated inverse experiment, let $G_d=\{y:0<p_d(y)<\infty\}$ be its positive finite evidence fibers. The **expected information gain** is
$$\operatorname{EIG}(d):=\int_{G_d}D(\mu_d^y\|\mu_0)\,p_d(y)\,\nu(dy)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the integrand is defined to be zero outside $G_d$. Here $D(P\|Q)$ is the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence of probability measures, with natural logarithms.

## Definition references

[[def-ip-design-indexed-inverse-experiment|The predictive density and posterior probability measure on positive finite evidence fibers.]]

[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence|The directional relative entropy is an extended integral with a finite negative part.]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice|The general Radon–Nikodym convention used by the library KL definition assumes AC.]]

[[thm-kullback-leibler-is-nonnegative|KL divergence between probability measures is nonnegative.]]

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

[MacKay, §2](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

## Remarks

The value $+\infty$ is permitted. Before finite numerical optimization, either use the extended objective without subtracting entropies or impose and verify integrability for every design being compared. In particular, do not form a difference of two infinite prior and posterior entropies.

## Remarks references

[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence|The library KL definition controls the negative part and defines its extended integral without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.]]

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N_2(0,C)$ with $C=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)$. Compare two zero-cost one-sensor designs with independent unit-variance Gaussian noise: $d_1$ observes $A_1\theta$ with $A_1=(1,0)$, and $d_2$ observes $A_2\theta$ with $A_2=(0,1)$. Their expected information gains are $\frac12\log 10$ and $\frac12\log 2$, respectively, so the sensor measuring the higher prior-variance direction is uniquely preferred.

## Example references

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

[MacKay, §3.1](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the prior covariance $C=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)$, the two row operators, and independent observation noise with covariance $1$ for both designs.

[A1] AC is inherited from the EIG/KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$, $\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det(I+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2})$. [[thm-ip-linear-gaussian-information-gain-logdet]]

[F2] The natural logarithm is strictly increasing and $\log1=0$. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Example.

1.1 For $d_1$, $A_1CA_1^T=9$ and $\Gamma_1=1$, so [F1] gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d_1)=\frac12\log(1+9)=\frac12\log 10$. For $d_2$, $A_2CA_2^T=1$ and $\Gamma_2=1$, so [F1] gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d_2)=\frac12\log(1+1)=\frac12\log 2$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 The costs are equal and $10>2>0$, so strict increase of the logarithm [F2] gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d_1)>\operatorname{EIG}(d_2)$. Thus $d_1$ is the unique maximizer among the two candidates. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $0<a<b$, let $\phi\in C_c^\infty((a,b))$ be nonnegative and not identically zero, define $U(r)=\int_r^b\phi(s)\,ds$ for $r\ge0$, and set $u^\dagger(x)=U(|x|)$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Choose $h\in C_c^\infty((a/2,2b))$ with $0\le h\le1$ and $h=1$ on $\operatorname{supp}\phi$, put $z(x)=h(|x|)x/|x|$ extended by zero at the origin, and let $q=\operatorname{div}z$. On real $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ define the Bessel blur $A=\mathcal F_2^{-1}M_m\mathcal F_2$, where $\mathcal F_2$ is the unitary Fourier transform with phase $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$ and $M_m$ multiplies by $m(\xi)=(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}$. Let $f=Au^\dagger$ and define $p=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\bigl((1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\widehat q(\xi)\bigr)$. Then $A$ is bounded, self-adjoint, and injective, $p\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$, and $A^*p\in\partial TV_2(u^\dagger)$. Thus $u^\dagger$ is the unique minimum-TV exact solution satisfying the full-space source condition; for zero noise the parameter ratio $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n$ is zero.

## Example references

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|A certificate is an adjoint image in the TV subdifferential at an exact minimum-TV truth.]]

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The full-space regularizer is the extended distributional-TV functional on L².]]

[Iglesias, Mercier, and Scherzer, *A note on convergence of solutions of total variation regularized linear inverse problems*, §§5.1–5.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06495)

[[thm-plancherel|Plancherel extends the unitary Fourier transform to L².]]

[[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls|A smooth cutoff exists around the compact radial support of $\phi$.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The nonzero nonnegative radial profile $\phi$, the radial truth $u^\dagger$, the Fourier multiplier $m$, and full-space $TV_2$.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the Plancherel supplier. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[thm-plancherel]]: $\mathcal F_2$ is a unitary map on complex $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ and preserves inner products.

[F2] [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]: for integrable $q$, $\widehat q(\xi)=\int q(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx$; integration by parts gives the displayed derivative transform.

[F3] [[lem-schwartz-space-is-dense-in-l-two]]: complex Schwartz functions are dense in complex $L^2$; taking real parts gives density of real Schwartz functions in real $L^2$.

[F4] [[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation]]: $TV_2(v)$ is the supremum of $\int v\operatorname{div}y$ over compactly supported smooth vector fields with $\|y\|_\infty\le1$.

[F5] [[def-ip-banach-convex-subgradient-and-dual-pairing]] and [[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate]]: $q\in\partial TV_2(u)$ when $TV_2(v)\ge TV_2(u)+\langle q,v-u\rangle$ for all $v\in L^2$, using the real Hilbert pairing.

[F6] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: a smooth cutoff can equal one on the compact radial support of $\phi$ and vanish near the origin.

[F7] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: on real-valued functions, the complex $L^2$ inner product equals the real Hilbert pairing.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** Fourier multiplier verification and a calibration field.

The real-valued subspace is closed in complex $L^2$: if $g_j$ are real-valued classes and $g_j\to g$ in complex $L^2$, then $\|\operatorname{Im}g\|_2=\|\operatorname{Im}(g-g_j)\|_2\le\|g-g_j\|_2\to0$, so $g$ is real-valued as an $L^2$ class.

1.1 The multiplier $m$ is real, even, and satisfies $0<m\le1$, so [F1] makes $A$ a contraction on complex $L^2$. For real Schwartz $g$, the integral formula [F2] gives $\widehat g(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat g(\xi)}$, and multiplication by $m$ preserves this symmetry. Approximate $m\widehat g$ in $L^2$ by Schwartz functions using [F3], then replace each approximant $s$ by $\tfrac12(s(\xi)+\overline{s(-\xi)})$. These symmetrized approximants remain Schwartz, converge to $m\widehat g$, and have real inverse Fourier transforms by [F2]; [F1] and the closedness observation above pass this property to $Ag$. Density of real Schwartz functions and boundedness of $A$ extend real-valuedness to real $L^2$. By [F7], the complex Plancherel pairing restricts to the real Hilbert pairing. Multiplication by the real function $m$ is self-adjoint, so $\langle Au,v\rangle=\langle u,Av\rangle$ for real $u,v$, and $A^*=A$. If $Au=0$, then $m\widehat u=0$ almost everywhere; strict positivity of $m$ and injectivity of the unitary Fourier transform give $u=0$. Thus $A$ is bounded, self-adjoint, and injective. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 Because $\phi$ is supported away from zero and from $b$, $u^\dagger$ is constant near the origin, smooth across radii $a,b$, and zero for $|x|\ge b$; hence it is a compactly supported smooth real function. Its gradient is $\nabla u^\dagger(x)=-\phi(|x|)x/|x|$ wherever $\phi(|x|)\ne0$ and is zero elsewhere. The cutoff in the Statement exists by [F6] and gives $z\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)$ with $\|z\|_\infty\le1$. Integration by parts gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^2}u^\dagger\operatorname{div}z\,dx=-\int_{\mathbb R^2}z\cdot\nabla u^\dagger\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\phi(|x|)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\nabla u^\dagger|\,dx.$$
For every admissible test field $y$, the same integration by parts gives $\int u^\dagger\operatorname{div}y\le\int|\nabla u^\dagger|$, while the field $z$ attains equality. Thus $TV_2(u^\dagger)=\int u^\dagger\operatorname{div}z$. Setting $q=\operatorname{div}z$, [F4] gives $TV_2(v)\ge\int vq=TV_2(u^\dagger)+\langle q,v-u^\dagger\rangle$ for every $v$, so $q\in\partial TV_2(u^\dagger)$. [F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]

3.1 The vector $q$ is smooth and compactly supported, so $q,\partial_1q,\partial_2q\in L^2$. Integration by parts using [F2] gives $\widehat{\partial_jq}=2\pi i\xi_j\widehat q$, and Plancherel [F1] yields
$$\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)|\widehat q(\xi)|^2\,d\xi=\|q\|_2^2+\|\nabla q\|_2^2<\infty.$$
Therefore $\widehat p(\xi):=(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\widehat q(\xi)$ is in $L^2$, defining $p=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\widehat p\in L^2$. The integral formula [F2] gives Hermitian symmetry of $\widehat q$, and the real even multiplier preserves it. As in step 1.1, approximate $\widehat p$ by Schwartz functions, symmetrize them, apply inverse Fourier transformation, and use Plancherel continuity and closedness of the real subspace to conclude that $p$ is real. By construction $A^*p=Ap=q$, so [F5] gives the required source certificate. Injectivity from step 1.1 makes $u^\dagger$ the unique exact solution, hence the unique minimum-TV exact solution. [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Step 3.1 provides a certificate at the unique minimum-TV exact truth. For every positive $\alpha_n$ and zero noise $w_n=0$, the parameter ratio is $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n=0$. Thus this example verifies the source condition and the zero-noise parameter side of the full-space deblurring setup without asserting existence of a regularized minimizer. [step 1.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

id: lem-figure-eight-character-and-longitude-traces
kind: lemma
title: Figure-eight character curve and longitude trace
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 10
deps:

  - thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctness

  - def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude
  - lem-figure-eight-two-meridian-presentation-and-preferred-longitude-word
  - lem-two-generator-sl2-word-traces-reduce-to-three-coordinates
  - lem-sl2-character-trace-coordinate-algebra
  - thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient
justified_by: []
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: Léo Bénard, François Florens, and Adrien Rodau, A slope invariant and the
        A-polynomial of knots, Example 3.20
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151
    - title: Kathleen L. Petersen, A-polynomials of a family of two-bridge knots,
        §§3–4
      url: https://nyjm.albany.edu/j/2015/21-39v.pdf
---

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $K=J(2,-2)$ be the figure-eight knot. Use the two-bridge group presentation $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle u,v\mid v w=w u\rangle$, where $w=uv^{-1}u^{-1}v$, and take $\mu=u$. On the one-dimensional irreducible character component, define $x(\chi)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(u))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(v))$ and $y(\chi)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(uv))$. Then
$$2x^2+y^2-x^2y-y-1=0,$$
and the preferred-longitude trace is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\lambda))=x^4-5x^2+2$. The displayed curve equation is irreducible over $\mathbb C$, and $x$ is nonconstant on it.

## Statement references

[Bénard, Florens, and Rodau, Example 3.20](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151)

[Petersen, §§3–4](https://nyjm.albany.edu/j/2015/21-39v.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the standard figure-eight knot, its positive meridian and preferred longitude, and the two-bridge group presentation in the Statement.

[F1] The four-crossing figure-eight code gives a one-component Wirtinger presentation ([[lem-explicit-unknot-and-figure-eight-oriented-wirtinger-codes]]; [[thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctness]]).

[F2] [[lem-figure-eight-two-meridian-presentation-and-preferred-longitude-word]] derives the exact two-meridian presentation from that actual four-crossing code and proves, using its crossing traversal and zero writhe, that the preferred longitude is $C=X_4u^{-1}vX_3^{-1}$ with $X_3=uvu^{-1}$ and $X_4=v^{-1}uvu^{-1}v$. It is not inferred merely from commutation and zero exponent sum.

[F3] [[lem-two-generator-sl2-word-traces-reduce-to-three-coordinates]] proves the actual four-matrix word table. In the equal-generator-trace case, every word trace is a polynomial in $x=\operatorname{tr}u=\operatorname{tr}v$ and $y=\operatorname{tr}uv$.

[F4] Word traces generate the character coordinate algebra by [[lem-sl2-character-trace-coordinate-algebra]]. The actual quotient is onto and any finite algebra generators give its closed affine coordinate model by [[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]].

## Proof

1.1 **Every irreducible pair has the required concrete matrix form.** Let $A=\rho(u)$ and $B=\rho(v)$. Relation $vw=wu$ makes them conjugate, hence of equal trace $x$. Choose an eigenvalue $M\ne0$ of $A$ and an eigenvector for it, and choose an eigenvector of $B$ with eigenvalue $M^{-1}$. The two lines are distinct; otherwise they form a common invariant line for the two generators. In this basis $A$ is upper triangular and $B$ is lower triangular, with respective diagonals $(M,M^{-1})$ in both cases. The upper entry of $A$ is nonzero, for otherwise the second line is common; the lower entry of $B$ is nonzero for the same reason on the first line. Rescale the second basis vector to make the upper entry of $A$ equal to one. Thus every irreducible representation is conjugate to $$A=\begin{pmatrix}M&1\\0&M^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}M&0\\t&M^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad t\ne0.$$ This works also at $M=\pm1$; no distinct-eigenvalue hypothesis was used. A scalar adjustment of the conjugating basis matrix gives determinant one if desired. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **All relator entries are computed.** Put $a=M^2+M^{-2}-3=x^2-5$ and $F=t^2+at-a$. Direct multiplication gives $$W=AB^{-1}A^{-1}B=\begin{pmatrix}t^2+(M^2-2)t+1&M+M^{-1}(t-1)\\t\bigl(M+M^{-1}(t-1)\bigr)&1+M^{-2}t\end{pmatrix},\qquad BW-WA=\begin{pmatrix}0&-F\\tF&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ Thus the representation relation is exactly $F=0$, not a condition obtained after discarding an extra entry. Conversely a pair with $F=0,t\ne0$ is irreducible. At $M=\pm1$ its two nontrivial unipotent matrices have distinct invariant lines. Otherwise a common line besides the two chosen eigenlines can occur only when $t=-(M-M^{-1})^2$; solving the two eigenvector equations gives this equality. But $F$ evaluated at that value is $1$, since $(M-M^{-1})^2=a+1$. So it never occurs on $F=0$. When $t=0$ the pair is upper triangular and reducible. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **The trace equation and its actual image.** Matrix multiplication gives $$x=M+M^{-1},\qquad y=M^2+M^{-2}+t=x^2-2+t.$$ Substituting $t=y-x^2+2$ into $F$ gives $$f(x,y)=2x^2+y^2-x^2y-y-1.$$ Every irreducible representation therefore maps to $f=0$. Conversely, if $f(x,y)=0$ and $t=y-x^2+2\ne0$, choose a root $M$ of $M^2-xM+1=0$. It is nonzero, and step 2.1 constructs an irreducible representation with those traces. The excluded points with $t=0$ have $x^2=5,y=3$, hence are only two points. In particular this is an actual dense realization of the curve, not merely a necessary trace equation. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **There is exactly one component containing irreducible characters.** The discriminant of the monic quadratic $f$ in $y$ is $$(x^2+1)^2-4(2x^2-1)=(x^2-1)(x^2-5).$$ Each of its four zeros is simple, so it is not a square in $\mathbb C(x)$: a rational square has even zero order. Thus $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb C(x)$ as a quadratic in $y$, and is irreducible in $\mathbb C[x,y]$. Indeed a factor of $y$-degree zero would divide the leading coefficient one, and two positive-$y$-degree factors would give a factorization over $\mathbb C(x)$. By [F3] and [F4], $x,y$ generate the whole character algebra and give its actual closed planar model. Reducible representations have common triangular diagonal characters; the relation makes their $u,v$ diagonal characters equal, so they lie on $y=x^2-2$. Every point on this parabola is realized by the diagonal pair $A=B=\operatorname{diag}(M,M^{-1})$. Step 3.1 realizes all of $f=0$ except its two intersection points with that parabola, which are also realized diagonally. Hence the full closed character model is precisely the union of that parabola and $f=0$. The latter is the unique irreducible component containing irreducible characters, and $x$ is nonconstant on it because the monic quadratic $f(x,y)$ has a complex root for every $x$. [F3, F4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.2 **The preferred word, not an unspecified centralizer element, is evaluated.** Use exactly the preferred word $C=X_4A^{-1}BX_3^{-1}$ of [F2], with $X_3=ABA^{-1}$ and $X_4=B^{-1}ABA^{-1}B$. Their matrices and the displayed $A,B$ give the Laurent polynomial identity $$\operatorname{tr}C=\bigl(M^4-M^2-2-M^{-2}+M^{-4}\bigr)+F\bigl(x^2(t+1)-tF\bigr).$$ This identity is obtained by the four indicated matrix products and the entry formula for determinant-one inverses; equivalently multiply out with $a=M^2+M^{-2}-3$ to get $\operatorname{tr}C=(x^4-5x^2+2)+F\bigl((a+5)(t+1)-tF\bigr)$. It is an identity before imposing the relator, so no denominator, exceptional parabolic point, or extra component has been canceled. On $F=0$ it gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho(\lambda)=x^4-5x^2+2$ for every irreducible representation. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Word traces are regular functions in the actual character model by [F4]. The irreducible characters are dense in the irreducible curve by steps 3.1–4.1. Consequently the longitude-trace identity of step 4.2 holds on that entire component, including its reducible intersection points. Steps 3.1–4.1 supply exactly the irreducible curve and nonconstant coordinate required in the Statement, with its original full-AC branch retained. No generic trace-model, eigenvalue-image completeness or preferred-longitude calculation remains assumed in this finite computation. [F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, construct] ∎

    - title: "Shahar Mendelson, Holger Rauhut, and Rachel Ward, Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions, §2.1"

## Statement

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$ use the one-based labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$. For $T\subseteq[n]$, $x_{T^c}$ agrees with $x$ off $T$ and is zero on $T$. Define $\sigma_s(x)_1:=\min\{\|x_{T^c}\|_1:T\subseteq[n],\ |T|\le s\}$. Define $\operatorname{supp}(z):=\{j\in[n]:z_j\ne0\}$ using the one-based labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$. Then
$$\sigma_s(x)_1=\min\{\|x-z\|_1:z\in\mathbb R^n,\ |\operatorname{supp}(z)|\le s\},$$
and this sparse-vector minimum is attained.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-best-s-term-l1-error|Finite minimum of coordinate-tail errors]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one-norm]]

[[lem-finite-sum-laws|Splitting a finite sum over disjoint coordinate sets]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §2.1 Definition 2.2, printed p. 42](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

[Mendelson, Rauhut, and Ward, *Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions*, §2.1, printed p. 5](https://www.mathc.rwth-aachen.de/~rauhut/files/circulant-independent.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A vector $x\in\mathbb R^n$, positive integers $n,s$ with $1\le s\le n$, and the coordinate-tail quantity $\sigma_s(x)_1$.

[F1] [[def-ip-best-s-term-l1-error]]: $\sigma_s(x)_1=\min\{\|x_{T^c}\|_1:T\subseteq[n],\ |T|\le s\}$, and the finite nonempty indexing family has a minimizing member.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|x-z\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^n|x_j-z_j|$.

[F3] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums of nonnegative terms are nonnegative and split over disjoint coordinate sets.

## Proof
1.1 Let $z$ be any vector with $|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\le s$, and put $T=\operatorname{supp}(z)$. For every $j\in T^c$, $z_j=0$, so $|x_j-z_j|=|x_j|$. The terms over $T$ are nonnegative; splitting the finite sum by [F2,F3] gives $\|x-z\|_1=\sum_{j\in T}|x_j-z_j|+\sum_{j\in T^c}|x_j|\ge\|x_{T^c}\|_1\ge\sigma_s(x)_1,$ where the final inequality follows from [F1] because $|T|\le s$. Thus every admissible sparse vector has error at least $\sigma_s(x)_1$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], choose a minimizing set $T_0\subseteq[n]$ with $|T_0|\le s$. Define $z_0=(x_{T_0})$, equal to $x$ on $T_0$ and zero on $T_0^c$. Define $z_0$ coordinatewise by $(z_0)_j=x_j$ for $j\in T_0$ and $(z_0)_j=0$ otherwise. Then $\operatorname{supp}(z_0)\subseteq T_0$, so it is admissible, and direct coordinate summation gives $\|x-z_0\|_1=\|x_{T_0^c}\|_1=\sigma_s(x)_1.$ Together with step 1.1 this proves equality and attainment. The proof chooses one witness from a finite nonempty set and uses no choice axiom. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Hahn–Banach theorem, and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space, and let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element with law $\mu$. Define its covariance by $C\ell=\mathbb E[\ell(W)W]$ for $\ell\in B^*$, let $N=\{\ell:\mathbb E[\ell(W)^2]=0\}$, and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/N$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=\mathbb E[\ell(W)m(W)]$. Let $i:E\to B$ be the canonical injection extending $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{x\in B:\|x-z\|_B\le r\}$. Then for any $h_1,h_2\in E$,
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow \exp\!\left(\frac{\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2}{2}\right) \qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
The denominator is positive for every $r>0$.

## Statement references

[[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space|a centered Borel Gaussian random element has centered normal continuous-linear projections]]

[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs|the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin Hilbert space]]

[[thm-cameron-martin-translation-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law|the Cameron–Martin change-of-measure formula]]

[[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs|the support is the Banach closure of the Cameron–Martin space]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, HB, countable choice, a real separable Banach space $B$, a centered Borel Gaussian random element $W$ with law $\mu$, and its covariance-induced Cameron–Martin Hilbert space $E$ with canonical injection $i$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the Cameron–Martin and support interfaces below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] HB and countable choice are assumed for the norming-family interface used to justify symmetry on the centered ball. [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] $W$ is Borel measurable, and every $\ell\in B^*$ applied to $W$ is a centered real normal variable. [[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space]]

[F2] The Cameron–Martin space is the completion of the covariance quotient, its canonical injection is continuous and injective, and the range of the covariance quotient is dense in $E$. [[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], [[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]]

[F3] For each $h\in E$, the law of $W+ih$ has density $\exp(z_h-\|h\|_E^2/2)$ with respect to $\mu$, where $h\mapsto z_h\in L^2(\mu)$ is linear and isometric, $z_h$ is centered normal with variance $\|h\|_E^2$, and $z_{C\ell}=\ell(W)$ almost surely. Since the covariance range is dense in $E$, this also makes $z_h$ an $L^2$ limit of continuous-linear Gaussian coordinates. [[thm-cameron-martin-translation-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]], [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

[F4] A separable Banach space is Polish, every Borel probability on a Polish space is tight, and the support of a centered tight Borel Gaussian is $\overline{iE}$ in $B$. Thus $0$ belongs to the support and every open ball about $0$ has positive $\mu$-mass. [[def-polish-space]], [[thm-every-borel-probability-on-a-polish-space-is-tight]], [[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]]

[F5] For every $h\in E$ and $r>0$, $\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r))\le\mu(\overline B_B(0,r))$. [[lem-ip-banach-gaussian-cm-shift-ball-bound]]

[F6] A real separable Banach space has a countable family $(\ell_j)$ with $\|x\|_B=\sup_j|\ell_j(x)|$. [[lem-separable-banach-has-countable-norming-family]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** use the Cameron–Martin formula on a centered ball, approximate each Cameron–Martin coordinate by a continuous linear functional, and control the residual exponential by the shift-ball bound.

1.1 Put $A_r=\overline B_B(0,r)$. By [F4], $\mu(A_r)>0$ because it contains the open ball of radius $r$ about the support point $0$. Let $(\ell_j)$ be the norming family from [F6], and define $A_{r,n}=\bigcap_{j\le n}\{|\ell_j(W)|\le r\}$. The sets decrease to $A_r$. For fixed $n$, the vector $(z_s,\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$ is centered Gaussian: [F3] makes $z_s$ an $L^2$ limit of continuous-linear Gaussian coordinates, so adjoining the finitely many displayed coordinates gives a centered Gaussian limit. Its law is invariant under simultaneous sign reversal, and $A_{r,n}$ is invariant under that reversal. Hence
$$ \mathbb E[e^{z_s}\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}]=\mathbb E[e^{-z_s}\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}], \qquad \mathbb E[z_s\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}]=0. $$
The variables $e^{\pm z_s}$ are integrable by the Gaussian moment formula in [F3]. Dominated convergence as $n\to\infty$ therefore gives conditional symmetry and conditional mean zero on $A_r$. Thus
$$ 1\le \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_s}\mid A_r]\le e^{\|s\|_E^2/2}. $$
For the lower bound, conditional Jensen applies. For the upper bound, [F3] applied to $-s$ gives
$$ \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_s}\mathbf 1_{A_r}] =e^{\|s\|_E^2/2}\,\mu(\overline B_B(is,r)), $$
and [F5] bounds the last probability by $\mu(A_r)$. [A1, A2, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 For any $h\in E$, choose $\ell_n\in B^*$ with $h_n:=C\ell_n\to h$ in $E$, possible by the completion in [F2], and put $s_n=h-h_n$. The Cameron–Martin formula [F3], applied to the translate by $-h$, gives
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r))}{\mu(A_r)} =e^{-\|h\|_E^2/2}\,\mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r]. $$
Since $z_{h_n}=\ell_n(W)$ almost surely and $z_h=z_{h_n}+z_{s_n}$, the bound $|\ell_n(W)|\le r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}$ on $A_r$ and step 1.1 imply
$$ e^{-r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}} \le \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r] \le e^{r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}}e^{\|s_n\|_E^2/2}. $$
For fixed $n$, let $r\downarrow0$; then let $n\to\infty$, so $\|s_n\|_E\to0$. The two bounds show $\mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r]\to1$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 Applying step 1.2 separately to $h_1$ and $h_2$ yields
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} =e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} \frac{\mathbb E[e^{-z_{h_1}}\mid A_r]}{\mathbb E[e^{-z_{h_2}}\mid A_r]}. $$
Both conditional expectations tend to $1$, so the ratio has the stated limit. Positivity of the denominator follows from [F4], since each closed ball contains the corresponding open neighborhood of a support point. [F4, step 1.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty simple Riemannian background of dimension $n\ge2$, let $T>0$, and let $q_1,q_2\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ;\mathbb R)$ be static potentials. Let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M$ be a maximal unit-speed geodesic with $0<L<T$, and choose a time shift $t_0$ with $0<t_0<T-L$. In a nonsingular geodesic-polar tube about $\gamma$, there are conjugate eikonal phases and transport amplitudes, with a transverse cutoff of width $\varepsilon_\lambda=\lambda^{-1/(n+8)}$, that produce approximate forward and terminal solutions for the two wave operators. After solving the transport hierarchy through the required finite order and correcting the residual by the zero-data energy solver, the exact solutions have remainders $R_{j,\lambda}$ satisfying
$$\|R_{j,\lambda}\|_{L^\infty(0,T;H^1(M))}\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{4,\infty}},\qquad \|R_{j,\lambda}\|_{L^2((0,T)\times M)}=O(\lambda^{-1/2}),$$
where $\chi_\lambda$ is the stated transverse cutoff and $C$ is independent of $\lambda$. The normalized product of the forward and terminal exact solutions converges against every compactly supported smooth spacetime test function to integration along the null ray $(t_0+s,\gamma(s))$, $0\le s\le L$, with the Gaussian normalization fixed so that the limiting transverse integral is one.

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-simple-geodesic-polar-extension]]

[[def-ip-simple-riemannian-background]]

[[thm-ip-variable-metric-wave-ibvp-energy-wellposedness]]

[[lem-ip-riemannian-green-boundary-traces-and-wave-lifting]]

[[def-countable-choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The simple background, maximal geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to M$, time shift $t_0$, $L<T$, and real smooth interior potentials from the statement.

[F1] [[lem-ip-simple-geodesic-polar-extension]] gives global nonsingular polar coordinates from a boundary point and the unit radial eikonal identity; [[def-ip-simple-riemannian-background]] gives absence of conjugate points and transverse boundary intersections.

[F2] [[thm-ip-variable-metric-wave-ibvp-energy-wellposedness]] supplies exact zero-boundary energy correction and smooth classical solutions for smooth forcing vanishing near the prescribed temporal endpoint. [[lem-ip-riemannian-green-boundary-traces-and-wave-lifting]] supplies the classical boundary convention.


## Proof

1.1 Extend the central geodesic a distance $\delta>0$ through both boundary endpoints in the no-return extension used by [F1], and take the polar centre $p=\gamma(-\delta)$ outside $M$. Choose $\delta<t_0/4$ and $\delta<(T-t_0-L)/4$. The polar differential based at $p$ is nonsingular along this extended ray for sufficiently small $\delta$: on a short initial segment this follows from the identity differential at the origin, and on the remaining compact segment it follows by continuous dependence of the Jacobi matrix and the nonsingularity in [F1] as $\delta\downarrow0$. It is injective on a sufficiently narrow ray tube as well. Otherwise a sequence of collisions in shrinking tubes has limits on the central ray; that ray is embedded by [F1], so its two limiting parameters agree and one local inverse chart excludes the collision. Thus there is a nonsingular polar tube containing the whole ray, with its two radial ends outside $M$. In the tube write $x=(r,\theta)$, $r=\delta+s$ along the ray, and $dV_g=m(r,\theta)drd\theta$. The Gauss orthogonality proved in [F1] gives $g=dr^2+g_{\alpha\beta}d\theta^\alpha d\theta^\beta$ and $\Delta_gr=m^{-1}\partial_rm$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $\phi=t-r$, $z=t-r-(t_0-\delta)$, and $D=\partial_t+\partial_r$. Then $\phi_t^2-|\nabla\phi|^2=0$ and, for $L_q=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q$, direct differentiation gives $$L_q(e^{i\lambda\phi}a)=e^{i\lambda\phi}(i\lambda\mathcal T a+L_qa),\qquad \mathcal T=2D+\partial_r\log m.$$ The variable $z$ and the angle $\theta$ are constant along $D$, and $D(m^{1/2}a)=m^{1/2}\mathcal T a/2$. Consequently $$a_0=m^{-1/2}\chi_\lambda(\theta,z),\qquad a_{1,q}=\frac{i}{2}m^{-1/2}\int_{r_*}^{r}m(\sigma,\theta)^{1/2}(L_qa_0)(\sigma,\theta,z)\,d\sigma$$ solve $\mathcal T a_0=0$, $\mathcal T a_{1,q}=iL_qa_0$, where all functions in the integral are expressed in $(r,\theta,z)$ and $r_*$ is a fixed exterior radial start. Extend the smooth metric coefficients and the interior potentials over this slightly longer tube. Integration in $r$ preserves support in $(\theta,z)$. The same recursion $\mathcal T a_{j,q}=iL_qa_{j-1,q}$ supplies every higher requested finite order; two amplitude terms already suffice for the stated bound. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Choose the angular and $z$ supports sufficiently small. Transversality of the entry and exit makes the tube's part in $M$ lie between smooth nearby entry and exit radii; all these packets are zero on $M$ near $t=0,T$. Put a radial cutoff equal to one near the entire tube intersection with $M$ and supported with its radial derivatives outside $M$. Then $$v_{+,q}=e^{i\lambda\phi}(a_0+\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}),\qquad L_qv_{+,q}=\lambda^{-1}e^{i\lambda\phi}L_qa_{1,q}\quad\text{on }Q.$$ On the fixed compact nonsingular tube, coefficient derivatives, integration lengths, and coordinate Jacobians are bounded independently of $\lambda$. The formula in step 2.1 and the chain rule therefore give $\|a_{1,q}\|_{C^k}\le C_k\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{k+2,\infty}}$ and $$\|L_qv_{+,q}\|_{L^1_tL^2_x}\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{4,\infty}}.$$ For the opposite phase use $v_{-,q}=\overline{v_{+,q}}$ (real $q$), obtaining the identical estimate. In particular the cutoff creates no residual inside the measurement domain. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F2] to $-L_{q_1}v_{+,q_1}$ with zero initial and boundary data, and to $-L_{q_2}v_{-,q_2}$ with zero terminal and boundary data. The smooth right sides vanish near the relevant time endpoints, so the regularity part of [F2] makes the corrections smooth. The resulting $u_1=v_{+,q_1}+R_1$ and $u_2=v_{-,q_2}+R_2$ are actual forward and terminal classical solutions, with smooth boundary traces compactly supported in time. The energy estimate gives $$\|R_j\|_{L^\infty_tH^1_x}+\|\partial_tR_j\|_{L^\infty_tL^2_x}\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{4,\infty}}.$$ Thus the remainder here is the correction to the complete two-term approximate solution, including its $\lambda^{-1}$ transport amplitude. [F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 In local coordinates about $(\theta_0,0)$ let $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\int\zeta^2dy=1$, choosing a cutoff Gaussian and dividing by its $L^2$ norm. Set $$\varepsilon=\lambda^{-1/(n+8)},\qquad \chi_\lambda(\theta,z)=\varepsilon^{-n/2}\zeta((\theta-\theta_0,z)/\varepsilon).$$ For bounded small $\lambda$ enlarge the constants and keep the support inside the tube; all asymptotic assertions concern sufficiently large $\lambda$. Then $\|\chi_\lambda\|_2=1$ and $\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{k,\infty}}\le C_k\varepsilon^{-n/2-k}$. For $k=4$ the exponent is exactly $\lambda^{1/2}$, so step 4.1 proves $\|R_j\|_{L^2(Q)}=O(\lambda^{-1/2})$. Also $\|a_0\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C$ since its squared metric density cancels $m$, and $$\|\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}\|_2\le C\lambda^{-1}\varepsilon^{-n/2-2}=o(1).$$ This verifies every normalization and derivative loss used in the correction estimate. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 For a smooth test $A$, the leading product is $a_0^2=m^{-1}\chi_\lambda^2$. Since $dt=dz$ at fixed $r$, $$\int_Q A a_0^2\,dV_gdt=\int \chi_\lambda(\theta,z)^2\left[\int_{r_-(\theta)}^{r_+(\theta)} A(r+t_0-\delta+z,x(r,\theta))\,dr\right]d\theta dz.$$ The nearby entry and exit radii are smooth by transversality. The bracket converges uniformly as $(\theta,z)\to(\theta_0,0)$ to $\int_0^L A(t_0+s,\gamma(s))ds$. The change of variables $(\theta-\theta_0,z)=\varepsilon y$ and $\int\zeta^2=1$ prove the required ray limit with coefficient exactly one. The terms containing a $\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}$ vanish by the $L^2$ bounds in step 5.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz; the terms containing $R_j$ vanish by the same inequality and step 4.1. These arguments also apply to any smooth function on the closed cylinder, not only a compactly supported interior test, because all approximate packets are supported away from the temporal endpoints and the global correction errors have vanishing $L^2$ norm. Thus the exact forward/terminal product has the asserted normalized limit. [step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a finite Wirtinger presentation by words in generators and their inverses, and let $\mu,\lambda$ be its marked meridian and preferred-longitude words. Let $\mathcal E_K\subset(\mathbb C^*)^2$ consist of the pairs $(M,L)$ for which some representation $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ has a common eigenline for $\rho(\mu)$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ with eigenvalues $M$ and $L$. Then the Zariski closure of $\mathcal E_K$ is defined over $\mathbb Q$: its radical vanishing ideal in $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$ is obtained by extending scalars from a radical ideal in $\mathbb Q[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$.

## Statement references

[Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long, and Shalen, §§2–3](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~culler/papers/PlaneCurves/curves.pdf)

[Tillmann, §§4.2–4.8](https://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/tillmann/papers/course.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a finite presentation of $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ over $\mathbb Z$, and the marked peripheral words $\mu,\lambda$.

[F1] The representation variety is cut out by polynomial matrix equations with integer coefficients after inverse letters are replaced by adjugates ([[lem-sl2-representation-variety-is-affine]]).

[F2] The meridian and preferred longitude are commuting peripheral words in the finite knot-group presentation ([[thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctness]], [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]).

[F3] An arbitrary subset of a finite-dimensional algebraic torus stable under all coordinatewise automorphisms of $\mathbb C/\mathbb Q$ has radical vanishing ideal equal to the scalar extension of a radical rational ideal, by the actual finite row-reduction argument in [[lem-automorphism-stable-laurent-ideals-descend-to-rational-coefficients]]. This applies to the point set itself; its image need not already be closed.

## Proof

1.1 Fix an automorphism $\sigma$ of $\mathbb C$ over $\mathbb Q$. If generator matrices $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ define a representation of the given presentation, then their entrywise images $\sigma A_1,\ldots,\sigma A_n$ do too: determinants and all relator equations are integer-polynomial equations by [F1]. Word evaluation commutes with $\sigma$, including inverse letters because their adjugate formulas have integer coefficients. Thus $\sigma\rho$ is again a representation, with peripheral matrices $\sigma(\rho(\mu))$ and $\sigma(\rho(\lambda))$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $(M,L)\in\mathcal E_K$. A common eigenline can be represented by one nonzero vector $v\in\mathbb C^2$, with $\rho(\mu)v=Mv$ and $\rho(\lambda)v=Lv$. Applying $\sigma$ gives the same equations for $\sigma\rho$, the nonzero vector $\sigma v$, and nonzero eigenvalues $\sigma M,\sigma L$. Hence $(\sigma M,\sigma L)\in\mathcal E_K$. Applying the inverse automorphism proves equality $\sigma(\mathcal E_K)=\mathcal E_K$. This treats both eigenline charts at once; it does not assume a preferred eigenvector, an algebraic section of eigenlines or a closed projection image. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], the radical vanishing ideal of the closure of $\mathcal E_K$ is the extension of its rational contraction, and that contraction is radical. This is exactly the stated meaning of being defined over $\mathbb Q$. In particular reduction of the image introduces no unproved field-of-definition step: it is the point-set vanishing ideal to which the finite-dimensional row argument was applied. The statement retains its full-AC branch through [F3]; all matrix and eigenvector operations in steps 1.1–2.1 are finite. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

---
id: lem-partial-projective-resolutions-determine-tensor-homology-in-degree-one
kind: lemma
title: Three projective degrees suffice for twisted first-homology comparison
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
deps:
  - def-projective-module
  - def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations
justified_by: []
proof_strategy: direct
axiom_use: The supplied projective lifting properties are used only finitely
  many times. Neither an infinite resolution, a global family of basis choices,
  nor a choice principle is assumed.
provenance:
  statement: ai-altered
  proof: ai-generated
sources:
  references:
    - title: Romyar Sharifi, Homological Algebra
      url: https://math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/homalg.pdf
      locator: Projective comparison argument; the finite low-degree version and
        coefficient-side bookkeeping are supplied locally below.
dependency_level: 0
---

## Statement

Let $R$ be any unital ring, let $S$ be a left $R$-module, and let
$$C_2\xrightarrow{d_2}C_1\xrightarrow{d_1}C_0\xrightarrow{\epsilon_C}S\longrightarrow0,\qquad D_2\xrightarrow{\delta_2}D_1\xrightarrow{\delta_1}D_0\xrightarrow{\epsilon_D}S\longrightarrow0$$
be augmented complexes of left $R$-modules, exact at $C_1,C_0,S$ and at $D_1,D_0,S$. Suppose each of the six modules $C_i,D_i$, $0\le i\le2$, is projective. No exactness at $C_2,D_2$ or further degrees is required. There are augmentation-preserving chain maps through degree $2$ between these complexes lifting $1_S$. For every right $R$-module $N$, any such comparison induces the same isomorphism of abelian groups
$$H_1(N\otimes_R C_\bullet)\ \cong\ H_1(N\otimes_R D_\bullet).$$
These isomorphisms are inverse under reversing the complexes, compose for a third such complex, and are natural in homomorphisms of right coefficient modules. In particular a supplied augmentation-preserving chain map through degree $2$ induces this isomorphism; its construction need not be the one chosen in the proof. Tensoring is not assumed exact, and $N$ need not be flat. This is a comparison of supplied algebraic complexes, not an assertion that a presentation complex is a deformation retract or a homotopy-equivalent spine of another space.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The possibly noncommutative ring, left augmented complexes and their exactness and projectivity as stated, and the right coefficient module $N$.

[F1] A projective left module lifts any map from it across a surjective left-module map ([[def-projective-module]]). Only a finite succession of such lifts will be needed.

[F2] The tensor product pairs a right module with a left module and is generated by finite sums of elementary tensors, with the balanced relation $(nr)\otimes c=n\otimes(rc)$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]). In this generality the result is an abelian group, not an automatically defined $R$-module.

## Proof

1.1 **Construct comparison maps in just three degrees.** Lift $\epsilon_C:C_0\to S$ across the surjection $\epsilon_D$ using projectivity of $C_0$, obtaining $f_0:C_0\to D_0$. The image of $f_0d_1$ lies in $\ker\epsilon_D=\operatorname{im}\delta_1$, because $\epsilon_Df_0d_1=\epsilon_Cd_1=0$. Regard $\delta_1:D_1\to\ker\epsilon_D$ as a surjection, and use projectivity of $C_1$ to lift this map to $f_1:C_1\to D_1$ with $\delta_1f_1=f_0d_1$. Now $\delta_1f_1d_2=f_0d_1d_2=0$, so $f_1d_2$ maps into $\ker\delta_1=\operatorname{im}\delta_2$. Lift it across $D_2\to\ker\delta_1$ by projectivity of $C_2$, obtaining $f_2$ with $\delta_2f_2=f_1d_2$. This gives all required chain and augmentation identities. Reversing $C,D$ produces a map $g$ in exactly the same finite way. No exactness in degree2 was used. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Uniqueness up to the homotopy needed in degree one.** More generally let $f,f':C\to D$ be any two comparison maps lifting the same $1_S$, and put $a_i=f_i-f'_i$. Since $\epsilon_Da_0=0$, projectivity of $C_0$ and exactness at $D_0$ give $h_0:C_0\to D_1$ with $\delta_1h_0=a_0$. The map $a_1-h_0d_1:C_1\to D_1$ has zero composite with $\delta_1$, because $\delta_1a_1=a_0d_1$. By exactness at $D_1$ and projectivity of $C_1$, it therefore lifts to $h_1:C_1\to D_2$ with $\delta_2h_1=a_1-h_0d_1$. Thus $a_0=\delta_1h_0$ and $a_1=\delta_2h_1+h_0d_1$. No further homotopy degree is needed for first homology. This construction applies in particular to the two comparisons $gf$ and $1_C$, and also to $fg$ and $1_D$. [F1, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Tensor the actual identities, without a flatness assumption.** For each left-linear map $u$ used above, define $1\otimes u$ on elementary tensors by $n\otimes c\mapsto n\otimes u(c)$. It respects the balanced relation since $u(rc)=ru(c)$, and it respects the additive relations in [F2]. Consequently these induced maps respect sums, differences, compositions and every chain identity above. If $z\in N\otimes_R C_1$ satisfies $(1\otimes d_1)z=0$, the second identity of step2.1 becomes $((1\otimes f_1)-(1\otimes f'_1))z=(1\otimes\delta_2)(1\otimes h_1)z$, an actual boundary. Chain maps preserve cycles and boundaries, so this proves equality of their induced first-homology maps. Apply it to $gf,1_C$ and $fg,1_D$ to show that the induced maps of $f$ and $g$ are mutually inverse. This uses preserved homotopy identities, not preserved exactness of the tensored augmented complexes. In particular no flatness of $N$ has entered. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Compatibility, finite choice use and limits.** A composite of augmentation-preserving comparisons is again such a comparison, so the uniqueness in step3.1 identifies its first-homology map with the unique comparison to the third complex. For a homomorphism $q:N\to N'$ of right modules, the tensor maps $q\otimes1$ commute with all $1\otimes f_i$ on each elementary tensor and hence on finite sums; this proves naturality. The same uniqueness shows that a separately supplied geometric or algebraic comparison induces exactly this isomorphism. Each lift in steps1.1–2.1 is supplied by the projectivity of its particular domain, and the proof takes only finitely many successive witnesses, including the reverse map and the two finite homotopies. No choice of lifts in all degrees, all objects or all coefficient modules is required: independence specifies a unique resulting map for each $N$. Zero modules, zero differentials compatible with the exactness assumptions, and the zero coefficient module obey the same equations. The proof neither constructs a topological spine nor assumes that arbitrary coefficient tensoring preserves exactness. This proves all the stated assertions with the prescribed left/right sides over an arbitrary ring. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $a>b\ge2$ be coprime positive integers. With the meridian-longitude and exponent conventions used for the enhanced A-polynomial, the enhanced A-polynomial of $T_{a,b}$ is, up to multiplication by a Laurent unit,
$$\widetilde A_{T_{a,b}}(M,L)=\begin{cases}1+M^{2a}L,&b=2,\\-1+M^{2ab}L^2,&b>2.\end{cases}$$
If $K$ is the unknot, then $\widetilde A_K=1$. The nontrivial torus-knot Newton polygon is therefore a line segment whose slope in the $(a,b)\mapsto M^bL^a$ convention is $ab$.

## Statement references

[[def-enhanced-a-polynomial|Enhanced A-polynomial convention]]

[[thm-torus-knot-group-presentation|Torus-knot group and peripheral words]]

[Baldwin and Sivek, Example 2.13](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

[Ni and Zhang, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1712.04012)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the oriented positive coprime torus knot and original meridian-longitude and Newton-coordinate conventions.

[F1] The actual torus-knot group/peripheral supplier gives $G=\langle x,y\mid x^a=y^b\rangle$, central $h=x^a=y^b$, positive meridian $\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta$ with $a\alpha+b\beta=1$, and preferred longitude $\lambda=h\mu^{-ab}$ ([[thm-torus-knot-group-presentation]]).

[F2] For exactly these group words, the complete irreducible peripheral eigenvalue-locus ideal is $(1+M^{2a}L)$ for $b=2$ and $(M^{2ab}L^2-1)$ for $b>2$. The proof supplies explicit irreducible matrix families with a cofinite set of meridian values and proves the exact radical ideal, including exceptional representations ([[lem-torus-presentation-irreducible-peripheral-eigenvalue-curves]]).

[F3] The crossing-free unknot has group $\mathbb Z$, by the actual one-generator, no-relator calculation in [[lem-explicit-unknot-and-figure-eight-oriented-wirtinger-codes]].

[F4] The enhanced A-polynomial defines the reduced union of one-dimensional peripheral eigenvalue-image closure components from irreducible characters, with primitive integer normalization ([[def-enhanced-a-polynomial]]).

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] with the given positive integers $a,b$. Its meridian and longitude are exactly the words required in [F2], including the sign and order of the positive meridian. For $b=2$, [F2] gives a single graph $L=-M^{-2a}$ with exact ideal $(1+M^{2a}L)$. For $b>2$ it gives the two graphs $L=\pm M^{-ab}$ with exact ideal $(M^{2ab}L^2-1)$. Each graph is a one-dimensional closed copy of $\mathbb C^*$ under its meridian coordinate; the exact graph ideals in [F2] prove that no additional isolated or other-dimensional image component contributes. The reduced union in [F4] therefore has precisely the displayed equation. These integer polynomials are primitive because their nonzero coefficients are $1,-1$, and square-free because [F2] identifies the graph ideals as distinct prime ideals with radical intersection. Thus they have the asserted normalization up to a Laurent unit. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For the unknot, [F3] identifies a representation with a single determinant-one matrix. Its complex eigenvector supplies a line invariant under that matrix and all its positive and negative powers. Hence there is no irreducible representation of the unknot group. The defining enhanced curve union in [F4] is empty, with unit vanishing ideal, so its primitive generator is $1$. This argument concerns only the unknot and makes no converse detection claim requiring instanton theory. [F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 In the specified exponent coordinates a monomial $M^jL^i$ corresponds to $(i,j)$. The two terms for $b=2$ give points $(0,0)$ and $(1,2a)$, so the segment has slope $2a=ab$. For $b>2$ the points are $(0,0)$ and $(2,2ab)$, so the slope is again $ab$. Multiplication by a Laurent unit translates both points and leaves the slope unchanged. The group/peripheral supplier retains its original full-AC hypothesis, whereas the new finite matrix calculation adds no choice principle. This proves every clause with the original positive-knot and peripheral conventions. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

id: thm-ip-exact-mmse-pnp-ista-stationarity
kind: theorem
title: "Exact-MMSE PnP-ISTA has monotone objective and vanishing gradient"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 5
deps:
  - lem-ip-tweedie-mmse-jacobian-and-prox-potential
  - def-ip-pnp-ista-with-denoiser
  - lem-l-smoothness-descent-inequality
  - def-lipschitz-holder-contraction
  - def-euclidean-inner-product
justified_by: []
forward_refs: []
proof_strategy: direct
axiom_use: "The local stationarity proof uses no choice axiom. It treats the analytic posterior-mean map as an exact plug-in map; it imports neither the AC-dependent Hilbert posterior-mean proposition nor a trained-network guarantee."
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Xiaojian Xu, Yu Sun, Jiaming Liu, Brendt Wohlberg, and Ulugbek S. Kamilov, Provable Convergence of Plug-and-Play Priors with MMSE Denoisers, IEEE Signal Processing Letters 27 (2020), arXiv:2005.07685"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.07685"
      locator: "§2, Assumptions 1–3 and Theorem 1; Appendix A.2, complete majorization and summable-residual proof."
    - title: "Rémi Gribonval and Mila Nikolova, On Bayesian Estimation and Proximity Operators, Applied and Computational Harmonic Analysis 50 (2021), 49–72, arXiv:1807.04021"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.04021"
      locator: "§2.5.1 and Appendix A.4, Gaussian posterior mean as a global proximity selection."
    - title: "Neal Parikh and Stephen Boyd, Proximal Algorithms, Foundations and Trends in Optimization 1(3) (2014)"
      url: "https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/papers/pdf/prox_algs.pdf"
      locator: "§4.2.1, equations (4.7)–(4.8), smooth quadratic majorizer for proximal-gradient descent; convex penalty assumptions do not cover h_{σ,γ}."
---

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $\sigma>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$ that is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane. Use the analytic Gaussian posterior-mean map $D_\sigma$ and potential $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ constructed from $\mu$ in the local lemma. This map is used as the exact MMSE plug-in map; no fitted parameter or training guarantee is assumed. Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and suppose
$$\|\nabla g(u)-\nabla g(v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2\quad(u,v\in\mathbb R^n)$$
for some $L>0$. Suppose the extended-real objective $f=g+h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ has finite infimum in $\mathbb R$, fix $0<\gamma\le1/L$, and run
$$x_t=D_\sigma\!\left(x_{t-1}-\gamma\nabla g(x_{t-1})\right)\quad(t\ge1)$$
from any $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Then $x_t\in X_\sigma$ and $f(x_t)$ is finite for every $t\ge1$; $f(x_t)\le f(x_{t-1})$ in extended-real order for $t\ge1$; the finite sequence $(f(x_t))_{t\ge1}$ converges; and $\|\nabla f(x_t)\|_2\to0$, where $\nabla f$ is the ordinary gradient of its restriction to the open set $X_\sigma$. This is a stationarity conclusion only: it asserts no global minimizer, objective rate, iterate convergence, posterior sampling, or trained-network guarantee.

## Statement references

[[lem-ip-tweedie-mmse-jacobian-and-prox-potential]]

[[def-ip-pnp-ista-with-denoiser]]

[[lem-l-smoothness-descent-inequality]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The integer $n\ge1$, the Borel probability prior $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^n$ not concentrated on any affine hyperplane, $\sigma>0$, the exact MMSE denoiser and potential constructed from $\mu$, a $C^1$ function $g$ with the displayed $L$-Lipschitz-gradient bound, a finite infimum for $f=g+h_{\sigma,\gamma}$, $L>0$, $0<\gamma\le1/L$, and an arbitrary initial point $x_0$.

[F1] [[lem-ip-tweedie-mmse-jacobian-and-prox-potential]]: $D_\sigma$ maps $\mathbb R^n$ into the open set $X_\sigma$, $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ is smooth on $X_\sigma$ and $+\infty$ off it, and $D_\sigma(z)$ is the unique global minimizer of $\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)$.

[F2] [[def-ip-pnp-ista-with-denoiser]]: a PnP-ISTA update takes $z_t=x_{t-1}-\gamma\nabla g(x_{t-1})$ and sets $x_t=\widetilde D_\sigma(z_t)$.

[F3] [[lem-l-smoothness-descent-inequality]]: if $g$ is $C^1$ with $L$-Lipschitz gradient, then $g(y)\le g(x)+\langle\nabla g(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|_2^2$ for all $x,y$.

[F4] [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]: an $L$-Lipschitz map satisfies $\|T(x)-T(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all points in its domain.

[F5] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the Euclidean gradient and norm use $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$ and $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$.

## Proof

1.1 For a point $s\in\mathbb R^n$, define the extended-real quadratic model $\mu_s(x)=g(s)+\langle\nabla g(s),x-s\rangle+\frac1{2\gamma}\|x-s\|_2^2+h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)$. By [F3] and $\gamma\le1/L$, its smooth part majorizes $g(x)$ and is tight at $x=s$. Adding $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ preserves the majorization; when $h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=+\infty$ both objective values are $+\infty$. Thus $\mu_s(x)\ge f(x)$ for every $x$, and $\mu_s(s)=f(s)$ in extended-real order. [given, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 For $t\ge2$ put $s=x_{t-1}\in X_\sigma$ and define $r_t(x)=g(s)+\langle\nabla g(s),x-s\rangle+\frac1{2\gamma}\|x-s\|_2^2-g(x)$. By [F3], $r_t(x)\ge0$ for every $x$, $r_t(s)=0$, and $\nabla r_t(s)=0$. Its gradient is $\nabla r_t(x)=\nabla g(s)+(x-s)/\gamma-\nabla g(x)$, so [F4] and the hypothesis on $\nabla g$ give $\|\nabla r_t(x)-\nabla r_t(y)\|_2\le(1/\gamma+L)\|x-y\|_2\le(2/\gamma)\|x-y\|_2$. On $X_\sigma$, $\mu_s-f=r_t$. [F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Completing the square gives $\mu_s(x)=\frac1{2\gamma}\|x-(s-\gamma\nabla g(s))\|_2^2+h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)+g(s)-\frac\gamma2\|\nabla g(s)\|_2^2$. By [F1] and the exact update in [F2] with $\widetilde D_\sigma=D_\sigma$, $x_t$ is the unique global minimizer of $\mu_{x_{t-1}}$. Hence $f(x_t)\le\mu_{x_{t-1}}(x_t)\le\mu_{x_{t-1}}(x_{t-1})=f(x_{t-1})$. Also $x_t\in X_\sigma$ for $t\ge1$, where $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ is finite, so $f(x_t)$ is finite. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The sequence $(f(x_t))_{t\ge1}$ is finite, nonincreasing by step 2.1, and bounded below by $\inf f\in\mathbb R$. It therefore converges: if $\ell=\inf_{t\ge1}f(x_t)$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $N$ has $f(x_N)<\ell+\varepsilon$, and every $t\ge N$ has $\ell\le f(x_t)\le f(x_N)$. [given, step 2.1]

3.2 Because $x_t$ minimizes $\mu_s$, step 2.1 and the identity in step 1.2 yield $0\le r_t(x_t)=\mu_s(x_t)-f(x_t)\le f(x_{t-1})-f(x_t)$. Summing from $t=2$ to $N$ gives $\sum_{t=2}^N r_t(x_t)\le f(x_1)-f(x_N)\le f(x_1)-\inf f$. The nonnegative summands therefore tend to zero. [F1, step 2.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F3] to $r_t$ with gradient Lipschitz constant $2/\gamma$ and point $x_t$, taking $u_t=x_t-\frac\gamma2\nabla r_t(x_t)$. Then $0\le r_t(u_t)\le r_t(x_t)-\frac\gamma4\|\nabla r_t(x_t)\|_2^2$. Step 3.2 implies $\|\nabla r_t(x_t)\|_2^2\le4r_t(x_t)/\gamma\to0$. [F3, step 1.2, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 For $t\ge2$, $x_t$ is a global minimizer of $\mu_s$ and belongs to the open set $X_\sigma$, where $\mu_s$ is differentiable. For every direction $v$, the global minimum gives nonnegative directional difference quotients along $v$ and $-v$ for small positive increments; taking limits gives $\langle\nabla\mu_s(x_t),v\rangle=0$. Thus $\nabla\mu_s(x_t)=0$. Since $r_t=\mu_s-f$ on $X_\sigma$, $\nabla r_t(x_t)=-\nabla f(x_t)$; step 4.1 now proves $\|\nabla f(x_t)\|_2\to0$. [F1, F5, step 1.2, step 4.1, choose] ∎
