## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $\mathcal V_n^{\mathbb C}$ be the $\mathbb C$-vector space of ambient-isotopy invariants of oriented knots with values in $\mathbb C$ and type at most $n$, where type at most $n$ means that the alternating resolution sum on every $(n+1)$-singular knot is zero; set $\mathcal V_{-1}^{\mathbb C}=0$. Let $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$ be the rational vector space on degree-$n$ circle chord diagrams modulo 4T and 1T; a weight system is a $\mathbb Q$-linear functional on this space. For an $n$-singular knot with chord diagram $D$, define $\sigma_n([V])(D)$ to be the $n$-fold alternating resolution sum of $V$ on that knot. Let $I_{\le n}(K)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}I_j(K)$ be the degree-$n$ truncation of the normalized unframed Kontsevich series. The degree-$n$ symbol map
$$
\sigma_n:\mathcal V_n^{\mathbb C}/\mathcal V_{n-1}^{\mathbb C}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}},\mathbb C)
$$
is surjective. In particular, every rational weight system has a complex-valued finite-type lift; no rationality claim is made about that lift or about the coefficients of $I(K)$. Moreover, for every $n$ and every $V\in\mathcal V_n^{\mathbb C}$ there is a complex-linear functional $\Lambda_V$ on $\bigoplus_{j=0}^{n}(\mathcal A_j^{\mathrm{un}}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C)$ whose degree-$n$ restriction is the degree-$n$ symbol of $V$ and such that
$$
V(K)=\Lambda_V(I_{\le n}(K))
$$
for every oriented knot type $K$. This recovery statement does not imply that distinct knot types have distinct Kontsevich series.

## Statement references

[[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative|Finite differences and type at most n]]

[[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations|Unframed 4T+1T chord-diagram module]]

[[thm-vassiliev-invariant-induces-weight-system|Weight systems induced by finite-type invariants]]

[[lem-kontsevich-integral-finite-type-truncation|Finite-type truncations and identity symbols]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §8.8.1, printed pp. 239–240](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Bar-Natan and Stoimenow, §§1.1 and 2.6, PDF pp. 3–5 and 16–17](https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-alg/9702009v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, the unframed finite-difference convention, and the normalized Kontsevich series with coefficients in the complexified chord-diagram completion.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: countable choice is the only axiom needed here, through ambient-isotopy invariance of the normalized series.

[F1] [[def-singular-knot-and-vassiliev-derivative]]: an invariant is of type at most $n$ when its $(n+1)$-fold alternating resolution sum vanishes on every $(n+1)$-singular knot.

[F2] [[def-framed-chord-diagram-and-four-term-relations]]: $\mathcal A_j^{\mathrm{un}}$ is the rational vector space on degree-$j$ circle chord diagrams modulo 4T and 1T.

[F3] [[thm-vassiliev-invariant-induces-weight-system]]: for an unframed invariant of type at most $n$, the $n$-fold derivative is a well-defined rational-linear weight system on $\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}}$; the conclusion holds for complex-valued invariants as well.

[F4] [[lem-kontsevich-integral-finite-type-truncation]]: $I_{\le n}$ is type at most $n$, and on an $n$-singular knot with diagram $D$ its $n$-fold derivative is $D$.

[F5] [[thm-kontsevich-universal-associated-graded-proof]]: for each $k$-singular knot, $D_kI$ has no homogeneous terms below degree $k$ and its degree-$k$ term is the chord diagram of that knot.

[F6] [[lem-kontsevich-braid-and-knot-isotopy-invariance]]: under countable choice, each coefficient $I_j(K)$ is a well-defined ambient-isotopy invariant of oriented knot types.

## Proof

**Given:** As above. Extend each rational weight system complex-linearly to the complexified chord-diagram module.

1.1 Let $W\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(\mathcal A_n^{\mathrm{un}},\mathbb C)$ be any weight system. Define $V_W(K)=W(I_n(K))$, using the complex-linear extension of $W$. By [F6] this is an ambient-isotopy invariant. Since $I_{\le n}$ is of type at most $n$ by [F4], each homogeneous coefficient, and hence $V_W$, is of type at most $n$. For an $n$-singular knot with diagram $D$, [F5] gives $D_nV_W(K)=W(D)$. Thus $\sigma_n([V_W])=W$, proving surjectivity; in particular this holds for rational-valued weight systems. [A1, F2, F4, F5, F6, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $V\in\mathcal V_n^{\mathbb C}$. Put $R^{(n)}=V$. For $k=n,n-1,\ldots,0$, define $W_k=\sigma_k([R^{(k)}])$ using [F3], and set $R^{(k-1)}(K)=R^{(k)}(K)-W_k(I_k(K))$. The type bound in [F4] makes $W_k\circ I_k$ type at most $k$. For a $k$-singular knot with diagram $D$, [F5] gives $D_k(W_k\circ I_k)(K)=W_k(D)=D_kR^{(k)}(K)$. Therefore $R^{(k-1)}$ has zero $k$-fold derivative and is of type at most $k-1$. At $k=0$, the residual is type at most $-1$, hence is zero by the convention in [F1]. Consequently $V(K)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}W_k(I_k(K))$. Define $\Lambda_V$ on the degree-$k$ summand by $W_k$ and extend complex-linearly over the finite direct sum. This gives $V(K)=\Lambda_V(I_{\le n}(K))$ for every knot type. No step uses separation of knot types by $I$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix a compact Hilbert inverse model $K:X\to Y$ and a family of reconstruction
maps $(R_\alpha)_{\alpha>0}$, with each $R_\alpha:Y\to X$, both held fixed. A
deterministic parameter-choice rule is a function
$\alpha:Y\to(0,\infty)$. It is **noise-level-free** (also called **heuristic**)
when the value $\alpha(z)$ for an observed datum $z\in Y$ uses only $K$, the
fixed family, and $z$; it does not take the exact datum or a noise bound
$\delta$ as input. Here $\delta\ge0$ is a valid noise bound for $z$ and an
exact datum $y$ when $\|z-y\|_Y\le\delta$. The resulting reconstruction is
$R_{\alpha(z)}z$.

## Definition references

## Example

Use $X=\mathbb R^2$ with its Euclidean metric, $Y=\mathbb R$ with its absolute-value metric, and $U=X$. Let $A:X\to Y$ be $A(s,t)=s$, and restrict the truth class to the half-space $C_+=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t\ge0\}$. For every datum $y\in\mathbb R$, the constrained fiber is $\{(y,t):t\ge0\}$, a continuous half-line of admissible truths; moreover $(C_+-C_+)\cap\ker A=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}\ne\{0\}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $X=\mathbb R^2$ and $Y=\mathbb R$ with the stated Euclidean and absolute-value metrics, $U=X$, $A(s,t)=s$ and the nonempty constraint class $C_+=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t\ge0\}$.

[F1] [[def-ip-admissible-constraint-class]]: $C-C=\{x-x':x,x'\in C\}$, $\ker A=\{x:Ax=0\}$, and restricted identifiability is injectivity on $C$.

[F2] [[prop-ip-constraints-can-remove-kernel-ambiguity]]: injectivity on $C$ implies $(C-C)\cap\ker A=\{0\}$.

## Verification

1.1 We have $\ker A=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}$. If $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2$ with $b\ge0$, then $(a,b)=(a,b)-(0,0)$ with both points in $C_+$. If $b<0$, then $(a,b)=(a,0)-(0,-b)$ with both points in $C_+$. Thus $C_+-C_+=\mathbb R^2$, so its intersection with $\ker A$ is the nonzero vertical axis. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Since this intersection is nontrivial, the forward implication in [F2] rules out injectivity of $A|_{C_+}$. Directly, $A(s,t)=y$ and $t\ge0$ hold exactly when $(s,t)=(y,t)$ with $t\ge0$; distinct such $t$ give distinct admissible truths with the same datum. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid representing one oriented knot, and let $\partial^-$ be the full filtered minus differential over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$. Call $O_i$ and $O_j$ consecutive when the $X$-marking in the row of $O_i$ lies in the column of $O_j$. Let $X_\ell$ be that marking and define the module map
$$H_\ell(\mathbf x)=\sum_{\mathbf y}\sum_{\substack{r\in\operatorname{Rect}^{\circ}(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\\X_\ell\in\operatorname{Int}(r)}}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n}U_a^{O_a(r)}\right)\mathbf y.$$
Then $\partial^-H_\ell+H_\ell\partial^-=(U_i+U_j)\operatorname{id}$. The map $H_\ell$ has Maslov degree $-1$ and does not raise the Alexander filtration. Consequently multiplication by any two variables $U_i,U_j$ is filtered chain homotopic, since the consecutive relation follows the single cycle of the knot grid.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot|Grid markings and the single-cycle knot condition]]

[[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex|The full filtered minus differential and variable gradings]]

[[lem-grid-rectangle-boundary-square-zero-and-filtration|Rectangle pairings, annuli, and grading changes]]

[[lem-grid-rectangle-differential-squares-to-zero|The full filtered minus differential is a chain differential]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, Lemmas 4.6.9 and 13.2.5](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A knot grid $G$, a consecutive pair $O_i,O_j$, and the associated marking $X_\ell$.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] gives one $O$ and one $X$ in each row and column and a single cyclic $O\to X\to O$ marking route for a knot grid.

[F2] [[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex]] defines $\partial^-$ by summing all empty-state rectangles with coefficient $\prod_aU_a^{O_a(r)}$; each $U_a$ has Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$.

[F3] [[lem-grid-rectangle-boundary-square-zero-and-filtration]] proves that each non-annular two-rectangle domain has two decompositions with equal total $O$-weight and that the only returning domains are thin horizontal or vertical annuli.

[F4] [[lem-grid-alexander-grading-integral]] proves $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$ and the Maslov rectangle-change formula.

[F5] [[lem-grid-rectangle-differential-squares-to-zero]] establishes that $\partial^-$ is a differential.

## Proof

1.1 The sum defining $H_\ell$ is finite because there are finitely many states and at most two torus rectangles for each ordered state pair. It is $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$-linear by its coefficient formula. For each counted rectangle $r$, [F4] gives $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$; the coefficient has Maslov degree $-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$ by [F2]. Therefore each term of $H_\ell(\mathbf x)$ has Maslov degree $M(\mathbf x)-1$. Also [F4] gives $A(\mathbf y)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)=A(\mathbf x)-n_{\mathbb X}(r)$, and $X_\ell\in\operatorname{Int}(r)$ implies $n_{\mathbb X}(r)\ge1$. Thus $H_\ell$ does not raise the Alexander filtration. [F2, F4, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Expand $\partial^-H_\ell+H_\ell\partial^-$ and group its terms by their two-rectangle domain $\psi$. If $\psi$ is non-annular, [F3] pairs its two decompositions. In each decomposition, when $X_\ell$ has multiplicity zero neither ordered term is selected; when it has multiplicity one exactly one of the two rectangles contains it and exactly one ordering is selected; when it has multiplicity two both rectangles contain it and the two possible placements of $H_\ell$ cancel in characteristic two. The paired decomposition has the same domain, $O$-weight, and multiplicity at $X_\ell$, so every non-annular contribution cancels. [F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 A returning two-rectangle domain is a thin horizontal or vertical annulus by [F3]. The only thin annuli containing $X_\ell$ are the horizontal one in its row and the vertical one in its column. In the horizontal annulus the unique $O$-marking is $O_i$, so its coefficient is $U_i$; in the vertical annulus the unique $O$-marking is $O_j$, so its coefficient is $U_j$. Each annulus has one decomposition and contributes its coefficient times the input generator. Hence the returning contribution is $(U_i+U_j)\mathbf x$. Together with step 1.2 this proves the chain homotopy identity. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The marking route in [F1] orders the variables cyclically, and each adjacent pair in that cycle is consecutive as defined in the statement. Any two indices are joined by a finite path of adjacent pairs. By [F5], each multiplication map is a chain map for the differential; adding the homotopy maps from step 2.1 along the path gives a filtered chain homotopy between multiplication by $U_i$ and multiplication by $U_j$. [F1, F5, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a fixed finite-dimensional real inner-product space, $2\le p<\infty$, let $r>0$, and put $B_r=B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$. Let $Y_p(B_r;V)$ be the $W^{1,p}$ closure of smooth $V$-valued one-forms on the closed ball satisfying $a(\nu)=0$ on the sphere. Write $d^*a=-\sum_i\partial_i a_i$ and $(da)_{ij}=\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i$ for $i<j$. There is $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ such that every $a\in Y_p(B_r;V)$ satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_{p,V}\bigl(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p\bigr).$$
Every such $a$ satisfies the zero-normal integration identity $\int\langle a,d\phi\rangle=\int\langle d^*a,\phi\rangle$ for smooth $\phi$ on the closed ball. If $da=d^*a=0$, then $a=0$.

For $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with the Frobenius norm and $2\le p<4$, there exist $\rho_p>0$ and $C_p$ independent of $r$ such that, whenever $a\in Y_p$ satisfies $d^*a=0$ and $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$, its curvature $F_a=da+a\wedge a$, $(a\wedge a)_{ij}=[a_i,a_j]$, satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_p\|F_a\|_p.$$
All norms here are Euclidean coefficient norms; the class $Y_p$ states precisely the boundary approximation hypothesis.

## Statement references

[[cor-riesz-transforms-are-bounded-on-lp|Riesz transform bounds]]

[[thm-rellich-compactness-from-w-one-p-to-lp-on-an-extension-domain|Rellich extraction]]

[Tao–Tian, Proposition 3.5 and §9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0209352)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Riesz transforms are the $L^2$ Fourier multipliers $-i\xi_j/|\xi|$ and are bounded on every $L^p$, $1<p<\infty$ ([[def-riesz-transforms-on-euclidean-space]], [[cor-riesz-transforms-are-bounded-on-lp]]). Fourier differentiation and Plancherel agreement and injectivity justify multiplier identities for smooth compactly supported functions ([[thm-fourier-differentiation-and-multiplication-identities-on-tempered-distributions]], [[thm-fourier-transform-agrees-with-l-one-and-plancherel-transforms]], [[thm-plancherel]]).

[F2] Smooth Sobolev approximation and the weak smooth-factor product rule hold; smooth cutoffs between balls exist. Multiplying global smooth approximants by a fixed cutoff gives compactly supported smooth approximants to a compactly supported Sobolev class ([[thm-meyers-serrin-density-on-an-arbitrary-open-set]], [[lem-weak-leibniz-rule-with-a-smooth-factor]], [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]).

[F3] A $W^{1,p}$-bounded sequence on a bounded smooth ball has an $L^p$-convergent subsequence. Balls are extension domains, and for $2\le p<4$, $W^{1,p}(B_1)\hookrightarrow L^{4p/(4-p)}(B_1)$ continuously ([[thm-rellich-compactness-from-w-one-p-to-lp-on-an-extension-domain]], [[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]], [[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]]).

[F4] Distributionally harmonic locally integrable functions are smooth. The mean-zero Poincare inequality holds on $B_1$ and its rescaled balls ([[cor-locally-integrable-weakly-harmonic-functions-are-smooth]], [[lem-mean-zero-poincare-estimate-on-bounded-connected-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]]).

[F5] Holder, $L^p$ completeness and monotone convergence are available. Divergence gives integration by parts for smooth forms on the closed ball; [F2] and the extension theorem in [F3] give density of functions smooth near the closed ball in $W^{1,2}(B_1)$ ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]).

[F6] Full AC supplies the countable and dependent choices used by these analytic suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, $V$, $p$ and $r$. Work first on $B_1$.

1.1 **The whole-space first-order estimate.** For a compactly supported smooth one-form $b$ on $\mathbb R^4$ put $f_{ij}=\partial_i b_j-\partial_j b_i$ for all ordered indices and $g=\sum_i\partial_i b_i$. The identity $\Delta b_j=\sum_i\partial_i f_{ij}+\partial_j g$ and [F1] give $\partial_k b_j=-\sum_iR_kR_if_{ij}-R_kR_jg$: multiplication of the Fourier symbols proves equality away from zero frequency, hence almost everywhere in the $L^2$ transforms, and Plancherel injectivity identifies the functions. Riesz boundedness now gives $\|\nabla b\|_p\le C_{p,V}(\|db\|_p+\|d^*b\|_p)$. Approximate compactly supported $W^{1,p}$ forms by compactly supported smooth ones using [F2]; all displayed first derivatives converge in $L^p$, so the estimate extends to them. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 **Reflection of a tangential one-form.** For smooth $a$ on $\overline B_1$ with $a(\nu)=0$, put $\jmath(x)=x/|x|^2$ on $1<|x|<2$ and $b=\jmath^*a=D\jmath^T a(\jmath x)$ there, and put $b=a$ inside $B_1$. On the sphere $D\jmath=I-2\nu\otimes\nu$, so the boundary values match. This continuous piecewise smooth form has its piecewise first derivatives as weak derivatives, by cancelling the value-jump terms in integration by parts. Outside the sphere, differentiating and cancelling the symmetric second derivatives of $\jmath$ gives $db=\jmath^*(da)$. Also $D\jmath D\jmath^T=|x|^{-4}I$ and $\Delta\jmath_j=-4|x|^{-4}x_j$, whence $\operatorname{div}b=|x|^{-4}(\operatorname{div}a)(\jmath x)+4|x|^{-2}x\cdot b$. The inversion Jacobian is $|x|^{-8}$; these formulas on the bounded annulus show that its $b,db,d^*b$ norms are controlled by the respective inside $a,da,d^*a$ norms, with an additional $C\|a\|_p$ in the codifferential estimate. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **The estimate with a compact lower-order term.** Multiply the reflected form by a fixed cutoff equal to one near $\overline B_1$ and supported in $B_2$. Its exterior derivative and codifferential acquire only bounded smooth multiples of $b$. Apply step 1.1 to the resulting compactly supported $W^{1,p}$ form and restrict to $B_1$, using step 1.2 and the product rule. This yields $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p+\|a\|_p)$. It extends to $Y_p$ by its defining strong approximation. For the same approximants, integration by parts and zero normal value give $\int\langle a_j,d\phi\rangle=\int\langle d^*a_j,\phi\rangle$; passing to the limit proves the claimed identity for $a\in Y_p$. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 **The kernel has no nonzero elements.** Suppose $a\in Y_p$ has $da=d^*a=0$. The identity used in step 1.1 makes each component of $a$ distributionally harmonic, hence smooth in the ball by [F4]. Closedness gives a smooth $V$-valued potential $u(x)=\int_0^1\sum_i x_i a_i(tx)\,dt$: differentiating under the integral and using $\partial_j a_i=\partial_i a_j$ makes $\partial_j u$ the integral of $\frac{d}{dt}(t a_j(tx))$, so $du=a$. Normalize $u$ to have zero mean on $B_{1/2}$. For $1/2<R<1$, Poincare on $B_R$ gives $\|u-u_{B_R}\|_{L^2(B_R)}\le PR\|a\|_2$. Taking the mean over $B_{1/2}$ bounds $|u_{B_R}|\le |B_{1/2}|^{-1/2}P\|a\|_2$. Consequently $\|u\|_{L^2(B_R)}\le C\|a\|_2$, uniformly in $R$. Here $a\in L^2$ since $p\ge2$ and the ball has finite volume. Monotone convergence [F5] gives $u\in W^{1,2}(B_1)$ with $du=a$. The zero-normal identity of step 2.1 extends to every $W^{1,2}$ scalar test by [F5], since $a\in L^2$ and $d^*a=0$. Test with $u$ to obtain $\|a\|_2^2=0$. Thus $a=0$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Removing the lower-order term.** If no constant bounded the $W^{1,p}$ norm by $\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p$ on $Y_p$, choose $a_j\in Y_p$ with $\|a_j\|_{W^{1,p}}=1$ and $\|da_j\|_p+\|d^*a_j\|_p<1/j$. By [F3] a subsequence converges in $L^p$. Apply step 2.1 to its pairwise differences; their first-order data tend to zero, so the subsequence is Cauchy in $W^{1,p}$. Completeness follows componentwise from [F5] by passing the derivative test identities to the $L^p$ limits. The strong limit $a\in Y_p$ therefore has norm one, but $da=d^*a=0$, contrary to step 3.1. This proves $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p)$ on the unit ball. [F3, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, choose, contradiction]

5.1 **Critical nonlinear absorption.** For $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$, the Frobenius matrix inequality gives $|[X,Y]|\le2|X||Y|$ and hence $|a\wedge a|\le2|a|^2$. Fix $2\le p<4$ and let $p^*=4p/(4-p)$. By [F3] there is $S_p$ with $\|a\|_{p^*}\le S_p\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}$. For $d^*a=0$, step 4.1 and Holder give $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|F_a\|_p+2\|a\|_4\|a\|_{p^*})$, since $1/p=1/4+1/p^*$. Choose $\rho_p=(4C_{p,V}S_p)^{-1}$. Then $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$ absorbs the last term and gives $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le2C_{p,V}\|F_a\|_p$. All curvature products are in $L^p$, since $p^*\ge2p$ for $p\ge2$ on a finite-volume ball. [F3, F5, step 4.1, choose, algebra]

6.1 **All radii and conclusion.** Pull back by $y\mapsto ry$, so $b(y)=r a(ry)$. Smooth zero-normal forms pull back to smooth zero-normal forms, and strong approximation shows that $Y_p$ pulls back to $Y_p$. The $L^p$ norms of $\nabla b,db,d^*b$ scale by $r^{2-4/p}$, while $\|b\|_p=r^{1-4/p}\|a\|_p$. Also $F_b(y)=r^2F_a(ry)$ and $\|b\|_4=\|a\|_4$. Dividing the unit-ball estimates of steps 4.1–5.1 by $r^{2-4/p}$ proves both stated bounds. The integration identity rescales directly, and the kernel assertion follows from the estimate. Full AC is used through the exact Fourier, compactness and approximation suppliers [F1]–[F6], including the sequential choices in step 4.1. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The complete proof of Tao–Tian's Proposition 3.5 (PDF p.9), and the surrounding critical product estimates on pp.8–9, were read. Its Hodge estimate and boundary-reflection mechanism are implemented here for the ball using explicit inversion and the actual local Riesz bounds. The proof closes the ball's kernel and lower-order-term removal explicitly. The public Wehrheim introduction only states its Hodge theorem; it is contextual and supplies no unproved premise here. The boundary hypothesis is the precise approximation class $Y_p$, which is sufficient for the ensuing constructed Neumann gauge iteration.

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers and let $K=T(p,q)$. Choose generators $x,y$ for the two-generator presentation $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle$. Let $P_{p,q}$ be the two-dimensional presentation complex with one vertex, oriented edges $x,y$, and one two-cell attached along $r=x^py^{-q}$. The assignment $\phi(x)=q$, $\phi(y)=p$ defines an epimorphism $\phi:\pi_1(P_{p,q})\to\mathbb Z$; let $\widetilde P_\phi$ be its connected cyclic cover classified by $\ker\phi$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde{S^3\setminus K};\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module for the infinite cyclic cover classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the deck transformation of the positive meridian. Put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ and define
$$\delta_{p,q}(t)=\frac{(t^{pq}-1)(t-1)}{(t^p-1)(t^q-1)}.$$
Then $\delta_{p,q}(t)$ is a Laurent polynomial, $A_K\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$, and the Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K$, defined as a generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$, satisfies $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\delta_{p,q}(t)$, where $f\doteq g$ means $f=\pm t^k g$ for some integer $k$.

## Statement references

[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link|The positive-meridian infinite cyclic cover and deck action]]

[[def-alexander-polynomial-from-the-first-elementary-ideal|The Alexander polynomial as a generator of the zeroth elementary ideal]]

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, §§5.1.6–5.2.4](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

[Calegari, §4.3](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, the torus knot $K=T(p,q)$, its exterior, and the total-linking cover.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom used by the one-variable Alexander-module and polynomial definitions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[L1] Full AC implies Countable Choice, the hypothesis of the tubular-exterior retraction supplier ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] [[thm-torus-knot-group-presentation]] gives $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle$ and a positive meridian $\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$.

[F2] [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]] says $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is generated by $[\mu]$ and the positive meridian maps to $1$ in total linking.

[F3] [[lem-knot-tubular-exterior-and-boundary]] says the open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto the compact exterior $E_K$.

[F4] [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]] defines $A_K$ as the first homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover with positive meridian deck action.

[F5] [[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]] identifies cellular-chain homology with singular homology, and [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] identifies first homology with the abelianization of the fundamental group.

[F6] [[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]] defines $E_0$ by the maximal minors of a presentation matrix, [[def-alexander-polynomial-from-the-first-elementary-ideal]] defines $\Delta_K$ as its gcd generator up to units $\pm t^k$, and [[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]] supplies unique factorization in $\Lambda$.

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC and the data in the Statement.

1.1 Abelianizing the presentation in [F1] gives the relation $p[x]=q[y]$. The map $\phi(x)=q$, $\phi(y)=p$ is onto because $\gcd(p,q)=1$; its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(p,-q)$, exactly the abelianized relation vector, so the abelianization is $\mathbb Z$. The meridian in [F1] maps to $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, so the epimorphism $\phi$ in the Statement is precisely the positive total-linking homomorphism that classifies the cover in [F4]. [A1, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

1.2 For every integer $n$, $(z^n-1)/(z-1)$ is a finite Laurent sum; for $n<0$ it equals $-(z^{-1}+\cdots+z^n)$. In the lifted attaching word, a positive edge contributes the current deck translate and a negative edge contributes the negative of the preceding translate. The $x^p$ block therefore contributes $(x^p-1)/(x-1)$ to the $x$-edge coordinate. The following $y^{-q}$ block starts after the $x^p$ translate and contributes $x^p(y^{-q}-1)/(y-1)$ to the $y$-edge coordinate. These are the complete signed edge contributions of the two-cell in $\widetilde P_\phi$. [given, algebra]

2.1 The cyclic cover in the Statement has cellular chain groups $C_2=\Lambda$, $C_1=\Lambda^2$, $C_0=\Lambda$. Its first boundary is $d_1=(t^q-1,\ t^p-1)$ because lifted $x$- and $y$-edges end $q$ and $p$ deck steps from their starts. Evaluating the two edge contributions in step 1.2 at $x=t^q$, $y=t^p$ gives the second boundary column; the $y$-coordinate is $t^{pq}(t^{-pq}-1)/(t^p-1)=-(t^{pq}-1)/(t^p-1)$:
$$d_2(1)=\left(\frac{t^{pq}-1}{t^q-1},\ -\frac{t^{pq}-1}{t^p-1}\right)^T.$$
This is the cellular boundary of the lifted two-cell. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 In $\Lambda$, $\gcd(t^p-1,t^q-1)\doteq t-1$: for positive exponents the Euclidean algorithm gives this because $\gcd(|p|,|q|)=1$, and negative exponents differ from the positive ones by units. Hence $a=(t^q-1)/(t-1)$ and $b=(t^p-1)/(t-1)$ are coprime. The kernel of $d_1$ is the free rank-one submodule generated by $(b,-a)^T$: if $au+bv=0$, unique factorization implies $a\mid v$, and then $(u,v)$ is a multiple of $(b,-a)$. The column in step 2.1 is $\delta_{p,q}(b,-a)^T$. To show $\delta_{p,q}\in\Lambda$, replace signed exponents by $m=|p|$, $n=|q|$, which changes each factor only by a unit. Set $A=(t^m-1)/(t-1)$ and $B=(t^n-1)/(t-1)$. They are coprime; since $m,n$ divide $mn$, both divide $(t^{mn}-1)/(t-1)$. Unique factorization gives $AB\mid(t^{mn}-1)/(t-1)$, hence $\delta_{m,n}=((t^{mn}-1)/(t-1))/(AB)\in\Lambda$, and the signed quotient is a unit multiple. If $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, this quotient is a unit, so the same cyclic presentation gives $A_K=0$. [F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F5], $H_1$ of the cyclic cover of $P_{p,q}$ is $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_2\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$. The presentation complex and $E_K$ have the same fundamental group and the same homomorphism $\phi$; the fundamental groups of their cyclic covers are the corresponding kernels, and the deck action on their abelianizations is conjugation by a preimage of $1\in\mathbb Z$. Hurewicz therefore identifies their first-homology $\Lambda$-modules. Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3] by [L1]; the deformation retraction then identifies the cyclic-cover homology of $E_K$ with that of $S^3\setminus K$. Thus $A_K\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$. [A1, L1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 The one-by-one presentation $[\delta_{p,q}]$ of $\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$ has $E_0$ generated by its sole $1\times1$ minor, namely $\delta_{p,q}$. Isomorphism invariance of the Alexander module and the definition [F6] give $E_0(A_K)=(\delta_{p,q})$ and hence $\Delta_K\doteq\delta_{p,q}$. [F4, F6, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$ and positive mass on some bounded Borel subset of $D$. Give $D$ the relative norm topology and trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $\Phi,\Phi_N:D\to\mathbb R$ be finite continuous potentials indexed by integers $N\ge1$, let $M_1,M_2:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Borel and nondecreasing, and let $\psi_N\ge0$ satisfy $\psi_N\to0$. Suppose for every $u\in D$ and every $N$,
$$\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_X),\qquad \Phi_N(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_X),\qquad |\Phi_N(u)-\Phi(u)|\le M_2(\|u\|_X)\psi_N,$$
and
$$J:=\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\bigl(1+M_2(\|u\|_X)^2\bigr)\,\mu_0(du)<\infty.$$
Define the pointwise fixed-data evidences and posterior updates by
$$Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu_0(du),\quad \Pi(du):=Z^{-1}e^{-\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du),\qquad Z_N:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_N(u)}\,\mu_0(du),\quad \Pi_N(du):=Z_N^{-1}e^{-\Phi_N(u)}\mu_0(du).$$
Then $Z,Z_N$ are positive and finite, and there are $C<\infty$ and $N_0$ such that
$$h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\le C\psi_N\qquad(N\ge N_0),$$
where $h$ is the library root-L2 Hellinger distance. This is a fixed-data assertion and makes no sampling-law or conditional-law version claim. In a separate branch, if AC is assumed for the library density/total-variation comparison convention, then $\|\Pi-\Pi_N\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\le C\psi_N$, where $\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal B(D)}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-prior-on-a-forward-domain|A prior is a Borel probability with full mass on its declared forward domain.]]

[[def-banach-space|A Banach space is complete for its norm metric.]]

[[def-separable-space|A separable space has an at most countable dense subset.]]

[[def-norm-and-normed-space|A norm induces the metric used on the parameter space.]]

[[def-borel-sigma-algebra|The Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets.]]

[[def-probability-measure|A probability measure has total mass one.]]

[[def-continuous-map-top|Continuity means inverse images of open sets are open.]]

[[def-extended-reals|The extended real line adds two infinite endpoints to the real line.]]

[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line|The extended-real Borel sigma-algebra uses the order topology and restricts to the real Borel sets.]]

[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces|A function is measurable when inverse images of measurable sets are measurable.]]

[[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law|Fixed-data evidence and the normalized potential update are defined fiberwise when evidence is positive and finite.]]

[[thm-ip-function-space-posterior-propriety|A common integrable lower envelope and continuity at support points imply positive finite evidence.]]

[[thm-hellinger-tv-comparison-under-library-convention|Under AC, library total variation is at most the library root-L2 Hellinger distance.]]

[[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability|Arithmetic and absolute-value operations preserve measurability of real-valued functions.]]

[[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral|The nonnegative integral is additive on sums of nonnegative measurable functions.]]

[[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space|The root integral of a square defines the norm for square-integrable functions.]]

[[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals|Minkowski’s inequality gives the triangle inequality for square-integrable functions.]]

[Dashti and Stuart, full lecture notes, §4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.6989)

[Cotter, Dashti, and Stuart, full paper, §2 and Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0909.2126)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Borel prior concentrated on the forward domain, finite continuous potentials $\Phi,\Phi_N$, a shared lower envelope, a pointwise error envelope $M_2\psi_N$, and the weighted integrability condition in the Statement.

[F1] Each finite continuous potential has a continuous section; under a common integrable lower envelope on a Borel full-measure forward domain in a separable Banach space, its fixed-data evidence is positive and finite and the normalized update is a probability measure. [[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-banach-space]], [[def-separable-space]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-probability-measure]], [[thm-ip-function-space-posterior-propriety]]

[F2] For a finite potential $\Phi$, the fixed-data evidence is $Z=\int_D e^{-\Phi}\,d\mu_0$ and the posterior density relative to $\mu_0$ is $e^{-\Phi}/Z$ when $0<Z<\infty$. [[def-ip-prior-on-a-forward-domain]], [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F3] For supplied densities $p,p_N$ relative to $\mu_0$, the library distance is $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)=\|\sqrt p-\sqrt{p_N}\|_{L^2(\mu_0)}$, with no factor $1/\sqrt2$. [[def-hellinger-distance-for-dominated-laws]]

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Choice only for the optional generic density/TV comparison branch. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] Under [A1], for two probability laws with a common sigma-finite dominator, $\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|\le h(P,Q)$ in the library conventions. [[thm-hellinger-tv-comparison-under-library-convention]], [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]

[F5] The derivatives of $t\mapsto e^{-t/2}$ and $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ are $-\tfrac12e^{-t/2}$ and $-e^{-t}$; the real mean value theorem bounds their increments by derivative magnitude times interval length. [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[lem-mean-value-theorem-on-closed-interval]]

[F6] The nonnegative integral is monotone and positively homogeneous. [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]

[F7] Continuous finite potentials on the Borel subspace $D$ are Borel; via the real-line inclusion they are measurable as extended-real-valued potentials. The norm map and real exponential are continuous, so composing Borel radius envelopes with them gives measurable integrands. [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-extended-reals]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]], [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], [[lem-metric-reverse-triangle]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]

[F8] Sums, differences, and absolute values of measurable real-valued functions are measurable. [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]

[F9] The nonnegative integral is additive, monotone, and positively homogeneous. [[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]

[F10] For square-integrable real functions, the root integral of the square is the $L^2$ norm and satisfies the triangle inequality. [[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space]], [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and pointwise posterior convention in the Statement.

1.1 Since $M_2\ge0$, $e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\le e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}(1+M_2(\|u\|_X)^2)$, so [F6] gives $\int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}d\mu_0\le J<\infty$. Apply [F1] to $\Phi$ and, separately for each fixed $N$, to $\Phi_N$; this gives $0<Z<\infty$ and $0<Z_N<\infty$ for every $N$, and defines the displayed probability updates. [F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $u\in D$ and $N$. Both potential values are at least $-M_1(\|u\|_X)$, so every real between them has that lower bound. By [F5] and the potential-error assumption, $|e^{-\Phi_N(u)}-e^{-\Phi(u)}|\le e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}M_2(\|u\|_X)\psi_N.$ Integrating and using $M_2\le1+M_2^2$ gives $|Z_N-Z|\le J\psi_N.$ The absolute difference of the integrals is bounded by the integral of the absolute difference: apply monotonicity and additivity to $e^{-\Phi_N}\le e^{-\Phi}+|e^{-\Phi_N}-e^{-\Phi}|$ and its reverse. Since $Z>0$ and $\psi_N\to0$, there is $N_0$ such that $J\psi_N\le Z/2$ for every $N\ge N_0$, and then $Z_N\ge Z/2$. [F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.2 The same mean-value argument for $t\mapsto e^{-t/2}$ gives $|e^{-\Phi_N(u)/2}-e^{-\Phi(u)/2}|\le\tfrac12 e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)/2}M_2(\|u\|_X)\psi_N.$ Squaring and integrating yields $\|e^{-\Phi_N/2}-e^{-\Phi/2}\|_{L^2(\mu_0)}\le\tfrac12\sqrt{J}\,\psi_N.$ [F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Put $a=e^{-\Phi/2}$ and $a_N=e^{-\Phi_N/2}$. The square roots of the posterior densities are $q=a/\sqrt Z$ and $q_N=a_N/\sqrt{Z_N}$ by [F2]. Add and subtract $a_N/\sqrt Z$ and use the triangle inequality in $L^2$ to obtain $\|q-q_N\|_2\le\frac{\|a-a_N\|_2}{\sqrt Z}+\frac{|\sqrt{Z_N}-\sqrt Z|}{\sqrt Z}.$ By [F3], the left side is $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)$. Also $\|a_N\|_2^2=\int_D e^{-\Phi_N}\,d\mu_0=Z_N$, which gives the displayed second term after applying [F10]. The first term is at most $\sqrt{J}\psi_N/(2\sqrt Z)$ by step 2.2. The second equals $|Z_N-Z|/[\sqrt Z(\sqrt{Z_N}+\sqrt Z)]$, so by step 2.1 and $Z_N\ge Z/2$ it is at most $J\psi_N/Z$. Therefore $h(\Pi,\Pi_N)\le\left(\frac{\sqrt J}{2\sqrt Z}+\frac{J}{Z}\right)\psi_N,$ which is the claimed bound with a finite constant independent of $N\ge N_0$. [F2, F3, F10, step 2.1, step 2.2, given, algebra]

4.1 Under the separate assumption [A1], apply [F4] to the two explicit posterior densities relative to $\mu_0$. This gives $\|\Pi-\Pi_N\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le h(\Pi,\Pi_N)$, and step 3.1 gives the optional TV consequence without adding an axiom to the Hellinger estimate. [A1, F4, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$, and put $a=|p|$, $b=|q|$. For $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, define
$$\delta_{a,b}(t)=\frac{(t^{ab}-1)(t-1)}{(t^a-1)(t^b-1)}.$$
Then $\delta_{a,b}(t)$ is a polynomial in $\mathbb Z[t]$, the Alexander polynomial $\Delta_K$ defined as a generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of the positive-meridian infinite-cyclic-cover module satisfies $\Delta_K(t)\doteq\delta_{a,b}(t)$, and the knot genus is $g(K)=(a-1)(b-1)/2$. Here $f\doteq g$ means $f=\pm t^k g$ for some integer $k$.

## Statement references

[[def-coprime-torus-knot|Parameterization and sign conventions for torus knots]]

[[lem-torus-knot-alexander-polynomial-from-presentation|The Alexander module and polynomial from the torus-knot presentation]]

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|The minimum genus of a connected oriented spanning surface]]

[[cor-knot-alexander-normalization-symmetry-and-genus-bound|The Alexander degree-width bound for knot genus]]

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, §§5.1.6–5.3.2](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

[Calegari, §§3.1–3.3 and 4.3](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[Akbulut and Ozbagci, §2](https://msp.org/gt/2001/5-1/gt-v5-n1-p10-p.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, coprime nonzero integers $p,q$, and $K=T(p,q)$.

[A1] Full AC means every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[L1] Full AC implies Countable Choice, the hypothesis of the spanning-surface and genus definitions ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] [[def-coprime-torus-knot]] defines the oriented primitive-slope knot $T(p,q)$ and identifies sign changes with the stated mirror and orientation conventions.

[F2] [[thm-torus-knot-group-presentation]] gives $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle$ with the positive meridian word determined by $p\alpha+q\beta=1$.

[F3] [[lem-torus-knot-alexander-polynomial-from-presentation]] proves that the positive-meridian Alexander module is cyclic with order $\delta_{p,q}(t)=(t^{pq}-1)(t-1)/((t^p-1)(t^q-1))$, a Laurent polynomial, and hence $\Delta_K\doteq\delta_{p,q}$.

[F4] [[lem-torus-knot-unit-slope-is-unknot]] says $T(p,q)$ is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot whenever $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$.

[F5] [[lem-torus-knot-sign-changes-give-mirror-or-reversal]] identifies the mirror and reversed-orientation curves obtained by changing parameter signs; [[lem-knot-genus-invariant-under-mirror-and-reversal]] proves that these operations preserve genus.

[F6] [[lem-positive-torus-knot-hopf-plumbing-surface]] constructs a positive Hopf-plumbed Seifert surface of genus $(a-1)(b-1)/2$ for $T(a,b)$ when $a,b\ge2$.

[F7] [[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]] defines $g(K)$ as the minimum genus of a connected compact oriented spanning surface under Countable Choice.

[F8] [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]] identifies the Alexander polynomial with the Seifert determinant under the positive-push convention; [[cor-knot-alexander-normalization-symmetry-and-genus-bound]] gives $\operatorname{width}(\Delta_K)\le2g(K)$.

## Proof


**Given:** The data in the Statement and [A1].

1.1 Apply [F2] to identify the exterior group presentation and its positive-meridian homomorphism. The Fox-module calculation [F3] applied to that presentation gives $\Delta_K\doteq\delta_{p,q}$ and proves $\delta_{p,q}\in\Lambda$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

1.2 Suppose $a,b\ge2$. For the four possible sign patterns, $T(p,q)$ is obtained from $T(a,b)$ by no operation, the mirror, orientation reversal, or both, according to [F5]. The genus invariance in [F5] therefore gives $g(K)=g(T(a,b))$. [L1, F1, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 For every positive integer $n$, $t^{-n}-1=-t^{-n}(t^n-1)$, so each signed factor $t^{p}-1$, $t^q-1$, and $t^{pq}-1$ differs from its absolute-exponent factor by a unit of $\Lambda$. Therefore $\delta_{p,q}$ is a unit multiple of $\delta_{a,b}$ as a rational function. By [F3] this places $\delta_{a,b}$ in $\Lambda$. Its defining rational function is finite at $t=0$, because numerator and denominator both have constant term $1$; a Laurent polynomial finite at $0$ has no negative powers. Thus $\delta_{a,b}\in\mathbb Z[t]$, and $\Delta_K\doteq\delta_{a,b}$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 By [F6], $T(a,b)$ bounds a connected oriented surface of genus $g_0=(a-1)(b-1)/2$, so the minimum in [F7] satisfies $g(K)=g(T(a,b))\le g_0$. [L1, F6, F7, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 If $a=1$ or $b=1$, the quotient defining $\delta_{a,b}$ cancels to $1$. By [F4], $K$ is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, which bounds a disk; an ambient isotopy carries spanning surfaces to spanning surfaces of the same genus in both directions. Since genus is nonnegative by [F7], the minimum is $g(K)=0=(a-1)(b-1)/2$. [L1, F4, F7, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

3.2 Since $\delta_{a,b}\in\mathbb Z[t]$, its degree is $ab+1-a-b=(a-1)(b-1)$: the numerator and denominator have leading coefficient $1$, and the quotient is polynomial by step 2.1. Its constant coefficient is $1$, since the numerator and denominator both have constant term $1$. Hence its exponent width is $(a-1)(b-1)=2g_0$, and multiplication by a unit does not change width. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 By the Seifert-determinant theorem and the genus-bound corollary [F8], $\operatorname{width}(\Delta_K)\le2g(K)$. Step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{width}(\Delta_K)=2g_0$, so $2g_0\le2g(K)$. Together with step 2.2 this yields $g(K)=g_0$. The formulas hold in the nonunit case, and step 3.1 handles the unit case. [F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

Thus these closed domains\nare not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.\n\n**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle\n$S^1=\\mathbb R/\\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,\nregarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a\n**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold\n$C=S^1\\sqcup\\dots\\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\\in\\mathbb N$)\ndiffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual\nsummands, and the number of components is $k$.\n\n**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$.           "source": "def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data",
          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary, let $x_0\\in X$, and put $G=\\pi_1(X,x_0)$. A **finite relative disk-embedding datum** consists of proper generic immersions $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\\looparrowright(X,\\partial X)$, $1\\le i\\le n$, whose boundary circles are embedded and pairwise disjoint, together with framed generic immersions $g_i:S^2\\looparrowright\\operatorname{int}X$ that are algebraically dual to the disks. A topological generic immersion has the local models of a smooth generic immersion: at a point with one inverse image its image sheet is locally flat, with a proper half-space chart at boundary points in which the disk is a half-plane and its boundary lies on the ambient boundary, and each of its finitely many self-double points has exactly two preimages and the coordinate-plane model $\\mathbb R^2\\times\\{0\\}$ and $\\{0\\}\\times\\mathbb R^2$ in a chart of $X$. All mutual intersections among the disk and sphere maps are also required to be finite and transverse, so the equivariant intersection sums below are finite. Proper means that the inverse image of $\\partial X$ is exactly the domain boundary. Each disk $f_i$ is supplied with a specified normal framing along $S^1$, equivalently the framing of its boundary attaching solid torus; this boundary framing is part of the datum and need not extend over $D^2$. Each sphere $g_i$ is supplied with a trivialization of its normal microbundle over $S^2$. Choose paths from $x_0$ to the immersed surfaces and orient the surfaces.           "quote": "The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.\n\n> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function\n> (Choice function).\n\nWritten out: for every set $\\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,\nthere exists a function $g$ with domain $\\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \\in S$ for\nall $S \\in \\mathcal{F}$.\n\nAn equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if\n$X_i \\ne \\emptyset$ for every $i \\in I$, then $\\prod_{i \\in I} X_i \\ne \\emptyset$.\nHere $\\prod_{i \\in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that\n$f(i) \\in X_i$ for every $i \\in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by\nitself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.",

          "quote": "Let $X$ be a set and let $R \\subseteq X \\times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.\nCall $R$ **entire on $X$** when\n\n$$\\text{for every } x \\in X \\text{ there is } y \\in X \\text{ with } x \\mathbin{R} y .$$\n\nThe **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\\mathrm{DC}$, is the following\nstatement.\n\n> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every\n> $a \\in X$, there is a function $x : \\mathbb{N} \\to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \\in f$ and $(a,c) \\in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \\to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,\n> The natural numbers $\\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with\n> $$x_0 = a \\qquad \\text{and} \\qquad x_n \\mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \\ \\text{ for every } n \\in \\mathbb{N}.$$\n\nHere a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily\na real-valued sequence. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is\nthe principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the\nfirst $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are\nexactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built\nalong the choosing.           "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.\n\n> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function\n> (Choice function).\n\nWritten out: for every set $\\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,\nthere exists a function $g$ with domain $\\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \\in S$ for\nall $S \\in \\mathcal{F}$.\n\nAn equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if\n$X_i \\ne \\emptyset$ for every $i \\in I$, then $\\prod_{i \\in I} X_i \\ne \\emptyset$.\nHere $\\prod_{i \\in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that\n$f(i) \\in X_i$ for every $i \\in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by\nitself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.",

          "quote": "If $f,g:X\\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\\geq 0$ and\nevery abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:\n$$H_n(f_\\#)=H_n(g_\\#):H_n^{\\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\\to H_n^{\\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$",

          "quote": "Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).\n\n### Finite sums of vectors\n\nBy axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence\nin particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). ### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite

[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same

it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$

nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and

reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.",

          "quote": "Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is

what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the

[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].",

          "quote": "Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].",

$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)

$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value

[[def-metric-space]].

with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.",

**The order.** For $a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ declare

$$a \le b \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad a = -\infty \ \text{ or } \ b = +\infty \ \text{ or } \ \big(a, b \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and } a \le b \text{ in } \mathbb{R}\big),$$

with $\mathbb{R}$ ordered as in Order on the reals, and write $a < b$ for
"$a \le b$ and $a \ne b$" as usual (Partial order and partially ordered set).

**$(\overline{\mathbb{R}}, \le)$ is a totally ordered set, and the inclusion of
$\mathbb{R}$ preserves and reflects the order.** All four checks are immediate
from the displayed clauses.

- *Reflexive.* For $a = \pm\infty$ one of the first two clauses applies; for
  $a \in \mathbb{R}$ the third does, since $a \le a$ in $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Antisymmetric.* Suppose $a \le b$ and $b \le a$. If $a = -\infty$ then
  $b \le a$ forces $b = -\infty$, since the clause $a = +\infty$ fails and $b, a$
  are not both real. Symmetrically $b = -\infty$ forces $a = -\infty$, and
  $a = +\infty$ or $b = +\infty$ forces the other to be $+\infty$. In the one
  remaining situation $a$ and $b$ are both real and antisymmetry is that of
  $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Transitive.* Let $a \le b \le c$. If $a = -\infty$ or $c = +\infty$ the
  conclusion is one of the first two clauses. Otherwise $a \ne -\infty$ forces,
  in $a \le b$, either $b = +\infty$ or $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$; and $c \ne +\infty$
  forces, in $b \le c$, either $b = -\infty$ or $b, c \in \mathbb{R}$. The value
  $b = +\infty$ is incompatible with the second alternative pair, so $b$ is real,
  hence so are $a$ and $c$, and transitivity is that of $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Total.* If $a = -\infty$ or $b = +\infty$ then $a \le b$; if $b = -\infty$ or
  $a = +\infty$ then $b \le a$; otherwise both are real and the order of
  $\mathbb{R}$ is total.
- *Preserved and reflected.* For $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ the first two clauses fail,
